## Volume Front Matter

### Series Title Page

**Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal Library—complete, uniform, comprehensive, convenient, economical—of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the times of Innocent III; a chronological reprint of all the surviving monuments of Catholic tradition throughout the first twelve centuries of the Church, prepared with the utmost care according to the most accurate editions, collated with one another and with a number of manuscript codices; continuously elucidated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by the discovery of all works completed after the extensive editions owed to the last three centuries; furnished with separate analytical indexes following each volume or each author of importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the subject matter below; expanded by works both doubtful and apocryphal, and by works possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever any one of the Fathers has written on any topic may be seen at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which the reader may readily learn which Fathers commented on the individual texts of the books of Scripture, and in which passages of their works they did so.**

**The most accurate edition, and easily preferable to all others when the following are taken into consideration: the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the reprinted works, the very convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the entire work, the low price, and above all this collection, which is unified, methodical, and chronological, bringing together for the first time in our library six hundred fragments and minor works previously scattered here and there, drawn from works relating to every age, place, language, and literary form.**

**Second Series**, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and Writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III, edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or Complete Courses in the several branches of ecclesiastical learning. Patrology has been printed in two editions, one Latin and the other Greek-Latin. — One thousand two hundred volumes of the Latin edition are sold for one thousand francs; the Greek-Latin edition for one thousand three hundred francs. — The Latin edition embraces all authors, both Western and Eastern; the latter, however, are presented in it only in Latin translation.

# The Eleventh Century

**The Complete Works of St Bruno, Bishop of Würzburg; St Odilo, Abbot of Cluny; and Bern, Abbot of Reichenau, now collected for the first time in one volume, revised according to the better editions, systematically arranged, enlarged, and corrected.**

**Added are:**

The letters and diplomas of Gregory VI, Clement II, and the Roman pontiffs;

the historical minor works of Rodulfus Glaber and Wipo the Priest.

Interspersed are the surviving writings or fragments of the writings of Guido of Châtillon, archbishop of Reims; Oliva of Ausona; Wazo of Liège; Gerard I of Cambrai; Hugh of Langres; Halinard of Lyon; and Jordan of Limoges, bishops;

and of Seifrid, abbot of Tegernsee; Odorannus, monk of Saint-Pierre-le-Vif; Helgaud of Fleury, monk; and Anselm, monk of Saint-Remi of Reims.

# In the Year of Our Lord 1045: Saint Bruno, Bishop of Würzburg

## The Works of Saint Bruno

After the editorial work of Reyser and Cochlaeus, revised by Heinrich Denzinger, professor of theology at the University of Würzburg.

[Col. 0009]

# Prolegomena

## I. The Life and Deeds of St Bruno

[Col. 0009A]

### 1

St Bruno (Brun), bishop of Würzburg, or Herbipolis, was born of the illustrious lineage of the dukes of Saxony, Franconia, and Carinthia, which produced the Ottonian and Franconian emperors. His father was Conrad I, duke of Carinthia, and his mother Mathilda, daughter of Hermann II, duke of Alamannia. Among his relatives were Gregory V, supreme pontiff, and the emperors Conrad II and Henry III. To make this genealogy evident at a single glance, we set out the entire family tree below.

[Col. 0009B] That our Bruno was the son of Conrad I and Mathilda is clear from what Hermann the Lame reports concerning his lineage under the year 1034 [Note: [Col. 0009B] Ussermann, edition I, p. 206.], namely, that he was the son of Conrad, duke, by Mathilda, when this is compared with what he records under the year 1024 concerning the younger Conrad [Note: [Col. 0009B] Ibid., p. 201.], namely, that he likewise was the son of Conrad, duke, by Mathilda. From this Father Aemilianus Ussermann correctly concluded [Note: [Col. 0009B] *The Bishopric of Würzburg*. San-Blasien Press, 1794, vol. I, p. 47. Cf. Hübner, *Genealogical Tables*, Leipzig, 1744, table 27.] that our Bruno and Conrad II, duke of Carinthia, were sons of the same father and mother.

Hence it is clear how greatly mistaken are those who make Conrad II the father of Bruno [Note: [Col. 0010B] Bruschius, Fries in the *Chronicles of Würzburg*, Heiron, and Megiserus in the *Annals of Carinthia*.], for this is also shown to be false by the fact that this Conrad died an untimely death in 1039, as the Hildesheim annals state [Note: [Col. 0011A] In Pertz V, p. 103.], whereas Bruno, already gray-haired, died in 1045.

It is further evident that it is entirely false that Bruno descended from the counts of Querfurt [Note: [Col. 0011C] Thus some say in Fries.], or that his mother was Mathilda of Querfurt, daughter of Gebhard of Querfurt and Sophia of Mansfeld, as others have asserted [Note: [Col. 0011C] Thus Bruschius, Elias Reusnerus in the supplement to his genealogical work *Basilikōn* (“Imperial Matters”), p. 45; and, following them, Henschenius in the *Acts of the Saints* under 17 May, and Pagius, *Critical Notes on Baronius* under 1045, no. 2, and others. Trithemius makes him a Saxon.]. Although this tale is reported by many important authors, it rests upon no monuments of antiquity; indeed, it is refuted by the genealogical tables of the Querfurt family [Note: [Col. 0011C] Cf. Hübner, cited work, vol. II, table 334.] and arose from the fact that some confused our Bruno with St Bruno, bishop and martyr and apostle of Prussia, who was killed for the faith in 1009 and who truly was a count of Querfurt [Col. 0011B]; while others, although distinguishing the two, were deceived by that report that Bruno of Würzburg belonged to the same stock of Querfurt and composed a genealogy entirely without foundation.

From the same genealogy of our saint it is highly probable that he received the name Bruno from his paternal uncle Bruno, who later became Pope Gregory V.

### 2

What Bruno did before becoming a bishop has been completely lost to memory, except that we learn from the account of a monk of Hammersleben concerning the basilica of Goslar and its provosts [Note: [Col. 0011C] In Leibniz, *Writings on Brunswick Affairs*, vol. II, p. 507.] that he was provost of Goslar’s high church [VII in the source; reading uncertain].

### 3

When the Emperor Conrad II was holding an assembly at Würzburg during Lent in 1034 [Note: [Col. 0011D] Anonymous historical record in Ludewig, *Writings on Würzburg Affairs*, in the notes to the Chronicle of Fries.], he arranged, with the unanimous consent of the clergy [Col. 0011C] [Note: [Col. 0011D] Bruschius.], for his paternal cousin Bruno to be placed over the church of Würzburg in the place of the deceased Meginhard; and, to honor him, at the same assembly he confirmed the privileges of the see in the most ample terms [Note: [Col. 0011D] An old record in Baum, in the sermon delivered at the Bruno jubilee of 1745.].

Bruno, however, took possession of the place of St Burchard on Easter Day [Note: [Col. 0011D] Hermann the Lame, under 1034.], which then fell on 14 April, as its nineteenth bishop. It is further handed down that on the Thursday after Easter he received the homage at Meiningen [Note: [Col. 0011D] Old record in Ludewig, cited work.] and that he was formally installed by Gebhard IV, count of Henneberg, who was performing the office of marshal according to custom [Note: [Col. 0011D] Spangenberg, *Chronicle of Henneberg*, fol. 74; cf. fol. 81.].

There are some who say that he was made bishop in 1033 [Note: [Col. 0011D] Bruschius; two chroniclers in Gropp, *Newest Collection of Writings on Würzburg Affairs*, I, 819, 823; two old records in Ludewig, cited work.] and give a different date for the beginning of his episcopate [Note: [Col. 0011D] Fries argues that he obtained the episcopate on 14 March; records in Ludewig maintain that he was at Meiningen on Thursday after Easter, 26 April 1033.].

But all the most reputable authors agree on the year 1034 [Note: [Col. 0011D] Hermann the Lame; the Hildesheim Annals in Pertz V, 99; the Augsburg Annals, ibid. V, 125; the Chronicle of Bernold, ibid. VII, 425; and the Chronicle of Würzburg. The Baluzian chronicle, ibid. II, 244, places the death of the predecessor—concerning whose date there is the same disagreement—on 21 March 1034. Finally, there are two records superior to every objection: the acts of the consecration of the church of St Burchard at Würzburg in 1042, in which that consecration is said to have been completed in the eighth year of Bruno’s consecration (in Gropp, *Chronicle of Würzburg*, vol. II, 206), and the acts of the consecration of the crypt of the cathedral church, celebrated on the twenty-first day after Bruno’s death and said to have taken place in the eleventh year of his consecration.] Since it is certain that Bruno died on 27 May 1045, and furthermore that he occupied the Würzburg see for eleven years, one month, and fourteen days, there can be no doubt that he obtained the episcopate in 1034, since exactly that amount of time elapsed from 14 April 1034 to 27 May 1045.

### 3*

After being promoted to the episcopate, Bruno showed that he had truly been given by God, as the Hildesheim Annals call him [Note: [Col. 0012D] Pertz V, 169.] [Col. 0012B]: “He was,” says Trithemius [Note: [Col. 0012D] *Annals*, vol. I, p. 169.], “in all things acceptable to God and human beings, just, learned, and an utterly blameless cultivator and propagator of Christian law.” Having become bishop, the same abbot of Sponheim continues, “he diligently devoted himself at all times to complete holiness and justice, and every good thing that he taught in words he first demonstrated by his conduct.”

Above all, however, there shone forth in the virtue of this most holy man a particular zeal for divine worship. Hence the laboriously prepared work on the Psalms, which we introduce below: he offered it to St Kilian and presented it as a gift to his cathedral church. To this church he either consecrated temples with the greatest solemnity or built and adorned them with the utmost generosity.

In the year of Christ 1034, on 7 September, Bruno consecrated the chapel of St Benedict at the monastery of Schwarzach, built by Abbot Wolfger [Note: [Col. 0012D] Anonymous record in Ludewig, *Writings on Würzburg Affairs*, p. 467; Bruschius, *Century of Monasteries*, fol. 145; the *Chronicle of Schwarzach* in Ludewig, *Writings on German Affairs*, vol. II, p. 16, which dates the event to the sixth day before the Ides of September, 1038. In the Schwarzach church, recently destroyed by the Vandals, there was formerly a stone on which the bishop, standing, offered the church to the seated St Peter; beneath it were carved words of this kind: “Bruno, bishop + St Peter the apostle.” I have this information from the excerpts of a certain Fabricius, who in the past century collected with great diligence many materials relating to our history, now preserved in the University Library.].

In 1036, on 8 days before the Kalends of June, Bruno attended the dedication of the church at Bustorf near Paderborn, having been summoned by Bishop Meinwerk together with St Bardo of Mainz and Herimann, archbishop of Cologne. Meinwerk, bishop of Paderborn, testified in a charter of donation that, with their advice, he had built the church together with its college of canons [Col. 0013A] [Note: [Col. 0013C] Schaten, *Annals of Paderborn*, vol. I, 498; *Life of St Meinwerk* in Leibniz, *Writings on Brunswick Affairs*, vol. I, p. 563.].

In the same year, on 15 August, he offered to God and St Kilian—that is, he donated to his cathedral church, which was then called St Kilian’s—a certain estate in the Paderborn diocese called Sunrgk, which he possessed from his paternal inheritance after dividing it with his brother [Note: [Col. 0013C] Fries, *Chronicle of Würzburg*.]. According to Fries, it yielded nearly 200 marks of silver [Note: [Col. 0013C] An anonymous record in Baum, cited work, p. 112, says that it produced 1,100 marks.]. He also arranged that a double tribute from the same village should be paid each year to the church and its clergy.

We have appended the authentic charter of this donation in full to our prolegomena. To make the matter still more secure, Bruno not only publicly announced on the feast of St John the Baptist, after preaching to the people, that he would do this [Col. 0013B], so that anyone who had an objection might have an opportunity to bring it forward freely; but, while traveling to Mainz, he also invited the Emperor Conrad II, who was staying there, and the bishops St Bardo of Mainz and Rotho of Paderborn to celebrate the feast of the Assumption of the Virgin with him at Würzburg and to act as witnesses to the donation [Note: [Col. 0013C] Fries; Schaten, I, 507.]. Indeed, he arranged for a bronze tablet bearing the inscription to be affixed in the church at Sunvyk.

Those estates, however, later passed to the bishops of Paderborn, and by the beginning of the sixteenth century they were no longer in the possession of the people of Würzburg [Note: [Col. 0013C] Fries; Schaten, I, 510. The latter testifies that the place was situated in a fertile region near Borgentreich, but that in his own time nothing remained except certain ruins of the church. Ibid.].

On Pentecost of the year 1042 he dedicated the Würzburg church of St Burchard, begun in 1033 by Willemuth, abbot of that monastery, and only recently brought happily to completion, in honor of the Holy Trinity, the Holy Cross, Mary the Mother of God, St Andrew the apostle, St Burchard, and St Remigius. He was assisted by Suidger, bishop of Bamberg, who later became Pope Clement II; Heribert of Eichstätt; Severus of Prague; Cadalus of Zeitz; and Ehrenfrid of Buhl [Note: [Col. 0013C] Fries; Reinhard, *Chronicle of Würzburg*, in Ludewig; Hofmann, *Bamberg Annals*, in the same author, vol. I, p. 67 of the *Bamberg Writings*. The acts of the consecration, formerly preserved in the chapter of St Burchard, are cited by Gropp, *Chronicle of Würzburg*, vol. II, 206.].

In the same year, 1042, on the day sacred to St Burchard, namely 14 October, he was invited by Gozonannus, bishop of Eichstätt, and attended the dedication of the church of St Walburgis. Since that bishop was carried off by a premature death on the third day afterward, Bruno received the duty of burying him [Note: [Col. 0013C] Bruschius, *Catalogue of the Bishops of Eichstätt*, fol. 183 [Col. 0013D] verso; Gretser, *Catalogue of the Bishops of Eichstätt*, vol. X of the *Works*, p. 845, from the anonymous Hasenried chronicle of 1075.].

Finally, he either built numerous churches and schools in his own diocese or endowed them with revenues [Note: [Col. 0013D] Bruschius; Kettler’s sermon delivered at the Bruno jubilee in 1745.].

The cathedral church itself, however, claimed the greatest diligence of this most holy prelate [Col. 0014B]. Finding it badly constructed and falling into ruin through age, in 1042 he undertook to raise it from its foundations [Note: [Col. 0013D] Fries.] and spent his entire patrimony on building and adorning it [Note: [Col. 0013D] Trithemius in the *Annals*; Fries.]. Finally, in 1043, he completed the presbytery and the crypt beneath it [Note: [Col. 0013D] Himmelstein, *St Kilian’s Cathedral at Würzburg*, 1850, p. 7.]. Hence his monogram can still be seen carved on the exterior part of the apse, of which we shall say more later.

Yet the most devout prelate did not achieve his desire to consecrate to God himself the church whose restoration he had arranged. Before undertaking the journey to Hungary—which was to be his last—he had already prepared the dedication of the crypt; but, overtaken by death, he left the completion of the work to another, namely St Bardo, called Chrysostom, archbishop of Mainz.

Accordingly, on 15 June 1045, which was the twenty-first day after Bruno’s death [Col. 0014C], it was consecrated [Note: [Col. 0013D] When the crypt altar was removed in 1699, a golden capsule was found into which Bruno had placed the relics and which he had sealed with his seal. On the lid were engraved the words “BRUNO EPS.” This, together with the act of consecration and three grains of incense, had been placed in a leaden box sealed with Bardo’s seal. In 1743, when Frederick Charles of Schönborn, then Bruno’s successor, consecrated the court church, all these objects were deposited in the high altar. This is taken from the diary of Johann Bernhard Mayer, bishop of Chrysopolis and auxiliary bishop of Würzburg, preserved in the chapter archive, vol. II, p. 13, and from B. Neumann’s description of the dedication of the court church in 1745, pp. 7–9, where each item is represented in copper engraving.

The act of consecration is of great importance for the chronology of Bruno. According to the copy, or facsimile, in Neumann, it reads as follows:

“In the year of the incarnation of the Lord 1046, in the fifteenth indiction, while the most glorious King Henry was reigning, in the seventh year of his reign, but in the seventeenth year of his ordination, and in the eleventh year of the ordination of Bruno, venerable bishop of the Würzburg church, on the twenty-first day of his death, namely the sixth day before the Kalends of June, this crypt was dedicated in honor of the Holy Trinity, the Holy Cross, holy Mary ever Virgin, St Stephen the protomartyr, and all the holy martyrs, and in honor of those whose relics are contained here.

“These are: hairs of St Stephen the protomartyr and the stone with which he was stoned; a veil of Glodesindis V, brought and placed beside the altar of St Stephen by an angel, in which relics of the bone of St Stephen’s shoulder are wrapped; a sandal and tunic of St Stephen; the blood of St Stephen; relics of St Vitus the martyr; relics of St Lambert the martyr; relics of Saints Celestine and Taurinus; relics of St Marcellianus the martyr; relics of St Blaise; relics of St George the martyr; relics of the Holy Innocents; relics of the holy martyrs Marcellinus and Peter; relics of Saints Dionysius and Pancratius; St Sixtus the martyr; St Stephen, pope and martyr, and St Cyriacus; St Maurice the martyr; St Laurence the martyr; St Apollinaris the martyr; relics of the holy martyrs Protus and Chrysogonus; St Alexander; and a piece of the gridiron of St Laurence.”

It must nevertheless be noted that there is an error either in the original itself or in the copy, since the reading should be the year 1045, in the thirteenth indiction, as our distinguished and celebrated historian Father Gropp has excellently demonstrated—unless one wishes the act itself to contradict itself.].

[Col. 0015A]

### 4

St Bruno’s care for the poor was no less great. From the revenues of the same estate called Sunryk, with which he had enriched the cathedral church, he ordered twelve poor people to be fed each year throughout the whole of Lent and also to be clothed on Good Friday [Note: [Col. 0015C] See the charter of donation. Thus the ancient manuscript cited by Baum in the sermon mentioned above.].

### 5

Bruno’s virtues made him, even more than his ties of blood, highly esteemed by the emperors Conrad II and Henry III. Yet Bruno was not the sort of man who followed the royal court in the manner of politicians and sought his own advantage through royal favor. Rather, he used the authority with which he was endowed to benefit the churches and advance every noble cause, as we shall prove by the following examples.

When an assembly was being held at Augsburg in 1040 [Col. 0015B], through the intervention of our Bruno and other bishops King Henry assigned the church at the monastery of Rinchnach, belonging to Altach, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of February [Note: [Col. 0015D] Hansiz, *Germania Sacra*, vol. II, p. 169. The diploma survives in the Altach materials appended to Gewold.].

Shortly afterward, on the ninth day before the Kalends of February of the same year, through the intervention of Bruno and Thietricus of Metz, Henry granted the county of Hasbania to the church of Liège [Note: [Col. 0015D] The letters are preserved in Chapeauville I, 279, and in Aubertus Miraeus, *Diplomatic and Historical Works*, vol. I, p. 264, second edition, Brussels, 1723.].

In the following year, 1041, he conferred another outstanding benefit upon the same church of Liège. For when Wazo, a pious and learned man, had been elected bishop there, and had been sent to the king, who was staying at Regensburg preparing to attack the Bohemians, in order to obtain royal approval, many courtiers argued that the election, having been made without royal favor, was invalid and that one of the royal chaplains should be promoted—someone who knew how not merely to preside but also to benefit the church.

[Col. 0015C] The young king’s mind was already inclined to send someone else to the people of Liège, unless Bruno alone, together with Herimann of Cologne, had resisted the whole assembly and drawn the king and the nobles toward a sounder decision [Note: [Col. 0015D] Anselm, *Deeds of the Bishops of Liège*, in Pertz IX, 220.].

On 3 January 1042, at Heeresheim, King Henry granted Bruno and his church various estates in the district of Kochergau, situated along the Kocher, namely in Sindringen, Suemeilendorf, Gerolzhagen, and Buch [Note: [Col. 0015D] Fries and others; Lang, *Bavarian Regesta*, I, 83.]. We have also added the record of this donation in an appendix.

In the same year, at Bruno’s urging, Gozmannus, a cleric of Würzburg from the counts of Rothenburg [Col. 0016A], was promoted to the see of Eichstätt, which had become vacant through the death of his brother Heribert [Note: [Col. 0015D] Thus the anonymous Hasenried chronicle in Gretser, *Catalogue of the Bishops of Eichstätt*, vol. X of the *Works*, p. 847, which also says that Heribert had been promoted at Bruno’s request. Since this would have had to occur in 1021, when Bruno had not yet had any connection with the people of Würzburg, we leave the judgment of this matter to others.].

After returning from Pannonia in 1043, King Henry held a general conference at Ulm. He came to Constance during the time of the synod with a great many bishops. On the day of pardon, which is Thursday in the Lord’s Supper, ascending the steps with the bishop of Constance, he urged his subjects to peace and confirmed the peace by an edict; and, in accordance with the institution of Christian law, he publicly pardoned all who had injured one another [Note: [Col. 0015D] Cf. Hartzheim, *German Councils*, III, 110, and the authors whom he cites. That this event belongs to 1043, as Hermann the Lame records it, rather than to 1044, as the Hildesheim Annals and Hartzheim have it, is excellently demonstrated by Father Neugart, *The Bishopric of Constance*, I, 353.].

The records by which we could specifically prove that our Bruno was among the authors of so remarkable an edict have indeed disappeared. Nevertheless, since he attended the councils as a prince of the empire, it must be presumed; and from similar events it is very likely that he should be counted above all among those who persuaded the king to undertake a measure so unprecedented and so contrary to the customs of the Germans of that age.

Many also attribute to our Bruno a notable act of the same kind, which took place during the siege of Milan in 1037 [Note: [Col. 0016C] The authors disagree about the year in which this occurred. Bruschius; Spangenberg, *Chronicle of Henneberg*, book II, chapter 1; the chronicle in Gropp, *Newest Collection*, I, 823; and another account in Fabricius’s excerpts, fol. 130 verso, assign it to 1034. Hermann the Lame, Conrad, abbot of Ursperg, the Hildesheim Annals in Pertz V, 99, the Augsburg Annals V, 125, and the Melk Annals XI, 498, refer Conrad’s journey to Italy to 1037. This must be accepted as the year in which the event actually occurred, since Muratori, *Italian Historical Authorities*, vol. I, p. 609, preserves a diploma of Conrad dated during the siege of Milan on the vigil of Pentecost 1037. Sigebert of Gembloux, who places it in 1039, must be entirely rejected.].

They relate that the Emperor Conrad imprisoned certain rebellious bishops of Lombardy, including the bishop of Milan. When the latter escaped from custody, the king pursued him, besieged Milan for an entire year, and installed another in his see.

While Conrad was besieging a certain fortress of St Ambrose near Milan called Curbitum, on Pentecost, although the sky had previously been clear, a terrible storm arose, with such violent flashes of lightning that [Col. 0016C] many men and horses in the camp were killed and some were even driven out of their minds by terror. Those who had been outside the camp, however, said upon returning that they had felt nothing of the storm.

The emperor, however, was attending Mass at the same time; Bishop Bruno, Bertulfus the emperor’s secretary, and others testified that they had seen St Ambrose threatening grave things against the king unless he abandoned the siege.

Wipo the priest, the emperor’s intimate associate, who wrote Conrad’s life, mentions the storm but says nothing about the vision [Note: [Col. 0016D] In Pistorius, *Writings on German Affairs*, vol. III, p. 481; likewise Hepidanus in Goldast, *Alamannic Affairs*, vol. I. Hermann the Lame and Conrad, abbot of Ursperg, also omit the storm.].

Many mention Bishop Bruno without qualification [Note: [Col. 0016D] Sigebert of Gembloux in Pistorius I, 833, and Pertz VIII, 358; Ricobald of Ferrara in Muratori, *Writings on Italian Affairs*, vol. IX, p. 120; *Deeds of the Bishops of Cambrai*, Pertz IX, 487; Alberic, monk of the Three Fountains, in Leibniz, vol. II of the *Historical Additions*, p. 70.], without specifying his see, although there were many bishops named Bruno in that period.

All the people of Würzburg, however, unanimously say that it was our Bruno [Note: [Col. 0017C] Chronicle III in Gropp, *Newest Collection*, vol. I, 843; an old record by an unknown author in Ludewig, p. 468; Bruschius; Fries; Reinhard; Johann Müller. Spangenberg, however, *Chronicle of Henneberg*, book II, chapter 1—whether relying on a historical record or drawing his conclusion from the Würzburg chronicles, I do not know—states that Poppo VIII, count of Henneberg, was summoned by Bruno in 1034, as his vassal, to follow him into Italy; but he says nothing about the event itself.] and that he then sang Mass in the emperor’s presence. This story was even admitted into the lessons of Würzburg itself and depicted in our churches.

There is, however, a writer of the Hildesheim Annals whose words were also inserted into the Saxon Annalist [Note: [Col. 0017D] Hildesheim Annals, Pertz V, 10; Saxon Annalist VIII, 680.] and who raises some suspicion that our Bruno may have been confused with Bruno of Minden (1037–1045).

These writers relate that Bruno of Minden, on that very day of Pentecost which was disturbed by the storm, received episcopal anointing from Herimann, archbishop of Cologne, in a field near Milan, with the king and nobles present. They are silent, however, about Ambrose’s appearance and his being seen by Bruno [Col. 0017B].

Father Aemilianus Ussermann therefore spoke too hastily [Note: [Col. 0017D] *The Bishopric of Würzburg*, “On St Bruno,” no. XIII.] when he said that others attributed that vision to Bruno of Minden, although they certainly do not speak to him of an Ambrose seen by the bishop of Minden. The editors of Pertz likewise acted too hastily when, in the index or notes, wherever “Bishop Bruno” was mentioned without qualification in the writers’ text, they identified him as Bruno of Minden.

We do not deny, nevertheless, that some uncertainty arises from this. Since, however, it is highly probable that our Bruno followed Conrad into Italy, since the emperor compelled him to perform that vassal’s duty, and since we see that Bruno repeatedly followed the king’s court; furthermore, since during the consecration of that prelate he could have experienced the divine event, and since nothing decisive stands in the way, we judge that what has until now been handed down and accepted in our church should not be disturbed in its possession.

[Col. 0017C] Some circumstances, however, will remain uncertain [Note: [Col. 0017D] It is certainly entirely false that the king was crowned at that time during the solemn celebration of Mass. Ussermann, quoting Sigebert’s words, thinks that the text should read: “while the emperor was staying in a small church beside the city,” rather than “was being crowned.” If our Bruno saw Ambrose during the Mass—namely, the Mass of the consecration—the opinion that he himself sang the Mass could easily have arisen.].

### 6

Finally, when Bruno was accompanying Henry III on his journey to Hungary to restore King Peter, that most unfortunate accident occurred which snatched the holy prelate from his flock.

When the king, around the feast of Pentecost, had withdrawn to a fortress beside the Danube opposite the town of Ips, called Besenburg (Boesenberg, S. Poersenburg), he climbed onto an old gallery [Col. 0018A] together with Bruno of Würzburg, Alamannus, abbot of the monastery at Süssenstein, situated not far from the fortress, and Reichhildis, widow of Albert, count of Ebersberg, who, after her husband had died during the preceding Lent, was then mistress of the castle.

While the countess was asking the king to grant her nephew on her brother’s side—namely Welf III—the fiefs formerly held by her husband, the gallery collapsed because of its excessive age. The king fell into the bath beneath it and escaped unharmed; Reichhildis and Abbot Alamannus were killed instantly; Bruno, gravely injured, survived until the seventh or eighth day, which was the Monday after Easter.

Thus report Aventinus and Fries [Note: [Col. 0017D] Aventinus, book V of the *Bavarian Annals*, no. 30; Fries, [Col. 0018C] in the *Chronicle*, from an account sent to him by a monk of that monastery while he was attending the Augsburg assembly in 1530. The Augsburg Annals in Pertz V, 126, give a brief account. What Bruschius and others after him relate—that all the king’s courtiers were present and that the king seized a window—was added later by popular rumor, which enlarged and embellished the event.].

Yet these authors, and Johannes Müller of Würzburg, Adlsreiter, and Brunnerus Boicus, the chroniclers who followed them, are mistaken when they admit a certain tale about a specter that, shortly before Bruno’s fall, foretold the disaster. For they relate that, when the ship on which the bishop was traveling had reached that whirlpool which makes the Danube dangerous in that region, a specter of black appearance stood upon the mountain and addressed Bruno as follows:

> “I am, O bishop, your evil spirit; you shall be mine wherever you go. For the moment I shall spare you, but soon you will see me again.”

They say that a tower stood on that very spot until 1530, which people called the Devil’s Tower. In his notes to the Roman Martyrology, Baronius sharply criticized Aventine over this little tale, because it was prejudicial to Bruno’s holiness, commended by the Roman pontiffs. The story was plainly invented by the common people, who, unable to bring themselves to believe that so holy a man had perished in so unfortunate an accident, could find no other explanation than that it had been brought about by hatred of the devil.

The day of Bruno’s death was 27 May 1045, and there is no doubt about the year. The authors indicate the day in different ways, but the weight and number of the historical records make 27 May entirely certain [Note: Thus three chronicles in Gropp (Novissima Collectio I, 817, 819, 823); Bruschius; the Abbot of Ursperg; Trithemius; both fifteenth-century editors of the Reyser Psalter; the Onoldine Necrology in Eckhard, Commentary on the Affairs of Eastern France I, 490; Ekkehard’s Würzburg Chronicle in Eckhard I, 818; the Würzburg Chronicle in Pertz VIII, 30, in Baluze, Miscellanea I, 501; and the calendar in the ceremonial book of the cathedral church, in Pertz II, 244, which later passed into the Schlimbach Library and belongs to the fifteenth century. Also the Mortuary Book of Paderborn, preserved in the cathedral of Trier and dating from the twelfth century; and the Saxon Annalist, Pertz VIII, 687. To these may be added public documents of unquestionable authority: Bruno’s own epitaphs, the charter of the consecration of the cathedral church’s crypt, and finally the charter of the translation in 1257, which we shall discuss below.]

Hermann the Lame, and Bernold after him [Note: In Pertz VII, 425], say that he went to heaven on 26 May. This could indeed have been passed over, had not Andreas, bishop of Würzburg, enacted in his synodal statutes of 1314 [Note: Councils of Germany IV, 248] that Bruno’s anniversary was to be celebrated “on the Saturday after Saint Urban’s Day, on which he happily closed his final day.” This law was later adopted word for word by Wolfram in his statutes of 1329 and by Gottfried IV in 1446. Those who favor this date further say that in that year the day in question was 26 May.

But this is completely and demonstrably false. For the Annals of Corvey [Note: In Pertz V, 6] report that Pentecost in that year fell on 26 May; consequently Saint Urban’s Day, which is 25 May, was itself the Saturday vigil. Moreover, Frisius testifies that Bruno died on the Monday after Pentecost. I therefore have no doubt that Andreas either made a mistake or that the text is corrupt [Col. 0019B], and that it should read “on the day after, or the second day after, Saint Urban,” on which day Frisius testifies that the anniversary was celebrated in the cathedral, in agreement with the very ancient ceremonial book of the cathedral church.

Finally, through an error propagated through a long succession of authors, it happened that in the Galessinian Martyrologies, and after them in Baronius and Canisius [Note: German Martyrology, in the unfinished third edition], the feast of Saint Bruno was assigned to 17 May. Indeed, the church of Würzburg, that most faithful daughter of the Roman Church, followed the Roman Martyrology and adopted the same day, although another day must be accepted from its own records.

Bruno therefore sat in the chair of Saint Burkhard for eleven years, one month, and fourteen days. Some give twelve years or two months [Note: Some authors cited by Frisius]. But the most trustworthy records [Note: Two chronicles in Gropp (Novissima Collectio I, 817, 819); Baluze’s Würzburg Chronicle; Ekkehard’s Würzburg Chronicle; the chronicle in excerpts of Fabricius, fol. 117; the charter of the translation in 1357. The Saxon Annalist under the year 1045, the charter of the consecration of the crypt, says that this was celebrated on the twenty-first day after Bruno’s death, in the eleventh year of his consecration] have left this as established fact.

### 7

Bruno’s sacred body was transferred to Würzburg by the officials, and they say [Note: Baum, sermon cited above, p. 114, from an ancient manuscript] that they concealed the manner of his most grievous death for some time, lest the people be disturbed by excessive grief. He was buried in the crypt of the cathedral church, which he himself had built and had already begun to prepare for consecration. His epitaph was as follows:

> “In the year of the Lord 1045, on 27 May, Bishop Bruno, the founder, died.”

[Note: That first sarcophagus of Bruno, with the epitaph just mentioned, still exists and is the altar-table which they call the Deans’ Altar. See Himmelstein, work cited, p. 33, and the record of the elevation and translation of 1699 in Gropp (Novissima Collectio II, 113).]

Other monuments of Bruno also remain, and they deserve mention. Above all there is his chasuble, preserved in the cathedral church, enclosed on every side, violet in color, and once gilded with Phrygian embroidery. It ought to be described more fully, if vandal hands had not ravaged it. This chasuble was used on the anniversary which was celebrated in Bruno’s memory until 1616 [Col. 0020A].

Another object that has greatly occupied scholars is his monogram. It is carved on the outer part of the apse of the cathedral church and occurs on the coins of the bishops of Würzburg, who were also dukes of Eastern Franconia and, from Bruno’s predecessor Meginhard onward, exercised the right of minting money until the end of the fifteenth century. It has this form:

We shall not repeat here what various writers have said about its meaning. Instead, on this matter we refer the reader to [Note: Here the reference is to G. Keller, a man highly skilled in the study of our coinage, in the Archiv für die Geschichte des Bisthums Würzburg VI, fasc. 1, p. 68], who has solved the problem admirably and explained the force of this sign so that the words are: “Bruno, bishop.”

[Col. 0020B] They say, on no known basis, that his house stood in the place called Braunshof, not far from the cathedral church. Bruno was of very great stature, as may be inferred from his remains; his head was not especially large in proportion to his body, and when he died his hair was already gray [Note: See the record of the elevation and translation of 1699]. The king and the people of Würzburg also honored his memory in this respect: they appointed his nephew Adalbero as his successor [Note: See the Würzburg additions in a manuscript of the Saxon Annalist, in Pertz VIII, 551].

## II. On Bruno’s holiness and cult

### 8

After his death Bruno left behind a great reputation for holiness. He is already listed among the bishops of that age distinguished for holiness and learning by the author of the Life of Saint Meinwerk in Leibniz [Note: Rerum Brunsvicensium I, 556], and from the accounts of the miracles which we give below it follows that, at the end of the twelfth and the beginning of the thirteenth century, he was commonly called a saint by the Christian people and invoked as a saint.

Later he is very frequently called “blessed” [Note: Acts of the translations of 1257 and 1423; the second epitaph of 1257; the Martyrology prefixed to the Passionary of the Carthusian monastery of Würzburg, 1485], and “saint” [Note: Laurentius of Bibra in a letter to the people of Baunach, discussed below], as well as “given by God” [Note: Annals of Hildesheim in Pertz V, various pages] and “venerable” [Note: The act of the consecration of the crypt, drawn up immediately after Bruno’s death, and the statutes of Bishop Wolfram in 1329].

The editor of the Reyser Psalter, at the end of the fifteenth century, calls him “a distinguished bishop, holy in religion and life,” and says that he “shone forth through works of virtue and always nourished, both by his work and by his example, the flock entrusted to him by the Lord.” We have given above the judgment of Trithemius, Bruno’s contemporary, which he also repeats in his book On Ecclesiastical Writers.

All the Würzburg chroniclers agree, except for one, Johannes Müller, who, with shameless boldness, dared to say that Bruno was not numbered among the saints despite the words of the devil appearing in the form of a specter. We reject this, together with that little tale, with indignation; even if it were true, the conclusion would not follow from it. Nor did Aventine himself, who was the first to tell the story, infer anything contrary to Bruno’s holiness from it.

But God himself offered greater testimony to the holiness of his servant than human testimony could provide, through the miracles by which Bruno shone forth both while alive [Note: Trithemius, in his Catalogue of Illustrious Germans Living Today] and after his blessed death.

### 9

When people began to flock to his tomb, and frequent miracles were being performed there, they were recorded by public authority as early as 1202 under Conrad of Ravensburg; we have added the document of that proceeding to the prolegomena.

Hermann I of Lobdeburg (1225–1254) sent a solemn embassy to Rome in 1237 to obtain his canonization from the Supreme Pontiff [Note: Frisius and the papal letters]. Gregory IX, who then occupied the chair of Peter, sent in 1238 a brief to the abbots of Brombach and Schönthal, of the Cistercian order, and to the prior of the Friars Preachers of Würzburg, entrusting them with the examination of the miracles.

That this examination was carried out by them is clear from letters sent to the same men by Innocent IV, who had meanwhile occupied the Roman See in 1246. In those letters he says that the miracles were fully established by the report of the commissioners. The report may perhaps have been based, in addition to the record of 1202, on the document which we give second in the appendix. The date at which the first miracle is said to have occurred agrees with this: namely, the year 1237.

Nevertheless, the Pontiff required that evidence concerning Bruno’s virtues also be produced from reputation and written documents, since eyewitnesses could not be brought forward.

Meanwhile Hermann, bishop of Würzburg, preparing the elevation of the sacred body and the solemn canonization, collected money from pilgrims and others and undertook to restore and adorn the presbytery and crypt of the cathedral church in which Bruno lay. Indulgences were also granted by bishops and cathedral chapters in various parts of Germany to those who contributed alms toward Bruno’s canonization and the restoration of the cathedral church [Note: See Lang, Regesta Boica II: the letters patent of Hermann, bishop of Würzburg, 1 September 1237, p. 265; the letters patent of the provost and dean of Würzburg, 1237, p. 271; the mandate of the provost and dean of Bamberg, 8 May 1237, p. 263; the indulgence of Engelhard, bishop of Naumburg, May 1237, p. 265; of Siegfried of Mainz, 28 April 1237, p. 263; of the bishop of Hildesheim, 13 July 1237, p. 265; of the bishop of Worms, 25 May 1237, p. 273; and of Hermann, bishop of Würzburg, 1 January 1240, p. 279. Baum, in the sermon cited above, p. 119, testifies that in his time the ecclesiastical government archives contained letters of indulgence issued by the bishops of Mainz, Bamberg, Worms, Speyer, Naumburg, Merseburg, Hildesheim, and Halberstadt to promote the canonization of Saint Bruno]. Nevertheless, all the money was spent on repairing the buildings, and the entire undertaking came to a halt.

### 10

As a result, Bruno has not been formally canonized, as the expression goes, even down to the present day. Thus there is insufficient foundation for what Trithemius says in his book On Ecclesiastical Writers: that Bruno had been entered in the catalogue of the saints. Nor is there sufficient basis for the conjectures of Henschenius in the Bollandist Acta Sanctorum [Note: Under 17 May, p. 39] and of Gropp [Note: Novissima Collectio II, p. 109], namely, that only the papal diploma had perished and that Bruno had been solemnly numbered among the saints around the year 1257.

For it is absolutely certain that no cult was offered to him in this church of ours before his name was admitted to the Roman Martyrology. On the contrary, his anniversary continued to be celebrated throughout the entire diocese until 1616, with only certain special ceremonies added in the cathedral—ceremonies not customary in ordinary funerals [Note: Gropp describes them (Novissima Collectio II, 110), following the calendar and the Schlimbach ceremonial of the cathedral church, as follows. On the preceding day, after Vespers, a procession was made to the crypt. Two boys dressed in red copes, carrying banners of the same color, went in front, together with the sacristan; the canons followed, along with the lords of Haug and the New Monastery, who had been invited for the occasion. Bruno’s tomb was incensed, with candles placed upon it. On the day itself, vigils and a Mass for the dead were sung in the crypt, but the celebrant wore violet—that is, Bruno’s own chasuble—and the altar was more richly adorned. Frisius testifies that the relics of Saint Kilian were also brought into the crypt in the evening and morning and remained there, exposed during the Mass].

There is no mention whatever of Bruno in the printed Würzburg Missals and Breviaries of the fifteenth, sixteenth, or seventeenth centuries [Col. 0022B]. Indeed, Laurentius of Bibra, bishop of Würzburg (1490–1519), explicitly testified to this in a letter sent to the inhabitants of Baunach. They had asked him to permit them to honor as a saint a certain Victor, who lay there and, as they said, shone forth through miracles.

The extremely cautious bishop did not grant their request. He said that he was especially moved to this decision by the example of his own cathedral church:

> “Although Bishop Bruno is renowned for many miracles, since it has not yet happened that he was canonized, our choir does not honor him as a saint; nevertheless, it does not omit him from the appropriate offices for the dead” [Note: In Gropp, Novissima Collectio II, p. 110].

The clergy and people of Würzburg nevertheless did not fail to display signs of the highest veneration for their most holy pastor [Col. 0022C], until at last, with the consent of the universal Church, they were permitted to honor him as a saint according to ecclesiastical custom.

On 13 September 1257, during the episcopate of Iring, Bruno’s old stone sarcophagus was enclosed within a new, larger, and more ornate one. The latter rose above the old tomb and was open at the top, so that access to it was available—a form of tomb then customary for altars beneath which saints lay. Later people used this arrangement to crawl through the tomb and apply to themselves the power proceeding from the saint.

The following epitaph was carved upon it:

> “In the year of the Lord 1045, on 27 May, blessed Bruno, founder of this church, died. He sat for two years, one month, and fourteen days.”

On the same occasion the sacred bones were wrapped in purple silk, and they placed inside the tomb the following document, sealed with the chapter’s seal:

> “In the year of the Lord 1045, on 27 May, blessed Bruno, bishop of Würzburg and founder of this church, died. He sat for eleven years, one month, and fourteen days, and was transferred from the place where he had been buried to this place in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1257, on 13 September, in the third year of the pontificate of our lord Pope Alexander and in the fourth year of the episcopate of our lord Iring, bishop of Würzburg.”

In the fifteenth century the tomb was opened again, as is clear from a paper document discovered in 1699. It read as follows:

> “From the day on which the relics of blessed Bruno were deposited in this place, the sarcophagus had not been opened until the year 1423 [Note: Gropp (Novissima Collectio II, p. 114) reads 1450; Johann Bernhard Mayer, suffragan bishop of Würzburg, gives 1443 in his diary. The date must be read as 1423, for Richard of Masbach was dean from 1422 to 1435 and from 1450 to 1454, while Heinrich Weckmar was vicar general in 1416 and 1423], on the day after the Assumption of the glorious Virgin, by Richard, dean, Johannes Giltmar, custodian, and Heinrich of Wechmar, canons and prelates of this church, for the honor of the aforesaid relics.”

Saint Bruno was honored above the other deceased bishops especially because his successors ordered that his anniversary be celebrated throughout the entire diocese. Thus Andreas, bishop of Würzburg, decreed in a synod held on 17 May 1314:

> “Likewise, we order that the anniversary of the reverend lord Bruno, formerly bishop of Würzburg, be observed by our subjects of the city and diocese on the Saturday after Saint Urban’s Day, on which he happily closed his final day, according to custom, humbly and devoutly” [Note: Statute 8, Councils of Germany IV, p. 246].

This was again emphasized in the statutes of Wolfram in 1329 and of Gottfried IV in 1446.

### 11

Finally, Cardinal Baronius, relying on the papal letters cited above, entered the name of Saint Bruno into the Roman Martyrology, revised with the authority of Clement X and reprinted at Antwerp in 1590.

As a result, beginning in 1616 people again seriously considered introducing a public cult of Bruno throughout the diocese. In that year the anniversary customarily celebrated each year in the cathedral in Bruno’s memory was abolished. The procession on the preceding day and the incensing of the tomb remained, but the funeral rite was removed; in place of the Mass for the dead, a solemn Mass of the Most Holy Trinity was substituted. These practices were retained until 1699.

[Col. 0023D] In the following year, 1617, the Roman Martyrology was printed at Würzburg for the use of the people of Würzburg. In 1616 Bruno’s miracles were made public in print from the document of 1202; the same was done again in 1657.

Nevertheless, the bishops of Würzburg were so observant of the ecclesiastical laws that, even after Bruno had been entered in the public calendars of the Church—a step which certainly seems equivalent to canonization—they nevertheless considered it a religious duty to honor him with the honors proper to the saints.

Although the Roman rite was introduced into the diocese by Johann Philipp of Schönborn, and although he arranged for the Würzburg Proprium to be printed in 1665 according to the norm of the Roman Breviary, Bruno’s feast was not included among the offices of our saints. The earliest monument of an office instituted in Bruno’s honor that has come to our notice is the 1689 Proprium of the Canons Regular of Saint Augustine at Heidenfeld, where Bruno’s office is found, though it differs from the one used today.

Finally, in 1699 Johann Philipp II of Greiffenklau ordered Bruno’s sacred body to be raised [Col. 0024B] and decreed that his feast, together with an office, should be celebrated throughout the diocese.

The sacred bones, which, according to Philipp Wilhelm Virtung of Hartung, then professor of medicine at the Alma Julia, emitted a pleasant odor—an odor which he judged should by no means be considered natural—were properly arranged, joined together, and clothed in episcopal vestments. On 29 September they were placed upon a new altar in the crypt, constructed by Georg Heinrich of Stadion, dean of the chapter.

In 1745, seven hundred years after the death of Bruno, under the rule of Friedrich Karl of Schönborn, a jubilee was celebrated with the greatest solemnity from 17 May through 23 May. Later, from 1749 onward, when the crypt was again renovated and enlarged, the stone sarcophagus that had first served as Saint Bruno’s tomb [Col. 0024C] was moved into the church to serve as the altar-table which they call the Deans’ Altar. The saint himself was placed upon that same altar; soon afterward, however, the sacred body was transferred to the altar of Saint Martin, where it remains buried in peace to the present day and is visited by the devotion of the faithful [Note: What has been set out thus far concerning Saint Bruno’s cult has been taken from Henschenius, Acta Sanctorum, under 17 May, p. 38 ff.; Gropp, Novissima Collectio II, p. 108 ff., from the diary of Johann Bernhard Mayer, suffragan bishop of Würzburg, preserved in the chapter archives, II, pp. 13–16; Himmelstein, Saint Kilian’s Cathedral, p. 22 ff.; Grebner, Compendium of Universal History, 1764, III, pp. 1217 and 1396; and Balthasar Neumann, Description of the Brunonian Jubilee of 1745].

## III. On Bruno’s writings

### 12

What we observed so often while describing Bruno’s life—namely, that because many Brunos distinguished for learning or virtue lived in that age, he was confused with others who bore the same name—appears above all when we investigate his writings.

We should therefore establish as a firm foundation that no other writing of Bruno has come down to our age or is commended by reliable testimony from antiquity [Col. 0024D], apart from the commentary on the Psalms, the canticles, the Lord’s Prayer, and the Creeds, which we have undertaken to publish after repeated efforts.

An anonymous writer of Melk, in On Ecclesiastical Writers [Note: Chapter 81], also claims that Bruno wrote against simoniacs. We, however, must most certainly admit that this is an error, since no other trace exists by which this work can be attributed to Bruno [Col. 0025A]. Trithemius, who in the fifteenth century was abbot of Saint James of the Scots in our city of Würzburg, already testifies:

> “If he wrote anything else, it did not come to me.”

Georg Galopinus is plainly mistaken when he published at Douai in 1608 a commentary on the Pentateuch under the name of our Bruno. Anyone who reads what is said there [Note: Deuteronomy 25:11] about the dispute between the author and the archdeacon of Benevento concerning the church of Siponto will acknowledge that it belongs to Bruno of Aosta, abbot of Monte Cassino and later bishop of Segni, who lived at the end of that same century.

Those who attribute commentaries on Paul’s Epistles or on Solomon’s Proverbs to him, such as Wilhelm Eisengrein [Note: In his Catalogue of Witnesses to Catholic Truth], either confuse him with that same Bruno of Aosta or with the founder of the Carthusians.

The verses against wicked and heretical priests must also be attributed to the latter. Ludewig, in his notes to Frisius’s chronicle, cited them from Selneccer and Aegidius Periander as though they were the work of our Bruno.

### 13

Having disposed of these false attributions, let us consider what sort of genuine work his work on the Psalms is, what its purpose is, and what its value.

A school flourished at Würzburg in the House of the Savior, under Bernulf, then a most distinguished teacher. Before him there had been an Italian summoned to Würzburg by the bishop, followed by a whole succession of men who were, for the conditions of that age, highly learned. Thus the fame of the Würzburg school spread far and wide, and many bishops of churches emerged from it.

Nevertheless, it must be presumed that a considerable part of the clergy, given the barbarism of the times, was of a kind that required various forms of instruction. Something similar occurred in the diocese of Verona, where there were many people for whom Ratherius, bishop and most rigorous reformer of his church, prescribed in his Itinerary [Note: In D’Achery, Spicilegium I, p. 376]:

> “That each person, if possible, should have with him in writing an exposition of the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer according to the tradition of the orthodox.”

As the conditions of the age required—when the intellectual powers of earlier peoples had grown old, while those of more recent peoples were still in infancy, so that they could do little except collect the work of others—so Bruno’s work too is a mere compilation, gathered from the writings of the Fathers on every side. Nevertheless, we cannot deny that judgment and critical ability shine through in the manner of his collecting.

We shall assign the parts of Bruno’s preface to their proper authors in the appropriate place [Col. 0025D]. His commentary on the Psalms itself was compiled from the following authors, whose names are indicated by initial letters placed before the passages:

- Augustine (A);
- Pseudo-Bede (B), who occurs frequently in the arguments but less often in the commentary;
- Cassiodorus (C), whom he used most extensively;
- Gregory (G), who occurs only six times;
- the Breviary on the Psalms attributed to Jerome (H).

In the Canticles, Origen (O) is cited several times and Rabanus Maurus once. According to the Reyser editor [Col. 0026A], scarcely thirteen times is the sense of an author reported without reproducing the author’s complete words.

After each psalm, following a very ancient custom [Note: See Blessed Cardinal Thomasius, Psalter with Canticles, Rome 1697, preface, p. XI], a prayer has been added which in a certain way gathers together the fruit of the psalm. This had been prescribed by the Council of Agde in 506, canon 30, so that after the antiphons prayers of collection should be said in order by bishops or priests.

That this custom existed in Spain is apparent from the Mozarabic liturgy; but there can be no doubt that the same practice was also followed in Gaul. The prayers found in Bruno appear for the first time in Alcuin’s Offices for the Ferias [Note: Patrologia Latina CI, columns 509 ff.], then in our Bruno, afterward in Ludolf of Saxony, a fourteenth-century author, in his commentary on the Psalms, and in George Cassander’s collection of ecclesiastical prayers.

Blessed Cardinal Thomasius concludes that they are older than the eighth century because they follow the reading of the Roman Psalter, whose use in Gaul had ceased long before Walafrid Strabo. Blessed Cardinal Thomasius restored them from Vatican manuscripts in his Psalter. But since our task was to publish Bruno, we have everywhere retained Bruno’s reading.

Saint Volbodonius, bishop of Liège, who died in 1020 and was therefore Bruno’s contemporary, did something similar in this respect. Rainerus, the monk who wrote his life, says that Volbodonius wrote by his own hand a book of psalms in which he placed beneath each psalm a prayer composed from that psalm and dictated by himself. Nevertheless, if Volbodonius really was the author of those prayers, they must have differed from ours.

The exposition of the Lord’s Prayer and the Apostles’ Creed, arranged through interrogations and questions, closely resembles the catechism used at that time in the examinations preceding baptism. Examples of this can be found among the collections of liturgical monuments.

### 14

It was of the greatest importance for us to investigate what sort of Psalter text Bruno placed beneath his commentary, since it is an exceedingly ancient and in many respects entirely unique exemplar of our Vulgate.

Above all, it must be noted that Bruno himself distinguishes this text in his critical observations, which occur here and there [Note: Psalms 44:19; 67:33; 86:3; 87, title; 88:19; 104:22; 104:27; 106:40; 134:13], from Jerome’s Roman Psalter and from the version which Jerome translated directly from Hebrew. Indeed, once he distinguishes it even from the Gallican Psalter [Note: Psalm 146:1], calling it “our translation,” as though it differed from all others.

The Reyser editor, a man of exceptionally keen vision, also recognized this. In his preface he observes:

> “This Psalter of the most blessed bishop Bruno of ours sometimes agrees in its wording with the Hebrew truth or the Roman interpretation, while it differs from the customary words of our Gallican translation. Its punctuation too, which in this Psalter has been made from the glosses of Jerome, Augustine, and Cassiodorus—men certainly most learned—and which is sometimes made from one gloss differently from another, differs in many places from the common and customary punctuation.”

Nevertheless, if the matter is examined more carefully, one will perceive that Bruno’s text is Jerome’s Gallican Psalter, although in many places it differs from that most customary form which we chant. Therefore Blessed Cardinal Thomasius [Note: Psalter with Canticles, Rome 1697, preface, p. XI] and the editors of Jerome’s divine library [Note: Volume X of Jerome’s works, Patrologia Latina XXIX, column 119, note c] were not mistaken when they said that the Gallican Psalter, marked with obeli and asterisks, was first published with the commentary of Bruno, bishop of Würzburg.

The only qualification is that Bruno very often has readings which the editors did not receive into the text of their edition, but which they nevertheless add in the notes as variant readings of manuscripts, especially the Palatine codex [Col. 0027B].

It is also entirely true that Bruno’s text more often differs from the Gallican Psalter, whatever the manuscript, and follows the Roman Psalter. Indeed, there are variant readings which can be reduced to neither of the two.

Three possible explanations for this peculiarity presented themselves. Either Bruno himself corrected the Psalter; or he followed a text corrected by Alcuin; or finally the Gallican Psalter text found in Bruno was the form that had gradually developed in Britain and had been brought here by the earliest apostles of our homeland, who had come from the British islands.

That Bruno himself corrected the text does not seem likely, since in the critical notes mentioned above he nowhere acts as a corrector, but appeals to a translation already established by usage.

We therefore undertook a comparison of Bruno’s text with Alcuin’s works on the Psalter and with the commentary on the Psalms falsely attributed to Bede, which must nevertheless be presumed to be of British origin.

But the Psalter text in Alcuin’s work entitled Offices for the Ferias appears to have been thoroughly altered according to the standard of the present day. In his commentaries on the penitential Psalms, the gradual Psalms, and Psalm 118, we found a few places in which he departs from the Gallican text together with Bruno and the Roman Psalter, but many more in which he differs from Bruno.

The comparison with Pseudo-Bede produced better results. We certainly admit that the proof would have become still more evident if Bede’s text had not been altered by copyists and others, so that his genuine reading must generally be taken from the commentary itself, and if a considerable portion of the Psalms had not gone without exposition in that commentary.

Nevertheless, we found nine places in which Pseudo-Bede agrees with Bruno against the Gallican and Roman Psalters:

- Psalm 4:5: “and in your beds”;
- Psalm 92:7: “in length”;
- Psalm 53:14: “he drives away”;
- Psalm 103:13: “a voice”;
- Psalm 105:37: “slain”;
- Psalm 118:145: “with my whole heart,” without “my”;
- Psalm 118:150: “with iniquity.”

Two of these are passages [Note: Psalm 68:31, “their pains”; Psalm 76:6, “I was digging”] in which he indicates that Bruno’s reading was known to him, although it occurs nowhere else in manuscripts of the Gallican or Roman text.

Furthermore, there are four places [Note: Psalm 26:17, “path”; Psalm 32:7, “into a wineskin”; Psalm 40:6, “his heart” transferred to the first stich; Psalm 117:34, “who are to come”] in which he departs from the Gallican together with Bruno and the Roman translation.

Bruno’s text therefore seemed to us to exhibit the form of the Gallican Psalter as it had developed over time in the British islands, when it was brought from there into these regions of ours by Boniface, Burkhard, and others. This may perhaps also explain what Walafrid Strabo says [Note: On Ecclesiastical Affairs, chapter 25], namely, that some Germans possess the Gallican Psalter.

### 15

Bruno must have composed his work within the four years preceding his death, since in the preface he cites the grammarian Papias [Note: Note 1], who wrote in 1041. On him, see Oudinus, On Ecclesiastical Writers I, column 621, Leipzig edition.

Alberic says of him in his Chronicle:

> “In the year 1053, the thirteenth year of the emperor Henry, son of Conrad, Papias published his book, namely, The Elementarium, an introduction to learning. This is proved by the number of years where, in the first letter, he discusses the ages of the world and, by counting, reaches this year.”

But Alberic was mistaken. For if one counts Henry’s years in this way, Papias could not have been cited by Bruno, who died in 1045.

King Henry had been crowned while his father Conrad was still alive, in 1028. Consequently, there is a double reckoning of his years: one counting from his coronation, including the period during which he reigned with his father; the other counting from his father’s death, when he began to reign alone.

Alberic followed the latter reckoning [Col. 0028C], when he should have used the former. If this is done, the year 1041 will be Henry’s thirteenth year.

## IV. Critical resources—what has been accomplished in this edition

### 16

Among Bruno’s manuscripts, the first place was certainly held by the autograph codex formerly preserved with great reverence in the cathedral church, to which the author had donated it. It was written with great expense, as the Reyser editor testifies. In Cochleus’s time, in 1533, it still stood, as he himself says, in the cathedral church of Würzburg’s rich library of ancient volumes.

But during the Swedish war—or, as others believe, because of disturbances caused by peasants in the sixteenth century—the library was hidden beneath the roof of the cathedral church and was not discovered until a long time afterward. The precious codex, which would have spared us the long labor of critical study, almost perished [Col. 0028D].

Next comes the Sagan Codex, which Cochleus used in publishing Bruno, supplied by Paul Dulciarius, dean of the chapter of Bautzen. We do not know what became of this manuscript either.

The Ebrach Codex, from the fourteenth century, is preserved in the library of the University of Würzburg. It gives an abbreviated but complete Bruno, and we collated it in preparing this edition.

[Col. 0029A] Bibliographers have indicated the number, place, and date of the editions with no small number of errors. We arranged for the most exact investigation in the libraries both of this city and of Munich, and were unable to discover any editions apart from the following.

The first Reyser edition was apparently printed at Würzburg in 1480, in small folio. Experts believe that this was the second work of Georg Reyser printed in this city, after the breviary. This edition was printed from Bruno’s autograph, as the editor himself notes.

Antonius Koberger reprinted Reyser’s edition in quarto; his editions are usually regarded as the earliest.

Koberger’s First Edition, 1494, Nuremberg [Note: [Col. 0029D] Cf. Roeder, *Catalogue of Books Printed in Nuremberg in the Fifteenth Century*, nos. 210, 250, 403, who places before these two a third edition of 1483, which appears to be Reyser’s.]—or Cologne, as Cave has it.

Koberger’s Second Edition, 1497, Nuremberg—or [Col. 0029B] Augsburg, as Reimmaun maintains [Note: [Col. 0029D] *Catalogue of the Theological Library*, p. 357.]

Cochleus’s edition, published at Leipzig in 1533 in quarto by Johann Cochleus, the well-known adversary of Luther, and dedicated to Conrad von Thüngen, bishop of Würzburg, under the patronage of George, Duke of Saxony and most steadfast defender of the orthodox faith; of Johann von Schleyer, bishop of Meissen; and of Paul Dulciarius, dean of Bautzen, who wished it to stand as a legacy left by him for poor priests [Note: [Col. 0029D] Lelong reviewed another edition of Cochleus, in folio, at Würzburg in 1521 [Col. 0030D], *Bibliotheca sacra*, Boerner edition, vol. I, p. 647; it is found nowhere else and appears to be Reyser’s.]. Johann Baptist Riederer preserved two letters from Cochleus concerning this edition, dated 1532 [Note: [Col. 0030D] *Nachrichten zur Kirchen-, Gelehrten- und Büchergeschichte*, vol. I, part 2, no. XXXII.].

This edition of Cochleus was reprinted in the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, Cologne 1618, vol. XI, and Lyon 1677, vol. XVIII.

Finally, in 1721 there appeared at Würzburg a *Psalter of David with the Notes and Commentaries of Saint Bruno, formerly Bishop of Würzburg*, offered to the major academic congregation of the Blessed Virgin Mary Annunciata at Würzburg, in duodecimo. It can scarcely, however, be counted among Bruno’s editions, since the commentary was entirely altered from Leblanc and others.

### 17. On the value of the sources consulted for establishing the text

As regards the value of the editions examined, we must first exclude all secondary editions. There remain Reyser’s and Cochleus’s editions for comparison, together with the Ebrach manuscript, which alone was available to us.

Among these, the first place unquestionably belongs to Reyser’s editor, a most discerning man who followed, in his own time, principles of sound criticism that were scarcely known. He understood very well that it is not the editor’s task to correct his author, or to show what the author ought to have said, but what he did say. Accordingly, he explained at length in his prolegomena:

“Psalters are not to be emended merely because of differences in wording arising from differences of time.”

“This Psalter is not, merely because of differences in punctuation and diction, to be corrected according to the form of other Psalters, nor are other Psalters to be corrected according to it,”

and similar principles.

Cochleus followed entirely different principles. He had set himself the aim of preparing a certain suitable and concise commentary on the Psalms for clerics and religious who were obliged to recite them. With the greatest care and diligence he preserved the reading and punctuation of the autograph that he had before his eyes, and therefore says that he labored hard over this Psalter. Yet he corrected whatever had not been expressed according to strict grammatical norms, softened harsher constructions, and added or altered obeli and asterisks.

This is clear from a comparison of the two editions. Reyser consistently preserves the reading that is less elegant and less adapted to the rules of grammar; in the [Col. 0030B] text, however, he preserves the reading that is less customary. His authority is strengthened by the fact that the Ebrach manuscript consistently agrees with him wherever it has not abridged Bruno. For these reasons we did not hesitate in the least to restore Reyser’s text for the most part, even though by doing so we would depart substantially from Cochleus’s familiar reading.

We also removed what Cochleus added on his own: the commentaries on the canticles, the comparison with the Hebrew text, and other material of the same kind, since it is Bruno, not Cochleus, whom we are publishing.

The restoration of Bruno’s preface was a work of especially great labor. Cochleus had substituted his own preface for it; the manuscript had omitted some things and added others; and Reyser himself had inserted certain material of his own in this section, though in such a way that it can be distinguished from Bruno’s material. Thus, in the absence of other aids, we restored the text of the preface in the best way possible. In passages drawn by Bruno from the Fathers, however, we retained Bruno’s reading.

Now we believe that we have completed everything that had to precede Bruno’s work. Nothing remains except to offer public thanks to those who assisted us by their advice, labor, and writings, especially the Reverend Lord Antonius Ruland, doctor of theology and chief librarian of our Julia University, a man most skilled in antiquarian and literary matters.

“And to you [Note: [Col. 0030D] These are the words of Reyser’s editor.], O blessed father, thrice and four times blessed, and pontiff venerable throughout all ages, happy Bruno, we return thanks. Obtain that we too may correspond worthily in our conduct. For to give the worthiest thanks is faithfully to serve God and to imitate the life of the saints. It is likewise to sing psalms worthily to God and to advance in the Psalter.””

[Col. 0031]

## APPENDIX OF DOCUMENTS

### I. Charter by which Saint Bruno donates to God and Saint Kilian his own village, called Sonnenryk. 15 August 1036.

[From Lunig, *Specilegium ecclesiasticum des deutschen Reichs-Archivs*, vol. XVII, p. 718, and Schaten, *Annales Paderbornenses*, vol. I, p. 508.]

[Col. 0031A]

Bruno, by the favor of divine grace bishop of Würzburg.

We wish it to be known, now and forever, to the royal authority and to every pontifical dignity, likewise to illustrious men, dukes, margraves, counts, and all the faithful of Christ, but especially to our successors, that we have offered to God and to his holy martyr Kilian, in hope of eternal reward, a certain estate situated in the diocese of Paderborn, called by its proper name Sunrike—that is, “a singular kingdom”—which we possessed by paternal inheritance, together with all its appurtenances, namely ministerials, liti, slaves, cultivated and uncultivated fields, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses, fisheries, mills, woods, roads and trackless places, outgoings and incomings, things acquired and yet to be acquired, forever and ever.

Since we wish this offering, made from sincere devotion, and our rightful conveyance of it to be equally clear in what manner and at what time it was made, we confirm it in writing. On the day of the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist, in the church, after the sermon to the people had been completed, with clergy and people listening, we disclosed the proposal concerning the aforesaid estate. We postponed carrying it into effect until the day of the Assumption of the Holy Virgin Mary, so that, if anyone should wish to oppose our will and deliberation by contrived arguments, he might then present himself before us.

After taking counsel on this matter with the prudence of our faithful, we decreed that, each year while we lived, on the feast of our blessed patron, the martyr and apostle, fifty marks of silver should be provided to our brethren for their clothing, and that the aforesaid estate’s aforementioned revenues [Col. 0031C], together with the other matters not yet set forth and not to be set forth on this page, should be recorded in legible letters engraved on two linked bronze tablets placed in the chapel of Sunryke, where the full amount is always to be found.

The outgoings and revenues from cultivated and uncultivated lands, and from each of the things named above, which are owed to the priest who presides over that chapel while serving God and his people, and which are owed to us or to our chief steward, are recorded there. The persons belonging to our property by the right of ministerial service are also listed on the same tablets by name, so that their descendants may not be alienated from their right.

Those persons likewise are listed by name, of either sex, who are to pay two wax-pounds each year and are thereafter to remain free from every private and public exaction as long as they live. The legal obligations of the liti are also recorded, as usefulness and necessity require, each matter separately, so that they may remain in memory from generation to generation.

Furthermore, we have decreed that unmarried liti shall possess the following right: in one year they shall redeem their service by two solidi of light coin or shall serve; in the alternate year they shall neither serve nor redeem their service, but shall attend to their own need and advantage. For the female sex we have established redemption by light money.

To our ministerials we assign this duty: each year, during harvest time, only four of them are to come to the aforesaid estate and advise the steward, so that together with him they may collect and receive the proper dues from all revenues. One of them, Richbold by name, who was more familiar to us than the others, we transferred into the fellowship and legal status of the ministerials of our church [Col. 0032A].

When he had lawfully married a certain free woman, Richere by name, born of free parents, we granted him two manses at Natefingam, with all the appurtenances of both, as a benefice. Moreover, since she too had judged it appropriate, we granted that she and her descendants should enjoy her freedom and the same benefice.

Having thus arranged these matters, to which our earnest desire for the heavenly kingdom made us especially devoted and attentive, we decree that, after our death, the faithful brother of episcopal dignity who succeeds us in the Church of Würzburg shall come each year on the feast of Saint Michael with two of his canons and ten soldiers to Sunrich. There he shall remain for three weeks or longer, as he pleases, conducting business. The steward, together with the subordinate stewards, shall serve him from all the Vovcwerken with abundant provision; and, after summoning the ministerials and the entire household, he shall have them share a banquet on Saint Michael’s Day.

Taking two canons with him, the bishop shall order two colts [Col. 0032B] to be given to him, and thus each year, beginning with the highest and senior members of his church and continuing down to the lowest, he shall extend the same favor. The ministerials who, during harvest time, have served with the steward as inspectors of all revenues and dues shall likewise be given two colts.

He shall examine the laws and regulations recorded in the aforementioned bronze tablets, and shall demand at the same time the entire due payable from the 308 manses and from the many other things belonging to the estate; its total is 203. From this he shall pay six sufficiently large salmon and fifty marks at the appointed time to the households and brethren.

From the same revenues he shall also provide, for twelve poor persons in need of grace and mercy, forty [uncertain reading: the Latin appears defective here], and each day for each of them, for the remedy of our soul, one sufficiently large loaf of fine wheat bread, three *batarii* worth of beer, three herrings, and on Good Friday ten ells of linen cloth, a belt of deerskin, a knife and sheath, and two shoes of goatskin.

In addition, we have assigned two marks of silver [Col. 0032C] to be given to our venerable brother Bishop Rodhard and to all the bishops of the Paderborn Church who shall follow him by divine grace—or, alternatively, a horse of equal value—on the condition that they protect all the goods of our church which are situated far too distant from our protection but conveniently located for them.

After all these provisions had been composed through the careful deliberation of our heart, and after the counsel of the canons of our church, both younger and older, since the term fixed by us—the day of the Assumption of the Holy Virgin Mary—was already approaching, we met our most serene lord Emperor Conrad, Archbishop Bardo, our brother Rodhard, and Bishop Rodhard of Paderborn in the church of Mainz. By many supplications we induced them to promise that they would come to Würzburg to celebrate the solemnities of the aforesaid day, and this was fulfilled.

On that very day of the Assumption of the Holy Virgin Mary, while we were celebrating Mass, after the sermon to the people had ended, in the presence and testimony of Christ and of the aforesaid princes—namely Emperor Conrad, Archbishop Bardo, and the whole church—we fulfilled our vows to God and Saint Kilian in the offering mentioned above, without contradiction from any human being.
