We confirmed them by the ban of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, by that of the bishops already named, by our own ban, and by that of all souls consecrated to God.

Thus, whoever he may be, whatever his condition or authority, if he should presume to alienate from the use of the Church the estate of Sunrike, which is our offering, or in any way alter our laws and regulations as contained in this document and in the bronze tablets, let him be bound by the chain of perpetual anathema and subject to eternal damnation with Judas the betrayer.

Therefore, by the force of obedience, we enjoin upon our brethren, both present and future, that if anyone should presume to act so rashly and irrationally as to alienate our offering from the house of God, they shall report the excommunication pronounced against him to apostolic authority and endeavor, by apostolic authority, to have him struck again with anathema.

Wishing this irreproachable ordinance of ours always to remain firm and unshaken, we recorded on the frequently mentioned bronze tablets what was done and how it was done, inscribed it in order on the pages of this present charter, and confirmed this attestation by the lead impression of our seal, so that it might be a memorial from generation to generation.

We also asked our brother P., the Paderborn bishop [Col. 0033B], a man in every respect worthy of approval, to bear witness to this action of ours on this present page by his signature and the impression of his seal, so that the authority of his holiness might also confirm what we have granted to his church and ours.

I, Rodhard, by the grace of God bishop of Paderborn, bear faithful witness to the action of this present page, established in every respect with reason, both by the attestation of my signature and by the impression of our seal. I confirm it by the ban of the episcopal authority which I exercise, so that this settlement may not be rashly violated by anyone unless his transgression is punished with anathema.

This was enacted in the year 1036 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the fourth indiction, on the day of the Assumption of the Virgin Mary.

### II. Henry III, king, grants to Bruno, bishop of Würzburg, and to his church the estate of a certain Herold, situated in Sinderingun, Sunichilendorf, Geroldeshagen, Buoch, and Meggendemuli, in the district of Cochengowe and the county of Count Henry.

[*Monumenta Boica*, vol. XXIX, part I. Munich, 1831.]

[Col. 0033C]

[Chrismon.] In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Henry, by the favor of divine clemency king.

We wish it to be known to all the faithful of the holy Church of God and of ourselves, present and future, how, for the love of God and for the remedy of our soul, and also at the intervention and request of our nephew Bruno, bishop of the holy Church of Würzburg, we have donated and assigned to the same aforesaid church—namely, to holy Mary, mother and ever-virgin of God, and to holy Kilian, precious martyr of Christ—the estate of a certain Herold, which came by lawful judgment into our royal right and power.

It is situated in the places called Sinderingun, Sunichilendorf, Geroldeshagen, and Buoch, in the district of Cochengowe, in the county of Count Henry at Kolvingun, together with all its appurtenances: lands, meadows, pastures, fields, cultivated and uncultivated woods, mills, waters [Col. 0033D] and watercourses, outgoings and revenues. We also add a certain portion of the same estate, situated in the place called Meggedemuli, with all the male and female slaves belonging to the aforesaid estate.

And so that this conveyance of ours may be believed by all to be true forever and may be more diligently preserved, we have confirmed below with our own hand this charter written concerning it and ordered it to be marked with our seal.

The sign of Lord Henry III, the unconquered king. [Monogram.] [Special sign.]

L. S.

Eberhard, chancellor, acknowledged it as deputy of Bartho, archchaplain.

Given on the third day before the Nones of January, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1042 [Col. 0034A], in the tenth indiction, in the fourteenth year of Lord Henry III’s ordination and the third of his reign, at Herestheim. Happily, amen, happily.

### III. Letter 56 of Pope Gregory IX concerning the canonization of Saint Bruno. 1 May 1238.

[From the Vatican Register, published by Henschenius in the *Acta Sanctorum* under 17 May.]

To the abbots of Brannebach and Schöntal of the Cistercian order, in the diocese of Würzburg, and to the prior of the Friars Preachers of Würzburg.

God is wonderful in his saints: he wonderfully manifests the power of his virtue and mercifully accomplishes the cause of our salvation. He frequently honors in this world his faithful, whom he always crowns in heaven, producing signs and wonders at their memorials, through which heretical depravity may be confounded and the Catholic Faith confirmed.

Therefore, although not as many as we ought, we offer to almighty God as many acts of thanksgiving as we can, because in our days, for the confirmation of the Catholic Faith and the confusion of heretical depravity, he visibly renews signs and changes wondrous portents, causing those who held the Catholic Faith in heart, word, and deed to shine with miracles.

For, as our venerable brother N., bishop, and our beloved sons the dean, chapter, and people of Würzburg have informed us through their messengers and letters, the Lord has bestowed such glory upon Bruno, bishop of Würzburg, of blessed memory, that his tomb shines with so many and such great miracles that it would be unworthy not to invoke his intercession among those of the other saints.

For this reason they humbly petitioned us to have testimony received concerning the miracles which the Lord performs through him. But because in so holy a matter one must proceed only with prior deliberation and gravity, placing full confidence in your circumspection before the Lord [Col. 0034C], we command you, after associating with yourselves religious and God-fearing men, to investigate most diligently the excellence of his conduct and the truth of the signs—namely, his deeds and miracles—and to preserve, until it pleases us, the depositions of the witnesses received, enclosed under your seals.

If not all, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the Kalends of May, in the twelfth year.

### IV. Letter 364 of Pope Innocent IV concerning the canonization of Saint Bruno. 5 November 1246.

[From Henschenius, in the work cited above.]

Some time ago, when the venerable brother N., bishop, and our beloved sons the chapter of Würzburg informed our predecessor, Pope Gregory of blessed memory, that Bruno, bishop of Würzburg, of holy memory, who once, while living in the world, was distinguished by great merits, now living in heaven shone with so many miracles that his sanctity was demonstrated by clear signs, and that it would be unworthy not to invoke his intercession among those of the other saints [Col. 0034D], they petitioned him to enroll Bruno in the catalogue of saints for veneration.

That same predecessor therefore instructed you by letter, after associating with yourselves religious and God-fearing men, to investigate most diligently the excellence of his conduct and the truth of the signs—namely, his deeds and miracles—and faithfully to send to the Apostolic See, enclosed under your seals, the depositions of the witnesses received.

Although, therefore, the investigation made by you concerning these matters, which you transmitted to the Apostolic See at our command, fully establishes the miracles of that saint—through which a person may appear to be regarded as a saint among human beings in the Church militant—nevertheless, in order that someone may be a saint before God in the Church triumphant, perseverance alone is sufficient, according to the words, “Be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life” (which that long robe of Joseph evidently prefigured).

Thus merits and miracles must bear witness to one another, since neither merits without miracles nor miracles without merits fully suffices to provide testimony to sanctity among human beings. And because, on account of the length of time, no one can be found in Germany (Teutonia), as is asserted, who can give eyewitness testimony concerning these matters [Col. 0035A], we, considering that in so holy and pious a matter one must proceed with the greatest gravity and deliberation, command you to investigate diligently, not only through witnesses but also through report, hearsay, and authentic writings concerning his life, conduct, and merits—whether by yourselves or through other trustworthy persons—and to transmit to us under your seals whatever you discover.

If not all, etc.

Given at Lyon, on the Nones of November, in the fifth year.

### V. Testimony concerning the miracles of Saint Bruno, formerly bishop of Würzburg, written in the year 1202. Moon 22.

[From an old charter now preserved in the royal archive. Printed in *Regesta Boica*, II, 5, Würzburg 1616 and 1657, and in Henschenius.]

[Col. 0035B]

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1202, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of July, on the twenty-second day of the moon, miracles were seen in the crypt of the holy martyrs Kilian and his companions and of the blessed Protomartyr Stephen.

The first is that, when a certain poor woman named Gepa had been crippled for eight years or more, on Sunday morning, while Mass was being celebrated, the same woman happened by chance to attend Mass beside the tomb of Saint Bruno, bishop of Würzburg. In the sight of many, she recovered the use of her legs.

On the same day, the large goiter around the neck of a certain woman named Adelheid was reduced to nothing and no longer appeared. On the Wednesday of that same week, she vomited poison in great quantity and was completely cured.

On that night, shortly before dawn [Col. 0035C], a certain virgin from the city of Würzburg, Richeidevin, recovered the use of her legs, with many testifying.

On the Thursday of that same week, a certain woman from Eltmann, at midday, with her priest bearing witness for her, recovered her sight.

Toward nightfall, a certain virgin named Bertha of Würzburg, who had been crippled from childhood, recovered the use of her legs.

On the vigil of Saint John the Baptist, a certain woman from Limbach named Demut, so crippled that she crawled on the ground, freely recovered the use of her legs.

On the following day, a certain woman from Leinach, who had come in a cart, recovered the use of her legs.

A certain boy from Büttelbrunn named Henry, crippled in one hand and one leg, was cured.

A certain crippled girl from Bleichfeld named Irmengart was raised upright. These things occurred with many bearing witness.

On the feast of Saints John and Paul, a woman named Adelheid, who had been deaf, mute, and crippled, was cured.

On the same day, a certain woman from Alhusen was cured of a very large hump, in the sight of everyone.

On the following Thursday [Col. 0035D], Henry of Lougingen, who lacked sufficient testimony, swore that he had been crippled in one leg for a long time and was cured.

On Friday, a certain boy who had been crippled and ill for a long time was cured.

On the same day, a certain virgin from Gorbolsdorf, the daughter of a knight, who, while she was supposed to be learning the Psalter, had often been tormented by a demon, lost her speech for seven days. As she came toward our city, she recovered her speech on the way, with many bearing witness.

On the vigil of Saint Kilian, after Matins, a certain woman from Windsheim named Weudelmut, whose hand was crippled, was cured.

On the holy day of Saint Kilian and his companions, a certain man from Himmelstadt who had been blind for a long time recovered his sight.

At midday, a certain boy from our city who was crippled in one hand was cured.

On the Division of the Apostles, a certain woman named Bertha of Ochsenfurt, who was crippled, was raised upright.

On the same day, two girls from Wertheim and Geilenhausen, on good testimony, were [Col. 0036A] raised upright.

On the following day, a certain woman named Mechthild, who had been crippled for five years, was raised upright.

A certain young servant of a canon of our church, named Reinhard, who had been crippled from childhood, was raised upright.

A certain virgin from the city of Bamberg, named Agnes, had stayed for two years beside the tomb of Saint Kunigund. On the night of the virgin queen, at midnight, she was cured. She had been crippled for five years in such a way that she crawled on the ground using both hands and both feet.

A certain woman from Iphofen named Kunigund, who had been crippled in one leg for a year and a half, while she was at Bamberg beside the tomb of Saint Kunigund, saw in a dream how Saint Bruno was to cure her. When she was on the way and wished to come to the city by boat, she freely recovered the use of her legs.

A certain six-year-old boy from Ense was seized by a wolf in the evening, carried by it to the forest, and covered with eleven wounds. His mother, with her hair disheveled and her clothes torn, followed with great cries while invoking Saint Bruno, and found the boy half alive near the wolf. When she invoked Saint Bruno three times, the wolf withdrew from the boy, and thus the boy escaped through Saint Bruno.

A certain woman from Worms, deaf and mute from childhood, recovered hearing and speech, with many honorable men who were present—and who later came as well—bearing witness.

A certain woman from our city, named Gisela, was freed from a demon.

Another woman from our city, named Irmengart, recovered her sight.

On the following day another woman, named Jutta, was given sight.

On Good Friday, a three-year-old boy was submerged in water until midday and was found dead. While his father and mother invoked Saint Bruno, he was restored to life through the invocation, with many bearing witness.

A certain girl from Retzstadt, who had been tormented by a demon for four years, was freed.

A certain boy was captured by thieves and placed in fetters. When he was alone, he invoked Saint Bruno and touched the fetters, and he was released.

A certain man had been captured, though he was innocent. While he was being hanged, he invoked Saint Bruno, and, although suspended, he hung from the third hour until evening without being able to die. When those hanging him dragged him by the feet so that he might die more quickly, it did no good. Later a passerby released him, and thus he escaped.

A certain woman who was possessed was freed beside the tomb of Saint Bruno.

A certain possessed woman, who was the mother of eleven children and had been tormented by a demon at each birth, was finally completely possessed for seven days, so that she became insane. At the tomb of Saint Bruno she was freed.

A certain crippled man from this city was raised upright at the tomb of Saint Bruno, with many bearing witness.

A certain merchant from this city named Eberhard, bound in fetters, was freed through Saint Bruno and escaped.

A certain boy from Schmalkalden had crawled continuously on the ground for under six years. During the Passion of the Lord he recovered the use of his legs.

A certain boy from Tubera, who had been submerged in a well, emerged alive toward evening, although he had been dead from the first hour until noon [Col. 0036D].

A certain blind virgin was given sight on the vigil of the Lord’s Ascension at the tomb of Saint Bruno.

The son of Ulrich, a nobleman of Ehrenbreitstein, suffering from a stone, was brought to the tomb of Saint Bruno and was freed, with many bearing witness.

A certain paralytic who had been so for six years or more, and who had many relatives in the city, was cured.

A certain man from Fulda who had been innocently hanged escaped through the help of Saint Bruno.

A certain woman named Erdlindis, the almsgiver of Lord L. of Sphippe, was bound with three chains. One fell beside the tomb of Saint Kilian, another at Mergentheim, and the third on the vigil of Saint Kilian at the tomb of Saint Bruno. Thus she was freed and escaped cured.

A certain boy from Heidingsfeld had been so weakened in the knees from childhood that he could not walk. His parents brought him to the tomb of Saint Bruno, and there he recovered the use of his legs.

Another boy from Karlburg, whose left hand was crippled, was cured in the presence of many.

The wife of the *scultetus* of Kissingen, lame and crippled in one leg, was carried to the tomb of Saint Bruno. When she invoked his grace, her leg was suddenly raised upright and she recovered the use of her legs; and her child, who suffered from stones, was freed from the stone.

### VI. A second document concerning the miracles of Saint Bruno

[Edited from a manuscript of the Heidenfeld collegiate church by P. Ignatius Gropp in the *Newest Collection of Writers and Matters of Würzburg*, vol. II, p. 117.]

First. Mechtild, who lives beyond Mainz, swore and said that she had had one foot crippled toward the ground, so that she could not walk but was carried over the ground on her knees, and that this had lasted two years. In the third year she took crutches under her armpits and came on them to the tomb of Blessed Bruno.

She placed her crippled foot upon the tomb of Blessed Bruno but did not dare approach the tomb, because she considered herself unworthy. She said these words: “Lord Jesus, help me. Blessed Bruno, help me for the sake of your sweet soul.”

Immediately the foot moved back and forth, and she felt great pain in the foot. At once she was cured, in the presence and sight of many. When they wished to lead her around the tomb, she said, “I am happy, because I can walk by myself.” She did not allow herself to be led by them, but went straight on her own, without anyone’s assistance, and thereafter remained upright and healthy.

Asked about the time, she said it was around the time when the Church of Bamberg was consecrated, in the year of the Lord 1237.

Second. The widow Chunegund, assisted by oath, says that she saw a certain woman who had long walked through the city on stools. One day, when the witness herself was hearing Mass in the crypt where the tomb of Blessed Bruno is located, at the altar of Saint Stephen she saw the same crippled woman near the altar of Bruno, placing her stools upon the tomb. While she was hearing Mass, the witness heard the crippled woman crying out: “Ah! Ah! Ah! Saint Bruno, help me.”

Then she began to stretch out her legs. The witness said to the woman who was beside her, “Let us go and see what this is.” They went to her, and between their hands and those of an honorable man, now deceased, she was completely raised upright and cured. They saw her rise from the ground and led her around the tomb.

Then she sat down and after a little while said, “If someone would help me rise, I would walk well and by myself.” The witness and her companion then helped her rise, and she walked straight on her own and remained healthy. The witness saw and heard this and was present at the events described.

Asked about the time, she said it was thirty-three years ago; asked about the day, she said it was on the feast of Saint Vitus.

Third. Otto the acolyte, assisted by oath, says that he saw a certain woman who had long been crippled and was carried on stools through the city. She was frequently received at the tables of lords as a poor woman.

When the witness was one day at the court of Lord Berno, he heard a servant saying, “There is a great cry in the crypt.” He quickly ran to the church and entered the crypt. He saw that the said crippled woman had moved from the place of the tomb, was raising herself, and was crying, “Saint Bruno, help me.”

Then she raised herself further. The witness seized her by the arm and helped her rise, then immediately let her go. She walked straight by herself as far as a statue and stood upright, holding the statue with her hands.

The garment that had been long when she was crippled had become so short that it scarcely reached the middle of her thigh. The witness then saw the hollow behind the knee of the crippled woman, as though her veins and tendons had been ruptured.

She was then led around the tomb three times. The lords then came and sang the Lauds. The witness afterward saw her healthy and upright. He saw and heard this and was present.

Asked about the time, he says it was in the summer; about the hour, during High Mass. Asked how long ago, he says it was when the cemetery of the Preachers was being blessed.

[Col. 0038A]

Fourth. Fridunis, wife of Hevold the smith, assisted by oath, says that she saw Reinhard, who had long been crippled, and saw him upon the tomb of Blessed Bruno. She heard him invoking Blessed Bruno and immediately saw him raised upright and cured. She saw him led away from the tomb with praises, and afterward saw him healthy and upright for almost five years. She saw and heard this and was present.

Asked about the time, she says it was in the summer; about the day, she does not remember; about the hour, she says it was before the first hour. Asked how long before, she says two years before the killing of Bishop Conrad.

Golebald, son of Wolckenand, swore that he knew and had handled Reinhard when he was crippled, and afterward saw him cured.

Asked whether he had been at the tomb when Reinhard was cured, he said no, but that he had run to the sound of the bells when the miracle occurred. He also says that the miracle itself took place through the invocation of Blessed Bruno and at his tomb.

You will find further testimonies concerning this miracle below.

[Col. 0038B] **Fifth. Concerning Master Albert, canon and scholasticus of Würzburg.** Heinrich, parish priest at Ochsenfurt, under oath testified that, while he belonged to the household of Master Albert the scholasticus, who was suffering from dropsy, he heard Master Albert himself say privately that he had been dropsical and had been cured at the tomb of Blessed Bruno and through invocation of him. Asked about the time, he said it was in summer; concerning the length of time, he said about thirty years.

Concerning the same Albert, Frederick, cantor of the Major Church and a priest, likewise testified that he had seen Master Albert the scholasticus healthy, and afterward dropsical and abandoned by the physicians; later he saw him cured through the merits of Blessed Bruno, as was said. Asked how he knew this, he said that he had seen the pustules through which the fluid flowed out, had seen the fluid flowing, and had heard Albert himself say: “Bruno did this for me.” Asked how long ago he had fully regained health, he said about thirty years.

Concerning the same Albert, Burchard, bell-ringer and servant of Saint Kilian, testified under oath [Col. 0038C] that he had seen Master Albert, an old man and suffering from dropsy, who, on the advice of Dean Perseus—as this witness himself had heard—had himself carried to the tomb of Blessed Bruno and was cured. Asked how this happened, he said that fluid like water began to flow out through certain pustules. Asked whether he had been present when Albert was cured, he said that, while he was above the tomb, fluid which previously had not flowed began to flow out through the merits, as is believed, of Blessed Bruno; thus he was cured within fifteen days.

Heinrich the priest likewise testified concerning the same Albert that, when he had become dropsical, he had himself carried to the tomb of Blessed Bruno. After he had lain there for several hours, invoking the help of Blessed Bruno, suddenly two blisters arose: one on the leg, the other on the foot of the other leg. When they burst, pus began to flow out there, and all the dropsical fluid poured through them onto the tomb of Blessed Bruno, and he was delivered from his illness. This witness was present at the miracle and heard what occurred.

**Other witnesses to the miracle, placed fourth.**

[Col. 0038D] Godefrid, parish priest of the Major Church of Würzburg, testified under oath that he had seen the aforementioned Renhard, had seen and touched the tendons that were contracted, and knew from the report of others that he had been cured at the tomb of Blessed Bruno. He had seen the contracted man, once cured, go to the high altar and to the altar of Saint Mary, and had heard the community sing, after his cure, “We praise you, O God” (*Te Deum laudamus*) because of his healing. Asked about the time, he said it was in summer. Asked how long ago it had been, he said more than thirty-six years; concerning the place, he said it was in the crypt where the tomb of Blessed Bruno is.

Herebard, cantor and priest at Haugen, testified under oath concerning the same Renhard in every respect as Godefrid, parish priest of the Major Church of Würzburg, except that he did not touch the tendons.

Likewise Arnold, custodian of the Major Church of Würzburg, testified under oath that he had seen the same Renhard contracted for a long time and had often seen him visit [Col. 0039A] the tomb of Blessed Bruno. When he was cured at the tomb and the bells were rung because of the miracle, Arnold ran up with the other clerics and saw the said contracted man standing upright at the tomb. Then, with the other canons and clerics, he sang “We praise you, O God” (*Te Deum laudamus*). He saw this and was present. Asked about the time, he said that he did not remember, since he had been a boy, except that he said it had happened in summer.

Likewise Heinrich, a citizen of Würzburg, testified under oath that he had seen the same Renhard contracted for six years. When this contracted man was visiting the tomb of Blessed Bruno, Heinrich—the custodian of the tomb and a witness to the miracle—wished to drive him away from the tomb. The contracted man replied: “I need the grace of the Savior and of Blessed Bruno just as the others do.” When the custodian went to investigate whether there were thieves in the church, he immediately returned and found him standing upright and cured at the tomb of Blessed Bruno. Later he saw him healthy, both here in the city and in Thuringia; he also saw him in the service of Bishop Heinrich Caseus. He saw and heard these things. Asked about [Col. 0039B] the time, he said it was in summer; concerning the day, he said it was on the night of Friday; concerning how long ago it was, he said that he did not remember, but that it happened while Bishop Conrad was alive. [Col. 0040A]

Heinrich the priest at Hervelstadt likewise testified under oath that Lord Berno, a canon of Würzburg, had a contracted porter—*portenarium*, as the term reads—named Renhard, mentioned above, who had been afflicted from infancy and moved about on crutches. He too was raised upright at the tomb of Blessed Bruno through invocation of him; afterward he was seen healthy and strong. This witness likewise saw it.

Otto, a priest from Memmingen, testified under oath that he had seen the same Renhard, whose legs were contracted and who could not walk but was carried on crutches. When the crutches were taken away from him, he could not move from the spot. He saw that this contracted man was cured beside the tomb of Blessed Bruno through invocation of him; all who were present invoked Blessed Bruno, and the cured man walked away. He saw him for a long time afterward healthy and standing upright; he saw and heard these things and was present. Asked about the time, he said that it was thirty-six years or more ago, and in summer; [Col. 0040B] concerning the hour, he said it was around the brief ninth hour.

# THE EXPOSITION OF THE PSALMS, CANTICLES, THE LORD’S PRAYER, AND THE CREEDS BY BLESSED BRUNO

[Col. 0039]

## VERSES OF SAINT BRUNO, DEDICATORY TO SAINT KILIAN

[Note: [Col. 0039C] He was a regional bishop in the Würzburg territory and apostle of eastern Franconia; in the year of Christ 689 he fell as a martyr beneath the swords of the ungodly.]

May he be a companion of your lot, Father Kilian,

the bishop who honors you through this gift.

[Col. 0039]

# PROLEGOMENA OF SAINT BRUNO (C)

## I. Preface of the Priest Jerome on the Psalms, which follows

[Note: [Col. 0039C] Thus manuscript R. The manuscript, however, has the following: “Here begins the letter of Blessed Jerome to Paula and Eustochium concerning the Psalter, [Col. 0039D] which he had again corrected according to the edition of the Seventy; in it he explains what an obelus and an asterisk are.” Compare *Patrologia*, vol. XXIX, cols. 117–120. This manuscript added three prayers of Bruno to this letter, which are given below, and presents Alcuin’s preface to the book *On the Use of the Psalms* in full (*Patrologia*, vol. CI, col. 468).—Furthermore, we note that in these passages from the Fathers, and elsewhere in the material collected by Bruno, we have retained the Brunonian reading [Col. 0040D].]

[Col. 0039C]

When I was formerly at Rome, I had corrected the Psalter and, according to the Seventy translators, had revised a large part of it, though hastily. But because you see that it has again been corrupted through the fault of scribes, and that the ancient error has proved stronger than the new correction, you compel me, as though I were cultivating a field that had already been plowed, to work the land again and to uproot the thorns growing back in crooked furrows. You say that what repeatedly grows up badly ought to be cut down still more frequently. Therefore, in my customary preface, I admonish both you—who may perhaps be exhausted by this labor—and those who wish to possess copies of this kind, so that what I have carefully corrected may be transcribed with care and diligence.

Let each person take note either of the recumbent line or of the radiating signs: that is, either of the obeli ÷ or of the asterisks +. Wherever he sees a preceding stroke, extending from it to the two points that we have printed in red, let him know that the Greek translators of the Seventy have more text. But wherever he sees something resembling a star, let him know that it has been added from the Hebrew books [Col. 0041A], likewise extending to the two red points, and according only to the edition of Theodotion, who does not differ from the translators of the Seventy in the simplicity of his language.

Knowing that I have done this for you and for every diligent student, I do not doubt that there will be many who, whether through envy or haughtiness, would rather despise excellent things than see them [Note: [Col. 0041D] Thus R.; the manuscript, however, reads: “to despise and see excellent things rather than to learn.” It should be read: “to despise and envy excellent things rather than to learn.”], and would rather drink from a muddy stream than from the purest spring.

Jerome, too, in his letter to Sunnia and Fretela [Note: [Col. 0041D] Letter 106, no. 7, vol. XXII of *Patrologia*, col. 840. This passage and what follows, as well as sections II–VI up to “David, son of Jesse,” are absent from the manuscript.] concerning the difference between the translators of the Seventy and the Hebrew truth, speaks as follows about the obelus and the asterisk: “Wherever something is lacking in the Greek”—and in the translation of the Seventy [Note: [Col. 0041D] The words “and in the translation of the Seventy” were added by Bruno.]—“compared with the Hebrew truth, Origen added it from the translation of Theodotion and placed the sign of the asterisk, that is, the star, which illuminates and brings into the open what had previously seemed hidden. But wherever something that is not in the Hebrew is found in the Greek manuscripts, he placed an obelus, that is, a recumbent stroke, which we can call a spit (*veru*) in Latin; by this it is shown that what is not found in the authentic books ought to be cut down and pierced through. These signs are also found in the poems of the Greeks and Latins.”

But lest it be thought that these signs had been added without necessity or usefulness, Blessed Jerome added in the same letter [Note: [Col. 0041D] No. ss., col. 857.], saying: “These signs—namely, the obeli and asterisks, or, as Papias says, the asterisci [Note: [Col. 0041D] These words were added to Jerome’s letter. This Papias was a grammarian, of whom Alberic relates in his manuscript chronicle that he produced an elementary work of instruction, which was a kind of glossary. See Oudinus, *On Writers*, vol. I, col. 621, edition of Leipzig [Col. 0042D]. *Asteriscus*, however, is a plant in Pliny, *Natural History* XXII.17, not the critical sign, the little star. For more concerning the Papias cited by Bruno, see the prolegomena, no. 15.]—when, through the negligence of scribes, they are left by most people as though they were superfluous, a great error arises in reading.”

Let no one, therefore, despise what, even when unknown, causes harm.

## II. Jerome on the *diapsalma*, or *diapsalmate*, in a letter entitled *To Rufinus*, elsewhere *To Marcella*

[Note: [Col. 0042D] This is the complete Letter 28 to Marcella (*Patrologia*, vol. XXII, col. 430).]

What you have received must be returned with interest; delay in repaying a debt gives birth to usury. You had asked for my opinion concerning the *diapsalma*. We pleaded the brevity of the letter and alleged that the matter could not be explained in writing. But what benefit is my silence, when your desire is stirred by silence into an even greater longing? [Note: [Col. 0042D] It should be read: “What benefit is it to my *ergodiōktēs*? Your desire is stirred by silence.”] Therefore, so that I may not detain you longer, accept a few things in place of many.

Some have said that the *diapsalma* is a metrical commentary; others, a pause for breath; some, the beginning of another sense. There are also those who say it marks a division of rhythm, and that because the psalms were then sung in joined voices to the accompaniment of an organ, it indicated a certain musical variation [Note: [Col. 0042D] The printed editions add: “who suppose it to indicate silence.”]. None of these explanations seems correct to us. Aquila, who is the most painstaking interpreter of Hebrew words, always translated *sela*—that is, *diapsalma* [Note: [Col. 0042D] The printed editions add: “which is written with samekh, lamed, he.”]. We also find *diapsalma* placed at the end of psalms, as in the third: “You have crushed the teeth of sinners; salvation belongs to the Lord, and your blessing is upon your people, *sela*”—that is, “forever.” And in the twenty-third: “Who is this King of glory? The Lord of hosts, he is the King of glory, *diapsalma*”—that is, “forever.” Conversely, in psalms of many verses it is not found at all, namely in the thirty-sixth, the seventy-seventh, and the one hundred eighteenth. Again, the ninth psalm is divided by the refrain of the *diapsalma*, although, as some think, the *diapsalma* could be nothing other than an indication of silence.

From this we observe that the word connects what precedes with what follows, or at least teaches that what has been said is eternal. Thus in the third psalm: “Many say to my soul, ‘There is no salvation in his God’”—“forever.” And again: “With my voice I cried to the Lord, and he heard me from his holy mountain”—“forever.” And in the fourth: “Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood? *Sela*.” And below: “What you say in your hearts, and in your beds be pierced with remorse”—“forever.” And in Habakkuk: “God will come from the south, and the Holy One from Mount Paran”—“forever.” And below: “The oaths to the tribes that you spoke”—“forever.”

We must know, moreover, that among the Hebrews one of three things is customarily appended at the end of books: either *amen* is written, or *sela*, or *shalom*, which expresses peace; hence Solomon is called “the peaceful one.” Therefore, just as we customarily place at the completion of a short work, to distinguish it from what follows, *explicit*, or *happily completed*, or something of that kind, so the Hebrews strengthen what has been written by saying *amen*, or refer to what has been written and what is still to be written by placing *sela*, or testify that what has been completed has ended happily by adding peace at the end.

We have drawn these things from the innermost spring of the Hebrews, not following the little streams of opinions, nor frightened by the variety of errors with which the whole world is filled, but desiring both to know and to teach what is true. If it does not seem burdensome to you, I shall report word for word what Origen thought concerning the *diapsalma*. Writing to someone who asked him what the word *diapsalma* meant in the psalms, or what use it served, he says among other things [Note: [Col. 0042D] The words “Writing to someone” through “he says among other things” were added by Bruno or by some glossator [Col. 0043D]; but he inserted them so unfortunately among Jerome’s words that the words beginning “And because—you may be led” appear to belong to Origen.]: “Since you despise new wine, at least let yourself be guided by the authority of the old. Often seeking the reasons why the *diapsalma* is inserted in certain psalms, I examined the Hebrew most carefully and compared it with the Greek. I found that wherever the Hebrew language has *sela*, while the Greek has *semper* (‘forever’) or something of this kind, there the Seventy, Theodotion, and Symmachus translated *diapsalma*.

“Nor is it harmful to confirm what we say by examples. In Psalm 74, whose beginning is, ‘We shall give thanks to you, O God; we shall give thanks to you and invoke your name,’ after the words ‘I have strengthened its pillars,’ the Seventy, Theodotion, and Symmachus have *diapsalma*. Aquila has instead, ‘I weighed its pillars, forever.’ In the fifth edition: ‘I am the one who prepared its pillars, forever.’ In the sixth: ‘I strengthened its pillars continually.’ In Hebrew, after *amudā*, which means ‘its pillars,’ there is *sela*.

“Again, in Psalm 75, whose beginning is, ‘God is known in Judea; his name is great in Israel,’ after ‘shield and sword and battle’ we find *diapsalma* in the Seventy and Theodotion; in Symmachus, likewise after ‘shield and sword and battle,’ *diapsalma*. Aquila has instead, after ‘shield and sword and battle,’ ‘forever.’ In the fifth edition, after ‘shield and spear and battle,’ ‘forever.’ In the sixth, after ‘shield and sword and battle,’ ‘to the end.’ In Hebrew, after *umalāmah*, which means ‘and battle,’ there was *sela*.

“In the same psalm, after the passage ‘to save all the meek of the earth,’ the Seventy have *diapsalma*; Symmachus likewise has *diapsalma*, and Aquila has ‘forever’; the fifth edition also has ‘forever,’ while the sixth has ‘to the end.’ In Hebrew, after *anwe arets*, which means ‘the meek of the earth,’ there was *sela*. And so, when we had found such to be the understanding of each edition, we made these notes. Whether those who translated *diapsalma* understood it as a change of some musical song and rhythm, or understood something else, I leave to your judgment.”

Thus far Origen. In this discussion alone, we preferred to follow his ignorance rather than to possess the foolish knowledge of those who do not know.

## III. What the *diapsalma* is, by Cassiodorus

[Note: [Col. 0043D] This is chapter 11 in full of the preface to the Psalter, vol. LXX of *Patrologia*, col. 17.]

Among interpreters of the psalms, a certain diversity of opinion concerning this term is known to have arisen. Jerome, the most learned investigator of the Hebrew language, maintains that it is a continuation of the Holy Spirit, because *diapsalma* means “forever.” Blessed Augustine, however, the most subtle investigator of obscure matters, proceeding without stumbling through difficult questions, is known to have preferred the view that it is rather a division, examining the character of the term itself.

For *sympsalma* is a Greek word meaning the joined combination of voices; *diapsalma*, however, means the interrupted continuation of words, indicating that wherever it is found there is a change either of persons or of matters. Properly, therefore, this term is inserted where either meanings or persons are shown to be divided. Accordingly, we too shall make divisions wherever the *diapsalma* is found in the psalms; elsewhere we shall investigate as the opportunity permits, wherever the authority of this term can be established.

## IV. What the Psalter and the psalms are, and why they are so called, by Cassiodorus

[Note: [Col. 0044D] Cassiodorus, preface to the Psalter, chapters 4–8, in the same place, cols. 15–16. The titles of chapters 5–8 are absent here.]

The Psalter, as Jerome says, is a resonant hollow wooden instrument formed in the shape of the letter delta. It has a broad belly at the upper part, where the strings are fastened; struck rhythmically with a plectrum, they are said to produce a very sweet melody. Its arrangement appears to be opposite to that of the lyre, since what the latter contains at the bottom, the former, in reversed fashion, bears at the top.

This kind of singular and sonorous instrument is adapted to the body of the Lord the Savior: for just as this instrument sounds from the higher parts, so that body celebrates the heights of glorious institution; as he himself also says in the Gospel: “He who is from the earth is from the earth and speaks from the earth; but he who comes from heaven testifies to what he has seen and heard.” Hence some define this work of David as being called “psalms,” because they are known to resound from a heavenly summit. Know, however, that only those contained in this volume are called psalms because of their excellence.

The prophet Daniel also testifies that the Psalter is a kind of musical instrument when he speaks of “the sound of the trumpet, flute, sambuca, lyre, psalterium, and symphony, and every kind of music.” The Book of Chronicles likewise explains this when it speaks of steps made from thyine wood [Note: [Col. 0044D] The printed editions add: “which are commonly called ebony.”] in the house of the Lord and in the royal house, and also of lyres and psalteria for the singers.

This musical instrument, the psalterium, is called *nablum* among the Hebrews; the term has nevertheless been made familiar by frequent repetition in the book mentioned above. The word *psalm* itself is certainly Greek; some wish it to be derived ἀπὸ τοῦ ψαύειν, that is, “from touching.” We also call women who play the lyre *psaltriae*, since with a trained thumb they produce musical modulations.

[Col. 0044D] A psalm, then, is a certain sweet and tuneful modulation produced by the musical instrument alone, that is, by the psalterium.

A canticle is what is sung to the honor of God when someone uses the freedom of his own voice and is not joined in harmonious modulation to any loquacious musical instrument; this is what is now performed in the praises of the Divinity.

A psalm was a canticle when, with a musical instrument leading the way, a singing chorus responded with joined voices, adhering exclusively to divine words.

A canticle was a psalm when, with the chorus singing first, the art of the musical instrument was jointly adjusted to a single harmony, and the words of the divine hymn resounded in a sweet union [Note: [Col. 0045D] The following words are added here to Cassiodorus’s text: “Concerning this distinction you will also find something below, in the gloss on Psalms 66 and 67.” I do not know whether these words are Bruno’s or the editor Reyser’s.].

## V. How one should understand the Lord Christ in the psalms, by Cassiodorus

[Note: [Col. 0045D] Cassiodorus, same place, chapter 13, but not in full, col. 17.]

For the instruction of the faithful, the psalms speak of the person of the Lord Christ in three ways.

First, by what is known to pertain to his humanity, as in the second psalm: “The kings of the earth stood forth, and the rulers gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ”; and also in the twentieth psalm: “You granted him the desire of his soul, and you did not deprive him of the will of his lips.”

Second, by what shows him to be equal and coeternal with the Father, as in that same second psalm: “The Lord said to me: You are my Son; today I have begotten you.” And in the one hundred ninth: “With you is dominion on the day of your power, amid the splendors of the holy ones; from the womb, before the morning star, I begot you.”

Third, through the members of the Church, whose leader and head is Christ, as in the twenty-first psalm: “Far from my salvation are the words of my transgressions”; and in the sixty-eighth: “O God, you know my foolishness, and my transgressions are not hidden from you.” This must be understood as spoken on behalf of each of the faithful. As for Christ, transgressions are proved to be utterly alien to him; hence Tichonius discussed this matter at greater length and with care in his *Book of Rules*.

If we keep this in mind, we are not disturbed by confusion, because the greatest error arises when what is clearly spoken concerning one person is inappropriately assigned to another [Note: [Col. 0045D] Thus it should be read with Bruno, not “elsewhere,” as in the printed editions.].

For if he had spoken in only one manner, who could have recognized his genuine substance, when even now, amid so evident a distinction, some strive through sacrilegious will to confuse the divine and human natures of the Lord Christ? He also teaches many things according to the literal sense and commands many things spiritually; he suitably changes persons suddenly, so that now Christ—God, the incarnate Word and man, the head of the Church—seems to speak, now the Church itself, now the righteous man, now the penitent, in order to touch upon and encompass everything necessary.

Everywhere the holy discourse vibrates with the fullness of heavenly things, and through the manifold diversity of virtues the merciful Redeemer discloses the mysteries of his kingdom, in order to bestow salvation upon the human race.

We have prefaced these remarks so that, when the reader comes to passages of this kind, he may fearlessly hear what he recognizes that he has already learned for his salvation.

## VI. Sayings of Saint Augustine in the prologue to the Psalter and of others concerning the virtues of the psalms

[Note: [Col. 0045D] This prologue to the Psalms, formerly attributed to Augustine, is actually Basil’s preface to his commentary on the psalms, in Rufinus’s translation (*Patrologia*, vol. XXXVI, col. 63). Although Bruno imitated it, he drew only a few things from it. Compare also Ambrose on Psalm 1 [Col. 0046D].]

The singing of the psalms adorns souls, summons angels to our aid, puts demons to flight, dispels darkness, and produces holiness in the sinful person. It is refreshment for the mind; it erases sins and is like the almsgiving of the saints. It increases faith, hope, and charity. As the sun gives light, as water cleanses, as fire burns away, and as oil soothes, it attacks the devil, reveals God, and extinguishes carnal pleasures.

It is the oil of mercy, the lot of joy, the chosen portion of the angels. It drives away harshness, suppresses every fury, and breaks anger. It is the continual praise of God. It is like honey. The singing of the psalms is a chosen song before God. It drives away every sin and joins the bond of charity. It penetrates all things, fills all things, teaches all things, and signifies all things. It magnifies the soul, purifies the mouth, gladdens the heart, builds a lofty tower, and glorifies the human being.

It opens the understanding, kills every evil, and reveals perfection. Whoever keeps its memory and love also has the fear and praise of God in his heart; he will never fall from it, nor will his prayer perish, but at the end he will rejoice before God.

It is tranquility of mind and the standard-bearer of peace, because the psalms pray for future things, groan over present things, and repent of past things. They rejoice over good works and recall the joy of the heavenly kingdom. Through the regular practice of singing, one often acquires a shield of righteousness against demonic powers. They show the light of truth. They are consolation for the old, an ornament for the young, and the old age and perfection of the mind.

With the help and gift of the one who established these things through prophetic mouths and taught us to entreat him through their continual use: to him be praise, honor, magnificence, blessing, and glory, wisdom, thanksgiving, power, and strength, together with God the Father and his only-begotten Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, throughout infinite ages of ages. Amen.

## VII. Concerning the institution, author, singers, number, and titles of the psalms

[Note: [Col. 0046D] These words are taken from the commentary on the Psalms falsely attributed to Bede (*Patrologia*, vol. XCIII, col. 477D), where the title is: “An exposition of how the Holy Spirit dictated the Psalter.” In our Ebracensian manuscript, however, they appear in a form so different both from Reyser’s edition and from Bede that we preferred to add them here in full, although we do not doubt that the text given above is genuinely Bruno’s.

“David, son of Jesse, while he was reigning in his kingdom, chose four men to make the psalms: namely Asaph, Heman, Ethan, and Jeduthun. Thus eighty-eight sang the psalms, and Abiuth played with two hundred [persons?], under the psalmody (*sympsalma*) and with the lyre [the syntax and referent are uncertain]. When David brought the ark to Jerusalem, after it had been brought back from Azotus twenty years later and had remained in the house of Aminadab, he placed it upon a new cart and brought it to Jerusalem with seventy thousand chosen men from every tribe of the children of Israel. From the tribe of Levi there were two hundred seventy-eight thousand men. From these he appointed four leaders over the *causationes* (“causes”; read *cantationes*, “songs”): Asaph, Heman, Ethan, and Jeduthun, assigning to each of them seventy-two men to respond in praise to the songs of the Lord. One struck the cymbal, another the lyre, another, rejoicing, the horn trumpet. In their midst David himself stood holding the psalterium. The ark went before, accompanied by seven choirs, and a calf was offered as sacrifice; the whole people followed after the ark.

“All the psalms of David number one hundred fifty. Of these, David himself made nine; thirty-two are not superscribed; seventy-two are attributed to David; twelve to Asaph; twelve to Jeduthun; nine to the sons of Korah; one to Moses; two to Solomon; and two to Haggai and Zechariah. Thus all the psalms of David total one hundred fifty. The *diapsalma* occurs seventy-five times, and the Songs of Ascents number fifteen.

“The first psalm is assigned to no one because it is the head of them all. Who else, then, is understood in the second except the Firstborn, for whom no inscription was rightly necessary? Moreover, since that psalm speaks of Christ—‘against Christ’—it has no need at all of an inscription merely to explain the person. We read that the historical order has been altered in the titles of the psalms. But just as the psalms are read not according to history but according to prophecy, so the order of the titles cannot disturb the order of the psalms. All the psalms that are inscribed with David’s name pertain to the mystery of Christ, because David is called Christ.”]

[Col. 0046D]

When David, son of Jesse, had been firmly established as king in his kingdom, he chose four leaders of psalmody: namely Asaph, Heman, Ethan, and Jeduthun. They taught two hundred eighty-eight psalms and canticles of the Lord. There are one hundred fifty psalms in all. Of these, nine are inscribed with David’s own name; seventy-two are attributed to David; thirty-two have no superscription; twelve are superscribed with Asaph’s name; twelve with Jeduthun’s; nine with the sons of Korah; two with Haggai and Zechariah; one with Moses; and one with Solomon.

There are seventy-five *diapsalmata* in the Psalter. The Songs of Ascents number fifteen; these too bear this title, but not the name of an author. For not all the psalms have titles, nor are all superscribed with the names of authors, singers, performers, or any other persons [Col. 0047B].

The first psalm, moreover, bears no title. But the first psalm has a different status from the other psalms: the first psalm is assigned to no one because it is the head, beginning, and, in a certain sense, title of all the psalms [Note: [Col. 0048D] Compare Pseudo-Bede, Commentary on Psalm 1, col. 483C.]. Who else, then, is understood in the second except the Firstborn Son of God, before whom, as the beginning, nothing ought to be placed? An inscription was likewise unnecessary for him because the psalm itself speaks of Christ: “against your Christ.” Since it expresses the person, it had no need at all of an inscription. Therefore it also has a title marked with an obelus.

We also read that the historical order has been altered in the titles of the psalms. But the psalms are read not according to history but according to prophecy; thus the order of the titles cannot disturb the order of the psalms. All the psalms inscribed with David’s name pertain to the mystery of Christ, because David is called Christ.

The prayers that follow precede the beginning of the psalms [Note: [Col. 0048D] In the manuscript these prayers have been transferred to the beginning of the preface. At the end, however, three other prayers are placed: “Christ, who are the true giver and bestower of eternal light”; “Lord, who command us to ask and make us find you”; and “Therefore I beseech you, Lord, remember,” and so forth.]

Benevolent and merciful God, who recalls those who wander and saves the penitent, who grants healing to the sick and a crown of glory to those who persevere: hear me, your miserable and unworthy servant, imploring your mercy through these psalms, so that, whatever I humbly ask here, I may deserve to obtain through your generosity. Through our Lord.

### Another prayer

I implore your mercy and compassion, Lord Jesus Christ, Son of the living God. I know that you are gracious and merciful, patient and exceedingly kind. I adore you, I praise you, I beseech you. For you have heard your saints and elect from the beginning of the world to its end. Hear me also, unworthy and sinful, praying and entreating you. Receive my prayer and petition, and make acceptable to you every spiritual meaning of these psalms, which I humbly pray or sing before you. You who live.

### Another prayer

Receive, merciful and compassionate God, this offering of psalms, which I, a sinner and guilty of every crime, offer for the remedy of my soul, and for those of either sex who are joined to me by blood or friendship, and for those who have entrusted themselves to our hands or have confessed to us, or whose alms we have received, and for the entire Christian people, living and dead. I beseech you, most gentle God, that it may benefit them for the pardon and remission of sins. Amen.

[Col. 0049]

# EXPOSITION OF THE PSALMS BY SAINT BRUNO, BISHOP OF WÜRZBURG (C)

[Col. 0049A] In the name of Christ begins the Psalter from the translation of the Seventy translators, corrected anew by Saint Jerome.

The origin of the prophecy of King David: one hundred fifty psalms [Note: [Col. 0049C] We added this from a manuscript. I have no doubt that it is genuine, since the same title appears in the manuscripts of the Gallican Psalter, which clearly underlies Bruno’s edition: “Here begins the Psalter from the translation of the Seventy translators, corrected anew by Saint Jerome the presbyter.” The Roman edition, however, was called “the Psalter corrected anew,” that is, “corrected from the beginning.” See Martianaeus’s note, vol. XXIX of *Patrologia* [Col. 0050C], col. 119.]

# PSALM ONE

[Note: [Col. 0050C] It should be noted that Bruno consistently followed this order: first came the title and its exposition, then the number and subject of the psalm. Here we have retained Cochleus’s order because it is more convenient [Col. 0050D].]

**C. B.** This psalm has no title because nothing ought to be placed before the Head, our Lord and Savior, of whom it is going to speak explicitly. For it signifies his holy incarnate life and the punishments of the ungodly. Hence the subject of this psalm is the same as that of the entire book, namely Christ in his wholeness: that is, our Redeemer as head together with his members, namely all the righteous and holy.

[Col. 0049B] **1** Blessed is the man who has not gone in the counsel of the ungodly, who has not stood in the way of sinners, and who has not sat in the seat of pestilence.

C “Blessed is the man”—*beatus* is understood as “well fitted” (which is Christ), to whom all things desired or hoped for come to pass—“man” he added excellently. For *vir* is derived from *vires*, “strengths”: a man is one who does not fail through enduring adversity, nor vaunt himself through any arrogance in prosperity. Here he shows that human errors arise in three ways: in thought, in deed, and in speech. One departs through sinful thought; by an evil deed one stands far from God. Through speech—whether of evil teaching, boasting, or habitual sin—one sits in the chair that infects with pestilence.

A Therefore blessed is the one who has not departed from God in thought into the distant region of unlikeness—that is, who has not sinned in thought. [Col. 0049C] Although he was placed in the council of the wicked—that is, although the wicked plotted that he should depart, just as Christ, although he associated with sinners, nevertheless did not depart into their way—Adam departed when he consented to his wife, who had been deceived by the devil. The wicked who plotted this are the devils, the Scribes and Pharisees, or all evil people. Christ, just as he did not enter their way, so did not stand in it. For the lure of the world and of sins did not hold him, nor did he sit in the chair of pestilence—that is, in evil practice, or rather in evil teaching—for he taught wholesome doctrine, and Christ left posterity no examples of evil teaching.

C A chair is properly called the seat of teachers, the tribunal of judges, and the throne of kings.

H Thus the meaning of this verse is: Blessed is the one who neither thought, did, nor taught evil.

2 But his delight is in the law of the Lord: And on his law he will meditate day and night.

C The law of God is the holy precept concerning the avoidance of sins; it was in this that the will of the one who committed no sins was found.

A C Observe that he says “in the law” a second time, not “under the law,” because Christ was in the law, since he had no sins; other mortals are under the law, since they are weighed down by offenses.

C It is called *law* because it binds our minds and holds them subject to its statutes. No one is able always to meditate on the law of the Lord except Christ; but the one who is his member will also meditate continually on the law of God, fulfilling it with all purity insofar as he can.

H Whether he eats, drinks, or sleeps: doing everything in the name of the Lord, he will meditate on the law of God day and night.

C *Day* is so called from the gods of the pagans. *Night* is so called because it harms our sight or our actions.

3 And he will be like a tree that is planted ÷ … beside streams of water: Which will give its fruit in its season.

C Christ is rightly compared to a fruitful tree, because of the cross which he endured for us. “Planted,” that is, preached, beside streams of water. Just as earthly water is the life of trees and of things that grow, so the water of baptism is salvation for those who believe in the Crucified One. [Col. 0050C] “He will give fruit,” that is, he will establish churches; “in its season,” that is, when he received the sacraments of the blessed Incarnation. *Fruit* is derived from *to enjoy*.

H The tree—to which Christ is compared according to his members, that is, according to all true Christians—means, I think, wisdom, concerning which Solomon also speaks: “It is a tree of life to those who follow it”; and the Apostle calls Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God. Thus the true Christian will be like a tree—that is, having been conformed to Christ the Son of God, to the body of his glory, namely, to Christ.

4 [Col. 0051A] And its leaf will not fall: And everything that he does will prosper.

C Understand “its leaf” as his words of promise, which do not fall from the truth through any mishap; rather, he brings everything that he does to completion in the prosperity of action. All these things are to be understood as fruit and leaves—that is, deeds and words.

5 Not so the wicked ÷ not so …: but like dust Which the wind casts ÷ from the face of the earth.

C “Not so the wicked”—this is the voice of one terrifying, just as “blessed is the man” is the voice of one inviting; for the wicked will not be as he said above that the blessed are. Dust is the dissolution of earth, to which the earthly man is compared when he is inflated by the wind of pride and, because of its lightness, is cast away from the firmament of God’s commandments. Dust is scattered here and there; so also the wicked person, who has once denied God, is led wherever the breath of the devil draws him, and is brought there through error.

6 Therefore the wicked will not rise in judgment: nor sinners in the assembly of the righteous.

C The wicked are those who in no way confess the Holy Trinity.

C H The wicked will rise, but not in judgment, because they have already been judged.

C The righteous rises in order to judge; the sinner, in order to be judged; the wicked, in order to be punished without judgment. Sinners are Christians who are subject to sins. For this reason they do not rise in the assembly of the righteous—that is, in the judgment of the righteous—because their sins have already been forgiven by grace through confession, namely, by those righteous persons. The saints too belong to this number, because no one is without sin except God.

B On Job: Here four orders are noted concerning the day of judgment: the saints, who have already been judged worthy of the kingdom and come with Christ to judge; and the wicked, who have already been adjudged to punishment. To sinners who have done penance it is said, “Come, blessed”; and to those who have not, “Depart from me.” “In the assembly,” that is, in the eternal good, which it was the saints’ purpose to follow.

C Or “in the assembly,” that is, in the judgment, so that they may judge with them. For the judgment is in the assembly, since, as though by the counsel of assessors, different sins will be punished with different penalties.

7 For the Lord knows the way of the righteous: but the path of the wicked will perish.

[Col. 0051D] C He says that God knows the way of the good—that is, their works—and that the path of the wicked will perish, as though the Lord were somehow unaware of it. But the meaning is this: the Lord knows what will remain in blessedness; he does not know what will perish—that is, the devil with his followers, who is the path of the wicked in everlasting punishment.

A Therefore he said “will perish” in place of “he does not know”; but it is also stated more plainly, because not to be known is to perish, while to be known is to remain and exist.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM I

Make us, Lord, like a most fruitful tree before your sight, so that, watered by your rains, we may deserve to please you through the abundance of sweet fruits, through our Lord, etc.

# PSALM II

[Col. 0052A]

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM II

C The Prophet speaks about the gathering of unbelievers against Christ in his Passion. And the Lord Christ speaks about his omnipotent kingdom and his ineffable generation.

TT. ÷ A psalm of David …

C This psalm is to be regarded as first in its title, second in order; hence in the Acts of the Apostles it is called the first.

H Or because among the Hebrews this and the first are counted as one psalm, without a title. By “title” is understood the meaning of each psalm. For what is a title except, so to speak, a key? One does not enter a house except by a key; so also the meaning of each psalm is understood through a key—that is, through its title—namely, in whose person it is sung, whether in the person of Christ, the Church, or the Prophet, and what its subject is.

1 Why did the nations rage, and the peoples meditate on empty things?

C Here the Prophet rebukes the peoples—not only the Jews but also the Gentiles—for raging against Christ, which is properly characteristic of wild beasts. They raged with bestial fury because they lacked right reason. They meditated on empty things, not understanding that his coming would bring benefit to all believers.

2 The kings of the earth stood forth, and the princes gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ. [Col. 0052C] ÷ A pause …

C By “the kings of the earth” he means Herod, who killed the infants, and another Herod, his nephew, who consented with Pilate to Christ’s death. By “the princes” he means the Pharisees. A prince is so called as one who takes the first place. They came to one will, not to one assembly, against the Lord—that is, the Father—and against his Christ—that is, the Son.

3 Let us break their bonds, and cast ÷ … their yoke away from us.

C These are the words of deranged Jews. They thought that they would break their bonds—that is, the evangelical commandments—if they rose up with malicious intent against the author of the law and his apostles, and that they would cast away their yoke, although the Lord’s yoke is easy [Col. 0052D] and his burden light (Matt. 11). Deceived by an empty will, they thought his dominion exceedingly burdensome and hastened to cast it off, although through it they could have been saved.

4 He who dwells in the heavens will laugh ÷ at them … and the Lord will mock them.

C Here he calls the saints “the heavens,” in whom Christ dwells. “He will laugh” and “will mock” are to be understood according to human usage. In reality, God neither laughs at anyone nor mocks with his expression; rather, by his power he accomplishes whatever he has determined.

5 Then he will speak to them in his anger, and in his wrath he will trouble them.

C “Then he will speak” signifies the time of the coming judgment. The anger and wrath of God are therefore called the repayment of sins; for Divinity does not undergo those emotions, but here speaks according to human custom.

H He does not say “he will punish,” but “he will trouble,” so that the one who has been troubled may be corrected without punishments. For anger is sometimes a necessary correction, as that of a father toward his son or of a physician toward a sick person.

6 But I have been appointed king ÷ by him … over Zion, his holy mountain, proclaiming his commandment.

H “But I”—the voice of Christ—“have been appointed king by God the Father” according to the condition of the flesh.

C Zion in the Hebrew language is called *specula* in Latin, “watchtower,” and here signifies the Church, which he also calls a mountain because of the height of its honor and the firmness of its faith. “Proclaiming his commandment”—

H C that is, the Gospel.

7 The Lord said to me: You are my Son; today I have begotten you.

C “The Lord” signifies the Father. “You are my Son,” as in the Gospel: “This is my beloved Son” (Matt. 3:17). By saying “today,” he shows the coeternity of his majesty. “I have begotten you” signifies that birth of which it is said: “Who will recount his generation?” (Isa. 53).

8 Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession the ends of the earth.

C “Ask of me,” that is, obey so that you may be able to ask. Here he is commanded to ask, so that he may request according to his humanity and possess what he receives. “Nations” signifies peoples; *gens* is so called from *genus*, “race.” When he says “your inheritance,” he shows the nature of his divinity. *Inheritance* is derived from *herus*, that is, “lord,” because one who possesses it rules over it with free authority. When he says “possession,” he signifies all the nations that will believe. “The ends of the earth” is to be understood as the substance of all creatures in this world.

9 You will rule them with an iron rod, and like a potter’s vessel you will shatter them.

C “You will rule them”—that is, you will take away their tyrannical power. For those who are saved are ruled. The iron rod is the strength of equity. “You will shatter,” that is, through the zeal of conversion you will crush their earthly desires. The sinner is rightly compared to an earthen vessel, so that his shattering may show both its ease and his earthen life; yet he is restored for the better when divine [Col. 0053D] grace leads him into a spiritual person.

10 And now, kings, understand; be instructed, ÷ you who … judge the earth.

C “Now, kings”—he calls kings those who rule over vices and who, with the Lord’s help, are able to understand and fulfill these things.

H To be instructed is to be taught. For those judge the earth—that is, the Church—well who teach others the good things they understand.

C Earth is so called from *terere*, “to wear down.”

11 Serve the Lord in fear, and rejoice ÷ to him … with trembling.

A “Serve the Lord.” And so that they may not become proud, he adds, “in fear.”

C For just as the fear of God excludes offenses, so security admits faults. But lest servitude seem wretched because of fear, he adds, “and rejoice”; yet lest one again fall into recklessness, he adds, “with trembling.” Thus, lest rejoicing make us elated, he adds “with trembling,” so that God may be served reverently.

12 Embrace discipline, lest at some time the ÷ Lord … become angry and you perish from the ÷ righteous … way.

C The one embraces discipline who fortifies himself through true repentance against harmful vices. “Lest at some time,” through the long patience of God, he perish from the righteous way—that is, from Christ, who is the true way of those walking rightly toward life, the guide of those who go, and the path of those hastening toward blessedness.

13 When his anger burns briefly, blessed are all who trust in him.

[Col. 0054B] C For his anger burned briefly in that brief judgment, where there is no separate examination of individuals, but the Judge judges everything at once.

H Blessed are all who trust not in human beings or in themselves, but in God. This psalm ends where the preceding one begins, namely, with blessedness; therefore among the Hebrews they are counted as one.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM II

Break, Lord, the bonds of our sins, so that, bound to the yoke of your service, we may be able to serve you with fear and reverence. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, etc.

# PSALM III

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM III

C Christ speaks to the Father about his persecutors. The faithful people are instructed not to fear death, because their author, by rising again, has displayed the hope of a true resurrection.

## TITLE OF PSALM

A psalm of David, when he fled from the face of Absalom his son.

C This entire psalm is referred to the person of Christ. It ought to occupy the third place because it contains within itself the mysteries of the Holy Trinity and of the three-day resurrection. For through David’s deliverance the resurrection of Christ is signified.

1 Lord, why have those who trouble me become so numerous? Many rise up against me.

C The Prophet speaks these words in wonder: why had the Jews and the nations troubled the Lord, from whom they ought to be saved? For so many rose up against Christ that Judas, one of the disciples, was added to the number of those who ought to be saved by him.

2 Many say to my soul: There is no salvation for him in his God ÷ … A pause.

C He repeats “many say” to show the exceedingly dense and foolish madness of the wicked. Therefore they say, “There is no salvation for him”; for they thought that the Father did not love the Son, whom he permitted to be killed in the flesh.

3 But you, Lord, are my protector ÷ … my glory and the one who lifts up my head.

C Here the Son calls the Father his protector according to the form of a servant, and likewise calls him the glory and exaltation of his head, so that the divine and human substance might be one person without any confusion.

4 [Col. 0055A] With my voice I cried to the Lord, and he heard me from his holy mountain. A pause.

C When he says, “With my voice I cried to the Lord,” this means: “Father, glorify your Son.” “He heard me,” as in: “I have glorified, and I will glorify again” (John 12). “From the mountain,” that is, from the highest summit of divinity.

5 I slept and was overcome with sleep ÷ … and I rose again, because the Lord received me.

C “I slept,” he said—that is, after the Passion I rested in the tomb, because he rose again quickly. “I was overcome with sleep” signifies secure sleep. For sleep is sweet rest and the pleasantness of slumber. “I rose again” with eagerness, mortality having been laid aside. Divine [Col. 0055B] power received the Son, because human nature could not rise again by itself.

6 I will not fear the thousands of the people surrounding me. ÷ Arise … Lord, save me, my God.

C He could not fear the unrighteous people, since he possessed the greatest protection in his divinity. The Son does not say “Arise, Lord” to rouse the Father; rather, tropologically and figuratively he asks for the Father’s help in the resurrection. A trope is an expression transferred from the place where it is proper to a place where it is not proper. It is therefore customary in the divine Scriptures, to clarify the matter through tropology, to say certain things about God according to our human custom.

7 For ÷ you … have struck all those opposing [Col. 0055C] me without cause; you have crushed the teeth of sinners.

C The Lord the Father struck those opposing the Son—that is, heretics, who persecute the Catholic rules without cause, that is, without reason. He crushed their teeth—that is, the biting words of those who disparage divine doctrines. God is so called from *demere*, “to take away,” because teeth take away everything.

8 Salvation belongs to the Lord, and ÷ upon your people your blessing. + A pause …

II Salvation belongs to the Lord—that is, it comes not from a human being but from God the Father—and the Lord’s blessing descends upon the Christian people.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM III

Pour out, Lord, your blessing upon your people, so that, fortified by your resurrection, we may not fear being surrounded by thousands of hostile vices. Through Jesus Christ, etc.

# PSALM IIII

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM IIII

C The Church prays that her prayer may be heard, rebuking unbelievers because they follow vanity, and admonishing the whole human race to offer a sacrifice of righteousness to God, from whom it may receive immense benefits.

[Col. 0056A]

TT. A psalm of David, for the end, a song.

C “The end” signifies not only the completion of something but also perfection; therefore it is to be referred here to Christ, who is the end of the law [Col. 0056A] (Rom. 10). A psalm is a musical instrument with a head of sounds, or rather a melody by which divine praises were sung. A song is that which resounded with heavenly praises through human voices.

1 When I called, the God of my righteousness heard me; in tribulation you enlarged me.

C The voice of the Church addressed to Christ. Although she knows that she has been heard, she does not cease to pray. Tribulation enlarges the holy Church of God in martyrdom, when confessors and martyrs are crowned at the same time, and the entire multitude of the righteous is continually increased through afflictions.

2 Have mercy on me and hear my prayer.

C The devout mother says that she ought to receive mercy if her prayer for her children is heard, because whatever is granted to the members is without doubt granted to the whole body.

3 Sons of men, how long will you be heavy of heart? Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood? A pause.

C He calls those sons “heavy of heart” who, having recognized the truth—that is, Christ—have nevertheless chosen rather to worship idols of vanity. Vanity is a general name for vices, but properly that is called vain which is judged alien from God. “Falsehood,” that is, an idol; they rightly received such a thing, because idols have been erected against the truth. We ought to love what is profitable, not what is harmful.

4 And know that the Lord has made his holy one wondrous: the Lord will hear me ÷ … when I cry to him.

C Here the Prophet indicates the secret of the holy Incarnation. He calls him “holy,” that is, the Son. He rightly says that he has been heard, because he preached Christ to the peoples. He cries to Christ, to whom he pleads through good works.

5 Be angry and do not sin. What you say in your hearts, and in your beds be pierced with remorse. A pause.

C We ought to be angry at past sins—that is, by repenting—so that we may shudder at having sinned. When he says “in your hearts and in your beds,” he shows that God recognizes human thoughts. A bed is so called from *cubare*, “to lie down”; it is the dwelling place of beasts. The meaning is: Abandon evil thoughts before you commit crimes—that is, before you bring evil thoughts into deeds; while they are still in your heart, extinguish them.

H Or: at night expiate through tears what you sinned by thinking during the day.

6 Sacrifice the sacrifice of righteousness and hope in the Lord. Many say: Who will show us good things?

C The most merciful mother Church first warned that the ancient sacrifices and worship of idols must be abandoned; now she urges Christians also to sacrifice themselves, not animals, to God by living rightly. We are taught to hope in God, so that we may obtain his saving promises. “Who will show us good things?” many say [Col. 0057A] in doubt—although they ought not to be few—namely, whether the resurrection is to come and whether there are rewards for the good. To this question the holy mother immediately responds, saying: “The light of your countenance has been marked upon us,” and so forth.

7 The light of your countenance has been marked upon us, Lord; you have given gladness in my heart.

C The light of your countenance has been marked upon us because, just as a coin bears the image of the emperor, so the signs of the heavenly King are impressed upon the faithful in baptism and in the other sacraments—that is, the seal of the holy cross, by which the devil is driven away. The light of God’s countenance is the impression of the cross, because it continually enlightens those who do not defile themselves with any perversity. He speaks of the gladness of right faith, for we rejoice truly when we believe rightly.

A Or that light is the grace of God, [Col. 0057B] infused into the mind to restore it, by which reason is marked like a coin with the king’s image; and this light is the whole and true good of the human being.

8 They have multiplied from the fruit of their grain and wine ÷ and their oil …

C He admonishes those who are evidently devoted to bodily things. For they have multiplied in the worst deeds, that is, they have been filled with worldly pleasure. Therefore he added “their own,” because sinners use these earthly fruits not according to God’s commandments but according to their own desires.
