Or “their own,” that is, Christ’s: his bread, which is living, and his wine, which intoxicates, and his oil, which is the head—that is, which fattens the mind. Grain is so called from *frumen*, the upper part of the throat; for the ancients called the top of the throat *frumen*.

9 In peace, in the same place, I will sleep and rest.

C Lest you think that temporal peace is signified, he means unchangeable and heavenly peace remaining in the heart. Therefore he says “in the same place,” so that you may understand that true peace is not altered within itself by any change. “I will sleep,” that is, I will end my life in that peace. “I will rest” in future blessedness, when rest and glorious repose will finally be given to the saints.

10 For you, Lord, have established me uniquely in hope.

C The Church’s hope is unique in her members, because she alone receives the kingdom of God, which the wicked cannot attain. When he says “you have established me,” he signifies a worthy and deliberate judgment, which here we possess in hope and there possess in reality.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM IIII

Hear us, Lord, and have mercy on us in our tribulations; and you who alone are magnified among the peoples, grant spiritual joy to us who have been established in hope of future gifts. Through our Lord, etc.

# PSALM V

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM V

C The Church, asking that her prayer be heard, declares that heretics and schismatics are to be excluded from the Lord’s gift, while also recalling the happy rewards of the blessed.

[Col. 0058A]

TT. A psalm of David, for her who receives the inheritance.

C “For her who receives the inheritance” signifies the Church, whose person is introduced in this psalm, because, when Christ rose again, spiritual goods came to her: faith, hope, and charity.

1 Give heed to my words ÷ with your ears … Lord; understand my cry.

C This psalm, like the preceding one, belongs to the Church of Christ. By saying “my words,” he signifies the psalmody of the mouth. By asking “understand my cry,” he opens the affection of his heart. This threefold repetition signifies one thing when he says “give heed,” “understand,” and “attend,” through the figure of *metabole*, which is the repetition of one matter under varying words. *Ear* is derived from hearing.

2 [Col. 0058B] ÷ Attend to the voice of my prayer … my King and my God.

C He now says “attend to the voice” in order to declare that this prayer is perfect, inflaming the affections of the mind. “My King and my God,” and “because I will pray to you, Lord”: this sentence is distinguished according to the persons, yet unity in nature is to be believed. Although he names three, he does not say “attend” in the plural but “attend” in the singular, as though he were speaking to one.

3 For to you I will pray, Lord; in the morning you will hear my voice.

C “To you I will pray,” that is, not to another, as the pagans and unbelievers do. Then the Church rightly believes that she will be heard in the morning, when she has broken forth into the light of heavenly conduct and the enlightened mind has begun to recognize the truth at the beginning of good actions. The one who is known to live in a bright manner prays in the morning; for we speak of morning when, the darkness having been dispersed, the arrival of bright light shines forth.

4 In the morning I will stand before you and will see, for you are not a God who wills iniquity.

H He repeats “in the morning,” that is, when the light of virtues begins in my soul, when I begin to stand before you, not before another. Not sitting, not lying down, but standing; and when you have set my feet upon the rock, then through these stages I will deserve to see you. Or: “I will stand before you” by living rightly, and “I will see”—understand, with the eyes of the heart.

C The order is: You are God, who is known not to will iniquity. For what else can God will except what he himself is shown to command? As Isaiah says: “I am the Lord, who speak righteousness and announce upright things” (Isa. 45).

5 The wicked will not dwell near you, nor will the unjust remain before your eyes.

C Those who are destined to be condemned to the torments of Gehenna cannot dwell near Christ in the blessed kingdom.

H They are rightly said not to remain before him because they will be deprived of his kingdom. For if God is fire, and a consuming fire, whoever is straw, whoever is wood, flees from the fire lest he be consumed. But if he is gold, he does not flee the fire by which he is purified (Deut. 4).

6 You hate all who work iniquity; you will destroy ÷ all … who speak falsehood.

H He did not say “those who worked iniquity,” but “those who work iniquity.” For those are hated by the Lord who persevere in sins to the end of life; those who amend what they have done badly are loved. “You will destroy them” signifies heretics, who kill as many people through falsehood as they bring into heresy.

7 The Lord will abominate the man of blood and deceit; but I, in the multitude of your mercy—

C A man of blood is one stained by human blood; similarly, one who deceives a living person in grace, as heretics do. A deceitful person is one who knowingly seeks to bring about another’s ruin, so as to deceive him through fraud. Deceit properly lies in an action, fraud in a word. Those people are abominated who do not deserve to attain Christ’s rewards.

[Col. 0059B] A For the disinherited are commonly said to be abominated. But the one who obtains the heavenly inheritance rejoices in hope, saying: “But I…”

8 I will enter your house; I will worship toward your holy temple in your fear.

H C The righteous will enter Christ’s house—that is, the holy Church, or the heavenly Jerusalem.

C The holy temple is the body of the Lord, which the Church rightly worships in fear. For faith is then firm when the divinity is worshiped with chaste love and fear.

A Or the heavenly temple: I worship toward it as I draw near to it by good works and prayers; I do not worship within it but near it and toward it, worshiping the glory of God while I do not see it.

9 [Col. 0059C] Lord, lead me in your righteousness because of my enemies; direct your way before my sight.

C The mother Church asks the Lord to lead her to eternal joys, since here she is wearied by various anxieties. It is right that Christ should wish to receive those who plead in his righteousness, because of his enemies—that is, heretics and pagans. One is called an enemy because he curses through perverse doctrine, the other because he does not believe.

H By “the way” he means Holy Scripture, lest one fall in it through understanding it badly.

A Or receive “the way” as the commandments by which one goes to you. “Direct this way of yours,” that is, show it before my sight, so that I may have the commandments before my eyes and be governed by them.

H “Direct my way before your sight” is found neither in the Septuagint nor in Aquila, Symmachus, or Theodotion, but only in the common edition. In Hebrew it reads: “Direct your way before my sight.” For, as in the Lord’s Prayer we ask that the Lord’s name be hallowed—not that it should be made holy by our praying, since it is holy of itself, but that what is holy by its nature may be hallowed in us—so now the Prophet asks that the Lord’s way, which is straight in itself, may also be made straight for him.

10 For there is no truth in their mouth; their heart is empty.

H C It is rightly said that there is no truth—which is Christ—in the mouth of heretics, whose heart was possessed by vanity, because he is not in their heart either. And not only is there no truth in their mouth, but also a tomb, and so forth.

11 Their throat is an open tomb. They acted deceitfully with their tongues; judge them, O God.

C The throat of one who lies is the tomb of the dead, because just as a foul odor comes from a tomb, so perverse doctrine comes from the mouth of a heretic. “Open”: if it were closed, it would stink less; if he had remained silent, he would have harmed less. They acted deceitfully with their tongues because they showed malice not only in speech but also in action. The Church did not desire this through a curse, but foretold what would happen.

H “Judge them, O God,” so that they may experience you as judge, since they do not wish to experience you as Father. You who will judge at the end, judge even now, so that they may know that you regard human affairs.

12 Let them fall from their counsels; according to the multitude of their impieties drive them out, for they have provoked you, Lord.

C One properly falls who is defrauded by the loss of his hope. Therefore let the enemies fall, lest they increase impieties by impieties.

H Drive them out from their impieties, or from the Church.

C For a sinner is made farther from it in proportion as he is enlarged by numerous crimes. Evil sick people provoked the good physician—that is, Christ—because they rejected the remedies of their salvation.

13 But let all who hope in you rejoice; they will exult forever, and you will dwell in them.

C “Let them rejoice and exult forever,” those who hope in the Lord, because although the wicked also appear to rejoice in this world, only the righteous will rejoice in the world to come.

H Blessed are those who deserve to be the dwelling places of Christ.

A Therefore let those rejoice now who hope in the Lord in this world, because after death they will exult forever.

14 But all who love your name will glory in you ÷ … for you will bless the righteous.

C “All will glory” signifies that those who enjoy the Lord’s vision will be happy in that homeland. “You will bless the righteous”: lest anyone think that the rewards of joy mentioned above are attributed to him because of his own merits, they are to be understood as resulting from the Lord’s blessing.

A Therefore those who love here will then glory, because they will possess for enjoyment what they love. This is the eternal inheritance after which the psalm is titled.

15 Lord, with the shield of your good will you have crowned them.

C The Lord will protect us with the shield of his good will when he enriches us with unspeakable gifts and leads us to be crowned in the everlasting kingdoms.

A Thus God’s good will and mercy are a shield protecting us in the present, and a crown in the future.

C He says “good will,” not “just will,” showing that we are saved by God’s goodness alone, not by our righteousness.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM V

Compassionate Lord, who understand the groaning of an afflicted heart before it is uttered, make us, we ask, a temple of the Paraclete, so that we may deserve to be crowned with the shield of heavenly benevolence. Through our Lord, etc.

# PSALM VI

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM VI

B The faithful pray that he may become a favorable judge for them, recounting the troubles by which they are afflicted and groan, and separating themselves from the fellowship of sinners, with whom they desire to have no share.

TT. For the end, with hymns, for the eighth, a psalm of David.

C “For the end” is already known. A hymn is praise of the Divinity composed according to the law of a certain meter. Indeed, a hymn is properly a song of praise—not of just anyone, but of God. If any one of these elements is lacking, it is not called a hymn. Whether it is not sung, or is sung but not in praise, or is sung in praise but not of God, it does not deserve to be called a hymn.

“For the eighth” signifies the coming of the Lord, when, the week of the world having ended, he comes to judge the world. Hence this psalm begins with the greatest trembling, saying: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger, nor correct me in your wrath.”

1 Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury, nor correct me in your anger.

C This psalm is the first of the penitential psalms. It is followed by 31, 37, 50, 101, 129, and 142. There are seven because sins are forgiven in seven ways: through baptism, martyrdom, almsgiving, forgiving a brother’s sins, converting a sinner, an abundance of charity, and pure repentance; the communion of Christ’s body must also be added. A careful inquirer may perhaps find other means of forgiveness, but you should not think that the elders brought the penitential psalms to the number seven without reason.

C The Prophet does not beseech the Lord not to rebuke him, since it is written, “Those whom I love, I rebuke,” but asks that he not be condemned in the severity of judgment. Anger is prolonged indignation; fury is the swift kindling of the mind, though anger is more vehement. The Lord will never be moved by these emotions, but remains in righteous tranquility even when punishing. These things are therefore said of God in transferred language.

2 Have mercy on me, Lord, for I am weak; heal me, Lord, for my bones are troubled.

C The confession of weakness moves God’s mercy, from whom remedies are easily obtained when the wounds of sin are revealed. Here “bones” signifies the strength of the mind. When that strength fails, all vigor of mind slips away, just as the whole body becomes weak when the bones of the body are shattered.

3 And my soul is greatly troubled; and you, Lord—how long?

H He said that his soul was troubled, namely, through repentance for the sake of amendment.

C “Greatly”: he said this so that merciful Christ would not delay his help any longer. “How long?” Understand: How long do you delay having mercy, when you are not accustomed to forget the prayers of suppliants even to the end?

H Or: How long will you not rescue, correct, or amend my soul, which is greatly troubled?

4 [Col. 0062A] Turn, Lord, and rescue my soul; save me because of your mercy.

C When he says “turn,” he asks that vengeance be relaxed, so that God may not exact the punishments we deserve. “Rescue me” from the punishment that threatens. He asks to be saved not according to his own merits but because of divine mercy; when hope is fixed in that mercy, pardon is more easily obtained.

5 For there is no one in death who remembers you; but in hell ÷ … who will confess to you?

C We rightly call the perfidious those who are forgetful of God, since they have no confidence in confession. H Thus “death” means mortal sin; “hell,” the blindness of despair. C Or, after temporal death there is no confession for obtaining forgiveness, much less in hell; therefore [Col. 0062B] he added: “Who will confess to you?”—that is, for the sake of forgiveness in hell, where no remission is found.

6 I have labored in my groaning; Every night I will wash my bed; I will water my couch with my tears.

C A groan is so called from doubled mourning, when we remember our evils and are shaken by fear of the punishment to come. “Bed” signifies bodily pleasure, which a person can wash with tears if he happens to lament it through heavenly inspiration. “Couch” signifies the heap of sins, which a person waters with tears so that his sins may be wiped away by that same most wholesome rain. A bed (*lectus*) is so called from choice and soft herbs, upon which in ancient times the bodies of those resting were laid down into sleep. To water something more abundantly [Col. 0062C] signifies more than to wash it: whoever waters his couch daily with tears cannot allow the pomp of lusts to steal into his thoughts.

7 My eye is troubled by fury; I have grown old among all my enemies.

C The eye is so called as if from *ocior lux*, “swifter light,” because it quickly looks upon what it fixes its attention on, or because it is hidden by concealing eyelids. Hence here he says that the eye of the heart is troubled, that is, H all the ruling part of my heart trembled. “I have grown old,” that is, C I have remained in the antiquity of the old man Adam. “Among enemies,” that is, among demonic spirits, or among our sins, which are called enemies because they lead our souls down to Tartarus and ferociously flatter us for that purpose.

8 Depart from me, all you who work iniquity, [Col. 0062D] for the Lord has heard the voice of my weeping.

C The prophet asks the company of the wicked to depart from him, so that he may serve his Lord more securely, and so that, when he who had sinned through fellowship with the wicked has driven such people away from himself, he may appear most devoted to the Lord’s commands. In this way too he proves that he has come to complete correction, because he wished to separate himself from the company of the wicked. Hence it follows: “The Lord has heard.”

9 The Lord has heard my supplication; the Lord has received my prayer.

C Supplication is frequent prayer offered with devotion; and supplication by itself is prayer that is excessive, fittingly persistent, and wins over the one addressed. Nor is it without significance that, in one petition, he says three times that the Lord granted what he asked, namely, so that [Col. 0063A] he might show the Holy Trinity to have been present to his petition.

10 Let my enemies be ashamed and troubled [the source’s + … .. mark spans *vehementer omnes*, “greatly all”]; let them turn back and be utterly ashamed very quickly.

C When he says, “Let them be ashamed,” he wishes sinners to be illumined by such great compunction that they may be ashamed of and amend the things they formerly did. Let them be troubled, that is, by fear of the future judgment. When he says “my,” he has relaxed his hatred, since a multitude of faults had been forgiven. “Let them be turned away,” that is, let them not be permitted to go where they are heading, namely, to sin. H “Let them be ashamed”: not lightly, but greatly; not tomorrow, but quickly. C And observe how this penitent, immediately heard and freed from sins, obeying the rule of the Gospel, prays for his enemies, that they may be converted: so that, just as he himself received forgiveness, his carnal enemies too may return to the Lord’s grace.

## Prayer from Psalm VI

God who hears all, hear the suppliant voice of our weeping, and grant perpetual health to our infirmities, so that, while you graciously regard the groaning of our labor, you may always console us with your mercy. Through him.

# Psalm VII

## Argument of Psalm VII

C This Psalm pertains to Christ’s humanity, who, in that by which he became humble, asks to be judged according to his justice and truth.

[Col. 0063C] TT. A Psalm of David, which he sang to the Lord because of the words of Chusi, son of Jemini.

H It must therefore be known that *Chusi* is interpreted as “Ethiopian,” and that this entire psalm was written against Saul, whom he calls an Ethiopian because of his dark character. *Jemini* means the family of Benjamin, from which Saul arose. C Or, as Father Augustine teaches, *Chusi* is interpreted as “silence”; “son of Jemini” is interpreted as “son of the right hand.”

1 O Lord my God, in you I have hoped; Save me from all those who persecute me and deliver me.

C The prophet asks to be delivered from all enemies, especially from spiritual wickedness, because carnal enemies attack the body, whereas spiritual ones strive to kill [Col. 0063D] souls. “Save me” from sin; “deliver me” from the devil, so that we may be removed from his power when the Lord’s mercy cleanses us from the filth of our offenses.

2 Lest he seize my soul like a lion, while there is no one who redeems or saves.

C The devil is compared to a lion, and Christ too is compared to a lion: the one because he seizes for destruction, Christ because he snatches away for salvation. “There is no one who redeems,” that is, when Christ ceases to come to our aid because of the obstacles created by our sins, at that time the devil prevails in seizing us.

3 O Lord my God, if I have done this; if there is iniquity in my hands.

H This verse and the next pertain to Christ, who committed no iniquity, and to David, who returned no evil to Saul, even though Saul twice fell into his hands.

4 If I have repaid evil to those repaying me evil, may I deservedly fall empty-handed before my enemies.

C No one repays unless he has first received something. But this man, full of God, exceedingly firm and benevolent through the virtue of patience, asks that, if he has returned evil for evil, he may fall empty-handed before his enemies, that is, emptied of the fruit of great gentleness. And not only this, but also—what is more serious—if I have repaid, and so forth, let the enemy pursue me.

5 Let the enemy pursue my soul and seize it; let him trample my life upon the earth, and bring my glory down into the dust. *Diapsalma.*

[Col. 0064B] C He calls the enemy the devil, who crushes the souls he has seized, since human beings can persecute only the body, but the devil also persecutes the soul, which is more. It is as though he had said: If I have returned evil to my enemies, contrary to your prohibition, let him bring the honor of the man assumed—which is established as having been made in the image of God—into that dust which the wind casts away from the face of the earth, that is, let him reduce it, as it were, to nothing.

6 ÷ Rise [the source marks the prefix *ex-* of Latin *exsurge*] .., O Lord, in your anger, and be exalted at the boundaries of my enemies.

C May the Lord rise up in anger, though he has no anger—that is, for vengeance. H Yet this vengeance, which is called anger, ought rather to be directed against the devil, who is punished whenever a sinner is snatched from him, so that the enemies may thus experience through vengeance the one whom they did not wish to experience through benefits. C God is exalted when, after sinners have been converted, the confession of praise is offered to Christ; and this occurs “at the boundaries,” that is, in the possession of the devil, in which Christ is certainly exalted while he is praised by the converted.

7 * And: rise up ÷, O Lord my God .., according to the commandment that you gave, and the assembly of the peoples will surround you.

C The Lord commanded in the commandment—that is, in the Gospel—to the disciples: “On the third day I will rise; I will go before you into Galilee.” He said the past concerning the future for the certainty of prophecy. “Assembly” here signifies the gathering of the reprobate, which surrounded Christ by not believing, on account of the rebellious Jews who persecuted [Col. 0064D] Christ. H Or “assembly” signifies the people of the faithful, who, by believing, surrounded Christ after the resurrection.

8 And for its sake return on high; the Lord judges the peoples.

C “For its sake,” that is, for the sake of the assembly in which Christ could not dwell because of unbelief. To return means to go back by a repeated journey to the place from which one came. When he says, “He judges the peoples,” the majesty of the almighty Father is revealed.

9 Judge me, O Lord, according to my justice and according to my innocence that is in me.

C When “judge me” is said, the humility of Christ’s humanity is expressed, which was assumed [Col. 0065A] from Mary’s womb. It is also certain that he had no sin whatsoever, because he committed no sin; therefore he displays his innocence.

10 Let the wickedness of sinners be consumed; and you will direct the righteous, searching hearts and reins, O God.

C The prophet, in the person of Christ, asks that the wickedness of sinners be brought swiftly to an end, that is, that the flesh may soon be crucified for us, so that his ascent may quickly be glorified. The righteous man was directed when he rose from the dead and ascended to the kingdoms of heaven. It belongs to God’s power both to examine our hearts and to understand bodily pleasures—that is, to search the heart and the reins.

11 My just help is from the Lord, who saves the upright in heart.

[Col. 0065B] A “Just help,” because it is now bestowed upon the just, and is like a medicine preserving health. C The humanity also says that its help is from God the Father, so that it might grant those who believe in it the hope of his compassion; to the upright in heart it grants both forgiveness and salvation.

12 God is a just, strong ÷ and .. patient judge. Will he be angry every day?

C God is called a just judge because at the end he gives each person what he has done. He is strong because no one can resist his will. And he is patient because he waits daily for the sinner to turn himself toward repentance (II Cor. V). He is said to become angry in the manner of judges, although anger is not found in the divinity. “Every day” means at every moment in which we commit sins; for where would his glorious patience be if his vengeance immediately followed guilt? [Col. 0065C]

13 Unless you are converted, he will brandish his sword; he has bent his bow and prepared it.

C “He will brandish his sword”—the prophet terrifies the obstinate Jews who served the cults of idols—that is, he will send his only Son in shining glory. We call that “brandished” which displays now light, now trembling shadows; this evidently arose from Christ’s incarnation, when he showed darkness to the perfidious and the light of his divinity to the faithful. By “bow” we understand the Scriptures of the New and Old Testaments, by which the obstinate are terrified. He said “he bent it,” lest his patience be thought slack. “And prepared it”: this can be said of God, so that the very manner of archers may be fully represented.

14 And in it he prepared instruments of death; he made his arrows for those who are burning.

C We have said that the bow is the Old and New Testament, from which the effect of death comes to the wicked, who sometimes seize an occasion of death from the Scriptures; yet life is granted through its arrows. From this bow the arrows went forth, namely, the apostles, who sent saving commandments like arrows to souls most eager—that is, burning— by which the impious are wounded and the faithful healed. “He made,” that is, he worked. And who made this? God; yet behold, and so forth.

15 Behold, he is in labor with iniquity: ÷ he conceived pain, and gave birth to wickedness.

C The Jewish people labored with iniquity when, seeing the Lord performing miracles, they plotted his death. It conceived pain when he rebuked them through various parables and turned them from their perversity. It gave birth to wickedness when it said, “Crucify him”; the order is reversed. First, through the devil’s suggestion, sin is conceived; then it is brought forth and born.

16 He opened a pit and dug it out, and he fell into the hole that he made.

C A pit is so called because its bottom lies hidden; here it stands for deceit, which the wickedness of the Jews opened, because it was the first to wickedly begin deceit against Christ. He dug it out when he completed it in his own condemnation. He fell into the hole, that is, into the place of death. A The deceiver is first harmed by the loss of innocence before he harms another through the loss of money.

17 His pain will return upon his own head, and his iniquity will descend upon his own crown.

C “Pain” is so called as if from “tameable horror.” Here we must understand “head” as the soul, to which sins are subjected and made liable when they are restrained from being committed. “Crown” is so called because it turns the hair to the right and left; it signifies reason, which rises above the mind. If this soul is bent downward by sins, it is necessary that iniquity descend upon the crown, that is, above its reason. For when their own sins descend upon the impious, they are consigned through their crimes to the punishments they deserve.

18 I will confess to the Lord according to his justice, and I will sing psalms to the name of the Lord Most High.

C Confession is spoken of in two ways: when we condemn our sins through satisfaction, or when with exultation we celebrate praises worthy of God. His justice resists the proud and gives grace to the humble, because it makes the proud endure their crimes, whereas it graciously absolves the humble. To sing psalms is to carry out the Lord’s commandments and to sing hymns with the voice and from the innermost heart.

## Prayer from Psalm VII

God who searches hearts, deliver us from those who persecute us, and, as we await your judgment, grant us steadfast guardianship of mind, so that we may not repay evil to our enemies with evil. Through our Lord Jesus, and so forth.

# Psalm VIII

## Argument of Psalm VIII

[Col. 0066D]

C The Church, singing the praises and majesty of the Lord Christ, says that his human nature has grown toward the heights of great things.

TT. For the end, concerning the winepresses; a Psalm of David.

C We have already said that “for the end” signifies the Lord. “Concerning the winepresses” declares the Church, which at its first entrance joyfully sings the Lord’s praise. A The Church is called a winepress for the same reason that it is called a threshing floor. The same reality is often suggested in Scripture through many different likenesses. On the threshing floor grain is separated from chaff; in the winepress wine is separated from grape-skins. Thus in the Church the good are separated from the wicked, not by place but by disposition.

1 O Lord, our Lord, how wondrous is your name in all the earth!

C The name of the Lord sounds as an ineffable title; hence, when he says, “How wondrous it is,” he cannot explain what he feels. “In all the earth,” because his holy religion is spread throughout the whole world. H That you became human for us, that you died, that you rose again, has been proclaimed among all nations; and also that you were lifted up, and so forth.

2 How exalted is your magnificence above the heavens!

C God’s magnificence is the mystery of Christ’s Incarnation. It was exalted when Christ, rising again, ascended into the heavens, as it is said in another psalm: “Be exalted, O God, above the heavens, and your glory over all the earth” (Psalm LVI). [Col. 0067B]

3 From the mouth of infants and nursing children you have perfected praise because of your enemies, so that you may destroy the enemy and the avenger.

H This prophecy was fulfilled in the Gospel, when the children cried out in the Temple: “Hosanna to the Son of David; blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Matthew XXI). C The meaning is that you are worthy of praise not only from the perfect and learned, but are also wondrously proclaimed by the mouths of beginners and little ones. By “infants and nursing children” we are to understand not children nourished with material milk, but the little ones in faith, who, instructed in the rudiments of faith, do not yet receive stronger food (I Cor. III; [Col. 0067C] Hebr. V). “Enemies” designates pagans and blasphemers. “Defender” means the perfidious Jew, C H or the heretic, A or the devil, the defender of his sect and of sin. Heretics too say that they defend the Christian faith, and sinners the truth, when they excuse sins. C By “enemy and defender,” or “avenger,” he specifically means the perfidious Jew, who, while he thinks he is defending the Father, proves himself an enemy of the Son. Thus it happened that, as if he were God’s defender, he was shown to be God’s most open adversary.

4 For I will see your heavens .., the work of your fingers +: the moon and the stars which ÷ you .. established.

C “I will see the heavens,” that is, the evangelical books. The finger of God means the effect of divine operation. By “moon” he means the Church; by “stars,” righteous people. “You established,” so that we may understand all things to have been founded in God’s predestination.

5 What is man, that you are mindful of him, or the son of man, that you visit him?

C “What is man?” must be pronounced with contempt, that is, the fragile and perishable follower of Adam, who has been mingled with the old sin through shared perversity. The Lord is mindful of him when he forgives his sins through his mercy. By “son of man” he means the son of the Virgin Mary; A because he visited us by assuming the body of our humility, and thus freeing us from the old sin, the Son of God visited the son of man when the Son of God became the son of man.

6 You made him a little lower than the angels; you crowned him with glory and honor, and you established him over the works of your hands.

C He was made lower, not by necessity but through compassion and voluntary will, accepting the form of a servant. He was made lower than the angels in that respect in which he accepted the cross for the salvation of all. He rightly said “a little lower,” because, although he assumed mortal flesh, he nevertheless had no sins. H “With glory,” when the lower regions shone at his descent. “With honor,” when he conquered death. “Crowned,” surrounded by the choir of the saints, he returned from the dead. C When he says “the works of your hands,” every creature is shown to be subject to him.

7 You subjected all things beneath his feet: all sheep and oxen, and also the beasts of the field.

[Col. 0068B] C When he says “all things,” he shows that both earthly and higher things are subject to him. “Sheep” signifies the chosen people. “Oxen” means preachers. “Also,” that is, not only the saints but also sinners—whom the beasts signify—are subject to him; they are rightly called beasts while they feed upon the pleasures of this world. They are sheep, however, when they are enclosed within God’s folds.

8 The birds of the heavens and the fish of the sea, which travel along the paths of the sea.

C Birds of the heavens, so called from their frequent flight, are proud people who, puffed up by the wind of boasting, fly as if through the empty air and despise humble things. By “fish” he means philosophers, who investigate the nature of this world with wandering curiosity. Like fish swimming in the sea [Col. 0068C], through excessive curiosity they do not contemplate heavenly things but, amid the waves of this age, searching out the hidden straits of flowing things, suppose that eternal life exists. These too are subject beneath Christ’s feet when they are converted. For although all things are rightly subject to Christ, we properly call those subject who have deserved to attain his easy burden.

9 O Lord, our Lord, how wondrous is your name in all the earth!

C The holy Church fittingly repeats this verse of praise to the Lord, which it spoke at the beginning, because he himself said, “I am Alpha and Omega,” that is, beginning and end (Revelation I).

## Prayer from Psalm VIII

Almighty Lord, we humbly beseech you concerning your wondrous name: since you have subjected every creature of the world to human use, graciously deem us worthy to perform the service of your worship. Through our Lord, and so forth.

# Psalm IX

## Argument of Psalm IX

C The prophet says that he will joyfully sing psalms to the Lord, because he has confounded the devil and avenges the blood of the poor; and, declaring that sinners together with the Antichrist will perish, he prays that the time of judgment may come swiftly, so that no one’s iniquity may prevail any longer.

[Col. 0069A] TT. For the end, concerning the hidden things of the Son; a Psalm of David.

C “For the end, concerning the hidden things of the Son: a psalm.” We have said that this “end” signifies him—not an end in which one fails, but one in which one grows; he is for us the beginning of good and the end of evil. “Concerning the hidden things of the Son” signifies the person of the Savior, whose mysteries and judgments are hidden from us. This entire psalm is sung by the prophet in the person of the Church.

1 I will confess to you ÷, O Lord .., with all my heart; I will recount all your wonders.

C He confesses God with his whole heart who is tossed by no worldly thoughts; this belongs to the perfect. “I will recount,” and so forth. H It is as though he had said: As much as you have taught me, so much will I recount. Whoever recounts as much as he understands recounts all God’s wonders, although there are more of them in themselves.

2 I will rejoice and exult in you; I will sing psalms to your name, O Most High.

C To exult is more than to rejoice. To exult is to delight with the most joyful freedom through a greater movement of mind and body; to rejoice is to expand in mind through gladness. For *laetitia*, “joy,” is as if from *latitia*, that is, the breadth of the mind, and is spoken of in relation to joy. “I will sing psalms,” H I will fulfill in deed. The Son is the name of the Father. He himself, God, is the Most High.

3 When my enemy turns back, they will grow weak and perish before your face.

H He calls the enemy the devil, to whom the Lord said: “Get behind me, Satan” (Matthew XVI). Some think that he spoke not to Peter but to the devil, who was suggesting things to Peter concerning the Lord: “Get behind me, Satan,” that is, adversary or enemy. “They will grow weak.” Here he includes in the plural all the devil’s satellites, who were previously strong because of our sins, but are now weak; whereas we are strong in God. “They will perish before the face.” C That is, before the grace [or “face”] of Christ.

4 For you have executed my judgment and my cause; you have sat upon the throne ÷, you who .. judge justice.

H “You have executed my judgment”: the voice of the Church, as though it said, “You chose the nations and rejected the Jews.” “My cause,” that is, you acted on my behalf against my adversaries, avenged me, and made my cause good. C *Throne* is Greek; in Latin, *sede*, “seat,” because each person is God’s seat. C H Here the present tense, “you judge,” is used for the future, because he will judge with equity.

5 You rebuked the nations, ÷ and .. the impious perished; you erased their name forever and for ages ÷ of ages ..

H You rebuked the nations through the apostles, because they worshiped idols. “And the impious perished,” because through preaching he was made pious from being impious. “You erased their name,” that is, the name of impiety. C “For ages of ages” signifies the kingdom to come, which will end in no age and at no time. It is an eternal age after this mutable age; it is “the age,” that is, the eternity following this age: when this age has ended, another begins.

6 The swords of the enemies have failed utterly; and you have destroyed their cities ÷ ..

C “Of the enemies” is a genitive, that is, of the devil, whose sword he testifies has failed when the devil’s power will be destroyed at the end by the judgment of the Almighty. *Framea* is a Hebrew word; in Latin, “sword.” “Cities” means the unbelieving peoples whose hearts the devil possessed in this age; he says that they have been convicted at Christ’s final manifestation.

Their memory has perished with a great crash, but the Lord remains forever.

C “With a great crash” means with the loudest outcry, as happens when prosperous circumstances are closed by a most grievous end, so that neither their power nor their name appears to remain. And behold the beautiful and most fitting contrast: earlier he said that the impious would perish; now he says that the Lord remains forever.

8 He prepared his throne for judgment, and he himself will judge the world in equity; he will judge the peoples in justice.

C “He prepared,” namely, God made human, so that the one who was judged here in humility might come there to judge in majesty. And it is certainly the Lord Christ who will judge. By “the world” we must understand holy men. These are to be judged in equity, since they will hear: “Come, blessed of my Father” (Matthew XXV); for equity is customarily used for a gentle and mild judgment. By “peoples” he means sinners. These are to be judged with justice, to whom it will be said: “Go into eternal fire” (ibid.).

9 And the Lord became a refuge for the poor, [Col. 0070C] a helper in times of opportunity, in tribulation.

C It is a great consideration for joy to have as judge the very one who is also a refuge. The poor of God is the person who despises earthly things and desires heavenly things. That help is sweetest which is provided in an opportune moment, that is, in necessity. “In tribulation,” when the mind of the afflicted is more eagerly stirred toward compunction.

10 And let those who know your name hope in you, for you have not abandoned those who seek you, O Lord.

C “Let them hope in you”: let them not look toward the flatteries of the world, but trust in your promise—those who know the name, that is, who venerate your majesty with the holiest devotion. A For God’s name is “Lord,” or “He Is.” The one who knows it is the one who willingly serves him who truly is. [Col. 0070D] Therefore let no one hope in transitory things, which possess nothing except “was” and “will be.” For what is future in them, when it comes, immediately becomes past; it is awaited with desire, lost with grief, and not held with certainty. C The reason why they should hope in God follows: he does not allow those whom he sees fleeing to him to be abandoned.

11 Sing psalms to the Lord ÷ who .. dwells ÷ in .. Zion; proclaim his purposes among the nations.

H “Sing psalms to the Lord,” that is, preach the Lord and fulfill in deed what you preach. Zion is called “watchtower,” that is, the Church, in which Christ dwells. “Proclaim”: the prophet’s voice admonishes preachers to proclaim his purposes, that is, Christ’s commandments.

12 For, seeking their blood, he remembered them; he has not forgotten the cry of the poor.

C Since above he said, “Preach to the nations,” lest anyone think that the blood of the martyrs would go unavenged, he said “seeking their blood,” so that vengeance might terrify persecutors and the promise might comfort martyrs. “He has not forgotten” is said lest they think that God forgets to repay good things to Christ’s poor because the future judgment is delayed.

13 Have mercy on me, O Lord; see my humiliation because of my enemies.

C The prophet asks to be helped in such a way that he may be seen by Christ the King, because Christ’s regard is aid. He again begs the Lord to understand his humility in the face of the pride of his persecutors, because the persecutors seem to be exalted precisely as the martyrs are humbled.

14 You who exalt me from the gates of death, so that I may proclaim all your praises at the gates of the daughter of Zion.

C The gate of death is the devil or alluring vices, through which one enters eternal death. “You exalt me,” that is, you put me far from such things. Freed from those gates of death, he promises to proclaim the Lord’s praises at the gates of Zion, that is, throughout the entire world of God’s holy Church. A For the gates of the Church are the apostles, and likewise all the best practices through which one comes to the vision of peace in the Church. H The gates of death are also heretics and every evil teaching. The gates of Zion are the good preachers of the Church and [Col. 0071C] holy doctrine.

15 I will exult in your salvation; the nations are fixed in the destruction that they made.

C Rightly, then, the prophet says that he rejoices in him, that is, in Christ, where joy has no end. He says that the nations are fixed who are not held by fear of the Lord, that is, as though bound by certain nails of sins, so that they cannot shake themselves free. We not improperly say that this pertains to the Jews: thus the perfidious Jews are fixed in their own evils, just as they decided to nail the Lord to the cross. For each person’s iniquity is also his punishment.

16 In the trap that they hid, their foot was caught.

C They concealed the trap as much as they could [Col. 0071D], yet they were unable to hide anything from Christ. We call those “caught” whom a knotted snare binds tightly. So it was with their foot, that is, the step of their mind and the perverse desire that made them walk toward vices. A The hidden trap is deceitful thought; the foot of the soul is love, which, if perverse, is called desire, and if upright, charity. By it the soul moves as toward the place to which it is heading, whether good or evil delight.

17 The Lord will be known when he executes judgments; the sinner has been caught in the works of his hands. A song of the *diapsalma*.

C The Lord will be known when the human race, whether on the left or on the right, has been separated by God’s judgment. The sinner has been caught in his own works when he receives a fitting punishment according to the quality of his deed.

18 Let sinners be turned into hell—all the nations that forget God.

C “Let sinners be turned,” he says, that is, let them be taken away from the pleasure of this world, so that they may no longer be able to rejoice in their enjoyment. Hell is so called from the fact that souls continually perish there; without doubt those will reach it who despise the Lord’s commandments. To forget the Lord is to be entangled in the errors of superstition and the mire of pleasure. Conversely, those remember him who do not seek such things.

19 For the poor will not be forgotten forever; the patience of the poor will not perish forever.

C The poor will not be forgotten when the Lord comes at the end of the age to judge the world. He also says that the patience which crowns the faithful will not perish. For if a person lacks patience, his soul is not perfect. “Forever.” H For although help for the saints is delayed, it is nevertheless not withheld, but comes.

20 Rise up, O Lord; let man not prevail; let the nations be judged in your sight.

C The prophet foresaw the coming of the Antichrist and proclaimed: “Rise up, O Lord; let him not prevail”—that is, let the most wicked man, namely the Antichrist, not prevail, whose wickedness human nature cannot endure. He also asks that the nations be judged at his swiftest coming, since they will commit great crimes with the Antichrist.

21 Establish a lawgiver over them, O Lord, so that the nations may know what kind of men they are. *Diapsalma.*

C By “lawgiver” he means the Antichrist, so that such a ruler may be given to sinners—not one who governs them, but one who perishes together with them. H “So that they may know,” when the nations have been condemned, and so forth, because they placed their hope in a human being and not in God. C Yet the only truest lawgiver is God; the Antichrist, however, will be an evil and false lawgiver.

22 Why, O Lord, have you withdrawn far away? Do you despise us in times of opportunity, in tribulation?

C Christ has not withdrawn far away, because he is wholly present everywhere; but he is thought to have withdrawn when he delays to help. We think that we are despised if we are kept from God’s help even for the briefest time. The prophet said this out of the anxiety of those who groan. But he provides more generously at that time when he supplies us with the consolations of great patience.

23 While the impious man is proud, the poor man is set on fire; they are caught in the schemes they devise.

C “The impious man is proud.” When he has proudly accomplished the deeds of his evil will, then the poor Catholic is more greatly inflamed toward the pursuit of virtue, because, when he sees the sinner excessively exalted, he easily recognizes that he will fall. But these impious men are caught and punished with the penalties they deserve. A Or, they are caught in the counsels of evil thoughts with which they plot to seize the saints in order to afflict them. And why is the impious man proud? He adds: “Because he is praised,” and so forth. [Col. 0073A] This is God’s great anger against the impious: that correction is absent and flattery is present; for the tongues of flatterers bind souls in sins.

24 For the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, and the wicked man is blessed.

25 The sinner has provoked the Lord; according to the abundance of his anger he will not seek him.

C The evil man, when he is praised by another sinner, is exalted in his desire for praise and does not think about correction, since the one praising him is found to flatter him. The argument for his iniquity follows: the one who is known to act evilly is blessed instead, deceived by the falsehood of flatterers. C “The sinner has provoked the Lord,” that is, he has stirred him to anger by his unspeakable pride. This is properly understood of the Antichrist, who provokes the Lord when, through his deception, he will proclaim himself not only an earthly king but also the God of all things. Yet this will lead to his ruin; therefore, as a false god, he will be punished with fitting flames. The Antichrist will not seek God so that his cruel sins may be forgiven, because he does not have God before his eyes. Therefore it is added: “There is no God,” and so forth.

26 God is not before his eyes; his ways are defiled at all times.

C O what profound blindness—not to have God before one’s eyes! He says of the Antichrist that all his paths are polluted, that is, his filthy thoughts and deeds. For whatever is befouled under the pestilential leadership of the devil must necessarily be contaminated.

27 Your judgments are removed from his sight; he will rule over all his enemies.

C God’s judgments are removed from the heart of the impious when he sees that what he deserved to endure swiftly is coming more slowly. This too increases his destruction: he is said to hold dominion over his enemies, and through this boast he will be readier for crimes, since he knows that no one will stand in his way.

28 For he said in his heart, “I shall not be moved from generation to generation, without evil.”

C The Antichrist says, “I shall not be moved,” that is, “I will leave no nation untouched, but will proceed from nation to nation until I am avenged.” He displays his deeds in one word when he says that he will do nothing without evil.

29 His mouth is full of cursing, bitterness, and deceit; under his tongue are toil and pain.

C His wickedness is described by a twofold perversity. In his mouth he will have blasphemous cursing when he falsely claims to be the Son of God. “Bitterness” will be present when he announces the punishment of death to those who oppose him and orders them to undergo torments. “Toil” is present when he afflicts the innocent with various disasters. “Pain” is present when he makes martyrs. These things he has in his mouth, which he will speak publicly; but these things he has under his tongue, which he thinks. He thinks of toil and pain, because without these the crown of martyrdom cannot be completed.

30 He sits in ambush with the rich in secret places, to kill the innocent.

C When he says, “He sits in ambush,” he compares the Antichrist’s actions with the custom of robbers, who hide themselves in order to kill the innocent. Here “rich” is understood in an evil sense, just as “poor” is understood in a good sense. A By “rich” he means the people of the world, whom he will enrich so that their glory may deceive others. C To kill the innocent is to turn a religious person into a sacrilegious one and condemn his soul to everlasting death.

31 His eyes look upon the poor; he lies in ambush in secret like a lion in his den.

C When it says “his eyes are upon the poor,” that is, that he looks upon them in spirit, [Col. 0074B] it must be understood that he does not look upon the poor man in order to benefit him, but directs his attention to him in order to kill him. H He calls the Antichrist a lion; the devil, too, is called both lion and dragon: a lion when he persecutes openly, a dragon when he does harm secretly. C What he says, “like a lion,” pertains to force; but what he adds, “in his den,” pertains to the deceit by which he will tear Christians to pieces.

32 He lies in wait to seize the poor: to seize the poor while he draws him away.

C The repetition of the ambushes shows the enemy’s excessive cunning. “To seize the poor” signifies the soul’s sudden danger. “While he draws him away,” that is, while he attempts to turn him back from the truth and endeavors to lead him to the worship of his own name.

33 In his snare he will humble him: [Col. 0074C] he will bow down and fall when he has gained dominion over the poor.

C The snare signifies the deceit by which the hearts of the simple are captured. He will humble them when, through the devil’s persuasion, they fall from the true religion and are led into unsound doctrine. The tyrant will bow down when, ceasing from such great persecution and having been sated by the excessive acquisition of the lost, he relaxes his mind into some period of inactivity. After the punishments and afflictions of the righteous, the utterly wicked one will fall, together with his followers, from his presumption when sudden destruction overtakes him; for the wretched man does not know the end of the age, since the Lord has placed it in his own power. H Therefore, when he expects that he will still live for a long time, sudden destruction will overtake him.

34 [Col. 0074D] For he said in his heart: God has forgotten; he has turned his face away, so as not to see to the end.

C This is an exceedingly foolish thought: to suppose that the Lord does not wish to regard his faithful, for whom he endured suffering, since for his sake they are taught to endure every punishment and adversity.

35 Rise up [÷ marks the Latin prefix *ex-*], O Lord God. Let your hand be exalted: do not forget the poor.

C “Rise up, God,” that is, come quickly; “let your hand be exalted” signifies the exercise of judgment. For the Prophet desired the coming of that by which the Antichrist could perish. “Do not forget” is now a plea that, contrary to the tyrant’s expectation, he not forget the poor [Col. 0075A] at the end of the age, when the recompense of merits is to come.

36 Why did the wicked provoke God? For he said in his heart: He will not seek an account.

C It must be stated in the form of a question: Why did the wicked provoke God? The answer is: because the wicked supposed that God could not call him to account for his deeds and for the wrongs done to the poor, as though God, walking around the hinges of heaven, did not consider our affairs. But in the future he will find him mindful whom he had expected to have forgotten.

37 You see that you consider labor and sorrow, in order to deliver them into your hands.

C The Prophet speaks to God: “You see that no one mocks you”; for you consider the labor and sorrow that the treacherous man held under his tongue, that is, revolved in his thoughts. “In order to deliver him,” that is, once delivered over to judgment he will not escape, but will receive what his deeds deserve, when he is tormented by eternal damnation.

38 The poor man is left to you: you will be the helper of the orphan.

C When he says, “the poor man is left to you,” he shows that the one who is left to the Lord is deprived of no benefit. For to be entrusted to a merciful ruler means to be handed over to every good thing. The poor man is so called from *paulum lare* [“a little dwelling”]. By “orphan” he means not one whose natural father has died, but one whose father has been buried, that is, the world, which he did not love. “You will be the helper” means that, when you see them afflicted bodily, you should not doubt that they will be delivered.

39 Crush the arm of the sinner and the wicked man: his sin will be sought, and it will not be found.

C The Prophet’s eyes return to the wickedness of the Antichrist, and he asks: “Crush his arm,” that is, reduce to nothing the power that sinners were using wickedly, since they were committing conspicuously impious deeds. He is called “wicked” because he will be an unjust persuader, so that those whom he cannot pervert by terror he may at least try to turn aside by harmful rewards. H “His sin is sought, and it will not be found”: that is, he is not worthy to come to correction. C He added “and it will not be found,” because there is no doubt that the criminal power, whose author is to be condemned, will perish. A Thus sin and the sinner are found for condemnation, though they are not found for correction.

40 [Col. 0075D] The Lord will reign forever and unto the age of the ÷ age .. You will destroy the nations from his land.

C Once the Antichrist has been killed, the Prophet returns to the order of future events, where the security of the saints and the eternal kingdom belong to Christ God. By “nations” he means sinners and impious people who live like beasts. “From his land” signifies the Savior’s kingdom, which the blessed alone enjoy.

41 The Lord has heard the desire of the poor: your ear has heard the preparation of their heart.

H By “the desire of the poor” he means the Church’s wish that he grant it the kingdoms of heaven. C And “the preparation of the heart,” that is, the longing that reveals the strength of the spirit through the ardor of the mind. H He calls the ear of God divine mercy.

42 To judge the orphan and the humble, so that a man may no longer presume to magnify himself upon the earth.

C Behold, by prophetic authority we are warned that the humble orphan is especially pleasing to God. When the orphan is called humble, the most righteous person is approved, so that he may no longer presume—that is, H so that the Antichrist may no longer exalt himself over God’s elect, because C then all evils must come to an end, when the author of death is condemned together with his people. These are the hidden things of the Son, which the title of this psalm proclaims.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM IX

Merciful God, open a gracious ear to our confession—you who have never been accustomed to abandon those who hope in you—so that, raised up from the gates of everlasting death, we may be able to escape unharmed the hidden ambushes of the tempter. Through our Lord.

# PSALM X

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM X

C The Prophet speaks concerning heretics who strive to convert Catholics to their own depravity, threatening them with the Lord’s judgment and declaring what they must endure in that recompense.

**TT. To the end ÷ A psalm .. of David.**

C It must be understood that this psalm has been approved for the destruction of heretics.

### 1 I trust in the Lord: how can you say to my soul, “Migrate to the mountain like a sparrow”?

H “I trust in the Lord”: the voice of the Church against heretics. C It is as though he had said: “While I am established upon the fixed summit of religion, how can you advise me, ‘Migrate to the mountain,’ that is, to heretical depravity, pretending that Christ is there, where no truth is found?” The mountain signifies the exalted pride of the mind, by which heresy alone is incurred, since heretics, unwilling to agree with the humble, attempt to raise themselves above the Church. The sparrow signifies the heretic, who is carried toward the most wicked preaching by the fickleness of an unstable mind. For the sparrow is an unsettled bird: some dwell in holes in walls, others in dewy valleys, and some in barren mountains.

### 2 [Col. 0076D] For behold, sinners have bent the bow; they have prepared their arrows in the quiver, to shoot in darkness at those who are upright in heart.

H “For behold, sinners,” that is, heretics, “have bent the bow,” that is, their mouths against the Church. “They have bent the bow,” that is, the power of their verbosity. C “They have prepared arrows,” that is, poisonous words. “In the quiver,” that is, in the heart. H “To shoot,” and so forth, means that when they see people in the Church darkened by ignorance or simplicity, they ensnare them by deceitful or hidden traps. C Those who are upright in heart are so called because they cannot be deceived by any wicked persuasion; or “in darkness” means in their dark and ambiguous assertions, or when the Church is disturbed by dreadful persecutions. When people are thought more easily to be changed by fear of bodily danger.

### 3 For they have destroyed what you have perfected: the just one ÷ but .. what did he do?

C The same Prophet says that heretics destroyed the law of God through false interpretations, turning into death what had been prophesied by the Lord for salvation. The defense of the Lord Christ follows: “What did the just one do?” H That is, Christ redeemed the world. C Or, if they wish to subvert the Scriptures, what did the just one do to them, that they should even persecute him?

### 4 The Lord is in his holy temple: the Lord’s throne is in heaven.

C For God’s holy temple is what you are (1 Cor. III), so that the heretic may know that he can be scattered by God, by whom the hearts of those who believe rightly are known to be possessed. Heaven signifies holy men, in whom the divine nature deigns to dwell. Thus the Prophet seeks to terrify heretics from the seduction of the good by the Lord’s judgment, so that, if they do not fear to seduce the righteous, they may at least fear him who is in and dwells among the righteous.

### 5 His eyes look ÷ upon the poor ..; his eyelids question the children of men.

H The Lord’s eyes, that is, the aspect and mercy of the Godhead, look upon the poor Christian people in order to help them. C The eyelids, so called from *palpitare* (“to flutter”), signify the subtlety of divine judgment and God’s hidden judgments, in which he questions us—that is, knows what each person possesses.

### 6 The Lord questions the just and the wicked: but whoever loves iniquity hates his own soul.

H “The Lord questions,” that is, knows and tests, the just and the wicked. C This is said so that each person may examine his conscience, concerning which he knows that God alone can pass judgment. For the just person is not the one whom human beings call just, but the one whom God proves to be just. What is it to love iniquity except to follow the devil? Whoever follows the devil persecutes himself, since he wishes to walk along those paths that lead to the places where punishments are to be escaped.

### 7 He will rain snares upon sinners: fire + and .. brimstone + and .. the spirit of storms, the portion of their cup.

C He will rain down, namely, words of preaching, which are showers for the devout but fiery snares for the faithless. It is also fire when the burning care of desire consumes them. H Brimstone is the corruption of sins. C The spirit of storms is present when they are thrown into confusion by a tumultuous mind; “the portion of their cup” means the measure by which they become drunk with polluted acts. H Or: fire is desire, brimstone the corruption of sins, the spirit of storms eternal punishment; and those whom fire burns up, the tempest deprives of life.

### 8 For the Lord is just and has loved justice: his face has seen equity.

C He says that the just Lord loves justice because he knows how to regard no others except those who know how to preserve justice—that equity, namely, which he himself graciously grants. The face of God signifies his favor.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM X

Direct the eyes of your mercy upon the humble person of our poverty, almighty Lord, and surround us with the arms of faith, so that, rescued from the arrows of iniquity, we may be able to preserve equity and justice. Through our Lord.

# PSALM XI

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM XI

C The Prophet asks to be saved from the perversity of this world, since the deceitful and proud denied God’s power with criminal insults; and, declaring that the Father’s promise was to be fulfilled through the Son, he praises the Lord’s utterances in concise form.

**To the end, for the eighth day. A psalm of David.**

C “To the end, for the eighth day,” as has already been said in the sixth psalm, pertains to eternal rest. The Prophet therefore asks that the iniquity of the world be destroyed, so that he may reach the truth of the future promise.

### 1 Save ÷ me .., O Lord, for the holy one has failed: for truths have been diminished among the children of men.

C “Save me,” the Prophet cries out to the Lord; he asks to be saved by the one from whom he knew that true medicine could be obtained, saying that the holy one was lacking. For the holy one could not otherwise fail unless truth had been diminished among human beings. Yet when he says “diminished,” he clearly shows that God’s gifts were corrupted by human faults and that the benefits bestowed were stained by their own perversity. He says “truths,” speaking of human truths; there is one truth of God, by which holy souls are enlightened.

### 2 Each one spoke vain things to his neighbor: with deceitful lips and a heart and a heart ÷ they spoke ..

C “Vain things” signifies falsehoods: when they sought false testimonies against the Lord, then truths were diminished. He calls them neighbors not so much because they were related by birth as because they were joined in participation in crime. “With a heart and a heart”: whenever we wish to show people to be deceitful, we disclose that their hearts are double; but when they are simple, we testify that there is one heart in them. “They spoke,” with evil things understood.

### 3 May the Lord destroy all deceitful lips: the boastful tongue.

C “May he destroy” is spoken against the Jews, so that they may perish everywhere, since they had gathered themselves together in one perversity. The boastful tongue is one that assumes some great power for itself. And lest you understand “boastful tongue” here in a good sense, he first mentioned deceitful lips. Consider, however, the piety of the speaker: he curses not human beings—for some were to be converted—but the vices themselves.

### 4 They said: “We will magnify our tongue; our lips are our own. Who is our lord?”

C He explains that these are people who, boasting in prosperous circumstances, presume to exalt their own glory and attribute to themselves what they received not from God. “Who is our lord?” is the language of sacrilegious people who contradict God, and of the proud. A It is also the language of hypocrites and philosophers who think that the sciences and eloquence acquired through talent and study are possessed by themselves, despising those who do not possess them. Therefore he adds:

### 5 Because of the misery of the needy and the groaning of the poor, now I will arise, says the Lord.

C “I will arise,” the Prophet says in the person of the Father concerning the Son; “I will arise,” that is, “I will appear and be manifested in the Son,” H so that he may redeem those who are in misery in the world.

### 6 I will place him in salvation: I will ÷ act .. confidently in him.

H “I will place him in salvation” is the Father’s voice: that is, he will place the salvation and consolation of the poor, perhaps of the nations, in the Son; [Col. 0079B] he is joy in place of groaning. “I will act confidently in him,” C that is, in the Son, because he is the Father’s power; confidence belongs to the Son, whose will no one can resist, because “the utterances,” and so forth.

### 7 The utterances of the Lord are pure utterances: silver tested by fire, proved upon the earth, purified sevenfold.

Here the utterances of the Lord are praised—utterances darkened by no lie and no adulterous falsehood—when he says, “pure utterances.” Earlier, human speech is condemned when he says, “they spoke vain things.” Silver of the earth tested by fire is customarily most pure when it has been cleansed by repeated smelting; so the utterances of the Lord are pure, beautiful, and rare. “Purified,” or “tested,” is set in opposition to what he says about sinners: “deceitful lips in the heart,” and so forth. “Sevenfold” signifies the sevenfold Spirit, that is, fear of the Lord, piety, knowledge, fortitude, counsel, understanding, and wisdom. A Through these the divine utterance shines forth, when the preachers of God’s word and those who live according to his utterances gleam with these gifts.

### 8 You, O Lord, will preserve us, and you will guard us from this generation forever.

H “You, O Lord, will preserve us forever”—the Church asks this—“that is, you will preserve us in faith. And you will guard us from heretics or Jews, whether from sinners or from the dialecticians and philosophers of this world forever.” C Here he preserves us so that we may not perish; there he makes us rejoice forever and crowns us.

### 9 The wicked walk about on every side: according to your exaltedness you have multiplied the children of men.

C For the wicked to walk about on every side is to live by crooked ways, since they never walk along the straight path, having abandoned Christ, who is the true way. “According to your exaltedness,” not according to human merit but according to the power of the divine will, the Church is multiplied; that is, it receives what Christ has promised in recompense through his piety and mercy.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM XI

Have mercy on our frailty, most holy Father, and grant us to retain your utterances with a chaste heart, so that we may be able to avoid the deceitful loquacity of the deranged. Through our Lord.

# PSALM XII

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM XII

C The Prophet, seeing the world enslaved to idolatry, asks that his faith be fulfilled through the coming of the holy Incarnation, so that, at least in this way, the Gentiles, confounded, might recognize their Creator.

**TT. To the end, a psalm of David.**

C “To the end”: here it signifies the time of Christ’s incarnation. C This entire psalm speaks of Christ’s love. Filled with love for the Lord, the Prophet confidently says that he is being delayed longer than he should be from his expectation and from the coming of the one whom, although he firmly believed would come, he nevertheless complains was slow to arrive. He was not yet worthy to see that long-awaited coming sooner, since delay is exceedingly burdensome to anyone who longs.

### 1 How long, O Lord, will you forget me to the end? How long will you turn your face away from me?

C When he says “how long,” he asks for Christ’s manifestation, which he saw in the spirit; “how long,” that is, “until when, for how long, will you not set me free?” H Any penitent person groaning under sins may also say with the Prophet: “How long,” and so forth. For demons and wicked people persecute most harshly those who truly repent and desire to keep Christ’s commandments. C “To the end,” that is, until Christ’s coming.

### 2 How long shall I set counsels in my soul, sorrow in my heart by day?

C When he says “how long,” the greatest ardor of one awaiting God’s coming is expressed. H It is as though he said: “I suffer this distress until I see you, as you promised that you would come.” A By “counsels” he means thoughts and deliberations about how and when he might be freed from the slavery of sin and the devil through the coming of the Savior; and because the hope of salvation is prolonged, desire increases into sorrow. C “By day,” that is, each day the love of your coming has been turned into mental sorrow by your delay.

### 3 How long will my enemy be exalted over me? Look upon me and hear me, O Lord my God.

C He calls the enemy the devil, who is said to have been exalted before the Lord’s coming, when he rejoiced over human captivity. “Over me,” that is, over my faith. “Hear me”: he asks for help not only for himself but for all the faithful. “Look upon me” is to be referred to the words, “How long will you turn your face away from me?” [Col. 0080D] “Hear me” is to be referred to what he says at the beginning of the psalm: “How long will you forget me to the end?”

### 4 Enlighten my eyes, lest I ever sleep in death, lest my enemy say: “I have prevailed against him.”

C When he asks that his eyes be enlightened, he means the eyes of the heart. They sleep in death when, once the light of faith has been buried, they are closed by carnal pleasure; for this is the sleep in which the enemy rejoices. By “the enemy” he means the devil and his angels, whose custom is to mock when they capture people and to rejoice when they discover that those deceived by them are in their possession.

### 5 Those who trouble me will rejoice if I am moved; but I have hoped in your mercy.

C “They will rejoice if I am moved,” that is, if I am separated from you through unbelief or sin; then the enemies become glad. He says “in your mercy” because whoever places his hope anywhere other than in God has an empty faith. O the power of faith and the great firmness of one who believes in him from whom he knows with certainty that he can be saved!

### 6 My heart will rejoice in your salvation; I will sing to the Lord who has granted me ÷ good things ..; ÷ and I will sing psalms to the name of the Most High ...

C The inner person had seen God’s salvation, which he desired to behold with bodily eyes. “I will sing,” namely, in the heart, where immense joy was being fulfilled. “I will sing psalms through good works,” which the Godhead seeks above all.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM XII

Do not turn your face away from us, almighty God, lest our enemies be exalted against us; but so pour the joy of your salvation into our heart that you may make us escape the sleep of the second death. Through our Lord.

# PSALM XIII

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM XIII

C The Church rebukes the Jews who, although they saw the Lord, did not believe in him at all. It says that those who refused to know the fruitful fear of the Lord are confounded by empty terror, and it foretells their conversion at the end of the age.

**TT. To the end ÷ a psalm .. of David.**

C “The end” signifies Christ; therefore it is frequently repeated, [Col. 0081C] so that the mind of the listener may always be lifted up toward the Almighty. C This psalm chastises the Jews’ madness with vehement rebuke: harsh in its attacks, terrifying to the profane, bitter to the unbelieving, so that this rebuke may rightly be given to the Church.

### 1 The fool said in his heart: “There is no God.”

C Seeing that Christ had come humbly among the Jewish people, he said, “There is no God,” and did not understand that he was the one foretold by the prophets. For this reason it is even more serious: they said this not with their lips but in their heart, so that unbelief might be joined to an evil intention and made worse. A Or the Gentile also is called a fool, thinking that there is no God; corrupted in mind, he makes a piece of wood his god.

### 2 They are corrupt and have become abominable in ÷ their .. pursuits. There is no one who does good; ÷ there is not even one ...

H For if they had possessed knowledge of God, they would not have been corrupted by unbelief and become abominable, that is, hateful. “There is not even one.” C Truly, there is only Christ, without whom no one is able either to begin or to complete any good. Another text has: “They are corrupt in their wills.” The will is so called from *volatus* (“flight”), because the mind is carried with great speed toward whatever it wills. The Jews, therefore, are corrupt: abandoning the soundness of the Scriptures, they fell into vicious interpretations, and, thus stained by the most wicked unbelief, they became abominable even to God as punishment for their sin.

### 3 The Lord looked down from heaven upon the children of men, to see whether there was anyone who understood or sought God.

C “The Lord looked down,” namely, so that he might send us his only-begotten Son. “Upon the children,” that is, upon the human race. H So that he might make his saints visible, through whom he looks and in whom he dwells, to see whether there is anyone wise. C The wise person understands in his mind that God is truly God and man, and seeks God through action, following his commandments so as not to depart from his will. But what the saints of God saw, through whom God is said to see, he states next: “They have all turned aside,” and so forth.

### 4 They have all turned aside; together they have become useless. There is no one who does good; there is not even one.

[Col. 0082B] C Here he says “all,” that is, the whole, while signifying a part. They have turned aside, namely, from God’s grace, and have become useless to themselves and to others. So many and so numerous were the impious among the Jews that almost all seemed to be faithless and lost. A The same may be said of the Gentiles: therefore none understand or seek, but both Jews and Gentiles have turned aside.

### 5 ÷ Their throat is an open tomb ...; ÷ they acted deceitfully with their tongues ...; ÷ the poison of asps is under their lips.

C Their throat is rightly called a tomb, since they brought forth poisonous speeches, just as a tomb exhales foul odors. They acted deceitfully with their tongues, with which they spoke deadly words. The asp is a monstrous kind of serpent, which, by natural obstinacy, is said not to admit the words of enchanters and cannot be turned from its purpose; nor can it be soothed by any incantation, as other kinds of serpents can. This signifies the deadly deafness of the Jews. It is called poison because it runs through the veins; so the designs of the wicked creep forth through hidden thought.

### 6 ÷ Their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness ..: ÷ their feet are swift to shed blood ...

C “Their mouth,” that is, the mouth of the Jews, when they blasphemed Christ in response to good admonitions. “Bitterness,” when they plotted his death. He calls the advances of their counsel “feet,” by which we move from an undertaking toward the outcomes of events. When he says “swift,” he shows that they lacked counsels of moderation. “To shed blood,” that is, the blood of the Lord the Savior and of his people, so that the enormity of their criminal deed might increase as they also lay their wicked hands upon the Lord the Savior.

### 7 ÷ Destruction and misery are in their ways ..; ÷ and they have not known the way of peace ..; ÷ there is no fear of God before their eyes ...

H “Destruction,” namely of the Jews’ bodies; “misery,” of their souls. “In their ways,” that is, in their deeds. Why? Because they did not know the way of peace, that is, Christ, either through faith or through works. Why? Because there is no fear of God in their understanding; for they do not fear the coming judgment. C The way of the impious is destruction, because it wears down and is itself worn down; and misery is in it, because through it one never reaches anything except disastrous punishments.

### 8 Will not all those who work iniquity understand, who devour my people like a morsel of bread?

H “Will they not understand?” It is as though he said: “If they do not now understand the vengeance that is to come, they will understand it in judgment, those who now do evil.” “They devour my people”: that is, heretics seduce the Christian people, or the wicked kill the good, or idolaters devour believers. Just as no hungry person can be properly filled without bread, so heretics are never satisfied with their iniquities unless they persecute Christians. A Or they are satisfied by the persecution of Christians, just as the hungry are satisfied by food.

### 9 They did not call upon the Lord; there they trembled with fear ÷ where there was no fear.

H They did not call upon the Lord; for if they had called upon him, they would have been saved. There they trembled amid idols and the empty rites of images, though they ought to have feared God. C And when they said concerning Christ, “If we release him in this way,” and so forth.

### 10 For God is in the just generation; you have confounded the counsel of the poor, because the Lord is his hope.

H “For God is in the just generation,” that is, in the Christian people. C “You have confounded Christ’s counsel,” that is, you refused to accept the counsel of him who said, “Repent.” H Christ is called poor because he became poor for us. “The Lord is his hope”: the Father is the hope of the Son, since his humanity was strengthened by the Godhead. A Or it may refer to any member existing in Christ, for the Lord is his hope; he is therefore despised precisely where he ought to be more greatly revered.
