### 11 Who will give salvation to Israel from Zion? When the Lord turns away the captivity of his people, Jacob will rejoice and Israel will be glad.

C When he says, “Who will give,” he wishes the Lord Father to be understood, who deigned to send the Lord Christ to Zion, that is, to Jerusalem. He is the eternal salvation of Israel, that is, of believers. “When he turns away,” that is, when he condemns the devil, who hastens to persecute and take captive God’s people. “Jacob will rejoice,” that is, the people of Jews and Gentiles gathered together by God’s grace. “Israel will be glad,” [Col. 0083D] that is, the universal Church.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM XIII

Deign, O Lord, to look down from your holy heaven upon the children of men, and grant us to recognize the way of peace, so that, once the captivity of vices has been turned away, we may enjoy the dwelling place of the heavenly Jerusalem. Through our Lord.

# PSALM XIV

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM XIV

C The Lord responds to the Prophet’s question: following the example of the Decalogue, one reaches the courts of his blessedness through ten virtues.

**TT. A psalm of David.**

C This psalm is not veiled by obscurity, but the Lord responds to the Prophet’s question: following the example of the Decalogue, one reaches the courts of his blessedness through ten virtues.

### 1 O Lord, who will dwell in your tabernacle, or who will rest upon your holy mountain?

C “Tabernacle” is formed from two nouns, namely *taberna*—which is the dwelling of the poor, because it was not yet covered with tiles but only with beams—and *coenaculum*, because they dined there, as was the ancient custom of taking food once a day. It signifies the Catholic faith, in which the holy Church of God dwells. The mountain signifies the future Jerusalem. A He does not ask who dwells absolutely in the Church, in which both good and evil people are found, but leaves “worthily” to be understood: who dwells in it worthily? This is proved by what follows: “or who,” and so forth.

### 2 He who enters without blemish and practices justice.

C To enter the tabernacle without any blemish belonged only to the Lord. He practiced justice when he drove the sellers and buyers from the temple. H But for his members, it means to walk without mortal sin and to enter through baptism without any blemish, since we cannot be without the smallest faults.

### 3 He who speaks truth in his heart, who has not acted deceitfully with his tongue.

H Many speak truth with their lips but not in their heart; they appear to speak truth, but their heart does not agree with their lips. Christ did not do this. Christ did not choose deceit, because what he spoke with his mouth he fulfilled in action. He acts deceitfully who does one thing and says another.

### 4 He has done no evil to his neighbor and has not accepted reproach against his neighbors.

H All human beings are our neighbors, and we must do evil to none. He does not accept reproach, that is, slander, against his brother who does not first believe evil about him before proving it. Whoever completes the things summarized above dwells in eternal life.

### 5 The wicked man is brought to nothing in his sight, but he glorifies those who fear the Lord.

H The wicked man is brought to nothing—that is, the devil—because among the saints he is regarded as nothing. The Lord magnifies those who fear him with holy fear. C Or he was brought to nothing when he said to him, “Get behind me, Satan; you shall not tempt the Lord your God.”

### 6 He who swears to ÷ his neighbor .. and does not deceive; who has not lent his money at interest; and has not accepted gifts against the innocent.

C To swear is so called as if from *juste orare* (“to speak justly”), that is, to speak rightly. A He does not deceive his neighbor who swears to give and assist his neighbor and fulfills his promise. H Or the soul does not deceive its neighbor, that is, the body, if it observes the commandments of God that it promises to observe. Just as visible money is forbidden to be lent at interest, lest the one who receives it be stripped rather than helped, so the word of God must be freely conveyed not only to the rich who nourish others but also to the poor. He does not accept gifts against, that is, contrary to, the innocent, who does not overturn a just judgment for the sake of some gift.

### 7 Whoever does these things will not be moved forever.

C He did not say, “Whoever sings,” but “whoever does these things.” That person will dwell in the Lord’s tabernacle and rest in his holy kingdom. Thus, by inserting this rule, he binds us to active virtue, lest, intent only on songs, we sing psalms vainly while neglecting the secret demands of so great a ministry.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM XIV

Grant us, most merciful God, to enter your church without blemish, and turn us away from the deceits of our neighbor and from usury, so that, while we observe these things according to your commandment, we may never be moved into hostile punishments. Through our Lord.

# PSALM XV

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM XV

C Christ, in the humanity he assumed, asks the Father to preserve him and gives thanks to him who by his power overcame the iniquity of this age; and, after the glory of the resurrection, placed him in the delights of his right hand.

**Inscription of the title ÷ to him .., David.**

C “Inscription of the title: to him, David.” Since this inscription of the title ought to be referred not to any other person [Col. 0085C] but to Christ, “to him, David” has been added, and this can appropriately be referred to the Lord the Savior. Here the nature of the assumed humanity prays to be preserved for our protection from the Jews.

### 1 Preserve me, O Lord, for I have hoped in you. I said to the Lord, “You are my God,” for you have no need of my goods.

C He says that he has always hoped in the Lord. “I said to the Lord”: the Son speaks from the form of a servant to the Father, with whom he is equal in divinity. H According to his majesty, the Father did not need the incarnation, passion, or resurrection, which pertain to the Son according to his humanity, in order to redeem us. But he adds for whom these things are beneficial: “to the saints,” and so forth; these things are necessary for them.

### 2 To the saints who are in his land; he has made + all .. my desires wonderful in them.

C He signifies the saints who are in the land of the living: the innocent and the just. H In the Church, which is called his land. C Through them the Savior’s desires were wonderfully accomplished, when, because they obeyed and did what Christ commanded, he made them eternal instead of mortal. A Or “he made wonderful,” when he magnified them through miracles, by which miracles it was shown that their preaching, faith, and works were the will of God.

### 3 Their infirmities have been multiplied; afterward they hastened.

H “Their infirmities have been multiplied among the nations,” that is, their idols, which, when the Lord came in the flesh, they abandoned and turned back to him most swiftly. For the Hebrew text has: “Their idols have been multiplied.”

### 4 I will not gather their assemblies from blood; nor will I remember their names with my lips.

C He says that these nations are not to be gathered by the blood of animals or by the customary offering of victims, but by the sacrifice of Christ’s body and blood. Christ therefore did not remember the names by which they had previously been called—sons of wrath, sons of the devil—but he remembers the new names by which they are now called Christians and sons of God. Christ’s lips signify the two Testaments, since both proclaim the kingdom of God and, in concordance of one sound, are joined like lips.

### 5 The Lord is the portion of my inheritance and my cup; [Col. 0086B] you are the one who will restore my inheritance to me.

C The Lord is the portion of the inheritance and of the cup. The Son says to the Father—not inferior in divinity, but subject in humanity—that the Father is the portion of his inheritance, namely, in the faith of the nations believing in the Father and the Son. The cup signifies the Lord’s will and distribution. “You will restore” is said because, through the devil’s action, the human race had perished. A The inheritance itself was restored when he drew his elect to immortality. C It is called an inheritance from *herus*, that is, “lord.”

### 6 The measuring lines have fallen for me in pleasant places; for my inheritance is pleasant to me.

H “Ropes” signifies the patriarchs, prophets, and apostles, or whomever Christ has called; he receives them “in splendid places,” that is, among the best. C The inheritance [Col. 0086C] of Christ is the multitude of the saints, which is called splendid for Christ, although it is despised by worldly people, because it has been chosen by him. He said “fell” instead of “came.”

7 I will bless the Lord, who has granted me understanding; Moreover, even until night my kidneys have reproached me.

C The Son blesses the Father, who according to his humanity granted him understanding, by which he discerned everything true and holy, so that human weakness might not attribute anything to itself without the Father’s grace. H “Night” signifies the time of the Passion. C “Kidneys” signify the kindred of the Jews, from whom Christ was born according to the flesh, and by whom he was frequently reproached even unto death. H Or, “kidneys,” that is, the pleasures of the flesh, reproach at the time when they urge one to sin. And thus [Col. 0086D] this is the voice not of the head but of Christ’s members, or of the head speaking on behalf of the members.

8 I kept the Lord always before me; For he is at my right hand, so that I may not be shaken.

H For whoever always gazes upon the Lord with the eyes of the mind is in no way turned toward sins. He gives the reason why he is not shaken: because the Lord is at his right hand. Indeed, when the Lord assists at the right hand, the left cannot prevail to do harm; but if the Lord does not hold the right-hand side, the devil will immediately occupy it.

9 Therefore my heart rejoiced, and my tongue exulted: ÷ moreover .. my flesh will rest in hope.

C Because he stood at the right hand, he testifies that he possesses gladness in his heart and exultation of tongue. II “Flesh” signifies the Church, which rests for a time in hope of the future resurrection. For the Church is the flesh of Christ; therefore Christ speaks: “The Church, which is my flesh, now rests in hope of the resurrection, so that where the head has gone before, the members may follow,” and so forth. C Or it is understood of the flesh of Christ as man, which he assumed for our salvation and which rested in the tomb in hope of the resurrection accomplished on the third day.

10 For you will not abandon my soul in the underworld; Nor will you allow your Holy One to see corruption.

C Behold, the Son gives thanks to the Father because his soul was not abandoned in the underworld according to the common manner, but was glorified by a swift resurrection. Here he rightly denies that corruption, that is, decay—which consumes human flesh—could occur. For Christ’s flesh could not decay in the tomb.

11 You have made known to me the paths of life; You will fill me with joy in your presence; Pleasures are at your right hand ÷ unto .. the end.

II The voice of the righteous: “You have made known to me,” that is, “You have caused me to know the commandments of Christ.” Then joy will be complete, when the body, that is, the Church, has been joined together in the kingdom of God, where it beholds the face of God. C He says “at his right hand,” because he never departed from contemplation of the Father. “The end” signifies perfection and eternity, so that “unto the end” means perfectly and eternally.

ORATION FROM PSALM XV

[Col. 0087C]

Preserve, O Lord, those who hope in you, and accomplish your will with us, so that, glorified by the joy of your resurrection, we may deserve to delight with all the saints at your right hand. Through our Lord, etc.

PSALM XVI

ARGUMENT OF PSALM XVI

C In this psalm a threefold prayer is drawn from Christ’s humanity. First, he asks that what is owed to him according to justice be restored. Second, he asks that his purity be delivered from the plots of the Jews. Third, he prays for a very swift resurrection, lest his enemies be permitted to insult him any longer.

TT. A prayer of David.

H “A prayer of David.” This psalm is sung against the Jews [Col. 0087D] in the person of Christ, or against heretics in the person of the Church.

1 Hear, O Lord, my justice; attend to my supplication.

C The voice of Christ in the Passion, and the voice of the Church in tribulation. Christ asks that his justice be heard because he was obedient to the Father unto death. There is a difference between supplication and prayer: prayer is holier, being made on behalf of the devout so that they may persevere; supplication, however, is made for one’s own or another’s sins. Or, supplication is something stronger than prayer.

2 Give ear to my prayer; not with deceitful lips.

H The Son prays—from the weakness of the flesh, not from any diminution of divinity—that what he asks may be heard. “Not with deceitful lips,” as is the prayer of those who unjustly condemn me and mine, such as the Jews. A For from the Jews came the false sentence, among whom the innocent man was condemned and the robber was known to have been released.

3 Let my judgment come forth from your face; let your eyes see equities.

C “Let judgment come forth from your face.” This is an unusual expression, since a sentence normally comes from the mind, not from the face. But it is fittingly applied to Christ, because the one who judges sees what he judges, and he alone knows all hidden things. “Let my eyes see equity”: here “equity” signifies divinity itself, which the Son always beholds, since he is equal to the Father. Another text reads this way. Ours has: “Let your eyes see”; and then equity signifies not [Col. 0088B] divinity but the merits of Christ and the Jews.

4 You have tested my heart ÷ and .. visited me at night; you have examined me by fire, and in me no iniquity has been found.

5 So that my mouth may not speak of human works; because of the words of your lips I have kept difficult ways.

C Here “testing” signifies the Passion, when amid dangers of death he displayed the finest proofs of endurance; “visitation” signifies the resurrection. He was visited at night, when his soul was not abandoned in the underworld. “Examined by fire,” that is, by the tribulation of the Passion. No iniquity was found in him that any burning could consume.

[Col. 0088C] C “Difficult ways” are those which human beings ought to imitate, although the path of vices is easy for them. For when sins are avoided, the ways are difficult for a person; these are the ways along which Christ, unstained by sins, walked. A Or “difficult ways” are called human works, which human works, namely, deserve. For evil works are human works, not God’s; those works, however, deserve the punishment that Christ endured.

6 Perfect my steps in your paths, so that my footprints may not be moved.

C Therefore Christ asks that his steps be guarded, that is, the human actions of his faithful members. “In your paths,” that is, in your commandments. “Perfect,” that is, make them persevere. “Footprints” are the marks of feet; these signify the apostles, for whom Christ asks that, by imitating him, they may not be moved away from the Father. A Or “footprints” are his teaching, left behind by him after the Ascension. He asks that it not be moved, since it has been so firmly established that even heaven and earth will pass away, but Christ’s words will not [Matt. XXIV].

7 I cried out, for you have heard me, O God; incline your ear to me ÷ and .. hear my words.

C “I cried out.” Christ cried out to the Father, that is, he prayed, because he confidently knew that his prayer would be heard by the Father. He asks that the Father incline, because human weakness cannot reach him by itself. He hears when he has graciously shown himself kind.

8 [Col. 0089A] Make your mercies wonderful, you who save those hoping in you.

H He made his Father’s mercies wonderful when through the apostles and the other saints he healed the infirmities of the needy. C “You save,” that is, “You establish in eternal life those who hope in you.”

9 Guard me from those resisting your right hand, as the apple of the eye.

C For the Son is the Father’s right hand, and the Jews dared to resist, that is, oppose, him. The pupil is a part of the eye by which we discern the qualities of things; it is called this because of its smallness, as though “little.” Christ is compared to it, since in his judgment he sees the righteous to be separated from sinners. He most appropriately asks to be guarded as the pupil, since through it we discern visible things, and nothing more excellent is found in our body.

10 Protect me under the shadow of your wings, from the face of the ungodly who have afflicted me.

C The Father’s wings are mercy and charity, by which the holy Church of God begs to be protected. C “From the face of the ungodly” signifies the demons and their followers, who accumulated the heat of their plots against the Lord’s death or against the saints. “Face” signifies the urgency of the ungodly, or their savage presence.

11 My enemies have surrounded my soul; they have shut themselves in with their own fat; their mouth has spoken pride.

C By “enemies” he means the Jews. By “soul,” temporal life, which they wished to seize when they surrounded him with swords [Col. 0089C] and clubs. They “shut themselves in with fat,” for those who grow fat through great greed; so the Jews, made thick by the excess of their crimes, spoke proudly against Christ in their wickedness. H Or against the Church, C defending their evil deeds.

12 Now, casting me out, they have surrounded me; they have set their eyes on turning toward the earth.

C “Casting me out,” namely, Christ outside the city. “They surrounded me,” not in service but in fury, on the cross. The wicked turn their eyes toward the earth when they turn over some evil thought in their minds. H Or they set their eyes to turn toward the earth when they thought about earthly things and did not meditate on heavenly things.

13 They received me like a lion ready for prey, and like a lion’s cub dwelling in hiding places.

[Col. 0089D] C “They received me,” that is, the Jews received Christ from Pilate, when he said: “Take him and crucify him.” The lion is understood as the devil, to whom these Jews are rightly compared, since they even appeared worse than he: he dared to tempt the Lord, whereas the Jews crucified the Lord. The lion’s cub signifies the remaining Jewish people, who made themselves sons of the devil. “Dwelling in hiding places,” that is, in concealed plots; for it is the custom of evil people to conceal evil desires, so that their plans may thereby come to fulfillment.

14 ÷ From .. arise, O Lord; go before him and trip him up. Rescue my soul from the ungodly, your sword from the enemies of your hand.

15 [Col. 0090A] O Lord, divide them from the earth, few as they are, during their life; their belly has been filled from your hidden things.

H The voice of Christ to the Father, asking him to anticipate him, lest his soul be harmed by the devil, the prince. The power of divinity went before him, bound him, and led him to the underworld. C “Sword” sometimes signifies a spear, sometimes a breastplate, sometimes a double-edged sword; all these things, nevertheless, certainly belong to the equipment of arms. H For the Father’s sword is the Savior’s soul, through which he conquered the devil. C For the devil’s enemies are the Lord’s hands, which always tear the human race apart against the Lord’s will by a perverse will.

C The Son also asks the Father that the believers be divided [Col. 0090B] from the few, that is, from the apostles, so that they may be converted to the Lord from the earth, namely, from the vices of this world. “During their life,” that is, in this world, where there is a place for repentance, so that they might believe in Christ. “From your hidden things.” Every sin is abominable to him and, as it were, hidden from his sight, because it is alien to him. Hence he says that their belly, that is, the understanding of the unbelievers, has been filled. A C Or, I divide the Jews from their own land throughout the entire world, and this during that life of theirs which they alone think is theirs, despairing of eternal life. But what will there be in the future then?

16 They are satisfied with children, and they have left their remnants to their little ones.

H “They are satisfied with children,” namely, the Jews, who have multiplied through the begetting of children [Col. 0090C] and through the things of the world. They left the remnants of the curse, that is, the vengeance they deserved when they said: “His blood be upon us and upon our children.” They left them to their children because those children, like their fathers, have been blinded and scattered.

17 But I ÷ shall .. appear in justice in your presence; I shall be satisfied when your glory appears.

C He says that he will appear in the presence of the Father with justice because he had fulfilled his will. “I shall be satisfied” by the belief of the human race, when the number of the saints has to be completed. The Father’s glory is manifested in the judgment of the Lord the Savior, when each person receives according to his deeds.

ORATION FROM PSALM XVI

[Col. 0090D]

Turn, O Lord, the eyes of our hearts toward perceiving the truth of your judgment, so that, while we are tested here by spiritual fire, we may be satisfied forever in your presence with the fruit of justice. Through our Lord, etc.

PSALM XVII

ARGUMENT OF PSALM XVII

C The prophet gives thanks to the Lord because he delivered him from grave dangers, and the Church speaks of the countless calamities it endured before the Lord’s coming. The voice of Christ is also introduced, where his virtue and power are described.

[Col. 0091A] TT. To the end; for David, the servant of the Lord, who spoke to the Lord the words of this song on the day when the Lord rescued him from the hand of all his enemies and from the hand of Saul; and he said.

This entire psalm pertains, under the person of David, to Christ, who is “the end,” who is called “servant,” and who is strong of hand, which is what “David” signifies. The song pertains to contemplation of heavenly things.

1 I will love you, O Lord, my strength; the Lord is my firmament, my refuge, and my deliverer.

C Whoever obeys the Lord’s commandments loves the Lord. “I love” is said as though from “I choose from among all things.” He rightly confesses that the Lord is his strength, by whose gift David was made stronger than his enemies. The prophet beautifully shows who his Lord is, proclaiming him with individual and varied words: he declares what the Lord is, being at one time strength, at another firmament, refuge, helper, protector, deliverer, and horn of salvation—all of which Christ is for the Church.

2 My God is my helper, and I will hope in him.

C For he says specifically that he hopes for the future, since in the past he had experienced him as his helper.

3 My protector and the horn of my salvation, and my supporter.

H “My protector,” because you protect and defend me. “The horn of my salvation,” because you will strengthen weakness, C in order to scatter enemies. Horns are the weapons of beasts, with which they carefully defend their safety in combat. “My supporter,” because Christ was received by the Father.

4 Praising, I will call upon the Lord, and I shall be saved from my enemies.

C He says that he calls upon the Lord while praising him, and attributes his entire victory to him—not to himself—who has deigned to provide everything. Therefore he says that he is to be saved from his enemies, because he did not appear to have attributed his victory to himself but to the Lord. For whoever acts otherwise is made captive to his vices, even if he seems to have overcome his enemies.

5 The pains of death surrounded me, and torrents of iniquity troubled me.

[Col. 0091D] H They surrounded Christ, who were groaning in the underworld. A torrent is called a river swollen by winter rains, and it signifies the swift-moving crowd of the wicked, who rush toward iniquity, trouble the Church, and swell like a torrent in the winter of tribulation; but with the Lord’s help they soon fail and flow away.

6 The pains of the underworld surrounded me; the snares of death came upon me beforehand.

C The order of the words in this verse is as follows: “The pains of the underworld surrounded me.” He speaks of the pagans, who will be the pains of the underworld, that is, those who will be tormented there with the pain they deserve. David says that the snares of death came upon him beforehand, that is, the guilt of original sin, which makes us liable from the very moment of conception, before we are born into the world. A Or Christ speaks these words in the person of his members.

7 In my tribulation I called upon the Lord, and I cried out to my God.

H Humanity called upon divinity in the Passion, and the Church called upon Christ. C To cry out is more than to call upon. The expression grew as desire advanced, and the kindled spirit sprang more eagerly into a cry.

8 ÷ And he heard from his holy temple ÷ .. my voice, and my cry entered into his presence, into his ears.

H The temple is the Lord’s body, where humanity was heard by divinity. C This cry is the justice of the cause, which could enter into God’s presence, because it was pleading for the disasters of the world.

9 The earth was shaken and trembled, and the foundations of the mountains were troubled and shaken, because he was angry ÷ with them ...

C Now the prophet reaches the mysteries of the Incarnation and describes the very sequence in a wondrous narrative. II “The earth was shaken” when earthly people came from unbelief to faith at Christ’s coming and trembled at their sins. C The foundations of the mountains signify the presumptions of the proud, that is, riches, honors, and the other human things upon which they rely. God was angry with them because human vices are shown to be hated by the Lord.

10 Smoke rose up in his anger, and fire blazed from his face; coals were kindled by him.

C Here “smoke” is placed in a good sense: when kindled, it poured forth the tears of repentance. “His anger” signifies the disturbance of fear of the future judgment, by which sinners are so troubled that they are brought to the remedy of repentance. Fire is the charity of God, which proceeds from the Lord’s face, because by his illumination charity is granted to those who cease sinning. He calls sinners “kindled coals,” because, like dead coals, they had previously been dead through sinning, but they live again, kindled by the fire of repentance. How dead coals are kindled he teaches next, namely, by the coming of the Lord the Redeemer, because he inclined, and so forth.

11 He inclined the heavens and descended, and darkness was beneath his feet.

[Col. 0092D] H The heavens, that is, the angels, were inclined when Gabriel came to Mary. “And he descended,” namely Christ, that is, he came in the flesh. Darkness is the depth of the Scriptures, which God gave to the feet, that is, to the apostles, or to the other saints. C Or darkness is the devil, by which he clouds minds.

12 And he mounted upon the cherubim and flew; ÷ he flew .. upon the wings of the winds.

C “Cherubim” is interpreted as “fullness of knowledge.” Christ mounted upon the cherubim when, in the sight of the apostles, he ascended into heaven. “He flew,” that is, his fame ran through the world’s regions more swiftly than the wind, when, while he lay in the cradle, the brightness of the star announced him more widely. For what can be said to be swifter than he, who, as soon as he was born, was seen in another part of the world? Then the speed of the winds was surpassed, although nothing in the world appears to be swifter than they.

13 ÷ And .. he made darkness his hiding place; his tent was around him; dark water was in the clouds of the air.

C By “darkness” he means the mystery of his Incarnation: since he could not be seen in his divinity, our Redeemer appeared veiled in human flesh. “His hiding place” signifies the secret of his majesty, which he reveals to the righteous when they will see him face to face in glory. “Around him” signifies the nearness of the tent, that is, the dignity of the blessed saints, so that those who faithfully persevere in his Church may dwell beside him in heaven. By “water” he means Scripture, which is dark, that is, obscure, in the prophets and in the preachers of the word; for even if someone thinks he understands their words, he can scarcely reach the power of those words in its entirety, as it truly is.

14 Before his presence the clouds passed by with brilliant light; + hail and coals of fire ...

C “Brilliant lights” is a plural nominative agreeing with “clouds.” The clouds are the preachers of the divine Word. The meaning is: Those clouds that contain God’s water, that is, the divine utterances, appear in this air as dark, that is, obscure, but before God they are brilliantly luminous, that is, radiant, because there everything is completely clear that is obscure here. “The clouds passed by,” that is, the preachers went to the Gentiles, leaving the Israelite people. “Hail” is the rebuke of the preachers, by which the hearts of unbelievers are goaded. “Coals of fire” are the fires of charity by which the minds of the faithful revive.

15 And the Lord thundered from heaven; the Most High gave his voice: + hail and coals of fire ...

C “He thundered” is the voice of the almighty Father: “I have glorified, and I will glorify again” [John XII]. Hence many thought it was thunder. The Most High gave his voice when he said: “This is my beloved Son,” and so forth.

A Or, the Lord thundered through the apostles and preachers with threats, which concern eternal punishments; and through those same men he gave a sweet voice, which concerns eternal rewards. For the clouds passed by, threatening eternal punishments to unbelievers and promising eternal rewards to believers.

16 And he sent his arrows and scattered them; he multiplied his lightning and troubled them.

C By “arrows” he means the evangelists, flying along straight paths on the wings of virtues—not their own, but those of the one by whom they were sent. “He scattered them” to whom they were sent, that is, he separated them by receiving the faithful and rejecting the ungodly. “He multiplied his lightning,” that is, he performed many miracles. H “He troubled them,” because through the apostles’ miracles they were pierced and brought to repentance.

17 And the springs of waters appeared, and the foundations of the world ÷ of the earth were revealed ...

H By “springs” he means the apostles. C They poured forth waters, that is, proclamations of eternal life, from their mouths. H He says that the “foundations” are the prophets and apostles, who were revealed. C Upon them the building of the world, that is, of the Church, was constructed. For when Christ came, what the obscurity of the divine utterance had concealed became clear.

18 From your rebuke ÷ .., O Lord, from the breath of the spirit of your anger.

H “From your rebuke,” when he said: “Unless the Son sets you free, you will die in your sins” [John VIII]. C By “the spirit of your anger” he means the preachers, who, inspired by the Holy Spirit, rebuked sinful peoples; or “the rebuke of the prophets” indicates the just reproof of sinful peoples.

19 He sent from on high and took me; and he lifted me up from many waters.

[Col. 0094B] C The voice of the Church: the Father therefore sent from on high, that is, the Son from heaven, and took the Church and joined it to himself. He lifted the Church from the waters when he acquired it through the regeneration of baptism. Or the Church was gathered from many waters, that is, from many peoples.

20 He rescued me from my strongest enemies and from those who hated me, because they had grown strong against me.

C H By “the strongest enemies” he means persecutors and heretics, who continually afflicted the holy Church. C He therefore says that it was rescued all the more because its enemies had grown strong against it in temporal affliction. For it deserved to grow when the enemy afflicted it through the power given from above. O truly divine [Col. 0094C] providence: the enemy is destroyed by his own efforts, and the more he thinks he is harming it, the more necessary it is that, even through his fiercest persecution, he should benefit it.

21 They came upon me beforehand on the day of my affliction, and the Lord became my protector.

C The false apostles came beforehand, attempting to subvert the hearts of the simple, before the preachers of Christ. “On the day of affliction,” when Christians endured martyrdoms. Therefore God was the protector, because a human being had become the attacker; for God protected the Church during the persecutions.

And he led me out into a broad place; he saved me because he desired me.

C The Church was brought into a broad place when it clearly grew in number through the savagery of its persecutors [Col. 0094D]. “Because he desired me,” that is, “He chose me,” who freely calls all people and makes those subject to him safe. No one is unaware that this is the custom of the faithful in the Catholic Church: the more it is constricted by persecutions, the more widely it expands through an increase of faith. For then invincible spirits rise up through God’s grace; then the fire of charity burns brightly; and, forming a battle line, those who desire the rewards of eternal life rush gladly upon the swords.

23 ÷ And .. the Lord will repay me according to my justice, and according to the purity of my hands he will repay me.

C “According to my justice,” that is, according to my will, given to me by you as good through grace. “The innocence of my hands” means works of piety, which the virtue of the saints continually practices by divine gift.

24 For I have kept the ways of the Lord, and I have not acted wickedly against my God.

C The ways of the Lord are love of God and of neighbor; those who do not wish to turn aside from God’s commandment are known to keep them. Whoever presumes to turn aside from the Lord’s commands acts wickedly.

25 For all his judgments are before my eyes, and I have not rejected his justice from me.

C He has God’s judgments before his eyes who continually considers his terrible judgments. He has never rejected God’s justice from himself, for Christ, or justice, always remains in his heart. Those reject God’s justice who, overcome by the weakness of the flesh and failing through long observance of the commandments, abandon the equity they had begun to keep.

26 And I shall be blameless with him, and I shall guard myself from my iniquity.

H “I shall be blameless,” that is, “I shall persevere in that innocence of Christianity in which I was called.” “I shall guard myself,” so that I may not turn back to the unbelief in which I previously was, but may firmly persevere in that Christian faith which I hold.

27 ÷ And .. the Lord will repay me according to my justice, and according to the purity of my hands before his eyes.

[Col. 0095C] C “My justice,” which you, God, have given. H By “eyes,” the sight of divinity is understood. C For just as the righteous always contemplate God in their hearts, so divine power continually regards them and renders to each person according to the purity of good deeds.

28 With the holy man you will be holy, and with the innocent man you will be innocent.

C With the holy man, that is, with the Lord the Savior, through his provision we can be holy. We are also commanded to be innocent with his innocence. For human conduct often becomes similar to that of those whom people have had as teachers and instructors.

29 ÷ And .. with the chosen you will be chosen; [Col. 0095D] and with the perverse you will be perverted.

C We must ask that we may be chosen together with Christ’s election—he is called “chosen” by Isaiah [Isaiah XLII]. This happens to us when we obey his commands. “With the perverse,” that is, “you will be overthrown with the devil,” who is perverse through his own iniquity. For he makes the utterly wicked like himself when he turns them toward obedience to him.

30 For you will save the humble people, and you will humble the eyes of the proud.

C He will save the people when, on the day of judgment, he places the humble at his right hand. By “the eyes of the proud” he means the arrogant, H who disdain to repent; C he will humble them when they descend into the depths of Gehenna.

31 [Col. 0096A] For you illuminate my lamp; O Lord my God, illuminate my darkness.

H The lamp is the understanding of the soul, which is illuminated by Christ. By “darkness” he means ignorance of the heart, which he asks Christ to illuminate.

32 For in you I shall be rescued from temptation, and in my God I shall cross over a wall.

C “In you I shall be rescued,” not by myself. “Temptation” signifies the devil, who tempts at every moment. He rightly said, “I shall cross over a wall,” that is, the obstacle of sins, which is a wall of death, not of salvation, which the wickedness of mortals has built between God and human beings.

33 My God ÷ .. his way is undefiled; the utterances of the Lord are examined by fire; [Col. 0096B] he is the protector of all who hope in him.

C “His way is undefiled,” that is, the Incarnation of the Word, which clearly had no pollution of sin. H The utterances of God are his commandments, tested by the fire of faith or tribulation; therefore they please God like gold tested by fire. Those who believe in Christ are protected. C No one has been abandoned except the one who neglected to hope in him.

34 For who is God besides the Lord? And who is God besides our God?

C This is said against the madness of the pagans, who fashioned gods for themselves with manifold vanity. He says “Lord,” because we are his servants and worship him. For this God is the inseparable Trinity, distinguished only in persons, not in the substance of divinity.

35 [Col. 0096C] God, who girded me with strength and made my way blameless.

H When he says “he girded me,” he means the Holy Spirit, who arms us against the powers of iniquity. C “My blameless way” is the utterly pure way without the stain of sin, along which only the one who committed no sins walked, and he caused others to walk along it.

36 He made my feet like those of deer, and he set me upon high places.

C Christ crossed over the sins that prick in this world and the deepest gulfs of sins, like a deer crossing thorny thickets. God set him upon high places, that is, the Father set him above every height of creatures, as the Apostle says: “And he gave him the name that is above every name.”

37 [Col. 0096D] He teaches my hands for battle, and you have placed my arms like a bronze bow.

C To be taught is to be made cautious against impending plots. “Hands” signify actions; “battle,” the struggle against the devil. Christ’s arms, however, are the prophets and apostles, through whom he accomplished the desire of his will. He compares these to a bronze bow because God’s servants do not become pliable in preaching; rather, remaining in heavenly strength, they pierce the hearts of devout people with saving words sent out like arrows and shot from afar.

38 ÷ And .. you gave me the protection of your salvation, and your right hand received me.

C “The protection of salvation” signifies the glory of the resurrection, when, having laid aside mortal flesh, he took it up again incorruptible [Col. 0097A]. “The right hand” is the power of divinity, which established the humanity it had assumed in eternal majesty.

39 ÷ And .. your discipline corrected me unto the end ..; and your discipline itself will teach me.

H The voice of the Church. For “the one whom God loves, he reproves,” and your teaching itself—as another text reads—will teach me, because while we are here it is necessary always to remain under instruction. Hence Paul says that all instruction in the present does not seem to be a matter of joy but of grief, whereas in the future it yields abundant fruit.

40 You enlarged my steps beneath me, and my footprints were not weakened.

II “You enlarged my steps,” that is, my understanding, in the breadth of your charity. A Because you made charity broad, working gladly even in these mortal things and members that are beneath me. H “My footprints were not weakened,” that is, his examples, to be followed by successors, and his teaching.

41 I will pursue my enemies and overtake them, and I will not turn back until they fail.

H “I will pursue,” the voice of Christ: that is, Christ will pursue the Jews or Gentiles who unjustly became his enemies. Or the Church pursues carnal desires and will overtake them before they overtake it; and “I will not turn back,” namely, from this purpose. “Until they fail” means until such carnal desires in me fail, or until the Jewish enemies and all the wicked fail in their malice or evil thoughts.

42 [Col. 0097C] I will crush them, and they will not be able to stand; they will fall beneath my feet.

H “I will afflict them,” as another translation has, namely, with many evils, as we now read happened to the Jews in the time of Titus. They could not stand because they had been raised up in pride. They will fall either to humble themselves in worship or to be trampled down as the condemned.

43 ÷ And .. you girded me with strength for battle; you cast down those who rose up against me beneath me.

C Christ was girded with strength when, through patience and courage, he overcame the adversities of his enemies. He cast them down when those who swelled with insane conspiracy against him were undoubtedly destined to be subjected to his judgment, so that they might perish with their instigator, since they refused to believe their author. For this is said of the unclean spirits who, through the Jews, stirred up wicked battles against Christ.

44 ÷ And .. you gave me the backs of my enemies, and you destroyed those who hate me.

C H “Back” signifies the conversion of those who, resisting the name of Christ, first turned their backs toward Christ rather than their faces, but afterward were converted and became Christians, like the Apostle Paul. C Or they gave their backs when they were defeated and converted; their flight—which is signified by the back—became Christ’s glorious victory. Thus Saul, having been defeated [Acts IX], became the victorious Paul, because he conquered others by converting them, after first being himself conquered. He scattered those who hated him when he left the Jews in their unbelief, saying: “His blood be upon us” [Matt. XXVII]. For this is the cause of their dispersion, namely, the blood of Christ.

45 They cried out, but there was no one to save them, to the Lord; and he did not hear them.

H The ungodly and the Jews will cry out to Christ at the future judgment, when they see that their hope in the devil has collapsed. C He will not hear them, because their repentance is fruitless where their condemnation is already known to be just.

46 And I will crush them like dust before the face of the wind; like the mud of the streets I will wipe them away.

C Let the proud and grandiloquent understand that they will be crushed like dust, those who plot to oppose the Lord with perverse minds. “Before the face of the wind,” so that they cannot remain at rest once they have been reduced to fragments [Col. 0098B]. He rightly compares sinners to mud, because they are stained by foul sins. “I will wipe them away,” that is, I will remove them from the midst of the saints, which pertains to the mud of the streets; for mud, because it is very soft, is easily removed.

47 You will rescue me from the contradictions of the people; you will establish me as head of the nations.

C Christ was rescued from the contradictions of the people when, after the faithless Jews had been cast out, he was transferred to the faith and devotion of the nations. He was established as head of the nations when he was received through their faith, because they caused the standards of the cross to shine upon the foreheads of the nations.

48 A people whom I did not know served me. ÷ In .. the hearing of the ear it obeyed me.

[Col. 0098C] C The people serve Christ—that is, the Gentiles believed in Christ, whom they previously did not know, because they believe in him. H “It obeyed by the hearing of the ear,” because, without seeing God’s wonders or his bodily presence, they afterward heard and, obeying their teachers, believed and fulfilled their faith in practice.

49 Foreign sons have lied to me; foreign sons have grown old; and they have limped from their paths.

H. “Alien sons”—sons of the devil, to whom he himself said: “You are of your father the devil” (John 8). C. “They lied to me” when they said: “Teacher, we know that you have come from God, and that in truth you teach the way of God” (Matthew 22). For to lie is to speak contrary to one’s mind, and to utter with the tongue what one plainly does not possess in the heart. A H. “They have grown old,” that is, they remained in the old person, whom I came to renew. “And they limped.” C. For we call those who are weak in one foot “lame.” H. He limps who believes in the Father but does not believe in the Son. C. The Jews limp: understanding one part of Scripture—the Old Testament—carnally, they reject the other, namely, the New Testament, and thus do not possess it.

50. The Lord lives, and blessed is my God. And let the God of my salvation be exalted.

H. The Church rightly says: “The Lord lives”—the one whom the Jews had shut in the tomb. C. God is called blessed when praise is rendered to him with worthy devotion. “Let him be exalted,” that is, let him be believed throughout the whole world. He could not otherwise be exalted who alone is called, and is, the Most High.

51. God, who gives me vengeance, and subdues peoples beneath me: my deliverer from my angry enemies …

H. “God, who gives me vengeance,” by overthrowing the Jews; or, God who gives vengeance to the holy apostles and to their successors in the Church, granting them the power to loose and correct. And he gave preachers authority to govern unbelieving peoples. He calls God the deliverer. The Church asks to be delivered from heretics or sinners, and this from the angry, C. that is, from those inflamed by burning wickedness. The Church is said to be avenged when her enemies are brought back into the inner sanctuary of true religion.

52. + And … from those rising up against me you will exalt me; [Col. 0099B] from the unjust man you will deliver me.

H. “From those rising up,” that is, from persecutors. “From the unjust man,” that is, from the devil, as in the Gospel: “An enemy has done this” (Matthew 13); C. or from any schismatic.

53. Therefore I will confess to you among the nations, O Lord, and I will sing a psalm to your name.

C. “Because of those things that were said above: ‘I will confess to you,’” that is, I will praise you through Christian peoples. “Psalm” signifies an actual work, through which divinity is praised more effectively by deeds than by words, and which God hears more readily than words. Hence he says: “I will confess to you,” that is, “I will praise you and act.”

54. Magnifying the salvations of his king, and showing mercy to his Christ, David, and to his seed forever.

C. The Father magnifies his king, that is, the Son, who is to reign throughout the whole world. “Christ” is interpreted as “anointed.” H. “David”: strong of hand. C. He showed mercy to David because he delivered him from the ferocity of his persecutors. “His seed” signifies the Lord the Savior. “Forever,” that is, unto eternity. Mercy was shown to Christ, the seed, when he rose again and ascended into heaven, and now sits at the right hand of the Father, king forever.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM XVII

Most merciful God, foundation of hope and refuge in distress, save us from enemies and from the snares of death, so that, rescued from the multitude of tribulations surrounding us, we may sing psalms most devoutly to your holy name with purity of innocence. Through our Lord Jesus Christ your Son, etc.

# PSALM XVIII

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM XVIII

C. While praising the preachers of the Lord, the Prophet most beautifully describes his incarnation; and, magnifying the precepts of the New and Old Testaments, he asks the Lord to cleanse him from hidden vices.

**Title.** To the end: a psalm of David.

C. The inscription of this title has often been explained. Throughout the psalm, therefore, they are the Prophet’s words speaking about Christ.

1. The heavens declare the glory of God, and the works of his hands proclaim the firmament.

C. The heavens are the apostles and prophets, who proclaim the glory of Christ’s coming. “The works of his hands,” that is, the human being fashioned by Christ’s hands. “They proclaim the firmament,” that is, the preaching—namely, of Christ’s incarnation—through which the solidity of our faith was strengthened; and therefore it ought to be said in the plural: “they proclaim.” But according to the wording that has “they proclaim,” it is necessary to understand the firmament as the apostles and prophets, who proclaimed the works of God, that is, the deeds of his power according to his humanity, such as his incarnation, death, and so forth.

2. Day pours forth the word to day, and night declares knowledge to night.

H. “Day”: Christ or the apostles. C. It “pours forth the word” when, by shining upon the hearts of the apostles, he made known the pure heavenly words; or when the apostles illuminate the hearts of the faithful with radiant preaching. “Night declares knowledge to night” when Judas betrayed Christ to the Jews and handed him over to be killed.

3. There are no speeches or discourses whose voices are not heard.

H C. “There are no speeches.” By denying, he says that there are no discourses or speeches that the apostles could not speak. C. “Discourses” refers to ordinary narratives; “speeches” to public exhortations. It is entirely certain that the apostles did both.

4. Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world ÷ earth …

C. “Earth”: here we must understand the human being. “Sound,” however, is the fame of miracles. “The ends of the earth” are kings; that is, the words of the Gospel reached not only the lowly but also the rulers of the nations, and taught all human beings with saving doctrine.

5. He has placed his tabernacle in the sun, and he himself, like a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber.

C. “He has placed it in the sun,” that is, in manifestation, because he came openly. He calls his body a tabernacle. “And he himself” refers to Christ the Lord, who, like a bridegroom for his Church, came forth from his chamber, that is, from the virginal womb. Christ is appropriately called “bridegroom,” from *spondendo*—“promising”—because he was promised so many times by the prophets.

6. He rejoiced like a giant to run his course ÷ his own … His going forth is from the highest heaven.

C. Christ is rightly compared to a giant: surpassing human nature by the greatness of his power, he struck down all the vices of the world together with their most savage author. Here “course” signifies the course of his life, since, born as a human being, he grew, taught, and suffered. “From the highest” signifies the Father. “His going forth” is the birth of the Son—not temporal, but coeternal with the Father.

7. His meeting is even to its summit, and there is no one who can hide from his heat.

C. “His meeting” is said according to his humanity, because after assuming flesh, Christ, remaining in both natures, proceeds even to the summit, that is, to the seat of the Father’s majesty, where the Son is always equal to the Father. His heat is the Holy Spirit, from whom no one can hide, because by the power of his divinity he knows the heart of each person.

8. The law of the Lord is immaculate, converting souls; the testimony of the Lord is faithful, giving wisdom to the little ones.

H. The law of the Lord is Christ, irreproachable because he had no sin. “Converting souls”: from captivity into liberty. C. The testimonies he gave to the Israelite people were faithful, because they were known in the fullness of truth. H. “Giving wisdom to the little ones”: not to those lacking understanding, but to the humble and innocent. C. Or the law of the Lord is the Old Law, immaculate because it was approved by the New Law.

9. The judgments of the Lord are right, rejoicing hearts; the commandment of the Lord is bright, enlightening the eyes.

The judgments of the Lord are truly right, because the Lord did not do otherwise than he taught. They are “right” because there is not one thing in the mouth and another in the deed. Hearts are made glad—“of the righteous” is understood. He calls the commandment bright because it is sincere and pure. It enlightens the eyes—not these bodily eyes, but the inner ones.

10. The fear of the Lord is holy, enduring forever ÷ and ever … The judgments of the Lord are true, justified in themselves.

C. The fear of the Lord, mingled with dread, is charity; with unshaken constancy and not trembling confusion, it remains holy. This fear, in worldly usage, is called reverence. “The judgments of God” means the commandments of God, written in the Old and New Testaments; they remain in themselves because their state is not changed by any variation.

H A. Nor do they require the authority of anyone else—so that they may be held firm—except that of the Lord, who can deceive no one.

11. More desirable than gold and much precious stone, and sweeter than honey and the honeycomb.

C. “The judgments of the Lord” are desirable, that is, the commandments of the New and Old Testaments, more desirable than gold, which human greed most greatly desires to possess. He added “precious stone,” which is worth much despite being a very small pearl. But because there might be people who despised riches, he added flavors: honey and the honeycomb. [Col. 0101D] The Old Testament surpasses honey; the New surpasses the honeycomb.

12. Indeed, your servant keeps them; in keeping them there is great reward.

C. When he says “your servant,” he signifies the just and devoted person, who keeps God’s commandments because reward follows those who obey. They are rightly said to be “great,” because all that God has prepared for those who love him cannot be comprehended.

13. Who understands offenses? Cleanse me from my hidden ones ÷ … and spare your servant from the alien ones …

H. “Who understands offenses?” Except the searcher of hearts, God, who is also able to forgive them. “From the hidden ones,” that is, from past sins. C. That is called hidden which is original sin, in which we are conceived and born, and by which we sin with secret intention. “Alien” is what is committed at the persuasion of wicked people or of the persuading devil, but it becomes one’s own because our punishable consent is added from our own free will; and from that stock of mortal beings corrupted by the spiritual enemy, a person is swiftly overthrown without the grace of God, because it is shown to have been corrupted in the first human being through disobedience. For how easy it is for the ancient ambusher to persuade the infected to what is forbidden, when by his cunning he was able to deceive those who were free and incorrupt? Thus “alien” are those acts that are done by others through our persuasion or fault, or that we do at the persuasion or assistance of others.

14. If they do not rule over me, then I shall be immaculate, and I shall be cleansed from the great offense.

H. Offenses are so called when a servant becomes a servant of sin. If I do not commit these sins, I shall be immaculate. “And I shall be cleansed from the great offense,” that is, from pride. C. By it the devil also fell, dragged down humanity, and emptied it of the blessedness that had been granted. A. He therefore does not ask that absolutely all sins be taken away from him, which is impossible, but that they not rule over him.

15. And the words of my mouth will be pleasing, and the meditation of my heart in your sight ÷ always …

C. The words of the mouth can please the Lord if the human being is made free from the vices mentioned above. The meditation of the heart that can reach God is hope, charity, and faith.

16. O Lord, my helper and my redeemer.

C. He calls God his helper in good actions, and his redeemer from evil, so that no one may attribute to his own merits what he has received by heavenly generosity.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM XVIII

Most merciful God, who, coming forth from the virginal chamber and having freed us, ascended to the right hand of the Father, we beseech your immense mercy: that, converted by your law, enlightened by your commandments, and instructed by your testimonies, we may deserve to be cleansed both from alien and from hidden sins. You who, with the Father, etc.

# PSALM XIX

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM XIX

[Col. 0102D] C. The Prophet asks that the Church be heard, requesting that her counsel be confirmed by the Lord, and saying that the faithful are to be magnified not by worldly power but by divine strength.

**Title.** To the end: a psalm of David.

C. The words of the title are already familiar. Now in this psalm the Prophet asks that prosperity come to the holy Church of God, which he foresaw would be possible through the Lord’s coming after a long period, saying: “May he hear,” and so forth.

1. May the Lord hear you in the day of tribulation; may the name of the God of Jacob protect you.

C. “In the day of tribulation” indicates a time of most severe affliction. When he says, “May the name of the God of Jacob protect you,” the Prophet asks the Lord to grant such a blessing to the Christian people as the holy patriarch Jacob once received from him, when he was preferred to his brother Esau. We are known to be heard when we obtain something in every respect.

2. May he send you help from the sanctuary, and may he protect you from Zion.

He says “may he send,” expressing a wish; he shows that the Son was sent by the Father as an aid to the holy Church of God. For Zion signifies the mountain of contemplation, which is fitting to divinity, since all things are known to it.

3. May he remember all your sacrifice, and may your burnt offering become fat. *Diapsalma.*

C. The sacrifice of the holy Church is to be understood as the rite now being celebrated in the solemn offering of the Lord’s body and blood. A burnt offering is called something wholly consumed by fire, and it represents the same sacrifice just mentioned. It becomes rich and joyful when our offering of mind and body is received by the grace of divinity.

4. May he grant you according to your heart, and may he confirm all your counsel.

C. He says, “May he grant you according to your heart,” that is, according to the understanding you have concerning the Lord: that you believe him to be one of the Trinity, to have suffered in the flesh, to have risen, to have ascended into heaven, and so forth. “And may he confirm all your counsel,” that is, the counsel of the holy Church: to believe the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit to be one God, from whom all things are; and, by deliberate counsel, to despise all the delights of the world for this faith.

5. We shall rejoice in your salvation, and in the name of our God we shall be magnified.

C. For he declared that he would rejoice in the Church’s salvation—which is Christ Jesus—in order to show himself to be one of her body. And he declared that he would be magnified in his name, because Christians were to be called from him. To be magnified is to become great.

6. May the Lord fulfill all your petitions. Now I know that the Lord has saved his Christ.

C. “May the Lord fulfill”—there is again a grateful turning toward the Church. By saying “now I know,” he displays the great power of his prophecy, since he says that he now knows what was to be fulfilled after many ages. The Father saved the Son in his glorious resurrection and ascension into heaven.

7. He will hear him from his holy heaven; salvation is in the powers of his right hand.

C. The meaning is this: the Father will hear the Son from heaven, because salvation is in his right hand. Although he possesses it from his own divinity, he nevertheless appears to seek it according to the flesh. He says “in the powers” because he makes us powerful by guarding us with his grace in the present life, and in the future life in blessed eternity, which is understood by “the right hand.”

8. Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we will call upon the name of the Lord our God.

H. “Chariots” signify the pleasure or greed of the world, because the proud and greedy, like unstable wheels, rush mentally here and there. “Horses” signify the proud; they are the greedy. H C. Let us not glory in them, but in the name of God, which leads to eternal rewards.

9. They are bound and have fallen, but we have risen and stand upright.

C. The Prophet says that those bound by human honors or wicked desires have fallen—arrogant people who must suffer this, since they bind themselves with the chains of entangled errors. A Christian is said to rise in two ways: from the death of vices, and in that resurrection in which the righteous receive eternal rewards. It is clear that both are understood here.

10. O Lord, save the king ÷ and … hear us in the day when we call upon you …

C. It is said to the Father: “Save the king,” that is, so that Christ may rise from the dead. “Hear us”: this comes to the human race when it firmly believes in and joyfully beholds Christ’s resurrection; or, through the king, hear us in the day of our need.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM XIX

Fulfill, Lord, our petitions, and receive us as a most rich burnt offering, so that, with the chariots of our enemies bound, we may rejoice in the help of your salvation. Through our Lord Jesus, etc.

# PSALM XX

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM XX

C. In this psalm the Prophet sings of the Lord Savior’s incarnation first, and afterward of the deeds of his divinity.

**Title.** To the end: a psalm of David.

C. This title is rightly shared with the nineteenth psalm, since this psalm also speaks about the Lord Savior like the preceding one, though with some difference.

1. O Lord, the king shall rejoice in your strength, and he shall exult exceedingly in your salvation.

C. “O Lord” is addressed by the Prophet to the Father. “In your strength,” that is, in the omnipotence of your majesty, in which the Son also reigns. “The king shall rejoice”: Christ Jesus rejoices. “He shall exult,” that is, because through him you saved human beings, your Son, who is the Savior, shall exult. “Exceedingly” indicates the greatness of the joy: as abundant as the benefit is, so great is the joy.

2. You granted him the desire of his heart, and you did not deprive him of the will of his lips. *Diapsalma.*

C. The desire of his soul was to be killed for the salvation of all, so that his precious blood might redeem the world. The will of his lips was evident when he commanded unclean spirits, healed various illnesses by the authority of his word, and planted his preaching among the peoples. It is clear that his will was frustrated in nothing, since everything he ordered to be done was fulfilled.

3. For you went before him with blessings of sweetness; you placed upon his head a crown of precious stone.

C. “You went before him” signifies that his humanity was preceded by the grace of divinity. A. The blessing of sweetness was freedom from sin, with which Christ was endowed; for we are conceived in the bitterness of Adam. C. Or the blessing of sweetness was given when it was said: “This is my beloved Son.” The crown signifies the assembly of disciples; it was the crown of his head, the royal diadem, because the circle of the apostles surrounded him as he taught. That diadem was not placed upon him in order to adorn him, but rather to be adorned by Christ. The precious stones are the apostles.

4. He asked life of you, and you granted it to him: length of days forever and ever ÷ and ever …

C. “Life” signifies the resurrection, which he asked for when he said: “Father, glorify your Son.” The length of days signifies Christ’s eternity, which is enclosed by no end. “Forever and ever” indicates the unceasing stability of the future age. But remember that these and similar statements are spoken from the part of him that suffered.

5. Great is his glory in your salvation; you will place glory and ÷ great … beauty upon him.

C. “Glory” and “great beauty” signify the time of judgment, when the Most High will appear in his divinity, possessing glory from judgment and beauty from majesty. There is also great glory for the holy incarnation in “salvation,” that is, in the Word of the Father.

6. For you will make him a blessing forever ÷ and ever … You will gladden him with joy in your presence.

H. “You will make him a blessing,” because every creature blesses him. “You will gladden him with joy” when the multitude of the saints has been gathered together and the number of the saints has been restored. C. “In your presence” indicates that Christ is unquestionably one person, because his humanity rejoices in his divinity. Nevertheless, the statement can rightly also be understood of Christ’s members.

7. For the king hopes in the Lord, and he will not be shaken by the mercy of the Most High.

C. This is the king who, in his Passion, was written in three languages. He hoped in the Lord according to his humanity. He will not be shaken by the Father’s mercy, because he is the protector of those who have long hoped in him.

8. Let your hand be found by all your enemies; let your right hand find ÷ all … who hate you.

C. “Let your hand be found,” that is, let your work be discovered. H. So that the enemies, afflicted by your power, may turn toward the good. The Father’s right hand is the Lord Savior. Those who hate him are to be condemned to perpetual punishment and tortured without end with the devil and his satellites in eternal darkness. Thus God’s hand is found against his enemies in the future judgment.

9. You will set them like a furnace of fire at the time of your presence; the Lord will disturb them in his anger, and fire will devour them.

C. A furnace is the rounded form of a bronze vessel made for baking bread, burning within under consuming flames. It signifies sinners, who will be tormented in judgment both by anguish of soul and by penal torture. The time of God’s presence is the day of judgment. H. Here God’s anger does not punish but disturbs them toward repentance, and this fire of the Holy Spirit devours—that is, consumes—sins. C. Or, when they hear: “Go into the eternal fire,” then the judge’s sentence will disturb them, and the fire will devour them forever.

10. You will destroy their fruit from the earth, and their seed from the children of men.

C H. “Fruit” means the works of the wicked. “To destroy from the earth” means from the holy Church or from the land of the living. C. “Seed” means the vows or deeds of sinners. “From the children,” that is, you make them strangers to the saints, whom you are going to send into eternal inheritance by your generosity.

11. For they turned evil against you; they devised plans that they were not able ÷ to establish …

H. The Jews appeared to turn evil against Christ when they said: “He is worthy of death.” They devised a council, saying: “Therefore command that the tomb be guarded” (Matthew 27), unwilling and even unable to believe that Christ would rise again. They were unable to establish this, because Christ rose when he wished. C. We say that people turn evils upon others when, through repentance directed against some, they shift the cause of iniquity onto others. The Jews did this to Christ when they attributed the destruction of the city and nation to Christ’s life, saying: “If we let him go on like this” (John 11), and so forth.

12. For you will set them as your back; in your remnants you will prepare their face.

A. The Jews were set as a back when, because of their fault, understanding earthly things, they were not worthy to behold heavenly things. H. The remnants of the Jews will be prepared when, at the end, they are to believe through Enoch and Elijah. Then you will prepare their face—namely, of those who believe in you—so that the hearts of the fathers may be turned toward the children.

13. Be exalted, O Lord, in your strength; we will sing and psalm your powers.

[Col. 0106D] H. “Be exalted in strength,” that is, display your majesty and power in judgment—you who previously came in humility. C. To sing is to speak the Lord’s words with the mouth; to psalm is to fulfill the divine commandments steadfastly through good works.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM XX

Bless us, Lord, with the blessing of sweetness, and fulfill the desire pleasing to you in us, so that, while we continually sing your powers with sweet melody, we may attain the length of perpetual life. Through our Lord Jesus, etc.

# PSALM XXI

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM XXI

C. In this psalm Christ speaks to the Father about his Passion, and urges the faithful to praise the Lord because in his resurrection he looked upon the catholic Church.

**Title.** To the end, for the morning reception: a psalm of David ÷ …

C. “To the end”—whether “psalm” or “David” is signified has been explained. “Morning reception” is the time of the resurrection, when he assumed a mortal body glorified in great glory. It is called “morning,” as though *manu primitivum*—“the first beginning by hand”—a time clearly applied to the Lord’s resurrection in innumerable passages.

1. God, my God, look upon me ÷ … why have you forsaken me? The words of my offenses are far from my salvation.

C. “God” is a Greek word and is interpreted as “fear.” Hence one of the pagan poets said: “Fear first made gods in the world.” Therefore Christ, as though moved by the Passion that was near, cries out according to his humanity: “Look upon me,” beseeching the swiftest aid of the resurrection. H. When he says that he was forsaken, he does not speak from his own person but from that of his people, whose sins he himself assumed. C. He says that the words that produce offenses are far from him, and yet he calls our sins his own offenses, although he had no sins. A. Thus he says that he was forsaken in the person of his members, who do not receive what they ask, since their words are words of offenses: they either ask for what is contrary to salvation, or, when they are not immediately heard, they murmur and complain that they have been forsaken.

2. My God, I will cry out by day and you will not hear; and by night, and it will not be accounted folly to me.

C. The humanity of the Word cried out by day, because the darkness of sins did not surround it. H. It is not heard because of those destined for death, who are called by the name of night. C. “Not to folly”: “you will account it to me” is understood—that is, the Father to the Son. The mediator between God and human beings therefore asked not foolishly but wisely; nevertheless, he is not said to have been heard, because he was going to redeem the world through his petition and Passion. H C A. Or “day” signifies prosperity, and “night” adversity. In these circumstances God sometimes does not hear those who ask—not for their folly, but so that they may thereby become wise and learn to ask wisely, seeking not earthly things but heavenly ones, or earthly things for the salvation of the soul.

3. Yet you dwell in the holy place, the praise of Israel.

C. “You dwell in the holy place, the praise.” Through this the Prophet declared Christ’s incarnation, because the Father, who is the praise of Israel—that is, of the Church that sees you through faith—dwells in the Son as praise. He also shows that he was not heard, not because of folly, but for the salvation of the human race, which was made holy through his Passion, since the Father always hears the Son in whom he always dwells.

4. In you our fathers hoped; they hoped, and you delivered them.

H. The patriarchs hoped, and he delivered them from Egypt. H. They hoped in the desert and were delivered. How much more does a father deliver his son when he asks and wishes to be delivered.

5. They cried out to you and were saved; they hoped in you and were not confounded.

C. The martyrs cried out to Christ when bodily punishment consumed them and unbelievers thought that they were not heard. Rather, they were greatly heard, because they deserved to receive the crown. “They were not confounded”: it is clear that they came to the reward; for the one who attains the eternal kingdom is not put to shame.

6. But I am a worm and not a man, the reproach of men and the outcast of the people.

C. Christ is compared to a worm because he was mortal and born of flesh without the mingling of seed. A worm likewise is born without intercourse. “Not a man,” that is, not a sinner—for this could not exist in him. “The reproach of men”: when they spat upon him and struck him with slaps. “The outcast”: when they chose Barabbas and rejected Christ.

7. All who saw me mocked me; they spoke with their lips and shook their heads.

C. “All” is to be understood of the wicked. “They mocked” by not believing in Christ. H. “They spoke with their lips”: “If he is the Son of God, let him come down from the cross” (Matthew 27). “They shook their heads.” C. Out of anger, as threatening people do, not judging from the heart; for they spoke with their mouth, not with their heart, and their judgment did not proceed from firm deliberation.

8. He hoped in the Lord; let him deliver him; let him save him, since he desires him.

H. The Prophet’s voice: “He hoped,” that is, humanity hoped in divinity. “Let him deliver,” that is, from the Jews. “He desires him,” because God the Father wished to have such a Son, without sin, through whom he would take away the sins of the world. C. Or, better, this was said ironically by the Jews; in Latin this figure is called *irrisio*—mockery—when someone displays something other than what he is attempting.

9. For you are he who drew me from the womb; my hope from my mother’s breasts; upon you I was cast from the womb.

H. The voice of humanity: “You brought me forth from the womb,” that is, from the womb of holy Mary. C. Because then he was separated from the stain of original sin, he came forth from the chamber like a bridegroom. “My hope from the breasts”: H. that is, according to his humanity, according to which he did not disdain to suck his mother’s breasts. “Upon you I was cast.” C. He shows that he was separated from human iniquity.

10. From my mother’s womb you are my God; do not depart from me.

C. When he says “from my mother’s womb,” he shows that not even the conception of the flesh was without God. “Do not depart from me.” H. On the day of the Passion.

11. For tribulation is near, for there is no one to help.

H. “Tribulation is near,” as he himself said: “Rise, let us go; behold, the one who betrays me is approaching” (Matthew 26). “There is no one to help”—neither angel nor human being, except you, Father.

12. Many calves surrounded me; fat bulls besieged me.

C. “Calves” are the Jewish people, who, ignorant of the yoke of God, act wantonly with heedless insolence, at once petulant and foolish. They do not regulate their steps with any restraint, but, wandering and unstable, they rush by certain leaps toward wicked counsels. “Bulls” designate the rulers of the Jews. He added “fat,” because they surrounded Christ with swords and clubs in their ferocity; for an animal that has been fattened becomes restless and savage.

13. They opened their mouths against me like a lion seizing and roaring.

C. The Jews opened their mouths, saying: “Crucify, crucify” (Matthew 27)—their own mouths, that is, mouths opened not by wisdom but by criminal thought. “Seizing” pertains to the utterly insane sedition with which they seized him and dragged him to the tribunals. “Roaring” pertains to the blasphemous voices with which they said: “Crucify, crucify.”

14. I have been poured out like water, and all my bones have been scattered.

H. The bones of Christ are called the apostles, C. who were scattered and poured out like water. Satisfying the world with divine rain, they washed it from the filth of sins. A. Or Christ was killed so shamefully as water is poured out; the outpouring of his blood drenched and washed us, and his disciples were scattered at his death.

15. My heart has become like melting wax within my belly.

H. He called his heart his wisdom, which was not understood before his Passion. C. Once the Passion was fulfilled, every promised truth was revealed. The mysteries of the law are rightly compared to wax, which gives back the splendor of light when it is dissolved by heat; so, through the fire of Christ’s Passion, the mysteries of the law were illuminated. “Belly” refers to the Church.

16. My strength has dried up like a potsherd, and my tongue has clung to my palate; and you have brought me down into the dust of death.

H C. Christ’s strength is compared to a potsherd, because, as a potsherd becomes stronger when hardened by fire, so Christ’s strength was made firm in the Passion, though previously it appeared like clay to unbelievers. C. “His tongue” signifies the preachers, who cling to his palate while they keep his commandments. He says that he was brought down into the dust according to the will of the Jews, who strove for this and thought that they had accomplished it, because they refused to believe in his resurrection; but they thought that they had delivered Christ over to a common death, so that they believed him to have been brought all the way into the dust.

17. ÷ For … many dogs surrounded me … ÷ The assembly of the wicked besieged me.

H. It is the nature of dogs to love their masters and bark against thieves. The Jews, on the contrary, did not speak rightly against their own Lord but barked wickedly, and they chose the thief. C. “The assembly of the wicked”: when they planned to seize Jesus by deceit and drag him to death.

18. They pierced my hands and my feet; they counted all my bones.

H. “They pierced my hands,” that is, they fixed them with nails, and they found a great fruit—namely, the salvation of all the nations. C. “They counted his bones,” mystically, that is, the apostles or the rest of the Christians whom the Jews sought to destroy through persecution, lest they grow stronger in greater number. Or they stretched his body on the cross in such a way that his bones appeared countable.

19. But they themselves looked upon me and observed me; they divided my garments among themselves, and over my clothing they cast lots.

C. He says that the Jews looked upon him according to their cruelty, so that they might not appear to have acted casually or in passing, but to have carefully considered and observed what was happening; yet their stony hearts were not moved by so many miracles. “They divided my garments among themselves” (Job 19). H. This was fulfilled in Christ’s Passion, when four soldiers made four portions.
