The tunic, however, was not divided, signifying the unity of the Church, which is not torn apart, although heretics attempt to divide it.

20. But you, O Lord, do not draw my help far away; look upon my defense.

H. Here humanity speaks to divinity. C. He asks for a very swift resurrection, so that, when such glory comes, the unbelief of the faithless may be destroyed. “Help” signifies Christ’s resurrection, which was not delayed, since it came on the third day. C. “For my defense”: lest that [uncertain: *pars illa vocatis inferni*] prevail against me in any respect.

21. Deliver my soul from the sword ÷ and … my only one from the hand of the dog.

C. He asks to be delivered from the death he wished to undergo. “Sword” signifies a spear, or sword, or any kind of weapon; here it signifies the malice of the Jews. He said “from the hand of the dog,” although a dog has no hand, but he wishes the power of the Jews to be understood. H. He calls his soul “only,” because it has no sin; or he refers to the catholic Church. C. So that it may be understood that he rejected new doctrines and the assemblies of the lost.

22. Save me from the mouth of the lion, and from the horns of the unicorns my lowliness.

C. “From the mouth of the lion”: he speaks of the power of the devil, who is rightly compared to wild beasts, since he is always delighted with human beings. “From the horns,” that is, from the proud. “Of the unicorns”: those who rise up in excessive arrogance and cannot endure companions like themselves. Christ asked to be separated from such people, his own humble ones; for animals armed with a single horn are much stronger than those furnished with two.

23. I will tell your name to my brothers; in the midst of the Church I will praise you.

C. After the sacred Passion, he says that the glory of divinity is to be proclaimed throughout the whole world. “I will tell,” that is, I will cause it to be told. Those who love and are loved are called brothers. “In the midst of the Church.” II. In the midst of believing peoples I will preach you and praise you.

24 You who fear the Lord, praise him; all the offspring of Jacob, glorify him.

C The fear of God is just and upright; it generates praise, grants love, and kindles the ardor of charity. “The offspring of Jacob” means those who agree with Jacob in faith and devotion and are supplanters of vices. Praise, therefore, you who fear him—that is, who hold his name in reverence—for no one deserves to proclaim him unless he is known and feared.

25 Let all the offspring of Israel fear him, for he has not despised or scorned the prayer of the poor.

H “Let all the offspring of Israel fear him,” that is, each person reborn through baptism and seeing God with the mind. “For he has not despised the prayers of the poor,” that is, of the Son.

C As those who glory in the honor of this world are accustomed to do: to despise the poor and scorn those who plead, and to measure a person’s case by the quality of his clothing, so that if he is elegant in dress he is considered truthful, but if shabby in attire he is regarded as utterly deceitful.

26 He did not turn his face away from me; and when I cried to him, he heard ÷ me ..

H He did not turn his face away, but raised me from the dead. “When I cried,” he answered: “I have glorified, and I will glorify again” (John XII).

C Or otherwise: he cried out so that our death might be brought to an end by his death, and the sin of the old man might be redeemed by the price of his most holy [Col. 0111C] Passion.

27 With you is my praise in the great Church; I shall fulfill my vows in the presence of those who fear him.

C “With you” means “concerning you.” “My praise in the Church,” namely the catholic Church, is called great both in extent and in honor. “Vows” means the sacraments of the body and blood, which are offered in the presence of those who are subject to him in holy fear. Finally, he adds what these vows are: “The poor shall eat,” and so forth.

28 The poor shall eat and be satisfied: ÷ and .. they shall praise the Lord who seek him; their hearts shall live forever ÷ and ever ..

C “The poor” means those who hunger for the kingdom of God. For only those whom such hunger possesses can be satisfied. The poor, once satisfied, praise God; the rich exalt themselves.

H “Those who seek him”: by faith and by works, understanding that he himself is the bread that came down from heaven. “Their heart lives,” that is, their hope is nourished without wavering. We call that truly alive which perseveres in the grace of divinity.

29 All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord.

C We call those people “remembering” whom it is clear have returned to the true remedy after forgetting Christ. And when God is faithfully known by them, it is rightly said that they remember, so that they may truly return to him whom previously they neglected through perverse intention.

“All the ends” means the universal Church, which is now clearly spread throughout the whole world.

H And every day the preachers of the true Christ strive through religious teaching to convert others to the true Christ.

30 And they shall worship in his presence, all the families of the nations.

C Those worship in the presence of the Lord who entreat Christ with sincere faith and works. His presence belongs only to the most faithful and blessed. “All the families” includes all believers, excluding no one.

31 For the kingdom is the Lord’s, and ÷ he .. shall rule the nations.

C “For the kingdom is the Lord’s,” because the kingdoms of the nations are not their own but belong to the Lord, who by his power both changes kings and preserves them. And he must necessarily be worshiped everywhere, since he is understood to be the Lord of all things.

32 All the prosperous of the earth have eaten and worshiped; in his presence all who descend into the earth shall fall.

H “All the rich have eaten,” that is, the apostles and the other saints have eaten the body of Christ. “They have worshiped”: in faith and action. “Those who descend”: from the pride of the world, so that they may worship in pure humility.

H A Or here “the prosperous” means the rich of the earth, who also eat the sacrament of the body of Christ, but will not be satisfied like Christ’s poor. They worship, but do not possess the fellowship of charity; and because in mind they descend toward earthly things, they will fall into hell.

33 But my soul shall live for him, and my offspring shall serve him.

C He says that his soul lives for God the Father, because he passed through this world in an unstained manner of life.

H “My offspring”: the children of the Church serve Christ.

C Or: the works of Christ shall serve by praising God.

34 The coming generation shall be announced to the Lord, and the heavens shall announce his righteousness to the people who shall be born, whom he has made ÷ the Lord ..

H C The prophet speaks of the coming generation: the people of the nations, who were to be brought forth from water and the Spirit. This generation shall be announced to the Lord—that is, it shall be converted to the Lord by proclamation, that is, for the Lord’s honor.

H “The heavens announce”: that is, the apostles preach the Son of God; for he is the Father’s righteousness.

C It is appropriately said that the Lord made the Christian people, because he predestined them before the ages, created them, redeemed them, and by his holy body made them free from sins.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM XXI

God, head of mercy, who for our sake descended into the Virgin’s womb, was fastened to the wood, pierced with a nail, and with your garments divided by lot, and rose free from the underworld: we beseech you, mindful of this exchange, to be the deliverer of the peoples from the mouth of the lion, you who were formerly the liberator of the fathers who hoped in you. You who live, and so forth.

## PSALM XXII

[Col. 0113A]

### ARGUMENT OF PSALM XXII

C Throughout the psalm, the Christian reborn in baptism gives thanks because he has been led from the barrenness of sin to places of pasture and waters of refreshment.

### TT. A Psalm of David

C Throughout this entire psalm, the faithful Christian gives thanks to the Lord because, having laid aside his former condition, he has been brought, by the Lord’s generosity, to places of pasture and waters of refreshment.

1 The Lord shepherds me; ÷ and .. I shall lack nothing. He has placed ÷ me .. in a place of pasture.

L Here the Church speaks confidently through faith. “The Lord shepherds me,” because before Christ’s coming the devil shepherded the world. Nothing good will be lacking to the one who clings to God. “In a place of pasture”: that is, he will place him in future blessedness; but already, in hope, he has placed him in that same blessedness, or he has established my hope in the unity of the Church and of faith.

2 He led me beside waters of refreshment; he restored my soul.

H C “Waters of refreshment” are the washing of baptism, by which the barren soul is irrigated. “He led me,”

C that is, he gradually nourished me, like little ones and the newly reborn, by doctrine.

H Of the patriarchs and prophets, or of the apostles.

C He turned the faithful soul toward Christ, though previously it was found to be captive under the devil.

3 He led me along the paths of righteousness, for his name’s sake.

[Col. 0113C]

C The paths of righteousness are the two saving commandments: love of God and of neighbor. They are called paths because the way to the kingdom of heaven is narrow (Matthew VII). For his name’s sake, the servant of Christ rejoices that he has been led to that knowledge, so that he can proclaim God’s commands; and he acknowledges that this was granted to him not by his own merits but by divine grace—as though he were saying: “I have been led into the paths of the commandments, not because of my merit, but because of his name.”

4 For even if I walk in the midst of the shadow of death, I shall fear no evil, because you are with me.

C The catholic Christian says: if I walk among heretics, who are rightly called shadows of death, I shall not fear their perverse persuasions, because you, Lord, [Col. 0113D] defend me.

H Or among the darknesses, ignorances, and sins of the world. For sins are the shadow of death because they reproduce the likeness of death. Yet I shall not fear for this reason also: because your rod, and so forth.

5 Your rod and your staff: they themselves have comforted me.

C The rod pertains to the justice and strength of the Lord the Savior. The staff pertains to human assistance, by which a person is guided and sustained by God, just as a sick person is supported by a staff; by it the foot is planted cautiously, and the whole body is supported as it leans upon it. By these two things, therefore, the faithful person is comforted. One is discipline, which crushes vices and those evil people who desire to harm the good; the other is guidance, which sustains [Col. 0114A] the faithful.

H A Certainly the rod also comforts when, by correcting the sinner, it leads him onto the way of salvation.

6 You have prepared a table before me, against those who trouble me.

C “You have prepared,” that is, you have predestined the holy altar. It is called a table from *mense*, because on the first day of each month banquets were conducted according to the rite of the nations, and so forth.

H It signifies Holy Scripture. “Against those who trouble me”: that is, against heretics who trouble the Church, or against the persecutors of the Church and demons.

7 You have anointed ÷ in .. oil my head; ÷ and .. my cup, which makes me drunk, ÷ how splendid it is ..

H The voice of the Church. “You have gladdened my head,” that is, my mind, with oil—that is, with spiritual joy. The cup is understood as [Col. 0114B] the word of God, which intoxicates the human mind.

C It is splendid, therefore, because it leads to the kingdom of heaven. Or the cup is the blood of Christ, which is splendid for those who receive it worthily.

8 And your mercy shall follow me all the days of my life.

C Mercy follows the faithful person for protection, but goes before him to bestow grace. Unless the Lord’s mercy followed us, human frailty would easily be deceived, because the devil prepares ambushes behind us while we remain in this mortal body. Hence it is exceedingly necessary that God’s grace always go before us and mercy follow us.

9 + And .. ÷ that .. I may dwell in the house of the Lord for length of days.

[Col. 0114C]

A He confesses that these things, which have been stated, were granted to him so that he might dwell, and so forth. The house of the Lord signifies the future Jerusalem, which consists in length of days, because in it there is perpetual joy and blessedness without end.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM XXII

Rule us, Lord, with the gentle reins of your commandment, so that, having received the habitation of the eternal tabernacle, we may be filled with the fullness of the everlasting cup. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who, and so forth.

## PSALM XXIII

### ARGUMENT OF PSALM XXIII

C The prophet testifies that the whole world is subject to Christ’s dominion, defining by what virtues those established in his Church are endowed; and he exhorts the superstitious to serve the true Lord.

### TT. A Psalm of David ÷ On the first Sabbath ..

C “On the first Sabbath” signifies the Lord’s Day, on which the Lord rose and, by rising, came to the aid of this age; on that day he also created the world. Because of the excellence of so great a miracle, it is properly called the Lord’s Day, that is, the day of the Lord, although all days belong to the Lord.

1 The earth is the Lord’s and its fullness, the inhabited world and ÷ all .. who dwell in it.

C “The earth is the Lord’s,” that is, the Church, which serves the Lord especially with a pure mind. For although all things were made by him, we nevertheless say that what belongs especially to him is that which reveres him as its creator.

“Fullness” means the holy multitude with which the Church is filled. The person dwells in the Church who perseveres in right faith until death; for we call dwelling remaining.

2 For he founded it upon the seas and prepared it upon the rivers.

C What is it to found the Church upon the seas except to establish it in firm faith upon the trembling waves of vices?

“Rivers”:

H The powerful or the greedy of the world. The Church stands above these rivers so that it may preach to them and they may be converted.

3 Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord, or who shall stand in his holy place?

C Since he has taught that all things he created belong to the Lord, he next shows by questioning what sort of people those must be who desire to be called his own.

H It is the voice of the prophet asking: “Who shall ascend the mountain,” that is, the heavenly Jerusalem.

C Or righteousness, toward which we strive with great effort, because we are hindered by sins that oppose us.

H “Or who shall stand,” that is, who shall persevere in righteousness.

C For it is much more useful to stand in the holy place than to reach its summit.

H Because many ascend but do not persevere. “Who” is therefore used to indicate rarity.

4 One innocent in hands and pure in heart, who has not received his soul in vain and has not sworn deceitfully to his neighbor.

C “Innocent in hands” is the person whose action harms no one but strives to help.

“Pure in heart”:

H Holy in thought.

That person does not receive his soul in vain who performs good works.

C Therefore whoever intends to act otherwise than he promises swears deceitfully, believing that it is not perjury: he wickedly deceives the error of the one who trusts him.

5 ÷ He .. shall receive a blessing from the Lord and mercy from God his Savior.

C Therefore he receives the blessing not from another but from the Lord.

H The one who has guarded himself from the stains mentioned above.

H Our Savior, therefore, is Christ, from whom both blessedness is granted and sins are released.

H The one alone obtains mercy from God who considers himself wretched.

C No human being exists who does not need mercy shown to him.

6 This is the generation of those who seek him, who seek the face of the God of Jacob. *Diapsalma.*

H “Generation,” that is, the people of Christians, who lay in darkness but now, seeking the Lord, seek the face of God through faith and action—that is, the face of Christ through his illumination. He later gave primacy of honor to the one who was born later, namely the Christian people, which he secretly indicated by Jacob.

7 Lift up your gates, princes; and be lifted up, eternal gates; and the King of glory shall enter.

C The prophet commands the gates of death to be removed—that is, desire, malice, and the other vices that had been established by the prince, the devil. They are called gates because sinners pass through them, carrying their deeds, and through them the devil enters hearts. Indeed, *porta* is so called from carrying. Again he commands the gates to be lifted up, that is,

H faith and charity, which are called eternal because through them Christ entered the Church.

8 Who is this King of glory? The Lord, strong and mighty; the Lord, mighty in battle.

H The voice of the demons, as though they were saying: “We have the devil as our king. Who is this king?”

Again, the voice of the good angels: he is strong because he bound the devil (Luke XI); mighty when he conquered hell; mighty in battle when he despoiled Tartarus. Thus the demons appear to have asked this question after they had been driven from the hearts of the nations by Christ’s authority, preaching, and grace.

9 Lift up your gates, princes; and be lifted up, eternal gates; and the King of glory shall enter.

C Again he admonishes those dwelling in various errors to remove the bars of death,

H that is, pride, desire, and avarice, because through these three every person was descending into hell.

The eternal gates have been lifted up,

C that is, the grace of baptism, the honor of chrism, and the salvation of preaching, through which the King of glory deigned to enter.

10 Who is this King of glory? The Lord of hosts, he is the King of glory. + *Diapsalma* ..

H He is rightly called the Lord of hosts, because by his power he trampled the realms below and, returning in triumph, went to the realms above.

“King of glory”:

C He makes those glorious by glorifying them.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM XXIII

God, establisher of the earth, whom all the fullness of the world serves, restore us to innocence of life, so that with you going before us we may be able to ascend the mountain of sanctification. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, and so forth.

## PSALM XXIV

### ARGUMENT OF PSALM XXIV

C Throughout this psalm, the Church begs that she not appear contemptible before the Lord’s presence and before her enemies.

### TT. A Psalm of David, for the end.

1 To you, Lord, I have lifted up my soul; my God, in you I trust; I shall not be put to shame.

[Col. 0116D]

C Mother Church says that she has lifted up her soul to contemplation of heavenly things through hope, faith, and charity, because whoever has seen divine things easily despises human things. To be put to shame is to be confused by sudden disturbance of mind; this does not happen to the Church, because she trusts in God.

2 Let not my enemies mock me, for all who await you shall not be confounded.

C The kindly generally laugh, but mocking is always the act of adversaries.

H The Church’s enemies are demons, heretics, vices, and sins. Those who await the Lord shall not be confounded, neither here nor in the future.

C [Col. 0117A] To await is to endure God bravely under the burden of evils, so that when he comes in judgment he may give what the devoted soul expected.

3 Let ÷ all .. who act wickedly be confounded in vain.

H The prophet says “let them be confounded” not as a wish but as a prophecy. Those who persevere in wickedness to the end will indeed be confounded.

C We call that vain which is fruitless and empty, which is proved alien to the Lord.

A Or optatively: “let them be confounded” here for the sake of their sins’ healing. If they do not wish to be confounded here, then let them finally be confounded eternally.

4 Make your ways known to me, Lord, ÷ and .. teach me your paths.

C The ways are so called from carrying and signify the commandments. A path is called *semita*, as though “half-way,” because it is directed along a narrow track. It is not known to the multitude but traversed by a hidden route.

H By “path” is understood the narrow way that leads to life.

“Teach me”:

C This expression is understood to pertain not so much to a track as to the law.

5 Direct me in your truth and teach me, for you are God my Savior; ÷ and .. I have waited for you all day.

C “Direct me” pertains to life; “teach” to knowledge.

H That I may do nothing perversely.

C It is salvation for a Christian to believe that God is his savior.

“All day”: as though he were saying, “every day,” that is, with no day omitted, but throughout my continuous life I have awaited your mercy and recompense.

A Thus I have waited for you, whom people think has forgotten them while you delay, patiently awaiting the delay of your compassion in bringing help.

6 Remember your compassions, Lord, and your mercies, which are from the age.

C Here, in human fashion, “remember” is said of one who can never forget anything. “Compassions” pertains to pious actions; “mercy” to a compassionate nature, since compassion is a matter of action, mercy of the heart. “Ages” are so called because times continually revolve within themselves, and the word is said to derive from following.

7 Do not remember the sins of my youth and my ignorances.

C Some wish a transgression to be a lighter form of sin, as something abandoned, called so because it abandons the way of equity.

H “Of my youth,” that is, what I did in adolescence.

C He says “ignorances” because we do many things without knowing that they are evil. Therefore he prays that God not remember his transgressions but rather remember him through his mercy.

8 According to your mercy, remember me, you; because of your goodness, Lord.

H “According to your mercy,” that is, remember me not because of my merit but because of your mercy.

C His goodness is also rightly proclaimed, of whom it is said: “No one is good except God alone” (Matthew XIX).

9 The Lord is sweet and upright; therefore he will give a law to sinners on the way.

C He is called sweet because he provides the delightful gifts of heavenly life.

He is upright,

H because he repays each person according to his works.

He will give the law of charity, through which, when we forgive an offense, we are reconciled to God.

C “On the way,” that is, in the present life, where the law is established and we are admonished to live rightly.

10 He will direct the meek in judgment; he will teach the gentle his ways.

C A person is called “directed” who is made straight from being crooked.

The meek are so called as though “accustomed to the hand,” that is, those who tolerate injuries and do not repay evil for evil.

The gentle are those who are disturbed by no rage but persevere continually in gentleness of spirit. He directs them in judgment because he makes them attain the blessedness he has promised. The next verse explains what the Lord’s ways are.

11 All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth, for those who seek his covenant and his testimonies.

C All the Lord’s ways are mercy because he anticipates everything with his goodness. They are truth because he judges all things justly.

To whom can such things belong? It follows: “to those who seek his covenant.”

H That is, the new covenant; and his testimonies, that is, the sayings of the earlier prophets.

12 For your name’s sake, ÷ Lord .. you will be gracious to my sin, for it is great.

C This is appropriately referred to the person of the Church, which says that she has been saved because of the name of Jesus, which our tongue interprets as “Savior.” “For my sin is great,” because unless divine compassion comes to the aid, as life extends, so human frailty is entangled in sins; for it continually increases with the passage of time.

13 Who is the person who fears the Lord? He will establish a law for him on the way he has chosen.

C In his customary manner, the prophet asks: “Who is the person who fears the Lord?” A law has been established for him, lest he sin in the security of ignorance; “on the way,” that is, in the holiness of his purpose.

H Or, “on the way of faith”; for if he fears, he is not deceived by security.

14 His soul shall dwell among good things, and his offspring shall inherit the earth.

H The soul of the righteous shall dwell among good things, that is, it shall persevere in hope of future rewards.

C “His offspring,” that is, good works, shall inherit the land of the living. They shall be received into eternal security, and his possession shall no longer be disturbed by any expulsion. For whoever holds something as an inheritance rejoices in the firmest possession.

15 The Lord is the strength of those who fear him, and his covenant is made manifest to them.

H We are weak and feeble; if we fear the Lord, he will be our strength, so that we are not shaken by the waves of this age. And the law is made manifest to us in Christ, though previously it was veiled by the letter.

C It is exceedingly necessary for us that his law be declared to us by his own gift. Without this, we can neither understand anything good nor bring it to completion.

16 My eyes are always toward the Lord, for he will draw my feet out of the snare.

H “My eyes are toward the Lord,” that is, let the eyes of my heart, or my mind, always think upon the Lord, for he will draw my senses out of the devil’s snare, by which I was previously captured through the pleasures of the world.

17 Look upon me and have mercy on me, for I am solitary and poor.

C Above he said, “My eyes are always toward the Lord”; now he says, “Look upon me as I look upon you.”

Have mercy on me,

H because I am wretched.

The Christian people are solitary.

C They are solitary for him because they alone guard the sacraments of faith; poor because, separated from the allurements of the world, they are filled with no worldly ambition [Col. 0119B].

18 The tribulations of my heart have multiplied; deliver me from my necessities.

C The tribulations of the Church have multiplied while she extends her thoughts through the calamities of the world, in which she has been sown. For the one who suffers on behalf of many must necessarily be weighed down by a heavy burden.

He speaks of the necessities he suffered through the plots of persecutors and heretics. These are the ones who desire to inflict death upon Christians.

A Necessities are rightly called adversities, because they are necessary for those striving toward the kingdom of heaven.

G Or by “necessities” he means venial sins, without which we cannot live.

19 See my humility and my labor, and forgive all my sins.

A C “See,” that is, look upon me graciously.

The humility of the Church appears when she patiently teaches the undisciplined.

C Her labor is that she is wearied by many persecutions. It is rightly that she begs for all her sins to be forgiven, because the hard labor of endurance always awaits the judge’s mercy; that is, because of this humility and labor, she deserves forgiveness of sins.

20 Look upon my enemies, for they have multiplied, and they hate me with unjust hatred.

H “Look upon” is the voice of the Church concerning her persecutors.

C She prays that they may return, because whoever is looked upon by him is converted without delay.

“They have multiplied”: in sins.

“With unjust hatred” he added because there is also a just hatred, as in: “With perfect hatred I hated them” (Psalm CXXXVIII). But these people hate me not with that just hatred but with an unjust one.

21 Guard my soul and deliver me; I shall not be put to shame, because I have hoped in you.

H “Guard”: the Church’s voice begs that she be guarded.

A Lest she turn to imitate them, and deliver her from every evil.

H Lest I be confounded either here or in the future, because I have hoped in you and invoked you.

C For she has chosen to invoke the one whom she knows does not reject those who piously plead with him.

A Therefore, because I have hoped not in myself but in you, I shall not be confounded.

22 The innocent and the upright have clung to me, because I have waited for you.

C “The innocent” means the little ones regenerated by holy baptism. “The upright” means those who, already mature in age, have turned away from sins. The Church says that they have clung to her because she has waited for God, patiently enduring adversities.

23 Deliver Israel, O God, from all his tribulations.

C “Deliver Israel, O God,” that is, O God of those who see you.

A Or: O God, deliver Israel, that is, the people whom you have prepared for the vision of yourself.

C Because he regards as pleasing those to whom he grants the sight of contemplating him.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM XXIV

Deliver us from all our distresses, most gentle God, because we lift up our souls to you. Forget, we beseech you, the sins of our youth and our former ignorance, and if we sin through negligence in any matter, mercifully forgive us. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, and so forth.

## PSALM XXV

### ARGUMENT OF PSALM XXV

C The entire text of this psalm is to be applied to the perfect Christian, who, persevering in the Church through the praise of various merits, consoles himself with divine benefits.

### TT. For David himself: ÷ a Psalm ..

[Col. 0120C]

C This entire psalm is to be applied to the perfect Christian; nevertheless, when such a person sings the hymn, it is necessary that its meaning be referred to Christ the Lord by the power of interpretation.

1 Judge me, Lord, for I have entered in my innocence; and, hoping in the Lord, I shall not be weakened.

C “Judge me, Lord”: the holy man asks for judgments because he was confident in the Lord’s mercy. He enters in innocence, that is, living among sinners without sinning. He does not trust in his own strength but in God; therefore he will not be weakened.

2 Test me, Lord, and try me; burn my kidneys and my heart.

H The Church asks to be tested so that she may know herself and be known by others.

C There are two kinds of temptation: one from the Lord, by which he tests the good in order to instruct them; the other from the devil, which always leads to death.

“Burn my kidneys”:

H That is, apply the Holy Spirit to my desires.

“And my heart,” that is, apply the Holy Spirit to my thoughts.

3 For your mercy is before my eyes, and I have been pleasing in your truth.

C Because the prophet had the Lord’s mercy before the eyes of his heart, he did not fear the dangers of temptations.

To please is to merit eternal grace together with the saints.

H C “In your truth,” that is, in Christ, who is the truth. Therefore, illuminated by grace, he pleased God and himself in mind.

4 I have not sat in the council of vanity, and I shall not enter with those who act wickedly.

H “I have not sat in the council,” that is, I have not been joined to those who act vainly in council against my Christ. “Entering” here signifies the beginning of evil action, which the holy man declares foreign to himself.

The vain are those occupied with futile investigations and who waste time in superfluous narration. The impious are those who strive to corrupt the divine Scriptures with perverse questions, such as heretics.

5 I have hated the assembly of the wicked, and I shall not sit with the impious.

C It is not enough to avoid the perverse and wicked unless they are also displeasing in the mind; therefore he says: “I have hated the assembly of the wicked,”

H that is, of Jews or heretics, who are called wicked.

“And I shall not sit with the impious,” who not only conceived evil but completed it in action; I shall have no fellowship with them.

6 I shall wash my hands among the innocent, and I shall surround your altar, Lord.

C He has washed his hands: whoever has cleansed his own deeds through tearful satisfaction. The altar is so called from height, as though it were a high altar.

H It signifies faith. To surround it is to adorn it with good works.

C Or the heavenly altar, to which the Lord entered as priest on our behalf.

A Or the altar means the mind.

7 So that I may hear the voice of praise and recount all your wonders.

A “So that I may hear the voice of praise,” that is, so that I may learn how to praise you, not presuming upon myself because of the good in me.

C By the “voice of praise” he perhaps means that which is always sung in the heavenly temple before Christ: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of Sabaoth” (Isaiah XVI). And he says that he recounts the wonders that the blessed Church daily sings in the celebration of the Masses.

8 Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house and the place where your glory dwells.

H “Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house,” that is, the holy priests and other saints.

C In them the glory of God is known to dwell. “The place where it dwells” signifies the secret place of the human breast. “Your glory,” because Christ makes glorious whatever he deigns to inhabit. The beauty of God’s house and the place of his dwelling are therefore the same.

A To love the beauty of God’s house is to love the good in the Church, who adorn the Church.

9 Do not destroy my soul with the impious, nor my life with men of blood.

H “Do not destroy me with the impious,” namely the Jews, who in their impiety handed over the gentle one.

A Or all the wicked are impious.

C “Men of blood” are those who live carnally, or those who shed Christ’s blood. Such people perish from the future Jerusalem.

10 In whose hands are iniquities; their right hand is filled with gifts.

H “In whose hands,” that is, in whose works, are iniquities. Their right hand is filled with gifts when the traitor Judas accepted money for Christ.

A Or those who, if they do anything good, do it for the sake of gifts.

H A For what was given to them to receive eternal things they turn toward the gifts of the world, considering piety to be gain.

11 But I have entered in my innocence; redeem me and have mercy on me.

H “But I in my innocence”: the Church speaks on behalf of the good.

C And through the devotion of a holy life she has entered into spiritual treasures.

“Redeem me,” that is, at your coming, by your precious blood.

“Have mercy,” namely in this world, where you spare those who plead with you.

12 My foot has stood on the straight path; in the churches I shall bless ÷ you .. Lord.

H “My foot,” that is, my understanding or affection, has stood in Christ, who is the straight way.

“In the churches”:

C Among the Christian peoples, he says that he will praise the Lord [Col. 0122B] Christ.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM XXV

Bestow your mercy, Lord, upon your supplicating servants, and make us devoted to your truth, so that, with our actions restored to innocence, we may deserve to be delivered from the impious. Through our Lord Jesus Christ.

## PSALM XXVI

### ARGUMENT OF PSALM XXVI

C The voice of the prophet saying that he fears God and fears no one else, because amid the adversities of the world God himself is his refuge; and by the prophetic spirit he promises himself hope of future blessedness.

### TT. A Psalm of David ÷ before he was anointed:

H David was anointed once under his father Jesse in Bethlehem (1 Kings XVI), a second time in Hebron (2 Kings II), and a third time (2 Kings V) when he reigned over Israel. Of these three anointings, the middle one pertains to this psalm. David bears the figure of Christ; Christ was anointed in baptism.

1 The Lord is my illumination, and my salvation; whom shall I fear?

H The voice of the Church directed to Christ. She says that she does not fear being covered by any darkness, since the Lord always illuminates and saves her, nor can she fear anyone when such a defender protects her.

2 The Lord is the protector of my life; from whom shall I tremble?

H She confesses that the Lord himself is her protector; therefore she is not afraid to tremble before an enemy,

[Col. 0122D]

that is, before the devil, or a heretic, or a persecutor.

3 When evildoers draw near against me, to eat my flesh,

C “When they draw near against me”: here he shows the desires of savage enemies, who desire not only to destroy but also, in their avid fury, to devour human flesh itself with cruelty.

A Or “flesh” means the desires of the flesh, which are food for harmful enemy spirits and persecutors; or even the bodies of the saints, granted to them for persecution—flesh with which they take delight in feeding by persecuting.

4 My enemies who trouble me have themselves been weakened and have fallen.

H “Those who trouble me,” that is, demons or persecutors, were then weakened when Christ assumed our humanity.

C For those who hasten to devour innocent blood fall.

5 If armies should stand against me, my heart shall not fear.

C An army is a strong fortification, which the force of an attacking enemy cannot easily conquer. But he says that all these things are contemptible to him when he is fortified by divine assistance.

6 If battle should rise against me, in this I shall hope.

H “If battle should rise against me”: the Church calls the battles of demons “battle,” and she hopes in Christ’s help and defense.

C For in tumultuous battles the glory of the victor always appears. A virtue cannot be shown to lie hidden if it has not been tested in combat.

7 One thing I have asked of the Lord; this I shall seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life.

H “One thing I have asked”: some think this means one charity or grace, or else that he refers to the request itself, since in Hebrew the word “one” is neuter, that is, “the Lord.”

“this”: that is, I shall seek the Lord, and so forth.

“That I may dwell in the house of the Lord,” that is, in perpetual life.

C And this not for a short time, but throughout all the days of my life.

8 That I may see the will of the Lord and visit his temple.

[Col. 0123C]

H “That I may see the will of the Lord,” that is, the love of God.

C He also sees the will of the Lord who understands and keeps his commandments. He visits his temple who strengthens Christ’s Church with sacred admonitions.

A Or he calls the temple the contemplation of the Lord’s glory; another text has: “that I may contemplate the Lord’s delight.”

9 For he hid me in his tabernacle; on the day of evils he protected me in the hidden place of his tabernacle.

H Therefore Christ has hidden the Church with himself, lest the storms of temptations harm it; or, as the Apostle says: “For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Col. 3). He does not say that the days themselves are evil, but that evil days are so called because of our evil deeds. C “In the hidden place of his tabernacle”: that is, in the secret of his divine power, he has always protected us and continues to protect us. H Or, “in the day of evils,” when the wicked prevail. C To be hidden means not to be exposed to the eyes of those who seek; to be protected means to be freed from every fear and danger.

10 He exalted me upon a rock: And now he has exalted my head above my enemies.

“He exalted me upon a rock,” that is, in Christ through faith. He exalted this head. C A “Head” here stands for the mind, by whose animation we are able to remain steadfast. “Above my enemies”: H that is, above carnal movements. C Or, vicious desires, above which our mind is raised when it is kept pure by divine assistance.

11 I went around and sacrificed in his tabernacle a sacrifice of shouting: I will sing and speak a psalm to the Lord.

C “I went around,” that is, I examined in my mind by what power God made heaven and created all things from nothing. A He redeemed the human being and the world believing in him; and I found what I should offer, namely praise. C “And I sacrificed in his tabernacle,” that is, I offered in his Church the sacrifice of praise. He says “of shouting,” namely because of the greatness of the praise.

C C “I will sing,” that is, I will preach. “I will speak a psalm,” that is, I will fulfill it in deed. For to sing is to proclaim praises with the voice alone, whereas to psalm is to preach them through one’s actions.

12 Hear, O Lord, my voice with which I cried to you: [Col. 0124B] Have mercy on me and hear me.

C Now the Church again asks to be heard; for it cried out earlier when it said, “that I may dwell in the house of the Lord,” since there is no satiety in divine things. The more sweetly God is tasted, the more he is desired; or it repeats this because it dwells in eternal glory by hope, but not yet in reality.

13 My heart said to you, “My face has sought you”: Your face, O Lord, I shall seek.

C Thus the faithful man said that his heart—that is, his desire—spoke to the Lord, because what he was thinking seemed to be what he offered. A “My face,” that is, my presence, [seeks] your presence; or, the beauty of my soul, given by you, [seeks] your beauty. C Indeed, the one who seeks the face of God is the one who keeps himself through holy conduct. Of such people it was said: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.” He also repeats, “Your face I shall seek”: although it is one and the same matter, its repetition shows that he sought Christ with ardent devotion.

14 Do not turn your face from me: Do not turn away in anger from your servant.

C For the holy man asks not to be made alien from the face of God. Again he asks that God not turn away from him at the time when he grants the saints the vision of his majesty. He calls the time of judgment “anger,” when he separates the wicked from the good. A Or, he does not turn away in anger when he permits someone to fall so that he may rise more cautiously and more strongly.

15 You are my helper; do not abandon me: Nor despise me, O God my savior.

C The Prophet asks not to be abandoned by the Lord, for he knows that if the Lord abandons him, no power will be able to govern him. H Christ is our Savior; and the Prophet asks not to be despised by him—that is, not to commit any sins by which he might be despised by God. A As if he were saying: “You created me in vain, O God, and you redeemed me in vain, O Savior, if you despise preserving me in the good you gave me, since without you my effort is nothing.”

16 For my father and my mother have abandoned me: But the Lord has taken me up.

C He calls Adam, the first man, his father, and Eve his mother, from whom the human race descended. They abandoned me in this misery to which they exposed me. But the Lord, having taken flesh, [Col. 0125A] took me up in place of the true parent, for eternal inheritance.

17 Establish a law for me, O Lord, in your way: And guide me on a straight path because of my enemies.

C “Establish a law for me”: the Prophet asks that a law be established for him, that is, that the understanding of the Gospel be opened to those who were to come. “In your way,” that is, in Christ. “Because of my enemies,” that is, heretics who, with evil intent, tried to overthrow that path—that is, the understanding of the Scriptures. A Or: “O Lord, because I strive toward you and am already on the way to you, establish a law in it to guide me, lest I go astray, and lest your discipline abandon me when I wander; and guide me further in the straightness of narrow places, because of those lying in wait,” and so forth.

18 Do not hand me over to the souls of those who afflict me, for unjust witnesses have risen against me: And iniquity has lied to itself ÷ .. [Col. 0125B]

H “Do not hand me over,” that is, so that the spirit of the perverse may not be satisfied by the adversities that befall me. Unjust witnesses rose against Christ, saying: “This man said, ‘Destroy this temple, and in three days I will rebuild it’” (Matt. 26). “Iniquity has lied to itself,” because each person’s vice returns upon its own author. C He rightly said “to itself,” because the one who strives to bring false testimony receives the punishment for his own lie.

19 I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord: In the land of the living.

H The voice of the Church: although it is exposed to so many dangers, it nevertheless believes that it will see good things—that is, receive by faith the inheritance of the kingdom of heaven, in which the saints reign with Christ.

20 Wait for the Lord; act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened. And endure the Lord.

C “Wait for the Lord,” namely, the one who does not deceive by promising, who does not charge or reproach when granting. “Manfully”: acting is commanded not only to men but also to women. “Let your heart be strengthened,” so that it does not despair from weariness and exhaustion. “Endure the Lord,” that is, endure what you suffer; do not grow weary or depart, and await what you believe.

PRAYER FROM PSALM 26

Defend us from the camps and battles of the enemy, O God, helper of all, so that, enduring perpetually in your house, we may be worthy to receive your face through spiritual contemplation. Through our Lord, etc.

PSALM 27

ARGUMENT OF PSALM 27

C The Lord Christ, in that by which he is human, prays that his prayer may be heard, and gives thanks because he has been heard. He asks that, just as he himself was raised by the power of his divinity, so his people, who will believe in his name, may be saved.

TT. ÷ To David himself ..  

C David, as we said, is interpreted as “strong of hand,” and signifies the Savior, who is strong of hand indeed because he cast down the prince of darkness. It should therefore be noted [Col. 0126A] that this is the third of those psalms that briefly commemorate the Lord’s Passion and resurrection.

1 To you, O Lord, I shall cry: My God, do not be silent toward me: +Lest you be silent toward me .. and I become like those who descend into the pit.

C The Lord Christ cries to the Father at the time of his Passion, asking that he not be silent toward him—that is, that he not fail to grant the petitioner’s request, but rather answer him. H As if he had said: “If you are silent, I shall be like those who perish; if you are silent, you will not be recognized.” C The pit signifies this age, for a pit is so called because it lies hidden beneath the earth. The humanity of the Word therefore asks not to be like other human beings; for although he assumed the common condition of flesh, [Col. 0126B] he nevertheless surpassed all created things. H Or, the pit signifies hell.

2 ÷ From .. hear + O Lord .. the voice of my supplication while I pray to you: While I lift up my hands toward your holy temple.

H Christ prayed on the cross for the whole world. He lifted his hands—that is, he stretched them out on the cross. “Toward the holy temple”: that is, so that he might prepare a temple for the Father, namely the body of the Church. C Nor is it unreasonable to understand the temple as heaven, since divine Scripture shows it to be the Lord’s dwelling.

3 Do not ÷ together .. hand me over with sinners: And with those who practice iniquity ÷ do not destroy me ..  

H He speaks of the sinners among whom he hung, namely the thieves. [Col. 0126C] C With those who practice iniquity, he asks not to have any share.

4 Those who speak peace with their neighbor, but evil is in their hearts:

H They were speaking thus (Matt. 22). The Jews spoke peace with Christ, saying: “Teacher, we know that you are truthful.” There was peace on their lips, but wickedness in their heart. C They were rightly called evil, because they hastened maliciously to betray their neighbor.

5 Give them according to their works: And according to the wickedness of their schemes:

H He asks that they be given according to their works, not by wishing it, but by foretelling it. “And according to the wickedness of their schemes”: C that is, so that they might harm the innocent one who had come to save them, and hand him over to death.

6 + According to the works of their hands .. grant them. Repay their recompense to them.

C There are four kinds of recompense. The first is when evil is given for good, as with the Jews toward Christ. The second is when good is given for good, as God gives to the elect. The third is when evil is repaid for evil, as in the saying: “Go into the eternal fire” (Matt. 25). The fourth is when, as this passage says, good is given for evil: those who had been persecutors later become converts and praisers of Christ.

7 For they did not understand the works of the Lord, nor the works of his hands: You will destroy them and will not build ÷ them ..  

C They did not understand the works of God, namely when he taught the people the way of truth. “Nor the works of his hands”: certainly they did not consider them; if they had considered them, they would have been terrified rather than despising them. Thus he says that they will be destroyed so that they should not be built again. Yet this appears to have been said prophetically rather than as an expression of the quality of anger.

8 Blessed is the Lord, for he has heard the voice of my supplication.

C “Blessed is the Lord”: the voice of Christ to the Father, because he heard him—although he is blessed even if he does not hear the voice of supplication—saying: “I have glorified, and again I will glorify” (John 12). Yet he is properly called blessed when we give thanks by blessing; therefore he is aptly called blessed who deigned to hear.

9 [Col. 0127B] The Lord is my helper and my protector: ÷ And .. in him my heart hoped. And I was helped.

C “Helper” pertains to the dangers of life, which, with the Father’s help, he overcame in the Passion. “Protector,” because he surrounded him with his defense against diabolical snares. In death, the humanity hoped in the divinity. “I was helped,” in tribulation, so that I might rise again.

10 But my flesh blossomed again: And by my will I shall confess to him.

C The flesh therefore blossomed when it sprang forth sinlessly from the Virgin, like the beautiful adornment of a flower, as Isaiah says: “And a flower shall rise from his root” (Isa. 11). But it blossomed again when it rose from the dead. H “I shall confess to you,” as in: “I shall confess to you, Lord, Father of heaven and earth” (Matt. 11), and so forth.

11 The Lord is the strength of his people: And he is the protector of the salvations of his Christ.

C The Lord is rightly called the strength of his people when, with his help, all adversities are overcome. “Protector,” because he covers them and frees them from impending evils. “Of the salvations,” that is, of the righteous.

H He added “of his Christ,” for whoever has been baptized in Christ is himself also called Christ—that is, anointed.

12 Save your people, O Lord, and bless your inheritance: And rule them, and raise them up forever.

C The humanity of the Word prays for the Christian people—for whose sake it is shown to have been assumed—that it may be saved in this world through faithful satisfaction. He calls the Church Christ’s inheritance, which he acquired with his holy blood. H It belongs to the Father and to him, since he said: “All that is yours is mine, and mine is yours” (John 17). He asks that this inheritance be blessed, so that it may increase in virtues and in number. C He asks that devoted peoples be ruled, lest they desire carnal things; that they be raised up, so that they may advance in understanding the Scriptures and in holy works; that, cleansed of earthly vices, they may be brought to eternal rewards. And he asks that this be done until that eternal age, which no other age follows.

PRAYER FROM PSALM 27

O most powerful God, strength of all, save your people from those who descend into the pit, and bind us together unanimously in your holy temple, so that we may hold in our hearts the peace that we proclaim with our mouths to our neighbors. Through our Lord, etc.

PSALM 28

ARGUMENT OF PSALM 28

C The Prophet generally admonishes believers to offer sacrifices to the Lord with devoted minds, enumerating in a sevenfold account the virtues of the Holy Spirit.

TT. A psalm of David ÷ at the completion of the tabernacle ..  

C The completion of the tabernacle signifies the perfection of the Catholic Church, which is shown to have been established throughout the whole world. For this entire psalm is filled with praise of the Holy Spirit.

1 ÷ Offer to the Lord, sons of God .. Offer to the Lord the sons of rams.

H The voice of Christ admonishes the preachers who, through grace, have been called into adoption as sons. What does it admonish? That they offer preaching and example. H C The rams are to be understood as the apostles. C For a ram is so called as if from “rushing with its forehead,” that is, “demolishing.” H It has two horns on its head, just as the holy apostles had the two Testaments that they preached. “The sons of rams” are the successors of the apostles.

2 Offer glory and honor to the Lord: Offer glory to the name of the Lord: Adore the Lord in his holy court ÷ ..  

H “Offer glory to the Lord,” so that the eternal God may be glorified through your works. “Offer to his name”: the Son is the name of the Father; the Church is the glory of Christ. That is, through you may his name become known among all nations. “Adore in the holy court.” C That is, worship him with the purest conscience; for it is itself the royal hall and dwelling place of the Holy Spirit.

3 The voice of the Lord is over the waters: The God of majesty has thundered: The Lord is over many waters.

H “The voice of the Lord,” that is, the preaching of God—namely, of Christ through himself and his apostles—is over the waters, that is, over the peoples, as in: “Many waters are many peoples” (Rev. 17). “The God of majesty,” the God of power, has thundered. The Lord is over the waters, that is, he preached with terror from the tabernacle of the assumed body to the peoples, saying: “Repent” (Matt. 4). G Behold the first gift of the Holy Spirit: fear, which Christ gave to human hearts through preaching. For “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom and repentance” (Ps. 110).

4 The voice of the Lord is in power: The voice of the Lord is in majesty.

H Therefore the voice of the Lord is rightly said to be in power, because he speaks in each saint. C No obstacle can oppose him. “In majesty”: for what is more majestic than the Holy Spirit? When he illumines the heart, he makes it perceive so that good things are desired and every evil thing is fled. G “In power” signifies the gift of piety; “in majesty,” the gift of knowledge.

5 The voice of the Lord breaks the cedars: And the Lord will break the cedars of Lebanon.

H Cedars are called the proud or exalted. C The cedar is rightly compared with the proud: it produces no useful fruit, and so too does detestable arrogance, which brought sin into the world. The cedars that grow in Lebanon become taller than cedars growing elsewhere, and they signify the nobles and kings of this world, who despise the rest of humanity as though they were lowly shrubs. The Lord will break them when, having cast down the proud, he chooses the humble. G In the breaking of the cedars, the gift of fortitude is understood, since he makes those who have been broken—that is, humbled and converted—endure anything for Christ.

6 And he will crush them like a calf of Lebanon: And the beloved one like the son of unicorns.

H This calf signifies Christ. Just as a calf breaks tender branches with its horns, so Christ will break the Jews. He is also called the beloved Son of God through the assumption of the body, and “the son of unicorns,” that is, of the Jews, because according to the flesh he was from the tribe of the Jews. The Jews are called unicorns because of the one Law they had, through which they raised themselves up in pride. We have both Testaments; they receive only the Old. We have two horns, that is, both Testaments.

7 The voice of the Lord cuts through the flame of fire: The voice of the Lord shakes the wilderness: ÷ and the Lord will shake the wilderness .. Kadesh.

H “The voice of the Lord cutting through,” that is, his help amid persecutors, by which he assists his saints. Thus the persecution of the raging is understood as a flame of fire; or he calls lusts “flame,” which through confession and grace he makes cease. “The voice of the Lord shakes the wilderness,” [Col. 0129C] that is, preaching will move the soul that had been desolate. For a soul occupied by vices is called desolate; once those vices have been shaken off, it becomes habitable by God. C Those who have not yet received the gift of faith are called a wilderness. H The Lord will move them from unbelief to faith. C Kadesh is interpreted as “the movement of a moth.” G This cutting through of the flame indicates the gift of counsel, by which the consent to and action of sin or persecution are interrupted; in the shaking of the wilderness, the gift of understanding is signified.

8 The voice of the Lord prepares the stags, and will reveal the dense thickets: And in his temple all will say, “Glory.”

H “Stags” signifies the preachers whom he prepared when he gave them the Holy Spirit and sent them to preach. “He revealed the dense thickets,” that is, through the Holy Spirit he disclosed to them the obscure things of the divine Scriptures. G Thus by the stags the wise are understood, who, ascending to lofty places through contemplation, overcome and repel the poisonous tongues of heretics. You therefore have the seventh gift of the Holy Spirit, namely wisdom. C For this reason, in his Church all who possess these gifts give glory.

9 The Lord makes the flood dwell there: And the Lord will sit as king forever.

C “The Lord makes the flood dwell there.” Here the flood signifies baptism, or the waters of baptism, through which a human being is cleansed just as the world was cleansed through the flood; and the Holy Spirit dwells in them. H “And the Lord will sit” in the saints—for they are called his seat—forever, that is, unto the age of the age; or Christ will sit at the right hand of the Father.

10 The Lord will give strength to his people: The Lord will bless his people with peace.

H The Lord will give strength—that is, faith and courage against the storms of this world—to the Christian people. And he will bless them here and in the future, when he will say: “Come, blessed of my Father.” “With peace,” in himself, because he himself is our true peace.

PRAYER FROM PSALM 28

Give strength to your people, O Lord, and make us a temple of the Holy Spirit, so that with a pure heart we may prepare for you an acceptable burnt offering. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, etc.

PSALM 29

[Col. 0130B]

ARGUMENT OF PSALM 29

C The voice of Christ giving thanks to the Father after his most glorious resurrection.

TT. A psalm of the song of the dedication of the house of David.

C The house signifies the temple of the Lord’s body. The dedication signifies the resurrection of that same Lord of ours. He dedicated it when he rose from the dead; for then his body was brought into eternal glory. We call something “dedicated” when the newness of a house is assigned to the most distinguished use. The house of David is so named because of his offspring. From him the Savior derived the origin of his flesh.

1 I will exalt you, O Lord, for you have taken me up: And you have not delighted my enemies over me.

[Col. 0130C] H “I will exalt you, O Lord.” The voice of Christ to the Father, or the voice of the Church to Christ: that is, “I will praise you, for you have taken me up.” C Through the dispensation by which I rose from the dead. “You have not delighted,” because the Jews could not extinguish Christ as they wished. He used “you have delighted” in place of “you have caused to delight.”

2 My God, I cried to you: And you healed me.

H The prayer of Christ or of the Church: “You healed me,” that is, you caused me to rise again. C Christ was healed when, by rising, he placed the flesh of our weakness in the eternal joys of life and made us safe.

3 O Lord, you led my soul up from hell: You saved me from those descending into the pit.

[Col. 0130D] A H “O Lord, you led me up”: this requires no explanation. For it is evident that Christ’s soul, together with the souls of the saints, was recalled by God from hell. C Those descending into the pit are the ones who live in the iniquity of this age. He was therefore saved from such people, because he was freed from their fellowship when he rose from the dead.

4 Sing psalms to the Lord, his saints: And confess to the memory of his holiness.

H The Prophet urges the saints to praise the one by whom they were saved. He said “to the memory of his holiness” because he deigned to remember us, who were living in the shadow of death—that is, of sin. H That is, remember this benefit by which he freed you.

5 [Col. 0131A] For there is anger in his indignation: And life in his will.

C His indignation is the death of the sinner. H God’s indignation occurred when Adam sinned. His anger was the just vengeance by which he expelled him from paradise. “And life in his will”: whoever does the will of God remains in eternal life. And just as it happened in Adam, so it happens in each sinner.

6 In the evening weeping will remain: And in the morning, joy.

H “Evening” is understood as this entire present life, because on account of Adam’s sin all weep or groan until the end of the age, when they remember the good things of paradise that they lost in Adam. And “morning” is joy, when in the resurrection they come together into freedom; or “evening” is when Mary was weeping, and “joy” because Christ rose. A He says “will remain,” that is, “will remain for a long time,” because from the time of Adam’s sin until the end of the age—

7 But I said in my abundance: I shall not be moved forever.

C “But I said in my abundance.” There was abundance in the Son of the ever-virgin Mary, because the Word became flesh and dwelt among us. He rightly said that he could not be moved forever, namely by God, whose majesty granted him the gifts of confidence.

8 O Lord, in your will: You granted strength to my beauty.

C “O Lord, in your will.” The voice of Christ asserts that strength was given from above by the Father to him as man—strength, namely, that by which he is not moved by God. A Through this strength he is free from every sin and shines with the fullness of every grace. Likewise, he possesses that beauty of which it is written: “You are beautiful beyond the sons of men” (Ps. 44).

9 You turned your face from me: And I became troubled.

H God turned his face from Adam when he sinned. He was troubled when he was cast out of paradise under the curse. A Or, he turned his face from Christ when he exposed him to the Passion, and the humanity and weakness of the flesh began to be afraid, troubled, and sorrowful.

10 To you, O Lord, I shall cry: [Col. 0131D] And I shall pray to my God.

H “To you, O Lord, I shall cry”: the Lord Christ says this, who cried out on the cross when he interceded with the Father for the redeemed people.

11 What profit is there in my blood: When I descend into corruption?

C Christ therefore asks not that he should not die, but that his flesh, dissolved by corruption, should not be defiled. H As if the humanity had said: “There is no profit in my shedding blood unless I rise from the dead.” A For if I do not rise, I shall announce to no one and win no one; therefore he adds: “Will the dust …?”

12 Will dust confess to you: Or will it announce your truth?

H “Will dust confess to you?” That is, will the crowd of the impious, still moved like dust by every wind of doctrine, be able to be justified if I do not rise? Nor will it announce your truth—that is, your Christ, who is the truth.

13 The Lord heard and had mercy on me: The Lord ÷ became .. my helper.

H “The Lord heard,” that is, God the Father. “He had mercy,” because he caused me to rise from the dead. “He became my helper,” because he made me the firstborn of the dead.

14 You turned my mourning into joy for me: You cut apart my sackcloth and surrounded me with gladness.

H “You turned my mourning,” when I said, “My soul is sorrowful,” into joy, when I said: “Go, announce to my brothers” (Matt. 28). C The sackcloth—that is, the body of Christ—was cut apart when he himself deigned to die for us. H He girded it with joy, namely through the resurrection of immortality.

15 So that my glory may sing to you and I may not be pierced: O Lord my God, I shall confess to you forever.

C For we have said that singing properly pertains to the joy of the mind. Christ’s glory is the majesty of the Father, from whom he heard: “This is my beloved Son” (Matt. 17). A And the glory of the Son sings to the Father, since it is the cause of the Son’s glory: that the Father may be praised and loved. C And because he was pierced once—that is, crucified—he declares that he will not again be subjected to suffering. “I shall confess,” that is, with the saints I shall praise you with an eternal voice.

PRAYER FROM PSALM 29

Most merciful God, receiver of all, do not permit our enemies to delight over us, but strengthen us so firmly in your power that, with our mourning turned into joy, we may continually cultivate the memory of your holiness. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, etc.

PSALM 30

ARGUMENT OF PSALM 30

C A The voice of Christ placed upon the cross, praying to the Father that he be freed from impending evils; and giving thanks for himself and the faithful people.

TT. A psalm of David. For the end.

C We have frequently said that the words contained in the title are to be referred to Christ, to whom this entire psalm must be fitted, since it sings of his Passion and resurrection.

1 In you, O Lord, I have hoped; I shall not be confounded forever: In your justice deliver me.

C Christ prays to the Father from the nature of the humanity he assumed, asking that, cast down from his hope, he not suffer the reproaches of human insult, adding “forever,” where his contemplation remained fixed. “In your justice,” by which you are accustomed to assist those who pray. “Deliver me” pertains to removing the dangers of this world.

2 Incline your ear to me: Hasten to rescue me.

C He said “incline,” because of the lowliness of his members: since the human condition could not reach divinity, divinity, having inclined itself, descended to it. “Hasten,” that is, hasten to grant the swiftest resurrection.

3 Be for me a protecting God and a house of refuge: So that you may save me.

H The voice of the Church: “A protecting God,” that is, a defending God, because there are many so-called gods, but for us there is one God, one faith, one baptism. He himself is the house of refuge, in which the Father dwells.

4 For you are my strength and my refuge: And for your name’s sake you will lead me and nourish me.

C “Strength” pertains to enduring what he suffered; “refuge” to the end of evils, when he overcame the iniquities of this age through the glorious end of death. [Col. 0133B] The Lord was a guide in his humanity when he caused his name to be known throughout all nations. He says that he was nourished until the Catholic Church reached maturity by his gift. H A That is, by gradually gathering the saints, he increases his body—that is, the Church.

5 You will lead me out of this snare that they hid for me: For you are my protector.

C The Jews therefore hid a snare for Christ, because they plotted secretly to destroy him by ambushes. Hence he says that he is to be led out, that is, swiftly raised to heavenly things by the benefit of the resurrection. He calls the Lord his protector because, while the Lord protects him, no adversity can prevail.

6 [Col. 0133C] Into your hands I commend my spirit: You have redeemed me, O Lord, God of truth.

H “Into your hands,” that is, into your power. C It was therefore fitting that such a spirit should be entrusted to so great a receiver. He also added who this Lord was: he is the God of truth. For he is especially the God of those who love truth and do not mingle themselves with any falsehood.

7 You hate those who observe vanities in vain.

C Truth therefore rightly hated vanity, because vanity operates in falsehood. H God is said to hate what he rejects. He added “in vain,” since vanity is called not only empty but also superfluous. A The vanity of this age is false happiness, which is observed in emptiness because it is lost; and it is observed superfluously when people act wickedly in order to possess it.

8 But I have hoped in the Lord: I shall exult and rejoice in your mercy.

C “I have hoped in the Lord,” where there is nothing vain, nothing superfluous, but everything is secure. To exult is to rejoice with great exhilaration of spirit. To rejoice is to be comforted by a moderated affection of the mind.

9 For you have regarded my humility: You have saved my soul from distresses.

C There was humility in the Most High because humanity adhered to him from the very conception. A distress is so called because it is placed in death—that is, established in the straits of death. For when we are bound by the snares of sins and cannot be released by our own power, it is called distress. A Distresses, therefore, are sins from which a human being cannot free himself.

10 And you did not enclose me in the hands of the enemy: You established my feet in a spacious place.

C “You did not enclose me,” because he was made free from the power of the devil. “You established,” that is, you made firm. “In a spacious place,” that is, in the homeland of virtues, in the region of the blessed. He calls his feet the moral virtues by which he walked through this world with firm steps. A The spacious place is charity; the feet are the affections of the soul.

11 Have mercy on me, O Lord, for I am troubled: My eye, my soul, and my belly have been troubled in anger.

[Col. 0134B] H “Have mercy on me, O Lord, for I am troubled.” This is the voice of those who are troubled by any tribulation; Christ speaks here in their person. As above, when he said, “You did not enclose me,” it may be understood of those rescued from tribulation; so too it may be understood of Christ when he said: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matt. 26). C He used “anger” for the indignation of his enemies. “The eye” signifies understanding, which we always trouble when we fear impending dangers. He calls his memory his belly, where he had stored the things that the Lord had promised him concerning his glorification. He understands “soul” as sensuality.

12 For my life has failed in sorrow: And my years in groaning.

C To fail means gradually to become less and to reach an end through certain diminutions of health; here it signifies that disturbance of Christ’s flesh by which the life of the flesh failed in his Passion. “And my years in groaning,” because the pain was not slight, where continual groaning resounded. A All Christ’s years were in groaning, because he always saw the future death, and they were completed in persecutions.

13 My strength has been weakened in poverty: And my bones have been troubled.

C The strength of the soul is established in poverty within Christ’s members, because human weakness lacks all good things. “Bones” signify bodily strength, because there should be no presumption either in strength of spirit or in hope of the flesh. H The strength of the body also existed in want and abandonment during the Passion.

14 I have become a reproach beyond all my enemies, and very greatly to my neighbors: And a terror to my acquaintances.

C By “enemies” he means the Jews. Innocent Christ was held among them as a reproach, while they polluted themselves by their wicked crime. We call the opposite of upright “unrighteous,” that is, dishonorable and disgraceful. “Reproach” signifies a greatly abominable crime. He calls “neighbors” those who, joined to him in the city of faith, nevertheless did not believe perfectly. He signifies by “acquaintances” the apostles, who were troubled during his Passion. H A Or he calls bad Christians “neighbors,” since in wickedness they are worse than all Christ’s other enemies.

15 Those who saw me outside fled from me: I have been forgotten like one dead from the heart.

H The apostles fled during Christ’s Passion, leaving him. Christ was given over to oblivion by unbelievers when they considered him dead in the flesh as nothing. C “Like one dead”: he is not called dead by the faithful, whose divinity is truly judged impassible, but he was considered dead by the minds of unbelievers. A He dies from the heart whose memory departs from the heart, just as people customarily forget the dead.

16 I have become like a lost vessel: For I heard the reproach of many who dwell around me.

C A lost vessel is one that has been broken and is useful for no purpose, and is therefore always thrown away. Thus Christ, dead, was thought by the faithless Jews to be cast away like a broken vessel. “I heard the reproach,” that is, of the faithless Jews dwelling around me. Such people are rightly called “those dwelling around,” because they wish to regard God’s law not spiritually but carnally. A For they are like bark surrounding the pith: they hold to the letter, enter into the spirit of the Scriptures, but always remain on the outside, in the bark of the letter that kills.

17 While they gathered together against me: They plotted to take my soul.

C He says that the greater part of the Jews plotted together to hand God over to death. H All plotted together to seek the soul of Christ—or the soul of the Church, in the case of heretics. C Every crime is more serious when it is carried out by the counsel of many.

18 But I hoped in you, O Lord; I said, “You are my God”: My lots are in your hands.

C The Son hoped in the Father because he knew that the Jews had no power against him; but by him we exist as creator, and by his ordering we are kept alive. H “My lots are in your hands,” that is, in the grace of the Holy Spirit. A He freely chooses whomever he wills, without merit. The lots, therefore—that is, God’s gracious election—are in his hands, that is, in God’s power, not ours.

19 Deliver me from the hand of my enemies: And from those who persecute me.

C He asks the Father himself to deliver him from the hand of his enemies, that is, the Jews, and from his persecutors—that is, pagans or heretics, who attack the Church of God by deceitful plots. A Those who persecute the Church most of all are those who, although they are Christians, refuse to live well. Because of them the Church has reproach, and among them this groaning voice says: “Make your face shine,” and so forth.

20 Make your face shine upon your servant: Save me in your mercy, O Lord; let me not be confounded, for I have called upon you.

C “Make your face shine,” that is, make it evident that you deign to look upon me, so that, just as they despair concerning the one who is dying, they may thus put their hope in the resurrection. H So that I may not be confounded, but may be saved from these persecutions.

21 Let the wicked be put to shame and led down into hell: Let deceitful lips become mute.

[Col. 0136A] H “Let the wicked be put to shame,” whether they are wicked demons or any evil persons, when they see the saints crowned whom they held in contempt, and see themselves condemned. C And when they look upon themselves, established in grave danger, let them quickly fall silent.

22 Who speak iniquity against the just: In pride and abuse.

C Falsehood speaks against truth when the Arians call the Lord the Creator’s creature. He added “in pride and abuse,” that is, in contempt. For when this falsehood heard that He had been scourged, it immediately burst into blasphemous words. A There was abuse when they crucified Him who had come in the flesh on their account, abusing God’s benefit.

23 How great is the multitude of your sweetness ÷, O Lord .. which you have hidden for those who fear you.

[Col. 0136B] H The multitude of sweetness consists in the many rewards which He has prepared for His Church, so that she may reign forever with His angels. C What is here perceived as hidden will be revealed openly at the future judgment. A C There is also here a manifold sweetness of God, when He corrects the good or spares them, makes promises, or disciplines those whom He loves; yet the wicked does not perceive it, having lost the palate of his heart through the fever of iniquity.

24 You have perfected it for those who hope in you: In the sight of the children of men.

C He perfected that sweetness in those who seek it with steadfast mind. “In the sight of the children,” that is, in that resurrection when He will restore eternal rewards to His saints. H “You have perfected,” as though he said, “you will perfect,” or “in the sight of those who sought human things and not heavenly things.”

25 You will hide them in the secrecy of your face: From the disturbance of men.

C “You will hide them in secrecy,” that is, in that resurrection, when the righteous enjoy the contemplation of God and obtain eternal rewards—a glory which the wicked do not see. Here he calls all persecutors and schismatics “men,” because here they are accustomed to disturb the Christian people.

26 You will protect them in your tabernacle: From the contradiction of tongues.

C Here the righteous are protected in the tabernacle, that is, in the Church; for there they are protected, where the wickedness of evil people is by no means permitted to harm them, while the unharmed souls of the righteous are preserved under every bodily affliction.

27 Blessed is the Lord, for he has made his mercy wonderful to me in a fortified city.

H Blessed is the Lord, whom every creature blesses. Yet He is not blessed by us as though He needed our blessing; rather, we bless Him so that we may deserve to receive blessing from Him. “He has made mercy wonderful in a city,” H C that is, in Jerusalem, which all nations surround. H It is in the middle of the world, because there He was born, suffered, and rose again.

28 [Col. 0137A] But I said in the excess of my mind: I have been cast away from the sight of your eyes.

H The Church is in an “excess of mind” when she considers what she lost in paradise, how God spoke with Adam through the angel, and how Adam saw God with his inner eyes. He was cast away from God’s sight when he transgressed God’s commandments, and all posterity was cast away in him.

29 Therefore you heard the voice of my prayer: When I cried to you.

C Christ says that He was heard in His members, because God’s grace is not slow to help the one who humbly beseeches the Lord. Christ was also heard when the Father’s voice was heard saying, “This is my beloved Son.” And when He cried to the Father, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew XVII).

30 Love the Lord, all his saints ÷ for .. the Lord will seek truth: And he will repay abundantly those who act proudly.

C He says “Love,” now as though addressing friends, not servants (John XV): it is the part of servants to fear, but of friends to love. The Lord seeks truth, which heretics do not know, bound as they are by false errors. Here he does not mean one particular vice by “pride,” but whatever is committed through depravity of conduct. He repays abundantly those who despise God’s commandments.

31 Act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened: All you who hope in the Lord.
