C “Act manfully,” that is, persevere most steadfastly in good works; do not fail through feminine softness, you who constantly offer your hearts to the Lord. For the hearts of the faithful are strengthened when they confirm their hope by the Lord’s power.

PRAYER FROM PSALM XXX

Most merciful Lord, we humbly beseech you for the immense multitude of your sweetness, that while we seek your truth, we may crush the swelling of detestable pride. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, etc.

PSALM XXXI

ARGUMENT OF PSALM XXXI

C The voice of the penitent and the words of the Lord responding that He surrounds with His mercy those who hope in Him.

TITLE. David, with understanding.

C Why did he place “David, with understanding” in this title, when all psalms have been written so that their meaning may be understood? The answer is: first, he mentions David because of the Lord Christ, since whatever this penitent is about to say refers to Him. Then he added “with understanding,” so that, when divinity has enabled us to understand our sins, we may then beseech Him for their cleansing. For in another psalm it is said, “Who understands his offenses?” (Psalm XVIII). Thus he speaks of understanding sins.

1 Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven: And whose sins have been covered.

H Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven, that is, washed away by the Lord through confession. Or, “whose sins have been covered,” that is, by charity, which covers a multitude of sins (Proverbs X), or veiled through repentance so that they may not be revealed at the judgment (1 Peter IV). C “Iniquities” are those committed before the faith has been received; “sins” are those incurred after the profession of faith or the grace of baptism.

2 Blessed is the man to whom the Lord has not imputed sin: Nor is there deceit in his spirit.

H Sin is not imputed to the one who sufficiently purges himself in this world through repentance, or cleanses himself through martyrdom. What is covered is not seen; what is not seen is not imputed; what is not imputed will not be punished. There is no deceit in the mouth of the one who professes himself a sinner. C For when we blame ourselves, it is truthful speech; when we wish to praise ourselves, it is a lie. The one who displeases himself is pleasing to the Lord.

3 For I was silent, my bones grew old: While I cried out all day long.

H “I was silent” is the voice of the wicked, who conceal their sins and refuse to speak of them in confession; therefore all my strength, that is, my virtue, grew old in weakness. A C As with a bodily wound which, when hidden, festers away from the physician. “While I cried out.” H They cry out, that is, if they possess anything good, they display it through vanity. “All day long,” H A that is, throughout their entire life—which is brief—they are silent about their sins, while they cry out and boast of their merits.

4 For day and night your hand was heavy upon me: I was turned into misery + my .. while the thorn is driven in. + Diapsalm .. [pause] ..

[Col. 0138C] H God’s hand is heavy upon sinners, that is, the power of vengeance on the day of judgment. C “Day and night” signifies continuous time. A person is called miserable because he is very ruinous; for “ruin” is so called as though one were falling into the depths. “I was turned into misery”: the one who had fallen from pride, so that the one who was formerly proud has now been made humble. The thorn is what raises and holds up the body; it is rightly placed here for pride. When broken, it does not cast one down to destruction, but raises one to salvation. H Misery is wretchedness. A Or “the thorn is fastened” when the conscience is pierced and suffers.

5 I made my sin known + to you .., and I did not hide my injustice.

C He makes his sin known who brings it to true confession. To cover something is to conceal it deeply in silence, or to hide it through dissimulation of the heart. Fools do this, thinking that God is unaware of what they do. Some think that a delict is a light sin, as though something had been negligently abandoned. Injustice, however, is something enormous or savagely committed. Here too the purity of the one confessing is shown, because he does not wish to conceal what he believed to be venial.

6 I said, “I will confess my injustice against myself to the Lord”: And you forgave the impiety of my sin. Diapsalm.

H “I said” in the heart, where God sees; “I will confess,” C that is, “I will acknowledge it publicly,” so that a devout and faithful confession may lead others to imitation. The impiety of the heart consisted in his having decided to remain silent, so that he might conceal something from the One who knows all things before they happen.

7 For this every saint prayed to you: At an opportune time.

H “For this he will pray,” that is, for this iniquity or forgiveness, which he mentioned above. He says “every saint,” because no one is free from sins. C “At an opportune time,” namely, in this life of the world, where conversion is permitted. For in hell, as was said above, no one confesses profitably to the Lord.

8 Yet in a flood of many waters: They will not draw near to him.

C The flood of many waters is the error of the worst people, who, tossed about by various depraved practices, establish multiple doctrines for themselves. They will not draw near to the Lord, because they depart from true religion.

9 You are my refuge from the tribulation that surrounded me: My exultation, deliver me from those surrounding me. Diapsalm.

C A refuge is that to which one flees in order to avoid dangers.

H “My exultation,” says the Church, “because I rejoice in you.” C Deliver me from enemies, whether from carnal vices or from unclean spirits, who hasten with headlong speed to destroy us.

10 I will give you understanding, and I will instruct you in this way in which you will walk: I will fix my eyes upon you.

[Col. 0139C] C Sinners do not have understanding except when the Lord, appeased by their conversion, forgives them. To understand is to act well and turn one’s desires toward God’s commandments. “I will instruct you,” as though I were teaching one who does not know. “In this way in which you will walk.” H He says, “I will teach you the way of confession, so that you do not depart from it.” C “I will fix my eyes upon you,” that is, I will direct the light of my understanding toward you.

11 Do not become like a horse and a mule: In whom there is no understanding.

C A horse without discernment serves the rider’s will, and runs wherever anyone mounts it. A mule patiently bears burdens; and for this reason neither has understanding, because the horse does not choose whom it should obey, nor does the mule understand under what burdens it is weighed down. Therefore the prophet forbids people to be ensnared by the devil’s deceits and burdened by vices.

12 With bit and bridle restrain their jaws: Those who do not draw near to you.

C The bit belongs to the mule; the bridle refers to the horse. “Bridle” is so called from restraining the wild animal; the ancients called a wild animal *gabal­lum*. These two restraints therefore hold back the animals, so that they proceed at the command of the one ordering them and are not carried away by their own wills. The jaws are the animals’ instruments by which food is chewed. Allegorically, therefore, he says that the jaws of the disobedient must be restrained, that is, that food should be given to them more sparingly, so that, weakened by fasts, they may submit to the Creator’s command.

13 Many are the scourges of the sinner: But mercy will surround the one who hopes in the Lord.

C Obstinate sinners, unwilling to walk along straight paths, endure many scourges, so that what they do not do willingly they may be compelled to fulfill when blows are applied. But mercy will surround the one who hopes in the Lord, so that no place may be left through which the devil can enter them.

14 Rejoice in the Lord and exult, you righteous: And glory, all you upright in heart.

C Every righteous person rejoices in the Lord. For the one who rejoices in himself is deceived by false presumption; but the one who rejoices in the Lord enjoys perpetual delight. To rejoice is to be soothed by the sweetness of a silent mind. To exult [Col. 0140B] is to rejoice with the fervor of an excited spirit. And glory, you who are upright in heart, and believe that through God’s service they attain the rewards of eternal blessedness.

PRAYER FROM PSALM XXXI

Holy Lord, who, when sins are forgiven, grant blessedness to those who confess you: hear the prayers of your present household, and, when the sting of sin has been broken, pour over us spiritual exultation. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, etc.

PSALM XXXII

ARGUMENT OF PSALM XXXII

C The prophet exhorts the righteous to rejoice in the Lord and calls blessed those who have deserved to belong to His worship.

TITLE. A psalm of David.

C This title is entirely familiar, and therefore the reader should follow the earlier exposition concerning it.

1 Exult, you righteous, in the Lord: Praise is fitting for the upright.

C The prophet admonishes Christians not to exult in earthly pleasures, but in the Lord, where joys are perfected in continual sweetness. Praise is not fitting for wicked heretics, but for the upright. H For those who direct their hearts according to the rule of truth. C “Praise” is one praise from the mouths of many, because of the unity of the Church.

2 Give thanks to the Lord on the lyre: Sing to him on the ten-stringed psaltery.

[Col. 0140D] C The lyre is so called because it is struck with rapid repetition. H It has a hollow below and six strings above, and signifies the six works of mercy. Of those strings, some sing well and others murmur; so too among the saints, some are one way and others another. The psaltery has a hollow above and ten strings, and signifies the ten commandments of the Law, which come from above into the saints.

3 Sing to him a new song: Sing well to him with shouting.

C By “a new song” he means the Lord’s Incarnation, at which the angels of the Lord sang, saying, “Glory in the highest” (Luke II). H He sings well who fulfills in action what he teaches. “Shouting” is jubilation, because neither words, syllables, letters, nor any voice can express, nor can the mind comprehend, how much a person ought to praise God; this is the *jubilus*.

4 For the word of the Lord is upright: And all his works are in faith.

C The Lord’s word is therefore upright, namely, to direct human beings; for the one who makes others upright is truly called upright. H His works are in the faith of the saints, because God does not lie concerning what He promises the saints.

5 He loves mercy and judgment: The earth is full of the mercy of the Lord.

C He loves mercy in this world, where He spreads it far and wide: namely, where He endures sinners and patiently awaits blasphemers. “Judgment” means when He separates the devout from the wicked and distinguishes their merits by the balance of equity. H “The earth is full”: the whole world, or the Church, because just as He is everywhere, so mercy is everywhere with Him.

6 By the word of the Lord the heavens were established: And by the Spirit of his mouth all their power.

H C “By the word of the Lord,” that is, by the Son of God, the heavens were established, that is, the apostles. C “By the Spirit of his mouth,” namely, when the Holy Spirit manifested their teaching through signs and miracles. “Power” refers both to miracles and to their preaching.

7 Gathering the waters of the sea as in a wineskin: Placing the abysses in treasuries.

C A wineskin is the stripped hide of an animal, which serves human uses for gathering liquids; this wineskin is compared with the Church, because just as the wineskin contains liquids, so the Church encloses the unity of the believing people. The water of the sea signifies the Christian people. H C He places the abysses “in treasuries,” that is, in the divine Scriptures: the abysses, that is, the depth of meanings.

8 Let all the earth fear the Lord: And let all who inhabit the world be moved by him.

C Here “earth” signifies the sinner who is hardened in every respect, and who is rightly called earth because he loves only earthly things. H “Let all be moved,” that is, from unbelief to belief. Alternatively, the creatures themselves were moved in admiration of the Creator.

9 For he spoke, and they were made: He commanded, and they were created.

H “For he spoke.” Therefore let all things fear Him, because they were made and created by Him.

10 [Col. 0141D] The Lord scatters the counsels of the nations; but he rejects the thoughts of the peoples: ÷ And .. he rejects the counsels of princes.

C The Lord scattered the counsels of the nations when He did not allow them to continue any longer in the worship of idols. H He rejects the thoughts of the Sadducees and Pharisees, or of the remaining kinds of authorities. The counsels of the princes Annas and Caiaphas—and the counsel of all of them was always directed toward evil—the Lord destroyed by rising again.

11 But the counsel ÷ .. of the Lord remains forever. The thoughts of his heart from generation to generation.

H The Lord’s counsel was that He should rise from the dead, just as He did. [Col. 0142A] C Alternatively, by the Lord’s counsel we understand the mystery of the Incarnation, which was granted for the benefit of the human race. This is dissolved by no age, but remains forever. A C “The thoughts of his heart” signify predestination, in which all things that endure forever have been set. Thus the eternal predestination of the saints is called “the thoughts of his heart.”

12 Blessed is the nation whose God is the Lord: The people whom he chose as his inheritance.

C That nation is truly blessed which worships the Lord, who protects and governs it. The Christian people are Christ’s inheritance, because their Author possesses them; He acquired them through holy preaching and precious blood.

13 [Col. 0142B] The Lord looked down from heaven: He saw all the children of men.

C The Lord looked down from heaven when He granted the coming of His own Son. “He saw” signifies the grace of the One who shows mercy. “The children of men.” H That is, He absolved sinners, because His regard was never without mercy. C Note, however, that when God is said in Scripture to regard sins, He punishes; but when He regards a human being, He absolves.

14 From his prepared dwelling place: He looked upon all who inhabit the earth.

C “From his prepared dwelling place,” that is, from the future body of the Lord, which had been prepared in predestination. “He looked upon all,” that is, He ordained that He should come to the aid of the world in danger, which He had ordained to make.

15 He fashioned their hearts one by one: He understands all their works.

C He fashioned the hearts to which He generously gave the gifts of His understanding. “One by one,” that is, separately or distinctly, their hearts—namely, those of the saints who live in the fear of the Lord. He understands them when He restores fitting rewards to the deeds of the good. “All their works,” that is, their thoughts, words, and deeds.

16 A king is not saved by great power: And a giant will not be saved by the abundance of his ÷ own .. power.

C By “king” he means a continent person, who, although by divine mercy he rules his body, cannot be saved from carnal vices if he presumes upon his own strength. He also wishes the same person to be understood as a giant, strengthened by the greatness of his virtues and fighting bravely against the devil’s monstrosity. And although he fights so bravely, if he is lifted up by the vice of pride, he cannot be saved. “Giant” is interpreted as “earth-born.” Human strength is rightly abandoned by God when a good gift is attributed not to God the giver but to one’s own strength.

17 A horse is deceptive for salvation: And in the abundance of ÷ its .. power it will not be saved.

C He uses the horse for human happiness, which carries and receives people in the manner of a deceptive horse. For when it seeks the fields, it is accustomed to deceive the unwary who put their confidence in it; therefore it is called a deceptive horse.

18 Behold, the eyes of the Lord are upon those who fear him: And upon ÷ those .. who hope in his mercy.

C Therefore the eyes of the Lord are upon those who fear Him, because He protects those whom He knows to fear Him. He explains who those are who fear God: those who hope in His mercy.

19 To deliver their souls from death and to feed them in famine.

C He delivered the souls of the righteous from death when He removed them from the devil’s power. Food is so called as though it were nourishment of the mind. Those who are placed in famine are those who continually kindle themselves with desire for heavenly things.

20 [Col. 0143B] Our soul awaits the Lord: For he is our helper and protector.

C When he says, “Our soul awaits,” he signifies the Christian’s patience; this confirms every virtue in a human being. He is a helper when by His grace we strive to approach Him. He is a protector when we resist the adversary.

21 For our heart will rejoice in him: And we have hoped in his holy name.

H “Our heart will rejoice,” that is, our soul, because of hope for future recompense. The Son is the Father’s name; in Him we must always hope.

22 Let your mercy, O Lord, be upon us: Just as we have hoped in you.

[Col. 0143C] H Before singing this verse, each person ought to consider how to say faithfully, “Just as we have hoped in you,” lest his mind be empty elsewhere, but let his hope be firm so that he may truly say, “Let it be,” etc.; so that you who washed us through baptism may strengthen us through the infusion of the Holy Spirit. We see this happen in the Acts of the Apostles, when those who had been baptized received the Holy Spirit (Acts XIX).

PRAYER FROM PSALM XXXII

Feed, O Lord, your people with the hunger for the word, and deliver our souls from the death of sin, so that, filled with your mercy, we may deserve, through your granting it, to be gathered into the joys of the righteous. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, etc.

PSALM XXXIII

[Col. 0143D]

ARGUMENT OF PSALM XXXIII

C The voice of the prophet blessing God, admonishing the meek to persevere with Him in His praise and to abstain from pleasures; and saying that the righteous will be delivered through their righteousness, but the wicked will perish.

TITLE. A psalm of David, when he changed his appearance before Abimelech, and Abimelech sent him away, and he departed.

C When Saul was persecuting David, he fled to Achish the king. While he was there, they wished to kill him out of envy; but he deliberately changed his appearance, filling his mouth with saliva so that he might be thought insane and be left unharmed. When he fled from there, he sang this psalm (1 Samuel XXI).

1 [Col. 0144A] I will bless the Lord at all times: His praise is always in my mouth.

H By saying that he blesses God at all times, he teaches us neither to succumb in adversity nor to be elated in prosperity. C God’s praise is always in a person’s mouth when he thinks or says such things that he cannot be reproved for anything. Praise is named from the laurel, which used to crown victors.

2 In the Lord my soul will be praised: Let the meek hear and rejoice.

C The faithful servant is glorified when he is known to possess a praiseworthy Lord. “Let the meek hear,” H that is, the saints. C Those who habitually practice moderation in all things through outstanding charity.

3 Magnify the Lord with me [Col. 0144B] And let us exalt his name together.

C The Church calls her brothers and exhorts obedient peoples to magnify the Lord’s name in glorious fellowship, lest detestable envy be mixed among the duties of holiness. “Let us exalt his name together.” “Together” signifies ordered choirs, when they respond to the Lord’s psalmody in alternating succession.

4 I sought the Lord, and he heard me: And he delivered me from all my tribulations.

C I sought the Lord, not across a long distance of lands, but in my heart. And He heard me, because Christ’s understanding embraces all things: He understands everywhere that He is being sought, and He hears. By saying “He delivered me from all,” nothing is left that you could suspect remained opposed to me. A Therefore those who are not heard do not seek the Lord. For he did not say, “I sought gold from the Lord,” but “the Lord.”

5 Draw near to him and be enlightened. And your faces will not be confounded.

H Draw near to Him, not in place but in faith and action, and be enlightened, namely, in mind and understanding, because unless you believe, you will not understand (Isaiah VII). And your faces will not be confounded at the judgment, at which the wicked will be confounded unto condemnation.

6 This poor man cried out, and the Lord heard ÷ him .. And he saved him from all his tribulations.

H “This poor man cried out,” that is, Christ, who became poor for us and cried to the Father in His Passion. C When He cried out, He was heard for salvation; but He was delivered from all worldly afflictions, H when He raised Him from the dead.

7 The angel of the Lord will encamp around those who fear him: And he will deliver them.

H There is no doubt that those who fear the Lord are guarded by angels. Therefore another text has: “The Lord will send out an angel.” C An angel is a minister of the divine will. Therefore, if you wish to become an angel, do what he commands: free one in danger, rescue the innocent, assist the anxious, and so forth. Thus the divine authority commands. 

8 [Col. 0145A] Taste and see that the Lord ÷ is sweet .. Blessed is the man who hopes in him.

C “Taste” does not refer to the palate, but to the soul’s most delightful sense. H The one who fears God with a perfect heart and keeps His commandments, and thus perceives Christ, understands that He is sweet, because He is the living bread that came down from heaven. The one who hopes in Him, and not in the uncertainty of riches, is called blessed. He is therefore blessed because he possesses the One who possesses all things, that is, God.

9 Fear the Lord ÷ all .. his saints: For there is no want for those who fear him.

H “Fear the Lord” is commanded to all the saints, lest they be deceived by the security they have received. C Only the one enriched by the fear of God lacks nothing. For he possesses every good, because by fearing God he loves Him.

10 The rich have lacked and suffered hunger: But those who seek the Lord will not be deprived of any good. ÷ Diapsalm ... [pause]

C The rich are in need when they do not have right faith. They hunger when they are not at all satisfied by the Lord’s body: rich in belly, but always hungering in spirit. For what do those who do not possess the Lord have? Those who seek the Lord will lack no good, because they enjoy spiritual desire. For when we love the Lord, we find everything in Christ.

11 Come, children, hear me: I will teach you the fear of the Lord.

C A father’s voice sounds to those who are receiving their first rudiments, so that they may come to the Christian faith. By saying, “I will teach you,” he warns us not to fear what we have heard about fear. For this is not a fear that is dreaded, but one that is loved. Human fear has bitterness; this fear has sweetness.

12 Who is the man who desires life: Who loves to see good days?

H The prophet speaks by asking who desires to see eternal life, so that he may rejoice with the saints in God’s kingdom. If you wish this, do what follows and you will see—that is, you will possess eternal life and good and everlasting days.

13 Keep your tongue from evil: And let not your lips speak deceit.

[Col. 0145D] C Keep your tongue from evil speech. He added “lips,” which immediately follow the movement of the tongue. Deceit occurs when we deceive the hearer.

14 Turn away from evil. And do good: Seek peace. And pursue it.

H “Turn away from evil and do good,” that is, destroy vices and build virtues. “Seek peace.” C No one can reach the author of peace unless here he seeks Him diligently through pure works.

15 The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous: And his ears are toward their prayers.

C When he says that the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, he shows the continual grace of divinity. H “And his ears,” because God hears whatever good things the saints ask. C For how could there be delay in hearing, when God Himself, who hears, dwells within them?

16 But the face ÷ .. of the Lord is against those who do evil: To destroy their memory from the earth.

C Lest the worst people say, “He attends to the righteous, but does not look upon us; let us act securely, since we do not deserve to be seen by Him,” he therefore declares that the face of the Lord, that is, His understanding or consideration, is upon the wicked. He says that He will destroy them from the earth, that is, from the future homeland, which only those pleasing to God will possess. Their memory will perish, because among the righteous there will be no remembrance of the wicked. H Alternatively, here we understand “face” as fury, which, by threatening anger, removes the memory of sin from the earth.

17 The righteous cried out ÷ .. and the Lord heard ÷ them .. And he delivered them from all their tribulations.

C He says that the righteous cried out to God, and he always declares that they were heard. The martyrs too—whom God did not at all deliver from the torments of tyrants—were heard and delivered when they were led to the kingdoms of heaven and proved to have been freed from all tribulations.

18 The Lord is near to those who are troubled in heart: And he will save the humble in spirit.

H C “Near” signifies not place but assistance. C Those whose hearts are troubled: for many are afflicted, but not in heart; they do not grieve over sins, but are distressed by worldly losses. H “Humble in spirit,” that is, meek; Christ will save them by granting the heavenly kingdoms.

19 [Col. 0146C] Many are the tribulations of the righteous: And the Lord delivered them from all these.

C Truly, the tribulations of the righteous are many, because the devil pursues them with greater force. But in what follows—“the Lord delivered them from all these”—the power of the Creator is shown, for it delivers the righteous from every tribulation. H Since the tribulations of the righteous are many, the one who suffers no tribulation is not righteous.

20 The Lord ÷ .. guards all their bones: Not one of them will be broken.

C By “bones” he means the steadfastness of the faithful in virtues, that is, patience and gentleness, which cannot perish in the saints or be broken by the devil, because they are preserved under the Lord’s protection.

21 [Col. 0146D] The death of sinners is most evil: And those who hate the just will offend.

C Truly, the death of sinners is most evil, because eternal punishment accompanies it. It is called “most evil” as though it were utterly ruined, namely, by eternal punishments. “Those who hate the just,” H that is, Christ, hate Him without cause and offend, that is, they abandon God by hating what is good, and thus sin unto eternal death. Or “the just” means each individual saint.

22 The Lord will redeem the souls of his servants: And all who hope in him will not offend.

H The Lord will redeem them, namely, with precious blood. C For whoever rightly believes in Him is redeemed from the captivity owed on account of sins. Scripture frequently uses “souls” for human beings. He added “of his servants,” that is, of those who do not live in wicked freedom. C “And he will not offend,” namely, like the good shepherd. H Neither here nor in the future. C Those who hope in Him do not presume upon their own strength.

PRAYER FROM PSALM XXXIII

God, disposer of angels and of the whole creation, send out your angel around us; protected by his guardianship, may we deserve to be delivered from the most evil death of sins. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, etc.

PSALM XXXIV

ARGUMENT OF PSALM XXXIV

C Christ speaks to the Father concerning His Passion, asking to be delivered from the persecution of His enemies.

TITLE. To ÷ David himself ..

C David, as we have said, embraces two meanings: “strong of hand” and “desirable.” Both are certainly fitting for the Lord the Savior.

1 Judge, O Lord, those who harm me: Fight against those who fight against me.

C Christ cries out from human weakness, asking that those who harm Him be condemned, that is, the devil with his ministers; for to judge the wicked is to condemn them. The one who fights seeks to overcome. The one who is defeated is already utterly conquered. Unclean spirits are called fighters because, although they cannot conquer the saints, they nevertheless do not cease to contend with them.

2 Take up weapons and shield: [Col. 0147C] And rise to my assistance.

C “Weapons” derives from restraining, because by them we restrain the most violent enemies; by weapons, heavenly aids are signified; by the shield, divine protection. The shield is so called as though it were “sculpted,” because the ancients marked their deeds upon it. The Lord’s will alone is what protects the one in danger and conquers the adversary.

3 Draw out the sword and bar the way against those who persecute me: Say to my soul, “I am your salvation.”

H Here “sword” means the soul of Christ or of any saint, because God effected vengeance against the devil through Christ’s soul, and through the soul of any saint He effects vengeance, as He did through Peter against Ananias [Col. 0147D] and Sapphira (Acts V). “And close ranks.” The Church asks that He close in her adversaries, so that they may not be able to go out to cause harm. “Say to my soul,” so that it may recognize you, because you are its salvation.

4 Let those who seek my soul be confounded and put to shame.

C To be confounded is to blush for one’s deeds and change them for the better. Although those who are convicted may be called confounded for punishment, so that here you might understand the requested confusion as conversion, he added “and put to shame,” that is, once corrected, let them love the One whom they had thought must be persecuted. “Those who seek my soul” is said in the evil sense, namely, of those who seek it in order to hasten to separate it from the body.

5 [Col. 0148A] Let them be turned backward and confounded: Those who think evil against me.

C “To be turned backward” is said only of those who are judged in need of correction, as in the words to Peter: “Get behind me, Satan” (Matthew XVI). He spoke of those who think evil, whether Jews, heretics, or pagans; for all think evil who hasten to teach something contrary to the catholic faith with a depraved intention.

6 Let them become like dust before the face of the wind: ÷ And let the angel of the Lord confine ÷ them ..

H “Dust” refers to light and fruitless people, because just as dust is scattered by the wind, so sinners are driven away by the divine sentence on the day of judgment. “The angel of the Lord,” that is, an evil spirit—not by nature, but by its own invention. He confines them, that is, he persecutes them as far as he can, that is, as far as he is permitted. The devil has the will to harm, but he does not have the power to carry it out.

78 Let their way be darkness and slipperiness: And let the angel of the Lord pursue them.

C Let their way, that is, their works, become dark, so that they may dread doing evil. Let it be slippery, so that they may not be able to remain in the same things for long. And if they decide to linger longer, may the Lord’s power pursue them, so that He does not allow those who hasten to destruction to remain longer in their crimes.

8 For without cause they concealed for me the destruction of their snare: They reproached my soul needlessly.

C “They concealed for me without cause,” that is, without reason—namely, the Jews, as they thought. For because they did not believe in the power of his divinity, they thought that they had concealed destruction from him. He rightly says, “the destruction of their snare,” because that snare was not the destruction of the Lord, who was not dying, but the destruction of the sinner. “Needlessly,” that is, falsely, they reproached him when they charged Christ’s truthful sayings against him as though they were some crime. H And they acted uselessly, because this reproach achieved no benefit.

9 May the snare come upon him which he does not know, and may the trap which he concealed seize him: + And .. may he fall into the snare ÷ into it ..

H The Prophet threatens that ruin which came upon the Jews in the time of Vespasian. And the trap which they concealed seized them—that is, the sudden death which they were secretly plotting against our Lord.

10 But my soul shall exult in the Lord, and shall delight in his salvation.

C For the first blessedness of the holy soul is to exult in the Lord. “She shall delight in his salvation.” H Our salvation is Christ, because the Church shall delight in him.

11 All my bones shall say: Lord, who is like you?

C The bones signify strength of spirit and steadfastness of mind, and are rightly compared with bones, because just as bones strengthen the body, so these strengthen holy intentions. C “Who” is negative; “like you,” H that is, no one. Who can be like God?

12 Delivering the poor from the hand of those stronger than he, the needy and the poor from those who plunder him.

C Christ delivered almost the whole human race from that power of the devil who then ruled throughout the world. For man was poor because he was mortal; needy because he sought bread in labor and sweat; poor because, cast down from wisdom and purity by unclean spirits who plundered him, he possessed only a slight and shadowy remnant of reason.

13 Unjust witnesses arose: They questioned me about things I did not know.

C Now Christ recalls his own Passion. Witnesses suddenly rose up against him—truly unjust, because they were going to speak against equity. He added, “I did not know,” that is, they themselves reported to me things which I certainly did not know I had said.

14 They repaid me evil for good: Barrenness for my soul.

C They repaid me evil for good, because although Christ bestowed life upon believers, they preferred to return death in exchange. The barrenness of the soul occurred when the good Teacher could find in them no fruit of faith.

15 But when they troubled me, I put on sackcloth.

C When they troubled me—that is, when the Jews troubled Christ by insults and ambushes—he clothed himself in sackcloth. H That is, divinity clothed itself in flesh and, by sin, condemned sin (Romans 8). C Divinity truly clothed itself in flesh, that is, it concealed itself beneath the veil of flesh from darkened minds.

16 I humbled my soul with fasting, and my prayer shall return into my bosom.

C Fasting is so called as though it were “going without food,” because those who abstain are led onward even to hunger. Christ fasted for forty days on the mountain (Matthew 4). “And my prayer,” that is, while it was poured forth by the Lord on the cross, and the wretched Jews were by no means worthy to receive it, returned into his bosom—that is, into the secret place of his heart—from which it had gone forth.

17 As for a neighbor, as for our brother, so I was pleasing; as one mourning and sorrowful, so I humbled myself.

C Here the grammatical cases of the nouns have been changed, for accusatives have been placed instead of ablatives. He says, “As though concerning a neighbor, as though concerning our brother, so I was pleasing to myself,” that is, I rejoiced in their fellowship, although they were pursuing me with hostility. For the Lord was pleased with them when he taught them not to sin. Christ was mourning, sorrowful, and humbled, because he could not find faith in all the Jews, whom he loved as brothers and neighbors.

18 And they rejoiced against me and gathered together; scourges were gathered against me, and I did not know.

H The Jews rejoiced when they seized Christ. They gathered together in order to crucify him, not in order to believe. Scourges were gathered, as Pilate said: “Having corrected him,” that is, having scourged him, “I will release him” (Luke 23). “And I did not know,” that is, I had no consciousness of the sin for which I ought to have been scourged or crucified.

19 They were scattered and were not pierced with remorse; they tested me. They mocked me with mockery; they gnashed their teeth at me.

H They were scattered from the bond of charity, and were not pierced with remorse so as to repent. The Jews tested Christ in many ways. They mocked him, saying: “Hail, King of the Jews.” They gnashed their teeth, shouting: “Let him be crucified.” The movement of the body reveals the movement of the soul. H C Savage men gnash their teeth when they are defeated by reason; for when words fail them in defense of the truth, they angrily grind their teeth and silently declare their threats and intentions.

20 Lord, when will you look upon me? Restore my soul from their wickedness, my only one from the lions.

C “When will you look upon me?” is said according to the customary weakness of human beings, to whom whatever is still future seems tedious; as soon as they desire something, they hasten for it to be fulfilled. “Restore,” as though returning my soul, which has been snatched away. “From their wickedness,” because he is shown to have been killed unjustly. “From the lions,” H that is, from persecutors. “My only one,” he calls his soul, which is the only one without sin. C Or “my only one,” because, born of the Virgin, he is the only one—that is, the only one born of a virgin. Or “my only one” means his Church.

21 I will confess to you in the great church; in a weighty people I will praise you.

C We have said that there are two kinds of confession: one of praise and the other of repentance; but this passage pertains to praise. The great Church is the Christian people, established firmly in the true faith. “In a weighty people,” H because it is not frivolous in sinning, and is therefore firm in faith. A Thus the chaff, being light, is lifted by the wind, while the grain remains because it is heavy. Such is the good Christian, because he is grain.

22 Let not those who oppose me unjustly rejoice over me; those who hate me without cause and signal with their eyes.

C “Let them not rejoice over me,” that is, let the heretics not insult me when the holy Church loses some of the number of the faithful, because heretics are always opposed to Christ and the Church. “Those who hate me without cause,” that is, vainly, since I have harmed them in nothing. C “They signal with their eyes”: one signals with the eyes when he wishes silently and deceitfully to indicate something. H Thus the Jews acted, because they displayed nothing good in their deed. A They proclaimed by their expression what they did not carry in their heart.

23 For indeed they spoke peaceably to me, and in the anger + of the earth .. while speaking, they devised deceit.

H C They spoke peaceably, saying: “Teacher, we know that you are truthful” (Matthew 22). C “And in the anger,” as in the saying: “It is necessary that one should die for all” (John 11), as though they were begrudging the whole people of the earth. Someone can speak deceit without intending to kill—for example, if someone tries to take money away from his neighbor. Therefore he added, “in the anger of the earth,” so that it might be shown that their deceit was deadly.

24 And they opened wide their mouth against me; they said: “Aha, aha! Our eyes have seen it.”

C They opened their mouths wide, demanding in a loud voice: “Crucify him.” “Aha, aha,” as though they were saying to themselves concerning him on the cross: “Good, good! We see what we wanted to accomplish regarding you: that you, the preacher of the people, should hang on the cross with thieves.” H Or “aha, aha,” that is, “Good, good! Now we see that the miracles you previously performed were nothing, because you cannot help yourself on the cross.” C “Aha” is a derisive and insulting exclamation. It is as though they were saying: “Now our eyes have seen your deeds and wonders; why do you not come down from the cross? But now we see that you cannot.”

25 You have seen, Lord; do not be silent. Lord, do not depart from me.

C “You have seen,” that is, you have proved how cruel the people have been toward me. “Do not be silent,” do not delay in giving judgment—which certainly cannot be done by remaining silent, but by speaking.

26 Arise and attend to my judgment, my God, and my Lord, to my cause.

H “Arise, Lord,” that is, distinguish between me and the Jews. “Attend to my judgment,” how those judging condemned me to death. “My God, to my cause.” C This is his cause: that he who had come to give salvation to the human race should be judged worthy of death by the mad. “Attend to my judgment,” A that is, consider how I was tortured in labors and pains. But because the wicked also suffer these things, he adds: “Attend to my cause for which I suffer.” The punishment is similar for the wicked and the good, but not the cause. It is the cause, not the punishment, that makes the martyr.

27 Judge me according to your justice, Lord, my God, and let them not rejoice over me.

C Christ asks to be judged according to justice—that is, according to mercy—he who committed no sins, so that he might show us an example of supplication. “That they may not rejoice over me,” that is, that the Jews may not say: “We were able; we did it; we accomplished what we wanted.”

28 Let them not say in their hearts: “Aha, aha, for our soul”; nor let them say: “We have devoured him.”

C “Let them not say: ‘Aha, aha,’” that is, “Good, good.” These are the words of those rejoicing with a criminal mind. H Nor let them say: “We have devoured him,” that is, let their mouth no longer be opened to devour me—to reckon me as like themselves. For a person devours what he puts into his mouth; thus sinners strive to draw the righteous into their own wickedness, so that they may become like them and one body with them.

29 Let them blush and be reverent together, those who rejoice at my evils.

H “Let them blush,” that is, let the Jewish persecutors and the heretics who rejoiced when they persecuted me blush—not only those who persecuted me, but also those who consented to those who rejoice, and so forth. Let them blush in such a way that they willingly condemn their own deeds and thus be converted. And because someone may blush without having reverence, he added, “let them be reverent together,” so that he might make clear the signs of their conversion. For reverence is fear of the Lord mingled with love.

30 Let those who speak maliciously against me be clothed with confusion and reverence.

H Let them be clothed with confusion—that is, with eternal confusion. Hence he says: “Depart from me, you accursed” (Matthew 25), so that those who judged me as a human being may see the God who judges.

31 Let those who desire my justice exult and rejoice, and let them say always: “May the Lord be magnified,” those who desire the peace of his servant.

H Let them exult: namely, the saints who desire to fulfill God’s justice; let them exult and rejoice in the reward of eternal life. Let them say always—namely, the saints—that the Lord the Father may be magnified; he is our peace. C But when he said “his servant,” he referred to the form of humility: he who, having assumed flesh (Ephesians 2), is called the Father’s servant according to humility. Who, then, desire peace for Christ? Those who are made strangers to vices.

32 And my tongue shall meditate on your justice, and on your praise all the day.

H “My tongue”: the saints. They shall meditate on God’s commandments. “All the day,” that is, let them strive to praise God throughout all time. C Because those who consider the divine commands in all their desires always praise God.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM 34

Protection and salvation of our soul, cover us with the helmet of hope and the shield of unconquerable fortification, so that, aided by you in the circumstances of our need, we may deserve to be filled with joy and exultation together with those who love you. Through our Lord Jesus, and so forth.

# PSALM 35

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM 35

C The Prophet vehemently accuses the despisers of the Law and, under praise of the Lord, describes the gifts bestowed upon the blessed.

TT. A psalm of David, concerning the end and the servant of the Lord.

C “Concerning the end” signifies the Lord, and “the servant of the Lord” is said of him who, taking the form of a servant, became obedient unto death (Philippians 2). The psalm and David are already known through frequent exposition.

### 1 The unjust man said within himself that he should sin: There is no fear of God before his eyes.

H “The unjust man said,” that is, he determined that he ought to sin. C And he thinks in this way so that he may grant himself permission to sin. “There is no fear of God,” that is, he does not think that God cares, so that human beings ought to fear him. A Or any unjust person said—that is, deliberated—not publicly, but within himself. There he formed his plan, where no human being sees; and although God sees, he does not care, because there is no fear of God before his eyes. He fears human beings, lest he publicly profess his wickedness. But he does not fear God, and therefore, in his heart—where God sees and a human being does not—he deliberated that he should sin, that is, commit wrongdoing.

2 For he acted deceitfully in his sight, so that his iniquity might be found out for hatred.

C He acted deceitfully in God’s sight, that is, within himself, because there is no fear, and so forth. H The devil and the Jews, clearly, acted deceitfully in God’s sight. Or this pertains to Judas the traitor, whose iniquity was found out for hatred. A Similarly, the iniquity of all evil people is found out for hatred, because God hates iniquity while punishing it perpetually.

3 The words of his mouth are iniquity and deceit; he refused to understand so as to act well.

C Their words are iniquity and deceit: iniquity pertains to blasphemy, deceit to deceiving one’s neighbor. “He refused to understand” signifies those who received, in some measure, a spark of wisdom, but, turning away from true understanding, polluted themselves through their own fault with perverse errors.

4 He devised iniquity upon his bed; he stood upon every path that was not good; wickedness ÷ however .. he did not hate.

C “He devised iniquity,” namely, the heretic, and through long reflection considered error, producing perverse books. H “Upon his bed,” in the secret chamber of the heart, where the mind meditates good or evil. “He stood upon every path that was not good”; therefore he could reach no fruit of justice. “He did not hate wickedness,” but loved it. A That is the height of wickedness; for whoever cannot be entirely free from wickedness ought at least to hate it in his mind.

5 Lord, your mercy is in heaven, ÷ and your truth reaches to the clouds.

H “Lord, in heaven,” that is, in the holy angels who were established in heaven and did not fall. Or “in heaven,” that is, in the Church. A Or in any holy person there is the mercy of God, by which he is heaven and is not unjust, unlike the one of whom it is said: “And your truth reaches to the clouds.” C That is, Christ dwells in the apostles and in the prophets; through evangelical teaching they water parched hearts so that they may bear the fruit of faith, hearts that had been made barren by the dryness of sin. For Christ is the truth, and the apostles are clouds.

6 Your justice is like the mountains of God; your judgments are a great abyss.

C He compared the blessed apostles with mountains, because they became capable of the Lord’s justice through devoted minds. Here he uses “abyss” in a good sense. For the depth of waters is an abyss, which we can neither measure nor see completely within; so we can neither comprehend divine justice with the mind nor define it by any reasoning.

7 You will save human beings and beasts, Lord. How you have multiplied your mercy, O God.

H The Lord will save human beings and beasts, that is, he rules and saves rational and irrational persons. C God saves the wicked and irrational by granting temporal salvation, as to beasts; and the good and rational by granting both temporal and eternal salvation. Or you save both good and wicked, since you were willing Christ to suffer for all. H The Lord’s mercy was multiplied when he redeemed us with his own blood. From the beginning your mercy was flowing freely, but then it was multiplied.

8 But the sons of human beings shall hope under the shelter of your wings.

C The sons of human beings are those who are not beasts but live rationally; having obtained the grace of baptism, they are reborn into a new generation. H C The wings of the Lord are the commandments of the New and Old Testament. C Every righteous person is known to hope under their protection, since he shows himself obedient to them.

9 They shall be filled with the abundance of your house, and you shall give them drink from the torrent of your delight.

H “They shall be filled,” that is, these sons of God shall be filled from the richness of the grace of the Holy Spirit, so that they may possess understanding of ecclesiastical doctrines and, forgetting their crimes, be filled with virtues. C We call a torrent a swift river; the wisdom of Christ is well compared with it, because it is sudden and so rapid that it draws whomever it wishes to faith without any delay.

10 For with you is the fountain of life, and in your light we shall see light.

H “For with you is the fountain of life,” that is, you are it, and with you is the source of all good things. The fountain of life is the teaching of God, which is life for the soul. The light of the Father is Christ; in him we shall see light, that is, the illumination of the Holy Spirit.

11 Extend your mercy to those who know you, and your justice ÷ to those .. who are upright in heart.

C He said “extend,” that is, spread your mercy far and wide, so that those who know you may be able to walk more firmly in this age. He asks justice for these—that is, a life that remains just, or his commandments—that they may keep them by living them, those who are upright in heart, that is, those who by the Lord’s gift have deserved to live here with a right mind; namely, those who direct their heart in all things toward God’s will.

12 Let not the foot of pride come upon me, and let not the hand of the sinner move me.

C He prays that he may not depart in the step of his mind from the just path, lest, standing erect in pride, he fall. The foot is placed here for the inclination of the mind. The hand of the sinner is the action of one who gives evil counsel; it moves us from firmness of faith when it tempts us with wicked persuasion. I fear the foot of pride precisely because there, and so forth.

13 There have fallen those who practice iniquity; they have been expelled and could not stand.

C “There,” where he said above—in the foot of pride and in the wickedness of perverse persuasion—they fell; as though he were saying: the demons who still practice iniquity by giving evil counsel to human beings and continually leading them to pride have fallen into a deep pit. H “They have been expelled,” that is, from the kingdom of God. C “And they could not stand,” because they were not permitted to delay carrying out the Lord’s commands, but were immediately hurled down to the place where the penal flame prepared for them awaits. A Adam also fell there and was expelled from paradise; he too is said still to practice iniquity, since we are all born in his sin. Neither the devil nor Adam could stand by his own strength—

## PRAYER FROM PSALM 35

Glorify us with heavenly mercy, fountain and source of everlasting light, so that, filled with the abundance of your house, we may reject every iniquity and deceit together with the shamelessness of savage pride. Through our Lord Jesus Christ.

# PSALM 36

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM 36

C The voice of the Church admonishing us not to imitate the wicked, and concerning the punishments of the evil and the rewards of the blessed.

TT. ÷ A psalm .. of David.

H This psalm glorifies the person of the righteous, marks out the unjust, instructs in morals, teaches the goodness of God, and tears away perversity.

### 1 Do not emulate those who act wickedly, nor envy those who practice iniquity.

H “Emulation” has many interpretations; here, however, it teaches: do not become a participant with the wicked, neither toward jealousy—for jealousy is anger—nor toward envy, for envy is spite. “Nor shall you envy,” that is, imitate those who practice iniquity, who gather riches through wicked frauds and seek honors.

2 For they shall quickly wither like grass, and like the green herbs they shall soon fall away.

C Grass is beautiful while it blooms, but when it has dried, its color immediately changes and it withers. So are the wicked: shining with joy as though in flower, they dry up through a premature end. “Green herbs” derives from the pot in which, once gathered, they are cooked. Here it is shown, through the likeness of grass and herbs, that the wicked quickly fall.

3 Hope in the Lord and do good; dwell in the land. And you shall feed on its riches.

C Here the Prophet admonishes us to hope in the Lord; this is the entrance of faith and the beginning of salvation. C H “Do good,” that is, fulfill the commandments. H “Dwell in the land,” that is, rule the flesh; let the flesh not rule you. C “And you shall feed” pertains to satiety and everlasting sweetness. “In its riches,” that is, in contemplation of the Lord Christ. H A Or in the Holy Scriptures.

4 Delight in the Lord, [Col. 0155D] and he will give you the requests of your heart.

C When he says “delight in the Lord,” he wishes the remembrance of him to be sweet to you, so that you may love the one you fear. He will give you the request of your heart, not of your flesh. The request of the heart is faith, charity, understanding of God, and the practice of good deeds.

5 Reveal your way to the Lord and hope in him, and he himself will act.

C The density of sins is a kind of veil, by which our way—that is, our life—is surrounded with a dark covering. We reveal it when we confess our offenses most readily. H “Hope in him,” so that he may be able to forgive the sinner. “And he himself will act,” doing what follows.

6 And he will bring forth your justice like the light, and your judgment like midday. Be subject to the Lord and pray to him.

C To bring something forth is to lead it from darkness into light; that is, to lead it from the darkness of this age to the brightness of the future judgment, where all things will be made public. Then our justice will appear to human eyes. H “And your judgment,” by which you chose what is good, he will reveal before his angels like midday, in the full splendor of his grace. Be subject to the Lord, not to sin, and pray to him for your offenses.

7 Do not emulate the one who prospers in his way, the man who commits injustices.

H “Do not emulate him,” that is, let the brief prosperity of the wicked not terrify you.

C “The man who commits injustices,” that is, wickedness—one whose actions are shameful and whose dealings are filthy.

8 Cease from anger and abandon wrath; do not emulate in such a way as to act wickedly.

C Wrath is what inflames the mind with swift movement; anger is what persists longer. Therefore he commands us to abandon both, through which we can arrive at guilt. “Do not emulate in such a way as to act wickedly.” H Lest you yourself become wicked by provoking others to wickedness. C The ancients defined wickedness as voluntary evil, into which we do not fall by chance but in which we take pleasure. “Wicked” is derived from “not at all,” that is, one who is fit for nothing at any time.

9 For those who act wickedly shall be cast out; but those who wait for the Lord shall inherit the land.

C To be cast out is to be thrown beyond the boundaries, that is, to be deprived of that city of God. But those who wait for the Lord shall possess by inheritance the land of the living, because they despise the prosperity of the wicked, awaiting the Lord’s judgment and meanwhile enduring adversity patiently.

10 ÷ And .. yet a little while, and the sinner shall not be; and you will seek his place and will not find it.

C “A little while” derives from “fist” and signifies something small and slight, which can be enclosed in the hand with the fingers contracted. Here it signifies the time remaining until the day of judgment, which, in comparison with the days that have passed, is altogether very short. “And the sinner shall not be,” not because the one who sinned will not exist, but because he will cease to sin. “His place” signifies this world, which alone caresses sinners and is properly friendly to them. H Or “his place” means the pleasure of sin.

11 But the gentle shall inherit the land and shall delight in the abundance of peace.

C We call the gentle those who are accustomed to the hand, that is, patient and mild. H Whom no storm of anger agitates. C They shall possess the future Jerusalem and remain in it forever and ever. “In the abundance of peace”: the peace of the future age, where nothing adverse and nothing contrary can exist.

12 The sinner shall watch the righteous and gnash his teeth at him.

C The sinner shall watch the righteous when he sees that wicked man laboring over good conduct. H For through the works of the saints they are themselves tormented and tortured in the present life. He shall gnash with the teeth of wickedness and envy, by which he tries to devour him; through this movement of the body, he reveals the movement of the soul. A C Therefore he shall watch as though from hidden ambushes, in order to entice him. He watches from hidden ambushes because, when he sees the righteous, he thinks that he is being accused by him and therefore tries to make the righteous like himself. If he cannot do so, he shall gnash his teeth, and so forth.

13 The Lord ÷ however .. will laugh at him, ÷ because he sees that his day is coming.

H This does not mean that the Lord laughs at anyone, but that they are worthy to be laughed at in retribution. “Because he sees” means that the Lord knows when the day of his vengeance and destruction will come.

14 Sinners have drawn the sword; they have bent their bow.

C The sword of the sinner is every deceit that desires the injury of another; he draws it who, through wicked persuasion, desires to deceive innocent souls. To bend the bow is to await, through a fraudulent deed, the time when they can deceive the simple and innocent. A The sword indicates open persecution, while the bow indicates hidden persecution: whoever fights with a sword fights at close quarters, but whoever fights with a bow fights from a distance.

15 In order to deceive the poor and needy, in order to slaughter the upright in heart.

H “In order to deceive the poor,” not the world’s rich, but Christ’s poor. C He added “the upright in heart”; this can be understood of the martyrs, who are upright in heart but slaughtered in the flesh. A poor person is one who is not sufficient for himself; a needy person is one who has no help, whether from himself or from another.

16 Let their sword enter their own hearts, and let their bow be broken.

C A sword is so called because it is made for the slaughter of enemies. H And it signifies vengeance upon their own souls. C And their bow—that is, their hidden wickedness against the devout—is broken, because it will not be able to harm the faithful in the realm of the soul. A The wicked first injure themselves in heart and soul, before they injure the righteous in body and external possessions. They cannot injure the righteous in his heart. But if the righteous has been injured in his possessions, he says: “It is better,” and so forth.

17 Better is the little that belongs to the righteous than the great riches of sinners.

C “Little” here should be understood as humility; while our mind guards itself in it, it rises above the precious things of the world. The riches of sinners are accumulations of crimes. Let us therefore consider how much better it is to receive that little belonging to the righteous and not possess the mass of so many crimes. And truly it is much better, because the arms, and so forth.

18 For the arms of sinners shall be broken, but the Lord strengthens the righteous.

C “The arms of sinners” signifies perverse actions, which shall be broken—that is, diminished by continual grinding. H Or their strength shall be broken in retribution, so that they may not harm the innocent. But the Lord strengthens the righteous in faith. H A “Arms” signifies the power and strength of sinners. A The Lord strengthens the righteous through hope in adversity and through examples, especially that of the cross. For the cross has ended in punishment but remains in glory. From places of punishment it passed to the foreheads of emperors. He who gave such honor to his punishments—what will he do for his faithful?

19 The Lord knows the days of the blameless, and their inheritance shall be forever.

C The Lord knows the days of the blameless, that is, the ways which he established and which human ignorance cannot behold. Their inheritance is the heavenly Jerusalem, exceedingly rich in eternal peace; it shall be forever, because it is granted without end.

20 They shall not be confounded in an evil time, and in the days of famine they shall be satisfied, because sinners shall perish.

H C “An evil time” signifies the day of judgment. C When all flesh fears the repayment and recompense of its deeds, the blameless shall not be confounded at that time. “The days of famine” signify the time of this world, when the blessed hunger for justice and shall be satisfied through the Holy Scriptures and the Lord’s examples. “Sinners shall perish,” that is, they shall be condemned in that judgment. A Or by “evil time” he means the time of tribulation here, in which the good are satisfied by hope of future peace, while sinners, having been satisfied here, shall perish, to be tormented by eternal hunger.

21 But the enemies of the Lord, as soon as they have been honored and exalted, shall fade away; like smoke they shall fade away.

H But the enemies of the Lord—that is, the wicked—when they have been honored in earthly power and exalted in empty glory, will soon, when death arrives, see all their glory melt away like smoke or mist.

22 The sinner borrows and does not repay; but the righteous shows mercy and gives.

H C “The sinner borrows” when he receives various benefits from God, “and does not repay,” that is, he does not give God worthy thanks. But the righteous shows mercy; although he receives little here, he is nevertheless found ready to give alms.

23 For those who bless him shall inherit the land, but those who curse him shall perish.

C For those who bless the Lord—that is, those who give thanks in all things and keep his commandments—receive that land of the living as their possession. Those who curse him—that is, blasphemers or those disobedient to God’s laws—are removed from that homeland.

24 The steps of a person shall be directed by the Lord, and he shall desire his way.

H “The steps,” that is, the understanding of each person, shall be directed by the Lord. “And he shall desire his way,” namely, God’s way, so that he may come to him who is the way, the truth, and the life (John 14). “Steps” signifies works and inclinations, which God directs. A And by the fact that he is directed, the righteous desires the way of God, although it is hard. The way of the earth is not hard, but full of robbers. The Lord’s way, though hard, is safe. Or he shall desire the way of the righteous person, in which, when he has fallen, and so forth.

25 When he falls, he shall not be shattered, because the Lord supports his hand.

H When he falls because of the weakness of the flesh—for the righteous falls seven times a day and rises again (Proverbs 24)—he shall not be shattered, because the Lord immediately shows mercy to the repentant. Thus David and Peter cleansed their acknowledged sin with tears and were strengthened by the Lord.

26 I was younger, and indeed I have grown old, and I have not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his offspring seeking bread.

A C “I was younger” is the voice of the Church, when in the first ancestor it initially received the beginnings of the natural law. “It grew old” when it reached an honorable age, having deserved in the latter times to receive the Lord the Savior. H A C We have said that “offspring” means the works of a person, which he sows and reaps. H C Therefore the works of the righteous do not seek bread—that is, the word of God—because he has been filled with the word of God, by which he truly lives and is nourished inwardly. A Here the Church speaks as one person. H Or David speaks, who was small in wickedness and old in virtues.

27 All day long he shows mercy and lends, and his offspring shall be in blessing.

H At all times he shows mercy from the Lord and lends—he who ministers his teaching to others. And his offspring, the works he has done or the teaching he has taught, shall be blessed by the Lord.

28 Turn away from evil and do good, and dwell forever ÷ in the age .. of the age ..

H Turn away from evil, that is, from an evil deed, and do the good which God commanded. Dwell in the unity of faith. C “The age of the age” signifies the eternal kingdom, which will not be changed by any succession.

29 For the Lord loves judgment and will not abandon his holy ones; they shall be preserved forever.

H For the Lord loves judgment, namely, just judgment, by which he distinguishes the righteous and the wicked. And he will not abandon his holy ones, who trust in him with complete hope; they shall be preserved forever, that is, in perpetual life.

30 ÷ The unjust shall be punished .. and the offspring of the wicked shall perish.

H The unjust shall be punished in retribution. “The offspring shall perish,” that is, their works shall be punished with them in torments, and the vanity and pleasure sought in sins shall disappear.

31 But the righteous shall inherit the land, ÷ and they shall dwell in the age ÷ of the age .. upon it.

H But the righteous shall possess the land of the living. And they shall dwell in it, which is without end, from which sorrow and lamentation have fled (Revelation 21).

32 The mouth of the righteous shall meditate wisdom, and his tongue shall speak judgment.

H “The mouth of the righteous shall meditate wisdom,” that is, Christ. C By “mouth” we should here understand thoughts; for just as the heart shall meditate wisdom, so the tongue shall speak justice and judgment in all things. H This will happen when he recounts before the blessed what he understands of God with everything measured and without deceit, not with anger but with just judgment.

33 The law of his God is in his heart, ÷ and his steps shall not be supplanted.

C “The law of his God”: this pronoun indicates the grace of the Lord the Savior. For although he is the God of all, he is properly called the God of him whom he has deigned to liberate. “In his heart” signifies that the whole understanding of the blessed has been filled with such a good; namely, that the heart agrees with the tongue, so that the law of God is not only in the mouth but also in the heart and in every understanding. No one will be able to supplant his steps. To supplant means to set pits before the feet so that one who falls in cannot find a firm foothold; this cannot at all be said to occur where all things are secure and eternal. A Because the good guardian, Christ, keeps the word of God in his heart from snares.

34 The sinner watches the righteous and seeks to put him to death.

H The sinner watches the righteous: for the Jewish people looked upon the righteous Son of God, gnashed at him, and sought to destroy him, because his teaching was burdensome for them to hear and he himself was burdensome even to behold. So now also the enemy watches each one of us in order to destroy us; but if you resist vigilantly, what follows comes to pass.

35 The Lord ÷ however .. will not abandon him into his hands, nor condemn him when he is judged ÷ to him ..

H As the Lord did not abandon the righteous man into the hands of the Jews—that is, into their power—so he will not abandon any righteous person into the power of sinners with respect to the soul, so that they might harm the soul, that is, so that he might consent to evil in evil. Nor will he condemn him, C that is, the righteous man when he judges the wicked; rather, discerning their merits, he will receive the righteous man, while he will torment the wicked with the punishment he deserves.

36 [Col. 0160D] Wait for the Lord and keep his way: and he will exalt you ÷ so that you may inherit the land: When sinners have perished, you will see.

H Wait for the Lord, that is, act patiently, whether in prosperity or in adversity. C You who keep the Lord’s ways—that is, his most sacred commandments. H And he will exalt you, so that you may inherit that land of blessedness in which the righteous will be exalted. C Then the righteous will see sinners perish, when their punitive adversity has been observed; and, while those sinners perish, they will see themselves placed in supreme blessedness.

37 I saw the impious man highly exalted: And raised up like the cedars of Lebanon.

C He says that he saw the impious man—that is, that he grew—not toward honor, [Col. 0161A] but rather toward ruin. And lest you think that he was raised only above the humble, he added, “and raised up like the cedars of Lebanon”: his advancement in honor, riches, and power is exalted only so that his irreparable ruin may be displayed. H This may properly be understood of the devil, and also of Judas. And if it is explained of Judas, the following verse is interpreted as follows.

38 And I passed by, and behold, he was no more: I sought him, and his ÷ place was not found.

H “And I passed by”—let the apostolic assembly say this. “I passed by” at the time of Jesus’ passion; and when he had risen, Judas was no more, because he went away and hanged himself with a noose. “I sought him, and he was not found,” namely, the place of that wicked man in the apostolic body, which was failing with such speed. But when this is explained of Judas, the apostles are understood by the cedars; [Col. 0161B] and when it is explained of the devil, angels are signified by the cedars. When it is explained of wicked or powerful rich men—who, having abandoned God, trust in the riches of the world and, however much they flourish, however much they are exalted and raised up, will not be found when they depart from this world—the wicked who have been raised up in this world are then understood by the cedars. For just as a cedar appears exalted above the lofty mountains but often falls apart under the force of the winds, so also the impious man; the place of the impious man is impiety.

39 Keep innocence and observe equity: For there are remains for the peaceful man.

H Keep innocence: if you harm no one and quarrel with no one, you will see Christ, who is understood as equity, just as he is the way, the truth, and the life. C There are remains for the peaceful man when his hope is brought to completion through the Lord’s reward—that is, when what he hoped for is fulfilled. The remains, therefore, are what are left after death. A The righteous man, however, leaves behind after death a good memory of his righteousness, and God leaves eternal rewards for him. C A peaceful man is one who makes peace among those who are in discord.

40 But the unjust will perish together: The remains of the impious will perish.

C “But the righteous,” and so forth. For just as the righteous rejoice after this life, so the unjust will perish when this light has ended. “Remains,” as has been said, signifies the memory of the righteous, which they leave behind in this world after death. The impious can in no way deserve this, since, when destruction overtakes them, false praise and fragile life dissolve. A Their remains also—that is, their earthly possessions—will all perish.

41 But the salvation of the righteous is from the Lord: ÷ And .. their protector in the time of tribulation.

H Salvation comes from the Lord, because he himself is our salvation. C The time of tribulation is twofold: here tribulation is temporal, but at the final judgment it is eternal. That latter tribulation is evil, because it is eternal and comes upon the impious on the day of judgment. In this present time of tribulation, therefore, Christ is the protector, because he rescues the righteous from it.

42 And the Lord will help them ÷ and will deliver them .. and will rescue them from sinners: ÷ And will save them .. because they hoped in him.

[Col. 0162A] C “And he will help them,” that is, he helps faithful servants in this world when they are wearied by contrary struggle; he delivers them when he does not allow their faith to be perverted by wicked persuasion. He will indeed rescue them when he preserves them unharmed amid the opposition of this world. “Because they hoped in him,” that is, they placed their hope in the Lord’s kindness.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM 36

O God, the blessedness of all the righteous is certain—you who do not abandon your saints in hunger and do not permit them to be overcome in the arena of tribulations—we beseech you to fortify us with that right hand which you swiftly extend, prepared for them lest they fall. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, etc.

# PSALM 37

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM 37

[Col. 0162B]

C The voice of a penitent imploring the mercy of a kind judge, who says that he has been wounded in body and soul and confounded by the reproach of his friends.

TT. A psalm of David, for remembrance ÷ concerning the Sabbath ..

C By saying “for remembrance,” this title declares that, since we cannot escape sin, we ought at least always to keep the offense itself in remembrance, so that, with God’s help, we may restrain ourselves from future faults. H “Sabbath” is interpreted as “rest,” that is, when the Church will rest in paradise, which Adam lost.

1 O Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury: Nor correct me in your anger.

[Col. 0162C] H This entire psalm is spoken in the person of a penitent, but it can also be referred to Christ, as can Psalm 68. Fury is irrational vengeance with the bitterness of gall. Anger, however, is merely the soul’s agitation. Therefore this penitent, who knows himself to be a sinner, asks to be rebuked not in anger but through mercy, and not in fury but through patience.

2 For your arrows are fixed in me: And you have strengthened your hand upon me.

H The arrows are words of instruction, which strike the penitent’s heart like a dart, so that he may do penance. “You have strengthened,” and so forth: so that, like a good teacher, you might make him corrected by blows and restored to amendment.

3 There is no health in my flesh because of your anger: [Col. 0162D] There is no peace in my bones because of my sins.

H “There is no health in my flesh because of the face of anger,” that is, I saw the face of your anger, but not anger itself; that is, through the holy Scriptures I understood how greatly you threatened sinners, and I was afraid, asking that this anger not descend upon me. “There is no peace in my bones,” that is, I granted no rest either to my bones or to my limbs before cleansing my mind through repentance.

4 For my iniquities have risen above my head: Like a heavy burden they have been made heavy upon me.

C Our iniquities raise themselves above our head when they are heaped up beyond what reason, which is the head of the mind, is able to bear; and if iniquity oppresses reason, it immediately gives way, overcome. H “Like a heavy burden,” because the burden of sin is not light but ought to be heavy for everyone, since it imposes upon everyone the heavy burden of judgment.

5 My wounds have become putrid and corrupt: Because of my foolishness.

H The wounds of sins rot and stink for me as long as I lie in sins; and now I eagerly seek a physician through repentance. C A scar is so called because it shows a wound hidden within it, signifying hidden sins. H These a person may conceal because of his foolishness.

6 I have become wretched and have been bowed down to the end: All day long I went about sorrowful.

H “I have become wretched” until I was cleansed by confession, [Col. 0163B] because sins are not forgiven without shame and sorrow. “Sorrowful,” that is, considering myself unworthy even to raise my eyes toward heaven, but striking my breast, I said: “God, be merciful to me, a sinner” (Luke 18).

7 For my loins are filled with illusions: And there is no health in my flesh.

H The penitent confesses that he is filled and weakened by those illusions with which the devil daily entices and persuades the human race to sin. By the loins he designates the body’s tingling will, that is, the appetite of the flesh.

8 I am afflicted and humbled exceedingly: I roared because of the groaning of my heart.

H I am exceedingly afflicted and humbled for repentance, [Col. 0163C] and I roared, seeking forgiveness with mourning. The groaning of the body is one thing, and the groaning of the heart another. The groaning of the body is on account of earthly things; the groaning of the heart is on account of one’s own sins and those of others. C To roar properly belongs to beasts, namely lions. A Or: I have been afflicted and humbled by exceedingly great miseries and calamities because of sin; therefore I roar.

9 + O Lord .. all my desire is before you: And my groaning is not hidden from you.

C His desire was such that he might deserve to be before God; for the Lord embraces whatever he does not reject. That groaning is not hidden from God which is devoutly offered for the liberation of the soul. Groaning is so called as if it were “doubled mourning,” because it arises from the expression of great pain.

10 [Col. 0163D] My heart is troubled: My strength has left me: And the light of my eyes—even that is not with me.

C Now he comes to the gravest pains of the soul, after passing through bodily afflictions. Therefore he says that his heart is troubled, because strength has abandoned him. He says, “My strength has left me,” A the strength that I had before sin. But why has strength abandoned me? Because “the light,” and so forth. He declares that the light of his eyes is not with him. H Because, having set aside the light of truth, he had fallen into the darkness of sins.

11 My friends and my neighbors have drawn near and stood against me.

A Hitherto he has confessed what he suffers inwardly from himself; [Col. 0164A] now he says what he suffers outwardly from those among whom he lives. C Friends are those joined not by blood but by affection. “Friend” is so called as if meaning “equal in spirit,” that is, similar. Neighbors, however, are those connected to us by kinship. H “Friend” and “neighbor” may also be understood of the disciples, who, terrified during Christ’s passion, withdrew so far from the Lord that Peter himself denied him. Let others explain what follows of the penitent; from this verse to the end, I see my Lord Jesus surrounded by the Jews.
