12 And those who were near me stood far away: And those who sought my life used force.

H Christ’s disciples stood far away, of whom the evangelist says: “His acquaintances stood at a distance” (Luke 23). But the Jews used force. C Or the devil with his ministers, [Col. 0164B] who, the more they saw him persist in the love of God, the more they strove to inflict death upon his soul.

13 And those who sought evil for me spoke vanities: And all day long they meditated deceit.

H They meditated many deceits when they asked whether a woman caught in adultery should be stoned (John 8), whether it was lawful to pay tribute to Caesar (Matthew 22), and did similar things. But they openly plotted deceit when they brought forward false witnesses. They spoke vain things: “He casts out demons by Beelzebul” (Luke 11).

14 But I, like a deaf man, did not hear: And like a mute man who does not open his mouth.

H Christ always bore the reproach of the Jews as if deaf, and like a mute, when Pilate said: “Do you not answer me?” (John 19). C Nothing can be stronger or nobler than to hear harmful words and not answer with opposing words.

15 And I became like a man who does not hear: And who has no rebuttals in his mouth.

H Thus Christ, accused by the Jews, kept silent as though he had nothing that he ought to answer on his own behalf, giving an example to humanity that it ought patiently to bear blows for God’s sake. Therefore he did not rebuke those who unjustly reproached him.

16 For in you, O Lord, I have hoped: You will hear me, O Lord my God.

C Therefore he says that his petition will be heard, because he confidently declares that he has hoped in God. Such is the will of the saints, such their firm purpose of mind: they are captivated not by any advantage of the present time, [Col. 0164D] but only by the love of God.

17 For I said: Lest my enemies ever rejoice over me ÷ and, when my feet are shaken, they speak great things against me.

H The enemies would insult Christ and rejoice if he, humbled in his passion, had not risen again. “Feet are shaken,” that is, the apostles were shaken from faith to unbelief. The Jews spoke great things, saying: “If you are the Son of God, come down from the cross” (Matthew 27).

18 For I am ready for scourging: And my pain is always in my sight.

H Christ is ready to endure scourging, [Col. 0165A] the cross, the lance, gall, and vinegar, so that through this death he might free the perishing people by his holy blood. “And my pain,” as though Christ were said to suffer until he brought his victory into judgment against the Jews.

19 For I will declare my iniquity + And .. I will think upon my sin.

H “For I will declare my iniquity,” that is, just as Christ submitted to the curse in order to rescue us from the curse (Galatians 3), so he also professes himself a sinner, because he bore our sins. “And I will think.” For he was thinking, with a merciful thought, how he might cleanse within himself the offenses of the human race, which he reckoned as his own.

20 [Col. 0165B] But my enemies live and have been strengthened against me: And those who hate me unjustly have multiplied.

H His enemies live because they were not immediately punished by divine vengeance. They have been strengthened in the letter of the Law, in which they did not understand what had been announced spiritually. C Or: they have been strengthened in wickedness. They have multiplied in the greatness of their offspring, those who unjustly hated Christ. H And certainly they hated him not reasonably but unjustly, because, in this letter, they believed that their seed would be multiplied like the stars of heaven.

21 Those who repay evil for good slandered me: Because I followed goodness.

H They repaid evil for good because they gave vinegar and gall to him who brought the sweetness of eternal life. They slandered me, saying: “He saved others; he cannot save himself” (Matthew 27). “Because I followed goodness,” so that, fulfilling the Father’s will, I might accept death for the life of the people.

22 Do not abandon me, O Lord: My God, do not depart from me.

H “Do not abandon me,” Christ says, when I have entered the depths of hell. C Or the penitent asks this, so that, having been converted, he may not be abandoned by God and sin again. Do not depart from me either, because, when you are absent, it is necessary always to go astray from the straightest way.

23 Attend to my help: O Lord, God of my salvation.

H Therefore he says, “Attend to my help.” Since the struggles of the flesh are severe, attend to my help and be our salvation in the time of tribulation. C Behold, the rule of the penitent has been fulfilled: he rejoices that he has been saved by God’s grace.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM 37

Send forth your salvation into our weaknesses, O most powerful Healer, into our mortal wounds and scars, so that, lamenting before you all our groaning and pain, we may be able to overcome the insults of opposing vices. Through our Lord Jesus, etc.

# PSALM 38

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM 38

C The voice of the righteous man, usefully silent before his enemies and asking to know the end of his life, if perhaps he may be able to behold the Lord’s incarnation; and asking that harmful sins be forgiven him.

TT. For the end. For Jeduthun. A song of David.

C What “for the end” signifies has already been explained. Jeduthun is a Hebrew name, which in Latin is called “one who leaps across,” signifying him who transcends the vices of this world through his purity. A song, however, is the divine praise of a joyful human voice, and sometimes of one who is grieving, but never of one who is penitent.

1 I said: I will guard my ways: So that I may not sin with my tongue.

C “I said,” that is, I deliberated within myself, in my heart. “I will guard my ways”; he does not say from crimes, because he was already holy, but from superfluous words, which even the self-controlled can rarely avoid. For guilt is more easily avoided by silence than by speaking. H By “ways” he means actions and words.

2 I placed a guard over my mouth: When the sinner stood against me.

C The mouth is said to be the door of the tongue, and it will be saved safely if its entrance is guarded. When the sinner stands, H that is, the devil, who is the instigator of those who lie in wait for the saints. A But I was silent about proclaiming good things because of those who slandered my words.

3 I was mute and humbled, and I was silent about good things: And my pain was renewed.

H I was mute, lest I quarrel with those who quarreled with me. C “Humbled” signifies that, having been thrown down upon the ground, he remained silent against their reproaches. He was silent about good things because it is the habit of the wicked, however new the things they hear, in no way to acquiesce. His pain was renewed, that is, the pain of compassion by which he kept good things silent from evil hearers. A For the pain that had been present in speaking, from which he rested by keeping silent, was renewed through the silence by which he denied his fellow servants the provisions of life and the word of God.

4 My heart grew hot within me: And in my meditation the fire will burn.

C He said, “My heart grew hot,” that is, it was kindled on every side. H By the remembrance of his own sins. C “Within me,” in the inner man, where reason speaks silently. “And in my meditation.” H What are you meditating on? This, I say: how I might discover that fire, namely, that of the Holy Spirit, which consumes sins and illuminates the mind. A Or because I saw dangers on every side—things that must be kept silent in speaking and things that must be spoken in silence—my restless heart began to boil with divine heat.

5 I spoke with my tongue: Make my end known to me, O Lord.

C The Prophet proclaimed with the truthful tongue of his conscience to the Lord, before whom he had been silent because of deceitful enemies. Therefore, kindled by meditation on eternal things, he asks to know his end, that is, the Savior. For he himself is our end; to reach him is life. H The Prophet does not ask that the end of this life be made known to him, but that end in which, with death destroyed, he may be joined to Christ.

6 [Col. 0167A] And the number of my days. What is it? So that I may know what is lacking for me.

C Next the Prophet desires to know the number of his days, that is, so that it might become clearer whether he might deserve to behold Christ’s presence with bodily eyes. He added, “so that I may know what is lacking for me.” Truly, he judged that he lacked life if he had not deserved to see his presence. H That he is not speaking here about his own days is shown by what follows.

7 Behold, you have measured out my days: And my substance is like nothing before you.

H According to the old man, his days have until now been measured out, that is, they have been under the yoke of sin. Now, with a new desire, I seek one eternal, immeasurable day, which Abraham saw and rejoiced in (John 8), in which elsewhere we are urged to rejoice, in which the Lord God has shone upon us (Psalm 117). C He rightly says that his substance is nothing before God, since it was condemned when Adam sinned; unless divinity has conferred something upon it, it has nothing from its own substance in which it may presume. A He says “before you,” that is, in comparison with your substance, or before your knowledge, and in your knowledge and illumination. Before human beings it appears to be something, but before you it is like nothing in comparison with eternity.

Yet everything is vanity: Every living human being. Diapsalma.

C For vanity—as we have often said—signifies mutability, which every human being except Christ endures, since Christ was clothed in this flesh. Understand, however, [Col. 0167C] not bodily change, which Christ also endured, but instability of mind.

9 Yet in an image the human being passes by: But he is also troubled in vain.

C “Yet in an image the human being passes by.” The image of God is that condition which the human being received when it was said: “Let us make humankind according to our image” (Genesis 1). And he rightly said, “he is troubled in vain,” because those who are occupied with temporal desires lose purity of mind. For this is to be troubled: to be led away from purity of mind into the activities of the world—and this in vain, because it is without benefit, indeed with harm to the soul.

10 He stores up treasure: And does not know for whom he will gather it.

H Often many people store up treasure and gather many things, which either the laziness of their children destroys, or the treasury seizes, or strangers plunder. But blessed is the one who stores treasure where he may deserve to hear: “As long as you did it for one of these least ones, you did it for me” (Matthew 25), and where thieves do not steal or break in (Matthew 6).

11 And now what is my expectation—is it not the Lord? And my substance is with you.

C “And now what is my expectation?”—“Is it not the Lord?” He declares that the Lord Christ is his expectation, and that in perishable desires he has no other confidence except in him alone. “Substance” is spoken in a good sense, the substance that is remembered as existing before Christ, where there is nothing except what is perfect. A C He says that this substance is not what was contracted from Adam, nor temporal things, but the possession of a good conscience. It is with God; it is not with human beings, because it is not seen by them.

12 Deliver me from all my iniquities: You have made me a reproach to the foolish.

H He asks to be delivered from past, present, and future iniquities. C The holy man was a reproach to fools because they rejected what was unlike themselves. The wicked praise only those things that they seem to possess in common. A Because I say that everything human beings desire here is vanity, and that the greedy do not know for whom they gather and store up, I am mocked by them, and you make me a reproach to the foolish, the greedy. And although he said that I was raving in this way, nevertheless [Col. 0168B] I remained silent.

13 I was mute ÷ and .. did not open my mouth: because you did it. Remove your scourges from me.

C “I was mute,” namely, in the salutary silence that heavenly generosity granted. “Because you did it”: he himself did it, certainly, who gave the gifts of patience. The scourges are corrections by which we are beaten for our sins; the holy man desires those due punishments for committed faults to be removed from him.

14 By the strength of your hand I have failed: In corrections you chastised the human being because of iniquity.

C For a strong hand scourges severely, and it was necessary for anyone struck by that exalted hand to fail. H When the hand of vengeance also weighs upon him, the power of sin fails, as the Apostle Paul says: “When I am weak, then I am strong” (2 Corinthians 12). Every human being is rebuked because of iniquity, whom the divine majesty does not wish to destroy.

15 And you made his soul waste away like a spider: Yet every human being is ÷ troubled .. in vain. Diapsalma.

H The soul wastes away when the flesh is restrained from luxury and desire. “To waste away” means to be stunned by former sins. But the one who does those things that belong to worldly vanity weaves spiders’ webs; that is, day and night he is occupied with vain work and produces not useful things but things dissoluble and corruptible. But because the Prophet says that the soul wastes away like a spider, this [Col. 0168D] is to be understood as follows: the afflicted soul is refined through vigils and prayers by abstinence to such a degree that it is drawn out like those threads, so that it contains nothing dense or hard of sin. For the one who lives in vanities, this worldly disturbance is vain and useless. But for the one who lives in God, this worldly disturbance is likewise vain and useless.

16 Hear my prayer, O Lord, and my supplication: Receive my tears with your ears.

17 Do not be silent, for I am a sojourner with you: And a pilgrim, like all my fathers.

C Therefore he first mentioned prayer and afterward supplication. Prayer is the reason of the mouth, which we offer while prostrate, revealing our vows. Supplication is frequent and continual entreaty, brought forth from the hidden depths of the breast. He added tears, which are always forceful in prayers and draw the mind of the one who shows mercy toward compassionate kindness.

C “Do not be silent,” he said—that is, let me hear you saying: “Your sins are forgiven.” An inhabitant is one who cultivates another’s land for a time, as are all the saints established in this age. H For they too, while they were in the body, were pilgrims away from the Lord (2 Corinthians 5). C Sin made us all strangers from the divine city and held us captive in this region. Everyone who is received into eternal blessedness is also called a pilgrim, because he begins to be where he was not. “Pilgrim” is so called as though meaning “one who goes farther.” A Or, [Col. 0169B] the one living here is called a pilgrim because he is also with God through faith and love. C He adds “all,” lest anyone be thought exempt from this condition.

18 Forgive me, so that I may recover my breath, before I depart: And I shall be no more.

C Therefore he rightly asked to recover his breath in the security of the heavenly kingdom, since he was burning with the heat of so great a desire. He adds, “before I depart,” that is, before I leave this light. “And I shall be no more,” namely, in this world; or, I shall not exist after death if you cease to help me here, because to remain in eternal afflictions is not to exist. Therefore he rightly said that he would not exist if he understood that he would have no share with the elect, A because they alone are blessed immutably in God. Those who are in hell, therefore, in comparison with that existence, [Col. 0169C] do not exist, because they are in eternal corruption and unending pain.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM 38

Guard our way, O Lord, so that we may not sin with our tongue; so that, as a spiritual spark burns in our meditations, we may store up in this age what, by your gift, we may receive in heaven. Through our Lord Jesus, etc.

# PSALM 39

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM 39

C The voice of the Church giving thanks because it has been freed from the world’s sorrow, while the Lord himself expounds the holy incarnation and the righteousness of his preaching and implores the Father’s help.

TT. For the end. A psalm of David.

[Col. 0169D] C We have often said that “the end” and “David” signify Christ the Lord, to whom this psalm must be applied.

1 Waiting, I waited for the Lord: And he attended to me.

H “Waiting,” the voice of the Church. It says that it awaits the Lord in the promises of the prophets, because the Prophet foresaw through the Holy Spirit that Christ would come in the flesh. H “And he attended to me,” through the splendor of the Gospel, in which he enlightened me.

2 And he heard my prayers: And he brought me out of the pit of misery and from the mire of mud.

H “And he heard my prayers,” because he himself shone upon me in the New Testament. “And he brought me out of the pit,” in which I was immersed when I worshiped mute idols. [Col. 0170A] “And from the mire of mud.” C For just as the mud of a pit is foul-smelling and heavy, so human sins are muddy and bristle with foul odors. H Hence “from the mire of mud,” that is, from earthly desires. Or: the pit is the depth of unbelief; the mud, carnal desires.

3 And he set my feet upon the rock: And he directed my steps.

H “He set them upon the rock,” that is, upon Christ. “My feet,” my senses. “And he directed my steps,” that is, he directs the senses of good works in the Church, because each person is crooked on his own unless directed by Christ. Therefore he directed my steps, lest, when coming to him, I should look back behind me toward the earthly things I had left. Or: the feet are affections; the steps are works.

4 [Col. 0170B] And he put a new song into my mouth: A hymn to our God.

H “And he put a new song into my mouth,” namely, his own praise, because the new human being came into the world and gave the world a new law. “A hymn,” C that is, praise composed according to the rules of song. “To our God,” H so that I may no longer sing shameful and theatrical sounds, but may delight in the hymns of the living God through the harmony of the New Testament.

5 Many will see and fear: And they will hope in the Lord.

H Many will see that he has been announced as having come and as having performed many miracles, and they will fear because they understand themselves to be sinners. And they will hope that their former sins may be forgiven them.

6 Blessed is the man whose hope is the name of the Lord. And he has not looked upon vanities and false insanities.

H “Blessed is the man,” that happy soul which has firm faith and directed hope in Christ. C Hope is so called as if meaning “a steadfast foot.” The one who has firm hope in the name of God is the one who eagerly desires the Lord alone, not temporal things. Vanity is to change suddenly from holy religion. False insanities are forming a god from stones; they are called insanities because they deceive the mind. H And all the things for which human beings go mad so that they may sin—the works of the flesh named by the Apostle (Galatians 5)—are false insanities because they deceive.

7 You have done many wonders, O Lord my God: And in your thoughts there is none like you.

8 I have announced and spoken: They have been multiplied beyond number.

H “You have done many wonders”: the Prophet recounts the divine miracles, that is, you showed our fathers your many wonders. “There is none like you.” C Is it comparable to playing with flaming torches in a theater that three boys walked in a furnace of fire (Daniel 3)? A You see someone walking on a rope as though performing wonders; consider our Peter, not a rope-walker but, so to speak, a sea-walker (John 21). God performed these miracles; behold them with the eye of faith. There is none like him.

H Up to this point the people of believers have spoken. From here the Lord himself begins to speak to the Father in this way. “I have announced,” saying: “Repent” (Matthew 4). [Col. 0171A] C “I have spoken,” namely, when he lived among us and preached the Gospel. “They have been multiplied beyond number”: H the Jews in their wickedness are outside the number, because they are not worthy to be counted among the number of the righteous. H A C Or sinners—whoever are destined for condemnation, even those called Christians—are beyond the number of the saved, that is, outside it.

9 You did not desire sacrifice and offering; A but you perfected ears for me.

H He says that the Father did not desire sacrifice, because when the Lord came, the sacrifices of the Jews ceased. “But you perfected ears for me,” that is, for obedience to the Father. C Or: this signifies his holy incarnation, in which he was obedient to the Father unto death, and in which he offered the Father, for the sins of all, a sacrifice, offering, and holocaust acceptable to him.

10 You did not desire a holocaust or a sacrifice for sin: Then I said: Behold, I come.

H You did not wish a holocaust for sin unless I offered myself to you as a sacrifice for the sin of the whole world. “Then I said: Behold, I come,” that is, I will assume flesh in which I may suffer.

11 In the heading of the book it is written concerning me, that I should do your will. My God, I desired it, and your law is in the midst of my heart.

H A C “In the heading of the book it is written concerning me,” in this book of Psalms. He says that it is written concerning him in the heading when it says: “Blessed is the man who has not walked,” and so forth. H Or in the Gospel: “In the beginning was the Word.” [Col. 0171C] Or in the heading of the book of the Old Testament, where it says: A “In the beginning”—that is, through the Son—God created, and so forth. He did the Father’s will when he descended from heaven. He desired to endure death for the life of all. C The divine law was in the midst of his heart when he meditated on the Lord’s law day and night.

12 I announced your righteousness in the great church: Behold, I will not restrain my lips, O Lord; you know.

C He rightly announced righteousness, saying: “Not so are the impious, not so.” “In the great church,” that is, spread throughout the whole world. He did not restrain his lips, for he did not cease admonishing the people of the faithless by preaching; in this he calls upon the Father as witness, because he feared no dangers. H The lips of Christ are also holy; he does not restrain them from preaching, as Saint Paul says: “The word of God is not bound” (2 Timothy 2).

13 I did not hide your righteousness in my heart: I spoke of your truth and your salvation.

C The will of the righteous man is, when he is able to benefit, not to hide the truth. The Lord the Savior did this, since he rebuked crowds and reproved unbelievers. H “I spoke of your truth,” because you are truthful. “And your salvation,” because you are the salvation of all.

14 I did not hide your mercy and your truth: From the great assembly.

C He did not hide the Father’s mercy when he said: “If you, although you are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more your heavenly Father?” [Col. 0172A] (Luke 11). H Truth and salvation are Christ, whom the saints preach. C Christ also spoke the truth in a very large gathering when, taking and reading the book of Isaiah, he said: “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled” (Luke 4).

15 You ÷ however .., O Lord, do not keep your mercies far from me: Your mercy and your truth have always received me.

C Having recounted his holy works, he returns to the glory of his passion, where he rightly begs the Father not to keep his mercies far from him. Mercy was shown when he saved human nature, wounded by the fault of transgression, through his incarnation. Truth was shown when, by the benefit of the resurrection, he sat at the right hand [Col. 0172B] of the Father. “They received me,” namely, in order to glorify me.

16 For evils beyond number have surrounded me: My iniquities have overtaken me, and I was unable to see.

C He speaks of his members, of whom he is the head, saying that evils surrounded him, so that he might profess himself to suffer what the multitude of believers endured, and that their number was beyond counting, at least among human beings. He adds that iniquities overtook him. The Lord the Savior neither committed evils nor was subject to iniquities, but he said this on behalf of his members, who suffer such things. It was an act of compassion on the part of our head that, having said many things about himself, he should mention the faithful. H Iniquities overtook the human race, that is, original [Col. 0172C] sin, from which iniquities sprouted. “And I was unable to see,” because the light of truth had been taken away.

17 They have multiplied beyond the hairs of my head: And my heart has abandoned me.

C Iniquity itself was multiplied beyond the hairs, that is, beyond the human race. C But the heart abandons us when a person, sick with sins, does not desire what will benefit him. H Or when a person sins, he does not have his heart, as David said: “Your servant has found his heart” (2 Samuel 7).

18 May it please you, O Lord, to rescue me: O Lord, look upon my help.

C “May it please you,” that is, “may it graciously please you”; here the concord of the Trinity is shown. For what pleases the Father pleases the Son and also the Holy Spirit. He adds “to you,” so that you might recognize the holy [Col. 0172D] Trinity as one God. “Lord, look upon me to help me,” so that we may understand that his regard is our protection; for we cannot otherwise be delivered unless the Divinity mercifully looks upon us.

19 “Let them be confounded and ashamed together, who seek my soul in order to take it away.”

C “Let them be confounded,” he said—that is, let them be disturbed by consideration of his wonders. “And let them be ashamed,” that is, let them be corrected by the glory of the resurrection, so that they may confess as God the one whom they formerly thought had been killed. “Together,” that is, all who persecuted Christ. “Who seek my soul,” for death; “in order to take it away,” that is, those who strive to separate it from my body in death.

20 [Col. 0173A] “Let them turn backward and be ashamed, who wish me evil.”

C Christ’s voice says “backward” here in a good sense, so that those who have followed an evil course may return to the good. “Those who devise evil against me.” C He signifies the wicked intentions of the Jews, which were not evil against the Lord, but against their own authors. “Thought” is so called from *coagitare*, “to drive or force together.” H Not only those who speak or act, but also those who wish me evil: let the humble follow me, those who formerly went before in pride.

21 “Let them immediately bear their confusion, who say to me, ‘Well done, well done.’”

C He said “let them bear,” as though it were an immense weight; “immediately,” as soon as they begin to sin, lest by advancing farther they be burdened more dangerously by their sins. “Their confusion,” that is, their perverse thought, convicted by the truth. [Col. 0173B] “Who say to me, ‘Well done.’” Here he censures false praisers, who, by flattering, strive more to deceive than they could wound by reproaches. H The Church indeed has two enemies: flatteries and blasphemies. A For there are two kinds of enemies especially to be avoided: those who speak good things with an evil intention, of whom he said above, “who wish me evil”; and those who speak evil while deceitfully praising, of whom he says here—

22 “Let all who seek you exult and rejoice over you, and let those who love your salvation always say, ‘May the Lord be magnified.’”

C “Let them exult,” namely, the righteous, “and rejoice” in eternal joy. “Over you,” H that is, in Christ. C “Those who love,” that is, those who seek me with spiritual charity. [Col. 0173C] H “May the Lord be magnified” in his members; may the holy people be magnified, and may God be glorified in them. Hence he said: “Let them see your good works and glorify the Father who is in heaven” (Matt. V). A Therefore let those who love Christ, our salvation, always say, “Well done, well done”—not as the wicked do, praising me, but magnifying you, Father, in me.

23 “But I am needy and poor; the Lord is concerned for me.”

H One is called needy who possesses something but lacks something; poor is one who possesses nothing; destitute is one who is without work. C “Poor”: the Lord is called poor from what is ours, rich from what is his own. For this reason he assumed the poverty of humanity, in order to make us participants in his abundance. [Col. 0173D] A But observe the consolation of the poor: the Lord is concerned for them. They followed.

24 “You are my helper and my protector, my God; do not delay.”

C When he says “helper and protector,” he shows the endurance of various sufferings. Hence the psalm itself began in this way and is also concluded with the same thought; therefore the whole psalm is rightly assigned to the virtue of patience.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM XXXIX

O God, the sole expectation of your servants, whom the head of the principal book taught would come into the world, implant, we beseech you, your law in the midst of our heart, so that, proclaiming your judgments, we may be rescued from impending dangers. Who, with the Father, etc.

# PSALM XL

[Col. 0174A]

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM XL

C The voice of the Prophet proclaiming blessed the giver of alms, and concerning the passion and resurrection of Christ.

**TT. To the end; a psalm of David.**

C This title is already well known, but it enhances this psalm that it is recognized as placed among the number forty, a number frequently applied to cleansing and purification.

1 “Blessed is he who understands concerning the needy ÷ and the poor .. On the evil day the Lord will deliver him.”

A C “Blessed is he who understands,” that is, so that alms may be offered even to the poor who do not ask. For one who gives to a petitioner performs a good work; but one who understands the poverty of the silent poor undoubtedly gains blessedness. [Col. 0174B] The Lord will deliver him on the evil day, that is, on the day of judgment, which is called an evil day for the wicked because the punishment owed to sinners is then paid.

2 “May the Lord preserve him and give him life, and make him blessed upon the earth, and not hand him over to the soul of his enemies.”

C “Preserve,” he said—that is, he does not permit him to perish amid the evils of the world, but leads him to his grace. Those who do not separate themselves from the Christian faith are properly called living. “And he will make him blessed,” certainly in the resurrection, when he places him at his right hand and admits him into the homeland of the blessed. H “And do not hand him over” into their hands or to their soul, that is, into the powers of the devil, who is always hostile to our faith. A H Or “upon the earth,” [Col. 0174C] that is, the Church; or even while he is living here in hope.

3 “May the Lord bring him aid upon his bed of pain; you have turned his whole bed in his sickness.”

H “May he bring him aid,” that is, may he provide him assistance, upon the bed of pain—that is, in the infirmity of the flesh, in which he is wounded as though on a certain little bed by his pleasure. “His bed”: here the body is understood as the bed. C What you have turned, disturbed, and afflicted here through various calamities, so that he may attain the rest of eternal blessedness, as happened in Job.

4 “I said, ‘Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul, because I have sinned against you.’”

C The Prophet cries out, devoutly fearful, so that he himself may obtain the Lord’s mercy. [Col. 0174D] “Heal the soul”: every sin is a sickness of the soul, and as it increases, the health of the inner person is destroyed. H Or here the Prophet changes the order and thereafter speaks in the person of Christ, who asks that the soul of his people be healed from sin.

3 “My enemies spoke evil against me: ‘When will he die, and his name perish?’”

C His enemies spoke evil during Christ’s passion, when they uttered falsehoods. It was unnecessary for the impious to devise lies, since they raged at the devil’s instigation. “When will he die?” These are the words of the deranged Jews, as Caiaphas said: “It is expedient that one man should die for the people” (John XI). “His name has [Col. 0175A] perished,” but only for those who refused to believe in him.

6 “But if he entered in to see, he spoke vanity; his heart gathered iniquity for itself.”

C He explains that time of the Lord’s passion when Judas entered deceitfully, not to venerate the Lord but to betray him. The Jewish people spoke vanity when they cruelly deliberated about his death. H His heart gathered iniquity for itself, when the wicked band determined to crucify the Lord of all things, saying: “His blood be upon us” (Matt. XXVII).

7 “He went out; and he spoke to the same end.”

8 “All my enemies whispered against me; [Col. 0175B] they devised evil against me.”

C The Jewish people went out from the secret place of the upright faith; they could not remain within because, through unbelief, they differed from the faithful. “He spoke to the same end,” namely, of vanity—that is, of the unbelief into which he entered by going out from the bosom of truth. He spoke vainly and falsely, and thus he spoke according to the very thing into which he had entered: deceit and falsehood. A bad entrance, a bad exit.

C Whispering is the smallest sound of the mouth, confused speech without any distinction of voice. The expression is derived from bees, whose uttered sound is a buzz; this occurred among those who murmured mouth to ear. “All my enemies,” that is, the Jews mentioned above, who were always devising evil against the Lord.

9 [Col. 0175C] “They established an evil word against me: ‘Will one who sleeps not add to it that he may rise again?’”

“An evil word,” when they cried out to Pilate: “If you release this man, you are not Caesar’s friend” (John XIX). “They established,” that is, they decreed. H Saying: “Take him and crucify him.” “Will one who sleeps”—C let the Jews hear, and let the heretics hear as well, him who sleeps immediately add to himself that he may rise again, saying: “I have power to lay down my soul, and I have power to take it up again” (John X). For the Jews thought that, if they killed him, he would not rise again.

10 “For even the man of my peace, in whom I hoped, who ate my bread, magnified treachery against me.”

[Col. 0175D] C By “the man of my peace” he means Judas, who gave him a kiss of peace when he betrayed him. “In whom I hoped,” that is, in whom I was thought to hope, whom I knew before he was born. “He magnified” it when, while they did not know who he was, he himself pointed him out to them.

11 ÷ “But you, Lord, have mercy on me .. and raise me up, and I will repay him.”

C “But you, Lord”—there humanity asks for what divinity promises elsewhere, saying: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John II). H “Raise me up,” namely from death, Father, [raise] the Son. “And I will repay him”: this happened when the due destruction overtook Judas. Vengeance anticipated Judas when due destruction struck him. Or “I will repay them,” [Col. 0176A] namely, the Jews. What we now see happened; one manuscript has *ei*, “him,” another *eis*, “them.”

12 “By this I knew that you desired me, because my enemy will not rejoice over me.”

C “By this I knew”: he shows that he recognized the Father’s love from this, that a glorious resurrection was to follow. “Because you desired me,” with “to be glorified and exalted” understood. “Because my enemy will not rejoice”: this was what he meant by “because you desired me,” namely, because the enemy was not permitted to rejoice over him.

13 “But because of my innocence you received me, and you confirmed me in your sight forever.”

H The greatest innocence is shown when the just man dies for the impious. C And he did not defend himself by any dispute. H Because of [Col. 0176B] this innocence, having conquered death, he was received by the Father in the heavenly places and confirmed forever. C His power rules heaven and earth, and every knee bows to him—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth (Phil. II).

14 “Blessed is the Lord, the God of Israel, from age to age; let it be, let it be.”

C The Lord is blessed, even if all are silent, because he does not receive every good as something foreign, but it proceeds from him himself. “From age”: he signifies the present world; and “unto age” is to be understood of the future, where all things now endure eternally. H He adds, “Let it be, let it be,” which is what the Hebrews say: “Amen, amen.”

## PRAYER FROM PSALM XL

[Col. 0176C] Gentle forgiver of our sins, who graciously intimates that we may escape the evil day if mercy follows the needy, bring aid, we beseech you, to our pains, so that, while you mercifully rebuke bodily sins, you may graciously bestow the medicine of the soul. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, etc.

# PSALM XLI

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM XLI

H The voice of the faithful desiring the Lord, C and speaking to their soul, so that, with God as helper, it may not be troubled in this world.

**TT. To the end; for understanding; for the sons of Korah.**

C “For the sons of Korah.” *Korah* in Hebrew is said to mean “skull.” The Skull, however, is the place where the Lord was crucified. [Col. 0176D] Therefore the sons of Korah are rightly called those who were worthy to receive the glorious trophy of the heavenly King, that is, the sign of the cross. And therefore this psalm suits the Christian person who is kindled by love of the Lord and by the flame of the Lord’s charity. On this subject it is the first psalm, followed by the eighty-third and the hundred thirty-third.

1 “As the deer longs for the springs of waters, so my soul longs for you, God.”

C “As the deer longs”: this animal is not improperly compared with the faithful, for it is, first, harmless; second, exceedingly swift; third, thirsty. H C It draws serpents in through its nostrils; when it has devoured them, it hastens to a spring because of the venom burning within it. [Col. 0177A] C This admonishes us that, whenever we absorb the poisons of the ancient serpent, we should hasten to the fountain of divine mercy. For Christ is an ever-flowing fountain; therefore he did not say “to streams,” since streams can dry up, whereas a fountain always flows. H Thus the person of the Church, who had long lived in a poisonous way of life, when, seeing this grace of God, he desires to abandon it, cries out, “As …,” so that, washed by repentance, he may see the glory of God.

2 “My soul thirsted ÷ for .. the strong + and living God. When shall I come and appear before the face of God?”

H “My soul thirsted,” not for dead images, but for him who said: “I live, says the Lord” (Ezek. XXXIII). C “When shall I come?” For he will then appear openly, when he mercifully looks upon us in his judgment. [Col. 0177B] H Or “when shall I come?” when the time arrives for me to see you in your glory with the saints (John III), and thus appear before the sight of your divinity, seeing you as you are, because the Church desires to be dissolved from the body and to be with Christ (Phil. I).

3 “My tears have been my bread by day and by night, while it is said to me daily, ‘Where is your God?’”

H How can bread be made from tears? It can, because just as the body is nourished by bread, so the soul is nourished by tears, since through them it hopes to obtain forgiveness of sins. C “Day” signifies prosperity; “night” we must understand as sorrow. Through these two, all the time of this life is indicated. “When he says to me daily”: this was continually said to Christians in the time of persecution [Col. 0177C]: “There is no one to avenge you; endure what we wish and command, and see whether your God will deliver you.”

4 “I remembered these things and poured out my soul within me, because I shall pass into the place of the wondrous tabernacle, even to the house of God.”

C While I was considering the things they reproached me with, or even the sins they imputed to me, I poured out my soul in a sudden flood of tears. The soul is poured out into itself whenever, pierced by God’s prompting, it returns into itself. He then explains why he poured himself out: because he was entering into the place of the tabernacle, that is, the present Church, where he groaned more deeply, since the heavenly Jerusalem was still deferred. H In it [Col. 0177D] are many wondrous persons, endowed with sacred virtues, who, built upon the foundation of the apostles, are held as one house. Entering it in mind, he poured out his soul.

5 “Amid the voice of exultation and confession, the sound of one feasting.”

C How did this most holy man long to go there? “Amid the voice,” namely, “of exultation and confession.” Exultation refers to psalmody; confession to lamenting sins. These two make the perfect Christian. “The sound of one feasting” is a brief definition of what exultation and confession are: they are the sound of one feasting. For this sound nourishes the soul and grants it a feast with sweet delight.

6 [Col. 0178A] “Why are you sad, my soul, and why do you trouble me?”

C The son of Korah, that is, the son of the cross, speaks, saying to his soul: “Why are you sad?”—that is, “Why do you trouble me by your affliction?” It is necessary that, since you are sad and mournful, the infirmity of my body should be troubled; I will tell you a saving remedy.

7 “Hope in God, because + still .. I will confess to him, the salvation of my countenance and my God.”

8 “My soul is troubled within me. Therefore I will remember you from the land of the Jordan and Hermonim, from the little mountain.”

C “Hope in God,” because hope changes everything for the better. But lest the soul say, “How can [Col. 0178B] I hope in him while my infirmity resists me?” the Son of the cross—that is, the man crucifying the flesh with its vices and desires (Gal. V)—speaks in response to his soul: “I will confess to him,” that is, I will repent of my sins, so that I may not be hindered from devotion to you. But to whom do you confess? “To him who is the salvation of my countenance,” that is, Christ.

H He says that his soul was troubled by the remembrance of former sins. “Therefore I will remember you.” H This penitent remembered his soul in the humility of repentance; he did not exalt himself by boasting, but made himself small by repenting. C He also says from where he will remember: from the land of the Jordan, which is interpreted as “descent,” because there the Lord descended into the spring that he consecrated for us, and it signifies baptism, in which sins were forgiven. [Col. 0178C] He therefore remembers the Lord through the benefit of baptism and the renunciation of the devil. Hence he adds, “and Hermonim.” Hermon is a small mountain near the Jordan, and is interpreted as “anathema”; he says this to the devil, so that he may be anathema to him when true repentance comes to God. “From the little mountain,” because God did not choose the proud but the humble. From the little mountain, therefore, which is Hermonim, he remembers the Lord, not exalting himself.

9 “Abyss calls to abyss ÷ in .. the voice of your cataracts.”

C “Abyss” and “cataracts” are Greek words. A C For by the two abysses the two Testaments are signified, namely, [Col. 0178D] the New and the Old, which confirm one another by mutual testimony, when the Old foretells the New. H “The Lord will raise up for you a prophet” (Deut. XVIII). The New, however, recalls the Old, as Paul says: “They drank from the rock, and the rock was Christ” (I Cor. X). C The cataracts are the prophets and apostles, because just as a multitude of waters pours forth through cataracts, so the Lord’s commands flowed from their mouths.

10 “All your heights and your waves have passed over me.”

C By the heights and waves, let us understand the holy Scriptures. The righteous man therefore says that they have passed over him because, as an eager investigator, he had immersed himself in knowledge of them.

11 [Col. 0179A] “By day the Lord commanded his mercy, and by night his song.”

12 “With me is prayer to the God of my life; I will say to God, ‘You are my protector.’”

H “By day the Lord commanded,” that is, in the light of the holy Scriptures he promised his mercy. “And by night, his song,” that is, to those placed in tribulation he displayed that same mercy. A Or “by day,” that is, in prosperity, God commanded us to understand his mercy and to show it to others; and by night he commanded a song, that is, exultation in adversity. Hence the Apostle says: “Rejoicing in tribulations” (I Thess. I). C Or, in the day of prosperity he teaches it, but in the night of tribulation he reveals it more clearly.

C “With me is prayer,” as though he said: within me there is [Col. 0179B] a sacrifice that I shall offer to God, namely prayer, which God has not despised. “I will say to God,” and so forth: that is, when the grace of baptism has received me, praising you for your benefits, I always call you my protector.

13 “Why have you forgotten me? And why do I walk sorrowful while the enemy afflicts me?”

C “Why have you forgotten me?” The most holy man speaks in human fashion, as though he said: “Why do you delay so long that you do not lead me into that homeland which you promised to your saints?” “Why do I walk sorrowful?” We are sorrowful when we endure scourges in this world. “While the enemy afflicts me,” that is, the devil, when he tests us by his deceitful stealth, and when we endure the vices of the flesh against our will and with a resisting spirit.

14 [Col. 0179C] “While my bones are crushed, they reproached me—those who trouble me, + my enemies ..”

C The bones are broken when the strength of our patience is afflicted. Our enemies mock this when they see it and abhor us as though we were disgraceful. H Or the bones are the stronger members of the Church, who, when pressed by scandals and various punishments, cause the simple to grieve when they see it. A H Hence the enemies of the Church reproach good Christians in the martyrs or confessors, since they are permitted by God either to be killed or to be afflicted.

15 “While they say to me each day, ‘Where is your God?’ Why are you sad, my soul, and why do you trouble me?”

H “While it is said to me each day,” as though the holy man were saying to Christ: “When I desired to please you, Christ, through repentance and affliction of body and soul, my enemies said that I was doing this in vain, saying, ‘Where is your God?’ (Isa. LXIV), not knowing the hidden things that God has prepared for those who love him.” C Or the martyrs say this in the passion, when their persecutors reproach them by asking where their God is. H “Why are you sad?” Because my desire is delayed. This repeated exhortation is a consolation against frequent tribulations.

16 “Hope in God, because + still .. I will confess to him, the salvation of my countenance + and .. my God.”

[Col. 0180A] H “Hope in God, because I shall still confess to him.” Let our hope always remain attentive in him; may he calm all our waves, preserve us in temptations, satisfy our thirst through his contemplation, and give us life through the salvation of his countenance.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM XLI

Wondrous salvation of our countenance, whom the souls of the faithful servants ardently thirst for, grant that, while we seek you—nourished by the visible rain of tears—we may invisibly place you within the tabernacle of our heart. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, etc.

# PSALM XLII

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM XLII

C The voice of the Church praying that, at the final judgment, [Col. 0180B] it may be separated from the unbelievers, and concerning its entrance to God.

**TT ÷ To the end; a psalm of David ...**

C “Psalm,” as has often been said, signifies the melody of heavenly words. “David,” however, indicates for us the very strong and desirable Savior, toward whom this psalm is directed from the person of the most faithful Christian, while his mind and intention are desirously turned toward him.

1 “Judge me, God, and distinguish my cause, God, from an unholy nation; deliver me from the unjust and deceitful man.”

C “Judge me, God.” The Prophet does not ask that his sins be examined, but that he be freed from the company of the wicked. It would be dangerous to say “judge me” unless he had added “distinguish my cause,” that is, separate [Col. 0180C] my mingling from the impious. “From an unholy nation,” that is, from the perverse or those who live wickedly. The unjust man is one who does evil openly. The deceitful man is one who secretly contrives evil. “Deliver me,” lest my life be corrupted by them. All these words can also be explained with reference to the future judgment. H No one is more unjust and deceitful than the one who is the inventor of iniquity and the imitator of holiness, namely, the devil.

2 “For you are God, my strength. Why have you rejected me? Why do I walk sorrowful while the enemy afflicts me?”

H I know that I am weak and fragile, and I do not perceive that I have any strength by which I may be delivered unless you save me. Christ rejects us when we have sinned. “I walk sorrowful” because of my sins. And therefore [Col. 0180D] I am afflicted in various temptations by the enemy, the devil, who above was called the unjust man. Therefore, because the darkness of sins troubles me, I flee as a suppliant to you, who are the light of the world.

3 “Send forth your light and your truth; they themselves have led me and brought me to your holy mountain and to your tabernacles.”

C The Prophet asks that the Father send the Son to judge, who is light and truth, so that when he comes, every sorrow of confusion may depart from his saints, and they may attain the glory of eternal blessedness. H “They themselves have led me” from the error of sin and have brought me into the Church through faith. C “Tabernacle” also signifies the Church itself; and the mountain signifies Christ. H Or the eternal tabernacles in heaven, to which the one who has been on the mountain, Christ, will come through faith. [Col. 0181A]

4 “And I will enter to the altar of God, to God who gives joy to my youth.”

C An altar is so called as though from “high place,” as if he said: H There I will enter, where I shall no longer present calves and rams, but offer myself as a living victim to God. “To God who gives joy to my youth.” C Here he uses “youth” for the newness of life, because the Lord, restoring all things that had decayed through old age, returned them to the newness of firm faith, giving believers the strongest steadfastness.

5 “I will confess to you on the lyre, God, my God. Why are you sad, my soul, and why do you trouble me?”

[Col. 0181B] C He confesses on the lyre who, enduring the adversity of this world, does not depart from the praise of God. H Or he praises on the lyre who mortifies his flesh. C “Why are you sad?” He frequently warns that the sadness of this age must be avoided, because it is always opposed to good things. Through it the strength of patience is broken, the light of charity is extinguished, the desire and virtue of hope grow weak, and the whole of life is thrown into confusion. But sorrow for sins should be embraced, because it directs one toward perpetual salvation.

6 “Hope in God, because + still .. I will confess to him, the salvation of my countenance + and .. my God.”

H “Hope in God.” He confesses him, asks him to forgive his sins, and calls him the salvation of his countenance. We too, confessing him, ask that we may deserve to be enlightened by his light, guided by his way, corrected by his truth, and enriched by his life. [Col. 0181C]

## PRAYER FROM PSALM XLII

We invoke and beseech you, almighty God, fountain of perpetual light, that, having sent forth your truth, you may suffuse our hearts with the brightness of a new light. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, etc.

# PSALM XLIII

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM XLIII

C The words of martyrs or confessors, praying that at the future judgment they may be avenged upon their enemies.

**TT. To the end; for the sons of Korah ÷ for .. understanding.**

C What the sons of Korah signify has already been sufficiently stated. “For understanding” means that we should understand the one who, according to the flesh, had his beginning in time, though begotten before the ages. H A C Wherever “understanding” is placed in the titles, it indicates that a spiritual interpretation is to be sought. [Col. 0181D]

1 “God, with our ears we have heard; our fathers have proclaimed to us.”

C “God, with our ears we have heard.” These words are to be understood as spoken in the person of the martyrs or confessors, as though he had said H that they had come to know him through spiritual understanding, according to the saying: “He who has ears to hear, let him hear.” He called the apostles and prophets “fathers”; through their proclamation we were reborn to life.

2 “The work that you worked in their days, and in ancient days.”

A C “The work that the Lord worked in ancient days” [Col. 0182A], that is, when he led the Israelite people unharmed through the waters of the Red Sea.

3 “Your hand destroyed the nations and you planted them; you afflicted the peoples and expelled them.”

C By “hand,” as has often been said, power is signified. For God’s power destroyed the nations when, after the Amorites and Gittites had departed from their own lands, the Hebrews were planted in their settlements (Josh. V). He afflicted the peoples when, as the priests sounded the trumpets, the walls of Jericho collapsed; it is established that they were then expelled from the city.

4 “For they did not possess the land by their own sword, and their arm did not save them.”

C Lest the Hebrews think that they had been victorious through their own strength, he therefore said: “not by their own sword.” By “arm” [Col. 0182B] we mean strength, since battle is fought by its exertion; but their arm did not deliver them from their enemies. Divine power alone saved them.

5 “But your right hand, your arm, and the light of your countenance, because you were pleased with them.”

C The right hand signifies the prosperous side; the arm, strength; illumination, counsel. The Lord confers these things together when he deigns to grant victory to those who fight. He was pleased with them when that one nation alone was chosen from the whole world, from which the Savior came.

6 “You are he himself, my king and my God, who commands salvations for Jacob.”

[Col. 0182C] C “You are he himself, my king,” that is, you yourself; there is no other Lord and Savior, to whom the name “king” is clearly appropriate. He adds “and my God,” so that you would not doubt that the Lord Jesus Christ is the one who commanded salvation for Jacob, when he heard through the angel: “You shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel” (Gen. XXXII), that is, “a man seeing God.” A Or by Jacob the Israelite people are understood, to whom God commanded bodily salvations as through another, namely, an angel, and not through himself. A C For “to command” means to order or accomplish something through another. A Thus God was not seen by the ancient fathers directly and in his essence; they saw him through some creature and were saved.

7 “In you we shall scatter our enemies with the horn, and in your name we shall despise those who rise up against us.”

[Col. 0182D] C This statement, that the enemies will be scattered with the horn, H that is, in Christ, because C the ancient enemy is to be despised, concerns the future judgment, where the victory is such that all struggles are shown to have been overthrown. H Something is scattered with horns; thus Zedekiah, having made two iron horns, said: “Thus I will scatter all Syria” (III Kings XXII). Our horn, however, is Christ, who is also the name of the Father; in him our adversaries are either scattered or despised.

8 “For I shall not hope in my bow, and my sword will not save me.”

C The bow is the warrior’s protection, in which [Col. 0183A] human beings place their confidence; but one presumes more on the sword, since an arrow is often shot in vain, whereas a sword more certainly accomplishes the effect of death. Yet the multitude of the saints does not trust even in it, but in divine protection. He supplies the reason for this.

9 “For you saved us from those who afflicted us, and you confounded those who hated us.”

C There is no doubt among the saints that, at the Lord’s second coming, they will be delivered from the persecution of the most wicked spirits, who here afflicted them with many snares. Those who hated the blessed will also be confounded, when they are condemned to eternal punishment and the righteous receive the kingdoms of heaven. A C “You saved,” he says instead of “you will save,” because of the Prophet’s certainty concerning the future. C Or they speak of the future [Col. 0183B] confidently as though it were past, because they have no doubt that what they know will certainly come.

10 “In God we shall be praised all day, and in your name we shall confess forever. Diapsalma.”

C Those who say “we shall be praised” profess that they will be proclaimed in the future. “All day” indicates perpetual time, which has no night. They confess forever who strive continually to make the praises of the Lord resound here. H He says “in God,” because he himself is our praise and glory; and we Christians are called by his name, and in such a name we shall confess.

11 “But now you have rejected and confounded us, and you will not go forth ÷ God .. in our strengths.”

C By saying “but now,” the martyrs signify [Col. 0183C] that they spoke earlier about future times, because the present time is now here. “You have rejected,” that is, you have delayed for us that future blessedness which you promised us. “You have confounded”: that glorious confusion which the martyrs undergo when they are afflicted with various insults, beaten with clubs, and, as though guilty of crimes, handed over to death. Now also God does not go forth in the strengths of the martyrs when he subjects them to tribulations and permits them to undergo various sufferings.

12 “You have turned us backward before our enemies, and those who hated us plundered us for themselves.”

C To turn backward is to flee a bodily enemy. H We ought to keep our enemies before us, that is, before our eyes, so that we may know what we must [Col. 0183D] avoid. “They plundered us for themselves.” C This usually happens to those who flee: those unable to prevail against their enemies fall into plunder. H The persecutors plundered the martyrs when they tormented them with blows and other tortures. A Or “us,” because we are behind as though defeated; while the persecutors are in front, as though victorious, mocking and torturing us.

13 “You gave us like sheep for food, and you scattered us among the nations.”

C The meek simplicity of sheep is food for wolves, and it is rightly compared with the martyrs, who acquiesce in being killed by persecutors without resistance. “Among the nations”: the martyrs, when handed over, lost their freedom together with their possessions.

14 [Col. 0184A] “You sold your people without price, and there was no multitude in their exchanges.”

H Up to this point the martyrs have spoken; now they speak about the Jewish people, to whom it was said: “You were sold because of your sins” (Isa. L). “Without price,” because the blood of the Lamb was not poured out for them. H “There was no multitude in their exchanges.” C An exchange is obtaining something equal to what has been given. H But here the commodity that was sold was of less value than the price, and therefore no exchange was made. For the Lord, who did not purchase the people with gold but with his own blood (I Pet. I)—that is, who freed the human race lying in sins—

15 “You made us a reproach to our neighbors, a mockery and derision to those around [Col. 0184B] us.”

C When he says “you made,” he shows the fixed condition of the passion by which the saints suffer from their neighbors, that is, their persecutors. “Reproach” is set against what is good. For just as all good things are honorable, so disgraceful things are reproaches. Derision is a confused expression of joy, declaring its insult through uncontrolled hilarity. “Those around us” explains them as unbelievers and faithless people.

16 “You made us a likeness among the nations, a shaking of the head among the peoples.”

C The martyrs were made a likeness of Christ when the nations afflicted them with equal punishments. The shaking of the head also happened [Col. 0184C] to the martyrs—as it happened in the Lord’s passion—when the wicked blasphemed them H with mockery or a shaking of the head. But even now, Jesus, if anyone wishes to live devoutly in you, the wicked immediately blaspheme with mockery or a shaking of the head.

17 “All day long my shame is before me, and the confusion of my face has covered me.”

H The Lord speaks these words in the flesh he assumed, because throughout the day Christ suffered shame for us, and even confusion, up to the very cross and its execution. C Shame ordinarily comes for a moment and departs once calmed after a brief time; this shame, however, was extremely grievous, since it continued without interruption.

18 “From the voice of one reproaching and reviling, from the face of the enemy and persecutor.”

[Col. 0184D] H “From the voice of one reproaching,” when it was said to him: “If you are the Son of God, come down from the cross.” “From the face of the enemy,” that is, Judas; “and persecutor,” the Jewish people. C To reproach is to curse someone to his face; to revile is to disparage someone in his absence and maliciously wound him with words.

19 These things have all come upon us, yet we have not forgotten you, nor have we acted wickedly against your covenant.

H “These things have all come upon us”: the voice of the martyrs—all that you, Lord, endured, we too have endured. “Yet we have not forgotten you”: we have always confessed you. “Nor have we acted wickedly”: that is, we faithfully proclaimed your covenant and faithfully lived within the covenant. [Col. 0185A] “We have not forgotten.” C For those who keep him in mind cannot forget his covenant.

20 ÷ And … our heart has not turned back: And you have turned aside your paths from your way.

C The heart of those who despair of the Lord’s goodness turns back; this is what these people did not do, for they were proved to place their hope in the Lord. “Way” is derived from *violence*. “Path” is used here in an evil sense, since he says “our.” Human paths—namely, the pleasant and shady tracks along which human frailty walks—are rightly said to be divided from the heavenly way: those lead to death, whereas this way leads to the desired salvation. A Or “you have turned aside,” that is, you seem to have driven away from our persecutors our good paths, along which we walk amid tribulations, as is implied by what follows.

21 [Col. 0185B] For you humbled us in a place of affliction, and the shadow of death covered us.

H We have been humbled in a place of affliction—that is, in this body in which we dwell and suffer for Christ’s sake. C “The shadow of death” refers to the passage from this life, which is shown to be common to saints and sinners. That other death, however, is the true death by which the wicked are punished with eternal damnation. H Although the saints are afflicted here and destined for death, they nevertheless live for God; therefore this death is the shadow of death, not death itself.

22 If we have forgotten the name of our God: ÷ And … if we have spread out our hands to a foreign god.

[Col. 0185C] H “If we have forgotten the name of God,” that is, Christ. “If we have spread out our hands to a foreign god,” that is, to an idol.

23 Will not God inquire into these things? For he knows the hidden things of the heart.

C “Will not”—this must be pronounced with emphasis, since it is an exceedingly grave matter in God’s sight if one sins against his religion. We customarily inquire when we desire to recognize things that we know our conscience does not contain. This is not so with God, because he knows everything; but he is said to inquire when, punishing us for these things, he makes us remember them. And because the subject was religious devotion, which is practiced more in the heart than in bodily observance, he adds: “He himself knows the hidden things of the heart.” A And what those things are follows.

24 For your sake we are put to death all day long; we are accounted as sheep for slaughter.

C To be subjected to death is to find, through the long sufferings of the present life, an end for Christ’s sake. “All day long”: not by a death lasting only a moment, but by a departure for Christ’s sake prolonged throughout the whole course of life, he indicates the end of the faithful. A sheep has no weapons and does not fight with its teeth, but patiently yields to the hands of the robber. Thus Christ’s servants were accounted as sheep to be killed, because they seemed to be slaughtered without any resistance.

25 Rise up; why do you sleep, Lord? Rise up ÷ and … do not reject us forever.

C It is not that rising up properly belongs to God, who is never known to be capable of sleeping; but in human usage he is said to sleep when our expectation is prolonged by divine providence. “Rise up” is repeated so that he may not delay coming to the aid of those whose dangers he sees increasing. “Do not reject us forever”: that is, until the end, where the blessed receive their rewards and crowns are prepared for the martyrs. H “Forever”: namely, eternal death.

26 Why do you turn your face away? Will you forget our poverty and our tribulation?

H God turns his face away for a time in order to test his elect. C “Will you forget our poverty?” That is: the poverty to which you were accustomed to bring help, and which you love so much in others that you call yourself poor. He added “our tribulation,” whose compassionate observer Christ always is.

27 For our soul has been humbled in the dust; our belly has clung to the earth.

[Col. 0186B] C They humbled themselves in the dust who, after scattering ashes over themselves, torment their souls in remembrance of their sins. H “Our belly has clung to the earth”: when the flesh is weakened, but the mind is intent upon heavenly things.

28 Rise up, help us, and redeem us for the sake of your name.

C “Rise up” should not be applied to sleep, but rather to the resurrection, in which human captivity is recognized as destroyed. When he rose, we were helped—not because of our merit, but for the sake of his name. Therefore he is called Savior, because by the grace of his mercy he saves the weak.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM XLIII

Rise up, Lord, as our help, and rescue us from the reproaches of our vices. You who, before our fathers, conquered the kingdoms of hostile nations, rescue us from our persecuting enemies by the illumination of your face. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, etc.

# PSALM XLIV

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM XLIV

C The prophet, filled with the Holy Spirit, promises to pour forth the incarnation of the Lord Christ, and describes Christ’s bride, the Church, through mystical virtues.

**TT.** For the end, for those who will be changed, for the sons of Korah, for understanding. + A song for the Beloved …

C “For the end” signifies perfection, that is, the Lord Christ. “The sons of Korah”: that is, the sons of the cross, who will be changed by passing from the sadness of this world to eternal joys. “Song” signifies the text of the psalm; “for the Beloved,” that is, for the Lord Christ, of whom the Father said: “This is my beloved Son” (Matthew III). His spiritual marriage is now recounted.

1 My heart has poured forth a good word; I speak of my works to the king.

C We say that something “pours forth” when the fullness of food evaporates in wholesome digestion. Thus this holy man, filled with heavenly generosity, poured forth what the faithful people would be abundantly nourished by. “My heart”: understand the inner chamber of the mind. “A good word”: he calls the Son of God by this name. “Works”: the prophet’s little work and the beautiful composition of this psalm.

2 My tongue is the pen of a scribe, swiftly ÷ writing …

H “The pen of a scribe”: the scribe himself is Christ, who wrote faith, hope, and charity in the hearts of the saints. “Swiftly”: what he had said is not delayed, but is quickly fulfilled.

3 You are more beautiful in form than the sons of men; grace has been poured upon your lips. Therefore God has blessed you forever.

C Christ is called more beautiful than all human beings—not in bodily appearance, but truly more beautiful than the human race because he had no sins. We rightly call that beautiful which is adorned with the grace of the purest holiness. H “Grace has been poured forth,” because the law was given through Moses, but grace and truth came through Jesus Christ (John I). [Col. 0187B] C It is rightly said: “God has blessed you”—in the form of a servant, which endured suffering and reached the kingdoms of heaven. “Therefore,” because grace has been poured upon your lips—namely, the grace of preaching. H And also of healing: when by your word you cure the sick, make the sea grow calm, call Lazarus and he comes, and all that you say is accomplished by the grace of your lips.

4 Gird yourself with your sword upon your thigh ÷ …, most powerful one.

5 In your appearance and your beauty, advance prosperously, proceed, and reign.

C By “sword” here we should understand the word of divine preaching; by “thigh,” the incarnation. H Christ, girded with the sword of the word of preaching, divides the Son from the Father, and so forth. “Most powerful one”: not sluggishly or lightly, but manfully.

C “In your appearance”: this pertains to Christ’s humanity; “beauty,” to his divinity. “Pay attention,” so that from heaven you may look with mercy upon the perishing human race. “Prosperously,” because he was about to bestow the benefits of liberation upon the human race. C H “Proceed,” like a bridegroom from the virginal womb. “Reign,” that is, in the belief of human beings; display the power of your majesty.

6 For truth, meekness, and righteousness; your right hand will lead you wondrously.

C “For truth”: this signifies the saying, “Truth has sprung up from the earth” (Psalm LXXXIV). Meekness was shown when he prayed on the cross for his persecutors (Matthew X). Righteousness, because the pious teacher instilled saving commandments. “Will lead”: it preserves him unharmed throughout the course of this entire life. “Wondrously,” because he rose again on the third day. “Right hand” signifies the power of the word.

7 Your arrows are sharp; peoples will fall beneath you in the heart of the king’s enemies.

C The sharp arrows are the words of the Lord and Savior, piercing human hearts for their salvation; they wound in order to heal. “Sharp” pertains to the swiftness of transformation. “Peoples will fall beneath you,” not with the feet that support their bodies, but in their hearts they will fall into humility—those who had previously stood upright in pride. He calls those people Christ’s enemies who dissent from the heavenly law with a contrary will.

8 Your throne, O God, is forever and ever; the rod of uprightness is the rod of your kingdom.

C Here God’s throne pertains to the future judgment, in which all things are examined truthfully. “Rod” signifies the rule of divine equity: this rod governs the righteous and strikes the wicked. It is truly called upright because it is bent by no crookedness. Or the unconquered strength and inflexible discipline is the rod of uprightness. And he shows more clearly what this rod is by continuing:

9 You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions.

C No one perfectly loves righteousness unless he also curses wicked deeds. Christ was anointed as king and priest. H “With the oil of gladness,” that is, of resurrection and ascension. C This repetition—“God, God”—displays the proclamation of great love. “Above your companions” is said because Christ received this blessing above the whole human race, so that, uniquely anointed, he might anoint others.

10 Myrrh, resin, and cassia are upon your garments, from ivory houses; from them the daughters of kings delighted you in your honor.

C The holy body of the Lord is understood to have been a kind of garment of divinity, because the majesty of the Word appeared hidden from unbelieving eyes beneath the veil of flesh. From this garment—that is, from the mystery of the incarnation—myrrh, resin, and cassia are fittingly said to have come. Myrrh signifies Christ’s death. Resin, which is called ammoniac resin, is compared with the Lord’s incarnation. Cassia, which our people call *fistula*, grows in watery places and signifies the waters of baptism. Ivory is the tusk of an elephant, which mates temperately with its female and does not take a second mate. This is suited to chaste women, who are known to have dwelt in ivory houses while following God’s commandments through chastity. “Daughters of kings” are those who rule themselves and their souls. H Or “daughters of kings,” that is, souls converted through the preaching of the apostles. A Or “daughters”: they are the Churches founded through the preaching of the apostles.

11 The queen stood at your right hand in a gilded garment, ÷ surrounded by varied adornment …

H The Church is called queen, and she is a queen who rules her vices or sins. C She is said to have stood at the right hand because the right side is honorable. We should apply gold to charity. The Church is also adorned with variety: with the gold of the apostles, the silver of the prophets, the gems of virgins, the scarlet of martyrs, and the purple of penitents.

12 Hear, daughter, and see, and incline your ear; forget your people and your father’s house.

C He says “hear,” namely, the prophets who sang of the Lord’s incarnation. The Church is called the daughter of the prophets because she was born from their preaching. H “And see,” with the eye of the heart. C “Incline your ear,” that is, receive the prophet’s words with honor. “Forget,” that is, abandon the gatherings of the pagans. “House”: he means Babylon, that is, the world. “Father”: the devil, who truly possessed that house of confusion.

13 And the king will desire your beauty, for he himself ÷ is … the Lord your God, + and all will worship him …

C This king, then, is the Savior, who desired the Church, established in the devil’s lot. “He himself is the Lord your God,” not the one whom you called father, who had made you dark, but the one who removed your former ugliness and bestowed upon you bridal beauty. The Christian peoples will worship him.

14 ÷ And … the daughters of Tyre with gifts; they will entreat your face, ÷ all … the rich of the people.

C “Tyre” is interpreted as “distress.” H It signifies souls placed in distress, for that person worships through the gifts of the heart. We look toward the face of the Church—that is, toward the face of the Christian people—when, placed in distress, we entreat Christ’s majesty with devout tears. “All the rich”: not Tyre alone, but the united diversity of the whole world, so that the face of the Church may signify either faith or the majesty of divinity.

15 All her glory ÷ is … within, the daughter of the king; she is clothed all around with golden fringes and varied adornments.

16 Virgins will be brought to the king after her; those nearest to her will be brought to you.

C The glory of the Church is indeed manifest when the daughters of rulers—or of the righteous—are converted to the Lord and desire to offer themselves with the heart’s hidden devotion. “Within”: to offer themselves to Christ in the secrecy of their thoughts. Fringes are the edges of garments, by which the final stage of human life is signified. They are called golden because at the end there is complete perfection, where the fullness of charity is found like gold. “Clothed all around with variety”: he speaks of the various virtues of the faithful, which we explained above.

C “Virgins will be brought to the king,” then widows. Observe in these very names that there is no small distinction. He said that virgins would be brought because they are strong in bodily integrity. He said that widows would be brought forward because they are often broken by various anxieties and wearied by bodily weakness. They will therefore be brought near to Christ—that is, chaste widows, who are joined at an inferior rank. For while virginity possesses a hundredfold fruit, this state glories in a sixtyfold abundance.

17 They will be brought in joy and exultation; they will be led into the temple of the king.

C It is rightly said, then, that they will be brought in joy, because that frail sex overcame the gravest sufferings of the body. They were brought by the ministries of angels, not merely into his presence but also into the temple—that is, into the king’s inner sanctuary, namely, the future Jerusalem—where to have arrived is blessed joy and glorious security.

18 In place of your fathers, sons have been born to you; you will appoint them princes over all the earth.

C “In place of your fathers.” He now explains how greatly this bride has progressed: in place of the ancient fathers—that is, the worshipers of idols—sons, the apostles, have been born to her, whom she sent throughout the whole world as princes of preaching. But to the extent that these things differ, the Church is praised. The former were seducers into error; the latter, teachers of truth. The former sowed destruction; the latter urged people toward life.

19 I will remember your name in every generation and generation.

H They will therefore remember your name, because the apostles will always proclaim you or build up the generations of the saints. Or the Christian people, converted through the apostles’ preaching, will remember Christ’s name. The Roman translation—which Jerome and Cassiodorus follow here—has “those who remember.”

20 [Col. 0190B] Therefore the peoples will confess to you forever, and throughout the age ÷ of the age …

H Because of their preaching, the peoples will always confess their sins to Christ. Or “they will confess.” A C That is, in the confession of the Creed, when they publicly confess the Creed before the face of the Church. A Or they will confess by praising, throughout the age of the age, here and after this life forever. “The age of the age” signifies the future, when every adversity comes to rest and righteousness alone reigns, after the devil’s opposition has been destroyed. Then they will confess by fully declaring God’s glory.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM XLIV

Lord Christ, Word of the Father, through whom all things were created and are created, we ask you to guard your Church, gathered from the diversity of the nations, so that, while we love you with a pure heart through the righteousness of faith itself, we may merit the rule of the eternal age with the fathers.
