You who, with the Father, etc.

# PSALM XLV

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM XLV

C The voice of the faithful, fearing nothing amid the world’s turmoil because God is their protector.

**TT.** For the end; for the sons of Korah; a psalm concerning hidden things.

C “For the end”: it is known how this can be referred to Christ. “The sons of Korah”: Christian sons, in whose person this psalm is sung. “Concerning hidden things”: it signifies the Savior’s coming, which he arranged in wondrous secrecy for the salvation of humankind.

1 Our God is our refuge and strength, a helper in the tribulations that have found us exceedingly.

[Col. 0190D] C What a beautiful definition—as though the Christians, the sons of Korah, were asked, “What is our God?” Let them answer: “Refuge, strength, and helper.” He is the refuge of the faithful when he frees them from danger to the soul; strength when he firmly guards their minds from wicked error; helper in tribulations when divine mercy receives and defends us amid tribulations.

2 Therefore we shall not fear when the earth is disturbed, and when the mountains are carried into the heart of the sea.

C Therefore we shall not fear, because we believe in Christ. H C “When the earth is disturbed,” that is, the generation of the Jews, who think earthly thoughts; and when the mountains—that is, the apostles—are carried away, leaving the unbelieving Jews. “Into the heart of the sea,” that is, when they have passed over to preach to the Gentiles. C And one should observe that he compared the perfidy of the Jews to dry land, but the faith of the Gentiles to false waters, so that you might recognize those hearts as hardened in evil, whereas these were seasoned with evangelical salt.

3 Their waters roared and were troubled; the mountains were troubled in its strength. Diapsalma.

C He says that the apostles sounded forth their preaching of the Lord’s coming, at which time he declares that the waters—that is, the innumerable nations—were troubled and terrified by this proclamation and by amazement at the miracles. [Col. 0191B] “The mountains were troubled,” that is, the powers of the world, when the pagans brought sacrilegious laws against God’s religion. “In its strength,” namely in the strength of the apostles’ sound: for by the apostles’ loud-sounding preaching the whole world trembled and afterward, with a purified heart, returned itself to the Lord’s mercy.

4 The rush of the river makes glad the city of God; the Most High has sanctified his tabernacle.

C This river is Christ, and the river’s rush has blessed it, because its course admits nothing stagnant or sluggish when the power of his divinity has poured itself forth. The tabernacle of the Most High is the Church, or the glorious assumption of the human body.

5 God is in its midst; it shall not be moved. God will help it at the dawning of the morning.

[Col. 0191C] C “God is in its midst,” that is, in the Church; it shall not be moved. For the Church cannot be moved, since it is known to be founded upon the most solid rock, that is, upon Christ. He says “will help,” namely, while she labors amid the adversities of the world. H “At the dawning,” that is, by the holy vision which a pure heart will merit. Or “in the morning,” that is, at the beginning of a good work, and this “at the dawning,” that is, by the illumination of the Holy Spirit.

6 The nations were troubled and kingdoms bowed down; he gave his voice, and the earth was moved.

H “The nations were troubled,” namely by vices and crimes. C “The kingdoms bowed down,” that is, they were humbled to worship. “He gave his voice”: by preaching in person and through the apostles, at which those who are called earthly had necessarily to tremble, being sinners. Or: the idolatrous nations were troubled at the sudden sound of preaching concerning an unknown religion.

7 The Lord of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our protector. Diapsalma.

C “The Lord of hosts,” assuredly he whom the heavenly hosts serve. “With us,” because, having assumed flesh, he dwelt on earth. “Protector”: when he assumed flesh for the salvation of unbelievers. He says “our,” for he is not the God of Jacob alone, but of all who are devout with like faith.

8 Come and see the works of the Lord, the wonders he has set upon the earth, removing wars to the end of the earth.

C When he says “Come,” he exhorts them to draw near to the Lord by faith, since they could not see one who was far off. [Col. 0192A] H “The works of the Lord,” that is, the powers of God. C A prodigy is so called because it speaks beforehand. This occurred at the Lord’s Nativity, when a virgin gave birth and the star appeared to the Magi. “Removing wars,” that is, because at the Lord’s Nativity, while Augustus reigned, the whole world is recorded to have been at peace. H Many histories relate that all wars ceased at the Lord’s coming. Or understand the conflicts of vices.

9 He will break the bow and shatter the weapons; he will burn the shields with fire.

H “He will break the bow,” that is, the hidden snares of evil spirits. “He will shatter the weapons,” that is, present conflicts. “He will burn the shield with fire,” that is, he will consume with spiritual fire the fantasies of diabolical excuse, the defense of sins, or protection. [Col. 0192B] C Or understand this of the arms of the nations by which they attacked the faith and defended themselves: all these will be shattered when they are conquered by truth.

10 Be still, and see that I am God; I shall be exalted among the nations and exalted on the earth.

C The sons of Korah speak this verse in the person of the Lord. It is rightly said to those who armed themselves with worldly delusions and served the devil, “Be still.” “For I am God,” not the one who formerly armed you for evil, but he who “shall be exalted among the nations and on the earth,” that is, in the Jewish nation; for above he compared the Jews to the earth.

11 The Lord of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our protector. + Diapsalma …

[Col. 0192C] C The sons of Korah repeat this confession a second time in order that through it they may declare to us that deliverance has been granted. “The God of Jacob” is frequently added so that the victory of the Christian people may be declared: although later in time, it nevertheless surpasses the first people in faithful devotion.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM XLV

Merciful God, a manifest refuge in impending tribulation, sanctify the dwelling of our heart with the rush of the eternal river, so that, while you, God of hosts, work with us, we may confute earthly battles. Through our Lord, etc.

# PSALM XLVI

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM XLVI

C The voice of the Church praising God and proclaiming his Ascension.

**TT.** For the end, for the sons of Korah, a psalm.

[Col. 0192D] C In this psalm too the sons of Korah speak—those whom the Church, their mother, marks with the banner of the cross. First the nations are admonished that they ought to resound with praises to the Lord; then the Lord’s Ascension and his kingdom are briefly described.

1 Clap your hands, all nations; rejoice to God with a voice of exultation.

C Those clap their hands who give alms and serve the sick. To rejoice is to be glad; the word is said to come from *iuvando*, “delighting,” when we express the greatness of joy not in articulated speech but in an indistinct voice. A voice of exultation signifies psalmody, which is offered to God for the majesty of his name.

2 For the Lord most high is terrible, a great king over all the earth.

H The Lord is called most high because by his own power he ascended the heavens. C “A great king,” because he is King of kings and Lord of lords (Apoc. XIX). “Terrible,” because he will judge the world; and lest he be thought king only of the Jews, he calls him king of all lands.

3 He subjected peoples to us and nations beneath our feet.

C “Feet” here signify the most holy preachers, beneath whom peoples and nations were rightly said to be subjected.

4 He chose for us his inheritance, the beauty of Jacob whom he loved. Diapsalma.

[Col. 0193B] C “He chose for us”—one must supply “to give”—so that he who had come to save the Israelite people might bestow this still more upon the nations in his merciful generosity. “The beauty of Jacob”: Jacob, by lentils and a small exchange of carnal things, attained spiritual honor. This is the very beauty of Jacob which the Lord loved, so much so that he wishes his faithful likewise to do what Jacob by mystical signification warned them to follow: namely, to offer earthly things to God and acquire heavenly things. Thus we are truly called Christians. II Or, from the beauty of beloved Jacob—that is, from his stock—he chose the apostles.

5 God ascended amid rejoicing, and the Lord at the sound of a trumpet.

C The Lord’s Ascension is said to have taken place amid rejoicing because the astonished apostles were filled with ineffable gladness of heart at such a miracle. The sound of the trumpet likewise signifies the words of the angels saying, “Men of Galilee” (Acts I). These words thundered with a great din, like the crash of struck air.

6 Sing praises to our God, sing praises; sing praises to our king, sing praises.

C To sing praises is to sing God’s praises by good deeds. “To our king,” that is, to our God Jesus Christ—not to anyone alien, but to our God, to whom alone such praise is fitting.

7 For God is king of all the earth; sing praises wisely.

[Col. 0193D] C “For God is king of all the earth”: this is said against those who made diverse gods for themselves in individual places, such as Venus at Paphos, Mars in Thrace, Jupiter in Crete, and others in different places. “Sing praises wisely,” that is, let one understand what one sings. No one does anything wisely which he does not understand. H Or: understand spiritually what you sing according to the letter.

8 God has reigned over the nations; God sits upon his holy throne.

H The Lord has reigned over the nations, which he received as an inheritance from the Father. C “He sits upon his holy throne” signifies the Lord Savior, who sits at the Father’s right hand, reigning for ages of ages. H Or he sits in the angels, who because of their innocence are called God’s thrones; hence he said, “Heaven is my throne.”

9 The princes of the peoples have gathered with the God of Abraham, for the mighty gods of the earth have been exceedingly exalted.

[Col. 0194A] H “The princes of the peoples,” that is, the apostles, have gathered to judge with the God of Abraham, that is, with Christ, who is the God of Abraham. “For the gods.” C These are the Jews, who were mighty because they swelled with pride; through pride they became last, though through humility they could have been foremost. H Or “gods” are the saints, who here have been exceedingly exalted through faith and preaching and in judgment will be raised still higher and more gloriously—that is, the apostles thus gathered at judgment are exceedingly exalted as judges.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM XLVI

[Col. 0194B] God, King of all ages, whose kingdom is extended over all peoples, subject, we pray, the nations of vices beneath our feet, so that, while we sing praises wisely to you, our God, we may overcome them with your help. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, etc.

# PSALM XLVII

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM XLVII

C The voice of the prophet praising God, who has enlarged his Church.

**TT.** A psalm of a song for the sons of Korah, ÷ the second of the Sabbath …

C Let us now see what “the second of the Sabbath” signifies. By “Sabbath” we should understand the synagogue, that is, the assembly of the Jews, which seemed to observe the Sabbath. The second is the Catholic Church. Therefore the words of this psalm are assigned to priests, to instruct the Christian people, who may without doubt be regarded as sons of the cross and are manifestly second in time after the synagogue.

1 Great is the Lord and exceedingly praiseworthy, in the city of our God, on his holy mountain.

[Col. 0194C] C The Lord is called great because he does all things powerfully; praiseworthy because he does beautiful and wonderful things. He adds “exceedingly,” because it has no limit but always increases by its continuance. “In the city,” that is, in the Church. The holy mountain is Christ.

2 It is founded in the joy of all the earth: Mount Zion, the sides of the north, the city of the great king.

H The earth was founded in joy from Christ’s Ascension, though formerly it lay subject to curse and sins. “Mount Zion,” C the Jewish nation. “The sides of the north,” [Col. 0194D] the peoples of the Gentiles: it became the city of the king, that is, the Catholic Church, which is known to have been gathered from the whole world.

3 God will be known in its dwellings when he receives it.

C The Lord will be known in the dwellings, that is, in his most holy members; his virtue and power will be declared when, by his own gift, blessed men are shown to offer themselves to him in the Church.

4 For behold, the kings assembled; they came together as one.

C The kings of the earth here signify the rulers of the Jews, whom Herod assembled together while seeking where Christ was to be born; and they, assembled together, said, “In Bethlehem” (Matt. II). And they came together as one because all gave the same answer.

5 Seeing it thus, they were amazed; they were troubled, they were moved. Trembling seized them.

6 There were pains like those of a woman in labor; with a violent spirit you will shatter the ships of Tarshish.

H The Jews themselves, namely, on seeing the Redeemer’s glory, were amazed at such glory; troubled because they knew themselves sinners; moved from unbelief to faith. Trembling seized them (Isa. XXVI) from the consciousness of their sins, whence it is said: “At your fear we conceived and brought forth the spirit of salvation.”

H “There were pains” when they began to afflict their bodies by abstinence. “With a violent spirit,” that is, with the most mighty Holy Spirit, “you will shatter the ships”: you will humble the pride of the nations, because Tarshish has become proud through the traffic of navigation, signifying those who are carried about by the business of this world. C These, then, now broken, say in faith: “As we have heard.” A The pains are those of the penitent, like the pains of a woman in labor.

7 As we have heard, so have we seen in the city of the Lord of hosts, in the city of our God; God has founded it forever. Diapsalma.

H As we have heard through the prophets, so we see in the Gospel, which is the city of hosts. “In the city of God,” that is, in the Catholic Church. C God founded it, because it alone is truly called the city of God.

8 We have received, O God, your mercy in the midst of your temple.

[Col. 0195C] C They receive God’s mercy who are not only called through faith but are also chosen through hidden predestination for eternal blessedness. H “In the midst of the temple,” that is, in the Church. C Mercy, which is Christ, is received not by all but by those Catholics who have followed his commandments.

9 According to your name, O God, so also is your praise unto the ends of the earth; your right hand is full of righteousness.

C God’s name is undoubtedly believed worthy of worship throughout the whole world. Therefore his right hand is full of righteousness: it signifies the place where the righteous are to be placed. For at judgment they come to the right hand, because those who have merited to be righteous by his gift are received into that right-hand part. A Or: “According to your name,” etc., that is, as you are named throughout all lands, so you are praised throughout all lands. Those praise who live well, and there can be no praise except in his saints.

10 Let Mount Zion rejoice + and … let the daughters of Judah exult because of your judgments, ÷ O Lord …

C By Mount Zion he signifies the Catholic Church. H “Let the daughters of Judah exult,” that is, the souls of confessors, because Judah is interpreted “confession.” C They are to exult because of the Lord’s judgments, by which they know that they will come to eternal blessedness.

11 Surround Zion and embrace her. Proclaim in her towers.

[Col. 0196A] H “Surround Zion,” that is, defend the Church by your faith. “Embrace her,” in charity. “Proclaim,” that is, preach, “in the towers,” that is, among the rulers of the Church. For as a tower is strong and looks out on every side, so saints must be strong and preachers among humankind.

12 Set your hearts upon her strength, and distribute her houses, that you may proclaim it to another generation.

H “Set,” that is, direct your hearts, “upon strength,” that is, upon Christ’s charity. C No strength can be more excellent than this. H O teachers of the Church, distribute the houses—that is, the ranks of ecclesiastical order—so that you may proclaim it not only to those who believe but also to those who will believe. C By the other generation he signifies the Christian people, who are known to be second after the Hebrew people whom the Lord first chose. H Therefore, teachers of the Churches, distribute the ranks of his ordinances canonically and holily, not corrupted by rewards or fallen through flattering respect of persons, so that you may proclaim. And what shall we proclaim? “For this,” etc.

13 For this is God, our God, forever and unto the age ÷ of the age …; he himself will rule us forever.

H This verse explains what ecclesiastical priests ought to proclaim: “For this is God, our God.” C “Forever” is said against those who imagined temporal human beings to be gods. May he indeed rule us, because he himself is our king. H May he rule our slippery and crooked steps.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM XLVII

Praiseworthy and terrible God, who are found to be the glorious ruler in the heavenly Jerusalem, enlarge our mind by spiritual understanding, so that, having received your mercy in the temple of our breast, we may be accounted worthy to proclaim your name. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, etc.

# PSALM XLVIII

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM XLVIII

C The voice of Christ concerning the merits of the righteous, the punishments of the wicked, and that the rich are not to be feared in this world.

[Col. 0196D] **TT.** For the end, for the sons of Korah, a psalm.

C The words of this title are directed to the Lord Savior. For he himself signifies “the end,” is understood through the sons of the cross, and is without doubt declared through the psalmist. Throughout the psalm the words are those of the almighty Son.

1 Hear these things, all nations; give ear, all you who inhabit the world.

C The universal Church is admonished to come to hear Christ, because Christ does not wish to benefit only a few, but all who seek him with a pure heart. “Perceive with your ears,” that is, so that they may store these words in the recesses of their memory. “Inhabitants of the world”: we understand Christians and the righteous, who know how to dwell [Col. 0197A] in the world without becoming entangled in its wicked errors.

## 2. Both earthborn and sons of men: Rich and poor together.

C “Both earthborn”: this means that all inhabitants of the earth are called to hear the words of God. C “Earthborn” are sinners who pursue earthly vices. “Sons of men”: he calls the righteous so, since Christ himself was also called the Son of Man. H By “rich and poor,” the free and the slave are understood.

## 3. My mouth shall speak wisdom: And the meditation of my heart understanding.

C The mouth of Christ speaks wisdom, that is, in order to disclose the divine mysteries hidden from the [Col. 0197B] wise of this age. Understanding pertains to establishing approved conduct; thus every divine utterance is most fully indicated by these two virtues. H I shall always meditate in my heart so that people, abandoning foolish vanity, may follow the understanding of Christ.

## 4. I shall incline my ear to the parable: I shall open my proposition in the psaltery.

C Christ promised that he would incline his ear in order to learn whether the devoted people fulfilled his preaching. “To the parable”: a likeness is an imitation of the reality; the meaning is that we should promptly do, with devoted emulation and by the Lord’s assistance, what has been given to us as an example. He said that he would open his proposition in the psaltery, that is, that he would declare the commandments of the [Col. 0197C] divinity in the holiness of his own body, so that he might be shown to teach by word and by example. For the psaltery, as we have often said, is an apt likeness of the Lord’s body.

## 5. Why shall I fear? On the evil day the iniquity of my heel will surround me.

C “Why shall I fear?” This verse should be pronounced as a question followed by its own answer: that is, “Why should I be confounded by fearful thought on the evil day?”—namely, on the day of the Passion, which was evil for the Jews but good for the faithful. The one who is gnawed by the memory of sins ought to fear the end of life. Christ, however, could not fear death, since the iniquity of the heel did not surround him, as normally happens to a sinner at the end of life, when iniquity closes a wicked life with a wicked end. A Or any person, recognizing his sins, says: “Why shall I fear on the evil day?” that is, on the day of judgment. And he answers: “For this reason: the iniquity of my heel will surround me.” H That is, actual or original sin.

## 6. Those who trust in their own strength: And glory in the abundance of their riches.

H “Those who trust in their own strength”: they slip at the heel. C “And in the abundance of their riches”: such people must fear the end, since they are unwilling to abandon worldly things and dread the punishments of their sins. By “strength” he means bodily powers, firmness of spirit, and eloquence of speech.

## 7. A brother did not redeem; will a man redeem? He will not give his appeasement to God.

H “A brother did not redeem,” that is, Adam, because he himself died and did not rise again; or “a brother did not redeem,” that is, Moses. “A man will redeem,” that is, Christ will redeem those whom Moses did not redeem. He will not give appeasement to God if he does not practice repentance, through which Christ is appeased. C Or it should be read as a question of astonishment, thus: “Will a brother not redeem? Christ redeemed—will a man redeem?”—namely, Adam. It is as though he said: “If Christ has not redeemed or will not redeem, no one will redeem”; hence it should be read negatively: “No man will give to God,” and so forth.

## 8. And the price of the redemption of his soul. And he will labor forever and live + still: to the end.

## 9. He will not see destruction when he sees the wise dying: Together the foolish and the stupid will perish.

H “And the price of redemption”: “he will not give” is understood, because he did not give alms, through which sins are wiped away. “He will labor forever,” placed perpetually in torments, “and live to the end,” because he is not killed but continually restored for punishment.

H “He will not see destruction,” that is, he does not understand that torments are impending for him. When he sees a person wise in God depart from this world, he says: “What benefit did fasting, chastity, and almsgiving bring him? Is he not dead too?” Something similar was said by the Jews when they insulted our Redeemer: “Are you greater than our father Abraham?” (John 8). C The foolish person is one who refuses to heed the preaching of the prophets. He is called stupid because he does not wish to receive the Lord himself when he comes. These, therefore, will perish together, because they are to be condemned at the future judgment.

## 10. And they will leave their riches to strangers: + And .. their tombs will be their houses forever.

H Those who hope in riches and not in the Lord lose both—their riches and God’s assistance. They lose their riches because they placed them where thieves break through; they lose God’s assistance because they despised him. The riches they loved so greatly they will leave not to their own people but—as what will burn them more grievously—to strangers, for whose sake they committed every sin. And they build tombs for themselves out of marble: solid, large, and beautiful, as though they would remain houses forever. Behold also the pomp of the dying.

## 11. Their tabernacles are from generation to generation: They have called their names in their lands.

H This will be their perpetual dwelling, because they do not rise again to possess eternal life, but to be condemned to punishment. “They have called”: often pagans feast above the tombs of the dead, and, drinking in the names of the departed, sing certain empty songs with musical accompaniment. C They also invoke the names of the dead and believe that this benefits them. H But it benefits nothing those condemned in hell; thus “lands” are understood as tombs. [Col. 0199A] Another reading has “and they invoked,” which is explained here.

## 12. And man, when he was in honor, did not understand: He was compared with beasts ÷ without understanding .., and became like them.

H “Man, when he was in honor, did not understand” that he had been formed in the image of God. C “He was compared with beasts”: a fitting likeness is given to the witless, so that those who do not understand that they bear the image of God may rightly be compared with foolish beasts. For take away from a man the knowledge of God, and he is altogether a foolish animal—empty presumption and passing pride.

## 13. This is their way, a stumbling-block to them. And afterward they will be pleased in their own mouth. Diapsalma.

C “This way,” that is, the life in which we walk in this age. [Col. 0199B] But what this way does to the wicked is not left unsaid. It is certainly a stumbling-block to those who practice it, that is, a goad and a pain. For a sinner does nothing for his own security when the result of his action is torment. It is the custom of sinners that, after they have fulfilled their desire in sin, they immediately give thanks to the divinity—in their mouth, not in their heart. Hence he says: “Afterward they will be pleased in their own mouth,” giving thanks to God that they have prospered in sin.

## 14. Like sheep they have been placed in hell: Death will feed upon them.

C Just as sheep continually remain after the loss of their wool, so in them punishment always finds something to torment without diminishing their substance. H They are rightly consumed by death, because they refused to have Christ as their shepherd.

## 15. And the righteous will rule over them in the morning: And their help will grow old in hell, away from their glory.

C “And they will rule over them”: this belongs to the resurrection of the blessed, so that the good may prevail over the wicked; in this life, sinners possess the righteous. “In the morning,” when the glory of the resurrection has dawned. Their helps grow old like rotten rags, because their riches benefit them nothing. “Away from their glory,” which they had in this age. H That is, in comparison with the glory they had here: the more they gloried here, the more corruption they will suffer in hell (Revelation 18).

## 16. Nevertheless, God will redeem my soul from the hand of hell, when he receives me. Diapsalma.

C God delivered the souls of those who steadfastly believed in his coming. “From the hand of hell,” from the power of the devil, who had held souls captive before Christ’s coming. C “Rich” is derived from *divus*, since a rich person is believed, as it were, to need nothing like a god; by him here we should understand the impious person. When his glory has been multiplied, join this with what follows: “Do not be afraid.”

## 17. Do not be afraid when a man becomes rich: And when the glory of his house has been multiplied.

H Judas the betrayer became rich by selling his master, but he carried away with him when he died none of the price he had received. If, therefore, someone now becomes rich by oppressing the poor, do not be afraid: he soon passes away and takes nothing of what he had seized with him, as the Lord says: “Fool, this night they demand your soul” (Luke 12); “and whose will be the things you have prepared?”

## 18. For when he dies he will not take everything: Nor will his glory descend with him.

C Here the reason is given why the glory of the world should not be feared. Why, indeed, should we fear a rich man who dies poor and is able to carry nothing else with him except what can make him burn? He is rightly said to descend into the deepest pit, but without the glory of the world and without a crowd of attendants. The house you admired remains entirely behind, but the burdens you did not see send enormous weight with him into Gehenna.

## 19. For his soul will be blessed during his life: He will confess to you when you do good to him.

C This blessing does not concern sanctification but popularity. “He is blessed” is said on account of the tongues of his attendants, who praise their masters amid their feasts. “When you do good to him, he will confess,” that is, he gives thanks to God when he acquires some profit.

## 20. He will enter into the generations of his fathers: Forever he will not see light.

C Those who imitate the worst fathers in this age will be condemned to their company. “Forever he will not see light,” that is, the light of wisdom, both here and forever—the light that enlightens every human being, which only the saints will see in the divinity. For just as sins are dark, so they take away the light of wisdom from sinners. H Of such people it is said: “Cast him into the outer darkness” (Matthew 22).

## 21. Man, when he was in honor, did not understand: He was compared with beasts ÷ without understanding, and .. became like them. [The marked words are *insipientibus et*, “without understanding, and,” unlike verse 12.]

C The prophet concluded this most beautiful psalm with equality of verse, so that the sinner might remove himself from his evil purpose when, through repeated rebuke, he recognized his own stupidity.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM 48

Fill our mouth, O Lord, with your wisdom, so that, mindful that you became human and redeemed us from Tartarus, we may deserve to be adorned with the light of your countenance. You who, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, etc.

# PSALM 49

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM 49

C The voice of the synagogue concerning Christ’s first and second coming, and its admonition that the faithful offer him a sacrifice of praise.

**Title.** A psalm of Asaph.

H Asaph was an outstanding musician, whose name is interpreted as “assembly.” This psalm distinguishes the righteous from the impious, the heavenly from the earthly, and the holy from sinners. It also declares that it was not the prophet who spoke, but the Lord himself, saying, “God,” and so forth.

## 1. The God of gods, the Lord, has spoken: And he has called the earth.

C In the Greek language, “God” is called *fear*. H Thus, God is the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit in the Trinity. Yet he is one God of gods, for good people are called gods. He has spoken, C through the prophets and apostles. “And he has called the earth,” that is, the human race. H He wished believers to be called gods because he gave them power to become children of God (John 1). C They are therefore called sons as well as gods, because both are granted by grace, not by nature.

## 2. From the rising of the sun to its setting: From Zion, the beauty of his splendor.

C “From the rising of the sun,” through the course of the sun: he signifies the whole world, because his radiance rises and sets over the entire earth. “From Zion, the beauty”: Jerusalem, in which this mountain shines like a mass of gold for pure minds. For from this city the apostles went forth and proclaimed the beauty of its splendor throughout the whole world, as Isaiah says: “From Zion the law will go forth, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” (Isaiah 2).

## 3. God will come manifestly: Our God, and he will not be silent.

C The prophet now speaks of Christ’s second coming: “He will come manifestly.” Christ will then come manifestly, when he will no longer be crucified but will judge the world. For now he is silent through patience when we sin; then he will not be silent, when he says to the wicked: “Go into the eternal fire” (Matthew 25). He is called “manifestly,” as though the festive day were called from the morning, because the whole day would be devoted to the festival and sacrifices.

## 4. Fire will blaze before him: + And .. a mighty storm around him.

[Col. 0201C] H This fire has a twofold power: it illuminates and burns. Let the righteous rejoice, because they are illuminated by it; let sinners fear, because they will be burned by it. C This storm is not driven by winds nor stirred up by raging blasts; rather, a powerful spirit rises from divine power, so that the Lord’s threshing-floor may be winnowed by the sentence of his justice. Then he separates the grain from the chaff. This judgment is rightly called a storm because it will come unexpectedly and, with extreme speed, distinguish the good.

## 5. He summoned heaven from above: And the earth, to distinguish his people.

H “He summoned heaven,” that is, the apostles and the remaining saints, who, having despised earthly things, set their minds on what is above. But he distinguishes the earthly, so that when the heavenly are placed on the right, these may be set on the left.

## 6. Gather his saints to him: Those who establish his covenant above sacrifices.

C Now the synagogue of Christ speaks to the angels, who by their ministry at the end of the age will gather all the saints from the whole world. H “Those who establish,” that is, the saints who preach or fulfill the New Testament above the Old, so that by “testament” you may understand the new law, and by “sacrifices” the old one. H C Or “those who establish the covenant,” that is, those who give and perform things in due order, as Christ testified to those who practice works of mercy: they will receive an eternal kingdom, and in their acts of compassion God takes greater delight than in all sacrifices.

## 7. And the heavens will proclaim his righteousness: For God is judge. Diapsalma.

C By “heavens” he means righteous men, to whom the administration of the heavenly word is entrusted. “For God is judge,” as though he said: He cannot be deceived, and just as he knows all things openly, so he distinguishes without reproach. H Or the saints will preach righteousness, that is, his commandments, and will preach that he is judge of the living and the dead; therefore righteousness is to be feared.

## 8. Hear, my people, and I will speak: Israel, and I will testify to you: I am God, your God.

C “Hear, my people”: here Truth itself speaks in its own person. “People” signifies the devoted multitude. When he says “hear,” it means, “receive with a devoted mind.” “I will speak,” with “things that will profit” understood. “To testify,” that is, to give testimony. He will give testimony to the faithful when he says: “For I was hungry, and you gave me food” (Matthew 25). There is also a great mystery here when he says, “I am”: “I am” is properly a word of divinity, because divinity is always present and does not change with time. There is also another mystery there: the one syllable is contained in three letters, so that the holy Trinity may be taught to be one God.

## 9. I will not rebuke you for your sacrifices: Your burnt offerings, however, are always before me.

C “I will not rebuke you for your sacrifices”: he speaks to the Jewish people, saying that sacrifices of cattle are no longer to be sought, but a contrite heart. Burnt offerings are accepted in his sight when our mind, kindled by divine love, dissolves its sins through lamentation and affliction, so that all vices may be burned up and consumed through bodily suffering.

## 10. I will not accept calves from your house: Nor goats from your flocks.

C By rejecting these two things, he indicates that all the sacrifices of the former age are to be excluded in every way; the whole is signified through a part.

## 11. For all the beasts of the forests are mine: The beasts on the mountains and the oxen.

C “The beasts of the forests” signifies the nations. “The beasts on the mountains” signifies the simple within the Catholic Church, who are known to dwell on the summit of faith. “Oxen” signifies the apostles, prophets, and preachers who labor assiduously in the Lord’s field.

## 12. I know all the birds of heaven: And the beauty of the field is with me.

C Who can know all the birds of heaven except the divine majesty alone? In this verse he has embraced everything. H “The beauty of the field is with him,” because wherever he wishes, the abundance of all things is either administered or withheld.

## 13. If I were hungry, I would not tell you: For the world ÷ of the earth .. and its fullness are mine. [The marked source word is *terrae*, “of the earth.”]

H God’s hunger is not for bodily food, but that someone should do his will (John 4). Therefore he conceals his hunger from Israel, because he awaits the sinner’s conversion. “The world of the earth” is his, that is, the holy Church, as though he said that it was to be redeemed by his holy blood.

## 14. Shall I eat the flesh of bulls: Or drink the blood of goats?

C How could things that are not necessary be pleasing to God? H Here he declares that the old sacrifices must be abolished. Therefore he requires sacrifice in good conduct, saying: “Sacrifice,” and so forth. Yet these rejected sacrifices can benefit us when the needy receive such things from us—when the hungry are fed and the thirsty are given drink. In the poor God receives what he does not permit to be offered to him in sacrifices.

## 15. Sacrifice to God ÷ a sacrifice .. of praise [the printed *et laudis* literally reads “and of praise”]: And fulfill your vows to the Most High.

[Col. 0203B] C That person sacrifices a sacrifice of praise to God who has been separated from earthly vices and dies to the world, so that he may become an offering to Christ. He also fulfills vows to the Most High who has prepared for him such sacrifices as the merciful God himself commanded. H This is the acceptable sacrifice; this is the rich burnt offering: that God be praised by the human being whom he created.

## 16. + But .. call upon me in the day of tribulation: And I will deliver you, and you will honor me. Diapsalma.

C He commanded, “Call upon me,” so that no one might place his hope in earthly comfort, where everything is transitory. “In the day” when the adversary afflicts you. “I will deliver you,” as though he said: “Surrounded by the devil’s attendants, I will free you with the utmost speed.” “You will magnify,” or “honor,” me, that is, you will proclaim that I am great forever. The Roman translation has *magnificabis* (“you will magnify”), whereas the Gallican has *honorificabis* (“you will honor”); the meaning is the same.

## 17. But to the sinner God said: Why do you recount my righteousnesses? And take my covenant upon your mouth?

C Here the wicked who refuse to be converted are forbidden to presume to mingle themselves in divine discourse, because the mouth that presumes to recount the Lord’s righteousnesses must be righteous. “My covenant” signifies both the Old and the New, because when one is mentioned in an undivided way, both are recalled. H Let the teachers or bishops of the churches hear this—those who cut away the people’s sins by preaching but do not fulfill in their works what they preach.

## 18. But you hate discipline: And you have cast my words behind you.

C He hates discipline because, through wicked presumption, he murmurs against just corrections and does not wish God to punish in him what he has done wrong. He also casts God’s word behind him who disdains to follow the divine commands.

## 19. If you saw a thief, you ran with him: And with adulterers you placed your portion.

C We should understand this verse in such a way that, through these two prohibited acts, he appears to have forbidden every crime. The person runs with the thief who joins him with shared intent in committing the crime. He places his portion with the adulterer who offers him assistance by which to accomplish his desires. There, without doubt, he is recognized as having his portion.

## 20. Your mouth abounded in wickedness: And your tongue fashioned deceit.

C Here we should understand “mouth” as the thought of the heart. Thoughts abound in wickedness when, through various kinds of sins, they rage with an evil will. “And your tongue”: whoever falsely praises another makes deceit with his tongue.

## 21. Sitting, you spoke against your brother: And against your mother’s son you set a stumbling-block. You did these things, and I was silent.

C Sitting is the posture of one who lingers; therefore he sins more grievously who lingers in detraction of his brother. Here we should understand “brother” as every neighbor according to the flesh, since he is also going to speak of the spiritual one. “Son of your mother”: he means offspring of the Church. He therefore sets a stumbling-block for his brother who devises heretical perversions or other traps by which an innocent brother may be caught. “You did these things, and I was silent.” H Because I reserved them for future judgment to be examined: I was silent because I did not immediately punish, but endured.

## 22. You wickedly supposed that I would be like you: I will rebuke you and set you before your face.

C “You wickedly supposed”—that is, because God is silent and delays punishing sins, fools therefore believe that he approved human crimes. H “I will rebuke you” when you have been placed on the left side. C “I will set you before your face”: he said above that the sinner had cast his words—which he ought always to have kept before his eyes so that he might live according to them—behind him and away. At the judgment, therefore, the sinner will see before his face what he thought he had passed over through the benefit of forgetfulness. It is an immeasurable terror for people to see those things by which they know they are brought to eternal punishments.

## 23. Understand these things, you who forget God, lest he seize you and there be no one to deliver.

C “Understand,” that is, obey, you who forget God. He forgets God who, through wicked presumption, scorns his commandments. “Lest he seize,” namely, the devil. For when he seizes, there is no one who can deliver to salvation except the Lord through his great mercy. H Or otherwise: when Christ seizes those who forget him—that is, casts them into death—no one can deliver them from him. For when the devil seizes someone here, there is one who can deliver to salvation, namely Christ. But when the Lord seizes someone for punishment, no one can free the one condemned.

## 24. The sacrifice of praise will honor me: And there is the way by which I will show him the salvation of God.

H “The sacrifice of praise,” because God is honored through every good thing the saints do. Christ is the way through the works of the saints. The Son is the salvation of God the Father. C Or he calls the way the most blessed psalmody, which is traversed not with feet but with pure minds, and leads to Christ. H O glorious path, which leads to the creator of heaven and earth!

## PRAYER FROM PSALM 49

Lord of gods, we ask you to receive us in the sacrifice of praise, by which, recounting your righteousnesses without the burden of sin, we may walk along that way which shows your salvation. Through our Lord Jesus, etc.

# PSALM 50

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM 50

C The voice of one doing penance.

**Title.** To the end. A psalm of David, when the prophet Nathan came to him, when he entered in to Bathsheba.

H This fiftieth psalm contains the voice of a penitent, showing that whoever has fallen into some crime should return to salvation by confessing his evils.

## 1. Have mercy on me, O God: According to your ÷ great .. mercy. [The mark covers *magnam*, “great,” alone.]

C When the most powerful king heard himself rebuked by the prophet Nathan, he was not ashamed publicly to confess his sin (2 Samuel 12), saying to the Judge: “Have mercy on me.” This expression is not examined critically but is always heard in tranquility; it is the one thing by which we, though guilty before the Lord, can be defended without difficulty. H For God shows great mercy to the one who considers himself wretched because of his sins.

## 2. ÷ And .. according to the multitude of your mercies: Blot out my iniquity.

H “According to the multitude,” I take refuge in your mercies, so that you may pour the antidote or medicine of your mercy into grievous wounds. He says “mercies” because my sins are many and your mercies are many. C For only the one whose sins are all blotted out is enrolled in the book of life.

## 3. Wash me more thoroughly from my iniquity: And cleanse me from my sin.

H “Wash me more thoroughly,” as though he said: “You can forgive me more than I know how to ask you.” C He adds, “Cleanse me,” so that nothing unclean may remain in him. For someone may be washed without becoming entirely pure; therefore he rightly added, “Cleanse me.”

## 4. For I know my iniquity: And my sin is always against me.

C Those sins are stronger which we commit knowingly, rather than those we perpetrate through ignorance. He says that his offenses stand against him because, already placed here as though before the coming judgment, he dreads the most terrible sight of his offenses; and he says that his offenses stand against him as a kind of depicted image—not once or twice, but always.

## 5. Against you alone have I sinned and done evil before you: So that you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged.

C If someone from the people goes astray, he sins both against God and against the king. But when a king sins, he is guilty before God alone. This king therefore says that he sinned against God alone, because he has no human being who can judge his deeds. And because he knew that God was everywhere, he rightly lamented that he had done evil before him. The Lord’s words are rightly called justified, since undoubtedly his declarations are always fulfilled. Some apply the words “and prevail when you are judged” to the Lord’s Passion, since, when judged, he prevailed, and, though condemned, acquitted the world. But it can rightly be understood that God prevails when he is judged by human beings, because in every judgment God is proved just.

## 6. Behold, ÷ for .. I was conceived in iniquities: And my mother conceived me in sins.

H This verse explains the fall of the whole human race. A human being is conceived and born in original sin, which is drawn from Adam, but is purified by the grace of God in baptism.

## 7. For behold, you have loved truth: You have made uncertain and hidden things of your wisdom manifest to me.

C God is not pleased with our punishments but seeks a true confession of error. David, therefore, not denying his sin, confessed the truth, which God seeks and loves above sacrifices. The “uncertain and hidden things” are what God revealed to the prophet David in the manifestation of his Son: namely, that he might foretell his future Passion and announce the glory of his resurrection. Hence he says that he ought not to have sinned, since he had deserved to recognize such things. Properly speaking, uncertain things are those that cannot be discerned at all but are gathered through certain ambiguities. Hidden things are those that neither the eye sees nor the human mind judges.

## 8. You will sprinkle me, Lord, with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed: You will wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow.

H Just as hyssop—that is, a humble herb suitable for treating the lungs—is useful, so someone sprinkled with heavenly hyssop, that is, humility of heart, is cleansed from every malignity of pride. “You will wash me,” that is, through repentance. C By hyssop, therefore, he understands the blood of Christ, which not only wipes away stains but also displays the purity of the radiant soul above the whiteness of snow, because the spiritual soul shines far above earthly bodies, none of which is whiter than snow.

## 9. You will give joy and gladness to my hearing: And the humbled bones will rejoice.

H “To my hearing,” that is, when, lying in the infirmity of sin, I deserve to hear: “Man, your sins are forgiven.” You will give joy and gladness to my hearing. C Joy pertains to the absolution of sins; gladness to the possession of everlasting rewards. “Bones” signify the supports of the soul, which had to be humbled until the penitent could be absolved. H “Bones,” that is, virtues which had been humbled by sins; or the eternity of hope is the humbled bones.

## 10. Turn your face away from my sins: And blot out all my iniquities.

H “Turn your face away,” that is, do not see my sins, do not remember them; blot out all my past, present, and future iniquities.

## 11. Create a clean heart in me, O God: And renew a right spirit within my inmost being.

C The prophet asks that a clean heart be created in him, that is, restored—a heart that, though pressed by sins, can no longer be moved toward guilt. “And a right spirit.” For just as through Adam we are made old, so through the benefits of Christ the Lord we are renewed. H Or “a right spirit,” so that I may confess rightly; or a spirit made right for seeing and discerning, just as it was formerly right in me.

## 12. Do not cast me away from your face: And do not take your Holy Spirit from me.

H “Do not cast me away,” so that I may not become an exile from your power like Cain (Genesis 4). “And do not take your Holy Spirit from me,” but, when my sins have been consumed by him, establish me in your sight. Or “the Holy Spirit,” that is, the spirit of prophecy.

## 13. Restore to me the joy of your salvation: And strengthen me with a princely spirit.

H “Restore to me the joy,” that is, the exultation of your Christ, which I possessed in him before I sinned. “With a princely spirit,” he said, that is, so that he himself, and not vices, may rule in me. Or by “a princely spirit” understand the Father; by “a right spirit,” the Son; and by “the Holy Spirit,” the Holy Spirit himself.

## 14. I will teach the wicked your ways: And the impious will be converted to you.

H “I will teach the wicked,” that is, I will punish myself so that they may imitate my example. C For if the prophet is spared, the greatest hope of remission is granted to those who offend. I will therefore teach sinners, by the example of my remission, to hope; and by my word I will proclaim the wonders of your mercies.

## 15. Deliver me from bloodguilt, God, God of my salvation: ÷ And .. my tongue will exult in your righteousness.

C The prophet asks to be delivered from bloodguilt, which is expressed contrary to Latin usage; nevertheless, the translator is entirely worthy of praise, because he chose to place something contrary to secular art rather than depart from the truth that had been set down. For if he had said “from blood,” he might seem to indicate one sin; but by using the plural number, he undoubtedly confesses that there are many offenses. “God of salvation” signifies the Lord Christ, through whom salvation is given to those who devoutly believe. “My tongue will exult,” that is, if you deliver me from sins, my tongue will rightly speak your praise, because of what was said in the preceding psalm: “But to the sinner God said,” and so forth. Once absolved, he could rightly speak the word from which divine law had suspended the sinner.

## 16. Lord, you will open my lips: And my mouth will proclaim your praise.

H He asks that his lips, which had been closed by sin, be opened. For praise from the mouth of a sinner is not beautiful (Ecclesiasticus 15). C “Mouth” is also called the secret place of the heart, from which divine praise is sung truthfully.

## 17. For if you had desired sacrifice, I would certainly have given it: You will not delight in burnt offerings.

H Let the Jews hear this and understand that their sacrifices have ceased. C Even the offerings of cattle and the rites of sacred worship are to be rejected at the Lord’s coming.

## 18. A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit: A contrite and humbled heart, O God, you will not despise.

C After saying which sacrifices God rejects, he now says which ones he seeks. We give this pleasing sacrifice to God when we slay the spirit of pride through the humility of confession; from it there flows not blood but streams of tears. He says “a contrite heart,” meaning one severely afflicted by the labors of repentance. “Humbled before God”: the heart could not have been humbled unless it had been broken by continual tribulation. God does not despise such offerings.

## 19. Deal kindly, Lord, in your good will toward Zion: So that the walls of Jerusalem may be built.

C The prophet therefore supplicates that, since the synagogue sinned while placed under the law, Zion, succeeding it through the grace of Christ—that is, the Catholic Church—may be established. “And let the walls be built”: if you wish to understand this according to history, it perhaps signifies the time of Theodosius, when Eudoxia, his exceptionally religious wife, crowned Jerusalem with a more extensive circuit of walls.

## 20. Then you will accept the sacrifice of righteousness, offerings and burnt offerings: Then they will place calves upon your altar.

C “Then you will accept,” O Father, the sacrifice—that is, the most glorious Passion of your Son, who offered himself as a sacrifice for all; his Passion is the truest sacrifice of righteousness. “Offerings and burnt offerings” pertain to Christians who were to believe after the Lord’s coming; it signifies that the hearts of living human beings, not the limbs of dead animals, are to be offered. He placed “calves” either for the innocent or for preachers, whose image the evangelist Luke assumed in the figure of the calf. Or it refers to those who offered their souls as a pleasing sacrifice upon the sacred altars.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM 50

God, ineffable name of the Trinity, whose mercy flows abundantly: cleanse the cavern of the human heart from vices and make it brighter than the whiteness of snow. Renew, we ask, the Holy Spirit within us, so that we may proclaim your praise; and, strengthened by a right and princely spirit, may we deserve to be established in eternal dwellings in the heavenly Jerusalem. Through the same Lord.

# PSALM 51

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM 51

C The voice of the prophet concerning Judas or the Antichrist.

**Title.** To the end. An instruction of David, when Doeg the Idumean came and informed Saul and said to him: “Behold, David has come into the house of Abimelech.”

C This entire title is rightly to be referred to the Lord’s second coming, in the time of the Antichrist, since everything is suitably adapted to Christ’s manifestation, so that it may not appear to differ from its psalm.

H This psalm contains the voice of the prophet reproaching the sins of the Jewish people. He speaks to the people themselves, saying:

## 1. Why do you glory in wickedness: you ÷ who .. ÷ are .. mighty in iniquity. [The separately marked words are *Qui*, “who,” and *es*, “are.”]

[The supplied source ends here, mid-sentence.]

C “Why do you boast in evil?” Since divine Scripture does not say that one should glory even in good deeds, but commands, “Let the one who glories, glory in the Lord” [Col. 0209A] (2 Cor. 10), the Prophet now rebukes a wicked man who boasts only in malignity, asking why he wishes to glory in evils, of which he ought to have been ashamed.

2. “All day long your tongue devised injustice; like a sharp razor you practiced deceit.”

C “All day long” signifies the whole period of life, because the wicked man, without any interruption, always both does and devises evil. “He devised injustice”: here he says that the tongue devised it, because it is the habit of the worst people to speak with the tongue before they think in the heart—that is, to utter things without deliberation. He aptly compared the deceit of an evil man to a sharp razor, because just as a razor shaves the hairs without injuring the person, so deceit will not be able to harm the righteous soul when it strives to take worldly things away from it. For earthly goods are compared with hairs, because hairs are certain superfluities of the body, while temporal goods are superfluities of the soul.

3. “You loved evil more than goodness, injustice more than speaking righteousness.” Diapsalma.

C He loves who is known always to love sinning. “More than goodness”: that is, if goodness touches the mind of a malevolent person, he immediately casts it away as a detestable vice, and loves speaking injustice more than uttering words of righteousness.

4. “You loved every word of rashness, a deceitful tongue.”

C This is said of the Antichrist, who, with morals thrown into confusion, loves iniquity, runs toward every word of rashness, commands what benefits no one, and speaks everything deceitfully; consequently, nothing he says is judged beneficial to anyone.

5. “Therefore God will destroy you forever; he will tear you away and remove you from your tent, and your root from the land of the living.” Diapsalma.

H All these things were fulfilled in the Jewish people, which, destroyed from the letter of the Law, torn away from the city, and removed from God’s tent, was displaced in the times of Titus and Vespasian. C “Forever,” however, means that the one who will be destroyed is assigned to eternal punishments. “And your root”: just as the saints are called the holy ones, so the imitators of sinners are called their roots. The associates of the Antichrist were his roots, [Col. 0209D] and therefore he says that his root is to be torn up together with him, because neither the Antichrist nor his ministers will have any share in the kingdom of blessedness with the saints of the Lord.

6. “The righteous will see and fear, and they will laugh at him, ÷ and they will say ..: ‘Behold the man who did not set God as his helper.’”

“The righteous will see,” that is, they will then understand the future punishment of the wicked, and they will fear lest they desire such things in this age. Here the righteous weep; in the future they will laugh. C They will laugh at him who, with foolish will, despised God’s long-suffering. When it says, “Behold,” with an extended hand, the wicked man’s abominable fate is displayed.

7. [Col. 0210A] “But he hoped in the abundance of his riches and prevailed in his vanity.”

C Here we should understand “riches” as all the splendors of the world. Whoever places his hope in them and not in God has deceived himself. He prevails in his vanity because he acquires nothing that can benefit him. That is called vain which is empty, fragile, or perishable, and separated from the firmest truth.

8. “I ÷ however .. am like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God. I have hoped in the mercy of God forever and unto the age ÷ of the age ..”

H The Prophet compares himself with a fruitful olive tree because of the richness of wisdom. “I have hoped in mercy,” because human frailty has no power to save anyone by itself, but only through the mercy of the Lord.

9. [Col. 0210B] “I will confess to you forever, because you have done it, and I will await your name, for it is good in the presence of your saints.”

C Here confession has been granted to us, where we deserve to be absolved. “Because you have done it”: “mercy” must be understood here. “For it is good”: that is rightly called good where both the hope of salvation and the victory of the whole life are received. It was also added, “before the presence of your saints”—that is, when the common joy of the righteous has already arrived. H Or: “because you have done it,” namely, that I am a fruitful olive tree, that I have hoped in the mercy of God forever; and therefore “I will await your name,” and so forth.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM 51

Destroyer of all worldly vanity, Almighty God, make us flourish in your house like a fruitful olive tree, so that, hoping in your mercy, we may be saved from the curse of iniquity. Through our Lord, etc.

# PSALM 52

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM 52

C The Church reproves those who are corrupted in heart or deed, and urges the faithful to endure the troubles of the world with equanimity.

TT. “For the end, concerning Amalek. An understanding of David.”

C “For the end”: what this signifies is already known. Amalek was a nation that fought against God’s people. The interpretation of its name is as follows: “concerning one who is in labor” or “one who is grieving.” It signifies the Church, which, like a woman grieving and in labor, admonishes the people of the faithless [Col. 0210D] to cease from their iniquities.

1. “The fool said in his heart: ‘There is no God.’”

C Speaking belongs properly to the tongue, not to the heart. But because divine power understands our thoughts, it is rightly said that fools speak in their hearts: what could reach the Lord’s ears not for pardon but for vengeance. H He says “in his heart,” whether the devil or the Jew: “There is no God,” as though he were saying, “Christ is not the Son of God.” A Or, anyone who lives badly is a fool; if he thinks that evil pleases God, he says in his heart, “There is no God.” So too does the one who says that God spares everyone and always, for God is both his justice and his goodness.

2. [Col. 0211A] “They are corrupt and have become abominable in their iniquities; there is no one who does good.”

C “They are corrupt”: all heretics are marked by this one word, for not believing rightly in God is corruption. The most just punishment follows them, so that they become abominable in their pleasures. “There is no one who does good”: this is what the Church, full of pains, was bringing forth—that amid such a multitude of the lost there might be no one able to do or imitate good.

3. “God looked down from heaven upon the children of men, to see whether there is anyone who understands ÷ or .. seeks God.”

C The Lord looked down from heaven—that is, from each of his preachers—and looked upon the children of men with great compassion, so that he might not destroy those who were in error but save those who repented. “To see”: that is, to make the saints see who understands their preaching—who reads it within himself or seeks God by his deeds.

4. “All have turned aside; together they have become useless. There is no one who does good, not even one.”

C He says that all those have turned aside who, with hardened hearts, persisted in their criminal purpose. First they turned aside; then it followed that they became useless to themselves. When “not even one” is said, all are denied. For if he had wished anyone good to be understood, he would not have said “not even one,” but “except one.” H All these fools who did not seek God became useless because they do not wish to fulfill God’s commands, and therefore they are useless both to themselves and to others. For the one who does not perform anything good is useless and is consequently cast into the outer darkness, as the Gospel testifies (Matt. 22).

5. “Will they not know ÷ all .. who work iniquity, who devour my people as they eat bread?”

H The wicked know that they act perversely, and not only do they fail to correct themselves, but they also devour God’s people with the teeth of their malice, like bread as food, which is always eagerly used. For although at different times we are satisfied with various foods, bread nevertheless remains our constant nourishment; so the wicked always desire to devour the good. A Or: will not all the wicked know at the future judgment that God exists, though they now refuse to know it? They will certainly know through the experience of punishments.

6. “They did not call upon God. There they trembled with fear where there was no fear.”

C “They did not call upon God.” For those things that sinners do against God’s will vanish like smoke with the greatest speed, and they tremble lest they be deprived of the honors or riches acquired in this age. “Where there was no fear”: one must supply “righteous” fear. A Or, because they did not call upon God, they are soon to perish. Or therefore they trembled there, and so forth; but they trembled for this reason: because, O God, and so forth.

7. [Col. 0212A] “For God scattered the bones of those who please men. They were confounded, because God despised them.”

C God scatters the bones of the wicked—that is, their very hard obstinacies. H Or, the hope of their eternity: those who dared to rise up in contempt of him. Those who please men and not God are rightly said to be confounded, because God despised them. He is deservedly despised by God who has abandoned God; and because he abandoned him, he is justly confounded by him as one unknown, as the Apostle says: “The one who is ignorant will be ignored” (1 Cor. 14).

8. “Who will give salvation to Israel from Zion? When God turns back the captivity of his people, Jacob will rejoice and Israel will be glad.”

C “Who will give?” One must add: “unless you, Lord.” These are the words of one who believes, not of one who doubts. “From Zion”: he means that blessed contemplation in which God is seen. Even in this age he gives salvation to Israel from Zion when he consoles the labors of the saints with his benefits. H He also raised us from the captivity of vices, once turned away, into the freedom of virtues. “Jacob will rejoice”: that is, the Christian people, when it supplants the Jewish people and receives its blessing. “And Israel will be glad,” when it beholds God with the eyes of faith.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM 52

Most merciful God, looking down from your holy heaven, put an end to our folly, so that, rescued from empty terrors, we may please you alone in the wholeness of a pure heart. Through our Lord Jesus, etc.

# PSALM 53

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM 53

[Col. 0212C]

C The voice of the Church concerning heretics, addressed to Christ.

TT. “For the end, in songs, an understanding of David. When the Ziphites came and said to Saul: ‘Is David not hidden among us?’”

C “For the end” signifies Christ. For this song proclaims Christ’s praises. “An understanding of David” indicates the Lord the Savior, whose coming he usefully understood. The Ziphites were so called from a village in Syria where Ziph lived; they betrayed that David was hidden among them. H “Ziphites,” by interpretation, signifies “those who flourish,” which has been granted to sinners in this world. C David bore the figure of Christ; H he was hidden in the lower part of the earth, and the Lord in the womb of holy Mary, and among one Jewish people; [Col. 0212D] and divinity in Christ’s flesh.

1. “God, save me by your name ÷ and .. deliver me by your strength.”

C The Prophet prays that he may be delivered by the Lord’s name from the malice of his persecutors, hoping for safety from no other source than God; and again he asks that he may be delivered by his strength at the future judgment. H “By your name”: that is, by that name of humility which is salvation, namely, by the name of the Savior, by the name Jesus.

2. “God, hear my prayer; listen with your ears to the words of my mouth.”

C The Prophet again repeats the name of the Almighty, so that when God is frequently invoked he may not delay to bring him help. H “Listen with your ears”: the Lord is said to have ears when he deigns to hear. C Or, “with your ears,” that is, with your mind.

3. “For strangers have risen up against me, and the strong have sought my life; they have not set God before their eyes.” Diapsalma.

C Here he does not wish “strangers” to be understood as men of foreign race, but as those made alien from the Lord by their deeds. Since the Ziphites were from the tribe of Judah, he rightly sought help from them; yet among them he found rather the snares of betrayal. By “the strong,” understand Saul with his ministers. The lost do not set God before their eyes because they believe that he does not know what they conceive in their criminal minds.

4. [Col. 0213B] “Behold, God is my helper, and the Lord is the sustainer of my soul.”

C He said “helper” with reference to one who was suffering, so that he might be able to endure what the wicked were striving together to bring upon him. It follows also what this help is: “the Lord is the sustainer of my soul.”

5. “Turn the evils against my enemies; in your truth destroy them.”

C Therefore the Prophet prays that the evil will may be removed from his enemies, by which he knew they were being burdened. For when the wicked come to the truth, they perish from their former will; and unless they depart from their evil intention, they will have no place among good deeds. May Saul perish, so that he may not persecute the innocent; may the Ziphites perish, so that they may not betray the one who is hidden.

6. [Col. 0213C] “I will sacrifice to you willingly, and I will confess your name, Lord, because it is good.”

C He sacrifices willingly to God who prays for his enemies. To sacrifice willingly is to offer God the purity of a good will. Here “to confess” also signifies “to praise.” To wish to praise him is an immeasurable good. From this the holy mind is refreshed and every adversity of this world is driven away.

7. “For you have delivered me from every tribulation, ÷ and .. my eye has looked down upon my enemies.”

C The Prophet testifies that he has been delivered from every tribulation—something that cannot occur in this age except to those who persist in the love of the Lord. The Lord’s eye looked upon David’s enemies, that is, the Ziphites, when he did not allow them to accomplish their wicked intentions; for God, being often merciful, does not permit evil deeds to be carried out, so that we may be pricked in heart and compelled to plead concerning our errors.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM 53

Save, Lord, your Church, which confesses the protection of your name, so that, having despised its enemies, it may magnify you with willing confession. Through the Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, etc.

# PSALM 54

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM 54

C Christ asks the Father that his prayer not be despised, a prayer which he is shown to seek from the weakness of the flesh, and he reveals what is destined to happen to the obstinate Jews who persist in their crimes.

TT. “For the end, in songs, an understanding of David.”

C Christ is rightly called “the end,” because whatever we do rightly and faithfully is, without doubt, to be referred to him. “In songs” means “in praises.” This understanding is certain: when we call David the father of the Lord Christ—as the blind man says in the Gospel, “Have mercy on me, Son of David” (Luke 18)—we understand this according to the flesh; according to divinity, however, we confess that David himself is the servant of Christ, as he says: “The Lord said to my Lord” (Ps. 109).

1. “Hear, God, my prayer, and do not despise my supplication; attend to me and hear me.”

[Col. 0214B] C In the first part the Prophet asks that his prayer be heard; then he requests that his supplication not be despised. H Understand by this, O human being, that unless you supplicate God with a pure conscience, you will certainly not be heard by God.

2. “I was troubled in my exercise, and I was disturbed by the voice of the enemy and by the tribulation of the sinner.”

C The course of the Lord’s life is most beautifully set forth in one statement. We call that an “exercise” which rests in no leisure. He was exercised by miracles and the holiness of his teaching, and he was saddened because the madness of the obstinate people did not believe his saving preaching. H “By the voice of the enemy,” saying, “He is a Samaritan and has a demon” (John 8), “I was disturbed.” C The sinner’s tribulation existed when they spat upon him with their mouths, struck him with slaps, and inflicted many other things upon him.

3. “For they turned iniquities against me, and in anger they were troublesome to me.”

C They turned iniquity against the Lord because, unwilling to accept any explanation, they sought the shedding of innocent blood. Let the foolish Jews hear that they caused the Lord such great trouble, with anger kindled, that they prepared an everlasting ruin for themselves. H “In anger”: anger is the splinter; the beam is hatred. Anger disturbs; the beam blinds, as in the words, “My eye is troubled because of anger.” “Troublesome” means “fierce.” C Or, trouble exists when we are made restless by excessive insolence.

4. “My heart was troubled within me, [Col. 0214D] and the fear of death fell upon me.”

H “My heart was troubled within me,” according to the human being; but it was strengthened by divine power. “And the fear,” and so forth. C The parts are appropriately joined to their own parts: it was consequently fitting that fear of death should invade the one whose heart had been troubled. It truly fell upon him when it came over him, no longer destined to have the power it once had, because everlasting death was conquered by Christ’s death.

5. “Fear and trembling came upon me, and darkness covered me.”

H He speaks in human fashion: fear belongs to the soul and trembling to the body. Evil people are called “darkness,” because “the one who hates his brother is in darkness” [Col. 0215A] (1 John 2). They did cover me, but because I was light, they did not seize me.

6. “And I said: ‘Who will give me wings ÷ like .. a dove? Then I will fly and rest.’”

C “Who will give me?”—namely, unless you, Father, who lead human nature to the kingdoms of heaven. “Wings” comes from *pendendo*, “hanging.” Consider, however, that he did not ask for the wings of an eagle or hawk, but of a dove, which is called as if “a fosterling of the cell,” an innocent and gentle bird that rises against no animal with a venomous will. Christ rightly asked for that bird’s wings, in whose form the Holy Spirit appeared over him (Matt. 3). “I will fly”: that is, I will transport myself with the swiftest will, so that I may rest from the iniquity of those who persecute me—namely, the Jews.

7. “Behold, I have gone far away in flight; I remained in solitude.” Diapsalma.

H “Behold, I have gone far away” from the Jews, for salvation is far from sinners. And I remained with unbelieving nations, which I caused to flourish at my coming. Concerning them another prophet says: “Let the wilderness rejoice and flourish” (Isa. 35).

8. “I was awaiting him who saved me from faintheartedness of spirit and from the storm.”

C He declares that he is awaiting the Father’s protection, who could save him from bodily weakness; and because he earlier said that he was troubled, he now testifies that he is fainthearted. He calls “storms” the tempests of seditions that the Jews were stirring up.

9. [Col. 0215C] “Hasten, Lord; divide their tongues, for I have seen iniquity and contradiction in the city.”

C Here he beneficially invokes a curse upon the Jewish people: that by the division of tongues they might not fulfill the will of their malice, as happened at that tower which men, fearing a renewed flood, attempted to extend upward (Gen. 10). He therefore rightly asked that those be divided whom he knew to be wicked in their sacrilegious assemblies. For this reason he added, “because I have seen iniquity in the city,” that is, H in the assembly: iniquity, because they did not believe; contradiction, when they reproached him: “Is this not the son of the carpenter?” (Matt. 13), and many other things.

10. “By day and by night iniquity will surround it upon its walls, [Col. 0215D] and labor is in its midst, and injustice.”

H He says “by day and by night,” that is, surrounding it at all times—namely, Jerusalem. “Iniquity upon its walls”: as high as the machinery of the walls could rise, so much higher did the malice of the Jews extend itself. “Labor is in its midst,” and so forth: labor in the oppression of the poor, and injustice in judgments. By “the midst”—because the leading men wish to dwell in the middle of the city as though in an honorable seat—he designates their nobles and leaders, whom neither law nor reason possessed, but labor and injustice.

11. “And usury and deceit do not depart from its squares.”

C Notice that he did not say “secretly,” but that such things had been committed in the squares [Col. 0216A]—things which divine law condemned. H Usury is taking more than one gives. For everything prohibited in the Law grew toward increasing the accumulation of sin. In the Law, people are forbidden to receive usury. Hence the Prophet says: “I have not lent at interest, nor has anyone lent at interest to me” (Jer. 15).

12. “For if an enemy had cursed me, I would surely have endured it.”

C Here an example of great patience is shown: when enemies speak things contrary to us, we should strive not to burst into contention or resist with words, but to give room to their mad speech.

13. “And if the one who hated me had spoken great things against me, I would perhaps have hidden myself from him.”

[Col. 0216B] C In this verse, and in the preceding and following ones, the treacherous Judas is rebuked. He could have been guarded against if he had been a public enemy, speaking in human fashion. Yet Christ, had he wished, could have guarded himself from him, though hidden not from Christ but from others. H Here the Lord does not complain only about the Passion, but also about the betraying disciple, from whom he did not hide himself, although he had hidden himself from the Jews—as we read in the Gospel (John 8)—and had even admitted him to the holy meal.

14. “But you, a man of one mind, my leader and my acquaintance.”

C Judas is called “of one mind” because he was numbered among the apostles. “Leader,” because he was sent ahead to villages and fortified towns to instruct unformed minds [Col. 0216C] by preaching the word. “Acquaintance,” because his betrayal was known to Christ. H Or, because he was sent with the others to preach, he is called his acquaintance.

15. “For together with me you received sweet foods; in the house of God we walked with harmony.”

H “You received sweet foods together with me,” that is, the body and blood of Christ, which he received from him unworthily. He also often went with the Lord himself into Solomon’s temple in harmony of preaching. C This should be joined to the preceding verse, as follows: “Why do you betray me—you, a man of one mind, my leader, and the one who received sweet foods with me?” Why do you betray me?

16. “Let death come upon them, ÷ and .. let the living descend into hell.”

C “Let death come, and let the earth devour them alive.” This happened to Dathan and Abiron: fire suddenly came and they died. C In his customary manner, however, the Prophet asks his enemies to receive correction rather than destruction. For death is called the end of life, and whoever is converted to a better condition is judged to have found the end of his former way of life. The living descend into hell when they are terrified by their worst thoughts and are carried toward better desires. Then we descend into the lower regions as living people, when we are terrified by the remembrance of our evils.

17. “For there are iniquities in their dwelling places, in their midst.”

H For there are iniquities in the dwelling places of the Jews. Indeed, they are full of iniquity both in deed and in thought.

18. [Col. 0217A] “I ÷ however .. cried out to God, and the Lord heard me.”
