H Therefore Christ, in the form of a servant, continually cried out to God for the Christian people. It was consequently fitting that he should be heard, because he could not be separated from his majesty.

19. “Evening, morning, and noon I will recount and proclaim, and he will hear my voice.”

C “Evening” signifies the time of the betrayal, when Judas handed him over to the cohort. “Morning,” when he was led to Pontius Pilate. “Noon,” when he was hung at the sixth hour. “Noon” is so called as if it were “midday.” The following words correspond to these times: “I will recount” belongs to evening, when he foretold everything that the wicked Judas intended to do. “I will proclaim” belongs to morning, because in the morning he proclaimed this by answering Pilate: “For this I was born” (John 18), and so forth. “He will hear my voice” belongs to noon, when he said: “It is finished,” and gave up his spirit (John 19).

20. “He will redeem my soul in peace from those who draw near to me, for among many they were with me.”

H “He will redeem in peace”: he relates that God heard him quickly, when he rescued him from the tribulations of death in the Resurrection. “In peace,” that is, in himself. “From those who draw near”: bodily, not in life or merit. “Among many”: they were believers with me, and yet they did not believe. Or, “among these who are many,” that is, among the wicked and not among the few—that is, among the good, who are few. Or, “in many,” that is, in baptism and pretended faith. They are not “in the few,” that is, in firm faith, true hope, and charity.

21. “God will hear and humble them, who is before the ages.” Diapsalma.

H God will hear me as I bless, not them as they curse. And he will humble them, that is, the proud. “Who is before the ages”: certainly the Father, whom they did not recognize as remaining in me.

22. “For there is no change in them, and they did not fear God; he stretched out his hand in recompense.”

H “There is no change in them” from evil to good. And they did not fear God; for that reason God descended to vengeance, as follows: “He stretched out his hand in recompense.” For when it had been extended to them for help, they did not receive it. “In recompense,” therefore, means in vengeance on the day of judgment: because they refused to turn and receive grace from the hand of mercy, he extended toward them the hand of vengeance, so that those who refused to receive when he was giving might receive when he was recompensing.

23. “They defiled his covenant; they were divided from the anger of his face, and his heart drew near.”

C He defiles God’s covenant, so far as concerns him, who in no way obeys his commands. The faithless are also divided from the faithful people in the judgment and separated like straw burned by fire from the grain. [Col. 0218A] “Anger” here is used for vengeance, which the wicked will endure. “And his heart drew near in judgment,” when the Lord’s heart—that is, his will proclaimed through the prophets and apostles—becomes known to everyone. H Or, the Jews defiled the covenant because they did not understand the Lord Jesus promised in the Law, and whatever they do understand from the Scriptures they turn toward evil, because they do not believe in the Trinity; therefore they are divided from spiritual understanding. A And from their division and defilement, God’s will drew near to believers, so that they also understand in the Scriptures the will of God that had lain hidden.

24. “His words were softened beyond oil, yet they themselves are arrows.”

C The words of the faithless Jews were softened when they said, “Teacher, we know that you have come from God” (Matt. 22). “Beyond oil”: no comparison could be found equal to such great wickedness, because nothing is smoother than oil. They themselves were also arrows when they said, “He is guilty of death” (Matt. 16). H Or, the discourse returns to Judas, whose words—“Hail, Rabbi”—were beyond oil, and who betrayed him with a kiss. The good, fleeing such oil, invoke God in tribulation; therefore it follows: “Cast,” and so forth.

25. “Cast your care upon the Lord, and he himself will nourish you; he will not allow the righteous to waver forever.”

C When thought is cast upon the Lord, it not only does not consume us, as the thought of this age does, but also nourishes us. For God does not permit the most righteous person to waver forever—as he says here—when that person is known to reign with him in eternity.

26. “But you, God, will lead them into the pit of destruction.”

C He first spoke of the righteous; now he speaks of the wicked, who are to be plunged into the depths of Gehenna. A pit is an open chasm in the earth; but lest you understand this as a life-giving pit, he added “of destruction,” that is, a deadly ditch. O unheard-of mercy of the Judge! Everything is announced beforehand to human beings so that punishable guilt may be avoided. By the likeness of a pit he warns us to fear the torments of Gehenna.

27. “Men of blood and deceit will not halve their days; [Col. 0218D] but I will hope in you, Lord.”

C “Men of blood” does not properly refer to those who shed human blood innocently, since righteous judges also shed it justly. Therefore he added “and deceitful,” so that only those may be marked who seek another’s destruction through the most wicked deceit. He says that such men will not halve their days, because, while they promise themselves a long life, they find the end of the swiftest death. “Their” was added so that you might understand the days counted by their own choice—that is, those they thought or wished they would live, not those appointed by the Lord.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM 54

Lord Jesus, who remain before the ages and, taking on the human condition, were betrayed by a disciple of one mind with you and underwent death for the lost, hear the prayer of those who supplicate and grant that, praising you in the evening, morning, and at noon, we may deserve to be defended from the storms of this age. You who live with the Father, etc.

# PSALM 55

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM 55

C The voice of the Church placed in persecution.

TT. “For the end, concerning the people who have been made far from the saints. David in the inscription of the title, when the Philistines seized him in Gath.”

C “For the end” is already known. “Concerning the people who have been made far from the saints”: the Jewish people asked Pilate not to write the inscription of the title as it had been written by the prophets, unwilling that Christ should be called their king [Col. 0219B] (John 19). That will made them far from the saints, because the saints glory in Christ’s being called their king. “Gath” signifies a winepress, that is, the pressure which every Christian suffers from the Philistines, that is, from foreigners. For the Philistines—who are now called Palestinians—were also called by another name, “foreigners.”

1. “Have mercy on me, God, for man has trampled me down; all day long he has attacked and afflicted me.”

C The virgin mother Church asks her heavenly bridegroom with devout tears not to allow her to be oppressed by her enemies. H By the man who tramples and attacks, he shows the persecution of the devil or of the remaining spiritual wickednesses.

2. “My enemies have trampled me all day long, for there are many who fight against me.”

3. “From the height of day I will fear; but I will hope in you.”

C Wine does not flow unless the grape is trampled underfoot. So the enemy tramples the Church in her members, so that the glorious merits of the saints may arise from it. “All day long”: at all times her enemies rebel against her; but because some of them are converted, he does not say “all,” but “many.”

C “From the height of day” signifies this world, where the height of pride swells up. For just as Christ commands humility, so the devil persuades people toward the summits of exaltation. But from what she should not fear or fall, the Church adds: “I will hope in you,” who never deceive those who trust in you.

4. [Col. 0219D] “In God I will praise my words; in God I hoped. I will not fear what flesh can do to me.”

C He praises his words in God who strives to apply everything he says well to God, not to himself. “I will not fear”: although the hand of executioners may rage, the Church in her members nevertheless scorns every torment while awaiting the gifts of the Lord Savior.

5. “All day long they were cursing my words; all their thoughts were against me for evil.”

H All day long the Jews cursed Christ’s words, saying, “He is not a prophet, but he deceives the crowds” (John 7). The thoughts of the Jews were turned toward evil against Christ, and those of sinners against the saints.

6. [Col. 0220A] “They will dwell and hide; they themselves will watch my heel.”

7. “As they waited for my soul, for nothing you will save them; in anger you will shatter the peoples.”

C Deceitful Christians appear to dwell within the Church, but they hide the evil of their perversity and do not dare openly to betray that they know they do not possess apostolic teaching. They watch my heel in the manner of the devil, or of those who are his ministers, who look toward the end of our course with treacherous cunning, desiring to overturn us from the faith and bring us to the dangers of guilt, at least in our final moments.

H The Jews watched for Christ’s soul so that they might accuse him, once captured in his words, before the authorities. They are saved for nothing: since they are not changed toward glory, they are transferred to punishments. “In anger you will shatter the peoples,” because they have struck against the stone of stumbling and rock of offense (1 Pet. 2). A Or, although they wait for him for evil and make themselves unworthy of salvation by this, nevertheless you, whose mercy surpasses all sins, save them for nothing—that is, freely, with none of their merits preceding—so that, as though angry, you compel peoples wearied by many tribulations to return to you. You are angry and lead them down; you rage and save; you terrify and call. It appears to be anger, but it is paternal.

8. “God, I have declared my life to you; you have placed my tears in your sight.”

C He declares his life to God who is not ashamed to confess his own sins. The tears placed before the Lord are joyful, because they do not torment but free us from torments.

9. “And according to your promise: then my enemies will turn backward.”

C God’s promise is that he will not reject devout tears. H The Church expresses the wish that her enemies turn backward—that is, that those who are running toward hell may turn back to God.

10. “On whatever day I call upon you, behold, I have known that you are my God.”

C Here the Prophet proclaims the Lord’s clemency and wondrous mercy: on whatever day Christ is invoked, he always shows mercy and pardon. “On whatever day” signifies satisfaction at different times. One person supplicates the Lord throughout the whole period of life; another is converted in middle age. Another is saved at the end of life. “Behold, I have known.” H Some know God through the creation of heaven and earth, as Paul says: “Through the things that have been made, the unseen things are perceived by understanding” (Rom. 1); others through divine inspiration; others through signs, as he said to Thomas: “Put your finger here” (John 20); others through pardon, clemency, and help, as penitents do.

11. “In God I will praise the word; in the Lord I will praise the speech. In God I hoped; I will not fear what man can do to me.”

H The Prophet again praises this word or speech, which was in the beginning with the Father; and hoping in him, he does not fear the threats of the adversary, saying: “In me are your vows, God.” C Or, “speech,” that is, the Gospel spoken from Christ’s mouth.

12. “In me are, God, vows + of yours .. ÷ which .. I will repay to you as praises.”

H These are the Prophet’s vows: that he may diligently celebrate the Lord’s praise. He added why he does this: “because you have delivered.”

13. “For you have delivered my soul from death and my feet from falling, so that I may please God in the light of the living.”

C “For you have delivered my soul,” that is, the faithful peoples, “from everlasting death.” And rightly does the holy mother call her soul delivered, since she rejoiced in the liberation of her children. He says that the feet have been delivered from falling—not something accomplished here, but something that will be granted in the age to come. For while the righteous walk in this world, they are in danger of falling, but they are restrained by divine mercy. Thus it is written: “The righteous man falls seven times and rises again” (Prov. 24). H The Light of the living is Christ, who enlightens those who please him. C Or, the light of the living is the manifestation of the saints.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM 55

O excellent champion in invisible wars, who do not permit those who trust in you to be overwhelmed by their enemies, we beseech you, wipe away the tear of sin from our eyes, so that, while we suppress carnal battles, we may be deemed worthy to please you in the light of the living. Through our Lord Jesus, etc.

# PSALM 56

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM 56

C That Christ prays according to the humanity in which he suffered, recalls the glory of his resurrection, and sings praises to the Father.

**Title:** To the end: “Do not destroy”; David, in the inscription of the title, when he fled from the face of Saul into the cave.

C David is forbidden to be destroyed—to be destroyed by Saul. “In the inscription of the title”: this did not happen to David, but it happened to Christ in his passion, so that the title written by Pilate would not be changed (John 19). “When he fled,” and so forth: this action applies both to David and to the Lord. For just as David fled from the face of Saul into the cave, so the Divinity was hidden from the faithless Jews in the body of Christ.

### 1

Have mercy on me, O God, have mercy on me, for my soul trusts in you.

C Christ cries out to the Father because he knew that his future passion was approaching. This repetition reveals the danger of the coming death. He prayed, however, in order to show us the rule of holy prayer: he suffered for us so that no one might shrink from being willing to suffer for him.

### 2

÷ And .. in the shadow of your wings I will hope, until iniquity passes away.

H The shadow signifies the protection of the Divinity. For shade is sought from the heat of the sun; but by heat persecution or tribulation is understood. The two wings are the two Testaments or the two commandments of charity, by which the Prophet asks to be protected until iniquity passes away—that is, the devil with his minions.

### 3

I will cry to God Most High, to God who has done good to me.

C He cries out from the humanity he assumed—from him whom the heavenly creatures never cease to ask for help. “Who has done good to me” signifies the mystery of the Lord’s Incarnation, which was bestowed upon the human race by divine grace.

### 4

He sent from heaven and delivered me. He gave over to disgrace those who trampled me. Diapsalma.

C “He sent from heaven”: understand not an angel, nor any creature, but the aid of his own heavenly power. It was a disgrace to the persecutors when they saw him whom they thought they were destroying rise again, and faithful peoples rejoice in his resurrection.

### 5

God sent his mercy and his truth; ÷ and .. he delivered my soul from the midst of lion cubs; I slept while troubled.

H Mercy and truth are Christ, whom the Father sent from heaven into the world; neither could exist without the other. If there had been mercy alone, permission to sin would have resulted; and if truth alone, man could not have endured the punishment. C “Lion cubs” signifies the people of the Jews, whom the rulers and priests—who are the lions—begot with savage intent. He slept in the deepest repose upon the cross, troubled by the tumult of the Jews. [The reading *afrem itu* is uncertain in the supplied text.]

### 6

The sons of men: their teeth are weapons and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword.

C The sons of men are those who raged with impious intent at the Lord’s death. Their teeth were weapons and arrows—that is, wicked counsels and words flying toward the accomplishment of death. Those voices that said, “Crucify, crucify,” are compared with a sharp sword; for just as a sharp sword produces the effect of death most swiftly, so those words completed the sentence of destruction with haste.

### 7

Be exalted above the heavens, O God, ÷ and .. your glory over all the earth.

C “Be exalted”: so that, though hanging upon the cross, you may always be recognized as reigning in your majesty. He said “above the heavens” because the Lord is known to have the heavenly powers subject to him, and because, ascending above the heavens and sitting at the Father’s right hand, he was glorified. He was also glorified over the earth when the Church filled the whole world, and in it praises are continually sung to God.

### 8

They prepared a snare for my feet, and they bent down my soul.

H “They prepared a snare”: when they brought deceitful questions against Christ. They also wished to bend Christ down so that his name would not be mentioned.

### 9

They dug a pit before my face, and they fell into it. Diapsalma.

C The sentence of death is rightly called a pit, since it sends one to the pit. For they said, “He is guilty of death,” and therefore they are said to have dug a pit, because they appeared to have handed him over to death. And they themselves fell into it. Every unjust word condemns its own authors; before it harms another, it first condemns itself. H “They fell into it”: when, after the Lord’s resurrection, they were handed over to their enemies, captured, killed, and scattered.

### 10

My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready; I will sing and utter a psalm.

C The Son gives thanks to the Father through that by which he also rose from the dead. He says that he is ready to give thanks because he knew that the glory of the resurrection was coming to him. We have said that “to sing” means to return thanks with the voice; “to utter a psalm” means to praise him through an action worthy of proclamation.

### 11

Awake, my glory; awake, psalter and lyre; I will awake at dawn.

C “Awake” is said in the sense of “arise,” for the performance of a miracle: “awake, psalter and lyre.” The psalter was present when he carried out the divine commandments; the lyre signifies the glorious passion, which, with its strings stretched and its bones counted, sounded forth the power of endurance. He rose at dawn, which is between the darkness of night and the brightness of God.

### 12

I will confess you among the peoples, O Lord; and I will utter a psalm to you among the nations.

H “I will confess you”: that is, after I have risen, I will praise you among Christian peoples. C “I will utter a psalm,” because throughout all nations psalmody is offered to the Lord with devoted mind in various languages.

### 13

For your mercy has been magnified up to the heavens, and your truth up to the clouds.

H Mercy has been magnified because, through the Lord’s resurrection, all things in heaven and on earth have been reconciled to the Father. C The clouds signify the prophets, whom the truth of the Holy Spirit filled like abundant rain; and, satisfied from the heavenly spring, they poured out gifts of spiritual abundance upon barren sinners.

### 14

Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and your glory over all the earth.

H The Prophet says “be exalted” concerning Christ’s glorious ascension. His glory will be over the earth when he pours out the gift of the Holy Spirit upon all flesh (Acts 2).

## PRAYER FROM PSALM 56

Transfer, O Lord, the iniquity of the humble household that hopes beneath the shadow of your wings, so that, when your mercy has been sent from heaven, we may be rescued from the most wicked pits of ambush. Through our Lord Jesus, etc.

# PSALM 57

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM 57

C Christ reproaches the wickedness of the Jews and declares their recompense, as well as the joy of the righteous when they see the punishment of sinners.

**Title:** To the end: “Do not destroy”; David, in the inscription of the title.

C Pontius Pilate is therefore admonished not to destroy the written title that declared the Lord to be king. For who could abolish that king whom it is clear is the Creator of heaven and earth?

### 1

If indeed you speak righteousness, judge rightly, sons of men.

C The Jews falsely speak of the righteousness of the Law, since they are not going to judge rightly; for those who will do what is just speak truly of justice. Right speech ought to resemble life. Here the Prophet reproves their words when they deceitfully said, “Teacher, we know that you have come from God.” They did not judge rightly when they said to Pilate, “Crucify, crucify.”

### 2

Indeed, in your heart you work iniquities on the earth; your hands contrive injustices.

C “Indeed, in your heart,” as though he were saying: How could you judge me, when in your heart you work iniquities? There the crime is complete before it is carried out. He says “on the earth” concerning the secret place of the breast; by “hands” he signifies actual evil deeds, which are contrived by the mind when perversity, gathered from many sources, comes together within it.

### 3

Sinners have been estranged from the womb; they have gone astray from the uterus; they have spoken falsehoods.

C Therefore he rightly calls sinners cast out like miscarriages from the womb of the Church: they have not been perfectly formed by any strengthening of doctrine, but, like the foolish softness of a tender animal, they are shown to have been thrown not into the light of life but into the darkness of faithlessness. And rightly is the Church said to have a womb, since she has borne us through holy baptism into perpetual light. They went astray from the womb because they followed doctrines contrary to their mother. They also spoke falsehoods because they departed from her holy teachings.

### 4

Their fury is like the likeness of a serpent, like a deaf viper that stops up its ears.

C The fury of the obstinate Jews is irrevocable, like that of a serpent. Their evil habit is also compared with that of a viper, which, so that it will not hear the words of the charmer and leave its hiding places, is said to stop one ear by bending its tail over it and to press the other into the earth. Thus, with the ears of their hearts stopped, the Jews refused to hear Christ’s saving command, or the intelligible truth of Holy Scripture.

### 5

Which will not heed the voice of charmers, nor the spell of the wise enchanter.

C He speaks of the viper, which will not heed the voice of charmers and does not allow itself to hear a voice that could have drawn it into the light. So also the Jew, or any obstinate and malevolent person, is not drawn by a teacher toward the light of truth.

### 6

God will crush their teeth in their mouths; the Lord will break the molars of the lions.

C God crushed the teeth of the Jews when their deceitful words were reduced to nothing. They were lions when they cried out with bloodstained mouths, “Crucify, crucify.” Their molars were broken in their mouths when they could not answer his most truthful words.

### 7

They will come to nothing like flowing water; he bends his bow until they are weakened.

C O unheard-of savagery of the Jews! They are compared with such great evils, from whom we know monstrous dangers to arise. Flowing water is a torrent that soon fails. God also bends his bow against the wicked—that is, the threat of his power—and terrifies them until, weakened, they yield and turn to the salvation of confession.

### 8

As wax that melts, they will be taken away; fire has fallen upon them, and they have not seen the sun.

H As wax is dissolved by fire, so those who persist in their obstinacy are destroyed by the fire of the coming judgment. C “They will be taken away”: he says, from the sight of God. H “Fire has fallen upon them,” that is, the judgment of death. “And they have not seen the sun,” C that is, the Lord the Savior. They cannot behold him except those who gaze upon him with pure minds. A C Or, the fire of evil desire has fallen here upon the minds of the wicked, and therefore they cannot see what is just, good, and holy—that is, they cannot act rightly or discern rightly what ought to be done.

### 9

Before your thorns understood the buckthorn: as living, so in anger he will swallow them.

H Here he speaks to the sinful people. The buckthorn is a kind of thorn, exceedingly rough with prickles but very pleasing in flower. Through its flowers it signifies the recompense of the good, and through its prickles the punishment of the wicked. It flowers for the righteous as an adornment, but provides sinners with thorns to pierce them. C He says “as living” because they are believed to live, though they are dead. For every sinner dwelling in sins dies to the truth. “As in anger” signifies that, although the Lord is not angry, he appears to strike sinners as though he were angry. When “he will swallow them” is added, this signifies their sudden destruction under just vengeance.

### 10

The righteous man will rejoice when he sees vengeance; he will wash his hands in the sinner’s blood.

H The righteous man will rejoice because, when the wicked are condemned to punishments, the righteous are made joyful by rewards. C When the sinner’s blood is poured out, then the hands—that is, the deeds—of the righteous man are corrected. When the wicked perish, the righteous person is admonished to guard himself more cautiously and more diligently.

### 11

And the human being will say: Indeed there is fruit for the righteous; indeed there is a God judging them on the earth.

C Here he wishes it to be understood that the wicked are not entirely free from punishment in this age, even though they appear to flourish, because “whoever has not believed has already been judged.” Nor are the good excluded from benefit, although they are oppressed by worldly burdens. II Then there will be fruit for the righteous, when the Lord gives him kingdoms. Before the judgment they are judged on this earth, concerning whom it has been said: “Whoever has not believed has already been judged” (John 3).

## PRAYER FROM PSALM 57

Most just Lord, grant your people to follow justice and love what is right, lest, turning their hearing away from your truth, they be wounded by the bites of the poisonous serpent. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, etc.

# PSALM 58

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM 58

C Christ prays that his enemies may not prevail against him, and he says how the Jews will be converted at the end of the age; for them a prayer is also offered with marvelous devotion.

**Title:** To the end: “Do not destroy”; David, in the inscription of the title, when Saul sent and guarded his house in order to kill him.

“To the end” has already been explained as meaning without end. “Do not destroy David in the inscription of the title”: this too is frequently placed there so that the Lord’s passion may be declared through these indications. The house of David indicates the tomb, where he rested in a three-day death, which the Jews sent to guard with evil intent; nevertheless, this happened against their will for the glory of his name, lest it be said that he rose through deception.

### 1

Deliver me from my enemies, my God, and free me from those who rise up against me.

C The humanity of the Word asks that the devil or his ministers, the Jews, be turned away from him—the humanity that was assumed without the stain of sins. We, however, ask as those subject to sin that we may be freed from unclean spirits by divine mercy. H Christ’s enemies were the Jews when they secretly envied him. They rose up when they opposed his commandments.

### 2

Deliver me from those who practice iniquity, and save me from men of blood.

C He sets forth two kinds of enemies: namely, enemies who merely intended to harm, and those who were already rising up to do harm; now he adds a third kind, those who were already practicing evil. H They became workers of iniquity (Matt. 27) when they armed their hands for his killing. They were men of blood when they wished the blood of the righteous to come upon themselves and their children.

### 3

For behold, they have seized my soul; the mighty have rushed upon me.

C Here “soul” means bodily life. The soul of Christ, however, could be seized by no adversity; rather, through the soul being seized, the time of the passion is indicated. “The mighty” signifies here the devil together with his Jewish ministers.

### 4

Neither my iniquity nor my sin, O Lord; without iniquity I ran and directed my course.

C “Iniquity” here must be understood as malice or ill will; “sin,” however, as the performance of a crime—things that are shown to have been wholly foreign to the Lord. For Christ ran through worldly life by a straight path, and iniquity could in no way confront him, since it always twists the deeds of humanity. For him to be directed meant that he should return to the place from which he had come.

### 5

Rise to meet me and see; and you, O Lord, God of hosts, God of Israel.

H Here he speaks to the Father, from whom he asked in the Gospel to be glorified. “And see”: that is, cause me to be seen, so that they may believe me to be equal to you. “God of hosts,” that is, of angels and human beings. “God of Israel,” that is, God of souls that see.

### 6

Attend to visit all the nations; do not have mercy on all who practice iniquity. Diapsalma.

C Attend now to visit all the nations, so that your abundance may increase from the nations, because you have found barrenness of faith in the Jewish people. He says “all the nations” because people from every nation were going to believe with the Lord’s help. “Do not have mercy” shows that those who plead with pure devotion are to be pitied. Although all practice iniquity, those who flee to Christ with devoted mind are nevertheless to be spared.

### 7

They will return toward evening and suffer hunger like dogs; and they will go around the city.

C The future conversion of the Jewish people is declared here, and that countless people from among them will believe at the end of the world, so that, although late, they may nevertheless be saved by a saving conversion. H They suffer hunger for the word of God until the end of their life. C “Dog” is derived from *canendo*, “singing,” for it is the dog’s custom to defend those places where it knows it finds nourishment. Thus the Jews, once converted, will defend the city—that is, the Church—which they will go about as reformed preachers.

### 8

Behold, they will speak with their mouths, and a sword is in their lips; for who has heard?

C Certainly then they will speak with their mouths what now they do not deserve to have in their hearts. A C There will indeed be in their lips the heavenly sword of the word of God, which is called two-edged, striking through both testimonies. C “Who has heard?” must be spoken with weight, as though almost no gentile, or an exceedingly rare one, will hear their preaching—namely, the preaching of the Jews. For when the Jews are converted, almost all the Christians from the nations will adhere to Antichrist, so that at that time the Christian born from the nations will be exceedingly rare.

### 9

And you, O Lord, will mock them; you will reduce all the nations to nothing.

C He declares that those from the nations who remain in the wicked religion of Antichrist are to be mocked, because they refused to hear true preaching. It is well known that “nations” can be used both in a good and in a bad sense. The Lord regards them as nothing because they do not venerate him as the author of all creatures. It is a custom of Scripture, as here, to speak of the whole by a part: thus “all the nations” means not all of them, but all the unbelieving ones.

### 10

I will keep my strength toward you, for you are God, my protector; my God, his mercy will come before me.

C Christ says that the strength of his humanity is to be applied to the Father’s benefits. “Toward you I will keep”: with the syllable changed, this means “through you.” “I will keep my strength”: rightly does he declare that his strength is to be attributed to the one whom he also knew to be his protector. H The Father’s mercy came before him when the centurion confessed him before seeing that he had risen from the dead as God. Many also returned beating their breasts and saying: “Truly this was the Son of God” (Matt. 27).

### 11

God has shown me over my enemies: do not kill them, lest they ever forget my people.

C “God has shown me”: he speaks now of a second gift of beneficence, so that the power of his majesty may also be displayed among enemies, and so that blasphemers may become devout. “Do not kill them”: he therefore prays that the Jewish nation not perish utterly, but rather recognize that it has erred through a satisfaction worthy of repentance.

### 12

Scatter them by your power, and bring them down, my protector, O Lord.

H “Scatter them”: this was said concerning the Jews, so that, scattered throughout the whole world, they might not grow proud, or, in this dispersion, might lament their crime through repentance.

### 13

The sin of their mouth, the word of their lips; and let them be caught in their pride.

C “The sin of their mouth”—that is, the madness of their thoughts—was present when they formed a plan to hand the Lord over to death. The word of their lips was also detestable when they said, “He is guilty of death.” It is clear that they were caught in their pride when they saw rising again the one whom they had rejected while he performed miracles.

### 14

And from the curse and the lie they will be proclaimed in the consummation; in the wrath of consummation, and they will not be.

H They cursed the Lord when they called him the son of Joseph the carpenter. They also attached a lie to him when they said that he had a demon. “And they will not be”: that is, they will not be able to persist in their wickedness, but will be consumed in it (Matt. 13). C For he speaks of that consummation which each person suffers (John 8), when, mindful of his sins, he torments himself. Therefore they will not remain proud, but will be humbled through repentance.

### 15

And they will know that God will rule Jacob ÷ and .. the ends of the earth. Diapsalma.

C “And they will know”: when the Jews have been instructed in perfect religion, they will know that Christ is Lord of the patriarch Jacob, which at first they did not believe, and that he is Lord of the ends of the earth—that is, of the catholic Church spread throughout the whole world—which now, with hardened heart, they do not understand.

### 16

They will return toward evening and suffer hunger like dogs; and they will go around the city.

C After the interruption of the second *diapsalma*, he comes to the third division, where the conversion of the Jews and the Lord’s resurrection are shown. “Dogs” here signifies preachers converted from the Jews, such as Paul and others. “The city” here signifies earthly Jerusalem, which Paul gloriously went around preaching, together with many other Jews who believed. In the earlier division we said that “evening” signified the end of the age; but here it indicates the beginning of the sixth age, when the Lord came and, after his resurrection, a multitude of Jews believed.

### 17

They themselves will scatter to eat; but if they are not satisfied, they will murmur.

C Those who have deserved to possess true doctrine will scatter to eat—that is, spiritual food—so that the nations may be converted to the faith, just as it was said to Peter in a vision: “Kill and eat” (Acts 10). Teachers are satisfied when they see peoples eagerly receive their preaching. Conversely, they murmur when they do not know their words to bear fruit in the minds of the faithless.

### 18

But I will sing of your strength, and I will exult in the morning in your mercy.

H Christ sang—that is, preached—the Father’s strength, how he conquered the devil together with him. C He will exult in the morning when the dark night of this age has passed, when the Lord’s mercy already shines forth in the reward of the saints. There he himself will exult as king and Lord, where he sees his people rejoicing in him. This singing and exultation can also be more properly referred to the members. Christ sang of his strength in Peter and in the other apostles and martyrs.

### 19

For you have become my protector and my refuge on the day of my tribulation.

C Christ is received when the whole Church is saved. Then Christ also becomes an eternal refuge, when this most desired voice is heard: “Come, blessed ones of my Father.” But even now Christ is a welcome refuge when he is granted during a time of tribulation.

### 20

My helper, to you I will sing praises, for you, O God, are my protector; my God ÷ .. my mercy.

C He frequently repeats the benefits in order to show us how we ought to give thanks. “Protector” is a word concerning our humanity, which he deigned to join to himself in the womb of the Virgin Mary. “My God,” that is, “my mercy”: there all benefits are found, there all gifts are designated.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM 58

Almighty Lord, whose strength and mercy we praise at the morning hour, we pray and beseech you to be our strength, so that, rescued from every darkness of shadows, we may be adorned with the morning light. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, etc.

# PSALM 59

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM 59

C The people converted to Christ pray that, after the tribulations they have endured, they may be led to him.

**Title:** To the end: for those who will be changed, in the inscription of the title; David, for instruction, when he burned Mesopotamia of Syria and Syria of Zobah. And Joab returned and struck Edom in the Valley of Salt, twelve thousand.

C “They will be changed toward the end”: those who, having laid aside the error of the old man, serve the Lord Savior with pure mind. The inscription of the title signifies Christ the king. “For instruction,” that is, Christian instruction. The wars that follow are contained in the history of the kings and signify the victories of the Lord Savior, which he wages throughout the whole world against pagans and faithless people; their words this psalm will utter. Christ, strong-handed and desirable, subdued the rebellious world not with iron but through the zeal of conversion, not by visible fire but through the ardor of charity, by which the Divinity is accustomed invisibly to fight and conquer.

### 1

O God, you rejected ÷ us .. and destroyed us; you were angry and had mercy on us.

C This people, bound by ancient errors, recalls under the form of thanksgiving that it was rejected and destroyed. When it says “you rejected,” it shows that it was recalled by God’s grace so that its life would not end in perverse doctrines. This destruction overturned in order to build; it cast down in order to raise up. Therefore this destruction rightly leads to thanksgiving. He was angry when he overturned their superstitions; he had mercy when he brought them to the worship of true religion.

### 2

You shook the earth and disturbed it; heal its fractures, for it has been shaken.

C “Earth” signifies the entire assembly of sinners, who were shaken at the Lord’s coming when they recognized that their forms of worship were abominable to God. They were disturbed when, amid their doctrines, they heard others say: “Grasp instruction, lest the Lord become angry” (Ps. 2), “and you perish from the right way.” “Heal its fractures,” and so forth: the wounds are exposed to the heavenly physician so that medicine may come to the broken. This is the fracture that makes us stronger, because it has been shaken—that is, it has been transferred from its former error so that it may obey you, the Lord, who formerly served idols.

### 3

You have shown your people hard things; you have given us wine of compunction to drink.

C He showed hard things to the faithful righteous in this world in order to make them precious in eternity. Virtue is compared with wine, in which there is no abundance of vices but an abundance of compunction, which, in a good purpose, makes the effort of our unchanged will understand what is right while these things are fulfilled.

### 4

You have given a signal to those who fear you, so that they may flee from the face of the bow. Diapsalma.

C He gave a signal to those who fear him when, through the Scriptures, he taught the faithful to endure manifold sufferings in this troubled world. “The face of the bow” designates the day of judgment, where the whole people is judged beneath what are like the two bent arches of the New and Old Testaments. But the person who has devoutly cast himself down in the humility of confession does not receive the arrow from this bow—that is, the sentence.

### 5

So that your beloved may be delivered. Save with your right hand and hear me.

C This faithful people prays that, having now been freed from tribulations, the power of God may turn its tribulations into the gladness of joy. It also prays to be saved by the right hand, because those who will rejoice in perpetual happiness are to be established on that side.

### 6

God has spoken in his holy place: I will rejoice and divide Shechem; I will measure the Valley of the Tabernacles.

C The Father spoke in the Son, namely the evangelical truth through which the redemption of the faithful came. “I will rejoice”: the people rightly rejoiced, to whom the Lord spoke prosperous things. H “Shechem” signifies Samaria. Christ divides Shechem when he assigns one part to blessedness and places another with the faithless. C “He measured the Valley of the Tabernacles,” that is, from the Jewish collection he possesses no small portion in the catholic faith. It is called a valley because it is, as it were, a hollowed plain.

### 7

Gilead is mine and Manasseh is mine; and Ephraim is the strength of my head.

C Gilead is interpreted as “heap of testimony.” Witnesses are called *martyrs* in Greek. This heap of testimony signifies a great congregation of martyrs. Manasseh is interpreted as “forgotten.” Therefore the faithful people rightly says that the forgetfulness which was to come from the abolition of crimes belongs to it. Ephraim means “fruitfulness,” which is “the strength of my head”—that is, the Lord Savior, who bestowed abundant fruit upon us through his passion and resurrection, since “unless a grain of wheat,” and so forth, “it bears much fruit” (John 12). H All these things are spoken concerning the calling of the nations, whose various virtues are to be understood through the interpretation of their individual names.

### 8

Judah is my king; Moab is the pot of my hope.

C Judah signifies Christ, and this should be said with exultation: “Judah is my king,” since this is the glorious confession of the faithful. Moab is placed for the nations, from which he foretold that the Church would be gathered. “The pot of hope” signifies the tribulation that the saints endure in this age, which, by the Lord’s gift, is extended toward the hope of eternal life, as Paul says: “Hope does not disappoint” (Rom. 5). The pot is used here in a negative sense, because in a perverse understanding it boils up like the wave of a cooking vessel; but when sins have been boiled away and burned up, the blackness of the pot will be transformed.

### 9

Into Idumea I will extend my sandal; the foreigners have been subjected to me.

H Idumea is interpreted as “bloody” or “earthly,” as though he were saying: Upon such people I will extend my sandal—that is, the preaching of the Gospel. “The foreigners have been subjected to me,” namely, to Christ and the Church.

### 10

Who will lead me into the fortified city? Who will lead me as far as Idumea?

C The faithful people cries out to the Lord: Who will lead me into the fortified city—that is, the future Jerusalem—except you alone, O God? It is so fortified that it cannot thereafter be shaken by any persecution; the one who enters it does so under your guidance. “Who will lead me?” He himself, namely God. For the Church desires those peoples who have not yet deserved to be perfect to be joined to her, so that, when the number of the predestined has been completed, those who are earthly may arrive together with the saints at eternal joys.

### 11

Are you not, O God, the one who rejected us? And will you not go forth, O God, with our armies?

C By saying “are you not, O God,” he shows that the one of whom he spoke above—the only one who would lead—is the one who alone ought to be propitious to us as Creator. He says “who rejected us,” that is, who restrained us from evil so that we would not wander according to our own will. “God will not go forth with our armies”: while you thus defend us inwardly in the present age from our adversaries, you nevertheless afflict us outwardly with various trials for our testing. The enemies think that you do not go forth with our armies, although you protect us virtuously in mind.

### 12

Give us help from tribulation, for the salvation of man is vain.

C The Church prays that, from the tribulation of this world, which it continually endured, the Lord’s help might come beforehand to it, knowing that each person will be consoled there all the more greatly according to how severely he was afflicted here for the Lord’s name. “The salvation of man is vain”: no one but God can provide salvation for a human being; therefore a person ought not to hope in another human being.

### 13

In God we will perform valor, and he himself will reduce to nothing those who afflict us.

C He will perform valor in God who, persevering continually in his commandments, tramples down diabolical temptations through Christ’s mercy. For he brings the enemies of the faithful to nothing, since he erases them from the book of the living, where, in their pride, they seemed to themselves to be written.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM 59

Most merciful Lord, save your suppliant people by the help of your right hand; and while it is exercised in tribulations for the fruit of good works, may your grace always console it. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, etc.

# PSALM 60

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM 60

C The voice of the Church asking to be protected beneath the covering of Christ’s wings.

**Title:** To the end, in hymns; David.

C It is already known that “to the end” signifies Christ. “In hymns” is a Greek word and is interpreted “in praises,” because the whole Psalm resounds with Christ’s praises. David, moreover, signifies Christ himself, whose praise the Christian people sings.

### 1

Hear, O God, my supplication; attend to my prayer.

C Supplication is an earnest and common entreaty, offered both to God and to human beings. Prayer, however, is that which we rightly offer to the Holy Trinity; he asked that it be attended to, that is, regarded by the Lord and met with mercy.

### 2

From the ends of the earth I cried to you when my heart was distressed; you exalted me upon a rock.

### 3

You led me, because you became my hope: a tower of strength from the face of the enemy.

C The holy congregation cries from the ends of the earth, H that is, from the four parts of the world, C in which the Church of almighty God is established. It cries to the Lord in distress of heart when prayer and crying are more earnest—namely, when, with the soul in peril, remedies necessary to the soul are sought. The rock signifies Christ; it declares itself exalted upon this rock, upon which every Christian is built. C You led me into it, namely, into that future rest which the Lord promises to his blessed ones. The reason is also given why it was led to the reward: because it placed the Lord as its hope. The tower also signifies the Lord; for a tower defends a city’s walls and wounds attacking enemies from on high. So the Lord’s power defends his people; it fights by the word, not by battle, and that tower is full of virtues, not swords.

### 4

÷ I will dwell in your tabernacle for ever; I shall be protected in the covering of your wings. Diapsalma.

H I shall indeed dwell in that tabernacle in which we shall remain without end, continually contemplating God. C The Lord’s protection is therefore rightly compared to wings, which neither burden those beneath them nor fail to remedy the injury of every adversity.

### 5

For you, my God, have heard my prayer; you have given an inheritance to those who fear your name.

C He shows why he rejoices under the shelter of the Lord’s wings: namely, because his prayer has been heard. “You have given an inheritance” signifies the kingdom of the future age. This has no end; but once it has been received, it never departs from us through any change.

6 [Col. 0233C] You will add days upon the days of the king: His years through the day of generation and generation.

C “Days” signifies the eternity of the Savior, who is rightly called our king, since we are ruled by him. H The years and days of this king will also be added through these generations, until, after the elect have been gathered and the enemies overthrown, he hands the kingdom over to God the Father, reigning together with him and with the saints. C “Through the day of generation and generation,” that is, through the one eternal day in the glory of God, which is the day toward which every human generation has been ordered.

7 He remains forever in the presence of God: [Col. 0233D] Who will seek his mercy and truth ÷ for him ..?

C He will remain forever—namely, the holy people in blessedness, with death’s dominion no longer ruling in them. C “Who will seek mercy?” Mercy will not be sought there, where no one is wretched. Nor will truth be sought there, where all will see God. None of them will be unworthy of such blessings, since they will possess the kingdoms of heaven forever. It must therefore be read negatively: “Who will seek?”—as though he were saying, “No one.”

8 Thus I will sing the psalm to your name forever ÷ and ever ..: That I may fulfill my vows from day to day.

C “Thus” signifies “in this way,” as he explains in what follows. He says that the blessed peoples will always sing psalms to the heavenly name, not for a short time, but forever and ever. He also promises to fulfill his vows to the Lord, so that he may always render him eternal thanks. “From day to day” signifies “always”: here we fulfill our vows, and there we sing praises to the Lord with perpetual joy.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM LX

Most merciful God, consoler of our anxieties, protect your household from the face of the enemy, so that, fortified by you as by a tower of strength, it may deserve to dwell in eternal tabernacles. Through our Lord, etc.

# PSALM LXI

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM LXI

[Col. 0234B] C The voice of a convert declaring that his soul is subject to God and admonishing the erring to trust in the Lord more than in the fleeting prosperity of this world.

**Title.** To the end. A psalm of David for Jeduthun.

C Jeduthun is interpreted as “transcending them,” that is, the lovers of this age, whom the soldier of Christ surpasses by despising the world’s will and remains firm in the strongest hope in the Lord. Such a person sets forth “the end,” that is, follows the Lord Christ; and the psalm likewise signifies a commendable life that obeys the Lord’s rules—that is, submits to them.

1 Will not my soul be subject to God? For from him comes my salvation.

C “Will not” should be altered for greater clarity: let us say, “Will it not be subject to God?” One is subject to God who always humbly does what he has understood to belong to God’s commands, and whose blessed mind desires nothing apart from him. “For from him comes my salvation,” that is, the only-begotten Son, who is rightly called and is salvation for those who believe.

2 For he himself is also my God and my Savior: My protector; I shall not be moved any further.

C “For he himself is also my God”: he now invokes the God whom above he called salvation. But lest you believe the Son to be lesser than the Father, he says, “He himself is my God.” He repeats, “my Savior,” for Christ is the salvation of the human race, which had perished in Adam. H He added, “my protector,” in eternity; therefore, “I shall not be moved any further,” because once I enjoy the blessed vision, I will not fear falling. Nor does he have anywhere else to run, except toward God.

3 How long will you all rush upon one man? You all kill: Like a leaning wall and a tottering fence.

C The people of God speak to the persecutors of Christians: “How long will you rush in a mass upon innocent people?” H He added, “You kill all of yourselves,” because whoever has the will to kill a person kills him even if he has not struck him. C The comparison is most apt. Although a leaning wall does not move, it nevertheless falls, because whatever has been inclined from its solidity is tending toward collapse; and a tottering fence easily falls into ruin if it has been shaken by some force. H Thus, murderers, although you were created upright, you are driven headlong toward ruin, and the natural sense within you has been perverted. C A fence is a dry construction of stones, built up and assembled without any binding material.

4 Nevertheless, they planned to drive away my price: I ran in thirst: With their mouth they blessed, and with their heart they cursed. Diapsalma.

C This verse refers to the Jews and to false Christians. The unbelievers planned to drive away Christ, who is the head and price of the Church, when they opposed his being worshiped with a pure heart through sacrilegious doctrines. Then the holy man carried out the course of his life in the thirst of sterility, because he could not find anyone whom sacred doctrine might refresh. The cause of the thirst follows: they blessed with their mouth—those who pass over the law by deceitful correction and do not demonstrate in their works what they proclaim with their mouth. They cursed with their heart because they understood the holy Scriptures perversely.

5 Nevertheless, be subject to God, my soul: For my patience is from him.

C The Prophet now repeats what he said above: that his soul is subject to God, so that this repetition might impress faith upon our minds. For Christ is our patience; on his account we gladly endure adversity and rejoice in observing the rule we have undertaken.

6 ÷ For he is ÷ my God .. and my Savior: My helper; I shall not depart.

C Above he called Christ “patience”; now [Col. 0235C] he again says, “my God and my Savior,” because he already knew that the salvation of his soul would come through the Word who was to become incarnate. “I shall not depart,” namely, from the faith that I hold, either because of your evil persuasion or because of persecution.

7 In God is my salvation and my glory: The God of my help and my hope is in God ÷ ... 

C He repeats that salvation is in God, not as among the gods of the nations, in whom there is everlasting death. “And my glory,” so that not only salvation but also having believed in him may be glory. “The God of my help,” lest human weakness attribute anything to itself. Finally he says, “My hope is in God,” so that he might attribute both the things he had already received to the Lord and apply his future blessedness to him.

8 [Col. 0235D] Hope in him, every assembly of the people; pour out your hearts before him: For God is our helper ÷ forever ..: Diapsalma.

C “Hope in him,” that is, in the one whom he had professed to be both his God and the salvation of the whole assembly of the people. He pours out his heart before the Lord who confesses his sins with the most abundant tears. The heart cannot otherwise be poured out except by a frequent downpour of tears.

9 Nevertheless, the sons of men are vain; the sons of men are liars in the balances, so that they may themselves deceive by vanity into the same thing.

C He says, “The sons of men are vain,” so that humanity, recognizing its vice, may hasten by swift supplication to the author of salvation. People are called vain in comparison with the truth above. He refers to the liars who deceive the simplicity of buyers with unjust balances, or to those who deceive by pretending to holiness. “So that they may deceive”: they could refrain from deceiving if their wickedness could be detected. “In their own vanity,” namely, in the equity that they are falsely thought to possess, when they are believed to be just.

10 Do not hope in iniquity, and do not desire robberies; if riches flow in, do not set your heart upon them.

C He teaches those who have been corrupted not to hope where the fruit of a good desire cannot be found. He also speaks to the poor who, from necessity of sustenance, desire something obtained by theft. “Do not desire robberies”: need cannot remove the crime of robbery, nor can it excuse the guilt of one subject to punishment. He now returns to the rich, saying, “If riches flow in.” Rightly, therefore, he commanded the rich not to set their heart upon them and not to love what they possess, since Paul says: “Do not hope in the uncertainty of riches, but in the living God” (1 Tim. VI).

11 God has spoken once; I have heard these two things: That power belongs to God, and to you, Lord, mercy; for you will repay each person according to his works.

C God spoke frequently to our fathers, but he spoke once to his Son, saying: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Hebr. I); for it is clear that the Father spoke this to no one else. “I heard these two things” in the Gospel: “I have power to lay down my soul and to take it up again” (John X). The second follows: “And to you, Lord, mercy”—“it is pleasing” must be supplied. Both belong to divinity, so that he may act mercifully and show mercy with power. And so that you may understand more clearly that this was said of Christ, the time of judgment follows: “For you repay.” “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John V). Thus, from these three attributes assigned to Christ—his singular utterance, power, and mercy—it is shown that in judgment likewise he is one true God with the Father.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM LXI

Subject our souls to yourself, Lord, since you are true patience, so that, rejecting the uncertainties of riches and despising all worldly vanity, we may follow you alone. [Col. 0236D] Through our Lord Jesus, etc.

# PSALM LXII

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM LXII

C The Church, desiring to see the Lord’s power, gives thanks because, under the Lord’s protection, it has escaped the storms of the world.

**Title.** A psalm of David, when he was in the desert of Idumaea.

C Idumaea is the place where David, fleeing Saul’s persecution, is known to have hidden. Idumaea is interpreted as “earthly” and signifies earthly actions, which have been entirely stripped of spiritual goods.

1 God, my God: To you I keep vigil from the dawn.

C “God, my God.” In this repetition of the venerable name he displays the affection of pious supplication. One keeps vigil for him whenever one sleeps amid the ambition of the world. He adds “at dawn,” when the time of the Lord’s resurrection shone forth, so that he might sing praises when he had invigorated the human race by the example of his resurrection.

2 My soul thirsted for you: How manifoldly my flesh seeks you.

C The soul of the faithful thirsts for God when it desires his commandments and outstanding virtues, and longs to see him, from whom the streams of all good things are known to flow. H Therefore the flesh seeks God in many ways, because it is afflicted by many injuries.

3 In + a deserted ÷ land .., pathless and waterless, thus I appeared to you in the holy place: [Col. 0237B] So that + I might see your power and your glory.

C “In a deserted land,” as the title said, that is, in the neediness and barren sterility of this world. “In a pathless place,” because the world has no way within itself except the Lord Savior, who is the way of the blind. “And waterless,” that is, dry and unfruitful, so that the soul may rightly grow hard through excessive dryness. Thus, through these three names, the neediness of this world is indicated. The holy Church says that it appeared in a holy and faithful purpose when it recognized that Christ is the true God. It says, “I appeared to you, so that I might see your power and your glory,” because no one sees the truth unless he has first been able to appear before God. For if this sun makes us see when it shines upon us, how much more does divine power—which is necessary for us even to receive or retain anything good—make itself seen, if, illuminating us first, it causes us to appear before it?

4 For your mercy is better than life: My lips will praise you.

C By “mercy” he means the Lord’s rewards, which he promises to his saints in abundant goodness; this is far better than the present life. “My lips will praise you”: after the benefits he promised, he pledges the service of devoted praise, which he knew to be most pleasing to God. H Your mercy grants eternal life; the present life often produces death. G Or: “Your mercy is better than life,” that is, than any manner of living, however holy, because no one could be saved by his own holiness if God’s mercy were absent.

5 Thus I will bless you in my life: [Col. 0237D] ÷ And .. in your name I will lift up my hands.

C He blesses God perfectly in his life who lives by good works in this light. He lifts his hands in the Lord’s name who, devoting himself to holy works, prays to the Lord with outstretched hands, so that the prayer itself may represent the form of the holy cross.

6 As with fat and richness my soul will be filled: And my mouth will praise you with lips of jubilation.

C Fat is the thick covering of the viscera that covers the inner parts of the liver. Richness is the obesity of a fattened animal nourished by food; these things were formerly suitable for sacrifices. But the richness of the soul is knowledge of divine things, upright faith, and steadfast patience, etc. Thus the leanness of this age is overcome. And “lips of jubilation”: dry lips, dried out by sin, cannot praise God; but when the soul has received the richness of divine mercy, it will praise him with lips of jubilation. H Here there are prayers; in the homeland there are jubilation and everlasting joy.

7 Thus I remembered you upon my bed; in the mornings I will meditate upon you, for you were my helper.

C When the Church says, “Thus I remembered you,” it shows that it has always kept the Lord in memory and was not forgetful amid prosperity, when human hearts commonly fail to remember benefits bestowed. By “bed” it signifies rest, where we are accustomed to release our bodies into sleep. In the mornings also the faithful keep vigil, for even in prosperity they cannot forget the author of light. He was a helper in dangers, when the Church was in the pathless desert.

8 And under the shelter of your wings I will rejoice; my soul clung to you; your right hand received me.

H “Under the shelter,” that is, under the protection of heavenly help, the Church says that it rejoices. C It says that its soul clung after the Lord so that it may never depart from its good purpose. The right hand of the Father is Christ the Lord, who received the Church to be protected under the shelter of his wings.

9 But they sought my soul in vain: They will enter into the depths of the earth; they will be handed over to the hands of the sword; they will become portions for foxes.

H C “But they,” that is, the enemies, sought Christ’s soul in vain when they resolved to shed his blood on the basis of false charges. C It follows: They were not raised to the heavens, but the bowels of the earth swallowed them downward. The Jewish people was handed over to the hands of the sword when the Roman commanders Vespasian and Titus devastated it with slaughter and fire. The Jews also, refusing to believe heavenly things, became portions for foxes: either while they joined themselves by wicked intent to deceitful and fraudulent people, or while they were reduced under the power of such people. Or this refers to the time when, in the devastation of Jerusalem, their corpses became food for foxes and the remaining wild animals.

10 But the king will rejoice in God; all who swear by him will be praised: ÷ For the mouth of those speaking iniquity has been stopped ...

C By “the king” he means the Savior, for he is the eternal king who will rejoice in the Lord God the Father. He added, “All will be praised,” since the saints of God praise Christ: they themselves unquestionably become praiseworthy, because no one can worthily proclaim his praises except those who have deserved to attain the palm of forgiveness. They swear by him who promise him the inviolable obedience of their minds. H The mouth of the Jews and of the chief priests was stopped when the Lord rose and the testimony of the truth increased. C And the mouth of all the wicked will be stopped in the judgment, not in this age.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM LXII

Bestow perpetual light upon those who keep vigil for you at dawn, leader of eternal light, so that our lips may praise you, our life may bless you, and our morning meditation may glorify you. [Col. 0239A] Through our Lord Jesus Christ, etc.

# PSALM LXIII

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM LXIII

C Throughout this psalm Christ speaks of his passion.

**Title.** To the end. A psalm of David.

C The words of this title, as has often been said, refer to the Lord Christ, who speaks throughout the psalm. It is known to be the sixth among those that touch upon the Lord’s passion and resurrection through a brief revelation.

1 Hear, O God, my prayer when I plead: Rescue my soul from fear of the enemy.

C The Lord Christ, from the standpoint of the humanity he assumed, asked that his prayer be heard, since one requests with all one’s strength what one perceives to be beneficial. “From fear of the enemy,” that is, the Jew, H or the devil: he asked that his faithful be rescued.

2 You protected me from the assembly of the malicious: From the multitude of those working iniquity.

C He was plainly protected from the assembly of the Jews, because, while they collectively believed that he would die, they were shown to be confounded by the glory of his resurrection. He was therefore protected because by the power of his strength he overcame the plots of the wicked. He said “from the multitude” to express the activity of the passion. Above he said “from the assembly of the malicious,” which can refer to their counsels; but this refers to their action. Therefore he said, “Those working iniquity.”

3 For they sharpened their tongues like a sword: [Col. 0239C] They bent the bow—an embittered thing—to shoot the blameless in secret.

C The reason is now given why he was protected from those working iniquity. For to the extent that they had sharpened their tongues like a deadly sword, to that extent their iniquity was shattered, and they harmed themselves more than Christ. It is indeed the custom of sinners that those who hasten to burden another first harm themselves. They sharpened their tongues when with one voice they said, “Crucify him.” They bent the bow, that is, prepared hidden ambushes. O bitter thing, worse than every gall: a dining companion for betrayal, a disciple for death, and the keeper of money corrupted by a money-payment. “In secret” is to be understood as the Jews thought; yet their action could not be hidden from Christ, since it had frequently been foretold before it happened. Those who have been cleansed from sins by God’s mercy are also called blameless, but Christ alone is truly blameless, since he contracted no stain.

4 Suddenly they will shoot him and will not fear: They have strengthened an evil word for themselves.

“Suddenly,” as though unseen or unexpectedly. H So the utterly deranged Jews thought. When he says, “They will shoot and will not fear,” he shows the swift effect of an evil will. They strengthened it for themselves when they said, “He is guilty of death,” or, “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. XXVII).

5 They spoke so as to hide their snares; they said, “Who will see them?”

[Col. 0240A] C It is the custom of sinners that the one who prepares a deceit thinks he can deceive a human being. So the Jews, confused and thinking Christ merely human, did not believe that their wickedness was recognized by him to whom all things are open.

6 They searched out iniquities; those searching searched to exhaustion.

C The Jews searched out iniquities that they ought indeed to have passed over, since they could find there no fruit for their salvation. For they said, “If we let him go on like this” (John XI), “the Romans will come,” etc. “They searched to exhaustion,” because those who strive to reach the worst things always fail in their thinking.

7 A man will approach a lofty heart, and God will be exalted.

8 [Col. 0240B] The arrows of children became their wounds, and their tongues were weakened against them.

9 All who saw them were disturbed, and every person was afraid.

10 And they proclaimed the works of God, and they understood his deeds.

C The heart is deep when a person thinks about heavenly things and avoids earthly ones. Such a person does not fail like the one who searched to exhaustion; rather, he grows more and more, because God will be exalted in his heart, not himself. For God grows great in the one who grows in holiness.

C “The arrows of children”: these are empty weapons, such as fragile reeds that children accustomed to play throw in the manner of arrows. So it was with the Jews’ intentions, through a most savage but ineffectual wickedness: they did not inflict a death to be mourned, but a most glorious passion. H Their tongues were weakened because their speech gained no stability; rather, their deceit made them weak.

C Some of those who believed were disturbed by them when they came and said to the apostles, “What shall we do, men and brothers?” (Acts II). “And every person was afraid”: he gives the whole for the part, so that everyone may be understood who feared the future judgment of the Lord. He was afraid because he feared that the future judgment threatened him.

C “They proclaimed,” namely, the glory of the resurrection and the earlier miracles that he performed. “And they understood his deeds,” namely, that they were divine, because human weakness could not accomplish such things. H For, pierced in heart, they understood and proclaimed what they had understood to others, because they reverently feared God.

11 The just will rejoice in the Lord and hope in him, and all the upright of heart will be praised.

H “The just will rejoice.” Just as the impious fear because of their unbelief, so the just exult in the Lord because of their hope of eternity. C The upright of heart are those who walk along the Lord’s paths. They praise the Lord, and are they also praised by the truth itself? What is more praiseworthy than to hear from him: “Come, blessed ones,” etc.?

## PRAYER FROM PSALM LXIII

God, protector of all who believe, guard your Church from the assembly of the malicious, who strive to attack it with hidden arrows, so that, retaining you with a sound and upright understanding, it may rejoice forever in the merits of the just. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, etc.

# PSALM LXIV

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM LXIV

C The people freed from sin ask that their prayer be heard, proclaiming various praises of the Lord and his power.

**Title.** To the end. A psalm of David + a song .. ÷ of Jeremiah and Ezekiel concerning the people’s transmigration, when they began to depart ...

C “To the end. A psalm of David”: these are words already known. “A song” signifies the prophecy of Jeremiah and Ezekiel, who prophesied concerning the people of the Babylonian transmigration, that after seventy years they would return to their homeland. It signifies the people returning from Babylon: those who, having condemned the confusion of this world, strive to come to the heavenly Jerusalem.

1 Praise is fitting for you, O God, in Zion, and to you the vow will be fulfilled ÷ in Jerusalem .. 

C The people, returned to the Lord from captivity to sin, burst forth into great exultation, saying: “It is fitting to sing a hymn to God alone, not to throngs of demons, and nowhere except in Zion,” H that is, in the Church. C And it is fitting to fulfill the vow in Jerusalem, not as vows are fulfilled by unbelievers to Mars and Venus and the other demons, but to God alone in Jerusalem, that is, in the vision of peace, in which happiness always remains fixed.

2 Hear my prayer: To you all flesh will come.

[Col. 0241C] C The same people who had first said, “Praise is fitting for you,” now cry out to the Lord with a hymn-like supplication, saying: “Hear my prayer.” They ask that he spare them, so that he may not condemn them in the future. H “All flesh,” as though he were saying, “Every human being will turn to you.” C Or, every human being will come to you in judgment, receiving according to what he has done (2 Cor. V). Therefore I ask you to spare me here, by hearing my prayer.

3 The words of the wicked have prevailed against us, and you will be gracious toward our impieties.

C “The words of the wicked prevailed” when pagan parents persuaded their children to worship ancient rites and sacrileges. But divine piety came to the aid of these errors when, at the Lord’s coming, it granted salvation to the world and made him a sacrifice on the cross, through which he reconciled the world to himself (Eph. V).

4 Blessed is the one whom you have chosen and taken up: He will dwell in your courts.

C Blessed is the one whom the Lord has chosen, and who does not attribute that choice to his own merits. To be taken up means to be placed in eternal rest. H Therefore, whoever has shown himself worthy of Christ’s election dwells with the holy apostles in everlasting tabernacles.

5 We will be filled with the good things of your house: Your holy temple is wondrous in righteousness.

C “We will be filled,” as though according to our measure, as much as we are able to contain. We will be given drink, as with Paul: “To each is given grace according to the measure of Christ’s gift” (Rom. XII). H “The holy temple” is that human being in whom the fullness of divinity dwells (Eph. IV). C What he called “wondrous” refers to the man mentioned above, who will judge the world in righteousness. H Or because he wondrously disclosed the truth to the unbelieving Jews. C The Church may also be understood as the Lord’s temple. It is wondrous in the saints, who are endowed beyond searching with the virtues of righteousness.

6 Hear us, God our Savior, hope of all the ends of the earth and of the distant sea.

C God is called our Savior because in his goodness he brought salvation to the human race. The Lord’s hope is not local or limited to one nation, but belongs to all the ends of the earth. “And of the distant sea” either refers to the islands, which he seemed not to have included within the aforementioned boundaries, or to the habitation of the whole world, which is rightly called the distant or great sea, because this world is bitter with demonic falsehoods and the waves of disturbances.

7 Preparing the mountains by your power, girded with might; you who disturb the depths of the sea, the sound of its waves.

C “Preparing the mountains,” that is, the apostles, who were chosen for the word of preaching. The Lord prepared them in his power because through them he performed great miracles. “Girded,” that is, clothed, with power, that is, with his majesty. Through the preaching of the apostles he disturbed the depths of the sea, that is, the hearts of the Gentiles, who were the depths of this world—which is called the sea—because they had been more deeply immersed in errors. Their hearts were rightly disturbed when they saw their gods fall silent. “Its sound,” that is, the cruel words of the persecutors, which were the sound of the waves, that is, of the persecutions of the sea, that is, of the world. H Or the depths of the sea are the profound boastfulness of the world.

8 The nations will be disturbed, and those who inhabit the ends of the earth will fear your signs; the outlets of morning and evening you will make glad.

C The nations were disturbed when they saw the most faithful performing miracles while alive and fulfilling the requests of those who prayed for the dead. “All will fear your signs.” H That is, the power of the cross, which was foolishness to unbelievers. C Or “signs,” that is, the miracles of the apostles, such as they had never before seen or heard. “The outlet of morning” is when someone turns from the prosperity of the world to God. “Evening” signifies the sadness of those who mourn, which God turns into joy. H By morning joy is understood; by evening, sadness. A Therefore he makes morning and evening delightful, that is, makes them sources of delight, while he gains saints both through prosperity and through adversity.

9 You visited the earth and intoxicated it; you multiplied it so as to enrich it.

H He visited the earth by assuming the substance of a body, and intoxicated it not with the wine of luxury but with the infusion of the Holy Spirit. He enriched it with the resources of diverse graces. C One is called rich (*locuples*) when one holds many places.

10 [Col. 0243A] The river of God is filled with waters; you prepared their food, for such is its preparation.

H We who believe are already the river of God. We will be filled with waters, that is, with the mercy of God, which is compared with waters, or with the Holy Spirit. Or, when we are washed in baptism, we are enriched by the same rain of spiritual infusion, as we are irrigated with spiritual gifts. C This food is the bread of life (John VI). C The Lord prepared such food for us, which we consume when we drink from Christ’s blood and are nourished by his body.

11 Make its streams drunk; multiply its offspring; in its showers the one germinating will rejoice.

12 Blessing the crown of the year of your goodness, [Col. 0243B] and your fields will be filled with abundance.

C Here he calls the streams the apostles or other faithful, who were intoxicated with the Holy Spirit. “Multiply its offspring,” that is, its generations—the generations of that stream which flowed from the holy river—so that through successive generations the blessed preaching may not fail but multiply among the apostles’ followers. Showers are drops that fall from roofs. They penetrate not by their weight but by their persistence, and signify beginners, those into whom expansive teaching cannot enter. Of them Paul says: “I gave you milk to drink, not food” (1 Cor. III). H Then the earth—that is, the Church—will rejoice in its germination when this spiritual fruit springs from it.

C “The crown of the year” signifies this whole world, through which the Catholic Church is spread here, and which the Lord blesses. He calls the fields faithful and just people, who are called fields because of their righteousness, since fields are level. They are filled with abundance because, with the Lord granting it, they will produce a thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and hundredfold fruit.

13 The beautiful places of the desert will grow fat, and the hills will gird themselves with jubilation.
