C “The beautiful places will grow fat,” that is, the Church, through the preaching of the apostles, which previously stood parched in the desert of unbelief. The hills should be understood as the multitude of martyrs, because after the apostles they are the higher ones. H Raised by God through immense rewards, they will gird themselves with everlasting joys.

14 The rams of the sheep have been clothed, and the valleys will abound in grain; [Col. 0243D] for they will cry out—they will sing a hymn.

C The rams are the apostles, who were leaders of the good Christian people in doctrine and were clothed in that wedding garment, H that is, perpetual immortality. C “The valleys” signify humble peoples. These therefore abound in grain, H that is, they are nourished by the fruit of eternal life. “They will sing a hymn”: all the elect, for the gifts of their diverse offices, sing perpetual praise to God together. C But because he said “they will cry out,” lest you believe that he meant a confused shouting, he added, “They will sing a hymn,” that is, praise, which is known to be fitting for rational creatures.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM LXIV

Hope of all the ends of the earth, hear the supplication of your household, so that, while it celebrates you with harmonious applause and a melodious hymn, adorned by the infusion of the Paraclete, it may grow rich with abundant fruit. Through our Lord Jesus, etc.

# PSALM LXV

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM LXV

C The voice of the Church exhorting the whole world to rejoice together over the Lord’s resurrection.

**Title.** To the end. A psalm of David. A song ÷ of the resurrection ...

C The holy Church sang this song, promising in it the hope of resurrection, destined to dwell not only among the faithful from the Jews but among all nations.

1 Shout joyfully to God, all the earth: Sing a psalm to his name; give glory to his praise.

C The holy Church says that the whole earth, which was going to believe in Christ, should rejoice. Jubilation is an exultation of the heart which, because of its immensity, cannot be expressed in words. “All the earth” signifies all the faithful. H “Let it sing a psalm,” that is, let it fulfill it in its works. C He gives glory to praise who, through repeated exultation, celebrates together the proclamations of Christ.

2 Say to God: How fearful are your works, ÷ Lord ..? In the multitude of your power your enemies will lie to you.

H “Say to God,” that is, preach about him, so that they may not worship the creature but understand the power of the Creator in the things they behold, because they are fearful—that is, worthy of fear. “They lied to him in the multitude of his power,” because, seeing the signs in Egypt, they said, “Everything that you command we will do” (Exod. XXIV), but they did not do it. Therefore he said, “Iniquity lied to itself, and the enemies of the Lord lied to him.” C Or, when he healed the sick by his great power, they lied and said, “He casts out demons by Beelzebub” (Matt. XII); and when he rose in the multitude of his power, they said to the guards after giving them money, “Say that his disciples stole him by night” (Matt. XXVIII).

3 Let all the earth worship you and sing to you; let it sing a psalm to your name. Diapsalma.

H “Let it worship you; let it sing to you,” not the creature that you subjected to its uses. He inserts “Diapsalma” in order to turn the words toward us, saying, “Come,” etc. C “Let it sing,” that is, let it utter a psalmody; and “let it sing a psalm,” that is, let it show holy works corresponding to its psalmody.

4 Come and see the works of God, fearful in his plans concerning the sons of men.

C The Church invites the nations, so that, having observed the miracles of the Old Testament, they may come to faith. “Come” is properly said as to those who are still far away. “See,” that is, recognize with the light of the heart the works of God—not those which everyone sees alike, heaven, earth, sea, etc., but those which the most faithful have spiritually recognized. H He is fearful when one is rejected and another chosen: the Jews are rejected and the nations are chosen. C Or he made the sons of men fearful and worthy of dread when he displayed great miracles through them.

5 ÷ He who .. turned the sea into dry land; they will cross the river on foot; there we will rejoice in him.

C He now shows what works of God they ought to see. “He turned the sea into dry land” when he led the Hebrew people through the midst of the waves (Exod. XIV). “They will cross the rivers on foot” when, with the Jordan divided to the right and left, he led the Jewish army into the promised land (Josh. III). H But because he says “they will cross,” not “they crossed,” it is better understood of the preachers and apostles, who, baptizing in the Lord’s river and passing through the river of persecution, turned the bitter persecutors into a dry land thirsting for God’s grace. “There we will rejoice,” where the fountain and source of our joy, prepared for eternal salvation, is found. “In him,” that is, in Christ.

6 He who rules in his power + forever ..: his eyes look upon the nations; those who provoke him should not exalt themselves. Diapsalma.

C Certainly in him we shall rejoice who rules, and so forth. For earthly princes too may rule, but not by their own power nor forever. Therefore these two expressions have been added, so that the power of the omnipotent King may be displayed. “His eyes are upon the nations.” H So that the Jews may be rejected and the nations chosen. C He forbids those who ought to be found humble to exalt themselves in themselves. For the faithful ought to be exalted not in themselves but in Christ, where elevation is secure and the ascent will never fall.

7 [Col. 0245C] Bless, O nations, our God: And make the voice of his praise heard.

C He admonishes the nations to glorify the true God with united voice and proclamation. “Hear,” that is, receive with faithful belief. “The voice of praise,” that is, the voice which the Father speaks concerning the Son. For he says of him: “This is my beloved Son” (Matt. III).

8 Who set my soul toward life: And did not allow my feet to be shaken.

C There are two mysteries of our liberation. First, through baptism he leads us to life; then he does not allow us to be driven out from it, although we are tested by being burdened with grave vices. He does not permit our feet and steps to be shaken—he who extended his hand to Peter so that he would not sink (Matt. XIV).

9 [Col. 0245D] For you tested us, O God: You examined us by fire, as silver is examined.

C God causes us to be tested when he grants us endurance through various kinds of suffering. A person is examined by fire when love for Christ is kindled to such a degree that the torments of burning flames are overcome. The example of silver is given because it is smelted by fire in order to be made purer; so also the saints are cleansed by tribulations from every dross of sin.

10 You brought us into a snare: You placed tribulations upon our back: You laid men upon our heads.

C “You brought us in,” that is, you caused the martyrs to enter the chains of imprisonment, which bound the body but dissolved the bonds of the soul. The tribulation placed upon the back signifies the bodily pains that they endured from the blows inflicted upon them. “Men” signifies sinners who had pronounced capital sentences against the martyrs.

11 We passed through fire and water: And you brought us out into refreshment.

C The martyrs passed through fire when fire consumed some of them. Water devoured others, but he brought them into refreshment, that is, into the places of security of the eternal kingdom. For after burning anxieties there is refreshment: a delightful and pleasant security.

12 I shall enter your house with burnt offerings: I shall repay you my vows, which my lips have declared.

[Col. 0246B] C I shall enter that future Jerusalem where not the burnt offerings of animals but the purity of souls is sought. He repays his vows, that is, he continually sings praises. Those vows are declared by the lips when the saints praise the Lord and accuse themselves while placed in affliction; that is, they judge that by their sins they have deserved the afflictions they endure, and in them they give thanks, praising God and proclaiming his justice and mercy.

13 And my mouth spoke: In my tribulation.

C See the blessed holiness of endurance. Many sin in tribulations because of the weakness of the flesh and remain silent about God’s praises. But the saints, placed in tribulations, know how to praise the Lord with a pure mind, as holy Job did (Job I, 2). Hence, “my mouth spoke in tribulation” should be understood as “the praises of the Lord.”

14 I shall offer you burnt offerings rich in marrow with the incense of rams: I shall offer you oxen with goats. Diapsalma.

C Burnt offerings rich in marrow are sacrifices that we offer to God with a pure and inward heart. They ought to possess marrow, that is, right faith. Rams signify the apostles. He added “with the incense of rams”; he did not say merely “with incense,” but added “of rams,” because that most fragrant incense is pleasing to the Lord which is shown to have been joined to the traditions of the apostles. Oxen are understood as preachers. A goat—so called as though “hairy”—signifies those who serve the devil, who are clothed in the bristles of vices. The Church offers these together with the oxen when converted sinners confess Christ.

15 Come, hear, and I shall tell all you who fear God how much he has done for my soul.

H Come, you who fear the Lord, and consider how the souls of the blessed are established in everlasting blessedness. C Now the Church calls not the unformed, as before, but the faithful and devout. Let us also hear and learn to ask what we know that our mother has received from the Lord.

16 ÷ To him .. I cried with my mouth: And I exalted him beneath my tongue.

C When the two things expressed in this verse are carefully fulfilled, the Christian is made perfect. Thus he cries with his mouth who supplicates the Lord purely, with a right conscience and not with a perverse will. “Beneath the tongue” means in the conscience, because our heart is beneath our tongue. We seem to exalt him beneath our tongue when we praise him in silent thought—him who is always shown to be the Most High.

17 If I regarded iniquity in my heart: The Lord would not hear.

C Thus the words of the one praying are understood, provided they are not defiled by any filth of thought. For he says: “If I have done this, God will not hear,” showing that, if they pray in such a manner, they are deceived by empty visions.

18 Therefore God heard: [Col. 0247B] And he attended to the voice of my supplication.

C He says that he was heard because he had not looked upon iniquity in his heart. Therefore he attended to the voice, because that cry ascended to the Lord which contains no pollution from human affairs.

19 Blessed be God: Who did not remove my prayer and his mercy from me.

H For the loving ears of Christ are always open to the prayers of the righteous. But let us humbly entreat him to open his ears to our prayers and, having granted forgiveness of sins, himself rescue us from present hardships. C These two things are joined together: when God does not remove the prayer, he grants mercy without doubt; and when prayer is suspended, mercy is prolonged.

PRAYER FROM PSALM LXV

Impress upon our mind, O Lord, the glory of your praise, so that, while we avoid the fires of this age, under your guidance we may be transferred into eternal refreshment. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, etc.

PSALM LXVI

ARGUMENT OF PSALM LXVI

C The Prophet begs that he may deserve to be blessed together with the faithful, and says that praise must be offered to him who judges the peoples with equity.

TT To the end; a psalm of song, with hymns.

C This hymn which the Prophet now sings is prefaced with “to the end” because the whole prayer is directed without doubt to the Lord. A psalm of song is one that was sung only with the modulation of the human voice. When “psalm” stands alone, it signifies that it was performed with instruments and tambourines. We have said that a hymn is a metrical poem composed according to its rule. A hymn, therefore, is one thing, a psalm another, and a psalm of song another.

1 May God have mercy on us and bless us: May he illuminate his face upon us ÷ and have mercy on us .. Diapsalma.

H The first petition is that God grant us his mercy, and then his blessing. C This is the request for blessing: that he illuminate his face upon us. No human sense can see that face unless it has been suffused with the radiance of its splendor.

2 So that we may know your way on earth: Your salvation among all the nations.

C The Prophet asks that in this world we may know that way of truth (John XIV), that is, the Lord Savior, who leads us to the way on which no one can go astray except one who presumes to depart from his rules. His salvation, that is, Christ, is proclaimed among all the nations.

3 May the peoples confess to you, O God: May all the peoples confess to you.

C Let the peoples confess their sins to you; and again let them not cease to proclaim the glory of the Lord. Finally, the repetition of the very word in one verse teaches that you should understand that the faithful people must do everything: namely, first confess their sins, and then make the praises of the Lord resound.

4 Let the nations rejoice and exult, because you judge the peoples with equity: And you direct the nations on earth. Diapsalma.

H Let the nations rejoice because they have been freed from the captivity of the devil; because you judge the peoples with equity, since you do not show partiality toward one nation but are God of all; and you direct the nations so that they may walk along the right path, whereas previously they did not walk with a straight step.

5 May the peoples confess to you, O God: May all the peoples confess to you: The earth has given its fruit.

[Col. 0248C] C The earth also gave its fruit when a multitude of different nations received the Lord Savior; and it produced vital fruit when it obeyed the Lord’s commands and abandoned the thorns and thistles of the devil.

6 May God bless us. Our God. May God bless us: And may all the ends of the earth fear him.

H “May God bless us,” that is, God the Father; “our God,” that is, God the Son, who by nature is God of all but has become specifically our God by grace; thirdly, “may God bless us,” that is, the Holy Spirit. “And may they fear him”—C this concerns beginners, so that they may both begin to believe and carefully guard what they have believed. H To fear belongs to beginners; to love, to the perfected.

PRAYER FROM PSALM LXVI

Illuminate your face upon us, O Lord, and bestow upon us abundant mercy and blessing. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you, etc.

PSALM LXVII

ARGUMENT OF PSALM LXVII

C The Prophet announces the advent of Christ, the suppression of his enemies’ pride, and his assumption into heaven.

TT To the end; a psalm of song, of David.

C We must attend to the force of this expression, namely “to the end,” because although it is called “the end,” it is always placed at the beginning. For it signifies the head and eternal beginning of things, as he himself said in the Gospel: “I am the beginning” (John VIII). H “Psalm” signifies works; “song” signifies the understanding of the mind. C A psalm of song is, as has already been said, one that is customarily sung only with the human voice.

1 Let God arise and let his enemies be scattered: And let those who hate him flee from his face.

A The Prophet asks for the resurrection of Christ, in which his adversaries, namely the Jews, would be scattered. An immeasurable punishment of cursing follows: that they should flee from his face, whose repentance is established everywhere. “Those who hate him” signifies those who had persisted in their obstinacy.

2 As smoke fails, so may they fail: [Col. 0249B] As wax melts before the fire, so may sinners perish before the face of God.

C Smoke is a dark, compacted mass rising from a corruptible flame; the more it is lifted up, the more it is thinned through the empty air. Thus sinners produce smoky deeds which, although they rise to higher things through the agency of pride, must fail in their own exaltation. So also at the judgment sinners perish before his face, just as wax is consumed before the fire. He does not say that they can be utterly consumed, since they are to be tormented by everlasting fire, but that they will be removed from the face of God. H For although wax is dissolved by fire, it does not lose its nature. So sinners may become soft from the hardness of sin and flow into repentance, so that they may be saved.

3 And let the righteous feast and exult in the sight of God: [Col. 0249C] And let them delight in gladness.

H Let the righteous who remain in their righteousness, and who possess no vices, feast. Let them delight in the Lord. Let them exult in the sight of God. C So that they may rejoice under the power of him whom they rightly fear here, having been delivered by his gift. “In gladness,” because, knowing that their gladness will be closed by no end, they delight in it more sweetly.

4 Sing to God, sing a psalm to his name: Prepare a road for him who ascends above the setting-place; the Lord is his name.

C He sings to the Lord who always beholds him in contemplation with a pure and faithful mind. He sings a psalm who does the works that he commanded. “Prepare a road for him,” that is, prepare your purified hearts, which God may deign to enter, he who ascends above the setting-place. H [Col. 0249D] That is, above death, and returned victorious from hell. C “The Lord is his name,” so that no one would doubt that the one whom the Jews thought should be killed as an ordinary man is Lord, Savior, and God.

5 + And .. exult in his sight: ÷ they will be troubled before his face ..: Father of orphans and judge of widows.

C Exult not in the fleeting gladness of this age, but in his sight, where true gladness continually exists. Those who are troubled and greatly afraid are driven from the face of God—those who tear orphans and widows apart with savage greed—when they hear: “Go into everlasting fire.” He explains who this one is from whose face they are driven: namely, the father of orphans and judge of widows. [Col. 0250A] Concerning him it is also written elsewhere: “You will be the helper of the orphan and widow” (Ps. IX).

6 God in his holy place: God makes those of one way of life dwell in a house.

C “God in his holy place” should be understood as referring to one who preserves an unchangeable judgment, so that the holy one is called steadfast: he changes times but does not change his plans. H Or, “God in his holy place,” that is, in the faithful soul; for wherever holiness is, there is God’s dwelling-place. He makes those of one way of life dwell in the Church, pouring into those who faithfully remain in it the spirit of charity. They are of one way of life and do not change. Indeed, the righteous person does not change, because he has once judged that he should remain in his righteousness.

In Hebrew, however, it reads: “The Lord makes monks dwell in a house,” that is, solitary persons who, being separated from vices, are alone and in whom sin does not dwell. For “monk” is interpreted as “solitary,” so that he is alone and divided from every sin.

7 ÷ He .. brings out captives in strength: Likewise those who provoke him, who dwell in tombs.

C He brought out captives because, after binding the devil, he freed the captives from hell and raised them to the joys of the eternal kingdom. “Likewise those who provoke him,” that is, those who provoke the Lord to anger by blasphemy. These are those who dwell in tombs, that is, those who are buried in foul and carnal activity. H Or understand “captives” as those bound in sins.

8 [Col. 0250C] O God, when you go forth before your people, when you pass through the desert. Diapsalma.

C He goes forth before the people when those who dwell in tombs are raised. The faithful behold him when they recognize his mercy in his great works. He crossed through the desert when he came to the nations, which, like a wilderness, were desolate and rendered alien to the word of God. And then—“when you have done these things” should be supplied—you will be known.

9 The earth was moved: ÷ for the heavens dripped from the face of God, Sinai A from the face of the God of Israel.

C “The earth was moved,” that is, earthly people believed when they saw such great miracles. “The heavens dripped.” H Namely, manna. “Sinai” is interpreted as “temptation.” [Col. 0250D] C He who established it, when Moses received the law there on two tablets. H And he who then went before the Jewish people in the desert has today visited the deserts of the nations in the Gospel; and he who then gave manna has today given the manna of his body and blood.

10 You will set apart a voluntary rain, O God, for your inheritance: ÷ and it was weakened: But you ÷ indeed .. perfected ÷ it ..:

C He explains what he has already said: “The heavens dripped.” The voluntary rain itself was manna, not the rain that is generally spread everywhere. He set it apart because he did not give this to the other nations. His inheritance was the Hebrew people, which was weakened for a time by not believing in the Lord. He perfected it when he admitted the remaining nations as an addition to faith.

11 Your animals will dwell in it: You prepared in your sweetness for the poor, O God.

C Now he shows from where he perfected the weakened inheritance: from the nations. The nations were animals, emptied of true religion. They will dwell in it, that is, in the Church, when they receive the worship of religion. “You prepared” signifies those predestined. “In your sweetness” means in that sweetness in which God’s poor surpass the wealthiest kings—not in the sweetness of this age, where the saints suffer things that are rather bitter.

12 The Lord will give the word to those evangelizing: great powers.

[Col. 0251B] C “The Lord will give the word to those evangelizing,” that is, to the apostles, who proclaimed his word with venerable confession. “Great powers,” when they were granted the ability to heal crowds of the sick. For the Gospel itself is also known to possess many powers. What is stronger than saving a soul? A The Lord will also give the word to those evangelizing with great miraculous power, or with great strength, according to another translation, which reads: “The Lord will give to those evangelizing the word of great strength or power.”

13 The King of the powers of the beloved + beloved ..: And the beauty of the house shall divide the spoils.

C “King, father of the powers,” that is, of the angels. D Or of the saints of his beloved Son, as in “This is my beloved Son.” [Col. 0251C] C “And of the beauty of the house,” that is, of the beauty of the divine house, namely the Church, the Son is recognized as author when he brought the spoils of the devil—wicked people—into the Church to the faith. H Or when the apostles divided the spoils, that is, people, in the Church. They received them from the idols: one received Achaea, another Cappadocia, as his allotted share from the spoils, and so forth.

The Holy Spirit repeats “beloved” because of the love he has for the Son. For one who loves someone always has that person on his lips.

14 If you sleep among the middle divisions, the wings of a silvered dove: And the rear parts of its back in the pallor of gold. Diapsalma.

C “If you sleep,” that is, if you rest in the commandments of God between the two Testaments. [Col. 0251D] H C The two Testaments are called the divisions. H And the individual books of the Old and New Testament. C The wings signify the speed of virtues, which lead us to that homeland if here we deserve to rest in the law of God. “The silvered dove” signifies the Church, because it possesses the innocence of a dove and shines with the silvery brightness of divine utterances. He says that it is to be adorned with the appearance of gold in that future resurrection. Therefore, if you sleep in this way, the rear parts of its back in the pallor of gold—this must be supplied—will receive you. Hence the Church in this world is compared with silver, but in the final resurrection with gold. Therefore the rear parts of the Church are the Church’s final gifts.

15 When he separates the heavenly kings over it, they will be whitened with snow in Selmon: The mountain of God is a rich mountain.

C A king is so called from ruling; hence “kings” signifies the apostles. D The heavenly Lord separates them when he set Paul apart for the nations (Gal. II) and Peter for the circumcision; they will shine above the snow. C That is, they shine upon the whiteness of snow, those known to govern the Church faithfully. Selmon is interpreted as “shadow,” which here fittingly signifies divine power; it protects us from the heat of vices. “The mountain of God is a rich mountain” is understood as Christ, from whom perpetual and sweet streams descend.

16 A mountain coagulated, a rich mountain: Why do you suspect coagulated mountains?

17 [Col. 0252B] The mountain in which it pleased God to dwell: For indeed the Lord will dwell ÷ to the end ...

C Christ is called a coagulated mountain for the nourishment of little ones, who must be given not solid food but coagulated milk to drink. He is rich because he is exceedingly abundant in his fertility. Above he said that the mountain was to be understood as the Savior; now he says: “Why do you suspect coagulated mountains?” That is, why did you wish to understand the apostles as the mountain? For they are not this coagulated mountain, although you recognize that they too have been taught by God’s grace. Thus the Prophet reproves that interpretation by which someone might have wished to understand the apostles through “mountain,” showing that here only Christ is to be understood by “mountain,” although the apostles too are called coagulated mountains. Therefore he adds:

[Col. 0252C] C “The mountain”—namely, this one—is the mountain in which God was pleased. For Christ alone is the mountain in which the Father was pleased to dwell. Indeed, the Lord will dwell even to the end, namely in the apostles; for he is now speaking of them, that he will dwell in them until the most perfect consummation of his majesty, which is an end without end.

18 The chariot of God is multiplied by ten thousand; thousands of rejoicing ones; the Lord is in them, in Sinai, in the holy place.

C The chariot of God is the joined fellowship united by love. The unanimity of the saints, therefore, is the chariot of God: he sits upon it like a charioteer and guides it by the saving law toward the service of his will. To show that this chariot was attributed not to horses but to human thoughts, he says “multiplied by ten thousand,” which is understood to pertain to innumerable peoples, not horses. “Thousands of rejoicing ones”: this must certainly be understood of the faithful. The Lord is in them, that is, in his saints. “In Sinai, in the holy place.” Sinai is interpreted as “commandment.” He rests there where his commandments are fulfilled.

19 You ascended on high. You took captivity captive. You received gifts among men.

C “You ascended on high.” Christ ascended—certainly he who descended for our sake in order to rescue us. On high, namely above the heavens of heavens. H “You took us captive,” us who were held captive by the devil. C The Lord’s gifts were the great works of the Holy Spirit granted to the apostles. Or, as the Apostle says: “Grace was given to each one of us according to the measure of Christ’s gift” (Eph. IV).

20 Indeed, those who do not believe: That the Lord God should dwell.

C “Indeed, those who do not believe” requires the following to be supplied: “he converted them.” For those who do not believe that he dwells—those who neglect to reach the Lord’s inner chambers so that they may be able to dwell in his house with the faithful—the Lord converts. He mercifully grants his faith to the human race; for this is grace, which is given freely.

21 Blessed be the Lord day by day: God will make the journey of our salvation prosperous. Diapsalma.

C “Blessed be the Lord,” that is, he must be blessed on every day and at every time. “Journey” signifies the course of life, which has now been made prosperous because the world has recognized its Redeemer. H He says “salvations” in the plural, because from him we have as many salvations as we have committed sins; for we are saved by him. Be confident, sinner; do not doubt that you can bless God daily by your works, because God will make your journey prosperous—the God of our salvations. For one who advances daily can bless God daily. Yet it profits nothing to have blessed God yesterday and not today.

22 Our God ÷ is for saving ..: And the Lord + Lord .. are the exits from death.

C “Our God”—let us supply: “has the power to save us.” “The exits from death belong to the Lord,” that is, the hoped-for resurrection of the faithful. Truly, his exit was unique, because he himself came forth from the dead, and from there he will grant that we come forth.

23 Nevertheless God will crush the heads of his enemies: The crown of the hair of those who walk in their sins.

C The heads of the enemies are the Jews, who first persecuted the Church; or the heads of the enemies are the teachers of heretics, who rage even against divinity itself, if such a thing may be said. “The crown of the hair” signifies the cunning of the empty questions of those who abandon what is useful and seek what is unnecessary through detestable disputation, persisting in their sins—such as the Manichaeans and other heretics. For they seek such minute subtleties of accusation that they seem able even to walk over and scrutinize the crowns of hairs themselves.

24 The Lord said, “From Bashan I shall turn”: “I shall turn into the depth of the sea.”

C “The Lord said”—let us ask what he said, because what he promised is of unknown magnitude. Bashan is interpreted as “dryness,” which had possessed the human race through the aridity of sin. But the Lord turned it toward his own greenness when he poured rivers of salvation into it. H And likewise he turned peoples from the depths of vices and sins, from the sea, that is, from the world. A “I shall turn,” therefore, means either “myself” or “my mercy,” into the depth of the sea, that is, of the world or of sins, so that I may free people from there. And I shall turn in such a way that the foot may be dipped, and so forth.

25 [Col. 0254A] So that your foot may be dipped in blood: The tongue of your dogs from the enemies, from him.

C “Let your foot be dipped,” that is, let the action of a good purpose reach as far as the blood of glorious martyrdom. For these dogs do not cease barking on behalf of the Lord; they are called dogs from enemies because they were previously enemies, but afterward defended the Church of God with clamorous barking. “From him,” namely from God, who turned bitterness into sweetness. From him, and from no other, that tongue of dogs formerly made up of enemies became salutary.

26 They saw your processions, O God: The processions of my God, my King, ÷ who is .. in the holy place.

C “They saw your processions,” whether the form of the assumed body or the traces of preaching by which he walked in this world with holy steps. “Of my God, the King,” because he is the King whose title reads: “King of the Jews.” He says “processions” a second time because he specially entered this world. H Or they saw his ascent into heaven in the holy place, namely in the holy man, that is, in Christ; they saw his ascent into heaven.

27 The princes went before, joined with those singing psalms: In the midst of young women beating tambourines. Diapsalma.

C “The princes went before,” that is, all the apostles went before in the holiness of their teaching. He says that a multitude of those singing psalms was joined to them, those who now made the Lord’s praises resound not merely with their voice but with good works. He adds “young women,” that is, those flourishing in the first stage of life, who turned their tambourines—that is, their bodies—to the praises of the Lord. Afflicting themselves with fasts, rejoicing in the affliction of the flesh, and turning the exertions of the body to the Lord’s praises, they brought them to completion in martyrdom.

28 In the churches bless God the Lord, from the fountains of Israel.

C He speaks to the faithful: “In the churches bless God,” not in the perverse assemblies of pagans or heretics, but in the catholic Church, where there is right faith and true confession. “From the fountains,” that is, from Christian teaching, which the apostles poured into the nations. A fountain is so called from “nourishing,” because it restores our bodies weary from labor; or from “pouring,” because it pours out waters. Properly, a fountain is what flows.

29 [Col. 0254D] There is Benjamin, a young man: In an ecstasy of mind.

H C “There is Benjamin”: the Apostle Paul, who descended from the tribe of Benjamin. C He was a young man in an ecstasy of mind when he fell at the Lord’s voice, and the Lord, taking pity, thundered: “Saul, Saul” (Acts IX). He is called a young man from *adolere*, that is, “to grow.” H He is also called a young man because he was the last of all the apostles, converted in the ecstasy that overcame him while he was going to Damascus.

30 The princes of Judah, their leaders: The princes of Zebulun, the princes of Naphtali.

C “The princes of Judah” indicates the Lord, who descended from the tribe of Judah. H The apostles are the princes of Judah, that is, of the Lord Savior, with “Judah” taken as a genitive case. As he said: “Jacob: Judah, your brothers shall praise you” (Gen. XLIX). C “Their leaders,” that is, the leaders of the peoples who had been established in the Church. Zebulun and Naphtali were tribes from which the apostles traced their origin. Judah is interpreted as “confession,” Zebulun as “dwelling-place of strength,” and Naphtali as “my delay”—meanings which you will fittingly apply to the catholic Church if you examine carefully.

31 Command, O God, your strength: Strengthen, O God, what you have worked in us.

C Christ is the strength of the Father; he declares what is being commanded. “Strengthen this, O God,” and so forth. This is certainly a great petition: that God strengthen in us the faith which he has deigned to bestow. For it was the Lord’s work that the blind gentile world, flooded with the light of truth, should be able to recognize the true Lord and Savior. H Strengthen the gift of baptism by the infusion of the Holy Spirit, and grant help so that we may be able to walk and remain in virtues.

32 From your temple in Jerusalem kings offer you gifts.

C From the temple in Jerusalem kings offer gifts—those who live rightly in the Church of God offer the purity of their heart. H The gifts of Christ are the virtues of the saints; and those who rule themselves are kings. The temple, therefore, is the body of any saint, which becomes holy through right living. From it they offer holy works.

33 Rebuke the beasts of the reed: the assembly of bulls [Col. 0255C] among the calves of the peoples: ÷ So that .. they may exclude those who have been tested by silver.

C “Rebuke the beasts,” that is, reprove the proud and fierce who persist in an evil will and waver like a reed. “The council of bulls,” that is, of untamed heretics, who with raised necks lead innocent souls astray. H The calves signify the foolish souls of the people who follow the bulls. He says that they should be reproved so that those who are found proved righteous may not be excluded from the kingdom of God. Yet this explanation of Jerome rests on the Roman translation, which reads “so that they may not be excluded,” as does Cassiodorus’ exposition. But Augustine, explaining our translation, says: “so that they may exclude,” that is, “make those who were hidden appear,” those who have been tested by silver, that is, by the word of God. For, as the Apostle says, heresies must exist so that those who are proved may become manifest among us.

34 Scatter the nations that desire wars: Let ambassadors come from Egypt; Ethiopia will hasten to give its hands to God.

“Scatter the nations,” that is, the heretics who desire wars, namely disputes against the Church. The Prophet also urges the peoples of the nations to offer gifts through ambassadors—that is, those converted from error—namely their souls, cleansed from worldly filth. Thus Ethiopia is urged not to delay handing itself over to God, just as the defeated surrender themselves to victors with weapons cast down, hand to hand, so that they may escape the danger of death. Egypt and Ethiopia signify the world, full of heavy bonds and the darkness of sins. Therefore idolaters will hasten before the Jews to surrender their hands to God.

35 Kingdoms of the earth, sing to God: Sing a psalm to the Lord. Diapsalma.

C “Kingdoms of the earth” signifies the whole human race. “Sing” refers to the purity of the soul; “sing a psalm” refers to works that are acceptable and pleasing to the Lord.

36 ÷ Sing to God .. who ascends above the heaven of heaven: Toward the east.

C For he shows to which God the psalm should be sung: namely, to him who ascended above heaven. The Lord Jesus, who first descended from heaven to free the nature of our weakness, also ascended and sits at the right hand of the Father. “Toward the east” clearly indicates Jerusalem, which is situated in the eastern region. [Col. 0256B] Hence, in the sight of the apostles, the Lord ascended into heaven (Acts I). H Or “toward the east,” namely because he himself is the East, or because through him all rise toward life. It is also reported that the Mount of Olives (Luke XXIV), from which the Lord ascended, lies to the east of Jerusalem.

37 Behold, he will give his voice the voice of strength: Give glory to God over Israel: His magnificence and his strength are in the clouds.

H C He will also give his voice the voice of strength when, on the last day, he says that the human race should rise. What is stronger than recalling ashes to the body? Give glory to God; for whoever gives glory to God makes himself praiseworthy. H “Over Israel,” that is, honor God more than carnal Israel honors him, because they honor him with their lips, but you with your heart. [Col. 0256C] C “Magnificence,” because he always does great things. “Strength,” because his work or effect serves his command. “Clouds”: the apostles and prophets.

38 Wonderful is God in his saints: The God of Israel himself will give strength and power to his people ÷ his .. Blessed be God.

C He is wonderful either in angels or in holy human beings. The Lord will give his faithful the strength of endurance and the strength of faith, so that they may be able to reach eternal rewards. “Blessed be God”: he is able to give what he said above, that is, he who ought always to be blessed by every mouth for his benefits. Just as he always bestows benefits, so may he always receive blessings.

This blessing takes place in many ways. For the one who meditates on the Holy Scriptures blesses God; the one who fulfills his commands blesses him; and the one who confesses to him blesses God.

PRAYER FROM PSALM LXVII

Ruler and Lord, who, granting the righteous a spiritual feast, make them delight in gladness, grant your flock to understand your death and to confess you as the triumphant conqueror of death, seated at the right hand of the Father. You who, with that same Father, etc.

PSALM LXVIII

ARGUMENT OF PSALM LXVIII

C Christ entreats the Father to save him, because he has been hated by the Jews without cause. He asks that the hope of the faithful, placed in his resurrection, not be deceived; and, asking to be freed from the mud of this age, he declares what he knew would befall his enemies.

TT To the end, for those who will be changed, of David.

C “For those who will be changed.” This change signifies the Christian peoples, who, having laid aside the depravity of the old man, have been changed by the gift of new regeneration. The phrase “for those” shows that Christ’s passion took place for them, that is, for all the faithful. “David” has also been added so that the end and the beginning of the title might correspond to the Lord Christ, who is α and ω, that is, the beginning and the end. “To the end,” as has very often been said, signifies Christ; and “David” likewise denotes the same Christ.

1 Save me ÷ make .., O God: for the waters have entered [Col. 0257B] even to my soul.

C His humanity was asking the Father for the help of resurrection. Divine Scripture often testifies that “waters” should be understood as the uprising of the people and the movement of nations, as in: “Perhaps the waters would have swallowed us.” Here too the Jewish people are said to have entered even into the soul of the Savior when, with criminal intent, they presumed to crucify him.

2 I am stuck in the mud of the deep: And there is no substance.

C Human beings became the mire of the deep when they were held liable both for original sin and for daily sins. Through this mire Christ was fixed when the deranged crowd cried out, “Crucify him.” *Lime* is so called as though from “binding earth.” [Col. 0257C] H There is no means of escape unless you, Father, save me, because I am fixed in the ancient sins of this people, raging with criminal cunning.

**3** I have come into the depths of the sea: and the tempest has submerged me.

Here the depth of the sea is the people’s abundant madness. The same tempest is the uprising of the frenzied mob. It submerged the Lord when it brought him to the cross.

**4** I have labored, crying out: my throat has become hoarse; my eyes have failed while I hope in my God.

C He labored, crying out, when he said, “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees.” He also says that his throat is hoarse because the sacrilegious people did not listen at all to his words. Let us understand these eyes as the bodily eyes, which were closed in the death of his passion. He hoped in him—that is, in the Father. Note that *I have labored* is rightly said, signifying an unheard cry. For we say that someone labors when he has not achieved the aim of his cry—that is, when he is refused a hearing.

**5** Those who hate me without cause have become more numerous than the hairs of my head.

C Thus, to show that the number of unbelievers was greater than that of the devoted, he says that the treacherous Jews had multiplied beyond the number of hairs, that is, of believers. We are said to hate without cause when we curse someone without any offense on his part, as the Jews did to Christ.

**6** My enemies who persecute me unjustly have grown strong: what I did not seize, I then repaid.

C The Jews grew strong when they accomplished what they were striving to do. *Unjustly*—indeed, it was unjust that the one who had come to save the Jewish peoples should instead find them as enemies. Christ did not seize sins, for he washed away our offenses; nevertheless, he accepted the cross and paid for us what he had not justly incurred for himself.

**7** O God, you know my folly, and my offenses are not hidden from you.

C When he says, “O God, you know my folly,” he speaks on behalf of the members, for Christ cannot be foolish, since he is recognized as the Wisdom of God. [Col. 0258B] Those who have been converted to faith were formerly foolish, but now are wise in Christ. They are the ones of whom the title said that they would be changed—namely, from the folly of unbelief or sins to the wisdom of Christ. The same must be said of the offenses: they belong not to the head but to the members of Christ.

**8** Let those who wait for you, Lord, not be ashamed because of me: Lord of hosts.

H Christ therefore prays that those who were awaiting his resurrection with great longing may not be ashamed because of him. When he says, “Lord, Lord of hosts,” he shows that nothing is impossible for his omnipotence.

**9** Let those who seek you, O God of Israel, not be put to shame because of me. [Col. 0258C]

H “Let them not be put to shame”—that is, let the hope of believers not be emptied because of my passion; rather, let them recognize that I have come to do your will. C Or: let those who seek you, O God of Israel, no longer endure human insults concerning my sleep.

**10** For on your account I endured reproach; confusion covered my face.

Christ endured reproach when the Jews said, “He casts out demons by Beelzebul” (Matt. XII). H “Confusion covered my face” when the apostles denied him.

**11** I have become a stranger to my brothers and a foreigner to the sons of my mother.

C Christ became a stranger to the Jews when they refused to believe in him; here he calls them his brothers. By “the sons of my mother” he means the same people whom he previously called his brothers. But if they had truly been sons of the mother, the synagogue, they would have received Christ not as a foreigner but as a dearest brother.

**12** For zeal for your house has consumed me, and the reproaches of those who reproached you have fallen upon me.

H Zeal for the house of God consumed him when he drove them from the temple, because they had made it a den of thieves (Matt. XXVII). C They reproached the Father when they said, “These are your gods who brought you out” (Exod. XXXII). H Those who reproach the Father reproach the Son. C He said, “They have fallen upon me,” to show the effect of the death that he accepted through the dignity of the cross. They also reproached the Father when they called Christ the son of Joseph the carpenter and said, “You have a demon” (Matt. XIII); for an insult spoken against the Son returns upon the Father.

**13** I covered my soul with fasting, and it became a reproach to me.

C He covered his soul with fasting because he could not find the faith of human beings, which he greatly hungered for; therefore he surrounded his soul, afflicted by such fasting, as though with a cloak of sadness. The good are always a reproach to the wicked, because they do not assent to their crimes and deliberately disparage those with whom they have no fellowship.

**14** I made sackcloth my garment, and I became a proverb to them. [Col. 0259B]

C Sackcloth signifies sadness and tears, as when the Lord, moved by the weakness of the human race, wept while raising Lazarus (John XI), and the Jews said, “See how he loved him.” He also became a proverb to the Jews when he seemed to teach the carnal people through certain comparisons, as it is read in the Gospel: “Jesus spoke a parable to the crowd.” A parable is a comparison made between naturally unlike things under some likeness. He spoke in this way so that those unable to grasp heavenly things might understand through earthly comparisons.

**15** Those who sat at the gate spoke against me, and ÷ about me .. those who drank wine sang.

[Col. 0259C] C The gate is so called because everything is carried from it. Those who sit at the gate are people who mingle with gatherings of men through assiduous curiosity. Thus he says that his passion was a spectacle to the Jewish people. If understood positively, those who are guided by commendable conduct sing to God. Wine likewise is meant not as drunkenness but spiritually. Those who sang were the ones who drank deeply of saving doctrine through heavenly understanding. Thus Cassiodorus also interprets “sing” of the faithful and the good, as he does what follows. But according to Jerome, the scribes and Pharisees sat at the gate (Matt. XXIII), that is, in judgment; though they possessed the key of knowledge, they neither entered nor allowed others to enter. Filled with the wine of iniquity, they sang together about how they might kill him. H Or they were drunk with wine when, covering his face, they said, “Prophesy to us, Christ: who is it that struck you?” (Luke XXII). [Col. 0259D]

**16** But I direct my prayer to you, Lord: the time of favor, O God.

C That is the time of favor when, through the benefit of his Incarnation, he freed the endangered world from impending destruction. H Or the time of favor is the time of the passion, when Christ prayed while the Jews were crucifying him (Luke XXIII): “Father, do not hold this sin against them,” and so forth. For the redemption of human beings was supremely pleasing to the Father.

**17** In the abundance of your mercy, hear me according to the truth of your salvation.

C For if there had not been an abundance of mercy, we, who were liable to punishment, could never have been redeemed. It was no small mercy that overcame such enormous sins. “Hear me” is spoken by one asking the Father—not according to the nature of divinity, in which he is equal to him, but from the weakness of humanity, in which he is less than the Father.

**18** Rescue me from the mire, that I may not be fixed in it; deliver me from those who hate me and from the depths of the waters.

C Christ asks on behalf of the members that his soul be made alien to muddy desires, that is, to the cravings of this world. “Deliver me from those who hate me”—that is, from the Jews. “From the depth of the waters” refers to that people, which was deep both in its evil plotting and in its turbulent rebellions.

**19** Let not the tempest of the water submerge me, nor the deep swallow me, nor let the pit close its mouth over me. [Col. 0260B]

H “Let it not submerge me”—that is, let this tempest of the passion not hold him in the depth of the infernal abyss. C The deep, then, is sin, which devours the souls of the wicked so that they cannot return to repentance. We say *to close* for *to shut in*. H He therefore asks that the infernal entrance—or the devil—may not close its mouth over him.

C A pit is a depth dug into the earth; Scripture uses it both positively and negatively, but here it is understood negatively.

**20** Hear me, Lord, for your mercy is kind; according to the abundance of your mercies, look upon me. [Col. 0260C]

H He asks this according to human frailty, saying: “You who redeem others through my passion, regard me also with the mercy that goes before.”

**21** Do not turn your face away from your child, for I am troubled; hear me quickly.

C The Lord is frequently called a child because of the purity of his innocence, since early age possesses the benefit of not loving the world’s vices. “Hear me quickly”—H so that I may take back the spirit that I commended into your hands.

**22** Attend to my soul and deliver it; because of my enemies, rescue me.

C “Attend to my soul,” so that it may truly be free when the reconciled divinity looks upon it. He also asked for the swift help of the resurrection because of his enemies, so that those who had despised him crucified might believe in him rising on the third day.

**23** You know my reproach, my confusion, and my reverence.

C The Savior willingly assumed reproach, confusion, and reverence on behalf of the human race, just as he assumed death. He endured none of these things on account of his own guilt; he bore everything for us, so that, as a good teacher, he might mercifully instruct us by the example of his patience when we are placed in such circumstances.

**24** All those who afflict me are before you; my heart awaited reproach and misery.

H “You see, Father, what tribulations they inflict upon me [Col. 0261A] and what mockeries they display.” C His heart awaited reproach when he willingly endured the iniquities of the Jews and the various sufferings he underwent, receiving his passion with benevolence. H Or: the reproach of the passion and misery, that is, the insult of the cross.

**25** I waited for one who would grieve with me, and there was none; and for one who would console me, I found none.

H “I endured”—there was no one among that great multitude of wicked people either to share his sorrows or to become a consoler. C He speaks not of the faithful but of the unbelieving persecutors. Faithful hearers console the teacher when the words of his preaching prosper in them. The stubbornness of the Jews therefore did not console Christ, because it did not receive his words.

**26** They gave gall for my food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink. [Col. 0261B]

C Gall mixed with vinegar was offered to him, truly indicating the bitterness of the Jews’ deed in the drink. He himself said, “I thirst” (John XIX), because he desired to find faith in them; they offered him their exceedingly bitter character, since they were converted by no remorse.

**27** Let their table before them become a snare, a retribution, and a stumbling-block.

C These words are spoken not from a wish to curse but in the manner of one foreknowing what follows. The Lord’s table is the spiritual nourishment of both Testaments, which the Jews first possessed when they kept God’s commandments. But after they began to fast from faith, it was handed over before their eyes to the nations, so that they might grieve more deeply when they themselves saw the happiness taken away. “For a snare”—from the letter by which they tried to bind others, they themselves would fall and remain bound in it. It was a retribution for their evils that the table was taken away and handed over to the nations. And “a stumbling-block,” because, abandoning the author of peace, they stirred up quarrels and wicked pursuits for themselves.

**28** Let their eyes be darkened, so that they may not see, and always bend their backs.

C A fitting punishment is foretold: they would not see in their own Scripture the truest Sun of justice. This happened to them because, weighed down by the excessive burden of their offenses, they always bend their necks toward the earth, stooping, and are given no possibility of looking toward heaven. The back is so called as though from “descending downward.” [Col. 0261D] H Or, “bend them,” so that they may always serve the Romans, or remain under the burden of the law, which no one could bear according to the letter.

**29** Pour out your wrath upon them, and let the fury of your anger seize them.

C When it says, “Pour out,” the greatness of the anger is signified, descending abundantly like a river. Fury seizes them as condemned and terrified, so that they may not be permitted to escape what they are given to endure for their crimes.

**30** Let their dwelling become desolate, ÷ and .. let there be no one who inhabits their tents.

C “Let their dwelling become desolate, and in their tents,” and so forth: it is clear that both of these things happened to the Jews when the city of Jerusalem was destroyed through repeated captivities. The tents—the temple of God and the palace of the king—remained without an inhabitant. Note that he used *dwelling* for private houses, but *inhabitation* for God’s temple, because we dwell there bodily; here, however, we inhabit wherever we frequent a place with the devotion of an attentive mind.

**31** For they persecuted the one whom you struck, and they added to the pain of his wounds.

H Christ speaks these things about himself to the Father, referring to his passion. It is written, “I will strike the shepherd” (Zech. XIII); and in another prophet, speaking in the person of the Father, it is said, “Because of the sin of my people I struck him” (Isa. XIII).

H They persecuted the one who had been struck—that is, the one who had been handed over—and killed him with detestable savagery. [Col. 0262B] H They added to the pain when they persecuted either the Church or the apostles.

**32** Add iniquity to their iniquity, and let them not enter into your righteousness.

C Their first iniquity was that they extinguished the prophets. Iniquity was added to their iniquity because they preferred to crucify the Lord himself. The punishment of sin was added, so that they might not enter into God’s righteousness—that is, so that they might not become participants with Christ in that kingdom of righteousness.

**33** Let them be blotted out of the book of the living, and let them not be written with the righteous.

C He says to the Jews, “Let them be blotted out of the book of the living,” not because they had been written in it, but because they judged themselves to have been written there. For what is written there cannot be erased, because everything has been secured in predestination. “And let them not be written with the righteous”: he denies that this will happen to them because they have not been changed, as the title says, by pious acts of satisfaction.

**34** I am poor and suffering; your salvation, O God, has received me. [Col. 0262D]

C “I am poor”: he claimed this property for himself because no one else endured this poverty and this suffering for the guilt of the whole world. Thus salvation—that is, the Son’s form, in which he is equal to the Father—received humanity when he reconciled the world to the Father. H Or: he was poor and suffering in the passion, but salvation received him in the resurrection.

**35** I will praise the name of God with a song, and I will magnify him with praise.

C Our Head praises the name of God with a song when the faithful are united in the Church in hymn-like exultation. He himself praises and magnifies in us what he knows that we can truly praise.

**36** And it will please God concerning a young bull producing horns and hooves.

C Praise poured out from a pure heart is much more acceptable to God than the slaughter of animals under the old law can be. H Or: it will please God the Father concerning a young bull—that is, Christ—producing horns, that is, giving strength to the Church, and hooves with which he tramples and tears apart the sacrileges of the nations. Christ is called a young bull because he offered himself to the Father. Nor does *concerning* here indicate comparison; it indicates the offered substance. The meaning is that God will be pleased by such a new bull—not a carnal one but a mystical one, not an old foreshadowing but a new fulfillment prefigured.

**37** Let the poor see and rejoice; seek God, and your soul will live.

C Let the poor see that God rejects the offering of animals and seeks a perfectly clean heart; therefore let them rejoice, because the offering is placed in the affection of the mind, where even a poor person can be exceedingly rich. “Seek the Lord”: he urges the poor to seek food for the mind, by which the soul may be nourished. We properly call that “living” which consists in the joy of blessedness.

**38** For the Lord has heard the poor, and he has not despised his prisoners. [Col. 0263B]

C The poor are Christians, who despise the pleasures and riches of this world and choose the poverty of human circumstances so that they may be filled with spiritual banquets. He frees his prisoners from carnal snares, recognizing them as bound to his commands.

**39** Let the heavens and the earth praise him, the sea and all that creeps in them.

C By the mention of heaven, it is understood that all heavenly things should praise him. By the mention of earth, understand earthly things; by the sea, all things that swim. Thus whatever is recognized as part of creation is invited to the praises of the Lord.

**40** For God will save Zion, and the cities of Judah will be built.

[Col. 0263C] C Zion is a small hill joined to the Jerusalem temple, but it grows great through the character of its name; for it signifies the Church. H The cities of Judah are the souls of the saints, which through confession are carried into the holy temple like living stones.

**41** And they will dwell there, and they will acquire it as an inheritance.

C Christians dwell in this Church; they will acquire it as an inheritance when, by God’s mercy, they reach that eternal Jerusalem.

**42** And the offspring of his servants will possess it, and those who love his name will dwell in it.

C Here we must understand “offspring” as perfect work, not a bodily lineage, which will possess the future land that is no longer to be changed by any end. Those who love his name will dwell in it and enjoy perpetual happiness.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM LXVIII

Most gracious Lord, hear us according to the truth of your salvation, so that, rescued from the squalor of sin, we may deserve to be inscribed by a heavenly finger in the book of life. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, etc.

# PSALM LXIX

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM LXIX

C The voice of martyrs and confessors praying to be delivered from the dangers of their persecutors.

[Col. 0264A] **TITLE.** To the end. Of David, for a remembrance, ÷ because the Lord saved him ...

C “The end” and “David” signify Christ. “For a remembrance” signifies the hope of deliverance and the certainty of the future reward that he promised to his saints.

**1** O God, ÷ attend to my help; + Lord, hasten to help me.

C We ask for help when we are subjected to dangers, so that, raised up by such a remedy, we may be able to overcome the calamities of various sufferings. “Attend”—that is, look upon me favorably, because God recognizes everything even when he is not asked. “Hasten” is said as though divine mercy were slow, but help appears slow to the one who hastens to be freed from the disaster of this world.

**2** Let those who seek my soul be confounded and put to shame.

C “Let them be confounded”: the voice of the martyrs demanding the correction of their enemies. A person is confounded when he is disturbed by the deeds of his perversity. A person is put to shame when he recognizes that justice has been violated by his own action and fears to incur punishment for those deeds. The enemies sought the souls of the faithful not for good but to separate them from the body.

**3** Let them be turned backward and put to shame who desire evil for me.

C “Let them be turned backward,” because one who descends from wicked thought follows the Lord’s commands. Let those who desire evil for me receive this retribution, so that they may not persist in their iniquity. O pious saints: even what is thought to be adversity they wished better for their enemies than their enemies wished for themselves while situated in prosperity.

**4** Let those who say to me, “Aha, aha,” be turned back at once in shame.

C He asks that those who are ashamed of their purpose may quickly turn back. “Those who say, ‘Aha, aha’”: *aha* is the speech of one praising, but here it is irony. Or he rebukes those who praise the afflictions and punishments of the martyrs and do not refer to the glory of the author that which has been granted to them through abundant mercy.

**5** Let all who seek you exult and rejoice in you, and let those who love your salvation always say, “Let the Lord be magnified.”

[Col. 0264D] H After the iniquity and conversion of the persecutors, he turns to the glory of the blessed, so that those who seek the Lord through the tears of repentance may exult. C The Lord is magnified in us, although he has nothing in himself by which to grow, when we render praise to God with a pure mind; and our conscience continually increases when we praise Christ worthily. The word *let him be magnified* is also borrowed from human usage: the one who grows through praises and becomes great through a good reputation is said to be magnified.

**6** But I am needy and poor; ÷ I am .. O God, help me.

C He calls those needy and poor who always desire to acquire God’s grace. “O God, help me”—that is, in worldly tribulation, where we struggle against the adversity of vices.

**7** You are my helper and my deliverer; Lord, do not delay.

C My helper in necessities and my deliverer from the disaster of the world. “Do not delay”: it is customary for those in danger to judge help slow, even when it is provided most swiftly. Christ does everything according to measure, but we consider slow what we seek with great longing.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM LXIX

Eternal God of inexhaustible help, hasten to come to the aid of your suppliant household, so that, having overcome the reproaches of evil, we may always be fortified by your assistance. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, etc.

# PSALM LXX

[Col. 0265B]

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM LXX

C The voice of the devoted, who ask to be freed from human iniquities so that they may offer thanks to the Lord more freely.

**TITLE.** ÷ A psalm of David, of the sons of Jonadab and of the first captives ..

C Jonadab is interpreted as “spontaneous to God.” He was a priest of God and commanded his sons to dwell in God’s temple and serve soberly (Jer. XXXV); they are known to have done so, and they are now taken as representing the faithful. “And of the first captives”: these, though frequently admonished, refused to amend themselves; becoming obstinate toward God, they were subjected to the first, second, and third captivity. We are therefore warned by this title to possess the willingness and devotion of the sons of Jonadab, not the obstinacy of the Jews, who deserved to be captives.

**1** In you, Lord, I have hoped; I shall not be put to shame forever. In your righteousness deliver me and rescue me.

H Our mediator therefore prays that this confusion of death may not be prolonged, as it is for other human beings. God’s righteousness is that whoever does his will should pass from death to life; through this righteousness Christ here asks to be rescued. C Or it is the voice of the members of Christ asking that, although they may be put to shame temporarily and beneficially, they may not be put to shame forever. When he says “in your righteousness,” he shows that his own righteousness is insufficient and that he needs mercy. [Col. 0265D] God’s righteousness is to spare the repentant.

**2** Incline your ear to me and save me.

H The ears of the Lord are spoken of when he deigns to hear the humble person asking forgiveness for his sins.

**3** Be for me a protecting God and a fortified place, so that you may save me.

H “Be for me a protecting God,” because apart from him no refuge, fortification, or protection can be provided by anyone. Nor is it called a fortified place in order to suggest a local place, because the Lord is everywhere. C Rather, this place is divine protection.

**4** For you are my strength and my refuge.

C The Lord is called strength in this world, where endurance is also sought; a refuge in that blessedness where no danger is feared any longer.

**5** My God, rescue me from the hand of the sinner, and from the hand of the lawless and wicked person.

C The person who acts against the law is one who, having received the law, acts contrary to the rules of its commandments, as the Jews do. The wicked are the pagans, who are restrained by no law of the Lord but, like beasts, do whatever pleases them. Thus he embraces every sinner under these two categories.

**6** For you are my patience, Lord; Lord, my hope from my youth.

C First we must be tested through patience by God’s grace, and then, by his gift, we will deserve to possess that fruitful hope of which the Apostle says: “Tribulation produces patience, patience produces proven character, and proven character produces hope” (Rom. V). “From my youth” signifies from the time when a person begins to fight against the devil, because that age is directed toward combat. For whenever one comes to him, it is rightly called youth, because then we are established in him with our fullest strength.

**7** In you I have been strengthened from the womb; from my mother’s womb you have been my protector.

C God is our strengthening when we come to him through the gift of faith. He is our protector because he himself protects and defends us against the wickedness of the devil. Here we must understand the womb as that of holy mother Church, where we are first conceived through the rudiments of faith and then regenerated from water and the Holy Spirit.

**8** My song is always of you; I have become like a portent to many, and you are my strong helper.

C “My song is always” signifies both the present world and the future: here we sing to him for deliverance, while there we give thanks for eternal recompense. The faithful person will be a portent in this world when he pursues something other than what the multitude of sinners can love. Sinners seek riches; the faithful, poverty. Sinners seek banquets; the righteous, fasts. Finally, they seek joys, while these seek sorrow. But lest the path of goodness be thought too difficult to walk, he adds, “and you are my strong helper.”

**9** Let my mouth be filled with praise, ÷ so that I may sing your glory .. your greatness all day long.

C For if Christ does not fill our mouth, neither is the tongue moved nor are honorable desires kindled within us. When he says “all day long,” he signifies all time and that one must never cease from the praises of the Lord. The reason he asks for his mouth to be filled is that he may sing God’s glory; without his grace, all praise is unworthy.

**10** Do not cast me away in the time of old age; when my strength fails, do not abandon me.

C The faithful person begs not to be cast away by God in the time of his old age, when the exhausted strength of his body needs more help. He also asks not to be abandoned when the strength of endurance has failed, or when he grows weak beneath the burden of tribulation, while the soul’s strength grows old through repeated tribulations and martyrdoms—for with Christ he can endure everything, but without him nothing.

**11** For my enemies have said to me, and those who guarded my soul have taken counsel together.

C The reason is given why God’s mercy should be stirred to provide help: when they have seized upon weakness, the ardor of those lying in wait is inflamed, since they think it easy to deceive one who, with his strength failing, cannot resist. The enemies’ united gathering is always more savage, and what is not divided is carried more heavily as a single burden. He therefore indicates that the enemies are not insignificant. What sort of counsel they formed he discloses next.

**12** Saying, “God has abandoned him; pursue him and seize him, for there is no one to deliver him.”

C Carnal enemies, when they see a person worn down by repeated calamity, believe that he has been abandoned by God. Those who think divine grace is established only in bodily strength say, “God has abandoned him; pursue him, because he cannot flee, and seize him, because he will not be able to resist us with our overwhelming force.”

**13** O God, do not be far from me; my God, look upon me for my help.

Human weakness thinks that God has made himself distant when help is slow in coming. Therefore he asks that God’s grace not depart from him and prays that, through God’s help, a patience worthy of him may be granted.

**14** Let those who slander my soul be confounded and fail; let those who seek evil for me be covered with confusion and shame.

C “Let them be confounded,” he says, when they see that what you have ordained is not changed. “Let those who slander fail”—that is, those who vainly speak against him. He said “let them be covered,” as though their faces were covered by a veil or by shame; this usually happens to those who condemn their former actions through a better life. Those who seek evil attack minds with wicked flatteries and a hidden wound, while persuading them to preserve the flesh’s health to the destruction of the soul.

**15** But I will always hope, and I will add to all your praise.

C After the correction of sinners has run its course, he turns to his own delight and good: just as they despaired of divine power, so the faithful people says that it will always hope in God. “I will add praise”: when someone says that the Father’s Word made heaven and earth, he praises God with perfect devotion. But when he adds that the Word became incarnate for the salvation of all, he has added a wealth full of praises; thus praise is added upon praise.

**16** My mouth will proclaim your righteousness, your salvation all day long.

C The Savior is the Father’s righteousness, and he is called salvation because from him the salvation of the world proceeds through the glorious Incarnation. “All day long” indicates unbroken time. He therefore shows that he will proclaim the Savior to the nations. H Or it is spoken in the person of Christ the Head, who proclaimed himself in the apostles.

**17** For I have not known worldly learning; I will enter into the power of the Lord. Lord, I will remember your righteousness alone.

C “I have not known worldly learning”—that is, secular knowledge and empty eloquence, defiled by evil deeds. [Col. 0268B] Therefore I will enter into God’s power, that is, into the heavenly Jerusalem. I will remember then, when he separates the lambs from the goats and the wicked from the faithful.

**18** O God, you have taught me from my youth until now; I will proclaim your wonders.

C “You have taught me” may refer either to the divine books or to faith infused from heaven. Youth begins from the time when a person begins to reach divine grace. It was certainly wondrous that the unlearned should be taught, that the treacherous should become devoted, and that the sinner should become most righteous.

**19** And until old age and decrepitude, O God, do not abandon me.

C Among the Greeks these two names are different: they call *old age* “gravity,” while *decrepitude* denotes the bordering age. In Latin they are designated by almost similar names. The faithful people therefore asks not to be abandoned by the Lord either in mature age or in advanced old age. Since he has taught and guarded himself from youth onward, he asks that this continue into old age.

**20** Until I proclaim your arm to every generation that is to come.

C The Father’s arm is the Lord Savior. And lest you think that Christ was to be announced only to those who lived at the time when he deigned to become incarnate for us, he added “that is to come,” so that you might understand that this preaching must be carried out until the end of the world. The Church therefore asks not to be abandoned until the end of the world.

**21** Your power and your righteousness, O God, [I will proclaim] even to the heights—the great things you have done. O God, who is like you?

C “Your power”—here too the wording must be supplied: “until I proclaim your power,” and so forth. Power refers to the grace of the Incarnation. Righteousness refers to the judgment in which Adam was judged, that is, punished with death together with his descendants. “Even to the highest things”: because God, having become human, sits at the Father’s right hand, reigning with him through endless ages. Great deeds are called such because of their greatness: God is strong to punish, as in Adam, and no one is found like him to liberate, as in the case of the thief. God is also recognized as unique in his works; therefore he adds, “Who is like you?” This must be read with wonder.

**22** How many great and evil tribulations you have shown me! Then, turning, you gave me life, and again you brought me up from the abysses of the earth.

C “How many” must be read with wonder, as though referring to innumerable sufferings, because for the present he shows the faithful harsh tribulations. “Many” indicates quantity; “evil,” quality. “Turning”—that is, you caused me to turn, because I had been distorted by the law of sin. It must certainly be understood that “again” is said to indicate the frequent application of Christ’s remedy: through many acts of forgiveness he has brought us out of the abyss, that is, from the depth of sins.

**23** You have multiplied your magnificence, and, turning, you have consoled me.

[Col. 0269B] C He multiplies his magnificence when he deigns to help us through the various causes of our afflictions. “Turning, you have consoled me”: that is, you heal the mind wounded by different illnesses. You heal the mind by revealing yourself and consoling it through the address of the divine Scriptures.

**24** For I too will confess your truth to you with the vessels of the psalm, O God; I will sing to you on the lyre, Holy One of Israel.

C Here that joyful righteous person now confesses that he sings the truth. “With the vessels”—H that is, with the faithful of the Church; and “on the lyre”—C that is, through worthy conduct. The psalm signifies right faith; the lyre, right action. The psalm sends its melody from higher things, the lyre from lower things, up toward heavenly things. Or “the vessels of the psalm” means psalms, as though spiritual jars preserving the Lord’s wine with uncorrupted flavor. H Or he signifies those who, filled with the new wine of evangelical and apostolic teaching, understand Christ as proclaimed in the psalms.

**25** My lips will exult when I sing to you, and so will my soul, which you have redeemed.

C By “lips” he means the mouth of the inner person; for my soul also has its own voice, with which it silently cries out to its Lord. His soul therefore rejoices because it knows that it has been redeemed. And so that you might understand “lips” of the soul, he added, “and my soul,” and so forth.

**26** But my tongue will meditate on your righteousness all day long, when those who seek evil for me have been confounded and put to shame.

C Then the tongue will meditate on the praises of the Lord for all time, when it has received his kingdom in that resurrection. The enemies are confounded and awestruck in two ways: either when they do penance here, or certainly at God’s coming, when they see with their own eyes those things made manifest that they did not believe would happen. Then, therefore, is the time of secure exultation for the saints, when the impious will no longer possess a place of dominion.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM 70

O ruler of the lofty throne, immeasurable, who do not allow those who hope in you to be condemned to eternal confusion: fill, we ask, our lips with your praise, and, as the instiller of good things, continually train us in these meditations. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, etc.

# PSALM 71

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM 71

C The Prophet, foretelling the advent of Christ, says that he is to be worshiped by all kings, because he redeemed the human race from the power of the devil.

**TT. A psalm concerning Solomon.**

C Solomon is interpreted as “peaceful,” and signifies Christ, of whom the Apostle says: “He himself is our peace, who made both one” (Ephesians 2). His own words testify that he is peaceful, for he said: “I give you my peace” (John 14).

### 1. Give the king your judgment, O God: And your justice to the king’s son.

[Col. 0270B] C The Prophet, inflamed with desire, asks the Father to give judgment to the Son, which he knew was to come. For *judgment* is so called as though it were *juris dictio*, “a declaration of right”—that is, what is right is declared in him—or as though it were *juris indicium*, “an indication of right”—that is, what is right is indicated in him. And to show that the request was entirely truthful, he repeated the same thing: “and your justice to the king’s son.” This is what he had said above: “Give the king your judgment,” and this is according to the human nature by which he is lesser than the Father.

### 2. To judge your people in justice: And your poor in judgment.

C He explains why he asked that judgment be given to the Son: namely, so that he might judge the whole world through the Father’s justice. God’s poor are those who, having abandoned worldly pride, have submitted themselves entirely to humility.
