For if a poor man is proud, he is not God’s poor man; and if a wealthy man loves humility, he is not the world’s rich man. The desires of such people must be examined, not their names.

### 3. Let the mountains receive peace for the people: And the hills, justice.

C The mountains signify the apostles and prophets, who receive peace—that is, Christ—to proclaim to the faithful people. By the hills he means the other blessed ones who rightly appear to preach the Lord’s commandments. Christ is called justice because he conquered the devil through justice more than through power, and judges the world in justice.

### 4. He will judge the poor of the people. And he will save the children of the poor: And he will humble the calumniator.

C The poor of the people, that is, the humble in spirit, are the apostles. The children of the poor are the children of the Church, regenerated in Christ through the apostles’ preaching. The calumniator is the devil, humbled by Christ’s power. A calumniator is rightly so called—and is one—who attempts by carefully devised plotting to bring another’s innocence into guilt; and it is certain that the devil has done this from the beginning of the world to its end.

### 5. And he will remain with the sun and before the moon: Throughout generations of generations.

C The sun is read as the Word of the Father, who remains Christ, God and man, one person from two distinct and perfect natures. For the humanity remains always united with the sun, that is, with divinity. He remains before the moon, that is, before the sight of the Church, which always beholds him with the eyes of its heart. For the Church receives light from Christ, as the moon receives it from the sun.

### 6. He descended like rain upon a fleece: And like drops falling upon the earth.

C He explains the mystery of the glorious Nativity. For the Lord of hosts, before whose face the earth trembles and is shaken, willed to descend gently into the virginal womb, without any disturbance, like rain upon a lamb’s fleece. H For the earth of the human body was dry when he came, and could display no fruit of holiness; but he, fertilizing it with the drops of his preaching, filled it with eternal fruits.

### 7. In his days justice will arise and an abundance of peace: Until the moon is taken away.

C “It will arise” refers to the time of the holy Incarnation, when it was to be born through the Virgin’s childbirth. For justice is the Word of the Father. An abundance of peace exists when the Christian religion is spread throughout the whole world. “Until it is taken away,” that is, until the moon is raised up—that is, as long as the Church extends and increases, or until the number of the predestined is complete.

### 8. And he will rule from sea to sea: And from the river to the ends of ÷ the [lacuna] earth.

H The Prophet testifies that Christ the Lord will rule this entire world, acquired and subjected through his Passion. C “From the river,” namely the Jordan, from which the most salutary rule of baptism flowed throughout the whole world. A beautiful brevity, yet it has poured forth immense mysteries for us.

### 9. Before him the Ethiopians will fall: And his enemies will lick the earth.

C We should understand the Ethiopians as sinners, who fall before him when they prostrate themselves in the humility of repentance. His enemies are the Jews, who will lick the earth—that is, they savor earthly things and do not believe in Christ; for each person savors what he licks. He means those Jews who will remain in their stubbornness.

### 10. The kings of Tarshish and the islands will offer gifts: The kings of the Arabs and of Sheba will bring presents.

C The kings of Tarshish, that is, rulers of vices, offer gifts to God when they are shown to serve him with devoted hearts. The islands are those who have expelled from their bodies the vices of the world flowing around them. The kings of the Arabs are those who subject the blandishments of the body to strict discipline. All who offer God the sweeter gifts of the virtues are called Sheba—whence the Sabaeans—more fragrant than the spices that grow in that land.

### 11. And all kings will worship him: All nations will serve him.

C By “all kings” he wished to signify every nation. “All nations” means those divided throughout the whole world both by languages and by regions. There is no nation whose people, in their own portion, do not worship their own Creator. And observe that he says that kings will worship—the very people who were thought worthy of worship.

### 12. For he delivered the poor from the powerful: And the poor man who had no helper.

C He delivered the poor man, that is, the faithful people, from the powerful devil; and the poor man who had no helper, because the human race had turned to the worship of idols. And how could those who did not even possess the understanding of beasts help them?

### 13. He will spare the poor and needy: And he will save the souls of the poor.

C When he says “he will spare,” he indicates all sinful human beings in general; for those who are held in some guilt are spared. They themselves are saved who will possess the kingdom of God.

### 14. He will redeem their souls from usury and iniquity: And their name will be honorable before him.

[Col. 0272B] C Usury takes its name from use, since it continually produces an increase from money that has been lent. Thus, among those living in sins, the usury of evils increases when they receive eternal calamity in return for what they commit in their temporal way of life. Faithful souls are freed from these usuries when they are released through repentance. Their name is honorable—truly a celebrated name—that they should be called Christians and shine forth from their king with the dignity of this title. He also added “before him,” that is, before God, because they will live before him and in his kingdom.

### 15. And he will live, and there will be given to him from the gold of Arabia; and they will worship him continually: All day long they will bless him.

C When he says “and he will live,” he reveals the eternity of Christ, through which the holy Trinity lives—not by created life, but in blessedness. The gold of Arabia is said to be purer than that of other lands, and this rightly refers to wisdom. H For minds shining with holy purity, like Arabian gold with its most beautiful radiance, are offered to him. “And they will worship him” is clearly referred to his humanity, when by his own mouth he established how he should be prayed to. “All day long” indicates the whole span of our life.

### 16. There will be a stronghold in the earth: On the summits of the mountains he will be exalted above Lebanon + its fruit [lacuna]. And they will flourish from the city like the grass of the earth.

C Christ is the stronghold of the mountains. “The summits of the mountains” signifies the excellence of the prophets. H “He will be exalted above” means, namely, the grace of baptism, above all the heights of the world, through which sins are removed. C Therefore the righteous will flourish from the city, that is, from the Church of God, like grass—not in its age compared with the saints, but in its beautiful greenness. And note that he says “from the city they will flourish,” not “in the city,” because, after laboring in this city of the present world, they will flourish in that eternal blessedness when they are crowned.

### 17. Let his name be ÷ blessed [lacuna] forever: His name remains before the sun.

C “Let his name be,” as though he were saying, “Let God be glorified forever,” because he is known to be about to grant eternal glory. He professed that his name remains before every creature—as it is said in the Gospel, “In the beginning was the Word”—so that no one might entertain the blasphemous thought that God’s holy Son was temporal. A name is so called because it makes a thing known. Here he places the sun for all creatures, since it shines more pleasingly upon our sight; and here the philosophers are mocked, because they held the sun to be eternal.

### 18. And in him ÷ all the tribes of the earth will be blessed [lacuna]: All nations will magnify him.

C “In him they will be blessed,” namely, in the Lord Jesus Christ. When he says “they will magnify,” he certainly means “they will praise.” For he cannot otherwise be magnified, since all the highest things serve him.

### 19. Blessed is the Lord, the God of Israel: Who alone does wonders.

C The God of Israel, that is, the God of the whole earth, must always be blessed; he alone does wonders because he needs no assistance. For although angels and many righteous people perform wonders, they do not do so alone, but accomplish them with the Lord’s help. H Yet “God” ought to be placed twice, because the Trinity is also shown in the verse.

### 20. And blessed is the name of his majesty forever: And the whole earth will be filled with his majesty: Let it be, let it be.

H The name is blessed, namely because Christians are named from Christ; this title has filled the whole world with sacred veneration. Here he calls the saints “earth,” because they are to be filled with his splendor. To say “let it be” belongs to one who desires; but to repeat it and say “let it be, let it be” belongs to one who desires exceedingly.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM 71

Invoking your name, almighty God, blessed before all ages, we pray that, once the calumniator has been humbled, you may deign to grant peace and justice to your people. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, etc.

# PSALM 72

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM 72

C The voice of the Prophet wondering why such great prosperity comes to God’s enemies and to the pagans.

“The praises of David, son of Jesse, have ended.” **TT. A psalm of Asaph.**

H “The praises of David, son of Jesse, have ended” belongs to the conclusion of the seventy-first psalm. What follows, “a psalm of Asaph,” is the beginning of the next one. C Asaph is interpreted as “synagogue,” and he speaks throughout the psalm in the figure of the synagogue. “The praises of David have ended,” that is, the sacrifices of cattle and the immolations have ended; now the Church performs the holy sacrifice of Christ’s body and blood.

### 1. How good is the God of Israel to those who are upright in heart!

C God is good to those who are upright in heart, that is, to those who understand his works through devotion. H And they will see him, as the Lord says: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God” (Matthew 5).

### 2. But my feet were almost moved: My steps were nearly poured out.

C The foot signifies the mind’s judgment; he says that it was almost moved when his mind differed from true understanding. The step signifies human actions, which were nearly poured out when they began to differ from true thought.

### 3. Because I was jealous over the wicked, seeing the peace of sinners.

C He gives the reason why his steps seemed to be poured out: because he directed an inappropriate jealousy toward sinners, thinking them happy although it is certain that they are to be punished with eternal condemnation. “The peace,” he says, “of sinners”—which is thought to be peace but truly is not. For when sinners appear wealthy and seem to have nothing in the world to fear, they are thought to possess peace; but that peace is always at odds with conscience, quarrels inwardly, and struggles with itself.

### 4. For there is no regard for their death: And there is strength in their affliction.

C He continues speaking about the prosperity of the wicked: there is no regard for their death, that is, they do not foresee their death and do not turn to reform themselves. “And there is strength” should be understood with a negation: for if they happen to be afflicted by some adversity, sadness does not seem to remain long in them, and therefore they do not immediately have recourse to the true physician.

### 5. They are not in the labor of human beings: And they will not be scourged with other people.

C Here we should understand “human beings” as holy men, who endure labors in this world and suffer various scourges so that, corrected, they may return to the Lord. This does not happen to sinners, which is given for the salvation of the devoted, because in this world they do not receive fitting punishments.

### 6. Therefore pride seized them: They are covered with their iniquity and impiety.

C He says “seized,” that is, pride grasped them as though with certain hands, so that they could not escape. According to another translation he also says “their pride,” because in truth it belongs to the devil to perpetrate this crime. “They are covered with iniquity”—he did not say “they are clothed,” but “covered,” so that we may understand them to be entirely submerged. He added “impiety,” which is proved to be the extreme of all evils; for iniquity can be moderate.

### 7. Their iniquity came forth as though from fatness: They passed into the desire of the heart.

C Iniquity proceeds from fatness when those who, by God’s favor, have been filled with the abundance of the present world sin by speaking against divine things. A sin is fat which is committed more by choice than by necessity. Sinners passed into the desire of the heart, that is, they went astray when they served senseless idols. H Or “into desire,” that is, into lust, so that they might do their own will rather than God’s.

### 8. They thought and spoke wickedness: They spoke iniquity on high.

C It is a twofold evil to think wickedness and then openly produce it as though it were something good. They spoke iniquity on high: this is what their treacherous mind was bringing forth, so that it might utter blasphemous words against its Creator.

### 9. They set their mouth in heaven: And their tongue passed through the earth.

C He sets his mouth in heaven who thinks that Jupiter, Mercury, and the other monstrosities are like God. Their tongue passed through the earth refers to those who speak beyond what is fitting and, although they themselves are frail, consider themselves to possess immortal dignities; or to those who think that God does not punish sins. H Or to those who, through the pride of knowledge, spoke against the Dweller in heaven: they set their mouth in heaven, but their wicked speech was humbled down to the earth and passed away because it had no firm standing.

### 10. Therefore my people will turn here: And full days will be found in them.

C It is fitting to understand here those peoples who once remained in God’s received law but, scattered through various desires, later returned, once corrected, to God’s commandments. The days are full when Christ the Lord deigned to come in the fullness of time. H Or he speaks of any good people who, having seen what has been said, turn more fully to God.

### 11. And they said: How does God know? And is there knowledge in the Most High?

H For sinners are ignorant that God is able to know all things, miserable as they are, because nothing is hidden from his eyes.

### 12. Behold, these are sinners, and they abound in the world: They have obtained riches.

H Behold, these sinners, abounding in the riches of the world, have lost the gifts of paradise. C The fools thought that God did not know what evil they were doing because sinners possessed riches while the righteous did not—as though he had promised such things to the righteous and faithful, rather than having willed that those to whom he promised the kingdoms of heaven should be poor in the world.

### 13. And ÷ I said [lacuna]: Therefore I justified my heart without cause. And I washed my hands among the innocent.

C This is the voice of a wavering and anxious soul concerning the prosperity and abundance of sinners. The justification of the heart is pure thought; the washing of the hands is the work of uprightness. “Cause” is named from “fall,” and may often be good and often bad; this type of cause is called doubtful, because the mind is uncertain what will follow.

### 14. And I was scourged all day: And my chastisement in the mornings?

C The troubled soul continues to speak of its tribulation, which it endured in the present world as though throughout the whole day, as though it had endured it in vain, since it had not obtained the riches of the world despite its good works and tribulations.

### 15. If I said: I will speak thus: Behold, I have rejected the generation of your children.

H The meaning is as though the soul were saying: “While I accuse myself in my morning prayers, if I wish to speak in this way and thus investigate God’s hidden judgments, I begin to become alienated from your children, who through my preaching have become your children.” A Or, “I have rejected the nation of your children,” that is, all the patriarchs, prophets, and saints who said and wrote that you care for human beings and are just in your rewards.

### 16. And I thought in order to understand: This is labor before me.

H Here the Prophet speaks: “I thought,” that is, I examined everything; and although with great labor, I nevertheless thought with the Apostle that “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory” (Romans 8). C Or, at first I thought that I understood, when I was foolishly reasoning; but now, enlightened, I see that it is a great labor to investigate why God permits these things.

### 17. Until I enter the sanctuary of God: ÷ And I understand [lacuna] their end. *Diapsalma.*

C The sanctuary of God is God’s law, which he contemplates so that he might understand the final destiny of sinners, since in the future judgment human felicity will be condemned, although it is shown to flourish here for a time. From this final destiny the question is resolved why God permits the wicked to flourish here and the righteous to be troubled briefly, while in the final age he arranges the reward most fittingly.

### 18. Nevertheless, because of their deceits you set them in place: You cast them down when they were lifted up.

A “Nevertheless, because of their deceits”—that is, because they practice deceit, let them suffer deceit, so that, deceived, they may choose earthly things and abandon eternal ones. This happens when the reprobate are handed over to the desires of their hearts (Romans 1), so that they do what is unfitting. C Their elevation is their downfall: the higher they climb in ruin, the more dangerously they fall. For to be lifted up is already to fall.

### 19. How have they become desolation? Suddenly they failed: They perished because of their iniquity.

C “How?” is the voice of one who wonders how someone who possessed such great happiness could suddenly appear desolate. He also explains the manner of their desolation: they suddenly failed, which signifies the arrival of sudden death. They perished because the wicked fail in this world in such a way that they die again in perpetual ruin.

### 20. Like the dream of those who awaken: Lord, in your city you will reduce their image to nothing.

C By a beautiful comparison he says that the happiness of the wicked is like the dream of those who awaken. For the dead can no longer possess riches, just as those who awaken have lost their pleasures. The image of sinners also perishes when Truth itself, having withdrawn from them, removes itself from them in the heavenly Jerusalem; there the likeness of those who are to be sent into the separation of Gehenna will not be seen.

### 21. For my heart was inflamed: And my kidneys were changed: And I was reduced to nothing and did not know.

H Christ the Lord now speaks: “For my heart was inflamed,” and so forth. The heart of Christ was inflamed to do the Father’s will. His kidneys were changed so that no defilement of human thought might prevail over him. He also says that he was humbled, to show that he was a true human being. He says that he did not know because he does not know sinners and sins—yet he is deceived by no ignorance. C Or the same jealous person speaks, grieving over the temporal abundance of the wicked and stating why their image is reduced to nothing: my heart was inflamed with harmful envy because of them—that is, they cause the good to sin, so that eventually they doubt divine providence—and the kidneys, that is, the constancy of the minds of the good, is moved to seek temporal things in return for their labors, although eternal things are owed to them; and so I was reduced to nothing, that is, to sin, and so forth.

### 22. I became like a beast before you: And I am always with you.

H “I became like a beast” is said by Christ, bearing the sins of the people in the flesh; and “I am always with you,” as in the saying, “I in you and you in me.” C Or he speaks whose feet were almost moved. He rightly calls himself a beast, since carnal rivalry sat upon him like an irrational animal because of the prosperity of the wicked; and yet I am still with you in faith, although a sinner.

### 23. You held my right hand: ÷ And in your will you led me [lacuna]: And with glory you received me.

H The Father held the Son’s right hand when he descended into hell, because the devil’s left hand opposed him on earth. He led him in his will when he rose, and received him in glory when he returned to heaven. C Or, by the right hand the forgiveness of sins, the virtue of faith, and the desire for heavenly things are understood; and by your gracious will, not through my merits, you led me; and in your Incarnation you gloriously received my nature to the Father’s right hand.

### 24. For what is there for me in heaven? And what did I desire from you upon earth?

H “For what is there for me,” that is, in comparison with the heavenly grace that you prepared for your elect, how worthless and fleeting are the things that the human mind desired from you upon earth? Alternatively, I sought no other beside you, either in heaven or on earth; my will was fulfilled by you, so that every knee of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth should bow to me (Philippians 2).

### 25. My flesh and my heart failed: God, the God of my heart, and my portion, God forever.

[Col. 0277D] H The voice of the Church. C “Failed” refers specifically to the heart, from evil thought. “God of the heart” signifies good understanding, when it realizes that it has gone astray. God is the portion of that person who joins himself to his majesty through faith. He promised to cling to him forever; this belongs to the perfect.

### 26. For behold, those who distance themselves from you will perish: You have destroyed everyone who commits fornication away from you.

C They distanced themselves from him who served idols. To commit fornication away from God is to deviate from his chaste love through adulterous thoughts; and whatever is believed against the catholic faith commits fornication with polluted senses.

### 27. But for me, it is good to cling to God: To place my hope in the Lord God.

C He clings to divinity who joins himself to it through true faith and upright conduct, and always places his hope in God, because nothing can be more blessed than to entrust everything to him who knows how to grant what will benefit his worshipers.

### 28. That I may announce all your praises: At the gates of the daughter of Zion.

C Zion is interpreted as “watchtower” or “contemplation.” Its daughter is therefore clearly the catholic Church, where the one who believes with a pure mind truly gives the Lord praise. By “at the gates” he means the very entrance into Christianity, when the people of the new birth are brought to the true faith.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM 72

Make us, Lord, cling continually to you and fix all the strength of our hope in you, so that we may deserve to proclaim your praises at the eternal gates. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, etc.

# PSALM 73

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM 73

C The synagogue laments why its members were handed over to the nations.

**TT. The understanding of Asaph.**

C “Understanding” signifies divine contemplation, which this psalm proclaims. Asaph is interpreted as “assembly,” which is now called the Church.

### 1. Why, O God, have you rejected us forever? Has your anger raged against the sheep of your pasture?

C The people of the Israelites speak throughout the psalm, terrified and asking why the Lord’s sanctuary was destined to suffer such unspeakable devastation. “You have rejected” means “you have cast away,” as though you had made them strangers to your protection. “Forever” signifies the captivity that occurred in the time of Vespasian and Titus. By “sheep” he means the Jewish people.

### 2. Remember your congregation, which you possessed from the beginning.

C The congregation of the Jews grew exceedingly strong when he caused them to increase among the people of Egypt. “From the beginning” refers to the beginning of faith, namely the worship that had been handed down and which the Hebrew people received through Moses.

### 3. You redeemed the rod of your inheritance: Mount Zion, in which you dwelt ÷ in it [lacuna].

C The Jewish people were God’s inheritance as long as they served him with a pure heart. He also called this inheritance a rod because of Moses, his servant, who performed great deeds for the people through the rod. By Mount Zion he signifies the city of Jerusalem, in which the Israelite people dwelt.

### 4. Lift your hands against their pride forever: How greatly the enemy has acted wickedly in the holy place.

C God’s power was therefore raised up against those peoples when his grace changed their pride into humility, leading them to the end—that is, to the Lord Savior. “The enemy” signifies the Roman people, who at that time were renowned worshipers of idols. They acted wickedly in the holy places of Jerusalem when the priests and all the temple ministries were exposed to plunder, and the entire Jewish nation either fell by the sword or was subjected to captivity.

### 5. And those who hate you gloried: In the midst of your solemn feast.

H Sinners glory when, stirred by the devil out of hatred for God, they afflict the holy martyrs with punishments. C Or, the Romans gloried when they committed sacrilege even in God’s temple in Jerusalem.

### 6. They set up their signs ÷ signs [lacuna] and did not understand: As at the exit above the summit.

[Col. 0279B] C The Roman army set up its signs, namely eagles, dragons, and the other standards it customarily used in battle. He adds “signs” so that the repetition itself might move the judge to swift vengeance. “And they did not understand”: if they had understood, they would certainly have sacrificed to you and would not have chosen to return to the worship of demons. And they are said to have set their signs above the summit, in your holy temple, just as statues of rulers are placed in elevated locations in public squares, so that the memory of passersby may be instructed by such sights.

### 7. Like men cutting down a forest of trees with axes, they cut down its doors together: With axe and hatchet they cast ÷ it down [lacuna].

C A door is called *janua* from Janus, because through him, as idolaters thought, access to the year was provided. Therefore, to show that that city had been utterly devastated like a forest, he says that it was cast down by these instruments of the smith. By “its,” understand the temple.

### 8. They burned your sanctuary with fire: On the earth they profaned the dwelling place of your name.

C The grief increases as the calamity of the overthrow grows. That sanctuary was the temple that Solomon built with marvelous construction. This temple, which heavenly power visited, was polluted by the destroyer’s hand, and its summits were brought down to the earth—though they had been built for the praise of the Lord. The prophet’s narrative here increases the atrocity of the deed, so that such savage cutting down and devastation might be confronted by the almighty Judge.

### 9. Their kindred said together in their heart: ÷ Let us cease [lacuna]; let us cause all the feasts of God to cease from the earth.

C Here the words of the enraged Jews are reported. When they saw the holy city and God’s sanctuaries overthrown, they said furiously and foolishly: “Let us cast away God’s law.” And lest they appear to be few, he said, “their kindred together.” The evils enumerated above could have moved the Lord’s mercy, if obstinate pride had not still remained in the Jews. Therefore the calamity was rightly not withdrawn from their impenitent heart, because their mind did not retreat from blasphemies even amid punishments.

### 10. We have not seen our signs; there is now no prophet: And he will no longer know us.

C These are still the words of despairing Jews, saying that they themselves had not seen the signs granted to their fathers amid those calamities, that they had no prophets from whom they might be instructed, and that therefore they had been abandoned by God.

### 11. How long, O God, will the enemy reproach? Will the adversary provoke your name forever?

H These events already narrated happened according to the historical account, when Nebuchadnezzar led the Jews away to Babylon, or when Titus and Vespasian, after setting the city on fire, killed many. C “Provokes” is derived from dogs, whose barking—that is, the letter—makes a great deal of sound. Thus he asks concerning the Jews speaking against the Lord out of impatience: “How long will you allow them to reproach you in this way? How long will you not turn that enemy and adversarial people to a true confession of your praise? Forever,” namely until the end of the world, when that nation will be converted.

### 12. Why do you turn away your hand and your right hand? From the midst of your bosom forever?

Here the Church spiritually implores God the Father concerning his only-begotten Son, who is in the Father’s bosom and is also called the right hand and the hand, asking him not to delay sending him upon the earth. H C He is said to turn away his hand when he allows us to sin. C But he turns his hand when he corrects sins here. H God’s bosom is his sanctuary, his temple, or his protection. C Or, literally: Why do you turn your hand, that is, Christ, away from the bosom—that is, the Jews—until the end of the age, when you will again turn your hand toward your bosom, that is, convert the Jews to Christ?

### 13. But God is our king before the ages: He has worked ÷ salvation [lacuna] in the midst of the earth.

C “Ages” are so called because they roll time back upon themselves. So that no one might think the Lord temporal, he says that he is king before the ages. “In the midst of the earth,” that is, among human beings, who are signified by the name “earth”: with all the peoples looking on, he worked the salvation of the human race. H Or, in Judea, which is called the middle of the earth.

### 14. You established the sea by your power: You crushed the heads of dragons in the waters.

C He now shows that the same one who is Savior is the one who once performed wonders. For he established the liquid abysses of the Red Sea when he fixed them on both sides so that the sea became a dry road for passage. “The heads of dragons” are the pride of demons, which is brought to nothing when the saving fountain of baptism cleanses the souls they had polluted. In this verse he explains the mystery of the miracle just mentioned: the passage through the Red Sea signified baptism and the victory over the devil. Therefore understand “in the waters” as referring to the waters of baptism.

### 15. You crushed the heads of the dragon: You gave him as food to the peoples of Ethiopia.

C The head of the dragon, that is, Satan, was crushed when his pride was cast down from heaven and when vices were extinguished in baptism. We understand the Ethiopians as sinners, who, once converted to the Lord, began to have the devil as food, because Christians consume him through the bites of their reproaches. H Or, so that those whom he had previously devoured through empty persuasions might crush him by the sign of the cross.

### 16. You split open springs and torrents: + You dried up the rivers of Etham [lacuna].

C By “springs” he means sinners, whose evils continually flow; by “torrents,” those who, suddenly stirred up, rush violently through sin against the good. God split these apart when he separated them from the devil’s service. Etham is interpreted as “strong” and signifies the devil, whose rivers—that is, whose teaching—God dried up and reduced to nothing.

### 17. The day is yours, and the night is yours: You fashioned the dawn and the sun.

H “The day is yours,” that is, the brightness of the Gospel; and “the night,” that is, the obscurity of the Law, because both proclaim you. “The dawn” means that human being through whom those sitting in darkness saw the light. He calls the moon the Church, which shines amid the darkness of the world.

### 18. You made all the boundaries of the earth: You sang of summer and spring.

H We call the boundaries of the earth the apostles and prophets. “Spring” signifies the righteous, who flourish in this world through good works; through “summer” they receive the fruit of their labor. C Or, spring signifies confessors, who serve the Lord with even devotion and gentleness. Summer, however, signifies those who burn with the heat of martyrdom.

### 19. Remember this: the enemy reproached the Lord: And the foolish people provoked your name.

H “Remember,” namely, the martyrs who suffer such things out of love for your name. “The enemy” is the devil. “The foolish people” means the gentiles or heretics, who continually provoke the Lord’s name. C Or, the enemy is understood as the people of the Jews, who are rightly called foolish when they wished to make the feasts and law of their God cease from the earth and said such things as would provoke God.

### 20. Do not hand over to beasts the soul that confesses you: And do not forget forever the souls of your poor.

C The holy man supplicates, knowing what was destined to come upon the devoted Jews, that God not hand over the souls of the faithful, lest the devil attain his desires. He calls the devil and his ministers “beasts.” The poor are those who have brought themselves here into the holiest humility so that there they may become rich.

### 21. Look upon your covenant: For the dark places of the earth are filled with houses of iniquity.

C “Look,” he said, “and deign to fulfill what you are known to have promised beforehand,” because those who are filled are sinners immersed in the darkness of ignorance, since they have lost the light of wisdom. They are filled with “the earth of houses of iniquities,” or “the earth with houses of iniquities”—that is, with earthly desires [Col. 0282A] arising from the house of iniquity, namely, an evil conscience; for the houses of iniquities, that is, evil and dark consciences, are filled with earthly desires and wickedness.

22 Do not let the humble one who has been made confused turn away: The poor and needy will praise your name.

C The Prophet asks that the humble, who continually praise God, should not be confounded. Here the poor man is called God’s poor man, while the other is called rich in the world: the former belongs to the eternal King, the latter to fleeting time. This one, God’s poor man, praises God even when he seems to be silent; that proud rich man of the world is mute, although he sings psalms.

23 Arise, O God, judge your cause: Remember your reproaches, those which [Col. 0282B] the fool utters all day long.

H “Arise, O God, judge the cause” on account of these reproaches, which either you endured for us or which the Church now endures. “Remember,” so that those who always reproached you or your people may be confounded in the judgment. C Or, God judges his own cause when, converting those who err, he makes them recognize their error and proclaim what they previously denied. And literally, remember those reproaches mentioned above: “There is no longer a prophet,” and so forth, which were spoken by the foolish people.

24 Do not forget the voices of your enemies: The pride of those who hate you has continually risen.

C “Do not forget,” namely, in everlasting condemnation, the voices of the obstinate. C Or, let those who call upon you amid present afflictions be comforted on account of the voices of their persecutors. C For pride is what the Lord hates spiritually; through it the angel fell, and through it the blessedness of the first man departed. We appropriately understand this of the Romans, who, lifted up by pride, raised their standards over the temple of God and burned it itself.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM 73

Creator of all the elements, Lord, eternal King before the ages, remember your flock, which you redeemed by the pouring out of your own blood, and graciously hear the voices of all who seek you. Through our Lord Jesus, etc.

# PSALM 74

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM 74

[Col. 0282D]

C The voice of the faithful Jews, who profess that they recount Christ’s miracles, and concerning Christ’s future judgment.

**Title.** “To the end, do not corrupt. A psalm of Asaph, a song.”

C Asaph is interpreted as “synagogue,” that is, the congregation which believed from among the Jews, not the one that remained obstinate. Here this Asaph admonishes the Jewish people not to corrupt their faith “to the end,” that is, in Christ. We have said that the psalm is a song when we discern present realities through spiritual contemplation.

1 [Col. 0283A] We will confess to you, O God, we will confess: And we will call upon your name.

2 We will recount your wonders: When I receive the appointed time, I will judge justly.

C The Jewish people burst forth into a voice of confession. It follows again: “We will confess.” This repetition testifies to the firmness of the promise. For confession frequently made to God does not bring danger but salvation, although confessing crimes even once before an earthly judge often brings death. To confess also means to profess something with the confession of many.

C The voice of the faithful has been introduced, those who deserve to serve God with a pure mind. Then there is a change of person; God speaks, promising that “when I receive the appointed time”—namely, through that by which he became human—he will judge with justice, [Col. 0283B] so that mortal hearts, pierced with remorse before the time of judgment, might beg to be absolved, lest they endure the harsh sentence of the Judge in the future. H He is not now a judge, but he will be. For if he were now a judge, sinners would not rise up, and they would not obtain riches in this age.

3 The earth melted, and all who dwell in it: I established its pillars. Selah.

C The Lord says that before his coming the earth—that is, the human race—was melted, meaning that it had dissolved from the solidity of truth into the corruption of sins by serving abominable idols. He calls the apostles “pillars,” because they were strengthened in the resurrection of Christ, since they wavered during his Passion.

4 I said to the wicked: Do not act wickedly: [Col. 0283C] And to sinners: Do not lift up the horn.

C Through the prophets and apostles he spoke the admonitions of truth, so that criminals would not act evilly. Sinners are those who, presuming upon their own righteousness and exalting themselves in pride, disdain submitting their necks to the yoke of Christ. Or they lift up the horn when they excuse themselves for their sins, sometimes accusing the devil, sometimes blaming another as the instigator.

5 Do not lift your horn on high: ÷ Do not .. speak iniquity against God.

C He too lifts up his horn on high who murmurs against God with iniquity conceived in his heart. Someone speaks iniquity against God when he considers himself so constituted by God that he could in no way avoid sins, saying that he came to some crime not through his own fault but through necessity, although he sinned by his own will.

6 For neither from the east nor from the west nor from the desert mountains: For God is judge.

C “Neither from the east,” and so forth; “the Lord is absent” must be supplied, as though he could not recognize you. By “east” he means people made conspicuous by divine radiance; by “west,” sinners from whom the light of truth is still hidden; by “desert mountains,” false preachers, that is, heretics. Therefore, since God is shown to be present with all these as knower and righteous judge, no one should presume to do what could condemn him in the future judgment.

7 He humbles this one and exalts that one: For the cup is in the Lord’s hand, full of unmixed wine.

C He certainly humbles the proud and exalts the humble, because the former trusts in himself, while the latter trusts in God. H The cup is retribution; it is full of unmixed wine, that is, truth, because on the day of judgment each person will be given to drink what he deserves. Yet it is mixed with mercy and judgment.

8 And he inclined from this ÷ to this .. Yet its dregs have not been emptied: All the sinners of the earth will drink.

C Here he signifies two peoples, the Jews and the Gentiles, because he took it from the mouth of the unbelieving Jews. He inclined it to be drunk by the converted peoples of the Gentiles. The dregs here must not be understood as filth, but as the final faith, when the Jews, together with the other sinners, will have deserved to believe; yet many sinners will remain in their obstinacy.

9 But I will announce forever: I will sing to the God of Jacob.

C The voice of the Church glorifying God because of the future judgment. The Church sings to the God of Jacob when it sings psalms.

10 And I will shatter all the horns of sinners: And the horns of the righteous will be exalted.

C The horns of sinners are the kingdoms of the proud, together with all their power and boasting, which will be crushed in the future judgment. The horns of the righteous, however, are the gifts of the future judgment; they are truly raised firmly, because they will remain in eternal beauty.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM 74

[Col. 0284C]

Good Shepherd, who for the redemption of mortal sheep drained the cup of suffering, we suppliantly call upon your name, so that you may firmly establish us upon the pillars of wisdom through the sanctification of the sevenfold Spirit. You who are with the Father, etc.

# PSALM 75

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM 75

C The voice of the Church, exhorting the faithful soul to offer gifts to the powerful God.

**Title.** “To the end, with praises, a psalm of Asaph, a song ÷ for the Assyrians ...”

C The words of this title are known, but we shall speak of the Assyrians. They are interpreted as “those who direct”; they designate the faithful Jews, who, already instructed in the rules of faith, strive to walk along straight paths. Asaph addresses these people, singing God’s praise wondrously.

1 God is known in Judea: His name is great in Israel.

C Judea is interpreted as “confessing”—believing in that King who came through the virgin Mary from the tribe of Judah. Israel is interpreted as “a man seeing God.” He speaks to those who, illumined by true light, have been separated from the iniquity of the faithless and confess the Lord’s name with a pure heart—not to those who remain in faithlessness, Jews and Israelites in name alone.

2 And his place was made in peace: And his dwelling is in Zion.

C That person is shown to have peace with the Lord who follows the commands of the one who rules; for true peace is to be in harmony with one’s own character and to wage war against vices. Zion is interpreted as “watchtower,” through which God is seen by the hearts of the faithful. Indeed, the person who has deserved to behold him with a sincere mind himself becomes Mount Zion.

3 There he broke the powers of bows: Shield and sword and war. Selah.

C “There,” namely in that peace where the Lord deigns to dwell—the things mentioned here are broken. The power of bows signifies the malice of the proud. The shield here signifies conflicts undertaken through the devil’s deceit; the sword signifies manifest wounds; war is shown to be contrary to peace. All these things will be broken when the author of peace comes.

4 [Col. 0285B] You illumine wondrously from the everlasting mountains: The ÷ all .. foolish in heart were troubled.

C He says that the Lord illumines through the everlasting mountains because through the prophets and apostles he granted the Christian people illumination by their preaching. These mountains are called everlasting because they stand in perpetual and unchangeable sublimity. He calls the foolish troubled because, having withdrawn from the true light, they followed the world’s dark desires; from the same source by which the righteous were illumined, these people were troubled.

5 They slept their sleep: and all the men of riches found nothing in their hands.

C They slept as though, while awake, they were dreaming about good works. In the future those who leave behind here the riches that they ought to have distributed for their own sake will be found to have had nothing in their hands.

6 At your rebuke, O God of Jacob: Those who mounted horses slumbered.

C He says that the unbelievers slumbered because they refused to hear the holy admonitions of the Lord, who is the God of Jacob. They mounted horses because, lifted up in pride, they wander through the allurements of this world as though they were riding swift horses.

7 You are terrifying, and who will resist you? From that time onward, your anger.

He says that Christ is terrifying in that judgment when he will appear on the seat of his majesty. There no one among the rejected can resist; there they recognize that the Lord condemns every wicked deed. “From that time onward” means at the time of judgment, which is also called the day of wrath (Zeph. 1), because nothing will any longer be concealed through patience, when vengeance is finally taken upon the impious.

8 You caused judgment to be heard from heaven: The earth trembled and was still.

God the Father caused judgment to be heard from heaven when he sent his Son into the world for the redemption of the human race. The earth trembled because sinners, terrified at his coming, repented of their sins and thereafter ceased from wicked deeds. C Or, at the final judgment Christ will come from heaven and cause judgment to be heard—that is, he will make it heard.

9 [Col. 0286A] When God arose for judgment: To save all the meek of the earth. ÷ Selah ...

C “To arise” is taken from the judges of the world: when they have decided something with severity, they are said to arise, because they appear, moved to avenge the crimes committed. The meek of the earth are those who are inflamed by none of this world’s vices.

10 For the thought of man will confess to you: And the remnants of thought will keep a feast for you.

C Our thought confesses to the Lord when it condemns past sins through satisfaction. The remnants of thoughts are, after tears have been poured out, the remembered destruction and lamentation of past crimes. These keep a feast for God when the person feels that he has been freed by him from that destruction of sins.

11 Vow and repay to the Lord your God: All who surround him will offer gifts.

12 To the Terrible One, and to him who takes away the spirit of princes; to the Terrible One among the kings of the earth.

C There are certain things which, unless we vow them, we are bound to fulfill by no law—for example, to preserve virginity, to seek the desert, or to fast daily. But once they have been promised, he commands that they be repaid to God. The matter is carried out “in the circuit” when the faithful offer gifts at the sacred altars—that is, they offer them by going around the altar.

C God is called terrifying not to the rejected—for if they feared God, they would amend their lives—but to the devoted he is both terrifying and sweet. “He who takes away the spirit,” namely the spirit of pride or swelling, takes it away from those kings who have deserved, by God’s gift, to rule and govern their own body; that is, “vow and repay” applies to those from whom he removes the spirit of princes, namely pride, giving those exalted princes a humble spirit, so that thereafter they tremble at God’s words and truly become kings of the earth—that is, of their own body and of others. Or he is also terrifying to the rejected in the judgment, when he will be sweet to the faithful.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM 75

Grant fulfillment to thoughts that confess you, O terrifying God, so that, illumined by the everlasting mountains, while we receive the glory of your resurrection, we may escape the disgrace of the future judgment. You who are with the Father, etc.

# PSALM 76

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM 76

[Col. 0286D]

C This psalm concerns the congregation of the faithful, which, leaping over the vices of this age, reaches that end to which nothing can be found comparable.

**Title.** “To the end, for Jeduthun ÷ a psalm of Asaph ...”

1 With my voice I cried to the Lord: With my voice to God, and he attended to me.

C That person cries to God alone who asks him for such things as he promises to give the faithful. For one who asks him for transitory things is not known to cry out to God, although he may seem to seek him. “And he attended to me”: for his attending means to rescue and to bestow such great things as an eager petitioner cannot manage to request.

2 [Col. 0287A] In the day of my tribulation I sought God, with my hands by night against him: And I was not deceived.

H This statement is as though he were saying: “I have lost my son, I have become poor, my house has been burned; I do not seek what I lost, but I seek the Lord. If I find him, I have everything in him.” C By “hands” he means good works; by “night” he signifies the life of this world. Truly, the person is not deceived to whom God’s promises are fulfilled. H Or, “I was not deceived by the devil’s ambushes.” And observe: this man seeks God with his hands in tribulation; we, when we are afflicted, think and complain of nothing except the affliction itself.

3 My soul refused to be consoled; I remembered God and was delighted: [Col. 0287B] And I was exercised, and my spirit failed. Selah.

C It refused to be consoled in the present by transitory and passing things, so that it might receive eternal consolation in the future. “I was delighted.” For when we remember God, we are filled with the gift of every sweetness. This happens to those who do not wish to be consoled by transitory things. He says that he was exercised in that divine contemplation: as he considered with what wisdom God disposes all things, his spirit failed in that very consideration, unable to comprehend the innumerable and immense works of God.

4 My eyes anticipated the watches: I was troubled and did not speak.

[Col. 0287C] H “They anticipated,” that is, before anyone else kept watch, I was keeping watch. Therefore a monk who does not keep vigil cannot say this verse. “I was troubled,” as a human being; “I did not speak,” as befits a Christian. I had anger in my heart, but I did not express it in words. H Or, “I was troubled” by the remembrance of sinners, for whom I suffer in compassion. And therefore he adds the cause of his distress:

5 I considered the ancient days and kept the everlasting years ÷ in mind ...

C “I considered the ancient days,” namely those of Adam, when the human race was held subject to sins. And “the everlasting years,” because just as these ancient days in which we are pass away in an instant, so future days and [Col. 0287D] years abide in heaven with enduring permanence. In these, death rules; in those, perpetual life reigns.

6 And I meditated by night with my heart: ÷ And .. I was exercised and I scraped out my spirit.

C He also meditates with his heart who makes his soul consider something rationally. We are exercised when we burn with innumerable thoughts. H “I scraped out my spirit,” that is, I dug it like a field, so that I might plant there the seed of God’s teaching. Jerome likewise says in his letter to Sunnia and Fretela that it should be said and written, namely *scobebam*—“I scraped out”—that is, “I searched out and dug,” like someone looking for herbs in a field.

7 Will God cast off forever: ÷ And .. will he not add that he may be more favorable still?

C “Will he cast off,” namely the human race, so that he will not help it through the mercy of his coming? This “will” is not denying but affirming; for he will add, that is, he will grant that the human race may be pleasing to him. “Still” expresses expectation, not grief. H This was the whole of my thought: God made man and promised him eternal life; how, then, was he expelled from paradise, so that he would not add to it and make him pleasing to himself again?

8 Or will he cut off his mercy forever, from generation to generation?

C God’s mercy is that he deigned to be born from the Virgin Mary. The Lord did not cut this mercy off from one generation—namely the Jewish generation—to another, the generation of the Gentiles. H That is, he cut it off neither from the Jews nor from the Gentiles. C “Forever” signifies the fullness of time, of which John says: “Little children, it is the last hour” (John 2).

9 Or will God forget to show mercy? Or will he restrain his mercies in his anger? Selah.

C From this he declared that God would show mercy, because he foresaw his coming. God will not restrain his mercy in anger; rather, in his mercy he will withhold himself from anger.

10 I said: Now I have begun: This is the change of the right hand of the Most High.

[Col. 0288C] C He also says, “Now I have begun,” namely to understand or to perceive. He explains what it is that has now begun: I have begun to understand that the holy change of the Lord’s right hand—that is, Christ—customarily works in us, so that, changed from the condition of the world, we may deserve to be called his children. H Or, “this change” means that he mercifully shows compassion to the one justly lost.

11 I remembered the works of the Lord: For I will remember your wonders from the beginning.

H I remembered the works of God that he had done for Moses or other saints. C “I will remember from the beginning” what he did when he made Adam in his own image; then how he accepted the offering of righteous Abel; how in Noah’s ark he saved animals of various kinds as a mystery of the Church; how he displayed a type of his coming in the offering of Isaac through heavenly compassion; [Col. 0288D] and similar things which were wondrous from the beginning, in all of which, nevertheless, God’s mercy toward humanity is revealed.

12 And I will meditate on all your works: And I will exercise myself in your inventions.

H All my thought concerns your virtues, and I will exercise myself— C that is, I will devote myself with humble devotion to your saving commandments—or I will meditate on all your works, that is, on the divine Scriptures.

13 O God, your way is in the Holy One: What god is great like ÷ our .. God? You are the God who works wonders.

14 You made your power known among the peoples: You redeemed your people by ÷ your ... arm [Col. 0289A]—the sons of Jacob and Joseph. Selah.

C “Holy” is Christ the Lord; he himself is also the way. He is rightly called the Father’s way, because through him we receive the means by which the Trinity is worshiped. For he says: “Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28). H Gods are called holy according to grace, but you are God by nature, and you alone also work wonders daily by nature. God works wonders: a thief yesterday, a Christian today; another yesterday a fornicator, today continent; yesterday you stole what belonged to others, today you offer what is yours.

C “You made known,” namely when you sent the Lord the Savior into this world, who is the power of God and the wisdom of God (1 Cor. 1). He was known only bodily to the unbelieving peoples, but to the faithful also in his divinity, as he truly is: “Blessed are the pure in heart.” H C “He redeemed by his arm,” that is, by the Son. “The sons of Jacob,” the Jewish people; “and Joseph,” the Gentile people, who preferred to believe in him with a pure heart. Joseph is interpreted as “increase.” Thus the Jews went before, and we have been joined to the faithful.

15 The waters saw you, O God, the waters saw you and were afraid: And the abysses were troubled.

“The waters saw you,” that is, the peoples of the Gentiles feared by believing; “the abysses were troubled,” C that is, the dark human hearts, which were converted through this salutary disturbance. H Or, the waters are pure minds and souls [Col. 0289C] and they feared; but their fear did not arise from hatred, but from faith.

16 The multitude of the sound of the waters: The clouds gave forth a voice.

C There is a multitude of the sound of the waters when sweet psalmody is raised to the Lord, when guilt is washed away by groans and tears. The cloud signifies the preachers who gave forth a voice when they proclaimed God’s commandments throughout the whole world. From this proclamation the sound of these waters arises.

17 For your arrows pass through: The voice of your thunder is in the wheel.

C Here he calls the evangelists “arrows,” because through their preaching they pierced the devoted medicinally to the innermost parts of the heart—not with an inflicted wound, but with salvation. [Col. 0289D] By “the wheel” he means the whole world, which is enclosed in the round shape of a wheel, where the voice of preaching is scattered. But what those clouds and thunders accomplished is stated next.

18 Your flashes illuminated the world: The earth was moved and trembled.

C “Your flashes illuminated,” that is, the divine commandments radiating with the light of truth. He calls those people moved and terrified who, faithfully hearing the word of God, through Christ’s gift reached a zeal for amendment.

19 Your way is in the sea, and your paths in many waters: And your footsteps will not be known.

C “In the sea,” that is, in human thoughts, which fluctuate like the sea, where Christ has his ways when by his grace he has subjected them to himself. “Many waters” means the multitude of peoples who have been converted, among whom are God’s paths when he deigns to come to them. “Your footsteps will not be known” signifies the bodily presence which the Jewish people did not wish to acknowledge.

20 You led your people like sheep by the hand of Moses and Aaron.

C The Hebrew peoples were led by the hand of Moses and Aaron, that is, by the work they performed through the novelty of various miracles. And it says “like sheep,” not simply “sheep,” because by not believing they became goats. Moses is interpreted as “taken up”; Aaron as “mountain of strength.” Their names express the virtues they performed.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM 76

[Col. 0290B]

Immense worker of all wonders, who once, with the waters standing still at your sight, afterward changed them into wine: we humbly implore you, that, having received the voice of our cry, you may grant us mercy—which you will never forget. You who are with the Father and the Son, etc.

# PSALM 77

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM 77

C The voice of the prophet to the Jews, enumerating how many gifts God granted them or wonders he displayed, and what kind of vengeance came upon them.

**Title.** “An instruction of Asaph.”

C Asaph, as has been said, signifies “synagogue” in the Hebrew language and “collection” in Latin. But because he prefixed “instruction,” he made clear that the faithful synagogue is able to speak here.

1 Attend, my people, to my law: Incline your ear to the words of my mouth.

C At the beginning God speaks, the one who gave the law to the Hebrews through Moses. The person attends to what is heard who perceives the things said with a devoted mind. “My people” refers to those who obeyed his commandments. A person is recognized as inclining his ear who wishes to receive what he has heard with his whole heart. Thus, just as by saying “attend” he commands the application of understanding, so by saying “incline your ear” he commands an attitude of willingness to hear. H Or these and the words of the following verse are Christ’s.

2 [Col. 0290D] I will open my mouth in parables: I will speak propositions from the beginning.

C *Parabola* is the Greek word for “likeness”: it is when we indicate what we wish to be understood through certain comparisons. “Propositions” signifies obscure and hidden questions, which must be solved by means of argument. When he says “from the beginning,” understand this as referring to the Old Testament.

3 How many things we have heard and known ÷ them .. And our fathers have told us.

H “How many things we have heard”: this pertains to the apostles. “And we have known them”: from the patriarchs and prophets. C He calls Moses and the other prophets “their fathers,” for they spoke many things concerning the Lord’s coming.

4 [Col. 0291A] They were not hidden from their children: In another generation.

C “They were not hidden,” namely from the spiritual children who were their imitators. “Another generation” signifies not the congregation of the Hebrews but that of the Gentiles.

5 Telling the praises of the Lord and his powers: And his wonders which he did.

C To recount the Lord’s works is to praise him. When his deeds are recounted, his glory is always increased. By “powers” he means the deliverances he performed for the people when he freed them from Pharaoh; by “wonders,” that he fed them with manna in the desert and, with a small and very slight effort, subjected the most powerful nations to them.

6 And he raised up a testimony in Jacob: [Col. 0291B] And he established a law in Israel.

C He says that a testimony was raised up in Jacob when, wrestling with the angel, he was touched on one thigh and limped (Gen. 32). This signifies the Israelite people: partly standing firm in the strength of faith, partly departing from their salvation. He established a law in Israel to remind them to be devoted to their Lord. This is what he said above: “I will open my mouth in parables and speak propositions,” because this verse speaks figuratively.

7 How many things he commanded our fathers to make known to their children: So that another generation might know.

C This verse signifies that God’s commandments were transmitted through human generations, so that no one might think that what was given to one person was not granted to all. Here “another generation” signifies outsiders, not relatives, and the Gentiles, not the Jews.

8 Children who will be born and rise up: And they will tell their children.

C The Christian children are those who handed on holy teachings to their descendants for the salvation of souls.

9 So that they may place their hope in God: and not forget the works of God: And may seek out his commandments.

C He admonishes them that their descendants should not place their hope in the law, which punishes, but in the grace that has been granted, which liberates; and that they should not forget God’s works— H that is, despise them, as the faithless Jews did— [Col. 0291D] but should seek his commandments as Christians.

10 Lest they become like their fathers: A crooked and exasperating generation.

H Here the faithlessness of the Jews is noted: they were always murmuring against the Lord in the desert. C They are called crooked because they refused to receive the truth. H “Exasperating,” because they blasphemed against the Lord, provoking him to vengeance.

11 A generation that did not direct its heart: And its spirit was not believed with God.

H Israel is perverse to this day, and its spirit has not been directed with God. Since it did not receive the Son, therefore it does not receive the Holy Spirit. C A person directs his heart who corrects himself according to the divine commands. A His spirit is believed to be with God who believes in God.

12 The sons of Ephraim, stretching and shooting the bow: Turned back on the day of battle.

C Ephrem, or Ephraim, is interpreted as “fruitful.” He was Joseph’s younger son, whom his grandfather blessed in the first place. His own sons, growing through their father’s blessing (Gen. 48), fell away from the fruit of faith. They “stretched the bow” when, at Moses’ admonition, they said: “Whatever God has spoken, we will do.” But they “turned back” when they said to Aaron: “Make gods for us that we may worship” (Gen. 32).

13 They did not keep God’s covenant. And they did not wish to walk in his law.

C They did not keep God’s covenant; therefore they turned back on the day of battle.

14 And they forgot his benefits: And his wonders which he showed them.

C The Jews forgot God’s benefits and all his signs.

15 Before their fathers he performed wonders in the land of Egypt: In the field of Tanis.

C He recounts the miracles performed before their fathers, namely Moses, Aaron, and the other elders, so that they ought to have believed more firmly in manifest events. For this reason he also named the province and the place where these things occurred. The field of Tanis signifies the humble commandment that Christ, placed on earth, taught when he said: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble” (Matt. 11).

16 [Col. 0292C] He split the sea and led them through: And he made the waters stand as if in a wineskin.

C The sea was split when it remained on two sides, so that it seemed not so much a sea as a rock cut open. He led them to the promised land. He made the waters stand—that is, he caused the wave to stand motionless—as though it had been enclosed in vessels.

17 And he led them by a cloud during the day: And throughout the whole night by the illumination of fire.

C The cloud of the day mystically signifies the Lord Christ, because he himself is also the true day; nevertheless, he was concealed from the faithless by the cloud of his flesh. “And throughout the whole night” signifies the Christians, whom he guards during the night of this age by the brightness of his light.

18 He split the rock in the desert: [Col. 0292D] And he gave them water as though from a great abyss.

C The rock was split in the desert when he struck it and waters flowed. This was done to show that all creatures obey his commands: first the waters, here the rock. He said “he gave them water” so that he might seem to signify animals more than human beings, who refused to give thanks for such great benefits. By “a great abyss” he indicated the abundance of the very ample wave, which flowed forth so copiously as though from the abyss of the sea.

19 And he brought water from the rock: And he led waters down like rivers.

H Here the rock signifies Christ, struck on the wood of the cross by a lance; from his side flowed the sacrament of baptism.

20 [Col. 0293A] And they added still to sin against him: In anger they provoked the Most High in a waterless place.

C “They added,” that is, they proceeded further, so that amid so many miracles they would not believe. He called unbelief “sinning”; it is clearly a very wicked offense in those who, after receiving benefits, did not return thanks. “They provoked the Most High in anger”: although watered by so many miracles, they did not wish to believe in him because of the barrenness of their faithlessness. Thus “in a waterless place,” or “in a dry place,” signifies not so much the location where the miracles occurred as their state of mind.

21 And they tested God in their hearts: So that they might ask for food for their souls.

C “They tested”: we call it testing when someone asks for something through deceitful words, so that simplicity may appear in the words while there is malice in the heart. Thus they slyly requested food for their souls—not spiritual food, but bodily food.

22 And they spoke evilly of God: They said, “Can God perhaps prepare a table in the desert?”

C They certainly spoke evilly, because they falsely refused to believe that the one who gives food to all flesh could prepare a table in the desert. But this table signifies the Passion, in which we who hunger are refreshed.

23 For he struck the rock and waters flowed: And torrents overflowed.

H The waters mystically signify the gift of the Holy Spirit and the streams of divine preaching, brought forth from the rock, that is, from Christ. Or, the water signifies the apostles, and the torrents the other teachers of the Church; through their preaching we quench our thirst for the word of God. Or, when Christ, who is the rock, was struck on account of our sins, the waters of baptism and martyrdom flowed.

24 Can he also give bread: Or prepare a table for his people?

H The distrust of the Jewish people adds: “Can he also give bread,” and so forth. They even denied that the bread of heaven could be given to them, which is Christ, saying: “How can this man give us his flesh to eat?” (John 6).

25 Therefore the Lord heard and delayed: And fire was kindled in Jacob, and anger rose up in Israel.

C For God knows the thoughts of murmuring even while the tongue is silent. Yet he delayed vengeance so that, if he took it immediately, he would not be believed able to satisfy those who murmured. Again he delayed vengeance in order to display patience. “And fire was kindled in Jacob.” Jacob, who is interpreted as “supplanter,” signifies the Gentiles, who supplanted the Jews: when the former entered, the latter were expelled. In the Gentiles the fire of charity was kindled; in Israel, that is, in the Jewish people, formidable anger rose up.

26 Because they did not believe in ÷ God .. Nor did they hope in his salvation.

C He says that they did not believe in their God, to show that they were obstinate. Nor did they hope in his salvation, that is, in the Lord the Savior.

27 [Col. 0294A] And he commanded the clouds from above: And he opened the doors of heaven.

C Although what follows may appear to have happened according to the historical account, it must nevertheless be referred to Christ. Thus the clouds were commanded—that is, the preachers—so that through the doors of heaven, namely the sacred Scriptures, glorious preaching might announce the Savior’s coming.

28 And he rained manna upon them for food: And he gave them the bread of heaven.

C Manna is interpreted as “What is this?” We aptly apply this to the holy communion of Christ’s body, because, while this food is received with wonder, the gifts of the Lord’s body, Christ’s body, are revealed. The bread of heaven is Christ, from whom heavenly beings receive spiritual food and enjoy it with indescribable delight.

29 [Col. 0294B] ÷ Man .. ate the bread of angels. He sent them food in abundance.

C Christ is therefore rightly called the bread of angels, because they are nourished by his praise. This bread fills the angels in heaven, while it feeds us on earth. H “He sent food,” so that they might now be filled not with the barley of the letter but with the doctrine of spiritual wheat.

30 He transferred the south wind from heaven: And by his power he brought in the southwest wind.

C For we know that the South Wind and the Southwest Wind are southerly winds; when they blow, sluggish cold is driven away and a balanced atmosphere is produced. So also the words of the Lord, burning with the fire of charity, have provided the world with a salutary moderation.

31 And he rained flesh upon them like dust: And winged birds like the sand of the sea.

C He rained flesh upon them—that is, nourishment of doctrine, by which the souls of the faithful might be satisfied. This dust signifies the subtlety of understanding. The sand signifies innumerable prudence, seasoned with the salty taste of the sea. But the winged birds signify heavenly desires, by which the soul, as though filled with flesh, may grow fat. He also said “the sand of the sea,” which has a salty taste; for there is also the sand of rivers, which does not have this taste. Consider, therefore, that all these things, known literally, are spoken in parables when they are referred to Christ.

32 And they fell in the midst of their camps: Around their tents.

C Camps are so called from chastity, because an army occupied with wars had no leisure for foul luxury. For us, however, this signifies that within the enclosures of the holy Church we can receive all heavenly gifts, if we ask by God’s gift that our good desires be fulfilled.

33 And they ate and were filled exceedingly: And he brought them what they desired: They were not deprived of their desire.

34 While their food was still in their mouths: The anger of God rose against them.

35 And he slew their fat ones: And he hindered the chosen men of Israel.

C They fulfilled the desires of the flesh, with their reason fasting: full in the belly, but emptied in mind. “Fraud” is so called as though faith had been broken. They were therefore satisfied for their own ruin—not so that they might live from it, but rather that they might perish.

C Their food was still in their mouths, while they were eating manna and the flesh of quail (Exod. XXXII). Food is so called from eating. Then the anger of God rose, when the Lord, angry with Moses, said: “This people has sinned grievously by casting and worshiping the calf”; for by worshiping it, they were destined to bellow in punishment. For it follows:

C “He slew their fat ones,” that is, the strong men of the Jews. Because of the sin of the calf made by Aaron, twenty-three thousand of them are read to have been killed in a single day. Thus it happened that the wickedness of the sinners hindered the chosen men of Israel from entering the promised land—namely, Moses and Aaron themselves.

36 In all these things they still sinned: And they did not believe in his wonders.

H That people still sinned, which murmured against God’s servant Moses. The wicked sin daily when they disdain obeying God’s priests; and they sin until they fail—and they fail with haste.

37 And their days failed in vanity: And their years with haste.

C He says that their days failed, as though they had been consumed by a wasting sickness. The days of sinners pass swiftly, as it is written: “Men of blood and deceit shall not halve their days” (Ps. LIV).

38 When he slew them, they sought him and returned: And at dawn they came to God.

C It was not those whom he says were slain who sought God, but the remaining people pleaded by the example of such men. The Jewish people therefore feared and sought God when they saw their companions being destroyed. “They came at dawn”: H having been scourged in their sins, they returned; and, having shaken off the sleep of unbelief, they came in the morning to hear the word of God.

39 And they remembered that God is (÷ est) their helper: And that God Most High is (÷ est) their redeemer.

C They remembered when, as the Lord was angry, the farthest parts of the camp were consumed by divine fire. After this had happened, they asked Moses to plead with the Lord for them (Num. XVI). H They understood that no one else could bring them help in such danger except the one who had freed them from the slavery of Egypt.

40 And they loved him with their mouth: And with their tongue they lied to him.

C This happens to those who think they believe through fear alone. For unless the Lord is feared together with love, he is not sought with the whole heart. It is the greatest sin to confess him with the tongue while the depths of the heart disagree—as though he who searches the kidneys and hearts did not know everything that is done in darkness. H They loved him with their mouth when they said to Moses: “Whatever the Lord commands, we will do.”

41 But their heart was not right with him: Nor were they held faithful to his covenant.

C For the Lord also says of them through Isaiah: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isa. XXIX). One is faithful to God’s covenant who truly loves him; “faith” is so called from the fact that what is said is made true.

42 Yet he is (÷ est) [lacuna] merciful and will be propitious toward their sins: And he will not destroy (÷ eos) them [lacuna].

H “Yet he was merciful”: while he awaits repentance, he does not immediately punish the offender, because he does not desire the sinner’s death, but his conversion (Ezek. XVIII).

43 And he abounded in turning away his anger: And he did not kindle all his wrath.

C He abounded when, hanging on the cross, he prayed for the Jews: “Father, forgive them” (Luke XXIII). Through his supplication it came about that God’s anger toward them was appeased. For he became propitious toward their sins, since, for satisfaction made to him on the cross, many of them—but not all—were deemed worthy to return.

44 And he remembered that they were flesh: A spirit going and not returning.

H For God knows that flesh always resists God’s law. C Flesh is so called because it is dear to its own soul. “A spirit going and not returning” is to be understood as “in this world,” since it is established that he will return to his own body in the resurrection. Thus, with marvelous brevity, the temporal death of man is defined here: “a spirit going and not returning.”

45 How often they provoked him in the desert: They stirred him to anger in the waterless place.

H They provoked him in the desert through the unbelief and dryness of their hearts.

46 And they turned and tempted God: And they provoked the Holy One of Israel.

H They turned—that is, backward—and embittered the Holy One of Israel, namely Moses, who saw God with mind and eyes. Even now they provoke him when they hear that the Lord Christ will be born in the flesh.

47 They did not remember his hand: The day when he redeemed them from the hand (÷ de manu) [lacuna] of the oppressor.

C “To remember” means to recall to the heart. “His hand” means the Lord’s benefits, H by which he freed them from the hand of Pharaoh, who figuratively signifies the devil.

48 As he placed his signs in Egypt: And his wonders in the field of Tanis.

C Tanis is a city of Egypt, where the wonders that are recorded took place. Wonders are so called as though they were things speaking beforehand—that is, things that foreshadowed what was to come. For all those plagues signified something.

49 But he turned their rivers into blood: And their rains, so that they could not drink.

C Here the first plague of the Egyptians begins. For just as water is read to have been changed into wine (John II)—which signifies the transformation of peoples for the better—so here, when it is changed into blood, it signifies the Jewish people transformed for the worse. He calls the rain the heavenly preaching, which he likewise says was turned into blood, to show that those who ought to have understood spiritually understood carnally. For how could they understand spiritually when they were occupied with carnal perceptions?

50 He sent among them the dog-fly, and it devoured them: And the frog, and it destroyed them.

H In the dog-fly he indicated the sect of the Cynics, which proclaims lust and luxury to be the highest good. C The frog is the extremely talkative vanity of heretics, which, dwelling in muddy perceptions, never ceases to chatter with wicked cries.

51 And he gave their fruits to rust: And their labors to the locust.

C Rust is shameful love, secretly consuming integrity by gradual diminution. The locust is malicious detraction, gnawing at the deeds of others through envious disparagement.

52 And he slew their vineyards with hail: And their mulberry trees with frost.

C Hail is God’s threat, by which he chastises the obstinate. Frost is malice that runs ahead and anticipates, not permitting the labors of others to reach their fruit.
