53 And he delivered their cattle to hail: And their possessions to fire.

H In the hail divine chastisement is shown. C By the death of the beasts, the destruction of the foolish is signified. H These animals are also killed by this hail, so that the folly of those who gave the divine name to beasts may be exposed. C Fire too is sent, so that the hearts of believers may be enlightened and vices consumed. As the Lord says: “I came to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it burn?” (Luke XII).

54 He sent upon them the anger of his indignation: Indignation and anger and tribulation: An assault through evil angels.

C The order of vengeance is narrated with the truest description. First, the Lord becomes angry at human sins when people are not converted by any remorse. Then, in his indignation, anger, and tribulation, he abandons the human being to his own malice; and finally, stripped of divine protection, they fall as prey to the devil. For it is clear that all created things are subject either to the Creator’s permission or to his command. He says that this assault of evils was carried out through evil angels—namely, indignation, the swelling of pride; anger, boldness; and tribulation, despair. H Thus those who were not corrected by divine scourges might be struck by diabolical snares.

55 He made a way for the path of his anger: He did not spare their souls from death: And he shut up their cattle in death.

H Divine anger has a way when someone, handed over for the vengeance of sin, does not free his soul from the punishment of Gehenna; or when folly—which resembles cattle—is shut up in everlasting death. C When he says, therefore, that the Lord made a way by which he could reach the vengeance of the unbelieving, he shows that vengeance could not come upon them unless they had been deprived of the Lord’s protection. By the death of their souls, understand the destruction of those men who were killed in that catastrophe.

56 And he struck every firstborn in the land of Egypt: The first fruits of all their labor in the tents of Ham.

H Just as these events are related as having occurred in Egypt, so also by his holy advent the Lord destroyed the principalities and powers of demons—or of vices—in this world. He triumphed on the wood of the holy cross and drove them from the hearts of those who had been devoted to diabolical cunning, because Ham is interpreted as “cunning.” C By “the first fruits,” understand every firstborn; for the first fruits of labor pertain to the whole of whatever human ability could possess.

57 And he took away his people like sheep: And he led them like a flock in the desert.

C When he says “sheep” and “flock,” he signifies the Christian people, who are pastured in this world as in a desert if they do not follow the desires of worldly things. Although literally you may understand the Jews, led into the promised land, as sheep, nevertheless, since he said that he would speak in parables, you ought to embrace in your understanding the Christian people signified by these things rather than the sign itself. For it follows: “And he led them out,” and so forth.

58 And he led them out in hope, and they did not fear: And the sea covered their enemies.

C We too were led out in hope from the land of Egypt—that is, from the darkness of sins—when we received the light of faith. “And the sea covered their enemies”: when we were washed in baptism, the devil was plunged into the abyss with his servants. Thus all these things happened to them in figure (1 Cor. X), as the Apostle says, announcing signs of our salvation.

59 And he led them to the mountain of his holiness: The mountain that his right hand acquired.

C The mountain of holiness is the holy Church, raised up in the breadth of faith; or that heavenly Jerusalem above, into which the Savior introduced the people of God by his grace. Literally, however, Mount Zion, near which the temple was built, is the mountain of holiness.

60 And he cast out the nations from before them: And by lot he divided among them the land (÷ terram) [lacuna] in the cord of distribution.

C He casts out nations from before us when barbarous and savage errors are driven away from us. He divides the land when, by his grace, he gives each person a blessed portion of the kingdom of God. The cord of distribution is so called from those who divided the land by stretching out a cord.

61 And he made them dwell in their tents: The tribes of Israel.

C Mystically, he will give the tribes of Israel—that is, those who see God—to dwell in the tents that innocent angels once possessed before the fall of pride.

62 And they tempted and provoked God Most High: And they did not keep his testimonies.

C Now he speaks of the obstinacy of the Jews, who tempted the Lord and did not keep his admonitions, and of what happened to them when the Lord was angry, so that the disobedient should fear such examples.

63 And they turned away and did not keep the covenant: Just as their fathers turned aside like a crooked bow.

H They turned away—those whom neither divine strength nor benefits softened. But just as their fathers killed the prophets, so these pursued God himself (Matt. XXIII). C A crooked bow is the malice of sinners, which does not shoot wounds from a distance but turns the arrows directed at itself back upon itself. For while the deceitful person strives to inflict blows, he is shown rather to turn his own snares upon himself. H A crooked bow is one that shoots its arrows at the person drawing it; while it seems to shoot an arrow against enemies, it wounds the person holding it.

64 They stirred him to anger on their hills: And with their carved images they provoked him to jealousy (÷ eum) [lacuna].

C The hills signify the proud and swollen thoughts of human beings, against which the Lord is always found to stand. They also provoked him to jealousy when they bestowed his honor upon idols. H For, having abandoned God, they served idols, worshiping them even on the mountains.

65 God heard and rejected them: And he utterly reduced Israel to nothing.

H He rejected those who were Israel in name only and not in vision.

66 And he rejected the tabernacle of Shiloh: His tabernacle where he dwelt among men.

C Shiloh was a city where the ark of God is read to have been established. Shiloh is interpreted as “its tearing away” or “its abandonment,” and it signifies the priesthood of the Jews rejected by God.

67 And he delivered their strength into captivity: And their beauty into the hand of the enemy.

C The Jews were delivered into captivity when the ark was captured by the Allophylites—that is, the Philistines—and they were defeated. By “strength” and “fortitude” he means the ark of the covenant, through which they appeared invincible among the nations and outstanding in the highest glory of beauty.

68 And he shut up his people in the sword: And he rejected his inheritance.

C It followed that the people should fall by the sword into ruin, once the dignity of the ark had been taken away. He rejected his inheritance when, because of the enormity of their crimes, he cast away the people whom he had chosen.

69 Their young men the fire consumed: And their virgins were not mourned.

C Here we should understand fire as the anger of the combatants. To mourn belongs to those who are at leisure; for when everyone feared the imminent dangers, no one was permitted to perform the proper rites for another’s funeral. Laments are so called from the household tombs, as it was the ancient custom to bury within the homes.

70 Their priests fell by the sword: And their widows were not mourned.

C Thus, in that very captivity, the sons of Eli the priest are read to have been slain by the sword by the Allophylites. The wife of one of them, having become a widow, was overtaken by death after a sudden childbirth (1 Sam. IV). Thus it happened that she was not mourned, while a common destruction seized everyone, although there is no doubt that the same happened to many others.

71 And the Lord awoke like a sleeper: Like a mighty man overcome by wine.

C The Lord is awakened to vengeance when provoked by our evil deeds; his patience was thought to have been asleep. The Lord also rose from the dead as one overcome by the wine of his Passion. Literally, however, those who are overcome and drunk with wine customarily become angry when they are roused and display themselves as strong; so it is said of God by analogy.

72 And he struck his enemies in the rear: He gave them everlasting disgrace.

C He struck the Allophylites in the rear, so that even while alive they might be gnawed by mice in execrable filth (1 Sam. V); and this disgrace remains everlasting for them. Thus he strikes sinners in the rear when he does not remit their debts; and they are, as it were, consumed by mice when the hostile troop of demons surrounds them.

73 And he rejected the tabernacle of Joseph: And he did not choose the tribe of Ephraim.

H C Here the rejection of the Jews and heretics and the election of the holy Church are narrated. C Joseph is interpreted as “increase,” which here must be understood in the opposite sense, since he is evidently rejected. Ephraim means “fruitful” or “abundance.”

74 But he chose the tribe of Judah: Mount Zion, which he loved.

C Judah is interpreted as “confessing” or “glorifying.” He rightly loves that tribe which was humble in confession and praiseworthy in conversion. H C The mountain signifies the holy Church.

75 And he built his sanctuary like a unicorn: On the land that he founded forever.

H The unicorn is said to possess singular power. H C It signifies the one Church of Christ, which he founded forever.

76 And he chose David his servant: And he took him from the sheepfolds: From behind the ewes he took him.

H C David—interpreted as “strong of hand” or “desirable”—signifies Christ, taken from the Jewish people and transferred, as from flocks of sheep, to pasture the people of the Church. H Or, he was chosen and raised up from the flock of mortals. C He was taken “from behind the ewes,” that is, from the place behind the ewes—fertile and bearing sheep—for Christ is the shepherd of fertile sheep, who beget many children by spiritual grace in holy faith and in the Church. For the shepherd follows the sheep; therefore he is said to be “behind the ewes,” not before them.

77 To pasture Jacob his servant: And Israel his inheritance.

C By Jacob we can understand the Christian people, who dwell here on earth, H and trample down vices and carnal desires. C By Israel as an inheritance, however, understand the future congregation, which is to be fed by contemplation of the Lord.

78 And he pastured them in the innocence of his heart: And he led them by the understanding of his hands.

C The excellent Teacher pastured those whom he deigned to teach, as he himself said: “Man does not live by bread alone” (Matt. IV). The understanding of his hands signifies active holiness, to which he led his faithful, according to the measure he himself granted, through glorious imitation.

## Prayer from Psalm 77

Refresh us with the nourishment of spiritual manna, O Almighty and most abundant giver, so that, directed by the understanding of your hands, we may deserve to glory on your mountain, acquired by your right hand. Through our Lord, etc.

# Psalm 78

## Argument of Psalm 78

C The voice of the Jews, saying how much they endured in the persecution of Antiochus or of the nations, and supplicating that by God’s power they may be avenged according to their desire for correction. H Yet this persecution must be referred to the soul, which is often written of as a city.

**TT.** A psalm of Asaph.

C Asaph signifies the synagogue. Therefore this entire psalm is placed in lamentation: it mourns future times as though they were past. It mourns the persecution of Antiochus, which occurred in the time of the Maccabees—then still future, but represented in the prophetic spirit as past because of the certainty of the event.

1 God, the nations have come into your inheritance: They have defiled your holy temple: They have made Jerusalem a guardhouse for fruit.

H The Prophet speaks of the persecution of the nations against the Church of God, which is his inheritance, or against Jerusalem: “God, etc.” C A nation is so called because it has been begotten from one stock. They defiled it when impious nations placed detestable images in the most holy places of Jerusalem and the temple. H For just as apples, when they begin to ripen, are guarded more carefully and, once ripe, are more easily devoured, so the adversary guards the soul that has become his own until he is able to devour it completely. The holy soul is God’s inheritance. In its figure, the Prophet laments the captivity of earthly Jerusalem.

2 They placed the corpses of your servants as food for the birds of heaven: The flesh of your holy ones for the beasts of the earth.

C When the Prophet says “they placed corpses,” he signifies the martyrs who flourished in that captivity amid abundant persecution and chose to die rather than be defiled by foods forbidden by the Lord. To cast away the dead without burial to birds and beasts, although burial is an office of piety, is plainly an example of great cruelty.

3 They poured out their blood like water around Jerusalem: And there was no one to bury them.

C Literally, he speaks of the Jewish people, who were killed by the nations not only within the city but also around its walls, so that no one could fulfill the duty of burial, since a common fate had overwhelmed everyone both around the walls and in the heart of the city. H These things indeed happened in Jerusalem before Christ’s advent, but they prefigured the slaughter of the infants, whose flesh was exposed to beasts and birds—that is, to persecutors—and so great a quantity of blood was poured out that scarcely could all the little bodies be buried.

4 We have become a reproach to our neighbors: A mockery and derision to those who are around us.

C He says that the Hebrews became a reproach and a laughingstock, though previously they had been revered for their devotion to the Lord. H The saints also become a reproach to those who were formerly their brothers, who persecute those made better through the stimulus of hatred.

5 How long, Lord, will you be angry forever? Will your jealousy burn like fire?

C He asks the merciful Judge not to remain angry with the Jewish nation forever, but that his jealousy might be kindled in them, as in Mattathias (1 Macc. II), who, inflamed with zeal for the tradition of his fathers, killed a certain Jew who was sacrificing to idols upon the very altars.

6 Pour out your anger upon the nations that have not known you: And upon the kingdoms that have not invoked your name.

C Pour out your anger upon the adversaries of the Jews; send forth your indignation abundantly, so that, just as they oppress us, they may be overpowered by your strength. Nor is it without significance that he first said “upon the nations” and afterward “upon the kingdoms”: first he invoked punishment upon the peoples, then upon the kingdoms themselves, which commanded such things to be done.

7 For they have devoured Jacob: And they have desolated his place.

C By saying “they have devoured,” he shows the savagery of the impious nation. “They have devoured” means “they have caused to be devoured,” when they exposed the corpses of the dead to the bites of wild beasts. They desolated his place when they stripped the most beautiful city of the habitation of its citizens.

8 Do not remember our former iniquities; let your mercies quickly go before us: For we have become exceedingly poor.

H May your mercy, who is your Only-Begotten, go before us, we ask, O Lord, so that, coming, he may be propitious toward our iniquities and rescue us from sins. For his sake we have become poor in the world. C By confessing their sins, therefore, they make the Judge propitious to themselves. Whoever fears the Lord’s judgment rightly desires that his mercy should come first. They say that they have become exceedingly poor; for poverty is a lack of goods, and we have nothing to offer to justice if the rigor of equity begins to investigate.

9 Help us, God our Savior: And for the glory of your name, Lord, deliver us, and be propitious toward our sins for the sake of your name.

C He rightly understood his weakness, therefore, who invoked the Savior as physician with all his strength. And he suitably adds: “for the glory of God,” not for any merit of his own. He is called Savior because he saves those who hope in him and changes the impending punishments of sinners into rewards.

10 Lest they should say among the nations: Where is their God? And let vengeance become known among the nations before our eyes.

H Spiritually, the nations are the opposing powers that grow strong against us, saying: “Where is your God?” as the pagans often said to the martyrs. C “And let it become known” means, by implication, the vengeance that the Lord is accustomed to take upon the faithless, when he compels them to condemn their wicked desires. But when he says “before our eyes,” he asks for the vengeance to be swift, so that he may see accomplished what he knows can at some time be granted.

11 Let the vengeance for the blood of your servants that has been poured out enter your sight: Let the groaning of the bound come before you.

H Here he invokes the judgment by which the blood of the martyrs may be avenged by the Lord. Understand the apostles as the bound, who were imprisoned in chains for Christ (Acts V) and condemned to exile. C Or he means those whom irreligious paganism bound for the Lord’s name. Do not understand this as a vindictiveness of the heart being requested, but as vengeance directed toward the conversion of the enemy. Vengeance is the defense of right against injury through just retribution.

12 According to the greatness of your arm: Possess the sons of those who were put to death.

H Spiritually, the sons of those who were put to death are the faithful peoples regenerated in Christ through the preaching of the apostles. C Or he means their sons, those who were punished with death for his religion; for them the Prophet prays that they may advance by the virtue of their parents, and that the Lord may possess them so that they are not led astray by the devil’s power.

13 And repay our neighbors sevenfold in their bosom: The reproach with which they reproached you, Lord.

C The Church does not pray against them but for them. For the affliction of bodies brings salvation to souls. “Sevenfold” signifies the perfection of the heavenly gift that we receive when we are filled with the illumination of the Holy Spirit. “The reproach”: since they inflicted injuries, let them now speak praises; since they were unbelieving, let them become devoted; since they were proud, let them become humble. “In their bosom” means in their souls and in the secrets of their souls, where glorious conversion always takes place.

14 But we are your people and the sheep of your pasture: We will confess you forever.

H They are called sheep because of their innocence, or because they have Christ as their shepherd. C They are rightly called sheep who, confessing his glory, have remained firm in faith.

15 From generation to generation: We will proclaim your praise.

H “In generation,” that is, in the prophets; “and generation,” that is, in the Gospels: the praises of Christ will always be proclaimed. C Or, in this generation, here in the Church, and in the heavenly generation in our homeland, we shall praise you eternally with all the blessed.

## Prayer from Psalm 78

Go before us, Lord, with your mercy before the zeal of your anger grows fierce, so that, aided by the patronage of the blessed, whose blood was poured out for you, we may obtain your propitiation together with forgiveness of sins. Through our Lord, etc.

# Psalm 79

## Argument of Psalm 79

C The voice of the Prophet concerning the advent of Christ and the expansion of the vineyard, that is, the Church.

**TT.** “For the end, for those who will be changed, a testimony: a psalm of Asaph.”

C Christ is the end of the Law. Asaph is interpreted as “one who gathers,” and signifies Christ and the Church. By him all are gathered into the faith and changed—from worse to better, from oldness to newness of life (Rom. X).

1 You who rule Israel, attend: You who lead Joseph like a sheep.

C It is therefore rightly said that the King of heaven rules Israel, because he mercifully governs those who look upon him with a pure heart. “Attend,” as if he were saying: Pour upon us the light of your mercy. By Joseph he means the faithful people, who are led into God’s sheepfold as sheep are gathered to pasture.

2 You who sit upon the cherubim, manifest yourself: Before Ephraim, Benjamin, and Manasseh.

C Cherubim is interpreted as “fullness of knowledge,” and it is manifest that Christ sits in this fullness. When he says “manifest yourself,” he asks that Christ appear through the benefit of the holy Incarnation. Ephraim is interpreted as “fruitfulness”; Benjamin as “son of the right hand”; Manasseh as “forgotten.” These virtues are evidently present in the Savior. He made us fruitful when he rose; he is the son of the right hand, that is, of the almighty Father; he is called “forgotten” when, hanging on the cross, he forgot his injuries and prayed for his persecutors (Luke XXIII).

3 Stir up your power, Lord, and come: To save us.

C He pleads all the more earnestly because he knows that the Lord’s Incarnation will bring us the greatest benefit. He asks him to stir up his power—that is, to come to wash away the sins of the human race. What prayers, or what vows, could be sufficient to seek that which can save the world from its impiety?

4 God, convert us, and show us your face: And we shall be saved.

C He earnestly asks to be converted because he knew himself to be distorted. The Father shows his face through the manifestation of the Son when he says: “Listen to him” (Matt. XVII). In him we have also been saved; therefore he says, “and we shall be saved.” Or he showed his face when he became incarnate. God shows his face to no one except the converted.

5 Lord God of hosts: How long will you be angry with the prayer of your servant?

C He rightly called him the God of hosts, who alone prevails in freeing us from the death of unbelief. H God is not angry if we seek justice; but a guilty conscience thinks that God is angry because of our prayer. C The Prophet believed him angry because he delayed coming to the aid of the human race; from this, the Prophet’s piety and great desire become evident.

6 You will feed us with the bread of tears: And you will give us drink with tears by measure.

C The bread of tears is a life full of sorrows; yet even in that life we are fed by God’s mercy when we are not destroyed by calamities and hardships, but rather instructed by them. He shows, therefore, that no time can be free from tears, since even refreshment itself was accompanied by weeping. “By measure” means according to an allotted portion; he wishes to show what the Apostle says: that God does not permit us to be tempted and afflicted beyond our strength (1 Cor. X).

7 You have made us a contradiction to our neighbors: And our enemies have mocked us.

C That contradiction was the pagan opposition that rose against the preachers of Christ with wicked speeches. H The enemies—that is, heretics—mocked the teachers of Christ. Likewise, the Jews and all unbelievers who make a noise around the Church and attack us mocked them.

8 God of hosts, convert us: And show us your face. And we shall be saved.

C He repeats the verse because it is the custom of one who greatly desires something to repeat what he desires to come. That face is therefore the power of Christ, through which we escaped the snares of death; it is also the power that grants the kingdoms of heaven to the worthy and to those who confess him.

9 You brought a vineyard out of Egypt: You cast out the nations and planted it.

C He calls the Hebrew nation a vineyard, which is clearly established as a type of the Church. A vineyard is named from vines. He led it out of Egypt by great miracles and, after expelling the nations—that is, the Amorites and their other neighboring peoples—planted it like a marvelous farmer. By this vineyard, however, the Church is understood, as I have said. Here it produces excellent fruits in the saints; pressed by tribulations, they give forth a sweet flavor, and, dug and pruned by the hoe of suffering, they multiply like vines. For this is the Church’s unique distinction: that it grows through persecutions.

10 You were a guide on the way before it: And you planted its roots, and it filled the land.

C Christ is the guide of God’s holy Church. Its roots are the prophets, planted by the operation of the heavenly King. From them it extended blessed branches and occupied the whole world with the pleasant shades of faith. This is what the title says concerning those who have been changed: understand the Jewish vineyard as changed into the Christian vineyard; and understand that what is said here of the Jewish vineyard is fulfilled in the Christian vineyard.

11 Its shadow covered the mountains: And its shrubs the cedars of God.

H The Church protects those who are proved to be within her bosom—that is, the patriarchs, various teachers, and apostles. C She covers those whom she nourishes, because her shadow makes fruitful and causes those whom she shelters more closely to grow more abundantly. Hence the cedars of God—that is, the martyrs, who have been established among the loftiest heights in the Church—are also protected by the Church herself.

12 It stretched out its branches to the sea: And its shoots to the river.

C The branches signify the Lord’s disciples, to whom he himself said: “I am the vine; you are the branches” (John XV). The sea signifies the most holy faith of all the nations. He says that it stretched out because this preaching extended from Jerusalem into every part of the world. By the shoots he means the children of regeneration who flowed from the river Jordan, where the Lord deigned to be baptized as an example of our salvation.

13 Why have you destroyed its hedge? And all who pass along the way pluck it.

C Now concerning the first vineyard, that is, the nation of Judea, he wonders why God abandoned it and why its protection was overturned—that is, why God’s defense was removed. H The synagogue’s protection was removed when blindness came upon it, until the fullness of the nations should enter (Rom. XI). C “They pluck it,” that is, they plunder it—those who pass by, namely the nations, which, passing beyond the way—that is, Christ—remained continually in the sacrifices of idols. Isaiah also foretold this, saying: “I will destroy its hedge, and it shall be for plundering,” and so forth (Isa. V).

14 The boar from the forest laid it waste: And the solitary wild beast fed upon it.

C Some understand this boar as Vespasian, the Roman emperor. He was called a boar because he dwelt in rugged places. By the solitary wild beast, however, he refers to his son Titus. H C Spiritually, call the solitary boar the devil, who, coming forth from the forest of the Gentiles, exterminated the Jewish people because of their unbelief.

### 15 [Col. 0306D] God of hosts, turn back: Look down from heaven and see, and visit this vine.

C Here Asaph asks that the Farmer of the work might look graciously upon his suppliant Jews and come to the aid of those in peril. “Visit” asks for the coming of the holy Incarnation, so that, when the Cultivator is present, the planted vine may prosper. H Thus he says: “Lord, God of hosts, turn away from your anger, and convert the synagogue into the Church.”

### 16 And perfect it, which your right hand planted: And upon the son of man whom you established for yourself.

H “And perfect it,” namely, the Church, which the right hand or power—that is, your Son—founded in his resurrection. “And upon the son of man,” that is, the Son of the Virgin, whom you established for yourself and, after conquering death, placed at your right hand. H Perfect, therefore, this vine founded upon you and upon your Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, in the true faith—the one whom you established for yourself.

### 17 It was burned with fire and dug up: At the rebuke of your countenance they will perish.

C Someone is burned with the fire of desire when he has committed a shameful crime. The trenches, moreover, are dug by hand when, through wicked action, we prepare snares for others and wish to deceive those who are unaware, while we ourselves instead fall into the very pit. These sins, therefore, will perish at the rebuke of God’s countenance, when he says: “Go into the eternal fire” (Matt. XXV). H Or “burned and dug up” refers to the unbelieving Synagogue.

### 18 Let your hand be upon the man of your right hand: [Col. 0307B] And upon the son of man whom you established for yourself.

C “Let your hand be,” that is, may the holy work bring the promise to fulfillment. The Son of man is Christ himself, who is also the Father’s right hand and was established among human beings, as he says in the Gospel: “This is my beloved Son” (Matt. XVII). He therefore asks for the work of the holy Incarnation.

### 19 And we will not depart from you: You will bring us to life, and we will call upon your name.

H “We will not depart,” that is, if we cling to you in faith, then we are refreshed by that bread which you sent from heaven (John VI). C And we will call upon that very name in the Lord’s Prayer, H that is, upon him to whom you gave the name above every name (Phil. II). C Or: if you send your Son to become incarnate, we will not depart from you, since we have asked for him with such great longing; and while we do not depart, you will bring us to life, and so forth.

### 20 Lord God of hosts, convert us: And show us your face, and we shall be saved.

C In this verse he sets forth the rule of the whole religion: first, that the Lord convert us; next, that he show his face; third, that he make us safe. Through this verse also, in brief, we ask for whatever is shown to be beneficial for us.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM LXXIX

Visit, Lord, your vine, which by your powerful right hand you freed from the Egypt of tribulations, so that, brought to life by the regard of your countenance, it may rejoice in the abundance of the fruits of a good life. Through our Lord Jesus, etc.

# PSALM LXXX

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM LXXX

[Col. 0307D]

C The Prophet admonishes the faithful to magnify God with many kinds of voices, and that no one should worship idols, but God alone.

### TITLE

For the end; for the winepresses; of Asaph; ÷ of the fifth Sabbath ...

C The intention of the title is that “for the end” designate Christ; “for the winepresses,” the Church; “Asaph,” the congregation of the faithful; and “the fifth Sabbath,” the baptized, since on the fifth day God made the animals from the waters, and in baptism the new human being is generated.

### 1 Rejoice in God our helper: Shout joyfully to the God of Jacob.

C This Asaph, whom we have often said signifies the synagogue, [Col. 0308A] admonishes the faithful peoples not to cease giving praises with the greatest joy to God, who has deigned to rescue them from savage dangers. “To God our helper” he says in opposition to the fictitious gods of the Gentiles, who cannot even help themselves. “To shout joyfully” is derived from “to help,” that is, “to delight.” Jacob signifies the Christian people.

### 2 Take up a psalm and give the tambourine: A pleasing psalter with the lyre.

C The psalm pertains to the proclamation of divine words. “And give the tambourine,” that is, good works. He adds: “Give a pleasing psalter,” that is, holy preaching, “with the lyre,” that is, with mortification or action of the flesh. For the psalter signifies the same thing as the psalm, and the lyre the same thing as the tambourine.

### 3 [Col. 0308B] Blow the trumpet at the new moon: On the notable day of our solemnity.

H The Jews sounded the trumpet at Passover, Pentecost, and the Feast of Tabernacles; we do so especially at the beginning of evangelical preaching and at the beginning of faith, when we rise again in Christ and receive forgiveness, and at the dedication of the house of our heart, when it has been renewed after its fall.

### 4 For it is a commandment in Israel: And a judgment for the God of Jacob.

C Israel is the chosen people, seeing God through faith; and likewise Jacob, on account of both peoples, the one coming from circumcision and the other from the foreskin. For Christ made both one, gave the law, and made known the future judgment as belonging to his power.

### 5 [Col. 0308C] He established it as a testimony in Joseph ÷ when he came out of the land of Egypt ..: He heard a language that he did not know.

C Joseph is interpreted as “increase”; the interpretation of this name is a testimony concerning the Hebrew people, who came out of the land of Egypt increased in number. And just as he was cast out through the waves of the Red Sea, so we, freed from the land of Egypt—that is, from carnal vices—are reborn through the holy water that regenerates us. And just as that sea was red, so the water of baptism—which flowed together with blood from Christ’s side—may now be called red. “He heard a language,” H C that is, the evangelical commandments, which he had not previously known.

### 6 He turned his back away from burdens: His hands served in the basket.

[Col. 0308D] C God removes from the backs of Christians the burdens of sins when they prostrate themselves in fortunate humility. We call “baskets” the vessels by which we cast away filthy refuse. Those whose hands are occupied with the uncleanness of sins hold them. We are freed from this servitude when we are cleansed from the filth of our crimes.

### 7 In tribulation you called upon me, and I delivered you: I heard you in the hidden place of the tempest: I tested you at the water of contradiction. Diapsalm.

H C Here the person of God is introduced, speaking to the people. C For he himself frees us from tribulation; he himself hears, in the hidden place, the distress of our tempest. But he tests us amid the contradictions of heretics, who resist and attempt to alter the will of the elect, stirring the mind like blowing winds.

### 8 Hear, my people, and I will testify to you, Israel, if you will hear me. There will be no new god among you: Nor will you worship a foreign god.

C He is God’s people who does not know how to be confused with the wicked through any mixture of conduct. God testifies when, in the future judgment, he gives each person a sentence according to the quality of his deeds (Matt. XVI). He also said: “There will be no new god among you,” lest anyone think that the Father’s Word came into existence in time. For he is the one who, begotten before every beginning from the substance of the Father, exists coeternal with him in equality. “Nor will you worship” shows that it is almost as great a crime to regard God as a new deity as to serve detestable idols.

### 9 For I ÷ am .. the Lord your God who brought you out of the land of Egypt: Open your mouth wide, and I will fill it.

C I am he who long ago brought you out of the land of Egypt; now I have come through the power of the flesh, and I bring you out of the land of Egypt when, through the grace of regeneration, I free you from the most loathsome sins. “Open your mouth,” that is, proclaim and disseminate, by confessing or admonishing, what is worthy to be heard. H Do you wish to eat the Lord your God? Open your mouth; he himself urges us to eat him. Therefore, as widely as you open it, so much will you receive. If you wish, you will receive the whole; if you do not wish, at least receive a part. He receives the whole who, leaving everything for his sake, follows him.

### 10 And my people did not hear my voice: And Israel did not attend to me.

[Col. 0309C] C The Jewish people did not hear, for they refused to believe in Christ the Son of God. H “I stand at the door and knock” (Rev. III): I want you to open, and I will enter, but you do not want to open.

### 11 And I dismissed them according to the desires of their heart: They will walk in their own inventions.

C The fitting punishment of the sinner follows. For the one who is abandoned by the Lord’s protection is not dismissed without penalty. It is the recompense for every evil to be deprived of such goodness. The sinner thinks it a kind of benefit if he is allowed to be filled with his own pleasures, although the Apostle says of their punishment: “God handed them over to the desires of their hearts” (Rom. II). H Unhappy is the one whom God does not correct. If someone sins and is not struck, that person is wretched; therefore he dismissed them, because though often struck, they did not accept discipline.

### 12 If my people had heard me: If Israel had walked in my ways.

C He called them his people because he gave them the law and displayed great miracles, so that their guilt might increase when the chosen people sinned against him. That person walks in his ways who is not found opposed to his commandments.

### 13 Perhaps I would have humbled their enemies to nothing: And I would have laid my hand upon those who afflicted them.

C See, therefore, that if we resist God by doing evil, he does not oppose our enemies—that is, demons [Col. 0310A] or vices. Nevertheless, he sometimes permits even the righteous to be tested. But he permits the righteous to be tested in such a way that he does not abandon them; the wicked, however, he allows to be afflicted so that he may make himself alien to them.

### 14 The enemies of the Lord lied to him: And their time will endure forever.

C They lie who bind themselves by good promises and then relapse again into the worst errors. He added: “Their time will endure forever,” namely, the time of their punishment, when it is said to them: “Go into the eternal fire” (Matt. XXV). H These enemies are the Jews, who lied to him, that is, denied the Lord. “Their time” means the time of their conversion, which will last forever—that is, until the end of the age, when all Israel will be saved.

### 15 And he fed them with the fat of wheat: [Col. 0310B] And he satisfied them with honey from the rock.

C “The fat of wheat” is the sacrament of Christ’s body. For what does fat in wheat signify except divinity in flesh? The rock is Christ; honey is his sweetness, by which all believers are satisfied through holy preaching. But the faithless remained hungry, for, with their ears made dull, they refused to obey Christ. Literally: he fed them manna.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM LXXX

Widen, Lord, the mouth of your suppliants, so that they may announce your glory; and, leaving the works of Egypt behind, may we rejoice in confessing your name. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, etc.

# PSALM LXXXI

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM LXXXI

[Col. 0310C]

C The Prophet speaks against the Jews concerning the coming of Christ, warning them to understand that he is the Christ who, in assuming flesh, appeared to be poor.

### TITLE

A psalm of Asaph.

C Asaph—whose name is plainly placed in the title for its significance—speaks throughout the psalm against the Jews concerning the coming of Christ, warning them to understand that he is the Christ who, in assuming flesh, appeared to be poor.

### 1 God stood in the assembly of gods: And in the midst ÷ he judges .. gods.

C He is speaking of the bodily posture of Christ’s humanity. For one cannot say that the nature of divinity stands or sits, since it is confined by no limitation of place. He also adds “of gods,” so that you may understand more clearly that it was said of human beings, among whom Christ is known to have dwelt bodily. H He calls all the leaders of the Churches gods; the God of gods distinguishes and judges them not through others but through himself. C Or he calls the apostles and the righteous gods, whom God judges, that is, distinguishes from others. Angels may also be called gods.

### 2 How long will you judge unjustly: And take the faces of sinners? Diapsalm.

H “How long will you judge”—he rebukes the wickedness of the scribes and Pharisees, or of certain bishops, who accept persons and judge according to outward appearance rather than according to God. It is as though he said: If a poor man with a just case comes, and then a rich man with a perverse case, you look at the person rather than the case; you do not consider the judgment, but the persons of those who have cases.

### 3 Judge for the needy and the orphan: Justify the humble and the poor.

C He more insistently admonishes the Jews that they ought to have understood Christ, whom they saw made needy and poor for our sake, although everything in heaven and on earth belongs to him. “The orphan” is one to whom an earthly father did not provide support.

### 4 Rescue the poor, and free the needy from the hand of the sinner.

C Here, therefore, those are admonished who did not at all stain their hands with the Lord’s death: let them not cease to rescue from the wicked the one unjustly handed over, who accepted poverty and need together with humanity; for this reason he is rightly called poor and needy.

### 5 They did not know and did not understand; they walk in darkness: All the foundations of the earth will be shaken.

C It is a true judgment that says they did not understand the author of light, because they walked in darkness; for if they had known him, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory (I Cor. II). “The foundations will be shaken” refers to the sign that clearly occurred at the Lord’s crucifixion: the earth was shaken and the rocks were split (Matt. XXVII). Or it refers to the fact that at that time many sinners—that is, earthly people—believed when they saw such a miracle, like the centurion.

### 6 I said: You are gods: And all sons of the Most High.

H C See what dignity it is for the faithful to be called gods and sons. C All those who obey his commands are called his sons. This verse, therefore, concerns only the righteous.

### 7 But you will die like human beings: And like one of the princes you will fall.

C He also rebukes the unbelievers, who preferred to die through pride rather than live through obedience. By saying “like human beings,” he signifies sinners, who were redeemed at no price and were not freed from sins because of their faithlessness. “One of the princes” signifies the devil, who fell after being cast down from heaven and received the punishment for his perversity (Rev. XII).

### 8 [Col. 0311D] Arise, God, judge the earth: For you will inherit ÷ among all the nations.

C “Arise” is said to him who slept in the tomb in the sleep of three days. “Judge those who, by setting their minds on earthly things, are rightly compared with the earth.” You will inherit that earth, namely, the one that the blessed will possess. H Or: you will inherit through faith among all the nations, because the apostles’ sound has gone out into all the earth (Rom. X), and from all nations they will receive an inheritance in the kingdom of heaven.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM LXXXI

Give us, Lord, in accordance with your commandment, to turn aside from the judgment of iniquity and to come to the aid of the needs of the poor, so that we may deserve to be joined to the number of your sons. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, etc.

# PSALM LXXXII

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM LXXXII

C The voice of the faithful pleading that the Church may not be tormented any longer by the forces of Antichrist, but that their defiance may quickly be crushed.

### TITLE

A song of a psalm of Asaph.

### 1 God ÷ who will be like you ..? Do not be silent or restrained, God.

C Who indeed will be like him who completed heaven and earth, and everything in them, with the greatest speed? This man contemplated him as such a great and mighty one and therefore rightly professes that no one is like him. “Do not be silent” refers to that future coming. He also restrained his power when he suffered, allowing himself to be held as though guilty and handed over to Pontius Pilate. These things will cease at the future judgment, where the power of his divinity will shine forth.

### 2 For behold, your enemies have made a tumult: And those who hate you have lifted up their head.

C This verse applies to the times of Antichrist, when God’s enemies will resound with tumultuous uprisings. He said “they have made a tumult,” rather than “they have spoken,” so that they might be denied the speech of human beings, since they did not possess rational voices. He says “they have lifted up the head,” although he could have said “heads,” because all madmen have one head: Antichrist.

### 3 They have plotted wickedly against your people: [Col. 0312C] And they have devised plans against your saints.

God’s people are those who strive with all their strength to fulfill the commandments of truth. C He added “against your saints,” so that they would attempt to bring destruction not only upon ordinary people but even upon the heavenly men themselves.

### 4 They said: Come, and let us destroy them from the nation: And let the name of Israel be remembered no more.

C Antichrist will have such an intention that the Christian name may be utterly destroyed from the world, not knowing, wretched man, that while he desires to kill Christ’s servants, he will complete the number of the saints through continual persecution. “From the nation” signifies the Christian people, who, although gathered from many nations, are nevertheless one, because they are known to have been produced from the one fountain of baptism.

### 5 For they have conspired unanimously together: Against you they have made a covenant; the tents of the Edomites and the Ishmaelites.

H O misery! God’s people cannot possess as much agreement in good as the wicked possess in evil. See, therefore, what fights against the saints: “the tents of the Edomites,” who are interpreted as “earthly”; “the Ishmaelites,” who are said to obey themselves—that is, whatever the heart has and whatever evil thought it conceives, they immediately do. C In the divine Scriptures, “covenant” does not refer only to what has no validity except after the testators have died; every pact and agreement is called a covenant, even among the living.

### 6 [Col. 0313A] Moab and the Hagrites; Gebal and Ammon and Amalek; Foreigners with the inhabitants of Tyre.

H Moab is interpreted as “from the father,” that is, from the devil; the Hagrites are “newcomers,” namely, a people foreign to God’s people; Gebal is “a vain valley”—*ge* means “valley,” and *bal* means “vain”—that is, the present world, in which vanity reigns. Ammon means “turbulent people,” that is, heretics. C Amalek means “licking people,” that is, deceitfully flattering. H “Foreigners,” that is, the Philistines, who are called “falling through drinking”—that is, those who have been drunk from the devil’s cup. Tyre is called *sor* in the Hebrew language, which is interpreted as “anguish of soul.” Those who attack God’s people are these. But let us see what prince they have. For it follows:

### 7 [Col. 0313B] For Assur also came with them: They became a help to the sons of Lot. Diapsalm.

H Assur is placed here for the devil himself. C He truly came together with them to attack the faithful. H Lot is interpreted as “one who turns aside”; the sons of Lot are unclean spirits. C Hence such a name is rightly placed at the end, signifying turning aside, as though he said: All this crowd of the lost turned together toward evil; there is no one who does good.

### 8 Do to them as to Midian and Sisera: As to Jabin at the torrent of Kishon.

C Midian means “turning aside from judgment”; Sisera, “exclusion from joy”; Jabin, “wise according to the world”; Kishon, “their hardness.” All of them perished at the torrent of Kishon and at Endor.

### 9 [Col. 0313C] They perished at Endor: They became like dung of the earth.

H Endor means “fountain of generation,” namely, carnal generation, not baptismal generation. C “They became like dung of the earth” when their corpses dissolved in bodily decay.

### 10 Set their princes like Oreb and Zeb: And like Zebah and Zalmunna.

H Oreb is interpreted as “a hole,” into which a serpent enters; Zeb, “a wolf”; C Zebah, “a victim,” H or “a sacrifice,” namely, of the devil; Zalmunna, “perfect in wickedness.” C He applies all these names to the army of Antichrist, who will not be saved through any conversion.

### 11 [Col. 0313D] All their princes, who said: ÷ Let us possess by inheritance .. the sanctuary of God.

C Those named above said: “Let us possess the sanctuary of God,” that is, the Christian people. H But they did not accomplish it, because the Lord fought for his people.

### 12 My God, set them like a wheel: And like stubble before the face of the wind.

C The wicked, while they are driven about by evil thought, become like wheels, H having no foundation in their evil deeds. “Like stubble,” C so that the lightness of sinners may be carried away as by a passing wind. “The face of the wind” signifies his presence.

### 13 [Col. 0314A] Like a fire that burns the forest: And like a flame burning the mountains.

C He also introduced fire and flame for the time of judgment, when the thick forests of sinners and the mountains of pride are burned up. H Or by “forest” he meant sterile people, who lack fruits. Therefore let sterility perish in them, as well as pride, which is signified by the name of mountains.

### 14 Thus you will pursue them in your tempest: And in your anger you will trouble them.

C “Thus you will pursue them” refers to what he said above: that they must be exterminated in the manner compared earlier to stubble before the wind. “In the tempest” means at the time of judgment, which is rightly compared with a tempest: first, because it is unforeseen; then, because it suddenly troubles everything with a crash. We have often said that anger cannot properly be attributed to divinity, but the expression is taken from human beings, who, when they judge criminals, are moved with an angry spirit.

### 15 Fill their faces with disgrace: ÷ And they will seek your name, Lord ...

C He now turns to those who will believe in the Lord. Their faces are filled with disgrace because they have found no one to praise their sins, and immediately they seek to invoke the Lord’s name.

### 16 Let them be ashamed and troubled forever ÷ and ever ..: And let them be confounded and perish.

H Let them perish according to what is evil in them, so that they may be saved according to what is good. For this destruction does not signify annihilation, but salvation.

### 17 So that they may know that the Lord is your name: You alone are the Most High over all the earth.

C Everyone will know the omnipotence of God, whether destined for death or for life, and that he alone is the Most High. Once they have recognized him, he will spare those who have converted and condemn the hardened to eternal punishment.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM LXXXII

Dispel from us, Lord, every error of excess, so that, having abandoned the nations of vices, we may fear you alone, who dwell as the Most High over all the earth. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, etc.

# PSALM LXXXIII

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM LXXXIII

[Col. 0314D]

C The voice of the Church, earnestly desiring God and professing blessed the one to whom the Lord grants help.

### TITLE

For the end; for the winepresses; for the sons of Korah. A psalm.

C We have already said that there are three psalms designated “for the winepresses”: the eighth, the eightieth, and the eighty-third. This signifies that the mystery of the Church belongs to the holy Trinity, having been consecrated by the repetition of the number three. We have said that Korah is interpreted as “bald,” and the interpretation of this name announces the place where Christ was crucified; therefore Christians are called “the sons of Korah.” This psalm is sung from their perspective.

### 1 [Col. 0315A] How beloved are your tabernacles, Lord of hosts: My soul longs and languishes for the courts of the Lord.

H Many desire possessions, others the riches of the world, and others to appear in churches and possess glory. I have only this desire: to see the eternal tabernacles. They are beloved, certainly, because there is an assembly of virtues, not of vices. “My soul longs”—this is my only love and desire: to see your courts. C The mind necessarily languishes for that toward which it has been directed but which it cannot presently reach. For he was contemplating the joys of heaven, but he could not reach them immediately.

### 2 My heart and my flesh: [Col. 0315B] Have rejoiced in the living God.

C Here one must observe how remarkable this man was in holiness: not only his soul but even his flesh—which is shown to be more subject to the vice of transgression—burst forth in fortunate rejoicing in God, foreseeing the good things of the future age, which he trusted he would obtain through Christ’s grace.

### 3 For the sparrow found ÷ for itself .. a house: And the turtledove a nest for itself, where it may place its young.

C The sparrow is exceedingly swift, living in holes in walls; when it has found a dwelling, it rejoices greatly. So the soul rejoices when it realizes that its dwelling in the kingdom of heaven has been prepared. The turtledove, however, is a most chaste bird, content with a single union and known to build a nest for its young. It signifies the Church, which knows no companionship with another besides Christ the Lord.

### 4 Your altars, Lord of hosts: My king and my God.

C “Your altars”—to which what was said in the first verse must be joined: how lovable and beloved they are. There satisfaction always stimulates further desire, and blessed hunger never departs. “King” is derived from ruling, while “God” is derived from creating, although that name also indicates fear.

### 5 Blessed are those who dwell in your house: Forever and ever they will praise you. Diapsalm.

C What, then, will be the joy of that coming age, where it is granted to rejoice abundantly, never to depart from that joy, and to praise God without end?

### 6 Blessed is the man whose help is from you: He has set ascents in his heart, in the valley of tears, in the place that he established.

C He discloses difficult labors and struggles when he says, “help from you.” And because this ascent is arranged through free will aided by God’s grace, he added “ascents in his heart.” When someone conquers lust with God’s help, he climbs the first step; when he has mastered pride, he ascends another; when he has overcome greed, he climbs a third. He is raised by as many steps as he has been freed from vices. “The valley of tears” is the humility of the penitent; “the place that he established” signifies the future kingdom of God. [Col. 0316A] God established that place so that, keeping his commandments, we may be placed there eternally.

### 7 For the lawgiver will give blessings: They will go from strength to strength; the God of gods will be seen in Zion.

H Christ is the Lawgiver, who gives blessing here to those who fight well. “They will go from strength to strength”: those who have appeared strong here become stronger there. C He is called the God of gods, just as he is called King of kings and Lord of lords. H What joy it is to go from strength to strength, and to have this very reward: that we may deserve to see Christ. To see God is an infinite crown. He does not say, “They will go from weakness to strength,” but “from strength to strength,” because unless we have strength here, we cannot have greater strength there. Do you wish to be crowned there? Fight here.

### 8 Lord, God of hosts, hear my prayer: Give ear, God of Jacob. Diapsalm.

C The God of hosts and the God of Jacob is Christ Jesus, who is known to be the most merciful overthrower of his enemies when he causes their wickedness to reach the paths of virtue, directed toward them. He is called the God of hosts because from him we have the ability to go from strength to strength, and because all virtues come from him alone.

### 9 Our protector, look upon us, God: And look upon the face of your anointed.

H The Father looks upon the face of the Son when he deigns to look upon us through his grace, because Christ is the head and we are his members, and Christ is in us. Hence he himself says: “Whoever receives you receives me” (Luke X). And the Apostle says: “Do you seek proof of the one who speaks in me, Christ?” (II Cor. XIII.) Therefore, because Christ is in us, the Father is said to look upon the face of Christ when he looks upon us, because he looks upon us for Christ’s sake.

### 10 For one day ÷ in your courts .. is better: Than thousands.

C This day is eternal; it has neither beginning nor is it enclosed by an end. H It is one perpetual day, because it has neither night nor darkness (Rev. XXI). C “Than thousands” signifies this world, where thousands of days endure until the end; and that one day surpasses everything gathered together through the multiplication of these days.

### 11 [Col. 0316D] I chose to be despised in the house of my God: Rather than to dwell in the tents of sinners.

C The despised person is one who, in human estimation, is regarded as the lowest; but before God he is judged honorable, because for God’s name he appears despised among human beings. “The tents of sinners” are recognized as the present life, or the glory and pomp of the world. H Therefore I wished and chose to be least in the kingdom of heaven rather than first in this world.

### 12 For God loves mercy and truth ÷ ..: The Lord will give grace and glory.

H God’s mercy is that he makes the righteous from sinners; truth is that he does not deny a reward to the righteous. [Col. 0317A] He first gives the promised grace when the sinner turns to life; for “grace” is so called as something given freely. He will also give glory when, justified by the divine gift, we become sharers in the company of angels in the future.

### 13 He will not deprive those who walk in innocence of good things: Lord of hosts, blessed is the person who hopes in you.

C The innocent person is one who harms no one; such a person therefore cannot be deprived of Christ’s gifts. “Lord of hosts” should be read as an exclamation of wonder: he who does such great things that human beings cannot recount them. Blessed also is the one who has placed his hope in eternal happiness, H and who knows that he has not offended his God.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM LXXXIII

Eternal God, founder of the heavenly tabernacles, arrange, we ask, ascents in our hearts, by which we may deserve to rise without the fall of sin to your tabernacles. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, etc.

# PSALM LXXXIV

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM LXXXIV

C The Prophet gives thanks to God because, from the ancient stock of the Jewish nation, a people came forth for the worship of the Lord the Savior; and he asks for the coming of Christ, in whom human blindness received the light of faith.

### TITLE

A psalm of David, for the sons of Korah, for the end.

C We have often explained what Korah signifies. Here it is sufficient to recall that this psalm is said concerning those who have already believed in the Lord the Savior with sincere mind.

### 1 You blessed your land, Lord: You turned away the captivity of Jacob.

C You blessed the land, namely, that which was punished in Adam at your coming: the flesh which you deigned to assume, or humanity. Understand by Jacob the faithful people, who were freed from captivity to the devil when they deserved to be saved by God’s grace. H Or, “the land” means the blessed Virgin, or the sinful person who confesses his sins. Previously he produced thorns and thistles; afterward, having received the blessing of contrition, he bears the fruits of repentance.

### 2 You forgave the iniquity of your people: [Col. 0317D] You covered all their sins. Diapsalm.

C To forgive is to release a debt, not from some other source but from mercy: not through the intervention of any cause, but through sheer mercy. He covered our sins when he did not wish to see them for the purpose of vengeance, but pardoned them, H or covered them with virtues.

### 3 You have softened all your anger: You turned away from the anger of your indignation.

C He recounts the offenses which the perversity of the Jews committed against the Lord. He turned himself away from anger when he turned away the destruction of the Jews, when the physician came to the sick and the author of salvation came to those filled with pestilence. This is to be applied not merely to one nation but to the benefit of the whole world. H Or: you did all the things mentioned above when you sent the Son to become incarnate.

### 4 Convert us, God our Savior: And turn your anger away from us.

C Previously the Prophet gave thanks for past sins that had been forgiven; now he asks concerning the future, because he foresaw that they would commit great crimes in Christ’s Passion. He says “convert,” so that persecutors may become defenders, blasphemers preachers, and opponents disciples.

### 5 Will you be angry with us forever: ÷ Or .. will you extend your anger from generation to generation?

C He posits two generations. The first is, as some think, from Adam to Christ; the second, from Christ to the end of the age. He therefore asks that, although the Lord justly becomes angry with the first generation because of its guilt, he may not likewise wish to strike the second generation with perpetual condemnation.

### 6 God, when you have turned, you will bring us to life: And your people will rejoice in you.

C You will bring us to life for this reason: you promise the vow of conversion, so that we may be able to reach the entrance of life. When you have granted this, that people—which unhappily rejoiced in itself—will then rejoice in you because of its hope.

### 7 Show us, Lord, your mercy: And give us your salvation.

C The Father’s mercy is the Savior, whom the blessed company asked to be shown to them through the illumination of holy faith. He adds “give us,” so that he may be received in our mind through a heavenly gift in such a way that no temptations may take him away.

### 8 I will hear what the Lord God speaks ÷ in me .. For he will speak peace to his people.

C The Lord speaks within, that is, the Holy Spirit, so that the Psalmist may be seen to speak outwardly; he hears inwardly so that he may be heard outwardly. The peace of God is Christ, whom he says will speak to his people, that is, to the saints who have pleased God through approved conduct.

### 9 And upon his saints: And upon those who turn to the heart.

C The person who turns to the heart is one who, abandoning sins, rises to repentance and chooses to undertake the blessed service of Christ, having abandoned the world’s deadly freedom. H He also turns to the heart who strives to understand the law not bodily but spiritually.

### 10 Yet his salvation is near to those who fear him, so that glory may dwell in our land.

C Although the Jews alone, having received the law, appeared devoted to the true God, they nevertheless provoked him by various offenses, doing everything carnally. Therefore they were not truly said to fear him, but to fear him “near at hand,” because they received his law carnally rather than spiritually. Yet although they were such, the Lord the Savior chose to be born from their carnal race, and glory dwelt in their land—that is, Christ, shining forth through miracles.

### 11 [Col. 0319A] Mercy and truth have met one another: Justice and peace have kissed.

C For through Christ’s gracious agency the two Testaments have been brought into a single sequence of union. In the New Testament there is mercy, by which we are liberated; in the Old, truth, where the true proclamation of the prophets is contained. These have met one another to fulfill the promised grace of perfection. Peace and justice have kissed one another, signifying the same thing as mercy and truth kissing one another: that is, they have come together in agreement on a pleasing judgment. Such an embrace of love usually occurs when people, moved by affection, see one another after a long time and kiss.

12 Truth has sprung up from the earth: And justice has looked down from heaven.

[Col. 0319B] C Truth sprang up from the earth when the Word became flesh from the Virgin Mary. Justice looked down when the Son of God came to the aid of the endangered human race. H For it was just that the Savior should have mercy on his people.

13 For indeed the Lord will give goodness: And our earth will give its fruit.

C This verse is appropriately applied to the humility of the penitent. In his goodness God gives the disposition and love of confession—that is, a rain of tears—so that our flesh, watered by devout weeping, may produce the fruit of repentance. H Or, Mary—who is called “our earth” because she is our flesh—gave her fruit, and gave a just fruit; therefore he says: “Justice will walk before him.”

14 [Col. 0319C] Justice will walk before him: And he will set his footsteps on the way.

C Justice walked before them when, having recognized the truth about their evil deeds, they humbly ask that what they have committed by sinning be forgiven them. Then they truly set their footsteps on the way, that is, in Christ—those who previously went astray along detestable paths.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM 84

Forgive, Lord, the iniquity of your people; and show us your mercy, which, with justice going before us, may lead us into the way of peace. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, etc.

# PSALM 85

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM 85

[Col. 0319D]

C Christ’s prayer to the Father for himself and for his members, of whom he is the head.

TT. A prayer. Of David.

C It is called a prayer, as though “the account of the mouth”: throughout this entire psalm Christ prays to the Father for himself and for his members, of whom he is the head.

1 Incline your ear, Lord: ÷ And .. hear me: for I am needy and poor ÷ I ..

H According to the weakness of the body he assumed, he pours out a prayer to the Father. C By “ear” he does not mean a bodily ear, but that spiritual hearing by which he knows the petitions of those who ask. By saying that he is needy and poor, he shows the condition of humanity that he had assumed. Whoever has deserved to be emptied of the perversity of this world is also needy and poor; Christ was truly such.

2 Guard my soul, for I am holy: Save your servant, my God, who hopes in you.

C Christ is truly called holy, because by the conduct of a heavenly life he trampled underfoot the allurements of this world. He asks to be saved by his divinity, so that he might instruct us that salvation is not established in human powers.

3 Have mercy on me, Lord, for I have cried to you all day: Gladden the soul of your servant: For to you ÷ Lord .. I have lifted up my soul.

C The one and same God-man Christ Jesus [Col. 0320B] asks for mercy, though he is the one who grants it, teaching us always to plead with God, since we frequently offend through sin. When it says “all day,” it indicates the whole period of life. He asks that his soul be gladdened, the source of joy, in that aspect in which he is a servant. He wishes to be called a servant because he was born from the Virgin Mary, who confessed to the angel announcing it that she was God’s handmaid. Hence in another psalm he also says: “I am your servant and the son of your handmaid” (Psalm 115).

4 For you, Lord, are sweet and gentle: And of great mercy toward all who call upon you.

C He shows what God is: sweet to those who return to him after the bitterness of this age; gentle, because he bears with sinners; of great mercy, because although our sins are countless, his compassion is far more abundant. It forgives so many offenses and denies aid to no one who calls upon him.

5 Hear, Lord, my prayer: And attend to the voice of my supplication.

C When he says “hear,” he wishes not to be heard casually, but for the prayer to be stored within the boundaries of God’s majesty, just as something heard through the ears of a human being is shown to be fixed in the memory. He adds, “attend to the voice,” so that an attentive mind might open its hearing.

6 On the day of my tribulation I cried out to you, because you heard me.

H “On the day of tribulation,” that is, on the day of the Passion, I cried out from the cross; you heard me, so that you might restore to me my spirit, which I had commended to you.

7 [Col. 0320D] There is none like you among the gods ÷ Lord ..: And there is nothing according to your works.

C By saying, “There is none like you among the gods,” he signifies the idols of the pagans, which were still worshiped in the world with abominable devotion. “And there is nothing according to your works,” namely, nothing like you, who made heaven and earth.

8 All the nations which ÷ ever .. you have made will come and worship before you, Lord: And they will glorify your name.

C Since at that time only the Jewish nation appeared to worship the one God, he proclaims that all the nations, which were held subject to idols, would come to his worship. H Through my Passion they will recognize the greatness of your power.

9 [Col. 0321A] For you are great ÷ you .. and perform wonders: You ÷ are .. God alone.

C “Great” can be said only of God alone, whose power nothing can in any way equal. He is also called “alone,” because the Holy Trinity is one God, distinguished only in persons, not separated by a division of nature.

10 Lead me, Lord, in your way, and I will enter into your truth: Let my heart rejoice, so that it may fear your name.

H C Here the Prophet speaks, or Christ in the person of his members. The way of the Lord is Christ, and he is also the truth. The Church prays that it may walk in this way and truth, for without God’s help it cannot fulfill this. Thus let the heart rejoice under fear, and let it fear under hope. In this world, whoever fears a human judge is guilty; whoever fears God is holy. H When I have been instructed through sorrow for my crimes, then I will rejoice in you with spiritual joy.

11 I will confess to you, Lord my God, with all my heart: And I will glorify your name forever.

C That is true confession which is expressed from the whole secret place of the mind; and the person confesses with all his heart who places all his hope in God. “Forever” signifies that among his saints his praises will continually resound to the Lord, when he has received the blessedness that was promised.

12 For your mercy ÷ is .. great toward me: And you have delivered my soul from the lower hell.

[Col. 0321C] H The faithful people give thanks to God because his mercy is great, and say that their soul has been freed from the lower hell, that is, from the punishment in which sinners are condemned. The upper hell is sin; the lower is eternal punishment. A C Or, the lower hell is the punishment of the condemned; the upper is the limbo of the fathers, in which the rich man, placed in the lower hell, saw Lazarus placed in the upper (Luke 16).

13 God, the wicked ÷ in .. have risen up against me; and the assembly of the powerful have sought my soul: And they have not set you before their eyes.

C Once again Christ speaks according to his humanity. When he says “the wicked,” he signifies the Jews, who rose up against him, namely, to declare the innocent man guilty, and the mad crowd slaughtered its own king. [Col. 0321D] “The assembly of the powerful” is the gathering of the proud, who with bestial roaring wished to take Christ’s life. He adds, “And they have not set you before their eyes,” etc. For whoever commits a crime in every way does not set God before his eyes; if he had him present, he would immediately be recalled from the crime he had conceived.

14 And you, Lord God, are compassionate and merciful: Patient and of great mercy and truthful.

C God is compassionate because he shows mercy to each individual thing; merciful because the very nature of his divinity is always gracious; patient because he bears with sinners; greatly merciful because he forgives us more than our weakness deserves; truthful because, through no weakness of his own, he does not know how to withdraw from his promises—that is, to take them away or deny them.

15 Look upon me and have mercy on me: Give your authority to your servant: And save the son of your handmaid.

C The voice of Christ according to his humanity addressed to the Father. He is the Lord’s servant, of whom Isaiah says: “Behold my servant; I will receive him” (Isaiah 42). Christ is called a servant in the Scriptures because of the innocence of his mind. He is also called the son of the handmaid, who replied to the angel by saying that she was God’s handmaid: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord” (Luke 1). By “authority,” understand the power of judgment, because, as he himself testifies, “the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5).

16 Make with me a sign for good, so that those who hate [Col. 0322B] me may see and be confounded: For you, Lord, have helped me and comforted me.

C A sign is so called because it signifies what is to come. “Make, Father, a sign in the resurrection,” namely, “for good”: for the good of believers and the confusion of those who deny; or “for good,” so that the Jews may see and be confounded over their evil, and thus return and believe. “You have helped me” refers to the contradiction of the disputing Jews and to the unjust struggles in which they were always overcome by the testimony of truth. “You have comforted me” looks to the persecutions of the madmen, which he endured most patiently, as though they were a storm’s assault.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM 85

Gladden, Lord, the face of your household, and deliver our souls from the lower hell, so that, protected by contemplation of your face, we may trample underfoot the desires of the flesh through spiritual rule. Through our Lord Jesus, etc.

# PSALM 86

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM 86

C The voice of the Prophet concerning the heavenly Jerusalem, that is, the Church of Christ.

TT. A psalm-song for the sons of Korah.

C The sons of Korah signify Christians. The psalm, sounding of higher things, urges us to think of heavenly realities and to rejoice in them with hymnic exultation.

1 Its foundations are on the holy mountains: The Lord loves the gates of Zion above all the tents of Jacob.

C Christ is the foundation of the Church. He holds it together so that it cannot totter through any shaking. “On the holy mountains” signifies the apostles and prophets, who are called mountains because of the excellence of their holiness. Zion signifies the heavenly Jerusalem, whose gates are faith, charity, baptism, repentance, and whatever admits the acquired people into that city. Or, as some wish, they signify the twelve apostles. The tents of Jacob signify the catholic Church, which is always afflicted here. Rightly, that spiritual and heavenly city is said to be loved above this one: in it, it is declared, there is already nothing troubling.

2 [Col. 0323A] Glorious things have been spoken of you: City of God. Diapsalm.

D The City of God is the holy Church, concerning which glorious things have been spoken throughout the entire sequence of Scripture and by all the prophets. For Isaiah said: “Arise, Jerusalem” (Isaiah 51); and concerning it the Savior also said: “A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden” (Matthew 5).

3 I will remember Rahab and Babylon: Those who know me.

D Rahab is interpreted as “pride” or “breadth.” Thus by Rahab the breadth of the Church’s empire is signified, or the breadth of sin. Babylon means “confusion.” Both signify the people of the nations, who before Christ’s coming, walking proudly along the broad roads of this age, had been handed over to the confusion of idols and sins, but were enlightened through mercy. He says, “those who know me,” because at the judgment the Lord will not remember every Rahab and Babylon, but only those who know him through faith and charity. The Hebrew and Roman translations, however, have “those who know me” in the dative sense: “to those who know me.”

4 Behold, the foreigners, and Tyre, and the people of the Ethiopians: These were there.

C The foreigners are those who are strangers to the Jewish people; and while the Jews did not believe, these were received. H We are also these foreigners, and Tyre, and the people of the Ethiopians. C Tyre signifies the distress of penitents, which is produced from contrition over sins; the people of the Ethiopians, who had been most darkened by the obscurity of sins, were gathered into the city of God.

5 Will Zion say: “A man, and a man, was born in her”: And the Most High himself founded her?

Will Zion—that is, can any human being say to Zion herself, “How will a man be born in her?” And yet such a man will be born in her who is the Most High, namely God, and he himself founded her, namely Zion. “And a man was born in her.” C God, having assumed flesh, became man, and as God he himself founded the synagogue, though he was thought to be merely a man.

6 The Lord will recount in the Scriptures of the peoples and of the princes: Of those who were in her. Diapsalm.

[Col. 0323D] C The Lord frequently recounted in the Gospel what Moses had foretold concerning him (John 5). For they are the princes—Moses and the prophets—who were in her, that is, in the synagogue. H Or, in Zion, that is, in the Church, he recounted in the writings of the apostles, who, while living in the flesh, were its princes.

7 As of all who rejoice: Your dwelling is in you.

C “As of those who rejoice”: he speaks of that incomprehensible joy where the eternal dwelling of the faithful is. H Or rather, this is said of the Church, where the dwelling is not truly and fully that of those who rejoice, but is “as of those who rejoice.”

## PRAYER FROM PSALM 86

God, foundation of our faith, who establishes the gates of eternity in holy minds as upon lofty mountains, with justice strengthening them, grant us to believe gloriously in you and to confess proclaimably that, for our redemption, you became man. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, etc.

# PSALM 87

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM 87

C Christ, asking the Father for help, recounts the contempt he was to suffer from the Jews. He asserts that the dead are not to be raised so that they may confess to the Lord, and asks that his resurrection come with the greatest speed.

TT. A song of the psalm for the sons of Korah, to the end, for Melech, for answering; the understanding of Heman the Israelite.

[Col. 0324B] C Melech is interpreted as “choir,” singing divine words. Heman, his brother: by this name Christ calls those who obey his commandments. Israelites are those who see God, shining with God’s light through obedience. Jerome, in Origen’s commentary, has Melech, as do Augustine and Cassiodorus. But in Jerome’s translation from Hebrew into Latin there is neither Amalech nor Melech, but “through the choir”; in Hebrew this is called Mahalat, and not Israelites but Esraites. Cassiodorus, however, following Augustine, explained Melech and Israelites. In Jerome’s commentary “Israelites” is found written, but in Hebrew it is Esraite.

1 Lord, God of my salvation: By day I cried out, and by night, before you.
