[Col. 0324C] C Christ prays to the Father by that which was born from the Virgin Mary, indicating the humility of the human weakness that he deigned to assume. “By day” signifies joy, and “by night” declares adversity; by both times he demonstrates that God must be entreated.

2 Let my prayer enter into your sight: Incline your ear to my prayer.

C The Lord inclines his ear when, in his mercy, he deigns to hear through the wondrous operation of his power—not through a bodily ear.

3 For my soul has been filled with evils: And my life has drawn near to hell.

C He says that his soul has been filled with evils—not with his own, for he had no sins, but with the world’s offenses, under which humanity labored. “And my life has drawn near to hell” refers to Christ’s Passion, as in the Gospel: “My soul is sorrowful unto death” (Matthew 26).

4 I have been reckoned among those who descend into the pit: I have become like a man without help, free among the dead.

C “I have been reckoned”: he censures those who thought he had died in the ordinary way, as others die. By “the pit” he means either the place of the tomb or the deepest depth of hell. “I have become”: namely, in the eyes of those who, with mad minds, did not believe in his divinity. He alone was free among the dead, because he also broke the barriers of death itself. For only his death was free, since he committed no sin, and his death was also voluntary. Although he was free among the dead, he was nevertheless judged by the madmen to be like the wounded, etc.

5 Like the wounded sleeping in the tombs, whom you remember no longer: And they have been driven away from your hand.

C He still speaks of those utterly foolish people who thought that God, wounded by a spear, had been killed and likewise buried, as one of the wicked among human beings. “Whom you remember no longer,” that is, for whom you have no care, since through their sins they were made alien from you. Understand “care” with regard to their salvation. “And they have been driven away”: that is, they are shown to have been expelled from God’s hand, while they were made alien from his governance.

6 They have placed me in the lower pit: In darkness and the shadow of death.

C “Pit” is used for hell, for the hollow place of burial, and for the deepest calamity of this world; here he wished it to be understood in the latter sense. “In darkness,” that is, under the blindness of forgetfulness. “The shadow of death” indicates the place of sinners, since joy does not shine upon them, who will remain in the perpetual darkness of their sorrow.

7 Your wrath has been confirmed over me: And you have brought all your waves upon me. Diapsalm.

C The Jews thought that Jesus Christ had come into the dangers of the Passion through God’s wrath, as they were saying: “Let him save him, if he wants him” (Matthew 27). H By “waves” he wishes the anger of wrath to be understood, which the Father would have poured out upon all nations. “You have brought it upon me,” because I took their sins upon myself, as he says elsewhere: “Because of the sins of my people I struck him” (Isaiah 53).

8 You have put those who know me far from me: They have made me an abomination to themselves.

9 I have been handed over, and I did not go out: My eyes have grown weak from want.

10 I cried to you, Lord, all day: I stretched out my hands to you.

C He calls the apostles “those who know me.” Through his divinity he knew everyone, but he himself was known by few. These, therefore, who were especially known were put far away, as it is written: “I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered” (Zechariah 13). He was made an abomination when, after he had been crucified, they were saying: “Ah, you who destroy the temple of God” (Matthew 27), and similar things.

C He was handed over by Judas to the bands of the madmen; nevertheless, he did not go out when he showed as little as possible of what he was able to do—that is, when he concealed his divinity. Or, he did not go out from custody. “The eyes grew weak,” that is, the apostles. “From want,” because they had not yet received the Holy Spirit. Want is named by contrast, where there is no abundance.

C “I cried to you, Lord, all day”: here a division must be placed, so that this continuation of “all day” should pertain to prayer and to the work of good deeds. “I stretched out my hands”: by “hands” he wishes good works to be understood, which by good deeds he continually stretched toward God. For if we join these words to the cross, what follows will be inconsistent.

11 Will you perform wonders for the dead? Or will physicians raise them up, and will they confess to you? Diapsalm.

C He certainly did not perform wonders for the dead, that is, for unbelievers. Wonders are performed only for those who behold the great works of God with faith. “Or will physicians raise them up?” This is said negatively, because although physicians care for bodies, they cannot raise souls dead through sins, so that those who have suffered the wounds of their unbelief may be brought to life through a most truthful confession. Yet even physicians of the body cannot give health to the sick without God’s gift.

12 [Col. 0326B] Will anyone declare your mercy in the tomb: And your truth in destruction?

C The tomb signifies the minds of unbelievers, and rightly it is called a tomb, where the soul, dead through sins, is confined. Or will one who is in the destruction of sin declare your truth? For the living and faithful are accustomed to declare mercy in their actions. The person is said to proclaim the truth who is found to preserve it in his actions. Thus he marks those who will not truly believe, whose throat is an open tomb (Psalm 5).

13 Will your wonders be known in darkness: And your justice in the land of forgetfulness?

C “Will they be known?” because everyone who commits sin hates the light. C Nor can God’s justice be known by those oppressed in earthly forgetfulness, that is, by the thickest blindness of the heart and the densest darkness of vices.

14 But I cried to you, Lord: And in the morning my prayer will go before you.

C By saying “but I,” he signifies that he cried out with his members, of whom he is the head. He also said that in the morning his prayer had gone before him, when the Church was asking many ages beforehand for what we still await as future. We must not understand this as though prayer precedes God’s grace, since even what we pray for comes from grace.

15 Why, Lord, do you reject my prayer: Do you turn your face ÷ from me ...

C We think that our prayer is rejected and that God turns his face from us when he delays our requests. Although he acts for our benefit, delays nevertheless deeply distress us. This can appropriately be understood as spoken in the person of the martyrs, who in this world are wearied by such desires.

16 I am poor, and in labors from my youth ÷ my ..: Yet, having been exalted, I have been humbled and troubled.

C “I am poor”: the Church rightly says this, since from its youth it is wearied by the poverty and labors of the world. “Having been exalted”: when any believer considers human affairs with a proud heart. “Humbled”: when he reaches confession. “Confounded”: when in repentance he condemns the evil deeds he has committed.

17 Your wrath has passed over me: And your terrors have troubled me.

C “Passed over” is beautifully said, because they will not remain. For when a believer afflicts himself, having been chastised, he escapes the Lord’s wrath. By “terrors” he means those of the coming judgment, which every sinful flesh will fear at the judgment; yet even the good shudder at them in this life.

18 They surrounded me like water all day: They surrounded me together.

C “They surrounded me”: namely, the offenses condemned by the strictness of the Law and the Gospel. They are rightly compared with waters, which enclose us in a most abundant inundation.

19 You have put friend and neighbor far from me: And those who know me from misery.

[Col. 0327B] C By “friends” he means those joined to us in a city through honorable pursuits and conduct; by “neighbors,” those assigned to us by the order of kinship. By “those who know me,” those who are neither friends nor neighbors, but have learned of us only through sight or reputation. Suffering or calamity, which is feared by the faithful, has often put these classes of people far away.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM 87

Redeemer of all and ineffable God of our salvation, who, penetrating the regions below for our sake, became free among the dead, hear the morning prayer of your household, and deliver us from the worst slavery of the lurking enemy. Who with the Father and the Son, etc.

# PSALM 88

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM 88

[Col. 0327C] C The voice of the faithful, praising the Lord’s mercies and power.

TT. The understanding of Ethan the Israelite.

C Ethan is interpreted as “strong.” Israelite means “seeing God.” Since this psalm was going to recount God’s praises and promises, that name was assigned to him to indicate the unchanging firmness of the faithful words.

1 I will sing the mercies of the Lord forever.

H I will always sing those mercies by which you deigned, through the Son, to visit the human being dead in sin.

2 From generation to generation: I will proclaim your truth with my mouth.

[Col. 0327D] C “From generation to generation” signifies two peoples, namely the Jewish and the Gentile peoples, to whom he testifies that he will proclaim the truth. And it is rightly said, “with my mouth,” because what proceeds from the mouth quickly slips away, whereas what is continually uttered by the mouth is celebrated with enduring devotion. H That truth is Christ, or the promises of God.

3 For you said: “Mercy will be built forever”: Your truth will be prepared in the heavens + in them ...

H “For you said”: your compassion is always exalted and will never be destroyed. H A C “It will be prepared in the heavens,” that is, your truth will be proclaimed in the apostles. Here begins the Father’s voice: “I have appointed,” etc.

4 [Col. 0328A] I have established a covenant with my chosen: I have sworn to David my servant: I will prepare your offspring forever.

H “I have established a covenant with the chosen,” that is, with the teachers of the Churches, so that they may teach and instruct the people acquired through grace. C God most justly swears when he promises everything by his right. For we say “he swore,” meaning “he prayed by right,” that is, “he spoke justly.” God also swears justly for this reason: what he swears he can always fulfill. A human being, however, is rightly forbidden to swear or to promise by an oath, because it is not in his power to accomplish what he promises. Christ too is prepared, descending in the origin of his flesh from the seed of David, forever King of kings and Lord of lords (Revelation 19); this must be understood according to his humanity. H Or, the “offspring” is not only Christ, the head, but also his members, namely those who believe in him.

5 And I will build your throne from generation to generation. Diapsalm.

C “And I will build”: this promise concerns Christ. Every saint is his throne, upon which he sits through his grace as upon a most splendid seat. H Or, his throne is the Church, in which Christ sits forever. The meaning is the same as before, although the words are different.

6 The heavens will confess your wonders, Lord: And your truth in the assembly of the saints.

C “The heavens will confess”: the true preachers, how the Lord governs the world with how many wonders. [Col. 0328C] “And his truth”: because the Word became flesh and dwelt among us. They confess it not everywhere, as they do his wonders, but in the assembly of the saints, where it is believed that the truth has been fulfilled and that the Word became flesh. H Or, the apostles proclaim the wonders displayed in Christ’s Incarnation and Passion and those things accomplished through him, in the congregation of the saints.

7 For who among the clouds will be equal to the Lord? Who will be like the Lord among the sons of God?

C “Clouds” are the prophets, apostles, and preachers, who watered the peoples through the Holy Spirit; yet they were subject to the law of sin. Nor could anyone among the sons of God, that is, among the saints, be his equal. He is the Son of God by nature; the saints are so by grace. He is without any sin; they are proved to have been stripped of sin through him.

8 God, who is glorified in the counsel of the saints: Great and terrible above all who are around him.

H C The Lord himself, who is proclaimed by the saints, is called great because he is God, and terrible because of his wondrous power. “Those who are around him” are the saints, who draw near to him through the gift of his grace, by innocence and holiness of life.

9 Lord God of hosts, who is like you? You are powerful, Lord: And your truth is around you.

C “Who is like you?” Because you are Lord of powers and authorities. The saints are enriched with powers, but they do not rule; you command those things by which others become distinguished through your gift. You are powerful from yourself; they are powerful through you. They are enlightened by your truth; your truth is always within you.

10 You rule the power of the sea: But you calm the movement of its waves.

H You rule the power of the sea, that is, the powers of this age. “But the movement,” etc., when you turn and calm the fierce movements of persecutions against martyrs and saints for the benefit of the saints, and the temptations stirred up by persecutors against your servants. C He says “you calm,” so that they may be able to endure; he does not say “you remove,” because if he were to remove the movement of persecutions completely, the martyrs would have no crown.

11 You humbled the proud one like a wounded man: [Col. 0329B] With the arm of your power you scattered your enemies.

H “You humbled the proud one like a wounded man,” that is, the devil, wounded and humbled by the nails of your cross, after his spoils had been taken away. C By “enemies” he means the unbelieving Jews, who were scattered throughout countless nations by the arm, that is, by the power of the Lord Christ.

12 The heavens are yours, and the earth is yours; you founded the world of the ÷ earth .. and its fullness: You created the north and the sea.

C The meaning of this verse is as follows: Why did the foolish wish to rage against you, Christ, in this world of which you are the founder? “The world of the earth” refers to the whole extent of the world; “its fullness,” to all the creatures that are in it. By “the north” understand the devil, who said: “I will set my throne in the north” (Isaiah 14). H Or, the Antichrist, concerning whom the Lord says to Jeremiah: “From the north every evil will be opened” (Jeremiah 1). C “The sea” means the lofty and wicked powers of the people of this age. A creature must not grow proud against the Creator, because it was created by him.

13 Tabor and Hermon ÷ in .. your name will rejoice: Your arm with power.

C H Tabor is interpreted as “coming light,” which pertains especially to God’s coming. Hermon means “his curse,” that is, the devil’s curse, which, when the Lord came, he received from Christians. For it was fitting that, in the presence of the light, the dark devil should be accursed; hence the saints will rejoice in God’s name. “The arm with power” is Christ, who does what he wills in heaven and on earth. Enlightened by you, therefore, and abhorring the devil, they will rejoice in your name, giving glory to you.

14 Let your hand be strengthened, and let your right hand be exalted: Justice and judgment are the preparation of your throne.

H “Let the hand be strengthened,” that is, the works that you perform in this world. C “Let the right hand be exalted,” that is, let the number of the predestined be glorified, who are to be placed at the right hand. God’s throne is eternal and always prepared, but it will appear prepared to us when we behold him judging with justice. H Or, the saints are God’s throne; and unless someone first practices justice and judgment within himself, he cannot become God’s throne.

15 Mercy and truth will go before your face: Blessed is the people who knows jubilation.

C Mercy is that by which he spares those who have been converted; truth is that by which he restores the promises. Blessed is the people who understands or knows jubilation, that is, who is recognized to have placed its immense joy not in its own powers but in God’s power. Jubilation is an abundant exultation of the mind that cannot be expressed in words.

16 They will walk in the light of your face, God: And in your name they will rejoice all day: And in your justice they will be exalted.

C Here he first describes those who know jubilation. The Christian people walk in the light of his face when they continually persevere in contemplation of the Holy Trinity. When he says “in your name,” he forbids rejoicing in presumption of one’s own strength. “All day” indicates the whole period of life. They will be exalted in God’s justice when, in that resurrection, they have been placed at the right hand.

17 For you are the glory of their power: And in your good pleasure our horn will be exalted.

H For just as your commandments were pleasing to them, so it has pleased you in them that their horn, that is, their power, should be exalted in you.

18 For the Lord’s is + our .. assumption: And the Holy One of Israel is our king.

C Our assumption by the Lord is the Incarnation, which is shown to have been fulfilled by the Holy One of Israel. Having placed our hope in it, we are raised upward from the depths of sins, while his mercy lifts us up and places us in eternal joys.

19 Then you spoke in a vision to your saints and said: I have placed help in the mighty one: ÷ and .. I have exalted the chosen one from my people.

C Now the Prophet again speaks to the Father. God spoke to the prophets and the other saints in a vision when he caused them to see the things they were saying; hence they were called “seers.” “He placed help,” that is, as though he were saying: The Father bore witness to the mighty one, that is, to the Son, saying: “I have glorified, and again I will glorify” (John 12). By “the chosen one” he means Jesus Christ; “from my people,” from the Jewish nation. Or, “the mighty one” means the body of the Church, over which he placed Christ to rule. Or, as another translation has it, “in” or “upon the mighty one.” H That is, upon the devil, so that, placed against or above the devil, he might crush his pride.

20 I have found David, my servant: With my holy oil I have anointed him.

C By saying “I have found David,” he clearly indicates Jesus Christ, whom above he called “the mighty one,” and concerning whom it is said elsewhere: “God has anointed you with the oil of gladness” (Psalm 44).

21 For my hand will help him: And my arm will strengthen him.

C “Hand” and “arm” are placed here for God’s strength, which strengthened Christ’s humanity in the Passion.

22 The enemy will accomplish nothing against him: And the son of iniquity will not add to harming him.

C “The enemy will accomplish nothing,” that is, the devil, who is the insolent enemy of humanity. The son of iniquity was Judas the betrayer, who is rightly called the devil’s son, since the devil is the author of all iniquity. They harmed Christ’s purpose in nothing.

23 And I will cut down his enemies before his face: And I will turn those who hate him into flight.

C Christ’s face, when it deigns to look upon sinners, causes them to fall from their wickedness. They are also turned into flight when, abandoning an impious life, they begin to hasten to Christ’s remedies. Remembering their sin, they flee from their deeds and turn to the Lord’s benefits.

24 [Col. 0331B] And my truth and my mercy are with him: And in my name his horn will be exalted.

C The truth of the Father is the Son. This pertains to judgment; mercy, however, pertains to compassion, because he forgives sins. “Horn” signifies unconquerable power, concerning which he says, “All power has been given to me” (Matt. XXVIII). H Or, Christ is the truth: he has spoken what he heard from the Father. Mercy, because he heals those infirm in mind and body. “Horn”: the strength of his Church, redeemed by his blood, is meant.

25 And I will set his hand upon the sea: And his right hand upon the rivers.

C “The sea” signifies all the nations, among whom our Savior received the glory of dominion. H And “upon the rivers,” that is, his power over the principalities and powers [Col. 0331C] of this world. Or, “the sea” signifies the world; “hand,” action; or “rivers” indicate the waters of baptism.

26 He himself will call upon me, “You are my Father: My God and the protector of my salvation.”

H We read in the Gospel that he often called upon the Father (John XVII), as in: “Glorify me, Father, with yourself”; and there: “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit” (Luke XXIII).

27 And I will place him as the firstborn: The highest ÷ above .. the kings of the earth.

C He is therefore the firstborn, as in the Gospel: “I am the Α and the Ω.” And he says “I will place,” that is, “I will establish.” H “The highest above the kings of the earth”: that is, I subject all the kingdoms of the world to him. Or, he is called the firstborn from the dead; [Col. 0331D] also the firstborn of the eternal Father and of the Virgin Mother.

28 I will keep my mercy for him forever: And my covenant faithful to him.

C This is said of him in the form of a servant, because he received the Father’s mercy with eternal honor; to him power was given in heaven and on earth. The covenant is faithful because everything that the prophets foretold concerning him has been fulfilled.

29 And I will establish his seed for an age ÷ of the age ..: And his throne like the days of heaven.

C “An age of the age” signifies eternity. The seed of David is Christ; his throne is the power of the future judgment, in which the righteous will shine with heavenly splendor.

30 [Col. 0332A] But + if .. his sons forsake my law: And do not walk in my judgments.

C He speaks these two verses about the Christian people. They are called “sons” because Christians are regenerated through water and the Holy Spirit from the mother Church.

31 If they profane my righteousnesses: And do not keep my commandments.

C If the sons named above do not keep Christ’s righteousnesses, that is, his commandments, a fitting vengeance is promised to befall them in what follows.

32 I will visit their iniquities with a rod: And their sins with scourges.

C He visits with a rod when he judges strictly, as the Apostle says: “What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod?” (1 Cor. IV). He also visits with scourges when what we have done wrong is punished more lightly in us. Or, the rod strikes, while scourges beat.

33 But I will not scatter my mercy from him: Nor will I harm him in my truth.

C Above he spoke about the members; now, however, he speaks about the head. For the Father says that he will not scatter his mercy from Christ, but will pardon him in its entire fullness. “Nor will I harm him”: even if enemies were permitted to harm him, nevertheless the Son was not injured in the Father’s truth—he whose blood redeemed the whole world—and because everything that the Father spoke through the prophets was fulfilled in Christ according to the order of truth. Hence he also adds: “I will not profane,” and so forth.

34 Nor will I profane my covenant: And what proceeds from my lips I will not render void.

[Col. 0332C] C The Father did not profane his covenant, that is, Holy Scripture, by lying; rather, he made it honorable through the faithfulness of events, since nothing that proceeded from his lips—that is, through the holy prophets—was destroyed by any falsehood.

35 Once I swore by my holiness: “If I lie to David, his seed will remain forever.”

C It is the custom of human beings to swear frequently so that they may be believed in something. God, however, swears once, since he is not changed by any variation of time. We have said that his oath promises things yet to come. “If I lie to David,” that is, “I will not lie”; for if it is placed negatively, this is also supported by common usage.

The seed of Christ consists of all the saints and true Christians who will remain in holy conduct to the end [Col. 0332D] of this life and afterward forever.

36 And his throne is like the sun in my sight: ÷ and .. like the full moon forever: And a faithful witness in heaven. Diapsalma.

C The throne of God is the faithful soul, in which Christ truly sits and shines like the sun; and like the moon, that is, the structure of our body glorified after the resurrection. C And “a faithful witness”: Christ is the one who bore witness to the truth, which is himself, and to the Father’s work in the world. He says that he is in heaven because he is there after his Ascension. C Or, “in heaven,” that is, in the heavenly holy man: in him the very glorified flesh is the faithful witness of this fulfilled promise—not in a condemned man.

37 [Col. 0333A] But you rejected and despised: You delayed your Christ.

This rejection and despising occurred in the kingdom of Solomon, in his descendants.

But when he says “you delayed,” it is plainly not said of Solomon or David, but of Christ. A The Father delayed him from the Jewish people; he did not take him away, because a remnant will be saved at the end.

38 You turned aside the covenant of your servant: You profaned his sanctuary on earth.

C “You turned aside the covenant,” that is, you transferred it to another party, so that what had been promised to the Jews might pass to the benefit of the nations. For temple, priesthood, offering, or kingdom did not remain for them; rather, Christians obtained everything in full. “Covenant”: this is the promise of God’s birth. “Profane” means irreligious, because when Christ came, the sacrifice of animals and observance of Sabbaths were removed on earth—that is, throughout the whole world where the Church of Christ is.

39 You destroyed all his hedges: You made his stronghold fear.

H He destroyed the hedges, that is, the words of the law. C The stronghold [Col. 0333B] of the Jews is the protection of God and Christ, which you made a cause for fear, so that, when they committed faults, they would fear the Lord himself, by whose fortification they had been accustomed to be enclosed.

40 All who pass along the way plundered him: He became a reproach to his neighbors.

A C All who passed along the way, that is, the nations, plundered the city of Jerusalem. C The Jewish people also deservedly became a reproach to their neighbors because they did not wish to believe in Christ.

41 You exalted the right hand of those who oppressed him: You gladdened all his enemies.

C He exalted the right hand of those who oppressed him when the Jews, handed over to their enemies, suffered exceedingly great slaughter. For an enemy becomes glad when his adversary is humbled before him.

42 You turned away the help of his sword: And you did not assist him in battle.

C He turned away the help of his sword when that armed people was made as defenseless as if unarmed, so that whereas previously the few conquered the many, afterward the many were unable to resist the few.

43 You removed him from purification: And you struck his seat to the ground.

A C You destroyed him, that is, you removed those who preferred in the obstinacy of their mind to despise Christ. For he destroys from purification—that is, from the faith that purifies hearts—those whom he also decided to condemn. “Seat” here is also used for kingdom; it is rightly said to have been struck to the ground when the divided people was scattered throughout the whole world, destined to have neither king nor kingdom any longer.

44 You shortened the days of his time: You drenched him with confusion. Diapsalma.

C The days of the Jewish kingdom were shortened because it did not deserve to possess the promise made to Abraham concerning the eternity of the kingdom. They were also confounded, namely, by the filth of their unbelief, when they saw the nations turn to their Lord, whom they themselves had killed.

45 How long, Lord, will you turn away to the end? Will your anger burn like fire?

C Now the Prophet asks the Lord, in his compassion for the Jewish people, to forgive them. “To the end” signifies the end of the age, when the Jews will be converted. We burn with anger when we intend to take vengeance; but we are moderately angry when we reprove someone with words. Thus he added “like fire,” which consumes whatever is placed before it.

46 Remember what my substance is: For have you established ÷ all .. the sons of human beings in vain?

C The Prophet asks that the Lord deign to free this flesh, subject to sins, by the glory of his coming, because it was not created for him to permit it to perish as something worthless.

47 Who is the person who will live and not see death? Will he rescue his soul from the hand of the underworld? Diapsalma.

C “Who is the person?” must be read interrogatively, with “no one” understood. For all human beings, whether righteous or sinners, will see death, which was inflicted upon the first human being by the law of sin. “Will he rescue his soul?” Here likewise “no one” must be understood. “From the hand,” that is, from the power of the underworld—a power from which no one can be snatched except by the one who, through dying, struck down death.

48 Where are your ancient mercies, Lord, as you swore to David in your truth?

[Col. 0334C] C “Where are the mercies?” is not spoken in sorrow, but as though the Lord were being asked, in his delay, to provide quickly what the speaker knew he would do. He calls them “ancient” because he knew that God had shown them to Abraham; he would not call them ancient unless he recognized that they had occurred before the times of David.

49 Remember, Lord, the reproach of your servants, which I carried in my bosom from many nations.

C Reproach came upon the servants of God when the nations, out of love for idols, persecuted Christians. This was in the bosom of Christians, that is, in the secret affection of their minds, because they were afraid to speak openly; hence they were proved to be extinguished.

50 The reproach with which your enemies reproached, Lord: The reproach with which they reproached the alteration of your Christ.

H “They reproached”: namely, the Jews and Pharisees. C This is the alteration of Christ: he abandoned the obstinate and admitted the faithful to the gifts of his compassion.

51 Blessed is the Lord forever: Let it be, let it be.

C “Blessed is the Lord” is set against the curses of the nations, since what they say is transitory. The praise of the Lord, however, remains forever. Then follows “Let it be, let it be,” so that no one would doubt such great promises, where repeated confirmation follows.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM LXXXVIII

Rescue, Lord, our souls from the hand of the underworld—you who for our sake powerfully shattered the realms below—so that, singing of your mercies, we may be freed both from the confusion of crimes and from everlasting death. You who, with the Father and the Son, etc.

# PSALM LXXXIX

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM LXXXIX

C The prayer of faithful peoples to God for the Church.

TT. A prayer of Moses, the man of God.

1 Lord, you have become our refuge + you .. from generation to generation.

C That venerable Moses, as a type of the holy Church—which he carried in prefiguration—offers a prayer poured out to the Lord and gives thanks to him who became its refuge, since it is known to have been delivered from every danger. But [Col. 0335B] so that you might understand that this was said not only of one person but of the universal Church, he used “for us,” not “for me.” “From generation” refers to the time from which the human race began. “From progeny” signifies to the end of the age, as though he were saying, “always.”

2 Before the mountains were made, or the earth and the world were formed: From age to age, you are God.

C Here let us understand “mountains” as the exalted powers of heaven, as though he were saying: You existed before you formed the heavenly and earthly things. “From age to age” requires us to understand eternity. “You are” is appropriately said of God, because he has neither past nor future; thus he said to Moses: “I am who I am” (Exod. III).

3 [Col. 0335C] Do not turn the human being into humiliation: And you said, “Turn back, sons of human beings.”

C “Do not turn human beings toward humiliation,” that is, do not cast them into the desire and ambition of this world. Therefore he rightly asks that human beings not be abandoned amid slippery falls, to whom it was said: “Turn back.”

4 For a thousand years in your sight are like yesterday’s day, which has passed.

C A thousand years are not merely few in God’s sight; they are regarded altogether as yesterday’s day that has passed. He also uses the finite for the infinite, that is, “a thousand” for “all.”

5 And a watch in the night: Their years will be regarded as nothing.

[Col. 0335D] C Beautifully he compared human life to watches during the night, in which everything is carried on amid darkness and trembling, when the human mind, surrounded by carnal vices, is assailed. A night watch is completed in three hours; for four watches fill the night.

6 In the morning, like grass, let him pass away; in the morning let him flower and pass away; in the evening let him fall, grow hard, and wither.

H “Morning” is called infancy, childhood, or adolescence; “evening,” however, he calls the old age of a human being. H Our morning does not remain but passes away, that is, our youth, and perishes through old age; nor does evening itself remain, but falls.

7 [Col. 0336A] For we have failed in your anger: And in your fury we have been troubled.

C “We have failed” means that we have been exhausted by human weakness. “We have been troubled”: he means the thought of death, whose fear we all dread. H We lived for nine hundred and more years; and behold, our life has been contracted into a brief span, because we have failed in your anger.

8 You have set our iniquities before your sight: Our age in the illumination of your face.

H “You have set,” and so forth: nothing concerning our sins is hidden from you. “Our age in the illumination.” C Because as soon as we sin, we expect punishment. H Whatever we think we do even in secret is open through your illumination and before your eyes. The Hebrew truth has: “Our life is in the illumination of your face.”

9 For all our days have failed: ÷ And .. in your anger we have failed.

10 Our years will meditate like a spider’s web: The days of our years are seventy years.

C He says that the brevity of human life has come about because of the Lord’s anger. For when he says, “All our days have failed,” this concerns innumerable years; but what follows, “and in your anger we have failed,” refers to the tribulations and hardships that we endure within that very brief life.

C A spider is a weak and extremely delicate animal that, when flies pass by, weaves certain deceitful nets to prepare food for itself; so the years of those devoted to criminal works are occupied with empty and deceitful schemes. It is called *aranea* because it is dry and exceedingly fine. He said “will meditate,” not “will work,” because they lived without any fruit of their works, in empty reflection.

11 But if they are in strength, eighty years: And more than these are labor and pain.

H Although this should appropriately be understood historically, as referring to the brevity of human life, nevertheless neither number is devoid of spiritual significance. H C The seventieth number signifies the Law (Num. LXX, LXXX); the eightieth signifies the Gospel. C Whoever here exceeds the commandments of the Law and the instruction of the Gospel is entangled in labor in the present and pain in the future.

12 For gentleness has come upon us, and we shall be corrected.

C “Gentleness has come upon us,” that is, Jesus Christ; he rebukes and corrects us if we do not hasten to fulfill his covenant.

13 Who knows the power of your anger, and, because of your fear, can count your anger?

14 Make your right hand known in this way: And make us instructed in heart in wisdom.

C For just as God’s rewards cannot be fully understood, so neither can the measure of punishment be grasped. He rightly added “because of your fear,” as another prophet also says: “I considered your works and was afraid.”

[Col. 0337A] C By “right hand” he means the Lord Savior, asking that he become known to them, through whom we learn everything that will profit us. “And those instructed,” and so forth: that is, those who have understanding concerning the Lord Christ. Someone is called “instructed” (*eruditus*) as though drawn out from every field (*ex omni rure elicitus*). For he is the power of God and the wisdom of the Father, whom the speaker here asks to know—not with bodily eyes, but with an instructed heart.

15 Turn back, Lord—how long? And be gracious toward your servants.

C The Prophet asks the Lord to temper his justice with some gentleness, so that he may be entreated by sinners, toward whom he was rightly known to be angry. H How long will you delay, Lord—you whom the prophets said would come?

16 We have been filled in the morning with your mercy: [Col. 0337B] And we rejoiced and delighted in all our days.

C He says that he was filled with mercy in the morning, that is, in the bright contemplation of God. Since the holy man of the Lord foresaw the coming, it was necessary that his heart rejoice in praise and delight throughout all the days of his life.

17 We rejoiced in proportion to the days in which you humbled us: The years in which we saw evils.

C The Prophet says that he rejoiced in those tribulations through which he perceived that the people were being salutarily humbled. For he knew that pride was harmful to faithful men; therefore he rejoices in the tribulations through which humility is preserved.

18 [Col. 0337C] Look upon your servants and upon your works: And direct their sons.

C Here consider the words with which he invited the compassion of the good Judge: first saying, “Look upon your servants,” and then, “upon your works,” so that, even if they did not deserve to receive forgiveness for their own deeds, they might obtain it through the works of the Creator. Among rhetoricians this argument is called an appeal based on praise of the judge.

19 And if the splendor of the Lord our God is upon us, direct the works of our hands upon us: ÷ And direct the work of our hands ...

C The splendor of the Lord is upon us when we are adorned with the imprint of his cross. He directs our works upon us when he grants us forgiveness of sins, so that, when we have been perverse, we may be made wholly upright by his correction. A Or, the works of our hands [Col. 0337D] are directed upon us when we do not perform them for the reward of earthly things. “And direct the work of our hands,” that is, charity, upon us, so that all our works may be one work of charity, because it is the end of the commandment and of all our works (1 Tim. I).

## PRAYER FROM PSALM LXXXIX

Sower of the shining star, almighty God, who, when night has been driven away, will restore new light to the world: fill us, we ask, as your mercy remits our sins, so that, with you illuminating us, we may drive away every darkness of sin. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, etc.

# PSALM XC

[Col. 0338A]

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM XC

C The Prophet foretells that every faithful person is surrounded by God’s help and announces the praise of Christ.

TT. ÷ A song of praise of David:

C A song of praise is divine praise. “Of David” here refers to Christ himself, whom the Prophet will speak of in the first part of this psalm in sweet narration. We continually oppose this hymn to demons with devout confidence, so that they may be defeated by us precisely where they attempted deceitfully to say something against the Creator.

1 Whoever dwells in the help of the Most High: In the protection of God ÷ of heaven .. he will abide.

C “Whoever dwells”—for to dwell is characteristic of one who remains and does not depart. Whoever therefore places such hope not in his own strength but establishes it in the will of the Most High is protected by the Lord of heaven. He says, “Whoever dwells here will abide there,” that is, whoever does not depart from him in this world will remain with him forever in the next.

2 He will say to the Lord: My protector ÷ are you .. and my refuge, my God: I will hope in him.

C This will be said by the one who considers useful for himself only what heavenly compassion deigns to provide. When he says “my protector,” he confirms that he has cast his entire self upon his benefits. When he says “refuge,” he declares that he has no other help; but when he is shaken by the storms of this world, he testifies that he wishes to flee for refuge to the harbor of divine [Col. 0338C] mercy.

3 For he himself will deliver me from the snare of hunters: And from a harsh word.

C “I will hope in him”: he gives the reason why he ought to hope in him, because he can free us from the tricks of enemies, whether spiritual or bodily, who set snares, like hunters, in which they can entangle the unwary through deceitful ambushes. A harsh word is every word spoken against the divine ordinances.

4 ÷ In .. his shoulders he will overshadow you: And under his wings you will hope.

C The shoulders of God are the works of miracles, through which divine power is displayed as though by certain shoulders. The wings are the admonitions of the prophets; if received with a pure mind, they lead faithful souls even to heaven. And if you ask what this overshadowing provides, I say: that the sun may not burn you by day, nor the moon by night.

5 His truth will surround you with a shield: You will not fear the terror of the night.

H Truth surrounds us as a shield, that is, Christ, by his protection, so that we are not struck by the burning arrows of the devil. “You will not fear the terror of the night,” that is, the devil, who is always in darkness so that he may strike. Or he says this: even if you are in error, which is night, nevertheless you will not fear beneath the shield of truth, because it will protect you.

6 [Col. 0339A] From the arrow flying by day: From the business moving through darkness: From the attack and the noonday demon.

C “The arrow flying by day” is the manifest persecution of tyrants. “Business in darkness”: understand it as their wicked zeal. “The noonday demon” is the greatest danger, kindled by the heat of persecution, where ruin is generally feared when human weakness is overcome. “Ruin” is so called, certainly, as though it were repeatedly returning to the lowest places.

7 A thousand will fall at your side, and ten thousand at your right hand; but it will not approach you.

C He says that a thousand will fall at his side, namely, from that height of judgment at which the saints will judge with Christ as assessors. Those fall from there who promise it to themselves through false presumption. But because few do this, he adds “ten thousand at your right hand,” because many falsely imagine that they will be placed at the right hand, although they do not possess this in their merits. “It will not approach you” means that no one who deceitfully promised himself the kingdom of God and did not hasten to the remedy of repentance will approach you. He uses a finite number for an infinite one.

8 Nevertheless, with your eyes you will consider: And you will see the recompense of sinners.

C “With your eyes”: he means that divine sight by which human merits are judged. For that consideration will be the recompense of merits. “You will see,” that is, “you will cause it to be seen.” Thus the discernment of merits in God’s judgment is called God’s observation with his eyes.

9 For you are, Lord, my hope; you have made the Most High your refuge.

C “For you are, Lord, my hope,” because, when the Lord rose again, the remaining members received hope of recompense. But the Lord Savior himself, insofar as he died, is known to have placed his refuge in the Most High; therefore the Church rightly follows his example, making him her refuge whom he himself had as his refuge.

10 Evil will not approach you: And a scourge will not come near your tabernacle.

C Although Christ endured insults from the Jews, no evil was able to approach his body. [Col. 0339D] Here “scourge” is placed for that which chastises sins; such a scourge did not approach Christ because he had nothing to be chastised or scourged. Thus there is a hypallage, because he himself did not approach evil or a scourge; the sense of the psalm’s wording is thereby transformed. “Scourge” is also used for an act deserving of scourging.

11 For he has commanded the angels ÷ [suis mandavit de te, “he commanded his angels concerning you”] ..: To guard you in all your ways.

C That it is read that the angels were commanded to guard him belongs to the weakness of human nature. Hence it is also said in the Gospel: “An angel from heaven appeared to him, strengthening him” (Luke XXII). And to declare the very perfection of his human nature, he added: “Lest you perhaps strike your foot.”

12 They will carry you in their hands: Lest you strike your foot against a stone.

C “Lest you strike,” that is, lest he stumble against the law, which seemed to have been written on stone tablets—the one who had come to teach the nations the law and evangelical doctrine (Matt. V)—that is, lest he abolish the law, but fulfill it.

13 You will walk upon the asp and the basilisk: ÷ And .. you will trample the lion and the dragon.

C These names are applied to the devil. He is an asp when he strikes secretly; a basilisk when he openly spreads poisons; a lion when he persecutes the innocent; a dragon when he swallows the negligent with impious greed. But all these creatures lay prostrate beneath the Lord’s feet at his glorious coming.

14 [Col. 0340B] Because he hoped in me, I will deliver him: I will protect him, because he has known my name.

C He therefore calls blessed the man who dwells in the help of the Most High, saying that he has been delivered because he placed his hope in his strength; and for that reason he has also been protected from all the devil’s ambushes. He knows the Father’s name who does not think that the Son is lesser than the Father.

15 He called upon me, and I will hear him: I am with him in tribulation.

C The one who calls upon the Lord is heard when he grants him rewards that will profit him. He says “I am with him” when the mind, devoted amid distress, is afflicted with greater fervor. Once delivered from this world, the righteous will indeed be glorified [Col. 0340C] when he is placed in that blessedness where tribulation will no longer have a place.

16 I will deliver him and glorify ÷ him: I will fill him with length of days: And I will show him my salvation.

C The length of days is eternal life, which no end brings to a close. “I will show him my salvation”: this is what is promised to the faithful in the supreme recompense, because they will behold Christ the Lord as salvation; there the whole desire and hope of the blessed will be fulfilled.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM XC

Grant us, Lord, through invocation of your name, to trample the deadly poisons of the asp and the basilisk, so that, once your salvation has been shown to us, we may be fortified against the enemy’s ambushes by the shelter of a spiritual shield. Through our Lord Jesus, etc.

# PSALM XCI

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM XCI

C The voice of the Church concerning the exaltation of the righteous and the destruction of the impious.

TT. A song of the psalm for the Sabbath day.

C “A song of the psalm” admonishes us that in all our actions we ought to render thanks to the divinity. The Sabbath day is interpreted as rest, through which we are reminded to cease from every evil action.

1 It is good to confess to the Lord: And to sing psalms to your name, O Most High.

H “It is good to confess”: that is, first do penance and erase your sins; then sing to the Most High.

2 [Col. 0341A] To proclaim your mercy in the morning: And your truth by night.

C Wonderfully our life has been enclosed in two expressions. “Morning” signifies joy, and then we ought to proclaim his mercies. “Night” indicates sadness, and likewise then, amid tribulations, we are commanded to proclaim his truth, because we suffer justly and deservedly. For just as mercy is shown in prosperity, by which he gives to the undeserving and is good to the wicked, so in adversity truth is displayed, by which he said that sinners would be punished.

3 On the ten-stringed psaltery: With song upon the lyre.

C The ten-stringed psaltery is the ten commandments of the Law. Song and lyre are the joy of good work, [Col. 0341B] that is, the joyful generosity of almsgiving. The lyre sings when someone accomplishes good works without the harshness of sadness.

4 For you have delighted me, Lord, in your creation: And I will rejoice in the works of your hands.

C The mother Church says that she has been delighted in the Lord’s creation because whatever good she has received she attributes not to her own merits but to her Lord. She professes that she rejoices in God’s works, not in her own happiness but in his will, as the Apostle says: “For we are his workmanship” (Eph. II).

5 How greatly your works have been magnified, Lord! Your thoughts are exceedingly deep.

C The Prophet marvels intensely at the works themselves and at the Lord’s magnificence. His thoughts have been made exceedingly deep, so that, just as the devil fell through pride, so the human race might be freed through the benefit of humility. Who could fathom this and similar things?

6 An unwise person will not know: And a fool will not understand these things.

C An unwise person is one who, emptied of heavenly wisdom, proves to be full of human cunning. Such a person does not know God’s works because he believes that what happens is accidental. Thus certain philosophers said. But a fool is certainly one who recognizes neither divine things nor even the events of the world, which we commonly call brutish.

7 When sinners have sprung up like grass: And all who work iniquity have appeared.

C Here he says that sinners flourish like grass; [Col. 0341D] but in that judgment he asserts that they will quickly perish, and when they come to judgment their hearts will appear to human eyes—hearts that could not appear here.

8 So that they may perish for an age ÷ of the age ..: But you, Most High, are forever, Lord.

C He then gives the reason why they appear: certainly not for glory, but so that they may perish. The punishment of the condemned has been beautifully explained: they do not perish in such a way that they cease to exist, but they fail for an age of the age, since they are never stripped of their afflictions. “But you, Most High”: “you will remain” must be understood. H And nothing is good except what is eternal. Whatever good has an end should not be counted among good things. For what does it profit me if I was king before the day and today die in prison? Everything that is past and has an end is nothing.

9 ÷ For .. behold, your enemies, Lord + for behold, your enemies will perish: And all who work iniquity will be scattered.

C The enemies of God are worshipers of demons and all who strive to oppose his commandments. They will be scattered when they have been separated from the Lord’s flock.

10 And my horn will be exalted like that of the unicorn: And my old age in abundant mercy.

C Here the unicorn signifies the exaltation of unity. For that unity is an exalted strength in which the glory of the saints adorns the Church. Old age has a white head; this likeness is rightly given to the Church, because all the merits of the saints will shine with the purest light, like the white hair of the head; its old age leads to perpetual life.

11 And my eye looked down upon my enemies: And my ear will hear those who rise up against me, the malicious.

C The enemies of the Church are the workers of iniquity, whom God then despises when they recognize that they have been separated onto the left-hand side. Those who rise up are the malicious rich, who here despise poverty. The ears of faithful people will hear them when they say: “What did our pride profit us?” (Wis. V).

12 [Col. 0342C] The righteous will flourish like a palm tree: He will multiply like a cedar of Lebanon.

C The righteous is rightly compared to a palm tree, for on earth it is rough; but when it has grown upward, it is filled with the sweetness of the most delightful fruits. It is called a palm as though it were “a nursling of peace.” So the life of the righteous is full of harsh labors in this world, but in the heights it is most beautiful. The cedar, a sweet-smelling wood, most suitable and strong for bearing weights, and growing much higher than the palm—the tallest of which is found in Lebanon—signifies the righteous, filled with good works.

13 Planted in the house of the Lord: In the courts of the house of our God they will flourish.

[Col. 0342D] C “Planting” here means God’s predestination, because unless someone has been planted in it, he will not possess the happiest growth. A court is called the beginning of a dwelling; the righteous will flourish there when, at that beginning of the resurrection, he rejoices at the happiness he hears, that is, when he hears: “Come, blessed ones,” and so forth.

14 They will still multiply in abundant old age: And they will be well-enduring, so that they may proclaim.

C Human old age is dry; the Church, however, then begins to be most abundant when, by the Lord’s mercy, it has been brought to the end of the age. “They will be well-enduring,” because the sufferings of the blessed win the kingdoms of heaven. And then they will proclaim that the Lord is righteous and that he is upright, and so forth.

15 [Col. 0343A] For the Lord our God is upright: And there is no iniquity in him.

C “For the Lord is upright”: he fulfilled his promises to his servants, and there is no iniquity in him, as though in this world he had permitted those whom he would not crown there with reward to be endangered through martyrdom.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM XCI

Eternal exultation of the saints, God, who makes the righteous, refreshed by varied distributions of good things, flourish unfailingly in palm-bearing courts: we ask that, once the burdens of sins have been remitted, you may graciously grant us fellowship with them. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, etc.

# PSALM XCII

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM XCII

[Col. 0343B]

C The praise of the Church concerning the Incarnation and the kingdom of Christ.

TT. ÷ A song of praise to David himself on the day before the Sabbath, when the earth was founded ..

C A song pertains to the praise of divinity. “To David himself” is applied to Christ. “On the day before the Sabbath” is the sixth day, which precedes the Sabbath. Here “earth” signifies the human being, to whom it is said: “You are earth, and into earth you will go” (Gen. III), whom the Creator formed at the beginning of created things on the sixth day.

1 The Lord has reigned; he has clothed himself with beauty: The Lord has clothed himself with strength and girded himself.

C The Prophet, considering what was to come, celebrates with great exultation that the Lord would reign. He clothed himself with beauty, that is, he displayed the splendor of his majesty, when he was transfigured on the mountain before the disciples (Matt. XVII). The Lord clothed himself with strength because he crushed the devil. H And he girded himself when, surrounded by a multitude of angels, he returned to the Father (Acts I).

2 For he established the world ÷ of the earth ..: It will not be moved.

C He established the world of the earth, that is, the Church—as in the Gospel: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matt. XVI)—which will not be moved in any way, although it is frequently harassed by persecution.

3 Your seat is prepared from that time: [Col. 0343D] You are from eternity.

C The seat is prepared, that is, the mind of the faithful; as it says (Isaiah 66): “Upon whom does my Spirit rest, unless upon the humble, trembling at my words, and quiet?” “From that time,” that is, from Christ’s Incarnation. “From eternity” indicates the divinity in Christ, which, co-eternally reigning with the Father, does not know subjection to time.

4 “The rivers have lifted up, O Lord: The rivers have lifted up their voice.”

C The Lord’s rivers are, namely, the apostles, who have drunk from the Holy Spirit; they are rightly said to have lifted up their voices, since they salutarily offered their praises to the Author.

5 [Col. 0344A] + “The rivers have lifted up their waves ..: At the voices of many waters.”

C “The rivers have lifted up their waves,” that is, the apostles have raised up their watering discourses and elevated them most holily in their preaching. “At the voices of waters” signifies the nations, who gather to the Catholic faith while praising God.

6 “The uplifts of the sea are wondrous: The Lord is wondrous in the heights.”

C “The uplifts of the sea” signifies the wise peoples in the Catholic Church; their wondrous uplifts occur when they stand firm-minded in God’s commandments. “The Lord is wondrous in the heights.” H When he sits at the right hand of the Father.

7 “Your testimonies have become exceedingly credible; [Col. 0344B] holiness befits your house, O Lord, for length of days.”

C The prophets’ testimonies have indeed become exceedingly credible because they have been revealed through the Lord’s Incarnation, though they had been held concealed in the sacred books. The house is certainly the universal Church; holiness befits it, that is, the abundant blessing of Christ’s coming, by which coming he adorns it in such a way that he never abandons it. “Length of days” signifies eternity. For, as someone has said, “There is no length in which there is an extremity.”

## PRAYER FROM PSALM 92

Almighty Lord, who, girded with paternal strength, established heaven, sea, and earth, hear your suppliants and grant faith in your testimonies; clothe us with the strength and beauty of sanctification. You who, with the Father and the Son, etc.

# PSALM 93

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM 93

C A prayer of the faithful that they may be delivered from persecutors who do not know God.

÷ TT. “A psalm of David, for the fourth day of the Sabbath ...”

C “Psalm” signifies a holy work; “the fourth day of the Sabbath” means Wednesday, the day on which the luminaries are said to have been made in the firmament of heaven. Thus the elect are founded in the Church, and this psalm tells at length of their endurance.

1 “God of retributions, the Lord: The God of retributions has acted freely.”

[Col. 0344D] C “God” is indeed a fearful name, since it derives from the Greek term signifying fear. The Lord of retributions is he who will judge the world and afflict the obstinate with just punishments. “Has acted freely,” that is, without anyone hindering him, he will judge the whole world.

2 “Exalt yourself, you who judge the earth ..: Repay retribution to the proud.”

C He was exalted before the disciples when he clearly rose in his majesty to everlasting glory. “He will judge the earth” when, by the dominion of his majesty, he judges earthly people. The proud are those who perish in their own wickedness. Retribution is therefore repaid to them when they hear: “Go into the fire.”

3 [Col. 0345A] “How long, sinners, O Lord: How long will sinners boast?”

H It is not enough for them to be sinners; they also boast in their sins. The first unhappiness is to sin; the second is not to repent at the end of life, which commonly happens to those who boast in wickedness. C On the day of judgment, if they do not reform here, they cannot boast. Therefore he says, “How long will they boast?”—as though he were saying, “Until the end of life,” because afterward boasting and wickedness will cease.

4 “They will speak forth and utter iniquity: All who practice injustice will speak.”

C Who are those who speak iniquity except those who say: “What will it profit us if we have lived justly? Or what did it profit those who lived innocently in this life, [Col. 0345B] since they died like the others?”

5 “They have humbled your people, O Lord: And they have harassed your inheritance.”

C By “the people” he means faithful men, whom he says have been humbled because they hear insults being directed against God. A devoted servant must necessarily be tormented by grief when he hears something utterly irreverent spoken about God. By “inheritance” he means Christian peoples, who are known to have been harassed by innumerable calamities at the hands of proud persecutors.

6 “They have killed the widow and the stranger: And they have slain the orphans.”

H Allegorically, the widow is the sinful soul that has lost the true God. The orphans are those who do not have God as Father, whom heretics [Col. 0345C] kill; likewise, wicked rich men afflict the other humble people.

7 “And they said: The Lord will not see: Nor will the God of Jacob understand.”

C For, in their madness, they suppose that God has not seen their evils when they sin, since they do not feel themselves swiftly struck down, while that merciful ruler cries out: “I do not desire the death of the sinner” (Ezekiel 33). “The God of Jacob” means the God of the Christian people.

8 “Understand, you senseless among the people: And you fools, become wise at last.”

C He calls senseless those who, established in the Church, rejoice in the prosperity of this age. To the fools he says, “Become wise”—that is, you who are strangers to true religion and openly blaspheme, saying that God neither [Col. 0345D] sees nor understands human deeds: you, I say, fools and madmen, take note of God’s mercy.

9 “He who planted the ear, will he not hear? Or he who fashioned the eye, does he not observe?”

C These verses should be read as a rebuke. For they show that God possesses the powers of hearing and seeing, as though he were saying: “He who planted an ear for you, will he not hear? He will indeed hear. And he who fashioned an eye for seeing, does he not see?” H Certainly he is wholly eye, because he sees everything; wholly hand, because he works everything; and whatever our members are capable of, he himself accomplishes.

10 “He who reproves the nations, will he not rebuke? He who teaches knowledge to man?”

C He who reproves the nations, that is, he who instructs the nations [Col. 0346A] through his law and prophets—will he not rebuke? He certainly will rebuke. He who teaches knowledge to man—does he himself not possess it? He possesses it, of course, because the fullness of knowledge is in God.

11 “The Lord knows the thoughts of men: For they are vain.”

C The thoughts of such men are utterly vain. The Lord knows them, because they themselves cannot know them through their own powers, being occupied with wicked thoughts. We call vain whatever departs from the truth and whatever bears no useful fruit.

12 “Blessed is the man whom you instruct, O Lord: And whom you teach from your law.”

C In contrast with the vain, “blessed” is rightly placed. For just as [Col. 0346B] those others are mocked by their fleeting thoughts, so the just are strengthened by the truth of heavenly teaching and truly become blessed, because they have received the gifts of heavenly wisdom. H Hence he is certainly happy, because he uses God as his teacher. “From the law,” that is, from the holy Scriptures. The reading of that holy Scripture also alleviates tribulations; hence it continues: “That you may soothe,” etc.

13 “That you may soothe ÷ him .. from the days of evil: Until a pit is dug for the sinner.”

C It is clear that it is a benefit of the holy law that, amid the adversities of this world, a Christian learns patience, by which all adversities are soothed for him. “The days of evil” are the present world, in which the just person, by enduring patiently, awaits adversity until an eternal pit of condemnation is prepared for all sinners [Col. 0346C].

14 “For the Lord will not reject his people: And he will not abandon his inheritance.”

C By “his people” he means the most faithful Christians, who hasten toward the Lord with the whole intention of their minds. An inheritance is human property transferred to a successor upon the death of its former owner. Yet although Christ’s inheritance was acquired by his holy blood, it never loses its author; rather, it is always possessed together with him.

15 “Until justice is turned into judgment: And who are beside it? All who are upright in heart ÷ Diapsalma ...”

C Justice will then be turned into judgment when, with the apostles seated upon twelve thrones [Col. 0346D], eternal rewards will be given to the just, and the just will judge the impious. “And who are beside it?”—he asks, namely, beside justice. He answers: “All who are upright in heart.”

16 “Who will rise up for me against the wicked? ÷ Or .. who will stand with me against those who practice iniquity?”

C For Christ testifies that God alone is his helper against wicked spirits. It should be read interrogatively: “Who will rise up?”—that is, no one will stand forth to fight the demons on my behalf, while human beings instead follow them by wicked imitation. “Or who will stand?”—that is, no one will stand in battle to fight, as though he were to be wounded by various weapons, so that he stands not by defending but by suffering.

17 [Col. 0347A] “Unless the Lord had helped me: My soul would almost have dwelt in hell.”

C He says, “Unless the Lord”—the voice of Christ in the person of his members—as though he were saying: “I would immediately have fallen into that pit in which sinners are certainly able to perish.” “My soul would almost have dwelt,” that is, my soul could have been deceived by vain persuasions, unless it had deserved to be freed by the Lord.

18 “If I said: My foot has been moved: Your mercy, O Lord, was helping me.”

C Here the benefit of very swift confession is shown: when a person confesses that he has fallen into sins, divine gifts of forgiveness immediately follow. Therefore, if I said, “My foot has been moved,” that is, “I have sinned,” as soon as I said it with a true heart, your mercy was helping me. Hastened [Col. 0347B] confession has such power that the sin is forgiven before it is punished.

19 “According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart: Your consolations have gladdened my soul.”

H “According to the multitude,” that is, as great as the weight of repentance was, so great was the number of consolations. For when I repented and endured tribulation in the present life, then I rejoiced to be consoled in the future; and the more I repented, the more you consoled me. I shed one tear and deserved one consolation; I shed ten tears and deserved ten consolations. As many wounds as we suffer, so many crowns do we also deserve; and the greatness of tribulations [Col. 0347C] is the greatness of rewards.

20 [Col. 0347D] “Does the seat of iniquity cling to you: You who fashion labor in the commandment?”

C “Does it?” must be read negatively. The seat of iniquity is the pleasurable possession of this world, which cannot cling to the Lord. For the Lord’s commandment says: “Blessed are those who mourn and those who suffer persecution for the sake of justice, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5). The Lord’s commandment in the present age contains labor and sorrow, not rest or joy, because the way that leads to life is narrow and constricted. We call “to fashion” (*fingere*) “to form,” and one who lies seems to form something for himself. Here, however, “to fashion” is attributed to God: he formed labor in the commandment. H For no one is crowned while sleeping.

21 “They will lie in wait for the soul of the just: And they will condemn innocent blood.”

C He says “they will lie in wait,” as though they will deal treacherously, because persecutors cannot find a true cause of accusation against the martyrs. “And innocent blood” can refer to Christ, because, truly innocent, he received the sentence of unjust condemnation for our redemption.

22 “And the Lord became a refuge for me: And my God a help for my hope.”

C Here he shows that human persecutions have no power against Christ or against the martyrs, and he says that divine refuge came to him especially at the time when the pride of human persecution was inflated by its zeal [Col. 0348A]. For through this the blessed crown of victory is prepared. “And my God a help for my hope.” Since here we still have hope and do not possess the reality, we leave hope for the future, because we already possess our desire.

23 “And he will repay them their iniquity: And in their wickedness he will destroy them: + He will destroy them: The Lord our God.”

C “And he will repay them,” that is, he will recompense the wicked according to the desires of their depravity. Note that the word “wickedness” encompasses every crime, just as “charity” encompasses every virtue. “He will destroy them,” that is, he will make them aliens from his kingdom.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM 93

Instruct us, O Lord, according to the benevolence of your law [Col. 0348B], and be our refuge in tribulation—you who wisely instill knowledge in human beings, so that they may not abandon it. Through our Lord Jesus, etc.

# PSALM 94

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM 94

C The prophet urges the peoples to come to the praise of God.

÷ TT. “A song of praise to David ..”

C “Praise” signifies devotion of voice; “song,” gladness of mind. Both ought to be joined together in the work of psalmody. “To David” signifies Christ, for whom this praise is sung.

1 “Come, let us exult in the Lord. Let us rejoice aloud to God our salvation.”

C “Come” is said to those who are perceived to be far away, [Col. 0348C] who have not yet joined the faithful people in the integrity of faith. There is also an exultation of this age that occupies the souls of unbelievers. Therefore he added “to God,” in whom true exultation exists. We have often said that to rejoice aloud (*jubilare*) is a great form of gladness, for which speech is insufficient.

2 “Let us anticipate his face in confession: And let us rejoice aloud to him in psalms.”

C To anticipate is to do something beforehand, before the one believed to be coming can see it. By “face” he means Christ’s appearance in judgment, so that we may confess our crimes before his judicial coming. “Let us rejoice aloud in psalms,” H that is, singing psalms in our hearts, or giving thanks.

3 “For the Lord is a great God: And a great king above all gods.”

[Col. 0348D] C By saying “for God is great,” he shows him to be more powerful than all others. Here “great” is said only of one who is shown to hold the summit of supreme power. He also calls holy men “gods,” above whom the Lord is a great king, since he creates all things and rules the universe.

4 “For in his hand are all the ends of the earth: And the heights of the mountains are his.”

C “The ends of the earth” refers to all the nations, which are subjected to Christ in faithful devotion. “The heights of the mountains” are the powers of the world and earthly honors, which nevertheless are subject to the Lord and therefore are said to be his. H For with a fist—that is, with power—he encloses the whole breadth of the earth.

5 [Col. 0349A] “For the sea is his, and he made it: And his hands formed the dry land.”

C The sea signifies the nations, which in this world are shaken by various blasts of vices. The dry land is the faithful people, still thirsting for the springs of faith, whom Christ deigned to establish by the gift of his mercy. “Let us rejoice aloud to him” should be joined to all these words.

6 “Come, let us adore and fall prostrate, and let us weep before the Lord who made us: for he is the Lord our God.”

C The prophet now urges the Christian people to make satisfaction through repentance. “Let us adore,” that is, let us bend ourselves by lowering the body. “Let us fall prostrate,” so that we may throw ourselves down before him and stretch ourselves out with the complete surrender of our limbs. To weep before God is to pour out devout [Col. 0349B] tears and condemn our wicked deeds. For if we entreat with complete purity of heart, he who made us and restores us will readily receive us. He then gives a threefold reason for this adoration: because he himself made us, etc.

7 “And we are the people of his pasture: And the sheep of his hand.”

C He says what the faithful are: certainly, the sheep of the Lord’s pasture, because by a happy lot they are satisfied with eternal delights.

8 “Today, if you hear his voice: Do not harden your hearts.”

C Here he adds one condition that must necessarily precede their being truly Christ’s sheep, saying: “Today, if you hear his voice.” For whoever [Col. 0349C] does not hear the Lord’s voice is not called his flock, nor is he placed in his pastures. “Today” is used for any time, as though he were saying: Whenever or on whatever day you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts.

9 “As in the provocation: According to the day of temptation in the desert.”

C The Jewish temptation rose up against Moses with grave murmuring, saying that neither food was given to them in the desert nor drinkable water granted by divine generosity. Therefore the guilt of their ancestors is recalled here, so that the punishment they deserve may be feared.

10 “Where your fathers tempted me: They tested and saw my works.”

[Col. 0349D] C “Where” signifies “in the desert.” There the power of God appeared, when food came from the air and drink from the rock. There they tested my works, when manna rained upon the hungry, when a multitude of quail came, and when the rock gave water (Exodus 16). “And they saw” is said as a reproach to them. For they saw and yet did not believe.

11 “For forty years I was offended by that generation: And I said: They always err in heart.”

A “Forty years” signifies the whole period of the present life. For the number ten is perfect; when it is added to the four parts of the world, it reaches forty.

12 [Col. 0350A] “And they did not know my ways: So I swore in my anger: They shall not enter into my rest.”

C “And they did not know my ways,” because during the forty-year period they refused to acknowledge God’s benefits. God is said to swear in two ways: he swears when appeased and gentle; here he is said to swear while angry, because he is known to threaten punishment. What else is it not to enter God’s rest except to receive everlasting torments? Therefore “they shall enter” must be read negatively, that is, “they shall not enter.”

## PRAYER FROM PSALM 94

O Lord, the outstanding salvation of all peoples, look graciously upon the sheep of your flock, and, imparting to them the salt of wisdom, deign to lead these same harmless [Col. 0350B] harmful (*innoxias noxias*, reading uncertain) ones into everlasting rest.

You who, with the Father and the Son and the Spirit, etc.

# PSALM 95

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM 95

C The praise of the faithful concerning Christ’s Incarnation and the exaltation of the Church.

÷ TT. “When the house was being built after the captivity, a song here to David ...”

H C This house is the universal Church, in which Christ dwells. It is built up after being destroyed when the soul, after the captivity of sin, begins, by the Lord’s help, to return to understanding the truth; nor will it cease to be built until the number of the predestined is completed at the end of the age. [Col. 0350C] H For the whole mystery of this psalm is in its title; all the sacraments and salvation of our life are in the title.

1 “Sing to the Lord a new song: Sing to the Lord, all the earth.”

C The person who, having put off the old man, is happily renewed through the grace of baptism sings a new song to the Lord. “All the earth” signifies the Catholic Church, which is known to be spread throughout the whole world. A new house deserves a new song. Let the renewed soul renew its song.

2 “Sing to the Lord and bless his name: Announce his salvation from day to day.”

C We bless God’s name when we confess in every respect that he is our salvation. He is announced from day to day [Col. 0350D] when the prophets promised Christ’s coming and the evangelists declared that he had come. Thus it is established that two heavenly days announce his glory: the Old Testament and the New. H For Christ shines in both. Do not announce him only in the Old, lest you be Jews; nor only in the New, lest you be Manichaeans; rather, praise him in both.

3 “Announce his glory among the nations: His wonders among all peoples.”

C The Lord Savior was to be announced, and his glory was also to be preached among the nations, because they proclaimed the author of so great a miracle. “His wonders” signifies the mystery of Christ’s Incarnation [Col. 0351A]: although he is most high, he became most humble for us.

4 “For the Lord is great and exceedingly worthy of praise. He is fearful above all gods.”

C “Great” pertains to power, because he is more powerful than all; “worthy of praise” pertains to mercy, because he redeemed us; “exceedingly” pertains to both, because neither how great he is nor how worthy of praise he is can be expressed. Here we should understand the gods whom paganism fashioned for itself.

5 “For all the gods of the nations are demons: But the Lord made the heavens.”

C They are demons because they bestow no good on anyone, but always deceive those who believe in them. They are called demons [Col. 0351B], as though they were “knowers.” Yet that cannot properly be called knowledge which does not obey the Creator’s will; therefore we should understand them as “knowers” in the sense of non-understanders, just as the Apostle calls the wisdom of the world foolishness (1 Corinthians 1). “The Lord made the heavens,” that is, he established the apostles and holy men, who have been accustomed to command demons.

6 “Confession and beauty are before him: Holiness and magnificence are in his sanctuary.”

C Confession is rightly followed by beauty, because no one can be beautiful unless he has been cleansed by God’s mercy. Sins make us foul, but repentance restores our beauty. “Holiness and magnificence,” that is, honor and blessedness. “In his sanctuary,” [Col. 0351C] that is, in that saying of Christ: “Come, blessed ones.” Or better, A “in the sanctification of grace,” by which he sanctifies us and thus magnifies us. Do not be magnified before being sanctified—for that is to fall—but first be sanctified, and then you will be magnified by God, not by yourself.

7 “Bring to the Lord, O families of the nations, bring to the Lord glory and honor: Bring to the Lord glory for his name.”

C “Family” (*patria*) is so called as if from “the father’s halls” (*patris atria*). “The families of the nations” signifies the entire community of Christians, which he admonishes to bring glory and honor to the Lord. Those bring glory to his name who, through devotion and good will, are changed for the better and confess the consubstantial Trinity in all things.
