For the praise and honor of the Lord is the servant’s good conduct, as the Savior says: “Let the light of your good works shine before human beings, so that your Father in heaven may be glorified” (Matthew 5).

8 “Take up sacrifices and enter his courts: Adore the Lord in his holy court.”

C By “sacrifices” he means offerings of a pure conscience. Hence not blood but devout tears flow—that is, a contrite heart. Or works of mercy. The Lord’s courts are the apostles or prophets, through whom the faithful people enter to God. Christ is truly adored when one reaches the courts of the Catholic Church.

9 [Col. 0352A] “Let all the earth be moved before his face; Say among the nations ÷ that .. the Lord has reigned.”

C The earth is moved when the sinner, abandoning earthly vices, is led by the Lord’s mercy to repentance. “The Lord has reigned” through the trophy of the cross among the human race. Hence the Roman translation made from the Seventy Interpreters has: “He has reigned from the wood.” Or, “he has reigned,” that is, he appeared in the flesh as one who would reign, though he has always reigned. H Or, he has reigned in souls moved by repentance.

10 “For he has corrected the world of the earth, which will not be moved: He will judge the peoples in equity.”

C He corrected the world when, through the rule of faith [Col. 0352B], he converted the hearts of the pagans. The world, namely, will not be moved because it remains firm in the solidity of true faith. By “the peoples” he wishes the faithful to be understood; they will be judged under the tranquility of heavenly mercy when he restores to them the promised rewards. Equity pertains to the blessed, anger to the everlasting punishments of the impious.

11 “Let the heavens rejoice and let the earth exult; let the sea be moved and its fullness: The fields and all that is in them will rejoice.”

C “The heavens” means the apostles, prophets, and preachers; “the earth,” converted hearers; “the sea,” the world. By “the fields” he means men who are not swollen with pride, nor harsh with anger, but gentle [Col. 0352C] and filled with meekness, who rejoice when they have received the gifts of a good way of life. “All things” signifies the universal multitude of the nations.

12 “Then all the trees of the forest will exult before the face of the Lord, for he has come: + For he has come: to judge the earth.”

C “Then they will exult,” that is, at Christ’s second coming, when he is about to judge the world. All the trees of the forest—that is, the nations, which had previously been barren like trees of the forest but will then be brought to fruitful cultivation—will rejoice with great joy before the face of the Lord. “For he has come”: by this he wished us to understand only that coming which we are still known to await. H Therefore these trees will certainly rejoice because they are not liable to burning; [Col. 0352D] for he will subject sinners to punishments and reward the just with everlasting prizes.

13 “He will judge the world of the earth in equity: And the peoples in his truth.”

He came first to be judged; afterward he will come to judge.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM 95

God, maker of heaven and earth, creator whom the whole earth celebrates with the melody of a new song, we ask that, just as we suppliantly confess you reigning from the wood, so, having abandoned every error of paganism, we may await with attentive minds the glory of your future coming. You who, with the Father and the Son, etc.

# PSALM 96

[Col. 0353A]

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM 96

C The prophet speaks of Christ’s first coming, urging the faithful to rejoice in it and rebuking those who venerate idols.

÷ TT. “A psalm to David: when his land was restored.”

C David’s land is Christ’s flesh, which, after the sleep of death according to the common law, was restored to glory through the singular gift of the resurrection. Or certainly, the land is the Church, that is, the mystical body of Christ, namely, all the faithful.

1 “The Lord has reigned; let the earth exult: Let the many islands rejoice.”

C The Lord has reigned; therefore who else is to be worshiped [Col. 0353B] except him who alone is known to rule? “Let the earth exult,” that is, the human race in its restoration. “Let the islands rejoice,” that is, the churches of the nations. He says “many,” not “all,” because of heretical perversions.

2 “Clouds and darkness surround him: Justice and judgment are the correction of his throne.”

C In this verse the Lord’s character toward the impious and the religious is described. He is cloudy and dark to the irreverent, while their dark hearts shine with no brightness. “Justice and judgment are the correction of his throne,” that is, of those who believe in him and have deserved to become his throne; they are rightly called “correction,” because, stripped of perversity, they have become upright and the throne of God.

3 “Fire will go before him: And it will burn his enemies round about.”

[Col. 0353C] C Fire went before the Lord’s coming when the hearts of unbelievers raged at the preaching of the prophets, so that, kindled by the heat of anger, they plotted the death of the preachers. “It will burn,” namely, the impious against the elect. “Round about,” because, while the elect were few, an innumerable multitude of adversaries surrounded them.

4 “His lightning flashes have illuminated the world of the earth: The earth saw and was moved.”

C “His lightning flashes have illuminated it,” that is, the preaching of the prophets or the miracles of the holy. “The earth was moved,” that is, earthly people were terrified by the novelty of the preaching, so that they understood themselves to be worshiping senseless idols while they possessed the supreme Creator, worthy of adoration.

5 [Col. 0353D] “The mountains melted like wax before the face of the Lord: + Before the face of the Lord .. all the earth.”

C “The mountains melted,” that is, the powerful of this age were humbled once they came to know the Lord. “All the earth,” that is, the powers of the age, whether pagans or heretics, who, called away from error by the Lord and condemning their superstitious devotion, choose rather to submit to divine service.

6 “The heavens announced his justice: And all peoples saw his glory.”

C “The heavens” means the apostles or preachers, through whose holy preaching God’s justice became known to the world. “They saw” must be understood here not with bodily eyes but by the light of the heart; for glory is usually heard, not [Col. 0354A] seen. Or, as some wish, “they saw glory,” that is, Christ, who is the Father’s glory.

7 “Let all who adore graven images be confounded: Those who glory in their idols.”

C Here he rebukes the worshipers of idols. An idol is so called because it is itself a trick (*dolus*), that is, something discovered through human falsehood. An image (*simulacrum*) is composed from imitation (*simulatio*) of sacred things, because an alien honor is given to it. Thus both are shown to be avoided by the interpretation of their very names.

8 “Adore him, all his angels: Sion heard and rejoiced.”

C Let the good angel adore God, who recognizes his creator with an upright heart and does not allow himself to be worshiped by human beings. But the evil angel eagerly [Col. 0354B] seeks to be worshiped (Revelation 19). “Sion heard,” that is, the Catholic Church received the Lord’s judgments with a pure heart and therefore rejoiced. For whoever hears God’s word with a deceitful mind departs sad, because he hears what he does not believe against his will (Matthew 4).

9 “And the daughters of Judah exulted. Because of your judgments, O Lord.”

C The daughters of Judah signify devout minds and approved persons. They are called the daughters of Judah because they preferred to confess and believe in Christ, who descended from Judah. “Because of your judgments,” namely, because you turn the sadness of your servants into joy and cast down the proud devil before them through the strength of humility.

10 “For you, Lord, are most high above all [Col. 0354C] the earth: You are exceedingly exalted above all gods.”

C Here “earth” means sinners; “gods,” just human beings. Through these two terms he signifies that Christ rules both earthly creatures and heavenly beings.

11 “You who love the Lord, hate evil: ÷ The Lord .. guards the souls of his saints; he will deliver them from the hand of sinners.”

C Here he addresses the good and the faithful, so that they may be separated from the devil’s wickedness. He is rightly called evil, since through him all evil came. And lest anyone fear offending the devil, it follows: “The Lord guards the souls of the saints.” He also frees souls from the hand of sinners when he does not allow them to be overthrown by any wickedness. [Col. 0354D] Yet lest you understand that the Lord guards the bodies of the saints from punishments—for he often hands them over to punishments in order to give martyrs their crowns—he said “the souls of the saints.”

12 “Light has arisen for the just: And joy for the upright in heart.”

C He says that light has arisen for the just, that is, the most true faith, so that the enlightened person may believe such things as lead him to the kingdom of heaven. Joy arises for the upright in heart when, by God’s favor, they do such things as they know will benefit them.

13 “Rejoice, you just, in the Lord: And confess the memory of his holiness.”

C Here he urges the just to rejoice not in human desire or in the ruinous boasting of this age [Col. 0355A], but in the Lord. The just confess the memory of his holiness when they have been placed in that everlasting kingdom, remembering from how great a calamity of this age they were rescued by God’s mercy.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM 96

God, guardian of holy souls, whose kingdom is the perfect portion of the just, grant that prophetic and evangelical flashes may be implanted in our hearts; and if anything is covered by an ancient veil, let it be opened when the Holy Spirit reveals it. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son, etc.

# PSALM 97

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM 97

C The prophet urges the Christian people to rejoice with the exultation of a new song when the wondrous [Col. 0355B] coming of Christ has been granted.

÷ TT. “A psalm to David:”

1 “Sing to the Lord a new song: For he has done wondrous things.”

C The new man ought to sing a new song, not the old man who, having not yet laid aside Adam’s sins, persists in them. The new song is to relate or sing of the Lord’s Incarnation. It is new because the world has never heard anything like it. He did wondrous things when he gave light to the blind and movement to the lame.

2 “His right hand saved him: And his holy arm.”

H Christ is called the right hand and the arm. “Right hand” is used here for virtue; “arm” for strength. [Col. 0355C] By his right hand he himself saved humanity for salvation, humanity that had perished through its own fault. C Or, he saved himself, who said: “I have authority to lay down my life and to take it up again” (John 10).

3 “The Lord made his salvation known; in the sight of the nations he revealed his justice.”

B “The Lord made his salvation known,” that is, the Lord Savior, who is rightly called salvific because he is the author of all salvation. “And he revealed his justice,” that is, Christ, who had previously been proclaimed by the prophets under a certain veil. When that veil was removed at his coming, the very face of truth appeared. H Or, the justice of life, which had been obscured by human unbelief.

4 “He remembered his mercy: [Col. 0355D] And his truth toward the house of Israel.”

H “He remembered his mercy” with regard to the people of the nations. “And his truth” with regard to the people of the Jews, fulfilling by his work what he had promised to the patriarchs.

5 “All the ends of the earth saw: The salvation of our God.”

C “All saw,” that is, they perceived with the mind what is known to have been accomplished throughout the whole world. This vision must be referred only to faith, so that the truth of the words may be established for us; through faith all the ends of the earth saw Jesus.

6 “Shout joyfully to the Lord, all the earth: Sing and exult and sing psalms.”

[Col. 0356A] C “Shout joyfully” means to leap forth into the joy of the voice with great delight. “All the earth” designates the universal Church. To sing is to resound with praises through the office of the mouth; to exult is to declare the heart’s desires with great love; to sing psalms is to fulfill God’s commandments through good works.

7 “Sing psalms to the Lord on the lyre, ÷ on the lyre .. and with the voice of a psalm: With ÷ hammered .. trumpets and with the voice of a horn trumpet.”

H He sings psalms to the Lord on the lyre who presents himself as chaste in all his members. The sound of a lyre cannot be perfect if one string is missing; likewise, if a person is subject to one capital crime, he does not sing psalms to the Lord on the lyre, because one string is missing and the sound of the lyre is not perfect. C The voice of a psalm also pertains to [Col. 0356B] divine praise. “Hammered trumpets” signifies the faithful, who, struck by various sufferings, sounded more clearly by God’s generosity. The voice of a horn trumpet is steadfast endurance in patience, which persists like a horn.

8 “Shout joyfully before the Lord the King: Let the sea and its fullness be moved: The world ÷ of the earth and those who dwell in it:”

*[The supplied source ends here, mid-sentence.]*
C He said that they should rejoice; now he shows where: before the king. The sea is moved when, at the future judgment, the hearts of the wicked are shaken by the recollection of their sins. “And its fullness” is rightly said, because they have committed many sins. The world will be moved when it comes into a new form, as it was foretold: “There will be a new heaven and a new earth” (2 Peter 3). “And those who dwell in it,” that is, human beings.

9 [Col. 0356C] The rivers shall clap their hands together: the mountains shall exult before the Lord: for he has come to judge the earth.

C “Rivers” signifies holy men, who have flowed forth with the heavenly abundance of good works. “Together,” that is, with the Lord Savior, to whom they have presented the works mentioned above. H “Mountains”: the apostles. C They shall exult before the Lord at the future judgment, because he has come—namely, to judge sinners, who always desire earthly vices and are therefore rightly called “earth.”

10 He shall judge the world ÷ of the earth .. in righteousness, and the peoples in equity.

C These are to be judged under righteousness: those who will not be freed from their obstinacy by any remission. Those peoples, however, are to be judged in equity, because there they receive rewards who here endured the gravest dangers for the Lord’s name. [Col. 0356D]

PRAYER FROM PSALM 97

Send forth, Lord, your salvation into our minds. You who have revealed your righteousness to all the nations, grant that you, who once came to be judged on behalf of the lost, may, when you come, bestow mercy on behalf of those for whom you were judged. You who live and reign with the Father and the Son, etc.

PSALM 98

ARGUMENT OF PSALM 98

C The Prophet urges the peoples to confess Christ the Lord and to adore him, because he is gracious toward his faithful.

[Col. 0357A] TITLE. ÷ A psalm of David ..:

C In David we discern both the person speaking and perceive Christ, strong-handed and desirable. For in this psalm his honor, kingship, and power are sung.

1 The Lord reigns; let the peoples be angry; he who sits upon the Cherubim: let the earth be moved.

C When the psalm says, “The Lord reigns,” it explains that he has displayed the glory of his resurrection. For the one who rose again is himself the one who reigns. “Let the peoples be angry”: H either the Jews or the Gentiles who do not believe, C though they can do Christ no further harm. “Cherubim” is Hebrew and signifies fullness of knowledge, where God is manifested as sitting, as it were, upon his throne. “Let the earth be moved”: he calls sinners to be shaken toward conversion; H for as long as the earth—that is, the sinner—is immovable, he cannot be healed. But when he has been moved and trembles because of his sins, he receives healing. Hence it is said elsewhere: “Heal its contrition, for it has been moved” (Psalm 59).

2 The Lord is great in Zion: and exalted above all peoples.

C Zion is interpreted as “watchtower,” that is, the Church, in which the Lord is shown to be spiritually present. And he whom they despised with perverse mind rises as king, exalted above all peoples.

3 Let them confess to your great name, for it is fearful and holy; and the honor of the king loves judgment.

[Col. 0357C] C The name of Christ is called great because it has been proclaimed everywhere; fearful, because he himself will come to judge the living and the dead; holy, because he remained immaculate and heavenly in his way of life. “The honor of the king” is the glorious proclamation that we always offer him by confessing his just judgment. Or, “loves”: the honor—that is, the worship by which we honor God—loves and seeks attentive consideration, deliberation, judgment of oneself and lowliness, together with reverence for God.

4 You prepared straight paths; you performed judgment and righteousness in Jacob.

II God prepared ordinances among the peoples, but they were distorted by their own fault. C He performed judgment among the faithful people when he granted them the ability to distinguish good from evil; and righteousness when, having abandoned idols, they deserved to serve their Creator. “In Jacob,” that is, in each faithful person. [Col. 0357D]

5 Exalt the Lord our God, and adore his footstool, for it is holy.

The Prophet admonishes devoted peoples, by his preaching, to magnify and exalt the Lord’s name and to adore his footstool, H A C that is, the body of Christ, which he assumed from the Virgin Mary. C “Footstool” signifies the humanity of the divinity. “His feet” signifies the stability of the divinity. “For it is holy,” namely, the body of Christ, and glorious and worthy of adoration.

6 Moses and Aaron among his priests, and Samuel among those who invoke his name.

C “Moses and Aaron among his priests”—although Moses is nowhere else read to have been a priest. H And although one of them held the rule of the law and the other of the priesthood, nevertheless both, by priestly proclamation, announced the Lord’s coming, whether through legal observances or through your little bells.

C Samuel anointed David as king, yet he did not receive the office of priest, because he was of the tribe of Ephraim, from which priests could not be made. Therefore he is placed here not among the priests but among those who invoke the Lord’s name. He was, however, a Levite, because he wore that linen ephod. H This signifies that one can be made white who, invoking God’s name through repentance, has washed away the blackness of sin with tears. [Col. 0358B]

7 They invoked the Lord, and he heard them; he spoke to them in the pillar of cloud.

C How powerful the sincerity of prayer is has been stated briefly: those who faithfully invoked God, he effectively heard. At that time he spoke to them in the pillar of cloud; but for us he has deigned both to speak and to appear through the holy footstool, that is, through the Incarnation.

8 They kept his testimonies and the commandment that he gave them.

C He gives the reasons why the Lord deigned to hear them. Christ truly loves the one who keeps his commandments, as he himself says: “If you love me, keep my commandments” (John 14). Here “testimony” means a signification established through certain signs of a preceding event, as he said in the Law: “This shall be a testimony for you” (Deuteronomy 6). [Col. 0358C]

9 Lord our God, you heard them; God, you were gracious to them, and taking vengeance upon ÷ all .. their inventions.

C By saying, “You heard them; you were gracious to them,” he shows that the desires of the saints were fulfilled in good petitions. And “taking vengeance upon all,” etc., lest human exaltation be able to steal upon them. For although some are holy and faithful men, nevertheless it is necessary that punishment be exacted in them in due measure, lest their heart appear able to be led into pride. By “their inventions,” understand their pursuits and their deficient works. H Or take “taking vengeance” in a good sense, so that God is understood to take vengeance upon their inventions—that is, to act against their inventions—because their actions and inventions were pleasing to the Lord. [Col. 0358D]

10 Exalt the Lord our God and adore him on his holy mountain, for the Lord our God is holy.

C It must be noted that he commands the holy Lord to be adored on the holy mountain, because, just as his praise does not suit a perverse mouth, so the shamefulness of a place cannot be appropriate to his worship.

PRAYER FROM PSALM 98

Lord of the exalted throne, we entreat and beseech you: grant that, while the pillar of light shines upon us, we may, with you as our guardian, preserve the order of the priesthood. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, etc.

PSALM 99

ARGUMENT OF PSALM 99

C The Prophet admonishes the whole world to praise the Lord with rejoicing.

TITLE. A psalm ÷ of David in confession ...

C “Confession” is called almost *confacio*, whether it is repentance or the praise of many celebrated by the mouth. It is so called for this reason: to show that it now pertains to many. It is well known that *con* signifies “together.”

1 Rejoice in God, all the earth; serve the Lord with gladness.

C Rejoicing is to be moved by great joy of mind, though not to burst forth into articulate words, and to serve the Lord amid delight. “All the earth” is not to be referred to the soil but is allegorically understood as human beings. This gladness is certainly charity, of which the Apostle says: “It is not puffed up, it does not act improperly” (1 Corinthians 13). We must not serve the Lord while murmuring, for in that way we do not love God.

2 Enter into his presence with exultation.

H “Enter”: do not dissolve yourselves in shameful amusements, but do everything you do for the glory of God. “With exultation,” C that is, so that then you may take joy in humility, when he is proved to be fearful to all the proud.

3 Know that the Lord himself is God; [Col. 0359C] he himself made us, and not we ourselves.

C “Know,” that is, understand, O Jews, that this Lord, whom you in no way believed to be the Son of God, is himself God, who made heaven and earth and also formed us in his own image. H And he recreated us not only bodily but as a new human being; and this was not by our merit but by his gift.

4 We are his people and the sheep of his pasture. Enter his gates with confession, his courts with hymns; confess to him.

H He comes to the faithful people, showing by beautiful comparisons what they are. “Sheep,” because they are simple and he himself is their true shepherd. “Of his pasture,” that is, the sweet feast of the divine Scriptures. The Lord’s gates are humble repentance, holy baptism, charity, and other good and holy works. “His courts”—here you should supply “enter”—signifies the prophets and evangelists and all who preached rightly. Their words are clearly the Lord’s courts, because through them and through those words one goes to him, and he himself, if sought with devoted mind, is found in them. [Col. 0359D]

5 Praise his name, for the Lord is sweet; his mercy is everlasting, and his truth is from generation to generation.

C He gives the reason why Christ’s name should be proclaimed and praised: because he is sweet. For this sweetness does not know satiety. “Everlasting,” because once he has bestowed the eternal goods that are to come, they are always preserved unharmed by him. “Age of age,” or “from generation to generation.” This signifies both the age now being lived and the age that we believe will come: the age in the joy of the blessed. In that age God’s truth is fulfilled, and his promises are completed in the truth of the homeland.

PRAYER FROM PSALM 99

We rejoice in you, eternal Lord, with gladness and exultation, asking that, while the gates of our hearts are opened in your praises, they may always be opened to mercy and truth. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, etc.

PSALM 100

ARGUMENT OF PSALM 100

C The Church of God sings of judgment and mercy and rejoices that it dwells not with the wicked but with the faithful.

TITLE. A psalm of David himself.

C Where “of David himself” is placed, everything is applied to the virtues of Christ, so that you may understand nothing as referring to that earthly king but recognize that everything was spoken of the heavenly one.

1 I shall sing of mercy and judgment to you, Lord.

2 I shall sing and understand in the spotless way: when will you come to me?

C Let sinners who despair of salvation hear the merciful Lord; let the proud, who do not consider their evil worthy of punishment, understand the judge. In these two expressions the whole work of God and the edification of the entire Church are shown to have been described. [Col. 0360C] For all God’s works are mercy and judgment, that is, truth; in these two all virtues are comprehended. H The Prophet admonishes everyone to understand what he sings, to contemplate the sense of the psalm, and not to let the mind wander outward, so that the mouth may appear to sing while the mind remains without fruit. “In the spotless way,” C because Christ had no sins and walked through this world with spotless steps. Therefore he says: “I shall walk in this world without stain, so that the spotless one may come to me.” H “When will you come?” He speaks of his second coming, when the returning Lord will inquire into human deeds.

3 I walked in the innocence of my heart, in the midst of my house.

[Col. 0360D] H Nothing pleases God so much as simplicity and innocence. C From this it is understood that, because of its most pleasing simplicity, the Holy Spirit appeared in the form of a dove; and because of his gentleness, the Son of God chose to be called a lamb. Through this he signified that eternal Wisdom dwells in peaceful and humble hearts.

4 I did not set an unjust thing before my eyes. I hated those who commit transgressions.

5 A perverse heart did not cling to me; I did not know the malicious person who turned away from me.

C Therefore the holy congregation rightly says that it did not set an unjust thing before the eyes of its heart, since it had excluded it from the innermost recesses of its mind. Indeed, we rightly deny seeing those things upon which we do not gaze with any pleasure. “I hated transgressions,” because I continually regarded human transgressions as hateful. For although they come before our face, they are nevertheless not in the sight of our mind. [Col. 0361A]

C A perverse heart cannot cling unless it has been bound by the cords of sins. “The one who turned away from me,” that is, the heretic who dissents from the Catholic faith through perverse doctrines, “I did not know.” Even if he claims to have been baptized, divine love is not recognized in him, since he is proved blasphemous by the Lord. H Or, “the malicious one” may be understood as any bad Christian.

6 The one who secretly slanders his neighbor: him I persecuted.

C The heretic slanders secretly when he tears apart an absent Catholic by some insult, not daring to contend openly because he knows that he is defending irrational claims. He says that such people must be pursued, so that they may be stirred to the pursuit of truth. H Or understand this of anyone who slanders.

7 The one with a proud eye and an insatiable heart: I did not eat with him.

C He has a proud eye who is excessively swollen with perverse will. He has an insatiable heart (1 Corinthians 5) who does not withdraw from blasphemies. He says that such people must be avoided to such an extent that we must not even enter into a meal with them, lest the ears of Christians be polluted by detestable speech.

8 My eyes were upon the faithful of the land, that they might sit with me; the one walking in the spotless way served me here.

C The holy congregation now professes that it joins the eyes of its heart to the saints whom it turned away from the worst people. The faithful of the land are Christians who dwell throughout the world and sit together in the unity of faith. “Walking in the way”: this is the true and evident proof of Christians—to shine in one’s life and to rejoice in the conduct of good ministers, as he said above: “With the holy you will be holy” (Psalm 17). Although this has not been excluded from laypeople, it is nevertheless shown to have been imposed especially upon priests, so that they may have as ministers men who do not oppose the divine rules.

9 The one who practices pride shall not dwell in the midst of my house; the one who speaks iniquity has not prospered in the sight of my eyes.

C The faithful people deny that they had any share with the proud. From this we learn that we must exercise such judgments over our subjects that we never favor the worst people, nor let those seem pleasing to us who must be avoided because of the perversity of their conduct. “Has not prospered,” that is, has not advanced. We call those “prospering” who improve by drawing near or become better through some prosperity. This does not happen to those who devote themselves to walking along crooked paths.

10 At dawn I destroyed all the sinners of the earth, so that I might destroy from the city of the Lord all who practice iniquity.

[Col. 0362A] C After saying that he had fled the company of the wicked, he now explains how he expelled that tyrannical part from his innermost being—namely, the perverse suggestion of demons. “At dawn”: at the very beginnings, that is, when diabolical suggestions begin to appear to us like uncertain twilight. They must then be driven out by prayer, lest, gradually increasing in their harmfulness, they seize us like a most cloudy day. “The sinners of the earth” are demons, who are rightly called this because they make others sinners. The “city of God,” the fathers said, is the devout soul. The devil is destroyed from it when he is removed from his purpose. [Col. 0362B]

PRAYER FROM PSALM 100

Incomprehensible in power, O God, who mercifully impress upon your servants mercy and judgment, grant us to understand faithfully, to enter the right way, and to turn away from the vanity of detestable pride. Through our Lord Jesus, etc.

PSALM 101

ARGUMENT OF PSALM 101

C The Prophet speaks in the person of any poor righteous man, so that the Lord may attend to his prayers.

TITLE. The prayer of the poor man when he is anxious and pours out his prayer before the Lord.

H The poor man is the Christian—not one lacking the riches of this world, but poor in spirit. C Or also one needy in this age but rich in God, empty of vices and full of virtues. He is anxious who, placed in grave danger, does not know which course he ought to choose. “Before the Lord”: he wants us to understand such a prayer as is poured out from the purses of the soul before the royal feet, beautiful as though by an abundance of golden metal.

1 Lord, hear my prayer, and let my cry come to you.

C Seeing human errors increase before the Lord’s coming, the Prophet appropriately assumed the person of the poor man. First he placed “prayer” and added “cry,” so that you might recognize that the practice of supplication had grown, and perceive that his prayer had burst forth into a cry.

2 Do not turn your face away from me; on whatever day I am troubled, incline to me ÷ your ear

2 ..

C This poor man therefore begs that he not be made a stranger to God’s presence. “On whatever day,” that is, at whatever time he was pressed by the wounds of sins or when the detestable enemy oppressed him. “Incline your ear,” that is, grant a hearing. God’s ear stands for his clemency, by which he graciously hears the prayers of suppliants. For “ear” derives its name from hearing. Although he sees and hears everyone, he is nevertheless said to hear only those to whom he deigns to show favor.

3 On whatever day I call upon you, hear me swiftly.

H He prays “on whatever day” for present distresses, so that he may be rescued from them by divine contemplation. C And now he asks more confidently that he may deserve to be heard more quickly. For one who asks for speed does not distrust his clemency.

4 For my days have failed like smoke, and my bones have dried like kindling.

C Therefore the days of sinners are rightly compared to smoky globes. This especially refers to the pride of the world, which, the more it is lifted up like smoke, the more completely it vanishes. H “Bones” signifies the strength of the soul. If what is strong in me has dried up and become weak, how much more will what is naturally weak, such as flesh, do so. C For one who fears that he will burn in the future is already chilled by fear of that fire, as though in a frying pan.

5 I have been struck like grass, and my heart has dried up, because I forgot to eat my bread.

[Col. 0363B] C The human race is well compared to grass, which possesses the joy of greenness but, once struck, quickly feels injury. So long as we stand in God’s law, we flourish like very green grass; but as soon as we have been cut down from his commandments by the devil’s sickle, we immediately wither. He also gives the reason why his heart dried up: he did not eat the spiritual bread, that is, Christ, because of sin.

6 From the sound of my groaning my bone has clung to my flesh.

C This poor man was afflicted by that groaning, while lovers of the world rather mocked him. Therefore he added “my,” to show that he had been withdrawn from worldly desires. II Let penitents learn from this poor man how to perform repentance. Let them consider what he says: “It has clung,” etc., as though he had said: “I so afflicted myself that I was without flesh.” And “my skin clung to my bones”: he said “flesh” for “skin.”

7 I have become like a pelican of the wilderness; I have become like a night-raven in a dwelling.

C The pelican is an Egyptian bird, similar to storks in the size of its body. It consoles itself in solitary pleasure and is always wasted by natural thinness; for, with its intestine stretched through its innards, whatever food it takes passes through without any digestion. It signifies hermits. The night-raven, that is, the nocturnal crow, which some call an owl and others a screech owl, seeks food at night. So too the penitent, in this nocturnal time, seeks food for the soul by chanting, keeping himself in a dwelling withdrawn from public view.

8 I kept vigil and became like a solitary sparrow on the roof.

C The sparrow is a small bird, watchful with keen intelligence and not easily caught in snares. It runs to the roofs of houses so that it may not lose its young. Those who betake themselves to the enclosures of God’s Church, keep watch on its height, and persevere there in greatest safety are compared to it. These birds, differing in kind and unlike in the character of their habits, are compared to human beings by hyperbole. This argument is called “from greater to lesser”: a human being is greater than a sparrow.

9 All day long my enemies reproached me, and those who praised me swore against me.

C It is clearly the devil’s malice that servants of God whom tyrants cannot overcome by open threats are bent rather by mocking reproach. For it is the custom of the perverse first to praise good people in secular life and afterward, when they see them afflicted by repentance, to condemn them with an oath.

10 For I ate ashes like bread, and I mixed my drink with weeping.

Christ ate ashes as bread because he turned repentant sinners toward himself. C Or, “ashes,” that is, I consumed the remnants of sins and small sins through true repentance, so that nothing might remain that would impede the merit of the kingdom of heaven. “And my drink”: then that heavenly drink enters the innermost chambers of my soul when it is watered by devout weeping. H Or, I dipped my bread in ashes and thus ate it. If the Prophet did this, what should we do? “And I mixed my drink with tears”: nothing was sweet to me, neither bread nor drink; I desired only forgiveness and Christ, the heavenly bread.

11 Because of the face of your anger and indignation, for, lifting me up, you dashed me down.

C Anger and indignation do not have a bodily face, but they always appear under an imagined form to those who fear. Anger pertains to vengeance; indignation to a moderate movement of the mind. God lifts sinners up by his benefits when he bestows wealth and grants honor to them; and when they are exalted by this, he takes everything away, so that they may not perish but may be humbled and recognize from whom they had received those things.

12 My days have declined like a shadow, and I have withered like grass.

C This penitent very beautifully said that, after Adam’s transgression, his days had declined, because he himself had turned away from the Lord. Each person is diminished in proportion as he is separated from that fullness of light. It therefore followed that the days of one who was declining should wither like grass: when the life-giving benefit by which he was nourished is withdrawn, he is brought into the dryness of sin.

13 But you, Lord, remain forever, ÷ and your memorial from generation .. to generation.

[Col. 0364D] C After a most worthy satisfaction for sins, the penitent comes to the praises of God. This poor man began his praise with the Lord’s coming, through which he knew that the world was to be saved. “Memorial” was spoken of the saving promise concerning the future Incarnation of the Lord; it endures through endless ages, and no forgetfulness can change it.

14 You will arise and have mercy on Zion, because the time of having mercy on it has come + because the time ...

C He is said to “arise” as though from sleep, because he had delayed coming to its aid for so long. Zion is a mountain by which the Church is signified. God had mercy on it when he gathered it from the nations and founded it upon his teaching. [Col. 0365A] H Therefore let the one who practices repentance have confidence, because the time of having mercy and saving has come.

15 For its stones have pleased your servants, and they will have mercy on its earth.

C He calls the apostles the Lord’s servants. These regarded its stones—that is, Christians—as pleasing when they saw their preaching bearing fruit among them. “They will have mercy on its earth,” because through God’s grace those who had tasted only earthly things and were soiled by earthly stain were to be cleansed.

16 And the nations shall fear your name, Lord, and all the kings of the earth your glory.

C After the Lord’s saving coming had shone forth, the nations were converted through fear. Those who remain firm in the faith also recognize the Lord’s glory most truly. For kings are those who rightly govern their bodies, restraining them with divine rules. H Or, kings who once feared idols and invoked the names of demons will now venerate your name.

17 For the Lord has built Zion, and he will be seen in his glory.

C Zion has been built—that is, the mother Church has been constructed from living stones. This same Lord who built Zion will be seen in his glory when, on the day of judgment, he separates the goats from the lambs (1 Peter 2).

18 He has regarded the prayer of the humble and has not despised their supplication.

C He also says that the Lord has regarded the prayer of the poor, that is, of the faithful, because he beholds all incorporeal things, and nothing is hidden from his eyes. This is what it means for him to regard it: namely, not to despise it.

19 Let these things be written for another generation, and the people who will be created shall praise the Lord.

H “Let these things be written for another generation,” that is, in the New Testament; and the people—namely, the Christian people—who had previously been dead in sins and were recreated in it through the grace of baptism, this people shall praise the Lord. C In a new song, namely, as in: “Sing to the Lord a new song.”

20 For he looked down from his holy height; the Lord looked from heaven ÷ upon .. the earth.

C “He looked down from his height,” that is, from heaven, when he assumed the frailty of our humanity. From there he looked upon the earth, that is, upon the frailty of our body, which was held subject to the vices of the world. [Col. 0365D]

21 To hear the groaning of the prisoners, to set free the sons of the slain.

C Those prisoners or bound men are holy men bound by the chains of the commandments. The Lord deigned to hear them groaning and crying out to him, so that by the benefit of his compassion he might release the world entangled in its own sins and, by divine strength, free the sons of those who had been slain—those who had been killed by the devil’s deceit—from their fathers’ errors.

22 To declare the Lord’s name in Zion and his praise in Jerusalem.

C The name of the Lord Christ was proclaimed in Zion when there the apostles first spoke of God’s mighty works in various languages (Acts 2). From this it happened that, from the local Jerusalem, the complete commandments of God flowed throughout the universal Church. [Col. 0366A]

23 When peoples and kings are gathered together as one, to serve the Lord.

24 He answered him in the way of its strength: Make known to me the fewness of my days.

C He therefore says that peoples come together as one, so that the strength of Catholic unity may be shown. He adds “kings,” or, as another translation has it, “the kingdoms of the earth,” so that they may serve the Lord of heaven. They are then freer, when they have been bound to their Creator in faithful service.

C The holy Church, established in tribulations, answered Christ calling it to holy works of virtue. “In the way of his strength,” that is, in its religion: not with the tongue but with life; not with the voice but with faith; not with shouting but with the heart. It desires to know the end of the age, so that it may soon deserve to reach that blessedness which the Lord promised. It calls all the Church’s days up to the end of the age “few days,” looking toward eternity, because whatever must come to an end should not be called long.

25 Do not take me away in the middle of my days; your years are from generation to generation.

C He is taken away in the middle of his days who returns to his former sins. “The middle of his days” signifies youth itself, in which slippery pleasure is sought and, through the ardor of age, crimes are loved more intensely. “By years,” understand the Lord’s eternity.

26 In the beginning ÷ you, Lord .. founded the earth, and the works of your hands ÷ are .. the heavens.

C By saying “in the beginning,” he shows that the Creator existed before his creatures, without any beginning of his own. By “hands” we should understand the power of his command, as it is written: “He spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created” (Psalm 32).

27 They will perish, but you remain; and all things will grow old like a garment.

H “They will perish,” in accordance with the saying: “Heaven and earth will pass away” (Matthew 24). C “But you will remain,” in the glory of majesty. “Garment” seems to be applied to the frailty of the flesh; for what grows old like a garment is consumed by death.

28 And as a covering you will change them, and they will be changed; [Col. 0366D] but you are ÷ the same .. yourself, and your years will not fail.

C We should perhaps understand the heavens as the “covering,” since, in the manner of a veil, they cover the earth. They too will be changed like other things, afterward to remain under eternity. “The same” is set against what was said, because while those things are changeable, the Lord always remains unchangeable.

29 The sons of your servants shall dwell, and their offspring shall be directed forever.

C By “sons” he means the disciples of the apostles, whom they begot through the womb of faith by holy preaching. “They shall dwell”: this dwelling signifies the place of blessedness. “Offspring” means the works of the faithful, which are sown in this world, so that in that eternity their praiseworthy fruit may appear. [Col. 0367A]

PRAYER FROM PSALM 101

Hear graciously, Lord, the prayer of your suppliants, so that we who, held fast in sins, have withered like grass may be raised up by the regard of heavenly mercy. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, etc.

PSALM 102

ARGUMENT OF PSALM 102

C The Prophet exhorts the whole world to praise God and rejoices in the gift of the many benefits that he administers to his faithful.

TITLE. ÷ Of David himself ..

[Col. 0367B] C “Of David himself” is placed so that you will not understand the earthly king David. As has often already been said, it signifies Christ. This entire psalm is filled with praise of the Lord. It is luminous through the clarity of its title, so that we should understand its contents without difficulty.

1 Bless the Lord, O my soul, and all that is within me, his holy name.

C The Prophet speaks to his soul so that, when it has been freed from various disasters, it may remember the author of all benefits and not think that what has clearly been granted by God alone should be attributed to itself or to another. “The inward parts” are right thought and the virtues of reason.

2 Bless the Lord, O my soul, and do not forget all his rewards.

H The Lord has bestowed many rewards upon us. C He made us, who were deserving of punishment, worthy of honor; no one is permitted to forget this. What these rewards and benefits are, he subsequently recounts, so that a person, contemplating his benefits, may praise him with his whole mind. For the one who cannot forget the benefits bestowed never ceases to praise him.

3 He forgives all your iniquities; he heals all your infirmities.

C First he becomes gracious toward our sins, when, after our offenses have been forgiven, he deigns to receive sinners into peace. He heals infirmities when security and immortality are granted to the faithful in the resurrection.

4 He redeems your life from destruction; he crowns you ÷ with .. mercy and compassion.

C He redeems life from destruction when he removes us from eternal death, so that we do not hear: “Go into eternal fire.” He crowns with mercy when he restores worthy rewards to the blessed. H For, with mercy preceding, he grants victory so that he may bestow the palm. Hence it is said: “With the shield of your good will you have crowned us” (Psalm 5). He crowns with a shield when he protects and defends, and thus crowns. The shield, therefore, is mercy: what protects us is not our merit but his mercy.

5 He fills your desire with good things; your youth shall be renewed like the eagle’s.

[Col. 0368A] C He fills it when it is said to them: “Come, blessed ones.” The example of the eagle is introduced because, when this bird has reached advanced age, so much of its upper lip grows out in a horny curve that it cannot tear away food in its accustomed freedom. Understanding where the danger to its life might come from, it is said to sharpen its beak on a stone until it is able to eat; and thus, by its customary reception of food, it is restored to its former strength. So the soul, if it does not cease to sharpen its sins upon the rock—that is, upon Christ—returns to its former health; then it is able to receive health-giving food.

6 The Lord performs acts of mercy and judgment for all who suffer injury.

C He performs acts of mercy for those who have shown mercy, as he says in the Gospel: “Blessed are the merciful” (Matthew 5), etc. He promises judgment to those adorned with the gift of patience, to whom it is also said: “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay” (Deuteronomy 32). Here understand “judgment” as vengeance.

7 He made his ways known to Moses, his will to the children of Israel.

C He made his ways known to Moses so that he might walk in the Lord’s ways by the steps of perfect faith, write down his righteousness and law, and teach moral conduct. He made his will known to the children of Israel—not his ways—because many of them presumed to turn aside from the Lord’s way. They knew his will, but they did not wish to keep his commandments or walk in his way. Therefore it is not said that he made his ways known to them, but his will.

8 The Lord is merciful and compassionate, patient and greatly merciful.

C He is merciful who is shown to be most kind by nature; compassionate, who bestows the gifts of his mercy. No one is merciful, however, unless he is also proved to be patient. Therefore he adds “patient,” that is, enduring and sustaining sinners for a long time. Finally he adds “greatly merciful,” because he makes the sun rise even for those who blaspheme him and grants them and preserves for them the breath of life.

9 He will not be angry forever: Nor will he threaten for all eternity.

C He is not angry forever with those who are known to be devoted to repentance; nor will he threaten those who love with their whole mind.

10 He has not dealt with us according to our sins: Nor has he repaid us according to our iniquities.

H He has not dealt with us according to our sins, because he has granted us better things than we deserved. Nor will he repay us according to our iniquities. C For he is so compassionate toward those who beseech him that he immediately releases the penitent from sins.

11 For as high as heaven is above the earth: So has he strengthened his mercy over those who fear him.

C By this comparison it is signified that, just as heaven covers the earth and grants human beings necessary benefits—now rains, now clear weather, now winds—so also God’s mercy provides various benefits for our weakness. For he sustains in order to correct, chastises in order to educate, tests in order to grant benefit; and, to put it briefly, if it is possible for heaven not to cover the earth, it can happen that the Lord does not protect those who serve him with the greatest purity.

12 As far as the east is distant from the west: So far has he removed our iniquities from us.

C The east signifies the kingdom of God, while the west signifies Gehenna, which is as far separated from the dwelling of the blessed as that poor man says in Abraham’s bosom (Luke XVI): “Between us and you a great chasm has been fixed.” Or the east is the beginning of our good life; the west, the outcome of evil conduct.

13 As a father has compassion on his children, so the Lord has had compassion on those who fear him: For he himself knew our formation.

C A human father who wants his son to be properly instructed frequently rebukes and chastises him. So the Lord chastises every son whom he receives, and leads those who fear him toward the pursuit of good will (Prov. III). For he himself knew: that we had cast ourselves down from that natural dignity; we are shown to be a creature and the handiwork of the Creator.

14 He remembered that we are dust; man is like grass. His days: like the flower of the field, so he will blossom.

H As if he were saying: “You do not become angry in order to crush us, but remember that we are potter’s vessels, which, once broken, cannot be repaired except by you.” C By these transient things humanity is compared: it becomes beautiful like a flower and the grass of the field, but it is not brought to a very long life. And if you were to ask, “What is man?” the answer is: “He is one whose days are like grass, and who blossoms like the flower of the field, but the flower immediately falls, because the spirit,” and so forth.

15 For the spirit will pass through him and will not remain: And he will no longer know his place.

C He continues to describe what man is: a passing spirit, passing through the present world, in which he cannot remain for a very long time. “He will no longer know his place” means that he cannot return to this age so as to repeat his life.

16 But the mercy of the Lord is from eternity and unto eternity: Upon those who fear him.

C Through mercy we are made altogether everlasting, although in ourselves we are frail and perishable. “Unto eternity” designates God’s eternity, since he is shown to be merciful before the ages, in the age, and after that age. Yet I see that this perpetual mercy is extended only over those who fear him.

17 But his righteousness is upon children’s children: Upon those who keep his covenant.

C “Children’s children”: we must understand the action of each person. Those who keep the Lord’s precepts and fulfill his commandments in their works—these beget works, and works in turn beget recompense in eternal blessedness.

18 And they remember his commandments, to do them.

C The memory of his commandments is that by which the mind recalls what it has heard and recognizes what it has seen and done. These are the aforementioned children, who remember his commandments through their works, not through the practice of singing. For even if someone were to recite the entire Psalter aloud, he is not mindful of it unless he has done what is commanded. For this reason the words were spoken so that they might be done, not so that they might be sung merely with shouting.

19 The Lord has prepared his throne in heaven: And his kingdom will rule over all.

C “He has prepared his throne”: this refers to the fact that Christ ascended into heaven, from where he will come to judge the living and the dead. He says that the one who prepared his throne will himself rule, so that the pagans would not suppose that their demons would in any way reign.

20 Bless the Lord, his angels, mighty in strength: Doing his word, to hear the voice of his sayings.

C He also admonishes the angels and spiritual beings to approach the service of so great a majesty. They are mighty in strength because they obey his commands. Here “strength” means moral virtue, not power. “To hear the voice” means that they should be humble, not proud; for those are worthy to bless who both know and revere their own Creator.

21 Bless the Lord, all his powers: His ministers, who do his will.

H He admonishes his powers to bless God—that is, those who, strengthened by his power, minister the word to the churches through preaching. C Or, since he first admonished those who are mighty in strength, who do his word, to bless God, he added, “who do his will,” lest you understand “word” as the sound produced by human beings striking the air. For to the angels the word of the Lord is his will.

22 Bless the Lord, all his works, in every place of his dominion: Bless the Lord, my soul.

H Since the whole work of the Lord is the heavenly and earthly creation, he admonishes all things to bless their Creator. “In every place” signifies the Church, which, by the Lord’s favor, was destined to believe throughout the whole world. For if we always bless him, we are continually guarded by him. Therefore this is a worthy admonition, to be taken up against every circumstance like an unconquerable shield.

PRAYER FROM PSALM CII

Heal, Lord, the sicknesses of your people, you who always have compassion on sinners as a father has on children, so that, delivered from the destruction of everlasting death, our soul may bless you and our life glorify you. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, etc.

PSALM CIII

[Col. 0371A]

ARGUMENT OF PSALM CIII

C The voice of the Church magnifying God and praising him by recounting his innumerable works.

TT. ÷ Of David himself ..

C Here “David” is used only for the person speaking. Otherwise, it is clear that everything is to be understood as spoken about the Lord the Savior, who in the beginning made heaven and earth.

1 Bless the Lord, my soul: My God, you have been greatly magnified.

C The prophet invites himself to bless God. To bless God is to confess his great deeds. God is magnified among human beings when he has appeared to them as great and exalted, so that they recognize him as Creator, Redeemer, and Judge. He is greatly magnified when he is proclaimed by one who yesterday was blasphemous but today has been converted.

2 You have put on confession and beauty: Clothed in light as with a garment.

C He put on beauty when he assumed mortal flesh. He put on confession when, at his coming, the faithless departed from the worship of idols, and the confession and beauty of the heavenly majesty became known throughout the world. “Light” signifies the Church, which is rightly understood as the garment of the Lord the Savior, having neither spot nor wrinkle.

3 Stretching out heaven like a skin: You cover its upper parts with waters.

C Here we must understand heaven as every righteous person, whose upper parts—that is, the faithful soul—are cleansed and watered by the saving waters of baptism. Or heaven is stretched out when publicans and prostitutes are admitted. Heaven belongs to the righteous through righteousness, but by the generosity of grace it has also been made from sinners. A Or, as has been said, he calls the preachers heaven: they are stretched out like a skin through their preaching throughout the whole earth. And just as the skins of dead animals are more widely used, so, after the apostles’ death, their teaching through preaching came into greater use in the Church. The waters are the pouring out of grace and charity, or spiritual understanding.

4 You make the clouds your ascent: You walk upon the wings of the winds.

H C He made the cloud when, after the resurrection, the Lord ascended into heaven in the sight of the apostles. He walks upon the wings of the winds when he carries out his will more swiftly than the course of the winds can proceed. Or rather, we should understand the winds as the souls of the righteous, who, instructed in both Testaments, are transferred to heavenly joys as though on two wings. He walks upon them when he displays in them the mercy of his work. The clouds may also be understood as preachers, through whom Christ ascends in his members when they forgive the sins of their hearers.

5 You make your angels spirits: ÷ And .. your ministers a burning fire.

C “Angel” is a Greek word which is interpreted in Latin as “messenger”; for when angels are sent, they are messengers, although by nature they are known to be spirits. The order of the words is: “who makes his spirits angels.” Every person who carries out divine commands is a minister of God. Such a man becomes heavenly fire when he is shown able, through the word of preaching, to burn and consume the wickedness of sinners.

6 You founded the earth upon its stability: It will not be moved forever and ever.

C Christ founded the earth when he made the Church firm. “Upon its stability” means upon himself, who is the immovable foundation. “It will not be moved”: if we remain continually above him, we will in no way be moved.

7 The abyss, like a garment, is its covering: The waters will stand above the mountains.

C The abyss is a very great multitude of waters, which signifies persecutors; for just as a garment placed beneath covers what is underneath, so they covered the world with the most foul superstition. “The waters stood above the mountains”: that is, above the saints, who are called mountains because of the firmness of their faith, when they afflicted them with various punishments. For here the waters, like the abysses, signify the impious.

8 At your rebuke they will flee: At the voice of your thunder they will fear.

C The abysses—that is, the superstitious—will flee from the rebuke of the apostles. “At the voice of your thunder,” that is, of preaching, when they heard that the devil would perish with his followers.

9 The mountains rise up and the plains descend: To the place that you founded for them.

C The mountains—that is, the proud and impious—rise up for as long as the Lord permits them. Then again, when it pleased him, he made them sit in the humility of the valleys. They were mountains when they raged; plains when, having been appeased, they subsided; “to the place,” that is, to the Church, where they were permitted to serve.

10 You set a boundary which they will not cross: Nor will they return to cover the earth.

C The boundary, namely the rite and superstition of the pagans, is the advent of the Lord Christ. As his religion grew, all idolatry, together with its authors, collapsed. “Nor will they return”: H to the crimes in which they had previously lived. C Or, better, “they will not return” in order to cover the human race with the flood of their superstitions.

11 You send forth springs in the valleys: Through the midst of .. mountains the waters will pass ÷

C “Springs”: here we should understand divine Scripture, which wells up in the valleys—that is, among humble people. “Mountains” signifies heretics and the proud, among whom the Scriptures flow with perennial abundance, because hearing them here is common to the good and the wicked. “They will pass through”: because these waters do not reach such people; that is, they do not water them for any fruit.

12 All the beasts of the field will drink: The wild asses will wait in their thirst.

C By “beasts of the field” understand the nations, which were to be given the waters that the Lord promised to the Samaritan woman in the Gospel. The wild ass is a forest ass, signifying the Jews, who do not wish to be satisfied with the drink of life but await in thirst until the fullness of the nations has entered.

13 Above them the birds of heaven will dwell: From the midst of the rocks they will give voice.

C By “birds of heaven” he wishes the holy souls of pontiffs to be understood; they dwell above the peoples of the Lord through holy preaching. “From the midst of the rocks they will give voice” when they are known to preach certain things from the examples of the apostles and prophets—that is, to confirm their own words from their tradition.

14 Watering the mountains from his upper chambers: From the fruit of your works the earth will be satisfied.

H “Watering the mountains,” that is, the apostles. “From his upper chambers”: pouring out the Holy Spirit upon them. “The earth will be satisfied,” that is, earthly people will be satisfied with the benefits of Christ’s generosity. C Or “mountains”: all the good leaders of the Church are watered with heavenly teaching, and through their teaching and life the earthly, transformed for the better, are satisfied.

15 Bringing forth grass for cattle: And plants for the service of human beings.

C The prophet admonishes that the earth, satisfied by the heavenly rain, should bring forth grass—that is, should give alms—for cattle, that is, for the poor, for those who ask everywhere. “Plants for the service of human beings” means that what is necessary should be given to them. Of this it is written: “Let almsgiving sweat in your hand until you find a righteous person to whom you may give it,” that is, one who does not ask because of shame and patience. A Or, for ministers of the Church who minister the word of God, and for the poor.

16 So that you may bring bread from the earth: And wine may gladden the heart of man.

C Our bread is Christ, who is brought forth from the earth when something is provided for those in need out of love for him. “Wine gladdens the heart,” that is, the mind, when it has been consecrated into the blood of Christ and received with honor, because nothing blameworthy is found there.

17 So that he may brighten his face with oil: And bread may strengthen the heart of man.

C The face too is gladdened with oil when it is anointed with royal chrism. H Or mercy brightens the faces of the righteous with oil before God. “Bread” here should be referred to the soul, which makes Christians perfect. A Christ is that bread, or righteousness.

18 The trees of the field will be filled ÷ and .. the cedars of Lebanon that he planted: There the sparrows will build nests.

H “They will be filled” with the true religion of Christ. “Trees,” that is, rational human beings. “Cedars”: the saints who are loftier in merit, whom he planted in the unity of ecclesiastical faith. C The sparrow is a small and extremely cautious bird. It signifies the lowliness of monks, who are shown to build nests—that is, monasteries—in the cedars, that is, in the inheritance of the powerful, as though in certain branches. Sustained by their strength, like sparrows they continually sing the praises of the Lord with unceasing voice: a heavenly life on earth, the imitation of faithful angels, living in the flesh beyond the flesh.

19 The house of the heron is their leader: The high mountains are for deer. The rock is a refuge for hedgehogs.

H The heron is the greatest of all flying creatures; it overcomes and eats the eagle. It signifies a holy man dwelling in the house of God and providing aid to others for conquering the devil. For the eagle is often used to signify the devil. C The deer signifies the faithful, who devour the serpent—that is, the devil—when they turn his wickedness into the praise of God. They dwell in the mountains, that is, in the apostles and prophets. The hedgehog, which we call *ericius*, is a timid animal, naturally armed and living among rocks so that it may not be found. It signifies the sinner who, fearing the future judgment, flees for refuge to Christ the rock.

20 He made the moon for the appointed times: The sun knew its setting.

C The moon signifies the Church, which was made for the appointed times, since it can decrease and increase at various times. The sun is Christ. He knew his setting—that is, the glory of his passion—when he said to his disciples: “The hour has come, and the Son of Man will be handed over into the hands of sinners” (Matt. XXVI).

21 You set darkness, and night came to be: In it all the beasts of the forest will pass through.

C He set darkness at the time of the passion, when the sun was darkened. It was also night for those who, looking carnally upon Christ on the cross, thought that he was dying in a merely human way. In this night the beasts went out—that is, the demons, seeking to devour some. H When the sun of righteousness sets for us also, everything is darkness; then these beasts of the forest, namely the devils, pass through us.

22 ÷ The young lions .. roaring to seize prey: And seeking food for themselves from God.

C Lions signify devils because of their cruelty. “Young lions”—so called because they are skilled in the sense of smell—signify the ministers of the devil, who roar in order to destroy the guilty. They seek this food from God, for no one can be seized by unclean spirits unless, because of his own guilt, he has been abandoned by God. Nothing can be done by anyone except what God, in his secret judgment, has permitted to be done, either for testing or for vengeance.

23 The sun has risen, and they have gathered together: And they will be placed in their dens.

C Then the sun rose when Christ resurrected. At that time the devil’s satellites gathered together, unable to endure his majesty, and placed themselves in their dens—that is, in the hearts of the obstinate. He is called the sun because he alone shines in such a way that day comes from him.

24 Man will go forth to his work: And to his labor until evening.

C This is indeed the custom of mortals: as long as we are here, when day comes we are occupied with various actions. One cultivates the field, another exercises himself in wars; one studies, another teaches. Whatever mortality does is shown to be concluded by evening—that is, by the end of the age.

25 How greatly magnified are your works, Lord: You have made all things in wisdom; the earth is filled with your possession.

C The prophet says with wonder, “How greatly magnified,” for not only is this work of Christ difficult for human beings—since it exceeds human understanding—but it is also shown to be immeasurable to the angels themselves. This wisdom, therefore, is the Son of the Father. “Earth” signifies the Church, which was filled when the universal Church served the Lord. “Possession” signifies the faithful people in the Church. Hence another translation has: “The earth is filled with your creation,” namely, this creation generated in the newness of life through baptism.

26 This is the great and spacious sea + with hands: There are reptiles there, whose number is not known.

C The sea signifies the present world, where the malice of demons, like certain waves, stirs the unstable will of souls. It is called “sea” from *meando*, “going,” because it is always going and returning. “There are reptiles,” that is, evil spirits, innumerable to us but nevertheless capable of being comprehended by God.

27 Small animals with great ones: There the ships will pass through.

C “Small animals”: because among the evil spirits themselves some are shown to be greater in wickedness and others smaller. “Ships” signify the Churches, which escape the dangerous waves of the world through the wood of the glorious cross, carrying believing peoples.

28 This dragon whom you formed to mock him: All things await you, that you may give them food in due season.

C “This dragon” clearly signifies the devil, who is truly called a dragon because of the poison that he breathed into the first woman, Eve, by wickedly persuading her. He was formed by his sins in such a way that he might be mocked by the angels. But since the dragon is spiritual, and the food of its kind is the deception of human beings, do not fear it altogether as savage, because, unless the Lord permits it, it cannot accomplish anything by its own power. It therefore awaits food from God’s permission, as do all other things.

29 When you give to them, they will gather it: When you open your hand ÷ all things .. will be filled with goodness.

C He explains further that, although we are afflicted by diabolical iniquity, we should not believe that the devil presumes to act from his own power. Rather, we should flee to the one without whose permission he can do nothing; and, being defeated more swiftly, he departs. He says, “when you give to them,” so that you may understand that unless it has been given to them, they will not be able to gather it. The hand signifies power, through which he fills all things abundantly and arranges everything wondrously.

30 But when you turn away your face, they will be troubled: You will take away their spirit, and they will fail; and they will return to their dust.

C He now speaks of those who apply God’s gifts to themselves rather than to God. When God turns his face away from such people, they are stripped of protection and become troubled. “You will take away the spirit of pride,” so that, having received the Holy Spirit, they may be renewed and restored. And let them return to their dust—that is, to humble confession of sins, in which they acknowledge the poverty of their weakness; and, failing in you, let them return to the most salutary conversion, those who had been wandering in their presumption.

31 Send forth your Spirit, and they will be created: And you will renew the face of the earth.

C “Send forth your Spirit,” that is, so that they may be repaired for the better. Those who humbly acknowledged themselves to be dust have indeed been restored. The face will be renewed when the sinner is cleansed from the oldness of sins.

32 May the glory of the Lord endure forever: The Lord will rejoice in his works.

C “May the glory of the Lord endure”—not that of anyone else. “Forever,” that is, eternally, because there is no end to his praise. H The Lord’s joy is when we, his creatures, bless him on the day of resurrection.

33 He looks upon the earth and makes it tremble: He touches the mountains, and they smoke.

C He speaks of those who, illuminated by God’s grace, tremble at their past sins. Here he calls sinners mountains; when they have been struck by the Lord’s indignation, they run to saving tears and emit certain smoky clouds of sorrow, like incense of sweetness.

34 I will sing to the Lord in my life: I will sing psalms to my God as long as I am.

C When he says, “I will sing in my life,” he designates the time when he appeared to dwell in this world. When he adds, “I will sing psalms to my God,” he refers to the future age, where existence is perpetual and psalmody has no end.

35 May my speech be pleasing to him: But I will delight in the Lord.

C Our praise becomes pleasing to God in this way: if we delight in the Lord. For the one who loves is loved; the negligent person is despised; the one who desires is sustained.

36 Let sinners perish from the earth and the wicked, so that they may no longer exist: Bless the Lord, my soul.

C Sinners perish from the earth when, deprived of earthly desire, they are stirred by God’s grace toward better pursuits. In the same way the wicked perish when they cease to be evil. “Bless the Lord, my soul”: a worthy beginning to the psalm, and a worthy conclusion—to bless continually the one from whom we know that we continually receive gifts.

PRAYER FROM PSALM CIII

Illustrious and almighty God, you who have satisfied the dry earth with abundant fruit, grant us to contemplate with spiritual understanding the ascent of your glory, so that, while we behold you in heaven, we may always meditate upon the things that are heavenly. Through our Lord Jesus, etc.

PSALM CIV

ARGUMENT OF PSALM CIV

C The prophet warns the faithful not to place their hope in these transient things, but, following the way of the patriarchs, always to seek God spiritually.

TT. Alleluia.

C This adornment of a word began with the present psalm, and you do not find it placed earlier by anyone, although many writers of the Hebrews existed from the beginning. We must know, however, that *alleluia* is defined as neuter in gender. Saint Jerome also clearly indicates this in his exposition of the same psalm. It ought to remain one and undivided in translation, since it has not been altered by the presumption of any language. Among the Hebrews, *alleluia* is said to mean “praise God”: *alle* means “praise,” while *ia* signifies the invisible God.

1 Give thanks to the Lord ÷ and .. call upon his name: Announce his works among the nations.

C “Give thanks to the Lord,” that is, praise him, and acquire for yourselves the favor of divinity through good deeds. “Announce”: this is fitting for evangelists and apostles, and now for priests, so that they may announce the great deeds of Christ. When he says “give thanks” and then adds “call upon,” he teaches that those who wish to call upon God must first confess his praises.

2 Sing to him and sing psalms to him: Tell of all his wonders.

C “Sing” pertains to the hymns that are to be offered; “sing psalms” pertains to the practice of devout works. “All” signifies what he is about to say. For it is not within human power to tell all his wonders; rather, the whole signifies a part.

3 Glory in his holy name: Let the heart of those who seek the Lord rejoice.

C He does not forbid us to be praised, since such a thing cannot be denied to good deeds; but he commands us to glory in the Lord, who grants what we do well. “Let the heart rejoice,” and so forth: let the heart rejoice if it seeks the Lord and is praised in the Lord, but not if it is praised for its own ability.

4 Seek the Lord and be strengthened: Seek his face always.

C He exhorts those who have chosen to seek him to strengthen themselves for future rewards. This seeking is not to be brought to an end at any time, since he adds “always.” By “face” he means his presence.

5 Remember his wonders that he has done: His marvels and the judgments of his mouth.

C The wonders refer to the division of the Red Sea; the marvels, to the plagues that he sent upon Egypt; the judgments of his mouth, because he fulfilled everything that he promised to Moses his servant. For he judged Pharaoh and his people, just as he said to Moses.

6 The offspring of Abraham, his servant: The sons of Jacob, his chosen ones.

C Here what he said above—“remember”—must be supplied. He rightly calls the rebellious Jews servants, because through their unbelief they refused to be sons. By the sons of Jacob he signifies the most faithful Christians, who deserve to be heirs of the Lord.

7 He himself is the Lord our God: His judgments are throughout all the earth.

C By saying, “He himself is the Lord our God,” he admonishes us to understand that the one whom the Jewish people determined should be crucified is God, and that his judgments are to be made throughout the whole world, not in Judea alone.

8 He remembered his covenant forever: The word that he commanded for a thousand generations.

C He remembered it forever when he fulfilled his promises. “His covenant” signifies the preaching of the prophets, who foretold the incarnation of the Word. To command is to say something through another; he did this through them when they were given to prophesy future things. “A thousand generations” signifies the end of the age.

9 Which he established with Abraham: And his oath to Isaac.

C This answers what I said above concerning “his covenant.” For the things promised in the Old Testament to the patriarchs Abraham and Isaac are said to have been established and sworn, so that they might be shown to be firm.

10 And he established it as a commandment for Jacob: And for Israel as an everlasting covenant.

C This covenant, thus arranged, he established for Jacob—that is, he confirmed it as a commandment, that is, as the New Testament. It is properly called everlasting because no other covenant ever succeeds it; in it is the complete perfection of all the promises.

11 Saying: To you I will give the land of Canaan: The cord of your inheritance.

C Canaan is interpreted as “humble.” Therefore it appropriately signifies that Christians will receive the land of the humble, that is, of the blessed. The cord of inheritance refers to the twisted constraints of this world, which the Lord dissolved through his passion for our salvation. For the assumption of his flesh is shown to be our inheritance.

12 When they were few in number: Very few and settlers in it.

C He now recounts how great a power divine virtue provided for the patriarchs.

13 And they passed from nation to nation, and from one kingdom to another people.

H “They passed”: this does not refer to the captivity of the Jews, but to Abraham, who went out from the land of the Chaldeans and came to Mesopotamia, from Mesopotamia to the land of promise, and again into Egypt. We pass through many kingdoms in order to reach the promised land, and thus from the kingdom of Egypt, this world, to another people in heaven.

14 He did not allow anyone to harm them: And he rebuked kings for their sake.

H He did not allow Pharaoh to harm Abraham through Sarah (Gen. XII), nor Abimelech (Gen. XX), nor anyone to harm Isaac through Rebecca (Gen. XXVI); but he rebuked Pharaoh and Abimelech for their sake.

15 Do not touch my anointed ones: And do not act wickedly against my prophets.

H Behold, before the Law the patriarchs, who were not anointed with royal oil, are called “anointed ones.” Those are Christ’s who are anointed with the Holy Spirit. Let the Jews therefore be ashamed, since they say that the Lord Jesus Christ cannot be called Christ because he was not anointed with royal oil, when even those who lived long before Saul—by whom this royal and material anointing began—are called anointed ones.

16 And he called famine upon the land: ÷ And .. he crushed every support of bread.
