C “He called famine” in the time of Pharaoh, when famine raged in Egypt for seven years (Gen. XLI). “Every support,” that is, the grain harvest, he reduced to nothing; for bread is the support of human beings, as he said above: “And bread strengthens the heart of man” (Ps. CIII).

17 He sent a man before them: Joseph was sold into slavery.

C He sent Joseph before the patriarchs whom he mentioned above. He is rightly called a man because, like a man, he endured everything manfully. The order of the words is: “He sent before them the man Joseph, who was sold into slavery.”

18 They humbled his feet in fetters; iron passed through his soul: Until his word came.

C Joseph was sent to prison by Potiphar, the official of Pharaoh. It is not recorded that he received fetters, but it could have happened that one shut up in prison was bound with iron chains. Iron passed through his soul when he was sent into these narrow straits, so that amid the evils he unjustly suffered, the charges of falsehood would not prevail. Here iron indicates the tribulation of harsh necessity. “Until his word came” refers either to King Pharaoh, who freed him, or to Joseph’s word concerning the interpretation of dreams, which the king sought in him and which freed him. That word belonged to God rather than to Joseph.

19 The utterance of the Lord set him ablaze: The king sent and released him; the prince of peoples, and he dismissed him.

C It set him ablaze inwardly with the light of the heavenly flame, so that he might speak of future things with confidence in the truth. “The king sent”: Pharaoh released him from the guilt by which he was held bound. He is the prince—namely Pharaoh, whom he had earlier called king—and he dismissed him from the prison’s confinement (Gen. XLI).

20 He appointed him lord of his house: And prince of all his possession.

C He appointed him lord and prince when he made him ascend his chariot and had him proclaimed by the herald’s voice as second lord after the king and prince of all Egypt.

21 So that he might instruct his princes as himself: And teach wisdom to his elders.

C Pharaoh believed that he could instruct his princes so that they too might become worthy interpreters of dreams. Therefore he placed him over them, not only to govern but also to teach, unaware that the one from whom the knowledge of dreams comes—God alone—was teaching him.

22 And Israel entered ÷ into .. Egypt: And Jacob became a sojourner in the land of Ham.

C At Pharaoh’s command, Joseph’s kindred were led into the lands of Egypt. Jacob, by the variation of names, varied the words of his revelation. Therefore now he says “Israel,” now “Jacob,” meaning one and the same person. Canaan, however, was the son of Ham and grandson of Noah, from whom the Egyptians derived their origin. Our translation has “Ham,” but the Roman translation, which he follows here, has “Canaan.”

23 And he greatly increased his people: And he strengthened them over their enemies.

H He increased his people through the fertility of birth; he strengthened them when, as they multiplied, the multitude of the Egyptians was severely afflicted by the well-known plagues.

24 He turned their heart so that they hated his people: And that they might deal deceitfully with his servants.

C God turned the heart of the Egyptians toward hatred of the Israelite people by granting them prosperity. “And that they might deal deceitfully”: after hatred had been conceived, it naturally followed that the enraged people would resort to deceitful schemes, as happened with the bricks, when they doubled the work and denied them straw, and similar matters (Exod. I).

25 He sent Moses his servant: Aaron, whom he chose, himself.

C It is clear that God sent these men to Pharaoh as witnesses of a kind, so that he might permit the people pleasing to God to depart unharmed.

26 He placed in them the words of his signs and wonders: In the land of Ham.

C Signs are like certain traces of future or past events. Wonders, however, pertain to marvelous events that had not previously occurred in the order of things; for *prodigium* is said from the fact that it speaks of something “far forward.” Thus those marvelous events, when they occurred, spoke far ahead and from afar to the Christian people, so that something might be understood from them.

27 He sent darkness and made it obscure: And he did not embitter his words.

C It is recorded that they endured darkness among the plagues of Egypt, but we should rather understand that the hearts of those who despised the Lord’s commandments were darkened. “They embittered the words” means that they received them bitterly, or certainly rejected them with insulting abominations. Thus the Roman translation explains it, which has “because they embittered”; but ours has “he did not embitter,” namely God, meaning that he did not provoke them, but fulfilled his words by confirming them with miracles.

28 He turned their waters into blood: And he killed their fish.

C He turned the waters into blood because they were destined to perish amid the streams of the Red Sea. The fish were killed so that no hope of life would appear to remain for human beings, since even the fish had died—those that had been nourished in their native element.

29 Their land brought forth frogs: In the chambers of their kings.

H In the frogs are signified the songs of poets who, departing from the Catholic rule, fill the hearts of earthly kings with the fables of deceptions.

30 He spoke, and the dog-fly and gnats came: In all their territories.

C The dog-fly signifies a fly that bites more sharply than other flies and is more violent in its pestering. The gnats are a kind of mosquito, extremely troublesome with their fixed stings.

31 He made their rains hail: Burning fire in their land.

C “He appointed,” that is, decreed that the rain given to make the earth fertile should be changed into the destructive devastation of hail. The consuming fire signifies lightning, which, when a storm has been stirred up, is accustomed to rage violently.

**32** “And he struck their vines and their fig trees; and he crushed the wood of their borders.”

C When he says “he struck,” refer this to the hail or consuming fire. But lest you think that only the fig trees were struck, he added “every wood,” so that you would not doubt that the crops too had been destroyed, when you recognized that even the strength of the trees had been crushed. For greater things contain the meaning of lesser ones.

**33** “He spoke, and the locust came, and the caterpillar, whose number there was not.”

C The locust is the parent of the caterpillar, which it produces by a harmful fecundity; it descends with its offspring upon that plunder like an army summoned together.

**34** “And it consumed all the grass of their land; + and it consumed .. all ÷ the fruit of their land.”

C And lest you think that army had been brought forward pointlessly, he says that every fruit of the land was consumed.

**35** “And he struck every firstborn in their land, the firstfruits of all their labor.”

C He has come to the seventh plague set down in this psalm. Some are also troubled by the question why only seven are recounted in this psalm, whereas ten are related in the narrative of Exodus. This happened because he is immediately going to say that the Lord bestowed seven benefits upon the Hebrew people; he first stated that the Egyptians had suffered an equal number of plagues. A Or because, for one who is praising, it is sufficient to touch upon a few things from among many, whereas for one who is narrating, it is necessary to mention everything.

**36** “And he brought them out with silver and gold; and there was not one infirm among their tribes.”

C We read that the Israelite people, when departing from the Egyptians, received gold and silver at God’s command (Exod. XI), so that it might appear not to have been a sudden theft but the reward of long labor. The second benefit follows: there too, by his command, no one could be afflicted with bodily weakness.

**37** “Egypt rejoiced at their departure ÷; because the fear of them had fallen upon them.”

C Then those who had remained in Egypt rejoiced altogether, when those who had resolved to go after the Hebrews had been drowned. Why? Because they themselves had suffered nothing similar. And they were afraid because the elements themselves were fighting on their behalf: the water of the sea, the darkened air, the consuming fire, and so forth. Or, “Egypt rejoiced” because of the hope of liberation from death. For this reason they compelled them to leave, lest human beings and firstborn children should again be killed.

**38** “He spread a cloud for their protection ÷ ..; and fire so that it might be possible ÷ for them .. by night.”

C The cloud was given to moderate the heat of the sun; fire was granted so that it could remove the darkness of the night. And this is the third benefit that is acknowledged to have been granted to the Israelite people.

**39** “They asked, and the quail came; and he satisfied them with the bread of heaven.”

C The desires of those who asked were surpassed. They asked for meat and received quail (Exod. VI)—for without doubt meat is sweeter both in four-footed animals and in birds—and in addition they received the bread of heaven (Num. XI). These events are well known from the reading of Exodus, when the quail rained down in the manner of the densest showers. Manna likewise rained down so that the Jewish people might be satisfied; this is what he here calls “the bread of heaven,” and most fittingly it is called the bread of heaven as a figure of the sacrament. For manna is said to mean “What is this?”; and, as though responding to one who was asking, it was said: “The bread of heaven.” With this he satisfied them.

**40** “He split the rock, and waters flowed; rivers went forth in the dry land.”

C This too was enacted as a figure of the Lord Christ, so that the rock might pour forth nourishing waters. For Christ the Lord is the spiritual rock (1 Cor. X), who causes life-giving waters to flow forth. These waters “went forth in the dry land,” that is, among the sinners of the nations, who are rightly called dry because they were parched by burning offenses; but, watered by the Lord’s rain, they put forth shoots into the new human being.

**41** “For he remembered his holy word, ÷ which I had .. to Abraham his servant.”

H “He remembered the word” which he fulfilled from his offspring, that is, his promise concerning Christ, which he promised to Abraham (Gen. XV). C Or he now adds the cause of the miracles mentioned. For they are said to have been performed because they are acknowledged to have been promised to Abraham.

**42** “And he led out his people with rejoicing, ÷ and .. his chosen ones with gladness.”

C He led out his chosen ones with gladness, because those who murmured were struck by the Lord’s anger. Therefore he is not said to have led out those whom, in the wilderness, he struck down because their sins demanded it.

**43** “And he gave them the regions of the nations; and they possessed the labors of peoples.”

C He now comes to the seventh benefit. By “regions of the nations” he appears to mean the possession of lands; by “the labors of peoples,” however, riches gathered over a long period of time.

**44** “So that they might keep his ordinances and seek his law.”

C The ordinances of Christ are that we love God with our whole heart, love our neighbors as ourselves, and honor our father. His law was to rest on the Sabbath day and to sacrifice a lamb at Passover. But these things are to be sought spiritually; for this reason he added “seek.”

**Prayer from Psalm 104**

We beseech you, Lord, while invoking your name: as you nourished our fathers with angelic food, with the power of your name going before them, so also cherish and renew us with mystical nourishment. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, etc.

**Psalm 105**

**Argument of Psalm 105**

C Here the Hebrew people are introduced making confession, when, having abandoned the faithlessness of their fathers, they were led, through the Lord’s own mercy, to his piety.

TT. Alleluia, alleluia.

C Here the Hebrew people are introduced making confession, who, having abandoned the faithlessness of their fathers, were led, through the Lord’s own mercy, to his piety [Note: [Col. 0383D] It should not seem strange here if the same words recur twice, since this singular repetition—which Cochlaeus had emended, taking the argument from Cassiodorus—is required by the edition printed from the autograph of St Bruno and one manuscript, and is to be preferred to the other editions.], so that we may understand that, once converted, they too rightly sing alleluia for their redemption.

**1** [Col. 0383B] “Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good; for his mercy is for ever.”

C This confession is to be applied as a remedy of repentance, yet it undoubtedly also belongs to the Lord’s praises; for it is a greater glory of mercy to spare one who confesses than to preserve one who lives without offence. The Lord is rightly called good because he waits for the erring person and feeds the sinner. “For ever,” however, signifies the course of this life, in which all who sin are miserable.

**2** “Who shall speak of the Lord’s powers, or make all his praises heard?”

C “Who,” then, signifies no one. For who has either the ability to conceive or the tongue to utter such that the tongue can recount the greatness [Col. 0383C] of so great a majesty? “Make heard”: here too “who” must be understood. For those things can be heard which can also be proved and spoken.

**3** “Blessed are those who keep judgment and do righteousness at all times.”

C One keeps judgment who judges rightly among others; one does righteousness who shows it in action. Such persons are therefore rightly called blessed, since they keep God’s commandments with a pure mind at all times. For whoever perseveres to the end shall be saved (Matt. X).

**4** “Remember us, Lord, in the good pleasure of your people; visit us with your salvation.”

C The devout pray that they may be counted among those [Col. 0383D] who pleased the Lord by faithful works. They desire to be visited by God, by whose coming they knew themselves to be saved. H The Salvation is the Father’s Son. C He is the salvation of which blessed Simeon said: “My eyes have seen your Salvation” (Luke II).

**5** “That we may see the goodness of your chosen ones, rejoice in the joy of your nation, and be praised with your inheritance.”

C The aforesaid people ask to be visited by the saving Lord, that they may see his goodness, which he was to bestow upon his chosen ones by his own gift. “With,” or “in the joy [Col. 0384A] of your nation”: this is the Lord’s own nation, gathered from the diversity of the nations, that there might be one flock and one shepherd. H That we Jews, keeping your commandments, may praise you together with your inheritance—that is, with the Gentile people who will believe in you—so that with them we may be one people, praising you eternally; for Abraham our father saw you and rejoiced (John VIII). May we too see and rejoice in praising you.

**6** “We have sinned with our fathers; we have acted unjustly, we have committed iniquity.”

C There is no doubt that this people laments those sins which it is shown to endure through the wickedness of its fathers. For those sin with their ancestors who do not separate themselves from their offences. This is what “we have sinned” means: “we have acted unjustly”; “we have committed iniquity.”

**7** [Col. 0384B] “Our fathers in Egypt did not understand your wonders; they were not mindful of the multitude of your mercies.”

C Two things commend bestowed benefits: understanding and memory; and both are denied to have existed in the faithless. They saw the plagues of the Egyptians and God’s benefits, but did not recognize why they occurred. Nor were they mindful of God’s mercy: seeing Pharaoh’s army, they believed that they had lost all hope of escape before the sea was divided, forgetful of the earlier wonders.

**8** “And they provoked him as they went up to the sea, the + Red Sea ...”

[Col. 0384C] C “They provoked”: that is, they made God, who had been appeased, angry with themselves. “Going up” is plainly said from the geographical position, since Egypt is reported to be lower than all regions; and therefore, going up from there, they sought higher places.

**9** “And he saved them for his name’s sake, that he might make known his power.”

C By saying “for his name’s sake,” he designates the Lord Saviour, whose name accords with saving those in danger. He made his power known, of course, to eyes seeing by spiritual reflection.

**10** “And he rebuked the Red Sea, and it was dried up; and he led them through the depths as through a wilderness.”

C He called the hidden command of divinity a rebuke, because in Exodus we do not read that the sea was [Col. 0384D] rebuked by the Lord’s voice. The sea was dried, not throughout, but only so much as then opened a way for them. The depths are called, and are, a wilderness when they are deserted by the flood of waters; thus that way of streams dried so far that it could become a dusty road. For this reason these depths are compared to a wilderness.

**11** “And he saved them from the hand of those who hated them, and redeemed them from the hand of the enemy.”

C Christ saved the human race from the troop of demons, which both hates and strikes humankind with the goad [Col. 0385A] of sins. He redeemed guilty sinners from the devil’s dominion with precious blood: this is “from the hand of the enemy.” Literally, however, this does not seem to be said: when he freed the Jews, he did not give the Egyptians a price. Yet “redeemed” is used; it should therefore be understood prophetically.

**12** “And the water covered those who afflicted them; not one of them remained.”

H This likeness now occurs in our baptism, where a person is washed by water and the devil perishes with his attendants. C For one who knows the history, its literal sense is plain.

**13** “And they believed ÷ in .. his words, and sang his praise.”

[Col. 0385B] C “They believed” displays the hardness of their heart in this: they preferred to believe not before the event but after the miracle had happened. “And they sang,” namely: “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously honoured” (Exod. XV).

**14** “They quickly ÷ became .. forgetful of his works; they did not wait for his counsel.”

C “They quickly became”: as though he said, they were changed with the utmost speed, so that those who sang praise to the Lord for miracles bestowed afterward took up impious murmurings. They changed counsel into sin, despairing before his prepared benefits had arrived. They asked for food in distrust, although before this they had suffered no hunger, always being fed by divine bounty. So today many people, while providing for themselves with excessive [Col. 0385C] haste, unwittingly anticipate the ordering of divinity.

**15** “And they desired a desire in the wilderness, and tempted God in the waterless place.”

C They “desired desires” when, amid murmurings, they demanded that water and feasting be given them in the wilderness (Exod. XV). The doubling of the words shows the excess of their desire. “And they tempted [him] in the waterless place.” H It was dry for them because they did not acknowledge the watering of the Holy Spirit in the pillar of cloud which went before them.

**16** “And he gave them their request, and sent fullness into their souls.”

C We speak of the soul as satisfied in two ways: when it is refreshed with bodily food because of the weakness of the flesh, [Col. 0385D] and when it is filled with spiritual delight. But here he says that their souls were fattened with flesh and drink, so that their despairing will might be overcome by the arrival of what they wanted.

**17** “And they provoked Moses in the camp, Aaron, the Lord’s holy one.”

C Sedition followed fullness of belly, which often arouses the causes of ruinous dangers. By “to provoke” we mean to provoke someone to anger. Dathan and Abiram provoked the holy men to their own destruction (Num. XVI), because they spoke out of envy, which displeased the Lord. This is fittingly placed among God’s praises because he is declared to have avenged his servants.

**18** [Col. 0386A] “The earth opened and swallowed Dathan, and covered the assembly of Abiram.”

H “The earth opened”: these things occurred literally; but even now the earth devours those who savour earthly things and depart from God’s commandments, those whom the grace of the Holy Spirit does not enlighten but the flame of sin kindles.

**19** “And fire blazed in their synagogue; flame consumed sinners.”

C “Fire blazed”: this occurred against the two hundred and fifty associates of Dathan and Abiram, who unhappily followed their designs. “Flame” is so called from the lash-like tresses of its hair. Here “synagogue” signifies the gathering of Dathan’s and Abiram’s associates.

**20** “÷ And .. they made a calf in Horeb, [Col. 0386B] and worshipped a carved image.”

C Horeb is interpreted “skull-place,” where later the Jews crucified the Lord; so that, in that same name, already then in the wilderness of Horeb they violated God’s worship by impious presumption, whose descendants were to crucify the Lord at the place of the skull. “They worshipped a carved image,” not in the wilderness but later in the land of promise.

**21** “And they changed their glory into the likeness of a calf eating grass.”

C Their glory was the divinity they worshipped. Losing it by an unhappy exchange, they deserved to reach the point that, abandoning the Creator of heaven and earth, they made for themselves a god in the likeness of a calf [Col. 0386C] eating grass.

**22** “They forgot God who saved them, who did great things in Egypt, wonders in the land of Ham, terrible things in the Red Sea.”

H They forgot God, who struck Egypt with many plagues to free his people, and worked miracles in the land of Ham, or Canaan, when, driving out the nations, he planted them in their land. He also did terrible things in the sea, when, with Pharaoh destroyed, he thus afforded his people a passage.

**23** “And he said that he would destroy them, had not Moses his chosen one stood in the breach before him.”

H Attend to this, O priest: the people would have perished had Moses not softened God’s anger. And when you see [Col. 0386D] the people sinning, declare their sins to them and stand in the breach—that is, in danger—asking the Lord to turn his wrath from them.

**24** “That he might turn away his wrath lest he destroy them; and they held the desirable land as nothing.”

C They held the land as nothing because they always thought carnally about what they saw and heard. But observe how good that land was, since it was called desirable. H It is the land of the living, which he calls desirable; they held it as nothing because they loved this transitory land. C Or that holy physical land was desirable to those who understood it because of the mysteries of our redemption; but to those who perceived nothing spiritual in it, it was nothing.

**25** [Col. 0387A] “They did not believe his word, and murmured in their tents; they did not hear the voice of the Lord.”

C “They did not believe in his Word”: this signifies the Son, in whom that utterly impious people did not believe. Or literally, they murmured because they chose not to believe his promises at all. While they practised murmurings, they did not hear the Lord’s voice. He says “in their tents” so that this may seem to have happened not to those at work but to the idle. For it is a greater offence when murmuring occurs among the idle.

**26** “And he raised his hand over them, to cast them down in the wilderness.”

C “He raised his hand”: here the Lord’s justice is set first, so that the mercy which follows may be felt with greater glory. [Col. 0387B] For he says that the Lord’s power arose to punish transgressors, cast them down, and do the other things that follow.

**27** “And to cast down their seed among the nations, and scatter them through the regions.”

H The Jews were scattered in different parts, so that, humbled at some time, the chastened people might acknowledge their Lord. But one whose mind is carried about by every wind of vain glory or desire is also scattered.

**28** “And they were initiated to Baal-peor, and ate sacrifices of the dead.”

H “They were initiated”: that is, those who ought to have consecrated themselves to God were initiated—that is, consecrated—to the idol Baal-peor; and those who ought to have hungered for the living bread ate sacrifices of the dead.

**29** “And they provoked him by their inventions, and ruin was multiplied among them.”

H They provoked him by their inventions, namely perverse ones, and the ruin of idols occurred manifoldly. A Or, “ruin was multiplied among them,” because for their graver sins they were more grievously devastated.

**30** “And Phinehas stood and made atonement, and the scourge ceased.”

C “Phinehas stood”: this word “stood” shows firmness of mind; from divine zeal he killed the fornicators. H Thus the priest to whom souls are entrusted ought to draw the sword—that is, bring forth the word—and kill fornication and desires in both sexes, so that it may be reckoned to him as righteousness.

**31** [Col. 0387D] “And it was reckoned to him as righteousness, from generation to generation for ever.”

C What he did, as stated above, was reckoned to Phinehas the priest as righteousness both here and in the age to come. It is also reckoned as eternal righteousness to every priest correcting vices.

**32** “And they provoked him at the water of contradiction, and Moses was troubled because of them, because they embittered his spirit.”

H The water of contradiction is understood as the waters of baptism, at which the devil and his works are renounced. If anyone afterward defiles himself with vices, the priest will be troubled on his account, because that person has embittered the Spirit [Col. 0388A] of God whom the priest preaches, as Paul said: “Who is weak, and I am not weak?” (2 Cor. XI).

**33** “And he distinguished ÷ with .. his lips. They did not destroy the nations which the Lord told them [to destroy].”

H “And he distinguished with his lips,” so that he might continually pray for them. C Or, he distinguished that utterance of distrust from the former steadfastness of mind. They did not destroy the nations because, after the people entered the land of promise, forgetting God’s commands and precepts—which had commanded them to kill those nations because of their idol worship—they instead joined themselves to those nations in forbidden association.

**34** “And they mingled among the nations, learned their works, and served their carved images; [Col. 0388B] and it became a stumbling block to them.”

C They mingled among the nations in forbidden association so that they might defile themselves with their superstition, and it became a stumbling block to them. *Scandalum* is a Greek word meaning “leftward,” because by perverse imitation it led their minds to the left side. Behold: the land of promise became a stumbling block, although it had been bestowed by the Lord’s bounty as a great reward. Hence we are warned to use rightly benefits granted by divine generosity, lest we perish more through that by which we know that we have been raised up.

**35** “And they sacrificed their sons and their daughters to demons.”

H “They sacrificed their sons and their daughters to demons.” This is to be understood morally, of their senses and souls. C Or literally: not those who entered the land of promise, but their descendants.

**36** “And they shed innocent blood, the blood of their sons and daughters + of their own .., whom they sacrificed to the carved images of Canaan.”

C They shed blood; yet we do not read that the Hebrews who entered the land of promise shed human blood in sacrifices to demons. Still, there is no doubt that this could have been done by the following generation. Lest those innocents whose blood they shed should be thought strangers, he added “of their sons and daughters,” so that odium against them might grow and the crime become greater; and, to make it still greater, he added that this innocent blood was shed to carved images. This figure is called *auxesis* among the Greeks, when praise or blame grows and is enlarged by added expressions.

**37** “And the land was slain in bloods, and defiled by their works; and they committed fornication by their inventions.”

C By “the land slain” we must understand cruel people, who slaughtered themselves more by their wicked devotion in killing their children. For in a figurative expression “the land slain” means earthly people, killed in soul by their evil actions. In doing this they are also said to have committed fornication, for those are seen to commit fornication against the Lord who have defiled themselves with adulterous superstitions.

**38** [Col. 0389A] “And the Lord was angered with wrath against his people, and abhorred his inheritance.”

C The Lord is said, in a figurative expression, to be angered with wrath. “And the Lord was angered with wrath.” H Because he abandoned them, and what had once been God’s people became the devil’s band. C God’s abhorrence and turning away are plainly the extreme of all evils; for when that which holds things together is withdrawn, the ruin of the things held necessarily follows at once.

**39** “And he delivered them into the hands of the nations, and those who hated them ruled over them.”

C They were delivered to the disgrace of slavery, though they seemed to glory in idols. “Those who hated them ruled over them”: this is a very grievous dominion. One who always hates is always angry, and one who is always angry [Col. 0389B] is implacable. Thus it is a most harsh slavery to serve one who is always hostile.

**40** “And their enemies afflicted them, and they were humbled under their hands. Often he delivered them.”

C “And their enemies afflicted them”: it was a fitting requital that those unwilling to serve the loving Lord should, by just judgment, be proved subject to hating enemies. “Often he delivered”: so that we may understand that he both promises good things and again aids those who have been scourged. He promised benefits, and human iniquity did not cease; he brought punishment, and deigned to renew mercy toward the afflicted.

**41** “But they embittered him by their counsel, and were humbled in their iniquities.”

[Col. 0389C] H But they embittered him by the counsel they held, to abandon him and serve idols. And they were humbled not by God, but by their own offences.

**42** “And he saw when they were afflicted, and heard their prayer.”

H “And he saw when they were afflicted”: the customary compassion of the merciful God went before, and immediately heard the converted in their prayers. He teaches you also that, if you are converted and groan, the prayers of your humility at once draw near to his lofty ears.

**43** “And he remembered his covenant, and repented according to the multitude of his mercies.”

[Col. 0389D] H He remembered the covenant which he made with Abraham at the beginning of our faith; C it was hidden in the prophets but revealed in the time of the Gospel. “He repented” is said in a human manner, H because God always repents over those who repent, when he does not do the evils which he had said he would do. C Therefore God repents when he knows us to repent; for he becomes toward us such as he has found us to be toward him. God’s repentance here is not grief over something imprudently done, but remission of the punishment of sin.

**44** “And he gave them into mercies in the sight of all who had taken them captive.”

C He says that they were given into mercies because they received diverse gifts of charisms: from that people the grace of God caused prophets, apostles, martyrs, and confessors to flourish. Or literally, he made the Gentiles who had taken them captive favourably disposed toward them, so that they often even set free those whom they had formerly held captive.

**45** “Save us, Lord our God, and gather us from the nations.”

H Save us, lest vices rule over us. And gather us, because the Hebrew nation is scattered throughout the regions of the nations. C The people to whom we assigned the words from the beginning of the psalm now beseeches God to perfect his Church from the gathering of the nations.

**46** “That we may confess your holy name [Col. 0390B] and glory in your praise.”

C “That we may confess your name,” namely your Son, who is both your name and your praise. C “And glory”: not in human boasting, but in you, where glory is truly secure and joy without end.

**47** “Blessed be the Lord God of Israel from age to age; and let all the people say: Amen, amen.”

H Rightly blessed through the ages is he through whom the ages were made—not only made, but also redeemed. May he also now deign to restore us in the Salvation, that is, in Christ Jesus our Lord, who is blessed for ever. C He says that God is to be blessed from this age to that everlasting age, so that unceasing praise may never become wearisome [Col. 0390C].

**Prayer from Psalm 105**

Remember us, Lord, in the good pleasure of your people, and save us, freed from the slavery of sin, by the saving visitation of your Salvation. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, etc.

**Psalm 106**

**Argument of Psalm 106**

C Here the Christian people are admonished to render praises to the Lord for the benefits bestowed on them.

TT. Alleluia.

**1** “Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good; for his mercy is for ever.”

C “Give thanks to the Lord”: the Prophet urges both the disclosure of one’s sins and the sounding forth of the Lord’s praises [Col. 0390D]. He says “for he is good” so that sinners may have confidence, after making satisfaction, to pray to the Lord. “For ever,” that is, eternally, because there is no time found exempt from his mercy.

**2** “Let those redeemed by the Lord say so, whom he redeemed from the hand of the enemy and gathered from the regions.”

C Let them certainly say alleluia, as the title says, and console themselves with joyful exultations, those who deserved to come to the Lord’s grace. Yet it especially signifies the people of the nations, redeemed by God’s blood and, through his mercy, removed from the enemy’s power—that is, the devil’s [Col. 0391A]—who were called from diverse regions, or who were redeemed in Christ’s Passion.

**3** “From the rising and setting of the sun, from the north and the sea.”

C Having designated three quarters of the world, he put the sea in place of the fourth—that is, the south—meaning by that side the Ocean, which is said to encircle the whole boundary of the world.

**4** “They wandered in a wilderness, in a waterless place; they found no way to a city of habitation.”

C The nations wandered in superstitious teaching, dry of true doctrine and in a wilderness, since they were shown not yet to have any wholly true teachers. They did not find the way to the city—that is, the works by which one reaches the heavenly Jerusalem.

**5** [Col. 0391B] “Hungry and thirsty, their soul failed within them.”

C “Hungry and thirsty” signifies the most inquisitive people of this age, who sought out the paths of truth through diverse opinions; but because they did not believe the true author, they could not be found in true wisdom. Their soul failed within them when the vigour of their minds succumbed, wearied by their labours and studies.

**6** “And they cried to the Lord when they were afflicted, and he delivered them from their necessities.”

C In the preceding verses he described those wandering; now he speaks of those returning to God’s gifts. “They cried” signifies that they sought with great longing. H Then too we are heard by him when it is not a mere voice [Col. 0391C] but affliction that cries to God. But see what this cry accomplished: he delivered them from their necessities and made them know the paths of truth.

**7** “And he led them forth in the right way, that they might go to a city of habitation.”

C He led them forth in the right way, namely Christ, so that those who had formerly wandered in a trackless error, receiving the way of the most holy religion, might happily arrive through faith in Christ at the blessed courts of the Church.

**8** “Let them confess the Lord’s mercies, and his wonders to the children of men.”

C It is fitting and right always to confess the gracious Lord, who both frees us from dangers by his mercy [Col. 0391D] and enlightens us by the splendour of his piety. He says that his wonders, which he performed in the world through evangelists and apostles, are to be preached to posterity.

**9** “For he satisfied the empty soul, and filled the hungry soul with good things.”

C The souls of the Gentiles were then empty and vacant, when they were deprived of good fruits through idol worship; afterward, when admonished by the Lord’s mercy, they were satisfied while hungry, as they turned their desires toward the pursuits of repentance.

**10** “Those sitting in darkness and the shadow of death, bound in poverty and iron.”

C The nations sat in darkness because they were emptied of the light of faith. By saying “sitting,” he shows that they had long remained there. The shadow of death was the sinful life of this [Col. 0392A] age. “Bound in poverty,” that is, in want of good work, they were tied with the cords of sins. Iron signifies the hardness of evils.

**11** “Because they embittered God’s words and provoked the counsel of the Most High.”

C “Because they embittered”: he explains how those sitting in darkness sinned. Acting against the Lord’s words, they refused to live according to his rules and therefore provoked his counsels. H Which he had given them so that they might choose life. C God’s just counsel was also a most healthful medicine: that illness should be cured by its contrary remedy, the pride of the mind by distress of heart.

**12** “And their heart was humbled in labours; they were weakened, and there was none to help.”

[Col. 0392B] C Their heart was humbled in tribulations and distresses, so that those who had been proud in prosperity might be humbled in tribulations and labours. “They were weakened”: that is, they were cast down from worldly presumption. “And there was none to help”: supply “another,” for no one gives aid to one in danger unless almighty God commands that help be given.

**13** “And they cried to the Lord when they were afflicted, and he delivered them from their necessities.”

C They cried to the Lord, namely confessing their own offences. Earlier they were silent, established in pride, and like senseless beasts uttered no saving word. Compunction took place, and then they gave a useful voice; that is, he delivered those oppressed [Col. 0392C] by the devil’s slavery.

**14** “And he brought them out of darkness and the shadow of death, and broke their bonds.”

D He brought them out of darkness, that is, out of the blindness of faithlessness. The shadow of death is a life stained with sins, bearing the most foul image of that future death. He broke their bonds: when Christ came, the devil’s tyrannical power was so broken that it can never prevail to return to the dominion it once possessed.

**15** “Let them confess the Lord’s mercies, and his wonders to the children of men.”

C He urges them to give thanks to the Deliverer, because divine power shattered the gates of sins and the bars of every evil.

**16** “For he crushed the brazen gates and broke the iron bars.”

C Brazen gates are people’s vicious habits, which confine us so within the courts of sins that they cannot grant permission to leave. By iron bars he means unclean spirits, who do not cease to guard and close those gates of sins round about, lest departure be permitted. These two metals seem to have been used for the strength of offences.

**17** “He received them from the way of their iniquity; for because of their injustices they were humbled.”

H “He received,” that is, Christ freed those whom the devil had shut in with the strongest bolts of vices. For because of their injustices they were humbled, that they might be exalted in Christ.

**18** [Col. 0393A] “Their soul abhorred all food, and they approached ÷ even to .. the gates of death.”

C Here we must understand spiritual food, namely God’s law and saving precepts, by which the faithful soul lives; the mind of the wicked is fasting from it in ruinous hunger. A grievous sickness, an accursed calamity: not to have an appetite for divine law. For how can one live who has begun not to love his own life? Hence they came to those deadly barriers, unless they were freed by the Lord’s mercy.

**19** “And they cried to the Lord when they were afflicted, and he delivered them from their necessities.”

C This verse is plainly repeated because in a similar case one statement was fitting.

**20** [Col. 0393B] “He sent his Word and healed them, and delivered them from their destructions ÷ ...”

H He sent his Word, that is, the Father sent the Son, to restore and heal us. And he delivered them from the destructions into which they themselves had plunged. C See what a sickness it is to disdain the spiritual delights of God’s Word and of the prophets, such that only the presence of the heavenly physician, namely Christ, could remove so great a danger of illness.

**21** “Let them confess the Lord’s mercies, and his wonders to the children of men.”

The fourth section of the Psalm is introduced by repeated verses. He admonishes the priests to confess to the Lord—that is, to offer sacrifice to him—and not to cease proclaiming his wonders to the peoples.

### 22 [Col. 0393C]

**And let them sacrifice the sacrifice of praise: And let them announce his works with rejoicing.**

**C** He renders sacrifice to the Lord who joyfully offers a sacrifice of praise. For it is much more excellent to offer him, through good works, the rejoicings of psalmody than to immolate the victims of cattle. And let his preachers proclaim his works—that is, his benefits—with rejoicing. For we more readily consent to believe those things which we see teachers proclaiming with steadfast and joyful conviction.

### 23

**Those who go down to the sea in ships: Doing their work upon many waters.**

**C** “Those who go down to the sea” signifies the priests, who descend into the stormy conditions of this age. **H** “In ships,” that is, in the Churches, which carry Christ and are battered by the waves [Col. 0393D] of this world. “Doing their work,” **C** that is, preaching to the Christian peoples, who are signified by the many waters.

### 24

**They themselves saw the works of the Lord: And his wonders in the deep.**

**C** “They themselves saw”—those preachers themselves, who recognized his works through spiritual understanding. “In the deep”: **H** for in the profound darkness the light of truth shone through their preaching, so that, while God was at work, they might see the light of the most true Trinity shining amid the densest darkness.

### 25

**He spoke, and a storm-wind arose: And its waves were exalted.**

**C** “The spirit of the storm” signifies the tempests of our tribulations, which God in his merciful compassion holds back, lest we be overwhelmed as evils increase. “And its waves were exalted” in human minds when we suppose that what we see must be attributed to our merits, although we can be delivered by divine grace alone.

### 26

**They ascend to the heavens and descend to the abysses: Their soul was wasting away in evils.**

**C** These waves also ascend to the heavens when they are lifted up by the pride of the world; but they descend to the abysses when they fall into despair. “Their soul was wasting away in evils,” that is, in fear and in remembrance of the evils it had committed; for here “to waste away” is used in a good sense. **H** “They ascend,” by hearing; “they descend,” by fearing.

### 27

**They were troubled and shaken like a drunkard: [Col. 0394B] And all their wisdom was swallowed up.**

**C** “They were troubled” pertains to the sense of confusion. “They were shaken” pertains to anger immediately spewed forth. “And they were shaken like a drunkard.” **H** For their understanding possessed nothing stable, nothing sober. “Their wisdom was swallowed up.” **C** For it cannot appear among troubled minds, in which wisdom had previously seemed to dwell; wisdom can be found only among calm and undisturbed souls. **C H** Their wisdom is therefore rightly said to have been swallowed up: those who previously seemed to themselves to be teachers now, disturbed by the wisdom of God, recognize that they had been fools. Thus formerly the dragon of Moses swallowed the dragons of the Egyptians (Exod. 7).

### 28

**And they cried to the Lord when they were afflicted: [Col. 0394C] And he led them out of their distress.**

**H** They cried to the Lord so that, abandoning luxurious drunkenness, they might follow the wisdom of God. **C** Behold, those who were like drunkards, whose wisdom seemed to have been swallowed up, returned by a saving cry to life-giving counsels; turning to the Lord, they began at last to be sober. And he led them out of their distress in the manner that follows, by an allegorical description.

### 29

**And he set their storm into a breeze: And their waves were silent.**

**C** “And he set their storm into a breeze,” that is, that most savage tempest—which could not be endured by human frailty—vanished when commanded into the air. “And their waves were silent,” that is, **H** they were changed into tranquility for those who were doing penance, because **C** immediately that uproar of raging evils fell silent at the command of the one who rules.

### 30 ÷

**÷ And .. they rejoiced because they were silent: And he led them into the harbor of their desire.**

**C** “They rejoiced” refers to what usually happens to those sailing after dangers: they rejoice that they have been delivered from a great disaster when they begin to approach the safest harbor—that is, Christ. For “harbor” (*portus*) is so called from carrying ships (*portare*), and the soul tossed by agitation is carried in Christ and made peaceful. **H** When the waves of temptations have come to rest, those who were troubled rejoice because they have been freed; and God will lead the freed into the harbor of their desire—namely, those who have turned their undivided will toward him, for he himself is the true harbor.

### 31 [Col. 0395A]

**Let them confess to the Lord his mercies: And his wonders to the sons of men.**

**C** Observe here that he repeated the same verse for the fourth time, so that the fourfold division of the world, which he earlier described as extending from sunrise and sunset, from the north and from the sea, might correspond to these sections; thus the faithful confession might everywhere be sung as one and everywhere with the greatest renown: so that, just as there is one Church everywhere, there might also be one confession everywhere. **H** “Let them confess to the Lord his mercies,” by which he protects the human race, “and his wonders performed for the sons of men,” because he wonderfully restrains these waves.

### 32 +

**And let them exalt him in the assembly of the people: And in the seat of the elders let them praise him.**

**C** Here he calls the Church noble and endowed with true religion [Col. 0395B], since it always exalts the Lord through religious deeds. And by “the seat” he commands all teachers to resound with the praises of the Lord—those who sit in the seat of the elders, that is, those who have been found worthy to be successors of the ancient pontiffs. **H** “And let them praise him in the seat of the elders”—not in the seat in which the scribes and Pharisees sat, who, although they read the law, did not understand that the Lord was announced in it; but in that seat in which either the prophets or the patriarchs, beholding him with spiritual eyes, recognized him in his miracles, or sang of him in their oracles.

### 33

**He made rivers into a desert: And springs of water into thirst.**

**C** He now adds the reason for confession and exaltation: because, once the Jews had been rejected, the whole fullness of the water of the Holy Spirit came to the Christian people. Those rivers—namely, the prophets or apostles—passed over to the deserts of the nations because the Jews did not believe; and, like a diverted and irrigating spring, all divine speech was transferred to the nations. “And springs of water into thirst,” that is, into the nations, so that those who had previously been dried up by the aridity of sin might drink the heavenly waters with thirst. **H** They rightly exalt and praise God, who placed apostles in the Church that had previously been a desert and hated, so that they might both console it by their address and make it fertile by their overflowing stream. He also gave to thirsty souls the outflow of preaching, and filled with eternal fruits the bodily earth which had previously produced the thorns of bitterness.

### 34

**A fruitful land into saltiness: [Col. 0395D] Because of the wickedness of those who dwelt in it.**

**C** Judea was a fruitful land when it flourished in heavenly religion, but it became salty when it despised God’s commandments. For salty moisture is found to be hostile to fruits; wherever it has gained dominion, it interrupts the shoot of fertility. This happened to them because of the wickedness of those who seemed, with deceitful minds, to inhabit God’s tabernacle.

### 35

**He made a desert into pools of water: And a waterless land into springs of water.**

**C** This verse pertains to the Christian people, whose dryness was given the saving water of sacred baptism. I think “pools” is used for the fountains of the Churches; pools (*stagna*) are indeed so called from standing (*stare*). [Col. 0396A] “A waterless land” signifies the unbelieving hearts of the nations, which, after being watered by the stream of baptism and holy preaching, flourished. **H** “He made a desert into pools of water,” providing baptism in the Church. “And a waterless land into springs of water,” that is, he established preachers amid the aridity of the nations. “And he settled the hungry there,” so that they might be refreshed by heavenly goods.

### 36

**And he settled the hungry there: And they established a city for habitation.**

**C** “He settled the hungry there,” that is, those who embraced the Lord’s exceedingly glorious gifts with eager desire. “A city for habitation” is the Catholic Church, in which those who obey heavenly commands establish themselves firmly.

### 37 [Col. 0396B]

**And they sowed fields and planted vineyards: And they produced the fruit of their produce.**

**C** They sow fields and plant vineyards who, cleansing their bodies of the thorns of sins, purify them through heavenly instruction. “Fruit” is named from enjoyment (*frui*), and therefore those who produce spiritual fruit enjoy the blessing of God. But those whom he finds fruitless he will cut down like the barren fig tree (Luke XIII). A field (*ager*) is named from activity (*agere*), because various means of sustenance are carried out there.

### 38

**And he blessed them, and they multiplied greatly: And he did not diminish their cattle.**

**H** God blessed those who guard themselves from evil thoughts. **C** “And they multiplied greatly,” through the fruitfulness of merits. We should understand “cattle” as simple people [Col. 0396C], distinguished by the integrity of their faith, not renowned for eloquence, but better in life than in speech; greatly strong, not in tongue but in heart. They were not diminished, but restored for the better, because they obtained the great grace of God. **H** He blessed the apostles, because they always did what was pleasing to him, just as God blessed everything through the hand of Joseph.

### 39

**And they became few: And they were afflicted by the tribulation and pain of evils.**

**C** In these two verses he describes those who, deceived by heretical perversity, abandon the Church of God. These, therefore, are few, although they seem many to themselves; for when compared with that universal Church, they are proved to be utterly insignificant. “Afflicted”: when diabolical snares struck them, pain and tribulation followed, because they are known to have abandoned the author of salvation. **H** He explains this of the Jews, whom he says became few because the works of God were no longer multiplied among them; and they were afflicted by the tribulation of evils because they persecuted the innocent man, upon whose leaders contempt was poured out: so that those who had despised the Lord might themselves be despised, and he made them wander in Satan’s trackless place.

### 40

**Contempt was poured out upon the princes: And he made them wander in a trackless place and not on the way.**

**C** Here the priests of the heretics are briefly indicated, upon whom contempt was poured out because they contend not with saving doctrine but only with deadly loquacity [Col. 0397A]. They slip through trackless errors, since they abandon the way of salvation and linger in crooked paths. Thus Cassiodorus’s text has *contentio* (“contention”), as does his exposition. But all the translations—the texts of Origen, Jerome, and Augustine—have *contemptio* (“contempt”), and they explain it accordingly: **H** “those who had despised the Lord might themselves be despised.” **A** Or they wished to be princes, but were despised and rejected by the Church, like salt that has lost its savor.

### 41

**And he helped the poor man out of poverty: And he established families like sheep.**

**C** He returns to the humble Catholics. “He helped the poor man,” **H** that is, he satisfied the Christian people with eternal nourishment. “And he established families like sheep,” so that, hearing the voice of the true shepherd, they might follow in faith. **C** This poor man is the one who, having abandoned worldly allurements, knocks at the door of heavenly mercy, so that he may deserve to be admitted into that household of God which, like harmless sheep, is adorned with the dignity of simplicity.

### 42

**The upright will see and rejoice: And every iniquity will shut its mouth.**

**II** “The upright will see” those who have been converted by their preaching. “And every iniquity”—that is, the devil, or the Jews and heretics—will become silent, **C** when there is nothing that can be brought against the Lord’s elect.

### 43

**Who is wise and will guard these things? And will understand the mercies of the Lord.**

**C** “Who is wise?” As though he were saying: Whoever is truly wise guards the things that have been said, so that he may prefer to be Christ’s poor man rather than a prince among heretics. [Col. 0397C] **H** For if you consider wisely and understand spiritually, you will see in this Psalm mercies that were sought and mercifully granted. **C** Or you will see mercies in heaven and understand that they were mercifully granted; that is, you will receive as a reward mercies that can never be brought to an end. **A** Or “he will understand the mercies of the Lord”—not his own merits, not his own strength, not his own power, but that everything good he possesses has been bestowed upon him by the Lord’s mercy; that the nations have come to faith through mercy; and that all who have been saved and all who will be saved are blessed by mercy alone. For this reason he so often commanded that the Lord’s mercies be confessed.

## Prayer from Psalm 106

We confess, O Lord, your mercies, which you continually exercise toward our poverty [Col. 0397D], praying that you, who, exalted in the Churches, sit at the right hand of the Father on the throne, may grant us both to understand and to guard the mystery of such great compassion. You who live and reign, etc.

# Psalm 107

## Argument of Psalm 107

**C** Christ gives thanks to the Father because, after the triumph of the Passion, he rose again perpetually into glory.

**TT. A psalm-song of David.**

**C** We have often said that a “song” refers to the contemplation of divine things, whereas a “psalm” refers to actual works, which nevertheless are known to accord with divine commandments. David signifies the king Christ, who speaks throughout the entire Psalm.

[Col. 0398A]

**My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready: I will sing and make melody in my glory.**

**C** Christ was always ready for such things, since he had no obstacle of sin preventing him from fulfilling the proclamations of the Father. It follows: “I will sing and recite a psalm.” He rightly spoke such things about himself, whose speech and deeds accorded with divine ordinances. The very repetition shows confidence in the promise, since he says twice, “My heart is ready.” **H** “I am ready” not only in deed but also in heart and understanding; therefore I will sing in my heart and make melody in my works. If one string of a psaltery is broken, the psaltery is ruined; and if we transgress one commandment in our actions, our psaltery is broken.

[Col. 0398B]

Therefore I will make melody in my glory. For whatever I sing or chant to you, O God, I do not do to give you grace but for myself, since you have no need of my good things (Ps. XV). Therefore, the fact that I serve you is my glory; for if I fast or lie in sackcloth because of my sins, by doing this I offer you only that I save my soul. As a good physician, you rejoice in this; you rejoice in my healing, and I rejoice in my own benefit.

### 2

**Rise up, psaltery and lyre: I will rise at dawn.**

**C** “Rise up, my glory,” which is indicated by the psaltery and the lyre. The psaltery pertains to moral integrity; the lyre to the affliction of the body. Through these he shows both praiseworthy deeds and his most glorious Passion. “I will rise at dawn” can be understood of Christ’s resurrection, of his members, and of every faithful person who stands ready in the Lord’s Church to praise him through pious works. For although he praises him in the deep night, he is illumined at dawn by the proclamation of God.

### 3

**I will confess you among the peoples, O Lord: And I will make melody to you among the nations.**

**C** He says that he will confess among the people of the Jews, where he spoke in his own voice; but he will make melody among the nations, to which the Lord’s apostles were sent and fulfilled his commandments. Thus he says that he will make melody because he is known to have accomplished these things through his ministers. **H** “I will confess you among the peoples,” that is, among the Jews who first believed, and afterward also among the nations of the Gentiles.

### 4

**For your mercy is great above the heavens: And your truth reaches to the clouds.**

[Col. 0398D]

**C** His mercy was magnified up to the heavens when the heavenly powers enjoy his benefits. “Up to the clouds,” when preachers, like rain-bearing clouds, watered unbelieving peoples. **H** “For your mercy is great above the heavens.” There is no creature that does not need the mercy of God—not even Gabriel, Michael, the Cherubim, or the Seraphim. I do not detract from the angels, but I proclaim the Creator, over whom the angels also rejoice, namely, because the Creator is proclaimed. Or: your mercy lifts from earth to the heavens.

### 5

**Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and your glory above all the earth, so that your beloved may be delivered.**

**C** “Be exalted above the heavens, O God”: since the heavenly realms are sustained by your mercy, it is right that you should be exalted above the heavens. “And above all the earth,” when I have been exalted, **H** that is, when I have been crucified, “I will draw all things to myself” (John XII). “So that your beloved may be delivered”: the Lord is crucified and exalted for this reason, so that his beloved may be delivered. It happened as we asked: he was exalted, and we were delivered. “Be exalted above the heavens, O God”: God is exalted only above the heavens, not above the earth; for when we are earthly, we do not exalt God, but when our conduct is heavenly, we do.

### 6

**Save me with your right hand and hear me: God has spoken in his holy one.**

**C** “Save me”: in the Passion he prays that he may be saved, so that the multitude of believers may be delivered. “God has spoken in his holy one,” that is, in the Son, so that the Word made flesh might speak with the Father in one will.

### 7

**I will rejoice ÷ and .. divide Shechem: And I will measure out the valley of the tents.**

**H** Shechem is interpreted as “shoulder”; the shoulder signifies works. The meaning, therefore, is: I am crucified so that I may divide my works among my saints. **C** Or, after his resurrection, he says that he will rejoice and divide his works—that is, his graces—among the apostles and the faithful. And he adds “the valley of the tents,” which signifies the humility of the Churches. The Lord measured out this humility when he distributed gifts to each of the faithful as he willed.

### 8

**Gilead is mine and Manasseh is mine: [Col. 0399C] And Ephraim is the protection of my head.**

**C** Gilead is interpreted as “migration,” by which migration the nations, pierced by the Lord’s calling, happily migrated to God. Manasseh means “forgetfulness”; by this word he signifies the Jewish people, who, having forgotten the divine benefits, crucified Christ, yet by his mercy returned to his worship. Thus, by recalling these names, he testifies that both peoples belong to him. **H C** Ephraim is called “fruitfulness,” and signifies the crown of thorns; for this was more fruitful than all fruits, since by this humility it delivered us, and he placed protection in the place of a crown.

### 9

**Judah is my king: Moab is the cauldron of my hope.**

**C** He called Judah his king because he descended from his stock. [Col. 0399D] **H** Moab is said to mean “from the father”: *mo* is interpreted as “from,” and *ab* as “father.” And who is the one who is “from the father”? He is the one who by evil works lost the father and did not return to the father—namely, the devil. For he signifies the devil, who is the cauldron of the Lord’s hope. *Labes* is interpreted as “pot.” How is he the cauldron of the Lord’s hope? In this way: those who do not walk rightly are handed over to the devil, so that, tormented by him, they may be converted to the Lord.

### 10

**Upon Idumea I will stretch out my sandal: Foreigners have become my friends.**

**H** Idumea is interpreted as “earthly,” for the merciful God wishes to possess not only heavenly things but earthly things as well. **C** Stretching out his sandal—that is, his law and Gospel—he filled the world with universal preaching; the foreigners are the nations.

### 11

**Who will lead me into the fortified city? Who will lead me as far as Idumea?**

**C** “Who will lead me?” A question is first put forward from the perspective of his humanity, so that the answer that follows may be supplied. **H C** The fortified city perhaps signifies hell, which no human force could open except the one who broke its gates. This city is fortified against departure but open for entering. **H** Idumea is also interpreted as “bloody,” signifying the place of punishments where the souls of sinners are slain.

### 12

**Are you not, O God, who rejected us: And will you not go out, O God, with our armies?**

**C** Who could break the prison of death? Who could open [Col. 0400B] the gates of the fortified city, except Christ himself? “You rejected us”: the head speaks with the members, that is, “you delayed us,” because it is clear that Christ himself was also delayed in his glorification while he remained in this life. “And you will not go out”: this signifies the time when, held by the Jews, he endured spitting and scourging. For then, if the divinity had wished, it would have repelled them; but he delayed displaying the miracle in order to fulfill the order of his beneficial Passion.

### 13

**Give us help from tribulation: For the salvation of man is vain.**

**C** “Give us help”: here Christ’s humanity cries out with his members, so that at last the tempest of this age may come to rest. “For the salvation of man is vain,” that is, **H** “Cursed is the man who places his hope in man” (Jer. XVII), because we have hope in God alone.

### 14

**In God we will perform mightily: And he himself will bring our enemies to nothing.**

**H** “In God we will perform mightily”: he will be our strength, our bread that strengthens the heart, and our ruler. “And he himself will bring our enemies to nothing,” because he crowns us and conquers the devil; he fights in us, or rather, he himself conquers in us.

## Prayer from Psalm 107

Prepare our heart for yourself, O Lord, to confess your name, so that, understanding that you rose at dawn, we may rightly strive toward the place where you shine forth victorious in the kingdom. You who live and reign, etc.

# Psalm 108

[Col. 0400D]

## Argument of Psalm 108

**C** Christ rebukes the Jews, who repaid him evil for good; and he recounts the destruction of Judas and of the people themselves.

**TT. A psalm of David, for the end.**

**C** This Psalm must be referred to the heavenly king, since all its words tend toward Christ the Lord.

### 1

**Do not be silent, O God, regarding my praise: For the mouth of the sinner and of the deceitful man has been opened against me.**

**C** The Lord the Savior, according to his humanity, asks that the praise of his resurrection not be silenced, saying: “O God, do not be silent regarding my praise,” that is, do not cause it to be silenced. For, since the enemies were speaking lies, saying, “His disciples stole him” (Matt. XXVIII), it was fitting that throughout the whole world we should sing testimonies of the resurrection against them, so that the Jews might recognize the guilt of their own perversity. “The mouth that has been opened” clearly designates the insults that he endured from the Jews; for although he speaks of one by the singular name, in understanding they are known to be many within the one people.

### 2

**They spoke against me with a deceitful tongue: And they surrounded me with words of hatred: And they attacked me without cause.**

**C** They spoke, therefore, with a deceitful tongue when with deceitful words they assailed the holy simplicity of the Lord, saying, “Is it lawful to pay the census tax to Caesar?” (Matt. XXII). “And with words of hatred,” when in an evil conspiracy they said to Pilate, “Crucify, crucify.” “They attacked me without cause”: just as the righteous love God without payment, since they love him not for any temporal benefit but solely for his goodness, so the ungodly hate him freely, because they cannot find in him any cause for hatred. **H** Or “freely,” that is, without reason or benefit. For whoever persecutes someone and gains nothing does not accomplish his intention; he is said to have persecuted “freely,” that is, in vain.

### 3

**In return for loving + me .. they slandered me: But I was praying.**

**H** “In return for loving me,” that is, in return for the benefits that I had conferred upon them, they inflicted insults on me and repaid me evil for good. “But I was praying”: “Lord, do not hold this sin against them” (Luke XXIII). **H C** Observe the three degrees of sinners. The first is not to return good for good; the second is to return evil for evil; the third and worst is to inflict evil in return for good. The Jews chose that final and most vicious degree. Conversely, consider the three degrees of virtue. The first is to bestow good for good; the second is not to return evil for evil; the third and most perfect is to bestow good for evil. And just as the Jews chose the worst degree of vice, so Christ wished to hold the highest degree of goodness, so that he would even pray on the cross for those who crucified him. **H** “But I was praying”: “Father, forgive them.” I was praying not for vengeance but for their salvation.

### 4

**And they placed evils against me in return for good: [Col. 0401D] And hatred in return for my love.**

**H** “They placed evils against me”: he was praying for those crucifying him, while they were saying, “Ha! You who destroy this temple, save yourself” (Matt. XXVII). “And hatred in return for love”: consider, O Christian and monk, if Christ prayed for those who crucified him, what we ought to do for our brothers.

### 5

**Appoint a sinner over him. And let the devil stand at his right hand.**

**C** The prophet, most certain of future events, foretold that the devil would be appointed over Judas the betrayer. He is rightly called a sinner, since the sin of betrayal began with him. He adds, “And let the devil stand at his right hand.” He could not have his right hand free, since he was wholly carrying out the crimes of the left side. Thus each person is said to do something according to the one who holds his right hand.

### 6

**When he is judged, let him go forth condemned: And let his prayer become sin.**

**C** This is spoken of the future judgment, when sinners will be condemned by the voice of the judge saying, “Depart from me, accursed ones.” Let him go forth, namely, from the assembly of the righteous. **H** His prayer ought to have become repentance, but it became sin. Let heretics and Manichaeans hear this: although they pray, their prayer nevertheless turns into sin. Judas’s repentance too—that is, his hanging—became a greater sin than the betrayal; for he offended the Lord more by hanging himself than by betraying the Lord.

### 7 [Col. 0402B]

**Let his days be few: And let another receive his episcopate.**

**H** His days are few because the sun of justice withdrew from him and darkness was multiplied for him. **C** Or because he did not live as long in the apostolate as the other apostles. “And another received his episcopate” (Acts I), lest the most sacred number of the apostles be broken when Judas died. Episcopate is the highest rank in the Church; in Latin it is called “oversight.”

### 8

**Let his children become orphans: And his wife a widow.**

**A C** Although it is not recorded elsewhere that Judas had a wife or children, it is understood from this prophecy that he did have them. When he died, it undoubtedly happened that his wife, left behind, became a widow and his children became orphans, since they had lost their father. Spiritually, however, his children are called the Jews, who followed him in that betrayal. **H** And the synagogue is Judas’s wife, repudiated by the husband Christ and left to Judas the betrayer. **C** Or “wife” can be understood as his will, from which we generate works that may be called children.

### 9

**Let his children wander about trembling and beg: Let them be driven out of their dwellings.**

**H** The Jews were trembling after the Lord’s crucifixion because they are no longer in their own places. Here he speaks of a begging for spiritual things; for they have no prophets, no law, no priesthood, no sacrifice. They have truly become beggars through their lack of good things. This was prefigured in Cain, of whom it is said, “He went out from the face of God and dwelt in the land of Naid” (Gen. IV). Naid is interpreted as “agitation”; therefore, having gone out from the face of God, he did not stand firm but dwelt in agitation and instability.

### 10

**Let the creditor search out all his substance: + And let strangers plunder his labors ..**

**H** “The creditor”: here the devil is understood. This is now prophesied concerning Judas in the optative form, that he may be given into the devil’s power and stripped of all good things. **C** The strangers are also the unclean spirits, whom the devil commands like slaves to do harm. They plunder the labors of those who transgress God’s commandments, when, having received permission, they deprive them of every good. **H** Or the strangers were the Romans, who, laying them waste, plundered their labors and riches.

### 11 [Col. 0403A]

**Let there be no helper for him: Nor anyone who has pity on his orphans.**

**H** “Let there be no helper for him.” At that time the Jewish people had a helper, when they were in Babylonian captivity for seventy years; for they had the prophets Ezekiel and Daniel there. Although they were then worshiping idols, their God nevertheless had mercy on them. But now it has been four hundred years since Christ’s killing, and they do not worship idols. Why, then, did the Lord abandon them? Because they killed Christ, and therefore they have no helper. **C** They are called “orphans” as though they were “little ones” (*pusilli*), because through the smallness of their age they are shown to be weak in governing themselves.

### 12

**Let his offspring be brought to destruction: In one generation let his name be blotted out.**

**H** O prophecy, O mystery of prophecy! “In one generation let the name of the Jews be blotted out.” Forty-two years passed after the Lord’s Passion, and that people was blotted out and Jerusalem was destroyed. Yet in this there was the mercy of God, because he gave them forty-two years for repentance; afterward none of them remained in that region.

**Let the iniquity of his fathers return to remembrance in the sight of the Lord: And let the sin of his mother not be blotted out.**

**H** Judas is cursed so that in Judas the Jews may be cursed. The Jews sinned in the desert, but God forgave them; now he prays that what they then sinned may be reckoned against them like a new crime, for their destruction. **C** “The sin of his mother” is the manifest insolence of the synagogue [Col. 0403C], which killed the prophets. She is called the mother of the betrayer in that respect because she shed the blood of the innocent—not in the respect in which she is called his mother because she produced holy men, but in the respect in which, as has been said, she shed blood. In this respect Judas imitated her as a son.

### 14

**Let them always be against the Lord. And let their memory perish from the earth: Because he did not remember to show mercy.**

**C** Sinners are therefore always made against the Lord when, alienated from his kingdom and separated from him, they are to be sent into Gehenna. For since he is eternal blessedness, those who are condemned to everlasting punishment are said to be made against him. Their memory perishes from the land of the living because they are not seen in the blessed homeland [Col. 0403D] and obtain no further mercy. “Because he did not,” and so forth: he states the reason for the most just vengeance, since one who despises showing compassion to others cannot find compassion himself. Through the singular number, however, we should understand not Judas alone but the whole people as one in Judas’s crime.

### 15

**And he persecuted the needy and poor man: And to put the brokenhearted to death.**

**C** In his customary manner the Lord recalls that he is poor and needy: needy from what is ours, rich from what is his. **H** “Brokenhearted,” as in the Gospel: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matt. XXVI). Alternatively, he was grieved because those who persecuted him were unwilling to repent. **A C** Or, since brokenness properly arises from sins, this is understood of Christ’s members, such as Stephen, Paul, and others whom the Jews persecuted in Christ [Col. 0404A].

### 16

**And he loved the curse, and it will come to him: And he did not wish blessing, and it will be far from him.**

**C** He still speaks of the faithless people, because it loved the curse when it said, “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. XXVII). It did not wish blessing when the man who had been enlightened said to them, “Do you also wish to become his disciples?” (John IX). But they, as though provoked by the sharpest curse, said, “You be his disciple; we are disciples of Moses.” By this statement the blessing was prolonged away from them, when, after they had been abandoned, it came to the faith of the nations.

### 17

**And he put on the curse like a garment: And it entered like water into his inmost parts. [Col. 0404B] And like oil into his bones.**

**C** The aforementioned people clothed themselves with a curse like a garment when, instigated by the devil, they gave their consent and preferred to hand the Lord over to Pontius Pilate. There he was clothed, as it were, with the burden of a garment, where he wrapped himself in such a will. The curse entered like water when he resolved to do what had been suggested to him by a most wicked inspiration; for when water is received by diseased entrails, it always enters to do harm. “Oil” here signifies delight in the crime. Thus iniquity flowed a third time into his bones like oil, when he completed the deed with unheard-of perversity, so that it entered not only into the flesh’s interior parts but also into the bones.

### 18 [Col. 0404C]

**Let it be to him like the garment with which he is covered: And like the belt with which he is always girded.**

**C** Above he said “he put on,” which pertains to a tunic; now he says “he is covered,” which seems to suit a cloak. The doubled garment signifies the burdens of enormous sins. “And like the belt with which he is always girded”: by this comparison he says that this people was bound by sins as by cords, so that, burdened by the weight of its obstinate faithlessness, it might never escape its burdens. These are the garments that make sinners burn, not keep warm; they cast them into flame rather than protect them from the cold.

### 19

**This is the work of those who slander me before the Lord: And who speak evil against my soul.**

[Col. 0404D]

**C** We should understand this verse not only against the Jews but also against all the faithless. The Arians slander the Son before the Father when they say that he is lesser. The Apollinarists speak evil against the Lord’s soul when they say that his divinity assumed only the flesh of a man and not a soul.

### 20

**But you, Lord, Lord, act with me for the sake of your name: For your mercy is sweet.**

**C** “But you, Lord”: that is, if Judas betrayed, if the Jew crucified, you show mercy, so that in opposition to what was done a glorious resurrection may arise. Or he says “with me” for this reason: everything the Father does, the Son also works. For mercy is sweet in the vessels of mercy (Rom. IX), and in these vessels the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit together perform this mercy. Or it is sweet in the assumption of flesh.

### 21

**Deliver me, for I am needy and poor: And my heart is troubled within me.**

**C** “Deliver me” from the Jews’ most savage Passion. He calls himself needy and poor because of the humility of the flesh. His heart was troubled, as he himself acknowledged: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Mark XIV).

### 22

**Like a shadow when it declines, I have been taken away: And I have been shaken off like a locust.**
C Here he shows the speed of the persecution: for he was snatched from the midst of the disciples with as great a speed as the shadow of night is accustomed to depart when the light of the sun arrives. “Shaken off like a locust”: a locust, avoiding the hand of one trying to seize it, flies away in certain leaps. H C Thus Christ, fleeing from the frequent persecutions, seemed to change places, so that the people might not fulfill their zeal before he himself had willed to die.
