23 My knees have been weakened by fasting: And my flesh has been changed because of the oil.

A The strong seem to me to be represented by the knees in the Church, as the apostles were. Therefore, C “my knees have been weakened” means when his apostles were scattered in the Passion. For what could have been weaker than that Peter should deny him and the rest of the faithful crowd should have hidden? H Here “oil” is an image of the brightness of God. C Or it signifies divine grace, which changed the weakness of the flesh into the glory of immortality. A That oil is the fullness of grace in Christ, which changed dead human nature into the glory of the resurrection.

24 [Col. 0405C] I have become a reproach to them: They saw me and shook their heads.

C Christ became a reproach to the Jews, who said, “Ha! You who destroy the temple of God” (Matt. XXVII), and the rest of what seemed to their deranged minds to be reproaches; but these very things proved to be what brought us healing. “They shook their heads”: this belongs to the customary behavior of those who are excessively angry, because by the turbulent movement of their heads they threaten.

25 Help me, Lord my God: Save me according to your mercy.

C The weakness that he assumed asks to be helped. H C For he himself asks for mercy who also grants help: he asks as a human being, he provides as God; therefore he asks for the resurrection of the body.

26 [Col. 0405D] And let them know that this is your hand: And you, Lord, have made it.

H “And let them know,” that is, let the Jews understand, that they did not prevail over Christ, but that it was the will of himself and of the Father that he should endure the cross for us, because “this is your hand.” C That is, your power—and one must supply, “has wrought this.” H Or “this is your hand,” namely, in my Passion and resurrection. A And let those who now persecute me know this afterward, when they believe in me.

27 Let them curse him, and you will bless: Let those who rise up against me be confounded: But your servant will rejoice.

C “Let them curse him,” namely, those who, shaking their heads, passed by and blasphemed him. The Father blessed the Son when he said, “I have glorified, and I will glorify again” (John XII). The Jews rose up against the Lord in order to hand him over to death. They were confounded when they learned of the miracles of his resurrection. “Servant”: according to his humanity, as Isaiah says, “Behold my servant, I will receive him” (Isa. XLII). H “Let them curse him”: to this day they do so; they curse him in the synagogue, while Christ blesses in the Church.

28 Let those who slander me be clothed with shame: And let them be covered, like a double cloak, with their confusion.

H C “Let the slanderers be clothed with shame”: that is, let them understand their error and be confounded by shame, and from there begin to come to repentance. For whoever is clothed with shame is near salvation: if someone is truly ashamed, he begins to repent. H A C *Diplois* is a kind of cloak, namely, a double cloak. C He therefore asks that they be clothed with the understanding of both covenants, since they are now stripped of both through their unbelief. For the confession of the Jews is that they do not understand the Law, which so often foretold that the Savior would come. Or “with a double cloak,” that is, with a twofold confusion, namely, before God and before human beings.

29 I will confess greatly to the Lord with my mouth: And in the midst of many I will praise him.

C This is said with reference to the members, because after the resurrection the holy Church of God, spread throughout the whole world, entreats God both with mouth and with confession. “In the midst of many” also designates the Church itself, which, although unbelievers still surround it, does not cease to confess God. A *Nimis* is customarily said, according to Latin usage, of what is more than it ought to be. Its opposite is *parum*, “too little,” which is less than it ought to be. But *nimis* is called *agan* in Greek. This verse, however, does not have *agan*, but *aian*, which some of our writers have translated sometimes as “very much,” sometimes as “exceedingly”; but *nimis* should here be understood in the sense of “very much.” Hence the Hebrew translation also does not have *nimis*, but “vehemently.”

30 He stood at the right hand of the poor: To save my soul from those who pursued me.

C He says that the Father stood at his right hand because he had no sins; but he also stands beside the faithful when he has forgiven their offenses. His soul was saved from those who pursued him when it consented in no way to the wickedness of his persecutors.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM 108

O God of singular mercy, you who deigned to submit to the curse in order to rescue us from the curse of the Law, we ask that you show mercy toward us for the sake of your name, and deign to free us from the vices that pursue us and from the slanders of evil people. You who live and reign, and so forth.

# PSALM 109

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM 109

C This psalm sings, fully yet briefly, of the Lord’s incarnation and of his divinity.

[Col. 0407A] TT. A psalm of David.

1 The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand.

C The most holy Prophet, raised into the secret heights of contemplation, shows in the first verse both the nature of divinity and that of humanity. When he says, “The Lord said,” he shows the nature of divinity. “To my Lord”: he spoke of the coeternal Son, who is called David’s Lord and son because he arose from his seed. “Sit at my right hand”: it is confessed and offered to the victorious Son, the conqueror of the whole world through the incarnation, so that by this position the glory of the humanity he assumed might be declared. H But he says that the right hand was given to the Son so that the one who commands and says, “Sit,” might not appear greater than the one to whom the command is given.

2 Until I place your enemies: As a footstool for your feet.

C A footstool is so called because it is climbed, that is, ascended. “Until” is used in place of an indefinite expression, for it is the usage of Scripture to employ that word both of a short period and of eternity. The Lord’s feet signify his eternal stability; for those enemies are subjected beneath these feet who, abandoning the sins of their vices, turn to the Lord and submit themselves to his preaching as to a footstool beneath his feet.

3 The Lord will send forth the scepter of your power from Zion. Rule in the midst of your enemies.

C “The scepter of power” is the staff of royal authority, by which he sustains the faithful and afflicts unbelievers. He said “your,” because the power proper to him is his own divinity and is coeternal. The Lord sends this forth from Zion: he is certainly the almighty Father, while the Son too is called “Lord from Zion.” He rules when the multitude of sinners turns to him. H He said “rule”; he did not say, “Kill your enemies,” but “rule,” that is, make those who were enemies and strangers begin to be yours; in other words, deign to be Lord of your enemies.

4 With you is sovereignty on the day of your power, amid the splendors of the holy ones: From the womb, before the morning star, I have begotten you.

C Here the almighty Father speaks of the almighty Son: “With you is sovereignty.” For the Father is the beginning, and the Son is the beginning; yet there are not two beginnings, but just as there is one God, so there is one beginning. “On the day” signifies eternity; there is one day where the divine brightness is already seen by the blessed. The “splendors of the holy ones” are when they will shine like the angels of God in the resurrection. “From the womb”: the Father speaks of the Son as coming from the secret place of my substance, namely, from divinity itself. H When he says “before the morning star,” he names one creature and indicates that the Son precedes all creatures. Nor could the Father indicate himself as Father in any other way unless he spoke in human words: “I have begotten you,” and “from the womb.” But what he says, “from the womb,” should cause no one scandal. The Father does not have a womb; but he cannot indicate himself as Father in any other way unless he speaks in human terms, so that, against Arius, Christ may be believed not to be a creature made by hand, but the natural Son of God, who is born from the womb and is not adopted.

5 The Lord has sworn and will not repent: You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.

H C When the Lord swore, he did not swear to the one who was begotten before the morning star, but to the one who was born from the Virgin after the morning star. Nor will he repent; C for all things rejoiced at so great and such an arrangement. “You are a priest”: this properly and truly ought to be applied to Christ, who, in the offering of bread and wine, consecrated his body and blood for us unto salvation. Christ is properly called a priest, for he offered himself once to be sacrificed for us (Heb. IX). God alone also swears lawfully, because he alone can provide what he promises; a human being cannot do so except with God’s help.

6 [Col. 0408B] The Lord is at your right hand: He has shattered kings on the day of his anger.

C H “The Lord is at your right hand.” At the beginning it says, “Sit at my right hand.” If he himself sits at the Father’s right hand, how does the Father in turn sit at the Son’s right hand? C This was said so that, when this reciprocal equality is presented, nothing greater or lesser might in any way be understood here. H That is, so that the Father might be shown equal to the Son. C “Kings”: he signifies those who gathered together against Christ; he shattered them when he cast down their pride.

7 He will judge among the nations; he will fill the ruins: He will crush the heads in the land of many.

C He is said to judge the nations on account of their common sins. He “fills the ruins” when he causes sins to collapse from human hearts and to perish through the most salutary correction. “He will crush the heads”: namely, the heads of those who have not Christ as their head, but the devil. When they have been corrected, their head is undoubtedly crushed. “The land of many” is the land that abundantly nourishes sinners. H Or he says “of many” with respect to the vengeance of condemnation, not “of all,” so that he may not remove hope; for if he had said “of all,” no one would hope for life.

8 He will drink from the torrent on the way: Therefore he will lift up his head.

C The torrent was the turbulent persecution of the Jews, which the Lord Christ drank on the way, that is, in this life, while he endured it in the body. “He will lift up his head.” H That is, the one who had humbled himself—the same one, not another—lifted up his head, who is the head of all.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM 109

Begotten before the morning star, you who are the beginning of all creation, we ask and entreat that, just as, seated at the Father’s right hand, you subjected your enemies beneath your holy feet, so you may deem us worthy of your service, with the condemnation of sin removed. You who live and reign, and so forth.

# PSALM 110

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM 110

C The assembly of the righteous, gathered from every direction, says that it confesses and praises God.

TT. Alleluia.

C Although this word of praise, “Alleluia,” appears to be general, nevertheless it is especially placed where there is rejoicing with great exultation.

1 I will confess ÷ to you, O Lord, with my whole heart: In the counsel of the righteous and in the assembly.

C Both those who lament their sins and those who give thanks to Christ confess; but the former do so in tears, the latter in joy. Here the faithful people exult with overflowing gladness, portraying a kind of image of the age to come, where they always celebrate the Lord’s praises with devoted mind, and where these words and voices continue without interruption. “The counsel of the righteous” is, A, what the righteous deliberate. The righteous deliberate to praise God and serve him for eternal goods. Therefore the one who praises and confesses in the counsel of the righteous does so not rashly, but with reason and holy deliberation, for eternal things, as all the righteous do. “The assembly” is the blessed crown gathered together from different parts of the world.

2 Great are the works of the Lord: Sought out according to all his wills.

H “Great are the works of the Lord”: he calls those who were formerly sinners upright. C For what is more magnificent than to make a righteous person from an ungodly one, a son from an enemy? “Sought out,” that is, singularly accomplished, such that nothing similar can be found. For he also permits the devil to rage, so that from his wickedness he may find servants most faithful to himself. Thus everything is accomplished according to all his wills, most perfectly, so that nothing better—or even anything at all—can be conceived in each individual case.

3 Confession and magnificence are his work … [Col. 0409C] And his righteousness endures forever ÷ and ever.

C “Confession,” that is, praise and glory and magnificence, is his work. For the things the Lord has done are exceedingly praiseworthy and beautiful. His righteousness endures forever and ever, when he says to sinners, “Go into the eternal fire” (Matt. XXV), or when he calls the faithful, “Come, blessed ones” (ibid.); thus, in both groups, the righteousness of God remains perpetual and unchangeable.

4 The merciful and compassionate Lord has made a memorial of his wonders: He has given food to those who fear him.

He made a memorial of his wonders when he displayed very many new and unusual wonders. “Merciful” shows the nature of his compassion; “compassionate,” when at his coming he assisted the human race with generous kindness. “He gave food,” certainly spiritual nourishment; for who would think that ordinary food was given to the faithful as a reward, since it is known to be granted indiscriminately even to sinners? H Therefore “he gave food,” that is, the bread that came down from heaven.

5 He will remember his covenant forever: He will announce to his people the power of his works.

C “Forever” signifies eternity, because he keeps the words of his covenant with the most solid truth: just as Christ was promised in the Old Testament, so he came in the New. The power of his works is what he says in the Gospel: “The blind see, the deaf hear, lepers are cleansed, the dead rise” (Matt. XI). He announced that power to his Christian people, so that from it they might understand and believe that he is God; and the reason follows.

6 So that he may give them the inheritance of the nations: The works of his hands are truth and judgment.

C He gave them—that is, the Christian people—the inheritance of the nations when he built the Church from all nations as living stones. “The work of his hands is truth and judgment”: truth, because he restored what he promised to the faithful; judgment, because he threatens the impious with the future punishments that are due to the wicked.

7 All his commandments are faithful, confirmed forever and ever, made in truth and equity.

C His commandments are faithful, because they are not altered by any falsehood, but firmly guard us when, with God’s help, we hasten to observe them. “Confirmed”: for the speech spoken by truth knows no wavering. He said that they were made in truth because what is said is fulfilled, and in equity because they are proclaimed according to the weight of justice; all his commandments possess both truth and the equity of justice.

8 The Lord sent redemption to his people. He commanded his covenant forever.

C For the Father sent the Son to redeem the human race. “He commanded forever”: we say that one commands when one sends words to those who are absent through intermediaries. This was accomplished when he transmitted the New Testament to the nations through the apostles, so that it might be preached by their successors forever; for no other covenant succeeds it, as the New succeeded the Old. [Col. 0410C] It is rightly called eternal, therefore, because it is recognized as needing nothing else.

9 Holy and terrible is his name. The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.

C “Holy”: the name refers to the incarnation, as he says, “Guard my soul, for I am holy” (Ps. LXXXV). “Terrible”: it refers to the omnipotence of his divinity. These two are joined together so that either love alone may not make us negligent or such great fear make us despair. What fear is, however, he shows: namely, the beginning of wisdom.

10 Good understanding belongs to all who do it: His praise endures forever ÷ and ever …

C This good understanding, that is, true and salutary understanding, which is proved to be intent upon the fear of the Lord, is useful and fruitful, since from it is born what is proved to lead to enduring glory. His praise is worthy, because here it frees sinners and in the future crowns them; his praise is not enclosed by any limit, because the benefit bestowed cannot have an end. H C Therefore “Alleluia” is rightly written in the title, because the psalm both began with the praise of God and ended in his praise.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM 110

Glorious confession of all the saints, grant us fear of your name—which you declared to be the beginning of wisdom—so that, admitted into the councils of your servants, we may be nourished with the banquets of your mercy. Through our Lord Jesus, and so forth.

# PSALM 111

[Col. 0411A]

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM 111

C The Prophet speaks of the blessedness of the righteous, of Christ’s incarnation, and of the condemnation of the wicked.

TT. Alleluia ÷ of the conversion of Haggai and Zechariah …

C The title “of the conversion,” or “return,” of Haggai and Zechariah is woven into this title because, just as they, having returned from Babylonian captivity and seeing the Lord’s temple being restored, poured forth the Lord’s praises with great exultation, so Christians, after the forgiveness of sins and having returned from the devil’s captivity into God’s grace, ought to sing with the most perfect eagerness. For this psalm shows, after the liberation from sins, how great are the goods of the faithful and what recompense awaits sinners.

1 [Col. 0411B] Blessed is the man who fears the Lord: He will greatly delight in his commandments.

H He does not yet say, “Blessed is the man who loves the Lord.” Fear of God belongs to beginners; love of him, to the perfect. “He will greatly delight in his commandments”: whoever fears the Lord and is blessed willingly keeps and fulfills his commandments. But observe that he also did not say, “He does his commandments,” but “he will greatly delight.” For many do keep the commandments, but from fear of punishment, not from desire of the will. The blessed person, however, also wills them and longs to do them.

2 His seed will be powerful in the land: The generation of the upright will be blessed.

C Let us ask in what land the righteous are said to become powerful, since here they are proved to be objects of ridicule. In that land, namely, in which the saints are going to reign with the Lord. “Seed” signifies good works, which are cast here like seeds so that the fruit of the future harvest may grow. “The generation of the upright” is not this generation of the flesh, but that which is known to be propagated through imitation of the righteous, by the likeness of its works.

3 Glory and riches are in his house: And his righteousness endures forever ÷ and ever …

C The house of the blessed is the secret place of the mind, where whoever fulfills the Lord’s commands stores holy riches and perpetual glory. A person’s righteousness is called that which is accomplished by the Lord’s generosity. And lest anyone think that, by keeping God’s commandments, he becomes blessed only temporarily, he added, “it endures forever and ever.” [Col. 0411D] He then adds the cause of this blessedness: “Light has arisen,” and so forth.

4 Light has arisen in the darkness for the upright: Merciful and compassionate and just.

C For the light has come that surpasses every light. And to make this light more welcome, he added, “in the darkness.” But these darknesses are inward, in the heart, where the worldly sun cannot enter; that light expelled them, the light that conquered death. “Merciful,” namely, toward those who confess him; but those who despise him will endure him as the just judge.

5 The merciful and lending man is joyful: He will order his words in judgment, because he will never be shaken.

C Here “joyful man” is said not so much of one accepted by human beings as of one pleasing to God. “Who is merciful,” that is, who gives his goods to the needy. He seems to lend when a person gives temporal things and is going to receive eternal ones. “He will order” means that he will judge with a tranquil mind how he might double the talent entrusted to him by the Lord. He therefore orders his words who proves that he has doubled God’s goods, saying, “Lord, you gave me five talents” (Matt. XXV). “He will not be shaken” means that he will in no way be separated from the Lord’s glory. H C He also orders his words in judgment who preaches the divine Scriptures with discernment, so that he does not cast pearls before swine (Matt. VII), nor by silence withhold good things from those who are able to receive them.

6 The righteous will be in eternal memory: He will not fear an evil report.

[Col. 0412B] C “The righteous will be in eternal memory,” because he is called to his reward; for it is said to the wicked, “I do not know you.” He will not fear that evil hearing which the wicked will hear: “Go into the eternal fire.” For that hearing appears evil to them, since they will be punished with just severity.

7 His heart is prepared to hope in the Lord: His heart is confirmed; he will not be shaken until he looks down upon his enemies.

C Here “heart” stands for the affection of a sound mind. The heart of the righteous is therefore confirmed when it is softened by no prosperity of the world. “Until he looks down upon his enemies”: in that future judgment the adversaries who despised the righteous here will be utterly despised. In this world God permits his righteous ones to see their enemies powerful, so that there they may behold them humbled. H Or “enemies,” that is, sins, heretics, the devil and his powers, and sinners: these he will despise.

8 He scattered; he gave to the poor: His righteousness endures forever ÷ and ever … His horn will be exalted in glory.

C “He scattered”: this sentence refers to that commandment, “Go, sell everything and give to the poor” (Matt. XIX). Whoever does this performs righteousness, because he fulfills the Lord’s commandments. H And this endures forever and ever, that is, the works themselves remain. C Or, because their reward remains eternally, they are said to remain forever and ever. H “His horn,” that is, his kingdom, will be exalted in glory, because he will reign forever with the Lord. [Col. 0412D] C For “horn” is used for power or for kingdom, as Daniel says: “The four horns are four kingdoms.”

9 The sinner will see and be angry; he will gnash his teeth and waste away. The desire of sinners will perish.

C The sinner will see on the day of judgment the Lord rewarding his chosen ones. Then he will be angry, because he is punished for his wickedness; he will also gnash his teeth and already bite himself with his own teeth, chastising himself with his own pain and demanding from himself the torments that here he forced the innocent to endure. And he will waste away in his destruction, while the desires of sinners, cut off, will wither.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM 111

God, everlasting light of upright hearts, grant us to love, to rejoice in your glory, and so to scatter our goods in this age that we may avoid the harsh hearing in the future. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, and so forth.

# PSALM 112

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM 112

C The Prophet exhorts the devout to utter praises to God continually from every part of the world.

TT. Alleluia.

C The following psalm explains the words of its own title. For since the title is “Alleluia,” “praise the Lord,” it too makes this its beginning, so that by its beginning it may explain the title. H This psalm also teaches us, after laying aside our former wickedness (1 Pet. II), to glory in the praises of God like newborn infants.

1 Praise the Lord, children: Praise the name of the Lord.

C “Children” refers to all the innocent faithful, because of purity of mind and simplicity of heart. It is not age that is chosen here, but purity. He praises the name of the Lord who celebrates his virtues with holy preaching; but he praises the Lord who commends him through a worthy way of life.

2 May the name of the Lord be blessed: From this time forth and forever.

H “May the name of the Lord be blessed.” It was blessed before only among the one nation of the Jews, because they alone blessed and believed; but now he is believed in and blessed among all nations. “From this time forth,” namely, from the time when they began to believe; “now,” that is, in the present; “forever,” that is, without end.

3 From the rising of the sun to its setting: The name of the Lord is praiseworthy.

C “From the rising of the sun”: for the whole world is declared here by the sun’s course, and the world is represented as though by a certain line. This signifies the Church, in which the faithful ought to make the praises of Christ resound throughout the whole world.

4 The Lord is exalted above all nations: And his glory is above the heavens.

C “Above all nations,” that is, above carnal human beings. We should understand “heavens” spiritually, so that the Most High may be perceived as above all creatures, he who is recognized as the creator of all things.

5 Who is like the Lord our God, who dwells on high: And looks upon the lowly in heaven and on earth?

“Who is like the Lord?” H C As if he said, “There is no one like him.” “Who dwells in the heavens”: H that is, in the saints. “And looks upon the lowly,” as he himself said, “Upon whom does my Spirit rest, except upon the humble?” “In heaven and on earth”: C thus humility pleasing to God is found both in heaven and on earth, just as pride is shown to be hated (Isa. LXVI). Where, then, do the proud think there is room for pride, when they see heaven and earth occupied by humility?

6 [Col. 0414A] Raising the needy from the earth: And lifting the poor from the dung heap.

C Let not the needy and poor claim this benefit for themselves alone. Whoever is raised by God’s grace from the stain of the body is lifted from the dung heap and from poverty. Finally, the worldly king is needy of God’s gifts and rolls in dung, since the vices of the flesh rule him.

7 So that he may seat him with princes, with the princes of his people.

C The princes of the people are the patriarchs and prophets, the apostles, and all who have pleased God by a worthy way of life. There the poor and needy person of Christ will be seated. He adds “of his people,” which signifies the Church. Do not understand “principality” here as an honor sought by human approval, but as that which is bestowed by the Lord, who is exalted through humility.

8 He makes the barren woman dwell in a house: A joyful mother of children.

C The holy Church was barren before the coming of her bridegroom, but through the preaching of the apostles she became a joyful mother of children, regenerating them through water and the Holy Spirit. The Lord makes her dwell in his house, H that is, in himself. C He makes her joyful through the birth and number of the saints.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM 112

As we praise your blessed name, almighty God, we ask that, placed in the bosom of mother Church, you may bind us together in the stability of your love. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, and so forth.

# PSALM 113

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM 113

C The Prophet recalls the benefits that the Lord bestowed upon the Hebrews and upon the Christian people, and demonstrates that the idols of the nations are vain.

TT. Alleluia.

C The Prophet recalls the benefits that the Lord bestowed upon the Hebrews; he demonstrates that the idols of the nations are vain, and goes on to explain how vital and salutary the religion of the Lord is for his own worshipers.

1 When Israel went out from Egypt: The house of Jacob from a barbarous people.

[Col. 0414D] C We should understand here that exodus by which we happen to leave the bonds of sins. Then we are freed from the Egyptians, that is, from the darkness of ignorance and the crowd of demons. “Barbarian” is said to derive from “beard” and “countryside,” because one who had never lived in a city was recognized as having always lived in the fields like a wild animal. We become the house of Jacob when we keep God’s commandments. H For Jacob is interpreted as “supplanter,” and we must first supplant vices and confess them—or the faith of the Trinity, which “Judah” signifies.

2 Judah became his sanctuary, Israel his dominion.

C We may understand “Judah” to refer not only to the nation of the Hebrews but also to all the faithful. For the true Judah is the Lord the Savior, in whom the power of the Israelites—that is, of those who see God—is known to be everlasting. Therefore those who follow him with circumcised hearts are truly called Israel. For Israel is interpreted as “a man seeing God,” A or, more accurately, “seeing God.”

3 The sea saw and fled: The Jordan turned back.

C “The sea,” that is, the Gentile world, saw the holy supplanters of vices—that is, the preachers—and fled; that is, it could not resist the apostles, because God was in them. Jordan is interpreted as “their descent,” namely, that of the baptized, who descend into baptism; that is, the baptized humble themselves. They turned back, A namely, toward God, from whom they had arisen and from whom they had withdrawn through sins. H For many who believed, when they saw the martyrs suffer, turned back—that is, from paganism to faith—and God became for them the one before whom they had placed their backs; and thus, forgetting their former sins, they reached forward to what lies ahead (Phil. III).

4 + The mountains exulted like rams …: And the hills like lambs of sheep.

C “Mountains” refers to the apostles, who exulted in their works like rams—that is, like preachers leading the faithful flock into the Lord’s folds. “Hills” are so called from *colere*, “to cultivate,” and signify those of middling rank converted by the apostles, who worship the Lord in truth.

5 What is it to + you, O sea, that you fled? And you, Jordan, because you turned back?

[Col. 0415C] H The Prophet questions himself and answers himself, as if he said: “What happened to you, Gentile world, that you fled? And you, Jordan—that is, what happened to you Christians, that you turned back? I know: you saw the holy preachers and were afraid.”

6 + Mountains, you exulted like rams; and hills like lambs of sheep?

H The mountains exulted—that is, the holy preachers—when they saw those who had previously been blasphemers converted. The rams exulted—that is, the leaders of the flocks who beget flocks: these are the apostles, one of whom says, “My little children, for whom I am again in labor” (Gal. IV), and again, “Through the Gospel I begot you” (1 Cor. IV).

7 The earth was moved at the presence of the Lord: At the presence of the God of Jacob.

C “The earth was moved.” Hear, you who have been converted; hear, faithful Christians, this movement—that is, the transformation—that has happily occurred in the earthly human race. It was not the trembling of mountains, but the prosperous conversion of peoples, so that, having been converted to the worship of God, it might remain fixed. This is the fitting response that follows upon both preceding verses, because each verse should be read as a question, according to Cassiodorus.

8 He turned the rock into pools of water: And the cliff into springs of water.

C “Rock” here refers to the hardness of the Jews, which he changed into the sacred pools of baptism when he caused them to come to the peaceful religion. “Cliff,” that is, the dry and hard hearts of the Gentiles, he caused to pour forth irrigating springs of divine speech.

9 Not to us, Lord, not to us: But to your name give glory.

C “Not to us, Lord.” Since he bestows good things on the undeserving, it is proved that the glory belongs to him, not elsewhere. It is an earnest and entirely true petition that, for the sake of his name, he should grant useful things to the human race, which he could not find to possess any merits among sinners. Hence he adds, “Because of …”: because of your mercy and truth, give glory to your name and perform wonders.

10 Because of your mercy and your truth: Lest ÷ ever the nations say: Where is their God?

[Col. 0416B] C “Mercy” is when he forgives the sins of the wretched and the delinquent; “truth” is when he restores the promises of blessedness. “Where is their God?” This is what the persecutors of the righteous say. For whenever martyrs are afflicted, this is the voice of tyrants: “Where is their God?”—as though he were unable to rescue those whom, in order to crown them, he allows to endure torments. For this reason also God performed wonders among the children of Israel, so that the nations would not say, “Where is their God?”

11 But our God is in heaven: He has done everything whatsoever he willed. Diapsalma.

C Against the words of the senseless, who say, “Where is your God?”, the most truthful knowledge is set forth: that our God is in heaven and is able to accomplish everything whatsoever he wills, in heaven and on earth.

12 The idols of the nations are silver and gold: The works of human hands.

H An idol is so called because it is fashioned in the likeness of some human being. C For although idols of bronze and wood are also found, he chose the material that the Gentiles judged more worthy of reverent worship, so that they might blush to worship cheaper things, whose preciousness is also proved to be mocked.

13 They have mouths and will not speak: They have eyes and will not see.

C “They have mouths”: in these verses the worshipers of idols are most truthfully marked and mocked. For, I ask, what use was a mouth to those who could not speak? What use were eyes that were unable to see anything? And what use were the other limbs, with which they were unable to perform any work?

14 They have ears and will not hear: They have nostrils and will not smell.

[Col. 0416D] C What use also was an ear to one who could not hear? What use was a nostril to one who could in no way perceive fragrance? “Nostrils” are said to derive from *gnaritas*, “knowledge,” because they enable us to recognize through smell.

15 They have hands and will not touch. They have feet and will not walk: They will not cry out with their throat.

C What use are hands to one who does not know tangible things? What use is a foot that cannot move itself? The mockery is increased by the addition, “They will not cry out,” because beasts and dumb animals have voices, but the cry of these is confused. These idols, however, possess neither human and articulate speech nor the confused cry that beasts have.

16 Let those who make them become like them: And all who trust in them.

C Those who have decided to follow such things become like them: they follow things without sensation and become without sensation themselves. For whoever follows another’s corrupt practices is bound up with them in confusion and evil. Therefore the worshipers and makers of such things are bound by equal guilt. For it is a similar wickedness to deceive others by one’s works and to bind oneself to the worst forms of worship.

17 ÷ The house of Israel hoped in the Lord: He is their helper and protector.

C “The house of Israel” signifies the Church, which sees God with the mind. “Helper”: because he helps those laboring in the flesh in this world insofar as he knows it to be beneficial. “Protector”: because he does not allow holy souls to be overthrown by any demonic deceit.

18 The house of Aaron hoped in the Lord: He is their helper and protector.

C The house of Aaron also signifies the faithful of Christ, because he made us a kingdom and priests for his God and Father (Rev. 1); and again: “But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood” (1 Pet. 2). Since Aaron was the first priest chosen among the Jewish people, what he had previously said in general he now unfolds concerning priests, in a fitting repetition, so that the lofty order of high priests might be praised with a special proclamation.

19 Those who fear the Lord have hoped in the Lord: He is their helper and their protector.

[Col. 0417C] II Those who fear the Lord—that is, all who fear him, love him, and hope in him—he protects with true protection and defends. C Thus he explains what he said above: “the house of Israel” and “the house of Aaron.” They are the ones who fear the Lord and hope in him, for these are the two things that make people blessed; and what he added also follows them, namely, that the Lord is both their helper and their protector.

20 The Lord remembered us: And he blessed ÷ us .. Diapsalma.

C When he says, “he remembered us,” he displays the grace of divine compassion, because he sent his Son to become incarnate; he came for this reason, to teach peoples who had gone astray and to save those who had been converted by his blessing. H He remembered us, therefore, when he delivered us, sent his Son, and blessed us with every spiritual blessing.

21 He blessed the house of Israel: He blessed the house of Aaron.

C He blessed the house of Israel by being born of holy Mary the Virgin. He blessed the house of Aaron, girded with the honor of the priesthood, as it is said of him in another psalm: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. 109).

22 He blessed ÷ all .. who fear the Lord: The little with the great.

C He blessed all; he did this among fishermen, and he did this among kings. No class of human beings who believe in him is shown to have been excluded or alien from his gift. Thus, after the particular blessings, he descends here to general ones, where all are blessed together. H “The little,” that is, those lesser in merit, and likewise those greater in merit, are blessed.

23 May the Lord add to you: + To you .. and to your children.

C “May he add,” whether a blessing or peoples faithful to our number; he does this also in our times and does not cease to work until the end of the age, until all the faithful, gathered into one flock, rejoice together. H Or, “may he add” other preachers of his over you, because at first there were few, but afterward they became many.

24 You are blessed by the Lord, who made heaven and earth.

[Col. 0418B] H C “You are blessed,” namely, the just and holy, by the Lord. C Observe the kind of blessing: he said “by the Lord,” because that is the perfect blessing—not prepared for oneself but for the Lord, from whom future blessedness can arise. By “heaven and earth” he signifies the little and the great.

25 The heaven of heavens belongs to the Lord: But the earth he gave to the children of men.

H The higher heaven signifies the apostles, because they heard preaching from Christ himself and received the illumination of the Holy Spirit. The heaven is also the apostles’ successors, whom they preached. “Earth” signifies the simple, who were earthly, nourished with milk and not yet with solid food (1 Cor. 3). C It is called “heaven,” moreover, because it contains all things within itself.

26 The dead will not praise you, O Lord: Nor all who descend into hell.

C “The dead” are sinners, for when a sinner has come into the depth of evils, he despises. Nor will all—that is, the inhabitants of hell—praise the name of the Lord.

27 But we ÷ who live .. bless the Lord: From this time now and forever.

C For the Lord, or God, is the God of the living, as it is read in the Gospel, not of the dead (Matt. 22). “The living,” however, should be understood not as those living this common life, shared by good and evil alike, but as those of whom it is said: “I shall please the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. 114). H We, the faithful who live—that is, who hold the right faith and possess good works—praise the Lord. [Col. 0418D] “From this time,” namely, from the time when we began to understand. “Now,” that is, at the present time; “forever,” that is, without end.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM 113

Ineffable Light, God the Trinity, who by the sight of your light terrified the waters of the Jordan, grant that those whom you renewed after washing them in holy baptism you may never allow to be stained by forbidden idols of images. You who live and reign, etc.

# PSALM 114

## TITLE OF PSALM 114

C The Prophet, showing that he has been delivered from the deep pit of sins, gives thanks to God because he recognizes that he has been heard.

[Col. 0419A] TT. Alleluia.

1 I have loved, because the Lord will hear the voice of my prayer.

C David does not exult joyfully in the greatness of his kingdom or in worldly prosperity, but rejoices that his prayer was received in his distress by the most merciful Lord; he continually felt that this was beneficial to him. Therefore, in saying “I have loved,” he testifies that he had love of God in his heart. H But observe that he does not say “I will love,” but “I have loved.” He did not promise that he would do it, but that he had done it. But why did he love? Because he will hear me praying in tribulations. Nor does he say “because he heard,” but “because he will hear.” Great, therefore, was this love.

2 Because he inclined his ear to me: And in my days I will call upon him.

[Col. 0419B] C “Ear” is named from hearing. How rightly, then, is God said to incline it toward us, since no human merits seem able to reach him so that he might deign to hear us? He inclined the ear of compassion when he became incarnate. And because he perceived abundant compassion toward himself, while he was placed amid many tribulations, he says that he will call upon him in his days. We call those our days in which we sin through our own iniquity and endure anxious pains in evil thoughts.

3 The pains of death surrounded me: And the dangers of hell found me.

H The pains of death are evil thoughts. The dangers of hell are wicked deeds, which surround the soul and urge it to sin. At first there are pain and labor; [Col. 0419C] here, however—that is, in wicked deeds—the danger is close to death.

4 I found tribulation and sorrow. ÷ And .. I called upon the name of the Lord.

H Every saint seeks not rest but tribulation, for he knows that “tribulation produces endurance, endurance produces testing, and testing produces hope, which does not disappoint” (Rom. 5). “And I called upon the name of the Lord.” C Through his assistance both sorrow and tribulation would be gloriously overcome. H He therefore states something new: he does not say, “I found rest” or “satisfaction,” but “tribulation.” He sought tribulation, for nothing is found unless it is sought.

5 O Lord, deliver my soul. The Lord is merciful and just: [Col. 0419D] And our God has mercy.

C When the Prophet says, “Deliver my soul,” he undoubtedly confesses that it has always been captive. He is merciful because he inclined his ear to him; he is just because he rebuked the sinner so that he might seek pardon. He has mercy when he receives the son whom he chastises (Prov. 3).

6 The Lord preserves the little ones: I was humbled, and he delivered me.

C The little ones are those who are most certainly small in their own estimation, but grow great through the Lord’s generosity. The excellent shepherd guards them when he defends them from the attack of the ravenous wolf; he does this when he finds them humbled.

7 [Col. 0420A] Return, my soul, to your rest: Because the Lord has dealt graciously with you.

C Let the devout people sing this—the people redeemed by precious blood, who through the Lord’s generosity have deserved to reach the desired rest. Therefore the Prophet exhorts his soul to return to the Lord, from whom both tranquil rest and the abolition of sins come to it. He calls its rest the conscience that was given to it by grace, not possessed as payment for merits. Therefore he adds, “because the Lord has dealt graciously with you.” H Christ is also our rest. Whenever we are in the distress of sin, let us say: “Return, my soul, to your rest.”

8 Because he rescued my soul from death: My eyes from tears, [Col. 0420B] my feet from falling.

C He now states the reasons why he said, “because the Lord has dealt graciously with you.” “He rescued” displays the benefit of divine power, for no one could have been delivered from perpetual death except by his power. “My eyes from tears.” H That is, I wept so that I might laugh; I mourned so that I might rejoice forever. For whoever does not weep in the present will weep in the future. C When he says “from falling,” he shows that sin is slippery and steeply sloping, and he believes that he has been snatched from it. H C The Prophet speaks of that rescue—from death, from tears, and from falling—by the power of foreknowledge, from the future, in the land of the living; for here we are not fully delivered from these things.

9 I shall please the Lord: In the land of the living.

[Col. 0420C] C He said “I shall please,” namely, now secure. Although the just please the Lord here also, they are nevertheless insecure; but the just will please the Lord securely then, when they will fear nothing further from the hostility of sins. “In the land of the living,” that is, in the congregation of the saints, where every living person is truly gathered and separated from the lot of the dying.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM 114

O Lord, cleanser of sins, because you swiftly console those who faithfully call upon you with great devotion, we ask that, after rescuing us from the dangers of hell, you restore us to the land of the living, with the death of sin removed. You who live and reign, etc.

# PSALM 115

## TITLE OF PSALM 115

[Col. 0420D]

C The voice of unconquered martyrs who endured a glorious death for the name of Christ.

TT. Alleluia.

C “Alleluia”: the voice of the faithful, the speech of the blessed, the holy melody of singers. Through it the hearing is soothed and the weary soul refreshed.

1 I believed, therefore I spoke: But I ÷ was .. humbled exceedingly.

H I believed—what? Since the preceding psalm ended, “I shall please the Lord,” I believed this, and therefore I spoke: “But I was humbled exceedingly,” because I considered myself to be earth and ashes, and yet, by the mercy of God, I would be in the land of the living. Therefore I was rightly humbled exceedingly, marveling at the Lord’s mercy. A Or, “I believed” is said against those who speak of divine things before they believe them in deed; to them God says: “Why do you recount my righteousness?” (Ps. 49). He says on their account: “I believed, therefore”—that is, because I believed—“I spoke the divine mysteries.” A Or, because I believed perfectly, I spoke; for one who does not speak what he believes and confess it with his mouth has not believed perfectly. But because I also spoke with my mouth what I believed, I was humbled exceedingly—that is, I suffered much for the word of God. C Therefore he says that he was humbled because, as holy religion increased, the martyrs themselves, who spoke on account of the faith, appeared to be subjected excessively to temporal punishments.

2 I said in my ecstasy: Every human being is a liar.

[Col. 0421B] C “I said in my ecstasy,” that is, in an intellectual rapture into divine contemplation. Great prudence it is for someone to consider himself imprudent and, when we are liars through the frailty of the flesh, to acknowledge that this belongs to us; but when we are truthful, to attribute it to divine gifts. “For every human being is a liar,” A that is, a sinner; a liar from himself, but truthful from God. For his not departing from the faith amid persecutions is from God.

3 What shall I repay the Lord: For all that he has repaid me?

C We speak of repaying when we return good for good and render good for evil. The Lord repays us good for evil when, though he was struck on the face, he granted us hope of resurrection, promised the kingdoms of heaven, and endured passion for our sins.

4 I shall receive the cup of salvation: And I shall call upon the name of the Lord.

C A worthy promise if it is promised by God’s gift; but if it is placed in human strength, it is dangerous presumption. “I shall receive the cup,” that is, passion and martyrdom, with desire. But who can give confessors patience amid torments except Christ, who deigned to receive the cup of passion for us? “And I called upon the name of the Lord,” trusting in whose assistance he believed that he would accomplish what he desired. Therefore I shall call upon the name of the Lord, because without his assistance I cannot receive the cup.

5 [Col. 0421D] + I shall pay my vows to the Lord before all his people: Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints.

A C “My vows,” which I conceived in my desire to suffer, I shall afterward fulfill in action before all the people, so that they may take from me an example of suffering. I shall do this because the death of the saints is precious in the sight of the Lord. H The vows, however, are the prayers of the martyrs. C It is rightly said that the death of the saints is precious, since it is known to have been purchased by the Lord’s blood. It was glorified by his passion, so that it might be extraordinary in his sight; and in order to be precious, it is not made so by offered riches but purchased by the shedding of blood. O life-giving death, O destruction to be sought, O glorious passage, which makes Christ’s members imitators of their Head.

6 + O Lord, because .. I am your servant: I am your servant: ÷ And the son of your handmaid:

C O Lord, he marvels that he has received such benefits as the Lord himself deigned to assume for the redemption of the world. He added, “and the son of your handmaid,” to indicate humility by repeated confessions, calling himself twice a servant and, third, the son of the handmaid. By calling himself the son of the handmaid, he confessed himself to be a son of the Church, which is a handmaid while she serves and a bride when she is joined to him.

7 You have broken my bonds: I shall sacrifice to you a sacrifice of praise: + And I shall call upon the name of the Lord ...

[Col. 0422B] C “You have broken”: here he explains the power of martyrdom, by whose triumphant force all the bonds of sins are broken. For no stain can remain in a person that the merciful blood has not washed away. This verse was believed to possess such power that some said all sins could be forgiven if, at the end of one’s life, one repeated it three times in confession. And because the bonds of sins have been broken, he rightly says that he sacrifices a sacrifice of praise. Thanksgiving is an exceedingly acceptable sacrifice to God.

8 I shall pay my vows to the Lord in the sight of all his people, in the courts of the house of the Lord, in your midst, Jerusalem.

C When he says, “I shall pay my vows to the Lord,” he promises to offer himself in return. For the vow of all the faithful is to offer themselves to Christ and to stand firm in his Church with right belief. “In the sight of”: it is fitting that the one who deigned to suffer for the salvation of all should be praised publicly. “In the courts of the house of the Lord,” that is, in the Church; and he names the Church still more aptly when he says, “in the midst of Jerusalem,” where peace rests and the unity of the people rejoices in the contemplation of God.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM 115

May the life of us who supplicate be, we ask, O Lord, such as the precious death of the saints is in your sight, so that, freed from the bonds of sin, we may deserve to taste in advance the joys of the future Jerusalem. Through our Lord Jesus, etc.

# PSALM 116

## TITLE OF PSALM 116

[Col. 0422D]

C This psalm suits the person of the martyrs, who, having undergone a glorious passion, rouse all nations to the praises of the Lord.

TT. Alleluia.

1 Praise the Lord, all nations: Praise him, all peoples.

C That chorus of the saints cries out that all nations ought to praise the Lord. The joint praise is the praise of all the faithful gathered into one. All nations are generally urged to praise the Lord, lest anyone say that he was overlooked in God’s judgment.

2 Because his mercy has been confirmed over us: [Col. 0423A] And the truth of the Lord ÷ remains .. forever.

C His mercy was confirmed among the Christian people when the one who granted it himself preserves us by his mercy. Here “the truth of the Lord” signifies the Son, as he himself says: “I am the way and the truth and the life” (John 14). It accords both with our salvation and with the truth to confess the Son, coeternal and consubstantial in all things with the Father.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM 116

Most almighty Ruler, who are praised by the mouths of all nations, we beseech you to enlarge our mind by your truth and confirm your mercy over us. Through our Lord Jesus, etc.

# PSALM 117

## TITLE OF PSALM 117

[Col. 0423B]

C The voice of the faithful confessing the Lord and trusting in him alone, who ask that the gates of righteousness be opened to them, adding that the cornerstone is the Lord the Savior.

TT. Alleluia.

C At the beginning of this psalm, he concludes four verses with the same ending, so that, according to the Gospel number, he might remind us that the whole world ought to render praises to the one Lord. He will do this explicitly throughout all the verses of Psalm 135.

1 Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good: For his mercy is forever.

H This confession does not concern the remission of sins, [Col. 0423C] but pertains to the praise of the deity. “For he is good”: C properly and by himself only that one is called good who makes good people fulfill what they are good for. “Forever” signifies the eternity to come, where there is one age and one day, and no change follows.

2 Let Israel ÷ now .. say: For his mercy is forever.

H “Let Israel now say,” that is, the man who sees God, who was previously blinded by sins but now contemplates God’s glory with a serene mind.

3 Let the house of Aaron ÷ now .. say: For his mercy is forever.

H “Let the house of Aaron now say,” which had formerly sacrificed to idols but now, attracted by the goodness of the Most High, performs a priesthood worthy of its soul.

4 Let those who fear the Lord ÷ now .. say: For his mercy is forever.

H “Let those who fear the Lord now say,” that is, you who formerly feared mute and deaf images, now sing the mercy of the almighty Lord with reverent fear.

5 From tribulation I called upon the Lord: And the Lord heard me in a spacious place.

C The tribulation of the present age will end; but the spaciousness of blessedness knows no limit. The spaciousness of eternal joys rescues from temporal evils, and those whom the narrowness of tribulations weighed down in this brief world will be welcomed by the boundless joys of rewards.

6 [Col. 0424A] The Lord is my helper: I shall not fear what man can do to me.

C “The Lord is my helper”: when he says that, with the Lord’s help, he does not fear man, he signifies carnal enemies who visibly persecute the purpose of religious people.

7 The Lord is my helper: And I shall despise my enemies.

H “The Lord is my helper”; therefore I shall despise heretics. C Or the Jews, or even the devil together with his other ministers.

8 It is good to trust in the Lord: Rather than to trust in man.

C We ought to trust in God alone, not in man: in the one who truly promises, not in the one who deceives himself with false presumption, saying, “I do what I want, and I do not have the Lord of my will.”

9 It is good to hope in the Lord: Rather than to hope in princes.

H It is good to hope in the Lord, who bestows eternal life, rather than in princes, whose power passes away with this world. C Here we may also understand the prince to be the devil, as in the saying: “For the prince of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me” (John 14).

10 All nations surrounded me: And in the name of the Lord + because: I have avenged myself ÷ upon .. them.

C The voice of the Church concerning the persecution of the nations, which first persecuted the head, who is Christ, [Col. 0424C] and afterward his body, which is the Church. But when he said “nations” and added the masculine form “I have avenged myself upon them,” this either belongs to the interpretation, because “nations” signifies peoples, or it is a schema of *exallage*, that is, an alteration, because he changed the gender of the noun. He has avenged himself upon them when, after being converted, they exacted from themselves the penalties of repentance that they had previously inflicted upon the innocent.

11 They surrounded me; yes, they surrounded me: And in the name of the Lord + because .. I have avenged myself ÷ upon .. them.

C “Those surrounding,” namely, the Jews, surrounded Christ in his passion. Yet in them he was avenged in the name of the Lord, when many of them, repenting after the evils they had committed, deserved to take upon themselves the name of Christians.

12 They surrounded me like bees, and they burned like fire among thorns: And in the name of the Lord + because: I have avenged myself upon them.

C Christ himself, surrounded by the raging Jews, poured the honey of his passion throughout the whole world. They are called “bees,” as if from *pedes* (“feet”), because the bee is born without feet. H They burned with envy when they wished to burn me. C The thorns signify the sins of the people; but he was avenged among them when they too were most sweetly filled with that honey. What happened to the Jews was like what happens to bees: they surround the honeycomb and store honey in waxen houses; and while they think they are storing provisions for themselves, they produce something by which human beings can satisfy their desires. So the Jews, through bitter efforts, made something most sweet for the whole world.

13 I was thrust down and overturned so that I might fall: And the Lord received me.

C A person falls when the Lord’s strength is withdrawn from him. But the body of the faithful, though thrust so that it might fall, did not and does not fall, because it is held by the Lord’s right hand. He therefore says that he did not fall even though overturned, because he was strengthened by the Lord’s reception. The faithful were handed over to torments and overturned from temporal rest so that they might fall from the faith; but the Lord received them, so that they would not fall from the faith.

14 The Lord is my strength and my praise: And he has become my salvation.

[Col. 0425B] C One who has been thrust down cannot fall when the Lord’s help is seen to provide strength. He himself is the strength, the praise, and the eternal salvation of the blessed.

15 The voice of rejoicing and salvation: In the tents of the righteous.

C That joyful chorus of the faithful exults in the tents of the righteous, that is, in the hidden places of the human heart, where the saints are always joyful, although they are afflicted outwardly. They exulted there when their persecutors thought that they were being consumed by grief and exhausted by tribulation. And so that you might recognize the source of their joy, he adds: “The right hand,” and so forth.

16 The right hand of the Lord has shown strength: The right hand of the Lord has exalted me: + The right hand of the Lord has shown strength ...

[Col. 0425C] C “The right hand of the Lord,” that is, Christ, through whom the Father exercised power in the exaltation of the saints. Christ exalts the saints when he grants the kingdoms of heaven to earthly people, and thus he showed strength in earthly people. For what is more powerful than clothing mortals with immortality and giving victory over the strongest enemy to the weak?

17 I shall not die, but live: And I shall recount the works of the Lord.

C “I shall not die” is the voice of the faithful against persecutors: I shall not die, as you think, but I shall live with a life you do not know, a life that those swollen with pride in mind cannot attain. “I shall recount the works,” because the endurance of the martyrs has been proclaimed throughout the whole Church.

18 The Lord chastising has chastised me: [Col. 0425D] And he has not handed me over to death.

H The Lord chastises us for correction with many blows, so that, once tested, he may rescue us from perpetual death. C The one whose faults committed here are cleansed is the only one not handed over to death; for he recalls that he has been well chastised here. Thus, lest the arrogance of the persecutors claim any credit for itself, he confirms that their torments were the Lord’s chastisement.

19 Open to me the gates of righteousness: I shall enter them and give thanks to the Lord. This is the gate of the Lord; the righteous shall enter through it.

C To whom are the words “Open” addressed, if not to the prophets and apostles, who received the keys of heaven through mystical powers? For, introduced through these gates of doctrine, we now stand inside and truthfully give thanks to the Lord. H C This gate is Christ, through whom one enters to the Father, as he himself says: “No one comes to the Father except through me” (John 14). C Thus he called the prophets and apostles “gates”; but because these open through and toward Christ, he adds one gate through which all entered, including those who were called gates. H But no one enters through it except the righteous.

20 I shall give thanks to you, because you heard me: And you became my salvation.

C This is the voice of a rejoicing people. Christ healed its wounds of sin, and he is said to have become its salvation; or he became salvation for those against the unjust enemy when the Redeemer of the nations appeared to human eyes.

21 [Col. 0426B] The stone that the builders rejected: ÷ This .. has become the cornerstone.

C Christ is called the cornerstone because he joined two peoples coming from opposite directions to himself in one solid grace; the Jews rejected him (Eph. 2). “Corner” is derived from the Greek word *gōni*, which in Latin is called *genu*, “knee”; when bent, the knee forms the shape of a corner through a corresponding quality. The Jews were building, H that is, they were erecting the letter of the Law. C Or, they were building because formerly they alone believed in the true God.

22 This + has been done .. by the Lord: And ÷ it is .. marvelous in our eyes.

C When he says that this was done by the Lord, [Col. 0426C] the nature of humanity is revealed. H C This stone is marvelous in the eyes of the faithful, who not only see it bodily but also, illuminated in mind, perceive it. The Jews saw it too, but not as marvelous, because they looked only upon the flesh and did not perceive the divinity within. Therefore he said “in our eyes,” namely, in the eyes of the faithful.

23 This is the day that the Lord has made: Let us rejoice and be glad in it.

C Although God created all days, he is nevertheless said to have made one day uniquely—the day sanctified by Christ’s birth. In it it is fitting to rejoice and be glad, because on it the devil lost his claim and the world received salvation.

24 [Col. 0426D] O Lord, save me; O Lord, grant prosperity: Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.

H “O Lord, save me as I come to you.” C So that here I may be rescued from the death of sins and there be placed in everlasting rest. To prosper is to make something harsh tranquil. Therefore the pains that they endure here for love of the Lord are unquestionably made prosperous there, when they have already reached eternal joys. It is clear that the one who is blessed—that is, the Lord Christ—is the one who deigned to come to us in the name of the Lord. As in the Gospel: “I have come in my Father’s name, and you did not receive me” (John 5); if another, namely Antichrist, comes in a name not the Lord’s but his own, him you will receive.

25 [Col. 0427A] We have blessed you from the house of the Lord: God is the Lord, and he has shone upon us.

H “We have blessed you”: the saints from the heavenly Jerusalem bless the little ones of the Church. C Or the apostles and leaders of the Churches say to the faithful people: “We have blessed you from the house of the Lord,” that is, from the Catholic Church, from which saving baptism comes and holy communion proceeds. From it, therefore, every blessing proceeds, and the Lord God has illumined our darkness by his resurrection.

26 Establish the solemn day amid the dense crowds: Up to the horn of the altar.

C “Establish” means: preserve with deliberate judgment and ready willingness the solemn day that has been consecrated by the honor of God and the confession of the saints. “Amid the dense crowds” means amid the frequent gatherings that the crowd makes dense in the worship of God. “Up to the horn of the altar” means that they should not depart before they have worthily received communion at God’s altar. Through this, therefore, what many are accustomed to do is forbidden: leaving after hearing the Gospel reading.

27 You + are .. my God, and I shall give thanks to you: You + are .. my God, and I shall exalt you.

C It is right that we call him our God whom we do not cease to worship with a pure mind. What he says, “I shall give thanks,” pertains to thanksgiving. “I shall exalt you,” because God is exalted through the preaching of the saints.

28 ÷ I shall give thanks to you, because you heard me ..: ÷ And you became my salvation ...

[Col. 0427C] H I shall give thanks to you, Lord, because you heard me and became my salvation, namely, so that you might join me with your saints in the heavenly Jerusalem.

29 Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good: For his mercy is forever.

C This verse too is shown to have already been said at the beginning of the psalm, so that, just as he made the beginning from Christ, the ending might also appear to correspond to him. For he himself said: “I am the Alpha and the Omega” (Rev. 1). Thus throughout our whole life we ought to take up confession and end in his delight.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM 117

Most merciful Lord, consolation of our tribulations, who fills the tents of the righteous with joy and rejoicing, exalt your Church by the strength of your mighty right hand, so that it may become a gate of righteousness and so be joined with the stability of the cornerstone, shining by your mercy. Through our Lord Jesus, etc.

# PSALM 118

## TITLE OF PSALM 118

C Throughout this entire psalm the universal chorus of the saints speaks: those who existed from the beginning of the world, who exist now, or who are believed to be future. Among them are found apostles, prophets, martyrs, confessors, ecclesiastical orders, and all who serve the Lord with holy integrity. It is depicted in the Hebrew letters in this order: eight verses begin with each letter; the first letter, [Col. 0428A] Aleph, is interpreted as “doctrine.” B And first, to the blameless in the way of the Lord, eternal blessedness is promised.

TT. Alleluia. H Aleph: doctrine.

1 Blessed are the blameless in the way: Who walk in the law of the Lord.

C Let us now see what spiritual fruits grow in this heavenly paradise. The saints become blameless when they receive the gifts of forgiveness; otherwise, in himself, no one is blameless except God alone, for he alone is naturally blameless. “In the way,” that is, in Christ. To walk there is the action of the righteous—not with bodily feet but through right conduct. “In the law of the Lord,” that is, those who either do not sin or amend themselves by the grace of God and provide themselves with worthy satisfaction. Nor is it without purpose that he says “in the law of the Lord,” to distinguish it from the law of sin, in which sinners walk.

2 Blessed are those who search his testimonies: They seek him with their whole heart.

H Blessed are those who search, namely, so that when they have sinned they may understand that they transgressed before witnesses and recognize the law of God as witness to their sins. “They seek him with their whole heart,” H that is, not lightly or sluggishly. C But those who devote their whole heart to the holy Scriptures do not pursue the display of falsehood, as heretics do, nor do they desire worldly joys. Therefore he first said, “who walk in the law of the Lord,” and then, “who search,” because no one is worthy to search the testimonies of God unless he is known to conduct himself in a commendable manner.

3 [Col. 0428C] For those who work iniquity have not walked in his ways.

C They are rightly said not to walk in the ways of the Lord, those who work iniquity. The working of iniquity is consent to evils; yet this is shown to be alien from the hearts of the saints by God’s gift.

4 You commanded: That your commandments be kept exceedingly.

C This is the venerable precept of the Lord’s command: that his commandments be kept not only diligently but also exceedingly. “Exceedingly” signifies greatly and infinitely. Therefore to exceed our strength is a divine service, because everything there ought to be excessive, since that which we ask to be granted to us is itself infinite.

5 [Col. 0428D] If only my ways were directed: Toward keeping your justifications.

C “If only” is always the expression of one who wishes. “Ways” signify the actions we carry out in this life. But when he says “may they be directed,” he shows that, insofar as human weakness is concerned, our ways are crooked. Yet when he adds “toward keeping,” and so forth, he explains here what he desired above: no one could attain to keeping the Lord’s justifications unless the Lord’s mercy were shown to be granted.

6 Then I shall not be put to shame: When I have looked upon all your commandments.

C “Then I shall not be put to shame,” namely, if I have looked upon all God’s commandments. To look upon them means always to keep God’s commandments before one’s eyes, so that if anything crooked is committed, it may immediately be corrected. When he says “in all,” he warns that one must sin in nothing, as it is written: “If anyone does not fulfill even the least part of the law, he is guilty of the whole law” (Jas. 2).

7 I shall give thanks to you with an upright heart: ÷ In that .. I have learned the judgments of your righteousness.

C This confession signifies praise. Uprightness of heart is the holy rule of faith, with which the distorted cunning of heretics cannot confess him. When he says “I have learned,” he indicates that the discipline was handed down to him by the blessed Fathers, not invented through a desire for perversity. They are “the judgments of righteousness,” because he delivered his servants who were suffering under diabolical persecution.

8 I shall keep your justifications: [Col. 0429B] Do not forsake me utterly.

C The holy Church promises to keep the Lord’s justifications. And because she knew that diabolical temptations surround her on every side, she asks to be guarded immediately by the Lord, lest the enemy’s savagery find an opportunity to inflict harm.

## TITLE OF THE FOLLOWING EIGHT VERSES

C B The faithful people explain in the sayings of the Lord the delights with which they are refreshed, showing themselves to be the house of the Lord and the receptacle of his commandments, whose mystery the second letter contains.

H Beth: house.

9 By what means does a younger person correct his way? By keeping your words.

“In what way does he correct.” H Here the Prophet says that not only advanced age needs correction; he also teaches that youth must be instructed and disciplined, and that divine words must be kept in such a way that, even if an old fault has been lamented, one now takes care that no thought consent to sin. C For he keeps God’s words not merely one who retains them in memory, but one who holds them in action.

10 With my whole heart I have sought you: Do not repel me from your commandments.

C This too is the Lord’s work: that he claims to have sought him with his whole heart. For no one would seek God unless he had first been sought by him. “Do not repel me”: he asks not to be rejected as unworthy from understanding the divine law. H See, therefore, that you seek God not partially but with your whole heart, lest you be repelled from his commandments.

11 [Col. 0429D] In my heart I have hidden your words: So that I may not sin against you.

C “In my heart I have hidden your utterances.” H For just as it is fitting for the faithful to proclaim God’s precepts, so they ought to be hidden from unbelievers, as in the Gospel: “Do not give what is holy to dogs” (Matthew 7), nor pearls to swine. C For it is a kind of sin to proclaim the Lord’s utterances to the obstinate.

12 “Blessed ÷ are you .., Lord: Teach me your ordinances.”

A “Blessed are you, Lord”: here “blessing” signifies praise. For when we bless God, we praise his deeds; when he blesses us, he sanctifies us. “Teach me,” that is, grant me to do what you customarily use to justify your elect; that is, grant me not merely to know and understand your ordinances intellectually, but teach me to do what I understand.

13 “With my lips I have proclaimed all the judgments of your mouth.”

C That chorus of saints says that it has proclaimed all the judgments of the Lord’s mouth: those which he spoke through the prophets and apostles, and those which Christ preached with his own mouth. “All the judgments,” however, signifies those which he learned through writing or speech. Yet it cannot literally proclaim all of them, since no knowledge is powerful enough to grasp everything; figuratively, therefore, he has said “the whole” for a part.

14 “I have delighted in the way of your testimonies, as in all riches.”

C “The way of your testimonies” is the Lord Christ, in whom the chorus of saints declares that it will rejoice. Here we must understand spiritual riches, concerning which the Apostle says: “For in everything you have been enriched in him, in every word,” and so forth (1 Corinthians 1).

15 “I will exercise myself in your commandments, and I will consider your ways.”

H “I will exercise myself”: exercise is persistent practice. C For one exercises himself in the divine commandments who strives to fulfill them through frequent practice, and thus merits reaching the innermost chambers of their meaning. No one merits contemplating so great a secret unless it has been granted to him to draw near to heavenly gifts through a good way of life. H By “ways,” however, he means prophetic and apostolic teachings.

16 “I will meditate on your ordinances; I will not forget your utterances.”

C He says that he will meditate on God’s ordinances so that he may in no way forget what ought to be retained.

ARGUMENT OF THE FOLLOWING EIGHT VERSES.

C H The holy people, who are resident aliens on earth, ask that the grace which they lost in their first parent be restored to them; but they also say that what their persecutors are doing must be repaid to them.

B Gimel: retribution or fullness.

17 “Repay your servant: give me life, and I will keep your utterances.”

C By “repay,” he does not mean “return according to merits,” but “give again”: since you have granted the disposition to ask, grant also the fulfillment and performance of the request. For no one can be called Christ’s servant unless he attributes whatever good he does not to his own merits but to divine grace. To keep the divine commandments is truly the act of one who is alive. Conversely, the person who does not keep the commandments is called dead in the Gospel, when the Lord says: “Let the dead bury their own dead” (Matthew 8).

18 “Unveil my eyes, and I will consider the wonders of your law.”

C “To unveil” means to remove a veil. For the inner sight is covered by a kind of covering of ignorance; and unless his mercy removes this veil, we cannot behold the Holy Scriptures with the light of the heart. The wonders of the law are mysteries contained in its spiritual meaning. H Unless the veil of the letter is drawn away, we cannot understand them.

19 “I am a resident alien on the earth; do not hide your commandments from me.”

C On this earth the righteous are resident aliens, who do not possess in the world a dwelling-place proper to the mind, as the Apostle says: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3). We have said that the commandments are: “You shall love the Lord your God,” and the like. He asks that these should in no way be concealed from him, though they are shown to be hidden from sinners.

20 “My soul has coveted to desire your ordinances at all times.”

C An unbeliever too can desire a good thing for a certain period; but it is clear that what he adds—“at all times”—belongs only to the perfect. To covet is to desire, for no one desires unless he covets. Therefore the doubled declaration indicates a completely full will, namely, both coveting and desire.

21 “You have rebuked the proud: cursed are those who turn aside from your commandments.”

H “You have rebuked the proud” so that you might lead them back to the holy humility which you taught. Or you rebuke wicked people through your teachers. Those who turn aside from God’s commandments are cursed; but they will be fully cursed when he says: “Go, you cursed, into the eternal fire” (Matthew 25). C We say “to rebuke” as if it meant “to burst forth from silence” and to leap into biting words; God frequently does this through the divine Scriptures.

22 “Take away from me reproach and contempt, because I have sought your testimonies.”

C We must consider why the martyrs ask that reproaches be removed from them, though they knew that through them they were to be crowned. Yet this prayer is poured out for the persecutors, so that they may be converted. For when they have been converted, reproach is removed from the martyrs: when the persecutors themselves honor the religion which they had thought ought to be persecuted in the saints.

23 “For rulers also sat and spoke against me, but your servant was exercising himself in your ordinances.”

H What the Prophet says here about himself he saw as destined to occur in the apostles and the other martyrs, who, as the Lord foretold, suffered many things before kings and governors; they exercised themselves in righteous deeds and God’s ordinances, even to the cutting off of their heads. C They were exercised in torments for their advancement, not tortured as punishment: they softened the awareness of their pain with thoughts of eternal reward, and their torments advanced them toward eternal joys.

24 “For your testimonies were also my meditation, and your ordinances were my counsel.”

H Christ’s testimonies were the saints’ meditation, especially amid these pressures. His ordinances were their counsel, because they promise them eternal life. C Thus the testimonies of the Lord, meditated upon, became counsel against the counsel of the malicious and against the fury and sufferings of the wicked. Their thought indeed alleviates every kind of pain.

ARGUMENT OF THE FOLLOWING EIGHT VERSES.

B The faithful people, constrained by worldly poverty, open themselves to the door of true riches; and through frequent meditation they offer their inmost hearts to God’s commandments as though they were tablets.
