H B Daleth: poor person, tablets, or door.

25 “My soul has clung to the pavement; give me life according to your word.”

C He says that he has clung to his flesh, which is undoubtedly vicious; for if the soul clings to the body, it favors sins. H Therefore, lest sin grow strong in me, I ask you to give me life, knowing that the desire of the flesh brings about death. C “Pavement,” then, is used for the body. For pavement is a solid surface constructed on the ground with extreme smoothness; our body likewise is polished with a similar smoothness.

26 “I have declared my ways, and you have heard ÷ me ..; teach me your ordinances.”

H “My ways,” that is, the works of my sin. “I have declared”: through confession. “And you have heard me”: because you have forgiven my sins. Now grant the teaching by which I may be instructed in your ordinances. C And “teach me your ordinances”: not merely so that I may hear them, but so that I may do them. For one is shown to be learned in divine matters when he is shown to have done what was entrusted to him.

27 “Instruct me in the way of your ordinances, and I will exercise myself in your wonders.”

H “The way of your ordinances,” that is, I will receive spiritually the ordinances brought forth by the letter of the law. “And I will exercise myself in your wonders,” that is, in the apostolic and other ecclesiastical teachings which were prefigured in that law. C For understood things produce wonder when they are set forth in the present in such a way that they seem to signify things far in the future.

28 “My soul has fallen asleep from weariness; strengthen me in your words.”

H “My soul has fallen asleep”: in the station of this mortal dwelling. “From weariness”: from bodily weakness. “Strengthen me”: so that, once the sleep of sin has been removed, I may remain constantly awake to these precepts. C To sleep belongs to the forgetful and sluggish; to doze belongs to the weary and the one who waits. H Cassian calls this drowsiness acedia.

29 “Remove from me the way of iniquity, and have mercy on me in your law.”

H “The way of iniquity”—that is, the desire by which one comes to sin—remove from me. “And in your law”: for this law has been established with you, that you should always have mercy.

30 “I have chosen the way of truth; I have not forgotten your judgments.”

H “I have chosen the way of truth,” that is, Christ the Son of God, whom I heard was to come into the world. “I have not forgotten those judgments” which he brought forth in the Gospel when he said: “This is the judgment, that whoever believes in the Son may have eternal life” (John 6). C To choose is to select one from many.

31 “I have clung to your testimonies, Lord; do not put me to shame.”

H Because I have clung to your testimonies, and by clinging to them I have merited the forgiveness of my former crimes, I therefore ask: help me, so that I do not fall back again into my former sins. Do not allow me to be put to shame by the repetition of sin, and then openly to suffer disgrace at your judgment.

32 “I have run the way of your commandments, when you enlarged my heart.”

H I ran the way when I suffered many things for your word, because of hope in future blessedness. “You enlarged my heart,” namely, in the breadth of charity, hope, and faith. C Or it is said to have been enlarged in the breadth of knowledge. For when the soul receives the light of truth, it opens itself to manifold understandings and becomes broader through the virtues it has come to know.

ARGUMENT OF THE FOLLOWING EIGHT VERSES.

C B The blessed people ask that they should be preserved by the gift of the Lord’s law. B And rightly it is called “receiving,” since it says, “Give me understanding.” It is also rightly called that which, persisting always in the same intention, turns its eyes away from the vanity of the world.

B He H B “She” or “receiving.”

33 “Establish the law for me, Lord, the way of your ordinances, and I will seek it continually.”

H The Prophet speaks in the person of the Church: “Establish the law for me,” that is, Christ, for Christ is the law—as if he were saying: Establish yourself for me; that is, deign to come, and I will always seek you, so that I may keep your commandments. C Or, since above he said, “Have mercy on me in your law”—which was said of the Old Testament, which could save no one by itself—he now speaks of the law of the New Testament, whose coming he desires.

34 “Give me understanding, and I will search your law, and I will keep it with my whole heart.”

C All understanding is granted by God, but it is nevertheless sometimes turned toward depraved pursuits. H Here, however, the Church asks to understand the distinction between good and evil, between the letter and the meaning, so that it may keep the law with its whole heart, that is, with complete love. C But since he previously said, “I ran the way of the commandments,” why does he ask again for what he remembered having received earlier—namely, the law and the way of the commandments? Because the Lord’s gifts must continually be requested so that they may be preserved; for he always gives who preserves what has been given.

35 “Lead me in the path of your commandments, because I have desired it.”

H A path is narrower than a way: that is, it is the narrow and constricted way, meaning the more exacting commandments which lead to life, because the broad and spacious way leads to death (Matthew 7). “Because I have desired it,” as if he said: I have desired nothing else but to fulfill your commandments. C The path is the New Testament; the way is the Old. For he asks for the spiritual grace which leads to heaven.

36 “Incline my heart toward your testimonies, and not toward avarice.”

C He asks that his heart be inclined toward the Lord’s testimonies, to which one arrives not through rapacious avarice but through praiseworthy humility granted by the Lord. The company of the saints knows that avarice is capable of containing every vice, and therefore asks that it be removed from it. For avarice is an utterly burning desire for temporal things.

37 “Turn my eyes away so that they may not see vanity; give me life in your way.”

C The blessed people pray that the eyes of the heart may be turned away from worldly delights, for there is no doubt that we sin through our eyes when we are led astray by ambition for various things. But an appropriate petition is added: that he may deign to give life in his way, that is, in Christ. Here those who occupy themselves with various spectacles are indicated, as are those who are seized by the foul love of women and do not wish to turn their eyes away from them.

38 “Establish your utterance for your servant, in your fear.”

C “Establish” means, as it were, “make it stand”: that is, implant, strengthen, and confirm it, so that we may not lose the holy utterance through fleeting forgetfulness. For many receive the Lord’s utterances negligently and, as though they were useless stories, refuse to hear them. Therefore he added, “in your fear,” where guilt is never acquired and one never reaches the dangers of sloth.

39 “Cut away my reproach, which I have suspected: ÷ because .. your judgments are pleasing.”

[Col. 0434C] A C He rightly asks that the reproach arising from suspicion be cut away from him. Often we judge someone to be of a certain character on the basis of suspicion, though he is not so; we are then found to be liars and thereby incur reproach. He asks that such reproach and shame be removed, through which he could be found guilty. Suspicion is very often proved uncertain, and it is not fitting for a Christian. In explaining this, “because” must be taken as a conjunction. “Your judgments are pleasing”: first he confessed his weakness; now he praises the Lord’s judgments, whose word is true and whose sentence is true. Therefore the lover of truth rightly calls the Lord’s utterance pleasing to himself, through which he knows that he will obtain rest and a crown.

40 “Behold, I have desired your commandments; give me life in your righteousness.”

[Col. 0434D] C In this verse the holy company says that it has attained the fullness of graces, because it has desired the true commandments of God, which confer true prudence and salvation. “Righteousness” is the Word of the Father, in which he asks to be given life.

ARGUMENT OF THE FOLLOWING EIGHT VERSES.

C B The holy congregation asks that the saving Lord be granted to it, so that it may put its enemies to shame through so great a reward and advance through continual meditation on the Lord’s law. B Therefore the Lord and Savior himself is designated by the name of the letter Vau, that is, “and he himself”—namely, the one to whom it is said, “But you are the same” (Psalm 101), that is, eternal.

B Notice how fittingly the fifth letter is now called the sixth letter, “he himself,” namely the one to whom it is said, “But you are the same” (Psalm 101), that is, eternal. Through faith in him the Church itself has also merited to be “the same,” that is, to reign with him here and in the future in one and the same devotion.

H B Vau: “And he himself.”

41 “Let your mercy come upon me, Lord, your salvation according to your utterance.”

C The holy congregation therefore prays that the Lord and Savior may come upon it, he who is the mercy of sinners and the life of the faithful. To show that this mercy is Christ, he added, “your salvation.” He is rightly called salvation, through whom salvation came to the nations and who grants the sick world the medicine of his compassion. “According to your utterance,” that is, according to the promise which you made through the prophets.

42 “And I will answer those who reproach me with a word, because I have hoped in your words.”

C Those who call the Son lesser reproach the Word. Or they are those who altogether refuse to believe that he suffered in the flesh. For this reason also he says that an answer must be given. “Because I have hoped in the words of God,” in which he said: “When you come before kings and governors, do not consider how or what you should speak; for what you should speak will be given to you” (Matthew 10). Unbelievers also reproach martyrs in their suffering and torments, saying the word of faith: “Where is your God?”

43 “And do not take the word of truth altogether from my mouth, [Col. 0435C] because I have hoped beyond measure in your judgments.”

C And do not take from me this word of faith, concerning which the Apostle says: “This is the word which we preach” (1 Corinthians 1). He therefore asks that no punishment and no terror extort the confession of truth from his mouth, but that he remain constant in faith. For the wicked despair when they are afflicted; but holy men, if they are afflicted, receive an even greater hope of his love.

A C But when he says “altogether,” he signifies that the word of truth was taken away from some for a time, as from Peter when he denied three times; yet it was not taken away from him altogether, since he washed away his fault with tears and cleansed it through the shedding of blood.

44 “And I will keep your law always, for age and age ÷ of the age ...”

[Col. 0435D] C He says that he will always keep the Lord’s law, because it is wicked to vary from it. Sometimes “always” means “until the end of this age”; but here, when he says “for age of age,” he signifies that eternity which has no end. For he knows the custom of the angels and powers: to praise the Lord without end.

45 “And I walked in breadth, because I sought your commandments.”

C This breadth is charity, concerning which it is written: “The love of God has been poured out in our hearts” (Romans 5). He merited it because he sought the understanding of the commandments. H For he sought and examined them diligently for this purpose: that he might believe and understand.

46 “And I spoke of your testimonies before kings, and I was not put to shame.”

C I spoke of God’s testimonies because he had asked and received the ability to answer those who reproached him with a word. Strengthened by this firmness, he says that he was not put to shame among the kings of the world, but brought forth in fearless speech the truth which he had conceived in his mind. He is put to shame whose words are overcome by argument; but the one strengthened by the testimony of truth itself cannot be brought to disgrace.

47 “And I meditated on your commandments, which I loved.”

C Here he shows the ardor of habitual meditation. For no one can meditate on the commandments unless he has traversed them through constant reading; and to make this frequency clearer, he added, “which I loved.” For a person can never neglect what he loves.

48 “And I lifted my hands toward your commandments, which I loved, and I exercised myself in your ordinances.”

C To lift one’s hands signifies to occupy oneself with good works. He lifts his hands toward the commandments who gives alms, as the commandments order. He exercises himself in the ordinances who seeks to advance through the frequent practice of good works. H Or, he does so who strives to find the spiritual meaning in those things indicated by the letter.

ARGUMENT OF THE FOLLOWING EIGHT VERSES.

[Col. 0436C] C B The chorus of saints, commending the hope of the Lord’s promises to our understanding, asserts that the faithful endure the adversities of the world, to whom eternal life is promised. B This life, therefore, which is received here in hope and there in reality, is expressed under the name of the olive, which the letter Zai designates: for here too the faces of the saints are gladdened with oil, and there they grow rich through the more perfect eternal vision of the Holy Spirit. The name of fornication, however, suits sinners who abandon the Lord’s law.

B Zai: olive or fornication.

B And because the grace of the Holy Spirit is sevenfold, the seventh letter is rightly called the olive.

49 “Remember your word to your servant, in which you gave me hope.”

[Col. 0436D] C “Remember” is said to God according to human usage, though he can in no way forget anything. He does not say this because it was fitting to attribute the insult of forgetfulness to that majesty, but he prays that God may quickly grant his servant the promise which he made in the Gospel: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matthew 5). “To your servant” must be understood as “fulfill the promise.” “In which”—that is, in that promise of your word—you gave me hope.

50 “This has comforted me in my humiliation, because your utterance gave me life.”

C When he says, “This has comforted me,” he shows that amid the afflictions of the world this was his consolation: that he should be afflicted in the present life and rejoice in the promise of the future. “In my humiliation”: because holy humility is proved by patiently enduring everything for Christ. “Because your utterance gave me life”: he gives the cause of his consolation. The promise of so great a judge strengthened the soul of the one enduring, and the hope of consolation gave life to the afflicted.

51 “The proud acted wickedly against me to the utmost. But I did not decline from your law.”

C He recalls that the proud—that is, the malicious and tyrannical—acted cruelly against him; they are to be given life not, but rather put to death. “I did not decline from your law,” contrary to what they thought when they persecuted the innocent; rather, he signifies that he remained continually in the judgment of truth.

52 “I remembered your judgments from the beginning, Lord, and I was comforted.”

C He remembers the judgments who does not presume to commit punishable sins. For the one who remembers the Lord’s judgment is recalled from sin by fear of punishment. “From the beginning” signifies the time when the world began to be governed. “I was comforted”: for divine power never abandons its servants.

53 “Despondency seized me because of sinners who abandon your law.”

C It is necessary that the fault of another should grieve a holy man, and that he should say that he has been weakened by sorrow, while his devout spirit desires all to be saved. He grieves for the one whose destruction he does not wish for, when he knows that punishments threaten him. Hence the holy company of martyrs was tortured not so much by its own punishments as by the excesses of tyrants. H Therefore he does not wish anyone to sin, but desires all to recognize the way of truth.

54 “Your ordinances were songs for me in the place of my pilgrimage.”

C When he says “songs,” he signifies that psalmody is to be performed with great delight. Song always lightens labors and does not allow weariness to steal upon the soul. The place of pilgrimage is the world, in which all who are devoted to the Lord Christ are pilgrims.

55 “I remembered your name in the night, Lord, and I kept your law.”

A C There is no doubt that this world can be signified by “night,” since the darkness of sins reigns in it. C But would that it closed only the bodily eyes and did not more dangerously blind the lights of the heart. In this night he remembers the name of God who attributes his benefits not to his own merits but to divine gifts; and through this he keeps God’s law. A Or “in the night of adversity,” when it is more necessary to give thanks than in the day of prosperity.

56 “This happened to me because I sought your ordinances.”

C “This”—namely, this night—happened to me as consolation. The reason follows why the night became consolation for him: because I sought your ordinances. It says “your ordinances,” not “my ordinances”; and therefore he could not be blinded by the darkness of the world, because the night of tribulations became his night—that is, it was made for his benefit and advancement. For we say that something happens to someone when it is beneficial to him.

ARGUMENT OF THE FOLLOWING EIGHT VERSES.

[Col. 0438A]

H B The blessed host desires to see the face of the Lord because it is known to have obeyed his commandments. B And because this desire will be fulfilled in the glory of the resurrection, the eighth letter rejoices in the name of life.

H B Heth: life.

Heth means life, which is found in the divine Scriptures and is Christ.

57 “My portion, Lord: I said that I would keep your law.”

C “Portion” is derived from “part.” We belong to the part whose wishes we obey; hence God is rightly called the portion of the godly. “I said,” that is, I established, resolved, and promised to keep God’s precepts; and thus he became part of the Lord’s portion.

58 “I entreated your face with my whole heart; have mercy on me according to your utterance.”

C The faithful people ask that the mercy of Christ’s coming should be fulfilled, by which he could appear as salvation to the world. “According to your utterance,” namely, that utterance in which he promises the saints his exceedingly blessed and altogether incomparable vision.

59 “I considered my ways, and I turned my feet toward your testimonies.”

C He sets forth the order of human conduct. First one must consider one’s ways, that is, weigh human actions with strict judgment, and then turn one’s feet toward the Lord’s commandments. If someone walks in them, he can have firm footsteps. By saying “I turned my feet,” he shows that they had previously been perverse.

60 “I am ready and I have not been disturbed, so that I may keep your commandments.”

C He testifies that he is ready to keep God’s precepts who fears neither persecutors nor the allurements of this age, having driven them from his senses. “I have not been disturbed” means that he is ready to endure tribulation for Christ. Unexpected things disturb, but a deliberate decision does not allow the mind to be troubled. He also indicates what he said he was ready for: to keep God’s commandments. They are kept wholly when no adversity is feared.

61 “The cords of sinners have encircled me. ÷ And .. I have not forgotten your law.”

C When he says “the cords of sinners,” he shows that there are as many snares as there are sins we commit. This must be referred to bodily depravity: it could happen that the flesh was bound by the cords of sins, while the mind, resisting the incentives of vice, did not forget God’s law. Cords are entangled and twisted bonds; such too are sins, by which sinners continually bind themselves.

62 “At midnight I rose to give thanks to you, because of the judgments of your righteousness.”

C He knows that at midnight the firstborn of the Egyptians were struck down (Exodus 12); he knows that the chains of Peter and Paul were loosed; he also knows that the bridegroom will come at midnight (Acts 12). Therefore he rises at that same time for praise, lest the door remain closed to him among the foolish virgins (Matthew 25). It is not without significance that he says “I rose,” for the one who always hastens to proclaim God’s praises rises. “To give thanks” means to praise the judgments of Christ’s righteousness.

63 “I am a participant with all who fear you and who keep your commandments.”

C Whoever walks in newness of life will be a participant with Christ. And because he said “all who fear,” lest you think he meant only those who dread God’s judgments with servile fear, he adds, “and who keep your commandments”: these are proved most devoted, with the purest fear and reverent love.

64 “The earth is full of the Lord’s mercy; teach me your ordinances.”

C When he says that the earth is full of the Lord’s mercy, he certainly indicates the spread of the Christian faith, which he filled so mercifully that it is shown to have emptied everywhere the name of utterly vain superstition. “Teach me your ordinances,” H that is, your commandments, so that I may understand them, proclaim them, and fulfill them in action.

ARGUMENT OF THE FOLLOWING EIGHT VERSES.

C B The blessed people give thanks that they were humbled in order to reach the Lord’s ordinances, and, explaining the name of the present letter, they call it their good to meditate humbly on the word of God.

H B Teth: good.

65 “You have dealt well with your servant, Lord, according to your word.”

A C Now he confesses the gifts bestowed upon him by the Lord. For the good Lord grants goodness to his servants. He explains below what that goodness is when he says: “It is good for me that you humbled me.” For he gives thanks for salutary affliction, not for worldly happiness. He understood that goodness ought to be called that from which one advances, not that in which one rejoices with empty exultation. Thus the physician does good when he cuts wounds, and thus a father when he beats his son. “According to your word,” namely, the word which says: “Whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Matthew 23). H Or, “You have dealt well”: when you redeemed us in the flesh. “According to your word”: which you promised to Abraham and the other patriarchs.

66 “Teach me goodness, discipline, and knowledge, because I have believed in your commandments.”

C God teaches goodness by inspiring the desire for charity; he teaches discipline when he grants patience in tribulation; he teaches knowledge so that a person may know how to distinguish between good and evil, between life and death. “I have believed,” C that is, I have obeyed your precepts, H or, I have fulfilled them in action. He places discipline before knowledge, so that a person should first practice discipline in himself and afterward teach it to others.

67 “Before I was humbled, I sinned; therefore I kept your utterance.”

C See how human life is described in this verse. First he says that he sinned, since he was subject to original vice; afterward he declares that he was humbled, so that he might be free from the guilt which he had contracted at the root of sin; finally, he kept God’s utterance because he merited being humbled, as the Apostle says: “But he gives grace to the humble” (1 Peter 5). And, to restrain the license of those who transgress, he says that after his humiliation he kept the Lord’s utterance—that is, the Holy Scriptures—by the Lord’s gift.

68 “You are good, and in your goodness teach me your ordinances.”

C He asks the good teacher to deign, in his goodness, to teach the disciple, so that he may know through practice the ordinances which he had learned by reading. The commandments are learned perfectly only when they are put into practice.

69 “The iniquity of the proud has been multiplied against me; but I will search your commandments with my whole heart.”

C He says that the iniquity of his persecutors has been multiplied against him, and therefore he asks that his devoted humility not be stained by the severe punishments of the proud. Rather, to the extent that they strove to seduce the saints, to that extent the saints should be seen to cling to the Lord’s commandments and become still more diligent searchers of them. Thus it happened that those who attempted to overcome the saints through temporal punishments and tried to separate them from God’s law made them all the more diligent searchers of the commandments.

70 “Their heart has become curdled like milk; but I have meditated on your law.”

C By “curdled milk,” he wishes the hardened iniquity of the proud to be understood: it had been contracted, after the manner of milk, into a thicker substance. Milk is named from its liquid quality, because it flows as a natural liquid from an inner substance; for a is changed into i, as in amicus and inimicus, and similar cases. “But I have meditated on your law,” [Col. 0440C] that is, to the extent that they hardened in evil, to that extent he could not be separated from God’s law.

71 “It is good for me that you humbled me, so that I may learn your ordinances.”

C He calls it good for him that he was subjected to the punishments of those who raged, not considering present things but desiring future ones. For he had begun to taste that heavenly sweetness which surpasses all delights. Such humility touches the glorious heights of the heavenly Jerusalem. For just as pride plunges one into Tartarus, so this humility raises one to heaven. “So that I may learn your ordinances,” that is, so that I may do what you taught. They are learned perfectly only when the precepts of God are demonstrated by faithful action.

72 “The law of your mouth is good for me, [Col. 0440D] more than thousands of gold and silver.”

C When he says “the law of your mouth,” he no longer testifies that the commands of the prophets or apostles are most precious to him, but the evangelical precepts spoken by Christ’s mouth. “More than thousands,” as if he were saying, “more than all the thousands of gold and silver”; this is something infinite and incomprehensible. For this love deserved to be judged so great that nothing could be compared with it, and all abundance of gold and silver could become worthless beside it. He said “thousands of gold and silver,” for whatever you name, it always surpasses it. Thus he has made a comparison without likeness, a price without measure, a love without end.

ARGUMENT OF THE FOLLOWING EIGHT VERSES.

C B The glorious company asks that understanding of the commandment be granted to it, so that it may enjoy the gift of true life; and it asks that it be made spotless by the Lord’s mercy, so that it may not be put to shame in that judgment. B And rightly the letter is called knowledge or beginning, in which the faithful seek understanding from him from whom they received the beginning of life.

H B Ioth: knowledge or beginning.

73 “Your hands made me and fashioned me; give me understanding, so that I may learn your commandments.”

C “Your hands” show the power of God’s action. And what is added, “they made me,” some wish to refer to the soul; “they fashioned me,” to the body, which is known to have been formed from the clay of the earth. The creature rightly cries out to its creator: “Give me understanding,” from whom I am known to have been fashioned. But what kind? Not the kind by which human beings seem wise to themselves, but that by which he may know the Lord’s commandments, so that what Adam lost through disobedience the holy company may gain through obedience. He therefore asks for that pure, contemplative, and devout understanding which Adam possessed before sin, H by which God’s commandments are understood and kept.

74 “Those who fear you will see me and rejoice, because I have hoped beyond measure in your word.”

H “Those who fear you” is the voice of the Church: those who fear God and see others observing God’s commandments will rejoice with great joy, because I hope in your word, H C that is, in Christ, C in whom hope never deceives. The Church therefore asks that such things be brought about in it that the devotion of all may be increased. For examples of praiseworthy things, when set before us, always advance us through imitation. It is as if it said: If you grant me that grace, so that I may diligently perform and complete your precepts, those who fear you will see this, and so forth.

75 “I have known, Lord, that your judgments are righteous, and in your truth you humbled me.”

H “Righteousness” belongs to Christ, in that he rebukes sinners for their offenses; “truth,” in that he humbles the proud from their prosperity. Therefore, because you humbled me in order to correct me, let your mercy now come to console me. C Thus he says, “I have known,” that is, I have experienced—namely, in my sufferings and benefits—that all your judgments are equitable in punishing and sparing.

76 “Let your mercy be made, so that it may console me, according to your utterance to your servant.”

[Col. 0441D] C Consolation occurs when he grants patience amid miseries, tempers their torments, and strengthens the sorrows of the afflicted soul with the promise of blessedness. “According to your utterance”: supply, “let it be made”—that is, according to the promise by which he pledged in the Gospel that he would not abandon those who suffered torments.

77 “Let your mercies come to me, and I shall live. For your law ÷ is my meditation …”

C Through Christ’s mercies he wishes to attain eternal life, because only that is properly called life which no trouble disturbs and no fear of death saddens. “For your law”—for that meditation makes blessed which acquires the kingdom of heaven through good works. We therefore do not become blessed merely through the meditation practiced by repeating the reading, but through that which is fulfilled in works.

78 “Let the proud be put to shame, because they have acted wickedly against me unjustly; but I shall exercise myself in your commandments.”

C “Let them be put to shame” pertains to correction, not punishment. A sinner’s conscience is then rightly put to shame when its former evils are condemned by its own will, and it begins to hate what it previously seemed to love. “Because they have acted wickedly against me”—for what is more unjust than their wishing to persecute those who seemed to be occupied with God’s commandments? “But I shall exercise myself”—he sets forth a saving remedy, namely, the practice of the commandments against cruel persecutors; for it is patience alone that conquers them in torments.

79 “Let those who fear you turn to me, and those who know your testimonies.”

C “Let them turn to me,” that is, to you. One is rightly understood to turn to the Lord when one has begun to take part in the ecclesiastical assembly. “And those who know,” that is, those whom divine reading has already imbued, but whom saving works have not yet instructed. Such are beginners in right living, whom he asks to be turned in this way.

80 “Let my heart be blameless in your justifications, so that I may not be put to shame.”

H Here “heart” stands for soul, as though he said: Let my soul be without mortal sin, and let this be so in your justifications—that is, let me not be guilty in the justifications, but clean from transgressing them. Or: let me be blameless, and let this not come from myself but from your justifications. “So that I may not be put to shame,” that is, so that I may not suffer eternal shame. Let the proud indeed be put to shame for correction, but let me not be put to shame for eternal punishment.

## Argument of the Following Eight Verses

C B The pilgrim people on this earth confess their very great longing for the Lord’s coming, recounting how great a persecution by the proud they have endured. B The devotion of this mind is signified by the letter Caph, which is interpreted as “hand,” through which the works either of the heart or of the body are expressed.

H B Caph, “hand.”

B Caph is interpreted as “hand” in such a way that it signifies the palm or hollow of that same hand: not contracted, but open and extended with outspread fingers. Therefore it signifies the works of the hand, whether of the body, the heart, or the inward love itself. Its opening signifies what the Prophet commends when he says: “Reveal your way to the Lord and hope in him,” etc. (Psalm 36).

81 “My soul has languished for your salvation, and I have hoped exceedingly in your word.”

C “My soul has languished” signifies that it has grown weary and exhausted, as often happens through excessive longing. It is characteristic of human nature that whatever we desire utterly seems to make us weary and fail. But, to show where this failing is directed, he adds: “For salvation,” which in the Hebrew language is called *Jesus*; and lest anyone doubt that this should be understood and interpreted in this way, he adds: “And in your word,” that is, in the only-begotten Son, who is the power of God.

82 “My eyes have failed for your word, saying, ‘When will you comfort me?’”

The eyes of the heart have failed. And observe that he says they failed “for” the word, not “from” the word. To fail from the word of God is the deprivation of every good; but to fail for his word is continual increase. “Saying”—although it is ordinarily the tongue that speaks, he says that the eyes have spoken, to show that the luminous desires of the heart proclaim with a kind of silent speech, fail before their most ardent cry, and that he endured this failing for so long until the awaited incarnation of God appeared to the eyes of the heart.

83 “For I have become like a wineskin in the frost; I have not forgotten your justifications.”

C Here he gives the reason why he asks to be helped and comforted. The wineskin signifies the mortal body; the frost displays the heavenly benefit of conversion, through which it comes about that our wanton flesh is contracted by the affliction of repentance. A wineskin in the frost, deprived of its natural color, is contracted by icy cold; so the body of the saints, emptied of the heat that incites vices, is drawn inward by the benefit of conversion. When it has thus been happily chastened, what follows comes to pass: they are utterly unable to forget God’s justifications.

84 “How many are the days of your servant? When will you execute judgment on those who persecute me?”

[Col. 0443C] C Knowing that the company of the saints is subject to the devil’s temptations until the end of the world, he asks when this world will end, so that the prepared vengeance against the persecutors—that is, the devil and his ministers—may be completed. He does not ask to know the length of his own life, but seeks the hastening of the future judgment, in which there will already be rest for the blessed and joy that will endure without end.

85 “The wicked have told me tales, but not according to your law.”

H A C The wicked are heretics, Jews, or pagan philosophers. C Their teaching is compared to empty tales because it wholly disagrees with God’s law and departs from catholic truth.

86 “All your commandments are truth; the wicked have persecuted me—help me.”

[Col. 0443D] C Truth always speaks what is true, but the faithless strive to obscure it with certain clouds. “They have persecuted me” by commanding perverse things and persuading what is false. He adds, “Help me,” as though he were asking for aid against a savage beast and a most cruel enemy, against those who speak such tales.

87 “They nearly finished me on earth, but I did not abandon your commandments.”

C By saying “nearly,” he both shows the enormity of the persecution and declares that, nevertheless, by God’s gift he did not fail. “On earth,” that is, in this age. “But I did not abandon your commandments,” because he showed and maintained his steadfastness in martyrdom to the end of his life.

88 “According to your mercy, give me life, and I shall keep the testimonies of your mouth.”

C He said “give me life” according to mercy—that is, establish me in that eternal life where the life of the saints is. “That I may keep”—H either the things you commanded in the law, or those which you proclaimed in the Gospels. A Martyrs would in no way keep the testimonies of God, that is, martyrdoms—for a martyr is called a witness—unless the Lord’s mercy gave them life. They were given life so that, by loving life, they would not deny life, and by denying life, lose life; and thus those who did not wish to abandon the truth for the sake of life lived for the truth by dying.

## Argument of the Following Eight Verses

C B The faithful people, describing the Lord’s power and deeds, say that all temporal things can come to an end, but that his commandments find no end whatsoever. B Subject to the discipline of these commandments, the people proclaim: “I shall never forget your justifications.”

A B Lamech, “discipline.”

B Therefore Lamech signifies “discipline,” because the faithful people are most willingly subject to the discipline of God.

89 “Forever, O Lord, your word remains in heaven.”

C Therefore God’s word remains forever in heaven, that is, in each of the saints, whom he makes live from death—that is, makes them live eternally through temporal death. Heaven is in them, or they are heaven, because they are known to conduct themselves in a heavenly manner. Or “in heaven” means in the angels, in whom God dwells. God’s word therefore always remains in them, because they continually remain in God’s service and praise with the firmest resolve.

90 “From generation to generation your truth; you founded the earth, and it remains.”

H C “From generation to generation” signifies the times in which two peoples believed in the Lord: one belonging to the law and the prophets, the other to the Gospel and the apostles. C In them is truth, that is, the Lord Christ himself. “You founded the earth,” that is, you established the saints, who are so founded that they remain in faith in Christ. This is why truth exists from generation to generation: because the earth, that is, believers, has been founded. For if he himself had not founded the earth in this way—that is, confirmed it—neither the earlier nor the later generation could have believed in Christ or remained in the faith.

91 “By your ordinance the day perseveres, because all things serve you.”

C Whenever “day” is placed in the singular, it signifies the day that is to come, which is one and eternal and has no night. Of it is written: “And the Lord will be their everlasting light” (Revelation 21). And lest anyone ask in doubt how this could happen, he adds that all things serve the Creator, who according to his will orders both temporal and eternal things.

92 “Unless your law—my meditation—÷ were, then … perhaps I would have perished in my humiliation.”

C The meditation of the law is that which commands us either to think or to act, so that, strengthened as though by an inward counselor, one may courageously overcome raging torments. By “humiliation” he means afflictions, which he endured with devout willingness and from which he rejoices to have been delivered when he merited reaching holy martyrdom. Some undergo this humiliation from necessity; others, such as the saints, undertake it willingly.

93 “Forever I shall not forget your justifications, because through them you have given me life.”

C No believer ought to forget those benefits of the Lord from which we are known to have received the gift of life. These benefits are the justifications that have granted us the life of the soul in faith. Other things may perhaps fall from the memory, but no believer forgets the benefit in which life is bestowed.

94 “I am yours; save me, for I have sought your justifications.”

C “I am yours” cannot truly be said by one who knows that he serves sin. The servant of vices does not deserve to have the Lord of the saints. Consider, however, that although the holy company has professed itself to be the Lord’s, it still asks to be saved—certainly in that future judgment, when the blessed enter everlasting rest. But why this salvation is continually requested he adds below: “For I have sought your justifications.” Some seek honors, others the joys of the world, others marriage; I seek your justifications.

95 “Sinners waited for me, to destroy me; I understood your testimonies.”

[Col. 0445C] C “They waited for me,” namely, evil persuaders, flattering me. They did this in order to wound my soul with the injury of perversity. By saying “they waited,” he shows that the punishment of martyrdom was neither hastened nor precipitated, so that a prolonged punishment might be more grievous than a sudden one. This persecution is more grievous, for it both delays the martyr’s crown and does not cease persuading the soul to death. But since this man understood God’s testimony, he could not be led into abominable vices. Hence only those are freed from such danger who are strengthened by the Lord’s illumination.

“I understood” should be explained as “I acted,” as it is said in another psalm: “Blessed is he who understands concerning the needy” (Psalm 40), that is, assists the needy. For one who acts according to the testimonies cannot, as we have said, be led into abominable vices.

96 “I have seen an end of every consummation; your commandment is exceedingly broad.”

C Consummation is the perfection of all virtues, and Christ is the end of that consummation. He says that he has seen him when, with an enlightened mind, he believed that Christ would come. “The broad commandment” signifies charity, which we are commanded to have toward God and our neighbor. For what can be called broader than that which embraces the whole law and the sayings of the prophets? As the Savior taught, “On these two commandments depend the whole law and the prophets” (Matthew 22).

H The Prophet therefore foresaw in the spirit that Christ would consummate everything written about him in the law, the prophets, and the psalms. For this reason he said on the cross: “It is consummated” (John 19).

## Argument of the Following Eight Verses

C B The blessed people, advancing through meditation on the prophets and the Gospel, assert that they have understood the divine commandments better than their teachers and elders. B Therefore the letter *Mem* is interpreted as “from which”: it signifies “from which,” that is, what is said [H B]: “How I have loved your law, O Lord!”—that is, from what affection of sweetness and love, so that it may signify “from within.” But what is said “from them” signifies that love for the Lord is to be conceived from the Lord’s commandments themselves; hence he says, “From your commandments I have understood.”

H B Mem, “from which” or “from them.”

97 “How I have loved your law, O Lord! [Col. 0446B] My meditation ÷ is all day …”

C By saying “how,” he promises that he will explain in what manner he loved God’s law with exceptional attention and willingness. “All day” signifies continuous time: one meditates on God’s law throughout the whole span of life when everything one does is done to God’s praise. If someone receives food temperately with fear of God, if he takes sleep appropriately, he meditates on God’s law in everything, since he commends himself through honorable and commendable action.

98 “You have made me wiser than my enemies by your commandment, because it is mine forever.”

C The enemies are to be understood as obstinate Jews, heretics, and pagans, who do not practice God’s precepts. He says that he was made wiser than these because he devoutly fulfilled God’s commands. But from what he became wise, he adds: “by your commandment.” Since he faithfully obeyed it, he surpassed all who were wandering astray. He adds: “because it is mine forever”—namely, your commandment, that is, the love of God and neighbor.

99 “I have understood more than all my teachers, because your testimonies ÷ are my meditation …”

C Let us attend to the preceding verse, where he did not say “above fathers,” but “above enemies.” Here he censures teachers, namely, the Pharisees, because they clung to the letter and neglected spiritual understanding. Therefore, above all such teachers, the holy company rightly says that it understood better, because it received the sincere teaching of God. But it also explains why it understood better: because your testimonies are my meditation.

100 “I have understood more than the elders, because I sought your commandments.”

“I have understood more than the elders.” Here he calls them elders not in mind but in body. The new people, who happily received Christ, therefore understood better than that older Jewish people which judged him contemptible. He adds why it understood more than the elders: “Because I sought your commandments”—I did not keep the commandments of perverse human beings.

101 “I restrained my feet from every evil way, so that I might keep your words.”

C “From every evil way” signifies the wicked persuasions of heretics, with which they flatter people, or the wicked deeds of all evils. “My feet” signifies the consent of the mind, which, as though by a footprint, leads us toward guilt unless God’s mercy draws us away. “So that I might keep your words”—he could not otherwise keep God’s words unless that deadly persuasion had been expelled.

102 “I have not turned aside from your judgments, because you established a law for me.”

C “From your judgments” means from that which your will established and gave as a rule of living; from this I certainly did not turn aside. “Because you established a law for me”—this is the Gospel, which granted the effect of complete fullness. The old law, which has the function of a pedagogue, is therefore not intended here.

103 “How sweet your words are to my throat, sweeter than honey to my mouth.”

C “How sweet,” that is, sweeter than all things and supremely sweet. H After honey—or another food—has passed across the palate, it has no further taste; but God’s words, whether in the mouth, the throat, or the hidden recess of the heart, are always sweet to those who meditate on them. C Although every bodily taste exists only in the palate and throat, the Lord’s words, swallowed down, become sweet in the throat of the heart.

104 “From your commandments I have understood; therefore I have hated every way of iniquity.”

C Taught God’s law, he understood the saying: “My son, do not walk with the ungodly” (Proverbs 1). He had also heard: “You have destroyed all who commit fornication away from you” (Psalm 72). When he heard such things in God’s commandments, he understood that the way of iniquity was to be utterly abhorred and could not please the just Lord.

## Argument of the Following Eight Verses

C B The blessed company rejoices that the light of the Lord’s word shines upon its feet. B It seeks the Lord’s everlasting rewards, on account of which this letter received the name “eternal.” Moreover, since it is interpreted as “fish,” it points to the one who seeks the light of the word amid the waves of the world.

H B Nun, “eternal” or “fish.”

105 “Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths.”

C The blessed company testifies that God’s word—that is, the holy Scriptures—shines upon its feet, lest, in the absence of true light, it fall into ruin, which it could not avoid by its own foresight. “And a light to my paths”—H so that, with this light going before us, while we walk the paths of this life, we may be led to that which is the true way. Thus the holy Scripture of the prophets is called a lamp, and the Gospel a light—or both are called light and lamp.

106 “I swore and resolved to keep the judgments of your justice.”

C To swear is to pray by right, that is, to speak equity, lest anyone turn what he has promised in another direction. To swear here therefore does not mean to make an oath—in which, by invoking divinity, we call it as a witness to the truth—but to swear means firmly to resolve in one’s mind to fulfill a good purpose. The judgments of justice are those by which he raises the humble and casts down the proud.

107 “I have been humbled exceedingly; Lord, give me life according to your word.”

C The members of Christ say that they have been humbled in every respect. They show that they have endured the dangers of many persecutions, and in their humility they ask to be given life according to God’s promises. That word may be understood as: “Come to me, all you who labor,” etc. (Matthew 11).

108 “Make the free offerings of my mouth pleasing, O Lord, and teach me your judgments.”

C The free offerings or pleasing sacrifices of the mouth are to offer the devotion of praise, not with a view to any worldly advantage, but out of regard for one’s own will. He therefore asks that these be made acceptable to God, so that, pleased by this offering, he may teach him his judgments, which he deigns to open to faithful minds.

109 “My soul is always in my hands, and I have not forgotten your law.”

H “My soul is in my hands”—that is, I always keep my soul ready in good works, according to what your law commands; or, I am ready to endure martyrdom for you. C This is prescribed everywhere and we are especially admonished of it: that we return in this way to the law and do not depart from the law. Through “hands,” therefore, either works or power is understood, or readiness for martyrdom and suffering.

110 “Sinners have set a snare for me, but I have not gone astray from your commandments.”

H What are these snares except the devil’s traps or his suggestions? C In this forest of the world you find as many snares as you behold vices. The remedy follows, which is recognized as fighting against these poisons: namely, that I did not at all turn aside from God’s commandments. One who does not turn aside from them is caught by no deception, because the ambushes are beside the commandments, not within them. H A snare is set beside the road, not on the road; and if you leave the road of the commandments, you fall into the snare.

111 “I have acquired your testimonies as an inheritance forever, because they are the rejoicing of my heart.”

C This inheritance is a profitable, eternal possession. [Col. 0448D] The testimonies are the most holy precepts. He rightly called the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom the rejoicing of his heart: for he deserves to reach it, as is proved by the fact that he rejoices in such an acquisition. H Your testimonies and precepts are the inheritance of the righteous, here and in the future, forever.

112 “I have inclined my heart to do your justifications forever, because of the reward.”

H “I have inclined my heart,” namely, toward humility. For I inclined—that is, humbled—my heart so that I might deserve to understand you, because the proud do not incline their hearts toward humility. He adds toward what he inclined it: namely, toward doing the justifications. These are your commandments, which I have freely resolved to perform for the sake of the reward of eternal life.

## Argument of the Following Eight Verses

C B The catholic assembly says that it has hated the wicked but loved the Lord’s law, and the holy people ask that, received by him, they may escape the evils of the world. B It explains the name of the letter when it says, “Help me, and I shall be saved.”

H B Samech, “help.”

113 “I have hated the wicked and loved your law.”

H “I have hated the wicked”—not the nature by which they were human beings, but the vices and sins by which they were opposed to God’s law. I love that law as you commanded, so that I might fulfill it in practice.

114 “You are my helper and my protector, and I have hoped exceedingly in your word.”

H “Helper” in the present; “protector” in the future age. C “Helper” pertains to fulfilling the commandments, since without his help we can neither begin any good thing nor bring it to completion. Or “protector” refers to when he assumed our nature. “And I have hoped in your word.” H This means in Christ. C He is the supreme protection.

115 “Depart from me, evildoers, and I shall scrutinize the commandments of my God.”

H “Depart from me, evildoers”—these are demons, vices, and sins. As long as they prepare traps and wicked suggestions for you, you cannot scrutinize the commandments of your God. C Nor can we be found fit to scrutinize them unless we devote all the powers of our soul to them. H Therefore, if you too wish to practice perfect repentance, separate yourself from the companionship of all evil people and flee to another place.

116 “Receive me according to your word, and I shall live; and do not put me to shame in my expectation.”

C The holy company asks to be received by the Lord after the faithless have been driven away, so that it may be saved by his promise. When he says “I shall live,” he indicates the future time. Here one does not truly live, where one sins through the frailty of the flesh. The expectation of the saints is also to earn the kingdoms of heaven and the company of angels and, above all, to behold continually him who always grows sweet in the hearts of the blessed.

117 “Help me, and I shall be saved; and I shall meditate on your justifications always.”

H The Prophet asks that help come to his soul from Christ. He adds: “And I shall meditate on your justifications.” C He gives the reason for this obedience. Since, as long as we are in this world, we cannot be free from sins, it is fitting that we always prostrate ourselves in this justification—which takes place in the confession of sins—and meditate on his will.

118 “You have despised all who depart from your judgments, because their thought is unjust.”

C They are rightly despised by the Lord who depart from his justification, which takes place in the confession of sins. Their thought is unjust: they wish to sin and refuse to submit to the most just Judge. [Col. 0450A] The proud are therefore rightly despised by the Lord, because they disdain to be healed and justified by the remedy of repentance.

119 “I have regarded all the sinners of the earth as transgressors; therefore I loved your testimonies.”

H All who existed before Christ’s coming were transgressors, because they were held under the debt of the transgression of Adam, the first man, and all descended to hell. “Therefore I loved”—so that I might not appear a transgressor among them.

120 “Nail my flesh with your fear, for ÷ … I have feared your judgments.”

C The holy Apostle therefore prays that he be nailed by the fear of the Lord, so that he who formerly died by living may live by dying. Happy is the one who is fastened by this nail and wounded by such a wound. He was fastened by that nail who said: “For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Philippians 1). H By the fear of judgment, God nails the flesh of the one who crucifies all the desires of the flesh and wishes to die and be buried with Christ (Romans 6), so that he may rise and live eternally with him.

## Argument of the Following Eight Verses

C B The members of the Lord, living forever, seek the coming of the sacred incarnation. B For he, namely Christ, is the living fountain who is sought; he is the pure eye that seeks.

H B Ain, “fountain” or “eye.”

121 “I have practiced judgment and justice; do not hand me over to those who slander me.”

[Col. 0450C] C Whoever judges against himself and condemns his own perversities before the Lord’s judgment with righteous abhorrence practices judgment. But lest you think this judgment flattering rather than true, he adds: “and justice,” because by it we judge ourselves when we become the avengers of our sins. “Do not hand me over”—the holy people ask not to be handed over to their persecutors, that is, to the devil and his ministers. The unclean spirits were angry with them because they saw their persuasions and attacks condemned.

122 “Receive your servant for good; let not the proud slander me.”

C We are received by the Lord’s mercy when we are struck by compunction for our sins. “Servant” is derived from “saving,” because the hand of his compassionate Lord saved the captive from impending destruction. Having been freed from danger to his soul by Christ’s mercy, he calls himself Christ’s servant. “Let them not slander me”—namely, the unclean spirits, who wickedly oppose and slander us. For although they deceive us, they also continually accuse us.

123 “My eyes have failed for your salvation and for the word of your justice.”

C He says that the eyes of the heart have failed because of the coming of Christ, whom he awaited with such great desire that he could have had no rest in waiting. Christ is the salvation. “And for the word of your justice,” that is, the evangelical words which he was going to speak to the believing people.

124 “Deal with your servant according to your mercy, and teach me your justifications.”

C He asks that mercy be shown toward him, because it is right that the one who is offended when not asked should be entreated continually. “Your servant,” because the one who wishes to belong to another immediately falls. Observe that he asks to be taught the justifications which he had already devoutly received. Throughout the psalm he frequently asks in one place for what he confesses elsewhere that he has received, so that God may preserve what he has given; for one must never grow weary of asking. This persistence is also signified by the Lord’s Prayer, which says: “Give us this day our daily bread.”

125 “Your servant ÷ am … I. Give me understanding, so that I may know your testimonies.”

C “I am your servant; give me”—you who are accustomed to grant what is rightly and confidently requested. “So that I may know,” that is, so that I may retain what I have received. To know means that, once something has entered our awareness, it is erased by no forgetfulness. Although everything beneficial must be requested from the Lord in continual prayers, the understanding of the divine Scriptures must especially be sought without interruption: the more it is received, the sweeter it is found.

126 “It is time to act, O Lord; they have destroyed your law.”

A The faithful people cry, “It is time to act”—that is, for you to appear to the world, dissolve sins, and overthrow the devil himself. He adds the reason for the action he has requested: the Jews have destroyed the law which he commanded them to keep inviolate. To destroy the law is to live otherwise than the law commands and to do what the law condemns.

127 “Therefore I loved your commandments above gold and topaz.”

H Just as gold surpasses the value of all metals, so topaz, possessing in itself the beauties of all gems, surpasses all their honors. Therefore the Prophet loved God’s commandments above all these things, because in them he found the coming of the Lord, who redeemed the world, announced.

128 “Therefore I was directed toward all your commandments; I hated every way of iniquity.”

[Col. 0451D] C One who loved God’s law above gold and gems necessarily appeared directed toward all his commandments. It was fitting that he should hate every iniquitous way who had deserved to love the most upright one. The iniquitous way is that which leads us to vices; the straight way is that which draws us toward salvation and virtues and grants forgiveness and salvation.

## Argument of the Following Eight Verses

B The holy people assert that they have opened their mouth and drawn in the spirit, so that their prayer may be heard. (C Therefore the letter received the name “mouth.”) In it, each little and humble person opens the entrance of the heart and absorbs the spirit of divine charity and mercy.

H B Phe, “mouth,” from *os* meaning mouth, not from *os* meaning bone.

129 “Your testimonies are wondrous, O ÷ Lord …; therefore my soul has searched them out.”

C He summed up the definition of the testimonies in one word by calling them wondrous. Wondrous indeed, because through them heavenly power became known to earthly human beings, and they gave understanding to the little ones, with which the angels are filled in blessed delight. They may always be scrutinized and sought through constant meditation. One need not fear what is said: “Do not seek what is too high for you, and do not scrutinize what is too strong for you” (Ecclesiastes 3). For what was commanded to be sought cannot be called too high.

130 “The explanation of your words gives light and grants understanding to the little ones.”

C God’s words are those which the authority of the righteous prophesied, as in: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive” (Isaiah 7), and elsewhere: “All flesh shall see the salvation of God” (Isaiah 40). The illumination of his coming explained these words, because through him the things held hidden in the sacred writings were made manifest. “Little ones” does not refer to age, but to simplicity and humility of conscience.

131 “I opened my mouth and drew in the spirit, because I desired your commandments.”

C “Mouth” means the entrance of the mind, which is opened when we take care to learn something. He draws in the spirit—that is, the power to act—which he could not obtain by himself. The spirit is drawn in when the mind is filled with the affection of saving desire and begins firmly to will what it previously desired. “Because I desired your commandments”—he indicates that he possessed ardor for the commandments; for this reason he opened his mouth, because he desired the commandments.

132 “Look upon me and have mercy on me, according to the judgment of those who love your name.”

C The Lord often looks in anger in order to destroy, as he did upon Sodom. He also looks favorably, as he did in the gifts of Abel. Therefore, lest he be received in the adverse sense, he adds: “and have mercy on me.” God’s judgment is to grant the help of mercy to those who love his name. According to that judgment, therefore, he asks that mercy be shown to him.

133 “Direct my steps according to your word, and let no iniquity rule over me.”

C “Steps” signifies the movements of the soul. Just as by bodily steps we transfer ourselves from place to place, so by certain steps we progress either toward better things or toward worse. “According to your word”—the holy company asks to be directed according to the commands and precepts whose observance makes it possible for no iniquity to rule over it. Observe how cautiously he asks: he does not ask that he be assaulted by no iniquity, because this cannot happen here under the common condition of life. It can, however, happen that not merely one iniquity, but every iniquity, does not rule over him.

134 “Redeem me from the slanders of men, and I shall keep your commandments.”

C Slanders are disputes against the honor of truth, or quarrelsome accusations brought forward. The holy company rightly prayed that these be removed from it, so that, once adversities had been taken away, it might investigate God’s commandments. A slander is an invented charge of dangerous falsehood, which the wicked zeal of perversity always brings against good people, attempting to stain what they have done with an upright conscience and thus make it possible to accuse them. Or more briefly: H A Slander is a false accusation of a crime.

135 “Make your face shine upon your servant, and teach me your justifications.”

C The holy company desires the coming of the Savior, by whose face dark sins are illuminated and who grants life to the dead and most certain remedies to the despairing. Or let it mean: illuminate me so that I may be able to see your illuminated, unveiled face. When Moses brought forth the law, the Jews could not look upon his face (Exodus 34), because they heard the law with veiled hearts. The face of Moses was the radiance of the law; because the Jews could not look upon it, he veiled his face, and in this way they were able to look upon him. Here he asks that the veil of the heart be removed, so that he may recognize the clear truth of the law.

136 “Streams of water have run down from my eyes, because they did not keep your law.”

C “Streams of water” signifies abundant tears, which we pour out when we are pierced by the recollection of our sins. If we kept the Lord’s commandments, we would certainly have joy, not the burning of weeping. Observe that he says satisfaction came through the eyes, through which we frequently draw in the enticements of this world; rightly, therefore, guilt is cleansed through those by which excess is also committed.

## Argument of the Following Eight Verses

C B The company of the saints, triumphant over its flesh, confesses the Lord’s justice according to the name of this letter; and it says that it venerates his fiery words with continual love.

H C Sade, “justice.”

137 “You are righteous, O Lord, and your judgment is right.”

C “You are righteous, O Lord,” who command sinners to afflict themselves so that your medicine may save them. For it is just that the offender be corrected through satisfaction and that God’s justice be declared by humble confession. Otherwise, if the sinner continually flourished unharmed, it would seem to have been granted on the basis of his own merits.

138 “You commanded justice concerning your testimonies, and your truth exceedingly.”

C “You have commanded”—that is, you have ordered them to be observed—“exceedingly,” that is, very greatly. The testimonies are those proclaimed under the form of testimony, that is, the commandments. They contain justice and truth: justice, because they distinguish everything equally; truth, because they grant what has been promised. H Or, everything that we suffer at your command is just, right, and true, because it either comes upon us on account of our sins or occurs so that we may be shown to have been tested. A Or he says that God’s testimonies are justice and truth: he proves himself just by commanding, and truthful; therefore he wishes them to be observed exceedingly.

139 [Col. 0454A] “My zeal has consumed me, because my enemies have forgotten your words.”

C Consumption is the constricting effect of some illness, which gradually causes us to waste away as it destroys the body’s solidity. He testifies that this happened to him when he could not endure the law of the Lord being violated by the tearing apart inflicted by the faithless. Here “zeal” is good. Sometimes, however, it is used in an evil sense, as there: “Zeal and envy consumed the house of Jacob.”

140 “Your utterance is exceedingly refined by fire, and your servant has loved it.”

C The Lord’s utterance is refined by fire because it purifies the hearts of mortals, which are heavily soiled with the filth of the world. And so that you would not believe this to be for death but for salvation, he added: “And your servant has loved it,” [Col. 0454B] for he certainly loved what he knew conferred life and honor, not what brought death. C And just as the utterance of the commandments consumes sins, so it enlightens the sinner if he turns back.

141 “I am young and despised; I have not forgotten your statutes.”

H This verse is to be referred to the Christian people, who, formerly despised and expelled from their father’s house, recalled God’s statutes, received the firstborn inheritance of the former people, and became first.

142 “Your justice is justice forever, and your law is truth.”

C This verse distinguishes the Lord’s justice and law from human justice and law. Human justice, however great it may be, is temporary. But God’s justice [Col. 0454C] remains forever, because whoever observes it will rejoice in eternal happiness. The same must be understood of the law: whoever is granted the ability to understand it is filled with heavenly truth, for Christ is the truth of the law.

143 “Tribulation and distress have found me; your commandments are my meditation.”

C Tribulation and distress are great gifts to holy men, because they know that, pressed down by the weight of such things, they sweat out their sins and advance toward eternal joys. “They have found me,” as though he were waiting for them, fixed and prepared for their struggles. He then adds the help by which he knew he had been healed amid various sufferings, saying: “Your commandments,” and so forth, because his mind was always occupied with the divine Scriptures. [Col. 0454D]

144 “The equity of your testimonies is forever; give me understanding, and I shall live.”

H God’s testimonies are equity, because they distinguish everything equitably. Therefore he asks to be given life, so that through understanding them he may attain eternal life. C Thus he briefly defined God’s testimonies as equity forever, in opposition to tribulations and distresses, which are known to be temporary, so that temporary hardships might be despised in hope of this kind.

## Argument of the following eight verses

C B The most reverent choir, in accordance with the name of this letter, cries out to the Lord with all its heart, diligently seeking his statutes.

[Col. 0455A] H B *Coph*, “calling.”

145 “I have cried with my whole heart; hear me, O Lord. I shall seek your statutes.”

C Understand this crying not as the voice of the body but as that of the spiritual mind. C It is the devoted affection of the mind, expressed with the great concentration of the heart. For the Most High has heard those thoughts that are revolved with pious intention. “With my whole heart” is said so that you would not suppose that something else should be contemplated when one cries to the Lord. For the whole spirit ought to be occupied in religious thought alone, lest a divided mind be unable to obtain what it asks. And consider what he cries for: not riches, honors, or pleasures, but “I shall seek your statutes”—not by reading alone but by practice.

146 [Col. 0455B] “I have cried to you; save me, and I shall keep your commandments.”

C “I have cried to you”: for he cries to the one who has poured out his petition worthily with the whole affection of his heart. When he says, “Save me,” this is to be understood of the soul, not the body. He could not have been asking for bodily safety who willingly submitted to bodily sufferings.

147 “I anticipated the time of maturity and cried out, because I hoped beyond measure in your words.”

C “I anticipated the time of maturity”: whoever, in the years of childhood, anticipates the sobriety of old age and assumes a very grave mind before he can grow gray through the number of his years. “Because I did not cease to hope in your words”—that is, in the Son. A Or, in the words of the prophets [Col. 0455C] and of God, who is powerful to do what he promised; for in his words he promised to send the Redeemer.

148 “My eyes anticipated you at dawn, so that I might meditate on your utterances.”

C “My eyes anticipated you”: this signifies that the eyes of his heart believed in the Lord who was to come in the flesh before his advent shone upon them. For Christ is the day, and his advent and incarnation are the dawn; dawn signifies the beginning of the day. “So that I might meditate”: he gives the reason why his mind rose before dawn—not to cultivate a field, but to meditate on God’s utterances.

149 “Hear my voice according to your mercy, O Lord; according to your judgment give me life.”

[Col. 0455D] C He asks that his voice be heard according to that mercy which made the blessed from the wretched, the free from captives, and the living from the dead. By adding, “Give me life,” he confesses that he is dead under the law of sin. No one can be given life unless he has no life of his own within himself. When he says “according to your judgment,” understand the judgment by which he spares those who supplicate him and acquits those who condemn themselves.

150 “Those who persecute me have drawn near in iniquity, but they have gone far from your law.”

A C “Those who persecute me draw near” when, after everything, they seem to advance even to the tearing of the flesh. H “In iniquity they draw near,” that is, with iniquity—acting unjustly. For the martyrs were suffering evil in return for good. A But “these persecutors,” namely, “have gone far from the law,” etc., because H A C the more closely they approached the sufferings of the saints, the farther they withdrew from the law of the Lord. If, however, some text has “to iniquity” or “unjustly,” the sense remains the same: whoever persecutes the righteous approaches iniquity and acts unjustly.

151 “You are near, O Lord, and all your ways are truth.”

C When he says, “You are near, O Lord,” he confesses that God is present everywhere and knows when we act perversely, and that we cannot escape him when we flee. There is therefore one salvation: to hasten toward the one whom you cannot escape. “And all your ways”: a Jew cannot say this, since he refused to believe the truth; but one who believes in Christ and keeps his commandments can say it. A Even amid torments, he confesses that one does not suffer them undeservedly, but that God’s judgment in this matter is true. Thus Esther, thus Daniel, thus the three in the furnace, thus all the saints confess (Dan. III).

[Col. 0456A]

152 “From the beginning I came to know your testimonies, because you founded them forever.”

C “From the beginning”—he means from the beginnings of the world, when the name of the saints began with righteous Abel, who was killed by his wicked brother while innocent, as a figure of the Savior [Gen. IV]—the Church says, “I came to know the testimonies,” A namely, those by which you testified that you would give the Redeemer and an eternal kingdom. “Because they were founded forever.” A C For they pertained to Christ as their foundation. He himself is the foundation [Col. 0456C] on which all the words spoken and written in the Law, the prophets, and the Gospel are founded (Eph. II). Hence it is clearly understood that Christ was seen in mind by the ancients.

## Argument of the following eight verses

C B The people, victorious over vices, ask to be given life, because they have sought the Lord’s commandments with the greatest zeal. They also testify that the beginning of the Lord’s words is truth; and this is the “head” that the present letter displays.

H B *Res*, “head.”

153 “See my humility and deliver me, because I have not forgotten your law.”

A “See my humility and deliver me”: although this voice seems to belong to martyrs, no one who has been incorporated into Christ’s body should think it foreign to him. “And deliver me”—C namely, from the necessity of punishments and from the danger of death, from which the blessed martyrs ask to be freed, or from the danger of sins. “Because of your law.” H A C Namely, the law in which you said: “Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Matt. XXIII).

[Col. 0456D]

154 “Judge my judgment and redeem me; because of your utterance give me life.”

A C The choir of the saints asks the Lord to judge its judgment, that is, its case, since demons afflict and persecute it unjustly, and asks to be redeemed from them. He added, “because of your utterance,” C namely, the utterance where he promises: “Whoever believes in me will not die” (John XI).

[Col. 0457A]

155 “Salvation is far from sinners, because they have not sought your statutes.”

H C The Jews are therefore rightly far from salvation, since they rejected the author of salvation and did not understand the statutes of the law, because they did not recognize Christ in them. A Or, salvation is far from any sinners who despise God’s law.

156 “Your mercies are many, O Lord; according to your judgment give me life.”

[Col. 0457B]

C The Lord’s mercies are those by which he deigns to assist the afflicted and wounded in various ways. “According to your judgment give me life,” H lest anything be found in me that would incur the judgment of death. C For he neither shows mercy without judgment nor judges without mercy. Therefore, when he shows mercy, he judges; and when he judges, he shows mercy.

157 “Many are those who persecute and afflict me; I have not turned aside from your testimonies.”

C He recounts injuries and persecutions, through which the number of the elect increases; yet amid everything he testifies that he has in no way turned aside from God’s testimonies.

158 “I saw the transgressors and wasted away, because they did not keep your utterances.”

[Col. 0457C]

C I saw some denying the faith they had held during the persecutions. The holy choir, looking upon this, was afflicted, grieving that it had lost companions in faith. But he shows why he wasted away: the transgressor in no way kept the evangelical utterances, namely: “Whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. X). H Or, the Jews are transgressors, for they said to Moses: “Everything that the Lord has said we shall do” (Exod. XXIV), and they did not do it. We too are transgressors when, renouncing the devil and his works in baptism, we do what we have renounced. The saints grieve over this intensely.

159 “See that I have loved your commandments, O Lord; in your mercy give me life.”

[Col. 0457D]

C He rightly says, “I have loved the commandments,” namely, by enduring the sufferings of martyrdom even unto death. For the Lord regards the qualities of souls more graciously than the torture of the flesh. A martyr must therefore be cheerful. He rightly asked the Lord to give him life in blessedness, since for true religion he had despised the life of this world.

160 “The beginning of your words is truth; all the judgments of your justice are eternal.”

C The “beginning” seems to me to signify the beginning of the divine Scriptures, namely: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth.” That beginning of God’s words is shown to be the perfection of complete truth. And just as Scripture is true in the beginning, so it is at the end. For the truth that speaks truly from the beginning also shows its words to be true unto the end, saying: “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away” (Matt. XXIV). The judgments of his justice will undoubtedly be everlasting, when neither any passage of time will change his sentence nor any circumstance overturn it. He understands those judgments to be the ones pronounced when it is said: “Come, blessed of my Father,” and: “Go, accursed ones, into eternal fire” (Matt. XXV). These judgments will remain fixed forever. Thus in one verse he has concluded both the beginnings of our faith and the things yet to come, all of which will be fulfilled in truth. A Or, your words proceed from your eternal truth, and thus their beginning is truth. And because they proceed from that truth, they are truthful and deceive no one. And because they deceive no one, and the judgments of your justice are pronounced through them—life for the righteous, punishment for the wicked—these judgments of your justice will be true forever and will remain forever: the former in life, the latter in punishment.

## Argument of the following eight verses

[Col. 0458B] C B The assembly of the saints says that the persecutions of those raging against it for the love of the Lord are exceedingly welcome.
