B The “teeth,” however, which the name of this letter expresses, may be understood either as the saints who praise the Lord or as the persecutors, of whom it is said: “The sons of men, their teeth are weapons and arrows.”

H B *Sin*, “teeth.”

161 “Princes have persecuted me without cause, and my heart has feared your words.”

C Here we must understand “princes” as persecutors; thus we also call the devil a prince, since he claimed primacy for himself in crimes. “Without cause,” because the holy martyrs neither prevented them from receiving tribute nor withheld obedience from them; indeed, they even prayed for them. Yet they, without fearing the martyrs’ persecution, feared to transgress God’s commands. Hence he adds: “And it has feared your words.” H It feared that word in which he says: “Whoever denies me before men, I shall also deny him before my Father” (Luke IX).

162 “I shall rejoice over your utterances, like one who finds great spoils.”

C The Christian people finally rejoiced like one who finds great spoils when it seized God’s utterances from the unbelieving Jews for the benefit of its own salvation. The utterances of God are also H those in which he said: “When they persecute you and curse you, and speak every evil against you, falsely, because of me, rejoice” (Matt. V). The entire Gospel consists of God’s utterances, C as do all sacred admonitions.

163 “I have hated and abhorred iniquity; but I have loved your law.”

C He says that he hates iniquity, which is right, not the unjust person; and he abhorred it so completely that he made it far removed and alien from himself, so that he might love God’s law with perfect will.

164 “Seven times a day I have praised you, for the judgments of your justice.”

H He praises God seven times a day, his mind continuing in full radiance and hastening toward that seventh day which is the Sabbath of Sabbaths, that is, eternal rest. C Or, literally, he signifies the seven hours and times at which the Church praises God: morning prayer, the third hour, the sixth, the ninth, evening prayer, compline, and the night offices. A C Or [Col. 0459A] he signifies all time, as it is said elsewhere: “I will bless the Lord at all times” (Ps. XXXIII). “For the judgments,” C because he spares the one who supplicates him and is so gracious to the humble that he not only forgives their sins but also grants them eternal rewards.

165 “There is great peace for those who love your law, and there is no stumbling block for them.”

C “Great peace,” namely, of mind, along with purity and abundance of faith. Nevertheless, the one who loves the law and professes himself God’s servant is subject to tribulations in this world; amid them he remains with a tranquil mind. A “And there is no stumbling block for them,” namely, God’s law: they are not scandalized by the law where they do not understand it. Rather, they venerate it and affirm that they themselves do not understand it and that something great lies hidden there. Nor is anything human beings may do a stumbling block to those who love God’s law; that is, they are not scandalized by the evil deeds of human beings and fall, even if they see religious people sinning. They themselves do not sin.

166 “I awaited your salvation, O Lord, and I loved your commandments.”

A C The holy fathers of the Old Law awaited Christ’s coming, and they loved his commandments, that is, they loved God and neighbor. The righteous of the New Law also await Christ’s saving second coming, so that they may be crowned with him in glory. Therefore the whole Church, which loves God’s commandments, awaits Jesus the Lord, the salvation of all.

167 “My soul kept your testimonies and loved them exceedingly.”

[Col. 0459C] C “Kept” pertains to enduring martyrdom. A God’s testimonies are kept when they are not denied; this is the duty of martyrs. C “Loved,” however, pertains to charity, which is stronger than every torture, conquers flames, overcomes swords, and transcends all things by heavenly power. He says “exceedingly” because perfect love has no limit but is expressed through every effort of the soul, so that it neither ceases at any time nor grows sluggish through the soul’s torpor.

168 “I have kept your commandments and your testimonies, because all my ways are before you.”

H He keeps the commandments and testimonies who proceeds along God’s ways on a straight course and does nothing in deed, word, or thought that would be considered unworthy in the sight of divine contemplation. “Because all my ways are before you”: C therefore he says that he kept the commandments because the Lord deigned to watch over all his ways, so that he would not attribute his ability to his own strength but to divine power. His ways would have been confused in blind night unless the true light had deigned to look upon them. Therefore error could not prevail over the one who professes that the author of light watches over him.

## Argument of the following eight verses

C B The choir of the saints, as it is near the end of the psalm, so desires to draw near to Christ. Therefore, desiring the advent of the Lord Savior, it asks that he deign, in his mercy, to call back the lost sheep. B He is therefore for us the consummation of all virtues, because whoever is granted the sight of him will have nothing further to seek. His is the sign under which we, the redeemed, sing: “The light of your countenance, O Lord, has been marked upon us.”

H B *Thau*: “sign,” or “consummation.”

169 “Let my supplication draw near in your sight, O Lord; according to your utterance give me understanding.”

C When the choir of the saints asks that its prayer draw near to the Lord’s sight, it shows that the presence of sinners is far from that same God, because nothing comes near him except what has been purified by holiness. It therefore asks to understand according to God’s utterance, lest it be submerged by the vanity and perversity of human wisdom. A Or, “according to the utterance,” that is, the promise; for he promised: “I will give you understanding and instruct you” (Ps. XXXI). H Give me, therefore, such understanding that I ask for nothing except what I ought to ask. C For he is not asking for worldly understanding.

170 “Let my petition enter into your sight; according to your utterance deliver me.”

C The holy petition ascends by degrees. For the one who earlier said, “Let it draw near,” now says, “Let it enter.” First it was to draw near; then it was to be able to enter into God’s sight, so that we may know that everything is fulfilled through his grace and attribute nothing to human power. And the one who earlier said, “According to your utterance give me understanding,” here also says, “Deliver me,” namely, according to his desire, so that he may desire heavenly things.

171 “My lips shall pour forth a hymn when you teach me your statutes.”

[Col. 0460C] C The lips will pour forth a hymn when they have been filled with God’s Spirit and speech is ordered toward heavenly understanding of the divine meaning. “When you teach me”: he promises the devotion of his praise when he has received the Lord’s gifts. H For if my lips are opened by you through a pure conscience, then they will utter a hymn worthy of praise.

172 “My tongue shall proclaim your utterance, because all your commandments are equity.”

C There is nothing else in your utterances, O Lord, but peace, equity, and life. I shall believe this in my heart, speak it with my lips, and proclaim it with my tongue. C For it is exceedingly culpable, abandoning the divine utterances, to turn to the world’s foolish tales and idle words, which not only do no good but also do harm, since the Lord says: [Col. 0460D] “For every idle word people will give an account” (Matt. XII).

173 “Let your hand come to save me, because I have chosen your commandments.”

C When he says, “Let your hand come,” he designates the Lord Savior, through whom all things were made and are governed. He therefore asks the Lord Savior to come. By saying, “I have chosen your commandments,” he testifies that for the love of God he has set aside every danger.

174 “I have desired your salvation, O Lord, and your law is my meditation.”

A C Christ is the Father’s salvation, the one who saved us. The ancient saints desired him, and now the Church desires to see him eternally at the Father’s right hand. [Col. 0461A] For this reason I always meditate on your law, because in it I see the one whom I await.

175 “My soul shall live and praise you, and your judgments shall help me.”

C The Church promises that its soul will live forever, since it knows that it has believed for salvation. “I shall praise you,” it says, with a new song, which the human being renewed for salvation ought to sing. It says that those judgments will help it which he promised to carry out in his servants, namely: “Come, blessed of my Father.” For then it believes that it will be perfectly helped, when the number of the righteous is to be placed at the right hand.

176 “I have gone astray like a sheep that has perished; seek your servant, because I have not forgotten your commandments.”

C This is the voice of the Church and of all the elect, as is the whole of this psalm. For that universal human being who had gone astray in Adam and could not return by himself to God’s folds, because he had lost the gift of wisdom that he possessed, says: “I have gone astray,” as though to say, “I have departed from your way and, blind, entered the trackless solitudes of vices. Like a sheep”—this one sheep is the single congregation of all the faithful. And it is rightly said, “that had perished,” so that you might recognize that it had been restored by God’s mercy. “Seek” is said to Christ the Lord, because human weakness cannot seek you out. The reason for the seeking is also added: “because of your commandments,” and so forth, since the one who is not shown to have forgotten God’s commandments is rightly sought.

## Prayer from Psalm 118

Crown of all blessedness, God, who, as a gracious provider, instructs your faithful to walk in your law, search out your testimonies, and keep your commandments for salvation: grant us to seek your statutes with our whole heart, to understand your utterances, and to proclaim your wonders, so that we who until now have wandered like lost sheep may, restored upon your merciful shoulders, rejoice in paradise. You who live and reign, etc.

## Psalm 119

## Argument of Psalm 119

C B The Songs of Ascents are songs of ascent by which one climbs to things above. The prophet cries to the Lord that he may be delivered from the wicked, and he is grievously afflicted because, lingering too long in this life, he is weighed down by association with the evil.

TT. Song of Ascents.

C New and wondrous titles begin: “Song of Ascents.” When we hear of steps in the psalms, let us not suppose that bodily paces are to be climbed, but understand an ascent of the mind. For “song” was placed first so that we should apply this rather to the soul’s progress. These steps are ascents of humility, the first of which is the abandonment and confession of sins. A For in these songs we are taught nothing other than to ascend in the heart, in good affection, in faith, hope, and charity, and in the desire for eternal life.

[Col. 0462A]

1 “In my tribulation I cried to the Lord, and he heard me.”

C Thus the first step of the virtues begins, in which the prophet, with tearful confession, asks to be delivered from the tribulation of this world. Therefore he says that he was heard because he cried in tribulation. For the Lord does not know how to delay when he perceives someone supplicating him with a contrite heart. What the tribulation is from which he asks to be delivered follows: “O Lord, deliver my soul,” and so forth.

2 “O Lord, deliver my soul from wicked lips, ÷ and . . . from a deceitful tongue.”

C The prophet asks to be delivered from wicked persuasions, through which the human race fell. For when the serpent came to Eve, it said through wicked lips: “Why do you not eat from this tree?” (Gen. III). And when she had replied that God had forbidden it, it said through a deceitful tongue: “Eat, and you will be like gods” (ibid.).

3 “What shall be given to you, or what shall be added to you, against a deceitful tongue?”

C The prophet returns to his question. He asks what remedy he believed should be provided against so monstrous a crime; but lest Christ’s help be delayed, the remedy sought follows in the next verse:

4 “Sharp arrows of the mighty one, with desolating coals.”

C Behold, he finds the remedy that destroys wicked lips: “sharp arrows of the mighty one” are the words of the divine law, by which the hearts of adversaries are pierced as though by darts. “Desolating coals” means the worthy compunction that makes solitude, devastation, and desolation of sins in the mind and purges the stain of sins. A Or, these coals are the exemplary life of the saints.

5 “Alas for me, because my sojourning has been prolonged; I have dwelt with the inhabitants of Cedar. My soul has been a sojourner for long.”

C “Alas!” is the speech of one grieving that he is wearied by the length of this world. There is no doubt that the saints had this complaint. “Sojourning” signifies exile; for a sojourner is one who cultivates another’s land for a time and is far separated from his own country. This is rightly said of those whose citizenship is in heaven (Phil. III). *Cedar*, a Hebrew word, is interpreted “darkness,” and signifies the present world in which evil reigns, and its lovers, entangled in dark deeds. “My soul has been a sojourner for long,” because the mind of the saints suffers sojourning here, where it knows that it dwells with no joy.

6 “With those who hate peace I was peaceable; when I spoke to them, they attacked me ÷ without cause . . .”

C For he hates peace who does not love Christ. “I was peaceable with the enemies of peace,” fulfilling that evangelical saying: “Love your enemies” (Matt. V). He also spoke peaceably, not reviling; but he was attacked without cause when he suffered deceitful disputes from inflamed wickedness.

## Prayer from Psalm 119

[Col. 0463A]

Best mitigator of our tribulations, God, deliver the souls of the faithful from the lips of detractors, so that, fortified by your spiritual aids, they may not be overwhelmed by any attacks. Through our Lord Jesus, etc.

## Psalm 120

## Argument of Psalm 120

C The prophet, raising his eyes to the merits of the saints, asks to be helped by their prayers, lest his mind succumb to hostile attack, confidently promising himself what he knows he rightly asks.

TT. Song of Ascents.

“Song” pertains to knowledge, but “of ascents” to action. For he walks well who both sings [Col. 0463B] with knowledge and advances by the progress of ascents, that is, by ecclesiastical activity.

1 “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from whence help shall come to me.”

C This righteous man came to the second step, in which, after humble confession of sins and tribulation, he dared to lift his eyes to the mountains. The prophet says that he lifted his eyes, that is, he shows that he had advanced to some contemplation. Spiritually, he is believed to have lifted up the eyes of his heart either to holy men, to the divine books, or to the exalted angels, who are truly mountains by their greatness and firmness, from whom help is fittingly expected. But lest perhaps we should place our hope only in the saints, the following verse shows whence help can truly come to us.

2 “My help is from the Lord, who made heaven and earth.”

C “My help is from the Lord”; and lest you should suppose another Lord, since this is an equivocal name, he says: “who made heaven and earth,” signifying the Word through whom all things were made. True help comes from him, from whom the saints have power to help us.

3 “May he not give your foot over to slipping, nor may he who keeps you slumber.”

C The foot is the lowest part of the body. By moving us from place to place at the command of the mind, it signifies our thoughts, through which we approach good and evil courses. The prophet prays that these feet may not be turned by the slipperiness of sins, lest, while the body stands, the heart suffer a fall. God is said to slumber when we fail in faith in him; in the one whose faith does not sleep, Christ keeps watch. Therefore, when we do not look to God in faith, his protection is withdrawn from us.

4 “Behold, he who keeps Israel will neither slumber nor sleep.”

C If you are Israel—that is, a man seeing God—God does not slumber for you. Therefore God is not said to slumber over those who see God with a pure mind, because the kind of sight of him that is returned in us is truly such as the gaze of our mind toward him has been. For Israel is interpreted “a man seeing God.” Therefore the one who rightly believes in him will be a most true Israel, for whom God, keeping him, will not slumber.

[Col. 0464A]

5 “The Lord keeps you; the Lord is your protection at your right hand.”

H The Lord keeps you, he himself who made heaven and earth, because the gods that did not make it perish from it. “The Lord is your protection at your right hand”: he protects you lest the hostile party, that is, the devil, hinder your right-hand work, that is, your good work. Thus “the right hand” here means spiritual goods, which are hindered by “the left,” that is, temporal things, unless God keeps them.

6 “By day the sun will not burn you, nor the moon by night.”

[Col. 0464B] H The righteous person cannot be burned—that is, lifted up—in prosperity, nor cast down by adversity in this present life. Observe also that what is signified by sun and moon is signified by day and night. A C Or, “to be burned” means “to be scandalized.” Therefore the person who is scandalized neither by his neighbor’s good deeds nor by bad ones is burned neither by day nor by night.

7 “The Lord keeps you from every evil; may the Lord keep your soul ÷ . . .”

H The Lord keeps you from all the enemy’s snares. He keeps the soul lest the party of the adverse power rule it. By “evil,” therefore, understand not the temporary discomforts of the body, which the lovers of this age judge to be most grievous, but that evil which removes divine grace and destroys the soul. For God permits even the holiest men to be tortured by immense sufferings; but he keeps the soul. Therefore he adds: “may he keep,” and so forth.

8 “May the Lord keep your going in and your going out, from this time forth and forever.”

C “May the Lord keep your going in” is spoken of martyrs, whose entrance must be guarded by the Lord lest they yield either to the violence of tortures or to seductions by flattery. “And your going out”: there is the whole perfection, when true confession remains in them to the end of life. “From this time forth,” and so forth, because whoever perseveres will possess eternal benefits. H That is, one is guarded not only in this life but also afterwards from eternal punishment.

## Prayer from Psalm 120

[Col. 0464D] Protect your people, O Lord God, protector of Israel, neither slumbering nor sleeping; and, lest we be burned by day, defend us from the scandals of this world. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, etc.

## Psalm 121

## Argument of Psalm 121

C B The prophet rejoices that he has been reminded that he will come to the heavenly Jerusalem, where the saints already stand in secure prosperity; and he speaks to the citizens of Jerusalem, wishing them an abundance of peace.

TT. Song of Ascents.

1 “I rejoiced in the things that were said to me: We shall go into the house of the Lord.”

H He comes to the third step, in which he no longer merely [Col. 0465A] lifts his eyes to the mountains but, having conceived hope, rejoices that he will go to the mountains, to the society of the saints, and to the heavenly Jerusalem. C It must be asked who said these things to the prophet, by which he testifies that he rejoiced: namely, the Holy Spirit, who spoke to his heart with a silent voice, not by speech but by divine breathing. H Or, “were said” in the prophets, the Law, and the apostles. C This house receives only the righteous and contains angels. It is the heavenly Jerusalem, in which the maker of all creatures is beheld.

2 “Our feet were standing in your courts, + Jerusalem.”

C The prophet says that he stands in that heavenly house which he desires with utmost zeal to reach. For one stands there where one remains always with firm will. A court is the entrance of a house, in which those dwelling there cannot remain. But here courts are used for the interior rooms, and the part for the whole.

3 “Jerusalem, which is built as a city, whose participation is in the same thing.”

C Certainly the heavenly Jerusalem is built daily from living stones—that is, martyrs, confessors, and those who serve the Lord with a sincere mind. He adds “as a city” in order to show that it possesses the likeness of a city. For although every city is named from its citizens, that is more truly called a city which contains citizens of one mind. “Whose participation,” and so forth: H C that is, the participation of the city itself is in the Lord Savior, who is properly “the same thing,” signifying eternity, which never ceases to be what it is, but is always, in one and the same manner, unfailing power. Hence he also said above: “But you are the selfsame” (Ps. CI), and said to Moses: “I am who I am” (Exod. III). Therefore it belongs to the Creator alone to be “the same thing.”

4 “For there the tribes went up, the tribes of the Lord, the testimony of Israel, to give thanks to the name of the Lord.”

C By saying “there,” he signifies the city of Jerusalem, to which the blessed continually ascend—those who advance through unceasing practice. “Tribes,” that is, the saints who have truly confessed that Christ is God. But, in order to distinguish these tribes from unbelievers, he added “the tribes of the Lord.” They would not be called his unless they had believed with a pure mind. For the other tribes, namely those who do not believe, are plainly of the devil. He briefly indicates what sort these tribes of the Lord are by saying “the testimony of Israel”—that is, either the testimony of Israel itself, or testimony to Israel, or what is Israel itself: those who bear witness to holiness, that is, who bear witness to themselves that they are Israel, meaning those who see God. Indeed, the saints testify to this by their deeds. And he says this not in order to praise themselves, but “to confess,” that is, to praise the Lord. For it is the true testimony of Israel to sing the praises of the Lord with the deepest devotion. That testimony, however, will be greater after this life than it is here.

5 Because there the seats for judgment were set: Seats ÷ above .. the house of David.

C “There they sat,” namely those who ascended and will judge with the Lord. Honorable is that session, and wondrous that dignity: by God’s grace, human beings become judges, although they had been made guilty by their sins. The holy men are rightly the seats of God, because, sitting within them, he illumines them with the grace of his majesty. “Seats above the house of David,” that is, above the household of Christ. He has used the past tense for the future, because he is speaking of the final judgment.

6 Ask .. what: for the peace ÷ are .. Jerusalem: And abundance for those who love you.

H A C Here “ask” does not mean “entreat,” but “inquire.” Thus, “ask,” that is, “inquire what things pertain to the peace of this city”; H and follow after it, so that through love of peace you may obtain the fruit of eternal blessedness. Abundance belongs to him of heavenly goods who, having abandoned passing things, loves God above all; C or, it is evident that all good things abound in the heavenly Jerusalem.

7 Let there be peace in your strength: ÷ And .. abundance in your towers.

C “Peace” is so called from sparing or feeding, for such peace is bestowed there through Christ’s compassion that no wars shake it and no sedition disturbs it. “Towers,” however, here signifies the martyrs, who, by the resistance of their bodies, defend the city of God through devout confession and, like lofty buildings, are known to withstand the enemies of the faith.

8 For the sake of my brothers and my neighbors: I spoke peace concerning you.

C The Prophet therefore urges each person to teach not for the sake of his own praises or advantages, but to labor for the sake of his brothers and neighbors. By “peace” understand the peace of the Church, which the saints teach must be preserved in the bond of charity. But when he says “concerning you,” he indicates that he is speaking to Jerusalem, in which there is an assembly of the saints—that is, the union of the blessed and perfect peace.

9 For the sake of the house of the Lord our God: I sought good things for you.

C The house of the Lord is Jerusalem, in which God dwells, to whom whatever service of love is offered is rightly referred. A Or, “for the sake of this house,” namely, the Church, so that those who are still pilgrims might advance there; I sought and labored by teaching.

PRAYER FROM PSALM 121

Almighty God, grant in your mercy an abundance of peace to those who walk in the courts of your house, so that, while we confess you with the full eagerness of our hearts, we may receive your good things in the heavenly places. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, etc.

PSALM 122

ARGUMENT OF PSALM 122

C The Prophet, who previously raised his eyes toward the saints, now lifts the lights of his heart to the Lord himself, asking that the Lord grant him his help, because through diabolical instigation he was suffering many adversities from those who assailed him.

TT. A Song of Ascents.

1 To you I have lifted my eyes: You who dwell in the heavens.

C In the first psalm he had said, “I cried to the Lord when I was in distress,” and in the second song he lifted his eyes toward the mountains and also rejoiced, because he had been promised that he would enter the house of God. Now he advances to something greater, so that he even dares to lift his eyes to the Lord himself. C For the saints lift their eyes to the Lord, whatever tribulation they may be enduring, and look toward him, from whom they trust that they can truly be saved. H For they lift their eyes there, where they strive and desire to arrive.

2 Behold, as the eyes of servants: Are upon the hands of their masters.

C Servants attend to the hands of their masters, whether they hope to be nourished by them or whether, for their offenses, they are ordered to be beaten until they hear, “Spare them.” We too ought to do this, lifting our eyes always toward God when we suffer some need or when we are beaten for certain excesses. A For “hand” signifies power.

3 As the eyes of the maidservant are upon the hand of her mistress: So are our eyes toward the Lord our God, until he has mercy upon us.

C For a maidservant attends to the hand of her mistress just as servants attend to the hands of their masters; and thus, when it is said, “our eyes,” it includes both sexes. “Until” here always signifies duration, although it may appear to be spoken temporally. So also it is said in the Gospel, “He did not know her until she had borne her firstborn son” (Matthew 1), although it is clear that he never knew her as a man knows a woman; there likewise the word is used for all time. For after the Lord has had mercy, will our eyes not be directed toward him?

4 Have mercy on us, Lord, have mercy on us: For we have been filled exceedingly with contempt.

C The voice of the martyrs, by its doubled petition, laments that mercy must be shown them, because their bodies labored in sufferings while their souls labored under reproaches. “Filled exceedingly” signifies the abundance of their sufferings, which nevertheless they testify that they endured eagerly and willingly. The saints are despised by the wicked; they are torn by blows, burned by flames, and plunged into the deepest waters.

5 ÷ For .. exceedingly filled is our soul: With reproach from the prosperous. And with contempt from the proud.

C All who desire to live devoutly according to Christ suffer reproach from those who take pride in earthly prosperity and worldly abundance (2 Timothy 3). C For the rich always despise the poor, and the proud despise the humble. He did not say “from the rich,” but “from the prosperous,” so that you should understand those who abound in wickedness.

PRAYER FROM PSALM 122

God, dweller in the heavens, we lift our eyes to you, asking that, when the reproaches of the proud have been put to shame, you may mercifully grant us your customary compassion. Through our Lord Jesus, etc.

PSALM 123

ARGUMENT OF PSALM 123

C The holy confessors acknowledge that they have been delivered by God’s mercy from so many afflictions of the world. They give thanks that they were not deceived by their persecutors, but were rescued when their plots were shattered.

TT. A Song of Ascents.

C These ascents have been established on that journey where the King of the homeland himself is recognized as having provided the way. If, with his aid, we walk faithfully and humbly along it, we reach his holy tribunals.

1 If ÷ for .. the Lord was with us, let Israel now say: If ÷ for .. the Lord was with us.

C This is the voice of the holy martyrs, already rejoicing in the Lord in blessedness and saying that they could in no way have overcome the dangers inflicted upon them except because the Lord was with them. “Let Israel now say”: in a certain sense the holy martyrs command the other devout and righteous people to give thanks with them for the fact by which they themselves had been saved. For this is the power of charity and unity: if something favorable happens to one person, all should rejoice as though it had happened to them all; and, conversely, if something adverse is inflicted, all should grieve as though it had happened to everyone. A C Thus they ascend the fifth step who, in steadfast hope, rejoice with the holy martyrs already crowned in heaven that they are unconquered by tribulations and will be crowned.

2 When men rose up against us: Perhaps they would have swallowed us alive.

C When men—namely, wicked men—rose up against us, they would have swallowed us alive. It is not customary for human beings to swallow the living; yet we are swallowed alive when we are plunged into heretical perversities or into the pit of sins. [Col. 0468C] Those who are still in the faith of Christ are called living; those who have departed from the faith are called dead. This could have happened to holy men unless heavenly power had delivered them.

3 When their anger raged against us: Perhaps water would have swallowed us.

C He said “when it raged,” because they had no just causes; for anger and envy lack judgment when, with impetuous minds, they pursue their desires. “Water” here signifies wicked peoples or pagans. They wished to swallow the servants of God when they tried to lead them into the worship of their gods, but divine power delivered them. The ancients called water that from which all things come, believing that everything was generated from it.

4 Our soul has passed through the torrent: Perhaps our soul would have passed through intolerable water.

H The torrent is the death of the flesh, through which the holy martyrs pass and are brought into refreshment. A C Or, it is the suffering, tribulation, and persecution of the wicked. Water is called intolerable when our weakness is considered without God’s help. For no one can endure the whirlpools of sins and the storms of crimes unless he has fled to Christ’s protection. Everything becomes bearable when God dwells within us: then neither error steals upon us, nor lust drags us away, nor empty pride prevails, nor the suggestion of the malignant enemy.

Blessed be the Lord: Who did not give us as prey to their teeth.

H “Teeth” here signifies the multitude of vices, from which God’s grace rescues us so that we may not be captured.

6 Our soul has been rescued like a sparrow: From the snare of the hunters. The snare has been broken: And we have been set free.

H Snares are laid for us in our desires and through various deceptions of diabolical cunning. But once the devil, who is our snare, has been crushed beneath our feet, we fly away from him like a wise and shrewd sparrow.

8 Our help is in the name of the Lord: Who made heaven and earth.

H “Our help is in the name of the Lord”—that is, in the name which is above every name. By the help of this name, the snares of death are overcome, if we remain fixed in him.

C Thus they are rightly said to be on the fifth step, since, with the Lord’s help, they were able to overcome the bodily senses amid suffering.

PRAYER FROM PSALM 123

Close, Lord, the gaping mouths of the wicked who strive to devour us with the savage teeth of their slanders, so that we who distrust our own strength may be fortified by the help of your name. Through our Lord Jesus, etc.

PSALM 124

ARGUMENT OF PSALM 124

C The Prophet cries out that we must trust in the Lord, lest we labor in vain, asking that prosperity come to the upright and vengeance to the wicked.

TT. A Song of Ascents.

C Although this saving staircase seems to have been constructed as a suitable remedy, we nevertheless stand without any firmness unless we are held there by the Lord’s governance. This ascent, however, takes place in the mind, not in the body. For, sitting in one place and shut away in the confines of a little cell, we ascend these steps more effectively than if we were to fly through people’s mouths.

1 Those who trust in the Lord are like Mount Zion: He who dwells in Jerusalem will not be shaken forever.

A He ascends the sixth step who trusts wholly in the Lord and does not waver in faith in God because of the prosperity of wicked people, but continues his journey upward with steadfast steps. H “Zion,” that is, “watchtower,” signifies the holy congregation of the elect, placed at the height of contemplation. “The mountain,” according to Daniel, is the Lord Christ (Daniel 2). Whoever places all his hope in him will not be shaken forever, because he is made conformable to the body of Christ’s glory. C Here too we understand Jerusalem to be the heavenly homeland—which is the vision of peace—from which no one can be shaken who has deserved to be established there.

2 Mountains surround it, and the Lord surrounds his people: From this time and forever.

C Here “mountains” designate holy men who inhabit that heavenly Jerusalem. “And the Lord surrounds”: he encompasses with the assistance of eternal protection those whom he knows to be faithful to him. “From this time” signifies this present age. “Forever” refers to that age in which he will already appear to the saints in the majesty of his light. But why this protection is provided is explained next.

3 For the Lord will not leave the rod of sinners over the lot of the righteous: So that the righteous may not extend their hands toward iniquity.

C “Rod” signifies the power of good and evil, but here it is clearly understood in a bad sense. “The lot of the righteous” is the Christian religion, over which Christ does not permit the rod of sinners—that is, the wicked power of tyrants—to rise up for too long, lest they be able to crush the Church of God through a very lengthy persecution. “So that the righteous may not extend their hands toward iniquity,” H that is, so that they may not think: “What profit is there in my being righteous if the wicked are always persecuting me?” This means that they should endure the wicked and not do evil. For God does not leave such a rod over the righteous for long, although they may appear weak for a long time.

4 Do good, Lord: To those who are good and upright in heart.

C The Prophet therefore desires that good be done to those who do not know how to separate themselves from the Lord through a perverse will. The upright in heart are those who follow God and do not strive to go ahead of him. H They are also those who conform their own will to the divine will and do not wish to bend the divine will to their own.

5 But those who turn aside toward entanglements, the Lord will lead away with those who work iniquity: Peace upon Israel.

C The works of iniquity have been beautifully defined as entanglements that bind us with the chains of perversity, so that we cannot be free when we are constrained by such great snares. “Those who turn aside,” that is, those who do not pursue God’s commands. For those who strive to turn aside from the Lord’s commands and those who wish to practice wickedness perish under the same sentence. “Peace upon Israel”: this peace is the Savior, who always defends those who see him. H For, removing the dividing wall of hostility between Jews and Gentiles, he made both one in those who believe—what had previously been divided (Ephesians 2).

PRAYER FROM PSALM 124

Repel, Lord, the wickedness of those who rise up against the lot of the righteous, so that those who trust in you with their whole heart may not be shaken by any showers of temptation. Through the Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, etc.

PSALM 125

ARGUMENT OF PSALM 125

C The holiest men, delivered through the Lord’s mercy, give thanks because they have been received from the most savage bondage of sins into such great grace that they were found praiseworthy among the nations. They pray that their captivity may be turned into joy.

TT. A Song of Ascents.

1 When the Lord turned the captivity of Zion: We became like those who are comforted.

H The captivity of Zion existed when the Church was oppressed by the worship of idols. It was turned into liberty when, at the Lord’s coming, the bonds of hell were broken. C Observe, however, that he does not say, “We became comforted,” but “We became like those who are comforted,” because, once that captivity has been destroyed, it does not make us entirely secure while we remain in this mortal body. But in the blessed Jerusalem there will be certain and perfect consolation.

2 Then our mouth was filled with joy: And our tongue with exultation.

C Then the mouth—that is, the secret recess of the heart—was filled with joy at the coming of the Lord and Savior, when he changed our captivity into joy. “And our tongue with exultation,” since such things had been granted to it by the Lord’s gift.

3 Then they will say among the nations: The Lord has magnified what he has done with them.

C He does not say “the nations,” but “among the nations,” because at the Lord’s coming the nations did not believe universally. Rather, there were among the nations people who had become faithful from the nations, and with them the still unbelieving Gentiles saw the Lord perform great deeds.

4 The Lord has magnified what he has done with us: We have become joyful.

C And lest you think that the Gentiles, saying of the faithful, “The Lord has magnified what he has done,” spoke falsely, the faithful confirm their statement by saying: “The Lord has magnified”—that is, he determined to show us great to the nations through the gift of spiritual powers. “We have become joyful,” certainly because of such great grace.

5 Turn, Lord, our captivity: Like a torrent in the south wind.

C The faithful peoples ask that their sins again be forgiven. “Like a torrent.” H A For when the south wind—which is a warm wind—blows, the ice melts and makes the torrent run full of water. So, when the Holy Spirit blows, our sins are dissolved into tears after forgiveness has been received through lamentation. A C For we call winter streams “torrents,” and our sins freeze our hearts by making them cold; these sins are dissolved into tears by the warmth of the Holy Spirit. But, so that the fullness of the meaning may remain clear, “turn” must be pronounced as “convert,” since *convertere* is an ancient deponent verb: “turn our captivity, as a torrent in the south wind is turned into liquid.”

6 Those who sow in tears: Will reap in exultation.

C Spiritual sowing is always carried out in tears. For either the saints lament past sins, or they are tormented by fear of the future, or they are harassed by persecutions. But those who sow such seed will reap the joys of the future promise. Conversely, sinners sow in joy and reap in tears.

7 Going forth, they went and wept: Casting their seed.

C “Going forth”: the saints go forth by doing good. “They wept” when they looked upon the poor, constricted by cold and cruelly worn down by want, casting their seed. He says “their own,” so that you may understand that almsgiving should be made from one’s own labors, not from plunder. “Casting” means, understand, sending ahead into heaven, where our deeds arrive before we do. For these are our treasure, to be stored up in heaven. H Or, going forth by preaching the word of God, they wept over the hardness of the hearts of unbelievers.

8 But coming, they will come with exultation: Carrying their sheaves.

C “Coming”: those come with exultation to whom divine mercy is already granted, who here acted in the manner commanded by God’s injunctions and produced sheaves—that is, actions bearing the richest fruit. And happy is the one weighed down by wheat-filled burdens, lest the lightness of the stalks deceive the reaper’s hopes and he recognize the emptiness of his labor only when he can no longer act.

PRAYER FROM PSALM 125

Comfort your people, Lord, and free us from the captivity of the worst vices, so that what we sow here in tears, by your rewarding, we may reap with joy. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, etc.

PSALM 126

ARGUMENT OF PSALM 126

C The Prophet, foreseeing the grace of the New Testament, teaches that no one should attribute any good to his own powers, but to the Lord, the giver. He also speaks of the Lord himself and of the apostles, or of whoever fulfills his commands.

TT. A Song of Ascents of Solomon.

Solomon is interpreted as “the peaceful one” and signifies the Lord, of whom the Apostle says: “He himself is our peace” (Ephesians 2). The house of this Solomon is the Church of Christ, which is also his city.

1 Unless the Lord builds the house: Those who build it labor in vain.

C Those build the house who strive to construct the truth of the faith within each Christian. For they are the house of which the Apostle says, “You are the temple of God” (1 Corinthians 3). But if they think they can build by their own powers, they appear to labor in vain unless God’s grace grants the effect of true belief.

2 Unless the Lord guards the city: The one who guards it keeps watch in vain.

C The city of the Lord is understood to be the heavenly Jerusalem, part of which is still on pilgrimage on earth. In it the bishops strive to keep watch over their flock, guarding it with vigilant care. The same is said to them as to the builders: they must not believe that merely human watchfulness can prevail, since only divinity can ward off the dangers of invasion.

3 It is vain for you to rise before the light: ÷ Rise .. after you have sat down. You who eat the bread of sorrow.

C He is still addressing those teachers, so that the people may be corrected more effectively when they see that even their teachers have been warned. Those seek to rise before the light who, neglecting Christ’s humility, wish to be exalted before they have been humbled. “Rise,” that is, first endure humiliation, and afterward seek the rewards of joyful ascent. “The bread of sorrow”: perfected Christians eat it when they chastise themselves with faithful tears. Concerning them another psalm says, “My tears have been my bread” (Psalm 41). For sorrow is bread to those who refresh themselves through affliction and console themselves through worldly sadness. And he next indicates when those who were ordered first to sit should rise. For they will rise when he gives sleep to his beloved, etc.—that is, when they have died, not before death.

4 When he gives sleep to his beloved, behold, the inheritance of the Lord: The reward, the fruit of the womb.

C God’s beloved are those who seek him with extraordinary love. H When, having received the sleep of rest, they depart from this age, then they become the Lord’s inheritance, because they are no longer subject to temptations. “The reward, the fruit of the womb”: C that is, the offspring of the virginal womb. Its fruit is every human being who will rejoice eternally with God. This reward is called an inheritance—not an inheritance of the deity, but a reward of the humanity—as it is said in the second psalm: “Ask of me,” etc.

5 Like arrows in the hand of the mighty: So are the children of those who have been shaken out.

C “Arrows”: the holy apostles or the other preachers. “In the hand of the mighty,” that is, sent forth under Christ’s power for preaching. For just as a weapon or arrow sent by a mighty person comes most directly and quickly to its appointed place, so the apostles, sent into all the earth, quickly reached the places to which they were sent and fulfilled the commands given to them. “So are the children of those who have been shaken out”: that is, succeeding in the place of the prophets, and by interpreting and explaining their prophecy, examining it. To examine is to make something covered public. The prophets are therefore called “those who shake out,” because they disclosed heavenly secrets to the world. Their children are the apostles, because those who believed their words were, in a certain sense, generated through faith.

6 Blessed is the man who has fulfilled his desire through them: He will not be put to shame when he speaks with his enemies at the gate.

C He calls these apostles blessed when their labor has reached glorious fulfillment. H Or, the blessed man is the people who have fulfilled their desire through these apostles—that is, having been converted through their preaching, they desire the eternal things that were preached and have already fulfilled this desire through their deeds. Or, he fulfills his desire through them who desires what they themselves desired—namely, to be in eternal blessedness—and desires it himself. C The gate of the city Jerusalem is Christ. For the one who preaches rightly about the Lord speaks at that gate. From such a place he first causes sinners and unbelievers to go out, and makes the devout enter. Faithful preachers will not be put to shame at the gate, because it is opened to them; but it is closed to the wicked, and therefore they will be put to shame.

PRAYER FROM PSALM 126

God, builder of spiritual houses, we beseech you to guard us; fulfill our desire in you, and, according to our merits, join us to your elect. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, etc.

PSALM 127

ARGUMENT OF PSALM 127

C The Prophet enumerates the blessings of those who fear God and blesses them so that they may obtain eternal joys.

TT. A Song of Ascents.

C How magnificent the ninth step is, the number itself declares: extended through triple multiplication, it displays to us the holy summit of the Trinity.

1 Blessed are all who fear the Lord: Who walk in his ways.

C First he distinguished fear of the Lord from terror of this age. By saying “blessed are all who fear the Lord,” he showed that those are not blessed who anxiously fear the dangers of this world in the loss of temporal things. By saying “ways” in the plural, he signifies the apostles and prophets, through whom one comes to the one Way, that is, Christ. Therefore only those fear the Lord with that holy fear of God who walk in his ways—that is, in his commandments and in the things that the prophets, apostles, and evangelists preached. In the following three verses he enumerates the benefits of fear of the Lord.

2 + For .. you will eat the labors of your hands: You are blessed, and it will be well with you.

C “The labors of your hands” are the recompense of good works. And lest you think this nourishment is bodily, he added, “You are blessed.” No one is made blessed by bodily food, except one who is nourished by a spiritual gift. “It will be well with you” when you receive what eye has not seen, ear has not heard, and what has not entered the human heart—what God has carefully prepared (Isaiah 64).

3 Your wife is like a flourishing vine: Within the sides of your house.

C “Wife” is so called as if from “sister”; therefore here we should understand the wife as wisdom. The vine is the mother of grapes, pouring forth sweet wines that refresh our hearts. So wisdom, bearing joyful fruits, makes us glad with sweet delight. “The sides” are the two Testaments; “the house” is one’s own thought. For the mind is fixed in its thought as in a dwelling. Understand the two sides of this thought as the Law and the Gospel, in which the holy mind is made firm and solid, as though established upon the two sides of a house.

4 Your sons are like young olive trees: Around your table.

“Your sons”: H that is, good actions standing around Scripture and heavenly teaching, with the richness of peace and the shelter of virtue. C Or, “sons” signifies both sexes, spiritually begotten by the heavenly word; and “the table” is the Lord’s altar, where they are nourished with heavenly bread.

5 Behold, thus will the man be blessed: Who fears the Lord.

C When he says “behold, thus,” he signifies that he will be blessed as explained above; for the one who fears his creator deserves to be blessed in this way.

6 May the Lord bless you from Zion: And may you see the good things of Jerusalem all the days of your life.

C He says, “May the Lord bless you from Zion”—that is, Christ, who deigned to appear to human beings on this mountain. Because of the meaning of his name, he is always likened to an excellent shepherd. For Zion is interpreted as “watchtower,” while Jerusalem is understood as “vision of peace.” He therefore wishes him to see all the good things in Jerusalem. But lest you believe that these good things are seen temporally in the heavenly Jerusalem, he added, “all the days of your life”—that is, of eternal life.

7 And may you see the children of your children: Peace upon Israel.

C “The children of your children” signifies grandchildren. This can certainly happen to blessed men who beget many peoples through holy preaching. Peace is the Lord and Savior, who dwells in that blessed Jerusalem, makes all things good and blessed, and embraces whatever he encompasses by the power of his majesty. May you see that peace, and not merely the children of your children.

PRAYER FROM PSALM 127

Grant perpetual blessedness, Lord, to those who fear your name, so that our conduct and our life may be such as to carry a lofty merit from good fruits to the stars. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, etc.

PSALM 128

ARGUMENT OF PSALM 128

C B. The Prophet urges the Church to declare how many struggles it has endured from its enemies, so that none of the faithful may despair because of his own tribulations. He foretells to those same enemies what he knew would befall them at the future judgment.

TT. A Song of Ascents.

C Here the Prophet teaches us to endure the troubles of the world patiently, when he proves that the Church has often suffered.

1 They have often attacked me from my youth: Let Israel now say.

C The Prophet admonishes Israel, that is, the Church, to declare its battles. “Often” signifies the frequency of its sufferings. “From my youth” signifies the time when righteous Abel was killed by his perverse brother (Genesis 4), and the many others thereafter; the Church was also attacked in Christ’s own Passion. “Let Israel now say”—that is, in this age, when it is the time for repentance—so that the remaining faithful may be instructed to bear persecutions patiently here, since in the future life the saint is not attacked. “Let Israel now say” is also to be supplied through the following three verses.

2 They have often attacked me from my youth: Yet they have not prevailed against me.

C The Church rightly says that it was attacked from its youth, so that you may understand that the Church’s persecution by the wicked has never ended. It has been attacked so often, yet it grows through persecutions and becomes great through its own crushing. For if here it loses holy men, it acquires them for the future homeland. It cannot therefore be brought to an end, since it increases through its losses. Hence it says that those whom it recalled above as having attacked it nevertheless could not prevail against it, because it never consented to them in evil.

3 Sinners have built upon my back: They have prolonged their iniquity.

C The Church testifies that sinners have built upon its back: they hasten to devise deceit and carry out hidden persuasions, as though against the back of the Church, where they cannot be seen. They secretly strive to turn some people away from the holy faith, so that they may deceive at least a few, although they could not overthrow the whole Church. It also says that the very plots which the enemies continually inflicted upon the faithful have been prolonged. For this iniquity has been prolonged from Abel to the present and will be prolonged to the end of the age.

4 The Lord is righteous; he will cut off the necks of sinners: Let all who hate Zion be put to shame and turned backward.

C “Necks” stands for pride, which the Lord cuts down in those who attack in this way, when he permits them to return through humility and satisfaction to mercy. “Let them be put to shame” at the final judgment—those who now refuse to be put to shame through repentance. “And let them be turned back” to eternal punishment. For they themselves—the obstinate—are those who hate Zion, that is, the Church.

5 Let them become like the grass of the roofs: Which withers before it is uprooted.

C Grass growing on old roofs withers and perishes before the time of harvesting, because it has flourished without any firm root. Thus sinners are compared to that transient grass, since they too often perish here before they are taken away from this light. For they are born on the peaks of pride, where they stand without any solidity. H Nor do they produce any grain of goodness.

6 From it the reaper will not fill his hand: Nor the one who gathers sheaves his lap.

C The reapers are the angels, who on the final day of judgment store the grain of the elect in the granary of the heavenly homeland. But from these people—that is, the proud—they do not fill their hand, because they separate them as rejected from the fellowship of the saints. For it was said above of the righteous, “They will come with exultation, carrying their sheaves”; here it is said of the unrighteous that they bring neither a hand full of fruits. The hand pertains to action; the lap to the conscience. For in the deeds of the wicked, nothing fruitful can be found in either.

7 And those who passed by did not say, “The blessing of the Lord be upon you”: “We bless you in the name of the Lord.”

C Those who pass by are the saints of God, who pass beyond this world because they regard it as nothing and pass over with their whole love to those heavenly things. From them no blessing is bestowed upon criminals who labor in vain. But lest this blessing be thought to be applied by human powers, he adds, “We bless you,” etc. For that is the firm and true blessing which is carried out with the Lord’s name in mind, from whom comes everything that is beneficial.

PRAYER FROM PSALM 128

Defend your Church, Lord, from the wickedness of all who attack it, by the right hand of your power, so that, when its enemies have been turned backward, it may be filled with the sacred blessings bestowed by you. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, etc.

PSALM 129

ARGUMENT OF PSALM 129

C The Prophet cries out to the Lord to be freed from the depths of sins, seeking the goodwill of the good Judge concerning the calamities he has described.

TT. A Song of Ascents.

1 From the depths I cried to you, Lord: Lord, hear my voice.

C “Depth” is as though from *porro fundum*, “the bottom far below,” whose lowest parts are completely submerged. From this depth Peter poured forth glorious tears; the tax collector beat his breast (Luke 18); Jonah cried out silently (Jonah 2). “Lord, hear”: when he prayed from the depth, he quickly reached the gifts of the Redeemer on high. That depth, therefore, is the profound humility of repentance.

2 Let your ears be attentive: To the voice of my supplication.

H Here the Prophet does not ask for a bodily ear, since he knows that God is incorporeal; rather, he requests the power by which God deigns to hear his own.

3 If you observe iniquities, Lord: Lord, who will endure it?

C By “iniquity” he wishes every sin to be understood, whatever may be committed through some perversity. For what is not just is iniquitous. Seeing, therefore, that there is no one who does not either go astray in his thoughts, sin through idle speech, or become occupied with a useless action, the Prophet says that the human race is not sufficient for God’s justice unless mercy comes to its aid. No one could endure God’s justice alone.

4 For with you there is forgiveness: And because of your law I have endured you, Lord.

C Terrified, therefore, by God’s justice, he flees to mercy as his advocate. For it is not found in our deeds that we deserve to be acquitted; rather, it belongs to his forgiveness that he deigns to free the guilty person who confesses. This is the law—that is, the evangelical command—through which he rightly believed that he would be saved. “I have endured” indicates charity, which sustains everything and makes Christians perfect. Or, “your law”: the law is mercy toward penitents.

5 My soul has endured in his word: My soul has hoped in the Lord.

C “My soul waited for his word”: because he believed that the Lord’s Incarnation was to come. For Christ is this Word, which he awaited in the meantime, [Col. 0478A] patiently. And to show that he did not mean some passing word, he explains it next by calling that Word “the Lord”: “My soul hoped in the Lord,” namely, in him who is the Word of the Father. For my soul hoped that, in future times, he would deign to be born of the Virgin Mary, in order to remove the destruction of the human race.

6 “From the morning watch until night: Let Israel hope in the Lord.”

C “From the morning watch”: the morning watch is the resurrection of Christ, who rose at daybreak while the soldiers were guarding the tomb. From the time Christ rose from the dead, the hope of the Church was confirmed in the Lord. “Until night,” that is, until the end of the world.

7 [Col. 0478B] “For with the Lord there is mercy: And abundant redemption with him.”

C The reason is given—an extraordinary one—why Israel ought to hope in the Lord: because in his hand there is mercy, which can make the unjust just, the weak immortal, and the fleshly like the angels. He also added “abundant redemption”: H because he redeemed us not with gold or silver, but with precious blood. H Or he says “abundant” so that no one might despair of forgiveness, thinking that the price of redemption could not extend as far as himself.

8 “And he himself will redeem Israel: From all his iniquities.”

C Israel, therefore, he redeemed with precious blood, which purifies without making bloody, which does not stain but cleanses [Col. 0478C] from every blemish. But when he says “he himself,” he shows that apart from him escape is impossible, and that no one else could redeem us.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM 129

We beseech you, Lord, turn the ears of your mercy toward the prayer of your suppliants, because with you there is forgiveness of sins: so that you may not observe our iniquities, but grant us your mercies. Through our Lord Jesus, etc.

# PSALM 130

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM 130

C By his own example the prophet teaches the Christian people humility, imposing a very severe punishment upon them if they do not receive the Lord’s commandments with the greatest humility. He urges Israel continually to hope in the Lord, so that it may be able to endure the adversities of this world. [Col. 0478D]

TT. A Song of Ascents.

C This entire psalm is sung about gentleness and humility. Thus those whom the labor of the preceding confession had afflicted are refreshed by the sweetness of glorious devotion.

1 “Lord, my heart has not been exalted: Nor have my eyes been lifted up.”

C Here a hypothetical syllogism arises: the sense is, “If my heart has not been exalted, nor my eyes been lifted up, I am evidently made a stranger to pride.” Yet the meaning is also: “My heart has not been exalted, nor have my eyes been lifted up. Therefore I am made a stranger to pride.” [Col. 0479A] Thus, when the prophet denies in himself what is vicious, he confesses what is altogether praiseworthy.

2 “Nor have I walked in great matters: Nor in wonders beyond me.”

C Pilate walked in great matters when he said to Christ, “Do you not know that I have power to release you?” (John 19). Those walk in wonders who boast of the virtues they have received from God, or seek miracles rather than a miraculous life.

3 “If I did not think humbly: But exalted my soul.”

C He says that he did not meditate upon the Scriptures arrogantly. The prophet therefore advises everyone to meditate upon the divine Scriptures with a simple and pure heart—not like the Arians and Manichaeans. He says, then, that he thought humbly, [Col. 0479B] as the Apostle says: “Do not be high-minded, but fear” (Romans 11). Again, he denies that his soul was exalted to the summit of pride, but he does not deny that it was lifted toward divine preaching. For it is right to raise the soul in those matters by which it is fed with heavenly bread; it is not permitted in those proud investigations where death is found.

4 “As a weaned child upon his mother: So is the recompense in my soul.”

C Those are called weaned who have been deprived of milk. The comparison is fitting: just as infants suck their mother’s breasts, so the faithful, as little ones, are nourished by the simplicity of divine Scripture until they are prepared for solid food. The order of the words is: “If I did not think humbly, like a weaned child beneath his mother, but exalted my soul, then you will thus repay me”—that is, if I presumed to despise you, then you will rightly see me cast away.” [The Latin reading is uncertain.]

5 “Let Israel hope in the Lord: From this time forth and forever.”

C The prophet teaches each of the faithful always to place his confidence in the Lord. For he says, “from this time forth,” that is, from the present time to the future eternity, when one age will exist and the succession of times will be changed into perpetual unity.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM 130

Do not permit us to be exalted by the prides of the world, almighty Father; but since you are gentle and humble of heart [Col. 0479D] (Matthew 11), Father, [likewise] teach us to consent to humble things that please you. You who live and reign, God, etc.

# PSALM 131

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM 131

C This psalm describes the mysteries of the Lord’s Incarnation: its advent blesses the Church, glorifies the priests, confounds the enemies, and causes the eternal sanctification of righteousness to flourish over the Lord himself.

TT. A Song of Ascents.

C Although the prophet’s Songs of Ascents have all raised him toward the advancement of a higher hope, this one nevertheless lifted him in every respect, because it describes the mysteries of the Lord’s Incarnation.

1 [Col. 0480A] “Remember, Lord, David: And all his gentleness.”

C “Remember” is said of him in the human manner, although he could never forget anything, since all past and future things are present to him. That David, “strong of hand” and “desirable,” is the Lord Christ. “And all his gentleness”: by this the power of his immeasurable patience is shown.

2 “As he swore to the Lord: He vowed a vow to the God of Jacob.”

C The Lord, namely Christ, swore; that is, according to the etymology, he prayed by right. This means that he truly and firmly promised; and he promised that he would redeem the human race. He showed whom he meant when he said to Peter: “Put your sword back in its place. Shall I not drink the cup which [Col. 0480B] the Father has given me?” (John 18). And the same thing that he promised is said to have been vowed: the vow of the Son, therefore, was that through the advent of his Incarnation he would reconcile the human race to the Father. Yet this vow was not divided from the Father and the Holy Spirit, because their vow is one.

3 “If I enter into the tabernacle of my house: If I ascend upon the bed of my couch.”

C By “tabernacle” he means the heavenly dwelling, where, after the resurrection, he ascended in the assumed flesh in the sight of the apostles. His bed is to be understood as rest—namely, the most blessed completion of his Passion, because after the Passion had been completed there was rest. Christ promises that he will not ascend into heaven, nor give that rest to his flesh, until he has fulfilled what he promised to the Father. [Col. 0480C]

4 “If I give sleep to my eyes: And slumber to my eyelids.”

C This sleep is to be understood as the rest of death, since he accepted only a three-day repose, which brought no corruption to the body but rest. “Eyelids” derives from *palpare*, “to touch”: unless they rest in a certain trembling relaxation, sleep cannot enter the eyes. The same point follows, repeated in other words: truly, the temples of our head cannot have rest when the eyes, stirred by frequent movements, are known to remain awake.

5 ÷ “And rest to my temples … until I find a place for the Lord, a tabernacle for the God of Jacob.”

[Col. 0480D] H He professes that he gave no rest to his temples before, through his resurrection, he built in humanity a place worthy of the Lord the Father, or the assembly of the Church. C For his place is the tabernacle of the Christian breast and the courts of the Catholic Church, which he inhabits always as heaven. He himself found it because he sought the lost sheep; he himself discovered it because he built a tabernacle for himself from us and in us.

6 “Behold, we heard of it in Ephrata: We found it in the fields of the forest.”

C We heard of it, namely, of the promise that was to be fulfilled. Ephrata is Bethlehem itself. From this it clearly appears that it was heard that the Lord would be born in [Col. 0481A] Bethlehem, as the prophet Micah says: “And you, Bethlehem Ephrata, are by no means least; for from you the ruler Christ will go forth” (Micah 5). “The fields of the forest” are the hearts of the nations, which previously, because of their wild and thorny sins, were lairs of demons but are now called fields, since the Lord cultivates them and roots them out. They are called fields because of their capacity and broad expanse.

7 “We will enter into his tabernacle: We will adore in the place where his feet stood.”

H We will enter into the tabernacle of God, we who are gathered by the Lord into the unity of the Church. C The feet signify the evangelical commandments. His feet stood there where the truth of faith is recognized as founded; for the Lord’s feet stand fixed with the eternal solidity of truth. H There, therefore, we will adore where the apostolic preachings are heard, which support the whole body of the Church. This place, then, is the Church. [Col. 0481B]

8 “Arise, Lord, into your rest: You and the ark of your sanctification.”

H C “Arise, Lord,” that is, return from the underworld into the everlasting blessedness of your divinity. C “Your,” I say, which your majesty has assigned to you. “You and the ark,” that is, the Church, which you deigned to sanctify. The prophet says to Christ, “Arise,” because he already foresaw in the spirit that everything had been fulfilled in predestination which Christ had promised above. H It is as though he were saying: “You have now fulfilled the oath, repaid the vow, found a place for God, and brought forth the Church from your side; arise now, return to the tabernacle and [Col. 0481C] to your rest.”

9 “Let your priests be clothed with righteousness: And let your saints exult.”

H Let the priests of God be clothed with righteousness, so that, armed with the breastplate of righteousness (Ephesians 6), they may not be wounded by the enemy’s arrows. C And let your saints exult, those who have put on Christ in baptism. A Or: all the saints are called priests, adorned with that royal priesthood of faith and charity.

10 “For the sake of David your servant: Do not turn away the face of your Christ.”

H For the sake of him who took the form of a servant from David’s offspring, may the brightness of your image [Col. 0481D] not be turned away from the saints in whom Christ dwells, but may it illuminate them. A C Or the prophet asks that he not turn his face away from the Jewish people because of Christ’s death. The prayer was heard, because many from that people were saved (Acts 21), including the apostles and many others.

11 [Col. 0482A] “The Lord swore truth to David, and he will not frustrate him: Of the fruit of your womb I will set upon your throne.”

C What could be said more firmly than when he swears by him through whom oaths are sworn? He promises who cannot be deceived. To frustrate is to render promises void; here he rightly denies that this can happen, where there could be no place for deception. “The fruit of the womb” is the heavenly doctrine of Christ, from which the Christian people were generated, sitting upon his throne when they are shown to teach commandments like his. The successors of Christ, therefore—the apostles and others—were placed upon Christ’s throne. They were the fruit of Christ’s preaching, begotten by his word. David, therefore, signifies Christ, to whom the Father swore this, that is, firmly promised it according to his humanity.

“If your sons keep my covenant: And these my testimonies which I will teach them.”

C This is also said of the apostles and Christians, who deserved to be called sons of God through the integrity of faith, if they guard God’s covenant and all his teaching with pure devotion. “To sit always in the heavenly places and eternally,” that is, forever—namely, in the future heaven, whose end there will not be.

13 “And their sons forever: They will sit upon your throne.”

[Col. 0482B] H Our sons also will sit, that is, they will remember the good works which we performed in his sight for love of him.

14 “For the Lord has chosen Zion: He has chosen her as a dwelling for himself.”

H Zion is the holy Church. In it the Lord rests, that is, in the hearts of his elect—in holy souls sanctified by heavenly mysteries.

15 “This is my rest forever ÷ …: Here I will dwell, for I have chosen her.”

C It is his rest for the Lord himself to occupy as a special tabernacle the religious breasts of human beings, and thus to be everywhere that he may be said to dwell in them as immeasurable [Col. 0482C] and incomprehensible.

16 “Blessing her widow, I will bless her: I will satisfy her poor with bread.”

A The Father’s voice concerning his Son, “his widow,” etc. A C The Church is called Christ’s widow because, deprived of every worldly aid, she places her sole hope in the Lord. He blesses her when, by continual blessing, he sanctifies her. Truly, Christ’s poor are nourished with heavenly bread, since they always hunger amid worldly riches. Of them it is said: “Blessed are the poor in spirit” (Matthew 5).

17 “I will clothe her priests with salvation: And her saints will exult with exultation.”

C God’s priests are clothed with salvation when they receive the Lord [Col. 0482D] the Savior with the utmost integrity of faith and are clothed with his mercy. “They will exult with exultation” signifies the perpetual joy of the saints.

18 “There I will bring forth David’s horn: I have prepared a lamp for my Christ.”

C When “there” is said, that blessed rest is indicated of which he said above, “This is my rest,” etc. David’s horn is the strength of Christ’s power, to be displayed in that judgment where he grants eternal rewards to the saints. “I have prepared a lamp”—H, A C—that is, John the Baptist, or the light of his preaching, namely, of John the Baptist, who was the true lamp of Christ (John 5).

19 [Col. 0483A] “I will clothe his enemies with confusion: But upon him my sanctification will flourish.”

C Just as God’s priests are clothed with salvation, so his enemies—that is, heretics, pagans, and whoever lived against his ordinances—are clothed with the garment of confusion when they hear, “Come, you blessed,” while the others hear, “Go into eternal fire.” He said “will flourish” to express the holiness of the glorious Incarnation; for the Father’s sanctification always flourished in Christ, whatever he did or whatever he endured.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM 131

In all our entering, remember us, almighty God; clothe us with priestly righteousness, so that we may deserve to be led into the everlasting tabernacles. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, etc. [Col. 0483B]

# PSALM 132

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM 132

C After the most glorious preaching of the preceding psalm, the prophet proclaims blessed unity, so that those who bind themselves to the Christian religion may persevere in one harmony of charity.

TT. A Song of Ascents.

1 “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is: For brothers to dwell together.”

H Here he posits two things, namely “good” and “pleasant,” and joins in one expression what seemed contrary to itself, since martyrdom is good but not pleasant, while pleasure is pleasant but not good. C By saying “brothers together,” he signifies not brothers according to the flesh, but those who have been established under one Father by the fellowship of faith, having one heart and one soul (Acts 4).

2 “Like ointment upon the head: Which descends upon the beard, the beard of Aaron.”

C The ointment upon the head is the Holy Spirit, who descended upon Christ at baptism in the form of a dove (Matthew 3), and he is the head of the body of the Church. “Which descends upon the beard,” that is, the same Spirit upon the apostles, who are aptly called a beard because, fixed manfully beneath Christ their head, they persevere like a beard. He added Aaron, who bore the figure of Christ in his priesthood, so that you would understand not the beard of just any man, but Christ’s.

3 [Col. 0483D] “Which descends upon the hem of his garment: Like the dew of Hermon, which descends upon Mount Zion.”

C By the hem of God’s garment the Church is signified. Upon its hem this anointing descends, because the Holy Spirit descends upon it in baptism until the end of the world and sanctifies it by his mercy. H Hermon is the Hebrew name of a mountain situated beyond the river Jordan; it is interpreted as “anathema” and signifies the Jewish people rejected by God. “The dew of Hermon” is divine Scripture, first entrusted to the Jews and afterward passing over to Mount Zion, that is, the Church of Christ. A Or faith and the grace of God. This dew is that which descends from Judea to the nations, which now contemplate God by faith, and therefore are Zion.

4 [Col. 0484A] “For there the Lord commanded blessing: ÷ And life forever.”

C “There,” namely in Zion, that is, in the Church, which consists in the gathering of the brothers. “He commanded blessing,” that is, he sent the Savior, who is the life and perpetual blessedness of believers. C No blessing is bestowed upon those who are not in agreement. Therefore, where concord exists, there God’s blessing is commanded.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM 132

Pour into your Church, Lord, the charity of our brotherhood and peace, so that, sprinkled with the dew of spiritual ointment, we may rejoice in the grace of your blessing. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, etc.

# PSALM 133

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM 133

[Col. 0484B]

C After the exhortations to mutual love, he now appropriately urges that the blessed unity be stirred toward the praises of the Lord with the most fervent zeal of charity.

TT. A Song of Ascents.

1 “Behold ÷ now … bless the Lord: All servants of the Lord.”

C “Behold” is said so that, with matters certain and complete, not only speech but also a demonstrative indication might be supplied. “Now” is said, that is, in the eternal homeland, because, after so many steps have been ascended, he alone ought to be praised who wondrously granted so much. The Lord is then to be proclaimed with greater zeal, when by his generosity he makes people secure. Or “now,” [Col. 0484C] that is, in the present life, where the soul must be exercised so that in the future it may be occupied with eternal praises. “Bless,” that is, praise; for by blessing him we praise him, while by blessing us he sanctifies us. H The servants of the Lord are those over whom anger does not rule, in whom sins do not reign, and whom vices do not dominate.

2 “You who stand in the house of the Lord: ÷ In the courts of the house of our God …”

C They stand in the house of the Lord whose mind perseveres with firm footing in the worship of God. The court is the entrance to a dwelling, signifying those who have deserved to be either in the inner chambers or already at the entrance of the holy Church of our God—that is, not of the one whom paganism worships, but of the one whom true religion confesses.

3 “In the nights lift up your hands in the holy place: [Col. 0484D] And bless the Lord.”

C “In the nights” signifies the end of this world, a time always darkened by tribulations. For there the hands must be raised where good works deserve the Lord’s help. When he says “lift up,” this means: perform almsgiving and good works more abundantly. He adds “in the holy place,” namely, the Church, or “in the Holy One,” namely Christ, as it is in Hebrew, or in holy works, which exist only in the holy Church. For Christ accepts only that almsgiving which a faithful Christian offers in his name, that is, in the holy Church. But lest anyone claim anything for himself, he says that the Lord must be blessed, because he himself gives both a merciful soul and more abundant resources.

4 [Col. 0485A] “May the Lord bless you from Zion: He who made heaven and earth.”

H The Holy Spirit, or the prophet, speaks this verse to the one who ascended through fifteen steps to the blessing, so that he may receive his reward. “May the Lord bless you from Zion, he who made heaven and earth”: he says this to distinguish him from those who are false gods.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM 133

As we bless you, Lord, we beseech you: deign to illuminate us, covered by the night of this world, so that, while we raise our hands in good works, we may receive from you the most abundant blessing. Through our Lord Jesus, etc.

# PSALM 134

[Col. 0485B]

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM 134

C The prophet declares that praises are owed to the Lord, recounting his various mighty works and refuting the worshipers of idols by exposing the falsehood of idols.

TT. Alleluia.

C After the steps have been completed up to that summit which makes Christians secure, “Alleluia” is most fittingly placed, so that the holy Church may delight in the praises of the Lord, for whom such a gift is known to have been prepared. Therefore let us say “Alleluia” with sincere minds, so that by divine grace we may be joined to that holy people.

1 “Praise the name of the Lord: Praise the Lord, servants.”

[Col. 0485C] H Praise the name of the Lord, which through faith you have recognized to be above every name. “Praise, servants,” C that is, you who are his servants, devoted with willing submission and having abandoned service to the devil.

2 “You who stand in the house of the Lord: In the courts of the house of our God.”
