C “You who stand,” that is, you who remain in belief in him with persevering devotion. A court is called the first entrance of a very spacious house, where inhabitants were accustomed to make hearths. The courts were named from the black smoke, as though “blackened.” In these words he says that those ought to bless God who appear to have entered the first part of the Lord’s house.

3 “Praise the Lord, for the Lord is good. [Col. 0485D] Sing praises to his name, for it is sweet ÷ …”

H Consider that he placed “praise” three times, so that through the similar quality of praise he might show us the indivisible unity of the Holy Trinity. “For he is good,” who is not merely good but supremely good. To sing praises refers to good bodily works, so that in this way of life we may appear to praise the Lord for our uprightness.

4 “For the Lord chose Jacob for himself, Israel as his possession.”

C The Lord chose Jacob when he united the Church’s people from diverse nations. Israel possesses him when, in the resurrection of the blessed, he is shown to dwell in all things.

5 [Col. 0486A] “For I have known that the Lord is great: And our God is above all gods.”

C The most holy man saw that majesty, wondrous and ruling over the powers of heaven, and, as the Spirit revealed its greatness, he rightly called the Lord great above all gods, since all things were created by him. He did not call them gods because he believed those whom foolish paganism worshiped to be gods; rather, because they themselves called them gods, he mentions them by that name in order to mock them.

6 “The Lord has done whatever he willed in heaven and on earth: In the sea and in all the abysses.”

C “Heaven” stands for all heavenly things; “earth,” for everything generated from the soil; “sea,” for those channels which the journeys of travelers visit; “the abyss” signifies the Ocean, which is unknown to us because of its depth. In all these things the will of God is unquestionably fulfilled.

7 “Bringing forth clouds from the end of the earth: He made lightning into rain.”

C If you take what follows literally, it is true. But because he speaks below of the Hebrew people, it is also appropriate to apply this to human beings. A C “Bringing forth clouds,” that is, raising prophets from a lowly purpose and bringing them to the summit of preaching. “Lightning” is the preaching of the prophets, when it strikes sinners with fear; it becomes rain when it washes offenders [Col. 0490C] from their sins and pours in saving showers from which spiritual fruits may sprout.

8 “Who brings forth winds from his treasuries: Who struck the firstborn of Egypt, from man to beast.”

C By “winds” he means the apostles, whose preaching traverses the whole world like a very swift wind. “From his treasuries,” H that is, from the heavenly secrets. C God strikes the firstborn of the world, as though of Egypt, when by the inspiration of his power he corrects human beings born in original sin. “From man,” that is, from the wiser men of this age, down to gentle and simple men; for all are oppressed, unless they are liberated from the devil by the grace of the Lord, as by Pharaoh’s impious domination.

9 [Col. 0486D] “He sent signs and wonders in your midst, Egypt: Against Pharaoh and all his servants.”

C He sent signs when, at Christ’s Passion, the earth shook and the rocks were split. It is called a sign because it signifies something: just as, when an animal’s footprint is seen, we infer that the animal has passed by. Wonders are so called as though “speaking afar,” that is, proclaiming things at a distance; he performs them when he converts faithful souls through signs given beforehand. Pharaoh is interpreted as “dissipation” and signifies the devil. “Against all his servants,” that is, against those who serve him; for we are servants of the one whom we serve with willing mind. The devil is submerged with his servants when, through the saving font of baptism, the people are freed from the devil’s error.

10 [Col. 0487A] “Who struck many nations: And slew mighty kings.”

C By “nations” he means throngs of vices. We strike these when, through repentance, we wound them by satisfaction; what is a wound to them is salvation to us. By “mighty kings” he means unclean spirits, whom the Lord kills when he cleanses us from sins and makes them strangers to us.

11 “Sihon king of the Amorites and Og king of Bashan: And all the kingdoms of Canaan.”

C Sihon is interpreted as “temptation of the eyes”; the Amorites as “those who make bitter.” Truly, the vices that lead us away from that most delightful blessedness are bitter. These have the devil as their king, who is the temptation of the eyes when he transforms himself into an angel of light (2 Corinthians 11), so that by the appearance of good he may deceive the devout. God kills these when he frees us from their service. Og means “enclosure”; Bashan is interpreted as “confusion.” Thus the king of confusion is rightly called an enclosure. For the devil closed the heavenly kingdom to us and cast us into confusion. H Canaan is interpreted as “agitation,” because those kingdoms of the devil agitate us away from God. C He killed them—the one who accepted the cross for the salvation of all.

12 “And he gave their land as an inheritance: An inheritance for Israel his people.”

C That land is the one which Christians will unquestionably possess as an inheritance in eternal peace. Therefore he adds, “an inheritance for Israel his people.” This inheritance of blessedness is perpetual itself, H into which he admitted us by his grace.

13 “Lord, your name is forever: Lord, your memorial from generation to generation.”

C He therefore prays that his name should always remain among the human race, so that from Christ’s advent until the end of the world people may always be called and be Christians. H Or, with that name remaining forever, may this be our eternal inheritance. C God’s memorial is everything contained in the holy Scriptures as a most salutary reminder. “Age of age” signifies the everlasting day; where we have “from generation to generation,” Cassiodorus’s translation has “forever and ever.” H Or, “from generation to generation,” namely, of the Jews and Christians, so that what the shadow of the Law prefigured may be recognized in the Gospel. A Or, in this age and the future one.

14 “For the Lord will judge his people: And he will be entreated for his servants.”

C “He will judge,” that is, the Lord will condemn the unbelieving Jews, because they did not wish to be his, although he chose them from all the nations for possession. “And for his servants,” that is, for the faithful, to whom it was said: “Whoever believes in me will not be judged, but passes from death to life” (John 11). For them he will be entreated, that is, he will be propitious, granting them the eternal promises. He is entreated by those whom he also hears.

15 [Col. 0488A] “The idols of the nations are silver and gold: The works of human hands.”

C Here the idols are designated by the material from which they are made, namely, gold and silver, fashioned according to the qualities of metals, for the mockery of the nations. The pagans are rightly mocked when they think that their gods provide human beings with what they receive from human beings—namely, gold, silver, and so forth. People would better consult their own interests by breaking them; for then they are of some use, if they are reduced to money. Thus, while whole, their god does not hear them; but, when diminished, it is rather of use.

16 “They have mouths and will not speak: They have eyes and will not see.”

C What use is a mouth that does not speak? What use is an eye that does not see? They are merely empty names, not functions capable of providing benefit. [Col. 0488B]

17 “They have ears and will not hear: Nor is there any spirit in their mouths.”

C What use is an ear that does not hear? What use are nostrils that do not smell? Empty names without realities, a fleeting presumption. What use is a hand that does not touch? What use is a foot that does not move? What use is a throat that does not make a sound? These are harmful delusions, not firm truth. The idols of the nations have been mocked sufficiently.

18 “Let those who make them become like them: ÷ And all who trust in them.”

C It is fitting that those who made senseless gods for themselves should lack the senses they bestowed upon them. And observe that he embraces both the makers and all the worshipers of idols in one condemnation, when he says, “those who make them” [Col. 0488C] and “those who trust in them.”

19 “House of Israel, bless the Lord: House of Aaron, bless the Lord.”

C Here he admonishes the faithful that their praises ought to resound for the true Lord. By Israel every righteous person is signified who rejoices in the contemplation of God. In Aaron the holy priests are signified.

20 “House of Levi, bless the Lord: You who fear the Lord, bless the Lord.”

C In Levi also the holy ministers, that is, the deacons, are signified; finally, all who serve the Lord in whatever manner of life. Thus the whole people devoted to God is commanded to praise God through its various parts.

21 [Col. 0488D] “Blessed is the Lord from Zion: Who dwells in Jerusalem.”

C “Blessed is the Lord,” that is, Christ, who is Zion; that is, he visited his Church through a holy Incarnation. He is the one who dwells in Jerusalem, which is built by the gathering of diverse saints and rejoices with eternal happiness in the presence of its king.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM 134

God of supreme sweetness, whom the whole earth praises for the kindness of your gentleness, we ask that, once the error of empty superstition has been washed away from us, we may be joined to your will. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, etc.

# PSALM 135

[Col. 0489A]

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM 135

C Declaring the magnificence of the Lord, the prophet recounts the miracles he performed in Egypt and among the Jewish people, repeatedly impressing his mercy upon us, because everything we can do is due to his mercy, and everything by which we live is due to his clemency.

TT. Alleluia.

C A wondrous psalm, and exceedingly deep in power. Its power is shown in Chronicles, where it says: “When they began to praise God and say, ‘Give thanks to the Lord,’ etc., the house was filled with cloud and darkness, so that even the priests could not stand and minister because of the darkness; for the glory of the Lord had filled the house of God” (2 Chronicles 5). For although it is certain that the divine presence is present in all psalms when they are sung purely, this is nevertheless believed more strongly when it is confirmed by the authority of Scripture.

1 “Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good: For his mercy is forever.”

C “Give thanks” is understood both as confession of sins and as praise. The repeated refrain “his mercy” in each verse indicates that everything being said proceeds from God’s mercy; without it we can neither exist nor have strength. Therefore it ought not depart either from our mouth or from our heart, so that it may itself deign to preserve us by continual protection. He is called “good” because he graciously hears his praises and mercifully forgives those who plead. He adds, [Col. 0489C] “his mercy is forever,” because in the present he grants it to restore us, spares us in order to correct us, and in the future grants mercy in order to crown us.

2 “Give thanks to the God of gods: For his mercy is forever.”

C He is the God of gods in whom no equal is found. And the God of gods can be called none other than the Holy Trinity alone.

3 “Give thanks to the Lord of lords: For his mercy is forever,” etc.

C He alone is the Lord of lords, to whom all things are subject. He is also the Holy of holies, the King of kings, and the Lord of all powers.

4 “Who alone does great wonders: For his mercy is forever.”

[Col. 0489D] A C Throughout all these verses, until the end, “give thanks” is to be understood, so that the sentence may be complete. He says that he alone performed wonders—as though he had not performed wonders through angels and apostles—but here he recalls that he alone performed these wonders when he is shown to have fashioned the natures of things by his word, creating them without the ministry of any creature. Hence what follows: “Who made,” etc.

5 “Who made the heavens with understanding: For his mercy is forever.”

C He made the heavens with understanding because they were created neither in confusion, nor disorder, nor shapelessness, but distinct and ordered, accomplished in the wisdom of their Creator.

6 [Col. 0490A] “Who established the earth upon the waters: For his mercy is forever.”

C He established the earth upon the waters, namely, those of holy baptism. Our earth—that is, our body—is restored when it is strengthened by the stability of religion. Or literally, “upon the waters,” that is, beside the waters. Or also, with one part of itself above the waters.

7 “Who made the great lights: For his mercy is forever.”

C Although literally this is true of the stars, spiritually he made great lights when he created angels and Powers, Thrones and Dominations, which by their most holy devotion radiate with heavenly light.

8 “The sun for the dominion of the day: For his mercy is forever.”

[Col. 0490B] C The dominion of the day is the rising of the sun, because through it all visible creation is revealed. It may also be said of Christ, who illuminates the darkness of minds.

9 “The moon and stars for the dominion of the night: For his mercy is forever.”

C We should understand the Church as the moon, and its various orders as the stars, such as bishops, priests, and deacons, who are known to shine like stars through a heavenly way of life. They were given “for the dominion of the night,” that is, of this world, so that through them the darkened hearts of mortals might shine forth.

10 “Who struck Egypt with their firstborn: For his mercy is forever.”

[Col. 0490C] C Since the historical account is known, let us see what may be understood spiritually here. Christ struck the firstborn of Egypt when he condemned the glory of this age, which was thought to be pre-eminent. For luxury, pride, and greed are, as it were, the firstborn of the world: the belly itself first gives them birth and embraces them as dear children, while it rejoices in desire for these things. He struck these when he condemned them.

11 He who brought Israel out from among them: For.

C For he brought Israel out through the midst of the Egyptians when he freed his saints from association with the wicked and led them from the most dreadful dwelling of this world into the light of his truth.

12[Col. 0490D] With a mighty hand and an outstretched arm: For.

C “Mighty hand” pertains to invincible action. “Outstretched arm” pertains to the singular omnipotence of the Lord, which always manifests the creator of all things.

13 He who divided the Red Sea into divisions: For.

C The Red Sea is the mingled depth of this world, which we cross by many divisions when, turning toward the land of the living, we hasten onward: one crosses to God through almsgiving, another through constant prayers, another through virginity, another through charity.

14[Col. 0491A] ÷ And [lacuna] led Israel through its midst: For.

C “And he led Israel out”: since this verse has been repeated, the explanation given above is sufficient.

15 And he shook Pharaoh and his power into the Red Sea: For.

C “And he shook Pharaoh,” that is, the devil together with his ministers, in the fountain of salvation, that is, baptism, where by the power of his might he drives them away. He said “shook” (that is, as though he had thrown off dust) in order to show the speed and power of the divinity and to demonstrate that they are earthly filth.

16 He who led his people through the wilderness: For.

[Col. 0491B] C The world is called a wilderness because it was deprived of divine election; and it is rightly so called, because it did not receive the creator who came to it. Those, therefore, are led through it by Christ who pass through its evils unharmed.

17 He who struck great kings: For ever.

C He struck great kings when the heavenly physician extinguished impious desires in our hearts. For then we live, while those desires die. Conversely, we must succumb if it happens that those desires overcome us.

18 And he slew mighty kings: For ever.

C He slew mighty kings when he drives out from us demons raging through various assaults, whose evil will is extinguished when the souls of the faithful are removed from their power.

19 Sihon, king of the Amorites: For.

C Sihon is interpreted as “temptation of the eyes,” or “fruitless tree.” “Amorite” means “exasperation”; all these meanings seem to pertain to the devil. For he is the fruitless tree; he is the exasperation. But the Lord kills these things in us when he brings us to his ordinances through holiness of conduct.

20 And Og, king of Bashan: For.

C Og is said to be interpreted as “conclusion” or “one who heaps up.” Bashan means “confusion,” and signifies the devil. He is rightly called confusion because he confounds his followers, and he himself departs from blessedness at God’s judgment in confusion. He also heaps up our sins in order to accuse us, and closes off the way to God so that he may not be seen.

21 ÷ And he gave their land as an inheritance [lacuna]: For.

C That land of eternal blessedness, which had been promised to the Jews, was given to the Christian people. When they were cast out because of their iniquity, the rewards of the promised inheritance were bestowed upon the saints and faithful.

22 An inheritance for Israel his servant: For.

C When he says “his servant,” he means the Christian people. [Col. 0492A] For he separates those who resisted his commands, whether Jews or Christians.

23 For he remembered us in our humiliation: For.

C Christ himself showed us both the way of humility and the discipline of patience. Therefore he remembered those who were placed in humiliation when, at his coming, he freed them by his own blood. Humility also began to be more widely desired when the Lord Savior displayed it in himself.

24 And he redeemed us from our enemies: For.

C For he redeemed us from various injuries and from the power of the devil when, struck with blows, scourged, and beaten, he gave his blood as the price.

25[Col. 0492B] He who gives food to all flesh: For.

C He gives food to the flesh when he deigns to nourish and satisfy his faithful with his body and blood. If you understand it literally as well, by his mercy he sustains and feeds all things.

26 Give thanks to the God of heaven: For ever.

C “Give thanks to the God of heaven,” that is, render him the praises due to him, because he has changed us from earthly beings into heavenly ones.

27 ÷ Give thanks to the Lord of lords: For ...

C At the end he again recalls, by the very verse that he placed at the beginning, that thanks must be given, so that no one might believe that anything could be done apart from his praise and mercy.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM 135

[Col. 0492C]

Remembering our human condition, have mercy, almighty God, so that you who once gave our fathers the land of their adversaries as an inheritance may establish us, freed from sins, together with your inheritance. Through our Lord Jesus, etc.

# PSALM 136

## SUMMARY OF PSALM 136

B This psalm may be understood in three ways: of the Jewish captivity in Babylon; of sinners expelled from the Church; and of that expulsion by which our first parents were driven from paradise.

TT. ÷ A psalm of David [lacuna]

1[Col. 0492D] By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept, when we remembered Zion.

H Babylon is interpreted as “confusion” and signifies the present world. A river signifies each person who is beautiful for an hour, whose flower passes away like a river. C The faithful sit above the rivers, those who suffer captivity in this world and, sighing with longing for the heavenly homeland, Jerusalem, pour out bitter tears.

2 On the willows in its midst we hung up our instruments.

H The willow is a fruitless tree, and it is said that if anyone takes a drink from it or eats it, he does not beget children. The instrument is the human body. For just as an instrument is composed of many pipes, so our body consists of many organs and members; and through its very touch by the hands, that is, through works, we offer melody, songs, and hymns to God. It is also said that the willow has no root; yet if it is cut off and planted beside water, it immediately grows green. So the sinner, although he has sinned and fallen, nevertheless, if he is beside water—that is, if he reads the sacred Scriptures—his soul flourishes.

3 For there those who took us captive asked us for the words of songs.

H The demons who deceived us and led us captive now, as though boasting and mocking, say to us: [Col. 0493B] “Give us a word from your faith, and just as, when you were in Jerusalem, that is, in paradise, you sang a hymn to God, so now sing.” C For the law of sin holds us captive in our members according to the mind, so that we do not do what we wish but what we do not wish.

4 And those who led us away asked us: “Sing for us one of the songs of Zion.”

C “Those who led us away,” that is, carnal desires—which justly entangle us in captivity—often persuade us that we ought to sing the words of psalmody in unclean places.

5 How shall we sing the song of the Lord in a foreign land?

C “How shall we sing?” We must answer them: [Col. 0493C] “We who are established in sins?” “In a foreign land,” that is, amid vicious actions, which are alien to God. “The song of the Lord.” H For the sinner ought not to sing but to mourn his sins. For no one can praise God unless he is holy (Ps. 49; Sir. 15).

6 If I forget you, Jerusalem, let my right hand be forgotten.

C The Prophet therefore binds himself with harsh conditions and bonds not to let heavenly Jerusalem, the region of the blessed, depart from his mind. Whoever forgets it here is by no means placed in the kingdom of God. H The right hand consists of the upright works of the good. If you wish always to be mindful of God, perform the works of the right hand.

7 Let my tongue cling to my jaws, if I do not remember you.

[Col. 0493D] C Now a second penal condition is proposed. For what is proved to be worse than being unable to speak that by which healing is customarily provided? Psalmody is the consolation of those who weep, the care of those who grieve, the health of the sick; it is this remedy for the soul, and it is known to be the refuge of all the wretched. Therefore you must always remember Christ, lest you be deprived of such a gift.

8 + If I do not set [lacuna] Jerusalem at the beginning of my joy.

C The beginning of joy is always strong, always most abundant, because at the very beginnings the will is kindled toward joys. For everything sudden is violent, and whatever lasts long in this age grows lukewarm. Or, “the beginning of my joy”: the Son of God was born.

9[Col. 0494A] Remember, Lord, the sons of Edom on the day of Jerusalem.

C Some interpret Edom as “bloody,” others as “earthly.” H Who, then, is he except the devil? For the devil deceives the human race, and the Prophet asks that retribution be given him, so that he may feel the punishment which by his own malice he brought upon humanity, dragging and leading it into Babylon.

10 They who say, “Empty it, empty it, down to its foundation.”

C These are the words of the sons of Edom, who persecute the Christian people; they persecuted them down to the foundation, that is, to the death of martyrdom. To say “empty it” is to say, “Take away temporal light.” The words are drawn from the likeness of a cistern, which is emptied more and more the more it is drained. But what benefit is it to the wicked to empty the temporal possessions of Christians down to the foundation, which is Christ, when they cannot take Christ, the foundation, away or diminish eternal goods?

11 Daughter of Babylon, wretched one: Blessed is he who will repay you with the repayment that you repaid us.

C The daughter of Babylon is our flesh, which brings the confusion of sins upon us. It is called wretched because it constantly wounds the soul with the wound of sins through unlawful desires. To repay it means to subject it to virtues through fasting and various tribulations—since it stirred us to vices by its desires—so that what it dragged toward guilt may, with God’s help, be brought to glory.

12[Col. 0494C] Blessed is he who will seize them and dash her little ones against the rock.

C He still speaks to the flesh itself, declaring blessed the one who holds and restrains her children, that is, harmful vices, and does not allow them to injure him. “And he will dash them against the rock,” that is, against Christ, so that he may not linger while holding them, lest seductive pleasure steal upon him, but so that those things which were urging us on with the most dreadful impulses may immediately be shattered and perish.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM 136

Most powerful Liberator from our captivities, grant us to sing your praises with spiritual harmony, so that those whom the burden of guilt formerly made exiles may be restored as heavenly citizens by the relief of your mighty right hand. Through our Lord Jesus, etc.

# PSALM 137

[Col. 0494D]

## SUMMARY OF PSALM 137

C The universal Church, praising together the Lord’s benefits bestowed upon her, admonishes the kings of the earth to acknowledge the Most High God, and prays that he not despise converted sinners, whom he deigned to create.

TT. ÷ To him [lacuna], David.

C Although David signifies Christ, nevertheless, by adding “to him,” the text indicates something more. “To him” must be pronounced with greater reverence, as to the Most High, the Almighty, the heavenly King. Then “David” should be joined to it; this name does not derive from divinity, but is shown to come through the origin of the assumed flesh.

1[Col. 0495A] I will give thanks to you, Lord, with my whole heart, ÷ for you have heard the words of my mouth ...

H If someone does penance for all the vices and passions of his soul, that person gives thanks with his whole heart. But if someone confesses one vice—for example, that he is greedy—he confesses this, but does not confess that he is a fornicator or a slanderer. Because he does not confess with his whole heart, he is not heard by God. C He considers the merit of the prayer, so that he may declare all his words heard.

2 In the sight of the angels I will sing to you; I will worship toward your holy temple and give thanks to your name.

H See the perfection of the penitent: after confession and penance, he is deemed worthy to sing [Col. 0495B] with the angels and give thanks to God. C The temple of prayer is the advent of blessed incarnation, which the Church worships daily while it venerates his body and blood in the sacrament; but that worship is perfect which is accompanied by blessed confession.

3 Because of your mercy and your truth, for you have magnified above + every [lacuna] your holy name.

C Mercy is that he deigned to come to free us without any merits on our part. Truth is that he fulfilled the promises of his prophets. The name was magnified when the power of his worship became known to us. H Let the sinner hear “mercy”; but let the righteous and proud hear “truth.”

4 On whatever day I call upon you, hear me; [Col. 0495C] you will multiply strength in my soul.

C “Day” here means a clear and sincere petition, which neither desire nor any greed clouds, but which shines from that sun which cleanses all the darknesses of mortality. In such petitions the devout people pray to be heard. H “You will multiply,” that is, you make the soul subject to many anxieties. C For by this he shows that he will suffer innumerable things, against which he asks such manifold aids of the virtues.

5 Let all the kings of the earth give thanks to you, Lord, because they have heard all the words of your mouth.

C The kings of the earth are those who rule their bodies by the gift of divinity. For the one who is shown to serve vices is not truly called a king. “Because they have heard”: hearing belongs to those who are known to be obedient. We do not say that those have heard whom we know to be rebellious against sacred commands.

6 And let them sing in the ways of the Lord, for great is the glory of the Lord.

H The ways of the Lord are mercy and truth. Kings, religious people, and true Christians—the governors of the soul’s passions and desires—are commanded to sing and praise them. For the glory of the Lord is that those who reject the world do not cease to sing his praises.

7 For the Lord is exalted and regards the humble, but he knows the proud from afar.

C Although the Lord is exalted, he nevertheless regards the humble, so that none of his subjects might think that he is not seen by the exalted Lord when he recognizes himself as prostrate in great devotion. “The proud” signifies the lofty; he knows them from afar because they do not approach his grace at all. And lest the proud think that, because they are high, they do not see God, he says, “he knows.”

8 If I walk in the midst of tribulation, you will give me life; ÷ and [lacuna] you stretched out your hand against the anger of my enemies, and your right hand saved me.

C The people are therefore given life, that is, made joyful: when they are placed amid various distresses, they are refreshed by remembering the sweetness of eternal joys. Knowing that gold is tested by fire, that the greatest reward is given after labors, and that tribulations are to be overcome by the Lord’s power, they rejoice in tribulations and are [Col. 0496B] given life in mind. He stretches out his hand against anger when those enemies who have been converted are here more severely afflicted than they had afflicted the humble who were subject to them, and begin justly to persecute themselves, though previously they had refused to spare the innocent. “Right hand” means power, and is Christ.

9 The Lord will repay on my behalf. Lord, your mercy is forever; do not despise the works of your hands.

C “The Lord will repay” is a most perfect prayer, of the kind we are instructed to pour forth: to entrust one’s cause to the Lord, who knows how to repay each person with what is due. And lest you think it was said with an angry spirit, he adds, “Lord, your mercy,” etc., which you show even toward our persecutors when, after their conversion, you make them suffer much for your faith. Therefore what he says about mercy pertains to those who persecute us. “The works of your hands,” that is, our enemies, because they too are the works of your hands. Therefore the devout people pray for their enemies, that he may mercifully forgive those who sinned against him by persecuting, so that, having received pardon, they may be converted.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM 137

Multiply your strength, Lord, in the souls of those who implore you, so that, while we continually worship in the holy temple, we may glory in your sight with the holy angels. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, etc.

# PSALM 138

## SUMMARY OF PSALM 138

C Christ speaks to the Father about his repose and resurrection, explaining the power of the Father’s divinity, because, insofar as he is human, he cannot hide himself anywhere from the Father’s knowledge; and he asserts that the dominion of the saints has been strengthened above all.

TT. A psalm of David, for the end.

C This entire psalm must be referred to the person of Christ the Lord and to the Father, because it speaks of his repose and resurrection. A It may also be expounded of a penitent.

1 Lord, you have tested me and known me; you have known my sitting down and my rising up.

C The Father tested the Son when he made his humility manifest, when he willed him to be baptized by John. [Col. 0497A] He knew him, that is, made him known, when he said: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear him” (Matt. 13). “Sitting down” is aptly named: it is the Savior’s death, in which there was not punishment but rest. A Or, “you tested me” in the passion, and “you knew,” that is, made known, in the resurrection. For he repeats the point at which he made him known, namely, in his sitting down, that is, in his passion, because by sitting he humbles himself; and Christ humbled himself even to the death of the cross. In the resurrection he made him known to all. Thus the eternal Father tested, that is, showed as tested and known, his Son.

2 You understood my thoughts from afar; you investigated my path and my course.

C “From afar” signifies here not place but time, [Col. 0497B] because he foresees not only our deeds but also recognizes our thoughts before we ourselves suppose them. “Paths” pertain to silent thoughts; “course” to just judgments.

3 And you foresaw all my ways, because there is no word on my tongue.

C “Ways” pertain to human actions. His ways, that is, his works, were foreseen to such an extent that the works of Christ were known through prophecy long before, as Isaiah said concerning Christ’s gentleness: “He was led like a sheep to the slaughter,” etc. (Isa. 53). “There is no word” means, certainly, no word of falsehood, because Christ never spoke under any falsehood.

4 Behold, Lord, ÷ you [lacuna] have known all things, the last and the first; [Col. 0497C] ÷ you [lacuna] formed me and placed your hand upon me.

C What he says, “you have known all things, the last,” pertains to his incarnation, which took place in the last times (Gal. 4), as Paul says. John also says: “Little children, it is the last hour” (1 John 2). “The first,” that is, the eternal things, which are enclosed by neither beginning nor end. “You formed me” signifies “you begot me.” The Father placed his hand upon him when he displayed the power of his majesty in him.

5 Your knowledge has become wondrous because of me; it has been strengthened, and I cannot attain to it.

C The Father’s knowledge is that which has been proclaimed throughout the world through Christ. It became wondrous through Christ when the mysteries of the sacred law were related to earthly beings. [Col. 0497D] “I cannot attain to it”: he speaks from the standpoint of the humanity and weakness of the flesh, as elsewhere: “The Father is greater than I” (John 14). The meaning is: “I cannot make the human nature that I assumed equal to the divine substance.” A Or the penitent, cast down from divine contemplation by his sins, says that it has been strengthened above his frailty and wondrously exalted.

6 Where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your presence?

C By saying “where shall I go?” he signifies that the nature of humanity has nowhere to flee of itself, since the Holy Spirit is wholly everywhere. “Presence” signifies the substance of the divinity, which embraces all things, sees all things, and penetrates all things. A Or the penitent asks where he may flee from God’s anger.

7 If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present.

C He says, insofar as he is human: “If I ascend into heaven, you are there,” namely, where he was to be placed at the Father’s right hand. He also descended into hell when he broke open the places of the dead and the most merciful Redeemer came to the aid of the human race. “You are present,” because he rose with the speed of three days. A Or the penitent says: “If I become proud and exalt myself, you punish me there; and if I descend into the depth of sins, there too you take vengeance.”

8 If I take my wings ÷ [lacuna] at dawn, ÷ and dwell at the ends of the sea,

C By “his wings” he means the swiftness of the divine majesty, [Col. 0498B] because he raised his holy body to the heights. When he also says “my,” understand the glory of his own power, because the divinity, by its own power and not with angelic assistance, placed the humanity at the Father’s right hand. When he had taken these wings at the dawn of the resurrection and had dwelt at the ends of the sea—that is, beyond the vastest limit of this world—the Father’s hand led him there. A Or the wings are the two commandments of charity, by which the penitent, rising from sins at dawn, dwells at the ends of the world, that is, in heavenly joy. This is given after the end of this life, yet one already dwells in it through hope.

9 For there your hand will lead me, and your right hand will hold me.

C The Father’s hand led Christ; that hand is the Father’s right hand, which will hold the humanity he assumed and united to himself throughout the eternal ages.

10 And I said, “Perhaps the darknesses will trample me, and night will be illumination in my delights.”

C This verse must be spoken ironically. For how could darkness trample him who is the light of the world? Rather, he trampled darkness when he restored the blindness of the first man by the light of his mercy. “Night” signifies the prison of hell, which he certainly illuminated when he shattered the devil’s power. “Delights” signifies paradise, to which the souls of the saints returned through the Lord’s favor. A Or these are the words of a penitent who fears being seduced by the dark acts of those who give evil counsel.

11 ÷ For [lacuna] darknesses will not be darkened by you, and [Col. 0498D] night will be illuminated like day; its darknesses are like its light.

C The reason is given why night is illumination in delights. He calls the obscure and profound things of the divine Scriptures “darknesses.” They will not be darkened but illuminated by the Lord. What had been like night, spoken darkly under the mystical covering of the prophets, became clear at the Lord’s coming. “Its darknesses are like its light,” because truth was present in both, whether they appeared obscure or illuminated. A Or the penitent says: “The darknesses of sins are not made darker by you, but by me, when I wish to excuse sin; but if I confess, you illuminate the night and the darknesses.”

12[Col. 0499A] For you possessed my reins; you received me from my mother’s womb.

C “Reins” signifies bodily strength. Therefore he rightly says that his reins were possessed by the Father, because, standing firm in heavenly righteousness, he knew no sin of the fragile body. By “the womb of my mother” he says that he was received from the bosom of the Synagogue by the Father’s divinity, which in him is one with the Father. For if you wish to understand it of the virginal womb, he is shown by the Lord to have been assumed not only when he emerged from the most chaste womb but also when he was conceived by the Holy Spirit. A Or these are the words of a penitent.

13 I will give thanks to you, because you have been awesomely magnified; your works are marvelous, and my soul knows this exceedingly.

[Col. 0499B] C The Father was wondrously magnified when, at Christ’s passion, the earth trembled, the rocks were split, and the tombs were opened. It was necessary to recognize as wondrous the one whom Christ’s humanity saw to be the most merciful giver of such great benefits. Or the penitent says that God is wondrously and terribly magnified in the conversion of sinners. The following verses may also be expounded of the penitent.

14 My bone was not hidden from you, which you made in secret, nor my substance in the lower parts of the earth.

C By “bone” he signifies the divine mysteries, which before the Lord’s coming were hidden, such as holy baptism and the Lord’s body and blood, which became clear when he came. “The lower parts of the earth” were the practices of the nations. But the substance of God the Savior became known to them when, understanding divinity in him, they believed with devoted minds through apostolic teaching that he was God. The earth, therefore, is the human race. Its upper parts were the Jews, who rightly believed before Christ’s birth; its lower parts were the nations worshiping earth and stones. These have now been made higher through faith.

15 Your eyes saw my unfinished state; and in your book all will be written. Days will be formed, and no one among them.

C He said, in the person of the Church, that the Father saw her unfinished state, because she will be gathered and perfected until the end of the age; but the divinity has already seen what is still being preserved for the distant future. [Col. 0499D] And those who will rejoice in eternal blessedness will be written in the book. “Days will be formed,” that is, the saints in perpetual blessedness. “No one among them”: one must understand “will be formed,” that is, no one will be shapeless or defective in the heavenly homeland, because every weakness of the flesh will be consumed and perish.

16 But your friends, O God, have been exceedingly honored; their dominion has been exceedingly strengthened.

C By “friends” he means the holy apostles. “Exceedingly” means “very greatly.” Their dominion was strengthened, which they received through the Lord’s favor, to such an extent that they deserved to be rams of the flocks and leaders of faithful peoples.

17[Col. 0500A] I will number them, and they will be multiplied above the sand; I rose up, and I am still with you.

C The sand of the sea signifies the Jews because of the aridity of their faith; sand is so called from aridity. Therefore Christ promises that he will number the faithful people, which is found to be more numerous than the Jewish people. “I rose up” means from the repose of sleep. “I am still with you” does not mean that he will ever be separated from him, but that he who is now invisible to us, dwelling at the Father’s right hand in the heavens, will afterward appear to all the nations.

18 If you kill sinners, O God, men of blood, depart from me. 19 For they say in their thoughts: “They will receive their cities in vanity.”

C God kills the sinner when he dies to sin so that he may live to God, as Paul says: “I died to the law, so that I might live to Christ” (Gal. 2). “Men of blood” are those who live carnally and perform the works of blood; to them it is said: “Depart from me.” A C The order of the words, however, seems to be connected in this way: “If you kill sinners, O God, they will receive their cities in vanity,” C that is, if you transfer sinners from evil thoughts to good pursuits, they will receive their former habits and sins, in which they dwelt, in vain—that is, they will reject vain things—and say to those who still remain in those vain and evil things: “Depart from me, because you speak in your thoughts,” that is, you speak in your mind and murmur against those things which have been proclaimed to you by the power of the Holy Spirit. Therefore, because you speak thus in thought against God, depart from me. C “Because you say” means that you murmur against those things which have been proclaimed to you by the power of the Holy Spirit.

20 Did I not hate those who hate you, Lord, and waste away because of your enemies?

C We are rightly commanded to love our adversaries, whom we happen to offend through our own fault. But when God’s enemies are obstinate, they are condemned with appropriate and religious execration, because, although they were created by him and owe him everything by which they live, they nevertheless become rebellious toward their creator. Therefore such people are rightly objects of horror, since they were not mindful of their benefits. “To waste away” is an expression of great sorrow. For we say that those waste away who are afflicted by continual cares and nearly reach the destruction of life as their bodies fail.

21 With perfect hatred I hated them; they became enemies to me.

C Perfect hatred is to love human beings and always hate their vices. For hatred is so called, as it were, from rejection by the mouth. He also says that they became enemies to him because they stood opposed to the Father’s commands, in order to show the unity of his divinity with the Father.

22 Test me, God, and know my heart; question me and know my paths.

C “Test me”: no one can say this except Christ alone, who committed no sins. “Know my heart,” because I do not know how to abandon you in persecution. “Question me” pertains to the most minute inquiry. For he first said, “Know my heart.” One who knows questions sharply and cannot be deceived, because no one questioned by one who knows can deny what he has done. “Paths” pertains to good works, which he continually performed and completed in heavenly holiness.

23 And see whether there is a way of iniquity in me, and lead me in the eternal way.

C Therefore the human substance in Christ rightly asks to be led in the eternal way, since it turned away from the way of iniquity, that is, from demonic actions. When he says, “see whether there is,” understand that this is spoken not in doubt but with the security of knowledge, as though he were saying: “See whether there is,” that is, “You will see that there is not.”

## PRAYER FROM PSALM 138

[Col. 0501B]

God, observer of heaven and earth, at whose death the realms of hell were illuminated, at whose resurrection the multitude of the saints rejoiced, and at whose ascension the host of angels exulted: we ask for the excellent power of such great glory, so that, directed along the eternal way, we may be guarded by that arm with which your honored friends glory with you in heaven. You who live, etc.

# PSALM 139

## SUMMARY OF PSALM 139

C The Church beseeches the Lord to be freed from the wicked devil. It declares that vengeance will come at the future judgment upon those who persecute his poor with deranged assaults.

[Col. 0501C] TT. A psalm of David, for the end.

C “For the end” signifies the Lord Savior, who is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes (Rom. 10). In this psalm he is proclaimed as coming to us in the voice of a herald: a terrifying, almighty, merciful, and exceedingly desirable judge.

1 Deliver me, Lord, from the evil man; rescue me from the unjust man.

C The mother Church, knowing how much her members suffer from the devil’s snares, cries out to the Lord, who alone can overcome his wickedness, that she may be freed from his manifold temptation. She calls the devil “the evil man.” “The unjust man” is the human being who follows the devil. For two epithets could not simultaneously apply to one person, which is prohibited by the rule of eloquence.

2 They who devised iniquities in their heart; all day long they were preparing battles.

C The dangers that are hidden are always more serious. By this he signifies heretics, who burst into sacrilegious conflicts through perverse doctrines. “All day long,” he says, to show that their wickedness is continuous, so that neither weariness nor any length of time might moderate them.

3 They sharpened their tongues like serpents; the venom of asps is under their lips. Diapsalma.

C By “tongues” he signifies the words of heretics, with which they strive to wound the hearts of the faithful. The venom of asps—H because they seem to have words of friendship, but they are full of deadly poison.

4[Col. 0502A] Guard me, Lord, from the hand of the sinner; rescue me from unjust men.

C “The sinner” again signifies the devil, who deceives through many tricks and many snares. His ministers also follow, because what they cannot accomplish secretly by inspiring our minds, they attempt to accomplish publicly through their followers.

5 They who planned to trip my steps; the proud hid a snare for me.

C We are properly said to be tripped when the earth is withdrawn from beneath our feet, so that we fall heavily into dark caverns. The devil does this to us when he prepares pits of sins. “The proud” are heretics, who hasten to deceive peoples with perverse doctrines rather than teach them, and set snares for the holy people when they attempt to bind them with empty riddles.

6 And they stretched out ropes as a snare; beside the path they placed a stumbling block for me. Diapsalma.

C They themselves stretched out ropes, that is, twisted and deceitful objections by which they may capture human understanding, so that they appear to stretch a stumbling block for minds just as a snare is stretched for feet. He says “beside the path” because they capture only those who depart from the straight road of virtues. A snare or rope is placed for this reason: it always tightens its bonds more severely, nor does its embrace slip away with any gentleness, since it encloses those caught in certain knotted loops.

7[Col. 0502C] I said to the Lord, “You are my God”; hear, Lord, the voice of my supplication.

C The Church prays not to be handed over to the worst snares. The Church, called from the nations and shining with the purest faith, confesses the Holy Trinity with most truthful faith and says: “I said to the Lord,” etc. It continues: “Hear, Lord, the voice,” etc. It would have been sufficient to say, “Hear my supplication”; but wishing to make something deeper known, he said, “the voice of my supplication.” For the voice of supplication is the purity of prayer and that silent cry which rises to the Lord. The voice of holy action is the most eloquent cry of the deeds themselves—not known to human beings but known to God alone. Hence it is said to silent Moses, “Why do you cry out to me?” (Exod. 14), and to Cain: “The voice of your brother’s blood cries out to me from the earth” (Gen. 4).

8 Lord, Lord, strength of my salvation; you have overshadowed my head on the day of battle.

C This repetition, “Lord, Lord,” shows the feeling of devout prayer. When it says, “you are the strength of my salvation,” it demonstrates that patience and perseverance in the contest are the Lord’s gift. For *strength* is derived from *greenness* (*viriditas*), which does not know how to wither through any hardship. When the Church says that its head was overshadowed, it signifies the blessed passion of the Lord: he was so overshadowed in it—that is, protected—that neither his spirit endured the disgrace of shame nor his flesh the injury of corruption. “In the day of battle” is rightly said of the day of his passion and death: for when the devil had been conquered and hell broken, the captives were set free, and he returned triumphantly from death.

9 Do not hand over my ÷ desire .. to the sinner: they plotted against me; do not forsake me, lest they be exalted. *Diapsalma.*

C For the desire of this person who fulfills the lusts of the flesh is handed over to the sinner—that is, to the devil. Such a person desires only what the devil wishes, and therefore in his desires he is handed over to the devil for possession. And because the enemies plotted—that is, by forming a plan—against me, I rightly ask, “Lord, do not forsake me.” The most just reason for the petition and its being heard follows: lest the ungodly be exalted in the destruction of the righteous.

10[Col. 0503B] The head of their circuit: The labor of their lips will cover them.

A C God overshadows the head of the righteous, but the labor of their lips covers the head of the wicked. The order of the words is this: “the head of their circuit,” that is, it is the head of their circuit; in other words, the head of the ungodly is the devil, who always goes around seeking someone to devour (1 Peter V). The labor of their lips is a lie uttered by the mouth, which is always laboriously contrived, since it is fashioned by elaborate plotting. Truth is spoken without labor, because it is uttered without difficulty. A Or, the head of their circuit is their pride, which arises from the labor of their lips, that is, from lying.

11 Coals will fall upon them: into the fire you will cast them: [Col. 0503C] They will not endure in miseries.

C The coals of fire are the torments of repentance, although this burning arises from a shower of tears. They are cast into the fire when, already kindled by the flame of charity, they begin to burn with holy works. What happens to them is that they do not remain in the miseries of sins, since they are already transferred to the better side.

12 A talkative man will not be directed on the earth: the unjust man will be seized by evils unto destruction.

C “A talkative man” is one who produces many useless words. He is not directed, because by much speaking he will not escape sin. An unjust man is one who, despising the divine rules, is carried away by the fervor of his own will (Proverbs X). Evils will seize him, because he continually devises what is harmful to himself, since he turns away from the Lord’s commandments.

13 I have known that the Lord will execute judgment for the needy: ÷ and .. vengeance for the poor.

C He will therefore execute judgment for the needy when, in that judgment, he grants them what was promised; and then he avenges the poor when he separates their persecutors from his holy kingdom.

14 Nevertheless, the righteous will confess your name: and the upright will dwell with your face.

H For what is the face of God except Christ, his Son? Except the thought of his divinity? C With the very face of God, the righteous will also dwell eternally, when—as the Apostle says—they will behold him not through a mirror but face to face (1 Corinthians XIII). Observe also that when the righteous suffer persecution, they confess praises to God—for then it is a great virtue to praise God—and the enemy and the tribulation depart more readily; and after this life such people will behold the face of God eternally.

PRAYER FROM PSALM CXXXIX

God, the strength of our salvation, defend your Church from the deadly poison of those who dissent, so that, overshadowed by you, we may never be bound by the snares of the enemy. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, etc.

PSALM CXL

ARGUMENT OF PSALM CXL

C The prophet pleads to be freed from various errors amid worldly activities, lest he fall into the nets of sins.

[Col. 0504B] TT. A psalm of David.

1 Lord, I cried out to you; hear me: attend to my voice when I cry out to you.

C “Lord, I cried out.” Wishing to infuse the human race with the devotion of continual prayer, the prophet appears to have set down two apparently different times. He says, “I cried out,” in the past, which signifies completed prayer; and again, “when I cry out,” which is plainly placed in the future. Thus, just as no time is free from sins, so one must never cease from devout prayers.

2 Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight. The lifting up of my hands is an evening sacrifice.

[Col. 0504C] C “Let my prayer be directed to you like incense,” that is, let my prayer come to you straight, in the fragrance of virtues, possessing no filth or vices. C Incense is the sweet burning of fragrant spices, and spiritually it has this meaning here. H “Incense” means the prayers of the saints (Revelation VIII). C The evening sacrifice perhaps signifies that offering which religious devotion customarily presents to the Lord at the end of life; and therefore let no one despair if, at the last, he wipes away his sins with a fountain of tears. The lifting up of the hands signifies pious works; the lowering of those same hands signifies cessation from good work. Our evening also signifies the time near the end of this life.

3 Set, Lord, a guard over my mouth: and a door of restraint around my lips.

[Col. 0504D] C The prophet asks that he say nothing of such a kind as ought to lead to guilt. A door is so called from “restraining” (*obstando*). The prophet therefore saw that the place from which he knew sin came so easily had to be fortified with great prayers. If through weakness he should sin, at least he prays that he not excuse that sin; hence what follows:

4 Do not incline my heart to words of wickedness: to make excuses for excuses in sins.

C “Words of wickedness” are when someone, after his sin, falsely flees to excuses. For it is the habit of sinners, whenever they have been discovered, first to excuse themselves by some falsehood; and when they have been convicted of that, they assume other excuses along with the sin of falsehood, lest shameless obstinacy ever yield to the truth. At one time they attribute what they do to circumstances, at another to necessity, and at another to other people. This, however, is the greatest vice with which human beings struggle.

5 With people who work iniquity: and I will not share with their chosen ones.

H Here also the prophet asks to be freed from the company of those who work iniquity. For just as the Lord has his chosen saints, so the devil also has his chosen ones, such as the leaders of heretics, who among the rejected are thought to be chosen; and all who are chosen for wickedness are also called the devil’s chosen. C “And I will not share” refers both to the people who work iniquity and to their chosen ones. H Or the first part of this verse should be joined to the preceding verse, so that the sense is: “Do not incline [my heart] to make excuses for excuses in sins with people who work iniquity.”

6 Let the righteous correct me in mercy and rebuke me: but the oil ÷ of the sinner .. will not fatten my head.

C The holy man preferred the rebukes of the righteous to the flatteries of sinners. He indicated what the correction of the righteous is when he said, “in mercy,” since the holy man rebukes not in anger but through love. It is better to be rebuked by the righteous than praised by a sinner. For the oil of the sinner is the flattery of a deceiver and of pretended love; dangerous is the flattery that can exclude a person from the kingdom of God.

7 For still ÷ and .. my prayer is among their good pleasures. Their judges were swallowed up, joined to the rock.

H “For still,” etc.: they remain in their own good pleasures. But I prayed for them that they might be converted. C Or he shows himself still imperfect when, in praying, he wished such things to happen to him as were pleasing to the wicked. According to the first interpretation, Christ prayed to the Father for his enemies, that they might be converted. “They were swallowed up,” that is, the judges of the Jews—or of the Gentiles, such as Plato and Aristotle—or of the heretics, when they are joined by faith to the rock, that is, to Christ, and separated from the devil. A Or “joined,” that is, compared: philosophers appear to say something, but when their writings are compared with divine Scripture, they are swallowed up, are nothing, and lie there like foolish things.

8 They will hear my words, for they have prevailed: as the thickness of the earth has been taken away upon the earth.

C He says that his words were heard by heretics and tyrants; the text of the present book expresses these words, since in so many places they are rebuked so that they ought to be corrected. After being so often admonished, they were therefore able to recognize the will of God. “The thickness of the earth” is the pride of tyrants, which raged against the holy martyrs.

9 Our bones have been scattered beside hell, because to you, Lord, Lord, my eyes are turned: in you I have hoped; do not take away my soul.

C The prophet says that the bones are the martyrs, because it is clear that they are the strongest supports of the Christian faith. He says “beside hell”; observe the propriety of the words: he does not say “into hell.” For although they appear to die by the common lot, eternal life is nevertheless granted to them. “Do not take away my soul,” that is, from your good things; but let my hope be in you, and let my eyes always attend to you.

10 Guard me from the snare that they have set for me: and from the scandals of those who work iniquity.

C By “snares” and “scandals” the prophet has briefly embraced all the evils of the world. He asks to be guarded from them, lest he be deceived by their plots. H The demons also continually set snares for us, for vices are near to virtues. They set a snare in almsgiving: if I do it so that I may be seen. Nets are set for deer, and the holy are deer, leaping over thorns, lofty with their horns, [Col. 0506B] and killing serpents.

11 Sinners will fall into his net: I alone am until I pass over.

C Nets are so called as though they were things that hold fast. He falls into the devil’s nets who does not cut away his sins. He is “alone” who does not walk joined to wicked people—that is, bound to them—who confesses the Holy Trinity as one God, and who places his hope in God alone. “Until I pass over,” that is, for as long as I remain in this world; for the blessed are said to pass through this age like travelers, since they are not held in it by any worldly pleasure. A Or Christ says, “I am alone,” that is, “I am solitary until I pass over,” that is, until I die. For then, when the grain of wheat has died in the earth, it does not remain alone but bears much fruit (John XII), because afterward many believed and the whole earth belonged to Christ.

PRAYER FROM PSALM CXL

Set, Lord, a guard over our mouth, so that we may not utter empty things; and, corrected by your mercy, may we be protected from every scandal of iniquities. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, etc.

PSALM CXLI

ARGUMENT OF PSALM CXLI

C Christ cries out to the Father, setting forth the deceits of the Jewish persecution; he begs to be freed from hell, since the faith of all the saints depended upon his resurrection.

[Col. 0506D] TT. An understanding of David when he was in the cave: a prayer.

C The subject of the psalm is contained in the present title. David, son of Jesse, fled from Saul the ruler, and while he was hiding in a cave he prayed (1 Samuel XXIV); this signified that the Lord Christ in the body would do the same before his passion. H Since the title says “an understanding of David,” it shows spiritually that David and the psalm are to be understood. Saul, therefore, spiritually signifies the devil. The cave is this world, into which the devil introduces nothing good, but only filth and putrefaction. For it is a dark cave, and this world is dark with sins; nor do the saints possess in it the perfect light that will exist in the other world. Nevertheless, Christ came as light into this world and illuminated it in part. And just as David was hidden in Saul’s cave, so the Lord Jesus was in this world under the devil and suffered persecution like David.

1 With my voice I cried out to the Lord: with my voice I entreated the Lord.

H “With my voice to the Lord”: he speaks all these words in bodily humility, so that he may show himself to be a true human being. C And lest the cry be understood as momentary, he added, “I entreated,” which is carried out through repeated supplication. For to entreat is to supplicate frequently.

2 I pour out my prayer in his sight: ÷ and .. I declare my tribulation before him.

C How pure, how gracious is the prayer that was poured out in the sight of the Father like the abundance of a transparent spring? Certainly it was poured out not so that it might flow down to the depths, but so that his prayer might reach the height of heavenly mercy. He declares his tribulations before the Father so that he may obtain pardon for our sins. Note that in these two verses prayer is made in four ways, according to the Apostle’s exhortation, where he commands that petitions, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings first be made (1 Timothy II).

3 When my spirit failed within me: you knew my paths.

C What he says, “when my spirit failed,” must be understood with reference to the members of the body. Or it may be read this way: “when my spirit failed,” etc., depends on what precedes, as though he were saying: “I declare my tribulation before him when my spirit failed within me.” H The Father knew the paths, that is, the teachings that he taught.

4 On this way on which I was walking: they hid a snare for me.

C The devil hides a snare beside the way in order to deceive those who presume to turn away from straight paths. But since Christ never departed from his holiness, it was necessary that he suffer weak temptations on the very way of righteousness, as is read in the Gospel.

5 I looked to the right and saw: and there was no one who knew me.

C “I looked to the right” indicates the time when he was going to the cross, because he was unable to see any of the faithful there. They were not seen standing at the right because they had been scattered by bodily fear (Matthew IV). “There was no one who knew me”: namely, the divinity that willingly endured all these things in the flesh it had assumed.

6 Flight has perished from me: ÷ and .. there is no one who seeks my soul.

C Flight perished from Christ when he allowed himself to be killed by the hands of the wicked. No one sought his soul when no consolation was offered him; he was left alone for his passion, though he was about to die for the salvation of all.

7 I cried out to you, Lord: I said, You are my hope, my portion in the land of the living.

C He cried out and placed his hope in the Lord when he said: “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit” (Luke XXIII). “My portion”: the passage in which he said to the thief, “Amen, I say to you: Today you will be with me in paradise” (ibid.), proves this in particular. That is, in the land of the living; for paradise is the land of the living, which only the blessed will enter.

8 Attend to my supplication: for I have been humbled exceedingly.

C He rightly says, “I have been humbled exceedingly,” because he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant; and he was humbled still further, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross (Philippians II). For how could he have been crucified unless he had humbled himself by assuming our nature, he who created heaven and earth?

9 Deliver me from those who persecute ÷ me .., for they have grown strong against me.

[Col. 0508B] C He prays in order to show reverence to the Father, who was able to deliver him. He therefore prays to be delivered by divine power from the Jews who persecuted him. They were so much stronger in bodily terms that they laid hands on him and rejoiced at his death; but those wretched men did this without considering the power of the divine authority in him.

10 Lead my soul out of prison to confess your name: the righteous await me until you repay me.

H C Saying, “Lead out of prison,” that is, from hell, he asks the Father, in the respect in which he died and was afterward transferred from the lowest depths to the heights, swiftly to lead his soul out of hell’s prison to the resurrection of the body. And this is “to confess his name,” for this confession of praise offered to the Father is shown by the faithful when it is established that he was brought out of hell’s prison by the miracle of the resurrection. “The righteous await,” H that is, the apostles or the other saints. “Until you repay me” the glory that I had before the world existed (John XVII). C Or, “until you repay” resurrection in return for the passion. The apostles and others await this during those three days.

PRAYER FROM PSALM CXLI

Entreating you, Lord, with humble voice, we ask for your mercy, so that, helped by you, our hope, we may receive a portion with your chosen ones in the land of the living. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, etc.

PSALM CXLII

ARGUMENT OF PSALM CXLII

[Col. 0508D] C The prophet, supplicating on behalf of every believer that the Lord’s mercy come to his aid, asks the Lord Christ not to enter into judgment with his servant; he begs to reach forgiveness swiftly, lest he be handed over to the enemies’ snares.

TT. A psalm of David, ÷ when his son was persecuting him ...

C David signifies Christ; his persecuting son signifies the Jewish people, or Judas the betrayer.

1 Lord, hear my prayer: listen with your ears to my supplication in your truth: hear me in your righteousness.

H “Lord, hear”: words humble and full of humility and mercy, which deserve to reach the Lord’s ears. C For his truth and righteousness consist in this: that he not dispute with the one who begs, nor drag into judgment the one who first condemns himself here. The Lord brings the proud to examination, those who think they possess good causes.

2 And do not enter into judgment with your servant: for no living person will be justified in your sight.

C Nor should it trouble us that it is said to the judge, “Do not enter into judgment with your servant.” H However just someone may be, however perfect, he cannot enter into the Lord’s judgment unless it has been tempered with mercy; for the stars are not clean in his sight. C “Every living person” signifies every human being, even any infant not yet baptized, as Job says: “No one is clean before you, not even an infant of one day” (Job XV); that is, no one can be free except through divine grace. Therefore neither Abraham, nor Isaac, nor Jacob will be justified in the sight of God.

3 ÷ For .. the enemy has pursued my soul: he has humbled my life on the earth.

H C “The enemy” is the devil, who persecutes the human race. C He is humbled on the earth whose life is polluted by carnal pleasures, not by praiseworthy humility but by sinful deviation.

4 He placed me in dark places like the dead of the age; and my spirit was distressed within me: my heart was troubled within me.

H Sinners are placed in dark deeds, and they are the dead of the age. But they are “like the dead” while they begin to repent; for he is not yet dead, because he stands in repentance. But if someone who sins does not practice repentance, he is the dead of the age—not “like the dead,” but completely dead—until he practices repentance. The spirit is distressed because it is written: “If you merely sigh over your sins, you will be saved.” The heart is troubled, that is, my conscience, because I have sinned. C Or, the distressed spirit indicates the nearness of danger; and the troubled heart testifies that human wisdom has been confounded, so that henceforth he might place his hope in the Lord, since he had no confidence in his own strength.

5 I remembered the days of old; I meditated on all your works: [Col. 0509D] I meditated on the deeds of your hands.

C His heart had rightly been troubled, because he remembered his former enormous sins. Those ancient days are the days darkened by the antiquity of the old person. He calls the works of the Lord those by which he founded heaven and earth, did good to the patriarchs, and led the Hebrew people through the sea. He says that he repeatedly recalled these things through memory and reading, so that the sweetness of reading might drive out the bitterness of the world. Let us believe that this example was set down as the greatest remedy, so that a similar medicine may also save us.

6 I stretched out my hands to you: my soul is like dry land to you, without water. *Diapsalma.*

C Here, by the stretching out of the hands, he designated Christ on the cross. Hence also whoever prays with outstretched hands imitates the Redeemer’s cross. Although the cross was imposed on Christ by the faithless Jews as punishment, it was nevertheless granted to believers for salvation. A comparison follows, in which he says that his soul desires God as dry land desires abundant rains. He says “to you,” that is, not to another: such is my soul; that is, it clings thirsting to God alone.

7 Hear me quickly, Lord: my spirit has failed.

C This penitent asks that the rain of mercy come to his aid most swiftly; and, so that he might be heard more quickly, he says that his spirit has failed within him. This happens to those who are weighed down by the burden of various passions.

8[Col. 0510B] Do not turn your face away from me: and I will become like those who descend into the pit.

C It is consistent with God’s mercy that he look upon the humble, while he despises the hearts of the proud. Here “the pit” signifies hell. He therefore asks that he not become like the proud, he who bewails his sins here; for if he becomes like them, he too will descend with them into the pit.

9 Make your mercy known to me in the morning: for I have hoped in you.

C “Mercy made known” means the clemency of God, widely known throughout the world, by which he grants and forgives those who entreat him in affliction. “Morning” designates the time of forgiveness; for after the night of sins, morning is rightly named when guilt is loosened. He also adds the reason for being heard: “because I have hoped in you,” who cannot deceive the one who hopes. Or, “morning” points to the time of Christ’s resurrection.

10 Make known to me the way in which I should walk: for I have lifted up my soul to you.

C When he asks God to make the way known to him, he shows that this way is unknown to human beings. The lamp and light of the one who illuminates every person shows this path, as he said above: “I will give you understanding, and I will instruct you in this way in which you shall walk.” The prophet therefore asks that he be shown the way of salvation, so that he may always know it and it may never depart from his heart. A solemn confession follows: “for I have lifted up my soul to you,” etc. For what we ask is made worthy of being granted if we do not incline our soul toward the world but always lift it toward God.

11 Rescue me from my enemies, Lord; I have fled to you: teach me to do your will, for you are my God ÷ ...

C Our enemies are the demons, who continually surround the faithful so that they may take away from them the hope of divinity. He flees to the one who obeys his commands. “Teach me”: he did not wish to err at all, since he desired to be the disciple of so great a teacher and to obey his will. He adds the reason and explanation: “for you are my God”; therefore I rightly ask this of you, most merciful one.

12[Col. 0511A] Let your good Spirit lead me in a straight land: because of your name, Lord, you will give me life in your righteousness.

H C “The good Spirit” is designated by this name as God the Holy Spirit; for it is written: “No one is good except God alone” (Matthew XIX). Therefore, if the Holy Spirit is called good and is God, this necessarily follows. C He leads us in a straight land when he subjects our body to his rules. Or the straight land is in the future age, where the upright will walk. “Because of your name,” etc.: although Christ gives everything freely, it belongs to his righteousness to justify and enliven those who entreat him. Therefore he does not say “in my righteousness” but “in yours,” because it is not through my merits but through the grace of Christ’s name.

13 You will lead my soul out of tribulation: [Col. 0511B] and in your mercy you will destroy my enemies.

C Holy souls are led out of tribulation as from prisons when, forgiveness having been granted, they are ordered to leave this age in which they suffer tribulation. Enemies are destroyed in mercy when, through earnest contrition, they are withdrawn from criminal thoughts. This applies to those who escape their deserved punishments through the remedy of supplication.

14 And you will destroy all those who trouble my soul: for I am your servant.

C Here he says that the devil and all the ungodly who die in their obstinacy are to be destroyed in the future judgment. They had previously troubled righteous men because they knew them to be servants of God; and those who persecute innocent men precisely because they know them to be God’s servants must necessarily perish in the judgment.

PRAYER FROM PSALM CXLII

God, who made the joy of your sacred resurrection known in the morning, when, returning from hell, you filled with joys the earth that you had left in darkness: we ask the ineffable majesty of your power that, just as then you made the apostolic company rejoice in the sacred *anastasis*—resurrection—so you may graciously illumine this Church, which with outstretched hands implores your mercy, with the splendor of heavenly radiance. You who, with the Father and the Son, etc.

PSALM CXLIII

ARGUMENT OF PSALM CXLII

C This Davidic battle is set forth beforehand to signify the contest of the Lord the Savior: just as David struck down Goliath by combat with a stone weapon, so by the rock—which is Christ—the devil’s strength was to be conquered.

TT. David ÷ against Goliath ...

1 Blessed is my God, who trains my hands for battle: ÷ and .. my fingers for war.

H C He certainly means spiritual, not bodily, war, in which the soul of the righteous invisibly struggles against demons and carnal passions. C The hands signify action; the fingers signify saving counsels, which spring forth from our heart like rays, while they strive with a certain subtlety to secure necessary matters. [Col. 0512A] Sometimes the fingers also indicate the Trinity, as in the passage: “Who weighed the mass of the earth with three fingers” (Isaiah XL); sometimes the Holy Spirit, as in the passage: “Moses received two tablets written with the finger of God” (Exodus XXXIV).

2 My mercy and my refuge: my protector and my deliverer.

C The Lord showed mercy to David when he chose him, the last of his brothers, through Samuel for royal elevation (1 Samuel XVI). “Refuge”: when he gave him the counsel to strike down his enemy with a stone, since he could not do so with a sword. “Protector”: when he caused him to be received by Saul as a son-in-law. “Deliverer”: when he rescued him from the danger of the king’s anger.

3 My protector, and in him I hoped: who subjects my people beneath me.

[Col. 0512B] C “Protector”: when, while hiding in the cave, he received the right of vengeance against Saul the king. “And in him I hoped”: the holy man knows that one must never cease from such hope. “You subject peoples”: because he was destined to rule over many peoples.

4 Lord, what is a human being, that you have made yourself known to him: ÷ or .. what is a son of man, that you regard him?

C “What is a human being?” must be pronounced as a question and an expression of contempt, as though it meant: mere dust, which has no firmness when the wind blows. “That you have made yourself known to him,” that is, you have revealed to the upright in faith the immeasurable mystery of the Godhead through the flesh assumed. In the same way, “or what is a son of man?” must be asked, and the answer likewise supplied: “that you regard him,” certainly among your sheep, in the number of the predestined.

5 A human being has become like vanity: his days pass away like a shadow.

C He briefly explains what he said above: “What is a human being?” When Adam was created, he was simple, pure, truthful, and immortal; but after he sinned, he became like vanity, since he became changeable and mortal. For we call that “vain” which, falling away from its substance, vanishes into thin air, like a shadow or smoke. Hence he added: “His days pass away like a shadow.” Just as a shadow passes, so human life after Adam’s sin passes away, unless it is restored through confession.

6 Lord, incline your heavens and descend: touch the mountains, and they will smoke.

[Col. 0512D] C The inclination of the heavens occurred when the power and honor of the heavenly beings descended to humanity, namely, the Son of God. Here he calls the proud “mountains,” whom the Lord touched when he granted them compunction. “They will smoke” when they weep over their sins with frequent sighs; for thick smoke is vomited from the mouth when a person is moved to lamentation.

7 Flash forth lightning and scatter them: send out your arrows and trouble them.

C He gave flashes of lightning when, through the preaching of the prophets, he infused the light of his truth into sinners living in darkness. “He scattered” means that he dispersed them, so that those who had previously been worshipers of idols might afterward flee to the enclosure of the Church.
