He calls the apostles “arrows,” because by the truth of their preaching, like feathered darts, they pierced the breasts of human beings. “And you will trouble them,” namely, with the good disturbance of contrition, because those who were first troubled in this way will afterward be joyful. “Them” is to be referred to the mountains.

8 Send your hand from on high: rescue me and deliver me from many waters: and from the hand of foreign sons.

C Here he turns his words to the Father. He calls the Lord the Savior “the hand,” whom he begs to come from on high—that is, from the height of power where he reigns with the Father in equality of power and unity of substance—to free the world. “From the waters,” that is, from peoples surging like waves and stirred up like a most savage storm. “From the hand of sons”: from those who do not know how to spare the faithful, because they are generated from the devil, who oppose the sons of God. The devil’s sons are rightly called foreign to the sons of God, because they have no share with them in the inheritance of heaven.

9 Their mouth has spoken vanity: and their right hand is a right hand of iniquity.

C Their mouth speaks vanity because they presume to disagree with the divine rules; for everything contrary to the truth is vain. The right hand of the reprobate is their prosperity, from which, lifted up, they assume permission to sin.

10 God, I will sing a new song to you: on a ten-stringed psaltery I will sing praise to you.

C Christ’s song is rightly called new, because, since he was not received by the Jews—to whom he had been promised as one who would come—he passed over to the Gentiles. It is also new that he deigns to nourish us with his body and blood. The ten-stringed psaltery is the Decalogue given to the Hebrew tribes.

11 You give salvation to kings; you redeemed David your servant: rescue me from the evil sword.

C “Kings” signifies righteous and truthful people who rule their bodies. He gives these people salvation when he makes them free from vices. “You redeemed” refers to deliverance from the battle with Goliath, or, spiritually, from vices. “From the evil sword”: for the devil’s sword is evil because it separates from good things; Christ’s sword, however, is good because it separates from evil things.

12 And rescue me from the hand of foreign sons: their mouth has spoken vanity: and their right hand is a right hand of iniquity.

[Col. 0513D] C We have already discussed this verse. He repeats it in order to make wicked people more detestable by the very repetition; and now the words are to be understood especially of heretics. Although what follows, just as what precedes, is true when understood literally, nevertheless, since the literal sense is clear, certain things must be gathered mystically.

13 Their sons are like young plants: from their youth.

C He calls “sons” those who are generated by the preaching of corrupt doctrine. They are compared with young plants because they did not flourish through any ancient preaching handed down by the Fathers, but sprang up through new errors—errors handed down by their own fathers. H For the planting of the heretics is not old but young. It did not arise from the old Law, nor from the prophets, nor from the apostles, but from new teachers.

14 Their daughters are adorned: encircled with ornaments like the likeness of a temple.

H Their “daughters”—that is, the words of the heretics—are adorned, that is, decorated by secular wisdom; but because they are daughters, not sons, they possess no strength. “Encircled with ornaments like the likeness of a temple”: he beautifully said “the likeness of a temple,” for they do not possess the true Church or temple, but only the likeness of a Church. C For a likeness does not possess truth; it bears the image of some existing thing.

15 Their storehouses are full: bursting forth from this ÷ into .. that.

[Col. 0514B] C Storehouses are what ordinary people call storerooms, and they signify the hearts of heretics, where specimens of various things, or banquets of doctrines, are stored; from there they emit various and most evil eruptions. If you defeat them by authority, they turn to perverse interpretations. When they have also been overcome there, with the Lord’s help, they turn to the tricks and slanders of sophists. Thus they turn from one side to another, always wandering and unstable, because they cannot possess the root of truth.

16 Their sheep are fertile, abundant in their exits: their oxen are fat.

C According to the letter, these people are said to have fertile flocks, while they themselves are taught to be barren in faith. “Abundant” is derived from *unda*, “wave,” as though meaning overflowing. He also did not say that the very flocks they are seen to possess are in their entrances, but in their exits, because everything goes out from them when they themselves too are shown to be destined to perish. H He also beautifully said, “their oxen are fat,” whose god is their belly and whose glory is in their shame (Philippians III).

17 There is no breach in the wall: nor passage, nor cry in their streets.

H “There is no breach”: for it is difficult to find an ignorant heretic. They are all teachers, instructed in secular knowledge and fortified by the doctrines of the apostles. If they dispute with you, their words are brief and enclosed in such artful speech that it is difficult to escape from them. For when they have bound and enclosed you with their syllogisms, and have woven a wall, as it were, out of their syllogism, you are held enclosed; you cannot get out. There is no breach and no passage. When you have agreed with them and have been enclosed there, you will be in their streets and on the broad way that leads to hell, and not on the narrow way that leads to life (Matthew VII), which is the passage of the saints. Nor is there in the streets of the heretics the cry of Jesus, who calls everyone to himself; it is on the narrow way.

18 They called ÷ the people to whom these things belong blessed: Blessed is the people whose Lord is their God.

H Many, not knowing better, consider such people blessed and say, “Blessed is the people to whom these things belong.” We, however, should say, “Blessed is the people whose Lord is their God.” For that person is blessed who possesses Christ in place of all riches, loves him, and rules over him.

[Col. 0515A]

## PRAYER FROM PSALM 143

Teach us, Lord, by spiritual weapons to resist harmful faults, lest, subjected to worldly vanity, we be driven from the dominion of your authority. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, etc.

# PSALM 144

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM 144

C The prophet explains the praise of the Lord through various accounts.

**Title.** A praise of David.

### 1 I will exalt you, my God and king: And I will bless your name forever and ever ÷ of eternity ...

[Col. 0515B] C “I will exalt you” means: I will make known what you are by preaching. For how could God be thought to become higher through some praise, when divine perfection cannot be increased? H Yet I believe you to be equal to the Father. C “My king”: this is a profession of faith, since he said that he was ruled by the one whom he knew he served with a pure mind. To bless the name, however, is to entreat through the grace of psalmody; and whoever does this will also deserve to praise him in eternity. Therefore it adds, “forever and ever,” where there is no end.

### 2 Every day I will bless you: And I will praise your name forever and ever ÷ of eternity ...

C Whoever blesses God here every day will praise him there, in that single eternal day which is to come, with the blessed in continual [Col. 0515C] rejoicing.

### 3 Great is the Lord and exceedingly praiseworthy: And of his greatness there is no end.

H “Great is the Lord”: because he is great without end and praiseworthy without end. C His power is inexplicable, his mercy incomprehensible, his wisdom ineffable; his true definition is that he has no end in the praises of the saints.

### 4 Generation and generation will praise your works: And they will declare your power.

C “Generation and generation” should be applied to two peoples: one is the people of the Hebrews, the other is from the nations. For they are the ones who have received the Lord’s benefits, and rightly declare his power by praising him.

### 5 They will speak of the magnificence of the glory of your holiness: [Col. 0515D] And they will recount your wonders.

H These two peoples proclaim with devout speech his magnificence and the wonders that Christ works daily in the Church.

### 6 And they will speak of the power of your awesome deeds: And they will recount your greatness.

H Christ’s power is awesome when he takes vengeance on the ungodly, as in the case of Pharaoh. His greatness is shown when the righteous are delivered, as Israel was frequently delivered from its adversaries.

### 7 They will pour forth the memory of the abundance of your sweetness: And they will exult in your righteousness.

H They will pour forth the sweetness of Christ, with which he has deigned to cherish [Col. 0516A] them. “And they will exult in your righteousness”: by which he will take vengeance on the ungodly.

### 8 The Lord is compassionate and merciful: Patient and greatly merciful.

C That he is called merciful is a power of his very nature; that he is compassionate is the reason for salvation in view of our weakness. “Patient”: because through patience he bears human transgressions, for which we ought to have been punished. “Greatly merciful”: as he himself says, “I do not desire the death of the sinner.”

### 9 The Lord is sweet to all: And his compassions are over all his works.

C What could be more magnificent than that he is sweet to all, since nevertheless only those with devoted minds have tasted his gifts? But you ask, “Why then does he condemn sinners who have not done his works?” His mercy is said to be over all his [Col. 0516B] works—that is, God’s works. Through mercy he crowns what his grace works in us; but he condemns what is constructed through the devil’s plotting. Therefore the works of the Lord are always chosen, whereas our works, or the devil’s, are without doubt condemned.

### 10 Let all your works confess to you, Lord: And let your saints bless you.

H “Let all your works confess to you, Lord,” namely, so that through the saints, who continually bless and praise you, you may be understood to be the author and creator of all things. C Or all works—even stones and things without sensation—proclaim God their maker through their marvelous ordering.

### 11 They will speak of the glory of your kingdom: And they will speak of your power.

[Col. 0516C] H “They will speak of the glory of your kingdom,” that is, they will proclaim it, so that you may be loved and glorified by all. “And they will speak of your power,” so that you may be feared by all. H C Thus all created things indicate how much glory is owed to him who created them with unimaginable and incomprehensible wisdom, and they display his infinite power.

### 12 So that they may make your power known to the children of men: And the glory of the magnificence of your kingdom.

C Through holy preaching, the power of God and the glory of his kingdom have been made known, lest, if he were unknown, he perhaps be sought less. His power was made known when the apostles performed various miracles after invoking his name.

### 13 Your kingdom is the kingdom of all ages: [Col. 0516D] And your dominion is in every generation and generation.

H “Your kingdom is the kingdom of all”: for all ages revolve under the dominion of your kingdom. C Or, it does not last for a period of time like the other kingdoms of the world, but throughout the whole duration of the world. And not only throughout that duration, but also afterward, eternally. Hence the same statement is repeated more clearly: “and your dominion,” that is, the eternal perpetuity that remains in every generation and generation. A Or, “the kingdom of all ages, and in every generation and generation,” is the heavenly kingdom, where from every generation and age there will be one eternal generation and one kingdom, alone glorious eternally.

### 14 [Col. 0517A] ÷ The Lord is faithful in all his ways ..: And holy in all his works.

H “The Lord is faithful in all his words,” since he fulfilled everything that he spoke through the prophets. “Holy,” so that, just as he is holy, we too, who are his works, may be made holy in him.

### 15 The Lord lifts up all who fall: And raises all who have been thrown down.

C For he lifts up those who are falling, although they have not yet fallen completely. He raises those who have been thrown down, who are known already to have suffered a ruinous fall. And rightly he is said to do these things, since we are defended by his guardianship lest we fall; but so that, once prostrate, we may be able to rise, we are likewise lifted up by his power.

### 16 [Col. 0517B] The eyes of all hope in you: And you give them food at the proper time.

H “The eyes of all,” that is, the inward sight of the saints, receives in that future time the rewards that it awaits. C Or this may also be understood of all things: then “food” should be understood as the sustenance appropriate to each thing. Some seek bodily things, others spiritual things, but for all of them there is one food, the provision that is distributed.

### 17 ÷ You open .. your hand: And you fill every living creature with blessing.

H He opens his hand and fills every living creature—that is, every soul—with his blessing: the soul that has endured curses and the reproaches of the world for his name. [Col. 0517C] C Or, because all food is in his hand, by his hand we understand his power, in which the life of all creatures is established and continues to exist. But it is better to understand only the rational creature, which truly is capable of being blessed.

### 18 The Lord is just in all his ways: And holy in all his works.

C The Lord is truly just because, when he chastises us, he acts equitably, restoring what is due to sins. “Ways” refer to disposition; “work” refers to effect among us. In him, however, willing is the same as doing, and disposing the same as commanding. “Holy” signifies one who is also pious, patient, and the giver of every good, since whatever is brought about by him is completed with the praise [Col. 0517D] of virtues.

### 19 The Lord is near to all who call upon him: + To all who call upon him .. in truth.

H The Lord is near to those who call upon him in faith and action, as he himself says: “I am a God who is near, and not a God who is far away.” C He is called near—that is, close—when he is favorable; when angry, he is distant. For his presence is always and everywhere. “If I ascend into heaven, you are there,” and so forth (Psalm 138). But since those also call upon him who desire the fulfillment of their vain and harmful desires, it is added, “in truth,” because the one who truly calls upon him is the one who asks from him for what he himself taught us to request and knows to be beneficial.

### 20 [Col. 0518A] He will do the will of those who fear him: And he will hear their prayer. And he will save them.

H The Lord does the will of those who fear him when he delivers those who beseech him with a pure heart either from the devil’s instigation or from the heat of sin.

### 21 The Lord guards all who love him: And he will destroy all sinners.

H The Lord guards those who love him and who have preferred his love to worldly loves. But he will destroy those who have placed the love of the world before love for him. C By saying that he will destroy all sinners, he means those who persist in their obstinacy.

### 22 My mouth will speak the praise of the Lord: [Col. 0518B] And let all flesh bless his holy name forever and ever ÷ of eternity ...

H “My mouth will speak the praise of the Lord,” now and in the future time of recompense. “And let all flesh,” that is, the whole body of the Church, bless his name. We are that body, and we ought to praise, bless, exalt, and proclaim the Lord. He says “his mouth,” meaning the secret place of the heart, from which the Prophet knew that he was gladly heard. He also said “flesh” by synecdoche, meaning the whole human being.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM 144

Ruler of all the saints, Lord, who provide spiritual food for every soul at the proper time, grant us to bless you continually and confidently exalt your power with your elect. [Col. 0518C] Through our Lord Jesus Christ, etc.

# PSALM 145

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM 145

C The prophet says that one must place no confidence in human beings, but place all hope in the Lord, lest anything be asked of him half-heartedly if someone else is believed able to provide it.

**Title.** Alleluia.

### 1 Praise the Lord, my soul: I will praise the Lord in my life; I will sing psalms to my God as long as I exist.

C The psalmist gently urges the soul to praise the Lord, so that, having dismissed superfluous thoughts, [Col. 0518D] it may devote all its strength exclusively to this task. “I will praise,” he said, to indicate the future time, when this destiny will be shared by angels and righteous human beings. “I will sing psalms as long as I exist,” namely, in the present, insofar as this concerns good works. H See also: when we act justly, we exist; when we sin, we cease to exist. Hence he says, “I will praise as long as I exist,” because “there is no praise in the mouth of a sinner” (Sirach 15).

### 2 Do not trust in princes: In the sons of men, in whom there is no salvation.

C “Do not trust,” that is, do not presume either upon demons, who are called princes, or upon human beings. For there is only one Son of Man who grants salvation to each person. H Understand this also of the powers of the world: do not trust in the emperor, nor in prefects, nor in the judges of the world, who are sons of men and in whom there is [Col. 0519A] no salvation.

### 3 His spirit will go forth and return to his earth: On that day all their thoughts will perish.

C He gives the reason why one must not trust in these people. Here we should understand “spirit” as the soul. When it has gone forth from the body’s enclosure, the flesh returns to the earth from which it took its beginning. Therefore he added “its own,” because it was produced from there. On that day—that is, at the time of death—human thoughts will perish, though previously they had extended themselves into various pursuits. H Then also all confidence in princes and human beings will perish, as will the thoughts of those who had hoped in them.

### 4 [Col. 0519B] Blessed is the one whose helper is the God of Jacob: His hope is in the Lord his God, who made heaven and earth, the sea and all that is in them.

C Israel—that is, “a man seeing God,” a name suitably applied to all the elect—is a helper to those who, by his gift, strive to ascend the steps of virtue. “Who made heaven and earth”: what could be more magnificent than to have made heaven and earth and all that is in them? H Therefore the one who made heaven and earth—in comparison with which the human being, according to the condition of the flesh, is like an ant—can free the human being whom he made. Therefore our hope is rightly in him.

### 5 He keeps truth forever; he executes judgment for those suffering wrong; [Col. 0519C] he gives food to the hungry.

C “He keeps truth”: he is the Lord Jesus Christ. “He executes judgment,” because he is the true judge and eternal governor, and he avenges the wrong suffered by the afflicted. “And he gives food to the hungry,” that is, to those who hunger to hear the word of God. H If understood literally, he also gives food for bodies; he gives food—his body—in the sacrament; finally, he gives food, heavenly teaching, but only to the hungry. Such a one also sets prisoners free.

### 6 The Lord sets prisoners free. The Lord gives sight to the blind.

H C “The Lord sets free”: those who were previously bound in their sins were later converted to Christ and set free through [Col. 0519D] him. “The Lord gives sight to the blind”: C all vicious people are blind, because they are entangled in the darkness of sins. He alone gives them light, who enlightens every person.

### 7 The Lord raises those who have been thrown down: The Lord loves the righteous.

C “The Lord raises”: this too is beyond doubt, because Christ raises those who have been thrown down. For while the devil casts down, the Lord lifts up. And who is it whose role it is to love the righteous, except the one who is able to place them in eternal blessedness?

### 8 The Lord guards the strangers; he will receive the orphan and the widow: And he will destroy the way of sinners.

C “The Lord guards the strangers,” that is, those who have fled from Babylon [Col. 0520A]—the city of the devil—to Jerusalem—the city of God. He calls “orphans and widows” those who look toward the Lord with a pure mind, deprived of human consolation. Christ receives them in order to vindicate them, and he will destroy the devil, who is the way of sinners, just as Christ is the way of the righteous, and all who imitate him on that way.

### 9 The Lord will reign forever; your God, O Zion, from generation to generation.

C Then he will reign perfectly in the saints, when what is written is fulfilled: “God will be all in all” (Colossians 3). Although he reigns in the saints here, he does not yet reign perfectly, because their hearts are sometimes occupied by empty thoughts. “In Zion,” that is, in the Church in the future blessedness: he himself will reign, with it and in it, who is blessed forever. H Or, [Col. 0520B] he will reign in the generation of the Jews and the generation of Christians; or in this generation of the Church and the generation to come in heaven.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM 145

Glorious, almighty God, in whom the souls of the blessed place the whole confidence of their hope, grant us that, enlightened by your help, we may continually love you with a pure mind. Through our Lord Jesus, etc.

# PSALM 146

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM 146

C The prophet urges the devout people to praise the Lord, who grants beneficial gifts to those who beseech him, since those who trust in their own strength cannot please [Col. 0520C] him.

**Title.** ÷ Alleluia ...

### 1 Praise the Lord, for the psalm is good: May praise be pleasing + and beautiful .. to our God.

H “Praise the Lord”: he did not say “the psalm is good,” but simply “good,” that is, it is good to sing psalms and praise the Lord. But you should know that here Jerome followed not our translation but the Gallican one, which has, “For the psalm is good.” He says that one should sing not with the voice but with the heart. For how many have a good voice, yet, because they are sinners, sing badly? C Praise is pleasing to the Lord when voice and life come together in one fellowship. For what sort of thing is it for a psalm to speak of chastity while the singer does not withdraw from obscenity? Thus what is known to struggle against itself in contrary opposition cannot be properly received by the [Col. 0520D] Lord. H Therefore the one who sings in heart and conscience sings well; praise becomes pleasing to God not through the voice but through conscience.

### 2 The Lord builds Jerusalem: He will gather the dispersions of Israel.

C The Lord builds the city of Jerusalem when, gathering the dispersions of Israel—who are known to dwell throughout the whole world—he constructs the heavenly city from living stones, as it is written: “And he will send his angels with a trumpet and a loud voice, and he will gather his elect from the four corners of the earth” (Matthew 24). H Or he is already building it, while he heals the brokenhearted and does the other things that follow.

### 3 [Col. 0521A] He heals the brokenhearted: And binds up their wounds.

C When the heavenly physician finds the hearts of penitents broken by severe affliction, he binds and strengthens them—as though covering them with a bandage of his compassion—and leads them to the firmest hope of healing.

### 4 He numbers the multitude of the stars: And calls them all by name.

C He numbers the stars, that is, holy men. For they shine like stars in the night of this age, because they have deserved to be gathered among the number of the saints. We also know that God can call the saints by name when we read that they are enrolled in heaven. Or this may also be understood literally of the material stars of the firmament [Col. 0521B].

### 5 Great is our Lord, and great is his power: And of his wisdom there is no number.

C “Great is our Lord”: certainly, for neither can his deeds be numbered nor can praise adequately grasp him. His power is also great because he is unique, almighty, and the governor and creator of all things; the number of his wisdom cannot in any way be comprehended. Here “number” is used for “end,” because what is numbered is brought to an end.

### 6 The Lord receives the meek: But he humbles ÷ .. sinners to the ground.

C The meek are those who are patient and afflicted through many tribulations. It is also right that these should be received into heaven, while the proud are cast down to the earth, so that, by an exchange [Col. 0521C] in turn, from the place where the humble one was lifted up, the proud one may fall:

### 7 Sing beforehand to the Lord with confession: Sing psalms to our God on the lyre.

C “Sing beforehand” is said to those who are still known to be silent. He shows both how and to whom one should sing when he adds, “to the Lord with confession.” The lyre signifies virtues singing beforehand in harmonious action. They produce a true lyre when no string—that is, no virtue—is broken. For how could the lyre be whole if one string were broken? Nor is a perfect sound produced when the broken string does not sound.

### 8 He covers the heavens with clouds: And prepares rain for the earth.

[Col. 0521D] C We appropriately understand “heaven” as holy prophecy. By divine providence, obscurity, like clouds, covers it, so that it may stir our understanding to seek, since what is reached through wearied desire is received with greater pleasure. But what do these clouds bring forth? An abundance of rain, namely, the rich springs of divine preaching, although these things are also literally true and should be understood beneficially.

### 9 He brings forth grass on the mountains: ÷ and vegetation for the service of human beings ...

C This too can rightly be understood spiritually. For the mountains signify holy men, on whom the Lord brings forth grass—that is, strong preaching—and vegetation, that is, gentler admonitions, on which the simple beasts may feed.

### 10 [Col. 0522A] He gives their food to the beasts: ÷ And .. to the young of ravens that call upon him.

C “Beasts” signify the ecclesiastical flocks, which are fed with appropriate nourishment, some with milk and others with solid food. “Ravens” are irreligious and pagan men, clothed in the blackness of sins. The young of ravens—the children of pagans or of other wicked people—are fed by God when they call upon the God whom their fathers had despised. Hence he adds that he does not give the food of faith to all their young and children, but to those who call upon him, since only those call upon him who do not overturn the rules of Scripture through any heretical perversion.

### 11 He will not desire the strength of the horse: Nor will the legs be pleasing to him.

[Col. 0522B] C The horse signifies a proud and swollen human being, to whom divinity cannot be favorable, since God chooses the meek. H Here “legs,” as also “thighs,” signify lust, which can in no way please God in man or woman. But through the strength of the horse and the legs, presumption in one’s own strength may also be understood. A person does not please God through his own power, but through fear of God, as the following statement indicates.

### 12 The Lord is pleased with those who fear him: And ÷ with those who hope in his mercy.

C The Lord is therefore pleased with those who fear him, but not with an ignoble fear. For many fear, but because they despair of his mercy, [Col. 0522C] they are not loved, as Judas was. The fear that is acceptable to God is joined with the greatest love and devout hope. Therefore let each person fear, lest he sin; let him love, so that he may pray, but let him not despair.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM 146

Builder of the heavenly Jerusalem, God, who both encloses the multitude of the stars within their number and calls each one individually by name, we ask you to heal the brokenhearted, gather the dispersed, and enrich us with your innumerable wisdom. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, etc.

# PSALM 147

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM 147

C The prophet addresses Jerusalem—that is, the heavenly city—so that, now made secure in its citizens, it may praise the Lord with continual rejoicing. He recounts how many benefits the merciful [Col. 0522D] Lord has graciously granted to his people.

**Title.** ÷ Alleluia.

C We return, indeed, to the customary “Alleluia”; but let it in no way be tedious to repeat a word whose honor is so great that, although it is preserved in the Hebrew language, it is nevertheless not translated in any other language. The Greek, Latin, Chaldaean, Syriac, Persian, Arabic, and every nation of the earth retains it and venerates it with devout devotion. Therefore let us too sing it with a pure mind.

### 1 Praise the Lord, Jerusalem: Praise your God, O Zion.

C Jerusalem, as has often been said, is interpreted as [Col. 0523A] “vision of peace,” which properly belongs to that city that will have no fellowship with vices and scandals. Zion is also interpreted as “watchtower.” For in that city of God we will see him as he is. Therefore these two names rightly suit the future city.

### 2 For he has strengthened the bars of your gates: He has blessed your children within you.

C When he says that the bars of the gates have been strengthened, he shows that the doors of the blessed city have been shut. This happens when the bridegroom enters, and those who are prepared with him, for the wedding, as is said in the Gospel concerning the virgins (Matthew 25). No saint will thereafter go out, nor will anyone new enter afterward. Great indeed is the blessing of the children there. [Col. 0523B] It says “within you” because they will never be able to leave it, since they are consecrated by an eternal gift.

### 3 He has established peace within your borders: ÷ And .. he satisfies you with the fat of wheat.

C Just as blessed Jerusalem possesses peace, so unhappy Babylon will undoubtedly endure a battle of sorrows. By “the fat of wheat” he means the visible deity itself, by which the understanding of the righteous is so refreshed that it is known to surpass every fellowship.

### 4 He sends forth his word to the earth: His speech runs swiftly.

C The Lord’s utterance is the Word of the Father, which he sent to the earth when he assumed the humility of a devout incarnation. Then his speech ran so swiftly that knowledge of the Holy Trinity filled the world with marvelous speed, [Col. 0523C] converting the worshipers of idols through the manifestation of its truth.

### 5 He gives snow like wool: He scatters mist like ashes.

C “He gives snow like wool”: “gives” means “makes.” This happens when he leads hearts of mortals, chilled by sins, to the warmth of repentance. A person is snow when he withdraws from the Lord; wool when he comes to his healing. “Mist” signifies every sin, which is always carried out in murky darkness. But it is scattered like ashes when it is dispersed through pure confession by the grace of Christ.

### 6 He sends his ice like morsels: Who can stand before his face in the presence of cold?

C Ice is frozen water like glass, hardened through many [Col. 0523D] winters and brought to the hardness of stone. H C Those who are bound by the cold of unbelief and freeze more each day are compared to it. The Lord sends them forth like morsels when he makes converts proclaim his mighty deeds, so that the hungry people may feed on heavenly bread. “Before his face,” that is, before the presence of his cold, is said—not because that cold comes from him, but because he perhaps permits it to happen, as in: “God hardened the heart of Pharaoh” (Exodus 10). Before that cold, which God himself does not remove, no one can remain standing; no one can endure it.

### 7 He will send forth his word and melt them: His spirit will blow, and the waters will flow.

H C When the word comes—that is, preaching—God melts [Col. 0524A] them, so that, pierced with remorse, they begin to practice repentance. “His spirit will blow,” that is, the warmth of God’s love. “The waters will flow,” that is, streams of spiritual benefit will pour forth. This happened with the persecutor Saul, and it happens today with very many people.

### 8 He announces his word to Jacob: His righteousness and judgments to Israel.

C “Jacob” and “Israel” signify the Church. For even now whoever is faithful is an Israelite; and before Jacob there was one who pleased the Lord with pure devotion. To him he is known to have proclaimed his word and his righteousness.

### 9 He has not done this for every nation: And he has not revealed his judgments to them ÷ ...

C “He has not done this for every nation,” because although the Christian religion [Col. 0524B] has embraced all nations, he nevertheless spoke face to face with none of them, nor divided the sea, except only with the Israelite people. A Or “the nation of Jacob,” which descended from Abraham, in whose faith all Christians stand. To that nation alone he revealed his judgments.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM 147

Strengthen, Lord, the gates of your Church, establish peace within its boundaries, and graciously grant it the fat of spiritual wheat. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, etc.

# PSALM 148

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM 148

C Through the mention of a few creatures, the prophet urges all creatures to praise the Lord: rational and intellectual creatures by themselves, but those lacking understanding or sensation [Col. 0524C] through those creatures which praise the Lord’s works with the wisest discernment.

**Title.** Alleluia.

### 1 Praise the Lord from the heavens: Praise him in the heights.

C Since it is fitting for the creature to praise its Creator, he says, “Praise the Lord.” H Human nature alone is not sufficient for the praise of God; let the heavens also be joined to it. But he did not say, “Praise, heavens,” but, “You who are in the heavens,” that is, thrones, dominions, principalities, powers, and the others in the heights—that is, you who are exalted, worthily praise the Most High.

### 2 Praise him, all his angels: Praise him, all his powers.

[Col. 0524D] C “Praise him, all his angels.” The word “angel” is interpreted from Greek into Latin as “messenger”; angel is a designation of office, not of nature. “All his powers” is a general term, for it includes all those who are exalted by the dignity of the heavenly army.

### 3 Praise him, sun and moon: Praise him, all stars and light.

H The sun, moon, and stars praise him because they do not depart from their office and service; their service itself is the praise of God. He adds “light,” so that, just as he said of invisible things, “Praise, all powers,” so he says of visible things, “Praise him, everything that shines.”

### 4 Praise him, heavens of heavens: [Col. 0525A] And let the waters that are above the heavens praise the name of the Lord.

C Although we read in Genesis that one heaven was made, nevertheless in Paul and here they are also named in the plural. There is no doubt that the waters above the heavens are those that pour down, for Genesis also says, “The floodgates of heaven were opened” (Genesis 7). He says, “Let them praise the name of the Lord,” and commands that the Lord be praised from his works. And what is more fitting than that the created order should praise its own author?

### 5 For ÷ he himself spoke, and they were made ..: He himself commanded, and they were created.

C By saying “he himself,” he signifies the Lord the Savior. For he is the Word made flesh, by whose command [Col. 0525B] all things were created. “To make” and “to create” differ: we too can make, but we cannot create. Therefore, because he said, “They were made,” which is a general expression, he added what properly belongs to divinity: “They were created.” “He commanded” means that he established and formed them.

### 6 He established them forever and ever ÷ of eternity ..: He gave a command, and it will not pass away.

C “He established them” declares the Lord’s power and might, so that there can be no doubt that the Lord is almighty, since nothing that he establishes is altered by any change. “Command” means law or condition, so that all things may be known to be under his power. Therefore he added, “and it will not pass away.” What the Almighty establishes and truth promises cannot pass away.

### 7 [Col. 0525C] Praise the Lord from the earth: Dragons and all abysses.

C Mystically, we should understand dragons and abysses as savage and powerful persons who, converted here to what is good, glory in the Lord’s praises in that homeland. Yet even when understood literally, poisonous dragons praise God like the other creatures.

### 8 Fire, hail, snow, ice, storm wind: Which do his word.

C Mystically, fire, hail, snow, and ice signify people who in this age have been turned from turbulent and utterly wicked pursuits toward the Lord. Storm winds are those who have deserved to come from tempestuous and [Col. 0525D] irreligious works to the grace of confession.

### 9 Mountains and all hills: Fruit-bearing trees and all cedars.

C Mountains signify people raised up by an overly proud power; hills, people of moderate status; fruit-bearing trees, those who have been converted from the hardness of sins and produce the fruits of good conduct. “Cedars” signifies the proud without qualification.

### 10 Beasts and all cattle: Serpents and winged birds.

C “Beasts” signifies the cruel and untamed; “all cattle,” the common people; “serpents,” the poisonous and crafty; “birds” signify philosophers, who range through the natures of things with the speed of their thoughts. From all these Christ prepares elect persons who, in that resurrection and praise, may be gathered into the companies of the angels.

### 11 Kings of the earth and all peoples: Princes and all judges of the earth.

C Kings signify holy men who rule themselves; all peoples, the crowds that come together to God; princes, we understand as exalted powers; judges, noble and powerful people. For, as frequently happens, these suddenly abandon worldly power and love to undertake the service of the Lord.

### 12 Young men and virgins, old men with the young, let them praise the name of the Lord: For his name alone has been exalted.

C “Young men” are those who, fervent by the nature of their [Col. 0526B] age, turn themselves toward moderation. “Old men with the young” signifies an age composed of different stages. For from every sex and every age the powerful Lord is able to call forth whomever he wishes. The most just reason for praise is given here: “For it has been exalted,” and so forth. For it has been exalted when, as the Apostle says, every knee of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth bows (Philippians 2).

### 13 His praise is above heaven and earth: And he has exalted the horn of his people.

C “His praise is above heaven and earth.” This praise signifies that praise which, after the end of this age, is rendered to him by all rational creatures in blessedness. When he says “above heaven and earth,” he signifies that neither heavenly nor earthly things can be found equal to the praises of God. [Col. 0526C] “He has exalted the horn,” that is, the power, because the faithful people will be exalted where every glory is bestowed.

### 14 A hymn to all his saints: To the children of Israel, the people drawing near to him.

C “A hymn to all”: this expression is a promise and the complete perfection of all blessedness. And to which saints? To the children of Israel, who deserved to bear this name not only by descent but also by faith.

## PRAYER FROM PSALM 148

God, the supreme and transcendent power over all exalted things, grant your servants that, just as all the things we see were created at your command, so what you command may be preserved under your protection. Through our Lord Jesus [Col. 0526D] Christ, etc.

# PSALM 149

## ARGUMENT OF PSALM 149

C The prophet says that a new song should be sung to the Lord Christ, who through his compassion built the universal Jerusalem from the whole world. Describing the joys and virtues of the saints, and the vengeance against sinners, he says that glory belongs to the righteous.

**Title.** Alleluia.

### 1 Sing a new song to the Lord: His praise is in the assembly of the saints.

C For the prophet, established in this world only in body, was mingled in understanding and faith with the angelic multitude in that homeland, and he urges [Col. 0527A] the blessed people to sing a new song there. The new song is the mystery of the holy incarnation, the wondrous birth, and so forth. “His praise” is either in this Church or in that heavenly Jerusalem.

### 2 Let Israel rejoice in him who made him: ÷ And .. let the daughters of Zion exult in their king.

C Israel and Zion are different names, but the same reality of the saints. For Israel is interpreted as “a man seeing God,” and Zion as “watchtower.” Both apply to the blessed people, who are urged to rejoice and exult in their king, Christ the Lord.

### 3 Let them praise his name in the assembly: Let them sing psalms to him with the tambourine and lyre.

C What this choir is like, another psalm explains: “From the rising of the sun to its setting, praise the name of the Lord” [Col. 0527B] (Ps. CXII). The choir, therefore, is gathered from the multitude of human beings from the beginning of the world in faith; and it cannot be completely assembled except in that blessed homeland. The tambourine and psaltery signify approved deeds, which are referred to divine gifts, because these deeds, signified here by those instruments and practiced here, make us praise God eternally in the other life.

**4** Because the Lord has been pleased with his people: And he will exalt the meek to salvation.

C The Lord is pleased with his people when he has made them rejoice in perfect sweetness. The meek are the patient, who here have endured various wickednesses for the kingdom of God. He will exalt them to salvation, that is, to eternal life.

**5** The saints will exult in glory: They will rejoice in their chambers.

C For there is the exultation and joy of the saints, where they recognize that the good Lord is such that he grants pardon to the guilty, grace to sinners, and everlasting glory to those who do not deserve it. “In their chambers,” that is, in the secrecy of the heart, where only he knows who has deigned to grant it. H Or, “in their chambers,” in the heavenly homeland. For here the saints weep in their chamber and water their bed with tears (Ps. VI).

**6** The exultations of God are in their throats: And two-edged swords are in their hands.

C The saints have the exultations of God in their throats, because whether in thought or in speech they do not cease to praise him from whom they receive eternal gifts. The two-edged sword is the word of the Lord the Savior; it is two-edged because it contains the two Testaments. “In their hands,” that is, in the power of the saints, as it is written: “The word of the Lord came by the hand of Haggai the prophet” (Hag. I).

**7** To execute vengeance upon the nations: Rebukes among the peoples.

C They execute vengeance, for these things are truly accomplished when they will sit with the Lord upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel (Matt. XIX).

**8** To bind their kings with fetters: And their nobles with iron chains.

C This verse explains what that double-edged sword does: it binds the kings of the earth with fetters, from which it is not permitted to depart; it also places iron bonds upon the nobles of the world, so that they are heavy to bear and so that, in eternal condemnation, they can prevail by no power to break their links.

**9** To execute upon them the judgment that is written: Glory ÷ this .. belongs to all his saints.

C “To execute upon them the judgment that is written,” namely, the judgment of which the Apostle says: “We shall judge angels” (I Cor. VI). And lest you think that only the apostles will judge, he adds: “This glory belongs to all his saints.” For all the saints judge with Christ, those who do not oppose his ordinances. C “The judgment that is written”: that is, they will judge them in the manner established in the holy Scriptures.

## Prayer from Psalm CXLIX

God, author of all goodness—you who exalt everyone who humbly confesses you in meekness—grant that, just as you make the saints exult in glory, so you may deign to guard the present Church from the pleasures of this age. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, etc.

# Psalm CL

## Argument of Psalm CL

B The city of God is admonished that, gathered from the circuit of the world, it should sing praises to the Lord both with its mouth and with its mind. C B The fiftieth psalm concerns repentance; the hundredth, mercy and judgment; the hundred-and-fiftieth, the praise of God in his saints. For this is how we move toward eternal life: first by condemning our sins, then by living well, so that, after an evil life has been condemned and a good one lived, we may deserve eternity. For, when called, we renounce the devil through repentance, so that we may not remain under his yoke; justified, we are healed through mercy, so that we may fear judgment; glorified, we pass into eternal life, where we praise the Lord without end.

**TT. Alleluia.**

**1** Praise the Lord in his saints: Praise him in the firmament of his power.

H Praise the Lord in his saints, because he will place them in the glory of eternity after judgment has been celebrated. Praise him in the firmament, because, every weakness having been removed, he has brought to the saints the firmament of eternal strength. C He teaches, however, how the saints ought to be praised: namely, so that not they themselves, but the Lord, should be glorified through their preaching.

**2** Praise him in his mighty deeds: Praise him according to the multitude of his greatness.

H Praise him in his mighty deeds, because, having powerfully consumed death through immortality, he has bestowed upon them the glory of unchangeable life. Praise him according to the multitude, because he has granted his own such glory as “neither eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man” (I Cor. II). C Or, “according to the multitude of his greatness,” whose end, as another psalm says, does not exist (Ps. CXLIV). Therefore he is commanded to be praised eternally and without end, because he is commanded to be praised according to the multitude of his greatness.

**3** Praise him with the sound of the trumpet: Praise him with psaltery and harp.

C Here various musical instruments are set forth in an ordered and symbolic manner: let the trumpet resound for the king; let the psaltery sing for God; let the harp, together with the rest, sing for the bridegroom. All these things are figuratively said to sound forth the praises of the Lord. H In the psaltery and harp, either the Decalogue observed in deed or the mortification of the flesh—which is understood by the name “harp”—is signified. Because he has made the mortified flesh in himself alive, he is rightly praised with the harp; and with the psaltery, because through observance of the Decalogue he has attained the eternal crown.

**4** Praise him with tambourine and choir: Praise him with strings and organ.

H Praise him with tambourine, that is, in the mortification [Col. 0529B] of the flesh, in the harmony of charity, and in spiritual commandments.

**5** Praise him with cymbals ÷ that sound well ..: Praise him with cymbals of jubilation: Let every spirit praise the Lord.

H This praise is fulfilled in the cymbals when, corruption of flesh and blood having been driven away, those conformed to the image of the Creator, filled with the entire fullness of hope, shine in the kingdom of the Father. “Every spirit”: therefore, in that kingdom, no longer flesh or blood, no longer corruption, but the human being, having become wholly spiritual, should not cease to praise God in the Spirit, who is Spirit.

A God commands himself to be praised in the saints: in the firmament of his power, and so forth. And what are all those things? You, his saints: you are his power, but the power that he made in you; you are the firmament of his power and the multitude of his greatness, which he made and displayed in you; you are the trumpet, psaltery, harp and tambourine, strings and organ, and well-sounding cymbals of jubilation, because you are harmonious: [Col. 0530A] you are all these things. Let nothing here be considered worthless, transitory, or merely playful. And because to think according to the flesh is death, let every spirit praise the Lord.

## Prayer from Psalm CL

Most sweet melody of our harmony, you who command the melodies of our breast to be exercised now by breath, now by strings: grant that, while we sing together with that spiritual affection, inserted into everlasting choirs, we may praise you together with all the saints. Through our Lord Jesus Christ your Son, etc.

**THE BOOK OF PSALMS, NUMBERING ONE HUNDRED AND FIFTY, ENDS.**

# Psalm CLI (Apocryphal)

## Argument of This Psalm

[Col. 0530B] B This psalm is properly inscribed to David, outside the number of the psalms, when he fought with Goliath.

I was little among my brothers: And younger in my father’s house. I tended my father’s sheep: My hands made an organ: My fingers fashioned a psaltery: And who made this known to my Lord? The Lord himself, the hearer of all; he himself sent his angel. And he took me from my father’s sheep: And anointed me with the mercy of his anointing. My brothers were good and great: Yet the Lord was not pleased with them. I went out to meet the foreigner: [Col. 0530C] And he cursed me by his idols. But I drew his own sword from its sheath and cut off his head: And I removed the reproach from the children of Israel.

[Col. 0529]

# Commentary of Saint Bruno, Bishop of Würzburg, on the Canticles

## The Canticle of the Prophet Isaiah, Chapter XII

[Col. 0529D]

**1** I will confess to you, Lord, because you were angry with me: Your wrath has turned, and you have comforted me.

H This is what you formerly said when, proceeding from Egypt through the dry sea into the wilderness: “Let us sing to the Lord” (Exod. XV), and what follows. Now, after striking Egypt again because it blasphemed the Lord, and after drying up, cutting apart, and humbling its river, glorify God and say: “I will confess to you, Lord,” etc. For when the Lord was born, when a census was first conducted throughout the Roman world (Luke II), Augustus Caesar, king of the Romans, destroyed Egypt; and all Egypt was struck into seven streams, and the Nile, a river of many waters, which previously flowed in a single channel and was impassable, was divided into seven parts so that it could be crossed on foot. Therefore glorify the Lord, who avenged its sins upon Egypt, and say: “I will confess to you, Lord,” that is, I will praise you, or I will do penance, because you were angry with me on account of my sin. “Your wrath has turned,” that is, your indignation. “You have comforted me” through the absolution of sins.

**2** Behold, God is my Savior: I will act confidently and will not fear.

The voice of the faithful Jews. “Behold, God is my Savior,” who was promised to us in the prophets, who gave us salvation. “I will act confidently and will not fear,” that is, I have faith in him that he will free me, and I will proclaim him confidently, that is, without fear.

**3** For the Lord is my strength and my praise: And he has become my salvation.

“For the Lord is my strength and my praise,” because he makes me strong against the enemy’s snares; I will praise him, the Son of God. “And he has become my salvation”: that is, according to his divinity he was not made but begotten by the Father; but at the end of time he was made for eternal salvation.

**4** You will draw water with joy from the fountains of the Savior: And you will say on that day: Give thanks to the Lord and call upon his name.

The voice of the prophets to the Jewish people. “You will draw water with joy,” that is, you will receive the teaching of the Gospel and of the apostles with gladness. “From the fountains of the Savior”: the apostles and evangelists were the fountains of Jesus. “And you will say on that day”—O apostles, specifically to the Gentiles, your followers, at that time, so that they may praise the Lord—“Give thanks to the Lord and call upon his name,” with the implied purpose: so that you may be saved by him.

**5** Make known among the peoples his inventions: Remember that his name is exalted.

The voice of the apostles to the Gentiles who have already believed: make known among the peoples who still do not believe his inventions. The inventions of Christ are to humble the proud, exalt the humble, or justify sinners and condemn the obstinate. “Remember that his name is exalted,” as it is written: “Christ became obedient for us unto death; therefore God exalted him,” etc. (Phil. II).

**6** Sing to the Lord, for he has done magnificently: Announce this throughout the whole earth.

“Sing to the Lord,” that is, praise the Lord, because he has acted magnificently, namely, by assuming a human being, rising from the dead, and ascending into heaven. “Announce this throughout the whole earth,” that is, among all the nations: that he assumed a human being.

**7** Exult and praise, O dwelling of Zion: For great in your midst is the Holy One of Israel.

H “Exult and praise, O dwelling of Zion, for great in your midst is the Holy One.” O [Note: [Col. 0531D] That is, Origen.] inhabitant of Zion, exult and praise your God, because the great and holy one of Israel—that is, Jesus Christ, your God—who formerly seemed to be your God and was confined within the narrow limits of the small land of Judea, has now filled the whole earth and is invoked among all the nations. Alternatively: Zion, that is, the Church, praise, because Christ the Lord, the Holy One of Israel, dwells in your midst.

## The Canticle of King Hezekiah, Isaiah, Chapter XXXVIII

H Lest Hezekiah’s heart be lifted up after unbelievable triumphs, he was weakened and saw that he was going to die. He turned his face toward the wall of the temple, so as not to show his tears to others, and wept with great weeping because of God’s promise to David, which he saw would perish in his death, since he then had no children and despaired that Christ would be born from his offspring. After his health was restored, he wrote the following: “I said: In the midst,” etc. This writing is not properly called a prayer but thanksgiving for the benefit he received.

**1** I said: In the middle of my days I shall go to the gates of the underworld: I sought the remainder of my years.

H “I said”: he relates what he silently thought during the time of his illness. “I said,” he declares, in the despair of my heart. “I shall go to the gates of the underworld,” that is, either of death or of Tartarus, of which it is said: “You raise me up from the gates of death” (Ps. IX), and what follows. To them murderous and deceitful men will be led halfway through the course of life and through the darkness of error, men who will not complete their days (Ps. LIV); for they neither complete works of virtue nor repent of their sins. Alternatively: “I said: In the middle of my days,” that is, in the middle of the course of my life, in youth, “I shall go to the gates of the underworld,” that is, I shall descend into the underworld like the other saints. “I sought the remainder of my years,” that is, thinking that I would live no longer, I asked that the remaining time of my life be granted to me.

**2** I said: I shall not see the Lord God in the land of the living: I shall no longer look upon a human being or an inhabitant of rest.

“I said: I shall not see”—understand, if I descend into the underworld, I shall not see God in the company of the saints. “In the land of the living.” H Therefore the region of the saints itself is what is called the land of the living. This is what he fears above all: that, led to the underworld, he may not deserve to look upon God’s salvation. “I shall no longer look upon a human being or an inhabitant of rest.” Because of the ambiguity of the word, we formerly joined this to the following verse. For the Hebrew expression, if it is read *edel*, signifies “rest”; but if it is read *eled*, it signifies “the west.” He therefore fears that he will not dwell with the holy people of God in rest; that his generation will be dissolved like a tent; that, like a woven fabric, it will be cut off at the very beginning of the light; and that Christ will in no way arise from his offspring.

**3** My generation has been taken away and rolled up from me: Like a shepherd’s tent.

“My generation,” that is, the begetting of my children, has been torn away and removed. “Like,” that is, as a shepherd’s tent is moved. This holy man grieved in three ways: either because he knew that he would descend into the underworld on account of sin; or because he knew that he would not see the Lord there; or, certainly, because he was still without children and feared that the promised Lord would not be born from his offspring.

**4** My life has been cut off like a weaver’s thread: While I was still being formed, he cut me off. From morning until evening you will bring me to an end.

“My life has been cut off,” that is, the course of my life. “While I was still being formed,” that is, while I was young, he cut me off. “From morning until evening you will bring me to an end”: either I shall bear it more lightly, or I shall reach the end of life.

**5** I hoped until morning: Like a lion, so he crushed all my bones.

H “I hoped until morning,” like Job, who expected night in the daytime and light in the darkness (Job XVII), thinking that punishments might be changed by the change of seasons. He who burns with great fevers knows this to be true; his inner fire consumes all his bones like a lion, and because of the greatness of his pain he does not think that he will live any longer. “Like a lion, so he crushed all my bones,” that is, all my strength.

**6** From morning until evening you will bring me to an end: Like a swallow’s fledgling, so I will cry out; I will meditate like a dove.

“Like a swallow’s fledgling, so I will cry out,” that is, like a swallow I groan. Alternatively: like a swallow’s fledgling—while approaching death, illness weighing upon me, and pain breaking my bones like a lion—I joined days and nights in tears and groans, and I awaited help from God alone, who could come to my aid. I said to him: I suffer more than my merits require; but if I have gone astray, I will turn toward what is better. A swallow’s fledgling cries out to its mother for food; a dove groans. So will I act toward my God because of my sins, until he has mercy on me.

**7** My eyes have grown weak: Looking upward.

“My eyes have grown weak,” that is, they have failed through the outpouring of tears. “Looking upward,” that is, asking forgiveness.

**8** Lord, I am suffering violence; stand surety for me: What shall I say, or what will he answer me, when he himself has done it?

“Lord, I am suffering violence,” that is, my weakness is greater than my frailty can bear. “Stand surety for me,” that is, be my guarantor, so that, once health has been restored, I may not return to my former vices. “What shall I say, or what will he answer me?” Understand: the Lord himself. H “When he himself has done it,” or imposed this very illness. Alternatively: “Stand surety for me,” for “it is not of him who wills” (Rom. IX), and what follows. And again he turns back to himself: What shall I say, or what shall I plead against you, my creator? Or what will he answer me, since he himself has done what he wished? Therefore all things must be endured, whatever he has decreed. Or: when he himself has shown me mercy and promised forgiveness.

**9** I will recall all my years to you: In the bitterness of my soul.

H “I will recall all my years,” namely, I will remember my prosperity and joy in the bitterness of my soul, that is, when I was in the bitterness of illness. For no condition of mortals is lasting, and every happiness of the world is lost while it is being possessed. When the time of tribulation arrives, all the past happiness of the world does nothing to help the one who endures it. Therefore Hezekiah says that he considers all the years of his reign and of his former, as he thought, blessedness in his present bitterness. And because he is now secure and does not suffer the things he recounts, he philosophizes about the human condition and says: “Lord,” etc.

**10** Lord, if this is how one lives, and amid such things is the life of my spirit, you will correct me and make me live: Behold, my bitterness is most bitter in peace.

H “Lord, if this is how one lives,” that is, if human life is such that one becomes ill, “and in such things”—understand, in such changes of illness—“the life of my spirit,” that is, the life of my soul, “you will correct me,” understand, by giving illness, “and you will make me live,” by healing me again. “Behold, in peace my bitterness,” etc., that is, behold, in the peace of my people and my city there is for me a most bitter bitterness: while those people rejoice at deliverance, and I, departing through death, alone have entered the gates of death, because they have been freed from Sennacherib.

**11** But you have rescued my soul so that it would not perish: You have cast all my sins behind your back.

[Col. 0534B] H “But you have rescued my soul,” understand, from the underworld, “so that it would not perish. And you have cast all my sins behind your back,” so that you might not see them in order to condemn me, but in order to forgive. Or, even in the present life, you have rescued my life.

**12** For the underworld will not confess to you, nor will death praise you: Those who descend into the pit will not await your truth.

H “For the underworld will not confess to you,” that is, those who are in the underworld will not praise you—namely, the devils—“nor will death praise you. Those who descend into the pit will not await your truth,” that is, they will not await the truth of judgment but the mercy of deliverance, especially when Christ descended to the underworld to free the captives.

**13** The living, the living, he will confess to you, as I do today: The father will make your truth known to his children.

“The living, the living, he will confess.” Whoever lives by truly living in the heavenly homeland will praise you, as I do today—understand, I praise you. “The father will make your truth known to his children.” H He calls himself the father and those subject to him his children; or he means every generation that will come after him, though not begotten by him, because he begot Manasseh, a most wicked son, who is not read to have blessed the Lord or confessed the Lord’s truth, but to have cursed God by persecuting his saints. “Your truth,” that is, the truth of your mercy. Here “confession” is understood not as repentance but as glory and praise. Thus the father will make your truth known to his children, so that through successive generations the truth and justice of God may be proclaimed to posterity.

**14** Lord, save me: And we will sing our psalms all the days of our life in the house of the Lord.

H “Lord, save me” from all adversities. “And we will sing our psalms,” that is, our song of praise, “all the days of our life,” that is, as long as we live—all of us who believe in you and have been delivered by your help.

# The Canticle of Hannah, First Book of Kings, Chapter II

[Col. 0535A]

**1** My heart has exulted in the Lord: And my horn has been exalted in my God.

H Let the Church of Christ, the city of the great King, full of grace and fruitful in offspring, say what it recognizes as having been prophesied about itself long beforehand through the mouth of this devout mother. “My heart has exulted.” She added “in the Lord,” because she exulted not in herself but in the Lord. “And my horn has been exalted in my God.” Truly my horn has been exalted, because it has been exalted not in itself but in its Lord. Elsewhere it says: “The horns of the righteous will be exalted” (Ps. LXXIV), because these horns are bestowed upon the righteous from the points of Christ’s cross. With these we will scatter and destroy the hostile powers lying in wait for our soul. [Col. 0535B] Alternatively: “My heart has exulted in the Lord,” that is, my mind. “And my horn has been exalted,” that is, my son, in my God.

**2** My mouth has been enlarged over my enemies: Because I have rejoiced in your salvation.

“My mouth has been enlarged over my enemies,” understand, over Jews and heretics, because the mouth of the Church has been enlarged over them; before Jews and unbelievers she speaks without restriction according to the Gospel. Alternatively: A “My mouth has been enlarged,” because even amid the constraints of persecutions the word of God has not been bound (II Tim. II), nor has it been bound in its heralds. “And I have rejoiced in your salvation.” This salvation is Christ Jesus.

**3** There is none holy as the Lord is: For there is no other besides you: and there is none strong like our God.

“There is none holy,” understand, no one is holy as God the Father is. “For there is no other besides you,” namely, the true God. “And there is none strong,” understand, no other immutable God, as you are with the Son and the Holy Spirit. H Or: “There is none holy as the Lord is, and just,” etc., as he is holy and sanctifying, just and justifying. There is no one holy outside and apart from you, because no one becomes holy except by you.

**4** Do not multiply lofty speech: Boasting.

**RABANUS.** The voice of the Church: “Do not multiply speech,” that is, do not boast in the wisdom of the Law; understand “lofty words” as words spoken in boasting. Solomon also says: “Do not seek what is higher than you” (Ecclus. III), and elsewhere: “The Lord is in heaven and you are on earth” (Eccl. V); therefore let your words be few.

**5** Let old things depart from your mouth: For God is the Lord of knowledge, and thoughts are prepared by him.

“Let old things depart,” that is, ancient traditions. “For God is the Lord of knowledge,” that is, he not only gives knowledge to the saints, but thoughts themselves are prepared by him, that is, they are manifest. Alternatively. H “Let old things depart,” that is, let grandiloquence not come out of your mouth. “For God is the Lord of knowledge.” These things are said about those who presume upon themselves, who think themselves righteous and are therefore proud and not subject to the righteousness of God, because they think that they can please him by what is their own rather than by God. Therefore the Lord is the judge of consciences; and, seeing the thoughts of human beings, that they are vain if they are human thoughts and do not come from him from whom human beings themselves are, he allows the proud to fall and the humble to be exalted.

**6** The bow of the mighty has been overcome: And the weak have been girded with strength.

“The bow of the mighty has been overcome,” that is, the power of the Egyptians through the signs of Moses, or the power of the Jews. “And the weak have been girded with strength,” that is, the Jews freed from Egyptian slavery, or the Gentiles strengthened by faith.

**7** Those who were formerly full have hired themselves out for bread: The hungry have been filled.

H “Those who were formerly full have hired themselves out for bread,” that is, the Gentiles, who previously had no teaching. For the Jews were formerly full of bread, that is, of the teaching of the Old Testament, and they hired themselves out for bread, that is, for the teaching of Christ they separated themselves from the fellowship of the faithful. Alternatively, “they hired themselves out,” that is, they handed themselves over to the devil for the sake of their doctrines, unwilling to share in the body of Christ.

**8** Until the barren woman bore many: And she who had many children has grown weak.

“Until the barren woman bore many,” that is, the Gentile world bore many children. And Judea grew weak in giving birth to children of God.

**9** The Lord puts to death and gives life: He leads down to the underworld and brings back.

“The Lord puts to death and gives life”: the Father put the Son to death, permitting him to be handed over, and gave him life by raising him. H “He leads down to the underworld and brings back,” that is, he led the soul of the Son down to the underworld with joy and brought it back.

**10** The Lord makes poor and makes rich: He humbles and exalts.

“The Lord makes poor,” when he says: “If you wish to be perfect, sell everything you have” (Matt. XIX). “And he makes rich,” by generating virtues in him and returning a hundredfold. He humbles the saints in the present and exalts them in the future.

**11** Raising the needy from the dust: And lifting the poor from the dung.

H “Raising the needy from the dust,” that is, Christ from corruption, because his flesh did not see corruption (Ps. XV). “Lifting the poor from the dung,” that is, the apostles. Alternatively: raising the poor from the earth, that is, Christ, who, though rich, became poor for us, so that by his poverty or death we might be enriched (II Cor. VIII). “Needy” means the same as “poor.” By “dung,” from which he was lifted, the Jewish persecutors are most correctly understood.

**12** So that he may sit with princes: And hold the throne of glory.

H “So that he may sit with princes,” that is, with the apostles in judgment. “And hold the throne of glory,” that is, so that Christ may sit at the right hand of the Father; or, so that the apostles may hold the seat of glory that the Lord has given them.

**13** For the hinges of the earth belong to the Lord: And he placed the world upon them.

“For the foundations of the earth belong to the Lord,” that is, the boundaries, which are the apostles, because their sound has gone out into all the earth (Ps. XVIII). “And he placed the world upon them,” that is, the holy Church upon the teaching of the apostles.

**14** He will guard the feet of his saints: And the wicked will fall silent in darkness: For a man will not be strengthened by his own strength.

“The feet of his saints,” that is, he will guard their understanding or works so that they do not sin. “And the wicked will fall silent in darkness”: namely, the Jews, heretics, and false Christians, who wander by causing offense and run about together with demons. “For a man will not be strengthened by his own strength,” that is, no one becomes strong through his own strength. Alternatively: “The feet of his saints,” that is, he directs the works of his elect into the way of righteousness. “And the wicked will fall silent in darkness,” because they will be sent into the outer darkness, where they will fall silent, that is, they will cease from the arrogance of their pride. “For a man will not be strengthened by his own strength,” that is, by strength of his own; but through divine power there can be a man, that is, a people of believers.

**15** The adversaries of the Lord will fear him: And he will thunder over them from the heavens.

“The adversaries of the Lord will fear him,” that is, demons or wicked human beings. “And over them”—understand, over the wicked—he thunders: in the present, threatening them with eternal punishments in the books; or in the future, with hailstones and flashes of lightning.

**16** The Lord will judge the ends of the earth, and will give power to his king: And he will exalt the horn of his Christ.

H “The Lord will judge the ends of the earth”: on the day of judgment, all who dwell upon the earth, or each person according to his works, when he departs from this light into the kingdom of the heavenly homeland. “And he will give power to his king,” that is, to his body, which is the Church. Because of the anointing of baptism, it is called a king, just as those who were anointed as kings in the Old Testament were called kings. “And he will exalt the horn of his Christ,” that is, the power of the holy Church, which received the anointing of the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands in baptism. Alternatively: “The Lord will judge the ends,” that is, the final works of a human being, in which he is found, not merely his earlier works. “And he will give power to his king,” that is, to the Christian people, because he gives them the power by which they rule the flesh like kings. “And he will exalt the horn of his Christ”: for all those anointed with his chrism can rightly be called christs; [Col. 0537D] yet, together with its head, this whole body is one Christ.

# The Canticle of Moses, Exodus, Chapter XV

**1** Let us sing to the Lord: For he has been gloriously magnified: He has cast horse and rider into the sea.

“Let us sing,” that is, let us praise, because he has been magnified through the signs performed in Egypt. But he has been gloriously magnified by casting the horsemen and their riders into the sea, namely Pharaoh and his army. Spiritually, that praise signifies the praise now performed in the Church. They praised the Lord; let us also praise him, the Church says, because Christ, O, has been magnified in [Col. 0538A] assuming flesh, in being born of the Virgin Mary, and in conquering the devil through the death of the cross, casting horse and rider into the sea—that is, casting the devil and his ministers into the underworld—and, by rising again and ascending into heaven, he has been gloriously magnified.

**2** The Lord is my strength and my praise: And he has become my salvation.

“The Lord is my strength,” Moses says, because he made us strong against the snares of our enemies. “He is our praise”; praise him, who has become our salvation by redeeming us and freeing us from Pharaoh’s slavery. Spiritually, the Lord is the strength of the holy Church, because he makes it strong to endure the adversities of this world.

**3** This is my God, and I will glorify him: The God of my father, and I will exalt him.

“This is God,” that is, Christ, “and I will glorify him,” that is, I will praise him. “The God of my father,” namely, Abraham, “and I will exalt him,” that is, I will proclaim his greatness. There were heretics who said that there were two gods, one of the Old Testament and another of the New. They said that the God of the Old Testament was just and cruel, because he commanded justly and commanded that those who sinned be put to death, saying: “If anyone does this or that, let him die the death.” But they said that the God of the New Testament was just and merciful, because he called sinners to repentance, saying: “Do penance.” But all these people lied, since Moses shows that the very God of the Old Testament is also the God of the New.

**4** The Lord is like a warrior. Almighty is his name: He cast Pharaoh’s chariots and his army into the sea.

“The Lord is like a man,” battling Pharaoh then and the devil now. He is almighty because he alone can do all things. “Pharaoh’s chariots,” etc.: indeed, all the things spoken of and accomplished here in Pharaoh at that time were later also completed by Christ against the ancient enemy. These things are proclaimed here by the prophetic Spirit as future events, as though they had already happened.

**5** His chosen princes were drowned in the Red Sea: The abysses covered them: They descended into the depths like a stone.

[Col. 0538D] “His chosen princes,” that is, the principal vices are overthrown together with the lesser ones. “The abysses covered them,” that is, Gehenna, into which they descended like a stone. For both that one and this one—namely, Pharaoh and the devil—were weighed down by the hardness of their sins and were not living stones.

**6** Your right hand, Lord, has been magnified in strength: Your right hand, Lord, struck the enemy: And in the multitude of your glory you cast down my adversaries.

“Your right hand, Lord, has been magnified”: that is, let us magnify your right hand, Lord, namely your Son Christ, in the strength of victory. He struck the enemy of our freedom, casting him down from dominion over those he had deceived.

**7** You sent forth your wrath, which devoured them like straw: And in the spirit of your fury the waters were gathered together.

“You sent forth your wrath”—wrath, that is, vengeance; yet the divinity is not disturbed by anger. “Which devoured them like straw,” because, just as fire easily consumes straw, so it was easy for God to submerge them. “And in the spirit of your fury,” because to those who suffer it appears to be fury, although it is just judgment.

**8** The flowing wave stood still: The abysses were gathered in the midst of the sea.

“The flowing wave stood still,” that is, either the divided sea or the Jordan, as it is read (Exod. XIV). “The abysses were gathered together,” so that they would not harm the righteous or kill the unrighteous.

**9** The enemy said: I will pursue and overtake them: I will divide the spoils; my soul will be filled.

“The enemy said,” that is, Pharaoh: “I will pursue,” etc. These are the words of Pharaoh or of the devil, although a stronger one came upon him and carried away his spoils (Luke IX).

**10** I will draw my sword: My hand will kill them.

“I will draw my sword,” that is, swords; and “my hand,” that is, my power or the multitude of my army, “will kill them.” So too the devil says: I will draw my sword, that is, I will open every method of deception, and my hand will kill them spiritually.

**11** Your spirit blew, and the sea covered them: They sank like lead in mighty waters.

“Your spirit blew”: for by the spirit of your strength [Col. 0539C] they were submerged. “Like lead”: pliable toward evil and weighed down by wickedness, so that they cannot lift their soul toward what is good.

**12** Who is like you among the mighty, Lord, who is like you? Magnificent in holiness: Terrible and praiseworthy, and working wonders.

“Who is like you?” You do great things, because you are holy; you are terrible in judging, praiseworthy in forgiving sins for those who repent, and you work wonders: on the cross and in the conversion of sinners.

**13** You stretched out your hand: And the earth devoured them.

Extendisti manum, that is, your power, and the earth devoured them, that is, sand or earthly sins. [Col. 0539D] Or, those who always do earthly things are devoured by the earth: they speak of earth, quarrel over it, desire earth, and, devoted to lust, seek bodily pleasure.

14 You were their guide in your mercy: To the people whom you redeemed.

There you were their guide to the promised land; here, to the heavenly Jerusalem, for those who have been redeemed.

15 And you carried them in your strength: To your holy dwelling-place.
