And then you carried them, that is, you brought them there without their labor, where they would see the tabernacle and afterward the temple; just as now you introduce the saints into paradise, where they see your eternal holy dwelling-place forever.

16 [Col. 0540A] The peoples arose and were enraged: Pangs seized the inhabitants of Philistia.

The peoples arose: Israel. And they were enraged, that is, their adversaries were enraged against them. These things, however, are understood of the future. *Philistia* is interpreted as “those falling by the cup”; *Edomites* as “red” or “earthly.”

17 Then the princes of Edom were troubled: Trembling seized the mighty of Moab; all the inhabitants of Canaan grew rigid. Let dread and terror fall upon them: At the greatness of your arm.

*Moab* is interpreted as “from the father,” and signifies sinners who persecute the righteous—those intoxicated with sins and guilty of shedding Christ’s blood. Or it signifies those stained by murders, who are “from the father,” the devil; the salvation of the righteous is an object of envy to them, yet the Lord overcomes them. [Col. 0540B]

19 Let them become immovable as a stone; let your people pass through, O Lord, until this people of yours whom you have possessed passes through.

“Let them become immovable”: he either wishes or declares that the peoples named above will not be able to resist God’s people. Or, mystically, the Jews became immovable with regard to faith in Christ, until all the people of the Gentiles, whom the Lord possesses, should pass over and come to faith.

20 You will bring them in and plant them on the mountain of your inheritance: In your most firm dwelling-place, which you have prepared, O Lord. [Col. 0540C]

You will bring them in, into the promised land; and the Lord will also bring his saints into the heavenly Jerusalem and plant them there forever, that is, make them live in blessedness. The mountain is Zion, and the most firm dwelling-place is Jerusalem. Spiritually, however, Zion signifies heavenly contemplation, and the most firm dwelling-place signifies the heavenly Jerusalem, whose boundaries the Lord has established in everlasting peace (Ps. 147), where no weakness can exist.

21 Your sanctuary, O Lord, which your hands established. The Lord has reigned forever and beyond.

O “your sanctuary”: this is the holiness of the assumed flesh, which was not made by human hand [Col. 0540D] but prepared by the hands of God. “The Lord has reigned”: he reigns and will reign forever and without an ending. Alternatively: “And he will reign in eternity and beyond”—if anything exists beyond eternity.

22 For Pharaoh entered the sea with his chariots, and the Lord brought the waters of the sea back over them.

Or, “For he entered”: understood spiritually, whoever is an Egyptian and follows Pharaoh, that is, the devil, is drowned in the waves of vices.

23 But the children of Israel walked on dry ground in the midst of the sea.

Or, “But the children of Israel”: mystically, that is, the one who follows Christ; and just as Christ walked, so he too walks. [Col. 0541A] The waters and the wall become his right and left sides. He himself proceeds by the middle way on dry ground until he emerges into freedom and sings the hymn of victory, saying: “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously magnified; horse and rider he has cast into the sea.” This will occur when, after death, the soul enters the heavens in glory.

## THE PRAYER OF THE PROPHET HABAKKUK FOR IGNORANCES. CHAPTER III

1 O Lord, I heard your report, and I was afraid.

“O Lord, I heard”: the Savior says to his disciples, “Everything that I heard from the Father I have announced to you” (John 15), that is, I suffer shameful and adverse things in the flesh assumed for the human race [Col. 0541B]; and afterward, having conquered death, I will enter into my glory. The prophet heard this report in the spirit and was afraid.

2 O Lord, your work—in the midst of the years revive it [the reading *illua* is uncertain].

“O Lord, your work.” He says, therefore: I beseech you, Lord, that you unfold what you promised and, when the appointed time has ended, bring forth your Christ; and revive the work that you promised, that is, fulfill your promise.

3 In the midst of the years you will make it known; when you are angry, you will remember mercy.

“In the midst of the years”: when, he says, the fullness of time has come and you have fulfilled the promises through your work (Gal. 4), you will show that what you promised is true; and when you have been angry with us sinners, you will nevertheless remember your mercy toward those who do penance. [Col. 0541C]

4 God will come from the South, and the Holy One from Mount Paran. *Diapsalma.*

“God from the South”: Paran is a place near Sinai, where the Lord himself gave the law. He who deigned to be born from the Virgin at Bethlehem came from there, proceeding from the South; he was brought by his parents to Jerusalem (Luke 2), so that a sacrificial victim might be offered for him according to the law.

5 His glory covered the heavens, and the earth is full of his praise.

“He covered the heavens”: at the Savior’s coming, all things were filled with glory, as in the Gospel: “Glory to God in the highest” (Luke 2). And elsewhere: “O Lord, our Lord, how wonderful is your name in all the earth” (Ps. 8). And again: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth” (Ps. 18). [Col. 0541D]

6 His brightness will be like the light; horns are in his hands.

“His brightness”: like the sun, so the Sun of righteousness will shine with brilliant light. “Horns,” that is, the standards and trophies of the cross, are in his hands.

7 His strength was hidden there; before his face death will go.

“His strength was hidden there.” His strength was hidden in the cross, for he said: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Mark 14), and: “Into your hands I commend my spirit” (Luke 23). There the power of his divinity lay hidden, and the weakness of his humanity appeared.

8 [Col. 0542A] The devil will go out before his feet; he stood and measured the earth.

“He will go out”: when the Lord came forth from the waters of baptism, death—that is, the devil—met him. The ancient serpent came before his feet, since he tempted him in the desert (Matt. 4).

9 He looked and dissolved the nations, and the everlasting mountains were crushed.

“He looked and dissolved”: standing, the Savior saw all things with his eye and measured the whole world with his gaze. He dispersed the unbelief of the nations and thawed their hearts from their frost; he also crushed the demons and the proud, who are called “the mountains of the age.”

10 The hills of the world bowed down by the paths of his eternity.

[Col. 0542B] “The hills bowed down,” that is, the proud were humbled through repentance. Before the Savior’s coming they were proud and could be bent by no one. “Before the paths of his eternity”: through the assumed flesh, through his preaching and that of his disciples, and through inward inspiration—the ways by which the divinity deigned to come to us—the proud were humbled and converted.

11 Because of iniquity I saw the tents of Ethiopia; the skins of the land of Midian will be shaken.

“Because of iniquity,” that is, on account of iniquity. Those who ought to have been the temple of God become, because of the iniquity of greed, lust, and every kind of wickedness, the dwelling-place of Ethiopians, that is, of demons. Understand the tents of the land of Midian and of Ethiopia as referring to the same people. At the end, conscious of their sins, they will tremble and be shaken at the judgment. [Col. 0542C]

12 Are you angry, O Lord, with the rivers? Or is your fury against the rivers? Or your indignation against the sea?

“Are you angry with the rivers?” The names “rivers” and “sea” express the hearts of unbelievers, which are swept downward with the full force of their intention. There are good rivers and bad rivers; hence this passage and this question can be understood both affirmatively and negatively. God is not angry with good rivers, but he is angry with bad ones; and the sea likewise can be understood in both a good and a bad sense. Worldly or heretical eloquence and words are a bad river; God’s words, preaching, and sacraments are a good river, in which the sinner is washed.

13 [Col. 0542D] You will mount upon your horses, and your chariots are salvation.

“You will mount upon your horses”: not upon the hearts of those with whom he is said above to be angry, but upon the hearts of his elect. By the illumination of his grace, as in the apostles, riding in these chariots he enlightened and saved the whole world. Alternatively, the four Gospels are the chariot of salvation.

14 You will surely raise your bow; the oaths you spoke to the tribes. *Diapsalma.*

“You will surely raise it.” He calls the bow the unexpected coming in which he foresaw that the kingdoms of the world would be judged. Or he calls sacred Scripture the bow: he raised it when through it he awakened the dead in sins and fulfilled what he had promised to the tribes of the ancient fathers. [Col. 0543A]

15 You will cleave the rivers of the earth; the waters saw you and the mountains were in anguish; the flood of waters passed by.

“You will cleave the rivers,” that is, you will divide and scatter the kings of the earth who fight against your people. The exalted kingdoms and the lofty powers of this age saw you and trembled. “The flood,” that is, the persecution of those who afflicted your people, passed by.

16 The abyss gave its voice; the height lifted its hands.

“The abyss gave its voice”: after the flood of waters, that is, of persecutions, had passed—that is, ceased—after your Passion, O Christ, the lower world, that is, the saints in the limbo of the fathers, praised you. And the height, that is, the angels, proclaimed you victorious; and, as though by the applause of raised hands, they showed you to be victor and triumphator. [Col. 0543B]

17 The sun and moon stood in their dwelling-place; at the light of your arrows they will go, in the brightness of your flashing spear.

“The sun and moon”: after his Passion and resurrection, the Lord was exalted—the Sun of righteousness, namely, into heaven—and, having sent forth the Spirit, he illuminated the Church, which is called the moon. She then stood so firmly, having received the strength of the Spirit, that she did not fear even death. “Your arrows,” that is, your wounds and your instruction, gave light to your people. Christ is signified by the sun, and the Church by the moon.

18 [Col. 0543C] In fury you will trample the earth; in wrath you will stupefy the nations.

“In fury you will trample”: when you avenge the wrong done to your people, you will trample earthly kingdoms and make all the nations marvel.

19 You went forth for the salvation of your people, for salvation with your Christ.

“You went forth”: this is understood as spoken to the Father, because he went forth to save his people through Jesus Christ his Son: “For God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (2 Cor. 5). Or, he went forth from the synagogue of the Jews to the Gentiles.

20 You struck the head from the house of the wicked; you stripped the foundation as far as the neck.

“You struck the head”: when your Son came, you struck Antichrist from the house of the wicked, that is, in this age, because “the world lies in the evil one” (John 5). You made his hidden things open, even unto eternity. For his foundations, or hidden things, are his thoughts, which are laid bare either to everyone at the judgment or here through confession, as far as the neck—that is, as far as words and deeds. Alternatively, the devil is understood by “the head.” [Col. 0543D]

21 You cursed his scepters, the head of his warriors, when they came like a whirlwind to scatter me.

“You cursed”: you cursed not only his scepters, that is, the devil’s kingdom, but also the head of the warriors whom you had struck—those who came like a whirlwind to overthrow your people, O Lord. According to the literal sense, however, we understand the wicked Nebuchadnezzar, or all the adversaries who came like a whirlwind to scatter me, that is, to overthrow Israel and take it captive. [Col. 0544A]

22 Their exultation was like that of one who devours the poor in secret.

“Their exultation”: they exult while devouring the poor and the people subjected to them, and they do this as though in secret, that is, as though you, God, did not know. Thus you came to battle for your people, and, sending your chariots into the waters—that is, among many nations—you made a way for them, and so forth.

23 You made a way in the sea for your horses, in the mud of many waters.

“You made a way.” The horses are the holy preachers [Col. 0544B], for whom you made a way among the peoples of the nations; and through whose preaching the waters—that is, the hearts of the nations—were stirred. Spiritually, the sea is the world; mud is sins and empty cares; many waters are the many peoples.

24 I heard, and my belly was troubled; at the voice my lips trembled.

“I heard, and my belly was troubled”: at your threat, says the prophet, I tremble with my whole belly, that is, with my mind. The trembling of the lips indicates the fear of a troubled spirit. I therefore heard your vengeance upon sinners—the vengeance you have carried out here and will carry out more fully at the final judgment—and I tremble, lest I too be found rejected.

25 [Col. 0544C] Let putrefaction enter my bones, and let it seethe beneath me.

“Let putrefaction enter”: I not only willingly endure this trembling, but I will also willingly endure what Job suffered (Job 1), that is, bodily putrefaction, so that my flesh may seethe with innumerable worms, together with every hardship and tribulation in this life.

26 That I may rest on the day of tribulation, that I may ascend to our people girded for battle.

“That I may rest”: that here I may be cleansed of my own sins and delivered from them; and that on the day of tribulation—that is, the consummation of the age and the judgment, the day of wrath, calamity, and misery—I may rest and ascend to the company of those who preceded us in Christ and girded themselves to battle against the powers of the air [Col. 0544D], armed and equipped on every side with the weapons of the virtues. With them I will ascend into the joys of the blessed, and in this life from virtue to virtue (Ps. 83). “For the fig tree will not blossom,” but I will blossom.

27 For the fig tree will not blossom, and there will be no bud on the vines.

“For the fig tree will not blossom”: the fig tree, vine, and olive were the synagogue of the Jews, since it produced the sweetness of good works; but when the Lord came, it neglected to bear the fruit of virtue. This verse and the following two are similarly explained of wicked Christians.

28 The work of the olive will prove false, and the fields will yield no food.

“The work of the olive will fail”: of one who promises one thing and does another, saying to Moses, “Everything that the Lord has said we will do” (Exod. 24), yet refusing to believe in the one whom Moses proclaimed (Deut. 17). The fields also, that is, the land—Judaea, once situated among the holy mountains but now lying in the plain, dried up by the depression of sins—does not produce food, neither for the flock, that is, the simple, nor for the herds, that is, the leaders; and therefore it will be cut off. [Col. 0545A]

29 The flock will be cut off from the fold, and there will be no herd in the stalls.

“It will be cut off from the fold”: among the Jews are the stalls of the heavenly Scriptures, but because they do not savor the pasture of heavenly understanding, those who might bear the yoke of the Gospel are absent. *Armentum* (“herd”) is derived as if from *aramentum*, because it plows the earth under the yoke of the plow; or it is said from the weapons of horns, and signifies a leader or anyone who bears Christ’s yoke. [Col. 0545B]

30 But I will rejoice in the Lord, and I will exult in God my Jesus.

“But I in the Lord,” that is, not in my own righteousness but in faith in divine protection, will rejoice. “For they will suffer these things, but I will rejoice” (2 Cor. 1): having suffered with my Jesus here, I will rejoice with him elsewhere; they who rejoiced here in profane things will suffer eternally elsewhere. But I, having been afflicted here for my Jesus, will rejoice and exult after this life in the reality of what I now possess in hope—in God my Jesus. Let others exult in their idols, others in riches, honors, or lust; I will exult in my redemption, in my Savior and Jesus. [Col. 0545C]

31 The Lord God is my strength, and he will set my feet like those of deer.

“The Lord God is strength”: in him I trust that I will perform virtue. And just as deer cross thorny places, so with the Lord’s help I will cross over all the dangers of sins.

32 And he will lead me victoriously over my heights, while I sing in psalms.

“And over my heights”: he makes me transcend every worldly exaltation through contemplation of heavenly things, singing of his victory and triumph.

## THE SONG OF MOSES. DEUTERONOMY, CHAPTER XXXII

1 [Col. 0545D] Hear, O heavens, what I shall say; let the earth hear the words of my mouth.

“Hear, O heavens.” He calls the greatest elements as witnesses, so as to make the hearer attentive and to indicate that he is about to speak of great matters.

2 Let my doctrine gather like rain; let my speech flow like dew.

“Let my doctrine gather like rain,” and so forth: just as the drops of rain and dew are innumerable, so in this song I will discuss the unfathomable judgments of God. Or, just as rain and dew make the earth fruitful, so may my doctrine cause the fruits of the virtues to revive in you.

3 Like a shower upon the grass and like drops upon the herbage, because I will call upon the name of the Lord.

“Like a shower”: this verse has the meaning given above, because “I will call upon the name of the Lord,” that is, my discourse concerns the Lord. [Col. 0546A]

4 Give greatness to our God; God’s works are perfect, and all his ways are judgments.

“Give greatness,” that is, honor him worthily in faith and works. “God’s works are perfect,” because he is supremely perfect. “And all his ways,” that is, his works, are judgments, that is, arranged and accomplished with rational discernment—with the most provident reason and discretion.

5 God is faithful and without any iniquity, just and upright. They sinned against him, not his children in their filth.

“God is faithful” in all his promises, and just and upright in his judgments. “Not his children,” because they had degenerated from the true father by following idols. So also now those who follow sins are like degenerates, since they do not imitate the good father. [Col. 0546B]

6 A perverse and crooked generation: Is this what you render to the Lord, foolish and senseless people?

“A perverse and crooked generation,” namely in thought and deed. “Is this what you render?” that is, are these—namely, your evils—what you render? Or, “Is it not thus?” The people is called foolish and senseless because it is and has been ungrateful for the Lord’s benefits; crooked in affection, or perverse in understanding: foolish, thinking harmful what is beneficial; and senseless, not understanding that what is beneficial is beneficial to it. [Col. 0546C]

7 Is he not your father, who possessed you and made and created you?

“Is he not your father?” For all human beings naturally have God as Father, because God is said to generate something when he produces it anew or from nothing. Thus it is said: “These are the generations of heaven and earth” (Gen. 2)—not that he generated them from his substance, but that he produced them anew. “Who possessed you and made and created you” must be read in reverse order, namely, so that he first created by determining to make, and then made by forming. For how could he possess anything unless he had first created it?

7 Remember the days of old; consider the generations of each age.

“Remember the days”: remember how you were chosen in the patriarchs, and consider how he chose Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and many others.

8 [Col. 0546D] Ask your father, and he will declare it to you; your elders, and they will tell you.

“Ask your father”: ask the spiritual teacher and those who are greater in knowledge.

10 When the Most High divided the nations, when he separated the sons of Adam.

“When he divided”: namely, at the building of the tower of Babylon, when by the division of languages he divided the nations (Gen. 11); or by the division of the Red Sea, when he separated them from the Egyptians (Exod. 14). [Col. 0547A]

11 He established the boundaries of the peoples according to the number of the children of Israel.

“He established”: he speaks hyperbolically, saying that he established as many boundaries of the peoples, that is, of individual nations, as there were individual persons in the people of Israel. Or he says that as many individual nations were established as there were people from Israel who entered Egypt, namely seventy (Gen. 46). The other translation says that he established the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the angels of God. This is understood as follows: just as we read that a guardian angel is assigned to each human being (Matt. 18), so we should believe that angelic princes were appointed over the nations. For in Daniel we read of Michael as prince of the people, and of the angel of the Persians or Greeks (Dan. 10). [Col. 0547B]

12 But the Lord’s portion is his people; Jacob is the cord of his inheritance.

“But the Lord’s portion,” which he chose from all these peoples and nations, displayed his wonders to, and bestowed singular benefits upon, was his people, namely, the Jews. He says this to commend God’s benefits to them more forcefully: from so great a multitude of nations he chose for himself those descended from the stock of Jacob, so that they might be the cord of his inheritance, that is, as it were, his hereditary possession.

13 He found him in a desert land, in a place of horror and vast solitude.

“He found him in a desert land,” that is, on Mount Sinai [Col. 0547C], where he bound him with his laws (Exod. 20). “In a place of horror and vast solitude,” that is, Arabia, which lies around the desert.

14 He led him around and taught him, and guarded him like the apple of his eye.

“He led him around,” that is, he led him by the road of Mount Seir (Deut. 2). “And taught him,” namely, patience or his laws. And he guarded him with such careful attention as the apple of his eye, for the pupil is guarded more carefully than all the other members.

15 As an eagle urging its young to fly and hovering over them.

“As an eagle urging its young to fly,” and so forth. Natural philosophers report that the eagle places its young before the sun; whichever one it sees fixing its gaze firmly upon the sun’s ray, it nourishes, but whichever it sees growing sluggish, it abandons. So too the Lord teaches us always to direct the eye of understanding toward the sun of the divine majesty. Hovering over them, it also urges its young to fly; so divine compassion wishes us to advance from virtue to virtue. [Col. 0547D]

16 He spread out his wings and took him up, and carried him on his shoulders.

“He spread out his wings.” God, who is also the eagle, lifts up those who grow weary in him, for where we are least able to suffice, we hope for divine aid. He himself carries us, just as the eagle is said to carry its young on its shoulders, so that if it is shot at, it may receive the arrows before its young do. Thus Christ was wounded for us and defends us on the shoulders of his protection; and formerly he carried the Jews in this way. The Lord adapts himself to the weak so that we may understand his compassion for us; in the Gospel also he likened himself to a hen (Matt. 23). [Col. 0548A]

17 The Lord alone was his guide, and there was no foreign god with him.

“The Lord alone”: it belonged to his power alone to lead his people forth so gloriously, for none of the other gods was able to do this.

18 He set him upon a lofty land, that he might eat the fruits of the fields.

“He set him”: the land of promise is said to be the summit of the world; hence Jerusalem also appears to be the navel of the earth. The wise men of the world report that the earth is like a globe, convex on every side; but our land, that is, the Church, is loftier than all the virtues of the world. [Col. 0548B]

19 That he might suck honey from the rock and oil from the hardest stone.

“That he might suck”: this is said because of the abundance of all good things, for although the land was rugged with rocks, it abounded in honey and oil. Moreover, “honey from the rock,” that is, from Christ, signifies the sweetness of doctrine supplied to the faithful in this land before the Passion. “Oil from the hardest stone” signifies the time after the resurrection, when he had already become immortal. Christ poured out the oil of the Holy Spirit in that same land.

20 Butter from cattle and milk from sheep, with the fat of lambs and rams, the sons of Bashan.

[Col. 0548C] “Butter and milk”: he demonstrates an abundance of things, for the land of Bashan was extremely fertile for feeding flocks; therefore it was given to the Reubenites and Gadites, who possessed very many animals (Num. 32). For us, however, “butter from cattle,” that is, strong doctrine, is supplied from the patriarchs and prophets. “And milk from sheep”: gentler doctrine is supplied for the simple, with the fat of lambs and rams—that is, through the examples of teachers and subjects, spiritual desire, which is signified by fat, is provided. *Bashan* is interpreted as “fatness,” because the saints display the fatness of charity.

21 And goats with the marrow of wheat; and he drank the purest blood of the grape.

“And goats”: by goats we understand examples of repentance [Col. 0548D], for the saints live in the world as though they were always mourning their sins. Such is the life of hermits and true monks. “The marrow of wheat and the blood of the grape” signify the body and blood of Christ, “purest,” that is, most unmixed.

22 The beloved grew fat and kicked; he grew fat, became thick, and grew broad. He abandoned God who made him and departed from God his Savior.

“The beloved grew fat” because of the abundance of all things, “and kicked,” by following foreign gods; “he grew broad,” namely, in the propagation of his offspring. Or, he grew fat through pleasures, became thick with riches, and grew broad through honors and power; therefore he abandoned God, as though he no longer needed his help. [Col. 0549A]

24 They provoked him with foreign gods and stirred him to anger with abominations.

“They provoked him,” that is, by such deeds they incited him to anger and vengeance. Likewise, the one who turns to idolatry after baptism, or gives himself over to vices or evil spirits, arouses the Lord’s vengeance against himself.

25 They sacrificed to demons and not to God, to gods whom they did not know.

“They sacrificed”: this is clear.

26 New and recent ones came, whom their fathers had not worshiped.

“New and recent ones,” that is, because they were not steadfast in the worship of God, which they had learned from their fathers, they newly turned to worship gods whom their fathers had not worshiped. [Col. 0549B]

27 You abandoned the God who begot you and forgot the Lord your creator.

“The God who begot you,” that is, who formed you so that you might exist. But he also begets us in another way through baptism for the remission of sins.

28 The Lord saw and was stirred to anger, because his sons and daughters provoked him.

“The Lord saw”—nothing can be hidden from him—and rebuked them because of their sin, since they provoked him by worshiping gods whom he had adopted as sons and daughters.

29 And he said: I will hide my face from them, and I will consider their end. For they are a perverse generation, unfaithful children.

“And he said: I will hide”—that is, I will withdraw my help—“and I will consider their end,” that is, what kind of end they will reach. [Col. 0549C]

31 They provoked me with what was not God and stirred me to anger with their vanities.

“They provoked me”: just as they provoked me, the one God, with many gods, so I will take up many nations and reject this one.

32 And I will provoke them with one who is not a people, and with a foolish nation I will stir them to anger.

[Col. 0549D] “And I will provoke them with one who is not a people”: by this people he signifies all the nations, which in comparison with Israel were regarded as though they did not exist; or because the nations worshiping idols were not called God’s people.

33 A fire has been kindled in my anger, and it will burn to the depths of hell.

“A fire has been kindled”: my vengeance will begin in this age and burn to the depths of hell, that is, to eternal damnation. For the Lord sometimes begins to scourge the wicked and impious here, so that from temporal punishment they may pass into eternal punishment (Acts 12). We read that this happened to Herod and Antiochus (1 Macc. 8).

34 And it will devour the earth with its produce and burn the foundations of the mountains.

“It will devour the earth,” that is, it will devour sinners together with their works; and it will destroy the thoughts and confidence of the mountains, that is, of the proud. [Col. 0550A]

35 I will gather evils upon them and exhaust my arrows against them.

“I will gather”: the evils are punishments, which seem evil to those who suffer them but are just in the judgment of the one who inflicts them. “And my arrows”: that is, I will execute acts of vengeance.

36 They will be consumed by famine, and birds will devour them with the most bitter bite.

“They will be consumed”: we read that this happened to those whose corpses birds and beasts ate, and whom famine and the sword consumed. Sinners are also now consumed by hunger for the word of God and devoured by birds, that is, they are torn apart by evil spirits. [Col. 0550B]

37 I will send the teeth of beasts against them, with the fury of those that drag across the earth and of serpents.

“The teeth of beasts”: the savagery of the devil will be sent against them, and in God’s fury it will drag them across the earth, that is, overthrow them in worldly desires.

38 Outside, the sword will lay them waste; inside, terror.

“Outside, it will lay them waste”: while suffering punishments, they are tormented by their own conscience (Isa. 66). Hence it is said: “Their fire will not be extinguished, and their worm will not die” (Mark 9).

39 The young man together with the virgin, the suckling with the aged man.

“The young man together”: he will spare no age when taking vengeance. Allegorically, however, in the young man we may understand the lustful; in the virgin, one barren of good works; in the suckling, the dull-minded; and in the old man, one rendered useless through prolonged sloth. God’s vengeance will consume them all. [Col. 0550C]

40 And I said: Where are they? I will put an end among human beings to their memory.

“And I said, ‘Where are they?’”: he does not ask out of ignorance but makes others learn. “I will put an end among human beings to their memory”: either when the Jews no longer appear in the promised land, or when the wicked are separated from the communion of the saints and regarded as nothing. There are many examples of this.

41 [Col. 0550D] But because of the anger of the enemies I delayed, lest perhaps their enemies should grow proud and say: Our hand is exalted, and the Lord did not do all these things.

“But because of this”: these two verses must be joined. For this reason he often endured the former people, lest the surrounding nations blaspheme his name. So also he endures us sinners and does not immediately condemn those who sin, lest evil spirits glory in our destruction and boast that they have won the victory.

43 It is a nation without counsel and without understanding. If only they were wise, understood, and considered their final end.

“A nation without counsel”: the nation of the Jews and all the impious is without counsel for salvation, because they do not know how to provide for their future. [Col. 0551A]

44 How could one pursue a thousand, and two put ten thousand to flight? Was it not because their God sold them and the Lord shut them in?

“How could one pursue?” It could not have happened that one of the enemies pursued a thousand Jews, unless their God had sold them—that is, cast them away from himself, regarded them with hatred, and shut them up in the hands of their enemies.

46 For our God is not like their gods, and our enemies are judges.

“For our God is not like their gods”: the Lord our God is truthful and just, but the idols of the nations are false and useless. “And our enemies are judges,” that is, approvers. For all the nations, although they worship various idols, confess that the world is governed by the power of one God.

47 Their wine is from the vine of Sodom and from the outskirts of Gomorrah.

“From the vine of Sodom”: in Scripture the synagogue or Jerusalem is often compared with Sodom (Ezek. 16), because just as the Sodomites abused God’s gifts, so these people always proved ungrateful for God’s benefits. Sin is first in the heart through consent, second in the inward plotting by which the deed is carried out, and third in the outward act that has been committed. The first is called the vine here, the second the grape, and the third the wine. [Col. 0551B]

48 [Col. 0551C] Their grape is the grape of gall, and their cluster is most bitter.

“Their grape”: the vine—which is the house of Israel—was turned into bitterness (Isa. 5), that is, it conspired toward Christ’s death; and to him hanging on the cross they offered vinegar mixed with gall (John 19), producing a most bitter cluster of their wickedness.

49 Their wine is the gall of dragons and the incurable poison of asps.

“The gall of dragons”: just as dragons and asps conceal poisons in their gall, so their conscience is full of wickedness.

50 Are these things not stored up with me and sealed in my treasures?

“Are these things not stored up?” That is, are they not reserved with me and not consigned to oblivion? These things—namely, your sins—are not forgotten because I have delayed taking vengeance; rather, they have been stored up until the day of retribution. [Col. 0551D]

51 Vengeance is mine, and I will repay them in due time, so that their foot may slip.

“Vengeance is mine,” that is, at the time of vengeance I will repay them what they deserve. “So that their foot may slip,” that is, those who seemed to stand will perish.

52 The day of destruction is near, and the times hasten to arrive.

“The day of destruction is near,” because it is certain; or because, although this age may contain many thousands of years, it is nevertheless brief in comparison with eternity. The days of vengeance therefore draw near, and when we do not expect them, they are present (Matt. 24).

53 [Col. 0552A] The Lord will judge his people, and he will have mercy on his servants.

“The Lord will judge,” that is, he will distinguish his saints from the impious. For “judgment” can be understood as separation or condemnation. “And he will have mercy on his servants,” that is, he will show mercy on the day of vengeance. Those who faithfully served him will receive eternal rewards, not from works but from grace and mercy—for what do you have that you did not receive? (1 Cor. 4.)

54 He will see that the hand has grown weak, and that even the imprisoned have failed; [Col. 0552B] the survivors have also been consumed.

“He will see that the hand has grown weak,” that is, he will make it apparent that the works of the wicked were weak. “And even the imprisoned have failed”: that is, those captured by enemies have failed through their own strength. “The survivors”: those who depart from this life have afterward no opportunity to do anything.

55 And they will say: Where are their gods, in whom they trusted?

And the adversaries of those who captured them, and the demons, will say to wicked Christians—whose god was their belly, honor, and riches (Phil. III)—after death and in death: “Where,” etc. Or even the just and good, seeing God’s vengeance and wrath, will say: “Where,” etc.

**56** From whose sacrifices they ate the fat and drank the wine of their libations.

“From whose sacrifices”: in these words he includes all the vanities that people pursue, whether of idolatry or of sins; for the wicked are reproached with the vain things in which they lived. [Col. 0552C]

**57** Let them arise and help you; and in your necessity let them protect you.

Let the idols that you worshiped come and rescue you.

**58** See that I alone am, and that there is no other God besides me.

“See,” that is, understand that I alone am God.

**59** I kill and I make alive; I strike, and I heal; and there is no one who can rescue from my hand.

“I kill”: he kills in two ways and gives life in two ways, because he condemns some to hell and raises others to eternal life. In another way, he kills the old person in order to make the new person alive. “And there is no one who can rescue from my hand,” that is, no one who can resist my power. [Col. 0552D]

**60** I will raise my hand to heaven and say, “I live forever.”

“I will raise it to heaven,” that is, I will display the eternity of my power.

**61** If I sharpen my sword like lightning, and my hand takes hold of judgment.

“If I sharpen it like lightning,” that is, when my judgment comes swiftly. “And my hand takes hold of judgment,” that is, when my power begins to judge.

**62** I will repay vengeance upon my enemies, and I will recompense those who hate me.

“I will repay vengeance,” that is, I will exact vengeance upon sinners.

**63** I will intoxicate my arrows with blood, and my sword will devour flesh.

“I will intoxicate my arrows,” that is, I will display my vengeance in sinners; “and my sword will devour flesh,” that is, my judgment will consume the carnal. [Col. 0553A]

**64** From the blood of the slain, and from the captivity, from the stripped head of the enemies.

“From the blood of the slain”: the words “I will intoxicate my arrows” are understood—that is, in the destruction of the condemned. “And from the captivity, from the stripped head of the enemies”: according to the literal sense, captives were shorn and sold—for this is to sell “under the crown.” Spiritually, however, Antichrist, the head of the ungodly, will be destroyed by the power of Christ taking vengeance. In another sense, the Lord exercises vengeance upon the captivity of the head of the enemies when he destroys the arrogance of the minds of the wicked and their malice. [Col. 0553B]

**65** Praise his people, nations, for he will avenge the blood of his servants.

“Praise his people, nations,” that is, his saints; “for he will avenge the blood of his martyrs.”

**66** And he will repay vengeance upon their enemies, and he will show mercy to the land of his people.

“And he will repay vengeance upon their enemies,” namely, upon heretics, unbelievers, and persecutors. “And he will show mercy to the land of his people,” that is, to the Church, when he displays his mercy toward her.

# HYMN OF THE THREE YOUTHS, DANIEL, CHAPTER III

“Bless all the works of the Lord, O Lord,” etc.

[Col. 0553C]

After a general exhortation has first been given—that every creature ought to praise God (alternatively, “the Lord”)—the text proceeds by treating individual things in turn (alternatively, “is restricted to individual things”): the angels and the heavens; the waters and the powers; the sun and the moon; the rain and the dew; the spirit, fire, and heat; cold and summer; and the rest, which would take too long to enumerate. Thus it also summons springs and seas and the whales, birds, beasts, cattle, and the sons of men to the praise of the Lord. And after the whole human race, Israel; and from Israel itself, the priests and servants of the Lord; the spirits and souls of the righteous; the holy and humble in heart; and finally Hananiah, Azariah, and Mishael, who by a powerful benefit are summoned to praise the Lord.

Every creature, however, praises the Lord not with its voice but by its works, because the Creator is frequently understood from his creatures, and God’s magnificence is displayed in each of his works and effects. (The text of **BENEDICITE** follows; it differs from the Vulgate in nothing except at verse 67, “cold and summer.”) [Col. 0553D]

# CANTICLE OF ZECHARIAH, LUKE, CHAPTER I

**1** Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, for he has visited and accomplished the redemption of his people.

“Blessed”: for he speaks of two things, visiting and redeeming. To visit belongs to the sick, while to redeem belongs to captives; and both apply to the human race, since the human race was weakened by sins and was also held captive by the devil’s deception. When the Lord came, he visited the weak, because he freed them from sins; and he redeemed the captive, because he withdrew him from the devil’s power, and by redeeming him made him his own. B. It should be noted concerning this verse that blessed Zechariah, in prophetic manner, narrates as already accomplished what he foresaw as still future in the spirit and soon to be done, saying, “for he has visited,” that is, he has become incarnate. [Col. 0554A]

**2** And he raised up for us a horn of salvation in the house of David, his servant.

B. “And he raised up a horn of salvation”: he means the firm height of salvation. For all bones are enclosed in flesh, whereas a horn projects beyond the flesh. Therefore the “horn of salvation” is called the kingdom of Christ the Savior; by this expression a spiritual height is announced, one that surpasses the joys of the flesh and by which the world and the joys of the flesh are overcome. [Col. 0554B]

**3** As he spoke through the mouth of his holy prophets, who have been from of old.

“As he spoke.” He says “from of old” because the whole Scripture of the Old Covenant preceded as prophecy concerning Christ. For not only Jeremiah, Isaiah, and the other prophets spoke openly of his coming; rather, the father Adam himself, Abel, and Enoch bear witness to his dispensation.

**4** Salvation from our enemies and from the hand of all who hate us.

“Salvation” must be joined to the preceding verse: he raised up for us, namely, salvation from our enemies. By “all who hate us” he signifies either wicked people or unclean spirits.

**5** To show mercy to our fathers and to remember his holy covenant.

“To show mercy”: for he had said that the Lord would be born in the house of David according to the declarations of the prophets; and thus mercy was shown to them when the promise was fulfilled. [Col. 0554C]

**6** The oath that he swore to Abraham our father, that he would grant us:

“The oath”: he says that this same Christ, in accordance with the oath that God swore, would free us, in order to fulfill the covenant that he established with Abraham. For it was chiefly to these patriarchs that either the gathering of the nations or the incarnation was promised from their offspring. [Col. 0554D]

**7** That, having been delivered from the hand of our enemies without fear, we might serve him.

“That, without fear”: for whoever either withdraws from the service of the Lord before death, or strives to remain holy only before human beings and not before God, has not yet been perfectly freed from the hand of spiritual enemies and serves the Lord (IV Kings XVII); rather, following the example of the Samaritans, he attempts to serve both the gods of the nations and the Lord.

**8** In holiness and righteousness before him all our days.

“In holiness”: he plainly and briefly designates how the Lord must be served—namely, in holiness and righteousness, before him and throughout all our days. [Col. 0555A]

**9** And you, child, will be called the prophet of the Most High; for you will go before the face of the Lord to prepare his ways.

“And you, child.” Beautifully, while speaking about the Lord, he suddenly turns his words to the prophet, so that he might also indicate that this was a gift of the Lord. A. But how could he address the child when he could not yet either hear or understand? He could understand because he was full of the Holy Spirit. For if, while still enclosed in his mother’s womb, he recognized the coming of the Lord, once born he was able to understand.

**10** To give knowledge of salvation to his people, for the remission of their sins.

“To give knowledge”: when he mentions that knowledge is to be given, he prevents you from thinking that a carnal and temporal salvation is being promised; he says instead, “for the remission of their sins.” [Col. 0555B]

**11** Through the merciful compassion of our God, by which the rising from on high has visited us.

“Through the merciful compassion”: compassion refers not only to the vital organs of the inner body, but also to everything covered by hide and skin. By “compassion,” therefore, his hidden mercy is signified. “By which,” namely, by these hidden mercies, “the rising from on high has visited us.” He is rightly called “the rising,” because, opening for us the rising of the true light, he made the children of night and darkness children of light (I Thess. V).

**12** To enlighten those who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death, to direct our feet into the way of peace.

“To enlighten”: the Lord’s enlightening consists in impressing the rays of knowledge and love of himself upon those who have lived in sins and in the blindness of ignorance. Our feet are directed into the way of peace when the course of our actions agrees in every respect with the grace of our Redeemer and Enlightener. [Col. 0555C]

# CANTICLE OF SAINT MARY AT VESPERS, LUKE, CHAPTER I

My soul magnifies the Lord.

“My soul magnifies”: she says, “The Lord has exalted me with such an unheard-of gift that it can be explained by no service of the tongue, but can scarcely be grasped except through the innermost affection of the heart. Therefore I offer all the powers of my soul in the praises of giving thanks.” [Col. 0555D]

**2** And my spirit rejoiced in God my Savior.

“And my spirit rejoiced”: because my spirit rejoices in the eternal divinity of that same Jesus, that is, of the Savior, while my flesh is made fruitful by his temporal conception. To this is similar the Psalmist’s saying: “My soul will rejoice in the Lord and will delight in his salvation” (Ps. XXXIV).

**3** For he has regarded the humility of his handmaid. Behold, from this time onward all generations will call me blessed.

“For he has regarded.” She rightly rejoices that the one whose humility is regarded is to be called blessed by all. For just as through the pride of our first mother Eve death entered the world, so again through the humility of Mary the entrance of life was to be opened. [Col. 0556A]

**4** For he who is mighty has done great things for me, and holy is his name.

“For he has done”: only that soul to which the Lord deigns to do great things can magnify him with worthy praises. His name is called holy because, by the summit of his unique power, it transcends every creature and is set far apart from all that he has made.

**5** And his mercy is from generation to generation toward those who fear him.

“And his mercy”: as though she were saying, “Just as his mercy came upon me, who fear him, so also upon all who fear him.” Turning from particular gifts to the general judgments of God, she describes the condition of the whole human race and explains in alternating verses what the proud and the humble deserve, what the children of Abraham are by free choice, and what the children of God are by grace. “Therefore,” she says, “the one who is mighty has not done great things for me alone; rather, in every nation and generation, whoever fears God and practices righteousness is acceptable to him” (Acts X). [Col. 0556B]

**6** He has shown strength with his arm; he has scattered the proud in the imagination of their hearts.

“He has shown strength”: now she speaks of God the Father, who has shown strength with his arm, that is, in his own Son. For just as your arm is the means by which you act, so God’s Word is called his arm, because through the Word he made the world. B. Or “his arm” is called the power and dominion of his might, because he needs no assistance from another in acting. [Col. 0556C]

**7** He has cast down the mighty from their seat and has exalted the humble.

“He has cast down”: the mighty are called the exalted, as the Jews are, who have been cast down from the seat of the kingdom or from the understanding of the holy Scriptures. B. He calls the same people “mighty” whom he earlier called proud. They are therefore called mighty not because they truly possess power, but because, trusting in their own strength, they refuse to seek the help of their Creator. Those, however, are truly mighty who can say with the Apostle: “I can do all things in him who strengthens me, Jesus Christ” (Phil. IV).

**8** He has filled the hungry with good things and has sent the rich away empty.

B. Those who hunger for heavenly things are filled here with heavenly virtues and, after death, with eternal blessedness. Those who glory in earthly riches or honors, by which they know themselves to be filled, are left empty of virtues, and after this life they will suffer eternal poverty. [Col. 0556D]

**9** He has received Israel, his servant, remembering his mercy.

“He has received Israel”: Israel, that is, everyone who sees God through faith, is received by God when he is a servant—that is, humble and obedient. God therefore received Israel, his servant, when he took flesh from Israel and raised it up to union with the Word; he received it when he united it to himself in the person of the Virgin Mary in the womb. And this was not on account of our merits or those of Israel, his servant, but on account of his unspeakable mercy, which he remembered. [Col. 0557A]

**10** As he spoke to our fathers, to Abraham and to his offspring forever.

“As he spoke to our fathers”: for he was saying to the fathers and prophets that he would accomplish this mercy for Abraham and his offspring, that is, for everyone who imitates his faith.

# CANTICLE OF SIMEON, LUKE, CHAPTER I

**1** Now you dismiss your servant, Lord, according to your word, in peace.

“Now you dismiss”: you see that the righteous of not only the New but also the Old Testament possessed a desire, based on hope of the future life, to be released from the body; indeed, they regarded it as the way of peace to lay down the earthly burden, since they did not doubt that they would possess perpetual rest in Abraham’s bosom. [Col. 0557B]

**2** For my eyes have seen your salvation.

“For they have seen”: “Blessed are the eyes that see” (Luke X) what Simeon saw. “Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed” (John XX).

[Col. 0558A]

**3** Which you prepared before the face of all peoples.

“Which you prepared”: he says, “That very salvation which you afterward prepared for all nations, peoples, and tongues to behold with mind and faith, and which you foresaw as to be sought with hope and love—I, who had long desired it, now contemplate as your salvation with the eyes both of flesh and of the heart.”

**4** A light for the revelation of the nations and the glory of your people Israel.

“A light”: the salvation of God, that is, Christ prepared by God, is truly a light for both peoples. Yet he is called more particularly the glory of Israel, for whom he was long awaited (Rom. IX), and from whom he came when proclaimed. He is the revelation of the nations, whom he likewise deigned to visit and enlighten. [Col. 0558B]

[Col. 0557]

# OF SAINT BRUNO, BISHOP OF HERBIPOLIS: COMMENTARY ON THE LORD’S PRAYER, THE APOSTLES’ CREED, AND THE FAITH OF ATHANASIUS

# THE LORD’S PRAYER, MATTHEW, CHAPTER VI, AND LUKE XI

[Col. 0557C]

**1** Our Father, who are in heaven.

**Disciple.** How many petitions are contained in the Lord’s Prayer?

**Teacher.** Seven.

**Disciple.** What is the first?

**Teacher.** “Hallowed be your name.”

**Disciple.** How is this phrase, which comes at the beginning—“Our Father, who are in heaven”—to be understood?

**Teacher.** It is an invocation of the divinity, since we profess that we have God as Father, because we are all brothers and have God as our Father in heaven (Matt. XXIII).

**2** Hallowed be your name.

**Disciple.** In the first petition you mentioned, what is to be understood?

**Teacher.** “Christian” is derived from “Christ,” and therefore, when we are called Christians, we bear Christ’s name. We entreat that we may be able to perform the works of Christ and that his name may be sanctified in us through our good works. [Col. 0557D]

**3** Your kingdom come.

**Disciple.** What is the second petition?

**Teacher.** “Your kingdom come.”

**Disciple.** What is to be understood there?

**Teacher.** We pray that Christ may reign in us and not the devil; that is, that the Church of Christ may always increase, in which God reigns; and that the day of judgment may come, because then the devil ceases to reign in the world and Christ will reign forever with his saints (I Cor. XV). [Col. 0558C]

**4** Your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.

**Disciple.** What is the third?

**Teacher.** “Your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.”

**Disciple.** How is it to be understood?

**Teacher.** Just as the angels in heaven obey your will, so also let the righteous on earth do so; and just as your will is fulfilled in the saints, so also let it be fulfilled in sinners.

**5** Give us this day our daily bread.

**Disciple.** What is the fourth?

**Teacher.** “Give us this day our daily bread.”

**Disciple.** What is understood in it?

**Teacher.** Here “bread” is understood as all the foods by which we are to live. We also pray for the reception of Christ’s body; finally, we ask him to give himself to us, for he is the living bread (John VI). [Col. 0558D]

**6** And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.

**Disciple.** What is the fifth?

**Teacher.** “And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.”

**Disciple.** What should be understood by it?

**Teacher.** We also pray that he may forgive our sins in the same way as we forgive our debtors. [Col. 0559A]

**7** And do not lead us into temptation.

**Disciple.** What is the sixth?

**Teacher.** “And do not lead us into temptation.”

**Disciple.** How is this to be understood?

**Teacher.** We do not ask not to be tempted, because “the one who has not been tempted has not been tested” (Rom. V). Rather, we pray that he not lead us into a temptation that we cannot endure (I Cor. X), that is, that he not permit us to sin in temptation. God is said to lead someone in when he withdraws his help.

**8** But deliver us from evil. Amen.

**Disciple.** What is the seventh?

**Teacher.** “But deliver us from evil.” [Col. 0559B]

**Disciple.** How is it to be understood?

**Teacher.** That is, from the devil, from sin, and from every evil temptation.

**Disciple.** How is “Amen,” which comes at the end, to be understood, or to what language does it belong?

**Teacher.** “Amen” is said in Hebrew; translated into Latin, it means “truly” and “faithfully.”

# THE APOSTLES’ CREED

**1** I believe in God the Father almighty, creator of heaven and earth.

**Disciple.** I accept these things. But since, as you know, we all believe that we are saved through faith, I ask you to tell me how you understand your faith, or in whom you believe.

**Teacher.** I believe in God, the almighty Father, creator of heaven and earth.

**Disciple.** Why is he called almighty, and why creator?

**Teacher.** He is called almighty because he can do everything that he wills; creator, because he created everything—heaven and earth, the sea, and all things. [Col. 0559C]

**2** And in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord.

**Disciple.** Do you believe in Jesus Christ?

**Teacher.** I certainly believe in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord, who is true God and true man.

**Disciple.** How is he true God, and how true man?

**Teacher.** He is true God because he was conceived from the Holy Spirit; true man because he was born from the Virgin Mary.

**3** Who was conceived from the Holy Spirit, born from the Virgin Mary.

**Disciple.** Behold, he has been born. What happened afterward?

**Teacher.** After his holy birth, growing in age and wisdom, he completed thirty years (Luke III). At that age he also deigned to be baptized by John the Baptist, and after his baptism he taught for three and a half years. And he preached everything that pertains to eternal life. [Col. 0559D]

**4** He suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, died, and was buried.

**Disciple.** What happened after this preaching?

**Teacher.** During that very preaching he was seized by the wicked and faithless Jews. Because of their envy and because of our sins, he endured many blasphemies and many sufferings under Pontius Pilate, who at that time was judge in Judea.

**Disciple.** Why is he called Pontius?

**Teacher.** He received this name from the place where he was born. [Col. 0560A]

**Disciple.** What happened after this?

**Teacher.** He was crucified under him, died on that same cross, and then was buried.

**5** He descended to the underworld; on the third day he rose from the dead.

While his body remained in the tomb, his soul descended to the underworld. From that underworld he mercifully freed the holy patriarchs—Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—and the holy prophets Isaiah, Jeremiah, and the rest, as well as all the others whom he had chosen. And on the third day he rose victorious.

**Disciple.** After he rose, what did he do?

**Teacher.** After his most glorious and holy resurrection, he lived with his disciples for forty days and forty nights, and he ate with them, teaching and speaking many things about the kingdom of God (Acts I). [Col. 0560B]

**6** He ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of God the Father almighty.

**Disciple.** What happened afterward?

**Teacher.** After this, while they watched, he ascended into heaven, where he sits at the right hand of the almighty Father, in whatever manner and however he wills.

**7** From there he will come to judge the living and the dead.

**Disciple.** What will he do afterward?

**Teacher.** When the end of the world has come, he will come with the same body with which he ascended into heaven, to judge the living and the dead.

**Disciple.** What are the living, and what are the dead?

**Teacher.** The living are the righteous; the dead are sinners.

**8** I believe in the Holy Spirit, the holy catholic Church.

[Col. 0560C]

**Disciple.** Do you believe in the Holy Spirit?

**Teacher.** Without doubt I believe in the Holy Spirit.

**Disciple.** What is he?

**Teacher.** He is God and the third person in the Trinity, because the person of the Father is one, that of the Son another, and that of the Holy Spirit another. In this Trinity I wholly believe and confess one God.

**Disciple.** Do you believe in the holy catholic Church and in the communion of the saints?

**Teacher.** I believe the holy Church, but I do not believe in it, because it is not God but the convocation or assembly of Christians and the house of God.

**Disciple.** In what language is “Church” said?

**Teacher.** Greek.

**Disciple.** What does it mean in Latin?

**Teacher.** A convocation or assembly of Christians, as I said above.

**Disciple.** What does “catholic” mean?

**Teacher.** Universal, that is, spread throughout the whole world.

**The communion of the saints.**

[Col. 0560D]

I also believe that I have fellowship and communion with the saints—that is, the communion of the saints—if I hold the faith firmly and preserve it in my works.

**9** The remission of sins.

**Disciple.** Do you believe in the remission of sins?

**Teacher.** No; but I believe that there is remission of sins, because for this reason the Son of God deigned to assume flesh: so that we, who could not be saved on account of our sins, might be saved by his mercy.

**10** The resurrection of the flesh.

**Disciple.** Do you believe in the resurrection of the flesh?

**Teacher.** I do not believe in it; but I believe that the flesh which we carry in this life under mortal conditions will rise immortal, and that on account of its partnership the soul will have to give an account. [Col. 0561A]

**11** And eternal life. Amen.

We believe without doubt that we shall attain eternal life if we firmly hold and fulfill in our works the things we have explained up to this point.

# LAUDS AFTER THE NIGHT OFFICE

The hymn which Saint Ambrose and Saint Augustine composed together. (The text of **TE DEUM** follows.)

# THE CATHOLIC FAITH OF SAINT ATHANASIUS, BISHOP

**1** Whoever wishes to be saved must, above all, hold the catholic faith.

[Col. 0561B]

Here blessed Athanasius posited free choice, as he says in the psalm: “Who is the person who desires life?” (Ps. XXXIII); and again, in the Gospel, Truth itself says: “Whoever wishes to come after me” (Matt. XVI). So also here: “Whoever wishes to be saved.” He does not say, “Whether you wish it or not, you will be saved,” but “whoever wishes,” because almighty God draws no one to the faith unwillingly or by compulsion.

But whoever wishes to be saved eternally, in body or in soul, must hold the catholic faith. For before every work it is necessary that faith precede; before every action, before every undertaking, before every beginning, everyone must hold the catholic faith, as the Apostle says: “Without faith it is impossible [Col. 0561C] to please God” (Heb. XI). Hence the prophet Habakkuk says: “But the righteous person lives by faith” (Hab. II).

“Catholic” is a Greek expression; in Latin it is translated as “general” or “universal.” “General” means that it pertains to all people; “universal,” because it has been spread throughout the whole world. Faith is belief by which we truly believe what we are in no way able to see. Hence the Apostle says: “Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the proof of things not seen” (Heb. XI).

It is called *faith* (*fides*) because it is made (*fit*) between God and human beings. We must possess this faith, this belief, above all, because faith is the foundation of all virtues. Therefore we first build faith, which is the foundation, and upon it the other virtues, because no one can be saved without faith.

Faith is thus called belief or trust. It is called catholic, universal—that is, right belief—which the whole Church ought to hold. The true Church is called the assembly of Christians or the gathering of peoples. [Col. 0561D]

**2** Unless each person preserves this faith whole and inviolate, he will undoubtedly perish forever.

This faith—“each person,” that is, every individual—must be preserved “whole,” that is, complete and perfect, so that no one divides it through heresy or corrupts it through any schism. “Inviolate” means that one must not violate it by speaking evil of it or by preaching against it. If one does not preserve it whole and inviolate, one will undoubtedly perish in eternal damnation.

**3** Now this is the catholic faith: that we venerate one God in Trinity and the Trinity in unity.

He now explains what faith is and how each person ought to believe it: “that we venerate one God in Trinity and the Trinity in unity.” That is, we must believe in three and one: one in substance and three in persons. Because of the Trinity, we must not abandon unity; because of unity, we must not abandon the Trinity. We must venerate—that is, adore and worship—the one whom we worship as both one and three: one on account of the unity of substance, and three on account of the names of the persons. [Col. 0562A]

**4** Neither confusing the persons nor separating the substance.

To confuse is to mix together. We must not believe in only one person, as the heretic Sabellius asserted, but in three—that is, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. [Col. 0562B] Nor must we separate the substance, as the heretic Arius asserted. For he said that just as there were three persons, so there were three substances. He maintained that the Father was greater than the Son, the Son lesser than the Father, and that the Holy Spirit was their servant.

“Substance” is so called because it subsists from itself. Substance, moreover, is a common name for all things that exist: heaven, the sun, the moon, the earth, and trees; human beings too are called substances. God, therefore, is substance—indeed, supreme substance, the first substance, and the cause of all substances, because he is the creator of all things (Exod. III). “Essence,” therefore, is properly said of God: it is that which always is what it is, because it is unchangeable (James I). [Col. 0562C]

**5** For one is the person of the Father, another of the Son, and another of the Holy Spirit.

Here the persons are distinguished against Sabellius, who asserts that they are one. The Father in his person is not the Son, but only the Father; nor is the Son in his person the Father, but only the Son; and the Holy Spirit in his person is neither the Father nor the Son, but only the Holy Spirit, proceeding from both. “Person” is so called because it sounds through itself.

**6** But the divinity of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one; their glory equal and their majesty coeternal.

[Col. 0562D]

“The divinity of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one,” that is, their substance is one. “Their glory equal and their majesty coeternal,” that is, their glory and power are equal, without beginning and without end.

**7** Such as the Father is, such is the Son, and such is the Holy Spirit.

For just as the Father is eternal, almighty, and invisible, so also are the Son and the Holy Spirit.

**8** The Father uncreated, the Son uncreated, and the Holy Spirit uncreated.

“The Father uncreated”: here the preposition *in-* means “not,” as a negative formation. The Father is uncreated, that is, not created, because he himself is the Creator of all and was created by no one. [Col. 0563A] He is the maker of all and was made by no one.

The Son is uncreated, and the Holy Spirit likewise uncreated. The Son is uncreated, not a creature as Arius said, because he created all things together with the Father; the same is true of the Holy Spirit.

**9** The Father immeasurable, the Son immeasurable, and the Holy Spirit immeasurable.

The Father is immeasurable because no one can measure his greatness or extent, which is higher than heaven, deeper than earth, and broader than the sea (Job XI). He is unbounded, incorporeal, not confined to any place, wholly everywhere; there is no place where he is not, as he says in the psalm: “If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into the underworld, you are present; and if I go to the farthest limits of the sea, there your right hand will hold me” (Ps. XXXVIII).

He is within all things but not enclosed; outside all things but not excluded. [Col. 0563B] The same is true of the Son, who “reaches mightily from end to end” (Wis. VIII), of whom it is written: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established” (Ps. XXXII). In the same way, the Holy Spirit is immeasurable. Hence it is said: “The Spirit of the Lord has filled the world” (Wis. I).

**10** The Father eternal, the Son eternal, and the Holy Spirit eternal.

Here “eternal” must be understood as everlasting. God the Father is called eternal because he exists without beginning and without end; the same is true of the Son and the Holy Spirit. For just as there was never a time when the Father was not, so there was never a time when the Son and the Holy Spirit were not.

**11** And yet not three eternals, but one eternal.

And yet they are not three eternals but one eternal, namely, in substance. [Col. 0563C]

**12** Just as there are not three uncreated or three immeasurable, but one uncreated and one immeasurable.

For God is one in his substance.

**13** Likewise, the Father almighty, the Son almighty, and the Holy Spirit almighty.

The Father is called almighty because he can do all things—not from *suffering* (*patiendo*), which he does not will, but from *doing* (*faciendo*) everything he wills; nothing is impossible for him. The Son is almighty because whatever the Father can do, the Son can do; and the Holy Spirit likewise.

Therefore, if he can do all things, what is there that he cannot do? He cannot do what it is incompatible with omnipotence to do. He cannot be deceived, because he is truth and wisdom; he cannot become sick or weak, because he is health; he cannot die, because he is immortal; he cannot come to an end, because he is infinite and everlasting. [Col. 0563D]

**14** And yet not three almighties, but one Almighty.

Yet they are not three almighties, because omnipotence belongs to the substance, and their substance is one. Fatherhood, however, exists in relation to another. Hence the names Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are relative, because each refers to another, just as, for example, servant refers to lord, lord to servant, teacher to disciple, disciple to teacher, father to son, and son to father.

No one is called a father unless he has a son of whom he is the father; and no one is a son unless he has a father whose son he is. For if he had not had a Son, he would never have had the name “Father.” Similarly, the Holy Spirit is not Spirit from himself, but is the Spirit of someone.

There is also another designation by which the Holy Spirit is spoken of relatively, namely, “gift.” For he is called the gift of the giver, and the giver of the gift. I say that the Father is the giver, while the Holy Spirit is the gift; the gift is referred to the giver, and the giver to the gift. This, then, is the reason why the Holy Spirit is called relatively. [Col. 0564A]

**15** Thus the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God.

“God” is the proper name of the Trinity, belonging to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; it is borrowed from a Greek designation. For in Greek God is called *theos*, that is, “fear.” Hence the word *Deus* is derived from the fact that there is fear for those who worship him.

The proper name of the Father, however, is “Father,” because he alone is Father; the proper name of the Son is “Son,” because the Son alone is from the Father alone; and the proper name of the Holy Spirit is “Holy Spirit,” because he proceeds from both.

The Father is God because he is himself the fountain and origin of divinity. Likewise the Son is God, though not from himself, because he is not from himself but is begotten from the Father alone. In the same way, the Holy Spirit is not God from himself, but is God proceeding from the Father and the Son. [Col. 0564B]

**16** And yet not three gods, but one God. Thus the Father is Lord, the Son is Lord, and the Holy Spirit is Lord. And yet not three lords, but one Lord.

As it is written: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one” (Deut. VI). The Father is called Lord from lordship, because he rules and governs his creation; the same is true of the Son and the Holy Spirit. [Col. 0564C]

**17** For just as, in accordance with Christian truth, we are compelled to confess each person individually as God and Lord,

“Individually,” that is, distinctly or separately: I call each person God and Lord. If you ask me what the Father is, I answer, “God and Lord”; likewise, if you ask what the Son is, I say, “God and Lord”; and if you say, “What is the Holy Spirit?” I answer, “God and Lord.” Yet in these three persons there are not three Gods or three Lords; rather, in the three, as was already said above, I confess one God and Lord. [Col. 0564D]

**18** So we are forbidden by catholic religion to speak of three Gods or Lords.

“We are forbidden,” that is, we are prohibited.

**19** The Father was made by no one, neither created nor begotten.

The Father was made by no one because he himself is the maker of all; he was not created but is the Creator; he was not begotten but is the Begetter. For “Father” in Greek is called *genitor* in Latin.

**20** The Son is from the Father alone, not made, nor created, but begotten.

The Son is from the Father alone: not made, because he himself, together with the Father, is the maker of all things; nor created, because he is the creator of all things; but begotten, alone from the Father alone [Col. 0565A]. Each person also possesses something proper to that person which the others do not possess. The Father has as his personal property that he alone is Father; the Son has as his personal property that he alone is begotten from the Father alone. The Son also possesses another property that neither the Father nor the Holy Spirit possesses: he has eternity with the Father and the Holy Spirit, and he has, in time, birth from a mother—which neither the Holy Spirit nor the Father has—because the Father did not assume flesh in his person, nor did the Holy Spirit, but only the Son. In this way he showed us in himself that he has two natures: one before all ages, by which he was begotten from the Father, and concerning which Isaiah said, “Who shall declare his generation?” (Isaiah 53); the other in time, concerning which the apostle Paul says, “But when the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the law” (Galatians 4). “In him it pleased the fullness of divinity to dwell bodily” (Colossians 2). From the Father he is without beginning and without end; from his mother he has a beginning, yet is concluded by no end.

**21. The Holy Spirit is from the Father and the Son: not made, nor created, nor begotten, but proceeding.**

The Holy Spirit has as his property that he is neither the Father nor the Son, but the Spirit proceeding from the Father and the Son. You hear that this one is from both, the Son from one, and the Father from no one; and by this their properties are clearly shown. The Spirit is therefore called the Holy Spirit of God because he is the holiness of the Father and of the Son. For although the Father is Spirit, the Son is Spirit, the Father is holy, and the Son is holy, he alone is properly called the Holy Spirit [Col. 0565C].

**22. Thus there is one Father, not three fathers; one Son, not three sons; one Holy Spirit, not three Holy Spirits.**

There is one Father because he alone begot one Son for himself. There is one Son because he was singly begotten by the one Father. There is one Holy Spirit because one Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son.

**23. And in this Trinity nothing is earlier or later, nothing greater or lesser. But all three persons are coeternal with one another and coequal.**

Nothing is earlier or later because there is no one prior and no one subsequent; no one lower and no one higher. Rather, they are coeternal with one another and coequal. Therefore there is nothing there either greater or lesser.

**24 [Col. 0565D]. Thus, in all things, as has already been said above, both the unity in the Trinity and the Trinity in the unity must be venerated.**

We must worship and adore the Trinity in unity and the unity in the Trinity.

**25. Whoever therefore wishes to be saved must think thus concerning the Trinity.**

Here he exhorts and admonishes, and every teacher must retain this by heart, firmly believe it, and teach it to others by preaching.

**26. But it is necessary for eternal salvation that he also faithfully believe in the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ.**

For it is necessary for us to believe as we have said above [Col. 0566A]. If we wish to possess eternal salvation—that is, to reign with Christ without end—it is necessary that we faithfully believe in the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ. How faithfully? Not that he was an adoptive son, but that he was the proper Son of God, as the Apostle said: “God did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all” (Romans 8).

**27. This, then, is the right faith: that we believe and confess that our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, is equally God and man.**

Now he begins to explain what the right faith is concerning Christ according to his humanity. The right faith is that we believe this humanity in our heart and confess it with our mouth, as the Apostle says: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” [Col. 0566B] (Romans 10). God and man is one true Son of God, because according to his divinity he is neither greater nor lesser than God the Father; according to his humanity he is in no way less than man, except for sin.

**28. He is God, begotten from the substance of the Father before the ages; and man, born in the world from the substance of his mother.**

“From the substance of the Father” means from equality of nature. “Begotten before the ages” means before every creature, as it says in the psalm: “From the womb, before Lucifer, I begot you” (Psalm 109). “From the womb” means from my substance. “Before Lucifer” means before every creature.

He is also man, born in the world from the substance of his mother—that is, wholly man, with body and soul, like us in all things except sin (Hebrews 4). “From the substance of his mother” means from equality with the mother’s nature. “Born in the world” means born in these times; he assumed flesh from no other source than the seed of a woman, without intercourse with a man. Hence Solomon says: “Wisdom built herself a house” (Proverbs 9); that is, Christ built flesh for himself from blessed Mary. Elsewhere it is written: “Who was made from the seed of David according to the flesh” (Romans 1).

**29. Perfect God, perfect man, subsisting from a rational soul and human flesh.**

He is called perfect, that is, complete, lacking nothing; perfect man, because he lacked nothing that belongs to man, except sin. “From a rational soul”: Christ possessed a true soul, in which wisdom could increase, as it says in the Gospel: “Jesus advanced in wisdom and age” (Luke 2)—in wisdom, in the soul; in age, in the body. “And subsisting from human flesh”: because *humus* means earth, he assumed flesh from humanity [Col. 0566D].

**30. Equal to the Father according to divinity; lesser than the Father according to humanity.**

“Equal,” according to the saying: “I and the Father are one” (John 10). “Lesser,” in accordance with what he says: “The Father is greater than I” (John 14); and in that in which he is man, he is lesser than divinity.

**31. Although he is God and man, he is nevertheless not two, but one Christ.**

For this reason the Son of God willed to be joined to human nature in such a way that one person would arise from these two substances.

**32 [Col. 0567A]. One, however, not by a conversion of divinity into flesh, but by an assumption of humanity into God.**

It was not that the divinity by which he is the Son of God converted itself into humanity, so that what was divine became human; rather, by assuming our nature he became one in such a way that he did not lose what he was, but assumed what he was not. For he assumed humanity and did not lose divinity.

**33. One altogether, not by confusion of substance, but by unity of person.**
