There is no commingling of natures in him, so that either divinity might be changed into the nature of humanity or humanity converted into the nature of divinity. Rather, each nature retains its own property forever. Nevertheless, the union of the natures is so great that the same one who was eternally begotten from God the Father is true man, and the one who was born in time from the Virgin is true God: because of the God who assumes, he is true God, God the Son of God; because of the man who is assumed, he is true man.

We believe that the person of the Son of God exists not as a union of two persons, but from two natures; we avoid as a sacrilege saying that he is composed of two persons.

**34. For just as a rational soul and flesh are one man, so God and man are one Christ.**

For just as we speak of one man from flesh and soul, and each person has two men within himself—one carnal and the other spiritual; one visible and the other invisible; one mortal and the other immortal—so God and man are one Christ.

**35. He suffered for our salvation, descended into hell, and rose from the dead.**

He suffered in that in which he was seen, in which he was man, in which he was crucified, in which he died, in which he was buried, and in which he rose again; for divinity is incapable of suffering. Yet, because of the union of the person, the Son of God is said to have suffered, and the Son of Man truly suffered in his nature.

He descended into hell, namely, in soul together with the Word. After humanity had been assumed by divinity, it was not separated from the Word, but the soul itself was separated from the body; for if it had not been separated, the body could not have died. This descent therefore pertains only to the soul.

He rose from the dead in order to show us an example of resurrection, as the prophet says (Hosea 6): “After two days he will revive us, and on the third day we shall rise and live in his presence” [Col. 0567D].

**36. He ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of God the Father almighty.**

He ascended into heaven—namely, the very humanity that had suffered—as the angels said: “Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? This Jesus, who has been taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven” (Acts 1) [Col. 0568A].

According to his divinity he cannot ascend to any place, but is wholly everywhere. “He sits at the right hand of God the Father almighty”: the right hand of God is not fleshly or bodily, as human nature has a right hand; rather, in this passage the glory of God must be understood, as though he plainly said: “He reigns in the glory of God.” To sit is spoken of as to reign.

**37. From there he will come to judge the living and the dead.**

He will come in the same form in which he was crucified, died, buried, and rose again—not, however, in the humility in which he was formerly, but in glory and majesty. For this reason he will come in that same form: so that Herod and Pilate may see the one whom they judged; the Jews may see the one whom they handed over; the soldiers may see the one whom they crucified; and the impious may see the one whom they denied [Col. 0568B].

“The living”: those whom his coming will find alive in the body. “The dead”: those who have died from the beginning until that day. Or otherwise: “the living,” that is, the saints; “the dead,” that is, sinners.

**38. At his coming all human beings must rise with their bodies.**

At the Lord’s coming everyone, whether righteous or sinful, must rise with his own body.

**39. And they will give an account of their own deeds.**

To give an account does not mean a tale of words, but the recollection of everything one has done, whether good or evil; and according to this each person must receive: the good, good things; the evil, evil things.

**40. Those who have done good will go into eternal life; but those who have done evil, into eternal fire.**

“Into eternal life”: because the good will always reign in glory without end. “Into eternal fire”: because for the evil there will always be, without end, the punishment of hell, without any mercy, with body and soul—not to be consumed, but always to burn. They will never fail, but will remain in everlasting punishments.

**41. This is the catholic faith; unless each person faithfully and firmly believes it, he cannot be saved.**

“This is the catholic faith”: as we said above, this is the catholic faith [Col. 0568D]. By this he here asks and admonishes that every priest know and preach it. “Which”—that is, which faith—“each person,” that is, anyone. “Faithfully”: so that he does not doubt it. “Firmly”: so that no one can remove you from your faith, whether through schism or heresy. And if you do not believe in this way, you cannot be saved.

# In the Year of the Lord 1046. Pope Gregory VI

[Col. 0569]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE

*(In Eggs, *Pontificium doctum*, pp. 310 ff.)*

[Col. 0569A] Gregory VI, a Roman previously called Gratianus, a Benedictine monk, son of Peter Leo, a man of exceptional nobility, archpriest of the holy Roman Church and cardinal of Saint John before the Latin Gate, was acclaimed supreme pontiff by the votes of the Roman clergy and people on the Kalends of May in the year of salvation 1045, after the three usurpers of the sacred throne had been removed, as we said above.

He was truly regarded as a genuine and legitimate pontiff by the holiest and most learned men of his time, namely Hildebrand, later Gregory VII, and Peter Damian, together with other men like them, implacable enemies of simony. Gregory did not persuade the false pontiffs to withdraw from the Holy See out of ambition, but out of zeal for piety, although money was involved. Therefore the Roman citizens, and especially the clergy, remembering the benefit he had rendered, elected him supreme pontiff as the liberator of the Church of God.

Gregory himself, at the Roman council held in the year 1080 of our redemption, acknowledged this Gregory as a legitimate pontiff. Glaber too, an author of precisely that period—for his narrative reaches the election of Gregory himself—highly praises Gregory VI and says the following after Benedict had been expelled:

“Then, with the consent of the entire Roman people and by command of the emperor, Benedict was expelled from the see, and in his place was installed Gregory, a most religious man, distinguished for holiness, a Roman by birth. His good reputation plainly restored for the better whatever his predecessor had defiled.”

Peter Damian himself, as soon as he heard of Gregory’s elevation—and indeed of his canonical elevation—wrote to him and congratulated him that, through his election, the Church of God, cleansed of its filth, had regained its original beauty. Thus there should be no doubt about the legitimacy of his entrance upon office.

Let us now see what Gregory, created pontiff by the unanimous consent of all, accomplished. William of Malmesbury, who flourished and wrote somewhat later, reports the following; it is also attested by other contemporary writers [Col. 0569C]:

“Pope Gregory VI, formerly called Gratianus, was a man of great religious devotion and severity. He found the state of the Roman apostolate so diminished through the negligence of his predecessors that, apart from a few towns near the City and the offerings of the faithful, he possessed almost nothing with which to support himself.

“Cities and possessions situated far away, which belonged by right to the Church, had been taken by brigands. Public roads and highways throughout Italy were lined with robbers, so that no traveler could pass safely except with a large escort. Swarms of ambushers seethed along every road, and the traveler found no stratagem by which he could escape them; they robbed the poor just as they robbed the rich. The suppliant could obtain no favor, nor could the resistant endure the violence.

“Travel to Rome from every province ceased, because anyone would rather distribute his money among the churches at home than feed petty thieves with his own labors. What was happening in the City, once the single dwelling place of holiness? In the middle of the forum murderers wandered, a faithless and crafty breed of men. If anyone, wishing to see the apostle’s church at the risk of his life, had passed the watchers on the roads by some device, he would fall among murderers and could in no way return home without loss of property or life [Col. 0569D].

“Above the very bodies of the holy apostles and martyrs, swords were unsheathed over the sacred altars, and the offerings of those who approached, scarcely placed there, were snatched from their hands. Once seized, they were consumed in feasting and the abuse of prostitutes. Alas! A storm of such evils assailed Pope Gregory’s pontificate.

“What then did he do? At first he dealt gently with his subjects, more through love than fear, pressing the offenders with words rather than blows. He urged the townspeople to cease harassing pilgrims and robbing their own people. The former, he said, was contrary to nature: that one who lived on the common air should not enjoy the common peace. A Christian ought to move freely among Christians wherever he wished, since all belonged to one household, all were joined by the bond of one blood, and all had been redeemed by one price. The latter was contrary to God’s ordinance, which commanded that those who serve at the altar should live from the altar [Col. 0570B].

“Moreover, the house of God ought to be a house of prayer, not a den of thieves or a gathering place of gladiators. They should permit offerings to pass into the use of priests or the support of the poor. He himself would provide as a father for those whom poverty compelled to robbery, so that they might receive alms through some honorable occupation. Those driven by greed should, for fear of God and the honor of the world, impose restraint upon themselves.

“He invited the invaders of the Church’s patrimony, by commands and letters, either to return what they had taken unjustly or to prove before the Roman senate that they held it by right. If they did neither, they should recognize that they were not members of the Church, since they insulted the head of the Church, blessed Peter and his vicar.”

After Gregory had often preached such things, and had accomplished little or nothing among obstinate minds, he decided to confront the long-standing disease with harsher remedies. With the cautery of excommunication he therefore removed from the body of the Church all who either committed such acts themselves, failed to oppose those who committed them when they could, or finally participated in their feasts or even their conversations [Col. 0570C].

This was enough for him in the exercise of his office, but his diligence almost turned to ruin. Those wicked men, chastened by a mild admonition, became furious; they spread threats through the air and surrounded the walls of the City with the din of weapons, so that they nearly killed the pope.

Judging, therefore, that the sword of excision must be used, he gathered weapons from every quarter and enlisted soldiers and equipped cavalry. Above all, he occupied the Vatican basilica in advance and either destroyed or drove away the plunderers of the offerings. Then, seeing that fortune was favoring him, with God’s approval he advanced farther. After killing those who resisted, he restored to their former right all the estates, castles, and towns that had been lost for many years but recovered by him.

Thus peace and public tranquility, which had been exiled through the negligence of many, were brought back into the homeland by Gregory. Pilgrims then traveled safely along roads whose routes had long been unfamiliar; joyful, they feasted their eyes on Rome’s ancient marvels and returned home singing after making their offerings.

Meanwhile the Quirites, accustomed to living by robbery, called him bloodthirsty and declared him unworthy to offer sacrifice to God because he was responsible for so many killings. And, as commonly happens when the disease of slander spreads to all, even the cardinals approved the arguments of the populace. Malmesbury reports this, together with other writers who flourished in that age [Col. 0570D].

Since Gregory, moved by zeal for justice, was inflicting severe punishments upon robbers, murderers, and highwaymen, the Romans who shared in this sacrilegious plunder were offended. They therefore approached Henry III, surnamed the Black, with false complaints, persuading him to descend into Italy against Gregory under the pretext of eradicating simony—the crime of which Gregory was accused of having used to occupy the apostolic throne.

Leo of Ostia, a Benedictine monk and a weighty authority (Book II, chapter 78), explicitly narrates how matters stood in these words [Col. 0571A]:

“The aforementioned archpriest, to whom the name Gregory had been given in the papacy, had presided over the apostolic see for two years and eight months when the emperor Henry, son of Conrad, having heard of so many disturbances concerning the Roman and apostolic see, entered Italy in the year of the Lord 1047, inspired from heaven. He hastened to Rome.

“Desiring to cleanse the apostolic see of so great a heresy, he halted at Sutrium and, wishing to deliberate on so great an affair, arranged for a universal council of bishops to be held there. He therefore sent to everyone and, after a great multitude of bishops, abbots, and religious men had gathered, he courteously invited the Roman pontiff to preside over the council.

“What more need be said? Once the council had been held, Gregory the Simoniac, convicted by synodal and canonical judgments, voluntarily descended from the see, removed the pontifical insignia, and, prostrate upon the ground, humbly asked that indulgence be granted him for the honor he had usurped.”

The abbot Desiderius of Monte Cassino (Book III of the *Dialogues*), Hermannus Contractus, and Sigebertus in their chronicles agree with Leo.

Whether these proceedings were conducted legitimately and canonically is doubtful. Advocates stand on every side. It is certain that Henry Caesar, a layman, had no right to hear the case of the supreme pontiff. Nor did Henry himself attempt to hear or judge it; rather, he convened a synod and referred the matter to the Fathers for judgment. Thus he honorably received Gregory when he came to him, as Hermannus Contractus, Otto of Freising, and Leo himself testify [Col. 0571C].

Nevertheless, there appears to have been a twofold simony. The first was that an ecclesiastical dispute was settled with money as intermediary. The second was that sacred resources and Peter’s patrimony were squandered, to the scandal of the entire world, upon false pontiffs or invaders by a private man—namely Gratianus—who possessed no legal authority.

Gregory is nevertheless excused and vindicated by the fact that all this was carried out out of zeal for peace, religion, and unity. Above all, the Roman people applauded, praising the good deed with a religious encomium and exalting and greeting Gregory as the liberator of the Church from the hands of three tyrants.

Furthermore, Gregory was neither judged nor deposed in that synod. Rather, since his zeal did not fail him, he abdicated voluntarily when he saw that the peace he had desired above all could not otherwise be restored to the Church. Benedict, expelled from the throne he had usurped, was continually devising new schemes with his accomplices and waiting for an opportunity to seize the pontificate again, as we shall see in the life of Damasus II [Col. 0571D].

That Gregory relinquished the pontificate voluntarily, not under compulsion, is attested by Otto of Freising (Book VI, chapter 32), whose words are these:

“The king first received him honorably, as was fitting; afterward, having gathered an assembly of bishops, he persuaded him to withdraw from the pontificate on account of the notorious charge of simony.”

Hermannus Contractus says the same in his chronicle:

“When Pope Gratianus, whom the Romans had installed after expelling his predecessors, met King Henry as he came into Italy at Piacenza, he was honorably received. Nevertheless, afterward at Sutrium in the synod, he laid down the pastoral office without reluctance.”

Baronius, Ciaconius, and Oldoinus hold the same view, as do the Sanblasian records generously communicated to me, in approximately these words [Col. 0572A]:

“Moreover, Gregory VI, having established his pontificate as best he could, went to Sutrium at Henry’s request in order to restore the long-desired peace of the Roman Church and to set a memorable example for the other three who had invaded the Holy See. In the full council held there, he voluntarily abdicated the pontificate, which he had laudably governed for two years and eight months.”

Palatius writes in his *Life* that this occurred in the year of salvation 1047; others add the day, 30 December.

Concerning Gregory’s death and the place where it occurred, greater difficulty arises because of the disagreement among historians. It is certain that after his abdication and the election of Clement II, Henry Caesar, returning to his homeland, took Clement the pontiff with him, fearing that the Romans might plot something against a German. He also took the deposed Gregory with him, lest, while he was present, something harmful should be attempted or changed at Rome. Freising testifies to this (Book VI, chapter 32), clearly stating that Gregory was taken by Henry across the Alps [Col. 0572B] into Germany, and that Hildebrand, who later became Gregory VII, followed him out of regard for his honor.

Gregory VII himself likewise attests this in the council held at Rome around the year 1080, where he is reported to have spoken as follows: “For you know that I did not willingly enter the sacred order, and that unwillingly I went beyond the mountains with Lord Pope Gregory,” and so forth.

It is therefore certain that Gregory was taken away from Rome. Whether he returned, how he returned, or when, is uncertain.

William of Malmesbury alone, followed by Platina, writes that Gregory died at Rome, consumed by illness, after cleansing the Church from robbers by sword and fire. Since for this reason the populace called him a murderer and bloodthirsty, and since the cardinals themselves seemed not to disapprove the arguments of the people, he summoned them to him and rebuked them severely. Among other things, he said to them:

“So that you may know whether I acted rightly or wrongly in cleansing the Church from robbers, place my lifeless body, after I die, before the doors of the church barred with beams. If, by divine will, the church opens, you will judge me worthy of Christian burial; but if the opposite occurs, throw me wherever you please and consider me condemned.”

The cardinals carried out his instructions and waited anxiously for the outcome. Suddenly, through the force of a violent storm, the barred doors of the church opened, and, while everyone looked on in amazement, the body itself was carried into the middle of the church [Col. 0572C].

This is the account of an English author, but it is not greatly accepted by experts. Writers of no inferior standing, adhering to the traditions of the ancients, believe that Gregory either spent the remainder of his life at Cluny, where he had withdrawn with Hildebrand, and was buried there after dying a holy death; or else that he died in exile in Germany, where, as we have said, the emperor took him so that he would not cause trouble for Clement after his election.

Hear Baronius, weighing this very matter with some hesitation under the year 1044, number 15:

“The reports circulating about Gregory’s death, and about the miracle by which the doors of Saint Peter’s opened of their own accord to receive his corpse, do not win credence from everyone, since it is said that he died not at Rome but in Germany, where he was living in exile. Yet neither do we present these claims about the miracle with complete confidence. Let the responsibility for belief rest with the author.”

Everything in this matter therefore remains uncertain, and there is no one whom you can easily follow.

Nor do the things that Ciaconius adds, following Platina, deserve greater confidence. He writes that Gregory—whom he thinks was never taken away from Rome—after Henry’s return gathered a small army, expelled Clement II from the City, recovered the rights and estates, waged war against Caesar, and was not defeated by him. He supports his statements with the authority of Leo of Ostia and firmly writes that Gregory died at Rome and was buried in the Vatican after the miracle at the church doors.

With all due respect to so great a man, these things are not found at all in Leo of Ostia; they are cited falsely, as will be clear to anyone who examines the text.

[Col. 0573]

# LETTERS AND PRIVILEGES OF POPE GREGORY VI

## I. Bull of Pope Gregory VI for the Monastery of Farfa and Its Abbot Almeric (1045–1046)

*[Muratori, Rerum Italicarum Scriptores II, II, p. 443.]*

[Col. 0573A]

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Almeric, abbot, and to all the brothers subject to him in the monastery of Farfa: greetings and apostolic blessing.

Let it be known to all bishops, dukes, marquises, counts, and great and small persons dwelling in the Roman world that Almeric, abbot of the monastery of Farfa, together with the flock entrusted to him, petitioned our highness and charity that we confirm what the holy pontiffs of old had ordered and established in the monastery of Farfa of blessed Mary ever-virgin [Col. 0573B].

Therefore we confirm and strengthen these provisions: that the consecration of their churches and the ordination of their monks by whichever bishop the abbot or the monks of that monastery prefer shall take place with our permission and command. And, so that it may be believed more securely, we confirm it perpetually with our seal.

If anyone should oppose or violate this command of ours, let him pay ten pounds of gold to the treasury of the apostolic palace and ten to the treasury of blessed Mary the Virgin.

We establish this not only in the county of Amiternum, but also in the March, and in all the cells subject to the aforesaid monastery, or wherever it possesses any ecclesiastical property. The clerics also dwelling in the churches of that monastery, enjoying this freedom, shall likewise receive sacred orders from whatever bishop the abbot of Farfa prefers. Nevertheless, we command that these orders be conferred by good and catholic bishops.

Farewell.

## II. Letter of Gregory VI to All Christians (1045–1046)

He promises to celebrate Mass three times a year for those who had decided to contribute an annual sum for the repair and roofing of the churches of the city of Rome.

*[Mansi, Councils, vol. 19, col. 611.]*

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all who are counted among the Christian faithful and acknowledge the see of the blessed chief of the apostles as the mother of all Churches: greetings and absolution from all sins through the blessing and merits of the blessed Peter and Paul, chief apostles [Col. 0573D].

We wish it to be known to you, dearest brothers [Col. 0574A], that from the holy Roman Church, our common mother and teacher and mistress of all, not only did the splendor of holy religion illuminate the whole world, but she also distributed, with merciful care, what was necessary to many persons in need throughout various regions of the earth.

Now, however, because of the sins not only of ourselves but also of many peoples, religion has grown cold and she has lost most of her earthly wealth. Certain emperors, kings, princes, and persons of other ranks, seized by miserable greed and not fearing to incur a mother’s curse, invaded her possessions, sold them, and converted them to their own uses. Though struck by the sword of anathema and strangled, like the unhappy Judas, by the bond of sacrilege, they became senseless rather than return to repentance.

From this there arose poverty, devastation, robbery, and plunder against the very head of the Church, namely blessed Peter, and as it were within his own entrails. Therefore his own church, and that of blessed Paul—churches that shine throughout the whole world because of their bodies and summon all nations to themselves by their fragrance and piety—now, alas, to our grief, threaten to collapse [Col. 0574B].

Accordingly, although we are poor in merits and not rich even in material goods, we have begun, with God’s help, to come to the aid of so great a danger and to extend a helping hand for restoration.

When devout clerics and very many laymen saw this—and when the glorious William, duke of Aquitaine, began encouraging them to assist us—they resolved to give offerings from their possessions every year, specifically so that the necessities of his own church might be restored and built up. Thus may almighty God, both through their merits and through the special prayer of the holy Roman Church, deign to restore them by true repentance to that faith which they promised the Lord in baptism, and, restoring the ruin of the heavenly homeland, place them in eternal blessedness [Col. 0574C].

Seeing their devotion and their praiseworthy love toward our common mother, we have promised, both ourselves and our successors, to celebrate Mass three times a year generally with all the Roman churches, and to commemorate them especially seven times during the solemn celebrations of Mass. May almighty God, through the merits of the Mother of God, who with singular piety always protects the Roman Church, through the authority of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and through the prayers of all the saints, especially those resting at Rome, absolve them from all their sins and lead them to eternal life.

## III. Letter of Gregory VI to Roland, Provost of the Florentine Church (1046)

He grants the church of Saint Donninus to the canons of the Florentine Church on the condition that they pay one gold solidus annually to the Lateran palace.

*[Ughelli, Sacred Italy, III, 65.]*

[Col. 0575A]

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Roland, provost of the Florentine chapter, and to your successors: perpetual salvation in the Lord.

It is fitting to repay those who deserve well with worthy benefits and to heap gifts upon those whose service is known to be devoted. But you, dearest son, since you decided to ask something small of us, we have willingly decided to grant your request. Indeed, you have already endured much labor and much burden on our behalf, so much so that you are found worthy not of small but even of great gifts [Col. 0575B].

Your request is that the church of Saint Donninus, situated in the county of Florence beside the river Arno, in the diocese of Saint John, in the territory of the parish of Saint Martin in Brozzo, belonging to our holy Roman Church, together with all its appurtenances wherever they may be found, be granted by our apostolic authority to you and to your successors, the canons who will serve in your chapter perpetually.

This seems to us sufficiently little, since it cannot be an adequate recompense for your service. We therefore grant to you, to your chapter, and to your canonical successors who will serve in the same chapter, that very little church of Saint Donninus [Col. 0575C], with all its appurtenances and revenues, wherever they may lawfully and rightfully belong to it; but on the condition that every year you pay from it one gold solidus as a pension to our palace.

We establish by apostolic censure that none of our pontifical successors, nor any person great or small, dare act against this small gift of ours. If anyone should do so, let him not only be subject to our anathema, but also pay a penalty of three pounds of gold, half of which shall be delivered to our palace and the other half shall belong to you. If anyone proves a careful observer of this command of ours, may our blessing flow upon him more abundantly.

Written by the hand of John, our scriniarius and notary of the Lateran palace [Col. 0575D]. Farewell. Given on the twelfth day before the Kalends of March, through Peter, deacon, librarian and chancellor of the holy apostolic see, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Gregory VI, indiction 14.

## IV. Bull of Gregory VI for the Monastery of Saint Quintinus of the Mount, Issued in the Roman Council

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Waleran, abbot of Saint Quintinus of the Mount, and to your successors: perpetual salvation in the Lord.

If, by granting assent to just petitions, we offer our support to the resolve of the devout, we believe that we are serving the will of the Lord. Therefore let it be known to all the sons of the Catholic mother Church that our son, namely Henry, king of the Franks, sent to us, [Col. 0576A] humbly beseeching our fatherhood that we should fortify with the protection of apostolic authority a certain cell situated in the district of Vermandois, constructed in honor of the Holy Trinity and of Saint Quintinus the martyr. At the urging of the sons of the soldier Rotbert, of blessed memory, who possess that little abbey by right of benefice, he endeavored to raise it to the venerable observance of sacred religion and sought to have it strengthened by royal authority.

Rejoicing in their petition, we raised the hand of ecclesiastical power and, by the apostolic authority with which we are supported, decree that no secular person shall ever possess the aforesaid abbey, nor shall anyone usurp anything from the property of that church for himself. Neither king, count, bishop, nor any prince endowed with whatever power shall seize for his own dominion a village, manor, or field, or the customary dues or jurisdictions belonging to the land attached to the aforesaid abbey, except perhaps for the purpose of protecting and defending it—and even then only with the permission of the regular abbot of that place. If anyone, in order to obtain this, gives or promises money or any gift to the king or to any prince, he shall be subject to the curse that follows.

Let an abbot therefore be appointed for that church according to the rule of Saint Benedict, and let the monks be subject to regular discipline. With full authority we prohibit anyone from inflicting any loss upon them from the property of that church. The possessions of that church are as follows:

In the district of Vermandois, one estate called Aisiolcurt (Arizecourt); and in the same district, in the village called Curticulas (Courcelles), seven manors. At Hadoniscurt, one manor. At Duriacum, half of a church. The mill of Bellisasis (Belles aises), with its water and appurtenances; in the suburb of Perrona, twenty-seven small holdings, with a mill and vineyards; at Perronella, a church with its dependents. At Tegerihamum, two manors; in the village of Saint Radegund, three manors. The estate called Vivarius (Vivier), with its appurtenances. At Alania (Alaine), two manors. At Dodonicum (Douln), one mill with a third part of a meadow. In the district of Soissons, in the village called Alamans, two manors with Witbert’s allodial property. At Wadoniscurt, two manors.

Furthermore, the following are the properties given by the aforementioned Rotbert for the restoration of the aforesaid abbey: the allodial property of Baillos (Barlex). Likewise, the allodial property of [Col. 0576D] Tiliacum. Similarly, the allodial property of Ostricurt (Estricourt), with its church, and the allodial property of Barderi. At Scaincurt (Esquincourt), five dependents with land and woodland. Frigilcurt (Frigicourt), with its appurtenances. Salicellus, with its woodland. Curcellis (Courcelles), together with all its appurtenances. The church of Buriacum (Buires). Likewise, the church of Sterpiniacum (Esterpigny), with its fishery and the water of Sebodiscula (Sopotecluse). The church of Asciniacum (Assigny). Hubert’s Bridge. In Frisia, one manor with water. In the village of Atheis (Athies), one mill with three dependents. At Liniacum, two manors. At Guitardi’s court, one manor. At Habelinicurt (Ablincourt), one manor.

All these possessions, and others like them, and whatever else it may be able to acquire for itself with the Lord’s help, it shall possess freely and without any contradiction, protected by apostolic authority.

But if anyone, plotting something wrongful against the protection of this apostolic privilege, should wish to pervert any of the provisions stated above, then, with the help of our Lord Jesus Christ and the assistance of blessed Mary ever-virgin, mother of the same Lord Jesus Christ, with the blessed spirits of all the heavenly powers supporting us, and with the hosts of the holy patriarchs and prophets consenting, and by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, together with all the apostles and disciples of the Lord, and with the merits of the martyrs, confessors, and virgins likewise lending their support, with the assent of the bishops of the province and of the suffragan bishops of this holy [Col. 0578A] see, we excommunicate and anathematize him. Separating him from the thresholds of the holy Church of God, we cut him off from all Christian fellowship, so that, bound forever by the chain of this anathema, he may be held fast by the anathema maranatha and by the bonds of this our decree.

But whoever acts well toward the same monastery, let our blessing abound upon him, because he has preserved our decree unharmed.

Written by the hand of John, our chief notary of the Lateran palace, in the fourteenth indiction. Farewell.

Given on the fourth day before the Kalends of March, by the hand of Peter the deacon, librarian and chancellor of the sacred Lateran palace, in the first year of our lord Gregory, universal pope, in the fourteenth indiction.

## In the Year of the Lord 1047. Pope Clement II

[Col. 0577]

## Historical Notice

*(In Mansi, General Councils, volume XIX, column 619.)*

Pope Clement, a German by nation, the second of that name, formerly called Suidgerus, after the abdication of Gregory VI, was created pontiff at Rome, by the efforts and influence of King Henry, from the bishopric of Bamberg, with the unanimous consent of all—as though no one else could be found more worthy of so great an office—on the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord in the year 1046. Consecrated according to custom on the following Nativity of the Lord and called Clement II, he elevated King Henry and his wife Agnes with the imperial blessing.

As the emperor was departing from Rome, he brought with him into Germany Gregory VI, formerly pontiff, so that nothing might be changed at Rome while he was present. Hildebrand, his disciple, accompanied him; Hildebrand was a subdeacon of the apostolic see and later became Gregory VII. Clement also departed from Rome with him and, beyond the Alps, as Leo of Ostia testifies, died on the seventh day before the Ides of October, in the ninth month after his promotion. His body was transferred from Rome to Bamberg and buried at Bamberg. When this became known to Benedict, he invaded the apostolic see for the third time and held it for eight months, until the election of Damasus II. *(Leo of Ostia.)*

[Col. 0577]

# Letters and Privileges of Pope Clement II

## I. Bull of Pope Clement II by Which He Grants the Monastery of Saint Andrew, Situated at Rome beside the Church of Saint Mary at the Cradle, to the Church of Fulda  
*(1046)*

*[Mansi, Councils, volume XIX, column 624.]*

[Col. 0577B]

Clement, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our beloved and spiritual son Roingo, pious and religious abbot of the venerable monastery of our Lord Jesus Christ the Savior and Saint Boniface, situated in the place called Bochonia, beside the bank of the river called the Fulda, and through you to your successors in the same venerable monastery, forever: perpetual salvation in the Lord.

It is fitting for apostolic governance to come to the aid of those distinguished by pious religion with benevolent compassion and to grant the minds of petitioners assent with eager devotion. From this, without doubt, we earn the most excellent reward of profit from God, the Creator of all, when venerable places, suitably ordered, have unquestionably been brought to a better condition.

Therefore, because you have asked us to grant and perpetually reconfirm to you and to your successors the aforesaid monastery of our Lord Jesus Christ the Savior and Saint Boniface, situated in the place called Bochonia beside the bank of the river called the Fulda, with all its movable and immovable property that it now possesses and, with God’s help, will possess in the future, we grant it again. We also give, to you, our dearest and most beloved son, and to your successors as abbots forever, out of the great love and excessive affection that I have for you and ought to have for you for as long as I live, the monastery constructed in honor of Saint Andrew and of the saint called Exajulus, situated beside the church [Col. 0578C] of holy Mary, ever-virgin Mother of God, which is called “at the Cradle,” with all its dwellings, heated chambers, wine cellars, kitchen, vineyards, gardens, and various fruit trees, with its court, well, and entrance through its main gate from the public road, and with everything generally belonging to it, whether situated outside or inside the city, which is known to belong to it by right and reason.

Therefore, in this fifteenth indiction, we decree and, by decreeing, confirm that this most sacred monastery shall remain perpetually and specially under the immunity of our holy Roman and apostolic see, so that you and your successors may hold and possess all the places of that monastery from now until the end of the world with complete security and tranquility. Established under the right and authority of our holy Church, which by God’s appointment we serve, it shall not be subjected to the jurisdiction of any other church.

For this reason, favoring your pious desires, by this authority of ours we bring into effect what you request. We therefore prohibit any priest of any church from exercising any jurisdiction or authority in the aforesaid monastery apart from the apostolic see. Unless invited by the abbot of the monastery, no one shall presume in any way to celebrate the solemnity of the Mass there, so that it may remain firmly endowed, in accordance with the fact that it stands under the apostolic see’s authority through the security of this privilege. Its places and possessions—both those which it presently holds or possesses and those which divine piety may in future wish to increase as the property of that monastery through the gifts, offerings, and tithes of the faithful—shall be preserved with perpetual security, without contradiction from any person.

We also establish by the text of this decree that any prelate of any church, or any person endowed with whatever dignity, who attempts to violate this charter of our privilege, which we confirm by the authority of the prince of the apostles, shall be anathema, incur the wrath of God, and be cast out from the company of all the saints. Nevertheless, the dignity of the aforesaid monastery, granted by us, shall remain perpetually inviolate and supported by apostolic authority.

Written by the hand of John, our notary and secretary of the sacred Lateran palace. Farewell. Given on the third day before the Kalends of January, by the hand of Peter the deacon, librarian and chancellor of the holy apostolic see, in the year 1046 of our Lord Jesus Christ, in the first year of Clement II, pope, in the fifteenth indiction.

## II. Privilege of Pope Clement II for the Monastery of Fulda  
*(1046)*

*[Dronke, Diplomatic Code of Fulda, p. 357.]*

[Col. 0579D]

Clement, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most beloved son in the Lord, Roingo, venerable abbot: perpetual salvation in the Lord from our pontificate.

Concern urges us to favor the interests of all the holy Churches of God and to provide them with suitable assistance, according to the condition in which each is to remain. Therefore, dearest son, we perpetually confirm to you and to your successors everything which your predecessors appear to have rightly and reasonably requested from our predecessors.

We therefore grant, bestow, and confirm by the decree of our privilege to you and your successors the monastery of Fulda, which flourishes under the name of Saint Boniface, established in the place called Boconia beside the bank of the river called the Fulda, with all its cells, courts, jurisdictions, and everything belonging to it. This is on the condition that no future abbot shall ever presume to receive consecration except from this apostolic see of ours.

Among all the monasteries of the whole of Germany, we assign to you and your successors the first place of honor in seating, in judicial judgments, in all councils, and in every order. Nor shall any bishop, archbishop, patriarch, or anyone constituted in the clergy in any manner be permitted, rashly or presumptuously, without permission received from you, to celebrate the solemnity of Mass upon the principal altar of your monastery.

Again, no person in authority, nor any prince, shall presume for any reason to subject all or part of your monastery to any mortal, or to give it under the name of a benefice. Rather, at all times it shall serve freely and securely only the holy Roman Church of which we are pontiff.

If—which God forbid—any abbot established in that monastery should be infamous for some crime, we establish and decree by apostolic authority, indissolubly, that he shall suffer no peril of being summoned until our apostolic see imposes upon him the judgment of its sentence.

It shall be lawful for you and your successors forever, after the manner of bishops, by our gift and munificence, to appeal to the apostolic see for your defense and to defend yourselves against all adversaries with the shield of Roman majesty.

Finally, we grant and firmly strengthen this privilege: among all the monasteries of the whole world, our Fulda abbey shall forever be held in the most special affection of love.

But the use of sandals, stockings, and dalmatics, which the sacred canons forbid to your order, we order, by apostolic authority, to be entirely removed—not only from you and your successors forever, but also from all abbots of every monastery existing throughout the world, both those now living and those who will live.

Although there have been certain pontiffs in this supreme see who, compelled by the tyranny of evil men, unworthily granted this to your Church and to various other Churches, even though it is known to differ from the sanctions of the holy fathers, we, because we know that it was wrongly requested and very badly granted by the text of a privilege, not only do not wish to confirm it but desire to renounce it completely.

For if our monastery, which embraces the most sacred body of the blessed apostle Paul, did not deserve to obtain this superstitious custom from Saint Peter, how will any abbey in the world obtain it? Almost the whole world knows that our bishops and cardinal priests and deacons possess highly special dignities which the clergy of other Churches of comparable rank may not possess. Our cardinal priests wear dalmatics and use *naccae* in solemn processions. If this had seemed worthy to our most holy predecessors, the abbey of Saint Paul, which is known to be nearest and most familiar to our see, would freely and solemnly enjoy dalmatics and [Col. 0581A] sandals.

Therefore, what Saint Paul did not request from Saint Peter, let the other younger saints cease to obtain from our unavoidable authority.

Whoever therefore observes this privilege of ours, let him be filled with every blessing. But whoever in any way presumes to violate this decree of ours, unless he repents, shall incur the wrath of the undivided Trinity, be overwhelmed by the curse of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, be condemned by the sacred council of the three hundred and eighteen fathers, and, lost on the final day of judgment under the anathema *amaranatha*, shall not know the brightness of light but shall groan eternally with the devil and his accomplices amid the outer darkness.

This privilege was written by the hand of John, notary and secretary of the sacred palace. [Col. 0581B] + Farewell.

Given on the day before the Kalends of January, by the hand of Peter the deacon, librarian and chancellor of the holy apostolic see, in the year 1046 of our Lord Jesus Christ, in the first year of Clement II, pope, in the fifteenth indiction.

## III. Rescript of Pope Clement II to All the Sons of the Church  
*(1047)*

*[Ughelli, Sacred Italy, II, p. 361.]*

The dispute of the archbishops of Ravenna and Milan and of the patriarch of Aquileia is attested to have been settled on the first day of the synod, held “around the Nones of January,” to the effect that the archbishops of Ravenna should sit at the right hand of the Roman pontiff unless the emperor were present.

[Col. 0581C]

Clement, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the sons of the holy Church: perpetual salvation in Christ.

That those who had not entered through the door into the most sacred sheepfold entrusted by Christ the Lord to the prince of the apostles, Peter, but had crept in from elsewhere like thieves and robbers, seeking their own advantage rather than the humility of the flock, have been driven from the apostolic see is not to be ascribed to our merits but to the divine goodness, which chose what is not as though it were, so that what is might be brought to nothing.

Among the many matters dealt with at the beginning of our pontificate in the synod—which we hastened for the common good and which, by the Lord’s favor, we were permitted to celebrate around the Nones of January—one matter was determined there that had often been debated by earlier pontiffs, our predecessors, and had either scarcely or never been settled: namely, the dispute over seating in the synod that had arisen between the archbishops of Ravenna and Milan, about which the patriarch of Aquileia was also muttering at our synod.

Each (Latin *quisquis*; variant *quisque*) claimed for himself the place at our right hand, and it was uncertain to us to whom it was legally due. On the first day of the synod, however, the archbishop of Milan was not present from the beginning. As the day was already declining and the patriarch was sitting at our right hand, with the chair of our dearest son, the emperor Henry, interposed—he was expected to arrive at any moment—the elected archbishop of Ravenna had also been assigned a place at the left.

When the archbishop of Milan came into the midst, because he had requested the place at the right, the elected archbishop of Ravenna exclaimed that it belonged to him. The patriarch of Aquileia made the same claim, and thus an argument arose among them over a single matter.

The whole synod decided that the disagreement of the three parties should be deferred. Immediately a certain catalogue was produced containing the names of the archbishops who had attended the synod of Pope Symmachus. In it the archbishop of Milan was listed. In opposition to this, a privilege of the Church of Ravenna was displayed, explaining that this listing of names had occurred not through any right or legal fullness, but rather through a favor intended to express humility: namely, that the archbishop of Ravenna had permitted the archbishop of Milan to be listed before him only on that particular occasion.

Lest any error therefore arise in the future, Pope John, the successor of Symmachus, had decided that the privilege itself should be drawn up—not because anyone might thereby appear greater, although the right-hand place of the Roman pope was not always legally due to the archbishop of Ravenna. The only addition was that of the emperor, if he were present; in that case the archbishop of Ravenna was to move to the left.

After the privileges of the two disputants had been displayed, the privilege of the other disputant, namely the patriarch, was also displayed: it had been issued by Pope John XIX and likewise concerned seating on the right-hand side.

After these matters had been heard, the entire synod was questioned. First of all, the Roman bishops and Roman clergy, whose authority was greater and to whom the matter itself was known, were asked; then we gave our response. When, in due order, John, bishop of Porto, and Peter the deacon, chancellor of our apostolic see, praised the privilege of the Church of Ravenna on behalf of their respective sides, Poppo, bishop of Brescia, did the same, and the entire synod followed his voice. Thus, since the voice of all converged in one agreement, our assent was likewise given in the same manner.

But so that what was done might become known to everyone, it seemed good that it should be recorded in our apostolic letters and made known both to those now living and to those in the future, so that it might possess all the greater force, since it is known to have been heard from our own mouth.

However, lest henceforth either the archbishop of Milan or the patriarch of Aquileia again be permitted to raise any controversy over the seating at our right hand, we forbid, by our apostolic authority, that this be permitted to them in the future. If anyone should presume to do so, then, for violating our prohibition, he shall not only pay the ban of Saint Peter to our see but shall also incur the bonds of our excommunication and anathema.

We also order that the seat of the archbishop of Ravenna shall always be at our right hand and at that of our successors, according to the authority of the ancient constitution, unless the emperor should be present; then he too is to occupy the left-hand place, by the firmness of the supports of our authority—“with firmness” (*firmitate*, sic)—attached to this account of ours.

Written by the hand of John, notary and secretary of our sacred palace. Farewell.

## IV. Privilege of Pope Clement II for the Church of Hamburg  
*(1047)*

*[In Lappenberg, Hamburg Documents, I, 72.]*

[Col. 0583A]

Clement, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our beloved brother Adalbert, venerable archbishop of the Church of Ammaburg, and to his successors forever.

It is fitting for apostolic governance to come to the aid of those distinguished by pious religion with benevolent compassion [printed *successisse*, “to have succeeded,” for *succurrere*, “to come to the aid”] and to grant the minds of petitioners assent with eager devotion. From this, without doubt, we earn the most excellent reward of profit from the Lord, the Creator of all, when venerable places have suitably and unquestionably been brought to a better condition.

Therefore, because you have asked us to confirm to you in its entirety the archbishopric of the Church of Ammaburg, just as it was decreed by our predecessors Nicholas, Agapitus, and Benedict, bishops of this apostolic see, yielding to your prayers, we grant and confirm it by apostolic authority, with everything generally and specifically belonging to the same aforesaid archbishopric: namely, all that your predecessors acquired through their labors, or that the faithful worshipers of Christ have given or are giving there out of love for the eternal homeland.

This includes also those who in our own time have been converted to the faith of Christ by the protection of God’s grace—namely, the bishops among all the peoples of the Swedes and Danes, and likewise in those regions extending from the southern bank of the Elbe to the river Peene and the river Eider. We decree that, under you and your successors, archbishops of the Church of Ammaburg, no other person may claim any authority for himself in your diocese.

Indeed, we urge them and all worshipers of true religion to provide you assistance and support in every way, so that they may deserve to receive a full reward from the Lord for the grace of this benefaction. For we do not doubt that everything which is shown to be advantageous to the Church and does not oppose the divine commands ought to be carried out and provided by the authority of almighty God and of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

And by this decree of ours we decree, according to the sanction of the aforementioned Pope Nicholas, Pope Agapitus, and Pope Benedict, [lacuna] and to the bishops of the Churches of Minden and Verden, [lacuna] to establish in those regions, nevertheless, [lacuna] dearest brother Adalbert, that the power [lacuna] dearest brother Adalbert, of our authority [lacuna].

Furthermore, in accordance with your most worthy petition, we add that on the Nativity of the Lord and on the octave of the Lord, on the Epiphany of the Lord, on the Purification of Saint Mary, on Palm Sunday, on the Lord’s Supper, on the holy day of Easter, on the Ascension of the Lord, at Pentecost, on the feast of Saint John the Baptist, and on the feasts of all the apostles, on the Assumption and Nativity of Saint Mary, and on the Annunciation of Saint Mary, on the feast of Saint Michael the archangel, on the feast of Saint Martin the bishop, on the feasts of the blessed martyrs Laurence, Maurice, and their companions, and on the feast of All Saints, as well as on the feasts of those saints whose bodies rest within that archbishopric, and at the consecration of bishops and churches, and on the day of your ordination.

In addition to this, at the request of Henry, our most beloved son the emperor, we grant you permission to ride upon the *naccus* on solemn days, but only at your own see. We also grant permission to use the pallium at ecclesiastical ordinations and to have the cross carried before you, as your predecessors possessed these privileges.

May the Holy Trinity deign to preserve your fraternity unharmed for a long time and, after the bitterness of this age, lead you to everlasting blessedness. Farewell.

Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of May, by the hand of Peter the deacon, librarian and chancellor of the holy apostolic see, in the second year of Clement II, pope, in the fifteenth indiction.

## V. Letter of Pope Clement II to Goffred, Count of Anjou, and Agnes, His Wife, the Countess  
*(1047)*

He undertakes the protection of the monastery of the Holy Trinity at Vendôme, founded by Goffred, and confirms its possessions, on the condition that twelve solidi be paid annually to Saint Peter.

*[Works of Ivo II, 244.]*

[Col. 0584C]

Clement, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Goffred, count of Anjou, and Agnes, the countess, his wife: greetings and apostolic blessing.

Whenever the sons of holy Church offer something to almighty God, they ought not to suppose that it has been given as though it were a gift, but should rejoice in a faithful repayment. They return to their Creator a portion of the things they have received from him, so that from his own possessions they may make him their most generous debtor. For from him we all have our being and our life, and possess everything that we possess; and, what is more, [lacuna].

You, dearest children, recognizing this not ignorantly but faithfully, have taken care to build, from your own possessions, a monastery for the redemption of your souls and of the souls of your parents, at the castle of Vendôme, in honor of the divine Trinity. You have also offered that monastery, with all its possessions, to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, with this consideration: that it should always adhere in a special manner to the holy Roman Church, so that no person might stand between the Roman pontiff and this venerable place.

Supported by divine confidence, we confirm this in such a way that, by the authority of the apostles Peter and Paul, we prohibit every person of whatever dignity or order from standing between the pontiff of the first and apostolic see and the abbot of the venerable place of Vendôme.

We wish a census of eleven solidi of the coinage of our homeland to be paid to blessed Peter each year, for perpetual remembrance and acknowledgment, etc.

We also establish that, when the abbot of that place dies, a successor shall be chosen for him from the same [Col. 0585A] congregation, provided that a person worthy of the prelacy is found. But if such a person cannot be found among them—which God forbid—then the monks assembled there shall choose an abbot for themselves from Cluny, or from the Greater Monastery, or from wherever they can find someone better, according to the fear of God and the rule of blessed Benedict. Nevertheless, out of reverence for the place, when choosing a shepherd for themselves, they shall use the counsel of three abbots whom they can find to be the most religious from neighboring places.

As for consecration, so that the elected abbot will not immediately be wearied by having to come to Rome, he shall receive it from any prelate, but without any subjection, provided that the prelate has received the episcopate without payment and according to the canons. But if the bishop was elected, invested, or consecrated for payment or against the canons, or if he should prove suspect toward the aforesaid place of Saint Peter, the person elected shall have recourse to us or to our successors and shall receive from the see of blessed Peter the apostle [lacuna], as is its right, both the staff and consecration.

He shall in no way attend a council that has not been convened by the Roman pontiff himself, etc.

We also add that, both at the place of Vendôme and at the aforesaid church of the Savior beside the walls of Angers, no person except the Roman pontiff alone shall be permitted to exercise any power or dominion, or to excommunicate or place under interdict. Even if the bishop of Chartres or the bishop of Angers should be excommunicated for any offenses, those who have been excommunicated nevertheless shall not be received by the monks, etc.

Given on the Kalends of July, by the hand of Peter the deacon, librarian and chancellor of the holy apostolic see, in the [Col. 0585C] first year of our lord Clement II, pope, in the fifteenth indiction.

## VI. Privilege of Pope Clement II for the Monastery of Tharisse  
*(1047)*

*[In Ussermann, Sacred Germany, volume III, documents.]*

Clement, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Jacob, venerable abbot of the monastery of the most holy martyrs, the protomartyr Stephen and Vitus, situated in the place called Tharisse: perpetual salvation in Christ.

The strongest shield of the apostolic see is so great that it can withstand every attack of evildoers and is sufficient for all the sacred churches. For it was founded upon the firm rock, that is, Christ, so that not only the savagery of men but even the gates of hell might not prevail against it. To it is well applied what is sung: “The Lord is my strength and my praise,” because whatever praise it possesses comes from God’s strength, not its own.

Since divine favor has placed our humility over this most holy see, by his grace alone and not by our merits, we have decided to fortify your monastery, dearest son, with its rights in such a way that every effort of those who oppose it may be emptied of force.

Indeed, with God as author, we ourselves erected that monastery and enriched it with whatever goods we could, for the salvation of our soul and of the soul of our son, Lord Henry, Roman emperor Augustus. With his will and consent we began and completed the construction of that place while we presided over the holy Church of Bamberg, to which the place belongs.

In particular, by exchanging the church at Tharisse and the oratory at Wenckheim, together with the tithes of both places, which had previously been lawfully transferred to it in vicarious possession by our brother and fellow bishop Bruno of the Church of Würzburg, we bestowed them upon this monastery.

Therefore, by the authority given by Christ the Lord to the apostle Peter, our teacher and elder, and through him to his successors down to our most unworthy fatherhood, in the name of the same Lord Jesus Christ we enclose, defend, and fortify this monastery of the most holy protomartyr Stephen and his fellow martyr Vitus, together with all the movable and immovable goods of that monastery, which it now possesses and shall possess forever, against the rashness of all evildoers and the rapacity of the wicked.

We do this through the inviolable protection of our apostolic decree, so that no duke, no margrave, no count, no viscount, no patriarch, archbishop, or bishop—and especially not the bishop of Bamberg—nor any person, great or small, may injure our monastery or diminish its goods, which it now possesses and shall possess forever.

Whoever among them commits such an act, by this sanction of apostolic power proceeding from the authority of the apostle Peter, we curse, excommunicate, and also anathematize, so that he may be alien from the kingdom of God and share the lot of the devil, the head of the wicked, unless he repents and makes worthy satisfaction for the offense he has committed against that most holy place.

We order this decree of ours to remain inviolate, strengthened by our seal and subscription. Farewell.

Written in the month of September, in the first indiction. Given at Rome on the Kalends of October, by the hand of Peter the deacon, librarian of the sacred apostolic see, in the first year of Clement II, pope, and likewise in the first year of Lord Henry III, emperor.

## VII. Letter or Diploma of Pope Clement II to John, Archbishop of Salerno  
*(1047)*

He confirms John’s transfer from the bishopric of Paestum to Salerno and grants him the pallium.

[Col. 0586D]

Clement, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother in Christ, John, now archbishop of Salerno: perpetual salvation in the Lord.

Whenever circumstances require that, because of necessity and the greatest advantage, a bishop be transferred from his own see to another, the person must be examined with the greatest care to determine whether he ought necessarily to be transferred, so that a greater benefit may arise as a greater see is assumed.

But you, dearest brother, whom the unanimity of the clergy and people of the Church of Salerno, together with the most glorious prince Guaimarius, received from the see of Paestum and elected as their pontiff, we carefully examined, lest you had been elected because of your own ambition rather than because necessity demanded a greater advantage, or perhaps through the heresy of simony. This was denied by everyone so completely that no one was heard to utter such a charge.

Indeed, when we heard from everyone that you were praised by all and saw that you were loved by all, we blessed the Lord, who was able to bring about such harmony among such a diversity of people concerning you that no one appeared to disagree. For the same love existed in all toward you, the same intention, and a common desire in everyone.

Therefore, assenting to the petition and wish of them all, and especially of the aforesaid glorious prince Guaimarius, and since they have transferred you from your own see to theirs, moved by the merits of your character rather than by any act of rapacious greed on your part, we, with apostolic assent, by this privilege of our authority, incorporate and enthrone you in that Salernitan see, where you may exercise the dignity and honor of an archbishop.

For whatever report spreads about you has pleased us: namely, holiness, chastity, kindness, and everything that is pleasing to God.

Therefore, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, we have marked your belovedness with the archiepiscopal pallium by our apostolic hand. You shall use it as often in the year as it is established that your predecessors used it. Since it is made from the wool of a sheep, understand that you are the shepherd of sheep. And because you are girded with it and also wear it about your shoulders, recognize and look around on every side lest any sheep go astray and fall into the jaws of wolves. If at any time—which God forbid—this should happen, you must carry it on your shoulders back to the fold and reunite it with its former community. The fact that the cross of the Lord is placed before and behind it always teaches you to keep before the eyes of your mind the apostolic saying: “The world is crucified to me, and I to the world” (Galatians 6).

We also confirm to you in its entirety the archbishopric of Salerno, with all its adjoining parishes. Moreover, we grant you the license and authority to ordain and consecrate bishops in the places subject to you, namely, the bishopric of Paestum with its parishes and dependencies, the bishopric of Conza, the bishopric of Nola, and the bishopric of Maluito [otherwise, Malfitano and Amalfitano], as well as the bishopric of Acerenza [for Acherontia], together with the bishopric of Bisignano, and the bishopric of Cosenza [for Consentia], with all their parishes and dependencies. As for the pallium mentioned above, after your departure your successors shall come to the apostolic see and receive, according to the decree, the use of the pallium and consecration. Our successors shall not thereafter have the power to consecrate bishops in any of all the aforesaid bishoprics that we have granted to you by apostolic authority, just as it has been granted to you.

If anyone, however, with wicked daring—which we do not desire—should in any way wish to oppose this our grant and presume to violate everything written above and confirmed by us, let him be bound by the perpetual bond of anathema. And so that this our grant may remain firm forever, we order that it be marked with our bull [Col. 0588A] and seal. But whoever, moved by pious regard, proves to be the guardian and observer of this our privilege, may deserve to obtain from the just Judge, the Lord our God, the grace of blessing and heavenly recompense forever and ever. Amen.

Written by the hand of John, scribe and notary of the sacred Lateran palace, etc. Given on the twelfth day before the Kalends of March, by the hand of Peter, deacon, librarian, and chancellor of the holy apostolic see, in the first year of the lord Pope Clement II, in the fifteenth indiction.

## VIII. PRIVILEGE OF POPE CLEMENT II FOR THE BAMBERG CHURCH (Year 1047)

[In Mansi, *Concilia*, vol. XIX, col. 621.]

[Col. 0588B] Clement, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our most sacred Bamberg Church, in her sons and daughters—namely, clergy and people—perpetual salvation in the Lord.

The dispensation of the ages comes from the Prince of heaven, who, before the ages were made, foresaw how they would be ordered. Hence what could be foreseen by his eternal eye cannot fail to be fulfilled. The nod of so great a God has betrothed you, his most illustrious daughter of Bamberg, to us as a lawful bride, and, before kings, has granted you to us through his favor, insofar as it has depended upon us. Certainly no husband has purer faith or more ardent love toward his wife than we have toward you; nor has it ever entered our mind to abandon you and cleave to another. But—I do not know by what divine counsel—it has happened that I should be joined to your mother and to all the churches, while nevertheless not being entirely separated from you.

Behold, therefore: when that head of the world, that Roman see, was suffering from the disease of heresy, and the presence of our most beloved son, the lord H., august emperor, watched and pressed forward for this purpose, namely, to drive away such an illness, after those three men had been expelled whom robbery had invested with the same name of papacy, among the many ranks of holy Fathers who were present, heavenly grace in its condescension willed that our utterly unworthy mediocrity—resisting with all its strength—should be elected and exercise the office of the chief of the apostles.

And when I was then torn from your most beloved side, sweetest bride, what pain seized me, what grief overwhelmed me—how, I do not know, it can be expressed—since it seemed to us to exceed every measure that the mother should have more honor, more dignity, and more strength than the daughter, seeing that every earthly knee bends before her, at whose will the gate of heaven is opened and closed, against whom even the gates of hell do not prevail. Yet no desire for such domination entered the doorway of our mind or willingly bent the neck of our heart.

It was enough for us to lead an active life; we conducted the contemplative life in whatever way we could, especially since perfect love neither ever beholds the appearance of another nor looks upon wealth. We call the divine vision as witness: we are not composing an apology. For it searches the secrets of the heart, and no darkness obscures it. We also use conscience itself as a witness, where concern for you is continual.

Now such vast expanses of land, now so many intervening obstacles blunt the inner eye, so that I cannot watch over my friend, my sister, my bride, my dove, with sufficiently diligent care and make you secure on every side. By divine gift—not, as we have said, through our own merits—we have now received that apostolic authority which commands both heaven and earth. We have therefore judged it worthy and appropriate that you too should profit from our advancement, and that you should receive greater protection from the very source by which our authority is increased.

The lord H., august emperor, of pious memory, founded you, raised you up, and lifted you to a lofty summit. At his supplication, you were well enclosed against all impious hands by the impenetrable wall and defensive works of apostolic protection, through our predecessors, namely Pope John XIV and Benedict. Wishing to do the same ourselves, so that, surrounded by a threefold protection through the power of the Holy Trinity, you might never fear any injury or ever suffer molestation from anyone, but might remain always safe and peaceful among your sons and daughters, serving God always with devotion and obeying him devotedly, we establish through this our apostolic privilege that, from all those goods which the supreme generosity of that orthodox emperor, proceeding from his supreme devotion, piously bestowed upon you, dearest bride, most chaste virgin, most beautiful Church of Bamberg, and which he exchanged in name only through a most suitable and acceptable transaction, by the canonical and reasonable judgment of the bishops of Würzburg and Eichstätt [Col. 0589C], or which the religious piety of any of the faithful after him has offered or shall offer forever—whether movable or immovable—no emperor, king, duke, margrave, viscount, nor, moreover, any archbishop, bishop, abbot, or any human person, may dare, attempt, or presume to take away, diminish, or mutilate anything from them by violence, fraud, or theft.

But if anyone, driven by diabolical instigation [Col. 0590A], should not shrink from committing such an act with cruel recklessness and should neglect rather to make amends for what he has done, we not only exclude and drive such a person from communion in the most holy blood and body of our Lord Jesus Christ and from participation in all Christianity, but also pierce him with the sharpest lance of apostolic anathema. Thus, deservedly lost because of his evil deeds, he may mourn an eternal death, associated in hell, the lowest underworld, with the prince of demons, the inventor of death, and with sacrilegious and treacherous Judas; surrounded on every side by Tartarean dragons raging in vengeance, may he not rise to life at the final and terrifying judgment of God, but, taking up again his most cruel body, may he be crushed with a double destruction, seeking death in the most unhappy and miserable manner of life and not finding it.

But whoever, moved by pious regard, withdraws his own hands from such recklessness and, should circumstances require it, rises against all who attack and attempt to take away anything, defending for the benefit of you and your people, most holy Bamberg, those goods—namely, as was said, those bestowed upon you or hereafter to be bestowed upon you forever—such a person may be blessed by him who sits upon the cherubim and glories, because he has taken care to preserve unharmed this privilege of our authority and has strengthened it by his own power. This privilege, indeed, with the counsel and will, as well as the eager and ready consent, of our most illustrious son, the lord H., august emperor, already mentioned above, we have sent to you from our apostolic see, rejoicing with him on your account.

For just as your first founder, H. Caesar Augustus, planted you, so this second H., following in his footsteps, with the same name and equal dignity, has watered you with equal devotion, given you increase, and, while he lives, will continue—through God’s mercy and inspiration—to give you increase. In this we desire that you, sweetest bride, may grow, flourish, and thrive forever and ever. Farewell.

## In the Year of the Lord 1047: Oliva, Bishop of Ausona or Vic

[Col. 0589]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE

[In Antonio, *Bibliotheca Hispana vetus*, vol. II, p. 5.]

Oliva, son of Oliva Cabreta, count of Besalú, became a monk of Ripoll and abbot both of that monastery and of the monastery of Cuxa; from the year of Christ 1017 he was bishop of Ausona or Vic. His notable deeds were arranged and published by the distinguished Flórez—whose final work this was—and, after his death, by the distinguished continuator of *Hispania sacra*, Fr. Manuel Risco, vol. XXVIII, beginning on p. 122.

Some of his writings are presented in the appendix to the same volume, Appendix X, beginning on p. 265: namely:

1. A sermon on the feast of Saint Narcissus, bishop and martyr, followed by the *Narrative of the Conversion of Saint Afra*;
2. A letter to Gaucelin, archbishop of Bourges, p. 275;
3. Another letter to the monks of Ripoll, composed around the year 1023, recovered by Peter de Marca from the archives of Catalonia and published for the first time;
4. The consecration of the church of Vic or Ausona in the year 1038;
5. The synodal letter of the Council of Narbonne against invaders of sacred property;
6. A letter to Sancho, king of Navarre, called “the Elder,” sent in the year 1023 concerning the avoidance of an incestuous marriage, from the archive of Saint John of Peña.

In the same work, beginning on p. 275, one might add from the library of the king of France, vol. III, p. 343, col. 2, codex 2858:

7. A letter from Oliva to Sancho, king of Iberia, urging him to contribute something of his own toward constructing the church of Ripoll;

and, from the same royal library, vol. IV, p. 364, col. 1, codex 7476:

8. *On the Paschal Cycle and Ecclesiastical Computation.*

Regarding this work, Baluze, and after him the distinguished Flórez, vol. XXVIII, p. 139, note 59, wrongly express some doubt as to whether it belongs to another Oliva, likewise a monk of Ripoll, since the bibliographers know of no writer bearing the same name.

## WRITINGS OF OLIVA

[In Flórez, *España sagrada*, vol. XXVIII, p. 265.]

[Col. 0591]

## I. SERMON ON THE FEAST OF SAINT NARCISSUS, BISHOP, CONFESSOR, AND MARTYR OF CHRIST

[Col. 0591A] Because today, dearest brothers, the annual return of the feast of the holy confessor Narcissus and martyr of Christ has come around, let us rejoice. Today, indeed, the just man planted in the house of the Lord, who, like a palm tree, brought forth flowers on high, has presented ripe fruits in the royal palace. Today, clothed in the robe that he had often washed in the blood of the Lamb, invested with the dignity of the priesthood, crowned with the martyr’s laurel, and suffused with the rosy redness of his own blood, he entered the palace of heaven and was gloriously presented as a most valiant soldier to the heavenly Emperor.

Today he entered the senatorial house and, embraced by Christ the true King, deserved to be placed in his proper order. Therefore, let the righteous rejoice in the Lord, for praise befits the upright; and let them say to the just man: “It is well; he shall eat the fruit of his deeds” [Isaiah 3:10].

And you too, Felix, rejoice exceedingly; and be glad, Gerunda, because you have deserved a special gift which no neighboring city or place has been able to possess. For Africa, filled with the warmth of faith, sent you, by God’s arrangement, the most holy Felix, who directed Barcelona through teaching toward faith in Christ and its cultivation, freed the impure from the error of demons by preaching, showed the way of truth to those who did not know it, and, preaching the Gospel, rested in you in a glorious death with the triumph of martyrdom.

To you also the true East, the Sun of justice, sent Narcissus, the flower of paradise and herald of his coming. He illuminated various provinces and summoned to repentance souls deceived by diabolical fraud. While he instructed you through his preaching and cherished you with his most holy prayers, he remained in you a venerable martyr and forever fortified you with his companions, whose names are written in the book of life.

But, blessed Narcissus, flower of paradise and good fragrance of Christ abiding in every place [Col. 0592A], with what praises shall we exalt you? Shall we marvel first at your faith or at your virtues? At your faith, surely, since without it no one can please God. It armed you with a shield, protected you with the helmet of salvation, and fortified you with the sword of the Spirit, namely, the word of God.

As for the virtues with which Christ’s grace adorned you, we shall recount a few from among many, in keeping with the subject on which we began. Therefore, when you passed through the imperial city, your sanctity does not need testimony concerning what you did there or how you taught there; for the city, filled with your preaching and fortified by your holy prayers, still displays priests whom you established and martyrs.

There, finally, the prostitutes of the most wicked Venus, given over to brothels and various kinds of pollution, received you into their lodging, gazed upon your holiness for a very long time, and perceived in you the brightness of the heavenly light sent down from above. Through you they deserved to become true worshipers of our Lord Jesus Christ. You yourself snatched them from the jaws of the ancient dragon and, cleansed from the stains of mind and body, consecrated them to their Creator. Animated by your most holy preaching, you wonderfully introduced them among the choirs of martyrs with the crown of martyrdom.

You also, filled with the wisdom of Christ, most wisely confined that dragon, the enemy of the human race, so that, unless the dragon should kill his own friend-dragon, he himself would immediately suffer a most profound fall and plunge into the abyss. Meanwhile, the waters of the Julian Alps, which the envious enemy had polluted so that they would not benefit human use, your sweet prayer turned into sweetness and rendered fit for human use.

Thus Christ’s grace never abandoned you; rather, everywhere illuminating, it kindled you, and everywhere protecting, it surrounded you [Col. 0593A].
