Hence what is written in the psalm suited you well: that the Son of God held your right hand, led you according to your will, and, taking you crowned with martyrdom and transferring you to the palace of heaven, established you among the senators of the heavenly court in their company.

Therefore, dearest brothers, since the day of so great a solemnity of the confessor of Christ, our apostle and martyr, has dawned for us, let us render thanks and praises to the almighty Creator. Let us submit ourselves to the prayer of that aforesaid Narcissus, the flower of paradise; let us love what he loved, believe what he preached in word, and imitate what he displayed in his works.

Let our bishop rejoice, therefore, and let the clergy and the whole people rejoice together. For just as Rome, which is the head and mirror of the whole world, deserved from God to possess Peter, the first of the apostles and the prince of its salvation, so Gerunda also deserved to possess Narcissus, the flower of paradise and teacher of its salvation. Let this entire day be devoted to the praises of Christ and dedicated to his divine worship. Let quarrels cease, because the solemnity of the preaching of peace is being recalled; let feasting and drunkenness cease, because the one whose feast is celebrated today prohibited such pleasures to Christians.

[Col. 0593]

## II. HERE BEGINS THE CONVERSION OF SAINT AFRA, IN THE PROVINCE OF ARICIA, IN THE CITY OF AUGUSTA

[Col. 0593B] Narcissus was bishop at the time when the madness of Diocletian was raging. Not knowing where to enter, he came as a fugitive to a prostitute named Afra, together with his deacon Felix. When she saw respectable men approaching, supposing them to be immoral, she prepared a meal and everything that she was accustomed to prepare, according to her usual practice, with her girls.

But when the bishop came to eat, he began to pray and sing psalms. Afra, who had never heard or seen such things, was astonished and began to ask who he was. When she learned that he was a bishop of the Christians, she immediately fell at his feet, saying:

“Lord, I am unworthy, and in this city no woman more depraved than I can be found.”

Bishop Narcissus said to her:

“My Savior could not be defiled by contact with the most defiled woman, for his holiness has wiped away and cleansed all her filth. Defiled stains cannot defile the Lord’s brightness. When light comes, and the sun’s radiance is poured down from heaven around sewers and muddy streets, it comes down from heaven pure and returns to heaven pure. Therefore, daughter, receive the light of faith, so that, purified from every sin, you may rejoice with everlasting gladness at my entrance.”

Afra said to him:

“I, who have committed more sins than there are hairs on my head—how can I be cleansed from so many?”

Bishop Narcissus answered:

“Only believe and be baptized, and you will be saved.”

Then Afra summoned her girls and said:

“This man, a bishop of the Christians, tells me: ‘If you believe in Christ and are baptized, you can be cleansed from every sin.’ What do you think?”

Digna, Eunomia, and Eutropia answered [Col. 0593D]:

“You are our mistress; and if we have followed you into the pollution of crimes, how shall we not follow you into forgiveness of sins? You are our head; wherever you go, it is necessary for the members to follow.”

Meanwhile, as they were speaking, night began. The bishop began to sing to the Lord with his deacon and passed the whole night in prayer and psalmody, while Afra and her girls shared his vigil.

At daybreak, the persecutors began searching for Bishop Narcissus, and they said to Afra:

“Where are those who entered your house during the night?”

She replied:

“My guests were lovers, and they went away to sacrifice.”

Thinking that they had gone to the Capitol or to a temple, they fell silent. But one of them remained and said to her:

“I recognized those who came late, because they were Christians: at every hour they marked their foreheads with the sign of the cross on which their Christ suffered.”

Afra said to him:

“Would Christians enter the house of a prostitute such as I? No one comes to me except those who are like me.”

He went away and reported everything she had said and everything he had heard to those who were searching for them.

Then Afra went to her mother, named Hilaria, and said to her:

“A bishop of the Christians came to me, not knowing where to enter. Throughout the whole night he stretched out his hands to his God, singing to him what he knew, and made us pray together with him. Around cockcrow the candlelight went out, and I began to hurry to relight it, but I could not. Then his deacon said to me: ‘Do not seek a light that can be extinguished; now a light that cannot be extinguished will be shown to you.’ When the bishop heard this, he prayed, saying: ‘Come, true Light from heaven, and show us your face, and we shall be saved.’ Immediately a flash came from heaven like the sun, and it came like thunder, and it did not depart; rather, it remained there as long as it took for dawn to begin. When he had finished his prayer, he ordered us to answer him and say: ‘Amen.’ Then the light of that flash immediately withdrew from our eyes.

“After this I threw myself at his feet and said to him: ‘You have done me a great injury, because you entered my house; for I am a sinful woman.’ He said to me: ‘Where my God made me enter, there I entered.’

“Then, in the morning, around the third hour, those who had lain in wait before daylight so that they might seize and kill him as he came out showed themselves to me. When I came out, they met me. I had there torches made of flax, and I hid them. I fear that they may search the place itself. If you order me, mother and mistress, I will bring them here, because he promised me, saying: ‘I shall make you a Christian, so that all your sins may be blotted out.’”

When her mother heard this, she was filled with joy and said:

“May God grant that this happen to me!”

Afra said to her:

“Then, when night comes, I shall bring him here.”

Her mother replied:

“Even if he is unwilling, ask him.”

In the evening Afra begged Saint Narcissus, and he went to her mother. When Saint Narcissus the bishop entered the house, there was great rejoicing, so that Hilaria held his feet for three hours and said:

“I beg you, lord, make me clean from my sins.”

Then Bishop Narcissus said to her:

“Blessed is your faith, which, before you learned the word of truth, established in your mind truth itself, which people can scarcely recognize through the word. Yet because I see that you are capable of hearing the word of God, begin today to keep a fast. Fast for seven days while hearing the discourse of truth; on the eighth day you will be purified from every sin and will be like infants, without consciousness of any crime or any sin.”

Hilaria said to him:

“If you command us, we shall say what we worship; then teach us what we ought to worship.”

Bishop Narcissus said to her:

“It is evident that you can rightly receive what you ought to worship, since you clearly explain what you have worshiped. Tell me, then, about your worship.”

Hilaria replied:

“My parents were of Cypriot origin, and came from there. Since the rites of Venus—and Venus cannot be worshiped except by women who have become prostitutes—are such, I therefore consecrated my daughter to the rites of Venus and permitted her to remain in a brothel, as though she were to serve the goddess Venus and please her through prostitution. I believed that Venus would be favorable to me if I occupied my daughter with imitating her divine practices. For the priests of Venus assert that the more lovers a woman who serves Venus can have, the more she can please Venus.”

When the man of God Narcissus heard this, he groaned and shed tears. He said to his deacon Felix:

“Rise, brother, and let us mourn over such worship, and let us ask the Lord that, where iniquity has abounded, grace may abound still more.”

As they were praying, an Egyptian appeared, blacker than a raven, naked, and covered throughout his body with wounds and elephantiasis. He began to bellow and say:

“O holy Bishop Narcissus, what have you to do with my beloved? What have you to do with my maidservants, whom I have always kept in my friendship? Your God cleanses souls and loves clean bodies; these already belong to me and cannot belong to anyone else. Do I ever enter where chastity reigns? Do I find a place where the spirit of chastity is present? Why have you entered here, where bodies are defiled and souls polluted?”

Then Narcissus said to him:

“I command you, unclean spirit, to answer what I ask you. Tell me, condemned one: Do you know that my Lord Jesus Christ the Nazarene was tempted, scourged, struck in the face with spittle, fed with gall, given vinegar to drink, fastened to the cross, died, was buried, and on the third day rose from the dead? Do you know that this happened?”

The demon replied:

“Would that I had been permitted not to know it! For at the hour when he was crucified, our prince, fleeing from his face, cast himself into the temple of God. Therefore the veil of the temple was torn, because it could not endure the power of the one pursuing him. Then the solid rocks themselves were split, and the tombs [Col. 0596B] were opened, and holy men arose who saw this happen: our prince was seized by the one who had been crucified and bound with fiery chains.”

Narcissus answered:

“What is the name of your prince?”

The demon said to him:

“His name is Satan, which is interpreted as ‘beginning of death.’”

Narcissus said to him:

“Tell me, what did our Lord Jesus Christ do wrong, that he should suffer so much?”

The demon said:

“He never sinned.”

Narcissus said to him:

“Then why did one who never sinned suffer so much?”

The demon replied:

“He suffered not for his own sins, but for another’s.”

Bishop Narcissus said to him:

“From your own mouth you condemn yourself, unclean spirit. Since you know that my Lord Jesus Christ was killed not for his own sins but for the sins of others, depart from these women, because he suffered for those who fled to his faith and grace.”

The demon said to him:

“Why does the holy law teach and command that no one take another’s property? You, who are holy, why are you taking my property? Why are you taking from me the souls I have gained?”

Narcissus said to him:

“You are both a breaker of things and a thief, condemned and ancient one, from the beginning; for you separated these souls from their Creator and Lord. Now I hold you as a thief and restore the creature to its Creator.”

The demon answered:

“I too am his creature; therefore restore me also to my Creator.”

Narcissus said to him:

“You yourself have confessed with your mouth that Christ suffered for the sins of human beings. And if he suffered for human sins, and had also suffered for a demon, I would restore you to your Creator. But he suffered for human sins in such a way that he bound your prince in hell and plundered his dominion.”

The demon said to him:

“Show mercy to me and give one soul into my power.”

Narcissus said to him:

“If I give one soul into your power, what will you do with it?”

The demon said:

“I will kill the person and gain his soul.”

Narcissus said to him:

“At first light tomorrow I will give you this power, so that you may do this.”

The demon said:

“Before God, tell me that you will give me a soul enclosed within a body, which I may gain.”

Narcissus said:

“Before my God I promise that I will give you a soul placed in a body that eats, drinks, sleeps, and wakes again.”

The demon said:

“Now command me to remain here tonight.”

Narcissus said:

“If you can remain with us, remain.”

The demon said:

“If you stretch out your hands to heaven, bend your knees, and sing psalms to your God, I cannot remain here.”

Narcissus said:

“May you never prosper, unclean spirit. Not only I, but all these people with me, will bend our knees to the Lord throughout the night and sing praises to him with us.”

Then the demon, uttering a most terrible howl in a dreadful voice, disappeared without a trace.

Saint Narcissus the bishop then had Afra, her mother, and her girls eat after the fast. Because they were trembling on account of what they had seen and heard, he strengthened them with his admonitions and prayers. He himself, together with his deacon Saint Felix, did not eat, knowing that in the morning he would again have to fight with the demon [Col. 0597B]. He also spent the night filled with prayer and the singing of psalms.

When day had dawned, the demon appeared and said:

“Remember, holy bishop, the oath you made before God, and give me the soul whose body I shall kill, so that I may have the soul itself with me.”

Saint Narcissus replied:

“You too must swear to me in the name of my Lord that you will immediately kill the person whom I give you; and tell me that, if you do not kill him, God will command you to go into the abyss.”

The demon said:

“By him who conquered us and our prince I swear that I will immediately kill the one whom you give into my power; if I do not, may God command me to go into the abyss.”

Narcissus said to him:

“Go beside the spring of the Julian Alps, from which no one can drink water—not human being, beast, or any wild animal—because a dragon lives there, and by its breath all who approach the spring die. Go and kill this dragon, and bring its soul under your power.”

Then the demon cried out:

“O lying bishop! He has even bound me by an oath to kill my friend; and if I do not kill him, I shall be compelled to go into the abyss.”

Then the demon departed and killed the dragon, and the spring was freed for human use, as it remains to this day.

For many days he taught them the word of the Lord. Hilaria and her daughter Afra were baptized, together with their girls and all their loved ones. He made Hilaria’s house into a church and appointed as their bishop Zozimus, Afra’s uncle.

After arranging everything properly, Saint Narcissus departed for Spain nine months later and went to the city of Gerunda. There he won a great many people for the Lord over three years, and finally attained the palm of martyrdom with his holy deacon Felix. We shall speak of the glory of his passion below.

Blessed Narcissus, martyr of the Lord, distinguished preacher of the divine word, shone with the dignity of the priesthood and entered the palace of the heavenly kingdom as a victor in the triumph of martyrdom. He first showed the peoples of the East, and afterward those of the West, the light of the true faith, and rested in a glorious death at Gerunda.

When he was converting many to the faith of Christ, one day at Gerunda, amid the very mysteries of the sacrifices, he was slaughtered by persecutors. In his confession of the Trinity he was weakened by three wounds, namely, in the shoulder, throat, and calf. Finally, after completing the magnificent course of his venerable passion, he received from the Lord the crown of glory and reigns with him forever. His venerable body remains incorrupt to this day as a conspicuous miracle; his spirit, joined to the Lord, rejoices with him in the heavenly kingdoms.

Although Christ had sent his apostles everywhere throughout the world to preach, and although very many people were still occupied by the errors of paganism, nevertheless, through the mercy of God and the favoring kindness of our Redeemer, blessed Narcissus was sent to us as a teacher and apostle.

Therefore, beloved, imitate him, according to the excellent preaching of Paul: “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ.” If anyone, by God’s grant, feels a portion of justice in his heart, let him flee to the preaching of the eminent martyr, lest what appears upright within him fall in any way. But if anyone—God forbid—burdened by the enormity of his crimes, is heading toward the pit of despair, let him look to the repentance of the prostitute Afra and her companions and imitate it. Taught through Narcissus and saved through Christ, they deserved, by Christ’s gift, to receive the fruit of righteousness.

He who, like Elisha, turned the bitterness of water into sweetness through prayer can, by praying, drive away the bitterness of our sins and obtain forgiveness through Christ’s grace and mercy.

Meanwhile, beloved brothers, rebuke in this venerable worship the mournful, sacrilegious, and perverse people of the Hebrews, so that they may learn to venerate the solemnity of a martyr whom they have never willingly learned to love or believe in.

But, blessed Narcissus, flower of paradise, receive whatever and very meager praises we offer. You who remain always secure in your blessedness before the Lord, mercifully be concerned with the burden of our miseries. We who rejoice now in your celebration may deserve to share forever in your merits, through him who wonderfully crowned you for the praise and glory of his name and mercifully granted you as a counselor of eternal salvation and present welfare—Jesus Christ our Lord. To him, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, belong all praise, thanksgiving, power, might, and blessing forever and ever. Amen.

Blessed Narcissus suffered in the church of Saint Felix of Gerunda, which at that time was called Saint Mary’s outside the walls, together with his deacon Felix, in the year of the Lord 297, at the place where he now lies and where the cathedral church stood in the time of the unbelievers.

[Col. 0599]

## III. LETTERS OF OLIVA

### FIRST LETTER: OF GAUCELIN, ARCHBISHOP OF BOURGES, TO OLIVA (Year 1020)

[Col. 0599A]

G., archbishop and abbot, sends an abundant gift of salvation to the lord O., elevated by the grace of the same dignity.

“Your proclamation of holiness,” etc. The remainder is found in volume CXL of *Patrologia*, under GAUCELIN, at the year 1029.

### LETTER II: OLIVA TO GAUCELIN, ARCHBISHOP OF BOURGES

To Gaucelin, venerable archbishop of the holy first see of Bourges, and to all who dwell in the monastery of the blessed Father Benedict of Fleury, the small together with the great: O., bishop—although unworthy—and abbot of the holy Church of Ausona, together with the entire congregation dwelling with him, sends every blessing to those who live piously in Christ.

We give thanks to your venerable fatherhood and most loving charity, because you grieved with us in our sorrows, showed compassion as fathers toward sons, remembered us across so great a distance of land, and sent letters of great consolation. We received them with much longing for you and were greatly consoled by rereading them.

Our greatest consolation after God is this: if it pleases Christ that you commend his soul to him, for we desire that it, like the soul of each of us, should be with him. Commending you also to the almighty Lord, we entrust ourselves to your prayers, praying that God may eternally unite in himself those whom place separates from one another.

### LETTER III: OF THE SAME TO THE MONKS OF RIPOLL (Around the year 1023)

[Col. 0599C]

Oliva, bishop—although unworthy—and abbot of the holy Church of Ausona, sends to the entire community dwelling in the monastery of the Mother of God the desirable reward of the heavenly kingdom.

I am pleased to hear the news of your good health; this is what I always desire. Know, moreover, that I take delight in such things and am most grateful to be remembered by you. As for the construction of the walls, the chest, and the other things about which you wrote, they seem to me, on your part, no less than good works, since they are most pleasing gifts of the pious God. Regarding Witard’s absolution and his correction as well, I place my confidence in you, after the Lord [Col. 0599D] Jesus, and entrust the matter to you, so that you may release him according to your will and correct him as far as you are able.

Therefore, after we had departed from you, among the other matters we undertook, we appointed judges between the archbishop and the viscount of Narbonne to deal with [Col. 0600A] . . . [lacuna] matters, and we declared a pact of peace, [lacuna] prepared to bring it to an end, when the countess of Rouergue, awaited on account of this affair, comes to settle it. Meanwhile, I drew up an agreement between the counts Wifred, William, and Hugh. They will be brought together this week, if perhaps we can put an end to such great evils.

Occupied, therefore, with these and other affairs, we cannot inform you of the day of our return. We ask that, concerning the matters taking place around you, you make us fully informed as soon as possible by your letters. Furthermore, guard the swans and the gull (*gaviancum*), the lord’s delights, as carefully as possible; and whatever adverse or favorable event befalls them, record it immediately in a letter, so that we may either rejoice with you in their prosperity or be distressed by their misfortunes.

Good news, moreover: we also have a crane, which has already learned to fly through the air by leaps, to pluck out the eyes of asses and pigs, and which now seems to be reddening in the head, darkening in its feathers, and growing clearer in voice. You ought to rejoice with us in such great successes of its. Farewell.

## LETTER IV. THE SAME AUTHOR TO SANCHO, KING OF NAVARRE  
*(In the year 1023.)*

To the magnificent lord Sancho, most glorious king, cultivator of the orthodox faith, to be preferred above all in praise, Oliva, prelate and abbot—though unworthy—of the holy Church of Ausona, together with the community of the divine order dwelling with him, sends wishes that you may happily and triumphantly possess successes here and fruits in heaven that shall never end.

[Col. 0600C] If the prosperity of your magnificence is increased by the bestowals of the divine gift, nothing more desirable can be found for our hearts. But if it is advanced through any misfortunes, nothing can be found that we more strongly wish to avoid. We give countless thanks, as far as we are able, to the omnipotence of the Creator, who so binds the breadth of your heart with the bond of his love that, when undertaking what is greatest or even of middling importance among your works, you do not act solely on your own initiative, but with royal prudence seek out the counsels of those who fear him—namely, of those who are far away as well as those who are near.

We also offer you abundant praise, because you never disregard our lowliness, but, in doing good and in seeking counsel from us—as though from someone of great importance in your affairs—you make inquiry. Consequently, you have so joined our souls to your spirit [Col. 0600D] that none of us wishes anything better to happen to himself than to you. At this time we saw our lord abbot Pontius, our brother and son, together with García, your most faithful servant; they reported to us your command and the concerns of your mind.

### 2

Accordingly, concerning the matter about which your highness was pleased to inquire of our lowliness, we have endeavored to send before your eyes whatever we were able to gather from the Law and the Prophets, or from the other divine Scriptures.

How great a crime it is to join those related by blood in a marriage bond, the law of the Old Testament declares, the prophets cry aloud, the apostles demonstrate, and the holy Fathers after them indicate in their writings. What is condemned by the prophets in the ancient Law is likewise forbidden by the apostles; it is opposed and subsequently anathematized by the other possessors of divine knowledge.

Finally, the Lord himself cries out through Moses in the book of Leviticus:

> No man shall approach his near blood-relative, to uncover her nakedness. [Col. 0601B]

A little later he adds and says:

> You shall not lie with your neighbor’s wife, nor shall you be defiled by the mingling of seed.

Again, in the same book:

> Every soul that does any of these abominations shall perish from the midst of his people.

Again, shortly afterward, in the same book:

> Whoever lies with his paternal uncle’s wife or with his maternal uncle’s wife and uncovers her nakedness, both shall bear their iniquity and shall die without children.

The prophet Ezekiel also says concerning this, among other things:

> If a man fathers a son who sheds blood and defiles his neighbor’s wife, will he live? He shall not live. He shall die in the sin that he has committed.

From this point the prophet Hosea speaks in similar terms:

> Curse, falsehood, murder, theft, and adultery have overflowed, and blood has touched blood. Therefore [Col. 0601C] the land shall languish, together with everyone who dwells in it, and the beasts of the field, the birds of the sky, and the fish of the sea.

For blood touches blood when the profane mingling of an irrational union joins itself to blood-relationship and the marital intercourse passes into the bond of fornication.

Thus far concerning the ancients. The apostle Paul, the founder and teacher of the Christian religion after Christ, also detesting this kind of fornication, says in the First Epistle to the Corinthians, among other things:

> Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ? Shall I therefore take the members of Christ and make them members of a prostitute? Certainly not. Or do you not know that whoever clings to a prostitute becomes one body with her? “The two,” he says, “shall become one flesh.” But whoever clings to the Lord is one spirit with him.

Again, in the same place:

> Flee fornication. Every other sin that a person commits is outside the body; but the fornicator sins against his own body. [Col. 0601D]

The same apostle says elsewhere in the Epistle to the Thessalonians:

> For this is the will of God, your sanctification: that you abstain from fornication; that each of you know how to possess his own vessel in sanctification and honor, not in the passion of desire, like the nations who do not know the Lord.

And shortly afterward:

> For God did not call us to uncleanness, but to sanctification. Therefore whoever rejects these things rejects not man but God, who also gives his Holy Spirit in you.

### 3

What follows are examples from the canons, issued by the holy Fathers, who were filled with the divine Spirit. What they contain concerning this matter is shown by what they transmitted from themselves to posterity.

Concerning incest, from the Council of Lérida, chapter 4:

> Those who defile themselves with the pollution of incest and persist in this detestable cohabitation shall eat food with none of the Christians.

Again, concerning those who join themselves to their near relations, from the Council of Toledo, chapter 5:

> Let no member of the faithful join a close blood-relative to himself in marriage. If he does so, let him remain excommunicated from the body of Christ and from fraternal fellowship for as long as he has been polluted by this contagion.

Again, from the Council of Agde, chapter 12:

> For incestuous unions and illicit relationships we reserve absolutely no pardon, unless they have healed adultery through separation. We call incestuous those who have taken their brother’s widow, or their brother’s full sister, or their stepmother, or their cousin, or a woman from their own kindred up to the seventh generation, or their uncle’s wife, or their uncle’s daughter, or their paternal uncle’s daughter, or their stepdaughter; all such unions are forbidden as illicit.

Again, Pope Gregory the most holy said in the Roman Council concerning this, among other things:

> If anyone takes his cousin in marriage, or a woman from his own kindred, or one whom a kinsman had taken, up to the seventh generation, let him be anathema.

And all who were in the council answered three times:

> Let him be anathema.

### 4

These, therefore, O good king and most illustrious prince, are the evils of an incestuous marriage. These are the injuries caused by a union forbidden by God. We would have gathered many more examples from the authors on this subject, had the shortness of time, the hurried return of the messengers, and the length of the document not compelled us to desist from what we had begun.

We pray and implore you by the Lord Jesus to guard yourself in every respect against these execrable acts, and henceforth to give your consent in no way to such abominable practices. For, as the blessed apostle Paul says:

> Those who do such things deserve death—not only those who do them, but also those who approve those who do them.

### 5

But perhaps someone will say: “If the king does not deny the emperor marriage with his sister, then peace will continue, the pagans will be destroyed, and the churches throughout all their lands will be restored and corrected according to the law of God. But if he does not do this, discord will arise in peace, the pagans will be strengthened, and damage to the laws of God will continue in the churches.” [Col. 0602D]

This is an utterly futile thought—or, to speak more truly, an insinuation of the devil introduced into human hearts, entirely removed from every rational consideration of truth. For peace has never proceeded from such a union, nor has security of divine worship arisen from so incestuous a marriage.

Finally, the Holy Spirit, mocking the thoughts of such foolish people who suppose that peace results from this kind of unlawful agreement, introduces them in a certain passage as saying:

> Let us do evil, so that good may come.

Are these people not like them, and equal to heretics, who, by promising this union, introduce an occasion for obtaining peace and justice?

But we have heard and believed, and therefore we speak. For peace always proceeds from chastity and modesty. Thus Christ, who is our peace, came among human beings as the son of a chaste and most modest Virgin, to reconcile the things that are in heaven and the things that are on earth.

Certainly John the Baptist, the forerunner of that same Son of God, while prohibiting Herod’s illicit unions, lost his life by being beheaded for the sake of justice, but gained glory. And not he alone, but all the saints who have preceded us until now resisted the opponents of divine law even to the shedding of blood.

Therefore, if opposition from wicked people—whether Christians or pagans—rises against you for this reason, do not fear them or be terrified of them. Rather, sanctify the Lord Christ himself. He shall be your terror and your fear; he shall be a sanctuary to you, but a snare of offense and a stumbling-stone to all those who rise against you for this reason.

Their arm will be an arm of flesh, but with you will be the Lord our God, who is a helper in times of need and in tribulation. But if he permits you to be scourged by them to some degree, keep in your memory the eternal hope laid up for you, which without doubt he will grant you: the inheritance that eye has not seen, ear has not heard, and the human heart has not conceived, which God has prepared for those who love him.

For the good are not always afflicted, nor do the wicked always oppress the just, since their glory is dung and worms; they spend their days in prosperity and in a moment descend to the underworld.

### 6

We know that in your regions in former times [Col. 0603C] very righteous laws were promulgated and holy canons established by the most blessed Fathers. At that time your land was an example to the whole world in divine religion and earthly rule.

But now foreigners devour your region before your eyes [Col. 0604A], and it is laid waste as in an enemy’s devastation. For it is known to be subject, among other vices, to three most wicked evils: namely, incestuous marriages, drunkenness, and augury.

We have already spoken as best we could about the first. Concerning drunkenness the Lord speaks through Isaiah:

> Woe to those who are powerful for drinking wine and strong men for mixing drunkenness.

The apostle Paul also says that drunkards shall not possess the kingdom of God. Concerning augury, God commanded in the Law:

> You shall not practice augury, nor observe dreams.

The apostle Paul likewise says:

> You observe days, months, seasons, and years; I fear that perhaps I have labored among you in vain.

For the present, we bring the letter to an end. We ask you as our lord, implore you as our father, and admonish you as our son, not to disdain believing our words—or rather, the divine assertions—and not to permit the agreement of wicked men to prevail against the divine laws and the statutes of the saints, namely, in the ordering of the churches and the correction of monasteries, in the defense of orphans and widows, and in the most just administration of the peoples entrusted to you.

As long as we remain in this body, we shall always pray for you as for our own souls, that almighty God may mercifully rescue you from the snares of your enemies and grant you perseverance in holy works until the end of your life.

If you wish to command us anything concerning your service, give the order according to your will, for we are ready to obey according to our ability. What could not be written here has been entrusted to the mouth of lord [Col. 0604C] Pontius [lacuna].

Given by the hand of Arnallus, minister of this work, on the fifth day before the Ides of May, in the year 1023 from the Incarnation of Christ, in the sixth indiction.

[Col. 0603]

## IV. CONSECRATION OF THE CHURCH OF VIC  
*(In the year 1038.)*

[Col. 0603D] In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1038, the era 1076, in the fifth [sixth] indiction, lord Guifred, archbishop of the holy first see of Narbonne, a man of outstanding intellect and singular wisdom, came to the see of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles and Church of Ausona. With him came the venerable college of bishops of his diocese, together with a very great multitude of clerics of various orders; and a large crowd of people of varied rank and of both sexes came to meet them, for the consecration of the basilica of that see, built in honor of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

These things took place under the authority and in the presence of the lady Ermesindis, countess, a magnificent worker of the divine law, [Col. 0604D] and of her nephew, lord Raimund, count and marquis, a boy of excellent disposition.

The numerous throng of advocates flowing together in ranks, and the assembly of the reverend prelates whom we mentioned above, were prepared with the greatest zeal through the initiative, industry, and devout purpose of lord Oliva, the venerable bishop of the aforesaid see. He had energetically begun this church from its foundations, completed it with great expense and labor, and adorned it to increase its sanctity with the diverse relics of saints gathered from every direction. Together with the most distinguished company of bishops and the sacred order of the people, with divine grace assisting him, he dedicated it.

[Col. 0605A] Finally, the aforementioned lord Guifred, eminent archbishop of the Church of Narbonne and worthy of praise in many respects, together with the choir of bishops assisting him, after completing this mystery with the praises of joyful celebration, beautiful salvation, and divine consummation, granted this endowment-charter to the same church and promulgated it by pontifical decree as a law destined to endure forever.

In the name of the supreme and immutable God and our Savior Jesus Christ, I, Guifred, archbishop of the holy first see of Narbonne; and Oliva, bishop of Ausona; and Berengarius of Elne; and Guislabert of Barcelona; and Eriballus of Urgell; and Guifred of Carcassonne, with one mind and undivided judgment, all together grant and confirm this endowment of confirmation to the holy mother Church of Ausona, founded and consecrated in honor of the blessed [Col. 0605B] apostles Peter and Paul. So that it may remain unshaken by the inviolable perpetuity of the law, under the adjuration of the divine name and by the authority of our order, we decree the following.

First, we establish that the same church shall be entirely free and subject to the execution of no service whatsoever. Let it freely hold and securely possess all churches and all estates, however great or wherever located, justly granted to it as gifts by any of the faithful, or to be justly granted to it forever: namely, whatever it has hitherto possessed and now possesses, or whatever it may have possessed throughout all human time; a third part of the revenues of churches, woods, meadows, uncultivated lands, or *rafigae* [an uncertain term], which the common people of this land simply call “thirds,” just as it has hitherto possessed them or ought to have possessed them; and also whatever grazing dues it has or ought to have from any source. We confirm that it shall possess these forever without anyone’s impediment.

We establish and in every way strengthen that it shall always have the public mint of its region and the toll-duty from the markets of that place and of Manresa.

We also prohibit, in accordance with the statutes of the holy canons and the authority of the ancient Fathers, that any bishop presume to consecrate a church within the bounds of this bishopric, receive the penitents of its bishop, or ordain its clergy, unless the prelate of the aforesaid see should willingly give his consent.

Let no one dare conceal estates belonging to this church, wherever they are known to be owed to it; rather, as soon as anyone learns of them, let him not hesitate to disclose them immediately for its benefit. Let no prince, no power great or small, and no person of whatever rank, sex, or order presume to reduce the boundaries of this bishopric or attempt in any way to transfer or alienate anything to the detriment of the aforesaid see.

The boundary of the entire bishopric of the holy Church of Ausona begins at the borders of Berguedà, rises to the mountain called Eramala, then to Mount Suroca, and proceeds to the meadow of the Round Field. It runs through that mountain range, as the waters divide by the cliff of Latione, and descends [Col. 0606A] to the river Têder. It reaches the plantations, which are the boundary between Gerunda and the boundaries of Ausona, and extends to the stream of Ausona. It also rises through that mountain range to Gerundella; then follows the road that comes to Bellapolla, and advances to the boundaries between Joannet and Elzeta. It reaches the borders of Arbutia, then descends to the summit of the mountain called Sera, and to the pass called Eramala, and reaches the hill of Mount Niger. From there it comes to the stream of Congust and reaches the castle called Bertillis, then the top of the cliff of Saint Genesius, and from there Mount Saint Saturninus and Mount Calvus; from there it extends to Mount Serratus.

It advances through the middle of the boundaries [Col. 0606B] between the march of Barcelona and that of Ausona, as those marches are divided, and goes to the castle called Queralt. It proceeds through the middle of the division of those marches to the river Segre. Likewise, on the side previously written down at the borders of Berguedà, the boundary runs between the march of Ausona and the march of Barcelona, as those marches are divided, and proceeds to the river Segre.

As for the land itself, and all the churches, parishes, or estates of whatever kind belonging to the canonry of the same see of the blessed apostle Peter—namely, whatever it now justly possesses, or shall justly possess or acquire throughout all future time—by the authority of the blessed apostle Peter, prince [Col. 0606C], and through our order, we excommunicate and prohibit anyone from taking, alienating, transferring, or exchanging any part of it to the detriment of the aforesaid canonry, whatever his power, sex, or order may be, except insofar as our brother and fellow bishop, lord Oliva, shall release it.

We bind this very property, recognized as belonging by right to the canonry, under the following condition: whatever the aforesaid bishop Oliva releases from it, as stated above, shall remain released; whatever he does not wish to release shall remain excommunicated by pontifical decree.

Accordingly, we decree that this entire endowment of our constitution, promulgated above, shall endure as an eternal law. We bless every person who observes it and assists as far as possible in keeping it secure, and we pray that such a person may obtain both length of life in the present age and the perpetuity of the age that always remains.

But under adjuration of the divine judgment and the prohibition of anathema, we establish that if anyone, of whatever power or order, attempts to break or violate this, or does break or violate it, he shall remain excommunicated by almighty God, the blessed apostle Peter, all the saints, and us. He shall be excluded from the assembly of the holy Church and from all Christians, bound with infernal chains, and shall eternally suffer the punishments of hell.

If, however, he desists from what he has begun and makes satisfaction through worthy repentance together with correction, let him be released from this excommunication [Col. 0607A], and let this constitution of ours be held forever inviolable and unshaken.

This was enacted at the see of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, on the second day before the Kalends of September, in the eighth year of the reign of King Henry. Written by the hand of Ermemir, canon and priest of the same see, in place of Arnaldus, notary of Bishop Oliva.

Raimbaldus, archbishop of Arles; Pontius, archbishop of Agen; Guifred, archbishop of the holy Church of Narbonne: I dedicated this church of our metropolitan see; Oliva, bishop; Guislibertus, by the grace of God bishop of Barcelona; Eriballus, bishop; Arnallus, archpriest; Willelmus, archdeacon; [Col. 0608A] Godebalo of Bisaura; Foleo, viscount; Raimundus, count and marquis; Adalbertus the Levite, also provost; Ermesindis, by the grace of God countess; Wifredus, by the grace of God prelate of Carcassonne; Petrus, bishop; Arnallus, bishop; Berengarius, by God’s will prelate of the holy Church of Elne, confirm the foregoing.

Bernardus, by the grace of God bishop of Couserans; Bernardus T.; Gerallus, viscount; Ermemir, though unworthy, priest, who in the aforesaid year and on the aforesaid day wrote these things, stated above, at the command of the aforesaid bishops and nobles, and of Count Raimundus, and under T—

[Col. 0607]

## V. SYNODAL LETTER OF THE COUNCIL OF NARBONNE  
Against the invaders of sacred property, under Oliva, bishop of Ausona.

[Col. 0607B] Wifredus, archbishop of the holy first see of Narbonne, [lacuna]. A synod assembled at Narbonne sends dearest greetings and perpetual blessing to its most beloved sons in Christ: Bermundus, viscount of Ausona; Gerallus of Capraria; Bernardus of Gurb; Wisadus of Ellemar; Bermundus of Foratella; Witardus of Mauritius; Miro of Sallifor; Hugo of Cervulus; Eloricus of Auris; Seniofredus of Laus; Wifredus of Balcia; Bernardus of Renvir; Willelmus of Montaniola; Bernardus of Tov.

When we had gathered in the name of almighty God to deliberate on certain necessary matters [lacuna], our dearest brother and fellow bishop Oliva rose in our midst, reporting that you [unlawfully] usurp estates granted by the faithful as a gift to the blessed prince of the apostles, and do not fear to expend what belongs to God for your own purposes [Col. 0607C].

Therefore, dearest sons, we are greatly astonished at why you take God’s property from him in this way, or why you do not leave to him what little belongs to him, so that you may possess much of your own. Is the bishop who has been ordained for you so dispensing what belongs to God as to squander it in the crimes of a perverse will?

How, moreover, do you regard yourselves as sons of the pious mother Church, or render her the honor due and appropriate to a mother, if, after violently taking away what belongs to her, you divide it up in the manner of outsiders?

Consider how far what you are doing departs from every path of righteousness and plunges you into the snares of injustice, while you reduce to nothing what the strictest excommunication of the most holy Fathers has established as most firmly binding [Col. 0607D], so that—unless God avert it—such condemnation may possess you forever.

We therefore admonish you by the eternal and one divinity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; by the authority of the blessed apostle Peter, whose place we unworthily hold; by the power granted to us to direct you; and by the power of binding and loosing granted to all of us by God [Col. 0608B]. Remembering the evil that you commit, while you hold what belongs justly to God in an unjust manner, restore to God and to the mother Church what it has lost by the first feast of Saint John the Baptist that is to come, so that God may preserve for you your own possessions, which he has granted.

But if, God forbid, you disregard our admonition and neglect our rebuke, then, following in the footsteps of the holy Fathers, just as they forbade such things, we forbid them. By the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, unless you believe our words, we excommunicate you and those who have acted with you in such matters. We judge you strangers to the thresholds of the holy Church, and we likewise excommunicate all priests or clerics of whatever order who presume to perform ecclesiastical office either for you or in the church where you may be.

Whatever our brother and fellow bishop Oliva releases from this property, we release; whatever he binds, we bind.

But we exempt the lady Ermesindis, countess, and her son Berengarius from all this excommunication. At the same time, by God, we both ask and admonish her to render the honor due to Saint Peter and to her bishop, and, insofar as she can, not permit him to suffer loss of justice.

When she sees him wishing, as far as he is able, to carry out the divine work, let her take care to correct those harming him by her authority and assist him in every way, knowing that it will turn to her profit if she does not allow him to suffer the loss of her support [Col. 0608D].

Guifredus, bishop of the holy first Church of Narbonne. Adalbertus, bishop. Stephanus, bishop of Agde. Stephanus, bishop.

## In the Year of the Lord 1048. Rodulfus Glaber, Cluniac Monk.

[Col. 0609]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE ON RODULFUS GLABER

*(Monumenta Germaniae Historica, Scriptores, vol. VII, from G. Waitz’s preface to Rodulfus.)*
[Col. 0609A] In the tenth and eleventh centuries, when learning had advanced greatly in almost all the provinces of Germany, and especially when events both ancient and contemporary were more frequently committed to memory in various forms, Gaul produced scarcely one or two writers who emerged from the darkness under which the whole province lay and composed a history of their own times. After Flodoard, Richer, and Dudo, during fifty years you will find no one who performed this task, except Ademar of Aquitaine and Odorannus of Sens, who compiled only very brief and excessively meager annals. Finally, in the middle of the eleventh century, a certain Cluniac monk undertook to write a universal history, convinced that nothing of this kind had been attempted since the time of Bede and Paul the Deacon.

Rodulfus, surnamed [Col. 0609B] Glaber [Note: [Col. 0609B] That is, “the Bald One”; cf. de la Curne de St.-Pelaye in *Mémoires de l’Académie des inscriptions*, VIII, p. 549. That Rodulfus was in fact his name is shown by the *Life of William*, which bears only this name as its title; see below.], was apparently born in Burgundy. Already in his twelfth year he was entrusted by his uncle, a monk, with monastic discipline in the monastery of Saint Leodegarius called Campellis [Col. 0610A]. He seems to have learned his letters quickly and not without benefit; but because of his frivolous, turbulent, and fierce disposition, as he himself testifies, he was expelled by the brothers [Note: [Col. 0609B] V, 1: “For when I was once living in the monastery of the blessed martyr Leodegarius, which is called Campellis (in the diocese of Langres) … Meanwhile, I do not blush to confess that I was not only born in the sins of my parents, but also proved troublesome in character and intolerable in conduct beyond what can be told. By the force of a certain monk—my uncle, that is—I was withdrawn from the most perverse vanity of secular life, which I practiced more than anything else, when I was nearly twelve years old, and, clothed in a monk’s habit—alas, what grief!—changed only my clothing, [Col. 0609C] not my mind. For whatever modest and holy counsel was charitably offered to me by the fathers or spiritual brothers, I opposed, swollen with the pride of a fierce spirit and carrying the inflated shield of my heart, lest, at the prompting of arrogance, anything salutary should touch me. Thereafter, disobedient to my elders, troublesome to my equals, burdensome to my juniors, and, to confess the truth, a burden to everyone by my presence and a relief by my absence, I was finally expelled by the brothers of that place, provoked by these and similar faults, from the fellowship of their dwelling. Yet they knew that, because of my knowledge of letters, I would not lack some place in which to live.”].

Thus we see that he advanced through several monasteries, residing now at Saint Benignus of Dijon [Note: [Col. 0609C] He continues in the passage cited: “After this, therefore, having been placed in the monastery of Saint Benignus, martyr of Dijon, etc.”], now at Meleredense [Note: [Col. 0609C] In the passage cited: “And a third time, when I was staying at the monastery of the blessed and ever-virgin Mary, surnamed [Col. 0610B] Meleredense, etc.” (Moutiers in the diocese of Auxerre.)], at Saint Germanus of Auxerre [Note: [Col. 0610B] V, 1], and at Besua [Note: [Col. 0610B] IV, 6: “When his companions returned to us, they reported what we have said, while we were then staying at the monastery of Besua.” I would not think that he lived at the Majus Monasterium (Marmoutier near Tours). For the words of V, 1—“For it was the custom of that monastery, as we ourselves observed”—seem to refer to Cluny. In the other manuscript, “Majoris Monasterii” was written by a more recent hand in place of “Cluniense.”], and finally at Cluny. At Dijon he obtained the friendship of the celebrated abbot William, whom he accompanied to Italy in the year of Christ 1028 [Note: [Col. 0610B] IV, 3: “For I myself was present when I arrived there with the abbot so often mentioned.” He rebuked a certain impostor who had fabricated relics.], and whose *Life* he composed after his death, which we publish below.

During the final years of his life he lived in the Cluniac monastery, then flourishing under Odilo [Note: [Col. 0610C] III, 3: “For afterward, when I was living in the monastery of Cluny with the other brothers, many monks from Spain arrived there, men of honorable conduct who had long followed the customs of their own region.”], attached to that abbot. At Odilo’s command and in response to the prayers of the brothers, he was induced to complete the *History*, which he had begun on William’s authority [Note: [Col. 0610C] *Life of William*, ch. 27: “Once offended by the guilt of my crimes, when I perceived that William had become bitter toward me for a time, I withdrew to another monastery not at all subject to his authority. While I was there, he appeared to me one night with a peaceful countenance, and, laying his hand upon me and stroking my head, said: ‘I ask you not to abandon me, if you did not pretend to love me; rather, I wish you to carry out what you promised. For at his command I had already described, for the most part, the events and portents that occurred around and after the thousandth year from the incarnate Savior.”], [Note: [Col. 0610C] See the preface.] He intended to record events that had occurred throughout the four quarters of the world around and after the year 1000. At first he treated them more briefly, and later more fully, so that, up to the year 1044, [Col. 0611A] when he ended his narrative, he amassed much worthy of notice.

But he followed no order and no definite plan, greatly confusing the chronology, and often assigning plainly false years even to events close to his own age [Note: [Col. 0611B] In his final years he is always two years removed from the truth, placing Conrad’s death in 1041 (V, 1) and Henry’s marriage in 1043 (V, 1). Likewise, the lunar eclipse that he assigns to 1046 had already occurred in 1014, so that the narrative does not proceed beyond that year. Rivet did not sufficiently recognize this, *Hist. littér.*, VII, p. 401.]. He included many things that in no way illuminate history, especially by recounting miracles and prodigious events [Note: [Col. 0611B] He himself says that this was his purpose in the passage cited in note 9.]. He lingered over theological and, if I may misuse the term, philosophical investigations [Note: [Col. 0611B] Compare what he says at the beginning about the four ages being compared with the four elements, virtues, and rivers; what he argues against the heretics in III, 8; and many other matters of this kind.]. What precedes the year 1000 he seems to have drawn from hearsay. Certainly, as I have already said, he knew no historians after Paul himself; for the *Lives* of Saint Germanus of Auxerre, Saint Maurus, and Brendan, which he cites [Note: [Col. 0611B] II, 8; III, 5; II, 2. In the *Life of William*, ch. 15, he also cites Gregory of Tours’ book *On the Glory of the Martyrs* and the *Life of Saint Benignus*.], concern earlier times. The letters of Maiolus and William [Note: [Col. 0611B] I, 4; IV, 1. Compare another letter of William in the *Life*, ch. 19.] he could easily have obtained elsewhere. Later, too, he often learned events from vague rumor.

Although he devoted himself to letters and read not only ecclesiastical writers but also Latin poets [Note: [Col. 0611B] For example, Terence in III, 9. He also inserts verses into his narrative in III, 9; and while he was living in the monastery of Saint Germanus, when his fellow servants and brothers of that place asked him to restore the inscriptions of the altars, once composed by learned men but scarcely visible because of age, which causes almost everything to decay, he willingly did so.], he nevertheless committed ridiculous errors in determining the situation of lands [Note: [Col. 0611C] II, 3. He places Vesuvius in Africa. In IV, 8, he reports wholly unheard-of things about the geography of Germany.], and in explaining the names of cities and peoples [Note: [Col. 0611C] I, 5 (the Normans); II, 3 (Orléans); III, 5 (Cluny); IV, 8 (the Rhaetians and the Lutici).]. If to these faults you add his superstitious disposition [Note: [Col. 0611C] Compare III, 3; IV, 2 and 3 (the chapter entitled “That, because the sins of men demand it, miracles are sometimes performed by evil spirits with the Lord’s permission”); V, 1, etc.], and the inelegance—or, not to say, the repulsiveness—of his language [Note: [Col. 0612B] He very often uses a participle in place of a finite tense, and frequently seems to have entirely neglected the connections between verbs.], you may reasonably think him an author not greatly to be commended.

Nevertheless, whatever he himself saw or received from contemporaries [Note: [Col. 0612B] Besides the passages already cited, compare III, 3; IV, 3, 6; V, 1; also III, 6: “For so many witnesses to the matter we are about to relate existed as there were people living in that city at that time”; IV, 4: “as we ourselves afterward observed”; IV, 6: “What Odolric, bishop of Orléans, saw when he went there and related to us”; V, 3: “We learned this from Guido, archbishop of Reims.” What he reports about Odilo he could himself have known extremely well; compare II, 8; IV, 7; V, 1.], he faithfully committed to his tablets, with a sufficiently candid and just disposition [Note: [Col. 0612B] Thus he attacks the false cult of relics in IV, 3, and more than once inveighs against simony. Besides the passages printed below, compare II, 6, especially these words: “For the kings themselves, who ought to be proper judges of persons suitable for sacred religion, corrupted by the distribution of gifts, judge someone more suitable to govern churches or souls—namely, the one from whom they hope to receive greater gifts.” Also noteworthy are the words of II, 4: “Although the pontiff of the Roman Church, because of the dignity of the apostolic see, is held in greater reverence than the others established throughout the world, it is nevertheless not permitted him to transgress in anything the rule of canonical moderation. For just as every pontiff and bridegroom of the orthodox Church uniformly bears the likeness of the Savior in his own see, so it is generally fitting for no one to perpetrate anything arrogantly in the diocese of another bishop.”], he described the spirit of the age and painted its corrupt customs in vivid colors. In French history there is much that depends on his testimony; he also records events in Germany and Italy that one would seek in vain elsewhere.

[Col. 0611]

THE FIVE BOOKS OF HISTORIES OF RODULFUS GLABER, CLUNIAC MONK, CONCERNING HIS OWN TIMES, FROM THE ELECTION OF HUGH CAPET AS KING DOWN TO THE YEAR 1046, COMPARED WITH THE ANCIENT THUANUS MANUSCRIPT.

(Duchesne, *Hist. Franc. Script.*, IV, at the beginning.)

PREFACE OF RODULFUS GLABER.

[Col. 0611C] To the most illustrious Odilo, father of the Cluniac monastery, Rodulfus Glaber.

[Col. 0612C] I was moved by the most just complaint of studious brothers, and often still more by my own concern, that in the days of our [Col. 0613A] time there was no one who would commit to writing, in some form of stylistic record, the many things that appear to be happening both in the churches of God and among the peoples, so that they might not be hidden from those who come after us. This is especially so since, as the Savior bears witness, even until the final hour of the last day, with the Holy Spirit cooperating, he himself will continue with the Father to make new things in the world.

And since for nearly two hundred years no one had undertaken this task—that is, since Bede, the presbyter of Britain, or Paul of Italy, who each left something written for posterity in historical form—for each composed a history of his own people or homeland, it is nevertheless clear that many things occurred both in the Roman world and in the overseas or barbarian provinces which, if committed to memory, would be exceedingly useful to men [Col. 0613B] and would especially assist everyone in cultivating prudence.

No less, indeed, and even more abundantly, did the events that are related occur around the thousandth year after the year of the Savior Christ’s incarnation. Therefore, insofar as I am able, I obey your command [Col. 0614A] and fraternal will, intending first only to show—although the total reckoning of the years from the origin of the world, according to Hebrew histories, differs from the translation of the Seventy interpreters—that we can affirm with complete certainty that the thousand and second year of the incarnate Word was the first year of the reign of Henry, king of the Saxons. That same thousandth year of the Lord was also the thirteenth year of the reign of Robert, king of the Franks.

These two men were then regarded as the most Christian and most powerful rulers in our world on this side of the sea. The first of them, Henry, later assumed the Roman Empire. For this reason we have fixed their memory within the sequence of times.

Moreover, since we are going to relate events in the four regions of the earthly world, it seems—and it is dear to my heart, since we are speaking to religious men—that, with the Lord going before us, we should incorporate into the work undertaken the power of the divine and abstract quaternity and its corresponding harmony [Col. 0614B].

BOOK ONE.

[Col. 0613]

HERE BEGIN THE CHAPTERS OF BOOK ONE.

I. On the divine quaternity.  
II. On King Rodulfus.  
III. On King Lotharius.  
IV. Which men afterward became emperors at Rome.  
V. On the attacks of the pagans.

CHAPTER ONE. On the divine quaternity.

[Col. 0613C]

God, the creator of all things, distinguished what he made by many figures and forms, so that through what the eyes see and the mind understands he might raise the educated person to the contemplation of the one Godhead. In investigating and learning these things, the Catholic fathers of the Greeks, who were moderately skilled in philosophy, first became renowned. Since their senses were trained in many matters, they were likewise practiced in contemplating certain quaternities, through which the present lower world and the world to come, the higher world, are understood.

When these quaternities, reflected back upon themselves, begin to be steadily unfolded by us, they render more alert both the minds and the understanding of those who contemplate them. There are therefore four Gospels, which establish the higher world in our minds. There are also four elements, which complete this lower world. There are likewise four virtues, which hold primacy over the others and, through our wonder at them, shape us toward the rest.

In the same way, there are four bodily senses besides touch, which serves the other, more subtle senses. What the fiery element of the aether is in the sensible world, prudence is in the intellectual world: rising upward and breathing eagerly with the desire to be near God.

What air is in the bodily world is likewise strength in the intellectual world. Air invigorates all living things and strengthens them, advancing them toward every action. In similar fashion, what water performs in the bodily world, temperance performs in the intellectual world. For temperance is the nurse of good things, bringing forth an abundance of virtues and preserving faith through the desire for divine love.

Earth likewise bears in the lower world the likeness that justice bears in the intellectual world—namely, a subsisting and immovable establishment of right distribution. In all things the spiritual correspondence of the Gospels is recognized as similar.

Thus the Gospel according to Matthew contains the mystical figure of earth, because it shows more openly than the others the substance of Christ’s flesh as man. That according to Mark represents temperance, which bears the likeness of water, since it moderately proclaims repentance beginning with John’s baptism. That according to Luke displays the likeness of air and strength, because it is widely diffused and strengthened by many histories. That according to John expresses distinctly the form of the fiery aether and prudence, and is shown to be higher than the others, since it introduces the simple knowledge and faith of God.

The human being is fittingly joined to these contemplative correspondences—of the elements, the virtues, and the Gospels—for these things were granted for his service. The Greek philosophers called the substance of his life μικρόκοσμον, that is, a small world.

Sight and hearing, which provide understanding and reason, correspond to the higher aether, which is subtler among the elements and, in proportion as it is higher than the others, more noble and luminous. Smell follows, expressing by its nature the significance of air and strength. Taste, quite appropriately, signifies equally water and temperance. Touch, the lowest of all and more solid and stable than the others, most fittingly displays the indication of earth and justice.

Through these clearest correspondences among things, God is openly, beautifully, and silently proclaimed. For while, by a stable movement, each successively indicates the other, they seek their principal origin by proclaiming the one from whom they proceeded, so that they may again rest in him [Col. 0615B].

It is also clear, in accordance with the agreement of the foregoing exposition, that the river flowing from Eden in the East and dividing into four most famous streams should be contemplated with a careful mind. The first of these, Phison, which is called “opening of the mouth,” signifies prudence, which is always diffused among the best things and is useful. Through sluggishness paradise was taken away from man; he must recover it with prudence going before him.

The second, Gihon, understood as “a cleft of the earth,” signifies temperance, the nurse of chastity, which healthfully uproots the foliage of vices. The third, the Tigris, inhabited by the Assyrians—who are interpreted as “those who direct”—likewise signifies strength, which, rejecting transgressive vices, directs men through God’s help toward the joys of the eternal kingdom [Col. 0615C]. The fourth, the Euphrates, whose name also conveys abundance, plainly designates justice, which feeds and refreshes every soul that loves it eagerly.

Since the significance of these rivers contains within itself the forms of the virtues mentioned above, as well as the figure of the four Gospels, the periods of this worldly age, divided into four parts, likewise represent these same virtues figuratively.

From the beginning of the world until the vengeance of the Flood, prudence flourished among those alone who, by loving their Creator in the simplicity of nature, recognized him—such as Abel, Enoch, and Noah, and the others who, endowed with the reasoning of the mind, understood what useful things they should do.

From Abraham onward, and among the other patriarchs who enjoyed signs and visions—Isaac, Jacob, Joseph, and the rest—temperance is shown to have been formed. In adversity and prosperity they loved their own Creator above all things.

From Moses and the other prophets, men of great strength and supported by the instruction of the legal commandments, strength was established, since they are shown to have diligently practiced the arduous precepts of the Law.

Finally, from the coming of the incarnate Word onward, justice fills and governs the whole age, surrounding it as the end and foundation of the other virtues, just as the Truth said to his Baptizer: “It is fitting for us,” he said, “to fulfill all righteousness.”

Since we are going to speak of the distinguished men in the Roman world who flourished from the year 900 of the incarnate Word, which creates and gives life to all things, down to our own time, insofar as we have learned them from reliable reports or have lived to see them ourselves; and since we shall also relate the events and many memorable things that occurred both in the holy churches and among both peoples, we first turn our pen to that principal empire of the whole world, namely the Roman Empire.

When the power of almighty Christ had bent the rulers of the earth beneath his rule, the terror of the Caesars declined all the more as their laws were more truly shown to have arisen from fear of ferocity than from love of pious humanity. Thus their entire stock gradually became separated from and emptied of the aforesaid empire, so that the city of Rome and its people needed their own rule more than they had once been accustomed to issue laws and rights to foreign peoples and citizens [Col. 0616B].

Then many of the nations whom Rome had previously subdued began to harass her with frequent attacks. Some kings of the surrounding provinces even seized and usurped the name of the empire. At that time the more powerful and exceedingly great kings of the Frankish people excelled in the justice of Christianity, as well as in the skill of arms and military strength. The entire height of imperial power was triumphantly attached to their rule for many years.

Among them shone most brilliantly Charles, called the Great, and Louis, surnamed the Pious. By wise counsel and courage they subdued under their own rule all the rebels around them, so that the Roman world seemed to serve their emperors as a single household. The commonwealth rejoiced more in the advancement of its ancestral rule than it was ostentatiously exalted by fear of emperors.

But since we have not undertaken to recount their deeds or their genealogy in historical fashion, we have taken care briefly to explain to what end their line came in its reign and empire. Kings from their stock continued to be emperors both in Italy and in Gaul, down to the last king, Charles surnamed the Simple (Hebes).

This king had among the chief men of his kingdom a certain Heribert, whose son he had received from the sacred font as godfather. Yet Heribert could certainly have become suspect to him through his own cunning, had not the hostility of a contrived deceit intervened.

When Heribert had decided to deceive the aforesaid king, pretending that he had an occasion for deliberating some matter, so that, as he later did, he might entice him into one of his castles and imprison him in chains, certain people finally advised the king to act with great caution lest he become entangled in Heribert’s tricks [Col. 0616D].

But when the king, believing what he had heard, decided to guard himself against Heribert, it happened one day that Heribert came very promptly to the king’s palace with his son. The king rose and offered him a kiss. Heribert, however, humbling his whole body, received the king’s kiss.

Then, when he had kissed Heribert’s son, the young man, though aware of the plot, was nevertheless inexperienced in cunning and repeatedly bowed before the king. His father, seeing him standing nearby, struck the young man forcefully on the neck and said: “Know henceforth that one must never approach an elder and a king to kiss them with the body held upright.”

When the king and all who were present saw this, they believed from then on that Heribert was free of any deception or fraud against the king. Seeing that the king was favorably disposed toward him, Heribert nevertheless pressed his request that the king come to him to deliberate the matter he had earlier proposed. The king immediately promised that he would go wherever Heribert wished.

On the appointed day the king came to the place Heribert had requested, bringing only a small army, out of friendship. On the first day Heribert received him with great pomp. On the second, however, as though by the king’s order, Heribert commanded all those who had come with the king [Col. 0617B] to return to their own homes, as though he and his men alone were sufficient to serve the king.

When they heard Heribert, they withdrew, unaware that they had left the king in chains. Heribert kept the aforesaid king imprisoned until the day of his death.

The king had also fathered a son named Louis, still a child. When Louis learned what had been done to his father, he fled, crossed the Ocean, and remained there until he reached manhood.

CHAPTER II. On King Rodulfus.

At that time Rodulfus, son of Richard, duke of Burgundy, was a man well formed in body and capable in understanding. He had also taken a wife named Emma, distinguished in judgment and appearance, the sister of Hugh the Great, whose military skill directed the kingdom of the Franks.

When Hugh saw that the kingdom was without a king and knew that its restoration depended upon his choice, he sent to his sister, asking her whom she would prefer to choose for the royal throne: himself, her brother, or rather her husband, the aforesaid Rodulfus.

She replied prudently, as she had been asked: she would rather kiss the knee of her husband the king than that of her brother. When Hugh heard this, he gladly agreed and granted Rodulfus the throne of the kingdom.

Rodulfus, having no children, died as the sole member of his line to possess the royal dignity. This Hugh was the son of Robert, count of Paris. Robert, having soon been made king, was killed by the Saxon army. We have postponed recording his lineage because it is found to be exceedingly obscure in earlier times.

CHAPTER III. On King Lotharius.

Meanwhile all the leading men of the kingdom elected Louis, the son of the aforesaid King Charles, anointing him as their king, destined to rule by hereditary right. The aforementioned Heribert had already died a cruel death.

For when, tormented by a divinely inflicted illness, he was approaching the end of his life and his people questioned him both about the salvation of his soul and about the disposition of his household, he answered absolutely nothing except this one statement [Col. 0618A]: “We were twelve who, by oath, consented to Charles’s betrayal.” Repeating this many times, he died.

Louis, moreover, fathered a son named Lotharius by Gerberga, formerly the wife of Duke Gislebert. When Lotharius had been confirmed in the kingdom, being agile in body, strong, and sound in understanding, he tried to restore the kingdom to its former condition.

For Otto, king of the Saxons—and indeed emperor of the Romans—had bent the upper part of that kingdom, also called the kingdom of Lotharius, toward his own kingdom, that is, toward the kingdom of the Saxons.

Lotharius once attempted to capture Otto, the second of that name, the son of the first and greatest Otto, while he was staying in the palace at Aachen. But certain people secretly warned Otto, and at night he scarcely managed to reach safety by flight with his wife [Col. 0618B].

Then Otto, having gathered an army of sixty thousand soldiers and more, entered France and came as far as Paris. After remaining there for three days, he began to return to Saxony. Lotharius, in turn, having gathered a military force from all France and Burgundy, pursued Otto’s army as far as the river Meuse, and many of those who were fleeing happened to perish in that river.

After this both sides ceased hostilities, with Lotharius failing to accomplish what he had desired. Lotharius fathered a son named Louis, whom, when he had grown into an adult young man, he made king so that he might reign after him.

He also brought him a wife from Aquitaine. When she saw that the young man was less capable than his father, she chose, with the cunning natural to her mind, to arrange a divorce. She deceitfully advised him that they should return together to Provence, from which she had come and which was subject to her by hereditary right [Col. 0618C].

Not understanding the woman’s cunning, he prepared to go as she had advised. When they arrived there, the woman abandoned him and joined her own people. When this was reported to his father, he pursued his son and brought him back to himself.

Afterward the two lived together, and after several years both died without leaving any children. In these two men, therefore, their royal or imperial line came to an end in ruling.

CHAPTER IV. Which men afterward became emperors at Rome.

When the line of the kings mentioned above had been exhausted, the kings of the Saxons assumed the Roman Empire. The first of them was Otto, son of Henry, king of the Saxons [Col. 0618D]. Hugh, duke of the Franks, surnamed the Great, had taken as his wife Otto’s sister, named Hadwig.

This Otto was not inferior in the glory and strength of his empire to those who had governed the empire before him. He was also very generous in expenditures for churches and almsgiving.

During his imperial reign the Saracens boldly came out from the regions of Africa, occupied the more secure places of the Alpine mountains, and, remaining there for some time while devastating the surrounding countryside, passed the time by plundering in various ways.

It happened at that time that the blessed father Maiolus, returning from Italy, encountered these same Saracens in the narrowest passes of the Alps. They seized him and carried him, together with all his companions, to more remote parts of the mountain. The father himself was seriously wounded in the hand when he voluntarily received upon it the blow of a spear aimed at one of his companions [Col. 0619A].

After dividing among themselves everything that belonged to him, they asked whether he possessed such resources in his homeland that he could ransom himself and his companions from their hands.

Then the man of God, distinguished by the dignity of complete courtesy, replied that he possessed nothing of his own in this world and did not wish to become the owner of any private property. He did not deny, however, that many people were held under his authority who were regarded as lords of extensive estates and sums of money.

When they heard this, the Saracens themselves urged him to send one of his men to bring them the price of his own ransom and that of his companions. They also specified the weight and amount of money, which was one thousand [Col. 0619B] pounds of silver, so that one pound might be allotted to each of them.

The holy man therefore sent one of his men to the monastery over which he presided, namely Cluny, with a brief letter reading as follows:

“To the lords and brothers of Cluny, Brother Maiolus, miserable and captive. The torrents of Belial have surrounded me; the snares of death have overtaken me. Now, if it pleases you, send a ransom for me and for those who have been captured with me.”

When this letter was delivered to the brothers of the aforesaid monastery, it caused them incomparable grief and mourning for his life, as well as deeply sorrowful news throughout the whole homeland. They sold whatever possessions were found among the furnishings and equipment of the entire monastery and quickly gathered the ransom prescribed for the pious father.

[Col. 0619C] Meanwhile, although the holy man was being held captive by the Saracens as a secular person, his merit could not remain hidden.

At mealtime they offered him the food on which they themselves fed—meat and very coarse bread—and said, “Eat.” He replied: “If I am hungry, it is the Lord’s task to feed me; nevertheless, I will not eat these things, because they have not been customary for me.”

One of them, seeing the reverence owed to the man of God, was moved by compassion. He stripped his arms and washed them, and, in the presence of the venerable Maiolus, prepared bread very cleanly on a shield. He cooked it immediately and brought it to him with the greatest reverence.

Maiolus received it, and, after first offering the customary prayer, refreshed himself with it and gave thanks to the Lord.

Another of those Saracens, after smoothing a small wooden shaft with a knife, placed his foot without hesitation upon the holy man’s book, namely the Bible, which Maiolus was accustomed to carry with him at all times.

When the holy man saw this, he groaned. Some of the less savage among them noticed what had happened and rebuked their companion, saying that great prophets ought not to be treated as worthless, so that their words were placed beneath someone’s foot.

For the Saracens read the prophets of the Hebrews, or rather of the Christians, and also said that whatever the sacred seers had foretold about Christ, Lord of all, had already been fulfilled in one of their own people, whom they called Muhammad.

To prove their error, they even possessed among themselves a genealogy corresponding, as they said, to that of Matthew’s Gospel, [Col. 0620A] which recounts the genealogy from Abraham to Christ, descending through the succession of Isaac. In his offspring the blessing promised and foretold for all peoples was given, as it says: “Ishmael fathered Nebaioth,” and thereafter it descends to their erroneous fiction, which is as far removed from the truth as it is foreign to sacred and catholic authority.
