Moreover, so that the holiness of blessed Maiolus might become manifest, the man who had trodden upon his book had his foot cut off that same day on some pretext, truly by the judgment of God, when the others furiously attacked him.

Many of them then began to become more gentle and reverent toward Maiolus.

Finally, some of the brothers returned there with all possible speed and, after giving the Saracens the money previously specified, brought the father back to his homeland together with only the men who had been captured with him [Col. 0620B].

Not long afterward, those same Saracens were surrounded at a place called Fraxinetus by the army of William, duke of Arles, and all of them perished shortly thereafter, so that not even one returned to his homeland.

At that time, therefore, the aforementioned Emperor Otto died, and his son, namely Otto II, succeeded him and assumed the same empire, which he governed with considerable vigor for as long as he lived. While he was reigning, the venerable Bishop Adalbert, from the province which in the language of the Slavs is called Bethem, and governing in the city of Braga the church of the holy martyr Vitisclodus, went out to the people of the Brusci to preach to them the word of salvation. After preaching extensively among them, and after many of them had been converted to the faith of Christ, he foretold his companions that in that same region he would receive the crown of martyrdom. At the same time, so that they would not be afraid, he informed them that, apart from himself, none of them would be killed there.

It happened one day that, at the bishop’s command, a profane tree situated beside a river—and to which the entire populace superstitiously offered sacrifices—was cut down and uprooted. An altar was then constructed and consecrated in the same place, and the bishop himself arranged the solemn celebration of Mass from among the people. While he was engaged in performing the sacred rites, he was pierced by the weapons of the impious; and when the sacred service had finally been completed, he also brought the present life to an end. His disciples then took the body of their lord and, carrying it with them, returned to their native land. Through his merits, even to the present, he bestows many benefits upon human beings.

In the following period, after many noble deeds had been accomplished and the commonwealth properly ordered, Otto died, leaving his son Otto III, who was still a boy of almost twelve years. Though still very young, he was vigorous in strength and intelligence; by hereditary right he assumed the government of the empire.

At the beginning of his reign, it happened that the apostolic see of the city of Rome was vacant, lacking a pontiff. He immediately employed imperial authority, chose a certain kinsman of his own, the son of a duke, and ordered him to be elevated to the apostolic see according to custom. When this had been carried out without delay, it became the occasion of a very great calamity.

There was a certain Crescentius, a powerful Roman citizen, who—as is the custom of such men—the greater his burden of money, the more readily he served avarice. As events proved, he did not openly favor Otto’s party. For he expelled from the see the very pontiff whom, as we have said, Otto had ordered to be ordained, stripping him of every honor, and insolently installed another in his place.

But as soon as Otto learned of this [act], he was inflamed with anger and hastened to Rome with a very large army. When Crescentius learned that Otto was approaching the city, he climbed with his men into a tower situated outside the city across the Tiber. Because of its height, it was called Intercoelos—“Among the Heavens”—and he fortified it in order to defend his life.

When the emperor reached the city, he first ordered the capture of that ill-secured pontiff who had been established through Crescentius’s arrogance. Once he had been captured, Otto ordered that his hands, as though sacrilegious, be cut off, and then that his ears be severed and his eyes torn out [perhaps: “plucked out”].

Afterward, learning that Crescentius, as we have said, was fortified in the tower—which shortly thereafter was to deliver him over to a cruel death—he ordered the tower to be surrounded by a dense siege of his army, so that Crescentius would in no way be given a place of refuge. Meanwhile, at the emperor’s command, machines were constructed all around from the wood of tall fir trees, assembled with extraordinary skill.

When Crescentius saw that he could find no way of escape, he at last—though belatedly—devised a plan of repentance. Yet this did not win him an opportunity for mercy. One day, with certain men from the imperial army consenting, Crescentius secretly left the tower, dressed in a cloak and with his head covered. Coming unexpectedly, he fell at the emperor’s feet and begged that his life be spared through the emperor’s mercy.

When the emperor looked at him, he turned to his men and, being in a bitter mood, said:

“Why,” he said, “do you allow the prince of the Romans, the author of imperial decrees, the giver of laws, and the appointing authority of pontiffs, to enter the huts of the Saxons? Now take him back to the throne of his eminence, until we prepare for his honor an appropriate reception.”

They took him, therefore, as they had been ordered, and brought him back unharmed to the entrance of the tower. Once he had entered, he informed those who were shut in there with him that they would live only as long as the tower was able to protect them from capture by the enemy, and that they should no longer hope for any safety at all.

Meanwhile, the imperial army pressed forward from outside, driving the siege engines, and little by little they were brought up against the tower. Battle was then joined. Some fought to enter from above, while others burst through to the doorway of the tower and, sitting upon it, tore it away; then, advancing upward in competition, they reached the upper parts of the tower.

Crescentius looked back and saw that he was being held by those whom he had thought could be kept at a greater distance by fighting. After he himself had been captured and gravely wounded, and the others who had been found with him had been slaughtered, the soldiers sent to the emperor to ask what he should order concerning him.

He replied: “Throw him openly from the upper battlements, lest the Romans say that we stole away their prince.”

They threw him down as ordered. Then, after tying him behind oxen and dragging him for a great distance through the marshes and along the roads, they finally left him hanging from a high beam in sight of the city.

When these things had been done, the emperor summoned Gerbert, the archbishop of Ravenna, and appointed him chief pontiff of the Romans. This Gerbert was originally from Gaul. He belonged to a lesser lineage, but was extremely sharp-witted and thoroughly trained in the studies of the liberal arts. He had also previously been appointed pontiff of Rheims by Hugh, king of the Franks.

But because, as we have said, he was highly intelligent and prudent, and understood that Arnulf, archbishop of that same city—while Arnulf was still living, Gerbert had been ordained there with the consent of that same king—was striving to be restored to his former see, he cautiously set out and came to the aforementioned Otto. Otto received him with great honor and immediately elevated him at Ravenna and thereafter, as we have said, appointed him pontiff of the city of Rome.

At that time it happened that the same emperor, urged by that pontiff and by various others who were zealous for the advancement of religion and for the house of God, decided that those who were called monks only in name in the Church of Saint Paul, but who otherwise lived wickedly, ought to be expelled from it. In their place he was to install members of another institution, namely those whom we call canons, who would serve in that same place, as he had been advised.

When he was intent on carrying out this decree, the most blessed apostle Paul appeared to him in a dream at night and undertook to admonish the emperor in these words:

“If zeal for divine service truly burns within you for the sake of a good work, beware of presuming to alter this institution by expelling the monks. It is not at all expedient ever to cast aside or alter the proper institution of any ecclesiastical order, even if it has been corrupted in part. For each person must be judged according to the order in which he first vowed to serve God. Yet anyone who has become corrupt may be corrected within the same sphere of his proper vocation.”

Thus admonished, the emperor reported to his men what he had heard from the Apostle, and took care to consider how he might reform the institution of those same men, namely the monks, for the better, rather than expelling them from the place or altering it.

Meanwhile, following an ill-advised course, he took as his wife [a woman] of the aforementioned Crescentius John; shortly afterward, he divorced and dismissed her, just as thoughtlessly as he had married her. At last, while attempting to return to Saxony, he died in Italy when death overtook him.

When the army that he had brought with him saw that it had been deprived of its lord, they united themselves into a single column so that they would not be slaughtered by those whom they had oppressed in Italy. They placed the dead emperor’s body on a horse before them. Thus reaching their homeland safely, they buried him honorably at Aachen, in the monastery of the ever-blessed Virgin Mary.

After Otto III, therefore, the kingdom of the Saxons was assumed by his kinsman Henry, who, although not [lord] of his own kingdom, became emperor of the Romans.

Meanwhile, it is fitting to recall in part the successive disasters by which, during the times of the aforementioned kings, the Roman world was subsequently scourged, both by external and by internal enemies. It is clear from earlier history that the principal empire of the whole world had been divided, so that, just as Rome was to hold the primacy of the entire Latin world, Constantinople was both the particular head of the Greeks in the transmarine regions of the East and the head of the others.

But once it had learned to divide itself within itself, each part gradually learned thereafter to diminish, until the one was severely constricted by wars and became smaller, while the other sought to be governed by a foreigner. And since it more often happened that such men ruled by tyranny than by generous piety or by hereditary descent, it was fitting that the insolence of such rulers, together with their subjects, should be worn down by repeated blows of oppression.

## CHAPTER V. On the blows inflicted by the pagans

Around the nine-hundredth year of the incarnate Word, the Saracen king Algalif left Spain and came with a very large army into Italy, intending to hand over human affairs with his men as spoil, to be destroyed by sword and fire. When he arrived, he ravaged the whole region and advanced as far as Beneventum.

The leading men of only some of the cities of Italy assembled their forces and attempted to engage the aforementioned Algalif in battle. But when they saw that they were greatly outnumbered, they sought refuge in flight rather than in war—as is very often the custom of these modern Italians.

Meanwhile, the Saracens returned with their prince to Africa. From that time onward they did not cease attacking the region of Italy, although they had been challenged in many battles both by emperors and by the leaders and margraves of the country, down to their prince Altmuzor and the aforementioned Henry, emperor of the Romans.

At the aforementioned time, an equally great disaster befell the peoples of Gaul through the attacks of the enemy, namely the Normans. They received this name because, driven out at first by a love of plunder, they boldly set out from the northern regions and sought the western land. In their own language, indeed, *Nort* means “north wind,” while *Mint* means “people.” Hence they are called Normans, as though “northern people.”

At their first departure they lived for a long time near the Ocean Sea, content with meager wages, until they united into a considerable people. Later, traversing broad stretches of land and sea with hostile force, they reduced certain cities and provinces to their own lot.

As time went on, a certain man arose in the district of Troyes, from the lowest class of peasants. His name was Astingus, and he was from a village called Tranquillus, three miles distant from the city. As a young man, he was strong in bodily power but of a perverse character. In his pride he cast aside the lot of his impoverished parents and chose to live in exile, overcome by the desire to rule.

He secretly went out to the aforementioned Norman people and at first attached himself only to those who, devoted to continual plunder, supplied food for the others. They commonly call these men the Flotta. After serving this wicked way of life for some time, he began to surpass his evil companions in diligence precisely as he became more criminal.

Little by little he became stronger than the others in bodily power and possessions, and they all together made him their leader on land and sea. Once established in this position, he assumed still greater cruelty, disregarded the savagery of the past, and began to extend his sword into distant provinces.

Later, he set out with nearly the entire people over whom he ruled toward the upper regions of Gaul, although he was a pestilential parent who was wickedly seeking to revisit his native soil. When he arrived, he destroyed everything with sword and fire beyond all the devastation inflicted by enemies. Since no one resisted, he consumed the land for a long time.

At that time, all the houses of the churches throughout Gaul, except those preserved by the municipalities of cities or fortresses, were utterly dishonored and burned with fire. After traversing all Gaul and obtaining rich spoils of various kinds, he led his army back to its own country.

Thus, for nearly a hundred years, disasters of this kind were inflicted far and wide upon the peoples of Gaul, both by Astingus himself and by his successors, the leaders of that people.

The events we have recounted also occurred repeatedly, at intervals following the deaths of kings or emperors, both in Italy and in Gaul, before they were restored. But when the army of the aforementioned people later resolved, according to its custom, to advance into Gaul, the venerable Duke Richard of Burgundy—namely the father of King Rudolf, as we mentioned above—met them when they were already far removed from their native soil.

He engaged them in battle and struck them down with such slaughter that scarcely any of them escaped by flight and managed to return home. Although afterward the same Normans ravaged many islands and provinces adjoining the sea, they did not thereafter enter the regions governed by the lot of the Frankish kings unless summoned by those same kings.

Indeed, shortly afterward many Franks and Burgundians in turn entered peacefully into marriages with the aforementioned Normans, who had now become worshipers of the Catholic faith, and by common agreement resolved that they should be called and should be one kingdom under one king.

From them arose the most excellent dukes: William, and after him all those called Richard by paternal or ancestral right. The capital of their duchy was the city of Rouen.

Since the aforementioned dukes excelled above others in the weapons of warfare, they were likewise superior to others in the grace of common peace and in the virtue of generosity. For every province that happened to be subject to their rule lived in concord, as though it were the household or family of a single kindred, preserving unviolated faith.

Among them, anyone who in any transaction took more than was justly due, or falsely claimed that something was for sale and took it away from another, was regarded as a thief and robber. They also maintained constant care for all the needy, poor, and foreigners, like parents caring for their children.

They sent very generous gifts to holy churches throughout almost the entire world. Thus, even from the East—from the renowned mountain of Sinai—monks came to Rouen every year, returning to their own people with many gifts of gold and silver that they had received from the aforementioned princes.

Richard II sent one hundred pounds of gold to Jerusalem, to the tomb of the Savior, and assisted with immense gifts anyone who wished to make the journey there devoutly.

Moreover, during the succession of the aforementioned periods, through the fault of sinful people, discord arose between two kings, namely the Frankish and the Saxon. As this discord continued to burn for a long time, by the hidden judgment of God a terrible scourge again fell upon the peoples of Gaul.

The prince of the Hungarians, with the entire military force of that people, taking advantage of the evil occasion provided by this discord, invaded the borders of Gaul. Once and again he miserably ravaged the whole region, capturing persons of both sexes and carrying them away together with their possessions, plundering without anyone resisting.

This disaster raged until, through God’s favor, the princes of both kingdoms—the Frankish and the Saxon—were bound together by the bond of one faith and kinship.

When the line of the earlier kings had been exhausted and the quarrels had been quieted, the world began to flourish again under the peace of new kings, and the kingdom of Christ began, through the font of holy baptism, to subjugate tyrants to itself everywhere.

The Hungarian people itself, after committing so many crimes and inflicting so many scourges upon other peoples, was converted with its king to the Catholic faith. Those who had previously been accustomed to seize the property of others with cruelty now willingly distributed their own possessions for Christ. Those Christians whom they had once captured by plunder and sold wherever they were found to be dragged away as miserable slaves are now cherished by the same people as brothers or free persons.

It also seems exceedingly fitting and honorable, and an excellent provision for the preservation of peace, that no prince should rashly seek to bear the scepter of the Roman Empire, or be able to be called or be emperor, unless the pope of the Roman see has judged him suitable for the commonwealth and entrusted him with the imperial insignia.

For formerly, tyrants of every kind, impelling themselves forward insolently, were very often made emperors; and they were all the less suited to the commonwealth because it is clear that they advanced through tyranny rather than through the authority of piety.

In the year 710 of the Lord’s incarnation, although that imperial insignia had previously been represented in various forms, the venerable Pope Benedict nevertheless ordered that the same insignia of the imperial office be made in a highly intelligible form.

He ordered a golden orb to be fashioned, surrounded in a square with the most precious gems, and a golden cross to be inserted above it. It was made in the likeness of the form of the structure of this world, which is said to stand enclosed in a kind of roundness. Thus, whenever the prince of the earthly empire looked upon it, it would serve him as a lesson that he ought not to rule or wage war in the world except in such a way that he might be considered worthy to protect the banner of the life-giving cross.

In the adornment of the various gems, it was likewise signified that the summit of the empire ought to be adorned with the forms of many virtues.

When the aforementioned pope later came forth according to custom with a very large multitude of men and members of the sacred orders to meet the emperor Henry, who had come to Rome for this purpose, and when he had handed him this imperial insignia in the sight of the entire Roman people, Henry received it joyfully. After examining it, as he was an exceedingly perceptive man, he said:

“Excellent father,” he said to the pope, “by deciding to make this, and by implying what form our monarchy ought to take, you have taught us most carefully how it should govern itself.”

Then, holding the golden orb in his hand, he added:

“No one is more fittingly entitled to possess and contemplate this present gift than those who, having trampled underfoot the pomp of the world, follow the Savior’s cross with greater freedom.”

He immediately sent it to the monastery of Cluny in Gaul, which at that time was considered the most religious of all the others; he had also bestowed upon it many other gifts of ornament.

But this too must certainly be considered: although, as we have related, it has very often happened that the conversion of unbelieving peoples to the faith of Christ has taken place externally in the northern and western regions of the world, nowhere is anything of this kind heard to occur in the eastern and southern regions of that same world.

The clearest indication of this prophecy was that arrangement of the Lord’s cross when the Savior hung upon it at the place of Calvary. For when the savage East had previously hung behind the crown of his head, so to speak, and had been exceedingly harsh toward peoples, the West stood before his eyes, destined to be filled with the light of faith.

Thus the North, mild through faith in the sacred word, received his almighty right hand extended toward the work of mercy, while the South obtained his left hand among the tumultuous nations of the barbarians.

Although we have briefly recalled this sacred sign, the inviolable support of our faith—namely, the Catholic faith—nevertheless remains that, in every place and among every people without exception, whoever has been reborn in the sacred font, believing equally in the almighty Father, in his Son Jesus Christ, and in the Holy Spirit, one and only true God, will have any good deed performed in faith accepted by God, and everyone who perseveres in this way will live blessedly in everlasting life.

For it belongs to God alone to know why the human race becomes more or less capable of its own salvation in different regions of the world.

We have related these things for this reason: the Gospel of Christ the Lord, reaching even to the borders of the two aforementioned regions of the world—namely, the northern and western—established the peoples of those regions firmly upon the foundation of holy faith. By contrast, it has penetrated less deeply into the other two regions, namely the eastern and southern, and has found their peoples more tightly ensnared in the savagery of their own error.

But lest anyone therefore bring an insulting accusation against the dispensation of the good Creator in this matter, the sacred canon of the Scriptures must nevertheless be examined with greater care. In that canon, without any doubt, the whole pattern of the worldly age is expressed, so that the goodness and justice of its author may equally be demonstrated, both in those who are saved and in those who perish.

For just as the first father of the human race had initially been established by the author of all goodness as the arbiter of his own salvation, so salvation was generally offered by the same Redeemer to all according to their capacity for receiving it.

Yet his hidden dispensation—before which everything that existed was always and simultaneously present, and to which nothing was lacking—revealed himself gradually through the successive growth of the ages as the omnipotent, solely good, and truthful one, both through works of mercy and through the punishment of just retribution.

For the principal goodness is never without a work of mercy; indeed, it continually gathers many from the mass of the children of the transgressor into the bosom of the Son of his divinity. Since this is accomplished daily in the world, what else is shown to be at work than the goodness of the Almighty—immutably moving and movably immutable?

For this reason, the nearer the end of the present age approaches, the more frequently these things that are described come to pass.

One must also consider how, gradually from the very beginning of the human race, knowledge of its author was manifested. The first of human beings, Adam, together with all his descendants, proclaims God as his creator when, deprived of the joys of paradise through the guilt of transgressing his command and punished with exile, he cries out in mourning that he is wretched.

But as the human race increased and spread more broadly throughout the whole world, unless the providence of the goodness of its own creator had brought it back into the embrace of mercy, that entire race would long ago have been irreversibly plunged into the precipice of its own error and blindness.

Therefore, from its beginning, through the divine dispensation of the good Creator, miraculous marvels of events and portentous signs of the elements were brought forth for it, as well as divinely given oracles intended to instill both hope and fear through the wisest of men.

And just as that same Creator completed all the works of the world’s structure by bringing them forth over the course of six days, and rested after producing them, namely on the seventh day, so he worked throughout the span of six thousand years, displaying frequent and notable signs for the instruction of human beings.

Thus, throughout the past ages, no period was left entirely empty of these signs of miracles proclaiming the eternal God, until that greatest beginning of all things appeared in the world clothed as a human being.

This occurred in the sixth age of the present world; and, as is believed, its end will be in the seventh age of this worldly structure and its various labors, so that from the one in whom whatever came into being received its beginning, it may also find in him the most fitting end of its own rest.

[Col. 0628C] **THE FIRST BOOK ENDS.**

## THE SECOND BOOK

[Col. 0627]

## THE CHAPTERS OF THE SECOND BOOK BEGIN

I. On the election of Hugh as king.  
II. On the sea monster and the wars of the West.  
III. On Conan, duke of the Britons, and Fulk of Anjou.  
IV. On the monastery of Lucca.  
V. On the remarkable portent of the city of Orléans.  
VI. On the offices seized for sordid profit.  
VII. On the fires and deaths of nobles.  
VIII. On the death of Duke Henry and the devastation of Burgundy.  
IX. On severe famine and the attacks of the Saracens.  
X. On the raining of stones.  
XI. On Leutard, the heretic who went mad.  
XII. On the heresy discovered in Italy.

## CHAPTER I. On the election of Hugh as king

[Col. 0627D]

Just as someone traveling through any exceedingly vast region of the world, or penetrating a broad expanse of sea by rowing, often directs the gaze of his eyes toward the height of mountains or the loftiness of trees, so that, recognizing them from afar, he may reach without error the place toward which he had set out, so it also happens with us. When we wish to reveal past events to those of the future, we frequently extend the gaze of our speech and our mind toward the persons of great men, so that the account may thereby become clearer and appear more certain.

Therefore, when, as we have said, the line of great kings who had reigned and ruled in Italy and Gaul had come to an end—namely, Louis, Charles, and the other kings of his lineage—the monarchy of both kingdoms immediately passed to men of a single kindred.

For how Otto I, Otto II, and Otto III possessed the Roman Empire, down to the empire of Henry, we remember having already set out above. Now it remains for us to relate how the kingdom of the Franks was thereafter arranged.

When Kings Lothair and Louis had died, the government of the entire kingdom of France fell to Hugh, son of the duke of Paris—namely, that great Hugh whom we mentioned above. His brother was also the most noble Henry, duke of Burgundy.

Together with all the leading men of the kingdom, they appropriately had the aforementioned Hugh anointed king. As we have already recalled, they were related by kinship to the kings of the Saxons, beginning with Otto I, who was born from the sister of Great Hugh.

[Note: Rather, the wife of Great Hugh was the sister of Otto I.]

After Hugh had assumed the government of the Frankish kingdom, he soon perceived that many of his subjects—whom he had previously held under his authority everywhere—had become rebellious. Nevertheless, being vigorous in body and mind, he gradually subdued all who rebelled against him.

He had a son of great prudence named Robert, who was also highly educated in literary studies. When Hugh realized that his strength was already failing somewhat, he gathered in the royal city of Orléans the leading men of the Frankish and Burgundian kingdoms and, while he was still alive, made that same Robert, his son, king—in the thirteenth year before the thousandth year of the incarnate Savior.

After several years, King Hugh himself also died peacefully and happily, having laid aside the kingdom. At that time, as we have said, King Robert was still a young man, prudent and learned, distinguished for his eloquence and piety.

But through the merciful providence of God, the Lord of all things deemed it fitting at that particular time to appoint such a man to govern the Catholic people. For during his reign, with signs in the elements preceding them, no small disasters descended upon the Church of Christ. Unless that same king had wisely resisted them with God’s help, they would have advanced far into the future while multiplying their ravages.

## CHAPTER II. On the sea monster and the wars of the West

In the fourth year of the aforementioned thousand, a whale of extraordinary size was seen to have come down through the sea at a place called Bernovallis, proceeding from the northern region toward the West.

It appeared in the month of November, one morning at the first light of dawn, resembling an island. As it passed by, lasting until the third hour of the day, it caused the greatest astonishment and wonder among those who saw it.

And lest anyone perhaps doubt the account, although it was seen by many, a monster similar to this one is also found described by several writers.

For it is read in the deeds of the distinguished confessor Bendanus—of the eastern Angles, that is—that the same man of God, Bendanus, after spending some time living as a hermit among the islands of the sea with several monks, once encountered this beast or one like it.

As he was rowing around various islands situated in the sea, twilight came on. Seeing in the distance what appeared to be a maritime island, he turned toward it with all who were with him, intending merely to spend the coming night there.

When they had arrived, they came out of their small boats and climbed onto the swelling back of the beast, intending to spend only one night there as guests. After a brief supper, the other brothers gave their weary limbs over to rest. Only the man of the Lord, Bendanus, the ever-watchful guardian of the Lord’s flock and more constant than the others in singing psalms, carefully observed the force of the winds and the courses of the stars.

While he was doing this attentively in the silence of the night, he suddenly realized that the promontory toward which they had turned for lodging was carrying them toward the eastern region.

When daylight returned on the following day, the most diligent man summoned his companions who were present, gently exhorting and consoling them, and said:

“Most kindly brothers, let us offer tireless thanks to God, the creator and governor of all things, who in his providence has prepared for us, amid these sea waves, a vehicle requiring no human rowing.”

When the companions heard these words from the man of God, they were overcome with astonishment of mind. Immediately entrusting themselves to divine providence and relying upon the wisdom of the holy man, they began to await the outcome of this chance event with greater confidence.

For many days they continually saw themselves being carried—not by any propulsion of their own—toward the rising sun.

At last they reached an island more beautiful than the others and endowed with every delight. The arrangement of its trees and the variety of its birds were unlike those of all other places.

A worldly man who went ashore and approached it found there remarkable and numerous gatherings of monks, or rather anchorites, whose life and conduct shone forth as holier and nobler than the pursuits of all mortal beings.

They received the travelers with great charity. After remaining there for several days and being carefully instructed in many matters pertaining to true salvation, they eventually returned to their native land and recounted to their countrymen everything they had discovered.

Moreover, after the portent of the Ocean that we began to describe had been seen, warlike tumult arose throughout the entire western region of the world, both in the lands of Gaul and in the transmarine islands of the Ocean—namely, among the Angles, Britons, and Scots.

For, as often happens, because of the sins of the lowly people, their kings and other princes were turned to discord. Immediately they began to blaze forth in the devastation of the people subject to them, until they were driven even to the shedding of their own blood.

This continued for so long in the aforementioned islands that one of their kings alone came to possess the rule of the others by force.

After King Adalrad died, among those who are called Danes—he had married the sister of Richard, duke of Rouen—their kingdom was invaded by King Canuc of the western Angles.

After repeated efforts at war and the devastation of the country, Canuc established a pact with Richard and married Adalrad’s sister, thereby holding the monarchy of both kingdoms.

After this, the same Canuc set out with a very large army to subjugate the Scottish people. Their king was named Melculo, a man strong in power and arms and, most importantly, most Christian in faith and conduct.

When Melculo learned that Canuc was boldly seeking to invade his kingdom, he gathered the entire army of his people and powerfully resisted him, preventing him from succeeding.

Canuc continued for a long time to pursue such insolent quarrels, but at last, persuaded by the aforementioned Richard, duke of Rouen, and by Richard’s sister, he completely laid aside his ferocity for the love of God, became gentle, and lived in peace.

Moreover, he cherished the king of the Scots as a friend and received his son from the sacred font of baptism.

From that time it began to happen that, whenever a hostile emergency weighed upon the duke of Rouen, he obtained a large army from the transmarine islands for his assistance.

Thus the Norman people and the peoples of the aforementioned islands lived for a long time in the security of the most faithful peace, so that they themselves frightened many peoples of foreign provinces through fear of their power, rather than being frightened by others.

Nor is this surprising, since, once discord—the destroyer of good things—had been expelled from them through fear of God, the noble kingdom of Christ, preceded by peace, happily held its triumph among them.

## CHAPTER III. On Conan, duke of the Britons, and Fulk of Anjou
Therefore, during the period of the aforementioned days, tumult from civil wars nevertheless raged in the lowest parts of Gaul. [Col. 0631C] Many who discuss the configuration of the world assert that the region of Gaul is laid out in a quadrangular shape. Although, from the Riphaean Mountains to the boundaries of Spain, with the Ocean Sea on the left and the Alpine ranges extending here and there on the right, its length exceeds the measure of a four-sided figure, its lower and correspondingly most insignificant corner is nevertheless called the corner of Gaul. Its principal city is Rennes. It has also long been inhabited by the people of the Britons, whose only riches in former times were freedom from the public fisc and an abundance of milk. Entirely devoid of civilized refinement, they have uncultivated manners, a quick temper, and foolish loquacity.

Among these Britons there was once [Col. 0631D] a prince named Conan, who, after marrying the sister of Fulk, count of Anjou, eventually began to be more insolent than the other princes of his people. For, having placed a diadem upon his head in royal fashion, he exercised an immense tyranny recklessly over the people of his corner of the world.

Afterward an irreconcilable quarrel arose between this Conan and the aforementioned Fulk, count of Anjou. Harassing each other with repeated devastations and bloodshed, they finally engaged in close combat—civil though it was, yet unavoidable. After they had inflicted upon one another for a long time every evil they could, both decreed that at a place called Concretus [Col. 0632A], each arriving with his army on the appointed day, they would enter into battle.

The army of the Britons, having devised a treacherous trap, wickedly overthrew part of Fulk’s army. At the aforementioned place, where the battle was to be fought, the Britons arrived secretly beforehand and, with great cunning, dug there a deep and very long ditch. They densely covered it with tree branches, thus laying a snare for their enemies, and withdrew.

On the appointed day, in accordance with the agreement, when each side arrived there with its army and both battle lines appeared already prepared, the crafty people of the Britons, conscious of their own deceit, pretended that they wished to flee, so that they might plunge the enemy more eagerly into the hidden trap.

[Col. 0632B] When Fulk’s army saw this and desired to rush upon them swiftly, a considerable part of it fell into the pit that the Britons had contrived by their cunning. Immediately, however, the Britons who had earlier pretended to flee turned back and, rushing eagerly upon Fulk’s army, struck down many of them in an exceedingly savage slaughter. They even knocked Fulk, thrown from his horse, to the ground in his armor.

Rising, inflamed with immense fury, he encouraged and sharpened the spirits of his men with his words. Then, driving forward like a most violent whirlwind through dense grainfields, they slaughtered the entire army of the Britons in a brutally savage massacre. After almost the whole British army had been destroyed, they also captured Conan, their prince, alive, with his right hand severed, and handed him over to Fulk. Having won [Col. 0632C] the victory, Fulk returned to his own lands; afterward no Briton troubled him.

## CHAPTER IV. On the monastery of Lucacense

Much could have been said about the many deeds of that same Fulk, but, avoiding tediousness, we have passed them over in silence. One memorable matter, however, remains, which we shall now relate.

Since he had shed a great deal of human blood in various outcomes of battle throughout the surrounding regions, he was terrified by fear of Gehenna and went to the tomb of the Savior in Jerusalem. Returning from there—as he was exceedingly bold—with great exultation, he was made somewhat gentler in his accustomed ferocity for a short time.

Then he conceived the plan of building a church [Col. 0632D] at the finest site among his own estates and of gathering there a community of monks who would intercede day and night for the redemption of his soul. As he always acted with careful inquiry, he began asking various religious men in whose particular memory of the saints he ought to found this church, so that they might pray to the almighty Lord for the remedy of his soul.

Among others, his own wife, who possessed very sound judgment, suggested to him that he should fulfill the vow he had made in honor and memory of those heavenly powers whom sacred authority testifies to be higher—the cherubim and seraphim. He readily agreed and built a very beautiful church in the district of Tours, at a distance of one mile from the fortress of Lucacense.

As soon as the work on the basilica had been completed [Col. 0633A], he immediately sent to Hugh, archbishop of Tours, in whose diocese it had been established, asking him to come and consecrate it as he had decided. Hugh delayed coming, saying that he could in no way commit Fulk’s vow to the Lord by consecrating it, since Fulk had taken away no small number of estates and dependents belonging to the mother Church of the see entrusted to him.

Rather, Hugh said, it was appropriate that Fulk should first restore to someone whatever he had unjustly seized, and that only then should he offer to God, the just judge, his own possessions which he had vowed.

When these words were reported to Fulk by his men, his long-standing ferocity returned. Taking the bishop’s reply with extreme indignation, he threatened him severely and compelled him by every means at his disposal to accept his more powerful judgment.

Immediately [Col. 0633B] afterward, taking a large sum of silver and gold, he went to Rome and explained to Pope John the reason for his journey. Then, asking him for what he desired, he presented him with many gifts. The pope at once sent with Fulk to consecrate the aforementioned basilica one of those whom the Church of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, calls cardinals, a man named Peter. He also ordered him, as though acting with the authority of the Roman pontiff, to carry out fearlessly whatever seemed necessary to Fulk.

When the bishops of Gaul heard this, they recognized that the sacrilegious presumption had arisen from blind greed: one man was seizing, while another was accepting what had been seized, and they had thereby recently created a schism in the Roman Church. All alike detested it [Col. 0633C], since it seemed utterly unbecoming that the man who governed the apostolic see should be the first to transgress the apostolic and canonical rule.

Moreover, ancient authority has repeatedly confirmed that no bishop may presume to exercise such an act in another bishop’s diocese unless the bishop to whom it belongs compels or permits him to do so.

One day in the month of May, therefore, an innumerable crowd gathered for the dedication of the aforementioned church. Fulk’s terror, because of the pomp of his pride, compelled an even greater multitude to assemble there. Only those bishops who were oppressed by his power were forced to attend.

When the appointed day arrived, the dedication was begun and completed with considerable pomp, and the solemn celebrations of the Mass were performed according to custom. afterward everyone returned to his own place.

At the ninth [Col. 0633D] hour of that day, while the sky remained serene everywhere under gentle breezes, a very violent whirlwind suddenly arose from the southern quarter. It struck the church, filled it with turbulent air, and shook it violently for a long time. Then, when the ceilings had been torn apart, all the beams of the church, together with its entire roof covering, fell to the ground through the western pinnacle of the temple and were overturned.

When many throughout the region learned what had happened, no one doubted that the audacious insolence of presumption had rendered the vow void. At the same time, this was an evident warning to all present and future generations not to do anything similar.

Although the pontiff [Col. 0634A] of the Roman Church is held in greater reverence than the other bishops established throughout the world because of the dignity of the apostolic see, he is nevertheless not permitted to transgress in any respect the bounds of canonical regulation. For just as every bishop and bridegroom of the orthodox Church bears, in the same way, the likeness of the Savior in his own see, so it is generally proper for no one to act insolently in another bishop’s diocese.

## CHAPTER V. On the marvelous portent of the city of Orléans

In the year 888 of the incarnation of the Word, a highly memorable and terrifying portent occurred in the Gallic city of Orléans.

It is known that in that city there was an ancient monastery established in honor of the prince of the apostles, in which a community of consecrated virgins is known to have first served the almighty God. Since then it has also been called by the surname “the Girls’ Monastery.” In the middle of this monastery stood fixed a banner of the cross, bearing an image of the Savior himself, who suffered death for the salvation of humanity.

From the eyes of that image [Col. 0634B], for several days continuously and in the sight of many people, a stream of tears flowed. An immense crowd of people gathered to witness this terrifying spectacle. Many of them, when they saw it, carefully recognized it as a divine portent—namely, of the calamity about to come upon that city.

For just as the Savior himself, foreseeing the coming destruction of the city of Jerusalem [Col. 0634C], is said to have wept for it, so this image of him is proved to have wept, by an unmistakable representation, for the disaster that was shortly afterward to overtake Orléans.

A little later, therefore, an unprecedented event occurred in the same city, portending, as was believed, that very thing. One night the guards of the great church—the episcopal church—rose according to custom and opened its doors to those hurrying to the morning praises. Suddenly a wolf appeared, entered the church, seized the bell rope in its mouth, and, shaking it, caused the bell to sound.

Those who were present, struck with astonishment, finally raised a cry and, as unarmed men, drove it out of the church by every effort they could make. In the following year, the entire human habitation of that city, together with the houses of the churches, was dreadfully consumed by fire.

Thus no one doubted that the portent of the two events had preceded the occurrence of a single calamity.

At that time [Col. 0634D] the venerable Arnulfus was bishop of the aforementioned city. Noble both by birth and by his learned wisdom, and exceedingly wealthy from the revenues of his ancestral estates, he saw the destruction of his own see and the desolation of the people entrusted to him. Following better counsel and gathering a great supply of materials, he began continually to rebuild from the foundations the great church, which had formerly been dedicated in honor of the cross of Christ.

While he and all his men devoted themselves most vigorously to the work he had begun, so that it might be completed as quickly and as honorably as possible, divine assistance was very clearly granted to him.

One day [Col. 0635A], while the masons were examining the solidity of the earth in order to lay the foundations of the basilica, they discovered a large quantity of gold. It was certainly believed sufficient to restore the entire basilica, however large it might be.

Those who had found the gold by chance took it and delivered it intact to the bishop. Giving thanks to almighty God for the gift bestowed upon him, he accepted it, entrusted it to the overseers of the work, and ordered that it all be faithfully expended on the construction of that church.

It is said that this gold had also been hidden there for the purpose of restoring the church through the foresight of the blessed Evurtius, an ancient bishop of that see. This is especially plausible because, when that holy man once rebuilt the same church in a better form than it had originally possessed, he too happened to discover there a similar gift divinely reserved for him.

Thus it also came to pass [Col. 0635B] that the episcopal residence—the house of the church, that is—was rebuilt more elegantly than before. At the bishop’s urging, the buildings of the other basilicas in the same city, which had perished and were dedicated to the merits of various saints, were made better than their predecessors, and the observance of the divine offices in them was held in greater honor than anywhere else.

The city itself was soon filled again with buildings, and its people, relieved of their sins and aided by the Lord’s mercy, recovered all the more quickly because they had wisely accepted their own calamity as a punishment intended for correction.

That city had been [Col. 0635C] from ancient times, as it remains today, the principal royal seat of the kings of the Franks, on account of its beauty, the multitude of its inhabitants, the fertility of its soil, and the clear waters of its river. It also received its name from the Loire, its appropriate river, and is called Aureliana, as if “at the mouth of the Loire,” because it is situated on the bank at the mouth of that river.

It was not named, as some less cautious people think, after the emperor Aurelian, as though he himself had built it; rather, it was named from the river, as we have said, which is more fitting and more truthful.

## CHAPTER VI. On appointments obtained through sordid profit

With sacred eloquence warning us beforehand, it is clear as daylight [Col. 0635D] that, as the last days advance, when charity grows cold among human beings and iniquity abounds, dangerous times for souls are at hand.

For the assertions of many of the ancient Fathers also make it known that, when greed was rampant, the rights and orders of earlier religious institutions took from the very source from which they ought to have arisen for their growth the basis of their corruption and decline. What had been a benefit to some who used it legitimately was turned by others to the ruin of souls.

As we have said, when sordid greed rules, the discipline of justice is very often suffocated. Although this may be regarded as probable in the religious practices of various peoples and provinces [Col. 0636A], it is still more evident among the Levites and priests of the Israelite people. The more formerly wealthy many of them had been in comparison with others, the more insolent they became through proud greed; and for that reason they eventually became worse than everyone else.

Yet the institutions of the old law, clothed in the many riddling figures of its symbols, differ greatly from the clear and spiritual gifts of the mysteries of the new grace. There, gifts consisted only of earthly sacrifices; here, God himself is received as the reward. There, each person earned everything through the performance of servitude; here, each person is considered worthy solely on account of the sincere will of an excellent conscience.

We have prefaced these remarks because for a long time now, when almost all rulers have been blinded by unsuitable gifts, this pestilence has raged far and wide among all the prelates of the churches dispersed throughout the world.

In the end [Col. 0636B], they turned the free and venerable gift of Christ the almighty Lord into profit for greed, thereby increasing their own condemnation. Such prelates are consequently found to be all the less suited to perform divine work, since it is clear that they did not approach it through the entrance of the principal door.

Although the canon of sacred Scripture cries out in many ways against the insolence of such persons, it is now found to occur more frequently than usual in the various orders of the churches. For the very kings who ought to have been selectors of suitable persons for sacred religious office, corrupted by the distribution of gifts, judge someone more suitable to govern churches or souls—namely, the person from whom they hope to receive greater gifts.

Therefore [Col. 0636C], those who are insolent and puffed up with pride thrust themselves forward into every office, fearing less to incur the lapse of neglected pastoral care, since their entire confidence rests only on money gathered in their purses, not on gifts of wisdom received.

Once they have obtained authority, they devote themselves to greed all the more, since it is clear that by means of it they have fulfilled their own ambition. They serve greed as though they had set up an idol in place of God; fashioned by it, they rushed into such office without merit or good works.

This becomes a deceptive model for the less cautious and, consequently, a stubborn source of mutual envy. Whatever one of such men gathers by imitating another appears to have been stolen from the other through envy. And, as is always the custom of the envious, they continually desire to be tormented by the prosperity of others.

From this [Col. 0636D] arise the constant tumults of lawsuits, frequent scandals, and the disruption of the proper order of various ranks through transgression. It also happens that, while irreligion rages among the clergy, the desire for insolence and license grows among the people.

Then deceitful lies, frauds, and murders draw almost everyone secretly toward destruction. And because the eye of the Catholic faith—that is, the prelates of the Church—has been covered by the darkness of the worst blindness, its people, ignorant of the path of their own salvation, fall into the ruin of their destruction.

It is only just [Col. 0637A], therefore, that those very prelates should be afflicted by the people whom they ought to have held subject to themselves, and that they should experience the defiance of those whom, by their own example, they made stray from the road of justice.

Nor is it surprising that, when they are placed in some distress, they are less readily heard when they cry out, since they themselves have closed the door of mercy for themselves through the accumulation of greed. Nevertheless, it is held with complete certainty that, in return for such wickedness, common disaster very often threatens peoples and all living creatures, together with a great pestilence affecting the crops through disturbed weather.

Thus it has happened that those who ought to have carried the aid of salvation to the flock of almighty God entrusted to them instead placed before it an obstacle to the benefit customarily received.

Whenever [Col. 0637B] the religious devotion of bishops has been absent, the strictness of abbots according to the rule has withered, the vigor of monastic discipline has grown lukewarm, and the rest of the people, following their example, have become transgressors of God’s commandments, what else can happen but that the entire human race, by its own voluntary choice, again slips into the ancient chaos of the abyss and its own destruction?

From the outcome of such a state of affairs, that ancient Leviathan had undoubtedly conceived the hope that the flood of the Jordan River would fall into his mouth, so that the multitude of the baptized, abandoning the way of truth through the desire for greed, might be plunged into destruction.

And because, as is known to have been fulfilled according to apostolic authority [Col. 0637C], charity grew cold and iniquity abounded among people who loved themselves more than was right, these events that we have related occurred throughout all the regions of the world more frequently than usual around the thousandth year after the birth of the Lord and Savior.

## CHAPTER VII. On the fires and deaths of nobles

In the seventh year after the aforementioned thousandth year, Mount Vesuvius, also called the cauldron of Vulcan, opened its crater more violently than usual and spewed forth a mass of enormous rocks mixed with sulfurous fire; these rocks rolled as far as three miles away. Through its foul breath it began to make the surrounding province uninhabitable.

Nor, I think, should I pass over in silence why this occurs only in the African region. First, it is because of the earth’s emptiness caused by the sun’s excessive heat; and because the Ocean Sea slopes down toward it from the east [Col. 0637D], gathering immense whirlpools by raising waves within itself. Struck by these, the air is driven into the bosom of the earth.

Then, with fiery vapor, it exhales upward as strongly as it can. For just as air, according to the regular structure of things, penetrates the upper regions, so, because of its twofold nature—namely moisture and heat—when it is repeatedly agitated, it produces fire in dry places or ice in wet ones.

Meanwhile, almost all the cities of Italy and Gaul were devastated by fires, and the city of Rome itself was largely consumed by flame. While this was happening, the same fire seized the timbers of the Church of Saint Peter and began, beneath the bronze-paneled ceiling, to lick and consume the beams.

When the entire crowd of people who were present saw this and found no means whatsoever of restraining the disaster, they turned together and ran, crying out in a terrifying voice, to the shrine of the prince of the apostles. [Col. 0638A] They implored him that, if he were not at that moment a vigilant defender of his own church, many people throughout the world would abandon the profession of his faith.

At once the devouring flame abandoned the fir beams and disappeared.

During the same period, the leading bishops, dukes, and counts died in Italy and Gaul. First Pope John, then Hugh, the finest of the margraves. After this, the more prominent men throughout Italy also died.

In Gaul there were Odo and Heribertus: the former was count of Tours and Chartres, while the latter was count of Meaux and Troyes. At that time Richard, duke of Rouen, also died. He had built an exceedingly wealthy monastery at a place called Fécamp, where he also lies buried.

William [Col. 0638B], duke of Poitiers, likewise ended his life at about the same time. Many of the more religious bishops of Gaul also departed from this world: Manasses, a man full of holiness, bishop of Troyes; Gislebertus [also Engelbertus], bishop of Paris; and Geboinus, bishop of Châlons, together with many others.

Among them was the holy Maiolus, of blessed memory, who reached the end of his present life at the monastery of Silviniacum. The honorable character of his life is also commended by his precious passing. For men and women of both orders came in great numbers from throughout the Roman world because of the report of his holiness, and from there they carried away the grace of healing for various illnesses.

At that time [Col. 0638C] a terrible plague raged among human beings: a hidden fire which, whatever limb it seized, consumed it by burning and severed it from the body. The burning caused by this fire consumed many people even within the space of a single night.

Although remedies for this dreadful disease were found at many memorials of the saints, an especially great crowd gathered at the churches of three holy confessors: Martin of Tours, Odolric of Bavaria, and this venerable father Maiolus. There they found the benefits of the salvation they desired.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the death of Duke Henry and the devastation of Burgundy

[Col. 0638D] In the third year after the aforementioned thousandth year, Duke Henry died in Burgundy, at the fortress of Pulliacum on the River Saône. In the month of October he was entrusted to burial at Auxerre, beside the eminent confessor Germanus.

Then, in the following month of December, on the evening of Saturday before the day of the Lord’s Nativity, a marvelous portent appeared in the sky: the form or mass of an immense dragon, emerging from the northern quarter amid tremendous flashes of light, made its way toward the south. This prodigy terrified almost everyone who saw it in Gaul.

In the following year King Robert entered Burgundy with a large army of warriors. He also brought with him Richard, count of Rouen, with thirty thousand Normans, because the Burgundians had rebelled against him, refusing to receive him in the cities and fortresses that had belonged to Duke Henry, his uncle. Instead, they divided those places among themselves as their own.

The king first arrived [Col. 0639A] with his entire army at the city of Auxerre and surrounded it with a siege. After remaining there for a long time and being wearied by frequent assaults, he was unable to prevail against it; it is said that the city had never been overcome by fraud or by an enemy.

Abandoning the city, the king turned with all his military equipment to attack the fortress of the blessed Bishop Germanus, which, strengthened by a fortified rampart, clings to the city. The army of Count Landricus and the household men of that place had enclosed it with a rampart, fearing that the sacred flock might be torn apart by the enemy.

Meanwhile [Col. 0639B], the venerable abbot Odilo of the monastery of Cluny approached the enraged king, desiring to intervene between both sides: so that honor might be shown to the king, harmony among the princes strengthened, and peace in the country secured.

Seeing that what he had resolved could scarcely be accomplished, he urged the only eight brothers who had been left to guard the confessor—for the king’s order had forced the others to leave with their abbot, named Hilderic—to persist constantly in prayer, in the hope that the Lord’s mercy might deem them, and the place as well, worthy of deliverance from so great a siege.

At daybreak on the sixth day of the siege, the king, seized by immense fury, put on his armor and helmet, sharpened his entire army with his words, and also had with him Hugh, the bishop of that city, the only man in all Burgundy who favored the king’s side.

When the king was already prepared for battle [Col. 0639C], the aforementioned abbot Odilo confronted him, rebuking him and reproaching his leading men for rising with hostile force against so great a pontiff of God, Germanus—who, as is found in the account of his deeds, had been specially accustomed, with God’s help, both to restrain many wars and to resist the ferocity of kings.

Paying little attention to his words, they reached the place toward which they had been heading. Surrounding the aforementioned fortress in the form of a crown, they engaged in battle, each striving to conquer it.

After both sides had fought long and hard against one another, God’s immediate assistance suddenly came to the aid of his own household. For at the hour of battle the entire interior of the fortress was so filled with a most terrible mist that no enemy outside had any clear approach from which to shoot, while they could see themselves being struck down in a heavy slaughter by those fighting from within.

Thus [Col. 0639D], with especially many of their Normans cut down, they abandoned the fortress unharmed, although they repented—late, indeed—of having taken up arms against a place of such great merit.

It also happened that at the hour when the king’s army began to engage the sacred place in battle, a religious man named Gislebertus, a monk of that place, began celebrating the sacrament of the Mass upon the altar of the blessed Mary ever-virgin. That altar, more handsomely adorned than the others, stands at the summit of the same church, and he began the celebration just as he was accustomed to do every day at the third hour.

This event clearly corresponded to the victory granted from heaven.

On the following day the king departed from there and proceeded by burning [Col. 0640A] the possessions of the people, except for the most secure cities and fortresses, as far as the upper parts of Burgundy. When he returned to Francia, the Burgundians eventually came back to their allegiance, though only after some delay; nevertheless, he successfully gained possession of the entire region.

## CHAPTER IX. On the severe famine and the invasion of the Saracens
At that same time a severe famine occurred throughout the Roman world for five years, so that no region was heard of that was not poor and in need of bread. Many people, exhausted by hunger, perished. Then, in many parts of the world, this dreadful famine compelled people to eat not only the flesh of unclean animals and reptiles but also that of men, women, and children, with no natural bond even of parenthood standing in the way. For the cruelty of the famine had reached such a point that grown sons were now consuming their mothers, while the mothers themselves, setting maternal affection aside, were doing the same to their little children.

Afterward, the Saracen people, with their king named Almuzor, came forth from the regions of Africa, occupying almost the whole of Spain as far as the southern borders of Gaul, and inflicting great slaughter upon the Christians. Although his forces were inferior, Willermus, duke of Navarre, surnamed the Saint, nevertheless engaged them in battle repeatedly. At that time, because of the scarcity of the army, the monks of that region were also compelled to take up weapons of war. At last both sides suffered heavy losses; finally victory was granted to the Christians, though at the cost of a great loss among their own men, and the Saracens who survived fled to Africa.

It is also recorded that, in those long-continued battles, many religious Christians fell, who desired to fight rather out of love for fraternal charity than for any ostentatious glory or praise.

At that time there was a certain brother named Wlferius, exceedingly gentle in character, who lived according to the monastic way in the monastery of Reomagus, situated in the district of Tarnoder. One Sunday a vision appeared to him that was well suited to inspire belief. After completing the morning praises, he had lain down in the aforesaid monastery in order to pray, while the other brothers had withdrawn for a short rest. Suddenly the entire precinct of that church was filled with men dressed in white garments and distinguished by purple stoles. The gravity of their bearing, as he looked upon them, revealed much about their discipline.

The man who preceded them, carrying a cross in his hand, said that he was a bishop of many congregations and declared that on that very day he ought to celebrate the sacred rites of the Mass there. He also reported, both he and the others, that they had taken part with the brothers of that monastery in the solemn morning praises of that night. Moreover, they brought an office of excellent praise, which they had heard was appropriate to that day.

It was the eighth Sunday after Pentecost, on which, because of the fullness of joy over the Lord’s Resurrection and his Ascension, and over the coming of the Holy Spirit, it is customary in many places of various regions to sing responsories composed in words of great dignity, filled with sweet melody and, as far as human understanding can judge, worthy of the divine Trinity.

Meanwhile the bishop who presided began to celebrate the solemn Mass upon the altar of Saint Maurice the martyr, intoning an antiphon of that same Trinity. In the meantime the aforesaid brother asked them who they were, from where they came, and for what reason they had arrived there. They gave him this gentle reply:

“We bear the profession of Christianity; but, while protecting our homeland and defending the Catholic people, the sword in the war against the Saracens separated us from the dwelling of human bodies. Therefore divine calling now transfers all of us together to the lot of the blessed. We have been granted passage through this province for the reason that many from this region must shortly be added to our company.”

Furthermore, when the man who was completing the Mass had finished the Lord’s Prayer and was giving peace to everyone, he sent one of them to give the brother the kiss of peace. When this had been done, he also indicated to him that he should follow him. But when, having seen these things, he wished to follow them, they disappeared.

The brother understood that he himself would soon depart from this world, and so it came to pass. In the fifth month—that is, December—after he had seen the things we have related, he went, at the command of his abbot, to Auxerre to treat some sick brothers in the monastery of Saint Germanus, the confessor of Christ. He was trained in the study of medicine.

When he arrived there, he began to urge the brothers for whose sake he had come to carry out as quickly as possible whatever had to be done for their recovery. For he knew that his own end was near. When they replied, “Rest today from the fatigue of your journey, so that tomorrow may find you stronger,” he answered:

“If I do not complete today, as far as I am able, what remains to be done, know that tomorrow I shall do none of these things.”

Thinking that he was joking—for he was always cheerful and tranquil in spirit—they disregarded his warning. But when the following day dawned, seized by a sharp pain, he approached, as best he could, the altar of the blessed Mary ever-virgin to celebrate the sacred Mass. When this had been completed, he returned to the house of the sick brothers and arranged his already greatly aching limbs upon a bed. As commonly happens in such circumstances, his eyelids began to seek sleep amid his distress.

Suddenly a radiant virgin stood beside him, flashing with immense brilliance, and asked him what doubt he had in his mind. When he had looked upon her, she added:

“If you are afraid of the journey, there is no need for you to be afraid, for I shall be your guardian.”

Made more secure by this vision, he sent for the provost of the place, a very learned man named Achard, who later became abbot of that monastery. He related to him in order not only the vision that had just occurred but also the earlier one. Achard said to him:

“Take courage, brother, in the Lord. But since you have seen things rarely granted to human sight, you must pay the debt owed by all flesh, so that you may be admitted into the fellowship of those whom you saw.”

The other brothers were summoned, and according to custom they paid him their final visit. On the third day, as night was beginning, he departed from the body.

While all the brothers were preparing, according to custom, to wash him and lay him out in cloths, and were ringing all the monastery bells, a certain layman, though devout, who lived nearby, unaware of the brother’s death and supposing that the bells were being rung to announce the morning office, rose, as he was accustomed to do, to go to the church.

When he had reached a wooden bridge that lay almost halfway along the road, several people who lived nearby heard voices crying out from the direction of the monastery:

“Bring him out, bring him out, and bring him to us as quickly as possible!”

A reply was also made to these voices:

“For the moment I cannot bring this one out; but I shall bring out another, if I can.”

Immediately the man who was going to the church saw before him, upon the bridge, someone apparently one of his neighbors—though in truth he was the devil—coming toward him. He could have had no doubt about this. Indeed, calling him by his own name, the apparition warned him to cross carefully.

At once the evil spirit rose high into the air in the form of a tower, wishing to deceive the man, who followed the spirit’s false display with his eyes. But while he was looking at it, his foot slipped and he fell heavily upon the bridge. Rising at once and fortifying himself with the sign of the cross, he recognized the devil’s deceit, returned home more cautious, and shortly afterward died peacefully himself.

## CHAPTER X. On the Abundance of Stones

At that same time, in Burgundy, near the castle of Jaunniacum, a very strange and memorable portent occurred in the house of a certain nobleman named Arlebaud. For nearly three years, large and small stones continually dripped inexplicably throughout the whole house, either from the air or from the ceiling, so that even now heaps of stones cast out from it can readily be seen around the house.

Although they rained everywhere through the house by day and by night, they injured no one by their impact, nor did they break any vessel. Many people recognized among them boundary stones—called *bonnae* by others—from their own fields. Stones were also found there that had been carried from roads, houses, and various buildings, both near and far.

The outcome proved that this was an indication of the future destruction of that household and family. For the man mentioned above and his wife were descended from very noble parents. Consequently, serious disputes arose between his sons and grandsons over their paternal estates and the neighboring lands surrounding them.

Not long afterward it happened that they prepared with all their strength to recover for themselves a certain village called Allanto, situated in the district of Sens. It had come into their legal possession through a grant from the rulers of the monastery of Saint Columba the virgin; but soldiers living at Auxerre had seized it from them by force and plunder.

After the dispute over it had continued for several years, the two sides engaged in battle in that same village on a day during the vintage. Many from both sides were killed in the fighting. From the household mentioned above, eleven sons and grandsons fell. As time passed, with conflict impending and discord increasing, countless killings within that family and murders at the hands of their enemies continued into the thirtieth year and beyond.

## CHAPTER XI. On Leutard, the Heretic Who Went Mad

Around the end of the thousandth year, there was in Gaul, at a village called Virtus in the district of Châlons, a commoner named Leutard. The outcome of the affair showed that he might be considered an emissary of Satan.

The beginning of his madness and obstinacy was as follows. One day he was alone in the fields, engaged in some rural task. Overcome by sleep because of his labor, he dreamed that a great swarm of bees entered his body through the secret parts of nature. They then burst out through his mouth with a great noise, tormented him with repeated stings, and, as they kept agitating him for a long time with their goads, seemed to speak to him and command him to do many things impossible for human beings.

At last, exhausted, he rose and went home. He dismissed his wife, as though in obedience to an evangelical command, and divorced her. Then he went out as if to pray, entered a church, seized a cross and an image of the Savior, and smashed them. Those who witnessed this were terrified, believing—as was indeed the case—that he was insane.

He also persuaded them, since peasants are unstable in mind, that he was doing all these things by a marvelous revelation from God. He therefore overflowed with speeches devoid of usefulness and truth, and, wishing to appear a teacher, he sought to unteach the teacher of doctrine. He declared that giving tithes was altogether superfluous and empty.

Just as other heresies, in order to deceive more cautiously, cloak themselves in the divine Scriptures, although they are opposed to them, so he too said that the prophets had related some things that were useful and others that were not to be believed. His reputation, as though he were a man of sound mind and devout character, soon drew a considerable part of the common people to him.

When the very learned old bishop Gebuinus learned of this—for Leutard was in his diocese—he ordered him to be summoned before him. When he questioned him about everything he had been found to say or do, Leutard began to conceal the poison of his wickedness, wishing to appropriate for himself testimonies from the sacred Scriptures, though he had never learned them.

But the highly discerning bishop recognized that his claims were incoherent, indeed no less shameful than condemnable. He showed that the man had become a deranged heretic, recalled the partly deceived people from their madness, and restored them more fully to the Catholic faith.

When Leutard saw that he had been defeated and deprived of the favor of the crowd, he threw himself into a well and perished.

## CHAPTER XII. On a Heresy Discovered in Italy

At that same time an equally harmful evil arose near Ravenna. A certain man named Vilgardus devoted himself more assiduously to the art of grammar than to the other disciplines, just as the Italians have always been accustomed to neglect the other arts and pursue that one.

When he had begun to grow proud because of his learning in that discipline and had begun to appear more foolish, demons one night assumed the forms of the poets Virgil, Horace, and Juvenal. Appearing to him, they deceitfully thanked him because he embraced the words of their books more eagerly than others and practiced them, and declared that he was a fortunate herald of their posterity. They further promised that he would later share in their glory.

Corrupted by these demonic deceptions, he began to teach many things arrogantly that were contrary to the sacred faith, asserting that the poets’ statements were to be believed in every respect. At last he was found to be a heretic and was condemned by Peter, the bishop of that city.

Many others throughout Italy were also discovered during the time of this destructive doctrine, and they perished either by the sword or by fire. From the island of Sardinia as well—which is usually particularly full of such people—some emerged at that time and corrupted part of the population in Spain; they too were exterminated by Catholic men.

This portent corresponds to the prophecy of John, for he said that Satan would be released after a thousand years. We shall discuss these matters at greater length in the third book.

# BOOK THREE

## THE CHAPTERS OF BOOK THREE BEGIN

I. On Stephen, king of the Hungarians, and the wars of the Beneventans.  
II. On Robert, king of the Franks.  
III. On the comet-star, whose appearance foretold many things.  
IV. On the renewal of churches throughout the world.  
V. On monasteries rebuilt or founded successfully by Abbot Willermus.  
VI. On the relics of saints revealed everywhere.  
VII. On the destruction of the Temple of Jerusalem and the slaughter of the Jews.  
VIII. On a heresy discovered at Orléans.  
IX. On the sons of that same king.

## PREFACE

Now, since we have related some events of earlier times, let us begin the third book of this work from that year and thereafter, as we promised—namely, from the thousandth year after the birth of the Word who gives life.

As we have said, with that year approaching, almost the whole world was deprived of both religious and noble persons. Nevertheless, from that same year onward, men of both orders distinguished themselves in Italy as well as in Gaul, whose lives and actions can provide posterity with examples worthy of imitation.

Although two most Christian kings were reigning—namely Henry, king of the Saxons, and Robert, king of the Franks—their countries were free from attacks by foreign nations, but were very frequently worn down by internal wars. For just as honor is sometimes shown to the wicked out of fear, so fear is inflicted upon the good because of the respect due to them.

When Henry was accepted into the imperial authority over the Lombards by the entire Roman people, through the intervention of Pope Benedict, a most holy man, that people, accustomed to deceit, rebelled. They anointed and appointed for themselves a certain king named Arduin. Although they resisted for a long time and with great determination, they later submitted themselves to the imperial commands after the greatest slaughter of their own people.

When Henry came to Pavia, he had a palace of remarkable workmanship built for him by those same Lombards.
