After taking possession of the imperial authority in proper fashion, he took a wife in his kingdom, namely the daughter of Sigefred, duke of the Saxons. When he saw that he could not have children by her, he did not dismiss her on that account; instead, he gave to the Church of Christ all the patrimony that would have been owed to children.

He also built a monastery in Saxony at a place called Bavoberch—that is, Bavo’s Mountain. In the Germanic language, *berch* means “mountain.” The monastery, enriched with innumerable gifts by the Roman pontiff, the aforementioned Benedict, he caused to be dedicated in honor of the prince of the apostles. Following the advice of that pontiff, he also elevated the same church to an episcopal see and, after appointing a bishop there, made it wealthy through the revenues of very extensive estates.

## CHAPTER ONE. On Stephen, King of the Hungarians, and the Wars of the Beneventans

At that time the Hungarian people, who lived around the Danube, were converted to the faith of Christ together with their king. To their king Stephen, so called at baptism and suitably most Christian, the aforementioned emperor Henry gave his own sister as a wife.

At that time almost all those from Italy and Gaul who wished to go to the Lord’s Sepulcher in Jerusalem began to abandon the customary route across the strait of the sea and to travel through the territory of this region. He established an extremely safe road for everyone. He welcomed as brothers all whom he saw and gave them immense gifts. Moved by this generosity, an innumerable multitude, both nobles and common people, went to Jerusalem.

At that same time the emperor Basil of the holy Constantinopolitan Empire ordered one of his satraps, the man surnamed Catapontes because he lived beside the sea, to come from the overseas cities belonging to the Roman Empire and collect tribute. The man willingly agreed and sent a Greek fleet to seize Italian possessions.

This undertaking continued for two years, and a considerable part of the province of Benevento was also brought under Greek rule. At that time a certain very bold Norman named Rodulfus, who had incurred the displeasure of Count Richard and feared his anger, went to Rome with everything he was able to take with him and laid his case before the supreme pontiff Benedict.

Seeing that Rodulfus was exceptionally skilled in military combat, the pope began to tell him of the Greek invasion of the Roman Empire and of his great sorrow that there was no one of such ability among his own people to repel men of a foreign nation.

After hearing this, Rodulfus promised that he would fight against the overseas forces if some assistance were provided to him either by the pope or by those upon whom the native needs of their homeland pressed more heavily.

The aforesaid pope then sent him with his men to the leaders of Benevento, so that they might receive him peacefully, keep him in readiness always to fight, and obey his command unanimously. Rodulfus went out to the Beneventans, who received him as the pope had ordered.

Immediately Rodulfus attacked the Greek officials who were collecting taxes from the people, seized all their possessions, and slaughtered them. When their comrades heard this—the men who had already subjected several cities and castles to their own rule—they gathered their forces into one army and went into battle against Rodulfus and those who supported his side.

In that battle the greater part of the Greek forces fell, and they also abandoned certain castles empty; Rodulfus’s victorious army followed and took possession of them. When the Greeks saw the slaughter of their men, they sent to Constantinople asking that assistance be sent to them as quickly as possible by those who had dispatched them.

They immediately refitted their fleet and sent many more fighters than before. Meanwhile, when it was heard everywhere that a few Normans had won a victory over the arrogant Greeks, an innumerable multitude, including wives and children, followed from the homeland from which Rodulfus had departed. Count Richard not only permitted them to go but compelled them to do so.

As they went forth, they came boldly to the Alpine pass also called Mount Jovis. There the powerful men of the region, driven by greed, had placed barriers and guards in the narrowest paths to demand payments from travelers. But the Norman army broke through the barriers, killed the guards, and forced its way across. Once they had emerged, they provided Rodulfus with substantial assistance.

Thus both sides, having recovered their strength, entered battle for a second time, in which the armies on both sides suffered heavy losses. Victory nevertheless came to the Norman army. Shortly afterward, after a third battle had been fought, both sides, exhausted, withdrew.

Rodulfus, seeing that his own men were failing and that the men of that region were poorly suited to war, went with a few companions to Emperor Henry to explain the matter to him. Henry received him kindly and enriched him with various gifts, since the report he had heard about him had aroused a desire to see him.

Immediately the emperor gathered a large army and prepared to go in defense of the commonwealth. Meanwhile the Greeks, thinking that Rodulfus had fled the country, rushed upon the castles that he had taken from them in victory. But in vain: they also hastily surrounded the ancient city of Troy with walls and filled it abundantly with men and women.

The emperor then proceeded to the region of Benevento and conquered and subjected to his rule all the cities and castles that the Greeks had seized. When he reached the aforesaid Troy, those inside repelled him and resisted him for a long time. They hoped that Basil would come to their aid in the following summer, as the Greeks had promised. They further hoped that Henry would be humbled so far that, terrified by fear, he would receive the feet of Basil.

But Henry surrounded the city with his army in a siege and set up siege engines so that he might take it by force. The besieged came out at night, carrying torches coated with pitch and set alight, and burned the siege engines from outside.

When the emperor saw this, he was inflamed with anger. He had the stronger siege engines rebuilt and enclosed in rawhide, and ordered them to be protected by vigilant guards.

By now the third month of the siege had passed, and both sides were exceedingly exhausted by alternating slaughter. The emperor’s army had also been severely afflicted by dysentery. At last the besieged, adopting a better plan, found a way to escape their danger.

One day they took a solitary man dressed in monastic clothing—such men are especially numerous in Italy—gave him a cross to carry, and sent all the younger children of the city behind him. Crying out, “Kyrie, eleison” (“Lord, have mercy”), he came to the emperor’s tent.

When the emperor heard this, he ordered them to be asked what they wanted. When they replied that they were appealing for mercy upon the afflicted city, he said:

“He who knows hearts knows very well that the fathers of these little children are greater murderers than I am.”

Weeping, he ordered them to return safely to the city. They did as the emperor had commanded.

The next day, again early in the morning, they came out of the city as before, crying, “Kyrie, eleison,” until the sound of their voices reached the emperor’s ears. He immediately came out of his tent and, seeing the crowd of orphans, was moved by compassion. Being a most wise man, he used the words of the Lord and said: “I have compassion on the crowd.”

Earlier he had declared that, if he succeeded in taking the city, every male found in it would be hanged on gallows, while everything else would be burned and the walls of the city themselves pulled down to the ground.

The emperor also ordered those who ruled the others in the city that, if they wished to receive his pardon and appease his anger, they themselves should demolish that part of the city walls which appeared to resist his siege engines.

When they heard this, they eagerly fulfilled what had been commanded them. Afterward the emperor ordered them to come out to him peacefully and to have the city wall rebuilt by their own people.

Taking hostages for peace from all the inhabitants of that region, he returned to Saxony. The Normans, with their duke Rodulfus, returned to their homeland and were gratefully received by their own prince, Richard.

In the following year, in the month of July, the emperor Henry died in Saxony and was honorably buried in the monastery of Bavoberch, which, as has been said, he had built in honor of the prince of the apostles.

## CHAPTER TWO. On Robert, King of the Franks

At the time already described, while the kingdom of the Franks was being governed by King Robert, his own subjects inflicted many insolent insults upon him, especially those whom he and both Hugos—namely, his father and grandfather—had raised from a middling or even lowly status to the greatest honors.

Among them was Odo, the greatest of the rebels, son of Theobald of Chartres, surnamed the Deceiver, along with many others of lesser power. They became rebels against him precisely where they ought to have been more submissive.

The second Odo was no less rebellious: he was the son of the earlier Odo and, the more powerful he became, the more fraudulent he was than the others. When Stephen, count of Troyes and Meaux and son of Heribert, the king’s cousin, died without children, this Odo appeared against the king’s will and occupied all the broad estates that by right were destined to pass into the king’s domain.

There was also continual litigation and frequent warfare between this Odo and Fulk, count of Anjou, since both were swollen with pride and therefore hostile to peace.

Willermus, stepson of Duke Henry and son of Albert, duke of the Lombards, also at one point rebelled against the same king. Landric, count of Nevers, supported Willermus; he had married Willermus’s daughter. Bruno, bishop of Langres, also supported him; Willermus had married Bruno’s sister, by whom he had sons and daughters. Of these children, Landric married the eldest daughter, while the two Willermuses—namely, the one of Poitiers and the one of Arles—married the others. One of his sons, named Rainaldus, took as his wife a daughter of Richard, duke of Rouen, named Adeleda.

Although Willermus was an outsider and, as a child, had been secretly taken from Lombard territory and then cleverly restored to his mother in Burgundy through a certain monk, he grew so powerful that no one in the country was his equal in wealth or military strength.

But Hugo, son of Lambert, count of Chalon, a very honorable man, strongly opposed and resisted him. Among the many excellent things he accomplished, Hugo also built a monastery in the district of Autun called Paredo, in honor of Saint Mary and Saint John the Baptist. He lies buried there in honorable repose.

This Hugo was bishop of Auxerre and governed his father’s county by the king’s command, since his father had no male offspring other than him. For that reason he opposed the king’s enemies, because he obeyed the king most faithfully in all things.

The aforesaid king took as his wife his kinswoman, named Constance in both name and character, a renowned queen and daughter of William, formerly duke of Aquitaine. By her he had four sons and two daughters.

At one point, however, there was a certain Hugo called of Beauvais, who sowed wicked seeds of hatred between the king and his wife and, for the sake of his own reward, had made the queen hateful to him. He had gained such favor with the king that he was regarded as count of the palace.

It happened one day that the king went hunting in the forest, and Hugo, as he always did, went with him. Twelve very strong soldiers, sent by Fulk, count of Anjou and the queen’s uncle, arrived and killed the aforesaid Hugo in the king’s presence.

Although the king was saddened by this deed for some time, afterward he was reconciled with the queen, as was proper.

This king, as a most wise worshiper of God, was always a lover of the humble and, as far as he could, a hater of the proud. If any episcopal see in his kingdom was without its bishop, he took the greatest care to restore to the Church a useful shepherd, even if he was of low birth, rather than choose someone of noble rank adorned with worldly pomp.

For this reason he also found the leading men of the kingdom very stubborn, since, despising the humble, they chose proud men like themselves.

He was at peace with the kings situated around his kingdom, especially with the aforementioned Emperor Henry. Once they had come together to confer with one another upon the river Meuse, which is the boundary of their two kingdoms. Many on both sides murmured that it was improper for either of such great kings to humble himself by crossing over, as it were, to seek the other’s assistance, and that it would be most suitable for them to be carried together in boats to the middle of the river, where they could speak.

But each of these highly educated men kept in mind the saying: “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things.”

At first light the emperor rose and crossed with a few companions to the king of the Franks. They embraced one another and kissed each other with great affection. After the bishops had suitably celebrated the Mass in their presence, it was fitting for both kings to dine together.

After the meal, King Robert offered Henry immense gifts of gold, silver, and precious gems, as well as one hundred horses splendidly caparisoned, each bearing armor and a helmet. He further instructed him to diminish their friendship only to the extent that he left all of these things behind.

When Henry saw his friend’s generosity, he accepted from the gifts only a Gospel book set with gold and precious stones, and a similar reliquary containing a tooth of Saint Vincent the deacon and martyr. His wife received only an equal number of golden vessels. Henry departed with the rest, leaving everything behind as a sign of goodwill.

The next day King Robert again went with the bishops to the emperor’s tents. The emperor received him with great honor, and after they had dined together he offered Robert one hundred pounds of pure gold. The king likewise took from him only an equal number of golden vessels. Having confirmed their pact of friendship, they returned to their own territories.

He was also always treated with great favor by other kings: Adalrad, king of the English; Rodulfus, king of Austrasia; and Sancho, king of Navarre in Spain. They sent him gifts and requested assistance from him.

## CHAPTER THREE. On the Comet-Star, Whose Appearance Foretold Many Things

During the time of the aforementioned king, a star called a comet appeared in the western sky in the month of September, at the beginning of night, and lasted for three months. Shining with extraordinary brightness, it claimed for itself and illuminated a very large part of the sky, until it set around cockcrow.

Whether God newly sends forth a star, or whether he increases the light of an existing star for the sake of some portent, only he can know who, in his ineffable wisdom, orders all other things. This, however, is regarded as thoroughly established: whenever such a sign is shown to human beings in the world, something strange and terrifying is plainly indicated soon afterward.

It happened shortly afterward that the church of Saint Michael the archangel was burned by fire. It stood upon a certain promontory on the shore of the Ocean Sea and is still venerated throughout the world.

There one may also observe a most certain marvel: through the waxing and waning of the moon, in a wondrous ebbing and flowing around the promontory, the current—or movement—of the Ocean proceeds and returns. They call the increase of that sea the *malina*, and its decrease the *ledones*. For this reason above all, the aforesaid place is frequently visited by many peoples from various lands.

Not far from the aforementioned promontory there is also a small river called the Arduus. After these events it swelled somewhat and for a period of time became impassable, greatly obstructing those who wished to travel to the aforesaid church and for a while becoming an obstacle to that journey. Later, returning to its former course, it left the shore deeply furrowed by its flow.

After these events, the venerable Abo, father of the monastery surnamed Floriacensis of Saint Benedict, crossed into the province of the southern Gascons in order to extend monastic religion. When he arrived there and stayed in a certain monastery, diligently practicing the things of God according to his customary manner, he was revered by everyone with profound affection.

One day, however, in the courtyard of that monastery, the goads of anger in certain quarrelsome men began to burn, and an excessively violent disturbance arose. When the most reverend man, the aforesaid Abo, learned of it and came forward to calm the tumult, carrying writing tablets and a stylus in his hands, one of the crowd, inspired by a demonic spirit, attacked him and pierced his side with a lance, making him a martyr of Christ.

It is also said that the attacker was soon seized by a demon and ended his life miserably. The body of the aforesaid father was honorably buried there by his own people and by the other faithful of that province. There too the Lord later bestowed many benefits upon human beings to the praise of his name.

At that time, in Italy and Gaul, many bishops held synodal gatherings among themselves concerning various questions. Regarding the fasts that many of the faithful observe between the Ascension of the Savior and Pentecost, they decreed that they should not be imposed by priestly command, except on the Saturday of Pentecost; and that those who wished to observe them should not be forbidden to do so.

At the same time, a question arose as to why monks, for three or four Sundays before the Lord’s Nativity, or during the period of Lenten observance, sang the hymn *Te Deum laudamus* (“We praise you, O God”) contrary to the custom of the Roman Church. When both abbots and monks were challenged on this matter, they replied that they did so for no other reason than by the instruction of blessed Benedict, that most renowned and excellent Father; and that the acts and sayings of that same Father had also been written down and commendably confirmed by Gregory, the supreme Roman pontiff. Once the bishops had learned these things, the monks’ custom continued to prevail with authoritative force. [Col. 0651A]

A considerable question was also raised by the same pontiffs concerning the day of the Lord’s Annunciation, which is celebrated on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, as to whether it might more appropriately be observed at some other time outside Lent. For some maintained that the Lord’s Annunciation could irreproachably be celebrated, according to the custom of the Spaniards, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of January.

Later, when I was living at the monastery of Cluny with the other brothers, many monks from Spain arrived there, men of upright conduct who had long lived according to the custom of their own region. As the day of the Lord’s Nativity approached, these monks asked the venerable Odilo, abbot of that place, whether they might celebrate the Annunciation according to the custom of their own people. When they had done so, separated from the others, it appeared that same night to two elders of the place that one of the Spaniards took a fire-fork from above the altar and placed a child in a frying pan full of coals, while the child cried: “Father, father, what you gave to this man, they are taking away.” What more is there to say? Among us the ancient custom prevailed, as was fitting.

# Chapter IV. On the Renewal of Churches throughout the World

When the third year after the aforesaid thousandth year was already nearly at hand, it happened throughout almost the whole world, but especially in Italy and Gaul, that the basilicas of churches were renewed, although most of them, being suitably situated, had in no way required it. Nevertheless, each Christian people rivaled the others in enjoying a more beautiful church. It was as though the world itself, shaking itself clean, had cast off its old age and everywhere put on a shining garment of churches. [Col. 0651D]

At that time the faithful almost everywhere transformed the churches of episcopal sees, as well as the monasteries of various saints and the smaller oratories of villages, into better structures. At that same time, among the others, the monastery of Saint Martin at Tours stood out. It had been demolished by the venerable man Heriveus, arch-clerk of that place, and rebuilt before his death with marvelous workmanship.

If anyone could have recounted his life and conduct—what sort of man he was from childhood until the end of his present life—he would have shown him to humanity as entirely incomparable among the men of his age. He was descended from the nobility of the Franks, though nobler in mind himself, and, like a lily or rose among thorns, he came by blood from a fierce people. He was nobly educated, as is customary among the well-born, and afterward devoted himself to the liberal arts. But when he understood that many who studied these things became more obstinate than submissive to divine obedience, he considered it sufficient if he could gain the salvation of his soul from them. Abandoning the studies of worldly learning, he secretly entered a certain monastery and very devoutly asked to become a monk. [Col. 0652A]

But, as we have said, since he was of illustrious lineage, the brothers of that monastery, fearing the threats of his parents, in no way consented to do what he had requested. Nevertheless, while keeping him there, they gave him their word that, if his parents’ opposition did not prevent it, they would most willingly fulfill what he asked.

He remained there for some time, giving an indication of what he would later become in the holiness of his life and offering all who lived there an example worthy of imitation. When his father learned what he had done, he was seized with fury and came to the monastery to drag away his son, who was truly engaged in more valuable pursuits. After rebuking him at length and using force against him, he took him away with him to the king’s court. He then begged the king to turn his son’s mind away from this purpose by promising him worldly advantages.

When King Robert saw him—for he was pious and religious—he exhorted him with gentleness to strive to preserve his good purpose with an undivided mind. Yet he ordered him, for the present, to become arch-clerk of the church of Saint Martin, wishing later to make him a bishop whom others could imitate. This was attempted many times, but, because Heriveus refused, it came to nothing. He did accept responsibility for the church, as though compelled, and was clothed in white; yet, though at times living in canonical fashion, he fully retained the mind and life of a monk.

He was always clothed beneath his garments in an unbreakable hair shirt, mortifying his body by fasting, extremely sparing toward himself, generous to the poor, and constant in vigils and prayers. Moreover, this man, full of God, conceived the plan of enlarging and elevating in the grandeur of its whole structure the church whose guardian he had been appointed. Taught by the Holy Spirit, he directed the masons to lay the foundations of an incomparable structure, which he himself, as he had desired, brought to completion. [Col. 0652C]

When the work was finished, he summoned bishops from many cities and took care that the building should be consecrated to God. On that very day he fittingly deposited within it Saint Martin, God’s holy confessor. For on that day the former dedication of the basilica was celebrated, namely, on the fourth day before the Nones of July.

It is also said that, several days before this translation, the same man of God, Heriveus, had asked the Lord to demonstrate some miracle through Saint Martin, as he had done in former times, as a sign of his love for the church, his bride. While he lay prostrate in prayer, the same confessor appeared to him and addressed him gently:

“My dearest son, know that you can obtain from the Lord greater things than what you ask. But the miracles already displayed should suffice for this time, since the harvest is now near in which the seed formerly scattered will be gathered. Only the healing that raises souls should be prayed for by all. On behalf of these people I never cease to implore the Lord’s mercy. Know that I especially intercede with the Lord for those who now serve him continually in this church. Some of them, excessively entangled in the affairs of the present age and also serving under military arms, were slain and fell in battle. You should not be unaware that I scarcely obtained from the clemency of Christ that they might be rescued from the ministers of darkness and be allowed to stand in places of refreshment and light. As for you, complete the vow pleasing to the Lord, as you have begun.” [Col. 0653A]

When the appointed day arrived, and the bishops and abbots had assembled with an innumerable multitude of faithful people of both sexes and every rank, the most reverend Heriveus first took care to disclose to the holier priests who had gathered what had been revealed to him. After the consecration had been performed according to custom and all the furnishings had been properly arranged, the same man began to wear himself down by stricter mortifications and lived alone in a small cell near the church, devoting himself to psalms and prayers.

Four years later, when he realized that he would soon depart from this world and had begun to fall ill, many people came to visit him. They were also waiting to see some miracle occur at his departure, since they knew that he was a man of such great merit. But he, with a discerning mind, foretold and warned them to attend to other matters and not to expect a sign, which they would certainly not see. Rather, he begged them to pray more attentively for him to the most merciful Lord. As the hour of his departure drew near, he repeatedly raised his hands and eyes toward heaven and said: “Lord, have mercy; Lord, have mercy.” With these words he breathed out his final breath. He was buried in the same church, in the place where blessed Martin had first been buried and had rested.

# Chapter V. On Monasteries Rebuilt Well by Abbot William or Founded by Him

At that time the venerable abbot William was distinguished in the improvement of the houses of God mentioned above. Blessed Majolus had first appointed him Father of the church of the holy martyr Benignus. He immediately transformed that church through such remarkable planning that another like it could scarcely be found. He also flourished no less in regular discipline and proved in his time an incomparable propagator of this order.

But in proportion to the love with which he was esteemed by religious and devout people, he was slandered and plotted against by the fraudulent and impious. He was born in Italy and came from a noble family, though he was nobler still through the distinguished learning he acquired. In that same region, on an estate that belonged to him by right of inheritance from his parents, formerly called Vulpiam, he first built a monastery overflowing with every grace; afterward, when he changed its name, it was called Fruttuaria. Having enriched it with many kinds of benefits, he appointed there as Father of the monks a man named John, who imitated him in every respect.

The aforesaid William was sharp-minded and outstandingly prudent. For this reason he held the highest position in the courts of kings and other princes. Whenever a monastery was deprived of its own shepherd, he was immediately compelled by kings, counts, and bishops alike to accept its governance for the sake of improving it, since monasteries taken under his protection were seen to surpass the others in wealth and holiness.

He himself also firmly asserted that, if the substance of this institution were observed by monks anywhere, they would suffer no want of anything whatsoever. This was demonstrated most clearly in the places entrusted to him.

It is said that this institution and the practice of this custom had their origin in the monasteries or rule of Saint Benedict, and that they were brought by blessed Maurus, his disciple, to our territory, that is, to Gaul. There is also a reliable account that, after the death of blessed Maurus, at a later time monks were expelled by enemy attacks from the monastery called Glannofolium, which he had built, as is recorded in his deeds. They came to the monastery of Saint Savinus the Confessor in the territory of Poitiers and brought with them all the furnishings they could carry. There they devoted themselves for some time to the practices they had learned. [Col. 0654B]

Later, when the strictness of that discipline had grown cold, it is known to have revived several times after being received at the monastery of Saint Martin of Autun. Then, as though after a third migration, it occupied the monastery of Baume, situated in Upper Burgundy. Finally, when the aforesaid institution was almost exhausted, by God’s will it chose for itself a seat of wisdom at the monastery called Cluny, where it would recover its strength and bear fruit through many branches.

This place acquired its name from the sloping and low-lying character of its site, or, more suitably, from *cluere*, which we say means “to grow.” From its beginning, that place indeed obtained a notable increase of diverse gifts day by day. [Col. 0654C]

The aforesaid monastery was first built by Berno, Father of the monks of the monastery of Baume mentioned above, at the command of William, the most devout duke of Aquitaine, in the district of Mâcon, beside the little river Grosne. This monastery is said at first to have received no more than fifteen agricultural holdings as its endowment. Nevertheless, twelve brothers are recorded to have assembled there.

From them, as from excellent seed, a lineage was multiplied that is known to have filled a great region of the world with an innumerable army of the Lord. Because they clung incessantly to works belonging to God—namely, justice and piety—they deserved to be filled with every good thing and left behind an example for future generations to imitate.

After the aforementioned Berno, the wisest abbot Odo took charge of its governance. He was an exceedingly religious man who had been provost of the church of Saint Martin at Tours and was richly adorned in character and holy conduct. He became such a propagator of this institution that the better monasteries in Italy, from the province of Benevento, and in Gaul, all the way to the Ocean Sea, rejoiced that they were subject to his authority.

After his death, Heimardus, a simple man, succeeded him. Although he was not equally famous, he was nevertheless no unequal guardian of regular observance. After him, the holy and venerable Majolus was elected; we have mentioned him above. He foresaw Odilo as his successor and Father of the monks. Odilo was the fifth abbot of the aforesaid monastery of Cluny after its first abbot, Berno.

From that monastery, brothers were frequently requested from various provinces and appointed Fathers of monks; they acquired great profit for the Lord. Yet this Father William, with whom the present account began, was found to have produced more fruitful results than all his predecessors through greater labor and more abundant sowing in the aforesaid institution.

# Chapter VI. On the Relics of Saints Revealed Everywhere

As we have said, when the world had been clothed in white through the renewed basilicas of churches, at a later time—namely, in the eighth year after the aforementioned thousandth year after the Savior’s incarnation—the relics of many saints, which had long remained hidden, were revealed through signs of various kinds indicating where they lay. They appeared to the sight of the faithful by God’s command, as though awaiting an ornament of resurrection, and brought great consolation to their minds.

This revelation is known to have begun first in Sens, a city of Gaul, at the church of blessed Stephen the martyr. Its archbishop was Leotericus, through whose efforts remarkable relics of ancient sacred things were discovered there. Among many other objects that had lain hidden, he is said to have found part of the staff of Moses.

When news of this became known, faithful people gathered from everywhere—not only from the provinces of Gaul but also from almost all of Italy and from regions across the sea. Many sick people likewise returned from there healed through the intercession of the saints.

But, as has often happened, because human advantage commonly begins where greed later drives it to ruin, the inhabitants of that city, which—as we have said—had become exceedingly wealthy through the gathering of peoples for the sake of piety, conceived excessive arrogance over so great a benefit. When the count of that city, a very simple man named Frotmund, died, his son, a thoroughly wicked man, assumed the government and began to administer the civil affairs. [Col. 0655D]

Having become exceedingly depraved, he also attempted with all his power to defile the honor of the church. He loved the transgressive customs of the Jews so greatly that he ordered all his people to call him their king, since his own name was Rainard. Although he was deceitful in every other respect, he was also regarded as a treacherous detractor of the Christian faith. Therefore he pronounced judgments against the poor without any mercy, entirely removing human compassion. Indeed, there were as many witnesses of the deed I am about to relate as there were people living in that city at the time.

Once a certain criminal was caught committing theft and was brought before Rainard so that, after hearing the case, he might determine what should be done with him. Immediately, without any pity, he condemned the man to be hanged on the gallows. But the man who had been caught began tearfully to beg Rainard to spare his life for the present, promising that he would never again commit robbery. It was useless. For, becoming still more cruel, he even bound himself by oath that the wretched suppliant would live no longer.

Seeing that he could not alter the sentence pronounced against him, the condemned man obtained only this: that he might confess his crimes to the bishop, and that the bishop might mercifully absolve him, as he was about to die, through the ministry granted to him. Once this had been granted, the wicked attendants immediately forced him to be hanged.

Led to the appointed place, he repeatedly uttered these words: “Lord Jesus, who on this day hung upon the cross for the salvation of humanity, forgive me.” It was the sixth day of the week, which is therefore held in greater reverence by all the faithful. Thus, he was bound, lifted up, and hanged with his throat tightly constricted.

When everyone withdrew from this dreadful execution, as they thought it, he remained hanging like a corpse until the following day. Then, by divine command, his bonds broke, and the earth received the man as he fell—alive, though he had been compelled to undergo death and had been taken away into the empty air. When he entered the city, he became a spectacle that astonished everyone. But alas, what grief! He returned to his former wickedness and escaped punishment.

A similar event is said to have occurred in the city of Troyes not long before this. Some thieves, driving cattle before them, realized that the owners of the cattle were pursuing them. They entrusted the same cattle to an old and innocent man, pretending that they were seeking the necessities of life, but in reality using him as a means of escape.

As soon as they had done this, the old man was caught with the cattle. He was dragged away, beaten, and bound like a criminal. Brought before the ruler of the city, Count Heribert, he wished to have his case examined. He was not heard; rather, as though he were guilty of death because of his decrepit old age, the count condemned him to be hanged. This sentence was carried out without any delay.

But as soon as he had endured the hanging, a heifer of enormous size and great strength, standing upright, placed her horns beneath the feet of the hanged man and supported him in this way without pain for three days. When the three days had passed, the man who was hanging heard travelers passing nearby and speaking to one another. He shouted as loudly as he could and begged them to come quickly and take him down.

But when they heard him, they thought that this was a demonic illusion. When he called out more insistently and affirmed that he was alive, the men came, untied him, and took him down. After he had been brought into the city, people asked him how he had managed while hanging on the gallows. He replied:

“When I was younger and had already taken a wife, my wife and I received a godchild offered to us by someone from the sacred font. We had agreed to give him, from our small means, the one calf that we had received from its mother by a gratuitous gift. When I had just been released to hang from the high beam, it seemed to me that the calf had come forward, larger than all the others. Stretching out her body and raising her neck, she gently placed her horns beneath my feet and supported me in this way for as long as I hung.”

After the man who had been saved from death had reported this, countless numbers of calves were later given throughout the region to godchildren of the sacred font, after the manner of that example.

Furthermore, since Rainard, as we have said, was Judaizing—or rather, raging madly—the king was persuaded, for he had often rebuked Rainard because of his wickedness, to subject the rule of so great a city to royal authority, lest the scandal to the holy faith grow stronger if the evil man’s power continued to increase.

For this reason the king was compelled to send an army to drive the aforesaid Rainard from the city and to preserve it under his own protection. Those whom the king had sent arrived and captured the city with immense devastation; they also burned a considerable part of it. The enormity of the calamity surpassed the magnitude of the former joy that had been earned through those crimes. [Col. 0657C]

# Chapter VII. On the Destruction of the Temple of Jerusalem and the Slaughter of the Jews

At that same time, namely, in the ninth year after the aforementioned thousandth year, the church at Jerusalem that contained the tomb of the Lord and our Savior was completely destroyed by order of the ruler of Babylon.

The occasion of this destruction is known to have begun in the following way. Since a great multitude of the faithful from the whole world were traveling to Jerusalem to visit the distinguished memorial of the Lord, the envious devil once again began, through the Jewish people whom he habitually employed, to pour the poison of his wickedness upon the worshipers of the true faith.

There was a considerable Jewish population of this kind in the royal city of Orléans in Gaul. They were found to be more arrogant, envious, and audacious than the others of their race. By a wicked plan they corrupted a certain man with money: a wandering beggar in the guise of a pilgrim, named Robert, who was in fact a fugitive slave belonging to the monastery of Melleray of blessed Mary.

They carefully received him and sent him to the ruler of Babylon with letters written in Hebrew characters, on small tablets inserted into an iron staff so that they could not be removed from him by any chance. After departing, he delivered the letters to the aforesaid ruler. They were filled with deceit and wickedness and warned him that, unless he quickly overthrew the venerable Christian house, he would soon lose all dignity when the Christians occupied his kingdom.

When the ruler heard this, he was immediately seized with fury and sent his own men to Jerusalem to destroy the aforementioned temple completely. They came and did as they had been ordered. They also attempted to batter the hollow mound of the tomb itself with iron hammers, but were entirely unable to do so.

At that time they likewise destroyed the church of blessed George the martyr at Ramla, whose power had once greatly terrified the Saracen people. For it is said that, when they repeatedly wished to enter it, they were seized with blindness.

After the temple had been destroyed, as we have said, it soon became clear that the outrage had been committed through the wickedness of the Jews. When this was spread throughout the whole world, all Christians agreed that every Jew should be expelled completely from their lands or cities.

Thus, hated by everyone, they were driven from the cities: some were slaughtered by the sword, others drowned in rivers, and others killed by various forms of death. Some even killed themselves in different ways, so that, after an appropriate vengeance had been carried out against them, scarcely any of them were found in the Roman world. [Col. 0658B]

The bishops also decreed and prohibited that no Christian should associate with them in any business. If any of them wished to convert to the grace of baptism and reject every Jewish custom or practice, they decreed that only such people should be received. Many of them did so, compelled more by love of the present life and fear of death than by desire for the joys of eternal life. For all who had falsely claimed that they had become such converts soon shamelessly returned to their former customs.

After these events, the aforementioned bearer of the letters returned, badly secure, to his native land. He began diligently to search for someone who might be aware of his people’s fraud. When he found very few of them living in great fear in the city of Orléans, he once again began to associate with them more familiarly.

It happened that a certain pilgrim arrived there—a companion of his on the overseas journey and certainly aware of the entire affair. When he saw that Robert was again clinging too closely to the friendship of the Jews, he publicly revealed to everyone how great an evildoer the little man was and for what reason he had obtained the wealth of the Jews.

Robert was immediately seized and, after being tormented with sharp scourges, confessed the crime for which he himself was responsible. Soon afterward, at the command of the king’s ministers, he was taken outside the city in the sight of the entire populace, handed over to the fire, and consumed.

The Jewish fugitives and wanderers who had survived the aforesaid disaster by hiding in remote places began, after five years had passed since the destruction of the temple, to appear again in the cities, though only in very small numbers. Since it is necessary—even if only for their confusion—that some of them survive in the future, either to confirm their own wickedness or to bear witness to the blood of Christ, we believe that, by the dispensation of divine providence, the hostility of Christians toward them was for a time softened.

In that same year, through the clemency of God, the mother of the ruler himself—namely, the emir of Babylon—a most Christian woman named Maria began to rebuild, with polished and squared stones, the temple of Christ that had been destroyed by order of her son. Her husband also, like another Nicodemus, the father of the son who is the subject of this account, is said to have been a Christian in secret.

At that time an astonishing multitude of people from every part of the world traveled joyfully to Jerusalem and brought many gifts for the restoration of the house of God.

# Chapter VIII. On the Heresy Discovered at Orléans

In the twenty-third year after the aforementioned thousandth year, an extremely crude and unusual heresy was discovered in the aforesaid city of Orléans. It had long secretly germinated and, growing wickedly into a crop of destruction, cast many into the snare of its blindness.

This utterly insane heresy is said to have begun in Gaul through a certain woman who came from Italy. Since she was full of the devil, she seduced whomever she wished—not only ignorant and simple people but also many who appeared to be more learned and belonged to the clerical order.

When she came to the city of Orléans and remained there for some time, she infected many with the poison of her wickedness. Those who had received this evil seed also attempted with all their strength to scatter it among still more people.

There were two leaders of this perverse doctrine—alas, what grief!—who were thought to be the most influential in the clergy of the city by birth and learning. One was called Heribert, the other Lisoius.

As long as the matter remained hidden, they enjoyed the highest favor both with the king and with the nobles of the palace. For this reason they were able to deceive people more easily, since the minds of those people had been less firmly bound by love of the universal faith.

They attempted to spread their wicked doctrine not only in the aforesaid city but also in neighboring cities. Wishing to make a priest of sound mind in the city of Rouen a companion of their madness, they sent messengers to him who explained the whole secret of this perverse doctrine and instructed him in it.

They said that the entire people would soon fall into their doctrine. When the priest learned this, he immediately went to the most Christian count of that city, Richard, and explained to him the whole course of the matter as he had discovered it.

The count immediately sent word to the king, openly informing him that a clandestine plague affecting Christ’s sheep had arisen in his own kingdom. When the king, Robert, learned this—for he was highly learned and most Christian—he became exceedingly sad and sorrowful, since he truly feared both the ruin of his country and the destruction of souls.

Therefore he hurried as quickly as possible to Orléans and summoned many bishops, abbots, religious men, and laypeople. He began to investigate most rigorously who the authors of this perverse doctrine were and who, having already been deceived, agreed with them.

An inquiry was conducted among the clergy into how each person understood and believed those things that the Catholic faith, through apostolic teaching, unchangeably preserves and proclaims. The two men, Lisoius and Heribert, immediately revealed themselves as the sort of people they had long concealed themselves to be, not denying that they held different beliefs.

After them, many others declared that they adhered to their party and affirmed that they could not in any way separate themselves from their company.

When the king and the bishops learned this, they became still more sorrowful and questioned them privately, since until then they had been men of the utmost usefulness in moral integrity. Lisoius was held especially dear in the monastery of the Holy Cross of the clergy; Heribert held the chief authority over the school of the church of Saint Peter, called Puellaris.

When they were asked from whom or where this presumption had come to them, they gave the following reply:

“It is a long time since we embraced the sect that you have only now recognized. We have been waiting for both you and everyone else, whatever their law or order, to fall into it; and we still believe that this will happen.”

After saying this, they immediately set forth publicly the most foolish and wretched of all ancient heresies—the heresy that had deceived them.

Its reasoning was all the less supported by adequate arguments because it is plainly three times contrary to the truth. They declared that everything which the authority of the Old and New Canon confirms with clear signs and miracles, and which the ancient witnesses testify concerning the blessed Trinity and Unity of the Godhead, was mere delirium.

They also asserted that heaven and earth, as they are seen, had always existed without any author or beginning. In their madness, barking like dogs and worse than all heresies, they resembled the Epicurean heretics only in this respect: they believed that no punishment of retribution was assigned for the crimes of pleasure.

They judged every Christian work of piety and justice—which is considered worthy of eternal reward—to be useless labor.

While they shamelessly uttered these and many other insanities, faithful and competent witnesses of the truth were lacking who could answer them sufficiently concerning their blind and erroneous assertions, so that they might submit both to the truth and to their own salvation. [Col. 0660D]

But we too, according to the smallness of our understanding, have decided to respond, however briefly, to the errors of those whom we mentioned above. First, however, we exhort all the faithful that meanwhile their minds may be calmed by the Apostle’s prophecy, who, foreseeing such a danger in the future, declared: “There must be heresies, so that those who are of the faith may be tested.”

In this matter, therefore, the folly of these men is especially exposed, and they are recognized as wholly devoid of every kind of knowledge and wisdom, since they deny the Creator of all creatures, namely God. For it is evident that everything, whatever its size or magnitude, if it is surpassed in magnitude by something else, is understood to have proceeded from the greatest of all; and by the same reasoning this must be understood both of corporeal and incorporeal things.

It must also be understood that whatever thing—whether corporeal or incorporeal—is made different from the immovable governor of things through any accident, movement, or alteration whatsoever, plainly proceeded through him; and, if it should perhaps come to rest, it seeks its end. For since the Maker of the whole creation is immovable in his own essence, good and truthful in his own essence, distributing and ordering the modes of natures ineffably by his omnipotence, there is nowhere apart from him where they may seek rest unless they return to the place from which they proceeded.

It is also evident that nothing has been lost by the Maker among all things, except that which, impudently, has overstepped the order of nature established by him. And therefore every thing is so much better and truer in what it is known to be as it stands more solidly and firmly within the order of its own nature. Thus all things that unchangeably obey his disposition continually proclaim their Creator through their service. But if any thing, impudently departing from him, has fallen into a worse state, it has provided a lesson while the others rightly remain in their proper condition.

Among the creatures mentioned above there is a certain middle class, namely the human race, superior to all living creatures but inferior to the heavenly spirits. This race, as we have said, standing midway between those above and those below, becomes like whichever side it cleaves to more closely. For this reason it becomes so much better and more elevated among the lowest creatures as it imitates the nature of the heavenly spirits.

To human beings alone it was granted, in comparison with the other living creatures, to become blessed; and likewise, if deprived of that blessing, the human being alone becomes more wretched than all the others. The goodness of the omnipotent Creator, carefully foreseeing this order of things from the beginning, and frequently observing that the same human being, by abandoning what is above, was becoming excessively entangled in what is below, therefore repeatedly performed, at the appropriate times, many signs for his instruction and encouragement.

Every book, indeed every page, of the divine writings is a witness and proof of this. These writings, discovered through the teaching of the Almighty himself, bear in a special way manifold testimony to him and raise the mind, or understanding, of the human being instructed by them toward the knowledge and contemplation of his Creator. Finally, by showing human beings what they have been placed above and beneath what they have been placed, they instill in them an insatiable desire; for everything that is present begins to displease them to the extent that they grow ardent in love for what is absent. Thus they become better and more beautiful the nearer they approach these absent realities through love. [Col. 0661D]

And insofar as they become better, they become more like the Creator, who is supremely good. Therefore it is plainly understood that whoever among human beings has been empty of the desire born of this love will undoubtedly become more wretched and worse than a beast. For although the human being alone among all living creatures was able to attain the blessedness of eternity, no corporeal animal besides him will experience eternal punishment for its own error or wrongdoing.

But if anyone’s mind desires knowledge of its Creator, it is fitting that he first strive to understand how he ought to conduct himself, insofar as he is able. For, as authoritative teaching—by no means to be disregarded—testifies, the human being especially bears the likeness of the Creator in that he is able, more than the other living creatures, through the gift and power of reason.

And just as the good of reason is preserved by self-restraint and love of the Creator—that is, by true humility and perfect charity—so wicked desire and rage destroy its usefulness. By failing to resist these, the human being becomes like the beasts; by serving those virtues, he is conformed to the likeness or image of the Creator. Thus, through humility, he understands what he is; through love, he passes into the likeness of the good Creator.

For this reason also prayers and offerings are offered by human beings to him alone, so that they may preserve the gift of reason intact, or, if it has been corrupted, so that the goodness of the Creator may increase and restore it. Praise and blessing are likewise offered to that same Creator, so that they may become a testimony of his knowledge to human beings sound in mind and vigorous in reason. And the more each person progresses in knowledge of the Creator, the more that person discovers himself to have been made both greater and better through the same knowledge.

Nor can anyone who has been made wholly better through knowledge of his Creator be blasphemous in any work of that Creator. Therefore it is evident that whoever has been blasphemous toward his work has been a stranger to knowledge of him. Hence it is also most certainly proved that just as knowledge of the Creator leads every human being to the highest good, so ignorance of him plunges him into the utmost evils.

For many, through folly ungrateful for his benefits, mocking the works of his mercy and remaining unbelieving, have become worse than beasts and have been plunged forever into the darkness of their blindness. What happened to many as the greatest remedy for their salvation, others have instead made, through their preceding guilt, an eternal loss for themselves.

This is most clearly and emphatically apparent in the singular grace of the omnipotent Father, sent of his own will from heaven into the world for human beings through the co-eternal Son of his majesty and divinity, namely Jesus Christ. [Col. 0662C] He, together with the Father, showed himself plainly to believers as the equal origin of all life, truth, and goodness.

Unknown throughout the ages and wrapped in hidden mysteries, he was the complete fulfillment of the testimony borne concerning him by the Scriptures. In him, through truthful words and signs, he made it certain that he himself, his Father, and their Spirit are one and the same in three distinct and most certain persons—that is, of one eternity, one power, one will, and one operation—and that this whole reality is one goodness and an essence wholly co-equal.

From him, through him, and in him are all things that truly possess being: he is always full and equally subsisting, the beginning of things before all the courses of time, and his fullness is throughout all things and the end of all things. [Col. 0662D]

But when the Almighty had expressed his own image in one of the middle orders of creatures, namely in the human being, and had left him to his own free choice, and had moreover subjected all the best things of the world to his rule, the human being neglected the restraint prescribed by his own constitution and, supposing himself to be something greater or other than the Creator’s will had determined, immediately became so much worse as he became more presumptuous.

For the sake of his more effective restoration, therefore, the same Creator sent into the world the person of the Son of his divinity, destined to assume the image prefigured by him. This image was the more useful and fitting because it was the more subtle and wondrous. Many human beings, however, unable or unwilling to believe or love it, so that they might at last find in it the sufficiency of their salvation understood, instead became entangled in various errors and proved all the more rebellious against the truth as they were shown to be strangers to knowledge of it.

To this lot undoubtedly belong all heresies and sects of every kind of error throughout the whole world. For all of them, unless they are converted and follow Jesus in the fullness of his deeds, it would have been better not to have existed. But those whose minds, full of faith, obeyed him by loving and believing became so much better through him as they adhered more perfectly to him who is the beginning and perfection of all good.

From these, indeed, is composed the entire praiseworthy company of the saints, whose venerable memory adorns all the ages of time. To them also it has been granted to exist and live eternally and happily with the Creator of all things, and to become ever more blessed through the vision of his knowledge.

We therefore believe that, as we had promised, we have sufficiently answered, in these few words, the madness of those condemned men.

Moreover, when many people had labored with every ingenuity to induce them, having laid aside their faithlessness of mind, to receive the true and universal faith, and when they obstinately denied that they would do so in any way, they were told that unless they returned more quickly to a sound state of faith, they would immediately be burned in fire by the king’s command and with the consent of the whole people.

But those men, wickedly trusting in their madness—or boasting that they were not afraid—and promising that they would escape the fire unharmed, even mocked with disdain those who urged them toward better things. When the king and all who were present saw that they could scarcely be recalled from their madness, he ordered an enormous fire to be lit not far from the city, so that perhaps, terrified by it, they might abandon their wickedness.

When they were led toward it, driven on by rabid insanity, they proclaimed that they desired this in every respect and voluntarily thrust themselves toward the fire. Finally, when thirteen of them had been handed over to the flames and had begun to burn more fiercely, they began, with whatever voice they could summon from within the fire, to cry out that they had recently been horribly deceived by the devil’s art and had held wrong opinions about the universal God and Lord; and that, because of the blasphemy they had uttered against him, they were being tortured by temporal and eternal vengeance.

When many of the bystanders heard this, they were moved by human compassion and approached in order to rescue them, even though they were half alive; but they were entirely unable to do so, because the avenging flame consumed them and immediately reduced them to ashes.

If any followers of this perversity were later found, they were everywhere destroyed by a similar punishment. Moreover, the venerable worship of the Catholic faith, after the madness of these worst of madmen had been uprooted, shone more brightly throughout the world.

## CHAPTER IX. On the Sons of the Same King

The aforesaid king therefore had four sons by his wife mentioned above. Concerned for the succession of the kingdom, he chose his firstborn, named Hugh, to reign after him—a boy still, but distinguished by the brilliance of his character. When he had prudently consulted the more discerning nobles of the kingdom about the boy’s being raised to the dignity of consecration, they gave him this answer: “Leave the boy, if it please you, O king, to advance through growth into manhood, lest, as was done in your own case, you entrust the burden of so great a kingdom to an unsteady age.” The boy was then nearly ten years old.

He did not at all heed their words. With his mother especially urging him on, he summoned the principal nobles of the kingdom to the royal residence at Compiègne and, as he had decided, had the boy crowned according to custom by the bishops. In the course of time, when he had grown up and saw that from the kingdom in which he had been crowned he could command no particular authority beyond food and clothing, he began to grieve in his heart and complain to his father that he should grant him some share of power.

When his mother learned of this, she—being exceedingly avaricious and her husband’s instructor—resisted the request and, moreover, assailed the young man with insults and curses. As someone says: “I know the disposition of women: when you wish, she herself does not; but if you do not wish, she will desire it of her own accord.” For she who previously, lest she lack any royal dignity, had raised the boy against everyone’s decision when her husband’s misfortune pressed upon him, later disgraced him in word and deed with all the force of her mind, as though he were a foreign enemy.

Seeing that he could no longer endure such treatment with composure, he joined some young men of his own age and began to harass and plunder his parents’ property at will. Yet shortly afterward, by God’s will, he came to his senses and, returning to his parents, made them well disposed toward him by humble satisfaction. At last they granted him, as befitted an excellent son, authority and power over the kingdom everywhere.

But what kind and how great he later proved to be cannot be explained in the present style. How humble and sweet in speech, more obedient to his father and mother than any servant, a generous giver to the poor, a consoler of monks and clerics, and, before his father, the most faithful intercessor for all who made petitions; how abundantly superior to everyone in every excellence—what narrator could relate it?

His reputation, spreading rapidly through all the provinces, caused many, especially the Italians, to desire him as their ruler and to raise him to imperial power. Indeed, from the surname of his great-grandfather, everyone called him Hugh the Great.

While he flourished in incomparable beauty of mind and body alike, the sins of his ancestors demanded it, and envious death suddenly snatched him from the world. But what mourning befell everyone cannot be expressed in any speech. At the request of his brothers, I composed the following iambics about his funeral:

> Maker, spare the mourners throughout the world;  
> Let weeping come to the innermost griefs.  
> Let the sobs of sighs feed those who mourn,  
> While death snatches away human glory.
>
> He flourished in the world in youthful years;  
> He had reached only twenty-eight years.  
> Hugh, light of kingdoms, greatest of kings—  
> Him the mournful night begrudged to humankind.
>
> No other such man shines in our age,  
> Honored by kingdoms, chosen for empire.  
> May he be adorned with so great a triumph of wars,  
> May he possess equal strength of body.
>
> Through him the Frankish people flourished joyfully,  
> And all Gaul together in faith and peace.  
> All Italy, bowing down, demanded him,  
> That he might exercise the imperial rights of Caesar.
>
> But our times did not deserve you,  
> O most beautiful of young men—alas, bitter grief!  
> Times in which the miseries of evils overflow  
> And the strength of the good continually collapses.
>
> You are your mother’s grief and your father’s calamity,  
> A monument cruel beyond measure to your brothers;  
> Common sorrow in all the palaces,  
> And mourning for the peoples to the furthest bounds.
>
> When the Lion was oppressed, the Virgin had seized the sun,  
> When a dreadful pallor occupied your limbs.  
> On the tenth day, by fate, the seventh light appeared;  
> The report reached your father that you were lost.
>
> Now behold, best ruler of the ages,  
> Who may govern the Frankish people most safely  
> And be able to repel the savage enemy:  
> Grant him a pact of perpetual peace.

He was buried in the same church in which he had first been crowned, namely that of the blessed martyr Cornelius, at the royal residence of Compiègne.

After his death, the same king again began to deliberate which of his remaining sons ought most suitably to reign after him. He had decided that Henry, named duke of Burgundy and born after Hugh, should succeed Hugh, and he resolved to raise him to the kingdom in place of his brother.

But once again his mother, driven by womanly hostility, dissented both from the father and from the others who favored Henry’s party, saying: “The third son, who was also called by the name of his father Robert, is more excellent for governing the kingdom.” This was the seedbed of discord between the brothers.

Finally, after assembling the principal nobles of the kingdom at the metropolitan city of Reims, the king established Henry, whom he had chosen, with the crown of the kingdom. Then, after some time had passed, the two brothers, having formed a pact of friendship, began—chiefly because of their mother’s insolence—to invade by force the villages and castles of their father and to plunder all the property of his that they could seize in the surrounding regions.

The one whom he had made king took the castle of Dreux from him; the other took Avallon and Beaune [variant: Bellensem] in Burgundy. Deeply distressed by these acts, the king gathered an army and marched into Burgundy: a war more than civil was waged.

Meanwhile, when he had consulted the venerable Father William at the castle of Dijon about what he ought to do, and had asked him—as a man of complete gentleness and piety—to pray to the Lord for him and for his sons, he received this answer from him:

“Remember, O king, the injuries and insults that you inflicted on your father and mother in your youth. For, with God as the just judge permitting it, such things are being inflicted on you by your sons as you yourself inflicted on your parents.”

Hearing this, the king bore it with the greatest patience. Crying out that he himself was plainly guilty, he did not deny it. Then, after the siege and devastation of both provinces, they returned to peace and rested for a little while.

In the following year, in the month of July, King Robert died at the castle of Melun. His body was carried to the church of the holy martyr Dionysius and buried there.

Then once again a renewed cruelty of discord arose between the mother and her sons, and long-standing hatreds loosened the restraints of their former anger. They raged for a long time, devastating their own possessions, until Fulk, count of Anjou, their kinsman [variant: maternal uncle], rebuked their mother for exercising such bestial madness against her sons and brought both sides back to peace.

In the following year, in the same month and in the same castle where the king had died, she too died. From there she was carried to the basilica of Saint-Denis and buried beside the king.

King Henry, having taken possession of his father’s property, appointed his brother Robert duke of Burgundy.

Moreover, while the same king was managing the affairs of his kingdom with an active mind and vigorous body, it happened that Leoteric, archbishop of Sens, died. Henry ordered one of the nobles of his own people to be consecrated and installed in his place.

But Odo, exceedingly rich in possessions though poor in faith, had chosen another candidate in opposition, lest royal authority remain intact in this matter. For just as he had earlier seized many things from his living father Robert by both force and cunning, so he wished by similar craft to act against his sons.

After he had first taken from Robert the cities of Troyes and Meaux, together with many castles, after Robert’s death he seized the city of Sens from Robert’s wife and sons; he had also then fortified it against them as its infamous possessor.

When Henry saw this, he pursued him in battle with such fierce determination for so long that Odo finally bent the knee, surrendered to him, and obeyed under his authority.

This Odo was born from Berta, daughter of King Conrad of the Austrasians, although through the ancestors of his father he derived his lineage from an obscure line. Since King Rudolph, his maternal uncle, had no offspring who could be heir to the kingdom, Odo presumed, while Rudolph was still alive, to seize the reins of the kingdom by force rather than affection, additionally offering many gifts so that the leading men of the country might give him their support.

But all in vain: “The kingdom is the Lord’s, and he will give it to whomever he wishes.” There is also the proverb: “According to a man’s faith, so shall his friend be.” For the people, especially, of that kingdom held his profession of faith in contempt and regarded the pact as nothing.

After the death of Emperor Henry, who was the nephew of King Rudolph, there arose Conrad, about whom we shall speak later. He had married a niece of the aforesaid Rudolph and therefore strongly opposed Odo.

Their dispute caused the greatest devastation of both kingdoms. At last, when the measure of so great an evil had already exceeded the bounds of God’s sight, Odo gathered an enormous army from every direction and entered the region of Toul, which he had already often devastated. There he attacked and captured the castle of Bar, though the entire province was greatly ravaged and overthrown.

Having stationed nearly five hundred soldiers in the castle for its defense, he himself hastened to return to his own territories, being driven by innumerable concerns. Meanwhile envoys sent from Italy awaited him, bringing him, as they said, the pledge of leadership over the whole region of Italy.

For the Milanese had rejected their own ruler, the aforementioned Conrad, having conspired against him and joined to themselves as many men as they could from the surrounding cities. They also thought that Odo might obtain the kingdom of the Austrasians and come over to them to rule them.

But, as Manufortis, the distinguished chanter of the Lord’s battles, says: “You cast them down when they were rising up.” So it happened. For suddenly Gocilo, duke of the whole region of First Rhaetia on this side of the Rhine, attacked him with a very large army and put Odo’s entire army to flight, although a great multitude fell dead on both sides.

At last Odo himself perished most miserably. Roger, bishop of the Catalans, taking his mangled corpse from the slaughter, and accompanied by the venerable abbot Richard, returned it to his wife.

[Note: In one manuscript the following is added in the margin, but by a more recent hand.]

[Many also relate that his body could not be found, although it was sought for a long time, until his wife came and discovered it by this distinguishing sign: he had a wart between his genitals and his anus.]

When it had been found in this way, she took possession of it and sent it to Tours, where it was buried beside his father in the atrium of the upper monastery of Saint Martin.

Such was the end of Odo. We wished to weave him into this narrative so that it might be known in the present how the most just Creator of all things powerfully fulfills what he once promised to his lawgiver Moses:

“I am the Lord, who judge the sins of fathers in their sons to the third and fourth generation.”

For this third Odo, about whom we have just spoken, was the grandson of that Theobald, count of Chartres, whose surname was Trickster.

Once, together with Arnulf, count of Flanders, Theobald sent envoys to summon William, duke of Rouen, as though to a friendly conference for peace. He promised, on behalf of the king of the Franks—or of Hugh the Great, who had been the son of King Robert, whom Otto, duke of the Saxons and later emperor of the Romans, killed at Soissons—that he would say things useful to him.

William was an innocent man, although very powerful. When he learned where Theobald had arranged the meeting, he traveled by boat along the Seine and quickly came to him.

When they met and rushed into one another’s arms, one side acting in genuine simplicity, while the others were enticed by deceit, they mingled words of pretended peace and friendship. After the end of their deceptive conversation, as William had begun to depart and was already some distance away, Theobald called him back, as though he still intended to speak more privately with him or to bid him a dearer farewell.

William took an oar in his right hand and ordered none of his men who were leaving to follow him. He leapt ashore. Theobald approached him, as though about to say something, then immediately drew the sword he had brought for this purpose from beneath his cloak and, with a single blow, severed his head from his body.

Those who had come with William saw this, seized their escape by rowing away, and reported to the people of Rouen what had happened.

William had a son by a concubine, named Richard, still a young man. His followers received him and established him as ruler of the kingdom in place of his father.

After committing the crime, Theobald hurried to Herbert, count of Troyes, asking that his sister be given to him in marriage—the wife, that is, of the aforesaid William, whom he had murdered.

Herbert immediately promised that she would be given to him. Calling her to a private conference, although she had not yet borne a child, he handed her over to Theobald as though to console her for the loss of her husband. It was a thoroughly detestable marriage.

By her he begot Odo, the father of the man whose most horrible end we described above.

It also seemed appropriate to recall at the end of the third book how divine power, the avenger and moderator of all good, at the present time showed itself an avenger of the insolence of the human race.

Around the thousandth year of the incarnate Word, when King Robert had taken Queen Constance from Aquitaine in marriage, people began to flock, on account of that queen, into France and Burgundy from Auvergne and Aquitaine. They were exceedingly frivolous in every respect, distorted in manners and dress, disorderly in weapons and the trappings of their horses, shaven on the crown of the head, bearded in the manner of actors, disgraceful in their leggings and boots, and entirely lacking the bond of faith and peace.

Alas, bitter grief! The whole Frankish people, previously the most honorable of all, and the Burgundians, thirsting for novelty, seized upon their wicked examples until everyone became conformed to their depravity and shamefulness.

If any religious person who feared God attempted to restrain those who practiced such things, they branded him as mad. But the man of most upright faith and steadfastness, Father William, whom we have already mentioned, cast aside shame and took up a spiritual denunciation. He severely rebuked both king and queen for permitting such things to occur in their kingdom, which had long excelled other kingdoms in honor and religious observance.

He also rebuked people of lower rank or order and threatened them so forcefully that many, restrained by his admonitions, abandoned their superstitious vanity and restored themselves to their former practice.

The same abbot therefore declared that all these contrivances were the armor of Satan; and that if anyone wearing such armor departed from this world, he could scarcely be freed from the devil’s bonds.

Yet among many people this wicked custom grew stronger. I recorded its detestable description in a few heroic verses:

> In the thousandth year after the Lord was born on earth from the Virgin,  
> While human beings, driven by grave errors,  
> Desire to turn their attention to more and more outward appearances,  
> And delight in arranging their conduct according to abandoned practices,  
> An unwary novelty presents itself amid dangers.
>
> Behold, they laugh at former things for themselves,  
> And make a mockery of the ages of our time;  
> They join everything to disgrace and adapt it to their practices,  
> They do not recoil from shameful things, and trample serious matters underfoot.
>
> They reject the honorable things that governed upright men.  
> With a distorted body, this age now creates tyrants,  
> Men in truncated clothing, senseless without the pact of peace.  
> The state, loosened by womanly counsel, groans.
>
> Fraud, abduction, and every crime dominate throughout the world.  
> There is no honor for the holy, no reverence for sacred things.  
> Hence sword, pestilence, and famine ravage everywhere.
>
> Yet impiety did not spare humankind even after it had been corrected.  
> And unless the great mercy of God held back his anger,  
> Hell would consume these people with its earth-shaking mouth.
>
> Such is the effect of the unhappy habit of sinning:  
> The more a person sins, the less he fears to sin here;  
> The less a person sins, the more he fears to sin here.

# BOOK FOUR

[Col. 0669]

## CONTENTS OF BOOK FOUR

I. On the universality of the Church unjustly demanded by the Constantinopolitans.  
II. On a heresy discovered in Italy.  
III. That, because the sins of human beings demand it, and with the Lord permitting it, miracles are sometimes performed by wicked spirits.  
IV. On the very severe famine that occurred throughout the world.  
V. On the peace and abundance of the thousandth year from the Lord’s Passion.  
VI. On the gathering of the people of the whole world that took place at the Lord’s tomb in Jerusalem.  
VII. On the battles of the Saracens against the Christians in the regions of Africa.  
VIII. On the battle of the Leutici against the Christians in the northern regions.  
IX. On the sign that appeared in the sun.

## PREFACE

[Col. 0669B]

After the many miraculous signs that occurred throughout the world both before and after, though around, the thousandth year of the Lord Christ, it is clear that there were many industrious men of shrewd judgment who predicted that no lesser events would occur as the thousandth year of the Lord’s Passion approached. This indeed happened most conspicuously.

After the death, as we have already said, of the most pious Emperor Henry, who had no offspring to succeed him in the kingdom, certain men from among the leading nobles attempted to put themselves forward—not so much to exercise the government of the state and the administration of justice as to shine with the crown of the kingdom.
