Above all, therefore, there was a certain Conrad, whom we censured earlier, bold in spirit and mighty in strength, but not very firm in faith. After much and prolonged discussion about establishing a ruler of the kingdom, especially among the bishops, it seemed to them that Conrad himself ought to be chosen, except for one matter on account of which Henry had also hated him greatly.

He had a wife who was related to him, and whom a certain kinsman of his had previously married. The bishops, moreover, made known to him what he most preferred: whether to retain such a marriage, which manifestly conflicted with sacred authority, or, having dismissed her, to receive the imperial crown.

He immediately promised to dismiss this incestuous marriage, to follow their words with the greatest diligence, and to obey their counsels. Then they sent to the Roman pope, asking him to consent to what they had decided.

He readily agreed, instructing them in addition that, as soon as Conrad had received the scepter of Germany, he should go to Rome to receive the crown of all Italy. [Col. 0670B]

Meanwhile, after obtaining the royal insignia, Conrad went to Italy, taking with him the wife whom, as we said, he had taken in an illicit marriage. As he descended the Alps, at the town called, though corruptly, Curiam Gallorum [“the Gauls’ Court”; reading uncertain], the Roman pope met him at Como with the greatest display, as he had previously promised.

At that time certain Italian margraves gave him less support. For it is their custom, as we noted above, to act in this way at the deaths of emperors. The people of Pavia, too—the proudest of all—had demolished to the ground, at great expense and labor, the king’s palace constructed in their city.

When Conrad learned of this, he attacked fiercely. First he captured the city of Ivrea, then he subjected the others, together with all their castles, to his authority. Thus arriving at Rome, he received the imperial crown according to custom.

When the bishops urged him to repudiate his illicit marriage by the authority of the Roman pontiff, as he had promised them, he took the matter very badly and said that, having been made emperor, he ought in no way to be deprived of his wife. Thus, as he had foolishly begun, he continued.

## CHAPTER ONE

### On the Universality of the Church Unjustly Demanded by the Constantinopolitans

*[The supplied source ends here.]*
Around the year of the Lord 1024, therefore, the bishop of Constantinople, together with his prince Basil, and certain other Greeks, formed a plan whereby, with the consent of the Roman pontiff, the Church of Constantinople might be called and regarded as universal within its own sphere, just as the Roman Church was universal throughout the world. They immediately sent men to Rome bearing many and varied gifts, both for the pontiff and for the others whom they perceived to favor their side. When these men arrived, they presented to the pontiff the grievance that had occasioned their journey.

But what will blind love of gain not attempt? There is a proverb: “With a golden fist one breaks an iron wall.” And although, for a time, avarice may be called the queen of the world, among the Romans it nevertheless established an insatiable lodging. For as soon as they saw that the Greeks were bringing them glittering wealth, their hearts turned toward the byways of fraud, testing whether they might secretly grant what was being requested. But not at all. For the highest Truth cannot be deceived, since it promised: “The gates of hell shall not prevail against it.”

While the plotters were still imagining that, in the quietest murmur, they had discussed such matters in the inner chamber, swift rumor about them ran throughout all Italy. What tumult and violent disturbance then arose among all who heard of it cannot be said. Above all, however, the most prudent man, Father Willelmus, of whom we have already spoken, sent the Roman pontiff a letter concerning this matter—brief in body, but immense in subject and sharp in language—which contained the following:

“Willelmus, servant of the cross of Christ, to Pope John [variant: Gregory], who has attained, by the grace of God and reverence for the seat of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles—the most excellent of sees in the world—the seat of judgment with the apostles and the crown of the kingdom.

“We are instructed by the words of the Teacher of the Nations that an elder should not be rebuked. Yet he also says elsewhere: ‘I have become a fool; you compelled me.’ Therefore, with the diligence proper to a son, we urge your common fatherhood to imitate, in one matter, the thoughts of men, while looking to the provident Lord and Savior, so that you may say to someone of one mind with you, as he himself once said to Peter: ‘What do men say about me?’

“If his answer is given in faith, observe how it sounds. If it is clear, take care that it not be darkened. If it is obscure, the light of the world must be entreated, so that you may shine in such a way as to provide light to all who are established within the bosom of the Church, enabling them to walk along the path of God’s commandments.

“But there is a report concerning an event that has recently occurred among us, and whoever hears of it and is not scandalized should know that he is far removed from heavenly love. For although the power of the Roman Empire, which once exercised monarchy throughout the world, is now governed by innumerable scepters in different lands, the power of binding and loosing on earth and in heaven rests, by an inviolable gift, upon the teaching office of Peter.

“We have said this so that you may realize that the Greeks have obtained from you a request no different from the vainglory of which we have heard. For the rest, we wish you, as befits a universal bishop, to be all the more vigorous in the correction and discipline of the holy and apostolic Church, and to remain eternally and happily in good health.”

This John [Gregory] was called “the Roman.” He was the brother of that Benedict [John] whom he had succeeded in the episcopate; he had suddenly been made a bishop from the lay order, a neophyte appointed through the gift of money. The arrogance of the Romans has devised the following kind of absurdity disguised by cunning: whoever they presently choose at their pleasure for the office of pontiff, they decree that, after changing his former name, he should be called by the name of one of the great pontiffs. Thus, in truth, if he does not possess the merit of the office, at least the name may exalt him.

The men of Constantinople, meanwhile, returned to their own country, and their arrogant presumption, refuted on every side, subsided.

## CHAPTER II  
### On a heresy discovered in Italy

At that time, therefore, there was a fortress in the land of the Lombards which was called what it was: namely, Mons Fortis, “Strong Mountain.” It was filled with members of the nobility of that same people. Heretical perversity had so stained all of them that they preferred to meet a cruel death rather than in any way be recalled from it to the most saving faith of Christ the Lord.

They worshiped idols in the pagan manner and attempted, together with the Jews, to offer foolish sacrifices. Very often Mainfred, the wisest of the marquises, his brother Alricus, bishop of the city of Asti—in whose diocese the aforesaid fortress was situated—and the other surrounding marquises and bishops launched repeated attacks against them. They captured some of them, and when they could not recall them from their madness, they burned them in the fire.

It happened, then, that nearby there was another fortress belonging to our religion and faith. In it a certain soldier once fell ill and came almost to the point of death. To visit him, a prominent woman from the fortress of the heretics came, as was their custom. Indeed, her visit served rather to make the wickedness of their sect more evident. As soon as she entered the house where the sick man lay, he suddenly looked up and saw an innumerable army entering with the woman: they wore blackest garments and had most hideous faces.

After the woman had entered and, as custom required, examined the sick man’s forehead, felt the pulse of his chest, and performed the other customary examinations with her hand, she declared that he would soon recover. Then she left the house, and the entire household departed with her, leaving the sick man alone.

Immediately the throng of black beings whom he had seen appeared before him. Their apparent leader addressed him:

“Do you recognize me?” he said. The sick man’s name was Hugo.

When Hugo replied, “Who are you?” the other said to him:

“I am the most powerful of the powerful and the richest of the rich, and I have come to you. If you believe that I have the power to rescue you from the death that now threatens you, you will live for a long time. And so that you may believe with complete certainty what I promise, know that through my help and ingenuity Chuonrad has now been made emperor. You know very well that no emperor has so swiftly subjected all Germany and Italy to his rule as he has.”

“I know,” replied the sick man, “and for a long time it seemed wondrous to me and to the others.”

Then the author of the first deception added:

“Did I not also, in the lands across the sea, hand over the kingdom of the Greeks, after Basil, to Michael, who obeyed me? Therefore believe me, and I will do for you far greater things than you could hope for; I will restore you to health.”

At that time there was a report that this Michael had been Basil’s chamberlain and had secretly given him poison in his drink to kill him. Without doubt, after Basil’s death, Michael took the crown of the empire. His administration of the empire, as was to be expected, was not especially beneficial.

Meanwhile, the aforementioned Hugo came to himself and, attempting with his right hand to make the sign of the venerable cross, said:

“But I call Jesus, the Son of God, as witness. I adore, believe in, and confess him. I shall believe you to be no one other than what you were and are: a deceitful devil.”

Then the demon immediately cried out:

“Please do not raise your arm against me.”

And at once the entire throng vanished like smoke. Hugo cried out as loudly as he could, and the members of his household came running. He related to them, in order, what he had seen and heard. After he had said these things, he died that same day before sunset. No one can doubt that he saw these things for his own sake and for ours.

## CHAPTER III  
### That, because human sins demand it and the Lord permits it, miracles are sometimes performed by evil spirits

The divine authority delivered through Moses to the Jews warned them in the following manner:

“If there is a prophet among you,” it says, “speaking in the name of any of the gods of the nations, who foretells something that is to happen and it happens by chance, do not believe him, for the Lord your God is testing you, to know whether you love him or not.”

We therefore have, in the present matter, an example that is different in circumstance but not dissimilar in kind.

At the time prescribed above there was a common man, a most cunning peddler, though of unknown name and homeland. Seeking concealment in different places so that he would not be recognized, he fraudulently adopted different names and claimed to belong to whatever province suited him. He also secretly dug bones from tombs, removing them from the ashes of people who had only recently died. He placed them in various reliquaries and sold them to many people as relics of holy martyrs or confessors.

After carrying out innumerable such deceptions in Gaul, he fled to the Alpine regions, where uncivilized peoples often live, possessing many dwellings in the highlands. There he called himself Stephen, although elsewhere he had been called Peter and elsewhere John.

As was his custom, he secretly gathered at night the bones of an unknown man from a most desolate place. He placed them in a small chest and a bier, and said that an angelic revelation had disclosed to him that the bones belonged to a holy martyr whom he pretended was named Justus.

Immediately the crowd, as it is accustomed to behave in such matters, gathered at this report: all the lazy rural population flocked there. Moreover, people regretted not having some illness for which they could seek a cure. They brought the weak, offered little gifts, kept vigil through the night, and awaited sudden miracles—miracles which, as we have said, evil spirits are sometimes permitted to perform as a temptation, when human sins have preceded them. This was then made abundantly clear.

For many kinds of restorations of limbs were seen to have occurred there, and various remarkable votive offerings were hung up. Yet the bishops of Morianna, Utzetica, and Gratinona, in whose dioceses these profanations were taking place, made no effort to investigate the matter. Rather, establishing little councils, they demanded from the people nothing except foolish profit in some cases, and at the same time the favor of deceit.

Meanwhile Mainfred, the richest of the marquises, learning of this report, sent some of his men to seize by force the image that was being worshiped and bring it to him—the object they believed to be a venerable martyr.

The marquis ordered that a monastery be built in the fortress of Seutia, the oldest fortress among the Alps, in honor of almighty God and of his mother Mary, ever-virgin. He had also decided, once the work was completed, to place the image there together with many other holy relics.

A short while later, when the church had been completed and the day of its dedication had been appointed, the bishops living in the surrounding region were summoned. Among them came the often-mentioned abbot Willelmus, together with several other abbots.

By that time the aforementioned peddler had become very dear to the marquis, since he promised that he would soon reveal much more precious relics of saints. He deceitfully fabricated their acts, names, and contests of martyrdom, as well as everything else.

When the more learned men questioned him about how he had come to know such things, he answered with babble that was scarcely credible. I myself was present there, having arrived with the abbot mentioned so often.

“For an angel appears to me at night,” he said, “and tells and teaches me whatever he knows that I wish to learn. He remains with me until I compel him to depart.”

When we replied by asking whether he saw this while awake and sleepless, he continued:

“Almost every night the angel snatches me from my bed without my wife knowing. After many conversations, he bids me farewell, kisses me, and departs.”

Recognizing the lie stripped of its cunning, we understood that the man was not angelic, but rather a servant of fraud and wickedness.

Nevertheless, the bishops properly carried out the consecration of the church for which they had come, and they placed among the other relics the bones devised through that profane trick—though not without the great rejoicing of both groups of people, who had gathered there in immense numbers.

This happened on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of November [October 17]. The supporters of this error claimed that these were the bones of the martyr Justus who had suffered on that day in the Gallic city of Beauvais; they also claimed that his head had been carried back to Auxerre, where he had been born and raised, and was preserved there.

But I, who knew the novelty of the affair, declared that what was being said was frivolous. The more distinguished men, however, recognizing the fabrications of the deception, placed their faith in the assertion I had made.

On the following night, certain monks and other religious men saw monstrous apparitions in the same church. They also saw forms resembling black Ethiopians emerge from the little shrine in which the bones had been enclosed and leave the church.

Although many sane-minded people cried out that the detestable fabrication was abominable, the rural populace continued in its former error, venerating the corrupt peddler under the unjust name of Justus.

We have recounted these events so that people may beware of the manifold deceptions of demons and of human errors, which abound everywhere in the world—especially at springs and trees that the sick unwisely venerate.

## CHAPTER IV  
### On the most severe famine that occurred throughout the world

As the year 1033 of Christ’s incarnation approached—which was the thousandth year from the Passion of that same Savior—there died the most famous men in the Roman world and standard-bearers of holy religion: namely, Benedict, the universal pope [Note: [Col. 0675D] John XIX, not Benedict; he died in 1033], and, as we have already said, Robert, king of the Franks.

Fulbert, the incomparable bishop of Chartres, also died, as did the aforementioned father of monks and distinguished founder of monasteries, Willelmus. Much useful material about him would remain to be said, were it not already known to have been set forth in the little book that we composed about his life and virtues.

One thing nevertheless remains, which I know was not included there. The aforesaid Father departed from this world to the rest of the blessed in the regions of Neustria, namely in the monastery of Fécamp, situated above the Ocean Sea and lying approximately forty miles from the city of Rouen. He was buried, as befitted so great a man, in the finest place in that church.

Several days later, a boy of about ten years, overcome by a serious illness, was brought to his tomb in the hope of recovering his health. There his parents left him, and he lay alone. Suddenly he looked up and saw a little bird, resembling a dove, sitting upon the tomb. After gazing at it for a long time, he fell asleep.

Then, refreshed by gentle sleep, he awoke and found himself so completely restored that he felt as though he had suffered no illness at all. His joyful parents took him back, and the event became a common source of rejoicing for everyone.

Afterward, famine began to intensify throughout the whole world, and the destruction of nearly the entire human race seemed imminent. The condition of the air became so disordered that there was no suitable season for sowing, nor, especially because of the abundance of rain, was there any opportunity for harvesting. The elements themselves appeared to be waging a quarrelsome battle against one another, while undoubtedly exercising vengeance upon human arrogance.

The whole earth was so drenched by continual rains that for three years no useful furrows could be found for seed. At harvest time, wild grasses and the wretched darnel covered the entire surface of the fields. Where a measure of seed did best, it produced only a sextarius at harvest; and the sextarius itself scarcely yielded a handful.

This sterility of vengeance first began in the regions of the East. After laying waste to Greece, it reached Italy. Then spreading through Gaul, it passed to all the peoples of England.

The entire population was then bound by want of food; the great and the middling grew pale with hunger together with the poor. The plundering of the powerful yielded to universal scarcity. If any food was found for sale, the seller was free to raise or accept whatever price he wished. In many places a measure of grain cost sixty solidi; elsewhere a sextarius cost fifteen solidi.

After the animals and birds had been eaten, and the most savage hunger pressed upon them, people began to seize for food every kind of carrion and things horrible to mention. Some fled from death by taking refuge at the edges of forests and among river plants, but in vain. There is no escape from the anger of God’s vengeance except by turning to him.

It is dreadful to recount the forms of corruption that then befell the human race. Alas, for grief! What had once rarely been heard of was then compelled by raging hunger: human beings ate human flesh.

Travelers were seized by those stronger than themselves, divided limb by limb, cooked over a fire, and devoured. Many who moved from place to place fleeing hunger were received as guests, slaughtered during the night, and became food for those who had taken them in. Others lured children away by displaying an apple or an egg, then surrounded, killed, and devoured them in remote places. In many regions the bodies of the dead were dug out of the earth and likewise served to relieve hunger.

This madness of savagery grew to such an extent that it was safer for a flock of sheep to remain without a shepherd than for human beings to remain without a guardian against robbery. For it had almost become customary to eat human flesh. One man brought cooked human flesh for sale in the market at Tournus, as though it belonged to some animal. When he was caught, he did not deny the crime. Then, bound with straps, he was burned in the fire. Another man dug up that flesh, which had been buried in the ground, and ate it at night. He too was burned in the fire.

There is a church about three miles from the city of Mâcon, situated in the Castanedi forest, isolated and without a congregation, and dedicated to Saint John. Near it a savage man had built a hut. There he slaughtered crowds of travelers who either passed by or stopped with him, and turned them into the most abominable food.

One day a certain man and woman stopped there for lodging and rested briefly. Then, as he cast his eyes around the corners of the hut, the man saw the severed heads of men, women, and children. He immediately grew pale and wished to leave, but the pestilential owner of the hut resisted and forced him to remain.

Fearing the trap of death, however, the traveler prevailed and hurried with his wife to the city. When he arrived, he reported what he had discovered to Count Otto and the other citizens. They immediately sent a large number of men to investigate the truth. Going there swiftly, they found the most cruel man in his hut, together with forty-eight heads of those he had slaughtered; he had devoured their flesh with a beast’s mouth.

They led him back to the city and bound him to a stake in a certain granary. We later saw the place ourselves. There they burned him in the fire.

At that time people in the same regions also attempted something that we have never discovered anyone else to have done. Many dug up white earth resembling clay, mixed it with whatever flour or bran they possessed, and made loaves from it, hoping in this way to relieve the death of starvation. Their only hope in preparing it was to escape death, but the attempt was futile.

Pallor and emaciation held the faces of everyone, and in many people the skin appeared stretched by swelling. Human voices became extremely faint and imitated the chirping of dying birds.

At that time wolves, attracted by the numerous unburied corpses of the dead scattered everywhere, began after a long interval to prey upon human beings. And because, as we have said, the multitude made it impossible to bury the dead individually, people who feared God built in certain places structures commonly called charnel houses. Five hundred bodies, and more, or as many as the buildings could contain, were thrown in together without order, half-naked or without coverings.

Crossroads and the unused margins of fields served as cemeteries. If some people learned by hearsay that conditions were better elsewhere and set out for other fields, many died on the road from exhaustion.

The devastation of this pestilence raged throughout the world for three years, as human sins demanded it. The furnishings of churches were sold to pay the expenses of the needy, and their treasures were distributed—treasures which, according to the decrees of the Fathers, had originally been deposited there for this purpose.

Yet in many places the excess of the needy surpassed the treasures of the churches, so much did just punishment exceed what remained. Even the starving, overcome by extreme hunger, died immediately from distension when they happened to be filled with food. Others touched food with their hands and tried to place it in their mouths, but collapsed in convulsions, unable to complete what they desired.

No pen can express how great the pain then was, how great the sorrow, the sobbing, the lamentation, and the tears poured forth by those who witnessed such things—especially by men of ecclesiastical religion: bishops, abbots, monks, nuns, and all alike, of both sexes and every rank, who feared God.

It was thought that the order of time and the elements, which from the beginning had governed the ages, had fallen into perpetual chaos, and that the human race was coming to an end.

What was even more astonishing was that, amid such a hidden calamity of divine vengeance, scarcely anyone was found who, with contrite heart and humbled body, would raise his heart and hands to the Lord as was necessary and plead for help.

Then, indeed, the saying of Isaiah was fulfilled in our own time: “The people did not turn back to the one who struck them.”

There was in human beings a certain hardness of heart together with dullness of mind. For the supreme Judge and author of all goodness grants the will to ask him, and knows when he ought to have mercy.

## CHAPTER V  
### On the peace and abundance of the thousandth year from the Lord’s Passion

In the thousandth year from the Lord’s Passion, following the scarcity caused by the calamity just mentioned, the rains of the storm clouds subsided through the consideration of divine goodness and mercy. The cheerful face of the sky began to brighten, and the calm winds of the heavens, together with serene weather, began to display the Creator’s generosity.

The entire surface of the earth likewise became pleasantly green and, by pouring forth an abundance of crops, gave promise of completely driving away want.

Then, first in the regions of Aquitaine, assemblies of councils began to be gathered by bishops, abbots, and the other devoted men of sacred religion from the whole population. Many bodies of saints and innumerable reliquaries of holy remains were also brought to these gatherings.

Afterward, throughout the province of Arles and that of Lyon, and then through all Burgundy, as far as the furthest regions of France, it was proclaimed throughout all the bishoprics that councils should be celebrated at appointed places by the bishops and great men of the entire land, for the restoration of peace and the instruction of the sacred faith.

When the entire multitude of the people heard this, the greatest, the middling, and the least came joyfully. All were ready to obey whatever the shepherds of the Church might command, no less than if a voice sent from heaven were speaking to people on earth.

The calamities of the preceding period terrified everyone, and fear pressed upon them lest they should attain the prosperity of the coming abundance. A written register had been arranged item by item, containing both the things that were forbidden and those which they had resolved to offer to almighty God by a devoted pledge.

The chief matter concerned the preservation of inviolable peace: men of every condition, whatever offenses they had previously committed, were to go about without fear and without weapons. A robber or one who invaded another’s property was to be restrained by the severity of the law and punished most harshly, either through the surrender of his possessions or by bodily penalties.

The honor and reverence shown to the holy places of all churches were likewise to be such that anyone who sought refuge there, whatever his offense, would escape unharmed—except only one who violated the pact of the aforesaid peace. If such a person were captured at the altar, he was nevertheless to suffer the prescribed punishment.

The same protection was extended to all clerics, monks, and nuns, so that if anyone traveled through the region with them, he would suffer no violence from anyone.

Many other provisions were established in those councils, which would take too long to recount. One matter certainly deserves remembrance: all agreed that, by perpetual sanction, wine should be abstained from on the sixth day of every week and meat on the seventh, unless severe illness compelled an exception or a very solemn feast occurred.

If some necessity arose so that this rule had to be relaxed slightly, three poor people were to be sustained with food in compensation.

At those same gatherings innumerable healings were performed among the sick. So that no one might regard these things as trivial, when many who had recently been bent were raised to their former condition, the skin was broken and the flesh of their legs and arms torn, with much blood being shed. This furnished confirmation even in the other cases about which people might have doubted.

All those present were inflamed with such fervor that, through the hands of the bishops, they raised staffs toward heaven, and with outstretched palms toward God they unanimously cried: “Peace, peace, peace!” This was to be a sign of the perpetual pact concerning what they had promised between themselves and God.

They further agreed that, after five years had elapsed, the same observance should be carried out by everyone throughout the world, in a marvelous manner, for the sake of confirming the peace.

In that same year there was such an abundance of grain, wine, and other crops as could not have been expected to occur during the following five years. Every kind of human food, apart from meat and exquisite dishes, was available for almost no price. It was like that great ancient Mosaic Jubilee.

The same abundance continued no less in the following, third, and fourth years. But alas, for grief! The human race, forgetful of God’s benefits and inclined toward evil from the beginning, like a dog returning to its vomit or a washed sow to the mire, made the pact of its own pledge void in many places.

As it is written: “He grew fat and thick and kicked.”

The leading men of both orders, turning to greed, began to practice countless acts of robbery, as they had done before, or even more than before. Then the middling and lower classes, following the example of their superiors, fell into monstrous crimes.

Who had ever before heard of so many acts of incest, so many adulteries, so many unlawful unions between relatives, so many debaucheries with concubines, or so many imitations of evil?

Moreover, to complete the accumulation of such evil, since there were few or none among the people who corrected others by rebuking such acts, the prophet’s prediction was fulfilled: “As is the people, so is the priest.”

This was especially so because, at that time, both in secular authority and in ecclesiastical religion, the persons holding every office of government were of childish age.

Because of the sins of the people, the saying of Solomon then came to pass: “Woe to you, O land!”

The Roman universal pope himself—namely, the nephew of the two Benedicts and John who had preceded him—was a boy of about ten years when the Romans elected him, the matter being secured through the payment of money from the treasury. They subsequently expelled him frequently and received him back dishonorably, and he exercised no authority.

As we have already noted above, at that time the other prelates of the Churches were raised to prominence by gold and silver rather than by merit.

Shameful indeed! Scripture speaks most clearly of such men—indeed, the very mouth of God says: “They became princes, and I did not know them.”

## CHAPTER VI  
### On the gathering of the people of the whole world that took place at the Lord’s tomb in Jerusalem

[Col. 0680A]

During that same period, from every part of the world an innumerable multitude began to converge upon the Savior’s tomb at Jerusalem—such as no human being previously could have hoped for. First came the lower order of the common people; then those of middling rank; afterward the greatest of all—kings, counts, and bishops. Finally, something that had never happened before, many noble women also went there with women of humble station. For many had formed the desire in their minds to die before returning to their own lands.

It happened that a certain man named Lethbaldus, from the region of Autun in the parts of Burgundy, arrived there while traveling with the others. [Col. 0680B] When he had surveyed all the most sacred places, and it happened that he had reached that place on the Mount of Olives from which the Savior, ascending into heaven before so many suitable witnesses, was promised to return from there to judge the living and the dead, he threw himself down in the form of a cross. Prostrate with his whole body, he rejoiced in the Lord with tears and indescribable spiritual exultation. Rising again and again, he stretched his palms toward heaven and, with all the bodily strength he could muster, lifted himself upward; then he expressed the desire of his heart in words such as these:

“Lord Jesus, who for our sake deigned to descend from the seat of your majesty to the earth in order to save the human race, and who, clothed in flesh, returned to heaven from this place which I behold with my eyes, whence you had come: I beseech your all-powerful [Col. 0680C] goodness that, if my soul is to depart from this body in the present year, I may not leave this place, but that it may happen that I come to be in the sight of the place of your ascension. For I believe that, just as I followed you bodily in the manner in which I came to this place, so my soul, unharmed and rejoicing, may enter paradise after you.”

When he had finished speaking, he returned with his companions to their lodging. It was already the hour of the midday meal. While the others were reclining at table, he himself turned toward his little bed with a cheerful expression, as though he intended to rest for a little while in heavy sleep. Immediately falling asleep, it is unknown what he saw; but while still sleeping he suddenly cried out: “Glory to you, God; glory to you, God!”

His companions, hearing this, urged him to rise and eat. He refused; instead, turning onto his other side, he said that he was suffering some discomfort. Remaining in bed [Col. 0680D] until evening, he summoned his traveling companions, asked for the life-giving Eucharist, and received it as viaticum. After bidding them a gentle farewell, he gave up his spirit.

Without doubt, this man was free from the vanity for which many set out, merely so that they may be considered remarkable. On his journey to Jerusalem, in the name of the Lord Jesus, he faithfully asked the Father for what he received. His companions, returning while we were staying at the monastery of Besue, reported these things to us.

At that same time Odolricus, bishop of Orléans, was traveling there. What he saw and related to us seems not to be a miracle that should be passed over. On the day of that great Sabbath, when fire, coming by the wondrous power of God, is awaited there by the whole people, the same bishop was standing there with the others. [Col. 0681A] The day was already passing into evening when, suddenly, at about the hour when the fire was expected to appear, one of the Saracens—a most shameless jester, from the great multitude of them that customarily gathers there every year together with the Christians—cried out, as is the Christian custom when it first becomes visible, “Agios, Kyrie eleison” (“Holy One, Lord, have mercy”), and burst into mocking laughter. Stretching out his hand, he snatched a candle from the hand of a Christian and attempted to flee.

Immediately seized by a demon, he began to be tormented most grievously. The Christian pursued him and took back the candle. But the other, tortured with extreme violence, soon expired in the hands of the Saracens. This event cast terror over everyone collectively, but it brought joy and exultation to the worshipers of Christ.

Immediately, as is customary, the fire burst forth by God’s power [Col. 0681B] from one of the lamps—of which seven are seen hanging there—and, rushing out in a stream, kindled the others. The aforementioned bishop had purchased that lamp, together with its oil, for a pound of gold from Jordan, who was then patriarch; he brought it back with him and placed it in his own see, where it bestowed many benefits upon the sick.

He also brought King Robert a very large portion of the venerable cross of the Lord Savior, sent by Constantine, emperor of the Greeks, together with a quantity of silk garments woven entirely of silk. In return, that king had sent through the same bishop a sword with a golden hilt and a golden chest containing exceedingly precious gems.

At that time Robert, duke of the Normans, was also setting out for Jerusalem with a great multitude of his people. He carried with him many gifts of gold and silver [Col. 0681C] for distribution. On his return he died at the city of Nicaea and was buried and laid to rest there.

His people were plunged into the greatest mourning for this reason: he had no offspring by a lawful marriage to assume the government of the province, although it is well known that he had married the sister of Canute, king of the English, and had divorced her because he hated her. Nevertheless, he had fathered a son by a concubine, giving him the name William, that of his grandfather.

Before he departed, he bound all the leading men of his duchy by military oaths that, if he did not return, they would choose that son as their prince in his place. They later confirmed this unanimously, with the consent of King Henry of the Franks.

For, as we noted above, from the first arrival of that people in Gaul it had been customary for their princes to arise from such unions with concubines. Yet, lest this seem excessively abominable, I wish to introduce a comparison with the sons of Jacob’s concubines, who on that account were not deprived of paternal dignity but were appointed patriarchs among their other brothers. At a much later time, moreover, Constantine, the great proto-Christian of the singular monarchy of the empire, is reported to have been born of the concubine Helena.

Furthermore, when several of the more thoughtful men then living had been asked by many people what this great concourse of peoples to Jerusalem—unheard of in the former age—signified, some answered with considerable caution that it portended nothing other than the coming of that lost Antichrist, whose arrival near the end of this age, divine authority bearing witness, is awaited. At that time the road through the eastern region, from which he will come, will also be opened to all nations, and all peoples will advance without hesitation to meet him. Thus, in truth, the Lord’s prophecy will be fulfilled: “For then the elect also will fall into temptation, if it is possible.”

This is the limit of that statement. Nevertheless, we do not deny that the devout labor of the faithful will thereafter receive a reward or recompense from the just Judge.

CAPUT VII. On the battles of the Saracens against the Christians in the regions of Africa.

At the same time, a renewed treachery of the Saracens rose up in the regions of Africa against the Christian people. Pursuing them by land and sea, they flayed alive some of those whom they could find and slaughtered others. After a long and violent conflict between the two sides, with much slaughter and many defeats inflicted by both parties, it happened that, by mutual agreement, their battle lines came together for close combat.

The Saracens, presuming upon and trusting in the savage ferocity of their immense numbers, believed that they would be victorious. Our men, however, though very few in number, invoked the help of almighty God through the intercession of his Mother Mary, of the holy chief of the apostles Peter, and of all the saints; they confidently hoped to obtain triumph over them.

They had especially bound themselves by a vow made at the beginning of that war: if the Lord’s powerful hand should deliver that most treacherous nation into their hands, then, after triumphing over them, whatever gold, silver, or other property they happened to capture from them, they would send all of it without exception to the place of Cluny, to the chief of the apostles, Peter.

For long before, as we noted above, many religious men of that people had received the habit of the sacred institute in the same monastery and had stirred the entire nation to love that place.

But why say more? When the battle had begun, they engaged for a long time and fiercely. The Christians nevertheless appeared victorious and entirely unharmed. Finally, such a trembling of terror seized the Saracen army that, as though they had forgotten the battle, they attempted to flee—but in vain, for they were caught in their own arrows; indeed, struck motionless by God’s power, they remained fixed in bewilderment. The Christians, whose battle formation was strengthened by divine aid, slaughtered them in such numbers that scarcely a few escaped from their innumerable multitude.

Their prince Motget—whose name, like that of Moses, is pronounced in a confused manner—is said to have been absent from that battle. After collecting the spoils, they obtained from them many weights of silver amounting to talents, mindful of the vow they had made to God. It is the custom of Saracens going to battle to adorn themselves lavishly with trappings of silver or gold.

That circumstance also increased the devotion of our men, who immediately sent to the monastery of Cluny whatever proceeds came from it, as they had vowed. [Col. 0683A] From these, the venerable abbot of that place, Odilo, ordered a most splendid ciborium to be made for the altar of Saint Peter. He commanded that all the rest be distributed to the needy in a most renowned and fittingly liberal manner, down to the last penny. The tumult of the Saracens, shattered for the present, subsided.

CAPUT VIII. On the battle of the Leutici against the Christians in the northern regions.

Germany, extending upward from the Rhine River toward the northern region of the world, takes its beginning there and is inhabited by very many peoples, though they are exceedingly savage and mixed. Among them is one more cruel than the others, dwelling in the farthest part of the Second Raetia.

For although both regions are called Raetia from the Rhine, the First Raetia lies on the western side of that same Rhine. This is what is commonly called, in corrupted form, the kingdom of Lothair. In the other region, as we have said, lives the barbarous people of the Leutici, fiercer than all others in cruelty; their name is derived from *lutum*, “mud.” Their entire habitation is around the northern sea, in filthy marshes, and for this reason they are called Leutici, as though “mud-dwellers.”

In the year one thousand after the Passion of the Lord, they came out of their hiding places and, devastating the neighboring provinces of the Saxons and other barbarians with extreme cruelty, destroyed the possessions of the Christians down to the ground, slaughtering and exterminating men and women.

Against them Emperor Conrad set out with a very large army and brought down in slaughter a far greater number of them, though not without loss among his own men. For this reason the clergy and people of his entire kingdom afflicted themselves and prayed to the Lord to grant him vengeance against the madness of so barbarous a people, so that, for the honor of his name, victory over them might belong to the Christians.

Afterward, attacking them, he crushed the greater part of them. The rest, taking refuge in flight, escaped in great terror to the inaccessible places of their marshes.

Having gained confidence from this victory, the same emperor again gathered an army and proceeded to Italy. Advancing toward Rome itself, he restrained by force all the rebels who had attempted to rise against him, remaining there for a full year. He also established a pact of security and friendship with Henry, king of the Franks and son of Robert, just as Henry had previously dealt with his father. To him he also sent a very large lion as a token of friendship. That king later took as his wife a woman named Matilda, outstanding in character, from among the nobility of Conrad’s German realm.

CAPUT IX. On the sign that appeared in the sun.

In that same year of the one-thousandth year of the Lord’s Passion, on the third day before the Kalends of July, a Friday, with the moon twenty-eight days old, there was an eclipse, or darkening, of the sun, from the sixth hour of that day until the eighth, and it was exceedingly terrifying.

The sun itself became the color of sapphire, displaying in its upper part the appearance of a moon at the quarter of its reillumination. The faces of human beings appeared pallid, like those of the dead, as they looked at one another. Whatever objects could be seen beneath the sky appeared yellow in color. Then immense stupor and fear seized the hearts of the human race, because those who witnessed it understood it to signify that something grievous was going to come upon the human race in the form of an impending calamity.

On that same day—namely, the birthday of the apostles—certain Roman nobles conspired against the Roman pope in the church of blessed Peter, wishing to kill him but being unable to do so. Nevertheless, they expelled him from his own see. But, as we stated earlier, the emperor, setting out for that place, restored him to his own see, both on account of this affair and because of other outrages that had been insolently committed.

Many other things also occurred throughout the world, in ecclesiastical as well as secular affairs, perpetrated against justice and right. Under the impulse of swift greed, scarcely anyone’s faith in another was secure, although faith is the foundation [Col. 0684B] and support of all that is good. And, so that it might become more evident that the sins of the earth were striking heaven, as the prophet cries out on account of the people’s continual iniquities: “Blood,” he says, “has touched blood.”

Afterward, when insolence had begun to flourish in nearly every class of mortals and the force of just severity and steadfastness had grown lukewarm, the apostolic saying could most rightly have been applied as a condemnation of our people: “A wickedness is heard among you such as is not found even among the nations.”

When shameless greed invaded human hearts, faith was endangered everywhere. From this arose robberies and incest, quarrels born of blind desires, thefts, and monstrous adulteries. Shame upon it! It was horrifying for anyone to report what he felt about himself. Yet no one corrected himself on account of this from the wicked practice of evil.

Again, four years later, there was an eclipse of the sun, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of September, a Wednesday, at the sixth hour, and, as always happens, with the moon twenty-eight days old.

In that same year Conrad, whom we mentioned above, died at Saxony as emperor of the Romans. His son Henry, whom he had while alive appointed king in his place, became emperor.

William, count of Poitiers, having been released for a large sum of money from the captivity in which Fulk’s son Geoffrey—called Martel—had held him for three years after capturing him in battle, returned to his own lands and died that same year.

Hugh, bishop of Auxerre, a man of great renown, also died. Likewise Rainald, count of that same city and son of Count Landric, who had married the daughter of King Robert, was himself boldly killed by a certain soldier of the lowest birth.

Fearing, on account of his boldness, that an untimely death was approaching him, as indeed happened, he restored, while still alive, an abbey built in honor of the Lord Savior so that it might be possessed in perpetuity and in its entirety by the monastery of Saint Germanus. He was also buried there and lies at rest.

Moreover, Fulk, count of Anjou, about whom we have reported certain things above, had already traveled to Jerusalem three times. On his way back he died at the city of Metz. His body was carried to the monastery at Loches, which he himself had built, and was honorably buried there.

LIBER QUINTUS.

[Col. 0685]

CONTENTS OF BOOK FIVE.

I. Various questions. II. On a wondrously conducted battle. III. On a third eclipse of the sun. IV. On the dissension of the bishopric of Lyon. V. On the eradication of simony.

CAPUT PRIMUM. Various questions.

[Col. 0685A]

The ears and minds of nearly all mortals at that time were stunned and dulled or weakened by the changes of diverse things, the events of various occurrences, and also the attacks of evil spirits. Nevertheless, it was frequently reported that useful revelations had been made manifest to some through visions.

One night, at the hour when the signal for Matins was sounded, a certain monk seemed to see an exceedingly dreadful being appear before him. By persuading him, it introduced a conversation of this kind:

“Why,” it said, “do you monks undertake so many labors, so many vigils and fasts, as well as hardships, psalmody, and many other humiliations, beyond the common practice of other human beings? Do not countless secular people, persisting in various crimes until the end of their lives, nevertheless expect to receive the same rest that you await? One day, or even one hour, would be enough to earn the rewards of your eternal blessedness by your righteousness.

“For you yourself—I marvel at the reason why you are so anxious—no sooner do you hear the signal than you rise quickly from your bed and break the sweet rest of sleep, although you could indulge in rest until the third signal.

“There is also a very memorable secret that I shall disclose to you, although it is a loss to our side and a saving remedy for yours. It is known to everyone that each year, on the day when Christ, rising from the dead, restored life to the human race, all the underworld is stripped by him and its own inhabitants are led back to the heights. Therefore you have nothing to fear. You may safely pursue whatever pleasures of the flesh and desires you wish.”

The demon, being utterly deceitful, reported these and many other such things to the monk in mockery, and enticed him so far that he was absent from the common morning assembly of the brothers.

But what it deceitfully fabricated about the Lord’s resurrection is refuted by the words of the sacred Gospel, which say: “Many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep rose.” It does not say “all,” but “many.” And this is truly what the Catholic faith professes.

For although, at times, by the arrangement of the true foreknowledge of the Almighty, utterly deceitful demons foretell things that are not entirely false, nevertheless, insofar as such things proceed from their own deliberation, they fabricate them superficially and deceptively. Or even if some part of what they foretell should happen, it will not plainly benefit human salvation [Col. 0686A] unless divine providence intervenes, perhaps for the careful purpose of correction.

Recently, by God’s favor, I myself have openly experienced many things of this sort. Once, while I was staying at the monastery of the blessed martyr Leodegarius, which is called Cappellis, a most dreadful human form appeared to me one night before the morning assembly, at the foot of my bed.

As far as I could discern, it was of medium height, with a slender neck, emaciated face, very black eyes, a wrinkled and contracted forehead, flattened nostrils, a protruding mouth, swollen lips, a receding and exceedingly narrow chin, a goat’s beard, hairy and sharply pointed ears, erect and disordered hair, canine teeth, a pointed back of the head, a swollen chest, a humped back, swaying buttocks, dirty clothing, and a body feverish with effort and rushing forward in its entirety.

It seized the top of the bed on which I was lying and shook the whole bed terribly. Then it began: “You will not remain in this place any longer.”

Terrified and waking—as can suddenly happen—I saw the figure I have described. Grinding its teeth repeatedly, it kept saying: “You will not remain here any longer.”

Finally, immediately leaping from my bed, I ran into the monastery. I prostrated myself before the altar of the most holy Father Benedict, and, greatly afraid, lay there for a long time.

I began with the utmost intensity to recall everything that, from the beginning of my life, I had rashly or negligently committed as offenses and grave sins, especially since scarcely any satisfaction of repentance toward God, whether from love or fear, had followed from me afterward.

Thus, lying there wretched and confused, I had nothing appropriate to say except: “Lord Jesus, who came to save sinners, according to your great mercy, have mercy on me.”

Meanwhile, I do not blush to confess that I was not only born in the sins of my parents, but also that in character I was troublesome and in my actions intolerable, more than can be related.

By the force of a certain monk—my uncle, in fact—I was drawn away from the most perverse vanity of secular life, which I practiced more than anything else. I was nearly twelve years old and had been clothed in the monastic habit—alas, shame upon it!—for I had changed only my clothing, not my mind.

Whatever the Fathers or spiritual brothers charitably suggested to me as modest and holy, I opposed. Inflated by a savage spirit, I carried the swollen shield of my heart, and, under the dictation of pride, prevented salutary counsel from touching me.

Thereafter I obeyed neither my elders, was troublesome to my equals, and burdensome to my juniors. To speak truthfully, my presence was a burden to everyone, while my absence was a relief.

Moreover, stirred up by these and similar things, the brothers of that place expelled me from their common dwelling, although they knew that, because of my literary knowledge, I would not lack some place in which to stay. This also had often been experienced before.

Afterward, when I had been placed in the monastery of Saint Benignus, martyr of Dijon, something not different but rather the same appeared to me in the brothers’ dormitory.

At daybreak, a figure ran out of the latrine building, calling in this manner: “Where is my bachelor? Where is my bachelor?”

The following day, at nearly the same hour, a certain young brother named Theodoricus, extremely light-minded, fled from there. Having cast aside his habit, he lived as a secular for some time. Later, pierced in heart, he returned to his commitment to the sacred order.

A third time, while I was staying at the monastery of the blessed and ever-virgin Mary, surnamed Meleredense, one night, when the signal for Matins was sounded, I was tired from some labor and did not rise immediately, as I ought to have done, when it was heard. Some others remained with me, enticed by an evil habit, while the rest hurried to the church.

As I went out afterward, breathless behind the brothers, the aforementioned demon climbed the marked step. With its hands drawn back behind its back and clinging to the wall, it repeated two or three times: “I am he, I am he, who stands with those who remain.”

Awakened by that voice, I raised my head and saw and recognized the one whom I had already seen twice before.

On the third day afterward, one of those brothers who, as we said, had been accustomed to sleep secretly left the monastery brazenly. Stirred up by the aforementioned demon, he remained outside the monastery with secular people in disorder for six days. On the seventh day, however, he was seized and brought back.

Indeed, as blessed Gregory testifies, such beings appear to some for their detriment, but to others for the benefit of correction. I pray and desire that this may happen to me for salvation, through the Lord Jesus our Redeemer.

This, in particular, should be committed carefully to memory: when unmistakable prodigies are displayed in the body while people are still alive, whether through good or evil spirits, it is certain that those to whom it happens to see such things will not live long in this flesh. We have learned many examples confirming this assertion, and it seemed worthwhile to commit some of them to memory, so that whenever they occur they may bring caution rather than deception.

At the castle of Tarnodorum there was a certain priest named Fretterius, who lived a religious life during the time when Bruno held the bishopric of Langres.

One Sunday, as evening was approaching and he was about to dine, he went out for a little while to the windows of his house for relief. Looking out, he saw a line of horsemen emerging from the north, as if going into battle, an innumerable multitude traveling toward the west.

After he had gazed at them for a long time and with great attention, he became agitated and called one of his people to witness so great a portent. But when he began to shout for someone to come, they immediately disappeared as they grew thinner and more dispersed.

He himself was struck by such terror of spirit [Col. 0688A] that he could scarcely restrain himself from tears. Then he began to grow ill, and in that same year, after living an excellent life, he died.

The calamity foreshadowed by what he had seen was thus withheld from him, but those who experienced it became witnesses. For in the following year Henry, son of King Robert and the one who reigned after him, came to that same castle in anger with a huge army, and much slaughter of men was carried out there on both sides.

It is clear that what he had seen had foreshadowed something both for himself and for others, though in different ways.

We also remember that something wonderful happened at Auxerre in the church of Saint Germanus. A brother named Gerardus was there, who was accustomed to remain in the oratory after the solemn office of Matins.

One morning it happened that he fell asleep during his prayers. Immediately, overcome by heavy sleep, he was carried outside the monastery as though lifeless; how, or by whom, remains unknown to this day.

When he awoke, he found that he had been thrown into the cloister outside the monastery, and he was utterly astonished at what he saw had happened to him.

In a similar manner, something happened to a certain priest who was spending the night in the same monastery. While he was asleep in the lower crypts, where many bodies of saints rest, around cockcrow he found himself transported behind the monks’ choir.

A reliable report concerning that same church states that, if a light happens to go out at night, its custodians can obtain no rest until it has been rekindled.

Moreover, there was a certain brother who was accustomed to pray frequently at the altar of Saint Mary, which is of exceptional distinction, and to pour forth groans and tears of penitence.

He had one habit, common to nearly everyone: during prayer he frequently spat and discharged saliva from his mouth.

It happened once that he fell asleep, overcome by sleep. A certain figure appeared to him standing beside the altar, clothed in white garments and holding a cloth of the purest white in its hands. It burst forth with words such as these:

“Why,” it said, “do you strike and stain me with your own spittle? For I, as you see, receive the offering of your prayers and carry it before the presence of the most merciful Judge.”

Struck by this vision, that brother restrained himself and also took care to admonish the others to restrain themselves, as far as they could, in sacred places.

Although this happens as a result of nature’s prompting, nevertheless in many regions among various peoples people entirely refrain from spitting in church. Unless the spittle is received, it is then carried outside in certain containers. This practice is especially observed among the Greeks, where ecclesiastical discipline has always been maintained with the greatest care.

It is therefore clear that the aforesaid place has long shone through the merits of blessed Germanus and of the other saints resting there, by signs and wonders, both through gifts of healings and through avenging punishments directed against those who seize or plunder what belongs to it.

Whenever certain nobles of this country have arisen as invaders or plunderers of the possessions of that place, God, as their avenger, has been accustomed to bring their family, together with their possessions, into disgrace and almost to nothing.

Among the other proofs of our assertion, the evident punishment of the family of a certain Bavo, as well as of his son Aluvalon, and the frequent confusion of the most sacrilegious castle of Silliniacum, stand as testimony to this.

Moreover, I myself was once asked by the fellow servants and brothers of our own community to restore the inscriptions of the altars, which had formerly been composed by learned men but, through age, had disappeared like nearly everything else.

As was appropriate, I gladly endeavored to complete this task as best I could. But before I had brought the work I had begun to its conclusion, from excessive standing, as I suppose, I collapsed onto my bed one night and became so contracted in all my limbs by a jaundiced illness that I could neither raise myself nor turn onto my other side in any way.

On the third night afterward, while I was being held by severe distress, a venerable man with white hair appeared to me. In my dream he raised me by the arm and said: “Complete as quickly as possible what you have begun; do not fear that you will suffer any longer.”

Immediately I awoke. Astonished, I shook myself and rose from my bed, then ran to the altar of the victorious martyrs—Victor, Apollinaris, and George—for their oratory was adjacent to the house of the sick. There I gave the most humble thanks to God for everything and, full of energy, completed the solemn Matins office.

On the following day I was entirely sound in body and, in that place, composed an inscription bearing the proper names of those same martyrs.

The main church had twenty-two altars. As was fitting, I arranged for their inscriptions, written suitably in *synopi* [sic] from hexameter verses, to be restored, and for the epitaphs of the saints to be repaired. I also arranged for the tombs of certain religious men to be ornamented in the same way.

This was exceedingly pleasing to people of sound mind. But, as Father Odilo was accustomed to lament frequently, so it happened:

“Alas! Shame upon it!” he would say. “Although the blemish of envy rages among other human beings, nevertheless, in the boundaries of some who have professed to live the monastic life, it has established a dwelling for itself.

“For a certain man, hated by the brothers of his own monastery, departed and came to our community. As has always been their custom, they received him devoutly. But he infected the abbot and certain monks with the poison of envy and compelled them to such hatred against me that they destroyed all the aforementioned inscriptions of the altars.

“Yet immediately, with the Lord as avenger, the one who had been the instigator of fraternal discord received his punishment. He was struck at once with the damnable blindness of the eyes and, stumbling with his feet, remained irreparably afflicted until the end of his life.”

The outcome of this event caused no small astonishment both to those living nearby and to those far away.

At that very time it happened that some of the brothers departed from this light. One of them was named Walterius, surnamed Pusillus (“Little”), as his stature indicated, and very simple by nature. He died at the beginning of the night of the great Sabbath of the Lord’s Resurrection.

At the hour of his death, a fiery column of light appeared to innumerable men and women, extending from the summit of the monastery all the way to heaven. There was no doubt to them that this had been accomplished by the generosity of the most merciful God, who wished the soul of this brother to share in his glorious resurrection and to demonstrate to the living the way of innocence.

Some people commonly ask why, in the time of the new law or of grace, visions divinely granted and miracles of various kinds do not occur openly, as they did in ancient times.

A brief answer should be given to them from the testimonies of divine Scripture—provided, however, that their hearts are capable of the gifts of the Holy Spirit.

It is appropriate first to present the clear testimony of Deuteronomy. After the Hebrew people had been nourished for forty years by heavenly manna, and, having crossed the Jordan, had entered the land of Canaan, heaven ceased to rain it down, and the children of Israel no longer used such food.

What, then, does this event signify for us, for whom nearly everything occurs in figure, except that, after crossing our Jordan—that is, through the baptism of Christ—we should no longer seek heavenly signs of things to come? Rather, that living bread should suffice for us, and whoever eats of it will live forever, destined to possess the land of the living.

Again, by the Lord’s command Moses established that whatever vessels came to that people from the spoils of their enemies should be purified with water if they were wooden, and with fire if they were bronze.

In a similar figurative manner, this expresses that the vessels—that is, the same human beings who fell to the Savior as a portion of the spoils of the ancient enemy—were to be purified by the water of baptism and by the fire of martyrdom.

The rod-like serpent should also be understood typologically. It frightened Moses so that he fled from it; then, when he took it up again by the tail, it became a rod.

In this event, the power of the Godhead clothed in flesh from the holy Virgin Mary is signified by the serpent made from the rod. Through Moses is represented the Jewish people, who, seeing the Lord Jesus as true God and man, flee from him in unbelief; but they will receive him near the end of the age, which is expressed by the serpent’s tail.

That crossing of the Red Sea, in which the sea was divided and dried up, and afterward the nations were exterminated by the sword at the Lord’s command, clearly signify that the kingdom of the Israelite people, existing temporally, would wither and be brought to nothing.

At the beginning of the new grace, or of Christ’s kingdom, the Lord Jesus stood and walked upon the waves of the sea and allowed Peter, whom he had placed over his Church, to walk with him. What is signified to all the faithful by this, except that, after all the nations have been subdued but not utterly destroyed or exterminated, Christ’s kingdom will be established from among them and will remain throughout the ages?

For divine speech frequently bears witness that the sea represents the figure of the present age.

Often, therefore, when someone wishes to elucidate a very important matter in words, he diminishes it by failing in himself, as Scripture says: “He who is a searcher of majesty is overwhelmed by glory.” But why we have prefaced these remarks, we shall briefly explain. It is evident that the mystery of the Eucharist is clear to very few, while it is almost wholly unknown to mortals [Col. 0691A], just like the other things that are established by faith and do not demand the scrutiny of the eyes. This above all must be emphasized: the life-giving consecration of the body and blood of the Lord Jesus Christ is believed in no way to suffer loss in itself or to incur danger through any accident. Whenever it seems to collapse or perish through the negligence of those handling it, judgment of condemnation remains for them, unless they repent with zeal. Yet since the Lord said, “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life, and I will raise him up,” we must in no way suppose that any animal other than a human being can receive the resurrection of the flesh; nor does anyone receive the Eucharist for salvation except a believer.

Finally, in our own time [Col. 0691B], there was a certain man in clerical dress who was rightly accused of a crime. It happened that he boldly undertook, as a judicial test, to receive the gift of the Eucharist—namely, the blood of Christ from the chalice. Immediately, through the middle of his navel, there appeared to emerge the whitest portion of that same sacrifice which he had received, plainly giving evidence of the guilt of one who had received it unworthily. At once, confessing what he had previously denied, he duly repented.

In the district of Chalon, too, when disaster was imminent, we saw someone who saw true flesh made from the consecrated bread. At the fortress of Dijon, at the same time, while it was being carried by someone to a sick man, it accidentally slipped from the bearer’s hand. Though he searched carefully, he was entirely unable to find it. But after a year had passed, it was discovered beside the public road, where it had fallen [Col. 0691C] under the open sky, as white and undefiled as if it had fallen at that very hour. Finally, at the monastery of Barbares in Lyon, when someone—apparently intending to handle improperly the little box or pyx in which it was customarily kept—tried to take hold of it, it escaped from his hands and remained suspended in the air at some distance.

The chrismal also, which some call the corporal, has often been shown to provide very great remedies, provided that the faith of those who seek them is not doubtful. When it was frequently lifted against fires, it either extinguished and restrained them, or drove them back, or turned them aside in another direction. It also often restored the painful limbs of the sick to health; when placed upon those suffering from fever, it likewise brought them healing.

At the monastery of Réome, in the time of the venerable Abbot William [Col. 0691D], it happened that a fire was ravaging the areas surrounding the monastery. The brothers of that place seized the chrismal, mounted on a staff, and raised it against the flames of the fire, which were burning terribly. Immediately, the fire turned back upon itself and was no longer able to seize more than it had already invaded.

Nevertheless, that Lord’s bread, when a breeze was blowing, slipped from the staff and flew more or less two miles, as far as a village called Tivalgas, where it came down upon the house of a certain man and settled there. After it had been pursued, it was reverently brought back to the monastery. For in that same year, on Easter Day, in the church adjoining the monastery and dedicated in the name of blessed Paul, it had happened that the chalice of the life-giving blood slipped from the priest’s hands onto the ground.

But when the aforesaid father learned of this, being a man of alert intelligence, he ordered three of his monks to repent of the guilt of this offense [Col. 0692A], fearing, namely, that the guilt of the foolish priest might involve his own men with him in the punishment of vengeance. He would indeed have done so, had the foresight of that prudent man not intervened, as the outcome of the matter proved.

For this reason we have prefaced these matters: to state confidently that, wherever an accident involving this sacred and life-giving gift should occur through negligence, the disaster of divine vengeance threatens and follows; while, conversely, wherever it happens to be handled worthily, all benefits abound.

It is also well established in many instances how much the celebration of that magnificent mystery benefits the souls of the faithful departed. Nevertheless, from various examples, I wish to bring forward one here [Col. 0692B]. In the more remote parts of Africa there was a certain anchorite, of whom it was reported that he had kept himself wholly separated from the sight of any human being for a period of twenty years. He lived by the work of his hands and by the roots of plants.

It happened that a certain little man of Teiphalian origin, one of those wanderers through various regions who are never satisfied with experience and new places, traveled there and arrived. Having learned of the anchorite’s reputation, he entered the solitude of that sun-scorched region and searched for him for a long time, in case he might find him. At last the solitary elder saw him searching for him and called him to come to him.

When he had come to him, he began to ask him who he was, where he was from, and for what reason he had arrived there [Col. 0692C]. He immediately replied that he had come there, inflamed by the desire to see him, and that he was seeking nothing else besides him.

Then that theological man continued, saying: “I know that you have come here from the regions of Gaul. But please tell me whether you have ever seen the monastery of Major Monastery [or, Cluniacum], which is situated in those regions.”

He replied: “I have seen it, and I know it very well.”

Then he said to him: “Know that, above all places in the Roman world, it is especially powerful for liberating souls from demonic domination. For the frequent offering of the life-giving sacrifice is so vigorous there that scarcely a day passes on which it does not rescue souls from the power of wicked demons through such an exchange.”

Indeed, as we ourselves observed, it was the custom of that monastery, from the first light of day until the hour of the midday meal, because of the number of brothers, to celebrate Masses continuously. This was done so worthily, purely, and reverently that the service might be thought more angelic than human [Col. 0692D].

In the year 1041 from the Lord’s Incarnation, therefore, the paschal limit fell on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, and Easter Day itself on the eleventh. I thought it worth recording this because the common [cycle] never becomes more moderate, nor does the intercalation ever exceed the seventh day before the Kalends of May. Rather, within those thirty-five days the most sacred day of Easter is lawfully confined.

In that same year the Emperor Conrad also died. His son Henry succeeded him in the kingdom, having already been appointed king by that same father [Col. 0693A]. At that time, through the inspiration of divine grace, a pact began to be established, first in the regions of Aquitaine and then gradually throughout the whole territory of Gaul, out of both fear and love of God. Its terms were that no mortal should dare presumptuously to take anything from anyone by force, exact vengeance from any enemy, or even demand a pledge from a guarantor, from the evening of Wednesday until daybreak at the beginning of Monday.

If anyone happened to act against this public decree, he either had to make payment for his life or was expelled from the fellowship of Christians and driven from his homeland. It was also agreed by all, as it is commonly called, that this should be called the Truce of God [Treuga Domini] [Col. 0693B]. It was supported not only by human safeguards but also, very often, by divine terrors. For many madmen, with audacious recklessness, did not fear to violate the prescribed pact; among them, divine avenging anger or the human sword of retribution immediately appeared.

This happened so frequently and everywhere that, because of their great number, the cases cannot be recorded individually—and rightly so. For just as Sunday is held sacred on account of the Lord’s resurrection and is called the Eighth Day, so the fifth, sixth, and seventh days, out of reverence for the Lord’s Supper and his Passion, ought to be days of rest from wicked deeds.

It happened, however, that while this statute was being observed firmly throughout almost all Gaul, as we have already said, the people of Neustria refused to accept it [Col. 0693C]. The occasion for this was a dispute arising from the most arrogant quarrel between King Henry, son of Robert, and the sons of the aforesaid Odo—namely, Theobald and Stephen—who, mingling civil wars with fires and ravages, inflicted considerable harm upon one another and caused great slaughter among their people.

Then, by the hidden judgment of God, divine vengeance began to rage among their populations. A certain deadly fever consumed many, both among the nobles and among the middle and lowest classes of the people; others it left alive with parts of their limbs mutilated, as an example for the future. At that time nearly the whole world also suffered scarcity because of the rarity of wine and grain.

In that same year—that is, the forty-fifth year after the thousandth year of the Lord’s Incarnation [Col. 0693D]—the aforementioned Henry, son of Conrad, already king of the Saxons in fact and emperor of the Romans in hope, married Agnes, daughter of William, duke of Poitou. He also betrothed her in the city of Chrysopolis, which is commonly called Besançon.

A very great multitude of nobles gathered there on account of the love and goodwill of both parties, including twenty-eight bishops. The kingdom of the Austrasians had come into submission to the aforesaid king, since it belonged to him by hereditary right. At the same time he had appointed over the people of the Huns, by his own authority, a king named Abbo.

All the margraves and counts, both from Italy and from [Col. 0694A] Germany, far and wide, willingly desired that this same king should exercise dominion over them. And not without reason. He was exceedingly pleasing in affability, distinguished in generosity, and endowed with the grace of humility. Nor was he marked by any impulse of domineering pride. For this reason he was beloved by everyone around him.

In that same year, the aforesaid people of the Hungarians rebelled against his rule. He attacked them as enemies, defeated them powerfully, and subjected them to himself as tributaries. Yet, shamefully, there was one thing in him that was exceedingly blameworthy: he was disgraced by sexual incontinence. For among all human vices, this fault disturbs the order of things more than the others.

In the following year, that is, the forty-sixth after the thousandth, there was great abundance of wine and vegetables in many places [Col. 0694B]. Afterwards, on the sixth day before the Ides of November, when the moon was fourteen days old, with no epact in force and the concurrent number seven, there occurred a lunar eclipse greatly terrifying to human beings.

For at the eighth hour of the night, between the sun and the moon itself—whether this was something accomplished and shown by God, or whether it happened through the turning of the sphere of another heavenly body—how it occurred remains known to the knowledge of the Creator. The moon itself first became almost entirely like foul blood, gradually escaping until the dawn of the coming day appeared.

In that same month, at the fortress of Saint Florentin, which lies above the Armançon River, around the middle of a certain day, something fell from the sky which in Greek is called *selas* or *chasma*, or *palmatias*, when the radiance of an ethereal brilliance is emitted unusually toward the earth. For the foolish common people claim that a star falls from heaven [Col. 0694C].

Then, in that aforementioned month of November, in certain places of Gaul, the crops of the first sowing of August, contrary to ordinary practice, were brought to maturity and harvested in October. This happened not without great astonishment.

## CHAPTER II. On a Remarkable War
