At the same time, a great disagreement had arisen, even to the shedding of much blood, between Henry, king of the Franks and son of Robert, and the sons of the aforementioned Odo—namely, Theobald and Stephen.

After many slaughterings and disasters on both sides, it happened that the same king, having taken the lordship of the city of Tours from them, gave it to Geoffrey, surnamed Tudites, the son of the aforesaid Fulk, count of Anjou [Col. 0694D]. Gathering a large army, he surrounded the city with a siege for a year and more.

Against him, at last, the two aforementioned sons of Odo advanced with hostile forces to fight, genuinely intending to succor the afflicted and needy city with provisions. When Geoffrey learned this, he sought the aid of blessed Martin and humbly promised that he would make satisfaction for whatever he had seized by plunder from the possessions of that holy confessor and of the other saints.

Then, having received a banner and placed it upon his own spear, he went with a large army of horsemen and foot soldiers to meet those who were coming to fight against him. When both sides came close together [Col. 0695A], such terror seized the army of the two brothers that it was as though all of them had become unwarlike, bound by fetters.

Stephen took flight and escaped with some soldiers. Theobald, however, was captured from the rest of the army’s multitude and led to the city of Tours. He restored the city to Geoffrey and remained in captivity, together with all his men, who were scattered here and there.

No one doubts that, with blessed Martin’s aid, he whom Geoffrey had piously invoked became the victor over his enemies. For some who fled from the battle line reported that the entire phalanx of Geoffrey’s soldiers, both horsemen and foot soldiers, appeared to be covered in brilliantly white garments at the very outset of the battle. The sons of Odo were carrying the proceeds of their plunder from the poor belonging to that confessor [Col. 0695B].

He produced a terrifying astonishment for all who heard it: more than 1,700 armed men were captured in the battle without any shedding of blood.

## CHAPTER III. On the Third Eclipse of the Sun

In the aforementioned month of November, on the tenth day before the Kalends of December, at the third hour of that day, the third eclipse of the sun in our time occurred, when the moon was precisely twenty-eight days old. For there is never an eclipse of the sun except under a twenty-eighth-day moon, nor an eclipse of the moon except under a fourteenth-day moon.

An eclipse is called a deficiency or failure, not because the object itself is deficient, but because it is rather obstructed from us. In those same days, as we learned from Wido, archbishop of Reims [Col. 0695C], his people saw the star Phosphorus, also called Lucifer, being driven up and down in the evening, as though threatening the inhabitants of earth; its identity was unclear [the transmitted text reads *idemtitabat*].

Such portents, sent forth from heaven, terrified very many people concerning their wickedness, so that they might return through repentance to the path of correction. At that time, amid the other shortages of things, wine became so scarce that a single *modius* cost twenty-four solidi.

## CHAPTER IV. On the Dissension Concerning the See of Lyon

In those days there was a very great dispute after the death of Burchard, archbishop of Lyon, concerning the episcopate of that see. Many sought it not by just merit but at the prompting of proud arrogance.

First of all, the aforementioned Burchard’s nephew, who bore the same name and was excessively proud, abandoned his own see, that of the city of Augsburg, and insolently seized the see of Lyon. After committing many wicked acts, he was captured by the emperor’s soldiers and condemned to perpetual exile.

After him, a certain count arrogantly installed his own young son Gerard there, with presumption alone as his authority. Soon afterward, he himself disappeared in flight—not as a shepherd of sheep but like a hireling.

When all this had been reported to the Roman pontiff, faithful men advised him to use his authority to have Father Odilo, abbot of the monastery of Cluny, elected and consecrated pontiff there. For the devotion of the entire clergy and people was acclaiming him in this way [Col. 0696A].

The pontiff immediately sent that father the pallium and ring and ordered him to be archbishop of the aforesaid city. But the religious man, mindful of the purpose of his humility, refused in every way to become so. He accepted the pallium and ring and reserved them for one who would be worthy before God—for the future pontiff of that see.

From ancient times, the city of Lyon itself has been regarded as the chief herald of the true light for a large part of Gaul, because the first heralds of the Christian faith, sent by Saint Polycarp, a disciple of the apostle John, came there and enlightened the entire region.

It happened afterward, as we said above, that King Henry, having recovered the kingdom of the Austrasians, learned of the disaster caused by this dispute and grieved over it, seeking to discover what he ought to do [Col. 0696B]. When he had arrived at Besançon, both the bishops and all the people advised him to install at Lyon as pontiff a man equally worthy of such a ministry—namely, Odolric, archdeacon of the Church of Langres.

Immediately, as had been advised, he sent him to the aforesaid see, adorned with the most splendid vestments. At once the peace of the entire province, long desired, was restored with rejoicing.

Afterward, the people of the Hungarians, already in rebellion against the aforesaid king for a second time, prepared to fight against him. He went out against them and, although inferior in number, nevertheless trusting in God’s aid, did not fear to engage them.

There were no more than six thousand men in his army, while the Hungarian phalanxes were estimated to contain two hundred thousand armed men [Col. 0696C]. Many bishops and numerous clerics were also with the king; out of piety, they entered the battle with him unarmed.

In that battle such a cloud and darkness overwhelmed the Hungarian side that scarcely could any of them recognize someone standing beside him. The king’s army, however, appeared to be illuminated all around and beneath by the brightest sun.

Fighting bravely, he struck down and routed his adversaries in an immeasurable slaughter, while very few of his own men fell. After capturing the enemy’s booty and restoring the kingdom to the order in which it had first been established, the triumphant king returned home.

At that time it happened that the abbot of a certain monastery, in order to win the friendship of that emperor’s generosity for himself and for the place entrusted to him, presented him with a very fine horse [Col. 0696D]. The horse, unbeknownst to the abbot, had secretly been stolen from a certain soldier and sold to him for money.

The emperor gladly accepted it and assigned it to his own riding. One day, while he was traveling mounted on that horse, the soldier from whom the aforesaid horse had been stolen happened to meet him.

Approaching the emperor prudently, he burst into these words: “You, O king, who ought to uphold the authority of all justice, are seen to possess the horse that was just fraudulently taken from me.”

The king immediately gave him this reply: “If the horse is yours, as you say, take it together with its rider, lead it away with you wherever you prefer, and keep both until you receive compensation for the theft.”

The soldier, thinking that he was being mocked, stood there in amazement. But the king compelled him to lay hands on both and lead them into his own possession [Col. 0697A]. Those standing around watched and were struck dumb with tremendous astonishment.

“What thanks,” said the king, “are due to the man who so craftily ensnared me in this trap?” While everyone was cursing him horribly, the king said: “Bring him here, so that, according to the deception he practiced against me, punishment may be exacted from him.”

When the aforesaid abbot had been summoned, he said to him: “Lay down the pastoral staff of government, which you think ought to be borne through the gift of a mortal man.”

When he had thrown it away from him, the king took it and placed it in the right hand of the image of the Savior. “Go,” he said to the abbot, “and receive it from the hand of the almighty King. Do not henceforth be indebted to any mortal for it; use it freely, as befits the dignity of so great a name” [Col. 0697B].

He received it joyfully and brought great delight to many through this deed; thereafter he flourished with complete freedom.

## CHAPTER V. On the Eradication of Simony

Recognizing, therefore, that throughout Gaul and Germany the desire for Simoniacal love of money was raging, Henry summoned from his entire empire both archbishops and the other bishops and addressed them in these words:

“I begin by speaking to you in grief, you who have been placed in the Church in Christ’s stead, the Church which he betrothed to himself and redeemed at the price of his blood. For just as he was born among us through the Virgin, in gratuitous goodness from the bosom of God the Father, in order to redeem us, so, when he sent his apostles throughout the whole world, he commanded his own: ‘Freely you have received; freely give.’

“You, however, corrupted by avarice and greed—while you ought to impose the canon against this kind of transgression, by giving and receiving—are accursed. For my father also, whose soul’s peril I greatly fear, practiced damnable avarice excessively during his life.

“Therefore, whoever among you knows that he has been contaminated by this stain must, according to canonical ordinance, be excluded from the sacred ministry. It is therefore perfectly clear that, because of this offense, various disasters have come upon the children of men: famine, plague, and also the sword.

“For all ecclesiastical ranks, from the highest pontiff down to the doorkeeper [Col. 0698A], are oppressed by the price of their condemnation; and, according to the Lord’s word, spiritual brigandage is rampant everywhere.”

After the emperor had delivered these words with great severity, the bishops were stunned and had nothing to answer him. They feared losing their own episcopal sees because of this offense.

And since this most wicked depravity had not sprouted only in the Gallican bishoprics but had occupied all Italy to a much greater extent—for at that time all ecclesiastical ministries were regarded as for sale, like secular merchandise in a marketplace—the bishops, seeing themselves ensnared by so grave an accusation, begged for mercy.

The prince, moved by compassion, offered them this word of consolation: “Go,” he said, “and strive to put in good order what you have received unlawfully. Remember to intercede attentively for the soul of my father, who is held guilty with you of this offense, so that you may obtain from God forgiveness for this crime on his behalf.”

Then he issued an edict throughout his entire empire: no clerical rank or ecclesiastical ministry was to be acquired for any price; and if anyone presumed to give or receive one, he was to be deprived of every honor and punished with anathema.

He further made this promise, saying: “Just as the Lord has given me the imperial crown freely, solely through his mercy, so I too shall freely provide whatever belongs to his religion. I wish, if it pleases you, that you likewise do the same.”

At that same time, the Roman see, which by right is regarded as universal throughout the world, had been miserably afflicted by the aforesaid pestilential disease for twenty-five years [Col. 0698C]. A certain boy of about twelve years had been appointed to that see contrary to law and right. Money alone, in gold and silver, had commended him more than either age or holiness.

And because his entry had been unfortunate, he experienced an even more unfortunate exit. For it is dreadful to recount the shamefulness of his conduct and life. Then, with the consent of the entire Roman people and by the emperor’s command, he was expelled [or removed] from the see, and in his place was installed a most religious man, distinguished for holiness, Gregory, a Roman by nationality. His good reputation restored to a better condition whatever the former man had defiled.

[Col. 0697]

# LIFE OF SAINT WILLIAM, ABBOT OF DIJON, by the monk Glaber Rodulfus

(In Mabillon, *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, Sixth Century, Part I, p. 320, from the manuscript codex of Saint Benignus of Dijon, collated with another manuscript and with the printed editions.)

## PRELIMINARY OBSERVATIONS

[Col. 0697D] 1. Among the various writers of this century who committed the deeds of blessed William to writing, two are especially notable [Col. 0698D] for having undertaken this task deliberately: one, Glaber Rodulfus, a monk of Cluny; the other, the chronicler [Col. 0699A] of Saint Benignus of Dijon. Both were contemporaries of Saint William and perhaps even his disciples.

Hugh, abbot of Flavigny, praises the Life of William edited by Glaber Rodulfus in the *Chronicle of Verdun*, in volume I of Labbe’s Library. Glaber himself also acknowledges that he composed it in Book IV, chapter 4, of his *Histories*: “Moreover,” he says, “the aforesaid father of monks and distinguished founder of monasteries, William, concerning whom more would also have to be said, except that what has been said is known to have been set forth previously in the little book which we published concerning his life and virtues.”

This little book by Glaber Rodulfus, already published by Bollandus under 1 January, we reprint here from the manuscript codex of Saint Benignus of Dijon.

2. It is clearly inferred from Glaber’s own little book that William’s birth must be assigned to the year 961 [Col. 0699B], in which it is expressly affirmed that his death occurred in 1031, at the age of seventy.

He spent almost the whole of his life in exercises of monastic discipline. This is proved by the fact that, scarcely having passed his seventh year, he put on the monastic habit at the monastery of Luciacum. From there, having departed out of zeal for stricter discipline, he withdrew to the monastery of Saint Michael and soon afterward to Cluny in Gaul with Saint Majolus.

Luciacum—also called by some Lucedium or Locedium, and commonly *di Locedia*—was an ancient monastery of our order. It was first called Saint Michael’s and later Saint Januarius’s, because the relics of that saint were transferred there; the town surrounding it also took the name of Saint Januarius. It lies not far from the city of Vercelli, to whose diocese it once belonged [Col. 0699C].

Today it is subject to the bishopric of Casale, in the territory of Montferrat. It passed first from the Benedictine order to the Cistercians and finally, after various fortunes, fell to secular clerics, as Francesco Agostino della Chiesa observes in his *History of Piedmont*, chapter 33.

3. In the twenty-ninth year of his age—that is, in 990, in the third indiction—William was ordained abbot of Saint Benignus by Lord Bruno, bishop of Langres, says the Benignian chronicler.

Besides the privilege of Pope Benedict, which some think was granted to that same William, this statement appears to be contradicted by a certain fragment of the manuscript history of the monastery of Benignus [Col. 0699D]. In it, the church of Saint Benignus is said to have been begun by William in 982 and completely restored in 986.

But these considerations are not weighty enough for us easily to depart from the authority of a serious contemporary writer, especially since both Glaber Rodulfus and the *Chronicle* edited by Labbe agree with the Benignian chronicler. It is also established that the privilege of Pope Benedict should be assigned not to Benedict VII but to Benedict VIII, since Ughelli records that it was granted in the year of Christ 1015, in volume II of *Sacred Italy*, column 996.

4. “The aforesaid William,” says Glaber in Book III, chapter 5, of his *Histories*, “was sharp-minded and distinguished for prudence; for that reason he held the highest position in the palaces of kings [Col. 0700A] and other princes.”

Blessed Odilo, his fellow student under Saint Majolus, embraces his praise in a few words, though words superior to many books, in a little work on the deeds of that same Saint Majolus. There he says:

“And, to speak with the peace of the spiritual craftsmen laboring in the same structure, one in particular shone forth who has recently departed from human affairs and who labored more than all of us—namely, Lord Abbot William. Concerning his illustrious deeds, his praiseworthy life, and his wondrous conduct, our smallness is not sufficient to report fully what it perceives.”

Jotsaldus, in his *Lament on the Death of the Blessed Odilo*, celebrates William and Odilo together in the same verses, which we shall quote below in Odilo’s Eulogy.

The old author of the *Chronicle of Fécamp* writes that William was supremely well educated in the liberal arts, in ecclesiastical disciplines, and in all spiritual offices [lacuna], imbued and enlightened by the grace of the virtues [Col. 0700B].

Thus there was scarcely any monastery in the Roman Empire that was not entrusted to William’s care. He governed some of them himself or placed his disciples over them; the abbots of the others, who were already in charge, he led by his example and admonitions to an exact practice of regular discipline.

“As an abbot of blessed memory,” says the same author, “William illuminated all the regions of the Roman Empire through the abundance of his religious observance, and he reformed and kindled the lukewarm hearts of many abbots by the image of his fervor.”

Sigebert, under the year 1027, lists him among the notable abbots through whose work ecclesiastical religion flourished in the eleventh century [Col. 0700C]:

“In France and Burgundy … through William of Dijon, revered for his strictness.”

Finally, as Glaber says in the passage just praised, whenever any monastery was deprived of its own shepherd, William was immediately compelled by kings or counts as well as by bishops to accept its governance in order to improve it.

The same author asserts that he was placed over nearly forty monasteries. The Benignian chronicler lists most of them: besides Benignus, which he discusses, Verzy, Bèze, Réome, Tornodorum, Melun, Saint Arnulf of Metz, Saint Aprus of Toul, Gorze, Fécamp, Jumièges, Saint-Ouen of Rouen, Saint Michael on Mount Tomb, Saint Faro of Meaux, Saint Germanus of Paris, Fruttuaria, Saint Amator near Langres, and Saint Mary near Saxon Fountain [Col. 0700D].

Glaber adds the monastery of Saint Saturninus on the Rhône River, which has now been reduced to a priory and made subject to the monastery of Ambronay.

5. It is not permissible here to omit the distinguished passage of Wibert, archdeacon of the monastery of Saint Aprus at Toul. Concerning Saint Leo IX, he writes in Book I, chapter 13, of his Life:

“Since his devotion to the holy and glorious Aprus was all the greater, he soon placed over that monastery, under the title of abbot, the aforesaid Guidricus, a man of religious life and conduct [Col. 0701A], at the wish and request of Lord William, at that time the venerable father of that place.”

The continuator of Aimoinus, Book V, chapter 47, likewise testifies that, while the monks of Saint Germanus of the Fields were living their lives in a secular manner, the most devout King Robert, together with his wife, Queen Constance, summoned Lord William, abbot of the monastery of Dijon, and gave him the abbey of Saint Germanus. William established it according to the rule and died in the year of the Lord 1030—or rather 1031, counting the year from the month of January, as is clear from the fourteenth indiction, the Dominical Letter C, the sixth day of the week, and the Kalends of January.

On that day, in the old necrology of the monastery of Fécamp, it reads: “On the Kalends of January, the deposition of Lord William, abbot of this place, of blessed memory, and father of many monasteries.”

On 22 February his first translation is recorded, together with the death of his successor John, in these words: “On the eighth day before the Kalends of March, the translation of Lord William, abbot of blessed memory, and at the same time the deposition of Lord John, abbot, and of his father Robert” [Col. 0701B].

In the necrology of Saint Germanus of the Fields he is commemorated on the Kalends of January, where it says: “Lord Abbot William, solicitous with extraordinary religious devotion.”

It has not seemed worthwhile to discuss here the illustrious men who flourished under William’s instruction in the various monasteries subject to his governance, since they will be mentioned below in their proper places.

6. Although, so far as we know, Saint William was not honored in ancient times by any public cult, Arnold Wion and Hugh Menard nevertheless inserted him among the saints in the sacred calendars on his January natal day, in the Benedictine Menology and Martyrology [Col. 0701C]. All more recent writers followed them and bestowed upon him the title of saint—not without reason, since so many arguments are available to demonstrate his holiness that scarcely any more certain evidence can be found for any saint of this century: foreknowledge of death, the performance of miracles, and, above all, an entirely blameless life and singular observance of the monastic rule.

For this reason Glaber, the writer of his Life, a serious man of great authority, calls Saint William’s death, in the final chapter, a passage to the holy, deifying light. He also observes—and this is especially worthy of note—that the miracles he had performed while still alive continued after his death at his tomb.

He is to be heard in Book IV, chapter 4, of his *Histories*:

“One thing remains, which I know is not contained there [in the Life of Saint William]. For the aforesaid Father departed from the world to the rest of the blessed in the regions of Neustria, namely in the monastery of Fécamp … and was buried, as was fitting for so great a man, in the finest place of that same church.

“After several days had passed, it happened [Col. 0702A] that a boy of about ten years, worn down by a severe illness, was led to his tomb in order to recover his health. There, after being left alone by his parents, he lay down.

“Suddenly, looking up, he saw a little bird sitting upon the tomb, resembling a dove in form. Gazing at it for a long time, he fell asleep. Then, refreshed by a gentle sleep, he awoke and found himself healthy, as though he had felt no illness at all.

“His joyful parents therefore received him, and the joy became shared by everyone.”

## 7. Saint William’s body was buried in the major basilica at Fécamp

The author of his Life says that it was buried in full view of the brothers going and coming—that is, before the altar of Saint Taurinus, bishop of Évreux, which today is called the altar of Saint Benedict. From this place it was later transferred to the chapel dedicated to Saint Mary Magdalene [Col. 0702B]—at what time and for what reason is unknown—and placed on the Gospel side. There it is still preserved in a stone sarcophagus, three feet long and nine inches wide, enclosed within a chamber in the wall on the north side, with the following inscription on a lead tablet, discovered in the year 1638:

> Reader, know that a full abbot of days,  
> By name William, an aged man, lies here.  
> He had shone forth as the first shepherd of this place,  
> Where, by God’s gift, he established many monks.  
> On the first day of January his new soul shone forth,  
> And the whole of the new Jerusalem came to meet it.

The occasion for this discovery was the new church constructed in honor of Saint William by the Count of Saint-Martin and the Marquis of Aglia. Since he intended to enrich it with the relics of that saint, whom he counted among his ancestors, he obtained from the most illustrious Prince of Guise, the commendatory abbot, permission to inspect and visit them, Abbot Mondino, a most distinguished man and the most serene Duchess of Savoy’s ambassador in France, having acted first with him on his mistress’s behalf.

## 8. The first inspection

This first inspection took place on 28 October 1727. It was found that Saint William’s body had for the most part been reduced to dust, apart from the principal bones. When this was reported to the ears of the most illustrious Abbot Guise, he ordered the tomb to be opened again and arranged for four bones to be removed from the sarcophagus—two to be sent to the Duchess of Savoy and the other two to the monks of Benignianus. The remaining bones, together with the ashes, were enclosed once more in a lead chest and returned to the aforementioned sarcophagus.

From the public records we learn that this final opening of the tomb [Col. 0702D] took place on 6 December of the same year. Among these records is a petition submitted to the most serene duchess in the name of the monastery of Fécamp, asking her, in her own words, to request Saint William’s canonization from the Apostolic See. But the matter remained unfinished.

# PREFACE OF THE AUTHOR

[Col. 0701]

## 1.

To the venerable Fathers endowed with the sweetness of the Holy Spirit, and to the beloved brothers who everywhere serve, in charitable hope, the universal Church of God according to its teachings: the least of monks, Ralph, offers this small token of obedience.

We do not doubt, then, that your unanimity will be pleased if we undertake to commit to posterity something concerning the life and conduct of the one whom all of you love—namely, Lord William, priest and abbot—to the extent that divine goodness has deigned to grant us the ability. Much that we ourselves have seen, and still more that we have learned from utterly truthful witnesses, will shape the course of this narrative.

Therefore we beseech the virtue-producing charity common to the faithful: do not despise a simple utterance, nor reject, as though it were from a worthless basket, a pure lump of fine flour. If its material were worked by a prudent hand, it would be able to drive away every want and confer lasting health.

# HERE BEGINS THE LIFE

[Col. 0703]

## 2. William’s homeland; his grandfather; his parents; he is received from the sacred font by a queen

The religious man, Lord William, whom the merciful Lord appointed shepherd for the children of His Church and promoter of His law, was by nationality an Italian. His grandfather, however, a man named Vibo, distinguished for military prowess, was of Suevic origin. In order to avenge enmities, he left his native province and went to settle in Italy, where he prospered happily, becoming richly endowed with wealth.

He was the father of Robert, who took as his wife a woman from among the nobility of the Lombards, named Perenza [Note: [Col. 0703D] Her death is recorded under the Kalends of November in the Necrology of Saint-Germain-des-Prés in these words: “Our friend Perenza died, the mother of Lord William, abbot.”]. She bore him a fruitful offspring of children, among whom was William, desirable above all others.

At the very time of William’s birth, Berengar, king of the Lombards, died. Otto, the greatest of emperors, then sought to bring all Italy under his power by force of arms. When he learned that Berengar’s wife had taken refuge in a certain fortress situated in the lake of the city of Novara [Note: [Col. 0704D] Other editions read *Novitiae*, incorrectly], together with men whose conspiracy was rebellious toward the emperor, he immediately turned aside to that place and surrounded it with a fierce army.

Robert was in that fortress with his own wife and children, and each of them, together with their lady, had entrusted themselves to his care and protection. After the two sides had fought fiercely for a long time, the emperor, seeing that victory was being delayed, attempted secretly to bend the standard-bearer of his enemies by gifts. He promised him, in addition to very great presents, a high position at his court if, abandoning his own side, he supported the emperor’s party [Col. 0703D].

But the man did not yield in the least, being a sworn soldier. He replied that he would prefer the death of his own body to being regarded as a deserter from the faith he had pledged.

After several days, the two sides held a discussion of peace and voluntarily surrendered to the emperor. Then Robert, a prudent and energetic man, suggested to the emperor that he command the son whom his wife had borne during the siege of the fortress to be made a catechumen by the imperial hand. The emperor gladly agreed and ordered this to be carried out as he had been advised. With his own right hand he lifted up the child and gave him the name William. Later, the queen, the emperor’s wife, received him from the sacred font of baptism.

## 3.

As we have said, his mother was distinguished not only by noble lineage but also by the uprightness of her character. She was accustomed to relate the following words concerning the boy:

> “I saw myself one night clothed in a dalmatic robe, and immediately a ray of sunlight illumined my right breast. Then certain faces appeared, bearing an angelic likeness. They themselves took my son away from me and raised the little child higher, enveloping him in immense radiance. I, watching this in great terror, was so frightened that I could find nothing else to say except: ‘Holy Mother of the Lord and Savior, I entrust him to you; protect him.’”

## 4. His parents dedicate him to God; he is educated in a monastery

Many other signs of excellent promise were observed in him, but we pass over them to avoid weariness. Even the appearance of his tenderest age seemed so unlike that of others that it was regarded as extraordinarily remarkable.

Therefore both parents, with one accord and one will, and with the favorable encouragement of all their relatives, vowed him to Christ the Lord, so that he might serve continually in His house. When he was about seven years old, they brought him to a monastery consecrated in honor of Saint Mary and the holy archangel Michael, called Luciacum, where the bones of the blessed martyr Januarius were also held in veneration. There, according to the custom [Col. 0704D] of the regular rule, they presented him to the abbot of that place.

The abbot received him with great devotion and clothed him in the habit of sacred monastic religion. He taught him the first elements of letters and placed him under the care of a teacher. The teacher was overcome with immense astonishment, because the quickness of the boy’s understanding advanced to such a degree of insight that within a short time he surpassed all the studies of his fellow pupils. Thus, even then, he was held in no small admiration by both the abbot and the other brothers.

## 5.

Moreover, in a neighboring monastery an old woman, whose husband was already elderly, had a suitable dwelling. For the sake of familiar care and protection, the boy was taken there during the day and was sometimes received there for the repose of the night.

Once, while the old woman was nurturing him with care and holding him in her arms against her breast, her breasts—which hung loosely beneath wrinkled skin—suddenly became swollen and poured forth an abundance of milk. Since she was devout in spirit and feared God, she carefully reported the matter to certain religious persons, because the boy who had appeared to her, she said, was destined to be advanced in the excellence and dignity of a higher life [Bolland., “a diligent life”].

As time passed, when he had grown older and was striving to serve obediently in the fear of God, the goads of envy were not lacking. Though often assailed by them, he steadfastly endured the reproaches of those for whose advancement he had labored with all his strength.

Earlier, first in the city of Vercelli and afterward at Pavia, he had fully learned the rules of the grammatical arts under secure supervision. He was appointed the assiduous guardian of the divine office and head of the school of that place. Advancing through a fortunate increase of virtues, with God’s favor, he was entrusted with the care and administration of the secretariat, as well as of the entire furnishings of the sanctuary, and with the determination of affairs at home and abroad.

## 6. He leads his father into the monastic life

Meanwhile he began to consider how he might withdraw his father from the storm-tossed cares of this world and have him spend the remainder of his life with him in the monastery, laboring for eternal rest. His mother had already died in peace.

He therefore persuaded his father to do what he had been considering. His father immediately obeyed his beloved son—or rather, God, who had granted him such a son. William then brought him, with great care and many gifts, to the monastery. He was received there with the greatest devotion and, himself living devoutly in the habit of holy conduct, completed his life not long afterward with an excellent end, in the presence of his son.

## 7. He refuses to swear fidelity to the bishop when he is to be ordained; consequently he is harassed and considers leaving

Meanwhile William was being sought for promotion to the office of deacon. He had truly been so obedient to the commands of those in the lower grades that he could serve even the priests as an example worthy of imitation for undertaking a safe path.

The monastery, however, was situated in the bishopric of the city of Vercelli [Col. 0705D] and was subject to the authority of that bishop. A bad custom had also taken root through an ill-considered practice: no brother of that place was to receive the grade of the levitical order before promising, by an oath, that he would preserve fidelity to the bishop.

When William was urged to do this according to their custom, he replied—being, as he was, refined and courteous—that he could not properly answer that he should in any way offer a declaration of fidelity to their minister for things which ought freely to be rendered at the command of God alone [Bolland., “could not properly weigh”]. “On the contrary,” he said, “a terrible judgment of the Savior threatens such flatterers.”

After giving this reply, he entirely delayed doing what they had urged him to do. At once he was vigorously assailed by the gnawing slanders of those who had urged this upon him, reproved by the bishop himself, and regarded as defiant of his authority.

He considered such things worthless and bound himself more and more to the worship of God, so that almost the entire care and responsibility for singing psalms, reading, and ringing the hours, by day and by night, rested on him alone in that place. For he was chaste in mind and body and ready for every good work. He frequently considered whether he might perhaps find some place to which he could move and serve the regular precepts more devoutly. The fervor of regular discipline had already grown very cold there.

## 8.

Accordingly, on one occasion he obtained permission to go for the sake of prayer and visitation to the monastery of the blessed archangel Michael [Note: [Col. 0705D] This monastery appears to be none other than the one said to have been dedicated to Saint Michael on the summit of Mount Picheriano, twelve miles from Cinisio, as recorded in the *History of Piedmont* [Col. 0706D]; for many years it has passed from monks to clerics.]. It is known to be situated on the highest ridges of the Alps.

When he had reached the foot of the mountain and had almost completed the ascent to the monastery—for the path was difficult—his horse, which he was leading behind him by a rein held in his right hand, strayed slightly from the narrow track while placing its foot, the rein slipped free, and the animal plunged headlong down the entire enormous precipice.

Seeing this, the man devoted to God was terrified in spirit, though his face remained serene. He continued to the church, applied himself to prayer, and prayed there for a long time as though nothing adverse had occurred.

Then he went out and sent a servant to find out what had happened to the horse, if anything had happened contrary to their hopes, and to report back to him. The servant went out and found the horse standing unharmed in the place where it had fallen, so that there was no injury at all visible on it; nor did there appear to be any abrasion on the harness or on the wood of the saddle.

For the distance from the place where it had begun its fall to the valley where it had come to rest amounted to two miles and more. He recovered the horse brought back by the servant and returned it to the man who had lost it [or: dismissed it]. Then, giving thanks to almighty God, he joyfully returned to the monastery. This event caused astonishment in many people and served as a sign of holiness.

## 9. He moves to Cluny and refuses the priesthood

William had heard, as widespread rumor proclaimed, that there was a monastery called Cluny in the regions of Burgundy [Col. 0706D], where the order of holiness, the strictness of the rule, and the discernment that is the mother of virtues had flourished incomparably above all others from the beginning. His mind burned with an intense desire to go there and visit it.

While he was considering this, it happened that the most holy abbot of that place, Majolus, while visiting sacred churches according to custom, turned aside to the monastery of Luciacum. When Christ’s servant William saw this and understood that God had decreed the fulfillment of his desire, he approached the man of God privately and disclosed to him the secret of his heart.

Majolus promised him with great eagerness the assistance he desired in everything he had resolved to undertake in the worship of God’s work. He then proceeded to Rome, intending to return and take William with him to the place he had long desired.

Meanwhile William wisely considered everything that seemed to concern him. Like a soldier ready for battle, he feared that, as he hastened toward the contest of faith, things long freely enjoyed might obstruct him: the claims of his parents, the appealing presence of his blood brothers, or their villages, broad estates, and many castles; even the affection owed to his native soil or the general love of all people. He therefore committed himself entirely to divine providence, so that, free and unburdened from all these things, he might run the way of God’s commandments as he had resolved.

When the man of God Majolus returned from Rome, each remembering his own promise, he received William as a spiritual son of Christ and led him to the most holy monastery of Cluny.

When William arrived there, Majolus sent one of his men ahead, announcing to the brothers that they should come out to meet him in their customary ceremonial dress, because they were about to receive someone who was arriving with him and to whom honor was owed by divine appointment.

At last, William was received with solemn ceremony, as the saint had ordered, and was honorably advanced with the counsel of the brothers, who had all perceived in him the merit of his life. The man of God Majolus also frequently held private conversations with William concerning the things that lead to true salvation.

After he had spent about a full year in that place, he was considered more admirable and venerable than all others, and worthy of imitation by the more honorable. His spiritual father then judged him entirely worthy to exercise the priesthood, for he had already been consecrated to the levitical ministry.

But William humbly and fearfully withdrew, saying that he was altogether unworthy to handle the sacrament of so great a mystery [Note: [Col. 0707D] The most modest abbot remained for a long time in the levitical rank. Thus, in the letter of Bishop Bruno concerning Flavigny, he subscribed as “Wilencus the Levite”; and in the round church of Saint Benignus, which that bishop built, the same name and title can still be read. Nevertheless, he later became a priest, as appears from the prologue above, no. 1, and below [Col. 0708D], no. 16.]. The saint, unwilling to disturb the disposition of his spirit, agreed to his wish.

## 10. He is placed over the monastery of Saint Saturninus

Meanwhile a certain prior of the monastery of the holy martyr Saturninus [Note: [Col. 0708D] It is now a priory subject to the monastery of Ambronay, commonly called Saint-Saurin.]—which lies on the Rhône—came to ask the holy man Majolus to lend him one of his men who could instruct him and the brothers entrusted to him in recognizing the way of salvation.

The man of mercy, considering the matter from two perspectives—namely, the assistance of one man and the testing of another’s obedience—immediately entrusted Lord William to him [Col. 0707D].

William did not hesitate or resist in the least. He humbly went to obey the Father’s command, since the man had come for the sake of the soul’s benefit.

The aforementioned man had several brothers living with him. Yet all had one will, one common agreement, one manner of acting, one way of praying, singing psalms, and eating, and their entire conduct was uniform through charity, with William truly serving as their teacher, according to Cluniac custom [Col. 0708A].

Indeed, all their private property appeared to be held in common in the community. After William had been raised to greater responsibilities, he was accustomed to say that nowhere had he found a more desirable place for attaining the poverty he had resolved to embrace, or for reaching the highest degree of holiness.

## 11. Then over the monastery of Saint Benignus

At that same time, the memorable Father Majolus was approached by Bruno, bishop of Langres, of venerable memory. Bruno asked him to undertake the monastery of the distinguished martyr Benignus, anciently venerated beside the fortress of Dijon, in order to restore the order of divine worship, which had entirely failed in that place. As he had long been accustomed to do in many monasteries, Majolus was to strive to reform this one for the better as well.

Moved by piety, the holy man immediately sent for William, asking that he be brought back to him. William had already completed a year and a half of devout living with the brother to whom Majolus had entrusted him.

When William had been recalled, Majolus entrusted to him, by a gentle command, the paternal care of the flock of Christ in the monastery of the holy martyr mentioned above. He further promised that whatever assistance William desired for the advancement of this spiritual undertaking, he himself would willingly provide.

He also solemnly charged the bishop, in God’s faith and in his own, to be William’s advocate and guardian, helper and comforter in all things, as a most loving father. Obeying this instruction with complete fidelity, the bishop loved him beyond what could be believed.

Thus the gracious Lord William went to the monastery appointed for him to receive and govern it. Saint Majolus sent with him some of the more honorable brothers of Cluny. William was received there with honor and, according to custom, was consecrated by Bishop Bruno himself as Father of the monks.

## 12. Then over Verziacum and Besua; his humility

Since he subjected himself and those entrusted to him to the regular disciplines with the keenest and most watchful zeal for the love of God, it was not long before the venerable Duke Henry also entrusted to him the monastery situated beside the fortress of Verziacum, where the ancient confessor of Christ, Saint Viventius, rests.

That monastery, like the first, lacked regular governance. After he had reformed it for the better, he was likewise appointed Father by the same Bishop Bruno over a third monastery, which was also without proper discipline and a rule of upright living. It stood beside the source of the Besua and was dedicated to the prince of the apostles.

It was extremely ancient and had often been laid waste by the attacks of pagans and of every kind of wicked person.

While William was striving with all his strength to restore it, it happened that the aforementioned bishop was holding a peace conference with Count William, lord of a large part of Burgundy [Note: [Col. 0708D] Count Otto, surnamed William, adopted by Duke Henry. He is frequently mentioned in the *Benignian Chronicle*. He was advocate of the monastery of Benignus, to which, as well as to Besua, Fruttuaria, and other holy places, he contributed many gifts. He died in 1027 and was buried in the monastery of Saint Benignus. “He deserved,” says the chronicler, “that his memory should always be celebrated by the monks of this place.”], who was also related by kinship to the father about whom we are speaking.

After other matters had been discussed, the bishop whispered to the count that he should gently suggest to the abbot, since he was his kinsman, that he should beware lest pride seize him on account of his virtues or his wealth.

The count respectfully approached William and delivered the message as he had been instructed. Father William then gave the count this reply with a cheerful expression:

> “If I could know that an increase of earthly wealth or possessions would prolong the span of even a single day of our life, I could not be persuaded not to exert myself for their increase.”

When the count reported this reply to the bishop, they both admired William’s wisdom and rejoiced equally at his humble understanding.

## 13. He is placed over the monastery of Fécamp

Since the report of William’s holiness was now spreading more widely, the venerable duke of the Normans, Richard, learned of it and sent for him, respectfully begging him to come to him.

William eventually went to him willingly, as he had been asked, and was received by him with due honor. The duke, refreshed by William’s most holy words, being a lover of every good thing, begged him to take charge of and adorn with a monastic order the church dedicated to the name and honor of the holy and undivided Trinity. It had been constructed long ago at a place called Fécamp and had been restored with greater magnificence by the duke’s father, Richard.

There lived a small and frivolous group of clerics, following a worldly way of life and released from the yoke of the rule.

Father William, seeing the devotion of the duke’s spirit [Col. 0709C], promised that with God’s help he would fulfill what the duke requested. They came together to the place, and there the duke, with several bishops, solemnly entrusted William with authority and responsibility for governing the entire site.

The man of God then gathered there a regular company of monks, so numerous in persons and so rich in the pursuit of good works that it surpassed the number of the former clerics threefold.

When the prince saw this, he enlarged the place with gifts of many kinds and grants of possessions. He also frequently urged both the abbot and the other brothers to ask him for whatever they knew would benefit their community, since in this matter he possessed both the will and the power to fulfill their wishes.

## 14. He establishes schools there

Meanwhile the most watchful Father saw that not only in that place but throughout the entire province, and indeed throughout all Gaul, the knowledge of singing psalms and reading was failing and disappearing among the clerics, especially among the lower clergy.

He established schools for sacred service, where learned brothers would devote themselves continually to this office for the love of God. There the benefit of instruction was freely bestowed on all who came to the monasteries entrusted to him, and no one who wished to attend was excluded.

On the contrary, a uniform lesson of charity was offered to servants and free persons alike, to the rich together with the poor. Many of these students, being poor in material resources, received food from the monasteries. Some of them also entered the habit of monks living in holy fellowship.

This labor of instruction ultimately brought highly desirable fruit to various churches. For he adorned the aforementioned place, as we had begun to say, with cloisters, regular workshops, and every other abundance of good things, so that it might always flourish with happier growth than the other institutions of that province.

## 15. He restores the church of Saint Benignus and discovers his tomb

It later happened that a part of the church of the blessed martyr Benignus, over which William had first been appointed father by God’s authority, collapsed in ruin.

When the masons wished to restore it, that same section suffered an even greater collapse. Seeing this, the man devoted to God understood that a divine sign was being given to him: the whole church ought to be renewed from its foundations.

Immediately, with the greatest ingenuity of mind, he began to devise a splendid arrangement for restoring the church. He began rebuilding it according to a remarkable design, much longer and broader than it had been.

No one, however, knew the small place in which the limbs of the precious martyr Benignus had been enclosed. In ancient times he had been buried there with such careful attention that the martyr could be confidently venerated through the ages in the place where he had died a blessed death for God. Some careless persons even claimed that his relics were not there.

This ignorance greatly saddened Father William. In the midst of his anxiety over this defect, the martyr of God himself revealed his honorable tomb to him in a most beautiful vision.

For, as Gregory, bishop of Tours, the blessed author of many accounts of miracles, relates [Note: [Col. 0709D] Namely, in book I, chapter 51, of *On the Glory of the Martyrs*. [Col. 0710D] The *Life of Gregory of Langres* is found among the *Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 7.], it was a very large stone sarcophagus containing the martyr. The same saint relates that another Gregory, Gregory the bishop of Langres, had once been severely reproached because he did not believe this.

The ancient past had concealed the position of the tomb. It had been buried deeply in front of the principal altar of that monastery.

William immediately searched for it and found it. When he opened it, he was permitted to touch the most sacred bones of the distinguished martyr. A wound inflicted by an iron bar was also visible in the martyr’s brain, as is recorded in the account of his passion [Note: [Col. 0710D] The *Passion of Saint Benignus* was published by the distinguished Francis du Bosquet, then praetor of Narbonne, in his *History of the Gallican Church*.].

He reburied all the bones, intact in number, in the same sarcophagus, in the presence of the more distinguished bishops and of other persons of various orders and both sexes, accompanied by fragrant incense and choirs singing psalms. Then he moved the sarcophagus a little toward the east and placed it in a most beautiful and incomparable tomb [Col. 0711A].

Thereafter the venerable Father, inflamed with even greater devotion, hastened eagerly to complete the work of restoring the basilica, as he had resolved. For, as we have said—and as can still be seen—he intended to complete a basilica more remarkable than all the basilicas of Gaul and incomparable in its particular arrangement.

## 16. He reforms the monastery of Saint Arnulf at Metz; he goes to Rome and falls ill on his return

With the grace of almighty God cooperating in him, the fame of William’s holiness began to penetrate the neighboring provinces and those farther away.

Adalbero, bishop of Metz, respectfully summoned him and entrusted to him the governance and improvement of the monastery of Saint Arnulf the confessor, as he was accustomed to do. William accepted it and returned it corrected within a short time.

He then conceived in his devout mind the intention of visiting the most holy threshold of the prince of the apostles, Saint Peter. Having established suitable superiors and other officials in the monasteries entrusted to him, he went to Rome for the sake of prayer, as he had resolved.

After visiting the tombs and shrines of the saints, and personally celebrating the sacred solemnities of Mass—for the aforementioned Bishop Bruno had imposed the priesthood upon him—he returned to his homeland, comforted by the apostolic blessing.

He began to fall ill with a fever. When he had just reached the monastery of Saint Christina the virgin [Note: [Col. 0711D] The monastery of Saint Christina near Ollona, concerning which there survives a diploma of Louis the Pious, in the notes to the *Capitularies*, edited by Cointius, volume VII, under the year 822.], he lay down in bed.

After recovering somewhat, he reached Vercelli, where he again began to suffer a more serious illness. Then, as he himself was accustomed to relate—and as Gerbald of blessed memory, a monk of the holy Father Majolus and abbot of the aforementioned monastery of Saint Christina, also testified—while he was lying in the church of Saint Eusebius the bishop, he became so lifeless for a period of four or five hours that no breath at all could be detected in him.

It is unknown, however, what divine things he perceived at that time. For, when he gradually came to himself, he uttered in a trembling tongue, with whatever voice he could command, these words:

> “Lord Jesus Christ, King of eternal glory, receive me, if it pleases you, for you are good. I do not doubt that from this body I shall pass to you.”

It should be understood that, as the subsequent outcome of the matter shows, the duration of this illness was not so much an impediment as a grace yielding spiritual gain.

## 17. He founds the monastery of Fruttuaria

At last, three of his own brothers came to meet him there and carried him in a light conveyance to estates under their authority, so that he might recover his strength. They ardently desired to see him, because the absence of divine piety pierced their hearts.

When he had recovered from his illness, after several days all his relatives and several lords of the neighboring cities came to him. They began to persuade him, promising that they would make many gifts if he began to build a monastery in his native land, just as they had heard that he had done abroad [Col. 0712A].

Most importantly, two of his brothers, namely Godefredus and Nitardus, distinguished men, secretly approached him together with Count William, lord of a large part of Burgundy, who was also related by kinship to the father about whom we are speaking. They promised that they would abandon secular military service and that they and all their possessions would pass into the special dominion of almighty God.

When he heard this, the worshiper of God immediately and confidently began to consider the construction of the monastery for which they had asked him. Together, by common counsel and will, they searched for a suitable site and found one in their father’s countryside, four miles distant from the River Po, a solitary place called Fruttuaria.

There he ordered a basilica to be established [Col. 0712B] and, in the presence of King Arduino, commanded that it be consecrated by several bishops in honor of Mary, the Mother of God, Saint Benignus the martyr, and all the saints.

That same king rests buried there with his wife and children. William also gathered into it, from Rome and from various other regions, very many bodies of holy martyrs.

After the death of Emperor Otto III, the Italians, who were reluctant to see the kingdom of Italy transferred to the Germans, hailed Arduino, son of the marquis of Ivrea, as king. Henry the Pious pursued him with arms and eventually compelled him first to return to private life and afterward to enter the monastery of Fruttuaria [Note: [Col. 0711D]].

Within a short time a numerous community of God-fearing brothers assembled there, observing the institutions of the blessed abbot Benedict, which Father William himself had learned from Saint Majolus at Cluny.

## 18. He persuades Saint Odilo to enter the monastery

After these events, William returned from Italy and devoted every effort to gathering from various parts of the world men suitable for the service of Christ [Col. 0712C]. He persuaded them by speaking of the glory of heavenly life and at the same time threatened them with the punishments of hell.

The Lord had granted him, along with his other virtues, such power in the saving word that to all who received his teaching he imparted the greatest firmness of faith, an increase of good virtues, and correction of vices.

He offered this instruction to everyone as he knew it was useful, whether gently or with the greatest severity, but always charitably.

It happened that on one occasion he held a conversation concerning the true salvation of souls with a man desirable in every respect, namely Lord Odilo, who was still living in the canonical habit.

Recognizing that Odilo was striving toward the heights of holiness, William began to urge him more attentively to accomplish as soon as possible what he believed to be of the greatest importance—namely, to set aside the affairs of this world so that he might follow Jesus Christ more freely [Col. 0712D].

The distinguished man was immediately moved to compunction and willingly promised that he would do what Father William had advised. Not long afterward, he came honorably to the famous monastery of Cluny. There Saint Majolus received him devoutly and, according to custom, consecrated him as a monk in the habit of holy fellowship.

Odilo’s conduct afterward became so pleasing to God and so sweet to those who loved God that the most holy Majolus commended him to the flock entrusted to him, saying that after Majolus’s death they would have Odilo as their father and shepherd.

This happened most clearly and beneficially. The immense love that they had for one another while both were alive cannot be expressed: each preferred the other to himself [Note: [Col. 0713D] In the printed editions, many passages here had been transposed; with the assistance of our manuscript copy, we have restored each to its proper place.].

### 19. He Is Esteemed by the Roman Pontiffs

Moreover, Father William was held in such great veneration and reverence by the Roman pontiffs who presided in his time that, whatever he suggested to them—whether in person or through some embassy—they eagerly endeavored to carry out. For he also tried to admonish Pope John by letter, because the pope paid too little attention to spiritual gifts being sold throughout the world, especially in Italy, for a price of gold or silver. The letter contained the following:

> “Spare us, I beg you, spare us—you who are called the salt of the earth and the light of the world. It should be enough that Christ was once sold for the common salvation of all. For now, as deserters from the true light and shepherds in name alone, look behind you to see where the sheepfold of Christ, indeed his members, are going. If the stream is lukewarm beside its source, no one doubts that farther away it will stink. Therefore care is sold to some for their own destruction. I wish you all, shepherds and pontiffs, to remember the axe of the Judge who bears it and stands before the door.”

The pope gladly received this letter and returned thanks and blessings to so great a Father, glorifying God in him.

[Note: Besides this letter of William to John XVIII, the supreme pontiff, there is also another addressed to the same man, in which William warns him not to allow the Church of Constantinople to claim for itself the title “Universal.” Rumor had falsely spread that the patriarchs of Constantinople had already obtained this title through an embassy sent to John. The same Glaber mentions this letter, the embassy, and the whole affair in Book IV, chapter 1; Hugh of Flavigny also mentions them in his Chronicle under the year 1024, where this second letter is preserved.]

### 20. He Wins over the Emperor Henry

Finally, the following was also highly memorable in this Father: although many nobles had then been infected by the poisonous words of wicked men and had prepared insults against him, or quarrels to be returned in revenge, whenever they came into his presence they immediately marveled that they had become incapable of expressing what they had intended. Their former ferocity was lost, and whatever followed proceeded entirely from gentleness.

The emperor Henry had been told about him that William, disparaging the emperor and judging him contemptible, favored the party of Arduino, who had seized the kingdom of Italy from him, and defended Arduino to the best of his ability. For this reason the emperor had become angry with the man of God, although without cause. When William learned of it, he went to him, laid out the truth of the matter while clearing himself, and wiped away whatever hatred the emperor had in his heart. Thereafter the emperor loved him so greatly that he bestowed many gifts upon him and immediately granted whatever William wished to have done.

### 21. And King Robert of France

In the same way, it had been reported to Robert, king of the Franks, that William was giving advice to the aforementioned Bruno, bishop of Langres, who was less obedient to the king, and that this advice resisted royal authority too strongly. The king and his wife, the queen, were consequently angered against him and repeatedly threatened to inflict the greatest damage upon his monasteries.

William therefore approached them both fearlessly and so restrained their anger through the power of the divine word that he also obtained their highest favor and esteem. When their son—called Hugh the Great on account of the gracefulness and generosity of his youth—had died after being anointed king,

[Note: Hugh, son of Robert, was anointed king in 1017 and died in 1026, on 17 September. He was buried in the church of Saint Cornelius at Compiègne.]

and both parents were afflicted by grief and mourning almost to the point of death because of his loss, a spiritual physician came to them and said:

> “You ought not to consider yourselves unfortunate because you have lost such a man; rather, you should consider yourselves exceedingly fortunate, because you were found worthy to have such a son. I say that, among every rank of human beings, I judge that the very fewest will be saved from among kings.”

When they replied in astonishment, “What are you saying, Father?” he answered:

> “Have you not heard how the sacred canon reports that scarcely three good men were found among thirty kings? Therefore, I beg you, stop mourning this young man as dead; instead, rejoice with him, since he has been granted rest and freed from evils.”

By these words he consoled and pacified them so greatly that they seemed to have nothing left to mourn, and they said that God had visited them through the holy man.

### 22. Bishop Hermann Persecutes the Monks and Perishes

He sometimes interpreted the names of certain people, either for their advancement or for their harm. After the death of Bertoald, bishop of Toul, who had entrusted to him the monastery of Saint Aper the Confessor, a certain bishop named Hermann was appointed to that episcopate. Hermann began to hate the monks of this Father, together with his institution, so fiercely that he even attacked with his staff the most honorable brother named Widric, who later became the devout Father of that same place and who at that time was responsible for the others.

When this was reported to the Father, he alluded to Hermann’s name and said:

> “This bishop acts according to his name.”

For in the barbarian language *Herman* means “a wandering man” in our language. Then he continued:

> “If he had been Christ’s shepherd, he would certainly not have torn apart his little sheep. Leave him alone: the true Shepherd knows, and he himself will gather what belongs to him.”

Not long afterward Hermann traveled far away to collect secular revenues and died cruelly, receiving burial in a foreign land.

### 23. And Leo of Vercelli

Leo, bishop of Vercelli, was likewise hostile to all the actions of this Father because of envy. William also used to say such things about him:

> “This most cruel Leo is entirely without God, because, if God had been with him, he would have loved what belongs to God for God’s sake.”

He also asserted that Leo was condemned after death and would remain condemned eternally. For it became unmistakably clear in many cases that whoever hated William thereafter paid the penalty, while, conversely, whoever loved him received from Christ the reward brought about by William’s holiness.

### 24. He Presides over Forty Monasteries and Twelve Hundred Monks; Those Who Pray in William’s Faith Are Heard; He Teaches the Unlearned to Pray; His Care for the Divine Office

It became abundantly clear everywhere that this Father had earned fertile grace and the richest gifts from the giver of every good thing. But, to spare the reader’s weariness, we conceal many matters in silence.

There were about forty monasteries, coenobia, and monastic cells which, under his protection, safely abounded in every kind of good; the brothers living in them were certainly more than twelve hundred. They possessed an utterly steadfast faith that, as long as they devotedly practiced what they had learned from this Father, they ought to fear nothing in this world and suffer no lack of anything useful to them. He very often impressed upon them that they should hope for and believe this in God, and they also proved it by many experiences.

For example, when they were traveling by various roads through different lands and might have been disturbed by the appearance of unexpected events, they were accustomed to say:

> “Lord, in the faith of Father William, do for us as you will.”

No one who said this ever lacked assistance.

He also taught the simpler and uneducated brothers who came to him from the world a form of prayer consisting mystically of five formulas, so that, just as God is offended through the five senses of the human body, he might be entreated for mercy through an equal number of clauses.

It was as follows:

> “Lord Jesus, merciful King, gracious King, merciful God.”

After each phrase, “Have mercy” was added. It was counted out in such a way that, if it were devoutly recited three times and five times again in the nineteenfold sequence of the articulations, the entire series of the Psalter would be completed by repetition. Thus, as the Father taught them, it was regarded among them as a substitute for the Psalter and was called by that name.

Mortification of the flesh, rejection of the body, meanness of clothing, and the utmost moderation or frugality in food flourished among all his people as though naturally. The manner of his speech, too, was equally pleasing to everyone, so far as could be seen, because it was imbued with grace. He devoted an immeasurable amount of work to piety and mercy.

Together with the nectar of heavenly sweetness, he was also highly skilled and adorned with the principles of trained music. Whatever was sung in the chanting of his choirs, by day and by night, in antiphons, responsories, and hymns, he corrected and improved, directing it toward such complete correctness that no one in the entire Roman Church could chant more fittingly or accurately. He also embellished the harmony of the psalms by distinguishing it with a melody sweeter than all others.

### 25. The Monasteries Are Restored; the Church of Saint Benignus Is Dedicated; He Preaches There

As we have said, many large and small monasteries and coenobia were under his protection. He either renewed them all from their foundations or made them more honorable by enlarging them.

The basilica of the holy martyr Benignus, whose pastor he had first been appointed by God’s authority, had nearly been completed through incomparable workmanship. After Bruno’s death and Lambert’s succession to his see, it was decided that the basilica should be consecrated according to custom by pontifical blessing.

On the appointed day, Fathers came together at his request from different provinces—not only bishops, but also an innumerable multitude of ordinary people of every order. It was the third day before the Kalends of November, before the feast of the martyr. After everything had been properly and solemnly completed as was fitting, the bishops and all the religious men present asked Father William to offer, during the solemn celebration of Mass on so great a day of consecration, the alms of the divine word both to them and to the entire people.

As he was obedient to every good work, he did not delay. With a devout mind, a contrite heart, a cheerful countenance, and filled with the Holy Spirit, he burst into tears and said:

> “Brothers and sisters, you have gathered here, a flock redeemed at the price of Christ’s blood. You have gathered, I say, for the wedding of his bride, your heavenly and eternal mother, the Church. She is called universal because she is extended not only to all the ends of the world, but also because no enormity of sins overcomes her gifts of mercy—provided only that faith is present.
>
> “She was mystically foreshadowed by the figures of the patriarchs, shown beforehand by the predictions of the prophets, built through the authority and labor of the apostles, and consecrated by the blood of the martyrs. In her, washed and renewed from the guilt of our former offense through the saving water of baptism, you are clothed in the first robe of angelic blessedness, which you lost through the transgression of the first parent, the inhabitant of paradise.
>
> “Then you eat the flesh and drink the blood of that almighty Lamb who, forming and redeeming you above all other creatures of the world, chose you in unconquerable kindness to possess the kingdom of himself and of the Father, and the glory of the Holy Spirit. Beloved, I invite, admonish, and entreat you to strive toward that kingdom through the fire of charity and the continual guarding of humility and chastity.
>
> “I should have rejoiced in the devotion of your unanimity and in your gathering for this consecration. But excessive sorrow weighs down my mind because of the signs of Satan which are most clearly visible among the people of God. Do you not see, you whose minds are still sound, the most savage tearing and cutting of garments? The shaving of men’s necks? The shameful roughness of the cheeks upon the beard? The almost wholly foolish and insane behavior of nearly everyone? The wanton oaths shouted in a harsh voice during almost every conversation?
>
> “All these things, recent and newly thickened, have not proceeded from the religious character of Christianity [manuscript: ‘from the goodness of Christ’], but have arisen from the fury of diabolical superstition. From this also sprouts pride, the root of all evils, and the fuel of the other vices. Judge for yourselves whether you are not servants of the one whose insignia and scars you bear upon yourselves.
>
> “I am ashamed to say this, yet I regret remaining silent, because you expected the sweetness of the word, while I offer you instead the bitterness of general rebuke. I also admonish anyone in this entire assembly who has offered even five solidi or anything at all as a gift toward rebuilding this holy martyr’s church, which you see before your eyes, to report it publicly before everyone.”

When no one was found to have contributed anything, he continued:

> “See, beloved brothers, amid what thorns and fires of the worst men this hall of almighty God has, through faith in his witness Benignus, risen to such elegant heights, God himself cooperating. I wish you, if it pleases you, to remember constantly how quickly each person lays aside worldly care and ambition.
>
> “Therefore, I beg you, resist vices and the evil devil with the help of our Creator; take up and cultivate the splendid virtues; obey in everything the most merciful God, your Creator and Redeemer. Through faith, prayers, and the merits of all his faithful, may he make you worthy to enter with them into the kingdom of eternal glory, through Jesus Christ, his beloved Son.”

When he had finished speaking and everyone had answered, “Amen,” the sobs, tears, and groans that resounded throughout the church cannot be described. When everything had been properly completed, all returned joyfully to their homes.

From that day onward, many kinds of cures of different illnesses took place in the same basilica, especially at the tomb of the glorious martyr; their multitude makes it impossible to record them. Moreover, whoever asks in full faith for whatever is beneficial unquestionably obtains it, provided that he is such as to deserve it through the merits and prayers of the saints.

### 26. William Shines through Miracles and Raises a Man Punished with Death

We should not pass over the fact that, while many were restored in mind through Father William’s conversation, many more were restored in body through his touch, refreshed through his prayer, comforted through his visits, and strengthened through his blessing.

Although what was once customary among the followers of Christ—raising the dead—is now heard of less often, we shall nevertheless relate a few of the many things which, as we have testified, the Lord accomplished through this man.

Once, as William was returning from the monastery of Saint Vivian the Confessor and was already approaching the monastery of Saint Benignus, he met a crowd of ordinary people weeping and returning from the spectacle of a wretched man—one of the servants of Saint Benignus’s household—whom the magistrate had convicted of a crime and sentenced to death by hanging.

When the merciful man heard this, although he was a mile away, he left his horse and hurried there, saying only:

> “Jesus, Jesus, who spared the thief on the cross, have mercy.”

He ordered his men quickly to take down the unfortunate man whom they saw hanging from the beam, already stiff. Then he prostrated himself and devoted himself entirely to prayer.

When they loosened the ropes tightening the man’s throat, the lifeless body fell to the ground. The holy man approached him and said:

> “Rise; the Lord commands it.”

The man opened his eyes, raised himself, and marveled greatly that he was still alive. He left with the man of God and, while everyone rejoiced, lived for many more years at the monastery.

In various provinces William also freed many others from hanging and death, both through his intervention and by paying the price of their redemption.

### 27. Gentle in Collecting Revenues; He Appears to the Author of This Life

He often impressed upon the brothers responsible for the interests of the monasteries that they should exercise prudence in collecting what had been entrusted to them, lest the very poor be afflicted excessively for the sake of tax revenues. He used to say that he would rather give something to a needy person than demand anything from one who was indigent.

Whenever he traveled through cities and villages, wherever he was going, an immense crowd of poor and sick people had already gathered before him. He was generous and liberal in dispensing every kind of benefit. People of every rank and sex longed for his presence, as though he were one of the patriarchs or apostles of the Lord.

Some also reported that he had appeared to them in dreams and had rebuked them for their wicked deeds or warned them about the common salvation of souls.

I call Charity herself, the mother of the virtues, to witness that once, when he had been offended by the guilt of my crimes and, as I perceived, had grown bitter toward me for a time, I withdrew to another monastery not subject to his authority. While I was staying there, he seemed one night to stand before me with a peaceful expression, and, placing his hand upon my head and stroking it, he said:

> “I ask you not to abandon me [printed editions: ‘I ask you to learn from me’] if you pretended not to love me; rather, I wish you to practice what you promised.”

At his command, I had already described for the most part the events and miracles which took place around and after the thousandth year from the incarnation of the Savior. This was also the reason that compelled me to turn my attention to the present work. Therefore I ask everyone alike not to form a prejudice against me on this account.

### 28. Everyone Reveres Him

The blessedness of the outstanding Father William had grown to such excellence that his love and veneration penetrated all the provinces of Latium and Gaul. Kings regarded him as a father, bishops as a teacher, abbots and monks as an archangel, and everyone together as God’s friend and their teacher of salvation.

Who else ever held the Venetian people in such friendly intimacy? We speak hyperbolically, following the Apostle (Galatians 4:15), for if it had been possible, they would have torn out their own eyes and given them to him.

Their patriarch, Ursus, indeed resolved to become a monk under this holy Father. But William, considering the loss that would come upon that people from the absence of so great a man, persuaded him to remain in his purpose. He is also known to have done the same for many others for a similar reason.

### 29. He Returns from Italy to Gaul and Dies Devoutly at Fécamp

Now, more assiduous in God’s work than active in worldly affairs, he spent two years in Italy awaiting his departure from the world; nevertheless, summoned thence by pressing circumstances, he returned to Gaul with the greatest reluctance.

Out of affection for revisiting them all, he travelled as far as the monastery of Gorze, which he had formerly reformed with the others according to the pattern of the Rule, and took care to visit the places that remained. Then he came to the aforementioned Fécamp.

After several days he began to suffer severe pains. With the solemnity of the Lord’s Nativity already approaching, he foresaw the day of his summons by Christ. He called the brothers to him and, deliberating prudently and wisely in their presence about everything that depended upon his protection—what should be done and how it should be arranged—and having strengthened all, present and absent alike, with his blessing and commended them to God, he asked that the saving and life-giving Viaticum be given to him.

After the entire solemnity of eight days had been completed, he spoke nothing at all, but raised his eyes only to God, directing his attention to him alone and contemplating him alone in his mind. Now the blessed soul was already looking toward the God of majesty, to whom it would soon depart from the vessel of the flesh, in his glory.

In the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1031, in the fourteenth indiction, in the seventieth year from the birth of this Father and worshiper of God, and in the forty-first year from his arrival in Gaul from Italy, while Conrad was emperor and Robert was king in France, on the venerable feast of the Lord’s Circumcision, the eighth day of the Nativity, on Friday morning, when the dawn of the coming day was driving away the darkness, the happy and blessed soul passed from the holy body of this friend of God—this lamp of the world—out of the world into eternal and divine light.
