His own people mourned, but the angels rejoiced. With them he praised and magnified God, blessing him in whom everything that exists justly lives.

His sacred body was honorably buried in the bosom of that same church of the Holy Trinity, in sight of the brothers going and returning, so that they might have before their eyes each day a Father worthy of imitation—one whom they had received as their instructor toward the eternal reward of justice—and so that through his merits and prayers they might be able to receive the kingdom of eternal life and glory with all the saints, through the gift of the Lord Jesus Christ the Savior, who with God the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns through immortal ages of ages. Amen.

## In the Year of the Lord 1048. Seifrid, Abbot of the Monastery of Tegernsee

## Letters of Seifrid

*(In Pez, Codex Diplomatico-Historico-Epistolaris, column 236, Thesaurus Anecdotorum, volume V.)*

### First Letter: To Bishop N.  
*He sends two of his brothers and promises his own arrival.*

To his most special lord +, surpassing all people of our time in holiness and justice, S., an abbot only in name, together with those subject to him, wishes perpetual joy in the inner and outer man, with all heart and voice.

Most reverend Father, I know that in every way I ought to obey you with servile service as long as I live. To the extent that I am able, I most devotedly desire to fulfill this with all the strength of my body. But I grieve that I cannot show myself worthy of the benefits which your eminence has often bestowed upon my smallness.

Devotedly and without ceasing, I entreat Christ, King of kings, for your salvation. Although my earthly resources fail me for rendering you service, I hope that before you, just as before God, my good will will suffice.

For this reason, of my own accord, I am sending you the two brothers whom you ordered me to send, and I subject them to the service of you alone because of the indissoluble bond of charity between us.

Therefore, because of the desolation of my monastery, even if our senior, the emperor himself, ordered me to send them to serve him, he would certainly find that I would disregard his command, though not without danger to myself. For I confess that, when I weigh the matter in the balance of my heart, your love outweighs fear of him.

For this reason alone I earnestly beseech your piety, by the most genuine faith with which Christ has filled you and which has grown brighter than light in the knowledge of all the faithful, to cherish them with paternal affection and, as soon as you are able, to send them back to me with joy.

Behold, once again and again, my inmost heart begins to burn with inward love, because I increasingly desire to see your true angelic face. Therefore, with life as our companion, as soon as I am able to accomplish it, I shall come gladly to see you face to face.

### Second Letter: To Bishop W.  
*He excuses the prolonged delay in transcribing certain books.*

To the lord Bishop W., shining with the radiance of every virtue and illuminating all who are placed in the house of the Lord like the sun, S., by the grace of God abbot in the Tegernsee community, together with those subject to him, continually praying for perpetual joys of happiness in both the inner and outer man.

I call God as witness, most beloved bishop, that as long as I live I always wish to serve you with every kind of service, most devotedly of all men. Together with my brothers, I also continually entreat God with all the strength of my heart for the health of your body and soul.

The magnificent gifts which you have frequently presented to Saint Quirinus wholly remind us to beseech Christ for you, as though commemorating you before God. But I humbly implore your excellent goodness not to harbor any displeasure of mind against my monastery because of the long interval of time.

The books which you requested have not yet been transcribed there. The frequent change of abbots, as well as the emperor’s command concerning the copying of various volumes, greatly obstruct the brothers’ desire to fulfill your wishes by serving you.

### Third Letter: To the Abbot of Fulda, Apparently Widerad  
*He laments the miserable condition of the church of Fulda.*

To the venerable abbot +, superior in every virtue to all abbots of our time, + unworthily appointed by the title of shepherd over the Tegernsee fold, together with that same fold, continually praying for the joys of the heavenly assembly.

Most beloved Father, I do not cease to pray as far as I am able and know, with the deepest sighs of my heart, that the advancement of your inner and outer man may always prosper in the Lord according to your desire.

But I cannot say without tears how greatly the report that brings me sad news of your disasters usually afflicts me. For I learned some time ago that the monastery of Saint Boniface, hitherto rightly called the mirror of all churches, has been burned together with its adjoining buildings. This is lamentable to all who know of it and who hope that, by God’s grace, it may someday be restored to its former beauty.

The tears that arose in me from this had not yet dried when a second evil report announced that you, swollen with disease, were already near death. Since I cannot offer you bodily comfort or medicine in these misfortunes, but only supplicate Christ for your cure, I also offer you the consoling teaching of Saint James:

> “Consider it all joy when you fall into various trials.”

And you know that it is also written:

> “My son, do not despise the discipline of the Lord, nor grow weary when you are reproved by him.”

Still placed between hope and fear concerning the condition of your affairs, I send you this brief letter because I desire to learn the truth through the report of the messenger who is present.

I myself certainly would not delay in coming to see you if I could offer your holiness some pledge of affection, and if I were not occupied with building the monastery of Saint Quirinus and, as you know, hemmed in on every side by extreme poverty.

### Fourth Letter: To the Emperor Henry  
*He asks and entreats him not to grant the monastery of Tegernsee as a benefice to anyone, lest he wish to destroy all its works of diligence and piety.*

To the unconquered Roman emperor Augustus H., beautiful above the sons of men with the special diadem of virtues, S., holding the administrative office of Saint Quirinus over the community [read: “college”], together with that same community, wishes, after the long rule of your prosperous empire, the fellowship of the heavenly court.

Because the poor and needy, exceeding all number, run to you amid the miseries of their distress, and because, for love of him who appointed you his vicar in the Church, you act as a father to all these people, we too, exposed to the world and bearing the heavy burden of poverty, flee in our misery to the refuge of your holiness, most merciful Caesar.

For since, after God, we lack every comfort except yours, we hasten the ruin of our religion and salvation if we ever cease to commend you to the Lord in our prayers. Therefore know for certain that no one in the kingdom lives who is more eager than we are, day and night, amid tearful groans, to beseech Christ for your long-lasting safety and to ask that peace and victory be granted you from heaven, so that the security of Christianity may not be shaken by any storm of war.

But an evil report disturbed our intention in prayer by bringing us the bitterest lament: namely, that you wish to grant this monastery as a benefice, to the unceasing punishment or destruction of our small community.

If anyone claims these monks as slaves, every exercise of craftsmanship will certainly cease here, because afterward those who are weary of living will have no desire to paint or write. They will instead be scattered here and there, so that they may accomplish nothing for spiritual edification.

This monastery, the oldest in the province and once resplendent with varied adornment, was granted freedom by lawful donation through royal authority, with its original founders intervening; it was likewise elevated by your predecessors to a free condition with privileges.

Now, therefore, we earnestly beseech him who holds the hearts of all kings in his hand to inspire your heart not to despise our humble prayers. We entreat you with mournful groans, by the holiness of the name of him who, best of kings, brought you to such exalted greatness, and for the sake of the almsgiving and eternal blessedness of your parents and yourself, not to subject us, your little servants, to anyone’s servitude.

Instead, protect us in the service of Christ and of yourself beneath the shadow of your wings. If you deign to fulfill these petitions, know that your memorial will remain eternally in this place in blessing.

### Fifth Letter: To Sigefrid, Archbishop of Mainz  
*He congratulates him on his return from exile and explains at what cost he avoided the plots laid by a certain monk of his abbey.*

To the most pious of archbishops, S., the most faithful defender of the poor and especially of monks, S., abbot of the monastery of Saint Quirinus, together with his brothers, offers diligent prayer and devoted servile service.

As long as you were in exile, I and my brothers prayed daily to the Lord for your safety. Now, giving thanks to him for your desired return, we rejoice exceedingly.

Divine mercy has established you in our time as the honor of monastic life and a singular protection. I therefore know beyond doubt that, if you had been present at the royal court, you would have been a faithful helper to me amid the adversities I suffered.

A certain man—not merely a false monk but, so to speak, scarcely a Christian—from the monks of Saint Emmeram’s, using a large sum of money with my superior, sought to ensnare me. Thus he was eager to enter the fold entrusted to me not through the door but, climbing in from elsewhere like a thief.

For this reason I would have been deposed from the abbacy, although innocent, unless, on the advice of friends, I had given the king three pounds of gold promised by oath. Since I was unable to repay them from my own resources, alas, I was compelled to spend most of the treasury of the church of Saint Quirinus to obtain them.

Therefore I earnestly beg you to provide some assistance to my poverty in discharging such great sureties, so that, through the intercession of Saint Quirinus, you may receive a heavenly reward from Christ. May you also hold the service of my inner and outer man as your most devoted servant for as long as I live.

### Sixth Letter: Apparently by the Same Man, to N.  
*He excuses his lack of expertise in the liberal arts and judges philosophy useful to those who use it cautiously.*

To his lord N., made serene by the light of inward illumination, his N., unworthy to be called his servant, wishes him to be crowned with the rewards of his labors.

Since Wisdom’s mouth has proclaimed that those who are falsely praised must necessarily blush at their own praises, I too, being pursued by the commendations of your prayers—may they truly be spoken of me—blush at being praised beyond my deserts, since I see that none of the things you assert can be attributed to me.

The duties of the rhetorician, together with dialectical syllogisms, are unfamiliar and therefore unknown to me. They neither strengthen nor advance my mind with the defenses of eloquence, nor arm or sharpen the dull and long-inactive edge of my understanding with the arguments of sophistry. I could in no way climb to or attain the art of such knowledge, since I have neither absorbed the savory seasonings of grammar, nor clothed myself in the figurative garments of tropes, nor laid the foundations of Priscian’s breadth and solidity upon which it might more easily be built.

For one does not reach higher things except by ascending through lower steps; nor does a wall above remain firm unless it is supported below by a solid foundation.

But since you recognize, my lord, that all these things which you have assigned to me have taken up residence in you through the continual leisure of constant reading, you also believe that I, by contrast, abound in the same things. Whatever I drank in, burning with the waves of study from the distinguished streams of Liège, is almost entirely dried up, so to speak, by the frequent illness from which I suffer.

Therefore I burn with desire to have the stimuli of learning applied to me for restoring my faltering memory. If circumstances allowed, I would often wish humbly to visit my faithful teacher.

As for what you said—that worldly philosophy, which is foolishness before God, offers little benefit—when I consider the matter more deeply, I judge this to be true. Yet, if it is handled prudently, one can make some progress through it.

Although it often deceives the unwary and drags along with it a pit of sorrow, it is nevertheless recognized as a road and, so to speak, a preliminary exercise for those who are prudent and cautious, through which the trained leap toward higher and truer things.

But, to conclude briefly what my mind bears, I wish your holiness to know that no one of our modest circle is more devoted to you than I am or shall be. I also ask your charity that, through your prayers, I may be helped in the Lord against the illness threatening me.

Farewell.

## Epitaph of Seifrid

The outstanding abbot Sigefrid lies in this tomb;

While he lived, he abandoned all earthly things.

Freely he undertook the heavy burden of poverty,

So that by this price he might live rich with the Lord.

Yet while he governed the rule of abbots here

With merciful care and the authority of a judge,

He condemned no one, but made everyone joyful,

So that Christ might now be gracious to him.

Those who approach this place should say, sharing his compassion:

May he now be a fellow-citizen among the angelic choirs.

I ask that whoever reads these things—or submits to Adam’s law—  
say, “O Christ, [Lord] of creation, have mercy on your creature.”

In the year of the Lord 1048. Wazo, Bishop of Liège.

[Col. 0725]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE

(From Fabricius, *Bibliotheca medii et infimae Latinitatis*, vol. VI, p. 314.)

[Col. 0725A] Wazo, also called Wazo and Guaso, was first chaplain at Liège, then master of the schools, chaplain to the Emperor Henry III, dean of Liège, provost and archdeacon, and finally, in 1042, bishop of Liège. He died in 1048. Anselm, a canon of Liège, wrote his life, with additions by Giles, in volume I of Chapeaville, pp. 281 ff.; there, on p. 282, is also Wazo’s *Invective against John the Provost*, who was exercising his office with considerable violence; on p. 300, a letter to Emperor Henry, advising him not to go to Aachen; on p. 302, a letter to the bishop of Châlons, in which he urges that the heretics—who at that time were Manichaeans—not be punished. For, to add this in passing, heretics were judged solely by their pallor, so that many Catholics too were slaughtered on that pretext; on pp. 303–304, another letter to the Caesar, advising him not to interfere in the election of the pontiff. See Valerius Andreas, *Bibliotheca Belgica*, p. 849.

The life of this holy man [Col. 0726A] was written not only by Anselm, canon of Liège, but Alexander, another canon of Liège, also joined him in the work. In their continuation of the *History of the Bishops of Liège*, the two of them described the deeds of this bishop. After Chapeaville’s edition, P. Martène published this history again from another manuscript in the *Amplissima Collectio Monumentorum*, vol. IV, p. 894, etc. In both editions the letters mentioned here are reproduced; but, apart from the fact that Martène’s *Invective against John the Provost* is much more complete, the other letters also differ greatly in many places from those printed in the earlier edition. Moreover, our librarian omitted another letter by Wazo to Henry I, king of France, in which he advises him not to attack Henry the Black, who was occupied on the Roman journey he had undertaken in order to obtain the imperial crown. See the *Literary History of France*, vol. VII, p. 591.

[Col. 0725]

## THE LIFE OF WAZO, WRITTEN BY ANSELM AND ALEXANDER, CANONS OF LIÈGE, AMONG THE DEEDS OF THE BISHOPS OF LIÈGE

(Martène, *Amplissima Collectio*, vol. IV, p. 872, from an ancient manuscript of the monastery of Saint-Hubert at Andage, written six hundred years ago.)

## CHAPTER I—On the election of Wazo

[Col. 0725B]

After him (Nithard), Lord Wazo was elected according to canonical statutes. Although he protested for a long time and in many ways, he was at last scarcely dragged into accepting the episcopal staff by the force of the obedience imposed upon him by the archbishop. Yet long before this, while still not a bishop, he had governed the whole bishopric by his counsel and wisdom. I shall briefly explain how he did this and how he lived before becoming bishop.

## CHAPTER II—How he conducted himself as master of the schools

He was first chaplain under Noch­er, and afterward was appointed by him master of the schools. In their study he exercised discipline most vigilantly, both in conduct and in letters, placing far above the others those who possessed honorable manners, even if they were less learned, rather than those in whom, as commonly happens, literary knowledge had produced the folly of vainglory.

To all who arrived from different parts of the world he applied what is written, “Test the spirits to see whether they are from God”; and he made access to himself difficult for many. But if he recognized that anyone had truly come for study, he received him most gladly for as long as he wished to remain, and sometimes provided him with clothing. Some departed instructed in letters, conduct, and religion; others arrived to be instructed in the same way. You might have seen bees flying to this flower-bearing tree from different hives, so that each might carry back to its own cell what it could use to pour nectar of honey-bearing dew into its parched combs.

In the same way, from unknown and familiar regions alike, throngs of students flocked from every side to the man who breathed forth the good odors of Christ. Like another Solomon, he invited religious people of every kind to come and see him and hear him with longing. And when many, following the example of the queen of the South who traveled to Jerusalem bearing the most precious gifts, voluntarily offered presents to this Solomon of theirs lest they appear empty-handed, he sought to shake his hands free from every gift, [Col. 0727A] just as usurers, by contrast, customarily extort debts with interest. He kept in his heart and uttered with his lips the Gospel saying, “Freely you have received; freely give,” and also, “It is more blessed to give than to receive.”

There is no need to praise his generosity, for he was so attentive to guests and pilgrims that he seemed not to spend his wealth but to pour it out, drawn from a full torrent. This was not without the astonishment of his envious rivals, who were indignant that the less powerful man surpassed the nobler and richer in virtue and renown.

Why delay over many details? Although he was unwillingly elevated to the dignity of the deanery under Bishop Balderic, after laboring in the school’s office, he strove to conduct himself there with such modesty and to be so compassionate toward his subordinates that, against the proud and powerful, he stood upright at the summit of virtue, armed with the weapons of justice.

Thus it happened that he did not hesitate to rebuke in writing John the provost, formerly closely joined to him in friendship, because John had given too little thought to opposing the evil of arrogance arising from the empty title of provost and had arrogated to himself a tyrannical power, always profane toward religion, in arranging the affairs of the church according to his own pleasure. It will not be unwelcome to insert this writing into the present little work, since it is especially suited to refuting the obstinacy of bad provosts. But if anyone is angry with me for this, he will thereby testify against himself that he is bad. Accordingly, after being newly released from the administration of the schools, he wrote as follows to the aforementioned John.

## CHAPTER III—The controversy with John the Provost

[Note: [Col. 0727D] In many places it differs from the printed editions, especially toward the end.]

“To brother John according to his merits, Wazo, not his [friend].

[Col. 0727C] The memory of our old friendship compels me, brother, still to address you, although among us you deserve no gratitude. Until now, a certain knowledge of letters gave you some adornment; justice of reason also elevated you in the ordering of affairs. Now that you enjoy good fortune, you seem to me to confuse your former qualities with your present ones. Whatever good you previously possessed, we attribute to pretense, because fortune, when it comes upon good qualities, usually makes them better. [Note: [Col. 0727D] Printed edition: “make [them better].”]

“Indeed, we call riches neither good nor bad in themselves, unless their possessors demonstrate this in practice. [Note: [Col. 0728D] Printed edition: “are shown by transference.”] The archdeaconate and the other vanity of the world did not infect you by its contagion; rather, it revealed through your actions how slyly you had previously concealed yourself. [Col. 0727D]

“You would perhaps fear the punishment of an evil life if you did not place such great confidence in secular power. Although I could list many things in you that deserve punishment, I wish, if I can, to refute one that affects me. You say that you have been powerfully established as provost and that you will administer the cloister’s affairs in your house as you wish, without the counsel of the dean and the brothers. Since you do not wield a sword, why do you say ‘powerfully’ rather than ‘according to rule’? If your dignity is from God, why do you not commend it in writing? To my confusion, you say that prelate and provost are one and the same, serving flattery and opposing the truth, with no reverence. [Col. 0728A] What else, I ask, is it knowingly to defraud the truth than to make Christ suffer and crucify him a second time? Woe to those who call evil good and exchange truth for falsehood. Since Christ says that he is the truth, whoever injures the truth undoubtedly wounds Christ.

“The holy Fathers, burning with zeal for justice and divinely enlightened, composed the cloister’s rule. Adding nothing superfluous and removing nothing necessary, they turned neither to the right nor to the left. If you would moderate your ambition and I my envy, the offices of prelate and provost would remove every controversy between us. Tell me, I ask, if the rule names individually the bishop, prelate, provost, cantor, cellarer, porter, even bakers [Col. 0728B] and cooks: if prelate and provost are one, why does it omit the dean? Should he not have been written about more carefully, since he is more bound to serve religion? The rule would therefore seem irrationally composed if it did not carry out all the things necessary for the cloister according to its purpose. But who, being of sound mind, would dare assert this, since the Holy Spirit, author of the rule, avoids a fabricated discipline?

“Do not, brother, do not misinterpret the rule’s sufficient text. Whether you wish it or not, retain the necessary distinction between prelates and provosts. For if prelate and provost were one subject, one chapter rather than two would have been written; just as the bishop and the prelate, though two names, make one chapter, so would the prelate and provost, [Col. 0728C] if they were one. Since, therefore, two persons are understood by the terms prelate and provost, the writers of the rule rightly chose to append two statements.

“Above all, let the name ‘dean,’ which the rule did not include, not trouble you. Only military discipline and the rule of Saint Benedict use it frequently, deriving it from ten soldiers or monks, while the sacred writings remain silent about it. Since regular observance admits thirty, forty, or more canons together, it reasonably avoids applying the name ‘dean,’ which concerns a number greater than ten.

“The prelate, then, according to the administration of spiritual life, will be first in the cloister; the provost, consequently, will be second in rank because of his care for external matters. Spiritual things are rightly placed before secular things, just as the rational soul governs the foolish body. The Western cloisters and all the monasteries wherever they exist steadfastly preserve this arrangement.

“Since you esteem wealth more highly than religion, you honor the provostship while suppressing the dean’s distinction; and because you glory in being provost, you presume to administer the cloister’s affairs without consulting the brothers—not promoting the more useful brothers to these tasks, but those who enjoy your favor alone. [Col. 0729A] From this, alas, the ruin of divine religion arises, and the study of literary discipline is entirely abandoned. Who plants a vineyard and does not eat of its fruit? Who will devote himself to religion and discipline while gaining nothing from it? The heavenly Father did not plant this arrangement, nor did Mother Church animate it in her writings.

“It is therefore necessary to cut down the bastard shoots with the spiritual knife and to obey the regular admonitions in all things. For the rule commands the provost to act under the prelate and to administer what has been entrusted to him humbly and faithfully to the brothers, with the example of good conduct. But if he resists, he is to be removed from office and another, more suitable, appointed in his place.

“Consider these matters, brother, I ask you: the provost’s subjection, his fidelity, his humility, and also the danger of his ministry. If you presume to distribute the cloister’s goods without consulting the brothers, where are the subjection, fidelity, and humility of obedience? Whence comes such a lofty claim to rule, if you have so ready a capacity to lose your dignity?

“Will the brothers not be allowed to share in counsels when they can be the agents of your appointment and deposition? Especially since the lord pontiff—who alone is called ‘lord’—may not define ecclesiastical matters without the counsel of the clergy: how then will you, a subordinate minister, dare to dissipate the brothers’ goods according to your pleasure?

“Lord Abbot is commanded to bring the whole congregation into council and to decide everything by counsel. Yet you disdain consulting your fellow brothers about common goods? He is also commanded to divide the monastery’s goods among several persons, so that the provost alone, holding everything, cannot become proud. Otherwise, if you do this freely, you are no longer presiding over canons but over your servants and beneficiaries. Who, I ask, will be able to live in any way who is willing to enter into the wages of your charity? Why are possessions transferred in the name of the brothers if you alone claim dominion over them? Until now we were Christ’s poor, canons of Mother Church; what remains is for us to serve you as purchased slaves. Stop, brother, I ask you, stop acting insolently, and humbly recognize the limits of your office.

“See also what the rule especially assigns to the provost: namely, to enlighten his subjects by the example of canonical conduct. If, therefore, the regular command is that the canons frequent the choir, refectory, and dormitory, why, when you have the opportunity, do you withdraw yourself as though you were forbidden to share their fellowship? You are healthy, strong, and often even idle. Do not be ashamed to be religious, because whoever is ashamed of Christ and of his words will be punished on the day of calamity and misery.

“From morning to evening you are not ashamed to toil over secular business, yet you are embarrassed to attend the choir once a week and once a month? ‘Let the one who does not work not eat,’ the Apostle writes. You, doing nothing or little work, will collect everything for yourself alone? If even natural food is forbidden to the idle, what are you, a negligent provost, doing by ruling over the works of those who labor? Behold, through the Apostle, the fellowship of life is withdrawn from you; whence, then, such abuse of domination?

“If those who serve the altar must live from the altar, consequently, you who serve nothing ought to receive nothing. ‘The one who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly,’ and each person will receive his reward according to his own labor. Moreover, if you were most religious, you ought through humility to avoid this ambition for domination [ [Note: [Col. 0729D] The words enclosed in brackets are absent from the printed editions.] ], as Truth teaches the apostles: ‘When you have done everything that has been commanded you, say: We are useless servants.’

“Thus David, little in the eyes of God, is raised to be king; Saul, acting arrogantly, suffers a shameful death. ‘Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.’ [Col. 0730B] If Paul, laboring more than all, professes himself the least and an untimely birth, why do you, doing no work, seize exclusive dominion in the opposite manner? If Paul’s judgment is praiseworthy in all things, your presumption is universally detestable.

“You say that you are a powerful provost and that you will distribute all the cloister’s goods in your house as you wish, without the counsel of the prelate and the canons. What do you make of yourself? What do you have that you have not received? If you boast, boast in the Lord. For the one who commends himself is not approved, but the one whom God commends. May the mother of justice produce your glory, and may the guardian of humility not abandon it.

“Do not measure yourself by the tongues of flatterers. Examine carefully what you are, not what you are called. If God came to serve, not to be served, why do you seek to rule with such arrogance? Although he was God, he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant. Yet you, ashes and dust, strive to be called a powerful provost? Truly, you cannot be his disciple unless, first laying aside the eminence of domination, you become little.

“Certainly, if no cloistered provost may be appointed except from a regular canonical member [Note: [Col. 0730D] The printed editions read, ‘from the regular canon.’], you ought not to be provost unless you lead the canonical life of the cloister. There is therefore a distinction between a cleric and a canon: the cloister is owed to the canon, not to the cleric. Every canon is a cleric, but it does not follow that every cleric is a canon.

“The provost is regularly established from a canon, not from a cleric. Therefore, if you are provost, you must be constant in the choir, refectory, and dormitory, unless granted permission. Since you love the provostship above all, why do you disdain the cloister’s military service? Either you will have religion together with the provostship, or the dignity of provost will be turned into mere stewardship. There would be no need to appoint a provost from among the canons if the same ministry could equally be performed by a layman.

“Therefore, be a provost deliberately and with religion. At least be willing to love religious people, so that, just as the one who receives a prophet in the name of a prophet receives a prophet’s reward, so your irreligiousness may at least be commended by your love of the religious. [Col. 0731A] For it is exceedingly profane that both things should be true: that you are irreligious and that you harass the religious. [Note: [Col. 0731D] Printed editions: “that you are religious,” contrary to the author’s meaning.] [ [Note: [Col. 0731D] The words enclosed in brackets are absent from the printed editions, as are several others.] ]

“Moreover, brother, gather from the rule the provost’s subjection, fidelity, humility, and administration—not domination. Do not disdain to seek the counsel of the dean and the brothers concerning the goods entrusted to you. Through subjection and humility, seek counsel and even instruction; through fidelity and administration, return everything you find beyond the benefice. Why do you accept a benefice if you are not faithful in all other matters?]

[Whatever you have justly gained beyond your ministry, retain during your lifetime; but do not refrain from making this known openly to the brothers, lest you be accused of theft. [ [Note: [Col. 0731D] This passage too is omitted from the printed editions.] ] Thus you will gain the fruit of your reasonableness if you inform the brothers of the amount that has been accumulated through your efforts. But if you suppress it in silence, you gain a theft for your successor, not for the brothers.]

I, having justly gained the service of four hundred [Note: [Col. 0731D] Printed editions read “cooks’ holdings,” wholly corruptly.] manors from two estates entrusted to me against my will, announced it to the brothers and immediately rendered the service. Yet the more I hoped to enter joyfully because of my fidelity, the more I was overcome by tribulations and envy. The evangelical servant who doubled his talent was praised by his master and deserved to receive a gift; I, having quadrupled it, was attacked and ensnared in many ways and reduced to poverty. [Note: [Col. 0731D] The material enclosed in brackets was also omitted by the abridger.]

[Since you hold many cloister goods without question on small revenues, why do you punish our fidelity as though you were prosecuting a theft? You harshly punish the ministers of your own affairs when they act unfaithfully; why do you not pursue the cloister’s affairs with equal diligence? How can you be shown to love the brothers as yourself if you treat your affairs and theirs with unequal affection?

“If among the ancient Romans, idolaters though they were, fraud against the state was expiated by the penalties for sacrilege, by what punishment, devised by the laws, will fraud discovered in the cloister rightly be punished?”]

Therefore, brother, let us all together gird ourselves with humility and fidelity, act according to the rule, and handle the cloister’s affairs irreproachably, as is proper. The greater we are in the dignities of the world, the more let us humble ourselves in everything. Let us diligently flee the heights of greed and domination, which naturally tend to drive away religion and discipline.

[Col. 0731D] [Note: [Col. 0732D] Here too the abridger presumed to omit the text down to the words “provost and prelate,” etc.] Do not reinforce your defense of your presumption by the example of the Cologne cloister, for, as I have learned by experience, thanks be to God, nothing of that kind is found there. The lord archbishop himself, setting aside the eminence of his domination, often walks through the cloister and visits the schools. When questions have been proposed and resolved, he honors with favor and gifts those whom he finds more useful. Thus he wins everyone’s pleasure and nourishes their studies; amid a sea of riches, he steers himself with the rudder of humility.

The provost and prelate stand first in the choir and diligently take part in the office, so that no difficulty or negligence may arise. Each carries out his duties with particular care. The discipline of the cloister especially belongs to the prelate; nevertheless, the provost, when invited, is not absent when a difficulty arises.

The provost provides the daily allowance together with the other officials. If anything is lacking, the prelate exacts it without hostility. The cellarer receives food, wine, and dishes from the provost and distributes everything without penalty according to the orders of the prelate and the elders. The provost is free from the levies that he has assigned to the cellarer, and the cellarer likewise from those to whom he has been obedient under the prelate.

Thus the unanimity of prelate and provost cooperates in the building up of the cloister, because unambitious charity investigates the things that are God’s, not its own.

Our cloister’s newly arisen discord would have to be mourned more bitterly, brother, if the members who are sick did not also grow together in the health of the head. And lest I deprive you of any duty of brotherly consolation, I beg you to moderate for a little while the small glory of your archdeaconate.

Since divine mercy has granted you many goods by which you may reasonably be honored in the archdeaconate prescribed by ecclesiastical decrees, why do you exalt yourself? Because you are a deacon? Say where you get the name “archdeacon.” If you cannot, cease boasting any further.

The Church removed rural bishops (*chorepiscopi*) [Note: [Col. 0732D] The printed editions read, “co-bishops and archdeacons.”] on account of their insolence; consequently, the metropolitan city of Cologne and the entire province lack them to this day. The canon forbids a deacon to sit before a presbyter without authorization; yet you presume to judge and even beat presbyters? Do you have such authority in judging that no scripture and no rational consideration can resist it? Since your will must necessarily be law and rule for us, I ask you by God always to direct it with justice.

[Note: [Col. 0732D] Almost everything that follows is absent from the printed editions.] If the one who steals a cow is rightly excommunicated, what will happen to the one who sells or plunders justice? Since justice is better than every dumb beast, it necessarily follows that every robber of justice is worse than a robber of livestock. Since it is clearer than daylight that harassing justice is the worst thing, although I was in favor with four bishops when arrangements were being made for all the bishopric’s goods, I received not even the price of a single carob bean, however much you may charge me with it.

Since you cannot legally rebuke me for anything except sins—which are many—why do you habitually call me angry as a sign of your ill will? If the anger of man does not accomplish the justice of God, either name my injustice or your truth is void. But because I do not wish to surrender my words or affairs, after abandoning the law, to your wicked counsels, lest I be confounded, you charge me with doing this because of the magnitude of my anger and your own obstinacy.

I would rather be called angry and not be so than always be a disciple of your counsels. You could equally call me a thief, a sacrilegious man, or a murderer, since you can in no way establish the truth of my deeds.

These things, brother, as a pledge of our former intimacy, I have entrusted to you for thoughtful consideration in a spirit of generosity, so that nothing may have been said to the detriment of goodwill. We earnestly beg this because reason demanded it. If it does not please you, I have placed my soul in my hand, ready to suffer condemnation, beatings, and even death for the fidelity of the cloister.

I do this not as someone superior or equal to the provost—for, according to the rule, I can compare myself with the dean—but to show myself, in ordering the closed affairs of the cloister, a principal counselor in justice. If it is credibly established that the prelate is the dean, as cannot be refuted, I ask not to be forbidden to act regularly as prelate together with the cellarer.

Otherwise, if you strive to oppose the commands of the rule, you incur the greatest corresponding penalty of the Church. The priesthood is also proved to be held in greater esteem than the provostship and archdeaconate, since the latter can be taken away by individual bishops, whereas the former [the priesthood] cannot be taken away by fewer than six bishops. Whatever is more firmly established must therefore be shaken more vigorously.

Accordingly, I ask you to honor me regularly as prelate and priest, although unworthy—or, if you are unwilling to do so together with my rivals, at least do not trample me down, since I have done nothing unfaithfully.

I reasonably avoided the ministry of obedience in the schools, since there was no desire to learn and no power to discipline; do not condemn me for this. For, along with other difficulties, I could not endure an acolyte who had twice attacked me with intent to kill, who had been condemned for twenty confessed thefts, restored without my knowledge, and released from the schools. Although, as a veteran or emeritus, no portion of the customary benefice remained for me, I nevertheless rejoice at his release, lest the reputation of our discipline be corrupted by danger.

“Is the strength of stones my strength, that I should endure? Or is my flesh bronze, that I should act patiently? May God confound—confound—the counsel of Ahithophel and free David from the hands of the boy Absalom. May he who cast the proud Lucifer into hell reduce the power of the cloister to nothing, with the rule prevailing.”

## CHAPTER IV—What he suffered from the peasants

Writing these things wholly free from envy and hatred, while striving to recall one man from crookedness of conduct to the path of uprightness, he offered all provosts a model of irreproachable life to be impressed upon them. He most kindly provided a mirror in which they might foresee whatever they ought to avoid and whatever they ought to practice, seeking not his own interests but those of Jesus Christ. This was shown no less clearly shortly afterward in his administration of the provostship and later of the episcopate.

But John the provost, to whom he had written this, was thereby inflamed with still greater fires of envy against him. Through persuasive words of earthly wisdom, John also kindled the minds of the bishop and the other elders against him, regarding the things he had faithfully accomplished as arising from a contentious spirit rather than from devoted fidelity.

And, so as to leave no stratagem unattempted against the innocent man, he stirred up by a messenger the inhabitants of that estate whose administration Wazo had undertaken in order to increase the brothers’ supply of wine, urging them to rebel against his commands and to hold them in contempt.

The peasants had already been hostile to their administrator, because his vigilance left no opportunity to defraud the brothers of what was owed them. But, after receiving confidence from the instigation of the superior provost, they were led to such recklessness that, unexpectedly during the night, they eagerly attempted to surround on every side with weapons and burn with flames the brothers’ house where Lord Wazo was resting with his companions. [Col. 0734B]

But almighty God does not abandon those who hope in him. He wonderfully rescued the defender of justice and truth from the danger of the fire. For although clothing and various household goods were lost—including a considerable quantity of wine which, in his foresight, he had gathered in the lower parts of the same house for the use of the brothers—not one of the men, by God’s gift, succumbed to the crackling balls of flame blazing all around them.

The man of God was not at all broken by such adversity. Rather, he became firmer in his good purpose. Victorious over so many temptations pressing against him, he hoped for heavenly assistance all the more abundantly the more obstacles he had endured from human beings.

## CHAPTER V—How he became chaplain to Emperor Conrad

Although he was being harassed by intolerable plots among his own people because of the good and faithful way in which he had acted, he nevertheless bound certain religious men, together with many bishops, to his affection—though they were far away—by his steadfast intention toward good works. They greatly approved his efforts and did not cease to offer assistance at an opportune time and place, lest their aid prove ineffective.

These supporters of his, fearing that he alone might not be able to resist the envy of his people for long, devised a fitting plan: imperial authority might serve as a protection for his successful actions against his envious enemies. They therefore brought it about with Emperor Conrad that he should request and obtain Wazo from Bishop Reginhard as his chaplain. [Col. 0734D]

Thus, after the envy of so many adversaries had for a time subsided, this happened not because he yielded to adversity, but so that he might meanwhile restore his strength for his good purpose, by which he would eventually acquire effectiveness for his excellent undertakings without difficulty.

After a deputy had been appointed to the deanery with the consent of the brothers and the bishop, he was bound to the service of Emperor Conrad. There, for nine months, he worked not from any desire to obtain the episcopate or from any other ambition to rule, but rather to recover the church and its possessions into freedom.

Why linger over further details? He quickly became exceedingly pleasing to the emperor and, because of his outstanding holiness and wisdom, was esteemed by archbishops and bishops alike. They rejoiced to summon him as a teacher for resolving questions of Sacred Scripture and as an arbiter in disputes concerning other matters.

Two archbishops of the noblest character and lineage—Aribo of Mainz and Piligrim of Cologne—would rise in turn, alternately standing beside one another in their seats, and compel him to sit beside them, listening to him eagerly and repeatedly questioning him.

## CHAPTER VI—How he defeated a Jew in knowledge of the Old Testament

At that time a certain Jew, highly distinguished in the art of medicine and for that reason much esteemed by Emperor Conrad, was regarded as nearly perfect in the traditions of the ancestral law.

On one occasion, when he attacked Lord Wazo with questions from the ancient law, he carried the dispute with him so far that, having wagered a wine-jar, he promised to offer him a finger of his right hand to be cut off if his own opinion could not be proved by the testimony of Scripture.

What more need be said? They came to the volume of the Old Testament. The passage over which they were disputing was sought out, and when it clearly supported Wazo’s side, the defeated opponent himself admitting this, the finger was awarded to the victor. Since the defeated wagerer could in no way refuse to surrender it, Wazo was glad to keep it in his custody until he should wish to reclaim it.

Thus this warrior of Christ gloriously brought back a new trophy for the Christian name from the leading teacher of the Jewish people. It became celebrated at the royal court that the Jew renowned for wisdom had been defeated by Wazo.

[Note: [Col. 0735D] The abridger omitted what follows, although it is especially worthy of note.]

The same Emperor Conrad was considering replacing the deceased Archbishop Aribo with Wazo in the see of Mainz. But the mercy of almighty God did not wish to deprive the Church of Liège of its own alumnus. It had reserved this man, tested many times by the trials of dangers, as an excellent father for itself after having been a good son.

## CHAPTER VII—How, after the deaths of the provosts John and Lambert, he became provost

[Note: [Col. 0735D] This chapter differs entirely from the printed editions.]

While these things were taking place at the royal court, word suddenly arrived that John the provost had died. Lord Wazo had long wished to escape the turmoil of the court and shut himself away in the quiet of the cloister. Nevertheless, until he heard that someone had been appointed as John’s replacement in the provostship, although he had ample opportunity to depart, he neglected to return home, lest he seem to have returned not to seek quiet but rather to thrust himself forward for the provostship.

Not long afterward he heard that Lambert the archdeacon had become provost. Around autumn he revisited the cloister. Shortly afterward Lambert himself died, having been provost for only three months, and left the arrangement of his affairs to the good faith of Dean Wazo. [Note: [Col. 0735D] “Hands of good faith” means persons entrusted with the matter or executors of the testament.]

Otherwise, he was to have celebrated Christmas at Paderborn, as he had received orders from the emperor, [Note: [Col. 0736D] The abridger says absolutely nothing about this assembly at Paderborn.] unless the matter of the deceased brother, entrusted to his good faith, had delayed him in this way.

But, as we believe, a far different force—namely, the divine dispensation, unknown to him—was pressing him on. He had suffered so many and such great things from provosts on behalf of the cloister’s fidelity; therefore, he would be all the more vigilant in promoting the interests of the Church in the provostship entrusted to him, insofar as he had clearly recognized how destructive negligence combined with fraud had been in his predecessors.

From every side, the faithful sons of the Church flocked to Bishop Reginhard. All earnestly demanded that the provostship be given to Wazo, since no one more worthy of this office could be found.

On the other hand, there were some who at first attempted to dissuade the wavering bishop from doing this. They argued that it was not prudent to make a man of such strong resolve provost—one who, because of his unconquerable confidence in his own conscious virtue, might strive to equal the bishop or even consider making himself superior to him. They urged him instead to choose some milder man who would dare resist his will in nothing.

The bishop’s mind was tossed about like a wave between conflicting currents of speech. At last, however, it was strengthened by such solid counsel that he judged the provostship should be granted to no one other than Wazo. It is also reported that the bishop’s having incurred the emperor’s displeasure contributed substantially to this decision: by elevating the emperor’s beloved chaplain with such an honor, he would serve to mitigate that displeasure.

When these matters had been arranged with the bishop, no less effort was required to persuade Wazo to accept the provostship. His spiritual friends pressed him vigorously, though he had been freely invited, to undertake the dispensing of provisions to the Lord’s sheep. He resisted still more strongly, saying that he had enough and more than enough wealth and had absolutely no need of the provostship.

Foreseeing, however, that he would be necessary for the brothers’ interests, and recognizing that he was being invited to this office by an honorable vocation before God and human beings, after sixteen years in the deanery—during which he had walked the royal road, turning neither to the right nor to the left—and after long and strongly refusing the archdeaconate, he humbly consented to undertake the burden of the provostship.

## Chapter VIII — How he conducted himself after becoming provost, and how he improved the provision of the brothers

Amid these successive elevations, the man of God took such care to arrange the ladder of humility in his heart that, the greater he appeared, the humbler he was toward himself. He strove to preserve himself whole and undefiled from the vices into which men bearing his name commonly become entangled—especially pride and the seizure of ecclesiastical goods, faults which, when he had occupied a humbler position, he had not feared to point out in others. In place of pride he possessed the humility by which he was approachable to everyone; instead of indignation toward those who gloried in a false justice, he showed compassion, as the kindest imitator of Christ, to all who were afflicted in whatever way. Who was weak without his sharing that weakness? Who was scandalized without his being inflamed? Thus he felt compassion for another’s weakness as though it were his own.

What should I say about his distribution of the household of the Lord’s provisions? Nearly all who knew Liège bear witness that, whereas previously only one loaf was given daily to each brother and no more than forty cartloads of wine were expended annually for their drink, he added bread made from the white-colored meal called *simila*, weighing five marks; and he permanently assigned to the brothers’ cellarer one hundred and forty cartloads of wine each year, without any excuse of scarcity, so that the measure of drink might reasonably be increased from it and the remainder might provide for the brothers of the churches who had no wine. He used to say that the needs of the smaller churches should justly be supplied from the abundance of the greater church.

Thus he enlarged the brothers’ provision, previously neglected, by adding bread and wine and, moreover, a more generous allowance for clothing; from a poor provision he made it excellent.

[Note: The abridger also omitted this.]

## Chapter IX — How he administered external affairs

He established sufficient food each day for twelve poor people or pilgrims to be fed in the presence of the brothers, asserting that even this was little, since the tradition of the holy Fathers holds that half, or even the whole, of the church’s resources ought to belong to the poor and pilgrims.

Moreover, the hospital to which the ninths or tenths from the episcopal estates were assigned had been entrusted to his care. He took such faithful measures to secure its administration that thirty poor people could be comfortably supported from it each year; and, in addition to the twelve alms-recipients whom Lord Bishop Baldric had appointed to be maintained from the church, he added twelve more to be fed. All pilgrims who arrived without horses were received, while he considered it the bishop’s responsibility to receive those who came with horses.

He regarded it as sacrilege if he did not increase through his own labor the duties entrusted to him. Meanwhile, as though against a most hostile enemy, he imposed frequent abstinences upon his own body, while increasing his expenditures for Christ’s poor. Every day both groups sitting at his sides were refreshed: on one side, bands of clerics; on the other, bands of poor people. Food for both kinds of people was carried away from his table, while he himself, a cheerful host, ate very sparingly and almost fasted. Always hungering and thirsting for righteousness, he sent the others away sufficiently satisfied.

He preferred his wealth to serve the common good rather than himself, and desired to direct it toward every work of mercy. The sick lying in bed, the hardships of exiles, and those worn out by old age or fallen from riches into poverty all experienced his humanity and were continually supported by his assistance. Thus this ecclesiastical man, becoming all things to all people, was an eye to the blind and a foot to the lame. The orphans found in him a father; the widows, a husband. Such was his administration of external affairs.

## Chapter X — What he was inwardly

[Col. 0738A]

Inwardly, he cherished those subject to regular observance as his dearest sons; against rebels he acted as the most severe judge with the sword of discipline, preserving the compassion of his heart toward both—calling the former to better things and restraining the latter from wickedness.

The soldier of Christ did not fear offending a human being, provided that he did not displease the inward Judge by maintaining what was fair and right. He remembered the Apostle’s saying: “If I were pleasing human beings, I would not be a servant of Christ.” And that of the Psalmist: “Those who please human beings are confounded, because God has rejected them.”

Thus it happened that, in defending the truth—for which he did not even fear to die—he sometimes incurred the offense of others who seemed to be more exalted by the height of earthly power. Consequently, many kinds of traps were laid for him on this account, and his close associates had just cause to fear repeatedly for his life.

But, according to Solomon’s saying, “In vain is the net spread before the eyes of the winged,” this bird of God, through honor and disgrace, through ill repute and good repute, through insults, threats, dangers, and finally everything that opposed virtue, escaped every trial in free flight. At first he endured these things with equanimity; then, at the proper place and time, he refuted them reasonably, as he always used the weapon of reason to pierce the breasts of his adversaries.

For among the mortals of our time, this was in him both most praiseworthy and most remarkable: in whatever matter he undertook a controversy against anyone, he achieved victory fortified by the aid of unconquerable reason. This happened because, as a watchful creature of God, he had directed his eyes before and behind toward the intention of the good, and had fixed himself upon it together with truth and reason so firmly that neither hatred nor favor could move him from it. It was as though you saw him despising the winds, the rocks, and Rhodope; or as though the Marpesian crag stood against the storms.

He had ordered his life, known to God and to himself, so that, except for the hours of sleep and food, he spent both nights and days continually in God’s praises—either singing psalms, reading, or disputing for reasonable causes. Rarely, or hardly ever, did anyone approach him without carrying away something appropriate to his age and nature.

He gave milk to the weak and fed the strong with bread; he ate and drank wine and meat, as Abbot Poppo used to testify [Note: The abridger of our author omitted this also]. Poppo alone knew certain of his secrets, and he surpassed the abstinence of all the monks known to him. He considered not what he ate without desire, but how much he ate, and thus more cautiously avoided the evil of satiety, as one avoids viper’s blood.

He regulated his clothing so carefully that he was neither dressed more ambitiously than others nor excessively shabbily, and he steadfastly cast away from himself every puffed-up display. He considered it better to subdue the limbs of the body by the power of a strong mind than by the harshness of a hair shirt. He never, or only rarely, provided them with a bath or a soft bed.

And what we cannot recall without tears, he had a certain solemn secret practice: Christ’s truth is present as witness that I invent nothing. When, together with many other hardships, his body—already drained by old age—was pressing him down, he ordered himself on appointed days to be beaten with the harshest blows. He solemnly commanded his appointed corrector, on the authority of the Lord’s word, not to spare him and not to presume to reveal the secret.

The corrector kept it concealed for a long time, even after his death; but he did not refuse to reveal such a pledge of treasure to a servant of his holiness who was altogether unworthy of it.

Amid such an abundance of virtuous activity, he always strove, although never in this matter toward himself, to maintain the golden mean everywhere else. Truly, as a preeminent mirror of discernment, the lamp of his life showed beforehand the royal road to be followed midway between left and right.

## Chapter XI — How, after Reginhard’s death, Emperor Conrad wished to give him the bishopric

When Bishop Reginhard died, most of the sons of the Church ardently wished this man to become their bishop. To remove their opinion as far as possible from himself, he strongly rebuked those who had deprived him, as provost of the greater church, of the primacy in choosing a bishop; he elected Nithard the custodian as bishop and compelled all the clergy and people to adopt his decision.

Thus he vigorously asserted the authority of his primacy—not by placing himself first, but by placing a younger man above himself. He used the authority of his power to preserve his purpose of humility, not to seize a position of eminence.

[Note: The abridger omitted everything that follows.]

Without delay, he went with the elected man and the episcopal staff to Emperor Conrad, who happened at that time to be wintering in Italy. Having found him at the town of Nonantula, he faithfully presented the petition of our Church, acting as its representative and spokesman. After presenting the elected man, he affirmed that he was suitable to undertake this burden and that the clergy and people unanimously requested it.

The emperor replied: “This man whom you offer me I do not recognize at all; but this honor, of which you are not unknown to me, I gladly wish for you.”

The other, on the contrary, struggled by every means to have the bishopric conferred upon the elected man instead of himself. He declared that the other was more worthy and more suitable, being young, active, and ready for the execution of imperial service, whereas he himself was cold, worn down by the burden of old age, already a man at the end of life, and ought henceforth to think rather of the grave.

When the emperor refused to change his opinion and pressed him insistently to accept the bishopric, he said:

“May Your Majesty spare—spare, I beg you, this decrepit old man’s reputation, which by God’s grace has been carried to this age without a mark of disloyalty. If I had accepted an embassy from any one person, to whom our loyalty ought afterward to remain faithful, and then turned it to my own advantage, what would become of that loyalty? How much more so if I defraud the one people of Mother Church of its petition and election? I shall rightly be accused of fraud and disloyalty if, unworthy as I am, I presume to accept this dignity against the common consent of our people. But lest your mind be disturbed by any doubt concerning the elected man’s life and character, let everything be charged to me; let this be held against me.”

At last the emperor was scarcely overcome by the splendid excess of Vaso’s struggle to escape the episcopate. As requested, he granted the bishopric to Nithard.

Vaso, however, fearing that he might advance outwardly in honors and thus begin inwardly to decline in character, patiently and kindly rejoiced to become subject to the man whose teacher he had been. Forgetting what lay behind and stretching toward what lay ahead, he pursued the prize of the heavenly calling for fourteen years as provost.

## Chapter XII — How he was elected bishop

The Lord no longer wished such a great and exceptional athlete of his to remain hidden. He had made him perfect within the enclosure of a single monastery, but now ordered this vigorous soldier to go forth into the field of combat, so that, in the time of his anger, he might become reconciliation for a suffering people and a remedy for his homeland endangered by the storm of war and famine.

Previously he had refused the episcopate offered to him; as has been said, he had placed Nithard above himself. After Nithard’s death, he was again requested for the episcopate by the clergy and people.

On the other hand, it is impossible to believe how many delays he attached to his election and with what effort he strove to prevent it. He said that the election would displease the king, that it would carry little weight in the matter, and that the king’s decision ought rather to be awaited.

The opinion of this man who resisted and made excuses was not heeded. Against his will, he was unanimously elected by all and sent to Regensburg, where King Henry—later emperor—happened to be present, preparing to invade Bohemia with an army.

The episcopal staff was presented together with letters from our Church, and the matter was deferred until the following day. On the next day the king consulted the bishops and the other princes of the palace.

There was no shortage of flattering tongues asserting that an election made without royal favor would be invalid; that a bishop should rather be appointed from among the royal chaplains; and that Vaso had never labored at the royal court in order to deserve such an honor. They treated it as though it were a crime for anyone to be made bishop unless he had been shown to roam about at the royal court, and as though one ought not rather to choose a man trained in the obedience of the cloister, who had learned not so much to rule as to be useful.

The young king’s mind was easily influenced by this opinion of the flatterers, and he was preparing to impose some barbarian upon our necks. But, as we believe, by God’s inspiration, from the entire company of counsellors only Archbishop Herimann and Bruno, Bishop of Würzburg, dared to oppose such a useless opinion with sounder counsel.

The defenders of truth and cooperators with God did not desist until, at last and only with difficulty, they reconciled our petition to the royal majesty and brought the minds of the nobles over to their view.

Yet the wise architects still had a far more arduous labor before them. As though attempting to cut a column from a monstrous mountain, our good craftsmen pressed on with every effort to arrange that this man, entirely smooth and rounded in virtues, should consent to have the burden of the Church placed upon him.

That devout heart remained long immovable in its purpose of humility. Indeed, as blessed Gregory says, it would not be a devout heart if piety had not conquered it.

He understood that, if he did not accept the bishopric, it would fall to someone young in age and character who, if he aspired to the pontifical height, might perhaps disperse the provision of the Lord’s flock which, under his direction, had borne fruit to the praise of God.

Thus, while he fled in mind from a position of eminence, he was urged by the command and entreaty of the bishops and finally compelled above all by the necessity I have mentioned. At last he consented to become the Church’s shepherd.

Thus, indeed, he entered through the door into the sheepfold; he did not climb in from another direction to become shepherd of the sheep. And he who entered irreproachably undoubtedly lived irreproachably.

He was brought back to the episcopal see and received honorably, as was fitting. But when they came to the cathedral and solemnly seated him upon the episcopal chair, I would never have believed it had I not seen it myself: with what groaning he burst into tears, which he seemed to shed like a seven-year-old boy beneath his master’s rod.

Everyone present marveled that the breast of a man whom they had thought iron could be torn by such floods of tears. Those who did not know his earlier life thereby truly proved that their shepherd’s heart did not rejoice in such eminence but was tortured by a salutary grief.

## Chapter XIII — How, after becoming bishop, he diligently fulfilled the duties of holy religion

[Col. 0741C]

His episcopal consecration, delayed for some time, was requested from the archbishop upon his return from the expedition. For this purpose the man of God, accompanied by clerics of various orders, went to holy Cologne and struck the thresholds of the saints—whose number is granted to no place except Rome in equal measure—with devout prayers.

After three days he was anointed bishop with sacred chrism and, from being a good son, was confirmed as the bridegroom of his mother, the Church of Liège.

Then I cannot explain how steep a mountain of holiness he strove to climb in order to evangelize Zion; with what discipline he compelled the body to serve the spirit; indeed, with what effort he grew wholly toward the praise of God.

Abased in his own sight before God, he did not know himself to be a bishop among the humble and subject. He attended the schools, examining the studies of individuals. By proposing questions, he preferred to be defeated reasonably rather than to prevail; and, as though withdrawing there from the turmoil of cares, he rejoiced—as he himself confessed—to have found refreshment.

Although, by the privilege of an outstanding intellect, he knew how to investigate the secrets of divine law, he did not disdain to question schoolboys about the rules of Donatus or Priscian. In turn, he eagerly desired to hear them, favoring and praising those who had thought correctly; honoring the more useful with gifts and rewards; rebuking and correcting the slower; and encouraging all by the example of their superiors. Finally, he wished them all to become better and more acceptable to God, saying with blessed Moses: “Who will grant me that all the people may be prophets of God?”

Nor do I think that I should pass over his observance of the offices of vigils, matins, and compline. Every day, in the choir with the other brothers, no one arrived before him, no one participated more devoutly, and no one departed later.

He spent the remaining hours of the day in ecclesiastical affairs, although during Lent he refused in any way to excuse himself either from the choir or from any gathering of the brothers. During that season he knew no private room except the church. He used a stone seat for a bed and a mat for bedding. At the hour of eating, he sustained his aged weakness with a little oat bread and beans, taking beer as his drink and, more often, plain water.

[Note: Chapeaville attributes what follows to Giles, but incorrectly.]

Amid such severity of abstinence, his angelic face was not wasted away by emaciation, nor was the grace of its rosy coloring altered. Thus divine mercy satisfied with inward sweetness our man of desires—our Daniel, whom his own will afflicted in the likeness of Christ’s cross.

## Chapter XIV — How generous he was during the time of scarcity

[Note: The material enclosed in brackets is absent from the printed editions. The remainder differs substantially.]

I shall relate a few things and pass over many more. Some, I know, I neglect for the sake of brevity; others, which are unknown to me, must necessarily be left unmentioned, since I think no one has been granted knowledge of all this man’s virtues.

Immediately in the first year of his episcopate, a famine more cruel than any pestilence settled upon the land. It is known to have oppressed the people of Gaul and Germany for nearly six continuous years, and its shameful traces may still rightly be seen everywhere.

During that same period, our prudent Joseph took care to purchase grain from every direction and store it in secure granaries—not because he sought earthly profits from it, but so that, at the proper time, as a faithful steward, he might distribute food freely and in sufficient measure to the hungry household of the Lord.

In addition to the daily allowance of one pound of money for the poor, and many other provisions too numerous for me to list, he arranged through discreet intermediaries to send grain, according to each person’s circumstances, to those who, out of shame, refrained from begging: ten measures to some, twenty to others, thirty to others, sixty to others, and one hundred to others.

Nor did the generous munificence of this distinguished man overlook the private property of freeborn people, which had been diminished by that terrible necessity. Through his efforts and greatest assistance, it was not necessary to sell the dowry-gold, clothing, or estates of great households in order to obtain food.

[Note: Much of this, like many other passages, is missing from the printed editions.]

What should I say about the communities of clerics, monks, and nuns? His diligence as a good shepherd watched over their needs so carefully that whatever was lacking from their appointed food because of the anxiety of famine, he most willingly supplied from his own resources.

Nevertheless, the industry of the pious Father also considered the laborious poverty of the peasants. To alleviate their distress, throughout the entire period of famine he ordered two pence to be given to every tenant each week, so that under the pressure of immediate need they would not be forced to sell their oxen or abandon their native land, and thus either lead a wretched life by begging or, together with their entire household, suffer a death more savage than any sword.

## Chapter XV — Concerning the charity shown to the people of Verdun during the war

Another equally intolerable pestilence was added to this calamity: namely, the war which Godefrid waged especially against the Church of Verdun and our own.

[Note: The abridger omitted “and our own.”]

When the city of Verdun and the house of holy Mary, Mother of God, had been utterly overthrown, together with all their adornment, by plunder and fire, he, although far away, grieved deeply over the fall of that distinguished city. Though he himself was placed in fear of a similar danger, he was nevertheless a cheerful giver and did not delay in coming to the ruined city’s aid. Concealing his own name, he sent a message containing these words:

“Holy Mary of Liège sends fifty pounds of denarii to holy Mary of Verdun: half for the canonical brothers, and half for the repair of the church.”

The canons of that place, stripped of all their goods, received this remedy for so great a disaster as a gift from God. And, lest they prove ungrateful to so great a benefactor, they vowed perpetual public prayers for him both while he lived and after his death.

Thus the storm of wars of which we have spoken consumed what remained of the famine and afflicted rich and poor alike with a single calamity. It threatened the common ruin of the whole country. Without doubt illustrious Lorraine would then have fallen—indeed, I say, it would have fallen—into irrecoverable destruction, since it had no defender, or, worse still, into a king’s hands through the disloyal oath of perjury, unless the Lord strengthened his Joshua to resist the enemies of the Church and indicated that the sides of justice were to be defended against the factious.

## Chapter XVI — How he calmed the storm of war for the most part

The most savage plunderers had already invaded the Church’s property. They had also devastated everything which the prudence of the aforementioned bishop had previously gathered into the city. Each man treated as his own the estates of the Church that he had usurped.

Then, behold, the unconquerable and fearless warrior of Christ clothed himself in the breastplate of justice, girded himself with the spiritual sword, and used the cross of Christ before him in every danger as a lance, saying with blessed Martin: “Protected by the sign of the cross, not by shield or helmet, I shall safely penetrate the enemy’s ranks.”

That outstanding champion of piety and justice was thus inflamed with the zeal by which Mattathias, out of zeal for his father’s law, did not shrink from killing a transgressing Jew at the very altars. While the weapons of dukes and counts were ceasing everywhere, aided only by hope in grace, he bound a few followers to himself and to the Church’s fidelity by oath.

The first successes of the war, which proceeded favorably for a short time, carried many of our soldiers over to the opposing side. They vainly imagined that, if they became accomplices in this new crime, they would acquire at will by force the benefice—indeed, the whole bishopric.

But when matters turned against them, let us also follow the diligence of our defender. He fortified the city according to the circumstances of time and place, making it continuously secure against enemy attack through appointed guards in the citadel and gates constantly barred by their enclosures. He ordered the houses of both clerics and laypeople to be filled with weapons and sometimes commanded the citizens to remain armed.

He himself, continually stationed at the episcopal residence and neglecting none of his customary religious duties, investigated the enemy’s devices through knowledgeable scouts. Against all these he endeavored to protect himself and his people with the shield of prudence.

Thus, like Argus—if it is permissible to believe the story—marked by a hundred eyes, he restrained external evils so that he not only did not diminish internal goods but increased them. Day by day he eagerly desired good things, while diligently guarding against evils for Christ’s faithful, whom he feared for most.

In this alone, if I may say so confidently, his mind, divided among many matters, did not appear lesser in any one of them, but remained whole and powerful for all things, according to the Apostle who strengthened him.

When friends living far away warned him by letter to leave Liège and withdraw to Huy, a fortress made exceedingly secure by its situation, he replied:

“Far be it from me to abandon the Lord’s flock by fleeing, or to suppose that any place amid such a turmoil of affairs is safe without them. From them, together with the patronage of the saints before God, everything that seems to bring us advantage or honor in war or peace depends. If I abandon them, the bolder enemy will attempt to attack them and will mock our flight, not without great disgrace to us. Here, rather, we must live as long as it is possible; there, we must die. With those with whom we have rejoiced in good things, we shall also endure dangers.”

Bound, certainly, by the chain of religious devotion and charity toward his sons, he could not easily be torn from their presence.

## Chapter XVII — How he destroyed the castles of the plunderers

Piety, stirred by the misery of the needy and the groaning of the poor, eventually laudably broke the strictness of this resolve and compelled him to rise from his customary rest and hasten to their aid. It persuaded him that nothing could be more blessed or more pleasing to God than to restrain the savage fury of the plunderers from oppressing the innocent populace.

A large number of these men had fortified extremely strong refuges for themselves in marshes or on cliffs. Relying upon them, they had usurped the surrounding estates of others and subjected the inhabitants, deprived of their possessions, to intolerable servitude.

During this storm of war they raged through the entire surrounding region with all the more freedom and all the more widely. The avenger of God therefore resolved, if he could, to level these little strongholds—built many centuries earlier but then especially harmful—with the ground and to free the country, long exhausted by these robberies.

Inflamed by the spirit by which Samuel is known to have slain the Amalekite Agag and Elijah the Tishbite the prophets of Baal, our most courageous hero, content with only a small number of soldiers, proceeded to besiege now one fortress, now another.

Inside, however, the brigands, rashly relying upon valleys and marshes, first concealed and dismissed their fear of danger and mocked it. They taunted our men with insults and called them mad for coming to attack a house fortified by nature itself.

Our men, on the contrary, encouraged by the commands of so distinguished a leader, vied with one another in weaving wicker hurdles, carrying bundles, and constructing a new route for their siege engines through impassable places.

Thus, through strenuous labor combined with ingenuity, they soon overcame a task difficult by nature. The marsh, known only to frogs and fish, became solid ground and prepared a deadly device for the brigands, though it had previously provided them with secure hiding places.

When the device had been brought to a point from which the robbers’ den could be struck with accurate blows, they faced hostile days and nights without interruption.
