Our men relieved one another in the labor, never ceasing to shake the courtyards of the building and every one of the enemy’s inner hiding places with frequent showers of stones.

The bishop himself, present there, fulfilled his vows of vigils and psalmody to almighty God while engaged in such work.

Why say more? When Godefrid struggled in vain to come to the assistance of his men, the besieged negotiated for their lives and limbs. The fortress was captured and utterly destroyed. After that, one fortress after another was destroyed in a similar disaster, without reconsideration.

Nor do I think that I should remain silent about this: during the siege he often provided daily expenses for a thousand armed men, often for more, and rarely for fewer, according to the ancient custom of the Romans. In the meantime he allowed the common soldiers the use of slaughtered livestock, except for those animals necessary for agricultural labor. He himself fully compensated each owner for the loss, allowing no place for injustice even amid such great difficulties.

From this it is clear how tenacious he was of fairness and uprightness at other times, since even when he most needed to gain the people’s favor—as commonly happens in such an undertaking—not even the greatest necessity could pull this rigid Cato away from justice.

## Chapter XVIII — Concerning the distribution of the graces bestowed upon this man

I take pleasure in contemplating in this man the riches of divine goodness and in admiring, within the breadth of a single heart, the divisions of grace. He strove to administer them with such a well-ordered alternation of activities that, when he was occupied with one matter, he was repeatedly engaged in others as well—something that could scarcely be believed if it were not known.

For if I consider him as bishop, I seem to see a peer of Gregory; when I behold him engaged in military affairs, I find him not inferior to a Maccabee. In wisdom I regard him as Solomon; in disputation, as Augustine. In humility of heart, continence, and constant vigils, he resembled any of the holy anchorites who were poor in spirit.

He dealt with worldly matters more from necessity than from inclination, taking every possible care not to displease the Creator.

Considering himself useless and his old age full of evil days, he lamented it with frequent sighs, recognizing with blessed Job that human life upon earth is nothing other than temptation.

Therefore he was accustomed to sing with blessed David: “When shall I come and appear before the face of my God?” And with the Doctor of the Nations: “I desire to depart and be with Christ.”

There can be no doubt that, if he had lived in the time of Nero’s or Decius’s persecution, he would willingly have presented himself at the tribunals of the persecutors and stood ready for condemnation—superior in judgment and stronger in offering his neck to the sword.

Even when he was surrounded by armed bands prepared to assist him, he was ready, holding out only the cross of Christ in his hands, to place himself among armed enemies and, if it were God’s will, to meet death in that manner, desiring to imitate him who said: “The good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep.”

Terrified by the great courage of our defender, the adversaries’ madness gradually weakened. As they themselves still commonly testify, whenever they attacked us with savage intent, as soon as they could see our city and the oratories of the saints, their minds were immediately changed by divine power, so that they not only refrained from doing harm but even found it pleasing, out of reverence for the place, to shed pious tears.

Thus it happened that those who had yearned to invade the property of others at the risk of their souls were eventually content, scarcely preserving their own safety, to retain what belonged to them. Sometimes the venerable Father Wazo compelled them, sometimes entreated them, and finally urged them by every means to come to their senses.

Thus the mercy of almighty God graciously deigned, through the effective diligence of a prudent helmsman, to free his Church’s ship for a time from storms of this kind. Yet, amid such faction, there was also war against the emperor—though not, as before, a war to be feared, according to the reports of good men.

## Chapter XIX — How he became suspect to the emperor

In this matter, because the emperor had at one point raged rather madly against the men of our Church, as good men reported, the man of God was accused before the emperor of a false crime: it was alleged that, having given his pledge to Godefrid, he had made a pact against the imperial majesty and the safety of the kingdom and—something it is wicked to suppose of so great a man—had given him confidence to wage war.

Other venerable deeds of his loudly proclaim how far this was from the truth. But because it is difficult for the eye of the mind—pulled in different directions by glory and wealth on one side, by the various cares of administering the commonwealth on another, and by a thousand flattering tongues on yet another—not to be blinded at times to the light of truth, those who brought the report persuaded the emperor that, in the matters which Lord Wazo had truly and faithfully carried out, he had served not the common good or imperial loyalty but his own arrogance, out of a spirit of contention.

The priest’s freedom of speech added to the suspicion. Entirely free from every kind of duplicity, he knew how to deviate neither to the right nor to the left from the path of truth. In acting for the truth, he did not hesitate to incur anyone’s displeasure rather than assent to powerful favor through silent concealment of the truth.

I shall therefore relate one matter which, through his deacon, who had learned it from his own mouth, came to the knowledge of our humble selves. Some people thought that the emperor had been considerably angered against him because he had assigned cases concerning bishops and ecclesiastical orders not to the emperor, a layman, but to the supreme pontiff for judgment.

## Chapter XX — What he thought in the case of the bishop of Ravenna

[Note: See Ughelli, vol. II, p. 359, and Peter Damian, book VI, letter 2.]

A certain noble-born canon of Cologne, named Wigerus, had received the archbishopric of Ravenna from Emperor Henry himself. Before he was ordained bishop, he had celebrated the solemn rites of Mass for two years merely as a priest, wearing the dalmatic and sandals.

Accordingly, he was summoned to the palace on account of many things he had imprudently done there, and especially accused of this apparent presumption. The emperor severely charged him with having committed such an offense.

He replied that the priests of that Church had always been permitted to do this on the authority of the holy Fathers. Judgment concerning the matter was then sought from the bishops. Some responded according to the emperor’s wishes, while others hesitated, and the matter came to Bishop Wazo.

Wazo repeatedly excused himself, saying that an Italian bishop ought not to be judged by him, a bishop from across the Alps. But the emperor insisted vehemently that, in obedience to the command he had received, Wazo should pronounce a judicial sentence concerning the matter.

Compelled in this way, he finally disclosed his opinion:

“We owe obedience to the supreme pontiff, but fidelity to you. You are owed an account of secular matters; to him we must render an account of those matters that appear to pertain to divine worship. Therefore, in my judgment, whatever this man has done against ecclesiastical order, I declare that its examination belongs solely to the apostolic authority. But if he has acted negligently or disloyally in secular matters entrusted to him by you, it undoubtedly belongs to you to demand an account.”

The other bishops agreed with this judgment. On that day he would not have lost his bishopric by anyone’s judgment, had he not himself voluntarily returned the staff and ring to the emperor.

## Chapter XXI — How he was tested by the countess of Castrum Mons
[Col. 0747D] Moreover, I think it not irrelevant to report two further matters in which the justice of the man of God was manifestly tested in contrasting ways. In the one case, as though he were faithfully acting on behalf of the emperor, he was tempted to act unfaithfully against God and the Christian religion; in the other, although somewhat injured by the emperor himself, he was proved ready willingly to devote himself to loyalty toward the emperor.

At a certain time Herimannus, count and margrave of the place called Mount of the Castles, had confirmed a pact by oath with Baldwin of Flanders. His wife, however—more driven by the instability of a woman’s mind than by sympathy for the just cause (for woman is a changeable and mutable creature, as she herself is a most cunning contriver of a thousand frauds)—planned, as though thereby to release her husband from perjury, to pollute herself by betraying that same husband and to entangle the conscience of a priest of God in consent to this crime. Through a messenger she instructed him to come with armed men, and announced the place and time at which and when he should seize her husband and hand him over to the emperor.

He, abhorring the novelty of this crime beyond what can be believed, said: “We have learned neither by report nor by reading that a wife has ever handed over her husband with impunity, whether in truth or in pretence. For it is pernicious in every way to imagine anything so openly abhorrent to human nature.”

Thus the man of God, perceiving with the lynx-like eyes of prudence the wickedness disguised beneath the appearance of virtue, steadfastly rejected from his mouth, with an abundant seasoning of honeyed wisdom, the deadly poison which the enemy of the human race was preparing to administer through the customary vessel of his deceit. Indeed, the Lord wished to change the enemies confronting his champion and to display to spectators the manly strength of his fighter through the hard labors of combat, allowing the many forms of that ancient serpent to lie in wait for his heel all the more fiercely because, through divine aid, he himself had hitherto thrust the serpent’s condemned head beneath the feet of this warrior, powerless as it was.

## CHAPTER XXII. How he was urged by letters to resist the emperor

At another time, when it was being reported that the emperor was offended with him, letters were delivered to Lord Wazo, the bishop. We know little about where or from whom they were sent. They contained persuasive words intended to induce him to receive three thousand warriors [Note: The printed editions read “a company of armed men”] into the fortifications of his cities and towns; these men, by waging war, could easily avenge the troubles inflicted upon him by the emperor.

He, as he sometimes used pleasantly to relieve serious matters with playful diversions, mentioned the affair in conversation with some of his close associates, and most cheerfully repeated, with jocular emphasis, that he possessed sufficient means for waging war. When one of those with whom he used to speak more privately ventured, in the familiarity of friendship, to suggest that his gray hairs, which had been brought from the earliest years of adolescence to that age without complaint, ought never to be brought so low that, at the very end of life, he should apply his mind to counsels of this kind, he replied:

“Let no one suppose that I hold any other intention in my mind than the one you advise. Let no one doubt that I am faithful to the lord emperor according to my knowledge and ability, however he may treat me. Even if the movement of his anger had advanced so far that, at his command, I had lost my right eye, I would still not cease to turn whatever I could foresee with my left toward his honor and loyalty.”

Since this is so, let the wicked tongue of those who slander Wazo be silent together with the Jews who disparage Christ; and let them, with the good, marvel that in our time no bishop labored more vigilantly in the holy religion, nor did any leader, margrave, or count contend more zealously for the loyalty of the Roman Empire and the safety of his homeland. For who but he, with God’s help, prudently dispersed the conspiracy formed against the emperor? Who laid low castles fortified by nature and by art? Who disarmed Godefrid, together with the largest part of his faction of soldiers, terrifying him on the one hand with threats and soliciting him on the other with gifts and promises?

## CHAPTER XXIII. How he deterred the king of the Franks by letter from invading Aachen

But behold: while I feared that, in striving for brevity, I might succumb to the subject, I passed over many matters that ought to be told. Among them is one which I think unknown to many: that memorable deed by which, though he was far away and perhaps unknown by face, he softened the mind of the king of the Franks, who had already resolved in his heart to usurp Lorraine, and almost recalled him from the very impulse of his undertaking, following the example of Paul.

Let us explain what happened and how, retracing the sequence of events. Our king, Henry, not yet emperor, had set out for Italy and was approaching Rome, intending to receive the apostolic blessing from the supreme pontiff together with the insignia of the empire. Since soldiers were scarce among us and the secure peasantry feared no incursion in the meantime, they enjoyed a welcome leisure. Then our bishop, sitting with Mary at the Lord’s feet but not abandoning Martha’s diligence, was informed of great disturbances in the regions of western Francia. Certain men were persistently urging and advising their king to invade the palace at Aachen—with a large force of arms—which, as they said, had once been an appurtenance to their right. They argued that the king and our princes were absent, that the few soldiers present could accomplish nothing against them, and finally that nothing prevented them, once they had taken possession of the principal seat, from bringing the rest of Lorraine thereafter into their own kingdom.

At the news of the danger threatening his homeland, the concern of the holy father was alarmed. Since he had no power to resist by force the strength of a man who wished to exploit this opportunity, he understood that the man must be met with ingenuity and reason; and he was extremely eager to act on this immediately.

As has been said, humble letters were sent to the king, who was inflamed in spirit. They commended the ancient friendship between the two kingdoms and their rulers: if these two kingdoms remained at peace with one another, as they had previously been, they would be a terror to all the nations of the earth, fearing nothing except God. Peace between them was therefore necessary; through harmony small matters grew, whereas through discord even great ones fell apart.

At first he disregarded and despised the letters after receiving and hearing them. He accused our king of treachery, injuries, and other crimes which it is unnecessary to recount; but he declared that he wished to claim for himself the kingdom and palace that were owed to him by hereditary right from his predecessors. He even announced, with sufficient insolence, the day on which he had decided to do these things.

In reply, our Cicero wrote among other things as follows:

“Your Majesty’s excellence knows with what disgraceful punishment secular law condemns the commission of theft. If such a crime happens to be committed by powerful men, although among human beings it may appear to be dignified by another name, nevertheless in the sight of the inner judgment it remains equally—or rather, in the case of the powerful, even more—clearly condemnable, since they were driven by less necessity to commit it.

“Consider, therefore, I beg you, how hateful to God and unworthy of your royal generosity it is to wish to steal the seat and kingdom of an absent equal, who is very far away; and, I beg you, recall your mind from such an intention, which plainly conflicts with your dignity. Rather, if you have resolved to undertake anything brave or powerful against us, let the return of our king be awaited, so that what is expedient may then be done by you more appropriately.

“But suppose that the seat of the kingdom was taken from your predecessors by deceit and that you have a hereditary right to reclaim it. Will you travel alone, or without a multitude, across the vast stretches of intervening land? Certainly not. Rather, you will be accompanied by an innumerable army, incapable of sparing the wretched; and, even against your will and despite your futile attempts to restrain them, they will consume countless thousands of human beings in an incredible devastation.

“Be certain, therefore, that if you do not restrain your hand from the slaughter of the innocent which you have begun in your mind, you will be held guilty in the sight of the Most High for as many murders as human bodies will be deprived of life if you carry this out.”

When the king heard this judgment of the man of God, his tyrannical fury was immediately calmed. Suddenly changed in mind, he ordered an assembly of bishops to appear. He commanded the man of God’s letter to be read aloud in his presence. After it had been read, he declared that this was rightly called a priest, and that this was a true bishop: though a stranger to a stranger, he had given him, before all his loyal subjects, sound counsel as a matter of duty.

Perhaps, unknowingly, he imitated the emperor Theodosius, who by a truthful judgment preferred the blessed Ambrose to all the bishops of that time, even though Ambrose had publicly rebuked and excommunicated him. From the very insult he had received, the king found an opportunity to show the bishop greater reverence; a noble humility of heart, raised above royal dignity, prompted him to do so.

Thus, with God inspiring him, the letters of one man, though far away, were able to dissuade the king’s wavering mind from the deed toward which many thousands of retainers, eager for plunder, were driving it. They restored the love of peace to his heart so completely that, conceiving nothing further of this kind, he soon gave and received his right hand with an oath from the emperor when the latter returned from Italy.

## CHAPTER XXIV. The bishop of Châlons consults him by letter about what he thinks should be done concerning heretics

[Col. 0750D]

Moreover, the apostolic eminence honored our bishop with frequent visits by letter, which he was accustomed to receive with the greatest reverence; and if he happened to be questioned about anything in them, he replied humbly. Bishops also from various places frequently consulted this outstanding fellow-worker in wisdom by letter on various matters. None who asked him useful questions was deprived of a prudent answer to what he had inquired.

Among these was the bishop of Châlons [Note: Roger II, who governed the bishopric of Châlons from 1043 to 1062]. Because of the danger threatening the souls entrusted to him, he once considered it necessary to consult Wazo’s holiness, and acknowledged by letter that the matter was as follows.

He said that in one part of his diocese there were certain peasants who followed the perverse doctrine of the Manichaeans and frequently held secret meetings, performing at some solemnity of their own certain obscene and shameful acts that he could scarcely describe. They falsely claimed that the Holy Spirit was given through a sacrilegious laying-on of hands; and, to establish the credibility of their error, they dogmatized most falsely that the Spirit had been sent by God nowhere else than in their heresiarch Mani—as though “Manes” meant nothing other than the Holy Spirit. Thus they fell into that blasphemy which, according to the word of Truth, cannot be forgiven either in this age or in the age to come.

Such people, he said, compelled as many as they could to join their group. They abominated marriage; they not only avoided eating meat but declared it profane to kill any animal whatsoever. Presuming to take the Lord’s command in the Old Law—“You shall not kill”—as a protection for their error, they claimed that it prohibited killing.

If any simple and inarticulate people happened to join the followers of this error, he asserted that they immediately became more eloquent even than the most learned Catholics, so that the sincere eloquence of the wise seemed scarcely able to overcome their loquacity. He added that he grieved more over the daily corruption of others than over the destruction of the heretics themselves.

The anxious bishop consulted the sure chamber of wisdom about what ought to be done with such people: whether or not the sword of secular power should be used against them; for, unless they were exterminated, a little leaven could corrupt the whole mass. Our bishop replied as follows:

## CHAPTER XXV. The response: his judgment concerning this matter [Note: This chapter differs greatly from the printed editions, in which scarcely anything of the author’s words is found beyond the beginning of this response.]

[Col. 0751C]

“Regarding those about whom you have written, their error is indeed manifest. It was examined long ago by the holy Fathers and refuted by their most lucid judgments. To say nothing of their utterly insane blasphemies, by which they falsely claim the Holy Spirit for themselves, let your affection understand how many difficulties they deliberately bring upon themselves through a mistaken understanding of the Lord’s command which says in the Old Law, ‘You shall not kill.’

“Unless they understand this as prohibiting only the killing of human beings, they must similarly see that the eating of those things which they think they may lawfully consume—such as grain, legumes, and wine—is forbidden to them. These things, having grown from seeds entrusted to the earth, became what they are according to the manner of their life; and unless they were killed, taken from their green life, they could not serve human use.

“Setting aside secular writings, the Psalmist bears witness to this matter when he says: ‘And he killed their vines with hail’; likewise the Apostle: ‘Foolish one, what you sow is not brought to life unless it first dies.’ Truth itself also says: ‘Unless a grain of wheat, falling into the ground, dies, it remains alone.’

“They must therefore necessarily admit that those things which, as is evident, can be killed through accidental causes once lived. Let them choose, then, whichever they wish: either, following the Catholics, let them believe that ‘You shall not kill’ is written concerning human beings alone, and let them lawfully use with us the abundance of animals to be slaughtered; or, if they insist that this is denied to them, we too shall deny them, according to the very judgment of their error, the use of bread, legumes, and other things of this kind, since unless these were killed in their manner, they could in no way be adapted for human use.

“Although the Christian religion abhors this, and condemns it together with the sacrilege of the Arian heresy, nevertheless, imitating its Savior, who, gentle and humble of heart, did not come to shout or contend but rather to endure insults, spitting, blows, and finally death on the cross, it is commanded for the present to tolerate such people in some manner. As blessed Gregory says: ‘Abel would never have attained innocence had Cain’s wickedness not exercised him; nor does the grape become wine unless it is crushed beneath feet.’

“But so that it may be clear what the merciful and compassionate Lord wishes to be done concerning such people—he who does not immediately judge sinners but patiently awaits their repentance—let us hear what he deigned to teach his disciples, and through them us, when explaining in his Gospel the parable of the field of wheat and weeds.

“‘The man,’ he says, ‘who sowed good seed in his field is the Son of Man. The good seed: these are the children of the kingdom; but the field is this world. The enemy who sowed weeds over it is the devil. The weeds: these are the children of the evil one; the harvest is the consummation of the age; and the reapers are angels.’

“What is signified by the servants who first appear and wish to pull up the weeds, if not the order of preachers? While they desire the good to be separate from the wicked in the Church, they seek, as it were, to eradicate the weeds from the good crop of wheat.

“But under the great restraint of discernment, that master of the household checks their eager efforts: ‘No,’ he says, ‘lest in gathering the weeds you uproot the wheat along with them. Let both grow until the harvest; and at harvest time I will say to the reapers: Gather first the weeds and bind them into bundles to burn, but gather the wheat into my barn.’

“What does the Lord show by these words except his patience, which he desires his preachers to display toward their erring neighbors? Especially since those who are weeds today may possibly be converted tomorrow and become wheat.

“That you belong to the number of those servants is shown by the fervor of spiritual zeal burning in your breast for souls deceived by the devil’s fraud. Through this zeal you seek to cleanse the wheat crop of weeds with the hoe of judgment, lest the good be corrupted by the wicked. Yet divine judgment must rather be obeyed, so that this may not be done by you prematurely or before the proper time. Otherwise, while we think that we are exercising justice against transgressors, we may, through an appearance of severity veiling impiety, wrong the one who does not desire the death of sinners, does not rejoice in the destruction of the dying, but knows through his patience and long-suffering how to lead sinners back to repentance.

“Let the judgment of dust cease once the sentence of the Judge has been heard. Let us not seek to remove from this life by the sword of secular power those whom God, the same Creator and Redeemer, wishes to spare as he knows best, so that they may recover from the snares of the devil in which they are held captive to do his will.

“Thus, thus indeed, it is fitting for us to reserve such people for that final harvest of the master of the household, whatever he may command his reapers to do; and we must await it with fear and trembling concerning ourselves as well. For any of those whom the field of this world holds as weeds may perhaps be found by that harvest to be wheat; and those whom we now have as adversaries on the way of the Lord, almighty God may make superior to us in that heavenly homeland.

“Certainly we read that Saul, who raged more fiercely than all the others, was present among the stone-throwers who killed the blessed Stephen, the first martyr; and the one who had him here as a persecutor rejoices to have him there as an apostle and martyr, placed before him.

“Meanwhile, we must also remember that we who are called bishops do not receive at our ordination the sword, which belongs to secular power. Therefore, by God’s authority, we are anointed not to kill but rather to give life.

“There is, however, another matter that must be carefully undertaken concerning the schismatics mentioned above, one which you certainly do not ignore: they, and those who communicate with them, must be deprived of Catholic communion, and they must be publicly denounced to everyone, so that, according to the prophetic admonition, they may go out from their midst and not touch their utterly unclean sect. For ‘whoever touches pitch will be defiled by it.’”

The man of God strove to impress these points so insistently, following the example of blessed Martin, that he in some measure restrained the headlong fury of the Franks, which habitually thirsted for bloodshed. For he had heard that they marked heretics merely by their pallor, as though it were certain that those who were visibly pale must be heretics; and thus, through their error and fury together, many who were truly Catholics had at times been killed.

## CHAPTER XXVI. That heretics must by no means be killed [Note: This entire chapter is missing from the printed editions.]

Since these things are so, and since nothing can be opposed with equal reason to what is so openly supported by evangelical sanction and reason, let those who have leisure consider how irreprehensibly it was done when certain followers of this kind of error were discovered at Goslar. After a thorough investigation of their superstition and a just excommunication for their obstinacy in error, they were additionally condemned to hanging.

When we carefully inquired into the procedure of that investigation, we could discover no other reason for their condemnation than that they had disobeyed any of the bishops who ordered them to kill a chicken.

For I shall confess it and not remain silent: had our Wazo lived in those times, he would certainly never have assented to this sentence. He would have followed the example of blessed Martin, who, in order to intercede for the Priscillianists condemned by an edict distorted through the counsel of priests who shamefully flattered the greatest emperor, preferred to suffer the loss of his outstanding virtue rather than fail to provide for the rescue even of heretics.

We say this not because we wish to defend the error of heretics, but because we demonstrate our disapproval of something that has nowhere been sanctioned in the divine laws.

## CHAPTER XXVII. He replies to the emperor concerning what he thinks about choosing a pope

Amid these events, we should recall that when Pope Clement, elevated from the bishopric of Bamberg to the apostolic see, had departed this life, the emperor resolved to seek Wazo’s advice about appointing another in his place.

As he was in all matters, and especially in such matters, a diligent investigator, Wazo carefully reviewed these things with others with whom he had shared the work: on the one hand, the deeds of the Roman pontiffs; on the other, their decrees; and also the authoritative canons and the capitulary.

After these had been carefully examined, he could find nothing other than that the supreme pontiff, whatever his way of life might have been, ought to be held in the highest honor; that he should never be judged by anyone; and indeed that no accusation by one of inferior rank against someone superior should be admitted.

Since it had been agreed that this election of the apostolic pontiff would take place on the Lord’s Nativity, the boldest defender of pure truth sent his messenger there. He ordered that the following instructions be confidently delivered to the ungrateful emperor [Note: This response of Wazo differs entirely from the printed editions]:

“Let your serenity consider whether perhaps the seat of the supreme pontiff, removed by those who ought not to have removed it, has been divinely reserved for him, since the man whom you ordered to be appointed in his place appears to have yielded to the same man, who is still alive.

“Therefore, since it has pleased you to demand our opinion on this matter, let your eminence cease wishing to substitute anyone in the place of the man who survives. It is certain that neither divine nor human laws permit this, as the words and writings of the holy Fathers everywhere attest: the supreme pontiff must be judged by no one except God alone.

“I call the Lord to witness—and I call to witness the oath which I, an unworthy priest, swore to you—that on this matter nothing truer or more excellent can be conceived or found by me than this judgment.”

When the bishop’s aforesaid messenger was approaching the royal court, Poppo—who was also Bruno, bishop of Brixen, already elected some time earlier to the supreme pontificate and later called Damasus by the Romans—was uncertain what to do, since the matter had already been settled and he had received the instructions to transfer it to the emperor. Nevertheless, he went in and presented the emperor with other instructions, as amusingly as he knew how.

After everything else, he said: “There remains one further matter which the bishop wishes to be conveyed. Since the matter has been settled, it is not appropriate for me to explain it to you.”

When the emperor heard this—for he was curious to hear many things and gather the opinions of various people—he pressed the legate insistently to extract the matter from him, although the messenger repeatedly expressed his reluctance. The messenger, for his part, deliberately prolonged the delay and sought, as it were, diversions away from the subject. In silence, he was also trying first to win over the powerful man, so that, as he knew well, by anticipating events he might break any anger that could subsequently arise in his heart.

What more need be said? The king promised that, whatever the matter might be, he would not become angry; that he would forgive every offense against anyone who delivered even the harshest command; and finally, if any danger to the favor enjoyed by the sending bishop should arise because he had revealed what was meant to be concealed, he himself would entirely ward off the dispute.

At last, reassured, the messenger carried out the instructions he had been ordered to deliver. To a man inclined to measure his will by his own power, they would have been almost as offensive as they were true, had the prior agreement not prevented him from reacting in advance.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. What he did and replied when accused by the emperor

[Col. 0755B]

At another time, when an edict had been issued that the people of Frisia, who were resisting the emperor under their leader Theoderic, should be attacked everywhere by naval warfare, he, being as he was fatherly in his concern, feared both that soldiers with no experience of fighting from ships would achieve nothing and that they might fall into an ambush prepared for them by the enemy. Moreover, he had received the order to go to the appointed place for assembling the army within three days, traveling two hundred miles or more [Note: The abridger omitted this, although he ought to have reported it, since it excuses the holy bishop]. Faced with the difficulties created by so many reasonable considerations, he took counsel not to depart anywhere or trouble the faithful of the Church in vain.

The army therefore went into Frisia and returned equipped for naval warfare. Not long afterward, a conference was held. Our bishop was summoned to it and severely accused of violating the emperor’s edict and of having managed other matters either negligently or disloyally. Those who had often benefited magnificently from his generosity unjustly brought the accusations.

He was prepared to justify himself reasonably concerning each charge, if he had been given the opportunity to offer an explanation. But, with the uproar of flatterers on the royal side shouting from one direction and the assembled bishops who were presenting their counsels urging him from the other, he alone found himself caught in such a storm. He did not have the strength to resist the emperor’s will any longer.

At last, because it seemed that the anger of the powerful man could not otherwise be appeased, he reluctantly consented to bend at his feet and was compelled to pledge three hundred pounds of silver as security for the redemption of supposed offenses that had not in fact been committed.

He regretted having done this for the rest of his life. Although the emperor later became reconciled and graciously forgave him everything, Wazo nevertheless continued to grieve and repeatedly reproached himself, asking why he had not removed even to the point of bloodshed the suspicion of such a fault.

Yet although in this matter he seemed in some way to have yielded by obeying the counsels of the bishops, on that very day and in the same assembly of courtiers he was said to have used his priestly authority against the emperor in the following manner.

Since, during the long and exceedingly prolonged dispute, our bishop—burdened both by gout and by old age—had had no opportunity to sit, the insane clamor of those who interrupted had at last barely subsided. Then Wazo said:

“Even now, nevertheless, may your Majesty deign to grant a seat to me, decrepit and weak. For even if Wazo, worn out by wrinkles and old age, is unworthy of honor, it is nevertheless unbecoming for a priest, anointed with sacred chrism, to be wearied so dishonorably among ordinary people.”

The emperor, being the kind of man who sought to usurp power over bishops in an excessively carnal—not to say ambitious—way, replied:

“But I too have been anointed with sacred oil, having been given the power to rule above others.”

The bishop, however, inflamed by zeal for truth and fervor for justice, judged that the emperor should be briefly instructed in this way:

“Your anointing is different and far removed from the priestly anointing you claim. Through it you have been adorned for killing, whereas we, by God’s authority, have been adorned for giving life. Therefore, just as life is superior to death, so without doubt our anointing is more excellent than yours.”

Tossed by the storms of the wavering world, this skilled sailor turned his ship, laden with the fruits of virtue, toward the harbor of an innocent life and a good conscience. Strong in adversity and humble in prosperity, just as he could not be broken by the world’s allurements, so he could not be shaken by its terrors, saying with the Psalmist: “The Lord is my helper; I will not fear what man can do to me.”

## CHAPTER XXIX. Whom and what kind of prebendaries he appointed

Having trampled down the storm of the world, he returned to the folds of your sheepfold, blessed Mother of God, and to those of the martyr Lambert, more pleasing than all the palaces of kings. As a good shepherd, he strove to lead the Lord’s sheep toward the eternal pastures. Meanwhile, along the road of this life, planted thick with the harshness of many difficulties, he devoted his whole mind to binding up what was broken, strengthening what was weak, and guarding what was firm and strong, judging that he existed and lived wholly not for himself but for them.

We saw him grant twenty-five prebends in a single day. He appointed fifteen canonical servants in the church of the most victorious Cross and ten in the church of the apostle Bartholomew, using resources acquired for the most part by himself [Note: The following material is missing from the printed editions]. He asked nothing of them except upright conduct and usefulness in divine service. At the same time, with a threat of anathema, he declared that no provost or dean should dare to demand any other profit or emolument from them.

Moreover, whenever someone sought to be substituted in the place of a deceased brother—for with us the matter of establishing stipends pertains to the bishop—those who sought to make their relatives or sons canons often offered estates of fertile land or large sums of ready money.

The most merciful Father said to them:

“No. The Church to which you are trying to offer these things has abundant estates and money. Instead, we seek brothers who are useful and well behaved. When someone has given himself perpetually to the Church’s service, we have no need to demand from him what is inferior—namely, temporal goods.

“What, then? Can anyone give something more precious than himself? In my judgment, we would be unjust if, from one who gives himself, we insistently sought what is more worthless to him. Nevertheless, let us first be permitted to test with what diligence their affairs have been conducted. If it is established that they have been successful as they should, we are prepared to give freely what is requested.

“And lest we appear to have introduced an obstacle into the matter, let those who wish to approach us bring letters. We ask of them only this gift, that it serve as material for examination.”

This faithful benefactor offered such things to people of various ages, both freeborn and descended from the Church’s household; he also added further benefits beyond their stipends. Nor did he exclude from the door of his generosity boys whose age he saw was still incapable of full understanding, provided that they showed promise and, according to their capacity, some degree of learning.

Through such gifts of his piety, the minds of many were kindled to love study. We saw some who had devoted themselves to frivolity turn to their studies and, through their industry in labor, obtain with the grace of accomplishment a canonical livelihood from so great a benefactor.

## CHAPTER XXX. Concerning the expenses he gave for buildings, and the perfection of his life

If anyone from the clergy, or even from among the laity, intended to construct buildings, this cheerful giver wished to be admitted as a fellow-worker in the undertaking by extending a most generous and substantial hand of money.

I experienced his goodness, bestowed both most kindly and most generously, in a similar undertaking, although I was unworthy and undeserving. I received from so munificent a giver a gift of eight pounds, together with many other things necessary for the work. Not long afterward, when I expected nothing—since I had deserved very little—he added a further benefit sufficient for my modest circumstances.

What I have said is little; I shall recall greater things. Wretched man that I am, I scarcely dare to confess that when he deigned to address me in that sweet conversation seasoned with the salt of his outstanding knowledge and elegant intellect, I was sometimes not excluded from the privacy of his psalmody and prayer. Yet the more solitary he was, the more devotedly he was accustomed, night and morning, to devote himself to God alone in prayer.

Moreover, on certain days of the week, or certainly during the customary season of fasting, he was never delayed by any winter weather from going barefoot around the shrines of the saints. As he went, the almsgiving he carried in his hand was always active beside him until he encountered someone to whom, even without that person’s knowledge, it could be entrusted as to Christ.

At mealtime, whatever dishes had been prepared, as though for someone about to feast, with nothing reserved that could have been eaten that day either by him or by those dining with him, were all expended as food for the poor. Thus the hand of almsgiving, scorched by the fire of charity together with the vowed discipline of fasting, lifted the fragrant offerings of prayer toward heaven.

He strove to display his daily way of life irreproachably before God and human beings through perseverance and the moderation of constant abstinence, the power of vigils, and other labors undertaken for Christ. He allowed no time free from the work of God, either for himself or for those other intimate companions who frequently visited his private presence, in which he was not either singing psalms, praying, reading, discussing some useful matter, or debating questions of sacred Scripture.

How lively, effective, ready, and accessible he was in resolving these questions! Finally, in all his conversation, even when it relaxed from the seriousness of its subject, it was plainly possible to perceive what dignity and what delight it contained. He scarcely ever—or perhaps never—indulged in food or sleep except as much as the necessity of nature required.

But who, even if most learned, could encompass in writing all his words or deeds worthy of remembrance? Everything concerning his merits is diminished beside them; our inarticulate littleness scarcely suffices to explain anything about so great a man.

There are also other distinguished matters that could be said about the life of our pontiff. If we wished to enumerate them individually, we would no longer be undertaking the brief account that we promised, but would exceed the intended length of the book. It would be like someone who, overly confident, attempts to plow a stagnant lake in a small boat, unaware that he is swallowed by the threatening surges of the neighboring waters; and, looking back from the midst of danger, realizes too late how reckless it was to attempt great things with small supports.

For the present, while matters remain calm, it is better to turn our fragile skiff by the helm into the inlets of the shore, lest, if we attempt something beyond our strength, we seem not so much to complete our course as to be miserably overwhelmed by the waves.

## CHAPTER XXXI. Concerning the approaching dissolution of his body
[Note: [Col. 0757D] The material enclosed in brackets does not appear in the printed editions.]

[Omitting, then, as has been said, the many deeds and sayings of that venerable man which are especially worthy of remembrance, let us bring the account to its conclusion by setting forth the end of his life. By what death this man of God left earthly things and entered heaven, he departed happily; and the outstanding shepherd desolated the Lord’s flock, exhausted by unendurable grief, through the loss of his most gracious presence. No one who knew his life can doubt that he obtained this from almighty God through his prayers: frequent tears during prayer bore witness to it, and he himself sometimes declared in ordinary conversation with those most closely attached to him that his years were, as it were, filled with days of misery, and that the time had come for him to put off the unhappy man [Col. 0758D].]

He was in the sixth year from his ordination in the administration of the bishopric and, as has been said, faithfully dispensing the goods of the supreme master of the household, he rendered to each his due, maintaining discipline most diligently in everything. When the solemnity of the apostles Peter and Paul arrived, he joyfully attended their vigils; and after Masses had been solemnly celebrated on the preceding and following day in their respective churches, while bringing his religious service to its conclusion through those by whom the blessed mother Church took her beginning, he returned to the table. During the meal he was first seized by a trembling and then by a severe fever. As this gradually crept into his other limbs [Col. 0759A], although he had not risen before the dishes were removed, he was so exhausted by pain throughout his body that, contrary to his custom, he was absent from the vigils of the approaching night.

Yet, having once more recovered his strength, he attended the vigils and Matins of the following day, Saturday—as he had always, I believe, been accustomed to struggle against bodily illness beyond all other mortals. From that time onward he was no longer able to attend the choir and the beloved assembly of the brothers; nevertheless, within the innermost part of his house he refreshed his spirit with the familiar sweetness of psalmody and reading. His spirit, which most powerfully ruled his body as it wasted away with fever, was thus prepared for the long-desired end. He protested that he felt nothing throughout his body except weakness.

As the illness therefore grew more severe, while his spirit nevertheless remained, as we have said, wholly strong and sound, he was brought from Saturday to Wednesday [Col. 0759B], the day on which the octave of the apostles is celebrated. Early that morning he ordered the priest who was accustomed to keep watch with ecclesiastical vigilance to be summoned. He told him that they must soon be separated from one another and added that he willingly wished to receive the anointing which the blessed apostle James commands to be administered to the sick. He ordered the things necessary for this rite to be prepared. He instructed the abbots and priests, together with several clerics of lower rank, to enter the chapel adjoining his bedroom, so that, in their presence, he might make arrangements concerning the affairs of the Church, offer his confession to God with them as witnesses, and, while they prayed and sang psalms, receive the sacred anointing.

He himself, with only two witnesses to this secret—that is, the priest mentioned above and the subdeacon who was also his chamberlain [Col. 0759C]—having put away every pleasure of the flesh, since the flesh was afflicted even unto death, washed his body, which for many years had been unacquainted with bathing, in the sole hope of blessed resurrection. This strongest despiser of himself desired that, by adding a further burden to his illness, there should now be done to him what in health he had striven to avoid, lest he serve harmful pleasure.

After he had been washed and clothed in white garments, he entered the brothers’ presence in the aforesaid oratory without being supported by anyone who was waiting there. He was placed on the seat on which, sitting, he had been accustomed to devote himself to psalmody or reading. He heard Mass and fortified his blessed soul with the holy viaticum of the Lord’s body, preparing to open it to the Lord, who had long been knocking.

Meanwhile, the affairs of the Church were arranged through trustees. The faithful testator assigned one portion to his successor [Col. 0759D], another to the poor and to those serving God. The excellent Father, loving all the others equally in Christ, left nothing to any relative or friend.

[Note: The material that follows was entirely omitted by the abridging editor.]

When our predecessors respectfully urged him to give to his parents some of what God had granted him, and suggested that this had nowhere been forbidden by sacred authority, he replied:

“I commend my surviving parents to the one to whom our predecessors also left me, who possessed neither estates, slaves, nor inherited money. Whether that God and Lord of ours wishes them to live as private persons or otherwise, we leave more suitably to his mercy.”

Moreover, if he had judged anything too severely against anyone while he was still in good health, under the guidance of reason, he wished it not to be changed through fear of death, but rather to remain unshaken after his death. He retained this inflexible rigor of purpose bravely until death, conscious that he had done everything with a good intention of mind and that nothing in these matters could displease the just Judge to whom he was hastening. The Judge himself attests this in his Gospel:

“If your eye is single, your whole body will be luminous; but if it is evil, your whole body will be dark.”

By the name “eye” he signifies intention; by “body,” the actions that follow. Just as the footsteps of one who walks are guided by the eye, so, plainly, according to the intention that precedes them—if it is good, toward good, and if evil, toward evil—the deeds of the person who acts follow accordingly.

## CHAPTER XXXII. His confession and anointing

[Col. 0760B]

When everything had therefore been prudently arranged, Abbot Olbertus—his contemporary and companion from the very years of childhood, and likewise his fellow student in meditation on the divine law—put on priestly vestments to perform these Christian rites for him. He himself desired to become the companion of one departing to Christ, with whom he had shared companionship in the way of God through unanimous love.

When, through psalmody and prayer, they had reached the point at which the rite prescribes that oil be applied to the sick man, he was wholly vigorous in mind and spirit, although already dead in the flesh. With whatever slight effort he was able, he rose from his bed, knelt before the altar, and, as it is written, “The just man is first the accuser of himself,” confessed that he was a sinner and that he had not lived as a bishop and true Christian ought to live.

As he accused himself before God sufficiently and at length concerning other offenses as well—offenses without which the life of the saints can scarcely, or perhaps cannot at all, be lived irreproachably—the aforesaid abbot, relying on the boldness permitted by their holy intimacy, suggested that if he had ever sinned against the emperor either in words or even in hidden thoughts, he should not delay to confess it to God, so that, secure from every accusation by the enemy, he might deserve to be presented fearlessly before God, the searcher of hearts.

To this he replied confidently:

“My conscience does not reproach me throughout my whole life for having sinned in any way against the emperor. Rather, I have always desired, and do still desire, his honor, and we have labored, insofar as it depended on us, so that it might increase day by day with God’s help. As for the fact that, while most willingly serving his honor, we were less acceptable to his favor, we attribute this certainly to other sins.

“Yet I myself reproach myself for having done something especially deserving of penance: although I was free from every disloyal act against him, I fell at his feet before everyone as though guilty and, by such humiliation, planted in the multitude a suspicion of a guilt which, God being witness, did not exist, and thus stained the name of bishop with the mark of a false crime. But alas! I am ashamed and repent. When everyone, even religious men, cried out that I should make satisfaction to him, though deeply angered against me, I alone could not continue resisting for long; overcome, I confess, I shamefully yielded. Therefore, because by persisting unshaken I did not remove the suspicion of the falsely imputed crime [Col. 0761A], I grieve and lament bitterly.”

After saying this, he asked that he be forgiven if he had sinned against any of the brothers present. In response, the devotion of the clergy standing by asked the Lord God to forgive their bishop, and, insofar as it depended on them, most willingly granted him forgiveness, not without many tears; they also humbly begged that he do the same for them.

When this had been done, the abbot whom we mentioned above solemnly directed him, through the sacred anointing with oil, accompanied by the psalms and prayers belonging to that office, onto the road of peace and blessed rest.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. How Abbot Olbertus entreated that he might not survive him by seven days

[Col. 0761B]

Then, when each had returned to his own place, the man of God remained lying in bed, asserting that he suffered nothing except weakness. He awaited, as though he had never been more cheerful in health, the long-desired hour when he would depart to the Lord who was calling him.

The priests and chaplains who kept watch beside him, attending in expectation of his glorious departure, testified that psalmody and prayers were repeatedly recited by his already dying lips and trembling tongue at the very hours at which he had been accustomed to recite them while well. Clearly, what the living and healthy man had long been accustomed to do through practice, in obedience to the ruling spirit, the flesh now dying demonstrated.

Wednesday had passed, namely the day of the apostolic octave; Thursday then remained. When the hour of departure, as was thought, was already near and the elders who had gathered were awaiting it with the greatest devotion, they earnestly begged him to allow himself to be taken down from the bed, as is customary with Christians who are dying.

“Do not,” he said, “wear yourselves out uselessly today; instead, come to meet me tomorrow, when I shall depart in God’s name.”

All who were present heard these words. The aforesaid abbot, who had anointed him the day before, received this announcement of his foretold death with a pious groan:

“If you depart,” he said, “may the mercy of the Almighty not allow me to remain in this world seven days after you.”

We believe that these words of his prayer reached the ears of the merciful hearer, as the outcome proved. For, immediately returning to the monastery of blessed James—where, besides another flock that he governed at the monastery of Gembloux, he was the father of many monks—he felt an illness creeping through all his limbs. He perceived that his own bodily dissolution was approaching together with that of the bishop, his like-minded brother. He was already weary of the rough hardships of this life, which he would have had to tread further without the consolation of so great a fellow traveler. Rather, he longed to be satisfied with him by the manifest contemplation of Christ, with whom, while discussing the mysteries of sacred Scripture, he had been accustomed to sigh for the sweetness of Christ’s vision, known not yet in reality but in hope.

One was with us the crown of the clergy; the other, the glory of the monks. Although one, amid the storms of the fluctuating world, undertook more readily to direct the activities of the practical life, he was nevertheless suspended in divine contemplation and made inwardly dead to external things. The other, dead to the world both by profession and by the intention of his heart, fed a twofold flock of two sheepfolds for the Lord, and, while wisely dispensing with the most kindly generosity both ecclesiastical resources and counsels [Col. 0762A], was by no means lacking in assistance toward external things.

Both were imbued with divine and human wisdom; both were exceedingly strong pillars in the temple of God. Each, in both orders of those serving God, strove throughout his life to weave for the divine majesty of the Bridegroom a garment of gold, standing at the right hand of the queen, and to surround it with the most delightful distinction of varied colors. They diligently competed in carrying this out for as long as they lived.

Under such safe guardians and fortified by such powerful defenders, Legia rested amid the most honorable leisure of the liberal arts, fearing neither the secret ambushes of robbers nor the attacks of open enemies. At that time Legia was happy; now, having lost this happiness, she is far unhappier.

[Col. 0762B]

When Friday dawned, namely the eighth day before the Ides of July, our shepherd, as he had foretold, returned his blessed soul to the Creator. Seven days after him, as he had asked God, the soul of the aforesaid abbot, having obtained what he had requested, followed the bishop, so that it might be clearly evident that, through this mystical number of days and because of the equal merit of their lives, these two great fathers had been received from the abyss of this world into one rest of eternal blessedness.

The happy souls of the just, exercised in many works of devotion, depart—yes, they depart—to the Lord their Maker. Living stones are gathered for the building of the heavenly Jerusalem; and, because of the wickedness of those who remain, those who could still have benefited the tender flock for a long time are, alas, taken away far too soon [Col. 0762C].

## CHAPTER XXXIV. How Legia was deprived of so great a shepherd

The good shepherd thus leaves wretched Legia with her little ones—“a daughter from a mother, blessed by a son,” and afterward much more blessed by that same father (the syntax of this transmitted phrase is uncertain). Even if stones could shed tears, she could never sufficiently mourn the irreparable loss of Wazo, since, after God, she is known to owe him this: that, by the distinction of a unique name, she alone among the surrounding greater cities was called a fountain of wisdom.

What region on earth is so remote that, as fame flies everywhere, the name of Wazo’s Legia has not reached it? It is little that threefold Gaul knows you as exalted by so great a father. Germany, embracing Alpine lands [Col. 0762D], is by no means unaware of you. The Pannonians, and likewise the Iberians, have experienced your glory. Nor is it hidden from the Britons spread throughout the farthest world, or from the Aquitanians together with the Arverni, how high you raised your head through the authority of so great a ruler.

The most renowned cities all around yield to you through the virtue of your supreme bishop. Even powerful Rome of old does not consider it beneath her dignity to be surpassed by your glory, since in the present age she has had no survivor among the orthodox equal to yours.

But now, alas, deprived of so great a shepherd, you stand as a shadow of a great name. Still, following the continuity of your former reputation, you invite many lovers of study to the school of learning, expecting that through liberal study they may be sustained by free assistance with food and clothing.

[Col. 0763A]

For in that hope they declare that they have been drawn from their native lands, believing those who report such things—those who have experienced such support among us in former times. Often, after seeking the exercise of letters not without benefit, since Wazo alone used to receive everyone and provide everything, none of them is now supported by all of us at this needy place. The works of mercy which one person carried out unfailingly, all of us together, even if we wish to do so, cannot accomplish.

## CHAPTER XXXV. An address to Legia

Come, then, now, dear Legia: if you have any piety toward God at heart or any love of honor in this world, strive with the utmost eagerness, I beg you, at least to embrace the traces of your ancient religion. For although you have been deprived of your fathers [Col. 0763B], sons have nevertheless been born to you in their place, whom almighty God, though still tender and inexperienced, is able to form toward the summit of holy religion by the example of good fathers.

“For to you, Lord, the poor are abandoned; you will be the helper of orphans.”

Yet there is something that you must be reminded of amid these matters, dear nursing mother, in whose [Col. 0764A] lap I alone, an insignificant servant among the beginners in true philosophy, grew up: do not begin to claim as your own merits the gifts of your Lord, if you possess any; rather, in recognition of your weakness, lay yourself beneath the feet of all the Churches, and especially of your holy and venerable mother, Cologne, whom the Lord has honored after the city of Rome both by the countless number of saints of different kinds and by the most delightfully varied crown of holy religion.

Revere her as your lady, so that she may not disdain to acknowledge you as her daughter. Thus, on account of your humility and of her recompense for charity, that heavenly key-bearer, the leader and patron of both, may bring her and you, together with the sheep of both, into the joys of their Lord, and establish them in the seats of the heavenly Jerusalem to behold the God of gods in Zion.

May this be granted by that same living and true God, who alone in Trinity and thrice in Unity possesses immortality and dwells in inaccessible light. To him, the immortal King of the ages, invisible, the only God, be honor, praise, and glory forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0763]

# CHARTER OF WAZO FOR THE COLLEGIATE CHURCH OF SAINT BARTHOLOMEW AT LIÈGE  
*(Year 1046.)*  
He adds ten prebends to the number of twenty canons and assigns them substantial revenues.

[Martene, *Amplissima Collectio*, vol. I, p. 411.]

[Col. 0763D]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Let it be known to all that Count Lambert of Leuven, excommunicated for his offenses, gave to me, Wazo, an unworthy bishop, for his absolution, five fiscal manses at Villers in Hasbaye—four servile manses and a fifth belonging to the lord’s demesne—that is, being himself a free man, he gave an allod free from oppressive customs, adorned and planted with waters, woods, meadows, and pastures. He also gave me in the same place the county, together with the circuit of the whole village and its dependencies, in cultivated fields and variscapia, in both its own and others’ allods.

He also gave me the mother church of that village, with an excellent court and certain demesne rights in his tithe. I, following the footsteps of my predecessors, Baldric, Wolbodus, and Raynard, who increased the poor church of Saint Bartholomew by their acquisitions, conveyed there the allod together with the church and the county itself through the hands of Count Gozelo, who was the advocate of the altar. I also established him there as advocate for the redemption of his soul, forbidding under anathema that, except in the matters belonging to the circuit court, where he received the third penny, he should presume to burden that place or the church any further [Col. 0765A] with lodgings or exactions.

I also gave there whatever I possessed at Herlans and Tavers, at Haimetines, and the church of Marcha, as well as whatever I held at Francons-Court, Formale, and Roteleirs, to supplement the prebend of ten clerics whom I added to the twenty canons whom I found there.

The witnesses to this matter are: Lanzo, provost of Saint Lambert; Rotbert, archdeacon; Goisbert and John, prebendaries; Rotgerus; Asculphus; Theodericus; Bavo; and Onulfus. From the clerics of Saint Bartholomew: Erpo, provost [Col. 0766A]; Ailulfus, dean; Bernardus; Gozechinus; and many others. From the free men: Count Gozelo, who is also advocate; Count A. of Namur; the counts of Los, Emmo, and Otto. From the church household: Mainerus, Warnaeus, Fastradus, Adelinus, Lambertus, Wolbertus, and Godefridus.

This was enacted in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1046, indiction XIV, while Emperor Henry was reigning, Gozelo was duke, I, Wazo, was bishop, Gozelin was advocate of the place, Erpo was provost, and Ailulfus was dean.

# IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1048. ODORANNUS, MONK OF SAINT PETER THE VIGIL

[Col. 0765]

# HISTORICAL NOTICE ON ODORANNUS

*(Hist. litt. de la France, VII, 356.)*

[Col. 0765B]

Odorannus, whom Baronius [*Annals*, year 986, p. 856] makes to have flourished as early as 986, was not born until the preceding year [Odorannus, *Chronicle*, pp. 636, 638, 639]. He was still young when he embraced the monastic profession at Saint Peter the Vigil in Sens. There he found all the assistance necessary for a sound education. Archbishop Seguin, having restored this monastery several years before his death, which occurred in 999, had appointed Rainard as abbot. A man of great merit, Rainard successfully worked to revive exact discipline there, established a library, renewed the good studies, and personally took care to teach letters.

It was under this capable master that Odorannus studied, together with other pupils of great promise, the best known of whom was Thierry, nephew of Abbot Rainard and later bishop of Orléans [Robertus of Auxerre, *Chronicle*, p. 74; *Spicilegium*, vol. II, p. 740]. Through the penetration of his mind and his application to work, Odorannus made all the progress that his age could permit. He also acquired knowledge of the liberal arts, especially goldsmithing and mechanics. All this combined to make him a celebrated man who was useful to his monastery, to which he brought great advantages. He made there a Christ attached to the cross and a well, works regarded as worthy of being known by posterity [Odorannus, *Chronicle*, under the year 1031; Robert of Auxerre, cited above].

This kind of work occupied only a small part of Odorannus’s time [Col. 0765D]. His principal application was the study of the great truths of religion [Mabillon, *Annals*, book LV, no. 4].

Nevertheless, he experienced what sometimes happens to solitary men who love retreat and lead a serious and holy life in the company of persons of an entirely opposite disposition. Odorannus found false brothers of this character at Saint Peter the Vigil. His conduct became hateful to them because it was a living censure of their own. Consequently he was hated, insulted, slandered, and treated as a heretical anthropomorphite [Odorannus, *Chronicle*, cited above]. Matters were pushed to the point that, despite his just defenses, he found himself in danger of losing his life. He escaped only by yielding to violence and decided to withdraw to Saint-Denis near Paris. This occurred in 1022 or 1023; some time later he returned to his first monastery, where he was received with great honors [Col. 0766C].

His skill in the fine arts was so well known that in 1028 King Robert and Queen Constance, wishing to execute the design of a reliquary which the queen had vowed in 1016 to give for enclosing the relics of Saint Savinian, chose Odorannus for this pious work [Mabillon, cited above, book LVI, no. 44]. They summoned him to Dreux, where the court was then located, and gave him their orders for receiving the gold, silver, and precious stones necessary for the undertaking. Odorannus carried out the commission so perfectly, to the king’s satisfaction, that the prince entrusted him with another reliquary for Saint Potentian [Odorannus, *Chronicle*, cited above] and had the appropriate weight of silver provided for its execution [Col. 0766D].

The other events of the life of this illustrious monk are unknown. We know only [*Chronicle*, beginning] that he was still alive in 1045 [Col. 0767A] and that he was then only sixty years old.

From what Odorannus himself tells us [cited above] about his writings in general, it appears that there was a collection containing a certain number of them. Nevertheless, only the following are known.

1. He left a *Chronicle* of his own composition, beginning in 675 and ending in 1032. Besides passing over many years in silence, without recording any event, the author is very concise even for those years in which he does report events. He explains himself with appropriate fullness almost only concerning the years 999, 1031, and 1032.

What he says about the penultimate of these years, concerning the execution of Queen Constance’s planned reliquary, which has been mentioned, is repeated from the history of the translation of Saint Savinian’s relics. That history seems to have preceded the end of the *Chronicle*. This passage, which fills more than two folio pages, forms chapters 26 and the two following chapters of that history and brings it to an end. The *Chronicle* also nearly ends at this point. Only four verses follow, in which the author asks God for mercy for King Robert, whose death he had previously recorded, and commends himself to Saint Peter and Saint Savinian.

Then comes what he says about the year 1032, where he tells us that he had enriched with gold and silver the upper part of the reliquary of Saint Sanucian and Saint Beata, his sister.

[Col. 0767C]

Baronius and Father Le Cointe [Baronius, year 875, pp. 512–513; Le Cointe, year 704, nos. 8–14] show clearly enough that Odorannus’s chronology is anything but exact and that he confused certain events when reporting them. These defects were copied for the most part by Clarius, another monk of Saint Peter the Vigil, in the periods for which he followed Odorannus his fellow monk. Robert, monk of Saint-Marien at Auxerre, warns that he too drew from our chronicler [*Chronicle*, p. 74, 2].

Pithou had already published part of Odorannus’s writing when du Chesne published it more fully from a manuscript belonging to Alexandre Petau. It is impossible to say precisely why this *Chronicle* does not carry the history beyond 1032. Nevertheless, as is certain and as one reads at its head, its author lived at least until 1045 [Col. 0767D].

2. Dom Mabillon printed the history of the translation of Saint Savinian, of which a word has been said [*Acts*, vol. VIII, pp. 254–266], and accompanied it with preliminary observations in which he gives very plausible reasons for showing that it belongs to Odorannus. The way in which the author speaks there of Archbishop Leoteric proves that he wrote it before 1032, the year of that prelate’s death.

On this basis we have maintained that the portion read in the *Chronicle* of the same writer was detached from it, rather than transferred from the *Chronicle* into the *History*. Odorannus begins this second work by going back to the episcopate of Archbishop Wenilo in the ninth century. He included everything he knew concerning the discovery and the various translations of the holy martyrs Savinian and Potentian, together with accounts of the miracles that accompanied and followed them. He ends it with the transfer of the relics of Saint Savinian from the lead reliquary in which they had previously been kept into the one that Queen Constance had made under Odorannus’s own direction.

What makes this work more interesting are various details that it contains concerning the history of the archbishops of Sens and the abbots of Saint Peter the Vigil.

3. The slanders with which Odorannus found himself burdened led him to write an apologetic letter in order to justify himself. Dom Mabillon published its beginning from a manuscript of the cathedral of Orléans, where the continuation is missing [*Annals*, book LV, no. 4]. It is addressed to the scholasticus of the same church, to Aycfroi, abbot of Saint-Avitus, and to Hugh, archdeacon of the church of Sens.

[Col. 0768C]

4. In this letter Odorannus mentions another work that he had been obliged to publish on the same subject, entitled *Complaint*, or *Lamentation*: *in lamentatione mea*.

If the title of manuscript 1625 of the Vatican Library, among the manuscripts formerly belonging to the Queen of Sweden, is as genuine as it is plausible, one would find these two letters of Odorannus there [Montfaucon, *Bibliotheca*, bibliography, p. 51, 2]. At least, he announces them together with his *Chronicle* and other minor works.

[Note: These minor works, recently published by the most eminent Cardinal Mai, we have reprinted after Odorannus’s *Chronicle*. Editor of the *Patrologia*.]

5. Manuscript 167 of the library of Saint-Germain in Paris presents us with another work by the monk Odorannus, concerning the origin of the abbey of Saint Peter the Vigil. He attributes its foundation to Queen Theodechild, or Theudechild, daughter of Thierry, king of Austrasia, who married a foreign king. But it appears that this work is of very little substance, since Dom Mabillon did not consider it worthwhile to make any use of it in his history of the foundation of this monastery [Mabillon, cited above, book II, no. 29].

[Col. 0769]

# CHRONICLE OF ODORANNUS, MONK OF SAINT PETER THE VIGIL OF SENS

Which, already sixty years old, he collected together with his other minor works into a single volume in the year 1045.

[In Duchesne, *Writers of the History of the Franks*, vol. II, p. 636.]

[Col. 0769A]

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 675, Saint Emmo, archbishop of Sens, died. In the time of King Chlotar and his mother Balthild, he synodally granted the monks of Saint Peter, together with the provincial bishops, the privilege of freedom.

In the year 688, Pippin the Austrasian assumed the chief authority over the Franks as mayor of the palace. In his time Saint Vulfrannus, archbishop of Sens, began to preach in Frisia.

In the year 712, the elder Pippin died; and his son, called Charles Martel, usurped the chief authority.

In the year 721, Bede the priest, historian of the English, died.

In the year 741, Saint Vulfrannus departed to the Lord [Col. 0769B], and Prince Charles died. After his death, his sons Carloman and Pippin assumed the chief authority.

In the year 750, Pippin, small in stature, was elected king, and Childeric, who remained from the line of King Clovis, was tonsured. Here the kingdom of Clovis came to an end. At this time the most holy Ebbo, archbishop of Sens, departed to the Lord and was buried in the monastery of the holy apostle Peter, where he shines to the present day through glorious miracles.

In the year 764, King Pippin died, and his sons Charles, called the Great Emperor, and Carloman were elected to the kingship.

In the year 767, Carloman died.

In the year 804, Alcuin the philosopher, abbot of Saint Martin, died. Alcuin and Charles disputed about philosophy; the book survives.

In the year 814, Charles the Great, emperor, died; and his son Louis, called the Pious, assumed the kingdom of the Franks and the Roman Empire.

In the year 828, Jeremiah, archbishop of Sens, died. He obtained imperial decrees for the holy mother Church of Sens, for the monasteries and cells belonging to it, as protection and defense against all judicial authorities.

In the year 833, Louis the Pious lost the kingdom, and his son Lothar usurped it; in that same year Louis recovered it.

[Col. 0770A]

In the year 840, the emperor Louis the Pious died.

In the year 841, war was waged at Fontenay between King Charles, called the Bald, and Lothar, Louis, and Pippin.

In the year 847, the bodies of the holy martyrs Savinian, Potentian, Altinus, and Eodald were transferred by Archbishop Wenilo into the basilica of Saint Peter, on the eighth day before the Kalends of September.

In the year 865, Wenilo, archbishop of Sens, died. He had anointed Louis, the brother of Charles, king in Burgundy. Egil the abbot succeeded him.

In the year 870, Lord Egil, archbishop, died. He had granted Saint Peter a privilege concerning the altar of the village of Alson. With the permission of the younger Lothar and at the command of the bishop of Trier, he had been taken from that diocese and from the monastery called Promia and appointed abbot by King Charles in the monastery of Flavigny [Col. 0770B]. Later he became archbishop of Sens on account of his merits and rests in the monastery of Saint Peter. After his death, the venerable Ansegisus assumed the bishopric. He anointed Charles the Bald king.

In the year 874, Emperor Charles III, called the Bald, son of Louis the Pious, while making his second journey toward Rome, died on the journey itself on the third day before the Kalends of October, and his son Louis assumed the kingdom. In the time of this Charles, the Capitula were composed at Pontigny by Leo the apocrisiarius.

The holy synod, which was assembled in the name of the Lord, at the summons of Lord John, thrice most blessed universal pope, and by the command of Lord Charles, perpetual Augustus, at the place called Pontigny, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 876, indiction IX, in the thirty-seventh year of the reign of the aforesaid unconquered emperor and the first year of his empire, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of August, established the following chapters, appended below:

## CHAPTER I

When Louis, who governed the rights of the Roman Empire, died, Lord John, thrice most blessed pope, invited Lord Charles, then king, to the thresholds of the holy apostles through Jadericus of Velletri, Formosus of Porto, John of Arles, and Ansegisus of Sens, venerable bishops. He chose him as defender and protector of that Church, crowned him with the imperial diadem, and chose him alone and specially above all others to hold the scepters of the Roman Empire. Obeying his sacred ordinances as duty required, we have all confirmed with common consent what he confirmed.

## CHAPTER II

As Lord Pope John decreed, with the counsel, consent, and joint decision of Lord Charles, the most glorious emperor, perpetual Augustus, he granted Ansegisus, the venerable bishop of Sens, authority to act in his place and bestowed upon him the primacy over Gaul and Germany: to summon synods, to decide canonically whatever necessities might arise, and to refer to his knowledge any matters of greater importance.

We unanimously praise this with every devotion, and decree and sanction that he himself should hold the primacy over Gaul and Germany, and that all his successors should hold it in their own city.

[Col. 0771B]
