In the year 878, Pope John of Rome, coming to Gaul, first arrived by ship at Arles; then, passing through Lyon and other cities, he proceeded as far as the city of Troyes. There he conferred with Louis, the son of Charles, and returned to Italy.

In the year 879, Louis, king of the Burgundians and brother of Charles, died.

In the year 883, Ansegisus, venerable archbishop of Sens, died and was buried in the monastery of Saint Peter. He transferred to the monastery of Saint Peter the bodies of the holy bishops and confessors Leo, Ursicinus, Ambrose, and Agricus; and, bringing from the city of Rome the head of Saint Gregory the Doctor, enclosed in lead, together with the arm of Saint Leo the Doctor, he deposited them in the same monastery for preservation. In his time, the bodies of the holy martyrs Sanctianus and Augustine were transferred from the village called Sanceias by the brothers of the aforementioned place and by its priest, Eodaldus, to the same monastery on the eighth day before the Kalends of July [June 24]. Moreover, after the lord Ansegisus had obtained the primacy of all Gaul and had deserved, by heavenly providence, to be called a second pope, he expelled the Jews from the city of Sens for a specific reason, and also the nuns; and he forbade them, under the threat of anathema, ever again to have a dwelling there in which to remain.

In the year 886, Hludovicus, son of the emperor Charles III, died. In this year, on the second day before the Kalends of December [November 30], the Normans came from Paris to Sens. In the following month of May they returned to Francia, after the archbishop Ewrardus had died and Walterius had been appointed in his place. In that same year he anointed Odo king. The latter granted the monks of Saint Peter a privilege concerning the election of the abbot.

In the year 896, Richard, prince of Burgundy, seized Sens [elsewhere: Sennis] against Walterius the archbishop and Warnerius the count.

In the year 898, King Odo died, and Charles the Simple took possession of the kingdom.

In the year 922, Robert, the prince, was anointed king. In that year, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of July [June 15], a battle took place between Charles and Robert, in which Robert was killed. When Charles, victorious in the battle, was returning from the slaughter, Heribertus, the most wicked of the faithless, met him and, under the pretense of a feigned peace, compelled him to turn aside to a castle called Parrona for the purpose of lodging; thus he captured him by deceit and kept him there. While Charles was being held there, in the year 923 he raised to the kingship Rodulphus, the noble son of Richard, prince of Burgundy, together with Hugh the Great, duke of the Franks, and the Frankish nobles. After Rodulphus had died in the year 935, Hugh the duke summoned Hludovicus, son of the aforementioned Charles, together with the Franks, and, after receiving oaths from Otgiva, his mother, established him in the kingdom.

In the year 954, King Hludovicus died, and his son Lotharius succeeded him in the kingdom.

In the year 956, Hugh the Great, duke, died, and his son Hugh succeeded him in the duchy. Gislebertus, count of Burgundy, also died, and Otho, brother of Duke Hugh, received his office together with his daughter named Leudegarde, by whom he was later made a *pipicus* by Radulphus of Dijon. Robert, count of Troyes, took another daughter, named Werra, in marriage. After Otho’s death, his brother Ainricus succeeded to the duchy of Burgundy.

In the year 986, King Lotharius died, committing his young son Hludovicus, together with the kingdom, to Duke Hugh.

In the year 987, the young King Hludovicus died. He accomplished nothing, and the kingdom was given to Duke Hugh, who was made king by the Franks in that same year. In the same year, his son Robert, a most pious man, was appointed king. Here the kingdom of Charlemagne comes to an end.

In the year 998, King Hugh died, while his son Robert was reigning.

In the year 999, Archbishop Sewinus died. He restored to its former condition the monastery of Saint Peter, whose loss his predecessor, Archbishop Anastasius, had begun to remedy; and there, under strict observance of the rule, he appointed Abbot Rainardus, whose body is also buried in the same monastery. From the city of Rome, through the hands of Pope John, he received the archiepiscopal pallium with which his predecessors had been invested, as well as the primacy of Gaul. He also raised the monastery of Saint Peter of Melun from its foundations, sent monks there, and placed Walterius over them as abbot. He rebuilt from its foundations the mother church of Saint Stephen, which had been destroyed by fire, completed it entirely, and adorned it with bells and ecclesiastical ornaments. Then, together with Milo, bishop of Troyes; Eribertus, bishop of Auxerre; and Roclenus, bishop of Nevers, he dedicated it with the greatest solemnity. On that same day he assigned three altars, by a charter of privilege, for the support of the clerics serving God there. Afterwards, obtaining from Abbot Rainardus and the brothers of the monastery of Saint Peter, by much entreaty, the arm of Saint Pope Leo together with the fingers of Saint Ebo, he adorned them with gold and gems and presented them to that house of God.

In return for these gifts, and for the remedy of his soul, he granted to Saint Peter and his monks perpetual privileges, with the consent and approval of the Roman pope and his fellow bishops: concerning the altar of Saint Sabinianus, which is thirty paces from the monastery crypt; the altar of Saint Sanctianus, which is in the village of Sanceias; the altar of Saint Peter, which is in the village called Alsonus; and the altar of Saint Lupus, which is in the village called Naudus. He also decreed that the abbot of that monastery should sit first after the bishop in an assembly of abbots or clerics, and should hold primacy among the other abbots of that bishopric; but he himself was to conduct himself in such a way as to be worthy of such an honor. He also constructed a panel of gold and silver before the altar of Saint Stephen; a tower was later built before the monastery from it.

In the year 1002, Ainricus, duke of Burgundy, died.

In the year 1003, King Robert besieged Auxerre and ravaged Burgundy.

In the year 1015, King Robert recovered the city of Sens, and Rainardus, abbot of the monastery of Saint Peter, died. He renewed the monastery of Saint Peter from its foundations and completely rebuilt the cloisters of the monastery, together with the buildings belonging to it. He also constructed a golden and silver panel before the altar, made a golden cross with gems, and enriched the same monastery with bells, books, vestments, sacred vessels, and other ecclesiastical ornaments. Moreover, instructing the monks in the regular way of life, he taught them the liberal arts.

In the year 1023, the monk Odorannus, after making the crucifix and the well [Note: Perhaps *pluteum*—“screen” or “lectern”—as in Sidonius, Book II, Letter 9: “grammatical screens/lecterns.”] of the monastery, suffered attacks from false brothers because of his sins, but, by God’s mercy, scarcely escaped death. After spending some time at Saint-Denis, he was returned to his own dwelling with the greatest honor.

In the year 1031, the pious King Robert died. He had been humble, benevolent, and devoted toward God’s saints, and an outstanding lover of all religious observance. Having completed various restorations of churches and adorned the bodies of the saints, he decorated the holy body of Saint Sabinianus with gold, gems, and silver. How this was accomplished must be briefly related.

It happened that, when King Robert was traveling to Rome, Queen Constance remained at Tillo with her little son Hugh. When Queen Berta, whom the king had formerly repudiated on account of consanguinity, learned this, she pursued him, hoping that, with the support of certain courtiers, she might be restored to the royal bed by apostolic decree. Queen Constance, therefore, fearing that she would be removed from the king’s side, was held in indescribable sorrow. One night, overcome by an extraordinary tumult of thoughts on this account, she fell asleep. In a vision there appeared to her a certain man surrounded by indescribable splendor, adorned with angelic white hair, wearing priestly vestments, and holding a pastoral staff in his hand. Terrified by the sight, she asked who he was. He revealed that he was a bishop and that his name was Sabinianus. He also said:

“Be steadfast, Constance, because, by God’s mercy, you have been freed from the sorrow that threatens you.”

Terrified by so splendid a vision, she began in the morning to inquire anxiously of the clerics around her whether there was in those regions a bishop named Sabinianus. When they professed their ignorance, one of them, Theodericus by name, who had been raised in the monastery of Saint Peter and was destined, when the king returned, to become bishop of Orléans, answered on behalf of them all:

“There is, lady, in the monastery of Saint Peter, Sabinianus, the first archbishop of Sens, who, together with his companions, attained the prize of the heavenly kingdom through the triumph of martyrdom. If you devoutly approach the presence of this martyr, know that you will obtain without delay what he promised.”

Rejoicing at the counsel of so great a man, she immediately sought the threshold of Saint Peter together with her son. There she shed tears for a very long time before the body of the blessed martyr, committing herself with all her strength to his faithfulness. Strengthened by her visit to so great a patron, she joyfully returned home. The third day had not yet passed when, suddenly, in the dead of night, the king’s messenger appeared at the door, announcing that the king himself would soon arrive. Restored by God’s guidance to his own dwelling, and so proving the martyr’s promise utterly true, he thereafter loved his wife more than before and determined that, under her authority, all royal rights and everything he appeared to possess should remain.

She, however, by no means forgetting the saint’s promise, began to consider how his body might be adorned with gems and gold—his body, which had long been concealed beneath the earth, enclosed in lead by the ancient fathers. When she presented her wishes to the king, she found him, by God’s help, entirely ready to fulfill them. He therefore summoned Odorannus, a monk of that place who seemed suitable for completing the work, and entrusted this undertaking of such great piety to his care and to the queen’s.

At Sens, they first gave, through the hands of Waldricus the provost, four pounds of pure silver. Then, at Sens, through the hands of Willelmus the chamberlain, fifty-five solidi of pure silver. Afterwards they sent, through the hands of Odo the *paratgius*, thirty-seven solidi of pure silver. They also sent from Paris, through the hands of the monk Odorannus, seventeen solidi and eight denarii of gold, together with extremely precious gems.

Since these things have been accomplished, it remains for us to make known to Christ’s faithful the wonders of God that we saw with our own eyes in the construction of this work and partly touched with our own hands. To conceal them in silence would be to commit a crime.

The king, occupied with various worldly cares, therefore postponed for a while sending to the monastery the funds collected for the work already begun. When he had found peace of mind, he sent word through the aforementioned brother Francolinus that he should come quickly to Druis to receive the materials for the work. After completing the evening office and receiving, as is customary among monks, the abbot’s blessing, he set out for the heights of the castle of Druis.

After sunset he came to the harbor of Saint Columba and crossed the river Yonne with his companions. When he had paused briefly on the bank, he saw, among the other stars that illuminated the night, a certain star rising at the point where, in summer, the sun usually indicates the first hour of the day. Leaping from the place of its rising, by divine power it began to move swiftly through the air toward the higher regions of heaven, almost to the point where at that season the sixth hour usually occurs.

When his servant, with the horse prepared for him to mount, urged him to climb on because night was approaching, he said:

“Wait for me a little, and look with your companion upon the wonders of God, which until now I have not seen.”

Struck with astonishment by this miracle, the servants, not knowing what portent the sign concealed, armed themselves with the sign of the cross and, filled with fear, entrusted themselves wholeheartedly to God and Saint Sabinianus. The star remained for a little while at the place to which it had come; then, moving backward, it returned within the space of an hour to the place from which it had come. They watched it almost until the third watch of the night, and then saw it joyfully complete its customary course among the other stars, discussing among themselves what it might signify.

It occurred to them that they would complete the journey they had begun with favorable progress and, having attained their wish, would return swiftly home. Applying themselves more eagerly to the labor of the journey, they passed through the desolate Belsa and, as he rose from the table, reached the king’s palace.

After first greeting the king and queen, so that the star’s omens might prove completely true, the queen said to the monk:

“Receive the gifts we have arranged, as far as we are able, to send at present to Saint Sabinianus, and return quickly home, because we have decided to leave early tomorrow for elsewhere.”

Then, immediately producing thirteen gold solidi weighed according to the public Orléans standard, she said:

“If the weight of the coinage does not satisfy you, let repeated weighing provide confirmation to your own eyes.”

When it had been weighed, nothing was found except exactly what the queen had stated. The monk therefore returned to the monastery, having obtained what he desired. After conveying the king’s and queen’s greetings to the abbot and brothers, he brought forth the gift of refined gold sent to Saint Sabinianus from the purse.

It was publicly weighed, and, when the balance was applied by Francolinus the doorkeeper and Raimbertus the king’s cellarer, it was found to contain seven denarii more. The brother who had carried it was astonished, as were the others who witnessed it, and they understood with certainty that he who had deigned to show a miracle by changing the star during their journey, and who had made the whole world from nothing, had granted that the refined gold in the faithful purse should increase, in the number sevenfold, through the merit of the martyr.

He who, through the intercession of Elisha, caused the oil to overflow in order to redeem the widow’s sons had made the small gift of gold immense through the devotion of the king and queen. And God, the Head of Christ, who said through his prophet, “The silver is mine and the gold is mine,” owns whatever is bestowed upon his members—that is, his holy martyrs—and it belongs to no other.

Afterwards, at Sens, the king gave through the hands of the monk Odorannus eight ounces of gold and fifteen solidi of pure silver. In completing the work, so that frequent demands for gold and silver would not become a burden to the king, five ounces of gold and three pounds of pure silver were added from the Church’s treasury.

Having described the materials of this work, most worthy of God, it is worthwhile to record the miracle of the goose’s ploughshare, which God’s omnipotence deigned to accomplish in our presence during the translation of the holy martyr. The desired feast day was approaching—the day on which, by the ancient fathers, his venerable body, together with those of his companions, had been transferred to the basilica of Saint Peter. The king had remained for a while at Sens and was preparing to return to Paris.

He therefore summoned Archbishop Leothericus and humbly asked him to visit the monastery and transfer the body of the holy martyr from the leaden container in which it had been placed by the ancient fathers into the golden chest that he had prepared for it. On the Friday preceding the Sunday on which the feast was to be celebrated, Leothericus came to the monastery with the greatest reverence and, together with the brothers, fulfilled the king’s instructions. He placed the body of Saint Eodaldus, which he found there with it, together with the body of Saint Sabinianus; he also replaced the bones of a little child buried with them. After completing the solemn masses, he departed to eat.

The brother under whose direction and care the construction of the entire work proceeded was seated in the monastery choir, warming with soft wax the silver images that he had arranged to be placed upon the cover of the chest. Suddenly, led by a little boy, a certain blind man appeared, asking to be admitted into the crypt where the body of Saint Sabinianus had been placed.

When the monk asked who he was, where he came from, and for what purpose he had arrived, he declared that he was a peasant who had a dwelling in the Wastin district, in a village called Fontanas, and that his own name was Mainardus. He had been warned in a dream the previous night to come into the presence of Saint Sabinianus and receive the light of his eyes there. He had been blind for three years.

He was admitted to the saint and prayed for a long time, but on that very day he was not granted any light. Nevertheless, filled, as he himself said, with an exceedingly sweet fragrance, he returned home.

When Sunday arrived, the king came with his bishops and nobles, as well as with abbots, clerics, and an innumerable crowd, to transport the body of the holy martyr. Together with his son Robert, he received it and carried it with his own shoulders and hands, placing it where the faithful venerate it at the present time.

After the solemn office had been completed and the king had reclined at table while the monks were eating, the monk so often mentioned was sitting there—the same place where the blind man mentioned above had found him sitting the day before yesterday. Guided by God’s will, the blind man came again, led by the little boy, and said that he had once more been warned in a dream to seek the help of Saint Sabinianus as quickly as possible.

Throwing himself face down before the saint’s presence, he recovered his sight through the support of the saint’s merits. The child who had hitherto led him was now led by him, and the boy returned to the house.

The king, rising from the table for the sake of prayer, as was his custom, remained alone in the church. As he was praying, the aforementioned brother happened to enter the church. Seeing him from a distance, the king calmly beckoned to him to come nearer.

“Tell me,” he said, “what Saint Potentianus was to Saint Sabinianus.”

The brother humbly replied that he had been his companion in the labor of his journey, his successor in honor, and his fellow martyr.

Then the king began to lament bitterly and beat his breast with his fists because he had separated them bodily from one another. Promising that he would restore him to his companion, he entrusted thirty-three solidi of pure silver to that same brother, so that he might begin preparing the shrine of Saint Potentianus.

But while he was attempting to carry this out, he was overtaken by a heavenly summons and rendered to God the debt owed by our father Adam.

May God, merciful, pious, and benevolent, have mercy upon him.

And join him to the saints, almighty Lord.

Peter, may you always remember your servant Odorannus.

Powerful Sabinianus, look mercifully upon Odorannus.

In the year 1032, Archbishop Leothericus died. He gave Saint Peter the village called Arcia, together with two churches, namely those of Saint Michael and Saint Mary, and that of Saint Ebo together with its dependencies. He also gave the land of Tillido, which yielded two solidi in rent.

Through the hands of Pope Gerbertus, also called Sylvester, he received the archiepiscopal pallium at Rome and, through his staff, also received the primacy of Gaul. In his time, the body of Saint Beata, sister of Saint Sanucianus, which had been secretly transferred with him by the canon Heribertus with insufficient care, was more suitably placed together with his body by the monk Odorannus. The top of their shrine was adorned with gold and silver, which Odorannus had acquired, so to speak, by his own labor.

As for how or by whom the body of Saint Serotinus, disciple of Saint Sabinianus, was brought to the monastery of Saint Peter, let the diligent reader not suppose that its omission from the present chapter is due to our negligence, but rather to our ignorance. We know with certainty, moreover, that the basilica in which he first lay was overthrown and utterly destroyed by the Northmen. His body, however, transferred to the monastery of Saint Peter, rests there in peace and, shining with miracles, obtains from God what is necessary for those who devoutly ask.

# History of the Translation of the Holy Martyrs Sabinianus, Potentianus, and Their Companions to the Monastery of Saint Peter at Sens

By Odorannus, monk of Saint Peter the Living.

(From Mabillon, *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, based on a manuscript from Saint-Marien at Auxerre.)

## Preliminary Observations

### 1

No one doubts that Sabinianus, together with Potentianus and their companions, brought the Christian faith to Sens, and that they suffered martyrdom there and received burial. A church was built over their tombs. From its crypts, according to Odorannus, a monk of Saint Peter the Living, “in the year 847 the bodies of the holy martyrs Sabinianus, Potentianus, Altinus, and Eodaldus were transferred by Archbishop Wenilo to the basilica of Saint Peter on the eighth day before the Kalends of September [August 25].”

Clarius agrees with Odorannus in his *Chronicle*, in these words:

“The holy martyrs of Christ, Sabinianus, Potentianus, Altinus, Eodaldus, and Serotinus revealed themselves to Archbishop Wenilo and Abbot Anastasius. They raised them with great honor from the church where they had been buried and transferred them to the basilica of blessed Peter on the eighth day before the Kalends of September,”

“at which time angelic voices were heard in heaven.”

### 2

In the same year in which “Hludovicus, son of Charles the Simple, was anointed king at Laon,” Clarius continues:

“The Hungarians [lacuna], arriving at Sens, set fire to the monastery of Saint Peter and ravaged the entire region. Seeing this great evil, Abbot Sanson and the monks, after taking counsel, carried the bodies of the saints Sabinianus and Potentianus, together with the other holy bodies and the relics, with great honor into a church of that abbey constructed within the city walls in honor of Saint Peter. The body of Saint Serotinus, however, was left in the crypt behind the altar of Saint Peter.

“After ravaging the entire region, the pagans returned home, having burned the monastery of Saint Peter. Only the oratory of Saint Serotinus remained there, which they were unable to burn. But how Archbishop Willelmus wished to retain the bodies of these saints, and how he returned them, you will find more fully in the little book on the miracles of Saint Sabinianus.”

This little book is precisely the history that we present here.

### 3

Around the year 1015, Leothericus, archbishop of Sens, together with “Abbot Rainardus began to investigate where the bodies of the saints Sabinianus and Potentianus had been hidden. From the time of Archbishop Willelmus they had been concealed in caves out of fear of the pagans. Having found them through the information of a certain old man named Martinus, a servant of that place, they carefully placed them in leaden containers, while the power of the Lord performed many miracles there.”

[Note: [Col. 0779D; Col. 0779] This note appears at the foot of columns 779 and 780, but the callout number (3) has not been printed in the text.]

The leaden containers in which the bodies of the saints were placed are mentioned in these acts, and there is no doubt that Clarius drew his account from them.

#### Cited Fragment

The cited fragment reads as follows:

### Concerning the Translation of Saint Potentianus to the Monastery of Jouarre

In the year 847, at Sens, the holy martyrs of Christ Sabinianus, Potentianus, Altinus, Eodaldus, and Serotinus revealed themselves to Archbishop Wenilo and Abbot Anastasius, namely the abbot of the monastery of Saint Peter. They raised them with great honor from the church where they had been buried and transferred them to the basilica of blessed Peter on the eighth day before the Kalends of September [August 25]. This is found in Clarius, a monk, in the *Chronicle of Saint Peter the Living*.

Then it happened—as I read in certain notes concerning the translation of Saint Potentianus to the Jouarre convent—that the fame of his miracles, spreading far and wide, finally reached the ears of the nuns of that monastery. They had been worn down by prolonged afflictions, by storms and famine, while human help failed, and they awaited divine assistance alone.

At that time Wenilo was bishop of Sens, a man of supreme holiness and religious observance. In the monastery mentioned above, Hermentrudis, both in character and in name, presided as abbess; she was closely related to the same bishop. Partly compelled by necessity and partly encouraged by confidence in their kinship, she approached the bishop and begged him not to delay assisting her and her congregation, who were in the greatest distress, through his own intercession and that of the celebrated Saint Potentianus—that is, by granting them relics.

The bishop initially resisted. But at last, by God’s mercy and because of her excessive persistence, the abbess obtained what she asked. The holy and incomparable treasure was quickly given and carried to the place mentioned above, which was weighed down by misery and deprived of every consolation. After the congregation received it with great rejoicing and placed it in the monastery with the reverence and devotion that were fitting, that place thereafter suffered neither scarcity of food nor any storm of bad weather.

### 4

Finally, according to the same author, in the year 1020:

“Lord Ermenaldus succeeded Abbot Ingo. During his time King Robert and Queen Constance made for Saint Sabinianus a shrine adorned with gold, silver, and precious gems. In it they also placed with him the body of Saint Eodaldus, together with the bones of a little child buried with them in the leaden container in which they had previously been kept. During this translation a certain blind man received his sight; and rain, which had not fallen since the Lord’s Easter, descended abundantly. This translation took place on the eighth day before the Kalends of September [August 25].”

Thus far Clarius. His account agrees with that of our author, except that the final words of the history seem to suggest that these events occurred toward the end of Robert’s life. Both authors, moreover, silently pass over the relics of Saint Potentianus granted by Archbishop Wenilo to Hermentrudis, abbess of Jouarre.

Nevertheless, this is how the matter stood, if credence is given to the fragment published by us in Part II of the fourth century, p. 578 [Note: This note is absent from Migne’s printed edition.]. Since we have heard that some people accept it in the less favorable sense, we have thought it appropriate to examine it more carefully.

### 5

No one who has read the author just cited, as well as the chronicles of Odorannus and the monk of Auxerre, should imagine that the entire body of Saint Potentianus was given by Wenilo to Hermentrudis, abbess of Jouarre. Nor does the fragment cited above say this. It says only that Hermentrudis earnestly requested from Wenilo the celebrated intercession of Saint Potentianus, obtained it with difficulty, and that the holy and incomparable treasure was carried to her monastery.

We have never intended these words to designate the translation of the entire body of Saint Potentianus, but only of some portion of the saintly bishop’s relics. Besides the fragment cited above, certain ancient records also prove that some of this saint’s relics were granted to the nuns of Jouarre.

The first evidence is found in the following words of the Auxerre manuscript, which testify that the martyr’s relics were brought to Jouarre in Burgundy around the year 886:

“But when, some time afterward, the pagans occupied this monastery of Jouarre, two of the nuns related to the aforementioned abbess Hermentrudis, escaping the imminent danger, fled for protection to their father, a man named Norgaldus, a most noble and excellent man in Burgundy, who shortly afterward rendered his soul happily to God.

“The nuns themselves daily recounted to their mother Rothaida and to their brothers Agembertus, Samuel, and Algaudus the many miracles that almighty God deigned to perform through the merits of the most holy Potentianus. They were so inflamed by the remarkable fire of devotion that they thought continually, day and night, about obtaining such a precious treasure for themselves.

“Therefore Samuel and Algaudus went to the monastery of Jouarre and conducted the affair with such skill that they obtained from Gisla, at that time the most noble abbess of that place, the long-desired gift. Having immediately attained their wish, they carried it with the greatest honor and reverence to the monastery that had been constructed for the most holy bishop in the village of Lucy.”

Thus far the Auxerre manuscript, whose text we reproduce here—not because we wish to champion the case of the people of Lucy against the people of Sens or Jouarre, but so that the evidence for the grant made to Jouarre may be brought to light.

### 6

Another argument is drawn from the lawsuit that arose in the thirteenth century between the nuns of Jouarre and the monks of Saint Peter the Living at Sens. This dispute gave rise to a new translation of blessed Potentianus, who rested at Saint Peter.

Gautridus of Colone, a monk of Saint Peter the Living, records the dispute both in his chronological tables and in a manuscript booklet, *On the Sacred Relics of the Monastery of Saint Peter the Living*. The ascetics of that place preserve the booklet, written in an excellent hand, together with a series of abbots extending to the year 1289.

Gaufridus’s words occur in the chronological tables:

“In the year 1218, in the monastery of Saint Peter the Living, almost all the body of Saint Potentianus was displayed—this word ‘almost’ is worthy of note—in the presence of the reverend fathers Peter, archbishop of Sens; Herveus, bishop of Troyes; and certain other prelates, bishops, and abbots.

“The nuns of Jouarre said that they possessed the body of blessed Potentianus. But on that day, namely the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May [April 17], the aforementioned fathers found the contrary. For they found the aforesaid body of Saint Potentianus in the monastery of Saint Peter the Living beneath the high altar, behind and below the altar, and they established the matter fully through written testimonies to which complete credence had to be given.

“They transferred the aforesaid body together with the body of Saint Altinus onto the high altar, placing the relics in a silver chest. They granted great indulgences for eight days after the feast to all pilgrims who came to the feast of this translation, as is contained in the documents issued concerning it.”

Gaufridus himself relates almost the same thing in the aforementioned booklet on the relics. It is sufficient to excerpt this passage:

“The aforesaid body of Saint Potentianus was displayed above the abbey gate and in the church, together with written testimonies to which complete credence had to be given, because the nuns of Jouarre said that it was preserved in their monastery. But on that day the contrary was proved, as is contained in the books concerning the monastery of Saint Peter.”

We shall present below the letters of Archbishop Peter and the other prelates. For the present, the translations of all the relics resting in the monastery of Saint Peter must, insofar as possible, be supplied with chronological notes.

### 7

In the year 847, the first discovery of the relics took place under Bishop Wenilo. Shortly afterward he granted the people of Jouarre some relics of Saint Potentianus. In the year 936, the bodies of the same martyrs were brought into the city of Sens out of fear of the Northmen. After Archbishop Willelmus yielded, they were restored not long afterward to their former seat and carefully concealed in caves dug for this purpose.

While the sacred relics were being returned, Bernardus, archclerk of Saint Mary, seized from the unwilling monks a portion cut from Saint Sabinianus’s pallium; it was thereafter preserved in the cathedral church. Around the year 1015, the bodies of the saints were inspected in the caves, and Leothericus, the bishop, with the assistance of Abbot Rainardus, enclosed them in leaden containers.

After the year 1025, with Robert and Constance providing assistance, the body of Saint Sabinianus was raised and, together with the body of Saint Eodaldus and also the body of a certain child, was placed in a richly adorned shrine. According to Clarius, this translation took place on the eighth day before the Kalends of September [August 25]. King Robert intended to grant the same honor to the relics of Saint Potentianus, according to the acts related here, but death prevented him from carrying it out.

In the year 1228, Peter of Corbolium, bishop of Sens, summoned his suffragan bishops and undertook the celebrated translation of the same martyr. In a charter he explained it as follows:

“Peter, by the grace of God archbishop of Sens; Willelmus, by the same grace bishop of Auxerre; Herveus, bishop of Troyes; Willelmus, bishop of Meaux; and Willelmus, bishop of Nevers, to all to whom the present letters shall come, everlasting salvation in the Lord.

“Lest the truth should ever be obscured by a cloud of doubt, we wish it to be known to all present and future that, on the fourth day before the Kalends of August [July 29], in the church of Saint Peter the Living at Sens, the bodies of the blessed martyrs Potentianus and Altinus, companions of the most blessed Sabinianus, archbishop of Sens, were revealed in our presence.

“They were also transferred by our hands into a certain chest on the same day, in the year of the Lord 1218. Trusting in the mercy of Jesus Christ, in that of the blessed Virgin Mary, and in the merits of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul and all the saints, we mercifully remit to all Christ’s faithful who, being truly penitent, charitably offer their alms to the same church, from the octave of Saint Mary Magdalene until the seven days following, in veneration of those same saints: seven days of the penances imposed upon them; broken vows, if they return to them; forgotten sins; and offenses against fathers and mothers, without the laying on of hands.

“In memory of this matter, we have caused this page to be strengthened by the protection of our seals.

“Given in the year of grace 1218, on the third day before the Kalends of August [July 30]. May they endure forever.”

8. These statements are supported by various manuscript codices of the same place, together with Gaufridus Hiron, a monk of Saint Peter, who in 1216 added an appendix to Clarius’s Chronicle. There still exists the autograph copy of Bishop Peter, which, on 19 October 1680, was examined by the visitor of our province of Burgundy. In the year 1449, on 17 December, Louis of Melun, bishop of Sens, ordered Guerin, abbot of Saint Remigius of Sens, Peter, abbot likewise of Saint John of Sens, and James Hodouard, vicar general and official, to undertake a new translation of the body of Saint Potentian; this was celebrated on this day through the agency of William Quatran, abbot of Saint Peter. There exists a rescript of Pope Innocent VIII, issued in 1488, by which he grants the monks of Saint Peter permission to transfer the sacred relics of their monastery. I do not know whether they made use of this before the year 1680, when, by order of our general provost, the visitor of the province of Burgundy placed the bones of blessed Potentian in a new and more suitably adorned reliquary. I have thought it appropriate to present these matters in chronological order. As for the fact that we assign 25 August to this translation, although the narrative placed below specifies no day, we follow Odorannus and Clarius, who assign to this day the translation performed by Wenilo; indeed, Clarius also noted the translation described here under the same day once again. It remains for us to express our judgment concerning the author of this narrative.

9. He appears to be Odorannus, a monk of Saint Peter the Living, famous for the Chronicle published by Chesnius. For, besides the already-mentioned Chronicle, he is said, at the age of sixty, in the year 1045, to have collected other little works of his into a single volume, as its title in the Chronicle indicates—such as the manuscript codex from which it was excerpted undoubtedly bore. The principal reason for attributing the following history to him rather than to someone else is that at least the middle portion of the Chronicle, which includes this translation, is expressed here and there in exactly the same words. This fact clearly indicates that the two works have one and the same author. Moreover, since Odorannus’s Chronicle records nothing later than this history of the translation, if it had another author, Odorannus would have copied the narrative inserted into his Chronicle word for word from him; yet such plagiarism cannot be charged against a sensible man, as he was. Furthermore, Odorannus himself took part in a large portion of this translation: summoned to the court by the king and Queen Constance, he applied his hand to the work. Who, then, could have committed the matter to posterity better than one who had been involved in it? In addition, he speaks of himself in both places in such a way that, for anyone comparing the Chronicle with this History, the same spirit seems to breathe everywhere. The only exception is that here he occasionally turns aside into commonplaces, which, since they have no flavor, I thought best to cut away. Let the author himself now speak, whoever he may be. We owe his book, drawn from the library of Saint Marian, to the religious man Jean-Baptiste Oudinet, prior of that place and of the Premonstratensian order.

## HERE BEGINS THE HISTORY OF THE TRANSLATION

### Chapter I. The translation of Saints Savinian and Potentian and their companions

The most holy bodies of the blessed martyrs—namely Savinian and Potentian and their companions—were therefore faithfully buried by the hands of the faithful in a suitable place within that same church of the Lord Savior, except for the venerable body of the martyr Serotinus, which was suitably buried by his relatives separately in another basilica.

When their ashes had rested in their place for many years, it was divinely made known to Wenilo, the most prudent bishop of the people of Sens, and to Anastasius, abbot of the monastery of the holy apostle Peter, so that more diligent worship and reverence might be shown them by the people. With the pure resolve of an uplifted heart, they summoned thousands of people of both sexes and hastened to transfer them to the nearby basilica of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles—for they had until then lain before its doors and on its grounds. That church was higher in the summit of its house and buildings and more celebrated for divine services, especially since the care of the monks dwelling there regularly persevered in solemn vows and constant meditations.

The festival of this translation was held at the time when three illustrious princes, descendants of the emperor Louis of august memory, ruled under the most noble scepters of the Franks: Lothair, and likewise Louis and Charles. It was also in the sixth year of their reign, in the year 847 from the Incarnation of Christ, in the seventh indiction, on 19 October.

[Note: These chronological indications do not agree with one another. This may be excused in an author writing approximately two hundred years later, unless the error arose through the carelessness of copyists.]

### Chapter II. How, during the festival of their translation, angelic voices were heard from heaven

Nor must we pass over in silence the fact that, on the night of the vigils, on the following day of which their venerable relics were to be transported, angelic voices resounded from the stars in human ears, as though choirs were singing psalms.

The bishop had gone there in the evening, together with a large gathering of the clergy, to celebrate the solemn vigils. When these had been devoutly completed and the bishop had returned to the city, heavenly rites continued throughout the night. It is evident that not only the monks but also some of the common people keeping vigil there perceived the harmony of this melody.

In truth, they supposed that these voices were human and thought that various religious men were converging on the monastery for the impending festival and were producing such a joyful sound. Then, again astonished that they should hasten their arrival during the silence of the untimely night, they took care to send scouts all around to discover whose vigil it might be. But when those sent out had searched the neighboring places and found no one, while nevertheless hearing the sweetness of the melody without interruption, they realized that it was the solemn rite of a heavenly office.

Here it was shown by a clear sign that the company of angels wished to be present at their solemnities with devoted favor. They had learned that these saints had vigorously obeyed the commands of the Almighty; therefore the angels hastened to share in their deeds and unfailing joys, having seen that they had devoted themselves to the best pursuits with ineffable rejoicing.

From that time onward the aforesaid basilica possesses the bodies of the devout martyrs, whose spirits are held in the delights of paradise, participants in eternal recompense. The city of Sens rejoices temporarily in the profit of such great Fathers, for whose rejoicing the heavenly Jerusalem exults forever. The people frequently gather at their tombs to offer prayers and vows, because through their intercession the weaknesses of the limbs are restored by the relief of health, and the strength of hearts is nourished by perpetual banquets.

### Chapter III. Concerning the cloak and head of Saint Savinian the martyr

When, as indicated above, the body of this precious martyr Savinian was reverently turned over in preparation for its removal from the leaden place—or, in other words, for its translation—the cloak in which it had been wrapped was found to be entirely intact, as though new, although many years had passed. But his head, which is the glory of this country of ours, appeared as though it had been crushed by leaden blows on its right side at some former time [the Latin reading is uncertain].

The two wounds made by sword-strokes are still so bloody that the blows themselves seem recent, so that those who look upon them can scarcely do so without a flood of tears. That this same bishop truly received the crown of martyrdom is attested to him even today by the holy and venerable head, and by the blood that still appears fresh at the wound in that head.

Moreover, the discovery of the bodies of the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, which was made by Saint Ambrose, bishop of Milan—as that blessed man himself wrote with his own hand—relates that they too were found in marble sarcophagi drenched in fresh blood, as though their heads had been cut off with a sword on that very day.

But the head of our martyr was struck by three sword-blows: two remain bloody with gore to the present day; the third, which is thought to have inflicted the glorious death, contains no bloody gore.

### Chapter IV. Concerning the blind man who was given sight there

A certain blind man came to so great a solemnity with the rest of the people, and experienced the martyr’s power in receiving his sight. He prayed that Christ might show through this witness how great the man’s merit was in His sight, and, if what was being done pleased Him, might declare it through the miracles by which he had always shone.

The blind man’s eyes poured forth tears, and the lights of faith rose in the sharpness of his mind. His humble supplication penetrated heaven and inclined the face of the Godhead toward mercy. The undefeated soldier implored his commander and acted so that even now he might receive the reward of military service. He displayed his wounds, recounted his labors, reviewed the number of his sweat-filled exertions, and showed how much was owed him for these things.

Those near the blind man joined him in prayer, and what he could not obtain by himself he earned through the offering of their tears. From heaven a hidden medicine was sent down, and the affliction of his eyes was removed by the hand of compassion. The blind man, now seeing, looked upon his companions and marveled that he possessed what he had shortly before despaired of having.

The clemency of the Savior was praised together with him; the people rejoiced in the man’s recovery; reverence for the martyr was increased and spread. Such things made this distinguished day solemn for the people living nearby.

### Chapter V. Concerning the lamp that was accustomed to burn before his body as if of its own accord

It should not seem absurd to relate something about the lamp that was accustomed to burn day and night before his sacred body, and before the bodies of countless other saints of ours in the crypt, which is built of revolving stones and suitably strengthened by arches, as the testimony of those who saw it declares.

It often happens that, through the custodian’s laziness, the lamp’s light fails and goes out, and then suddenly, once lit again, it gives forth brilliant flames. It is said not merely to emit a very bright light for one hour or one day, but to drive away the darkness for three days and as many nights.

This lamp of the saints is therefore often kindled by divine power; and without any oil being poured into it, the rush-wick emits a very bright light, so that it shines more brightly than the other lamps which human hands light by pouring on oil, moistening the wick with liquid and applying fire beneath it, and so forth.

One of our brothers, whose face and name we know but whom here, out of consideration for him, we have not identified by name, once blew out the lights of that same lamp three times, for a necessary reason, as we have said. Each time it received back the light of its brightness by divine power, so that heavenly divinity supplied a greater illumination than the brother’s negligence had extinguished, and so forth.

### Chapter VI. Concerning the drought and the sending of rain, and concerning the fragrance at the translation of Saint Savinian

I think that I should commit to the memory of future generations in a few words the most merciful compassion of God, which the gracious ruler of God granted us, in view of the condition of our region, through the merits of the most holy martyr Savinian.

From the Lord’s Easter—the solemnity of solemnities and the glory and ornament of all Christians—not a drop of rain had fallen from heaven, and the soil, split by frequent cracks, was withering up to the day of his translation. Therefore, on the day when the body of the aforementioned martyr was lifted from the ancient place of its own rest, an abundant quantity of rain descended, and the earth was relieved of its drought.

It is now plainly understood that God, through Savinian the martyr, pleasing to Him by his merits, looked upon the humility of His poor and fully relieved the afflicted homeland, suffering from scarcity of rain, by an inundation of falling drops, and so forth.

### Chapter VII. Concerning the fragrance at his translation

As the distinguished doctor Paul says, “We are the good odor of Christ to God in every place,” so this precious martyr, while alive, was not only filled with a good fragrance—namely, he gave off the aroma of savory preaching and was wonderfully famous for miracles—but also exuded a marvelous fragrance at the translation of his body.

For the whole monastery was so completely filled with the sweetest fragrance that it seemed as though every kind of spice and all sorts of balsam had been present there. For fifteen days, indeed, the nostrils of everyone entering within the monastery’s enclosure were filled with fragrant sweetness, just as on the first day of his translation, and so forth.

Indeed, the bodies and clothing of the two priest-monks who were privileged to lift the holy body from the leaden place and place it in the chest where it is now kept continued for many days to give off such a fragrance that they seemed to be drenched in a nectar-like perfume, and so forth.

### Chapter VIII. Concerning the frequent appearance of the inner and outer custodians

Frequent visitation, constant protection, and manifest revelation are known to have occurred at this place of ours, as related by the custodians who were ordered to keep watch over this church.

Often, at the deep hour of night, when most welcome sleep usually overtakes people as they lie sleeping, the terrified custodians, awakened by excessive fear, were deemed worthy, with watchful eyes, of seeing things that mortals are permitted to behold.

For they frequently saw the whole church shining with splendid lights and an innumerable crowd of white-robed people of both sexes—bishops, clerics, laymen, boys, and girls—filling the entire circuit of the church.

On many occasions, the watchmen who are known to keep vigorous guard over this suburb of ours, entrusted with protecting it from the dangers of fire and the ambushes of robbers, appeared to run up while loudly striking the church doors and terrifying the sacristans with reproaches, saying:

“Why do you sleep, weighed down by excessive slumber, oppressed by wine and sleep? Rise, rise, and bring aid as quickly as possible to the sacred lights and the holy pledges of the saints. For, as it most clearly appears to us, the entire church, from its roof down to the lowest foundations, seems to be burning with heavenly fire.”

Then, as the brothers rose from their beds amid the tumult of fear, the visions very often disappeared, and the splendor of the fires, both inwardly for them and outwardly for those watchmen, gradually failed and diminished as they observed it. Fear was removed from both groups in equal measure.

Yet the gentle vision of the saints more often makes the brothers guarding the sacred basilica joyful by bringing them joy, while the fire, as though alive, terrifies those stationed outside. But afterward, when they see that the church has not been burned, they become still more joyful at this marvelous vision.

For just as in ancient times Moses, the giver of the old law, saw a bush burning without being consumed, so they feared that this monastery was on fire; but the fire was not harmful. It was a visitation of angelic power and of the saints, whose vast and indescribable multitude is retained there.

### Chapter IX. Concerning the woman deprived of the use of her feet and healed by the holy martyrs

Moreover, a poor young girl from the town of Melun, named Ingelberta, sought the threshold of the saints together with her mother. She was carried in a cart drawn in front by the strength of a worthless little ass, being entirely deprived of the support of her limbs.

She was supported from door to door by provisions and clothing; her limbs, wasted by corruption, pains, and hunger, were restored by the nourishment given by compassionate people. She was known to everyone for the importunity of her appeals, since she could not live without the aid of many people.

When the opportunity was given, she began deliberately to long for the assistance of the holy martyrs, so that they might bring healing to her weakness. She summoned her mother and said:

“I desire to visit the tombs of the propitious martyr Saint Savinian and of the other saints. I shall not delay, I say, in obtaining through them the desires of my heart.”

Her mother, inflamed by these words, carried out this great hope more readily. Brought before the saints, she humbly bowed her neck and worshiped them with a lowered head, asking them to be present to assist her.

Remaining attached to the pavement for a long time, she perceived that the God of compassion was present through the saints’ intervention. Immediately, healing came, preceded by the enormity of her pain; and help rejoiced the renewed, panting spirit. Her ardent soul was stirred toward many things, and she called her mother, saying:

“Come, joyful mother, you who silently lifted me, terrified, from the ground.”

After God had changed the ugliness of her limbs into the beauty of strength, she, enlightened by the saints’ assistance, ran on an unhindered foot and repeatedly called back to her mother.

The mother hurried after her, unaware of what had happened, and tremblingly searched for the little stools that her daughter had lost.

“With one blow,” said the girl, “health was divinely granted to me.”

A great many people surrounded her, and she looked upright upon the crowd flowing around her and rejoicing with her. For, by the common report of all, she had suddenly obtained health.

The cry of everyone rang out publicly, returning thanks to God, while the patronage of the holy martyrs was in full force.

### Chapter X. Concerning the hostility of the Northmen provoked by the people of Sens

At the time when William held the summit of the archbishopric of Sens, a man vigorous in intelligence and cunning, the people of the Northmen, provoked by the bitter exasperation of the citizens of that city, ravaged the borders and everything nearby in that region with the harsh excess of hostility.

For this people tore the inhabitants apart in a criminal slaughter that inflicted wounds. Terrified by the excessive persistence and savage violence of the persecution, the people from all around fled for protection into the city.

### Chapter XI. Concerning the bringing of the saints’ bodies within the city walls

At that time Charles the Simple was reigning; in Burgundy, Richard, father of King Rudolf, held the duchy. At that time Samson was abbot over the monastery of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, a man adorned with divine uprightness and a lover of sacred religion.

Disturbed by the pressure of the calamity confronting them, he summoned the monks to a most humble council, so that he might obtain sound advice from them. Finally, the common counsel and judgment of them all considered it useful that the bodies of the holy martyrs—namely Savinian, Potentian, Altinus, and Eodald—together with the other holy bodies and relics, should be transferred with the greatest increase of honor into the church of that same abbey, which had been built within the city walls.

The body of the holy martyr Serotinus, however, was left behind and suitably buried in a safer cave of the same place.

When this had been done, the aforementioned bishop deceitfully introduced schemes of rivalry among the monks, saying that it would be more advantageous for the relics of the saints to be carried within the walls of the holy mother Church of Sens, built in honor of Saint Stephen the protomartyr.

At the time, the simplicity of the devout brothers thought that these actions were being undertaken out of concern for holiness; but afterward these words were revealed as flattery.

### Chapter XII. Concerning the siege of the city and the oratory rescued from the fire

When the city had been besieged, it would take many pages to relate how much slaughter the enemy inflicted by overthrowing, ravaging, and plundering the churches and their possessions and estates. In particular, they burned with savage flames the basilica of Saint Peter, built with marvelous workmanship, seized its varied furnishings and all its equipment, and strove utterly to destroy it.

Alas, what grief! It must be said not without a groan: the aforementioned oratory of the martyr Saint Serotinus remained there, divinely rescued from the fire. Grieving over this, they added more and more fuel to the flames with all their effort; but it was preserved unharmed, for the strengthening of the people of God, by the living will and merit of God.

Through the saving intervention of the holy martyrs—Savinian and Potentian, Altinus and Eodald—the untouched mausoleum of Saint Serotinus the martyr was preserved, because the love of sincere affection had bound them together, and the absence of the saints’ limbs did not permit the one whom a single faith of charity had long before joined to them to be deprived of swift assistance.

### Chapter XIII. Concerning the return of the Northmen to their own country

At last, after many of the Northmen had been overcome and killed in various ways, the survivors returned to their own country.

The monks immediately hastened to ask the bishop that the bodies of the saints be brought back, unaware that they had been carried there by stealth. But he looked at them with grim eyes and, before hearing their request, said:

“Of our own free will, even though you are unwilling, yet through the outpouring mercy of God, we wish this right to be made known to all and bound by constitutions: the dignity of this see shall possess the bodies of these saints, whose martyrdom’s training has caused it to flourish and shine brilliantly.”

At this slanderous assertion, some of the more cunning clerics and the more powerful nobles were stirred up, unanimously asserting that the bodies ought to remain there, where the highest bishops had flourished.

To this the often-mentioned bishop added savage words:

“For the rights of the laws decree that the pontiff, who makes decisions for all, as well as the clergy, worshipers of the divine majesty, and all venerable lands and regions, ought to serve the vigils of such great martyrs. You, the common crowd, return to your monastic purpose with all your possessions recovered, knowing that from now on we shall be adorned by the presence of these saints.”

Then the tumult of the monks, groaning and pleading, rose up, and the sorrow resounded of the poor carrying earth-stained bodies [the reading is uncertain], and of people of both sexes, as they said:

“Why are we afflicted in this way? What evils have we deserved to suffer these things, if we flee to the protection of a common refuge? Why are we disgraced? Why are we deprived of the patrons given to us by God?”

At this, the bishop, carried away by the rashness of his wicked counsel, ordered them to be driven outside the walls.

### Chapter XIV. Concerning the monks’ persistent groaning, and the terrible vision shown to the bishop’s guards

The memorable abbot Samson almost died from continuous grief and abstinence. The whole unanimity of the community, weighed down by vigils, prayers, and fasts, suffered the same hardships.

Christ, therefore, the most impartial judge of all things, having compassion on the afflicted and aided also by the prayers of the holy martyrs, did not permit the monastery to remain any longer without the treasure of so precious a possession.

In the middle of the night, the guards of the church of Saint Stephen were shaken by the horror of a most violent disturbance. They hastened at once and filled the bishop’s ears with trembling cries:

“O bishop, bring aid to us who are desolate! It is to be feared that this basilica in which we dwell will collapse completely. A terrible crash resounds within, and lights of immense brightness dart through it.”

“What superstition,” said the bishop, “has disturbed your rustic minds? You have truly been deceived by the false suggestions of the monks and led astray by the empty hope of their promises.”

But the voice that testified to the truth could not be extinguished by the more terrible whirlwind of the disturbance.

On the following night, the bishop’s deployment of guards was disturbed; one of them, fleeing because of the magnitude of the terror, refused to remain there any longer. At the bishop’s command, both groups of guards were immediately assigned to the watch.

Persisting in this calamity, the bishop, cunning in character, appointed himself guardian of the church on the third night, surrounded by a huge troop of soldiers for the purpose of a genuine investigation. Blinded by the density of the flashing light, he began to rage violently and gnash his teeth, and insistently cried out that the bodies of the saints should be carried away.

### Chapter XV. Concerning the saints’ limbs brought back from the city

Finally, a modest troop of monks from Saint Peter arrived. Having recovered their patrons, they carried the saints back to their own basilica, happier than can be believed, amid a great chorus of those dancing and exulting.

For this reason Bernard, the arch-keykeeper of that see, inflamed by the poisonous zeal of envy, pulled away the cloak with which the tomb of the most holy apostolic patron Savinian was covered. Seizing an *artavus*, he cut it in half and said:

“If we are deprived of the relics of these Fathers, at least we shall retain a portion of this.”

A part of the cloak is still preserved in that same see in memory of posterity.

[Note: Clarius, in his Chronicle, calls him the arch-keykeeper of Saint Mary, contrary to this author. Was the arch-keykeeper of the cathedral church of Sens granted the title of Saint Mary’s abbey?]

[Note: An *artavus* is a tool suited for cutting cloth, either a kind of scissors or a kind of knife. This term is expressed in a manuscript of the Rule of the Order of Saint Victor cited in Du Cange’s Glossary: “Let him accept neither writing implements, nor *artavi*, nor little knives.”]

[Note: Namely, the monastery of Saint Peter.]

Everyone can clearly see how greatly this holy place had increased in sanctity, especially since they had consecrated it by the shedding of their own blood and since it was made most celebrated by the very frequent obsequies of the monks dwelling there.

### Chapter XVI. Concerning the caves constructed by Abbot Samson

Moreover, the venerable abbot Samson, endowed with more careful counsel of his own and of his brothers, wishing to secure salvation for those who would come later, constructed hidden caves for the limbs of the saints.

O laudable duty of devout Fathers! What people seeking the public welfare would deny that these men were shrewd and greatly worthy of honor, and that they possessed great power, since through the memory of the saints their intervention remains for long ages?

Although the limbs of the saints were covered in dense caves, nevertheless, because many people believed that the saints were present there, they were healed by their devout assistance from every disease-bearing pain.

### Chapter XVII. Concerning William’s death

When Bishop William had died, Bishop Gerlannus was praised in his place. He had followed the monastic way of life from earliest childhood and was strongly supported by the doctrines of philosophy. His family background was of moderate rank, but he distinguished himself as no sluggish follower of the liberal arts.

We think that this should be reckoned among the best works of his prudence: because he was very devoted to the often-mentioned monastery, he constructed a tower there with polished workmanship.

When his worldly course had finally been completed, he was summoned to the stars and departed, commanding that his remains be buried in the basilica of Saint Germanus of Auxerre.

Heldemannus was later elected to this pontifical throne. A monk of Saint Denis, he pleased everyone and Christ alike and was lovable and beloved.

During his rule Notrannus flourished as superior of the monastery of Saint Peter. A vigorous hoarder of treasures, he earned the dignity of the bishopric of Nevers through gifts.

But because the monastery of Saint Peter was weighed down by his prideful ambition, it nearly came to nothing.

At that time the same place was still being honored, enriched by God with the better parts of both kinds of property, through the devotion of Queen Techilde; but may the most merciful virtue wash away her offenses.

Bishop Heldemannus, for his part, died, seized by the final lot, and was incorporated into the heavenly assemblies.

### Chapter XVIII. How Archembald, struck by blessed Savinian in the ordeal of death, perished

Archembald was raised to the honor of the episcopate, prompted more by the scrutiny of his parents than by that of God.

Carried away by the frenzy of slippery youth, he devoted himself to shameful pleasure. Applying his energy to what was hateful to divine worship and embracing all that belongs to the perishing age, he utterly ruined the abbey of Saint Peter, which was exceedingly wealthy in every kind of possession: he sold and distributed all its best churches, villages, and lands, while keeping the remainder for his own uses.

We consider it a lengthy and impious task to expose all his lamentable excesses. We add only this: he was a horrible and hateful persecutor of those serving Christ and a most zealous lover of worldly things.

Warned by Saint Savinian, the most just martyr, in a night vision on two successive days, he refused to cease from his wicked work. On the third day the saint approached him again; when he refused to obey his commands, he struck him with an invisible blade:

“We shall not endure for long the trifles of your seductive activity, nor shall we allow you to lay waste the place consecrated by the shedding of our blood.”

He was found entirely naked of every covering of clothing in the brothers’ refectory, which he had claimed for himself and impiously taken away from their use.

The just judgment of retribution struck him with sudden death, for he had utterly destroyed the possessions gathered for the support of the brothers and for the assistance of the poor and of all who came there.

Let no one think it incongruous that he should end in this way, since he had first cast aside the care of pastoral dignity, and so forth.

### Chapter XIX. Concerning Bishop Anastasius and how he began to restore the same place

After that man had died such a cruel death, Anastasius, a man of uprightness and remarkable integrity, succeeded him in the episcopate.

Fearing the ordeal of that most terrible death, he became a willing restorer of the often-mentioned place. Anticipated by divine love, and especially by an appropriate warning in a vision of Saint Savinian himself, he began of his own accord to seek out the monastery’s lands, buy them back, educate monks, and reform the rule of sacred discipline there.

Supported by the grace of these and all other good works, he cast off human defilement and earned the fellowship of the saints in heaven. His remains lie buried in the same basilica.

### Chapter XX. How, after Anastasius’s death, Sewinus succeeded him

The metropolitan city of Sens, deprived of his protection, raised Sewinus to enhance the splendor of the episcopate. He was distinguished by nobility and shone through the integrity of his morals.

A vigorous obeyer of holy instruction, he strove to follow the excellent modest ways of his predecessor.

He overthrew the wicked schemes of rivals and sincerely sought the friendship of those who pleased Christ, eagerly embracing every distinguished spiritual gift and rejecting the transitory things of the malicious.

While he attempted to accomplish many works of virtue, he encountered what stands in the way of truth—namely, the savage incitements of the ancient enemy, who, an age-old thief, burns with envious seeds and pursues the joyful ranks of Christ, seeking how he may obstruct them.

He therefore stirred up the misguided minds of clerics who were wandering about and provoking others. The citizens of that same city also fought fiercely against him in hostile opposition, striving likewise to suppress what belonged appropriately to the sanctuary.

But the guiding protector of the aforesaid city, wishing to destroy those hearts swollen with evil once they had been torn away, set himself before them as a shield so that the footsteps of those who followed might remain safe and the house of God might be defended and raised to higher things.

At last, protected by Christ’s victorious defense, he sometimes softened the efforts of the wicked with gentle words; at other times he dragged them down and crushed them with threatening reprimands. Meanwhile, punishments of every sort subsided, and, with Christ’s favor, benefits of prosperity began to flourish.

### Chapter XXI. How, after Sewinus was placed in the see, he adorned the same place with an abbot and monks and restored its possessions

Meanwhile, the desire to ennoble the monasteries of the saints and restore their former honor, wherever they had been destroyed, began to burn within him.

Indeed, he ardently resolved to beautify the monastery of Saint Peter through the assistance of the saints, since he grieved that it had been overturned by the wickedness of many.

He therefore appointed as abbot over that monastery Rainardus, whose noble lineage was conspicuous and whose conduct was excellent and intelligence well developed. He restored half of all the possessions of that abbey.

This young man, of vigorous character, invested with the insignia of office through the favor of his neighboring government, surpassed all nearby rulers in the practice of integrity.

With a heart aflame, as befitted a nobleman, he immediately strove to restore the place. He determined that some monks should be distinguished by the learned teaching of all the liberal arts, recognizing this as the supreme good of all: that, instructed in these liberal disciplines and formed according to the purpose of sacred religion, the condition of the place might become more worthy and be magnified by all.

### Chapter XXII. Concerning the man who swore falsely upon the altar of Saint Savinian
At that time also an evident miracle occurred in the aforesaid monastery, which we certainly believe must not be concealed in silence. A certain man named Rothberthus, born in a neighboring village which antiquity called Masliacus-Major, profane in character and defiled by obscene desire, performed an unlawful sacrilege against Saint Savinianus in the church. Immediately afterward demonic madness enclosed him, and he was tormented in the presence of everyone by miserable suffering. At once some other, most dreadful spirits also appeared—those teachers of crimes and promoters of human salvation—who, secretly inciting him, drove him toward various forms of wickedness.

Finally, with his arms bound, and through the intercession of his parents, who acknowledged his crime, he was led to the caves of the holy martyrs, lest the trembling structure of his limbs should receive more deeply the demonic lamentation of its ravings. There, with his limbs exposed and wounded by many blows, he desired, as far as he was able, to ravage and tear apart all who held him. Through the openings of his scars he expelled blood as though disemboweling himself, and he mangled his bloody hands, exhausted by the straps, crying out terribly:

“O all-powerful martyr Savinianus, why are you killing me with dreadful torments?”

His relatives, overcome, openly confessed the sacrilege. For this reason they drew repeated sighs from the depths of their hearts and, through the intercession of the saints, implored that Christ’s assisting power might mercifully be present to them, so that the pestilential demonic force might leave the hiding places of this possessed man [Col. 0793C], and Christ’s renewed power might prevail.

They left him there entangled in ropes, their breathless effort relying in every way upon the saints’ help. He raged with burning spirit, rashly demanding that the name of the holy martyr Savinianus be spoken. Nothing was more pleasing than his severity, and nothing more severe than his pleasure. By then all the strength of his limbs had given way, and sleep had weighed upon the dislocated joints of his arms.

Thus, while he slept, a merciful vision came to him. He saw distinguished men descend from the stars, covered in an exceedingly bright light. They approached him with measured steps, but threatened him with harsh rebukes:

“Why,” they said, “have you, savage presumptuous man, entered our cave, you who, as a wanton reviler, have recently violated the place sanctified by the shedding of our blood?”

Terrified, he fled from their lordly gaze. The swift brilliance passed away and brought an end to his sudden danger; he remained as if dead. Then, when the mercy of the pious martyrs had been restored, it spared him, gentler toward the stupefied and nearly lifeless man:

“Because of the faith of your parents, who have entrusted you to us for healing, we command you to depart restored to health.”

Wonderful to relate! At once the bonds with which his hands had been tied fell away. Separated from the pillar to which he had been fastened, he completely recovered the vigor of his entire body. The healthier he became, the more joyfully he brightened his brow, now free of every cloud, and he became to everyone a truthful herald of the power wrought in him.

A crowd of rejoicing people therefore gathered around, singing hymns in corresponding melodies to the Creator of all things, by whose gift all things that appear marvelous are accomplished, and so forth.

## CHAPTER XXIII

How the bishop himself lay prostrate before the feet of the abbot and the monks, and restored the property that he still retained

Meanwhile, the prudent bishop Sewinus, adorned with the more radiant proclamation of his virtues, congratulated the same monastery. He spread joy across his face with a cheerful expression and carried sincere gladness within him. Then all the playfulness of his heart was removed from its depths; his former frivolous spirit became a seeker of the Godhead, and he seriously colored his former foolishness with the appearance of virtue.

Indeed, he poured out more fully and abundantly what he had held in his tenacious hands, since he did not hesitate to enrich himself by lending to the saints. He abhorred the savage monster of greed and, destitute and poor in possessions, preferred to serve Christ rather than, mortally wounded, be blinded by the allurements of treasures, especially when urged by a heavenly admonition from the holy martyrs Savinianus and Potentianus on the solemn feast of John and Paul.

Struck with awe, he went swiftly to the monastery of the heavenly key-bearer Peter, acknowledging himself guilty and criminal. Prostrate before the sight of all the brothers, he sought pardon with bowed head and the humblest voice. He therefore restored all his estates to the aforesaid abbey, retaining only a very small portion for his necessary needs.

From this arose a favorable breeze for the monks, and a powerful joy of those who praised Christ struck the whole city, and so forth.

## CHAPTER XXIV

How, after Sewinus’s death, Leothericus succeeded him, loved the clergy and people, and loved Abbot Rainardus and the monks

[Col. 0794C]

After Sewinus had been taken up into the ranks of the heavenly by the all-governing will of God, Leothericus was invested with the episcopal throne. He was distinguished in his actions, and love for his praiseworthy height of honor compels us to proclaim him, although eloquence is lacking in our discernment. His sincerity rightly caused the priestly dignity to increase, and under his guidance the customary excellence of the holy Church of God surpassed others, and so forth.

Moreover, we would consider it lengthy to attach to this little work the distinguished miracles that shone forth during his time. He frequently burned with affection for the aforesaid neighboring monastery, following with even greater zeal the useful interests of the diligent rector, Abbot Rainardus, for the common good. For he rejoiced that the goodness of his worthy predecessor Sewinus survived in Rainardus, and that Rainardus was his heir in the soundness of his conduct.

Finally, the most praiseworthy Abbot Rainardus, shining with the preeminent virtue of charity, had renounced every pleasure for himself and his own people and had acted according to the law of continence. He was a willing hearer of the apostolic assertion that, without chastity, it is impossible to please God, and also of that philosopher who says that nothing is earlier or better than the celibate life.

He did not hold this model of religion negligently. Rather, presenting also the mirror of good works that he had left behind, and embracing with ardent effort the rights of equity and the institutions of the ancient leaders, he shone as an honor worthy of admiration to many, and so forth. He carefully restored every ruined workshop together with its implements, ennobling them.

Meanwhile, his zeal of affection was revealed in connection with the solemn feasts of the holy martyrs, but he was wasting away more frequently because he did not know where the tomb containing the limbs of Saint Savinianus was concealed.

## CHAPTER XXV

On the tombs of Saint Savinianus and his holy companions, opened by Abbot Rainardus and Archbishop Leothericus

The bodies of the blessed martyrs Savinianus, Potentianus, and their companions, reverently buried inside the caves by Abbot Samson out of fear of the pagans, remained hidden there until the time of Lord Archbishop Leothericus and Lord Abbot Rainardus. Therefore, wishing to test the statements of the elders, he carefully reported their serious testimony, foreseeing with prophetic spirit that, through the intercession of the saints, many remedies of healing would be obtained.

They therefore adopted the salutary plan of opening the mausoleums of the saints, who were enclosed in the more secluded caves. When this had been done, an abundance of a wonderful fragrance immediately spread, giving them assurance of the saints’ presence. Praising God, they placed them there more fittingly on the eighth day before the Kalends of September [25 August].

Whatever sick or infirm people were given the potion with which the saints’ bones had been washed, they immediately obtained the benefit of healing. Through this, great things are magnified to the praise of Him who, by His all-governing protection, rules whatever He has created and gives life.

## CHAPTER XXVI

How Queen Constantia came to know Saint Savinianus

[Col. 0795C]

At that time Rotbertus, the most devout of kings, was reigning. After carrying out various restorations of churches and adorning the bodies of the saints, he decorated the body of Saint Savinianus with gold, gems, and silver. How this was done must be explained briefly.
