It happened that, when King Rotbertus was traveling to Rome, Queen Constantia remained behind with her little son Hugh Tillo. When Queen Berta learned this—she had previously been rejected by the king on account of consanguinity—she followed him, hoping that, with the support of certain courtiers and by apostolic command, she might be restored to the royal marriage bed. Queen Constantia therefore feared that she would be removed from the king’s side and was held by indescribable sorrow.

One night, overwhelmed by an excessive tumult of thoughts concerning this matter, she fell asleep. In a vision there appeared to her a man surrounded by indescribable radiance, adorned with angelic gray hairs, wearing priestly clothing and holding a pastoral staff in his hand. Terrified by overwhelming fear, she asked who he was. He thundered that he was a bishop named Savinianus, and said to her:

“Be steadfast, Constantia, for by God’s favor you have been delivered from the sorrow that threatened you.”

Terrified by so splendid a vision, she began the next morning to inquire anxiously of the clerics around her whether in those regions there was a bishop called Savinianus. When they confessed their ignorance, one of them, who had been raised in the monastery of Saint Peter and was destined to become bishop of Aurelianum when the king returned, replied for them all. His name was Theodericus [Note: [Col. 0795D] We reported his deeds under the year 1021.]:

“Yes, my lady. In the monastery of Saint Peter there is Saint Savinianus, the first archbishop of the metropolitan city of Sens, who, together with his companions, reached the prize of the heavenly kingdom through the triumph of martyrdom. If you approach this martyr’s presence with a devout mind, know that you will obtain without delay what he promised.”

She rejoiced at the counsel of so great a man. Very quickly, together with her son, she sought the threshold of Saint Peter. There she poured out tears for a long time before the body of the blessed martyr and entrusted herself to his faith with all her strength. Comforted by the visitation of so great a patron, she returned joyfully home.

The third day had not yet passed when, suddenly, in the dead of night, a royal messenger appeared at the door, announcing that the king’s presence would soon arrive. Restored by God’s guidance to his own residence, he confirmed the martyr’s promise as wholly truthful: from then on he loved his lawful wife more than before and determined that all royal rights and everything he appeared to possess should remain under her direction.

But she did not at all forget the saint’s promise. She began to consider how his body might be adorned with gems and gold. It had long been enclosed in lead and concealed by the ancient fathers beneath the atrium. She presented her wishes to the king and, with God’s help, found him entirely prepared to fulfill them.

He summoned Odorannus, a monk of that place who appeared suitable for completing this work, and entrusted to him, together with the queen, the task of such great piety. First, at Sens, through the hand of the provost Waldricus, they gave four pounds of pure silver. Then, at Sens, through the hand of Willelmus the chamberlain, they gave fifty-five solidi of pure silver. Later they sent, through the hand of Odo Paratgius, thirty-seven solidi of pure silver. They also sent to Paris, through the hand of the monk Odorannus, seventeen solidi and eight denarii of gold, together with extremely precious gems.

After these things had been accomplished, it remains for us to make known to Christ’s faithful the wonders of God that we saw with our own eyes in the construction of this work and partly handled with our own hands. To conceal them in silence would be a crime.

## CHAPTER XXVII

On the monk Odorannus’s journey to the palace and the gold received from the queen for the making of the reliquary

[Col. 0796D]

The king, occupied with various worldly concerns, delayed for a little while sending funds to the monastery for the work that had begun. When he had obtained leisure, he sent word through the aforementioned brother Francolinus that he should come quickly to Dreux to receive the contribution for the work.

After completing the evening office and, as is customary for monks, receiving the abbot’s blessing, he proceeded toward the heights of the castle of Dreux [Note: [Col. 0795D] The castle of Druense, more correctly Drocense, or in ancient form Durocassense, commonly Dreux, or a name renowned in itself.] When, after sunset, he came to the port of Saint Columba, he crossed the river Yonne with his companions. After stopping briefly on the bank, he saw among the other stars by which the night was illuminated a certain star rise in the place where, in summer, the sun usually indicates the first hour of the day.

Leaping from the place of its rising, by divine power it began to travel swiftly through the air, seeking the higher regions of the sky, almost up to the point at which, in that season, the sixth hour usually occurs. His servant, with the horse prepared for him to ride, urged him to mount because night was approaching.

“Wait for me a little,” he said, “and look with your companion upon the wonders of God that I have never before seen.”

The servants, astonished by this miracle and unaware of what omen it carried, fortified themselves with the sign of the cross and, terrified in heart, entrusted themselves to God and Saint Savinianus.

The star remained for a little while in the place to which it had come, then, traveling backward, returned within the space of one hour to the place from which it had come. They watched it almost until the third watch of the night and saw it joyfully complete its customary course among the other stars. As they discussed among themselves what it might signify, it occurred to them that they would complete their journey with prosperous steps and, having finally attained their desire, return quickly home.

They therefore devoted themselves more promptly to the labor of their journey and reached the king’s palace by way of desolate Belsa, after he had risen from the table.

After offering the king and queen the customary greeting, so that the star’s omens might prove entirely true, the queen said to the monk:

“Receive the gifts that we have presently arranged to send, as far as we are able, to Saint Savinianus, and return quickly home, because we have decided to leave for another place early tomorrow morning.”

Then, immediately producing thirteen gold solidi weighed according to the public coinage of Orléans, she said:

“If my weighing does not satisfy you, let repeated weighing before your own eyes provide assurance.”

Nothing other than what the queen had stated was found on the balance.

The monk therefore returned to the monastery, having obtained what he desired. After delivering the king’s and queen’s greetings to the abbot and brothers, he brought forth from the purse the bright gold gift sent to Saint Savinianus. It was publicly weighed by the hands of Francolinus the doorkeeper and Raimbertus the king’s cellarer. As the balance tipped, it was found to contain seven denarii more.

The brother who had carried it, and the others who marveled, therefore understood with certainty that He who had deigned to show a miracle through the star’s change during the journey, and who created the whole world from nothing, had caused the bright gold to increase in the faithful purse, for the martyr’s merit, according to the number sevenfold of the Spirit.

He who, through Elisha’s intercession, caused the oil to overflow in order to redeem the widow’s sons made the small gift of gold exceedingly great through the devotion of the king and queen. And God, the head of Christ, who said through His prophet, “The silver and gold are mine,” possesses whatever He bestows upon His members, that is, the holy martyrs; it belongs to no other.

Afterward, at Sens, the king gave through the hand of the monk Odorannus eight ounces of gold and fifteen solidi of pure silver. During the completion of the work, so that the king would not be burdened by frequent requests for gold and silver, five ounces of gold and three pounds of pure silver were added from the church treasury.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

On the translation of Saint Savinianus and the miracles performed in the presence of King Rotbertus

[Col. 0798A]

Having described the equipment for this work, most worthy of God, it is worthwhile to inscribe with the pen of Scripture the miracle that the omnipotence of God deigned to perform before us during the translation of the holy martyr.

The desired day of his feast was approaching, on which his venerable body, together with those of his companions, had been transferred by the ancient fathers into the basilica of Saint Peter. The king, having remained for a short while at Sens, was preparing to return to Paris. He therefore summoned Archbishop Leothericus and humbly asked him to visit the monastery and transfer the body of the holy martyr from the leaden container in which the ancient fathers had placed it into the golden reliquary that he had prepared for him.

On Friday, with the feast awaiting the following Sunday, the archbishop came to the monastery and, with the greatest reverence, fulfilled the king’s instructions together with the brothers. He placed the body of Saint Eodaldus, which he found with Saint Savinianus, beside the body of Saint Savinianus; he also replaced with them the bones of a small child buried there. After completing the solemn Masses, he departed to eat.

The brother under whose supervision and care the whole construction of the work was proceeding was seated in the monastery choir, softening with warm wax the silver images that he had arranged to be placed upon the lid of the reliquary. Suddenly, without warning, a certain blind man arrived, led by a little boy, asking to be admitted to the crypt where the body of Saint Savinianus had been placed.

The monk asked him who he was, where he came from, and for what reason he had arrived. He declared that he was a peasant and had a dwelling in the district of Wastinum, in a village called Fontanas; his own name was Mainardus. He had been warned in a dream the previous night to come into the presence of Saint Savinianus and receive his eyesight there. He had been blind for three years.

Admitted to the saint, he prayed for a long time, but on that very day he did not deserve to receive any light. Nevertheless, filled, as he himself said, with an exceedingly sweet fragrance, he returned home.

When Sunday arrived, the king came with his bishops and nobles, as well as abbots and clerics, and an innumerable people, to transport the martyr’s body. Taking it up together with his son Rotbertus upon his own shoulders, he placed it with his own hands in the place where it is venerated by the faithful to this day.

After the solemn service had been completed, while the king reclined at table and the monks were eating, the aforementioned monk was sitting in the place where the blind man described above had found him sitting two days earlier. By God’s prompting, the blind man then arrived again, led by the boy, and said that he had once more been warned in a dream to seek Saint Savinianus’s help as quickly as possible.

Throwing himself face down before the saint’s presence, he recovered his sight through the merits of the saint’s intercession. The boy who had until then led him returned home with him, now led by the man whom he had guided.

The king rose from the table for the sake of prayer, as was his custom, and remained alone in the church. While he was praying, the aforementioned brother happened to enter the church. Seeing him from a distance, the king beckoned calmly with his hand for him to come closer.

“Tell me,” he said, “what Saint Potentianus was to Saint Savinianus.”

The monk humbly replied that he had been his companion in the labor of the journey, his successor in honor, and his fellow martyr.

Then the king began to complain bitterly and beat his breast with his fists because he had separated them bodily from one another. Promising that he would restore him to his companion, he entrusted thirty-three solidi of pure silver to the same brother, so that he might begin preparing the reliquary of Saint Potentianus.

But while he was considering carrying this out, forestalled by a heavenly summons, he paid to God the debt owed by our father Adam.

## [MINOR WORKS]

### NOTICE ON THE FOLLOWING MINOR WORKS

*(Spicilegium Romanum, vol. IX, preface, p. XIV.)*

Among the codices of Christina, Queen of the Swedes, now in the Vatican, there is an old autograph manuscript, as I believe, containing the minor works of the monk Odorannus, who before the middle of the eleventh century was not unknown in Gaul under King Robert, at whose court he enjoyed great favor.

From this codex Chesnius once obtained from Senator Petavius, then its owner, the short chronicle that he published among the *Scriptores rerum Francicarum*, vol. II. Mabillon also published a mutilated letter of Odorannus (see Minor Work 13). No one had yet brought forth all the other works hidden in this very rare codex, although they are not lacking in historical learning and treat, not inelegantly, of biblical, musical, and physical questions and doctrines.

The genuine form of the episcopal election of that period in Minor Work 8 is especially pleasing [Note: [Col. 0799] Compare the Greek mandate to a recently ordained bishop in Leunclavius, *Jus Graeco-Romanum*, p. 429]. In Minor Work 9 there is a sermon to be pronounced before the people on behalf of an elected bishop; in Minor Work 11, a monastic exhortation; and finally, in Minor Work 12, a testament of fraternal unanimity.

As for the hymn to Saint Savinianus, I do not determine whether it belongs to Odorannus or rather to King Robert, who is known to have composed other hymns as well. Certainly, it is written in a different hand in the codex.

Finally, the epitaphs of Sens that we append somewhat increase the treasury of Christian inscriptions.

### THE MINOR WORKS OF ODORANNUS

*(Mai, in the place cited above, p. 58.)*

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0799B] … the locust grows fat, the caper bush is scattered [Note: [Col. 0799B] The prologue is acephalous in the codex. To explain these opening words, I record the gloss written above them: “The feet swell, or become thickened, with subcutaneous fluid; the hair of the head falls out; or venereal heat grows weak.”]. Before the golden cord fails [Note: [Col. 0799B] Gloss: “before the breath of the heart fails.”], before we rise at the voice of the dove, before the wheel over the cistern is crushed [Note: [Col. 0800B] Gloss: “the movement of the intestines, the stomach.”], before the dust returns to its own earth from which it came, and the spirit returns to God who gave it, we must remember, dearest one, the time of darkness and, with the utmost diligence, consider the future judgment of the strict Judge. We must provide our neighbors with an example of good action not only through the performance of good deeds but also through writings and words.

Therefore, from among the many things I have accomplished at different times, I have taken care to hand over to your fatherhood [Note: [Col. 0800B] He is speaking to the abbot.] a few minor works—not only useful to you, but also, without any suspicion of envy, useful to those who read them, with God, from whom all good things proceed, as their author.

First, I have decided to set down what I briefly composed concerning the origin and end of Lady Theudechild and the foundation of our place, at the urging of the most devout King Rotbertus and the admonition of Lord Archbishop Leuthericus [Note: [Col. 0800B] Odorannus was familiar with both men. See Mabillon, *Annales Benedictini*, under the year 1028. Leuthericus was archbishop of Sens.].

Next, wishing to show by the years of the Lord at what times and through which persons this place was enriched with the relics of the saints, I have touched upon the matter with the deepest humility, including, among other things, the miracles that I saw take place during the translation of Saint Savinianus. The remaining matters, attached to their own chapters, plainly reveal their contents to readers.

### THE PROLOGUE ENDS

### THE CHAPTERS OR TITLES OF THE MINOR WORKS OF ODORANNUS BEGIN

[Col. 0801]

[Col. 0801A] I. The origin, deeds, and end of Lady Theudechild the queen, and the construction of the monastery of Saint Peter.

II. A chronological demonstration, by the years of the Lord, of the times and persons through whom the monastery of Saint Peter was endowed with royal charters, episcopal privileges, and the relics of the saints; also, that the bishop of Sens holds primacy over Gaul and Germany and is called the second pope; and a display of the miracles of Saint Savinianus.

III. A thanksgiving addressed to William the abbot under the praise of charity. Also, concerning accusers and accused persons, or false witnesses. Concerning conspiracies and indictments as well. And concerning the restoration of the priesthood, from the writings of Gregory and Isidore.

IV. To the monk Eurardus, concerning three questions.

[Col. 0801B] V. To the monk Rotbertus, concerning the musical modes.

VI. On the division of the monochord, addressed to the monks of Saint Germanus of Auxerre who were staying at Saint Leodegarius.

VII. To the monk Arembertus, concerning the responsory “Aspiciens a longe” (“Looking from afar”), against Amalarius; and a resolution of the drama, together with a mystical interpretation of the Shunammite woman.

[Col. 0802A] VIII. An episcopal election issued by Odorannus.

IX. A sermon by the same author, to be pronounced publicly at the ordination of a bishop.

X. On injuries against priests and the excommunication of bishops.

XI. An exhortation of Odorannus to the monks of Masciacus, sent by Abbot Ingo.

XII. A testament of fraternal unanimity issued by Odorannus.

XIII. A letter of Odorannus to Ayrfredus, teacher of the holy Church of Orléans and abbot of the monastery of Saint Avitus, and to Hugh, archdeacon of the holy mother Church of Sens.

[Col. 0802B] Having recovered somewhat from his long and very serious ailment of the feet, in the year 1045 of the Lord’s incarnation, at almost sixty years of age, Odorannus gathered these works into a single body, lest the present minor works should perish through the cunning of the envious, and left them, out of love of charity, to diligent brothers for their exercise.

### THE ARGUMENT ENDS

## IN THE NAME OF CHRIST, THE BOOK OF THE MINOR WORKS OF THE MONK ODORANNUS BEGINS

[Col. 0801]

## MINOR WORK I

[Col. 0801C] After the Franks had been expelled from Sicambria by the emperor Valentinian and had begun to dwell in the remotest regions of the Rhine River, they chose for themselves by common agreement a king named Faramund, son of Marchomir, who was descended from the line of Priam, king of the Trojans.

After Faramund’s death, they made his son Clodio their king. When Clodio died, his son Meroveus was elevated to the kingship. When he too died, his son Childericus assumed the kingdom. After Childericus’s departure, the Franks established his son Chlodoveus as their king—a man clever in intelligence, vigorous in warfare, and prudent in counsel.

While still a pagan, he took as his wife a Christian woman named Chrochildis, daughter of Chilperic, king of the Burgundians, who was brother of Duke Gundebod; their father, Gundoveus, was king of the Burgundians.

After King Chlodoveus, at the urging of his wife and through the preaching of Saint Remigius, bishop of Reims, had been baptized in the name of the holy Trinity, Queen Chrochildis, at his command, built a monastery of magnificent workmanship south of the city of Paris, across the River Seine, in honor of the holy apostles Peter and Paul.

After Chlodoveus had conquered many great kings, he died in peace and was buried in the aforementioned basilica of Saint Peter, where blessed Genovefa also lies buried. He died in the fifth year after he killed Alaric, king of the Goths, in the thirtieth year of his reign. From the passing of Saint Martin to the passing of King Chlodoveus there were 112 years.

After his death, his four sons—Theodoricus, Chlodomirus, Childebertus, and Chlotarius—divided his kingdom among themselves. When Chlotarius the younger alone survived after the deaths of his three brothers, his sister, named Theudechildis, with his favor, built a monastery in the presence of the city of Sens, after the model of what their parents had constructed at Paris, in honor of the aforementioned apostles.

She established it so that, under holy religion and the authority of an abbot, monks might serve God there throughout all their days; and she ordered that her body be entrusted to burial there. Whatever she was able to possess on this side of the Loire—that is, in Francia—or beyond the Loire—that is, in Aquitaine—whether inherited or acquired, she bequeathed to this house of God under the terms of a testament.

If anyone wishes to know the matter fully, he will certainly be able to learn it if the archives of that monastery are opened to him as they actually are.

At that time, throughout almost all Gaul, Fortunatus the priest, an Italian by birth and a most eloquent man, was held in high renown. After King Chlotarius had cast off the human condition and his son Sigebertus had succeeded to the kingdom, Fortunatus composed certain works held by us in praise of that Sigebertus and of Queen Brunechildis [Note: [Col. 0803D] These works are extant in editions of Fortunatus.].

As for Lady Theudechild the queen, how abundantly she overflowed with the fountain of piety and how praiseworthy a life she led, the same Fortunatus clearly sets forth in verse when writing to her.

“Illustrious offspring, etc.,” as in the editions of Fortunatus.

Likewise, the epitaph of Theudechildis:

“Although with golden things, etc.,” as in the editions.

(Later, another epigram concerning Theudechildis follows in the codex, which I did not find among Fortunatus’s poems. It reads as follows:)

This place the queen Theudechildis built from its foundations  
for monks, ennobling it with her own possessions.

Although her body is now enclosed in this cavern,  
her spirit lives with God in the starry heaven.

Imploring “Well done!” from righteous shepherds,  
may God grant what is deserved to those who seize these things—alas!

## MINOR WORK II

[Col. 0803]

The second minor work contains the Chronicle of Odorannus, which Chesnius published from this very codex among the *Scriptores rerum Francicarum*, vol. II; for that reason we omit it here.

## MINOR WORK III

To the most holy and ever-pious Lord William, abbot of the monastery of the most holy martyr Dionysius, ever to be remembered in the heart of Christ: Odorannus, a brother exceedingly desirous of his honor, sends the prosperity of the present age and the joys of eternal happiness.

[Col. 0803B] Since the entire sequence of the Scriptures of the Old and New Testaments urges that God be honored by faith, hope, and charity, and since the Apostle openly demonstrates that charity is greater than these, it is clearly recognized that the love of God and neighbor fulfills charity, if, according to the command of divine speech, we love God with all our heart, all our soul, and all our strength, and our neighbor as ourselves.

For although what the Apostle James says may escape those who are less diligent—“If anyone keeps the whole law but offends in one point, he has become guilty of all”—a vigilant reader will nevertheless see that he was speaking of this one thing, charity, which is God, if he examines with the most subtle eye of the mind the words of the Apostle Paul writing to the Romans, where he says:

“Owe no one anything except to love one another [Col. 0803C]; for whoever loves his neighbor has fulfilled the law. For: You shall not commit adultery; you shall not kill; you shall not steal; you shall not bear false witness; you shall not covet your neighbor’s property; and if there is any other commandment, it is summed up in this one: You shall love your neighbor as yourself.”

You are recognized, most reverend Father, as burning so intensely with the fire of this charity that you appear admirable not only to those well disposed toward you but also to those hostile to your own welfare. Though supported by the honor of authority among your household, you are not at all exalted, but are among them as one of themselves. You do not hesitate to become like the Apostle by sympathizing diligently with those who grieve and are placed in bitterness.

Anyone who knows me personally will not doubt that you did this for my lowliness. When the cunning of the envious had almost caused the whole world to conspire against me, to such an extent that, as desire prevailed, I was denied a hearing, as soon as I was worthy to reach the threshold of blessed Dionysius [Col. 0804B], you received me honorably, beyond what my smallness deserved. In that congregation, with the consent of all the brothers, you deigned to appoint me not as an outsider and guest but as a citizen and member of the household.

After, by God’s favor, I was summoned by Lord Abbot Ingo, you sent me back to my own place, enriched with various gifts and with the greatest honor.

Therefore I cannot find anything worthy with which to repay you. Even if all my hairs were turned into tongues, I would not be able to express in words the thanks I owe you. But lest I be found wholly ungrateful, I offer you one thing whose value man does not know: whenever I receive the cup of salvation and invoke the name of the Lord, I offer a saving sacrifice to the heavenly Majesty for your health [Col. 0804C].

Moreover, because through the negligence of priests and the greed of those who administer public affairs—who pursue curiosities, as the Apostle censures, and are informers, whom worldly laws entirely exclude—such men rage with impunity, and because of this conspiracies and perjuries frequently boil over everywhere, and, what cannot be said without the greatest sorrow of heart, erupt within the ecclesiastical order, I thought it worthwhile to send you a few passages taken from ecclesiastical regulations contrary to this error.

I also decided to add something definite to this work concerning the restoration of the priesthood, so that, if the question should perhaps be debated by learned men, Your Holiness may know what ought to be decided concerning it.

Farewell.

[Col. 0804D] (Here the codex proceeds against the crime of calumny: 1. from the decrees of Innocent; 2. from the Council of Carthage; 3. from the Capitularies of Charlemagne; 4. from the Council of Chalcedon; 5. from Book IX of Roman law [Col. 0805A] [Note: [Col. 0805D] The following passage of Roman law does not appear in the edition of that law published by Canciani, vol. IV, where Book IX is printed on pp. 490–494. Similar statements, however, occur in the *Codex Theodosianus* IX.1.19.]. We shall quote only this fifth testimony:)

“If anyone, being angry, rashly brings some charge against anyone, it is not to be regarded as an accusation but as an insult; rather, after allowing time for reflection, let him acknowledge in writing that he will prove what he said in anger. But if, perhaps coming to his senses, he does not wish to repeat or write, after his anger, what he said, he is not to be held liable as guilty of the charge.”

Likewise: “Unless a formal written accusation has been lodged, no one is to be made a defendant or brought to trial; for just as punishment constrains the person convicted, so it also constrains the accuser if he has not proved what he alleged.”

Likewise: “The confession of those who are accused of crimes must not be believed against others unless they have first proved themselves innocent; for the confession of a defendant against anyone else is dangerous [Col. 0805B] and must not be admitted.”

Likewise: “Before a formal accusation, no one is to be called a criminal. Once the accusation has been properly lodged, the defendant is then to be received by the judge, with this proviso: the dignity both of the accused and of the accuser is to be assessed, and the judge is to have each of them kept in custody in such a way as their birth or dignity permits. Certainly, when those who have confessed their own crimes wish to speak about others, the judge must not believe them; for it has been established by law that a defendant does not make another defendant by voluntary confession, nor is credence to be given concerning another to one who has confessed himself to be a criminal.”

Likewise: “A slave accusing his master is not only not to be heard but is also to be punished, unless he has proved that his master was involved in a crime against the majesty of the state.” [Col. 0806A]

Likewise: “If a slave accuses his master, or a friend, household member, or freedman accuses his patron, or if anyone informs against a defendant, he is to be punished by the sword immediately at the very beginning of the accusation; for we wish such a voice to be silenced, not heard—unless he has proved that his master or patron was involved in a crime against the majesty of the state.”

(6. From the Council of Agde; 7. from the decretals of Pope Sylvester; 8. from the Council of Carthage, all of which we omit; 9. finally, the following are included.)

Concerning accusations or formal written charges, the emperors Theodosius and Constantine, Arcadius and Honorius, and the others established provisions against unscrupulous accusers, so that they might not take pleasure in accusing people of false crimes. Therefore, I, so-and-so, appear against you in public proceedings. If I have brought a charge unjustly and thereafter have been shown to be defeated, I bind and formally declare myself subject to the same penalty which I sought to impose upon you, and to be condemned and subjected to it in your interest. And, for the full security of the entire matter, I confirm this with my own hand and submit it for ratification by the judgment of good men.

(10. From Pope Gregory to Secundinus; 11. from a letter of Bishop Isidore to Bishop Masso, which begins, “When your servant came to us”; 12. from the Council of Ancyra. Finally, Odorannus’ letter concludes with these verses.)

Here, grant the monks pious prayers for long years,

and remain a shepherd, lest the sheep be torn apart.

## OPUSCULUM IV

[Col. 0805]

To Lord Eurardus, brother and fellow priest, Odorannus, the lowliest brother of the synkellites, wishes whatever he wishes for himself.

[Col. 0805C] Your Fraternity is not unaware, as I have learned, that every medicine is made either from similar things or from opposites. But although you surpass me in age and merit, you wish to be taught by me how every harmony is joined from similar and dissimilar elements, and from things neither wholly similar nor wholly dissimilar. Do not take it amiss, venerable Father, if I delay, because what you ask, unless I am mistaken, is not suited to your age or your health. Let it be enough for you, insofar as your ability permits, to know on the level surface of the monochord the beginnings and ends of the regular modes, their ascents and descents as well, and to be delighted by the sweet melody of low and high sounds. Nevertheless, since I have not forgotten your questions, I shall briefly explain what the distinguished teacher Augustine thought about Solomon’s apostasy, what Jerome, interpreter and expositor of the divine law, wrote about his repentance, and where Ambrose, defender of the Catholic faith, called him holy. [Col. 0805D]

In book X of his *Literal Commentary on Genesis*, Augustine says of him: “Solomon, a man of such great wisdom—can it be believed that he thought there was any usefulness in the worship of idols? [Col. 0806C] No; but he was unable to resist the love of women, which drew him toward this evil, doing what he knew ought not to be done lest he grieve the women whose pleasures he passionately desired and in which he was wasting away.”

Likewise, Jerome, in book XIII of his *Commentaries on Ezekiel*, says: “The house of Israel—that is, those who behold God in spirit—is shown a house, namely the temple, which Ezekiel saw situated on a mountain. And not merely on a mountain but, as it is now said, at the summit of the mountain. We must by no means suppose this to be the temple said to have been constructed by Solomon in the books of Kings and Chronicles; for that temple belongs to another order and measurement and differs greatly in its several features. It is so much inferior to the temple now shown to Ezekiel that not only its worshipers or custodians but even its builder, Solomon himself, sinned and offended God, although afterward he did penance, writing the Proverbs in which he says: ‘At last, therefore, I repented, and turned back to choose instruction.’” [Col. 0806D]

Ambrose also, mentioning him in his book *Hexameron*, says: “Since you see elephants subject to you and lions placed beneath you, know yourself, O man—not in the manner attributed to Apollo of Delphi, but in that of the holy Solomon, who says: ‘Unless you know yourself, O fairest among women.’” [Col. 0807A]

Concerning aborted fetuses, once they have begun to live in their mothers’ wombs, and the fact that they are held liable under the penalty of original sin, Saint Augustine says the following, among other things, in the book he wrote *On Faith to Peter the Deacon*: “Hold most firmly, and do not doubt in any way, that not only human beings who already use reason, but also infants—whether they begin to live in their mothers’ wombs or, already born from their mothers, depart from this world without the sacrament of holy baptism, which is given in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit—are to be punished with the everlasting punishment of eternal fire. For although they have incurred no sin through their own action, nevertheless through conception and birth in the flesh they have drawn upon themselves the condemnation of original sin.” [Col. 0807B] In the *Enchiridion* as well, the same teacher, writing to Laurence, discusses this question at greatest length.

With these matters thus explained, the question of the origin of souls remains to be resolved. So that I may not exceed the limits of a letter or give occasion for whispering to those who mock me while deceiving themselves, I shall append it separately, with the authors’ names indicated above. Here, however, is what blessed Pope Gregory the universal writes to the recluse Secundinus: “There has been no small inquiry among the holy Fathers concerning the origin of the soul; but whether it descended from Adam or is given individually has remained uncertain, and they have declared the question insoluble. If this comes into your hands, let your most loving affection for me not be disturbed; for, to speak in the words of him who was a dwelling-place of the Holy Spirit, we do not wish to affirm what we do not approve by clear testimonies.” [Col. 0807C]

Do not hesitate to read Cassiodorus’ book *On the Nature of the Soul* and the first book of Isidore’s *Sentences*. But lest, by weighing the opinions of different writers for too long, I seem to entangle myself in delays, the section will show what Isidore thought in his book *On the Definitions of Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, and what the most eloquent versifier Prudentius left written on this sort of question. [Col. 0808A] Farewell in Christ, radiant jewel of monks, and pray for me.

The following comes from Isidore, concerning the origin of the soul:

“Nothing incorporeal and invisible extends as far as human substance.”

Then follow verses of Prudentius:

“Here the doubting disputant comes forward, and this passage continues as far as:

‘That the divine power may not be permitted, ever full for itself and in itself.’”

Then Odorannus continues. Here ends the third question, concerning the origin of the soul. [Col. 0808B] Moreover, writers on natural matters state that the development of the human body is completed in forty-six days: for, during six days from conception, it has the likeness of milk; during the following nine it is changed into blood; then for twelve days it becomes solid; during the remaining eighteen it is formed until the complete outlines of all the limbs are present; and from that point onward, until the time of birth, it increases in size. Six, nine, twelve, and eighteen make forty-five; if we add one, namely the day of conception itself, we find forty-six.

The name Adam, written with four letters, signifies the same thing. For ἄρκτος (*arktos*), meaning “north,” begins with alpha; δύσις (*dysis*), meaning “west,” begins with delta; ἀνατολή (*anatolē*), meaning “east,” begins with alpha; and μεσεμβρία (*mesēmbria*), meaning “south,” begins with mu. These are the four regions of the world, beginning with these four letters; and if these letters are reckoned according to Greek numerals, they make forty-six. For alpha is one, delta four, alpha again one, and mu forty; taken together, they yield forty-six. [Col. 0808C]

You who read these things, I ask you to return words of greeting,

for to me a light sheet of paper will be the weight of love.

## OPUSCULUM V

[Col. 0807]

To Rotbertus, half of my soul, brother and fellow priest, his brother Odorannus, wrapped in the gravest sins, sends whatever one friend may send to a friend.

[Col. 0807D] That friendship is truly a fellowship of souls is testified, reverend brother—sweeter to me than the sweetest honey—by the most perfect affection of your soul. When I was recently placed in tribulation, it was not ashamed of me; rather, by often pouring forth tears from the depths of a devout heart and frequently sacrificing an offering of praise to the heavenly Majesty, it has always, as I hope, rendered the fearsome Judge favorable toward me.

Now, because in repayment for so great a kindness you ask me to demonstrate to you not the sluggish weight of riches—which, when the thirst for possession has blazed up, is in no way better equipped for wrongdoing, and which the victorious spirit has trampled beneath itself, finding nothing more worthless for merit—but the knowledge of singing correctly, which you esteem more highly than these things, I shall explain it to you clearly insofar as heavenly goodness has granted me the ability. [Col. 0808D]

First I shall set out the names of the musical strings, marked continuously by the alphabet; then I shall append the names of the regular modes together with their formulas. I indicate the names of the strings to you for this reason: if, with the help of heavenly grace, you should be able to acquire knowledge of singing on the regular monochord, you may be able to distinguish by how many intervals the tones differ from one another.

What follows is a modest treatise on musical tones, with musical notation and so forth. I leave this piece of late-night work to experts in that art, as it existed in the Middle Ages, to publish or elucidate. Odorannus concludes as follows:

Here you have, good man, an extended parenthesis, though I hope not an unprofitable one, in which the formulas for singing correctly have been handed down as lightly as I could manage. It remains that, if you have been unable to reach a higher knowledge of the musical art, you should at least know that the entire monochord consists of five tetrachords in three genera, namely diatonic, chromatic, and enharmonic. The first of these is called hypaton, the second meson, the third synemmenon, the fourth diazeugmenon, and the fifth hyperboleon. [Col. 0809A]

There are not, as some maintain, six consonances, but five. The first is the diatessaron, consisting of an epitrite proportion, that is, sesquitertian, as four is to three. The second is the diapente, consisting of a hemiolic proportion, that is, sesquialteran, as three is to two. The third is the diapason, consisting of a duple proportion, as four is to two. The fourth is the diapason together with the diapente, consisting of a triple proportion, as six is to two. The fifth is the bis diapason, consisting of a quadruple proportion, as eight is to two.

The epogdous, that is, the tone, taking the place of a point, consists of a sesquioctave proportion, as nine is to eight. The diatessaron consonance consists of two tones and a minor semitone. [Col. 0809B] The diapente consists of three tones and a minor semitone. The diapason consists of five tones and two minor semitones. Accordingly, the diatessaron contains four strings, the diapente five, and the diapason eight.

Above all, however, the singer must beware, in the formulas of the modes set out above, that every chant either begins with its differentia, or differs from it by an epogdous—that is, a tone—or by a full enharmonic interval, that is, two tones, or by a diatessaron or diapente. But if you wish to know what a differentia is: a differentia is a certain dissimilarity among similar things; or, a differentia is a sufficient distinction for discerning the matter you have undertaken to distinguish. [Col. 0810A]

You therefore have, O Rotbertus, sweet comfort of my labors, the knowledge of singing correctly contained in a brief document, which may prove somewhat useful to many if they apply themselves to it diligently. If it should fall into the hands of rivals and, reading it secretly, they mock it publicly while composing their own works, let them remember, if they are able, this saying of blessed Augustine: “It is necessary that many books be made by many people, in different styles but not with a different faith.” [Col. 0810B]

I also remind and exhort you to raise me up on the wings of your prayers, so that, by God’s mercy, I may deserve to be released from the bonds of my sins, by which I am miserably constricted as my own conscience accuses me, and may leave posterity something worthy of remembrance. Farewell in Christ, guardian, as I believe, of my soul.

## OPUSCULUM VI

[Note: [Col. 0809D] For understanding this work of Odorannus, nothing will be more useful than consulting, besides Boethius, Euclid’s *Introduction to Harmonics*, among the ancient musical authors edited by Meibomius.]

[Col. 0809]

To the brothers united with one another by the bond of perfect charity in the monastery of Saint Leodegarius, Valcherius and Rotbertus, who follow the master Rule with the foot of obedience, their brother Odorannus, in need of God’s mercy, sends whatever is fitting.

[Col. 0809B] The arduous and almost exceedingly difficult task which you wish to force from me I would by no means presume to undertake at present, unless, trusting in God’s help and in your prayers, I hoped to stretch myself toward what you request. This is especially so since I am staying within the river Arar, in a castle called [Col. 0809C] Malliacus, with Archbishop Gilduinus [Note: [Col. 0810D] Namely, of the Church of Sens, from the year 1032.], whom I have undertaken to educate, and I lack books and instruments of the liberal arts. Yet, as we read long ago, nothing is so difficult that it cannot easily be done when someone does it willingly; so, recalling what I know, I shall satisfy your wish as far as I can.

The measurement of the regular monochord, dearest brothers, in which you ask to be instructed, may be carried out as follows, without prejudice to the authority of Father of the Fatherland, lord Boethius. Since a string cannot by its nature be divided or measured, let a square piece of wood be used, fully and carefully smoothed for this work, with a length of approximately two hand-feet and a thickness of approximately one palm. [Col. 0809D]

At the ends of this wood, using a geometric instrument—that is, a compass—draw two small circles, of equal measurement. Then take a carefully polished ruler and, with every precaution, draw it from the center of the first sphere to the center of the second, producing the straight diameter of those circles. Again take a compass and, fitted to the lower or upper part of the circles, let it touch the farthest ends of the first diameters, so that another pair of diameters is formed across the thickness of the wood. From these draw a straight line parallel to the first line of the diameters of the original figure, taking such care that it creates between itself and the other line a space equal to the measure of the fingernail of the little finger.

This plane surface, containing the force of a line, must be measured in this manner. Using a ruler with a compass, divide it into two equal parts. Again divide these same two parts into two others, so that the entire plane surface is divided from diameter to diameter into four equal parts. [Col. 0810C]

Let the string called nete hyperboleon therefore occupy the end of the third measurement, and let it be divided as far as the diameter into eight parts; add to it its own eighth part so as to complete the number nine. In this way a tone in the sesquioctave proportion is established between nete hyperboleon and paranete hyperboleon. In the same manner, to produce trite hyperboleon, preserve the ruler of the sesquioctave proportion from paranete hyperboleon to the point designated for it. [Note: [Col. 0810D] These and the following terms are also recited by Euclid, p. 3, and by Boethius, book I, chapters 20–25.]

The remaining semitone, needed to complete the diatessaron consonance, or to fill out the hyperboleon tetrachord, is to be determined as follows. Divide the hyperboleon string with a compass into three equal parts, and add one third of it to itself so as to produce a sesquitertian proportion. In this way the entire string will be called nete diazeugmenon.

Following the model of this first tetrachord, it is appropriate to construct the four tetrachords that follow in the diatonic genus. Again apply the compass to construct the diazeugmenon tetrachord, and divide nete diazeugmenon, which occupies the place of the semitone, into eight parts; add to it its own eighth part, occupying the interval of a tone, in order to construct paranete diazeugmenon. If someone wishes to proceed more easily and without great labor, let him divide nete hyperboleon into two equal parts and add half of it to the whole, so as to produce the diapente consonance, consisting of three tones and a minor semitone. Let him do the same with paranete hyperboleon, so that he obtains trite diazeugmenon, producing with it that diapente consonance. Let this method be observed in constructing the remaining tones, so that in the diapente consonance, which consists of a sesquialteran proportion, there are, as we have said, three tones with a minor semitone. [Col. 0811A]

Let us now see what the final string of this diazeugmenon tetrachord is. Divide nete diazeugmenon, following the model of the earlier tetrachord, into three equal parts with a compass, and add one third to it; thus the entire remaining string will be called paramese.

The synemmenon tetrachord is to be measured as follows. Divide lengthwise, by equal measurement, the little space contained between the two lines, each of which possesses a diameter on its respective side, so that the lower part belongs to diazeugmenon and the upper part to the synemmenon tetrachord. Let nete synemmenon occupy the place held by paranete diazeugmenon in relation to nete diazeugmenon—namely, the distance of a tone. This tone joins the hyperboleon tetrachord to the diazeugmenon tetrachord and separates the synemmenon from the hyperboleon; thus paranete diazeugmenon and nete synemmenon are almost one and the same. Similarly, let the distance occupied by trite diazeugmenon be a tone, and let paranete synemmenon be almost identical with it.

To obtain trite synemmenon through a consonance, divide trite hyperboleon into two parts and apply a sesquialteran proportion. Next comes mese, “middle” in power and name, connecting the conjunct and middle tetrachords. Let lychanos meson, immediately adjacent to it, be established by a sesquioctave proportion, taken from paranete diazeugmenon through a diapente consonance. Let the tone parhypate meson be tuned to this, preserving a sesquialteran relation to trite diazeugmenon. To find the end of this meson tetrachord, which displays the semitone, divide the meson string into three parts, and add one third of it to itself so as to produce a diatessaron consonance. [Col. 0811D]

Lychanos hypaton, which has already been said to contain a fourth part of the whole line and appears to be a sesquioctave distance from hypate meson, is to be made sesquialteran in relation to meson. Following its model, establish hypate hypaton, which preserves a diapente consonance in relation to lychanos meson and differs from it by a tone. Divide hypate meson into three parts, so that hypate hypaton, containing the semitone, is produced in a sesquitertian proportion. Next comes proslambanomenos, which also possesses the diameter of the left-hand sphere, a tone from meson, and a diapason. [Col. 0812A]

Thus far concerning the diatonic genus, which is more natural and harder. The remaining two genera are to be measured in the following way. Divide equally with a compass the interval containing a tone—that is, the interval between nete hyperboleon and paranete hyperboleon—and add half of it to itself; where the compass rests, let paranete hyperboleon chromatica be established. Trite diatonica is to be the same as trite chromatica. In the enharmonic genus, let paranete hyperboleon enharmonica be the same as trite hyperboleon diatonica. The semitone of the diatonic genus is to be divided in the enharmonic genus into diesis and diesis; and this is to be trite hyperboleon enharmonica.

It should also be known that every nete, paramese, mese, hypate, and proslambanomenos is immovable in all three genera, and serves as the beginning and end of the tetrachords; that the diatonic genus consists of two tones and a semitone; that the chromatic genus consists of three semitones, incomposite, and of major and minor composite semitones; and that the enharmonic genus consists of two incomposite tones and a diesis and a diesis. [Col. 0812B]

With these matters thus arranged, I humbly ask your holiness, beloved brothers, to pity me and sustain me with the oars of your prayers as I labor on the sea of this fleeting age, so that, with God as guide, I may deserve to reach the harbor of eternal salvation. If anyone desires to know fully the beginnings and ends, as well as the ascents, descents, and differentiae of the tones, let him diligently read for himself the letter I wrote to our brother and fellow priest Rotbertus. Contemplating the descriptions placed below with the eye of your heart, fare well and be happy. [Col. 0812C]

Then, with musical notes placed above them, the following verses appear:

By these signs a skillful person will be able to learn the marked chant,

without a singing teacher’s voice, from the diagrams written above,

if he distinguishes the *magada* string on the monochord.

[Note: Gloss in the manuscript: They call *magadam* what we call a *sesquisphaerium*, that is, a fourth part of a sphere.]

For the pleasant echo of the voice repeats this,

together with the consonances and tones, with a twofold *diaschisma*.

After this comes the *Greeting of the Apostles*, as it is inscribed, likewise with musical notation:

Hail, lights of the world,

Peter and Paul, most holy;

of whom one, joined to his Master

on the gibbet of the cross, while the other,

set at the sword’s throat, from heaven’s throne

governs the fabric of the world,

now almost near its end.

Ask for us wretched people, burdened

by the weight of sin, that with you

we may enjoy perpetual joy.

Various musical diagrams follow. Finally, the author continues: [Col. 0812D]

### The Ratio of All Consonances

It should be known that the proportion—that is, the comparison of numbers—which in arithmetic is called sesquitertian, that is, “one-and-a-third” (for *sescus* means “one other”), is called the diatessaron in music, from two and four, because, with two standing in the middle, the two extremes are joined to each other, as eight is to six. For eight contains the whole of six and its third part, namely two.

Similarly, what in arithmetic is called hemiolia or sesquialtera, that is, “one-and-a-half,” is called the diapente in music, as nine is to six. For nine contains the whole of six and its half, namely three. [Col. 0813A]

What in arithmetic is called duple is called the diapason in music, as twelve is to six; for twelve contains six twice over. And what in arithmetic is called epogdous, that is, taking the place of a point or unit, is called a tone in music, as nine is to eight; for nine contains the whole of eight and its eighth part, namely one. [Col. 0814A]

The triple proportion in arithmetic is called the diapason and diapente in music, as eighteen is to six; for eighteen contains six three times, and is twice double. Likewise, the quadruple proportion in arithmetic is called the bis diapason in music, as twenty-four is to six; for twenty-four contains twelve twice over and six four times, as the formula set out below demonstrates.

A diagram follows in the manuscript.

## OPUSCULUM VII

[Col. 0813]

To his brother Arembertus, Odorannus sends abundant greetings.

[Col. 0813B] Prompted by the encouragement of your delightful questions, I, your devoted servant, return these few answers to you. Amalarius, priest of the Church of Lyon, while criticizing the responsory of blessed Gregory whose beginning is “Looking from afar,” expresses wonder that the words of this responsory are nowhere found continuously, as they stand, in any of the prophets. If he had applied the subtle eye of his mind, he would surely have discerned several passages composed according to this same method, not only in the nocturnal but also in the daytime offices, such as “The Lord says, my words.”

Although the lord Gregory, vessel of election and dwelling-place of the Holy Spirit, has no need of our defense, we nevertheless explain briefly to those who are less diligent what we think about this matter. “Looking from afar” (understand: “I, Gregory”), that is, having contemplated [Col. 0813C] Christ’s coming after many ages: “Behold, I see the power of God coming,” that is, with the eye of true faith I behold fulfilled what the Psalmist says: “Awaken your power, O Lord, and come, that you may save us.” And as the prophet Isaiah says: “Behold, the name of the Lord comes from afar.”

“And a cloud covering the whole earth” (understand: “I see”), that is, the glory of the Lord filling the whole world, just as the Wisdom of God the Father confesses in its praise: “I caused an unfailing light to rise in the heavens, and like a cloud I covered the whole earth.”

“Go out to meet him” (understand: “all the faithful”), that is, with the Psalmist, go before his face with confession; “and say,” that is, believe in your heart and confess with your mouth, singing and making melody in your hearts to the Lord.

“Announce to us whether you are the one who is to reign over the people of Israel,” that is, reveal to us through your prophets your birth or the judgment to come, showing us your mercy so that we may be saved; or make known to us your salvation, you who reign over Israel—that is, over those who see God. [Col. 0813D]

This too, dearest brother, must be carefully observed: in the Psalms and the prophets, the future tense is set for the past, the past for the future, the present also for the past or future, and the past and future for the present. If anyone dislikes these things, let him seek more useful matters for himself.

Moreover, having resolved the question concerning *drama*, let us hasten to the mystical interpretation of the Shunammite. *Drachma*, *-ae*, of the first declension, is a kind of weight, an eighth part of an ounce, and is weighed by three scruples. [Col. 0814B] *Drama*, *-atis*, of the third declension, is called in Latin a “story” or “play.” Hence the antiphon is sung in honor of this virgin: “Sing for us the sweet songs of the *drama*.” By this we mean Solomon’s *Song of Songs*, in which, after many passages spoken in the person of the Church and suitably echoed in honor of the holy Mother of God, the synagogue proclaims in admiration of her:

“Return, O Shunammite; return, return, that we may look upon you.”

The repeated proclamation indicates that an excessive longing to see her is present in the heart of every believer.

Therefore, by the Shunammite—who, as we read in the Book of Kings, was sought throughout the whole land of Israel to serve King David and was found exceedingly beautiful, and in whose bosom the king is also said to have rested—blessed and ever-virgin Mary is represented. In her bosom the King of heaven is believed to have rested; and from her undefiled womb, having become human for our salvation, the same one, God and man, is proclaimed to have come forth like a king from his chamber.

It is rightly read concerning the Shunammite: “The king did not know her,” because blessed Mary, virgin before childbirth, virgin in childbirth, and virgin after childbirth, ineffably brought forth for us God and man without sexual union. [Col. 0814C]

Otherwise, what we have presented figuratively concerning the Shunammite remains to be understood mystically as referring to the holy Church, which has neither spot nor wrinkle. For when, with God’s gift, we strive to carve out from the divine Scriptures an understanding of some mystical meaning, we rub ears of grain with our hands together with Christ’s disciples.

*Sunam*, according to the true interpretation of Hebrew names, means “height.” Hence Abishag, beautiful among the daughters of Jerusalem, is described as having arisen; her name is interpreted as “ignorance of the will.” King David, whose name is interpreted as “strong of hand,” is said to have taken her to his side but not to have known her.

Adonijah, who is called the elder, is known to have sought her in marriage through Bathsheba, whose name is interpreted as “house of seven” or “house of those who administer the abbacy.” He is said to have been killed by the hand of Benaiah, whose name means “instructor” or “builder,” son of Jehoiada, whose name means “wise.”

Leaving these matters aside for a little while, with God leading us, let us return, according to the capacity of our small understanding, to the resolution of the mystical proposition. [Col. 0814D]

Through *Sunam*, which is interpreted as “height,” the eternal wisdom of God—the Word of the Father, through which all things were made—is rightly understood. Concerning it the Psalmist says: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established”; and: “You made all things in wisdom.” Concerning it Solomon also says: “All wisdom is from the Lord God, and it has always been with him, and exists before the age.”

The Apostle, having been caught up in mind to the third heaven and contemplating its excellence, proclaims: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments, and how unsearchable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor, or who first gave to him, so that he might be repaid? For through him, and with him, and in him are all things; to him be glory and dominion for ever and ever.” [Col. 0815A]

Through Abishag, whose name is interpreted as “ignorance of the will,” the holy Church of the elect is signified. Concerning it Solomon says: “Blessed is the barren and undefiled woman who has not known the marriage-bed in sin; she will bear fruit when souls are examined.” [Col. 0815B]

Anna too, the mother of holy Samuel, observing prophetically the fertility of the synagogue and the Church’s barrenness for a time, and finally the future fertility of the Church and the barrenness of the synagogue, declared: “The barren woman has borne many, and she who had many children has grown weak.”

For truly, once the ceremonies and animal sacrifices of the old law had ceased, our holy and undefiled mother, the Church of God, does not cease daily to beget children for God through the faith of believers and the regeneration of holy baptism.

Through King David, whose name is interpreted as “strong of hand,” the Son of God, who conquered the devil and the world, is rightly understood. Concerning him Daniel says: “I saw in a vision of the night, and behold, one like a Son of Man was coming with the clouds of heaven; and dominion and honor were given to him, and every people, tribe, and language shall serve him. His dominion is an everlasting dominion that shall not be taken away, and his kingdom shall not be destroyed.” [Col. 0815C]

He also restored humanity to paradise, as the Psalmist says: “You, O Lord, are the one who will restore my inheritance to me.” More particularly, Christ is called our inheritance, as the same Psalmist sings: “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance”; and: “Blessed is the people whose God is the Lord.”

To show that we are God’s inheritance, he added: “Blessed is the people whom the Lord has chosen as his inheritance.” [Col. 0815D]

Having said these things, let us turn our pen back to the order of the narrative.

Through the old age of King David the final period of the present age is rightly understood, in which God deigned to become human for our sake. Through his death, however, the true death of Christ hanging upon the cross for our redemption is signified. Moreover, through the Shunammite woman, who was sought out throughout all the regions of Israel and found to be exceedingly beautiful, who is also written to have been placed beside the king’s side to warm him, and in whose bosom the king rested, the holy universal Church is figured, as we have already said. Gathered from all nations, she is believed to be joined to Christ the true King through the unity of faith, as the Psalmist says:

[Col. 0816A] “The queen stood at your right hand in a garment of gold, clothed in varied adornment.”

In the gilding of the garment, the blood of Christ by which we were redeemed, or the anointing of sacred chrism, is signified; and in the varied adornment, the diverse distribution of the gifts of the Holy Spirit is marked. Christ rests in the bosom of the Church when, after his resurrection and about to ascend into heaven, he says to the apostles: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we shall come to him and make our dwelling with him.” Hence John also says: “If we love one another, God remains in us, and his love is perfected in us.”

Otherwise, Adonijah, whose name is interpreted as “elder,” designates the ancient people of the Hebrews. After seeing the Lord Christ suspended on the cross and dying, he wished, taking occasion from the old law, to subject the Church of the faithful to himself. He asks that the Shunammite woman be given to him through Bathsheba, when, wishing to subject Christ’s faithful to the carnal sacrifices of the temple, and also to the new moons and Sabbaths, he drives her away from Jerusalem.

The son of Jehoiada, however, Benaiah, who is called “wise” and whose name is interpreted as “instructor” or “builder,” attacks and kills him. This occurs while the wise architect of the Church and instructor of our conduct, the vessel of election, the apostle Paul, armed with the shield of faith, protected by the helmet of salvation, and strengthened by the sword of the Holy Spirit, rebukes the Jews, saying: “It was necessary that the word of God be spoken to you first; but since you rejected it and judged yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles.”

Writing to the Corinthians, he also says:

[Col. 0816C] “Was anyone called while circumcised? Let him not acquire foreskin. Was anyone called while uncircumcised? Let him not be circumcised.”

And to the Galatians he says:

“I, Paul, tell you that if you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing; for in Christ Jesus neither circumcision has any value nor uncircumcision, but faith working through love. And peace and the mercy of God be upon all who keep this rule.”

Simon Peter, James, and the other apostles are likewise read to have sent, by the hand of Barnabas and Paul, to those who had been converted from the Gentiles to faith in Christ through baptism, so that they would not be subjected to circumcision and the ceremonies of the old law, a letter of this kind in the Acts of the Apostles:

[Col. 0816D] “It has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us, brothers, to impose no further burden upon you beyond these necessities: that you abstain from the pollutions of idols, from blood, from things strangled, and from sexual immorality.”

Otherwise I declare [Note: [Col. 0815D] That is, Odorannus in the margin.] to all who are counted by the Christian name, but do not keep this law given to them by the Holy Spirit and by Christ’s disciples, that, unless they repent, they are not Christians. And if they are not Christians, then, as John testifies, they can certainly be called Antichrists, that is, those who stand against Christ. Concerning them we read elsewhere:

“They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would surely have remained with us.”

The followers of such people are called heretics, that is, alienated from God.

[Col. 0817A] On the other hand, King Solomon, whose name is interpreted as “peaceful,” of whom, as the history of the Kings reports, the whole earth desired to see the face, and by whose command Adonijah was also killed, may allegorically be understood as our peaceful King, Jesus Christ, Son of the living God, “into whom,” as the Apostle says, “the angels desire to look,” who through his blood made peace between the things in heaven and the things on earth.

He conquers the ancient enemy when he destroys the dwelling-place of his wickedness, Antichrist, the son of perdition, who is lifted up and exalted above everything called God or worshiped as God, as the Apostle declares: “The Lord Jesus,” he says, “will kill him with the breath of his mouth and destroy him by the manifestation of his coming.”

More [marginal note: “I shall say”]. Having dealt with those matters that seemed to belong to the mystical interpretation of the Shunammite woman, we thought it worthwhile to add a few things appropriate to moral interpretation.

In the Song of Songs already mentioned, under the person of the Shunammite, the words of the wise man prophesying about Christ and the Church run as follows:

“If you do not know yourself,” he says, “O beautiful among women, go out and follow the tracks of the flocks, and pasture your young goats”—whom another translation calls “lambs.”

The Church is called *ekklesia* in Greek and “the assembly of the righteous” in Latin. She is said not to know herself when, having renounced the pomp of original sin and set aside the worship of idolatry, she leaves the past behind with the Apostle and strives toward what lies ahead.

She is called beautiful among women when, compared with the gatherings of the synagogue, she is found purer through baptism.

She goes out with Abraham, the soul of the righteous leaving its land and its kindred, when, passing beyond the enticements of its own body, its pleasures, and the desires of its bodily senses, it hastens with humble mind toward higher things.

She proceeds after the tracks of the flocks when, following the footsteps of the preceding prophets and apostles, she desires to cling to the words and deeds of spiritual teachers.

She pastures her lambs when, ascending from virtue to virtue, she supplies nourishment for herself and her own by clinging to readings of the divine word.

To those who desire to pluck pasture from the divine word the Apostle says:

[Col. 0818B] “As to little ones in Christ, I gave you milk to drink, not solid food.”

And the Psalmist says:

“Taste and see that the Lord is good.”

The soul adorned with virtues such as these and similar ones deserves to be called a daughter of God, as the Holy Spirit suggested to her through the mouth of David:

“Hear, daughter, and see, and incline your ear, and forget your people,” by resisting idolatry or the ticklings of the flesh; “and the house of your father,” by fleeing the blemish of original sin or the pleasures of the body, lest they reach the point of consent.

Then you will be worthy to hear the bridegroom’s voice on the last day:

“You are wholly beautiful, my beloved, and there is no blemish in you. Come from Lebanon, come.”

May the charitable resolution of questions be a firm hope in Christ, the strength of our one faith.

## OPUSCULUM VIII

[Col. 0817]

[Col. 0817C] That every inequality, having proceeded from equality, returns in some manner to equality, may at times be doubtful among the learned; it belongs to a mind strengthened by purer reason to discuss it. But the common people, for whom doubt itself passes away, are plainly instructed by the Father of his country.

[Note: [Col. 0817D] Above, on col. 809, he called Boethius “Father of his country.”]

Therefore, in proportion to immortality, the providence of the Almighty created the human being at the beginning equal to the angels. Through disobedience to God’s commandments, however, he was changed from immortal to mortal and, alas, was expelled into the distress of this age that we endure.

But his Creator, unwilling that he suffer eternally, sent his Word and mercifully raised him not only to the equality of the citizens above but even exalted him above all created things, as the Prophet wonderfully says:

“You have subjected all things beneath his feet.”

Although this was specifically foretold of the man Christ Jesus, nevertheless that evangelical saying must be recalled attentively as applying to his members:

[Col. 0817D] “Whatever,” the same Lord said, “you bind on earth will be bound in heaven; and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven.”

This authority, with the cooperation of the Holy Spirit, was handed down through the intervals of time to the apostles and to their successors. The faithful must believe in their hearts and confess with their mouths that it remains unshaken.

[Col. 0818C] Strengthened nobly by this power, the holy Church of Sens, redeemed by the death of Christ Jesus and instructed by the words of the blessed martyr Savinianus, primate of the Gauls, and dedicated by the blood of the blessed protomartyr Stephen, now, together with the consent and will of that illustrious king [Note: [Col. 0817D] A general pronoun is used for a specific name, as happens in formulas.] of the Franks, and of the bishops, nobles, abbots, and clergy of the province, as well as the faithful of both sexes, proclaims that that lord [Note: [Col. 0817D] Likewise, as in the preceding note.] should become its supreme bishop. Rejoicing in his good works, it declares him worthy and suitable for this office, insofar as human frailty permits us to know.

Under his oversight, therefore, having dismissed every controversy, we resolve to serve in the service of the supreme Maker. We who fell to the depths through disobedience desire, by obedience, to become equal to the angels, so that, touched by the finger of discernment and struck by the plectrum of pious admonition, we may deserve to rejoice together with him upon the drum of abstinence and in the choir of unanimity.

And thus, joined in the harmony of the four principal virtues, may we always be able to praise God with this kind of concord:

“Let every spirit praise the Lord.”

(If the matter concerns an abbot, the appropriate wording of the place and persons should be honorably altered.)

[Note: [Col. 0818D] We observe in this and the following little work the custom and formula then prevailing in Gaul for proclaiming bishops. A different version is given by Acherius, *Spicilegium*, new edition, vol. III, p. 379.]

## OPUSCULUM IX

[Col. 0819]

[Col. 0819A] Elders and brothers, you ought to hear why you have been gathered here. When almighty God first created the human being, he granted him free will. But the human being, misusing free will by eating the forbidden fruit, was deprived of the seat of delights, while free will itself remained.

His followers, wandering from the way of truth for many ages and serving idols, were utterly ignorant of their Creator, until almighty God, appeased by the obedience of his servant Abraham, willed that he be circumcised. Afterwards, through his holy friend Moses, freeing Abraham’s descendants from Egyptian slavery and desiring Moses to preside over his people, he gave them the law through Moses’s hand.

After choosing Aaron and his sons, through the inspiration of his Spirit, for the honor of the high priesthood, God’s providence filled seventy men to preside over the people together with him. While their descendants continued through successive generations down to the prophet Samuel, God gave that people King David, of whom he says: “I have found David according to my heart.”

From David’s stock the Lord Jesus, by the will of the Father and with the cooperation of the Holy Spirit, took immaculate flesh from an immaculate Virgin, chose twelve apostles, and willed to be called by them Lord and Teacher.

To them the holy mother Church, the bride of the same Lord Jesus, was entrusted, and the power of binding and loosing was granted. As long as the circuit of this world revolves, that power remains stable and firm in their successors, namely, those who are called bishops.

Observe, therefore, dearest brothers, with what reason, piety, mercy, and moderation toward the human race almighty God acts, since he deigns to place over us not angels or archangels, but human beings naturally like ourselves.

It is therefore beneficial for you to please God by the performance of good works, so that you may have priests and rulers worthy of God, who by word and example may provide you with guidance for proceeding toward the heavenly kingdom.

Moreover, let your fraternity know that the holy Church of Troyes, widowed by the death of its bishop, has requested the presence of our lord Archbishop Gilduin [Note: [Col. 0819D] Concerning Archbishop Gilduin of Sens, see the *Annales Benedictini* under the years 1032 and following.] so that, according to the judgment of the holy canons, he might grant it a suitable bridegroom and shepherd.

Gladly agreeing to its petition, together with the consent and will of our lord Henry [Note: [Col. 0819D] From this we learn the date of this writing, namely, the reign of Henry I, who succeeded his father Robert, mentioned by Odorannus in the prologue, in the year 1031.] king of the Franks, and of his suffragans—namely, the bishops of Chartres, Orléans, Paris, Meaux, Nevers, and Auxerre—as well as of the nobles of the Franks and of the acclaim of the entire clergy and people, he gives it the lord Mainard, whom you see present, arch-keyholder of the holy Church of Saint Stephen, this holy mother Church’s pastor and bridegroom, born of noble stock and adorned with good morals.

[Note: [Col. 0819D] As if “supreme key-holder.” But I would prefer *arciclavus*, “one who holds the keys of the treasury.” For this Mainard was treasurer of the Church of Sens. See the cited *Annales* under the year 1032.]

Therefore, dearest brothers, we ask your charity to raise your voices on high and proclaim what pleases you concerning this matter.

This verse should be repeated three times, followed by the most fitting election of the clergy; then, if possible, by that of the metropolitan and all the bishops of the province; and finally by the blessing, with the metropolitan present, of no fewer than three bishops.

## OPUSCULUM X

[Col. 0819]

To Gilduin, archbishop of the holy mother Church of Sens, Odorannus, syncellus, detained by severe bodily illness, emulates the better gifts.

[Col. 0819C] The marvelous deeds of your predecessor, Archbishop Leutheric, of blessed memory, impel us to strive to obtain through the study of sacred readings the ability to bring forth things new and old. He always remained, in accordance with the Apostle, constant in prayer and indefatigable in meditation upon God’s law.

If it had been worthy for us at present to enjoy his bodily presence in this age, the new heresy of the Burgundians would by no means have sprouted [Note: [Col. 0820D] I would like a more thorough investigation of this Burgundian heresy.]. As you have informed me, they assert in a rebellious frame of mind that they owe nothing to their bishops if, when canonically summoned by them to come for the correction of their offenses, they delay coming.

To prevent them from remaining in so great an error, an antidote must be offered from the authority of the divine laws. Among other words of holy exhortation, the words of the Lord Jesus speaking with the apostles were as follows:

[Col. 0820C] “Whoever despises you despises me.”

Since priests hold the place of the apostles in the Church, they cannot be assailed by a greater insult than when, while supplying the divine word, they are despised by their subjects.

Lest ecclesiastical authority be weakened, worldly laws promulgated by Christian emperors under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit provide a contrary response. They prescribe that every insult against priests be compounded threefold.

The chapters of the glorious Emperor Charles, brighter than daylight, also contain the following:

“Concerning summonses made by bishops, we command that whoever neglects them shall pay threefold. But if an excommunicated person comes to make satisfaction, let him be received canonically.”

Having explained these matters, if you wish to know how the threefold payment is made, I shall state it briefly.

Every insult against any elder or advocate, whether contempt or scorn, excepting the king and priests, is punished by sixty solidi, that is, the value of three pounds. When the number three is multiplied by three, it therefore increases to nine. This is the law of the first episcopal summons, if it has been despised.

Nine multiplied by three produces the number twenty-seven. Consequently, this is the law of the second insult.

If the number twenty-seven is likewise increased threefold, it rises to eighty-one. And this is the law of the third priestly insult.

But if anyone—God forbid!—enslaved to the yoke of the devil and compelled by his sins, has been expelled from the Church according to our Lord’s command as a pagan and tax collector, and, in accordance with the Apostle, has been handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh so that the spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord, and if he wishes to return to the Catholic Church, let him first, as was said, make satisfaction to the priest; then, finally, by repenting, let him obtain reconciliation according to ecclesiastical custom.

Farewell.

## OPUSCULUM XI

[Col. 0821]

To the brothers of the monastery of Masciacum, worthy of desire and to be received with the greatest veneration, Ingo, abbot by the grace of God and not by his own merits [Note: [Col. 0821D] Concerning this man, Mabillon, *Annales Benedictini*, under the year 1014: “Ingo, a man of great nobility in the world and a fellow student of King Robert in Gerbert’s school, whom the abbacy of Saint Martin of Masciacum rewarded and afterward made illustrious in the world as abbot of Saint-Germain of Paris, as was fitting for so great a man,” says Helgaldus in his epitome of the life of King Robert.
