Yet he was unable to regulate the conduct of his monks so thoroughly that after his death they did not require correction. In the Chronicle of Clarius the monk, Ingo is called a relative of the king and is said to have become abbot of Saint Peter of Vivi the following year.” This, then, is the occasion on which Odorannus, who was a monk of Saint Peter of Vivi, wrote this epistolary exhortation in the name of Ingo, who had undertaken to govern badly behaved monks.]—offers the gift of perfect charity and the prize of eternal recompense.

[Col. 0821B] Disturbed, dearest brothers, by the various troubles of this age and afflicted by diverse evils, we ought to recognize the cause of those evils and, with the help of God’s mercy, avoid it once recognized.

The Holy Spirit reveals the cause of prosperity and adversity in these words:

“Justice exalts a nation; sin makes peoples wretched.”

The sin by which we are made wretched is credibly this: although we are Christians in faith, we sometimes destroy by our actions the profession of a monk. And because we prefer temporal happiness to eternal blessedness, we lose the latter unless we recover our senses, and we do not attain the former, however small it might be, if only we wished to be upright.

Since, therefore, God’s vengeance begins temporally in this life and continues into the next, which has no end unless conversion comes to our aid, let us all—whether superiors or subjects—lay aside every excuse.

And since each of us is conscious of the ways in which he has especially offended God, let us all listen to him together and obediently as he admonishes us:

“Return, transgressors, to your heart. Likewise: Wash yourselves; be clean; remove the evil of your thoughts from my eyes; cease to act perversely; learn to do good.”

Thus may you reach, through the salutary course of repentance, the safest harbor of forgiveness. In this way we shall be able not only to escape present evils but also to hope for those that are to come. Let us unlearn the desire for carnal things alone and at times think about attaining spiritual things.

And so that our desires may be restrained and keep some measure, let the swift passing of those whom we have seen flourishing greatly in the dignities of this age come to mind, and let us not forget that we follow them daily.

For without interruption we hasten toward death. Let us return to the customs by which the monastic order has until now grown and flourished. Let there be no pretenses, no conspiracies among us who invoke God as Father—among whom bishops say, “Peace be with you,” for whom all priests pray in agreement, “Mercifully grant peace in our days,” and, “May the peace of the Lord be always with you,” and to whom God deigns to promise:

“Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God.”

Let that threat of his not appear contemptible to us:

“Woe to the one through whom scandal comes!”

Lest, perhaps—may he himself avert it—mere affliction, as Isaiah says, eventually give understanding to the hearing, so that, placed in torments, we may learn by unhappy experience what we now do not believe or pretend not to know.

[Col. 0822C] Let none of us fail to recognize what learned men have proved and believed down to our own time: through harmony small things grow, but through discord even the greatest things fall apart.

Perhaps, while we desire to hold our possessions more securely or to climb more successfully toward the acquisition of transitory things, the ruin of the passing age—which we prepare for ourselves by our divisions—may, by God’s just judgment, overwhelm us and drag us into the destruction of soul and body.

When this little admonition of our humility, however slight, appropriate to the present time, reaches you, dearest fathers or brothers, I wish it to be read in the assembly of the brothers, so that through it our littleness may recall all the brothers to remembrance.

For I hope, once every doubt has been removed, that after the days of the feast of the Lord’s resurrection, if God grants me life, I shall be with you and remain among you for some time.

Farewell.

## OPUSCULUM XII

[Col. 0823]

[Col. 0823A] That every human being has been created to love and worship God is testified by Ecclesiastes at the end of his discourse in these words:

“Fear God and observe his commandments; this is the whole human being.”

That is, every human being was created for this purpose: to fear God and observe his commandments.

Our true preacher, the Lord Jesus, likewise offers his disciples, among other sayings sweeter than the sweetest honey, these words:

“What I say to you I say to all: watch!”

And:

“Fear him who can destroy soul and body in Gehenna.”

As his passion drew near, he also taught them to preserve the patience of unanimity in this way:

“I give you a new commandment: that you love one another as I have loved you.”

And as he ascended into heaven, he prayed to the Father, saying:

“I pray not only for these, but also for those who will believe in me through their word, so that they too may be one in us.”

Luke likewise thundered in the Acts of the Apostles concerning followers of this kind:

[Col. 0823B] “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul, and they held everything in common.”

Thus, while the holy Church of the elect, founded by the apostles, flourished in these and similar virtues through many cycles of years, the devil, envious of every good, poured the malignant poison of his invention into the minds of heretics, caused divisions to boil up among the faithful, and disturbed the virtue of unanimity as far as he could.

But the holy Church, well founded upon the firm rock—that is, Christ—could not be shaken by any disturbances of heretics. As the Holy Spirit moved through the hearts of spiritual teachers, she remained immovable.

[Col. 0823C] Among these teachers, the lawgiver Benedict, striving to gather people of one mind in the house of God, wrote a rule for monks, distinguished by discernment and brilliant in expression, in which the great power of unanimity is clearly shown.

Although, as the Apostle says, faith is not possessed by all, beneficence toward the brothers is nevertheless the duty of all. Although the holy universal Church is distributed among different orders, she is nourished and governed by the bowels of one charity.

Burning with love for her, the humble congregation of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, and likewise of the holy apostles Savinianus and Potentianus [Note: [Col. 0823D] See the *Lives of the Roman Pontiffs*. Since mention of these Lives has arisen here, I am pleased now to clarify somewhat a certain passage in the Life of Soter. It says there: “This pope decreed that a wife should not be considered legitimate unless she had been blessed by a priest.” From where did the biographer derive this very ancient authority? Certainly it is absent from the Isidorian letters of Soter, but it is present in the first Isidorian letter of Evaristus. I think our biographer took it from Burchard, book IX, chapter 7, who in fact cites Soter in place of Evaristus. The old author of the Lives of the Pontiffs, whom we commonly call Anastasius, does not recount that statement or law of Soter. Yet since Anastasius, in the Life of Saint Sylvester, orders that a bishop be made one who is the husband of one wife blessed by a priest, it is reasonably permissible to infer that a canon concerning marriages contracted in Christian fashion existed before Sylvester, relying upon which Sylvester issued his own law that a bishop should be chosen only from offspring of such marriages, as though those marriages were not pious and Christian unless they had been blessed by a priest.] and of their companions at the village of Sens, desires that the fellow-provincial priests or any faithful people suitable for undertaking this work be joined to its fraternity by the bond of charity, not only bodily but also spiritually.

This is to be done on the following terms: if any one of them falls ill, he is to be visited by the abbot or the brothers according to ecclesiastical custom, or by the other fellow priests; and if he dies, seven Masses are to be sung by each monk who is a priest, or by the other priests, for the salvation of his soul. In the assembly of the brothers, after the first hour of the day and before the litany is said, the Psalter is to be sung in its entirety.

In return for this arrangement, what has been prescribed for the priests is likewise to be done for the monks by those priests or monks.

And every year, just as a neglected fast or a neglected feast is made up on the feast of All Saints, so on the first following day the commemoration of all the faithful departed is to be solemnly celebrated in the same monastery by the abbot or the neighboring brothers, for the sake of God’s charity, with a public almsgiving to the poor and a bodily charitable meal afterward.

And so that this exhortation may endure perpetually (the manuscript reads *perpete*), we record the names of the present brothers and earnestly ask that henceforth the names of deceased brothers be designated.

The arrangement is to be firm as follows: according to ecclesiastical custom, after the priest has offered the exhortation of prayer after the offertory of the Mass, the subdeacon, standing behind the altar, is to recite at the proper place the names of the living household members and of the dead.

Moreover, it must be known that if difficulty—whether of place, time, or any other circumstance—arises in visiting the sick person, each individual should, in his own place, offer him the comfort of fraternal charity, as stated above; and if he dies, he should do likewise.

And if the monks become weary of singing the Psalter, let them celebrate a Mass for the dead in the assembly of the brothers.

On the very day on which this testament was confirmed in the chapter-house of Saint Peter by the text of the holy Gospel, alternately, it was decreed that twelve priests from among those who are outside should sing one Mass each week, one for each apostle; and that in the assembly of the monks a Mass should be celebrated once a week in honor of all the apostles.

The remaining priests or brothers, each week, are to sing one Mass individually for the souls of all the faithful departed, so that God may grant them rest, and grant us the tranquility of peace, the fertility of the earth, through the intercession of the apostles, and the happiness of life.

### How the things stated above are to be done

When the brothers have gathered together, after the reading has ended, the abbot is to say: “Let us bend our knees.” When the prayer has ended, he is to say: “Rise.”

Then, with everyone standing, the abbot, after the greeting—that is, “The Lord be with you”—is to say this prayer:

[Col. 0826A] “O God, who by the illumination of the Holy Spirit [enlighten] the hearts of the faithful, etc., as in today’s liturgy.”

Likewise another:

“O God, whose proper attribute is always to have mercy and to spare, etc., as in the present liturgy.”

Finally another:

“Grant, we ask, almighty and merciful God, forgiveness to all the faithful departed and indulgence to the living, so that, by your generosity, we may together deserve to attain eternal life. Through, etc.”

## OPUSCULUM XIII

[Col. 0825]

To Ayrfred, teacher of the holy Church of Orléans and archimandrite of the monastery of Saint Avitus, and also to Hugh, archdeacon of the holy mother Church of Sens, the unworthy brother Odorannus offers the gift of the prayers of the faithful through the mercy of God.

[Col. 0825B] If, while wandering around the cells of gyrovagues, I were serving the temptations of the belly and my own pleasures, or if, together with ox-drivers, I were turning the clods of the valleys with the hardest plow while frost and heat scorched them, perhaps no one would envy me.

But because, residing in a monastery, I desire diligently to investigate the truth of subtle things—things that exist and that receive an unchanging essence of their own—I suffer curses and insults from rivals. As though raised from some precipitous depth of mind, I am compelled to answer their slander.

Because, as I recall having written in my lament, I preferred to remain silent before the wicked rather than answer them, I would not have given a reply unless, while trying to pierce me with an arching blow, those wretched men had inflicted upon themselves with their poisonous tongues the deadly poison of the anthropomorphites.

Thus, while, driven by envy and senseless concerning the truth, they accuse me of saying—God forbid!—that, holding a wrong opinion about God, I have said that he is mutilated in his hands or disabled in any of his limbs, they rush headlong into the aforementioned heresy, asserting that God is composed of bodily features.

The blessed Augustine, offering the antidote of the Catholic faith, responds to them from the opposite side, saying that nothing bodily is to be believed to have been formed in God [Note: [Col. 0825C] Here this little work ends in the manuscript. Mabillon had indeed published this same work, written entirely by Odorannus and likewise mutilated, in the *Annales Benedictini* under the year 1022, book LV, no. 4. Nevertheless, I have retained it so that my edition of Odorannus might not lack this fragment, whatever its value.]

[Col. 0825] What follows in the manuscript is a prose hymn, or, as the Greeks call it, a *canon*, with musical tones, in praise of Saints Savinianus, Potentianus, and their companions. Its author appears to be Odorannus himself, since he later adds his own name in the manuscript, as we shall see below.

The *Annals of the Benedictines*, under the years 1016, 1025, and 1028, report that Odorannus made a precious shrine for Saint Savinianus at the command and expense of King Robert and Queen Constance, for the solemn translation of his relics. I think that he also wrote the hymn at that time.

In any case, no one has written more eloquently than Odorannus himself about all the honor bestowed upon the holy martyrs and the procession that was conducted, in his Chronicle under the year 1031.

## IN HONOR OF SAINT SAVINIANUS AND HIS COMPANIONS

### HYMN

[Col. 0825]

[Col. 0825C] Holy Savinianus, precious martyr of Christ, pray for us together with your companions, we ask. *Evovae.*

O wondrous initiation of the prelates of the Church of Sens, by which the flock enslaved to demons recognized the shepherd of shepherds! O glory of pontiffs and honor of those who strive, do not deny us, your servants, your assistance!

Let the company of holy faithful people rejoice in this temporal world by celebrating the solemnities of Savinianus and Potentianus; eternal Jerusalem, praising Christ, exults at their triumph.

Let us all praise the King of kings, the Lord, who chose Savinianus as his most holy one and made Potentianus his co-heir.

Savinianus was Hebrew by birth and was one of Christ’s disciples, whom he commanded to go forth two by two.

He [Col. 0826C] had been thoroughly instructed in the doctrines of the ancient law. From the Lord’s mouth he also learned words of salvation.

Charity joined to him, and uprightness united to him, men of distinguished merit, supporters of the true faith. Having become Christ’s forerunners, they were renowned for miracles and, together with the other disciples, brought peace to the peoples.

*Evovae.*

When Christ sought the stars, virtuous men were added to the prince of the apostles, obedient to his commands.

After Peter had obtained the seat of the chair of the city of Rome, he summoned Savinianus, urging him to visit the Gauls [Note: [Col. 0825C] Savinianus, Potentianus, and Altinus were sent from the city of Rome by the holy apostle Peter into Gaul to preach Christ; Serotinus and Odaldus, or Eodaldus, joined them. The author of the Lives of the Pontiffs, whom we have published in this *Spicilegium*, vol. VI, p. 6, relates this. The observations we made there concerning the Gallican Church’s origin from the Roman Church are confirmed by this hymn, written in the time of King Robert, in which the aforementioned apostolic men are named and celebrated for this very reason.].

*Evovae.*

Let us celebrate the solemn feast of the glorious martyrs of Christ, Savinianus and Potentianus, who, recalling Gaul at Sens from error, earned heavenly things by giving their own blood.

Bringing back to Christ the King and Lord a gift acceptable to him—the people who had been lost—they merited heavenly things, etc.

[Col. 0827A] The holy prince of the Church, Peter, instructed them to scatter the seeds of the divine word in Gaul. At his command they assailed this city with the bow of faith.

They draw the famous city of Sens away from the worship of the devil, and for the true and Catholic faith, [they assail] it with the bow [of faith], etc.

When the devout archbishop Savinianus approached the town of Sens, fortified on every side with spiritual weapons, he turned the minds of the unbelievers toward love of himself and placed upon their necks Christ’s gentle yoke and light burden.

For he crushed the profane efforts of the pagans and triumphed successfully over his enemies.

Endowed with the presage of the heavenly Spirit, the supreme bishop soon approached the metropolitan city of Sens.

*Evovae.*
The virtue of which the illustrious Potentianus and Altinus, the chosen soldiers of Christ, offer an example. Evovae.

[Col. 0827B] Moreover, with great-hearted effort they press upon the pagans, destroying their shrines and strengthening the rights of Christ. Evovae.

The profane host marvels at Christ’s unheard-of teaching and at the arrival of renowned leaders of wisdom. Evovae.

Then, as the proclamation of many miracles shines forth, the peoples eagerly seek to obtain Christ’s baptism. Evovae.

The grieving enemy, seeing himself crushed by their ancient triumphs, kills Christ’s athletes through the savage deceits of the wicked. Evovae.

Savinianus, poor in spirit, and the people of Senones, rich in the fatness of the earth, encountered one another on the road of this pilgrimage and were brought into harmony; the Lord cooperated with both, granting to the former constancy for instructing them in truth and faith, and to the latter the efficacy of believing and obeying. To both, [Col. 0827C] etc.

Golden Rome sends the illustrious bishop Potentianus and Altinus, the devout fellow minister of God’s word. Together they endure extraordinary sufferings for God, seeing in the supreme pontiff an example of patience and virtue. These two together, etc.

The praiseworthy Potentianus, running willingly toward every kind of torment and at last strengthened in faith in Christ, offers his neck and, crowned with blood, returns his soul to the Lord. His body, exposed to beasts and birds, remained untouched by God’s providence alone. His soul, etc.

The glorious athlete of the Lord, the pontiff Savinianus, having happily endured many struggles for Christ, at last—without delaying to be slaughtered by the sword of the pagans, as he had long desired—was taken from human affairs and departed to the rewards of his labors. For he was summoned to their pestilential council and condemned to death [Col. 0827D] for Christ; to human affairs, etc.

O happy and praiseworthy brief suffering of the saints, made a restoration of salvation for faithful peoples! Evovae.

While the people, rejoicing with blessed Savinianus, hastened by the thousands to baptism, the ancient serpent roused the ministers of his error against the holy bishop. [Col. 0828A] When the ancient enemy saw the worship of idols and the snares of his contrivance being undone, the ministers, etc.

The outstanding Savinianus, contending in the struggle, nobly underwent his final ordeal for the Lord beneath the dreadful sword of the impious, his head delivered up; immediately ascending to heaven, he was found worthy to receive the rewards of his labors. The funeral of the same man is carried by the hands of the faithful disciples to the mausoleum. The rewards, etc.

Today blessed Savinianus, with his company of brothers, ran the contests of the world; today, having shed his blood, he received the palm of glory; today, freed from the flesh, he follows into heaven the Lamb, the Son of God. Wonderful and blessed adornment of the saints, to be crowned in heaven and venerated on earth! Today, freed from the flesh, etc.

The pleasing retinue of his friends follows the athlete of the Lord Savinianus as he walks along the road of martyrdom: namely, the holy [Col. 0828B] Potentianus, the equally noble Altinus, the illustrious Eodaldus, and the holy Serotinus. For, having been afflicted by the danger of death at the hands of the impious, they were found worthy to attain the glory of martyrdom. The holy, etc.

Glory to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit.

The illustrious cultivators of the Lord’s harvest, Savinianus and Potentianus, brought back from Christ’s sowing seeds doubled. Evovae.

Shining with the gift of a twofold charity, they excelled completely in love of God and love of neighbor. Evovae.

Placed by the Lord among wolves like lambs, the holy martyrs of Christ, with minds most ready for Christ, scorned their purse, their bag, and their other provisions. Evovae.

Returning radiant with miracles, those same holy disciples rejoiced and said to the Lord: “Behold, the demons are subjected to us through the power of your might.” Evovae.

Christ said: “Do not rejoice that you rule over spirits, but rejoice because your names are written in heaven.” Evovae.

O most illustrious gem of the martyrs, Savinianus, obtain pardon for us through your holy intercession, and come to our aid in distress and affliction. Grant us, holy martyr, help in whatever tribulation, and come to our aid. Glory to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit.

Today the glorious athlete of the Lord, the pontiff Savinianus, followed by the pleasing retinue of his friends, departed to the rewards of his labors; may his devout intercession with God release us from every danger! Evovae.

Let us celebrate Christ with the festive rejoicing of praise, recounting the glorious trophy of Savinianus and likewise the triumphal dance of his companions, that through their prayer we may enjoy heavenly assistance. The outstanding conqueror Savinianus, together with his band of companions, is pursued by torments and struck down by the sword; having overcome these things, they rejoice without end in the presence of God.

[Col. 0827] END OF THIS WORK AND ADMONITION TO THE READER.

With God as author and governor, Odorannus, a monk nearly sixty years old, wrote this book, although his intellect was still vigorous while his eyesight was already dim and his limbs growing cold. You who read, pray for him.

[Col. 0829]

## SENONIAN EPITAPHS.

### [Note.]

On the following page of the same codex, five epitaphs of Senonian bishops are written in an equally ancient hand; in addition, there are two others of Senonian monks, namely Rainardus the abbot and Ludovicus, formerly a count. Whether Odorannus himself collected these in this codex—he was certainly younger than them all—or someone else, is uncertain. I scarcely doubt, however, that these epitaphs are known to learned students of Gallican antiquities. For the present, nothing prevents me from appending them here. I have added the years of each person’s death from the Benedictine Annals.

### EPITAPH OF LORD EGILO, ARCHBISHOP.  
*(He died in the year 870.)*

[Col. 0829A]

Here lie buried the limbs of the life-giving  
Bishop Egilo, whom the heavenly palace receives.

### EPITAPH OF ANSEGISUS, ARCHBISHOP.

[Note: [Col. 0829B] In the codex there is this ancient annotation: “In the year from the incarnation of the Lord 883, Ansegisus, archbishop, second pope of all Gaul and Germany, died happily on the seventh day before the Kalends of December.” Mabillon agrees concerning the year of his death in the *Benedictine Annals* under this year.]

Anseisus, bishop of the Senones, lies enclosed here;  
at Christ’s judgment he too will rise.

Primate of the Gauls (the codex reads *primax*), raised by Pope John,  
he deserved this through his outstanding merits.

Here he established King Charles as Roman emperor;  
he pleased the Frankish princes.

He brought here with him the head of Pope Gregory.  
A lover of peace, he himself died lamented by the devout.

### EPITAPH OF HELDEMANNUS, BISHOP.  
*[Note: [Col. 0829B] Here and in the following epitaphs, the persons are actually called bishops, not archbishops, in the codex. He died in the year 958.]*

[Col. 0829B]

Pastor of a beautiful congregation, and himself beautiful,  
behold Heldemannus lies in this tomb.

Formerly a monk of the outstanding martyr Dionysius,  
afterward an excellent bishop of the city of Senones.

His happy life offered comfort to the wretched;  
therefore he now enjoys the starry throne.

He died on the Nones of August. Pray, I ask, reader,  
that he may live forever with the Lord in heaven.

### EPITAPH OF ANSTASIUS, BISHOP.  
*(He died in the year 977.)*

Once a shepherd guarding God’s fold, Anstasius  
now places his spirit among the heavenly beings, while his ashes rest here.

He was devout, a strong fighter, and, supported by love of God,  
rich in the gracious conversation of the Word.

Whatever the world loves, he rejected with virtuous goodness;  
the Davidic prophet was present upon his pious lips.

When January had reached its sixth day before the Ides,  
he died. Therefore, I pray, spare your servant, O God.

### EPITAPH OF SEVINUS, BISHOP.  
*(He died in the year 995.)*

This humble tomb, deservedly venerated by all,  
contains the noble remains of Sevinus.

His blessed soul heaven possesses  
among the holy number of shepherds.

Gentle, he endured much while seated in this see  
for the honor of the holy religion.  
[Note: [Col. 0829B] Mabillon recounts some misfortune of Sevinus the bishop [Col. 0830B] in the *Benedictine Annals* under the year 995.]

Now, having grown old, he departed to the stars, there to be placed.  
We ask that the almighty Lord spare him.

### EPITAPH OF RAINARDUS, ABBOT.

[Note: [Col. 0830B] In an ancient hand in the margin: “He was the nephew through his sister of Sevinus the archbishop.” The monastery over which he presided was Saint Peter the Living at Senones, as is written in a later hand in the margin. He died in the year 1015.]

[Col. 0830B]

The jewel of fathers, and also the shining diadem of monks,  
is covered by this tomb in the office of death.

His name was Rainardus; gentle in mind,  
he was a sweet adornment to monks and servants.

No one flourishes through the ages better than he in piety,  
noble in body, nobler in merits.

May the almighty Lord, ever and everywhere merciful,  
grant him life after death without end.

### EPITAPH OF LORD LUDOVICUS, COUNT AND MONK.

Born from royal stock, he lies buried here,  
Ludovicus, who performed the office of count in the world,

whom Alamannia freely gave to us as a monk.

[Note: [Col. 0830B] Concerning this Ludovicus, count of the Alamanni and afterward a Senonian monk, see Mabillon, the work cited above, under the year 1015, which was Ludovicus’s final year.]

## IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1049. SAINT ODILO, FIFTH ABBOT OF CLUNY.

[Col. 0831]

# HISTORICAL EULOGY OF SAINT ODILO, BY MABILLON.

*(Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict, Sixth Century, p. 631.)*

## I. Writers of His Life.

[Col. 0831A]

### 1.

What we did in the preceding century concerning the first four abbots of the monastery of Cluny must also be done here by us in honor of blessed Odilo: besides the Life of him written by ancient authors, which does not adequately set forth the deeds of so great a man, we should compose his eulogy not only from ancient authors but also from various charters drawn from the Cluniac archive and from other ancient documents. In this way the illustrious actions of so great a man will be represented more easily and accurately; and so many ancient monuments will contribute no little to illuminating the history of the monastic order in this age.

### 2.

We begin with those who undertook to commit the deeds of the blessed abbot to writing for posterity. Saint Odilo had two principal writers of his Life, namely Jotsaldus and Cardinal Peter Damian, both his contemporaries.

Jotsaldus—for this is the consistent form found in the ancient codices, although in some printed editions he is incorrectly written as Lotsaldus—was the first writer of the Life. He was a monk of Cluny and a disciple of blessed Odilo, as he himself bears witness in the preface to his work, where he declares that he was nurtured by the instruction of the great Odilo and formed by his beneficence.

This man himself is, unless I am mistaken, Josaldus, one of the five monks who is found to have subscribed, together with Odilo the abbot and Robert the prior, a charter of a certain Girbaldus in the year 1032. Josaldus and Joserannus are likewise named as brothers in a charter of Bernardus and Ada, their father and mother, which was drawn up during the reign of Robert.

Furthermore, a notary Josaldus is read to have subscribed many documents of the Cluniac archive from this period; we do not think that he was a different man from ours. He also seems to be the Josaldus mentioned in a catalogue of the old books of the library of the monastery of Cluny, where it is said that he wielded his pen against Berengarius, the heresiarch, in the time of Henry, king of the Franks. That work has perished—or at least lies so unknown that no one has yet seen it or found it cited anywhere.

Finally, we have Jotsaldus the abbot, whose epitaph is read affixed to the outer wall of the old church of Saint Peter at Cluny in these words: “Here lies Lord Jodsaldus, abbot.” But whether one and the same Jodsaldus is praised in all these monuments, or different men of that name are being designated, is entirely uncertain.

### 3.

The Life of Saint Odilo written by Jotsaldus—or rather, a fragment of it—was published by Andreas Duchesne in the Appendix to the *Cluniac Library* under the name of the Anonymous of Silviniacum, and by Joannes Bollandus on 2 January. But here we present it in full from a manuscript of the Thuanean library, which Chiffletius testifies that he saw in the proofs of the *History of Tournus*. We also had the same work from two other manuscript codices, one belonging to the monastery of Crespy, the other to our library of Saint-Germain-des-Prés.

Moreover, the same Jotsaldus published a poem entitled *Lamentations* on the death of blessed Odilo, which appeared in the *Cluniac Library*. But since it contributes nothing to the elucidation of the blessed man’s deeds, we thought it best to omit it [Note: [Col. 0831C] We give the complete poem below. EDITOR OF THE *PATROLOGY*]; it is enough to select a few verses in which he sings thus of Odilo and William, abbot of Dijon:

At the same time William also departed, perhaps on the Kalends,  
himself a great Father of the monks of Dijon.

These men had at last been monks of holy Maiolus,  
flourishing in one period, in purity of body,  
and friends of the one faith and of true piety.

Faith joined them both; they had similar departures:  
their glory was not unequal, and the same crown follows them. [Col. 0832C]

At the end of the poem he asks Odilo to remember him and Almanius before God. Almanius, however, is perhaps the very man to whom Odilo had dedicated the Life of Saint Maiolus, together with Hugh. For there he calls him his dearest brother, and it is clear that he was a learned man from the fact that he asks him and Hugh, if anything should be found incorrectly stated in the Life, to correct it.

[Col. 0833A]

Farewell now, Odilo; remember Jotsaldus,  
and ever kindly attend to the prayers of your Almanius.

### 4.

The other writer of blessed Odilo’s Life was Saint Peter Damian, cardinal and bishop of Ostia, a man sufficiently renowned by his own name. At the urging of Hugh, abbot and successor of blessed Odilo, he undertook this work so that what was narrated more fully in the earlier Life might be recounted more briefly after unnecessary material had been removed.

Since this later Life contains nothing that Jodsaldus had not previously related, it seemed sufficient to retain the earlier one. Indeed, as Baronius himself attests, this Life is very slight and far from equal to the merits of so great a man. If anything worthy of notice should nevertheless occur in it, we shall present it when occasion arises in the eulogy or in the notes to the other Life.

Besides these [Col. 0833B] writers of the Life, many others celebrated the deeds of blessed Odilo in their writings. We shall not fail, as appropriate, to quote their words—or at least those of the more celebrated among them—in their proper places throughout this eulogy.

We also have at hand a discourse by an Anonymous on the praises of blessed Odilo, copied from a manuscript of the monastery of Silviniacum. But since it contains nothing that illuminates the history of so great a man, we thought it best to omit it.

## II. The Homeland and Parents of Blessed Odilo.

### 5.

Everyone unanimously acknowledges that Odilo was an Auvergnat by birth, and the commonly cited authors affirm that he came from the noble family of the Mercorii. There are, indeed, legitimate arguments to prove this.

Andreas Duchesne, a very learned man, offers proof of the matter in his notes on Odilo’s Life in the Appendix to the *Cluniac Library*. There he cites an old Necrology of the Church of Clermont, lent to him by Savaron, in which, on the fourth day before the Nones of January, it is said that Odilo of Mercorio, canon of Clermont and provost of Brioude, left forty solidi of annual revenue to that same church for the celebration of blessed Odilo’s feast in the church of Clermont.

“For what purpose,” the learned man adds, “would that Odilo of Mercorio have expended so large a sum of money, unless blessed Odilo had been his kinsman?”

Furthermore, Bishop Stephen, to whom Jotsaldus dedicated the Life of blessed Odilo, and whom the same author asserts to have been the holy man’s nephew, is the very man who appears in the commonly circulated catalogues of the bishops of Anicium, or Le Puy, under the name Stephen of Mercorio. Gisseius, in his *History of the Bishops of Le Puy*, the Sammarthani in *Gallia Christiana*, and other writers who have treated these matters explicitly affirm this.

All doubt is removed by an old manuscript Chronicle of Saint Peter of Le Puy, from which our Stephanotius copied these words:

“Stephen, pastor of Anicium, was born of a noble family from the castle commonly called Mercurio, the nephew of blessed Odilo, abbot of Cluny . . . . He died and was buried at the monastery called Volta, which he himself had built with blessed Odilo, his maternal uncle, on their own land. He died on 4 August, while Henry was reigning as king of the Franks; he departed to Christ amid the weeping of the peoples and the rejoicing of the angels.”

He then adds that Peter, the nephew and episcopal successor of Stephen, a bishop of blessed memory, was buried in the same monastery of Volta with his uncle. We shall say more below about the monastery of Volta.

Certainly Peter Damian observed in Odilo’s Life that blessed Odilo traced his origin to a most illustrious family of Auvergne, asserting that he derived his lineage from a knightly family. Jotsaldus likewise bears witness to this when he says that Beraldus, surnamed the Elder, the father of blessed Odilo, was the most noble among the leading men of Auvergne and exceedingly rich in possessions and earthly power. His mother he calls Girberga, distinguished no less by piety than by nobility; after her husband’s death, she survived him and, he writes, became a nun in the monastery of Saint John at Autun.

Odilo also had brothers, and quite a number of them, but Jotsaldus withheld their names. He praises his sister Blitsemodis as an abbess, but nowhere states which monastery she governed.

### 6.

We learn more about blessed Odilo’s family from two charters in which the holy man lists his brothers and some of their children.

The first is Odilo’s own charter, by which, before he assumed the monastic habit, he granted certain possessions to the monastery of Cluny. It is undated and is number 11 in the Cluniac cartulary commonly called that of Saint Maiolus. It reads as follows:

“To the most holy Church of God, the monastery of Cluny, dedicated in honor of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, I, Odilo, son of Beraldus, in the name of God, with the consent of my mother and my brothers, namely Stephen, Ebo, Beraldus, and Bertrannus, cede something from the property belonging to me, which came to me by lawful succession; and I will and desire that what has been ceded remain so forever.

“These possessions are situated in the land of Auvergne, in the county of Brioude, in the vicariate of Aurata, in the village called Saruciacus. In that village I cede to God and holy Peter, for the support of those serving the aforesaid church, the entire church built in honor of the Savior of the world, together with whatever share of my inheritance at that place has been granted to me.

“I further cede one holding cultivated by Leotardus, son of Gerbaldus. Long ago my mother, my brothers, and I gave it for the burial of our brother Hicterius; afterward I bought it back from my brothers, fathers, and lords, namely the canons of my most blessed lord and martyr Julian, and gave one hundred solidi as its price. I likewise cede this holding to the aforementioned church, not only for myself but also for my father, my mother, and my brothers, both living and dead, and for the salvation of all our parents and faithful.

“I cede these aforesaid possessions to the often-mentioned church on the condition that the pastor of that church, namely Lord Abbot Maiolus, for as long as he lives, and his successors for all time, together with the servants of that church, may have, hold, and possess them and may do with them whatever they wish in due order. Nevertheless, they shall not presume to alienate or sell them except to my brothers.

“If anyone—something I by no means believe will happen—should at any time arise, whether I myself after changing my will, or any of my heirs, or any person put forward or opposed for the purpose, and should presume to disturb this charter with any claim, let him incur the wrath of almighty God and the offense of the saints; moreover, let him be compelled to pay ten pounds of gold and an equal weight of silver to the person against whom he has brought the suit.

“And so that this charter may possess firmer force in the ages to come, I have confirmed it below with my own hand, and I have decreed that it be strengthened by the hands of other men.

“Sign of Odilo, who asked that this charter be written. Sign of Girberga, his mother. Sign of Stephen, Ebo, Beraldus, and Bertrannus, his brothers. Sign of Beraldus, Rotbert, Gozfret, Warinus, Bernardus, Miro, Gualterius, and Guitbertus, who wrote this charter.”

### 7.

The second charter, which is more important because it contains the foundation of the monastery of Volta, was issued in the year 1025. In it not only blessed Odilo’s brothers but also many of their descendants are listed.

We have therefore not hesitated to reproduce it here in full, though it is lengthy, copied from the Cluniac cartulary:

“It is rightly and soundly judged useful and fitting by all the faithful who think wisely that all affairs arranged for the worship of God and the advancement of ecclesiastical dignity should be commended by their very authors to the posterity of the faithful through legal testaments and written documents.

“Warned, therefore, by this authority, I, Odilo, monk and priest of the monastery of Cluny, in the name of God, wish and desire that the newcomers and inhabitants of this region and homeland, throughout the ages to come, should know that my brothers—men of most illustrious and most beloved memory to me and to all our friends—Beraldus, provost of the Church of Anicium, Bertrannus, Lord Stephen, an honorable elder, and Ebo, a man of good simplicity, resolved with a common vote and common desire to build a little monastery on a certain small estate of theirs and to order it to the service of God according to the measure of their ability.

“But some of them, alas, hindered by most bitter circumstances and misfortunes, and others overtaken by the lot of nature, could not begin and complete what they desired. After their death, their sons came together with me, along with my other nephews and kinsmen and many of their faithful. They also began to ask what they should do concerning the deaths of my aforesaid brothers, their fathers, parents, and lords, or whether we could find some counsel that might provide them with a saving remedy from the Lord.

“We could find no other remedy more salutary or more appropriate than to undertake the very beginning and completion, according to our ability, of what they had left for our deliberation: namely, to build a monastery on one of their small estates in accordance with their vow and to order it to the service of God according to our ability.

“When this plan had been determined and praised with eager voices by all our friends and neighbors, we began to build a church on a certain hill belonging to us, called Volta, because it is enclosed on three sides by the waters of the river Hilaris—the Allier—and, so to speak, is wrapped around like a winding curve.

“After a portion of the building had been completed, with the counsel of faithful neighbors we decreed that an oratory in that building should be consecrated by Lord Stephen, the venerable bishop of Auvergne. This was done on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of October, on the feast of the Exaltation of the Lord’s Cross and of the passion of the blessed Pope Cornelius and the most blessed and victorious martyr Cyprian.

“On the day of the consecration of that oratory, I first, brother Odilo, together with my nephews, the sons of my brothers and sisters—namely Lord Stephen, provost of the Church of Anicium, and his brother Beraldus; Lord Hildegarius, cleric and canon of the aforesaid church; Beraldus, son of my aforesaid brother Ebo; William, son of my late brother William, an honorable man, and his sons; and Geraldus, Rotbertus, Beraldus, Odilo, and Hicterius—with the counsel of our sisters, namely Lady Blismodis, the venerable abbess, and Aldegardis, a matron of the highest worldly nobility—we all together offer to almighty God, living, true, unchangeable, and eternal; to the most holy and undivided Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; to the most blessed Mother of God and of our Lord, the ever-virgin Mary; to the holy angels and archangels; and to all the citizens of heavenly glory, patriarchs and prophets, and the beloved of the Lord, John the Baptist and John the Evangelist, and the blessed apostles [Col. 0836C] Peter and Paul, and the remaining apostles and apostolic men, the Holy Innocents and all the holy martyrs, confessors, and virgins, certain possessions which our parents held by hereditary right, and certain others which they acquired from their most honorable lords through the most devoted service of fidelity.

“These possessions are in the county and bishopric of Auvergne. First, there is the aforesaid hill, as has been said, enclosed by the winding course of the aforementioned river, and the church consecrated on the other side of the river in honor of the holy martyr Cyricus; also a little village near the same place, called Forsanguis, and one holding adjoining that village, called Plania.

“There is also the church in the village of Saraziacus, together with the entire village itself, except for that part which fell by lot to the aforesaid nephew of ours, William. There is another village near the aforesaid church, called Saraziacellus by its diminutive name. This little village and the aforesaid estate called Forsanguis, our lord and dearest brother Stephen, while still alive and in good health, gave by a charter of donation for the completion of the work now in hand, and left them when he departed this life.

“There is another village in the same county, called Montaniacus, which came to us by inheritance from our uncle Golfaldus.

“There are also two other churches, belonging not to two parishes but to one, situated in the bishopric of Le Velay: one consecrated in honor of Saint John, the Lord’s forerunner, and the other in honor of blessed Peter the apostle.

“In the village of Lisacus, we offer in its entirety the part which Beraldus the provost and his brother Bertrannus are seen to possess; and at Capilliacus, whatever Lord Bertrannus is seen to possess.

“All these things written above, with everything belonging to them, we offer, as has been said, to God and to all his saints, for the liberation and rescue, salvation and rest, of the aforesaid men Beraldus, Bertrannus, Ebo, and Stephen, for whom this offering is made especially; and also for the salvation of their other brothers Hicterius, Eustorgius, William, and Hicterius; likewise for the salvation of their father Beraldus and his father Hicterius, most illustrious men; and of all their and our parents, kinsmen, and faithful, living and dead, of either sex, every age and rank; and of those who now offer counsel and assistance for completing, guarding, and establishing this work, and who in the ages to come shall offer them; and of all faithful Christians, so that the mercy, piety, and grace of the Lord may now and in the future have mercy on all of them and on us.

“We place the aforesaid place, and everything that appears to belong to it, as well as whatever faithful Christians in the ages to come may grant to the same place in estates, possessions of any kind, or offerings, under the protection and guardianship of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, the defense of the pontiffs of the Apostolic See, and the governance of the abbot and monks of Cluny; and we decree that it be free from every servitude and exaction of human wrongdoing.

“For we establish and desire with all our longing that the abbots and monks of Cluny should always hold and possess this place and order and arrange it for the service of God according to the rule of Saint Benedict, as they do the other monasteries properly belonging to them, for the worship of divine religion, as has been said.

“If anyone should perhaps [lacuna] against this decree of ours, let him know clearly that we judged it fitting that the holy congregation of that place should acknowledge that it possesses something of servitude from our poverty, out of reverence for and in recognition of the merit of that place, because someone from our family has been seen to have obtained honor according to God and according to the world, and because considerable benefits are known to have come to our parents and to us ourselves.

“Moreover, if anyone should at any time presume to bring any claim against the testament of our offering, let him acknowledge that he has acted against the judgment of divine justice and the rights of worldly laws. If he wishes to correct his offense by repentance, let him receive pardon; but if he does not wish to correct it and instead decides to persist in his wickedness, let him not obtain what he seeks, but receive what he deserves: namely, let him pay the penalties prescribed by the laws for such a crime here, and suffer everlasting punishments forever.

“Sign of Lord Odilo the abbot, by whose vow and desire this charter was written. Sign of his nephews, namely Stephen, Beraldus, another Beraldus, yet another Beraldus, Aldigerius, William, and Odilo. Sign of Peter. Sign of Bernardus. Sign of Pontius. Sign of Dalmatius. Sign of Pontius. Sign of Blismodis. Sign of Aldiardis. Sign of Auxilia.

“This charter was made in the year from the incarnation of the Lord 1025.”

## III. Odilo Becomes a Monk at Cluny, Then Abbot.

### 8.

As Jotsaldus relates, after spurning the fortresses of Brioude and Anicium, because in both cities or churches either he himself or others of his family held the principal dignities, Odilo withdrew to Cluny, a monastery renowned throughout the world for holiness and religious observance. There he was given the monastic habit by blessed Maiolus, the most holy abbot, to whom he was already well known.

Hugh, abbot of Flavigny, reports in the *Chronicle of Verdun* that this occurred in the year 991; the Cluniac Chronicle agrees, having been copied by our Stephanotius from the monastery’s ancient parchments.

No one, however, will readily persuade himself of this if it is true that in that very year Odilo, as may be gathered from several charters, was taken by blessed Maiolus into a share in the governance of the abbacy. Certainly Jotsaldus himself, and after him Peter Damian, seem not to depart far from this view, for they report that Saint Maiolus died nearly four years after Odilo had come to conversion.

It is certain that Maiolus died in the year 994. From this one may infer how great was blessed Odilo’s maturity and merit: while still a neophyte and almost at the very moment of entering religious life, he was judged worthy by Saint Maiolus himself to govern so great a congregation.

### 9.

That his election cannot have been delayed beyond the year 992 is proved by many charters issued in that very year [Col. 0838C], in which Odilo is called abbot.

In the second cartulary of the monastery of Cluny, charter 738, a certain field situated in the village of Bersoniacus is given to the monastery of Cluny, over which Abbot Odilo presides, in the fifth year of Hugh, king of the Franks—that is, at least in the year 992.

In that same year, in July, Girbaldus sold a small piece of a field situated there. Charter 539 is a donation of a courtyard and vineyard in the village of Morgonus, in the district of Mâcon, made to Odilo the abbot in the sixth year of King Hugh; charter 753 likewise bears that same year and was also made in favor of Odilo the abbot.

Several charters issued in the first year of Rodulfus, king of the Burgundians, would also have to be brought forward here, if it were universally established that this king ascended the throne before 993.

The charters cited above are supported [Col. 0838D] by the author of an old Chronicle, a manuscript of which we possess, where under the year 992 the following is recorded:

“In Burgundy, Odilo, formerly a cleric of Brioude, professed himself a monk and was placed in charge of the monastery of Cluny, which he governed and advanced for fifty-six years with marvelous religious fervor,” etc.

Moreover, since nearly all other authors have granted Odilo the same number of years in office, and since it is certain—as they themselves also attest—that he departed this world on the Kalends of January in the year 1049, their authority too ought rightly to be brought forward to confirm our opinion.

Nevertheless, Sigebertus, in his *Chronicle*, assigns the beginning of Odilo’s governance to the following year; Hugh of Flavigny assigns it to 994, but he pays attention only to the death of Maiolus. This is stated more explicitly in the *Chronicle of Maillezais*, where the holy man is said to have succeeded Abbot Maiolus in 994.

Indeed, besides the charters cited above, several others occur in the Cluniac cartularies that call Odilo abbot of Cluny while Maiolus was still alive. Such is a charter issued in the seventh year of King Hugh—that is, in 993—in which certain possessions at Visandon are bestowed upon the monks of Cluny.

In the preceding year, in December, a vineyard at the village of Dambinas, in the county of Mâcon, was given to Odilo, abbot of Cluny.

Finally, in that same seventh year of the same king, in March, and therefore in the year 994, shortly before the death of Saint Maiolus, Abbot Odilo received and gave land at the place called Scambium, in the village of Odgracum, likewise situated in the county of Mâcon.

[Col. 0839B] ### 10.

Maiolus had not yet, at that time, abandoned the governance of the monastery, as various charters prove—issued in the sixth and seventh years of King Hugh—which bear his name in the book of donations made under Saint Maiolus.

In charter 16, Maiolus is called abbot of Cluny in the sixth year of King Hugh, when he acquired certain churches by exchange in the county of Autun.

In the same year, in June, Landrada granted the Cluniac monks, where Maiolus is abbot, certain possessions situated in the district of Mâcon.

In the seventh year of the same king, Berardus the cleric granted to the monastery of Cluny, where, he says, “Maiolus is abbot,” half of the forest of Advolt.

From this it is clear that Odilo was Maiolus’s kind of vicar and coadjutor in governing the monastery. Hence, in a charter of a certain Bernardus, a nobleman who was freeing several of his serfs at the request of Vivianus the provost—Vivianus claimed that they belonged to his monastery—the following is found:

“He abandoned the claim which he had against the said place of Cluny, over which the lord and most reverend Father Odilo presides by the command of the holy Father Maiolus.”

11. In Volume VI of Acher’s *Spicilegium* we have the decree of the election of Saint Odilo as abbot of Cluny, which was carried out while Saint Maiolus was still alive. Besides Maiolus himself and 177 monks, King Rodulfus, Archbishop Burchard, several other bishops, numerous abbots, and noblemen subscribed to it. The document contains no indication of its date. But if Rodulfus did not obtain the kingdom of Burgundy before the end of 993, the election took place shortly before Maiolus’s death, which occurred on 10 May of the following year. From this it is clear that Maiolus, exhausted by old age, transferred his burden to Odilo, lest the vigor of regular discipline—which, because of his advanced age, he believed himself unable to supervise as necessary—should grow slack in the monastery of Cluny through his own fault.

“I,” he says, “Maiolus . . . . . worn out by age and weakened also in bodily functions, while I perceive myself to be less suited to pastoral care, having been forewarned by the concern expressed in the chapters of blessed Benedict regarding the appointment of an abbot, together with all my brothers, sons, and fellow servants, choose as a religious man and decide that he shall be abbot Odilo, formerly a cleric of blessed Peter, a brother and son to the monks; lest, through the insolence of our infirmity, the order should grow dull and suffer any setback, which, with God’s favor, is always to be advanced toward better things.”

From the same document we learn that Odilo accepted this dignity only reluctantly, because he considered himself unequal to so great a burden. Therefore the blessed old man summoned bishops and abbots, as well as noblemen, and arranged for the decree to be confirmed by their subscriptions.

“And lest,” he says, “he put forward some device of excuse—for just as someone who rashly aspires unworthily to the government [of a monastery], so one who is worthy yet refuses is rightly regarded as needing to be compelled—we have sought the counsel of the bishops and abbots,” and so forth.

The names of those who confirmed the election by their subscriptions have been given in the *Eulogy of Saint Maiolus*, under the year 994. It is therefore not useful to repeat them here; instead, in their place, we offer several verses apparently composed by a contemporary author about this election. They are found in a manuscript of the monastery of Cîteaux under the title “The Election of Lord Odilo.”

This venerable Father was soon called to the stars.

There is no need for our teaching to set forth fully

What kind of Father God chose as his successor:

How prudent he was, how richly endowed with moral excellence,

In human affairs and likewise in heavenly ones;

Christ alone knows, who grants him these gifts.

Odilo, renowned through illustrious fathers,

Fleeing earthly things while still young in years and seeking heavenly things,

Joined himself to Father Maiolus, with Christ as guide.

Received from the flock, destined himself to become leader of the flock,

He diligently fulfilled whatever the Rule commanded him.

Deigning to live in such a master’s place,

Chosen and desired by all the brothers as Father,

At his Father’s command he undertook the care of the sheepfold,

Like him in all respects, although he added the summit of honor,

And with devotion ordered everything in a manner pleasing to God.

Discreet in speech, and so modest in action

That he follows neither the left-hand path nor the right,

He skillfully measures out an equal rule in everything.

The authority of kings seeks his counsel,

And the highest nobles submit to his honor.

Thus he practices active life without abandoning contemplation.

Only in body is he on earth; in heart he moves in heaven.

But not to say more, he is not unequal in virtues

To Father Maiolus, resplendent in countless wonders.

As Maiolus was gentle, so this man too is acknowledged as divinely so;

When you see this man, you may say that the other is present before you.

O how powerful this place is, and how brightly it shines,

Since it deserved to acquire such fathers for itself;

Like two suns shining their rays upon us,

One glitters in the heavens, while the other flashes on earth!

Let it suffice to have come this far; for Holy Scripture says:

“Do not praise a man during his lifetime.”

12. Since the arguments by which it is proved that Odilo was elected abbot of Cluny while Saint Maiolus was still alive appear so certain and clear, it is surprising that, when Maiolus was near death in the monastery of Souvigny and the brothers asked him to whom he wished the government of the abbacy to be entrusted, he said absolutely nothing about Saint Odilo. This is attested by Syrus, his disciple and biographer. Indeed, in another *Life*, preserved in the *Appendix to the Cluniac Library*, Maiolus is said to have replied:

“It is not for us, dearest sons, to choose an abbot for you; but the Angel of Great Counsel will not allow you to remain long without advice,” and so forth.

Was it because Odilo refused to undertake the government of the abbacy, as we said in the preceding section, so that it became necessary to invoke the authority of King Hugh and the bishops? Certainly Adhemar says in his *Chronicle* that Odilo succeeded Maiolus unwillingly, and that he was elected both by King Hugh himself and by the entire congregation.

## IV. Events under Saint Odilo

13. In the preceding section we cited several charters dated in 992 or the following year. Since they were written during the joint administration of Maiolus and Odilo, it is not surprising if they bear the name of one or the other. How vigorous religious life was under such men may be gathered from a charter of Walter, bishop of Autun, issued at the same time, namely in the sixth year of King Hugh, in the month of May. In it he says that the monastery of Cluny was united to him by affection above all others, and that religion flourished there, and so forth. He then relinquishes to it whatever might belong to himself or to the archdeacons in the churches belonging to the said monastery, with the exception, however, of synodal offerings. He specifies these churches as those of Mont Algaie, Tresela, Saint Leodegarius, Mont Malard, Tervise, Vallis, and Saint Mary.

Besides Walter himself, Elinardus the abbot subscribed, followed by the provosts, the cantor, Erpertus the abbot, Ugo the abbot, and finally the archpriests and canons.

The same bishop, in the twenty-ninth year of King Lothair, had given Saint Maiolus the churches of Saint Mary of Mont-Melard and Saint Mary in the village of Vallis, as well as other revenues and tithes of the church of Saint Germanus of the village of Tyrinacum, where the Cluniac monks daily served in obedience.

We shall speak below of the monastery of Magabrense, which the same bishop entrusted to Saint Odilo to restore to better condition. For the present, we must discuss the donations made to Odilo after the death of Saint Maiolus. Since, under the government of this holy man, the reputation for holiness of the Cluniac monks was no less celebrated than in the time of their predecessors, bishops and other noblemen granted them many possessions. From their charters we learn many things of considerable use for illuminating history.

14. In the second year of Rodulfus, king of Transjurane Burgundy, in April, and therefore in 995—if it is true that Conrad, Rodulfus’s father, died on 19 October 993—Count Artaldus gave Saint Odilo the church of Saint Peter in the village of Marogliacum, with its priesthood, tithes, and all appurtenances, and so forth, in the territory of Lyon and Roanne.

He may perhaps be the same Artaldus who, in another charter without a date, donated the estate of Saint Praejectus at Memboli in the county of Valentinois. Pontius, son of Count Ademar, subscribed to that charter.

15. In the third year of the same King Rodulfus, Humbert, bishop of Grenoble, gave the monastery of Cluny, “where,” as he says, “Lord Odilo is abbot,” half of the castle of Visilia, together with the entire borough and the church of Saint Mary. He also gave the church of Saint Martin of Ponte-Roso, with its tithes, offerings, and cemeteries.

Frideburgis, the bishop’s mother, Wigo, his brother, and Humbert, bishop of Valence, his nephew, subscribed.

16. In the first year of King Robert of the Franks, who, after his father’s death on 24 October 996, began to reign alone, a certain Ayroardus gave the monastery of Cluny an indominicate estate in the county of Mâcon.

Also in Robert’s first year, Odilo exchanged certain properties with Maiolus, provost of Mâcon. This exchange was approved on 2 March, and therefore in 997, by Willelmus and Wido.

17. In 997 a charter of King Rodulfus is recorded in the Cluniac Library. In it, in the ninth year of his reign, after confirming several possessions to the monastery of Cluny, he grants it several others at the request of his wife Emma. It was issued at the estate of Ansa, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of July, in the third indiction, and so forth. Reamundus authenticated it in place of Ansus, bishop.

But this is an obvious error. For it is certain that the charter belongs to Rodulfus who, while Charles the Simple was being held in prison, was called king of the Franks in 923.

18. At the beginning of the year 998, which was the fifth year of King Rodulfus, the same king, after having previously issued several charters in favor of the Cluniac monks, issued one by which he confirmed various possessions to them in the counties of Lyon, Forez, and Vienne. It was issued at Paterniacum in 998, in the fifth year of King Rodulfus. The chancellor Padicius authenticated it in place of Purgardus, archbishop and archchancellor.

In the sixth year of his reign, therefore toward the end of that same year 998, the same king, through the intervention of his wife, Queen Agildrudis, and Archbishop Purchardus, confirmed all royal decrees and all charters or donations made by other faithful men to the monastery of Cluny within the limits of his kingdom. In the manner of his father of blessed memory, he renewed them all in every respect and listed them individually.

19. Also in 998 or the following year—for the charter is dated to the third year of King Robert, who, after his father Hugh’s death on 24 October 996, obtained the monarchy, as we believe—Bernard gave Odilo and the monastery of Cluny half of his allodial property in the village of Buxerias, for the soul of his brother Israel, who was still alive.

The same Bernard is described in another charter, dated to the fifth year of King Robert, as a knight and, according to the dignity of the age, a very illustrious man. Together with his wife Emma he gave, as a pledge for two hundred solidi, what he possessed in the village of Buxerias in the county of Mâcon.

Five years later, that is, in the tenth year of King Robert, this same Emma, Bernard’s wife, together with Maiolus, her husband’s brother, granted to the same monastery her share of the same village of Buxerias, which she had divided with Israel, Bernard’s other brother.

Finally, in another charter, where she is called the wife of the very illustrious knight Bernard, she gave, together with her son Gaucerannus and her daughter Emma, for her burial at Cluny, the property she possessed in the territory of Ammacum in the county of Mâcon.

It is therefore clear that this family was exceedingly generous toward Cluny.

This Bernard must be distinguished from another man of the same name who lived at the same time and in the same region and who was also beneficent toward Cluny, as is clear from his charter. In it, together with his wife Ada, he granted the monastery one estate in the territory of Milan, in the county of Mâcon, in the village of Curtilis.

He is there said to have had two sons, namely Josaldus and Joserannus. The former may perhaps have been Jotsaldus, later a Cluniac monk and the author of the *Life of Blessed Odilo*.

To these may also be added Bernard who, together with his wife Atta and their son Robert, gave a vineyard in the village of Noglas in the fourth year of King Robert.

It seemed best to report all these matters together, lest the similarity of the names should produce confusion among the persons. But now we must resume the sequence of years.

20. In January 999, in the sixth year of King Rodulfus, Odilo and Vivianus, the prior, leased to Peter the knight and Ermengardis, his wife, the castle of Condorcum with its appurtenances, in return for an annual rent. They received three estates as compensation.

A charter of Blismodis also bears this same sixth year of King Rodulfus. She calls herself a most noble woman and donates the church of Saint Maxima of Talusatis. She subscribed the charter together with her son Albuinus and other witnesses.

21. Around the year 1000, King Robert and Henry, the brother of his father Hugh Capet and duke of Burgundy, jointly issued a diploma forbidding anyone to build a castle within the specified boundaries of the monastery of Cluny.

The charter is undated in our copy, but it cannot be later than 1001, since Henry died in October of that year.

22. In the sixth year of King Robert, that is, in 1001 or the following year, if the reference is to his sole rule, Maiolus the cleric claimed that certain customary dues were owed to him from the lands of the monastery of Cluny. But he lost his case before Willelmus, count of Mâcon, and his wife Ermentrudis.

A charter issued in June also bears Robert’s sixth year, and therefore belongs to 1001. In it Arleis gives to Saint Maiolus and his monks, so that through his merits he may obtain eternal rewards, a portion of a middle planting in the county of Mâcon, in the village of Marsiacum, at a place called Trimblada.

If, however, Robert’s sixth year here is understood as the period when he reigned jointly with his father Hugh, the charter must be assigned to 993. Yet Arleis seems to have been seeking the protection of Maiolus after the latter’s death. For sacred honors were conferred upon him immediately after his death.

23. In 1004 the canons of the church of Vallavensis—that is, Le Puy-en-Velay—asked Odilo for certain houses to be relinquished to Gauslinus, so that they might acquire from him other houses which Gauslinus held from Kigonus and which would be useful for enlarging their workshops.

Odilo agreed, receiving in compensation other houses that had come from a donation of Wigo, the bishop of blessed memory.

The transaction took place in the city of Anicius, on the third day before the Nones of February, on Thursday, on the eighth day of the moon, in the year of the Incarnation 1004, in the second indiction. Beraldus, provost of Anicius, Robert the abbot, and another Robert, the sacristan, subscribed.

In this same year Ratburnus, the viscount, and Walda, his wife, gave the Cluniac monks the church of Saint Martin of Laudadis.

24. In 1005 Rodulfus, a nobleman who is said to have been the founder of the monastery of Paterniacum, exchanged one of his female serfs for another who belonged by right to the monastery of Cluny.

The charter was issued in 1005, in the twelfth year of King Rodulfus, in the third indiction. These chronological indications agree perfectly, provided that Rodulfus began to reign in October 993 after his father’s death.

25. The donation made to Saint Odilo by Count Lambert of one estate in the village of Latonai, in the territory of Mâcon, must be assigned to this same year, or at least to the year 1020, since only the third indiction is indicated during Robert’s reign.

The date is expressed as follows:

“Publicly enacted at the city of Chalon, while King Robert reigns, but among us our Lord Jesus Christ [reigns], in April, on Thursday, in the third indiction.”

[Note: [Col. 0843D] Note the formula “Christ reigning.”]

26. A certain Robert uses the same formula in the Celsinian cartulary. To that monastery, where Lord Odilo was then abbot, he gave, for his burial, a vineyard situated on Mount Dorensis.

The charter concludes:

“Issued while Robert, king of the Franks, reigns—or rather, while our Lord Jesus Christ reigns.”

The foundation of the monastery of Chauriacum, which is subject to Celsinianum, is dated by the same formula. Count Pontius likewise used it in a charter by which he gave the Cluniac monks several possessions in the county of Trevis, near the stream called Lota, in the places Villetas, Merdusana, and Mota.

That charter, however, has entirely different chronological indications from the preceding one:

“Issued in the castle of Torana, on Thursday of Septuagesima, in the seventh indiction, with an epact of fifteen, while Jesus Christ reigns.”

Lord Bishop Cono subscribed.

Finally, Beatrix, wife of the viscount Archimbaldus, who, as she herself says, had recently died, gave Cluny, where Odilo is abbot, one estate from her possessions situated in the county of Lyon, at a place called Salsetum.

The charter was issued at Cluny, “while the Lord Jesus Christ reigns,” in May.

Some people believe that this formula was used in these and similar charters because at that time the king had been placed under ecclesiastical prohibition on account of Bertha, whom he had married even though she was related to him by affinity.

It is certainly clear from Beatrix’s charter alone, which we have just cited, that this is false. For that charter was written after Robert’s death. Archimbaldus, whom Beatrix says had died, was still alive in 1037, as will be shown below from his charter, and indeed two years later he established monks in the cell of Saint Lawrence.

But this is not the place to discuss the formula; learned men have debated the question more fully elsewhere.

27. In the tenth year of King Robert, Bishop Letbaldus of Mâcon gave two servants at Odilo’s request. The charter was issued on a Monday in August and must therefore be assigned to the year 1007.

Moreover, in a certain charter of the Cluniac monks, Bishop Letaldus is said to have subscribed after Odilo the abbot and Vivianus the provost, before the other monks.

Was he Letbaldus of Mâcon, who, after leaving his see, withdrew for a time to Cluny?

28. In 1008, in the seventh indiction, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, Odilo granted certain houses situated at Arles on an emphyteutic lease. Many others subscribed with him, among them Hugo of Calviote and Redemptus of Botera.

29. In the twelfth year of King Robert, in April, and therefore in the year of Christ 1009, a certain Rodulfus gave Odilo and the monastery of Cluny a small estate and several other properties in the village of Aziacum, in the county of Mâcon.

30. In 1015 Gaufredus, bishop of Chalon, sitting together with the canons in a general assembly, transferred the church of Juliacum from the payment of tithes, at the request of Odilo the abbot. In return, Odilo gave the church of Saint Vincent—that is, the cathedral church—a church which had been donated to him by Goffridus of Semur.

Hugo, count and bishop—that is, bishop of Auxerre—and others subscribed together with Bishop Gaufredus.

The charter is dated to the twenty-sixth year of King Robert, but that year does not agree with 1015, the year in which these events are said to have occurred.

31. In 1017, while Robert was reigning, on the sixth day before the Nones of May, Willelmus, duke of the Aquitanians, returning from Rome, gave the monastery of Cluny in the city of Pavia half of the revenue from the fish caught around the island of Rado.

His two sons, Willelmus and Odo, subscribed.

32. In 1018, while Robert was reigning, the same Willelmus—whom some call “the Great” because of his outstanding qualities—gave the monastery of Cluny an estate in the vicariate of Marevennus.

Countess Agnes, Willelmus the Younger, Bishop Gislebertus, Count Fulco, and others subscribed to the charter with Duke Willelmus.

33. Gislebertus, the bishop mentioned in this charter, was placed over the church of Poitiers in 975, according to the *Chronicle of Maillezais*. He was succeeded by Isembertus the archdeacon, who subscribed to the same charter. Under their episcopates Arnaldus, also mentioned in it, administered the deanery of that church.

The same Willelmus also granted the mint of Niort to the Cluniac monks, as is clear from another of his charters. His wife Agnes and his two sons, Willelmus and Odo, subscribed to it with him.

34. Agnes, mentioned in both charters of Duke Willelmus, was his third wife, the daughter of Otto, surnamed Willelmus, duke of Burgundy.

Willelmus had received Willelmus and Odo from earlier wives: the first from Almodia and the second from Prisca, his second wife.

Both died without children and were buried in the monastery of Maillezais, which their father had founded. Their father too, shortly before his death, received the monastic habit there and was buried there, in 1030 or the following year.

Agnes, besides a daughter named Agnes, who married the Emperor Henry, surnamed “the Black,” bore Willelmus two sons who are famous in the history of Aquitaine.

She herself mentions them in a donation made to the monastery of Cluny after her husband’s death. It seems appropriate to insert it here from the Cluniac cartulary:

“To the sacred and venerable place of the monastery of Cluny, which was built in honor of the apostles Peter and Paul, and over which Lord Odilo the abbot presides, I, Agnes, and my sons Willelmus and Gauffredus, give to the inhabitants of the aforesaid place the entire mint which we possess in the village called Engeliacum; and in another village called Molgong, all the customary dues which we are accustomed to receive there, so that from them you may purchase the spits which we used to give you.

“We also ask that our names be entered in your Missal, in which your benefactors are commemorated, because we place the greatest confidence in the prayers of you and your congregation. And take into consideration this agreement which you have made with me.”

In this year the most noble Countess Agnes besieged the castle of Volventum and, as was her custom, captured it.

35. How greatly Agnes bound the Cluniac monks to herself by the benefactions bestowed both by her and by her relatives is clear from a certain public document, by which the Cluniac monks granted her Lasiacum as a memorial of their gratitude, as may be seen in the Cluniac cartulary.

36. On the ninth day before the Kalends of February 1019, at the request of his wife Irmingardis, King Rodulfus granted from his own inheritance to the Cluniac monks—those who then and thereafter obeyed the Rule of Saint Benedict—the church of Saint Blaise, together with the entire little settlement and its appurtenances.

The charter, which is also published in the *Cluniac Library*, column 411, was issued at the estate of Tabernae, otherwise called Urba, from the river flowing there.

But in that charter the thirty-fifth year of King Rodulfus is joined with the year 1019 of the Lord’s Incarnation, which is an error.

A charter of Leotbaldus—called Theobaldus in another copy—bishop of Mâcon, also bears the year 1019. In it he relinquishes to Lord Odilo the abbot and the Cluniac monks the tithes and other appurtenances of the church of Saint Sulpicius. It was issued at a synod of the clergy, on the fourth day before the Ides of November.

But Leotbaldus was already dead at that time, if we trust the published lists of the bishops of Mâcon.

Indeed, in that very year a court is said to have been held in the presence of Otto, count of Mâcon, and Gauslinus, the bishop who succeeded Leotbaldus. Humbertus, provost of the church of Cluny, attended with four or five monks of the same place, to recover for the monastery certain possessions which Raculfus claimed as belonging to him.

I believe that this was the very same court at which Humbertus, together with several other monks, complained at Mâcon before Count Odo and Bishop Gauslinus against a woman who had seized certain properties at Colongiae and other estates belonging to Cluny. That case is said to have been lost in October 1019.

Around the same time Hugo, bishop of Auxerre, gave Cluny, where Odilo was abbot, half of the estate of Givriacum in the county of Dijon, for the soul of his father Lambert, namely the count of Chalon, and of his mother Adheleidis, whom Rodulfus Glaber discusses.

The other half was likewise granted to the monastery by Hugo’s sister Mathildis, together with her husband Gaufredus and their sons Gaufredus, Hervaeus, Odo, Thetbaldus, and Lambertus.

Hugo himself subscribed to the donation together with Leotbaldus, bishop of Mâcon.

In another charter Hugo confirmed the same donation. Otto the count, Gauslenus the bishop, Ugo the viscount, Acelinus the abbot, and others subscribed with him.

It was issued in the year of the Incarnation 1019 and in the thirty-second year of King Robert’s anointing.

37. In the seventeenth year of King Rodulfus, in March, and therefore in 1020, Countess Tetberga gave one estate at a place called Camnium, in the county of Lyon, for the welfare of her lord Artaldus—that is, her husband—and of her sons Artaldus and Geraldus, who subscribed to the donation.

In that same year Wicardus, while staying at Cluny, gave the monastery the chapel of Saint Mary at Rocha, in the village of Quinciacum.

A repeated charter records the same donation in the thirty-third year of King Robert, that is, in 1028 if the reference is to his sole reign.

Other charters of this Wicardus and his relatives are preserved in the Cluniac cartulary, but without dates.

Wicardus’s sureties gave Abbot Odilo the church of Saint Martin in the village of Vallis, in the county of Lyon.

38. In 1021 Bernard gave the monastery of Cluny Silva Augusta in the county of Mâcon.

Count Otto subscribed to the charter, which was issued in the fourth indiction, in the thirty-fourth year of King Robert—that is, from the time when Robert began to reign jointly with his father. Otherwise it would indicate the year 1029, but the indiction would conflict, unless perhaps “twelve” is read for “four.”
