In the twenty-sixth year of the same king, which coincides with the year of the Incarnation 1021 and the end of the preceding year, the church of Blessed Mary of Bellimont was given to the monastery of Cluny in the county of Chalon, at the end of Senoium.

39. At the beginning of 1022, if it is indeed joined with the twenty-eighth year of King Rodulfus, Ademar gave the monastery of Cluny, where Odilo was abbot, the church of the village of Testor, with tithes, burials, firstfruits, and so forth.

The sons of the same Ademar—Willelmus, Stephanus the abbot, Wido, Pontius, and Armannus—subscribed.

40. In 1023 two brothers, noblemen named Leodegarius and Pontius, renounced the world and gave Abbot Odilo half of the castle of Altonum. Their father had previously given the other half to the monastery of Cluny.

The charter was issued in the year of the Incarnation 1023, on the Wednesday before the Ascension of the Lord, while Rodulfus was reigning.

Their brothers Feraldus and Petrus, bishops—apparently the bishop of Gap and the bishop of Sisteron—as well as Arnulfus, Geraldus, Rodulfus, and Rumbaldus, consented to the donation.

In the same year Gauslenus, bishop of Mâcon, exchanged certain properties with Odilo the abbot in the village of Lupiacum, in the county of Mâcon, and gave him several vine-lands in various places.

Walterius the provost and the other canons subscribed with the bishop, in the year of the Incarnation 1023, while Robert was reigning.

41. In the twenty-sixth year of King Robert, which must be understood as reckoned from the beginning of his joint reign with his father—for he did not reign alone for so long—and therefore in June 1023, Gibaldus gave Odilo the abbot forests, meadows, lands, and a mill on the river Absonus, in the diocese of Autun, in the county of Aval, at the village of Martiniacum, in the eighth indiction. This indication, however, does not agree with that year.

Ermuinus, bishop of Autun, Count Landricus, and his son Rainaldus subscribed.

In the same year of King Robert, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of July, on the thirteenth day of the moon, two estates in Villa-Francorum, in the county of Mâcon, were given to Odilo the abbot of Cluny.

Bishop Gauslenus and Wigo the viscount subscribed to the donation.

42. In the twenty-eighth year of King Robert, in March, and therefore in 1023, an estate in the village of Casotis, in the territory of Salornum, in the county of Mâcon, was given to Odilo, abbot of Cluny.

Count Otto subscribed to the charter. It is said to have been issued in the eleventh indiction, which does not agree with the chronological indications written above, nor with the twenty-eighth year of the same king if that year is calculated from the beginning of his joint reign with his father.

43. In the twenty-ninth year of King Robert, in June, and therefore in the common era 1024, Odilo the abbot and the Cluniac monks gave a certain Hebrew man named Solomon one vineyard, one meadow, and one vine-land in the village of Carniacum, in the county of Mâcon. In exchange, he gave them a vineyard in the territory of Fusciacum, in the village of Molonacum.

Count Otto, his wife Elizabeth, Bishop Gauslenus, and others subscribed.

The transaction took place on Friday, in June, with an epact of fifteen, in the twenty-ninth year of King Robert.

44. The charter by which both those kings confirmed several donations made to the monastery of Cluny at various times cannot be later than the thirty-first year of King Robert—that is, the year 1026 of the Christian era—when Hugh the Younger, Robert’s son, died.

It has no date in the Cluniac cartulary.

45. Under the same kings, Otto, count of Mâcon, gave or restored two estates to the monastery of Cluny, as he himself says in the charter:

“For the soul of my father Wido, and also of my grandfather Otto, surnamed Willelmus, and of my wife and my son Gaufredus, I return to the place of Cluny the estate called Aniscum from ancient times, situated near the river Arar, which formerly came to my county from the inheritance of Saint Vincent—that is, the cathedral church of Mâcon—just as Count Leotbaldus, my ancestor, had previously given it by the testamentary decree of King Louis to the apostle Peter and the Cluniac monks.”

He also donated another estate adjoining the first, called Asnerias, with its appurtenances, and so forth.

It was issued while Robert was reigning with his son Hugh.

Otto’s wife, whose name is not given in the charter, was Elizabeth. While Robert was reigning, she and her husband together gave the monastery an estate in the village of Fusciacum, in the county of Langres, in the county of Ouche.

Finally, Count Otto gave Abbot Odilo certain possessions in the village of Camavata, in the county of Mâcon, as well as a mill above the river Graona, beside Rocacavernosa.

Bishop Goslenus subscribed.

46. In the thirty-fifth year of King Rodulfus, that is, in the common era 1027, or the following year, the church of Saint George situated at Villa-Domina was given to Abbot Odilo.

A vineyard in the same place and one estate in the county of Grenoble were also given.

47. In the thirty-seventh year of King Rodulfus, Count Amedeus, son of Count Humbert, together with his wife Adalheida, gave the monastery of Cluny—where Lord Father Odilo presides—the church of Saint Maurice in the village of Maltacena, along with many other possessions, while reserving to himself and his successors the right of patronage.

This charter is preserved in the *Cluniac Library*, column 412. It is said there to have been issued in the thirty-seventh year, while Rodulfus was reigning, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1025, on the Kalends of November, on the twentieth day of the moon.

These chronological indications do not agree with one another, since the thirty-seventh year of King Rodulfus began in October of the common year 1029.

The same Humbert was also beneficent toward the Cluniac monks living at Maltacena, as is clear from two of his charters in Guichenon’s proofs for his *History of Savoy*, in which he grants many things to the same place.

Neither charter has a date, but both name Humbert’s three sons: Amedeus, Aymo, and Odo.

48. In the forty-second year of King Robert, reckoned from the time when he had been admitted by his father into a partnership in the kingdom, and therefore in 1029, an estate in the village of Sarciacum, in the county of Mâcon, was given to the monastery of Cluny. It was issued in the eleventh indiction, in February.

49. In the thirty-third year of the same king, which, if it refers to his sole rule, would be 1027 or the following year, the Cluniac monks were given the chapel of Saint Mary with its tithes and so forth, in the village of Quinciacum, in the county of Lyon, together with as much land beside the same chapel as would suffice for building a house, workshops, and a monk’s garden.

Another charter should be assigned to approximately the same time. By it seven vine-lands in the county of Mâcon were given to the monastery of Cluny while King Robert was reigning with his son Henry.

In 1027 Henry was designated by his father as partner in the kingdom.

50. In 1031, at the request of Robert, the prior of Cluny, Count Otto came to the chapter. There he released into mortmain all that they had so far received or purchased in the county of Mâcon, and confirmed the Cervia Forest, which his own ancestors had formerly given to the monastery.

Count Otto, his son Gaufredus, and Wido, son of Count Gaufredus, subscribed.

The transaction took place at Cluny on the third day before the Ides of August, in the year of the Incarnation 1031, in the fourteenth indiction, on the twenty-fifth day after the death of the glorious Robert, king of the Franks, in the fortieth year of his reign, which was the sixth year of his most devout son, Lord Henry, from the time when he was anointed king over the peoples of the Franks and Burgundians.

Labbe gives, and more correctly, the twenty-second day, the forty-fourth year, which was the fifth year of his son, and so forth.

51. A charter of Odilo himself, by which he granted some land under a rent to Joscelinus the cleric and his two heirs, seems also to belong to the same year.

Other monks consented. Five of them subscribed after Robert the prior, and after them Ugo the abbot.

It was issued at Saint Marcellus on the seventh day before the Kalends of November, in the first year of Henry, king of the Franks.

In charters of this kind no more than four or five monks usually subscribed. We nevertheless have one before us to which twenty monks subscribed, but it is undated.

52. In 1032, in the fifteenth indiction, on Thursday during Easter week, Girbardus the priest, coming to conversion, gave several possessions to the monastery. Three months later, Aia, a noble woman, obtained them on lease under a rent of three solidi, for her own life and that of her sons. She had paid forty solidi for them, together with a mule worth one hundred solidi and one bench.

Odilo the abbot subscribed, as did Robert the prior with five other monks. One of these was called Josaldus, perhaps the same man who wrote the *Life of Blessed Odilo*.

[Col. 0850B] 53. Before that time Berlio the knight had given Odilo, abbot of Cluny, the church of Saint Germanus the Confessor, situated in the district of Vienne, in the territory of Corsoriacum, on an island between Bulburus and Carusius.

The charter contains no date, but Leodegarius, archbishop of Vienne, and Aymo, bishop of Belley—that is, of Bellicum—subscribed to it.

54. Since in this very year, 1032, King Rudolf of Burgundy ended his life, it seemed appropriate to include here several charters which occur here and there with no other indication of time than that they were issued during his reign. Among these is the charter of Wigo, viscount, who, together with his wife Euphemia, daughter of Nardum, viscount, gave Odilo, abbot of Cluny, during the reign of Rudolf, lands in the counties of Lyon and Mâcon, situated on the Saône and Voiane rivers, in the village of Konneuco. Wigo made this donation for the soul of his father Berard, of his mother Blismodis, and of his brother Wichard.

Likewise, certain knights, under the same King Rudolf, gave the Cluniac monastery the churches of Saint John, Saint Antoninus, and Saint Leutherius, in the county of Venasque, in the territory of Dimont; they had received these from their lord, Count William—namely, William of Provence—and from his wife, Countess Lucia. Walter, archbishop of Besançon, granted, at the request of the Cluniac monks, the altar and tithes of the church of Saint Stephen in the village of Port, subject to the payment of the customary *eulogiae* and *paratae*. The charter was issued during Rudolf’s reign, and the canons, the dean, Abbot Robert, and others gave their consent.

55. Here, too, we may mention the charter of Otto-William, since it contains only the clause “during the reign of King Rudolf.” For since Count Otto himself died in 1027, and the others named in it died long before King Rudolf died, it cannot be assigned to the final years of Rudolf’s reign. In this charter Otto, surnamed William, says that he had long turned a deaf ear to the appeal of Saint Majolus and of his successor, Lord Odilo, concerning the two estates of Saint Peter of Cluny—namely, Ambariacum and Juliacum. At last, however, he declares that he is restoring them, together with all the forests, villages, and other properties belonging to them.

Otto, his son Rainald, Otto, Bishop Gauslenus, and Abbot Adselinus subscribed. Done at Lons-le-Saunier, during the reign of King Rudolf. In another copy of this charter another son of Otto-William is also recorded, named Wido. Otto himself calls Henry, duke of Burgundy, his lord, and adds many terrible curses against anyone who might at some time violate his benefaction. From this we understand that the charter cannot be assigned beyond the year 1001, when Henry, duke of Burgundy, died.

56. After the death of King Rudolf, Queen Ermengard, his widow, donated to the Cluniac monastery—where, she says, Lord Odilo the abbot presides—through her advocate, named Hubert, two *mansi* in the county of Geneva: one in the village of Silvigiacum and the other in the village of Cicuilatis, together with all the houses, smallholdings, vineyards, meadows, and other properties belonging to them. The charter has no date.

57. In the year 1036, William, most noble count of Provence, and his wife Lucia restored to the Cluniac monastery—where, they say, Lord Odilo the abbot presides—the inheritance of Saint Majolus, namely Diliada and the Seven Springs in the diocese of Riez. Done at the monastery of Podius-Olinus, on Monday, in the year 1036 from the Incarnation, indiction 5, while Emperor Conrad was reigning in his tenth year.

Another charter concerning the same matter reads: “The two brothers, counts of Provence, Geoffrey and Bertrand, renounced and surrendered to God and Saint Peter of Cluny, into the hands of Abbot Odilo, Diliada and the Seven Springs.” The witnesses were Raimbald, archbishop; Ferald, bishop; and many other noblemen. In another copy, between Ferald and Peter of Sisteron, another Bishop Peter also subscribes, but his see is not specified; and the charter is said to have been issued at Serrianum-Villa, on Thursday of the Ascension of the Lord, while Conrad was reigning in his tenth year.

Conrad, or Chuno, mentioned in these and similar charters, is the Emperor Conrad, surnamed the Salian, whom Rudolf established as heir to the kingdom of Transjurane Burgundy. Another charter bears the year 1037; it was likewise issued in the tenth year of Emperor Conrad, indiction 5, on the second day before the Kalends of November. In it Pontius, surnamed Valnerudis, his brother Armannus, and their cousin Rostagnus give to the Cluniac monastery—where Abbot Odilo presides—half of what they possess in the village of Salabaldemari, in the county and diocese of Die.

58. In the year 1037, Archimbald, viscount, gave Lord Odilo, abbot, the church of Saint Lawrence with all its appurtenances, in the county of Mâcon. He also gave as a pledge the forest of Planacassanea and a *mansus* in the village of Vigosetum, until he should return from Jerusalem. After his return, he also gave and confirmed the donation of the estate of Mommalardis, which his grandfather Hugh and his father Artald had given to Cluny, but only on the condition that he himself die without an heir.

Done at Cluny, in the year 1037, indiction 5, while Henry was reigning. Bishop Walter and others subscribed. Two years later, this same Archimbald established monks in the church of Saint Lawrence, as we shall relate in its proper place.

After Archimbald’s death, his wife, named Beatrix, gave to the Cluniacensians, over whom Odilo then presided, one *mansus* in a place called Salsetum, in the county of Lyon. The charter was issued at Cluny in the month of May, while Our Lord Jesus Christ was reigning.

59. A charter is said to have been issued in the year 1038 recording a donation made to Odilo of one small estate and three *raxarae* of vineyard in the county of Mâcon, in the vineyard of Manisiacum, in the territory of Itgiacum, on the third day before the Ides of January, indiction 5—which does not agree with the year stated—on Wednesday, while Emperor Conrad was reigning.

Since in this same year Emperor Conrad handed over the kingdom of Burgundy to his son Henry, we refer here a charter in which, while the same Conrad was emperor, with Odilo as abbot and Leutfrid as count, Richuinus and his wife Lanzede gave the Cluniac monks, in the county and diocese of Saintes, a quarter-share of the church of Dombasila and of the church of Gingivilla.

60. In the eighth year of Henry, king of the Franks—which, if the reference is to his sole monarchy, is the year 1038 or a subsequent year—Hugh, bishop of Auxerre, gave Abbot Odilo the church of Saint Cyricus on the Graon, together with the authority and forest belonging to it. Robert, duke, and John, abbot, subscribed. Done at Auxerre, dictated by Jotsald.

61. In the year 1039, the church of Saint Mary, with its tithes, lands, forests, and other properties, was given to the Cluniac monastery in the village of Silvago, in the county of Geneva. The monks were invested by means of the rope of the church bell. The charter was issued in the year 1039 from the Incarnation, in the first year of King Henry.

This Henry was the son of Conrad, surnamed the Black, who succeeded his father in the empire and in the kingdom of Transjurane Burgundy. In the same year Laeco gave Abbot Odilo of Cluny three *condaminae* situated in the village of Silvago. The charter was issued in the year 1039 from the Incarnation, indiction 7, while Henry, son of Emperor Conrad, was reigning, in the first year of his imperial rule. The boundaries of the *condaminae* are described in the charter according to the four winds; by this word, evidently, some portion of land is designated.

The same date is given for the donation of an allod called Germinata, in the county of Geneva. In the same year Dundinus, taking the monastic habit under the rule of the monastery of Saint Peter of Cluny, as he himself says, gave his possessions to the monastery: in the year 1039 from the Incarnation, indiction 7, in the first year of King Henry. This may perhaps be the same Dundinus who is called Divus in another copy, where it is recorded that, likewise in the year 1039, indiction 7, in the first year of Henry, emperor and son of Conrad, he became a monk at Cluny and transferred his property at the village of Ausiacum to the monastery.

62. In the year 1040, under Henry, king of the Franks, Wigo, son of William, gave Abbot Odilo of Cluny a small estate in the village of Berziacum, in the county of Mâcon. Count Geoffrey confirmed the donation.

In the same year Bernard, bishop of Cahors, and his brother Robert gave Abbot Odilo the church of Saint Saturninus of Carennac. Another chartulary contains two charters of this same Bernard, donating the same church of Saint Saturninus, with all its appurtenances, to Odilo, abbot of Cluny, to be placed under his direction. Besides the canons, two abbots, Stephen and Albert, subscribed these charters; but they have no dates.

The Bernard mentioned in these charters is absent from the catalogues of the bishops of Cahors, both in Cruceus and in *Gallia Christiana*. For Bernard, whom these authors mention, had already died by the time these donations were made. Deodatus, or Deusdedit, his successor, was present in 1028 at the dedication of the church of Saint Savior at Limoges and preached at the Second Synod of Limoges in 1034. According to the authors cited, he is said to have died around 1040.

63. In the twelfth year of King Henry—which, if the reference is to his sole monarchy, would be the year 1042 from the Incarnation—the chapel of Saint Mary of Bracmacum, in the county of Chalon, was given to Odilo, abbot of Cluny. Count Theobald and others subscribed.

64. In the year 1046, Hugh, archbishop of Besançon, confirmed to Hugh, an honorable religious man and cleric, and permitted him to unite with the church of Laon—which that same Hugh had built and enlarged—the churches of Saint Mary of Calx, Saint Albinus, and Saint Symphorianus, with all their appurtenances. Done at Besançon, indiction 6, while Henry was reigning, in the year 1046. But the year does not agree with the indiction.

65. Count Pontius and the knight Rotland gave to the Cluniac foundation, where Lord Odilo presides as abbot, the churches of Saint Mary and Saint John, with their tithes and the entire priestly benefice, together with twelve *sextarades*—so the text reads—of land, in a place called Heron, in the district of Trevis, in the diocese of Die.

The charter was issued in the tenth year of King Eyco—is “Erico,” or Henry, to be read instead? But even if Henry is read, it remains to be investigated whether the reference is to the king of the Franks or to the emperor who, as we have already said, then ruled the kingdom of Burgundy. It is difficult to resolve this question without the original charter.

66. To these we add several charters drawn up under Saint Odilo but without dates. One such is the charter of Gerald, father, I think, of Armannus, bishop of Viviers, who, together with his wife Valmode, gave the Cluniac monastery—where Abbot Odilo presides—the church of Saint John in the village of Meissano, in the diocese of Viviers. Harmannus, or Hermannus, administered the church of Viviers at the beginning of the eleventh century.

Aymo of Petrafortis, while engaged in secular military service, gave to the Cluniac monastery, over which Lord Odilo presides as abbot, ruling the flock, a village situated in the district of Grenoble, in the county of Saroges, called Mons-Ermenoldi, together with all that appeared to belong to it—vineyards, meadows, and fields. Hubert, count of Savoy, his son Amedeus, Burcardus, Odo, and others subscribed. The charter is found in Guichenon’s proofs for the *History of Savoy*, p. 5.

A certain Ansedeus gave the Cluniac monastery the church of Saint Nazarius, with its altar and all its appurtenances, and four chapels situated nearby, in the territory of Autun, near the castle of Bourbon; he held this church as a benefice from Count Hugh. He also gave the church of Saint Peter in the village of Leuma, the chapel of Saint Praejectus there, and the church of Saint Baudilius in Pistichianum, and so forth. Counts Hugh and Theobald subscribed the donation.

Likewise Margrave Rotbald and his wife Eimildis gave Cluny, where Lord Odilo is abbot, the castle of Podius-Dolinus in its entirety, with all its appurtenances, situated in the county of Orange. Countess Adalax, her son William, Rostagnus of Sabran, William the viscount, and others subscribed with them.

A woman named Tetha gave the Cluniac monastery, where Abbot Odilo presides, Durannus the cleric, her servant. Bishop Walter and Warulf, the bishop’s brother, consented to the donation. After Odilo’s death and Hugh’s election in his place—when Hugh was then residing at Saint-Marcel during Lent—the same Walter and Warulf, together with another Walter, son of that Warulf, confirmed the aforesaid donation.

This same Walter confirmed a donation made by his mother Tescenda of land in the village of Cueles, for the soul of Walter, brother of her son Warulf. The nephews of that bishop, Walter, Bernard, and Otto, consented, with Hugh, prior of Cluny, present.

67. Particularly noteworthy is the *werpitio*—the formal renunciation—made by Boso concerning the *comanda* of Polliacum. We have therefore decided to transcribe it here from a Cluniac copy, where it appears without any date:

“Boso came to the court, where very noble men were present with Count Gerald, and Boso swore this oath, speaking in his own hand—that is, personally:

‘I, Boso, neither I nor any dependent of mine, man or woman, acting at my command, by my contrivance, or by my design, shall seek any *comanda* at Polliacum or in its obedience, nor shall I make any seizure of an ox, a cow, or anything else. And if I, or any man or woman under my authority, should make any claim upon the *comanda* or seize anything, then, within fifteen days after I learn of it, or after I am summoned to account by you, Gerald, or by your messengers, or by the abbot who is now in office, or by whoever shall hold that office in the future, or by the monk who holds that obedience, I shall make restitution for what was seized. Afterward I shall come to you, Gerald, for mercy—or to the abbot or monk who is now in office or who shall hold it in the future.’”

68. A charter of Count Rainald follows in the same place, also without any indication of time. He gives the Cluniac monastery the estate of Belmont, with its lands, villages, and appurtenances, situated in the county of Nevers—perhaps the reading should be “Nivernais”—for the soul of his father Landric, his mother Mathildis, his wife Advisa, and his brother Wido. Rainald himself subscribed, together with his wife Advisa and their son William.

How favorably disposed this Landric was toward the monks can be inferred from another charter, which likewise has no indication of time. In it he speaks as follows:

“I have always desired that the monks should lead a peaceful life and fulfill their vows without impediment. Therefore I wished to settle the dispute which the Cluniac monks had with the noblewoman Adelaide concerning land that her brother Antelmus had given them in the county of Autun, in the village of Fontinellulas,” and so forth.

Rainald, son of Count Landric; Gauzfrid, husband of Adelaide; and his sons Gauzfrid, Robert, and Walter subscribed, as did Adelaide’s sons Girboldus, Obtrannus, Gauzfrid, and Hugh, and also Countess Hatewis.

69. In the chartulary of Celsiniacum, which we had in hand, there are several charters of donations made to that place under the rule of blessed Odilo, but in almost none of them is a date found. Some contain the clause: “which is governed . . . . . ,” or “under the rule of the most blessed father Odilo.” Most concern the acquisition of burial rights.

Among them is one by Hugh of Ucio, Durannus of Deibanio, and others, who give two *appendariae* for the burial of Bomparus, and so forth. In another, Stephen and Theotberga give a vineyard in the village of Samniacum for their burial. The priest Rotbert gives certain possessions so that, if at some time, by the Lord’s permission, he should wish to become a monk, he may be received; but if not, and he should die in that place, he may obtain burial there.

William gave the Celsiniac monastery a church built in honor of blessed Peter, called Casa-Meiana, with *mansi*, *appendariae*, and other properties, so that it might remain with Saint Peter of Celsinianas—so the text reads—under the protection of Saint Peter of Rome, without anyone’s opposition, and so forth.

Finally, to omit many others, Bernard of Turre ceded to the Celsiniac foundation, which is governed under the direction of Lord Abbot Odilo, many properties in the village of Plausiacum, together with the entire allod which, he says, his father Gerald possessed in that village of Plausiacum on the very day when he became a monk.

It is therefore clear that the famous Gerald of Turre, whom the illustrious family of the present princes of Bouillon recognizes as the first ancestor of its family of Turre, attached himself to the Cluniac community; most of his descendants did the same, as we learn from this same chartulary.

It should not be passed over lightly that in several charters of the same place another Odilo is mentioned together with Odilo, abbot of Cluny; this other Odilo was then prior of the monastery of Celsiniacum. Consequently, if charters bearing the name of Odilo should sometimes appear whose chronological features do not sufficiently agree with the lifetime of Saint Odilo, they should not for that reason be called into question, but should be attributed to Odilo the prior.

It has seemed worthwhile to present one charter of this kind:

“In the name of God: Odilo, unworthy priest and negligent monk of the monastery of Cluny; also Odilo, provost of the monastery of Celsiniacum; and the other brothers serving God there.

We wish it to be known to those present and to those who shall come after that we could not retain in lasting peace the estate which a nobleman of good memory, named Eustorgius, had given to God, the holy apostles, and the monastery of Celsiniacum, unless his uncle Rotbert, a noble and Catholic man and dean of the Church of Auvergne, had deigned both to confirm the gift of his nephew and to grant it on his own behalf. This he did through his goodwill and sweetest charity.

Therefore we considered it right to return grace for grace to him, just as he humbly sought it, asking and beseeching us to receive him into the fellowship of our brothers, together with his father, mother, brothers, and their relatives. We, attending to his vow and desire, received them into our fellowship and brotherhood, wishing, praying, and beseeching that in all that we and our entire brotherhood may do or say, with the intercession of the blessed apostle Peter and all the saints, almighty God may grant them a share and fellowship with us: that he may grant the living time for repentance and pardon of sins, and bestow on the dead rest and eternal life.

If that lord, Lord Robert, should wish to join the monastic order, we earnestly command and, in commanding, beseech that he be received with charity and treated with honor and reverence. If he should wish to have burial in our place, let him be buried wherever he himself orders.

V. Various Monasteries Established, Restored, or Reformed by Saint Odilo

70. Which monasteries were subject to the jurisdiction of the abbots of Cluny in the year 996 we learn from a bull of Gregory V, supreme pontiff, reproduced in the Cluniac Bullary, p. 10. In it are listed individually not only the various possessions belonging to that most illustrious monastery, but also the cells—or, as they are called, priories—dependent upon it.

Some of these cells were placed under the rule of blessed Odilo, while others had been subject to the Cluniac monastery long before. Here we shall discuss only those which were assigned to the Cluniacensians during Odilo’s time, reviewing them in chronological order insofar as the ancient records permit.

71. From the bull of Gregory V which we have just cited, it is clear that the monastery of Magabrense had already been joined to Cluny in 996; but in what year this occurred is not known. Although we are certain that it happened during the time of blessed Odilo, as we learn from a charter of Walter, bishop of Autun, in which he himself explains the occasion and reasons for this union, we present the charter in full from an ancient copy written approximately five hundred years ago:

“We wish it to be known to all Christians living under the rule of the Catholic faith that I, Walter, by the grace of God bishop of Autun, reflecting upon the goods of the Church entrusted to me by God, and considering how much the divine majesty may deign to grant to my ability, judged it necessary to gather what was scattered and preserve what had been gathered. For this reason I sought the counsel of Lord Odilo, abbot of the monastery of Cluny, and of Lord Vivian and the other brothers of the aforesaid monastery, concerning a certain monastery of ours called Magabrense, consecrated in honor of Saint Martin. In the time of our predecessors it had been deprived not only of regular discipline but almost of every useful resource; and I desired to restore it to its former state of monastic religion.

I did this because I believed that I could find no other counsel so salutary as to seek assistance from the aforesaid Lord Odilo, abbot of the Cluniac monastery, and from the venerable Fathers of that place who lived under his regular direction, and to entrust the aforesaid monastery of Magabrense to their governance.

They, therefore, granting assent to our requests, began to organize that monastery according to the rule, insofar as the resources of the place permitted, appointing brothers there to serve almighty God.

Let everyone, present and future, know that I began this undertaking with the intention that the love and fellowship of the aforesaid Cluniac house, which in the time of Lord Abbot Majolus of venerable memory remained joined to our house by the bond of charity, might likewise remain unshaken and firm forever.

Therefore I hand over the aforesaid monastery of Magabrense to our brother, Lord Odilo the abbot, and to his successors, and to the monastery of Cluny, to be governed and ordered according to the rule forever, with the counsel of our clerics and of the other sons of the Church entrusted to us by God. The purpose is, as I have said above, that the fellowship of our place and of the Cluniac monastery may always, through the ages to come, be bound and united by the bond of charity, and that there may perpetually be held there a worthy commemoration of both the living and the dead clerics of the Church entrusted to us. Likewise, may their memory be celebrated in our church.

In doing this, I do not wish—God forbid!—to appear a destroyer of the place entrusted to me. I am not removing the aforesaid monastery from the power of my successors and of the holy Church of Autun; rather, I have arranged it so that the abbot of Cluny, his successors, and the brothers of that place may, with the counsel of our succeeding bishops and canons, organize, hold, and possess it according to the rule.

We ask and beseech our successors, the bishops and canons, by our supplication and entreaty, since they share in our desire, always to strengthen and confirm this our arrangement more fully by their pontifical dignity and authority, and to govern and direct it according to the will of almighty God and the fitting disposition of this our arrangement. Let them always be, as is right, protectors of that place and its strongest helpers against the adversities of evil men.

We establish and absolutely decree that no bishop who succeeds me, nor any person exercising any authority, presume to appoint an abbot or provost there without the permission and consent of the aforesaid abbot of Cluny and his successors.

The abbot of Cluny, the brothers of that place, and their successors shall likewise organize and arrange the aforesaid monastery with the counsel of our succeeding bishops and canons, namely, men who are good and devoted servants of Christ.

We have decided to strengthen this our arrangement both by a privilege of Roman authority and by a royal decree.

Walter, sinful bishop.”

In another copy of this charter, Humbald, abbot; Hemericus, abbot; Autus, precentor; and Anscherius, archdeacon, are recorded as having subscribed with Walter, the sinful bishop, as he is called here.

72. Rodulfus, a nobleman, founded the monastery of Beracum and endowed it with his own possessions. Rodulfus himself explains the occasion of its foundation in these words:

“I, Rodulfus, therefore, in the name of God, hearing every day through the authority of the sacred Scriptures that punishments are threatened to those who act wickedly, while heavenly dwellings are promised to those who act justly, and desiring to find some refuge where I might avoid the snares of my sins, could find no counsel so salutary as to build, according to my ability, some monastery suited to monastic religion, where suitable service might daily be offered to God and his saints.

For the purpose of undertaking and completing this, I went to the monastery of Paterniacum, the monastery of the venerable Odilo, abbot of Cluny, and of the brothers living there, to seek their assistance. Strengthened by their counsel, in the year 998 from the Incarnation of the Lord, namely in the fifth year of the most noble King Rudolf, I summoned Lord Aindricus, bishop of the Church of Lausanne, to dedicate this monastery. He, being good and noble, kindly and nobly fulfilled our desire.

This monastery is situated on the shore of Lake Yverdon, in the diocese of the holy Church of Lausanne, in the county of Vaud; it is dedicated in honor of the holy apostle Peter. I give this monastery to God and Saint Peter. I also grant to that monastery these lands,” and so forth.

In another copy of this charter, the bishop of Lausanne mentioned here is called Amedeus, but the reading of our copy should be retained. For this is Henry—whose name is sometimes written Aindricus or Ainricus in ancient charters—who administered the Church of Lausanne at the end of the tenth century.

73. At approximately the same time, the church of Saint Maurice of Maltacena, otherwise called Burgetum, is believed to have been given to Saint Odilo. Cluniac monks were established there, as is clear from various subsequent donations made by Count Humbert and his son Amedeus, published in Guichenon’s proofs for the *History of Savoy*. In the Cluniac Library, col. 412, there is a charter of King Rudolf concerning this matter, issued in the year 1024.

74. To approximately the same period, as it seems to me, may be assigned the establishment of monks at Saint Victor in the city of Geneva. At that time the church of Saint Victor was famous; the author of the *Life of Saint Odilo* calls it ancient and noble. Indeed, in chapter 22 of Fredegar’s *Chronicle*, it is said to have been built by Queen Sedeleuba in the suburb of Geneva. This Seleuba was the sister of Clotild, wife of Clovis the Great, and daughter of Chilperic, king of the Burgundians.

When the Empress Adelaide visited this church a few years before that time, she found it almost deserted. Distressed by this, she persuaded Hugh, the bishop of that city, not to neglect a place so venerable and so well suited to the establishment of monastic religion.

The discovery of the body of the blessed martyr gave support to the empress’s wishes; this occurred at that time. The bishop mentioned above discovered the sacred remains, which had long been hidden, by some unknown circumstance, and, in the presence of King Rudolf, his wife Egildrud, and other leading members of the court, bishops, and counts, reverently placed them beneath the altar of the same basilica in a solemn procession.

But the resources of the place were not sufficiently ample for an abbot to be established there. Therefore, “it should be remembered”—these are the words of Bishop Hugh in the charter which he drew up concerning the matter—“that I summoned Odilo, abbot of the monastery of Cluny, to carry this out, and, with the permission of Lord King Rudolf, and also with the consent of his brother Burchard, archbishop of Lyon, and at the urging of the other counts and noblemen, I entrusted the aforesaid place of the holy martyr Victor to his governance . . . so that the aforesaid place might remain in religion forever, that the most excellent charity between our successors and the abbots of the Cluniac monastery might be firmly established, and that our memory might be specially preserved among them,” and so forth.

This charter, which Guichenon published in the *Bibliotheca Sebusiana*, century 1, no. 13, has no date; consequently, different scholars have assigned it to different years. The brothers Sammarthani infer from this charter, in their catalogue of the bishops of Geneva, that the Hugh mentioned here as bishop of Geneva lived in the year 930. But it can be demonstrated from this alone that they were mistaken: Odilo, to whom the church of Saint Victor is said to have been entrusted on this occasion, was not associated in the government of Cluny by blessed Majolus until 992 or the preceding year.

Guichenon conjectures that the charter was issued around 1019. If, however, the date of the charter of King Rudolf reported in the Cluniac Library, col. 411, is genuine, Agiltrudis, Rudolf’s first wife, who is mentioned in the charter concerning Saint Victor, had already died by 1019, since Rudolf there calls his wife Iraisinda.

Yet Rudolf is said to have confirmed, at the request of his wife Agiltrudis, his brother Bishop Burchard, and Abbot Odilo, all the privileges of the Cluniac monastery granted by his predecessors, in a diploma said to have been issued in 998. It therefore seemed preferable to assign the aforesaid donation of Saint Victor to the earlier years of that king.

75. In the year 999, Hugh, bishop of Auxerre and also count of Chalon, completely subjected to the Cluniac monastery the monastery of Aurea Vallis, otherwise Paredum. It had previously been built by his father, Count Lambert, with the assistance of Saint Majolus, but it was supposed to remain under its own abbot. This is clear from his charter, which Peraldus published from the original in his collection of Burgundian charters, p. 166:

“Issued in the month of May, indiction 12, in the year 999 from the Incarnation of the Lord, in the fourth year of King Robert’s reign. Udebaldus, though an unworthy priest and monk, wrote it. Done in the suburb of Chalon, in the monastery of blessed Marcellus, in the presence of King Robert.”

The king himself, however, did not subscribe, although Duke Henry and other counts and noblemen subscribed with Hugh, among them Bishops Rodgerius and Raynaldus.

We possess a copy of the same charter, by means of which several words that Peraldus could not read in the original can be supplied; the original had undoubtedly been worn away in certain places by age. In our copy, Ainricus is written for Henricus, as frequently occurs in ancient charters. The mother of Bishop Hugh is also called not Adellerdis but Adelaydis, a fact confirmed to us from other sources. Moreover, the person called Count Marcius among Peraldus’s subscribers is called Count Mauricius in our copy.

In the same copy, Hugh also mentions the donation of the church of Saint Marcellus, formerly made to Saint Majolus by Gaufredus, his mother’s husband. After the words “let the donation be made,” the charter reads as follows:

“Moved by the same vow and desire, and strengthened by the counsel and authority of the aforesaid princes and bishops, he transfers to the apostles and to the aforesaid abbot and the brothers entrusted to him, who inhabit the aforesaid Cluniac monastery, and likewise to their successors forever, the place of Saint Marcellus situated in the suburb of Chalon, namely where that holy martyr himself rests bodily, together with all that belongs to it, just as formerly it was entrusted by Count Gaufredus, husband of the mother of this same prelate, to Saint Majolus and his successors, to be possessed, organized, and administered by perpetual right, without anyone’s opposition.

This testament was pleasing,” and so forth, as in the published texts.

That this addition is not spurious is clear from a charter of Count Theobald of Chalon, the nephew of our Hugh. In it he testifies that the monastery of Saint Marcellus had been commended to Saint Majolus by Count Gaufredus, who had married Adheleidis, the widow of Lambert, Theobald’s grandfather, with the consent of Adheleidis and of Hugh, then a cleric and later bishop.

“Afterward,” he says, “while the most serene King Robert was reigning, my uncle, Lord Hugh, count and bishop, in the presence of that king, the counts, and the bishops of this region, gave the aforesaid monastery to Lord Odilo, abbot and successor of Abbot Majolus,” and so forth. Theobald himself confirms this donation; his complete charter on the matter was published in the previous century, p. 772.

[Note: [Col. 0859D] *Patrologia*, vol. CXXXVII, under MAIOLUS.]

Robert, king of the Franks, also confirmed the donation of the monastery of Aurea Vallis, or Paredum, to the Cluniacensians, as André Duchesne observed in his notes on the *Life of Blessed Hugh*, printed in the appendix to the Cluniac Library, col. 93. The same Bishop Hugh and count also gave that monastery the villages of Vivens and Moncellum, together with certain other properties, as is clear from another charter of his issued in the twentieth year of King Robert.

76. In this same year, 999, Emperor Otto III confirmed to the Cluniac monastery the monastery of Blessed Mary at Pavia, commonly called the Cell of Saint Majolus. A diploma concerning this matter is found in the Cluniac Library, col. 409. This place is called most noble in the *Life of Saint Odilo*, and the same holy man greatly advanced it.

77. In the fifteenth year of King Robert, in the month of September—and therefore in the year 1011 of the common era, if the reference is to his sole monarchy—Wido, a nobleman, subjected to Cluny the monastery of Thieru, which had formerly been held as a secular possession by his parents. Peter, abbot of that place, consented; the rights and prerogatives of the abbacy were reserved to him for the whole of his life.

Gregory of Tours discusses the relics of Saint Symphorianus, deposited in the altar of the church of Thigernum, in book 1, chapter 52, of *The Glory of the Martyrs*. He discusses the discovery made there of the martyr Genesius in chapter 67 of the same book.

78. At the beginning of the eleventh century, though the precise year is uncertain, the monastery at Valentiola in the diocese of Riez was founded. The occasion for this was the donation of an estate in the same place, which Gregory V mentions in the bull already cited by us. Since blessed Odilo judged it suitable for the construction of a monastery, he requested and obtained permission from the bishop, as is clear from an old record that we have transcribed from the Cluniac cartulary, where the following is read:

“Abbot Odilo sends monks to Almeradus, bishop of Riez, to ask permission to build a monastery beside the church in the village of Valentiola, which had been consecrated in ancient times in honor of the holy confessor Maximus. He consented and decreed that no person should exercise lordship or customary rights in the said place, and that the brothers residing there might receive what was offered by the faithful.”

No date is appended, but from this we conjecture that Almeradus presided over the Church of Riez at the beginning of the eleventh century, because he bestowed several possessions upon the monastery of Lérins, which at that time was governed by Abbot Warnerius. For Warnerius preceded Saint Odilo in the administration of the monastery of Lérins.

The same Almeradus—or, as he is written there, Helmeradus—in a certain charter, while Lord Warnerius was acting as provost of Cluny, acknowledged before the relics contained in an image of Saint Peter that he was not entitled to the tithes of his own labor from the lands of Valentiola and from the other possessions dependent upon Cluny. The charter was issued in the church of Valentiola itself, but is without a date, as is also a third charter in which the same prelate remits to Saint Odilo certain annual revenues that the church of Valentiola used to pay to the bishop.

Finally, a certain Archimbertus and his son Pontius relinquished to the Cluniac monks whatever they claimed to be theirs by right in the village of Valentiola, and so forth. This took place in the council held at the capu [sic; so our copy reads—should it be *campo* (“field”) or *capitulo* (“chapter”)?] of Saint Romanus, in the presence of Bishop Joscelin and many others, in the diocese of Friedun. The year is not given. What diocese Friedun was, over which this bishop presided, is unknown to us, unless perhaps it should be read as Forojuliensis, whose Church was governed around this time by Gaucelmus, or Gocelinus, who is said to have bestowed many possessions upon the monastery of Lérins.

[Col. 0862A]

79. In the year 1022, Odilo undertook the government of the monastery of Lérins and presided over it until 1028, when Amalricus was appointed in his place, as we learn from two manuscript chronicles in our possession. With their help, Vincent Barrulis, a monk of that place, should be corrected: in his *Chronology of the Saints of Lérins* he wrote that Odilo was placed in charge of the island of Lérins shortly after the death of Saint Maiolus. The same author cites two charters issued by Odilo as abbot of Lérins, but neither contains a date, nor do they in the Cluniac Library, where they have been published again.

80. The church of Juliacum underwent many changes, and it is therefore extremely difficult to assign the time when it was first inhabited by Cluniac monks. Certainly, we have already cited the charter of Otto, surnamed William, duke of Burgundy, issued during the reign of Rodulfus, in which, after confessing that he had long turned a deaf ear to the appeals of Abbots Maiolus and Odilo, he is said at last, moved by remorse, to have restored Juliacum.

[Col. 0862B]

81. After Otto William had restored Juliacum to the Cluniac monks, certain secular men attempted to appropriate the same place for themselves. Their efforts could be checked only by the gift of another estate from Count Raynaldus, Otto’s son. We establish this from an old record preserved in the Cluniac cartulary, in these words:

“Count Otto, who is surnamed William, restored to the monks serving God in the most famous monastery of Cluny the estate called Juliacum. After a long time had passed, Aymo and Otbertus, the sons of Aldo, arose and proclaimed that this estate was their inheritance. But this calumny ceased in the presence of Count Raynaldus, son of the aforesaid William, who, on account of this calumny, gave the aforementioned Aymo and Otbertus another estate, which they accepted, and they abandoned their complaint.

“Sign of Count Raynaldus. Sign of Adheleidis, his wife. Sign of Azelmus, abbot of Mont-Saint-Jean. These things were done at the castle of Dijon, in the year 1022, in the sixth indiction, under Robert, king of the Franks.”

Otto William, however, had not yet died in the year 1022; this is a copyist’s error. Robert, duke of the Burgundians, mentions both restorations in another old record from the same cartulary, issued in the time of King Henry, his brother. In this record Robert testifies that William and his son Raynaldus, by the authority and command of his father, King Robert, restored Juliacum to the Cluniac monastery, with the consent of Hugh, count of Chalon, and of many other noblemen of both military orders; Robert himself confirms and strengthens the restoration.

[Col. 0862D]

82. In the year 1025, blessed Odilo built the monastery of Volta on his paternal estate. What had been promised by his brothers many years earlier, but which they had been unable to fulfill, he himself completed together with his nephews, their sons. The inscription still exists, as Andreas Duchesne testifies in his notes to the *Life of Saint Odilo*, appendix to the Cluniac Library, p. 74, in verse above the door of the church of that place, through which access is gained to the cloister. It conveys the following in these few words:

> This temple, O King of kings, [lacuna]  
> Odilo founded for you.

The saintly abbot himself, however, sets out the entire sequence of events in the foundation charter, which we gave in full above, in paragraph two.

83. Around this time, the viscount Kadolenus, together with his wife and his son William, gave the Cluniac monastery a place called Saint John of Molgone. We gather that several documents concerning this matter existed from various records dealing with it in the Cluniac cartularies. The donation was made while King Robert was reigning and Duke William was governing Aquitaine, in the month of May.

Isembertus, bishop of Poitiers, subscribed to it, calling himself pontiff of the Aquitanians; with him were Jordan, bishop of Limoges, and Roho of Angoulême. Also subscribing were the viscounts Joffredus and Acfredus, and then William of Parthenay. Kadolenus, however, is nowhere said to have subscribed, perhaps because the documents concerning this matter were drawn up only after his death.

[Col. 0863B]

84. It is not clear when the monks began to inhabit the house of Sariano. Its beginnings are owed to a certain Leodegarius, a Cluniac monk, who built a church there by his own labor. Once it had been endowed, monks were established there. The church was dedicated by Regimbaldus, archbishop of Arles, who began to preside over this church around the year 1031.

We learn this from an old record, which we possess transcribed on ancient parchment. After a brief formula, it reads as follows:

“A certain servant of God, named Leodegarius, a brother and monk of the monastery of Cluny, in the village called Sarrianis—which the late William, once duke of Provence and father of his country, had assigned to the holy apostles Peter and Paul, to the monastery of Cluny, and to the place where he requested to be buried, and to blessed Maiolus while he was still living in the flesh, and which, while alive, he had designated and, at his death, had granted by donation—undertook to build a church. He requested that it be consecrated and dedicated by Lord Regimbaldus, venerable archbishop of the people of Arles, to the honor of God and the memory of the Lord’s victorious cross, of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, of blessed Marcellus, pope and martyr, of blessed Saturninus, renowned martyr,

[Col. 0863D]

and of all the saints living and reigning with their head, Christ, forever and ever. The aforesaid brother also gives to the aforesaid church, on the day of its consecration, one mansion, for the support and benefit, through succeeding generations, of those who serve God there.”

At the end, without anyone’s subscription, there is this clause:

“May all the faithful who praise this work of ours prosper.”

85. In the year 1029, Rodulfus, king of Transjurane Burgundy, at the request of Count Reinoldus, son of Otto surnamed William, granted the monastery of Vallis, situated in the diocese of Besançon, to the Cluniac monks, and confirmed to it everything that had been bestowed by Otto William and by Reinoldus, his son.

Perardus gives the charter in full, p. 177. It was issued at Logis in the year 1029, the thirty-fifth year of King Rodulfus. There it says:

“the monastery built in honor of God and our Savior Jesus Christ, and likewise of his mother Mary, and of the holy apostle Peter, and also of blessed Nicholas, the holy confessor, situated in the bishopric of Besançon beside Pollignac, in the place properly called Vallis.”

We learn that this monastery was built from its foundations by Otto William from a charter of Hugh, archbishop of Besançon. In it he confirms the donation of tithes, offerings, burials, chapels, and so forth, in the village called Mediolanum, and of the chapel of Saint Victor at Madriacum, made by his predecessor Walter to the church of Vallis. He says that Otto William had built this church,

[Col. 0864B]

and that Walter himself had consecrated it in honor of blessed Mary. In another copy, Hugh himself is said to have granted all these things with Abbot Odilo’s intervention. It was issued in the year 1033, on the feast of Saint John, and was subscribed by Provost R., Robert the abbot, two archdeacons, Abbot Radaldus, and many other canons and laymen.

86. The foundation of the monastery of Chauriaco must be assigned to a date before 1034. It was founded by Stephen, bishop of Clermont, under the rule of Saint Odilo, for the benefit of the monastery of Celsinacum. For in that year Renco, Stephen IV’s successor, was already presiding over the Church of Clermont, which he still governed in 1052.

We have an account of this foundation in the Celsinacum cartulary:

“Stephen, bishop of the holy Church of God at Clermont, and his mother and brothers, together with Rorgius and his son Faramundus, and all the canons of the holy Church of Clermont, gave to God and Saint Peter and to the place of Celsinacum, which is governed under the direction of Lord Odilo the abbot, three churches and six dependencies. The first church is called Chauriaco, so that a monastery may be built there; the second is Saint Mary; the third is Saint Marcella, together with tithes, baptisteries, burials, fields, meadows, and so forth. This donation was made in the month of December, on Tuesday, while our Lord Jesus Christ was reigning.”

87. Under the same episcopate of Stephen, and under nearly the same conditions, the monastery of Saint Flour among the Auvergnats was founded. Amblardus and Eustorgius, noblemen, granted it to the Cluniac monks residing in the monastery of Celsinacum under the rule of blessed Odilo. The document of their donation is preserved in the Celsinacum cartulary; Stephen, bishop of Clermont, and Robert, viscount, subscribed it together with the donors.

The monastery of Saint Flour remained under the obedience of the Cluniac order until the year 1317. At that time, after Gerard, abbot of Aurillac, had renounced the episcopal dignity, Raymundus Vehens, prior of Saint Flour, became bishop, and his monastery was converted into a cathedral. The monks nevertheless remained there until the year 1476, when Sixtus IV granted them secular dress.

[Col. 0865A]

88. In the year 1037, the monastery of Saint Marcellus at Salciacum, situated in the diocese and county of Valence, was handed over to the Cluniac monks so that regular discipline might be restored there, since it had not been possible to maintain it under the abbots appointed there.

We have the charter of this grant, which we produce from the Cluniac cartulary:

“After the first man transgressed, and so forth. I, Count Ademarus, and my wife, named Rotildis, together with our sons—namely Bishop Pontius, Hugh, Lambertus, Gontardus, and Geraldus—give to God and to the holy apostles Peter and Paul, and to the Cluniac monks, over whom Lord Odilo the abbot presides, a certain place called Saltiacum, situated in the bishopric and county of the city of Valence and consecrated in honor of Saint Marcellus the martyr. Until now it has been placed under certain abbots in a state of neglect regarding the care of souls, so that it may be converted to a condition of better rectitude, together with everything belonging to that place, namely lands, pastures, woods, vineyards, waters, mills, meadows, and all its dependencies, to possess and administer, and with hereditary right to do whatever they wish.

“We do this so that both we and all our relatives and friends, and also the soul of Lord Count Lambertus and the souls of all faithful Christians, may deserve to have fellowship and a share in the prayers of the servants of God who serve Christ in the monastery of Cluny or in all its dependencies.

“Publicly enacted in the year from the incarnation of the Lord 1037, while Emperor Cono was reigning, in the tenth year of his reign.

[Col. 0865C]

“Witnesses: Count Ademarus and his wife Rotildis, who made this donation and received ten ounces of gold from the monks for it; and the monk Edraldus, who rendered them great service by acquiring it for Saint Peter. Bishop Pontius, and his brother Hugh, and their brothers Lambertus, Gontardus, and Geraldus. Rainardus the priest wrote this, dictated by Raintardus.”

Bishop Pontius, the son of Ademarus, who is mentioned in this charter and subscribed it, governed the Church of Valence after Guigo. He was still seated in 1047, as can be gathered from several charters; but in what year he took up or relinquished this see is unknown to us.

89. Count Lambertus, mentioned there, was the father of Ademarus the donor. He had arranged for the monastery of Saint Marcellus itself, which had been entirely deserted, to be restored, as is clear from another charter in which he speaks as follows together with his wife Fuletrudis:

“We give from the property belonging to us to God and Saint Marcellus, and to the monks Oddo and Durannus, and to those who shall come to that place, for our sons Ademarus and Lambertus and for our parents, so that the church of Saint Marcellus may be rebuilt there and a monastery established there, and so that the place itself may be subject to no one except Saint Peter, prince of the apostles.

“Let no abbot be held or chosen in the said place of Saint Marcellus of Fellinis except one who observes and keeps the Rule of Saint Benedict and charitably compels the brothers subject to him to do the same.”

Because the leaf is damaged, no date is preserved. Its heading nevertheless says that it was made under King Conrad.

[Col. 0866A]

Indeed, the same Conrad confirmed this donation in the forty-sixth year of his reign, that is, in the year 983 of the common era.

90. The foundation of the cell of Saint Lawrence in the region of Mâcon must be assigned to the year 1039, as is clear from the charter of the viscount Archimbaldus. In that same year, in the seventh indiction, while King Henry was reigning, he gave Abbot Odilo a vineyard-estate situated in the region of Mâcon, on the condition that a community of monks living under the discipline of the abbots of Cluny should be established in the church of Saint Lawrence, which he had previously given to the Cluniac monastery. The estate, together with the other properties belonging to that church, was to be transferred for their use.

91. In the year 1045—but the eleventh indiction prefixed to the charter in the copy does not agree with it—the monastery of Saint Savior of Nevers was subjected to the Cluniac monks by Hugh, bishop of that city, with the consent of Adalelmus, the rector of the place, and the canons of the church of Saint Cyricus, to whose jurisdiction it had previously belonged. The document drawn up concerning this matter is preserved in the Cluniac cartulary. It was publicly issued in the holy synod, in the year 1045, in the eleventh indiction, on the eighth day before the Ides of November.

92. Under Henry, king of the Franks, though the year is uncertain, Peter, bishop of Toulouse and son of Roger, was staying at Cluny. Astonished by the holiness of the monks residing there, he bestowed upon them the church of Saint Columba, situated in his diocese.

We infer that monks were established there not only because many other churches, with estates and dependencies, belonged to this church, but also because in the diploma of Paschal II, in the Cluniac Library, p. 571, among the properties he confirms to the Cluniac monks, there appears the monastery of Saint Columba in the bishopric of Toulouse.

This same church, which had somehow been alienated from the Cluniac monks, was restored to them by Amelius, bishop of Toulouse, while Pontius was abbot of Cluny, as is clear from his charter, issued in the year 1110 under King Louis and preserved in full in the Cluniac Library, col. 578.

Anselm, canon of the church of Liège, writes in chapter 53 of his *Deeds of the Bishops of that Church* that blessed Odilo and his successors acquired many churches in the parish of Liège. In these churches, he says, devout monks were established by him under the name of priories; night and day they never cease to strike the ears of divine mercy on behalf of the welfare of the Church.

93. These were the principal monasteries which, as far as we have been able to learn from ancient records, were entrusted during Odilo’s time to the governance of the Cluniac abbots, apart from many others that had already been subjected to Cluny under his predecessors and that he restored or entirely renewed, as the author of his *Life* testifies.

Besides these, Odilo also brought various other monasteries back to better practice when, through the misfortunes of the times or the negligence of their abbots, they had fallen away from the fervor of regular discipline. These, however, were not subjected to the Cluniac monks. Among them were the famous monastery of Saint-Denis and many others throughout Gaul. In these places, especially through the agency of King Hugh, the holy man restored regular discipline, as Ademarus and the author of the *Chronicle of Saint Maixent* testify.

William, duke of Aquitaine, likewise, as Ademarus asserts, entrusted several monasteries under his authority to Odilo’s direction for the same reason. Thus, at the monastery of Angeriacum, he arranged for Raynaldus to be appointed abbot in place of Alduinus, who had died, and for Aymericus to be substituted for Raynaldus, who likewise died—although the author of the *Chronicle of Maillezais* says that Goffridus succeeded Raynaldus.

Such, indeed, was the opinion held by everyone of blessed Odilo and of the Cluniac monks living under his rule that many monks of other places, who possessed a love of regular discipline, embraced the customs of the Cluniac monks; indeed, they even received abbots from Cluny, although they remained independent and did not wish to be subjected in other respects to the Cluniac monastery.

This happened especially when the monks requested it, or when it pleased the bishops or princes under whose authority such monasteries were established. Thus, Durandus, who had been made abbot of Savigny at the recommendation of the Cluniac abbot and other abbots of the order, was succeeded by Iterius, a Cluniac monk, on the advice of Saint Odilo, as Burchardus, bishop of Lyon, testifies in a charter written concerning this matter, the original of which we have in our hands.

94. The fame of the Cluniac monastery and of its most holy abbot was not confined within the boundaries of Gaul. It provided the occasion for the Cluniac institution to be propagated among foreign nations.

We have a distinguished example of this in Sancho, king of the Spains. Since he was inspired by a desire to establish monasteries properly throughout his kingdom, he sent one of his own men to Cluny, on the advice of his bishops and nobles. His name was Paternus. Thoroughly instructed in regular discipline and in the holy customs of that place, he was later to return and ensure that those practices were observed in the monasteries of Spain.

We learn this from the same king’s diploma for the monastery of Oña, which our Yepes published in the appendix to volume V of the *Annals of our Order*. There the most devout prince speaks as follows:

“The monastic order, the most perfect of all ecclesiastical orders, was at that time unknown throughout our entire homeland. [lacuna] At last, with God inspiring me, I found salutary counsel among prudent and religious men. From their reports I learned that no one could display the perfection of that holy profession which I sought more perfectly than the congregation of the Cluniac monastery, which at that time flourished more clearly and perfectly than the other monasteries of Saint Benedict in regular religion, with God’s help and under the administration of the venerable Abbot Odilo.

“Therefore, concerning this matter, I sought the counsel of all our bishops and nobles, and sent one of our countrymen, a man as religious and God-fearing as it is possible for human beings to know, named Paternus, together with a devout company of religious companions, to the aforesaid monastery of Cluny, so that he might learn and understand there the perfection of the monastic life. Once sufficiently instructed in it, he was to return to our homeland and offer our thirsty homeland a drink of the monastic profession.

“By God’s gracious gift, what we had arranged was accomplished. For this same man, perfectly instructed in the teaching of regular discipline together with his companions, returned safely to us. We first appointed him teacher of the monastic life in the monastery of Saint John of Peña; and, so that the brothers might live regularly under him, we placed him in charge as pastor of souls. We strengthened the aforesaid monastery with royal gifts and the firmest privileges, so that it might persist securely in the stability of regular life, and so forth.

“After this monastery had been properly ordered through regular discipline, all the bishops and princes of the entire kingdom took counsel together. They came to me unanimously and urged that, just as I had adorned the monastery of Saint John of Peña with monastic religion, so I should also honor the monastery of Oña with the same regular profession of blessed Benedict. This monastery had formerly been built in honor of the holy Savior by the religious Count Sancho, and so forth.

“I sent to the monastery of Saint John of Peña and requested that Lord Paternus, whom we had appointed abbot of the venerable congregation there, come to us with a number of religious brothers. He graciously obeyed my just request, and without any delay I obtained from him what I had asked. After removing the women who were living in the monastery of Oña without any reverence, we established there, with the consent, will, and petition of all the bishops and clergy of our homeland, a congregation of religious monks. By the common acclamation of the brothers, we placed over them as abbot a man named Garsea, according to the Rule of Saint Benedict.

“After the abbot of the place had been carefully instructed and the congregation honorably arranged, we sent Lord Paternus back to his own monastery. Therefore, so that it might remain undisturbed …”

The king makes further provisions concerning the election of the abbot and the monastery’s immunity, for he wishes it to be subject to no one at all. If an abbot should at some time deserve to be deposed as guilty of grave offenses, this is to be done only by council.

The Paternus mentioned in the royal diploma is the same man to whom Odilo wrote the letter published in volume II of the *Spicilegium*, p. 386. There he calls him “Lord Paternus, fervent in the love of God, a prudent guardian of Christ’s flock with paternal affection.” From the same letter it can readily be inferred how deeply Odilo was bound to King Sancho and to his son Ranimirus: he arranged for the kingdom of Spain to be commended in the public assembly at every hour of the day through daily prayers.

The Cluniac order also possessed monasteries in Spain that were entirely subject to its jurisdiction, even during the time of Saint Odilo. Among these was the famous monastery of Saint Zoilus at Carrión, where Arnulfus is said by Spanish historians to have been appointed the first prior of the place by the saintly abbot himself. Several other monasteries were also subject to this one, and all of them venerated Cluny as their mother. In the year 1435, however, Eugenius IV bestowed the title of abbot upon the priors of Carrión, who had been withdrawn from the authority of the Cluniac monks.

### VI. The Affection of Supreme Pontiffs, Kings, and Other Princes toward Saint Odilo

95. So great was the reputation for holiness of the Cluniac monks under the rule of blessed Odilo that all faithful and devout men desired to bind them to themselves by benefits or donations, believing that nothing would be lacking to them if they were aided before God by the prayers and patronage of such men.

Hence we read of so many bulls of pontiffs and so many diplomas of kings and emperors issued in their favor, by which either ancient privileges were confirmed or new ones granted. We also read of so many charters of princes and other men, both noble and humble, by which either new monasteries were established for habitation by Cluniac monks, or monasteries already erected were enlarged with estates and various possessions, so that at least the number of those serving God under so holy a discipline might increase within them.

Pontiffs and kings seemed to compete over which of them would be more generous toward the Cluniac monks. The pontiffs, at the intercession of secular princes, granted privileges; the princes, for their part, at the recommendation of the pontiffs, defended by their authority the properties already acquired by the monastery and enlarged the old possessions with new donations.

96. This can be seen in the bull of Gregory V, in which he states that he granted the privilege at the intervention of the emperor Otto. He enumerated every possession of the Cluniac monastery so carefully and minutely that none might be without the benefit of his confirmation. It was published in the Cluniac Bullary, p. 10; for that reason we have not thought it necessary to reproduce it here.

The following, which Silvester II, Gregory’s successor, wrote to blessed Odilo, are worthy of notice in the same work, p. 11:

“Silvester to Odilo, beloved son and illustrious abbot, and to the entire congregation entrusted to him: loving greetings and apostolic blessing. We entrust ourselves at all times to your most holy prayers, and with earnest petitions we beg you to deign to receive us; for in whatever condition our own position may be, your advancement will in no way suffer any loss,” and so forth.

We possess two letters of Benedict VIII against the invaders of the Cluniac monastery’s possessions. In the first letter, addressed to the bishops of Aquitaine, Burgundy, and Provence, to whom it is inscribed, he urges them to act manfully in defending the Cluniac monastery, which had been built by William, the most noble prince of Aquitaine, and placed under the special protection of the Roman Church by him, with the praise and approval of the Roman emperor and of the kings of the Franks and Burgundians.

From this same letter we gather that Robert, king of the Franks, was greatly distressed by such harassment of the Cluniac monks, since the pontiff testifies that complaints concerning it had been brought to him in the presence of the God-devoted Lord Robert, king of the Franks, and of his princes and nobles, who had come with him to the threshold of the apostles.

The other letter of Pope Benedict is addressed to Stephen, bishop of Auvergne. He commands him not to delay binding with the bond of excommunication certain of the invaders listed in the preceding letter, whom he designates by name, because they had disobediently neglected to restore the possessions of the Cluniac monastery.

John XIX, as the title in the Cluniac Bullary, p. 8, indicates, at the intervention of Saint Henry the emperor, asserted all the rights, both spiritual and temporal, of the Cluniac monastery in a letter that he wrote to Odilo concerning this matter. Another letter of the same pontiff is praised there, in which, at the intervention of Emperor Conrad, he confirms all the possessions and rights of the Cluniac monastery.

The same pontiff, in a letter to Robert, king of the Franks, urges him to defend the same place against its invaders. He also wrote to Burchardus, archbishop of Lyon, and to Gauslenus, bishop of Mâcon, to assert the monastery’s immunity from every episcopal jurisdiction.

In a letter addressed to all the faithful, he testifies that, following in the footsteps of his predecessors, and with the consent of many bishops then gathered at Rome in synod in the presence of Lord Conrad, the newly crowned emperor, he confirmed all the privileges and immunities of the Cluniac monks.

It was issued on the fifth day before the Kalends of April, in the third year of Pope John, in the tenth indiction. These chronological indications agree very well with the year 1027.

Finally, Clement II wrote to the bishops, princes, and magnates of Gaul, commending to them in the same way the protection of the Cluniac monastery.

97. The esteem in which Odilo was held by the princes of this world is proved by the many charters of donations that we cited above and by the various diplomas issued in his favor. The bulls of the pontiffs testify to the same thing, in which the Roman pontiffs declare that they have undertaken the care of the Cluniac monks, moved especially to do so by the intervention of emperors or kings.

Certainly Otto III, under whose reign Odilo was appointed to govern the Cluniac monastery, confirmed to him the monastery of Saint Maiolus near Pavia, as is clear from the diploma issued concerning this matter, which we cited above from the Cluniac Library.

Adhelais Augusta, the wife of the emperor Otto I, honored Odilo above all others. The saintly man himself wrote her *Life*. It will suffice to quote a single passage, from which it will be clear how great and sincere this blessed woman’s veneration was for the holy abbot.

He speaks of the matter in this way, referring to himself without naming himself:

“There was indeed there, in her presence, shortly before she was to depart this life, a monk who, although unworthy to be called an abbot, was nevertheless thought by her to be a man of some importance. When she looked at him, and he in turn looked at her, both began to weep profusely. I would say that she did more than if I said that she had healed many sick people. For she humbly took hold of the rather unkempt garment in which he was dressed and kissed it with her most holy eyes and her serene face. Then she said to him humbly and in silence: ‘Remember me, my son, in your contemplations, and know that I shall no longer see you with bodily eyes. When I have departed from human affairs, I entrust my soul to the prayers of the brothers.’

“From there she proceeded along the road by which she had come and reached the place where, by God’s ordering, she had decided that a tomb should be prepared for her.”

Saint Henry, the protector of monks, succeeded Emperor Otto. He demonstrated his affection for Cluny by magnificent gifts. Among them, as Ademarus reports in his *Chronicle*, were a golden scepter, a golden orb, a golden imperial garment, a golden crown, and a golden crucifix, weighing together one hundred pounds, along with many other things.

The same author continues that he often held familiar conversations with Odilo, the abbot of that place, and took him with the leading men into the hall of his palace. The author of the *Chronicle of Saint Maixent*, or of Maillezais, repeats the same account.

98. The various diplomas of Hugh, king of the Franks, and of Robert, his son and successor, readily prove the veneration in which they held Odilo’s holiness and innocence of character.

Robert wished him to be present, together with the other bishops and nobles of the kingdom, at the translation of the body of Saint Aignan at Orléans, which the most devout prince desired to make highly celebrated. “The presence of Lord Odilo, the venerable abbot of the Cluniac monks, was not lacking,” says Helgadus, “nor that of other good men of no small merit, with whom he always desired to converse.”

We can understand how greatly Robert revered Odilo’s holiness from the *Chronicle of Dijon*. There we read that, when William, abbot of Saint Benignus, learned that King Robert—who was devastating everything in Burgundy—intended to come to Dijon, “the aforesaid Abbot William,” says the chronicler, “ordered the monks to withdraw to other monasteries, [lacuna] leaving only a few to guard the place and serve Saint Benignus, together with Lord Abbot Odilo. He had summoned him for this purpose, so that, if the king should perhaps attempt any harm against this place, he might be persuaded by Odilo’s prayers to leave it alone.”

And in fact Robert inflicted no harm upon the monastery.

Robert, duke of the Burgundians and son of the same King Robert, calls Saint Odilo a devoted and faithful friend of his salvation and honor.

William, duke of Aquitaine, revered him so greatly that, as Ademarus testifies, he said that he believed he saw in him a temple of the Holy Spirit and handed himself over to him, commended into his hands. For this reason, as we observed above, he subjected several monasteries in his territory to Odilo.

[Col. 0871D] **99.** Rodulfus, the third king of Transjurane Burgundy bearing this name, issued at the very beginning of his reign a charter in which he declared that he wished to be the monastery of Cluny’s most invincible protector, and called upon all the nobles and judges of his kingdom to do the same for him. This diploma is preserved in the Sebusian Library, century I, chapter 55. It would be superfluous to collect more material concerning this ruler, since we have frequently cited various of his charters above.

Odilo’s reputation among foreign peoples was no less than among the Gauls. We may infer that he was held in the highest favor by Sancho, king in Spain, and by his son Ramiro, from a letter of Odilo himself to Paternus, which we cited above. The same is clear from another letter, addressed to García, the son and successor of Sancho, [Col. 0872A] where he writes as follows:

> “Therefore, we know that, on account of the indissoluble intimacy and fellowship by which we were formerly joined to your father, we are so devoted to your loyalty, etc.”
