He implores García’s aid during the famine that had already been prevailing in Gaul for two years.

**100.** How great was Odilo’s authority among princes and the peoples subject to them may be demonstrated by that famous public treaty commonly called the Truce of God (*Treuga Dei*), which, as Hugh of Flavigny reports in his *Chronicle* under the year 1041, was established by Odilo himself and other pious men in response to divine revelations.

Ademar supplies another example of Odilo’s authority over peoples in his *Chronicle*. He reports that the citizens of Bourges resisted for five years Goslin, who, having been a monk of Saint Benedict, had been made archbishop of Bourges by King Robert, [Col. 0872B] because Goslin, although of royal descent, had nevertheless been born of a prostitute. But, says that author, when Odilo had finally intervened as mediator, the king’s will prevailed.

Some, however, regarded Odilo’s authority with hostility. Such was Adalbero, bishop of Laon, who, in a poem to King Robert published by Valesius, mockingly calls Odilo “king.”

**101.** Yet no one should suppose that Odilo won the favor of princes through flattery or gentle obsequiousness, or even among simple people through self-important arrogance. On the contrary, he acquired this great authority through the holiness of his conduct and his zeal for promoting what was good, sometimes by sterner words, sharp rebukes, and threats invoking divine judgment.

[Col. 0872C] Otto William, duke of Burgundy, the most powerful man of those times, testifies in a charter already cited by us above that he had for a long time passed over the cries of Saint Majolus and Lord Odilo with deaf ears, but had at last complied with them.

Rodulfus Glaber also relates, in Book II, chapter 8 of his *History*, that blessed Odilo met King Robert as he was hastening with his army to besiege the castle of Saint Germanus near the city of Auxerre. But, as the same author continues, when the holy man reproved the king and his leading men because they were rising with hostile force against so great a pontiff of God, Saint Germanus, and when they had disregarded the warnings of the man of God, immediately a divinely produced mist completely covered the castle. Protected by it, the besieged inflicted a great slaughter upon the besiegers. [Col. 0872D]

By an almost similar miracle, William, surnamed “Greased Mouth,” count of Mâcon, suddenly became lame after he had built a castle against Cluny; and Count Hugh, his enemy, captured and soon afterward demolished that castle, as Ademar relates in his *Chronicle* under the year 1020.

Countess Ermengard, who is said to have incited Odilo to sin, so deterred herself by rolling over burning coals that afterward she devoted herself to pious works and bestowed many gifts upon the monastery. Those coals are still preserved in the sacristy of the monastery of Souvigny. There Ermengard’s anniversary is recorded as having been solemnly celebrated in the necrology written by Geoffrey Cholet in 1453. It contains the following:

[Col. 0873A]

> “On XI Kalends, a full office shall be held for Lady Ermengard, countess, who, through the hand of the most blessed Father Odilo, gave the gift of Saint Maurice with its appurtenances to God and to the church of Souvigny, for the service and refreshment of the weak and sick brothers of the community of Souvigny. She also gave the ferry of La Ferté on the Allier. She also gave a large golden cross, two silver candlesticks, two purple cloths, and she performed and gave many other good things to this monastery in lands and meadows.”

### VII. He Defends the Liberties of the Monastery and Refuses the Archbishopric of Lyons

**102.** The great affection of pontiffs and princes for blessed Odilo and the men of Cluny could not restrain those who envied the monks from harassing them, both on account of their possession of temporal goods and on account of the privileges granted to them—privileges that some attempted with all their strength to tear away.

In the preceding paragraph we praised several papal bulls by which powerful men in the world were rebuked as invaders of the monastery’s possessions. But it was much more difficult to withstand the efforts of the bishops of Mâcon, who were distressed that the monastery of Cluny, built within the boundaries of their diocese, should be exempted from their jurisdiction.

For the Roman pontiffs had granted privileges to the men of Cluny by which, in accordance with the provisions of the founder William’s testament and with the consent of kings and princes, complete immunity was asserted for the monastery of Cluny: namely, that the monks of the monastery of Cluny [Col. 0873C] could be ordained by any bishop whom the abbot wished, and that the bishop of Mâcon should have no jurisdiction whatsoever in that place; indeed, he could not enter it unless invited by the abbot. These provisions are explicitly contained in the bull of Gregory V, cited by us in the preceding paragraph, and they were confirmed by subsequent pontiffs.

**103.** Armed with these privileges, Odilo invited Burchard, archbishop of Vienne, to celebrate ordinations at Cluny. When Burchard had done so, Gauzlin, bishop of Mâcon, lodged a serious complaint against him and referred the matter to the synod of Anse, held in 1025, at which Burchard was also present among the other pontiffs.

When Gauzlin accused Burchard before the Fathers on this matter, Burchard placed all the blame on Odilo. The holy abbot was therefore summoned and appeared with several of his monks. He produced the privileges that we have just reviewed, by which the abbot of Cluny was permitted, setting aside the bishop of Mâcon, to summon whichever bishop he preferred to celebrate ordinations in the monastery of Cluny.

But the Fathers who were present, after reading the canons of the Council of Chalcedon and the decrees of other ancient councils, judged that the privilege alleged by Odilo ought not to be placed above them. Therefore Burchard, having obtained Gauzlin’s pardon, promised that, as long as he lived, he would provide Gauzlin with as much oil as was needed each year to prepare the sacred chrism. [Col. 0874A]

This, unless I am mistaken, was the occasion on which Pope John XIX of Rome wrote letters to Gauzlin and also to Burchard of Lyons, severely reproving them for harassing the monastery of Cluny, which had been entrusted to the special protection of the Apostolic See, and Odilo, its most holy abbot.

Gauzlin died shortly afterward, but his successor Walter followed in his footsteps, as Peter of Saint-Julian and other writers relate in various places. From this, it seems, the same Pope John took the occasion to write to King Robert against those priests who were attempting to tear down the privileges granted to the monastery of Cluny by the Apostolic See.

Indeed, it is clear that the matter was brought before the synod held at Rome in 1027 from a letter of that pontiff to all the faithful. In it, after confirming the privileges of the monastery of Cluny with the consent of the pontiffs present, and in the presence also of Emperor Conrad, recently crowned, he forbids anyone to dare excommunicate the monks of Cluny, and explains other matters at greater length. These may be seen in the *Cluniac Bullary*, p. 9.

In any event, this controversy later broke out repeatedly under Odilo’s successors. But what was finally decided on this occasion at the Council of Reims under Callistus II may be read in Orderic Vitalis.

**104.** That the concern with which the holy man was bound to defend his monastery’s immunity cannot at all be attributed to ambition is clear even from the single fact that he consistently refused the most eminent dignities when they were freely offered to him.

[Col. 0874C] Rodulfus Glaber supplies a distinguished example of this in Book V, chapter 4 of his *History*. After recounting the various disputes that arose after the death of Burchard, bishop of Lyons, concerning the election of his successor, he adds:

> “When all these matters had been reported to the Roman pontiff, faithful men suggested to him that, by his authority, he should choose Father Odilo, abbot of the monastery of Cluny, to be consecrated pontiff there; for the devotion of the entire clergy and people was eagerly acclaiming this choice. He immediately sent that Father both the pallium and the ring, and commanded that he should be archbishop of the aforesaid city. But the religious man, considering the purpose of his humility, absolutely refused to become so, and, accepting the pallium and ring, reserved them for him who would be worthy before God, the future pontiff of that see.” [Col. 0874D]

Hugh, abbot of Flavigny, tells the same story in his *Chronicle of Verdun*, where he writes that this was done by Pope Gregory. An old author of the manuscript *Chronicle of Cluny* reports that this Gregory was the sixth of that name.

But Gregory was elected Roman pontiff in 1044, at which time Odelric, who was substituted for Odilo when he refused, had already been governing the Church of Lyons for several years. Hugh himself reports that Emperor Henry sent Odelric to Lyons with the pontifical ornaments in 1041; and it is otherwise certain that Odelric, from the time he was appointed bishop, held his see without anyone’s opposition.

Thus Garnerius, in his notes on chapter 4 of the *Roman Diurnum*, says that Odilo was elected archbishop of Lyons by Benedict IX. But, as we judge, it is more likely that this occurred during the pontificate of John XIX. For John himself, in a letter to Odilo, makes serious complaints against him because, neglecting the reverence he owed the pontiff, he had refused the government of the Church of Lyons when it was offered to him.

The complete letter on this matter is found in volume II of the Acherian *Spicilegium*, p. 87; no one will regret having read it.

**105.** Odilo nevertheless did not obey the pope’s instructions. He considered himself permitted to disobey pontifical commands in this one matter alone; in other circumstances he thought that he could do nothing of importance without their permission.

Thus, when a certain murderer who had killed Stephen of Clermont withdrew to Cluny and became a monk there, and when some people thought that he had washed away his crime with tears of penance—or even judged, on account of his outstanding gifts, that he was the sort of man who ought to be promoted to the priesthood—the most devout abbot did not dare to do this without a special mandate from the pontiff.

When the pontiff was consulted on the matter, he permitted no such thing to be done. He judged it sufficient that the murderer, deprived of Holy Communion throughout his life, should at the end of his life be given the Viaticum as an act of mercy. So testify the Fathers of the Second Council of Limoges, session 2, toward the end.

### VIII. Odilo’s Principal Virtues

**106.** We have already admired in Odilo an outstanding example of humility, which is the foundation of all the virtues. He shunned dignities with the same ardor with which most others ordinarily pursue them.

How deeply this virtue had taken root in his heart may be inferred from what happened to him at Monte Cassino. For when the blessed man once decided, as we read in Leo of Marsica’s *Chronicle of Cassino*, Book II, chapter 53, to visit that monastery, the sacred head of our order, he wished, out of reverence for the most holy Father, to climb the entire mountain on foot.

The monks of Cassino received so great a man with the honor that the fame of his supreme sanctity seemed to demand. But when, according to the monastery’s ancient custom, he had been led into the chapter house, he earnestly begged one favor from Abbot Theobald: namely, that, prostrated at the feet of all the brothers, he might be permitted to kiss their feet. Although he obtained this only with difficulty, he carried it out with the greatest humility and devotion of spirit.

During those days the feast of the holy Father Benedict happened to be celebrated. Taking this opportunity, Abbot Theobald in turn asked Odilo to grant him one favor: that he himself should publicly celebrate Mass on the sacred mountain during so great a solemnity. Odilo, although reluctant in spirit, finally consented.

When everything had been prepared and he was to proceed to the altar, Theobald offered the blessed man the staff that, according to the custom of abbots, he carried while celebrating. But no one could induce Odilo to take it. He declared that, in the presence of the representative of blessed Father Benedict—who is the abbot of abbots—it was not fitting for any other abbot to use a pastoral staff. This was conceded to the holy man’s humility.

Finally, as he was leaving the sacred mountain, Theobald and many of the brothers escorted him honorably. They obtained from him a promise that he would employ all his efforts to secure for the monastery of Cassino some relics of Saint Maurus; this was accomplished seven years later. For when the Fossatenses had granted him a bone from Saint Maurus’s arm, he entrusted it, enclosed in a silver reliquary, to six of his brothers, who carried it to the monastery of Cassino.

**107.** Odilo was no less humble at home among his own people than he was among outsiders. From this arose such gentleness toward those subject to him that some even tried to reproach him for seeming, in his conduct, more indulgent than was fitting for a superior.

But, as Peter Damian and other authors after him have written, he replied:

> “If I must be condemned, I would rather be condemned for mercy than for harshness.”

Thus, as the same author reports, in imposing forms of penance he was so compassionate toward those who had gone astray that he displayed not the strict authority of a father but rather a mother’s affection.

By this manner of acting, as the *Cluniac Chronographer* observes, he earned the illustrious title of “the most clement man,” and in the same place calls him “the most merciful Odilo.”

Nevertheless, he tempered all these qualities with prudence, the nurse of the virtues, so that the vigor of regular discipline suffered no loss through his leniency. Certainly, the Fathers of the Council of Limoges, assembled in 1031 concerning the apostolate of Saint Martial, praised his supreme prudence.

Yet he so humbled himself in his own eyes that, in the *Life of Saint Adheleid*, he declared himself the refuse of all the poor of Cluny.

**108.** The holy man’s chief concern was that charity should flourish unimpaired and inviolate among his own people. For this reason he so detested the evil of envy that, as Rodulfus Glaber testifies in Book V, he was often accustomed to lament that such an enormous crime was found among certain people bound by the monastic profession.

Those who attempted to weaken charity and unity among the brothers through whispering or flattery, or who were found murmuring, he so abhorred that he judged they ought to be expelled from the monastery. In this matter alone he was severe.

Abbo, abbot of Fleury, testifies to this in a letter to the monks of Micy, where he condemns such men. Mockingly, he calls them “historiographers,” because they were accustomed to disparage the conduct of their brothers. In this connection he praises the example of blessed Odilo, who had ordered several of his own monks stained by this vice to be beaten with scourges and expelled from the monastery.

> “Indeed,” says Abbo, “in our own profession also, the singular Odilo, ruler of the men of Cluny, recently expelled from his monastery such ‘historiographers’ when they had been discovered, after they had been beaten with scourges, and terribly branded with the iron of excision.”

**109.** The holy man so overflowed with the fire of charity that, although overwhelmed by an almost infinite multitude of affairs, he never omitted the exercises of piety by which that fire was nourished.

Neither the difficulty of journeys, nor the care of monasteries, nor any other circumstance could keep him from offering the most holy sacrifice of the Eucharist every day. He used to do so with an abundant outpouring of tears, preparing for so fearful an act by sacred vigils, fasts, and other mortifications of body and soul, so that he might approach the holy altar in greater purity.

He so carefully guarded his virginity that he was commonly called “the centenarian virgin,” as we learn from the *Chronicle of Limoges* and also from the *Chronicle of Senonais Saint-Pierre-le-Vif* in volume II of the *Spicilegium*.

From this arose his fervent devotion to the Blessed Virgin. Whenever the verse was sung in church,

> “You, who were to undertake the liberation of humankind, did not shrink from the Virgin’s womb,”

he would immediately fall prostrate upon the ground out of reverence, as Peter Damian testifies.

Jotsaldus observes in his metrical lament on the death of the same blessed man that he always honored the Blessed Virgin with tender affection. For this reason he implores her patronage and that of the other saints who were his protectors, asking that they deign to admit him into their company.

**110.** The holy man never failed to extend to his neighbor, whenever the opportunity arose, the charity that he possessed toward God. This shone forth especially during the famine. As it grew severe, he did not hesitate to dispose of and sell the sacred vessels and every costly ornament with which the church of Cluny was enriched by the gifts of kings and princes, in order to aid the needs of the poor.

On this occasion he even sold the imperial crown that Saint Henry had consecrated to the apostles Peter and Paul by placing it upon their altar, judging that nothing at all should be preferred to the life of Christ’s members.

Indeed, through such acts of generosity the monastery of Cluny was so drained during those extremely difficult times that it was forced to seek aid from foreign peoples, since nothing remained for sustaining the brothers of that place and assisting the neighboring populations.

This is clear from his letter to King García, where he writes on the matter:

> “Although not without shame, we are compelled to disclose to the generosity of Your Sublimity the necessity of our poverty, by which we have now been continuously afflicted for two years and more. For the general poverty of the entire kingdom, together with the calamity of famine and want, oppresses us, as it does the other inhabitants of our neighborhood. In order that we may escape this danger, we greatly need your assistance, if it pleases you.”

But nothing commends Odilo’s mercy toward the poor more than what he himself says in the prologue to the *Life of Saint Majolus* that he composed. There he confesses that he was so affected by the calamities of the province and by the great and lamentable suffering of the poor that he spent many nights without sleep.

Finally, once, while traveling during those wicked times of famine, he found two boys who had died of hunger in the middle of the fields. His heart was moved, and, since he had been unable to help them while they were still alive, he had them buried after covering their bodies with his own garments.

### IX. The Commemoration of the Faithful Departed First Instituted by Saint Odilo

**111.** Blessed Odilo is famous throughout the entire Church because he was the first of all to establish a particular day solemnly dedicated to the general commemoration of all the dead. After first instituting this rite in his own monasteries, the universal Church later approved it and prescribed by general decree that it be observed everywhere.

Certainly, even before this, the dead were commemorated on a fixed day in many places, as is clear from numerous ancient Martyrologies and Necrologies found here and there. This is also evident from Udalric, who observes in the *Customs of Cluny* that among the Cluniacs the commemoration of the dead had customarily been celebrated on the Monday after the feast of the Most Holy Trinity.

Thus, in a very ancient manuscript calendar of Auxerre, this commemoration is recorded on the tenth day before the Kalends of February. Long before that time, in the final chapter of the Rule of blessed Isidore, an offering is prescribed every year, on the day after Pentecost, for the souls of the dead.

But such prayers were offered only for those who had belonged to the same congregation or at least had been joined to it by some association, or certainly for those who had earned this favor through donations, kinship, familiarity, or other benefits. Odilo, however, whose charity could not be confined within such narrow limits, wished this grace to be extended to all the faithful departed without exception.

**112.** Jotsaldus and Peter Damian describe at length in the *Life* of the blessed man the occasion for instituting this commemoration. It has therefore seemed sufficient to present here a letter written on this subject by a certain monk named Burchard, which we possess from a manuscript of the Thuanean Library:

[Col. 0878D]

> “To the lords, fathers, and elders of the monastery of Cluny: Burchard, their poor and insignificant servant and monk, sends the gift of heavenly glory.
>
> “Because I know you to be most fervent proclaimers and extollers of the glory and crown of our common lord and father, Odilo, we make known to your holy ears what we recently heard from truthful witnesses concerning his praises.
>
> “A certain religious man and knight of the abbot of Volta went to Jerusalem for the sake of prayer at the Lord’s tomb. When he was returning to his own country, he lost the correct road. Entering a great forest, he wandered about, not knowing where he should go.
>
> “By God’s will, while he was wandering in the forest, he happened to find a certain old hermit, a most holy man. When the old man saw him, he asked who he was, what he was seeking, from where he had come, and where he was heading.
>
> “The knight humbly explained to him the cause of his having gone astray and where he was from, saying that he was returning from Jerusalem and had lost the correct road.
>
> “When the old hermit heard that he was from Gaul, he asked him whether the place called Cluny and the abbot of that place, the holy man named Odilo, were known to him.
>
> “The pilgrim knight replied that the place itself and its abbot were unknown to him, but that he had very frequently heard from his own senior abbot—namely, the abbot of Volta—that he belonged to the aforesaid place and abbot.
>
> “Then the elder said to him: ‘I shall tell you what divine mercy has revealed to me concerning him. The holy Odilo, abbot of the aforesaid monastery, is of such excellence and such merit before God that he has obtained from Him what has never been granted to any of the saints: that for two additional days—namely, Monday and Tuesday—all the souls of the faithful departed should be free from the torment of punishments and from all the fires and sufferings of Gehenna.
>
> “‘But you shall soon be restored to your journey, for, in order that you might hear these things from me, God’s will permitted you to stray from the road for a little while.
>
> “‘When you have returned to your homeland, wherever you can, you shall spread the name of this holy Odilo, announcing to all people, rich and poor, great and small, that each should strive according to his means to offer prayers and alms for the glorification of that soul through whose singular intercession God has granted even to sinful—or even condemned—dead people such unheard-of, kind, and immeasurable mercy.’
>
> “You, most holy Fathers, will know what ought to be done in consequence. Know, nevertheless, that no church remained in Germany where, after all the bells had been rung on the aforesaid two days, a public and most generous alms was not given for his charity.”

**113.** To this letter we append the decree concerning this celebrated institution, made by the blessed abbot and already published by Chesnius in the *Cluniac Library*. We present it here, however, from an old manuscript of the monastery of Cluny, in which it reads as follows:

[Col. 0879C]

> “It has been decreed by the most blessed Father, Lord Odilo, with the agreement and request of all the brothers of Cluny, that just as in the churches of God, built far and wide throughout the world, the feast of All Saints is celebrated on the day of the Kalends of November, so among us the commemoration of all the faithful departed who have existed from the beginning of the world until its end shall be celebrated in a festive manner, as follows.
>
> “On the aforesaid day, after chapter, the dean and cellarers shall give alms of bread and wine to all poor people who arrive, as is customary on Holy Thursday. Whatever remains that day from the brothers’ meal shall be received in its entirety by the almoner, except for the bread and wine that he will receive for the evening meal.
>
> “On that same day, after the evening assembly, all the bells shall be rung and Vespers for the dead shall be sung. On the following day, after Matins, all the bells shall again be rung and the Office for the dead shall be performed. At the morning Mass, the Office shall be performed festively, all the bells shall be rung, and the tract shall be sung by two brothers.
>
> “All the brothers shall offer privately, and publicly they shall celebrate a Mass for the repose of all the souls of the faithful; twelve poor people shall also be fed.
>
> “And so that this decree may possess perpetual force, we wish, request, and command that it be observed both in this place and in all places belonging to it. If anyone else should take an example from this faithful institution of ours, let him become a participant in all good vows.
>
> “Therefore, we have instructed and command how the memory of all Christians shall be observed once each year. We judge it altogether fitting that, for the souls of our brothers serving the Lord in monasteries under the rule of blessed Benedict, we should add something to the divine services beyond the ordinary, and we have likewise decreed that the memory of our dear Emperor Henry should be observed especially with them, as we ought, since we have been enriched by him with many possessions.
>
> “Thus, at the vigil of the dead, after the psalm ‘To the Lord when I was in distress,’ which is recited after the readings, let us say ‘Lord, why have they multiplied?’; at the morning praises, after ‘Out of the depths,’ ‘How long, O Lord?’; at Vespers, after ‘Praise the Lord, O my soul,’ ‘Unless the Lord had been with us’; at ‘[lacuna], O God, with our ears,’ after ‘Lord, you have been our refuge,’ ‘The Lord is my shepherd’;” at the Litany, ‘Judge me, O God, and distinguish my cause.’
>
> “And so, with divine grace favoring us, as we have stated above, let their memory be observed throughout all future times, both in this place and in all places belonging to it.”

**114.** Udalric mentions this institution in chapter 42 of the *Customs of Cluny*. After discussing the feast of All Saints, he adds concerning the following day that Father Odilo had decreed that, just as on the preceding day the commemoration of all the saints is customarily made, so on the following day the commemoration [Col. 0880C] of all the faithful departed should be made.

He then proceeds as follows concerning the occasion for instituting this custom:

> “Whoever has read his Life can there learn well what led this pious Father to establish this.”

These words of Udalric confirm what is found on this subject in both *Lives* of the blessed man.

Geoffrey, prior of Vigeois, also supports this account in chapter 12 of his *Chronicle*. He says that Odilo instituted the feast of the dead by divine revelation, celebrated it after the feast of All Saints, and commanded his entire order to celebrate it.

This institution soon became customary in other Churches as well, as Sigebert of Gembloux, a monk, testifies among others in his *Chronicle*. After recounting the vision mentioned above under the year 928 and Odilo’s establishment of the commemoration of the dead, he adds:

> “This rite, passing to many churches, caused the memory of the faithful departed to be solemnly celebrated.”

Anselm, a canon of the same church, notes in chapter 53 of his *Deeds of the Bishops of Liège* that this was received by Bishop Notger in the diocese of Liège. After explaining the occasion on which this solemnity was instituted by Saint Odilo, he adds that it was immediately adopted in various Churches, and then says:

> “This custom Bishop Notger, the Christ-bishop, also transferred to his own diocese and ordered it to be solemnly performed.”

**115.** In the old edition of the *Chronicle of Hirsau*, Trithemius records the decree made by Saint Odilo on this matter under the year 1010. Under that year he recounts the familiar story of the hermit said to have provided the occasion for this institution. He writes that the hermit lived in a desert near Mount Etna, or Vulcan, situated in Sicily.

He repeats the same account, somewhat more fully, in the new edition of the same *Chronicle* produced at Saint Gall, except that in place of the hermit he introduces a certain wandering monk from the Cluniac family. He then adds that this institution was confirmed by Pope John XVIII.

This should rather be referred to John XIX, if this very decree was made after the death of Emperor Henry Augustus, as is stated explicitly in the decree cited by us above. For John XVIII had already died several years earlier when Saint Henry died.

What appears in the old Martyrology of Ado, from the provostship of Saint Lawrence at Corbie, is even farther from the truth. It reads:

[Col. 0881B]

> “The fourth day before the Nones of November … likewise, on that day, the general memory of the faithful departed, established by blessed Odilo but authorized and confirmed by the most blessed Pope Leo, in the year 1002 from the Incarnation of the Lord.”

But in that year it was Sylvester, not Leo, who occupied the Roman see. Perhaps, however, this is a copyist’s error, because he carelessly omitted the word “fiftieth.” For in the fifty-second year of this century, Leo IX, a most holy man, governed the Roman Church.

### X. Odilo Promotes Learning: His Writings

**116.** That Odilo united learning in letters with uprightness of conduct in his own person is proved by what we have already said about his virtues and by the works he published.

We also learn that he approved learning among his own people from what we read here and there in ancient authors about the measures he took to promote it. Certainly Abbo, abbot of Fleury, a man renowned in those times for holiness and learning, wrote a lengthy letter in response to the request of an attentive and teachable Cluniac monk concerning the recurrence of similar numbers found frequently in the canons of the Gospels.

He testifies that he had committed this question to writing and explained it in a more extended discourse because he had been unable to provide an adequate answer extemporaneously, both on account of the difficulty of the question itself and because there had not been enough time for a complete explanation. From this it is clear that the monk had applied himself to unraveling more difficult questions of Sacred Scripture.

[Col. 0881D] The monks of Cluny also devoted themselves to the study of history under the rule of blessed Odilo, as is clear from the *History* of Rodulfus Glaber, dedicated to Odilo himself. Glaber testifies that he undertook to write it after being stirred by the complaints of earnest brothers, who were distressed that no one could be found to commend to posterity the events of their own times, both in the churches of God and among the peoples.

He also says that in this matter he showed himself obedient to Odilo’s instruction and to the brothers’ wishes. And lest anyone perhaps think that this *History* was not written for monks, Glaber explicitly affirms that he wrote it for religious men.

Syrus the monk wrote the *Life of Saint Majolus*, together with two books of Miracles of Lord Odilo, the revered abbot, in obedience to the paternal command.

We omit the rest in order to say something about the works and learning of the blessed abbot himself.

**117.** Abbo, abbot of Fleury, praises Odilo’s eloquence in the letter cited above. Jotsaldus, in the *Life* of Odilo, commends at length his learning in the Scriptures and his fluency in speech.

Peter of Blois praises his exhortations in Letter 123, addressed to Richard, bishop of London, where he cites several passages from the holy abbot concerning the most holy sacrament of the Eucharist.

Trithemius, who had seen only his sermons, nevertheless lists him among the learned men who flourished in the eleventh century. Platina likewise assigned him a place among men distinguished by birth and learning.

At the end of an old manuscript codex of the church of Anicium there are several verses praising Saint Majolus, addressed to blessed Odilo. We present some of them, in which the learning of the blessed man is praised:

> “To Lord Father Oydelio, revered for his goodness,
>
> “Clear in doctrine, strengthened by divine favor,
>
> “Whom the Greek name (*onoma*, ‘name’) gives us as the Phoebus of the Lord,
>
> “With the flock entrusted to him by the heavenly King,
>
> “All the brothers serving the Lord’s mother …”

They beseech Vallari and eagerly desire to reach him, etc. I omit the authors who compiled catalogues of illustrious men. Yet we cannot sufficiently marvel at the humility of this blessed man, who seemed so worthless and despicable in his own eyes that, concerning the Life of the empress Adelheid—which, after the manner of Basil and Jerome, he called an *Epitaphium*—he said that he had written it only in a humble and brief style [Col. 0882C], in order to provide some learned man with an opportunity to write about so holy an empress worthily, appropriately, and as the matter required. Guided by the same spirit, he composed the Life of Saint Maiolus, his predecessor, according to the smallness of his own understanding, as he himself said. He also composed several hymns and prayers for the divine Offices concerning Saint Maiolus and Saint Adelheid, to be recited on their feast days. All these works were published in the Cluniac Library together with his sermons, several letters, a profession of faith, and some prayers.

Our own Lucas Dacherius likewise published three letters of this same blessed man in volume II of the *Spicilegium*, which he had transcribed from the Cluniac archives. We also have before us one of his sermons that remains unpublished, which he composed on the solemnity [Col. 0882D] of the Holy Cross. His concern for preserving the charters of privileges and donations made to his monastery may also be included here: he took care that an accurate collection of them be made, as we learn from the collector’s preface in an old manuscript of the monastery of Cluny.

Finally, besides all these works, a certain ancient *Chronicle* is attributed to our Odilo by some manuscripts. But since no trace of this attribution exists among the ancient authorities, we conjecture that the name Odilo entered this manuscript in place of Odo. Indeed, the monk of the Greater Monastery who collected the deeds of the counts of Anjou, published in volume X of Acher’s *Spicilegium*, praises Thomas of Loches, who composed brief chronicles entitled in the name of Odo [Col. 0883A], abbot—apparently none other than those attributed to our Odilo.

Moreover, the humility with which the holy man was endowed shone forth no less in his writings than in the other actions of his life, so that he did not hesitate to entrust them for examination even to his own disciples. The most holy abbot himself bears witness to this: for that reason he dedicated the Life of Saint Maiolus, written by him, to Hugh and Almanno, monks of Cluny, as is clear from the letter prefixed to the Life. We omit it here for the sake of brevity, since it has already been published more than once.

## XI. On Some of the Blessed Man’s Disciples

### 118.

[Col. 0883B]

The yoke of Christ was so gentle under the rule of blessed Odilo that it is not surprising that many men distinguished by birth and other gifts, abandoning the splendors of the world, wished to be numbered among the Cluniacs at the time when he presided over that famous monastery. It is neither possible nor permitted by their multitude to list them all. It will be enough to mention some of the more distinguished, besides those whom we praised above from various charters in paragraph 4.

Among those distinguished by learning and devotion to literature, Syrus, Arlebaldus, and Jotsaldus must be given a place. Yet Saint Hugh, the successor both to his holiness and to his dignity, may stand for them all. Nor were there lacking bishops who preferred to lead a humble life under Odilo’s discipline rather than preside over others.

Certainly, after Odilo the abbot and Vivian the provost, a bishop named Ledbald subscribed a charter that we praised above under no. 27. Hence we conjecture that, having abandoned his episcopal see, he at that time embraced the monastic life at Cluny [Col. 0883C]. We know of no other Bishop Ledbald in that period except Ledbald of Mâcon, otherwise sufficiently well known, who, as we learn from various charters, bestowed several gifts upon the monastery of Cluny. Yet we do not dare assert, without further evidence, that this is the same man mentioned in that charter.

We also find in the letter of Pope Sylvester II, praised by us above, a certain bishop whose name he did not state, who had abandoned his see and withdrawn to Cluny. Whether he was Ledbald or Bishop Sancius is uncertain. From a letter of the blessed man, published in volume II of the *Spicilegium*, which he addressed to Bishop Paternus in these words—“Igne [‘Fire’], etc., Brother Odilo, together with the lord Bishop Sancius, and the entire congregation of the poor of Cluny, etc.”—we infer that Sancius came from Spain to Cluny after relinquishing his episcopate, where under Odilo’s rule he professed the monastic life [Col. 0883D].

### 119.

Jotsaldus praises a certain Bishop Richard once and again in book II, writing that he was a disciple of the blessed man and his companion on his journeys. Finally, Sanjulianus relates in his *History of Mâcon*, from an old catalogue, that Walter, Bishop of Mâcon, withdrew to the monastery of Cluny, where he died wearing the monastic habit. The Sammarthani likewise report the same in *Gallia Christiana*.

His disciples who became abbots could be listed in numbers nearly equal to the monasteries he recalled to better observance [Col. 0884A]. Among them, Adrald, abbot of Bremet, is praised in the Life published by Saint Peter Damian. Nor is there time here to repeat what we said above about the abbots Paternus and Garsia, who renewed in the monasteries of Spain the careful observance of the Benedictine Rule together with the institutions of the monastery of Cluny.

Others appear here and there among the published authors. Yet far more numerous are those who, though unknown to men, live in everlasting glory. Such would have been Walter, whose name and deeds would be entirely unknown to us had Glaber not made him known to us on what seems an almost accidental occasion. He was a man not greatly distinguished either by bodily appearance or by intellectual subtlety, but exceedingly acceptable to God for the holiness of his conduct and purity of heart, as became clear at the end of his life [Col. 0884B].

It is worth presenting the words of Rudolf Glaber himself, from book V, chapter 1 of his *History*:

> “It happened there”—at Cluny—“at that time,” during the time of Saint Odilo, “that some of the brothers departed this life. One of them, named Walter, surnamed Little, *Pusillus*, because of his stature, and by nature exceedingly simple, died at the beginning of the night of the Great Sabbath of the Lord’s Resurrection. At the hour of his death, a column of fiery light appeared to countless men and women, extending from the summit of the monastery all the way to heaven. They had no doubt that this had been brought about by the gift of the most merciful God, who wished the soul of this brother to share in his glorious resurrection and to show the living the way of innocence.”

Walter found a place in the Benedictine calendars under the title “blessed,” on 7 [Col. 0884C] April. Yet he was never granted any public cult. In the lament that he composed on the death of blessed Odilo, Jotsaldus congratulates him on being about to meet Christ the Lord at the future resurrection, surrounded by many disciples:

> Then Odilo, newly radiant with heavenly light,  
> Will walk among the saints and go forth to meet him,  
> Enclosed by a host of many fellow soldiers,  
> Whom he joined to the Lord by words and examples.

### 120.

Nor may we omit Casimir, son of Mieszko II, king of the Poles. The writers of Polish history say that after his father’s death, because the nobles of the kingdom could not endure the rule of his mother Richeza, he was driven from the kingdom while still young and withdrew to the monastery of Cluny. There, abandoning the splendors of the world, he professed the monastic life and was ordained a deacon [Col. 0884D].

But when divisions in Poland multiplied and public calamities grew so severe that no hope of restoring tranquility appeared unless the kingdom were restored to Casimir, everyone proclaimed Casimir king, even though he was absent. Envoys were appointed to summon him, wherever he might be hiding, for no one knew where he had withdrawn.

After various fortunes, they learned from Richeza that Casimir was professing the monastic life at Cluny and living with no thought whatever of earthly affairs. Nevertheless, they went to Cluny, greeted their king, and begged the abbot to give him permission to reclaim his kingdom, since no other means remained of rescuing so noble a portion of the Christian world from impending [Col. 0885A] destruction.

Odilo refused, declaring that the matter had not been placed within his authority; he replied that he would never permit it without a special mandate from the Roman pontiff. The envoys therefore hastened to Rome. After explaining to the pontiff—who was Benedict IX—the calamities of the kingdom, and accepting various conditions mentioned by these authors, they obtained what they requested.

Thus Casimir, released from his vow of chastity, returned to Poland as both monk and deacon. He was again proclaimed king, took a wife, and fathered children. Yet, mindful of his former condition, he is said to have devoted himself, insofar as his status permitted, to works of piety and to have built various monasteries for his Cluniac brethren.

[Col. 0885B]

So that the Poles might never become unmindful of so great a benefaction, it was decreed that, in addition to the annual census payment which the nobles of the kingdom were required to pay to the Apostolic See, they should also wear their hair in the form of a crown and provide other services, which the historians of Poland relate at greater length. We have been unable to find anything about this matter in the ancient documents of the monastery of Cluny.

[Col. 0885C]

Casimir is said to have begun his reign in 1041 and, dying in 1058, to have left it to his son Boleslaus II. Moreover, at the beginning of the fourteenth century, Pope Clement V released Władysław from his vows so that he might succeed the deceased Casimir, king of Poland. Władysław had first become a monk at Cîteaux and afterward at the monastery of Saint-Bénigne of Dijon. But in letters issued concerning this matter, preserved in volume VII of Acher’s *Spicilegium*, the pontiff indicates that his profession had not been free. Bucelinus commemorates Casimir with the title “blessed” in the Benedictine *Menology* on 28 November.

### 121.

It is remarkable how highly most of the prelates of Odilo’s time, together with other men distinguished by power and worldly honors, valued the counsels of blessed Odilo. Since their condition did not allow them to live in monasteries, they nevertheless entrusted themselves and all that they possessed so completely to the blessed man’s direction that they undertook nothing of any importance without his counsel or command.

Among these was Fulbert, bishop of Chartres, the most brilliant light of this eleventh century. Excusing himself for having been unable to visit the blessed man, he promises to do so as soon as he is permitted. “I shall come to you someday,” he says, “[Col. 0885D] you whom the Holy Spirit truly inhabits, to seek the counsel of the divine oracle, etc.” Certainly, both from the letter that the blessed abbot wrote to Fulbert and from those which Fulbert himself sent to him, preserved in the Cluniac Library, vol. 351, it is clear that Fulbert subjected himself to blessed Odilo so completely that he depended entirely upon his will.

For he sought Odilo’s counsel not about one matter or another, but concerning the whole course of his own life. In another letter he advises Leutheric, archbishop of Sens, to entrust himself wholly to the counsel of Odilo and his followers, if he wished to escape peril to his soul and also recover the glory and honor of the present life.

A certain monk H. laments his lot in a letter to the monks of Dijon, *Spicilegium*, volume II, p. 390—he is, I think, Halinard, abbot of Saint-Bénigne after William—because, being absent, he had received the news of Odilo’s arrival at Dijon too late to see him there [Col. 0886A]. Here are his words:

> “Because you informed me so late of the arrival among you of the lord, most holy Father Odilo, I have become deeply saddened; for I had resolved to seek him, though he was far away, through the sweetness of his most gracious and benevolent consolation, and now I shall not be able to see him visiting his native land,” etc.

On another occasion Alinard saw blessed Odilo, as Odilo himself testifies in a charter concerning a settlement made between himself and Elizabeth, abbess of Balma. For this matter Odilo, accompanied by several of his men, and the abbess, likewise accompanied by several nuns, had assembled at the designated place, as the custom of those times generally required [Col. 0886B].

Odilo relates the same event in an old record of the matter preserved in the Cluniac *Chartulary*:

> “I, Odilo, priest and monk of the monastery of Cluny, and the lord Robert, provost of the same place, wish it to be known that a dispute, with reason and peace, arose between us and Elizabeth, abbess of the monastery of Balma, over a small estate near the village of Givry. For this reason the said abbess and several servants of God with her, and we, assembled at the aforesaid place. Present there were the venerable abbots, the lord Allenard, the lord Guidric, the lord Otger, etc., who settled the matter, and the parties pledged mutual brotherhood.”

No date was attached to this charter, not even in the original. Nevertheless, we infer that it was made after the year 1030 [Col. 0886C], because Alinard succeeded William at the beginning of 1031. It is also clear from many charters, which we have cited in their proper place, that Robert was prior of Cluny at that time.

### 122.

Moreover, because Odilo attended not to his own interests but to those of Jesus Christ, he watched over the welfare of others no less than his own. Hugh, abbot of Flavigny, provides a splendid illustration of this in his *Chronicle of Verdun*. He relates that the blessed Richard and Count Frederick, having already abandoned the splendors of the world and being concerned to choose a monastery in which they might pass their lives religiously, approached blessed Odilo to receive his counsel on the matter. They were prepared to submit themselves to the blessed man’s discipline if he judged that preferable.

[Col. 0886D]

But the holy man, filled with the spirit of prophecy, persuaded them to return to the monastery of Saint Vitonus at Verdun, which they had already chosen. He “added,” says that author, “that in the course of time it could come about through them that the dwellings of God’s servants, now modest, would later grow, and that through their industry the place, which then seemed narrow and contemptible, would become distinguished.”

Afterward Hugh extols blessed Odilo’s charity at length, since by this action he had offered an example of sincere charity, being much more concerned for another’s good than for his own. Hence he concludes that the entire progress of the monastery of Verdun, whatever its extent, ought to be attributed to blessed Odilo.

## XII. Eulogies of Odilo from Various Authors

[Col. 0887A]

### 123.

Although the many and very distinguished virtues in which we have shown at length that Odilo excelled may seem more than sufficient to compose his eulogy, it will nevertheless be worthwhile to present here several tributes bestowed upon him especially by contemporary authors, so that it may be evident how highly such a man was esteemed by everyone.

Indeed, Odilo’s reputation for holiness, and that of the brothers who lived under his rule, was so great that the monastery of Cluny was commonly said to surpass others both in religious observance and in wealth. Hugh testifies to this in his *Chronicle of Verdun*. Pope John XIX of Rome, in the letter praised above, rebukes Gauslenus, bishop of Mâcon, for disturbing the monastery of Cluny, which shone forth in holiness before nearly all nations; he calls its abbot, the lord Odilo, a venerable Father even to unbelievers [Col. 0887B].

Benedict VIII implies that injuries inflicted upon that place redounded upon the whole Church when he wrote to the bishops of Gaul in these words:

> “The loss suffered by the monastery of Cluny is the common loss of all of us, because of the interruption of the prayers and other pious works that were regularly performed there for the welfare of the whole Church.”

Accordingly, Sylvester II valued the prayers of the Cluniac monks so highly that he wished to commend himself entirely to them. “To your most holy prayers,” he says, “we commend ourselves at all times, and with faithful petitions we entreat that you may deign to receive us.” He likewise calls Odilo an eminent abbot.

[Col. 0887C]

The other bishops followed in the footsteps of the supreme pontiffs. As we have just said, Fulbert, bishop of Chartres, venerated Odilo as his Father and was accustomed to call him the holy archangel of monks. The canons of Chartres said that he had been given to them as the clearest mirror in the world, and in their letter they call him “most holy Father” even while he was still living.

We have already noted that Abbo of Fleury called him singular in our—that is, monastic—profession in the letter praised above. But in a letter to Abbot G., he commends him as the standard-bearer of the whole religious life. The author of the *Chronicle of Saint-Maixent* testifies that he was not unequal to Saint Maiolus in virtues and the merit of his life.

[Col. 0887D]

Leo of Marsica calls him a man venerable for his life and reputation in his Cassinese chronicle. Peter of Poitiers congratulates the region of Auvergne on having produced such a fosterling, whom he calls the magnificent Odilo. For Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny—whom he addresses in a panegyric—he wishes for the spirit of Odilo and of the other Fathers.

Sigebert and other chroniclers praise him for having ruled and advanced the monastery of Cluny for fifty-six years with wondrous religious fervor. He then adds:

> “Who, besides his other qualities, distinguished in piety, shone forth during life not only through the examples of his life but also through miracles,” etc.

Our Magdeburg chronicler adopted these words in a manuscript. [Col. 0888A] The same Sigebert, under the year 1048, proclaims him among men religious and illustrious for holiness; and under the year 1027 he names him among notable abbots through whose work ecclesiastical religion flourished, singling him out as distinguished in piety.

Ademar likewise proclaims him the successor of Maiolus and not unequal to him in virtue. As we have already said, William, duke of Aquitaine, revered him as a temple of the Holy Spirit. Some commonly called him a “hundredfold virgin,” because they thought he produced a hundredfold fruit in the field of the Church. Others called him the most merciful Father, because he devoted himself entirely to works of mercy. [Col. 0888B]

Still others sought to celebrate his holiness and distinguished works with various other praises, whose words there is no time to report. It will be enough to conclude all this with the judgment of Saint Bernard, who in his *Apology to William, Abbot*, exhorts the Cluniac monks to reform their conduct by looking to Saints Odo, Maiolus, Odilo, and Hugh, whom they gloried in having as their princes and teachers.

## XIII. Blessed Odilo’s Final Illness and Death; His Sacred Cult

### 124.

What blessed Odilo did as he approached death and prepared himself for the journey to his heavenly homeland has been described so accurately by Jotsaldus in the Life that we shall provide below that scarcely anything seems necessary to add here.

Certainly, we possess a letter from the monks of Silviniacum to a certain abbot, in which they describe the death of blessed Odilo and report what they had seen and heard personally. Yet it contains almost nothing other than what Jotsaldus relates [Col. 0888C]. We have nevertheless thought it worthwhile to reproduce it here because it was written shortly after the blessed abbot’s death and may help to establish the authority of our Jotsaldus.

We have this letter from two manuscript codices: one belonging to Queen Christina of Sweden, formerly from Saint-Magloire in Paris, and the other from Saint-Maur-des-Fossés. The former gives it this title:

> “Letter of the monks of Silviniacum to A., abbot of Cluny. It begins, etc.”

The other has:

> “On the death of Odilo, abbot. Of all nobility, etc.”

We are convinced that the title attached in the Maglorian manuscript is not authentic, as is clear from the mere reading of the letter. Yet, if conjecture is permissible, the man designated in both codices as “abbot of abbots,” whether AL. or A., seems to have been none other than Albert, then abbot of the Greater Monastery. It will be sufficient for us to reproduce the letter here in full, exactly as we found it.

[Col. 0888D]

### Here begins the account of how the lord Abbot Odilo migrated to heaven, and of his virtues

> “To the lord AL. [Mag. cod. A.] abbot of abbots, resplendent with the light of all nobility and holiness, a fruitful olive tree in the house of God, the humble assembly of Silviniacum sends greetings in the King of heaven and his kingdom.
>
> “Since, most holy Father, we have learned that you greatly desire to know how many days the lord and abbot Odilo of blessed memory lay ill in his final sickness, what he did or said as the hour of his calling approached, and also what the benevolent mercy of God revealed at his tomb after he had departed to the heights, we have taken care to make everything known to you briefly.
>
> “[Col. 0889A] Two months after the lord abbot had come to us to visit the tomb of Saint Maiolus, his predecessor, and was wishing to return to Cluny, he was asked to visit a certain church and there, on a Sunday, to sing Mass in the presence of an innumerable multitude. On the following day, the thirteenth from the day of the Lord’s Nativity, while he was returning, his customary stomach pain seized him and did not cease tormenting him for six consecutive days.
>
> “Afterward, when the pain finally left him, he suffered only bodily weakness, as he himself reported. He could no longer take any food or drink except a little mulled wine, which even then he vomited shortly afterward.
>
> “[Col. 0889B] On the vigil of the Lord’s Nativity, he came to the chapter house and, weeping copiously by himself, prostrated himself when he heard the Lord’s birth proclaimed. Finally, after magnificently delivering a sermon, he began to judge himself very severely, saying that he had never done anything good, although by the grace of God he was a virgin in body. After absolving us and commending us to the supreme Shepherd, he admonished us with his blessing to celebrate that most sacred solemnity with spiritual joy and to omit nothing because of his illness.
>
> “At matins on that same night, he was carried into the oratory of the Blessed Virgin Mary. With the brothers chanting before him, he sang the psalms and responsories and pronounced the blessings. With all the strength he possessed, he proclaimed aloud, “We praise you, O God.”
>
> “[Col. 0889C] Indeed, since he had now abandoned earthly food, he received spiritual food every day, having the sermons of the holy Fathers read before him and imploring their assistance, so that through their prayers he might be taken up from this valley of tears.
>
> “On the vigil of the feast of Saint Sylvester, before the brothers rose for matins, he felt himself growing weaker and the end now approaching. He ordered the Lord’s Communion and the cross to be brought to him. When he saw the cross, he immediately began to draw long sighs from the depths of his breast. Weeping and singing certain prayers that he had committed to memory, he adored it, and then received Holy Communion.
>
> “[Col. 0889D] That same day, at the hour of vespers, he had himself carried before the altar of Holy Mary, Mother of God. There he solemnly sang vespers and pleaded with her for a very long time, with tears, that she might deign to have mercy on him.
>
> “Finally, he had himself carried back to the infirmary. After resting for a little while on his bed, he had himself raised and supported in a seated position, until suddenly he bowed his head. As soon as those standing nearby saw this, they summoned us. Meanwhile they placed him on a hairshirt and lit lamps, because night was approaching, the night on which the most sacred day of the Lord’s Circumcision is observed.
>
> “When we came immediately and raised our voices in heaven with tears over the loss of so great a Father, he signaled to us to be silent. When we had fallen silent, he asked those supporting him whether he had been placed on a hairshirt. When they replied, ‘Certainly,’ he added and said, ‘Drag me,’ looking at something unknown to us.
>
> “[Col. 0890A] Since some of us did not understand the word correctly, they immediately said to him, ‘Lord, are you saying that we should shave you?’ He replied to them in a very clear voice, ‘I never said what you claim.’
>
> “Then he looked fearfully toward the east, as though speaking with someone, and began alternately to be silent and to speak. Afterward, when his mouth seemed to move for a very long time as though laughing, his blessed soul migrated to heaven.
>
> “When his body had been washed, embalmed with spices, and clothed in the same garments that he himself had ordered during his lifetime, it was carried into the church and placed before the altar of the apostles Peter and Paul. Great grief and mourning were displayed there by those who kept vigil before his bier that night.”

> “[Col. 0890B] Meanwhile, a certain very devout brother named Gregory, seeking his bed, saw him standing beside him, as though in the same place where he had died. When he asked him how he was, recalling that he had already died, Gregory received the reply that everything good had come to him and that Jesus Christ, the King of glory, had met him.
>
> “He also said that at first the devil had appeared to him in the form of a horrible man, showing him toward which place—namely, the door of the latrines—he had departed in confusion, having found nothing in him.
>
> “Then, as the news of his swift passing resounded, an unbelievable multitude of people began to gather for his funeral rites. Everyone mourned him with a kind of brotherly and exceedingly sweet affection, and, we do not know through what divine prompting, grieved for him with deeper compunction, because they knew that he had pleased the Lord.
>
> “[Col. 0890C] A few days afterward, once he had been buried in the crypt on the left side of the church, near the altar of Saint Laurianus the martyr, the favor of our Savior began to reveal him to the world through signs of miracles.
>
> “In the village of Longoumnus there lived a widow whose only daughter, by a hidden judgment of God, had lost not only the use of her mind but also the functions of her tongue and ears. He therefore admonished her three times in dreams to bring the girl to his tomb.
>
> “The woman took the unfortunate child and led her to his tomb. As soon as she gave her wine to drink—the wine with which his most holy body had been washed—and poured some of it into her ears, the girl recovered speech, hearing, and the use of her mind.
>
> “While she was giving thanks to almighty God, a certain deaf man arrived and asked that some of the same wine also be poured into his ears. He immediately began to hear and returned to the deserted region from which he had come.
>
> “[Col. 0890D] A certain man from the territory of Bourges, who had lost the use of his tongue for ten years, came to his tomb and, after several days had passed since his arrival, was granted the ability to speak properly.
>
> “Finally, a very old man who had remained in the darkness of the longest blindness entered the crypt containing his tomb, on the vigil of Palm Sunday. He clearly told his guide that he could see, by the grace of God and through the merits of the man whose tomb he had sought.
>
> “[Col. 0891A] Then a certain woman from the castle of Montluçon, afflicted by a serious impairment of sight, had herself carried to his mausoleum. While she multiplied the words of her prayer and invoked God in faith, the general aid of blessed Odilo came to her, and the blindness that had deprived the woman was driven from her eyes, because he was a son of light and not a son of darkness.
>
> “From the castle of Dieuze a certain man came to his tomb. He not only recovered the power of speech that he had lost, but also the use of his right foot and hand, and so returned joyfully to his own home.
>
> “At Tours there was a certain old man deprived of the light of his eyes. When he came to his tomb a second time, he was deemed worthy to recover the sight he had lost.
>
> “We have briefly explained these things concerning the miracles of our Father to you. Many others are also reported, but they are not believed because they are related by contemptible persons. Farewell.”

*(Here the Fossat manuscript ends.)*

> “[Col. 0891B] If you wish to know about the election of our most illustrious Father, the lord Abbot Hugh, singing a new song, know that he was elected in accordance with the command of the blessed Father Benedict. He was endowed with every wisdom and learning and supported by uprightness, usefulness, and honor of conduct. He accepted the honor of the abbacy unwillingly, weeping and judging himself unworthy of such an honor.
>
> “Finally, he is greatly loved, honored, and exalted by the princes of Burgundy and Auvergne, indeed even by the supreme pontiff of the holy Apostolic See; and whatever had been under the authority of his predecessor is granted and given to him.”

[Col. 0891C]

Jotsaldus observes that, when the blessed man was at the point of death and the brothers asked him who would assume the rule of the monastery in his place—for they depended entirely upon his decision—he replied that he entrusted the matter to God’s providence and the brothers’ election.

Perhaps the blessed Father feared that, if he designated his own successor, the practice would become an example and eventually lead to the Cluniac abbots being created through such designations rather than through the election of the brothers, although the Rule of the blessed legislator prescribes this so explicitly.

All the abbots who had preceded blessed Odilo at Cluny had either been designated by their predecessors or, at least, while those predecessors were still living, had been taken into partnership in the government as assistants. Thus Odo succeeded Berno, Aymard succeeded Odo, and Maiolus succeeded Aymard, as was proved in Aymard’s own Eulogy. Finally, no one can deny that Odilo likewise first became Saint Maiolus’s colleague and then his successor [Col. 0891D].

Udalricus supports Jotsaldus in this matter. In book III, chapter 1 of the *Customs of the Monastery of Cluny*, he explains the procedure for the abbatial election and presents as an example what occurred after Saint Odilo’s death in the election of blessed Hugh, in these words:

> “When blessed Father Odilo was asked at the end of his life what he thought concerning his successor, he did not consent to name anyone.”

He nevertheless adds that the blessed old man designated several of the monastery’s more senior and reputable men, so that the others could follow their judgment and votes. As the same author continues, when the cloister prior first named Hugh, who was then prior, all the others approved the election by unanimous consent.

[Col. 0892A]

The author of the *Chronicle of Maillezais* perhaps intended to suggest this when he says under the year 1048 that Odilo, having reached a good old age at seventy-six years [should read: eighty-six], rested; “in his place,” he says, “by his command and by the election of all the brothers, Hugh was appointed, a noble shepherd, not unlike him in the merit of his life.”

### 125.

Since Jotsaldus explicitly wrote that blessed Odilo departed this life on the Kalends of January in the year 1049, no room for doubt can remain concerning the matter. Those who wrote that he died in 1048 must either be understood to have begun the year at Easter, or else, since the blessed abbot died during the very night that lay between the two years, they seem to have assigned his death either to the preceding day, which was the last day of 1048, or to the following day, which was the first day of 1049.

[Col. 0892B]

Indeed, since Odilo died on a Sunday, according to Jotsaldus, his death must necessarily be assigned to the year 1049, which in fact began on a Sunday.

There is likewise no difficulty concerning the period during which the blessed man presided over the monastery of Cluny. Those who assign him only fifty-six years of rule count them from the death of blessed Maiolus, although, as we explained more fully above, he had assumed the name and office of abbot in the monastery of Cluny at least two years earlier.

126. Although blessed Odilo departed this life on the very Kalends of January, his feast was nevertheless transferred to the following day, because on the day of his death the feast of the Lord’s Circumcision was celebrated. We infer that this was done shortly after his death from Book I, chapter 47, of Udalric’s *Customs of Cluny*, where he says that they arranged the deposition of Saint Odilo, so dear and familiar a saint, in such a way that the eighth day after the Nativity of Saint Stephen had only a commemoration, with merely one antiphon and one collect. Hence Henry, abbot of Cluny, in his Statutes, issued at the beginning of the fourteenth century, should be regarded as having confirmed an ancient custom rather than instituted a new one, when he decreed that thereafter the feasts of Saints Odilo, Hugh, Odo, and Maiolus should be celebrated with a double rite.

And certainly the Cluniacs’ affection for Saint Odilo was so great [Col. 0892D] that immediately after his death they caused a special commemoration of him, together with the other patrons of the monastery, to be made in those prayers commonly called the suffrages of the saints. Udalric himself bears witness to the same thing in Book I, chapter 5, already cited. In the Cluniac Library, col. 328, we possess a hymn and prayers that were recited in ancient times on his feast; and at his Mass, in addition to the three customary prayers, a fourth was added to be recited over the people.

So famous was Saint Odilo’s name already at that time among all people that in 1064 a chapel was built in his honor. We learn this from an old cartulary written while Saint Hugh was still alive. There, in charter 689, Achard, bishop of Chalon, is said to have dedicated, in the year 1064, indiction II, on Friday, the twenty-third day of the moon, on the Nones of December, a chapel in honor of blessed Mary and the most sweet Father Odilo, at a place called Alacarmeda, in the parish of Cidanis. From that time such a great multitude of people came to that oratory, although it stood in a very dense forest, that, when many had established their homes there, it later became necessary to create a parish in that place.

Gaufridus, prior of Vosius, lists Odilo among the four holy abbots of the monastery of Cluny in chapter 34 of his monastery’s *Chronicle*. Odilo of Mercœur, our saint Odilo’s kinsman, as we have already said in section 5, arranged for his feast to be celebrated in the church of Clermont. It seemed worthwhile to reproduce here the very words of the obituary, from Quercetanus’s notes to the *Cluniac Library*, col. 69:

> IV [Col. 0893B] Nones of January, the Octave of Saint Stephen, and of Odilo, abbot and confessor. For the celebration of this feast, Odilo of Mercœur, canon of Clermont and provost of Brioude, promised forty customary solidi, or to pay at one time forty pounds; and these are to be distributed at Mass and at Vespers on the feast day.

For the rest, the commonly circulated Martyrologies celebrate Odilo’s memory on 1 January, or at any rate on the following day, since in some it is identified as the day of his death, while in others it is identified as the day of his deposition, or rather as the commemoration of his feast. In the Martyrology of Saint Arnulf at Metz, Odilo is commemorated on the second day before the Kalends of January. In the obituary of the Church of Reims, however, on the very day of the Kalends of January, the abbot Oydelo is praised together with William, likewise an abbot.

## XIV. The Sacred Relics of Odilo and Their Translations

[Col. 0893C]

127. The sacred body of blessed Odilo was deposited in the nave of the church of the monastery of Silviniacum, where he died, near Saint Maiolus. His tomb is still visited today, although the sacred remains were removed from there many centuries ago and exposed to the public veneration of the faithful.

Certainly, if credence may be given to the *Book of Anniversaries of Silviniacum*, which Gaufridus Choleti, prior of that place, had made in 1453, Peter Damian was the first to raise and translate his body from the earth, and this occurred not long after the blessed abbot’s death. For there one reads:

> On the eighth day before the Kalends of February, a full office is to be celebrated, as for the Cluniac abbots, for Bishop Peter Damian, who raised the body of our blessed Father Odilo and placed it, with extraordinary devotion, in the place where it now rests. The sacristan is to provide the brothers’ refectory meal.

The obituary of the same place agrees, where on the eighth day before the Kalends of February the deposition of Lord Bishop Peter Damian is likewise commemorated.

Saussay, in the *Gallican Martyrology*, commemorates on 3 May the “Reopening of the body of Saint Odilo, abbot of Cluny.” The Bollandists adopted these words for the same day in their *Praetermissa*. Clement IV and Honorius IV, who governed the Roman Church toward the end of the thirteenth century, testify in bulls preserved in the Cluniac Library, col. 309, that the bodies of Saints Maiolus and Odilo, which rest in the church of Silviniacum, shone forth with many miracles in their own times. But they say nothing about the translation of Saint Odilo, although they approve the elevation of blessed Maiolus; perhaps that translation had already taken place long before.

128. Another translation of the relics of blessed Odilo was nevertheless carried out by Roger, archbishop of Bourges. We learn that it was solemn, since on that occasion several bishops and abbots assembled at the monastery of Silviniacum, from an ancient document preserved in the Cluniac Library.

129. Clement VI, at whose command this translation was carried out, granted indulgences to those who visited the church of Silviniacum on the feast days of Saints Maiolus, Odilo, and the other saints whom he lists, and also on the day of the translation of blessed Odilo. From this special commemoration of the translation we infer that it was more celebrated than the others.

But since this bull is dated, as it appears in the Cluniac Library, col. 312, to the second year of Clement—that is, to the common era 1343—either the pontiff is speaking of another translation, different from the one he himself ordered, which is unlikely; or Roger’s document was issued at least two years after the translation had taken place; or finally an error entered the chronological dates of the bull. Certainly the letter of Aymo the prior, by which he confirms that one of the blessed man’s ribs was given to the canons of Chartres, likewise assigns this translation to the year 1345. We reproduce that letter here in full from the papers of the distinguished Antonius Wion of Heroval.

130. For the rest, the sacred relics of blessed Odilo are still reverently preserved by our Cluniacs in the church of Silviniacum. His body is kept in a reliquary above the altar beside the church’s choir, opposite the other altar which, as has been said elsewhere, was constructed to preserve the body of blessed Maiolus.

Their heads, however, are enclosed in separate reliquaries. Gaufridus, the prior of that place, had them carried in these reliquaries on the joyous arrival of Charles, duke of Bourbon and Auvergne, when that prince first came to Silviniacum in 1434, as is clear from a public document drawn up concerning the matter and published in the Cluniac Library, col. 312. This Gaufridus, as it seems to me, is Gaufridus Choleti, whom we have already mentioned; he arranged for one chest to be made for enclosing Saint Odilo’s body and another for his head, together with a cabinet.

### Testimonial Letter Concerning a Rib of Saint Odilo, Confessor and Abbot of Cluny, Granted to the Canons of Chartres

[Col. 0894D]

> To the venerable Fathers, lords and ladies, and dearest friends, the lord dean and the other canons of Chartres: We, Brother Aymo of Saint-Gerand, humble prior of the priory of Silviniacum, and the entire convent of that place devoted to God, send greetings in him who is the true salvation of all.
>
> Since the reverend Father in Christ and lord, Lord R., by divine permission archbishop of Bourges, together with several bishops, abbots, clergy, and people, most of the population of the whole region having assembled at the said priory . . . . . and being present, on the second day before the Ides of April, in the year of the Lord 1345, raised the body of our devout and most glorious Father, blessed Odilo, for the praise of the entire court of Paradise and for the solemnity of that same saint, with the devotion, honor, and reverence that were fitting.
>
> After this raising had been completed, the venerable and discreet man, Lord Stephen Roger, your fellow canon and official of Bourges, humbly and with great insistence petitioned us to send you some relics of the most holy body mentioned above. We, consenting to his petition insofar as the Most High supplied us with the means, decided to send through him one of the ribs of the aforesaid Saint Odilo to your most holy college. You received it in your chapter with great reverence and solemnity, proposing to arrange and decree that, both in your cathedral church [Col. 0895B] and throughout your entire diocese, you would continually celebrate his feast of the translation, to the exaltation of that same saint, provided that by our letters patent we should testify that the said rib had been removed from the body of that same saint, as all these matters were more fully contained in the letters you sent us.
>
> To your devotion, dearest lords, for which, insofar as we can and ought, we give thanks for so devout and solemn a reception of the said relics, we make known by these presents that the said rib, delivered to you by the aforementioned Lord Stephen Roger, your canon, was extracted from the body of the most blessed Odilo and was entrusted to be carried to you by him in the presence of several trustworthy witnesses. Therefore, with devout and earnest prayers, we beg you to establish the feast of its translation in your church and to have it celebrated annually throughout the entire diocese of Chartres.
>
> In witness whereof, we have thought it right to affix our seals to this present letter. Given in our aforesaid priory, on the twenty-second day of July, in the year of the Lord 1347.

[Col. 0895]

# LIFE OF SAINT ODILO

## Here Begin the Chapters of the Following Life

### Chapters of Book One

[Col. 0895B]

Prologue of Jotsald, monk, to Stephen the pontiff. Also, a preface or lament on the death of the same Father. [Col. 0895C] On his noble lineage. Chapter I: How he began to serve God in his own childhood. II: How he joined the company of Saint Maiolus. III: How he abandoned the pomp of this world. IV: How Saint Maiolus chose him as his successor. V: On his bodily appearance, and that there was nothing artificial or affected in him. VI: That four principal virtues shone forth in him. VII: On justice, or how he was loved with the greatest affection by pontiffs, kings, dukes, and emperors. VIII: That he was generous toward the poor. IX: How he provided clothing for two boys who had already died, or committed them to burial. X: On a cleric marked by the contagion of leprosy. [Col. 0895D] XI: How hospitable he was, and how he won for Christ many people of different ages and kinds. XII: On fortitude. XIII: On temperance and the renewal of his establishments. XIV: On his death, how his blessed spirit left his earthly body and sought heaven. XV: Commendation of his soul. XVI: How the holy man appeared to a certain monk. XVII: On a similar vision.

### Chapters of Book Two

Chapter I: How, once a boy, he was divinely freed from a very serious illness. II: On a blind man restored to sight. III: On water changed into wine. IV: On a theft discovered at Pavia. V: Also, on another similar theft. VI: On crossing the very deep waters of the Ticino and lighting a lamp. [Col. 0896B] VII: On a similar miracle. VIII: On many people fed with a few little fish. IX: On wine overflowing in a small vessel on Mount Aventine. [Col. 0896C] X: On a certain man freed from fevers. XI: On wineskins emptied for the use of the poor and then filled again by divine power. XII: On a glass vessel broken and restored. XIII: On a certain hermit’s vision. XIV: On the revelation of Lord Pope Benedict. XV: On a certain boy cured of an illness of the throat. XVI: On books and other belongings soaked with water and not at all damaged. XVII: On a certain little boy who was a monk, freed from a very serious illness. XVIII: On a book and vessels found. XIX: On a certain powerful man freed from pain in the eye. XX: On a cleric cured of an illness of the arm. XXI: On a certain man deprived of his reason, or possessed by a demon, who was healed. XXII: On a certain mute man who was healed.
