XXIII: On a certain small vessel emptied of wine and later found full through the power of the saint.

### Chapters of Book Three

[Col. 0896D]

Chapter I: On a certain insane, deaf, and mute girl who was healed. II: On a deaf and mute man who was freed. III: Also, on another mute man. IV: On a certain paralytic who was also mute and was cured. V: On a mute priest. VI: On a blind man restored to sight. VII: Also, on a blind woman who was healed. VIII: Also, on another blind man restored to sight. IX: On a certain insane man restored to his senses. X: On a certain paralytic. XI: On a man freed from dropsy. XII: Also, on another man with dropsy. XIII: On a certain crippled woman who was healed. XIV: Also, on another woman healed in a similar manner. XV: On a certain poor woman cured in a similar manner. XVI: On a certain captive freed from his chains. XVII: On a certain holy man who was deprived of his reason.

## Here Begins the Prologue of Jotsald, Monk, to Stephen the Pontiff, on the Life and Virtues of Saint Odilo, Abbot

[Col. 0897]

[Col. 0897A] To the reverend Father Stephen, crowned with pontifical glory according to the interpretation of his name, the least of the servants of God, a monk in name only, Jotsaldus: whatever is more pleasing in either life.

The studies and writings of the ancient philosophers exalted the praises and memories of their predecessors, hoping by such indications to make immortal those whom they knew to have been mortal. Then, in a second rank, ecclesiastical discipline—its subject matter as much more sublime as it is more directly aligned with a surer hope—describes the glorious works of holy men, so that those who come after, and those yet to come, may always have examples to follow, and so that everything may be referred to him from whom virtue and prudence are given, and from whom fortitude and wisdom also flow. Following their model, I, however insignificant a little man, nourished by the instruction of the great Odilo and shaped by his beneficence, wished, after the manner in which Jerome wrote concerning Blaesilla and Nepotianus, to inscribe a sort of epitaph [Note: [Col. 0897D] Odilo himself likewise calls his book on the life of the empress Adelheid an *epitaphium*, following Jerome’s example.] concerning his death and virtues, and, as it were, to scatter flowers upon his tomb—flowers that might offer something of sweetness and grace to those entering, and that might give off, according to their nature, at least some small fragrance.

In this work I offer the devotion of my heart, and I provide material for those wishing to describe loftier things; I do not steal from them the opportunity to perform the task better. I decided to send this work to you, holy prelate, because I know that you are his nephew and were summoned through him to the glory of the priesthood, trusting that whatever cultivated or uncultivated speech may have written in his praise will please your judgment.

## Also, a Preface or Lament on the Death of the Same Father

[Col. 0897]

[Col. 0897B] Who will give water to my head and a fountain of tears to my eyes, that I may weep over the desolation not of one person, nor of two or three, but of many peoples, of mixed sex, varying condition, varying age, and varying rank? I shall weep, I say, over the devastation of the most noble congregation, the great household bereft through the death of its father Odilo. From his very inmost being, from his instruction and virtues, it hung as though bound by certain chains and ropes, and, so to speak, was sustained by indissoluble bonds of love.

What are you doing, awakener of the heaviest tears and messenger of so great a calamity [Mss. 2: desolator, “destroyer”]? Break forth and cry in the ears of the mixed multitude, saying: How has the helper of the wretched departed? How has the timely consoler of the sorrowful fallen silent? Or where has he gone, the desirable charioteer of many monks and the discerning governor and ruler of innumerable peoples?

O how uncertain is the condition of human life! O how changeable is the course of mortal affairs! While we thought that he was our companion in the common life, we now hold him dead; and him whom we hoped to have present, we mourn as absent. Yet if he ought to be mourned who has escaped sorrow; if he ought to be lamented who has passed from grief to joy, from darkness to light, from punishment to rest, and from death to life.

What shall we do, O soul? Where shall we turn? If we begin to magnify our grief too extravagantly, I fear that the sharpness of the mind may be struck back, and that, disturbed by immoderate sorrow, we may fail entirely to pursue what we wish to inscribe concerning his virtues. But first let us speak of the nobility of his flesh, which is included in the titles of holy men as an addition to their praise; and afterward, advancing step by step through the traces of his virtues, let us come, as though by certain stages, to repeated mournful lamentations over his funeral.

The precepts of rhetoricians require that the ancestors of the person being praised be remembered and that their lofty deeds be recalled; thus speech reaches him by stages, so that he may appear more illustrious through the virtues of his fathers and forefathers, and may be seen either not to have degenerated from the good or to have himself adorned those of only moderate distinction.

Let us not seek in the praises of his soul the advantages of the flesh, which he himself always despised. Nevertheless, since he descended from blood of no ordinary nobility, let us take up in his praise what we can. His father was among the most noble of the leading men of Auvergne: a man vigorous in arms, exceedingly wealthy in possessions and riches, prudent in counsel, and in every moral excellence of his time second to none. By the privilege of his authority and favor he was commonly called Major Beraldus.

In the virtue of faith he was so distinguished that what others found difficult to preserve under oath, he kept inviolate by a simple word. His conduct and appearance were far removed from anything that might now be seen in any prince, whatever his manner of action. He had a wife named Girberga, not inferior in birth or morals. How great her continence and chastity were, and what her disposition toward her husband had been, became evident to everyone after his death.

For, leaving her homeland, her relatives and children, and her great landed possessions and riches, she followed Christ like another Paula. At the monastery of Saint John at Autun [Note: [Col. 0897D] That ancient monastery still exists; it was founded by Brunichild under the title of Saint Mary, and Saint Gregory endowed it with a privilege. Others, however, think that the monastery founded by Brunichild is the one still famous today under the name of Saint Andochius. Both are bound to the Benedictine order.] [Col. 0898D] she took a place among the nuns and assumed the religious habit.

How commendably she persevered there in her purpose, how sweet and beneficial her life thereafter was to everyone there, and with what glorious end she completed her life, I heard with groaning recounted in a few words by those who survived her. Finally, these parents had other sons, powerful and noble, inferior to none in their own rank so far as worldly glory was concerned.

There was also a daughter who must not be passed over, named Blismodis, an abbess, who, serving God in holy virginity night and day, completed nearly a hundred years of life. Having described these matters briefly, let us turn our style toward him whom the nobility of his mind and the loftiness of his lineage famously commend.

## In the Name of the Most High God, Here Begins the Life of the Same Father

[Col. 0899]

### Chapter I — How He Began to Serve God in His Own Childhood

[Col. 0899A]

[Col. 0899B] Thus the most blessed man Odilo, born from a noble lineage, was consecrated to Christ from the very beginnings of his life like another Isaac, and at Brioude, at the church of Saint Julian the glorious martyr, was assigned to the clerical state. From childhood he delighted in humility, chastity, innocence, and purity; and, insofar as his age permitted, he devoted himself to works of mercy.

He surpassed his peers in wisdom and conduct, so that everyone already regarded him not as a boy but as an old man in maturity, though not in years. When the years of childhood had passed and the strength of youth began to follow, he silently deliberated within himself about abandoning the Egyptian pots and entering the promised land through the midst of the world’s dangers.

Good Jesus, how gracious is your calling, and how sweet the inspiration of your spirit! As soon as you have struck the mind, you transform the heat of the Babylonian furnace into love of the heavenly homeland. For behold, when you suddenly strike the heart of our young man, you change it and wondrously kindle it toward the true embraces of Solomon.

### Chapter II — How He Joined the Company of Saint Maiolus

Certainly, while he was meditating on such things in his heart, that great Maiolus, famous throughout almost the entire world, entered the territory of Auvergne. By divine disposition, the man of whom we speak was brought before him. When Maiolus perceived in him an outstanding elegance of body and nobility of birth, foreseeing with his inner eyes something great and divine in him, he wholly fell in love with him; and in turn the fire of divine charity was kindled more and more between them.

A familiar conversation arose between them. The younger man disclosed his desire to the elder; and the old man, so that he might carry out what he had conceived, instructed the younger man’s mind by every means available to him.

### Chapter III — How He Abandoned the Pomp of This World

When these matters had thus been arranged between them, the old man returned to his own place, while the young man’s determination was prepared to complete what he had begun. Not many intervals having passed, this new soldier, like another Benedict, likewise abandoned the strongholds of Brioude and Le Puy. He despised his ancestral wealth, relatives, and brothers; and, like the ancient Abraham leaving Ur of the Chaldeans, he sought Cluny as a kind of entrance into the promised land. Having once again laid down his old burden, he assumed the monastic habit.

Good Jesus! How delightful it was then to see the sheep shorn of its worldly fleece rising again from the bath of baptism, advancing with twin offspring of a twofold love, carrying nothing barren within itself [Col. 0900B] and meditating on nothing vain! Once he had taken the habit, you would see our sheep, first among the others in work and last in rank, seeking the pastures of eternal verdure, arranging the services of the lamps, keeping watch over the children entrusted to his care, sweeping the floors, and humbly performing every lowly duty.

But the pearl did not remain hidden for long; the strong athlete could not long be concealed in a private place.

### Chapter IV — How Saint Maiolus Chose Him as His Successor

After almost four years had passed, Saint Maiolus, following many labors endured for Christ, left the darkness of Egypt, crossed the dangers of the sea, entered Jerusalem, and was placed by Christ in eternal peace. As the moment of death approached, he chose Lord Odilo as his successor and left his own sheep to the Lord and to him.

Odilo resisted, and was unwilling beyond what can be believed; nevertheless, by the common vote and common judgment of all, he was appointed to the office imposed upon him and set over God’s people like another Moses.

What are you doing, beloved soul of God? Why do you resist? Why do you still wish to stand behind the wall and look through the lattice and windows? Come out now into the diffused light; come out. The bridegroom speaks to you as to his bride in the *Song of Songs*: “Rise, hasten, my beloved, my beautiful one, and come” (Song 2:10)—plainly saying: Rise from the bed of repose, in which you seek to care only for yourself; hasten and come to extend the care of salvation also to your neighbors through the diligent labor of preaching.

“Show me your face; let your voice sound in my ears. For your voice is sweet, and your face is beautiful.”

Having undertaken the duty of governance, he was conformed more and more to the example of the saints and adorned in all things by heavenly instruction. In him there shone a certain notable lesson, to be imitated and feared by his subjects; and the grace that shone within him declared outwardly what he was inwardly. For, as has been said before us, the disposition of the mind is seen in the condition of the body. And since this is so, let us now say a few words about the posture of his body.

### Chapter V — On His Bodily Appearance, and That There Was Nothing Artificial or Affected in Him

He was of medium height. His face itself was full of authority and grace: cheerful and gentle toward the mild, but toward the proud and those who offended him, terrifying to the point that he could scarcely be endured. Strong despite his leanness, adorned by pallor, and dignified by white hair, he had eyes that shone with a kind of brilliance and were both terrifying and wondrous to those who looked at him. They were continually filled with tears, because the virtue of compunction was often present.

In his movements, gestures, and manner of walking there also shone an appearance of authority, the weight of gravity, and the mark of tranquility. His arrival was like a ray of most welcome joy and an event of unusual delight. His voice was manly and so full of beauty that it greatly soothed the minds of his listeners with the sweetness of its modulation.

His speech was full of sweetness and grace, moderately measured according to the nature of each matter: neither exceeding the proper measure of speech nor, at an inappropriate time, deficient in foresight when explaining. There was nothing artificial, nothing affected in him; rather, nature wonderfully made him proportionate in bodily bearing and ordered in his way of life.

And although, according to blessed Ambrose, we do not place the seat of virtue in bodily beauty, we do not exclude grace. Leaving these matters aside, let us return to the composition of his character, by which he was adorned through divine grace.

### Chapter VI — That Four Principal Virtues Shone Forth in Him

So far as human judgment can determine, four principal virtues shone forth in the holy man with no ordinary brilliance: prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance.

Philosophers define prudence as consisting in the investigation of truth and in the desire for fuller knowledge. [Col. 0901C] In this kind of virtue he shone so brightly that he never ceased investigating the truth by day or by night. The book of divine contemplation was always in his hands; conversation about the Scriptures was always constant for him; and his labor for the edification of all was unceasing.

As Jerome instructs Eustochium, the sacred page sometimes received the face of the sleeping man, while repeated reading refreshed him when he awoke. Nothing in this life was sweeter or more beloved to him. Prayer continually followed reading.

What groans, what sighs, and what floods of tears there were in him, especially during that holy sacrifice of the immaculate Lamb, the Holy Spirit, author of that gift and grace, knows. I shall speak of something wondrous, and certainly true. Although sleep often overtook him while he was chanting the psalms in bed, the psalm nevertheless did not depart from the mouth of the sleeping man, so that, if you did not know otherwise, you would think him awake. When he awoke, he seized the psalm so hastily, as though he had not interrupted it. I believe that he was then speaking with the bride in the *Song of Songs*: “I sleep, but my heart is awake” (Song 5:2).

How learned he was in the Scriptures, how eloquent in speech, and how Catholic also in orthodox faith, his sermons and numerous letters attest. Like honeycombs of the richest sweetness, they seem to exhale the fragrance of prudent eloquence and the beauty of sweetness and grace.

### Chapter VII — On Justice, or How He Was Loved with the Greatest Affection by Pontiffs, Kings, Dukes, and Emperors

[Col. 0902A]

Justice is, as philosophers maintain, that which gives each person his due, does not claim what belongs to another, and neglects personal advantage in order to preserve the common equity. You should know that all these qualities shone forth in him not moderately but abundantly.

For he displayed the honor due to all ages, persons, and conditions, insofar as justice required; and he made himself so pleasing to everyone that he became dear to all, no otherwise than an angel—or rather, since that is how it must be said, precisely as an angel. In accordance with the apostolic teaching, he resisted none of the Christian princes and powers; instead, he made himself so friendly and dutiful [Col. 0902B] that, like another Joseph, he was loved and greatly revered by all.

Let King Robert of the Franks join in this affection; let Adelaide, mother of the Ottos, draw near; let Henry, emperor of the Romans, come; let Conrad and Henry—father and son, both Caesars and noble invincibles—be present. Through the friendship, services, and imperial gifts of all these men he was so honored that there was one heart and one soul between him and them.

What shall we say also of Stephen, king of the Hungarians, or Sancho, king of the western peoples? Although they had not seen him in person, nevertheless, hearing of his sanctity through the exchange of envoys and letters, they bound him to themselves through favors and abundant gifts, humbly commending themselves to his prayers and intercessions.

There was also, in the distant western regions, another Sancho, bishop of Pamplona, who attached himself to him in friendship and served him with abundant gifts. He even came to him from so distant a region and resolved to be made a monk by him.

The Odilo of blessed memory loved him so greatly that, even while dying, he mentioned him and, after his death, sent two brothers to visit him, carrying remnants of his garments, to announce to him the end of his life and to restore their former friendship with him after his own death [Note: [Col. 0901] These words, “and again to renew that same friendship with the living,” are absent from manuscript 2.], and again to renew that same friendship with the living.

Nor are those priests of the Lord and apostolic men to be passed over—Sylvester, Benedict, John, and finally Clement of pious memory. He so won their favor that he was like one of their brothers.

For what person, wherever he might be, would not desire to have Odilo as another Solomon, a friend and father, and an intercessor for him before God? Italy rejoiced when Odilo was present, and especially Pavia, which through his prayer and efforts was delivered, in the times of the emperors Henry and Conrad, from destruction by the sword and the danger of fire.

Rome also rejoiced, that mistress of the world, at the companionship of so great a man, who often visited it out of love and desire for the holy apostles. Officials, clerics, and monks likewise rejoiced at his arrival, so that they held him in intense affection as their dearest brother.

We have placed these matters under the heading of justice in order to show clearly that he gave each person his due and thereby earned everyone’s favor and love; and also so that it might be made clear to all that, since God had suffused him with grace, he necessarily had to be loved by everyone.

Thus everyone in common formed a good opinion of him, because everywhere he was an object of love and honor to all. As for those beneath him, he honored elders as fathers, younger men as brothers, old women as mothers, and virgins as sisters. Yet he considered everyone superior to himself, and toward all alike he offered familiar companionship and salutary conversation.

He was burdensome to no one, intrusive toward no one, desirous of no one’s honor, and he did not claim what belonged to another. Rather, he cheerfully gave to another what was his own. He neglected his personal advantage in order to preserve the common equity.

He retained benevolence and generosity, which are themselves also aspects of beneficence, or of justice [Note: [Col. 0893D] Thus manuscript 2. But Thuanus, together with the edition, reads: “Beneficence and . . . are themselves aspects of justice,” etc.], so that in these qualities alone he shone forth in our own times as uniquely distinguished in his order.

For he wished to do good to everyone in common; but toward those whom he could assist, he was generously liberal. He rejoiced more in what he gave than in what he received, knowing that the former belonged to happiness and the latter to need, and that, according to the saying of the Lord who is Truth, it is more blessed to give than to receive.

### Chapter VIII — That He Was Generous Toward the Poor

Toward the poor he was so generous that at times you would have seen in him not a dispenser but a lavish giver. Indeed, he took greater delight in making alms than anyone could take in acquiring money. [Col. 0903C] What more shall I say? He was the staff of the blind, the food of the hungry, the hope of the wretched, and the consolation of the sorrowful.

What more shall I say? He overflowed with the compassion of mercy beyond what can be expressed, and, insofar as it lay within him, he excluded no one from the benefit of mercy. And, as is written in the epitaph of Pope Sabinian:

> Here he removed the faults of men with gentle speech:

Nor was he a judge of faults, but rather a remedy. Certainly, he was so deeply immersed in this virtue that thoughtless people, judging his exercise of it, considered him excessive. But he was accustomed to allude gracefully to this objection: “I would rather,” he said, “be judged mercifully for my mercy than be condemned cruelly for my cruelty.” For, as Ambrose says: “A merciful man is good [Mss.: *bonum*]; while helping others, he helps himself, and through another’s remedy he heals his own wounds.” For he recognizes that he is human who knows how to forgive, and he follows the ways of Christ, who, having assumed flesh, preferred to come into this world as Redeemer rather than as judge. Therefore this holy man too, as we have said, preferred to be a remedy for faults rather than their judge.

Yet whatever was offered to him, he accepted most willingly, so that he might have something to distribute to the poor. The saying in the Gospel was always fulfilled in him: “To everyone who has, more will be given, and he will abound” (Matt. XIII, 12). For we often saw his purse so emptied that he had nothing to give the brothers, when suddenly, unexpectedly, a sufficient blessing came to him, by which the outcry of those urgently pressing him could be stilled. And lest, by speaking of these matters generally, we seem to overlook some of his particular works of mercy, certain deeds worthy of remembrance must be inserted here, so that they may lend credibility even to those which need not be recorded by name.

### CHAPTER IX — How he provided clothing for two boys already dead, or committed them to burial

At a certain time, as he was going to Saint-Denis near Paris and traveling along a public road, he came upon two boys who had succumbed to the torment of hunger and cold and, beneath everyone’s eyes—miserable to relate—lay naked and unburied in the middle of the road. For at that time there was a severe famine which, by its magnitude, had almost overwhelmed the provinces of Gaul and Aquitaine.

The holy man, therefore, pierced by horror at such a sight, dismounted from his horse, stopped, and hired undertakers. He pulled from his back the woolen garment commonly called a *staminium*, covered their nakedness with his own hands, buried them, and paid the service owed to the dead; then he continued the journey he had begun.

If Martin is celebrated throughout the world for having divided half his tunic with a poor man, why should this man not also be celebrated in his own way for an entire tunic given not to one living person but to two dead ones? Many similar examples could be brought forward, were the powers of our smallness not to fail. Yet, lest everything be buried in silence, at that time, and thereafter for many years while misery weighed upon the land, he broke up many ecclesiastical vessels and splendid ornaments for the use of the poor, among them even the imperial crown of the emperor Henry, judging it unworthy to deny such things to Christ’s poor, for whom Christ’s blood was poured out.

In the treasures of the Church given to the poor, Laurence is proclaimed marvelous by divine and human testimony. Although we do not dare to equate this man with him, nevertheless, among all the people of our own time whom we have seen—and I say this without prejudice to anyone—we rank him above all others, in his order, in this virtue. He helped those whom he could; and when he could not help them personally, he entreated others to show mercy.

For when he was unable to relieve the misery of everyone during the aforementioned periods of such bitter famine, we saw him go about the villages and churches wherever he could, persuading princes, the wealthy, and people of moderate means to give alms, gently stirring them to mercy, and freely promising them from heaven the fullest remission of sins.

[Note: [Col. 0903D] Undoubtedly to be referred to this passage is the blessed man’s letter to King Garcia, published in volume II of the *Spicilegium*, in which the holy man implores the aid of the pious prince during the famine.]

Thus, those whom he could not sufficiently support with his own resources, he assisted by persuading others through words of mercy. Certainly, by such counsel we know that many thousands of poor people escaped the peril of hunger and death. He passed over no one’s misery, despised no one’s need, and recoiled from no one’s infirmity.

### CHAPTER X — Concerning a cleric marked by the contagion of leprosy

Finally, a certain cleric of the church of the holy Mother of God at Anis, most noble according to the flesh but marked by the contagion of leprosy, had chosen for himself, as though necessary for so great a corruption, an isolated place beside a certain river, contiguous to a little monastery called Volta.

When the servant of God arrived there and learned of this, he sympathized with the sick man and ordered the brothers to comfort him in whatever ways were necessary. The wretched man himself sought a private interview with the holy man and humbly asked through an intermediary that he come to him.

The saint did not refuse to do so, recalling the example of the Lord’s humility, who, even without being asked, chose to come to the centurion’s servant. When he reached the man, he did not recoil from his misery; to our great astonishment, as we watched, he rushed to kiss him, embraced him, and shared a familiar conversation with him for a long time.

O man worthy of praise in every respect, who loved the privilege of human nature in a man more than he feared the misery caused by any disease!

[Col. 0905D] The manuscripts of Crespi and Saint-Germain read *juxta Ligerim*. But in the Thuanean manuscript one finds *juxta Alierim*, by which name the Elaver, commonly called the Allier, would be designated; Volta lies upon it, a place made famous by the monastery founded there by Saint Odilo himself. Indeed, the same codex below has *monasterio quod*, “the monastery which,” instead of *monasteriolo quod*, “the little monastery which.” The Cluniac Library supports this reading, where in this same Life one finds *juxta Alexim . . . monasterio*. Bollandus, from an old manuscript of Saint-Maximin, indeed has *monasterio*, but nevertheless calls the river the Loire. We have therefore preferred the reading that gives *Ligerim*. For, apart from that famous Volta which we have just mentioned, near the river Allier, not far from the city of Anis, we find on geographical maps, a little below that same city, a place called la Volte, situated above the Loire; we suspect that this is what is indicated here. Certainly, there may then have been there some small monastery, which our author called a *monasteriolum*, “little monastery.”

### CHAPTER XI — How hospitable he was, and how he gained many people of different ages and kinds for Christ

In receiving guests he was cheerful and pleasant. His generous spirit never supposed that anything was lacking for him, but in the abundance of Christ’s blessing he was lavishly generous to all.

He guarded the purity of his integrity so inviolate that he deserved to become a dwelling place of the Holy Spirit and a receptacle of the most chaste purity. So great was the perfection of humility in him that not even the slightest trace of pride was discerned. Innocence shone in him to no ordinary degree.

He measured everyone according to his own disposition; and just as he was free from the gall of malice, so he believed that others could not be corrupted by the plague of deceit. He excelled so greatly in the beauty of moral integrity that, in every action of his, the beauty of this virtue shone forth like the light of a certain radiance. For that holy soul wished neither to see nor to hear anything dishonest or unbecoming.

He kept the truth in his heart and uttered it with his mouth; but he avoided falsehood in every way, as though it were a deadly disease. Nor did he seek the favor of human praise, nor place his glory in the mouths of men. Whenever he was received or honored by brothers or bishops, according to ecclesiastical custom, with officious services of respect, I call Jesus, the advocate of his soul, to witness that he regarded such things as insignificant and counted them as a price of no importance.

Yet because he could not avoid this without causing scandal to many, outwardly he accepted fraternal attention, but inwardly he did not depart from his resolve of humble strictness. He remained steadfast in the brothers’ community until he reached the very extremity of death.

O how cheerfully he moved among the others! How joyfully he stood in the midst of that holy choir, looking to right and left upon the crown of the young plantation, mindful of that verse from David’s song: “Your children are like olive shoots around your table” (Ps. CXXVII).

And the more the number of the brothers increased, the more he showed by certain signs and clear indications the joy of his soul. And because he often saw that this was burdensome to some, he was accustomed to say: “Do not grieve, brothers, at the increase of the flock. For he by whose will and calling they are gathered will govern them by his providence and mercy.”

For he became the father of many monks, whom he gained for the Lord from different conditions, ages, and periods of life. He received some in childhood, others in youth, and others in old age. Although they came to him at different times, nevertheless, under one rule of moderation and discernment, he fostered and nourished them with maternal charity and paternal solicitude, gathering them from many different places and diverse dispositions into one body.

Wherever he went or proceeded, such a multitude of brothers followed him that you would have thought him no longer a leader and prince, but truly the archangel of monks. Fulbert, his intimate friend, the bishop of Chartres—praiseworthy in holiness and remarkable in wisdom, at whose death the study of philosophy perished in France and the glory of priests nearly fell—used to call him by this name in his sermons and letters.

### CHAPTER XII — Concerning fortitude

Having now to speak briefly of the fortitude of his soul and body, we must also give the definition of that virtue according to the judgment of the ancients. Fortitude is to drive the soul above fear of danger, to fear nothing except what is shameful, and to endure adversity and prosperity bravely.

Relying, therefore, upon this virtue, it seems difficult to say how brave he was in repelling the plots of enemies and how patient in enduring them. You could see in him this special quality of patience: like another David, he repaid those who had injured him with an even greater grace of kindness, and preserved a still greater benevolence toward those who hated him.

Adversity could not cast him down, nor prosperity lift him up. O how many attacks and how grievous persecutions that holy soul endured from those within and those outside; and, in addition to these, how harsh bodily punishments he imposed upon himself in fasts, vigils, and prayers! And—what may now be said openly, after the voyager’s safe passage—he had condemned his limbs, with God alone as witness, to certain iron bonds and fetters, so that scarcely could human flesh have endured it.

A very rough hair shirt always clung to him beneath; above it he appeared clothed in an ordinary and moderate garment. He endured many and various labors for the peace of the churches, for the condition of his houses, and for the benefit of his neighbors; and through his own dangers he sought tranquility for all.

You know, merciful and compassionate Jesus Christ, lover of men, what most grievous pains and bitter torments you secretly inflicted upon him to prove his patience. Yet amid them he kept his spirit unconquered, like good earth yielding fruit in patience, saying that he deserved punishments greater than those he suffered.

Redeemer of souls, Lord, who strike in order to heal and mortify in order to give life, according to the multitude of his former sorrows may the consolations of your healings and the joy of heavenly delights succeed one another for him.

### CHAPTER XIII — Concerning temperance and the renewal of his houses

Temperance, which is the last in the catalogue of the proposed virtues, observes in its definition the measure and order of the things that must be said or done. In the exercise of this virtue he was so effective that in all his actions and commands he maintained measure, preserved order, and displayed marvelous discretion.

According to blessed Jerome, he moderated his fasts in the manner of a charioteer, according to the weariness and strength of his body. He tasted each dish that was set before him in such a way that he avoided superstition while preserving abstinence. His dress itself was notable neither for elegance nor for squalor. He tempered the gravity of his manners with a cheerful expression.

In correcting faults he was severe according to measure and time; in remitting them, gracious; and in both he was balanced on an equal scale. These virtues which we have proposed shone forth in him, and all the others converged upon them. For you could see in him the complete examples of virtue.

Thus he excelled in each individual virtue as though he possessed none of the others; yet he retained them all so that none was lacking. He also showed himself so approachable and benevolent toward his subjects that he preferred to be loved rather than feared, and to be useful rather than to rule.

Who ever heard anything displeasing about this man? Who heard it and believed it? Who believed it without thereby marking himself more clearly as malicious and infamous? For he himself gave authority to himself, appearing in all his acts and actions well-formed and composed before God and men.

Besides these inward qualities, he also possessed outwardly glorious zeal in building and renewing holy places and in acquiring ornaments from every source. His principal house, Cluny, demonstrates this: in all its buildings, inside and out, apart from the walls of the church, he carefully renewed it in his own time and adorned it with many ornaments.

There, also, in his final years, he constructed a cloister wonderfully decorated with marble columns brought from the farthest parts of that province and transported, not without great labor, along the swiftest currents of the Durance and the Rhône. He was accustomed to boast of it, saying—for he had a cheerful disposition—that he had found it wooden and was leaving it marble, after the example of Caesar Octavian, whom history describes as having found Rome brick and left it marble.

[Col. 0907D] The Crespi codex reads *ligneum*; another manuscript, with Bollandus, has *ligneam*. Our reading seems better, since the author appears to allude to Augustus Caesar’s saying about the city of Rome.

He also began a canopy over the altar of Saint Peter, whose columns he clothed in silver with niello, beautifully worked.

[Col. 0907D] The manuscripts read *cum nigello*, “with niello”; Bollandus reads *cum jugello*.

But what shall I say of all his monasteries? Paterniacum, a place pleasing to him because of his love for the Mother of God; the monastery of Romanum, built from the foundations; the place of Saint Victor of Geneva, constructed entirely in his own time in addition to its ancient and noble church; Carus, a place; Amberta, a very celebrated church; Rivis, entirely rebuilt; Celsinanias; Silviniacus; Firmitas, transferred; the monastery of Saint Saturninus; and at Pavia, the most noble house of Saint Maiolus.

[Col. 0907D] The monasteries known from other sources require no fuller notes here. Paterniacum and Romanum, situated in the diocese of Lausanne, were received by Odilo from Adelaide. Carus, situated in the Mâconnais, was given to Saint Odo by Robert, bishop of Valence, and his brother Edward. Amberta belongs to the region of Lyon; Rivis, commonly Riz, and Celsiniae, Sauxillanges, to the Auvergne. Silviniacum, Souvigny, lies among the Bourbonnais; Firmitas, la Ferté, was a priory subject to Silviniacum. The rest has been discussed elsewhere.

Besides these, a great number of various churches were, through his industry, greatly enlarged in his time in buildings, possessions, and ornaments.

In the final years of his life he also built, on a small estate belonging to his parents, a monastery called Volta—la Voute—from the turning of the surrounding water. It was adorned with devoted care; from the revenues of his old friends and relatives, as he was able, he endowed it for the service of God, and furnished it suitably with books and ornaments.

If enemies mock, or friends criticize me for having included these things needlessly, let them know—indeed, let them know—that all these matters pertain to the virtues of his soul, and that through such deeds he happily earned the patronage of the saints and had already received from the Lord the crown of blessed recompense.

What are we doing now, my soul? Why do we weave such lengthy delays of circumlocution? Do we wish to postpone death and make life longer, as though we feared reaching the end? That sentence given to the first man still remains: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. III, 19).

All who came after him have passed away and paid the law of death. Patriarchs, prophets, and apostles have died; kings, emperors, princes, great and small—all who had a beginning in birth have the condition of dying. Elijah and Enoch are exceptions, and they too, in their own order, will die in the days of Antichrist.

The Son of God dies; we die in one way, he in another: he by power, we by condition; he by will, we by necessity—although he too died by necessity, because of our liberation. For unless he had died, we would not rise again; he dies so that after death we may hope for eternal life.

### CHAPTER XIV — Concerning his passing: how his blessed spirit left the earth and sought heaven

In the final years of his life, Odilo, of blessed memory, began for five years to be severely afflicted again by new and very grievous torments. When he already felt death approaching, he went to the thresholds of the holy apostles with this vow and hope: that there, under the protection of so many apostles, he might discharge the debt of death, as he had always desired.

But since a man’s way is not in his own power, things turned out otherwise than he had hoped. He remained there for four months, held by a very serious bodily illness. He enjoyed the desirable conversation of Clement, the pope of blessed memory whom we mentioned above, and his blessing of apostolic reverence. He also received the welcome visits of many monks and clerics, among whom Lord Laurence, archbishop of Amalfi, often came to see him.

[Col. 0909D] One should read *de Amalphia*, “of Amalfi”; Peter Damian has *Amalfitanus*. This was Laurence of Amalfi, archbishop, who, having become bishop of that church after being a Benedictine monk, administered it excellently until the year 1049, when, as we learn below in chapter 17, he died.

He was a man altogether most holy, eloquent in the Scriptures of both languages, Greek and Latin, and an intimate friend of our Father. The souls of the two men were joined together by an indivisible love of the spirit.

After he recovered contrary to hope, supported by the intercession of the holy apostles and fortified by apostolic blessings, he returned to his own places. He came to Cluny and remained there for almost an entire year, afflicting himself intensely, as far as his illness permitted, with fasts, prayers, and vigils. He instructed the brothers who lived there and those who arrived later with pious exhortations, and foretold that the swift laying aside of his body was near.

After this he decided to visit his monasteries and cells, to see the brothers, and, by instructing them with paternal admonitions, to summon them to better things; then, wherever he might withdraw, he would await his calling with watchful care.

When this work had begun, they came to Silviniacum, where his predecessor, Saint Maiolus, had died and lay buried. After remaining there for several days, when the approach of the Lord’s Nativity was already at hand, and, like a voice going before it, he publicly announced day after day in his sermon the joys of that great festival to the people, suddenly all his long-standing torments and ancient pains gathered together at his vital organs, and, alas, what grief! hope for his life was abandoned.

As ecclesiastical custom requires, the brothers came before him with psalms; according to the apostolic teaching, the prayer of faith was offered over him; the mystery of the life-giving body and blood was received; peace was given to the brothers; and finally that saving cross of our redemption, together with the image of our crucified Lord, was presented to him for prayer.

O Lord Jesus! What sighs and groans there were in that hour! What recollection and confession of sins, what glorification of your majesty, what invocation of your name, and what remembrance of your passion and our redemption! With eyes raised and filled with showers of tears, he contemplated and shared in the suffering of the image of your face, as though he were seeing you crucified and dying once again.

He stood wholly absorbed before you with Mary your mother, and the sword of the sharpest compunction passed through his soul. I do not know whether with bodily or incorporeal eyes he saw at his side the hostile enemy and plotter against the human race, who had not abstained from attempting his fraud even against the Lord himself.

You would have seen him—and heard him with an unrestrained cry—rebuking that enemy with certain terrible denunciations and commanding him in imperial words to withdraw far from him. To use his own words:

“To you,” he said, “enemy of the human race, I forbid, by the power of my Lord Jesus Christ and by the standard of the holy cross, to turn your engines and your hidden and open snares away from me, because the cross of my Lord is life to me and death to you. The cross of my Lord is with me; I always adore him, always bless him, and now commend my spirit into his hands.”

When these things had been completed, the solemnity of the Lord’s Nativity was already approaching. During those days it had always been his custom in life to appear more gracious and attentive.

When the vigil arrived, he proceeded with the brothers into the chapter house; he heard the announcement of the heavenly oracle and of the approaching festival; he bent his knees, adored, and completed the prayer. After this he delivered a sermon so festive and brilliant that he had never done better in his life. He consoled and relieved the brothers who were grieving for him, declared that they should hope in God’s mercy after his death, and then eagerly arranged to share with them in the joys of so great a festival.

But since he was now almost lifeless and could not attend the major church of Saint Peter, where the brothers’ community gathered, he remained in the church of God’s Mother and Virgin Mary with some brothers detained there with him. Like a festive precentor, he gave out psalms and antiphons, bestowed blessings, and joyfully performed all the offices appropriate to so great a festival, forgetting his bodily weakness.

Cheerful and festive, he wished to receive the coming Lord festively—not now through a mirror and in an enigma, but face to face—and he sighed for this with his whole desire. He was very anxious lest the end of the divine calling, already imminent, should find him insufficiently prepared.

His bodily strength having almost entirely failed, throughout the whole solemnity he was carried to the church by the hands of bearers at each hour of the day and night and at the celebrations of Mass. He was always refreshed by the life-giving mysteries, and he asserted with certainty that the day of his calling was approaching around the festival of the Lord’s Circumcision.

He recalled the death on that same holy Circumcision of that most perfect man, Lord William, abbot of Dijon, who therefore received the crown of divine recompense on that day because he had always piously sympathized with the tender wounds of the Lord’s blood—namely, according to Jerome, with the injury of the Circumcision.

In the same way, this man too had the same quality of affection toward the Savior’s humanity. Thus both men were moved by one and the same kind of piety, were called from this world at a similar time of the solemnity, and shine in heaven with no unequal brilliance. For while they lived, they were inseparable friends, equals in their holy profession, and not unlike in all moral integrity.

Suspended in such expectation, he passed almost all that time without food or drink. In a wondrous way he arranged both his private affairs and those of the community as though he suffered nothing; and, cheerful and lively, he gave instructions concerning how his body should be prepared and buried.

The feast of the holy pontiff Sylvester had arrived, together with the eve of the awaited Circumcision, when suddenly, before dawn, he began to be pressed more and more toward the end of death. He urgently requested the mystery of the Lord’s body and blood, recognized it faithfully, and received it devoutly. Again the cross was adored; again the devil was driven away and, lest he dare approach him with deadly intent, was forbidden in repeated imperial words.

As the day advanced, against the illusions of evil spirits and the assaults of wicked thoughts, the Creed was read before everyone as a shield of faith. Augustine was brought in as interpreter; he was listened to attentively; and the sermon was repeated with those standing by.

The reading was prolonged far into the day, and the spirit, placed in the final struggle, was strengthened in the power of faith. Meanwhile death gradually broke through and entered the barriers of the flesh.

The brothers came before him and were again greeted; they were instructed and fortified with paternal exhortations and blessings, and admonished to be mindful of their own calling. When consulted about his successor, he said: “I entrust this to God’s disposition and to the election of the brothers.”

After this the day was drawn out until evening. The brothers performed the evening offices, and he himself was carried by the hands of bearers, with his bed, before the holy altar of God’s Mother Mary.

A wondrous thing! He gave out the psalms; dying, he sang with those who sang. And when, amid such a spectacle of grief, the brothers, overcome by sadness at his death, omitted something while singing, he corrected it; what they forgot, he remembered.

When these things were completed, he indicated that the brothers should leave, and he remained for some time in prayer. Later, when he wished, he was carried back to the house.

He anxiously asked what the community of brothers was doing. It was Saturday. Night was already coming on, and he was concerned, by command, about the washing of the feet, lest the hour be prolonged for the brothers.

While these things were taking place, his spirit was released into death. Suddenly he was returned almost lifeless and was held in their hands. The brothers hastily spread the hair shirt on the ground, scattered ashes, and laid the holy body upon them.

At last, having recovered his breath, he asked where a certain bearer from among the brothers of his own age, named Bernard, was. When Bernard said, “Lord, in the ashes and hair shirt,” he replied, “Thanks be to God.”

Then he anxiously asked whether the children and the community of brothers were present. When he was told that everyone was there, he finally turned toward the cross standing nearby, directed the sight of his eyes to it, and silently uttered with the movement of his lips certain words of a final prayer.

And so, without any convulsion of the body or any sign of disordered emotion, with his eyes closed, he rested in peace.

The brothers whom he himself had ordered did so, washing, embalming, and arranging his body in the manner he had prescribed. They placed it in the bier customary to him, carried it to the church before the holy altar, and kept it there for three days because brothers were coming from everywhere to attend the burial.

For his funeral, not merely the village but almost the entire province came. You would have seen some grieving here and others rejoicing there, yet all weeping. Some wept for joy because they had been given so great a patron; others wept from sorrow because they had been deprived of the consolation of so great a father.

After three days, when the customary rites had been completed, he was carried by the hands of his disciples with a great choir of singers to the tomb in that same church and, as was fitting, buried decently in a new stone sarcophagus hewn from rock.

The holy man died on the night of the Circumcision of our Lord Jesus Christ, in the first watch of the night, which was also reckoned as Sunday, in the eighty-seventh year of his age, the fifty-sixth of his ordination, and the year 1049 of the Lord’s Incarnation.

### CHAPTER XV — Commendation of the soul

Now, Lord Jesus, we commend to you the soul of him whom, though dead, we cannot retain. We rejoice because we received such a gift from you; we grieve because we lost him so quickly.

We cannot bear his absence, but we are consoled by the hope that he is with you. For why, Lord, should he not be there with you who here never wished to be separated from you? Who ever loved you more than he did? Who ever glorified you more than he did, according to his desire and ability?

For your sake he shared the grief of those who grieved; for your sake he endured many labors; for your sake he supplied many things to the poor. And what shall I say, Lord? Although he did not shed his blood for you, he will not lack the fruit of martyrdom, because, had it been necessary, he would have endured it with all his strength [ms. 1: “would have wished it”]; and because this could not be, his own prolonged torments and labors will be made equal to the sufferings of your saints.

If any virtue or grace shone forth in him, Lord, it came entirely from you and from him: from you through grace, from him through voluntary obedience. Your grace went before; the effect of his work followed.

Now, receiver of holy souls, Son of God, Jesus Christ, be the perpetual rewarder of his labors, and be our most merciful comforter in him and through him—you who live and reign forever and ever. Amen.

### CHAPTER XVI — How the holy man appeared to a certain monk

On the same night on which the holy man died, a certain brother named Gregory, a Ninivite [Mss. 2: *Ninevita*. Could this be from Ninove, a town in Flanders midway between Brussels and Oudenaarde in the county of Aalst? Peter Damian, in Bollandus, has *Juveneta*.] by nationality, simple in nature and most innocent in life, returned to his own bed, weary and weakened by illness, after the saint, as we have said, had been carried into the church. He gave himself to rest and, before he had fully fallen asleep, saw that same Father standing beside him.

Then, in a presumptuous voice, he said: “What are you doing, lord?”

He replied: “Well, brother, very well. For my Lord Jesus Christ deigned to come in person to his servant. But at the hour of my departure, there in the corner”—and he pointed to the place as though with his finger—“I saw a fierce and extremely terrible figure which wished to frighten me with its horror and immense ugliness. But with my Lord present, it could not harm me.”

Having said this, he withdrew. The brother then arose and truthfully related to the brothers who were present at the time, and afterward to us, what he had heard and seen.

### CHAPTER XVII — Concerning a similar vision

When Lent followed, Lord Laurence, the archbishop whom we mentioned above, died at Rome. A certain cleric named Albero, German by nationality and most noble by birth, was devoutly present at his funeral. He had been exceedingly close to Father Odilo while he lived and had come to Rome at that time with Pope Leo, his near relative.

After the archbishop had died and been carried to the church, Albero, compelled by weariness, gave himself to sleep in a corner of that same church. Suddenly, while he was still almost awake, the blessed Odilo appeared to him.

Trembling and afraid, he said to him in a friendly voice: “Lord, when did you come here, and why?”

“I came,” he replied, “for the funeral of our brother, Lord Laurence the archbishop. When these rites were completed, I did not wish to leave here without seeing you.”

After he had said this, the vision disappeared. Albero later truthfully related these things to us and to many others.

Let the epitaph now come to an end, lest weariness from lengthy speech arise in the minds of the hearers. Nevertheless, let it be said briefly at the conclusion of the discourse that Odilo had long desired the end of his life, but, according to the Apostle, through the necessity imposed by his subjects, remained in the flesh so long by God’s grace.

Certainly, the present life was weariness to him, and death gain. He often grieved, even to the shedding of tears, that he had outlived his contemporaries and younger companions and remained behind to see the misery of sorrows. He seemed to himself a stranger among others, because only a few shared his measured and disciplined disposition.

He was often moved to compunction because almost all the beauty of integrity and the virtue of innate goodness had withdrawn from the world. “Woe is me, because my sojourning has been prolonged,” he frequently sang with David; and, according to the Apostle, he chose to depart and be with Christ, which is far better.

Since, therefore, he has now departed as he wished, let the mourning of his funeral be closed with this discourse; let his rest in Jerusalem be invoked again and again for all days, and repeated throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

Odilo, may you live always on high with Christ;

Odilo, holy one, may you receive the everlasting crown.

May the virgin-born Lamb go before you, Odilo;

May you be able to run after him joyfully and touch his footprints,

Wholly suffused with the fragrance of that ointment,

With which, when his name is poured forth, he refreshes holy minds [ms. 1: souls],

With whose fragrance Mary herself anointed the head of God,

A sinner in herself, made blessed by divine gift.

## HERE BEGINS THE PROLOGUE TO THE SECOND BOOK

[Col. 0913]

[Col. 0913D] In the preceding book, or rather in what was designated the epitaph, we spoke about the character of Father Odilo and the virtues of his spirit—not fully, to be sure, but according to what we were able to say. To those who inquire into signs and measure each person’s merit by the novelty of his miracles [Note: [Col. 0914D] Codex of Saint-Germain: “by the novelty of miracles”], it must nevertheless be said that the prerogative of divine love is placed not in the display of signs but in the perfection of virtues. For miracles and signs do not commend us to God; rather, the perfection of our works demonstrates that we are perfect. Judas, after all, performed signs together with the apostles, while the reprobate, excluded outside the kingdom on the day of judgment, will say: “Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and in your name perform many signs?” (Matthew VI). And the Lord himself says in the Gospel to the holy apostles returning from preaching: “Do not rejoice in this, that the demons are subject to you; but rejoice in this, that your names are written in heaven” (Luke X, 20). Since these things are so, it is vain to regard as something great what is known sometimes to be possessed by the reprobate together with the elect. Nevertheless, lest our Odilo also be excluded from this grace, a few of the many things that our Lord deigned to display before and after his death, for his own praise and glory and to commend Odilo’s merit to men, must be related.

# THE SECOND BOOK BEGINS

[Col. 0915]

## CHAPTER I.—How, when he was once a boy, he was divinely freed from a most serious illness

[Col. 0915A]

At the beginning of the account of his virtues, it must be told what happened to him while he was still a boy. Lest it seem incredible to anyone, I learned it from those to whom he himself was accustomed to relate it.

While he was still a very young child being raised in his father’s household, before he had even been sent to school, it happened that he was deprived of almost all the strength of his limbs, and the ability to walk or move by himself was denied him. One day his father’s household happened to be moving from one place to another, and the infant was carried under the care of his nurse by the service of household slaves. When, midway through the journey, they had turned aside toward a certain church consecrated in honor of Mary, the Mother of God, they set the little boy down with the bundles [Col. 0915B] before the door of that church. There were houses adjoining the basilica, where they needed to obtain some provisions.

While they were detained there for some time, the boy, seeing himself left alone, was moved by divine inspiration and began to test whether he might somehow reach the door and enter the church of the Mother of God. Thus, with whatever strength he possessed, crawling on hands and feet, he reached the door, entered the church, and came as far as the altar. He seized the altar cloth with his hands; then, stretching his arms upward with all his might, he tried to rise, but he was held back by knots that had long been badly tied. At last divine power prevailed [another manuscript: “nevertheless”], restoring the boy’s weakened limbs. In a wondrous manner, through the intervention of the Mother of God, he rose and stood healthy upon his feet, then ran here and there around the altar. The attendants, returning afterward to the bundles and not finding the boy, were greatly astonished and began searching for him everywhere. When he could not be found, they became exceedingly distressed among themselves. At last, by chance, they entered the church and saw him wandering and running through it. They recognized the power of divine strength, joyfully took the boy into their arms, reached the place toward which they had been traveling, and returned him safe and sound to his parents with great rejoicing.

Even then the Lord was showing in the boy how pleasing and acceptable he would one day be to him: although the child could scarcely yet speak or distinguish anything, God mercifully freed him from the bond of such crippling contraction. The church of the Mother of God was also a prophecy of what was to come, for when he reached mature understanding and age, he loved and honored it with all his desires and glorified it throughout his life with all his strength. It is also reported that, when he had reached adulthood, he entered a church consecrated in the same way in honor of the Mother of God and, with no one other than God as witness, dedicated himself to that same altar, saying:

“O most merciful Virgin and Mother of the Savior of all ages, from this day forward keep me in your service, and in all my affairs, as my most merciful advocate, always be present to me. After God, from now on I place nothing before you; and of my own free will I surrender myself forever to your service as to that of my own master, as though I were your personal servant.”

Let this suffice concerning his childhood. Now we must come to the things that, when he had reached a more mature age and had been ennobled by the governance of the abbey, he accomplished with the Lord’s cooperation.

But many of the things I am about to relate at the outset I did not see myself. I learned them from two of his monks: Peter, the provost of the monastery of Saint Maiolus near Pavia, a religious man, and Syrus, the abbot of a certain monastery [Note: [Col. 0915D] Some manuscripts read “Syrone.” He is Syrus the abbot, who committed the Life of Saint Maiolus to writing.], who reported them through a memorandum of Brother Boso, a monk of extraordinary simplicity and innocence, as I had requested when I began this work. Those brothers were both reputable men, very close to Father Odilo, aware of many of his secrets, and for a long time companions of his journeys and labors.

Therefore, what they report is credible to the extent that it is certainly established that they relate things they saw with their eyes, heard with their ears, and even handled with their hands, and that they entrusted them to prudent memory so that they might become known at a definite time to us and to many others. [Note: [Col. 0915D] Because a leaf is missing here from our Saint-Germain manuscript, the gap—which sometimes occurs in the Thuaneus manuscript up to chapter 5—could not be supplied.] For this reason we surround our account with the testimony of reputable men, lest our rivals judge that we invented these things through someone’s false flattery.

For, as Gallus relates concerning Martin in the dialogue of Sulpicius Severus and Postumianus, Odilo does not need to be supported by lies: Christ has already, as we piously believe, glorified him in heaven, and publicly commends him in the world through various signs of virtue. Far be it from me to invent or relate anything falsely about so great a man unless I had seen and experienced it myself, or it had been reported by faithful persons or suitable witnesses.

## CHAPTER II.—Concerning a blind man who was given sight

At a certain time, the most blessed Father Odilo went out from Cluny, that celebrated place, and came to a certain estate belonging to him, situated not far from the same monastery, called Besorniacum [another reading: Bersoniacum]. According to his customary practice, he sought the church in order to offer the vows of his prayers to Christ the Lord. From there he withdrew to a house that appeared to adjoin the church. Since it was cold, a fire was lit, and he began, while seated, to warm his frozen limbs.

Afterward, rolling his eyes here and there, he caught sight at a distance of a boy whose facial form the beautiful hand of the heavenly Craftsman had made handsome. He asked who he was. Those standing around replied: “He is held attached to your service, lord, by the bond of servitude.”

The saint said: “How so?”

“He is the son,” they answered, “of your steward. Although he appears handsome in appearance, he lacks the use of his eyes.”

The God-bearing hero was silent. Turning his mind toward hope, he invoked the mercy of the Thunderer in silent prayer. Calling the child to him, he imprinted the sign of the Lord’s cross upon eyes condemned to blindness, and, with God cooperating through his virtues, immediately supplied what nature had withheld. He then sent him home rejoicing and seeing.

For he loved children—not pursuing childish frivolity, but piously embracing in them the innocence of their age [lacuna] “for of such is the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew XIX).

Who can speak of the mighty deeds of God, dearest brothers? For we see fulfilled the truthful saying of Christ: “Whoever believes in me will also do the works that I do” (John V, 36). The right hand of the powerful Savior certainly performed a similar work while he dwelt in human flesh; and now he has deigned, through the same distinguished miracle, to magnify his servant in the age of our own time, so that anyone may easily learn how highly he must be esteemed who, through a similar work, with the Lord, ruler of the ages, cooperating, deserved to be exalted.

## CHAPTER III.—Concerning water changed into wine

At one time Saint Odilo was staying in one of his monasteries called Aurea Vallis, a religious place renowned for the holiness of the brothers who lived there. It was the first day of the fast preceding the Lord’s Pasch, on which the imposition of ashes upon the head is received and the difficult beginning of abstinence is undertaken by the faithful.

The worshiper of God, wishing to fulfill the customary observance, sat secretly at table with a handful of ashes, when, at about the ninth hour of the day, the brothers, having taken a little food, were giving themselves to reading. In accordance with the Psalmist’s saying, he began to restore his weary body with bread mixed with ashes. He signaled to a certain brother to bring him a drink of water, with which he might sustain his weakened limbs alongside the dry food.

The brother brought what he had been ordered to bring. But when Odilo brought it to his lips, suddenly the taste and fragrance of the water conveyed the flavor of wine. He stopped and, as though unaware of the reason, again motioned to the brother to bring water. The brother, astonished that he had offered water, indicated this to him. At last, after the vessel had been emptied, he brought the Father a second time one filled with water. Odilo barely touched it with his mouth, and once again it began to smell of wine instead of water.

The blessed man, perceiving God’s kindness toward him, did not refuse with humble devotion to take what God had sent. Behold, [lacuna] at Cana of Galilee he had provided wine from water for those celebrating a feast. Now, for his servant who willingly desired to mortify himself, he changed pale water into the taste of wine. With what joy of heart and confidence of mind must he then be thought to have exulted, when he realized that God cared for him in this way? He could then sing in the words of the Psalmist: “The Lord is mindful of me,” or, as it is said elsewhere, “The Lord cares for me.”

## CHAPTER IV.—Concerning a theft discovered at Pavia

At the time when King Henry was hastening to the citadel of the Roman Empire so that he might be advanced from kingship to imperial rule, the most blessed Odilo was traveling with him. At Pavia, the wealthiest town in Italy, they both celebrated the adorable Child of the most glorious Virgin.

When the sacred offices of hymns for that day had been completed, the elder sat at table with the brothers so that, after taking nourishment, they might recover their lost strength. Many were reclining, and there were also many attendants. Among them was a certain possessor of fraud who, pretending that he wished to serve, was watching with his eyes for an opportunity to steal something.

When he saw an elaborate cloth upon the table of the man of God, enticed by deadly greed, he was eager to carry out what he had desired in his wicked mind. After hunger had been removed by the meal and the tables had been cleared, while the others were attending to their own affairs, that evil man suddenly seized the cloth that he happened to find and hurried away, rejoicing in the booty he had discovered and unaware how great a loss of his limbs was soon to befall him.

The next day, when the table had been set at the proper hour, what was missing was sought. When a murmur of complaints arose among the attendants over the lost cloth, the generous Father, treating the matter as insignificant, said: “Bring another, and take care in future that something of this kind does not happen again [lacuna].”

Later, that wicked man brought the stolen object to the marketplace of saleable goods, together with the blessed man and the king; but he could not sell it in any way, because that wicked man did not deserve to possess it. Having tried once, twice, and three times in vain, he finally returned home, embarrassed by shame in his face, empty-handed.

And behold, divine vengeance immediately punished the criminal deed committed against the servant of God. Suddenly his hands and feet dried up, and the wretched and pitiable man was carried, together with the stolen object, to the church of Saint Maiolus [supplied: “to the church”]. He was placed upon the ground, while the cloth was hung above him. The people flocked together; the church was packed with an innumerable multitude; Odilo’s merit was recognized; and Saint Maiolus was entreated by everyone’s prayers to bring aid to the miserable man.

At last divine mercy, accustomed to compassion, raised up the wretched man, suffused his arms and hands with their natural moisture, strengthened his legs and soles, and he returned home with all the people, glorifying God.

## CHAPTER V.—Another similar theft

The savage mind of another thief also plotted to inflict upon the aforesaid Father the loss of a similar seizure. The aforementioned Father was staying in the city of Pavia when, behold, one night a thief entered the stable of the horses and led away one that he had recognized as the best of the lot, and upon whose back the blessed man was accustomed to sit.

But because in that city not only the man of God but also the things belonging to him were well known, the thief feared to remain there and fled to the town of Lodi, hoping to obtain there the price he desired from the sale of the horse. But because God always cares for his own, he so closed the hearts of all who saw the horse that no one showed any inclination to buy it.

When the thief saw this, touched by remorse of heart and recognizing that he had acted wickedly, he immediately returned to the place that had witnessed his fraud and restored the horse he had stolen to the grieving servants. This was announced to the man of God. He gave thanks to the supreme Creator of all things and, so that no harm might be inflicted upon the thief, calmed by commanding prayer the wills that were raging.

For he was not eager for vengeance; rather, through his heart’s excessive kindness, he always sought to repay evil with good. In accordance with the admonition of blessed Paul the Apostle, who is called the vessel of election, he never wished to return evil for evil to anyone, but to do good to all in common.

## CHAPTER VI.—Concerning the crossing of the exceedingly deep waters of the Ticino and the lighting of a lamp

At the time when a certain nobleman named Arduino had seized the kingdom of Italy, and the great Henry, most illustrious among others, was already in that Italian land and was seeking the monarchy of the kingdom with the consent of the princes of Italy, the aforesaid Father, traveling through Italy, came to a certain river which, flowing past the walls of Pavia on the southern side, is called Ticino, taking its name from itself.

He wished to cross it quickly, but there was no boat by which a river of such depth could be forded. Trusting in God, to whom he clung with his whole mind, he called one of his servants, named Wolveno, and ordered him, in the name of the Lord, to walk without hesitation through the deep waters of the river.

Wonderful to relate—but all things are possible to one who believes—the servant immediately obeyed, and his master followed him. Thus, with the entire company, without the aid of a boat and without any injury, under Christ’s guidance, they reached the farther bank.

Then the prophecy of the holy Habakkuk was fulfilled: “You made a way in the sea for your horses, in the mud of many waters” (Habakkuk III, 15). What seems more wondrous or more worthy of praise? Once the Israelite people crossed dry-shod through the divisions of the sea; now blessed Father Odilo cleaved a path across the waves themselves. But since both are gifts of God, in both cases God must be glorified by us.

Those who were present, seeing this, thought it was an ordinary crossing of the water and tried to attempt it on horseback. But before the horses’ first hoofprints could touch the bank, they would almost have been submerged unless they immediately turned back and pressed their steps rearward.

After witnessing so great a miracle, one of the bystanders ran to the holy man’s knees and begged him to use his house as lodging. The blessed man gladly consented, for the day was already turning toward sunset. He came with his companions to the house, was refreshed by the man’s charity, and went to sleep.

In the middle of the night, while the blessed man was already asleep, a wind suddenly blew through the openings in the house and extinguished the lamp with its breath. The chamber-servant who slept before him, named Deodatus, awoke, was terrified, and grieved that darkness had entered where he remembered leaving light.

He sprang from his bed, and, not knowing where to seek light, took courage from faith and began to pray to God, saying: “O divine Light, who illumines the whole world, hear me, unworthy [another manuscript: “wretched”], and through your Odilo drive the horrors of darkness from this house.”

Immediately light poured from heaven, filling him with joy and security and flooding the house with luminous brightness. And lest this seem incredible to anyone, faithful men and Christian brothers, it was the wondrous power of the Creator, who, seeing the devotion of his servants’ hearts, wished to glorify him in such a way that the light of his merits might be spread throughout the regions of the world.

## CHAPTER VII.—A similar miracle

The memorial day of divine visitation and human salvation—the feast, namely, of the Lord’s Nativity—was approaching. Saint Odilo of God had celebrated the first days of the Lord’s Advent at Paterniacum, a monastery dear to him.

From there he set out and gradually traveled through the mountains until he reached a certain village called Leodonium [Lons-le-Saunier], where salt, the seasoning of human food, is produced. With pious desire he was hastening to celebrate at Cluny—the dwelling-place of virtue and religion—the birth of the blessed Virgin’s Son.

Lord Peter had arrived from Italy and was traveling in his service; the pious Father rejoiced greatly in his companionship. After lodging in the aforementioned village, the elder ordered his men to be ready at dawn and to set out early, so that after a day’s journey they might reach the monastery of Saint Marcellus. For the day of Wednesday was approaching, on which both the solemn fast and the election of the Mother of God are proclaimed in the Church. [Note: [Col. 0919D] This monastery is situated in the suburb of Chalon-sur-Saône.] [Note: [Col. 0919D] Wednesday of the Ember Days in the third week of Advent, on which the Gospel “The angel Gabriel was sent,” and so forth, is read.] There he desired both to hear and to celebrate the festive message of the heavenly oracle sent to the blessed Virgin.

When morning came, they set out. The sky was already covered with clouds, spreading and driving upon the earth an immense quantity of rain and the discomforts of the winds [Note: [Col. 0920D] Another manuscript: “and filling it with the discomforts of the winds.”]. But these hardships could not turn the strong spirit of the man of God away from the purpose of his desire. Rather, he encouraged his companions not to lose heart but to complete the journey steadfastly. Since he did not allow himself to be conquered by pleasure, he showed himself unconquered by labor, because he remained free from every disturbance of spirit.

After a laborious journey and a great part of the day had passed, they came to a certain river that had swollen so greatly that, extending beyond the limits of its banks, it appeared impossible to cross. The companions ran about on every side and attempted many things, but could find no passable crossing.

Then the servant of Christ, placing his hope in God, called one of the servants, named Arbaldus.

“It seems to me,” he said, “that there is a course for crossing the river at this point. Therefore, enter confidently in God’s name, and by experience learn whether we too may cross.”

The man delayed nothing. He did what he had been ordered to do, crossed the river, reached the farther bank, and called out that he could lead all the others across.

The elder replied: “No; you must return to us.”

Through the Father’s intervention, he crossed back again, escaping the danger of the waters.

“Go before us, then,” he said, “in the name of the Lord.”

Thus, entering one after another in line, they crossed the vast flood, drenched by the water up to their thighs. But, as those who were present testified, the water did not reach the man of God even as far as the strap of his sandal.

All the companions were chilled by the water that had poured over them and by the excessive cold. At last, deep into the night, they reached the place they had long desired, dedicated to the honor of the outstanding martyr Marcellus. After praying, they sought a house, and, sitting around a large fire, some began to warm themselves while others changed their clothes.

Seeing their severe hardship, the sweetest Father’s heart grew warm, and he comforted their afflicted breasts with these words:

> O brothers, once strong through many dangers,
>
> do not break your hearts over your present circumstances.
>
> Through varied misfortunes, through so many hazards of life,
>
> we are making our way toward the kingdom of heaven and blessed dwellings.
>
> Endure, and one day it will bring joy to remember these things.

“Believe my littleness: the blessed Mother of God, for whose service you have assembled, will be the pious remunerator of this labor of yours.”

After they had taken food, they refreshed their weary limbs with the rest of sleep. On the following day, after completing the ecclesiastical offices, the gift of almighty God filled the brothers’ hearts with food and joy, and afterward he reached Cluny.

## CHAPTER VIII.—Concerning a few little fish by which very many were fed

Near Paris [Note: [Col. 0921D] From here through the words “of so great a man” we possess the text from a single Saint-Germain manuscript.] is the monastery distinguished by the honor of the glorious body of the martyr Saint Dionysius.
