This place had been entrusted by the Frankish kings Hugh and Robert to the man of God Odilo, so that it might be advanced for the better in monastic order and in the teaching of regular life.

The servant of God was once staying in this monastery, supplying the nourishment of life and the draught of salvation to his hearers with eloquent speech. The season of Lent had passed, and the days of the mystical supper and of Christ’s saving Passion had ended, when the light of joy—the triumph, namely, of the Lord’s resurrection—shone upon the world.

But on so solemn a day the eating of fish was lacking for the Father and the brothers. At that time the elder Ivo held the office of provost, an amiable man who strove to observe and honor the Father, who had deserved well of him. He was very sad and deeply distressed that the barrenness of the waters did not provide him with an abundance of fish. He kept trying to obtain such food from somewhere, but whatever efforts were made produced no success.

Divine providence was arranging that, on the new feast, a new guest of the deep should be sent to a new man—one renewed day by day, according to the Apostle, in the spirit of his mind—through God’s gift.

At the very dawn of that great day, after the brothers had solemnly completed the office of Matins, the aforementioned Ivo, possessing faith in God and relying upon the Father’s merits, set out from the church and went toward the servants’ quarters. He called those skilled in fishing, made many inquiries with them, and impressed upon them repeatedly the need to catch fish. He spoke now of the pious Odilo’s arrival, now of the day of the Lord’s resurrection, now of the brothers’ exhaustion from singing melodies.

Finally, in the power of Christ, he ordered them to seek the Seine River with their nets.

“Go,” he said, “and invoke the merit of Odilo and the name of Christ. For I believe that your hope will not be disappointed.”

Without delay, that most faithful company of servants cast their net into the river. Unexpectedly, the river yielded a fish of enormous size, called a sturgeon—a fish that fishermen could scarcely ever remember having caught in the river’s depths.

Thus those who had departed empty-handed returned laden. The new fish was presented: the river mentioned above was not accustomed to give such a fish, but the lavish hand of Christ had directed it to his servant. The holy Father held this unexpected miracle in such great wonder that he even ordered the schoolchildren, to whom a fish of such enormous size was strange and unknown, to come and see it. He increasingly kindled the elders, young men, and boys alike to glorify almighty God for this favor.

The solemn day was celebrated in glory of the Lord’s resurrection. The men rejoiced in the novelty of the deed accomplished through the merits of so great a man.

Near the monastery of Saint Dionysius is a small monastery consecrated in honor of Saint Martin, commonly called “at the Public Way.” [Note: [Col. 0921D] The church of Saint Dionysius de Strata, commonly Saint-Denys de l’Estrée, still exists there; very ancient tombs of Saint Dionysius and his companions can be seen there. No monks live there, although the revenues are extremely rich and are collected by the commendatory prior. Beside this church there is another, bearing the title of a parish, under the patronage of Saint Martin.] At this place the brothers who, because of illness or fatigue, cannot remain in the aforementioned monastery of Saint Dionysius sometimes withdraw.

One day the holy man arrived there fatigued and, turning aside from the monastery, went there for the sake of rest. The administrators of the larger monastery, recognizing this, sent him whatever was necessary. But as for fish—for none could be found among them—they sent very small gifts.

Meanwhile, while the man of the Lord thought he would have a private rest, suddenly, as a stream of monks always came to him wherever he was, two abbots arrived with several monks. He received them joyfully, spoke with them at length, and finally invited them to dine with him.

He then approached the cooks and those who served the food and asked what they had with which he could refresh the guests he had invited. They replied that they had the other things more or less adequately, but that there was almost no fish—nothing sufficient for so great a number.

“Children,” said the holy man, “leave your concern about this to him who was able to satisfy five thousand people with five loaves and two fish, and prepare a full meal for us and our guests.”

Having said this, he withdrew. They diligently procured what had been ordered, as best they could.

Why delay? They came to the table, and all reclined in their appointed places. I am about to relate a marvel, as those who were present truly testify. While the cooks served the fish and the servers carried it to the brothers at the table, that small quantity of fish and other food began to increase in the hands of the diners and the servers, until everyone had an abundant—indeed, more than abundant—share, and much remained for the servants.

At the end of the meal the holy man said:

“Children, you promised little and gave much; you feared hunger and refreshed us abundantly. Take care to preserve something of the fullness of our meal for yourselves.”

They, delighted with exceeding joy of heart, replied:

“Even now, lord, much remains for us, enough for us and for others if they should arrive. And if your holiness should thereafter propose anything, there will be no difficulty in our hearts about believing it. For, contrary to the expectation of our faintheartedness, what your confidence in God promised has happened.” [Another manuscript: “did not doubt.”]

To this the holy man replied:

“It was not my faith but your obedience and the merit of our guests that obtained this, so that what we took in charity, through the working of divine blessing, could suffice for all of us. Nevertheless, our hope—and yours—must always be placed in him with whom all things are possible that are impossible for human beings.”

## CHAPTER IX.—Concerning the overflowing of wine in a small vessel on the Aventine

A miracle not unlike this also happened at another time. In the city of Romulus, which by its size and beauty, as well as by its apostolic dignity, holds the citadel of the whole world, the venerable elder Odilo was staying for a certain period.

He had lodging in the monastery of the sacred Virgin who had given birth, situated on the Aventine Hill [Note: [Col. 0923D] Hildebrand, later Pope Gregory VII, was brought up there under his uncle, Abbot Hildebrand, as is said in his Life.]. This hill, possessing beautiful buildings above the other hills of that city and raising the summit of its position high into the air, makes the summer heat tolerable through the coolness of its breezes and provides a suitable dwelling.

A certain abbot named Armo, bound to the blessed man by a special affection, supplied the pasture of life to the spiritual sheep reclining within the enclosures of that monastery.

One day, therefore, Lord Odilo came to the table and asked whether he had at hand a wine suitable for his weakness. Those entrusted with this care replied that they had nothing of that kind that could be useful to him.

The man of God then turned to the aforementioned abbot, who was seated beside him:

“Good man,” he said, “if you have something that could be especially suitable, provide me with a charitable assistance from it.”

With a cheerful face and calm spirit, the abbot immediately ordered as much as Odilo desired to be brought.

Then the Father said: “Although this little vessel of ours appears small, let it be brought full.”

For he always strove to be generous with his own possessions and sparing with those of others.

A small vessel full of unmixed wine was brought and set before him. He began, like a cupbearer, to pour it out for himself and for the abbot reclining beside him. For as long as the meal lasted, each drank as much as he wished. The other brothers, stronger in body, drank another liquor, which nevertheless did not have a similar taste.

The food had now run out and it was time to rise from the table, yet that vessel, as though inexhaustible, still appeared to retain a little unmixed wine.

Then the lover of true piety, smiling gently, said:

“No, my brothers, I have not yet shown complete charity toward you.”

He immediately took a small glass vessel, poured the wine into it, and distributed a drink to each as a blessing.

Then an astonishing thing occurred. There were nearly twelve brothers; after cups had been drunk according to their number, the wine immediately ceased to flow any further.

While the brothers rejoiced among themselves and marveled at what had happened, the most prudent elder said:

“This guest of ours, through the abundance of his exceptional love, caused wine to overflow in a small vessel as an offering of charity.”

Thus the work, divinely accomplished in itself, testified that it had been brought about through the piety of another. For pure humility excelled in him, through which, as the Apostle says, he considered all others superior to himself and himself inferior.

## CHAPTER X.—Concerning a certain man freed from fevers

After leaving that illustrious City, he traveled along the public road and came to the town of Turin, where a certain man suffering from the burning of fevers prayed that a remedy might be given him through the washing of Odilo’s hands.

The sick man therefore secretly received from the attendants, without delay, the benefit of the holy man, while praising together the one Lord Jesus Christ, the eternal Father’s only Son. But, lest it reach the Father’s ears, the matter was concealed from everyone in profound silence.

## CHAPTER XI.—Concerning wineskins emptied for the use of the poor and filled again by divine power

From there he headed toward the Jovian Alps and, already climbing the arduous road, encountered a crowd of needy people who all cried out together for the necessary alms. Immediately the most munificent Father ordered the wineskins to be emptied of wine and given to the desire of the poor; and this was carried out without delay.

Not long afterward the proper hour arrived at which frail nature demanded the taking of food. They all reclined, and behold, the wineskins that had been empty of wine were found full of wholesome liquor. Everyone was astonished and offered solemn thanksgiving to the divine majesty for so great a gift.

## CHAPTER XII.—Concerning a glass vessel that was broken and restored solid again
When I was in Pannonia with Lord Abbot Hugh [Note: [Col. 0924D] Codex of Saint-Germain: “Lord and elder Hugh, abbot.”], one day I began a conversation with the venerable Bishop Richard, a protégé and monk of Father Odilo, about the virtues of that same Father. I was eager to question him and discover whether he knew any of them that he might disclose to me. For the bishop himself had been exceedingly close to him and for a long time [Col. 0925A] had been privy to his secrets and his companion on journeys and in labor.

Among other matters, mention was made of a certain vessel that had been broken and, as was said, restored through the Father’s prayers. Therefore, still uncertain, I anxiously inquired of him about the truth of the affair. He replied:

“Do you remember, brother, that dispute which Bishop Alberic of Como [Note: [Col. 0925D] That is, of Como, who is often called “of Cuma.” For among the bishops of Cuma in Campania of Italy no Alberic is found. But Alberic, Bishop of Como, is famous: he built a new cathedral church from its foundations, while the old one, which stood outside the city, was assigned to Benedictine monks; it later passed to the Cistercians and was eventually granted in commendam, and now has no monks, as Ughelli testifies in volume V of *Italia Sacra*, where he relates the history of the dispute mentioned here from the *Chronicle of Novalesa*. The same author gives further information about Bremet Abbey, now possessed by Olivetan monks. See also Lubin, *On the Abbeys of Italy*.] had with Odilo, the nephew of the elder Odilo, concerning Bremet Abbey?”

And I replied: “I certainly remember it, and remember it well.”

“While that dispute was taking place,” he said, “one day the aforesaid bishop and I were traveling together on the road and conversing with each other about many things. Among other matters I began to reproach him for having unjustly presumed to acquire the aforesaid abbey for himself, although he knew that it had first been given by Emperor Conrad to the administration of the aforesaid Father [Col. 0925B] Odilo. Among other arguments I began to set before him the holiness of the man, and the fact that many praiseworthy things were widely reported to have been done by him, including the reputed restoration of a certain broken glass vessel.

“‘I confess,’ Alberic replied, ‘that I know this better than you do. And because I see that you are uncertain about it, so that you may no longer doubt, hear the truth more clearly.’

“And I said: ‘I shall gladly hear it and store it carefully in my mind.’

“He then said: ‘At a certain time that elder of yours, as you call him, and abbot [Note: [Col. 0926D] Manuscript of Saint-Germain: “That elder and lord abbot of yours, as you call him.”] had come to the court of my lord, the Emperor Henry. While he was staying there, it happened one day that at the emperor’s table a most precious glass vessel of Alexandrian make [Note: [Col. 0926D] The same manuscript: “Alexandrian, with…”] containing ground spices was placed before him.

“‘He then summoned me and Landulf [manuscript: [Col. 0925C] Laudulf], later Bishop of Turin, and ordered us to carry that vessel, together with the powdered spices, to the table of our lord Odilo and to give it to him as a remedy for bodily health. We carried the vessel as the emperor had ordered, set it down before the abbot on Caesar’s behalf, and bowed humbly, as was fitting.

“‘He received it humbly, retained the vessel, and ordered us to return, and at the appointed time to come back to collect the little vessel. When we returned, however, as is characteristic of human curiosity—that people gladly wish to look at new and unusual things—the monks began handling the vessel among themselves, passing it from hand to hand. Then suddenly the vessel slipped from their hands and, being fragile, broke as it fell.

“‘Recognizing this, the man beloved of God was not a little distressed and said: “Brothers, you have not acted well. Through such negligence you may have deprived the young clerics, under whose custody the vessel entrusted to you had been placed, of the emperor’s favor. But so that no harm may come to those who are free from guilt, let us go to the church and beseech the Lord’s mercy concerning this.” At his command they hastened to the church, devoted themselves to psalms and prayers, and each person anxiously prayed on our behalf that no harm might come from this to us innocent men.

“‘When the prayer was finished, the holy man ordered that the vessel broken by them be brought to him. He examined it with his eyes and handled it with his hands; and behold, he found no sign of a crack or break. Angry with the monks, he said: “What did you think you saw, brothers? Surely your sight was held by some sort of darkness. You falsely imagined that the little vessel was broken, whereas now no sign of danger can be seen upon it.” But when the brothers saw this, struck dumb with astonishment at the miracle, they dared say nothing.

“‘Afterward, at the appointed time, my companion and I came to collect the vessel and asked its bearer for it. He took me aside, returned the vessel, and urged me to give it back to the emperor [Col. 0926B] as a great gift. When I asked him why he said this, he narrated in order everything that had happened.

“‘I returned with my companion full of joy, quietly reported to the emperor what I had learned, and filled him with great admiration and extraordinary delight at this miracle. For he loved that man beyond measure and humbly adhered to his counsel. After learning such things about him, he held him increasingly worthy of every veneration.’

“Thus Alberic, Bishop of the Church of Como, truthfully related these matters to me. I also learned with certainty from many other persons that they were true.

## CHAPTER XIII — On a Certain Vision of a Hermit

Lord Bishop Richard also related to me a certain vision, which I had once heard but at that time had not retained in my mind. He said:

“At a certain time a religious man from the district of Rodez was returning from Jerusalem. While crossing the sea that stretches from Sicily toward Thessalonica, he and several others encountered an exceedingly violent wind in mid-sea. The wind drove the ship to a certain island or rock, where a servant of God lived as a recluse. The aforesaid man remained there for some time, awaiting calm weather, and began to converse with that servant of God about many things.

“When the man of God asked him where he was descended from, he replied that he was from Aquitaine. Then the same man of God asked whether he knew a certain monastery called Cluny and its abbot, Odilo. [Col. 0926D]

“He replied: ‘I know it—indeed, I know it well—and I want to know why you ask.’

“‘I shall tell you,’ he said, ‘and I urge you to store in your mind what you hear. Near us are places which, by the manifest judgment of God, continually belch forth the most terrible fires. In them the souls of sinners undergo various punishments for an appointed time. A multitude of demons have been assigned to renew their torments continually; restoring their punishments day after day, they make their unbearable sufferings increasingly severe.

“‘Yet I have often heard them lamenting and making no small complaint, because through the prayers of religious people and alms bestowed upon the poor at various holy places, the souls of the condemned are very often released from their punishments by God’s mercy.

“‘Among other things, you should know that they made particular mention—and the greatest complaint—of that congregation of Cluny and of its abbot. Therefore, by God, I urge you: if you return safely to your people, make known to that congregation all that you have heard from me, and announce on my behalf that they should devote themselves more and more to prayers, vigils, [Col. 0927B] and almsgiving for the repose [Thuanus: redemption] of the souls placed in punishment, so that through these things joy may be multiplied in heaven and loss or mourning may be inflicted upon the devil.’

“Having returned to his homeland, the aforesaid man diligently reported these matters in order to the holy Father and the brothers [Note: [Col. 0927D] Codex of Saint-Germain: “When the aforesaid man had returned … it was reported to the brothers and religious men.”].

“When they heard this, they experienced no small amazement together with the greatest joy of heart. They gave thanks to the Lord, added prayers to prayers, alms to alms, and diligently labored for the repose of the dead.

“On this occasion, therefore, the holy Father established a general practice throughout all his monasteries: just as the feast of All Saints is celebrated on the first day of November, so on the following day a general commemoration should be held for the repose [Col. 0927C] of all the souls of the faithful; Masses should be celebrated privately and publicly with psalms and alms; and alms should be distributed in many ways to all the poor who came. Thus the adversary would grieve more and more over the loss inflicted upon him, while, conversely, the Christian laboring in this hope of mercy would rejoice.”

## CHAPTER XIV — On the Revelation of Lord Pope Benedict

Although it is always extremely foolish to observe visions and dreams, nevertheless faith should often be given to things that occur through divine providence, through the disclosure of past events, or through the revealing of future events. We have almost as many examples of these matters in the Old and New Testaments as there are books.

Therefore we judged it fitting to insert into this work a certain vision worthy of remembrance, known with a clarity brighter than daylight to many who are still living. Through it we may infer how much grace before God was merited by the man of whom we speak, while he still survived in this world. Elder Benedict once presided over the Apostolic See [Note: [Col. 0927D] Namely Benedict VIII, whose brother and successor was John XIX or XX; both were sons of Gregory, Count of Tusculum, as Leo of Marsi testifies in book II, chapter 27, of the *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*. See Baronius, under the year 1024.], outstanding in Roman nobility, exceedingly skilled in prudent judgment, and, so far as worldly eminence was concerned, most capable in civic affairs.

He loved the blessed Odilo with distinguished affection and honored him with the greatest devotion. Whenever the blessed man brought his presence within the walls of the Roman fortress, Benedict generously provided him with the assistance owed by a friend. [Col. 0928A]

When he had completed the course of mortal life, he returned his body to the earth and his soul to the power above. His kinsman by blood, John, then obtained the government of the Apostolic See.

A long time had passed while the soul of the aforementioned prelate, having not yet obtained a share in eternal light, was suffering punitive judgment for its offenses. Then, behold, the mercy of the compassionate God wished to reveal both that man’s punishment and the gift of His immense kindness, in order to make known the merit of the blessed Odilo.

The spirit of the aforesaid prelate appeared in a revelation to John, Bishop of Porto, [Note: [Col. 0928D] Sigebert relates this story in his *Chronicle* under the year 1025, but with many errors. I would, however, have it observed that he says the pontiff was freed from infernal punishments through Odilo’s intervention; by these words he intended nothing other than the cleansing flames of purgatory.] and to two others whose names I do not recall, indicating to them what was happening to him: namely, that he was held not in the splendor of light but in the shadows of punishment. He therefore urged them to go to his brother and quickly send a mission to the pious Odilo, for heavenly judgment had decreed that he would be rescued from his torments through Odilo’s intercessions.

When the darkness had withdrawn, those who had witnessed the vision approached the pope and reported what had been commanded them. Hearing this, the prelate grieved deeply for his brother, delayed no longer, and sent through the aforesaid Bishop John a sheet of writing containing the account of the vision to the blessed man.

Without delay the faithful messenger set out, reached Pavia, and, exhausted by the labor of the journey, disclosed to Lord Peter, superior of the cell of the blessed Majolus, what had been revealed and commanded to him. He earnestly asked Peter to act as the swift intermediary in this matter. [Col. 0928C]

Peter promptly sent the sealed letter to the most holy Father. By divine will it happened that the same servant of God was found at Cluny.

After reading the letter that had been brought to him, he summoned the noble senate of the monks and addressed them all in order. He opened the depths of his wisdom, repeated many arguments, and urged them not to regard such a mission as insignificant. Then he ordered that offerings of prayers and distributions of alms be solemnly made for the liberation of the universal prelate.

The elders therefore gratefully undertook the light burden of charity. Publicly and privately they appealed to the ears of the pious Creator with devout prayers. Not only in that monastery, but wherever communities of the brothers were scattered, a similar service was performed at the Father’s command.

The appointed period was now drawing to its end, when so many prayers [Col. 0928D] and offerings, together with generous almsgiving, had penetrated the entrance of divine kindness. Therefore the heavenly clemency was pleased to disclose the matter through an account beyond doubt.

In the aforesaid monastery there was an elder named Eldebertus, noble in flesh and nobler in spirit, who ministered to the needy by providing alms. A vision such as the following was revealed to him in sleep.

He saw a person of conspicuous beauty entering the monastery cloister with a great company of men in white, proceeding as far as the chapter house, where Lord Odilo sat with the holy senate, and humbly bowing his head at the knees of that same Father. When the brother asked who that radiant person was, he learned that it was Lord Benedict, Roman pope and bishop of the first see. Benedict was offering thanksgiving for his liberation, because through the intervention of Lord Odilo and the brothers he had escaped the immense abyss and flown up to heavenly blessedness.

After seeing this, the brother awoke from sleep. Retaining firmly in his memory what he had seen and heard, he related everything in order when day had dawned.

Then the holy senate rejoiced, and together with the pious Father made vows of jubilation resound to the eternal Majesty. It became evident to everyone how much the venerable Odilo could accomplish through the grace of the undivided Trinity: through him the womb of death [Col. 0929B] was able to empty the prey it had snatched away.

## CHAPTER XV — On a Certain Boy Healed of a Throat Illness

At a certain time, while the same holy man was staying at Paternacum, there was there a little monk named Rodulfus. That exceedingly dreadful illness which commonly occurs in the throat in those regions had disfigured and disgraced him so greatly, and had almost entirely closed off his voice, that in that part of the body there no longer seemed to be the appearance of a throat, but rather a kind of swelling pestilence.

The man of God took pity on so great a calamity. He called the boy to him, touched the place of the swelling with his hands, impressed upon it the sign of the cross, spoke certain healing words at the same time, and allowed him to depart.

In a marvelous manner, just as such a swelling in others, once it has afflicted them, usually grows day by day, so in this boy it began from that moment to disappear. The disfigured throat returned to its former shape, and to the present day he has enjoyed the desired health.

## CHAPTER XVI — On Books and Other Belongings Touched by Water but Not Damaged

In the Jura region, at Nantois, there is a monastery given by Count Gislebertus to the holy Father for the establishment of the order of regular life.

One day, setting out from there and traveling toward the city of Geneva, when the third hour of the day was already approaching, he crossed a river running through those mountains. A mule carrying his belongings, bearing the man of God’s bed together with his books, was crossing without a guide. It strayed from the public ford and had already begun to sink in the deep part of the river. Everyone rushed together, raising their voices and trying to help the creature that was perishing.

The animal, exerting great force, emerged from the water and reached the bank with its head extended. One of the servants ran forward and stretched out his hand to seize the halter, but in vain. The dumb animal understood nothing, turned back again, and by swimming through the deep water was driven out onto the opposite bank, giving nothing visible of itself except its head.

Then, behold, the magnanimous hero came walking across the level ground. Seeing what was happening, he uttered nothing mortal; covering his swan-like head with his cap, he advanced his step and continued the journey he had begun. [Col. 0930A]

Among the others who were being agitated by this commotion, the elder Peter was especially anxious. He had been entrusted with arranging the Father’s belongings [Note: [Col. 0929] Codex of Thuane: “He proceeded. Then Lord Peter, who was present, cried out.”]. He called out to one of the men to approach by some clever means and see whether he could somehow catch the animal.

The man did not delay. Extending his hand, he seized the halter and with strong effort pulled the mule from the water. Everyone ran together, quickly dismounted from their horses, unloaded the pack animal, and examined the Father’s belongings that had been brought out of the water—namely, his bed and books. All these things, as God and those who were present bear witness, were found so untouched by the water that not the slightest trace of moisture appeared upon them.

Everyone marveled with joy, glorified God, and raised the merits of so great a man with praises. They loaded the mule again and followed the elder with rejoicing. Lord Peter went ahead of the others and reported to the Father what had happened.

The Father, mildly indignant, said: “What are you saying? Can anything immersed in water appear not to be wet?”

When the journey was completed and the day had passed, they withdrew to the lodging of a certain little estate. Then he ordered his books and the other things that had been pulled from the water—namely, the cloths and towels—to be brought to him. These, being intended for ordinary use, were found then, as always, wet from the water and undamaged.

Then the most kindly man, praising God, began to speak to the brothers:

“O beloved brothers, do you see the marvelous kindness of our God toward us? He preserved unharmed those things which, if they had been soaked in water, we could not have recovered; but those things that could be soaked without risk of damage, he allowed to become wet.”

Thus, with faithful heart, he attributed nothing to himself but everything to God, who worked in him and through him. For his spirit was excellent and despised human things; he did not desire glory as the reward of deeds accomplished.

## CHAPTER XVII — On a Certain Little Monk Freed from a Most Serious Illness

Since we have made mention above of the monastery at Nantois, we must also relate what once happened there.

At a certain time, when the holy Father arrived there, he found a boy named Gerardus. That detestable illness of epilepsy tormented him day after day so greatly that in him there remained neither voice, nor memory, nor any function of his limbs [Col. 0930D], and he was scarcely distinguishable from a dead man.

Moved by such calamity, the man of God asked the brothers to pray to the Lord for him. He himself approached the holy altar to celebrate Mass, ordered the sick boy to be present, refreshed him with the divine mysteries, and compelled him, as was his custom, to drink sanctified water from the chalice of Saint Majolus.

Without delay, when the illness had fled, the desired health followed, and it remained whole in the aforesaid man until the present day.

## CHAPTER XVIII — On a Book and Vessels That Were Recovered

The true lover of God, Odilo, was once traveling through the Jura Alps. Suddenly a horse heavily loaded with many packages slipped and fell down the mountain slopes into the depths [Col. 0931A] of a valley among the harshest crags.

The Allobroges rushed down, striving in vain and attempting what was beyond their strength. At last, after many efforts of spirit, they found the horse unharmed, together with some of the small packages, but discovered that a book of Sacraments written in golden letters was missing, along with glass vessels fashioned in relief work.

This greatly saddened the man of God’s heart, but he continued the journey with the things they had recovered. As evening approached, they reached a certain cell subject by right to Saint Eugendus the abbot. The brothers living there received them honorably, and after showing them hospitality they rested.

Heavy rain mixed with snow was falling. The man of the Lord told the brothers what had happened to him and earnestly asked [Col. 0931B] them not to be reluctant to go and search those same places, in case they might somehow find the gilded book.

They promised with the readiest spirit to carry out his commands. Who would not yield to the prayers of so great a man, to whom even our God often seemed, so to speak, to give obedience?

When dawn appeared, he sent out the men, and the following day led them to the places [Note: [Col. 0931D] Thus the manuscript of Saint-Germain. The Thuane manuscript, almost exactly as Peter Damian has it in another Life, chapter 13, reads: “He led them to the places; they found the gilded book, which the protection of Christ had kept untouched by the storms; they found the vessels sound, which the immense kindness of our God had protected from breaking. Immediately they picked up what they had found and returned rejoicing, handing it over to the Father, whose joy may be understood by anyone who wishes from the immense praises poured out to God.” [Col. 0932D]], and they searched for the lost book and vessels. But, fatigued by their own labor, they returned home after a long time without result.

The mountains and surrounding hills were covered with such a deep mass of snow that no hope seemed to remain of recovering the aforesaid objects.

Almost two months later, when the severity of winter had vanished from the aforesaid mountains and hills, gradually uncovering their surface, and nearly all memory of the lost objects had disappeared, a certain priest named Ermendrannus happened by chance to visit the place where the aforesaid objects had been lost. He turned his eyes here and there, and, behold, against hope he found the book. The protection of Christ, through the merits of Father Odilo, had preserved it untouched by storms and the long duration of the snow.

He also found the vessels intact, which the kindness of our God had protected from being broken. Taking what he had found, he delivered it to Gauzerannus, abbot of Saint Eugendus. Later, at the abbot’s command, the aforesaid priest returned it to Father Odilo, joyful and exultant, when he was going back to that region of the Jura. Anyone who wishes to know how great was his joy may learn it from the immense praises poured out to God.

## CHAPTER XIX — On a Certain Powerful Man Freed from Eye Pain

Once, while he was passing through the district of Geneva and the castle of Albia, a certain elder named Siebodus, lord of that castle, a man of imposing stature and considerable power, approached him.

One day, while Siebodus was lying beneath a tree, a fragment of bark accidentally fell into his eye. It so disturbed and corrupted the function of that organ that it could neither be expelled nor could any remedy be found for it. Sleep had fled from his eyes, every kind of food was distasteful to him, and no possibility of recovery could be found.

The holy man learned the cause of so great a danger and, grieving for a man who was very close to him, took him aside. Over the place of pain he impressed the sign of the holy cross, with the breath of his mouth and the power of prayer, promising that when he reached his lodging he would offer a saving sacrifice for him.

Without delay, after the saint departed, sleep, long denied, compelled the aforesaid man to sleep. When he awoke, he found that the fragment of bark had been drawn from his eye together with a little down, and he felt no distress from the pain that had passed.

At once he also sought the food he had found entirely distasteful, and took it with appetite. Through a messenger he joyfully made known the cause of his deliverance to the man of God at Silvigiacum (so the text reads), where Odilo had already arrived. He gave thanks and thereafter held him in great veneration.

## CHAPTER XX — On a Cleric Healed of an Affliction of the Arm

At another time, while he was returning from Rome and was staying at the castle of Lucca [Note: [Col. 0932D] This refers to the distinguished ducal city of Lucca in Etruria, commonly called Lucques.], a mortal wound had grown on the arm of a canon of Saint Martin of Tours named Archimbaldus. It seemed to him no longer to threaten illness but almost death itself.

He therefore approached the saint and displayed the danger of his great need. But the saint, as though pretending not to see these things, secretly touched his arm with his own hand, invoked the protection of the holy cross, and impressed the sign of that same cross upon the wound. [Col. 0932C] He then dismissed him and instructed him to take careful precautions.

In a marvelous manner, when Archimbaldus departed and wished to look at or touch the place of the wound, he neither found nor felt any sign of the former pain.

Struck with astonishment at the miracle, he returned to the man of God and wished to make public what had happened to him. But when God’s servant foresaw this, he became very angry and rebuked him, saying that he had suffered nothing and did not know what he was talking about.

For Odilo feared human rumors like deadly poison, and he fled the desire for empty praise as though it were a pestilential evil.

When he was staying at a certain time in his monastery called Volta, and the wall of the church was still being completed, it happened [Col. 0932D] that one day, while the workmen were laboring to finish the work, the walkways on which they stood, their twisted fastenings having broken because of extreme age, fell downward. The masons fell with them from the height of the wall to the ground, and the collision of their limbs … [lacuna]

## CHAPTER XXI — On a Certain Man Possessed or Mentally Afflicted Who Was Healed

At another time, when we had come with him from the region beyond the Jura to Nantois, [Col. 0933A] of which we spoke above, we found there a certain young soldier named Mainerius, mentally afflicted and brought by his own servants.

He had abandoned military service and set aside every private and public concern. Miserable and naked except when he was restrained, he wandered here and there, uttering unknown sounds, remaining without food, and, as is customary with such people, having nowhere a safe dwelling or any rest.

The man of God took pity on so great a calamity and grieved for the man’s most promising youth. With the brothers he prostrated himself on the ground before the altar of Saint Peter, devoted himself to psalms, and sought the patronage of the saints with litanies.

Then he rose, approached the afflicted man, sprinkled him with sanctified water, compelled him to drink, and allowed him to depart.

After the saint departed, the man himself followed him as far as Cluny—not ill but healthy, not bound but free, not compelled but willing. He gave thanks to God and to the saint for the restoration of his health, brought gifts of fish as offerings of charity, and then returned home.

The following year Odilo sought him there again, but did not find him. On the day the saint died, the man himself arrived at Silviniacum. Sad and mourning, he attended the saint’s funeral, and, since he had been unable to do so while Odilo lived, he gave thanks again and again to the deceased for his deliverance.

## CHAPTER XXII — On a Certain Mute Who Was Healed

A certain religious abbot of the monastery of Brolio (Ebreuil), named Girbertus, had a nephew who was a vigorous soldier named Gauzfredus. For a long time Gauzfredus had lost the use of his tongue, although he retained, to no small degree, his ability to hear and the memory of the wise old man, just as is read of Zoe, the wife of Nicostratus.

He was warned in a vision to seek water with which the saint washed his hands and, by drinking it, to recover thereafter the power of speech.

He immediately summoned his household servants. As best he could and as far as he was able, he indicated with his hands what he wanted, making it known, though not without great difficulty. The aforesaid Girbertus sent him to Silviniacum, where the saint was then staying, to obtain this remedy on his behalf.

After certain servants of the man of God had been persuaded, a faithful theft was committed: water in which the saint had washed his hands was secretly taken. On the pretext of doing so, another water, marked by the man of God himself in the chalice of Saint Majolus, was added to it, and thus it was sent to the sick man.

After first changing his clothes, he entered the church and devoted himself to prayer. Then, with the greatest reverence, he took the water, and as soon as he drank it he completely recovered the function of his former voice. He spoke, and no longer indicated by hand gestures what he had seen, but related it all in order with words. With full mouth and full voice, he joyfully proclaimed his thanks to God.

## CHAPTER XXIII — On a Certain Small Vessel Emptied of Wine and Later Found Full through the Saint’s Power

Almighty God, the rewarder and glorifier of His faithful servants, who in this mortal and sorrowful life glorify Him according to their knowledge and ability, was pleased, through the merits of His faithful and beloved servant Father Odilo, who confessed and glorified Him before men in this valley of tears, to perform, among many other truly splendid deeds, a particularly delightful and wondrous work of power, here also glorifying him. The corrupt wording that follows appears to associate Brother Adraldus with several memorable signs of miracles. [Col. 0934A]

So that no one may be able to doubt this, since we have undertaken to commit it to writing for the memory of those who come after us, we have and present a truthful and faithful witness who relates it. He is so suitable to testify to it that it is clearer than daylight that the person who reports this is both a monk of this beloved Father of God and is called Adraldus by his own name, and that he alone, together with a certain layman, was at that time aware of what had happened.

At a certain time, then, the same man of the Lord, Odilo, returning from France and hastening toward Cluny, the place of all religious observance, unexpectedly and without warning arrived at a certain church called Tolonnis [Col. 0934B] (Toulon), where the aforesaid brother Adraldus was staying as its superior by reason of obedience; it belonged by right to the monastery called Golden Valley.

One of the brothers accompanying the blessed man, named Warnerius, went a short distance ahead of the Father and his companions. On arriving, he announced that Father Odilo was present.

The aforesaid Adraldus was astonished and amazed. At first he did not believe it; then he became sad and mournful, and, because he had not prepared himself for receiving the Father, he was terrified, calling himself a wretched man.

Nevertheless, strengthened in the Lord, he recovered his strength. He sent the household boys in every direction to seek what was necessary and, insofar as the shortness of time allowed, hastened to prepare whatever was suitable for receiving so great a Father.

Meanwhile, Father Odilo, beloved by God and men, arrived and was received by that same brother with great joy and cheerfulness. Adraldus affectionately and warmly kissed and embraced him, yet did not omit a humble and subdued complaint and rebuke concerning his unexpected arrival.

To this the sweetest Father began, as was his custom, to speak gently and pleasantly, both excusing himself and satisfying the brother. He said that the circumstance had arisen because of the time and place, and that he had by no means come seeking an expensive preparation.

Since that year the failure of the vineyards had made wine very costly and had denied its use to all but the wealthier, the prudent and moderate Father said that he would buy wine so as not to burden the brother. But the brother immediately objected, becoming not a little indignant:

“With what face, my lord,” he said, “could I allow you to do this in your own house?”

They then came to the meal. Food was set before the Father and all his companions in the greatest abundance and sufficient quantity, in a manner appropriate to their disciplined way of life. Wine was also brought out in a small, distinctive vessel that had been bought full.

The most discerning Father ordered that the monks be given two cups, while everyone else was to receive one. But the appointed measure was exceeded, and wine of precious price was generously served to everyone without any calculation.

After the meal had been eaten and the tables removed, thanksgiving and praise for the charitable refreshment followed from the gracious and honeyed mouth of the sweetest Father Odilo.

Night succeeded day, and Father Odilo relaxed his limbs in rest. When morning came, [Col. 0935A] Adraldus saw him on his way; but, ordered by Odilo to return, as soon as he entered his own house he summoned the steward and ordered him to examine carefully how much wine remained in the vessel and report it to him.

The servant obeyed his orders and inspected the vessel with particular care. Against expectation—and this is marvelous to relate—he found it full, though he had believed that most of it had been emptied.

Fear seized the man. For some time he turned the matter over in his thoughts in confusion, but upon returning he reported what he had found.

The matter seemed incredible to the brother when he heard it, and in reporting it the servant appeared almost deranged. The smallness of the vessel and the great number of people who had emptied it strongly suggested that very little liquid could remain in it.

Nevertheless, they went and investigated the matter through the more trustworthy testimony of their eyes, and found it to be so. [Col. 0935B]

Then astonishment mixed with fear doubled in the one who saw such things, which prompted him to say nothing before: “God is wondrous in his saints.” [Col. 0936A]

Truly wondrous, truly almighty, truly merciful is God in his saints. Establishing for himself the most august palace in their pure and sincere minds, he dwells there, reigns there, and from there arranges many great things. Through them he performs deeds altogether marvelous and not to be imitated.

Many similar things could be described from his virtues if they were recorded more carefully. Through God’s grace he accomplished much of this kind in secret, and never wished it to become public—especially among those suffering from fever, whom he always helped by the sign of the chalice of Saint Majolus. He said that such things were accomplished not by his own merits but by those of the aforesaid Father. Yet there could truly be no doubt that in such matters the disciple was a fellow worker with the master through his virtues. [Col. 0936B]

# HERE BEGINS THE THIRD BOOK

[Col. 0935]

[Col. 0935B] Thus, concerning the things he did while alive, we have said a little of much, reporting some matters that we ourselves saw and recognizing with certainty from reliable witnesses that other things were also true. Now, concerning the things that the Lord performs through him after his death, let us, with the Lord’s assent, speak of what we can, as we have learned from the testimony of truthful witnesses.

## CHAPTER I — Concerning a Certain Insane, Deaf, and Mute Girl

In an estate called Longovernis, adjoining Silviniacum at a distance of nearly four miles, there lived a pitiable mother who had a daughter afflicted by three conditions: she was insane, deaf, and mute. Three times in dreams she was admonished by a certain very beautiful and pleasant person to go to Silviniacum, to take her daughter with her, to seek the tomb of an old man—he said that he himself was that man—who had recently been buried, and, while traveling, she would see what would happen to her.

Thus admonished, as we have said, for three successive nights, she put faith in the words and began to go there with her daughter. While they were traveling, however, before they reached the appointed place, the portent of the vision began to be fulfilled. For as they passed through a certain forest quite near the aforesaid place, namely Silviniacum, the daughter, who had been deaf and mute for many years, said: “Mother, mother, from here I hear great peals of bells.” She was speaking of the bells of the monastery, which she heard. “From here I both see and hear oxen and the sound of the cymbals hanging from their necks.” When the mother heard this, she recognized the signs of the vision, led her to the tomb, offered an oblation according to her means, gave thanks, and then returned home with her daughter healed.

## CHAPTER II — Concerning a Deaf and Mute Man Who Was Liberated

Another miracle, not unlike this one, follows. From those vast Alps of inner Aquitaine, two young men came to the tomb of the man of God. One of them was deaf and mute, but had been brought by the other so that he might be healed. When they entered the tomb, the healthy one asked that water with which the blessed Father’s limbs had been washed be given to him. Having received it, he poured it into his companion’s ears and made him drink it; then both withdrew to their lodging, for it was evening.

On the following day, the man who had previously been deaf and mute returned to the tomb, hearing and speaking, with an offering in his hand. In a full voice he gave thanks for his liberation, and so returned home.

## CHAPTER III — Likewise, Concerning Another Mute Man

At the same time, a certain mute man came from the district of Bourges. As he later reported, he had completely lost the power of speech for seven years. Trusting in God’s mercy, he too approached the tomb and recovered the speech he had lost for so many years, as we have said. He told everyone what had happened to him and departed joyfully.

To establish whether what he had said was true, certain curious persons sent with him another inquisitive man, who carefully investigated the matter among neighbors and truthful witnesses. Having found that it was so, this man presented himself to us as a truthful and suitable witness to confirm it.

## CHAPTER IV — Concerning a Certain Paralytic Who Was Also Mute and Was Healed

In the district of Nevers, in the fortress of Dizet, paralytic illness had afflicted a certain man on one entire side of his body and had completely taken away his ability to speak. At the urging and with the assistance of neighbors and friends, he came to the memorial of the holy Father. He recovered the health of his limbs completely, obtained a tongue released for speaking, gave thanks to God, and so returned home. He was well known to many, who affirm in their own testimony that these things were so.

## CHAPTER V — Concerning a Mute Priest

Also from the district of Bourges, from the fortress of Briord, a certain mute priest came to the tomb of the man of God. Prostrating himself in prayer, he humbly asked that what he had lost be restored to him. But when he saw that his prayers were being delayed for a long time, he decided to return home.

When he arrived, however, he immediately merited receiving what he had sought for so long. His silence dissolved into words, and in a clear voice he recounted that he had obtained this through the power of the Lord and the intercession of Father Odilo. A certain wealthy merchant named Solomon, and many others, acknowledge by their testimony that this is true.

## CHAPTER VI — Concerning a Blind Man Who Was Given Sight

A certain old man, entirely deprived of light, had himself led by a boy to the urn of the most holy Father. Before he touched the threshold of the little door of the crypt in which the saint rests, he recovered the light he had lost. Now seeing, and moving swiftly, he went ahead of his guide; then he prostrated himself on the ground before the holy tomb, gave thanks for the light granted to him, and departed rejoicing. It was then the Saturday before Palm Sunday.

## CHAPTER VII — Likewise, Concerning a Blind Woman Who Was Healed

[Col. 0937B]

A certain blind woman was brought from the fortress of Lucius Mountain to the threshold of the holy Father. She remained there for a long time, persevering in prayer. When she saw that what she sought was being delayed for her too long, she despaired and, wishing to return home, approached the tomb once more and began tearfully to beg the saint’s permission to leave.

Amid these words and the deep sighs of her sorrowful heart, her badly closed eyes opened, light was suddenly restored to her unexpectedly, and thus she returned to the home of her relatives, seeing with her own eyes rather than through those of others.

## CHAPTER VIII — Likewise, Concerning Another Blind Man Who Was Given Sight

Another veteran, a native of the city of Tours, deprived of the light of his eyes, was admonished in a vision and resolved to visit the tomb of the holy Father, led by one of his daughters. When he arrived, he asked for and received water with which the saint’s limbs had been washed. He had it poured into his darkened eyes and prayed that his sight might be restored.

Because night was already approaching, he left there and sought lodging and food—he was poor—but found none anywhere. Thus, without food or lodging, he spent the entire night. On the following day he hurried back to the tomb and immediately recovered his sight. Rejoicing, he began to call out loudly, giving thanks to God.

The church was full of people, while priests and clerics were celebrating Mass. Everyone ran to witness such a spectacle, recognized the truth of what had happened, and all together blessed God. For so evident and manifest a miracle, they gave thanks together with the poor man.

## CHAPTER IX — Concerning a Certain Insane Man Restored to His Senses

[Col. 0937D]

In the town of Silviniacum, where the saint rests, there was a certain merchant named Rainaldus who, because of a long and very serious illness, had completely lost his memory and understanding. His brothers and relatives began to lead him to the tomb of so great a Father, but they could not persuade him either to protect himself with the sign of the holy cross or to beat his breast.

When they came to the memorial of the holy Father, they offered upon the tomb a certain gift for the sick man and promised to pay every year throughout his life the specified annual due. By this arrangement they brought home the man whom they had brought there insane and out of his mind, now sound in memory and completely healed.

## CHAPTER X — Concerning a Certain Paralytic

[Col. 0938A]

In the town of the city of Auxerre there lived a certain peasant named Rainaldus. From the loins downward he had lost all power in his limbs. Having heard of the miraculous powers taking place at the tomb of so great a Father, he had himself placed upon a cart and ordered his brothers and wife to bring him to the holy threshold.

When he arrived and approached the tomb of the holy Father, he asked to be given some of the frequently mentioned water, washed his infirm limbs, and devoutly prayed that health might be restored to him. After this, the pain gradually departed from his limbs, the desired health returned, and, increasingly trusting in God’s goodness and confident in the intercession of so great a Father, he had himself carried home.

After not many days had passed, he returned to the holy threshold—not in a vehicle, but walking on firm feet. He gave thanks for his restored health, made his vows, displayed to everyone the evidence of his healing, and so departed for home.

## CHAPTER XI — Concerning a Man with Dropsy Who Was Liberated

In the county of Flanders, in the town of the venerable Father Otmar, there lived a young cleric named Geraldus who was so afflicted by dropsy that he could take neither food nor drink without great pain. His belly had swollen so greatly that the skin stretched over it seemed almost ready to burst. He could neither stand nor sit without the greatest danger, and could scarcely walk.

And what more shall I say? He was so deprived of the functions of all his limbs that he preferred death to that most wretched life. By divine prompting he therefore came to Silviniacum with great difficulty. He asked to be brought into the tomb of the holy Father, prostrated himself on the ground in prayer, complained in a plaintive voice that he had come from far away, and tearfully begged the saint to bring help to him in his misery.

Without delay, while he prayed, he vomited from within, through his mouth, a stream of clotted blood, in the sight of everyone. Rising from there, he proclaimed by gestures and words that he would be healed. Gathering up his garment, he displayed the folds left by the skin that had previously been stretched and that, now that the swelling had subsided, remained loose and empty.

When these things had been accomplished, he returned home rejoicing.

## CHAPTER XII — Likewise, Concerning Another Man with Dropsy

Some time earlier, a certain old commoner had likewise been liberated from the same illness there.

## CHAPTER XIII — Concerning a Certain Holy Woman with Contracted Limbs Who Was Healed

[Col. 0938D]

At the extreme boundary of the territory of Autun stands the fortress of Moulins, situated on the river Allier. There a certain young woman lay beneath the solar of the most noble lady Ermengardis. For many years she had so lost the use of her limbs that she could not go anywhere unless she was carried.

Admonished in a dream to go to the memorial of the holy Father, she compelled the lady’s vicar, through excessive cries and persistent pleas, to have her placed in a vehicle and taken to Silviniacum. As soon as she arrived there, approached the saint’s tomb, and devoted herself to prayer, the functions of her limbs were restored. She who had come bent and contracted was raised upright, while all who knew her gave praise to God.

After this she began to return to the place from which she had come. But, by some hidden judgment, before she reached the far end of the village, she again became weak. Once more she was carried back to the tomb on the hands of others, and once more, through the mercy of almighty God and the intercession of Father Odilo, she was restored to her former health. Yet she did not thereafter go beyond the village, nor did she again attempt to cross the boundary of her weakness.

## CHAPTER XIV — Likewise, Concerning Another Woman Healed in a Similar Manner

A certain merchant named Rainaldus lived there at Silviniacum. He had a daughter weak in the legs, infirm, and, to complete her affliction, disabled in the upper part of her body. They carried her to the tomb of the holy Father. As soon as she had been brought there, she began to raise herself and gradually to walk. She remained there until she obtained, in full, the ability to stand and walk.

## CHAPTER XV — Concerning a Certain Poor Woman Healed in a Similar Manner

Another poor woman was also there at that time, likewise weak throughout her entire body for a long period. She too obtained the strength of complete health on that same day, in the sight of the assembled multitude.

For the feast of the holy apostles Peter and Paul had then arrived, and a crowd of many peoples had gathered there. When they saw these three miracles described above occurring at one and the same time, they were filled with overwhelming amazement.

Great joy arose, and the fame of the miracles flew through the ears of everyone. The church was filled with people of both sexes and shaken by diverse and immense shouts. The monks sang with the clerics in jubilation; the voices of the people rose to heaven, astonished and rejoicing at the miracle of so great a marvel.

Christ, ever wondrous in his saints, was proclaimed by all, and it was declared and celebrated by the mouths of everyone, through certain indications and manifest signs, how much his most faithful servant could accomplish through his grace.

## CHAPTER XVI — Concerning a Certain Captive Liberated from His Chains

A pitiable man, captured by a certain wicked person, was tightly bound in fetters. To guard him more carefully, they shut him in a chest, piled up a heap of stones above it, fastened the locks, and kept the wretched man there for a long time.

But the captive, retaining hope in God, humbly prayed to God from those hidden places of darkness—before whom obscure things are manifest—and called upon Father Odilo as his intercessor, asking that he cast him out from there and grant him permission to go free.

While he was speaking these words of his petition, he sensed and heard someone approaching the chest and calling to him to come out. Immediately, by divine power, the heap of stones was scattered here and there, the locks sprang open, and the fetters were released. Thus the imprisoned man, freed and unbound, came out of the darkness into the light. Rejoicing, he came as quickly as possible to the tomb of the holy Father and recounted to everyone, with clear proofs, what had happened to him.

## CHAPTER XVII — Concerning a Certain Man Deprived of His Mind Who Was Healed

Another man, a peasant belonging to Saint Maiolus and the monks, named Rotbertus, who had a wife and children, had been completely overcome by madness. His sons and relatives brought him by force to the memorial of the holy Father, although he resisted with all his strength. They offered an oblation for him and immediately brought him home, restored in mind and body.

[Col. 0939]

# THE LETTERS OF SAINT ODILO

## LETTER I — TO FULBERT, BISHOP OF CHARTRES

[Bibliotheca Cluniacensis, p. 349.]

[Col. 0939C]

To the lord and venerable, holy, and most beloved brother and fellow priest Fulbert, Brother Odilo sends greetings in the Lord.

Most beloved man, what does this question brought to us by one of your faithful clerics mean? He says that it pleased your fatherhood to make me, unworthy though I am, a judge of your life, by ordering me to set down in writing for you what I think of your blameless way of life, insofar as it is permissible to speak of it.

But eyes covered by the darkness of blindness cannot clearly behold the splendor of the firmament and the spheres of the stars of heaven. I call you the splendor of the firmament and the star; I shall also call you the morning star, using the testimony of the prophet Daniel: “Those who are learned,” he says, “will shine like the splendor of the firmament. And those who instruct many in righteousness, like the stars forever and ever.”

You, who are such and so great that I cannot even worthily conceive of you, are you to be judged by our judgment? We, oppressed by the darkness of ignorance and unable to recognize even ourselves, ought in no way to assess the life of the righteous according to our own discretion.

Every person rightly judges you so worthy of praise that it is more fitting to wonder at you than to say anything about you. The weight of your question would overwhelm the understanding of our smallness, were it not for the ready remembrance of the divine word.

To set an example for the faithful, the author of life and salvation, as you know better than anyone—for you are wholly evangelical—came into the region of Caesarea Philippi and asked his disciples: “Who do people say that the Son of Man is?” And a little later: “But who do you say that I am?”

He does not ask because he is ignorant of the one whom no one knows and from whom nothing is hidden, as though he himself did not know; rather, he provides the leaders of the Church with an example of asking about themselves. Therefore every superior of the Church ought to inquire of his subjects what reputation and opinion they have of him.

If he hears something good about himself, let him give thanks to God, from whom every good thing comes, and return thanks, so that, with God’s assent, he may advance successfully from virtue to virtue until he is able to see the Lord of hosts in Zion. If, however, he hears something unfavorable about himself, let him repent and thereafter strive carefully to correct it.

But if the example of teachers moves you to inquire about yourself, then we must proclaim the clarity of your wisdom, the purity of your faith, and the integrity of your diligence. Truth, indeed, is entirely incapable of silence; yet it cannot be proclaimed by a foolish and unlearned man as something pleasing to God and hated by the world.

I have spoken these things about you both now and at other times, and in ordinary conversation—not deceived by any fraudulent flattery, nor desirous of any gift, praise, or money—but because I sincerely believe them and most earnestly desire them to be true. I neither refuse nor shall refuse to say so.

But if you judge me a flatterer, hear Scripture: “My son, if sinners entice you, do not consent to them.” Yet it is not blameworthy if we praise those whom we believe worthy of praise, since Scripture says: “Let another praise you, and not your own mouth.”

If someone wishes to object with what Scripture says, “Do not praise a man during his life,” I agree, because I consider you dead with respect to mortal life, since you have heard from the Apostle: “For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.” And together with him, in words and deeds, you say: “If we live, we live to the Lord; if we die, we die to the Lord. Whether we live or whether we die, we are the Lord’s.”

For the rest, my dearest, as a certain Wise Man says: “A man can flee everything except his own heart.” No one can depart from himself. Wherever he goes, his conscience does not leave him. And the Apostle Paul says: “No one knows what belongs to a man except the spirit of the man that is in him.”

I would nevertheless say something by way of exhortation—but how should an unlearned man teach one whom spiritual anointing teaches about everything? Yet I shall keep silent about that evangelical saying: “You still lack one thing.” You know perfectly well what that is.

Farewell.

## LETTER II — TO PATERNUS, THE ABBOT

[Apud Acherium, *Spicilegii*, vol. III, p. 381.]

To the lord Paternus, fervent with the fire of divine love, prudent caretaker of Christ’s flock with paternal affection, Brother Odilo, together with Lord Bishop Santius and the entire congregation of the poor of Cluny, sends the reward of monastic labor from Christ.

If everything around you is prosperous and peaceful, we rejoice and exult, and with every good wish we pray that you may always progress from good to better.

For the condition of the kingdom, that it may be freed from the incursions of pagans and from the persecution of false Christians, we continually offer humble and persistent prayers to almighty God, with complete devotion of heart. We also beseech him through continual prayers and tireless petitions, day and night, to restore the firmest peace among the sons of the late Lord Santius, our divinely remembered king.

Above all, we pray for our most beloved Lord Redimirus, who is dear to us and bound to us by every bond of love and affection. Concerning his goodness and integrity, and the way he represents his father’s character in all things, the lord bishop—entirely faithful and devoted to him—came to us and recounted such great and remarkable things that he has bound us to his companionship and fidelity with indissoluble bonds of charity, so that his memory can never be torn from our hearts in the divine services.

For his bodily and spiritual peace and salvation, all of us recite daily after Matins the psalm: “Lord, how they are increased.” And at all the other hours: “I lift up my eyes,” asking that the Lord rescue his soul and body from every evil and guard his coming in and going out, not only in the present age but forever and ever.

We further ask that you escort these messengers whom Lord Bishop Santius and we are sending as far as Saint John. The lord bishop wishes to have with him all the things he left there.

He wants the silver, so that he may complete, as an everlasting memorial of himself and of the aforesaid deceased king, the work that we began on the altar of Saint Peter in his name and in the name of the late king. As for the ornaments consecrated for the divine services, he wishes to keep them with him for as long as he lives.

Of the gold that he brought with him when he came to us, he has already completed the two strips of the great altar table, the right and the left, which, as you know, had been destroyed. As for the lower one that remains, and concerning the cows that he has at Saint [lacuna].

## LETTER III — TO LORD GARSEA

[As above.]

[Col. 0942C]

To Lord Garsea—described in the damaged salutation as *religioni* [lacuna]—who fittingly governs royal scepters with integrity of character, Odilo, together with the flock of the poor of Cluny entrusted to him, sends peace in the Lord—firm peace with the brothers, friends, and all who are rightly subject to you—and victory with triumph over all your enemies.

We rejoice and give thanks to almighty God because we continually hear that you are growing and advancing nobly and gloriously, both in love and knowledge of him and in secular power.

We are bound to you by the indissoluble familiarity and companionship with which we were formerly joined to your father. Thus we are so devoted to your fidelity that we continually beseech God for your salvation and security, for the salvation and security of your people, and for victory over all your enemies. We ask his most merciful goodness so to arrange all your affairs according to his will that, after your present glory and happiness, he may lead you to heavenly joys.

Moreover, although not without embarrassment, we are compelled to disclose to your highness the need caused by our poverty, by which we have now been afflicted continuously for two years and more. For the general poverty of the entire kingdom, together with the calamity of famine and want, oppresses us as it does the other countrymen in our vicinity.

To enable us to escape this danger, we greatly need your assistance, if it pleases you. Our entire brotherhood both wishes and prays that the Lord grant you peace, victory, and everlasting life.

Farewell.

## LETTER IV — TO LADY R. . . .

[As above.]

[Col. 0943A]

To the most noble lady R., Brother Odilo sends faithful prayers.

I would be very surprised that you, lady, so often gladden an unknown and undeserving man with your greetings and enrich him with gifts, if I did not recognize and perceive in you that maternal goodness which has always been common and equal toward both those known and those unknown, toward the deserving and the undeserving alike.

Therefore I turn wholly not to wonder but to give thanks, namely for all the benefits that your charity has always been accustomed to bestow upon us and ours.

You have been pleased, through Brother Luitfrid, to commend yourself to the prayers of our brothers and of me. Know that in those prayers you have been received and enrolled with the greatest devotion—and not only you, but also our most beloved friend, your lord A. . . . . . . . . ., and his dearest brother E. . . . . . . . ., of whom I have always heard good things and, thanks be to God, still hear them.

I earnestly ask your charity to greet both of them most respectfully on our behalf.

Farewell; mindful of you, may you never be forgetful.

[Col. 0943]

# A BOOKLET BY SAINT ODILO, ABBOT OF CLUNY, ON THE LIFE OF THE BLESSED ABBOT MAIOLUS

(*Bibliotheca Cluniacensis*, p. 279.)

## PREFACE

[Col. 0943B]

To Hugh [Note: [Col. 0943] Hugh, who was elected abbot of Cluny after Odilo himself and was the sixth in succession.] and to my most beloved brother Almannus, Odilo the priest sends greetings in the Lord.

When I was sitting in the cloister of the Roman monastery during the past Easter season, on the day before the solemnity of our father Maiolus was to take place, one of the brothers, named John—who, in accordance with the fitting interpretation of his name, has been enriched with the gift of the Lord’s grace—began asking in which volume he ought to mark the readings for that night.

I replied to him: “It is fitting that, in memory of this father, the words of the most blessed Father Gregory should be read, since that father, while he lived, frequently and most diligently both heard and read them, and, whenever he wished, discussed them in eloquent speech.”

After the evening office had shortly afterward been completed and the time for the day’s service had been determined, both custom and necessity invited us to go to bed.

At that time I was mourning and lamenting not only the loss of my household property but also the grave danger of an unusual calamity and unheard-of misery, and, what pressed most heavily, the great and lamentable loss of the entire homeland and of all the poor.

The anxious thought of so great a danger and so great a sorrow had already kept me awake for many nights. But on that same night, when the customary gnawing thought sought to intrude itself importunately upon our minds, I began to implore the blessed Maiolus to ask the Lord for the help of consolation.

After a little while, the sweet memory of so great a father began to suggest to me, promising in a certain way, that if I would strive to occupy my mind with his praises, I could undoubtedly find the support of heavenly consolation very soon.

For this reason, most beloved lords and brothers, although not in proportion to his greatness but according to the smallness of our understanding, I took care to write the work that follows.

Whatever its quality, our brotherhood both wishes and prays that the fire of your spiritual understanding may examine, distinguish, and correct it.

## HERE BEGINS THE TEXT OF THE BOOKLET

[Col. 0943]

[Col. 0943C]

After the sacred, divine, and saving teachings of the apostles and evangelists, and after the glorious, victorious, and unconquered struggles of the blessed martyrs, divine favor, so to speak, provided its Church with new consolations in a third place: namely, lamps burning with love and shining with speech.

I mean apostolic priests and illustrious men, endowed with human learning—not vainly, but profitably—and filled with divine wisdom. Through their spiritual understanding and their most penetrating investigation of the divine Scriptures, the shadow of the Law might shine with light; the prophetic word, highest in its depth and deepest in its height, might proceed into the light when spiritually understood; and the glory, power, and majesty of the evangelical light might drive away the densest darkness of the whole world.

Through their most sincere diligence, the deeds of the apostles are explained and commended to the faithful. Through their most devoted zeal, the triumph and merit of the blessed martyrs are commended to the holy Church.

By the faith, wisdom, and persistent preaching of these men, the murmuring of those who whisper and bark against the Catholic faith is restrained and crushed; the clamor of schismatics is quieted and the mouths of those speaking vainly are closed; the power of idols is destroyed; the cruelty of the pagans is overcome; the madness of philosophers is despised, spat upon, and annulled.

The falsehood, treachery, unbelief, error, and rage of all heretics are blown away like a smoky stench and the foulest smoke, so that they can appear neither ever nor anywhere; they are dissolved, exhaled, and reduced to nothing.

After the joyful heavenly court had received such great men, its own citizens and the household servants of its King, divine governance wished, from that supreme and heavenly commonwealth, to provide for the Church’s little ones in a fourth place and in a fitting order. Thus the grace that it had deigned to provide through the exalted and strong later came to be provided through the humble, innocent, and simple.

Then the monastic order began to flourish—or, more truly, to live again. We know that it proceeded from the blessed Elijah and John the Baptist, and we rejoice that through the apostolic way of life and conduct, through the growth of the virtues, and through the spiritual exercises of the holy Fathers, it has come down to us.

Through them and from them, the perfection of that one and special evangelical—indeed, dominical—commandment was most perfectly fulfilled: the commandment that was lacking to the young man who asked the Savior about possessing eternal life, when the same Lord Christ answered him, saying:

“If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything that you have, give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; then come and follow me” (Matthew 19).

Among the most attentive hearers and vigorous executors of this saving commandment, the most blessed Father Benedict—blessed both in merit and in name—shone forth brilliantly like a certain heavenly star.

He was so great and such a man in life, conduct, and miracles that, by describing his birth, life, and death, the most holy Pope Gregory—entirely an apostolic man and bishop of the apostolic see—bore witness to him. Gregory is recognized as holding, among the foremost leaders of the Church, a distinctive and principal privilege both in life and in teaching.

In the course of time, after the departure of the most devout father mentioned above, nearly all Gaul received the beginning of that institution and religious observance through the blessed Maurus, his disciple.

[Note: [Col. 0945D] Through Blessed Maurus nearly all Gaul. Thus Peter the Venerable, *Letter 28, Book I*: “We read that Saint Maurus, the disciple of the blessed Benedict himself, was sent by him to these regions of Gaul to establish monasteries according to his teaching.” And Rodulfus Glaber, *Book III of the Histories*, chapter 5: “It is said that this institution took its beginning from the monasteries or rule of the holy Father Benedict and was brought by the blessed Maurus, his disciple, to our territory, that is, to Gaul.” Faustus, his fellow disciple under Saint Benedict and constant companion on his journey through Gaul, faithfully composed the complete history of the *Life of Saint Maurus*; it is preserved in Surius, volume I, under January 15.]

Then, through him and through those whom he instructed in righteousness, over the course of many ages the same religious observance grew toward the summit of perfection. But as they departed this life, righteousness grew scarce, wickedness increased, and discipline—the mother of all good virtues—grew lukewarm. The endeavors of the pious Fathers began to fail.

Just as the rule of holy institution had gradually received growth toward perfection through religious men filled with the fervor of the Holy Spirit, so through the negligent and sluggish it gradually fell into decline.

Thus the ruinous decline of the salutary purpose had crept in secretly until that time when, with the favor of William, the most Christian prince of Aquitaine, a blessed abbot named Berno began to build a monastery in the region of Burgundy, on the Mâconnais soil, in the district called Cluny. To the extent that he could, he labored diligently in this construction and, through arduous struggle, brought the devotion of his pious purpose to a praiseworthy completion.

Because of his merit and example, many who sought the tranquil harbor of the monastery were converted from the world. From among all these we recall one in particular—and in recalling him, we single him out—whom we have learned proved beneficial for the salvation of many.

That man was named Odo, a man praiseworthy in every respect, the most devoted and faithful servant of the blessed Martin, bishop of the Church of Tours, and a cleric and canon of that same Church [Col. 0946C].
