This honorable and humble man, thoroughly trained in regular discipline, succeeded the aforesaid father in governing the abbey after his departure from this life, being chosen by the common election of many faithful men. How he thereafter reached the summit of the virtues, the account of his labors has made known throughout the Roman world.

He was succeeded by a man of blessed memory named Haymardus, a son of blessed simplicity and innocence. He was exceedingly diligent in enlarging the estates and acquiring temporal resources, and sufficiently devoted in observance. He endured both the loss of his temporal sight and whatever adversity could befall him with the greatest patience, without any murmuring or indignation. Indeed, because of the merit of his simple patience and innocent life, this man was enriched by Christ with such and so great a gift that, in his time [Col. 0946D], he was deemed worthy to summon the blessed Maiolus, for the love of the monastic order, by the author of our salvation.

In bringing about this conversion, the sweet conversation and spiritual exhortation of the venerable man Hildebrannus were of great importance [Col. 0947A].

[Note: The venerable man Hildebrannus. There were many monks and priors, or superiors, of this name in the monastery of Cluny. John, a disciple of the second abbot Saint Odo and the writer of his Life, mentions one in these words: “Then the lord Hildebrannus, a truly truthful man and superior of the monastery of Cluny, was my teacher in the disciplines of the Rule.” There can be no doubt that this is the very man whom Saint Odilo mentions here, since he adds that he was “one of the earlier monks of Cluny and superior of that monastery, twice invited to accept the office of abbot, but unwilling to do so, because he always wished rather to obey than to command, and to be subject rather than to preside.” From Odo’s time until Maiolus, the abbey of Cluny was vacant twice: first at the death of Odo himself and then at the death of his successor Aymardus; after the latter, Maiolus, this Hildebrannus’s disciple, was finally elected. But there was also another Hildebrannus, both a monk and prior of Cluny under Abbot Saint Hugh; we shall speak of him elsewhere. For now it will suffice to add what the anonymous monk of Silviniacum says in chapter 5 of the Life of Saint Maiolus, since it seems clearly to illuminate this passage of Odilo: “Leaving behind the broad and spacious road of worldly choice,” he says, “he bound himself beneath the light yoke of Christ, and, at the admonition and exhortation of the lord Hildebrannus, the most religious father and prior of the monastery of Cluny, he sought the noble mastery of monastic discipline. Nurturing that father Maiolus with himself for many days in the service of Christ the Lord, he brought forth a perfect athlete of God.”]

Although he was one of the earlier monks of Cluny and superior of that monastery, he was twice invited to accept the office of abbot, but refused, because he always wished rather to obey than to command and to be subject rather than to preside. Perhaps someone will think that I have lost my senses because, when I was preparing to write about the blessed Maiolus, I have happened to say so much about those who came before him. But no one should think that this happened by chance; it was deliberately and carefully done. For whatever we have said above about just and holy men, we have recognized to be wholly, or at least to a great extent, reflected in the man of whom we now wish to speak.

This man was our most blessed father Maiolus, born of a distinguished lineage and nobly raised from earliest childhood by noble parents with vigilant care. [Col. 0948A] As the time of his childhood advanced, he was devoted to ecclesiastical studies, so that he might be imbued with spiritual learning. By heavenly prompting and divine providence it therefore came about that a boy of such good promise was then more closely intent upon divine works, so that he passed all the time of his adolescence without endangering his chastity; and thus it happened that throughout the whole course of his life he preserved the ornament of virginity in his body.

When he was already approaching the age of youth, he did not delay attempting higher and better things in divine studies, more demanding things in human studies, and more serious pursuits. Thus, trained in both kinds of learning, he did not fear to approach the altar at Lyon [Col. 0947C].

[Note: To approach the altar at Lyon. This altar was dedicated to the Emperor Augustus at Lyon during the consulship of Julius Antonius and Fabius Africanus, as Suetonius notes in his Life of Claudius, chapter 2. Florus also speaks of it in book III: “An altar,” he says, “was dedicated to Caesar at the confluence of the Saône and Rhône, and C. Julius Verecundatus Eubius, an Aeduan, was appointed its priest.” Strabo likewise says in book IV: “There stands an altar of extraordinary dignity, bearing an inscription of the sixty nations and a statue of each of them; another enormous altar has been placed nearby.” At this altar Caligula also held mixed contests, as the same Suetonius says in his Life of Caligula, chapter 20: “He also held a contest in Greek and Latin eloquence. In this contest, they say, the defeated were made to present prizes to the victors and to compose their praises. Those who had displeased the judges most were ordered to erase their writings with a sponge or with their tongue, unless they preferred to be beaten with rods or thrown into the nearest river.” Hence Juvenal, Satire 1:

“May he grow pale who, pressing with bare heels upon a snake,

is about to speak as an orator at the altar of Lyon.”]

Then, in that city, the nurse and mother of philosophy [Col. 0947D], which, by ancient custom and ecclesiastical law, not undeservedly retained the primacy of all Gaul [Col. 0948B], he wished to have Antony, an educated and prudent man, as his teacher in the liberal arts [Col. 0949A].

[Note: Which, by ancient custom and ecclesiastical law, retained the primacy of all Gaul. This shows that it is not so new a thing, as some assert, that the Church of Lyons is first among all the Churches of Gaul and enjoys the honor of primacy. William the Breton aptly suggests this when he says in the *Philippide*:

[Col. 0948C] “And Lyons, by whose primate all Gaul was wont,

as report has it, to be ruled.”

Likewise Frederick, emperor of the Romans, in a diploma issued in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1157: “When Heraclius, archbishop and primate of the see of Lyons, came to our court—a see which in ancient times excelled other cities, whether under the chief pagan flamines or the first teachers of the law, but now presides more widely through divine religion and imperial magnificence, and is first among all the Churches of Gaul and shines with the dignity of primacy—we received him with due honor.” Hence Peter the Venerable himself, Heraclius’s brother, writing to Peter, archbishop of Lyons, in Book II, Letter 2, calls him “placed by God upon the lofty watchtower of the Church, established among the leaders of the spiritual battle, distinguished not only by the name of bishop but also by that of primate or patriarch—indeed, superior in ecclesiastical dignity to all the Gallican Churches” [Col. 0948D].

Urban II confirmed this glory of primacy, granted to the archbishops of Lyons by favor of the Roman pontiffs, in his letter to Archbishop Hugh; in it he also ended the long-contested dispute between him and Richerius, archbishop of Sens, concerning that dignity. The letter begins: “URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HUGH, primate archbishop of Lyons, and to his successors to be canonically promoted, forever.” Near the end it says: “Accordingly, since the suffragans then present received our judgment with due humility and promised obedience, the long-standing complaint of the Church of Lyons was at last ended, with the Lord’s assent. Therefore, by this present document we confirm to your Church of Lyons primacy over four provinces” [Col. 0949C]. And shortly afterward: “The provinces which we confirm to you are Lyons, Rouen, Tours, and Sens, so that these provinces may render fitting obedience to the Church of Lyons and devoutly and humbly show the honor which the Roman pontiffs have prescribed in their own writings as due.” Paschal II likewise confirmed it in 1116, in the person of Gozeran, archbishop and primate, to whom these words occur in a diploma: “Therefore, venerable brother Gozeran, archbishop of Lyons, by the text of this present decree we confirm to your fraternity and your successors, and through you to the same Church of Lyons, primacy over the four primacies of Gaul—namely Lyons, Rouen, Tours, and Sens—as is established by our predecessors” [Col. 0950C].]

[Note: He wished to have Antony, an educated man, as his teacher. The monk of Silviniacum reports the same in the Life of this Maiolus: “Hence it came about,” he says, “that, urged on by his desire to learn letters, after hearing of a certain Antony who, devoted to the higher philosophy, directed the schools at Lyon, he turned his steps there and, assuming the role of a student, devoutly committed himself to the instruction of the master who presided over them.”]

Afterward, however, he followed far more the example of that great Antony, the sole disciple of Christ, than the studies of this Antony, a philosopher by secular profession.

[Note: In that city, the nurse and mother of philosophy. The antiquity of the schools of Lyon is sufficiently attested by what Pliny says in Letter IX: “I had not thought there were booksellers at Lyon”; and by what Ausonius writes in his address of thanks for the consulship to Gratian: “How Titianus, by alternating between the municipal school at Vesontio and that at Lyon, grew old—not indeed through age, but through lowliness.” But, so far as I know, no trace of the flourishing of philosophical study there is found anywhere, except in this statement of Saint Odilo [Col. 0948B] and in another passage of his Life of the Empress Saint Adalheidis, which reads: “Lyon rejoiced, that famous city once the mother and nurse of philosophy.” It cannot, however, be denied that at a much later time Lyon became renowned for the study of both civil and canon law, as is evident from the following words of the sentence given by the arbitrators in the monastery of Saint-Germain-des-Prés in 1290: “Likewise, when we found that there was disagreement between the aforesaid archbishop and chapter concerning the granting of permission to doctors wishing to lecture in the city of Lyon in canon or civil law, we determined the aforesaid disagreement,” and so forth.]

Thereafter, invited by the nobles and citizens of his homeland—namely, by his relatives and friends—he came from the aforesaid city to the city of Mâcon. Since he was a religious man, he remained among them for a little while in a religious manner. His praiseworthy life and admirable zeal could not remain hidden from the bishop of that city [Col. 0950D].

[Note: The bishop of the city of Mâcon. Perhaps Naimbodus, who held the see from 941 until 962 and was present at the testament of a certain prince named Sebo. In that document, recognizing that he had unjustly retained the priory, or little abbey, of Carilocus, which had been entrusted to Saint Odo, abbot of Cluny, “he restored it to the venerable abbot D. Aymardus of the monastery of Cluny for the remedy of his soul,” around the year 942.]

He was humbly invited by that bishop, with the advice of the clergy and citizens, not to disdain administering the office of archdeacon in that same Church. Since he was endowed with the grace of humility, he did not delay obeying what he recognized had been divinely commanded to him through the ministry of the bishop. As later became fully evident, the entire undertaking was directed toward an increase of greater usefulness.

After he had undertaken an office of such dignity, he conducted himself in a manner pleasing to God and to the world—not to the world lying in wickedness, but to the world reconciled to God the Father through the blood of Christ. The aforesaid city has a nearby monastery which many regard as most suitably adorned with spiritual studies. The senior already mentioned was frequently summoned there by the father of the monastery and the brothers, with whom he often conversed and shared spiritual fellowship.

Finally, amid these sweetest conversations and the mutual services of the most sincere charity, the brothers of the aforesaid monastery, seeing with the inward gaze of their mind his angelic face and hearing with the hearing of their heart his honeyed eloquence, desired to acquire him as their brother—one whom they later deserved to have as their father. The entire flock of the Lord was intent upon this, but that elder Hildebrannus, whom we mentioned above, labored most ardently to bring it about.

The grace of the Lord was already producing in him contempt for the world, in accordance with the desire and vow of the brothers of the aforesaid monastery. What more need be said? Having laid aside his ecclesiastical office, despised the pride of worldly nobility, and abandoned the companionship of secular associates, friends, and relatives, so that he might freely serve Christ, the true King, he submitted himself entirely to heavenly instruction.

Not long afterward, on the appointed day and at the agreed time, he came to the monastery. He was received with the greatest courtesy, introduced according to the Rule, and, as was customary, treated honorably and charitably. Our speech cannot fully express how great the brothers’ joy was at his arrival, how immense their gladness, how extraordinary their exultation.

From then on, he possessed a ready will for despising the world, the firmest charity for loving God, affectionate brotherhood in his love of neighbor, no difficulty in learning the order of regular observance, and celebrated eagerness in displaying obedience not only to the abbot but also to the brothers. In giving an example to all, pure simplicity reigned in him.

What his conduct among the brothers was at the beginning of his religious life became evident from their affection at the time of his most famous election. It was no longer necessary for anyone to instruct him in regular observance, since, as the holy Evangelist says, the anointing of heavenly grace taught him about everything (I John II).

Meanwhile, his life and teaching began to shine so perfectly that in the house of God he deserved to hold the first and foremost place in the praise of all the faithful. For it pleased the Divinity that he should ascend through the various stages of humility to the summit of monastic perfection, so that he no longer appeared to be merely one among others, but outstanding among and above them all.

In the sixth year, as the story goes, of his conversion from the world, the aforesaid abbot of blessed memory—namely, the lord and pious father Haymardus, whose monk the blessed Maiolus was, and whose admonitions and commands he always obeyed with the whole intention of his mind and the full capacity of his body, and had resolved always to obey—began to be entirely deprived of bodily health [interea], and, what was more grievous to him, although he bore it patiently, of his temporal sight.

When he already foresaw that he was turning toward sunset and recognized that he could not long continue to care for so great a monastery and so many spiritual sheep, he began to discuss spiritually with the spiritual and religious brothers the ordering of the monastery and the election of his successor, and to arrange it patiently and with tranquillity of mind.

An inquiry was made of everyone, and the election came to the man toward whom all the brothers’ wishes were directed—namely, the lord Maiolus [Col. 0951A]. Concerning the matter of this election, I am not capable of speaking in proportion to its greatness. But, to use the briefest possible expression, neither there nor anywhere else could a better man than the blessed Maiolus be found for that office, nor can one be found.

What more need be said? The chosen man was summoned; when invited, he resisted; when entreated, he objected; when adjured, he trembled; when forbidden to refuse, he remained silent. Therefore we give thanks to God, because the decree of resistance was overcome by the praiseworthy lesson of obedience.

Finally, he was elected by the brothers, acclaimed by the people, blessed by the bishops, and placed with great ceremony in the elevated position by the aforesaid father of the monastery. He was greeted with the greatest courtesy by the brothers and honored and revered by everyone as lord and abbot [Col. 0951D].

[Note: And honored by everyone as lord and abbot. This is taken from the Rule of Saint Benedict, where, in chapter 53, we read: “The abbot, because he is believed to act in the place of Christ, is to be called lord and abbot—not because he assumes it himself, but out of honor and love for Christ.” What we shall note is to be applied to the letters of Peter the Venerable.]

And he was not honored and revered only by his own people, but by all who were able to see and know him; beyond all the men of his time, he was held in every honor and veneration.

Let the statements of our forebears, expressed in distinguished language, suffice concerning his birth and life, his conduct, miracles, and death. Those who were able to speak of great things in the greatest manner magnificently described his most illustrious deeds and the merits bestowed upon him by the Lord.

I, however, the least servant of that servant, have dared, in no other manner than that in which those men themselves spoke, to note down in a poor style and in the briefest divisions, chapter by chapter and in some fashion, what they said, following Alcuin [Col. 0951D], the teacher of the Emperor Charles the Great—thus unequal to him as a sinner to the just, unlearned to the learned, and unable to speak to the most eloquent.

[Note: Following Alcuin, a pious and learned man, English by birth, the unique glory of the city of York, commonly believed to have been the first founder of the University of Paris, and abbot of Saint Martin of Tours. We shall soon publish all his writings, partly from older editions and partly from manuscript codices not yet printed, if God permits.]

That man, Alcuin, sent to us and to those like us the Life of the most exalted and incomparable man, the most holy priest Martin, written by Sulpicius Severus in the loftiest style and expanded with fuller expressions. Just as no one after the Apostles is equal to the blessed Martin, so I openly acknowledge myself greatly inferior to Alcuin.

He, being a great man, spoke great things about a great man; I, being small, shall speak small things about a great man. He spoke of his Martin as of a supreme priest and incomparable man; I shall speak of Maiolus as of a most pious father and most holy abbot, an outstanding and truly Catholic man.

This man, then, was born of the most distinguished ancestry and shone with a double nobility from both parents. He was sent forth, for the illumination of many, by the eternal Light of lights itself, like a brilliant star destined to rise over the human race [Col. 0951D]. Noble as he was, he had been nobly raised and carefully educated.

And, so that we may ascend from lower things to higher ones, the man already mentioned—often to be mentioned and often to be recalled—was grave in his bearing, lofty in speech, eloquent in expression, pleasant in appearance, angelic in countenance, serene in his aspect, and in every movement, gesture, and bodily action he displayed dignity. With the fitting arrangement of all his limbs, he was most becomingly adorned and seemed to me the most beautiful of all mortals [Col. 0952A].

He was firm in faith, confident in hope, filled with a double charity, distinguished in wisdom, wondrous in understanding, prudent in counsel, strong in courage, a tireless cultivator of spiritual knowledge, and a true lover of charitable devotion. The spirit of the fear of the Lord filled him—this fear which, as the prophet David testifies, is recognized as the beginning of wisdom (Psalm CX), namely, that wisdom whose radiance suffused the blessed Maiolus and enabled him to receive the gift of heavenly blessedness.

Enkindled by the light of this gift, our Maiolus wished to become poor with the poor in spirit, so that he might deserve to be enriched by the King of heaven with the heavenly kingdom. With the blessed meek he strove to become meek, so that with them he might possess the land of the living.

With the blessed who mourn, he desired to lament the negligence of his children and the dangers of the whole world, so that with all his own he might reach eternal consolation. With those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, he strove to join himself to that same righteousness by hungering and thirsting for it, and with them to feast at the heavenly banquet and always be satisfied with spiritual delights.

He strove to be merciful to the wretched, so that with the blessed merciful he might obtain mercy from the Lord. As a man continually intent upon heavenly desire, by just merits and constant prayer he deserved to attain divine contemplation, so that with the pure in heart he might become worthy of the vision of the Lord.

And, so that he might most truly deserve to be called and to be a son of God, he learned perfectly to be a peacemaker—not merely to possess his own soul through patience, but also, as far as he could, to recall all those who were at odds with one another to concord and peace.

For the sake of righteousness, he patiently learned to endure persecutions and sufferings from the ancient enemy and wicked men, so that, blessed among those who suffer for righteousness and are poor in spirit, he might be joined to them in receiving and possessing the kingdom of heaven (Matthew V, 3–11).

Adorned with the three virtues mentioned above and surrounded on every side by the eight blessings of the Gospel, the most blessed father Maiolus also strove with fervent desire to acquire the four cardinal disciplines and to live out what he had acquired through just works.

Through prudence, he would provide for his own salvation and that of those entrusted to him in the future; through temperance, also called moderation, he would arrange the spiritual tasks entrusted to him with the moderation of just discretion; through fortitude, he would be able to resist the devil and his vices and, by resisting him and fighting lawfully, overcome the author of evil manfully; through justice, which is diffused through every kind of virtue and seems to be the seasoning of those same virtues, by living soberly, piously, and justly (Titus II), fighting the good fight, finishing the course, and keeping the faith, he would deserve to receive from the one who is the giver and author of all virtues the crown of righteousness laid up for him (II Timothy IV)—the blessed God before and above all things, forever.

The abundance and gracious kindness of whose blessing granted us the gift of enjoying such a great and eminent shepherd. In him we have an example to follow, and in him a pattern has been set before us according to which we may be formed, just as Blessed Gregory says concerning our head, Jesus Christ our Lord. In the propagation of that body, the blessed Maiolus deserved to occupy, as it were, the place of a most healthy member.

When someone hears the foregoing statements concerning the life and virtues of his soul, he may perhaps wish to inquire about visible miracles and bodily signs, by which the faith of those who are accustomed to doubt the merits and rewards of the elect is supported and strengthened. To them we should respond in the words of Blessed Gregory: “Faith has no merit where human reason supplies proof.”

And lest anyone doubt his sanctity and glory, let him learn from those who knew him by sight and hearing how he lived, how he taught, and how, full of days and adorned with virtues, he departed from this light. When he has learned from the testimony of the faithful that he lived holily and taught rightly, let him believe without doubt that, with Christ as his guide, he reached the glory of all the saints.

How many miracles the Lord deigned to display through him, both before and after his departure, is attested by volumes composed by highly learned men, written with Catholic understanding and rhetorical pen, and in certain places varied in dactylic meter [Col. 0953C]. Since almighty God allows no time to pass without a testimony to his kindness, he frequently renews examples of holiness in order to correct the negligence of our weakness. This, too, has happened in our own time, and more frequently than usual.

Among all those bearing the title of holiness who shone forth in our times, the blessed Maiolus appeared preeminent. Concerning his honorable conduct and the virtues of his honorable life, we shall say a little for the present. To confess the truth, he was useful in everything and praiseworthy in every respect.

There was dignity in his actions, sobriety in his habits, humility in prosperity [Col. 0954A], and patience in adversity. He was approachable to the gentle, terrifying to the proud, sparing when he ought to be, and generous when it was fitting. He was not peculiar in dress, nor confused in conduct. As far as human beings are concerned, he was always one and the same.

He strove to be a devoted imitator of the saints and an attentive hearer of them above all, submitting himself to their service and discipline in order to obey and serve. That sevenfold chain which the Apostle Peter arranged with brilliant order in a threefold and fourfold number, he did not merely hear with a deaf ear and learn by listening; he also taught it thoroughly with tongue and hand, supplying virtue in faith, knowledge in virtue, self-restraint in knowledge, patience in self-restraint, godliness in patience, brotherly affection in godliness, and charity in brotherly affection (II Peter I).

He preferred the praiseworthy lesson of apostolic simplicity to dialectical syllogisms, rhetorical arguments, and all the devices of all philosophers, saying with Paul: “I have learned to be self-sufficient in whatever circumstances I am. I know how to be humbled, and I know how to abound. In every situation and in all things I have been instructed both to be filled and to hunger, both to abound and to suffer want. I can do all things through him who strengthens me” (Philippians IV).

Thoroughly instructed by the wisdom of such teachers and divine philosophers, and illumined by the teachings and virtues of the entire ecclesiastical discipline, he became, as the ecclesiastical text says of Moses, “beloved by God and by human beings, and therefore his memory is in blessing” (Ecclesiasticus XLV).

Father Maiolus truly was beloved by God and by human beings, because through the love of God and neighbor which he held firmly he pleased God and human beings. He strove to please human beings in such a way that he would not displease God, and to please God in such a way that he would benefit human beings.

He pleased God by living well and teaching rightly. He pleased human beings by displaying spiritual and temporal benefits to them as far as he was able. Truly, we recognize that his memory exists in blessing when we recall and still clearly see that through him and through those whom he begot in Christ the buildings of the heavenly structure have grown, have increased, and continue to grow.

And, if I may speak with due regard for the spiritual craftsmen laboring in that same structure, one man shone forth above all: he recently departed from human affairs and labored more than all of us—namely, the lord and abbot Willelmus [Col. 0955A]. Our insignificance is not sufficient to report fully what it knows of his illustrious deeds, praiseworthy life, and admirable conduct.

[Note: The lord and abbot Willelmus, who, at Maiolus’s command, reformed the monastery of Saint Benignus at Dijon and was appointed its abbot and rector. This is shown by the Chronicle of that monastery in these words: “When the lord Bishop Bruno saw that the condition of the place was uncertain, he humbly approached D. Maiolus, abbot of the monastery of Cluny, and earnestly begged him that, with his help, he might restore both its interior religious life and its exterior possessions to a better condition. Moved by his prayers, the venerable Abbot Maiolus gave him twelve monks, chosen from the entire congregation, instructed in the discipline of holy religion, learned in divine and human wisdom, and distinguished by noble birth. He placed over them as abbot a man named Willelmus, and appointed him spiritual father to the sons who requested one. This man was born in Italy, of a sufficiently elevated origin and noble lineage. The aforesaid D. Maiolus, when he came to Rome, found him in the monastery called Lanciacum, where he had been educated from childhood; and, taking him with him at his request, brought him to Cluny in the flower of youthful age. He was ordained abbot by Bishop D. Bruno in the year of the Lord 990. After accepting the office of abbot, he began to exercise himself in divine virtues. He was chaste in body, devoted in mind, approachable in speech, endowed with prudence, distinguished by temperance, firm in inward strength, steadfast in the judgment of justice, constant in long-suffering, strong in patience, gentle in humility, and full of the grace of good works,” and so forth.

“Having heard of his reputation for religion,” the same Chronicle says, “Henry, duke of Burgundy, entrusted to him the abbey of Vézelay, which had been reduced almost to nothing, so that he might restore it to its former condition; and he did so with God’s help. The lord Bishop Bruno also entrusted all the monasteries in his diocese to his care: namely, the abbey of Beze, dedicated in honor of the apostles Peter and Paul; the monastery of Saint John called Réomans; the site of Saint Michael the Archangel near the castle of Talmay; and the abbey of Molesme, where Saint Valerius, archdeacon and martyr, rests.”

Asson calls him “most devoted to God” in book II of the History of Abbot Berchorius, where he also says that “with the assistance of Bruno, bishop of Langres, he renewed the Church of Saint Benignus at Dijon with remarkable workmanship, both in its religious life and in its walls.”

Glaber Rodulfus also highly praises his zeal in either reforming monasteries or founding them anew, in book III, chapter 5, of the History of the Franks: “At that time,” he says, “the venerable abbot Willermus became distinguished in improving the aforesaid houses of God, having first been appointed by the blessed Maiolus father of the Church of the holy martyr Benignus.” A little later he adds: “The aforesaid Willermus was sharp in intellect and remarkable in prudence; for this reason he held the highest position in the palaces of kings and other princes. Whenever any monastery was deprived of its own shepherd, he was immediately compelled by kings or counts as well as by bishops to undertake its governance for the sake of improving it, since the monasteries entrusted to his protection were seen to surpass all others in wealth and holiness.”]

How clearly the memory of the most blessed Maiolus and his disciples exists in blessing may be answered by the monasteries built by them—some constructed from their foundations, others restored from corruption to a better condition through an increase of virtues.

How greatly this man of whom we speak pleased God, the Lord deigned to demonstrate openly to human beings through the signs and miracles which he worked through Maiolus’s merits. For, as the most trustworthy report attests, many faithful people afflicted with various illnesses, even those who had despaired of life, were visited by him and restored by the Lord’s grace to their former health.

Many, after the darkness had been removed from their eyes, began through his merit to see more clearly [Col. 0955B]. Many afflicted by fevers of various kinds were freed through his prayers by the Lord’s gracious aid. Many, as is reported, were granted a saving remedy from the venom of serpents, the bites of wolves and dogs, and the attack and deception of demons through the sign of the Lord’s cross traced by his right hand.

Many in dangers upon rivers, from blows of lightning, and from other troubles were delivered through his intercession. At times candles that had been extinguished at night before his bed, either through the negligence of the chamberlain or because of some unforeseen event, were, as those who were present testified, restored by divine power to light.

When he was once in the monastery of the most holy martyr Dionysius, reading at night—as was his custom—the book *On the Celestial Hierarchy* by that same martyr, an admirable philosopher in both language and condition, a heavy sleep came upon him, and the candle fell from his hand onto the page of the book. Then something marvelous and unusual occurred. The fire, carrying out its natural function, consumed the wood [or: flax] and the wax, but left the page unharmed.

Even if he did not raise the bodies of the dead, the Lord performed through him other miracles that were more important and more glorious. If the soul is more than the body (Matthew 6), much greater and more excellent is the restoration of souls to eternal life than the resurrection of bodies returning to the hardships and dangers of this life. How many he raised from the death of the soul and the abyss of vices, and led by his example into the paths of life, their number—known to God alone—does not permit us to count.

Through these and similar virtues he became illustrious before God and beloved among human beings. Many Catholic and honorable clerics, religious monks, and venerable abbots revered him as a most holy Father. Holy and learned bishops treated him as a dearest brother. Emperors and empresses, kings, and princes of the world called him elder and lord. He was honored by the pontiffs of the Apostolic See, and in truth he was at that time the leader of monastic religion.

The lord Caesar, Otto the Great, loved him with all his heart. His wife, the divine Adelaida, Augusta Empress, loved him with the most sincere charity and most devoted affection.

[Note: “The divine Adelaida, Augusta Empress.” Saint Odilo himself wrote her *Life*, and several letters of Gerbert—later Roman pontiff, called Sylvester II—addressed to her are also extant.]

Their son, the Emperor Otto, loved him with humble devotion, affection, and a like purpose; so did Chuonradus, brother of the aforementioned empress, a noble and peaceable man, and his most noble wife Mathildis. The more frequently they saw his face, the more deeply they grew in love for him.

What shall I say of the most noble Henry, duke of the Burgundians? What of Lambert, a most illustrious man and most noble count? What of William? What of Richard, the bravest dukes of Aquitaine and Normandy? What of the Italian princes and marquises?

[Note: “What of William, duke of the Aquitanians.” He was the son of Eblo, count of the Auvergnats and Poitevins, who was surnamed Caputstupae, as Ademar teaches in his *History of Aquitaine*: “His son Eblo, sprung from Ranulf, was advanced as count simultaneously among the Auvergnats and Poitevins; and, having taken Adela, daughter of Rosius of Rouen, in marriage, he fathered William Caputstupae by her.” And later: “William Caputstupae, son of Eblo Ranulf, count of Poitiers, advanced as count of the Auvergnats, Vellay, Limousin, and Poitiers, became duke of Aquitaine.”]

[Note: “What of Richard, Norman.” This Richard was Richard I by name, son of Duke William; he too left a son, also called Richard, heir to his duchy.]

How much William, governor of Provence, honored him, his life and death demonstrate.

[Note: “William, governor of Provence.” He had Bosso, the first count of Provence, as his father, and was himself the father of Constance, wife of Robert, king of the Franks. He was undoubtedly that William whom the *History of the Counts of Anjou* calls count of Arles in these words: “The aforesaid King Robert took as wife the niece of the aforesaid Fulk,” count of Anjou, “a renowned queen named Constance, daughter of William, count of Arles, born of his sister Blanca; by her he had four sons and two daughters.” Hence it is clear that those are mistaken who make Blanca, the mother of Queen Constance and wife of this William, the sister of Godfrey surnamed Grizaetunica, grandfather of Fulk.]

Through William’s merit and faithful service he was also deemed worthy to receive the habit of blessed Benedict.

Archeanbaldus too, administrator of the place of Silviniacum, most faithful, most distinguished among his own people, and a father to the neighboring country and a most vigorous protector of the poor, showed how greatly and in what manner he was devoted to blessed Maiolus. The aforesaid place proclaims this in many ways: before and after Maiolus’s death, Archeanbaldus continually adorned and ennobled it with buildings, wealth, and various kinds of ornament, so that it would have been fitting had such a thing been done by one of the kings.

[Note: “Archeanbaldus.” He was called of Bourbon and was the offspring of that great Count Archimbaldus who lived under Clotaire I, king of the Franks, as some assert.]

[Note: “Administrator of the place of Silviniacum.” Perhaps rather the son of its founder. The Archeanbaldi are said to have been the first benefactors of the monastery of Silviniacum. Pope Urban II testifies to this in a letter given to the monks of Silviniacum in 1097, in which, among other things, he writes: “For this reason, we also caused the distinguished knight Archimbaldus, under the pledge of his own hand, to promise into our hand, over the tomb of his parent, that he would preserve intact throughout his life everything that his father or grandfather had bestowed upon your place, both in possessions and in immunities and customary rights.” This is also clearly confirmed by a public document concerning the joyful arrival of Charles of Bourbon, count of Auvergne, drawn up in 1434, where his ancestors, namely Archimbaldus, lord of Bourbon, are called “founders and protectors of the monastery of Silviniacum.” But when and which of those ancient Archeanbaldi first built and endowed this monastery is by no means certain, since, when Silviniacum was destroyed in the time of Stephen, abbot of Cluny, most of the monastery’s charters perished, as Pontius, bishop of Clermont, teaches in a diploma beginning as follows: “In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, in the year 1173 from the Lord’s incarnation. I, Pontius, by the grace of God bishop of Auvergne, taking pity on the desolation and destruction of the monastery of Silviniacum, solely out of divine regard for the good of peace and stability, and also by mandate and consent of Stephen, abbot of Cluny, and of the whole chapter, and afterward confirmed by that abbot in the presence of Lord Louis, king of the Franks, undertook the burden and labor of restoring the monastery, which had long been weighed down by great debts. For this reason, when we came to Cluny, we carefully heard, in our presence, the monks and townsmen who disagreed concerning the customs of the town and monastery,” and so forth.]

But the one who now survives, heir to his honor and name, treats that place well and inflicts no harm upon its inhabitants.

So greatly was blessed Maiolus magnified and glorified, by the grace of the Lord going before him, in the sight of kings and princes and before all the people, that we may undoubtedly say of him what the scriptural discourse says of Moses, God’s servant: “He glorified him in the sight of kings and showed him his glory” (Ecclesiasticus 45).

Hugh, king of the Franks, whenever he saw him, received him with humble devotion and treated him with great honor. At the time of his calling, he asked him to come to him, intending that the monastery of Saint Dionysius might be better ordered through his counsel and assistance than it then was.

[Note: “Hugh, king of the Franks, asked that the monastery of Saint Dionysius might be better ordered through his counsel.” King Hugh did indeed make the request, but death overtook Abbot Maiolus, and he left its fulfillment to his successor, as is clear from Ademar’s words: “The monastery of blessed Dionysius, which had already corrupted its former monastic rule, King Hugh restored more honorably according to regular propriety, as was right in the churches of the Lord, through the hand of the venerable Abbot Odilo; and he restored several other monasteries of the saints to the beauty of their former discipline.”]

Knowing the Lord’s saying, “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Matthew 22), and the Apostle’s command, “Fear God, honor the king” (1 Peter 2), he gladly undertook the journey for that task and reached the place of Silviniacum.

[Note: “He reached the place of Silviniacum.” All who have written about Maiolus’s death report that he died at Silviniacum and that innumerable miracles occurred at his tomb. Because of the glorious presence of his body, Roman pontiffs fortified that place with the special protection of the Apostolic See, and the kings of the Franks likewise honored it by granting the special right of striking coins. Through the kindness of Lord Savaron, president of Auvergne, we saw some of the bronze coins bearing the inscription and image of Saint Maiolus, impressed in the following manner. We also saw smaller ones with the same inscription, but with a different representation and position of the pastoral staff. Their value, if anyone wishes to know it, is recorded as follows in the registers of the General Mint of Paris:

“The coinage of Sauigny, belonging to Monsieur Louis of Clermont and to the Prior of Sauigny, must be of three deniers and sixteen grains of the king’s silver standard, and of nineteen sous and six deniers in weight to the Paris mark. Likewise, the small coins of the said coinage must be of three deniers of the king’s silver standard and of sixteen sous and six deniers’ weight of double small coins to the Paris mark. They may produce no more than a tenth in small coins—that is, nine livres of deniers and one hundred livres of double small coins—and the deniers and the small coins mentioned above shall be worth, one among the other, in small tournois and half-tournois, twenty deniers less per livre than the small tournois. That is to say, the seven deniers of the said coinage shall be worth only twelve small tournois. Monsieur Louis of Clermont and the Prior of Sauigny must make the die of their coinage with two crosses and two piles.”]

There, when the Lord called him, full of days and holiness, he died from this life on the fifth day before the Ides of May, at dawn on Friday, after the celebration of that most sacred solemnity on which Christ Jesus our Lord, having subdued the prince of death, ascended to the right hand of the Father and showed his faithful Maiolus the path by which he too would ascend after him.

After his death, the aforementioned King Hugh honored his funeral and tomb by his personal arrival and royal gifts. At that tomb, where, by the Lord’s grace, many miracles have been performed and continue to be performed, innumerable benefits have been granted and continue to be granted to countless people. The number and greatness of these things exceed the capacity of our memory to relate them all in order.

But to use the briefest conclusion: at the tomb of this most holy man of whom we speak, whose life and merits we strive to commend to the charity of the faithful, many who were afflicted by any illness have been and are being healed by the grace and mercy of Christ. There the paralyzed are raised up and the lame walk; there those suffering from fevers and the blind are healed; there those possessed by demons are cleansed; and those terribly and miserably burned by some kind of fire unknown to us are set free.

[Note: “Those terribly burned by a kind of fire unknown to us are set free.” Glaber reports the same thing in Book II, chapter 7. Since his words seem in some way to explain this passage, it will not be burdensome to transcribe them here:

“Among the bishops in Gaul who had withdrawn from the world in greater holiness was the blessed Maiolus of revered memory, who reached the end of the present life at the monastery of Silviniacum. The nobility of his life is also commended by his precious death. For, when the fame of his holiness spread, very many men and women of both orders flocked from the whole Roman world, and from there carried away thanksgiving for the restoration of various illnesses. At that same time a most grievous plague raged among human beings, namely an occult fire which, having seized whatever limb it touched, consumed it and severed it from the body. Many were even consumed by the burning of this fire within the space of a single night. But although remedies for this dreadful pestilence were found at many memorials of the saints, an especially great concourse gathered at the churches of three holy confessors: Martin of Tours, Odolric of Bavaria, and this venerable father Maiolus; and the remedies of the desired health were found.”]

And whoever comes there devoutly and faithfully seeks help in whatever need returns home safe and joyful, having obtained what he prayed for, through our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns, God in the unity of the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

When I wished to bring this account to an end—an account in which, with faithful boldness and humble presumption, I have attempted to say something about the life and character of blessed Maiolus—a memorable prophecy came to mind. I had heard from the report of certain faithful people that something of this kind had happened to his father. Some say that the father himself was accustomed frequently to relate it in a pleasant manner.

But I feared inserting it into this work, lest it seem incredible to someone. After I began to recall certain events that occurred in his time and that clearly supported the prophecy, I resolved without hesitation to say something about it. Yet the novelty of the unusual matter resisted my beginning, because I feared that, on account of its greatness, I might be unable to complete it.

As I considered these things, my own thought said to me: “Who could so aptly relate how a good man’s ingenuity deceived the wolf’s most savage rage, as the man who wrote the *Life of Blessed Jerome*, interpreter of the divine law and a most learned, highly educated, and Catholic man, related the gentleness and obedience of a lion?”

As the time approached when an immense and most savage multitude of Saracens, boiling forth from the borders of Spain, came by sea as far as the territories of Italy and Provence, and in both kingdoms slaughtered people of every order, sex, and age; then, destroying monasteries and laying waste cities, villages, and estates, advanced swiftly through the Julian Alps as far as the ridges of the Pennine Alps; there, loosening the reins of their impiety, they afflicted Christian peoples for a long period with various attacks and calamities—killing some, taking others captive, stripping others of all their possessions—and thus fulfilled the desires of their impiety through tyrannical violence.

Among the other evils committed by that most wicked people, they seized the most blessed Father Maiolus, returning from the threshold of the Apostles, by fraud and ambush; stripped him of all his possessions, bound him in chains, and afflicted him with hunger and thirst. But he was eventually freed by divine intervention and, after being ransomed with money from his monastery, escaped from their hands unharmed under the Lord’s protection. His unjust capture became the occasion of their expulsion and perpetual destruction.

Just as, after Christ’s Passion, the Jews were driven into exile from their own land, so, after the capture of his servant and most faithful servant Maiolus, the Saracens were expelled from the borders of the Christians. And just as through Titus and Vespasian, princes of the Romans, the Lord exercised vengeance upon the Jews, so through William, a most illustrious man [Note: “Through William, a most illustrious man.” The count of Arles or Provence, mentioned above] and a most Christian prince, he removed the yoke of the Saracens from the shoulders of the Christians. He also wrested from their tyrannical rule, by powerful valor, extensive lands that they had unjustly possessed.

But after saying these things, we must return to our subject.

What is the subject we proposed? A certain memorable prophecy corresponding to the events that occurred in the time of blessed Maiolus.

What were those events? The unexpected arrival of the Saracens; the affliction of the Christians; the destruction of monasteries and cities; the capture, ransom, and liberation of blessed Maiolus; and, with Christ’s help, the expulsion of that same fierce nation from the borders of the Christians.

What, or what kind, was that memorable prophecy? Before the most savage Saracen invasion, there had occurred an unheard-of fury of wolves, especially in those regions where, after crossing the sea, the full force of the Saracens raged.

We have described, according to our ability, how the multitude of the faithful was freed from the persecution of the Saracens. Let us now describe, as best we can, by what means the country was freed from the infestation of wolves.

At that time there was a certain soldier in those regions named Folcherius, vigorous in arms, exceedingly wealthy by hereditary right and through other possessions and riches, and—as we said of his most noble offspring—shining with a double nobility from both parents. He was a man of great counsel and prudent, shrewd intelligence, namely the father of this most holy Father of ours, Maiolus, of whom we speak.

[Note: “A soldier named Folcherius.” He was the father of Maiolus. The anonymous author calls him Fulcherius, changing a single letter, in these words: “Blessed Maiolus, born in the region now called Provence, a fosterling of the townsmen of Avignon, distinguished by Gallic nobility, born of Fulcherius, shone forth as the nobler offspring of a noble lineage.”]

In his territory and neighborhood the aforementioned rage of wolves had grown especially fierce. Among these wolves, one appeared stronger in body than the others, swifter in running, more savage in tearing apart, and more voracious in devouring, to such an extent that through its appetite it swallowed whole the limbs of human bodies.

Then that man, hearing and seeing such a plague and such a calamity increasing daily, began to consider within himself, and to think most intensely, not only of his own need but also of that of others: how he might free himself and his fellow citizens from so great and terrible a danger.

At last, warned by divine prompting and strengthened by heavenly counsel, he ordered hedges to be raised and enclosures constructed, and rams, sheep, and lambs to be brought into them—something no one at that time dared to do because of the wolves’ fury. Then, dressed in military armor, namely a coat of mail and helmet, and covered completely above with sheep skins, he began at night to sit beside the sheepfolds.

One night there was an attack of wolves upon those same sheepfolds. By God’s will it happened that the wolf which was the fiercest sprang upon the man who was waiting for it. It leapt upon his back, placed both feet upon his shoulders, and began to search all around for the easiest way to kill the ram, which was not there.

It found his throat and neck protected by mail, his head covered by a helmet, and his body enclosed by the protection of armor; it could harm him nowhere. The man immediately extended both hands, seized both of the wolf’s feet, and, strong as he was, firmly clasped the wolf’s limbs with his own. He then returned swiftly to his companions, who had been waiting a long time and were uncertain how the contest would end, and presented to their eyes the great wolf as a great prize.

It was kept alive until the following day and displayed to the people whom it had always afflicted. It was killed and cut open, and whole human limbs were found among its entrails. The dead wolf was hung from a trunk, and, when one had been killed, all the others fled from those regions.

If anyone wishes to understand these things intelligently, he may infer something spiritual from them. By the wolves’ fury, I believe the savagery of the Saracens was foretold. By that man in secular dress, admirable in many respects, who deceived the wolf and killed it by deceiving it, I understand his son also to have been prefigured: the one who, after overcoming by the power of Christ the invisible wolf, namely the ancient enemy, despising him together with all his vices and illusions and subduing him by heavenly power and spiritual arms, rescued many faithful souls from his authority by his example, teaching, and merits, and led them into the way of salvation, life, truth, and justice.

Going before him, accompanying him, and following him was the One who is the way, the truth, and the life, namely the Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns as God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0961]

## Four Hymns of Saint Odilo for the Vigil of Blessed Maiolus

(*Cluniac Library*, p. 291)

### At the Vigil of Blessed Maiolus

#### Hymn at Vespers

By the blood of the victorious Lamb,

this day has been made sacred,

poured forth beneath the final light,

powerful with a double lamp.

Behold, paschal joy

shines through every age.

Let clergy and people,

and above all the monastic flock,

sing the passing of great Maiolus,

his life as well as his merit,

than whom, while he was placed on earth,

nothing was sweeter.

Christ, suffering, goes before;

Maiolus, confessing him,

follows by the straight path,

being preceded by God’s gift.

He honored by his deeds

the steadfast faith of the patriarchs;

what the choir of prophets sang,

he believed with faithful faith.

Following the sacred doctrines

of the apostolic order,

he himself became a renowned father,

an apostolic man.

His clear confession

is crowned with martyrdom,

as he contends lawfully,

having subdued the prince of the world.

He consecrated as a virgin temple

his own breast;

a messenger of heavenly life,

he is rightly called an angel.

May our excellent Father,

who rejoices in these names,

join us to them in heaven,

with the grace of Christ assisting.

To him who takes away the sins of the world

be praise and glory,

with the Father and the Holy Spirit,

through everlasting ages. Amen.

#### Hymn at Matins

Christ, way of all, light of the saints,

through the sacred prayers of the venerable Father,

great Maiolus, send to your faithful people

the joys of peace

from heaven, and grant forgiveness

for our sins. [lacuna]

And may the enduring grace

of the life-giving Spirit be present with us.

Protected by whose powerful gift,

and by the examples and lofty merits of the fathers,

may we likewise deserve to climb

the narrow height of the kingdom.

Glory to the Father, and to the begotten Son,

and to you, equal to both forever,

life-giving Spirit, one God,

through every age of the world. Amen.

#### Hymn at Lauds

Maiolus, companion of the nobles,

who please the King of kings,

among the heavenly courtiers

who know the Godhead,

joined by the privilege of honor

to the monastic assembly,

you also enjoy, with the angelic choirs,

the palace of light.

Therefore, Father, look upon us,

oppressed by the weight of sin;

lay down the heavy burden,

make the conscience light.

Here, once our burdens have been laid aside

and we have been freed from the bonds of death,

join us, your little servants,

to the most excellent monks,

with whom may we possess

perpetual joys,

with the grace of Christ assisting,

through endless ages. Amen.

#### Hymn at Second Vespers

Christ, life-giving God,

vine of all your branches alike,

grant us to celebrate

the feast of so great a patron, Maiolus.

You were pleased to glorify him

in our days,

before kings and crowds of people,

by many signs and worthy merits.

Grant that we may thus participate

in these perpetual and abundant joys,

so that, because of our guilty deeds,

we may not deservedly be unable to lack them.

We ask you, Ruler, author of compassion:

may this our pastor be your intercessor,

so that in your mercy

you may forgive all our sins.

At so great a feast, it is fitting for us,

continually singing his devout vows,

to render you besides

double praises for Easter.

Trinity, one and supreme God,

to you, King, be everlasting glory,

who in such great goodness rule all things

through every age. Amen.

## Epitaph of the Empress Adalheidis, by Saint Odilo

(*Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, edited by D. Pertz, Historical Writers, vol. IV, p. 633)

### Prefatory Notice

Saint Odilo, fifth abbot of Cluny and the most celebrated reformer of the monasteries of his time, was born in Auvergne around 962. In 995 he succeeded Maiolus in governing the monastery of Cluny and, after accomplishing many memorable deeds, died in 1049.

Well trained in sacred letters and a constant reader of Jerome’s books, Odilo composed an epitaph for the Empress Adalheidis, who had died in 999 and with whom he had been joined by intimate affection during the final years of her life. He wrote it to rescue the blessed woman’s life and principal deeds from oblivion by setting them out concisely and—as he himself admits—to encourage someone more capable of undertaking the task to write the empress’s life.

You should therefore not expect a complete and exact history of her life. Only the principal events in the distinguished woman’s life are briefly reviewed [Note: Chapters 1–8], her pious works are enumerated [Note: Chapters 9–12], and the final year of her life, during which the author appears to have accompanied Adalheidis, is treated at greater length [Note: Chapters 13–23]. These things, however, are related by a man who should be considered to have learned them either from Adalheidis herself [Note: Chapter 2: “For she often discussed with her faithful intimates how great and what kinds of things she had suffered,” and so forth] or through personal presence [Note: Chapter 5: “What we say about her we know not only by hearing but also by sight and experience. We heard many words of healing from her and received very many gifts,” and so forth; compare chapters 15 and 19].

The book was written immediately after the empress’s death and sent by Odilo to Abbot Andrew and the congregation at Pavia, perhaps also to the other monasteries founded by Adalheidis, at Paterniacum and Saltz. Certainly the people of Saltz knew the epitaph; in the middle of the eleventh century [Note: Apparently in 1056, that is, before 1057, the year of the death of Duke Otto of Schweinfurt, whom the author celebrates while still alive] they added a second book recounting the miracles of Saint Adalheidis [Note: Chesnius noted that Leopold of Babenberg praised Odilo’s book in his *On the Faith and Religion of the Ancient Princes of Germany*].

And why would he have passed over Paterniacum, where he himself had stayed with the empress during the last year of her life? Moreover, all the copies of the epitaph that could be found present a threefold text, which I believe was altered in this manner so that, after Odilo had first offered his book to the people of Pavia, he sent it, revised in a second edition, to Paterniacum, and, with several other minor corrections, to Saltz.

Copies of the Pavia manuscript therefore exist as follows:

1. The Oxford manuscript among the Bodleian books, no. 2690 (817, Bodl. Sup. D. Art. 91), designated C. It is a parchment folio manuscript of the eleventh century, which I used myself in 1827. It contains the *Life of Odo, abbot of Cluny*; the *Credulity of Odilo*; Odilo’s *Life of Maiolus*; Peter Damian’s *Life of Odilo*; Odilo’s *Life of Adalheidis*, whose final eight pages are missing because they have been cut out; a fragment of the *Life of Saint Simeon*; and six sermons of Odilo [Note: See our *Annals*, VII, pp. 418–419]. The text is, on the whole, complete and good. It is joined by:

2. C., formerly of Saint Martin of the Fields, which Martin Marrier, a monk of that monastery, copied with such diligence in the *Cluniac Library* bearing the name of André Duchesne, pp. 353–362, that it appears to be a reproduction of the manuscript now missing from the books of Saint Martin of the Fields deposited in the Royal Library of Paris. The epitaph of Otto I and of Henry II is appended. Chesnius sprinkled this edition with a few notes.

3. C., formerly of Vallicella, now distinguished among the Royal Brussels manuscripts as no. 7460; and

3*. C., formerly of Saint-Salvator of Anchin, now no. 792 of the Douai Library. Both, according to Bethmann, contain many lives of saints, are parchment folios of the thirteenth century in a very large format, and derive from an older manuscript written at the command of Attala, daughter of King Robert and Constance, countess of Flanders. After the monastery of Watten, near Saint-Omer, had been built and she had received the widow’s habit at Rome from Alexander II, she died at Messina.

The following verses are found at the end of the *Life of Adalheidis*:

“By what manner of life Queen Adalaida lived at Rome,

Odilo the abbot saw and recorded in writing.

Countess Atala ordered these things to be written for us,

that by this example she might win for herself in life

the resolve to reject evil, but to choose the good life.

May that woman, ever worthy of praise, reign with the Lord,

who avoids the wicked and desires to imitate the just.”

[Note: The verses of Garinus the cleric are inscribed in the Brussels manuscript.]

Bethmann copied the Brussels manuscript for our use.

These four manuscripts, with very few exceptions, agree with one another, and alone among all the manuscripts preserve Odilo’s letter to Andrew; all the others depart from them at definite places.

Closer, however, to the Pavia manuscripts are three others that may be called Paterniac manuscripts:

4. C., of the Royal Library of Paris, among the Latin Supplements, no. 854, parchment, a long folio of the eleventh century. It contains the lives of Saint Amalberga, Hilduin, archbishop of Trier, Adalheidis, Odilia, Liutwin, archbishop of Trier, and Willehaldus, together with the lives of Albanus and Celsus written by another hand [Note: Its text agrees with our edition of the *Lives of the Saints*, II, pp. 377 ff.]. Waitz converted it for our use in the preceding year.

5. C., of the University Library of Würzburg, among the Theological manuscripts in folio, no. 34, parchment, of the eleventh century, formerly belonging to Saint Peter at Weissenburg. It places Otto’s epitaph before the epitaph of Adalheidis. I used it in 1835. The learned Bollandists entered readings from the same manuscript in the seventeenth century into their notes; Bethmann saw those notes still preserved in Royal Brussels manuscript no. 8978.

6. C., of the Palatine Library of Vienna, among the secular historical manuscripts, no. 994, now designated no. 622, parchment of the eleventh century. Pages 1–3 contain Otto’s epitaph and pages 3–26 the epitaph of Adalheidis. In some places the text has been scraped away. Our colleague Chmel had it transcribed for our use.

The Saltz manuscripts again depart from these in several readings and by the addition of the *Book of Miracles*:

7. C., formerly of Saints Maurice and Germanus at Speyer. Bethmann found a copy made in the seventeenth century for the use of the learned Bollandists in Royal Brussels manuscript no. 8976, and copied it, as he did the next manuscript. The end of the manuscript, beginning with the word *fulgorem* (“brightness”) in chapter 22, is missing.

8. C., formerly of Bodec, in Westphalia, represented by the Bollandist copy in the Royal Brussels Library, no. 8977; and

9. C., formerly of Saint Magnus at Regensburg, copied by Canisius in *Ancient Lessons*, vol. V, part II, p. 395, and in the second edition, vol. III, part I, p. 73. It presents a less pure text, which Leibniz repeated in *Scriptores Brunsvicenses* I, pp. 262 ff.

Last to be named is:

10. C., the Einsiedeln manuscript, parchment of the fifteenth century, incorporated by Hartmann into the *Annals of Einsiedeln* in 1612. It agrees in large part with the text of Canisius.

A brief excerpt from the *Life and Miracles*, under the title *Life of Saint Adelhaydis*, appeared in four octavo leaves at Durlach in the fifteenth century.

I used these excellent resources as follows: I placed the readings of the Pavia manuscripts in the text, added at each chapter the Paterniac and Saltz readings that occur in all seven manuscripts, and incorporated into the list of variant readings those found only in the Saltz manuscripts or in one or another individual manuscript. I retained the division into chapters found in the Vallicella manuscript, rejecting that of Canisius.

## Epitaph of Otto the Great, Emperor

[Note: “In the Palatine Library manuscript of Vienna: ‘of the most great Emperor Augustus.’”]

Here in this little tomb lies the divine and greatest Otto [variant in manuscript 2: “Otto shone forth for the world, divine or greatest”],

mighty in empire [manuscript 2: “mighty in death”], like David in ancient times [manuscript 2: “in”],

renowned like wise Solomon himself and a friend of peace.

He prays [variants: *Obta* in manuscript 2; *Obtat*, in the manner of Hezekiah, in manuscripts 5 and 6], endowed with a hope greater than Hezekiah’s [cf. 4 Kings 19:15 ff.; Isaiah 38:10],

that peace may come and truth increase through the ages [manuscript 2: “that the age may shine brightly”].

He is said, behold, to have made the Passover [variant: *Fase* in manuscript 2; i.e. *Pascha*, “Passover”; cf. 4 Kings 23:22 and 2 Chronicles 35:18] very celebrated,

and, like Josiah, first beneath the sun to have celebrated his festivals.

Not that alone, but he brings to light the mystical deeds of those who went before,

first ruling kingdoms and reforming the sacred rights of laws,

and, in celebrating, crowns the world [variant: “Otto”].

Whatever best thing the land of Germany ever possessed,

fortunate Italy, you began to possess with the blessed woman [Adalheidis].

He carefully tamed the swollen rhinoceros [Berengarius?],

who had subdued many kingdoms, and made him gentle;

he conquered the Sarmatians and compelled them to serve Christ,

to drive out the demon and to mark the triumph of the cross.

Warring against the Hungarians [manuscript 2: “Ungros”] and bringing back victorious standards,

he rescued innumerable peoples worthy to be called to the sacred faith,

who had been oppressed by dreadful [manuscript 2: “great”] peril.

You, once fortunate and splendid mistress [manuscript 2: “ruling”],

Rome, Otto, together with his holy wife, granted to you

that you might regain, as usual, the scepter and diadem of the world.

The whole world [manuscript 2: “all worlds”] rejoices beneath so great a Caesar [manuscripts 5 and 6: “Ezekiah”].

Peace, once taken away, perishes when the great Otto departed.

While May repeats [variant: “recites,” in witnesses 2 and 6] the mournful Nones in due order,

the pious Caesar Otto is carried up to the heavenly ranks,

to be joined on high with his own Maurice, who leads him,

to him to whom he yielded the palace that you behold as his own.

With you, illustrious wife—for you are blessed in your offspring—

the world rejoices when Otto the Second is born.

He reigns as the Third; heaven resounds with jubilation.

But now your lineage, under clear governance,

protects, enlarges [variant: “augments,” in witnesses 2 and 6], enriches, exalts, and honors the world;

to him your father, called by the name HEINRICUS,

had yielded this name, and to him you too yield the honor.

As long as the radiant East and the farthest earth shall endure,

the sea and the stars of the heavens, the regions of the universe shall mourn you. [This entire verse is written in a larger hand in witness 5.]

[Col. 0967] HERE ENDS [the word is absent in witnesses 2 and 5. In witness 2 the following verses are added after the death of Heinrich II:

Let everything mourn that is known to be able to mourn.

May God, who does not know how to mourn, attend these laments,

so that he may relieve the disasters which the world suffers under its prince—

alas, at his death. For his sake, brothers, pour forth prayers!

Caesar Heinrich, named after the fathers,

is mourned: august, divine, distinguished, and handsome,

victorious and unconquered, flashing with the radiance of God.

Let lamentation, poured forth in Jeremiah’s utterance, proclaim him;

let Davidic songs commend him to the Lord Christ;

let them join Solomon’s kisses to the virginal bridegroom,

in whose service he built, with a kindly heart,

very many things suited to divine worship.

Among them is a temple roofed with splendid design,

adorned within and without with a twofold beauty;

the world feared him, and he lies buried in it in the flesh.

His blessed spirit rejoices in the heavenly court.

He laid down the clay which he had assumed in time, about to receive it again,

so that with the saints he might receive the rewards of true life.]

## HERE BEGINS THE PREFACE TO THE LIFE OF LADY ADALHEIDA

[The entire preface is absent in witnesses 4–10. Variant heading: “Prologue”; in witness 3, “in the Life of the Empress”; Adalheida is sometimes written Adaleida in witness 1.]

To the venerable lord ANDREAS, abbot, and to all the brothers entrusted to him, serving devoutly our Lord and Savior in the suburb of the city of Ticinum, brother ODILO, the very refuse of all the Cluniac poor [that is, “filth,” “the lowest of all”; this reading is found in witnesses 1–3 and in Odilo’s own foundation charter of the monastery of Volta (1025), in Mabillon, *Acta SS. O. S. B.*, VI, 1, p. 634], sends prosperity in the present life and everlasting joys.

I have taken care to transmit to your fraternity, written in a poor style, the epitaph of our lady Adalheida, the august empress, judging it appropriate that her continual memory should be preserved among you—she through whose diligence and prudence the buildings of your monastery grew from their foundations, and by whose abundant and continual munificence you are sustained.

For we have not compressed such a great subject into a short and humble discourse because our speech is sufficient to praise such virtue and nobility, but so that some man of such learning might take from it an occasion for writing, and might unfold so eminent a matter in more eminent language, so that it might resound in the ears of empresses and queens. Thus, when they hear great things about great women and strive to follow in the footsteps of honesty the woman of whom we speak, at least through them domestic care may flourish, just as through her the commonwealth flourished far and wide.

[Col. 0969] HERE ENDS THE PREFACE [variant: “Prologue”; witness 3: “The first Life of the most noble Empress Adaleida”; witness 4: “Here begins the Life of Saint Adalheida Augusta”; witnesses 5–6: “The Epitaph of Lady Adalheida Augusta”; witnesses 7–10: “Here begins the Prologue to the Life of Saint Adalheidis, empress.”]

## HERE BEGINS THE TEXT OF THE SAME BOOK

### 1

In the days of our present age, therefore, the Lord, who orders all things and bestows every honor and every form of goodness, while Otto the First was prosperously exercising the scepter, granted to the Roman commonwealth a venerable glory in the female sex.

For the empress Adalheida, of divine and celebrated memory [variant: “celebrated,” in witness 3], was, after God, the author of many good things and virtues that then came to pass. As we endeavor to commend her in writing to the memory of those who will come after, I fear that I shall rightly be censured [variant: “wrongly,” in witness 3], because we, scarcely capable of it, attempt to explain with a poor style the substance of such nobility and virtue.

Whoever censures us as deserving censure [variants: “for censure,” “with censure,” in witnesses 4–10], whether on account of our uncultivated speech, or because of the novelty of the undertaking, or because of the simplicity of our natural eloquence, should know—indeed, should know [absent in witness 3]—without any doubt that it was not desire for human praise that invited us to this task, but the feeling of true and most sincere love [variant: “and,” in witness 4].

If, as you rightly ought, reader, you wish to recoil from the rusticity of our little talent, attend to the nobility of mind and body of the woman whom we have begun [variant: “wish,” corrected in witness 1; “began,” in some witnesses] to commend.

For if you wish to wait for a man endowed with such eloquence or wisdom as could suitably describe the life of this woman, it is necessary either that Cicero the rhetorician be recalled from the dead, or that Jerome the presbyter be sent down from heaven [variants: “from the heavens,” in witnesses 7–10].

For if that holy and incomparable Jerome, learned in divine and human wisdom [the words are absent in witnesses 7–10], had lived in the time of this august woman, and had undertaken to commend Paula [variant: “Paulum,” in witness 1], Eustochium [variant: “Eustochium,” in witnesses 1–10], Marcella, Melanie, Fabiola, Blesilla, Laeta [variant: “Letta,” in witness 1], and Demetrias [variant: “Demedriadete,” corrected to “Demetriadem” in witness 1], who was struck seven times [the note concerns a woman of Vercelli struck seven times; see Jerome, Letter 49 to Innocent, vol. III, letter 7, Duchesne], in books and letters, he would certainly have commended this woman in no small number of volumes.

If no such man as Jerome, or anyone else so learned in the liberal disciplines that he could worthily describe the character and life of such a woman, is available, let us, though unlearned, undertake the task with God’s help [variant: “with God’s gift,” in witness 4], according to our ability.

[In witnesses 7–10: “To the extent possible. Here ends the Prologue. Here begins the Life.”]

### 2

She, sprung from a royal and religious lineage [the Welfs in Burgundy], while still a young girl and in the sixteenth year of her age [“sixth,” according to Leibniz], by God’s gift obtained a royal marriage [the words are absent in witnesses 7–10], being joined, namely, to King Lotharius, son of Hugh, the very wealthy king of Italy.

From this union she had a daughter [Emma], from whom Lotharius [variant: “Hlotarius,” in witnesses 4 and 5], king of the Franks, begot King Louis [variants: an uncertain reading in witness 4; “Ludowigum,” in witnesses 7–10]. He died without children and is known to have been buried at Compiègne according to royal custom.

When the aforesaid Lotharius [variant: “Hlotarius,” in witnesses 4 and 5] died about three years after he had married Lady Adalheida [variant: “Saint,” in witnesses 7 and 8], she was left widowed, deprived of her kingdom [the words are absent in witnesses 7–10], and without marital support [variants: “counsel,” in witnesses 4 and 7–10; “counsel and support,” in witness 6].

A biting persecution came upon her, which is accustomed to purify the elect as a furnace purifies gold [the note in some witnesses adds: “Therefore such a thing did not happen to her because of sins personally demanding it, but, as we believe, rather because of the gifts arising from divine providence”].

There came upon her, as I truly confess, by divine will, an outward bodily affliction [variant: “of the body,” in witness 3], lest the lustful impulses of the flesh, as she was still a young woman, burn her inwardly [variant: “should have burned,” in witness 3].

The Lord willed that she be worn down by so many blows [variant: “For the Lord willed,” in witnesses 7–10], lest, according to the saying of the Apostle Paul, she should be “a widow who lives in luxury and is dead” (1 Timothy 5:6).

For he willed, with paternal affection, that she endure so many dangers [variant: “suffer,” in witnesses 7–10], lest she prove unworthy of that divine sonship [the wording “divine sonship” is found in witnesses 4–10] of which Scripture says: “The Lord chastises every son whom he receives” (Hebrews 12:6).

For she often gave thanks to God for this [variant: “indeed,” in witnesses 7–10], and with faithful intimates [absent in witnesses 4–10] discussed how many and what kinds of things she had suffered at that time [variants: “had been,” in witness 2; “had suffered,” in witnesses 7–10], and how mercifully the Lord had delivered her from the hands of her enemies [variants: “had delivered,” in witnesses 2, 5–10].

For she judged it more advantageous for her to have been occupied for a time with temporal anxieties than, while living in luxury, to have been subjected to the laws of perpetual death.

### 3

After Lotharius, her husband, died (950), a certain man named Beringarius [variants: “Berangarius”; “Berengarius,” corrected to “Berengerus” in witness 4; “Berengerus,” in witnesses 7–10] obtained the honor of the Italian kingdom. He had a wife named Willam [variant: “wife,” in witnesses 7–10].

Taken innocently by them in an improper manner [the words are absent in witnesses 4–10], she was tormented by various hardships, her hair being torn out [variants: “her hair removed”; “with her hair pulled out,” in witnesses 7–10], frequently battered with fists and kicks [variant: “beaten,” in witnesses 4–10], and finally shut up with only one female servant-companion in loathsome prisons (20 April 951).

Freed by divine intervention, she was afterward raised, by God’s ordering, to the imperial heights.

On the very night when she was being led out of prison [the castle of Garda, according to Donizo], she fell into a certain marsh [variant in witnesses 4–10: “a certain bed of reeds”; variant in witness 8: “a marsh with one maidservant”]. There she remained for days and nights without food or drink, persevering and begging God to send her help [variant: “to come to her aid,” corrected from “to come” in witness 1].

While she was held in such danger, a fisherman suddenly came by boat, carrying in a little vessel a fish called a sturgeon (20 August) [variants: “a fisherman carrying a sturgeon”; “a fisherman bearing a fish in a boat,” in witnesses 4–10].

When he saw them [that is, the fisherman saw them], he asked who they were or what they were doing there. They gave him an answer quite suited to their immediate need:

“Do you see that here we are wandering without human assistance, strangers and abandoned [the words are absent in witnesses 7–10], and—what is harder—that we are endangered by solitude and hunger? If you can, give us some food; but if you cannot, at least offer us consolation” [variants: “offer us consolation”; “give us consolation,” in witnesses 4–10].

Moved by compassion for them, as Christ himself—by whom he had been sent—had once been moved by compassion for the poor suffering from hunger in the desert, he said to them:
