“We have nothing here for the necessities of food except only fish and water.”

He had fire with him, as those who practice the business of fishing commonly do. The fire was lit, and the fish was prepared. The queen took food; the fisherman and the servant attended her.

### 4

While these things were happening [the wording “these things” is preserved in witnesses 7–10], a certain cleric arrived who had shared her captivity and flight, announcing that an army of armed soldiers was at hand.

They received her joyfully and led her with them to an impregnable fortress [Leo of Ostia and Donizo name Canusium].

Afterward, following the counsel of the Italian princes and with God’s grace preceding her, she passed from the throne of the kingdom to the citadel of empire (2 February 962).

For she is worthy to be called and venerated as the most august of all Augustae:

No one before her

so enlarged the commonwealth—

haughty Germany

with its princes,

and noble King Otto,

by whom she bore a son—

and subjected fertile Italy

to Roman citadels.

Over Rome she set a Caesar,

most worthy of empire.

[Variant in witness 6: “subjects.”]

### 5

Let what has been said about the nobility of her flesh suffice. But how and in what manner she exercised the nobility of her mind, no mortal is sufficient to tell. Yet, to speak briefly according to my ability:

Filled with steadfast hope and faith, and completely with twofold charity [variant: “filled with certain hope and faith, and filled with twofold charity,” in witnesses 4–10],

she was exceedingly just, brave, prudent, and most modest;

she lived happily while she governed the ages,

with the help of the Lord who rules the regions of the universe.

Yet the utterance of wise Solomon [variant: “utterance,” in witnesses 2, 9, and 10] aptly suits this most holy woman:

“She opened her hands to the needy, and extended her palms to the poor. She will not fear the cold for her household, for all her domestics are clothed in double garments. She made herself a quilted covering; linen and purple are her clothing [variant: “garment,” in witnesses 3 and 10]. Her husband is noble in the gates, when he sits with the senators [variant: “elders,” in witnesses 1 and 2] of the land. Strength and beauty are her clothing, and she shall laugh on the last day. She opened her mouth with wisdom, and the law of kindness is on her tongue [the remainder is absent in witness 4]. She considered the ways of her household, and did not eat her bread in idleness. Her sons rose up and proclaimed her most blessed, and her husband praised her. Many daughters have gathered riches; you have surpassed them all” (Proverbs 31:20–29).

These things which we say about her we learned not only by hearing, but also by sight and experience [the words are absent in witnesses 4–6]. We heard many words of salvation from her and received very many gifts.

For often she made those who lacked a coin rich in gold [the words “made rich” are absent in witnesses 1–3]; those who sometimes lacked their daily expenses she made distinguished by honors [the note indicates omissions in witnesses 3–6].

As the wife of the first and greatest Otto, the emperor most famous throughout the whole world [“most famous,” feminine, in witnesses 7–10; “emperor” is absent in witnesses 5 and 7–10], and as the mother of many emperors, she deserved to receive that blessing which we read that Tobias deserved to enjoy in the book of the same father: namely, that he should see his children’s children to the third [“third and fourth,” in witness 4] generation.

### 6

After the most august Otto entered the way of all flesh (973), the Augusta governed the monarchy of the Roman Empire prosperously for a long time with her son.

But after, by divine will, the principate of the Roman Empire had been strengthened through the merits and industry of that Augusta [variant: “the Roman Empire,” in witnesses 4–10], there were wicked men who attempted to sow discord between them [variant: “to spread discord,” in witnesses 7–10].

Deceived by their flattery, the Caesar withdrew in heart from his mother.

If we were to commit to writing how many and what kinds of things she suffered at that time [variant: “suffers,” in witnesses 7–10; absent in witness 4], we might seem to detract from the dignity of so great a lineage. For we ought not to touch with our pen what a humble reconciliation soon pacified.

Loving her son and unable to endure the authors of discord, in accordance with the Apostle’s command to “give place for a little while to anger” (Romans 12:19), she resolved to seek her paternal kingdom (978).

There she was received kindly and honorably by her brother, King Chuonrad [“Conrad” in witness 1], and by his most noble wife Mahtilde [daughter of Louis IV, king of the Franks].

Germany grieved at her absence; all Burgundy rejoiced at her arrival; Lyons, that renowned city, once the mother and nurse of philosophy [the words “that renowned city” are absent in witnesses 7–10], exulted, as did noble Vienne, a royal seat [the words are absent in witness 4].

### 7

Afterward Caesar Otto, led by repentance, sent an embassy to his royal uncle and to Maiolus, a father of holy memory (980), earnestly begging with the utmost haste that, through their intervention [variants: “intercession,” in witness 4; “interventions,” in witnesses 7–10], he might obtain the grace of his mother, which he had lost through faults of his own [variant: “through his own merits,” in witness 4].

He prayed and entreated them again to hasten, as soon as they could, to meet him at Pavia together with his august mother [variant: “and,” in witness 4].

Having made use of the counsel of such men, at the appointed time [variant: “at the established time,” in witnesses 7–10] the mother met her son at Pavia (December). [The note states that Otto stayed at Ticinum on 5 December 980 and that an ancient Halberstadt source, the *Saxon Chronographer*, reports that he celebrated Easter 981 at Rome with his mother and wife.]

When they saw each other, they began to greet one another humbly, weeping and shedding tears, prostrate on the ground with their whole bodies.

In the son there was humble repentance; in the mother there was generous forgiveness [variant: “liberal remission,” in witness 5]. Thereafter an undivided bond of perpetual peace remained between them both [the words are absent in witnesses 6–10].

### 8

Not long afterward (983), deprived of her only son [“she was deprived of her only son,” in witnesses 7–10], to whom Otto the Third, born of the Greek woman, succeeded, she was for a long time afflicted by renewed blows [variant: “recurrent,” in witnesses 5–10].

We cannot recount one by one how many and what kinds of troubles followed upon the death of her son.

Although that Greek empress had been sufficiently useful and excellent for herself and for others, she was nevertheless, in part, opposed to her Augusta mother-in-law.

At last, following the counsel of a certain Greek [John of Calabria] and other flatterers, she threatened her, gesturing as though with her hand and saying:

“If I live a full year longer, Adalheida shall not rule over the whole world, which cannot be encircled by one palm” [the negation is absent in witness 4; witnesses 7–10 read *quin*, “so that … not”; variant: “by one hand,” in witness 1].

Divine judgment caused this imprudent statement to become true. Four weeks earlier, the Greek empress had departed this light (15 June 991); Augusta Adalheida survived and remained fortunate.

She continued to mourn and lament the dangers of the world, while necessarily administering the affairs of the Roman Empire.

Otto the Third, her only son’s son, was most happily and honorably raised by the leading men of the kingdom, and did nothing toward her except what was fitting both for her and for him.

Therefore, through the merits and industry of his grandmother [variant: “the merits of his grandmother,” in witness 3], he obtained the Roman principate (21 May 996).

From her earliest age the aforesaid empress had endured many things from outsiders and from members of her own household [variant: “from her earliest age,” in witness 3], so that she could say with the Prophet:

“Often they have fought against me from my youth” (Psalm 128:1), and so forth [the continuation is absent in witness 4].

For she often said that apostolic saying [variant: “the apostolic word,” in witnesses 4–10]:

“For I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy of the glory that is to come, which shall be revealed in us” [variant: “which shall remain,” in witness 2] (Romans 8:18).

“If we suffer together, we shall also reign together” (2 Timothy 2:12); and again:

“If we are companions in sufferings, we shall also be companions in consolations” (2 Corinthians 1:7) [variants in witnesses 4–10: “suffering … consolation”].

She repaid good for evil to many [variant: “good things for evils,” in witnesses 4–10], and, according to the Lord’s command [variant: “the Apostle’s command,” in witnesses 7–10], she forgave those who sinned against her before sunset (Ephesians 4:26).

She kept nothing for herself from the insults inflicted upon her, but entrusted everything to the Lord, knowing that the Lord had said through the prophet:

“Vengeance is mine; I will repay” (Romans 12:9) [variant: “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay,” in witnesses 7–10].

Spare, I beg you, those whom she spared!

And let us say, as the occasion permits, in what adversities and with what endeavors she strove to serve during prosperity.

For as many kingdoms as, with God’s favor, she had possessed first with the Caesar, then with his son and his son’s son—namely, the Augusti and Caesars named Otto—so many monasteries she founded from her own resources in honor of the King of kings.

### 9

In the reign of her father, namely the most noble King Rodulf [variant: “Ruotholfus,” in witness 4], and of her brother Lord Chuonrad [variant: “Chunradus,” in witness 4] [the words “in the reign of her father … and of her brother” are absent in witnesses 7–10], at the place called Paterniacum [Peterlingen, west of Fribourg in Switzerland; see the royal charters issued for the monastery from 974 onward in Schoepflin, *Alsatia diplomatica*, I. The monastery had in fact been founded in 961 by Bertha, Adalheida’s mother; see the charter in Guichenon, *Bibliotheca Sebusiana*, p. 1 and following], where she buried her mother, Queen Bertha [“by name,” in witness 3; daughter of Burchard, duke of Alamannia], devoted to God in all humility [variant: “goodness,” in witness 2 and witnesses 4–6], she founded a monastery in honor of the Mother of God.

By her munificence and by the command of her brother, King Chuonrad, she entrusted it perpetually to the most holy Father Maiolus and his successors for its governance [variant: “permitted it to be governed,” in witness 1]. Compare Otto II’s charter dated 25 July 979, in Schoepflin, *Alsatia diplomatica*, I, 124.

Afterward, in Italy, near the city of Ticinum, she began a monastery from its foundations (981), completed it honorably by imperial authority in honor of the Savior of the world through her most lavish donation [variant: “of the most lavish,” in witness 1], and enriched it abundantly with estates and ornaments [the words are absent in witness 3 and perhaps in witnesses 7–10]. She entrusted it to the aforesaid Father Maiolus for regular governance [the note refers to Otto II’s charter of 30 September 981, in Margarinus, *Bullarium Casinense*, II, 53; earlier donations of Otto I and Adalheida are confirmed there, though their charters do not survive].

In Saxony, after the departure [variant: “death,” in witness 6] of the aforesaid ruler of the commonwealth, with the cooperation of her only daughter, most wise and prudent [Mahtildis, abbess of Quedlinburg], she bestowed very many gifts upon the monasteries of nuns.

### 10

About twelve years before her death (987), at the place called Salsa [Seltz in Alsace; see in Schoepflin, *Alsatia diplomatica*, the royal charters granted to it in 992 and following years], she decreed that a town should be established under Roman liberty [the charters granted to the monastery show that the place was given royal immunity by Otto III and Heinrich II and exempted from episcopal jurisdiction by John XVI; it was subject to the Roman Church “not by the power of donation, but only for the sake of liberty.” I therefore understand “Roman liberty” as the royal immunity of the place. See also Eichhorn, *Staats- und Rechtsgeschichte*, §224]. Later she brought this intention to complete fulfillment.

In that same place she also founded a monastery from its foundations with marvelous workmanship, and, in honor of God and the prince of the apostles, ordered it to be consecrated most augustly and devoutly by Widerald, bishop of the city of Strasbourg, while her nephew Otto the Third was reigning and present with her [variants: “her own,” in witnesses 4–10; “standing beside her,” in witness 2] on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of December (18 November 996). [The date is 996; on 19 November 995 Otto signed charters at Aachen.]

And so that the sacred place might be supported with greater authority through succeeding ages [variant: “through succeeding times,” in witnesses 7–10], a gathering of bishops was also summoned together with the aforesaid Caesar by the often-mentioned and often-to-be-mentioned Augusta Adalheida, grandmother of that Caesar.

In the monastery itself she prepared a cloister well suited to monks and resolved to organize it according to the Rule of Saint Benedict.

She appointed there as abbot a man named Eccemagnus [variants: “Ecce magnus,” “Eccmannus,” “Ecemagnus,” “Essemannus,” “Ezemannus,” and “Ezzemannus” in the witnesses; Ezemannus appears in a charter of Heinrich II], a man of good reputation, learned in human knowledge and divine wisdom, whom she wished to have as a continual teacher in the divine Scriptures.

She enriched and ennobled the monastery so greatly with estates, buildings, gold, gems, precious garments, and various other furnishings of adornment [variants: “equipment,” in witnesses 1, 4, and 6], that nothing was lacking there for those serving God [the words are absent in witnesses 7–10].

For the four years [“three years, rather,” according to the note] that she survived, giving herself and her possessions to her Creator, she acquired the poor of Christ and his servants as friends for herself, so that when temporal things failed, they might receive her into eternal dwellings [the words are absent in witness 1; variant: “welcome her,” in witnesses 7–10].

### 11

Although she was occupied with the highest offices of the commonwealth, she did not disdain to provide aid for the various anxieties of the wretched and needy.

Although she was able, as befitted imperial dignity, to adorn her body with magnificent garments and crown her head with the most precious gems, she did not wish to burden herself with such encumbrances [variants: “be burdened,” in witnesses 4–10]. Rather, she either decided that they should be distributed to the poor, or prepared from them to adorn the standards of the Lord’s cross [absent in witness 1] and the Gospels of Christ [variant: “the Gospel books,” in witness 5].

She was a diligent imitator of her Redeemer, who, although he was highest of all, did not disdain to undergo the lowliness of humanity [the words are absent in witnesses 7–10].

Moreover, she bestowed very many benefits [variant: “gifts,” in witness 4] upon countless monasteries of canons, monks, and nuns established throughout various regions of the world, so that the hosts of those serving God, refreshed by her generous abundance, might more freely implore intercession for her and for the commonwealth from God [compare the *Annals of Quedlinburg* under the year 999].

### 12

In all that she did she maintained the form of justice and preserved a common generosity, believing without any doubt that he would be the future judge whom hidden things do not deceive [variant: “do not escape,” in witness 4], disgraceful things offend, and honorable things delight [variant: “delight,” in witnesses 1 and 3].

Therefore she was seen to be eminent in justice, most pleasing in generosity, and to place works of beneficence upon Christ [variant: “above Christ,” in witnesses 2 and 5], whom the blessed Apostle establishes as the foundation [the words are absent in witnesses 1–3; further words are absent in witnesses 7–10], understanding wisely that faith is the foundation of all virtues [variant: “he called it the foundation of all,” in witness 3].

She therefore practiced perfect generosity, so that she might conceal her work in silence as far as she could and desire to assist the needs of individuals. Thus not her own lips, but the mouths of Christ’s poor, would praise her, so that what is spoken by the blessed Job might already be seen to have been fulfilled in her:

“The blessing of the perishing came upon me” (Job 29:13) [the note explains: “that is, it came to me”].

She strove to weigh carefully, in accordance with the assertion of that prophet, that a poor person should never leave his roof with an empty lap [variant: “never,” in witness 2] (Ecclesiasticus 29:12).

By such dealings she sought to acquire, in the land of the living, an inheritance of the heavenly lot [the words are absent in witness 4].

### 13

Now, in the very last year of her life (999), since, as I believe, it was not hidden from her that she was about to depart from the world, she visited her paternal land—as always a friend of peace, and for the sake of peace and charity [the words are absent in witnesses 6, 9, and 10].

Since the faithful of her grandson King Rodulf [variant: “Ruotholfus,” in witness 4] were quarreling among themselves, she established treaties of peace among those whom she could; those whom she could not reconcile, in her accustomed manner, she entrusted entirely to God.

To unfold how diligently and devoutly she visited the holy places is beyond our ability [witnesses 4–10 add: “it is beyond our capacity to explain”].

At that same time she visited the monastery of Paterniacum, which she herself had nobly founded in honor of the Mother of God, for the healing of the soul of her mother resting there, from both her own resources and those of her mother [the words are absent in witnesses 7–10].

Whatever at that time was lacking, because of temporal need, to the brothers serving God there, she supplied with a most generous hand, as she was always accustomed to do [variant: “provided,” in witness 2].

### 14

At that time something unusual happened, which we judged should be inserted into this work [variant: “But at that time,” in witness 3].

Exhausted from the journey, she could not, as was her custom, give alms to the poor with her own hand [compare the *Annals of Quedlinburg* under the year 999]. She called one of the brothers and instructed him to distribute coins to the poor in her place.

At her command he went to the poor. The number of the poor exceeded the number of coins. The servant feared that he had fewer than could suffice for those in need.

What more is there to say?

The power of the one who

satisfied five thousand of the people

with five loaves [variant: “with five loaves each,” in witnesses 4–10]

was present through the merits of the Augusta.

When the coins had been multiplied, the poor departed happily with their gift [variant: “the coins were multiplied; then they departed,” in witness 5].

## Textual apparatus supplement

- **Opening elegy (Cols. 0967–0968C).** Witness 2 omits both complete verses beginning *Mauricio ducente suo*, “with his own Maurice leading him,” and *Ipsi, cui cessit*, “to him to whom he yielded.” Printed *Conjuge tu celebris* means “illustrious in your spouse”; witnesses 2 and 6 have *Conjunge*, “join,” an imperative that yields “Join, you illustrious woman.” Printed *Dum stabit*, “as long as [the radiant East] shall stand,” appears as *Cum stabit*, “when [it] shall stand,” in witness 2 and as the spelling *Qum stabit* in witness 6. Printed *agustat*, “enlarges,” is *augustat*, likewise “enlarges/exalts,” in witnesses 2 and 6. Witness 5 writes the whole final verse, “the sea and the stars of heaven—the regions of the universe shall mourn you,” in a larger hand. Witnesses 2 and 5 omit *Explicit*, “Here ends”; witness 2 then adds the fully translated lament for Henry II printed above.
- **Prefatory letter (Cols. 0967C–0970A).** Witness 2 spells printed *peripsima* as *peripsema*; both name Odilo “the refuse/lowest one” of all the Cluniac poor. Printed *sustentamini*, “support,” is *sustentamine*, also “support,” in witness 2. Beside *larga continuaque munificentia*, “abundant and continual generosity,” witness 3 reads *continuatim*, “continuously,” and a second hand writes *continuat*, “continues.” Witness 3 has *magnam materiem*, “a great subject,” for printed *grandem materiem*, “so great a subject.” Witness 1 has *ea de qua loquimur*, “she of whom we speak,” for printed accusative *eam*, “the woman whom we speak of.” The closing headings remain distinct: witness 3 has “The first Life of the most noble Empress Adaleida”; witness 4, “Here begins the Life of Saint Adalheida Augusta”; witnesses 5–6, “Epitaph of Lady Adalheida Augusta”; and witnesses 7–10, “Here begins the Prologue to the Life of Saint Adalheidis, empress.”
- **Chapter 1 (Cols. 0969B–0970D).** Witnesses 7–10 read *totius honoris*, “of every honor,” where the printed text has *totiusque honoris*, “and of every honor.” Witnesses 5–6 spell *auctrix*, “female author,” as *autrix*, with the same meaning. Witness 4 replaces *Quisquis nos reprehenderit*, “whoever censures us,” with the abbreviated reading *Q. ergo n.*, “Who, therefore, [censures] us.” Printed *reprehensionis dignos* means “worthy of censure”; witness 4 has dative *reprehensioni dignos*, likewise “worthy of censure,” and witnesses 5 and 7–10 have ablative *reprehensione dignos*, “deserving in respect of censure.” Witness 1 deletes the first *s* in *exspectare*, “to wait,” leaving *expectare*, the same verb in alternate spelling. Witnesses 7–10 have *ex superis*, “from the heavenly regions,” for printed *e superis*, “from heaven.” Witness 1 deletes *-que*, “and,” from *septiesque*, leaving *septies*, “seven times”; witnesses 7–10 likewise read *septies*. The concluding addition in witnesses 7–10 is “As far as possible. Here ends the Prologue. Here begins the Life.”
- **Chapter 2 (Cols. 0970C–0971A).** Printed *sextum decimum aetatis suae ageret annum* means “she was passing the sixteenth year of her age”; witness 3 has *duceret*, “was spending/passing,” for *ageret*. Witnesses 7–10 omit “she obtained a royal marriage.” Witness 4’s damaged form of Louis’s name remains uncertain; witnesses 7–10 read *Ludowigum*, “Louis.” When Lotharius dies, witnesses 7–10 omit *privata regno*, “deprived of the kingdom”; witnesses 4 and 7–10 have *consilio*, “counsel,” for printed *solatio*, “support,” and witness 6 has both *consilio et solatio*, “counsel and support.” After *fornax*, “furnace,” witnesses 4–10 add: “Therefore this did not happen to her because her own sins demanded it, but rather, as we believe, from gifts arising through divine providence”; they then resume with “There came upon her.”
- **Chapters 3–5 (Cols. 0971B–0973A).** In chapter 3 witnesses 4–10 omit *A quibus indecenter*, “by whom, improperly”; witnesses 7–10 read *caesariei distractis*, “with her hair torn out,” while witness 4 has *capillorum … detracta*, “deprived of her hair.” Witnesses 4–10 read “a certain reed bed” for the printed “a certain marsh,” and witness 8 specifies “a marsh with one maidservant.” Witness 1 corrects *venire*, “come,” to *subvenire*, “come to her aid,” and corrects the damaged *de tanto* to *detenta*, “held.” Witnesses 4–10 describe “a fisherman carrying a sturgeon,” rather than the printed fisherman “carrying in a little boat a fish called a sturgeon.” Witnesses 7–10 omit *humano consilio peregrinamur*, “we wander without human assistance.” At chapter 4, witnesses 7–10 have *Dum haec ita agerentur*, “while these things were happening thus,” for printed “while these things were happening”; witnesses 4–10 use *ejus*, “of her,” rather than *ei*, “with her,” for the cleric’s association with her captivity and flight. Witnesses 4–10 have *deduxerunt*, “conducted,” for *duxerunt*, “led,” and witnesses 6–10 have *in quoddam … castrum*, “into a certain fortress,” for *ad*, “to.” In chapter 5 witnesses 4–10 rearrange the opening as *speque fide certa, gemina caritate referta*, “filled with sure hope and faith and with twofold charity.”
- **Chapters 6–8 (Cols. 0973A–0975A).** At chapter 6 witnesses 4? and 5–10 make *solidatum* agree with *principatum*: “the principate of the Roman Empire had been strengthened”; witnesses 4–10 also place *imperium* before *principatus*, preserving “the principate of the Roman Empire.” Witnesses 7–10 have *disseminare discordiam*, “to scatter discord,” for *seminare*, “to sow,” and read *passa sit*, “she may have suffered,” for *passa fuerit*, “she had suffered.” At chapter 7 the embassy asks intercession for faults described as *propriis*, “her son’s own,” in witnesses 7–10 and *meritis*, “deserts,” in witness 4; *interventu*, singular “intercession,” appears in witness 4, while witnesses 7–10 have plural *interventionibus*, “intercessions.” Witness 4 reads “again praying and beseeching them,” and witness 1 inserts *et*, “and,” before “as quickly as possible.” Witnesses 7–10 have *constituto tempore*, “at the appointed time,” for *statuto tempore*, with the same sense; witnesses 6–10 omit “the undivided bond” from the restored perpetual peace. At chapter 8 witness 3 has *succedit*, “succeeds,” for *successit*, “succeeded”; witnesses 5–10 have *recidivis*, “recurring,” for the equivalent printed *reciduis*. Witnesses 7–10 read *quin possit*, “that she could not,” for printed *quod non possit*. For Otto III, witnesses 4–10 explicitly read *Romani imperii … principatum*, “the principate of the Roman Empire.” The printed citation in the vengeance sentence is Romans XII, 9; witnesses 7–10 add *et ego*, “and I,” producing “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay.”
- **Chapters 9–14 (Cols. 0975A–0977D).** In chapter 9 the Paterniacum note identifies Payerne west of Fribourg, cites royal charters from 974 in Schoepflin, and states that Bertha, Adalheida’s mother, founded the monastery in 961, citing Guichenon; a second note identifies Bertha as the daughter of Burchard, duke of Alemannia. At Ticinum, witness 3 has singular *fundamento*, “foundation,” for *a fundamentis*, “from the foundations,” and witnesses 3? and 7–10 omit “she enriched it most fully with estates and ornaments”; the charter note cites Otto II’s charter of 30 September 981, which confirms earlier lost donations of Otto I and Adalheida. In chapter 10 the Salsa note identifies Seltz in Alsace; the long note explains from its charters that “Roman liberty” means royal immunity and records that the place was subjected to the Roman Church for liberty, not as a donation. The abbot’s name appears as *Ecce magnum* in witnesses 1–3, *Eccmannum* in 4 and 6, *Ecemagnum* in 5, *Esemannum* in 8, *Ezemannum* in 7, and *Ezzemannum* in 9–10; Henry II’s charter calls him Ezemannus. Witnesses 7–10 omit “the monastery itself” from the endowment sentence, witnesses 4–10 omit “and” before its precious garments, and witnesses 2–4 and 7–10 have a damaged omission from the sentence about the years she survived. In chapter 11 witness 2 has *valebat*, “she was able,” for *valeret*, “she might be able”; witness 1 corrects the damaged *redi-* to *radiare*, “to make [her head] shine,” with precious gems; witnesses 4–10 use passive *gravari*, “to be burdened,” for active *gravare*, “burden herself”; witness 1 omits “the standards of the Lord’s cross,” and witnesses 7–10 omit “to endure the abject things of humanity.” In chapter 12 witness 4 has indicative *fallunt*, “deceive,” for subjunctive *fallant*, “may deceive”; witnesses 1 and 3 likewise have *delectant*, “delight,” for *delectent*, “may delight.” Witnesses 1–3 omit “whom the blessed Apostle sets,” and witnesses 7–10 omit the words after “foundation” through “faith is.” In chapter 13 witnesses 6, 9, and 10 omit the second *pacis*, “of peace,” from “for the sake of peace and charity”; witnesses 4–10 expand “it is not possible” to “it is not within our power”; witnesses 7–10 omit “as much from her own as from” in the description of Paterniacum’s endowment. In chapter 14 witness 3 begins *Accidit autem tunc*, “But then it happened,” and witnesses 7–10 have *Ex ejus jussu*, “at her command,” for printed *Ejus jussu*. Witnesses 7–10 read present *excedit*, “exceeds,” for past *excessit*, “exceeded.” Witnesses 4–10 have *quinis*, “five each,” for *quinque*, “five”; witness 5’s corrected reading is *multiplicati denarii*, “the coins having been multiplied,” for *Multiplicatis denariis*, “when the coins had been multiplied.”

15. Having departed from there, she sought the place of Agaunum, where a rock [variant: *rupis*, “of a rock,” in witnesses 4–5] holds the bodies of countless most blessed martyrs [the text is lacking in witness 3]. With what devotion, with what reverence [lacking in witnesses 7–10], did she ask the aid of the great martyr Mauritius and his companions! How many sighs [lacking in witnesses 7–10] were hers there! How many [lacking in witnesses 7–10] breaths! How much mourning! What rivers of tears [lacking in witness 10]! Never, I think, were there any sins that did not then deserve eternal remedies.

For if you had looked upon the august woman’s face, you would have said that it surpassed human appearance [variant: “you would have believed,” in witnesses 7–10]. If she uttered anything else with her lips, you would have believed that she was doing nothing other than unfolding that prophetic passage [the text is lacking in witnesses 9–10]:

> I pour out my prayer in his sight [variant: “my prayer and my tribulation,” in witnesses 7–10];  
> I declare my tribulation before him.  
> *(Psalm 141:3)*

Her greatest tribulation was her charitable compassion for all who turned aside from God’s law, so that she could say [variant: “saying to the Lord with the prophet,” in witness 3], with the Prophet:

> Faintness has seized me because of sinners.  
> *(Psalm 118:53)*

And with Paul:

> Who is weak, and I am not weak?  
> *(2 Corinthians 11:29)*

[The witnesses 4–10 continue: “I am not weak? and so forth.”]

Thus she lamented the sins of others in a manner in which many cannot lament their own misfortunes. She rejoiced in the steadfastness and progress of those who had gone before; every day she grieved over the failings of those living in the present, and especially over those of the future. When I speak of the future, I undoubtedly declare that she possessed the spirit of prophecy. There would be a deficiency in my account if I had not learned this from public evidence [variant: “It would be so,” in witness 10; “unless,” in witnesses 7–10].

16. When she was about to depart from that holy place and had withdrawn into a corner of the church for the sake of prayer, a messenger came to her from Italy and announced that Franco, bishop of Worms [variant: “Vangionensis,” in witness 1], had died at Rome [variant: “announcing that he had died,” in witness 4; cf. Thietmar, *Chronicle* IV.39]. Since he was a man of good reputation, the august lady loved him greatly, as she was accustomed to love all good men [variant: “him,” in witness 10]. As soon as she heard of his death, she summoned one of her attendants and humbly asked him to pour out prayers to the Lord for him [the words are lacking in witness 10; variant: “to offer prayers,” in witnesses 7–10]. Then, as if beside herself, she began:

> “What shall I do, Lord, or what shall I say about that old man of ours and my nephew [the words “and my nephew” are lacking in witness 3]? Many in Italy, I believe, will perish with him; after them, alas, wretched me, the noble Otto will perish, as I fear. I shall remain deprived of every human consolation. Far be it from me, O Lord, King of the ages [variant: “of heaven,” in witness 3], to survive such a mournful loss!”

Then you would have seen the august woman prostrate upon the ground with her whole body [the word “ground” is lacking in witness 4]; you would have believed [variant: “you would have seen,” in witness 9; lacking in witness 10] that with all the effort of her mind she was intent upon heaven and, as though she had already found the footprints of the martyr Mauritius, was licking them with tearful lips [variant: “with a fevered mouth,” in witnesses 4–6; “with a fevered mouth,” in witnesses 7–10; “to reach them,” in witness 2].

After a little while she rose from prayer; she gave gifts to the martyrs and alms to the poor.

17. Thereafter she went to the city of Geneva [variant: “the Genevan city,” in witnesses 4; “Geneva,” in witnesses 7–10], wishing to see the shrine of the most victorious martyr Victor. From there she came to Lausanne [variant: “Lausannia,” in witnesses 7–10], and there she most devoutly worshiped the memorial of the Mother of God. In these places she was honorably received by the king and by the bishops, her nephews; then she came to a village called Orbe [the text reads *Urba*; editorial note: “Orbe”].

After remaining for some time in that village [the words are lacking in witness 4], she gave whatever necessities she could to the poor and wretched who came to her [the words are lacking in witnesses 9–10; variant: “she supplied,” in witness 10]. She discussed with the king and the leaders of the region matters of peace and propriety [variant: “and with the king,” in witness 4]. From there she also sent varied and diverse gifts to holy places. For what church, what monastery of monks joined to her by kinship or proximity, did not deserve to receive gifts or presents [variant: *xenia*, “guest-gifts,” in witnesses 2 and 4–10] from her?

To say little of much, at the very time when her final day was approaching [variant: *supremus*, “highest,” in witness 1], she visited the most blessed Father Benedict at Monte Cassino [editorial note: “Cassino”], although with small gifts, yet with gifts of her own. She also visited Father Maiolus of blessed memory, already crowned with heavenly glory, whom, while he remained in this mortal flesh [variant: “in this life,” in witnesses 7–10], she loved above all mortals in that order [the phrase is lacking in witnesses 1 and 7–9; variant: “from that order,” in witness 10].

She had not forgotten Cluny, the monastery so familiar to her [the text is lacking in witness 4; variant: “she had not forgotten Cluny,” in witness 3]. Therefore, for the restoration of the monastery of the most blessed confessor of Christ, Martin of Tours [editorial note: “at Tours”], which shortly before had been consumed by fire [the text is lacking in witness 4; editorial note: “in the year 997, on 25 July”], she sent a considerable amount of silver [the text is lacking in witness 4], and, for the honor of the altar, part of the cloak of her only son, the august Otto [the text is lacking in witness 4; variant: “part of the cloak,” in witness 4].

18. To recall her most sweet words to the person charged with delivering them, she said, among other things:

> “I beg you, dearest, I beg you to address the most holy priest [variant: “the most holy priest of Christ,” in witness 4; “the most holy confessor,” in witnesses 7–10] in this manner:
>
> “‘Receive, priest of God, as my service, these small gifts which Adalheid, handmaid of God’s servants, a sinner in herself but empress by God’s gift, has entrusted to you. Receive part of the cloak of my only son, the august Otto, and pray for him to the Christ whom you clothed in the poor man when you divided his garment.’”

On the day when she was about to leave the place mentioned above [the text is lacking in witnesses 4 and 10], at one and the same hour, while we sinners stood nearby [variant: “were standing nearby,” in witness 2], she both left us an example of perfect humility and showed that she possessed the spirit of prophecy—not arrogantly, but humbly.

19. A certain monk was there in her presence who, although unworthy to be called abbot [variant: “to be called,” in witnesses 7, 9, and 10], was nevertheless considered by her to be a man of some importance [the words are lacking in witnesses 9–10; editorial note: “He was Odilo”]. When she looked at him [variant: “when she observed him,” in witnesses 7–10], and he in turn looked at her, both began to weep profusely. I shall say that she did more than if I said that she had healed many sick people [variant: “I shall say that she then did more,” in witnesses 4–10; “if I said,” in witnesses 7–10].

She humbly took hold of the rather unkempt garment in which he was dressed and, kissing it, pressed it to her most holy eyes and most serene face; then she said to him humbly [variant: “familiarly,” in witnesses 4–10] and silently:

> “Remember me, my son [variant: “sons,” in witness 10], in your prayers of contemplation, and know that I shall not see you again with bodily eyes [variant: “that you shall not see me again,” in witnesses 2, 4, and 7–10]. When I have departed from human affairs [the words are lacking in witness 1], I entrust my soul to the prayers of the brothers.”

From there, traveling by the route by which she had come, she reached the place where, by God’s ordinance, she had determined to prepare her tomb [editorial note: “Seltz”; variant: “to be prepared,” in witnesses 4 and 6–10; witness 5 corrects *parare*, “to prepare,” to *parari*, “to be prepared”].

20. Thus, on the final journey of her temporal course [variant: “of her temporal time,” in witness 4], she raised herself above herself as far as she could, so that, having rejected the turmoil of worldly affairs, she might freely devote herself to divine contemplation. The business of familiar matters was even burdensome to her [variants: *familius*, “more familiar,” in witness 1; *familiarius*, “more familiarly,” in witnesses 2, 3, and 7–10]. She had already admirably completed the activity of Leah and Martha [variant: *laudabile*, “praiseworthy,” in witnesses 5–6; the words “she had completed vigorously” are lacking in witness 3]; she longed to attain the desirable leisure of Rachel and Mary.

Therefore, intent upon readings and constant in prayers [variant: “constantly,” corrected from “constant,” in witness 1], she rejected earthly things and, with her whole mind, yearned for heavenly things. If anyone interrupted her with worldly business, she did not answer on that subject; rather, she mournfully turned over in her heart the apostolic words:

> Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from this body of death?

And, secure in the hope of divine recompense, she would say:

> The grace of God through Jesus Christ.  
> *(Romans 7:24)*

Then, instructed by heavenly teaching, she came to the place where she was to surrender her last breath to God [the word “last” is lacking in witnesses 1 and 3]. The day was approaching on which the annual devotion was performed for the memory of her son, the august Otto. From the neighboring places, crowds of poor people had gathered to her, as they always did.

21. It was her custom, on the anniversaries of her friends and household members, to distribute a spiritual gift to her spiritual soldiers—I mean Christ’s poor, by giving alms [the text is lacking in witness 4]. A multitude of needy people had been arranged in orderly ranks at the place [variant: “places,” in witness 10].

She went to them and, following the example of the patriarch Abraham [the words are lacking in witness 2], not doubting that God was among them, humbly worshiped. Forgetting her weakness, she attempted, beyond her strength [variant: “beyond her own strength,” in witness 9], to approach them [variant: “to undertake it,” in witness 2; “to approach,” in witnesses 5–6]. With her own hand she gave to each one, and to those whom she saw to be more pitiable she gave clothing [the text reads “she clothed them with garments and gave other things,” in witness 4] or other small gifts.

When this spiritual task was finished, she had Masses celebrated for her son by a certain venerable archbishop [editorial note: “Willegis of Mainz”; variant: “she requested,” in witnesses 6–10]. That very night she was seized by a fever [variant: “already,” in witness 3], and as the burden of her illness grew worse over several days, she was brought to the very end [variant: “was led,” in witnesses 6–10].

Nevertheless, she remained devoted to prayer as far as she could, and, with eyes longing for Christ, deigned to look upon nothing else. When her bodily strength had recovered somewhat, she asked to be fortified more attentively with the Church’s mysteries. Then, having been anointed with sacred oil, she humbly and most devoutly received the sacrament of the Lord’s body, worshiping him in whom she had always hoped and believed.

Strengthened by such defenses and nourished by such a banquet [the words are lacking in witnesses 7–10], she told the elders who stood nearby [variant: “were standing nearby,” in witness 2] and the clergy to sing the penitential psalms [variant: “the psalms of penitence,” in witness 4] and to recite the names of the saints according to ecclesiastical custom. When this had been done, she sang with those who sang and prayed with those who prayed, until that point where she prayed that God might be present to her in mercy.

She was unskilled, with the sister of Moses, in holding the tambourine and leading the dance, or, with David, in the strings and organ; but, taking up well-sounding cymbals and following the Lamb [the words are lacking in witnesses 7–10], she was already wholly absorbed in jubilation.

22. As the year one thousand from the Lord’s incarnation was approaching [variant: “the year,” in witness 3], longing to see one day that knows no setting in the courts of the Lord above thousands, she often said with the Apostle:

> I desire to depart and to be with Christ.  
> *(Philippians 1:23)*

As she awaited even in the present with spiritual joy the feast of the nativity of that same Lord Jesus [the phrase is lacking in witness 2], when blessed December was completing its sixteenth day [editorial note: “Thus, because she died at midnight, her death is entered in obituaries and annals under either 16 or 17 December”], she too, having happily laid down the burden of the flesh, flew forth into the radiance of the purest ether [the passage ends here in witness 7].

With her household she had grave cheerfulness; with outsiders, most honorable seriousness; toward the poor, tireless compassion [the text is lacking in witness 3]; toward churches of God, overflowing generosity; toward the good, enduring kindness; against the wicked [variant: “the impious,” in witnesses 8–10], generous severity; in seeking, fear; in what she sought, strength [the words “in her strength and in what she sought” are lacking in witnesses 8–10]; in prosperity, true humility; in adversity, patient endurance; in daily food, sobriety; in clothing also, moderation; in readings and prayers [variant: “in prayers and,” in witness 8; “in prayers and in,” in witness 10], in vigils and fasts, perseverance; in giving alms, one and the same will.

No exaltation hindered her because of the nobility of her flesh [the text is lacking in witness 2], nor could desire for human praise draw her to herself because of the goodness [variant: “power,” in witnesses 8–10] granted to her by God [variant: “from,” in witness 10]. No presumption concerning the virtues granted to her by God [the whole clause is lacking in witness 10], and no despair persuaded by her own failings [variant: “ill-persuaded,” in witnesses 4 and 8–10; “badly persuaded,” in witnesses 5–6], ruled her. No ambition concerning the honors, riches, and delights of the world [variant: “of this world,” in witness 3] held mastery over her [variant: “over her,” in witnesses 4–6 and 8–10]. Rather, in all things, the mother of every virtue, discernment, accompanied her [the words are lacking in witnesses 7, 9, and 10].

She possessed secure firmness in faith, firm security in hope, and, in the love of God and neighbor, charity, the root of all good things and the chief cause of virtues [variant: “the principal cause,” in witness 4; the phrase “in love … charity” is lacking in witnesses 8–10].

But, to speak the truth, divine power revealed through the miracles that shone forth at her tomb how great and what kind her life was [variant: “how great and what sort of life she had,” in witnesses 8–10]. If these were described in order [the remainder is lacking in witnesses 8–9], they would require a volume of their own, for they cannot be explained in our language. Yet, lest they remain wholly concealed in silence, I have chosen, avoiding prolixity, to encompass them in a brief chapter.

23. At her tomb, the blind recover the light they had lost, and the paralyzed recover bodily health. Those suffering from fever are healed there. Many sick people afflicted with various illnesses are restored through the grace and mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ [the manuscripts add various conclusions: “to whom are glory forever and ever. Amen”; “to whom are honor and glory forever and ever. Amen”; “who rules the circuit of heaven throughout all ages of ages. Amen”; “who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns, God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen”; “The Life of Saint Adalheid, august empress, composed by the venerable Father Otto, abbot of the place of Cluny, ends.”]

# Appendix: Book of Miracles

[From the Codex of Bodeken, Canisius, and Hartmann.]

## Prologue to the Second Book

Since it is clearly evident from the preceding style with what diligence this handmaid of God imitated blessed Martha, it is also necessary to bring forward certain signs of heavenly contemplation [variant: “judgments,” in witness 10], by which we may infer that she more perfectly attained the state of her sister Mary. Moreover, we can easily understand how, by keeping her body chaste and pure in accordance with the Apostle’s command, she deserved fully to become a temple of the living God [the word “God” is found in witness 10; “living” is lacking in witnesses 9–10].

For although throughout her whole life she abounded in royal riches and resources worthy of her lineage, from the beginning of her widowhood she subdued her flesh with a hair shirt and trampled underfoot the summit of worldly glory by contempt of mind. She is known, through her desire for heavenly contemplation, to have devoted herself so completely to Christ alone, namely Justice [variant: “namely, and Justice,” in witnesses 9–10] that she agreed with the Psalmist in his sweet voice, who concluded that his good was not to enjoy the delights of a kingdom but to cling to God.

*The prologue ends.*

# Miracles of the Same Adalheid, Queen

[The words “these miracles” are lacking in witness 10; witness 9 begins: “The book of miracles.”]

1. One day (in the year 994), while she was seated for the refreshment of the body in the honorable company of both clergy and laity, and the purest dishes were satisfying everyone’s needs [variant: “while she was already seated, and,” in witness 10], she—following the custom of holy minds, which display one thing outwardly to avoid favor while doing another inwardly—pretended to be eating and held a knife in her hand for some time. Thus, not for her own pleasure but according to the will of others, she prolonged the meal. Suddenly, however, the color of her face changed together with the disposition of her mind, and the iron fell from her hand onto the table [variant: “fell down,” in witnesses 9–10]. With a sigh she indicated that this was not a mark of insolence but that she had perceived something extraordinary through divine revelation [the words are lacking in witnesses 9–10].

While the whole crowd wondered what this might portend, yet did not dare to ask, she concealed from the multitude [variant: “from the crowd,” in witnesses 9–10] the significance of the secret, in keeping with the beauty of evangelical perfection. Only the bishop of Augsburg, named Dudo [editorial correction: Liutold, who held office in 989–996], who because of his merits in life was familiar to her and devoted to her by constant service, did she deign to address with this introduction [the words are lacking in witnesses 9–10]:

> “Now, venerable Father, there is great need of consolation for you, because the wall of your western mother church has fallen through divine ordinance [the words “which is your” are lacking in witness 10]. Such a great loss does not impose upon your prudence a concern for its restoration more than it has brought a cloud of grief upon my mind because of your distress or the common damage to our church [witnesses 9–10 join the phrase “of our church” to the preceding words].
>
> “But I command and urge you to console yourselves in the tranquility of the divine nature, which alone inhabits inaccessible light without any change, permitting all things in some manner to be moved because of our guilt, but restoring more things [variant: “whole things,” in witness 10] to a state of wholeness through its ineffable clemency.”

The bishop, disturbed both by the prophecy and by the material loss, carefully noted the time of the aforesaid collapse and hastily sent a messenger to the Augusta to test the matter and learn the truth. From his report he learned that the disaster had occurred and the hour had corresponded exactly with the handmaid of God’s prediction.

2. At another time, a portent similar to this prophecy was revealed through her. It was all the more worthy of wonder because it differed in place, time, and outcome.

Her son, elected prince of the Roman state, had taken a Greek woman as his wife. Deceived by her perverse character and worse counsel [variant: “by her character and evil counsel,” in witness 10], he attempted to obtain the kingdom of the Greeks. Accordingly, having gathered an army from every available resource [variant: “from all his resources and efforts,” in witness 10], he crossed the borders of Italy (in the year 982), thereby giving the king of the Greeks an opportunity to wage war and bringing loss of reputation and life upon himself and his men.

Meanwhile his pious mother, devoting herself day and night [variant: “night and day,” in witnesses 9–10] to divine worship, undoubtedly fulfilled the devotion of blessed Anna [the name is glossed in witness 8 as “anima,” that is, “soul”; witnesses 9–10 read “Anna, the widow”], and according to canonical rule performed the duties of widowhood with all diligence.

One day, striving with the utmost devotion for the safety of her only son and the condition of the entire kingdom, she sacrificed herself to God as a living offering in her usual manner, standing before the crucifix. She was seized in ecstasy and appeared, to human eyes, to be dead. Returning to herself after an hour, she retained in her memory what she had seen. She made known that the fate of the aforesaid battle had been shown beforehand to her in a spiritual vision—not by describing the event, but by mourning the slaughter of good men.

From these signs it can plainly be inferred with what purity of heart she shone, or rather with how much freedom of spirit she served Christ in secret. With the prophets, the Lord revealed future things to her; with the patriarchs, he strengthened her faith; with the apostles, he taught her the perfection of the Gospel; with the martyrs, he granted her endurance of tribulations; with priests, he instilled in her care for the Church; with holy virgins, he increased the sincerity of her most holy mind; with monks, he displayed his familiar presence to her [variant: “and with them,” in witnesses 9–10]; and with apostolic disciples—I mean widows chosen by Peter and Paul and appointed to the service of religion—he endowed her on earth with devotion [variant: “he preached,” in witness 10] and exalted her in eternal glory.

She deserved such abundant grace in healings through the work of benevolence [variant: “through the work,” in witnesses 9–10] that, just as she relieved the poverty of the needy by the generosity of alms, so also she restored the health of the sick and weak by a powerful gift.

Yet, in a wonderful manner, fleeing human knowledge to avoid presumption, and desiring secretly to please the giver of so great a gift [variant: “of so great a gift,” in witness 10], she either seized the efficacy of the signs entirely by furtive speed [variant: “in every possible way,” in witness 9–10], or, if she could not prevent some of her attendants from knowing, she acted by command [variant: “she issued a command,” in witness 8; the phrase is lacking in witnesses 9–10] that they should not spread the matter anywhere in casual conversation. She constantly revolved beneath her vigilant heart that saying of the teacher of the nations [2 Corinthians 1:12]:

> This is our glory: the testimony of our conscience.

And what the Lord himself commanded—that the work of the right hand should be hidden from the left [Matthew 6:3]—she fulfilled with simple prudence in all her conduct. Yet a city set upon a mountain could not remain hidden from everyone [variant: “hidden in everyone,” in witnesses 9–10; cf. Matthew 5:14]. One of these signs, burning brightly, reached our knowledge, and we are taught that the power by which it was performed was the cause of many virtues.

3. At a certain time, while she was sitting in a private room occupied with heavenly meditation [variant: “seated,” in witnesses 9–10], and everyone in authority was absent except a lame man [variant: “everyone’s jurisdiction being absent,” in witness 8], a steward named Hicemannus [variant: “Huozemannus,” in witnesses 9–10], acceptable to her for his fidelity and silence, brought her a gift of beautiful apples.

Receiving it with a serene face [variant: “a most sincere face,” in witness 8], as she was a friend of cheerfulness [variant: “as she was,” in witness 10], she selected one from among the many and ordered the others to be presented to the keeper of such things. By chance, however, an apple slipped farther away from her hand. The lame man was immediately ordered to bring it back, but he refused the service because the crutches with which he pretended to walk were being held by the lady [variant: “by a gift,” in witness 8].

While he resisted and reasonably offered the weakness of his body as an explanation for his disobedience, she finally bowed her head reverently in the saints’ domestic oratory before the venerable relics [variant: “the domestic [saint],” in witness 8], which she always kept before her [the words are lacking in witness 9; witness 9 adds: “whom she used to worship”], and affirmed that her lords wished the lame man to walk.

> No sooner said than done, the lame man rose from the ground;
>
> Obedient to the command, he became sound in his whole body;
>
> Ordered to keep silent about so great a sign,
>
> He displayed his joy; such grace could not remain concealed.

4. At the time when the blessed woman departed from the world, Duke Herimann of Swabia, who had taken the daughter of her brother Conrad in marriage, wished by hereditary right to seize the possessions belonging to the monastery of the handmaid of God [editorial note: “Seltz”]. But she proved to him and to all who lived around him by manifest signs that she left no heir except the apostles and the monks who served them.

At that time, a man who had recently lost his sight happened to be with the same duke. Formerly trained in the art of bloodletting, he had for that reason enjoyed the blessed queen’s generous favor. Since he had learned by experience [variant: “through experiences,” in witness 10] the abundance of her beneficence and the brilliance of her holiness, he came to her tomb in a spirit of prayer and invited her to assist him with prayers and tears.

For an entire week he visited the place of the sacred body with persistent supplication. On one occasion, weary and sad, he sat down upon the pavement and, overcome by the weariness of his languishing soul, was drenched with the moisture of sleep. Then holy Adalheid appeared to him in a dream, adorned with a remarkably reverent countenance and beautiful beyond human appearance. In a terrible voice she asked why his lord Herimann was usurping the private possessions of the apostles into his unjust dominion [variant: “jurisdiction,” possibly intended, in witness 8].

When he confessed his ignorance—or rather added an account of the duke’s tyranny—she said:

> “See to it that, if through our merits you recover the health of your eyes, you also approach the prince as the faithful interpreter of our embassy and plainly instruct him, with a sign, to abandon this wickedness altogether. Otherwise, let him know that I and my lords, the twelve apostles, judges of the entire world, will pursue our rightful claim, and let him learn beforehand that he and his men will be scourged by an unavoidable blow of vengeance.”

After these words, the man immediately awoke. Rejoicing at the memory of the vision and the speech, he followed the departing woman’s feet as far as the tomb. There he prostrated his whole body and lay devoted to prayer until the monks’ choir had celebrated the offices of Mass.

As soon as the cantor began the Introit, the blind man received his sight and mingled his joy with the singers. When the miracle was immediately announced by the sound of the bells, the entire people ran together. The man was recognized and marveled at [the words are lacking in witnesses 9–10], the handmaid of God was venerated, and the finder of light—indeed, the confirmer of the created order [variant: “the first creation,” in witness 8; “restorer,” in witnesses 9–10]—was praised by people of every sex and condition.

Afterward, having gained his sight and remembering the testimony and embassy entrusted to him, he returned at a joyful run to his lord. He explained what he had been warned of in sleep [variant: “what he had been,” in witness 10] and testified that his restoration of sight was evidence of divine judgment: if he himself, or any powerful person, or anyone at all should thereafter presume to inflict harm upon the ecclesiastical benefices of the glorious woman in the Lord.

Struck with fear, the duke therefore took care to correct whatever, in his unjust undertaking against God’s will, he had foolishly done concerning the possessions of God’s handmaid. He also added to the aforesaid monastery an estate for producing salt, situated near the town of Marsal [editorial note: Marsal in Lorraine, already famous at that time for its saltworks].

5. It seems worthy of report how King Heinrich, a singular devotee of the holy martyr George [the word “holy” is lacking in witnesses 9–10], became a suppliant worshiper of this most holy widow [variant: “became,” in witnesses 9–10].

When he came to the aforesaid place after obtaining the imperial power, it happened that he rested there on a bed placed where the most holy soul had been freed from the prison of the flesh. The emperor was suddenly struck by so great a burden of illness that, unable to rise from his bed, he sought the various opinions of his attendants concerning the cause of so great and sudden a pain.

All declared with one voice [the words are lacking in witnesses 9–10] that the reverence due to that holy place was the cause of such an affliction. He pondered this within himself for a long time, reconsidering whether he had offended the venerable Augusta in some other way. Moved to repentance, he ordered himself carried to the chapel of the tomb.

Since her merits could not be celebrated without a decree of the apostolic see and the consent of the clergy, he promised that he would build an oratory to blessed Mary at the aforesaid place and freed the abbot of that monastery from imperial service, as she herself had established [the words are lacking in witness 8; editorial note: “Perhaps the charter of Heinrich III, issued at Speyer on 29 September 1002, belongs here”].

6. At about the same time (in the year 1008), a reckless knight came to the same place. While he was hospitably received in the house of a poor man, he began, at the devil’s prompting, to mistreat the man’s small possessions. Among the other injuries he inflicted upon his host, he killed the household birds and had food prepared for himself from another’s property [variant: “prepared,” in witness 9; the word is lacking in witness 10].

The master of the house, together with his wife, poured himself into prayers and tears. First he begged the man, through his lord the abbot, to spare him; finally, by the reverence due to holy Adalheid, he implored him to abandon such insolence.

The knight persisted in his brazen undertaking, indeed adding greater evils, and said:

> “I, alive, rule over you and yours this night [variant: “over you and your masters,” in witness 8]; but Adalheid, being dead, is powerless to provide you with protection.”

No sooner had he said this than, scourged from above for such calumny, while he hastened to eat the food wickedly obtained, he began to bite his hands and the rest of his limbs. Immediately bound because of his helplessness and the guilt of his rage, he endured throughout that night a harsh imprisonment of mind and body.

At first light, he was unwillingly dragged by the hands of those leading him to the tomb of Christ’s handmaid. There, in the presence of the brothers, he recovered the health of his senses. For that most compassionate woman, who had powerfully avenged the offense, afterward generously forgave the penitent man.

7. A certain religious woman named Frowessa [variant: “Eruowela” in witnesses 9–10; alternatively “Eruovvezza”; Canisius has it in the margin as “Eruovvela”] had been lame in both feet from early childhood. In the year following the memorable passing of the Augusta, she was belatedly gladdened by healing.

When news of this virtue first reached the ears of the people, an assembly of the entire populace took place in great joy. Placing a cross and a candle in her hands, they went about through various churches proclaiming divine praises [variant: “even to her hands,” in witness 10].

8. It also seems that the following should not be passed over in silence: it is known to have happened to an unknown man for the spreading of her merits.

While he was traveling through a forest called in the rustic language Biwalt [editorial gloss: “a vast forest beyond the River Lauter, between Luterburg and Weissenburg, today called Bienwald”; witness 10: “Biwald”], he happened by chance to be accompanied by a horse grazing nearby as far as the town of Seltz. For this reason he was accused of theft by a powerful man named Heimo [variant: “Hermon,” in witness 10], who at that same time had come there with the aforesaid Emperor Heinrich.

The man, pronouncing a definite sentence on uncertain evidence, ordered the accused to be scourged in a miserable manner, stripped, and blinded. As soon as the stranger had been blinded, he raised his mind and hands to heaven and said:

> “If I, innocent of theft and deceit, have undeservedly suffered such evils, you, holy Adalheid, restore my sight through your prayers and merits!”

After this, a certain man named Benno received him into his household and care. A few days later, when the pain had diminished, he approached the shrine of the precious treasure. After declaring his innocence, he recovered the health of his eyes.

Nevertheless, with the pupils of his eyes divided through the middle, he later displayed traces of true blindness.

9. Among the other gifts that this handmaid of the saints bestowed upon holy Peter [Note: [Col. 0988D] At Seltz; the monastery was dedicated to Saints Peter and Paul.] was a certain household [Note: [Col. 0987] *famula* in 8.], an inhabitant [Note: [Col. 0987] “designated” in 8.] of a district called Nortgowe. When a certain man, in insolent presumption, attempted to enslave this household for himself and his descendants, and no one could in any way subdue the person who resisted, he imprudently seized and blinded one of this class, named Benzon [Note: [Col. 0987] “Bezonem” in 8; “Penzonem” in 9 and 10.]. After learning that the man had recovered some sight a few days later, he captured him again and finally tore out all his remaining sight. Without delay, the blind man, disfigured by a bloody and pitiable face, while the wound was still raw, approached the monks, asked for the venerable tomb of his mistress, and, in the manner of rustic simplicity, began to reproach her for the cause of so great a calamity. Thus he did not cease accusing her amid weeping and lamentation until he recovered the integrity of his pupils together with the clearest use of his eyes—something that we know is not unheard-of, but rather rare, among the saints.

10. A certain woman also came from the territory of Metz (in the year 1038), upon whom, by divine providence, the affliction of blindness had grown. As she wandered through various places in her desire to obtain healing, she was warned in dreams by the saint herself to seek her assistance. But while she was seeking only the healing of her eyes, she obtained a double grace. For at that same time it happened that Chuonrad, the glorious prince of the Roman Empire, arrived with Gisila, his partner in bed and kingdom. When the venerable queen saw the woman standing there enlightened, magnifying God, the author of good things, with worthy praises, and rejoicing with her august kinswoman in holiness [Note: [Col. 0987] “herself and the queen” in 10.], she received into her own generous care the person who had been visited by the light of the blessed woman [Col. 0989A].

11. There was also in the regions of Gaul a powerful countess who had sadly become the mother of a mute son. For this reason, as she devoutly visited many monasteries, having heard so great a reputation for miracles, she eagerly sought the holy place and devoted herself there to prayers for three days. Afterward, having despaired through the long passage of time of receiving the gift of healing [Note: [Col. 0989] “from the Lord by healing” in 8.], when she was preparing to return home, she prostrated herself with the boy before the altar consecrated at the head of the life-giving body. The mother, intent upon tearful prayer, confessed that she alone was unworthy and bereft, and declared that she had come rejoicing in hope but would return in sadness. Meanwhile, the boy [Note: [Col. 0989] absent in 10.] was released into a sudden and peaceful sleep. After an hour had passed, he awoke of his own accord and rose happily; he grasped his mother by the garment and, with his first words, asked whether this was the tomb of Saint Adalheida, who, appearing to him in sleep, had released the bond of his tongue. In this way the matron, who had been about to depart in despair, spent the rest of the day there in joy. Devoted and grateful for her son’s recovery, she offered gifts to the brothers as they praised God in their sacred rites.

12. A certain man born in Burgundy had been so lame and bent from his mother’s womb that the soles of his feet seemed joined to his buttocks and his hands to his knees. When he was freed from this disabling infirmity through the merit of Saint Sulpitius [Note: [Col. 0989D] Of Bourges.], he was, by divine providence, permitted to be afflicted by another calamity, so that, when he was healed through the prayers of this most devout and holy woman [Col. 0989C], the power of the illustrious confessor might be matched. It happened [Note: [Col. 0989] “therefore” in 9; absent in 10.] that this man was living with the abbot of the aforesaid place, Gerbert, a man of blessed memory, among a crowd of other needy people, and was present at the morning praises on the feast of blessed Peter the apostle with ears that could hear but to no purpose. For, forgetful of both evils and blessings, and also contemptuous of the venerable time and place, he began to exchange obscene words with men and women, and thus, with gatherings of fools, obstructed the divine praise.

Then suddenly, with astonishing speed, both his arms sprang tightly backward onto his back, and both his hands were bent back upon themselves with such force that, when the joints of his fingers burst, those standing nearby were drenched by the spray of blood. Nor was he struck by any lesser punishment inwardly, for he was seized by a most evil demon. Bound by this double penalty, he moved the entire people to tears [Note: [Col. 0989] “weeping” in 9 and 10.] and lamentation as they watched the pitiable spectacle. But while the choir of monks celebrated the praises of God during Mass, and the whole people, in mournful tones, invoked the merits of Saint Adalheida in prayer, at last, when the knots of his arms had been loosened [Col. 0990A], he regained the integrity of mind and body. Nevertheless, after several days he became mute, and at the tomb of that most blessed mother he recovered the use of his tongue.

13. In the time of the third Emperor Heinrich [Note: [Col. 0989] “Henry” in 9.], there occurred an extraordinary event involving a single sign, through which we recognized, by the truest proof, her spiritual power as belonging to the company of the saints. A certain man named Burchard [Note: [Col. 0989] “Burcardus” in 10.], faithfully serving Liudpold [Note: [Col. 0989] “Liudolfus” in 8.], archbishop of Mainz [Note: [Col. 0989D] He held office from 1051 to 1060], belonged, by the servile condition of his family, to the dominion of the venerable empress. Through her most generous [Note: [Col. 0989] “Most abundant” in 9 and 10.] kindness, he had been given an estate belonging to his ancestors, which he possessed by hereditary right without any doubtful dispute; and for that reason he was accustomed to venerate his benefactress and mistress with the utmost devotion [Col. 0990B].

It happened, however, that Otto, duke of the Alamanni, of Swinvorth [Note: [Col. 0989D] Duke from 1048 to 1057.], although he followed many examples of justice and other virtues, nevertheless, inflamed by the fires of insatiable greed, began unjustly to claim for his own authority the aforesaid little estate, which perhaps bordered on his vast possession [Note: [Col. 0989] “of his possession” in 10.], in the manner of Ahab—or rather of Jezebel.

Thus, when the man had suffered such a violent and unlawful [Note: [Col. 0989] “Not legally” in 10.] loss of land and despaired of human protection against the height of so great a power, he recalled in his mind the privilege of the generous gift and faithfully approached the protection of the mistress who had bestowed it. Bringing with him, in pitiable attire, the charter drawn up concerning the aforesaid possession, he placed it upon the sacred tomb. With the convenient ringing of bells and a plaintive [Note: [Col. 0989] “Lamenting” in 9 and 10.] outcry, he declared in rustic fashion that he was awakening his mistress, who was sleeping, and urged the congregation of the brothers to pity his misfortune [Note: [Col. 0989] “To lament” in 8.] and provide him consolation [Note: [Col. 0989] “And” in 9 and 10; “for the sole consolation” in 8.] through the pious patroness.

Strengthened, therefore, by the promises of fraternal consolation, he returned home fortified, with the anchor of hope amid the waves of such adversity. Afterward, when the aforesaid duke had been struck by a very grave illness, blessed Adalheida appeared to him in the silence of night, with a face both severe and dignified, and forcefully threatened him with the dreadful fires of hell unless he quickly restored to her servant the estate unjustly taken from him.

The prince, shaken by the threatening rebuke of so sensible and venerable a person, brought the injured man, who had endured intolerable wrong, through a swift embassy. After first relating the wondrous vision and the exceedingly fearful threat of sudden death and eternal punishment, he readily restored to him the right to the lost possession. At once, the man who had suffered such great losses and obtained such benefits [Note: [Col. 0989] “So many” in 10.], rendering worthy thanks to the Lord God and Saint Adalheida, hastened joyfully to her monastery. He bestowed many gifts suitable either for ecclesiastical ornaments or for the needs of the brothers [Col. 0991A] [Note: [Col. 0991] “And” in 10.], and, after recounting the circumstances and manner of the restoration, never ceased praising Saint Adalheida and almighty God [Note: [Col. 0991] Here the text of 8 ends. “The Life of Saint Adalheida, august empress, ends” in 9.—In 9 and 10 the following is added:

**Hymn for Vespers:**

When the year has completed its course,

the festive light of Adalheida

has shone forth for us in blessedness,

she who now rejects the world.

Instructed by the teachings

of apostolic doctrine,

she uses royal power

as though she had never used its emblems.

She poured forth the most abundant riches,

filling the churches with gifts;

the great resources of the kingdom,

distributed, fed the multitudes.

She had resolved to follow Martha,

and had completed the work by hand

(the phrase “and had completed the work by hand” is absent in 10);

she loves Mary in her heart,

secure in beholding Christ.

To the almighty Thunderer

be eternal glory through the ages,

may join us through sacred solemnities

to the joys of heaven. Amen.

The office of Blessed Adalheida’s Mass follows; in 10 there are also offices for Vespers, Matins, and so forth.]].

[Col. 0991]

**SERMONS OF SAINT ODILO**

(*Bibliotheca Cluniacensis*, p. 371.) (C)

**FIRST SERMON: ON THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD OUR SAVIOR**

[Col. 0991B]

As we celebrate the most sacred day of the Lord’s Nativity, dearly beloved brothers, we ought to direct the gaze of our mind toward his divine eternity and eternal divinity, and, so to speak, toward the inimitable and ineffable splendor proceeding from God the Father. At his temporal birth, those things that are in heaven and those that are on earth necessarily and uniquely rejoice with spiritual exultation.

We have rightly said that the things in heaven and the things on earth rejoice at the coming of their Creator, because we know that, in the beginning, God made two creatures capable of understanding and praising him—namely, the angelic and the human. Compared with their author, these creatures are nothing; nevertheless, they exist much more excellently and happily than the other creatures, because they especially received from him the privilege of praising and knowing their Creator. The rest of the world’s structure praises God not by itself but through us, when, as we contemplate it, we marvel either at its beauty or at the wondrous wisdom of its Craftsman. And when we behold all that has been created, we are lifted up into admiration of the Creator.

We, however, who, by the gift of his grace, have been made companions of the angels in knowing and praising God, let us, at the birth of the Lord Christ, sing with the angels, “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will,” and let us say with the Prophet, “Come, let us exult in the Lord; let us rejoice in God our salvation.”

Humanity had been created to contemplate its Creator, so that, always seeking his appearance, it might behold him, and, beholding him, might seek him, and might remain without end in the solemnity of that love. After the condition of human nature, persuaded by the apostate angel, lost the light of invisible things in its first parent and poured itself entirely into love of visible things, it was blinded to inner contemplation in proportion as it was deformedly scattered outwardly. Though it would have become spiritual in the flesh had it chosen to keep the commandment [Col. 0992B] of its Creator, by abandoning its Author it became carnal in mind.

Hence it happens that it knows nothing except what it learns, so to speak, by touching with the eyes of the body, and thinks only of those things that it draws into the mind through bodily images. While the mind, having expanded itself, gazes upon its entire being in these things, it grows coarse and dull with respect to the subtlety of inward understanding. And because it can no longer raise itself to the heights, having lost heavenly beauty, it willingly lies deformed in these lower things.

But almighty God, who created humanity in his own image, did not wish it to perish eternally in its deformity. He sent his Son, who also appeared among human beings beautiful in form beyond the sons of men, so that the human being whom he had wondrously formed by the power of his divinity, he might mercifully reform through the presence of his humanity, and transform from an unformed shape into a beautiful form.

The Lord assumed the form of a servant in order to reconcile us to God the Father. He wished to appear visibly in our flesh so that, with him as our guide, we might return to the love of invisible things. O sign of great compassion! O ineffable mystery of divine mercy! Almighty God determined to redeem humanity; and, in redeeming humanity, he also showed himself bodily. He himself, so to speak, following after the traces of his fugitive, the Place came in order to redeem the human being whom he had lost.

For if the Creator could in no way be called a place, the Psalmist, praising God, would never have said, “The children of your servants shall dwell there.” We say “there” only when we specifically designate a place. Our Creator, although he is the place of all things and yet is without place, when he came into the world had no proper place on earth, just as he himself said: “The Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.” And according to the evangelist Luke, he was placed in a manger, because there was no place for his most pure mother in the lodging.

Who has ever seen anything like this? Who has ever heard of anything comparable? For as great as was the humility in the humanity he assumed, so great was the sublimity in his divine majesty. How sublime in what belonged to him, how humble in what belonged to us: he lay in a manger, yet he sat in heaven; lying in his mother’s lap, yet sitting at the right hand of the Father. Though before all ages he was the only-begotten of God the Father, in time he became the Son of the Virgin. Without losing what he was, he became what he was not. He became a sharer in our mortality so that he might make us sharers in his life.

Today has been fulfilled that prophecy of the prophet Isaiah who says: “A branch shall go forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root.” Again, he himself says more plainly: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son.” Again, the same prophet says: “A child is born to us; a son is given to us.” Exceedingly sweet is that he was born; exceedingly salutary is that he was given. When you hear that Christ was born for you, rejoice. When you also hear that he was given to you, rejoice much more.

But between the Father and the one born, and between the giver and the gift, according to the divine nature, do not suppose that there is any difference.
