For, according to the essence of divinity, the Father and the one born, the giver and the gift, are of one substance. He who was given is as great as he from whom he was given. And he who was begotten is such as he from whom he was begotten. The Begetter did not precede him in time; the one begotten is not inferior to the Begetter.

The Holy Spirit also is believed and proclaimed to be of the same nature, power, and majesty. By his coming upon her, the womb of the most holy and ever-virgin received the Word of God; today the whole world commemorates her unique childbirth. For the grace of so great a reality, and of so divine and ineffable a mystery, causes not only the righteous on earth to exult, but also the ministers of the supreme divinity on high to rejoice.

Therefore, although burdened by our own transgressions, let us anticipate his presence with confession of the Lord, and let us rejoice to him in psalms. Let us attend upon him with humble devotion, so that he may attend upon us with merciful compassion, and so that we may confidently say: He is present with us—he who, as has been said, was born and given for us.

Without doubt, the Lord will be present with us; and according to his divine nature, wholly and everywhere, he is present in all places. For he who, according to his unbounded substance, always possesses being cannot fail to be present with us who serve him, just as he said to his disciples: “Behold, I am with you all days, until the consummation of the age.” If he promised that he would be with his faithful on every day, how much more will he be present with us on the day of his birth, if the service of our devotion is more ready for him!

He speaks through Solomon: “I came forth from the mouth of the Most High, the firstborn before every creature.” And again: “The Lord possessed me at the beginning of his ways, before he made anything from the beginning; before the ages I was established.” And he who says through Isaiah, “I fill heaven and earth,” is today, through the wondrous mystery of his arrangement, placed in a manger.

The one whom Solomon shows to have existed eternally before the ages, Isaiah affirms to be absent from no place. He who always is and is everywhere cannot be absent from us. I have said boldly: he cannot. He cannot do this powerfully. Such impotence is omnipotence. This impossibility is supreme possibility.

How true and faithful are the testimonies of the ancient prophets concerning the eternity of Christ and his divine, unbounded presence—the flowing, heavenly, loud-sounding trumpet proclaims with a great voice. “Jesus Christ,” it says, “yesterday and today, he is the same also through the ages.” And elsewhere, using a testimony from David: “But you are the same, and your years shall not fail.” And the Savior himself says in the Gospel to the Jews: “Before Abraham came to be, I am.”

But although he eternally existed with God the Father before Abraham—or, to speak more truly, before every creature—he nevertheless willed to be born in time from the seed of Abraham. For God the Father said to Abraham: “In your seed all the nations of the earth shall be blessed.”

The blessed patriarch David also merited the distinguished privilege of such a promise. To him God the Father, revealing the uncertain and hidden things of his wisdom, said: “From the fruit of your womb I shall place upon my throne.” The prophet Jeremiah likewise affirmed this when he said: “Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I shall raise up for David a righteous shoot.”

Considering the magnificence of this most noble shoot and the sublimity and excellence of this sweetest fruit, the prophet Isaiah, anticipated by the Holy Spirit, foretold it, saying: “On that day the shoot of the house of the Lord shall be in magnificence, and the fruit of the earth shall be exalted.”

These two men, who more openly than the other patriarchs received the promise of the Savior’s coming, rightly obtained the first and principal place in the account of the Lord’s generation according to the evangelist Matthew, whose beginning is as follows: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham.”

The oracles of the prophets and the apostolic words agree with these sacred words of the evangelist. That the Mediator of God and human beings was born according to the flesh from the seed of Abraham, the prophet Isaiah very clearly sought to commend, speaking in the person of God the Father: “And thus, Israel, my servant, Jacob whom I have chosen, the seed of Abraham my friend, in whom I took hold of you.”

And the outstanding preacher writes in the Epistle to the Hebrews: “He did not take hold of angels anywhere, but he took hold of the seed of Abraham.” And that he was born from the seed of David, the eminent teacher began his letter to the Romans in this way: “Paul, servant of Jesus Christ, called as an apostle, set apart for the Gospel of God, which he had promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures, concerning his Son, who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh.”

And writing to Timothy, he says: “Remember that the Lord Jesus Christ rose from the dead, from the seed of David, according to my Gospel.”

Whoever, freed from the darkness of ignorance and enlightened by the light of faith, called the Son of God “Son of David” in the Gospel, merited to receive not only spiritual but also bodily light. The Lord Christ wishes to be called by this name because he knows that there is no other name in which the world can be saved.

Therefore, dearly beloved brothers, so that we may merit being saved by him who is the Savior, let us all say, let each one say: “Lord, Son of David, have mercy on us.” Amen.

**SECOND SERMON: ON THE EPIPHANY OF THE LORD**

[Col. 0995A]

O fraternal love and fellowship pleasing to God, we ought to know that the feast of the present day, which already revealed the devotion of the Gentiles through the affection of the Magi, has also been adorned with other mysteries and supported by manifold privileges; therefore it is rightly proclaimed celebrated throughout the whole world.

Today, through the sign of the new and manifest star, the ministry of the virginal birth and the joy of the Lord’s Nativity are openly revealed. For the radiance of God which, as the Gospel says, surrounded the shepherds when Christ was born, today brought the Magi from distant regions of the earth to that manger in which the Virgin who had given birth placed the infant God.

It is God who was then born in a human being; it is a human being who, assumed by God, is today worshiped by the Magi. Perhaps you are astonished that I have said that God was born in a human being, or that a human being was assumed by God. Hear the Apostle saying: “A vessel of election, full of God.” “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself.”

Blessed Augustine understands this in the following way and left it written in his works: “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself. God hidden, from God the Father; human, manifest, from the human virgin. The shepherds recognized him, taught by the angel; the Magi worshiped him, led by the new star.”

The fact that the shepherds saw angels, went to Bethlehem, and found the infant lying in a manger and wrapped in swaddling clothes, as had been told them, teaches those who are shepherds of spiritual sheep always to cling to God through contemplation of the heavenly life, to eat of that Bread which was born in Bethlehem, and to provide that bread of life to those entrusted to them.

The fact that the Magi, seeing the new star, came from the East, sought the newborn King, found him in their search with Mary his mother, opened their treasures, and offered gifts, teaches all the faithful always to strive to please God through the practice of holy conduct and the sacred work of the active life.

Spiritual joys follow, dearly beloved brothers, upon spiritual joys; sacred solemnities are joined to sacred solemnities. Thus virtues and rewards are heaped upon the faithful, if they consider carefully.

That most learned Gregory, who among the Greeks is called “the Theologian,” began his sermon on this solemnity in the following way: “My Jesus, and again, the mystery.” Not long ago we celebrated the day on which he who had become human came forth from the virginal womb like a bridegroom proceeding from his chamber. Today we celebrate the day on which he made himself openly known to the world.

On that day he was acclaimed by the songs of angels; on this day he was honored by the gifts of the Magi. Just as on that day peace was announced by the angels to people of good will, as the Gospel bears witness, so today, as the oracle of David affirms, light has arisen for the righteous and joy for the upright of heart.

If, then, at Christ’s coming light and joy arose for the upright of heart and the righteous—that is, for the shepherds and Magi, for Zechariah and Elizabeth, for Simeon and Anna, and for many others who devoutly awaited the salvation of the world—then for the unjust and wicked, namely Herod and the scribes and Pharisees who consented to his cruelty, there came immense grief and sadness.

What joy the coming of Christ brought to the righteous, dearly beloved brothers, and what exultation it brought, if you wish to know fully, the most faithful and sincere account of blessed Luke the evangelist will show. What anger and indignation, by contrast, befell the unjust and wicked, the sacred reading of today’s holy Gospel makes clear.

How fearful and breathless was the wicked Herod’s suspicion concerning the newborn King is testified by his deceitful and frightened speech to the Magi. He said to them: “Go and inquire carefully about the child,” and so forth. The deceiver promised that he would worship Christ, whom he was secretly plotting to kill. The impious man sought to destroy the one through whom every righteous person desires to live and without whom no one can exist.

In the meantime, by killing many, he destroyed them, but he could not find the one whom he sought to discover, not understanding, poor wretch, that the words had been spoken against him: “There is no wisdom, there is no prudence, there is no counsel against the Lord.”

Blessed Pope Gregory, that festive preacher, in the homily for the present day, spoke as follows in order to denounce the cunning of Herod and those like him: “Those who falsely seek God cannot find him at all.”

How Herod was deceived, when the angel gave warning, is shown by the Magi’s return by another road. How, after being deceived, he became enraged and revealed the mourning and groaning of little children and mothers. How arrogantly he raised himself against the Lord is shown by the precious death of the saints. How evil he was to himself, how wicked to his own people, and, to repeat the words of the fathers, how most wretched was the end of him and his followers, is thereby demonstrated.

The prophet Isaiah, foreseeing the joy of Christ’s witnesses and the exultation and gladness of the pious innocents, as well as the punishments and destruction of Herod and all the wicked, summed it up in a brief statement, saying: “The gentle shall increase their joy in the Lord, and the poor among human beings shall exult in the Holy One of Israel, because he who prevailed has failed. The deceiver has been confounded, and all who watched for iniquity have been cut down.”

How blessed is the prophet who condemns the impious by prophetic authority, rewards the pious by divine promise, and, so to speak, marks both classes of human beings—the good and the wicked—with an appropriate sign.

O wondrous prophet, who, as blessed Jerome says, should be called not so much a prophet as an evangelist: he fully discloses all the mysteries of our salvation, announcing some things still future through prophecy and proclaiming others as though they had already occurred through evangelization.

He promises that a virgin will give birth; he introduces a branch proceeding from the root of Jesse; he asserts that a child has been born for us and shows that a son has been given to us; and, by assigning such names to him, he thoroughly teaches that he is God. “And his name,” he says, “shall be called Wonderful, Counselor, God, Mighty, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace.”

He clearly declares that he will sit upon the throne of David and that he will establish and strengthen his kingdom in judgment and justice, now and forever. He urges Jerusalem to rise and announces that her light has already come. He commands her to lift her eyes and see, and to rejoice because all those gathered in faith have already come to her. In a clear voice he proclaims that nations will proceed in her light and kings in the splendor of her rising—something that the whole world today celebrates as fulfilled.

King David, from whom, as the most victorious Cyprian says, Christ’s birth according to the flesh arose, and who merited so great a grace that, as blessed Ambrose writes, a Virgin was chosen from his family to give birth to Christ for us—this David, in the psalm that was recited, favors those who devoutly celebrate the most sacred days of the Epiphany and fully proclaims what is appropriate to each feast.

Desiring to recount the mysteries of the Lord’s incarnation, he began in this way: “He shall descend like rain upon fleece,” and so forth. Foreseeing that peace with justice would come to the world at the time of his birth, he says: “In his days justice shall arise, and abundance of peace.”

For he knew that God had determined, through the humanity he assumed, to subject the whole world to himself: “And he shall rule from sea to sea,” and so forth. And because not only the Jews but also the Gentiles were to be called to faith and, covered in the darkness of sins, converted to the light of truth, he added, saying: “Before him the Ethiopians shall fall.”

Considering the mystery of the present day, he proclaims in a clear voice: “The kings of Tharsis and the islands shall offer gifts,” and so forth. And, still marveling at the greatness of his power, he says: “All kings shall adore him; all nations shall serve him.”

At the beginning of this humble discourse of ours, we stated that the feast of this day had been consecrated by many privileges of divine mysteries. Your fraternity may know that this is true because the authority of the Catholic faith commends it in many ways.

Today Christ appeared manifest to the world; today he received the sacrament of baptism, and by receiving it consecrated it through his presence. Today, as the faith of believers holds, he changed water into wine at the wedding. Spiritually, wine is made from water, because, when the letter of the Law ceases, the grace of the Gospel shines forth through Christ.

Christ is baptized; the world is renewed. Christ is baptized; the old human being is stripped off, and the new human being is put on. The first human being, earthly from the earth, is driven out; the second, heavenly from heaven, is put on.

When Christ was baptized, the mystery of holy baptism was consecrated by the presence of the entire Trinity. The voice of the Father thundered: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.” The Holy Spirit appeared in the form of a dove. And just as the Son alone willed to be baptized by blessed John.

Concerning this statement, blessed Hilary writes as beautifully as he understands it correctly: Although the whole Trinity accomplished the incarnation of the Word and the mystery of baptism, nevertheless only the Son was baptized by John, just as only he was born from the Virgin; and he passed through all the sufferings of the mortality he assumed without sin, while according to the nature of his divinity he always remained incapable of suffering.

But let us return to what came before. This day, as we have often said, is festive enough in itself, but it is especially conspicuous because it is known to be close to the Lord’s Nativity. When God is worshiped in a child, the honor of the virginal birth is cultivated. When gifts are brought to the human God, the dignity of the divine childbirth is worshiped. When Mary is found with the child, the true humanity of Christ and the integrity of the Mother of God are proclaimed.

For the evangelist says: “And entering the house, they found the child with Mary his mother; and falling down, they worshiped him; and opening their treasures, they offered him gifts: gold, frankincense, and myrrh.”

The gifts that the Magi offer reveal hidden mysteries concerning Christ. By giving gold, they proclaim him a king; by offering frankincense, they worship God; by presenting myrrh, they acknowledge him as mortal.

Let us therefore believe that Christ assumed our mortality in such a way that, through his single death, we may recognize our double death as abolished. How Christ appeared mortal and paid the debt of death, you have written in Isaiah: “He was led like a sheep to the slaughter.”

And in the person of Jeremiah we read that the Jews said concerning him: “Let us condemn him to a most shameful death.” Concerning that most shameful death, that is, the death of the cross, the Apostle says: “He became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross.”

And elsewhere: “Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more”; and: “In that he died to sin, he died once”; and: “Because he died for our sins.” Blessed Peter also says of his passion: “Christ suffered for us”; and, “When he suffered, he did not threaten.”

That we should believe Christ to be king, we establish by divine authority. For he himself says of himself in the psalm: “But I have been appointed king by him,” that is, by God the Father. And the patriarch David says: “O God, give your judgment to the king.”

And that he is the King of kings, he himself says through Wisdom: “Through me kings reign, and princes decree the laws of justice.”

And that he is truly Christ, God, and Lord, the whole world, created through him, bears witness on every side. For he himself says in the Gospel: “All power has been given to me in heaven and on earth.”

And the Apostle asserts that God the Father gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth.

And elsewhere the Apostle says: “Because through him and in him all things were created, and he is before all things, and all things hold together in him.” And the blessed evangelist says: “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made.”

If all things are known to have been made through him and to hold together in him, it follows that all things should be believed to have recognized his coming.

What shall I say about rational creation—that is, angelic and human creation? The closer it is to its Creator through thought, [Col. 0998D] the more joyfully it rejoiced at his coming. And not only did rational creation recognize that God had come in the flesh, but even irrational creation declared by certain signs that he himself was its Author and in some manner rendered him the service of obedience. To mention a few things among many, as the authority of our predecessors relates, when he was born, heaven produced a new star. The sea offered itself to his feet as something that could be trodden; at his command, the wind fell silent; when he died, the earth trembled. The sun withdrew the rays of its light; rocks and tombs were opened; the dead rose; and many who had been held captive departed free from the underworld. John Chrysostom speaks quite appropriately about these things: “Everything necessarily serves [Col. 0999A] him from whom it received the beginning of its existence.”

Therefore, brothers, we have said—and still wish to say—so much about Christ’s divinity that, while we behold him placed in a manger, wrapped in swaddling clothes, a humble human being among all things, we may have no doubt that he is the true God and Lord above all things. Yet that unique name of divinity, “God,” is very often referred to the Father in the divine writings, and occasionally to the Son. How often it is referred to the Father, the human mind cannot in any way determine; but that it is sometimes referred to the Son, we are taught by many testimonies. Hence there is the saying: “God, a righteous judge.” When we say, “God, a righteous judge,” we do not doubt that this was said of the Son. For he himself said: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son.” And elsewhere the Psalmist, after saying, “Lord,” added: [Col. 0999B] “God of my salvation.”

Jesus is interpreted as “Savior” or “saving one.” Scripture likewise cries out: “The Lord himself is God; the Lord himself is God.” How frequently Christ Jesus is called Lord, every page of divine Scripture bears witness: “The Lord who shatters wars”; “The Lord is his name”; and the Psalmist says: “The Lord is my illumination and my salvation.” He is our illumination because, as the evangelist said: “He enlightens every person coming into this world.” And as blessed Peter the apostle says: “He brought us out of darkness into his marvelous light.”

Christ is our salvation, as that same shepherd of the Church says, using the testimony of Isaiah: “By whose bruise we have been healed.” And blessed Peter says: “Lord, to whom shall we go?” And elsewhere he himself says: “Lord, it is good for us to be here.” Thomas, after [Col. 0999C] his resurrection, said: “My Lord and my God.”

Just as Christ Jesus is very often called both Lord and God, so at times he is called King and God, and at times Lord and King. “King and God” occurs in the fifth psalm: “My King and my God”; “Lord and King,” as in the twenty-third: “The Lord of hosts—he is the King of glory.”

Therefore, dearest brothers, instructed by these and other testimonies of divine Scripture, if we believe that our Lord Jesus Christ, mediator between God and human beings, Son of God and of a human being, was mortal in our flesh; if we proclaim him King of kings; if we adore him as God of gods and Lord of lords; if by right belief and good works we avoid the errors of vices, walk along the paths of justice, put our flesh to death with its vices and desires, despise visible things, and desire invisible things—[Col. 0999D] then, together with those three Magi and their three aforementioned kinds of gifts, we bring gifts to his manger every day in a spiritual manner.

To him be glory and power, honor and dominion, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON III. ON THE PURIFICATION OF HOLY MARY, THE MOTHER OF GOD

The almighty Word of almighty God the Father, coming from royal seats, appearing among human beings as a human being, clothed in bodily covering, willed to fulfill the decree of the Mosaic law, so that he might erase the record of the ancient transgression. For just as on the eighth day after his birth [Col. 1000A] our Lord willed legally to be circumcised by his parents, so, when the number of forty days had been completed, he willed to be presented in the temple by his Virgin Mother with the sacrifices prescribed by the law.

At that time circumcision cleansed the circumcised from original sin, and the legal offering provided purification for boys and mothers who needed purification and who had been polluted at the root of Adam. But neither our little child nor his most holy and pure Mother needed any of these things. Truly, the Son of God did not need legal circumcision, since he had not been formed through carnal union, but was conceived in the Virgin’s womb through the coming of the Holy Spirit and the power of the Most High, as the angel announced.

For he is the stone that Daniel saw cut from the mountain without hands—namely, Christ, born from the people of the Jews [Col. 1000B] without any human work intervening. Nor did the Mother of God need bodily purification, since she conceived not through the work of a man but through the power of the Most High and the illumination of the Holy Spirit. But for this reason he willed to submit himself and his Mother to the decrees of the law: so that he would not appear to be a despiser of the law, since he was the giver and author of both Testaments.

For the command of the law required that the child be circumcised on the eighth day and, on the fortieth day, as has been said, be presented in the temple, and that his parents offer on his behalf a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons if they could not find a lamb. In both animals, the grace of the saving mystery shone forth. The turtledove, according to those who discuss the natures of animals, is an exceedingly chaste creature; the dove is exceedingly gentle and patient.

[Col. 1000C] It is fitting that a turtledove or dove be offered for Christ, because he is the author of patience and gentleness, the guardian of virginity and lover of chastity. Coming to us and assuming a true body from the Virgin, he consecrated virginity in his Mother; dying for us, he left us an example of patience.

Today, as Luke relates, the child Jesus is presented to the Lord in the presence of his flesh, although he never departed from the Father’s throne through the presence of his divinity. Rich in what was his, poor in what was ours, he is remembered today as presented in the temple that David’s prudence and Solomon’s diligence had once prepared for him. Rightly did he determine to establish a house for himself through those from whose stock he wished to choose his Mother.

Fittingly, the Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary was born from the lineage of the richest, wisest, and strongest of all kings, [Col. 1000D] because she was to give birth to him who is the power of God, as the apostle Paul proclaims, and the wisdom of God; and, as Paul himself testifies: “In him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.”

This same woman who had given birth was poor in earthly possessions, but full of heavenly blessing. She was descended from a royal lineage, yet was so poor in temporal income. Poor in goods, she was filled with divine gifts. So poor that she did not possess the lamb offered for sin; so rich that, while preserving her virginity, she was able to give birth to the Lamb who takes away the sins of the world.

It was one and the same matter: Christ willed to be born both of a poor mother and of a betrothed Virgin, [Col. 1001A] so that the divinity present in the man might remain concealed from the devil and the rulers of the world until the time appointed by God. For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory; yet this was entirely necessary. If Christ had not been crucified, the human race would not have been liberated.

The Son of God himself, made for a little while lower than the angels, also became poor for us, so that by his poverty he might enrich us. O blessed poverty, which made us rich! O fortunate want, which made us wealthy! How great and of what kind is this poverty, which is announced by angels, revered by shepherds, most dutifully greeted and adored by Magi, and before which every knee bows!

What great and immeasurable riches did that aged, righteous, and God-fearing Simeon recognize in that child through the insight of his mind! Once he was granted the joy of seeing him, he desired to see nothing apart from him, [Col. 1001B] nor did he wish to remain alive in this life. If that old man Simeon had not recognized that through Christ and in Christ he could attain eternal life, he would not, after recognizing him, have so willingly sought temporal death.

As the evangelist Luke testifies, he had received an answer from the Holy Spirit that he would not see death unless he had seen the Lord’s Christ. After that old man Simeon saw the Lord’s Christ according to the promise of the Holy Spirit, and recognized that the saving light had come into the world, he blessed God and said: “Now, Lord, you dismiss your servant in peace, because my eyes have seen your salvation.”

Therefore, dearest brothers, following the example of this most holy elder Simeon, let us believe that the Lord Christ has come into the world. Let us faithfully embrace the remembrance of his coming in the arms of the sincerest [Col. 1001C] love, and let us be joined to him, as members to their head, so that we may not be separated from him until we are worthy to see him in the temple of his glory.

Let us also flee this deceptive and fleeting life and strive with the whole desire of our minds toward that life which is true and enduring, with the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, who, as he himself says, is the way, the truth, and the life: the way of those who walk rightly; the truth of those who love truth; the life of those who live well.

He lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON IV. ON THE LORD’S INCARNATION

[Col. 1001D] The mystery of the Lord’s incarnation and our restoration, which the faith of believers recalls on this day, although by its greatness and excellence it surpasses human and angelic understanding, was nevertheless announced in its entirety—as much as the devotion of the elect could or ought to comprehend and know—through the ancient fathers, that is, the patriarchs and prophets of the Old Testament; and the Majesty of divine condescension deigned to narrate it through the apostles and evangelists, suitable ministers of the new law.

How many and what great testimonies shone forth in the sequence of the Old Testament, so greatly favoring and so clearly corresponding to this sacred mystery, our smallness and ignorance cannot fully gather. Whatever the Gospels, the apostles’ Epistles, and the Acts say, [Col. 1002A] all acknowledge that Christ came to human beings through the Virgin.

From the sayings of our predecessors, therefore, the Catholic teachers, we know that the fathers of both Testaments, although separated by places and times, nevertheless unanimously held the same understanding concerning the glory of the Lord’s coming. And so that we may know this beyond doubt, blessed Pope Gregory declares that, like a heavenly constellation—the Pleiades named by divine Scripture, whose seven stars do not stand together in one place but shine together—the divine authors, though separated by places and times, shone forth in one faith and truth to explain the mysteries of our salvation.

Authority in David’s speech calls these not only stars but also heavens, saying: “The heavens declare the glory of God.” For these heavens, these stars, [Col. 1002B] and the other spiritual and rational heavenly bodies, shining by the Word and burning with love, received from their author—not from themselves—the ability to shine in speech, to burn with love, and, with the Holy Spirit teaching them, to narrate what they understood about him.

Some of them spoke more fully, others more briefly; some more openly, others more obscurely, about the divine mysteries revealed to them. Among them, just as Isaiah obtained a distinguished privilege among the ancient fathers in foretelling divine benefits, so Luke deserved to hold the foremost place in narrating the hidden mysteries of the incarnate Word and the Virgin’s birth.

This most divine man, and, as his whole account has revealed, most learned in every wisdom and knowledge, did not wish to begin the order of his narrative at first with those matters about which he was chiefly going to speak and toward which his entire [Col. 1002C] devotion was directed. Instead, he wished first to describe the surrounding miracles: the generation and birth of the Lord’s precursor; his wondrous life; his holy conduct; his abstinence, unheard of through the ages, in food and clothing; his steadfastness and constant perseverance in every kind of virtue; and his most vigorous freedom in reproving vices. He also wished to describe clearly the outstanding nobility and blameless justice of his parents.

After he believed that he had spoken sufficiently about these matters, he devoted himself entirely, with the light of heavenly grace preceding him, to explaining what he had in mind, saying: “The angel Gabriel was sent by God to a city of Galilee named Nazareth, to a virgin betrothed to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house [Col. 1002D] of David; and the virgin’s name was Mary.”

We have heard, brothers, that an angel was sent by God the Father to a Virgin; we have heard that the Virgin was greeted with a new form of salutation, and that, in the salutation itself, she was troubled, as the Gospel says. We have heard that the archangel Gabriel addressed her with words of consolation so that she would not fear, because she had found grace with the Lord. Then he declared that she would conceive and bear a son, whom he commanded her to call Jesus.

He foretold that this one would be great and the Son of the Most High, and that, according to his humanity, he would receive the throne of David, the house of Jacob, and an everlasting kingdom without end. According to his divinity, however, he had always possessed and ordained these things eternally with God the Father and the Holy Spirit, before the world existed, in his eternal [Col. 1003A] foreknowledge.

After this most dutiful and joyful word of consolation, the most holy Virgin began to inquire by asking, or rather by hesitating, how it could happen that the angel would presume to announce an unusual and unheard-of event with such authority. The angel thoroughly explained that this event—which nature had not produced and for which there was no example—could take place when the Holy Spirit came upon her and the power of the Most High overshadowed her.

O unheard-of and marvelous example of unique humility! She rejoiced that she had conceived the Lord and Creator and did not doubt that he would be born from her. She could have recognized herself as the mistress of all believers without any loss to her most sincere humility; yet she did not delay to call herself the handmaid of her Lord, saying: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to [Col. 1003B] your word.”

See, brothers, the humility of the Virgin conceiving the Word of God. See the obedience of the Lord coming to us through the Virgin. See the glory and love of God the Father toward the human race, as he sends an angel to the Virgin named Mary.

The exceedingly sweet interpretation of this most noble name clearly demonstrates the glory of her merits and virtues. For Mary is interpreted as “star of the sea” or “Lady.” She is rightly called Lady because, preserving her perpetual virginity, she was worthy on this day to conceive and, at the appointed time, give birth to the Lord of all creation.

To him God the Father gave all power in heaven and on earth, as the patriarch David testifies in the psalm, saying: “All power in heaven and on earth has been given to me,” and so forth. [Col. 1003C] Concerning him the same Prophet says: “The earth is the Lord’s and its fullness.” Likewise, in the same psalm: “The Lord is strong and powerful; the Lord is powerful in battle.”

And so that we might believe him strong and powerful, the archangel Gabriel—whose name means “strength of God”—was obliged to announce that he would be born from the Virgin. The almighty Father sent his only Son, like a giant of twofold substance, to defeat the prince of destruction and destroy the dominion of death.

It follows, then, that Mary, the Mother of God and ever-virgin, is called the star of the sea. Just as those who labor amid the waves of the sea through the practice of navigation desire, with the stars serving them by God’s appointment, to come to the harbor of rest, so whoever is endangered in the perilous shipwreck of this age, when destructive waves rush upon him, whether his soul’s [Col. 1003D] life or his bodily life is at risk, must direct the eyes of his mind toward the contemplation of this star. Through her merit and grace he may confidently believe that he can be freed from every danger.

For the stars, as you know, are ordered by divine command to shine at night and to precede the sun of day. And this bright and morning star of ours was prepared while the darkness of ignorance still weighed upon us and was already, by God’s favor, about to diminish, so that through her Christ our God, the sun of justice, might come forth to us. Of him it is written: “Behold, a man whose name is Dawn.”

The prophet Zechariah testifies that God the Father promised to send him for the illumination of the faithful, saying: “Behold, I send you Dawn, [Col. 1004A] my servant.”

Who has ever heard such a thing? Or who has seen anything like it? The Virgin, about to give birth to the Lord, calls herself the Lord’s handmaid; God the Father calls the human being who is to be born a servant and Dawn. Insofar as he is human, he is a servant; insofar as he is Dawn, he is the coeternal, consubstantial, and only Son.

Concerning him the prophet Malachi says: “For you who fear God, the sun of justice shall rise.” And Zechariah in the Gospel says: “The Dawn from on high has visited us.”

O how great and glorious a star the Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary proved to be! From her that radiance, that light, that illumination—the Word made flesh—came forth to us. He not only, as the evangelist John proclaims, “enlightens every person coming into the world,” but also governs, disposes, and orders the stars, the moon, the sun, and every creature that he made.

He lives and [Col. 1004B] reigns as God with God the Father and the Holy Spirit throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON V. ON THE LORD’S RESURRECTION

The resurrection of the dead, divinely promised to Christians, is held with the greatest certainty. For Truth itself promised it, and Truth cannot lie. The promise of the resurrection of bodies is therefore true, because Truth, which does not know how to lie, must fulfill everything it promised.

To make us know with complete certainty that this resurrection of bodies is to come, the Lord himself deigned to demonstrate it in his own body. Christ rose so that the Christian would not doubt that he too will rise. What went before in the head follows in the body.

We must know, [Col. 1004C] dearest brothers, that there are two deaths and two resurrections. There is a first death, and there is also a second. The first death has two parts: one by which the sinful soul departs from its Creator through guilt, and another by which, when God judges, it is excluded from its body through punishment.

The second death is the death of the body and the everlasting punishment of the soul. Through the first death, the soul of every good and evil person is separated for a time from its body. Through the second death, the soul of the evil person alone is tormented eternally with its body.

Thus the first death held every human being bound, because the transgression of nature made each person liable through the propagation of sin. But the Son of God, immortal [Col. 1004D] and righteous, came and, in order to die for us, assumed mortal flesh from us. Since that flesh could have no sin, he endured the punishment of sin without guilt.

Therefore the Son of God accepted for us the second part of the first death—that is, the death of the body alone. Through it he wiped away from us both the dominion of sin and the penalty of eternal punishment.

This is what Christ mercifully works in the world now: he gives those whom he urges to live well the faith by which they believe rightly and grants charity by which they willingly persist in good works. On the last day he will deign to raise them bodily for this purpose: to bestow eternal blessedness upon them.

Therefore, dearest [Col. 1005A] brothers, raised in soul through faith, let us live with justice, so that we may also rise bodily to eternal joy. We shall experience the gift of the first resurrection that Christ has granted us, so that, when we have risen bodily, we may deserve to reign without end with the Savior himself, when death will be swallowed up in victory and true life and true joy will be given to the faithful, when the same almighty God, according to the merits of faith and good works, will give his faithful the kingdoms of heaven.

He lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON VI. ON THE SAME RESURRECTION OF THE LORD

Although, dearest brothers, our devotion was directed toward this end—that a discourse, indeed slight or small, expressed in simple words, might proceed from our ministry to you—[Col. 1005B] the venerable mystery of this day nevertheless imposes upon us a silence more appropriate to the occasion. Yet when we fear to speak about so great and such a matter, the singular joy of the present day gives us boldness to speak.

And because this is judged to be our duty, although we are less than adequate, we must nevertheless not appear entirely ungrateful to this sacred assembly. The affection of your charity invites us to speak: ready to believe, devoted to hear, vigorous in action. The awe-inspiring service of the angels around the Lord’s tomb stirs us to exalt the sacred mysteries of this most excellent feast. The deeds and words of the most holy persons of both [Col. 1005C] orders exhort us to perform the same task without failing.

The unfailing devotion of the holy women invites us to narrate the greatness of this day. Indeed, while we seek God, so that no worldly failing may disturb our desire, the most worthy running of the disciples urges us on—a sight most pleasing, a sound most sweet, wondrous to behold, delightful to hear. For the Gospel says: “The two were running together, and that other disciple ran ahead, faster than Peter, and came first to the tomb.”

Who would not desire to seek Christ seated at the Father’s right hand and, so that he may find him by seeking, to run spiritually, when he recalls with delight that such great apostles also ran bodily to his tomb?

But so that he himself may aid our desire, let each of us cry out longingly with the words of the Song of Songs: “Draw me after you; [Col. 1005D] we will run,” so that afterward, with David and the apostle Paul, we may rejoice that we have run well, competed lawfully, and completed the course.

The final part of the verse written above clearly indicates the goal toward which such running tends. After saying, “Draw me after you; we will run,” it adds: “In the fragrance of your perfumes.” To run in the fragrance of perfumes means, restored by the holy fragrance of virtues, always to advance toward our Creator with the step of the mind.

These most devoted women ran this praiseworthy course. As the Gospels relate, they had followed the Lord from Galilee and, even when the disciples departed, remained faithfully attached to him until the time of his Passion. It is clear that they ran in the fragrance of perfumes both spiritually and according to [Col. 1006A] the letter, because, as Mark testifies, they bought spices to anoint the members of the Lord’s body.

How vigilant and diligent was the holy women’s search for the Lord’s body is clearly shown by their discovery—late, indeed, but certain. If the sincere affection of their charity toward the Lord from the beginning of their conduct is praiseworthy, much more praiseworthy is the service of their most devout attentiveness at his burial.

We read in the Gospel according to Luke that they received the Lord Christ with the greatest devotion in a certain village. And, as the holy Evangelist relates, they confidently invited him for the raising of their brother, namely Lazarus. From there they followed him all the way to the cross and the tomb, so that they might offer to him when dead, if it were permitted, the loving [Col. 1006B] care that they had shown him while alive.

If we consider it worthy of admiration that the holy women, with diligent care, performed the funeral rites of one whose teaching had brought them from vices to virtues and from darkness to light, and whose wondrous power had enabled them to receive their brother Lazarus back alive from the dead, what speech or eloquence could adequately describe with what devotion, of what kind and how great, his most pious Mother, the Mother of that same God and Lord, stood before the cross, as the holy evangelist relates, awaiting with pious eyes not the death of her child but the salvation of the world?

The mind cannot conceive, nor can any spirit comprehend, with what love and desire she would have wished to see him [Col. 1006C] whom she sought with all the ardor of her mind, turning here and there and circling the places of the Lord’s Passion and resurrection.

She knew that the one whom holy David foresaw as free among the dead could not be made subject to the laws of death. She knew that death could in no way hold him, since she knew that, for the restoration of the world, he had both willed and been able to be born ineffably from her, with no contagion of death intervening and her virginity remaining intact.

Together with the others, she sought her son in the tomb, but with a very different desire—just as, if I may put it this way, her profession differed from the purpose of the others, and fruitful virginity from the good of continence. The others sought him in order to embalm the body; she believed that he had already been brought back from death by God the Father.

For this reason, brothers, we have taken care to recount briefly the steadfast service of Christ’s male and female disciples around the Lord’s [Col. 1006D] burial, so that by their examples we might stir ourselves, according to our ability, to narrate the joys of the Lord’s resurrection. For, as blessed Gregory says, it is exceedingly unworthy that the tongue of flesh should be silent about the due praises on the day when the flesh of the Author rose again.

The glorious resurrection of so great an Author, and his triumphal encounter with the ancient enemy, also compels us to say something because of its magnitude. By the noble and wondrous victory of this encounter, that strong armed man who guarded his own court was powerfully overcome when a stronger one arrived. He lost the weapons and spoils in which he had trusted, because at the very beginning of the world he both perished first and caused the loss of others.

That one, supported by angelic majesty, after he saw the human being made in the image [Col. 1007A] of God, burst forth in malicious envy. He did not cast down another before he himself was cast down; he was taken captive before he captured; he was ruined before he ruined. While he robbed the human being of the grace of the immortality that had been given, he himself also lost what he had previously been. And while he sought to swallow up life by biting it, his bite became death to him—perpetual death—as the destroyer of death, giver of life, and mighty warrior Hosea spoke through prophecy: “From the hand of death I shall free them; from death I shall redeem you.” And again: “I shall be your death, O death; I shall be your bite, O underworld.”

Together, then, with this author of death, [Col. 1007B] death is subdued and driven out today; today, through Christ, life is restored to mortals. Today demonic slavery is expelled; today the Lord grants freedom to Christians.

For today the condescension of divine mercy brought a unique remedy to the world: when Christ rose, true light shone from above upon the human being who had been lost and surrounded by the darkness of death. The mass of the human race, which at the very root of its origin had been miserably corrupted by the cunning of the livid serpent and the fault of the first human being, has today been wonderfully and mercifully restored by the grace of the second human being.

By pride the author of death was cast down and struck down the human being; by humbling himself, the giver of life today raised the human being up. The ill-advised presumption of our first parents made us mortal; today the transformation brought by the heavenly right hand has restored us to life.

The apostate angel perished irretrievably for this reason: he naturally possessed no material for sinning in himself, but of his own will, deceived by [Col. 1007C] himself, he grew arrogant against his Creator. Divine compassion, however, grieved for the human being because it recognized that he had fallen not solely through his own will but through the prompting of another.

Hence holy David sings beautifully enough in the psalm: “When he falls, he will not be shattered, because the Lord supports his hand.” And this is the transformation of the heavenly right hand that we mentioned above. Truly, I say, it is a transformation of the heavenly right hand, because the order between guilt and grace is different. He who brought us forth by nature made us exiles from life; he who brought us forth by grace made us participants in life.

Let us hear what the first human being, expelled from paradise, heard: “The earth shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you.” Let us hear what the patriarch David, foreseeing the grace to be given through Christ, said: “The Lord will give goodness, and our earth will give its fruit.”

Let us also hear [Col. 1007D] what that Adam, made mortal and disobedient to his Creator, heard. Let us hear what the thief, hanging on the cross and confessing life, obtained through Christ’s mercy.

To the former it was said: “By the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread”; to the latter it was said: “Today you will be with me in paradise.”

Let us fear what, because of sin, we deserved in our first parent: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go.” Let us love what, through the working of justice, we trust was said to God the Father on our behalf by our Head: “Father, I will that where I am, they also may be with me.” And elsewhere: “Where I am, there also will my servant be.”

And the apostolic saying: “For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God. When Christ, your life, appears, then [Col. 1008A] you also will appear with him in glory.” That is the glory of which the Prophet says in the psalm: “I shall be satisfied when your glory appears.”

And let us also be satisfied, nourished by the sweetness of so many promises—we who once were in danger, worn down by fear of such great threats. Let servile fear depart; let divine love be present. Let the trembling of the old slavery withdraw; let the exultation of the new freedom draw near.

That is the exultation which the oft-mentioned Prophet sang in the psalm as destined to come to him: “But my soul shall exult in the Lord and shall delight in his salvation.”

And what pertains especially to the hope of the Lord’s resurrection and our own is shown clearly by the preceding and following statement. The preceding verse wishes a precipice upon the ancient enemy—the precipice that he had prepared for the human race through Christ’s death. [Col. 1008B] The following statement introduces the bones of the human body crying out to the praise of God: “All my bones shall say: Lord, who is like you?”

It is as though they were saying: “When you rise from death, you will grant us the hope of rising.” You rescue the needy from the hand of those stronger than he, the poor and needy alike from those who plunder him.

Because of their groans and miseries, you promised in another psalm that you would rise again. The Lord promised and fulfilled it. He died and rose again. He died because of our sins; he rose again because of our justification. Let us die for him, so that we may be raised by him. “If we suffer with him,” says the Apostle, “we shall also reign with him.”

Let us believe that the Lord Jesus was raised from the tomb by God the Father, and we shall find grace and salvation [Col. 1008C] in timely help, as the apostle Paul bears witness and promises: “If you confess and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved.”

In him, as that most blessed shepherd of the Church, Peter, says, “though you do not now see him, you believe; and believing, you exult with inexpressible and glorified joy, receiving the outcome of your faith,” knowing that you were not redeemed from your former empty way of life, inherited from your fathers, with corruptible silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ, like that of an unblemished and spotless Lamb, foreknown indeed before the foundation of the world but manifested in the last times for your sake.

Through him you are faithful in God, who raised him from the dead and gave him glory, so that your faith and hope might be in the Lord.

Therefore, [Col. 1008D] instructed by the teaching of so great an Author, let us believe in Christ and exult with inexpressible joy. But let us rejoice especially in this Paschal solemnity, in which, as the chief of the apostles says, “we have been redeemed from our empty way of life by the holy blood of the unblemished and spotless Lamb.”

We ought also to rejoice greatly in this: today the yoke of our captivity has been broken; today the hammer of the whole earth has been crushed. “This is the day that the Lord has made; let us exult and rejoice in it,” because the snare has been broken and we have been set free.

And, according to Zechariah’s prophecy, today we have been brought out of the pit in which there was no water, by the blood of the covenant. Moses prefigured this very thing when he sprinkled the tabernacle [Col. 1009A] and all the vessels of ministry with blood, saying: “This is the blood of the covenant that God has commanded for you.”

Almost everything is cleansed by blood according to the law, and it says that there is no forgiveness without the shedding of blood. This openly demonstrates that the abolition of sin would not take place unless the Passion of our Lord Jesus intervened, and unless he himself were an offering for sins, through whom the forgiveness of all sins is given to us.

O what a mystery, at whose coming every sin ceases! O what a sacrifice, at whose fragrance every offense flees! O what a priest, who offered himself so that by his death he might make ungrateful servants free from perpetual death!

Having made them free, he also calls them brothers and sons. Come, dearest brothers, let us strive with the whole affection of our minds to be peacemakers, so that we may deserve to be called [Col. 1009B] and to be sons of God.

Let us do, insofar as he grants it, the will of God, so that, having received this power, we may become his adoptive brothers—of him who, according to the faith and confession of the first of the apostles, Peter, is the natural and only Son of the living God.

With him God lives and reigns throughout infinite ages, in the unity of the Holy Spirit. May he preserve us in perpetual peace and grant that we may continually celebrate his Pasch with worthy reverence. Amen.

## SERMON VII. ON THE SAME RESURRECTION.

Today, beloved brothers, with our Lord Christ risen and bringing back to the world the hope of immortality, while triumphing in victory over the conquered prince of darkness, what for centuries had seemed difficult to unbelievers and impossible to the faithless [Col. 1009C] has, by divine help and mercy, been transformed into complete assurance. Let minds return to rejoicing, since the storm of deadly oppression and the cloud of ancient blindness have been dispersed, and the tranquillity of eternal rest and the brightness of the divine light have shone forth. Praises must be given to God, and such great benefits and gifts of his—so great that they cannot be greater—must be celebrated with thanksgiving. For we, brothers, who ought to love God with our whole heart, soul, and strength, must always and everywhere proclaim his blessings and praises with glory. But now it is especially fitting that this should be done, because the day desired in the prayers of all the faithful has arrived, and after the horror of the long night and the darkness over the earth, the world, illumined by the Lord’s light, has shone forth.

The coming of this light [Col. 1009D]—namely, perpetual brightness—and the sacred mysteries of its coming itself, prefigured from the very beginning of the world by the deeds of the ancient Fathers, proclaimed in many prophecies, promised by true testimonies, and displayed when that same light appeared in human form: just as we worship and hold them in reality, so the ancient Fathers worshiped them in certain hope. In such certain hope, indeed, that of the things they believed and proclaimed, they announced some as still to come, while they rejoiced as though they had already received others and as though they had already arrived for them. Did not the patriarch David already believe that he possessed the joy of this day in the present, when he said: “This is the day that the Lord has made; let us exult and rejoice in it”?

[Col. 1010A] From where did such great joy and exultation come to him in expectation of this day? He knew that through the sacrament of this day he would pass from the valley of tears and the mourning of ancient lamentation to the joy of eternal blessedness. Moreover, he knew without doubt that, in the hope of Christ’s resurrection, the sackcloth of prolonged penitence having been torn away, he would be stripped of the garments of mortality and corruption—which our first parents had sewn from skins and with leaves had covered their shame—and clothed with the robe of immortality and the garment of joy and gladness, which the divine utterances had promised him. He also said that, after the glory of the Lord’s resurrection had been revealed, and after Christ had risen—our resurrection having been promised at the end of the age—he could no longer be pierced by any sadness, but would eternally serve his Lord God with glory, filled with divine songs and heavenly confession full of praises. Therefore, joining with his own person the whole rejoicing company of the faithful, singing praises and giving thanks to the Lord, he said:

“You have turned my mourning into my joy; you have torn off my sackcloth and clothed me with gladness, so that my glory may sing to you and I may not be pierced with sorrow. Lord my God, I will confess to you forever.”

This kind of confession pertains more to proclaiming the mercies of the Lord and Savior than to exposing the wretchedness of the sinful human being, just as the same Savior shows in the Gospel when he says: “I confess to you, Father of heaven and earth”—that is, “I praise and glorify you.” And the saint in the Psalms says: “Confess to the Lord, for he is good.”

The Lord Jesus Christ became the minister and witness, giver and revealer of this immeasurable [Col. 1010C] goodness: minister by being born, witness by dying, giver by rising again, revealer by ascending. For he himself, who is the highest and eternal good, became its minister when he was born, its witness when he suffered, its giver when he was brought back from death, and its revealer when he was taken up to the right hand of the Father.

These are the four particular benefits of the divine gift, selected from all the Lord’s benefits and disclosed to the faithful through the four books of the Gospels, the four evangelists, and the four regions of the world. Since we faithfully believe them, firmly retain them, and recall them with such veneration as we are able—because from them above all we learn the Lord’s goodness—it follows that, as the Davidic word admonishes us, we should do this:

“Confess to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy is everlasting.”

The world, reconciled to God the Father by the blood of Christ—namely, the Catholic Church spread throughout the whole world—proclaims his mercy forever, since it does not doubt that by the gift of that same mercy it can be freed from the miseries of this age. The whole fullness of the faithful proclaims the Lord’s mercy forever, since through Christ’s resurrection, which today it celebrates with singular and most devout veneration, it confidently hopes to attain the glory of the resurrection to come and the joy of eternal blessedness, and on today’s [Col. 1011A] festival to see face to face the glory of its Redeemer, rising from death.

Let us therefore confess to the Lord, for he is good, by humbly accusing ourselves of our sins and sublimely proclaiming his goodness. Let us confess that he is merciful, praising his mercies without end, so that in this age he may preserve us by his goodness, grant us to enjoy forever both his mercy and his presence, and bring it about that, just as by the eyes of faith we see him rising in the flesh which he assumed from the Virgin Mother, so in the divinity which he has from God the Father we may see him reigning face to face, together with that same God the Father and the consubstantial and coeternal Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON VIII. ON THE ASCENSION OF THE LORD AND SAVIOR

[Col. 1011B]

After our Lord and Savior, through the most holy triumph of his passion and death, had abolished the record of sin, crushed the sting of death, and destroyed the tyranny of demonic cruelty, he alone, free among the dead, having conquered death, restored to freedom the human race, which had been held captive by death. The body which he had taken from the Virgin without any danger of sin, and which he had subjected to the laws of assumed mortality not by necessity but by power, he displayed, on returning from the underworld, glorified by the glory of the resurrection and, so to speak, restored to life before the eyes of the apostles.

He deigned first to appear to a woman who was seeking him with the greatest devotion—not without an admirable reason and a reasoned wonder. For it was fitting that the sex which, when deceived by the devil, had deceived the first man and suggested to him the destruction of death, should first announce to human beings the remedy of life. And, to take my argument from matters of greater importance, it was fitting that the sex which, when Christ was born without the contagion of sin, had gone before him while preserving the seal of its perpetual virginity, should, when Christ had risen, itself justified from sins, become the messenger of perpetual salvation.

There is no doubt that the Lord appeared to Peter, the leader of the apostles; through apostolic testimony and evangelical description it is held to be entirely certain. The Lord wished to appear to him individually before the other apostles, so that he would not despair because of his denial. He did not wish him to remain long under suspicion, lest he despair of being able to receive the privilege of the apostolic dignity. Therefore the Lord permitted him to fall, as the festive preacher Gregory said, so that through the gift conferred upon him he might learn how he ought to show mercy to others.

On the very day on which he rose from the dead, he wished to appear to two male disciples and two female disciples. To the women, greeting them festively, he said, “Hail”; to the men, as they walked with him and doubted about him, he opened the mysteries of the divine Scriptures and, in the breaking of the bread, fully taught them that he had truly risen. Then, as often as the most sacred and excellent office required it, he appeared generally to his disciples and manifested to them in person that the peace which, through the angels, he had foretold would come into the world had now come, saying: “Peace be with you.”

To certain disciples who doubted about him [Col. 1012A] he showed the scars of his wounds, offered his body, restored from death, to be touched, and wiped away the stains of doubt from their hearts. He also wished to appear to seven disciples who were laboring unsuccessfully in fishing. What was difficult for them he made possible by his bodily presence and divine majesty, so that at his command they caught the indicated number and a multitude of fish. If you were to see that number arranged according to arithmetic, you would know that a mystery shone forth in it to no small degree; and if you desire to know it fully, it is set forth at sufficient length in blessed Augustine.

For, so that the truth of the resurrected body might be evident in Christ the Lord, and so that the solemnity of the most worthy resurrection might, beyond doubt, add the glory of the accomplished resurrection to the fullness of true faith and most sincere belief, he ate a roasted fish and a honeycomb. In the roasted fish he showed that he had suffered; in the honeycomb, that he had truly been raised by God the Father.

We, most beloved brothers, believe that the Lord Jesus Christ reached the glory of the resurrection through the bitterness of his most bitter passion. But, so that we might know with complete certainty that the Lord’s bodily resurrection will take place in us, he deigned to demonstrate it in his own body. Christ rose so that the Christian would not doubt that he too will rise. In the passage of time, after the mystery of his resurrection had been accomplished, the Lord Jesus Christ ascended into heaven, so that the Christian might trust that he can ascend there, since he does not doubt that his head has gone before him.

[Col. 1012C] The authority of the Old Testament foretold the nobility and glory of this Lord’s ascension long beforehand in many ways; the angelic sublimity declared it as he ascended, exulting; and the majesty of the evangelical account and apostolic preaching narrated it clearly throughout the whole world.

Apostolic preaching, as has been said, vigorously recounts the mysteries mentioned above. The blessed apostle Peter declares himself an adequate witness of all the matters about which he speaks and, supported by apostolic freedom, proclaims them in the most open speech, as was appropriate, saying:

“We must obey God rather than men.”

He immediately added, and said to those with whom the event was then taking place:

“The God of our fathers raised Jesus, whom you killed by hanging him [Col. 1012D] on a tree. God exalted him by his right hand as Prince and Savior, to grant repentance to Israel and forgiveness of sins. And we are witnesses of these words, and so is the Holy Spirit, whom God has given to those who obey him.”

And in another place the same shepherd of the Church, relying upon the Davidic prophecy [fretus, “relying upon”; the text reads fruitus], says:

“Therefore David, being a prophet and knowing that God had sworn to him with an oath that he would set one from the fruit of his loins upon his throne, foresaw and spoke of the resurrection of Christ: that he was neither abandoned in the underworld nor did his flesh see corruption. God raised this Jesus, and of this we are all witnesses. Therefore, exalted at the right hand of God and having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, he poured out this gift, which you see and hear. For David did not ascend into the heavens. But he himself says: ‘The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand.’”

Finally, the distinguished preacher Paul, wishing to commend this mystery of our salvation to his hearers, addressed them with the thoughtful and spiritual circumlocution of one expressing a desire and offering a prayer, saying:

“May the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, give you a spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him, enlightening the eyes of your heart, so that you may know what is the hope of his calling, what are the riches of the glory of his inheritance among the saints, and what is the surpassing greatness of his power toward us who believe, according to the working of the might of his strength, which he worked in Christ, raising him from the dead and setting him at his right hand in the heavenly places, [Col. 1013B] above every principality, authority, power, and dominion, and every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the age to come. And he subjected all things under his feet and gave him as head over the whole Church, which is his body.”

And, as the same Apostle writes to Timothy: “The pillar and foundation of truth.” And plainly:

“Great is the mystery of piety, which was manifested in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, appeared to angels, preached among the nations, believed in the world, taken up in glory.”

Thus the evangelical account resounds through Mark and Luke. Luke, when he wrote to Theophilus, says that he had composed an account of all that Jesus began to do and teach, until the day on which, after giving commandments through the Holy Spirit to the apostles whom he had chosen, he was taken up. And Mark says in today’s reading:

“The Lord Jesus, after he had spoken to his disciples, was taken up into heaven and sits at the right hand of God.”

How, or in what manner, the angelic sublimity declared the joys of this present solemnity when the Lord ascended, human weakness cannot say with its mouth or conceive in its heart. Nevertheless, we have thought it worthy to insert into this little discourse one admirable and joyful testimony, as Luke narrates it, to be recited with such festive solemnity in the services of the Church:

“While the apostles were watching him go into heaven, behold, two men stood beside them in white garments, and they said: ‘Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? This Jesus, who has been taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven.’”

It is said that angels appeared in white garments as the Lord ascended because the human race, which had been covered by the darkness of deadly blindness, deserved through the grace of Christ to receive the garment of eternal gladness and fellowship with angelic dignity.

As we proposed, it is clear that the authority of the Old Testament foretold this long beforehand in many ways, for those who read the holy Scripture diligently and understand it faithfully. What does the divine Scripture proclaim to have been translated through Enoch, and to have been carried away in a fiery chariot through Elijah, except that the Lord Christ has today been lifted up to the right hand of the Father’s majesty? As he himself says to the Father through the Prophet in the Psalm:

“You have held my right hand; in your will you have led me, and with glory you have taken me up.”

Behold, the saint in the Psalm wished to call this journey of the Lord and Savior through the stars a course. What David calls a course, Solomon in the Song calls a leap:

“Behold, he comes, leaping upon the mountains, bounding over the hills.”

And the other says:

“His going forth is from the end of heaven, and his circuit reaches to its end.”

The one whom David foretold as running, Solomon foresaw as leaping.

O most prudent prophets! O most fortunate parents of so great an offspring, who have deserved through prophetic proclamation to become his parents and witnesses! For from your root the prophet Isaiah foretold that a shoot would come forth with a flower. Concerning him he says elsewhere:

“In the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord will be prepared at the summit of the mountains, and it will be lifted above the hills.”

And in another place:

“There will be a shoot of the house of the Lord in magnificence, and the fruit of the earth will be exalted.”

Whom, brothers, should we understand as the mountain prepared at the summit of the mountains, except the mediator between God and human beings, the man Jesus Christ, surpassing the nature and merit of human beings? Whom should we understand as the magnificent and glorious shoot of the Lord and the exalted fruit of the earth, except that same Son of God and human being, taken up today above the heavens of heavens and above the dignity of all the angels to the right hand of God the Father?

Therefore, most beloved brothers, fleeing the phantoms of every vice, loving the graces of all the virtues, let us seek him of whom we speak with the whole affection of our hearts; let us love him with all the ardor of our minds; let us follow him with the steps of love and faith, so that through him and with him we may reach the One who, through him, wished to restore the corrupted nature of the human race and, having restored it in him, deigned on this day to call it back to himself. He lives and reigns with him, God, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON IX. ON THE DAY OF PENTECOST

The inexpressible and immense majesty and glory of this present day, with the Word presiding and tongues giving their assent, demands by the force of its own power that we say, as far as we are able, how much divine mercy has cared for human misery. You know that whenever any undertaking has been brought to its conclusion, those who have carried it out are somehow compelled to gather themselves together and reflect at the same time on what sorrow or joy happened to occur along the course of the undertaking. This matter itself judges that such reflection is especially appropriate, so that the person rescued may give thanks to the liberator, cling with every desire to the giver of joy, and cry out with the Prophet:

“But for me it is good to cling to God, to place my hope in the Lord God.”

If we are urged, through careful reflection, to recall to mind the weakness of our mortality, our daily offenses, and the precipitous courses of a life of uncertainty, much more ought we, with the highest reverence, to remember the works of mercy which the author of salvation has performed for our salvation.

Let us contemplate the leaps which the incarnate divinity made for us [Col. 1015A]. Let us consider what God accomplished in a human being, and what the human being assumed by God, appearing temporally and bodily, endured. No one who firmly holds the Church’s faith can doubt that all the mysteries of the Lord’s coming were accomplished by the will of God the Father. That the Holy Spirit, coeternal with the Father and the Son, was their co-worker and the author of the humanity assumed by the same Son of God is made clear by the beginning of so great a mystery.

When Christ mercifully came to human beings, the Holy Spirit came upon the Virgin. When Christ magnificently sat at the right hand of the Father, the Holy Spirit descended upon the apostles, just as the universal Church, gathered in that same Spirit, recalls today with the greatest reverence and devotion.

When our Lord and Redeemer had been sentenced to the punishment of the cross, he was given vinegar to drink and said, “It is finished.” He wished this to be understood by us in two ways, as though he were saying: “It is finished”—namely, the Old Testament—and the New has been begun. Or: “The mystery of my coming has been completed up to this death which I endure for you.”

In the Lord’s passion many works of his piety were completed, while some were still to be completed afterward, such as the glorious resurrection after three days; then, in the passage of time, the wondrous ascension; and, today, the spiritual outpouring in fiery tongues upon the apostles, visible to the whole world.

Today, through the clearest testimony, we recognize that by the power of the divinity the dispensation of Christ’s assumed humanity has been completed with the coming of the Holy Spirit upon the apostles. For if, as we said earlier, we necessarily recall to mind the cause of every undertaking, comparing joyful things with sorrowful ones, rejoicing that we have escaped hardships and attained prosperity, what is as useful, what as fitting, as on this day—on which Christ’s bodily matters reach their completion and on which spiritual gifts become manifest in clear light—to recount, by recapitulating in a certain way, all that has previously been accomplished?

We do not presume or claim to be worthy ministers of so great a matter in a boastful manner, as the blessed Apostle did humbly and wisely. But, to confirm our faith and stir up your devotion, our smallness has judged it appropriate to say in what ways, as stated above, divine mercy has cared for human misery [Col. 1015D].

Christ was born from an incorrupt Virgin so that corrupt human birth might be transferred into a spiritual origin. He wished to receive legal circumcision in order to show himself the author of that same law, and so that we, circumcised by his example for spiritual joys—that is, instructed in heavenly disciplines—might be found fit for the construction of the heavenly building.

Then, worshiped by the Magi, he received three significant kinds of gifts, so that he who had become mortal for us might be believed to be King and Lord of the ages. He also wished to be presented in the temple; he wished a turtledove and a dove to be offered for him, giving us an example that, when we approach the altar, we should sacrifice victims of chastity, innocence, and the other virtues [Col. 1016A].

At twelve years of age he remained in the temple without the knowledge of his Virgin Mother. Shortly afterward, he was sought with ardent diligence and hurried steps and, as Luke reports, was found sitting in the midst of the teachers—not teaching, but learning and listening. When his mother asked why he had remained without her knowledge, he replied that he had to be in his Father’s house.

These childish deeds are supported by the firm foundation of the Catholic faith. When Jesus is sought by his mother, he is plainly recognized as a true human being. When he declares that he ought to be in his Father’s house, he is believed by all the faithful to be the true and only Son of God. Sitting among the teachers, listening to and questioning them, he signifies that no one should presume to undertake the office of preaching before reaching mature age.

It should moreover be understood that the Church’s piety approves nothing more concerning the Savior’s infancy than what the divine word declares [Col. 1016B]. Nevertheless, he passed through the weaknesses of assumed mortality—as the faith of the faithful believes—without any contagion of sin. The hidden God always remained impassible in the human being. And although the Son of God had no need to be cleansed or purified, nevertheless, at the appointed day and time, namely in the thirtieth year of his age, he received that singular and uniquely saving mystery of baptism. By receiving it he sanctified it, and by sanctifying it he gave it to all the faithful so that they might be sanctified through it, as though he had bestowed a heavenly gift.

But while he granted ministers of the Church the ability to baptize, he reserved to himself, claiming it as a kind of distinction, the power to baptize, as the divine voice announced to blessed John, a man of great merit, when Christ did not delay coming to him for the grace of baptism:

“He upon whom you see the Spirit descending and remaining over him is the one who baptizes.”

For he was the friend of the Bridegroom, the faithful and humble Forerunner, greater than whom, according to the testimony of Truth, no one born of women has arisen; he baptized and preached baptism, as the sacred Gospel records. For he says:

“I indeed baptize you in water, but the one who is to come after me will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire.”

How he baptizes in the Holy Spirit and fire, today’s solemnity approves clearly and ceremonially. As the blessed evangelist Luke narrates in the Acts of the Apostles, we learn that divided tongues appeared to the apostles as though of fire, and the Holy Spirit sat upon each one of them [Col. 1016D].

Therefore, most beloved brothers, I have wished to say a little today about the sacrament of baptism, because Christian religion is accustomed to celebrate it more and more at this season.
