Christ is baptized, and he is approved as the beloved Son not only by the prodigies of the patriarchs or the oracles of the prophets, but by the Father’s voice:

“This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.”

Concerning him the Psalmist says: “The beloved King, the beloved.” And Solomon in the Song says concerning him: “The beloved from the Beloved.”

Then, led by the Holy Spirit, he sought the desert. Having completed [exacto, “having completed”; the text reads exempto] the forty-day fast, he hungered as a true human being and overcame the devil’s temptations by divine power. Then, as a true Son of God, he made use of angelic ministry. Afterward, as the prophet Isaiah had foretold long before, he went to the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali. To those dwelling in the region of the shadow of death and sitting in darkness he displayed the light of truth—namely, himself, who said: “I am the light of the world,” and of whom the holy Evangelist says: “He was the true light that enlightens every human being coming into this world.”

Having called his disciples, he handed on to them the perfection of heavenly discipline, explaining the eight kinds of blessedness. He declared himself to be the source of all blessedness. He proclaimed openly the things upon which we should be built and proposed obscure things by which we should be stirred.

By certain movements of the assumed flesh, but entirely free from sin, he showed himself to be the Son of Man; through extraordinary miracles divinely performed, he testified that he was the Son of God [Col. 1017B]. Thus, joining human things to divine and divine things to human, Christ is proclaimed from two substances in one person, true God and human being.

Let us see how humanity served the divinity, and how divinity favored humanity. In raising Lazarus, he did what belongs to God; in weeping for his friend, he did what belongs to a human being—and so with the rest. To mention a few things from many: when healing the sick, he groaned; when feeding the hungry, he lifted his eyes to heaven; when addressing his disciples, he went up onto the mountain; when healing the weak, he stood in the plains; when hungry, he overcame the enemy; awakened from sleep, he commanded the sea to be still; when thirsty, he offered salvation to the Samaritans; when he wished to be captured, he caused his enemies to fall backward; when dying, he endured death, and at his death all creation groaned together.

At Christ’s death the lights of heaven grew dark and the veils of the temple were torn. The underworld releases captives; the earth gives back resurrected corpses. In the danger of death recognize the human being; in the operation of power understand God.

When he rose from the dead, he restored life to the world and granted his faithful the hope of rising again. In the power of his divinity he entered to the disciples through closed doors; in his restored body he displayed the marks of his passion as tangible proofs, showing that we shall rise in that same flesh and live forever in greater glory.

And so that no one would doubt the glory of the resurrection, when the Son of God ascended into heaven he placed at the Father’s right hand the flesh which he had assumed from us, so that we might believe that we shall ascend to the place where we know that our head has gone before us [Col. 1017D].

Today, from there, the love of God is sent to the faithful in the Holy Spirit, which the Apostle calls charity:

“The charity of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us.”

For the Holy Spirit, coeternal and consubstantial with the Father and the Son, is not sent as a lesser or unwilling being, but as one equal to them, sent by his own will from God the Father and the Son, because, as Truth says: “The Spirit breathes where he wills.”

Let those who dream that the Holy Spirit is lesser within the divinity be silent, as well as those who count him among created things as a created being. He cannot be lesser who is read and believed to be the co-worker of the entire divine work. Nor can he be counted among created things who is the creator and renewer of the whole structure of the world [Col. 1018A].

If I proclaim the Holy Spirit creator and renewer, I willingly agree with the prophetic words:

“Send forth your Spirit, and they will be created, and you will renew the face of the earth.”

If I declare him the co-worker of the whole divine work, I do not dissent from the authority of divine Scripture. When God established the structure of the world through the Word, the Holy Spirit was borne over the waters, as the divine page makes known to readers of divine things.

After the first grace had been taken from the first human beings through the devil’s envy, when divine mercy wished to recall perishing humanity to the knowledge of God, the Holy Spirit instructed the patriarchs, filled the prophets, overshadowed the Virgin when the angel announced that she would bear the Son of God, appeared visibly over the same Christ after his baptism in the form of a dove, and descended today in fiery tongues upon the apostles. Those whom he found to be merely human, he made gods—or rather, sons of God—through the grace of adoption.

The Holy Spirit is beautifully called God and Lord, creator and renewer, because those whom he recreates in baptism through divine regeneration he renews from the contagion of the old human being by remitting sins, and by renewing them he transforms them into the likeness of the second human being.

Concerning this same Spirit the Psalmist says:

“By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the spirit of his mouth all their power.”

And Solomon says of him:

“The wisdom of all things taught me.”

For, as the Apostle says:

“No one can say ‘Lord Jesus’ except in the Holy Spirit.”

And:

“No one speaking in the Spirit of God says ‘Anathema to Jesus.’”

O how great is this craftsman, how powerful, how effective! Just as, together with the Father and the Son, he created all things from nothing, so, whenever he wished, he was able to restore what had been corrupted.

In those homilies which the two Gregorys of the highest authority composed for the glory of the present day, certain principal works of the Spirit shine forth. They are called principal because they were festively set forth by such great authorities.

They say that the Holy Spirit raised David, a boy who played the harp and was endowed with his manifold grace, to the height of kingship. He enriched Amos, a rustic man who was pruning sycamores, with wondrous power and prophetic authority. He made Peter, skilled in the catching of fish, the shepherd of the whole Church; he made Matthew, a public tax collector, an evangelical writer [Col. 1018D]. He made Paul from Saul, and from a wolf a lamb, from a persecutor a teacher.

Brothers, how great is it for a human being to speak about God! What more shall I say? I shall nevertheless say what I feel. Whatever exists, whatever has existed, whatever may ever rightly exist, will not be without the gift of this craftsman. For whatever preserves the order of justice, whatever supplies the progress of prudence, whatever grants victory to virtue, whatever makes temperance honorable, whatever is upright in faith, certain in hope, and perfect in charity—all of it receives its beginning and increase from him who wondrously consecrated the present day by the presence of his coming.

By whose grace we have been made gracious, illumined by whose light, and comforted by whose consolation, let us love our Lord Jesus Christ by keeping his words, so that we may deserve to become worthy of the love, coming, and dwelling of God the Father and the Son and of that same Spirit, the Paraclete. Thus may the whole Trinity come to us and, by dwelling within us, perfect us as the temple of its glory: the one, living, and true God, who without beginning and without end lives and reigns throughout infinite ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON X. ON THE WONDERFUL NATIVITY OF JOHN THE BAPTIST, THE FORERUNNER OF CHRIST.

Celebrating the birth of the Lord’s Forerunner, dearest brothers, we ought faithfully and devoutly to consider how many praises we owe to God, with thanksgiving, on account of his memory. To repel and drive away the thick and terrible darkness of death and [Col. 1019B] ignorance, which the author of darkness had poured over the world, the light that would illuminate the whole world was about to come. Therefore it was fitting that a multitude of temporal and rational lamps should precede that ineffable and eternal light. I speak of the fathers of the ancient religion, by whose virtues, examples, and teachings faithful peoples, their perpetual blindness dispelled, were enlightened and instructed, so that, when he came, they might recognize him, if not wholly, at least in part.

Thus, as we have said, they were lamps—not from themselves, nor from elsewhere, but illuminated by that supreme illuminating light—namely, observers of the heavenly commandments: some before the Law, some under the Law, and others in the times of the judges, kings, and prophets, proclaiming beforehand the mysteries of the Lord’s birth, passion, resurrection, and ascension. [Col. 1019C] After them the Lord’s Forerunner, John, shone forth. He brought into public view, in clear light, all the proclamations of the patriarchs and the prophecies of the prophets.

For this holy man was not only just, but also arose from just parents: just in preaching, just in his entire way of life, and just in his passion. His birth, justice, holiness, and all his most sacred deeds were announced by the archangel Gabriel and fully set down by the evangelist’s pen.

It was entirely fitting that a child endowed with such dignity should be called by such a name. For, as the authority—or wisdom—of our elders testifies, John is interpreted as “the grace of God,” or “in whom there is grace.” No human discourse can express how great was the holiness and heavenly grace with which the Lord’s Forerunner was endowed. And because human discourse cannot express him, it must not remain silent about what was said concerning him and to him.

What is accomplished for so great a man when so little a human being speaks of him? What can human smallness contribute here, since the supreme and ineffable Trinity speaks of him? God the Father speaks of him in the psalm; the same God speaks in the Gospel. In the psalm: “I have prepared a lamp for my Christ.” Concerning this the holy evangelist says: “He was the burning and shining lamp.” In the Gospel: “Upon whom you see the Spirit descending and remaining, he is the one who baptizes.”

Certain testimonies that the Holy Spirit, through Isaiah and Jeremiah, especially utters concerning the person of the Lord the Savior, heavenly teaching and catholic understanding declare suitably to pertain to his Forerunner. The Holy Spirit also bore witness to him much more openly when, filled with the Spirit, he wonderfully leaped for joy at the coming of the Lord’s mother, while he was still enclosed in his mother’s womb, as the Gospel relates—not by nature’s power, but by grace’s assent.

The Lord Christ himself, to whom John bore witness, saying, “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sin of the world,” said of him during his preaching: “Among those born of women there has not arisen anyone greater than John the Baptist.” And having declared him greater among those born of women, Christ made it known that John was free from the fault of frivolity and the allurements of pleasure. He asserted that John was a prophet and more than a prophet. He taught that the man whom, by the power of his divinity, he had consecrated with the privileges of such great virtues and graces, so that he surpassed the merits of all mortals, had been called an angel by God and sent before him to prepare the way of salvation, as the oracle of the prophet Malachi reports.

For if *angelos* is Greek for what is called in Latin *nuntius*, “messenger,” blessed John is rightly called an angel. By being born of a barren mother, he announced that one would be born of a virgin mother; by preaching, he announced the one who would preach; by baptizing, the one who would baptize; by suffering, the one who would suffer; and by his suffering, the one who would redeem the human race.

He lives and reigns with God the Father and the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XI. ON THE VIGIL OF THE APOSTLES PETER AND PAUL

At the beginning of the vigil of the apostolic solemnity, [Col. 1020C] you heard that boy harpist—I mean David, the mighty king and most valiant leader of the Israelite people—singing. He was endowed with such great grace and providence from God that from his descendants the Virgin was chosen, from whom the Son of God would assume the body of our redemption. With him you sang, in joyful voices and devout affection:

> “The heavens declare the glory of God,  
> and the firmament announces the work of his hands.”

We heard of the heavens; we saw the firmament: the heavens declaring God’s glory, the firmament announcing it. Let us seek and see who these heavens are, how they declare God’s glory, what the firmament is, and how it announces the work of God.

The prophetic discourse would not introduce “the heavens declaring God’s glory” or “the firmament announcing the work of his hands” unless it wished the apostles and apostolic men to be understood spiritually, established immovably upon the foundation and firmament of faith.

If, however, we wish to understand the prophetic discourse literally, let us say that the heavens declare God’s glory when they present the sun, moon, and stars, arranged within themselves, in marvelous order at their appointed times; and that the firmament announces the work of God when it shows the stars of heaven shining and moving within it.

But we should not understand the passage in this way as its primary meaning; rather, we ought to understand it spiritually. These elements can more properly bear the figure of the heavens and firmament—that is, of spiritual teachers—than fully display God’s glory and the work of his hands. For these elements are mute [Col. 1021A] and irrational, although arranged rationally and wisely by heavenly power and divine wisdom.

Since our understanding can no longer discern the meaning of the psalm already proclaimed according to the letter, which kills, it is necessary that the Spirit, who gives life, teach us to understand it spiritually.

It is perfectly clear that the spiritual heavens were and are the holy apostles. If we call heavens those whom we know to be most eminent among their contemporaries in the order of teachers through different ages, then these are the heavens of heavens, the teachers of teachers, the princes of peoples, the sons of those cast out. On account of the merit of the great faith of Abraham, the supreme patriarch, they became sons. Concerning them the Holy Spirit speaks to the Church in the psalm:

> “In place of your fathers, sons have been born to you;  
> you will appoint them princes over all the earth.”

When we call Peter and Paul heavens, we do not exclude the other apostles from that exalted name. All the apostles, therefore, are rightly called heavens, through whom the world came to know the teaching of true faith. Thus we call Peter and Paul heavens and acknowledge each of them as the firmament.

First, let us see by what authority of the divine Scriptures they are called heavens, by what scriptural declaration they are called the firmament; then let us see how and in what manner they declare God’s glory, and how greatly and profoundly they announce the work of his hands.

The apostles are not called heavens without reason, since the Lord says through Isaiah: “Heaven is my throne”; and Scripture says again: “The soul of the just is the seat of wisdom.” If the soul of the just is the seat of wisdom, and heaven is the seat of God, then the souls of Peter and Paul are seats of God and seats of wisdom. Paul himself asserts that the Lord Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God.

And if the Lord promises that he will rest upon the humble, peaceful, and trembling person who receives his words, then without doubt he established the seat of his divinity in these men. Sitting and dwelling in them, he makes the world subject to himself and, through them, shows faithful peoples the way of salvation and the path of true humility.

We have learned, with Scripture as witness, that Peter and Paul are spiritual heavens. Let us see them declaring God’s glory—not in our words, but in their own most sacred words.

Did Peter not declare God’s glory when he said that he had been made a witness of heavenly and divine greatness, and that he had received from God the Father honor and glory through a voice descending upon him from magnificent glory:

> “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased”?

And again:

> “We ourselves heard this voice brought from heaven when we were with him on the holy mountain.”

Was Peter not the firmament when he said:

> “We must obey God rather than human beings”?

When he addressed the gods, standing in the midst of the people and established upon the firmament of true faith, he said:

> “Men and brothers, you know what took place throughout all Judea, beginning from Galilee after the baptism that John preached: Jesus of Nazareth—how God anointed him with the Holy Spirit and with power. He went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, because God was with him. And there is salvation in no one else, nor is there any other name under heaven given among human beings by which we must be saved.”

Paul likewise is believed to have been and to be a heaven or firmament when these words are read as having been spoken by him:

> “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments and unsearchable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor? For from him and through him and in him are all things; to him be honor and glory throughout the ages of ages. Amen.”

And elsewhere:

> “Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword? For I am certain that neither death nor life, nor angels nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor strength, nor height nor depth, nor any other creature will be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.”

If anyone wishes to know that what we have briefly proposed is true, let him read the Acts of the Apostles and the Epistles of both men more diligently. When he finds them declaring God’s glory more extensively, abundantly, and clearly, and announcing the work of his hands, let him believe with complete certainty that they were the firmament and the heavens.

Paul is not inferior to Peter, although Peter is the foundation of the Church. Paul too was a wise architect, knowing how to establish the footsteps of believing peoples; nor, I say, was Paul unworthy of the apostolic fellowship. He can easily be compared with the first apostle and is second to no one. For the grace of God going before him made equal the one who knew himself not to be unequal.

Both were called by Christ; both lived faithfully in Christ; both were crowned most gloriously by Christ. One was called from the shore; the other was summoned from heaven. The one from fishing, the other from persecution. For this reason they are worthy of double honor, because together they labored in word and preaching.

Moreover, brothers, lords, elders, and fathers, whose beginning in pious conversion and whose progress in faith and holy conduct we proclaim, it is fitting also to speak of their admirable and praiseworthy end.

For we know that Rome—as it itself boasts and proclaims, together with the whole world subject to it—was instructed by their preaching, consecrated by their blood, and transformed from various errors into the unity of faith through their merits and presence. [Col. 1022D] In the conflict and contest of the saints there was firm faith, certain hope, and most victorious charity. Against them stood the impious cruelty of Nero and the most abominable falsehood of Simon Magus. Through their persecution Peter was fastened to the cross and Paul was beheaded: the one suffered on a cross, the other was severed by the sword.

The place of their suffering was the same; their burial chamber was alike. They were equal in merits and alike in passion, heirs of the heavenly kingdom and co-heirs with Christ.

Those whom he called—as one of them asserts—he also justified; those whom he justified, he also magnified; and those whom he magnified, he also glorified.

By imitating their justice and magnifying their greatness through praise, may we deserve to reach that glory to which we proclaim and believe that they arrived on this day. Amen.

## SERMON XII. ON THE ASSUMPTION OF THE MOTHER OF GOD, MARY

It seems entirely appropriate and fitting that the Fathers ordained that, in commemoration of the Lord’s Mother, that Gospel reading should be recited which tells how those two sisters in mind and flesh received the Lord Jesus as their guest.

For the one for whom she prepared, at his coming into the world, a temple consecrated by heavenly power and dedicated to perpetual virginity, these two, as the Gospel relates, prepared a house for a temporary dwelling and offered the service of devout humanity and most sincere charity.

Their life and conduct were so marvelous and so celebrated in the memory of the faithful [Col. 1023B] that catholic and most learned interpreters of the divine Scriptures affirm that they preserve the figure of two ways of life.

Martha, therefore, who managed the household and provided what was necessary for such a great and distinguished guest and for his disciples, represented, as we have said, the active life. Through Mary, however, who sat at the Lord’s feet and listened most attentively to his words, the contemplative life was plainly prefigured.

Come, dearest brothers: let us see whether our Lady, the Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary, fully practiced both ways of life—both the praiseworthy active life that Martha cultivated by her work and the excellent contemplative life that Mary attained by listening and choosing.

Indeed, just as we know from the sacred sequence of his writing that the beloved disciple of the Lord, John the theologian, said and wrote little about the human and bodily actions of the Lord Jesus but much about the nature, power, and majesty of his divinity, so we believe that the Lord’s Mother was not so intent upon active conduct as to give herself wholly to divine contemplation. Rather, she raised herself with all the affection and desire of her mind toward the contemplative life.

She did not restrict herself to active life beyond what was fitting for the Lord’s mother. Yet, so that she would not be entirely deprived of active life, after she had been chosen by the Lord, greeted by the angel, overshadowed by the Holy Spirit, and made fruitful by the Word of God, she rose from her place and, traveling by a difficult path over the steep mountains to bring to her relatives the laborious service of active life, entered the house of Zechariah the prophet and greeted Elizabeth. [Col. 1023D]

She recognized in the spirit the noble pledge deposited in Elizabeth’s womb, and in these few actions, as we have said, she fulfilled Martha’s role.

If Martha was blessed, since she represented the active life, how much happier were those holy persons of whom we speak, who deserved to become recipients of such great joys and gifts?

What greater happiness can there be than when, in the Mother of the Lord—and, so to speak, in a royal palace—fruitfulness reigns in a virgin womb together with virginity? What greater happiness than when barrenness, sterile with age, generates and gives birth, and when an age that has earned the name of old age receives the honor of a new fatherhood?

And, as blessed Jerome pursues the matter in a delightful discourse, John also leaped and danced at Mary’s entrance. Through the Virgin’s mouth he heard the words of the thundering Lord, and from his mother’s womb he longed to burst forth to meet him.

How, how greatly, and in what manner Mary submitted herself, together with the other Mary, to the duties and services of the contemplative life—let the testimony of the archangel Gabriel affirm and the narrative of the Gospel discourse, for the speech of our smallness fails in recounting these things.

We know one thing with certainty: her entire life and conduct were always directed toward the Lord.

And just as it was said of the other Mary, “She chose the better part,” so the Mother of God, before all women, offered her virginity to God. For this reason she deserved that the Son of God, at the angel’s announcement, should assume from her the body of our redemption.

We have said that she was always intent upon divine contemplation, but we ought to establish this in catholic words.

To speak in ordinary human terms: where was she bodily when the angel was sent to her by the Lord? Certainly, in her parents’ house. Where was she in spirit? Truly, as we have said, in that vision of divine contemplation.

What was she doing? Living irreproachably, without prejudice to anyone, as was proper to her vocation, she prayed and read.

How did she pray? The song that she sang, exulting as with a tambourine, cries out:

> “My soul magnifies the Lord.”

What did she read? Perhaps the testimonies of the divine Scriptures came before her—testimonies that unquestionably referred to the ineffable mystery taking place within her.

Did she not believe that the Mosaic prophecy could be fulfilled in the pledge she carried?

> “The Lord,” he says, “will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers, like me; you shall listen to him.”

And she clearly perceived many other sayings of the prophets, in which the truth of so great a sacrament and mystery was foretold and plainly declared.

Did not the testimony of the patriarch Jacob appear to refer to this?

> “The scepter shall not be taken from Judah, nor the ruler from his thigh, until he comes who is to be sent, and he himself shall be the expectation of the nations.”

What could be clearer than what Balaam, a diviner false-speaking by his own nature but truthful by God’s command, confessed?

> “A star shall rise from Jacob,  
> and a man shall arise from Israel.”

The Mother of God, raised to the citadel of divine contemplation and instructed by David’s testimonies, knew that the Lord would proceed from her as a bridegroom from his chamber, and that he would be beautiful, as the same prophet foretold, beyond the sons of men.

Illumined by the light of the Holy Spirit, she did not doubt that these words of the prophet Isaiah referred to her:

> “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son”;  
> and: “A branch shall go forth from the root of Jesse,  
> and a flower shall rise from his root.”

What could be clearer? What could be more joyful? The noblest of the prophets announces both that a virgin will give birth and that a branch will arise from the root of Jesse.

It pleased me, therefore, to insert into this little declamation of ours a passage from the eighty-sixth psalm, which blessed Ambrose—a man praiseworthy in every respect and a true defender of the catholic faith—wished to expound so splendidly in connection with the memory of the Lord’s Mother and the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation and birth.

For this reason, as I said, I wished to append the opinion of so great a bishop to my impoverished work, so that what the poverty of my little intellect could not adequately pursue might be ennobled and commended by the authority of so great a bishop’s judgment.

For, according to the ancient interpretation, the most learned teacher already mentioned says:

> “Mother Zion shall say: ‘A man and a man was born in her, and the Most High himself founded her.’”

According to his divinity, he could not have a mother who is the author of the Mother. He was made not by divine generation but by human generation. Because he was made man, God was born.

Thus elsewhere you have:

> “A child is born for us; a Son is given to us.”

In “child” there is the name of age; in “Son” there is the fullness of divinity. Made from a mother, born from a father. Yet consider the one who was both born and given not as different, but as one. For there is one Son of God, born from the Father and born from the Virgin.

The order differs, but the two converge in one name, just as the present reading also teaches: “A man was born in her, and the Most High himself founded her.” Man in body, certainly; Most High in power.

Although God and man differ in nature, the same one—not another—is present in both. One aspect is proper to his nature; another he shares with us. Yet in both he is one, and in both he is perfect.

It is therefore not astonishing that God made him both Lord and Christ. He therefore made Jesus—the one who received his name from a body—the one of whom the patriarch David also writes:

> “Mother Zion shall say: ‘A man, and a man was made in her.’”

He was unlike the Father, not in divinity but in body; he was not separated from the Father, but received in the gift.

For the grace of this gift the virgin Mary merited, at the angel’s announcement, by conceiving the Lord; she obtained it by giving birth; and, remaining perpetually a virgin after childbirth, she possessed it without corruption.

Filled, as we rightly believe, with the gifts of this same grace, she spent the entire period of the Lord’s infancy, childhood, and adolescence with him. As a true mother, she ministered the service of maternal tenderness to the true Son of her humanity.

What were their conversations with one another? How sweet and loving they must have been, when virginity shone in the mother and fruitfulness rejoiced; when humanity appeared in the Son and divinity remained hidden!

What was that divine and virginal companionship, in its extent and character? It surpasses entirely the understanding not merely of us, but of all human beings.

Then the same one who was the only-begotten Son of the Virgin Mother, when he wished to appear as the only Son of God the Father, showed this through the majesty of the Trinity at the time of his baptism. The Father was heard in the voice; the Son was seen in the name; and the Spirit deigned to appear in the form of a dove.

A great man named John, sent by God, is a witness to this greatness, greater than all others. This man, who until then had been wondrously aware of the secret of the Lord’s incarnation and birth, became the wondrous minister of this mystery.

Therefore, brothers, so that we may believe in our hearts and confess with our mouths that the three named and distinct persons—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—are of one divinity, deity, lordship, essence, and simple substance, and likewise of equal majesty, power, honor, authority, eternity, immensity, and glory, let the most truthful words of truth and the truthful testimonies of the prophets, apostles, and evangelists admonish and teach us.

And so that the unity may be believed, confessed, and adored as supreme, simple, eternal, and incomprehensible in the three persons, and the Trinity likewise believed, confessed, and adored as supreme, simple, eternal, and incomprehensible, let the sincerity of the holy divine Scriptures invite us, and let the faithful authority of the catholic Fathers teach us—those in whose understanding and writings the devotion and truth of faith do not waver.

When the mystery of baptism had been accomplished and consecrated by the presence of the whole Trinity, the Lord Jesus went into the desert, not by another’s spirit but by his own and by his own will, where the evil spirit found him to tempt him. Overcome by the Lord’s power, the evil spirit withdrew from him in confusion while angels ministered.

Afterward he was found by blessed John and, because of his incomparable innocence, was called by him “the Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world.”

And so that the light kindled by God would not be placed under a bushel or remain hidden any longer, he went forth into public view. Because he found the whole world subjected to sins, he prescribed the remedy of healing for all and said that the kingdom of heaven had drawn near at his coming.

Thus the prophecy of Isaiah might be fulfilled:

> “The people sitting in darkness have seen a great light.  
> Upon those dwelling in the region and shadow of death,  
> light has arisen.”

Then, with the light of his divinity going before him, he called disciples from the various occupations and circumstances of this life, as the Gospels relate, and chose twelve from among them, whom he also called apostles. Through them he showed the human race the way of salvation.

The most holy Virgin always remained attached to their sacred assembly and noble fellowship. She always lived with them and rejoiced to present herself frequently before the Lord’s gaze.

The excellent part that Mary, Martha’s sister, possessed in hope and figure, the Mother of God held most firmly in reality. With the apostles she discussed the human actions of Christ, which she knew more truly and particularly, so that they might learn from her how to believe the secret of so great a mystery themselves and proclaim it more clearly to others—and, when the proper time came, transmit it to the world in writing without any ambiguity.

As the holy evangelist John reports, she was sometimes present at the Lord’s miracles. In these and in his other works and powers of divinity, she rejoiced beyond what can be expressed.

And if Mary, once a sinner, to whom he was merciful in forgiving sins, listened attentively to words from his mouth, how much more ardently did this woman, holy in mind and body, listen—she to whom he was both Lord and Son?

Moreover, so that the prophecy of the just Simeon might be fulfilled—“And a sword will pierce your own soul”—at the time of the Lord’s passion, the beloved disciple received this instruction concerning her:

> “Behold, your mother.”

As for the Lord’s burial, they say that she was much more concerned than those holy women. If I am not mistaken, that opinion seems to be supported by the good Sedulius, the evangelical poet, eloquent orator, and catholic writer.

If we wish to know what the Mother of God was doing after the Lord’s resurrection, before he ascended into heaven, there can be no doubt that she frequently went around visiting the places of the Lord’s birth, passion, burial, and resurrection. In those same places she shed tears and imprinted the sweetest kisses of her most holy mouth.

Then, nourished by the sight of the Lord’s places, she returned joyfully to the refuge known to her: the apostolic fellowship.

We believe that she was present at the joy of the Lord’s ascension and that, on the holy day of Pentecost, she received with the holy apostles the grace of the Holy Spirit—a grace which she plainly possessed in its fullness from the very conception of Christ.

If anyone, moved by devotion or by a pious desire for knowledge, wishes further to investigate what she did after the Lord’s ascension, how holily and justly she lived, and with whom she dwelt, this seems to be known only to God and to the archangel Gabriel, to whom her entire care is said to have been entrusted by the Lord; to the angels who rejoiced with her and spoke with her; and also to John, the beloved disciple of the Lord, who received her from the cross itself into his solicitude and care—namely, so that a virgin might serve a virgin and render to the Lord’s mother the service of devotion and love, since she had made him worthy of her affection above the others.

Her most pure life and conduct were not unknown to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, or to the other apostles; nor was her holy, admirable, and praiseworthy way of life unknown to them. For she was always with them from the beginning of their conversion until the day on which the only-begotten Son of God, a man truly born from her, wished to rescue her from the labors of this life and, as is believed and proclaimed, deigned to raise her above the choirs of angels to the glory prepared for him from the ages.

The whole world celebrates the joy of this day today. Today, because of the veneration of the Assumption of the Lord’s Mother, the angels rejoice; virgins give thanks; patriarchs and prophets offer thanks to God, because they recognize that their prefigurations and prophecies have been fulfilled through this same Mother of the Lord; and the apostles and evangelists exult when, in their true faith, they declare in their writings that the Lord came in the flesh and was born of a Virgin.

Today the martyrs also glory, celebrating the solemnity of the Mother of their Lord with worthy praises. The supreme pontiffs, confessors, and catholic teachers rejoice, while through their teaching the faithful believe and worship that the Son of God assumed what he was not and did not lose what he was; and they proclaim that the Lord’s Mother bore as a virgin and remained a virgin after childbirth.

I shall say something more, if I dare; I shall say it with faithful confidence, with pious boldness. Today the whole world rejoices and is glad with fitting jubilation. Only Tartarus howls, roars, and mutters beneath its breath, because the joy and gladness of this day offers some remedy and refreshment even to those enclosed within the prison houses of hell.

As I think, the ministers of Tartarus do not dare today to touch their captives, whom they remember to have been redeemed by the blood of him who deigned to be born of a Virgin for the salvation of the world.

Concerning the merits of this Virgin and her most glorious Assumption today, the interpreter of divine law—namely, holy Jerome—and other outstanding teachers were able and willing to say such great things that we neither dare nor ought to add anything to them.

Anyone who wishes to know fully the glory of today’s solemnity should read the sermon that the aforementioned Father Jerome composed and sent to holy Paula, to Eustochium, her virgin daughter, and to the other virgins—not only those present, but also those who would come afterward.

In that sermon, virgins—women who are virgins, and not only women but also men who are virgins—can learn how they ought to serve the Virgin of virgins in virginal and manly fashion.

Today, most reverend Fathers and dearest brothers, lords and elders, most devoted mothers and sisters, let us celebrate the feast of the blessed Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary, so that through her singular merit and through the prayers of all the holy men and women who are virgins, we may deserve to have the Virgin’s Son and the Bridegroom of virgins, our Lord Jesus Christ, as merciful and favorable toward us.

He lives and reigns with God the Father and the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

The Mother of God, who today is believed, venerated, and worshiped as having been assumed into the glory of heaven, above the choirs of angels and even into the presence of the highest divinity, is the one whom some of our people, addressing her with humble devotion, have been accustomed to call:

> “For you are the royal palace, the form of modesty”—that is, of bashfulness, which is always the inseparable companion of whole virginity and continuous chastity.
>
> “For you are, after God, the chief cause of human salvation.
>
> “You are the unique mother; you are the perpetual virgin.
>
> “You are the untouched mother; you are the fruitful virgin.
>
> “You are the mother without a man; you are the virgin without equal.
>
> “You are a mother who gives birth without loss of your integrity.
>
> “You have received so many divine gifts; you are adorned with such great heavenly gifts.
>
> “You are so abundantly filled with God’s grace that, through the flower of your virginal womb, the almighty Father overcame the prince of darkness and author of death, and removed from the entrance of paradise the flaming and turning sword.
>
> “Through the one whom your virginity brought forth, he opened for the faithful the gates of the heavenly kingdom, which the cunning of the ancient enemy and the presumptuous rashness of our first parents had closed.
>
> “Through these gates, as the firmness of the faithful believe, he assumed you to the throne of his eternity amid the multitude of angels. The Divinity incarnate from you festively came to meet you, just as the celebration of your glorious Assumption today displays it to the whole world.”

For the completion of this little declamation of ours, we have composed not a hymn, but, in the manner of hymns, a sufficiently modest and poor composition.

## SERMON XIII. ON THE BIRTH OF THE BLESSED VIRGIN MARY

**[Beginning missing]** childbirth. For the angel found her intent upon such services and greeted her.

As a truly modest virgin, she blushed. Strengthened by him, she believed what was said; and by believing she brought forth Jesus Christ, the Lord our Savior, whom the patriarchs and prophets had foreseen and foretold as destined to be born of a virgin.

The apostles saw him and proclaimed in true faith that he had already been born of a Virgin, and that he was made according to his humanity who had always existed according to his divinity.

What was he? What was he made? He was God; he was made man. He assumed humanity; he did not lose divinity. Made humble, he remained exalted. He was born a man, yet did not cease to be God. He was born a little child, while the Great One lay hidden.

Whoever gladly embraces God born as a man does not recoil from the Virgin’s childbirth.

God, the creator of man and the Son of man, says: “What is it that troubles you about my birth?” I was not conceived through the desire of lust. I made the mother from whom I would be born; I prepared and cleansed the way for my journey.

This woman whom you despise, Manichaean, is my mother, but she was fashioned by my hand. If I could have been defiled when I made her, I could have been defiled when I was born from her.

Just as her virginity was not corrupted by my passage, so my majesty was not stained there. If a ray of the sun knows how to dry the filth of a sewer without knowing how to be defiled, how much more does the splendor of eternal light, in which nothing defiled is found? Wherever it shines, it can cleanse; it cannot itself be polluted.

Fool, from where could there be filth in the Virgin, where there was no intercourse with a human father? From where could there be filth in one who experienced neither lust in desiring [or conceiving] nor pain in giving birth? From where could there be filth in the house to which no guest had access?

The Lord and maker alone came to her. He put on the garment that he did not previously have, and left her closed just as he found her.

Just as he was born alone among the dead, free, so the modesty of the mother from whom he was born alone remained intact.

Eve, disobedient, deserved punishment; Mary, obedient, obtained grace. The former was cursed when she tasted what was forbidden; the latter was blessed when she believed the angel. The former brought death upon us; the latter bore life for us.

What are you doing, Manichaean? You attack Christ’s mother; you do not defend Christ.

Let the unclean … [lacuna] … because from the most pure Virgin was born [the …] of the world … [lacuna] … To whom, with God the Father and the Holy Spirit, belongs equal honor … [lacuna] … and glory without distinction, co-eternal majesty.

Throughout infinite ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XIV. ALSO ON THE BIRTH OF THE BLESSED VIRGIN MARY

*[In Martène, Thesaurus Anecdotorum V, 621, from a manuscript codex of Silviniacum.]*

[Col. 1029D]

So let Mary’s life be set before us as an image of virginity, from which, as from a mirror, the appearance of chastity and the form of virtue shine forth. Here you may take examples for living: in her, as in a model, the principles of uprightness are expressed, showing what you ought to correct, what to avoid, and what to retain. The first enthusiasm for learning is the excellence of the teacher. Who is nobler than the Mother of God? Who is more splendid than she whom Splendor chose? Who is chaster than she who brought forth a body without bodily corruption?

For what should I say about her other virtues? She was a virgin not only in body but also in mind, never adulterating her sincere affection through any deceitful artifice. Humble in heart, dignified in speech, prudent in spirit, [Col. 1030A] sparing in speaking, more devoted to reading, placing her hope not in the uncertainty of riches but among the poor, intent upon work, modest in conversation, seeking the judgment of her mind from God, not from human beings. She harmed no one, wished well to all, rose before her elders, did not envy her equals, fled ostentation, followed reason, and loved virtue.

When did she ever offend her parents, even by her expression? When did she disagree with her relatives? When did she disdain the needy? She was accustomed to visit only those gatherings of men at which compassion would not blush and modesty would not be passed over. There was nothing harsh in her eyes, nothing bold in her words, nothing immodest in her conduct; her gestures were not languid, her walk was not unrestrained, her voice was not wanton. Thus the appearance of her body was itself an image of her mind, a figure of uprightness.

For a good house ought to be recognized [Col. 1030B] at the very vestibule, and should make clear at the entrance that no darkness lies within, so that our mind, hindered by no bodily barriers, may shine outward like the light of a lamp placed within. What, then, shall I say of her frugality in food and abundance in service—of the one exceeding nature, and the other falling almost short of nature itself? There, no hours were allowed to pass unused; here, days of fasting were doubled. Whenever the desire to restore her strength arose, food was generally taken in such a way as to ward off death, not to provide delights. The desire for sleep never came before necessity.

Yet when her body rested, her mind kept vigil. Frequently, while sleepless, she either repeated what she had read, continued what sleep had interrupted, carried out what she had planned, or declared what was to be done. She did not go out [Col. 1030C] of the house except when she went to the church. Even then, she went with her parents or relatives: at home, diligent and withdrawn; in public, surrounded by attendants—but with no better guardian than herself. In her walk and demeanor she was worthy of reverence; she raised not so much the imprint of her feet as the step of virtue. And although she had others as guardians of her bodily person, she herself was the guardian of her conduct.

There will be many from whom she may learn, if she teaches herself—she who has teachers of virtue—for whatever she did was instruction. Thus Mary attended to everything as though she were being admonished by many. Thus she fulfilled every duty of virtue, so that she seemed not so much to learn as to teach. Such did the Evangelist display her; such did the angel find her; such did the Holy Spirit choose her.

Why should I linger over each detail? Her parents loved her, strangers praised her, and she was worthy to give birth to the Son of God. At the very entrance of the angel, she was found at home in an inner chamber without a companion, so that no one might interrupt her concentration or disturb her. For she did not desire female companions, since she had good thoughts as companions; indeed, she seemed less alone when she was alone. For how could she be alone when so many books were with her—so many archangels, so many prophets?

In the end, Gabriel found her where he was accustomed to visit her. When the angel appeared in human form, Mary trembled, as though moved by the sight; yet, having heard his name, she recognized him as one not unknown. She was a stranger in the presence of a man, but not a stranger in the presence of an angel, so that you may recognize religious ears and modest eyes. [Col. 1031A] At last, when greeted, she fell silent, and when addressed, she replied. But she who had first been troubled in feeling afterward promised obedience.

How religious she had been toward her kinswoman is signified by the divine Scripture. For she became more humble when she learned that she had been chosen by God, and immediately proceeded into the hill country to her kinswoman. Certainly, she did not go in order to believe as an example what she had already believed through the oracle. “Blessed is she,” it says, “who believed,” and she remained with her for three months. Over so long an interval, faith was not being sought, but devotion was being displayed. And this was after the child in his mother’s womb leapt up at the presence of the Lord’s mother … [lacuna]. The remainder is lacking.

## SERMON XV. ON THE HOLY CROSS

[Apud Marten., as above, from a Cluniac manuscript.]

[Col. 1031B] After that singular, marvelous, universally proclaimed, and saving triumph of the Lord’s Passion, after the glory of the resurrection of that same our Lord, and after the most holy Paschal feasts, there is recalled, with the greatest dignity and appropriateness, that most celebrated day on which the insignia of the Lord’s Passion are found, to the honor and glory of God’s name and for the salvation of the human race: namely, the cross on which the author of our salvation hung, and the nails by which that most sacred body was fastened—the body which the Son of God deigned to assume from the undefiled Virgin, having been ineffably begotten by God the Father before all temporal ages.

With good reason, therefore, the entire faithful household of the Church most solemnly commemorates, over the course of the years, the finding and exaltation of the saving gallows, because [Col. 1031C] through the cross it learned that the dominion of death had been destroyed; through the cross it recalls that it escaped the destruction of eternal death; and through the cross it rejoices that it found the support of eternal life. For when the finding of the Lord’s victorious cross is celebrated, the resurrection of the crucified Lord is most clearly recalled; and when the exaltation of that same cross is honored, it is recognized that the Lord Jesus Christ, crucified upon it, ascended into heaven.

To confirm the greatness of this matter, certain corresponding praises are found in Scripture, so that when like things are joined to like, no one may be found unbelieving in what is said about God. A woman, deceived by a serpent’s falsehood, brought death to her husband, indeed to the whole human race; the humble devotion of holy women, with an angel’s truthful proclamation, announced to the apostolic company that the Lord [Col. 1031D] had risen. You have heard that the disobedient man was expelled from paradise through the tasting of wood; you have heard that the confessing thief was led into paradise through humble confession. A wanton woman, wickedly recommending divorce, pointed out the way to hell; an intact virgin directed the straight path to heaven. A corrupted woman brought death upon her offspring; an undefiled virgin bestowed perpetual life upon the human race.

Mary Magdalene, once a sinner, brought joy concerning that same resurrection; the empress Helena, through the discovery of the cross and the other insignia of the Lord’s Passion, displayed joy and gladness to the faithful peoples then living and to those who would come afterward. Mary, the Lord’s mother, at the time when her only-begotten Son, the Lord, [Col. 1032A] was suffering, stood before the cross and, with devout eyes, as the catholic teacher Ambrose writes, awaited not the death of her beloved Son but the salvation of the world. The evangelical poet Sedulius likewise asserts that, concerning the Lord’s burial, she was more solicitous than the other women.

Helena, on the other hand, the ruler of the Roman Empire, diligently and earnestly devoted herself to seeking and discovering the instruments of the Lord’s bodily punishment and the insignia of our salvation. With devout affection and sincere fulfillment, she labored with all her desires to find what she sought; and once it was found, she eagerly wished to honor it to the Lord’s honor and glory.

For carrying out this undertaking she had as a most energetic helper her son Constantine, prince of the Roman Empire, who, first among the rulers of the world, with the counsel and zeal of the aforementioned and frequently mentioned Helena, granted liberty and privilege to the Roman Church. From that time, with the Lord’s approval and through the action of the prince just mentioned, without anyone’s opposition, the honor and power of Christ, the faith and victory of the crucified Lord began to be publicly proclaimed throughout all the regions of the world to which the power of the Roman Empire extended—not merely to the boundaries of the Roman Empire, but as far as the majesty of the divine and incarnate Word is proclaimed, and as far as the authority of the holy Gospel, which saves the world, resounds with living and unhindered voice, proclaiming the honor and glory of the cross and the deeds and wonders of the crucified Lord.

What are we wretched people attempting to say in praise of the cross? What do we unlearned persons presume to utter, when we know that so many and such great things are spoken daily by our elders and betters, so that the wisdom of the newly faithful proclaimed what was known most firmly to angels, human beings, and all the faithful? The Son of God mercifully deigned to assume a human being from the Virgin; having become human, he wished to appear among human beings; and through the human being whom he assumed, he wished to free the human race from the destruction of perpetual death and to lead it back from darkness to light, from death to life.

And he knew—as he knows all things—that the presumption of our first parents could not be corrected unless divine condescension assumed our humanity. But the proud rashness of our first parents would always reign in the world, as we have said, nor could the guilt that had spread through the world by the unlawful tasting of wood be dissolved, unless Christ, hanging upon the wood of the cross, erased with his blood the bond of mortal condemnation. [Col. 1032D]

It is necessary, dearest brothers, that whoever rejoices to have been redeemed by Christ’s precious blood should strive to fortify himself with the sign of the Lord’s cross and, as blessed Jerome commands, should trace the cross with his hand at every action, at every step, against every danger, just as all do who faithfully dedicate themselves to God through the mystery of the cross.

In another place, the same most eloquent speaker, preaching brilliantly in praise of the cross, adorns the banners of soldiers, the purple robes of kings, and the diadems of Caesars with the image of the saving punishment. Everyone who, from the time of the Lord’s Passion, resolved to suffer or die for Christ wished to reach Christ through the punishment of the cross.

Peter desired to reach Christ [Col. 1033A] through martyrdom on the cross. Therefore Christ foretold to him how he would have to reach the kingdom: “When you were younger,” he said, “you girded yourself and walked where you wished; but when you grow old, you will stretch out your hands.” By the stretching out of his hands, he signified that Peter would obtain what he desired: the gallows of the cross.

Andrew faithfully preached the mystery of the cross, and through the punishment of the cross reached triumph. Paul, though he was not crucified in body, carried the Lord’s cross, as blessed Pope Gregory teaches, in both heart and body through a twofold devotion. He said: “Far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ.” He also rejoiced that he had reached the summit of knowledge and wisdom because he gloried in knowing nothing except Jesus Christ, and him crucified.

Whatever anyone suffers for Christ, following the example of the Lord’s Passion, is called suffering and torment for the sake of honor and glory. The woman in the Book of Kings who, when Elijah prophesied, took care to gather two pieces of wood in the form of the cross—as interpreters of the divine Scriptures maintain—prefigured the Church. For the two pieces of wood gathered by the woman just mentioned have been spiritually understood by the Fathers, as we have said, as a figure of the cross.

To those who desire spiritually to understand the most holy mysteries of this cross, that desirable saying of Paul speaks and, by speaking, admonishes those who possessed and still possess love, devotion, honor, and glory under its discipline, and who desire to receive its most salutary instructions:

“May the Lord God grant you, according to the riches of his glory, to be strengthened with power through his Spirit in the inner person, and may Christ dwell through faith in your hearts; rooted and founded in charity, so that you may be able to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth, length, height, and depth” (Ephesians 3:16). According to the Apostle’s saying, we believe this to pertain to the mystery of the Lord’s cross.

The breadth of the cross, from the top of one arm to the top of the other, we can, I think, understand without danger to a simple interpretation. Its height, we say, extends from the foot of the cross to the wood placed transversely, according to the reliable teaching of our venerable elders. Its depth, however, is the lowest part of the cross, fixed in the earth and unable to be seen by bodily light.

We believe its sublimity to be the excellence of the highest and principal virtue, which is faith in God [Col. 1033D] and concerning God; without its sincerity and integrity, it is impossible to please him. In another interpretation, we can understand breadth as the good works of charity, length as perseverance to the end, height as hope of heavenly rewards, and depth as the inscrutable judgments of God, as the faithful and most widely accepted testimony of the Fathers reports.

Under the rule of Helena Augusta and her most august son Constantine, the cross is said and believed to have been found; and under the reign of the most victorious king and most Christian ruler Heraclius, its triumphant and celebrated exaltation is said to have been adored and honored.

What are we, who, ignorant in knowledge, unlearned in wisdom, and faltering in speech, presume to say anything in praise of the cross? How many, how great, and what kind of men there were who could speak grandly about so great a matter! Our sluggish smallness is not sufficient to recount their merits and endeavors; nor, with ignorance obstructing us, can the frailty of our memory fully grasp even what they say, let alone their number of noble utterances.

All the catholic teachers of the Church have also endeavored to declare what was necessary concerning the mystery of the cross and the Lord’s Passion—some more obscurely, others more openly, others at greater length. Among them John Chrysostom spoke far more abundantly than the rest.

Long afterward there shone forth a certain monk, and after his monastic life, bishop of the city of Mainz, named Rabanus: abundantly learned in secular knowledge, catholic in faith, and fully instructed in specialized learning. He began, wove, and completed such a work in praise of the cross that nothing more precious to look upon, more delightful to read, sweeter to retain, or more difficult to write can be found or ever will be found.

It pleased me to insert whole into this brief declamation the judgment on the praise of the cross of the most blessed John, surnamed Chrysostom, the most illustrious patriarch of the royal city, in such a way that what our rusticity could not adequately recount might be ennobled by his simple and sublime authority.

For that already-mentioned man once wrote a statement concerning the Lord’s cross, in which he addressed one of his friends, saying among other things:

“And if you desire to know, dearest friend, the power of the cross, and how great are the things I can say in its praise, listen:

The cross is the hope of Christians; the cross, the resurrection of the dead; the cross, the guide of the blind; the cross, the way of the despairing; the cross, the staff of the lame; the cross, the destruction of the proud; the cross, the consolation of the poor; the cross, the restraint of the rich; the cross, the punishment of those who live wickedly; the cross, triumph over demons; the cross, the defeat of the devil; the cross, the tutor of the young; the cross, the support of the needy; the cross, the hope of the desperate; the cross, the helmsman of sailors; the cross, the harbor of those in danger; the cross, the wall of the besieged; the cross, the father of orphans; the cross, the defender of widows; the cross, the counselor of the righteous; the cross, the rest of the afflicted; the cross, the guardian of little ones; the cross, the head of men; the cross, the end of the aged; the cross, the light of those sitting in darkness; the cross, the magnificence of kings; the cross, the perpetual shield; the cross, the wisdom of fools; the cross, the freedom of slaves; the cross, the philosophy of emperors; the cross, the law of the impious; the cross, the proclamation of the prophets; the cross, the announcement of the apostles; the cross, the glorying of martyrs; the cross, the abstinence of monks; the cross, the chastity of virgins; the cross, the joy of priests; the cross, the foundation of the Church; the cross, the safeguard of the world; the cross, the destruction of temples; the cross, the rejection of idols; the cross, the stumbling block of the Jews; the cross, the ruin of the impious; the cross, the strength of the weak; the cross, the physician of the sick; the cross, the cleansing of lepers; the cross, the rest of paralytics; the cross, the bread of the hungry; the cross, the fountain of the thirsty; the cross, the protection of the naked.”

May Christ crucified be for us the way, the life, and salvation—he who always saves us and governs all ages. May the cross be the strength and refuge of us all, with the aid of him who endured the punishment of the cross for the salvation of human beings, [Col. 1036A] who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 1035]

## THE CREDO OF SAINT ODILO

(Bibliotheca Cluniacensis, p. 369.)

[Col. 1035A] I adore, praise, glorify, and bless that eternal and unbounded unity of the supreme divinity, just as all the holy angels and archangels and all the saints adore it in heaven. I believe and confess the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit: three in persons, one in divinity and substance; and I believe and confess them as the holy patriarchs [Col. 1035B] and prophets foretold, the angel Gabriel, sent from heaven to the Virgin, declared, the holy apostles announced, the Evangelists proclaimed, the martyrs preached, the confessors taught, and the holy virgins confessed.

I believe and confess that Word which was in the beginning, which was with God, and which was God. For my liberation and redemption and that of the whole world, he was temporally conceived and born from the most sacred and undefiled Virgin Mary, in the reality of our body and without human lust. According to the law of Moses, on the eighth day he was circumcised with the imposition of the name Jesus; on the fortieth day he was presented in the temple by his mother with offerings and gifts; he was manifested to the Magi; baptized by John; tempted in the desert by the devil but not overcome.

After many innumerable benefits of miracles and healings had been granted, and after the preaching of the Gospel, at the appointed and foreordained time he was betrayed by his own disciple, seized by the Jews, bound, scourged, struck on the cheek, covered with spittle, crowned with thorns, given vinegar to drink, crucified, dead, and buried. On the third day, having conquered the devil and despoiled hell, he was raised from the dead by his own power. For forty days he was manifested to the apostles in the flesh in which he had been crucified. On the fortieth day, while those same apostles and many other faithful people watched, he was raised above the heavens. From there he will come to judge the living and the dead and the age by fire.

I also believe in the Holy Spirit, who descended upon that same Lord of ours in the form of a dove and upon the holy apostles in tongues of fire, distributing among them knowledge of all languages and giving them unconquerable steadfastness against the persecution of all enemies.

I believe in the holy, catholic, and apostolic Church. I confess one baptism for the forgiveness of sins, and I await the resurrection of the dead and the life of the age to come. Amen.

[Col. 1035]

## SACRED POEMS AND PRAYERS OF SAINT ODILO

(Bibliotheca Cluniacensis, p. 406.)

### I. HYMN ON THE ASSUMPTION OF HOLY MARY

[Col. 1035C]

The day of joy is here,

Pleasant with every light,

On which the Queen of virgins

Climbs the starry path,

Surrounded on every side

By the shining ranks of angels,

And followed by the renowned

Company of holy virgins.

As all ought to believe,

Christ, radiant with a heavenly crown,

Born from her,

Comes forth to meet her.

Beyond the glory of the angels,

He brings back with him

To the Father’s throne

The excellent pledge,

Unacquainted with the bed of sin.

The city of the heavenly kingdom,

And all its dignity,

Honors the parent

Of its Prince

With fitting prayers.

With them, in great joy,

Let us celebrate together

The joys of this day,

Praising God in supplication.

Let us pursue

The most brilliant proclamations of this feast,

Supplicating with the affection of the mind,

And rejoicing with the expression of the voice.

The remainder is wanting in the manuscript.

### II.

[Col. 1037A]

A renowned star rises,

Illuminating every age,

Through which day and time

Take on the lights of life.

The remainder does not survive in the manuscript.

### III. PRAYER FOR THE ADORATION OF THE CROSS

In whose name every knee bends—of those in heaven, on earth, and beneath the earth—to him I now bend my knees. I confess my guilt to the Father of lights, possessor of all spirits, who commands both earthly and heavenly things.

And to you, enemy of the human race, I issue this prohibition: you who prowl about seeking someone to devour, turn away from me [Col. 1038A] your devices and hidden snares, because the cross of the Lord, whom I always adore, is with me.

The cross is my refuge; the cross is my way and strength; the cross is an unconquerable sign; the cross is an invincible kind of weapon. The cross repels every evil. The cross drives away darkness. Through this cross I shall undertake the divine journey.

The cross is life to me; death to you, enemy. May the cross of our Lord be my exaltation; may his blood remain in me as true redemption. May his resurrection be for me a firm faith and certain hope in the resurrection of the righteous. May his glorious ascent into heaven be for me daily progress toward the heavenly desire; and may the outpouring of the Holy Spirit into our hearts be the forgiveness of all our past sins. Amen.

[Col. 1037]

## THE STATUTE OF SAINT ODILO CONCERNING THE DEAD

(Bibliotheca Cluniacensis, p. 338.)

[Col. 1037B] It was decreed by the most blessed Father, Lord Odilo, with the agreement and request of all the brothers of Cluny, that just as throughout the churches of God built far and wide across the world the feast of All Saints is celebrated on the day of the Kalends of November, so among us also, in festive fashion, a commemoration should be held of all the faithful departed who have existed from the beginning of the world until its end, in the following manner.

On that aforementioned day, after the chapter, the dean and cellarer shall give alms of bread and wine to all poor people who arrive, as is customary on the Lord’s Supper. Whatever remains that day from the brothers’ meal for lunch, the almoner shall receive in its entirety, except for the bread and wine, which he shall receive after supper.

On that same day, after the evening synaxis, all the bells shall be rung, and the Office for the Dead shall be celebrated. At the morning Mass, the Office shall be conducted festively, and all the bells shall be rung. The Tract shall be sung by two brothers. All the brothers shall offer; privately and publicly they shall celebrate Masses for the repose of all the faithful souls; and twelve poor people shall be fed.

And so that this decree may retain perpetual force, we wish, ask, and command that it be observed both in this place and in all places belonging to it. If anyone else takes an example from this faithful institution of ours, may he become a participant in all the good things of our vows. Thus we have advised and commanded how the memory of all Christians is to be observed once a year. We consider it thoroughly fitting that, for the souls of our brothers serving God in monasteries under the rule of blessed Benedict, we should increase the divine services beyond the customary measure.

Moreover, because we wish the memory of our dear emperor Henry to be celebrated especially with them, we establish the following, as we ought, since we have been enriched by him with many resources. At the vigil of the dead, after the psalm “To the Lord when I was in distress,” which is recited after the readings, let us say, “Lord, why have they multiplied?” At Matins, or afterward, “Out of the depths” and “How long, O Lord?” At Vespers, after “Praise, O my soul,” [say] “Unless the Lord [had been with us]” and “O God, we have heard with our ears”; after “Lord, you have been our refuge,” [say] “The Lord shepherds me.” [Col. 1038C] At the litany, “Judge me, O God, and distinguish [my cause].”

And thus, by divine grace, as we have stated above, may their memory be celebrated throughout all future times, both in this place and in all places connected with it. The authority of divine law admonishes us that in the house of the Lord, which is the Church of the faithful, each of the devout should strive, according to the strength granted him by the Lord, to offer something, lest, like the lazy servant, he justly be condemned by the Lord for hiding his talent, but rather, like the good servant, be rewarded with a worthy recompense for faithfully multiplying his profit.

## APPENDIX TO SAINT ODILO

[Col. 1039]

## CERTAIN PRECEPTS CONCERNING SOME CHURCHES AND PLACES GRANTED TO THE MONASTERY OF CLUNY DURING THE TIME OF SAINT ODILO, ABBOT OF CLUNY V

(Bibliotheca Cluniacensis, p. 409.)

### I. The Precept of Emperor Otto concerning Saint Maiolus of Pavia  
*(Year 999.)*

[Col. 1039A]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Otto, by the grace of God emperor Augustus of the Romans.

Let it be known to all our faithful that, at the petition of Lord Odilo, venerable abbot, and for the salvation of our soul, by this our precept we confirm to a certain cell dedicated in honor of Saint Mary, situated in the city of Pavia and belonging to the monastery of Cluny by the gift and transfer of Gaidulf and his heirs, formerly called the chapel of Gaidulf but now called by all the cell of Saint Maiolus—all the possessions and properties [Col. 1039B] belonging to that same cell, within and without, which it possesses or which God may grant to it in the future, with cultivated and uncultivated lands, waters, mills, fishing rights, and all movable and immovable goods.

This is on the condition that the aforesaid cell shall have, hold, and firmly possess them, and shall always remain under the administration and disposition of the abbot of Cluny, just as Gaidulf arranged. Moreover, by our donation and authority, and by our imperial power, we command that no duke, archbishop, bishop, margrave, count, judge, viscount, or any great or small person of our empire presume to interfere in the aforesaid cell or its dependencies, or to arrange or administer anything concerning them, without the command and consent of the abbot of Cluny.

If anyone should violate this precept of our stability, let him pay one hundred pounds of gold, half to our treasury and half to the monastery of Cluny. And so that it may be believed more truly and observed forever, we have strengthened it with our own hand and ordered it sealed with our seal.

The sign of Lord Otto, most illustrious emperor Augustus.

Given on the Ides of April, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 999, indiction XII, in the fifteenth year of Otto’s reign as king and the third of his imperial rule, successfully at Rome.

### II. The Precept of King Rodulf concerning Chaviniis, Blenosco, Saint Victor, and other Chapels  
*(Year 997.)*

[Col. 1039D]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Rodulfus, [Col. 1040A] by the merciful favor of God, pious Augustus and most invincible king.

Just as it is unquestionably certain that no power exists except from God, so it necessarily follows that whoever, by his disposition, is raised to the height of earthly power should humble himself beneath the powerful hand of that same giver and strive to please him with his gifts. Therefore let it be known to all who succeed one another through the courses of time—namely, to kings as well as counts, to magistrates of every rank, and to administrators of the commonwealth—that, at the entreaty of Emma, consort of our rule, and of certain other faithful people of ours, I transfer certain possessions to the monastery of Cluny, for the love of God and of the holy chief apostles, Peter and Paul.

This is on the condition that the brotherhood of monks dwelling there shall possess those properties perpetually and by right, without opposition from any king, count, or person of any lower rank, and, reserving them to that place for the memory of us, shall continually implore the mercy of Christ and the patronage of the aforementioned apostles, both for us and for the welfare of our kingdom, and likewise for those who permit this donation to remain unshaken.

These possessions are situated in the county of Mâcon, in the vicariate … [lacuna], and the estate is called Chivineas, which we give with all its dependencies, together with one-third of the fishpond called Osa, with its serfs and the other properties belonging to the same fishpond, so that the same monks may always possess half the catch.

We also confirm the donation made by the good man Levibald of Blenosco, and likewise that concerning the chapel of Saint Victor, which is in Absgogia, as well as the other properties that Altaldus or others, by transferring them to the aforesaid chapel, assigned to Cluny.

We therefore confirm these properties, with the chapels, male and female serfs, vineyards, meadows, waters, mills, woods, cultivated and uncultivated houses, and everything that is demonstrably attached to them or is to be acquired by the aforesaid monastery through our concession.

We also judge valid the document which Bishop Berno made for the aforementioned monks concerning their tithes, so that no one may be permitted, by any recent authority, to remove anything from the tithes that have belonged to them from ancient times.

All these things we confirm by a precept of our authority and mark with the impression of our seal, admonishing our successors with this saying: “Cursed is the one who moves the boundaries,” that is, the ordinances of his neighbor.

The sign of Rodulfus, most glorious king.

Beamundus recognized this on behalf of Bishop Ansusius.

Enacted at Ansavilla, eleven days before the Kalends of July, indiction III, in the ninth year of the reign of Rodulfus, most glorious king.

### III. Charter of the Same King concerning Saint Blaise at Viculis, with All Its Dependencies  
*(Year 1019.)*

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Rodulfus, by the grace of God king.

[Col. 1041B] Since the whole order of religious life, according to the decrees of preceding kings, was beginning its holy way of life, and since, for perseverance in it, the public royal table supplied sustenance for those who disciplined themselves more strictly and more intimately in God’s service—sufficiently to some and less sufficiently to others—and since in this way the condition of the holy Church has been extended through long courses of time until the present, it is nevertheless fitting that we, who labor as though among the last workers in God’s vineyard, should not allow those same workers to fail in the exercise of God’s work. Rather, insofar as our strength permits, we should strive to bring them to completion in every detail.

Therefore let all those departing in the present time and succeeding in the future know how I, Rodulfus, at the request [Col. 1041C] and earnest desire of my beloved wife Irainsanda, give from my hereditary possession a certain small estate, for the remedy of my soul and that of my aforesaid wife, to the monastery of Saint Peter called Cluny, and to the abbot of that monastery and its monks, who now and henceforth obey the precept and rule of Saint Benedict and serve God there: namely, the entire church of Saint Blaise at Viculis, with everything belonging to it there: mountains and plains, fields, meadows, pastures, woods, tithes, male and female servants, and all its equipment.

I and my aforesaid wife give this to the monastery written above, so that if we have performed the office imposed upon us by God less worthily, we may not receive the loss of our sin and negligence according to our deserts, [Col. 1041D] but, through the prayers of those whom we support by supplying temporal goods, we may be rewarded with an everlasting recompense as we run the race.

So that this may be believed to have been done by us and not violated by our descendants, [Col. 1042A] we have strengthened it with our own hand and caused it to be sealed.

The sign of Rodulfus, pious king.

Albicer, an unworthy priest, wrote this at the king’s command.

These things were enacted at the estate of Tabernis, which is also called Utba because of the river flowing there. Given eighteen days before the Kalends of February, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1019, while King Rodulfus was reigning, in the thirty-first year of his reign.

This little benefice—that is, the aforesaid church, which we give to the brothers dwelling at Cluny—lies in the district and county of Geneva, with the villages attached to it there.

### IV. Charter of Count Amadeus concerning the Church of Saint Maurice in the District of Maltacena  
*(Year 1025.)*

[Col. 1042B]

In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, in the thirty-seventh year of Rodulfus’s reign, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1025, two days before the Kalends of November, on the twentieth day of the moon.
