I, Amadeus, son of Count Humbert, and my wife Adalegida, have ordered this charter of donation to be made concerning the church of Saint Maurice, situated in the district called Maltacena, and concerning all the lands that we now give and shall give in the future, for the honor of the Lord God and of the Church of Saints Peter and Paul, the monastery of Cluny, over which Lord Father Odilo presides, for the redemption and salvation of our souls.

With the permission and confirmation of Lord Malenus, bishop of the Church of Grenoble, and of Bishop Humbert [Col. 1042C] and all the canons of that city, we give to the Lord God everything mentioned above, and to his blessed apostles Peter and Paul, to the monastery of Cluny, and to all the monks dwelling there, so that we may be able to share in their prayers. We reserve to ourselves the right called the right of patronage, and the right of presentation, for ourselves, our children, and their successors, for as long as it shall be our will, and so forth.

If anyone should wish to disturb this donation, let him pay one hundred pounds of gold in the king’s court and, in addition, incur the curse of the bishop of Grenoble, and so forth.

The seal of Count Humbert and of his wife Ancillia. The sign of Count Amadeus. The sign of his wife Adelidis.

They made this donation, ordered this charter to be drawn up, and requested that it be confirmed in the king’s court.

The sign of King Rodulfus, of Ermingardis, of Odo, and of Ancelin.

[Col. 1041]

## HYMN ON SAINT ODILO

(Bibliotheca Cluniacensis, as above, p. 328.)

[The reader will miss the first three verses of the immediately following hymn, whose opening is “Commend the flock to the Lord,” because the membrane in the manuscript is torn.]

### DIVISION

[Col. 1041D]

O man noble everywhere,

… [lacuna] … with spoils:

[Col. 1042D]

By which the Tartarean spirits

Mourn that their prey is taken from them.

[Col. 1043A]

You, the glory of the Church,

Rescue us from the storms of the world:

While the waters fear you,

You restrain the forces of nature.

Certainly, the limbs of the weak

Restore their former strength;

The washed hands: the cup

Restores speech to the mute.

[Col. 1044A] You, pour light into our minds

Through holy prayers:

You who restore sight to the blind,

And drive away our darkness.

Let there be praise to the unbegotten Father,

Let there be honor to the Only-Begotten:

Let there be supreme majesty

To the Spirit equal to both. Amen.

[Col. 1043]

## Mass of Blessed Odilo

*(As above.)*

### Prayer

[Col. 1043B]

O God, who granted blessed Odilo to keep watch over the guardianship of your flock, grant, we ask, that your household may be formed by the example of him whose teachings established it. Through the Lord.

### Secret

May the sacrifice offered to you, Lord, be commended by the prayer of blessed Odilo; may it both protect us from adversities and kindle us unceasingly to your love. Through the Lord.

### Post-Communion

[Col. 1044B]

Grant, we ask, almighty God, that, through the intercession of blessed Odilo, your confessor, the vigor of the heavenly table may raise up those whom the burden of their own guilt weighs down. Through the Lord.

### Over the People

Grant, we ask, almighty God, that through blessed Odilo we may direct our footsteps toward you, since you have deigned to instruct us by his teaching. Through the Lord.

[Col. 1043]

## Lament of the Monk Jotsald at the Passing of Lord Odilo, Abbot of Cluny

*(Bibliotheca Cluniacensis, p. 329.)*

[Col. 1043C] Let the string extend its sonorous chord toward voices of mourning;

Let the instruments of all modes be turned according to their lot.

Mourn, peoples; mourn, tongues, stars of heaven;

Let the sun’s shining orb plunge into darkness;

Let the radiant horns of the moon wholly fail;

Let the entire world lament, its body stretched out:

Now I shall rouse the lands, the sea, the mountains, and the forests;

I shall move all four-footed creatures, two-footed creatures, and creeping things.

Let them grieve for Odilo, the Father now taken away,

Let their applause be cut short, let their inward parts be pierced by weeping,

And let them pour forth these tears in varied voices:

Odilo, sweet glory, glory of the age to come;

Odilo, sweet glory, friend of brotherly peace;

Odilo, sweet glory, renowned for the lamp of your merits.

You are rest for the weary, medicine for the sick,

[Col. 1043D] A staff for the weak, the greatest strength of the wretched.

Where has that radiant face gone, where has your golden speech withdrawn,

You who composed human conduct so excellently?

Where is your holy hand, where finally your flashing gaze?

Where does it lie in the expanse, or in what cavern does it rest?

Reason, answering these questions, says:

In funeral order the limbs are enclosed in the tomb;

This is the law imposed upon mortals by an everlasting covenant.

The parent of nature, creator and author of all things,

[Col. 1044C] Ordered the dying to go into the western darkness.

Whatever receives its beginning in light moves toward sunset;

The learned and the unlearned depart by an equal lot;

The shadow of death receives the rich and the poor alike;

The structure of ashes is dissolved and turned into ash:

What cannot be undone must be endured patiently.

### Revelation of Grief and Consolation in Death

Muse, tell me the causes by which I may dissolve my sorrows,

Laying aside barren tears and taking up joys.

Odilo does not die, but spurns death’s funeral rites;

Odilo does not die, but lived an honorable life;

Odilo does not die, but received life through death.

He reigns forever, rejoicing to behold Christ,

Whom he served, taught, sought, and glorified,

Whose glory was the cross, and Christ crucified.

[Col. 1044D] Virgin Mary, how greatly he served your honor!

He held you in all his prayers as Lady of the world and gracious Lady of heaven;

He chose and loved you above all, firmly remembering the God born from you,

And drew tears from himself because of your holy breast—

The breast that heaven marvels to have suckled God, and the world adores!

How dear to him was Christ’s holy circumcision,

Which brought the knife’s wounds upon his tender limbs,

The groans poured forth in the light of his eyes bear witness.

[Col. 1045A] On this day, deservedly, the flesh is dissolved in the tomb;

He suffers with Christ and now lives, radiant, in him;

He dies with Christ and at last rises with Christ.

On the same day Lord William departed from this light.

William also died on these same Kalends,

He too, the great Father of the monks of Dijon.

These had ultimately been monks of the holy Majolus,

Flourishing at one and the same time, pure in body,

United in one faith, friends of true piety.

Faith joined them both; they had similar departures,

Their glory was not unequal, and the same crown follows them.

### Here the beloved one is prepared for his bed, and various mystical objects are offered.

Beloved Odilo, now white and ruddy,

[Col. 1045B] Follows Christ’s footsteps with confident stride.

A flowery and snowy bed is carried for him,

Which lofty cedar covers and fragrant cypress adorns;

Violets are scattered, and every lily is spread out.

Then you may see him paint rose-colored flowers for himself,

And look upon various plants with kindly eyes.

Balsams are not absent, nor many spices ground together;

Nard and myrrh shine, and powerful cinnamon gives off its fragrance,

And the strips [or fragments] of the cross are mingled with all the choicest

Ointments of aloe, stacte, and precious henna.

There are a thousand substances, and even more varied fragrances;

A nectar-like flavor fills heaven itself above.

### Here he is joined to the Bridegroom.

Odilo enjoys these delights and is renewed;

Near the Bridegroom, he shines with a clear light.

[Col. 1045C] He now celebrates kisses and confirms the covenant of the bride.

Songs now resound, and paschal drums play;

Now, joyful, he sees the Lord and God face to face.

### The beloved is compared to a tower and fortified with mystical arms.

Odilo, while he lived, scattered the fragrances of virtues;

He was a strong tower, a shield fortified by heavenly things,

Around which seven battlements were encircling;

From them hung the weapons of valiant men,

And no hostile enemy could overcome it.

### The beloved is sought.

Where are you feeding, reclining, beloved of my desires?

### Here he is found.

You occupy the southern place; like the sun, you touch the heights.

### A dish is offered to the beloved.

[Col. 1045D] The mystical Solomon serves you holy dishes;

Lebanon provides these, untouched by any corrupting impurity.

Solid columns are fashioned from silver;

Its resting-place is of gold, its ascent is purple;

At its center it is paved with love of piety.

### How he sings musically.

In alternating melodies you now sing wedding songs,

And run through mystical teachings in sweet rhythms.

### How sweetly he says that he is resting.

Now I rest beneath the desired shade of him

Whom I desired, served, sought, and always loved.

[Col. 1046A] His fruit is sweet to my throat,

And his love grants me, whose limbs now lie in the dust,

Sleep made pleasurable by an exceeding sweetness.

### To the daughters of Jerusalem, that they may not awaken the beloved.

Daughters of Jerusalem, I appeal to you, friends of peace:

Grant him rest, and do not forbid him to lie down,

Until he himself wishes it, and until the shadow passes,

And the day arrives to which no night succeeds.

### Here, awakened, he rises again.

Odilo looks toward the final triumph over death;

Now the first palm shines again, and the second is preserved,

When the judge of the world comes, with the heavens divided,

To see the causes and deeds of all human beings.

Then the sign of the cross will appear, lofty before everyone,

The cross which the Lord Jesus sanctified by hanging upon it in death.

[Col. 1046B] Then the angelic host will be afraid, and every

Power of heaven, resounding, will fall silent in trembling.

The shining sun will flee; the paling moon will withdraw;

Then bodies will come forth from opened tombs.

The glory of the saints will be separated from the lot of the wicked:

For the good will rise to the light, and the evil to the fire.

Then Odilo, renewed and radiant with heavenly light,

Will walk in the midst of the saints and go forth to meet them,

Surrounded by a host of many fellow soldiers,

Whom he joined to the Lord by words and examples.

### Prayer for the beloved.

Virgin Mary, then, taking pity, receive your servant,

And powerful Baptist, look upon him who remembers you.

May the angelic Spirit snatch him away once the enemy has been put to flight.

Blessed Peter, provide for him a gracious dwelling in heaven,

[Col. 1046C] He who was always devoted and dutiful toward you.

Blessed apostolic assembly in the splendor of the Lord,

Purple-clad witnesses at the highest hinge of heaven,

Order of priests, leader and light of peoples,

Virgin choir sanctified in Christ:

May our Odilo have you as intercessors,

So that together he may rejoice in heaven throughout the ages. Amen.

### Epilogue of Salutation

Odilo, live and farewell, dearer to me than the whole world,

Clearer than glass, brighter than shining gold,

With conspicuous face and gleaming, snow-white hair,

Whiter than a swan, more beautiful than a red star.

While I recall you, good man, I am wet with the dew of tears,

I who was bound to you by the bonds of an especially deep love.

[Col. 1046D] How illustrious were your eyes, filled from the fountain of compassion,

how often were sweet groans revealed in me!

Whom shall I seek as your equal? Whom shall I hold as your equal?

Then peace and rest, and the sure hope of life, remained;

You were a tranquil harbor for me returning from the sea.

You were a tower from which I looked out upon terrors;

A healing antidote by which I drove away every poison.

You were foot, you were hand, and you became all things in everything.

And lest I make excuses for producing many verses,

Odilo, now farewell; remember Jotsald,

And always graciously attend to the prayers of your own Almannus.

[Col. 1047]

## Translation of the Body of Saint Odilo, Carried Out by Roger, Archbishop of Bourges, in the Year 1345

*(Bibliotheca Cluniacensis, p. 345, from the chartulary of Silviniacum.)*

[Col. 1047A] Roger, by divine permission archbishop of Bourges, to all the faithful of Christ: eternal salvation in the Lord.

Know that, with the permission and mandate of the most holy Father in Christ, our lord, Lord Clement, by the worthy providence of God sixth pope, we, together with the reverend Fathers in Christ, the bishops of Capitulien., of the Augustinian Order, and of Saulonien., of the Order of Preachers, and with very many abbots, prelates, and ecclesiastical persons summoned for this purpose, gathered together in the church of Silviniacum of the Cluniac order, in the diocese of Clermont, solemnly raised the venerable body of the blessed confessor Odilo from the place where it had until then been buried, according to the form, ordinance, and procedure handed down to us by the holy Roman Church.

[Col. 1047B] We saw the head of that holy confessor and the other members of his body, and with our own hands touched, held, and examined them; then we placed and honorably and decently enclosed them in a chest.

Indeed, having considered the merits of this holy confessor, which devoutly led and attracted us to his revelation, and desiring with all our strength to advance his praise and honor, so that he might be adorned and venerated by the faithful of Christ with suitable honors and praises, [Col. 1048A] and so that the said church might be visited and frequented all the more willingly by those faithful of Christ for the sake of devotion, relying upon the mercy of almighty God and upon the authority of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul and of blessed Stephen, our patron, we mercifully grant in the Lord to all truly penitent and confessed persons who visit that church each year on the feasts of the blessed confessor, especially on the day of his raising, and throughout its octave, a remission, for future and perpetual times, of forty days from the penances imposed upon them.

Moreover, we wish and grant by special favor that any preacher who preaches the divine word to the people present in the aforesaid church may, on our behalf and by our authority, grant and bestow twenty days of indulgence upon [Col. 1048B] all truly penitent and confessed persons who are present at such preaching, whenever and as often as he happens to exercise the office of preaching.

In witness of all these things, we have caused this present letter to be strengthened by the protection of our seal.

Given at Tolon in the diocese of Clermont, while visiting our province, on 21 June in the year of the Lord 1345.

Signed: William Vincent.

## In the Year of the Lord 1048: Berno, Abbot of Richenau

[Col. 1047]

## Historical Notice

*(From John Egon’s book On the Illustrious Men of Richenau, in Bernard Pez, Thesaurus, I, III, 687.)*

[Col. 1047C] I consider Berno—whom others prefer to call Bernard—who, formerly a monk of Prüm, was placed by the emperor Saint Henry in charge of the monastery of Richenau, to be rightly compared with the most distinguished teachers of Richenau, or even preferred to most of them. For among the poets of his age he was outstanding. He was an eloquent rhetorician, an excellent philosopher, and so skilled in music that he illuminated it with highly learned commentaries; he was also so nobly instructed in sacred letters that he carried everyone away into no small admiration of him.

He composed many treatises, of which the authors who published books on ecclesiastical writers—such as Trithemius, Bellarmine, Arnold Wion, and Antonius Possevinus—make mention. They are as follows:

- One book On the Office of the Mass, which, though printed many times, was recently included in volume XI of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*.

- One book On the Life of Saint Ulrich, published in volume IV of Surius.

- One book On the Coming of the Lord, addressed to Aribo, archbishop of Mainz.

- One book On the Fast of the Four Seasons.

- One book On the Fast of Saturday.

- One book of Sermons, both for brothers and for others.

- One book of Letters to Various Persons.

- One book On Music, addressed to Pilgrim, archbishop of Cologne, whose original manuscript Trithemius writes that he possessed.

- One book On Musical Instruments.

[Col. 1049B]

- One book On the Measurement of the Monochord.

- One book On the History of the Alemanni, as Trithemius reports in the prologue to his Hirsau Chronicle, asserting that he inserted much from it and from other historians into his own Chronicle. I, however, have never succeeded in seeing this History of the Alemanni.

He is also said to have written several other works, among them, as some have thought, the Life of Saint Meginrad the Martyr, whose author I above identified as anonymous; but concerning this I now suspend my judgment.

[Col. 1050A] Berno, insofar as this also seemed relevant here, was especially dear to the emperor Saint Henry and was his inseparable companion on the Italian expedition and Roman journey. Thus it happened that he administered the affairs of the monastery of Richenau extremely well and enlarged it with distinguished privileges obtained from the Apostolic See.

He also built a new basilica for Saint Mark, the patron of Richenau, and had it consecrated in the year of Christ 1048, on the day before the feast of Saint Mark.

Here, too, a serious error of Ekkehard of Saint Gall must be corrected. Excessively favoring the honor of his own people, he says that Berno had been a monk at Saint Gall before his prelacy. But since he alone writes this without reason, and since he is not so ancient an authority, I do not think that he deserves credence from anyone—especially since he is opposed by Hermann the Lame, who knew Berno and had him as his teacher at Richenau, by the German Annals of Richenau, and by Arnold Wion, all of whom expressly testify that Berno was a monk of the monastery of Prüm.

[Col. 1050B] At last good Berno died, equally mature in years and merits, not without the firm reputation of great holiness, in the year of Christ 1048, on the second day before the Ides of June, and was buried in the basilica of Saint Mark that he himself had built.

[Col. 1049]

## Literary Notice

*(In Oudin, Commentaries on Ecclesiastical Writers and Writings, II, 598.)*

[Col. 1049C] Berno, abbot of Richenau, was initially a monk of Saint Gall in Germany, of the Order of Saint Benedict. After he had served there laudably for a long time under the discipline of the Rule, and had cultivated his mind through knowledge both of music and of ecclesiastical histories, he was promoted in 1014, renowned for his merits, to the abbacy of Richenau near Constance on the Rhine.

Berno flourished during the period of Henry II and Conrad II and the first five years of Henry III. He himself says that he attended the coronation of Henry II, in chapter 2 of *On Certain Matters Pertaining to the Office of the Mass*.

What he accomplished in the Church’s chant will be shown by Ekkehard the Younger in the *Life of Blessed Notker the Stammerer*, chapter 10.

Gerard John Vossius, in book II, chapter 44, p. 367 in my edition, falsely makes this Berno a disciple of Hincmar, archbishop of Reims. An indication of this seems to be Hincmar’s own letter to Aeneas, bishop of Paris, which Baronius reports from the Vatican Library in his *Annals*, under the year 912.

[Col. 1049D] Yet Vossius is plainly mistaken and causes others to be mistaken: this must be understood of another Berno, one hundred years older, the first abbot of the Church of Cluny. When he went to Burgundy in 912, he appointed Odo of Tours—who had become a cleric, musician, and archdeacon of the Church of Tours in 901—to head the monastery school at Balm, the monastery he had recently founded, after clothing him there in the monastic cowl.

The statements of the above-cited Ekkehard in the *Life of Notker the Stammerer*, chapter 10, must also be understood of this same Berno.

Indeed, the period of Berno, abbot of Richenau, cannot at all be reconciled with the age of Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, or with his supposed discipleship.

There exists a short work written by him, *On Certain Matters Pertaining to the Office of the Mass*. It was first published among the writers *On the Divine Offices*, collated with manuscript copies through the study and care of Melchior Hittorp, at Cologne in 1568 and Paris in 1610, p. 661 in folio. It was also printed separately at Venice in 1572, in octavo, together with other works of the same subject.

From there it was transferred to the Paris edition of the *Bibliotheca Patrum* of 1575, volume IV, col. 572; the edition of 1589, volume VI, col. 709; the edition of 1610, volume X, p. 697; the Cologne edition of 1618, century or volume XI, p. 51; likewise the Paris edition of 1624, volume X, p. 697; and the Lyon edition of 1677, volume XVIII, p. 56.

He also polished, in more elegant Latin, the *Life of Saint Ulrich*, bishop of Augsburg, which is found in Surius under 4 July. Two others had composed it before Berno: the first anonymous, or Gerard the priest, a disciple of Saint Ulrich; the second Gebhard, bishop of Augsburg, who may also have seen him.

[Col. 1050C] Of these earlier authors Gerard John Vossius writes as follows in book III of *On Latin Historians*, part IV, *On Historians Omitted*, chapter 5, p. 764:

> “During the times of Otto I and II there was a certain Gerhard who first, though in a rough style, wrote down the Life of Saint Ulrich, bishop of Augsburg. His period is indicated by the fact that he lived with this Saint Ulrich, who became bishop in the year of Christ 924 and died on 4 July 973, in the fiftieth year of his episcopate, having lived eighty-three years. From this writer Gebhard, bishop of Augsburg, and the abbot of Richenau drew material for their Life of Saint Ulrich. They labored to make what had previously been expressed by the anonymous author in rustic diction more elegant and polished, so that it might delight more readers; and they acted in such a way that the source itself was greatly neglected, indeed remained unknown for several centuries, until Marcus Welser at last discovered it, previously unknown, and presented it to the literary world. For he was the first to draw that Life of Saint Ulrich out of darkness and make it public.”

The same author writes on page 766:

> “Gebhard, bishop of Augsburg, was a contemporary of Dietmar. He began to occupy the see in 1006 and governed the Church for nine years. This is the Gebhard who converted the church of Saint Afra, built by Saint Ulrich and in which he had wished to be buried, into a monastery and abbey by bringing monks of Saint Benedict there. Above we said of him that he expressed more neatly and elegantly the Life of Saint Ulrich, which had been written by his contemporary in a rustic and inelegant manner, just as it was again done somewhat later by Berno, abbot of Richenau. Berno also wrote the Life of Saint Meginrad, bishop and martyr, which John Mabillon published in volume II, p. 63 and following, of the fourth century of The Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict.

[Col. 1051A] “There also exist, among the philosophical manuscript books of the Paulina Library at Leipzig, in the Philosophical Repository 1, series 2, among the mathematical and astronomical books in folio, codex 30: Berno, abbot of Richenau, A Tonary Book. His Antiphonary and Music are also there. In codex 31: Berno’s Music, A Tonary Book, and The Measurement of the Monochord. From these little works it is evident that he excelled in music and chant.”

These are the words of Joachim Feller in his *Catalogue of the Manuscript Codices of the Paulina Library at Leipzig*, printed on p. 328, codices 30 and 31, of the 1686 edition, Leipzig, in duodecimo.

The following authors discuss Berno, abbot of Richenau, who died in the year of grace 1045, on the seventh day before the Ides of January, after governing the monastery of Richenau for thirty-nine years: Gerard John Vossius, book II of *On Latin Historians*, chapter 44, p. 367 in my edition; I myself, in the *Supplement to Bellarmine On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under the year 1030, p. 327; William Cave, in his *History of Literary Affairs* under the year 1014, p. 599; and Antonius Possevinus, volume I of the *Sacred Apparatus*, under “Berno, Abbot of Richenau.”

[Col. 1051]

## Second Literary Notice

*(Bernard Pez, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, volume IV, Preface, p. VII.)*

[Col. 1051C] No one has treated the life and writings of Berno, abbot of Richenau—whom Sigebert of Gembloux writes was distinguished in human and divine knowledge—more accurately or elegantly than John Egon in book II, chapter 27, of *On the Illustrious Men of Richenau* (see above). We therefore refer the reader who wishes to know more about Berno, who died in the year of Christ 1049, to that work.

Here we shall discuss only his little works, now being committed to the press for the first time.

The first is addressed to Aribo, archbishop of Mainz, who presided over his Church from approximately 1020 to 1031, as Nicholas Serrarius reports in book V of his *Mainz Affairs*, p. 729. The subject of the book is: *How the Advent of the Lord ought to be celebrated in a year in which the Nativity of the Lord falls on Monday.*

At that time there was not one opinion shared by all on this matter:

> “For, as Berno says to Aribo in chapter 1, so that you may recognize more clearly what we are asking about, we inform you of something which we nevertheless scarcely believe has been unknown to you for a long time: whenever the Nativity of the Lord falls on Monday, as in the present year, a great error spreads through the Churches of God. Some say that no more than four Sundays should be celebrated together with the most sacred vigil of the Lord’s Nativity; others, on the contrary, contend that the Advent of the Lord ought rather to contain four full weeks, dedicating a fifth Sunday especially to the Lord’s vigil. They have no other argument or reason for their position, as far as we have been able to investigate, except that the four offices found in the nocturnal Antiphonaries, or the readings from the holy Gospels and from the Apostle, may be more fully completed.”

[Col. 1052C] In this little work Berno adopts the first opinion and confirms it by the authority and custom of famous Churches.

Especially noteworthy is the conclusion with which he closes the discussion of chapter 2:

> “This custom, as it is said, is observed throughout almost all Gaul and in Rome itself, once mistress of the world. We learned this from most truthful informants, especially Adalbold, a bishop of holy memory, who, when challenged by our writings and residing at Rome, investigated this matter there. Although afterward, I do not know for what reason, they acted otherwise, I nevertheless learned at the same time, both by hearing and seeing, that Piacenza and other cities of Italy observe the rule of the ancient institution. Abbot Heriger too, a man of no small authority in our times, composed a little book of his own on this matter, in which, as those who have read it assert, he proves by more probable arguments that those who celebrate more than four Sundays of the Advent of the Lord act against the institutions of the Fathers.”

[Col. 1053A] The Adalbold praised here by Berno is without doubt that celebrated bishop of Utrecht whose little work *On the Thickness of the Sphere* we published in volume III, part II, of the *Patrologia*, volume CXXXIX.

Moreover, the little book of Abbot Heriger of Lobbes concerning the present controversy, mentioned by no one so far as we know, appears to have vanished completely.

Berno’s little work is followed by a *Response of Aribo*, archbishop of Mainz, in which he wholeheartedly favors Berno’s treatises: works discovered well and skillfully, arranged excellently, expressed eloquently, and finally pronounced with firm memory. If the authority of so slight an episcopate possesses any force, he lays his hand upon them, as Berno requested.

The little work comes from a manuscript codex of the illustrious monastery of Saint Emmeram at Regensburg, in quarto, six hundred years old. We also saw the same work in the parchment volume of the cathedral church of Freising, whose script appeared to reach back to Berno’s age.

[Col. 1053B]

The second little work of Abbot Berno, which we now bring to light for the first time, is entitled in the aforementioned codex of Saint Emmeram: *General Explanation of the Beginning of the Advent of the Lord According to the Authority of Bishop Hilary*, although none of the ancient or more recent writers has mentioned this little Bernonian commentary under that title.

This work is slight, but, as we hope, it will be very welcome to learned men for two reasons. First, it excerpts the book of the Offices of Saint Hilary, a glorious author of the Church and distinguished teacher—that is, that celebrated bishop of Poitiers—although no record of this book survives in the catalogues of ecclesiastical writers.

[Col. 1053C] Second, shortly before its end it discloses to us a new synod of Orléans at which the proper rite for beginning the Advent of the Lord was discussed, although, so far as I know, no mention of it is made by the collectors of councils and synods.

So true is it that no monument of antiquity should readily be despised.

The subject of the *Dialogues on the Fasts of the Four Seasons*, etc., dedicated by Berno to Aribo, archbishop of Mainz, is summarized by Sigebert of Gembloux in book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 156, in these words:

> “But I shall not pass over what he wrote about the fasts of the Four Seasons, concerning which there is disagreement among many as to their celebration. Some, according to the consideration of the seasons, assign to the fast the Wednesdays and Fridays of February, May, or September, and end the fast when the Saturday falls on the Kalends; others, without considering the seasons, fast only when the Wednesday and Friday of the fast, together with the Saturday, fall in March, June, or October. Many authorize this manner of fasting, and especially the Germans, by these writings of Berno.”

[Col. 1053D] We have nowhere yet found what Aribo replied to Berno concerning this little work, according to his custom. Nevertheless, it is sufficiently clear that it pleased him, from the Council of Seligenstadt, which Aribo held in 1022 concerning ecclesiastical discipline. Its second chapter is worded as follows in volume VI, part I, col. 828 of Harduin’s edition of the Councils:

[Col. 1054A]

> “Regarding the uncertain fast of the Four Seasons, we establish this certainty: if the Kalends of March fall on Wednesday or earlier, the fast is to be celebrated in that same week. But if the Kalends of March extend to Thursday, Friday, or Saturday, the fast is to be postponed to the following week. Likewise, if the Kalends of June fall on Wednesday or earlier, the fast is to be celebrated in the following week. And if they fall on Thursday, Friday, or Saturday, the fast is to be reserved for the third week. This must also be known: if at any time the fast of the month of June falls, according to the aforesaid rule, on the vigil of Pentecost, it is not to be celebrated there, but in the solemn week of Pentecost itself,” and so forth.

[Col. 1054B] This is precisely the teaching of our Berno on this matter throughout almost the whole little work, especially chapter 4, which should be consulted.

I excerpted this little work from a very ancient parchment codex of the celebrated monastery of Benediktbeuern, with the most learned and dear Father Karl Meichelbeck dictating it to my pen; our *Thesaurus* is indebted to him under many titles. Later I also found it in the codex of the imperial monastery of Saint Emmeram mentioned above, from which I supplied the prologue that was lacking in the Benediktbeuern codex.

John Trithemius, in chapter 311 of *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, attributes three works to Berno by which he illuminated music: namely, two books *On Music or Tones*, the first of which begins, “Thus every regular Mo. …”; one book *On Musical Instruments*, whose beginning is “Music should not be despised …”; and one book *On the Measurement of the Monochord*, whose beginning he does not quote.

I strongly suspect that the first two little books and the last one are entirely one and the same work.

Certainly, Sigebert of Gembloux, in chapter 156 of *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, speaks of Berno’s musical discoveries in such a way that it would be difficult for anyone to extract from his words several works by Berno on this subject:

> “I pass over,” says Sigebert, “what he wrote on human knowledge. Among these works, this is especially distinguished: excelling in the art of music, he wrote about the rules of harmonies and tones; and, in measuring the monochord, going beyond the rule of Boethius, but with the agreement of the lesser Boethius, Guido, he placed one tone beneath the tetrachord hypaton, and, contrary to the practice of the ancients, usefully inserted the synemmenon in that same tetrachord hypaton.”

Nor does the Anonymous of Melk discuss more than one musical work by Berno in chapter 81 of *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, where he composes the following eulogy of the abbot of Richenau:

> “Berno the musician, a pious and learned man, lived at the monastery of Prüm under a monastic profession. Later the pious emperor Henry appointed him abbot of Richenau. Welcomed gladly by the brothers, he gathered together those who had been scattered, and, consecrated by Lambert, bishop of Constance, governed as a man distinguished by great piety and learning for forty years. He wrote a book *On the Institution of the Mass* and an outstanding work *On Music*.”

Thus the Anonymous of Melk, unaware of several works by Berno on music.

[Col. 1055A] But whether the books *On Music or Tones* and *On the Monochord* are distinct from one another, as Trithemius holds, or not, Berno’s work *On Tones* exists in the Melk codex now marked N, no. 3. It is no earlier than the fifteenth century and was copied very badly indeed.

Another copy of his Tonary is preserved in a parchment codex at Tegernsee, approximately five hundred years old.

When we were examining the ancient and distinguished books of that monastery, we also encountered another excellent work *On Music* by Theoger, or Dietger, one of our bishops of Metz. The Anonymous of Melk writes of him in chapter 109 of *On Ecclesiastical Writers*:

> “Dietger the abbot, called Theogorus by the Latins and by some Germans Theokarius, was first a disciple of Lord William, abbot of Hirsau; then the third abbot of the monastery of Saint George; and finally bishop of Metz. After administering the bishopric for some time, he was buried at Cluny. He too wrote a treatise *On Music*, in which he discusses its invention, numbers, and propositions briefly but with sufficient subtlety, according to the mathematicians.”

We do not hope to do anything unwelcome to our reader if we give here the whole prologue of Theoger’s work, which is brief. Here it is, therefore, from the Tegernsee codex:

### Here Begins the Music of Theoger, Bishop

> “The philosopher Pythagoras is said to have been the first among the Greeks to discover the art of music. Boethius, illustrious by birth and learning, is said to have translated it, and to have been the most profound investigator of that same art according to numerical proportions. The monk Guido, however, was a most diligent investigator of voices. The Monochord exists as the clearest demonstration of this art; its first institutor is also said to have been the aforementioned Greek philosopher.”

### The Work Begins

> “The Monochord is a musical instrument which in ancient times naturally and sufficiently consisted of eight strings,” and so forth.

[Col. 1056A] These matters concerning Theoger’s *Music* have been mentioned only incidentally, on the occasion of Berno of Richenau’s Tonary. Since that work is distinguished and illustrated with ancient figures and unfamiliar forms of letters and musical notation, which our printers would imitate only with the greatest difficulty, it seemed best to publish here only the prologue.

John Trithemius also praises Berno’s book of *Letters to Various Persons*, which one of our friends recently discovered in a famous library of Germany.

Berno’s letters are of great importance, especially letter eleven, in which he sets out at length the errors of John Cassian concerning free will from Cassiodorus and Prosper, and concludes that “Cassian, although approved in other matters, was rightly censured in this respect.”

From this you may readily gather that the monks were not so influenced by Cassian’s authority that, from his *Conferences*—which they constantly had in their hands—they commonly imbibed Pelagian or Semi-Pelagian errors together with the milk of sound doctrine. This is what the otherwise very celebrated man Jean-François Buddeus, doctor of theology at the University of Jena, recently argued in book III, chapter 2, of his *Institutions of Dogmatic Theology*, not without injury to the holy men of the Catholic Church and to entire religious orders.

For what sort of claim is this?

> “This happened especially”—namely, that Pelagian errors spread more widely from day to day—“when, in the thirteenth century, Francis and Dominic established new orders of monks, which afterward attained great renown in the Roman Church. For Cassian especially pleased Dominic; hence he also caused his doctrines to be revived eagerly in the monasteries,” and so forth.

It is regrettable that such a statement escaped our learned friend! See Edmund Martène, a man distinguished for piety and learning, in his *Commentary on the Rule of Saint Benedict*, pp. 10 and 24.

[Col. 1055]

## Berno’s Little Book on Certain Matters Pertaining to the Office of the Mass

[*Bibliotheca veterum Patrum*, volume XVIII, p. 56.]

### Chapter One: How the Celebration of Mass Was Conducted in the Ancient Times of the Apostles

[Col. 1055D]

Therefore, at the beginning of the Church’s birth, the solemn celebrations of Mass were not conducted in the manner or order now customary. This is also attested by the most blessed Pope Gregory, who, among the many useful things he established—both in the celebration of Masses and in the various uses of ecclesiastical affairs—ordered the Lord’s Prayer to be sung in the preparation of the body and blood of Christ [Col. 1056D], as it is written of him: “He judged that the Lord’s Prayer should immediately be recited over the offering, after the Canon.”

When he perceived that certain people were murmuring about this and other matters, the most pious Father did not disdain, among other things, to give the following explanation, saying: “We say the Lord’s Prayer immediately after the prayer because it was the custom of the apostles to consecrate the sacrificial offering by that prayer alone. And it seemed to me very inappropriate [Col. 1057A] that we should say over the offering the prayer which Scholasticus had composed, while not saying over Christ’s body and blood the tradition which our Redeemer himself composed.”

But as the state of religion increased, so too did the dignity of ecclesiastical honor. Nevertheless, the Canon itself was not composed in its entirety by one person alone; rather, at different times one person inserted or added one thing and another something else, as we read concerning this most holy pope. He added to the Canon: “And dispose our days in your peace, and rescue us from eternal damnation, and command that we be numbered among your elect.” Concerning Pope Alexander also, who was seventh in succession from Saint Peter, we read as follows: “He introduced the Lord’s Passion into the priests’ prayer when Masses are celebrated.” Pope Leo established that the following should be said within the action of the sacrifice: “The holy sacrifice,” and so forth. [Col. 1057B]

Then Gregory, the third pope of that name, having built an oratory in the basilica of the Apostle Saint Peter in honor of all the saints, established that the daily solemn celebrations of Mass should be held there, and likewise ordered the priest to say in the Canon: “Whose solemnity is celebrated today in the sight of your majesty, Lord our God, throughout the whole world.” Since this pertains specifically to that celebration, it was not recorded in the Canon, which is said generally.

These things have been said about the Canon, which is also called the Action. Let us now consider the other matters that the Lord grants us to discuss. Pope Celestine established that the one hundred and fifty psalms of David should be sung before the sacrifice, arranged as antiphons from the whole Psalter. Previously this was not done; only the Epistle [Col. 1057C] of Blessed Paul and the holy Gospel were recited.

The Litanies—that is, “Kyrie eleison” and “Christe eleison,” which follow—are believed to have been taken from Greek usage. The prayers which we call Collects are believed to have been composed by various authors, especially Gelasius, bishop of Rome, and the blessed Pope Gregory. Hence we read in his Life:

“He also abridged the Gelasian book concerning the solemnities of the Mass, removing much, altering a little, and adding certain things, and compressed it into the volume of a single little book. He entitled this volume the Book of Sacraments.”

Perhaps in the earliest times only the Epistle of Paul was read; later, other readings were interspersed, not only from the New but also from the Old Testament, according as the order of the solemnities required.

Here it should be noted that, just as we believe Saint Gregory to have arranged these chants—whoever composed them—in the Book of Sacraments and the Antiphoner, so too we believe the blessed Jerome to have been the arranger of the Lectionary, as its preface, placed at the beginning of that same *Comes*—for so he called it—attests.

Later, when Graduals and Alleluias began to be used frequently between the apostolic and Gospel readings, the Spaniards, as though struck by the novelty of the matter, resisted strongly, saying:

“In certain churches of Spain, praises are sung after the Apostle and before the Gospel is preached, whereas the canons prescribe that after the Apostle not praises but the Gospel should be announced. For it is presumptuous to place first what ought to follow. Praises follow the Gospel because of the glory of Christ, which is proclaimed through that same [Col. 1058A] Gospel.”

Nevertheless, by the authority of the holy Roman Church it was later established that Responsories and Alleluias should be sung before the holy Gospel.

The same Spaniards also decreed in the Council of Toledo (Council of Toledo IV, canon 11) that the hymn of the three youths should be sung from the pulpit every Sunday and on the solemnities of martyrs. The Romans, however, do not do this except four times a year, on those Saturdays which are entitled “with twelve readings.”

The Creed of the Catholic faith is also recited after the Gospel, so that through the holy Gospel it may be believed in the heart for righteousness, while through the Creed confession may be made with the mouth for salvation (Romans 10). We sing it, however, not according to the Council of Nicaea but according to the Constantinopolitan version, translated as it is. The Council of Toledo also decreed [Col. 1058B] (Council of Toledo III, canon 11) that it should be sung every Sunday, following the custom of the Eastern churches.

Pope Sergius established that the clergy and people should say “Agnus Dei” during the breaking of the Lord’s body. The Offertory, which is sung during the offering, is said to have entered Christian usage from the custom of the earlier people; nevertheless, we do not clearly read what he specifically added. The same may be said of that angelic hymn, “Holy, Holy, Holy,” and of the antiphon said after Communion. We may sincerely believe that the earlier saints offered or received Communion in silence, as we still customarily do on Holy Saturday of Easter—although there are some who assert that Pope Sixtus added the aforesaid hymn, “Holy, Holy, Holy,” to the Mass. [Col. 1058C]

In all these matters, however, we must observe that, just as the most wise Pope Gregory most carefully corrected the Book of Sacraments according to the rule of truth, so too he composed and ordered, with considerable usefulness, the harmony of musical modulation.

## CHAPTER II. On “Glory in the Highest”

Now let the style of our discussion turn to the question toward which the whole preceding argument was directed: namely, why priests may not sing every Sunday or on the birthdays of the saints that hymn which the angels sang to the Lord born in the flesh, saying: “Glory to God in the highest,” and so forth.

If it has been permitted to sing it at Easter, according to the heading of the Missal, I consider it no less lawful at the Nativity of the Lord, when it first began to be heard by human beings on earth how it was sung by the angels in heaven. Let those who object bring forward where this was prohibited by the holy Fathers or by the most holy Pope Gregory himself; and if we cannot answer these points, we rightly surrender.

For whoever wishes to confirm something from the authority of Sacred Scripture ought to show, from the oracles of the prophets, the sayings of the apostles, the councils of the ancient Fathers, and their writings or deeds—and, greater than all these, from the truth of the holy Gospel—the passage by which he wishes to support his opinion. Hence we customarily say, “It is written in this or that place,” and we read in the decrees of the pontiffs or in such-and-such a council, in [Col. 1059A] such-and-such a chapter.

But since we nowhere read that Saint Gregory prohibited this hymn, let us also introduce suitable witnesses, so that their testimony may establish whether it ought rightly to be sung. For since it is written, “Every word shall stand on the testimony of two or three witnesses” (Matthew 18), I shall first produce two, and afterward many.

Pope Telesphorus, eighth in succession from Blessed Peter, established that before the sacrifice the angelic hymn should be said, namely: “Glory to God in the highest.” The martyrdom which he endured for the Lord testifies how his testimony should be regarded.

Concerning Pope Symmachus we likewise read: “He established that the hymn ‘Glory in the highest’ should be said every Sunday and on the birthdays of martyrs.” What sort of holiness this man possessed will be sufficiently clear to those who wish to read about his good works in the *Book of Dialogues*. There the blessed Pope Gregory relates that a certain Paschasius, a deacon of the holy Roman Church, had such merit before God that, when a demon-possessed man touched his dalmatic after his death, he was freed from the demon. Yet because Paschasius had resisted the ordinance of so great a pontiff, he appeared visibly—not in a dream—to a certain devout man while undergoing the punishments of purgatory, and made known for what fault he was suffering them.

Behold, two suitable witnesses have been found concerning this angelic hymn, and, I think, no one can refute them. But if a third is still sought, I now bring forward not the testimony of one person but of sixty bishops, who, gathered in the name of the Lord at the Fourth Council of Toledo (Toledan Council II, p. 730), promulgated a decree on this and other hymns of the same kind, in chapter 12:

“Concerning hymns, which are also to be sung, we have the example both of the Savior and of the apostles. For the Lord himself is said to have sung a hymn, as the evangelist Matthew testifies: ‘And after singing a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives’ (Matthew 25). And the Apostle Paul wrote to the Ephesians, saying: ‘Be filled with the Holy Spirit, speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs’ (Ephesians 5).

“And because they saw that certain people in the Church despised those hymns which appeared to have been composed by human ingenuity in praise of the apostles and in honor of the triumphs of the martyrs, they vigorously rebuked them with words of this sort, saying: ‘Then let them also reject that hymn composed by human beings which we say daily, in public and private worship, at the end of all the psalms: “Glory, honor to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit, for ever and ever. Amen.”’ In its place we sing: ‘Glory to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit, unto the end.’

“And afterward they add: ‘For that hymn also which the angels sang to Christ born in the flesh—“Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will”—is angelic. The remaining words which follow there were composed by ecclesiastical teachers. Therefore those words too ought not to be sung in churches, since they are not found in the passages of the holy Scriptures. Masses, prayers, orations, commendations, and impositions of hands are composed; if none of these were sung in the Church, all ecclesiastical offices would be idle.’ [Col. 1060A]

And shortly afterward:

“Therefore, just as no one should henceforth disapprove of prayers composed in praise of God, so no one should disapprove of hymns composed in his praise. Rather, let Gaul [or: Galicia] and Spain celebrate them in the same manner, and let those who dare reject hymns be punished by excommunication.”

Hence the holy Father Benedict commands us monks to celebrate hymns at all the regular offices—hymns which he calls Ambrosian.

Someone may object that at that time the Gauls and Spaniards had not yet adopted the custom of the holy Roman Church in the celebration of their Masses. We do not deny this either. The abbot Hilduin, a man highly learned in divine law, attests it in the letter which he sent to the Emperor Louis concerning the Passion of the holy martyr Dionysius and his companions. Among other matters which seemed relevant to his account, he added:

“This appears to be supported by very ancient Mass books, almost worn away by extreme age, which contain the order of the Mass according to Gallican custom—a practice observed in this western region from the beginning of the received faith until it accepted the form now in use, namely, the Roman one. In the archive of our monastery there is also a Missal arranged in a manner quite different from the usage of the Roman Church.”

And, greater than all these considerations, since there is one faith, why should the churches of Gaul differ from the Roman Church in the celebration of Mass? When Augustine asked this, Gregory replied:

“Your Fraternity knows the custom of the Roman Church, in which you remember having been brought up. But it is my pleasure that, whether you have found something in the Roman Church or in any other Church [Col. 1060C] which may please almighty God more, you carefully select it and pour it into the Church of the English, which is still new to the faith, as a special instruction gathered from the many Churches. For things are not to be loved because of places, but places because of good things. Therefore, from each of the Churches select whatever is devout, religious, and right; gather these things as if into a vessel, and make them customary among the minds of the English.”

These examples sufficiently instruct us that we do nothing wrong if we faithfully preserve those practices which we have received as established by the authority of pontiffs who preceded that holy man in time, or which we have borrowed from the usage of the Gallican or Spanish churches, imitating the praiseworthy humility of that most blessed pope.

When certain people criticized him because he followed the custom of other Churches, he acknowledged, among other things, saying [Col. 1060D]:

“If either the Church of Constantinople itself or any other Church possesses something good, I am ready to imitate it for the good, together with my subordinates, whom I shall forbid to do what is unlawful. For he is foolish who thinks himself so advanced that he refuses to learn the good things he sees.”

For if, as has often been said, we are prohibited from singing that angelic hymn on feast days because Roman priests do not customarily sing it, then in the same way we could remain silent about the Creed after the Gospel, which the Romans did not sing at all until the time of the Emperor Henry of blessed memory.

But when they were asked why they acted in this way, I heard them give the following answer in my own presence [Col. 1061A]: namely, that the Roman Church had never been infected with the filth of any heresy, but had remained unshaken in the solidity of the Catholic faith according to the teaching of Saint Peter. Therefore the Creed was more necessary for those who might at some time have been stained by heresy, so that they might repeat it more often by singing it.

But the lord emperor did not desist until, with everyone’s agreement, he persuaded the apostolic lord Benedict to have it sung at the public Mass. Whether they still observe this custom, however, we cannot affirm, because we do not know it with certainty.

In the same way, many things can be alleged which appear to have been introduced [variant: added] for the sake of ornament after the time of Saint Gregory, whereas the Psalmist says: “I will add [Col. 1061B] to all your praise” (Psalm 70).

It also seems very strange that, although it has been clearly determined what belongs exclusively to a bishop and not to a priest—namely, the ordination of clerics, the dedication of churches, the preparation of sacred chrism, the sacred imposition of hands for giving the Holy Spirit the Paraclete—there could be any other matter among the divine sacraments which priests do not share with bishops, especially since the most excellent thing in all the sacraments, namely the holy body and blood of Christ, is consecrated daily by priests just as by bishops, and the body and blood consecrated by the former is not holier than that consecrated by the latter.

Hence Saint Jerome says concerning these same priests:

“For in blessing they share with bishops [Col. 1061C] in the mysteries, and no difference is to be believed to exist between you and bishops in the preparation of Christ’s body and blood, since, if necessity demands it, they too ought to receive the Eucharist previously blessed by priests.”

And shortly afterward:

“For if anyone recalls this as an insult, thinking that he ought not to receive the Eucharist which a priest blesses, he is plainly perverse, believing that God had two bodies, one greater and one smaller: that which the bishop consecrates being greater, and that which priests consecrate smaller. Whoever thus divides Christ insults God.”

Moreover, when we read at the beginning of the Missal, concerning when Roman priests customarily sing or do not sing “Glory to God in the highest,” only the heading is given. Nowhere, however, do we find that it was prohibited to us either by the blessed Pope Gregory or by any of the holy [Col. 1061D] Fathers. Therefore, I think that we are permitted to sing the aforesaid hymn frequently every Sunday or on the birthdays of the saints, for the increase of divine praise.

## CHAPTER III. On the Octave of Pentecost

Having arranged these matters as best we could, it does not seem inappropriate to say something about the octave of Pentecost. When I was still residing among the Gauls, I learned that considerable controversy had arisen in those regions. Some maintained that, just as the Nativity and Resurrection of the Lord are celebrated, so the octave of Pentecost ought also to be celebrated, especially since we frequently read in our liturgical books [Col. 1062A] “after the octave of Pentecost.” Others, on the contrary, argued that in this solemnity—because the Holy Spirit appeared upon the apostles in fiery tongues—no more than seven days ought to be observed, in accordance with the gifts of that same Holy Spirit.

But, with the assistance of the Holy Spirit himself, let us settle this dispute between the two parties and show which side we ought rightly to favor.

When the outstanding doctor Saint Augustine was discussing the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount and comparing the individual Beatitudes with the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit—for the first Beatitude begins, “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5)—when he reached the eighth, he continued as follows:

“The eighth returns, as it were, to the beginning, because it shows and proves what has been completed and perfected. Thus the kingdom of heaven is named in the first [Col. 1062B] and in the eighth. When it is said, ‘Who will separate us from love? Tribulation? Or distress? Or persecution? Or famine? Or nakedness? Or danger? Or the sword?’ (Romans 8), there are seven things which bring perfection; for the eighth glorifies and reveals what has been perfected, so that through these stages the others may also be perfected, as though beginning again from the head.”

It seems to me, therefore, that the sevenfold operation of the Holy Spirit, of which Isaiah speaks (Isaiah 11), corresponds to these stages and statements.

And somewhat later:

“This eighth statement, which returns to the beginning and declares the perfected human being, perhaps also signifies circumcision on the eighth day in the Old Testament, and the Lord’s resurrection after the Sabbath—which is certainly the eighth day and also the first day—and the celebration [Col. 1062C] of the octave-days which we celebrate in the regeneration of the new human being, as well as in the number of Pentecost itself. For when the number seven is multiplied by seven, producing forty-nine, one is added as if an eighth, so that fifty may be completed. Thus we return, as it were, to the beginning, on the day when the Holy Spirit was sent, on which we are brought into the kingdom of heaven, receive our inheritance, are consoled, are fed, obtain mercy, are cleansed, and are made peaceful; and, thus perfected, we endure all external afflictions for the sake of truth and righteousness.”

From these words of Saint Augustine it can plainly be understood what may be thought concerning the octave of Pentecost.

For the present, however, let us speak briefly about the sacrament of our baptism, which is administered in the likeness of Christ’s death, burial, and resurrection. The Apostle [Col. 1062D] testifies to this when he says:

“All of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death. For we were buried with him through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life. For if we have been grafted into the likeness of his death, we shall likewise be united with his resurrection” (Romans 6), and so forth.

Hence the blessed Pope Leo also says:

“In the rule of baptism, death is present through the killing of sin; immersion imitates the three-day burial; and being lifted from the waters resembles the one rising from the tomb.”

Therefore the holy Fathers most rightly established only two legitimate times for baptism, unless necessity intervened: namely, Easter Saturday and Pentecost Saturday. Both [Col. 1063A] are celebrated for eight days. Those baptized on Saturday are rightly buried with Christ, so that they may be able to rise with him on Sunday. For just as the Sabbath signifies the rest of souls, so the Lord’s Day, which is both the first and the eighth, signifies the resurrection of bodies.

If, then, our baptism is celebrated for eight days because of a definite mystery, so that on the eighth day the baptized change their garments, why should the baptism of the apostles not be celebrated even more for eight days?

That the apostles were baptized on the holy day of Pentecost through the coming of the Holy Spirit, who appeared in fire, is attested in the Gospel by John the Baptist, who said to the crowds flocking to him:

“I indeed baptize you in water for repentance. But he who is to come after me is mightier than I, whose sandals I am not worthy [Col. 1063B] to carry. He will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire” (Matthew 3).

And the Lord himself said to the apostles:

“John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days from now” (Acts 1).

Concerning this solemnity of the octave of Pentecost, a certain distinguished teacher says:

“The eighth day is also the first, according to the pattern of the eight Beatitudes. The first Beatitude says: ‘Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven’ (Matthew 5). The eighth says: ‘Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven’ (ibid.).

“These statements pertain to those who have been regenerated: those who are poor in this life for the sake of the kingdom of heaven must persevere to the end of life, so that they may receive the kingdom for which they labored here.” [Col. 1063C]

The baptism of neophytes, although it takes place on Saturday, pertains to the baptism which the apostles received on the holy day of Pentecost, whose octave is the following Sunday, which we customarily call the octave of Pentecost.

And again, somewhat later:

“The work of the sevenfold Spirit is celebrated for seven days, and on the eighth day comes the completion, manifestation, and glorification of that same work. If this is so, the eighth day rightly recalls that same glorification in our offices: it returns to the beginning and is also the first day.

“Therefore, just as we celebrated the majesty of the Holy Spirit at Pentecost, let us celebrate it also in the octave of the same feast, so that, by recalling his gifts most frequently, his love may deign to pour itself more abundantly into our hearts.”

From all these considerations it is clear [Col. 1063D] that those who celebrate the octave of Pentecost act more rightly than those who refuse to do so. Therefore, with the greatest justice and correctness, the solemnity of Pentecost’s octave is celebrated, venerated, and honored by the holy mother Catholic Church, spread throughout the whole world. But whoever contradicts this sound definition divides the unity of that same mother Church.

Having finally brought to an end the discussion with which we have occupied ourselves until now, I wish to begin another line of argument.

## CHAPTER IV. On the Advent of the Lord

The first Sunday of the Advent of the Lord; the second Sunday; the third Sunday; the fourth Sunday, which is immediately before the Nativity of the Lord.

In the Lectionary, however—the book which he called the *Comes*—the arrangement is different [Col. 1064A]: the fifth Sunday before the Nativity of the Lord, which Amalarius called the preparation for the Lord’s Advent; then the fourth Sunday before the Nativity of the Lord; the third Sunday before the Nativity; the second Sunday before the Nativity; and the first Sunday before the Nativity.

Thus, in reverse order, what Jerome calls the first Sunday, or the one immediately before the Nativity of the Lord, Gregory calls the fourth Sunday of the Advent of the Lord. This is not unreasonable, in my view, on account of the five ages of this world, during which the human race was held captive under the yoke of the devil until he appeared in the flesh, being born from the womb of an inviolate Virgin, who would abolish the sins of the flesh through the offering of his body and sanctify the beginning [Col. 1064B] of the sixth age that followed.

Or it may be because our inner person is corrupted through the five bodily senses, so that death works within us, as the prophet says: “Death entered through your windows” (Jeremiah 9). Thus, during these five weeks, a dwelling is prepared in the mind for our King, whom the prophetic reading in that fifth week announces as coming in these words:

“Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will raise up for David a righteous Branch; and he shall reign as king and shall act wisely, and he shall execute judgment and righteousness in the earth” (Jeremiah 23).

The number four, which, as Saint Gregory noted above, he placed in the four Sundays of the Advent of the Lord, is celebrated with the following symbolism: since the human being consists of four elements, he awaits the Lord’s Advent [Col. 1064C] during four weeks. Through three orders of books—namely, the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms—he knows that the One formerly promised has been presented with certainty to this world for the salvation of the human race through the fourth order, that is, the beginning of the Gospel, in which the angel narrates to the holy ever-virgin Mary the conception and birth of the Lord.

And lest this small testimony of my own insignificance—which I have drawn more from the opinions of others than from my own—seem unworthy of consideration, let the statements of our predecessors be brought forward, so that from them at least it may clearly be established whose practice is more correct.

Amalarius, a not unworthy investigator of the divine offices, says:

“In the ancient books of the Missals and Lectionaries we find written: ‘the fifth week before the Nativity of the Lord.’ For we have an equal number of readings [Col. 1064D] in the Lectionary and an equal number of Gospels, beginning from the time mentioned and extending through the Sundays until the Nativity of the Lord.

“The Antiphoner has three daytime offices and a fourth on the Sunday which is vacant after the twelve readings; it has four offices at night, as I said above, on the Sundays.

“The author of the Lectionary arouses our faith so that we may recall the proclamation of our Lord Jesus Christ, who was to come into the world, through the five ages of the world.

“The author of the Missal called the Gregorian, and of the Antiphoner, touches us so that we may recall the Nativity of the Lord, celebrated through the three orders of books—namely, the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms—and also through the fourth, that is, the beginning of the Gospel. In that Gospel Gabriel the archangel [Col. 1065A] is described as sent to Zechariah, announcing the forerunner of the Lord’s Nativity, as well as the prophet Zechariah’s prophecy concerning the Lord’s Advent, and Gabriel’s being sent to the Virgin Mary (Luke 1), announcing to her the conception of our Savior, and other matters of this sort up to the Nativity itself.

“The fourth week itself—namely, the one immediately before the Nativity of the Lord, or the week in which it is celebrated—is distinctive. In the office of Matins it has proper antiphons for the psalms on each weekday.”

In another way, the author of the Lectionary teaches us how powerful the Lord is who is to come to us and enter our house in order to dwell in it—a house which we customarily defile through our five senses.

Attractive forms enter through the eyes; evil suspicion of a brother through the ears; a lustful odor [Col. 1065B] through the nostrils; gluttony pollutes us through the mouth; cruelty through action. The coming King does not wish to dwell in filth. Unless the dwelling is cleansed so thoroughly that not even the dust of such fantasies remains, the coming guest will not deign to enter it.

Therefore the author of the Lectionary writes five readings for the five weeks, to exhort us to circumcise our five senses from every vice and prepare a worthy dwelling for the King, the Lord, and the true Prophet.

Concerning the King himself the first reading says:

“Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will raise up for David a righteous Branch; he shall reign as king, and he shall act wisely” (Jeremiah 23).

But concerning the Lord it says:

“And this is the name by which they shall call him: ‘The Lord our righteousness’” (ibid.).

And again, in the Gospel, concerning the Prophet:

“For this is truly the Prophet who is to come into the world” [Col. 1065C] (John 6).

The author of the Missal or Antiphoner urges us to make this same preparation during four weeks. Just as the inner human being acts well or badly upon the soul through the five senses, so through the four elements he either falls into evil works or rises to good ones.

Therefore, as I said, the aforesaid author exhorts us: if until now we have been sluggish through negligence, let us henceforth rise to cleanse our house, so that the one who was not awakened in the fifth week may at least rise in the fourth.

The reading which is read in the fourth week says precisely this:

“We know that it is already the hour for us to rise from sleep” (Romans 1), and so forth.

For this reason I do not doubt that, in the aforesaid week, the cantor raises his voice with his trumpet:

“To you I have lifted up my soul,”

so that he may awaken those who in the fifth week were overcome by the sleep of negligence.

The reading mentioned below shows how we ought to prepare our house:

“Not in revelry and drunkenness, not in bedrooms and wantonness, not in strife and jealousy; but put on the Lord Jesus Christ” (Romans 13).

The Sacramentary impresses the same preparation upon the altars [variant: ears] of our hearts:

“Let us receive your mercy, O Lord, in the midst of your temple” (Psalm 47), so that we may precede the coming solemnities of our restoration with fitting honors.

This is the reason by which the opinion of the Fathers is supported [perhaps something is missing here: “who arranged three daytime offices in the Antiphoner,” or something similar]. For every dispensation of the humanity of the almighty Word is the indivisible work of the Holy Trinity. And although the assumption of humanity pertains to the Son alone, the effective completion of our redemption pertains to the whole Trinity.

Therefore it is judged entirely fitting and advantageous that only three weeks be observed in the Advent of the Lord. If anything has been added beyond this, it is understood synecdochically, lest the order and rule of so great a mystery be presumptuously—God forbid—abolished.

There is also another account of the same matter, by no means to be despised, which the glorious author and outstanding teacher of the Church, Hilary, employs in his book *On the Offices*:

“Just as that householder in the Gospel visited the fruitless fig tree three times (Luke 13), so the holy mother Church, through the annual recurrence of the Savior, has stirred herself during the hidden period of three weeks. For the Son of Man came to seek and save what was lost (Luke 19).

“He came before the Law, because through natural understanding it became known what each person ought to pursue and what ought to be done. He came under the Law, because through the examples of the patriarchs and the proclamations of the prophets he confirmed the legal decrees for the seed of Abraham. He came third, after the Law, through grace, for the calling of the Gentiles, so that from the rising of the sun to its setting they might learn to praise the name of the Lord—those whom he does not cease, until the end of the world, to exhort to worship his majesty.”

## CHAPTER V. On the Mass, “Our Supplication,” and the Harmony of the Sunday Offices
### [Col. 1066C] On the Mass *Hear Our Supplication*, and on the Harmony of the Sunday Offices

“Mercifully hear, we ask, O Lord, our supplication,” which in certain sacramentary books is customarily placed twice: first, after the week of Pentecost has been completed, following the offices of the fast of the fourth month, which in the Missal is entitled “The Sunday Is Vacant”; and secondly, after two Sundays, when the third begins.

Here, I think, one must ask in which place it is more properly said. For after the fast of each of the four seasons has been completed, the following Sunday is free from the office, although Masses composed for it are not lacking. And since the offices of the fast of the first month, in the first week of Lent, and of the fast of the fourth month, in the week of Pentecost, are found written down, although they always arrive at the same order, nevertheless, just as after the first week of Lent has been completed the Sunday that is placed there [Col. 1066D] is celebrated, and the readings from the Apostle and the holy Gospel are read, so it ought rightly to be done here as well—especially since the same Mass, the reading from the Apocalypse of John, and the Gospel that are read on that day agree with one another in a wondrous manner.

For the priest, in his own voice and that of the Church, beseeches that the disposition to make supplication and the assistance of protection be granted him; and in the reading it is written: “And the twenty-four elders fell down before him who sat upon the throne, and worshiped him who lives for ever and ever. Amen” (Rev. 4). And in the Gospel, Nicodemus, a ruler of the Jews, came to Jesus by night (John 3), asking and inquiring about the salvation of his soul.

After this, from the end of that same week until the Advent of the Lord, an equal number [Col. 1067A] is found both of offices and of Masses. For twenty-three weeks are counted, so harmoniously arranged that sometimes all the chant—namely, the antiphons called Introit chants, the Graduals, the Offertories, and the Communions—agrees with the apostolic and Gospel readings in such a way that, like a kind of organ, they produce a harmonious symphony from voices differing among themselves.

To give, by way of example, a few instances out of many, let us consider the first Sunday after the octave of Pentecost. Its Introit begins: “O Lord, I have hoped in your mercy” (Ps. 12); and the Responsory: “I said, O Lord” (Ps. 30), with the verse: “Blessed is he who understands concerning the needy” (Ps. 41). The Offertory likewise says: “Attend to the voice of my prayer” (Ps. 5).

Does it not seem to you that, in these words, the prophet—speaking in the voice of poor Lazarus [Col. 1067B] or in the person of the holy Church, poor and afflicted at this time—cries out to God, asking that he graciously take pity on his members in this valley of tears? And what does the reading from John on that day contain except the fullness of the honey of charity, when it says: “God is love, and whoever remains in love remains in God, and God in him” (1 John 4)? And a little earlier: “God loved us, and we ought to love one another” (ibid.).

What does the holy Gospel proclaim except that it urges us to works of mercy, when it shows the patience of poor Lazarus rewarded in Abraham’s bosom and the avarice of the proud rich man condemned (Luke 16)? On account of this, the priest beseeches him who is the strength of those who hope in him, asking him graciously to be present to our invocations. And because, without him, our mortal weakness can do nothing—just as Lazarus could do nothing without his help—may he grant us the assistance of his grace, so that, in carrying out his commandments, we may please him in will and action by loving him with all our heart, with all our soul, and with all our strength, and by loving our neighbor as ourselves. Then, when at last we have been received into Abraham’s bosom after the end of this life, may each one of us be able to sing with Lazarus in joyful exultation of heart: “I will declare all your wonders; I will rejoice and exult in you; I will sing praise to your name, O Most High” (Ps. 9).

In this manner, throughout the twenty-three weeks, if the Mass mentioned above is omitted in the third place, either all things agree with all things, or some with some—especially, if one examines carefully, the Masses agree with the Gospel [Col. 1067D] readings.

And so that a lengthy discourse may not produce weariness in the reader, after passing over many matters, let us still say a few things by way of example. It is not difficult to investigate how the Gospel reading in which the Lord says beforehand to Peter, “Do not be afraid; from now on you will be catching men,” and he, having brought the boats to land, followed him with his companions (Luke 5), agrees with the prayer of the Mass, which is composed in this form:

“God, who have prepared invisible good things for those who love you, pour into our hearts the affection of your love, so that, loving you in all things and above all things, we may attain your promises, which surpass every desire.”

So that we may be worthy to attain all these things with the apostles, Peter urges us in the reading to be “all of one mind in prayer” [Col. 1068A].

Again, the Mass corresponding to the Gospel reading in which the Lord fed four thousand people with seven loaves and a few small fish is this:

“God, whose providence is not deceived in the ordering of your creation, we humbly beseech you: remove all harmful things and grant us everything that will benefit us.”

For God foresaw what he would do for the hungry people. Rightly refreshed by the nourishment of divine generosity, they joyfully sing with the prophet Daniel: “As in the holocaust of rams,” asking that the sacrifice be made in the sight of the Lord in such a way that it may please him (Dan. 3). And because these words belonged to the legal sacrifices, and now testify that those sacrifices have been changed into the mystery of the body and blood of Christ, the Secret prayer begins in this way:

“God, who have established the distinction among the legal sacrifices by the perfection of a single sacrifice” [Col. 1068B].

The prayer corresponding to the Gospel in which the Lord wept over the city of Jerusalem (Luke 19) is:

“God, who manifest your omnipotence especially by sparing and showing mercy, multiply your mercy upon us” (Luke 18).

The Gospel of the two men and the apostolic reading that is read on that day agree well, when the Apostle says: “I am the least of the apostles, who am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God” (1 Cor. 1). And the tax collector, standing far off, did not dare to raise his eyes to heaven, but beat his breast, saying: “God, be merciful to me, a sinner” (Luke 18).

Standing between these two, the priest prays and says:

“Almighty and everlasting God, whose abundant goodness surpasses both the merits and the petitions of those who beseech you, pour out your mercy upon us, so that you may forgive what the conscience fears and add what prayer does not presume to ask” [Col. 1068C].

Now let us see what harmony may be found in the office of the twelfth Sunday after the octave of Pentecost. On that day, in the Gospel according to Mark, we read how they brought to the Lord a deaf man who could scarcely speak, and begged him to lay his hand upon him; and shortly afterward: “Immediately his ears were opened, and the bond of his tongue was loosed, and he spoke correctly” (Mark 7).

Observing this, the Prophet, speaking in the person of the sick man at the Introit, beseeches God, saying: “O God, attend to my help; O Lord, hasten to help me” (Ps. 69). The title of that psalm also agrees with this; it is inscribed: “For the end, of David, for remembrance, because the Lord saved me” [Col. 1068D].

Seeing that this grace of healing occurs only through a divine gift, the priest prays to the Lord in the following words:
