“Almighty and merciful God, from whose gift it comes that you are worthily and laudably served by your faithful, grant us, we ask, that we may run without stumbling toward your promises.”

Hence, in the reading, the Apostle professes that he has confidence through Christ toward God. And in the Responsory, as though the bond of the tongue had already been loosed, the Prophet promises to offer praises to God, saying: “I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise shall always be in my mouth. In the Lord my soul shall be praised” (Ps. 33).

The name of Moses is introduced in the reading; and in the Offertory: “Moses prayed before the Lord for [Col. 1069A] the sins of his people,” so that, just as in the Gospel the Lord heals the body that is sick, so here he may heal in soul the people who are languishing. Hence it is written: “And the Lord was appeased concerning the evil that he had said he would do to his people” (Exod. 32). And in the Verse: “The Lord said to Moses: ‘You have found grace in my sight, and I know you above all others’” (Exod. 33).

Thus both peoples, of the New and of the Old Testament, healed by divine benefits, commemorate those benefits, singing with the Prophet: “From the fruit of your works, O Lord, the earth shall be satisfied, that you may bring forth bread from the earth, and wine may gladden the heart of man” (Ps. 103). The earth which, in the first man, brought forth thorns and thistles after being cursed now, watered by heavenly rain and filled with the fruit of good works, produces that bread which came down from heaven. By its taste we are refreshed, and by the cup of wine, in the mystery of Christ’s blood, we are given to drink, so that the oil of divine mercy may gladden the face of the inner man, and that same bread may strengthen the human heart [Col. 1069B].

The Gospel in which a lawyer questions the Lord about the commandment, and he answers: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, with all your strength, and with all your mind, and your neighbor as yourself” (Matt. 22); and in which the Samaritan cares for the wounded man, gives him to the innkeeper, and promises him a reward (Luke 10)—to this Gospel the following prayer to the Lord corresponds:

“Almighty and everlasting God, grant us increase of faith, hope, and charity; and, so that we may be worthy to attain what you promise, make us love what you command.”

These and other matters, whether omitted, stated, or still remaining, if observed with diligent care, are brought to a harmonious conclusion—provided that the office “Exult in God” is sung on no Sunday. For since the other Sundays that are free after the fasts have assigned readings and Gospels, while this Sunday, which is here free, does not have them, that office is rightly omitted, so that harmony may be preserved in the others.

But if someone objects, asking why the office of Wednesday is not likewise sung here, as in the Advent of the Lord and in Lent, we reply that, since four weeks are appointed in the Lord’s Advent before Christmas, and separate offices are established for each day in Lent, so that the fourth day in Advent and the second Sunday in Lent are free, ecclesiastical men rightly determined how those two days should be supplied by the offices of the Wednesdays [Col. 1069D].

But after the week of Pentecost has ended, and the following Sunday is free, the office of Wednesday is no longer repeated; rather, “The Spirit of the Lord” is sung. Likewise, after the fast of the seventh month has ended, I think that the Wednesday office should not be repeated. Instead, if it is necessary to observe some office and no feast of the saints occurs, it is more fitting to repeat the office of the preceding week, as is customarily done in the churches of Gaul, than to disperse the harmony of the Gospels and the offices.

Nor can I sufficiently marvel at what reason prevents a single office, if circumstances require it, from being sung over two weeks, just as a single history with its Responsories may be sung over two, three, or four weeks [Col. 1070A]. For after the free week has ended, in the Introit of the Mass the cantor asks peace from the Lord, so that his prophets may be found faithful. And the Responsory gives the words of the prophet David: “I rejoiced in the things that were said to me: We shall go into the house of the Lord” (Ps. 121); and in the Verse: “Let peace be in your strength” (ibid.).

In the Gospel the Lord mentions the prophet Moses, saying: “The scribes and Pharisees have sat upon the chair of Moses” (Matt. 23). The following Offertory begins: “Moses sanctified an altar to the Lord,” and its first Verse is: “The Lord spoke to Moses”; its second Verse: “Moses prayed to the Lord.”

And in the Communion the Psalmist urges us, together with Moses, to take up sacrifices, enter the courts of the Lord, and worship the Lord in his holy hall (Ps. 95). And because we cannot please God either in sacrifice or in the offering of sacrifices without his help, nor enter his courts or worship him in his hall, the priest rightly beseeches God in his own voice and ours, saying:

“May the working of your mercy direct our hearts, O Lord, we ask, because without you we cannot please you” [Col. 1070B].

On the following Sunday, he himself consoles us in the Introit, saying: “I am the salvation of the people,” and so forth. Hence, in the Gospel he not only heals the paralytic whom they brought to him lying on a bed, but also forgives his sins, saying to him: “Take courage, son; your sins are forgiven” (Matt. 9).

Therefore, rightly we ask the Lord in the prayer of the Mass that almighty and merciful God, being reconciled to us, may drive away everything that opposes us, so that, just as the paralytic walked with free steps through God’s mercy, so we too, freed in mind and body, may carry out the things of God with free spirits [Col. 1070C].

And because the Apostle knew that certain scribes had said within themselves, “This man blasphemes,” he warned them beforehand in his Epistle, saying: “Therefore, speak the truth, each one with his neighbor, and do not give place to the devil” (Eph. 4).

Then comes the Sunday on which the Gospel is read about certain people invited to the wedding of the king’s son who neglected to come, as it is written: “One went to his farm, another to his business; and the rest seized his servants, treated them with insults, and killed them.” Wishing to guard us against this, the Apostle admonishes us in his Epistle, saying: “Do not become drunk with wine, in which there is debauchery, but be filled with the Holy Spirit” (Eph. 5).

There also, when the king saw among those reclining at table a man who was not dressed in a wedding garment, he ordered him to be thrown, with hands and feet bound, into the outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth (Matt. 22).

Observing this, the penitent people say: “We sat by the rivers of Babylon and wept when we remembered you, O Zion.” And the cantor, wishing to appease the Just Judge and make him favorable, begins to sing, confessing in these words: “All that you have done to us, O Lord, you have done in true judgment, because we have sinned against you” (Dan. 3), and so forth.

In the Responsory, already aspiring to the banquet of God, he sings: “The eyes of all hope in you, O Lord, and you give them food in due season” (Ps. 144). On account of all these things, the priest asks the merciful Judge, once appeased, to grant his faithful forgiveness and peace [Col. 1071A], so that they may all be cleansed from offenses and serve him with a secure mind.

And in the Communion, the Prophet, inspired by a certain hope through the divine gift, joyfully sings in the person of the faithful: “Remember your word to your servant, O Lord, in which you have given me hope; this has comforted me in my humiliation” (Ps. 118).

The harmony between the Gospel and apostolic readings, the Offertory, and the Mass in the week that follows is evident. In the Gospel the Lord heals the official’s son (John 5), while the Offertory recounts concerning blessed Job how Satan asked the Lord to test him and, after receiving power over his possessions and his flesh, destroyed all his substance and his children and afflicted his flesh with a grievous ulcer (Job 1).

To resist such ambushes, the Apostle urges us, by the example of blessed Job, to be strengthened in the Lord and in the power of his might: “Put on,” he says, “the armor of God, so that you may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil” (Eph. 6), and so forth, to the end of the reading [Col. 1071B].

And in the Gospel we read that, after the father learned that the boy had been healed at the hour when Jesus told him, “Your son lives,” he himself believed, and his entire household (John 4). His household means his family. On behalf of this family—that is, the Church gathered from the Gentiles—the priest prays in these words:

“Guard your family, we ask, O Lord, with continual mercy, so that, protected by you, it may be free from every adversity and devoted to your name in good works.”

In the Responsory the Prophet recalls the benefits and power of the Just Judge, saying: “O Lord, you have become our refuge” [Col. 1071C] (Ps. 89), and so forth, to the end of the following verse. Hence, in the Introit the cantor confesses that all things are placed in the will of the Lord and that no one can resist his will.

In the Communion also, the Prophet, speaking in the person of blessed Job or of the holy Church subjected to persecutions of many kinds, prays to the Lord, saying:

“My soul is in your salvation, and in your word I have hoped greatly, when you will pass judgment on those who persecute me. The wicked have persecuted me; help me, O Lord my God” (Ps. 118).

It remains only to speak of the twenty-second Sunday after the octave of Pentecost, and of how the entire office agrees with the Gospel in which the person of a king is introduced, who wished to settle accounts with his servants. When a debtor who owed ten thousand talents was brought before him and had no means of repaying, the king, moved by compassion, forgave him the debt. But because that man refused to show mercy to his fellow servant, the angry lord reclaimed the debt he had forgiven and handed him over to the torturers until he should repay the entire debt (Matt. 18) [Col. 1071D].

The Lord plainly declares the purpose of this parable, saying: “So also my heavenly Father will do to you, if you do not each forgive your brother from your hearts” (ibid.).

Fearing this sentence, the Prophet cries out to the Lord in the Introit, saying: “If you observe iniquities, O Lord, Lord, who will endure it?” (Ps. 129). And because he knew that the Lord was a just judge, he endeavored by this utterance to make him favorable: “For with you,” he says, “there is forgiveness, O God of Israel” (ibid.).

Therefore, the priest confidently asks the Lord, saying:

“God, our refuge and strength” (Ps. 45), be present to the devout prayers of your Church, you who are yourself the author of mercy, and grant that what we faithfully ask we may effectively obtain.

For we ask faithfully only if we have forgiven the debts of our fellow servants, so that we too may be able to be absolved by the Lord from our debts.

The apostolic reading also sufficiently admonishes us concerning the observance of the unity of fraternal charity, when the Apostle sets himself forth as an example and says, among other things: “God is my witness, how I long for you all in the mercies of Jesus Christ. And this I pray: that your charity may abound more and more in knowledge and in all understanding, so that you may approve what is excellent, that you may be sincere and without offense for the day of Christ, filled with the fruit of righteousness through Jesus Christ, to the glory and praise of God” (Phil. 1) [Col. 1072A].

The Responsory commends this charity, saying: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together as one” (Ps. 132).

In the Offertory, blessed Esther, bearing the figure of the Church, asks the Lord to remember her and to place a right word in her mouth. For if a right word sounds in our mouth—namely, when we confess our sins, repent, and forgive the debts of our neighbors—then immediately, in the Communion, the divine promise is directed toward us:

“I tell you: there is joy among the angels of God over one sinner who repents” (Luke 16).

As for the twenty-third Sunday, since I have treated it in a certain letter that I composed for Archbishop Aribo concerning the Advent of the Lord, I shall now refrain from saying anything about it.

## CHAPTER VI

[Col. 1072C]

Amid these matters, I think it worth asking why the author of the offices placed only twenty-three Sundays between the octave of Pentecost and the Advent of the Lord, whereas the arranger of the Lectionary placed twenty-five readings, apart from those customarily read on the octave of Pentecost, on the fifth Sunday before the Nativity of the Lord, and on the feast of the Holy Trinity. If these are added, the number twenty-eight is completed.

The one who arranged the offices took account of the embolismic years in the nineteen-year cycle, in which Easter usually occurs later and shorter intervals of time are completed between the octave of Pentecost and the Advent of the Lord; the other took account of the common years, in which the same Paschal feast customarily occurs earlier.

Let us give an example. When the final Paschal limit falls on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May, and Easter itself occurs on the seventh day before those same Kalends, whoever wishes to calculate carefully will be able to find no more than twenty-three weeks from the octave of Pentecost until the Advent of the Lord. And so it happens that the office “O Lord, in your mercy” must necessarily be sung in the very week of the octave of Pentecost.

But when the first Paschal limit falls on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, and holy Easter itself occurs immediately on the following day—that is, on the second day before the Kalends of April—then from the octave of Pentecost until the Advent of the Lord the number of twenty-eight weeks is completed, according to the reckoning of the Lectionary.

This is certainly a fitting number to stand between these solemnities of the Holy Spirit and the Advent of the Lord, because it is recognized as perfect not only according to the wise men of this world, since it is complete in its parts, but even more because of the mystery of the sevenfold grace and of evangelical teaching. For when seven is multiplied by four, it grows into this sum of perfection, so that just as six is perfect within the number ten, so this number is found perfect within the number one hundred.

A skillful calculator will easily understand this if he carefully gathers together the divisions of its parts. No one doubts that seven pertains to the Holy Spirit, while four pertains to the Gospel, because through the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit the Gospel is preached throughout the four regions of the world.

If anyone should contentiously attempt to object that, in the offices mentioned above, not everything agrees completely with everything else, let him receive this answer from Blessed Augustine:

“Not everything that is narrated as having happened should necessarily be thought to signify something; rather, they are added on account of those things that signify something. For the earth is plowed only by the plowshare; but, for this to be possible, the other members of the plow are also necessary. Likewise, only the strings of harps and similar musical instruments are fitted for singing; but, so that they may be fitted, there are also the other parts in the joining of the instruments, which are not struck by the singers, but to which those that resound when struck are attached. Thus, in prophetic history, certain things are also related that signify nothing, but they adhere to and are, in a certain manner, bound together with things that do signify.”

## CHAPTER VII. On the Fast of the Four Seasons

[Col. 1073C]

The Catholic Fathers established from the beginning the boundaries of right faith and holy doctrine, which it is altogether unlawful to transgress. Yet many ecclesiastical customs are also found to have been established by the holy Fathers within the limits of canonical regulation, such as Advent of the Lord, Septuagesima, Sexagesima, Quinquagesima, Lent, the greater litany, the days of Rogations before the Ascension of the Lord, the vigils of certain saints, and these very fasts of the Four Seasons now before us, together with many others. All these we are bound by perpetual right to observe without transgression of any kind and to hold as law, as Saint Augustine says to the presbyter Casulanus concerning the fast of Saturday:

> For in matters about which divine Scripture has established nothing certain, the custom of the people of God or the institutions of our ancestors must be held as law. [Col. 1073D]

Moreover, nothing is found to have been established without reason in ecclesiastical customs by the holy Fathers, if the cause is carefully investigated. As may be understood from the sermons of the ancients, and especially of Saint Augustine, it is necessary for our religion to celebrate the Four Fasts annually. For the year turns through four seasons: spring, summer, autumn, and winter. These four seasons, through their attractions, are accustomed to draw us back from love of the Creator. Therefore one must fast in each season, so that our four elements may be chastened and not be seduced by the world’s pleasure.

The four elements themselves are joined to the four seasons of the year. Spring is moist and warm, and in it we undertake one fast so that the element of moisture in us may be chastened and may not consent to the false beauty of spring. For the beauty of the earth arises from moisture and warmth. Summer is dry and warm; in it we undertake a second fast so that the element of warmth in us may be chastened and may not consent to the fire of the flesh. The third fast takes place in autumn, which is cold and dry, lest we wither and waste away through some languor of spirit and be found without the fatness of oil in the eternal tabernacle—for in that season we gather what we shall enjoy in the future. The fourth fast takes place in winter, which is cold and moist, lest our limbs be loosened by indulgence and dissipation in eating and drinking, and through this the love of God be neglected. [Col. 1074A]

But because the four seasons of the year hinder us from attaining the love of God [variant: draw us away from the love of God], we undertake four fasts, one in each season, each appropriate to its own time. In a similar way, the four daily cycles—morning, midday, evening, and night—hinder us from love of heavenly things. Through these also we are daily drawn away from love of eternal realities. Each has three days. Since each season has three months, individual days are consecrated to fasting for each month. Yet because daily sins weigh us down, one fast for each season is not sufficient; therefore we introduce the Lenten season, in which daily sins are afflicted.

These fasts of the Four Seasons are customarily celebrated on Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday. Wednesday is observed because on that day the Jews took counsel to kill Christ; Friday because they killed him; and on Saturday, by the authority of the holy Roman Church, the fast is concluded because of the sorrow that the apostles experienced over the death of our Redeemer, as Pope Innocent relates in his Decretals:

> Reason most clearly demonstrates that one must fast on Saturday. For if, on account of the venerable resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ, we celebrate the Lord’s Day not only at Easter but also repeatedly on that day throughout the cycles of the weeks, and if we fast on Friday because of the Lord’s Passion, we must not pass over Saturday, which seems to lie between the sorrow and the joy of that time. [Col. 1074C]

On that Saturday the consecration of ecclesiastical orders is also celebrated. Saint Augustine explains the reason for this consecration in his letter to Januarius:

> Saturday, he says, was commended to the former people for bodily observance in rest, so that it might be a figure of sanctification in the repose of the Holy Spirit. For nowhere do we read in Genesis of sanctification on all the preceding days; only of Saturday is it said: “God sanctified the seventh day” (Genesis 2). Therefore, because “the love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us” (Romans 5), sanctification is commemorated on the seventh day, where rest is commended.

Now let us consider the readings. On Wednesday two readings are read, so that those who are to be consecrated on Saturday may be admonished to possess knowledge of the Law and the Prophets, which flourished especially in the fourth age. On Friday only one is read, because the Law and the Prophecy are recapitulated in the one Gospel, which is now preached and read in the sixth age of the world.

Concerning the twelve readings assigned to Saturday in the Sacramentary, the following is found written in the letters of the Fathers:

> Six readings were formerly read by the Romans in Greek and Latin. This custom is still observed at Constantinople for two reasons: first, because Greeks were present who did not know the Latin language, and Latins were present who did not know Greek; and second, because of the unanimity of both peoples. The readings are called twelve because of the twelve readers, not because of twelve varieties of meaning. There are only six readings in terms of their content. For if we say “Amen” twice, we must not on that account understand two truths, but one.

But enough concerning these matters; let us now return to the subject at hand. If I remember correctly, your question was whether one ought to fast immediately on the first Saturday of March, even if that month begins on Thursday, Friday, or Saturday, or whether the fast should be deferred to another Saturday because of the Wednesday. To this I answer you from the custom of the holy Church, which must be held as the highest authority: one must always await the Wednesday of that same month, without opposition of any kind, because the fast that begins on Wednesday ends on Saturday. It is assigned wholly to March, not to February, so that our first fast may be consecrated to the Lord in the month in which the beginning of the year and creation itself began.

Accordingly, this limit must be firmly observed: no one should determine a fast before the fourth day before the Nones of March, or after the sixth day before the Ides of that month; but within these seven days, whenever the first occurrence falls, it will be lawful to fast. From this, as though by an intellectual thread, the straight line of the most correct rule extends for fourteen weeks to the second Saturday of June, and from there for another fourteen weeks to the third Saturday of September; then, whether for thirteen or fourteen weeks, to the Saturday immediately before the Nativity of the Lord, so that the limits of those Saturdays may be found without error.

To demonstrate this, let the seven weekdays be set out together with the same number of days in March—that is, from the fourth day before the Nones through the seventh day before the Ides—during which the limits of the first Saturday are customarily varied. Once these have been examined, the matter itself will become clear to us. Beginning with the last case: March either begins on Thursday, and the Saturday on which one must fast falls on the sixth day before the Ides; or the month begins on Friday, and the Saturday falls on the seventh day before the Ides; or it begins on Saturday, and the Saturday falls on the eighth day before the Ides; or the month begins on Sunday, and the Saturday falls on the Nones; or, if it begins on Monday, the Saturday falls on the day after the Nones. If it begins on Tuesday, the Saturday falls on the third day before the Nones; but if March begins on Wednesday, the Saturday falls on the fourth day before the Nones. [Col. 1076A]

If, by calculation, you direct your attention correctly from each of these individual limits to the limits of September across fourteen weeks, you will clearly see that in the fourth or seventh month the Wednesdays are fewer than their corresponding Saturdays in proportion to their number, except in September, when it begins on Thursday, in June when it begins on Wednesday, and in March when it begins on Tuesday. A prudent calculator will find it by no means difficult to investigate how this comes about.

From all this the reasoning is clear: the argument gathered from the number of weeks is firmer and more stable and never falters, whereas the argument compiled from consideration of weekdays sometimes wavers.

Concerning the tenth month, nothing else need be said except that the Saturday immediately before the Nativity of the Lord must always be observed, except when the vigil falls on Friday. I know that I have stated this as certain; and how true it is even in the matter presently under discussion, I shall try to demonstrate, with whatever brevity I can, from what has been said.

Thus Amalarius, that most diligent investigator of the divine offices, whose statements shine fortified by the judgments of Catholic men, says among other things when discussing these same fasts:

> The first apostolic men always administered consecrations in the month of December, in which the Nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ is celebrated, up to Simplicius, who was the forty-ninth after blessed Peter. He was the first, if I am not mistaken, to consecrate in February, for no other reason than to signify that those who are advanced through the sacred mystery should be joined more closely to Christ’s body. [Col. 1076B]

> This could in no way be done more suitably than if they were generated through those patriarchs from whom Christ was born. What is impossible according to the flesh is worthy and suitable according to the spirit: namely, that through the interpretations of the patriarchs’ names they should be born in the mind, since they appear to be more familiarly joined to Christ’s genealogy. And because it is incongruous that, just as a single week is assigned to each generation, a consecration should likewise be celebrated in every week, spiritual consecration is celebrated at each season for an appropriate reason, according to the virtues and interpretations of the patriarchs who are placed in the several sections of the genealogy.

> Through three annual groups of fourteen, forty-two weeks are formed. According to Matthew, there are that many generations of Christ with Christ himself; for that many weeks are found from the first Saturday of the first month to the fourth Saturday of the tenth month. The first consecration is celebrated on the first Saturday of the first month, which, as it were, generates Christ in the place of Abraham. Abraham is interpreted as “father of many nations,” to whom it was said: “In your offspring all nations shall be blessed” (Genesis 22). If a consecrated person stands among the offspring of many who are converted to God through his example, he is begotten from the first patriarch, Abraham; that offspring itself is Christ, in whose offspring it was promised to Abraham that all nations would be blessed.

> This consecration is celebrated in spring, a season suitable for generation. Abraham also belonged to the third age of this world, an age compared with adolescence, which is suitable for the generation of children. [Col. 1077A]

> The second consecration is in the fourth month, on the second Saturday, which is the beginning of the second catalogue of fourteen weeks. This is assigned to the place of the sons of David. David is interpreted as “strong of hand”; he struck down Goliath, that is, humility struck down pride. Those who are consecrated are consecrated so that they may be strong and, through humility, overthrow pride. This consecration is celebrated in June, when the sun’s great heat is over the earth. Everyone knows that David was warlike; the season of June is suitable for wars.

> The third consecration is celebrated in September, on the third Saturday, which is the beginning of the third catalogue. This is assigned to the generation of Jechoniah. Jechoniah is interpreted as “the preparation of the Lord.” No one doubts that, if all ought to be prepared for the Advent of the Lord, this is especially true of those who are consecrated. Nor is this without reason: if the catalogue of the final group of fourteen is counted and Jechoniah is counted only once, no more than thirteen generations are found with Christ; if he is counted twice, fourteen are found. [Col. 1077B]

> Saint Augustine declares that, for the sake of the mystery, Jechoniah—whose name means “the preparation of the Lord”—is counted twice, at the end of the earlier catalogue and at the beginning of the following one, signifying the cornerstone, that is, Christ. In him God the Father prepared to join two peoples, like walls, into one house.

> Blessed Jerome, however, relates that the matter was confused among Greeks and Latins through the fault of copyists and the passage of time. He asserts that the father who is called Joachim in Hebrew was not led into Chaldaea but died in his own land, and that Joachim’s son, returning from captivity, fathered Salathiel. [Col. 1077C]

> Therefore the aforesaid teacher wished it to be understood that the thirteen and fourteen weeks prefigured in mystery the fact that Jechoniah was placed in the catalogue once or twice. In fact, thirteen are found in every year except in those years when March falls on Tuesday or Wednesday and the Nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ falls on Sunday or Monday.

Concerning this fast, which the ancients used to celebrate on the very vigil, the aforementioned Amalarius said:

> This consecration ends on the very Nativity of Christ, as is still the custom, I do not know whether of all or only some Italians, to do—as I myself learned when I was present there. [Col. 1077D] But among our Churches the practice has grown of anticipating it in the preceding week, because the two offices of the fast and of the Nativity of the Lord cannot suitably be celebrated together. And just as we anticipate this one by bringing it forward, so, if the second Saturday of June coincides with the vigil of Pentecost, we defer it by prolonging it to the following Saturday, although our predecessors used to celebrate both together on the holy vigil itself, as we have clear testimony in the headings of the books.

> Why should we now inquire into something that has begun to be forgotten after so long a time? Nevertheless, lest you be deprived of this knowledge, the following heading concerning the matter is found in our books:

> If twelve readings fall on Holy Saturday of Pentecost, then on Wednesday let the antiphon “Hear, O Lord” be sung and read; Mass [prayer]: “We ask, O Lord, hear our prayers.” Seek in the first week of Lent. Reading: “Solomon said.” Likewise, prayer: “The devotion of the people.” Reading from the prophet Isaiah: “Hear, Jacob.” Alleluia: “Lord God of salvation.” Gospel according to Luke: “The disciples approaching.” Offertory: “Men of Galilee.” Communion: “Father, while I was with them.”
>
> On Friday: antiphon “Hear, O Lord”; Mass [prayer]: “Be favorable, O Lord.” Reading: “Rejoice, daughters of Zion.” Alleluia: “Lord, you have become our refuge.” Gospel according to Luke: “A man named Jairus came to Jesus.” Offertory: “Men of Galilee.” Communion: “Father, while I was with them.”
>
> On Saturday, once everything is prepared, let them first sing the litany. Then: “Lord, have mercy”; “Glory to God in the highest.” Afterwards, prayer: “To our minds.” Another: “By that fire.” Third: “God, who [works] toward souls.” Fourth: “Grant, we ask, almighty God, that by saving fasts…” Fifth: “Grant, we ask, almighty God, thus [deal with] us.” [Col. 1078B]
>
> The readings with their graduals follow: “Merciful,” “Protector,” “To the Lord,” “Let my prayer be directed,” and “Bless.” At Mass: “Grant, we ask, almighty God, that of splendor…” Reading: “While Apollos was at Corinth.” Alleluia: “Give thanks.” Tract: “Praise the Lord.” Gospel according to John: “If you love me.” Offertory: “Send forth your Spirit.” Communion: “At the last.”
>
> This is certainly according to the ancient custom. The graduals are included not only in our books but also, as I found them prescribed in a certain order according to the authority of Pope Gelasius. [Col. 1078C] This custom, as we have discovered, is still preserved today in the holy Roman Church.

The account also seems to be supported by the fact that in the authentic Antiphonaries only two alleluias are found written down, namely “You will send forth the Spirit” and “The Spirit of the Lord”; the others, however, were composed by modern writers. Therefore one must consider this: if the singing of alleluias abounds in monasteries, what do the simple priests of the villages do, who scarcely know two of them? To use the common proverb, either they sing what they know, or they are compelled to keep silent about what they do not know.

In writing this, I do not prejudice the authority of the most holy priests, whom I once heard, gathered in the Holy Spirit, establish in their synodal decrees that alleluias ought rather to be sung more abundantly. I have simply taken care to answer the questions according to what I was able to understand, wishing also, if I can, to assist the ignorance of those like myself who do not know how to sing so many alleluias.

In a certain little book concerning this order I read that, at each prayer, we ought to show humility of mind by bending the knees, except during the period from Easter to Pentecost. At the single prayer concerning the fiery furnace, we do not bend the knees, when Nebuchadnezzar was compelling the people to worship the statue he had made, so that our prayer to the one God may be separated from the error of the nations. For a similar reason, on Good Friday we do not bend the knees for the unbelieving Jews, who bent their knees before God in mockery, [Col. 1079A] lest we seem to imitate those who were eager to perform a good work badly. In the same way, we then abstain from the kiss because of the example of the betrayer Judas, who handed over the Lord Jesus Christ through a kiss of feigned peace.

If anyone wishes to celebrate the fasts of the Four Seasons in their lawful order, let him not neglect to observe the argument written above and gathered from the judgments of the holy Fathers. Carefully mark the first Saturday of March, together with the preceding Wednesday of that month, and count fourteen weeks from it to the second Saturday of June; then count another fourteen weeks from there to the third Saturday of September, which in no way deceives you. From there always observe the Saturday immediately before the Nativity of the Lord, whether there have been fourteen or thirteen weeks. On each of these four Saturdays the lawful fast will come to you without any error—the fast which the books of the Sacramentary prescribe as to be celebrated with twelve readings. If the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord falls on Saturday, the same fast must be anticipated in the preceding week.

[Col. 1079]

## Book of Berno, Abbot of Richenau, on How Advent of the Lord Is to Be Celebrated When the Nativity of the Lord Falls on Monday

*(Pez, Thesaurus Anecdotorum IV, II, 39.)*

[Col. 1079B] Here begins the letter of Berno, abbot of the monastery of Augia, to Aribo, archbishop of Mainz, concerning how Advent of the Lord ought to be celebrated this year when the Nativity of the Lord falls on Monday.

To Aribo, archbishop exalted to the summit of the highest dignity, through whom the measure of wheat is faithfully administered to fellow servants in the threshing floor of the Lord, Berno, although a lowly servant of the Mother of God, wishes the “Well done” of the good servant as his preface.

Whenever we are less than harmonious in the rite of ecclesiastical order, we ought to turn to the counsel of teachers, through whom, as Scripture testifies, divine Wisdom has searched out the depths of rivers and brought hidden things into the light. The Lawgiver also commands this: “Ask your father, and he will tell you; your elders, and they will explain it to you.” [Col. 1079C]

For this reason, most pious Father, we have judged that you above all should be consulted concerning the matters that have come into doubt regarding the celebration of the Advent of the Lord. Heavenly providence has granted you such fullness of knowledge that, through the water of the divine Scriptures, it has led you not only as far as the ankles, or the knees, or even the loins, but also as far as the very torrent which you cannot cross:

> For, it says, the waters of the deep torrent had swollen, and it cannot be crossed on foot.

Although it cannot be crossed, it is nevertheless possible, with the help of that divine Wisdom signified by the torrent, to reach it. Therefore touch, to some extent, the water of this torrent, which no mortal can cross, and offer some taste of understanding to our thirsty hearts. [Col. 1079D]

## Chapter I. The question at issue is proposed, different opinions are brought forward, and it is established that only four weeks are to be assigned to the celebration of Advent.

[Col. 1080B]

So that you may understand more clearly what we are asking, we inform you of something that we do not at all believe has long been hidden from you. Whenever the Nativity of the Lord falls on Monday, as in the present year, great error spreads through the Churches of God. Some say that no more than four Sundays should be celebrated together with the vigil itself of the most holy Nativity of the Lord; others, on the contrary, contend that Advent of the Lord ought rather to have four full weeks, dedicating a fifth Sunday especially to the vigil of the Lord. So far as we have been able to investigate, they have no other argument or reason in their defense except that the four offices found in the nocturnal Antiphonaries, or the readings from the holy Gospels and from the Apostle, may be completed more fully. [Col. 1080C]

In response, others put forward an opinion supported by a fuller rationale and by the authority of the ancients—namely, of blessed Pope Gregory and the presbyter Jerome. One of them, in the Sacramentary, that is, the Missal, placed the following headings:

> First Sunday of Advent of the Lord; second Sunday; third Sunday; fourth Sunday, which is immediately before Christmas.

The other, in the Lectionary, which he called the *Comes*, wrote:

> Fourth Sunday before Christmas—which the presbyter Amalarius called the preparation for Advent of the Lord—then fourth Sunday before Christmas; third Sunday before Christmas; second Sunday before Christmas; first Sunday before Christmas.

Thus, in reversed order, what Jerome calls the first or the Sunday immediately before Christmas Gregory calls the fourth Sunday of Advent of the Lord. [Col. 1080D]

This is not inappropriate, as I judge, because of the five ages of this world, during which the human race was held captive under the yoke of the devil, until the one who was born in the flesh through the womb of the untouched Virgin appeared, abolishing the sins of the flesh through the offering of his body and sanctifying the beginning of the succeeding sixth age. Or it may be because our inner person is corrupted through the five bodily senses, so that death works in us, as the prophet says: “Death has entered through your windows.” Thus, during these five weeks, lodging may be prepared in the mind for our king, whom the prophetic reading in that fifth week announces in these words as coming:

> “Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will raise up for David a righteous Branch.”

Again, in the daytime Antiphonary, after three offices the fast immediately follows; then the Sunday is left vacant. From this it is plainly demonstrated how greatly those also err who, in the present year, place the fast that ought to have preceded it after the vacant Sunday, beginning Advent of the Lord on the sixth day before the Kalends of December. [Col. 1081B]

If, to avoid this, they fast earlier, they nevertheless act against the institutions of the Fathers, who established that the fast of the tenth month should always be celebrated on the Saturday immediately before Christmas.

As for the number four, which, as we noted above, Saint Gregory assigned to the fourth Sunday of Advent of the Lord, celebrating it with this sacramental meaning—that a human being, who consists of four elements, should await his Advent through four weeks—through the three orders of books, namely the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms, he was formerly promised, and through the fourth, that is, the beginning of the Gospel, when the angel narrates to holy Mary, ever-virgin, the order of his conception and birth, we know with complete certainty that he was presented to this world for the salvation of the human race.

And lest such testimony from my own littleness—which I have offered more from the judgment of others than from my own—seem worthy of little regard, let the sayings of our predecessors be placed before us, so that from them at least it may plainly be proved whose usage is more correct.

## Chapter II. The same point is confirmed from Amalarius, Fortunatus, and Bede.

Amalarius says—the not-to-be-dismissed investigator of the divine offices (Book III of *Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 40):

> “In ancient books of Missals and Lectionaries it is found written: the fifth week before Christmas. For the Lectionary contains that number of readings, and that number of Gospels from the time mentioned through the Sundays up to the Nativity of the Lord. The Antiphonary has three daytime offices and a fourth on the Sunday that is vacant, after twelve readings; it has four nighttime offices, as I said above, for the Sundays. The author of the Lectionary arouses our faith to recall the proclamation of our Lord Jesus Christ, who was to come into the world, through the five ages of the world. The author of the Missal called the Gregorian, and of the Antiphonary, touches us so that we may recall the Nativity of the Lord celebrated through the three orders of books, namely the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms, and also through the fourth, that is, the beginning of the Gospel, in which Gabriel the archangel is narrated as having been sent to Zechariah—the announcement of the birth of the Lord’s forerunner. [Col. 1082A]

> “There is also the prophecy of Zechariah concerning the Advent of the Lord, and Gabriel sent to the Virgin Mary, announcing to her the conception of our Savior, and other such matters up to the very Nativity.

> “The fourth week itself, that is, the one immediately before Christmas or in which Christmas is celebrated, is distinctive. In the morning office it has proper antiphons in the psalms for each weekday. In another way the author of the Lectionary teaches us how powerful the Lord is who is to come to us and enter our house, so that he may dwell in it—a house we are accustomed to defile through our five senses. Alluring forms enter through the eyes; evil suspicion of a brother through the ears; lustful odor through the nostrils; gluttony pollutes through the mouth; cruelty through touch. The king who is to come does not wish to dwell amid filth. Unless the lodging is cleansed, so that not even the dust of such phantoms remains, the coming guest will not deign to enter it. Therefore the author writes five readings for five weeks, to urge us to circumcise our five senses from every vice and prepare a dwelling worthy of the king, the Lord, and the true prophet.

> “The first reading speaks of that king: ‘Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will raise up for David a righteous Branch, and the king shall reign and be wise.’ And again concerning the Lord: ‘And this is the name by which they will call him: The Lord our righteous one.’ And again in the Gospel concerning the prophet: ‘For this is truly the prophet who is to come into the world.’

> “The author of the Missal or Antiphonary urges us to make the same preparation through four weeks. For just as a human being acts well or badly toward the soul through the five senses as messengers, so through the four elements he either falls into bodily evils or rises toward good things. Therefore, as I said, the aforementioned author urges us that, if until now we have been sluggish through negligence, we should henceforth rise to cleanse our house, so that the one who did not awaken in the fifth week may at least rise in the fourth. The reading that is read in the fourth week says precisely this: ‘We know that it is now the hour for us to rise from sleep,’ and the rest. [Col. 1082C]

> “I do not doubt that for this reason the cantor raises his voice with the trumpet in the aforementioned week: ‘To you I have lifted up my soul,’ so that he may awaken those who have been overcome by the sleep of negligence in the fifth week.

> “The reading mentioned next shows how we ought to prepare our house: ‘Not in revelries and drunkenness, not in beds and wantonness, not in strife and rivalry, but put on the Lord Jesus Christ.’

> “The Sacramentary impresses the same preparation upon the ears of our heart: ‘Let us receive your mercy, O Lord,’ it says, ‘in the midst of your temple, so that with fitting honors we may go before the coming solemnities of our restoration.’

> “If anyone wishes to invalidate our statements, as though there were not four full weeks from the Sunday mentioned to the Nativity of the Lord, he seems to me to be ignorant of the rule of Sacred Scripture, which commonly fulfills the whole from a part.” [Col. 1083A]

These words make it sufficiently clear that those who count not four but five Sundays at the Nativity of the Lord transgress this rule of Sacred Scripture, which signifies not only the whole from a part but sometimes also a part from the whole.

This account is supported by the argument of the famous and most learned calculator, namely Lord Bede—if indeed it is granted that it belongs to him and not to someone else—which, I think, is known to almost the entire world:

> “Let it be known to all people that whoever wishes to celebrate Advent of the Lord diligently should see to it that he begin neither before the fifth day before the Kalends of December nor pass beyond the third day before the Nones of that month; but within these seven days, wherever the Sunday occurs, he may without doubt celebrate.”

This custom is observed, it is said, throughout almost all Gaul and in Rome itself, once mistress of the world. We learned this through the most truthful informants, and especially through Adalbold, bishop of blessed memory, who, having been challenged by our writings while present at Rome, investigated the matter—although afterward, I do not know for what reason, they acted otherwise. The people of Piacenza, however, as I myself learned at that same time by hearing and seeing, and other Italian cities, preserve the rule of the ancient institution.

The abbot Herigerus, a man of no small authority in our time, also composed a little book of his own on this subject. In it, as those who have read it assert, he refutes with probable arguments those who contend that more than four Sundays of Advent of the Lord should be celebrated, showing that they act against the institutions of the Fathers. [Col. 1083C]

## Chapter III. An objection to the foregoing is dissolved.

The objection raised by the opposing side—that four Sundays, apart from the vigil of the Lord, ought to be celebrated so that the four nighttime offices, or the reading from the holy Gospel or the Apostle on the Sunday that is vacant, may be completed—can easily be weakened by a reply. Who does not see that it would be highly incongruous for the mystical principles of the four weeks to be nullified on account of three or four responsories, which may, if that should seem appropriate, be sung on the weekdays of the preceding week; or on account of the reading from the holy Gospel or the Apostle, which may be completed on the Tuesday before the fast, as we ourselves have heard and seen done in the regions of Italy, or rather on the Sunday itself, when the vigil is celebrated with the morning hymns?

The fourth Sunday of Advent of the Lord would certainly not be vacant if it had its own proper office. The Introit “Remember” (*Memento*) is found in no authentic Antiphonary; the office itself was added by someone at his own pleasure. Therefore it need not be regarded as of the highest importance if, for a more reasonable cause, it is occasionally omitted.

This Sunday is vacant, just as the other three Sundays are, which are similarly placed after the twelve readings. Nevertheless, they do not lack readings from the Epistles and Gospels needed to complete the number of fifty-two Sundays in the year. There are four Sunday offices between the Nativity of the Lord and Septuagesima; from Septuagesima to Easter there are eight—the ninth is vacant in the middle—and from Easter to the octave of Pentecost there are eight. Then twenty-three follow up to Advent of the Lord. In Advent of the Lord only three are assigned, the fourth being vacant, as we said above. Four and eight, then eight and twenty-three, and three make forty-six. Add the four vacant Sundays, one that is the preparation for Advent of the Lord, and the Sunday of the Holy Trinity, and you will see that the total of fifty-two Sundays has been completed. [Col. 1084A]

But more Masses are found added in the Sacramentary: three, for example, after Theophany; one after the octave of Pentecost; and one in the seventh month, when the fast is to be celebrated. This is not, I think, an inappropriate arrangement, so that the number five, which here exceeds the number fifty-two, may nevertheless be joined by words of supplication to the fifth Sunday before Christmas. For the priest prays:

> “Stir up, O Lord, we ask, the wills of your faithful,” and so forth.

In some books of the Missals another Mass is also found, composed by I know not whom. If more are found in certain books, they are not in the authentic books.

With matters standing thus, I gladly ask those who strive this year with such zeal to add one week to the Sunday of Advent what they think should be done when Easter falls on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April and Septuagesima on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February. In that case the two offices—“All the earth” (*Omnis terra*) and “Worship” (*Adorate*)—will remain unused as though less necessary, unless perhaps they make room for the first, namely “All the earth,” in such a way that before Epiphany they sing “Upon the lofty throne” (*In excelso throno*) contrary to custom, although in all authentic Antiphonaries it is prescribed precisely as follows:

> “First Sunday after the Epiphany of the Lord.” [Col. 1084C]

Not only this, but also the responsories *Domine, ne in ira* (“Lord, not in anger …”) will be unable to reach any Sunday, since the octave of the Epiphany will fall on the Tuesday immediately before Septuagesima. If this is so—and indeed because it is so—they must understand that one of two things is necessary: either they must entirely omit as practically unnecessary all these items, namely the offices, the responsories *Domine, ne in ira* (“Lord, not in anger …”), [Col. 1084D] four lessons, and five Masses; or, wherever they can, they must insert them and concede to us that we may perform this with only one Mass and one apostolic or Gospel lesson, which they think themselves permitted to do in very many cases. Otherwise, let them move the Paschal limit far enough forward that those two offices—not to mention the lessons and Masses—may find a place between the Epiphany and Septuagesima; and we will concede to them that they anticipate the Advent of the Lord, so that the Sunday which is otherwise unoccupied may, with the whole week intact, precede the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord this year.

If they reply that this is forbidden by canonical authority, we for our part truthfully say that [Col. 1085A] we have unquestionably received from the holy Fathers Gelasius, Gregory, Jerome, and Hilary the rite by which we celebrate the Advent of the Lord. These authorities stand like foundations in the structure of the holy Church, and to refuse to accept their judgments is a transgression of divine law.

## CHAPTER IV. Berno invokes the authority of Aribo, so that he may permit no more than four Sundays of Advent to be celebrated

Although we believe these things to be so, we shall nevertheless not easily persuade others. Therefore, let a decision proceed from the authority of your holy see, one which determines to preserve the institutions of the holy Fathers, lest the sons of holy Mother Church, divided into schism, be able to dwell in the house of the Lord with less than complete unanimity. For at last we desire to drink pure draughts of this knowledge from the sweetest fountain of your sacred heart, lest, for too long, we stray from the truth through the various [Col. 1085B] streams of error. May you thus be granted that reward which the Lord deigned to promise through the prophet in these words: “Blessed are those who sow upon all waters.”

May the beloved Bridegroom of the Church, who daily descends into his garden, to the bed of spices, gather you—feeding in the gardens of virtue, among the lilies of the valleys of chastity—into [Col. 1086A] his granary after the end of this life! The humble little company of the brothers of Reichenau salutes you, always mindful of you amid the sacred offerings of prayer.

## Reply of Archbishop Aribo

Desiring to preserve your holiness undefiled throughout everlasting ages, we rejoice in your watchful concern for the things that belong to the Lord. At last, too, we wholeheartedly approve your treatises, so well and skillfully conceived, so excellently arranged, eloquently expressed, and finally recited with a firm memory; and, if the authority of so insignificant a pontificate has any force, we lay our hand upon them, as you requested. May the Lord make such grace in you fruitful and increase it, so that, if you should still perceive any obstacle remaining which might offend the Church, you may wish to drive it away [Col. 1086B] with the same caution and diligence.

Furthermore, we desire to be refreshed by your prayers and by the holy swarm which, under your governance, produces honey; and we earnestly ask that you—who now feed, under the form of the cross, on a portion of roasted fish so that you may someday be deemed worthy of a honeycomb—may by your prayers call back me too, who fight feebly from afar and sometimes, abandoning my post, yield ground.

[Col. 1085]

# Berno, Abbot of Reichenau: General Account of the Beginning of the Advent of the Lord According to the Authority of Bishop Hilary

*(In Pez, at the place cited above, p. 49.)*

[Col. 1085C] It must certainly be known, and must be carefully retained in the memory by all orthodox believers, that, just as the principal seasons of the current year are contained within their proper limits according to a fixed arrangement—namely, the season of Septuagesima, which is completed in a period of seventy-three days; the season of Lent, which consists of forty-two days; and likewise the limit of the Paschal solemnity, which varies over a period of ten and eleven years from 12 Kalends of April to 14 Kalends of May—the limit of the Rogation days, which at every time is sought from the day before the Nones of May and is the twentieth day of the moon in May; and the limit of Pentecost, which is always sought from 13 Kalends of June and is the fourth day of the moon in June—so, then, the limit for beginning the Advent of the Lord is fixed by an immovable boundary, according to the faith of the Council of Nicaea, from 5 Kalends of December to 3 Nones of that same [Col. 1085D] month. For the seven intervening days, which vary, plainly indicate the Sunday on which, without any deviation, the holy Church throughout the world begins to proclaim the Advent of the Lord each year.

And so it happens that, if this same limit is fixed on 6 Kalends of December, as is the custom of certain Churches, the entire week immediately preceding the Nativity of the Lord is found to be superfluous, and not at all uncertain. For it has been decreed by the mystical authority of the Fathers that the desirable Advent of the Lord should be completed only by waiting through three weeks. But if a fourth week grows in because of the variation of the four days contained within the aforesaid limit [Col. 1086C], it is counted by the figure of synecdoche—that is, the whole is counted from the part—because the whole week is not spent in idleness, but on its Saturday the vigil of the Lord is finally celebrated.

“What reason is there,” they say, “for four weeks to be completely fulfilled in proclaiming the Advent of the Lord, with the vigil of the Lord being observed upon the arrival of the fifth? If it begins on 3 Nones of December, where the last Sunday of that limit is found, only three complete weeks are spent in the Advent of the Lord, even when the solemnities of the lawful fast have been celebrated; finally, as the fourth week dawns, the vigil of the Lord occurs on Sunday.”

The reason, however, is that the aforesaid judgment of the Fathers supports it. For every dispensation of the incarnate Word of the Almighty is the undivided work of the Holy Trinity. [Col. 1086D] And although the assumption of humanity pertains to the Son alone, the accomplishment of our redemption belongs to the whole Trinity. Therefore it is judged entirely equitable and fitting that only three weeks be observed in the Advent of the Lord. If anything has been added beyond this, it is understood synecdochically, lest the rule of so great a mystery—God forbid—be presumptuously annulled.

There is also another explanation of the same matter, by no means to be disregarded, which the glorious author and outstanding teacher of the Church, Hilary, employs in his book *On Offices*: “Just as,” he says, “[Col. 1087A] the master of the household in the Gospel visited the unfruitful fig tree at his threefold coming, so holy Mother Church, through the recurring cycle of the year, hastened for herself the coming of the Savior through the mystical span of three weeks [the text has plural *spatia*, “spans”; another manuscript has singular *spatium*, “span”]. For the Son of Man came to seek and save what had been lost. He came before the Law, because through natural understanding it became known what each person ought to do and what each ought to follow. He came under the Law, because through the examples of the patriarchs and the proclamations of the prophets he confirmed the legal decrees given to Abraham. He came third, after the Law, through grace, for the calling of the Gentiles, so that from the rising of the sun to its setting children might learn to praise [*discerent*, “might learn”; manuscripts: *discernerent*, “might discern”] the name of the Lord; until the end of the world he does not cease to exhort them to worship his majesty.” These are the passages which, while I was staying among the Gauls, I not unprofitably gathered for myself from the book *On Offices* [Col. 1087B] of Saint Hilary.

## Confirmation of the Same Judgment

But lest what we have so far reported by following the footsteps of the Fathers perhaps appear ambiguous [*amphibola*, thus the manuscript], we thought it worthwhile to relate how this same authority was also supported in our presence, near the city of Orléans, by the assembly of many bishops and the determination of spiritual Fathers.

For it happened in a certain year, midway through the course of the nineteen-year cycle, that the canons of Orléans, owing to negligence, [Col. 1088A] began the Advent of the Lord on 6 Kalends of December. When that week had passed, the eighth day arrived, namely 3 Nones of December. We brothers of Fleury, monks of the most blessed Father Benedict, began the Advent of the Lord. On the following day, 2 Nones of December, the feast of the translation of that same Father was being celebrated; the aforesaid canons, as was customary, came together for so great a feast, while we, according to monastic custom, celebrated the morning Mass of the Advent of the Lord, which we had begun the previous day [another manuscript omits “the previous day”]. The men of Orléans began to murmur greatly among themselves and to accuse us rashly.

But because the solemnity of so great a Father held us back from replying, the matter was thoroughly discussed on the following day. Since it could not be settled [Col. 1088B] without the presence of the bishop of that city, all the bishops of the Franks agreed without delay to hold a council concerning the Advent of the Lord in the city already mentioned. We of Fleury were present, armed with the authority of the Fathers and fully prepared for the contest; and by contradicting them in every respect we so thoroughly refuted them that we imposed eternal silence upon them concerning this matter. From that day onward, no presumptuous person has been found among the Gauls or Germans who was willing to oppose so sound a determination. Therefore, if there is one Lord, one faith, and one baptism, let there also be one unanimity of the Church.

[Col. 1087]

# Berno, Abbot of Rich Reichenau: A Dialogue on How the Fasts of the Four Seasons Are to Be Observed on Their Saturdays

*(In Pez, at the place cited above, p. 53.)*

## Prologue of Berno, Abbot, to Aribo, Archbishop of Mainz, for the Dialogue on the Observance of the Ember Fasts

[Col. 1087C] To the most beloved lord Aribo, fragrant flower of bishops, Berno, the least of the servants of the Mother of God, as a pledge of discerning faith and likewise as the payment of due service.

Doctrine and truth, which display their beauty in the breastpiece upon your chest [the printed *in rationabilis peccatoris tui* is corrupt; apparently *in rationali pectoris tui*, referring to the priestly breastpiece], led my mind to regard you above all others as worthy to commend to your judgment the sequence of that account which I recently composed, [Col. 1088C] in the form of question and answer, concerning the fasts of the Four Seasons. For I have invented nothing from my own resources; rather, whatever I was able to discover that the ancient Fathers had expressed with good grounds on the subject, I committed to memory by writing it down with careful arrangement.

But now, O ornament, I beg you to weigh this little work in the scales of equitable judgment and pronounce whether it is worthy of approval; for it will be sufficiently validated if it has been strengthened by the authority of so great a bishop.

# Here Begins the Dialogue Held between Berno, Abbot of the Monastery of Reichenau, and the Monk Gerung, on How the Fasts of the Four Seasons Are to Be Observed on Their Saturdays

[Col. 1087]

## CHAPTER I. On the Diversity among Those Who Celebrate the Fasts of the Four Seasons

[Col. 1087D]

**G.** Although I do not doubt that during these sacred days of fasting you wish in every way to enjoy the leisure of the sweetest rest in bed, [Col. 1088D] having stripped off the garment of worldly activity, so that you take pleasure in saying, “I sleep, but my heart is awake,” [Col. 1089A] nevertheless I thought you should be roused by whatever prayers might awaken you, so that you may unbolt the door to your beloved Bridegroom, Christ, in our persons, and extend your hand to lead us into the chamber of sacred doctrine, where you may also break the bread of understanding for the little ones who ask for it. For you are then salutarily awakened for a time from the sleep of contemplation if you compassionately bend down to the needs of your neighbors.

**B.** You have defined this very admirably, my son. But I suffer all the more because I feel nothing of this kind within myself: no feather of virtue lifts me to the heights; rather, the heavy burden of worldly care sinks me to the depths, and the sluggishness of an undisciplined mind drags me through the sleep of repose toward harmful things. Thus I fear that I may be found among those of whom the Psalmist says: “They slept their sleep, and found nothing.” [Col. 1089B] Yet because Solomon says, “The lizard clings with its hands and dwells in kings’ houses,” although slow in understanding, I nevertheless place my trust in him who faithfully gives to everyone who asks him and reproaches no one. With whatever effort I can, I shall try through him to raise myself toward him, who also gave understanding to the rooster. So now, at last, set forth what you are so eager to investigate.

**G.** This, namely: although one faith commends the unity of holy Mother Catholic Church, why does she sometimes disagree among her children because of a diversity of customs? To bring one particular matter into the middle, I have now decided to inquire about the fasts of the Four Seasons, in the observance of which some appear to disagree. For while the books of the Sacraments are headed and arranged in this way—[Col. 1089C] that on the first Saturday of the first month twelve lessons are to be celebrated with fasting; in the fourth month, on the second; in the seventh, on the third; and in the tenth, on the Saturday immediately before the Nativity of the Lord—some think it should be understood as follows: if March begins on Thursday, Friday, or Saturday, they immediately celebrate the fast on that Saturday, although its preceding Wednesday, or sometimes even Friday, falls in February, and in the same manner observe the second Saturday in June and the third in September, without any consideration of the Wednesday or Friday. Others, on the contrary, do not wish to assign the first Saturday in March to the fast unless the Wednesday of that same month precedes it, and they apply the same arrangement to the Wednesdays in June and September [printed *quatuor ferias*, apparently for *quartas ferias*, “Wednesdays,” as the subsequent discussion shows]. Therefore reason requires you to disclose [Col. 1089D] whether an argument or rule was established by earlier generations concerning this matter, so that, instructed by its authority, we may discern which of these practices ought rather to be followed.

## CHAPTER II. In Uncertain and Doubtful Matters, the Institutions of Our Elders Must Be Maintained

**B.** It is right to take pleasure in the decisions of our predecessors, who surpassed us in age and wisdom, decisions which restrain the understanding of the mind within the boundary of its lawful course; whoever crosses that boundary is held liable to guilt. Hence Scripture beautifully admonishes us, saying: “Do not transgress the ancient boundaries which your fathers established.”

**G.** Pause your step here for a little while, and disclose to me the meaning of the testimony you have cited.

**B.** I do so willingly, since I see you present with such attention. [Col. 1090A] From the beginning, the Catholic Fathers established the boundaries of right faith and sound doctrine, and it is wholly unlawful to transgress them. Many ecclesiastical customs, too, are found to have been established by the holy Fathers within the limits of canonical rule, such as the Advent of the Lord, Septuagesima, Sexagesima, Quinquagesima, the Greater Litany, the Rogation days before the Ascension of the Lord, the vigils of certain saints, and these very fasts of the Four Seasons that are now before us, together with many others. All these we are rightly bound to observe perpetually, without any transgression, and to hold as law, as Saint Augustine says to the presbyter Casulanus concerning the fast of Saturday: [Col. 1090B] “For in those matters concerning which divine Scripture has established nothing certain, the custom of the people of God or the institutions of our elders must be held as law.” Furthermore, nothing is found to have been established by the holy Fathers in ecclesiastical customs without reason, if the cause is diligently investigated.

**G.** It is undoubtedly believed to be as you assert. For that reason it seems all the more fitting that you explain by what reasoning these fasts of the Four Seasons were established; why especially on these three days of the week; why two lessons are read on Wednesday, but only one on Friday; and why Saturday is headed for twelve lessons when no more than six are read. Then, too, I wish to ask what I originally set out to inquire: in what order [Col. 1090C] the often-mentioned and still-to-be-mentioned fasts are to be celebrated on their Saturdays.

## CHAPTER III. By What Reason the Fasts of the Four Seasons Were Established, Why Especially on Three Days of the Week, and Finally the Reason for the Greater or Lesser Number of Lessons

**B.** [Col. 1090C] *(Amalarius Fortunatus,* Ecclesiastical Offices, *book II, chapter 2.)* As can be understood from the sermons of the ancients, especially those of Saint Augustine, it is necessary for our religion to celebrate four fasts annually. For the year turns through four seasons: spring, summer, autumn, and winter. These four seasons customarily draw us away from the love of the Creator through their delights. Therefore we must fast in each season, so that our four elements may be chastened [Col. 1090D] and not be seduced by the pleasure of the world. The four elements themselves, joined in their nature, correspond to the four seasons of the year. Spring is warm and moist; in it we undertake one fast so that the element of moisture in us may be chastened and may not consent to the false beauty of spring. For from moisture and heat the beauty of the earth arises. Summer is dry and hot; in it we undertake a second fast, so that the element of heat in us may be chastened and may not consent to the burning of the flesh. The third fast is held in autumn, which is cold and dry, so that we may not wither and waste away through some weakness of spirit and be found without the richness of oil in the eternal tabernacle. For in that season we gather what we are to enjoy in the future. The fourth fast is held in winter, which is both moist and cold, so that our limbs may not be loosened by excess and indulgence [Col. 1091A] in eating and drinking, and thereby the love of God be neglected.

But because the four seasons of the year hinder us from the love of God, we undertake four fasts—one fast in each season, each corresponding to its season. In a similar way, the daily cycles hinder us four times from the love of heavenly things: in the morning, at midday, in the evening, and at night. Through these periods we are daily drawn away from the love of eternal things. Each seasonal fast has three days, because each season has three months. For each month, one day is consecrated to fasting. But because daily sins grow heavy upon us, one fast in each season is not sufficient; therefore we introduce the Lenten fast, by which daily sins may be afflicted.

[Col. 1091B] These fasts of the Four Seasons are customarily celebrated on these days, namely Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday. Wednesday, because on that day the Jews took counsel to kill Christ; Friday, because they killed him; and Saturday, by the authority of the holy Roman Church, the fast is concluded because of the sorrow which the apostles had over the death of our Redeemer, as Pope Innocent relates in his Decretals: “The reason,” he says, “most clearly demonstrates that one must fast on Saturday. For if on Sunday, on account of the venerable resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ, we celebrate not only Easter but also, throughout the cycles of the weeks, repeatedly represent the image of that day; and if we fast on Friday because of the Lord’s Passion [Col. 1091C], we ought not to pass over Saturday, which appears to lie enclosed between the sorrow and joy of that time.” On this Saturday, too, the consecration of ecclesiastical orders is celebrated. Saint Augustine also gives the reason for this consecration in his letter to Januarius: “Saturday,” he says, “was commended to the former people to be celebrated bodily in rest, so that it might be a figure of sanctification in the rest of the Holy Spirit. For nowhere in Genesis do we read of sanctification on all the preceding days; rather, it is said of Saturday alone: ‘God sanctified the seventh day,’ because the love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us. Therefore sanctification is commemorated on the seventh day, where rest is commended.” [Col. 1091D] Now let us consider the lessons.

On Wednesday two lessons are read, so that those who are to be consecrated on Saturday may be admonished to possess knowledge of the Law and the Prophets, which flourished especially in the fourth age. On Friday only one is read, because the Law and prophecy are recapitulated in the one Gospel, which is now preached and read in the sixth age of the world. Concerning the twelve lessons which are headed in the Sacramentary for Saturday, this is found written in the books of the Fathers: *(Amalarius Fortunatus,* Ecclesiastical Offices, *book II, chapter 1):* “Six lessons were read by the ancient Romans in Greek and Latin—a custom still observed today at Constantinople—for two reasons. One was that there were Greeks [Col. 1092A] who did not know the Latin language, and Latins who did not know Greek; the other was for the sake of the unanimity of both peoples. They are called twelve lessons because of the twelve readers, not because of twelve varieties of meaning. There are only six lessons in terms of their content. For if we say ‘Amen’ and ‘true,’ we must not therefore understand two varieties, but one.” But enough of this. Let us now return to the matters proposed.

## CHAPTER IV. Whether One Should Fast Immediately on the First Saturday of March, Even If That Month Begins on Thursday, Friday, or Saturday, or Whether It Should Be Deferred to Another Saturday Because of the Wednesday

If I remember your question correctly, it was this: whether one should fast immediately on the first Saturday of March, even if that month begins on Thursday, Friday, or Saturday, or whether it should be deferred to another Saturday because of the Wednesday. [Col. 1092B] To this I reply, on the basis of the custom of the holy Church—which must be held as possessing the greatest authority—that without any deviation one must always await the Wednesday of that same month. For the fast which begins on Wednesday and ends on Saturday is assigned wholly not to February but to March, for this reason: so that our first fast in that month may be consecrated to the Lord in which the beginning of the year and the creation of the world itself began. Therefore this limit must be firmly observed: no one should establish a Saturday for fasting before 4 Nones of March or after 6 Ides of that same month, [Col. 1092C] but within these seven days, wherever the first one occurs, one may lawfully fast. From this, as though by an intellectual thread, let the straight line of the most correct rule be drawn across fourteen weeks to the second Saturday of June, and from there through another fourteen weeks to the next Saturday before the Nativity of the Lord [the printed sequence omits a September stage, although the following discussion includes it], so that the limits of these Saturdays may be found without error.

**G.** You seem to have spoken sufficiently about the first month. But there is still something that troubles me concerning the fourth and seventh. When you said that fourteen weeks must always be counted from Saturday to Saturday, you did not add whether, after the fourteenth week has ended, the second Saturday of June, the fourth month, [Col. 1092D] should be preceded by two Wednesdays, and the third Saturday of September by three, since this appears to be precisely what gives rise to the question. I ask you to make clear how this usually comes about.

**B.** To demonstrate this, let the seven weekdays be set out together with the corresponding days of March—that is, from 4 Nones through 6 Ides—during which the limits of the first Saturday customarily vary, so that, when these are examined, the matter itself may disclose its character to us. Let us begin from the last. March either begins on Thursday, and that Saturday on which one must fast falls on the Ides [15 March as printed, inconsistent with the preceding stated range]; or the month begins on Friday, and the Saturday falls on the seventh day before the Ides; or March begins on Saturday, and the Saturday falls on the eighth day before the Ides; or the month begins on the first day, which is Sunday, and the Saturday falls on the Nones. Or, if it begins on Monday, the Saturday falls on the day before the Nones. If it begins on Tuesday, the Saturday falls on the third day before the Nones. Or if March begins on Wednesday, [Col. 1093A] the Saturday falls on the fourth day before the Nones.

If, applying calculation from each of these individual limits to the limits of June, and again from those to the limits of September, you direct your line accurately through fourteen weeks, you will clearly see that in the fourth or seventh month the appropriate number of Wednesdays is not lacking before the respective Saturdays—except in September, when September itself begins on Thursday, June on Wednesday, and March on Tuesday; and also when September and June coincide in this respect, with September beginning on Friday, June on Thursday, and March on Wednesday. It will not be difficult for a prudent calculator to investigate how this comes about.

From all these considerations, reason plainly teaches that the argument gathered from the number of weeks is firmer and more stable, never wavering, than the argument assembled from consideration of the weekdays, [Col. 1093B] which sometimes becomes unstable. Concerning the tenth month, nothing else need be said except that the Saturday immediately before the Nativity of the Lord is always to be observed, unless the vigil happens to fall on Saturday.

## CHAPTER V. The Foregoing Matters Are Further Explained and Confirmed

**G.** Although your speech has persuaded me that nothing is truer than what you assert, I would nevertheless like to be thoroughly instructed by what authority this argument discovered from the number fourteen weeks ought especially to be regarded as valid—particularly since I remember that you said above that nothing in ecclesiastical customs was established by the holy Fathers without being supported by some reason.

**B.** I know that I certainly said this, [Col. 1093C] and I shall now endeavor to demonstrate, as briefly as I can, how true it is also in this matter, which is the subject of the present discussion, from the statements of our elders. Amalarius, therefore, the most diligent investigator of the divine offices, whose statements shine forth fortified by the judgments of Catholic men, said the following, among other things, when discussing these same fasts *(On Ecclesiastical Offices, book II, chapter 1):*
