“The first apostolic bishops always administered consecrations in the month of December, in which the Nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ is celebrated, down to Simplicius, who was the forty-ninth after blessed Peter. He was the first, if I am not mistaken, to consecrate in February, for no other reason than to signify that those who are advanced through the sacred ministry should be joined more closely to the body of Christ. This cannot be done more suitably than [Col. 1093D] if they are generated through those patriarchs from whom Christ was born—a thing impossible according to the flesh, but worthy and fitting according to the spirit. That is, through the interpretations of the patriarchs’ names, they are born in mind, since they appear to be more familiarly associated with the genealogy of Christ.

“And because it is unsuitable that, just as a single week is assigned to each generation, a consecration should likewise be celebrated in each week, a consecration is celebrated in each season for an appropriate reason, according to the virtues and interpretations of the patriarchs who are placed in the sections of the genealogy. Through three fourteen-week periods (*tesseres decades annuales*, thus the manuscript) there are forty-two weeks in the year. There are as many generations of Christ [Col. 1094A] according to Matthew, including Christ himself; and likewise forty-two weeks are found from the first Saturday of the first month to the fourth Saturday of the tenth month.

“The first consecration is celebrated on the first Saturday of the first month. It is, as it were, in the place of Abraham, who generates Christ. Abraham is interpreted as ‘father of many nations,’ to whom it was said: ‘In your seed all nations shall be blessed.’ If a consecrated man stands in the seed of many who convert to God through his example, he has been begotten of the first patriarch, Abraham; that seed itself is Christ, in whom it was promised to Abraham that all nations would be blessed. This consecration is celebrated in spring, a season suitable for procreation. Abraham, too, belonged to the third age of this world, an age compared with youth, [Col. 1094B] which is suited to the generation of children.

“The second consecration takes place in the fourth month, on the second Saturday, which is the beginning of the second catalogue of fourteen weeks. This is assigned to the place of the sons of David. David is interpreted as ‘strong of hand.’ He struck down Goliath—that is, humility struck down pride. Those who are consecrated are consecrated for this reason: so that they may be strong and, through humility, overthrow pride. This consecration is celebrated in June, when the sun’s great heat is upon the earth. Everyone knows that David was warlike and burned intensely for battle. The season of June is suited to wars.

“The third consecration is celebrated in September, on the third Saturday, which is the beginning of the third catalogue. It is assigned to the generation of Jeconiah. Jeconiah is interpreted as ‘the preparation of the Lord.’ There is no doubt that, if all must be prepared for the coming of Christ, [Col. 1094C] those who are consecrated must be prepared above all. This consecration has its end in the Nativity of Christ. Sometimes it ends in the third week, because the days of the Nativity of the Lord have been anticipated, and then it has thirteen weeks; sometimes it ends in the fourth, because of lateness, and then it has fourteen. Nor is this without reason. For if the catalogue of the last group of fourteen (*tesserecedecadis*, thus the manuscript) is counted, and Jeconiah is counted once, no more than thirteen generations are found with Christ. If he is counted twice, fourteen are found.”

There you have what you wished to know: namely, why the argument for the four fasts is to be gathered from the reckoning of fourteen weeks.

**G.** I give thanks to God and to you, since I now possess this explanation. [Col. 1094D] But I think it is not fruitless to ask further what is meant by the statement: “If Jeconiah is counted once, no more than thirteen generations are found with Christ; but if he is counted twice, fourteen are found.”

**B.** Saint Augustine says that this was done because of the mystery: Jeconiah, whose name is interpreted as “the preparation of the Lord,” was counted twice, being placed at the end of the preceding catalogue and at the beginning of the following one, signifying the cornerstone—that is, Christ—in whom God the Father prepared to join two peoples, like walls, into one house. Yet blessed Jerome reports that, because of scribal error and the passage of time, the matter became confused between the Greeks and Latins. He says that the father [Col. 1095A] who is named Joachim in the Hebrew text was not led into Chaldea but died in his own land, and that his son Joachim, returning from captivity, fathered Salathiel. Therefore the aforesaid teacher wished it to be understood that the thirteen and fourteen weeks prefigured in mystery the fact that Jeconiah was placed once or twice in the catalogue.

## CHAPTER VI. When Thirteen or Fourteen Weeks Occur, and So Forth

**G.** I hope you will not now be burdened by telling me when thirteen weeks and when fourteen weeks usually occur.

**B.** For the sake of your love, I shall certainly not be burdened to disclose what I have been able to learn as true. [Col. 1095B] In fact, thirteen occur in every year except when March falls on Tuesday or Wednesday, while the Nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ falls on Sunday or Monday. Concerning this fast, which the ancients used to celebrate on the vigil itself, the aforementioned Amalarius said that the consecration ends on the Nativity of Christ, as is still the custom of certain Italians—whether of all of them I do not know—as I myself learned while staying there. But in our Churches the practice has developed of anticipating it in the preceding week, because the two offices of the fast and the Nativity of the Lord cannot suitably be celebrated together. For just as we anticipate the former by bringing it forward, so, when the second Saturday of June falls on the vigil of Pentecost, we defer it by extending it to the following Saturday, [Col. 1095C] although our predecessors used to celebrate both together on the holy vigil itself, as we have clear evidence from the headings of the books.

**G.** I wish to know by what propriety these two offices can be celebrated together.

**B.** Why is there any need now to investigate what has already begun to be forgotten over such a long period? Nevertheless, so that you may not be deprived of this knowledge, the following rubric is found concerning the matter in our books:

“If twelve lessons fall on the Saturday of holy Pentecost, then on Wednesday let the following be sung and read: ‘Hear, O Lord, our prayers.’ Seek in the first week of Lent. Or from the Books of Wisdom: ‘Solomon said.’ Likewise the prayer: ‘The devotion of the people.’ Or from the prophet Isaiah: ‘Hear, Jacob.’ Alleluia (‘Praise the Lord’). Office chant (*Off.*): ‘Lord God of my salvation.’ [Col. 1095D] Gospel according to Luke: ‘The disciples approaching.’ Offertory: ‘Men of Galilee.’ Communion: ‘Father, when I was …’

“Friday: ‘Hear, O Lord.’ Prayer: ‘Be favorable, O Lord.’ Lesson: ‘Rejoice, daughters of Zion.’ Alleluia: ‘O Lord, our refuge.’ Gospel: ‘There came to Jesus a man whose name was Jairus.’ Offertory: ‘Men of Galilee.’ Communion: ‘Father, when I was …’

“On Saturday, once all are prepared, let them first sing the litany: ‘Kyrie eleison’ (‘Lord, have mercy’). ‘Glory to God in the highest.’ Then the prayer: ‘To our minds.’ Prayer: ‘With that fire.’ Prayer: ‘O God, who [acts] toward souls.’ Prayer: ‘Grant, we beseech you, almighty God, that thus we…’ The lessons with their graduals follow. Gradual: ‘Be merciful.’ Gradual: ‘Protector.’ Gradual: ‘To the Lord.’ Gradual: ‘Let my prayer be directed.’ Gradual: *Bened…*, “Bless …” [abbreviated incipit]. Prayer: ‘Grant, we beseech you, almighty God, that …’ [the incipit continues *ut clar…*, with the last word abbreviated]. Or: ‘While Apollos was…’ Alleluia: ‘Give thanks.’ [Col. 1096A] Tract: ‘Praise.’ Gospel: ‘If you love me.’ Offertory: ‘Send forth your Spirit.’ Communion: ‘On the last day of the feast.’”

## CHAPTER VII. Whether, When the Fast Is Deferred to Another Saturday or Falls within the Holy Week of Pentecost, the Graduals or the Alleluias Should Be Sung

**G.** If the fast itself is deferred to another Saturday, as you said a little earlier it should be, or if it falls within the holy week of Pentecost itself, should the graduals or the alleluias be sung?

**B.** According to the ancient custom, certainly the graduals. This is found inserted not only in our books but also, as I found it headed in a certain order according to the authority of Pope Gelasius; and, as we have learned, [Col. 1096B] this custom is preserved to this day in the holy Roman Church. The fact that only two alleluias are found written in the authoritative Antiphonaries also seems to support this account, namely: “Send forth your Spirit” and “The Spirit of the Lord.” The rest were composed by modern authors.

Therefore one must consider this: if singing alleluias abounds in monasteries, what are the simple village priests to do, who scarcely know two of them? To use a common proverb: either they sing what they know, or they are compelled to remain silent about what they do not know. In writing this, however, I do not prejudice the authority of the most holy priests, whom I heard long ago, gathered in the Holy Spirit, [Col. 1096C] establish in their synodal decrees that the alleluias ought rather to be sung. I have simply taken care to answer the questions according to what I was able to understand, wishing, if possible, also to provide counsel for the ignorance of those like myself, who do not know how to sing so many alleluias.

G. Since it is the Church’s custom on these days that we pray standing, I wish to learn whether, if the fast so often mentioned should occur during this week, we ought to kneel at Mass or not.

B. In a certain little book concerning this order I read the following (Amalarius Fortunatus, *The Ecclesiastical Offices*, book II, chapter 3):

> At each prayer we ought to show humility of mind by genuflection, except during the period after Pentecost. Only during *De camino ignis* do we not kneel, when Nebuchadnezzar compelled the people to worship the statue he had made, so that our prayer, which is directed to the one God, may be distinguished from the error of the Gentiles. For a similar reason we also do not kneel on Good Friday on behalf of the faithless Jews, who, in mockery, knelt before the Lord, lest we seem to imitate those who strove to perform a good work wickedly. In the same way, at that time we abstain from the kiss because of the example of Judas the betrayer, who through a kiss of feigned peace betrayed the Lord Jesus Christ.

## CHAPTER VIII  
### Summary of the doctrine explained thus far, and the prescribed manner to be observed in fasting

G. Since you have satisfied my inquiry in every respect, all that remains is for you, from the connection of the conversation we have had up to this point, to gather together a brief summary, by which those whose ears are wearied by lengthy speech may be instructed in this subject.

B. If anyone desires to observe the fasts of the Four Ember Seasons in their proper order, let him not neglect to follow the argument written below, gathered from the opinions of the holy Fathers. Mark carefully the first Saturday of March, together with the preceding Wednesday of that same month, and count fourteen weeks from that point onward, up to the third Saturday of September—which cannot mislead you in any way. From there, always observe the Saturday immediately preceding the Nativity of the Lord, whether there are fourteen weeks or thirteen. On each of these four Saturdays, without any error, that fast will properly occur which is designated in the sacramentaries as being celebrated with twelve readings. But if the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord falls on a Saturday, that same fast must be anticipated to the preceding week.

G. Since you have now determined the times of the fast in a regular manner, I ask that you also describe, even if briefly, some rule of abstinence, so that our outward man may be guarded against either wasting away through excessive starvation and becoming feeble, or growing insolent through an immoderate appetite for food; lest Nabuzardan, the chief of the cooks—that is, the most wicked glut of voraciousness—overcome us, and the walls of our Jerusalem collapse within us, as it is written: “The chief of the cooks destroyed the walls of Jerusalem.”

B. Since the table of Sacred Scripture, concerning which the Psalmist says to the Lord, “You have prepared a table before me,” is placed before every petitioner and is filled with the varied teachings of every discipline, it seems strange that you should ask me for something which you can discover for yourself. Nevertheless, lest at the conclusion of this little work I prove to be a harsh creditor, after having thus far shown myself ready to serve you in the duty of giving, I shall provide, on my behalf, one supplier of heavenly food from among many as a guarantor—I mean Saint Augustine—so that you may be instructed by the mastery of his art in the manner you should employ in abstaining.

# Berno’s Short Works on Music

*(In D. Martin Gerbert, abbot of the monastery of St. Blasius in the Black Forest, ecclesiastical writers on music, vol. II, p. 61.)*

[Col. 1097]

## Editorial Notice

We publish Berno’s prologue to the *Tonary* of the monk of Reichenau, from a twelfth-century manuscript of St. Blasius, collated with the manuscripts of Leipzig, Saint-Emmeram, Admont, and Ottobeuren. It was dedicated not to Grinoverus but to Piligrinus, archbishop of Cologne, as I restored with my own eyes from that twelfth-century manuscript of Villingen—the one consumed by flames in 1768 together with the monastery of St. Blasius—the true reading against the erroneous one, “To the beloved son Grinoverus,” which misled Mabillon and planted a stumbling block for the editors of *Gallia Christiana*, vol. III, p. 659, who clearly recognized that there could have been no place for Grinoverus among the archbishops of Cologne at that time.

The Roman uncial letters in which this entire title or inscription was written had been embellished, in the varied strokes and curls customary to the age—ornaments which even idle typographers of our own day are beginning to employ. These led the copyist astray, so that instead of *Piligrino vero* he wrote *Filio Grinovero*. The matter is rendered certain by the other manuscripts which we consulted.

We give the *Tonary* from Vatican manuscript no. 1344 of the Palatine Library, dating from the eleventh century, collated with the Admont manuscript. It nevertheless differs considerably from the beginning onward. The Vatican manuscript reads as follows:

> “The authentic *protos* consists of the first species of the *diapente* and, above it, of the first species of the *diatessaron*. Its final syllable in *saeculorum Amen* lies higher than the final by an interval of a *diatessaron*.”

The Admont manuscript, however, reads:

> “The authentic *protos* has eight differentiae; the first of them ends its *saeculorum Amen* on the *lichanos hypaton* at an interval of a *diatessaron*.”

We also present a letter by Berno himself, entitled “On the Various Modulation of Psalms and Songs,” addressed to Meginfrid, Eipennon, and his beloved brothers in Christ, from an eleventh- or twelfth-century manuscript of Salem; and, from an eleventh-century manuscript of St. Gall, a letter “On the Consonant Diversity of the Tones,” dedicated to Burchard and Kerung, together with the others engaged in the school of the Lord at Reichenau.

[Col. 1097]

# Berno’s Music  
[Note: [Col. 1097] Leipzig manuscript: Bernhard.]

## Or Prologue to the *Tonary*

### Summary

1. The musical scale.  
2. The nine modes of sound.  
3. Musical consonances.  
4. The tetrachord, especially that of the finals.  
5. The species of consonances.  
6. The eight musical tones in ecclesiastical use.  
7. Their limits.  
8. The ascents and descents of sounds.  
9. Median and common tones, from which some establish twelve modes.  
10. Indifferent tones.  
11. Songs concerning the regular composition of modes.  
12. The differentiae of the tones.  
13. The *Noanneane* formulas, and so forth.  
14. Irregular tones and songs to be avoided.  
15. The position of the semitone, to be carefully observed.

## Berno’s Letter to Piligrinus

[Col. 1099A] To the lord and beloved of God, Piligrinus, truly a stranger and pilgrim in this world: Berno—though slight in merits, nevertheless a servant of the Virgin Mother of God—[wishes] citizenship in the citadel of divine contemplation.

The splendid form of Christian faith shining brilliantly in you proves with distinction that your soul is the seat of wisdom. For the dignity of moral discipline so orders the natural movements of your spirit that, through a rational progression, you are borne upward to heavenly things by the love of divine contemplation. There, amid the joyful exultation of your heart, may it delight your soul to proclaim to its Bridegroom:

> “Draw me after you; we shall run in the fragrance of your ointments,”

as though among those who hold harps in their hands and sing the song of Moses, the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb.

When I consider this, I can hardly discover [Col. 1099B] what reason there could have been for you—whom not only the contemplation of the four mathematical disciplines renders complete, but whom also the melody of heavenly harmony continually keeps intent upon divine praises—to command me, so to speak, half-voiced, indeed almost mute and tongue-tied in the arts, to say something about the tuneful modulation of music.

This is especially remarkable since, exalted by God in the Church of the people and praised in the assembly of elders, you continually receive with joyful inward hearing the way in which wise and fortunate Cologne, under your episcopal rule, with the blessed sons of its Church, while the prince of the apostles modulates, in a certain manner, the plectrum of all languages, sings to the Lord God upon a ten-stringed psaltery with song and harp.

Yet, urged on by nature itself, I do not doubt that you wished to request this of me with such ardor because, since the entire structure of our soul and body is joined together by musical harmony, your own spirit might also be delighted more sweetly by the sonorous sweetness of this art. For, as Cicero says, nothing is more desirous of things like itself, nor more rapacious, than nature.

And since, through that affection of charity with which you have always freely cherished me, you imposed upon me this work of obedience [Note: [Col. 1099D] Leipzig manuscript: *genus* (“kind,” instead of *opus*, “work”).], I know well, to use someone’s words [Note: [Col. 1099D] Leipzig manuscript: *cito* (“quickly,” instead of *sat*, “enough”).], that if I obey well enough, I gladly offer the little book customarily called a *tonary*, choosing rather to presume beyond my strength than to deny anything to charity, which hopes all things.

Trusting in you, O glory and ornament of prelates, I ask that with the calm moderation of your discernment [Note: [Col. 1099D] Leipzig manuscript: *quod* (“which,” instead of *quo*, “with which”).] [Note: [Col. 1099D] Leipzig manuscript: *moderamine* (“governance,” instead of *moderatione*, “moderation”).] you correct my errors and, if anything has been worthily stated, defend it without envy.

Nevertheless, it seems appropriate that certain preliminary matters first be set forth [Col. 1099D] [Note: [Col. 1100D] Leipzig manuscript: *proponantur* (“be proposed,” instead of *ponantur*, “be set forth”).], by which those less capable of understanding may meanwhile be exercised, as it were before the doors, and may finally be admitted to the inner chambers of the science itself.

May divine mercy preserve your Blessedness here unharmed for a long time, and afterward lead you to the heavenly kingdoms, where, established among the choirs of those singing psalms, you may joyfully chant:

> “As we have heard, so have we seen, in the city of the Lord our God, on his holy mountain.”

# Prologue to the Following Tones

[Col. 1100A]

## 1. The Musical Scale

Every regular construction of the monochord, according to the distinguished instruction of the highly eloquent Boethius, consists of fifteen strings, through which the power of the entire harmony proceeds in a secure arrangement, provided that the *synemmenon* is not absent. These are divided into four tetrachords, distinguished by the following names: the tetrachord of the graves, the tetrachord of the finals, the tetrachord of the superiores, and the tetrachord of the excellentes.

The tetrachord of the graves is so called because it lies below the finals and produces the lowest sound of all. The tetrachord of the finals is so called because the ending of all legitimately proceeding tones lies in it. The tetrachord of the superiores is so called because it is placed higher; the tetrachord of the excellentes because it surpasses the sounds of the other three.

In the middle of these there is usually inserted a fifth tetrachord, called the *synemmenon*, that is, “joined” [Note: [Col. 1100D] From here through no. 2, the Ottobeuren manuscript is defective.].

Since every song, however, is woven in an orderly manner not from arbitrary voices but from definite and determined sounds—which the Greeks call *phthongoi*, “sounds,” as though by analogy with speech—so that, just as every sequence of speech is arranged through the elements of letters, the harmony of a melody may likewise be produced through a rational quantity of sounds, we think it worthwhile to say something, even briefly, concerning the modes of these sounds, following the tradition of our predecessors, for the sake of those less learned in this art.

## 2. The Nine Modes of Sound

There are nine modes, as antiquity discovered through shrewd investigation, corresponding, as I believe, to the human voice, which consists of nine functions: the striking of the tongue as a plectrum; the impact of the four teeth; the repercussion of the two lips in the manner of cymbals; the cavity of the throat; and the assistance of the lung, which receives and releases air like a bellows. For a similar reason they also assign nine Muses to Apollo [Note: [Col. 1100D] Here the Ottobeuren manuscript ends.].

Let us now attempt to explain the modes themselves as best we can.

The first mode occupies the very briefest space between two voices and is made in a semitone, as is clear from this example, in low and high pitch, in the antiphon: “Gabriel was sent,” up to the place “Mary,” and likewise “virgin.”

The second has a more perceptible interval and is made in a tone, as in this antiphon: “Gabriel was sent.”

The third is somewhat more extended, namely by a tone and a semitone, as in this antiphon: “Gabriel was sent to Mary the virgin.”

The fourth is still more extended; it is made in two tones, as in: “Blessed are those who walk.”

The fifth is broader still, namely by two tones and a semitone, as in: “Do not be afraid, Mary.” Likewise, in the antiphon: “On that day they shall flow.”

The sixth is no less broad, namely by three consecutive tones, as in this responsory: “Now his body.” “Whose father a woman.”

[Col. 1101A] The seventh surpasses these in extent, consisting of three tones and a semitone, as in this antiphon: “Blessed Agnes amid threats.”

You will find the eighth, as though more rarely, in four tones, though not complete, as in this responsory:

> “You, man Symphorian, to be hung upon the torments,”

for from the note that descends to [Note: [Col. 1101D] “down to”] the note that rises to *in* there are a semitone, three tones, and another semitone. These two semitones joined together do not make a complete tone. Likewise, in:

> “The princes persecuted.”  
> “He coveted much spoil.”

[Note: [Col. 1101D] The material enclosed in brackets is absent from the Leipzig manuscript.]

The ninth, extended over a longer span than all the others, reaches the limit of divisions of this kind. For you will find no division of musical voices either broader than this or narrower than the first. It consists of four tones and a semitone, and you have an example in this antiphon: “To you I have lifted up my soul, my God.” Likewise, in the responsory: “Among those born of women, none.” Likewise, in the responsory: “This is the virgin; she entered.” Likewise, at the high point of the antiphon “He recognized this,” in the passage: “And he was found in.”

Beyond this final mode, if you seek voices separated from one another by alternating intervals, you will find none in any rational song until you reach the consonance of the octave. There, what occurs is rather a change of voice than a progression into a broader mode, because even the possibility of human vocal production does not permit a suitable sound to be produced at intervals so far separated from one another.

## 3. Musical Consonances

Among all these, only the fifth and seventh modes are found among the consonances of musical art: namely, the *diatessaron*, which is in the ratio of four to three, and the *diapente*, which is in the ratio of three to two. Consonances arise when a male and a boy’s voice sound together at the same time—or, rather, in that manner of singing which is commonly called *organizing*.

In the remaining modes there are not consonances but intervals and certain distinctions between voices.

There are also other consonances, such as the *diapason*, namely in double proportion, and the triple proportion, which is formed from the *diapason* and *diapente*. The combination of *diapason* and *diatessaron*—although the Pythagoreans deny that it is a consonance, because it consists neither in a multiple nor in a superparticular ratio, which is characteristic of the consonances of musical art, but in a multiple-superpartient ratio—is nevertheless a consonance.

For the proportion is such as eight to three, a proportion called in arithmetic “double super-bipartient.” The number eight contains the number three twice and two of its parts, namely two units.

Nevertheless, since the eminent teacher Boethius approves Ptolemy’s judgment on this point, we must necessarily acknowledge it to be the greatest consonance, because the *diapason* is such a harmony that, whatever other consonance it receives, it preserves and does not alter it, nor does it make a consonance dissonant.

“As,” he says, “whatever is added to the number ten, when placed within it, remains whole and unharmed, whereas this does not occur in other cases, so it is also with this consonance. For if you add two to three, you immediately produce five, and the form of the number is changed. But if you add the same numbers to ten, you make twelve, and the two, joined to ten, are preserved.”

From these words it is sufficiently clear that it is one thing to weave a song through simple consonances together with intervals of sounds, and another to resume the same voices, whether above or below, through compound consonances by a change of position. To speak of these matters belongs to another time and place.

There is also the double *diapason*, that is, the quadruple proportion.

## 4. The Tetrachord of the Finals

Having said these things briefly, let us attempt to present a few points concerning them which we think necessary for the task undertaken. First, the tetrachord of the finals must be examined more carefully. It possesses such a certain natural power of sounds that the whole authority of the modes or tones appears to proceed from the origin of its four strings.

Nor has this power been divinely granted to the number four alone without reason. For everything we call a beginning can only be the beginning of something; similarly, the end of something is the end. But wherever there is a beginning and an end, there is necessarily also a middle—[Note: [Col. 1102D] The material in brackets is absent from the Leipzig manuscript.] [“so that it consists of beginning, middle, and end,” or] “so that one proceeds from the beginning through the middle to the end.”

Therefore, for anything to be complete, it consists of beginning, middle, and end.

The number one, then, is not so much a number as a beginning, a source, and an origin of all numbers. It lacks a middle and an end, unless, on account of its perfection, it may be called an end as well as a beginning.

The number two, however, has no end to which one ought to arrive through a middle, because it is entirely without a middle. It remains, therefore, for it to be called a beginning, so that this may be a second beginning derived from the first, while the first is derived from nothing.

The first beginning is that from which all numbers arise; the second is that through which all numbers are discovered.

But if two are joined to one, the number three appears: the first odd number, which has beginning, middle, and end. In it, the single intervening middle has equal endpoints. For it is enclosed on both sides by unity, and what the joined extremities accomplish, the doubled middle accomplishes: one and one make two, and these joined together—that is, two and two—make four.

The first of all numbers, therefore, is three, to which a middle was added between two extremes so that it might be bound together.

The number four, however, because it possesses two middles, and because the outermost parts are bound more tightly when the middle is doubled, was rightly chosen by nature, at the command of the Creator, as the number by which it might bind together, with an indissoluble bond, the elements that oppose one another, and conform the three kinds of music—the cosmic, the human, and that which is produced by instruments—according to the fixed law of modulation.

Rightly, I say, has this number been assigned to musical harmony. It reconciles lower things with higher, binds the condition of soul and body through a fitting union of proportions, restrains the beastlike movements of human beings, orders their morals, calms—or rather drives away—the anger of demons, and even joins the earth, through the concord of its sounds, in a certain manner to heaven.

[Col. 1103A] If you add the number four itself to the natural numbers preceding it—that is, to one, two, and three—you will make the sum of ten. From this perfection of the number ten, too, we may become accustomed to sing upon the ten-stringed psaltery, so that our praise may be pleasing and beautiful to our God.

So greatly did the ancients also think this number relevant to the perfection of the soul—if their opinion is to be trusted—that the Pythagoreans made a religious oath by it, saying:

> “By him who gave to our soul the number, the fourfold one.”

Moreover, this same number four is generated from the number two, which we said above is a beginning; from it also the number eight, which is the first cube, is produced. For twice two, which is four, makes a surface; twice two times two makes a solid body, which is eight.

Under the mystery of this number, the harmonious sound of the Evangelists went out into all the earth, and their most sweet voice of preaching proceeded to the ends of the world. The Psalmist knew that this kind of harmony was most pleasing to God when he invited human minds to sing to the Lord four times, saying:

> “Sing to our God, sing; sing to our king, sing wisely.”

Therefore, whether from these few things we have brought forward, or from other matters that do not presently come to mind or lie wholly hidden, it is sufficiently clear that, not without the great prompting of a divine gift, this power has been implanted in the number four, so that the harmony of the whole should arise from it [Col. 1103C] and return to that same number as to the origin of its beginning.

In the same way, those eight tones always return, two by two, to one of the four strings of the finals, as though to a parent, under the direction of a certain justice.

Hence the ancients beautifully called this same number eight “justice,” not only because of the harmonic reason mentioned above, but also because it is the first of all numbers to be divided into equally even numbers—that is, into four and four—while the division itself can nevertheless be divided into equally even numbers, namely two and two.

## 5. The Species of the Consonances

Now, as divine grace may inspire us, let us attempt to explain how each authentic tone, or its own plagal, proceeding from its final, returns again to that same final, although it may extend itself upward or downward into various sounds.

First, we must state how many species there are of the *diatessaron*, the *diapente*, and the *diapason*. The *diatessaron* has three species, the *diapente* four, and the *diapason* seven [Note: [Col. 1103D] Leipzig, Ottobeuren, and Saint-Emmeram manuscripts: eight.].

Different musicians arrange these species in different ways. Following the teaching of the masters, however, we place them in an orderly manner according to the logic of the tones, so that anyone who has even slight knowledge of this art may easily understand.

The first species of the *diatessaron* consists of a tone, a semitone, and a tone. It begins at the *lichanos meson* and ends at the *lichanos hypaton*. If you add a tone above it, the first species of the *diapente* arises.

The second species consists of two tones and a semitone. It begins at the *mese* and ends at the *hypate meson*. If you add a tone above it, it becomes the second species of the *diapente*.

The third consists of a semitone and two tones. It begins at the *trite diezeugmenon* and ends at the *lichanos meson*. A tone must be added below it in order to form the third species of the *diapente*.

The fourth species of the *diapente* consists of the first species of the *diatessaron*, with a tone added below—not by the string of the same name [Note: [Col. 1103D] The enclosed words are absent from the Leipzig manuscript.] [but by the form of the same species], but by another: it begins at the *paranete diezeugmenon*, descends through a tone, semitone, and tone to the *meson*, and, with the lower tone taken up, completes the fourth species of the *diapente*.

It is easy to discern the species of the *diapason*. If you begin at the *proslambanomenos* and proceed up to the *mese*, it will be the first species; and so, continually repeating the sequence by ascending a semitone or tone, the end of the seventh species will be at the *paranete hyperboleon*. But if you take your beginning at the *hypate hypaton*, the end will be at the *paramese* [Note: [Col. 1103D] Better: “at the *nete hyperboleon*,” as corrected by a later hand in the Leipzig manuscript.].

[Note: [Col. 1104D] The Leipzig, Saint-Emmeram, Ottobeuren, and Admont manuscripts omit the material enclosed in brackets through no. 7.]

This, then, is the arrangement of the species in the consonances according to certain ancient authorities. The more careful modern writers agree with them to some extent concerning the *diapente* and *diapason*, but assign a different beginning and order to the species of the *diatessaron*.

Since the *diapason* consists of a *diapente* and a *diatessaron*, and since the first species of the *diapason* extends from A to a—that is, from the *proslambanomenos* to the *mese*—while the first species of the *diapente*, beginning at the *mese*, ends at the *lichanos hypaton*, they considered it incongruous that the tetrachord of the graves, which extends from that same *lichanos hypaton* to the *proslambanomenos* and contains the *diatessaron*, should be excluded from these species as idle and useless.

For this reason they determined that the first species of the *diatessaron* should extend from A to D, and that from this same D the first species of the *diapente* should rise to the high a. Thus the first species of the *diapason* is contained in these two species from A to a.

The first species of the *diatessaron* is therefore A B C D, namely from the *proslambanomenos* to the *lichanos hypaton*, consisting of a tone, a semitone, and a tone.

The second species is B C D E, consisting of a semitone and a ditone.

The third is C D E F, namely a ditone and a semitone.

And so, counting through the entire sequence of strings—that is, through four letters—you will find these three species alternately in groups of four, except in two places: between the *parypate meson* and the *paramese*, and between the *trite synemmenon* and the *nete diezeugmenon*.

The first species of the *diapente*, as stated above, is contained in D E F G a: a tone, a semitone, and a ditone.

The second is E F G a: a semitone and three tones, namely from the *hypate meson* to the *paramese*.

The third is F G a c: three tones and a semitone, from the *parypate meson* to the *trite diezeugmenon*.

The fourth is G a c d: a ditone, a semitone, and a tone, from the *lichanos meson* to the *paranete diezeugmenon*.

If you examine these species carefully, you will find the positions of the tones and semitones to be different and arranged alternately through the sequence of voices in the construction of the entire monochord, except in three places: between the *hypate hypaton* and the *parypate meson*; between the *hypate meson* and the *trite synemmenon*; and between the *paramese* and the *trite hyperboleon*.

Since the *diapason* is completed from these two consonances, it has as many forms as are contained in them. It therefore contains seven species: four on account of the *diapente* and three on account of the *diatessaron*.

The first lies between A and a, that is, between the *proslambanomenos* and the *mese*.

The second extends from the *hypate hypaton* to the *paramese*.

The third ends at the *trite diezeugmenon*, beginning at the *parypate hypaton*.

The fourth extends from the *lichanos hypaton* to the *paranete diezeugmenon*.

The fifth is bounded by the *hypate meson* and the *nete diezeugmenon*.

The sixth rises from the *parypate meson* to the *trite hyperboleon*.

The seventh descends from the *paranete hyperboleon* to the *lichanos meson*.

If you inspect the position of the tones and semitones, you will see that all these species are distinct from one another. If you add an eighth by ascending from the *mese* through the *paramese* and *trite diezeugmenon* to the *nete hyperboleon*, you will see that it does not differ from the first. But if you ascend from that same *mese* through the *trite synemmenon* and *paranete synemmenon*, you will recognize it as identical with the fifth.

Thus the *diapason* has seven species, one fewer than the voices in which the different arrangement of the eight modes takes place. The following account will make this clear.

We know from Boethius’s *On Music* that originally there were only seven modes according to the species of the *diapason*, but that Ptolemy added an eighth. Since we are concerned with brevity, let us explain their names and differences according to ecclesiastical usage.

## 6. The Eight Ecclesiastical Modes

The ecclesiastical order uses eight kinds of song, which we improperly call “tones.” The four higher voices of the monochord are called as follows:

- authentic *protos*, that is, the first master;
- authentic *deuteros*, that is, the second master;
- authentic *tritos*, that is, the third master;
- authentic *tetrardos*, that is, the fourth master.

For the Greeks call *authentoi* “masters,” as though they were endowed with authority, since their authority is pre-eminent. Hence, by comparison with the higher rank, usage has established that these modes should be so called.

The other four, occupying lower positions, are called:

- *plagis proti*, that is, “the lateral mode of the first,” with *authenticus* understood, as though it were contained at his side and were lower;
- *plagis deuteri*;
- *plagis triti*;
- *plagis tetrardi*.

But when giving their rules, let us use Latin names: let us call the higher modes masters and the lower ones disciples.

Before we begin to describe their ascents and descents, let us identify the final strings of all of them.

There are four voices called finals because regular songs end on one or another of them: D E F G, which are the *lichanos hypaton*, *hypate meson*, *parypate meson*, and *lichanos meson*. They were chosen as finals from among all the others because they are more sonorous amid the distinctions of the seven voices. If any old or new song ends outside them, it is undoubtedly judged irregular and illegitimate.

The song of the master and his disciple—that is, the first and second modes—ends on D.

The song of the second master and his disciple—that is, the third and fourth modes—ends on E.

The song of the third master and his subordinate—that is, the fifth and sixth modes—ends on F.

The song of the fourth master and his disciple—that is, the seventh and eighth modes—ends on G.

Since we have stated their names and finals, let us explain the limits of their ascents and descents.

## 7. The Limits of the Modes

[Note: [Col. 1105D] Here the remaining manuscripts resume.]

The *protos* [Note: [Col. 1105D] The words in brackets are absent from the cited manuscripts.] [that is, the first authentic master] consists of the first species of the *diapente* and, above it, the first species of the *diatessaron* [Note: [Col. 1105D] The words in brackets are absent from the cited manuscripts.] [not because its first species begins there, but because the form and likeness of that first species, which lies below, is contained here in the arrangement of those strings—namely, tone, semitone, and tone]. Its plagal consists of the same species of the *diapente* and the same species of the *diatessaron* below.

What I mean is this: the first tone has permission to ascend from its final, that is, from the *lichanos hypaton*, through the *diapente* to the *mese*, and from the *mese* to the *paranete diezeugmenon*, which is the first species of the *diatessaron* [Note: [Col. 1105D] The cited manuscripts add: “consisting of a tone, semitone, and tone.”], in the manner stated above.

The second tone, which is called its plagal, ascends through the same *diapente*, but through the same species of the *diatessaron* below, descending from the *lichanos hypaton* to the *proslambanomenos* through a tone, semitone, and another tone [Col. 1106C].

The *protos* sometimes legitimately takes one tone above the *diatessaron* [Note: [Col. 1105D] The Admont manuscript adds: “and rarely a tone and a semitone.”]. Similarly, so do the other authentic modes, except the *deuteros*, which admits only a semitone.

The *protos* also descends below its final [Note: [Col. 1106D] The Admont manuscript adds: “The *protos* descends below its final through a *diatessaron*, sometimes through a *diapente*, similarly into the neighboring sound, and so forth.”] into the sound next to it, sometimes into the third, but never, in legitimate songs, into the fourth. The other three authentic modes behave similarly, according to the order of their finals.

The *deuteros* consists of the second species of the *diapente* and the second species of the *diatessaron* above, in the manner discussed above. Its plagal consists of the same species of the *diapente* and the same species of the *diatessaron* below; you can understand this also from the preceding discussion.

The authentic *tritos*, which is the fifth tone, consists of the third species of the *diapente* and the third species of the *diatessaron* above.

The authentic *tetrardos* [that is, the seventh tone] consists of the fourth species of the *diapente* and, above it, the form of the first species of the *diatessaron*, in the manner stated.

Its plagal consists of the same species of the *diapente* and the first species of the *diatessaron* below [Note: [Col. 1106D] The Leipzig manuscript adds: “Its plagal consists of the same species of the *diapente* and the same species of the *diatessaron* below.” The enclosed words are omitted there.] [according to some authorities; in reality, however, it is the form of that first species].

Every plagal tone therefore has the same *diapente* and *diatessaron* as its authentic counterpart. They differ in this: the authentic has the *diatessaron* above the *diapente*, whereas the plagal has it below.

## 8. Ascents and Descents of the Tones

[Note: [Col. 1107D] In the cited manuscripts all of this is absent until below, at no. 9.]

The first mode or tone rises to high d, that is, the *paranete diezeugmenon*, and more rarely to e, which is the *nete diezeugmenon*. It descends to C, that is, the *parypate hypaton*, and very rarely to B, which is the *hypate hypaton*. Between D and d it possesses the fourth species of the *diapason*, with one note above and below it and, as stated, very rarely two notes below.

The second mode rises to a, that is, the *mese*, and more rarely to b or [the notation is defective], that is, to the *trite synemmenon* or *paramese*. It descends to A, which is the *proslambanomenos*, and sometimes one sound lower still, which modern writers, as stated above, added and marked with the Greek letter Γ.

This mode possesses between A and a the first species of the *diapason*, with, more rarely, a note above it and a note below it. These are the first master and his disciple.

The song of the master—that is, of the first tone—begins on six strings, namely C D E F G a, with its *cola* and *commata*, that is, its members and divisions, which we call the distinctions of the song, on those same strings.

The song of the disciple—that is, of the second tone—has four legitimate beginnings, A B C D, though six are commonly used by many: A B C D E F. It likewise has its *cola* and *commata* on these.

If you begin the song of the first mode on C, D, E, or F, it must rise no less than to high c [Note: [Col. 1108D] Read: “rise to high c.”], that is, the *trite diezeugmenon*, so that by its ascent you may discern what kind it is.

But if you begin the song of the second mode on those same notes, you must descend at least to B, so that by its descent you may show to which mode it belongs [Col. 1107C].

In making this judgment, however, only four beginnings will be assigned to each disciple.

The third mode rises to e, that is, the *nete diezeugmenon*, and more rarely descends to D, which is the *lichanos hypaton*. The principal song has distinctions on six strings, D E F G a, possessing between E and e—that is, between the *hypate meson* and the *nete diezeugmenon*—the fifth species of the *diapason*, and extending above and below the voice.

The fourth mode rises to [the notation is defective], that is, the *paramese*, and more rarely to c, which is the *trite diezeugmenon*. It descends to B, possessing between B and [the upper note] the second form of the *diapason*, and extending above the string.

Its song begins, according to some authorities, on six strings; legitimately, however, on four: B C D E. It has six distinctions: B C D E F G.

These are the second master and his disciple.

If you begin the master’s song on D or E, its ascent must reach no lower than d, that is, the *paranete diezeugmenon* [Note: [Col. 1108D] Perhaps: “likewise.”]. If it is the disciple’s song, its descent must reach at least to C, so that by ascending or descending you may discern what kind it is.

The fifth mode rises to e, which is the *trite hyperboleon*, and more rarely to g. It descends to C, that is, the *hypate meson*. Between F and f it contains the sixth species of the *diapason*, extending above and below the voice. Its song has six beginnings and distinctions: E F G a b c, from the *hypate meson* to the *trite diezeugmenon*.

The sixth mode ascends to c, which is trite diezeugmenon [Col. 1108A], but rarely to d, that is, to paranete diezeugmenon; and it descends to C, which is parypate hypaton, possessing between C and c the third octave species, and sometimes, above, the string. Its legal melodic beginnings are four, C D E F; according to some, six, as are also its distinctions, C D E F G a; and these are the third master and his disciple. If you begin the master’s chant on E or F, let the smallest degree of ascent be to e, which is nete diezeugmenon; but that of the disciple should be to B in descent, so that it may become clear to which of them such a differentia ought to be assigned.

The seventh mode ascends to g, that is, paranete hyperboleon, and descends to E, that is, parypate meson, containing between G and g the seventh octave species, and, above and below, the voice. The beginnings and distinctions of this chant are six: F G a c d. The eighth mode ascends to d, that is, paranete diezeugmenon, but rarely to e; it descends to D, that is, lichanos hypaton, possessing between D and d, according to the first master, the fourth octave species, and, above, the string. For Ptolemy added this mode, and because the octave lacks an eighth species, he obtained the fourth as the first did; although it has the same species, it has a different final and does not have the same descent to C. The legal beginnings of this chant, like those of the other disciples, are four, D E F G; the customary ones are six, as are its distinctions, D E F G a. These are the fourth master and his disciple. If you begin the master’s chant on F or G, let the smallest degree of ascent be to f, that is, trite [Col. 1108C] hyperboleon; but that of the disciple, because of the difference mentioned above, should be to E in descent.

This is the rule of ascent and descent for the eight modes, and this is the law that must be followed for them. The careful and prudent diligence of modern writers has set it down through the dissonance of the proper chants of each tone. In ancient times, although the authentic modes were not intensified equally with the plagal modes, all were nevertheless indiscriminately reduced to the fourth or fifth string; and the indiscriminate descents of many chants between the authentic and subordinate modes still testify to this. Hence, in many cases, there is often uncertainty concerning the ascent, but especially concerning the descent, whether the property belongs to the authentic mode or to its plagal.

For this reason, the younger writers, judging more subtly and more sharply, and distinguishing more certainly and more lawfully, neither agree entirely with the ancients nor entirely disagree with them. They say that there must be definite differences among the modes, so that we may be able to recognize the chants as belonging to whichever mode they are. But if the first mode descends from the high e to A—that is, from nete diezeugmenon to proslambanomenos—and the second is lowered from paramese, which is [lacuna], to the same A; if a chant that does not exceed the range between A and a—that is, between mese and proslambanomenon—is composed and regularly ends on D, the final of both, it is uncertain to which it should rather be assigned. The same occurs in the other modes. To drive away this uncertainty, we approve the rule prescribed by the younger writers [Note: [Col. 1109D] Here again the material already set out above on p. 1106 is repeated, namely, “Protus consists of the first …” through “the first mode, therefore,” p. 1107, no. 8.].

**9.** [Note: [Col. 1109D] Admont. “It must now be observed that every authentic mode, beginning from its final, may freely ascend to the ninth sound, sometimes to the tenth or the eleventh; this occurs only in the deuterus, which ascends to the eleventh, but descends only to the fourth, sometimes to the fifth; whereas its subordinate mode ascends to the fifth place, and sometimes descends to the tone, to the fourth, and also at times to the fifth. From this an easy recognition follows, etc.”] [Note: [Col. 1110D] Here the manuscripts continue.] It must now be observed that every authentic mode, beginning from its final, may freely ascend to the ninth sound—not that this always occurs, but that such is its capacity for ascent—and may descend only to the neighboring sound and sometimes to the third, as we have also touched upon above. Its subordinate mode, however, should ascend to the fifth place and descend to the fourth, and sometimes also to the fifth; and from this it is easy to recognize an authentic mode or its subordinate. [Note: [Col. 1110D] Here the Ottoburanus manuscript ends.]

What should be thought concerning those chants that do not reach the diapente [Note: [Col. 1110D] The closing words are missing in the Lipsiensis and Saint-Emmeram manuscripts.] [nor admit a lower diatessaron], or that do not have a diatessaron above the diapente, but do not reach a lower diatessaron either; or those that do have a lower diatessaron and something above the diapente, but do not ascend all the way to the diatessaron? The following order must be observed concerning such chants.

If a chant does not reach the diapente from its own final and, because of its brevity or imperfection, does not have a lower diatessaron, we customarily designate it as subordinate. For example, between protus and its subordinate: the antiphons “May God, God bless us”; “Blessed mother”; “Heavens of heavens”; “Into all the earth”; “Justly and piously”; “Judge justly.” Between deuterus and its plagal: “Let the earth bless the Lord.” Although, to the judgment of the ear, it sounds more suitably like the third than the fourth, not only does the present rule oppose this, but even if you wished to begin it according to this sonority, you could in no way reach the final by singing in a direct course. But if you end it as the differentia of the fourth tone, “Saeculorum. Amen,” and begin a semitone higher—that is, from parypate meson—you will be able to reach the final without injury.

If, however, a chant does reach the diapente but has neither a diatessaron above nor below it, then, because the diapente is common to both, the chant too should be common to both; nevertheless, it should be assigned to whichever of them has the more frequent usage. Thus we sing to protus these antiphons, or ones like them: “Living for two days”; “Light has dawned.” But those that begin in a similar way, ascend to the same place, and descend to the same place—namely, “O Lord, save”; “He was offered”—we sing as belonging to its subordinate mode.

[Col. 1109D] Some call such chants “middle tones.” Since such chants can be found between each of the four authentic modes and their subordinate modes, they add these four to the eight and attempt to count twelve tones.

If a chant ascends above the diapente but has no lower diatessaron, it will be authentic. This commonly occurs more often than to require an example, although the rule does not hold everywhere, as may be observed in the antiphon “This man knew,” which ascends a semitone and a tone above the diapente but descends two tones below the final. Nevertheless, we adapt it to the fourth tone because, since the euphony of the third opposes us, we cannot do otherwise.

Likewise, the antiphon “Caesar said to Hippolytus,” although it ascends a tone and a semitone above the diapente, is governed not by the seventh tone, as the rule would prescribe, but by the eighth—not because the discipline of the art dictates this, but because the sound of the voice compels it.

But if it has a lower diatessaron, it will be subordinate, as in the antiphon “In a spirit of humility,” where, at the passage “so let it be,” it exceeds the diapente by a tone; but because it has a lower diatessaron at the passage “today,” it will be subordinate, as we have said.

Or certainly, if it is found to have both a diatessaron above the diapente and one below it, it ought rather to be assigned to the authentic mode. Yet this rule has been thoroughly corrupted in many cases, partly through the ignorance of singers and partly through long-established usage—both in the daily antiphons composed from the psalms and in many other chants, namely, nocturnal and diurnal chants. This could to some extent be corrected if established custom could in any way be removed from the mouths of singers, as the few examples set out below will make clear.

The antiphon “But Peter was kept,” although it belongs to the first tone and, through its interval or system—that is, through its cola and commas—always returns to the final of the first tone, is sung in this manner: “But Peter was kept in prison” [Col. 1110C] [Note: [Col. 1110D] With musical notation.], and likewise, “And prayer was made for him without ceasing by the Church.” Here, on the syllable *a*, some begin to deviate from the proper course and decline into the third or fourth tone. This can nevertheless be corrected by such neumes, if anyone takes care to do so, so that it is sung, “by the Church to God.”

Likewise, the antiphons “And looking upon them” and “The good shepherd,” although more properly belonging to the third tone, are assigned by most people, less regularly, a conclusion in the eighth. This can be corrected if, at the end of these antiphons, where “Alleluia” is to be sung, the first syllable—that is, *al.*, which falls on mese—descends through the diatessaron to the final, counting the intervening notes, in this way [Note: [Col. 1110D] With musical notation.]: “Alleluia.”

For this reason, we govern these antiphons rather by the authority of the third tone, because according to that tone they have a diatessaron above the diapente; whereas according to the eighth they lack a lower diatessaron, although they extend a tone higher above the diapente.

**10.** Sometimes, in a remarkable way, it happens that one and the same melody can be sung equally suitably and appropriately in this tone or that, as with these antiphons: “Glorious princes”; “The wicked, wickedly”;” “The Lord knows”; [Col. 1111A] “No one condemns …”;” “He who hates.” These are governed and concluded both by the sixth and by the eighth tone.

Some attempt to force them, more violently than accurately, into the third tone. Likewise, the responsory “To a sinful people” is governed by the sound both of the tritus and of the tetrardus. Hence its verse is sung by some according to the tritus, that is, the fifth tone, in this manner: “Be propitious” [Note: [Col. 1111D] With musical notation.]; but by others according to the tetrardus, as follows: “Be …”

The antiphons that begin uniformly with O, such as “O Wisdom,” “O King of the nations,” and their like, stand as if at a crossroads between protus and its subordinate, because in all cases they exceed the diapente by a tone, while in some they have a lower diatessaron and in others they do not. More frequent usage has prevailed in favor of the subordinate mode, because in such a chant not only a diatessaron but sometimes also a lower diapente is found, as in the antiphon “O King of glory,” at the passage “spirit”; but this is according to some authorities. Nevertheless, those who assign to protus only those antiphons that do not have a lower diatessaron are not in error.

**11.** On account of such and other winding paths of error, the skilled singer must carefully examine whether a chant begins according to the regular order from its final, whether it proceeds lawfully, lest anything made discordant by a corrupted natural quality arise; whether the consonances agree properly according to the established measurement of tones and semitones, lest it begin its singing below or above the proper limit; whether it returns to its final by the direct path of the law; and which finals belong to it.

The finals, therefore, are lichanos hypaton, hypate meson, parypate [Col. 1111C] meson, and lichanos meson. Thus every melody of protus and its subordinate—that is, of the first and second tones—is governed and concluded by the authority of lichanos hypaton. That of deuterus and its subordinate—that is, of the third and fourth tones—is governed and concluded by hypate meson. Tritus with its subordinate—that is, the fifth with the sixth—is governed and concluded by parhypate meson. Tetrardus with its subordinate is governed and concluded by the sound of lichanos meson. This, then, is their rule for beginning any melody: they should never begin above the fifth higher place or below the fifth lower place, but should restrain their beginnings within those eight sounds, or sometimes nine.

It must also be noted that there is always a certain concord between the finals in the fifth higher place and the lower finals, so that some melodies seem to end in them almost regularly. Such is the responsory “It happened when he was lifting up,” which, although beginning regularly, ascends beyond the ninth to the tenth sound, outside the rule, and does not end on the final lichanos hypaton but on its associate, mese. In the same way are concluded “Terrible is” and the communion “I will sing to the Lord.”

This bond of association, therefore, joins lichanos hypaton with mese, hypate meson with paramese, parhypate meson with trite diezeugmenon, and lichanos meson with paranete diezeugmenon. They also have a similar relationship with the lower fourths and, in some cases, the fifths, although this usually pertains more to their beginnings [Col. 1112A] than to their endings.

It also happens, in a remarkable way, that the finals have not only their associates in the fifth regions, as we have said, but also find their counterparts in the higher fourth places. Thus, just as the members of chants, which are cola and commas, often stand through arsis and thesis in the finals and in the fifth places, so they also stand in the fourths.

Furthermore, if every mode—whether authentic or plagal—is carefully considered at the fourth place from its final, a marvelous and divine concord is found, so that if a chant is transposed from its final to the fourth place, it seems to proceed lawfully under the same mode or tone and to end regularly in the same place as though in its final. Indeed, many melodies, if begun from the finals themselves, whether to the right or to the left, do not fit well because of the semitones lacking in those places; but if begun from the higher places, they proceed evenly without any diminution of sound and end honorably in their associated notes.

To make this clearer, let us take the following examples from the fourth tone: “I have become”; “O death, I shall be”; “Sion, renew”; “Sion, do not fear”; “Go now.” If you wish to begin these antiphons at the third place from the final, that is, from lichanos meson, you fail in singing because you do not find the semitone where it ought to be. But if you attend to the fourth place, that is, mese, and, after inserting the first semitone in synemmenon and then a tone, begin the same antiphons at the third place thereafter—that is, at paranete synemmenon—you will see the entire chant proceed without injury until, at the end, it reaches its final’s associate, namely mese.

Similarly, with antiphons of the same mode—namely, “To you, Lord, I have lifted up,” and “From Egypt I called”—if you insist on beginning from the final, you will see that they fit less suitably in the middle. But if they begin at the fourth place, that is, mese, they are sung without loss of neumes until they obtain their ending there. Some, failing to attend to this, think that these and similar chants are governed more by the seventh than by the fourth tone, although they do not deny that they obtain their ending in the fourth.

The same defect of neumes occurs in the communion “Blessed is the servant,” which belongs to the third tone, unless it is transposed from hypate meson to mese.

Many also err considerably concerning the antiphons “Before me none was formed” and “From the time when it was made.” They think that these ought at the beginning to be governed by the seventh tone because of the similarity of the chant that they appear to share with the preceding examples at their beginning. Yet it is perfectly clear that they also begin suitably from the final of the first tone itself, proceed lawfully through intervals and systems in the fourth or fifth places, and regularly obtain their conclusion on the same final.

In the eighth tone also, if you begin the communion “From the fruit of works” from the final, you will recognize that in the middle the chant fits less suitably through its limmata or semitones. But if you begin after two tones and one semitone, at the fourth place, you will perceive the whole sequence of this chant, through an orderly progression, to belong to its associated ending.

The same commonly occurs in the fifth places. For example, unless the antiphons “I have other sheep” and “Lord, those who have worked,” which belong to the sixth tone, are transposed to the fifth place—that is, from parhypate meson to trite diezeugmenon—they will not be able to preserve their order on the regular monochord.

Let these few examples suffice. Moreover, just as synemmenon necessarily sometimes assists in the higher places in such deficiencies, so at times it appears to oppose them—only in those chants that proceed through synemmenon in the lower places, whose position they cannot supply in the higher places; and even this occurs sometimes, not always.

The following must be observed in such cases: if a chant begins from the final, it should nevertheless be able to begin at the fourth place; but if it begins below or above, at whatever place it is there from the final tone, here it should begin from the fourth associate.

One must also consider that, although in all subordinate tones the ascent extends as far as the diapente and beyond, protus too can in such cases ascend as far as the ninth sound [Note: [Col. 1113D] “And beyond it, it may sometimes ascend,” etc.], and the other three authentic modes—namely, the fifth and the seventh—may fail to reach the place regularly assigned to them because the strings are lacking. The learned singer should then, whenever reason demands it, return lower, so that through the octave places he may recover the sounds that he had not found above.

But when the individual authentic modes or their lateral forms are separated from their finals above or below by their differentiae in the interval of the sounds, or when we come to explain what relation or measurement of spaces they have to the final syllable of “Saeculorum. Amen,” we shall show this more fully when we explain it in its proper places in the book of tones, because whatever is set before the eyes is more firmly committed to memory.

For the present, however, this must be briefly noted: every principal sound, whether it belongs to any authentic mode or to its plagal mode, should always begin from its own final, on which it regularly ends.

**12.** The differentiae, which were devised at the discretion of skilled singers for the sake of ornament, have been arranged by us in the following manner. The differentia of each tone, if it begins at the final itself, occupies the first place; the second occupies the next lower place, and so it proceeds downward as far as it is found. Then it begins to run again in its proper order at the next higher place where it occurs, until it reaches the fifth place, where each final finds its associate. Thus the final itself, sitting in the middle like a leader, chief, and governor, establishes the law of beginning for the differentiae on either side of it.

Some call these differentiae “definitions.” In this regard, care must be taken: when someone hears the word “definition,” he must not understand it in the sense in which learned men have defined a definition as an account that explains what the thing defined is. Here, “definition” means nothing other than a differentia, by which the beginnings of a chant or of “Saeculorum. Amen,” whether by extension, by descent, or by beginning in the same place, differ from the sound of the principal tone with a certain pleasant and harmonious variety.

We, however, think that they ought more properly to be called differentiae than definitions, especially since we are not there explaining through discourse what something is, but by singing “Saeculorum. Amen” in different ways and beginning the melody differently, we distinguish one sound from another [Note: [Col. 1113D] Here the prologue ends in the Admont manuscript, followed by a tonary under the name of Guido, somewhat different from Berno’s tonary.].

**13.** There are also melodies established in antiquity for investigating the force of each tone, such as *Noan Noeane. Noeis Noeane* [Note: [Col. 1114D] Saint-Emmeram and Leipzig: *Noeais, Noeoeane*.]. In these we understand syllables suited to melodic performance rather than meaningful signs of things. Together with other little verses found by modern writers both for antiphons and for introits and communions, we have placed them at the head of each tone, so that through them an inexperienced singer might have an easier way of understanding.

**14.** If a chant begins contrary to the law of the finals, or varies in its progress contrary to the rule, and does not reach its proper ending, so that it begins in one tone and ends in another, it must be judged spurious rather than legitimate.

Therefore, not only must these and other faults of this kind be avoided in chants, but one must also observe with extremely vigilant care the neumes: where the pauses of the sounds are rare [Note: [Col. 1114D] Leipzig: “regular,” rather than “rare.”] and shorter, and where they must be measured longer, lest you hurriedly and for too short a time utter what the authority of the masters commands to be sung more slowly and at greater length.

Nor should we listen to those who say that it is entirely without reason that, in a song of suitable rhythm, we sometimes make a pause more quickly and sometimes extend it. If any grammarian reproves you when, in a verse, you shorten a syllable at a place where you ought to lengthen it, although there is no other natural reason why you ought to lengthen it except that the authority of the ancients has so decreed, why should not the principle of music—which governs the rational measurement and rhythm of sounds themselves—be offended if you do not observe the proper quantity of pauses according to the character of the places?

If something badly pronounced, which lies outside you, could at some time offend you, how much more something that lies within you? [Note: [Col. 1114D] So all manuscripts read, but the word should certainly be “within,” not “below.”] For we have perceived that it is not grammar but music that makes a human being stand upright—which, to use the words of a most learned man, anyone who descends into himself understands.

Accordingly, just as a verse is woven together in meter by a definite measurement of feet, so a chant is composed through the apt and harmonious joining of short and long sounds. And just as, in a hexameter verse, when it proceeds lawfully, the mind is delighted by the sound itself, so, if in the wrong order it admits a spondee in the penultimate foot and a dactyl in the final foot, or if someone pronounces a word of the second conjugation with an acute accent on the antepenultimate syllable, as *dócete*, or a word of the third conjugation with a circumflex on the penultimate, *legîte* [Col. 1115A], the ear itself languishes at the novelty.

So, in a chant joined together according to the authority of the ancients through a suitable and measured fitting-together of melodies, the whole structure of soul and body is delighted; conversely, it withdraws from the pleasure of hearing if it perceives anything corrupted in the chant.

Therefore, whoever thinks that he can sing well without knowledge of this art, but, when questioned about the number or intervals of high and low sounds, does not know how to answer, and wishes to trust only the sense of the ears and not to reason, their teacher, although the judgment of both must be sought—and indeed more that of reason, which, insofar as possible, comprehends the truth and integrity of things in nature through the gift of the omnipotent Artificer—such a person, I say, should be compared more to a nightingale, which in spring sings as though rhythmically and sweetly, than regarded as a skilled singer.

Accordingly, let the chant of our music be marked by a measured quantity of sounds, weighed and wisely joined together through the gravity of the neumes, modest, simple, and manly, not effeminate, so that, touched by its sweetness, we may be moved gladly to sing psalms to the Lord, always mindful of the Psalmist’s admonition: “Sing psalms wisely.”

**15.** Indeed, we sing psalms wisely if we observe not only every interval suitably fitted to the musical sounds, but also, if we attend carefully to the harmonic distance by which the authentic modes and their subordinate modes differ from one another, lest any confusing interchange occur among them that would render the result more discordant.

Because tritus and deuterus are distinguished from one another by a discernible interval, namely a semitone, while the others are separated by a tone and therefore their properties are less clearly recognizable in sound, we have taken care to mark below the diapente of each of the four modes together with the melodic movement of the words, so that from the order of their arrangement the character of any one of them may more easily be understood.

Since every diapente consists of three tones and a semitone, one recognizes most clearly whose diapente it is by carefully observing at which place the semitone occurs. The diapente of protus admits the semitone after two tones; the diapente of deuterus after three tones; the diapente of tritus has the semitone in the first place; the diapente of tetrardus after one tone.

From this one may gather how truthful is the statement that a certain wise man makes about these matters. “Protus and tetrardus,” he says, “are opposites, because the diapente of protus first has two tones, then a semitone, and finally a tone; whereas the diapente of tetrardus first has a tone and a semitone, then two tones. They agree in the first species of the diatessaron, except that in tetrardus it is higher.

“Deuterus and tritus are altogether opposites, since the diapente of deuterus first has three tones and then a semitone, whereas that of tritus first has a semitone and then three tones; and the diatessaron of deuterus consists of two tones and a semitone, while that of tritus consists of a semitone and two tones.

“If you reverse the diapente of protus, it becomes the diapente of tetrardus; and again, when the diapente of tetrardus is reversed, it sounds as the diapente of protus. Their diatessaron, however, cannot be reversed. If you reverse the diapente of deuterus, it becomes the diapente of tritus; and again, when the diapente of tritus is reversed, it sounds as the diapente of deuterus. Their diatessaron can likewise be reversed.”

Now, as we promised above, let us set out the diapente of each mode, beginning each from its proper final, and ascend through five syllables, counting the sounds that lie in between; then let us descend in the same way through another five syllables all the way to the finals. Thus we sing the diapente of protus: “I am the beginning and the end”; that of deuterus: “There are two commandments of charity”; that of tritus: “There are three precious gifts”; and that of tetrardus: “The name of the Lord is tetragrammaton.”

With these matters thus arranged, let no one think that I deserve to be struck by the dart of reproach without regard for shame because I have not added to this work certain differentiae used by some modern writers. Let him know that I wished rather to observe the constitutions of those who, before us, were more correct in age and knowledge than to follow novelties of sounds.

And lest I leave these altogether untouched: in the first tone, others use differentiae from ours for the antiphon “Living for two days,” ending “Saeculorum. Amen,” and likewise for “O blessed pontiff,” ending “Saeculorum. Amen” a tone lower; and there are many similar cases. In the fourth tone, they use them in the antiphon “We know”; in the seventh, in “They were speaking,” they sing certain foreign sounds; and so in any similar cases that may be found.

But if they burn with such desire for this new sonority, let them act as they wish. I shall now cease speaking at length, so that the prologue may end.

# BERNON’S TONARY

From the Vatican Library Palatine manuscript, collated with the Admont manuscript.

[Col. 1115]

[Col. 1115D] The authentic protus consists of the first species of the diapente and of the first species of the diatessaron above. [Col. 1116D] Its final syllable in “Saeculorum. Amen” lies above the final by the interval of a diatessaron.

**NONANNOEANE.**

[Col. 1117A]

“Seek first the kingdom of God.”

“Saeculorum. Amen.”

Lichanos hypaton.

A. “The angel of the Lord announced,” etc. [Note: [Col. 1117D] Admont. These antiphons do not begin on the final, but a tone and a semitone higher, that is, on parhypate meson. A. “Blessed is the man whose delight is in the law of the Lord,” etc.]

The first differentia [Note: [Col. 1117D] Admont: “second.”], which indeed begins from the final but soon ascends to the fifth sound, so that, just as the antiphon is separated from the final syllable of “Saeculorum. Amen” in the low register, so the second neume is separated from the first by a diapente in the high register.

“Saeculorum. Amen,” lichanos hypaton; ant. “Lord, our Lord,” etc. These antiphons begin a tone lower, with the following differentia, in this manner: “Amen,” but with the higher one they immediately rise through a tone to the diapente after the contiguous tone. Therefore we have placed them midway between the two, so that you will not err in assigning them to either one. Ant. “Friend, I am not doing you an injustice,” etc.

The second differentia descends from the final syllable of “Saeculorum. Amen” through the diatessaron, counting the intervening sounds, all the way to the final; thus it begins a tone lower.

“Saeculorum. Amen”; ant. “Amen, I say to you,” etc. Although these antiphons begin from the final, because they are sung through quilismata—which we call stepped neumes—they are performed more by the action of the throat than by the function of strings or any instrument. They should therefore be sung according to the sound of this differentia rather than according to the principal mode of the authentic itself.

“Saeculorum. Amen”; ant. “You are a column”; ant. “Well done, good servant.”

[Col. 1117C] These antiphons begin a tone and a semitone above their final under the sound of the same differentia. This same differentia also has, in these and other similar cases, a certain proximity to the differentia that belongs to the plagal protus.

Parhypate meson. Ant. “Ananias, Azarias,” etc. The “Saeculorum. Amen” of this third differentia lies at a diatessaron interval from the final; the differentia itself begins a tone and a semitone higher than that same final, and a tone lower than the Amen.

“Saeculorum. Amen”; ant. “When the treasures had been opened,” etc. The fourth differentia is arranged at the same place as the preceding one, but is better distinguished by the sound of the voice in the Amen at the end.
