[Col. 1117D] “Saeculorum. Amen”; ant. “I am the vine, alleluia,” etc. The fifth differentia places its final syllable Amen at the fifth place above the final, but begins the melody in the middle of the diapente [Note: [Col. 1118D] Admont: “that is, at parhypate meson.”].

“Saeculorum. Amen”; ant. “Those surrounding me.” The sixth differentia places Amen at the fourth place above the final in the high register, but begins the singing a tone lower, at parhypate meson. Some, however, begin this higher, at lichanos meson.

“Saeculorum. Amen”; ant. “Hail, Mary,” etc. The plagal protus consists of the same species of diapente as its authentic counterpart and of the same species of diatessaron below [Col. 1118A]. It ends “Saeculorum. Amen” on the same final on which it begins.

The second is similar to this.

Ant. “Jesus assumed.”

This one differentia lies a semitone and a tone above the final in the high register; the distinction is produced more by the interval than by the sound.

“Saeculorum. Amen”; ant. “From eternity it has not been,” etc. The authentic deuterus consists of the second species of the diatessaron [Note: [Col. 1118D] The reading seems to be: “The authentic deuterus consists of the second species of the diapente and the second species of the diatessaron.”]; it ends “Saeculorum. Amen” a semitone [Col. 1118B] and a tone higher.

**Noeane.**

“It is the third day since these things happened.”

“Saeculorum. Amen”; ant. “The Lord, receiving seven.” The first differentia begins a semitone and a tone higher, and there it also ends its final syllable.

“Saeculorum. Amen”; ant. “Deal kindly.”

The second differentia begins its Amen a semitone and a tone higher; from itself it ends a tone away, and from the final it ends at the interval of a diatessaron.

“Saeculorum. Amen.” Lichanos meson; ant. “Lord, you have searched me.”

The third differentia begins the melody on the same string as the preceding ones, but determines the final syllable of Amen at the sixth place from the final.

[Col. 1118C] “Saeculorum. Amen”; ant. “Simeon receiving,” etc.

The melody of these antiphons begins at the sixth place from the final contrary to the art, and there Amen also ends. Ant. “As I live”; ant. “I have done one work.”

The fourth differentia has the same place for beginning as the preceding one, but does not produce a similar sound in the penultimate Amen. Hence a person does not err greatly if he sings either the preceding antiphons with the tenor of this sound or these with the sound of the preceding differentiae.

“Saeculorum. Amen,” or in this manner, “Saeculorum. Amen”; ant. “Take these things away,” etc.

The plagal deuterus consists of the second species of the diapente, like its authentic counterpart, and of the second species of the diatessaron [Col. 1118D] below.

**Noeais.**

“The fourth watch came to them.” “Saeculorum. Amen”; ant. “Announce,” etc.

The first differentia determines “Saeculorum. Amen” a semitone higher than the final, but begins the melody a tone lower.

“Saeculorum. Amen”; ant. “They will walk with me.” The second differentia begins two tones below the final; the Amen syllable rests midway between the two strings.

“Saeculorum. Amen”; ant. “They approached Jesus,” etc.

[Col. 1119A] The third differentia places its final syllable Amen a semitone and a tone beyond the final in the high register, but takes the beginning of the singing one tone below. Thus it properly joins the beginning and the ending, that is, the Amen, by a diatessaron.

“Saeculorum. Amen”; ant. “Before the bed.”

The fourth differentia places Amen on the final and begins a semitone higher; but in some cases it occupies the final place and in others the third place from the final.

“Saeculorum. Amen”; ant. “He was distressed.”

Under the same differentia these begin from the final, except that in the antiphons “To you, Lord, I have lifted up” and “From Egypt I called,” the semitone occurs less correctly if the melody begins from the final. I have taken care to explain more fully in the preface how they can be sung without loss of neumes. Ant. “To you, Lord, I have lifted up,” etc. These, however, begin a semitone and a tone higher under the same sound. Ant. “Blessed is the Lord,” etc.

The fifth differentia begins on the third string from the final, where it places Amen. Lichanos meson.

“Saeculorum. Amen”; ant. “From an unjust man.”

The sixth differentia begins a semitone and a tone higher and concludes Amen at a diatessaron from the final.

“Saeculorum. Amen”; ant. “I have become like.”

This antiphon sounds a diatessaron to the final at its last syllable Amen and a diapente above; nevertheless, through a certain sweet and melodious reversal of the throat, it distinguishes itself from the sound of the other differentia.

“Saeculorum. Amen”; ant. “Unless you diligently,” no, etc.

The authentic tritus consists of the third species of the diapente [Col. 1119C] and of the same species of the diatessaron above.

“Five prudent ones entered for the wedding,” etc.

“Saeculorum. Amen”; ant. “There is still much.”

Some begin the antiphon “Sing praise” from mese, etc. The first differentia begins two tones above the final, and there Amen also ends.

Saeculorum. Amen; antiphon: “The Spirit exulted,” etc.

The second differentia, where the preceding *amen* also ends, begins melodically a fifth above the final.

Saeculorum. Amen; antiphon: “Alleluia, whom you seek.”

The plagal third mode consists of the same species of fifth as its authentic counterpart, and of the same species of fourth below.

[Col. 1119D] *Noeais.*

“At the sixth hour he sat beside the well.” Saeculorum. Amen; antiphon: “As he ascended.”

This alone begins a tone higher in some sources: antiphon “The mother, not knowing.”

These begin again where the preceding ones begin: antiphon “He made known,” etc.

This begins a semitone and a tone lower, on the same note: antiphon “If I am the true Christ.”

This differentia of the sixth tone ends its *amen* a tone higher; but it takes its point of departure for beginning from the final itself. *Parhypate meson.* Saeculorum. Amen; antiphons: “Blessed is the Lord”; “He blessed.”

The authentic fourth mode consists of the fourth species of fifth, and of the first species of fourth above.

[Col. 1120A] *Noeoeane.*

“There are seven spirits before the throne of God”; saeculorum. Amen; antiphon: “Blessed are you,” etc. This antiphon begins one tone higher; antiphon: “He himself will go before.”

The first differentia begins from the final in the manner of the principal tone, and its *amen* ends a fifth higher, at the fifth degree; but after the beginning of the chant it distinguishes itself from the principal mode by varying its course.

Saeculorum. Amen; antiphon: “She has been assumed,” etc.

The second differentia begins from the final and lowers its *amen* by a tone.

Saeculorum. Amen; antiphon: “Receive the Holy Spirit,” etc.

The third differentia likewise begins from the final and immediately rises to the third degree, where it also places its *amen*.

Saeculorum. Amen; antiphon: “I ascend to.”

The fourth sings the final syllable of the *amen* at the fifth above the final, and, by a reciprocal movement, returns from that final to the same consonance.

Saeculorum. Amen; antiphon: “Water burns.”

Although these antiphons, after ascending to the fifth, soon change into another mode, they nevertheless belong to the same differentia: antiphons “Silver and gold,” etc.

The fifth differentia begins two tones higher and ends the *amen* a fourth above the final.

Saeculorum. Amen; antiphon: “Blessed daughter.”

The sixth differentia ends its *amen* at the fourth degree above the final and begins there as well.

Saeculorum. Amen; antiphon: “Many waters.”

[Col. 1120C] The seventh differentia is separated from its final by a fifth at the high point of the *amen* and begins at a fourth. It differs from the preceding one in this respect: the preceding one rarely reaches the fifth from the final, whereas this one not only reaches the fifth freely but sometimes proceeds beyond it, contrary to the rule.

Saeculorum. Amen; antiphon: “God of gods,” etc.

The eighth, rare and almost barbarous, is placed last as an extraordinary form. It lowers the *saeculorum. Amen* four degrees below the final; but it sometimes begins the melody at the fifth degree, so that it is separated from its final by a fifth, and sometimes at the fourth, as the examples below will make clear.

“As it was in the beginning, and is now, and ever shall be, and unto the ages of ages. Amen” [Note: [Col. 1119D] With musical notation]; antiphons: “The angels of the Lord”; “The martyrs of the Lord.”

These are intoned in a similar manner, although they begin lower: antiphons “We who live”; “In the churches, bless.”

But the following, although they begin at the same place, correspond more closely to the principal note by a fifth.

Saeculorum. Amen; antiphons: “In the furnace of fire”; “Wisdom cries aloud”; “The righteous shall stand.”

In these three, the melody is inflected from the first highest note to the ninth, so that from the final—which is *lichanos meson*—it extends, touching each successive string, to the fifth *phthongus*, carried through both regions.

[Col. 1121A] The modes or tropes that we customarily call tones, although the nocturnal responsories begin from different positions of the strings, nevertheless each one readily reveals its identity through the uniform modulation of its verses. This is plainly evident from the few examples we have set down below. Unless, perhaps, someone wishes to adorn the modulation of those verses more suitably by multiplying the neumes [Note: [Col. 1121D] f., variety].

## AUTHENTIC FIRST MODE

R. “Blessed are you, Mary.” V. “Hail, Mary, full of grace; the Lord is with you.” R. “It has been confirmed.” V. “O King of heaven, to whom…” Glory be to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit.

## PLAGAL FIRST MODE

[Col. 1121B]

R. “Holy and immaculate…” V. “Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb.” R. “Christ, the Lamb of God.” R. “Let the heavens rejoice.” R. “Hear, Israel.” Glory be to the Father.

## AUTHENTIC SECOND MODE

R. “Rejoice together.” V. “They have taken away my Lord, and I do not know where they have laid him; if you have taken him away, tell me.” R. “After they had been fulfilled.” V. “Awaiting the Savior…” Glory be to the Father.

## PLAGAL SECOND MODE

R. “Our King will come.” [Col. 1121C] V. “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world.” R. “Like a cedar.” R. “When he had crossed over.” R. “Ascending on high.” Glory be to the Father and to the Son.

## AUTHENTIC THIRD MODE

R. “Blessed is he who…” V. “The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone; this was done by the Lord, and it is marvelous in our eyes.” R. “The angel of the Lord spoke.” R. “Today the heavenly…” Glory be to the Father and to the Son.
