We once brought forth these compositions for Zion with a rejoicing spirit, singing them as best we could; but now, sitting as though beside the rivers of Babylon, embittered by misfortunes, we have hung up our instruments, crying out tearfully and saying: “How shall we sing the song of the Lord in a foreign land?” For the land has indeed become foreign to us, since in it we are not permitted even to live, let alone sing. The prophecy has been fulfilled in us which once threatened wretched and unhappy Judah in these words: “Your land is deserted, your cities are burned with fire; foreigners devour your region in your presence, and it will be desolate as in a hostile devastation” (Isa. 1:7). Therefore the joy of our heart has failed, our chorus has been turned into mourning, the crown has fallen from our head (Lam. 5:15), so that we are compelled to say: “Woe to us, for we have sinned” (ibid., 16); and, as a certain wise man says: “At this time the powerful are free to oppress, the private citizens to destroy, and the wretched to weep.”

But what remains to be done amid these circumstances except that in that prophetic book in which lamentation, song, and woe are written, we should meditate day and night, so that when miserable daughter Babylon (Ps. 136)—that is, the multitude of those who persecute us in their wickedness—receives from the Lord the recompense which she rendered to us (ibid.), namely, everlasting woe, we may, through lamentations worthy of power [Note: [Col. 1129D] variant readings: “mel.”; “of repentance”], truly deserve to sing a song of joy, with the merits of the Prince of the Apostles assisting us. For love of him, most blessed Father, we have labored in this work to obey your commands.

[Col. 1131]

# BERNO OF AUGIA. ON THE VARIOUS MODULATION OF THE PSALMS AND SONGS

From the Salem manuscript, eleventh or twelfth century.

## SYNOPSIS

1. Ezra restored Holy Scripture.  
2. The Seventy Translators.  
3. Other translations of Scripture.  
4. The Gallican and Roman versions of the Psalter.  
5. Differences between the Roman and Gallican versions.  
6. Differences in Isaiah and the other prophets.  
7. Nothing should be sung in the Church except from Holy Scripture or from works treated by wiser men.  
8. The words of Holy Scripture must not be altered.  
9. Nothing contrary to its faith should be introduced.  
10. Antiphons beginning with “O” in Advent, and certain others on the feasts of the Nativity.  
11. The office of Septuagesima, when the *alleluia* is laid aside.  
12. Responsories whose verses do not correspond sufficiently.  
13. Or which abound in other errors.

[Col. 1131A] Berno, who is what God wills, to Meginfrid and Eipennon, beloved brothers in Christ: the enduring adornment of unfading glory.

It seems reasonable to me that those whom one Spirit binds together by the bond of charity should not be separated by the text of letters, but rather joined by a letter—those whom the fellowship of dear friendship cements together. Therefore, compelled by the request of your brotherly affection, Meginfrid, I first wish to write something for you about the various modulation of the psalms and songs, which is customarily performed differently or confusedly in the Church. Before doing so, however, I desire to recall something about the translations of the interpreters, so that, by casting this as a kind of foundation of discourse, the structure of our account may rise more solidly.

### 1

For, as the authority of our forefathers confirms, all the Scripture of the Old Testament was originally written in the Hebrew language. But after Jerusalem had been destroyed and the Law burned by the Chaldaeans, when the Jews returned from the Babylonian captivity to Jerusalem, Ezra, a scribe learned in divine knowledge, restored the entire library of the Old Testament and all the books of the Law and the Prophets; he established, corrected, and arranged them in twenty-two volumes, according to the number of the Hebrew letters. Following his example, many gentiles collected the deeds of others and established libraries. Among them, a certain Pisistratus is said to have flourished; afterward Xerxes, then Seleucus and Alexander the Great.

### 2

Ptolemy, too, surnamed Philadelphus, surpassing all learned men in zeal, brought into his library not only the writings of the gentiles [Col. 1131C] but also the divine Scriptures. For, as is reported, seventy thousand books were found at Alexandria in his time. He also requested from Eleazar the high priest that the Scriptures of the Old Testament be translated from Hebrew into Greek, and obtained the Seventy Translators to fulfill his desire.

Some make a marvelous claim about those same seventy Translators: that, divided individually among separate cells, they translated everything through the Holy Spirit in such a way that nothing was found in one of their codices that differed from the others, even in the order of the words. Saint Jerome strongly opposes this opinion, saying:

“I do not know what first author constructed by his lie the seventy cells at Alexandria, in which, divided from one another, they supposedly wrote the same things, since Aristaeus, the *hyperaspistes*—which means ‘faithful protector’—of that same Ptolemy, and, much later, Josephus report nothing of the kind. Rather, they write that the translators were gathered together in one basilica and compared their work, not that they prophesied. For it is one thing, he says, to be a prophet, and another to be an interpreter. The former foretells what is to come through the Spirit; the latter transfers, through learning and abundance of words, what he understands.”

A little earlier, after recalling what had been omitted by the Seventy Translators, he says:

“The Jews say that this was done by prudent design, lest Ptolemy, a worshiper of the one God, should discover even among the Hebrews a dual divinity; and they did this especially because he seemed inclined toward Plato’s doctrine. Finally, wherever Scripture bears sacred witness concerning the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, they either translated it differently or remained entirely silent, so as both to satisfy the king and not make public the secret of the faith. Read the prologue of that same blessed Jerome on the book of Genesis.”

### 3

There were also other interpreters who translated the sacred utterances from Hebrew into Greek, such as Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion. There is also the Common translation, whose author is not apparent; for this reason it is called the fifth edition without the interpreter’s name. Origen and Eusebius of Caesarea call it *koinē*—that is, “Common” or “Vulgate.” Origen discovered it with extraordinary labor and compared it with the other editions.

But many Greek commentators also translated and corrupted it in various ways. Many Latins, and especially Romans, received this version before Saint Jerome and continue to use, retain, and preserve it. Wishing to correct their diversity, or rather their error, blessed Jerome, being skilled in many languages, translated the whole of the Old Testament from Hebrew into Latin. His translation rightly takes precedence over the others, as Isidore says, for it is more faithful to the words and clearer in the distinctness of its meaning. Pope Saint Gregory likewise asserts that his translation is more truthful than the others.

There is also a sixth edition, concerning which blessed Jerome says:

“I briefly admonish you to know that there is one edition which Origen, Eusebius of Caesarea, and all the Greek commentators call *koinē*, that is, Common and Vulgate; and another, that of the Seventy Translators, which is found in the *Hexapla* codices and was faithfully translated by us into Latin, and is sung in the Churches of Jerusalem and the East.”

A little later he adds again:

“Just as in the New Testament, whenever a question arises among the Latins and there is a difference among the copies, we hasten to the source of the Greek language in which the New Testament was written, so in the Old Testament, whenever there is a difference between the Greeks and Latins, we flee to the Hebrew truth, so that we may seek in the streams whatever proceeds from the fountain. This *koinē*, that is, the Common edition, is itself the edition of the Seventy; but the difference between them is that the *koinē*, through place and time and the will of the scribes, is an anciently corrupted edition, whereas the one contained in the *Hexapla* and translated by us is the very translation of the Seventy preserved incorrupt and undefiled in the books of learned men. Therefore, whatever differs from it unquestionably also departs from the authority of the Hebrews.”

Thus far Jerome. This same great and eminent man was once carried up before the tribunal of the eternal Judge, where he was admonished by a divine rebuke to devote himself to divine studies and serve the benefit of the holy Church.

### 4

Among other works, from the corrected translation of the Seventy Translators [Col. 1133C] he translated the Psalter from Greek into Latin and gave it to all the Churches of Gaul and to certain Churches of Germany to be sung. For this reason they call it the Gallican Psalter, while the Romans still sing the Psalter from the corrupted Common edition, from which they composed their chant and transmitted to us the custom of singing.

Hence it happens that words which, according to the custom of singing, are modulated in the daily or nightly offices are intermingled and inserted confusedly into our psalms, so that the less learned can scarcely discern what belongs to our edition and what to the Roman edition.

Perceiving this, the devout father and learned teacher Jerome arranged three editions in one volume: he placed the Gallican Psalter, which we sing, in one column; the Roman in another; and the Hebrew in a third. Wherever something had been inserted in our version that is not found in the Hebrew, he marked it with an obelus, that is, a spear, using this sign: ÷. But wherever he added something from the Hebrew, he caused it to shine forth with an asterisk, that is, a star, using this sign: +.

### 5

Although I am far inferior in learning to this supreme teacher—for, in comparison with him, I do not think I even possess a language—and although I follow his footsteps from afar, I nevertheless wish, for the sake of your affection, to distinguish something of what we sing by modulation in antiphons, responsories, graduals, offertories, and communions, and of what we say by distinct enunciation in the Churches.

Since I am small in understanding and slow in intellect, and although advanced in age, already weakened by old age, I begin, like children who after their first lessons learn the songs of the psalms, by taking my beginning from fear: for “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. 110:10), so that through fear we may arrive at charity, which “casts out fear” when it is perfect (1 John 4:18). And I shall try to note not only differences in the chant but also certain other places where our edition and the Roman edition appear to differ in their words.

Thus the antiphons or communions which, according to the Roman Psalter, are sung as “Serve the Lord in fear, and rejoice in him with trembling,” we sing, according to the correction of blessed Jerome, as: “And rejoice in him in trembling.”

In the third psalm, where they sing, “I slept and took sleep,” we sing: “I slept and was overcome by slumber.”

In the fourth psalm, where they sing, “When I called upon you, and you heard me, O God,” we say: “When I called, the God of my righteousness heard me.” As for the fact that it suddenly changes from the first person to the second, saying, “In tribulation you enlarged me,” it follows the practice of all the prophets, who very often change tenses and persons and observe the order of their reasoning in this way.

In the fifth psalm: “Direct my way in your sight.” As blessed Jerome says, this is found neither in the Seventy nor in Aquila, Symmachus, or Theodotion; only the *koinē* edition has it. Finally, just as it is written in Hebrew, all translated it with the same wording: “Direct your way in my sight,” according to what is said in the Lord’s Prayer: “Our Father, who are in heaven, hallowed be your name.” It is not that, when we pray, his name is made holy in us; therefore here too the Prophet asks that the Lord’s way, which is straight in itself, may also be made straight for him.

In the sixth psalm, where they sing, “Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger, nor correct me in your fury,” we sing: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury, nor correct me in your anger.” Likewise, where they have, “Turn, Lord, and rescue my soul,” we say: “Turn, Lord; rescue my soul.”

In the seventh psalm, where they sing, “Rise up, Lord my God, in the commandment,” we say: “And rise up, Lord.”

In the eighth psalm, “I see your heavens” is not found in the Greek; but in the Hebrew one reads *samecha*, which is interpreted as “your heavens,” and it was added from Theodotion’s edition to the Seventy with an asterisk [Col. 1134D] +.

Where the Romans sing, “For to you the poor man has been abandoned; you will be the helper of the orphan,” we, leaving aside “for,” say: “To you the poor man has been abandoned; you will be the helper of the orphan.”

In the psalm beginning, “The fool said,” after the verse has ended, the three verses that follow—“Their throat is an open tomb; destruction and misery…” through “there is no fear of God before their eyes”—are not found in the Hebrew. They were inserted into our translation from the Greek by blessed Jerome.

They sing, “Guard me, Lord, as the apple of the eye”; we sing: “Guard me as the apple of the eye.”

But where the words of that psalm do not precede or follow, there is no harm if we say only in the verse, “Rise up, Lord”; as in the verse, “Save your people, Lord, and bless your inheritance,” our Psalter has: “Save the people and bless your inheritance.”

Where they sing, “But I shall appear with righteousness in your sight; I shall be satisfied when your glory is revealed,” we say: “But I shall appear in righteousness before your sight; I shall be satisfied when your glory appears.”

In Psalm 17: “Because of the brightness before his sight the clouds passed by.” Blessed Cassiodorus says: this verse must not be passed over lightly. “Because of the brightness” is one part of speech, that is, a plural nominative, and it corresponds with “clouds.” The clouds, as was said above, are to be understood as preachers of the divine word.

In Psalm 18: “He rejoiced like a giant to run his way.” Neither the Greek nor the Hebrew has “his”; it was added by blessed Jerome under the obelus, that is, with this sign: ÷.

In the same psalm, where they sing, “The law of the Lord is blameless,” we sing: “The law of the Lord is immaculate.”

At that offertory: “The ordinances of the Lord are upright, gladdening the heart,” since the words placed in the Psalter continue up to “and sweeter than honey and the honeycomb,” we would sing more correctly: “The ordinances of the Lord are upright, gladdening the heart, and sweeter than honey and the honeycomb.” In that tract where the Romans sing, “The heavens shall proclaim his righteousness,” we do not say “the heavens,” but sing, “They shall proclaim his righteousness.” Where the Romans sing, “And your cup that makes drunk—how splendid it is!” our edition has, “And my cup that makes drunk—how splendid it is.” The Romans sing, “Make your ways known to me, O Lord, and teach me your paths”; we, however, sing, “Show me your ways, and teach me your paths.” In that psalm where they sing, “Hear, O Lord, my voice, with which I cried to you; my heart said to you: ‘I sought your face; your face, O Lord, I shall seek,’” we say instead, “Hear, O Lord, my voice, with which I cried; my heart said to you: ‘My face has sought your face; your face, O Lord, I shall seek.’” At that offertory: “In you I have hoped, O Lord; I said, ‘You are my God; my times are in your hands’”; in place of “times” we have “my lots.” In that psalm, “I have been turned in my distress,” the word “my” is not found in the Greek, but was added from the Hebrew and from the translation of Theodotion under an asterisk, that is, the star-sign `+`.

[Col. 1135D] In that antiphon or Communion where they sing, “Rejoice, you righteous, in the Lord,” we sing, “Exult, you righteous, in the Lord.” In that Introit where we chant in the song, “And from all his tribulations he delivered him,” we say while chanting the Psalter, “He will save him.” In the same psalm, where they sing, “Fear the Lord, all his saints, for those who fear him lack nothing,” we say, “There is no want for those who fear him.” Where they say, “They shall not fail,” we say, “They shall not be diminished in any good thing.” In Psalm XLI, where they sing, “As the deer longs for the springs,” our translation has, “Just as the deer longs”; and in another verse, “My soul thirsted for the living God,” we have, under an asterisk `+`, “for the strong God.” It should be known that in this psalm “The salvation of my face, my God” occurs twice; but in the second occurrence, that is, at the end of the psalm itself, it reads, “The salvation of my face and my God,” with the conjunction “and” added from the Hebrew and Theodotion under an asterisk `+`. In the same psalm: “My enemies who afflict me reproached me,” which is not found among the Romans, but is written in the Hebrew: “My enemies reproached me.”

In Psalm XLIII, according to the Roman text, it is written, “And you shall not go forth, O God, in our powers”; but “God” there is superfluous. Again, in the same psalm, when we chant in the song and verse, “Rise up, O Lord, help us, and deliver us for your name’s sake,” according to our edition we say only, “Rise up, help us, and redeem us for your name’s sake.” Where the Romans sing, “God will help her with his countenance; God is in her midst; she shall not be moved,” we say, “God will help her at the break of dawn.” They say, “God has ascended in jubilation” (`in jubilatione`); we say, “God has ascended in rejoicing” (`in jubilo`). They say, “As we have heard, so also have we seen”; we say, “As we have heard, so have we seen.”

In Psalm XLVIII, the verse “When a man was in honor” occurs twice. In the first occurrence it has the conjunction “and” added, thus: “And when a man was in honor”; at the end it has no conjunction, but reads: “When a man was in honor.” They say, “Call upon me in the day of your tribulation; I will rescue you, and you will glorify me”; we, however, say, “And call upon me in the day of tribulation; I will rescue you, and you will honor me.”

In their edition of Psalm L, it reads: “Wash me yet more from my injustice, and cleanse me from my offense”; ours reads: “Wash me yet more from my iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin.” Theirs reads: “For I acknowledge my iniquity, and my offense is always before me”; ours: “For I myself know my iniquity, and my sin is always against me.” Theirs: “For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and my mother bore me in offenses”; ours: “For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and my mother conceived me in sins.” Again, theirs: “I will teach the wicked your ways”; ours: “I shall teach the wicked your ways.” Near the end of the psalm they sing: “A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit; a contrite and humbled heart God does not reject”; we, however, say: “A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit; a contrite and humbled heart, O God, you will not despise.”

[Col. 1136D] In Psalm LII, which begins, “The fool said,” the second verse has added: “There is none who does good; there is none, not even one”; we end the verse simply: “There is none who does good.” But to the fourth verse, which begins, “All have turned aside,” we add at the end: “There is none, not even one.” They chant: “Will not all who work iniquity understand, who devour my people as though eating bread?” and shortly afterward: “They trembled with fear where there was no fear” (`Trepidaverunt … erat`). We, however, say: “Will not all who work iniquity know, who devour my people as food of bread?” and at the end of the verse: “Fear trembled where there was no fear” (`Trepidaverunt … fuit`). They say: “When the Lord turns back the captivity of your people”; we: “When the Lord turns back the captivity of his people.” [Col. 1137A] They end the first verse of the following psalm: “And by your strength deliver me”; we: “And by your strength judge me.” They sing: “Hear, O God, my prayer, and do not despise my supplication; attend to me and hear me”; we: “Attend to me and hear me.” In the same psalm, where they chant: “Fear and trembling came upon me, and darkness covered me,” we say: “Fear and trembling came upon me, and darkness covered me.” Nor should it disturb you that interpreters, following the rule of grammatical art, used the singular number—“darkness” (`tenebra`)—instead of the plural, since, as Saint Gregory testifies, the words of the heavenly oracle are not to be bent according to the rules of Donatus. Thus the same Prophet, not fearing the grammarians’ rod, wrote: “Deliver me from bloods” (Psalm L, 16); and in the Gospel of John: “Who were born not from bloods, nor from the will of the flesh, nor from the will of man, but from God” (John I, 13). Just as there he used the plural for the singular, so here he used the singular for the plural, following the harmony of the Hebrew truth, which says: “Fear and trembling came upon me, and gloom covered me.” Where they sing, “Cast your thought upon the Lord,” we sing, “Cast your care upon the Lord.”

In Psalm LVI, the verse “Be exalted above the heavens, O God” is placed both in the middle and at the end. In the middle it reads, “and your glory over all the earth” (`et in omnem terram gloria tua`); at the end, “and over all the earth is your glory” (`et super omnem terram gloria tua`). Where we sing antiphonally in the choir, “God has shown me over my enemies; do not kill them, lest my people forget,” they say: “My God has shown me good things among my enemies; do not kill them, lest they forget your law.” And in the following verse, in place of what we sing, “Bring them down, my protector, O Lord,” they say, “Destroy them, my protector, O Lord.”

In Psalm LIX it reads: “Judah is my king; Moab is the vessel of my hope”; in Psalm CVII: “Moab is the cauldron of my hope.” Where we say, “Foreigners are subjected to me,” the Romans say, “Allophyles” (`Allophyli`, foreigners) “are subjected to me.” At the end of this psalm we sing, “And he himself will bring down to nothing those who afflict us”; in the other version: “And he himself will bring down to nothing our enemies.” In the verse, “Let all the earth worship you and sing to you,” where they conclude, “let a psalm be sung to your name, O Lord,” the Roman edition has, “to your name, O Most High”; ours simply, “let a psalm be sung to your name”; the Hebrew sings, “to your name.” Where they sing, “God is in his holy place; God makes those of one mind dwell in a house,” we say, “God makes those of one way dwell in a house.” Regarding this verse, which is read among us as “They saw your entrances, O God,” Saint Jerome says: “Therefore it should be read by us in this way: ‘They saw your entrances, O God,’ and the copyist’s error should be left aside, since he put the nominative in place of the accusative.” Where they sing, “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive and gave gifts to men,” we sing, “You ascended on high, you took captivity, you received gifts among men.”

[Col. 1138A] In that psalm, “Save me,” where we sing, “Confusion covered my face,” they say, “Reverence covered my face.” We say, “I have become a stranger to my brothers and a foreigner to the sons of my mother”; they say, “A guest to the sons of my mother.” In that psalm, “O God, give your judgment to the king,” they sing: “All the kings of the earth, all the nations shall serve him”; we: “All the nations shall serve him.” In the same psalm Saint Jerome says that in the Greek “God” is not found twice in “Blessed is the Lord, the God of Israel,” although in the Hebrew and among the Septuagint it very clearly reads “the Lord God”—an appellation that signifies the mystery of the Trinity—that is: “Blessed is the Lord God, the God of Israel.” They sing: “Because I was zealous among sinners”; we: “Because I was zealous against the wicked.” In the same psalm: “You held my right hand, and by your will you led me, and with glory you took me up”; we, however: “And with glory you received me.”

In Psalm LXXII, when Saint Jerome was explaining the verse, “Look upon your covenant, for they have been filled,” he explained it as follows:

“Because they have been darkened by the thickets of iniquities—the thickets,” he says, “are interpreted as thorns—therefore those who darkened your land by their persecutions have been filled with thoughts of iniquity. But you, O Lord, who through your covenant—whether Old or New, since both proceeded from you—promised to protect us, now cut down the thorns and rescue us.”

In that psalm, where they sing, “Vow and repay to the Lord your God, all you who offer gifts around him,” we say: “You who will bring gifts around him.” At that offertory they sing: “The earth trembled and was still”; we: “The earth feared and was still.”

In Psalm LXXVII, in the verse where many sing, “And I meditated at night with my heart, and I swept my spirit”—or “I scrubbed” it—Jerome writes: “And I dug out my spirit.” This means, he says, “I dug it like a field, so that I might put there the seed of the Lord’s teachings.” In the verse where it is sung, “Their priests fell by the sword,” many say: “And their widows shall not be mourned,” using the future tense; but we think it more correctly said in the past tense: “They were not mourned,” because the prophet recounts past statements as already completed, and the Hebrew agrees with this sense when it says: “His priests fell by the sword, and his widows were not wept for.” Where they say, “They placed the mortal remains of your servants,” we say: “The corpses of your servants.” Where they say, “You who sit upon the cherubim, appear before Ephraim,” we say: “You who sit upon the cherubim, manifest yourself before Ephraim.” In that Introit, “Exult in God our helper,” where they sing, “Sound the trumpet at the beginning of the month,” we sing: “Blow the trumpet at the new moon” (`neomenia`; the text has `comenia [neomenia]`). In that verse where they sing, “With his shoulders,” we say, “Upon his shoulders.” They sing, “As one passing through the dark places of the fields”; we: “From the assault and from the noonday demon.” They: “He called upon me”; we: “He cried out to me.” Where they sing, “The righteous shall flourish like a palm tree; he shall multiply like a cedar that is in Lebanon,” we say: “The righteous shall flourish like a palm tree; he shall multiply like a cedar of Lebanon.” They sing: “The Lord has reigned; he has clothed himself with beauty; the Lord has clothed himself with strength and girded himself with power”; we: “The Lord has reigned; he is clothed in beauty; the Lord is clothed in strength and has girded himself.”

In Psalm XCV, which begins, “Come, let us exult in the Lord,” where they sing, “For the Lord will not reject his people,” our edition does not have this. Where they sing, “For in his hand are all the ends of the earth, and he himself beholds the heights of the mountains,” we: “For in his hand are all the ends of the earth, and the heights of the mountains are his.” They: “And his hands formed the dry land”; we: “And his hands fashioned the dry land.” They: “Let us weep before the Lord who made us”; we: “Let us weep before the Lord, who made us.” They: “But we are his people and the sheep of his pasture”; we: “But we are the people and the sheep of his hand.” They: “As in the provocation”; we: “As in the irritation.” They: “They tested and saw my works”; we: “They tested,” and we add “me” under an obelus `÷`, “and they saw my works.” They: “For forty years I was near to this generation, and I said: ‘They always err in heart’”; we: “For forty years I was offended by that generation, and I said: ‘They always err in heart.’” They: “To whom I swore in my anger: ‘If they shall enter into my rest’”; we: “As I swore in my anger: ‘If they shall enter into my rest.’”

Where the Romans sing, “Praise and beauty are before him; holiness and magnificence,” we say: “Praise and beauty are before him; sanctity and magnificence.” They: “Take up offerings and enter his courts; worship the Lord in his holy hall”; we: “Take up offerings and enter his courts; worship the Lord in his holy court.” They: “For he made the world firm, which shall not be moved; he shall judge the peoples in equity and the nations in his anger”; we have only: “He shall judge the peoples in equity.” They: “The Lord has made his salvation known before the nations”; we: “In the sight of the nations he has revealed his righteousness.” They: “All the ends of the earth have seen the salvation of our God”; we: “All the boundaries of the earth have seen.”

In Psalm CI, where they sing, “I have been struck like grass, and my heart has withered, because I forgot to eat my bread,” we say: “It has been struck like grass, and my heart has withered, because I forgot to eat my bread.” They sing: “I was mixing my drink with weeping”; we: “I was mixing my cup with weeping.” In the verse, “This is the great and spacious sea with hands,” “with hands” is not found in the Greek; it was added from the Hebrew and from Theodotion’s edition in the Septuagint under an asterisk `+`, that is, the star. The phrase is spoken metaphorically of the sea, as though it had outstretched hands and received everything into itself. Among the Romans it is sung, “Rise up, my glory”; among us only, “Rise up, O psalter.” For “my glory” is found neither among the Hebrews nor in any interpreter, but only in Psalm LVI.

In Psalm CIX, which begins, “The Lord said to my Lord,” the first name “Lord,” as Saint Jerome says, is written in Hebrew with the letters by which the Lord Father is designated; the second name “Lord” is written with the letters by which human beings ordinarily call a lord. Therefore the Lord Father commands the man who was assumed by God to sit. We have said this against the Arians and against those who say that the Father who commands him to sit is greater than the one to whom the command is given. All the Gospels resound concerning the person of the man, and now no proof is necessary, because all things that seem lowly refer to the flesh.

That psalm which begins, “I will confess to you, O Lord, with my whole heart”—in it, there is something superfluous [the Latin does not identify the word]. Where the Romans sing, “Light has risen in the darkness for the upright in heart,” we do not have “in heart.” The Romans: “The righteous shall be in eternal memory; he shall not fear an evil report”; we: “He shall not fear an evil hearing.” Regarding “Because he inclined his ear to me, and in my days I shall call upon you,” Saint Jerome says in his letter to certain persons:

“You say that `te`—‘you’—is not in the Greek, and it is rightly to be removed from your copies. In the same psalm: ‘I shall please the Lord in the land of the living,’ for which you say you have read in the Greek: ‘I shall please in the sight of the Lord’; but this is superfluous.”

In that psalm, “Give thanks to the Lord,” the Romans sing: “Surrounding, they surrounded me, and in the name of the Lord I shall avenge myself upon them”; we: “And in the name of the Lord, because I have avenged myself upon them.” Again, in the same psalm they say: “O Lord, save me; O Lord, give prosperity”; we: “O Lord, save; O Lord, give prosperity.”

In Psalm CXVIII, where the Romans sing, “How sweet are your words to my palate, O Lord, more than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth,” we say: “How sweet are your words to my palate, more than honey to my mouth.” “My soul is always in your hands.” Concerning this verse Saint Jerome says to Sunia and Fretela:

“For this you say that you have read in the Greek: ‘My soul is always in your hands.’ But it should be known that among the Septuagint and all other interpreters it is written: ‘In my hands,’ and not: ‘In your hands.’ All the ecclesiastical interpreters among the Greeks explain this passage in the same way, and its meaning is briefly this: ‘Every day I am in peril, and, as it were, I carry my blood in my own hands; yet I do not forget your law.’”

In the same psalm: “The streams of waters flowed from my eyes, because they did not keep your law”; for this you say that you have read in the Greek: “because he did not keep your law.” But this is superfluous, since in the Hebrew also it reads: “Streams of waters flowed from my eyes, because they did not keep your law.”

The Romans sing: “I saw those who did not keep the covenant, and I wasted away”; we: “I saw transgressors, and I was wasting away.” In the verse, “O Lord, deliver my soul from lying lips and from a deceitful tongue,” you say that you have read in the Greek, “and from a deceitful tongue”; therefore this is superfluous. In the following psalm, where they sing, “I lifted my eyes to the mountains,” we say: “To the mountains.” Where they sing, “Except that the Lord,” we: “Except because the Lord.” In the verse, “Blessed is the man who has fulfilled his desire from them,” it is said in the Greek that “man” is absent; but this is plainly contained both in the Greek and in the Septuagint.

In Psalm CXXXIV, where the Romans sing, “Praise the Lord, for he is gracious,” we: “Praise the Lord, for the Lord is good.” Where they sing, “For the Lord will judge his people and will be compassionate toward his servants,” we: “He will plead their cause.” Regarding “He who made the great lights,” Saint Jerome says to those whom you mentioned above that you found “great” alone in the Greek; but this belongs to the preceding verse, where we read, “He who alone does great wonders.” It should therefore be read there, and here it is superfluous [Col. 1141B] and should not be written. In that psalm, “By the rivers,” where they sing, “When we remembered you, O Sion,” we say: “When we remembered Sion.” They sing: “Remember, O Lord, the sons of Edom”; we: “Be mindful.” At that offertory, “If I walk,” where they sing, “You will stretch out your hand,” we: “You stretched out your hand.” In that tract, “Deliver me, O Lord,” where they sing, “Free me from an unjust man,” we: “Deliver me.” They: “Those who thought up evils in their heart”; we: “Those who thought up iniquities.” They: “Free me, O Lord, from unjust men”; we: “Deliver me.” They: “Snares”; we: “A snare.” They: “And they stretched out cords as a snare for my feet”; we: “And they stretched out cords into a snare.” They: “Shade my head”; we: “You shaded my head.” In that responsory, where they sing, “Lead my soul out of prison,” we: [Col. 1141C] “Lead me out of custody.” Where they sing, “My spirit was distressed within me,” we: “My spirit was distressed over me.”

In Psalm CXLIII, where the Roman edition has, “You who give salvation to kings, who delivered your servant David from the evil sword,” ours has: “You who give salvation to kings, who redeemed his servant David; from the evil sword deliver me.” The reader should not be disturbed by the sudden change of person or tense, because the prophets, taught by the Holy Spirit, customarily pass from person to person and from time to time, and in this way utter the divine words. In that Introit, where they sing, “Your saints, O Lord, shall bless you,” we: “May your saints bless you.” In that Gradual, “The Lord is near to all who call upon him,” where it is sung: “My mouth shall speak the praise (`laudem`) of the Lord, and let all flesh bless his holy name (`nomen sanctum eius),” we say: “My mouth shall speak the laudation (`laudationem`) of the Lord, and let all flesh bless his holy name (`nomini sancto eius`).” In that psalm where they sing, “Praise the Lord, O my soul; I shall praise the Lord in my life; I shall sing to my God as long as I exist,” we: “I shall sing to my God as long as I shall exist.” In Psalm CXLVI, which begins, “Praise the Lord, for the psalm is good,” there is disagreement among some as to whether it is more correctly said, “Praise the Lord, because he is good,” or “Praise the Lord, because the psalm is good.” But from the Hebrew, where it says, “Praise the Lord, for the song is good,” we can observe that it is more correctly said: “Because the psalm is good”—that is, singing psalms is a good thing—as Saint Jerome explains. “To sing psalms,” he says, “is not with the voice but with the heart. How many have a good voice and, because they are sinners, sing badly? He sings psalms well who sings in his heart, who sings Christ in his conscience.” Let these few remarks about the psalms suffice, however inadequately expressed.

### 6

Now I shall attempt to turn my hand to Isaiah, who, as Blessed Jerome says, should be called not so much a prophet as an evangelist and apostle. For he himself bears witness concerning himself and the other evangelists, saying: “How beautiful are the feet of those who announce good things, who announce peace!” And again concerning himself: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me; for this reason he anointed me and sent me to evangelize the poor.” And because “apostle” means “one who is sent,” God speaks to him as though to an apostle: “Whom shall I send, and who will go to this people?” And he replied: “Here am I; send me.”

And because many who are not only less perfect in literary knowledge but also trained in the liberal arts commonly divide the readings in this prophet, or pronounce the words in song, very differently from the truth of the text, I have decided to note briefly the passages where they divide the sentences less correctly or pronounce the words otherwise than the true text has them.

Let us first consider what is written: “What use to me is the multitude of your sacrifices? says the Lord.” Since it should be connected and punctuated as “I am full”—that is, “I need nothing,” in accordance with what is written elsewhere, “The earth is the Lord’s and its fullness”—some wrongly join the ablative to this little sentence, “I am full”: “with the burnt offering of rams and the fat of fattened animals.” Then they add the accusative: “And I did not desire the blood of calves and lambs and goats,” whereas the preceding words, “the burnt offering of rams and the fat of fattened animals,” should be pronounced in the accusative, just as what follows: “And I did not desire the blood of calves and lambs and goats.”

Again, in the passage where it is written, “At the first time the land of Zabulon and the land of Nephtali were lightened, and at the last the way of the sea beyond the Jordan of Galilee was made heavy,” some attach the word “of the nations” to the following sentence, thus: “The people of the nations who walked in darkness,” although it should be divided quite differently. For there are two Galilees: one beyond the Jordan, in which Solomon gave Hiram, king of Tyre, twenty cities in the territory of the tribe of Nephtali; the other is near the lake of Gennesaret, in the tribe of Zabulon, around Tiberias. To distinguish it as the one located in Judea, the text now says: “Beyond the Jordan of the Galilee of the nations.” Then it continues: “The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light.” And where it is written, “And you have overcome the scepter of the exactor, as on the day of Midian,” some erroneously use the plural instead of the singular ablative and say: “As in the days of Midian.”

In that Introit which we sing on the day of the Lord’s Nativity, “A child is born for us, and a son is given to us,” our translation, according to the Hebrew truth, has: “A little one is born for us; a son is given to us.” And in place of what we sing, “whose government is upon his shoulder,” the Hebrew truth has: “And the principality has been made upon his shoulder.” And in place of what we sing, “And his name shall be called the angel of great counsel,” the Hebrew has six names: “Wonderful, Counselor, God, Mighty, Father of the age to come, Prince of peace.” Here it should be noted that the names are not to be joined in pairs, as many think, so that we read “Wonderful Counselor” and again “Mighty God.” Rather, “Wonderful” is to be read separately, “Counselor” separately, and “God” separately, followed by “Mighty”; afterward the two names “Father of the age to come” and “Prince of peace” are to be joined.

In that reading, “Climb upon a high mountain,” some manuscripts have the masculine form: “You who evangelize Sion, and you who evangelize Jerusalem,” although according to the Hebrew it should be pronounced in the feminine: “You who evangelize Sion, and you who evangelize Jerusalem.” Sion and Jerusalem are commanded to climb upon a high mountain—that is, to the heights of the virtues—and to raise their voice with strength, announcing without fear and saying to the cities of Judah: “Behold your God,” and the rest that follows.

In the antiphon that some chant, “The saints who hope in the Lord shall have strength; they shall take wings like eagles; they shall fly and shall not fail,” the Hebrew has: “But those who hope in the Lord shall change their strength; they shall take wings like the wings of an eagle; they shall run and shall not grow weary; they shall walk and shall not fail.” This signifies that the saints, having taken up the wings of the virtues, just as eagles customarily revive in old age through the changing of their feathers, so will continually run in the service of God and not grow weary; they will walk and not fail, as it is written of them: “They shall walk from strength to strength,” so that after the end of this life, having assumed an immortal body, they may see the God of gods.

In that responsory, “Shine, shine, O Jerusalem; your light has come,” it is written in the Hebrew: “Arise, shine, for your light has come.” The name “Jerusalem” is not found in the Hebrew, to signify that what is written and promised pertains not only to Jerusalem and the Jews but generally to all generations that were to believe in Christ. And below: “Your sons shall come from afar, and your daughters shall suck milk.” Some divide this in such a way that they say “from milk” and then add “they shall rise,” thinking that the word “from afar” should be answered by the other expression “from milk.” But Blessed Jerome gives another sense, saying: “Your daughters shall suck milk,” meaning souls nursing in Christ, in the baptism of little ones, as the Apostle Peter says: “Like newborn infants, desire the rational, guileless milk”; or, like little children, let them meanwhile suck milk—that is, the apostles’ teaching—until they are able to take solid food, the nourishment of perfect doctrine. Alternatively, as some manuscripts have it: “Your daughters shall rise from the side.” For either it should be read, “Your daughters shall suck milk,” or, “Your daughters shall rise from the side.” This signifies that, just as Eve, the mother of all, was formed from the rib of Adam’s side, so the Church was built from Christ’s side when, according to John’s Gospel, one of the soldiers opened Christ’s side with a lance, and immediately flowed forth the blood of our redemption and the water of baptism. These are so joined that we are baptized with water and redeemed with blood.

In Hezekiah’s song, in the verse “I said: I shall not see the Lord,” some manuscripts have “the Lord God,” but this is written falsely. “Lord” must be repeated twice, “Lord, Lord,” as Saint Jerome says. They divide and conclude the verse “I shall not see man any longer, nor the inhabitant” in such a way that the following verse begins: “My generation has ceased.” Blessed Jerome, indeed, because of the ambiguity of the word, first translated it in this way, but later corrected it: “The inhabitant of quiet.” True rest and true exultation are eternal life; eternal life, moreover, is the contemplation and vision of the Trinity. Who is the inhabitant of eternal life except almighty God himself and his elect?

In the verse “O Lord, I am oppressed,” some manuscripts have “Answer for me,” but this is written falsely. It is better, as the interpreters say, to read: “Guarantee me,” as though he were saying: “If I have done anything wrong, guarantee me; that is, be my surety, and receive me into your faith and protection.” For it depends “not on him who wills or on him who runs, but on God who shows mercy” (Romans IX, 16). Again, in the same passage, “O Lord, thus one lives,” some manuscripts have “If thus one lives.” But it is not so, as Saint Jerome says. The king philosophized about the condition of this life by saying: “O Lord, thus one lives”—that is, “Human frailty is so fragile and fleeting.”

Again, in that Introit where it is sung, “You who thirst, come to the waters, and you who have no price, come,” some sing, “Drink with gladness.” But according to the prophet it should be said: “Eat,” not “drink.” Yet how can we eat water? Sacred Scripture is food in some passages and drink in others. Wherever it is grasped with difficulty, it is food; wherever it has an easy meaning, it is drink. The sense is this: “O Gentiles, who thirsting desire knowledge of the Old and New Testament, come to the waters of baptism or to the gifts of the Holy Spirit. And you who have no silver—that is, the sayings of the Lord, of which the Psalmist says, ‘The sayings of the Lord are pure sayings, silver tested by fire, proved’—hurry and come quickly to my faith. Buy the gifts of the Holy Spirit and the water of baptism, not with the price of gold or silver or anything of that kind, but by believing and doing good. Eat that water itself—that is, the spiritual teaching or the gifts of the Holy Spirit—by hearing, reading, meditating, and retaining it in your heart.”

In that reading where it says, “You shall no longer be called Forsaken, and your land shall no longer be called Desolate,” some manuscripts add: “But you shall be called My Will in the Age.” This is false. For it is customary among the Hebrews always to assign names from things, as with Abram, who was previously called “exalted father”; again, when he heard through the promise, “In your seed all nations shall be blessed,” he was called Abraham, that is, “father of many nations.” The Lord and Savior, among his other names, was called Emmanuel, which means “God with us.” So now the Church is called in Hebrew `Ephiba`, which means “my will in her.” The sense is: “You shall no longer be called Forsaken by God, and your land”—that is, your dwelling—“shall no longer be called Desolate, because Christ shall dwell in your midst. But you shall be called My Will in Her,” that is, the Church of Christ; and it shall be said of you: “This is the Church of Christ, which does the Lord’s will.” Therefore let us ask the Lord that, by doing his will, we may be called and truly be sons of his holy mother, the Church, so that we may be able to remain with him and in him forever and unto ages of ages.

### 7

Now, therefore, I wish to note certain chants that appear to have been composed in the holy Church without the authority of Sacred Scripture, or compiled extraordinarily according to human custom and the whims of the flesh. Those who sang such things did not heed that the Lord cries out through the prophet by command: “Sing wisely” (Psalm XLVI, 8). It was also established in the African Council that prayers and supplications should not be said unless they have been approved, and that none of them should be sung at all in the Church except those that have been examined and approved by wiser men in synod, lest something should have been composed against the faith, whether through ignorance or through deliberate effort.

Here it should briefly be considered that not only those things composed deliberately out of unbelief, but also those composed in simplicity and ignorance against the rule of faith, must be rejected with equal scrutiny. Blessed Jerome too, when explaining the Apostle’s command, where he says, “Be filled with the Spirit, speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and psalming in your hearts to the Lord” (Ephesians V, 19), says among other things: “Therefore we ought to sing, psalm, and praise the Lord more with our mind than with our voice.” Hence the holy father Benedict commands us, saying: “Let us stand at psalmody in such a way that our mind agrees with our voice.”

How does our mind agree with our voice when, by musical modulation, we raise the voice high, while either remaining wholly silent about Sacred Scripture or changing its words or meaning into another interpretation, thereby fulfilling rather that Virgilian line, “He gives sound without mind,” than the apostolic command that we quoted above?

### 8

And, strangely enough, while some wish to appear and be wise according to this world, through superstitious interpretation they try to adapt the words of Sacred Scripture to their own meaning. They alter in song and speech the words that the Power of God and the Wisdom of God themselves uttered, or that the Holy Spirit foretold through the mouths of the prophets and apostles, changing them according to Donatus and Priscianus, although all worldly philosophy and the teaching of secular learning derived their origin from the authority of Sacred Scripture.

What consistency is there in listening to Priscianus while despising the truth, which is God? For Terence, Virgil, Cicero, and the other followers of the liberal arts have earned this in their writings: that their expressions should remain undisturbed as they are—such forms as `advortite`, `diunt`, `ipsus`, `optumus`, `maxumus`, `olli`, and many similar examples. How much more, then, should the oracles of heavenly words remain within their own rule!

For some, in the Gospel where it is written, “And I say to this one, ‘Go,’ and he goes; and to another (`alio`, dative singular), ‘Come,’ and he comes,” wish to correct it to `alii` (“another,” nominative singular): “And another, ‘Come,’ and he comes.” And where the holy Gospel says, “For power was going out (`exiebat`) from him and healing all,” they correct it to: “For power was going out (`exibat`) from him.” And where Zacchaeus says in the Gospel, “If I have defrauded (`defraudavi`) anyone,” they say: “If I have defrauded (`defrudavi`).”

But in that offering for the dead in which we sing, “Deliver the souls of all the faithful departed from the hand of hell and from the depth of the lake,” some, with a kind of mental affectation, sing “from the depth of the lake” (*lacus*), paying insufficient attention to the fact that the noun *lacus* normally bears that form of the genitive according to both declensions, that is, the second and the fourth. In accordance with the idiom of Sacred Scripture, however, *laci* is more often used than *lacus*, especially where the deep pit, abyss, or depth of hell is indicated. Thus the prophet Isaiah, who says of himself, “And one of the Seraphim flew to me, and in his hand was a live coal which he had taken from the altar with tongs, and he touched my mouth and said: ‘Behold, this has touched your lips, and your iniquity shall be taken away, and your sin shall be cleansed,’” himself, I say, declared: “Nevertheless you shall be dragged down to hell, into the depth of the lake” (*laci*); and again: “Those who descend to the foundations of the lake,” that is, of hell. We therefore rightly judge that we ought rather to follow the authority of him whose lips were cleansed by heavenly fire than the teaching of some grammatical author. [Col. 1146B]

Daniel also agrees with this meaning: “One stone was brought and placed over the mouth of the lake”; and again: “They had not yet reached the floor of the lake when the lions seized them and crushed all their bones.” We therefore ask in song that the Lord free the souls of his faithful from the depth of the lake, that is, from hell.

We ought therefore to hold firmly to the sequence of Sacred Scripture and inviolably observe its tenor in all things, attending to what a certain wise man admonishes when he says: “Prudent reader, always beware of superstitious interpretation, so that you do not accommodate the Scriptures to your own understanding, but join your understanding to the Scriptures.” Therefore it must be established that we preserve, hold, and guard unchanged the sacred words of the Gospel, the oracles of the patriarchs and prophets, and the writings of the apostles, with complete faith and fitting devotion, just as they are found in authentic books; adding nothing, removing nothing, and changing nothing, if we wish to escape that threat which the Holy Spirit appears to utter near the end of the Apocalypse: “If anyone adds to these things, God will add upon him the plagues written in this book; and if anyone takes away from the words of the book of this prophecy, God will take away his share from the book of life, from the holy city, and from the things written in this book.” [Col. 1146C]

Therefore, if anyone wishes to sharpen his intellect through the rules of grammatical art, let him exercise himself in the schools and, if he wishes, use Donatus and Priscian as teachers, provided that, while preserving the integrity of true interpretation, he does not refuse to maintain the honor due to the divine utterances. But enough of this. Let us now consider the remaining matters. [Col. 1146D]

### 9

Finally, I was unable to find in the whole sequence of Sacred Scripture where that responsory which is placed first in the antiphonary, “Looking from afar” (*Aspiciens a longe*), or that introit, “Upon the lofty throne” (*In excelso throno*), or that responsory sung concerning holy Mary, ever-Virgin, “I saw the beautiful one, like a dove, ascending above the streams of waters” (*Vidi speciosam sicut columbam ascendentem desuper rivos aquarum*), is written—unless, perhaps, there are some who say that at the beginning of the nascent Church there were many interpreters who translated Sacred Scripture from Greek into Latin, and that these texts were taken from them, before Blessed Jerome, interpreter of the divine law, translated the whole Old Testament from Hebrew into Latin and delivered a corrected edition of the Seventy Interpreters to Latin ears. [Col. 1147A]

But we do not dare to prove anything from a source concerning which we possess no certainty, although blessed Jerome himself, in a sermon which he composed for Paula and Eustochium concerning the assumption of holy Mary, Mother of God, ever-Virgin, testifies that the words of this responsory are found in the Song of Songs, saying:

> “With regard, certainly, to her ascent to the heavens, the contemplator of heavenly secrets follows, with much wonder at the sight, in the Song of Songs: ‘I saw,’ he says, ‘the beautiful one, like a dove, ascending above the streams of waters,’ and so forth.”

But where he found those words, and whether he himself translated them, we do not know. We know for certain that, according to the edition which we possess from him, we can find them nowhere. [Col. 1147B]

I am completely ignorant of where the passage sung concerning Saint Michael in that antiphon or alleluia—“The sea was shaken and the earth trembled”—where the archangel Michael descended from heaven, ought to be sought and found. The antiphon which some sing in the Church, “You are holy, says the Lord; I will multiply your number, so that you may pray for my people in this place,” is not easily found in the place where the Lord is said to have spoken these words. But since God is truth, the one who presumes to utter such things on his behalf ought to have spoken the truth, without fearing what the Lord threatens through the prophet: “Have you not seen a vain vision and spoken a lying divination? And you say, ‘The Lord says,’ when I have not spoken” (Ezekiel 13:7). [Col. 1147C]

In that responsory, “Receive the Word, Virgin Mary” (*Suscipe Verbum, virgo Maria*), at the place where it is written, “You shall conceive through the ear,” and in that responsory, “It was announced by the archangel Gabriel to the Virgin Mary concerning the entrance of the King, and he entered through the shining region of the Virgin’s ear to visit the palace of the womb, and he returned through the golden gate of the Virgin,” the statement is sufficiently childish and simple—would that it were not equally un-Catholic. [Col. 1147D]

For if, as they assert, she conceived immediately upon hearing the angel’s words, what do they make of the delay represented by all the sentences between the place where the angel said, “Hail, Mary, full of grace, the Lord is with you; blessed are you among women,” and the place where it is said, “When she heard this, she was troubled at his saying”; and, “Do not fear, Mary; behold, you shall conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus. He shall be great and shall be called the Son of the Most High,” up to the place where holy Mary said to the angel, “How shall this happen, since I do not know a man?” [Col. 1148A]

The angel answered her, foretelling not the present but the future: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy one who shall be born will be called the Son of God,” until Mary concluded in these words: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord”—not indicating but desiring it—“Let it be done to me according to your word.”

These words make it sufficiently clear that no one ever could, can, or will be able to know how the Son of God entered through the womb of an untouched virgin for the salvation of the human race and came forth with the seal of holy chastity closed. For, according to Ezekiel’s prophecy, she was prefigured as that gate continually shut, accessible only to God. Through the ineffable cooperation of the Holy Spirit, the Virgin conceived the Son of God; in the unity of one person, the Virgin bore the true God and true man; and after giving birth she remained a virgin. [Col. 1148B]

Therefore, in that responsory, “Receive the Word,” where we sing, “You shall conceive through the ear,” we would more correctly say, “You shall conceive in the womb.” But that text, “It was announced by the archangel Gabriel,” is rightly judged by wise men to have been rejected. Likewise, what is sung on the very holy night of the Nativity, “He descended from the heavens, sent from the citadel of the Father; he entered through the Virgin’s ear into our realm,” is deservedly rejected. In its place, in many churches of Gaul, what we have written below is sung as follows:

> “The true God, begotten from the Father, descended from the heavens; he entered the Virgin’s womb, so that he might appear visible to us, clothed in the human flesh of our first parent Adam; and through the closed gate God and man, light and life, the Creator of the world, came forth.”
>
> **Verse:** “Like a bridegroom.” [Col. 1148C]

That responsory also which is sung on that most sacred night and begins, “Holy and immaculate virginity, with what praises I should speak of you, I do not know, because the one whom the heavens could not contain you have carried in your womb,” can easily be seen to deserve just criticism. For it addresses virginity as though it were a woman, saying, “Holy and immaculate virginity,” although virginity is not a woman but a certain virtue, named from the noun *virgo*, “virgin.” And when the responsory has ended, it turns in direct address to Mary herself, saying, “Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb.” The same responsory would more correctly and more Catholicly be sung as follows: [Col. 1148D]

> “Holy and immaculate Virgin Mary, with what praises I should speak of you, I do not know, because the one whom the heavens could not contain you have carried in your womb.”
>
> **Verse:** “Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb.”

The antiphon sung at the vigil of that same Lord’s Nativity, “When the sun has arisen from heaven, you shall see the King of kings,” is found written in certain books as, “coming forth from the Father like a bridegroom from his bridal chamber,” although the words “from the Father” have been erased by modern copyists. For God, the Son of God, did not proceed from God the Father like a bridegroom from his bridal chamber; rather, he joined human nature to himself in the Virgin Mother, and thus proceeded from the Virgin’s womb like a bridegroom from his bridal chamber. Therefore it is more correctly sung: “You shall see the King of kings coming forth from the Mother like a bridegroom from his bridal chamber.” [Col. 1149A]

### 10

Now, although in an inverted order, it is appropriate to consider those antiphons which begin with the letter O in order to invite the Lord, and which proceed in the order of that same letter. For, as was established by the holy Fathers, that most desirable coming of the Lord was appointed for a period of three weeks before the Lord’s Advent; these weeks were prescribed and arranged for each day with various antiphonal chants.

Three offices were also established for each of the three Sundays of those weeks. Since the same period of the Lord’s Advent ordinarily extends from the fifth day before the Kalends of December to the Nones of that month, one, two, or three days—or sometimes a whole week—remain over from the fourth week. It pleased the arranger of the antiphonary, during each night of that fourth week whenever such days remained, to compose morning praises and to arrange antiphons for inviting God at the evening praises, beginning on Sunday and extending through Friday. [Col. 1149B]

The first antiphon begins, “O Wisdom, who came forth from the mouth of the Most High,” and concludes, “Come to teach us the way of prudence.” The second is “O Adonai”; the third, “O Root of Jesse”; the fourth, “O Key of David”; the fifth, “O Rising Sun, splendor of eternal light”; the sixth, “O King of the nations”; and the seventh, “O Emmanuel.” All of them end with the word “Come.”

I have taken care to record these so that it might be clearly understood that these alone appear regularly and correctly to belong to the invitation of the Lord’s Advent. Let those who wish examine and understand whether those which are sung in imitation of these agree in meaning and words. [Col. 1149C]

In the antiphon sung on the octave of the Lord, “A wonderful mystery is declared today,” we found written, “The natures are renewed.” I cannot help wondering what those natures are which are said to have been renewed. God, begotten from the substance of the Father before the ages, appeared among human beings as true God and true man, born in time from the substance of his mother, subsisting in two natures—that is, divine and human—and in one person.

Thus we read in a certain synod held in the city of Spalatum [Hispalis]:

> “Therefore, if anyone is unwilling to believe and preach that in our Lord Jesus Christ there are either two natures or one person, or if anyone is unwilling to confess that he is both God and man—that is, the incarnate Word, truly born from the Virgin Mary for our salvation—he is so condemned and shown to be foreign to the Catholic faith that he resists the sacrament of human redemption with ingratitude.” [Col. 1149D]

It is therefore evident that the divine nature exists invisibly, impassibly, and immutably; it could neither be changed, restored, nor renewed. The true God, the Son of God, assumed human nature in the unity of his person, without division or mixture, and redeemed, restored, and renewed us on the wood of the cross. Consequently, renewal pertains solely to the nature of man. Therefore it could more correctly be said, “The nature is renewed”; or, as some prefer, “God, having become man, is the renewer of nature.” [Col. 1150A]

That responsory, “The Holy Spirit was seen in the form of a dove, and the Father’s voice was heard: ‘This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased,’” ends and concludes there. Some add, “Hear him!” But that voice was not heard at the baptism; it was uttered by the Father on the mountain, where the Lord was transfigured, and therefore it ought not to be joined to this responsory.

### 11

It now seems necessary to discuss something concerning the solemnity called Septuagesima, which begins at evening and, contrary to ecclesiastical custom, ends at morning prayers. For all festivals established for solemn celebration ordinarily begin with the preceding evening, proceed through the nocturnal and morning hours in the regular course of the whole day, and thus reach the second evening.

This one alone, as was said above, begins at evening and scarcely reaches the morning hours. Hence it may be inferred that some, touched by the sweetness of melodious praise, established this boundary for the modulation of the alleluia. Consequently, some criticize the author of this nocturnal office because, without testimony from Sacred Scripture, he attempted to weave such a musical narrative by addressing the alleluia as though it were a person. [Col. 1150B]

But we do not wish to leave unmentioned those things which we know to have been taken in some way from authentic Scriptures. For in the Book of Judges we read that someone addressed his son-in-law, who wished to depart, in these words:

> “Consider that the day is declining toward sunset and drawing near to evening. Remain with me today also, spend a joyful day, and tomorrow you shall depart to go to your house.”

Taking the opportunity provided by this sentence, he began to say to the alleluia as follows: “Remain with us today,” and the rest that follows.

In the Book of Wisdom we read:

> “O how beautiful is a chaste generation with glory! For its memory is immortal, because it is known both to God and to men. When it is present, they imitate it and desire it; when it has withdrawn, it triumphs forever crowned.”

And in the same book:

> “Good is the delight in the works of his hands, and unfailing nobility.”

We also read in Tobit that he said to his wife concerning his son: [Col. 1150C]

> “For I believe that the good angel of God accompanies him and orders well all that concerns him, so that he may return to us with joy.”

We believe that the responsory, “May your years be multiplied by the Lord,” was written from the Proverbs of Solomon on the occasion of this discourse:

> “Hear, my son, and receive my words, so that the years of your life may be multiplied; I shall show you the way of wisdom and lead you along the paths of righteousness.”

Likewise, that responsory which we sing, “Alleluia; a good name is better than great riches,” is also found in the Proverbs of Solomon. I have not yet found the Scriptural passages from which the remaining texts, except those composed from the Psalms, can be taken. [Col. 1150D]

It would therefore seem more correct to me that the singing of the alleluia itself should begin at evening on Friday, be celebrated throughout Saturday, and conclude at evening with the singing of the Alleluia in praise of the Lord. I offer this according to my own judgment, without prejudging the wisdom of others, whom I know to be devoted to the praise of God.

That some wish to place in this Sunday night, which is called Septuagesima, those responsories which are arranged after the Lord’s resurrection and begin, “If I should forget you,” seems to me unreasonable. For if the author of the antiphonary had wished them to be sung there in the first place, he would certainly have written them there, rather than placing them after Easter. [Col. 1151A]

In the reading taken from the Book of Ecclesiasticus, which begins, “In all things I sought rest,” one verse is found in certain books as, “Like cinnamon and balsam giving fragrance.” In others it reads, “Like cinnamon and aromatic aspaltum, I gave forth fragrance.” [Col. 1151B]

That responsory, “Our salvation,” which is sung in Lent, is concluded by some as follows: “So that we may serve you securely.” But it is more correctly sung as it is found in Genesis: “May your mercy look upon us, so that we may securely serve the King.”

### 12

Let us now turn our style to those responsories whose verses do not agree with them at all, but differ greatly in meaning and words.

To the responsory “Hail, Mary, full of grace,” they attach the verse:

> “Lift up your gates, O princes, and be lifted up, you everlasting gates.”

But those gates, those princes, and those everlasting gates which are commanded to be lifted up pertain more properly to other persons than to holy Mary, ever-Virgin. Since the angel said to Mary, “Hail, Mary, full of grace,” she replied in the verse by asking:

> **Verse:** “How shall this happen, since I do not know a man?”

And the angel answered her:

> “The Holy Spirit.” [Col. 1151C]

The following are examples of responsories and their verses:

> **Responsory:** “Behold, the Lord will come.”
>
> **Verse:** “Behold, the Lord will come with power, and the kingdom, power, and authority are in his hand. Over all.”
>
> **Responsory:** “Jerusalem, you shall plant a vineyard.”
>
> **Verse:** “Rejoice, daughter of Zion; exult, Jerusalem. Arise, Zion.”
>
> **Responsory:** “Bethlehem, city of the Most High God.”
>
> **Verse:** “He shall speak peace to the nations, and he shall rule from sea to sea. And there shall be peace.”
>
> **Responsory:** “Receive the Word, Virgin Mary.”
>
> **Verse:** “You shall indeed bear a son and shall suffer no loss of virginity; you shall become pregnant and shall remain forever an untouched virgin. That she may be blessed.”
>
> **Responsory:** “Egypt, do not weep.”
>
> **Verse:** “Behold, the Lord of hosts, your God, will come in great power. To deliver.”
>
> **Responsory:** “The Lord shall descend like rain.”
>
> **Verse:** “All kings shall adore him; all nations shall serve him. He shall arise.”
>
> **Responsory:** “Behold, the Root of Jesse.”
>
> **Verse:** “The Lord shall give him the throne of David his father. And he shall be.”
>
> **Responsory:** “The Lord shall teach us his ways.”
>
> **Verse:** “Come, let us ascend to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob. Because.” [Col. 1151D]
>
> **Responsory:** “Sound the trumpet.”
>
> **Verse:** “Announce it to the ends of the earth, and say to the distant islands: ‘Behold, God.’”
>
> **Responsory:** “Return, Virgin Israel.”
>
> **Verse:** “With everlasting love I have loved you; therefore I have drawn you, taking pity on you. For salvation.”
>
> **Responsory:** “I have sworn, says the Lord.”
>
> **Verse:** “My salvation is near, that it may come, and my righteousness, that it may be revealed. And the covenant.”
>
> **Responsory:** “Cry out with strength.”
>
> **Verse:** “Climb upon a high mountain, you who evangelize Zion; lift up your voice with strength. Behold, God.”
>
> **Responsory:** “A star shall arise from Jacob.”
>
> **Verse:** “All kings shall adore him; all nations shall serve him. And all shall be.”
>
> **Responsory:** “The Lord shall go forth.”
>
> **Verse:** “And he shall be exalted above all the hills, and all nations shall flow toward him. And they shall stand.” [Col. 1152A]
>
> **Responsory:** “The Forerunner enters on our behalf.”
>
> **Verse:** “He is the King of righteousness, whose generation has no end. The High Priest.”
>
> **Responsory:** “The nations shall see.”
>
> **Verse:** “And you shall be a crown of glory in the hand of the Lord and a royal diadem in the hand of your God. And he shall be called.”
>
> **Responsory:** “The Root of Jesse.”
>
> **Verse:** “Before him kings shall shut their mouths; the nations shall implore him. And he shall be.”
>
> **Responsory:** “Rejoice with me.”
>
> **Verse:** “All generations shall call me blessed. Because.”
>
> **Responsory:** “He is held in the bosom.”
>
> **Verse:** “He is carried in a mother’s arms, he who had carried his mother; the angelic princes surround him in a faithful company. Through whom.”
>
> **Responsory:** “They have been opened.”
>
> **Verse:** “For the death which the Savior deigned to suffer for all, he first returned to the Savior. And therefore.”
>

### 13

In the midst of these matters it should be known that, although certain verses agree with their responsories, they become somewhat devalued and cause weariness through the excessive frequency with which they are repeated. Such are “God shall come from Lebanon,” “from the rising of the sun,” “who rule Israel,” and many others of this kind.

For this reason we have set down not only those verses which we were able to find in more corrected antiphonaries for the sake of emendation, but have also taken care to record others newly composed in place of the earlier ones.

The verse belonging to the responsory which is sung, “In the sweat of your face,” begins:

> **Verse:** “Because you obeyed the voice of your wife.”

Some sing *plusquam me* (“more than me”), whereas it should more correctly be *plusquam meae*, that is, “You ought to have obeyed my voice more than your wife’s voice.” [Col. 1154A]

The verse, “And when Reuben had gone to the well and had not found him,” is sung by some as:

> “And having torn his garments…”

But the conjunction *and* is superfluous there, and it is more regularly said:

> “Having torn his garments, he went to his brothers and said…”

One responsory still remains which seems to me not to be passed over. It begins, “While the Lord was walking in paradise,” and the following verse is attached to it:

> “O Lord, I heard your report and was afraid.”

It is then joined to what is found in the prophet Habakkuk:

> “I considered your works and was terrified.”

But the expression which follows in Genesis would be more correct:

> “O Lord, I heard your report and was afraid because I was naked, and I hid myself.” [Col. 1154B]

Nor should it be passed over that God sought the lost man in the breeze after midday and found him naked. At midday the sun is usually hotter, and afterward declines toward a breeze. The first man fell away from the heat of the Sun of righteousness when he did not remain in love of his Creator; he declined toward the breeze after midday when he fell into the guilt of faithlessness.

But let us, fervent in divine love and always walking clothed in the wedding garment, seek the heavenly Bridegroom at midday, saying with the bride:

> “Tell me where you pasture, where you lie down at midday, you whom my soul loves.”

Thus, remaining in the fervor of the twofold love, may we always rejoice and celebrate with Christ. [Col. 1154C–D]

[Col. 1155]

## On the Consonant Diversity of the Modes

*From a contemporary manuscript of Saint Gall.*

Bern, by the grace of God—and, if not by merit, nevertheless by office—abbot, to his most beloved sons in Christ, Purchard and Kerung, together with the others engaged in the academy of the Lord’s schools at Reichenau: may they advance daily from virtue to virtue, so that they may be able to behold the God of gods in Zion. [Col. 1155A]

Recently, urged by the persistence of your prayers to hand over to your keen diligence certain little verses composed concerning the consonant diversity of the modes for you to learn, I did not immediately turn my mind to doing so. I believed that I would provide laughter for posterity if, amid the abundant treasures of wisdom and the copious streams of divine and human literature flowing like a torrent, I, lacking all eloquence, presumed to mutter something. I was not without fear that this saying might rightly be directed against me:

> “Do not carry wood into the forest, or fish into the sea.” [Col. 1155B]

But, considering again that saying of the Lord which declares, “Give to the one who asks you, and do not turn away from the one who wishes to borrow from you,” I did not dare wholly refuse—not as though I were giving to those who asked, but at least as one wishing to lend. I hoped to gain no small interest if, in exchange for the chatter of a wordy little composition acquired from one source or another, I might deserve to share in the learned sobriety of your domestic eloquence.

It is therefore clear that music consists of eight modes. Through them the consonances of musical modulation, which for the sake of brevity we now pass over, appear to agree with one another through a certain friendly affinity of conjunction. [Col. 1155C]

Among us their names took their beginnings from the authority of their order, from the first through the eighth. Four of them—the first, third, fifth, and seventh—are called *authentic* in Greek speech, because they appear to preside over the others, namely, the second, fourth, sixth, and eighth, with a kind of authority of mastery. For *authentic* signifies “author” or “teacher.” Thus, just as the higher modes are called authentic, the lower are called *plagal*, as though they were parts proceeding from the side of the higher modes. [Col. 1155D]

For this reason the mode which those instructed in this art commonly call “the first” in Latin speech is called *authentic protus*, as though “the first authoritative mode”; the second, *plagal protus*, or *plagal*, that is, “the part of protus”; the third, *authentic deuterus*, because it has the second authority; the fourth, *plagal deuterus*, or “the plagal mode of deuterus”; the fifth, *authentic tritus*, taking its name from the number three and from its authority; the sixth is subordinate to it according to the rule stated above. The seventh is called *authentic tetrardus* from its order, for *tetra* means “four.” Then comes the eighth, which is subordinate to the seventh; hence it is called *plagal tetrardus*, or “the plagal mode of tetrardus.” [Col. 1156A]

The first, third, fifth, and seventh are rightly called authentic or principal, since their sound is higher and their ascent greater. Each of them, beginning from its final, can freely ascend as far as the ninth degree, while in descending it sometimes reaches the third sound adjacent to it. The lower modes, however, ascend only as far as the fifth and descend to the fourth sound.

Thus the lower modes—the second, fourth, sixth, and eighth—do not wholly depart from the higher modes, as disciples do not wholly depart from their teachers. Joined to them by a neighboring sequence of sounds, they display a certain form of discipleship, since, as we noted above, their ascent is shorter and their descent lower. [Col. 1156B]

Leaving aside the distinctions of the individual modes, which appear to differ slightly in certain notes according to the varying practice of teachers, we have attached to each little verse, by way of example, the principal character of its sound, both in antiphons and in responsories. We have also taken care to add further verses of the same rule belonging to introits and communions, together with their differences, since these are fewer and more certain. If it pleases your charity to append, according to your custom, the differences or definitions of the antiphons, know that this would greatly please us.

For the rest, I earnestly ask for your obedience, that you receive these things with the same affection of charity with which they have been composed by me, and that, as good sons, you retain in Christ the memory of your father.

Farewell. [Col. 1156C]

# LETTERS OF BERNO, ABBOT OF REICHENAU (*AUGIA DIVES*)

(From R. P. Bernard Pez, *Codex diplomatico-historico-epistolaris*, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, vol. V, part III, p. 201.)

## LETTER I. TO ABBOT VO
