He would never wish to be separated from him.

[Col. 1157D]

To Lord Vo., worthy of the highest veneration and a splendid mirror among abbots, Berno, the least of the disciples and dependents of Saint Benedict, sends whatever a son owes a father and a servant owes a master.

Having once been breathed upon, most blessed Father, by the sweetest fragrance of your virtues, I would never, if it could be avoided, wish to be deprived of the most delightful constancy of your company. Hence, day and night, nothing can bring relief to such an ardent desire except the presence of your most eagerly desired face. Since I cannot now greet you in person, I at least salute you for the moment through the service of this letter; and amid the wounds of love—for, as the Bride says, “I am wounded with love”—I use these words with the Psalmist: “Who will give me wings like a dove, and I shall fly away and rest?” Where else but under the shadow of your roof? If there I might now nest and rest with the sparrows—that is, with the true poor of Christ—I would not despair of one day becoming one of their number, of whom Isaiah speaks, saying: “Those who hope in the Lord will renew their strength; they will take wings like eagles, they will fly and not grow weary.”

You, who are unquestionably the sweet glory of us all and the crown of all monks, have already, scorning the desires of this world, changed your strength like an eagle and come to life again with those of whom it is said, “They will go from strength to strength.” Taking up the wings of virtue, you have flown to the heights; and, though you do not fail through bodily weakness, you rather advance with the Apostle, saying, “When I am weak, then I am strong.” And because you have deserved to possess that divine promise which says, “I will raise you above the heights of the earth,” hear me, I beg you, crying out to you: “Draw me after you,” so that, running after you in the fragrance of your ointments, I may deserve to share with you in that inheritance which the Lord deigned to promise you: “And I will give you,” he says, “the inheritance of Jacob your father.”

## LETTER II. TO GERON, OR JERON, ARCHBISHOP OF MAGDEBURG

He congratulates him on the peace of the empire, commends the affairs of his monastery to him, and sets forth rules for the holy administration of the episcopate.

To G., archbishop of Parthenopolis, raised to the summit of apostolic dignity, Berno, servant of God’s Mother and Virgin, offers the homage of inward devotion, filled with perfect integrity of faith.

The angels rightly sang glory to God in the highest when recently, through your vigilance and with God himself as its author, so great a peace shone forth on earth for people of good will. Although this gift of saving peace ought to be desired by all whose hopes and vows are directed toward heaven, it must nevertheless be sought especially by Christ’s priests—not merely sought, but, in the words of the Psalmist, pursued above all: “Seek peace,” he says, “and pursue it.” The Apostle, mindful of this, also says: “Pursue peace and holiness, without which no one will see God.” The mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, likewise, after completing the dispensation of the flesh and returning to the Father, earnestly commended this peace to his disciples, so that, divinely consoled by such a sweet pledge as by a final farewell, they might one day deserve to enjoy the vision of the Redeemer in the heavenly Jerusalem, which is interpreted as “vision of peace.”

[Col. 1160A]

Since we have learned, both from the report of the peoples and from the evidence of events themselves, that your mind is devoted to the pursuit of this peace, we render immense thanks to the giver of all things. We rejoice all the more abundantly in the progress of your virtues because, through the effect of true charity, we are bound more closely to your mind by love. Therefore, by this letter, in which we salute your blessedness most warmly, we have taken care to remind you earnestly not to neglect exercising inwardly, among your own people, for the peace of God’s servants and handmaids, the good of peace which you necessarily establish outwardly in the world; so that, through their merits and intercessions, you may one day be able to reach the realms of heaven.

[Col. 1160B]

For the moment, however, we set these matters aside and inform you of the troubles that lie close at hand for us. You should know that we are exposed to the plots of many rivals who utterly envy our desire for peace. With every kind of cunning ingenuity they strive, if somehow possible, to poison the pious and religious ears of royal majesty with malicious reports by lying about us and our affairs, and in one way or another to seize something belonging to our use, as is partly clear and evident to you. What is more grievous and must be lamented with the deepest sighs of our hearts is that those who appear most conspicuous in this regard are chiefly people who, under the appearance of reverence, outwardly display the semblance of holiness. For if the integrity of their conduct truly corresponded inwardly to their outward appearance, they would not still, through vice, be preserving their allegiance to the world. Whatever their order or condition, we humbly ask that the shield of your foresight be set against their crafty and hostile evasions, lest our innocence before our lord be harmed by their wicked artifice.

At the end of this brief note, please attend for a moment to our admonition, even if it is less sweetened with the honey of eloquence. For we are inflamed by an excessive fire of love for you, and it is sweet to us to address your kindness at greater length, since the sweetness of the most delightful memory of you has been unable, from the first moment of our acquaintance, to be erased from the tablet of our heart by any stylus of forgetfulness. We congratulate you on your temporal glory, but rather wish you to be fitted in every way for eternal blessedness. This can rightly come about for you only if you diligently attend to the duty of your dignity; if, through vigilant meditation, you seek what sort of person an apostolic reading declares a bishop ought to be; and if, while bodily necessity keeps you in the world, which lies in the power of the evil one, you dwell in the heavens through contemplation of the mind, so that you may proclaim with the Apostle: “Our citizenship is in heaven.”

You must also return, with profit, to the Lord from whom you received it the talent of royal intimacy by piously and mercifully assisting, through the aid of intercession, those who are in misery and affliction. Strive with all your strength to fulfill this rule of conduct: while you spend the day in the active work of labor, recover the night for the use of quiet contemplation through the persistence of prayer. Likewise, when dawn returns in the morning, before beginning any work, devote yourself to divine reading, so that, exercised in turn by these studies—reading in the morning and prayer in the evening—you may, with Christ as your guide, discern with a purer eye of the mind the affairs that arise amid your active duties during the day.

But since a person’s way is not in himself, and his steps are directed by the Lord, he must be invited by constant prayer to seal the heart and direct the steps of one’s works. In the *Song of Songs* he deigned to exhort his bride, namely the holy soul, saying: “Set me as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm.” Thus, inwardly, through the thought of the heart, there may be love from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith; and outwardly this same devotion of the heart may be shown through good works in condescension toward one’s neighbors, so that, seeing your good works, they may glorify your Father who is in heaven.

With such seals, beloved shepherd, continually mark the thoughts of your heart within and the works of your arms without, so that, in heart and body, like a vessel of election cleansed and sealed, you may receive from the Lord the promise spoken to Zerubbabel and directed to you: “I will take you, my servant, and set you like a seal, because I have chosen you, says the Lord.”

But since our account began with the good of peace, it is pleasing to bring the discourse to an end by recalling the same peace. If the word *Salem* is joined to your name, Jero, it seems without doubt to signify “vision of peace,” with only one letter O placed in the middle in place of U, as a definite sign of the future crown. From this it may clearly be understood that, if your holiness diligently labors in this valley of tears for the peace and unity of the Catholic mother Church, then, just as you now share in the name of peace, so you may one day enjoy its vision as your reward.

## LETTER III. TO THE EMPEROR HEINRICH II

He celebrates his virtues, thanks him for granting him the prefecture of Richenau, and prays that all may go well for him.

To his lord, the orthodox propagator of the Christian religion, Heinrich, august emperor, and also lord of lands and sea, honorably raised up and crowned by God, Berno, the least in the merits of his servants, offers the service of the deepest devotion together with persistent prayers.

With immense rejoicing of heart we rightly pay every kind of thanks to the Lord, who has caused the magnificence of your dignity, like a lofty pyramid, to rise above all kingdoms. It may justly be compared with the beauty of this most beautiful figure, since the fame of your glory, towering above all rulers everywhere among the nations, rises to such a height that it draws everyone’s gaze to its admiration. For, ascending to the citadel of your mind, the pattern of every virtue offers itself to all as a mirror in which to behold themselves. There faith of the patriarchs shines, the hope of the prophets gleams, and the surpassing charity of the apostles prevails. Thus, with God’s help, you bravely vindicate kingdoms with David and govern empires peacefully with Solomon.

If, while still tossed upon the sea of the present age, you endure the various outcomes of war, and, in accordance with what is said of the patriarch Jacob, they seem to provoke and quarrel with you, while those who possess weapons envy you, days will nevertheless come when, according to that same patriarch, your bow will rest upon the strong—that is, upon God—and the bonds of their arms and hands will be loosed by the powerful hands of Jacob. For although the victory of your triumph is now proclaimed everywhere throughout the world, you will nevertheless enjoy the gift of perfect peace more abundantly when, after subduing the enemies of holy Church, you are able to hear with the people of God: “The Lord will fight for you; you shall be silent.” The blessing of Joseph will then be directed to you: “The God of your father will be your helper, and the Almighty will bless you.” Then also, according to Isaiah’s prophecy, the Lord will make the pride of the unbelieving cease and humble the arrogance of the strong; the firstborn of the poor will feed, and the poor will act with confidence. Indeed, that King of whom Solomon says, “He who sits upon the throne of judgment scatters all evil with his gaze,” will look upon you with the regard of heavenly mercy and, granting you the tranquil quiet of the times, will deign to crown you with the crown of justice.

[Col. 1162C]

Meanwhile I too, your humble dependent, mindful of the benefits by which, although unworthy, you wished to raise me from the dung of poverty and, with God as author, place me among the leaders of the people in a certain seat of dignity, pour out all my hope to God day and night in prayer, together with the entire flock entrusted to me. May the prosperity of the present life smile upon you according to your desire, and may the happiness of future blessedness become your reward.

Through the bearer of this letter, inform us about the peaceful condition of the empire, the varying outcome of your military campaigns, and—greater than all these things—about the health of your body and soul, so that we may joyfully render thanks to the giver of all good things. May the sublimity of your imperial rule prosper here through many courses of years as you govern well, so that afterward you may sweetly gather the fruit of your works amid the delights of paradise. Farewell.

## LETTER IV. TO H., ABBOT OF SAINT SAVIOUR’S

As he is about to depart, he bids him farewell and commends the needs of his brothers to him.

To Abbot H., joined to me most sweetly by the affection of brotherly charity, Berno, half of his own soul, offers himself in complete fidelity.

Since, from almost the very cries of infancy, we have grown together into one through the solid bond of dear friendship, it follows that this shared honor between us is indissoluble. For we shall be able to have one heart and one soul in Christ if, in accordance with the Apostle, we bear one another’s burdens.

Therefore, as you know well, since I am about to undertake a journey of greater length, I began to consider how neither you should remain without a greeting from me nor I depart from you without a gift. Receive, then, this little letter sent in the place of a friend. It both performs for me the duty of greeting and reminds you to come to my aid, now that I am placed in such great need—not as though a benefit were only now joining those whom beneficence united long ago, but, in accordance with the Apostle, that your abundance may supply our want out of your equality, so that our abundance may likewise be the supplement of your want—when will that be? Yet, although we speak thus, you are rich.

Otherwise, as Tully says, it is too narrow and meager a way of reckoning friendship, to require the balance of what has been received and given to be equal. “True friendship,” he says, “seems to me richer and more abundant, and does not strictly observe whether it gives back more than it has received. There is no fear that something may slip away, or flow down to the ground, or even be heaped up excessively in friendship.”

Mindful, therefore, of this saying, and finding nothing in the entire treasury of friendship that seems more precious to me, I give myself wholly to you. I (do not) doubt that you especially wish to enjoy this gift, so that I too may in the same way enjoy you in the Lord. Therefore, amid the sacred solemnities of Masses and the libations of prayers, I ask you to remember me, as I remember you; and, after offering an appropriate greeting from me to the entire flock of Saint Saviour entrusted to you, take care to commend me and all our people to them with whatever affection of charity you can. [Col. 1163C] Farewell.

## LETTER V. TO THE BROTHERS OF RICHENAU

He determines what further should be offered by his people for the soul of the deceased monk Heinrich.

Berno, servant of God’s Mother, sends true love in Christ to the community of the brothers of Richenau.

The text of your letter has sufficiently disclosed what affection remains for me in the hidden places of your hearts. Although, overflowing everywhere with honeyed sweetness, so to speak, it greatly gladdened us concerning your prosperity and your conduct worthy of God, it also brought no little sadness to our hearts when it recalled the lamentable death of our brother Heinrich. We mourn him not so much as dead, since we knew him to be mortal, as we grieve that he was taken from us so suddenly—alas! Yet, since now, to use someone’s words, the time is for a remedy rather than a complaint, let tears be wiped from our cheeks; let mourning withdraw, and sorrow and groaning flee. Let Christ be our common consolation, both for him and for us.

For the absolution of his soul, although we do not doubt that you have already fulfilled the customary duty owed to human destiny, we nevertheless thought it necessary to add something. We judged it entirely equitable that he who, according to the testimony of your profession, had served well in external action for the common benefit of us all here, as Martha served, as long as he lived, might now, through the support of your prayers, be able to possess with Mary the better portion in Christ.

Therefore, gathered together as you are, and with my spirit joined to yours, we fraternally ask you to count thirty continuous days, allowing none to pass without the saving Sacrifice being offered for the soul of this brother, together with an equal number of psalters and vigils. On the first day let one hundred poor be fed, on the third two hundred, on the seventh three hundred, and on the thirtieth four hundred, so that the sum of this thousandfold perfection may bring complete remission there where “one day in the courts of the Lord is better than a thousand.”

For you, our brothers, and also for the clerics stationed in our cells, we judge that suitable and fitting refreshment should be prepared on the four days mentioned above as an act of charity. We wish Lord Tietbald to be the organizer and provider of this arrangement, and we appoint Brother Alawicus, together with those who are ministerials outside, as his assistants. Farewell.

## LETTER VI. TO ABBOT BURCHARD

He announces to him the death of Heinrich, the monk of Richenau.

To the uniquely beloved Abbot Burchard, Berno, least in the merits of the hooded monks, a pledge of undivided faith.

Although apostolic authority forbids us to grieve over the [death] of those dear to us who sleep in Christ, nevertheless the affection of piety stirs the breast to sorrow. A fitting measure must be maintained in both respects, so that piety may compel us to weep over the condition of death inflicted upon us, while hope of the future glory of blessed immortality leads us to rejoice.

This is what we now believe must necessarily be done concerning the laying aside of the body of our dearest brother Heinrich. We can no longer recall him to us by tears; indeed, if that could help, the tears of the Lord alone, first of all, would be sufficient through his mercy. Almost the entire palatine company also mourns for him and draws sighs. Therefore, let the tears be wiped away and constant prayers for his rest be poured out to God. Let consolation not be hidden from our eyes, because he who dried up the veins of death and broke the passage dividing our brother from the underworld has, as we hope, rescued him from among mortals for this reason: that he might exchange death for a better life.

Therefore, as sorrow perishes, let joy succeed it, especially since, as Solomon bears witness, the day of death is better than the day of birth: for when the sinner dies, he ceases to sin; while the just person will be in eternal remembrance and will not fear evil report.

My innermost love, I beg you with every kind of prayer: since we have not so much lost the intermediary of our love as sent him before us to the Creator, let us henceforth be bound more tightly in the bond of brotherly charity, so that we may no longer live as two but always as one in Christ. Farewell.

## LETTER VII. TO H., A BISHOP

He complains that access to him was denied at the appointed place and time, and asks him to allow himself to be loved.

To H., a venerable bishop, a radiant mirror of great men, Berno, as though an unworthy servant of God’s Mother and Virgin, offers the service of sincere devotion.

[Col. 1165A]

If that old saying is valid—that friends have everything in common—then all the rights of friendship are likewise common. Whoever loses them rightly loses the name of friend, since he does not safeguard the spirit of the one who, to use a customary expression, is his other self. For, as your Tully says, there ought not to be satiety in friendships, as there is in other things. I said “your,” not “your [plural],” because, while preserving your reverence separately for the moment, I have decided to address you not as a bishop now but as a friend of former times.

You seem to me to have forgotten both this name and its duty and to be devising certain new ways of acting. For, according to the saying of that familiar friend of yours, the oldest things, like wines that have acquired age, ought to be the sweetest. And, according to his testimony, that saying is true which declares that many bushels of salt must be eaten together before the duty of friendship is fulfilled.

Although we have already spent much time in the age of our friendship, we have not yet consumed the equivalent of even one sextarius, let alone a bushel, in the custom of such long-standing acquaintance. Yet you, as though the duty of so honorable a virtue had already been fully performed between us, suddenly withdraw yourself from friendly conversation so completely that you will not even allow me to greet you.

After we recently parted from one another, bidding farewell with exchanged kisses as you departed, I preserved the words of your promise—that on your return you would seek me especially—as a most sweet pledge in the treasury of my heart. Day and night I remained suspended in expectation of the most desired news of your return. Then suddenly, together with a mission of congratulatory purpose, I received the commission to meet you on the appointed day.

But, by what fate I do not know, I remained disappointed in my hope. I opened the latch of my door in the heart dear to you; but you had turned aside and passed by, and, without greeting me, left behind in place of the traces of your love the goads of sorrow. I, on the contrary, aflame with the fire of your love, was ready to cross ice and waters to you, so that in me, through the zeal and duty of goodwill, the saying might be fulfilled: “Many waters could not extinguish love, nor could rivers overwhelm it.”

Therefore, repay a friend with the gift of grateful reciprocity, and give yourself to me more quickly, wholly, for greeting, conversation, and embrace, so that we who began to love freely, with goodwill alone intervening between us, may henceforth be able to have one heart and one soul more closely in the charity of Christ. Otherwise, consider what you yourself testified that Tully said: “When charity and goodwill have been removed, all joy from life has been removed.” Farewell.

## LETTER VIII. TO A., A BISHOP

He warns him not to act rashly in choosing the successor of Emperor Heinrich, but to conduct everything after consulting others.

To the glorious bishop A., Berno, servant of God’s Mother and Virgin, offers the service of due obedience and the gift of prayer.

Although, because of the fault of our first parent, we are compelled continually to mourn the death of those dear to us, nevertheless it is fitting to find consolation in him who is the firstborn of the dead and prince of the kings of the earth. Thus, having obtained at least some small consolation concerning the [death] of our most beloved savior, King and Emperor H., we have sent these consolatory letters to your holiness, earnestly urging you both always to preserve a worthy memory of him and not to neglect the condition of your kingdom.

You do this rightly if you do not hasten too precipitously in your counsels. As wise men, you ought to await the associates of your kingdom, so that now once again the dear fellowship of one king may unite them, his authority govern them, and civic concord render them glorious—those whom no Alpine ruggedness has hitherto been able to separate, nor any public or private matter to set apart.

Know that the public assembly of us all will be held on the day before the Nones of September beside the Rhine, at a place called Kambe. If anything beneficial for our kingdom is deliberated there, with the Lord’s help, it will also be advantageous to you. For everything that is ours is yours, and, in turn, everything that is yours is ours.

You, illustrious Italy, are greeted by your sister Francia, which counsels the treaties of unity, so that you may be able to exchange mutual kisses and so that the God of peace and consolation may quickly crush Satan beneath your feet. For the common good will stand firmly among you if that ancient agreement of yours—having the same will and the same refusal—does not waver in any way.

Nature has handed this law of friendship to you above all as a kind of solidarity: beginning with the Charleses and ending with the Ottos in Heinrich, so that there might be, as it were, one mind among many of you.

Therefore act prudently, preserve the law of friendship, and await the angel of great counsel, because it is written: “Do everything with counsel, and afterward you will not regret it.” These are the few things I wished to recall in goodwill; receive them in friendship. Greet on our behalf your—and indeed our—most courageous Leo, firm in faith, and Heinrich, a man of ancient virtue. For this reason, A., we give you particular thanks, because we have learned that you protect our affairs as though they were your own.

## LETTER IX. TO H., A BISHOP

He asks him for relics of Saint Ursus the Martyr, whose body he had heard was to be transferred.

To H., flower of bishops and ornament of every kind of virtue, Berno, servant of God’s Mother and Virgin, together with the entire brotherly community of the monastery of Richenau, offers the highest and unfailing good.

If there can be any distinction among the soldiers of the heavenly court, those who have deserved to reach, by the crimson ascent, the golden resting place of our peaceful King seem certainly to excel. Here the thresholds of the apostles are worn down; from here the intercessions of the martyrs are sought; peoples assemble, make vows, and fulfill them, so that through “the calves of their lips” they may offer a sacrifice pleasing to God.

And because the middle of that litter, by which one ascends to the resting place mentioned above, is paved with charity, whoever aims at that true being of the faithful ought rightly to hope through another for what he is unable to attain himself. Apostolic authority testifies to this when it commands: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ”; and James says: “Pray for one another, so that you may be saved.”

If such salvation can be obtained through those whose bodies are still subject to corruption and weigh down the soul, then, with God as author, we ought all the more to hope to be saved through those whose souls already rejoice with Christ in heavenly glory, where, in the dwellings of the just, the voice of exultation and salvation resounds.

For this reason, most reverend Father, we believe that this letter should be sent to you, through which we confidently hope to obtain the gifts of charity. For a sweet fragrance of renown has spread around us, and we have learned that you wish to transfer the [body] of the holy, thrice and four times blessed martyr Ursus, your patron. You should know that this would be a source of complete joy to us.

Therefore, first venerating you, who by the merit of your faith and the privilege of your episcopal see are rightly the chief minister of so distinguished an office, and then greeting with the deepest affection of heart all who are gathering for that same purpose in devotion to religion, we devoutly and humbly beseech you that, as a gift of blessing, we may deserve through you to be presented with relics of so great a patron.

If, with God’s guidance, we obtain the fulfillment of this desire, we also earnestly wish that the day of his passion, or any deeds of that same martyr that are preserved among you, be sent to us, so that now, in the presence of the blessed martyr’s memory, we may cast together, as though in the Lord’s field, the seeds of prayer with tears, and through his intercession may deserve at the end of our good works to carry rejoicing sheaves to the heavenly threshing floor. Farewell.

## LETTER X. TO CUONO

He requests from him relics of the same holy martyr Ursus.

[Col. 1167C]

To Cuono, a man of virtues and therefore worthy of the name Cuono, Berno, servant of holy Mary, ever Virgin, together with the congregation entrusted to him, offers the duties of brotherly charity.

Since we have learned that you are, in very deed, four-square in the fourfold kinds of virtues, we do not hesitate to disclose to you the desire of our petition. We have nearby a place that is to be prepared for divine worship. Wishing to endow it with some rare adornment of sacred relics, we have sent you this little letter through our brother P., humbly begging that, as a kindly gift of your charity, we may be permitted to touch some portion of the most sacred body of the blessed Ursus, martyr of Christ and your patron, so that together we may possess something from which we may always rejoice in common in the Lord.

For such a recompense, we promise you in the meantime an inviolable pledge of undivided faith, until you receive the Lord himself as your reward, if you now take care to satisfy our desire for his love.

## LETTER XI. TO FRIDERICUS

Why Cassian the collator is criticized by so many, etc.

Berno to his own Fridericus: as to a rich man in true peace, who always kisses mercy and truth, he sends the good beyond which there is none greater.

[Col. 1168A]

That perpetual fire of which the Lord commands the lawgiver never to allow it to fail from the altar burns continually upon the altar of your heart, from which the incense of devoted prayer sends forth a sweet fragrance. Drawn by its scent, among the other men of your friendship, I cannot, even if I wished, be forgetful of you, especially since the words of your wisdom, in accordance with Solomon’s saying, are for me like nails firmly fixed in a high place, and I myself am refreshed by their memory.

When we had gathered at Cologne in the present year, and a certain pleasant discussion of sacred Scripture had taken place between us, you suddenly raised the question of why Cassian, who composed many useful works on the instruction of monks, should nevertheless be found to appear especially to be his own critic [apograph: *reprehensores esse videantur*, “critics seem to be”]. Come, then, and attend to what I say.

Cassiodorus, a monk formerly a senator, a man learned in divine and human letters, after expounding the first verse of Psalm 69, which begins, “O God, come to my assistance,” added:

“But, since he is not to be followed generally in all things, the most eloquent Cassian celebrates this passage with such great honor in the tenth Conference, explaining at length the usefulness of this same verse, that whatever monks undertake, they do not begin without a threefold repetition of this verse.”

Likewise, in another work addressed to the brothers of his monastery (*On the Institutions of Divine Letters*, chapter 29), he says:

“Read diligently and listen willingly to Cassian the presbyter, who wrote on the instruction of faithful monks. At the very beginning of the holy undertaking he says that eight principal vices must be avoided.”

And shortly afterward:

“Nevertheless, he was rightly criticized by blessed Prosper concerning free will. Therefore we warn you that, since he exceeds the bounds in such matters, you should read him with caution. Victor, the African bishop of Martyritanum [Codex: Mataritanus], with the Lord’s help, so purged his statements and added what was lacking that the palm of victory in these matters may deservedly be awarded to him.”

He is criticized by three authorities, whose testimony proves that he erred: Cassiodorus says that he is not to be followed in everything; he affirms that blessed Prosper rightly blamed him concerning free will; and he praises Bishop Victor for purging his statements.

You have already heard to some extent what he was criticized for, by whom, and on what grounds: namely, concerning free will. Now let your charity carefully attend to where that heretical error lies hidden in his writings.

In his book entitled *On the Protection of God*, Cassian introduces a certain man named Chaeremon disputing about grace and free will, and shows that he approved and accepted Chaeremon’s opinion in every respect. From the passage where he says, “Divine protection is therefore always inseparably present with us,” almost to the end of that same Conference, he appears to depart from the line of truth. For, by a kind of alternating interpretation, he gathers from sacred Scripture certain statements opposed to one another, and, after making a general division of all the faithful, endeavors to affirm that some are those whom God saves by grace, while others are those whom nature justifies through free will.

Accordingly, he says of God:

“When he has perceived in us a certain beginning of good will, he immediately enlightens and strengthens it, and urges it toward salvation, granting increase to that which either he himself has planted or has seen arise through our effort, etc.”

But if you object that nothing deserving criticism can now be found in him because, as we said above, Cassiodorus testifies that he was corrected by a bishop, know that we by no means possess him in corrected form, just as Cassiodorus himself did not possess him at the time when he wrote these things. Hence he also says:

“We believe that this book, namely, among others, will soon be sent to us from the regions of Africa. But you, dearest brothers,” he says, “with God’s help, read those sections that he is known to have praised for their soundness.”

Unless, perhaps, you possess a copy in which you do not fear that thorns of error may be found amid the fragrant roses of sweet opinions, nor think that Virgil’s words ought there to be admitted to the ears:

“[…] Flee, boys; the snake lies hidden in the grass.”

But, lest we seem to burden the reader if we wish to expose all the doctrines of such falsehood within the brevity of a letter—especially since a Catholic book exists, composed by the blessed Prosper so often mentioned, in opposition to these same absurdities of heretical perversity that strive to attack God’s grace—it is pleasing to set down a few of the many words of this defender of divine grace, so that it may become clear, by contrast, which of them rightly carries the palm from this field of battle.

[Col. 1169C] After the aforementioned teacher, having taken his stand in the Catholic battle-line, had attacked the enemy of God’s grace with the armor of Sacred Scripture and shattered the wall of unbelief with the battering ram of faith, he says this near the end of his book:

> “I now rightly consider it necessary, before concluding the volume, briefly and jointly to arrange the points we have shown not to agree with Catholic truth, so that those matters which, amid our responses, may escape the reader’s recollection may be recalled together with greater fidelity.”

**A.** In the first definition, therefore, it was said (PROSPER):

> “The beginning not only of good actions but also of good thoughts is from God, who both inspires in us the beginnings of holy intention and grants the power and execution by which we may accomplish what we rightly desire. For every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, descending from the Father of lights, who both begins what is good, carries it out, and brings it to completion in us.”

This we too embrace wholeheartedly and profess to be Catholic.

**B.** In the second definition it was said (CASSIAN):

> “Divine protection, therefore, is inseparably present with us, and so great is the Creator’s compassion toward His creature that providence not only accompanies it but continually goes before it. The Prophet, having experienced this, confesses it when he says: ‘My God, His mercy will go before me.’ When He has observed in us the emergence of some good intention, He enlightens and strengthens it, and urges it [Col. 1170A] toward salvation, granting it growth—whether He Himself planted it or saw it spring forth through our effort.”

(PROSPER.) Here he descends from the preceding definition, and what had all been attributed to grace is now assigned in part to free will.

**C.** In the third definition it was said (CASSIAN):

> “Except that in all these matters both God’s grace and freedom of the will are made manifest: for sometimes a human being can extend his desire toward the virtues by his own impulses, yet he always needs to be assisted by the Lord. For no one enjoys health whenever he wishes, nor is freed from the disease of illness merely by the desire of his own free will.”

As though our physician did not also grant the sick this: that they should truly desire health.

**A.** In the fourth definition it was said:

> “But so that it may become more evident that, even through the good of nature which has been bestowed by the Creator’s favor, the beginnings of good intentions sometimes arise—although, unless they are directed by the Lord, they cannot reach the completion of the virtues—the Apostle testified, saying: ‘To will is present with me, but to accomplish the good I cannot.’”

As though the Apostle, who professes that his sufficiency for thinking comes from God, possessed a good will from natural inclination and not from the gift of grace.

In the fifth definition it was said:

> “And so these things are in a certain way mixed and confused with one another, that among many people it is debated at length from what one depends upon the other: that is, whether God has mercy on us because we have supplied the beginning of a good will, or whether, because God has mercy, we obtain the beginning of a good will. For many, believing these individual points and asserting them more strongly than is right, have become entangled in various and mutually contradictory errors. If we say that the beginning of a good will is ours, what was there in Paul the persecutor, or in Matthew the tax collector, one of whom, occupied with the bloodshed and punishments of the innocent, and the other with public violence and plunder, was drawn toward salvation? But if we say that the beginnings of a good will are always inspired by God’s grace, what shall we say about the faith of Zacchaeus, or about the piety of the thief on the cross, who, by their desire exerting a certain force upon the heavenly kingdom, anticipated the special summons of their calling?”

(PROSPER.) The one who says that a good will is born from grace, and the one who says that grace depends upon a good will, are both said to be in error; yet both opinions are declared acceptable, since the form of the one is set forth in Paul and Matthew, and of the other in Zacchaeus and the thief.

**In the sixth definition it was said (CASSIAN):**

> “These two things, then—grace and free will—seem indeed to be opposed to one another; but both are compatible, and we conclude, on grounds of piety, that we ought equally to accept both, lest, by taking one of them away from humanity, we should appear to have exceeded the rule of ecclesiastical faith.”

(PROSPER.) As though both should be accepted in such a way that in some people the will precedes grace, while in others grace precedes the will, rather than in such a way that in everyone the will follows grace. For, according to them, if free will is removed when grace precedes it, grace is removed when free will precedes it.

**In the seventh definition it was said (CASSIAN):**

> “After the transgression, therefore, Adam acquired knowledge of evil, which he had not possessed; but he did not lose the knowledge of good, which he had received.”

(PROSPER.) Both statements are false: for Adam had learned beforehand, at God’s warning, from how great an evil he ought to abstain; and, while he was established in how great a good, when he believed the devil he forgot it. Just as the worst knowledge of evil is to be evil, so the worst ignorance of good is not to be good.

**In the eighth definition it was said (CASSIAN):**

> “Therefore we must beware lest we refer all the merits of the saints to God in such a way that we ascribe nothing to human nature except what is evil.”

(PROSPER.) As though nature before grace were not under condemnation, were not in blindness, were not wounded; or as though those whose merits derive from the same source as their righteousness had not been justified freely.

**In the ninth definition it was said (CASSIAN):**

> “It cannot, therefore, be doubted that the seeds of the virtues are naturally present in every soul, implanted by the Creator’s gift. But unless these have been awakened by God’s assistance, they will not be able to advance toward the growth of perfection.”

(PROSPER.) As though Adam had lost nothing of spiritual goods through his transgression, and virtue were not something to be given in order to be possessed, but merely something to be encouraged so that it might more easily attain perfection.

**In the tenth definition it was said (CASSIAN):**

> “We also read that divine justice provided for this in Job, its most proven champion, when the devil sought him for single combat. For if he had entered the contest against the enemy not by his own strength but protected solely by the grace of God assisting him, and if, without any strength of his own patience, sustained only by divine assistance, he had endured those many masses of temptations and afflictions sought with all the enemy’s cruelty, how could the devil not more justly have repeated against him that slanderous accusation which he had previously uttered: ‘Does Job worship God for nothing? Have you not fenced him in, and his whole household and all his possessions around him? But take away your hand—that is, allow him to fight with me by his own strength—and he will surely curse you to your face.’ But since, after the contest, the slanderous enemy does not dare to repeat any such complaint, he confesses that he was defeated not by God’s strength but by Job’s. For although it must be believed that God’s grace was not wholly absent from him, He granted the tempter as much power to tempt as He knew Job possessed strength to resist.”

(PROSPER.) If God merely knew what Job could do, and did not also grant him the ability to do it, He was a witness to his patience, not its helper. And in what matter will the assistance of grace be necessary, if so great a victory was accomplished by human powers alone?

**In the eleventh definition it was said concerning the faith of the centurion (CASSIAN):**

> “The Lord marvels at him and praises him, and places him above all those who had believed from the people of Israel, saying: ‘Amen, I say to you, I have not found such great faith in Israel.’ For he would possess no praise or merit if the Lord had preferred in him that which He Himself had bestowed.”

(PROSPER.) An impious idea, which supposes that the person to whom God has given nothing is happier than the person to whom He has granted everything.

**In the twelfth definition it was said (CASSIAN):**

> “That is why, when we pray, we call the Lord not only our protector but also our receiver. Insofar as He first calls us and draws us, ignorant and unwilling, toward salvation, He is our protector and Savior. But insofar as He is accustomed to bring aid to us when we strive, and to receive and defend us when we flee to Him, He is called our receiver and refuge.”

(PROSPER.) Only one who does not wish to be saved by Christ can assent to this opinion.

Thus, in these definitions, this is taught, this is written, this is proclaimed in published disputations: that, when Adam sinned, his soul was not wounded, and that what enabled him to sin remained sound in him—since he did not lose the knowledge of good which he had received, nor could his descendants lose what he himself had not suffered to be damaged; that the seeds of the virtues are naturally present in every soul, implanted by the Creator’s gift, so that whoever wishes may, by natural judgment, precede God’s grace and earn His assistance, by which he may more easily arrive at perfection; that no one has praise or merit who is adorned with bestowed goods rather than with his own; and that one must beware of referring all the merits of the saints to God as though human nature could of itself do no good, when its integrity in the virtues is so great that even without God’s assistance it can fight against the devil himself and his savagery all the way to the final punishments.

This possibility is naturally present in all human beings, but not all wish to make use of the virtues innate within them. The Creator’s goodness toward all human beings is so great that some, because they come willingly, are received and praised by Him, while others, because they resist, are drawn unwillingly; and therefore He is the receiver of those who will, but the Savior of those who do not will. And when one part of the Church is justified by grace and another by free will, those whom nature has advanced are more glorious than those whom grace has freed, because in Adam’s descendants the will is as free for every good work as it was in Adam before the sin.

*(Thus far Prosper.)*

For the present, dearest one, let these points suffice in answer to what you asked. But if you desire to know more fully about this matter, read the book composed by blessed Prosper on the subject, and you will clearly establish that Cassian, although approved in other respects, was rightly censured in this matter.

Now, then, let my pen turn toward you, my love from the depths of my heart, so that, because you are carefully preserved in the ark of my breast, you may be greeted with the service owed by charity. I desire you to be concerned in all things for yourself and, in accordance with the saying of the Wise Man, to know yourself. Behold, the world lies in the Evil One. Whoever loves the world loves the Evil One. Whoever loves the Evil One does not love God. It remains, therefore, that whoever loves God must not love the world.

Hence John also admonishes us, saying: “Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him.” Happy is that conscience which uses the resources of worldly substance—without which the present life cannot be lived—for necessary use, but does not abuse them for luxury! With the mind’s pure gaze foreseeing the deceptive nets of heretical deceit, it avoids the deep abysses of the devil’s earthly pit; and it investigates the snares of the crafty enemy, lest they secretly creep in, so that it may escape his traps, like the one who said: “Our soul has been rescued like a sparrow from the snare of the hunters; the snare has been broken, and we have been freed. Our help is in the name of the Lord.”

Trusting in whose help, engage the enemy without fear, always turning this over in your mind: that a crown is owed only to a lawful contest. Therefore, may four rows of stones be continually enclosed in the rational breast of your heart, each row inscribed with the names of three patriarchs, so that, marked by the excellence of the four principal virtues, you may confidently confess faith in the Holy Trinity. For by carrying day and night in the sanctuary of your breast the memory of the holy Fathers, as a kind of adornment of good works, you will be worthy to be chosen from the midst of your brothers, so that you may exercise the priesthood before God. Established in this degree of dignity, may you always become upon the altar of your heart a saving victim for God: a victim seasoned with the salt of wisdom and consumed by the fire of the Holy Spirit. Concerning this fire and salt the Lord seems to have said in the Gospel: “For everyone will be salted with fire, and every sacrifice will be salted.”

Farewell.

[Col. 1173]

FRAGMENTS OF BERN’S LETTERS.

I. TO KING HENRY.

[In Mabillon, *Annals of the Benedictines*, book LVIII, no. 91, for the year 1045, where he printed the following fragment, interwoven into his narrative, as it is presented here.]

[Col. 1173B]

Henry the king was perhaps still staying at Zurich when Bern, abbot of Reichenau, wrote him a letter with this superscription: “To my lord, Henry the most unconquered of kings, peaceful, most glorious promoter of the orthodox faith: BERN, though by the quality of his merits the least of all his servants, offers the gift of devoted service and continual prayer.” In this letter Bern praises Henry because he had opened the bosom of his compassion to King Peter, who had fled suppliantly to him; and because he had not only exacted no vengeance for the offences Peter had committed against him [Col. 1173C], but had cherished and assisted him with a marvelous affection of charity, until, with Christ’s help, he had restored him to his kingdom. He then adds: “These few things I had to say for the present, impatient as I am of your love, and to send kindly to the excellence of your majesty. I have also appended two sermons, one on the Epiphany, the other on the Lord’s Supper, in which I have discussed something concerning repentance—not as I ought, indeed, but as I was able—humbly beseeching that, if you judge it worthy, you may order them to be attached to our writings.” After these sermons he returns again to Henry’s praises; then he pleads for Hirmingard, abbess of Zurich, who had been deposed from her rank for sexual misconduct. “I speak,” he says, “of Hirmingard, once abbess at Zurich, but now deservedly cast down because of her fault. Once united to her heavenly Spouse, she could sing that sweet epithalamium of the divine song: ‘Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.’ Now, like an adulteress and a prostitute, she is compelled to bewail the loss of her virginal beauty.” And below: “Now therefore I appeal to the royal glory of your mercy and humbly entreat that you do not deny to this wretched and unhappy woman the work of mercy which, by divine inspiration, you have granted to all remaining in your kingdom [Col. 1174B] [lacuna]. Behold, she has now turned to God with her whole heart and labors in groaning; every night she washes her bed [lacuna]. Let the intercession also of my lady Queen Agnes be added, that through love of God she may obtain from you for her the restoration of her former honor.” These things we once excerpted hastily and selectively from the manuscript of Villingen.

II.

[Published by Martène, *On Ancient Ecclesiastical Rites*, vol. IV, book II, chapter 15, no. 3, entitled “Which version of the Psalter was formerly used in ecclesiastical chant.” We give Martène’s words preceding and following the fragment.]

“Now, since several ancient versions of the Psalter have existed, someone may perhaps wish to know which in particular was formerly used in the divine offices. Saint Jerome, writing in Letter 135 to Sunnia and Fretela, states that the version of the Seventy Interpreters, [Col. 1174C] ‘such as,’ he says, ‘is found in the Hexapla and is kept uncorrupted and undefiled in the books of learned men, [lacuna] is chanted at Jerusalem and in the churches of the East.’ Besides this version, there was another, less corrected in Jerome’s judgment, which was called the Common, the Vulgate, and Lucian’s edition, and which the Romans used in celebrating the divine praises. Having translated the accurate Septuagint version into Latin, Jerome set aside the Vulgate; the Gallican Church then adopted this translation, and it was accordingly given the name Gallican Psalter. On this matter Walafrid should be heard at the end of chapter 15 of his book *On Ecclesiastical Matters*: ‘Although the Romans still retain the Psalms according to the Seventy Interpreters, the Gauls and some Germans chant the Psalter according to the revision which Father Jerome made from the Septuagint edition. Gregory, bishop of Tours, is said to have borrowed it from the Roman Fathers and brought it into the churches of Gaul.’

“The opinion of Bern, abbot of Reichenau, is the same, although he differs from Walafrid about the time when this version was received by the Gauls. For in a manuscript letter to Meginfrid and Bern, speaking of Saint Jerome, he says: ‘Among other works, from the corrected translation of the Seventy Interpreters he translated the Psalter from Greek into Latin and handed it over to be sung in all the churches of Gaul and in certain churches of Germany. For this reason he called it the Gallican Psalter, while the Romans still sang the Psalter from the corrupt Vulgate edition; from it the Romans composed their chant and handed down to us the practice of singing. Hence it has happened that words which are customarily modulated in the daily or nightly offices are intermingled and confusingly inserted into our Psalms, so that the less learned can scarcely discern what belongs to our Roman edition. Observing this, the pious Father and expert teacher compiled three editions in one volume; he arranged the Gallican Psalter, which we sing, in one column, the Roman in another, and the Hebrew in a third.’

“Our brethren published such a triple Psalter from a manuscript codex of the monastery of Saint Peter at Chartres in volume I, or the *Sacred Library of Saint Jerome*. Thus Bern of Reichenau differs from Walafrid in that Walafrid writes that this version was introduced into Gaul by Gregory of Tours, whereas Bern says that it was introduced by Jerome himself. Mabillon, however, after accepting both accounts, maintains in his investigation of the Gallican cursus, [Col. 1175B] [Col. 1176A] no. 22, and draws arguments for confirmation of his opinion from Gregory himself, who, when he cites verses of the Psalms in many places, especially book V, chapter 14, and book VI, chapter 5, uses a version different from the Gallican. By the same mode of argument some formerly wrote that Saint Benedict used the Gallican Psalter, as Peter Boherius teaches in his second Commentary on the Rule of Saint Benedict, because he adduces in the Rule verses of Psalms wholly conformable to the Gallican Psalter. Moreover, from Bern’s letter cited above you may infer that in his time—that is, the middle of the eleventh century—the Romans still adhered to their own version. Yet this Roman Psalter was used in the churches of the City down to the pontificate of Pius V, by whose command the Vulgate, or Gallican, edition was everywhere received, except in the one Vatican church at Rome and, outside the City, at Milan; both retain their ancient Psalter, as does the church of Saint Mark at Venice.”

[Col. 1175]

THE LIFE OF SAINT MEGINRAD, HERMIT AND MARTYR AMONG THE HELVETIANS. By Bern, abbot of Reichenau.

(Mabillon, *Acts of the Saints*, century IV, part II, p. 63, from Christopher Hartmann and Bollandus.)

PRELIMINARY OBSERVATIONS.

[Col. 1175C] 1. Among the pious and holy men of the monastery of Reichenau, whom I commemorated in the latter half of the third century in connection with the Life of Saint Pirmin, Saint Meginrad or Meginratus holds a foremost place. Some call him Meinrad; others, corruptly, Meinard, Meinrard, or Meinhard. He was first a monk on the island of Reichenau, then a hermit in the Black Forest near Lake Zurich, and finally was called a martyr according to the custom of those times. For, as I have observed elsewhere, the practice then prevailed that anyone who ended life by a bloody death was called and venerated as a martyr, provided he had otherwise been upright in character and life. The cause of Meginrad’s death is not sufficiently clear. It appears to have been nothing other than the savage cruelty or greed of two assassins, to whom the holy man’s life, and perhaps also his rebuke, [Col. 1175D] was burdensome. His Life was written by an anonymous author, whom Christopher Hartmann, a learned monk of Einsiedeln, judged to be Bern. I too accept Hartmann’s conjecture, if he means Bern, abbot of Reichenau. What moves me to think it should be assigned rather to Abbot Bern than to Benno, the second inhabitant of Saint Meginrad’s cell (to whom Bollandus attributes that composition), is that under Abbot Bern, who governed Reichenau from 1008 for forty years, Saint Meginrad’s body was raised from the tomb and by this rite enrolled among the saints by the authority of Pope Benedict IX, as Hartmann writes. I therefore suppose that on this occasion Bern committed the holy hermit’s deeds to writing, in order to make his sanctity known to the pope and others. Surius first published this Life of Saint Meginrad with slightly altered wording; then Hartmann in his excellent *Annals of the Hermitage of Blessed Mary*; and finally John Bollandus in his January volume with commentaries.

2. Meginrad’s commemoration was inserted in the sacred calendars of the Roman and Benedictine Martyrologies and other more recent ones on 21 January. But in the Benedictine Martyrology this deserves notice: that Meginrad the hermit is commemorated on the said day, and Megimad, abbot of Einsiedeln, on 17 February; and that our Menard, in book II of his *Observations*, calls Megimad the founder of the monastery of Einsiedeln, saying that he flourished about the year 860, as Miraeus teaches in the *Benedictine Chronicle*. For Meginrad the hermit and the man who gave rise to the monastery of Einsiedeln were one and the same; Miraeus corruptly calls him Megimad.

3. The monastery of Einsiedeln was founded in the place where Saint Meginrad lived as a solitary. That place remained without inhabitant or cultivation for at least forty-four years after Meginrad’s death, until Saint Benno, a canon of Strasbourg, withdrew there and repaired the little chapel, which had collapsed through neglect and rainwater. Then Saint Eberhard, likewise formerly provost at Strasbourg and now a hermit, added a monastery, becoming the first abbot of the place; and he enclosed in a larger basilica the chapel of Blessed Mary, first founded by Meginrad and restored by Benno. Saint Gregory succeeded as the second abbot; he is said to have been descended from the royal stock of the English, and through his efforts the monastery’s resources increased no less than its esteem and [Col. 1177A] renown. Meginrad’s body, which had been buried at Reichenau, was brought back there, at least for the greater part, in 1039, according to Hermann the Lame, monk of Reichenau, whose words are: “The church of Saint Meginrad’s cell is dedicated on 13 October; the relics, the body of Saint Meginrad.” This is the reading of the Canisian edition. I think it should be read: “and the body of Saint Meginrad was translated into it.” But perhaps, because not the whole body but only a part was translated there, the monks of Reichenau substituted *relics* in the manner of a gloss, lest they should seem to be deprived of any part of it. From the time of Saint Meginrad it was called [Col. 1178A] Saint Meginrad’s Cell, or Meginrad’s Cell; then the church of Saint Mary in Saint Meginrad’s Cell; and the monastery in the Black Forest, sometimes Eberhard’s Cell, after Eberhard the second hermit; finally, the monastery of the Hermitage or of the Hermits, in German Einsiedeln, and the monastery of Blessed Mary in the Hermitage, because of devotion to the Mother of God, which is continually frequented there by pilgrims. The monastery is situated in the diocese of Constance, between Lakes Zurich and Lucerne, on a high mountain clothed on every side with forest.

THE AUTHOR’S PROLOGUE

[Col. 1177]

[Col. 1177B] 1. Being about to relate the passion and death of the venerable man Meginrad, hermit and martyr, I wish briefly to turn my pen back and to set forth beforehand, in brief, at what time he was educated, where and by whom, to what place or to whose care he was first entrusted for learning letters, under what abbot he undertook to observe the monastic life, and how he also left the brotherly battle-line for the single combat of the hermitage. I shall therefore return to deal with each of the matters I have proposed.

THE LIFE BEGINS.

[Col. 1177]

[Col. 1177B] 2. In the time of Charles, the most glorious emperor of the Franks, who was the first among them to receive the name of Caesar, the aforesaid man was born in Alamannia, in [Col. 1177C] the district which antiquity called Sulichgewe after the village.

[Note: [Col. 1177D] Today Sulgovia, commonly Sulgen, by others Sulgaw, near the Danube.]

His parents were Alamanni, distinguished more by nobility of character than by perishable wealth.

[Note: [Col. 1177D] Hartmann calls his father Berthold, count of Sulgovia.]

When he had reached the age at which he could be fitted for literary studies, his father took him to the island which the ancients called Sindlochesau, after the name of a certain priest.

[Note: [Col. 1177D] Rather, a count, who gave the place to Saint Pirmin in the time of Charles Tudites, father of King Pippin. Read the Life of Saint Pirmin in Century III.]

This Sindloch first built monks’ dwellings there and, by command of Berchtold, the most noble duke of the Alamanni, brought Pirmin and his companions there to live, in the time of Pippin, king of the Franks; and he gave the island its name from his own. The aforesaid boy, then, was brought there by his father and entrusted to Erlebald, a monk of every excellence of character.

[Note: [Col. 1178D] Hermann the Lame: “In the year 822, when Hatto, abbot and bishop of Reichenau, adopted a private and quiet life, Erlebald, the thirteenth abbot, presided for thirteen years.” See Walafrid Strabo’s poem on Wettin.]

Erlebald was also related to the aforesaid boy by blood. [Col. 1177D] Seeing that the little child was of good disposition, he gladly undertook to rear him, taught him diligently, and advanced so far in instructing him that he imparted knowledge of the Holy Scriptures. For from earliest childhood the boy avoided the games and errors in which tender age is accustomed to become entangled, and applied his mind to receiving the things his teacher taught.

3. When he reached his twenty-fifth year, through the agency of this same teacher he was raised to the office of deacon and, not long afterward, to the rank of priest. At that time, while Louis Caesar, son of Charles, reigned, an abbot named Hatto was on that island, a man very eminent in learning, good works, and nobility of character; he was also bishop of the [Col. 1178B] church of Basel. Rejecting the business of the active life and transferring himself to the beauty of the contemplative life [Col. 1178C], the aforesaid Erlebald was chosen by all with Louis Caesar’s permission and placed over the said island and brethren, being appointed to the office of abbot. As soon as he had received this authority, he urged the often-mentioned venerable man Meginrad to take up the yoke and undertake the rule of monastic life to be observed. He accepted this wholesome counsel and made the promise; with all earnestness he labored to keep what he had promised—ever ready to obey, strict in fasting, constant in prayer, generous in works of mercy, and above all humbled beneath everyone.

4. While he flourished in these virtues, the aforesaid abbot sent him to a certain cell belonging to the monastery already mentioned, situated beside Lake Zurich, through which the river Limmat flows, so that he might preside there over a school and distribute among many, for the Lord’s gain, the talent with which he himself had been endowed.

[Note: [Col. 1178D] Hartmann calls it Bollingen and places it on the right shore of Lake Zurich, above the village of Jona.]

Some time passed while he was occupied in these duties. One day he took with him the pupils he had trained and, crossing the said lake by boat, entered the wilderness adjoining the lake’s shore and extending as far as the Pennine Alps and the village of Cham, for fishing and to examine the places of the wilderness. They came, therefore, to a river flowing through that solitude, and there the blessed man occupied his companions in fishing, while he himself walked alone, contemplating the solitude; for he was exceedingly inflamed with love of a solitary dwelling. After feeding his mind for a long time on this contemplation, he returned to his [Col. 1179A] companions and found them laden with no small catch of fish. He addressed them thus: “Thanks to the Giver, who has mercifully enriched us with His gifts. Now, sons, if it please you, we should return to visit our own homes.” They returned and came to a village situated not far from the shore.

[Note: [Col. 1179D] Namely Altendorf, at the foot of Mount Etzel, according to Hartmann.]

5. Entering the lodging of a certain matron there, they rested a little and refreshed themselves with food and drink. Seeing that the aforesaid matron was full of the fear of God and very ready to serve guests, the man of God disclosed to her the hidden ardor of his mind, beginning with these words: “Woman dear to Christ, if you were willing to listen, I would reveal to you the secret of my heart. But before I do this, I ask that you conceal my words and intention until you see whether what I believe I have conceived with a devout mind can be fulfilled in deed. I delight in dwelling in this wilderness beyond all riches, and I would now place my little dwelling in it, so that I might devote myself more intimately to prayers, if I could find someone willing for love of God to supply my bodily necessities. But because I am still deprived of this comfort, for the present I ask that what I desire be concealed.” Inspired by God, as I believe, she replied: “I shall reveal your secret to no one against your will; but know that, if you wish to persevere in what you have begun, I shall supply you with necessities for the Lord’s sake and satisfy your desire as far as I can.”

6. Giving thanks in return for her promises, he went back to the cell from which he had departed, and everywhere, through continual fasts and prayers [Col. 1179C], asked God to deign to confirm in his heart whatever pleased Him concerning this undertaking. Finally strengthened by divine inspiration, he left the cell and the school over which he presided, and revisited his hostess, wishing to discover whether or not she was willing to remain firm in her promise. When he found that she had persisted in supplying the promised assistance, he constructed a dwelling for himself in the wilderness not far from that village in which the same woman lived, and there, tireless in fasts and prayers, served the Creator; the aforesaid matron, and other devout men as well, supplied his necessities.

[Note: [Col. 1179D] There is still there a chapel of Saint Meginrad, called “in Etzel.” Hartmann dates this withdrawal to 832. I prefer 828, provided that he died in 860; for he lived seven years in the wilderness of Etzel and twenty-six years in the Black Forest.]

7. Having there performed the service of the heavenly King for seven years, and unable to bear the multitude of people coming to him, he changed his place. Four miles from the shore of the aforesaid [Col. 1179D] lake he found a plain among the mountains, very difficult of access.

[Note: [Col. 1180D] Hartmann relates from Reichenau records that he carried with him from the cell at Etzel the Rule of Saint Benedict, Cassian’s writings, a Missal, and a book of Homilies.]

There, aided by devout men and especially by an abbess named Heilwiga, he built the dwellings necessary for his purpose and remained in that place for the rest of his life, afflicting himself with severe fasts and praying without interruption so far as human frailty allowed. Everything that faithful [Col. 1180A] men and women sent him he distributed as alms to those who came to him.

[Note: [Col. 1180D] Hartmann understands this as Hildegard, daughter of King Louis the German, for whom her father was then building at Zurich the monastery called Fraumünster.]

8. It happened meanwhile that one day, while he was praying, so great a multitude of demons spread themselves about him on every side that, as these ministers of darkness obscured it, he could not even see the light of day itself. As they wearied him with terrible threats and extreme terror, he lay prostrate in prayer and, as the situation required, commended himself with all earnestness to the merciful Lord. When this had continued for a long time, he saw a light from the East. An angel followed that light and came to him where he lay praying amid the evil spirits; with great authority the angel commanded the wicked host to depart and no longer dare to inflict upon him any temptation or terror. When the enemies had departed [Col. 1180B], the aforesaid angel comforted him kindly and departed; from that day, as the venerable man related, he suffered no further terror from evil spirits.

9. It happened afterward that a certain brother from the aforesaid monastery came to visit him. He received him kindly and showed him, together with the companions who had come with him, all the hospitality due to guests, as far as means permitted. When evening had come and the shining stars invited sleep, they refreshed themselves with pleasant conversation, and after Compline went to sleep: the visiting brother in a separate place, his companions apart as well, and the venerable man himself in a private little dwelling. After briefly refreshing his body with sleep [Col. 1180C], the man of God rose and devoted himself, wakeful, to his customary prayers. The aforesaid brother too, although resting in bed, spent almost a sleepless night. As he curiously turned his eyes this way and that, he saw a boy in white garments coming forth from the place of the oratory, of marvelous beauty, as it seemed to him, and seven years old. The boy went in to the man of God and prayed with him as he prayed, and spoke various things with him. Though the aforesaid brother heard the sound of their conversation, he did not understand its meaning. The boy also stood beside the brother, who was fully awake, and warned him concerning certain matters which the brother said had altogether been forbidden him to disclose publicly. I pass over many things, seeking brevity, which the reliable testimony of very many people shows to be wondrous concerning him. [Col. 1180D]

## 10

When, therefore, he had spent his twenty-sixth year in that very wilderness, serving the Lord in fasts and abstinence from all worldly things, it happened that—at the instigation of him who entered into the serpent, deceived our first parents through its mouth, and drove them from paradise—two men hastened to his cell with the intention of killing him. When they had come to a certain village situated on the shore of Lake Zurich, they asked to be shown which route was passable for approaching his cell.

[Note: Namely, Endigen, where afterward the town of Rapperswil was built, together with its castle, as Bollandus notes from the German Life.]

Once the route had been shown to them, they rose early during the night and set out along the path indicated to them, driven on by the most dreadful spirit that had filled them. For a long time, however, they were led astray from the straight path that went to the cell itself; at last, after being tormented by the demon, they reached the place they sought, when most of the day had already passed.

### 11

Meanwhile, he himself, intent upon his customary prayers, was devoutly offering the solemn celebration of Mass to the Creator. Before the wicked men entered the cell itself—one of them was called Richard and was an Alemannian by birth, while the other was Peter, born of the Rhaetian people—the chickens that the venerable man had raised in that place, seeing them approaching nearby, fled through the wilderness as though pursued by a fox. Their unusual cries and unheard-of commotion filled the forest with echoing noise, so that even the robbers greatly wondered and were astonished at this, judging by their own reasoning that the event must belong to the realm of prodigy.

### 12

Nevertheless, they were not diverted from what they had begun. They approached the chapel in which, as has been said, the man of God was pleasing the Lord with abundant prayers, and, as one who knew the future, had received the Lord’s Body with a pure heart and devoted mind as provision for his death.

When the man of God perceived that his killers had arrived, he did not immediately present himself to them. Instead, delaying for a little while longer, he did not open the closed door of the chapel, so that he might remain somewhat longer in prayer. Thus he completed his prayer with vigor, and, taking each reliquary into his hands and kissing it, commended his struggle to the Lord and to the saints whose relics he reverently embraced.

The wicked men who had come watched him doing this through a certain opening in the wall. Then the strong athlete, strengthened by God, came out to fight and did not deny his presence to his killers. First he addressed them with words of greeting, and then added:

“Friends, why have you come so late? Why did you not hasten to come to hear the Mass of my littleness, so that I might pray to the common Lord on your behalf? But enter even now, to ask that the Lord and his saints may be favorably disposed toward us; afterward return to me, so that I may give you whatever blessing God may enable me to offer you for his love. In this way complete the work for which you have come.”

They therefore entered the oratory, not intent upon what they had been urged to do, but upon committing the evil for which they had come; and immediately they returned to him. The man of God gave them his tunic and cowl, and added bread and drink, saying:

“Receive these things from my hands. After you have completed what you came to do, you may yourselves take whatever you wish of the things that are here. For I know that you entered to kill me. But I ask one favor of you: when you have brought the course of my present life to an end, place one of the candles that you see—and which I fashioned for this very purpose—burning at my head, and the other at my feet. Then leave this place quickly, lest those who come afterward, as they customarily visit me, seize you and you suffer the punishment for your crime.”

### 13

Immediately the aforementioned Richard, with polluted hands, seized the blessed man around the middle and tightly clasped his emaciated little body in his arms, then menacingly ordered his companion to strike the saint with a staff. When the latter had weakened him by striking him for a long time around the side and the calves, while the saint extended his hands toward the Lord, the other said:

“Sluggish man! Why do you not strike him on the head, so that he may receive a mortal blow? If you delay inflicting it, I shall deliver it most swiftly.”

At once he seized the staff and swung a very powerful blow at his head. Struck in this way, the holy man fell half alive to the ground; and they immediately rushed upon him and strangled his throat with their hands until he breathed out his spirit.

As his soul was departing, at the very moment of his final breath, an odor of such sweetness spread forth and filled the entire cell, as though the fragrances of every kind of perfume had been poured out there.

### 14

Afterward they stripped him of the garment in which he was clothed, carried him, and placed him on the bed where the man of God was accustomed to rest. Beneath the naked body they placed a felt covering, and also laid down certain fragments.

[Note: That is, they placed it over him; this meaning is also occasionally found in other authors of the Middle Ages. In Ekkehard the Younger, chapter 1, it is said that Grimald placed a cross covered with gilded silver upon the nocturnal lectern—apud Goldastum, p. 38—or is this perhaps a scribal error?]

[Note: Goldastus, in his notes on chapter 5 of Ekkehard, interprets *filtra* as threads or cords, citing the *Catholicon* of Balbi. More correctly, the distinguished Carolus Fresnius says in his *Glossary* that *feltrum* or *filtrum* is compressed wool, commonly called felt. Bernard, Prior of the Gates, in his letter to the Recluse, counts *filtrum* among the furnishings of a bed.]

They also took the candles, as the man of God had requested while still alive. They placed one at his head, while others hurried to the chapel to bring back the light that burned continually in that oratory. When they returned to the little body of the deceased, they found the candle that they had placed there, though extinguished, burning brightly.

A great fear immediately seized them, so that they did not dare touch anything belonging to the service of the altar. Taking some of his garments and certain bedclothes, they hurried back to the place from which they had come.

### 15

As they fled from there, the ravens that customarily used to come to the servant of God while he was alive and receive food from his hands followed the robbers, as though wishing to avenge the man who had been killed. With loud cries they filled the forests, and, flying as close as they could to the men’s heads, exposed the crime that had been committed.

Not long afterward the wicked men themselves were captured, and the crime they had secretly committed was brought to light, since God did not wish the punishment they had deserved for the killing of his servant to be delayed. For when the judges and the Christian people under Count Adalbert had decreed this, they were burned alive.

[Note: I think this was Adalbert, whom King Louis of Germany is said to have defeated in Rhaetia in the year 841, according to Hermannus Contractus. Hepidannus speaks of another Adalbert in these words: “In the year 906 Adalbert, the glory of the Franks, was killed.”]

### 16

The candle that they had placed at the head of the man of God, and which had been lit from heaven, continued burning until it reached the straw that had been placed over the little dead body. The fire also seized part of the straw and reached the limbs of the deceased. When it touched them, just as it had been kindled by divine power, so by God’s command it was extinguished.

Immediately the news of his death was spread. When the venerable abbot Waltherus learned of it, he and the brothers living under his authority removed the body of the man of God from the wilderness and carried it to the monastery of Augia, where they buried it with due honor.

[Note: Waltherus succeeded Folcwinus as abbot of Augia in the year 848 and died in 864, according to Hermannus.]

The holy martyr suffered on the twelfth day before the Kalends of February, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 863, while Louis was reigning over the East Franks, in the twenty-eighth year of his reign.

[Note: Hermannus Contractus and Trithemius assign Meginrad’s death to the year 860; Hepidannus, a monk of Saint Gall, and Marianus Scotus assign it to the following year. The reasoning of both sides is the same. Since Meginrad was killed in January, those who reckoned the beginning of the year from March or Easter counted it as the year 860; those who reckoned from January counted it as 861. I therefore prefer to follow the authority of those writers who had read this Life—as is highly probable—for perhaps the numerals had once been written differently in it. Surius, moreover, seems to have read the year 860.

“In the year 1039,” writes Hartmannus in chapter 6 concerning Abbot Embrico, “on the day before the Nones of October, the relics of Saint Meginrad were returned to the people of Einsiedeln. At that same time Pope Benedict IX had enrolled among the saints him whom many miracles had already made famous.”
