In the year 1599 the name of Saint Meginrad was inserted into the new Breviary of the Church of Constance, together with an appointed office, as is customary for martyrs, in the double rite; but it was assigned to 23 January because of the feast of Saint Agnes, which is celebrated on the 21st, as Bollandus observed.]

---

# LIFE OF SAINT UDALRIC, BISHOP OF AUGUSTA  
### By Berno, Abbot of Augia

## Berno’s Prologue

### 1

To the most reverend Father Frideboldus, and true foster-son of the holy mother Afra, Berno (alternatively, Bern), servant of the Mother of God, together with the entire fellowship of the brothers of Augia, sends the highest and unfailing good.

The remarkable power of charity, flowing from the sweet fountain of your heart, imposed upon my littleness this duty: that I should make lucid, by a more polished style, a little book concerning the life of our thrice-and-four-times blessed patron Udalric, which had been composed in a truthful but simpler manner than was fitting. The pious intention of the one who commands is indeed present, but the fulfillment of the command will not be equally easy, since slowness of understanding and the cares of external affairs, seasoned—as one may say—with a bitter flavor, prevent me from undertaking so arduous a work.

There is also the fact that Gebehardus, of venerable memory, who was the fourth after the blessed man to govern the Church of Augusta Vindelica, second to none among the learned men of our time, undertook the same task out of a desire to correct it, but, forestalled by death, left it unfinished. If he himself had put the final hand to the work, my littleness would have placed a finger upon its mouth altogether in this matter.

What he composed, although it breathes the beauty of eloquence, raises itself so high through the sublimity of its words and sentences that scarcely anyone can understand anything from it. The other work, on the contrary, although supported by the truth of its subject matter, seems almost to lie upon the ground, so that anyone among the wise who has once been able to taste something from it will be reluctant to incline himself to it again.

Therefore, reverend Father, it has pleased you and your people to impose this burden upon me, so that, walking midway between the two, I may compose the material in a moderate style. Then those who come to it from either side may find, upon the middle ground spread with charity, both milk for the little ones to suck and food for the strong to eat.

I would shrink from this in every way if I did not know that it is written: “Obedience is better than sacrifice” (Ecclesiastes 4:17). But now, if you promise, by extending the hand of your intercession, to guide my hand, I shall attempt to obey, relying upon the merits of the blessed man joined with yours, and upon the help of the omnipotent Word, who opened the mouths of the mute and made the tongues of infants eloquent.

I shall begin the narrative with the infancy of that man of God and carry the course of my discourse through to the end, adding nothing of my own except examples from the ancient Fathers and sayings of the sacred Scriptures, which customarily adorn the sequence of words with their own beauty.

This alone I have imposed upon myself from my own labor: to restrain more closely, with modest brevity, what has been spread more broadly; to expand, with measured length, what has been arranged too compactly; and to correct what has been expressed less regularly along the line of rectitude. All these matters, however, await the judgment of your scrutiny, so that under your kindly judgment they may be able to stand as approved.

I wish, most blessed Father, that you may prosper in Christ and always remember me.

[Note: In the Cologne manuscript, forty-two chapters follow at this point. We possess an accurate copy through the generosity of the religious man Wuillelmus Vulfratus, formerly prior at Saint Pantaleon.]

# The Life Begins

## Chapter I

The distinguished confessor of Christ, Udalric, was descended from the lineage of the Alamanni. His parents, namely Hupaldus and Teotbirga, were both illustrious and noble according to the dignity of this world, but far more illustrious and noble in faith and divine religion.

When God had enriched them with the fertility of such a great and excellent offspring, they immediately entrusted the child to a faithful nurse for rearing, as Moses had been entrusted. Even amid the earliest beginnings of his birth, heavenly signs were not lacking. For although he was nourished with tender affection, a certain unsightly emaciation nevertheless appeared in his face.

For this reason his parents became exceedingly sad, and great anxieties revolved in their troubled hearts. A certain foreign guest, a cleric by office, was kindly received by them—as their door was always open to the traveler—and was treated humanely for some time. Then one day, while he was sitting at the hour of refreshment, he heard the aforementioned infant, who had not yet fully completed twelve weeks from his birth, uttering a sound amid his wailing.

Being perceptive of future events, he delivered this oracle:

“Unless this infant is weaned more quickly,” he said, “he will not be able to survive.”

Although they were warned once and then a second time, they were reluctant to carry out the words of so great a herald. Finally, on the third day, when he had perceived through the ear that the aforementioned infant—who still had to be mentioned again—was even weaker, he uttered this prophetic declaration before everyone:

“Know for certain that, unless he is immediately withdrawn from the milk, he will die this very night. But if he is rescued from death in the manner I have prescribed, he will one day be great before the Lord.”

How the mysteries of this prophecy were to be fulfilled does not require the labor of our pen to explain; it can be demonstrated.

## Chapter II

At last, once he had been removed from the milk, he began to advance in body and soul so greatly, to the admiration of all and to the joy of all who lived around him, that what is written about Isaac and his father Abraham may not inappropriately be applied to him as well:

“And the child grew, and was weaned; and Abraham made a great feast on the day of his weaning.”

Rightly did that great patriarch make a great feast at the weaning of his son, whom he had received from God by promise. Rightly did the heavenly Father make a great feast for the children of holy mother Church at the weaning of this child, inviting them in these words:

“Eat, friends, and drink deeply, beloved ones.”

This child, then, destined to become a steward of God’s mysteries, already needed to be strengthened with solid food, so that, one day standing at the table of Christ’s altar as at a heavenly banquet, he might in due season give the measure of wheat to his fellow servants.

He was already beginning to conduct himself modestly among his peers, to possess the fear of God, to show honor to his parents, and to avoid wantonness. As far as was possible at such an age, he was already revealing outwardly—in the movement of his body, his gestures, and his manner of walking—the kind of character being formed inwardly in his mind.

When his parents saw such a great grace of God shining in him, they entrusted him to the religious brothers of the monastery of Saint Gall, so that under their instruction he might be trained both in the studies of secular letters and in heavenly disciplines. There, among outstanding teachers of regular discipline, he daily tasted the sweet fruits of contemplation, turning into deeds at once the words he read in the sacred books.

He was already touching the summit of that ladder of Jacob by ascending the steps of the virtues. He was already hearing from the Savior:

“Go, sell all that you have and give to the poor, and come, follow me.”

And he would already have assumed the habit of monastic life, had he not been admonished by divine revelation and desisted.

## Chapter III

At that time there was in the same monastery a certain handmaid, enclosed for the sake of Christ, named Vuiberata. Devoting herself day and night to fasts, prayers, and vigils, she prepared in the secret chamber of her heart a chaste temple for the Lord, in which she continually offered a pleasing holocaust to the Creator of all, saying with the Psalmist:

“In me are your vows, O God, which I shall repay with praises to you.”

When the holy youth disclosed to her the secret of his desire, she resolved to seek the matter from God and requested a delay of three days for this purpose. After the three days, instructed by the divine Spirit, she gave this answer:

“No, religious man,” she said, “it is not the will of God that you remain in this place. Rather, there is a region in the East where a certain river divides two territories, and there, by God’s command, you must ascend to the height of episcopal dignity.

“Although you will suffer many adversities from pagans as well as from bad Christians, nevertheless, trusting in him who said, ‘Take courage; I have overcome the world,’ you will overcome everything, saying with the Psalmist:

‘Through God we shall act bravely, and he himself will bring our enemies to nothing.’”

Hearing and pondering these words, he secretly revealed them to certain men who clung to him more closely out of friendship, and he urged them to keep silent about them for the time being.

He himself, meanwhile, like the most prudent of bees, gathering flowers of meaning through the various fields of the sacred books and storing them in the hive of his heart, began to strive with all his strength to prepare spiritual honey, which later it would befit him to pour forth among the peoples, according to the Psalmist’s saying:

“How sweet are your words to my throat, more than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth!”

And as it is said of preachers:

“They shall pour forth the memory of the abundance of your sweetness.”

Thereafter, fully trained, he returned to his home with the goodwill of all the brothers.

His parents, rejoicing greatly in his progress and giving thanks to God, again entrusted him to Adalbero, the venerable bishop of the Church of Augusta, a man preferable to many in the gift of faith and the merit of his life. They did so so that, constantly attending upon his revered presence, he might see in him, as in a mirror of discipline, whether anything still needed to be corrected in his conduct.

When the aforementioned bishop of God recognized him as firm in faith, strong in hope, rooted and grounded in charity, and adorned with every moral excellence, he admitted him to closer intimacy and began to use him as a counselor in everything, both at home and abroad, so that his prudence might arrange the affairs of the entire bishopric, public as well as private.

## Chapter IV

Meanwhile, it pleased the mind of the man of God to journey to Rome and visit the thresholds of the apostles, so that he might commend himself and all that belonged to him more earnestly to their prayers and to those of the other saints.

When he arrived there, he was courteously received by the bishop of the apostolic see, named Marinus, a man magnificent and glorious before God and human beings. When Marinus asked who he was and from where he had come, he replied that he had been born of the stock of the Alamanni and was a cleric of Adalbero, bishop of the Church of Augusta.

Then the Apostolic said:

“Do not take what I say harshly, for the same man of whom you have spoken, your bishop Adalbero, has already departed from this world. By the working of God’s ordinance, it is necessary that you undertake the care of this government.”

But he, conscious of his own weakness—and indeed mindful of the command, “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things”—judged himself unworthy to bear the burden of so great an honor.

Then the pope, filled with the divine Spirit, said:

“If you now evade this by hiding yourself, so that you will not steer the ship of the Church in this time of peace and tranquility, a day will come when you will be unable in any way to pass by the decrees of God. Rather, amid the many waves of arduous labor, sorrow, and anxiety, you will be compelled to undertake its governance and, with God as your guide, bring it to the shore of peaceful rest, as one who is exceedingly weary.”

After hearing this, he went to his lodging and, amid sacred offerings of prayer, commended both himself and the soul of his deceased master to God and his holy apostles with tears.

Thus, on the following day, without the pope’s knowledge, he secretly departed, following in this also the example of the Lord’s action of which Saint John the Evangelist relates that, when they wished to seize him and make him king, he immediately fled.

But as soon as Adalbero of blessed memory had departed this life, Hiltinus succeeded him in the episcopate. When Hiltinus, after fifteen years, had been taken from this light, the Lord willed to fulfill what had previously been foretold about his servant Udalric through the mouths of his faithful. With the entire clergy and people joining together in one vote, and King Henry’s will agreeing to the same, that holy man of God was elevated to the episcopal throne in this city.

## Chapter V

After he had obtained the honor of so great a dignity, no discourse will be able fully to explain what sort of man he was or how great.

He was wholly devoted to prayer, wholly devoted to reading, and especially attentive to the virtues by which the Apostle described a bishop as being blameless, as God’s steward: not arrogant, not irritable, not addicted to wine, not violent, not greedy for dishonest gain, but hospitable, kind, sober, just, holy, self-controlled, holding fast to the faithful word that accords with the teaching, so that he might be able to exhort in sound doctrine and refute those who contradicted it.

He practiced these two virtues in such alternating succession that, unless some unavoidable necessity intervened, he allowed no time to pass idle without applying himself either to prayer or to reading. Thus he almost always enjoyed the desired embraces of Rachel, unless the intervention of Leah temporarily drew him away from the sweetness of such diligence.

He was greatly concerned with repairing the walls of the church and rebuilding the houses and the buildings of the city itself, which in the time of his predecessors had either fallen into ruin through excessive age or been consumed by fire.

Moreover, the greater part of the household had been killed by pagans, and the portion that remained was suffering greatly from poverty. Amid these circumstances, the venerable hero, as one with eyes before and behind, began to look around with careful attention of mind and to exercise provident care for all things.

Using wise counsel, he placed prudent and suitable masters in charge of the material buildings. But he himself, like a wise architect, laid Christ as the foundation with the Apostle, building upon it gold, silver, precious stones, and other such things, so that the building of holy souls, constructed through his preaching, might grow into a holy temple for the Lord.

To all whom he prepared for such a building through word and example, he also continued to provide the other services of humanity, as their resources allowed—not only extending the hand of mercy to those who were present, but also ministering to those who were far away, prevented by illness or confined in prisons.

## Chapter VI

He was therefore miserly toward no one but generous toward all, so that he could say with blessed Job:

“The blessing of the perishing came upon me, and I comforted the heart of the widow.”

And shortly afterward:

“I was eyes to the blind and feet to the lame; I was a father to the poor.”

And again:

“I wept once over the one who was afflicted, and my soul had compassion on the poor.”

Accordingly, at the daily meal, a dear crowd of poor people was always present at his table. He fed them with food and clothed them with garments.

He chastised himself with excessive austerity, so that he did not eat meat and wore a woolen garment next to his bare skin, proclaiming through his conduct the Apostle’s words:

“I chastise my body and bring it into servitude, lest, after preaching to others, I myself should be rejected.”

At night he remained wakeful in prayer and sacrificed himself upon the altar of his heart through his devotion to prayer. By day he offered to the Lord upon the visible altar a saving sacrifice, so that his offering might be pleasing and acceptable to the Redeemer of all.

By day he served the Lord with Martha in the Lord’s members; by night he sat with Mary beside the feet of Jesus and listened to his word, knowing what is written:

“Those who draw near to his feet shall receive his teaching.”

It was his solemn custom, after Compline, to take no food or drink and to cultivate silence. For he knew that the Lord had said:

“By your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned.”

Therefore he continually asked of the Lord:

“Set, O Lord, a guard over my mouth, and a door of restraint around my lips.”

But whenever it was necessary for him to speak, his speech was seasoned with the salt of wisdom, modest, humble, and useful for persuasion. As a certain Wise Man says: “Weight in speech, and measure in words.”

When his limbs, wearied in God’s service, required some rest and refreshment, he did not indulge himself in the softness of feathers, but allowed himself a little sleep upon a mat, a carpet, or a blanket laid beneath him.

To summarize briefly, he carried out the external office of a priest in such a way that inwardly he did not neglect the discipline of monastic life.

He also practiced measured moderation in food and a certain distinctive form of abstinence by which he used religious ingenuity to outwit those who dined with him. Very often, when they hoped that he would eat with them, he would rise from the table after the removal of the meat dishes and go to the church, where he celebrated the solemnities of Mass.

Thus it is still reported by many, as though it had happened in recent memory, that one day the venerable Father was seated at lunch with Conrad, bishop of the Church of Constance of blessed memory, at the shrine of Saint Afra the martyr. After both men had finished their meal and departed, a matter arose that required the aforementioned bishop to send a messenger to the man of God.

When the bishop’s messenger arrived, he found him standing at the holy altar and offering the saving sacrifice to the Lord. When this was completed, he heard the message and allowed the messenger to return to his master.

When the messenger returned and was asked why he had been delayed so long, he replied that he had waited for the man of God until he had celebrated the solemnities of Mass three times.

The bishop seized upon that very word and said:

“He celebrated the solemnities of Mass?”

Then, as if smiling, he added:

“And truly no one more satiated than he approached the table of the altar today.”

Whether he said this in jest or in earnest, what he said was nevertheless true. The Lord had fed him with the bread of life and understanding and given him to drink of the water of saving wisdom, so that he could rightly proclaim with the Psalmist:

“My heart has poured forth a good word.”

And again:

“And your intoxicating cup, how excellent it is!”

The voice of psalmody resounded so continuously and sweetly in his mouth that not only he himself, but also those who were accustomed to sing it with him with pure intention of mind, conceived from it such purity of heart that through divine revelation they came to know certain hidden things, which they then made known to others.

For this reason I shall set down below, by way of example, certain instances, so that the truth of what I say may be confirmed.

## Chapter VII

At one time, when the craftsmen wished to repair the crypt of the church for the better, there was a certain cleric named Rambertus who was devoted to the service of the holy man.

One day, falling into an ecstasy of mind, he seemed to himself to be singing psalms in the customary manner with his lord the bishop. He also seemed to see Adalbero, the former bishop whom we mentioned above, standing nearby on the northern side of the same crypt, dressed in sacerdotal vestments and signaling to him to come to him.

Struck in mind and uncertain and hesitant between life and death about what he should do, he finally fixed his frightened gaze upon the living bishop, as though asking what he should do.

Then the bishop said:

“Why are you staring at me in this way?”

He replied:

“Behold, my lord Bishop Adalbero stands ready to celebrate the divine mystery and calls me to him.”

The bishop said to him:

“Hasten to go and obey all his commands.”

As soon as Rambertus had approached more closely, he heard Adalbero say:

“Rambertus, tell your lord that he will receive a great reward from the Lord for the prayers and almsgiving that he has faithfully offered on my behalf.

“Let this also be a sign for him: I and Fortunatus, if God permits, will sanctify the holy chrism with him at the coming Lord’s Supper.

“Moreover, the construction of this crypt will collapse very soon. But for this reason he must not desist from the work he has begun; rather, he should strive to secure it upon firmer foundations.

“Take care also to warn the brothers that the prayers they voluntarily promised to make for me have by no means been fulfilled as they promised. Unless they take care to correct this, let them know that they will have to render an account of it before the Lord.”

When the bishop returned from the royal city—for at that time he was residing there—he found that what had happened to the crypt was exactly as it had been shown to Rambertus in the vision.

Then the bishop, impatient of delay, did not cease from his labor until he had restored everything to a better condition.

On another occasion, when the aforementioned Rambertus was singing psalms in the customary way with the holy man in the town of Währingen, he began to be shaken by great terror. Turning his eyes aside, he saw the bishop who was worthy of God.

When the bishop asked him what was wrong, he replied that he saw his former master Adalbero, prepared just as before, commanding him to assist him as he celebrated the mystery of the sacred altar and to perform the service of his customary ministry.

The prophecy was truly fulfilled which says:

“With the holy man you will be holy, and with the innocent man you will be innocent.”

## Chapter VIII

I do not think it should be passed over how the Lord also wished to glorify him through a vision of a heavenly sign.

On the solemn holy day of Easter, while a great crowd of brothers stood present and the holy priest was celebrating the divine mysteries, a certain heavenly right hand appeared. Together with the bishop’s own right hand, it sanctified the sacraments.

When the solemnities of Mass had been completed, a certain priest named Henry, who had served as cantor that day and had witnessed so great a miracle, followed the bishop as far as his chamber, fell at his feet, and, in the presence of the assembled people, explained the same vision rather imprudently.

The man of God said to him:

“It would be better for you to remain silent than to bring such things to the ears of the common people.”

Immediately Henry, covered with shame, went out and sat in the vestibule of the chamber. He shed such abundant tears that, overcome by their flooding, he was compelled to endure an impairment of his sight.

The man of God, mindful of his own weakness, guarded against human praise, lest he fall into the precipice of pride. He always gave thanks to God for his indescribable gift. And, as it is written of his saints, “They go from strength to strength,” he advanced like a heavenly creature before his own face, so that in mind he might ascend to wherever the impulse of the spirit led him.

Having advanced to higher things by these steps of virtue, on a certain night preceding the holy day which the Christian religion is accustomed to call the day of indulgence, or the Lord’s Supper, a voice spoke to the blessed man in a vision:

“Bishop Udalric, know that you are going to receive guests.”

When he awoke, he began wondering with himself who these future guests might be. That sleep was not the empty slumber that sometimes deceives human minds, but rather the kind of sleep of which the bride says in the Song of Songs:

“I sleep, but my heart is awake.”

While the man of God was enjoying such repose in sleep, he again merited hearing a voice say:

“Udalric, your prayers and almsgiving are acceptable to God. He has commended you to your two predecessors, Fortunatus and Adalbero, so that today and henceforth, while you celebrate the sacred mysteries, they may assist you and bless them with you.”

When morning came, at the hour when the illustrious minister of the mysteries celebrated the divine sacraments, the right hand of the Lord appeared again before certain people who were worthy to see it. Together with the holy bishop, it consecrated the same sacraments by imposing the sign of the cross.

When those same people approached the sacred altar to receive holy Communion, the saint of God knew through the Spirit that they were aware of this secret. Therefore, when he offered the Lord’s bread to each of them, he placed a finger upon the mouth of each, so that they might understand that they must not disclose what they had seen.

Moreover, after the sacred service had been completed, he summoned them to himself and explained the order of the mystery revealed to him during the preceding night. He forbade them, under threat of their present life, to tell anyone either this or what they themselves had seen for as long as he remained in the flesh.

## CHAPTER IX

At another time, when once again, beneath the silence of a certain night [Col. 1192A], he was commending his limbs to rest, Saint Afra the martyr appeared, beautiful of face, splendidly clothed, and girded with a tunic. She said to him, “Rise and follow me.” Immediately she led him out into a field called Lecfelt, after the name of the river flowing there. There he found Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, seated as though in a synodal assembly, together with a great multitude of bishops and other saints—some whom he had once seen in the flesh, and others whom, by divine grace revealing them to him, he then began for the first time to recognize.

Among the other matters under discussion, a cry arose then concerning Duke Arnulf of the Norici, who was still alive, just as in the Apocalypse of Saint John a voice was once heard from the souls seeking vengeance against those who had slain them. The saints cried out because of his destruction of churches [Col. 1192B] and monasteries, whose possessions he distributed as benefices among laymen. Accordingly, by the judgment of all, he was condemned to punishment.

Two swords were also brought forth into their midst: one with a hilt, the other without a hilt. Concerning these, the prince of the apostles said to the blessed man: “Tell King Henry: the sword without a hilt signifies the man who reigns over the people without anointing; the other, the one with a hilt, signifies him who has been divinely crowned through the rite of sacred blessing.”

When the assembly of the saints had ended, the holy martyr of God mentioned above also showed him the places where King Otto later established his camp. There, holding a general conference with his men, he received King Berengar of the Lombards, presented together with many others, under his dominion. She also foretold the savage invasion of the Hungarian people and their most bitter engagement with our countrymen, as well as the places where the battles would occur. Although with great loss to his own people, she nevertheless promised the Christian people the triumph of victory.

O blessed man, worthy of a heavenly vision, and in such matters comparable to the holy apostles Peter and Paul! The one learned through a vision, on a sheet let down from heaven, about the election of the nations; the other asserts that, whether in the body or outside the body, he was caught up to the third heaven, where he heard and saw the hidden things of God. This holy man, too, both in the manifestation of the sacred right hand upon the altar, and in this vision, and afterward in others—as will become sufficiently clear before the end of our account—saw and heard the hidden things of God, and learned not only the salvation of his own [Col. 1192D] people but also that of many nations.

He did not then spread these things indiscriminately among the ears of the common people in empty self-display. Rather, he privately revealed them to a few whom he judged worthy of this knowledge. Yet, recognizing that divine grace had anticipated him to such an extent, he did not exalt himself, but referred everything to the One from whom he had received whatever good he possessed or could possess, saying with the Apostle: “By the grace of God I am what I am.”

## CHAPTER X

He therefore began to care for the flock entrusted to him, not to bury the talent committed to him in the earth, tied up in a cloth, but, as a good steward of the word of God, to put it out at interest. For this reason he frequently inspected the boundaries of his diocese and, summoning clergy and laypeople before him, diligently sought to investigate above all how the priests of the churches themselves lived with their ministers: whether they taught the people rightly and according to Catholic doctrine, and whether they fulfilled in deed what they preached with their mouths, lest perhaps, while preaching to others, they should themselves become reprobate and for this reason be despised by their hearers.

Next he examined whether the laypeople obeyed their teaching, whether on Sundays and the other solemnities of the saints they abstained from unlawful work, whether they devoutly visited the thresholds of the churches as they ought, and whether they paid tithes correctly, along with many matters of this kind. After investigating these things, he praised and confirmed whatever was sound and well ordered; whatever he found otherwise, he corrected and amended.

He warned that the heresy of the simoniacs was to be avoided like a destructive plague, asserting that those who endeavored to incline their minds toward this most wicked heresy would be handed over to everlasting punishment [Col. 1193B]. Accordingly, he never accepted any gift for the ordination of clerics or the consecration of churches. Just as, in the anointing with sacred chrism, he freely gave the Holy Spirit the Paraclete through the laying on of hands, so he granted these things freely as well, knowing the Lord’s command: “You received without payment; give without payment.” Only if the founders of the churches themselves, out of goodwill, asked him to accept something—and this as an expression of gratitude—did he perhaps receive it.

He established that the lawful right of the household of Saint Mary ever-virgin, granted anciently by his predecessors, was to be preserved inviolably. He permitted no one living under his authority to be harmed by the oppression of officials. Rather, he corrected everything among his people with such perceptiveness according to the rule of equity and justice that he allowed no one to inflict upon another what he would not wish done to himself, in accordance with the commandment: “What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another.” And the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whatever you wish that people would do to you, do the same to them.”

## CHAPTER XI

When the envious devil, the enemy of all good, saw the holy man continually ascending through these and similar stages of virtue toward higher things, he began by every means he could to strive to hinder his mind, however little he was able. It happened at that time that, through the instigation [Col. 1193D] of Satan and the persuasion of wicked men, a quarrel and hatred arose between Liudolf, son of the emperor Otto the Great and ruler of the Alamannian people, and his uncle Henry, duke of the Norici. When the emperor was unable to summon them to reconciliation, he supported the brother against the son.

At that time a certain Count Palatine Arnulf appeared, the son of the former Duke Arnulf. The aforesaid Duke Henry had entrusted to his loyalty all Bavaria, together with its metropolis, Regensburg, and had gone to Saxony to the emperor. While he remained there, Arnulf, like a treacherous deserter, placed himself, together with the city and a multitude of its people, under Liudolf’s power.

When these events became known to the holy bishop, he left the soldiers guarding the city of Augsburg and hastened into the region of the Norici, where he heard that the emperor was then stationed with his army. The tyrant mentioned above [Col. 1194A] went to Augsburg, plundered the surrounding possessions, captured some of the bishop’s soldiers, and, laden with booty—or, more truly, weighed down by the burden of sin—returned to Bavaria.

Meanwhile, after learning that the servant of God had returned from royal service, he did not fear to besiege him in the fortress called Montachinga. But his presumption against God’s servant did not prosper. For after a short interval of days, he was compelled to withdraw from the siege by Count Adalbero and the bishop’s brother Thietbald, at the cost of his own men. Covered with the shame he deserved, he returned to his homeland; there, too, his brother Herimann was captured.

The very brave warrior Adalbert, like another Maccabee, also fell in that same [Col. 1194B] battle while fighting fiercely for the Church of God—truly, as we ought to believe, passing through the loss of mortality into the gain of immortality. Saint Udalric carried his body to Augsburg and buried it in the church of Saint Mary ever-virgin; his spirit he commended to the Lord through the sacrificial offering.

## CHAPTER XII

After this, such fear seized the minds of all that no one dared presume to usurp anything belonging to the church of Saint Mary ever-virgin at Augsburg. For none of those who had previously unjustly taken anything from it, or had offended against the holy man of God, escaped unpunished—except those who, through worthy satisfaction and by the mercy of God, obtained absolution through the bishop’s intercession.

To offer a few examples from many, one of them, while his neighbors truthfully testified against him, tore his own hands for so long in a state of deranged mind that he finally died. Another stole a certain book from the city of Augsburg and, from its price, acquired a horse. When he had brought it home, he said to his wife: “It would have been better for me to have bought this horse, so beautiful in appearance, than to have left in Augsburg the book by which I bought it.” She replied: “As I hope, it would have been more useful to you if your hand had never touched that book.”

When he wished to caress the horse with a gentle touch along its hindquarters, as is customary, he was immediately struck by it and died. Not long afterward, the aforementioned Arnulf also felt the anger of the just Judge for the injuries he had inflicted upon the man of God. When the city of Regensburg had been besieged, he went out prepared for battle [Col. 1194D], and there he was killed and died.

A certain man from the bishopric called Eichstätt unjustly seized and carried away with him a piece of a very cheap tablecloth from the possessions mentioned above. But immediately, possessed by a demon, he could find no place, either inside or outside the church, in which to hide. Even when sprinkled with blessed water, he could not rid himself of the demon’s presence; he always seemed to see him remaining beside him as an inseparable companion. At last he returned to Augsburg, restored what he had unjustly taken, and earnestly begged to be corrected.

The bishop, who was wholly filled with the compassion of his inmost heart, both granted him pardon for the love of Christ and, after freeing him from the demon, allowed him to return home.

## CHAPTER XIII

Meanwhile, the conflict that had arisen, as we said above, between Emperor Otto—because of his brother Henry—and Liudolf had grown so great that it could be ended only by the sword. The battle lines of both sides had already been drawn up, so that the fighting was about to begin at close quarters. Then Udalric, the athlete of God, knowing that blessed are the feet that bring peace, and recalling what the Lord Himself says in the Gospel, “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God,” took with him Hartbert, the devout bishop of the Church of Chur, and thrust himself into their midst.

They addressed them with such skill in persuasion, while the Spirit of the Father spoke through the mouths of both, that they easily recalled them to a treaty of peace and firmly established the gift of true charity in their hearts. Otto then received the repentant Liudolf just as the father in the Gospel once received his returning son. For each son had been dead and came to life again; he had been lost and was found.

Great joy and exultation arose throughout the whole army. Praise and thanksgiving resounded from everyone’s lips, because through His servants the Lord had delivered His people.

## CHAPTER XIV

In the following year, that is, in the nine hundred and fifty-fifth year of the Lord’s incarnation, the Hungarian people, more savage than any wild beast, just as had previously been revealed to the man of God from heaven, burst forth with an innumerable multitude. They devastated and occupied the entire region of the Norici, from the Danube to the Black Forest, which extends toward the mountains, and part of the province of the Alamanni as far as the river Iller.

After crossing the Lech, they burned the church of Saint Afra with fire and surrounded the city of Augsburg with a siege [Col. 1195C]. But the holy bishop of God, seeing so many wolves, did not abandon the guardianship of his flock by fleeing like a hireling. Instead, he opposed himself to them and entrusted the entire matter to the Lord.

While the soldiers fought fiercely against the enemy all around the walls and before the gate, he sat upon a horse and walked fearlessly amid a rain of stones and arrows, protected neither by shield nor helmet but clothed in a stole. You might have seen a new Joshua carrying the ark of the Lord and sounding the trumpets—except that Joshua remained outside the walls of the city of Jericho, whereas this man remained inside, in the house of Rahab, who had been converted to God, that is, in the Church, and assaulted the city of the devil standing outside.

Under Joshua’s leadership, while the priests carrying the ark of the Lord sounded the trumpets and all the people shouted with the loudest cry, the walls of Jericho collapsed completely. With this man carrying the ark of the Lord in a pure heart, while the priests and Levites sounded their trumpets—that is, psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs—and all the people cried out in fervent prayer to God and to His holy mother Mary ever-virgin for their deliverance, the Hungarians, who were the city of the devil, fell.

The rest took flight. The Christian army pursued them, striking them down, until their leaders, together with many others, were captured and brought to Regensburg, where afterward, to the disgrace of their nation, they were hanged on gallows.

When these things had been accomplished, the venerable bishop, giving thanks to God in all things, began, as though from a citadel of the mind, to look down and consider the needs of his subjects. He did not judge it right to seek only what belonged to himself while neglecting the causes of his people, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying: “Anyone who does not provide for his own, and especially for those of his household, has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever.”

Therefore he kept with him the communities of his clergy, which had been reduced to such poverty by the plundering of the enemy that they could retain nothing for their daily sustenance. As far as he was able, though poor himself, he supplied the poor with the necessities of the present life. And not only to them, but to all who asked him, he extended the hand of mercy according to what he possessed, in accordance with the Lord’s command: “Give to everyone who asks of you.”

## CHAPTER XV

At that time he was admonished in a vision not to delay repairing the church of Saint Afra, which had been burned by the pagans, and also to provide a suitable roof for the tomb of Bishop Simpert, which was situated beside the steps in the choir.

Thereafter the servant of God began, with fasting and prayers and with contrition of heart, to offer himself to God. He also took other religious men with him and devoutly begged that almighty God, through His mercy, might deign to reveal to him the place where the body of His most holy martyr was buried, and whether a crypt should be built in the eastern part, at the place toward which his own inclination urged him.

Thus the Lord confirmed the truth of what He had spoken through the mouth of holy David: “Behold, the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and His ears are toward their prayers” [Col. 1196C]. And elsewhere: “He will fulfill the desire of those who fear Him, and He will hear their prayer.”

One night Saint Afra appeared to him in a vision and showed him the place of her body in the church. But she forbade a crypt to be made there because of the relics of the saints who, resting there in peace, await the coming of the just Judge.

Instructed by this revelation, he began to devote himself vigilantly to the work appointed. He restored the walls of the church and built the crypt on the western side. He did not cease from his labor until, in a short time, he had completed everything with perfect beauty.

It is now fitting to demonstrate with what veneration that place deserves to be regarded, in which the holy martyr of God forbade a crypt to be built. There was a certain gardener who, walking among the grass there, discovered a cave [Col. 1196D]. Inside it he saw a small structure built underground and altered or transformed in appearance. He came and reported it to the bishop, saying: “If it pleases your holiness, my vegetables and other things I need can be stored here.”

The bishop said to him in the Spirit: “If you do this, you will immediately lose your senses and the health of your limbs.” But the wretched man disregarded these words, gathered his belongings into the cave mentioned above, and immediately lost his reason, sight, and hearing.

He was brought to the holy man of God. When he acknowledged his guilt, he asked for forgiveness and obtained pardon together with restored health. I shall relate something marvelous. From that hour onward, the gardener was never able to find the cave he had discovered. From that time the man of God began to visit that holy place more frequently [Col. 1197A] and to prepare a tomb there for himself. Whenever he was at home, he used to offer the saving Host to the Lord there every Friday.

## CHAPTER XVI

Meanwhile, for the sake of prayer, he went to Rome, where he obtained the head of Saint Abundius the martyr and brought it back to Augsburg with religious devotion.

He used to visit holy places, especially the monastery of Saint Gall, where he had been raised and educated. At one time, having gone from there to the cell of Saint Meinrad to visit the servant of God Everhard, after the sacred offering of prayers and the sweet words of fraternal conversation, the holy bishop, having exchanged the customary kisses, decided to return home. He expected that on that occasion he would never see the servant of God again. He had already begun to leave when Everhard, hastening breathlessly, ran after him [Col. 1197B] and, repeating the kisses of charity, burst into tears and said:

“From this hour we shall not see one another again in this life, until, freed from our bodies, we may be granted to see one another in the presence of God.”

The bishop said to him: “Venerable father, do you now know for certain that the time of my dissolution is at hand, when I must depart from this life?”

He replied: “The end of your life has not yet come. But the outcome of the matter will prove that what I say is true.”

Then they parted. Yet before the bishop visited that same cell, the servant of God Everhard departed from this world.

After some time, he also went for the sake of prayer to the place of the Agaunian martyrs, where Saint Maurice rests with the sacred legion, and obtained no small number of relics of the Theban martyrs. He brought them to Augsburg with the greatest honor [Col. 1197C] and devoutly placed them in the oratory of the holy Mother of God amid hymns and psalmody.

In those same days the venerable hero came to the monastery of Insel, which is called Reichenau, where at that time a venerable man named Aluwigus governed the flock of the Lord. Receiving him with the honor that was fitting, Aluwigus gave him many relics of the saints, for the sake of which he had come there, and so allowed him to return home rejoicing.

## CHAPTER XVII

It must not be passed over that, on account of his merits, very many benefits were granted to the sick. In particular, those afflicted by epilepsy were freed from that great affliction through his blessing.

He took care to conceal this for the sake of humility. If some of them openly requested this grace of healing [Col. 1197D], he would withhold the gift of blessing, asserting that it belonged more properly to apostolic dignity than to his own insignificance.

Through oil consecrated by him on Maundy Thursday, people afflicted by various illnesses were restored to their former health. Those whose eyes had been darkened by blindness also deserved to be enlightened through the anointing with this holy oil.

It is worthwhile to relate how he himself likewise obtained the grace of health through the efficacy of this holy liquid. Once, when he came to the monastery of Kempten, he was afflicted by such a serious illness that he could move nowhere except when supported in the hands of others, nor could he take any food to restore his strength.

Then word was sent with all speed to Augsburg, and oil consecrated by him was brought. On the ninth hour of the day, during the very vigil of holy Pentecost, he was anointed with it. Through God’s grace, contrary to everyone’s expectation, he suddenly recovered so completely that he refreshed himself with food and, in good health, took part with the brothers in the evening assembly. He celebrated the entire day of the approaching feast with spiritual joy. Thus, while everyone rejoiced together, he returned in good health to his see.

## CHAPTER XVIII

Once, when the man of God was about to cross the river Vindex, he found that its channel had risen so high that none of his companions dared cross it. His fellow travelers then went away, seeking a ford wherever they might find one. He remained alone with one cleric [Col. 1198B] and crossed the river without any hesitation in the name of the Lord.

And, more astonishing still, although the cleric was seated on a taller horse and was completely immersed in the water from the waist downward, he saw that not even a single hair of the bishop’s socks—made from a woolen cloak and worn because of the cold—was wet.

When the cleric expressed great amazement at this, the bishop sternly warned him, saying: “Take care, while I still remain in the flesh, to tell no one of this,” following the Teacher of humility, who commanded His disciples not to tell anyone what they had seen until the Son of Man had risen from the dead.

These are Your works, O Christ, the signs of Your graces. In Your saints You still cause ancient miracles to shine forth. For just as You once provided a dry path for the ancient Hebrew people when the Red Sea was divided [Col. 1198C], so You led this servant of Yours through the same element with his clothes dry.

The waters stood as walls for them on the right and left, so that they could cross through the middle on dry footprints. But this man crossed through the midst of the waves, reached the shore under Your guidance, and was not wet in the least.

At another time, while traveling by boat along the Danube toward Regensburg, through the negligence of the sailors the ship struck some piece of wood. As a result, cracks opened and the vessel gradually began to fill with water.

Terrified, the sailors hurried toward the shore. When they arrived, they carried out everything that was in the ship but forgot the bishop, who was sitting in the stern. Then one of the clerics, sighing from the depths of his heart, said: “Woe to us wretched men, for in such great danger we have forgotten our lord.”

As he said this, he ran back more quickly, lifted the bishop onto his shoulders, and carried him to shore. Once he had disembarked, the ship sank at the stern. In a marvelous manner, the vessel, which had floated upon the water while full of people and other belongings, could not remain afloat any longer after the man of God and his companions had left it, but sank. From this it was understood that almighty God had held it with His hand while the man of God and his companions were in it.

On another occasion, when the man of God wished to travel to Rome, he came to a river called the Tar. He found it so dangerously swollen that no one could cross it either on horseback or by boat. But the holy bishop, placing his trust in God, celebrated the solemnities of the Mass on the bank of that river and then crossed the river on foot safely, together with all his companions.

## CHAPTER XIX

In those days the chosen bishop of God, stirred by devotion to sacred religion and inflamed by the fire of divine love, began to gather religious women in the church of Saint Stephen, the first martyr of Christ, situated outside the city walls. He did this so that they might serve God in their holy vocation with greater freedom, the farther they were removed from the labor of worldly affairs.

When a certain matron came to that monastery to enter the religious life and had been received by the community, she remained devoted to the service of God. Although she was not well instructed in letters, she was sufficiently capable of supervising external affairs.

For this reason the sisters wished to entrust her with the office of cellarer, but she refused to consent. The matter was then brought before the bishop. When he ordered her to obey, she refused and persisted in her obstinacy.

The following night she was rebuked in a dream in these words: “Because you did not obey the bishop’s commands, you will lack the use of walking until you deserve to be absolved by him.”

When she awoke, she remained completely weak and lame. When the bishop returned to the city, she was carried on a bed into his presence; by him she was both rebuked for her disobedience and healed.

As soon as she felt herself healed, she ran ahead of the bishop before he reached the church, praising and blessing God.

Once, when the servant of almighty God was traveling to a synod of bishops that was to be convened in the royal villa called Ingelheim, he encountered a poor man named Rotbert, who carried his own internal organs, which had fallen out through his abdomen, in his lap.

When he saw him, he was moved by compassion and ordered a denarius to be given to him, saying: “Receive this in the name of the Lord, and go in peace.”

As soon as he received the alms, the man departed and began to improve so much that after some time he was completely restored to health. After the man of God’s death, when Rotbert was again afflicted by other illnesses, he came to his tomb and deserved to be healed, as the reader will be able to find more fully recorded in its proper place.

## CHAPTER XX

Thus the holy man of God, inflamed by a heavenly desire, began to grow weary of the things of this world and to place the profits of earthly matters after the love of Christ. Although he was held here in body, in mind he dwelt in heavenly things, so that he could rightly be counted among those who might say with the Apostle: “Our citizenship is in heaven.”

Therefore, possessing zeal for God, though not according to knowledge, he began to exert himself with all his strength before earthly authorities so that a certain cleric named Adalbero, the son of his sister, might assume responsibility for the entire bishopric, while he himself, under the habit of monastic religion, might devote himself to God alone. He obtained this arrangement.

But the wretched man, either unaware or unwilling to know what the most wise Solomon had said—“An inheritance to which one hastens at the beginning will lack blessing at the end”—immediately subjected the bishop’s soldiers and entire household to himself by an oath, and publicly carried the pastoral staff in his hand.

The other bishops, indignant at this, summoned both men to a synod. They accused the aforementioned Adalbero of heretical presumption because, while his lord was still alive, he had not feared to usurp such things.

When he wished to clear himself of the charges brought against him, everyone determined that this could not be done unless, with the books of the holy Gospels brought into their midst, he confirmed by oath that he had not known it to be heresy to presume to do such things.

When everything pertaining to this matter had been completed, the bishop and Adalbero both returned home. They received such consolation from the holy synod that, when the bishop departed this life, no one else was to be ordained in his place except Adalbero.

But there is no wisdom, prudence, or counsel against the Lord. For in that same year, after several months had passed, one day, as evening was approaching, the aforementioned cleric sat at table with the man of God, having recently undergone bloodletting and suffering some discomfort from the incision. Suddenly he rose from the middle of the gathering and went to bed; that very night he brought the present life to an end.

The bishop immediately learned this through the spirit. When the man who had entered to announce the death came in, the bishop forestalled him and said: “I know that Adalbero has died. Hurry and have a vehicle prepared, so that we can carry him to Augsburg.”

At that time they were staying in the fortress called Dillingen. The holy bishop carried Adalbero’s lifeless body to Augsburg [Col. 1200C] and buried it in the church of Saint Mary.

Among the other works of mercy he performed for the repose of his nephew’s soul, he also acquired for himself the abbey called Uttenburg, which Adalbero had held as a benefice while he was alive. He kept it until, through his efforts, it was granted the privilege of liberty.

## CHAPTER XXI

One day, while the holy man of God was traveling, a certain man came before him and gave the most certain report of the death of Conrad, bishop of Constance.

Those who were present expected that he would immediately wish to celebrate the customary offices of the funeral for the repose of the deceased. But he, knowing through a secret messenger accustomed to attend him what the truth of the matter was, said to them: “In the meantime, remain more composed; tomorrow you will learn what you ought to believe about this.”

The following day, at daybreak, a man came from Constance and announced that the aforementioned man was alive and well.

Although the servant of almighty God knew that the time of his own dissolution was already approaching, he nevertheless continued, for as long as he could, to be carried in a vehicle and to sow the seeds of the divine word in the hearts of his hearers.

He had followed this manner of traveling even while he was still healthy: wherever he had to go, he would sit alone on a seat placed upon a wagon, accompanied only by one cleric with whom he could devote himself more freely to the chanting of psalms, without the impediment of others.

He was eager to enter the walls of the city of Augsburg as quickly as possible, so that there, like a good hired laborer, he might await the end of his work.

When he arrived there [Col. 1201A], for as long as his strength permitted, he outwardly offered the saving Host to the Lord amid the daily solemnities of the Mass, while inwardly he sacrificed himself as a victim upon the altar of his heart.

He sat at table with others; while they ate and drank, he remained entirely fasting. His food was either the sweet pleasure of the psalms or the continual reading of sacred texts. Among these, he especially delighted in hearing from the fourth book of Saint Gregory’s Dialogues how many people, after being released from their bodies, were carried away in spirit and then returned.

Meanwhile he ordered the administrators of his possessions to divide into three portions everything they could find in every place that properly belonged to his jurisdiction. While he was still alive, they were to distribute one of these portions to priests and the poor [Col. 1201B].

One day he ordered himself to be carried into the church to hear Mass. After hearing it, he had a carpet spread before the holy cross and devoted himself to prayer upon it. After rising, as though after half an hour, he ordered everything he possessed in the way of household goods to be brought before him, except for the furnishings of one house and its tables, and one covering, which he left for the service of his successor.

When he saw the rest, he groaned and said: “Ah! What need have I of all these things?” There were only a few shirts, seven or eight tablecloths, two sacks, and ten solidi in silver. He immediately ordered the official to distribute the coins among the poor and the rest among the clerics.

Thus he diligently prepared himself, so that when the one who knocked came, he might immediately be able to open the door.

## CHAPTER XXII

While meditating on such things, he was several times carried away in spirit to the heavenly realms, and he saw and heard certain things that he also related in part to those attending him.

For he announced to Wernher, abbot of Fulda, who had come to visit him, that if two people agreed with the others in his election, Wernher would succeed him in the bishopric.

On another occasion, as though awakened from a deep sleep, he said before everyone: “Alas, alas, that I ever saw that Adalbero, my nephew! Because I consented to his desire, they do not wish to receive me into their company without punishment.”

We read of something similar in Saint Gregory’s book of the Dialogues. He relates that a certain Paschasius, a deacon of the Apostolic See renowned for extraordinary holiness, whose dalmatic, placed upon his bier after his death, touched a demoniac and healed him, was assigned to a place of punishment for no other reason than that, in the dispute that arose between Pope Symmachus and Laurentius, he had chosen Laurentius for the papal office.

Although the unanimous judgment of all had overcome him, he nevertheless persisted in his own opinion almost until the day of his death, loving and preferring the man whom the judgment of the bishops had rejected as head of the Church.

Since the fault of the two men had been almost alike—for just as Paschasius chose Laurentius even after Symmachus had been ordained, so this man, while he himself still remained in the flesh, looking upon the matter with an eye that was simple but insufficiently discerning, wished Adalbero to become bishop against the decrees of the Fathers—we may understand the same thing concerning this most holy man as Saint Gregory understood concerning Paschasius.

When Peter questioned him about this—how one who had possessed such holiness that the touch of his burial garment could drive an evil spirit from a possessed man could nevertheless, after death, be led to a place of punishment—he replied:

“In this matter the great dispensation of almighty God must be recognized, as well as its manifold character. By His judgment it was arranged that the same man, Paschasius, should both suffer inwardly for a certain time the penalty for what he had sinned, and yet perform marvelous deeds through his body after death before human eyes. Before his death he had performed pious works known to those who witnessed them, and after his death he performed miracles through his body. Thus those who had seen his good deeds would not be deceived in their estimation of his almsgiving; nor would the guilt that he himself did not believe to be guilt, and therefore did not extinguish with tears, be left unpunished.

“So once, that great leader of the Israelite people, Moses, with whom, as Scripture relates, the Lord spoke face to face, as a man speaks with his friend, and Aaron his brother and priest, because of the guilt of unbelief, deserved to hear from the Lord: ‘Because you did not believe in me, to sanctify me before the children of Israel, you shall not bring these peoples into the land that I will give them.’

“This was so that certain weaker people might understand by what punishment the strict Judge strikes serious offenders at the final judgment, since He corrects even those whom He predestined before the ages for the number of the elect.”

But enough of these matters; let us now return to what we interrupted.

## CHAPTER XXIII

For a venerable day had come for the whole world, namely, the birthday of Christ’s precursor. The man of God, overcome by the grievous languor of his illness, as though awakening from sleep, began to say to those standing by: “Clothe me, and provide shoes for my feet.” Although they thought that he was giving such orders in a fit of mental disturbance, they nevertheless hastened to obey.

Moreover, dressed in pontifical vestments and accompanied by the entire clerical office, as is customary, he went out in public contrary to everyone’s expectation. Coming thus to the church of blessed John the Baptist, which he himself had built, he remained there undefeated and without anyone’s support until he had celebrated twice, as had been appointed for that day, the solemn rites of the Mass.

When these had been duly completed, he sat down and said before the clerics who were standing by:

“I undertook the celebration of this office not through the capacity of my own strength, but by the divinity and command of Christ. For today, while I was resting in sweet sleep, two young men of handsome appearance stood before my bed. One of them said to me: ‘Why do you not rise? For today you must celebrate Mass at Saint John’s.’ The other replied to him: ‘How can this happen? For, because of the weakness of his strength, he has not yet completed Prime.’ Then the one who had spoken first said: ‘Rise, and hasten, according to my command, to perform the divine mystery in the aforementioned church, for today no one there will sing except you.’”

After saying this, he returned to his chamber and joyfully awaited the approaching day of his calling. Repeatedly he uttered the Psalmist’s words: “When shall I come and appear before the face of my God?”

Meanwhile, when he was questioned by the man who served before him in the office of reader, whether, in view of the illness by which he was afflicted, he expected to depart from this world, he replied:

“I know with complete certainty that I shall soon depart from this world.”

When the man, grieving, asked him which of the bishops he wished to summon for his burial, especially since none of the neighboring bishops remained who had not been invited to the royal conference in France, he said:

“You know how to commend earth to earth. When the time comes, do only what belongs to you; it belongs to God to provide someone to commend my body.”

## CHAPTER XXIV

After a few days had passed, on the vigil of the Apostles, which that year fell on a Wednesday, he most certainly expected to depart from this life. Although he did not express this explicitly, he disclosed it in certain words and made it clear by evident signs.

Indeed, when all the bells around were ringing for Vespers, he himself, having bathed and clothed himself in the sacred vestments prepared for this purpose, prostrated himself on the ground, as though he were about to die at that very hour. When the evening synaxis was finished, he rose with the help of others and, as though somewhat dismayed in mind, said:

“O holy Peter, you have not acted now as I thought you would.”

O blessed man, worthy to be praised with every commendation, whose spirit indeed was willing, although the flesh was weak; for him, to live was Christ and to die was gain. Therefore, abhorring so greatly the burden of bodily habitation as though it were a prison, he desired to be dissolved and to be with Christ.

Restored again in spirit, he remained tranquil for five continuous days, asking pardon from everyone and giving his blessing. When the Thursday of the fifth day had ended and evening was dawning into Friday, while the dawn was already illuminating the breadth of the earth, and while the clerics were singing and weeping, he commended his spirit into the hands of the Lord.

In the year of the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 973, in the eighty-third year of his age and the fiftieth of his ordination—like one in a jubilee, that is, a year of complete remission—the true Hebrew passed free from the Egypt of this world, to live forever with his Lord.

He departed on the fourth day before the Nones of July, in the time of Otto II, emperor Augustus.

When his body had been stripped according to custom for washing, so great a fragrance of the sweetest odor flowed from it that it filled the nostrils and breasts of all who were standing there. The sweetness of that odor remained until he had been entirely clothed and carried into the church.

After this, when the venerable Wolfgang, bishop of the city of Regensburg, arrived, the body of the holy man was buried with great honor in the church of Saint Afra the martyr, where, while he was still alive, he had prepared a tomb for himself.

At that place, through his merits and by the gift of Christ’s grace, many miracles continually occur and many benefits are granted to the sick. He lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

These matters await the examination of your judgment, so that under you as a kindly judge they may be able to stand confirmed. I desire, most blessed Father, that you may prosper in Christ and that you may always remember me.

*(A certain edition of the Life written by Berno contains the following chapter. Although Surius did not publish it, and although it is not certain to me that it is Berno’s, nevertheless, because it concerns the history and explains the form of the image of Saint Ulrich, I have decided to add it here.)*

At a certain time, when the same holy bishop was seated at Saint Afra to dine with the blessed Conrad, bishop of Constance, of happy memory, the two of them, continually conversing about heavenly matters and forgetful of corruptible food, refreshed in spirit, continued their divine conversation until the following Friday, paying no attention to the meat that had been set before them.

It happened, therefore, that a certain servant of the dukes of Bavaria approached the holy man. When the business for which he had come had been settled, as he was leaving the bishop gave him a piece of meat, without noticing that it was Friday and that the day was to be observed.

When the messenger returned to his own lord, wishing, driven by malice, to defame the holy bishops as though they had not abstained from eating meat on Friday, he immediately produced as evidence the piece of meat that he had received from the holy man. And behold, wondrous to relate, the appearance of the meat was changed into the appearance of a fish, condemning the rash servant’s slander and displaying the innocence of the holy men.

For this reason, in the glorious image of the bishop, a fish is customarily depicted forever, as a memorial of this miracle.

[Col. 1203]

## VERSES OF BERNO

Prefixed to the Saxon Book of Sacraments preserved in the Boherian Library.

*(Mabillon, Benedictine Annals, book LV, no. 27.)*

Receive the little book written with a pure mind,  
which Bern, the last of your servants, brings,  
who, although unworthy, is always your faithful fosterling,  
ready for service, kindly with devoted heart,  
while he flourishes and is strong, while he lives in a healthy body.

# [POEM ON THE TROJAN WAR]

[Col. 1205]

## NOTICE FOLLOWING THE POEM

*(Literary History of France, vol. VII, p. 587.)*

Perhaps one would be entitled to attribute to Berno a poem on the destruction of Troy, published by Goldast and Barthius. What seems to authorize this attribution (Fabricius, *Bibliotheca Latina*, book II, p. 625) is, on the one hand, that in Goldast’s edition the piece bears at its head the name Bernard of Fleury, and, on the other, that it is ancient and was composed before the end of the twelfth century (Barthius, *Adversaria*, book XXXI, chapter 7), which suits an author presumed to belong to the preceding century, such as this supposed Bernard.

Now, since no Bernard of Fleury is known in those times, while it is known that Berno was then a monk there, and since his ordinary name Bern was often expanded into Bernard, there is considerable basis for crediting him with this poem.

It consists of eighty-eight elegiac verses, rhyming both in the hemistich and at the end, so that the rhyme is the same in the pentameter and the hexameter. This must have cost the poet considerable labor, although it made the piece more curious than interesting. Although his verses retain several marks of roughness and barbarism, others can be found in them that have merit. One must conclude that Berno’s Muse was better mounted when he worked on this poem than when he composed the preceding inscription that has been discussed.

Goldast was the first to draw it from the dust (Fabricius, cited above). He published it among poems falsely attributed to the poet Ovid.

Afterward Barthius, who did not know that edition, unearthed the piece in manuscripts and had it reprinted without an author’s name, with several observations of his own.

[Col. 1205]

## POEM ON THE TROJAN WAR, APPARENTLY BY BERNO

*(In Barthius, *Adversaria*, book XXXI, p. 1432.)*

Some remarks on rhythm introduced into verse by ancient Greek and Latin writers. Also published is a sufficiently ingenious rhythmic poem on the capture of Troy, in many passages pursuing the sound of syllables, although scarcely Latin.

Anacreon clearly cultivated rhythm among the Greeks in poetry of the highest elegance. I believe that not a few Latins followed him; their writings have now perished utterly, except for a few fragments preserved by grammarians who cited them for other purposes.

But here we call rhythm the consonance of syllables at the ends of verses, not what the very learned Victorinus and other writers on the art of grammar teach. That the genuine Romans did not reject this kind of rhythm, although it would become a principal cause of the corruption of Latin in later centuries, even in other kinds of verse, is shown by these deliberately composed verses of Marcus Varro:

“Ὄνος λύρας” — “Ass of the lyre” —  
“And he carried off the orthophallian psalteries,”  
on which sayings resound in Greece,  
those who place the beginnings of tales.”

Other passages of the ancients could also be brought forward on this subject, if we wished to copy out our poetic miscellany. The authority of Terentianus is sufficient, however; he distinguishes rhythms from meters in such a way as to acknowledge that both kinds were in use.

The final age knew this distinction as well, sinning through deliberate choice, not ignorance. Eccard, in his book *On the Life of Notker*, chapter 17, authenticated all the litanies and songs that they had made—rhythmically, metrically, or in prose—as well as the disciplines that they had taught.

Here, however, we shall publish an unpublished poem of the later age that ingeniously composed a double rhythm, and not without a third and fourth. Gaspar Gevartius, with whom I enjoy the closest friendship, gave it to me when he learned that I intended to assemble a complete edition of the poets of the later age.

I am not inclined to bring into that collection poets who barbarously break into rhythms, according to the custom and law of lesser languages, verses conceived in Latin measures—such as Bernhard of Morlaix, whom one might call the chief of such writers; Goffrid of Viterbo; the *Quirinalia* of Metellus, composed in hexameters; and the poems of Peter of Blois, Abbot Willeram, Wippo, and a thousand others. This poem, however, seems to me to have been written with a distinctive genius and not unworthy of being treated separately.

It is written on the Trojan War in the following words:

I wish to mourn Pergama,  
seized by deceit alone.  
Paris is without equal;  
he dares to attempt it.  
He goes and approaches;  
the sailor goes alone.  
The safe desire of the sea  
is unknown to the citizens.

[Col. 1206]

Given by fate to the Danaans,  
captured, reduced to the ground.  
He seeks, sees, dares to love;  
theft, dangers, the sea.  
Secretly he carries her off and secretly departs;  
flight occurs, the robber returns.  
He offers incense to the altars of desire,  
for Paris prepares weapons.

[Col. 1207]

After Helen’s abduction,  
a thousand ships are filled.  
Thinking himself superior,  
stripped of his treaty,  
the Greek commander  
for the partner of his bed,  
the divine Pergama nearby  
is attacked by the adulterer.

At Juno’s nod  
it is destroyed by gifts;  
full of evil offspring,  
it is wiped out by deceit.

Then the Greeks give everything to death;  
they harden themselves.  
From this point the houses burn  
through varied slaughter.

She is punished with slaughter  
and with her own disgrace,  
the woman worthy of death,  
restored to the victor.

“Cruel one, why do you escape?  
Why are you guilty of disaster,  
having just endured Paris  
and intending to keep faith?”

“The report of an old matter—  
tomorrow these things may happen;  
a woman overcome by wine—  
I do not hope it will happen.”

The slaughter completed,  
she is treated foully.  
On the face of the Dorians  
the whip follows.

She lives, though unwilling,  
and has deserved lamentation.

“Juno, what are you doing?  
Do you think so many blows  
will be enough?”

“Then you will kill again,  
then you will kill again.  
You find no one remaining?  
Rather, you pursue them.”

“No one rebels;  
he is pursued in war.”

“Do not strike me, Juno;  
bring about a swift death.”

“Until now I have wept;  
what remains of life—”

“The anger of God has persisted.  
I marvel that he thirsts.”

“No one remembers me;  
no one makes a covenant with me.”

Fear shakes the bones  
while renewing the tears.

The city, once lofty,  
becomes one of the least.  
A fortunate city—  
if only fate could have allowed  
kingdoms sufficiently blessed,  
rich in honored things,  
kingdoms sufficiently blessed,  
the robber of pleasure.

The city, once long celebrated,  
behold, bare ground.  
Ancient Troy, you perish;  
soon, soon you will belong to cattle.

A good city, full of good,  
endowed with a protector,  
full of power,  
most fortunate in power.

If we should commend  
the highest worship,  
wine from the vineyards,  
payment in coin,  
a court full of persons,  
land with its own gifts,

an old and famous city,  
so good, so renowned—

[Col. 1208]

Larissa and Mycenae run forward,  
without strong allies.  
The widower, bereaved,  
joins his side with the sword.  
Grief forbids fear  
whether to live or to die.

The Greek pitches his tents  
and constructs the horse.  
By the wicked fraud of Sinon,  
the city now full of goods  
gives birth to an enemy,  
a populous city.

Blind with desire for plunder,  
their hearts closed to entreaty,  
Diomedes cuts off  
arms, legs, and feet.

Paris, the robber, by Diomedes  
returns the fosterling of Leda.  
He returns from his former love  
and from the delights of the marriage bed.

You hand over what was not otherwise surrendered;  
you do not fall only in disaster.  
Through the same means, once before, Theseus—  
do not return to the same thing.

The future will make shameful things feared,  
as yesterday did;  
what drunken truth clings to,  
I shall not be surety for.

Hecuba is added above to the booty;  
she is forced to go on foot,  
her beautiful hair torn,  
through the theatrical forum.

Because she lives a life of poverty,  
she cries out in this manner:

“After the deaths of such slaughter,  
could anything more be added?  
Those whom Atreides killed?  
Those whom you see to have died?

Nor do you thus pity anyone,  
the remains of ashes.”

But Juno wages war;  
the blade is sated with blood.

“By striking, you can show mercy;  
let an aged body be worn away.  
Seize the misfortunes of the light  
with a brief end.  
Let the rest be given to destruction;  
there is no mention of me.

Let the sword that ends the rest  
allow me to survive.”

The spirit becomes restless,  
again the cause of fear,  
and, abundant in excellent things,  
is utterly annihilated.

If it could conquer fate,  
it would judge it less severe.

A city of the first nobility,  
giving without gifts,  
until they harmed the blessed,  
and the ill-gotten ship—

While chance ends the game,  
he will be food for cattle.  
Now Troy no longer seems to me  
pasture and lair for wild beasts.

Outside and inside, with citizen and colonist,  
that one endowed with the throne,  
most celebrated and worthy of report,  
with prince, citizen, and constitution—

What we customarily commend:  
countryside, field, water, grove—  
the joyful farmyard gave food,  
and the ship the straits.

The city gave citizens, the fields colonists,  
the granaries were full of good things.  
Very good things, so good and rare,  
become a cattle pen.

[Col. 1209]

Rich from ancient times,  
it perishes in a short time.  
The cause of such a matter  
was a fatal woman.

[Col. 1210]

While she is borne along by hostile fate,  
something comes from nothing.  
She was a destructive prostitute,  
a woman pregnant with evils.

[Col. 1209]

I do not deny that this age could have done without possessing this monument, so rich in elegance. Nevertheless, I am also willing to affirm that it matters to one who seeks complete learning not to be ignorant of the literature of every age.

Moreover, although in language, phrasing, and style this poem may seem barbarous, solecistic, and affected, we nevertheless learn from it what people did at that time, when they could not aspire to our felicity.

This poem was written before the year 1200. For Nicolaus of Rievaulx, a not incompetent poet of that age, expressly places the beginning of the second distich in this form:

“Paris, unequaled in form, the one flower of the world.”

The very learned J. Picard produces his verse in his work addressed to William of Newburgh, book II, *On English Affairs*, chapter 27.

The genre is indeed new, and I do not think anything of this kind had previously appeared in public.
