Only one thing might seem a sufficiently worthy reason for suppressing it: the imitation of badly cultivated minds. But if they have decided to play the fool, let them do so at their own risk. We did not wish to rage against a fetus not yet properly born.

There is an error in these words:

“Do not strike me, Juno; by striking you can show mercy.”

It should read: “Me, me,” as the following distich clearly proves. It alludes to the Maronian line:

“Me, me—I am the one who did it; turn the sword upon me.”

Other matters ought to have been noted, but leisure could be put to better use.

# IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1051. WIPPO THE PRIEST, CHAPLAIN OF THE EMPERORS CONRAD THE SALIAN AND HENRY III

[Col. 1213]

## HISTORICAL AND BIBLIOGRAPHICAL NOTICE ON WIPPO

*(Literary History of France, vol. VII, p. 443.)*

[Col. 1213C]

Wippo, historian of the Emperor Conrad the Salian and panegyrist of the emperor’s son, Henry the Black, is commonly considered to have been German by nationality (Oudin, *Scriptorum*, vol. II, p. 644; Basnage, and others).

But this opinion belongs among those based only on prejudices unsupported by examination. Anyone who pays even a little attention to the reading of his writings will agree that he was from Transjurane Burgundy.

When he speaks of that region himself, he does so with an affection and a detailed account of circumstances that visibly show that he was more particularly interested in it than in any other province of the empire. When this is brought together with the passage in which, inviting King Henry to visit it before he was proclaimed emperor, he calls it his homeland, it proves that this was in fact the country where he had been born—something that cannot apply to that prince.

“You enlighten your homeland, if only you should visit it.”  
[Note: Fabricius nevertheless observed (*Bibliotheca mediae et infimae Latinitatis* VI, 326, under Wippo, on this verse): “In the Middle Ages, *homeland* likewise meant ‘region.’”]

[Col. 1215B]

Emperor Conrad the Salian conquered this province and united it to the empire in 1033. It was most probably then that he took Wippo into his service.

Wippo, who was a priest, entered it as chaplain and continued to perform those duties under Emperor Henry the Black. In dedicating to Henry the history of his father, he describes himself as a priest by the grace of God and servant of the servants of the lords of this world—that is, of Conrad and his son Henry.

Although he was very sickly, he devoted himself greatly to study and often practiced versification, which seems to have held a particular attraction for him. He had read the historians and ancient philosophers and knew them reasonably well for his time.

What he tells us about his access to the councils of Emperor Henry and public assemblies suggests that he was an intelligent man, familiar with the conduct of affairs of state.

Wippo flourished under the two emperors already mentioned, a period of more than thirty years, from 1024 to 1056, the date of the death of Henry III, surnamed the Black. But there is every appearance that he did not live until that final date.

He had intended to write the history of the latter prince, as he had already written that of his father, but it does not appear that he carried out this plan. His final work was in fact published before Henry attained the empire, that is, before the year 1046. In it he calls him only king, although he announces that he would soon be emperor:

“Pious king and future Caesar.”

Thus one may doubt whether our panegyrist lived beyond 1050 or 1051.

Before Pistorius and Canisius published their collections, Wippo and his writings were unknown in the republic of letters. It has since been learned that he composed:

### 1. The History of the Emperor Conrad the Salian

He dedicates it to Henry, his son, in a letter followed by a preface in which he plays the philosopher to some extent. In both pieces one sees the motives that induced him to undertake the work and the purpose he had in view.

He was so concerned with accuracy that he asks his readers to attribute any errors found in the work to those who supplied him with information, since his frequent illnesses did not allow him always to remain with the court. Consequently, he was obliged to rely on others to learn what had happened there.

At the conclusion of his work he congratulates himself that he has omitted nothing of what he had learned or seen for himself concerning matters relevant to his subject. Several other historians before Wippo had already treated the same material, but this did not prevent him from undertaking it after them.

He begins his History with the general assembly held immediately after the death of the holy Emperor Henry, in order to give him a successor to the crown of Germany. He then proceeds to the election of Conrad that took place there and to the ceremony of his coronation—three events on which he dwells at greater length.

He next reports, with fairly good order, the other more memorable actions of his hero, ordinarily taking care to mark their dates. The History of Conrad is not so completely Wippo’s principal subject that he does not also touch upon the great deeds of Henry, his son, by then emperor, as he had initially undertaken to do.

Although he enters into a certain amount of detail concerning the history of both men, his narrative is nevertheless somewhat concise; he says that he adopted this practice so as not to burden his readers. If he succeeded better than several other historians of his time, he nevertheless followed the inclination of most of them by occasionally inserting verses into his prose.

Wippo’s work is interesting not only because it teaches us several historical details that escaped the historians who preceded him, but also because it informs us of the true ancestry of Conrad and of the Empress Gisela, his wife, which had previously been unknown.

The public owes the work to Jean Pistorius, who brought it to light among his other *Historians of Germany*. As is known, that collection was printed several times at Frankfurt, in the years 1582, 1584, and 1607.

### 2. The Panegyric of King Henry the Black

Wippo composed a panegyric of approximately three hundred hexameters in praise of King Henry the Black, who was not yet emperor. He therefore published it before the year 1046 and dedicated it to Henry himself in a short prose letter, in which he calls it a *Tétralogue*.

It is so called because it is divided into four parts, corresponding to the number of speakers: the Poet, the Muses, the Law, and the Graces.

Elsewhere he tells us that he presented it to the king at Strasbourg, where Henry was celebrating the feast of Christmas. Although this Panegyric is almost entirely a work of imagination, it nevertheless contains several facts that may be useful to history.

But the author does not show himself a better poet in it than the other versifiers of his age. At the end a short elegiac poem is added, which was presented at the same prince’s table. It concerns the mystery of Christmas and contains, besides, no poetic beauty.

Canisius was the first to draw these two products of Wippo’s muse out of obscurity. They appear in the second volume of his *Lectiones antiquae*, from which they were transferred to volume III of the new edition of the same collection by M. Basnage, who added a few slight observations.

**3º** At the end of the *History of the Emperor Conrad*, the author added a mournful song on the death of that prince. In speaking of the person who composed it, he designates him only by the words *quidam de nostris* (“a certain one of our number”). But this can be none other than Wippo himself, who uses [Col. 1217B] the same expression to designate the author of the *Tetralogue*, or panegyric of King Henry. On this occasion he reports two verses that are read somewhat differently in the body of the poem; this suggests that he revised it in a second edition produced after his *History of Conrad the Salian*. Wippo presented this mournful song to King Henry when he was at Constance. The piece contains nine [Col. 1218A] stanzas, each of ten short rhymed verses. But the editor, when having it printed, joined two verses together on the same line, so that at first glance they might be taken for long verses, and the stanzas for containing only five.

**4º** M. Fabricius, at the very end of Book III of his *Latin Library of the Middle Ages*, published a collection of Proverbs that the priest Wippo dedicated to Henry, son of the Emperor Conrad, as the title indicates. They are brief, selected maxims intended to shape good morals, which the author expressed in one hundred and fifty kinds of short rhymed couplets, though without any consistent meter. The final twenty-five proceed by as many antitheses concerning vices and virtues, whose character [Col. 1218B] is represented fairly well in each case. The work is ingenious and highly instructive.

**5º** We learn from Wippo himself that he had also composed another poem of one hundred verses on the extreme severity of the cold that occurred in 1033, when Conrad, to whom he presented it, was occupied in Burgundy with recovering the places seized by Odo, count of Champagne. This poem is lost.

[Col. 1217]

## LIFE OF CONRAD THE SALIAN, EMPEROR

By Wippo, priest.

(*In Pistorius, Ancient Writers of German Affairs*, vol. I, p. 421.)

## WIPPO’S LETTER TO KING HENRY, SON OF THE EMPEROR CONRAD

[Col. 1217C] To the most glorious Emperor Henry III, king fit for peace and war: Wippo, by the grace of God a priest, servant of the royal servants who rule as lords of this world.

I considered it appropriate, lord emperor, to write the illustrious life and renowned deeds of your father, the Emperor Conrad, lest the lamp remain hidden beneath a bushel, lest the sun’s ray be obscured by cloud, and lest the virtue preserved in memory be covered by the rust of oblivion. For unless his deeds had preceded as splendid and very brilliant, they might in some measure seem obscured by the excessive splendor that follows from your virtues. As for me, your little servant, my intention is—if God grants it—to recount the deeds of both men that occurred during my lifetime, distinguishing them between us in such a way that I may truthfully say that one beneficially came upon the commonwealth—namely, the Roman Empire—while the other rationally restored it to health. If in this respect I write or say something more, less, or otherwise than the integrity of events warrants, it will not be the fault of the writer [Col. 1218C] but of the narrator, since, when I was very often ill, I could not frequently be present in the chapel of my master Conrad.

Concerning what I myself saw and received from others, I shall disclose it, relying on the pen of truth, for you who wish to gather its fruit. And since there are certain things that you commendably did while your father was alive, I had judged that these should be placed among your father’s deeds. But what you gloriously did after his death I decided should be arranged separately. If some detractors object that this work is superfluous, since others have also written on the same subject, I shall reply—even though I had not yet seen anything written on it—“In the mouth of two witnesses every testimony shall stand”; and that the words of Christ in the Gospel are disseminated in the Church not through one witness alone but through four reliable witnesses.

To you, [Col. 1218D] supreme emperor, I dedicate this work; to you I present your father’s deeds, so that whenever you yourself contemplate performing the most illustrious actions, you may first envision your father’s virtues as in a mirror, and so that what you inherited from your paternal roots may flourish more abundantly in you [Col. 1219A]. Just as you surpassed all your predecessors in certain divine and worldly matters, so may you, with the favor of almighty God, deserve to hold your kingdom and empire longer than all of them. Farewell.

# HERE BEGINS THE LIFE

[Col. 1219]

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 1219A]

I considered it useful and fitting to bind the fleeting memory of passing things with the bonds of writing, and especially not to let the praises of the Christian Empire pass by in idle silence. For those who administered it well in this life thereby retain a certain glory of perpetuity; and for posterity, should they wish to emulate their parents, an example of good living is set before them. A useful example generally makes the mind of the imitator readier and firmer in the conduct of affairs.

It also commonly happens that from praise of one’s ancestors one may easily recognize the shame and disgrace of descendants, if they have at least failed to equal them, even though they have praised their deeds under the instruction of fame. For just as virtue ennobles many commoners, so nobility without virtues makes many nobles degenerate.

Moreover, it seems impermissible to remain silent about the victories of Catholic princes while proclaiming in resounding words the triumphs of unbelieving tyrants. It is sufficiently ill-advised to write and read about proud Tarquin, Tullius and Ancus, Father Aeneas, the fierce Rutulian, and others of this kind, while entirely neglecting our own Charleses and three Ottos, the Emperor Henry II, the Emperor Conrad, father of the most glorious King Henry III, and that same King Henry, triumphant in Christ.

Modern writers should fear becoming contemptible before God through the fault of sluggishness, since the primitive authority of the Old Testament—which carefully recorded the histories of the Fathers through fruitful labor—prefigures and teaches that the fruit of new events should be stored in the granary of memory. Thus we commemorate that Abraham rescued his cousin Lot in war; thus we learn that the sons of Israel overcame various enemies. Thus, because of the abundance of their writers, we have before our eyes the battles of King David, the counsels of Solomon, the strategies of Gideon, and the wars of the Maccabees.

[Col. 1219D] The ancient philosophers served the commonwealth in various ways. They often reported plausible dreams, by which they led their listeners toward what they had undertaken to affirm. Sometimes, for the same purpose, they invented fabulous narratives veiled beneath respectable things and names, since such fictions were not contrary to philosophy. Often, through open disputation, they established for the rulers of the commonwealth the truth that human souls are immortal. And, as Macrobius reports, Socrates said that the soul does not perish after the body; indeed, nearly all philosophers taught without hesitation that the fruit of human endeavor does not end with life itself, but that all who have aided their homeland and preserved its law enjoy everlasting happiness throughout eternity, while punishment is reserved, by the judgment of the just Creator, for those who despise justice [Col. 1220A].

They proved the immortality of the human soul by many arguments, including this: while confined within bodily bonds, it enjoys such freedom that, now through the celestial regions, now through earthly places, and sometimes through the hidden depths of the sea—things it had never physically seen—it travels by the living movement of thought. At times, while the body is awake, and at other times while it rests, it gathers many future events through its own vision, not another’s, and retains them in memory. Once freed from the cloudy veil of flesh, it enjoys the same vivacity much more freely. They said that believing this—or rather, knowing it—would be of the greatest use to princes, who, often growing sluggish through arrogance, pay too little attention to the advantages of the life to come.

For this reason the ancients made statues and very magnificent monuments for victors, and judged that their deeds ought to be inscribed upon them, so that honor might remain for the dead, for the perpetual memory of posterity, since they believed that their souls lived forever. Although they investigated the immortality of the soul by human wisdom alone—an immortality not yet promised or revealed to them by Christ—they were nevertheless led by this belief both to practice justice themselves and diligently to impress it upon the rulers of their homelands in their writings.

They considered the deeds of the commonwealth to die together with its rulers unless what happened was recorded. They held that, through the negligence of silence, the greatest ruin would result if from surviving writings it were not evident that every person is followed after death by that to which, while alive, he had devoted himself.

But from us, whose sluggish silence has been driven out by the word of truth, which says, “What I tell you in darkness, speak in the light; and what you hear in the ear, preach upon the housetops,” why should Christian princes and defenders of the evangelical faith be denied what pagans voluntarily offer? For if our Catholic kings, defenders of the true faith, govern without danger of error the law and peace of Christ that he handed down to us through his Gospel, then those who make their good deeds known in writing will be doing nothing other than preaching the Gospel of Christ.

Although the mind of a writer may hesitate to undertake difficult matters accomplished with mature judgment, moral seriousness, and the utmost constancy—and although, if such things are done with foolish extravagance, feigned boldness, or shameful ambition, they are matters in which every writer must be involved—both the deeds and the omissions of those whom he records ought to be made public, insofar as the capacity of his intellect permits. From this, religion will have stirred the good toward virtue, intention will have commended them, the homeland will benefit, and blessing will accrue to posterity.

What has passed is readily available; but what is still to come is not foreknown. Moved by this consideration and hope, I wished to write these things for the common benefit of readers, so that they might be pleasant to those who hear them. For if anything dishonorable is presented in them, it will plainly lie within the reader’s power whether to imitate it. I do this also for my own advancement, so that, with God’s prompting, I may avoid idleness—an enemy of the soul—by occupying myself with these tasks while many vices press upon the body.

Since I am prepared to speak of public deeds, I chiefly embrace the acts of two kings: namely, the Emperor Conrad and his son Henry III, whom nearly all wiser men call Henry “the line of justice.” The deeds of the father that occurred in my time I shall depict with a writing pen, as I myself saw them or learned them from the reports of others, for successors who do not know them. But the most illustrious deeds of the son, since by God’s grace he still lives and reigns, I shall not cease gathering for as long as I live.

If it should happen that, just as I was granted entry into this life before the king, so I am granted departure from it, and in this way leave my work unfinished, I beg the writer who comes after me not to be ashamed to set his walls upon my foundations, not to disdain raising up my falling style, and not to begrudge my beginnings, just as he would not wish anyone to begrudge his unfinished work. For if the one who began possesses the middle, there ought not to be anyone ungrateful at the completion of this work when he finds the beginning prepared.

These matters I have set out as a brief preface. Now I shall turn to the emperor’s deeds; but first I shall say a little about how suitable his election was. To make my account more credible, I shall first recall which bishops and other princes at that time provided support for the kingdom.

## ON THE ASSEMBLY OF THE PRINCES

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1023, the Emperor Henry II, after putting the affairs of the Empire in good order and beginning, after long labor, to reap the mature fruit of peace, while the Empire remained secure and his mind sound, was seized by an illness of the body. As it grew worse, he departed this life on the third day before the Ides of July. His body was carried from Saxony for burial to a place called Pabemberg, where he himself, with commendable zeal and devotion, had founded a bishopric distinguished by every ecclesiastical adornment. For its dedication he summoned the apostolic lord, Benedict, by whose authority he confirmed public privileges for the protection of the place through a formal charter.

After the emperor’s death, the commonwealth, deprived of its father and seemingly desolate, soon began to totter. Thus the best men were filled with fear and anxiety, while the worst hoped that the Empire would fall into danger. But divine providence entrusted the anchors of the Church to episcopal men and to such governors as at that time needed to remain in order to steer the homeland without loss into the harbor of peace.

For since the emperor had died without sons, each of the most powerful secular princes relied more on force than intelligence, striving either to become first or, by whatever agreement might be made, to become second to the first. As a result, discord invaded almost the entire kingdom, so thoroughly that in many places killings, fires, and plunderings occurred, had not the momentum of these illustrious men been checked by restraint.

The Empress Cunigunda, although deprived of her husband’s vigor, nevertheless aided the commonwealth to the best of her ability, on the advice of her brothers, Theodoric, bishop of Metz, and Hetzilo, duke of Bavaria; and she directed the acumen of her intellect toward restoring the Empire through anxious and careful deliberation.

The subject requires me to mention the names of certain supreme men, whether bishops or secular princes, who at that time held power in the kingdoms. Francia was accustomed to elect kings through their counsels, so that what I am about to relate may not appear to have happened by mere chance, but may be believed to have been accomplished by the deliberation of the wisest men and therefore to have been useful, honorable, and excellent.

At that time Aribo, a Norican by nationality, noble and wise and suited to royal counsels, governed the archbishopric of Mainz. Pelegrinus held the archbishopric of Cologne; he was Aribo’s kinsman, prudent and fit for that office. Poppo governed the archbishopric of Trier, the brother of Duke Ernest, a pious and humble man who at that same time held his brother’s son, Duke Ernest, under his guardianship together with the duchy of Alemannia.

The noble Theodoric, vigorous in virtue, possessed the bishopric of Metz. Bishop Werinharius presided over the city of Strasbourg, a man noble and devoted to divine and secular duties. Marcelinus [Macelinus], a wise and faithful man in ecclesiastical dignities, occupied the Church of Würzburg. Eberhard, the first bishop of the Church of Bamberg, governed the bishopric of Pabemberg; he was a man greatly needed by the commonwealth for his intelligence and character.

Heimo was prelate of the Church of Constance, a man wise in God, modest, and prudent in worldly affairs. Bruno, brother of the Emperor Henry, governed Augsburg; he was useful and distinguished in intelligence, had he not been obscured by the fraternal hatred with which he opposed the emperor.

The Church of Juvavum, called Salzburg in the common tongue, was governed by the archbishop Gunther, of blessed memory, brother of Counts Eberhard [or Eccard] and Hermann, gentle and good before God and men. Burkhard [or Kebehardus] was bishop of the Church of Regensburg, distinguished for his benevolence. Bishop Albert [Agilbertus] governed the Church of Freising, a prudent administrator of his clergy and people.

With these men many other bishops and abbots from the same regions were present, but naming each individually would make the work tedious. I pass over the prelates of Saxony because I did not know what details concerning their lives or names it would be appropriate to add, although I undoubtedly learned that they were present, offering counsel and assistance in these great affairs.

I pass over Italy, whose princes could not assemble in time for the royal election. Later, when they met the king in the city of Constance together with the archbishop of Milan and the other princes, they became his men and willingly swore allegiance to him.

The dukes who were contemporaries of the men mentioned above were these: Benno, duke of Saxony; Adalbero, duke of Istria; Hetzilo, duke of Bavaria; Ernest, duke of Alemannia; Frederick, duke of Lotharingia; Gozelo, duke of the Ripuarians; Cuno, duke of Worms and of the Franks; and Udalric, duke of Bohemia.

For Burgundy had not yet been subjected to the Roman Empire as it is now. Its subjection is attributed to the glory of three kings. The Emperor Henry II first intended—or attempted—to subject it, and persevered successfully in this undertaking. Then the Emperor Conrad, with courageous force, expelled the Franks from it by war and subdued it. Finally, the pious and peaceful King Henry, “the line of justice,” governed that same Burgundy magnificently in war and peace. What he accomplished there through divine providence, in the counsels, deliberations, and assemblies of both peace and war—some of which I myself attended—I shall relate elsewhere.

Now I return to my subject. Hungary, which that same King Henry III subdued through a noble and extraordinary victory, and after his victory secured for himself and his successors through the wisest policy, would at the time in question not even listen to us.

The bishops and dukes mentioned above, together with the other powerful men, judged that no other means would enable them to escape the threatening danger more effectively or quickly. They therefore employed all their strength and remarkable skill so that the commonwealth would not continue to totter without a ruler.

Private counsels and the inclinations of individuals—whom each would support, oppose, or wish to have as lord—were conveyed through the convenience of letters and envoys, and not in vain. For it is the work of providence to prepare inwardly what one needs outwardly; and counsel before action is the seed of the fruit that follows. You wait in vain for help from another if you do not know [Col. 1223C] what you want.

To deliberate secretly in difficult matters, to consider gradually, and to act swiftly will produce a good outcome. At last a day was agreed upon and a place designated; a public assembly took place, such as I do not remember having seen before. I shall not delay in writing what was done at this assembly, for it deserves remembrance.

## ON THE ELECTION OF THE KING

Between the territories of Mainz and Worms there is a place of broad, level extent, capable of receiving a very great multitude. It is secure and suitable, among the hidden parts of islands, for conducting secret business; but I leave it to topographers to speak more fully about the name and location of the place. I shall return to what I began.

When all the chief men had gathered there—so to speak, the strength and vital organs of the kingdom—they pitched their camps on both sides of the Rhine and around it. Since the river separates Gaul [Col. 1223D] from Germany, the Saxons, together with the Slavs adjacent to them, the East Franks, the Noricans, and the Alemanni assembled on the German side.

From Gaul came the Franks who live above the Rhine, the Ripuarians, and the Lotharingians. The supreme matter was debated, and uncertainty about the election caused hesitation. Suspended between hope and fear, those related to one another and those joined by personal ties spent a very long time examining their conflicting desires.

For they were not deliberating about some moderate matter, but about one which, unless it were heated and thoroughly considered with fervent hearts and the greatest devotion, would bring the entire body of the kingdom to destruction. To use common proverbs, it is better to cook food thoroughly, since food eaten raw produces danger; and, as they say, medicine intended for the eyes must be prepared with care.

In the same way, while there was a prolonged contest over who ought to reign, one candidate was rejected because of an age either too immature or excessively advanced, another because his ability was untested, and certain others because of evident arrogance. From among the many, a few were chosen; and from those few, exactly two were set apart. Upon these the final examination of the leading men, deliberated with the utmost care for a long time, finally came to rest in complete agreement.

There were two Cunoes. One, being older, was called the elder Cuno; the other was called the younger Cuno. Both were among the most noble men in Teutonic Francia, born of two brothers. One was called Hetzel and the other Cuno. We have learned that they were sons of Duke Otto of the Franks, together with two others, Bruno [Col. 1224B] and William. Bruno became pope of the Roman Church of the apostolic see and, changing his name, was called Gregory. William, made bishop of the Church of Strasbourg, raised it to remarkable heights.

The two Cunoes mentioned above, being, as stated, most noble on their fathers’ side, were no less distinguished through their maternal ancestry. The mother of the younger Cuno was Matilda, born from the daughter of Conrad, king of Burgundy [Lombardy]. The mother of the elder Cuno was Adelberta [or Adelbera, or Adelheida], descended from the most noble [most glorious] house of the Lotharingians.

This Adelhayta was the sister of Counts Gerhard and Adalbert, who, constantly contending with kings and dukes, were at last scarcely reconciled on account of their kinsman, King Conrad. Their ancestors, as is reported, came from the ancient race of the Trojan kings, who under the blessed confessor Remigius submitted their necks to the yoke of the faith.

Upon these two men—that is, the elder and the younger Cuno—the rest of the nobility long remained divided. Although nearly everyone, through more secret counsel and eager desire, chose the elder Cuno because of his virtue and probity, each nevertheless cleverly concealed his own inclination on account of the younger Cuno’s power, lest they disagree out of ambition for honor.

At last, by divine providence, it happened that they reached an agreement with one another through an arrangement quite suitable to so uncertain a matter: if the greater part of the people praised one of them, the other would yield to him without delay.

I think it worthwhile to relate how the elder Cuno revealed his intention—not because he despaired of becoming king, for he already perceived that God’s will was being inspired [or: inspired] in the hearts of the princes, but so that he might strengthen his kinsman’s spirit and prevent him from being disturbed by the new situation.

He therefore addressed him in this most excellent speech:

“Joy proportionate to prosperity neither exceeds the bounds of gravity nor permits one to be ungrateful for benefits received. Just as harmful faintheartedness in adversity draws a person toward worse things, so honorable happiness in prosperity leads a person toward better things. And little is the fruit of attained happiness if it does not nourish the soul of the laborer with measured cheerfulness.

“In this way I feel the vigor of my spirit increased by great joy, because the equal consensus of this vast assembly foresaw that only two of us would be placed at the royal summit, one of whom it would set in the royal seat. We ought not to think that we surpass our kinsmen in nobility or wealth, nor should we exalt ourselves in words or deeds as though we had earned anything deserving such veneration.

“Our ancestors preferred to display their glory through deeds rather than words. It will be fitting for all who are among equals to be content with a common life. Whatever it is—in other words, whatever makes us seem more capable than the rest—let us give thanks for it to God, its author.

“We must therefore take care lest we who have been judged worthy of such honor by the consent of others appear unworthy of this grace through our own private and familial dissension. For it is foolish to abuse another’s power excessively as though it were one’s own. In every election no one is permitted to judge himself, though he may judge another.

“If this were permitted to anyone concerning himself, how many petty kings, not to say kings, would we see? The votes, devotion, and agreement of the Franks, Lotharingians, Saxons, Noricans, and Alemanni, who possessed the best intentions, were directed toward us as toward the offspring of a single stock, as toward one house, as toward an indivisible family. No one would suspect that those joined together by so many bonds could be dissolved by enmities.

“It is fitting that all whom nature has bound together should agree, since nature joins those related to one another in friendship. But if we reject something voluntarily offered by others because of some impediment—in other words, if we disagree with one another—it is certain that the people will then wish to abandon us and seek some third person for themselves. We shall not only be deprived of the highest honor, but shall fall into the disgrace of cowardice, which is more detestable to every good man than death—as though we were unable to sustain the virtue required for so great a government, and as though one of us, which I consider a great crime among blood relatives, were unwilling to trust the honor of the other.

“Thus the greatest honor and supreme power still revolve around us, and they have come to us in such a way that, if we wish, they may remain in one of us. Therefore it seems to me that, if this honor remains concentrated in one of us, the other should not thereafter be deprived in some fashion of sharing in the same honor.

“For just as, when one’s relatives enter upon kingship—even though not all are kings—some transmission of honor flows to them, so those who have been enrolled and named for power, even if they do not attain it, will not be entirely without a certain honor derived from it; they would not be summoned to their own dignity undeservedly.

“Furthermore, if the relatives of kings are honored on account of the kings, and if everyone wishes to be such toward us, then, provided we are of one mind with one another and one man’s advancement depends upon the other, who could be happier than we if one of us reigns? The other will, through his goodwill, in a sense render the commonwealth’s service to the one who reigns.

“Let us therefore be cautious. Let us not prefer what is foreign to what is related, or uncertainty to certainty, lest this day—which until now has been sufficiently joyful and pleasant because of such a choice—bring us prolonged misfortune. Thus we would badly handle among ourselves the goodwill conceived by so great a people.

“To prevent this, dearest of all my kinsmen, I wish to say what I think of you. If I learn that the people wish and desire you as their lord and king, I shall not by any evil stratagem withdraw this goodwill from you. Rather, I shall choose you more eagerly than the others, to the extent that I hope to be more pleasing to you than they are. But if God looks favorably upon me, I have no doubt that you will repay me with the due return.”

To this the younger Cuno replied that the entire proposal was acceptable to him, and he most certainly promised that, as his dearest kinsman, if the supreme matter called him, he would show him every royal loyalty. During these words, the elder Cuno bowed slightly before many witnesses and kissed his kinsman. By that kiss it was first discovered that each of them had yielded to the other.

“Having thus established a judgment of concord, the princes sat down. A very great crowd of people stood around:

> Then what each had long concealed, veiled in his heart,  
> He rejoiced that the time had come to bear openly.

The archbishop of Mainz, whose opinion had to be received before that of the others, was asked by the people what he thought. With a full heart and cheerful voice, he praised and elected the elder Cuno as his lord and king, ruler and defender of the homeland.

The other archbishops and the remaining men of the sacred orders undoubtedly followed this judgment. The younger Cuno, after briefly conciliating the Lotharingians, immediately returned and, with the greatest enthusiasm, elected him as lord and king. The king took him by the hand and made him sit beside him.

Then individuals from each kingdom repeatedly spoke the same words of election. A shout arose from the people; all unanimously joined the princes in the election of the king. Everyone desired the elder Cuno and persisted in supporting him. Without hesitation they placed him above all rulers and judged him entirely worthy of royal power. They demanded that no delay occur in his consecration.

The aforementioned Empress Cunigunda willingly [or: without reluctance] offered the royal insignia that the Emperor Henry had left to her, and, insofar as the authority of her sex permitted, strengthened him for kingship.

I certainly believe that the favor of the heavenly powers was not absent from this election, since among men of singular power so many dukes and margraves, without envy and without dispute, chose the man who, although inferior to no one in birth, virtue, or personal possessions, nevertheless possessed little benefit or authority in the commonwealth in comparison with such men.

Although the archbishop of Cologne, Duke Frederick, and certain other Lotharingians departed in an unreconciled state on behalf of the younger Cuno, as rumor had it—indeed, at the instigation of the enemy of peace, the devil—they soon returned. For the sake of those whom the common condition of death had carried off, they came into the king’s favor and willingly accepted whatever he commanded. The archbishop Pelegrinus, as though to make amends for his earlier fault, obtained from the king permission to consecrate the queen in the Church of Cologne.

I shall speak of her in what follows; for now I return to the king. Truly, he was chosen by God’s will, in whom God himself had foreseen the testimony that he later received from men. For he was a man of great humility, prudent in counsel, truthful in speech, vigorous in action, very little given to avarice, and the most generous of all kings in giving. I shall speak more fully of his character later.

This alone must nevertheless be said here: it could not turn out otherwise than that he should become a prince and the greatest of princes, since the vigor of the greatest virtues was present in him. For since it is written, “Humility precedes glory,” he rightly preceded the glorious men of this world, because the queen of virtues clung to him. Therefore it was not right for anyone on earth to wage war against the man whom almighty God had predestined to rule over all.

## ON THE CONSECRATION OF THE KING

After the election had been completed, everyone hastened with the greatest splendor to follow the king to Mainz, so that there he might receive the most sacred anointing. They went rejoicing; the clerics sang psalms [Col. 1227B], and the laymen sang, each in his own manner. I had not yet discovered that God had received such praises from men in one day and one place.

If great Charles had been present alive with his scepter, the people would not have been more enthusiastic, nor could they have rejoiced more at the return of so great a man than at this king’s first arrival.

The king reached Mainz. There, received with the honor due to him, he devoutly awaited his consecration, which all desired. On the day of the Nativity of Holy Mary, when the archbishop of Mainz and all the clergy were solemnly preparing to bless him, during the sacred offices of the royal anointing the archbishop addressed the king in these words:

“Every power of the unstable world flows with utmost purity from a single source. It commonly happens, however, that when several streams proceed from the same origin, they are muddy at one time and clear at another, while the principal fountain remains pure. In the same way, insofar as human nature dares to compare Creator and creature with one another, we wish to draw an analogy between God, the immortal King, and earthly kings.

“For it is written: ‘All power is from God.’ When that almighty King of kings, author and source of all honor, pours the grace of some dignity upon earthly princes, it remains pure and clean insofar as it belongs to the nature of its source. But when it reaches those who have handled this dignity unworthily and polluted it with pride, envy, lust, avarice, anger, impatience, and cruelty, they will offer themselves and all their subjects a dangerous drink of iniquity, unless they cleanse themselves through repentance.

“Let the whole Church of the saints pray and intercede with the Lord, so that the dignity which today is given by God, pure before the Lord and our present king Conrad, may be preserved inviolate by him insofar as human capacity permits.

“Our speech is addressed to you and on your account, lord king. The Lord who chose you to be king over his people first wished to test you and afterward to make you reign. For he chastises everyone whom he receives; he deigned to correct the one whom he wished to receive; it pleased him to humble the one whom he intended to exalt.

“Thus God tested his servant Abraham and glorified him after he had been tested. Thus he permitted David, his servant, to suffer the anger, persecution, and injuries of King Saul, as well as hiding places in the wilderness, flight, and exile; afterward he made him the most glorious king in Israel. Blessed is the one who endures temptation, for he receives the crown.

“God did not discipline you without cause; he has sweetened in you the fruit that follows. He permitted you to lose the favor of your predecessor, the Emperor Henry, and to regain that same favor, so that now you may know how to show mercy to those who lose your favor. You suffered injuries so that now you may know how to show mercy to those who endure injuries. Divine piety wished you to be without discipline so that, after receiving heavenly instruction, you might assume Christian rule.

“You have reached the highest dignity; you are Christ’s vicar. No one is a true ruler except his true imitator. You must think, upon this throne of kingship, about everlasting honor. It is great happiness to reign in the world, but the greatest is to triumph in heaven.

“Since God requires much from you, he desires above all that you practice judgment, justice, and peace for the homeland, which always looks to you; that you be the defender of churches and clergy, and the protector of widows and orphans. Through these and other good works your throne will be established here and forever.

“And now, lord king, the entire holy Church joins us in asking your grace for those who have hitherto sinned against you and lost your favor through some offense. Among them is one named Otto, a noble man who offended you. For him and for all the others we ask your clemency: forgive them for the love of God, who today has transformed you into another man and made you a participant in his divinity, so that he himself may deign to repay you in kind for all your sins.”

Moved by mercy at this speech, the king groaned and overflowed with tears beyond what can be believed. Then, as the bishops, dukes, and the whole people pleaded, he forgave everyone for whatever they had done against him. The entire people received this gratefully. All wept for joy at the king’s manifest piety:

> He would be made of iron who could not weep.

Such great power forgave such great offenses. And although, had he never become king, he could have avenged his wrongs, nevertheless, relying on no confidence in such great power, he reserved nothing for vengeance. After the divine offices and the royal consecration had been completed with the greatest dignity, the king proceeded; and, as it is written of King Saul, he went “higher than all the people from his shoulders upward,” and, transformed into a certain appearance never before seen in him, returned to his chamber with the sacred retinue, cheerful in countenance and dignified in bearing. From there he was escorted to the table with royal splendor and passed that day, the first of his royal state, with the utmost courtesy.

## ON THE COURTLY ARRANGEMENTS AND ON THE QUEEN

I think it unnecessary to say much about the oath of fidelity made to the king, since frequent usage bears witness that all bishops, dukes, and the other princes, the leading soldiers, the common soldiers, indeed all free men of any consequence, swear fidelity to kings. Nevertheless, all submitted by oath with greater sincerity and willingness. Likewise, in the arrangement of the court—whom the king should appoint master of the household, whom he should designate as masters of the chamber, purveyors, cupbearers, and the other officers—it is not necessary to linger long, since I can say this briefly: I neither remember nor have read of any predecessor whose ministries were more suitably or honorably provided for.

In this matter he greatly valued the ability and advice of Bruno, bishop of Augsburg, and of Wernher, bishop of Strasbourg. So, too, he relied on the counsel of the soldier Werniharius, whom the king had long experienced at his side as cautious in counsel and bold in war. Through the cherished queen Gisela’s prudence and advice, all the proud were kept in check. Her father was Heriman, duke of Alemannia; her mother, Kerbirga, was the daughter of Conrad, king of Burgundy, whose parents descended from the stock of Charlemagne. Hence one of our number, in a little book which he called the *Tetralogus* and later presented to King Henry III while he was celebrating the Nativity of the Lord in the city of Strasbourg, composed among other verses these two:

> When the fourth line is counted after the tenth,  
> From Charlemagne proceeds the prudent Gisela.

Although she possessed such great nobility and a most becoming appearance, she was entirely free from arrogance; she was reverent in God’s service, constant in prayers and almsgiving, and attended to these as secretly as she could, mindful of the Gospel injunction not to perform one’s righteousness before men. She was generous in disposition, distinguished in intelligence, eager for glory rather than praise, fond of modesty, patient in feminine labor, not at all wasteful in vain things, abundantly generous in honorable and useful matters, wealthy in estates, and skilled in managing the highest honors.

The envy of certain people—an envy that often rises like smoke from those below against those above—prevented her consecration for several days. Whether she endured that hatred justly or unjustly remains still a matter of dispute. Nevertheless, masculine virtue prevailed in the woman, and, consecrated with the consent and at the petition of the princes, she followed the king as his necessary companion.

For the moment I have abbreviated what concerns the queen. Passing over the royal deeds, I shall now return to them.

## ON THE FIRST DEEDS OF KING CHUONRAD

Returning in my writing to the deeds of the illustrious King Chuonrad, I must relate certain things that he did on the very day of his consecration. Although they may seem small, they are nevertheless richly endowed with a certain mystery. But since this is a public history, which seems more suited to directing the reader’s attention to the novelty of events than to figures of speech, it is better to pursue the matter in full than to intermingle mystical interpretations indiscriminately.

During the king’s procession, three people came before him, each with a complaint. One was a tenant of the Church of Mainz, another was an orphan, and the third was a widow. When the king began to hear their cases, some of his princes tried to turn him away, telling him not to delay his consecration and to hear the divine offices at the appointed time. Looking toward the bishops, he replied in a thoroughly Christian manner, as Christ’s vicar:

“If it is my duty to devote myself to government, and if it is the mark of a steadfast man not to postpone what can suitably be done, it seems more right for me to do what I ought than to hear from another what ought to be done. I remember that you have often said that it is not the hearers of the law but the doers who are justified. But if, as you say, we must hasten to the consecration, then I ought to plant my steps more cautiously in God’s work, the closer I recognize myself to be approaching an arduous dignity.”

Saying this, he remained at the same station where those afflicted persons had first met him, and, without moving his feet, set the law before them. Proceeding a little farther, someone came before him and said that he had been expelled from his homeland entirely without fault. The king seized him by the arm, drew him through the crowd of bystanders to his own throne, and there carefully entrusted the poor man’s case to one of his princes.

A happy beginning to a reign is evident when there is greater haste to administer justice than to bless the king. The king’s zeal for compassion was greater than his desire for consecration: when he sought royal honor, he walked along the path of justice. He could say with the Psalmist: “My foot has stood on the right path.” He established himself through the goodness of grace before he ascended the judicial throne. He feared being thrown down if there were no support beneath him at the height of kingship. Amid new joys and the king’s delightful ceremonies, it was most praiseworthy to hear so many cries of the poor and settle their cases.

He did not wish to neglect what he could quickly govern; he refused to delay justice, because that was what ruling meant. He postponed his blessing for the sake of royal honor, for it is written: “The honor of the king loves judgment.”

> In all things nothing can be so beneficial  
> As the king’s judgment applied to its duty.

Thus, in such cases—the very cases for which royal authority is chiefly invoked, namely, the defense of churches, widows, and orphans—the king prepared for himself on that day a path toward the rest of his government.

## ON THE KING’S JOURNEY THROUGH THE KINGDOMS

I have not thought it especially necessary to recount all the king’s journeys and the places where he annually celebrated the principal feasts of the Nativity of the Lord and of Easter, except that I must mention whatever notable and distinguished event occurred in any place. If I wished to record everything, my strength would fail before the material did.

As soon as I can, I shall come to his most illustrious deeds, in which so much glory shines forth that no one will resent my silence about lesser matters. Having gathered his royal retinue, King Chuonrad first traveled through the region of the Ripuarians and reached the place called Aachen Palace. There the public royal throne, established by the ancient kings and especially by Charles, is regarded as the chief throne of the entire kingdom.

Seated there, he organized the commonwealth with the greatest distinction. Holding a public tribunal and general council, he distributed divine and human laws usefully. His reputation drew its strength from his virtues. Everyone regarded him as more distinguished than the day before in maintaining peace, dearer because of his goodwill, and more honored because of his royal retinue.

Although he was ignorant of letters, he prudently instructed the entire clergy—openly, with affection and generosity, and privately, with appropriate discipline. He greatly won the hearts of the soldiers by refusing to allow the ancient benefices of their parents to be taken from any of their descendants. Moreover, because of the frequent gifts by which he compelled them to dare brave deeds, they judged that no one like him could be found anywhere in the world.

It is tiresome to relate how generous he was, how pleasant, how steadfast in spirit, how fearless; how gracious to all good men and severe toward the wicked; kind to his subjects and harsh toward his enemies; effective in all that he undertook; and how tireless he was in whatever served the kingdom. He made such progress in a short time that no one doubted that, since the days of Charlemagne, no one more worthy of the royal throne had lived. Hence there is the proverb: “The seat of Chuonrad has the stairways of Charles.”

One of our number, in a little book he called the *Gallinarius*, brought forth this verse in his fourth satire concerning that proverb:

> Chuonrad treads the stairways of King Charles,

Such signs carried the king’s name and glory beyond the regions of nations and across the waves of the sea. Everywhere the virtue that continually flowed from his inexhaustible vigor was proclaimed.

Returning from the Ripuarian region, the king came to Saxony. There, according to the will of the Saxons, he confirmed with steadfast authority their exceedingly harsh law. Then, exacting tribute from the barbarians who bordered Saxony, he collected every fiscal due. From there he passed through Bavaria and eastern Francia and reached Alemannia. In passing through these lands, he most firmly enclosed the kingdoms within the treaty of peace and royal protection.

## HOW THE KING HELD A TRIBUNAL WITH THE ITALIANS

In the first year of his reign, King Chuonrad celebrated holy Pentecost in the city of Constance. There Heribert, archbishop of Milan, met the king with the other leading Italians. He became bound to his cause and swore fidelity to him by the pledge of oaths and hostages: when the king came with an army to subjugate Italy, Heribert himself would receive him and publicly praise him as lord and king with all his people, and would immediately acclaim and crown him.

The other Lombards had made a similar arrangement because of the people of Ticinum, who are also called Papians. Their envoys were present with gifts and friendly intentions, attempting to appease the king for the offense of their fellow citizens, although they could in no way obtain from the king what they desired.

I shall briefly explain the offense. In the city of Pavia stood a palace once constructed by King Theoderic with marvelous workmanship and later excessively embellished by the Emperor Otto III. When the Pavians learned of the death of the Emperor Henry, the predecessor of King Chuonrad, they immediately—following the usual human tendency to behave immoderately in new circumstances—rushed imprudently against the defenseless court.

> With unlawful boldness they broke the king’s walls,

and they dug up the entire palace down to the lowest foundation stone, so that no king might ever again decide to establish a palace within that city. Because of this bold act, a great dispute continued for a long time between the king and the Pavians.

The Pavians said: “Whom have we offended? We preserved fidelity and honor toward our emperor to the end of his life. After his death, when we had no king, we cannot rightly be accused of having destroyed our king’s house.”

The king, on the contrary, replied: “I know that you did not destroy your king’s house when you had no king at that time; but you cannot deny that you demolished a royal house. If the king has perished, the kingdom remains, just as a ship remains when its helmsman falls. These were public buildings, not private property; they belonged to another, not to you. Those who seize another’s property are liable to the king. Therefore you were trespassers upon another’s property, and consequently you are liable to the king.”

After the king had insistently pressed many arguments of this sort upon them, the envoys abandoned the peace they had unsuccessfully sought and departed. The other Italians, however, were honored with very great gifts by the king and dismissed in peace.

The king, having properly organized the kingdom of Swabia, proceeded to the castle of Turicum, where he received into his dominion certain Italians who had not come to Constance. A few days later he reached the city of Basel.

## THAT KING CHUONRAD APPOINTED A BISHOP AT BASEL

The city of Basel lies at a threefold frontier, namely, of Burgundy, Alemannia, and Francia; the city itself, however, belongs to Burgundy. The king found the city without a bishop, since its administrator, Adalbero, had departed this world three months before the king’s arrival.

There the heresy of simony suddenly appeared and quickly vanished. For the king and queen accepted an immense sum of money for the bishopric from a certain cleric, a nobleman named Udalric, who was then made bishop there. Later, moved by repentance, the king bound himself by a vow not to accept any more money for a bishopric or abbey. He almost faithfully kept this vow. But his third son, Henry, who later became king and Augustus, admirably and without scruple made amends for his father’s vow, since throughout his entire life he is not said to have accepted even the value of a single penny for any ecclesiastical dignity.

King Chuonrad, after holding a royal conference at Basel and carefully taking possession of the Burgundian borders beyond the will of Rudolf, king of Burgundy, reached Saxony by way of the Rhine.

Why I have mentioned King Rudolf I shall briefly explain. In his old age this Rudolf, king of Burgundy, governed his kingdom leniently, thereby arousing the greatest envy among the princes of his realm. He invited Emperor Henry, the son of his sister, into the kingdom and designated him king of Burgundy after his own death, making the princes of the kingdom swear allegiance to him.

To secure this arrangement, Emperor Henry spent an immense amount of money, again and again. But after the Emperor Henry’s death, King Rudolf wished to invalidate his promises. King Chuonrad, intent on increasing rather than diminishing the kingdom and wishing to reap the labors of his predecessor, brought Basel under his control, so that he might see whether King Rudolf would honor his promises. Queen Gisela, the daughter of King Rudolf’s sister, later reconciled them well.

## ON BOLISLAUS, DUKE OF THE SLAVS

In the same year mentioned above, Bolislaus the Slav-born, duke of the Bolonians, arrogated to himself the royal insignia and royal name as an insult to King Chuonrad. Death quickly emptied his boldness of substance.

His son Misico, likewise a rebel, drove out his brother Otto into the province of Ruhnia because Otto favored the king’s party. How King Chuonrad later restrained the insolence of this Misico and the treachery of a certain Udalric, duke of Bohemia, I shall relate in its proper place.

## ON THE ENMITY BETWEEN THE KING AND DUKE ERNEST

At the same time, at the urging of the devil, the enemy of peace, Ernest, duke of Alemannia, Chuno, duke of Francia, Frederick, duke of the Lotharingians, and many others joined together against King Chuonrad. They plotted many things and prepared many fortifications in vain, achieving nothing except the calamity that was to come.

King Chuonrad paid no attention to them and set out for Italy with his forces. But Duke Ernest humbly followed him as far as Augsburg. Through the intervention of his mother, the queen, his brother Henry, who was still a child, and other princes, and despite the king’s great reluctance, he was scarcely received back into the king’s favor.

## THAT THE KING RETURNED TO ITALY WITH AN ARMY

In the year of Christ’s incarnation 1026, King Chuonrad, at the counsel and request of the princes of the kingdom, designated his son, the boy Henry, as king after him and entrusted him to Bruno, bishop of the Church of Augsburg, for protection.

Carefully setting his aforementioned enemies against one another through his son and his other faithful men, he himself began to march into Italy with a numerous army. In this expedition, the aforementioned Ernest, duke of Alemannia, serving the king for a time, received the abbey of Kempten from the king as a benefice, although it was contrary to law and right for him to possess it freely rather than serve generously; he was then honorably sent back to protect his homeland.

## THAT THE KING AFFLICTED THE PAVIANS

The king entered Italy through Verona, between Milan and Pavia, and came to Vercelli, where he celebrated holy Easter. During those Easter days Leo, bishop of that city, a very wise man, departed this world, and Harderic, a canon of Milan, succeeded him.

The king had by then subjugated almost the whole plain of Italy to his authority. He could not suddenly capture the city of Pavia, since it was very populous. He refused to receive the Pavians back into his favor because they still refused to rebuild the palace they had destroyed on the site where it had previously stood. Instead, he began to crush their defenders—Margrave Adalbert, Wilhelm, and the other princes in those territories—with remarkable force.

He destroyed their castle called Urba and dismantled many other castles and extremely strong fortifications. At that time a great evil occurred in Italy because of the conflict with the Pavians. Many of their churches, together with the castles around them, were burned, and the people who had taken refuge there perished by fire and sword. The fields were devastated and the vineyards cut down. The king blocked all exit and entrance, seized their boats, prohibited commerce, and afflicted all the people of Ticinum in this way for two years, until they had completed everything he commanded, postponing nothing at all.

## ON THE SEDITION THAT TOOK PLACE AT RAVENNA

At the same time King Chuonrad entered Ravenna and ruled there with great authority. One day the wretched Ravennates provoked a quarrel with the king’s army. Trusting in their numbers, they attempted to drive the army from the city and, through the narrowness of one of the gates, prevented those outside from bringing aid to those within.

When the tumult had arisen, the fighting began to grow more violent everywhere. Some attacked their guests in the houses; others fought in the streets; others besieged the gates; many from the walls, and many from the high towers, engaged in a cowardly battle with stones and clubs.

The Germans, on the other hand, resisting with arms and ingenuity, formed lines in front and behind and surrounded the Ravennates. As their swords raged and opened a path toward one another, they left those who had been caught in the middle dead, wounded, or fleeing.

A certain count named Eppo, an excellent soldier from Bavaria, left the city with Panon and subdued those who were holding the bridge. Many of them, thrown headlong from the bridge by that one man, were drowned in the water.

King Chuonrad, who was in his chamber, learned of the sedition, seized his arms, called for his horse, and left the palace courtyard. When he saw the Ravennates defeated in battle, fleeing to the churches, and seeking hiding places everywhere, he took pity on them, since both sides were his subjects. He recalled the army from pursuing the citizens and withdrew himself into the palace.

When morning came, the surviving Ravennates, wearing sackcloth and barefoot, with drawn swords, as their law required, came before the king after the defeat of their fellow citizens and, as he commanded, made satisfaction in every way.

There King Chuonrad showed his customary great generosity toward a wounded German. The man’s foot had been completely severed in battle, together with a large part of the leg above the ankle. The king ordered his leather boots to be brought, commanded that both be filled with coins, and ordered them placed beside the wounded soldier’s bed.

## THE KING WITHDREW INTO THE MOUNTAINS BECAUSE OF THE HEAT

At that time an extreme heat afflicted Italy, so that many animals and a great number of people were endangered by it. King Chuonrad, yielding to no one except God and the waves of the heat, withdrew beyond the river Atim into the mountains because of the shade and the temperateness of the air. There he received royal sustenance lavishly from the archbishop of Milan for two months and more.

Leaving from there in the autumn, he traversed the Italian plain again, held councils and royal conferences in suitable places, and sent rebels into chains. Thus he pacified the kingdom and, proceeding onward, reached the border of Italy and Burgundy.

## THAT THE ENVOYS OF KING RUDOLF CAME TO KING CHUONRAD IN ITALY

At the beginning of the year of Christ’s birth 1027, King Chuonrad celebrated Christmas in the royal city of Ipo. Envoys of King Rudolf of Burgundy came there, promising that Rudolf would come to Rome for King Chuonrad’s imperial election and consecration.

The king gladly accepted this, dismissed the envoys with gifts, and himself crossed the Po and began to make his way toward Rome. When he reached the city of Lucca, he found it opposed to him, together with Margrave Reginher. After remaining there for a short time, the king received the city and the margrave into submission a few days later. He quickly subjugated all Tuscany to himself, and thus, triumphing, visited the Roman citadel.

## THAT KING CHUONRAD BECAME EMPEROR AT ROME

King Chuonrad entered Rome in the same year, as stated above—that is, from the Nativity of the Savior in 1027, in the tenth indiction—and was magnificently received with royal honor by Pope John and all the Romans.

On holy Easter Day, which in that year fell on 26 March, he was elected emperor by the Romans and received the imperial blessing from the pope,

and was called Caesar and Augustus by the Roman name. Queen Gisela likewise received there the consecration and title of empress.

After these events had been completed, and the divine office had ended, the emperor, positioned between the two kings—Rudolf, king of Burgundy, and Cnut, king of the English—was honorably escorted to his chamber.

During those same Easter days, a great sedition arose between the Romans and the Germans over a trivial matter. Two men were quarreling over an oxhide. When they began striking each other with their fists, the whole imperial army was aroused, and armed horsemen and foot soldiers gathered from both sides.

On our side, a certain young man named Berrengar was killed, the son of Count Lutold of Alemannia, a man of very noble birth and exceedingly warlike. The Romans resisted for a long time, but at last, defeated, they fled, and countless numbers of them perished.

Because the emperor had loved the aforementioned young man and held him as a close companion, he ordered him to be buried beside the tomb of Caesar Otto. On the following day the Romans who had caused the sedition came before the emperor. The free men were barefoot and carried naked swords; the slaves wore withes around their necks, as though prepared for hanging. As the emperor commanded, they made satisfaction.

## THAT THE EMPEROR CAME INTO APULIA

After peace had been made between the Romans and the Germans, the emperor proceeded into Apulia. He subjugated Benevento, Capua, and the other cities of that region, whether by force or voluntary submission. He also granted the Normans who had gathered in Apulia—driven from their homeland, I do not know by what necessity—permission to live there, and united them with his princes to defend the borders of the kingdom against the stratagems of the Greeks.

Since everything was turning out properly and successfully for him, the emperor returned, passing through Rome, and again traversed Italy.

## ON THE TYRANT THASSELGART

At that time there was in Italy a certain tyrant named Thasselgart, who had committed many crimes in the kingdom during the reign of Emperor Henry. He had escaped Emperor Henry’s persecution through the sea-retreats and other fortifications he possessed, which were extraordinarily secure.

He was noble by birth, contemptible in person, disgraceful in morals, and a great plunderer of churches and widows. Emperor Chuonrad pursued him most diligently and opposed him in every way with ambushes before and behind.

When Thasselgart wished to flee from one of his castles to another, he was captured by the emperor’s soldiers. When the emperor heard this, he hurried with great speed, so that he traversed almost one hundred Latin miles within a day and a night. For he was thinking that, as usual, the man might escape again.

When the emperor arrived, the tyrant himself was brought before him. On seeing him, the emperor is said to have asked:

“Are you not that lion who devoured the beasts of Italy? By the holy cross of the Lord, such a lion shall eat no more of my bread.”

With these words, and after all the princes of the kingdom had adjudged him, he ordered him to be hanged on the gallows. Once he had been hanged, peace and security, which had long lain hidden, emerged throughout that entire province together.

## ON THE CONSPIRACY OF CERTAIN GERMANS

Meanwhile, while the emperor remained in Italy, great envy, many schemes, and many factions against him broke out in vain among the Germans.

To begin with the lesser and proceed to the greater: a certain count in Swabia named Wolff, rich in estates and powerful in arms, and Bruno, bishop of Augsburg, engaged in conflict with one another and inflicted much harm upon the kingdom through devastation and fires.

At last the aforementioned count burst into Augsburg itself, plundered the bishop’s treasury, and ravaged the entire city. Later, compelled by the emperor, he restored everything and made compensation to the bishop.

Chuno, duke of Worms and the emperor’s cousin, was neither faithful to the emperor nor, nevertheless, very harmful to him, and meanwhile remained quiet.

Frederick, duke of the Lotharingians and stepfather of the aforementioned Chuno, was overtaken by his own death while acting as an enemy of the emperor.

Ernest, duke of Alemannia and stepson of Emperor Chuonrad, had recently been elevated by him through benefices and gifts. But after departing again, and at the devil’s prompting, he plotted rebellion. On the advice of certain soldiers of his, he ravaged the province of Alsace and destroyed the castles of Count Hugh, who was related to the emperor.

Then, having gathered a large army of young men, he invaded Burgundy. Beyond the castle of Solothurn he began to fortify an island with an embankment and ditch. But King Rudolf of Burgundy, fearing to receive an enemy of the emperor, prevented him from carrying out the undertaking.

Returning from there, Ernest fortified a certain castle above Zurich. By excessively plundering the Church of Reichenau and the abbey of Saint Gall, he inflicted no small damage upon the homeland. Thus, setting aside law and justice, he persisted in his wicked efforts until the emperor’s return.

## WHERE DUKE ERNEST SURRENDERED HIMSELF AGAIN

After peace had been confirmed throughout Italy, Emperor Chuonrad returned successfully to Alemannia. At Augsburg he held a familiar conference with his faithful men and began to discuss the traitors of the homeland.

From there he came to the town called Ulm, where a public conference had been arranged. Duke Ernest came there, not with a humble plea, but trusting in the multitude of his soldiers, whom he had selected as the best. He intended either to make peace with Caesar according to his own pleasure or to depart from there by force.

After conferring with his men, he first reminded them of the faith they had promised under oath. Then he urged them not to abandon him or cause him to lose his honor. It was not fitting, he said, that they should forget that the histories of their fathers always testified that the Alemannians were men of good faith and steadfastness toward their lords. If they remained faithful to him, their rewards and the glory and honor of their descendants would be assured.

When he had spoken thus, two counts, Frederick and Anselm, replied on behalf of the others:

“We do not deny that we would firmly promise you our support against all, except him who gave us to you. If we were servants of our king and emperor and had been assigned by him to your authority, it would not be lawful for us to separate from you.

“But since we are free, and since we have as the supreme defender of our freedom our king and emperor, if we abandon him, we lose the freedom which, as someone has said, no good man loses except together with life itself.

“Since this is so, whatever honorable and just thing you require from us, we are willing to obey you in it. But if you wish to act against this, we shall freely return to the place from which we came to you conditionally.”

When he heard this, the duke realized that his own men were abandoning him. Without any agreement, he surrendered himself to the emperor. Caesar had him exiled to Saxony, upon a certain rock called Gibichenstein, so that, once chastened for his rebellion, he might cease from it thereafter.

## THAT THE KING OF BURGUNDY MET THE EMPEROR AT BASEL

The emperor crossed Alemannia, receiving into submission all who had rebelled against him and demolishing their fortifications. When he reached Basel, he addressed Rudolf, king of Burgundy, who had come to meet him outside the city near a village called Mitthena.

After holding a familiar conference, the emperor led the king into the city. Peace was confirmed between them, with Empress Gisela meditating all these matters. The kingdom of Burgundy was handed over to the emperor under the same agreement by which it had previously been given to his predecessor, Emperor Henry.

The king, enriched again with gifts, returned with his men to Burgundy. The emperor, meanwhile, went down by way of the Rhine into Francia. There his cousin Chuno, who had earlier rebelled, surrendered himself. The emperor kept him for a while in lenient custody as a punishment; then, after destroying his excellent fortifications, he received him back into favor and restored everything to him in honor.

A short time later Adalbero, duke of the Istrians or Carinthians, convicted of treason, was defeated by the emperor and exiled with his sons. The emperor gave his duchy to this Chuno; it is said that Chuno’s father had held that duchy long before.

Thus Duke Chuno remained faithful and served well Emperor Chuonrad and his son, King Henry, for as long as he lived.

## ON THE EMBASSY OF THE BISHOP OF STRASBOURG

At the same time, Wernher, bishop of the city of Strasbourg, was sent by the emperor as an envoy to Constantinople.

Although he pretended, as we thought, that he was going to Jerusalem for the sake of prayer, he was wonderfully prevented by the judgment of the Lord, whom no one can deceive. For he was leading with him a large retinue of men and an even larger number of mute animals—horses, oxen, sheep, and pigs—as well as an excessive quantity of worldly luxuries.

When he reached Hungary, King Stephen barred his way. Nothing of this sort had happened to any farmer at that time. From there he returned through Bavaria, crossed into Italy with his entire retinue, and remained for a long time near the borders of Verona. At last, with the greatest difficulty, he entered the Adriatic Sea by way of Venice and reached Constantinople in an unfortunate voyage.

When he had been honorably received by the Greek emperor and was treated by him with considerable familiarity, he began to desire to visit Jerusalem with the emperor’s assistance. But, since something always intervened to prevent that desire, he was never able to attain it.

In the following period he died and was buried in the same city. His bishopric was assumed by Wilhelm, a canon of Strasbourg. The Greek emperor later wrote the reason for the embassy to Emperor Chuonrad in letters written in gold.

## THAT THE EMPEROR HAD HIS SON HENRY CONSECRATED KING

In the year of the Lord 1028, in the eleventh indiction, Emperor Chuonrad had his son Henry, an eleven-year-old boy of great intelligence and good character, raised to the royal dignity by Piligrim, archbishop of Cologne, at Aachen Palace, with the princes of the kingdom and the entire multitude of the people approving it.

He was then consecrated and crowned on the principal Sunday of Easter, and thereby tripled the joy of Easter. For whereas in earlier years the world had honored two crowns, namely those of his father

and his mother, now a third was added:

> The hope of peace that the king made with Caesar,

especially since the one crowned was of an age worthy of such a long course [the wording is uncertain].

Afterward, as they traveled through the various kingdoms, the emperor acting in person and the king, under the guardianship and direction of Bruno, bishop of Augsburg, subdued all rebels and everywhere successfully confirmed treaties of peace.

## ON THE DEATH OF THE BISHOP OF AUGSBURG

In the following year the emperor celebrated Easter at Regensburg in Bavaria. There Bruno, bishop of Augsburg, died. The empress accompanied his body, and, together with her son King Henry, had it honorably buried at his own see of Augsburg.

That bishop Bruno was himself very noble. Since he was the brother of Emperor Henry, he was the son of the empress Gisela’s maternal aunt [the printed text is corrupt here]. His sister, married to Stephen, king of Hungary, was the cause of the Christian faith’s first establishment among the Pannonian people.

Eberhard succeeded to the bishopric of Augsburg.

## HOW DUKE ERNEST RECEIVED THE DUCHY AND IMMEDIATELY LOST IT

In the year of the Lord 1030, Emperor Chuonrad celebrated Easter at Ingelheim. There Ernest, the duke of Alemannia mentioned above, was released from custody and received back his duchy, on the condition that he would pursue his soldier Wehelon, who had disturbed the realm through many factions, as an enemy of the commonwealth, together with all his men, and that he would confirm under oath that he would do so.

When the duke refused to carry this out, he was judged a public enemy of the emperor and, having completely lost the duchy, departed with a few followers.

The emperor gave the duchy of Alemannia to the younger Herman, Ernest’s brother, and entrusted him to Warmann, bishop of Constance.

By the common counsel of all the princes of the kingdom, the emperor had that Ernest and all who resisted justice and peace excommunicated by the bishops, and ordered their property to be confiscated.

The empress Gisela herself—something marvelous to say, but praiseworthy in action—put her rash son after her wise husband and publicly gave her word to all that, whatever happened to him, she would exact no vengeance and would harbor no ill will on that account.

## THAT THE EMPEROR CAME WITH AN ARMY AGAINST THE HUNGARIANS

At the same time, many disputes arose between the Pannonian people and the Bavarians, though they were caused by the fault of the Bavarians. King Stephen of Hungary consequently made many incursions and raids in the kingdom of the Noricans, that is, the Bavarians.

Moved by this, Emperor Chuonrad came against the Hungarians with a great army. King Stephen, being entirely unequal to the emperor, called for prayers and fasts throughout his kingdom and sought only the Lord’s protection.
