The emperor was unable to enter a kingdom so strongly defended by rivers and forests. Nevertheless, by many raids and fires around its borders, he sufficiently avenged his wrongs, then withdrew, intending to carry out his undertaking at a more suitable time.

But his son, King Henry, still a very young boy and entrusted to Eigilbert, bishop of Freising, received an embassy from King Stephen, who was asking for peace. Acting justly and wisely, he received into friendship a king who had been unjustly injured and who of his own accord was seeking mercy.

## HOW DUKE ERNEST SOUGHT AID FROM COUNT ODO

Meanwhile, while these things were happening, the aforementioned Ernest, deprived of the dignity of the duchy, spent great efforts in vain, thinking and undertaking many things to determine how he might resist the emperor. Taking with him his knight Welfone and a few others, he went into Latin Francia to Count Odo, his kinsman; for Odo’s mother and the mother of Empress Gisela had been sisters. When he asked him for counsel and assistance, Odo—whether he was unwilling or dared not—gave him no support against the emperor.

## HOW DUKE ERNEST PERISHED

Duke Ernest, having returned, came again into Alemannia. There, in a certain wilderness called the Black Forest, remaining in very secure places, he lived for some time by pitiable plunder. At last, when he was being hemmed in on every side by the emperor’s soldiery, certain men who favored the emperor ambushed in the pastures the horses that the duke and all his men possessed, the best of their animals.

The duke, having lost the horses in which he had placed his confidence and having nothing more to rely upon, was uncertain what to do amid such confusion. Nevertheless, gathering from every side whatever horses he could obtain, he left the forest with all those whom he then had, reflecting that it was better to die honorably than to live shamefully.

When they had reached the forest passes in that region of Alemannia called Bara, they saw an abandoned camp which the enemy had occupied the previous night. They immediately realized that an ambush was being prepared for them. For Count Manegold, an imperial knight who held from the emperor a large benefice of the abbey of Augia, had been stationed there under the protection of Warmann, bishop of Constance, who at that time governed Alemannia in place of Duke Herman, so that Duke Ernest might commit no plundering or arson in the region.

At once Duke Ernest and his followers became exceedingly eager, thinking that they would quickly avenge their injuries upon the enemy. Taking the road, they began to pursue those who were pursuing them. With the same intention, Count Manegold and those who had been with him advanced here and there, carefully watching the duke’s movements. On this occasion the two sides came so close together that they could see and address one another. There were, however, many more knights on Manegold’s side than on the duke’s.

Without delay they engaged in battle, and all those on the duke’s side fought fiercely, impelled by anger, ferocity, and boldness; those on the other side were moved by the promise of glory and reward. The men who had been with the duke, giving no thought to their lives, were all hastening toward death. But the duke, since he spared no one, found no one who spared him in this battle. Wounded by many men, he was finally killed and fell.

There Count Wecilo [also Wehelo], the duke’s knight, fell—the cause of all these events. Adelbert and Iwerin, noble men, and many others were killed there. On the other side, Count Manegold himself, the author of this encounter, fell, together with many others.

The body of Duke Ernest was brought to Constance and, after first receiving absolution from the episcopal authority for his excommunication, was buried in the church of Saint Mary. The body of Manegold was buried at Augia.

This ever-grievous and disastrous battle occurred on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of September [18 August]. When this was announced to the emperor, he is said to have remarked:

> Rarely will rabid dogs multiply their offspring.

## KING RUDOLF OF BURGUNDY DIED, AND ODO [also UDO] INVADED HIS KINGDOM

In the year of the Lord 1032, Rudolf, king of Burgundy and maternal uncle of Empress Gisela, died in peace. Count Odo [also Udo], a Frank and the son of his sister, invaded his kingdom and captured certain very strongly fortified castles or cities, whether by treachery or by war. He did not dare to make himself king, but neither was he willing to relinquish the kingdom. Someone reported that he had often said that he never wished to become king, but always wished to be the king’s master.

In this way he disrupted a large part of Burgundy, although the kingdom of Burgundy had been confirmed by oath to the emperor Conrad and his son King Henry by King Rudolf, for the time after Rudolf himself should no longer survive. But while Count Odo was doing these things in Burgundy, the emperor Conrad was conducting an armed campaign in Sclavonia. What he did there, and how he later drove Odo out of Burgundy, I shall relate in due course.

The aforementioned Boleslav, duke of the Poles, died and left two sons, Misico and Otto. While Misico was pursuing his brother Otto, he had driven him into Russia. After living there miserably for some time, Otto began to ask the emperor Conrad for mercy, so that, with the emperor ruling and helping him, he might be restored to his homeland.

When the emperor wished to do this, he decreed that he himself should attack Misico with forces from one side, while Misico’s brother Otto attacked from the other. Unable to withstand this assault, Misico fled to Bohemia to Duke Udalric, with whom the emperor was then angry. But Udalric, wishing in this way to appease the emperor, intended to hand Misico over to him. Caesar rejected this wicked arrangement, saying that he did not wish to purchase an enemy from an enemy.

Otto was restored to his homeland and made duke by Caesar. After some time, however, when he was acting less cautiously, he was secretly killed by one of his own household. Then Misico sought in every way to gain the favor of Empress Gisela and the other princes, so that he might deserve to return to the emperor’s grace.

Moved by mercy, Caesar forgave him. Dividing the province of the Poles into three parts, he made Misico tetrarch and entrusted the other two parts to two other men. Thus, as his power was diminished, his rashness became less dangerous. After Misico’s death, his son Casimir faithfully served our emperors up to the present time.

## HOW THE EMPEROR WENT INTO BURGUNDY WITH HIS SON HENRY

In the year of the Lord 1033, the emperor Conrad celebrated Christmas in the city of Strasbourg with his son, King Henry. From there, having gathered an army, he entered Burgundy by way of Solothurn. Coming to the monastery of Payerne on the Purification of Saint Mary, he was chosen to govern Burgundy by the great and small of the kingdom, and on that very day was crowned king. He then besieged certain castles which Odo had invaded, but was greatly hindered by the excessive severity of the winter that had then set in.

Because of this extraordinary cold, one of our men composed a hundred verses and presented them to the emperor. In them, extraordinary things are related: that the horses in the camp around the castle of Murat, if they had planted their feet in the earth and attempted to do something during the warmth of day, became so frozen during the night that they could not be pulled from the surrounding frozen ground except with axes and poles.

One man, having no assistance, killed his own horse when it had become fixed in this way, stripped away its hide from the legs upward, and left the remainder embedded in the frozen earth. Human beings, too, were greatly disfigured by this cold. The faces of young and old alike were the same: all were gray-haired and bearded day and night because of the dreadful harshness of the ice, although many of those present were young and beardless. And yet:

> Scarcely was this the reason that Caesar abandoned the wars. [The text is corrupt or incomplete.]

The emperor returned and reached the castle of Turicum. There, many Burgundians, the widowed queen of Burgundy, Count Hupertus, and others, unable to come to the emperor because of Odo’s ambushes in Burgundy, encountered him as they traveled through Italy. Having pledged faith by oath to him and to his son King Henry, and having been magnificently rewarded, they returned.

## HOW THE EMPEROR CAME AGAINST ODO WITH AN ARMY

In the summer of the same year, the emperor came with his army into the lands of the Franks against Count Odo, saying that if Odo unjustly sought the property of others in Burgundy, then, with God’s help, he ought to lose something of his own.

Then, in the kingdom of King Henry of the Franks—but specifically in Odo’s estates and benefices—the emperor wrought such devastation and arson that Odo himself, compelled by necessity, came humbly to seek pardon, promising to relinquish Burgundy and to make satisfaction according to the emperor’s command. Thus the emperor returned with his honor preserved and Odo’s loss accomplished.

## HOW THE EMPEROR DROVE ODO OUT OF BURGUNDY

In the year of the Lord 1034, the emperor celebrated holy Easter at Regensburg in Bavaria. In the summer of that year, when the aforementioned Odo failed to keep his promises and still held a certain part of Burgundy, which he had unjustly invaded, the emperor Conrad, having mobilized the Germans and Italians, swiftly entered Burgundy.

The Germans came from one direction; from the other, Archbishop Heribert of Milan and the other Italians, under the leadership of Count Hupert of Burgundy, assembled as far as the river Rhône. When Augustus came to the city of Geneva, he subdued Gerold, the prince of that region, the archbishop of Lyons, and many others.

He then returned and besieged the castle of Murat, fortified by Odo with very strong soldiers. He captured it by force and led away as prisoners those whom he found inside. When the other supporters of Odo heard this, they fled solely out of fear of Caesar. Caesar pursued them and utterly expelled them from the kingdom. Taking many hostages from the princes of Burgundy, he returned through Alsace to the empress.

For while he was going into Burgundy, the empress had followed him as far as Basel. From there she returned to the city of Strasbourg and awaited the emperor’s return. At that time Mathilda, daughter of the emperor Conrad and Empress Gisela, a girl of extraordinary beauty and betrothed to King Henry of the Franks, died at Worms and was buried there.

## HOW KING HENRY SUBJUGATED THE SCLAVIANS

Meanwhile, while the emperor was doing the things related above in Burgundy, his son King Henry, although still in his boyhood, diligently provided for the commonwealth in Bohemia and in the other regions of the Sclavians. There he vigorously subdued Duke Udalric of Bohemia and many others who were opposing Caesar. When he met his returning father, he produced double joy among the people through his double victory.

Afterward, having gathered forces from Saxony against those called the Lutici [also Lintici], who had once been partly Christian but had now, through apostate wickedness, become entirely pagan, the emperor came against them. There he wonderfully brought an implacable conflict to an end.

At that time many disputes and incursions were taking place between the Saxons and the pagans. When Caesar arrived, he began to inquire which side had first violated the peace that had long remained unbroken between them. The pagans said that the Saxons had first disturbed the peace and offered to prove this by single combat if Caesar ordered it.

The Saxons, on the other hand, likewise promised the emperor a single combat to refute the pagans, although they were making an unjust claim. After consulting his princes, the emperor—although he was not acting with sufficient prudence—allowed the matter to be decided between them by a duel.

Immediately two champions, each chosen by his own side, engaged. The Christian, trusting in faith alone—which without works of righteousness is dead—and failing to attend carefully to the fact that God, who is truth, arranges all things in true judgment, making his sun rise upon the good and the evil and sending rain upon the just and unjust, began to fight boldly.

The pagan, however, keeping before his eyes only the truth of his cause, for which he was fighting, resisted fiercely. At last the Christian was wounded by the pagan and fell.

As a result, the pagans became so elated and bold that, unless the emperor had been present, they would immediately have attacked the Christians. To restrain their incursions, the emperor built the castle of Wirbina, stationed garrisons of soldiers there, and bound the princes of Saxony by oath and imperial command to resist the pagans unanimously. He then returned to Francia.

In the following year, however, the same castle was seized by the pagans through treachery, and many of our men who were inside it were killed by them. Moved by this, the emperor again came with forces as far as the river Elbe.

When the pagans prevented his crossing, the emperor secretly sent part of his army across by another ford of the river. After the enemy had thus been put to flight, he himself entered the region along the undefended bank and humbled them everywhere with immense devastation and fires, except in places that could not be conquered. As a result, they afterward paid the tribute imposed by the ancient emperors and increased by the emperor Conrad.

For the emperor Conrad had labored greatly, both previously and at that time, among the Sclavian people. Therefore one of our men composed a brief poem about it and afterward presented it to the emperor. It relates how the emperor sometimes stood in marshes up to his thighs, fighting in person and urging the soldiers to fight; and how, after the pagans had been defeated, he slaughtered them with excessive harshness because of a most abominable superstition of theirs.

For it is said that at one time the pagans had treated a wooden image of our Lord Jesus Christ crucified with criminal mockery: they spat upon it and struck it with blows, and finally gouged out its eyes and cut off its hands and feet.

In vengeance for this, the emperor mutilated a very great multitude of captured pagans in the same manner on account of a single image of Christ, and destroyed them by various forms of death. For this reason Caesar is called in those same verses “the avenger of the faith” and is compared with the Roman princes Titus and Vespasian, who, in vengeance for the Lord, exchanged thirty Jews for one coin, since the Jews had sold Christ for the same number of denarii.

When the emperor returned, he imperiously swept aside whatever obstacle he found in the kingdom. In the same year Adalbero, duke of the Carantanians, lost the emperor’s favor, lost his duchy, and was sent into exile.

## ON THE CONSPIRACY OF THE ITALIANS

At the same time, a great disturbance, unheard-of even in modern times, arose in Italy because of the conspiracies that the people had formed against their princes. All the valvassors of Italy and the ordinary soldiers had conspired against their lords, and all the lesser men against the greater, so that they would not tolerate anything being done to them by their lords against their will without taking revenge.

They said that if their emperor did not come, they would make a law for themselves by themselves. When this was announced to the emperor, he is said to have replied:

> If Italy now hungers for law, then, with God’s permission, I shall satisfy her abundantly with laws.

Preparing himself in the following year, he entered Italy with his forces. Meanwhile, the Italian princes, knowing that their badly conceived conspiracy might generate danger, assembled together with the lesser men and first attempted to destroy this new evil by exhortations and counsels.

When this did not succeed, they tried to overcome them by war. But when battle was joined, the incredible multitude of the lesser men prevailed by the sheer pressure of their masses. There the bishop of Asti perished at his dishonorable post; the others fled and, utterly confounded, anxiously awaited the emperor’s arrival.

## HOW KING HENRY TOOK THE DAUGHTER OF KING CUNITTO [also CHUNO] IN MARRIAGE

In the year of the Lord 1036, King Henry, the emperor’s son, took as his wife Chunelinde, daughter of King Cunitto of the English, who had been consecrated as queen, in a royal marriage.

In the same year, as has been said, the emperor Conrad entered Italy with his son King Henry and an army, and celebrated Christmas at Verona in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1037. From there, coming to Milan, he was magnificently received by Archbishop Heribert in the church of Saint Ambrose.

On that very day—whether by whose counsel we do not know—almost a serious riot arose among the people of Milan, who were asking the emperor whether he wished to favor their conspiracy. Angered by this, the emperor ordered everyone to come to the city of Pavia for a general assembly.

When this had been done, despite the protests of all, the emperor enacted a law. At that assembly a certain Count Hugh and many other Italians accused the archbishop of Milan on many charges by which he had offended them.

The emperor summoned the archbishop and ordered him to satisfy everyone. When the archbishop refused, the emperor realized that the entire conspiracy of Italy had been formed on the archbishop’s advice. He immediately seized him and held him in his power.

He then entrusted him to the custody of Poppo, patriarch of Aquileia, and Duke Chuno of the Carantanians, who transported him under imperial guard as far as the city of Piacenza.

One night, one of the archbishop’s household placed himself in the bed in which the archbishop usually slept and hid beneath the coverlet, so as to deceive the guards. The archbishop, having obtained a horse from someone, escaped. Coming to Milan, he was received by his own people with great joy.

Thereafter he omitted nothing that he could contrive against the emperor. The emperor destroyed every castle opposed to him and, having restored just law, abolished Italy’s wicked conspiracies. He came to Ravenna and celebrated holy Easter there.

In the same year three bishops—the bishops of Vercelli, Cremona, and Piacenza—were accused before the emperor in Italy. The emperor seized them and sent them into exile. Many were displeased by this, since priests of Christ had been condemned without judgment.

Some people reported to us that our most devout King Henry, the emperor’s son, secretly condemned Caesar’s presumption toward the archbishop of Milan and toward these three bishops, with all due reverence for his father. And rightly so: just as no honor should be shown after a judicial sentence of deposition, so before judgment priests are owed great reverence.

In the same year, the aforementioned Count Odo of Francia invaded certain places in the emperor’s kingdom. In a battle fought against him by Gozelo, duke of the Lotharingians, and his son Godfrey, together with Count Gerard and the soldiers of the bishop of Metz, Odo was killed while fleeing. His banner was brought to Caesar in Italy and testified that the enemy had been slain.

At that time the emperor afflicted the Milanese severely. Since he could not capture their city, which was fortified by ancient construction and a very large population, he consumed by fire and sword everything around it.

## ON THE MIRACLE THAT OCCURRED ON THE DAY OF PENTECOST

At the same time, while the emperor was besieging a certain castle of Saint Ambrose called Corbitum, near Milan, an event occurred there which many regarded as a miracle.

On the holy Sunday of Pentecost, before the third hour, lightning suddenly burst forth from a completely clear sky with thunder of such force that a large part of the men and horses in the camp perished. Some, overcome by such terror, fell into a state of mental disturbance, so that their senses scarcely returned even after several months.

Those who came from outside the camp, however, said that they had neither seen nor heard anything of the kind.

At that time the emperor gave the archbishopric of Milan to Ambrose, a canon of Milan, although this gift proved of little benefit to him. For the citizens of Milan demolished everything that Ambrose possessed in their territory, while they retained their own archbishop Heribert in honor until his death. Nevertheless, they did so with the favor of Henry, the emperor’s son, as I shall relate more fully, if God wills, in the deeds of the king.

At the same time the pope came to meet the emperor at Cremona. He was honorably received and dismissed, and returned to Rome. After dispersing the army throughout the regions, the emperor himself withdrew to mountainous places for relief, since great heat prevailed that summer.

## ON THE SEDITION THAT OCCURRED AT PARMA

In the winter of the same year, having gathered an army, the emperor crossed the Po and came to the city of Parma. There he celebrated Christmas, as the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1038 began.

On the very day of the Nativity of the Lord, a great sedition arose between the Germans and the citizens of Parma. A certain wealthy Conrad, the emperor’s food-provider, was killed together with others.

Angered by this, the army attacked the citizens with swords and fire. After the burning, the emperor ordered a large part of the walls to be destroyed, so that this ruin might show other cities that their presumption had not gone unpunished.

The emperor then crossed the Apennine mountain and proceeded toward Apulia. The empress came to Rome for the sake of prayer and from there returned to the emperor.

When the emperor reached the frontiers of his empire, he established Troia, Benevento, Capua, and the other cities of Apulia in law and justice. By a single command he settled the disputes that existed between the foreign Normans and the natives. With every offense removed from the kingdom, he returned successfully and came to Vienne.

There he arranged sieges and ambushes against the Milanese, who were still rebellious toward him. Having settled the other affairs of the kingdom according to his will, he decided to revisit his homeland.

At that time, because of the excessive heat, a severe pestilence invaded the army. It spared neither age nor person. There Queen Chunelinde, wife of King Henry, died on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August [18 July], as though standing upon the threshold of life and entering death. She left the king only a single little daughter, whom her father later betrothed to Christ and caused to be consecrated as an abbess.

The empress’s son Herman, duke of the Alemannians, a young man of good character and vigorous in military affairs, was afflicted by the same plague and died among the hands of the most skilled physicians on the fifth day before the Kalends of August [28 July], not without great loss to the empire.

In that and the following month, a very great multitude of the army, infected by the disease, perished. The queen’s tender and delicate body, embalmed with spices, was taken with the king and empress to Germany and buried in the provostship of Lutburg.

It had been decided that the body of the duke should be taken to the city of Constance in Alemannia, but because of the excessive heat it was buried at Trent.

## HOW THE EMPEROR HANDED BURGUNDY OVER TO HIS SON, THE KING

In the same year King Stephen of Hungary died, leaving the kingdom to Peter, his sister’s son.

When the emperor returned to Bavaria, he restored his ailing army with medicines and counsel. Having found the whole kingdom illumined by the serenity of peace, he went to Burgundy in the autumn of that same year. He summoned all the princes of the kingdom and held a general assembly with them. At that time he caused the law of Burgundy, long neglected and almost obliterated, to be revived for the first time.

After three days had passed, on the fourth day of the general assembly, while the leading men of the kingdom and the entire people praised and petitioned him, the emperor handed the kingdom of Burgundy over to his son King Henry and made him swear allegiance anew.

The bishops and the other princes led him into the church of Saint Stephen, which serves as the royal chapel at Solothurn, praising God with hymns and songs. The people cried out and said that peace would produce peace if the king reigned together with Caesar.

The emperor returned by way of Basel, descended through eastern Francia and Saxony, and revisited Frisia,

> strengthening peace and making law.

## ON THE DEATH OF THE EMPEROR

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1039, when the emperor Conrad trusted that the affairs of the kingdom were well placed in the hands of his son King Henry, and the hope of the empire likewise securely established, and when he saw nearly everything throughout the kingdom inclined according to his will, he celebrated the holy day of Pentecost that year at the city of Utrecht in Frisia.

There, while he proceeded magnificently to the table with his son and the empress, crowned and venerating the most sacred sacrament, he was seized by a moderate pain. Nevertheless, so as not to disturb the joy of so great a day, he concealed his suffering.

On the following day, when the fatal illness pressed upon him with great force, he ordered the empress and his son the king to leave the chamber and go to dinner.

Meanwhile, sensing that his end was approaching, the emperor remained in his final moments no less constant and vigorous in faith than he had always been when healthy. He summoned the bishops and had the body and blood of the Lord, together with the holy cross and relics of the saints, brought to him.

Raising himself up, with very abundant tears and profound emotion, in pure confession and earnest prayer, he most devoutly received communion of the saints for the remission of sins. Bidding farewell to the empress and to his son King Henry with faithful admonitions, he departed this life on the eleventh day before the Nones of June [3 June], a Monday, in the seventh indiction.

The emperor’s entrails were preserved at Utrecht, and the king enlarged the place of burial with gifts and estates. The remainder of the body was wrapped and enclosed by the empress and the king as carefully as could be devised, and carried to Cologne. It was transported through all the monasteries of that city, as well as those of Mainz and Worms and those situated between them, with all the people following and praying.

Incredible prayer and great [also: many] alms were offered for the redemption of his soul. On the thirty-eighth day after he had fallen asleep, he was honorably buried in the city of Speyer, which the emperor himself, and afterward his son, had greatly exalted.

For God added this grace to the emperor Conrad: we have neither seen nor heard of such universal lamentation, so many prayers, or such almsgiving being offered for the unburied body of any emperor. And, as we learned from Bishop Henry of Lausanne, who, together with the other Burgundians, accompanied him from his death to his burial, Caesar’s son, King Henry, placed his shoulders beneath his father’s body at every entrance of the churches and finally at the burial itself, with extraordinary humble devotion.

Not only what a son owes his father in perfect love, but also what a servant owes the Lord in holy fear, the king most diligently rendered to his dead father.

We have written briefly about the deeds of the emperor Conrad. If in them we have omitted anything altogether untouched, let this be regarded as unknown to us. If anything has been stated more briefly than the magnitude of the events demanded, we shall truthfully affirm that this was done for the convenience of the reader.

For this reason one of our men composed a song of lamentation, which he afterward presented to his son King Henry in the city of Constance. Since these laments belong to the same work, we have thought it not inappropriate to insert them here.

[Col. 1247]

## VERSES ON THE DEATH OF THE EMPEROR CONRAD

### 1

Whoever possesses a clear voice,  
Let him sing this song,  
About the year of lamentation  
And the immeasurable loss.

Every person mourns,  
Outside and within the house;  
The people sigh for the Lord,  
Keeping vigil through sleep.

King God, guard the living,  
And have mercy on the dead.

### 2

In the year one thousand  
And thirty-nine  
From Christ’s nativity,  
The nobility fell far and wide,

And Caesar, head of the world,  
And with him many of the highest.  
The emperor Conrad fell,  
The lover of law.

King God, guard the living,  
And have mercy on the dead.

### 3

At almost the same time  
Glory went down;  
The morning star fell,  
Queen Chunelinde.

Alas, how cruel the year!  
Herman had fallen,  
The empress’s son,  
A duke feared [also: to be feared] by his enemies.

Chuno, duke of the Franks, fell,  
And a great part of the elders.

King God, guard the living,  
Have mercy on the dead.

### 4

May the emperor’s glory  
Remain in our memory;  
Through fresh remembrance  
May the man of good character live.

May the worthy ruler  
Be made new by frequent song;  
May distinguished fame after death  
Grant him fellowship with life.

King God, guard the living,  
Have mercy on the dead.

### 5

Born of the blood of kings,  
He surpassed everyone completely,  
Glorious in person,  
Handsome under his crown [source order: *sub sua corona*; variant: *fuit sub corona*].

Scepter, kingdom, and empire  
Were suited to no one more.  
He ennobled the commonwealth;  
For its sake he labored.

King God, guard the living,  
Have mercy on the dead.

### 6

After he had filled Francia,  
Through an abundance of peace  
He softened the Alemannians  
And all the tyrants of the kingdom.

Upon the Saxons and Noricans  
He imposed the bridle of law.  
A prosperous Italy  
Saw his great deeds.

King God, guard the living,  
Have mercy on the dead.

### 7

Rome first submitted herself;  
From the highest to the lowest,  
The people of Ravenna  
Experienced his supremacy in war.

The Veronese felt  
The swords of the unconquered Caesar;  
Hesperia threw herself prostrate  
And supplicated the ruler.

King God, guard the living,  
Have mercy on the dead.

### 8

Returning to Alemannia,  
He found calumny there.  
Here Caesar made it vanish  
Like wind, like dust.

All those who had been plunderers  
And most distinguished citizens  
Perished together;  
For that reason they were made exiles [also: were exiled].

King God, guard the living,  
Have mercy on the dead.

### 9

The emperor delayed nothing;  
Everywhere he was the giver of peace.  
He brought war upon the pagans,  
So that they might not harm Christians.

Neither marsh defended them,  
Nor was there safety in any water.  
He effectively restrained the Sclavians,  
The barbarians, and all the wicked.

King God, guard the living,  
Have mercy on the dead.

[Col. 1249]

## WIPPON’S PANEGYRIC, WRITTEN IN VERSE FOR EMPEROR HENRY III, SON OF EMPEROR CONRAD

First published from the Augsburg manuscript by Heinrich Canisius

(*Lectiones antiquae*, vol. III, p. 162).

## JACOB BASNAGE’S OBSERVATION ON WIPPO

Canisius had the following concerning Wippo in the preface to the second volume of the *Antiquae Lectiones*:

> “I had never before heard the name of Wippo, even by hearsay. From Urstisius I know only that he was chaplain to Henry III and that he wrote a history of the life of Conrad II, Henry’s father, which still lies hidden in some library.”

### I

Since that time Wippo has become somewhat better known. For Pistorius first brought to light the *Life of Conrad the Salian*, written by him (*Hist. Germ.*, book I, p. 21), so that it no longer remains hidden in the corners of libraries. He represented the deeds of the father to the son and then inserted into his father’s history the distinguished deeds accomplished by his son Henry III.

### II

From the dedicatory letter of this history we learn that Wippo was not only chaplain to Henry III but also to his father Conrad:

> “Since at that time I was ill for a very long period, I could not often be present in the chapel of my lord Conrad.”

He was therefore Conrad’s chaplain and, in that capacity, an eyewitness to his deeds whenever illness did not detain him. Before him many had written a history of Conrad, but he was not deterred by the difficulty. He says that he saw “the words of Christ in the Gospel expanded not through one alone, but through four suitable witnesses”—a statement which, unless I am mistaken, he uttered more boldly than was proper.

[Col. 1251]

### III

The following verse gave rise to the suspicion that Wippo belonged to the Burgundian people:

> You illumine the homeland, if you will only visit it.

For he is speaking of Burgundy, which was demanding the emperor’s presence. Unless perhaps one should say that Burgundy was Henry’s homeland because he was the grandson of Rudolf, king of the Burgundians: for he had Gisela as his mother, and she was Rudolf’s granddaughter.

Wippo therefore appears concerned and anxious about Burgundy because he had originated there. He himself testifies that he enjoyed weak health.

### IV

Wippo wrote those poems immediately after the beginning of Henry III’s reign, since he mentions Burgundy, which had recently been subjected:

> Moreover Burgundy sends you this command, O king: Rise  
> And come quickly. Newly subjected, she totters  
> At times, when her lord has long been absent.  
> Although Burgundy now holds peace through you,  
> She nevertheless seeks to see in you the author of peace,  
> And longs to feed her eyes upon the king’s countenance.

Rudolf had already written Henry as heir to his kingdom before Conrad’s death, namely in the year 1032. From this arose wars, with Odo asserting his maternal rights over the Burgundian kingdom. Disputes also arose concerning part of the kingdom between Henry I, king of the Franks, and Conrad, Henry the emperor’s father.

Peace was finally achieved in 1034, and Henry entered upon his inheritance, so that Burgundy could be called “newly subjected” around the year 1040, when Henry began to hold the reins of the empire.

Since Henry could not go into Burgundy, he held an assembly with the Burgundians at Greater Augia in the year 1048. Thus it should be read in Hermannus Contractus, not “with the Burdiones,” as the text has it.

### V

The work is divided into four parts and is called by its author a *Tetralogus*, because it introduces four persons—namely the Muses, Law, Grace, and the poet himself—to sing the emperor’s praises.

From this it is clear how great the ignorance of the Germans was at that time. For he asks the emperor to promulgate a law by which wealthy boys might be educated in the humane letters:

> Then issue an edict throughout the land of the Germans,  
> So that every wealthy man may educate all his children  
> In letters, and teach them his law,  
> So that they may know how to plead before princes.  
> Let each man provide them with a model from his own books.  
> Only to the Germans does it seem empty or shameful  
> To teach anyone unless a cleric is engaged.

## HERE BEGINS THE PROLOGUE TO THE KING’S EPILOGUE

[Note: It should read *Tetralogus*.]

[Col. 1251]

To the lord King Henry III, Catholic in faith and speech, most glorious in deeds, Wippo, the least of his servants:

> As the dew of Hermon [Note: Psalm CXXXII] is to the lofty mountain of Zion…

The accessible loftiness of your holy piety, lord king, makes my weakness hasten toward the desirable summit of your grace; and just as the stellio, which strives to dwell in the king’s palaces [Note: [Col. 1252C] Proverbs 25], so I, although obscure in every respect, nevertheless desire to frequent the joys of your brightness in my writings. And since, as Solomon testifies [Note: [Col. 1252C] Proverbs 30], it is the glory of a king to investigate a matter, I have composed for you, my lord king, this brief Tetralogus, by which you may sometimes lighten your sleepless cares [Col. 1252A] for the commonwealth and rouse your mind toward those things that have been commended to you. A tetralogus is the speech of four persons. In it the poet first urges the Muses to praise you. The chorus of the Muses blesses and praises you, the lord king. Then the Law addresses you with counsels sufficiently suited to your dignity. Finally, Grace, in gentle speech, will temper what the Law has urged you to do by right. To read these things through with you, let Jesus Christ the Savior, mediator of law and grace, be present; his kingdom and rule shall not fail forever. Farewell, my most pious lord king.

Here ends the prologue.

[Col. 1251] THE POET

[Col. 1251B]

Learned Pierian Muses, bring forth memorable praises;

Tell me, I beg, of Henry in everlasting songs.

May the poems of the king prolong his immeasurable renown.

May a thousand generations proclaim his joyful deeds.

May this glory of genius outlast two ages of the world;

[Col. 1252B]

Though the world perish, may the king’s wisdom live.

If as boy and youth he has flourished in all his deeds,

What fruits will this man yield when brought to mature age?

Compose; the king supplies material fit for praise;

Dictate to me, and I shall write down what you dictate.

[Col. 1251] THE MUSES

[Col. 1251B]

First we bless the almighty King,

Who is the head of kings, through whom their glory increases;

Who, as Father in the Son and equally with the Holy Spirit,

[Col. 1251C]

Shall reign under the eternal Law, and beyond it.

[Col. 1252B]

Let us piously praise him, for we possess the highest subject of praise;

Let this gift belong to him who reigns, threefold and one.

But our king, Henry the Third, a man endowed with perpetual gift,

[Col. 1252C]

Reigns as a friend of the virtues.

[Col. 1253A]

Second after Christ, he rules the world around us.

Let us praise him, for we have reasons to praise him.

And now let pious Henry be blessed through us,

With the king’s name repeatedly recalled above all in our verses,

So that whenever the saints rise, summoned on behalf of the king,

The king may each time please Christ through the name joined with theirs.

King Henry, be most dear to the God of kings.

King Henry, be most dear to holy Mary.

King Henry, be beloved by the leader Michael.

King Henry, shine in the heavens through John’s fountain.

King Henry, may Peter be your doorkeeper in heaven.

King Henry, may Paul’s good epistle strengthen you.

King Henry, may Andrew direct your actions.

King Henry, may the virgin John care for these prayers for you.

King Henry, may Thomas turn you toward everything that is right.

[Col. 1253B]

King Henry, may Philip be your guide to the heights.

King Henry, may the equals of James redeem you.

King Henry, may you please God through Matthew’s gift.

King Henry, may Simon strengthen your court.

King Henry, may Thaddeus grant you a pious life.

King Henry, may you hold fast to God through Bartholomew.

King Henry, may Matthias prepare the ways for you by his mouth.

Pious king, may you always rejoice on high with Stephen,

And may all Stephen’s companions bless you in their order.

Good king, may Silvester be your right hand forever,

And may all his companions bless you in their order.

May you please the sacred virgins in all your deeds;

May all the saints redeem you from the world’s crime.

May the king of saints be your patron and that of your people.

These things, O king, we Muses sing to you with ringing voice,

[Col. 1253C]

And our chorus continually renews your songs,

So that your praise may increase while the sun and moon shine forth.

We offer our service by which the glory of your deeds may grow;

Our gifts make Maro’s words manifest:

What pious Aeneas, what Turnus could accomplish in arms;

The Muses’ pipe dictated songs to Flaccus,

So that he made Maecenas everlasting through praise.

The same pipe taught Lucan to sing of the wars,

The final struggles of Caesar and of the great age.

From our counsels the author Statius learned

To distinguish the Theban youths amid the mournful flames.

The whole world had recited Ovid’s work;

From our care he adorned his writings with figures.

Once we sang praises to ancient kings,

[Col. 1254A]

And the practice of writing about princes grew.

Never did it please us so to praise any powerful man

As the lord king, whom his noble name proclaims

To be descended from the great stock of the ancient Henrys.

King, we sing to you; for you we prepare the gifts of praise.

Receive them, so that you may live, though dead, in our writings.

We shall take care that the world may say:

Henry the Third was once a friend of peace.

The fame of his merit shall outlast the ages of the world.

Thus the one whom the world will yet bring forth shall sing of you.

[Note: In the manuscript these words stood in the margin: “THE KING’S EXHORTATION.”]

Are not great honors deservedly owed to you,

And the people’s favor, and, after all things, a share of heaven?

For he who is beloved by the people has very often pleased Christ—

A king whom such an abundance of virtues illuminates.

Is anything lacking that the king’s glory could seek?

[Col. 1254B]

All advantages have come through you, in hope or in reality.

If we seek peace, you, king, will provide it;

If we desire war, you, king, will undertake it;

If we seek counsel, you, king, will give very useful advice;

If we wish for learning, you, king, are the glory of learning.

You, king, know how to surpass all generous men.

Among the merciful, you, king, stand as the more merciful.

Thus, king, you chastise those who must be corrected with reason.

Whatever equity consists in human conduct,

God has created either wholly or in part within you.

What a prudent craftsman, who first chose the material

From which he would fashion such great goods;

The man whom the Lord, the creator, would select from the nation,

As afterward more suitable than any other for this rule!

Appearance, ancestry, and probity all accord with the king;

[Col. 1254C]

All things fit him; everything converges through him.

He alone possesses all that many men once enlarged.

Hail, assured rest of the peoples in our age;

Hail, peace of the world, strongest tower of the earth,

You who always lay the enemies of the Church low in abundance;

Through whom the world foresaw the honor of its head.

You are the head of the world, and the ruler of Olympus is your head,

Whose members you govern by the just moderation of law.

The Lord desires such men, in whom this greatest virtue is found:

A very humble mind, with which we know you were born.

A bowed neck is fitting to receive a crown.

The humble king grows whenever the day rises,

And the elevated man falls, always ready to rage.

## EPILOGUE

[Col. 1253]

[Col. 1253D]

King, read through a few of the songs of your Muses;

Let this place be left for others to return duties of praise to you.

If your servant Wippo wishes to preserve time

So that he may write for the king what the Law has dictated to him,

[Col. 1254D]

He has persuaded us to bring these verses to an end.

May you be the concern of Christ, pious king and future Caesar.

And may you live in health, growing gray for a hundred years.

## THE SONG OF THE LAW IN PRAISE OF THE KING

[Col. 1253]

[Col. 1253D]

The Law raises both ears toward the king’s praises.

As fields grow through rains, so I grow through these praises.

Honeyed flowers do not delight bees more as they lick them

Than the king’s praise delights me, upon which the compact of law rests.

[Col. 1254D]

Let these words be for me as they are for grass green with dew,

When spring days restore the joys of the world.

What is more fitting for the Law than to say such things to the king?

Hail, flower of the fatherland, through whom the world does not doubt

That it will possess the fruit of peace, since you reign second in the world.

After the Lord of heaven, worthy to protect earthly things;

Hail, stock of kings, to be venerated by peoples throughout the ages.

There was a great root, which such a branch enlarged;

There was a noble shoot that adorns the world with flowers.

The virtue of one man will often accomplish much,

And probity, once displayed, commends a certain quality exceedingly—

The quality produced by many men when they possess one king as their head;

If one wished to count them, the series would become long in due order.

Yet six virtues from among all the rest will magnify the king,

And they know how to surpass the others sufficiently:

A humble mind, love of piety, peace sent throughout the world,

Nobility and fitting appearance, and confidence in war.

These I call pre-eminent and suited to the king’s honors;

Through these Henry, the friend of Christ, shines forth.

[Col. 1255B]

Now I come to what the world knows in him:

What I shall say is mine, because I am the Law and he is my king;

And whoever despises me, his king lays low in battle.

Whoever observes my rights, the king knows how to defend him.

The king, dear to Christ, will lay no one waste in greed.

He considers learning worthless if someone gathers together

Whatever he can possess, without seeking the right to possess it;

He is very rich who despises riches.

A deaf-eared love obstructs the cries of the wretched.

Money will sell laws and capture kings,

And will steal from princes the practices of justice.

But King Henry, a prudent man, takes care of this:

That he should attend to wealth when it oppresses no one.

Gifts do not bend the king against the law.

He acts as a learned man; what king is more learned than he?

[Col. 1255C]

What Caesar can better know, if the rubric has forbidden something,

Than he who began to learn it in his earliest years?

May his father, revived in eternal praise, be blessed—

Emperor Conrad, whom the greatest purpose overtook,

So that he might know that his son was prepared for the kingdoms through study,

A public ruler able to discern the world.

May his mother also be blessed, worthy of remembrance in song,

Gisela, proceeding from the blood of Charlemagne.

For if the fourth line is counted after the tenth,

She herself will be born noble after Charlemagne the Great.

She had devoted herself to this: that the king should study the Law.

She had persuaded him that books must be read,

So that, skilled in judgment, he might distinguish varied customs.

The light of learning directs the darkened world.

Roman power conquered hostile peoples

[Col. 1255D]

Once through counsels; it did not always conquer by arms.

It is sufficiently proven how much wisdom can accomplish—

Wisdom that bends the governance of kingdoms by the force of the word.

King, hail once more. May praise be yours together with your mother,

[Col. 1256A]

At whose request wisdom grants you everything,

So that you may be able to preserve the glory of empire through laws.

Rejoice together; let discord not reign,

The discord that formerly disturbed the joys of our kingdom.

May there be peace without end of days with the lords of the world’s affairs.

O holy conduct, when you return honors to your mother.

You have hope of life, if through you she has glory.

Whatever there was, God himself rightly transferred it.

From then on no human being can dissolve the bond

That God joined, he who created the gifts of peace.

May the sweetness of your mother’s name endure in you,

Since you are always able to acquire other friends.

No mother shall ever again come to you in this life.

But I shall tell you something else, king, as your counselor—

Your Law, so do not refuse to remember it after it has been spoken:

[Col. 1256B]

When almighty God has made the world secure for you,

And no one dares despise the yokes of the commandment,

And the pacified world lies silent under a strengthened treaty,

And, through your empire, your flying word—

The written word of the Augustus’s illustrious name—

instructs the people,

Then issue an edict throughout the land of the Germans:

Let every rich man educate all his children

In letters, and explain the Law to them,

So that, when the practice of pleading before princes comes,

Each may produce an example for them from his books.

Long ago Rome lived honorably by these customs;

Through these studies it was able to bind such great tyrants;

All Italians preserve this practice from their earliest childhood;

And the whole of youth is commanded to labor in the schools.

Only among the Germans does it seem empty or disgraceful

[Col. 1256C]

To teach anyone unless he is accepted as a cleric.

But learned king, order everyone throughout your kingdoms to be taught,

So that wisdom may reign with you in these regions.

Moreover, Burgundy gives you this command, king: “Rise

And come; hurry, for those newly subjected [Note: See the preceding observation.]

are wavering,

Sometimes with their lord absent for many years.

The ancient saying has proved entirely true:

Whatever is absent from the eyes is removed from the heart’s sight.

Although Burgundy now maintains peace through you,

It nevertheless seeks to see the author of peace in you,

And longs to feed its eyes on the king’s face.

Come here, and make the kingdom serene by your arrival.

If the sun set when Caesar left the kingdoms,

Shine upon the fatherland, if only you visit it.

You once subdued these kingdoms through great labor;

[Col. 1256D]

Now make use of the peoples who are ready to serve you, king.

Let this be an easy road, which the course of peace prepares;

May you come here favorably, and see all things prosper.”

## THE SONG OF GRACE IN HONOR OF THE KING

[Col. 1255]

[Col. 1255D]

All things are full of blessings. Thus Wippo’s Muse wishes.

I, the Law, have sung these things to the king in devoted song.

Hear, hope of the world, what the innermost heart says,

What this sequence intends, and what praises Grace will add.

Grace praises you; Grace sings thanks to you.

You perceive the songs springing from the mind’s vein.

[Col. 1256D]

After the just Law, let Grace accompany the king [leg. “let Grace accompany,” for *comeretur*];

And after judgment, let the sweetness of forgiveness follow.

Just as we customarily bring medicine to wounds,

So let the custom of piety come to the aid of the condemned.

The Law generates force for the king by striking the guilty,

[Col. 1257A]

So that, if the king is also dear, Grace may give counsel.

A man wrote the Law; Grace descended from heaven.

The Law teaches service; Grace shows how to rule.

The Law will condemn, but Grace will justify.

In saying this, I do not at all deny that the Law is good;

But, while praising forgiveness, I commend it to kings.

One is not sufficient if the other does not remain with it.

One is broken, though strong; the other is despised, though gentle.

There is a good balance in what Law and Grace blend together.

If joined, they will produce love of peace.

I do not praise a burden that no one will be able to bear.

After examining their strength, Grace will burden those who have fallen.

The Lord, King of heaven, showing mercy,

Hiding judicial punishments, protects converted enemies.

[Note: In the manuscript’s margin: “THE COUNSEL OF GRACE.”]

Imitate him, I ask, pious King Henry, the Thunderer,

[Col. 1257B]

Who spares the wretched and, by sparing, punishes crimes.

Thus teach both goods to reign in the patron,

Through whom the Law may strike and through whom Grace may heal the Law.

This the order of consecration will have foretold to you, venerable one,

When the bishop girds the sword around the curve of your thigh:

When you are an angry king, rest in mercy.

Let hard things be softened by waters; let soft things grow hard in flames;

And let moderated justice alternate its turns.

Thus hard adamant will be dissolved by gentle blood;

Glass is better joined by bonds of lead;

Iron melts with clay in a glowing mass.

Nature commands that sorrowful things be changed by gentle ones:

After sour things, it is pleasant to taste sweetness;

After sweet things, to mingle sour flavors again.

I have not prepared these words for you, king,

[Col. 1257C]

Because anyone doubts that you are a merciful lord and father of the kingdom,

But because I wish to chastise those who are moved by law alone,

To whom I offer these pious teachings.

When almighty God created all things in the world,

Only man received the gifts of the Creator as a free being.

Soon his wandering mind corrupted that first freedom.

The wretched began to misuse the gift of reason;

And nature learned that it could do evil through practice.

Behold, God added the Law to restrain this,

So that its transgressor would not depart unpunished,

And, fearing punishment, perverse will might return

And recognize through judgment how wicked it is to sin.

Thus the merciful Lord wished to recall his servants.

Man could not endure it, burdened by the punitive Law,

So that through vengeance he might restrain guilt;

[Col. 1257D]

And the mortal yoke hurt his injured neck.

“Let the murderer be killed,” the Law said, “once he has committed homicide,

And let the adulterer be stoned immediately together with the adulteress;

Let tooth fall for tooth; let eye go for eye;

[Col. 1258A]

Let foot be repaid with foot; let one hand yield to another;

Let wounds strive to return an answer to wounds.

Let him who curses his parents die;

He who commits theft shall not remain without punishment;

Let five oxen redeem one taken away by fraud;

He who steals a sheep shall repay one with four;

If a man curses, let him die for the curse.”

Thus the Law, bending the weapons of its words,

Terrified many and compelled them to despair.

The people, pressed beneath so great a burden, cried aloud;

The wretched man shouted, bound by a hard fetter,

That he could not bear this, and that the time for mercy had come.

The Lord heard those crying out, and the Creator,

In his accustomed compassion, answered the groans of the wretched.

He came into this world clothed in flesh beneath a veil,

[Col. 1258B]

Both the fashioner and the redeemer of the human race.

He did not reject the Law, but, giving it just moderation,

Placed forgiveness alongside the Law, so that man would not die;

So that, while the Law promises death, Grace promises life;

That Grace may raise up the humble, while the Law scatters the rebellious.

Once converted, let no judge refuse forgiveness.

Thus almighty God had once spoken through the prophets:

“I do not desire the death of the sinner, nor do I rejoice in punishment.

Let him be converted,” he says, “and live; let him himself serve me—

The preserved man whom I restore to his former place.”

Now the same Lord, coming in the covering of flesh,

Says: “I command this to all disciples; learn it:

Let them repent of their crimes, and live with everlasting life.

Let sin perish; let the sinner learn to live.

He who converts is not the person he once was.”

[Col. 1258C]

I shall not say here what true mercy in life is:

What is given freely is rightly called mercy.

Who would call that forgiveness which the recipient has earned?

If someone wishes to show mercy to a converted sinner,

And, sparing the wretched man, does not know how to exact vengeance,

He grants forgiveness; thus Grace rejects punishment.

Let a man show favor to a brother fallen into sin.

He who falls and rises has hope that he may live.

We all sin; let us do for sinners

What the Lord, who is merciful toward his enemies, does for us.

When I praise forgiveness, I do not seek to despise the Law.

The good Law, if it strives to carry forgiveness on its back,

Benefits from Grace when the Law has preceded it.

Let there be Law for the one who resists, but Grace for the one who returns:

Thus the world will be able to stand in both goods.

[Col. 1258D]

Now may the peace and mercy of Christ be yours, king.

May you, prince of the world, be strong through Christ’s gift.

May you, lord of the kingdom, live in everlasting peace.

Thus wills your servant Wippo, with faithful heart.

[Col. 1257]

## WIPPO’S VERSES FOR THE KING’S TABLE AT THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD

[Col. 1257D]

May the royal assembly rejoice at this season,

When light rises for the peoples in darkness.

[Col. 1258D]

Amid rejoicing, reason urges us to remember

That God was born, that the Son himself was given.

[Col. 1259A]

Little Bethlehem gave bread from a great stock,

Bread able to satisfy whatever exists everywhere.

Grace extended bread from heaven to the world;

The living bread is present, an everlasting food.

A fountain of leaping water, cups of life poured forth;

Whoever drinks from it shall not thirst again.

The sweetness of honey flowed from heaven through Christ,

So that servants might taste the delights of the Lord.

[Col. 1260A]

The ox refused hay when it saw the noble grain,

And the manger of God guarded the ass’s mouth.

Virgin Mary, behold; marveling at such things, rejoice:

See God born from you through the Word.

Pious heavenly King, descend upon our festivals;

Grant the fruit of peace, as you do everywhere.

Be pleased to show favor to King Henry,

So that he may carry out his duties with joy.

[Col. 1259]

## WIPPO’S PROVERBS, PUBLISHED FOR HENRY, SON OF THE EMPEROR CONRAD

*(In Martene, Amplissima Collectio IX, 1095, from a five-hundred-year-old manuscript of St. Matthias at Trier.)*

[Col. 1259B]

Here begins the composition containing one hundred proverbs.

It is fitting for a king to learn the Law.

Let the king hear what the Law commands.

To observe the Law is to reign.

Knowledge of letters is the light of souls.

He who does not heed the light more often gives offense.

He who possesses knowledge adorns his judgment.

Wisdom is better than worldly power.

A single understanding is worth more than multiple revenues.

He is very wise who loves the worship of God.

The faithful man is crowned in heaven.

He believes well who harms no one.

He who is faithful draws near to the honor of his elder.

He who trusts in God is strong as a lion.

It is better to hope in God than to gather riches.

[Col. 1259C]

The strongest hope makes one’s affairs blessed.

Unfeigned charity hates offenses.

He who loves his brother pleases God and the Father.

The kingdom of heaven does not belong to the envious.

It is better to be humbled than exalted.

The humble man triumphs in his house.

He who travels through difficult places often falls.

Gentle men reject quarrels.

Those who quarrel constantly are loved by few.

To endure the wicked for God is to overcome.

The gift of peace is good for everyone.

Those founded in peace are not uprooted.

The conflagration of wars is the corruption of morals.

The chaste man is a friend to his soul.

Where luxury is frequent, want will not be absent.

[Col. 1259D]

Worldly pleasure is always vain.

The judge’s sentence ought to follow mercy.

It is sometimes better to forgive than to demand vengeance.

He who shows mercy will obtain mercy.

The word of truth will aid those judged.

The false man in speech lacks honor.

He who lives by falsehood destroys everything.

The cheerful giver is loved by the Savior.

Every miser is dear to no one.

To bestow good things is not to diminish them.

[Col. 1260B]

Where holy prayer contends, there tribulation is conquered.

To pray without ceasing is to cleanse offenses.

He prays well who weeps in his heart.

A strong fast frees one from the second death.

He who cannot fast should learn to give alms.

He will rejoice well who does not cease from goodness.

It is sometimes better to sleep than to serve the devil.

Sleep does not greatly brighten the face.

He who confesses himself guilty placates God.

Where there is true repentance, there is God’s mercy.

For one ought to spare those who have long been placed in prison.

He is greatly deceived who is never corrected.

A friendly rebuke is not condemnation.

The oil of the sinner is the praise of the flatterer.

[Col. 1260C]

Where drunkenness is prolonged, piety is brief.

Much and strong wine is little removed from death.

Through gluttony of food and drink the whole man perishes.

Through moderation one reaches abundance.

Nature rejoices in more things when they are moderate.

A proverb: “Nothing in excess” is praised above all.

An energetic young man becomes a glorious old man.

He who grows sluggish while he is vigorous is worth nothing when cold.

He who is idle in youth is troubled in old age.

Brave men are marvelous to everyone.

Kings and governors ought not to be idle.

Let the rulers of the world make their conduct equal to their name.

Pontifical men are equal to the saints.

Let physicians of souls stray little.

To watch against the wolf is to avoid being carried off.

[Col. 1260D]

He who defends a widow advances toward Christ the King.

He who vindicates an orphan, God crowns him.

The consoler of the poor is a lover of eternal life.

One ought to beware lest one see vanity.

The eye sets the heart ablaze as a little fire sets straw ablaze.

Unseen pleasure will more quickly be cut down.

He who gladly hears good things applauds God in his heart.

It is better to listen to a poor man than to the sound of a lyre.

He hears the wretched in vain who closes his mouth and hands.

A conciliatory tongue is comparable to the tree of life.

A deceitful tongue is always hateful.

[Col. 1261A]

He who speaks moderately is free from plague.

A hand without work will quickly beg.

The labors of the hands provide honors.

He who does good work, may he be blessed by God.

Blessed are the feet that visit the homes of the sick.

To walk with God is to save the soul.

He who departs to the eternal dwelling does not stumble.

It is unjust to return punishment for a benefit.

He who returns evil for good is unworthy of a gift.

To overcome evils with good is a ladder to heaven.

Contempt for the world has been discovered by God.

He who loves the present world follows a fleeing thing.

Heavenly counsel is better than the help of this life.

The heavenly homeland possesses beautiful halls.

The son and brother advance when the Father calls them.

The joys of feasts are always in heavenly gold.

Why do you flee from him who encloses all things in his handful?

O whoever you may be who wish to join your mind to heaven,

Where the just dwell, beautiful with garlands and palms,

Despise the world’s threats and subdue its pleasing things beneath your feet.

### Pride says:

No one in all your deeds will be equal to you.

### Humility:

You are a rotten worm; why, mortal man, are you proud?

### Vainglory:

For the sake of reputation, do whatever good you can before human beings.

[Col. 1261C]

### Fear of God:

Desire that the good things you habitually do remain hidden.

### Hypocrisy:

Strive to conform yourself outwardly to a holy person.

### Religion:

Woe to you whitewashed on the outside, who pretend to be tombs.

### Disobedience:

What should he do who is far inferior to you?

### Submission:

“Whoever despises you,” God says, “despises me also.”

### Envy:

Why do you not in some way go higher than he?

### Rejoicing with another:

Rejoice with your brother, and bring help to one who is advancing.

### Hatred:

[Col. 1261D]

How can anyone love one who stands opposed to him?

### Charity:

True love of a brother is the brief fulfillment of the Law.

### Detraction:

Who could tolerate that he should remain silent about the venial things that man commits?

### Just Correction:

You must never rebuke anyone secretly.

### Anger:

Why do you not resist when something is done to you that you do not want?

### Patience:

What would you not endure for Christ, who was crucified for you?

### Insolence:

Always be harsh and severe toward the sinner.

[Col. 1262A]

### Gentleness:

Rebuke, compel, ask, Timothy; persist shrewdly.

### Fear of the mind:

God himself knows what it is; do not concern yourself with any judge.

### Satisfaction:

You will be suspected if you do not confess your offenses.

### Sadness:

How can you rejoice when you freely endure so many evils?

### Spiritual joy:

Why does what gives you no joy now make you sad?

### Torpor or sloth:

You are deprived of sight if you weep continually.

### Exercise of virtue:

Death comes without delay; labor night and day.

### Wandering:

[Col. 1262B]

Depart from this place; that place is happier than this one.

### Stability:

Since God is everywhere, remain everywhere at peace.

### Despair:

You will not rise, weighed down entirely by the burden of sin.

### Confidence of hope:

Mary’s forgiven sins give you hope of pardon.

### Greed:

Multiply interest, and you will not beg in poverty.

### Contempt of the world:

However much you possess, when dying you will carry nothing away from here.

### Hard-heartedness:

From where do you feed your own people, if you scatter your own goods?

### Mercy:

If you have anything, give it; let your will be generous toward you.

[Col. 1262C]

### Fraud and Theft:

Have you nothing to give? Seek it by theft or fraud.

### Innocence:

It is better that nothing be given than that you steal through fraud.

### Deceit and Falsehood say:

By deceiving, accomplish what you do not wish to say truthfully.

### Truth:

A mouth that lies is proven to be the soul’s death.

### Gluttony of the Belly:

Why are you not satisfied with the feasts given by the Maker?

### Moderation in Food:

Spare yourselves in every kind of food, lest you perish with the Sodomites.

### Foolish Joy:

Make your companions rejoice and cause them to laugh.

[Col. 1262D]

### Moderated Sorrow:

Where is your laughter, since here you are a wretched exile?

### Excessive Speech:

There is no sin in saying very many things, if they are good.

### Discreet Silence:

You will never avoid guilt if you speak much.

### Uncleanness:

Not every pollution [Note: Namely, when it is involuntary.] of the flesh is a grave fault.

### Bodily Integrity:

The heavenly gate of the kingdom is closed to the unchaste.

### Lust:

Use lust? You do not know what the future life is.

[Col. 1263A]

### Unblemished Chastity:

If you are chaste, you will enjoy life without end.

### Spiritual Fornication:

Pleasure conceived in the mind is not a great offense.

### Purity of the Flesh:

Certainly you commit adultery when you are desirous of a woman.

### Love of the Present Age:

What can be more beautiful than this sweet life?

### Love of the Heavenly Homeland:

If this is a prison, O God, what must your dwelling be like?

Here end the proverbs.

In the tongue’s plectrum, death and life are entrusted to you.

Do not be double-tongued, lest you give examples to the wicked.

He will be least dear who broadcasts everything he knows.

He will be dear to the beloved who does not keep silent about entrusted matters.

The whisperer’s tongue is worse than a dragon’s bile.

Words bless the just; a hundred blows do not teach the fool.

[Col. 1264A]

No plague can be worse for a servant than a wicked man.

The learned man differs from the unlearned by eight virtues.

A virgin who has fallen will not solidify her ruin afterward.

The strong mind of a man falls through feminine fickleness.

Various modulations of the voice break the force of the heart.

An overdrawn bow is very often broken.

A drop hollows a stone; a ring is worn away by use.

Do not grow sluggish in psalms and the praise of God.

The people’s joys are a pious and kindly ruler.

The nobler the man, the more flexible his neck.

What is often shut out at the door we forget within.

Rewards are with you; death carries away the rest with it.

To have set a limit to riches is no final praise.

The gifts a dying man gives are not truly gifts;

He would scarcely give them to anyone if he could live longer.

It is a boy’s virtue to observe the commands of his teacher.

## ABOUT THE SAME TIME: HELGAUD, A MONK OF FLEURY

[Col. 1263]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE ON HELGAUD

*(Literary History of France, vol. VII, p. 405.)*

[Col. 1263B]

Helgaud [Note: Possevin (*App.*, vol. I, p. 720) calls him *Helgacitus*, or *Helgalcidus*, following the reading of Vossius [Col. 1264D] (*Hist. Lat.*, book II, ch. 44, p. 116, col. 2), but this is a corruption.] or Helgald, who would deserve the title of panegyrist more than that of historian, tells us himself (*Life of Robert*, *Patrologia*, vol. CXLI) that he had been a monk of Fleury under Abbot Gauzlin, who united that dignity in his own person with that of archbishop of Bourges and died in 1029. From this it may be presumed that Helgaud had studied under Abbo, or under Constantine, his successor in directing the schools of Fleury. But although he made progress there in other literary knowledge, he scarcely benefited from their lessons in learning how to write well. His style is in fact so unnatural—or, more accurately, so affected, harsh, and obscure—that no one would ever recognize in it a disciple of Abbo.

[Col. 1263C]

Moreover, one cannot help acknowledging that Helgaud was a man of merit and piety. This is what one may infer from the singular share he had in winning the favor of King Robert, who ordinarily formed close bonds only with persons of this character. Not only did he have free access to the prince, whom he regarded as his father; he even dares to call him his friend—“friend of a friend, beloved of a beloved one” (*amicus de amico, dilectus de dilecto*). Robert, moreover, truly loved Helgaud as [Col. 1264B] his son, “with fatherly affection” (*affectu diligebat paterno*). The proofs our writer gives of this are conclusive and leave no room for doubt. Helgaud had another illustrious friend in the person of Odolric, bishop of Orléans, on whose friendship he could rely to the point of obtaining from him anything consistent with the rules of equity.

Gauzlin also showed Helgaud particular consideration. He chose him to supervise the construction, on the estate of the abbey of Fleury, of a chapel under the invocation of Saint Denis and his companions. Helgaud initially made it of wood. King Robert, having gone to visit it out of devotion, made gifts there and shortly afterward enriched it with some relics of the holy martyrs. Then an unexpected fire reduced it to ashes, but Helgaud found a way to rebuild it in stone. And, so that those who went there to pray might learn that it was his work and might be encouraged to remember him in their prayers, he placed on the right and left of the altar two inscriptions in verse, in which he took care to name himself and to claim the suffrages of those who would read them. From this one may infer that Helgaud was a priest, since he was charged with serving this chapel. Among his other good [Col. 1265A] qualities, he held gratitude in especially high esteem. He shows this by the prayers he offers for the eternal happiness of his benefactors when he speaks of their kindness toward him.

It would be difficult to determine precisely the end of his life. It is certain that he lived beyond 1033, the date of the death of Odolric, bishop of Orléans, whom he speaks of as a person no longer in this world. There is even considerable reason to think that he wrote only after 1042—that is, after King Henry, Robert’s son, had distinguished himself against Stephen, count of Champagne, Waleran of Meulan, and the rebels of Normandy, who refused to recognize William the Bastard as their sovereign. The reason for this conclusion is the ending of Helgaud’s work, [Col. 1265B] where, speaking of those who would undertake to write of King Robert’s military exploits, he says that they would find material there to make the father and his sons appear as great commanders crowned with glory. Several modern writers (*Oudin*, *Scriptores*, vol. II, p. 644; Le Long, *Bibliothèque française*, p. 340, col. 2) suppose that Helgaud flourished around 1050, but one may reasonably doubt whether he lived beyond 1048. His death is marked on the twenty-ninth day of August in the necrology of Saint-Bénigne at Dijon, and on the preceding day in that of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, which gives him the title of priest (Montfaucon, *Bibliotheca bibliothecarum*, p. 1163, col. 2; *History of Saint-Germain*, appendix, p. 117, col. 2).

The only work of Helgaud’s composition that remains to us [Col. 1265C] is an abridgment of the life of King Robert (Du Chesne, vol. IV, p. 59). It has been added to this title that the writing was taken from the work of another monk who had treated the same subject more fully before our historian. But M. de Sainte-Palaye (*History of the Academy of Inscriptions*, vol. X, p. 556) has shown with strong arguments that this addition, which reduces Helgaud to the status of a mere abridger, is entirely without foundation and should be regarded as a rash product of the copyists’ ignorance. If, therefore, this Life bears the title “abridgment,” it is not because it is an excerpt from another, more extensive work, but because it is merely a concise history of the prince whose deeds the author undertakes to write. Helgaud himself in fact warns us that he did not intend to speak [Col. 1265D] of the wars in which Robert distinguished himself, or of political affairs, and that he leaves it to historiographers to transmit their memory to posterity.

By this omission the author excluded from his work what was most interesting for the history of King Robert’s life. He limited himself (Hist. de l’Acad. des insc., ibid., p. 558) to giving us a long declamation concerned solely with this prince’s piety; his devotion to the saints; his fasts, mortifications, and prayers; his charity toward the poor; the affection he [Col. 1266A] bore toward monks; the possessions with which he enriched them; the great foundations he established within the Order of Saint Benedict, especially at the abbey of Fleury; and, finally, several miracles attributed to him. Thus it is less a history than a sermon or funeral oration in the taste of that period, in which the author inserted many minutiae and entered into the smallest details. The whole is composed in a style of the kind already described, in which frequently affected consonances take the place of good taste. Nevertheless, these details, which often concern the interior life of the households of our kings, offer us a very naïve and singular picture of the simplicity of the customs of that age.

This work is preceded by a short notice concerning the [Col. 1266B] foundation of Fleury and the testament of Leodebode, its founder—pieces that are visibly out of place here with regard to the Life of King Robert, to which they have no connection. Hence the learned and judicious M. de Sainte-Palaye conjectures, with considerable justification (Hist. de l’Acad. des insc., ibid., p. 557), that the author had a more extensive design and intended to write the history of the abbeys of Saint-Aignan of Orléans and Fleury. Afterwards, not wishing posterity to be unaware of the great possessions they had received from King Robert, he took occasion to add to it, as a supplement or continuation of this history, the Life of that prince, most of whose [Col. 1266C] contents in fact concern what he did in favor of these two monasteries. Anyone who takes the trouble to read attentively the preface placed at the beginning of this Life, in order to connect it with the preceding work, will agree that the conjecture is as sound as it is ingenious. In the course of time, the negligence of copyists evidently caused the missing portion of the body of the History to be lost.

Helgaud’s work, as it has come down to us, was first printed together with the Life of Saint Louis by William of Nangis and Gaguin’s History of France (Bib. cath. Rot.). This folio collection appeared at Frankfurt in 1577. It seems that this edition was unknown to our bibliographers. Pithou (Scri. Fr., vol. I, pp. 59–79) later reprinted [Col. 1266D] our author’s work after Glaber’s History, in the first volume of his Historians. The Duchesnes published it again in the fourth volume (pp. 59–79) of their Collection, after the same Glaber.

Vossius (Hist. Lat., bk. II, chap. 44, p. 116, 2) attributes to Helgaud the Life of Saint Abbo, abbot of Fleury. But this opinion, peculiar to that critic, is entirely devoid of plausibility. The work belongs to Aimoin, Abbo’s disciple, as was shown in the article devoted to him.

[Col. 1267]

## HELGAUD’S LIFE OF ROBERT, KING OF THE FRANKS

(See volume CXLI of the *Patrologia* under ROBERT, king.)

## IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1051, OTHERWISE 1048. GERARD I, BISHOP OF CAMBRAI

[Col. 1267]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE ON GERARD I

(In D. Leglay, *Cameracum Christianum*, p. 22.)

[Col. 1267A] Gerard, son of Arnold or Arnulf, the lord of Florennes, whom Alberic in his *Chronicle* surnames of Ruvigny, was by nationality a native of Liège. Educated at Gerbert’s school in Reims under the direction of Archbishop Adalbero, at the request of Emperor Henry, whose chaplain he was, he became bishop in 1013 and was consecrated on the day after the Purification. Alberic calls him “the Great” and reports that he founded the abbey of Florennes with his brother Godfrey, where he established a double monastery: one, under the name of Saint Gingulf, for clerics; the other, in honor of Saint John the Baptist, which he placed under the discipline of Richard, abbot of Saint-Vanne of Verdun.

In 1015, indiction XII, on the fourth day before the Ides of May, he subscribed the council of Reims together with Archbishop Arnulf, Adalbero [Col. 1267B] of Laon, and Fulk, bishop of Amiens. He confirmed the gift of Robert, son of the lord of Béthune, and in 1018 subscribed the foundation of a certain collegiate church in the town of Rozoy. In 1046 he founded and endowed the abbey of Saint Andrew in the castle of Cambrai, a town belonging to the episcopal jurisdiction. He also kept there for some time the body of Saint Humbert, which had been brought to the place. This saint had formerly built the monastery of Maroilles on his own estate, but after the monks had been expelled, clerics occupied it. When Gerard, while visiting the churches of his parish, came to this place, he found the buildings almost destroyed and everything dispersed, as though the monastery had been plundered by an enemy army. Accordingly, when the pious bishop understood that these evils had arisen from the insolence of the clerics, and after he had tried in vain to bring them back to better conduct, he took care to restore the monastic order there. But the expelled clerics, like brigands, burst into the place and, breaking open the chests, carried away every valuable object, especially the body of Blessed Humbert, to their hiding places. They were, however, compelled by the bishops to restore these things. Shortly afterward, at Gerard’s command, the body of Saint Humbert was transferred to the church of Saint Andrew, built by this bishop in the castle of Saint Mary of Cambrai, where there was a community of monks established by the same prelate; for he considered this place safer for preserving the sacred relic. Later, however, it seemed preferable to him to return it to its former see, namely Maroilles. Mabillon discusses these matters under the year 1018.
