Around the year 1022 he attended the synod of Aachen, where he supported the case of Durand, bishop of Liège, against Piligrim, archbishop of Cologne, who was claiming for himself a certain monastery belonging to Durand’s diocese. Shortly afterward he accompanied Emperor Henry as he departed for Italy, from which he returned victorious after defeating the Greeks and Saracens, as far as the monastery of Santas [Note: [Col. 1267C] Setten or Santen, in the Duchy of Cleves; it is thought to be Tacitus’s *Vetera Castra*, where Civilis was defeated by Cerealis.]

In 1023 Gerard and Richard, abbot of Verdun, served as envoys from Emperor Henry to Robert, king of the Franks. A synod was held at Arras in 1025, after Epiphany, at which Gerard, a learned bishop and a student of the school of Reims under Archbishop Adalbero, whose kinsman he was, refuted the Manichaean heretics and brought them back to the Catholic faith. The acts of Gerard’s synod and disputation, which he dedicated to Reginald, bishop of Liège, are found in volume XIII of the *Spicilegium*, p. 1 and following.

[Col. 1268C] In 1013, when the decree commonly called the Truce of God [Note: [Col. 1267C] The Truce of God, devised as a remedy for private wars, stipulated, among other things, that no one might attack his enemy from Saturday at the hour of None until Monday at Prime. It was also forbidden ever to assault an unarmed cleric or monk who was traveling, or a man going to or returning from church with women, or the surrounding houses up to a distance of thirty paces.] was promulgated, it was prescribed, among other things, that every Friday should be observed by fasting on bread and water, and that on Saturday one should abstain from meat—something not yet customary—and remission of all sins was promised only to those who carried out these requirements. Gerard strongly opposed this, especially in a very learned letter that he wrote to Berald, bishop of Soissons, and Warin, bishop of Beauvais, as Sigebert and Balderic report. Later, however, he yielded to the judgment of the advocates of the Truce of God. His name is found subscribed to a document concerning the advocacy of the abbey of Marquillies, belonging to Baldwin, margrave of Flanders, in 1008, and in a diploma of Emperor Henry for the monastery of Nivelles in 1040.

He is praised for having restored, through his efforts, the monastic religious order, which had been almost annihilated in the monastery of Maubeuge, by Ansoald, a virgin of great holiness [Col. 1270A] and no less learning, who had taught the first elements of letters to her brother Theodoric, later abbot and reformer of Saint-Hubert, as the author of Theodoric’s Life relates. Together with Wazo, bishop of Liège, he removed Engroband from the government of the monastery of Lobbes because he lived in a worldly manner and squandered its goods; Richard, abbot of Verdun, was substituted for him, according to Balderic, book III, chapter 15. He restored the household possessions and ascetic discipline of the monastery of Saint-Ghislain, which had been ruined by its abbot Simon, in whose place he appointed Verricus. He also did the same at Hautmont by restoring Benedictine observances, as Bartholomew Fitzen of the Society of Jesus teaches in *Flores Leodienses*, p. 5.

[Col. 1269]

## ACTS OF THE SYNOD OF ARRAS AGAINST THE MANICHAEANS

(*Acts of the Ecclesiastical Province of Reims*, vol. II, p. 6.)

## NOTICE

A leaven of the Manichaean heresy, which was believed to have been destroyed at Orléans in 1022, was fermenting secretly in the diocese of Arras. These pernicious doctrines did not escape the vigilance of Gerard, bishop of Cambrai and Arras. He had the sectarians sought out, interrogated them, and summoned them to the synod that he held in 1025 in the cathedral of Arras. Other prelates had allowed themselves to be deceived by the artifices of these heretics. To halt the progress of the evil, Gerard wrote to one of these prelates, believed to have been Reginald, bishop of Liège, and sent him the acts of his synod.

## GERARD’S LETTER

[Col. 1269B] To R., a bishop distinguished by the dignity of his name and the prerogative of his merits, Gerard, a fellow bishop of no merit: whatever is most excellent for blessed life.

When I consider your noble intellect and prudence, I am not so greatly astonished that wicked men, bewitched by the spirit of error, could have conspired in some madness of perverse doctrine. But I am utterly amazed that, when you investigated them, they could have concealed themselves well enough to deceive you. For, as you yourself know, we reported to your charity that certain men of this kind had lived among your people, as we established by true indications. Because, through fear of punishment, they feigned an appearance of religion, you allowed them, as though they were harmless, to depart without being convicted. This proved all the more effective in those men at subverting the simple, while it planted in the simple the doubt that they ought not to be heard, when they heard that the men had been examined by a true inquiry and that no ground for punishing them had been found. Yet those also who had been sent by them to carry out such seduction and had come to us resisted capture with great dissimulation, to such an extent that no punishments could compel them to confess. At last, however, they were convicted by those whom they had already almost imbued with the same magical error, and they partially disclosed to us the discipline of their sect.

After certain further matters which they claimed to hold from evangelical and apostolic doctrine, they said that the mystery of baptism and the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood did not exist and should therefore be rejected unless administered as a pretense; that penance contributed nothing to salvation; that married people could in no way belong to the kingdom; and other things indicated in what follows this little work [Note: [Col. 1269C] It is observed that this heresy was already attacking the points later opposed by Luther and Calvin: justification, baptism, penance, the Eucharist, [Col. 1270C] purgatory, the invocation of the saints, the veneration of images, and so forth.] We report this to you so that you may not listen to their simulated religion or contrived words.

## ACTS OF THE SYNOD

[Col. 1271]

[Col. 1271A] I. In the year 1035 of the Lord’s Incarnation, indiction VIII, while Lord Gerard governed the Church of the city of Cambrai or Arras, it happened, according to an annual custom, that after the solemn observances of the days of the Lord’s Nativity and Epiphany had been completed at Cambrai, the same prelate was required to hold his station for several days at Arras. There, while he was dealing as circumstances and time required with ecclesiastical matters, it was reported to him that certain men had come to that place from the regions of Italy. Introducing a certain sect of a new heresy, they were attempting to pervert the discipline of evangelical and apostolic authority, and, putting forward a certain form of justice, were asserting that men were purified by this alone and that there was no other sacrament in the holy Church by which they could attain salvation. Having heard this, the lord bishop ordered the men to be sought and brought before him. When they learned the reason for the investigation, they secretly prepared to flee, but the investigators anticipated them and dragged them into the bishop’s presence. Since he was then greatly occupied with deciding other cases, he asked them only a few questions about their faith for the moment. Perceiving that they were held by some error of perverse doctrine, he ordered them confined in custody until the third day; on the following day he enjoined a fast upon the clerics and monks, so that divine grace might grant them repentance through the reception of the Catholic faith.

On the third day, which was Sunday, Bishop Segmentatus, with his archdeacons, crosses and Gospel books prepared, proceeded to the church of Blessed Mary to celebrate the synod, surrounded by a multitude of the entire clergy and people. After the antiphon *Let God arise* had been begun, they completed the entire course of that psalm. Finally, when the bishop had taken his seat in his tribunal, and abbots, religious men, archdeacons, and the rest had seated themselves on either side according to the rank of their order, the men were brought out of custody and introduced into the midst of the assembly. First the bishop addressed the people generally concerning these matters. Then, turning to the men, he said:

“What is your doctrine, your law, and your religious observance? And who is the author of your discipline?”

They replied that they were hearers of a certain Gundulf, a man from the regions of Italy, and that they had been instructed by him in evangelical commands and apostolic teachings. They accepted no writing apart from this one, but held to it [Col. 1271D] in word and deed. Yet the bishop had learned that they utterly abhorred the mystery of holy baptism; rejected the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood; denied that penance benefited those who had fallen after their profession; abolished the Church; execrated legitimate marriages; recognized no gift of virtue in holy confessors; and maintained that no one except apostles and martyrs ought to be venerated.

Questioning them about these matters, the bishop said:

“How can it be consistent for you to hold to evangelical and apostolic institutions while preaching things contrary to them? For the evangelical text relates that when Nicodemus, a ruler of the Jews, confessed from the signs and miracles that Jesus had come from God, the Lord immediately replied that no one could merit the kingdom of heaven by this confession alone unless he were born again of water and the Spirit. You must therefore either fully accept this mystery of regeneration or contradict the evangelical words, since it is certain that Jesus truly spoke them.”

They gave the following answer:

“Our law and discipline, which we received from our teacher, will appear to contradict neither the evangelical decrees nor the apostolic ordinances if anyone wishes to examine it carefully. It is this: to leave the world; to restrain the flesh from its desires; to obtain our livelihood through the labor of our hands; to seek injury for no one; and to show charity toward all who are devoted to this zeal for our way of life. If this justice is preserved, baptism is of no use; but if it is violated, baptism contributes nothing to salvation. This is the substance of our justification, to which the use of baptism can add nothing, since all apostolic and evangelical instruction concludes with such an end.

“If, however, anyone says that some sacrament lies hidden in baptism, this is nullified for three reasons. First, the wicked life of those who administer baptism can offer no remedy of salvation to the baptized. Second, whatever vices are renounced in the font are afterward found again in life. Third, in the case of a little child who neither wills nor runs, who knows nothing of faith and is ignorant of his own salvation and advantage, in whom there can be neither a request for regeneration nor a profession of faith, another’s will, another’s faith, and another’s profession do not seem in any way to apply.”

To this the bishop replied:

“If you attribute authority to this justice of yours from evangelical and apostolic teaching, we can easily refute it by powers drawn from elsewhere. Evangelical and apostolic authority testifies that the Son of God, born of the immaculate Virgin, was held untainted by any corruption of sin. But, as the Apostle teaches, he is himself just and justifies all things—not because he had received the gift of justice from outside himself, through participation in which he would be called just, but because he is just principally and substantially. Thus we must necessarily say that in him the just and justice are identical and one. Otherwise the Apostle is mistaken in saying, ‘justifying all things.’ For if he received justice from elsewhere in order to be just himself, he would possess a weaker and lower justice than the one from whom he received it; and he would not be justifying all things. Rather, that one from whom he received it would be the one by whom both he and all things were justified.

“But he himself receives from himself that he may be just and justify all things; without him there is no saint and no one who is just, through whom every holy and just thing exists, and from whom every grace and every gift of justice descends, as blessed James says: ‘Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, descending from the Father of lights’ (James I). The fact that he says that the ‘gift’ descended ‘from the Father of lights’ should not trouble you, because when it descends from the Father, it also descends from the Son, since he himself says: ‘I and the Father are one’ (John X). Rightly, therefore, the Apostle says that he is ‘just and justifying’ all things (Romans III)—not just comparatively, as though his justice could be increased or diminished, but immutably and essentially just.

“Nevertheless, this Son of God, so great and such, as the evangelist relates, came in Galilee to the Jordan, to John, in order to be baptized by him. When John, conscious of his own weakness, refused the ministry, the Lord said to him: ‘Allow it for now; for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all justice’ (Matthew III). What does this mean? He in whom was the fullness of all justice, who was immutably and incomparably just and justifying all things—did he lack something of perfect justice, so that he needed the ministry of flowing material water and of the one baptizing in order to fulfill justice? Moreover, if he needed this ministry of baptism to supplement his justice, he was not perfectly just and was not justifying all things. For nothing is fulfilled unless something is lacking from its supreme fullness. Fullness cannot receive increase. Therefore he was not perfectly just—which it is impious to judge concerning God.

“But if he was just, he could receive nothing from baptism by which to supplement his justice; he was immutably, perfectly, and supremely just. Therefore he did not need to be baptized. Why, then, did he say, ‘Thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all justice,’ when he neither needed to be baptized nor possessed any justice lacking fullness that could be supplemented through baptism? He needed it [Col. 1273C] certainly—not for himself, but for us. He sought to fulfill justice—not his own, but ours. For the restoration of the human race always remained in his eternal purpose. Having distinguished the observances of the sacraments in a more spiritual manner, he willed that what was useful and necessary for the effecting of our restoration should be administered visibly through the hands of stewards, but fulfilled invisibly through the work of the Holy Spirit.

“For this reason the provident Lord established many sacraments in the holy Church, [e] among which he first established the use of baptism for the mystery of regeneration. Now *baptism* is rendered in Latin as *tinctio* (“dipping” or “immersion”), because there a person is changed for the better by the spirit of grace and becomes something quite different from what he had been. Previously we were hideous through the deformity of sins; in the immersion itself we are made beautiful through the whitening of virtues. This mystery is completed in no other way than through the designation of the Trinity, that is, through the naming of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Hence the Lord says to the disciples: ‘Go,’ he says, ‘teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit’ (Matthew XXVIII).

“This mystery is called a sacrament from hidden powers or from sacred things. It is fruitfully performed within the Church because the Holy Spirit, descending in it, secretly produces the effect of the same sacrament. Therefore, whether it is administered within the Church by good or by wicked ministers, because the Holy Spirit mystically gives it life, it is neither increased by the merits of the good nor diminished by the vices of the wicked: ‘Neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the growth’ (1 Corinthians III).

“Thus the minister himself does not say over the baptized person, ‘I,’ but rather: ‘Almighty God, Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has begotten you from water and the Holy Spirit and has given you remission of all sins, he himself has anointed you with the chrism of salvation unto eternal life.’ In this it is clear that the minister’s life detracts nothing from those who receive the power of sanctification from the Holy Spirit, especially since we read that Judas, who was to become the Lord’s betrayer, baptized among the other disciples. We also know that all those whom John the Baptist had baptized in water were rebaptized by the Lord’s disciples; yet we find no one whom Judas baptized being washed again in a second font.

“For if the betrayer’s wicked life had harmed those being baptized, surely he who had come to save everyone would not have allowed baptism to perish in that one man alone. But because human wickedness cannot diminish the work of divine power, he did not repeat what a man had administered and the Spirit had sanctified.

“Moreover, as divine Scripture testifies, we have heard that there were great kings in Jerusalem who administered certain affairs belonging to Babylon, while certain citizens of Babylon administered affairs belonging to Jerusalem. Thus we know that citizens of the good city administered the affairs of the evil city, and conversely that citizens of the evil city administered the affairs of the good city. If, then, the commonwealth of the good city could be administered by citizens of Babylon without being corrupted, how much more is the sacrament, which receives the power of sanctification through the invisible operation of the Holy Spirit, not corrupted by wicked ministers, since one thing is what is performed outwardly by the minister and another what is inwardly given life by the Holy Spirit.

“This is why, when John said in the Gospel, ‘The Pharisees heard that Jesus was baptizing, although Jesus himself was not baptizing but his disciples’ (John IV), he wished a distinction to be understood between God’s working and the ministry of the administrator: namely, in saying that Jesus baptized, he indicated the invisible operation of divine power; but in adding, ‘although Jesus was not baptizing, but his disciples,’ he meant not the working power but the visible administration carried out by those performing the rite. Therefore, in the baptism of the faithful, one thing is invisibly effected through the working Spirit, and another is visibly presented through the obedient minister.

“As for the fact that baptism is given through material water, the reason is this: the Lord willed that the invisible reality should be bestowed through a corresponding but certainly tangible thing and visible element, over which the Holy Spirit was borne in the beginning. For just as the body is outwardly cleansed by water, so the soul is secretly purified through its mystery. When God has been invoked, the Holy Spirit descends from heaven and, having healed the waters, sanctifies them from himself. They receive the power of purification, so that in them flesh and soul polluted by sins may be cleansed.

“Thus, through Christ’s death and resurrection, the power of baptism creates a new creature from the old, so that in those who are reborn both Christ’s death and his life may work. Blessed Paul says: ‘Do you not know that all we who have been baptized in Christ Jesus have been baptized into his death? For we were buried with him through baptism into death, so that just as Christ rose through the glory of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life’ (Romans VI).

“Hence it should be noted that, in the rule of baptism, death also intervenes through the killing of sin; the threefold immersion imitates the three-day burial; and the lifting from the waters represents the one rising from the tomb. Then the infant is drenched with the anointing of sacred chrism, from whose name Christ is called, and the person is sanctified after the washing. For just as remission of sins is given in baptism, so through anointing the Spirit is bestowed. Although this is administered bodily, it nevertheless benefits spiritually. The grace of baptism itself is likewise a visible act in that the person is immersed in water, but it becomes spiritual in that the person is cleansed from sins.

“The laying on of hands takes place so that the Holy Spirit may be summoned through blessing. Then the Paraclete willingly descends from the Father after the bodies have been cleansed and, as though recognizing the water of baptism as his former seat, rests upon it. For we read: ‘In the beginning the Spirit of God was borne over the waters’ (Genesis I).

“This is the first sacrament of our restoration. To confirm it, the Lord, needing no remission of sin and no remedy of rebirth, possessing nothing that could be cleansed by water, nevertheless hastened to John to be baptized in the waters of the Jordan, as the evangelist teaches. When John refused, he said: ‘Allow it for now; for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all justice’ (Matthew III), as though he were saying: ‘To provide an example of all justice, so that all the faithful may learn that no one can be justified without baptism, however innocently and justly he may live.’

“John, however, said: ‘And I did not know him’ (John I), as though he were saying: ‘At first I did not know him; but when I saw him retaining baptism for himself, I understood that he was the one who would baptize in the Holy Spirit and for the remission of sins.’ As he himself said: ‘Upon whomever you see the Spirit descending and remaining upon him, he is the one [Col. 1275D] who baptizes in the Holy Spirit’ (ibid.).

“Therefore it must be noted that it is impossible for anyone to aspire to perfect justice without the mystery of regenerating water, especially since works of justice could not grant this grace to Cornelius of Caesarea until Peter renewed him and his entire household with the saving water. The Holy Spirit fell upon them before baptism, in an unheard-of example of preceding grace, so that Peter, animated by this manifest power of God, might open the kingdom of God to the Gentiles. The Lord had previously warned him and the other disciples not to go along the way of the Gentiles.

“Since this is so, you are plainly convicted of contradicting yourselves: you say that you hold evangelical and apostolic commands, yet you preach things contrary to them. For the evangelist also relates that ‘Jesus came, and his disciples, into Judaea, and there he remained with them and baptized’ (John III). He established the sacrament of baptism and the power of regeneration when blood of redemption and water of baptism flowed from his side. Hence the apostle John says: ‘There are three that bear witness on earth: the Spirit, the water, and the blood’ (1 John V).

“Peter, to whom the Lord had granted primacy in the Church, when the promised coming of the Holy Spirit had filled the number of believers, consecrated with baptismal water the three thousand people converted by his preaching, as Luke testifies, saying: ‘When they heard these things, they were pierced in their hearts and said to Peter and the other apostles: What shall we do, men and brothers? Peter said to them: Repent, and let each one of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins, and you shall receive the Holy Spirit’ (Acts II). He exhorted them with many other words, saying: ‘Save yourselves from this corrupt generation’ (ibid.). Those, therefore, who received his word were baptized, and about three thousand souls were added on that day.

“Paul also, whose doctrine you profess to hold, having been afflicted with punishments for the injury he had done to God, was baptized by Ananias. He himself later says that he baptized Crispus and Gaius and the household of Stephanas. Philip also baptized in water the eunuch of Queen Candace, who was returning from Jerusalem, as the Book of the Apostles indicates (Acts VIII). This is the tradition received from the apostles that the Catholic Church still preserves.

“Hence it follows that, however justly and innocently anyone may seem to live, he nevertheless cannot be saved without the washing of the divine font. Yet, whether held bound by the guilt of original sin or by the fault of his own actions, once reborn in the font he is cleansed and purified from every stain of sin. He is so renewed that the one who had descended into the font as a son of the devil rises reborn as a son of God; the one who had descended as a son of transgression rises as a son of reconciliation.

“And, to gather everything together: just as the wisdom of the Creator first fashioned the original man from a virgin mass of earth, so the mercy of the Redeemer brought this man forth from the purified womb of the font. Unbelievers customarily chatter against this, saying that the first man, if he had not sinned, would have been endowed with the gift of immortality, whereas this man, however justly and innocently he may live, cannot avoid the loss of death; and therefore it is far from the truth to say that, just as the first man was fashioned by the Creator, so this man is regenerated from the font.

“It is easy to bend their objection toward its consequence if one can consider the purpose of divine mercy. From one and the same source of divine reason came both the wondrous creation of that man as immortal and the merciful restoration of this man, subject to death. It would have been easy for this man to be endowed with the glory of immortality, just as the first, had it been included in the Creator’s plan. But because free will and security from mortality deceived the first man, and through the guilt of transgression drew him into death, God invites this man to true life through the unavoidable event of death, lest, deceived by the hope of immortality, he devote himself too ardently to temporal pleasures.

“Because the first man, secure from death, despised the Creator, opened his ear to the tempter, and perished at once through the audacity of pride, the Redeemer’s mercy willed that this man should remain suspended under the sentence of death, so that through the guardianship of humility he might avoid the enemy, hear the Creator, and thus ascend to the things above. Nothing, therefore, contradicts the truth in saying that this man, regenerated from the font and invited by death to life, is formed in the same way as the first would have been formed had he not sinned—the first whom presumption of immortality soon compelled to undergo the ruin of death.

“But perhaps you object to me how much the gift of immortality benefited him, since the Creator did not fail to know that the cause of his ruin would arise from it. It had benefited him greatly, namely, if he had wished to remain without sin and not taste death, both he and his offspring would always have had the angels as fellow citizens. But when he neglected the Creator’s command, deceived by his own freedom, he was excluded from paradise and transferred the posterity of his kind to unknown regions. By begetting, he transmitted to his descendants the punishment that he himself had incurred as a transgressor. He could not have been delivered from it unless Christ had relieved him by his coming; through the mystery of new regeneration, Christ purified every past fault by the washing of his baptism and restored the condition of the original freedom.

“Therefore, to avoid the assaults of the wicked seducer, when infants or young people first come to the sacraments of regeneration, they do not approach the font of life until the unclean spirit has been driven away from them by the exorcisms and breathings of the priests. Thus it may truly be shown how the prince of this world is cast out, and how the strong man is first bound and his vessels are plundered and transferred into the possession of the victor, who leads captivity captive and gives gifts to men.

“If you refuse to believe that, when those who receive from the font a little child ignorant of faith, unaware of his own salvation, and not concerned for regeneration, the faith or confession of those people benefits that child, it follows that you must also deny that the faith of those who brought the paralytic benefited him. The evangelist says that ‘when Jesus saw their faith, he said to the paralytic: Take courage, son; your sins are forgiven you’ (Matthew IX).

“Nor would you consider acceptable what we read in the Gospel about the Canaanite woman, whose faith benefited her in obtaining salvation for her daughter. Another evangelist says that people brought little children to Jesus so that he might lay his hands upon them; and he embraced them, laid his hands upon them, and blessed them (Mark X). From this it is understood that it was not the faith of the little children—for they did not yet possess any—but the faithful belief of those who brought them that obtained the children’s blessing, just as the Lord said to the centurion who asked for the healing of his servant: ‘Go, and as you have believed, so let it be done for you.’ And the child was healed in that hour (Matthew VIII).”

Finally, you who think that nothing should be done bodily in the holy Church—so that, in this mystery of baptism [Col. 1278A], there should be no water, chrism oil, the ministry of the priest, or the other things that the Catholic Church preserves to this day—I ask you: what does that material washing of water mean, which you customarily offer to one another for the washing of your feet? For if you say that you received this from the Gospel, because the Lord, washing the feet of the disciples, is said to have left them this example, and that you likewise say you do this for that reason, it is foolish—indeed sacrilegious—to reject the other and much greater things that were established by the Lord himself, the author of all things, proclaimed by the Gospel, and handed down by the apostles, without which the fullness of our salvation cannot stand. These things the Lord himself instituted for his disciples to observe, both before and after the resurrection.

## II. On the Body and Blood of the Lord

[Col. 1278B]

Certainly, there would have been enough that could be said about these matters, if time permitted; but because the day, inclining toward sunset, admonishes each of us to return home, let us now, leaving these things aside, pass on to that sacred and immutable sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood which you, to your own confusion, are attempting to overthrow by attacking it against divine and apostolic tradition—unless you repent. It is impossible to investigate by the insight of human reason what weight of power this mystery contains in itself, however great that weight may be. What is beyond the human soul cannot be confined within human understanding. Human eloquence, therefore, is not sufficient to comprehend it. For this is that holy and wondrous [Col. 1278C] exchange by which heavenly things are joined to earthly things, the realms below are despoiled, paradise is opened, and the exiled human being is restored to the ancient garden; through it, too, the angels recognize the human being as their fellow citizen, and adore the human being—God—placed above them. But since time urges us, trusting in the grace of him of whom we speak, we shall declare as much as the perception of our weakness apprehends.

Sacrifice is so called as though it meant “a sacred act,” because it is consecrated by mystical prayer in remembrance of the Lord’s passion, undergone for us. Therefore, at his own command, we believe it to be the body and blood of Christ: although it comes from the fruits of the earth, it is sanctified and becomes a sacrament, through the invisible working of the Spirit of God. I have called it a sacrament for this reason: it is, as it were, a viaticum [Col. 1278D] introducing us to the contemplation of eternity. The Greeks call the sacrament of this bread and cup *Eucharistia*, which in Latin is interpreted as “good grace” (*bona gratia*). For what is better than the body and blood of Christ? This sacrifice, made from bread and wine mixed with water, is consecrated upon the altar by ineffable sanctification, by the cross and by his words. There, a saving remembrance of his passion, resurrection, and ascension into heaven is enacted; and it becomes the true and proper body of our Lord Jesus Christ, and his true and proper blood, although it appears to be something else.

It appears to be material bread, but it most truly becomes the body of Christ, as we have learned through the testimony of Truth itself. For on the very night when he was [Col. 1279A] voluntarily about to hand over his body to death for us through the mystery of the passion, as the evangelist relates, “He took bread, and blessed it, and broke it, and gave it to his disciples, saying: Take, this is my body. Likewise, taking the cup, he blessed it and gave it to his disciples, saying: Drink from this, all of you; this is the cup of the New Testament, which will be poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins” (Matt. 26; Mark 22; Luke 22). When he adds, “Do this in remembrance of me,” he referred this to what he commanded to be done daily by the faithful through the ministry of priests, while the remembrance of his passion is enacted and holy bread and the consecrated cup are offered under the sacrament of the sharing of his flesh and blood.

To this spiritual nourishment, to this mystical and [Col. 1279B] divine banquet, the Lord invites us. He indicates to us such a necessity of consuming this food that we cannot otherwise have life in ourselves unless we have eaten his flesh and drunk his blood.

But perhaps someone, hearing this too carnally, might object that no one can have life in himself, since Christ did not distribute for anyone to eat the flesh that he carried in his own body, but is said to have entered heaven with his body perfect and entire. Or perhaps—something impious to say—that the Lord incurred the fault of lying in this statement, since many appear to have life in themselves who do not remember ever having tasted his flesh or blood. With God’s will, we resolve this matter as follows.

[Col. 1279C]

Human beings can indeed have this temporal life in the present age without this food; but they cannot have eternal life, which is promised only to faithful people who worthily receive the flesh and blood of Christ. Hence he himself says: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves” (John 6)—namely, the life of the soul, Christ himself, who elsewhere says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14). He called himself the Son of Man, whose body is daily sacrificed by priests upon the altar. Concerning this the Apostle says: “The bread which we break, is it not the body of the Lord? And the cup which we bless, is it not the sharing in the blood of the Lord?” (1 Cor. 10.)

Therefore, when the Lord said [Col. 1279D], “I am the living bread which came down from heaven; if anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever,” the Jews argued among themselves, saying: “How can this man give us his flesh to eat?” (John 6.) They did not understand this bread; hearing of flesh, they recoiled. For they were not members of Christ, and therefore they were scandalized by the flesh of Christ.

Likewise, when the disciples, understanding his words carnally, said, “This is a hard saying; who can hear it?” (ibid.), the Lord replied: “Does this scandalize you? What then if you should see the Son of Man ascending where he was before?” (ibid.) The sentence was suspended and seemingly incomplete. For the disciples thought that Christ would have his flesh, with which he was clothed, cut into pieces and distributed to believers; and, supposing that it was contrary to nature for human beings to consume human flesh as food, they said of this exceedingly difficult and impossible matter: “This is a hard saying; who can hear it?”

Therefore the Lord said [Col. 1280A], “If you should see the Son of Man ascending where he was before,” implying: “Then you will see that I do not distribute my flesh to believers in the manner you suppose. Rather, by giving myself to them through spiritual grace, I transform them into my body. This grace is not consumed by bites or worn away by teeth; it is received by the palate of the inner person—that is, by reason and the understanding of the mind.”

Thus the sharing of the Lord’s body, as we said above, is called in Greek—but in a term customary among Latins—*Eucharistia*, that is, “good grace.” [Col. 1280B]

The holy bread by which the Lord’s body is consecrated and which is visibly received by the mouth can be seen; but the power of the Word of God—that is, his divinity—by which the soul of the recipient is sanctified cannot be seen.

Christ therefore ascended with his body perfect and left us the sacrament of his body. Finally, lest they think that eternal life was promised to them in this food and drink in such a way that they would no longer die bodily, after saying, “Whoever eats my flesh,” he immediately added: “And I will raise him up on the last day” (ibid.). For whoever worthily eats Christ’s flesh and drinks his blood, although dead in body, possesses eternal life meanwhile according to the spirit. As for the body, it too will not be deprived of eternal life, because it will be raised on the last day and will no longer die.

[Col. 1280C]

In this way, therefore, the word of Truth was without the fault of lying when it said that no one has life in himself except the one who is nourished by the spiritual food of sharing in his flesh and blood.

It might, however, appear to weak hearers that what follows contradicts this statement: “The flesh profits nothing” (John 6), since above he had said that no one has life in himself without receiving his flesh. But it must be understood in this way: “If you wish to understand my words carnally, so that you eat my flesh as you would any other food, the flesh profits you nothing.”

[Col. 1280D]

For who could distribute his body in this way throughout the many churches spread across the whole world, distributing it for consumption by so many innumerable peoples, over such long periods of time, each day and to each person, without ever diminishing?

To this we reply, since we hear you confessing the evangelical faith and apostolic tradition. The Word who in the beginning was with God became flesh at the end of time. How was he wholly with the Father always, and how did he confine his whole self within the Virgin’s womb? If he was wholly in the Virgin, how was he wholly with the Father?

But hear the mystery of such great power. As the Son of God was about to ascend into heaven, he promised the disciples, who were anxious at his departure, that he would remain with them all the days until the consummation of the age—although shortly before he had foretold that he was going to the Father. [Col. 1281A]

Human understanding would recoil from believing this unless the power of discernment were applied.

A human being, bounded by the body, cannot remain in one place or depart from a place except through the succession of time. But the eternal essence of God is confined neither by time nor by place. For just as it always is, so it is always everywhere. His remaining, therefore, means that he is wholly absent from no place; his returning means that he withdraws from them the body taken upon earth.

Thus he said that he would remain with them and go to the Father, while he carried up to heaven the body that he had assumed, now exalted in the glory of incorruption, and promised that through the presence of his majesty he would remain everywhere with them. Therefore, since he went to the Father, with whom he always is, and remained with the disciples, it is not impossible for him to preserve in heaven the body that is eternal and incorruptible, while on earth he offers us the sacrament of his body for communion.

[Col. 1281B]

As for your objection that it is consumed daily in so many places, times, peoples, and by so many people, without being diminished, this causes no scandal of unbelief if anyone wishes to contemplate with the eyes of faith what the Lord said while extending the bread and cup to them: “Do this in remembrance of me.”

Christ suffered once and died once; yet daily in the Church he suffers for us, daily he dies for us, while, at his command, the memory of his most holy passion is enacted and, through the ministry of priests, the saving mysteries of his body and blood are renewed. These are invisibly vivified by the same Spirit through whose working the Son of God was incarnate in the Virgin’s womb.

[Col. 1281C]

This may be understood from the words of the blessed apostle Andrew, whose teaching you profess to imitate among the other apostles. When he was compelled to sacrifice to idols, he said: “To the almighty God, who is one and true, I sacrifice every day—not the smoke of incense, nor the flesh of bellowing bulls, nor the blood of goats, but every day I sacrifice upon the altar of the cross the spotless blood. After all the people of believers have eaten his flesh and drunk his blood, the Lamb who was sacrificed remains whole and alive.”

Although he was truly sacrificed, and his flesh was truly eaten by the people, and his blood was truly drunk, nevertheless, as I have said, he remains whole, undefiled, and alive.

[Col. 1281D]

When Aegeas asked how it could happen that a Lamb who had been killed should live, and, having been sacrificed and eaten, should remain whole and undefiled, the Apostle replied: “If he believed by imitating the example of the disciples, it would be easy for him to learn; but otherwise he could not attain to the investigation of the truth.”

It will likewise be impossible for you to contemplate this unless, laying aside the rigidity of unbelief, you receive the example and faith of the disciples. But because we have taught that this must be contemplated with the eyes of faith, if anyone is more edified by visible things than stirred by the power of invisible realities, we shall relate a few of the many things that the Lord deigned to show regarding this very sacrament of his body and blood, so that the minds of carnal people might be strengthened by what could be observed with bodily eyes.

[Col. 1282A]

At the time when the blessed Gregory was serving as pastor of the Roman Church, a certain married woman, moved by religious devotion, was accustomed to make offerings and to bring them familiarly to the supreme pontiff at the church. One day, as she customarily approached in due order to receive communion from the bishop’s hand, and the pontiff extended to her a portion of the Lord’s body, saying, “May the body of our Lord Jesus Christ benefit you for the forgiveness of sins and eternal life,” she smiled.

When the man of God observed this, he withdrew the communion and, placing it separately upon the altar, entrusted it to a deacon for safekeeping while the others communicated. After the sacred mysteries had been completed, the bishop asked the reason for her laughter. She replied that she recognized that little portion as part of the offering that she herself had made with her own hands [Col. 1282B] and presented to the bishop, and that she had laughed because he had called it the Lord’s body.

The bishop therefore addressed the people and urged them all to pour out a common prayer to the Lord, asking that, to strengthen the faith of many, he might restrain the woman’s unbelief through a manifest sign of his power. And so it happened.

When everyone had risen from prayer and they were pressing forward to behold the heavenly spectacle, the bishop uncovered the corporal pall and, while the whole people and the woman looked on, found a portion of a little finger stained with blood. Turning to the woman, he said: “Now that you have experienced the miracle of divine power, do not delay in hearing the Truth say: ‘The bread that I give is my flesh, and my blood is truly drink.’”

[Col. 1282C]

But the Creator, who foreknew our weakness, by the power through which he made all things from nothing and fashioned for himself a body from the flesh of the Virgin through the working of the Holy Spirit, transforms bread and wine mixed with water, while their proper appearance remains, into his flesh and blood through the sanctification of his Spirit and through the catholic prayer, for our restoration.

Finally, when everyone had again prostrated themselves in prayer, they implored divine power to restore the holy mystery to its former form, so that it might become possible for the woman to consume it. And so it happened. Having therefore received a share in the Lord’s body, the woman thereafter advanced in holy devotion and faith; and all who were present grew fervent in the love of Christ and in belief.

[Col. 1282D]

At another time, a certain man of the highest nobility and, according to worldly standards, great power, asked the blessed Gregory to send him relics of the blessed apostles and martyrs. He was familiar with the bishop and, through his admonition, had been sufficiently instructed in the worship of God.

He therefore received the envoys honorably and kept them with him for some time. After making commemorations of the apostles and martyrs for this purpose, and completing the solemnities of the Mass while consecrating the relics, he divided into portions the cloths upon which he had celebrated the sacred rites and placed each portion separately in small boxes. After securing them with seals, he handed them over to the envoys, who then departed.

As they were traveling and did not know what they were carrying, they began to reproach themselves rather anxiously for being completely ignorant of what they were bringing to their lord. Why delay the account? Having broken the seals and opened the little boxes, they saw nothing but pieces of cloth.

[Col. 1283A]

Indignant, they returned to Rome, accusing the bishop of having valued their lord’s request and the labor of their journey so little that he had sent him pieces of cloth in place of relics, as though such material could not be found among them.

The bishop patiently endured their folly and ordered them to attend the celebration of the mysteries. When the point in the service for the sermon was reached, he urged the people of God to pray and to implore the saints, asking that God deign to display the power of his might in this matter, so that those who did not understand what faith deserved might come to recognize it.

After the prayer had been offered, and after taking the knife from the man who had broken the seals, he pierced one of the pieces of cloth on the altar of Saint Peter and cut it through the middle. [Col. 1283B]

From it—an astonishing sight—blood flowed and stained the entire piece of cloth.

As the envoys and the others present stood astonished at the miracle concerning the secret of the sacred faith, the blessed bishop said to those who had thought little of the holy relics: “Know, brothers, that at the consecration of the Lord’s body and blood, when offerings were placed upon the holy altar for the sanctification of the relics in honor of the apostles and martyrs of Christ to whom they were specially assigned, their blood—which was poured out for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ—always entered these cloths.”

Thus Saint Gregory sent the envoys back to their lord, rejoicing and strengthened in faith.

[Col. 1283C]

Consider, therefore: If the blood of Christ’s martyrs entered the cloths in their memory, how much more do the blood and body of Christ transform the holy bread and wine whenever the memory of the Lord’s passion is enacted? One further matter remains to be said, a wondrous one and useful for refuting the unbelief of the wicked.

A certain man venerable for his virtue, named Plexis, watched over a flock of monks with tireless care. It would be enough to speak of his virtues and miracles alone. But hear one thing that usefully concerns the present matter.

One day, as he customarily stood before the most holy altar with humble devotion and, celebrating the solemnities of the Mass, consecrated the venerable mysteries of the Lord’s body and blood, when the time of the fraction arrived, he suddenly saw what must be believed faithfully and admired with believing hearts: namely, [Col. 1283D] the portion of the consecrated bread being transformed into an infant, while an angel of the Lord divided it into portions. This was a manifest sign of the truth, showing that what we take from the altar under the sacrament of sharing in the flesh and blood is the true body and blood of Christ.

Often, too, while these sacred mysteries are being celebrated, many have seen choirs of angels surrounding the altar table on which the holy things are consecrated, as soldiers standing in attendance upon their king.

At these words of the lord bishop, all the faithful who stood around, with tears rising in their eyes, praised God’s power and God’s mercy. Then he turned to those who had been led astray by heretical perversity and said: “Tell me [Col. 1284A] if you have anything by which you think these things can be refuted.”

But they, stunned by the weight of his words and the power of the heavenly miracles, with lowered faces and displaying something like repentance, sighed deeply and gave a single groan, saying that they heard nothing here except what was divine—something that made them mute and almost speechless.

Falling to the ground and beating their breasts, they confessed their guilt. Raising their voices, they declared that they marveled at God’s patience, since he had tolerated them for so long to the disgrace of the Christian name. They said they could hope for no forgiveness for their error, since, by plunging into such a depth of unbelief, they had not only immersed themselves but had also killed many others by hurling them into the precipice of the same ruin.

The bishop said to them: “You who have until now barred the fallen from the path of forgiveness and judged [Col. 1284B] that no fruit of reconciliation was to be hoped for in penance—it is hard for you to seek this from the one who calls sinners to repentance and rejoices more over one repentant sinner than over ninety-nine righteous people, unless by the price of a better faith you strive to seek it from him; for he is certainly always ready to open the bosom of his mercy to those who repent.

“But if you reject the hardness of your faithlessness by accepting the Catholic faith, and, laying aside the rigidity of unbelief, receive the teachings of the Christian faith, I confidently promise you forgiveness from God.”

## III. On the Holy Church, Which Is the House of God

But I still perceive in you certain shadows of unbelief. As long as you permit them to remain in your hearts, you cannot hope for any visitation of the light from above. [Col. 1284C]

These are the shadows that cause you, condemned by the blindness of unbelief, to rise up against the holy Church of God and to attack the house of the living God with disgraceful verbal blows.

You say that there is nothing in the temple of God worthy of any religious worship more than the chamber of one’s own dwelling; that nothing in it is holy except the cement and stones arranged by the work of craftsmen; and that the table of the Lord, upon which the offerings of his body and blood are presented, contains no other sacrament in itself than a heap of stones.

If what we said earlier about his body and blood is faithfully held, there is nothing here that the human mind can rightly doubt. For just as our Lord and Redeemer instituted which things were to be used in sanctifying these mysteries and by which ministers they were to be consecrated, so he also chose the place in which they were to be specially sacrificed—namely, in the holy Church, which is specially called the house of God, because there is no place for true sacrifice outside the Catholic Church.

[Col. 1284D]

This place has been consecrated for the performance of divine worship. Concerning it the Lord himself says: “My house shall be called a house of prayer” (Luke 19). On the fortieth day after his birth, he desired to be offered there with sacrifices; there Simeon received him, having attained the fulfillment of his long desire; there Anna the prophetess recognized the Redeemer of Israel. In praise of her holy purpose and steadfast widowhood, she received this singular commendation from the Gospel reading: she “did not depart [Col. 1285A] from the temple.”

Finally, when the Lord was a boy of twelve, he remained in the temple without his mother or relatives knowing it. When they sought him, he said: “Why were you looking for me? Did you not know that I must be in the things that belong to my Father?” (Luke 2.)

As the hour of his passion approached, he went to Jerusalem and immediately entered the temple, showing us the pattern of religious conduct that we ought to follow: whenever we enter a town, a fortress, or any place where a house of prayer has been consecrated to God, we ought first to hasten to it, where, after offering the vows of our prayer, we may commend ourselves to God.

Having entered the temple, he began to drive out those who were selling and buying there, saying: “My house is a house of prayer” (Luke 19).

[Col. 1285B]

That house of God had first been built by Solomon, and later by Jesus the priest and Zerubbabel—not because God dwells in temples made by human hands, but so that his name might be invoked there, so that he might hear the prayers of his devout people there, receive their vows, and accept their gifts and prayers.

A little later the evangelist says of this place: “The blind and the lame came to him, and he healed them in the temple” (Matt. 21). After expelling the unworthy and profaners from the temple, he healed the blind and the lame there—not because he lacked the power to heal in the street or in the city, but because he exercised the power of his might for a definite symbolic purpose: plainly to show that outside the Church no one has access to a place of salvation, and that this is the place in which divine benefits are more abundantly granted to those who seek them.

[Col. 1285C]

Here the sinful tax collector came and returned justified. Concerning this the Book of the Apostles also says: “Every day they continued with one accord in the temple” (Acts 2). A little later: “Peter and John went up into the temple at the ninth hour of prayer” (Acts 3). Of this the Lord says: “Two men went up into the temple to pray” (Luke 18).

Moreover, the sick man whom the Lord had healed after he had wasted away through a long illness beside the Sheep Pool could not recognize the author of his salvation while he was sitting amid the crowd, until Jesus found him in the temple and there wished to be recognized by him. He thus plainly taught that if we desire to recognize the grace of our Creator and to attain to his vision, we must devoutly hasten to the temple of God, where we should strive to give him thanks for benefits already received and to implore him for those yet to be received, and should take care to prepare ourselves as the temple of God in which he may mercifully deign to come and make his dwelling.

[Col. 1285D]

It had always been the Lord’s familiar custom that, whenever he entered any city, he would immediately turn aside to the temple. Hence the evangelist John says: “Jesus went to the Mount of Olives, and at dawn he came again into the temple” (John 8). The evangelist Luke says: “Jesus entered the synagogue according to his custom, and rose to read” (Luke 4). When you hear “synagogue,” understand “temple,” where the Jews’ assembly was.

[Col. 1286A]

This seat had always been especially pleasing to the Lord, so that whenever he entered it he would address the people and deign to disclose the mysteries of his divinity. Although we know that no place is empty of the presence of his majesty, nevertheless he grants the benefits of his grace more fully and more abundantly here to those who ask, where the most holy mysteries of his body and blood are celebrated and divine praises and vows are offered.

In the temple the Lord appeared to Solomon in the cloud of his glory, saying that there he would grant relief from every tribulation and distress to those who asked him, and that, against storms and mortality, the sword and famine, drought and every disorder of the air, whatever was sought there by those who asked would be accomplished by God’s grace.

[Col. 1286B]

Certainly, every day the Lord enters the holy spiritual Church—not because he delights in the height of its walls or the variety of its pavements, but because the assembly of believers takes place there. There he receives thanksgiving from the faithful for the benefits he has bestowed; there he receives hymns, spiritual songs, and sacrifices of devoted praise; and there he grants the holy sharing in his body and his blood.

Finally, Luke, writing to Theophilus, says that the Lord Jesus “after his passion presented himself alive to the disciples by many proofs, appearing to them for forty days and speaking about the kingdom of God” (Acts 13). What is speaking about the kingdom of God except arranging matters concerning the condition of the Church, which is called the kingdom of God?

You insist, then, that the house of God—which we call the Church—has been built by piling up stones, and that nothing holy derives from its stone material; and therefore that there is no difference, but that prayers made in your dwellings and private [Col. 1286C] homes are just as effective as those made in God’s holy temple. Against this, we must consider why the Lord commanded Moses to make the tabernacle of the covenant for himself with such worship, in which his glory appeared more specially than in all other places, and in which, uniquely, he was consulted in doubtful matters and set forth judgments and the law for the children of Israel.

Hence the Apostle says to the Corinthians: “Do you not have houses for eating and drinking, or do you despise the Church of God?” (1 Cor. 11.) A little later he says: “Therefore, my brothers, when you come together to eat, wait for one another; but if anyone is hungry, let him eat at home, so that you do not come together for judgment” (ibid.).

[Col. 1286D]

Paul thus shows that we come together in the Church in order to pray and to eat the Lord’s supper. You have heard two reasons why the people come together in the Church: one from ancient tradition, so that they may receive judgments and knowledge concerning matters; the other from the New Testament, so that they may eat Christ’s body.

We seek both in the Church: namely, to hear there judgments concerning our evil or good conduct, and knowledge of God, and to eat Christ’s body.

But because certain men grew their hair long, while women proceeded into the Church with uncovered heads, glorying in their hair—which was not only indecent but also provided fuel for lust—the Apostle restrained them from this custom, saying: “Is it fitting for a woman to pray to God in the Church without being veiled? And does not nature itself teach you that if a man grows his hair long, it is a disgrace to him, whereas if a woman grows her hair long, it is her glory?” (ibid.)

[Col. 1287A]

Finally, you ought to listen to the blessed martyr Urban—if you truly believe that martyrs ought to be imitated—who dedicated the house of Saint Caecilia to the name of the holy Church.

Hence the distinguished teacher Augustine says, on Psalm 80: “These structures, which are built for a time to receive the bodies of either the living or the dead, are necessary, but they pass away with time. Will we raise these buildings into heaven after God’s judgment? Nevertheless, without them we cannot at this time do what pertains to possessing heaven.”

The house itself is therefore called a church because it contains the Church—that is, the people called together by him who makes them dwell with one accord in a house. It is sanctified by the bishop so that the coming of angels may be in it, and so that people entering it may know that they must restrain themselves from every shameful word, vulgarity, and useless thought.

Let those who enter the Church hear what Moses heard when he wished to see the burning bush. The Lord said: “Do not come near; remove the sandals from your feet, for the place on which you stand is holy ground” (Exod. 3). And the angel said to Joshua: “Remove the sandals from your feet, for the place on which you stand is holy ground” (Josh. 5). The Apostle says: “The temple of God is holy, which you are” (1 Cor. 3).

As we enter the house of God, the Church, where the Lord and his angels are, we ought therefore to remove the sandals of dead works, to think [Col. 1287C] about the conduct of the angels and the presence of God’s majesty, and by constant hymns and spiritual psalms to invoke the name of the Lord, so that what the Psalmist says may be fulfilled in us: “Strengthen, O God, what you have worked in us, from your holy temple, which is in Jerusalem” (Ps. 67).

## IV. On the Sacred Altar

As for the stories you invent about the Lord’s table and its material structure—that it is nothing other than a heap of stones, and that therefore it is venerated through an empty religious observance—this is not the voice of a human being but of the devil. For there is no other place in the world where the venerable offerings of his body and blood can be duly sanctified. Whoever does not believe that the heavenly mystery remains upon the altar does not understand the price of the cross.

The Lord commanded through Moses that an altar of earth be made for him, upon which holocausts and sacrifices were to be offered. The Book of Leviticus testifies that the Lord had commanded this same Moses that the priest who had been anointed should place some of the blood of the victim upon the horns of the altar of incense, most pleasing to the Lord, which was in the tabernacle of testimony.

This altar, in the new tabernacle—that is, in the holy Church—holds the image of Christ’s body and of the tomb in which the blood of the true and undefiled Lamb, Christ, who offered himself as a sacrifice to God the Father, is daily offered by the faithful.

This was first consecrated by the patriarchs and later, as we said, by the Lord through Moses. For we read that Noah, after the flood, “built [Col. 1288A] an altar to the Lord, and taking from the clean cattle and birds, offered holocausts upon it; and the Lord smelled the fragrance of sweetness” (Gen. 8).

Likewise Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob did so. Jacob, departing from Beersheba, saw a ladder extending from earth to the heavens, by which the angels of God were ascending and descending; he also saw the Lord speaking to him.

Rising in the morning, he said: “Truly, the Lord is in this place, and I did not know it.” And, afraid, he said: “How terrible is this place! This is nothing other than the house of God and the gate of heaven.” Rising in the morning, he took the stone that he had placed beneath his head and set it up as a pillar; then he poured oil upon it and made a vow to the Lord (ibid., 28).

There he offered tithes and sacrifices. In imitation of this, altars are still anointed with sacred oil in the holy Church.

Concerning this the Lord says in the Gospel: “If you offer [Col. 1288B] your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there” (Matt. 5). And elsewhere: “Which is greater,” he says, “the gift, or the altar that sanctifies the gift?” (ibid., 23.)

Luke says of this: “When Zacharias was serving as priest in the temple, an angel of the Lord appeared to him, standing at the right side of the altar of incense” (Luke 1). And John says in the Apocalypse: “I saw beneath the altar of God the souls of those who had been slain” (Rev. 6). Again: “Another angel came and stood [Col. 1288C] before the altar, holding a golden censer, and much incense was given to him, so that he might offer it from the prayers of the saints upon the altar that was before the throne” (ibid., 8). A little later: “The angel,” he says, “took the censer and filled it with fire from the altar” (ibid.).

### On Incense.

Since, in speaking of the sacred altar, we have also mentioned incense and frankincense, whose use we read was observed both in heaven through the ministry of angels and on earth by the ancient and modern Fathers, we possess the following authority from divine institution.

Among the other things that the Lord ordained to be made for the worship of the tabernacle, he also commanded Moses as follows: “You shall make me an altar for burning incense, of acacia wood” (Exod. 30). And again: “You shall place the altar opposite the veil that hangs before the ark, before the mercy seat, where I shall speak with you; and Aaron shall burn fragrant incense upon it in the morning. When he arranges the lamps, he shall burn it; and when he sets them up in the evening, he shall burn the perpetual incense before the Lord” (ibid.). Then, in what follows, he says: “Take for yourself spices—stacte, onycha, and fragrant galbanum—and the clearest frankincense; you shall make incense compounded by the art of the perfumer, carefully mixed, pure, and sanctified for remission” (ibid.).

“To proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord and the day of recompense” (Luke 4). And shortly afterward, when they were gazing at him, he said: “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing” (ibid.).

Paul, too, who always teaches us to pass from the old things to the new, inserted many passages from Moses, the prophets, and the Psalms into his writings, as in the passage from Genesis: [Col. 1289A] “The first man, Adam, was made a living soul” (1 Cor. 15). What then? Is he to be said to have rejected the Old Testament, when in the Epistle to the Hebrews he writes in this way: “The first tabernacle was made, in which were the lampstand, the table, and the presentation of the loaves, which is called the Holy Place; behind the second veil was the tabernacle called the Holy of Holies, having a golden censer and the ark of the covenant covered on every side with gold” (Heb. 9), and the other things that he discusses in that same Epistle concerning the Old Testament?

Therefore, following the examples of the holy Fathers, the apostles and their successors transferred many elements of that ancient observance for use in the ministry of the New Testament, to be administered by the ministers of the Church, [Col. 1289B] such as this very anointing with sacred chrism and oil, about which we began to speak, with which priests and kings were formerly anointed at the Lord’s command.

For it is written in Exodus that the people should offer oil, the Lord saying: “Command the children of Israel to offer [or bring] you the purest oil from olive trees” (Exod. 27). For, as Isidore says, the olive itself is the tree, the olive is its fruit, and oil is its juice. The olive tree is especially a tree of peace; it possesses richness by which the limbs of the weary and weak are restored, and it provides the grace of light. Its juice, when offered by the people, is a simple liquid; but through the blessing of priests it is transferred into a sacrament, just as we previously taught concerning baptismal water.

People governed by the senses, however, cannot perceive these things; faith must understand what [Col. 1289C] bodily eyes cannot contemplate, so that what the Apostle says may come to pass: “His invisible attributes are understood and perceived through the things that have been made; his eternal power and divinity also” (Rom. 1).

Hence blessed Augustine, explaining Psalm 44, says: “Visible oil is a sign; invisible oil is a sacrament. Spiritual oil is invisible. God can bestow spiritual oil by himself, without bodily oil; but because of people governed by the senses visible things are enacted, so that invisible things may be grasped more easily.”

Finally, the apostles used this practice of oil in the restoration of the sick, and apostolic men used it in the signing of neophytes. Thus it is written in the Gospel: “Going out, they preached that people should repent, and they cast out demons, and they anointed many sick people with oil, and [Col. 1289D] healed them” (Mark 6). Hence the Apostle James says: “Is anyone among you sick? Let him summon the presbyters of the Church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord; and if he is in sins, they will be forgiven him” (James 5).

Thus it is clear that this custom was handed down by the apostles themselves to the holy Church: that the possessed and all other sick people should be anointed with oil consecrated by pontifical blessing. Neophytes are also signed with it, as we have said. At the exorcism of this oil, the devil is commanded to depart from the catechumen, who is still regarded as dead because he has not yet been baptized. The anointing with chrism, however, sanctifies the living person who has been brought back from the dead and invites the grace of the Holy Spirit into adoption as a son.

[Col. 1290A] In the Old Testament, moreover, Aaron was anointed by Moses, as were his sons, who were to minister in the tabernacle of God, just as the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: “Take Aaron and his sons and bring them to the entrance of the tent of testimony; and when you have washed the father and his sons with water, you shall clothe Aaron in his garments and pour the oil of anointing upon his head” (Exod. 19).

And again: “The high priest—that is, the chief priest among his brothers—upon whose head the oil of anointing has been poured, whose hands have been consecrated for the priesthood, and who has been clothed with the holy vestments, shall not uncover his head or tear his garments; he shall not enter at all where there is any dead person. He shall not make himself unclean even for his father or mother, nor shall he depart from the holy places, lest he pollute [Col. 1290B] the sanctuary of his God, because the oil of the holy anointing of his God is upon him” (Lev. 21).

Hence the Psalmist says: “The Lord your God has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Ps. 44). When he mentioned “companions,” whom else did he have in view except bishops, whom, as the vicars of Christ, he foresaw through the prophetic spirit as governing the holy Church, and who were to receive this grace of anointing from him who is the true priest according to the order of Melchizedek?

Christ is our head; therefore the pontiff is anointed on the head, since he is made Christ’s vicar. By imitating him who is the head of the whole Church, through this mystery of anointing he himself is also made the head of the Church entrusted to him. And just as Christ intercedes for the universal Church, so the bishop intercedes for the Church entrusted to him.

[Col. 1290C] In the statement that the prophet says Christ was anointed above his companions, he indicates the gift of spiritual grace by which Christ was anointed above his companions—that is, above the other saints. His anointing was fulfilled at the time when he was baptized in the Jordan, and the Holy Spirit descended upon him in the form of a dove and remained in him. But in saying that Christ’s companions were anointed with oil, he indicates the grace of material anointing with which Christ’s vicars, that is, the pontiffs, are poured over.

For if Christ alone had reserved for himself the singular anointing of priestly grace, the Apostle would by no means have taught that the other priests possessed this grace when he said: “Many have become priests, because they were prevented by death from continuing” (Heb. 7).

[Col. 1290D] Therefore the holy Church still preserves this custom of anointing when bishops are ordained. The bishops themselves also anoint the hands of presbyters when they consecrate them, with oil, so that they may be pure for offering sacrifices to God and generous in the other duties of piety. Oil signifies both things: the grace of healing and the charity of love, concerning which the Apostle says that “the charity of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us” (Rom. 5).

But if someone objects: Since God can heal the sick, drive out demons, and sanctify his own without oil, why is the rite of consecrating oil observed with such devotion? We reply: Could not the ancient righteous please God without circumcision? [Col. 1291A] Certainly they could; but after they had been commanded to be circumcised, if they did not do so, they were held by the bonds of sin. Hence blessed Augustine says: “For the ancient righteous, if they were not circumcised, it was not a sin; but after God commanded Abraham and his descendants to be circumcised, it became a grave sin if it was not done.”

## V. On signs

The use of signs, too, was taken from the Old Testament. There the Lord commanded through Moses that hammered silver trumpets be made. When the Levites sounded them during the sacrifice, the people, summoned by the sweetness of their sound, would hasten to the tabernacle of the covenant to worship. By their blast they were also summoned to war and would overthrow the weapons of their adversaries; [Col. 1291B] the strength of the enemy, terrified by that sound, would collapse upon itself.

For we read that, before the ark of the covenant, the walls of Jericho, by which the army of the adversaries was enclosed, fell at the sound of the trumpets. In the same way, bells are now made in the holy Church, so that through their ringing the faithful may be invited into the bosom of Mother Church and, laying aside the occupations of worldly care, may learn to arm themselves against spiritual assaults.

And just as, when the sound of a war trumpet is heard, soldiers are stirred more courageously to battle and the hostile attack, scattered by fear, is dispersed, so, when the harmful crowds have been terrified, the people summoned by the sign may be strengthened for the Lord’s battles; and, when the aerial powers have been driven far away, the assembly of the Church may be preserved by an angelic hand.

## VI. On the sacred orders

[Col. 1291C] We must now come to the most sacred orders, which we hear you reject with the obstinacy of a deranged mind. Concerning them, it must first be noted that the Apostle names those who are most necessary in the Church and portrays their conduct—those without whom the offering at the altar cannot properly be celebrated, namely, Levites and priests.

For just as a priest watches over the offerings without interruption, a deacon is necessary to minister the things that the priest requires. The other orders are subject to these. As the Church grew, the ecclesiastical office also grew; so that the multitude of the Church might be assisted, lower orders were added to aid those placed in authority.

Among these are the doorkeepers, that is, gatekeepers, who with vigilant care guard the door of the holy Church and [Col. 1291D] watch over the treasures of the house of God. Through them we gain access to the temple of the Lord, who says: “I am the door” (John 10). They admit those whom the privilege of faith invites and exclude those who have been separated from unity; to them the Lord will say: “I do not know you.”

Next are instituted the readers, that is, narrators of the Lord’s word, concerning whom the Apostle says: “To another is given the utterance of wisdom according to the same Spirit” (1 Cor. 12). These are the ones who, singing distinctly and orderly in the church, instruct the faithful by their holy conduct.

Then there are the exorcists, who through the laying on of hands and priestly blessing receive the power to cast out unclean spirits and the grace of healings. Concerning them the Lord says in the Gospel: “They will cast out demons [Col. 1292A] in my name” (Matt. 7).

Formerly, certain people, wishing to usurp this power of driving out demons, though endowed with no laying on of hands or privilege of priestly blessing, attempted through exorcism to cast demons out of possessed bodies, as the Book of the Apostles relates concerning the Jewish sons of Sceva. When they were exorcising unclean spirits in the name of Jesus whom Paul preached, they were suddenly afflicted by the fury of the indignant spirit and, paying the penalty for their rash undertaking through an avenging spirit, heard this reply of rebuke: “I know Jesus, and I know Paul; but who are you?” And immediately the unclean spirit leaped upon them (Acts 19).

By the punishment inflicted upon them by that fury, it was clearly shown that they were not among those to whom this gift of grace had been granted by priestly authority.

[Col. 1292B] These are followed by the acolytes, that is, the candle-bearers, who by preaching minister the fire of the heavenly word, by which the brethren may be enlightened to recognize God and inflamed to love him.

The subdeacons are those who receive the offerings from the people in the temple of the Lord and perform the duties of the Levites in offering the vessels of the Lord’s body and blood and administering the things carried out in connection with the services of the altar.

Anyone who has the leisure to read through the Old Testament will find that these orders took their origin from it, no less than those who remain, namely, the Levites and priests. Since their rank is higher, we must dwell a little longer upon them.

For, as the Book of Numbers reports, the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: “Bring forward the tribe of Levi and make them stand before Aaron [Col. 1292C] the priest, so that they may minister to him, keep watch, and observe everything that pertains to the worship of the multitude before the tent of testimony; and let them guard the vessels of the tabernacle, serving in its ministry.”

Concerning these it is written in the Acts of the Apostles that, “calling together the whole multitude of the disciples, the Twelve said: ‘It is not right for us to abandon the word of God and serve tables. Therefore, brothers, choose from among yourselves seven men of good reputation, full of the Holy Spirit and wisdom, whom we may appoint over this work; but we will devote ourselves to prayer and the ministry of the word.’ And the statement pleased the whole multitude, and they chose Stephen, a man full of faith and the Holy Spirit, and Philip and the others, whom they set before the apostles; and after praying, they laid [Col. 1292D] hands upon them” (Acts 6).

From that time the apostles, or the apostles’ successors, ordained seven deacons throughout all the churches, who, in a higher rank than the others, stood around the altar of Christ like the columns of the altar.

Concerning them Paul, whose teaching you claim to hold, wrote to Timothy.
