After stating that a bishop must be blameless, sober, prudent, and dignified in conduct, he immediately added: “Deacons likewise must be dignified, not double-tongued, not addicted to much wine, not pursuing dishonest gain, holding the mystery of faith with a pure conscience. And let them first be tested, and then let them serve, being without accusation” (1 Tim. 3).

[Col. 1293A] The order of presbyters also took its beginning from the sons of Aaron, who were then called priests in the Old Testament but are now called presbyters. They preside over the Church of Christ and, in the making of the Lord’s body and blood, share with the bishops, as they do likewise in teaching the peoples and in the duty of preaching.

Concerning them the Apostle Paul writes to Titus: “For this reason I left you in Crete, that you might correct what remains to be done and appoint presbyters in every city, as I directed you: if anyone is blameless” (Titus 1). And in the First Epistle to Timothy: “Do not neglect the grace that is in you, which was given to you through prophecy with the laying on of the hands of the presbytery” (1 Tim. 4).

Therefore, when presbyters are ordained, they receive the gift of priestly grace through the laying on of hands. Concerning them it is written in the Book of [Col. 1293B] Numbers: “Gather for me seventy men from the elders of Israel, whom you know to be elders and teachers of the people; and bring them to the entrance of the tent of the covenant and make them stand there with you, that I may come down and speak with you, and take from your spirit and give it to them” (Num. 11).

And shortly afterward: “The Lord came down in a cloud and spoke to him, taking from the spirit that was in Moses and giving it to the seventy men” (ibid.).

Concerning these also it is written in the Acts of the Apostles that, when the Apostle Paul had come to Miletus, he sent to Ephesus and summoned the presbyters of that Church, to whom, among other things, he said: [Col. 1293C] “Take heed to yourselves and to the whole flock, in which the Holy Spirit has placed you to shepherd the Church of the Lord, which he acquired through his own blood” (Acts 20).

Peter also says in his First Epistle: “I appeal to the presbyters among you, as a fellow presbyter and a witness of Christ’s sufferings, and a sharer in the glory that is to be revealed: shepherd the flock of God that is among you, watching over it, not under compulsion but willingly, according to God; not for the sake of dishonest gain but willingly, and not as domineering over the clergy, but becoming examples to the flock from the heart. And when the chief Shepherd appears, you will receive the unfading crown of glory” (1 Pet. 5).

Finally, the order of pontifical priesthood took its beginning from Aaron, as Isidore says, although Melchizedek had earlier offered sacrifice, and after him Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; but these men did so of their own free will, not by priestly authority.

[Col. 1293D] Aaron, however, was the first in the Law to receive the priestly name, and the first to offer victims clothed in the pontifical vestment, the Lord saying to Moses: “Take Aaron and his sons and bring them to the entrance of the tent of testimony. And when you have washed the father and his sons with water, you shall clothe Aaron in his garments, that is, the linen garment, the tunic, the ephod, and the breastpiece, which you shall fasten with a belt; and you shall place the tiara upon his head, and the holy plate upon the tiara, and pour the oil of anointing upon his head” (Exod. 29).

In the New Testament, however, after Christ, the pontifical order began with Peter. For to him the pontificate in the Church of Christ was first given, as the Lord says:

“You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build [Col. 1294A] my Church” (Matt. 16).

He therefore was the first to receive the power of binding and loosing, and the first to bring the people to faith through the power of preaching. Indeed, the other apostles also received, together with Peter, an equal share of honor and power; and, when the apostles ordained them, bishops succeeded them. These bishops were established throughout the world in the seats of the apostles. They are no longer chosen from a people of flesh and blood as at first, but according to each person’s merit, which divine grace has bestowed upon him.

That bishops are ordained through the laying on of hands by their predecessors, the priests of God, is an ancient institution. [Col. 1294B] Thus the patriarch Isaac, placing his hand upon Jacob’s head, blessed him; Jacob did likewise for his sons; and Moses, laying his hand upon the head of Joshua, gave him the spirit of strength and leadership among the people of Israel.

In the same way, our Lord Jesus Christ, the fulfiller of the Law and the prophets, blessed the apostles. In the Acts of the Apostles, at the command of the Holy Spirit, hands were laid upon the apostles Paul and Barnabas for the episcopate, and they were sent to evangelize.

The head signifies the principal seat of the mind; and just as the body is governed by the mind, so the Church, which is the body of Christ, is governed through the bishops.

Concerning them the Apostle Paul says to Titus: “A bishop must be blameless, as God’s steward” (Titus 1). And to Timothy he says: “If anyone desires the episcopate, he desires a good work; for a bishop must be blameless, sober, prudent” (1 Tim. 3). And again: [Col. 1294C] “I remind you to rekindle the grace of God that is in you through the laying on of my hands” (2 Tim. 1).

Moreover, that secular men should by no means be admitted to the ministry of the Church, the same apostolic authority teaches and says: “Lay hands hastily on no one” (1 Tim. 5). And again: “Not a recent convert, lest, being puffed up with pride” (1 Tim. 3), he should think that he has obtained not so much a ministry of humility as an administration of secular power, and, like the devil, fall through the arrogance of pride into condemnation.

For a secular man will not be able to fulfill the teaching office of the priesthood, since he has neither held its office nor learned its discipline; nor can he teach what he has not learned.

[Col. 1294D] Since this is so, it becomes foolish and abhorrent to all Catholics that you think you can give what you have not received. You make no distinction concerning the places in which, or the ministers by whom, some gift of grace is to be given; but in groves, in shallows (*breviis*), or even within the shameful confines of latrine buildings, you perform your fantasies and sacrilegious incantations over those whom you can draw into fellowship with your error, as though this were some mystery of sanctification.

In this matter you will find the Apostle Paul, whom you falsely claim as your teacher, to be your accuser instead. Writing to Timothy, he says: “Fight the good fight of faith; seize eternal life, to which you were called and for which you confessed the good confession” (1 Tim. 6).

## VII. On burial

[Col. 1295A] We shall also speak about burial, which you attribute to the greed of priests, though it offers no benefit of salvation. You assert that it makes no difference whether the dead are buried in the courtyards of the house of the Lord or in any other places, pretending that no mystery of holiness is involved, except that the priests amass money for themselves from the price paid.

But if you presume to deny the faithful who are alive the bosom of Holy Mother Church, it is no wonder that you also wish to deny it to the dead. Since we have already treated the Church with complete certainty, let us say something about burial as well.

When faithful Christians spend their temporal life together in the unity of the Holy Spirit, under the mystery of the Catholic faith, in this temporal Church, so that through it they may reach the heavenly Church, where, I ask, should their bodies more properly be buried after dissolution than in the bosom of Mother Church?

[Col. 1295B] For just as, while living temporally, they adhere to the temporal Church through faith, so, while dying temporally, they rest in her bosom, awaiting the day of resurrection and the glory of the eternal Church. This is the mother of believers, who regenerates those born for death into immortality. She preserves the bodies of her children for a time, asleep in peace, yet destined to be raised to unfading glory in the general resurrection.

If, therefore, amid so great a light of truth you do not cast away the darkness of error, tell us from where you promise yourselves the spirit of eternal life. In the holy Church we are reborn to God and offer ourselves; through her, according to the quality of our devout way of life, we advance toward eternity. But when we are dissolved, we rest buried in her, and according to the likeness of death we imitate the future blessedness of resurrection.

[Col. 1295C] Whoever, therefore, does not embrace this single pledge of Christian faith is undoubtedly torn away from the structure of Christ’s body.

The patriarch Abraham knew that he was to be gathered into the unity of this faith when he purchased a double burial place from Ephron. Although he could have had it without payment, he nevertheless judged it better to purchase it, lest he appear to share in the company of the wicked. There he buried his wife Sarah, and afterward he himself was buried there, as were Isaac and Rebekah.

Jacob also, when he was about to die in Egypt, instructed his sons to carry him back there for burial. His son Joseph, [Col. 1295D] before he died, said to his brothers with a kind of prophetic insight: “After my death, God will visit you and bring you up from this land to the land that he swore to our fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. When you go up, carry my bones with you from this place” (Gen. 50), namely, to the ancestral place of burial. And they did so.

Tobit, a man full of the Holy Spirit, instructed his son that, when he himself died, he should arrange his funeral and bury his wife beside him. It must be noted that the holy Fathers wished to be separated from foreigners not only in life but also after death, since they foreshadowed the unity of the future Church, which, gathering the faithful separately, rejects profane worship.

[Col. 1296A] If Abraham purchased a grave for himself at a price, although he could have had it free of charge, why should we not also give the holy Church some gift at our burials—something that may benefit the living as a remedy and the dead for the obtaining of pardon?

But if you object that this is demanded more by the greed of priests, we do not deny that some may act in this way; indeed, some do. Yet it is not right that the good should be corrupted because of the vice of the wicked, or that divine mysteries should be disgraced. Whatever is done in the name of the Lord will not be without reward.

O blind and wandering people, I rebuke you with the Lord’s words! Since you do not know the Law, why do you not search the Scriptures? [Col. 1296B] The Book of Kings clearly records that all the kings of the people of Israel were buried in one place, except the wicked and the unrepentant. If those who repented corrected their offenses, they shared burial with the others.

From this it is understood that, since Solomon was buried with the others, he had obtained pardon for his crimes, although his repentance is not recorded.

Moreover, among the many other mysteries concerning burial that present themselves, the providence of the Savior himself was also present in this: that the holy cross on which he hung was, as the teachers relate, fixed above the tomb of the first parent Adam.

Nor is it without significance that the field called Haceldama was purchased with the price of his blood, where the bodies of foreigners are buried. Truly, the Church is purchased with his blood, and in her bosom the poor of Christ rest.

## VIII. On repentance

[Col. 1296C] Since you have said above that the mystery of regeneration is nothing, on the ground that whatever works of Satan a person being baptized professes to renounce, he later does not fear to take up again in life, by this opinion you appear to disparage repentance and the other remedies that God has provided for reconciling sinners. It remains for us to labor further over this matter.

For we have not yet reached the deepest point of the wound of unbelief; it must be opened by the instrument of the healing word, so that the pus of hidden corruption may break out into the open.

Divine providence certainly knows that no one renewed by the grace of baptism is fully capable of overcoming the devil’s snares and conquering the desires of the flesh. [Col. 1296D] Therefore, lest anyone fall after his lapse into the pit of despair, it has reserved suitable medicines of restored salvation for each wound of vice: humility for the proud, charity for the envious, self-restraint for the lustful, moderation for the gluttonous, repentance for the fallen, and appropriate medicines for every other vice. Through these, the sinner may be reconciled to God as though through a kind of baptismal regeneration.

But, to say nothing of the rest, since you reject repentance while claiming to be hearers of the Gospel, I ask what the Lord intended when he said in the Gospel: “I rejoice over one sinner who repents more than over ninety-nine righteous people who have no need of repentance” (Luke 15). And elsewhere: “I have not come to call the righteous but sinners to repentance” (Matt. 9).

[Col. 1297A] Examples of repentance certainly abound, and abound more than enough. Through them, Scripture revealing it, we know that many have been raised from the tomb of vices and the death of the soul. We know that many who had persisted in wickedness before their election came to their senses through repentance, and that very many who fell after their election were later restored through the remedy of repentance to their former grace.

Among these we first bring forward blessed Peter, who, while repenting and weeping over the guilt of his denial, not only regained his former grace but also received primacy over the whole Church, both on earth and in heaven.

We have also heard in the Gospel about the prodigal son, who had been deprived of his father’s grace: by repenting, he not only returned to his father’s favor but also received again the first robe that he had lost. When you hear “first,” do not understand “new,” but “former,” because by repenting he recovered the garment of his former innocence, from which he had stripped himself by sinning.

[Col. 1297B] Finally, since you accept apostolic teaching, you ought to hear how Paul summons a fornicator brother to repentance: “It is actually reported that there is fornication among you, and such fornication as is not even found among the Gentiles, so that someone has his father’s wife. And you are puffed up, and have not rather mourned, so that the one who has done this deed might be removed from your midst. I, though absent in body, am present in spirit, have already judged the one who has acted in this way: in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, when you are assembled and my spirit is present with the power of the Lord Jesus, to hand such a person over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Cor. 5).

And elsewhere: “I fear that, when I come, God may humble me before you, and that I may mourn over many of those who sinned before and did not repent of the impurity, fornication, and shamelessness that they committed” (2 Cor. 12).

For what else does it mean to hand a person over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved, except that he should cleanse through the tribulation of the flesh, by repenting, what he had committed through the lack of restraint of the flesh, so that, after the rust of the flesh’s enticing touch has been burned away in the furnace of repentance, the spirit may be saved purer for the day of the Lord?

Hence he himself later says that he fears mourning over the destruction of those who did not repent of their impurity and fornication.

[Col. 1297D] Finally, in ecclesiastical history we heard of a certain young man at Ephesus who had been shut away in a monastery by the blessed Apostle John. Instructed in Catholic disciplines and having received the grace of baptism, after many examples of a religious way of life, he was driven by the spirit of diabolical persuasion to abandon the monastery. Among forests and lairs of wild beasts, he was corrupted by murders, thefts, and every kind of wickedness.

When the apostle sought him out and recalled him to the Church, the wretched man said that, because of the magnitude of his crimes, he had no hope of recovering salvation. Blessed John promised him the hope of pardon under oath. Then, through fasts and prayers, he restored him within a short time so completely that he surpassed the others in holiness, and the Apostle entrusted to him the governance of that very Church, [Col. 1298A] thereby offering great examples of true repentance, an immense lesson in regeneration, and conspicuous signs and trophies of visible resurrection in him.

But observe how the same Apostle John writes to the angel of the Church at Ephesus: “Remember from where you have fallen, and repent, and do the first works; otherwise I will come to you and remove your lampstand from its place” (Rev. 2).

There is one example that is sufficient to commend the power of repentance. A certain man, driven by the madness of desire, once loved to such an extent a virgin consecrated to God, the daughter of a senator, that he consulted an unclean spirit through sorcerers. When the evil spirit promised to fulfill his desire if he would renounce Christ, he not only consented but also gave the spirit a written document of renunciation in his own hand.

[Col. 1298B] Thus, by the art of his sponsor, he obtained the virgin’s embrace; but not long afterward he bitterly wept that, as the price of his fornication, he had denied his creator. At last he confessed the whole sequence of events to blessed Basil, bishop of the city of Cappadocia, and was shut away in a certain room for three days as a penitential satisfaction, where he suffered many insults from the spirit that tormented him.

Meanwhile the blessed man summoned a multitude of clergy and people into the church and did not cease praying to the Lord until, through the most powerful struggle of prayer, he wrested the document from the devil’s hand and, with everyone looking on, received the sheet as it descended through the air.

[Col. 1298C] Let it therefore be far from the minds of the faithful to listen to your execrable teaching, by which they are to believe that repentance is of no benefit to those who fall after election! For it is clearer than daylight that, after crimes have been committed, people return through it to innocence.

We have found repentance so effective and so powerful for abolishing sins that, even if someone repents of his offenses at the last breath of life, and his crimes are disclosed through public lamentation, he nevertheless does not lose the fruit and hope of saving pardon. For the purpose that resolved to save what had perished cannot be changed; and because his will is not changed, even if time for amendment is not granted, nevertheless, if a person dies with a humble confession, pardon is not denied to his faithful resolve by him who does not desire the death of the sinner, but that he turn away from perdition through repentance and, saved by the Lord’s mercy, live.

[Col. 1298D] As for what could be objected concerning the sin unto death, for which no consolation of pardon is apparent, that applies to those who, falling into the pit of despair, have left themselves absolutely nothing by which they might be rescued from it.

## IX. That repentance may benefit after death
But, lest anyone believe that repentance benefits the living alone and not the dead, we learn from the testimony of Scripture that many who had departed this world were relieved from punishments through the piety of the living, when the Mediator’s sacrifice is offered for them, or alms are given, or when someone fulfills a substitute act of repentance on behalf of a dead friend—when a living friend supplies what the sick man, overtaken by death, could not do.

Since, blind in the light of faith, you not only refuse to believe this but attempt utterly to destroy it [Col. 1299A], you are not, as you claim, truly hearers of the Gospel. For Truth itself says: “If anyone speaks blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, it will not be forgiven him, either in this age or in the age to come” (Matt. XII). In this statement, blessed Gregory says in his *Dialogues*, it is understood that certain faults can be forgiven in this age and certain others in the age to come. For when forgiveness is denied of one thing, the consequent meaning plainly shows that it is granted for certain others. But this must be understood of small and very minor sins, such as continual idle talk, immoderate laughter, or some other [lacuna] of household care, and so forth—things without which human life is not conducted—which continue to burden people after death if they have not been loosened while they were still living in this life. Shortly afterward he says that these are cleansed after death by purgatorial fire, if, while still in this life, someone earns by good works what he is to obtain there [Col. 1299B].

Hence it is rightly called purgatorial fire by the holy teachers, because certain sins are purged through it, insofar as the living can obtain this either by alms, by sacrifices, or certainly, as we said above, by fulfilling a substitute act of repentance. Thus Paul also says: “The most valiant man Judas, having made a collection, sent twelve thousand drachmas of silver to Jerusalem to offer them for the sins of the dead, thinking rightly and religiously about the resurrection; for if he had not hoped that those who had fallen would rise again, it would have seemed superfluous and vain to pray for the dead.” Then he says: “Therefore it is a holy and salutary thought to pray for the dead, so that they may be released from sin” (2 Macc. XII).

[Col. 1299C] It is therefore established, as we said, that the dead can be absolved from sins through the price of such works. Otherwise the Apostle Paul—whose hearers you falsely claim to be—should by no means be heeded when he says that wood, hay, and straw, that is, the smallest and lightest sins, are easily consumed by purgatorial fire. These would surely be subjected not to purgation but to eternal punishments, unless by such offerings they had earned release in purgatorial fire.

## X. On Marriage

As for marriage, which with sacrilegious intent you judge abominable, contrary to the decrees of the Gospel and the Apostles, saying that married people are by no means to be counted among the faithful, there are many examples of the holy Fathers sufficient to refute the blasphemy of this unbelief. Concerning these, [Col. 1299D] we must bring the vessel of our discourse under the guidance of a certain discernment, lest, as though suffering shipwreck between two rocks, we give occasion in either direction—either by frightening everyone indiscriminately away from marriage or by encouraging everyone indiscriminately toward it.

Now, just as there is a certain distinction of rank between secular and ecclesiastical men, so their manner of life must also be preserved according to a certain principle of discernment. For once an ecclesiastical man has abandoned the service of the world and been counted among the Lord’s people, he cannot, without violating the belt of his profession, again bind himself to the marriage bed. But for secular men, who are subject to no yoke of ecclesiastical governance, neither the evangelical nor the apostolic decrees [Col. 1300A] prejudice legitimate marriages—provided that they know the pleasure of marriage must always be subject to them, and provided that they distinguish the appointed times for intercourse: when they should come together and when they should abstain from their wives.

For such marriages are not pleasing to God when people are provoked to lust and sensual pleasures like animals, excluding God from their minds and devoting themselves to their desire, like horse and mule. But whoever uses marriage in such a way that, with fear of God, he is concerned rather with the love of children than with satisfying the appetite of wanton flesh will not, because of the fault of marriage, be excluded from the company of the faithful.

Those who assert, therefore, that married people must be driven from the kingdom of God are mistaken, especially since we have testimony of this kind in the Gospel, and apostolic tradition [Col. 1300B] confirms such a law of human custom in many places. On this matter we bring forward this one testimony from the mouth of Truth.

When the Pharisees tested him by asking whether it was lawful for a man to dismiss his wife for any cause whatsoever, he answered: “Have you not read that he who made them made them male and female from the beginning, and said: ‘For this reason a man shall leave father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh’? Therefore they are no longer two but one flesh. What therefore God has joined, let no man separate” (Matt. XIX). When they asked why Moses had commanded that a bill of divorce be given and the wife dismissed, he said to them: “Because Moses permitted you to dismiss your wives on account of the hardness of your hearts; but from the beginning it was not so. I say to you that whoever dismisses his wife, except on account of fornication, and marries another, commits adultery” (ibid.).

Peter, in his Epistle, says: “Let women be subject to their husbands, so that even if some do not believe the word, they may be won without a word through the conduct of their wives” (1 Pet. III). And shortly afterward: “For in this way formerly the holy women who hoped in God also adorned themselves, subject to their own husbands, as Sarah obeyed Abraham, calling him lord” (ibid.). And again: “Husbands likewise, living with them according to knowledge, granting honor to the female vessel as to the weaker” (ibid.).

Hence blessed Paul also says to the Corinthians: “It is good for a man not to touch a woman; but because of fornication, let each man have his own wife, and let each woman have her own husband. Let the husband render the debt to his wife, and likewise the wife to her husband” (1 Cor. VII). And shortly afterward: “To those who are joined in marriage I command—not I but the Lord—that a wife should not depart from her husband; but if she has departed, let her remain unmarried or be reconciled to her husband; and let the husband not dismiss his wife. If any brother has an unbelieving wife and she consents to live with him, let him not dismiss her; and if any woman has an unbelieving husband and he consents to live with her, let her not dismiss her husband; for the unbelieving husband is sanctified through the believing wife” (ibid.).

And again, when he said that he had no command of the Lord concerning virgins, turning to married people he said: “I consider this good because of the present necessity, for it is good for a man to be so. Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek release. But if you take a wife, you have not sinned” (1 Cor. VII).

He writes to the Ephesians as follows: “Let women be subject to their husbands as to the Lord, because the husband is the head of the wife, just as Christ is the head of the Church” (Eph. V). And again: “Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ also loved the Church” (ibid.). And again: “He who loves his wife loves himself” (ibid.).

He also writes to Titus in this way: “Teach the young women to love their husbands, to love their children, to be prudent, self-controlled, managing their households, subject to their husbands” (Tit. II). And to Timothy: “Avoid younger widows; for when they have become wanton against Christ, they wish to marry, having condemnation because they have made their first faith void. I therefore wish younger women to marry, bear children, be heads of households, and give no occasion for reproach; for some have already turned back after Satan” (1 Tim. V). And to the Colossians: “Husbands,” he says, “love your wives and do not be bitter toward them” (Col. III).

Since, therefore, this law of human custom is supported by such great institutions of divine authority, your heretical doctrine must plainly be rejected and utterly trampled underfoot. For if marital union were a cause of perdition for human beings, he who came to restore the lost would have given no example and no command concerning this union. Finally, Paul, who burned with such a great fire of charity that he wished even to become an anathema for his brothers, [Col. 1301C] would have given no advice on this matter if he had understood it to threaten the soul’s destruction. But enough has been said for the present on these matters.

## XI. On Confessors

Who, indeed, does not see that in this matter you are guilty before the divine judgment and the Christian communion, since with sacrilegious audacity you stir up a rebellion of perverse doctrine against the most blessed confessors of Christ, saying that no one besides apostles and martyrs should rightly be venerated, that confessors possess no gift of virtue, and that no grace of salvation can be expected from them—whose bodies, reduced to ashes, seem to differ in no way from those of dead animals?

The Apostle Peter certainly received from the Lord the power of binding and loosing; he also handed it on to blessed Clement, and likewise to Linus and Anacletus. The other apostles too left the same grace to their successors, that is, to the holy teachers and confessors. Some of these fell by the sword, while others rested in the peace of the Church.

They are not therefore unjustly venerated by human beings because they did not feel the sword of an executioner. Rather, if the circumstances of the times could not provide martyrdom, they nevertheless do not lack the glory of martyrs, because both by their desire and by their virtue they were able to be martyrs and wished to be so. For they endured many sufferings of human affliction in hope of eternity: hunger, vigils, nakedness, fasts, the insults of the envious, the attacks of the wicked, care for the sick, concern for those in danger, lamentation for those perishing, weeping with those who wept, and burning with those who caused scandal.

Moreover, in the various contests against human and spiritual wickedness, the strength to conquer, the patience to await, and the evenness to endure always shone forth in them. Although an executioner was absent, they themselves supplied the executioner’s service. For what else could the executioner strike in them except the body? Certainly, what the executioner would have done in a moment, they inflicted upon themselves through prolonged torment, killing the desires of the flesh within themselves and removing whatever had been pleasant, sweet, or pleasurable.

Furthermore, a punitive prison was not lacking for them, since they enclosed themselves within the confinement of a narrow and austere life, away from the allurements of the world. Their mind was most luminous, their hands [Col. 1302B] full of purity, because as they celebrated the most holy mysteries of the body and blood at the altar table, they did not cease to offer in the inner chambers of their hearts a living sacrifice pleasing to God—that is, themselves, without blemish or admixture of evil works.

And, as we have said, although they did not feel the sword of an executioner, nevertheless, being made worthy of God by the merit of their life, they are not deprived of martyrdom, because martyrdom is accomplished not only by the shedding of blood but also by abstention from sins. Otherwise what was spoken by Truth to the two brothers, the sons of Zebedee, would seem far removed from the truth: “You shall indeed drink my cup” (Matt. XX), although we read that one of them fell by the sword and the other rested in the peace of the Church.

Nor do they demonstrate by any example of the authorities that blessed Mary, Mother of God, ended her life by the sword. Yet if the prophet Simeon had foretold through the Holy Spirit that she would suffer, saying, “And a sword will pierce your soul” (Luke II), blessed Jerome says that the sword pierced her soul in this respect: she felt the sword of compassion and grief at Christ’s death, making Christ’s death her own through the force of her extraordinary love.

We also read that the Apostle Philip and the evangelist Luke departed from this world not through the struggle of suffering but in peace. Finally, who is so stony-hearted that, when he sees the sick come to the tombs of these men and return with swift healing, he would not believe that their merits live before the eternal Judge? Who, after the apostles, is more powerful in miracles than Martin, or than Benedict?

[Col. 1302D] But perhaps you object that many performed miracles in Christ’s name and yet were afterward rejected by the Lord. Concerning these, the Lord says in the Gospel: “Many will come saying: ‘Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and in your name cast out demons?’” (Matt. VII). To them the Lord will say: “Truly I tell you: I do not know you; depart from me, all you workers of iniquity” (ibid.).

Their life did not agree with their words, and for that reason they were rejected by the Lord. But what they appear to perform is attributed not to their merits but to Christ’s name. For the demons that were expelled had fled not from them but from Christ’s name. This was once made clear in the case of the sons of a certain Jew named Sceva, who, as we said above, attempted by exorcism to cast demons from possessed bodies in the name of Jesus whom Paul preached. Afflicted by the swift fury of the indignant spirit, they heard: “Jesus I know, and Paul I recognize; but who are you?” And immediately the unclean spirit leapt upon them (Acts XIX).

The punishment inflicted by that fury plainly showed that they were not among those whose holy life agreed with their holy preaching. The bodies of the two parties, committed to the earth, reveal what each had been in life: the former seem to live daily through miracles, while the latter appear able to display no sign of virtue from themselves.

For the holy Church is filled with books overflowing with miracles that are seen to occur at the tombs of holy confessors. But the rejected, after their souls have been shut up in hell and their bodies placed in tombs, leave no indication of holy merit. For this reason the devil sometimes displays signs of illusory light at their bones in order to deceive people, inviting deluded minds through this means to practice veneration. We read that this was demonstrated in the time of blessed Martin, who, finding a monastery dedicated by popular error over a robber as though in honor of a martyr, commanded by the authority of his word that the buried man confess that he had shared nothing with the saints but was being tormented in hell with the demons for the guilt of his crimes.

Therefore, if anything similar happens in such places, about which the memory of the elders provides no certainty, consecrations are forbidden, lest shrines of idols built long ago according to the rites of the Gentiles be venerated as sacred; nor may divine offices be rashly performed for the buried unless the life of the deceased has been examined by the provincial bishop to determine whether it accorded with the Gospel of Christ.

## XII. On the Duty of Singing Psalms

Who could doubt that you are driven by an unclean spirit when you reject what was brought forth and instituted through the Holy Spirit—namely, the practice of singing psalms in the holy Church—and charge it as a superstitious and erroneous form of worship?

The ecclesiastical order therefore adopted this manner of singing not from playful or comic performances but from the fathers of the Old and New Testaments. Thus we read of David in the Book of Kings that, when he was bringing the Lord’s ark back from the land of the Philistines, he laid aside his royal insignia, took up a lyre, and began to sing psalms before it [Col. 1303D], since he understood that no more suitable sacrifice of heavenly grace could then be offered. By the sweetness of this music he also freed King Saul from a demon, whom the art of physicians had given up as hopeless.

Certainly we also read that the signs of this musical praise are celebrated among the citizens above, as in the Apocalypse of the Apostle John: “Each holding a harp, and they sang a new song” (Rev. V). And again: “And the voice that I heard was like the voice of harpists playing on their harps” (Rev. XIV).

From this it must be understood how pleasing to God is the duty of singing psalms when it is performed with an attentive mind, since by it we seem to imitate the choirs of angels, who are known to resound the praises of the Lord without interruption. Hence the Psalmist often admonishes us, saying: “Sing a new song to the Lord, and sing psalms to him well with a shout” (Ps. XXXII). And again: “Sing a psalm to his name; give glory to his praise” (Ps. LXV). And in Matthew’s Gospel: “And after singing a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives” (Matt. XXVI).

For through the Holy Spirit the Psalmist had seen that such a sacrifice is pleasing to God above the fat of bulls or the blood of goats, when he said: “Shall I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats? Offer a sacrifice of praise to God” (Ps. XLIX). And again: “The sacrifice of praise will honor me” (ibid.).

Finally, he commands not only irrational creatures but all created things to praise their Creator continually with the sound of psalmody, when he says: “Praise the Lord from the heavens” (Ps. CXLVIII), and so forth, until the end of the psalm, which he concludes: “Let every spirit praise the Lord” (Ps. CL).

Therefore, lest the Psalmist be said to summon irrational or lifeless creatures vainly to praise the Creator, what cannot speak is then truly seen to raise itself in praise of God when, through the movements of its nature, it conforms itself to the will and command of the Creator. Or rather, he appears by this to admonish rational minds to remember to give praise to the Creator for divine benefits, by whose gift creation itself seems to serve human uses.

Paul too, whose imitators you claim to be, urges us to join in psalmody, saying: “Speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody to God” (Eph. V). And elsewhere he says: “I will sing with my mouth; I will sing with the spirit and with the mind” (1 Cor. XIV). Indeed, many copies of divine Scripture teach that angels sang the sound of psalmody at the passing of holy men.

It is therefore clear that those who judge this duty of singing psalms not to belong to divine worship must be expelled from the bosom of the holy Church. As for their belief that, by singing psalms, we invoke many adversities upon ourselves whenever the Psalmist turns the eye of his mind against evildoers—for example, “Why do you glory in wickedness?” (Ps. LI), and “Let their eyes be darkened so that they may not see” (Ps. LXVIII), and other such passages—they are mistaken, not knowing that he looks with prophetic spirit upon what was to come upon those whom he had seen exulting and glorying while swelling with rage against Christ’s death and that of the holy martyrs, and who, refusing to turn away from the perversity of their wickedness, rejoice in evil things and delight when they have done wrong.

It is therefore evident that such people do not dissent from their head, that is, the devil, who is the head of all the wicked and who, even while understanding Holy Scripture, attempts to distort it through a sinister interpretation.

## XIII. On Venerating the Lord’s Cross

Since you pour forth the poisons of a serpentine doctrine against the Lord’s cross and the life-giving wood, saying that it is the result of human error that people venerate it, since it contains no greater power in itself than the other trees of the forests, except that it was fashioned by human hands and therefore deserves no veneration, we shall state a few of the many things that seem useful to this matter.

We know that every substance that is not God is a creature, and that whatever is a creature is not God. We therefore attribute nothing divine to wood when we judge it worthy of worship, since among the other creatures that are not God it possesses the substance of its own nature. But if you carefully investigate the reason for the mystery, you will see that the standard of the Lord’s cross is honored not only by human beings but also by angels, and that it disclosed a sacrament they did not know.

For the first Adam was killed by the sword of disobedience through the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, and he dragged us with him into death. The second Adam passed through the palm of obedience from the cross into eternal life, and he led us with him. Nevertheless, we do not say that the tree of the knowledge of good and evil had death in itself according to its nature; rather, it served as the occasion on which our parent’s obedience was tested or his disobedience punished. In contrast, the tree of life is the cause of eternal life.

Our Lord Jesus Christ brought this tree to you through the wood of the cross in our Church, so that we who were debtors to death through the tree of the knowledge of good and evil might be made capable of life through the wood of the holy cross. And just as that tree did not have death in itself by its nature, so the wood through which life is granted to us did not possess this power in itself, but from the power of him who was weak in our condition yet lives by the power of God.

Death and the devil reigned through disobedience to the tree of the knowledge of good and evil; that same death and devil were overcome through obedience to the wood of the holy cross. Who, then, would dare deny that the cross is rightly venerated by human beings, since through it the devil was conquered and the world was saved by God’s work?

Who, unless driven by the madness of insanity, would deny that the standard and power of the Lord’s cross should be honored, when he hears blessed Andrew—whom you falsely claim to imitate among the other apostles—proclaiming with such love for its suffering and such devoted veneration:

“When he had come,” says Scripture, “to the place where the cross had been prepared, seeing it from afar, he cried out in a loud voice, saying: ‘Hail, cross, which have been consecrated in the body of Christ and adorned from his limbs as with pearls. Before our Lord ascended you, you possessed earthly fear; now, receiving heavenly love, you are embraced according to my desire. Knowing what great joys you contain within you, I come to you secure and rejoicing, so that you too may receive me, exalting me as the disciple of him who hung upon you, because I have always been your lover and desired to embrace you. O good cross, which received beauty and splendor from the limbs of the Lord: long desired, carefully loved, sought without ceasing, and at last prepared for a desiring heart! Receive me from among human beings and return me to my Teacher, so that through you he may receive me who through you redeemed me.’”

And the Apostle Paul says: “Far be it from me to glory except in the cross of my Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal. VI).

[Col. 1306A] Therefore, when we glorify the Lord’s cross, we invoke Christ in our minds as though he were hanging upon it. Whom we invoke, we worship. We prostrate our bodies before the cross, but our minds [before] God. We venerate the cross through which we were redeemed, but we entreat him who redeemed us.

## XIV. On the Image of the Savior on the Cross

The reasoning concerning images made in churches can also be understood more readily if an analogy is drawn from the Old Testament. As the people of Israel journeyed through the desert, they were sometimes wounded unto death by the bites of fiery serpents. When the Lord was consulted about this, he commanded a bronze serpent to be made and raised upon a tall pole; those who had been bitten were quickly healed when they looked at it.

And we, journeying from Egypt—that is, from a carnal way of life—through the desert of worldly exile toward the land of heavenly promise, empty the venom of the ancient enemy from our hearts by looking upon the Mediator hanging on the cross. Whoever sees Christ through the image of the Son of God and his Passion will be able to escape the poisons of the ancient enemy.

This is certainly indicated by the words of the Lord himself: “Just as Moses exalted the serpent in the desert, so the Son of Man must be exalted” (John III). The bronze serpent was appropriately suspended from wood, so that the Lord might be signified both as dead in the serpent and eternal in the bronze—dead, namely, in humility; eternal through divinity.

There is also another reason for this. The simpler and uneducated people in the church, who cannot perceive what is contained in the Scriptures, contemplate it through certain lines of a painting: namely, Christ in that humility in which he wished to suffer and die for us. When they venerate this image, they worship Christ ascending the cross, Christ suffering on the cross, Christ dying on the cross—Christ alone, not the work of human hands.

For it is not a wooden trunk that is worshiped; rather, through that visible image the inner mind of a person is stirred, and Christ’s Passion and death undertaken for us are inscribed as though upon the membrane of the heart, so that each person may recognize within himself how much he owes his Redeemer. Thus, in accordance with the Savior’s judgment, what bears Caesar’s image is rendered to Caesar, and what bears God’s image to God.

The same reasoning may be applied to images of the saints, which are made in the holy Church not so that they should be worshiped by human beings, but so that through them we may be inwardly stirred to contemplate the operation of divine grace and draw something from their deeds for the conduct of our own lives.

For example, when we look upon an image of blessed Mary, Mother of God, we certainly recall through her the benefits of divine condescension, by which God recreated the mass of reconciliation from the mass of perdition. Through her zeal for obedience and her example of humility, she urges us to seek the heavenly homeland, which the pride and disobedience of the first virgin had closed.

Likewise, when we contemplate through external images the angels attending their Creator in ministry, we are inspired to join their number through the zeal of our conduct, according to the glory they receive from God. When we look upon the portrayed images of the apostles and holy martyrs, what else are we commanded through them except that, trampling worldly cares underfoot and despising our bodies, instructed by their teachings and strengthened by their glorious struggle, we may deserve to be crowned among the triumphators over the world?

Similarly, when we gaze upon images of confessors and virgins, we are warned by their example to avoid the desires of the world, trample down the enticements of the flesh, and offer ourselves to God as an immaculate sacrifice. Thus, when the ranks of the other saints are viewed, they instruct us to emulate their virtues, just as once the brave deeds of men, through the praise bestowed upon them, kindle others to undertake every courageous act.

## XV. On the Orders of Ecclesiastical Governance

But I can no longer tolerate the swelling of your rebellion raging [Col. 1307B] against divine ordination, by which you strive to reduce the order of ecclesiastical administration to nothing.

The holy Church, which blessed Paul the Apostle calls the Jerusalem above, our mother, the abiding city, and a house from God, not made by hands, consists of angels and human beings. Part of it, enjoying the fellowship of the angels in distinct orders, already reigns with God in heaven; another part, also distinguished in orders, still journeys on earth and sighs for the heavenly fellowship, where, according to the Apostle, there is a tabernacle not made by hands and not of this creation, after the likeness of which the tabernacle was made through Moses. Concerning it the Lord said to him: “Make everything according to what was shown to you on the mountain” (Exod. XXV).

In that heavenly and true tabernacle, which God and not man fashioned, our High Priest of confession, “having an everlasting priesthood, entered once for all into the holy places through his own blood, having obtained eternal redemption” (Heb. VII, IX), into the inner part of the veil—that is, into heaven itself. Sitting at the right hand of the Father, that is, in the glory of the Father’s majesty, he intercedes for us not by voice but by mercy.

Finally, “King of kings and Lord of lords” (1 Tim. VI), through whom kings reign and lawgivers decree what is just, governing the heavenly and earthly principality—that is, the whole commonwealth—and arranging and directing the entire host, both heavenly and spiritual and earthly and temporal, in distinct orders, presiding over the heavenly and worldly court, distributes in marvelous order the ministries of angels and human beings according to the variety and suitability of times. He determines what is appropriate to each particular time or person, whether through his hidden inspiration, evident illumination, or revealed command.

We therefore read that sacred orders were arranged by God in heaven and on earth, in both the Old Testament and the New, from whom, according to the Apostle, every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named. Hence blessed Dionysius the Areopagite, bishop and venerable father, as he had learned from the Apostle Paul, who was caught up to the third heaven and saw heavenly secrets, wrote two books on angelic and ecclesiastical governance.

Hence blessed Gregory also said that the providence of the divine disposition established ranks and distinct orders for this purpose: that the lesser might show reverence to the greater, and the greater offer love to the lesser; that unity of concord might be woven together through diversity; and that the administration of each office might be carried out properly. For the whole could not subsist in any other way unless such a great order of distinction preserved it.

Since creation cannot be governed or live in one uniform equality, the example of the heavenly armies instructs us. For although there are angels and archangels, it is clear that they are not equal, but that one differs from another in power and order. This is made plainly intelligible by the fact that, in carrying out the ministry from above, some spirits send others, as the prophet Zechariah testifies: “Behold, the angel who spoke with me was walking, and another angel went out to meet him and said to him: ‘Run and speak to that young man, saying: Jerusalem shall be inhabited without walls’” (Zech. II).

When one angel says to another, “Run and speak,” there is no doubt that one sends the other. Those who are sent are lesser, and those who send are greater. This interpretation also seems not inappropriately supported by what is said through Daniel: “A thousand thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times a hundred thousand stood before him” (Dan. VII). For to minister is one thing, and to stand before another is something else.

If, then, such a distinction exists among those who are without sin, how much more must this principle of governance be maintained among those whom we know cannot be without sin? Blessed Gregory says that all human beings were born equal by nature, but that the varying order of merits places some below others because of fault. The very diversity that arose from vice is administered by divine judgment, so that, since no human being can stand equally secure, one is governed by another.

Hence blessed Paul says: “Let every soul be subject to higher authorities; for there is no authority except from God, and whoever resists authority resists God’s ordinance” (Rom. XIII). The Apostle Peter likewise says: “Be subject for the Lord’s sake to every human institution, whether to the king as supreme or to governors as sent by him” (1 Pet. II).

We therefore read that orders existed in the Church of the ancient people, commonly called the Synagogue, arranged by God through Moses. These orders determined who should appoint others, and how and when; who should be appointed by others; who should govern others or be governed by others; and how much each should minister in the several offices.

But now, in the Church called the kingdom of heaven, we read and understand that, in the likeness of the heavenly orders, the ministers of the Lord have been distinctly arranged by divine institution and apostolic tradition. Among them there is a certain greater dignity and, corresponding to the distinction of honor, a certain distinction of authority. Through their care, those of lower rank are gathered into one body of the Church as though from a certain diversity, lest the cause of transgression enter under the pretext of liberty.

For this reason, a rule established by the apostles and their successors remains to this day, by which the affairs of the entire ecclesiastical governance are administered through bishops and archdeacons, and also through deans and provosts. Since this is so, there is nothing by right that you ought to oppose against it.

## XVI. On Their False Justice

But since you attempt to introduce a doctrine of false justice, placing it so far above divine grace that you attribute everything to your own merits, we shall shake this impious error of presumption with the blows of divine authority. For there is no justice and no merit of goodness that has not received whatever it possesses from the fountain of heavenly grace.

Hence John himself—concerning whom the Lord testifies that no one born of women is greater—says of himself: “A person cannot receive anything unless it has been given to him from heaven” (John III). The Apostle says: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, descending from the Father of lights” (James I). Paul says: “Wretched man that I am, who will free me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom. VII). And again: “By the grace of God I am what I am.” And again: “But I labored more than all of them—not I, however, but the grace of God with me” (1 Cor. XV).

He himself instructed us in this confession when he said that no time passes in which we do not need his help. Through the transgression of the first human being we lost natural ability and innocence, and no one can rise by free will from the depth of that ruin unless the grace of the merciful one raises him up.

[Col. 1309C] Whatever holy thought, pious counsel, or movement of good will there is in our hearts or in our will descends from the gift of his grace, because through him we can do some good, without whom we can do nothing, as he himself says to his disciples: “Without me you can do nothing” (John XV). For all human merits are preceded by his grace, through which it comes about that we begin both to will and to do something good. Indeed, by what works of righteousness was sinful Mary forgiven her sins, Zacchaeus justified, and the thief received into the joys of paradise, except by the grace of divine mercy alone? Concerning this the Apostle says to the Romans: “Where sin abounded,” he says, “grace abounded still more” (Rom. V). And elsewhere: “For all have sinned and lack the glory of God, being justified freely by his grace” (Rom. III).

[Col. 1309D] And again: “We too,” he says, “were by nature children of wrath, even as the rest” (Eph. II).

Therefore we hold with complete certainty that all human beings by themselves can attain not only perfection but not even the beginning of righteousness, and that all who become good are preceded by divine grace. For he himself freely prepares good will in human beings, freely grants it, himself assists it, and himself brings it to completion. So that we may “deny ungodliness and worldly desires and live soberly, righteously, and devoutly in this present age” (Tit. II), he says: “The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom. VII). His grace is an inexhaustible generosity of compassion: it makes the foolish wise, grants faith to unbelievers, calls the wandering—not only calls them, [Col. 1310A] but also recalls them—expels earthly desires and inspires desire for the heavenly kingdom, uproots wickedness by implanting goodness, drives out envy through the gift of kindness, and pours the gift of love into those who are hateful and those who hate one another. Thus, in order that we may be good instead of evil and burn with the fire of holy charity, the work of spiritual grace is begun in us and brought to perfection in us by its operation.

Therefore every Christian ought to know that the beginning of saving grace rests neither on the powers of nature nor on legal precepts, but on the illumination of the heart and the voluntary gift of the divine will. Through this, what God commands can be not only recognized by us but also loved and performed. Rightly, therefore, the person who mercifully stirs us to good works is ascribed to the gratuitous benefit of divine goodness, so that he may have something which he ought justly to crown in us. Just as by mercy he prepared for them the gratuitous gift of justification, so by justice he prepared the reward of eternal justification. Thus the work of grace in all the predestined is begun by gratuitous mercy and brought to completion by just recompense.

As for the contrary matter that might be raised concerning the unjust: for them he prepares eternal fire by a just judgment—not unjustly—for he had foreseen them as worthy to undergo punishments, yet he did not predestine them to commit sins. God predestined what divine equity would repay, not what human iniquity would lose. Therefore he prepared for the guilty person not the fault that he hates, but the judgment that he loves; for it is written: “For God loves mercy and judgment” [Col. 1310C] (Ps. LXXXIII).

Accordingly, the good works that God mercifully grants, he justly crowns; but the works that he himself does not grant, he justly punishes. In the former, divine generosity is crowned; in the latter, human transgression is condemned. Therefore the one has nothing that he can ascribe to his own merits, nor does the other have anything by which he can rightly detract from divine judgment. Thus, in accordance with the Apostle, the creature has no grounds to say to the one who fashioned it, “Why have you made me thus? Does the potter not have power over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?” (Rom. IX). He therefore displays the riches of his goodness in the vessels of mercy, but his power and judgment in the vessels of wrath, preparing the former for glory and enduring the latter as they go toward destruction.

What, then, is this righteousness of yours, which ascribes everything solely to merits, yet owes nothing to grace? Moreover, Paul already bears witness against you that you have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge: “For, being ignorant of God’s righteousness and seeking to establish your own, you have not submitted yourselves to the righteousness of God. For Moses writes that the person who does the righteousness that comes from the law will live by it” (Rom. X). How much more, then, will the righteousness that comes from Christ’s Gospel and apostolic authority give life? For what else did the apostles teach except what they received from the mouth of Truth? What else does the holy Church hold except what it received from blessed Peter and the other apostles?

Who does not know, or fail to perceive, that what was handed down to the Roman Church by Peter, the prince of the apostles, [Col. 1311A] and is preserved by all to this day ought to be observed, and that nothing should be superimposed or introduced that either lacks authority or appears to take its example from elsewhere? Especially since it is evident that throughout all Italy, Gaul, Spain, Africa, Sicily, and the intervening islands, no one founded Churches except those whom the venerable Peter or his successors appointed as priests. Let them read whether another of the apostles is found or recorded as having taught in these provinces. If they do not read it, because they find it nowhere, they ought to follow what the Roman Church preserves, from which it is beyond doubt that they received their beginning, lest, while pursuing foreign assertions, they appear to lose the source of their institution.

## XVII. Conclusion

[Col. 1311B]

The day was already inclining toward sunset, and the lord bishop, with those who had gathered to listen standing around him, said:

“What it was necessary for us to say concerning these matters in order to strengthen your faith has been sufficient, brothers. But lest we burden you further with words, let this suffice. Preserve this one thing as the undefiled seal of your faith, recalling what the Apostle Paul had foretold: that ‘in the last days some shall depart from the faith, giving heed to deceitful spirits and doctrines of demons, speaking lies in hypocrisy and having their conscience seared; forbidding marriage and commanding abstinence from foods which God created to be received with thanksgiving by the faithful’ (1 Tim. IV).”

[Col. 1311C] At these words of the lord bishop, those who shortly before had seemed to themselves unconquerable in argument and incapable of being constrained by any form of speech were so astonished by the weight of his words and the manifest power of God that they stood as though they had never learned any speech with which to contradict. Speechless, they could answer only that this seemed to them to be so, and that the whole substance of Christian salvation could consist in nothing other than what the bishop had just set forth.

To them the bishop said: “If you believe these things to be so, lay aside such faithless unbelief and, condemning with us this heresy and its authors—unless they repent—excommunicate them.”

Then the bishop, all the abbots and archdeacons who were present, and the entire clergy together, with the people’s support, began as follows:

[Col. 1311D] “We condemn and anathematize this heresy, which today has been found to have conspired against the true and catholic Church: the heresy that maintains that baptism contributes nothing to washing away the stain of original sin and actual offenses; that professes that sins can in no way be remitted through repentance; that regards the holy Church of God, the most sacred altar, and the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood as nothing other than what is seen with bodily eyes, and treats this as a worthless affair; and that avoids lawful marriages. We condemn and anathematize this heresy and all who affirm it.

“For, according to evangelical faith and apostolic tradition, we profess that no one can be saved except through the water of regeneration, as the Lord himself says: ‘Unless a person is born again of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God’ (John III). But the sins that people contract after baptism, at the devil’s prompting and by their own will, we profess are not only remitted through repentance, but that through repentance divine grace itself can be merited, since through it we see sinful Mary cleansed, Zacchaeus justified, Peter restored after his fall, and the thief received into paradise.

“We believe that the holy Church is the common mother of all the faithful, and that no one can reach the Church which is in heaven unless he has first been gathered into this Church which is on earth. We confess that the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood is from God the pledge of our redemption and salvation. Concerning it the Lord says: ‘Unless you eat my flesh and drink my blood, you shall not have life in yourselves’ (John VI). And again: ‘My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink’ (ibid.).

“Concerning this body and blood, in accordance with what he himself says—‘Take and eat, all of you, for this is my body’ (Matt. XXVI), and ‘Drink from it, all of you, for this is the cup of my blood’ (ibid.)—we profess without doubt that it is the same flesh which, born of the Virgin, suffered on the cross, was raised from the tomb, exalted above the heavens, and now sits in the glory of the Father’s majesty. Whoever hears this and remains unbelieving has neither Christ born, nor Christ suffering, nor Christ buried for him, nor will he obtain with Christ a share in blessed resurrection. This mystery cannot be sanctified anywhere except upon the most sacred altar, which the Lord established through Moses to be made for him from the earth.

“As for marriages, the Lord, his disciples, and the teacher of the nations both granted permission for them and instituted the observance of lawful marriages, etc. . . .

“If anyone thinks contrary to this catholic institution, he shall not be able to have a place among the faithful.

“Since those who shortly before had been held by heretical unbelief could not adequately understand what was being said in the Latin language, after they had heard through a vernacular interpreter the sentence of excommunication [Col. 1312D] and the profession of the sacred faith had been explained, they declared by unanimous assent that they would renounce what had been condemned and believe what was believed by the faithful. But, to confirm the testament of their faith, each of them wrote, in the form of a cross, a +certain character, so that this sign might be presented to them at the final judgment for salvation if they kept this faith, but might become a sign of their shame if they violated it.”

Thus, giving thanks to God together and having received from the lord bishop the gift of his blessing, they all returned happily to their own [the supplied text breaks off here].

[Note: [Col. 1311D] The acts of the Synod of Arras were not inserted into the major collections because they had not yet been published. Father Hardouin, whose edition is later than Labbe’s, merely indicates them in the table of contents of volume VI. These acts were made public by D. L. d’Achery in his *Spicilegium*, volume XIII, in quarto, and volume I, in folio.]

[Col. 1313]

# LETTERS OF GERARD I, BISHOP OF THE CHURCH OF CAMBRAI

(*Acts of the ecclesiastical province of Reims*, vol. II, p. 49.)

## FIRST LETTER: TO THE ARCHDEACONS OF LIÈGE  
*(A.D. 1030.) Concerning the proper treatment of excommunicated persons.*

[Col. 1313A]

Gerard, by the grace of God, though unworthy bishop, to the archdeacons of the holy Church of Liège: to supply by blameless conduct what the prerogative of your title requires.

Since I am always fraternally concerned about the works of your charity, I wish to admonish you, without prejudice to the purpose of charity, not to attempt to usurp any unreasonable innovation by which you might appear to differ from the custom of ecclesiastical and apostolic institution. I mean especially what has been firmly and irrefutably confirmed by prophetic and evangelical authority, as well as by apostolic [Col. 1313B] tradition and that of the holy fathers.

You must not judge that those who, from the very cradle completing the whole course of their lives in evil deeds, swelling with mad fury against the holy Church of God, were never able to soften their purpose of wickedness, and who, even at the very end of their lives, showed no correction of repentance through any change of circumstances, but died hardened and excommunicated with the same intention of evil will—those who, excluded by just judgment from the bosom of the holy mother and deprived of the burial owed to the faithful, I say, ought to be granted the favor of absolution and buried among the faithful in undivided communion.

I trust that you would not do this rashly if you were willing to take the law of all your observance from the source from which you receive the consecration of your honor, and if the see of the blessed apostle Peter, which is the mother of your priestly dignity, were your teacher in ecclesiastical discipline.

On the present occasion, insofar as my insufficiency permits, I am prompted to urge you toward that see, setting forth a few judgments—few indeed, but not to be avoided—from prophetic and evangelical decrees. For what could arise more clearly or more effectively against such conduct than what the Lord declares by the prophet Ezekiel in rebuke:

“If the righteous person,” he says, “turns away from his righteousness and commits iniquity, according to the abominations that the wicked person is accustomed to commit, shall he live? None of all the righteous deeds that he did shall be remembered; in the transgression by which he transgressed and in the sin which he committed, in these he shall die.”

And shortly afterward: “In his injustice which he has committed,” he says, “he shall die” (Ezek. XVIII).

I therefore propose that you consider this: if the former righteousness of a person—righteousness which perhaps existed in some measure—does nothing to remove the stain of subsequent evils, how much less, indeed how entirely nothing, can those former righteous deeds avail this man, for whom no such deeds existed throughout his whole life, and for whom certainly no time passed that was free from devotion to wickedness?

But the Lord himself, the Lord of the prophets and Mediator between God and human beings, when the blessed Peter asked him about a sinful brother, concluded the rule of correction in such a way that, if the brother could not be admonished by one person alone, one or two others should be brought in; and if they made no progress, the matter should immediately be reported to the Church. If he did not listen even to the Church, he was to be regarded as a pagan and a tax collector.

To this judgment he immediately added: “Amen I say to you, whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven.” And again: “I say to you that if two of you agree on earth concerning anything whatever that they ask, it shall be done for them by my Father” (Matt. XVIII).

What, then, has been bound in heaven by the sentence of Truth through those who, by God’s authority, hold the primacy of heavenly judgment, receiving from God the authority to bind in his place? Who is so rash in mind and so disordered in understanding as to dare not only to make the censure of this binding void, but even to assert that it is void?

Yet, because it often happens that a pastor is moved toward a particular neighbor by hatred or favor, the prophet rightly says: “They put to death souls that do not die, and they give life to souls that do not live” (Ezek. XIII). Hence blessed Gregory says in his homilies (Homily 26 on the Gospels): “He puts to death one who is not dying when he condemns the righteous; and he attempts to give life to one who will not live when he tries to absolve the guilty from punishment.”

The cases must therefore be weighed, and only then should the power of binding and loosing be exercised. It must be seen what the fault was and what repentance followed the fault, so that those whom almighty God visits by the grace of compunction may be absolved by the pastor’s sentence. The absolution of the one presiding is true when it follows the judgment of the inner Judge.

This is well signified by the raising of the four-day-dead man: it shows that the Lord first called and restored the dead man to life, saying, “Lazarus, come forth”; afterward, the one who had come out alive was loosed by the disciples. The disciples loose Lazarus alive, whom the Master had raised dead. For if the disciples had loosed Lazarus while he was dead, they would have displayed the Creator rather than his power.

From this consideration it must be understood that we ought to loose through pastoral authority those whom we know our Creator has brought to life through his reviving grace. Conversely, we must consider that those cannot be loosed by our judgment whom the inner Judge has not animated by any spirit of satisfaction.

But let us hear what the Lord’s beloved John says concerning such people—John himself, I say, who declares: “Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John III). “This,” he says, “is the confidence that we have toward God: that whatever we ask according to his will, he hears us. We also know that we have the petitions which we ask of him. Whoever knows that his brother has sinned a sin not unto death, let him ask, and he will give life to the one who sins not unto death.”

And immediately he adds: “There is a sin unto death; I do not say that anyone should pray for it” (1 John V).

It is as though he plainly said: that one should pray for a sin not unto death belongs to the will of him who does not desire the sinner’s death. He confirms this in what follows when he says, “because he hears us.” But by adding, “There is a sin unto death; I do not say that anyone should pray for it,” he clearly wishes it understood that to pray for such a person is rather to resist the divine judgment, as blessed Augustine says: “To pray for those who are openly impious—what else is it than to provoke God to anger?”

The Lord himself also says through the prophet: “I shall judge each one according to his ways” (Ezek. XXXIII). And elsewhere: “As I find you, so I shall judge you.”

Blessed Gregory says in his *Dialogues* (Book IV, chapter 39) that as each person departs from this life, so he is presented at the judgment, although shortly afterward he says that certain lighter faults, such as idle speech and immoderate laughter, can be remitted.

Scripture also says: “If a tree falls toward the south or toward the north, in whatever place it falls, there it shall remain” (Eccles. XI). What it is like to pray for such a person, the Psalmist has proclaimed with terrifying force in the spirit, saying: “Let his prayer become sin” (Ps. CVIII). And the Lord, under the figure of the Jewish people, restrains the prophet from praying for such persons, saying: “Do not take up praise or prayer for them” (Jer. VII).

Moreover, what the Apostle writes in the First Epistle to the Corinthians is surely well known to you. “I wrote to you in my letter,” he says, “not to associate with fornicators—not, of course, with the fornicators of this world, or with the greedy, or with the robbers; otherwise you would have had to leave this world.” Then he adds: “If the person who is called a brother is a fornicator or a robber, with such a one do not even take food” (1 Cor. V).

In this matter it must be considered: if the Apostle gives such a strict warning that the company of these people must be avoided, with what hope based on our own judgment should we think to restore to the communion of the faithful someone who, right up to the end of his life, was free from no kind of wickedness; who never ceased from seditions, bloodshed, or arson; who never refrained from sacrilege; who never kept his hands from robbery; and who, rather, at the very end of his life, with his belly full of plunder but empty of the nourishment of righteousness, breathed out his spirit?

Struck by the manifest judgment of God, he neither obtained the pardoning grace of confession nor received the viaticum of salvation. We had repeatedly summoned him to satisfaction because his sins demanded it, but he resisted with greater obstinacy, and we struck him with the rod of apostolic authority. Thus, even when placed at the point of death, he showed no mention or sign of seeking pardon.

Therefore, lest we delay you longer, let your charity observe what Pope Leo says in his decretals concerning such excommunicated persons who die in this condition (Epistle 92, chapter 6, to Rusticus): “Their case,” he says, “must be reserved for the judgment of God, in whose hand it lay that the death of such persons should be deferred until the remedy of communion. But we, who did not communicate with them while they were alive, cannot communicate with them after their death.”

But perhaps someone may be led to suppose that the price of absolution and burial should be sought either in money or in estates donated for ecclesiastical uses, on the claim that palaces are built and churches restored by such resources. But listen briefly to how Ambrose Autpert refutes this opinion:

“To those who say such things,” he says, “we answer truthfully that palaces fall more because of this, and churches are overthrown, precisely where, according to your opinion, they seem to stand. From this one nation rises against another, one kingdom against another; from this arise disasters, famine, destruction, and dangers; and by what an earthly lord is appeased, the heavenly Lord is provoked to anger.”

But since it is not hidden from your knowledge that certain people, under the pretext of equity and justice, allege that something of this kind was done by the elders of our own time, for that reason, my brothers—and among you I address our dearest brother John in particular—I urge you not to claim this standard of bad custom as something to be preserved for yourselves on the authority of its supposed authors.

For those people should not be called authors who do not preserve what the holy Church received from the Lord and the holy fathers, but who establish as worthy of observance whatever occurs to their own will. Rather, consider what the Lord answered when the scribes and Pharisees complained that his disciples were transgressing the traditions of the elders: “Why,” he said, “do you also transgress the commandment of God for the sake of your tradition?” And shortly afterward: “In vain,” he says, “they worship me, teaching human doctrines and commandments” (Matt. XV).

But if perhaps you object that he was your parishioner and on that account claim for yourselves the unrestricted power of absolving, let what was decreed concerning this at the Council of Meaux be brought forward. It is as follows:

“Concerning those who have a benefice or inheritance within one parish but are parishioners of another bishop, and who, while traveling from place to place, commit robberies and depredations, it has pleased us that they be excommunicated and not leave the parish before they have made worthy satisfaction for what they committed. Their excommunication is to be reported to their lord and to their own bishop, so that they do not receive them before they return to the place where they committed the robbery and make full satisfaction for everything” [Note: [Col. 1317D] Council of Meaux, A.D. 845, canon 2.]

For the present, enough has been said about this. Now, out of fraternal love, we exhort and ask you: since up to now good practice and everything belonging to the general observance of ecclesiastical dignity have been preserved by you and in this place, take the greatest care during the remaining time that the nobility of the ancient religion not be adulterated by any innovation of invention [Note: [Col. 1317D] “Imposturetur,” for “adulteretur”—“be adulterated.”].
