Nor should you be pleased to advise your elder, who is also our brother and, by the grace of God, our fellow bishop, anything contrary to equity and goodness—something which he may perhaps have failed to consider adequately, and which we rightly complain that you have not sufficiently attended to—namely, concerning Erlebold.

As you yourselves know, after being informed by your elder and our brother, we excommunicated Erlebold for the incest he had committed with a religious woman, as well as for the many other evils he had perpetrated in our diocese. Yet our brother has now received him, after absolution, into communion without our counsel or admonition [Note: [Col. 1317D] The canons forbid one bishop to absolve a person excommunicated by another bishop. Apostolic Canon 33. See the Council of Reims of A.D. 1148, canon 1.].

Our parishioners, whom we had separated from communion because they had burned churches and committed robberies, were taken from our parish into yours—that is, into Nivelles—despite our protests, and admitted to burial. Your own people, concerning whom we had brought a complaint before you, and who likewise had been excommunicated by us for arson and other offenses, nevertheless still lie buried in that same place, neither cleansed by satisfaction nor granted absolution [Note: [Col. 1317D] Balderic, *Chronicle of Cambrai*, Book III, chapter 28.]

## SECOND LETTER: TO ADALBERON, BISHOP OF LAON  
[Note: [Col. 1318D] Adalberon had made a kind of simoniacal agreement with Guy, nephew of the bishop of Soissons, to secure for him succession to the bishopric of Laon. Gerard succeeded in preventing this plan through the letters he wrote to Adalberon, to Ebale, and to Berold.]  
*(A.D. 1031.) Concerning Adalberon’s choice of a successor to the see of Laon.*

[Col. 1317C]

To Lord Adalberon, bishop of the holy Church of Laon, Gerard, by the grace of God a fellow bishop.

Although until now we had not been troubled by the various rumors of the people concerning you, since we saw that you displayed no little wisdom both in the observance of ecclesiastical discipline and in the exercise of public administration, nevertheless a certain astonishment now disturbs and, so to speak, almost deprives our mind of life, when we hear that so remarkable and unheard-of a crime has arisen from you in the holy Church: namely, that the governance of one Church should be handed over to two shepherds and that you should claim for yourself the right to choose your successor.

You know well that this was granted to no one in the entire canon of the Old Testament or in the apostolic Church. But even if we have heard that some saint foretold a successor through the Spirit, it is not for us to turn this into an example, because, as blessed Gregory says (*Moralia*, Book VI): “God’s miracles are not to be turned into examples, but admired.”

We therefore beg your charity not to think it so great a loss of honor to change your purpose that you should oppose the divine ordinance. Do not submit Scripture to yourself; submit yourself to Scripture. Do not, by loving your own opinion too greatly, leave future generations an opportunity to usurp the priesthood, to which the material for sedition would truly succeed.

For we think that nothing would be lacking, if such a practice grew, for the sees of Churches to become objects of sale and the highest office of the priesthood to be sold for the profits of commerce, so that every wealthy person might aspire to the height of pastoral governance. What we say to you out of fraternal charity, we ask you not to take amiss [Note: [Col. 1318D] Balderic, *Chronicle of Cambrai*, Book III, chapter 29.]

## THIRD LETTER: TO EBALE, ARCHBISHOP OF REIMS  
*(A.D. 1031.) Concerning the same matter.*

[Col. 1318B]

To Ebale, archbishop, Gerard, a fellow bishop of no merit.

Since we have heard that a certain novelty of detestable usurpation is growing within your diocese—namely, that one Church should have two bishops and that one should have unrestricted freedom to appoint the other as his successor—we now seem to behold an open abyss, from which the smoke of rash usurpation rises and foretells a future conflagration of schism, through which disputes will arise and the Church will be loosened from the unity of her peace.

But since we have heard that you have given no assent to this opinion, we give thanks to God, from whom this gift has come to you: that no one has been able to drag you into this precipice of heresy.

Therefore we forewarn your fatherhood and implore you by him who willed us, though unworthy, to be shepherds in his Church: never give your consent to this invention, which is contrary to the ordinance of the Holy Spirit and to the institution of the whole catholic Church.

As for the fact that you recently sent word that you wished us to meet for a discussion, we have left that to your will, and we think that it should be dealt with more deliberately, because such great dangers to the holy Church of God arise from the fact that we consult too carelessly together for its welfare [Note: [Col. 1318D] Balderic, *Chronicle of Cambrai*, Book III, chapter 30.]

## FOURTH LETTER: TO BEROLD, BISHOP OF SOISSONS  
*(A.D. 1031.) Concerning the same matter.*

[Col. 1318D]

To Berold, a bishop in name and merit, Gerard, a fellow bishop of no merit, whatever is most excellent for living blessedly—

Since we have heard that a certain novelty of detestable custom is growing within the holy Church—namely, that one Church should have two bishops and that one should have unrestricted freedom to appoint the other as his successor—we now seem to behold an open abyss, from which the smoke of rash usurpation rises and foretells a future conflagration of schism, through which disputes will arise and the Church will be loosened from the unity of her peace.

But since we have not yet heard whether you have given assent to this matter, we forewarn your fraternity and implore you by him who willed us to be ministers and shepherds of his Church: if it is indeed your counsel, consider that you ought rather to yield to the divine ordinance than to act according to your own judgment; let not carnal love carry you away toward what is wrong, but let spiritual fervor kindle you toward zeal for righteousness.

If this is not so, then may no one ever drag you into this precipice of heresy, so that you give your consent to this invention, which is contrary to the ordinance of the Holy Spirit and to the institution of the whole catholic Church [Note: [Col. 1319D] Balderic, *Chronicle of Cambrai*, Book III, chapter 31.]

## FIFTH LETTER: TO LEDUIN, ABBOT OF SAINT-VAAST  
*(A.D. 1031.) Concerning the burning of the cathedral church of Arras.*

Gerard, a bishop in name but not in merit, to Leduino, abbot, and to the entire congregation of our holy father Vedast living under him, and to all who devoutly read this page: may life and peace be multiplied by God, who is life and glory to all who believe in him.

[Col. 1319C] Since we have learned that you are a son of holy Mother Church, and since, by imitating your father, the merciful God who begot you for himself as a son by adoption, in the likeness of his goodness, we greatly rejoice with God and with your charity. For, before the other sons, you have at this time shown due honor, through the compassion of your heart, to that same mother Church, afflicted by God’s judgment. For we read in the Books of Kings that King and prophet David blessed the men of Jabesh-gilead who buried King Saul, although he had been cast down and rejected by God, saying: “Blessed are you by the Lord, because you have shown mercy to your lord Saul and have buried him” (II Kings 2). If those men deserved a blessing from King and prophet David because they showed mercy to Saul, although he had been cast down and rejected by God, [Col. 1319D] how much more do you, who have shown mercy to your mistress, the mother of us all, namely holy Church?

If the love of God the Father is shown in the Son, who through the death of the flesh laid down his life for the human race, the image of that same Son is likewise displayed in the one who, out of compassion, has mercy on his neighbor in distress. But if this exchange of charity is granted to the one who comforts his neighbor, how much more to the one who has shown merciful honor to the Church, the universal mother of the faithful, and, moreover, to Mary, the mother of God the Redeemer of all?

But lest the feeling of my mind remain concealed from you for long, I shall disclose it to you in no lengthy speech. For there steals over me more than usual a fear and grief which, although old for me through experience, nevertheless always becomes new through increase. For whenever I look upon myself according to the quality of my life, I am immersed in bitterness, because I fall short in good things and persist in evil ones. But whenever I raise the eye of my mind to contemplate the things that are in the world, I see that all are placed in evil. I plainly observe by what sword the world is struck and by what blows the people perish; and therefore I fear that still greater things are coming, because I confess that this happens through our priestly sin, as the blessed apostle Peter bears witness in the words of Scripture: “For it is time that judgment should begin from the house of God” (I Peter 4). And in Ezekiel: “Begin from my sanctuary” (Ezekiel 9).

For example, as is manifest at the present time in the church of Saint Mary of the people of Arras, which, on the third day before the Kalends of August, a fire coming from heaven entirely consumed while everyone looked on. Hence I greatly fear that this was a judgment of divine punishment coming upon the children of men: just as once, before the Lord’s coming, two white fleeces are read to have fallen in that place as a sign of mercy, so, as a sign of the divine vengeance that is to come upon the children of unbelief, fire would come with sulphur, terrifying the elect so that they might flee from the face of the bow, and burning the impious and sinners who continually disparage Christ before the children of the Church.

For they are accustomed to say of us, the ministers of the Church: “These are the shepherds of the people, who are not truly shepherds but wolves. For they consume the sins of the people, since they receive the Church’s revenues as their daily stipend; yet they labor not at all, neither through devotion to prayer nor through the word of preaching. Therefore, whatever adversity there is in the world—namely mortality, pestilence, and famine—they say is deserved, and begins from the sanctuary.” And truly, from the sanctuary, according to that prophecy of Jeremiah: “The stones of the sanctuary are scattered at the head of every street” (Lamentations 4).

But whether it is a heretic or a false Christian who brings these charges against the faithful, let him be answered with what the blessed Peter says in his Epistle: “If these things begin first with us, what will be the end of those who do not believe the Gospel of God? And if the righteous will scarcely be saved, where will the impious and the sinner appear?” (I Peter 4).

And again with what the Lord said in the Gospel to the Galileans who had reported to him that Pilate had mingled the blood of their people with the sacrifices of idols: “Do you think that these Galileans were sinners above all the other Galileans, because they suffered such things? No, I tell you; but unless you repent, you will all perish likewise.” And again, concerning the eighteen upon whom the tower in Siloam fell and killed them: “Do you think that they were debtors above all the inhabitants of Jerusalem? I tell you, no; but if you do not repent, you will all perish likewise” (Luke 13).

What more need be said? These things, dearest brothers, must be answered, according to the Gospel of God and the apostle Peter, to their folly, for the sake of the fidelity and honor of the Church; and yet we cannot deny that many things they daily strive to spread abroad in insult against us are true. For, as the blessed Gregory says (Homily 17 on the Gospels): “The world is full of priests, but in God’s harvest a rare one is found.” And again: “As the people are, so is the priest.”

Therefore we have judged it necessary that, because through the example of our life Christ’s flock rushes toward destruction, through the merit of our life it should be recalled to Christ, by preaching that evangelical message: let all who have fallen through guilt repent. You, therefore, dearest brothers, who have renounced the world and stand in the Lord’s harbor, help us who labor in the sea, praying to God with prayers and fasts, lest the judgment of God’s wrath come upon us.

[Note: [Col. 1321B] Balderic, *Chronicle of Cambrai*, book III, chapter 32.]

## LETTER VI. TO FULCO, BISHOP OF AMIENS. (In the year 1031.) Concerning the unjust expulsion of the Bishop of Thérouanne.

[Col. 1321B]

To Fulco, lord bishop of the people of Amiens, Gerard, by the grace of God bishop of the people of Cambrai, wishes both innocence in this life and heavenly glory with the angels.

[Col. 1322A] That our confrater Drogo, bishop of Thérouanne, is assailed by Count Baldwin with such injuries is something to be lamented not only by us, his confraters, but also by all faithful Christians. Certainly, as we have heard, we bear this with grief, no differently from the one who suffers, out of regard for brotherly charity. For who could be so savage or hard-hearted as not to mourn an ecclesiastical see left widowed while its shepherd is still alive?

Therefore, in God’s name we admonish and beseech you to strive, by whatever means you can, to come to the aid of your deposed brother. For, thanks be to God, no one can do this better, and certainly you ought to do so, because he was formerly your cleric and was raised to the grace of so great a dignity by your support. You ought to remember how liable to both canonical and apostolic sanctions is anyone who, when able, delays assisting a bishop in shipwreck.

We therefore humbly implore your charity that, after summoning the lord archbishop together with the other brothers, your fellow bishops, you vigorously rouse the king to support your brother. You should make clear to him that, if he permits the holy Church to be mutilated, heavenly wrath will tear his kingdom apart.

[Note: [Col. 1322B] Balderic, *Chronicle of Cambrai*, book III, chapter 34.]

# In the Year of the Lord 1051. Hugh, Bishop of the Church of Langres.

## Historical Notice

(From *Gallia Christiana*, volume IV, p. 554.)

[Col. 1321C] Hugh of Breteuil, son of Gildwin, count of Britoglium or Britolium in the territory of Beauvais, and brother of Valerian, who, having been wounded in the knee in the battle fought at Bar, later embraced monastic life in the monastery of Saint Vanne, where he was appointed abbot after Richard, as Hugh of Flavigny reports in his *Chronicle of Verdun*, was a canon of Chartres and subsequently bishop of Langres.

The *Chronicle of Saint Benignus* relates his elevation to this office as follows:

“After Richard’s death, the king, provoked to anger by the queen’s counsels, again gave the bishopric to a certain cleric of the Church of Chartres. This was Hugh, who would have been a useful vessel in the house of the Lord had he taken care to avoid youthful desires and trample down pride. But he, adding cruelty to these faults and proceeding by right and wrong to the extreme, after he had troubled the clergy and people of Langres for eighteen years, was driven from his see.”

The chronicler of Bèze agrees:

“When he had obtained the bishopric, he was not, as was fitting, a diligent promoter of the churches of God’s concern, but, on the contrary, was negligent and destructive.”

He specifically complains that his monastery was worn down by many afflictions: Abbot Ulger, who resisted, was badly treated, deposed, and led captive to Dijon, to Saint Benignus, together with several of his monks.

When Hugh was seeking the see of Langres, Henry, his contemporary, chose to be present so that no violence might be inflicted upon him, as had been inflicted upon his predecessor, and placed him in the cathedral, fearing Richard’s fate, says the *Chronicle of Langres* after the Besançon chronicle. Meanwhile King Robert breathed his last, and Henry returned at a rapid pace; nevertheless nothing was taken away from Hugh, who, supported by the patronage of both the deceased and the new king, ruled peacefully.

[Col. 1322D] It is difficult to determine what judgment should be formed concerning him. Even the chroniclers already cited suggest that his beginning was not so bad. He conferred many benefits upon many religious communities, especially upon the people of Dijon, the canons of the Holy Twins, the nuns of Poligny, and the monks of Bèze, to whom he assigned the chapel of Saint Genulfus at Langres as a priory.

He brought it about that the property situated in the district of Floriacum on the river Ouche was restored to Saint Marcellus of Chalon at a public gathering of the nobles of Burgundy at Paluellum. He also gave to the same church the church of Saint George at that Floriacum, with Alvisius as prior.

I do not know why he treated the monastery of Bèze and its abbot Ulger so badly. But I do know that he had as companion and collaborator Halinard, then abbot of Saint Benignus and later archbishop of Lyon, a man everywhere esteemed as most holy.

As for the affliction of the clergy and people of Langres, one might say that they deserved it, and that it was imposed upon Hugh by the kings so that they might avenge Richard’s unfortunate and undeserved fate and death. One might also add in his defense that he was sometimes earnestly praised by those who had so greatly condemned him. Thus the chronicler of Bèze speaks of him:

“With Hugh happily presiding in the pontifical chair and piously governing the Church of the see of Langres, his deposition and the accusation of dreadful crimes restrain the true pen.”

At the beginning of his episcopate, when Robert, duke of Burgundy, had claimed for himself an estate called Vivarium on the river Ouche, and the monks of Saint Benignus demanded it back, saying that it had been granted to them by Count William for the salvation of Duke Henry’s soul, Hugh restored it to them and issued a charter of restitution signed by our Hugh, in which he says:

“I, Hugh, have appended what follows, by which I excommunicate and anathematize … and, anathematizing, excommunicate, so that no person of a king, duke, bishop, abbot, count, and so forth, may on any pretext dare to take any possession or customary right in the aforesaid Vivarium. Through the gift of the renowned Hugh, bishop of the Church of Langres, the Church of Saint Genulfus was assigned to Besançon.”

But also, “the village called Bannus was granted in perpetual right,” says Harduinus in a charter of the year 1059.

Perardus reports a charter in which Hugh speaks as follows:

“While at a certain time we were carefully deliberating about establishing the commonwealth of the Church of Langres, so that, with Christ’s assistance, we might be improved and advanced to higher things, our faithful man Wido came before our greatness, asking that, through the ministry of our authority, he might be permitted to place in a certain church dedicated in honor of blessed Stephen such clerics as would, by living there together, devoutly submit themselves to the canonical rule … We satisfied his desire and handed over to the aforesaid canons the altar of that church, together with everything that had previously been accustomed to be paid to us, except subjection and the census of three solidi, which we established should be rendered to our see each year …”

“Done publicly at Langres, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1032, indiction 20, in the first year of Henry, king of the Franks, and of Hugh’s pontificate.”

In the following year, indiction 1, he gave to Warner, provost of Saint Stephen, at the request of the knight himself, a certain church of Saint Florentin, which a knight named Aymo held from him by beneficiary right, together with serfs, market, toll, and so forth, for the use of the clerics residing there, on the condition that they not neglect to show submission to the prelates of the abbey of Saint Stephen.

At the request of Aymo, his faithful count, he returned to the monastery called Pulchrada or Saxon’s Fountain, Saint Benignus and its abbot Halinard, the Church of Saint Peter situated in the village of Mora.

Done publicly at Langres, while Henry was king, in the eighth year.

If we reckon Henry’s reign from his first coronation, this diploma belongs to the year 1034; if from his father’s death, to 1038. Mabillon assigns to the year 1042 the charter by which Robert, duke of Burgundy, remits burdensome customary dues in the village of Gilly to Saint-Germain of the Meadows, and to which our Hugh subscribes.

There is, however, considerable difficulty in the dating. Duchesne gives it as follows: “While Henry, king of the Franks, was reigning in the tenth year, Hugh, bishop of Langres, presiding in the episcopal chair, in the fifth year.” Their reign and episcopate would thus begin together, if Henry’s starting point is taken as his father’s death and if Hugh was installed at Langres and placed in possession of the see. Consequently their tenth years must run together if Henry’s reign is reckoned from his father’s death.

But if it is reckoned from the year 1027, when he was crowned while his father was still alive, as Mabillon proves, his tenth year would not be 1042 but 1036, which was also the fifth year of Hugh’s pontificate.

I know that here we assume that King Robert was taken from the living in the year 1032. Holgandus indeed asserts this, but the most learned men deny it, assigning his death, some to the year 1031 and others to 1033. Yet here we cannot depart from the records of our own region.

William, abbot of Saint Benignus, died in 1031 on the very feast of the Circumcision, that is, on the first day of the year 1032 according to our way of reckoning the year. In that same year 1031, in August, Lambert had died; Richard was substituted for him by Robert and held the office for slightly more than five months. Therefore, already at the beginning—according to our reckoning—in February of the year 1032, he was removed by poison.

Since Hugh was appointed bishop by that same king only afterward, King Robert certainly did not leave this life until 1032. [Col. 1324D] He is mentioned in the same year 1036, indiction 4, in a document by which the knight Richard gives “one mansus” in the place called Fontanellas.

In the year 1037 he subscribes a charter by which Count Reginald gives to the monastery of Flavigny, at the village of Salins, one chest with a cauldron.

Count Rainald of Châtillon, taking monastic habit in the monastery of Saint Benignus, grants it certain things, and Hugh is a witness to the grant in the year 1038, indiction 6, in September, on the second day of the month, a Saturday, while Henry, king of the Franks and brother of Robert, duke of Burgundy, was reigning, in the eleventh year of his reign.

In that same year Hugh issued a charter in which he states that, when he often visited the monastery at Dijon, attended the assembly of the monks, and saw God’s service being constantly performed by them, he was moved by piety to give Saint Benignus “the church situated in the village called Itzium,” and so forth.

We possess this charter. His mark is appended to the diploma by which Robert, duke of Burgundy, remits to Saint Benignus the safeguard payments of three villages in the year from the Lord’s incarnation 1043, indiction 11, in the second week of Lent, on Tuesday, the first day of March, while Henry, king of the Franks, was reigning in the thirteenth year of his monarchy.

A charter by which the cleric Gibuinus gives to Saint Peter of Bèze his inheritance in a village called Blaniacum ends as follows:

“Done in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1044, indiction 12, on the third day before the Ides of June, the feast day of Saint Barnabas the apostle, while Henry held the kingdom of France; and Hugh, who later deserved to be expelled from the episcopate of the holy Church of Langres, now presiding under the name of shepherd.”

In that same year he subscribed the diploma establishing the canons of Saint Paul, which Chifflet calls his testament.

He wrote a “Treatise on the Body and Blood of Christ against Berengarius,” which our Dom Lucas d’Achery published from two manuscripts, one royal and one Corbie manuscript, at the end of Lanfranc’s works. It begins:

“Hugh, the least of the bishops of Langres, to Berengarius, in certain respects a most reverend priest: to understand God.”

From this we learn that Berengarius was a priest. Hugh also wrote a concise account of the Acts of Saint Victor.

Finally, in the year 1049, a council of twenty bishops was celebrated at Reims by Pope Leo IX, together with nearly fifty abbots and very many others of the ecclesiastical order. Our Hugh was present. In the first session he accused the abbot of Pultaria of several crimes; when the abbot could not clear himself, he was deposed.

In the second session Hugh was proclaimed a defendant instead of an accuser. He was accused by Peter, a deacon of the Roman Church, of having obtained the bishopric by simony; of conferring sacred orders simoniacally; of carrying weapons; of homicides and adulteries; of tyranny toward clerics; of oppression of the people; and of other crimes. “By these words,” says the history of the council, “many informers who were present gave testimony.”

The bishop, greatly disturbed, asked permission to bring several men into the council and chose the archbishops of Lyon and Besançon. He asked the latter to undertake his defense. But when that man attempted it, he immediately found himself rendered speechless by divine power. Therefore the archbishop of Lyon was compelled to assert that Hugh confessed to having sold orders and extorted money from a priest, while utterly denying the remaining crimes.

When judgment had been postponed until the next day, the bishop withdrew that very night. Consequently he was excommunicated by the entire assembly and deposed from the priesthood.

Later, however, he returned repentant to Leo and, with immense tears, publicly confessed his crimes and voluntarily accepted penance. Then he followed the pontiff on his return to Rome, traveling barefoot. He entered the synod then being held naked and unshod, his face drenched with tears, carrying in his hand rods with which he might be beaten, and imploring forgiveness and mercy in a lamentable voice.

At such a spectacle everyone wept, uttered sighs, and begged for pardon. The pontiff, moved by compassion, granted indulgence to the suppliant; and, like a merciful father to a repentant son, restored to him the best robe and ring of the episcopate he had lost, together with the sandals, and even restored the episcopate itself, provided that the Church of Langres, or any other church, should be willing to receive him as bishop.

On his return to his homeland he fell ill and asked for and received the monastic habit from certain Cluniac monks who were accompanying him on the road, under the name of the monastery of Saint Vanne, which his brother Valerian governed. He died devoutly at Biternum, says the author of the Life of Garnerius, provost of Saint Stephen of Dijon, and was enrolled in the catalogue of the brothers of Saint Vanne, as Laurence of Liège, a native of that place, testifies.

It therefore seems that he did not die at Verdun, as most people think; nor at Biterris, as may be inferred from the words of Dom Fiot in his notes on the Life of Garnerius. Nor did he die here, since he departed this life while returning to his homeland, and Rome’s road back to it certainly did not pass through the city of Biterris. Nor did he die at Verdun, for there he would have received the monastic habit from the Cluniacs, not from the abbot of Saint Vanne or from monks of that monastery.

He therefore died on the journey, in a certain village called Biterna. Wibertus relates, in the Life of Leo, that on his return, excessively worn out by fasts and exhausted by other works of penance, he ended his present life in good perseverance.

His anniversary is celebrated on the seventh day before the Ides of February.

[Col. 1325]

# Hugh’s Treatise on the Body and Blood of Christ against Berengarius

(*Works of Blessed Lanfranc*, edited by Dom Lucas d’Achery, Appendix, p. 68, from two Corbie manuscripts.)

[Col. 1325D] Hugh, the least of the bishops of Langres, to Berengarius, in certain respects a most reverend priest: to understand God.

[Col. 1326D] If you had rightly perceived the nature of existing things, most discerning man, and if you had examined the judgments of the Fathers with an effort not so much feeble as perverse, you would not believe that the sacrament of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ is celebrated in such a way that you say it is a body while proclaiming it incorporeal.

Likewise, if you weighed the fact that the breadth of divine power exceeds the circles of the senses, and that what forms the senses within you cannot be encompassed sensibly, you would contract a mouth too widely opened, correct one that had been contracted, and finally restrain one that had been corrected.

For, speaking far too expansively, you say that in this kind of sacrament the body of Christ exists in such a way that the nature and essence of bread and wine are not changed; and you establish as intellectual the body that you had said was crucified. In this it is most clearly evident that you confess it to be incorporeal. In this matter you scandalize the universal Church and offend your own author, who offered something tangible that you affirm to be incorporeal.

For if the nature and essence of bread and wine remain, after consecration, with real primacy, nothing can be understood to have been transferred; and if what has been added is only an operation of the intellect, truly it cannot be grasped how, or from where, or in what way it is the same thing that still does not subsist. The intellect is an examiner of essences, not their maker; a judge, not their institutor. And although it may display or represent images of things, it produces no body with material origin.

But if the sacrament of bread and wine, solely for the sake of the power of salvation, is one and the same with the one who was born and suffered, then, by the same judgment, the same understanding, it makes no difference to the author whether this sacrament is, or is said to be, baptism, or whatever else is celebrated beneficially in the sacraments, as is evident in many cases. It would be as if, from a distance, you called someone “the same as the kings,” and then referred this to a patrician, or to Caesar, if you wished.

But if you apply Christ’s body to the sacrament in this manner, then, from the fact that this is a common virtue and a public strength, it follows that it is a common and public evil. Moreover, if by their essence or nature they do not possess the power of salvation, they possess its contrary; and thus, while they remain in their own nature, the sacrament will be powerless.

From this it clearly follows that Christ’s body is weak if he says that the bread, which has remained in its own nature, is the body. Therefore it is necessary either that you remove bread altogether from its nature or that you not presume to call it Christ’s body.

But if you should say that it retains its own nature and yet is not a powerless sacrament, you speak against reason. If you grant it a nature, you remove adherence [or: “inherence”]. For all things, while they remain in their own nature, do not depart from the properties inherent in that nature.

What, then, do you say about water changed into wine? Will you say that it remained in its own nature and yet is wine, or will you say that it is not wine, just as neither is bread the body except by the power of taste? Whichever of these you say, you rob wonderfully, pour out most deeply, and drink in solitude.

You call something “worn down” that is incorruptible [variant: “incorruptible”], and you construct an inference that certain elements destroy. For, not understanding well, you think that everything worn down consequently perishes. But see: beaten fire is not destroyed, and air does not suffer from an arrow.

And if you say that it is increased because it is sacrificed day by day, you will not say that the oil-cruse is not diminished when something is taken from it each day. But if you present it as not diminished and confess it to be both consumed and whole, then, if Elijah could do this, why could God not do it?

The grain of the woman of Sarepta prefigured these unleavened things. The loaves themselves, by which thousands were fed, prefigured this: not only was their fullness preserved, but twelve baskets overflowed. If you ask how they were freely obtained [variant: “tasted”], or from where they were increased, we answer that this occurred through the same power. And your own confession concerning them is the most certain faith of the sacrament.

For stable nature, through long-established possession, often releases the freedom of its constancy and the compact of its power, by which it rules in things, through the very means by which it possesses them [variant: “through which it possesses them alone”]. Otherwise, unless you concede this, you would appear to oppose the unconquered God—something that the one who grants to you those things that you rashly urge concerning the sacrament of Christ’s body cannot take away from himself [variant: “from you”].

In this matter you indeed surpass others, but you arm their madness, those who, detracting from divine power, say that nature is the maker of things [variant: “the thing-making power”].

Therefore, O man most reverend in all other respects, take faith for yourself, because “the righteous person lives by faith” (Romans 1:17), and by faith hearts are cleansed, as it is written: “Cleansing their hearts by faith.” It must be held above all in the mysteries because, as is written elsewhere, even the doubt of the mind, although the one who receives may be of good life, excludes him from reaching the understanding of that sacrament.

Reflecting on this frequently with you, I beg you not to argue any further about divine omnipotence. For just as you do not grasp how the Word became flesh, so you cannot grasp how this bread is changed into flesh and the wine transformed into blood, unless the faith of omnipotence teaches you.

Otherwise you are wrestling with God—not in the arms of the patriarch, nor with the dawn; indeed, your entire wrestling is nocturnal, more like that of one who wrestles treacherously than of one who embraces amicably. Such wrestling not only fails to merit anything but brings loss; nor is it free from the guilt of error, as though, unwilling—or variant: “willing”—to persevere, you should run into death.

Therefore I advise your philosophy to hold fast to what is written: “Take the crown from the wrestler; he will lie sluggishly in the arena.” Cease, then, to be a soldier of error; cease attacking the heavenly mystery. Consider that God’s will and word surpass every nature, and believe that he who is powerful in making things is powerful to transform them, as it is written: “You will change them, and they will be changed” (Psalm 101). For God’s willing is the accomplishment itself.

Therefore strip off the covering of error and prepare your mind with the pure veil of faith. Remember what is read in Ambrose concerning the sacraments (*On Initiation*, chapter 9): “The body which we make is from the Virgin.” When he says that it is from the Virgin, he speaks of birth, and not of something similar to another thing, as you judge it to be through power.

I understood this clearly when, beginning a discussion with you about the mysteries, I investigated your faith with curiosity [variant: “more inquisitively”]. I am prepared to prove how far you are from your own witnesses, Ambrose and Augustine—whom you indeed invoke, but who do not bear witness in the manner you claim—since I see them contradicting your assertions through their own words, especially those by which you authorize yourself through them.

For they, truly free and not possessing error as a veil of malice in the meanings of their words, compare this heavenly banquet with nothing and call it like nothing else. One of them says that God is to be judged by his own words, not by the assertions of others; that, through the Word by which it is distributed, the efficacy of flesh and blood proceeds from the edible sacrament through a spiritual secret; and that I should believe, plainly and simply, that the flesh itself is no other flesh and the blood itself no other blood than that from which he appeared incarnate.

As he once received the form of a servant, so he receives this creature in himself daily for us, making it his body by renewing it through a certain hidden power. Thus says blessed Augustine in the fourth book [variant: third book] *On the Trinity* (book III, chapter 4, vol. III), where he recalls that the apostle Paul preached by signifying Christ:

“We call it the body and blood of Christ, but only that which, received from the fruits of the earth and consecrated by mystical prayer, we rightly take for spiritual salvation, in memory of the Lord’s passion for us, while the Spirit of God works invisibly.”

As it is written in the Book of Wisdom:

“The creature, serving its Maker, is extended into torment against the unjust and becomes gentler in doing good to those who trust in you. Therefore, then, transforming itself into all things, it served your grace, which nourishes all things, according to the will of those who desired you” (Wisdom 16).

Although this example is suitable to other assumptions or transformations—as when visible forms are assumed by incorporeal things, or when transformations of things occur, as true water is changed into true wine—it applies especially to this sacrament. In it, the creature of bread and wine is shown to serve God in such a way that, with invisible swiftness, it changes the persistence it had displayed according to nature, and, transforming itself into all things—that is, into him in whom all things exist, or who is the man Christ of all things—becomes his body through the very Restorer [variant: “Creator”].

May it be extended into the torment of judgment against the unjust, that is, against those who receive it unworthily; and may it be gentle toward those who trust that they will find life in the power and truth of the mystery.

Through the statement “according to the will of those who desired you,” those who receive the sacraments of life carelessly and ignorantly ought to be instructed. For this reason they are not incorporated into him into whom the sacraments themselves pass. “When you sit,” as we read in Solomon, “at the table of a powerful man, know that you must prepare such things.” Explaining this, Saint Augustine says (*Tractate 84 on the Gospel of John*): “What is the great table, unless it is the table from which we receive the body and blood of Christ? What does ‘know that you must prepare such things’ mean, unless it means what blessed John explains?” Just as Christ laid down his life for us, so we too must lay down our lives for our brothers (1 John 3).

We must run with desire to this saving banquet, because Christ himself celebrated it with desire, as he said to his disciples in the Gospel: “With desire I have desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer” (Luke 22:15). Inviting the Jews to this table, Augustine says in his book *Against the Classes of Enemies* (*Book Against Five Classes of Enemies, or On Five Heresies*, chapter 7):

> “You raged, O Jews; you killed; you shed the blood of Christ. What must you do now except be baptized as believers? And what must you drink except the blood which you shed as believers? There is no reason for you to shudder: the blood of the physician has been shed, and it has become medicine for the madman.”

As Augustine says concerning Paul, he patiently endured a madman: “He endured me while I struck him; he granted that I should be struck by him.” What, I ask you, is there that is vile in that very creature which passes into Christ’s body? For even the body which Christ assumed from the Virgin was, by nature, corruptible; and although it was not corrupted through intercourse, it nevertheless came from the same element from which the fruit of the sacraments proceeded. Although the Virgin gave birth, she was not born in the same manner as she gave birth, nor did she descend from virgin parents; rather, she was born under the condition of birth that remains common to all mortals. She came forth in one way to give birth, and in another way she generated the incarnate Word—not from anything other than earthly substance—as Augustine says in his book *On the Words of the Lord*:

> “When divinity,” he says, “came into the womb of the Virgin Mary, by that same authority by which he had formed Adam in paradise from the clay of the earth, he fashioned flesh for himself from the substance of Mary herself.”

From this same material we also know the fruits of the sacraments to be produced. We confess that, once offered in the Catholic manner, they are made the flesh and blood of Christ by the hidden power of the Godhead, through the holy and invisible Spirit. Hence Augustine is again quoted:

> “Who makes these things,” he says, “except the one who commanded that the earth should produce them, and who by that same word creates, governs, and acts upon the things he created?”

For the immutable Word of God, humbly made flesh, has transferred us mortals—who, like ourselves, are incapable and inadequate—through faith in the sacraments into a new creation. No one can see this except one who does not merely consider the distinctions of the limbs in us. Thus, by his supreme power, he incorporated into himself the very matter of the mysteries; and this must be believed invisibly because it was made invisibly. For just as the Word of God was invisible in the flesh, although it had indeed been made flesh, so this flesh itself, because it now subsists in the Word, has in a certain manner become invisible. Yet, by another necessary and pious arrangement, it is concealed beneath certain qualities of bread and wine, to assist our taste. Nevertheless, with spiritual eyes the reality of the flesh is not denied.

Otherwise faith in so great a mystery would have perished if blood became visibly present in the chalice, and if Christ’s flesh reddened openly in the slaughterhouse; scarcely anyone on earth would not recoil from that sight. But since eternal life is promised only to the one who eats, those who did not dine with Christ would be consigned to perpetual death. Just as a physician makes a harsh potion pleasant for a fastidious patient by tempering it with other sweet substances, and does so the more carefully the more he knows it will benefit him, so our Provider and prudent host adapted the meal of his flesh to those who recoil from it. By preserving the appearance of the former creature, he ensured that it would be received more boldly through the sight of its outward form.

Likewise, although God in his immortal essence knew that the human race could not be restored unless the one who could not die in his divinity died according to the flesh, he concealed himself beneath the garment of our flesh and suffered through the members he had assumed, without the appearance of the Word. Although, as I believe, no one saw him, no one will say that he was absent.

In this matter, just as he arranged for the immortal and invisible one to die through the body, so he made that same body, by nature inedible, edible through its form and appearance. lest abstinence itself, recoiling from the bloody [body], condemn those whom sacred refreshment, having freed them from death, would satisfy.

For what has become so desirable in its mode of existence as to be nourished by that bread itself and refreshed by it—the bread which feeds us with such power that, incorporated into Christ, we are fattened to our very marrow and the inner man grows spiritually rich? We are nourished in order to receive and eat him. Through him we are suckled by faith and fed by appearance—or perhaps by hope (*spe*). Through him we are already children of God, as it is written: “We are children of God through grace, through faith, through the sacrament, through the blood of Christ, and through the redemption of the Savior.”

He is immortal and holy food, through whom we are strengthened, while he himself is not diminished. This bread is like light, which feeds the eyes of many and yet remains as great as it was. The sacrament of the faithful, which only the faithful recognize, is life for each person when what is visibly received as a sacrament is spiritually drunk in its very reality. Otherwise the mind would not be satisfied; otherwise the soul would not be refreshed, as Augustine says:

> “God would not satisfy me at all unless he promised to give me God himself.”

Where, then, is this promise? “The bread that I shall give,” he says, “is my flesh for the life of the world” (John 6:52). But you will say that this is bread, and that God is not promised. Hear again: “I am,” he says, “the living bread which came down from heaven” (ibid., 6:51). He is living and gives life. For again you have this statement: “If anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever” (ibid., 6:52).

You have heard that it is life. But what kind of life? A life that is distinguishable, discrete, and separate. Why? Because it is perpetual, eternal, saving, ignorant of corruption, and full of blessedness: through it one lives eternally, through it one lives in health, through it one lives without corruption, and through it one lives happily. Is this not to be loved with longing, and, by loving and worshipping, believed? In this respect it also differs from our life. For active life is neither perpetual nor worthy of honor; it is subject to destruction. As Augustine says: “This life is vapor, appearing for a little while and afterward destroyed.” And elsewhere: “Human life, even if long, is like one drop in relation to the entire sea.” Again, he says: “Even the days themselves do not stand still; why do you wish to stand with them? What will it matter to you hereafter if you believe contrary to them, differently, otherwise, or in opposition?”

Are the things which proceed from the Truth not true? Or has the Truth itself deceived us? Far from it! Rather, you disturb the Truth and accuse it as though it had lied. Nor do you fear Scripture, which says that the things promised by the Truth must be believed without being seen. For the Truth itself says: “This is my body” (Matthew 26:26).

You admit that he said this, but you do not cease resisting it. You say that it is a body, yet not a body; his own, yet not his own. How you may say this—or may not say it—I think I have explained above. Therefore consider this statement of Augustine (*Sermon 2, On the Words of the Apostle*, chapters 1 and 10):

> “The faithful recognize the sacrament of the faithful. But what else does the one who hears hear except what he hears? That man will possess conduct but not life if he considers Life a liar.”

For they are words of life, because Life itself spoke them; and they are life itself. The Truth spoke them, and they are themselves true; and he speaks to those to whom he speaks because he himself is the Word of the Father.

Why does the appearance that remained scandalize you? As I believe, if the slain Christ had bloodied you, the scandal would have been greater, as John Chrysostom says (*Homily on the Betrayal of Judas*, near the end):

> “You will blush,” he says, “at the hidden offering: Christ has been set before you as one slain.”

Thus the mystery is now with you; it is now concealed within the mystery. For if you do not walk by faith, what will become of the mystery? “We walk by faith, and not by sight” (2 Corinthians 5:7). Otherwise one does not come to the altar, which is both priest and sacrifice. All these things are in Christ. For he is the sublime altar of the Father (Hebrews 13:10), as it is written:

> “Do you think that the altar where Christ the high priest stood is anything other than his body, through which and into which the vows and faith of the faithful are offered to God the Father?”

Hence the Psalmist says: “I will go in to the altar of my God” (Psalm 42:4). He added what he meant by this: “to God, who gives joy to my youth.”

The same point appears in Ambrose (*On the Sacraments*, book 4, chapter 2):

> “The form of the body,” he says, “is the altar, and the body of Christ is on the altar.”

For he himself is the priest, as Scripture says: “It is terrible for an unclean person to approach them.” There is the priest who has power to destroy body and soul in Gehenna (Matthew 10:28). And there is also the Psalmist’s statement: “You are a priest forever” (Psalm 110:4). Paul likewise says that, because he remains forever, he possesses an everlasting priesthood. Hence he also says: “We have such a high priest, who has sat down at the right hand of the Majesty in the heavens” (Hebrews 7:1).

To show that he was the sacrifice, therefore, when entering the world he says: “You did not desire sacrifice and offering, but you prepared a body for me; then I said, ‘Behold, I come.’ In the heading of the book it is written concerning me, ‘to do your will’” (Hebrews 10:5–7). In that will, as the Apostle says, “we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ” (ibid., 10:10).

But so that nothing at all might be lacking to one coming to Christ, he himself is the tabernacle, reserved for this mystery alone, so that all things might be under grace through the fullness of loving-kindness. Henceforth no one is to slaughter for himself anything other than him in whom sacrifices have their end; through him not only are we preserved for life, but also all those things that were offered in sacrifice.

For no flesh now smokes for synagogues or for idols; the people [who offered] those very sacrifices is saved with the saved people. For where the anointing ceased, the sacrifice also ceased.

Therefore become dim-sighted, and in a certain way blind, so that you may see the one whom you did not see. Just as, through a good sense of shame, your outward sight is restrained, so that what it sees it does not see, so conceal the acuity of your elevated judgment through fear of God, lest outward appearance, confronting you through the external features of the mystery, deceive your mind and the flattery—or perhaps corruption—of a perverse intention corrupt your pure understanding.

Do not presume to think individually what the whole community does not affirm. For, as we read in Ambrose, these mysteries belong not only to individuals—or perhaps to angels—but also to the whole community. For that reason they ought to possess a common judgment according to Catholic and canonical interpretations. What you perceive outside these is therefore, as I have judged, something “external,” because you see such matters outside the common eyes, as you discussed with me at your table. I speak from experience: I happened to hear it, for I would not have believed it. Having abandoned unity, you exalt yourself on the basis of a faction.

## In the Year of the Lord 1052: Halinard, Bishop of Lyons

[Col. 1333]

## Historical Notice Concerning Halinard

*(Gallia Christiana*, volume 4, page 84)

[Col. 1333B] Halinard, also called Helmard and Almard, was born of a noble Burgundian family, with a father from Langres and a mother from the Aedui. He was exceptionally well educated in letters, chiefly through the care of Walter, Bishop of Autun, whose son he was in baptism. When he became a young man, his father entrusted him to Bruno, Bishop of Langres, and he was enrolled among the canons. There he listened to philosophers and ecclesiastical men devoted to sacred studies, and under their discipline he made astonishing progress.

His chief concern, however, was his character, to such an extent that even then he displayed the qualities of a monk. He was anxious to preserve himself whole and sincere from the vices by which that age is usually contaminated, to seek the companionship of the good, and to avoid that of the wicked. Lambert, Bishop of Langres and Bruno’s successor, wished to promote a man endowed with so many and such great gifts to ecclesiastical dignities. But the pious young man had a very different intention: fleeing the world, he assumed the monastic habit in the monastery of Saint Benignus at Dijon. By his perseverance he compelled his parents and the bishop to consent to his pious purpose. Under Abbot William, in that institution, he rejoiced like a giant to run the way of perfection. Shortly afterward, the most pious father appointed him provost over the monastery; and finally, after William’s death, he was established as abbot.

In that dignity he displayed such brilliance in virtue and knowledge that his fame spread far and wide. For this reason he was highly esteemed by the Frankish kings Robert and Henry. For this reason also he appeared worthy to Henry III, called the Black, of the bishopric of Lyons as early as 1041—an office which, as we have seen in Odolric’s account, he avoided with remarkable humility.

After Odolric’s death, however, he was demanded by the unanimous voice of clergy and people. Envoys were sent to the emperor to seek his consent. Caesar agreed, granted a diploma, and even issued an order, but in vain: with unconquered spirit Halinard refused to have so great a burden imposed upon him. At last the people of Lyons took refuge with the supreme pontiff. Gregory VI, complying with their wishes, sent to him and commanded by pontifical authority that he obey the petitions of clergy and people.

Trembling at such a command, the most pious man yielded. Having given his consent, he went to Henry’s court, accompanied by legates of the suffragan bishops, archdeacons, and clerics of the church of Lyons, so that he might receive the royal temporalities from him. Caesar did not refuse him, but ordered him first to swear the oath of loyalty owed to the emperor.

Halinard refused to do this, saying:

> “If I put aside the commands of the eternal King and of the Rule which I have promised by oath, what faith will remain to me, so that I ought to keep the oath sworn to the emperor? For the Lord says in the Gospel that one must not swear at all (Matthew 5:34); and the Rule of Father Benedict commands a monk not to swear and to make himself a stranger to the affairs of the world.”

This matter greatly disturbed the German prelates, because he refused to do what they themselves had willingly done. If Menestrier is to be believed, if he showed himself pious at court, he certainly did not show himself either a learned theologian or an expert in canon law when he refused to swear an oath that contained nothing contrary to God’s law—since it was required not in respect of ecclesiastical duties but in respect of the civil affairs with which bishops were honored.

Nevertheless, the king admired his steadfastness and piety, and, moved by the pleas of certain prelates, said:

> “Persuade him, if he does not wish to swear the oath, to conduct himself in such a way that he may appear to have sworn it, lest the custom of our country be annulled.”

The sincere man replied:

> “If I pretend to have done it, it will be the same as if I had done it. Far be this from me.”

At last the king released him from the oath, content with his word and promises. In his presence he had him ordained, giving him whatever was necessary for priestly blessing. He was ordained by Hugh, Bishop of Besançon, at Herbestein, in the year 1046 from the incarnation of the Lord.

“Having attained and equaled apostolic honor,” says the San-Benignian Chronicle, “he led an apostolic life in deeds and in name.” The same virtue of humility remained, while his works of charity multiplied; and throughout his life he shone before all by word and example, although, according to the custom of those times, he retained the governance of the monastery of Dijon until his death and scarcely resided in his bishopric, being summoned elsewhere for various affairs of the Church.

In the first year of his ordination, he followed the emperor to Rome with Hugh, his ordainer, and took part in the deposition of Gregory VI and the promotion of Clement II. After Clement’s death, the Romans asked the emperor to make Halinard Roman pontiff, says the San-Benignian Chronicle.

“ In 1048,” says Alberic, “when the emperor and the Romans were discussing the election of the supreme pontiff, Halinard, Archbishop of Lyons, was requested for the papacy by one party. The Romans loved him greatly because of the eloquence of his speech and the graciousness of his conversation. He expressed the native sound of each people’s speech as far as the Latin tongue penetrated, as though he had been born in that same country. But when he learned the will of the prince and the people, in his great humility he concealed his intention of going to the court until, while he delayed, Bruno, Bishop of Toul, was elected and called Leo IX in 1049.”

Summoned to Rome by Leo, Halinard was present at the council against the Simoniacs. In that same year he accompanied the pope to Reims and took part in the council held in the basilica of Saint Remigius, where, being free from simony, he condemned by his vote those guilty of so great a crime. He again joined Leo’s retinue when the pope returned to Rome and confirmed by his subscription Leo’s diploma in favor of Milo, Abbot of Dervensis. He is also mentioned in the privilege granted that same year to the monastery of Saint Maurice of Agaunum.

He took part in the Roman council of 1050, at which Saint Gerald was enrolled among the saints and the Berengarian heresy was condemned. In the autumn he accompanied the pontiff when he set out for Gaul. He was present at the elevation of Saint Gerald at Toul among the Leuci; and when he came to Langres, he ordained Lord Arduin as bishop in the pope’s presence.

In 1051, when Leo left the city, Halinard accompanied him to Benevento, Capua, and Salerno. He was selected for this purpose because he was powerful in speech and his tongue was capable of persuading people to anything: he was to serve as legate and mediator of peace between the Normans, who ruled those regions, and the pope himself.

The following year, when Leo was leaving Rome to travel to Hungary, he left Halinard at the monastery of Saint Gregory on the Clivus Scauri, which the pontiff had assigned to him for instruction. While the holy bishop was staying there, one day, as he reclined at table, a false friend offered him a fish infected with poison. As a result, he himself, two monks of that place, and all the others who ate it died within eight days.

The holy prelate died on the fourth day before the Kalends of August in the year 1052, in the seventh year of his pontificate and the twentieth year of his governance of the monastery of Saint Benignus. He had chosen burial for himself in the aforementioned monastery of Saint Gregory. But noble Romans arranged for his body to be carried to the basilica of Saint Paul, where it was honorably buried on the left side of the church, beneath an arch erected over his tomb.

All the sacred furnishings with which he had served in divine worship, together with silver vessels and a considerable quantity of gold, he sent to Dijon, to his monastery, which during his lifetime he had adorned with many ornaments, books, and buildings.

In the chartulary of Athanacum there is a document of Halinard’s which might be regarded as his testament. It was addressed to the canons of Lyons. In it he first asks them to pardon whatever negligence he had incurred among them. He declared that, if God prolonged his life, he would devote every effort to their advancement.

Second, concerning the appointment of his successor, he gives advice. Above all, he urges them not, as they had done until then, to wander through various places and others for this purpose, but, after offering prayers and fasts, to beseech God to appoint from among them a bishop worthy of the office. For this duty, considering the circumstances of the time, he judged the provost Um—possibly an abbreviated or corrupt reading—to be suitable.

Third, he begs Pontius the Seneschal to grant part of his possessions to the monastery of Athanacum. “For I am greatly indebted to them,” he says.

Halinard has not yet found a place in the sacred calendars, but he is given the title “Venerable” in the Benedictine *Menologium* on 29 July. The Bollandists mention him among those passed over under 26 April. In the necrology of Saint Benignus at Dijon the following is found:

> “The fourth day before the Kalends of August: the deposition of Lord Altinard, Archbishop of Lyons and abbot of this place.”

[Col. 1337]

# Life of the Venerable Halinard, from Abbot of Dijon to Archbishop of Lyons

By an anonymous disciple of his

*(In Mabillon, Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict, sixth century, part 2, page 34)*

## Preliminary Observations

1. After regular discipline had been restored by blessed William in the monastery of Saint Benignus at Dijon, men distinguished by nobility and learning flocked there from neighboring and distant regions, so that under the governance of so holy a Father they might embrace the monastic life.

Among these was our Alinard, or Halinard. He first served under the same blessed Father in the office of prior, afterward succeeded him in the dignity of abbot, and finally, having become Archbishop of Lyons, shone before the whole Church because of the holiness of his life and the renown of his learning.

His deeds were carefully described by the anonymous author of the Chronicle of Saint Benignus of Dijon. Since that author admits that Halinard had received him into the monastery and instructed him in the exercises of regular discipline, he deserves complete credibility, having written what he had either seen himself or learned from those who had been present at the events. We have already discussed this author in the fourth century, part 2, under the year 878, where he described the discovery of the body of Bertilio, Abbot of Dijon, which took place under our Halinard and was reported there.

2. Several deeds of Halinard can also be collected from various donations which Perard records in his *Collection of Burgundian Charters* as having been made to the monastery of Saint Benignus during Halinard’s time. Some of these are mentioned below by the chronicler, number 10 and following.

In the charter of Duke Gerard concerning Wulfereicurta, dated 1030, the monastery of Saint Benignus is called, under Abbot Halinard, the most famous religious monastery of our time. In a charter of Hugh, Bishop of Langres, the church of Saint Peter in the village of Mora is restored to the monastery known as Pulchrada or Saxon’s Fountain, so that this place might be reformed or improved under Halinard’s care with monastic dignity.

Bruno, Bishop of Toul and later Leo IX, gave two altars at Bertiniacicurta when he dedicated the church in the presence of Halinard and Widric, Abbot of Saint Aper. The same Halinard wrote to John, the Roman pontiff, and to the vestiarian of the Sacred Palace, against the canons of Dijon, who were attempting to transfer the right of the cemetery from the suburb of Saint Benignus to the castle of Dijon. For these letters and others, see Perard.

3. Halinard’s name has not yet found a place in the sacred calendars, and therefore it has been sufficient to call him “Venerable.” Bucelin gives him no other title in the Benedictine *Menologium* on 29 July. The Bollandists mention him among those passed over under 26 April, because Ferrarius praises him on that day.

He nevertheless died on the fourth day before the Kalends of August, as is certain from our chronicle. We have Severtius as witness that he was indeed recorded on that day in the obituary book of the Church of Lyons, and the old necrology of our monastery of Saint-Germain-des-Prés agrees with him.

There is no need to refute here the errors of Severtius and others who wrote about the affairs of Lyons when assigning the period of Halinard’s governance, since it is sufficient to produce the text of this author’s Life, which they had not seen. Hugh, Abbot of Flavigny, mentions Halinard in the Chronicle of Verdun, where he places his ordination in the year 1026.

The author of the Chronicle of Bèze also discusses him, although he does not praise him, because Halinard, while abbot of Dijon, had attempted to subject the monastery of Bèze to himself after regular discipline had been extended from the monastery of Saint Benignus to Bèze. But now let us hear our author from volume 1 of the *Acherian Spicilegium*, where the entire Chronicle is reproduced from a manuscript.

## The Life Begins

[Col. 1337]

### 1

Lord Halinard was serving in this place in the office of prior. In the time that followed, he also attained the name and merit of abbot and shepherd. It is fitting that we commit his memory to writing, since he instructed us with gentle and fatherly teachings.

He was born in Burgundy, sprung from the lineage of noble men. His father was a man of Langres, while his mother was a citizen of the Aedui. From the earliest beginnings of childhood he was handed over to the study of letters, and by heavenly providence he shone with exceptional effectiveness in a twofold knowledge.

He was loved with paternal affection by Walter, the venerable bishop of the city of the Aedui, whose son he was in baptism. For that reason Walter educated him with greater care, so that he might later be made a lamp in the house of God.

As time passed and his childhood ended, when adolescence had already begun to claim him, his father entrusted him to Lord Bruno, bishop of Langres. Seeing that he possessed a generous intellect, Bruno took care to associate him with the college of canons.

In that city, as he listened to philosophers and ecclesiastical men, he was, by the inspiration of divine grace, inferior to none of his companions in wisdom. The richness of his eloquence was restrained by the gravity of wisdom. From the substance of this combination he began to become a vessel of election; and since his mind was capable of all things, he left nothing unattempted and, in the end, nothing unabsorbed.

When he began to be clothed in the flowering blossoms of youth, he so formed his adolescence in good conduct that even then he seemed to be a monk. With complete vigilance he guarded himself whole and sincere from all the vices by which people of that age are accustomed to be polluted.

For he feared being imbued with them, lest, infected by them in tender youth, he should later be unable to free himself from them even when he wished, in accordance with what is written: “A young man, according to his way, will not depart from it even when he grows old” (Proverbs 22:6).

He obtained the companionship of good men, especially of the prudent, and hated followers of disgrace.

### 2

Since he was loved by Lord Lambert, Bishop of Langres, because of his benevolence, which made him dear to everyone, and since that bishop desired to elevate him by conferring ecclesiastical orders upon him, Halinard rejected the unstable and fleeting glory of the world. He sought to fulfill in deed what the Lord commanded in speech:

> “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Matthew 16:24; Luke 9:23).

Thus, scorning all the rewards of earthly possession for the sake of hope in the promise of the future, he assumed the habit of holy conduct.

But there he did not lack the trial of tribulation. His parents pursued him and, with the bishop’s consent, forcibly dragged him away from the monastery. Stripped of his monastic habit, they led him publicly through the streets, so that, because of this shame, he might hate what he had embraced so ardently.

But the cunning art of the Evil One accomplished nothing against the teaching of the Holy Spirit. They could in no way recall him from his intention. After a short time, he fled, so that he might complete outside his homeland what he was not permitted to accomplish in his native land.

But again he was pursued, captured, and brought back to the bishop, who tried to soothe him with many promises and flatteries, hoping somehow to turn his mind away from this intention. When the bishop saw that he persisted in his judgment, he finally permitted him, though only with difficulty, to do what he wished.

Having thus obtained what he desired, Halinard thereafter lived under another’s authority and, as far as he could, deviated in nothing from the purpose of holy discipline. Having banished slothfulness and murmuring far from himself, he stood out above the others in the singular virtue of obedience, fulfilling among the brothers what Saint Benedict says:

> “The good of obedience is to be shown not only to the abbot; the brothers must also obey one another” (*Rule*, chapter 71).

As an imitator of blessed Benedict, whose discipleship he had entered, he embraced the wise foolishness of God, according to the Apostle’s command:

> “If anyone among you wishes to be wise in this world, let him become foolish so that he may be wise” (1 Corinthians 3:18).

Just as philosophers devote the full attention of their minds to the arguments of syllogisms, so he devoted himself to learning those things which had to be carried out daily in the monastery. Having carefully learned all these matters and committed them to memory through experience, he began to appear more learned than everyone else.

### 3

When the aforementioned Father William recognized that Halinard was already so prudent in the monastic order, he placed him in charge of the community of brothers and entrusted him with the care of souls. He fulfilled this ministry with such authority and such solicitude that he was both an example and a source of fear to all who lived with him.

Content with regular observance, he was so devoted to moderation that he seemed in no way to differ from the fellowship of the common table. When he saw the vices of some that needed correction, he first sang the praises that could be found in each person; afterward, like one who knew them, he reproved them.

Nevertheless, he more often warned everyone to present themselves inwardly to God as people whom human opinion considered them outwardly to be on account of their religious habit.

Thus, having been tested in every office of the monastery and having diligently fulfilled the service of every ministry, he first administered the office of provost under the authority of the abbot for four years. Finally, after the death of the aforementioned father, the entire community of brothers compelled him to undertake pastoral care, since the teaching of justice required it.

Although he accepted this ministry unwillingly and reluctantly, once he had been devoted to the cultivation of God’s vineyard, so that he might show himself to be its laborer, he sought the common benefit of many more than his own. He was kind to all and just toward everyone. He harmed no one and strove to benefit those whom he could.

Sound doctrine was indeed present in him, because he carefully did what suited his condition, in accordance with the Apostle’s words:

> “Giving no offense in anything, so that our ministry may not be blamed, but in everything let us show ourselves as God’s ministers” (2 Corinthians 6:4).

Because he was filled with holy and modest speech, his hearing was entirely closed to obscene and shameful things, in accordance with what is written:

> “Hedge your ears with thorns, and do not listen to a wicked tongue” (Sirach 28:28).

He was so devoted to reading that, while traveling, he often carried a little book in his hands. Thus, even while riding, he refreshed his mind by reading.

When he read philosophers and books of secular wisdom, he pursued with shrewd diligence what the divine voice commands through the lawgiver concerning a captive woman. Whatever useful things were found in the books of philosophers, these he deemed worthy of his memory. Whatever was superfluous—namely, the love of worldly things and care for secular matters—he scraped away as poisonous and deadly. In the one case he made her bald; in the other, as with fingernails, he cut these things off with an extremely sharp knife.

Through his constant reading, therefore, he was formed by the authority of Scripture. He was so strong in canonical and monastic institutions that no one seemed his equal in the decrees of the laws or in philosophical arguments.

Then, composed in virtue and wisdom, and also richly endowed with the most honorable fluency of speech, he adapted himself to individuals so that he might be loved by all, fulfilling the Apostle’s statement:

> “I have become all things to all, so that I might save all” (1 Corinthians 11:22).

Whatever he said was composed with the gravity of wisdom. His speech was seasoned with salt; because of the weight of his virtue it was brief and uncommon, and because of its prudent sweetness it was regarded as precious. Therefore, whenever he delivered a sermon for moral edification, he was considered as welcome as he was eloquent.

Governing the flock entrusted to him with provident devotion, he urged them to fight, in united and holy combat, against the worst enemy of all the saints, and he exhorted each of them not to cease doing whatever good he could, lest he wish to do it at a time when it would no longer be permitted.

He also frequently brought forward the admonitions of blessed John—or, as another reading has it, Paul—who says in his Epistle:

> “Pursue peace with everyone, and holiness, without which no one will see God” (Hebrews 12:14).

### 4

He was greatly loved by the Frankish kings Robert and Henry. The emperor Conrad and his son, Emperor Henry, also honored him with extraordinary affection. Consequently, when the see of Lyons was vacant, Emperor Henry himself, because Halinard had once been known to him and was greatly loved for his religious conduct and reputation for holiness, offered him the honor of that bishopric.

Halinard, however, avoided the heavy burden of that stormy eminence by guarding his humility, pleading that, as a monk, he was entirely unfit for so great a burden.

At that time there was among the clergy of Langres a certain cleric named Odolric, advanced both in age and in holy conduct and exceptionally well educated in letters. He was then present at the king’s palace, although he was not yet fully known to the prince.

Our lord Father Halinard urged that Odolric be sought for this office; the richness of his wisdom and the dignity of his old age recommended him. When these words had been reported to the king, he was astonished both that Halinard so despised the honor of the priesthood when it was offered to him and that, while refusing it for himself, he sought it so earnestly for another. He consented and granted the dignity of the bishopric to the aforementioned Lord Odolric.

Halinard himself escorted him to the see and provided everything appropriate to his service as though he were one of Odolric’s own household. Odolric governed the Church of Lyons for five years, instructing the minds of his subjects by word and the example of good works.

Later, after suffering the plots of certain malicious and envious men, those who could not kill him with the sword did not shrink from killing him with poison. Thus murdered, he was joined to the other holy bishops who rested there.

5. At last the voice of the entire clergy, with the consent of the people, urged him to bow his neck to accept this high office, and begged him to undertake the care of the flock entrusted to him. They sent an embassy to the emperor, asking that the lord Halinard be given to them as bishop. An imperial command was sent ordering that the lord Halinard be enthroned. But his spirit, strengthened by divine power, was in no way swayed by these demands, until the letter of the apostolic pope arrived.

John, surnamed Gratianus [Note: Here he took the name Gregory VI. In 1046, after being driven from the Roman see together with Benedict IX and Sylvester III, he was replaced by Suidger of Bamberg, bishop, under the name of Clement II, as will be related below.], was then seated in the apostolic see. When he learned that Halinard was unwilling to yield to the petitioners’ wishes, he sent to him, commanding by pontifical authority that he obey the requests of the clergy and people.

Thus having attained and equaled the apostolic dignity, he led an apostolic life in deeds and in name. The same virtue of humility remained, while his works of charity multiplied. He seasoned everything he did with the savor of virtue. Just as a person is accustomed to examine himself by looking into a mirror, so he examined his inner self through divine reading; and from this he fashioned himself adorned in mind. If anything disfigured was discovered, he corrected it by the rule of justice.

Whenever he joined learned men and, as commonly happens, some matter from Scripture was proposed, he listened willingly and replied wisely and modestly. If anything perverse was proposed, he refuted it not harshly but with frank modesty—not defeating his opponent by clever argument, but teaching him kindly through the examples of venerable teachers. He brought forward the statements of the orthodox together with evangelical authorities. In this way he showed himself both highly learned and apparently eager to avoid boasting either of pride or of learning.

He scrupulously avoided swearing, lest he should perhaps commit perjury. Consequently, what he did at the emperor’s palace must not be passed over in silence.

6. The emperor Henry III governed the kingdom of Burgundy. For Rudolf, king of Burgundy, being without children, had made the emperor Henry II heir to the kingdom. After him the empire passed to Conrad; he took as his wife the sister of the aforesaid king, named Gisela, by whom he fathered Henry III. By paternal succession, the kingdom of Burgundy came to Henry by right.

The city of Lyons lies within the bounds of that kingdom. King Lothar of the Franks had given it as a dowry to his sister, Queen Matilda, whom he had married to Conrad, king of Burgundy and father of the aforesaid King Rudolf.

Accordingly, because of the grant of the bishopric, the lord Halinard, who had been chosen for this purpose, went to the court of the emperor Henry. With him were the bishops who were his suffragans, legate archdeacons, and the clergy of Lyons, who were seeking a pastor for themselves. As was customary, the emperor, on account of the honor of the episcopal office bestowed upon him, demanded from Halinard the oath of loyalty owed to him.

The lord Hugh, archbishop of Chrysopolis, acted as intermediary and mediator in this matter. When Halinard heard these words, he replied:
