“If I set aside the commands of the eternal King and of the Rule which I have promised under oath, what trust will there be that I ought to keep the oath of the emperor? For the Lord says in the Gospel: ‘Do not swear at all’ (Matthew 5:34). And the Rule of our father Benedict commands the monk ‘not to swear, and to keep himself apart from the affairs of the world’ (chapter 4).”

These words were reported to the emperor. Admiring and embracing Halinard’s firmness of spirit, yet wishing to test his perseverance, he said that he would by no means give him the bishopric unless he obeyed his commands.

But Halinard replied: “It is better for me never to accept the priesthood than to transgress God’s command.”

At this, the bishops of those regions, and especially Sigebald, bishop of Speyer, where these events took place, persisted, saying: “Who is this man who has presumed not to obey the commands of the prince in his palace, when none of us has ever dared to do so? Either let him swear loyalty to the king, or let him be rejected.”

The bishop Theodoric of Metz, however, Bruno, bishop of Toul, and Richard, bishop of Verdun, who were his friends, advised the prince not to trouble on this account a religious man whose constancy in faith and in the other virtues they knew.

Then the emperor said: “Persuade him, if he does not wish to take the oath, at least to present himself in such a way that he may appear to have taken it, lest the custom of our country be annulled.”

Halinard replied: “It is exactly the same if I pretend as if I had done it. Far be this from me!”

When the emperor saw that he was so firm, he did not wish to disturb him further. Assenting to his faithfulness expressed in word and promise, he granted him what had been requested. In his presence he had him ordained and gave him whatever was necessary for the episcopal blessing.

He prepared everything not only for Halinard and the other bishops, but also for the deacons and ministers of the altar—vestments, books, linens, and every necessity—as though he were not a prince but a servant. For that devout king was deeply ecclesiastical and most devoted to divine worship.

7. The venerable father Halinard was ordained by the hands of the lord Hugh, archbishop of Chrysopolis, at a place called Herbrestinc in the Teutonic language, a name which in our language means “good dwellings,” in the year 1046 from the Lord’s incarnation.

In that same year the aforementioned prince went to Rome, where on Christmas Day he received the imperial crown from the hands of Pope Clement. The emperor himself had ordered Clement to be ordained, and he had John, who then occupied the chair, as well as Benedict and Sylvester, deposed; when their guilt was examined in the council then held, they were found to be not only simoniacs but also usurpers of the Church of Christ.

The lord archbishop of Lyons and the aforementioned Archbishop Hugh attended this council, together with many other bishops assembled from various regions.

It had frequently been Halinard’s custom to travel to Rome for the sake of prayer, so that he might seek the patronage of the holy apostles and martyrs who protect that city. Indeed, it was his desire that, if possible, he might give up his soul to God there. Therefore he was not deprived of his desire; rather, the Lord granted it to him as he had wished.

After the aforementioned Pope Clement died, the Romans asked the emperor for Halinard. The emperor had exacted from the Romans a considerable sum of money so that no pope would be elected without his permission. When Halinard learned the will of the prince and the people, he pretended to delay going to court until, while he lingered, another man might be elected.

The Romans loved him greatly because of his eloquence and the affability of his speech. He pronounced the native sound of every people’s language as far as the Latin tongue extends, as though he had been born in each of those countries.

8. When the lord Bruno, bishop of Toul, who was called Pope Leo, had been ordained [Note: Leo entered the see in 1049; in that same year the Council of Reims was also held.], the lord Archbishop Halinard was summoned by him to a council at Rome. All the bishops of Gaul were summoned as well, to deliberate there concerning the state and correction of the holy Church.

In that same year the lord pope went to France and held a council of bishops at Reims. Our aforementioned father was there with him. At that time, the body of Saint Remigius was translated by the lord apostolic and the bishops who were present, and the church itself was consecrated.

For a third time the aforementioned pope held a council in the city of Rome, which the aforesaid prelate attended. When the pope set out again for Gaul, Halinard accompanied him inseparably.

When they came to the city of Langres, Halinard ordained there, in the pope’s presence, the lord Arduin as bishop, in place of the man who had been expelled.

Again, in the following year, while traveling to Rome, he journeyed with the lord apostolic to Benevento and Capua, to Monte Cassino, and to Monte Gargano, to Saint Michael the Archangel. The aforesaid pope went to those regions in order, if possible, to relieve their inhabitants in some way from the oppression under which they were being heavily burdened by the Normans.

Because the lord Bishop Halinard was powerful in speech and his tongue was sufficient to persuade people of anything, the lord apostolic took him with him as mediator and ambassador of peace between the Normans and himself.

On his return, since he was hastening to meet the emperor, who at that time happened to be in the region of Hungary, the aforesaid pope ordered Halinard to remain in Rome until he returned. The bishop of Langres, Hugh, was in his company.

Hugh, repenting of the things he had done no differently [variant: blindly], sought the lord pope to ask for a measure of penance for his offenses and absolution from his sins. The apostolic pope, being merciful and kind in spirit, saw that he was truly penitent and distressed, sympathized with him, and immediately forgave him, saying that what he had suffered was sufficient as penance. After absolving him from his offenses, he also rewarded him most generously as he departed, granting him permission to receive a bishopric.

9. When they came to Rome, the lord Halinard, intending to take leave of the pope and his other companions, reclined at table with them. There a fish was offered to him by a false friend, infected with poison.

All who partook of it—Halinard as well as the others—either died within eight days or perished after being consumed by a long illness. Two monks from this place who were with him were killed by this food.

He died on the fourth day before the Kalends of August, in the year 1052 from the Lord’s incarnation, after seven years in the episcopate and twenty years governing this place.

He had ordered that he be buried at Saint Gregory by the Clivus Scauri, for the lord pope had granted him that place as a residence. But Roman nobles who had come to visit him while he was still alive ordered that his body be carried to Saint Paul. There he was honorably committed to burial, on the left side of the church, and an arch was built over his tomb.

[Note: Bucelinus praises his epitaph in the *Menologium*, expressed in these two verses:

> Having become a participant in and equal to the apostolic honor,  
> He led an apostolic life in deeds and in name.]

He sent all the ornamentation that he used for sacred ministry to his holy protector Benignus, together with a considerable quantity of gold and the silver vessels that belonged to his office.

He greatly increased the adornment of this church, among other things having a golden cross decorated with gems made. He also ordered many books to be written, renewed the workshops of this monastery, and, although he was learned in every branch of knowledge, devoted himself especially to geometry and natural philosophy.

What was increased in this place during his lifetime in lands and possessions must not be passed over in silence.

10. Hugh, archbishop of the see of Chrysopolis and Halinard’s close and intimate friend, gave the church situated in the suburb called Salins, which his parents had built from the foundations. It was consecrated in honor of the holy martyrs Symphorianus and Agatha, and Saint Anatolius the confessor rests there.

He placed the deed of this gift upon the altar of Saint Benignus on the feast of that martyr, intending to celebrate Masses there. In the presence of all the people who had gathered, he bound by the sentence of excommunication anyone who should remove that place from the authority of the abbot and monks of Dijon.

This donation was made in the year 1037 from the Lord’s incarnation, in the fifth indiction, in the sixth year of Hugh’s episcopate.

By episcopal privilege he granted another church, situated in the same suburb and dedicated to the honor of Saint Mary. Count Rainald had given this church to Saint Benignus for the repose of the soul of his father Otto, called William [Note: More about this Otto is found in the *Life of Saint William of Dijon*, which was published in the earlier part of this century.]; in return for his gift, while Halinard was still prior, he received a considerable sum of money from the lord Halinard.

11. The aforementioned Count Rainald gave a site in the aforesaid suburb for the construction of a church. A chapel was built there in honor of the apostle Saint Andrew; because it was made of wooden materials, it was later reduced to nothing through neglect.

At Evoregio he gave the land that had belonged to Theudebert. The monks possessed it for some time, but because of the opposition caused them by Odilo, they relinquished it until the aforementioned count restored it to them, when they already possessed the site of Saint Anatolius.

This took place in the year 1026 from the Lord’s incarnation, after the death of Count William, who died in that same year.

Of the inhabitants of that town, some—clerics and laymen—who came to this monastery for monastic conversion gave their possessions to our holy protector Benignus. Others, offering their sons, likewise contributed from their property. Among these was my father, who, when he offered me, gave—apart from other things—a house beside the well and the site of a cauldron, which was later granted in return for a rent, on the agreement that whoever held it would pay forty-six shillings each year.

12. Some time afterward, when a period had passed, the same Count Rainald gave, near the castle called Vesoul, a church consecrated in honor of Saint George, so that a monastery might be built there and four monks installed, who would serve God there perpetually and pray for the repose of the souls of his father, mother, brother, himself, and all his family.

He gave vineyards and lands for their support, together with whatever was necessary, and also fishing rights with the men who served him in that work.

The aforementioned Archbishop Hugh was present at this donation. With the staff which he was accustomed to carry in his hand, he gave the altar of the aforementioned church to Abbot Halinard; in memory of this act, they exchanged their staffs.

Count Burchard likewise gave the site called Offonisvilla, formerly a noble abbey and consecrated in honor of Saint Leodegarius. He earnestly begged the aforementioned Abbot Halinard to restore the monastic order there.

13. Roger, lord of the castle called Wangionumrivus, also gave the church built by his father Wido in honor of Saint Stephen, intending that, after the canons had been expelled, monks might be placed there to serve God day and night.

Rainald, likewise lord of the castle called Châtillon, when he came to the point of death and took the monastic habit, gave the lordship of Saint Julian, together with all the lands and serfs belonging to it, and the church dedicated to that saint’s name. He requested that monks be installed there to pray to God for his soul and for the souls of all the faithful [Note: This was done in 1038, as is clear from the charter of that date, which Perardus presents, together with the other donations mentioned here, in his *Collection*.].

In a similar manner, Count Albert of Metz gave the estate called Wlfereicourt, together with male and female serfs. He had resolved to make the gift during his lifetime, but after his death his son, Duke Girard, fulfilled it [Note: In 1033, according to the charter preserved by Perardus.].

A certain noblewoman named Letgardis, sister of Bishop Lambert, also gave the church situated in the village called Islo, on the River Meuse in the county of Bassigny.

[Col. 1345]

# The Letters of Halinard

## First Letter to Pope John XIX

[Col. 1345D]

[See under John XIX, for the year 1038, in *Patrologia*, volume CXLI.]

## Letter II: To Eiquocus, Treasurer of the Sacred Palace

[*Mabillon, Annals of the Order of Saint Benedict*, IV, 729]

[Col. 1346D]

To that lord Eiquocus, treasurer of the Sacred Palace, first senator and sole duke of the Romans, his own abbot, nominally, sends the service of continual fidelity.

Those whom the bond of true charity unites are not separated by distant stretches of land. Therefore let your highness know that, although distant from you in body, I am always present with you in mind and spirit. Not only do I myself, but also my brothers who diligently serve Saint Benignus, and indeed our own elder, continually strengthen your well-being by holy prayers, as though present with you in every prosperity. As long as life remains, you will soon have me at your service, not forgetful of your benefits.

Moreover, because we have great confidence in you, we openly disclose and earnestly ask that, if one of our neighboring rivals should wish to contrive anything against our place before the lord pope, you prevent it, as you are well able to do.

We seek nothing unjust. We wish the ancient law of our place to remain intact and inviolate, which they are striving vigorously to transfer elsewhere. Thus may the one formerly known to you now appear still better known; if you take good care of him, you will make us mindful of you.

## Letter III: To the Canons of Lyons  
*(Around 1051)*

[*Gallia Christiana*, volume IV, appendix, p. 8]

Halinard, unworthy bishop, sends to the lords, the canons of Lyons, the support of his prayers.

Let it be known to your brotherhood that I must soon be stripped of the prison of the flesh. Therefore, though absent, I beg you in person, on my knees, to pardon compassionately whatever negligence I have incurred toward you.

For if the Lord grants me the present life, as he is able to do, all my concern will constantly watch over your advancement.

Furthermore, I offer you counsel concerning the appointment of a faithful pastor to succeed me. Do not henceforth, as you have done until now, search distant and foreign places for this purpose. Rather, after offering prayers and fasts, ask the mercy of the Almighty to appoint from among you as prelate one whom he, who is able to raise up children for Abraham, judges worthy.

For this office, according to the circumstances of the present time, the provost Vin. appears suitable. If you are able, as I hope, to persuade him to accept that preeminence—for I am witness to his conscience—… I urge him to succeed me. Finally, truly … to will and arrange everything …

To you also, dearest Ponce the Seneschal, I make every kind of prayerful request: grant part of my possessions to Saint Stephen and part to the monastery of Athanacum, for the salvation of my soul, since I am greatly indebted to them.

Moreover, I forbid everyone to inhabit, cultivate, or perform divine service in the church of Veisa, except the monks of Athanacum, until they peacefully possess that church and its lands, as Robert agreed with them.

Next, I command Robert himself, by the faith which he pledged to me, to offer for my redemption or favor one half of the eight ounces of gold which he owes—one half to Saint Stephen and the other to the monks of Athanacum.

I also forbid and anathematize, by the authority of God the almighty Father, blessed Peter, all the saints, and myself, that anyone should oppose the monks of Athanacum on account of the money of the Jews who were formerly killed there.

Farewell.

IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1052: JORDAN, BISHOP OF LIMOGES.

[Col. 1347]

# Historical Notice

*(From* Gallia Christiana, *volume IV, p. 514)*

[Col. 1347D]

Jordan of Loron [al.: of Laron, as it is read—and more correctly—in the *Deeds of the Bishops* by Bernard Gui], provost of Saint Leonard, a nobleman, was elected bishop when the leading men of the Limousin region were competing, not without simony, to obtain the bishopric of the city of Limoges. The election took place in an assembly held at Saint Junianus by the most prudent Duke of Aquitaine, William, at the end of January.

The duke, taking with him certain bishops and nobles, led the elected man into the city of Limoges and, in the major church of Saint Stephen, invested him freely with episcopal honor and the pastoral staff.

Afterward Jordan was ordained deacon and priest at Augeriacum on the Saturday of Mid-Lent, and on the following Sunday was consecrated by Islo, bishop of Saintes and assistant to the archbishop of Bordeaux, together with three other bishops: Boso, Arnald, and Isembert.

Then William, son of Duke William, and Arnald, bishop of Périgueux, installed him in the see of Saint Martial.

Meanwhile, Gauslin, archbishop of Bourges, indignant that he had been despised by Jordan—for Jordan ought to have been ordained by his own metropolitan—assembled a synod before King Robert. Seven archbishops with their suffragan bishops attended, and Gauslin excommunicated the entire Limousin region … and prohibited Jordan from exercising the episcopal office.

Jordan claimed that he had avoided the laying on of hands because Gauslin demanded money for it, money which he had requested and received from another person. Nevertheless, in order to make satisfaction, Jordan went barefoot to the see of Bourges with one hundred clerics and monks, all likewise barefoot.

The archbishop came to meet him with the clergy, and, bringing forward honorably those whom he had previously bound, absolved them.

In 1024, on the day before the Nones of March, in the seventh indiction, he approved the foundation of the cell of Liziniacum, established by Hugh of Liziniacum, a most noble man.

Before his journey to Jerusalem, he dedicated the monastery of Arnacum, where the body of Saint Pardulf rests, on the Ides of July in the year 1028 of the Lord’s incarnation. There were present Guido de Turribus, a nobleman of Limoges, with his venerable wife Engalsia [al.: Emallia], and Ademar of Loron [Learum], Gerard, Ebo of Comborn, brother of Archambald surnamed “Rotten Chamba,” together with Adenar, son of Guido the viscount, according to Geoffrey of Vigeois, *Chronicle*, chapter 9.

In that same year the royal basilica of the Savior at Limoges was consecrated on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of December by eleven prelates: Geoffrey, archbishop of Bordeaux; Jordan of Limoges; Isembert of Poitiers; Roho of Angoulême; Arnald of Périgueux; Peter of Girona; Deusdedit of Cahors; and others.

In 1031 he attended the council of the province of Bourges, held at Limoges, where the question of Saint Martial’s apostolate was discussed and he defended it in the assembly of the Fathers. Yet previously he had written a letter to Pope Benedict VIII arguing that this saint should not be counted among the apostles.

From what Jordan pronounced at the aforesaid council, we learn that another synod had been held at Limoges in 1029, or rather 1028, at which the same matter had already been debated and decided, and which he had attended.

Concerning this apostolate of Saint Martial, John XVIII [al.: XIX or XX] wrote to Jordan, declaring that those who denied that this saint was an apostle were insane.

At the council of 1031 Jordan publicly denounced the soldiers who plundered the possessions of the sanctuary and oppressed the poor. Against them the Fathers pronounced these anathemas:

> “We excommunicate those soldiers … cursed are they themselves and their helpers for evil; cursed are their weapons and their horses. May they be with Cain the fratricide and with Judas the traitor … and just as these lamps are extinguished before your eyes, so may their joy be extinguished in the sight of the holy angels, unless before death they come before their bishop’s judgment for satisfaction, amendment, or worthy penance.”

In the following year Jordan also attended the synod of Poitiers mentioned in the *Chronicle of Maillezais*.

In 1047 the church of Saint Mary of Saintes was dedicated by many bishops, among whom Jordan is recorded.

In 1048 he attended the consecration of the church of Uzerche with Gerald of Périgueux and William, bishop of Angoulême. At that time he witnessed the donation made to this monastery by a nun named Aalberga, called Bonasia, and by her son Boso.

From the chartulary of the church of Limoges we transcribed a letter of this bishop in which he grants many possessions to Saint Stephen for the common fund; but the names of his parents are scarcely legible. From the same chartulary we obtained the agreement made between him and William, count of Poitiers.

Jordan’s death is assigned to the year 1052. He was buried in the church of Saint Augustine.

Ademar of Chabannes dedicated to him and to many bishops and abbots an apologetic letter in defense of Saint Martial’s apostolate in 1029. Mabillon published it in volume IV of the *Annals*, in the appendix. From it we learn not only the year in which it was written but also the date of the earlier synod of Limoges held in support of this apostolate, namely 1028.

[Col. 1349]

# Letter of Jordan to Benedict VIII, Roman Pontiff

After Benedict’s death, John XIX gave the reply.

(See under John XIX, for the year 1033, in *Patrologia*, volume CXLI.)

[Col. 1351]

# Two Charters of Jordan

(*Gallia Christiana*, volume II, appendix, pp. 171–172, from the chartulary of the Church of Limoges)

## I. Letter of Jordan, Bishop of Limoges, by which he grants many possessions to the chapter of Limoges

[Col. 1351A]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, I, Jordan, by the grace of God bishop of the see of Limoges, considering the fall of human frailty, give and grant from my allodial property, which came to me by hereditary succession, for the remedy of my soul and of the souls of my parents Marbod and Odolgardis his wife, and of my father Gerard and his wife Odolgardis, to Saint Stephen at the see of the city of Limoges and to the canons of that see, as an allod in common for the canons, without contradiction from any person:

namely, the new castle, the upper tower and the place where the donjon stands, as it is commonly called, together with the houses; those pleas which belong to my division; the upper meadow by the spring; the forest called Serra; one quarter of the chapel of Saint Michael and Saint Quintin, with all the land belonging to the chapel; and the estate of Cursatea, as it is held from the fief of the count of Poitiers.

Count William himself gave me that entire fief as an allod outside the bishopric.

If anyone should contradict this aforesaid donation or seek to bring a claim against it, let him be anathema and be plunged into hell with Dathan and Abiram.

The sign of Bishop Jordan, who confirmed this charter and ordered it to be written.

This charter was made in the month of February, while Henry was king of the Franks and William duke of the Aquitanians.

## II. Agreement Made between Jordan, Bishop of Limoges, and William, Count of Poitiers

[Col. 1351C]

We believe that those skilled in the ancient constitution are not unaware that the supreme craftsman of all creation fashioned the structure of the human being under this condition of law: that he should rule over all living creatures which move upon the earth.

Nature created all human beings equal, but by an expanded arrangement of God, when he was able to hold each thing subject to its own right, he placed some below others—not because nature had arranged it, but because the order of merits had been altered by fault.

Indeed, kings, counts, and prelates began to preside over other people by ruling them, as the Psalmist says: “You have placed men over our heads” (Psalm 65:12); and blessed Pope Gregory says: “By the grace of God we are above men.”

Strengthened by these testimonies, William, count of Poitiers, came to the city of Limoges for the sake of peace. After peace had been established in the presence of noble clerics and laymen, he made the following agreement with Bishop Jordan:

If the count of Poitiers should appoint a bishop to the bishopric of the see of Limoges, it should in no way be done without the election and counsel of the canons of Saint Stephen, and without the counsel of Aimeric of Niort together with one of his sons, if he is alive; or, if he is dead, with his two sons; likewise with the two sons of Alduin of Nobiliacum, if they are alive; and, if they are dead, with the counsel of those who hold the towers of Niort and Nobiliacum.

For the commendation of the bishop, this election must not be made for earthly gain or because of anyone’s friendship, but for the salvation of Saint Stephen of the see of Limoges, with the knowledge of those men.

The bishop who comes after Bishop Jordan must provide the same security and guarantee that Bishop Jordan and his predecessors provided to the canons of Saint Stephen concerning the bishopric and their common property—or such security as they themselves should agree upon, and without force.

Count William, together with Bishop Jordan and the canons of Saint Stephen, made this agreement under oath: that he would neither give away nor diminish anything belonging to the bishopric, nor would his successor who came after him.

If the community of Saint Stephen should be threatened on account of this agreement, and he did not come to their aid within eleven days against those who had done the wrong, and if the community of Saint Stephen were thereby released from remaining in his allegiance, then, for the sake of providing assistance, Count William gave as hostages Aimeric of Roncum and Albert of Cambo.

If these men should die, others of equal worth must be substituted in their place.

On account of the agreement and election concerning the bishopric, these are the hostages: William of Roca, William of Kartes, Hugh of Lacella, Gerard of Volvent, son of Raymond, Vivian of Brederium, and Peter of Niort.

If any of them should die, he must be replaced within fifteen days after the count of Poitiers has been notified. The person who gives the notification shall suffer no penalty.

If this is not done within fifteen days after notification, they shall enter the castle of Saint Stephen, which is enclosed by wall and ditch, without malicious intent, and shall not leave it without the absolution of the five clerics who are hostages … the count of Poitiers, if they are alive; and, if they are dead, for the absolution of those who hold that honor, with the counsel of the other five clerics who are on the spot and for the welfare of Saint Stephen, with their knowledge and without preventing the notification.

This charter was made on the third day before the Nones of August, while Henry was king of the Franks and William duke of the Aquitanians, and while Jordan was bishop of the see of Limoges. They ordered this charter to be written and confirmed.

[Col. 1353]

# Acts of the Second Council of Limoges

[Note: Binius had published fragments after Baronius; now the complete text is brought to light from a manuscript in the library of Thuanius. That it was held in 1031, not 1034, is proved beyond question by the very day on which it began, namely the first day before the Kalends of December, which, as these acts testify in column 1362, fell on a Thursday.]

Held under Jordan on 18 November 1031. It concerns the apostolate of Saint Martial and many matters relating to discipline. Interspersed are speeches by Jordan himself to the Fathers of the synod, namely:

1. A brief narrative of the events conducted at the synod of Limoges in 1028;
2. A homily on these words from Luke: “The Son of Man came to seek and to save what was lost”;
3. A eulogy of the monasteries of the diocese of Limoges.

(From Labbe, *Councils*, volume IX, column 869.)

## Session I. Held on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of December

[Col. 1353A]

At that time, by God’s will, on the feast of the dedication of the temple of the Lord Savior, which falls on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of December, a council was assembled near the city of Limoges.

Thus, early in the morning on the very day of the dedication, all the bishops assembled together with the priests and deacons in the church of the blessed protomartyr Stephen.

The same basilica had been solemnly decorated the day before for the gathering of the council, as had the church of the Lord Savior, in which the anniversary of the dedication was duly celebrated by the entire people of Limoges.

Seats for the bishops were therefore arranged in the form of a crown in that holy church of Limoges, which is the first of all the churches of Gaul.

When prayers had been offered and the bishops had taken their seats, after the archdeacon had delivered a reading, Bishop Jordan said:

“By the inspiration of divine grace, the bishops present have deigned to come to our assistance at our summons, concerning whatever matters may be necessary. Therefore we admonish all of you, beloved clerics, that in this holy council no one knowingly conceal the truth; no one, through fear or favor, gift or hatred, presume to disturb right justice.

“First we must speak about our own order, so that whatever needs correction may, with God’s help, be corrected, superfluities cut away, and what has been approved by all strengthened, so that firm unity of peace may remain among us.

“For we know that God is not in divisions of mind, and that God rejoices in unity. Those deserve to possess his grace who do not separate themselves from one another through the scandals of factions.

“If anyone appears uncertain about something, or perhaps thinks that the others are blameworthy in any matter, let him come forward and speak freely, so that he may either teach or be taught, and so that disparagement may be removed from the brotherhood of the Church.

“Therefore we seem to have been gathered here in the name of Jesus so that justice may find a place among us and injustices may be rejected.”

After some brief discussion of divine matters, the bishop again said:

“I reveal to you the grief of my heart, O venerable bishops and other ministers of the Lord, and I raise a complaint against the secular powers among my parishioners. They do not allow the Church of God to remain at peace; they invade the possessions of the sanctuary; they afflict the poor entrusted to me and the ministers of the Church; and they refuse to hear of peace from me, who am their pastor.”

All the bishops said with one voice:

> “Whoever troubles you will bear judgment, whoever he may be. For it is right that such men, who presume to oppose you, should be cut off from communion with the Church. For whoever troubles those subject to you troubles you; and whoever troubles you troubles Christ, whose place the bishops occupy in their legation. Therefore they deserve the severity of divine and apostolic discipline and must be punished by a just anathema from our council until they come to their senses through fruitful repentance.”

Then Odolricus, the most reverend father of the monastery, clothed in sacred vestments as he sat beside the pontiff, rose in the circle of the bishops. When silence had been established, he said to the pontiff:

“We beg, excellent pontiff, by the reverence due to your rank, that before anything else is discussed, the question of your Church concerning the apostleship of blessed Martial may be prudently debated and here find peace according to the rule of truth. For this is chiefly the matter over which you and I have brought this council together. Behold, the holy bishops present with you are here in the name of the Holy Spirit; behold, many learned in divine and secular writings are present. Let anyone who wishes to contradict us in this matter—whereby we profess blessed Martial to be an apostle and everywhere render his memory the apostolic honor in divine worship—come forward confidently before you and either prove by reason that we are liars, in which case we shall gladly accept his judgment; or—and this we believe with God’s help—find us truthful and accept the truth in peace.

“Time and again we have asked you to establish this rule firmly in all the churches and monasteries throughout the Limousin. Time and again you have excused yourself, saying that you were unwilling to do so until, after the letter of Pope John, the matter had been heard at a council before this see by the bishops of the province and judged worthy, just, and reasonable on the authority of the ancients—so that you would not seem to act without consulting the neighboring bishops, nor be called by ill-disposed persons arrogant or presumptuous.”

The pontiff replied:

“Just as this was first approved, praised, and confirmed by the Roman pope, and again by the Council of Bourges, at which, at the beginning of this November, you represented me as president, so I now wish the matter concerning blessed Martial to be judged justly and canonically in this holy see, with me present, so that by this third authority the entire schism throughout the Limousin may henceforth be removed by a decree of our authority. Therefore, let an examination of blessed Martial’s apostleship be conducted in the presence of the bishops, to determine whether he truly is an apostle or not.”

At this, Engelricus, a canon and priest of the church of Anicius, a highly learned man, rose before them and said:

“The countless multitude of unlearned people contradicts the claim that he was an apostle for this reason: he was not one of the Twelve. When many repeatedly hear of the twelve disciples, or of the twelve seated upon twelve thrones, they suppose that no one is an apostle except the Twelve. Nor do they think that the other seventy-two were apostles, but only simply disciples. Against this, let the authority of that man be brought before your council who faithfully translated the Old and New Testaments from Hebrew and Greek into Latin, who was an expositor of the sacred books, and whose authority it is sacrilegious for anyone to question, since among all teachers after the apostles he is the Church’s strongest pillar.”

The codex was then brought forward and examined, and the bishops had Jerome’s commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians read aloud before them. There Jerome writes as follows (Jerome, on the opening of chapter 1 of Galatians):

“As for the fact that, besides the Twelve, certain men are called apostles, the reason is that all who had seen the Lord in the flesh and afterward preached him were called apostles. Thus Paul says: ‘He was seen by the eleven; then he was seen by James; then by all the apostles’ (1 Cor. 15)—that is, by the seventy-two whom the Lord sent out in pairs to preach. Others too were appointed apostles by those whom the Lord chose, as he says to the Philippians: ‘I considered it necessary to send to you Epaphroditus, my fellow soldier, but your apostle’ (Phil. 2). And concerning such men it is written to the Corinthians: ‘Whether they are apostles of the churches, for the glory of God’ (2 Cor. 8). Silas and Judas too were called apostles by the apostles.”

To this Engelricus added:

“If those who saw the Lord in the flesh and afterward preached him are apostles, how much more is Martial an apostle, who was the Lord’s disciple in the flesh and became a great laborer and fruit-bearer in preaching, so that Gaul itself is the sign of his apostleship? All Aquitaine knows that Martial was the first enlightener of Gaul, and no one can contradict this. Since, therefore, he was the Lord’s disciple, just as Cleophas was, and since this western region bears the sign of his apostleship, he is unquestionably an apostle in the same order as Paul and Barnabas.

“Even if this better-founded institution seems harsh to certain people because of the custom familiar to them, by which they normally celebrate his memory as that of a confessor, I say confidently that no one can by any reasoning contradict those who choose rather to celebrate his memory as that of an apostle.”

At this, Father Azenerius of the monastery of Masciacum, a man learned in letters, rose in the presence of the bishops and gave his testimony:

“Since I was thoroughly trained among grammarians and later at the palace, I have never heard Martial—who dedicated this first church before all the churches of Gaul—recited in any of our monasteries throughout Francia except with the other apostles. And rightly so, because he was the first to beget the peoples of Gaul in Christ Jesus through the Gospel.

“But after, at King Robert’s command, I assumed the direction of his monastery in Bourges alone, I there first encountered another improper custom in this matter, which I immediately abolished. For I promptly entered his name and memory in the rank in which God had placed him, namely, among the apostles.

“For long ago, before I took the monastic habit, when I was traveling to Jerusalem and was attending the solemn service on the Saturday of Pentecost in the basilica of Hagia Sophia at Constantinople, I remember hearing the Greeks pronounce Martial in the Greek litanies, after the Twelve, among the other apostles.”

Odolricus then began to explain, saying:

“Let the pontiffs and elders who stand here before me listen. I need not testify that from antiquity Martial has always been pronounced an apostle in many places of the greatest learning, lest I perhaps be judged a flattering witness on behalf of the administration of his Church. Men from foreign places are present who will give true testimony of this before you.

“Nevertheless, I must not remain silent about the fact that, when long ago I was being instructed for several years in the liberal arts at the monastery of Saint Benedict in Francia, I found an ancient rule of the monastery according to which Martial was pronounced in the litanies with the other apostles. The father of that place, Abbo, most distinguished in philosophy—whom many of you know, the most renowned master of all Francia in every divine and secular authority, and afterward crowned with martyrdom by the sword of the persecutor in Gascony—what he wrote about Martial and what testimony he bore concerning him is known to the clergy of this city.

“After him there was a father of that same monastery, distinguished both by his great age and by his birth, as well as by his eloquence and liberal learning, and finally raised to the archiepiscopal see of Bourges.

[Note: Gauzlenus, abbot of Fleury and archbishop of Bourges.]

“Many of our people know what testimony that man bore to the holy servant of God. For while King Robert was still alive, when my predecessor Hugo was assisting him at the palace in Paris in the company of a multitude of nobles and learned men, a dispute of this kind began before the king between the Franks and the Limousins; I too was present there at the time.

“They said: ‘You Franks are acting wrongly, because you pronounce Martial with the apostles; we are acting rightly, because we recite him among the confessors. You call him the last of the apostles; we call him the first of the confessors in the litanies.’

“The aforementioned archbishop, Gauzlenus, restrained their quarrel, saying:

“‘Unless both sides in this matter are made uniform, one side is more just than the other, and it is necessary that the more just and reasonable side should always prevail. For all who pronounce Martial among the confessors seem to me not to be acting well, justly, or perceptively. He belongs more to the apostolic order than to the order of the confessors.

“‘Therefore those who remove his name from the rank in which God placed him and put it where God did not place it are not acting rightly. He belongs rather to the apostolic company than to the order of the confessors, who come after the martyrs.

“‘Certainly, if someone were to pronounce the name of the king who is present not among the names of kings but among the names of subordinate counts, he would either be called a rustic or a malicious despiser of the king. If this were done with rustic simplicity, the king would not be disturbed in spirit but would readily forgive the rusticity. If, however, it were said not simply but contemptuously, there is no doubt that the king’s spirit would be inflamed to anger because of the contempt. If the contemptuous person persisted in such an intention, he would receive sentence against himself as one maliciously contemptuous; indeed, not only the king but his subordinate counts, princes, and friends would be angered against the offender.

“‘Truly, the whole of this region knows that that preacher of Aquitaine belongs not to the rank of the confessors, who come after the martyrs, but to that of the apostles, who come before the martyrs.

“‘For my part, if I were to remove his name from the apostolic order, I would fear incurring in this matter the indignation of the apostle Peter and the others, who once in the world and now in heaven have their illustrious colleague and companion Martial seated among them in the apostolic ranks.

“‘And if I were to transfer his name to the catalogue in which I pronounce Saint Benedict, Hilary, and Martin, I would fear incurring the anger of Saint Benedict, Hilary, Martin, and the others, who rejoice that he shines in heaven in the apostolic order.

“‘There can be no envy or quarrel among the saints there, because the unity of charity reigns in all; and what individuals do not possess in themselves, they possess in all through charity, where God is all in all.

“‘Certainly, if there are other apostles besides the Twelve—and without doubt there are—then he is truly an apostle who received from the Lord, together with the other Twelve apostles, the whole gift of grace.

“‘Certainly Martial is not now, nor will he be, anyone other than the one he once was; and the one he was, he is now, and he will always be. He was God’s friend, he is God’s friend, and he will be God’s friend. He was an apostle, he possesses apostleship—for Gaul is the seal of his apostleship—and he will possess the honor of an apostle in heaven forever. He was an apostle in office; he is an apostle in reward; he will be an apostle forever in glory and honor.

“‘In the flesh he is of the lineage of Abraham; he is the Lord’s disciple; he was baptized by Peter at Christ’s command; he is joined by kinship of the flesh to that same Peter, keeper of the keys of the kingdom, and to Stephen, the first martyr; he was sent by the Lord; through the Lord’s breathing upon him he was consecrated by the Holy Spirit and exalted with the power of binding and loosing; on the day of his ascension he was sanctified by the Lord’s episcopal blessing; on the day of Pentecost he was filled with the Holy Spirit in Zion; he knew the languages of all nations; he first brought to these western peoples the testimony of the living God; he proved an unconquered witness of Christ’s resurrection.

“‘Therefore, when raising the dead, he always set before the barbarians as a witness the crucified one and his resurrection, saying: “In the name of the Lord whom the Jews crucified, and who rose from the dead on the third day, arise, you who lie dead.”

“‘His name itself seems to resound with this testimony to God. For the name Martial is interpreted by a Greek term as “testimony,” or “witness of life,” or, as others wish, “immortal power,” because by the power of the resurrection he caused a disciple to rise from death after six days when touched by Peter’s staff; or “the power of immortality,” that is, the preacher or witness of him who alone, the immortal King of the ages, possesses immortality. For this reason he proved an unconquerable witness of Christ’s resurrection.

“‘Clearly, if there is no apostle except the Twelve, as the heretical Ebionites preach—and it is impious even to think this, for they accept no apostle except the Twelve and reject Paul because he is not one of the Twelve, as Bede says in his Commentary on Mark—then Paul and Barnabas are not apostles. To think this is madness.

“‘We Franks preserve as established the custom concerning this matter that our fathers, who first shaped the monastery of Saint Benedict by their teaching, handed down to us as supported by complete reason. Whoever wishes to imitate us in this matter will hold to the straight line of truth.’

“When the archbishop had finished speaking, he fell silent, and the king, together with all the clergy and princes of rank who were attending him, applauded the archbishop’s words.

“When we returned to this city, we immediately arranged to search through the ancient books of our own place concerning this matter. We found countless copies, both among us and in various churches of Aquitaine, in which Martial was written as an apostle. In ancient volumes of the Martyrology as well, we still found two of his disciples, Alpinianus and Austriclinianus, written as apostles.

“For this is how it is read in certain very ancient books: ‘On the day before the Kalends of July, the feast of Saint Martial, teacher and apostle of Aquitaine, together with the two apostles Austriclinianus and Alpinianus, whose life shone forth exceedingly through signs and miracles.’

“But do not be surprised, most reverend prelates, that I have brought this testimony before your council as though we wished his disciples themselves to be recited as apostles. We do not wish this, lest—as some say—the apostolic name become cheapened if the Church were to produce so many apostles, since we know that some people find even this claim about Martial displeasing.

“Rather, we have said these things so that those present at the council may easily understand that, if the ancient fathers long ago did not hesitate to acknowledge Martial’s disciples as apostles, they knew and believed their master to be an apostle all the more certainly.

“Let the elders of the monasteries throughout the Limousin be questioned about this antiquity, so that we may fulfill the prophetic saying: ‘Stand upon the ways, ask about the ancient paths of the Lord; seek which is the right way, and walk in it’ (Jer. 6).

“The father of the monastery of Tulle bears witness to us that, ever since that place was founded in the time of Charles Augustus, it has always retained the customary practice of commemorating Martial as an apostle.”

Meanwhile Geraldus, father of the monastery of Solignac, seated solemnly in the council and clothed in sacred vestments, said before everyone:

“I know that we possess extremely ancient codices containing ancient testimony that Martial was proclaimed an apostle by the ancients. But as the negligence of churchmen gradually increased, when other things that were right had also begun to be corrupted, this too was corrupted by younger men, so that he was no longer called an apostle because he was not one of the Twelve. For many even today, failing to notice the fact, think that Paul and Barnabas were among the Twelve.

“Therefore they changed his name in the litanies from the apostolic order to the series of confessors. Having a good zeal, but not according to knowledge, they thought that their patron would be honored better if they called him not the last of the apostles but the first of the confessors; for this reason, in some places they wrote him down as a confessor in accounts of his deeds. But the most ancient codices prove that this was by no means written on the basis of his deeds.

“On this matter it is more prudent to write him everywhere as an apostle than as a pontiff or confessor, because the holy apostles who were bishops, whether killed or not killed by the sword, are all called both pontiffs and confessors when they are called apostles. Yet there are countless pontiffs and confessors who are not apostles.

“If, at episcopal consecration, a bishop is called an apostle, when it is said, ‘You are Urban; you are Christ’s apostle; let the Church be your mother; let the apostles be your brothers; let the angels guard the rank of your apostleship,’ how much more is he an apostle who was sent and consecrated by the Lord himself and exalted with apostolic power—that is, the power of binding and loosing?

“But let Ambrose of Milan, a strong pillar of the Church, come before your council, O prelates; let us hear his authority on this matter.”

The codex was then brought forward, and the following was read from the commentary on the Epistle to Timothy, where Ambrose says:

[Note: The passage is falsely cited.]

“At the beginning of the Church’s birth, all presbyters were called bishops, or presbyters, and all bishops were indiscriminately called presbyters or bishops; likewise, all bishops were called apostles. Why, then, are these terms now distinguished, so that bishops are no longer called apostles or presbyters, but only bishops, and presbyters before episcopal ordination are not called bishops but only presbyters?

“The bishops who governed the churches after the death of the apostles, when they saw that they did not possess the same grace that the apostles had in the power of signs, in the force of miracles, and in the raising of the dead, considered it a serious matter to claim the apostolic name. Therefore they divided these two names between them, so that the greater priests would be called bishops alone, while the lesser priests would be called only presbyters.

“If, then, those bishops who once lived after the apostles and were called apostles, though inferior in the power of signs to the apostles who had seen the Lord, and who governed the churches after the death of the apostles, were called apostles, how much more is he an apostle, and rightly called an apostle, who received from the Lord every gift of grace together with his companions and was powerful in the working of signs, as a true apostle?”

When he fell silent, a certain priest named Peter said:

“This same thing was testified many years ago by Regembaldus, father of the monastery of Milbec. For when you, venerable pontiff, were seated in this basilica during the week of Pentecost at your synod, in the presence of a multitude of priests, you addressed the synod, saying:

“‘Some novelty has arisen among us concerning our patron Martial, and it is sufficiently harsh and burdensome to me. Some celebrate his memory as that of an apostle, others as that of a confessor; some testify that he is an apostle, others a co-apostle. What, then, brothers, do you think about this?’

“But that man, venerable in his gray hair and distinguished in learning and conduct, immediately began to cross himself in amazement and answered first:

“‘I have never heard anything like what I hear now. Certainly, pontiff, you are introducing a greater novelty to my ears. In our monastery, and in the others where from my childhood until now I have lived throughout the provinces of Bourges and Tours, I have never heard Martial recited except with the other apostles.’”

Meanwhile, at that council, when one of the clerics of the city of Périgueux was disputing with the father of the monastery of Solignac and said, “In the same way we can call Saint Fronto an apostle,” the latter answered him before everyone:

“Be silent, brother, I say; it is better that you keep silent. When we were drinking honey and milk in the schools of our teachers, you were chewing only beans. The new account of Saint Fronto, on whose authority you rely, was published by our Gauzbertus for the sake of profit. Under Hildegarius, bishop of this see of Limoges, he served as our chorepiscopus.

“But how can that man be an apostle who was a native of Périgueux? Surely, if he learned the psalter there as a boy, as his deeds relate, and became a cleric there, then priesthood and Christianity already existed there, as did schools of the divine Scriptures and the clerical order. He is said to have lived rather as a hermit than as a bishop. You do not know what signs he performed in order to convert the people of Périgueux.

“Rather, it was Martial who won them for God, bringing all Aquitaine to the faith together with Stephen, prince of the Gauls. Neither Fronto, nor Saturninus, nor Dionysius is said to have raised the dead. Yet without the raising of the dead and the display of signs, the first pagans could not have believed, as the Lord says: ‘Unless you see signs and wonders, you do not believe’ (Acts II [sic]).

“Likewise it is said elsewhere: ‘They went out and preached everywhere, while the Lord worked with them and confirmed the word by the accompanying signs’ (Mark 16:20).

“No one was an apostle except one who went forth from Jerusalem, as Isaiah says: ‘From Zion the law shall go forth, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem’ (Isa. 2:3). Likewise the Lord says: ‘It was necessary that Christ should suffer and that repentance and forgiveness of sins should be preached in his name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem’ (Luke 24:46–47). And elsewhere he says: ‘You shall be my witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth’ (Acts 1:8).

“Where is the place where Fronto is said to have raised Georgius? By contrast, at Else the place is always shown where Martial raised Austriclinianus.

“Martin of Tours is said to have received from God, after the apostles, such great grace that he became the raiser of three dead men. His disciples are said to have traveled throughout the world, in case they might find some young man who could match Martin in raising three dead people; but they could not find one.

“Tell us, brother: which martyrs, which confessors, which virgins have you read of raising more than three dead after the apostles? Certainly, in this matter too Martial is shown truly to be an apostle, because, in order to win a great multitude of pagans for God and bear abundant fruit, he raised six dead people as a true apostle.

“We can point to those six dead as witnesses of the truth, in the monuments where they lie. We know where Austriclinianus, the son of Nerva, two priests of idols, Stephen’s armor-bearer, and the son of Arcadius lie awaiting the resurrection of the dead. In addition to these, he raised a girl who, torn by a demon, had become as if dead.

“Likewise, at a maritime town near Mauritania, he raised nine men at once who had lain as if dead at his feet, so that the entire people believed them to be dead. I speak the truth; I do not lie. Unless Martial had received such a great grace of signs from him who gave his disciples power to raise the dead, he would not have won so great a multitude of pagans for heaven. By such signs the barbarians could easily receive the faith and the name of Christ.

“Yet we are so steadfast and solid in the Catholic Church, with God’s help, that although Martial performed all these things in the office of an apostle, we would in no way acknowledge him as an apostle—that is, God’s legate—unless this too had been anticipated by our ancient fathers. For unless he truly were Christ’s legate, that is, sent by Christ to preach, the ancients would never have acknowledged him as an apostle, nor would they ever have written his name for us to recite together with the names of the other apostles.

“Ancient codices brought from Francia, Spain, and the English people demonstrate this; so do the treatises of earlier teachers who composed certain worthy works in his praise. We know that God does not delight in falsehood and that his saints do not rejoice in flattery. The Lord seeks truth, and for the sake of truth the saints attained the kingdom.

“And, lest I make you, venerable fathers who are present at this council, endure a longer speech, I shall touch briefly on this one point: never, up to this present day, which is Thursday (the fourteenth day before the Kalends of December, Thursday), has a book been produced anywhere in the world that has the names of Fronto, Saturninus, Dionysius, Julianus, Austremonius, Ursinus, or any of the other fathers who came to Gaul after Martial written among the apostles in the litanies.

“Martial’s name, however, as I have already said, is found inscribed among the other apostles in countless litanies in the most ancient books of Aquitaine and Francia, as well as of Spain and other peoples.

“Finally, those who wrote him in the series of the Twelve Apostles in the Canon of the Mass and elsewhere, just as they wrote Paul, Barnabas, Luke, Mark, and Cleophas, would certainly not have done so unless they knew him truly to be an apostle, belonging to that order in which Paul and Barnabas are said to be apostles.”

At this, one of the clerics from Angoulême, who was less learned, objected, saying:

“If Martial’s name were found in the Acts of the Apostles, that would be sufficient for us.”

Immediately another of the Angoulême clerics, a learned man who had come from Angoulême to the council with Bishop Rohon, answered him:

“We have heard the bishops adjure everyone at this council not knowingly to keep silent about the truth. Therefore I dare not refrain from answering you on this matter before everyone.

“The names of the seventy-two are found neither in the Gospels nor in the Acts of the Apostles, and Martial is undoubtedly one of those seventy-two. When Luke, Paul’s disciple, wrote the Acts of the Apostles, Martial had already been in Aquitaine for thirty years.

“Luke was silent about Peter’s arrival at Antioch; he was silent about Peter’s arrival at the city of Rome. If he had treated these two matters fully and had not mentioned Martial by name, you would rightly be astonished. But since Peter came to Antioch and afterward to the city of Rome with Martial, and first sat as bishop at Antioch and afterward at Rome, and since Peter and his fellow disciple Martial came to Rome fourteen years before Paul, while Luke said nothing about them, there is no reason for you to be astonished or doubtful.

“For if you doubt this on the assumption that Martial did not belong to the time of the Lord’s preaching, you do not believe his deeds; and for that reason you are rightly judged a brute animal if you suppose that so many great and distinguished fathers—most learned, both ancient and modern—who have received and continue to receive his deeds with the highest reverence, could have wavered in this matter.

“What I heard some people say long ago I must now bring forward in this council. Some people, I do not know whether truly or falsely, think that Martial was the young man who, according to Mark, followed the Lord during the Passion after all the disciples had fled. They think this because Martial was then a young man and had ministered to the Lord on that very night at the Supper. He was fifteen years old when the Lord called him and commanded him to be baptized by Peter.

“Others suspect that the young man was John the Evangelist. Mark says:

“‘Then all the disciples deserted him and fled. A certain young man was following him, clothed in a linen cloth over his naked body; and they seized him. But he, abandoning the linen cloth, fled from them naked’ (Mark 14:50–52).

“On this matter Bede says in his Commentary on Mark:

[Note: This is Bede’s sense, not his exact words.]

“‘Whether this young man was John or some other person whose proper name is unknown to us, it is certain that he possessed a great ardor of love for the Lord.’

“Others likewise think that Martial was the disciple who, according to John, was known to the high priest, spoke to the doorkeeper, and brought Peter in. They think this because he is said to have been of noble birth and therefore known to the high priest.

“Others deny this and assert that the disciple was John. Augustine, however, says the following in his commentary on this matter:

[Note: This is also from Augustine.]

“‘We do not know who this disciple was who was known to the high priest. For we cannot assert that he was John, because wherever John mentions himself, he adds, “whom Jesus loved” (John 13:23); here, however, he omits this.’

“I have also seen others who thought that Martial himself was Matthias and that, because of the similarity of the names, he had easily begun to be called that by the language of the Aquitanians, or perhaps because it is not easy to discover where Matthias’ body lies.

“I, however, hold it as certain that if Matthias were not one person and Martial another, neither would be written in the order of the apostles in our books or in those of the English people. For in the litanies of ancient volumes of the English people, who received the beginnings of their faith and ecclesiastical institutions from Pope Gregory, Matthias and Martial are both inscribed with the other apostles. Gregory therefore did not fail to know that Matthias and Martial were not the same person.

“While questioning a learned Greek, I learned from him that Matthias preached in Lesser Armenia and there departed in peace. But let the holy assembly of the fathers listen willingly to me.

“Many years ago, certain brothers from Mount Sinai came by God’s providential will to this western region. They were grave in conduct, overflowing with the Catholic faith’s learning, entirely honorable in life, and skilled in both languages. After they had remained with us at Angoulême for a long time, awaiting the city’s prince, and we saw that they were perfectly versed in Greek and Latin letters, we arranged to question them about this matter.

“At that time the rule concerning the apostle’s memory was commonly observed in this city, having been restored rather than newly begun, while King Robert and Gauzlenus, archbishop of Bourges, were still alive. I was then staying at Angoulême, where I had also been brought up from early childhood. Although I appeared among the others as something of a learned man, I opposed this rule firmly, above all others, thinking it vain and false, or perhaps born of pride, because I heard Martial being proclaimed in this Limousin city as an apostle. Carelessly, I accommodated my understanding to the opinion of rustics, thinking that there was no apostle except the Twelve.

“So I approached those Greeks and asked whether the Easterners knew Martial. One, named Simeon, and the other, named Cosmas, answered with one voice:

“‘Of course we know Martial the apostle, one of the seventy-two.’

“When we said to them, ‘We know no apostles except the Twelve,’ they asked us:

“‘Do you have in these western churches the evangelist Luke, who writes that another seventy-two were chosen by the Lord after the Twelve Apostles?’

“When we said that Luke was indeed present, but that we did not believe those seventy-two had been apostles, only disciples, they immediately fled from us and fortified themselves with the sign of the cross. They began to denounce our words, saying:

“‘Go far away from us, wretches, because you are heretics, since you do not believe the words of the Lord, who said to them: “Go; behold, I send you as lambs among wolves” (Luke 10:3). Do you not believe that those whom the incarnate Lord himself sent to preach were apostles? He sent the Twelve in pairs, and afterward he likewise sent another seventy-two in pairs.

“‘The Greeks were always wiser than the Latins, and the Latins’ Scriptures have flowed from the Greek source. Therefore we truly know Martial, whom we call ὁ ἅγιος Μαρτιάλιος (“Saint Martial”), to be one of those seventy-two who went with Peter to the West to preach. We possess at Mount Sinai, in our language, the deeds of him and of all the seventy-two.’

“After receiving this testimony from the Greeks, I began to turn many things over in my mind. Carefully searching the hidden contents of ancient volumes, I more and more frequently found Martial pronounced an apostle by the ancients.

“I also observed that Paul and Barnabas, Silas and Timothy, were apostles, though they were neither of the Twelve nor of the seventy-two. I saw that Timothy, Paul’s disciple, is called an apostle by Jerome. Mark and Luke, Silas and Onesimus, and certain others too are called apostles in ancient writings, and apostolic honor is rendered to their memory.

“Thus, by God’s revelation, I began clearly to understand that he truly is an apostle who, being Hebrew by birth, the Lord’s disciple, the Lord’s minister at the Supper, filled with the Holy Spirit by the Lord’s breathing upon him, exalted by the Lord with the power of binding and loosing, and sent by the Lord to preach, deserved to become a most fruitful laborer in the apostolic office.

“From then on I judged this rule reasonable, full of the authority of the ancients, and inspired by God’s will; and I began to defend with all my strength what previously, in my ignorance, I had attacked with all my strength.

“For our bishop of Angoulême, Hugo, a man learned in every respect, who died forty years ago, while his successor died fourteen years ago, spoke as follows about Martial in one of his works:

“‘In those times,’ he says, ‘the city of Limoges surpassed all the cities of Gaul, holding the stronghold of the Aquitanian kingdom. Blessed Martial reached it, sent by the Lord through the legation of blessed Peter as an apostle to the peoples of Aquitaine.

“‘As he was traveling to the city of Bordeaux to preach to the Basques, he passed through the city of Angoulême. After staying there for a long time, he converted the people of Angoulême to the living God and ordained as its first bishop a man named Ausonius, a native of that region, whom he himself had baptized.’”

And when certain members of the council said, “Why is Dionysius, who came to Gaul long after Martial, named in the book of the Acts of the Apostles, whereas Martial is not expressly named there?” he replied:

“Because Dionysius was a Gentile disciple of Paul, and Luke was Paul’s companion; in that book he recounts chiefly those deeds of Paul which he himself witnessed. But as for the names of those who flourished at that time in preaching, I do not see what bearing it has on us, either for controversy or for benefit, since many are named there, or in Paul’s Epistles, whose memory we nevertheless do not know in particular on their feast days. As for that ancient disciple Jason, Philip the evangelist, Apollos, Epaphras, and the others expressly named there, although we either do not know or omit mentioning each of them individually and specifically, it is nevertheless certain that those peoples to whom they were given as patrons do not negligently venerate their memory.

“For even if Martial’s memory is not celebrated annually and specially among certain peoples, nevertheless for us Westerners, who were enlightened by his coming with heavenly brightness, who know him to be patron in heaven and on earth of the western peoples, his memory must always be kept joyfully on suitable occasions, and not without honor. [Col. 1365C]

“Moreover, concerning Dionysius the Areopagite, who is mentioned in the Acts of the Apostles, I used to think that he was the same man who later came to Gaul with Rusticus and Eleutherius, after the deaths of the apostles Peter and Paul and of Martial. Recently, however, I happened by chance to read Bede’s commentary on the book of the Acts of the Apostles, where it is written as follows:

> ‘This Dionysius the Areopagite is the same man who was afterward made bishop of Corinth, ruled the Church with the greatest glory, and, renowned for his eloquence, wrote many books for the benefit of the Church.’ (Bede, on Acts XVII)

“Jerome, mentioning this Dionysius in his Chronicle, said:

[Note: Jerome is cited falsely.]

> ‘Dionysius, bishop of the Corinthians, renowned for his eloquence, flourished under the emperor Antoninus, at which time Polycarp, the disciple of John the Evangelist, suffered martyrdom. Under Trajan, however, who was the fifth emperor to rule after Vespasian, the apostle John fell asleep in peace, and Pope Clement, having been thrown into the sea, was crowned with martyrdom.’

“Gregory mentions this Dionysius in one of his homilies, saying:

> ‘It is reported that that ancient and venerable father Dionysius the Areopagite said that from the lesser ranks of angels they are sent forth to perform ministries, either visibly or invisibly.’ (Gregory, Homily XIV on the Gospel)

“But concerning this Dionysius of Francia, where he was originally from, I believe that a faithful account is preserved in the Passion of Saint Marcellus. For it reads there:

> ‘A certain boy, Marcellus, was being educated under the instruction of the blessed Sixtus. When the boy saw Sixtus the bishop being tormented with punishments, he began to be afraid. Then Saint Laurence, strengthening the boy in his infancy, said to him: “Marcellus, your father Aegeas was unwilling to believe in Christ. But your mother Marcellina, and your brothers Saturninus and Dionysius, at the command of Saint Clement, pope of the city of Rome, have been sent to the regions of Gaul to instruct the peoples in the Christian faith. Go to them, lest you perish at the hands of Decius.”’

“And further it says:

> ‘Marcellus set out with Anastasius, his fellow soldier and Christian, to go where his brother Saturninus the bishop was. He reached Argentomagus, where he was seized by the governor and questioned as to who he was, or from what province or city he had come there. The boy replied: “I am a Christian. I came out from the city of Rome, and I am hastening to the city of Toulouse, where my brothers Saturninus and Dionysius dwell.” The governor Heraclius said to him: “Tell me the name of your father or mother.” The boy replied: “My father is named Aegeas, and my mother is named Marcellina.”’

“But if the bishops wish, the Passion itself can promptly be brought before their council. These things do not seem to me inconsistent with the writing concerning the deeds of Dionysius that is kept among us at Engolismas. For there it is read that Clement ordained a certain Philip as bishop and sent him to Spain to preach; but to Dionysius he entrusted the seeds of the divine word to distribute among the nations. He sent him to Gaul and gave him as companions Saturninus, Marcellinus, and Lucian, as well as Rusticus and Eleutherius.

“When they had all arrived together at the harbor of the city of Arles, Marcellinus went to Spain; Saturninus, however, proceeded to Toulouse; and Dionysius, with Rusticus and Eleutherius, went to Paris. Lucian the presbyter, for his part, went to the city of Beauvais. Julian of Le Mans also, as we find in his deeds, was Roman by birth.

“Saturninus, however, as his Passion teaches, suffered under Diocletian and Maximian, when Decius Germanicus and Gratus were consuls. Yet I hear that some people are occasionally troubled as to how the account given in the deeds preserved at Toulouse can be reconciled with this. For if he first came to Toulouse under Diocletian and Maximian, in the consulship of Decius Germanicus and Gratus—or, as seems more truthful to me, if he suffered under Decius, according to the Passion of the aforementioned Marcellus, and suffered under their rule—how could he have been ordained bishop by the apostle Peter and sent to Toulouse?

“For from the Passion of the blessed Peter, which, according to Jerome’s exact account, occurred in the thirty-seventh year after the Lord’s resurrection, that is, in the thirteenth year of Nero, until the first year of Decius there were 182 years. From the first year of Decius until the first year of Diocletian there were 32 years. From the resurrection of the Lord until the last year of Diocletian there were 265 years.”

At these words, while certain members of the council were conducting a subtle investigation concerning the agreement of the Chronica, on account of Martial’s arrival in Aquitaine, the Engolismian cleric added, saying:

“If it pleases you, let Jerome’s Chronicle, which cannot lie, be brought before the council and carefully examined on this question.”

Accordingly, after scrutinizing the book, he spoke:

“Although Bede, in his commentary on the Acts of the Apostles, says that Peter came to Rome in the fourth year of Claudius and suffered in the thirty-ninth year after the Lord’s resurrection, nevertheless, according to Jerome’s carefully calculated Chronicle, the following is found.

“The Lord suffered in the eighteenth year of Tiberius. After Tiberius, Gaius reigned, and after him Claudius. In the second year of Claudius’s reign, Peter, the prince of the apostles, and his fellow disciple Martial came to Rome. In the fourth year of Claudius, Mark in Egypt and Martial in Gaul began to preach the Lord.

“After Claudius, who ruled for thirteen years, seven months, and twenty-eight days, Nero assumed the imperial power; he likewise ruled for thirteen years, seven months, and twenty-eight days. He reigned for thirteen complete years and died in the fourteenth, after more than half of it had passed.

“In the first year of Nero’s reign, Stephen, king of the Gauls, went to Rome with legions of Gauls, as he had been commanded by letters sent to him through couriers. In the second year of Nero, the apostle Paul first came to Rome, that is, fourteen years after the blessed Peter’s arrival. Paul had not yet been in Rome when Stephen went to Nero. Paul was sent to Rome in chains by Festus, governor of Judea, because he had appealed to Caesar. [Col. 1367C]

“Likewise, in the first year of Tiberius, Herod the tetrarch began to reign among the Jews. He reigned for twenty-four years, that is, until the first year of Gaius Caligula, Tiberius’s successor. Under this Herod the Lord suffered; he was the brother of Archelaus, that is, the son of that Herod under whom Christ was born.

“After Herod the tetrarch, Agrippa reigned for seven years. This is the Herod who killed James and arrested Peter, and who was struck by an angel. In the fifth year of this Herod, that is, in the second year of Caesar Claudius, Peter and Martial, as we have already said, first came to Rome.

“After Agrippa Herod, his other son Agrippa reigned for twenty-six years, that is, until the second year of Vespasian, when the kingdom of the Jews came to an end.

“After Nero, Vespasian ruled. In the third year of his reign, Martial died at Limoges. He survived Peter by four years. For, as we have already said, Peter suffered in the thirty-seventh year after the Lord’s resurrection, that is, in the thirteenth year of Nero’s reign; and in the fortieth year after the Lord’s resurrection, that is, in the third year of Vespasian, Martial was taken up.

“All these matters are calculated with such care that, if Peter suffered in the thirty-ninth year after the Lord’s resurrection, as some say, then Martial survived Peter for one full year and, on the following day—that is, on the first day of the next year as it began—ascended into heaven with Christ. In that same year in which he dedicated the basilica where his body rests in honor of the apostle Peter, he received temporal death two months later. [Col. 1368A]

“But if, according to Jerome, Peter suffered in the thirty-seventh year after the Lord’s resurrection, that is, in the thirteenth year of Nero, then Martial survived Peter by four years.”

When these and similar matters concerning the agreement of the years had been satisfactorily settled, and the Engolismian cleric again said that there was nothing surprising in Luke’s not naming Martial expressly, since Luke does not give the names of the seventy-two, nor does he in any way record Peter’s arrival in Antioch and Rome, Father Odolricus again addressed the council, saying:

“Lest anyone perhaps say that we are now declaring a new apostle, previously unheard of, I shall again bear true testimony, venerable bishops, to the antiquity of his apostleship, since it was long ago anticipated and attested by the ancients.

“Behold, two priests from among our brethren are present here. Long ago, for this very reason, I sent them to Britain, so that they might investigate more carefully the ancient law which, as I believe, Gregory established for the English, and might report it back to us after removing every falsehood.

“When they reached the English, they found Martial written down as an apostle from ancient times both in their Martyrologies and in their litanies. They then came to a certain large monastery in which Augustine, the first bishop of the English, lies bodily buried. There they discovered that the book of the deeds of the blessed Martial was not present; nevertheless, through the litanies and Martyrologies they found in that same place that he was honored with the apostolic name as their patron.

“When they asked the father of the monastery, saying, ‘Why do you proclaim Martial as an apostle in your litanies, when you say that you do not possess his deeds?’ he replied:

> ‘Because, he said, from the time when the name of Christ was first heard in this province, our fathers have observed this practice, and we cannot in any way alter their tradition. We know, indeed, that our earlier teachers derived from Gregory’s instruction. Nevertheless, we often discuss among ourselves, inquiring who this apostle is whose name we do not see at all in the Gospels or in the Acts of the Apostles.

> ‘And because we did not possess the authority of his deeds, we were not a little uncertain about him. For that reason we thought that his name should repeatedly be erased from the apostolic memory. But, on the other hand, when we realized that our ancient fathers had not written him down as an apostle for no reason, we did not dare in any way to remove his name from the company of the apostles.

> ‘But you, Gallic pilgrims, who know of his apostleship and announce his deeds to us, have utterly cast out from our hearts every doubt concerning him. On this account we had long and frequently prayed to God that we might be made certain. Nor, at your arrival, do we seem to have been abandoned in our hope. Rather, we ought to rejoice over so eminent a disciple of our Lord Jesus Christ.’”

They told us that they had discovered many other truthful witnesses among the same people of the English concerning the antiquity of this authority.

I should also mention that seven years ago the king of the English sent royal gifts to the duke of Aquitaine, together with a book written in golden letters, containing the names of the saints, distinguished by images.

[Note: Here Cnuto was surnamed “the Great.”]

[Note: Willelmus.]

Long ago, when the same question was being debated at the council of Poitiers, Duke Willelmus, having been informed by letters, displayed this volume to the bishops as testimony to its antiquity. Martial was indeed placed there in the catalogue of the other apostles.

This highly learned prince said to the archbishop of Bordeaux and to the other bishops who were present:
