“We can infer how eminent in authority is the blessed patron of the Aquitanians, concerning whom Gregory, in that people among whom he carried out his labor, established this rule to be observed. Surely it belongs to the ignorant to doubt concerning one about whom holy Pope Gregory did not doubt.

“You see, bishops, that in this book, which was written among the English, Timothy, Cleopas, Silas, and others whose names are read in the Gospels, the Acts of the Apostles, or Paul’s Epistles, and whom you call apostles besides the Twelve, have been omitted. Yet our patron has not been omitted, although he was the first bishop of Gaul and his name is passed over in the Gospels.

“This was so that we might know that he truly was God’s disciple in the flesh and that, together with the first twelve chosen disciples, he received from God the greatest grace of apostleship: the sign of possessing this western people forever.

“We see this done in the case of Martial, just as the ancients did and the moderns still do in the cases of Barnabas, Luke, and Mark. For some celebrate their memory among the confessors, not among the apostles, solely because they are not among the Twelve. Others, judging more rightly, commemorate them not among the confessors but among the apostles and proclaim them apostles, because, born according to the flesh from the stock of Israel, they were sent by other apostles to preach.

“Thus those who commemorate Martial as a confessor seem to do so because he was not one of the Twelve. But those who remember him as an apostle judge more rightly, because although he was not one of the Twelve, he was nevertheless born from the lineage of Abraham, that is, from the tribe of Benjamin; he saw the Lord in the flesh and was his disciple. He was also deemed worthy to receive from the Lord, together with the Twelve, every gift of grace.

“Furthermore, he was sent by the Lord through the blessed Peter to preach to the Gauls, where he possesses clear signs of apostleship. For the fruitfulness of his preaching among the other apostles is proved to have been very great. Indeed, apart from Paul and the Twelve, we do not know of another apostle who bore fruit in such abundance as Martial bore through preaching.

“When the duke had concluded with these and similar arguments, and no one could oppose his words, one of the learned clerics said to those who were seated in the council:

‘We know that Matthias had previously been one of the seventy-two and afterward, through Peter’s appointment, became one of the Twelve. But another, whom the lot did not admit into the Twelve, nevertheless remained an apostle among those who were outside the Twelve. This is the man afterward called Judas the apostle, who at that time was called Joseph Justus or Barsabas.

“He is the one who was sent with the apostle Silas by the other apostles. Hence Jerome, the interpreter of divine law, writes as follows: “Silas and Judas also were called apostles by the apostles.”

“If they were called apostles by the apostles, then they truly were apostles. For the earlier apostles did not regard as apostles without reason those whom they called apostles; nor would they have called them so unless they were apostles.

“Moreover, the apostle Paul, in whom Christ was speaking, would not have called them apostles in addition to the Eleven unless they truly were apostles in addition to the Eleven. For Paul did not speak any word in vain or falsely: “He appeared,” he says, “to the Eleven, then to all the apostles” (1 Cor. XV).

“I have brought forward these arguments on account of certain people who are arguing in the council, saying: “What if Martial was an apostle at that time? Why was he not placed in the position of Judas when Matthias was chosen?”

“Let them know, therefore, that not only Matthias but also Barsabas was chosen and appointed by the apostles; and that, by a hidden lot, Matthias was selected to take the place of Judas, so that there would no longer be eleven but twelve principal witnesses of the Lord’s resurrection.

“Barsabas, however, did not lack the apostolic name, because others besides the Twelve had long before been appointed to the apostolic ministry, as the Lord said: “Go; behold, I send you like lambs among wolves” (Luke X).

“But who would say that Martial was not a witness of the Lord’s resurrection? But was not Barsabas, because he was one of the seventy-two, as Matthias was, an apostle at that time and afterward still an apostle? Is he not the one whom, as I have already said, we now call Judas the apostle together with the apostle Silas?

“For just as Matthias was first an apostle among the seventy-two and afterward became one of the Twelve, so Barsabas, being an apostle, remained an apostle, although he was not one of the Twelve. In the same way, if Martial was one of the seventy-two, then he was an apostle at that time and afterward remained an apostle, when Matthias had been transferred into the Twelve.

“As someone has said, ‘Apostle’ is the name not of a number but of an office.

“In reality, those two were appointed to complete the number of the Twelve who had seen the Lord’s works from the baptism of John until the day of his ascension and who were of mature age. For if the Lord himself did not begin to preach before the age of thirty, how much more was it fitting that the twelve disciples should not be public witnesses of the Lord to the Jews before reaching mature age?

“Moreover, if Martial had not yet reached his twentieth year when the Lord ascended into heaven, what prejudice can we find in the fact that he was not substituted in Judas’s place, especially since the earlier twelve witnesses were either advanced in years or mature in age, whereas his bodily maturity had not yet been completed?

“If David, while still a young man, was chosen by the Lord for kingship and anointed at his command with royal consecration, yet did not begin to reign before completing thirty years of age, what is surprising if Martial, still a youth in age, received from the Lord, together with the other apostles, the anointing of the Holy Spirit for the power of binding and loosing, and the other gifts of grace belonging to the apostolic office?

“When he had reached mature age, that is, thirty years, he received from the Lord, through the embassy of the blessed Peter, the apostleship of the Aquitanian Gentiles, and carried it out with the greatest effectiveness.

“What the Lord commanded Peter—to send Martial to preach in the provinces of Gaul—is very similar to what the Holy Spirit said to the teachers residing at Antioch: “Set apart for me Paul and Barnabas for the work to which I have appointed them.” After they had prayed and fasted, they laid hands on them and sent them away (Acts II).

“And just as those men were sent by the Holy Spirit, although through the ministry of the disciples, so Martial was sent by the Lord to Gaul, although through the embassy and counsel of the blessed Peter.

“When the Lord called and chose him, Martial had completed only fifteen years of age. He remained with him for three years, that is, until the Passion and Ascension. After the coming of the Holy Spirit upon the apostles in Zion, he spent five years in Judea; afterward he remained seven years with Peter in Antioch. Then, in the following year, at the Lord’s command, he entered Aquitaine, where he is known to have labored in preaching for twenty-eight years. For he departed this life in the third year of Vespasian.”

By these words, the stubbornness of the opponents, which had been springing up, was easily extinguished. All the learned acclaimed that it was entirely fitting that the first twelve apostles who were chosen should have possessed mature age. Meanwhile, the council at Poitiers ceased discussion of this article.

The same venerable elder who had delivered this speech also added:

“What need is there to say more, beloved? You see that nothing here is truly harmful except the unsuitable custom of many—a custom not made clear by reason but, as usually happens, grown old through sluggish negligence among a great number of people.

“Let us see from what source this tradition, which has prevailed among many, descended. We have learned from the trustworthy report of our fathers that long ago—from the time of the Lord’s own disciple, when he died in peace under the emperor Vespasian, even until the time of the grandsons of Charles Augustus, when the canonical order was changed into the monastic order by the brothers Pippin and Charles, sons of Louis, in the place where I am rector—our predecessors throughout Aquitaine recited him as a disciple of Christ together with the other apostles and commemorated him as an apostle.

“This continued until younger men, as though showing greater zeal—or rather exercising worse judgment—began to introduce a novelty, saying: “It is permitted us to move the patron of Aquitaine from the place of the apostles, where he is now last, so that he may be more honored by us, if we call him first in the series of confessors. Let him be the beginning of confessors, not the end of apostles. We choose for him to be first before all confessors rather than last among the apostles.”

“Thus, supported by no rational basis, this human judgment gradually produced, down to our own times, such a custom, though not in every place. For certain churches even today appear to retain an older observance in this matter. Although others may have changed it on earth, they have nevertheless been utterly unable to diminish or obscure his glory in heaven, where he eternally possesses immense apostolic honor, shining in the glorious choir of the apostles before the sight of the majesty of God’s glory.

“If, therefore, with God’s inspiration, we recover the earlier and more ancient institutions of our fathers, according to truth and reasonable authority—institutions long ago removed and corrupted by human inventions—and if we do this by restoring rather than presumptuously introducing something new, why are we blamed as transgressors of our fathers’ boundaries, concerning which it is written: “Do not transgress the ancient boundaries which your fathers established” (Prov. XXII)?

“Why, I ask, should this seem harsh to some, if we follow the straight line of truth, if in this matter we imitate our more perceptive ancient fathers, and if we judge it unworthy to follow those who were less discerning?

“Do not Father Azenerius, Benedict, rector of the monastery of Cluny of Saint Michael, and many other highly learned and most reverend abbots and bishops, both present and absent, together with the Roman Apostolic See, bear witness with us to this judgment and consider it good, just, and pleasing to God?

“Why should we appear to obscure—or, God forbid, to falsify—the great deeds of such a patron by heedlessly lending an ear to the opinion of the many? For by what reasoning can we deny that he was a disciple of the Lord and followed him in the flesh?

“Who, then, would rashly dare to deny that he was sent by the Lord to preach and was promoted, together with the other apostles, to the power of binding and loosing, and that, by Christ’s command and gift, with the counsel of the blessed Peter, he received a special share of the vast Gentile population in the western region as his apostolic lot?

“Those who either do not believe him to be an apostle or, if they believe it, do not willingly accept it deny all these things about him. They seem to deny these things, I say, who judge him to be merely a confessor—not like John the Evangelist, but like Pope Sylvester or one of those who did not follow or see the Lord in the flesh.”

Then one of the bishops sitting in the council, a man advanced in character and age—namely, Aemilius, pastor of the Church of Albi—after silence had been made, said:

“We judge in every respect that this radiant illuminator of the Aquitanian homeland, who first came to this region to save our fathers, and whom Christ the Lord and the blessed Peter directed for the salvation and illumination of the nations of Gaul, who were sitting in darkness and the shadow of death—the one commanding, as master and Lord commands a disciple and servant; the other exhorting, as a fellow disciple and kinsman exhorts a fellow disciple and kinsman—ought to be honored as highly as we can, yet according to the straight rule of truth.

“Let us retain in him what does not exceed the truth; and, neither omitting nor surpassing what is true and most evident in his case, let us honor him as much as we can.

“For if he was truly sent by the Lord to preach, if he was his disciple in the flesh, if he was one of those to whom it was said, “Blessed are the eyes that see what you see” (Luke X), then it is certainly clear that whoever denies him to be an apostle omits—and indeed attacks—the truth.

“But if he were called an apostle in such a way that he was not a disciple of the Lord from the stock of Israel and had not received from the Lord the power of binding and loosing, that would exceed the truth. If someone says that he was one of the Twelve, he goes beyond the truth.

“But whoever calls him an apostle in this sense—that he was sent by the Lord, not one of the Twelve but one of the seventy-two, like Paul and Barnabas, who became chosen apostles after the Lord’s ascension—neither despises nor exceeds the truth. Rather, deviating neither to the left (laevam) nor to the left (sinistram), he walks along the straight road of justice.

“Therefore, if any portion of the most ancient fathers is found to have called him an apostle and to have pronounced his name together with the other apostles, it seems good to me that we should hold firmly to their path, so that our successors may thereafter not hesitate to accustom themselves to the straight way.”

While he was saying these and similar things, another of the bishops, namely Isembertus, rector of the Church of Poitiers, began to explain, saying:

“Whoever stirs up controversy over this word is looking for a knot in a reed. We are not Ebionites, who accept no apostles besides the Twelve and reject Paul as a transgressor of the Law.

“For piercing our adversaries, this extremely sharp arrow is sufficient: the sole judgment of the blessed Jerome. Likewise, with the strongest sword of the apostle Paul, which no skill or force can ever blunt, every contentious party must be destroyed.

“Paul says that the Lord appeared to the Eleven, then to all the apostles (1 Cor. XV), so that we may know that all those whom the Lord sent to preach while he still dwelt in the flesh were apostles.

“Jerome says, as has just been read in the present lesson: “All who saw the Lord in the flesh and afterward preached him were apostles,” and so forth.

“It is plainly evident that Martial saw the Lord in the flesh and afterward preached him. It is good for him to be called an apostle, although it is not wrong for him to be called a confessor.

“For if the apostle Peter is called a confessor, that is not wrong, since confession of the truth is always common through the mouths of all the saints, both in the Old and in the New Testament.

“Although it is good for this patron to be called a confessor, it is nevertheless better for him also to be proclaimed an apostle, lest his glory appear hidden under a bushel—the glory by which he is proclaimed both a disciple of the Lord and one who shares in the apostolic lot.

“But whoever contentiously calls him a confessor does not seem to me to be acting rightly, because he appears almost to deny what properly belongs to him and creates hostility in the Church.

“Therefore, lest an occasion be given for a division in the Church of God, we must take the greatest care that all, with one heart and voice, proclaim the one thing that is better. Let the sole custom that seems offensive to the ears be received in a better sense, and let schism, murmuring, and doubt be utterly removed from our common assembly.

“If anyone presumes to oppose this peaceful harmony, let him be judged one of the contentious and schismatic.”

To this the venerable Jordanus replied:

“Beloved, much inquiry has been made concerning this matter over the past years, until this controversy reached the ears of the holy Apostolic See of Rome. On this subject Pope John deigned to send us a copy of a letter, strongly bearing witness to the glory of his apostleship and reproving all who contradict that he is an apostle. This sacred letter has been preserved and is readily available; in it the true testimony of the Roman See is plainly evident.”

Aimo, archbishop of Bourges, replied to him, saying:

“We had the text of Pope John’s letter, addressed to all the bishops of Gaul, read aloud before us fifteen days ago at the council of Bourges, where many bishops had gathered. A large company of learned men was present there. After examining this dispute with great discernment, they found that what Pope John established in the Roman See, and what you, under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, established in this Church, the first of all the churches of Gaul, concerning this most just matter, was sound.

“No one denies that he was one of the seventy-two. The Lord said to those men: “Go; behold, I send you like lambs among wolves” (Luke X). It is therefore clear that those whom the Lord called apostles truly are apostles.

“And it has always appeared that many of the ancients pronounced this first leader of Gaul not among the confessors but among the apostles. Therefore, with a very large company of learned men agreeing, before the entire people in the major church of Bourges, we bore witness that the blessed Martial is an apostle of the truth.

“For we took care not to oppose the decree and command of the Roman Apostolic See. As a testimony to the truth, we requested that a written document be prepared at that same council, which we confirmed with our own hands, so that it might be known to all that we have no desire to depart from the Roman See on this matter, since it is not right to do so.

“Moreover, as soon as this same matter was preached before the entire Church, all the people there, as one man and with one voice, immediately blessed the Lord for the glory of their patron.

“Therefore, just as the Roman Church bears witness—a church whose testimony it is unlawful to contradict—and just as we bore witness at the aforementioned council of Bourges, so in the present general assembly we testify that this judgment is just and necessary for the holy Church.”

Then the God-beloved Jordan replied [Note: [Col. 1375D] Acts of the First Council of Limoges, in the year 1029]:

“I should like briefly to recall how, some years ago—that is, in the first year of the dedication of this basilica of our Redeemer at Limoges, which this city today joyfully commemorates with us—this see of Limoges received this declaration, not without an extraordinary manifestation of divine authority, while the most learned king of the Franks, Robert, and your predecessor Gauzlenus, the metropolitan, were still alive.

After many disputes within this chapter, some agreeing and others resisting, and after many litanies had been offered on this matter, so that this declaration, unless it were God’s good will, might in no way remain established in the concord of this see, a synodal assembly came to this church [Col. 1375B]. On the third day of the synod, the whole body of priests and the great number of the other clergy, together with us and with an assembled multitude of noblemen and teachers of the law, received, I believe under God’s guidance, one heart and one will at the third hour of the day. Everything was so inspired in all that, peacefully, willingly, and voluntarily, with good obedience, this decision was accepted by everyone and thereafter observed immutably throughout our diocese.

It pleased everyone that we should receive this will pleasing to God in such a way that, just as its novelty seemed strange to the multitude, so another new but magnificent and glorious matter should be established against all its opponents. Accordingly, after a very great assembly of the people had gathered, we lifted the most sacred body of our patron from its tomb [Col. 1375C] and, with most devout service, transferred it onto this holy altar, which he himself consecrated in honor of the protomartyr Stephen.

This took place on the Sunday of the Lord’s Resurrection [Note: [Col. 1375D] In the year 1029, in which 3 August was a Sunday.], on the very solemnity of the discovery of the body of blessed Stephen and of the consecration of this holy church, which that same patron first dedicated to God in all Gaul, after the idols that paganism had previously worshiped in this place had been destroyed.

This seemed fitting to us: just as, while alive, he had made this see of his the fountain of baptism and of evangelical illumination for the whole people of Aquitaine, so, by visiting and traversing it in his body, he might here give us the beginning of this observance, and its members might not hesitate thereafter to preserve the institution whose beginning had been taken from its head.

Accordingly, on that same day, over this altar, we solemnly celebrated the mysteries in honor of his apostolate. We ordered that they should always thereafter be celebrated both here and throughout all the churches and monasteries of our diocese, so that henceforth the memory of our patron might be observed by all in concord, not as that of a confessor but as that of an apostle.

We also established that this day should be commemorated every year: the day on which the outstanding shepherd was transferred to his own see, and on which his cathedra—that is, his ordination or the beginning of his episcopate—also occurred. This does not mean that he was consecrated bishop on that day—for on the day of the Lord’s Ascension he received episcopal consecration from the Lord together with the other bishops, when the Lord, raising his hands, blessed the disciples and was carried up into heaven [Col. 1376A]. Rather, just as there is the cathedra of blessed Peter at Antioch and likewise his cathedra at Rome—not because he was then consecrated bishop, since he had received pontifical consecration from the Lord long before, but because on that day he first sat in those churches to receive pastoral governance over the people of God—so on this day, the third day of August, he made this house a temple of Christ out of a shrine of demons, and in this very church he first sat, assuming the care and governance of a shepherd over the people.

It is believed that two priests of God, Austriclinianus and Alpinianus, his disciples, enthroned him on the cathedra of this church, in keeping with the testimony of truth, so that where two or three were gathered in the name of the Savior, the Lord might be there in their midst [Col. 1376B].

For Linus and Cletus, priests and disciples of blessed Peter, indeed together with them blessed Martial himself, a fellow disciple of that same blessed Peter, are also believed to have enthroned him at the first Roman Church. According to some, this first church is at the title called *Ad primum*, and is in honor of the Levite Stephen, the first martyr; according to others, it is at the Lateran, because the patriarchal palace is there.

Thus, on the following day, the day after the dedication of this most holy basilica and the discovery of the relics of the protomartyr Stephen, the transfer of our patron to his see, or the feast of his cathedra, began from that time to be celebrated in this same holy church of Limoges.

On that same day, after the mysteries had been completed with rejoicing [Col. 1376C], and after the whole clergy and people had been joined together in peace through the institution of the apostolic commemoration, we carried the most sacred body of our patron back to its own monument. We placed under anathema those who thereafter in our diocese should presume to disturb this decision [Note: [Col. 1376D] Thus far the First Council of Limoges.].

After a long time, however, when murmuring arose about this declaration in certain churches throughout Gaul, and some people said, ‘How can he be an apostle when he is not named in the Gospels, nor is he openly mentioned in the Acts of the Apostles?’ while others thought that this had never previously been said, but had only recently and—God forbid!—been arrogated by us for the first time, and when a serious dispute was again beginning to grow, by God’s providence a letter on this matter was sent to us [Col. 1376D] by Pope John of the apostolic Roman see.

Then, by unanimous counsel, we decreed that, because of this declaration, an assembly of bishops and learned men should be gathered in this city to decide whether it should again be accepted or not. If, therefore, you decide that this opinion should not be accepted, neither must it be accepted by me any longer, but rather opposed. But if you accept it, then I too accept it, just as I had accepted it before, so that whoever thereafter presumes to cause scandal in our diocese concerning it may be restrained by both your discipline and ours.”

Then the archbishop said:

“Just as I have already said, and now declare openly to all once again, in the same way that the Roman Church accepts this and commands its acceptance through the text of the letter, and in the same way that the Council of Bourges has most recently commended this very matter, so I commend it as good, accept it in peace, and earnestly ask and exhort the brotherhood of this holy council to accept it without schism. But if anyone does not yield to our exhortation, let him have God as his judge and the witness of every conscience. Nevertheless, if our fellow provincials do not accept it, they must be admonished [or perhaps: admonished to] obey the Roman see, their head, compelled by our severe authority.” [Col. 1377A]

To this the venerable Jordan replied:

“As I see that this declaration is being accepted by us in God’s good will and in peace, we give thanks to Jesus Christ our Lord and Savior; and blessed is God, who has ennobled this holy Church of Limoges through the priesthood of blessed Martial, and who has drawn this western people back from slavery to idols into true liberty through his fruitful preaching [Col. 1377B].

To the Father of our Lord we offer thanksgiving, who did not wish a burning lamp to be hidden under a bushel, nor a city set upon a mountain to be concealed; but what our earlier fathers are proved to have seized upon from antiquity, he now deigns to grant us to see, wisely sifted in our own days, clearer than light.

Truly, heaven and earth will pass away, but the words and promises of God will not pass away. And if blessed Martial was called by the Lord the light of the world, it is impossible that the Lord’s same promise should not be fulfilled in him, since he shone with great light in the office of apostolate and preaching. Therefore, in the very name, he rightly gleams [Col. 1377C] with apostolic radiance.”

Turning again to the archbishop, he said:

“Now, if it pleases you, venerable father, let today’s council be concluded, lest the festive people be wearied by our delay. Tomorrow and on the third day, with God’s help, we shall discuss other matters.

Let us all proceed together now to the church of our Savior, where a great crowd awaits us. Let us celebrate a festive station there, and let one of us offer the sacrifice to God for the solemnity. The rest of us shall stand around him there, admonish the people concerning the present council, and proclaim blessing to those who desire peace and a curse to those who desire war, according to the law of the Lord.”

At these words the bishops rose from their seats [Col. 1377D] and proceeded in fear of God, ascending to the place of the church to hear the solemn rites of the most holy basilica.

At the request of the venerable Jordan, the metropolitan of Bourges, wearing the sacred pallium, approached to celebrate the holy rites. During the praises, which in Greek are called *tropoi*—“turns” or “variations” in ordinary melody—when the singers cried out the verse of the Holy Trinity, all the bishops immediately approached the great altar together with the archbishop, the deacons, and the other ministers. They prayed and, as is customary, exchanged peace with one another and with the ministers of the altar. Then they sat around the altar in the seats prepared for them.

Meanwhile, when the angelic hymn, with its *tropes*, that is, festive praises, had been completed with great adornment, the archbishop gave the first prayer for the solemnity of the church [Col. 1378A]; then, with the whole church listening, he added a second prayer commemorating blessed Martial. The prayer runs as follows:

> Almighty and eternal God, who willed blessed Martial the apostle to preside over your holy Church, we ask that, through the support of his merits, you grant us the grace of your mercy.

He especially wished to pronounce this prayer publicly before everyone so that he might clearly appear as an open and unmistakable defender of the testimony to the apostolate of blessed Martial.

This prayer, together with the Secret, the Preface, and the prayer called the *ad complendum*, is said to be Gregorian because it had long before been sent by Pope John of Rome to the people of Limoges.

Finally, after the Gospel had been read, when silence had been established among the people [Col. 1378B], Bishop Jordan, turning his face toward the people and standing before the altar in a more elevated place, began to address them as follows:

“We have heard, beloved, the words of the holy Gospel: ‘For the Son of Man came to seek and to save what was lost’ (Luke 19). For this reason our Lord Jesus Christ is called the Savior, because he wishes to call all sinners back to salvation, as the Apostle says: ‘The saying is trustworthy: Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the first’ (1 Timothy 1).

After saying a few words about the faith of Zacchaeus, who restored fourfold what he had defrauded, and after turning his speech toward the soldiers who were plundering the property of the sanctuary and of the poor, oppressing the people either through false accusation or through power, so that, imitating faithful Zacchaeus, they might justly restore what they had seized [Col. 1378C], he added at the end:

‘Behold, beloved, for the sake of your peace the shepherds of the churches are here, our holy brother-bishops, who have deigned to assemble in this city to lighten the burden of my office and to save and pacify you, following the example of our Lord Jesus Christ, who came “to seek and to save what was lost.”

Concerning this one matter I admonish you with them, adjuring you in the Lord Jesus, so that none of you should presume to disobey them, and none should withdraw by excusing himself from this council. Rather, let all the princes and leaders of the people from the province of Limoges come to us tomorrow and on the third day in peace, and let no one withdraw from our common assembly unless dismissed by us of our own will [Col. 1378D].

When you assemble at the council, let no one presume to harm another on account of any hostility, whether in his possessions or in his house, neither while he remains here, nor while he returns to his own place, nor for seven days after he has returned.

Let no one stir up sedition in this assembly or outside the city. Let no one seize anything by force. Let no one, as is customary, decide to enter into combat under the pretext of just grievances. Let no one undertake here any military expedition or cavalry action to be carried out later. Let everyone seek nothing here except peace, if perhaps quiet peace is granted to us by the Lord, because this assembly is properly the Lord’s assembly: to seek peace and to console the holy Church of God.’

To everyone who observes these things, as to a son of peace, indeed from our Lord Jesus Christ and his holy apostles, we grant absolution from sins and eternal blessing, so that, just as the Lord deigned to grant blessed Peter, this blessed Martial, at whose most sacred body we are standing, and the other apostles power and authority to bind and loose, so he may deign to free from the bonds of sins those who hasten to obey God and us, who, though unworthy, exercise his office, in matters of peace and justice.

But those who do not accept our peace, following not God but the devil, shall be subject to the condemnation that we shall now order to be recited before them. Our peace, however, will return to us, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “If there is a son of peace, your peace will rest upon him; but if not, it will return to you” (Luke 10).’

Then [Col. 1379B], at the bishops’ command, the same deacon who had proclaimed the Gospel began to read aloud from a written roll, before the people in the tribunal before the altar, the curse, as follows:

> **Excommunication of the Seditious.** By the authority of God the Father almighty, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, and of holy Mary, Mother of God, and of holy Peter, prince of the apostles, and of blessed Martial, and of the other apostles, and of all God’s saints:
>
> We bishops, specially assembled in the name of God—Aymo, archbishop of Bourges; Jordan, bishop of Limoges; Stephen of Le Puy; Renco of Auvergne; Ragamund of Mende; Aemilius of Albi; Deusdedit of Cahors; Isembertus of Poitiers; Arnaldus of Périgueux; and Roho of Angoulême—excommunicate those soldiers from this bishopric of Limoges who are unwilling, or have been unwilling, to confirm peace and justice to their bishop, as he demands.
>
> Cursed be they and their helpers for evil; cursed be their weapons and their horses. May they be with Cain the fratricide, with Judas the betrayer, and with Dathan and Abiron, who entered alive into hell. And just as these lamps are extinguished before your eyes, so may their joy be extinguished in the presence of the holy angels, unless before death they come to the judgment of their bishop for satisfaction, amendment, or worthy penance.

All the bishops and priests, holding burning candles in their hands, immediately threw them onto the ground and extinguished them. At these words the people’s hearts were greatly terrified [Col. 1379D], and all cried out:

> “So may God extinguish the joy of those who are unwilling to accept peace and justice.”

When this had been said, Lord Jordan addressed the people:

“These words of the curse were very recently spoken in the holy Council of Bourges against the enemies of peace. Just as, by God’s gift, peace was established among the people of Bourges, so we desire that peace be made among the people of Limoges.”

After this each of the bishops, and finally the archbishop, admonished the people concerning peace, saying:

“Just as your shepherd has foretold peace to you, so we confirm his words with one heart and one agreement, by the authority of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, and of blessed Peter, and of blessed Martial, and of the other holy apostles, to whom the Lord himself specially granted the power of binding and loosing [Col. 1380A].

Whatever this shepherd, given to you by God, confirms, we confirm; whatever he destroys, we destroy. Those whom he binds, we bind; those whom he blesses, we bless.”

When these and similar matters had been brought to a conclusion, silence was made. When the time came for the breaking of the Lord’s body, and the archbishop, according to custom, was pouring out a blessing upon the people, he inserted a mention of blessed Martial, saying:

“May almighty God bless and preserve you, and deign to illumine this house with the presence of his gift [variant: his divine majesty], and to open over it the eyes of his mercy by day and by night. Amen.

And may he graciously grant that all of you who have gathered today for the annual solemnity of the dedication of this basilica, through the intercession of the apostle blessed Martial and of his other saints, whose relics are venerated here with devout love, may be able to carry away from here the forgiveness of your sins with you. Amen.

So that, through their intervention, you may yourselves become a temple of the Holy Spirit, in which the holy Trinity may continually deign to dwell, and, after the course of this fleeting life has run its course, may deserve to attain happily to eternal joys”—and the rest that is customarily pronounced in an episcopal blessing.

Nevertheless, that second verse of the blessing in this manuscript, as also in certain others, contained the name of blessed John the Evangelist. But, as I have said, because the occasion of the feast at this place made it appropriate, and with the agreement of the learned men present, the archbishop deliberately spoke these words with reference to blessed Martial’s own dignity and glory [Col. 1380C]. This greatly pleased the whole Church, with the greatest love and rejoicing.

For we hold it as most certain that those things please the Holy Spirit which, through the agreement of many of the faithful, converge in one will, according to what is written: ‘The multitude of those who believed was of one heart and one soul’ (Acts 4).

As daylight came to an end and the evening solemnities were finished, Bishop Aemilius, angelic in his venerable gray hair, gave the people this blessing in the same basilica because of the patronage of blessed Martial, saying:

“May he who has granted you to stand upon apostolic foundations deign to bless you, through the intervening merits of his apostle, blessed Martial” [Col. 1380D]—and so forth, as follows.

After counsel had been taken, the bishops admonished one another to assemble again for the council very early the next day, with all delay removed; and the day dawned as Friday. We shall reserve for the following account a brief description of how this was done, asking the Lord our God and Lord Jesus Christ—who with the Holy Spirit has glory together with the Father throughout immortal and everlasting ages—to deign to bring to our memory the useful things that we ourselves saw with our eyes and heard with our ears while present, so that they may be committed to writing. Amen.

## SESSION II

Celebrated on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of December. —An account is inserted here of the events that took place at the First Council of Limoges in the year 1019.

[Col. 1381A]

Meanwhile, on the second day of the council, after the annual solemnity of the Lord’s basilica had concluded, the bishops rose before dawn to sing psalms. When the dawn gave the first beginning of light to the day, they performed the mystery of the altar for the Lord, and very early, before it grew fully light, assembled at the basilica of the holy see and entered the council in an orderly and properly arranged procession.

The aforementioned Lord Azenerius, venerable father of the monasteries of Saint Martin of Massay and Saint Benedict of Fleury, who had come to the Council of Limoges together with the bishop [Col. 1381B] of Bourges, led the litany for them on those three days. In these litanies he proclaimed blessed Martial among the names of the other apostles on each day.

This was an ancient custom of his and of his communities, as he himself publicly proclaimed before everyone at the council. He was especially learned in the liberal arts, and said that it was extremely improper for one who had received from the Redeemer, together with the other apostles, the power of binding and loosing to be proclaimed among those saints who had not received it.

Although all bishops possess the power of binding and loosing, nevertheless the others did not receive it individually from Christ, except only those who saw him in the flesh with blessed eyes, followed him, and were sent by him to preach; for the Lord said: ‘As the Father sent me, so I send you.’ When he had said this, he breathed on them and said: ‘Receive the Holy Spirit. Whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven; and whose sins you retain, they are retained’ (John 20).

After they had all prayed together, and the archdeacon had given an appropriate reading, and then, in the proper order, the one who delivered the address, at the bishops’ command, had proclaimed teaching from the divine Scriptures and concerning the catholic faith, a discussion again took place among the bishops about seeking the truth and observing it until death, recognizing and reducing falsehood to nothing, and about justice, peace, and the inviolable maintenance of the statutes of the Fathers.

First, therefore, before any discussion took place among the bishops, one of the leading men came forward and said to the archbishop:

“Dearest Father, we have discovered that certain men from the clerical order are now in this see and this city who, not for reasons but out of frivolity, are preparing not to obey your words, which were debated at yesterday’s council concerning blessed Martial, teacher of Aquitaine: namely, that he ought rightly to be proclaimed by all among the apostles rather than among the confessors. Concerning this matter, certain people are still murmuring in corners, as though they had found an opportunity in its novelty.”

The archbishop replied:

“None of us is unaware that yesterday [day], before everyone, it was rationally determined that the testimony to blessed Martial’s mission had been anticipated and attested by the ancients. And since, just as our head, the holy apostolic Roman see, approves it, so we, its members, ought to accept and embrace it with every form of veneration [Col. 1382A]; and since those who specifically received from Christ, while he was still dwelling on earth in the flesh, the power of binding and loosing are without doubt apostles; and since no one can contradict the truth, blessed Martial received from Christ, while he was still dwelling on earth in the flesh, the power of binding and loosing together with the other apostles.

The holy doctors and our ancient fathers, stronger pillars of the Church, also proclaim that all who saw the Lord in the flesh and afterward preached him were called apostles. And who would deny that this patron of ours saw the Lord in the flesh and afterward preached him?

Paul, the teacher of the nations, also writes that there were others, besides the Eleven, who were apostles, saying: ‘He appeared to the Eleven; afterward to all the apostles’ (1 Corinthians 15) [Col. 1382B]—that is, to the seventy-two, one of whom we unquestionably believe blessed Martial to have been.

Moreover, when the Lord said, ‘Did I not choose you twelve?’ (John 6), did he say, ‘Did I not choose you twelve apostles?’ Rather, ‘disciples’ is understood, as the evangelist John testifies when he says: ‘Many of his disciples went back and no longer walked with him’ (ibid.). Thus Jesus said to the Twelve—‘disciples’ being understood: ‘Did I not choose you twelve?’ That is, ‘Did I not choose you twelve disciples?’

It is certainly established that there was a multitude of the Lord’s disciples, and that those whom the Lord himself chose and sent to preach were specially apostles. Were not those who were chosen for preaching the men of whom the evangelist Luke says: ‘The Lord appointed seventy-two others and sent them, saying: “Go; behold, I send you like lambs among wolves”’ (Luke 10)?

But since they argue about blessed Dionysius and the other ancient Fathers of Gaul, did Dionysius and Saturninus, Gentiles by race, receive from Jesus himself, before he ascended into heaven, the power of binding and loosing together with those who saw and followed the Lord in the flesh? Are the names of Dionysius and Saturninus found anywhere to this day—since they raise the issue of novelty—written in litanies among the names of the apostles?

The truth is perfectly clear: in the most ancient codices, preserved in countless places and among distant peoples, blessed Martial is written together with the other apostles. Therefore, let him be an apostle for us, since he was also one for the ancients.

Finally, what I have said concerning blessed Dionysius and Saturninus, understand to have been said in the same way concerning Ursinus, Austremonius, Fronto of the Petracorian people, Julian of Le Mans, of Roman origin, and the others who saw or could have seen the apostles in the flesh, and who were sent to preach in Gaul after blessed Martial, whether by blessed Peter or by blessed Clement or their successors.

They did not receive the power of binding and loosing specifically from Christ, but from those who consecrated them in the order of the episcopate, just as I too received this power, not through my own merit but by God’s grace, from the one who bestowed the grace of the episcopate upon me, my consecrator—namely, the lord Jordan, pastor of this holy see of Limoges, who is present here.

But why is it still necessary to recapitulate more of what has already been more fully and perfectly determined in due order by the ancient Fathers, by the holy Roman and apostolic see, recently by the Council of Bourges, and here yesterday through the discussion of learned men? Nothing therefore remains except that, here in the presence of the council, all clerics from among our fellow provincials who, after this council, presume with a rebellious spirit to proclaim blessed Martial, the first teacher of Aquitaine, in any order or commemoration other than that of the apostles, should be publicly condemned by excommunication.” [Col. 1383A]

As the metropolitan, with stern expression, was about to pronounce the bond of condemnation, Lord Jordan addressed him:

“We ask your authority, venerable father, to suspend this judgment today with regard to the clerics of this holy see. For today, according to the Lord’s word, I shall admonish them between myself and them alone. If they listen to me, I shall have gained my brothers. But if they do not listen to me, I shall take with me one or two more of the present fellow bishops, our brothers, so that ‘every word may stand on the testimony of two or three witnesses.’

If they do not listen to them, I shall speak to the Church, publicly before the present council, so that all may hear as witnesses. But if they do not listen to the Church—that is, to this holy council now present—they shall be to me as a pagan and a tax collector. Then, by the word of your authority, bind them as disobedient not to men but to the Holy Spirit.

For, as Augustine says, the Holy Spirit, who once spoke through the apostles, now also deigns to speak through us whenever, while discussing divine matters, we speak the truth.” [Col. 1383C]

Trusting these words of the primate, the archbishop said:

“Then, with the Lord’s help, let the other matters pertaining to the council be discussed.”

After they had explained the ecclesiastical rules at length, Lord Jordan said:

“It is pleasing that the chapters of the Council of Bourges should be brought forward, in case these same provisions are merely adapted to the people of Limoges, or whether our clergy might prefer them otherwise, or whether other suitable provisions should be added.

For one and the same law cannot always suit all churches, peoples, cities, or nations. Rather, certain practices are brought into custom according to the character of places, peoples, and minds, in different yet suitable arrangements. A difference of local custom does no harm, provided it is supported by reason or authority.

Reason, however, ought to prevail more than authority, for the Gentiles worship idols on the authority of their ancestors, although they rely on no reason. Some authority appears to exist without reason, whereas reason of itself confers the dignity of authority. Therefore the authority of many elders has often been changed for the better or entirely disregarded because it is supported by too little reason.

It is a grave fault if anyone presumes arbitrarily to despise authority that is full of reason. Rational authority, therefore—or reason together with authority, and authority together with reason—must always present and distinguish itself as worthy.

The use and observance of diverse customs among peoples and in different places, provided they are not contrary to faith, hope, and charity, seem to do nothing contrary to Christian dignity. Indeed, that custom is always believed to benefit religion which, according to place, time, necessity, dignity, reason, and authority, appears to please the brothers dwelling together in unity by their unanimous consent.

For what of it? Can the canons criticize monks because of the twelve readings, or monks criticize the canons because of the number nine? Both practices are sound in reason and authority: three times four, representing the four parts of the world subject to the Holy Trinity, gives glory to the Holy Trinity; while three times three, representing the nine orders of angels, gives glory to the Holy Trinity.

The number twelve was approved by that man full of the spirit of all the righteous, the holy pope Gregory, first a monk and afterward apostolic [Col. 1384B]. The nine were handed down by Ignatius the martyr, a disciple of blessed Peter, who heard in heaven readings and psalms uttered by the angelic choirs according to the number nine. Then the Council of Nicaea, and afterward holy Gregory himself, observed this number in psalms, readings, and responses.

What of the custom among Eastern or Western clerics of shaving the beard or not shaving it—does it seem to impair religion? The former have the apostle Peter as the author of this custom, and they maintain it with authority and reason, saying that it is reasonable for clerics to differ from laymen, in bodily appearance as in life.

Therefore this custom is clearly more beneficial than harmful to religion.

The others choose the custom of not shaving the beard, taking the apostles Paul or James, the brother of the Lord, as their authority [Col. 1384C]. They join reason to their authorities—for our obedience ought indeed to be reasonable—and say that it is reasonable for clerics, like laymen, to preserve a manly beauty in the face, according to the dignity of the human condition created by God, who willed that only a man should have a beard for the sake of beauty, and that the sign of the clerical state should be shown only on the crown of the head.

They add another reason for themselves: our Lord the Nazarene willed to be unshorn; no iron came upon his head, except that he deigned to endure the crown of thorns upon his crown. In imitation of him, the crown of clerics is represented on the crown of the head by the cut of the iron, so that the kingship and priesthood of Christ may also be foreshadowed by the shaving itself on the heads of clerics.

Thus, just as our custom in this matter possesses authority, and at the same time reason and an increase of religion, so among the Greeks their custom, differing from ours, contains authority together with reason and a fruit of religion. In this matter neither can they criticize us, nor we them, just as the Apostle says concerning believers who ate meat:

‘Let the one who does not eat not despise the one who eats, and let the one who eats not judge the one who does not eat. For the one who eats, eats for the Lord; and the one who does not eat, does not eat for the Lord’ (Romans 14).

Those who observe authority together with reason may rightly criticize those who preserve authority without reason; but the latter cannot criticize the former in any way.

Accordingly, those who put the blessed teacher of Aquitaine among the confessors, possessing the authority of their elders without reason, say: ‘Those who came before us, this one and that one, proposed him thus.’ They rightly deserve criticism from those who show reason together with authority, proposing him together with the other apostles and saying: ‘Those ancient Fathers, at those authoritative places, and the apostolic Roman see, and those most learned men, proposed him in the order of the apostles.’

It is reasonable that the one who, among others, received from the Lord the power to preach the Gospel, the power of binding and loosing, and knowledge of all languages, and who has Gaul as the seal of his apostolate, is therefore an apostle and should rightly be proposed together with the apostles, while his memory should always be confirmed in the glory of the apostolate.

Thus they may justly rebuke those people in this matter, not those people them [Col. 1385B]. I have said these things so that the diverse customs and laws of different peoples, if they possess reason, may not generate scandals.

We must take the greatest care, before all things and above all things, to hand on to the people for observance God’s commandment, not our traditions; to establish nothing to be done except what is supported by the authority of the divine Scriptures; and, God forbid, to presume to establish, teach, or command anything from our own hearts or outside the commandment of the Lord and the holy Fathers.

Whatever we hand on to others, we must first do ourselves, lest we be among those who sit upon the chair of Moses, of whom the Savior said to the crowds and to his disciples: ‘They say and do not do’ (Matthew 23); and again: ‘They themselves do not wish to move them with their finger’ (ibid.).”

After these words, the archbishop turned to Azenerius the abbot, who sat at his right on another cathedra, dressed in sacred vestments, and said:

“We ask you, dearest brother, to set forth before this holy council the chapters of the Council of Bourges, just as Lord Bishop Jordan commands, since you yourselves were present and heard them.”

Then he began to recite them, saying:

These are the chapters concerning which the holy mother Church of Bourges had been corrupted at that time. Therefore, following in the footsteps of the Fathers, the bishops who were present there—Aymo of Bourges, Stephen of Le Puy, Renco of Auvergne, Ragamund of Mende, Aemilius of Albi, and Deusdedit of Cahors—decreed that the following provisions should be observed by the churches entrusted to them.

[Col. 1385D] “First of all, that throughout all …,” etc. (See the Council of Bourges, 1031.)

When the elder had finished speaking at length on these matters, Lord Jordan said:

“All these things please us well. Only concerning the changing of the Body of the Lord: because of the priests who cannot be present at their own churches every Sunday, it pleases us that the matter be regulated so moderately that it can be observed by everyone without excuse. For the provisions established in the Church ought to be so moderated that all may carry them without an unbearable burden, that souls may be saved, that each person may perform what the Church enjoins without murmuring, and that disobedience may find no place.

“Therefore, it pleases us that the Body of the Lord be renewed twelve times a year in all those churches where it is customarily kept continually: namely, at Easter, at Pentecost, at the Nativity of Saint John, at the Feast of Saint Peter’s Chains, at the Assumption of Saint Mary, at the feast of Saint Michael, at All Saints, at Saint Andrew’s feast, at the Nativity of the Lord, at the Hypapante, in Lent, and at Mid-Lent. By these divisions of the year all the priests are able to return to their own churches, and the Body of the Lord, which is renewed, must be received only by clean ministers of the Church.

“As for the regular monasteries of monks, since they attend more carefully and more scrupulously to everything pertaining to the worship of the altar, we leave these matters to the discretion of their abbots, as we do their other rules. Those who desire to enter life by the narrow and difficult gate more strictly than we do, who break their own will, who bear the yoke from youth, and who obey the commands of bishops with the greatest diligence in all things ought not to be bound by our laws. Such men, I say, ought not to be subjected to the laws of councils, unless perhaps they have become open to blame or contempt.

“So the Apostle says: ‘The law is not laid down for the righteous but for the unrighteous and the disobedient, the ungodly and sinners, the wicked and defiled, those who kill their fathers and mothers, murderers, fornicators, men who have intercourse with males, kidnappers, liars, perjurers, and whatever else is contrary to sound doctrine, which accords with the gospel of the glory of the blessed God entrusted to me’ (1 Tim. 1).

“I do not compel regular abbots to come to the synod of this see so that they may be accused, but so that they may offer me counsel concerning the administration of ecclesiastical affairs. Thus, while these spiritual men assist me, scattered as I am among the many cares of different people, in lightening my burden, they may share with me in the reward of the crown. For concerning ecclesiastical worship and reverence for the Body of the Lord, I myself have seen with my own eyes the regular monks of the Limousin keeping the altars and books, vestments, chalices, linens, and everything pertaining to the altar daily in the utmost cleanliness and with reverence.”

When much more had been said on these and similar matters, and the archbishop and everyone else approved, certain elders became just accusers, saying in the council:

“At the place of the monastery of Saint Peter of Belloc [corrected: Belliloc], the holy Church of Limoges is suffering violence. This place was once illustrious in the regular order, but now it has been so trampled underfoot by secular persons [Col. 1386D] that a secular abbot, without the monastic habit, rules over the monks of that monastery.”

Everyone in the council cried out:

“This is a great destruction: that a blind man should lead those who see, and a fool teach the wise. By this conduct discipline dies, a place is given to hypocrisy among the monks, and the opportunity to possess property privately is stolen from them—things by which, deceived, they may perish. When the head is diseased, the whole body is useless; and because of such destruction of God’s places, wrath goes forth from the face of God against the peoples.”

Then the monks of the aforesaid monastery were summoned. Standing before the bishops, they said:

“Let a suitable abbot be appointed for us according to the Rule, and we shall be at peace. For while we were mourning, this man seized tyranny over us. So that it may be known to the bishops present: Rodulf, formerly archbishop of Bourges, built this monastery on his own estate in the time of King Charles, and endowed it most nobly with his estates and many gifts. After he had passed to heaven and a long period had elapsed, the count of Toulouse, finding an opportunity, subjected the monastery to his own power and granted it as a benefice to the count of Périgueux. The latter in turn granted it to the viscount of Comborn, who has now imposed a layman upon us, for this reason: Bernard, a monk of Solignac and later bishop of Cahors, but our abbot, was his predecessor and his maternal uncle.”

The bishops said:

“Ecclesiastical offices ought to be distributed not according to carnal origin but according to the excellence of one’s merits.”

Then that cleric—an abbot but not a monk, great in secular nobility and lineage—was immediately summoned and stood before the bishops as an accused man. Kneeling, and being judged on this matter according to the canons, he replied:

“O most reverend Fathers, I beg you to correct this matter by a just judgment, and I willingly consent.”

The Fathers said:

“Bring before Lord Jordan someone suitable from among the regular monks, so that he may canonically appoint him abbot to govern this place. As for you, remember to remain outside it not as its destroyer but as its defender and provider.”

Accordingly, after the bishops had spoken at length about these matters, they entrusted the affair to the primate of Limoges, under the testimony of the council and of William, duke of Aquitaine, in the following terms [Col. 1387C]: by the feast of the Nativity of the Lord, which was expected in the sixth week, he was to appoint in that place a worthy shepherd according to the Rule. If he found opponents who would not permit this to be done, he was to bind both them and the place itself with canonical excommunication until the place was restored to its former dignity.

When certain people asked whether any of the monks might perhaps wish to move from that secular place to another regular one, and whether this was permitted to them, the learned men present judged that such a course was right.

“Such men,” they said, “strive to please God. For even if one who is good among the wicked is perfect, nevertheless it is praiseworthy and very beneficial to attain the fellowship of the good. As the Holy Spirit says through the Psalmist: ‘With the holy man you will be holy, and with the innocent man you will be innocent, and with the chosen man you will be chosen; but with the perverse you will become perverse’ (Ps. 17). And again the Apostle says: ‘Bad conversations corrupt good morals’ (1 Cor. 15). Scripture says again: ‘Whoever touches pitch will be defiled by it, and whoever associates with the proud will put on pride’ (Sir. 13).

“For although a lily shines among thorns, it is nevertheless burdened by the thorns and grows more gloriously among pleasant things than among thorny places. If a regular abbot happens to be appointed over secular monks, and cannot turn them away from illicit practices, and has no good men to help him endure the wicked patiently, it is better for him to abandon them and live alone with himself than to lose the tranquility of his heart through their incorrigible harshness.

“According to the Lord’s word, it is better for him to enter life one-eyed or lame than, possessing two eyes or two feet, to be cast into Gehenna. That is: it is better for him to gain himself alone than, through the wicked whom he loves uselessly, to suffer loss. The Holy Spirit speaks of such men through the prophet, saying: ‘Son of man, unbelievers and subverters are with you, and you dwell among scorpions’ (Ezek. 2). Job likewise says: ‘I was a brother to dragons and a companion to ostriches’ (Job 30). And David says: ‘Who will give me wings like a dove? Then I will fly away and rest’ (Ps. 54).

“Indeed, blessed Benedict abandoned the secular or rustic monks who had tried to kill him with poison, so that he would not cloud the tranquil eye of his mind with their utter vileness. As the holy Fathers said, whatever can disturb the peace or tranquility of heart by which we ought continually to think upon God must be cast away, however useful or necessary it may be; for a heart disturbed by any vice cannot think upon God.

“In saying this, we do not condemn those who sometimes live in the midst of false monks or necessarily dwell among wicked superiors, provided that they fulfill what is written: ‘Do what they say, but do not do what they do’ (Matt. 23); and again: ‘As a lily among thorns, so is my beloved among the daughters’ (Song 2). The Apostle was tested by dangers among false brothers, and one must fulfill the pastor’s commands in everything, even if—God forbid—the pastor himself acts otherwise.

“Blessed Peter also cites Lot as an example in this regard, saying: ‘He rescued righteous Lot from the conduct of the wicked, who lived among them and tormented his righteous soul day after day by their lawless deeds’ (2 Pet. 2). These words apply not only to monks but generally to all Christians who live among the wicked. Paul likewise says to his disciples concerning such people: ‘Among a crooked and perverse generation, among whom you shine like lights in the world’ (Phil. 2). Hence John says to the Church of Pergamum: ‘I know where you dwell, where the seat of Satan is; yet you hold fast to my name and have not denied my faith’ (Rev. 2).

“Therefore, as Gregory says, a good man is not one who refuses to tolerate the wicked. The wicked must be tolerated all the more as they become more numerous. We call those monks regular who, unwilling to do what is illicit, live under the authority not of themselves but of another; everything they have is held in common, and they possess nothing that the abbot has not given or permitted.

“It may happen, however difficult it may be, that one regular monk lives among many rustic monks, provided that he keeps himself from illicit practices and is content with those things suitable for the needs of this life, with the permission or gift of the one who governs him, as the Apostle says: ‘Having food and clothing, we shall be content with these’ (1 Tim. 6).

“We call secular monks those whom regular monks will judge on the day of judgment, just as the Ninevites—or the queen of the South—will condemn the unbelieving Jews at the Lord’s saying; or as the twelve apostles will judge the twelve tribes of Israel, because those who believed refused to believe. So these monks will judge those others, because while these lived according to the Rule, the others refused to live according to the Rule.

“Thus monasteries are established and flourish under righteous leaders, but under vicious ones they fall and languish. Therefore the bishop to whose diocese the monasteries belong, together with the abbots and the neighboring Christians, will incur evil unless they prevent unworthy men from entering pastoral leadership, just as a good reward from God awaits them if they appoint worthy stewards over the household of God.”

When these and similar matters had been expounded to the listeners in a lofty, mystical, and useful discourse, Lord Jordan said:

“I give thanks to God because several monasteries in the diocese of Limoges proceed along the right path and spread examples of good fragrance far and wide, as the Apostle says: ‘We are the good fragrance of Christ to God among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing’ [Col. 1389B] (2 Cor. 2).

“I praise these abbots of Limoges who are present at this holy council and testify before the Lord Jesus that, conducting themselves according to the Rule with their subjects, they devote themselves more to winning souls than to caring about perishable and transient things. For it is fitting that all who undertake the governance of souls should prepare themselves to render an account.

“First of all, I do not fail to recognize that the household of blessed Martial in this city, the monastery of Cambon of blessed Valeria, a possession of blessed Martial, and the other monasteries that have been subject to it by right of perpetual possession since ancient times live according to the Rule. Likewise, I rejoice that the most noble monasteries of Solignac and Uzerche, as well as the monasteries of Saint Martin and Saint Augustine in this city, the community of virgins in the basilica of the blessed Mother of God, and the other communities of God’s servants throughout the Limousin, regularly observe the reverence due to the holy order.

“How greatly the communities of God’s servants avail in the sight of almighty God to intercede for the salvation of peoples, blessed Gregory showed when speaking of a community of nuns. He said: ‘Rome could by no means have survived amid so many Lombard swords in our times, unless the communities of consecrated virgins in this Roman city had resisted such great hostility by their prayers.’ And again: ‘Therefore,’ he says, ‘we must provide for the monasteries of God’s servants, so that we may supply them abundantly with aid, lest, burdened by any want, they should in some measure succumb to their vocation.’

“For Gregory also wished the monasteries of monks throughout the whole world to be free and undisturbed, so that if he discovered any bishop excommunicating or troubling them for whatever reason, he might punish them severely; this can readily be seen in his letters. We too desire the monasteries of God’s servants to be defended, peaceful, and secure, following in the footsteps of so great a Father.

“Nevertheless, if a fault of pride or disobedience is found in abbots, it must be pursued canonically. I have said this because of the abbot of the monastery of Uzerche, whom they say has despised the decrees of the holy council this year. Some have reported to us that he buried at his monastery the excommunicated viscount of Albuciens, who had been killed while engaged in plunder. If this is true, it grieves my heart.

“For everyone knows that it has been established in holy councils that if someone excommunicated by his bishop is killed, or dies a natural death without reconciliation, he is under no circumstances to be buried in a Christian burial, unless the bishop, after his friends or relatives have made satisfaction on his behalf, grants absolution and permission. Nor is prayer to be offered for him, nor are his goods to be received as alms, until he has been absolved by the bishop.

“Likewise, if any excommunicated person has been wounded unto death or struck by illness and brought to his end, and asks for penance from the heart or seeks to become a monk, his penance is indeed to be accepted and the viaticum granted to him out of mercy. Nevertheless, he is under no circumstances to be buried, nor is prayer to be offered for him after his death, until he has been absolved by his bishop [Col. 1390B].

“For, as blessed Gregory says in the second book of the *Dialogues*: ‘Christ granted such great power to his Church that those who still live in the flesh can absolve those already freed from the flesh, whom they had bound while alive. For the Lord said to Peter: “Whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven”’ (Matt. 16).

“Saint Benedict absolved after death two holy women and one of the brothers who had died bound. Pope Gregory likewise bound a physician who was a brother at the very moment of his death. He permitted neither consolation nor prayer for him at the end, nor allowed him to be buried in the church cemetery; yet long after his death he absolved him out of mercy and established that prayer should be offered for him.

“Nevertheless, as the blessed pope writes, it is exceedingly dreadful when someone departs from the world unreconciled. Moreover, if one bishop binds someone and another thinks that he can absolve him, the one who receives him is deceived, and the one who is received perishes. On this pretext of false mercy, the councils of the Fathers are destroyed, God is despised, and peace is driven from the Church.

“For the person who receives an excommunicated man perishes together with him because he receives a similar punishment of excommunication. As blessed Peter says in the writing of blessed Clement, whoever consents to an excommunicated person or participates in conversation with him is himself one of those who destroy the Church of God.”

When certain people in the council asked whether excommunication must be observed in the case of someone whom a bishop had perhaps bound unjustly and without fault, Father Odolric said:

“As blessed Gregory testifies—and his authority must by no means be despised—if a shepherd binds someone, whether justly or unjustly, whether because of guilt or without guilt, the excommunication must be observed, lest the person who has perhaps been unjustly bound should deserve that very excommunication on account of another fault. Nor should a sheep rashly rebuke its shepherd, lest through the pride of such swollen rebuke a fault that did not previously exist should arise.

“He says concerning bishops that they deprive themselves of this power when they bind or release someone out of hatred or favor rather than according to the merit of the case.”

To this the pontiff added:

“A priest who knowingly receives an excommunicated person is removed from the clerical order because he excommunicates himself by consenting to the excommunicated person.”

[Col. 1391A] Then all the bishops said:

“We establish canonically that anyone who has unknowingly received an excommunicated person and later discovers this must immediately turn to penance in the presence and judgment of his bishop. But anyone who has done this knowingly—whether during the person’s life or after his death, or who is proved to have accepted any part of the condemned person’s property as alms—must cease from the priestly order and may not recover his rank unless, after making satisfaction, he is reclothed by his bishop in the sacred vestments.

“If he is not a priest, he must be deprived of Eucharistic communion and of attendance at Mass until reconciliation with the bishop.

“When a bishop deposes a priest, he shall proceed as follows: first he shall order him to be clothed in all the priestly vestments; then with his own hand he shall remove his maniple, then his chasuble; then he shall turn back half of the stole from his neck between his shoulders beneath his right side—and he is deposed from the priesthood into the diaconate.

“When he excommunicates anyone, he shall go publicly to the church door and close the door against him. When he absolves him, he shall walk with him as far as the church doors and open them so that he may enter. Otherwise no excommunicated person may enter a church, because this is sacrilegious and illicit.

“Priests are to excommunicate for unknown causes; bishops, for known causes, lest the power of bishops be cheapened.”

After these statements, when they asked the accused abbot what he had to say, he replied to the lord primate:

“Lord Father, the truth concerning the matter of which I am accused has not been reported to you. Far be it from me ever to receive an excommunicated person without your permission. For the higher our order is, the more subject and ready it must necessarily be to obey bishops. In bishops we honor or despise God himself, as he says: ‘Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever rejects you rejects me’ (Luke 10).

“Behold, I produce suitable witnesses: after that excommunicated viscount was killed while engaged in plunder—for counts who engage in plunder are openly excommunicated in all councils—his soldiers carried him to our monastery without my knowledge. We neither received nor buried his body, but ordered it to be carried back beyond the water, where the soldiers themselves buried it without any cleric being present.”

When they heard this, the bishops gave judgment, saying:

“If this is so, the excommunicated man was not buried, and the abbot of the monastery cannot be judged guilty.”

Then the bishop of Cahors began to relate the following:

“Very recently, after the Council of Bourges, a knight who had been excommunicated was killed in our diocese. At the request of his friends and relatives I absolutely refused to absolve him, so that the others might be afraid; for he had been guilty of the grave offense of plundering. Accordingly, without the ministry of a priest and without my command, he was buried by soldiers near a certain church of Saint Peter.

“But when morning came, his body was found cast far outside the cemetery and lying naked on the face of the earth. The mound where he had been buried was found untouched, exactly as it had been left before. The soldiers opened it again and found nothing in it except the clothes in which he had been wrapped. They buried the corpse there again and carefully closed the grave beneath an enormous weight of earth and stones. Yet on the following day they saw the corpse cast out and the grave untouched, as before. They buried him five times, and as many times they saw him thrown out in the same manner. Finally, overcome by such a great marvel, they buried the body far from the church cemetery beneath the earth. Struck with terror by this, the military leaders did not delay in establishing with us the peace that we desired.”

The council replied:

“What else can this mean except that, before human eyes, the Judge of all affirms the authority of his Church, because the burial of the excommunicated is rightly separated by bishops from Christian burial? Such men deny the faith while pursuing brigandage rather than peace. For they should not be called Christians, of whom the Apostle says: ‘They profess to know God, but deny him by their deeds’ (Tit. 1). James likewise says: ‘Faith without works is dead’ (Jas. 2).

“Certainly Dathan and Abiron perished from the midst of the multitude because they despised their shepherds. Thus, if someone despises God in his bishop, he is rightly separated from the Church and left unburied if death happens to overtake him in the bond of excommunication.”

Meanwhile, the venerable Father Odolric, head of the household of blessed Martial, sitting in a chair beside the primate of Limoges and wearing the sacred vestments as usual, began to give the bishops counsel:

“Here, dearest brothers, you ought to determine what remedy you will apply against the general disease. For if the military leaders of Limoges oppose you concerning the maintenance of peace, as you desire, what should be done against this?”

The bishops said:

“Dearest brother, in this matter we ask you yourself to give counsel.”

He replied:

“Unless they agree to peace, bind the entire land of Limoges with public excommunication, in this manner: no one is to be buried throughout the whole Limousin except a cleric, a poor person who begs, a pilgrim who has arrived, or a child of two years or younger; nor is anyone to be carried to another bishopric for burial.

“Let the divine office be performed secretly in all the churches, and let baptism be granted to those who request it. Around the third hour, let the bells sound in all the churches, and let everyone prostrate himself face down and pour out prayers for the tribulation and peace.

“Let penance and the viaticum be granted at the approach of death. Let the altars in all the churches be stripped as on Good Friday, and let the crosses and ornaments be hidden, because this is a sign of mourning and sorrow for everyone. The altars are to be vested only for the Masses that each priest celebrates with the church doors closed, and after the Masses they are to be stripped again.

“No one is to take a wife during the excommunication. No one is to give another the kiss of peace. No cleric or layman, whether resident or passing through, is to eat meat anywhere in the Limousin, nor any foods other than those permitted during Lent.

“No layman or cleric is to have his hair cut or his beard shaved until the strict princes, the heads of the peoples, obey the holy council in everything. If anyone is proved in any way to have violated this bond, he is not to be received except with fitting penance. For the excommunication of bishops must be observed with the greatest care, lest perhaps the Lord’s anger grow still greater against us and against the people.”

Then the council asked whether, if one or two of the leading men obeyed, the bishop ought to pardon them without the others, or not. Bishop Aemilius and Abbot Azenerius resolved the matter in this way:

“If, out of a hundred wicked men, we cannot bring back any except one, we ought to receive that one alone with joy.”

Father Odolric replied:

“If one of a hundred who are lost is won for salvation, there is joy before the angels of God. Finally, if anyone, after the death of disobedience, hastens to obedience to the bishop, he is already being inwardly brought to life by God, and therefore it is necessary to absolve him.
