“For concerning those who do not receive the penitent and contrite, but absolve the hardened either out of fear or through secular affection, the Holy Spirit says through the prophet: ‘They kill the souls that should not die and bring to life the souls that should not live’ (Ezek. 13). And again: ‘Woe to those who call evil good and good evil, who make darkness light and light darkness’ (Isa. 5).

“Therefore, if even one of the leading princes obeys you, while all the others remain rebels with brazen faces, receive the peacemaker in the peace of Christ and assist him in everything. Permit his land and honor, rejoicing in absolution, to remain free. But let the other regions of the land of Limoges that have rebellious princes remain under the aforesaid anathema until a worthy correction is made, so that there may be a distinction between good and evil, as between light and darkness.

“If all the greater powers of Limoges consent to peace, so that everything is absolved, but some private soldiers or lesser princes are found disobedient to the council, let such men be privately excommunicated in this manner: they shall be separated from communion in the Body and Blood of the Lord; they shall have no permission to enter a church; they shall neither eat nor drink nor walk with Christians; they shall not wear linen; they shall not eat meat or drink wine; they shall not cut their hair or shave their beards; they shall not presume to go to any prayers; if they are ill, no cleric shall visit them.

“If they die while under this excommunication, they shall not be removed from the place where they died, nor covered with wood, stone, or any other protection. No one shall accept any of their property as alms for their souls.”

The following was stated in the council:

“If any bishop should at times, through fear, affection, or money, be induced not to restrain by justice, in accordance with the council, someone whom he ought and is able to restrain; or if he absolves, whether living or dead, someone whom he ought not to absolve; or if he is proved to violate in any respect the council that he established together with the other bishops, he shall be deposed by those same bishops for the period of time that they shall unanimously determine.”

All the bishops said:

“This proposal pleases us; so let it be done. The same shall be done with a bishop who receives an excommunicated person belonging to another bishop, whether living or dead, or permits or consents to his being received in the diocese by anyone.”

Meanwhile, while the bishops were discussing these matters, a complaint was raised in the council by those who said:

“In the monastery of Saint Martial above, baptism is administered at Easter and Pentecost, and there servants are granted freedom by their masters. The clerics of this see wish this to be administered nowhere else but at this see.”

Those who were of sound judgment opposed this with the following response:

“In the oratory of Saint John the Baptist, which lies to the south, above and beside the basilica of the Savior, fonts have been prepared since ancient times, and baptism has always customarily been administered there only at Easter and Pentecost. At other times throughout the year, infants from that upper parish are baptized in the church of Saint Michael. Until now this holy see has in no way raised complaints on their account.

“The parishioners of the church of Saint Peter of Cairognes, and all the princes throughout the Limousin who wish to do so, bring their sons to this see for examination during Lent and for baptism at Easter or Pentecost. The parishioners of the church of Saint Michael, the church of Saint Mary of the Sands, and the other churches subject to the basilica of blessed Martial, together with any princes from throughout the Limousin or from the external cities of Aquitaine who wish it, send their children upward to the hall of the Redeemer for baptism.

“Finally, it has always been the custom that anyone who wished could grant freedom to his servants above, either before the altar of the Redeemer, before the body of blessed Martial, or before the body of a deceased neighbor. If, therefore, something has always been permitted to us until now and has never before been prohibited, in what way will it now become illicit? Let the bishops present judge by a just judgment what is equitable in this matter.”

The bishops said:

“It would be sacrilegious to remove from blessed Martial the privilege established for him in ancient times. This see of blessed Martial is the head and mother of all the churches of Gaul, because it was consecrated to God first of all the churches in Gaul. Therefore, all the churches of the Limousin should especially show it honor in all things as their proper head.

“But this see and mother must not remove from her other daughter churches the institutions justly granted to them from ancient times, nor forbid the honor owed to them. A bishop ought to rejoice and give his assent when the churches subject to him continue in their ancient honor.

“Therefore, at the monastery of blessed Martial, as was customary in ancient times, it is rightly appropriate to celebrate baptism—both because the proper order of Easter must not be neglected, since it draws the minds of carnal people toward higher things, and because of the threefold litany and the station at the fonts—but only for no fewer than three infants, and only at Easter and Pentecost.

“By the same reasoning, it is fitting for this to be done in other monasteries and churches where it has been customary since ancient days, provided that the greater number of those to be baptized is at this mother church.

“Those baptized in other churches within this city are to be brought on that same day before the bishop at this see, with lights, for confirmation. For where the Paschal candle is consecrated and baptism is administered, the Easter rite is completed more honorably, and the three litanies—which can in no way be omitted on the Saturdays of Easter and Pentecost, lest, God forbid, the authority of the Holy Spirit be diminished—are more suitably performed.

“After six readings, the seventh is sung solemnly in the choir by several singers clothed together in their vestments. Then the singers, priests, and other ministers proceed in groups of three to the fonts. After baptism has been administered to only three infants—for the others, if there are more, are baptized by another priest who has remained there—they return from the fonts in groups of three: those assigned to the choir go to the choir, and those assigned to the altar go to the altar, with the candles not yet lit, while all the bells sound.

“When the procession of three has ended and the ringing of the metal bells has ceased, the priest immediately proclaims the hymn of the angels in a loud voice, with the whole church now illuminated, after the singers have cried out: ‘Light them.’”

“That is enough concerning baptism. Now we must speak of the freedom of servants, since this may be carried out either at this see, or before the body of blessed Martial, or at any church of the Lord they choose, before witnesses, or before the body of a recently deceased relative, as we often see done in many cities; provided, of course, that the designated chancellor of this see writes the instrument of freedom.

“For we also see legitimate grants of freedom made before the king at the royal palace, or wherever the king may be. Indeed, the Salic Law states that wherever the master of a servant wishes, he may release his servant.”

When certain people spoke about preaching to the people and about proclaiming fasts and litanies as circumstances required, saying that these matters ought to be established and announced only at the see, the bishops said:

“Preaching must be diligently practiced not only at the see but also in all the churches wherever the will of the Lord inspires an energetic teacher to offer it. For it is greatly to be lamented that laborers in God’s harvest are exceedingly rare. Many may be willing to hear good things, but few are willing to speak them.

“All priests entrusted with a parish ought to admonish the people by preaching on every Sunday and feast day, according to the saying: ‘Reprove, entreat, rebuke’ (2 Tim. 4). For if a priest proceeds without the sound of preaching, he is guilty of death under the divine threat. A bishop, moreover, must urge those whom he sees to be learned and suitable for the office to undertake so sublime a work, not only by command but also by request.

“No one, whether monk or cleric, may undertake this office unless he has been ordained by the bishop to the rank of lector.

“Concerning the proclamation of litanies or fasts, it is written as follows in the Book of the Capitularies of Charles: ‘When tribulation comes upon the people, whether through mortality, hostility, famine, unseasonable weather, or anything of this kind, and we are not present, let none of us wait for an edict. Rather, clerics or monks should exhort one another and, together with the people, hasten through litanies or fasts to incline the mercy of the Lord toward our kingdom.

“‘Therefore, if such things are instituted by another church without consultation with the see, out of necessity and not rashness—or, God forbid, out of the arrogance of pride—there is no reason for the clerics of the see to be indignant. Nevertheless, let everything be regulated in mutual agreement among all the neighboring communities, so that peace and unity between the see and the other churches may remain unshaken.’”

The bishop of Périgueux then raised an inquiry concerning one of his canons, merely a cleric, who had taken a wife. He asked them to judge what should be done with him. The council answered:

“Let the canons judge. For how can we judge anything according to our own discretion, when everything has already been judged by those who came before? Nothing should be said that has not been said before.”

Then the Apostolic Canons were read, where chapter 27 says:

“Which clergy may be joined to wives.—We command that those who have advanced to the clergy while unmarried may, if they wish, take wives, but only readers and singers.”

And again it was said:

“The Toletan Canons also judge as follows: when those brought up in monasteries reach the age of adolescence, they are to be given the free choice whether they wish to vow the monastic profession or remain among the laity. Those who wish may marry; but those who, being left to their own discretion, have vowed the profession may no longer look back toward the world. For the Council of Bourges, as we have heard, judged that whoever abandons his clerical office is to be separated from the other clergy.”

A question was also raised concerning certain abbots who, on the greater feast days, have a chaplain and several deacons, like bishops, to celebrate Mass. After careful consideration, it was determined that this was done not by way of usurpation but in honor of the solemnity. It also seemed permissible that the same practice be observed not only for abbots but for other priests in many churches where there are large communities of monks or canons, out of reverence for the solemnity. Nevertheless, no more than three deacons are employed for abbots or other priests at solemn celebrations. Bishops, however, are sometimes to have three, sometimes five, and occasionally seven deacons at their disposal, according to the requirements of the feasts and for all public Masses. For it is known that in the monastery of Blessed Martial the ancient custom has always been preserved and is still observed today, and must never be omitted: namely, that at Easter and the more important feasts throughout the year three deacons and a chaplain minister to the abbot at the public Mass, while on other days or lesser feasts there are only a chaplain and one deacon.

Then certain men were accused who had given money for the rank of presbyter; others who had had two wives before the diaconate; still others who, while in the clergy, had amputated their own genitals; and others who had committed homicide while still laymen and afterward, having become monks, had received the rank of deacon. Concerning these it was said at the council:

“No mercy can be shown them without deposing them all. For if we absolve those whom the holy Fathers condemn, we offer them false mercy and eternal death.”

Then the Apostolic Canons were produced, where chapter 30 reads:

“If any bishop, presbyter, or deacon has obtained this dignity through money, let both him and his ordainer be deposed, and let him be entirely cut off from communion, just as I, Peter, deposed Simon Magus.”

Likewise, chapter 31:

“If any bishop, using secular powers, has obtained the episcopate or a church through them, let him be deposed and separated, together with all who communicate with him.”

Likewise, chapter 17:

“If anyone, after baptism, has entered into a second marriage or has kept a concubine, he cannot be a bishop or a deacon, nor at all belong to the number of those who serve in the sacred ministry.”

Likewise, chapter 18:

“If anyone has taken a widow, a divorced woman, a slave-woman, or any woman belonging to those who are exhibited in public spectacles, he cannot be a bishop, presbyter, or deacon, nor belong to the number of those who serve at the altar.”

Likewise, chapter 21:

“If a eunuch was made so through the ambushes of men, or if his genitals were amputated during persecution, or if he was born so, and is worthy, let him become a bishop.”

Likewise, chapter 22:

“If anyone has mutilated himself—that is, if anyone has amputated his own genitals—let him not become a cleric, because he is his own murderer and an enemy of God’s creation.”

Chapter 23:

“If anyone, while he is a cleric, mutilates himself, let him be utterly condemned, because he is his own murderer.”

Chapter 24:

“A layman who mutilates himself is to be deprived of communion for three years, because he has proved an attacker of his own life.”

Concerning homicides it was said:

“If anyone commits homicide voluntarily and not through necessity, and afterward becomes a monk, he cannot be promoted to the degrees of the altar. For when monks are advanced to ecclesiastical orders, the abbot who presents them to the bishop must take the greatest care that they are suitable and approved, in accordance with what Saint Benedict says: ‘If any abbot asks that a presbyter or deacon be ordained for him, let him choose from among his own men one who is worthy to perform the priestly office.’”

For that man who is still alive, who treacherously killed Bishop Stephen, when he could find no penance sufficient for so great a crime, sought the monastery of Cluny and became a monk there. Since he knew how to read and sing like a trained cleric, Abbot Odilo was considering presenting him to the bishop for the degrees of the altar. But the venerable abbot, acting prudently, sent a letter to the Roman pope requesting his advice and informing him of the monk’s crime. The pope sent him this reply:

“It is impossible for such a man to be advanced to any order; nor can he offer an oblation into the hands of a priest, lest perhaps, on account of that one man, the fury of the Lord descend upon many. Nor may he receive holy Communion. At the end of his life, however, let the viaticum be given to him as an act of mercy. Here let him do nothing but mourn, if perhaps he may find mercy there. Thus let him live henceforth, remaining in the mourning of penance, neither offering nor receiving Communion.”

The matter of the times for ordinations was also investigated, since some bishops now conduct ordinations throughout the entire year, something earlier bishops did not do. The statutes of the Fathers were therefore reviewed, and it was found that ordinations to the various orders are rightly performed in March, June, September, and December—namely, on the Saturday of the Twelve Readings, when the fasts of the Four Seasons are observed. If there is such a large number of ordinands that the bishop cannot consecrate them all on Saturday, those who remain are to be ordained on the following Sunday, from morning until the sixth hour.

At other times ordinations are in no way to be conducted, except in a case of great necessity, and then only to the diaconate or presbyterate. Nor may they take place on any feast except Sunday, and even then only when a general fast has preceded it on Saturday. A bishop himself may likewise be ordained only on Sunday, around the third hour of the day. It is certain concerning Saint Gregory that he never performed ordinations except in March. Blessed Peter the Apostle, however, did so in December and nowhere else; in June only blessed [lacuna]; and in September, and not at any other time, blessed [lacuna].

Again, the matter of the excommunicated men of Aquitaine was investigated [perhaps: complained of]. They receive penance and absolution from the Roman pope without the knowledge of their own bishops, and for this reason peace and the council in Aquitaine are being destroyed: those whom these bishops justly bind, he unjustly absolves. In response, the venerable Engelricus, a canon of the church of Saint Mary of Le Puy, began to explain, saying:

“Some years ago Stephen, bishop of Auvergne, bound Count Pontius of Auvergne with excommunication because of his lawful wife, whom he had dismissed and had taken another woman. Since he was unwilling to absolve him by any means unless he had made amends, the count obtained absolution at Rome from the lord pope, while the pope was unaware that he had been excommunicated. The bishop took this very seriously and sent a letter of complaint to Rome to the apostolic, who sent him this reply:

‘What I did unknowingly, dearest brother, is not my fault but yours. For you know that whenever anyone from the whole Church of God, which is throughout the entire world, comes to me seeking a remedy, it is impossible for me to neglect his care, since the Lord said specifically to blessed Peter: “Peter, feed my sheep” (John 21). How, then, could the Apostolic See exclude anyone from healing without a reasonable cause? You ought certainly to have made his case known to me in writing before that sick sheep came to Rome; then I would have rejected her in every way and, by confirming your authority, struck her back with the blow of anathema. For I confess to all my fellow priests throughout the world that I am their helper and consoler rather than their opponent. May schism be far from me and from my fellow bishops. Therefore, the penance and absolution that I unknowingly gave to your excommunicated man, and that he fraudulently accepted, I declare invalid and void, so that he may expect nothing from it except a curse until you justly absolve him after satisfaction has been made.’”

The bishops therefore said to one another:

“In vain does this complaint dare to murmur against our head. The apostolic is without fault, and rather we are culpable unless we make known to him by our letters the persons whom we do not wish to be absolved. When such men deceive the apostolic so that they are fraudulently absolved by him, that absolution is invalid for them and therefore is to be confirmed neither by him nor by us.”

Someone at the council said:

“Recently I witnessed the matter concerning the bishop of Angoulême, who is present here, and I shall relate it. One of his parishioners, having been excommunicated by him and refusing to make satisfaction, was unable to obtain penance from him. Without the permission of his own bishop, he secretly obtained from the Roman pope a rule of penance and brought the bishop a letter in the pope’s name on Maundy Thursday. In it the apostolic asked the bishop to confirm for the man the penance that he had supposedly imposed.

“The bishop, recognizing the fraud, said to the man: ‘The roles are reversed: what I ought to have requested from the apostolic, the apostolic is requesting from me. I cannot believe that this command originated with him. It is of no benefit to you. Until you receive penance either from me or, at my command, from the archdeacon of this see, remain in excommunication.’ And he drove him out of the church.”

The bishops said:

“We hold it as established by the Roman apostolics themselves and by the other Fathers that, if a bishop imposes penance upon his parishioner and sends him to the pope to judge whether he is worthy of penance for such a crime, the authority of the pope may confirm it, lessen it, or add to it. For the judgment of the whole Church is especially established in the Roman Apostolic See.

“Likewise, if a bishop sends his parishioner to the apostolic, with witnesses or letters, to receive penance—as often happens in the case of very serious crimes, when bishops hesitate to impose a penance appropriate to the offense—that man may lawfully obtain a remedy from the pope. But no one may receive penance and absolution from the apostolic without consulting his own bishop.

“To give an example: Blessed Martial, the apostle of Aquitaine, had already imposed penance upon King Stephen of Gaul, who under Nero possessed authority to govern Gaul as far as the Pyrenees, for the killing of the virgin Valeria and other crimes. He had already purified him in the baptismal font, through which all offenses are wiped away. Nevertheless, because the ruler was required, at Nero’s command, to hurry to Rome with the Gallic legions, he visited the blessed Apostle Peter—after, as we believe, being forewarned by blessed Martial—and asked him to absolve him for the killing of the virgin.

“That absolution of the ruler by blessed Peter was certainly a confirmation of the absolution and penance that blessed Martial had imposed upon him. Indeed, if blessed Peter had known that he was bound by excommunication from blessed Martial, he would have condemned him rather than absolved him.

“In the same way, the Roman apostolics ought to confirm the judgment of all bishops, not dissolve it. For just as the members must follow their head, so the head must not distress its members.

“I shall relate for edification what once happened to a soldier in Gascony. At the command of Sancho, duke of the Gascons, he beheaded his lord, although unwillingly: terrified by the duke’s madness, he had done it because the enraged duke threatened him, saying, ‘Unless you kill this man, I shall kill you.’ With a single blow he beheaded his own lord. Filled with the most grievous sorrow, he hurried to his bishop for penance.

“The bishop, moved by compassion, said to him: ‘You ought to have accepted death for your lord before laying hands upon him in any way, and thus to have become a martyr of God for such faithfulness. But you have committed a most serious crime, one unheard of among us. I do not know how to advise you concerning penance, but go as quickly as possible to the Roman pope. If he grants you penance, I shall rejoice and confirm it; if he rejects you, you will never find penance either from me or from anyone else.’”

The man promptly carried this out and took with him letters from his bishop, together with witnesses. When the apostolic was celebrating the sacred rites at Saint Peter’s on the Monday after Easter and had sat down after the Gospel, the guilty man began to cry out before him, in the presence of the whole Church, weeping and sighing bitterly:

“Penance I want, lord; penance I want, lord.”

The apostolic said to those standing beside him on his right and left:

“Ask for what offense.”

When questioned, the man said nothing other than:

“I have offended my Creator; I have offended my Creator.”

The apostolic said to him:

“Why, then, did you not seek your bishop?”

He replied:

“My bishop sent me to you.”

Then the witnesses explained the crime to the apostolic and presented him with the bishop’s letter. The apostolic therefore spoke to the bishop who was standing at his right, saying:

“Consider the divine authority: by what penance can this dead man be brought to life?”

The bishop replied:

“The Lord says in the Gospel: ‘Everyone who has left house, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or fields for my name’s sake shall receive a hundredfold’ (Matthew 19) [lacuna].”

The rest is lacking.

## In the Year of the Lord 1053. Guido, Archbishop of Reims

## Historical Notice Concerning Guido of Châtillon

*(Gallia Christiana, vol. IX, p. 65.)*

In the year 1033, in the month of July, Guido of Châtillon entered upon the archiepiscopal dignity. Andreas Quercetanus has carefully traced his lineage in his genealogical History of the House of Châtillon. He had two brothers, Gervasius of Châtillon, vice-lord of the Church of Reims—the office at that time being held by laymen—and Miletius of Châtillon.

Entrusted to the school of Reims from childhood, he diligently trained himself for several years in the canonical life and ecclesiastical rites. In the second year of his episcopate, he gave the altar of Saint Stephen to the nuns of Saint Peter of Reims; in 1040, he gave the altar of Crusciniacus to the monks of Saint Remigius.

In that same year, when a dispute arose between the Church of Reims and Richard, abbot of Saint Vannes of Verdun, over the coinage of Mouzon—which Archbishop Ebalus had joined to the Reims mint—Guido reasserted the church’s prior possession by entering into an agreement with the abbot. To compensate him for the loss, he generously granted him the parish of Vineyards.

In 1043 he gave the church of Germereium to the monastery of Mouzon. In 1047 he subscribed King Henry’s judgment in favor of the monastery of Saint Medard against Robert of Couches. In 1048 he attended the council of Senlis.

In 1049 he received Pope Leo IX with great pomp in his metropolitan city, accompanied by the archbishops of Trier, Lyon, and Besançon. There the most holy pontiff dedicated the basilica of Reims on the sixth day before the Nones of October and, on the following day, celebrated a council in the same church attended by twenty bishops and fifty abbots. A dispute arose in Leo’s presence between the churches of Reims and Trier concerning the primacy of the see and the prerogative of seating; it was debated but not resolved. For this reason, so that every opportunity for contention might be removed, the seats of the prelates were arranged in the form of a circle.

What was established at that synod is shown by the canons enacted against the heresy of simony and certain other vices, by which many, both bishops and counts, were struck with anathema. But since Baronius has reported the complete acts of the council from the archive of the Church of Reims, as well as a longer history for this same year, it is sufficient to touch briefly, from the Sammarthani, upon the matters more closely concerning Guido.

“They say that on the fifth day before the Nones of October the bishops, twenty in number, assembled in the aforementioned basilica, together with forty abbots and many others of the ecclesiastical order. There the old dispute between the clerics of the archbishops of Reims and Trier was immediately renewed. The former maintained that the archbishop of Reims was primate in Gaul and that the synodical arrangement therefore belonged to him; the others, by contrast, tried to ascribe the same dignity to the archbishop of Trier and to grant him the first seat after the prelate of the Roman Church when the council was celebrated, and so forth.

“After this, everyone sat in the order established by the archbishop of Reims. The lord pope sat in the middle of the choir, facing the tomb of Blessed Remigius; the archbishop of Reims sat on his right, and the archbishop of Trier on his left. After the archbishop of Reims sat Beroldus of Soissons, Drogo of Thérouanne, Frollandus of Senlis, and Adelbero of Metz.

“On the southern side sat Haimardus, archbishop of Lyon; Hugo of Langres; Joffridus of Coutances; Ivo of Sées; Herbert of Lisieux; Hugo of Bayeux; Hugo of Avranches; and Theodoricus of Verdun. On the northern side sat Hugo, archbishop of Besançon; Hugo of Nevers; Eusebius of Angers; Pudicus of Nantes; the bishop of the English; and John of Porto.

“Behind them the abbots likewise sat in a circle, in this order: Herimarus, abbot of Saint Remigius; Hugo of Cluny; Sigefridus of Gorze; Fulco of Corbie; Rotbertus of Prüm; Rainoldus of Saint Medard; Girvinius of Saint Richarius; Gotfridus of Vézelay; Arnoldus of Pultaria; Rodolfus of Mouzon; Oylardus of Châlons; Milo of Der; Norgaudus of Hautvillers; Albertus of Saint Thierry; Stephanus of Saint Urban; Wlricus of Saint Augustine of Canterbury; and Alwinus of Saint Benedict in the land of the English.

“When they had taken their seats, Peter, a deacon of the holy Roman Church, rose at the pope’s command and set forth clearly the matters to be discussed at the synod: the many illicit practices carried on in the regions of Gaul contrary to the decrees of the canons—namely, the heresy of simony; ecclesiastical offices and altars held by laymen; the depraved customs that they exacted in the churchyards; incestuous marriages; those who, abandoning their lawful wives, became entangled again in adulterous marriages; monks and clerics who abandoned their holy profession and habit; clerics devoted to worldly warfare; the Sodomitic vice; and certain heresies that had sprung up in those same regions.

“After presenting these matters, he admonished everyone present to deliberate with him prudently and to offer counsel, together with the pope’s timely assistance, on how these weeds—the seed of a corrupt crop—might be uprooted before they choked everything.

“After this he turned his speech to the bishops and, under threat of the anathema of apostolic authority, urged them that if any of them had obtained his position through simony or had advanced anyone to the same dignity for a reward, he should disclose it by public confession.

“First the archbishop of Trier rose in response to these words and declared that he had neither given nor promised anything for obtaining the episcopate, nor sold sacred orders to anyone. Then the archbishops of Lyon and Besançon rose and professed themselves free from such guilt.

“Then the aforementioned deacon turned to the archbishop of Reims and asked him to state what he had to say concerning the matters from which the others had purged themselves. Rising, he asked for a delay until the following day, saying that he wished to speak privately with the lord apostolic. When this was granted, all the others rose in order, following the words of those who had gone before, and cleared themselves of such suspicion, with only four exceptions: the bishops of Langres, Nevers, Coutances, and Nantes. Their case was left for examination that day, and the deacon turned the course of his speech toward the abbots who were present, admonishing them to confess if perhaps they too had entered the Lord’s fold from somewhere else, rather than through the door.

“Herimarus, abbot of Saint Remigius, rose first and cleared himself of such guilt with an appropriate answer. Then Hugo of Cluny followed and added this account of his purification, saying: ‘In order to obtain the honor of the abbacy, with God as my witness, I neither gave nor promised anything; my flesh indeed desired it, but mind and reason resisted.’

“After him some attempted to excuse themselves suitably; others, answering nothing, preferred to conceal their guilt rather than disclose it.

“Then the bishop of Langres rose and complained at length about the abbot of Pultaria, his diocesan, alleging that, living in the stench of lust, he engaged in many disgraces, had refused to pay each year the tribute owed to blessed Peter and to his vicar, the pontiff of the Roman Church, to whom that abbey belonged, and, although excommunicated for this reason, had presumed to celebrate the mysteries of the Mass and, while still subject to excommunication, had attended that same synod. When he was examined and proved unable to clear himself of the crimes charged against him, he was deposed from the dignity of his office, and so forth.

“On the following day, when the bishops had gathered at the aforementioned basilica, the pope withdrew with some of them into the oratory of the Holy Trinity. There, after the bishop of Reims had held a private conversation with him concerning his confession and they had spent a long time discussing the advancement of ecclesiastical religion, the apostolic proceeded forth in the same order as on the preceding day.

“After they had taken their seats, the aforementioned chancellor instructed the archbishop of Reims to give an account of the heresy of simony, concerning which he had obtained a delay the previous day. He also accused him of many other crimes that, as he asserted, he had learned through widespread report.

“The archbishop rose in response and requested that he be granted the opportunity for consultation. After this was granted, he summoned the bishops of Besançon, Soissons, Angers, Nevers, Senlis, and Thérouanne and held a private consultation with them. Returning from it, he obtained permission from the pope for the bishop of Senlis to plead his case.

“The bishop of Senlis rose and replied that the archbishop was not guilty of the heresy of simony. After hearing this, the apostolic ordered the archbishop to prove by oath that this was so. But he requested canonical time for deliberation and promised that, once it had elapsed, he would do what the requirements of his defense demanded.

“When this was granted, it was decreed that he should attend the council to be held at Rome in mid-April. As for the other charges brought against him, since they seemed to lack the testimony of a legitimate accuser, it was decreed that for the present they should remain unexamined.”

The acts of the council narrate these matters in precisely these words. Anyone who wishes to know more about the remaining events should consult Baronius.

After returning from this synod, Guido celebrated, in 1051, at his metropolitan church, the marriage of Henry I, king of the Franks, and Anna, and consecrated Lietbert as bishop of Cambrai.

In 1052, on the sixth day before the Nones of May, in what they call the twenty-ninth year of his episcopate—or rather the nineteenth—he celebrated the elevation of the body of Blessed Bertin in the monastery of Sithiu. Drogo of Thérouanne and the abbots Herimarus of Saint Remigius, Alfred of Saint Wilmar, Gervinus of Saint Richarius, Fulbert of Saint Bavo, and Rumold of Saint Winoc were present, as was Adela, daughter of Robert, king of the Franks, and wife of Baldwin of Lille, who generously supplied the cloth in which the relics were wrapped.

In the same year he subscribed a charter issued by King Henry I in favor of the new monastery of La Chaise-Dieu. In 1053 he granted the altar of the basilica of La Cour to the monastery of Saint Remigius, where he had chosen burial. In that same year he confirmed the gift that Manasses, the son of his brother, had made to the same monastery at a place called Urillo. He was also present at the discovery of the sacred bodies in the church of Saint-Denis near Paris.

Finally, after giving his assent to the restoration of the monastery of Sparnacum, he ended his days on the Kalends of September in the year 1053 and was buried at Saint Remigius.

## Diplomas of Guido

### I. Privilege of Guido Granted to Odila, Abbess of the Monastery of Saint Peter  
*(Year 1035.)*

*[Dom. Marlot, Metropolis Remensis, II, 84.]*

In the name of God. Amen.

I, Guido, archbishop of Reims, wish it to be known to all worshipers of the Christian faith, present and future, what common settlement of our agreement we made with Odila, abbess of Saint Peter, and with the nuns, concerning the altar of Saint Stephen.

After Dodon’s death, the aforementioned altar came into our hand and power. When the abbess heard of Dodon’s death, she went as quickly as she could into the presence of our [lacuna] familiarity and requested that I grant the aforesaid altar to Saint Peter without personal tenure.

[Note: “It is granted to be held impersonally, that is, without a person who succeeds as its true title-holder; thus perhaps the altar is granted together with its burden.”]

We assented to the petition of the abbess and the nuns on this condition: for as long as we remain alive in this world, they are to remember us in their prayers at every hour.

After the final day, having taken away the light, has closed our eyes, our anniversary is to be observed by them each year, as the agreement provided, so that on that day, for the remedy of our soul, a vigil is celebrated and the commemoration of the dead is made. Twelve presbyters are to be summoned, and the same number of Masses sung that day. For the remedy of our soul, thirty poor persons are to be fed in the refectory and gathered together in memory of us; and, as has been said, they are to be refreshed in the name of Christ on account of the aforesaid altar, because it is written: “What you have done for one of the least of mine, you have done for me.”

And so that this written instrument of our authority, which we have made, may remain unshaken for all days, we confirm it completely by our authority. Moreover, for Saint Peter, the key-bearer of the kingdom of heaven, to whom we have granted the aforesaid altar, we ourselves have confirmed this document and caused it to be strengthened by the hands of our faithful men.

Executed at Reims, in the eighth year of the reign of King Henry and the second year of the episcopate of Lord Guido.

Witness-signature of Harduinus, archdeacon.

Witness-signature of Richardus, archdeacon.

Witness-signature of Conrannus, dean.

Witness-signature of Albertus, chamberlain.

Witness-signature of Albericus.

Witness-signature of Harduinus, provost of this place.

Oldaricus wrote and subscribed this in the place of Harduinus the chancellor.

### II. Charter of Archbishop Guido by Which He Grants the Altar of Crusciniacus to the Monks of Saint Remigius  
*(Year 1040.)*

*[D. Marlot, Metropolis Remensis, II, 85.]*

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. I, Guido, by the grace of God archbishop of Reims, wish to make known to the faithful of our Church, present and future, how, at the repeated prayers and entreaties of Lord Abbot Theodoricus and the others, I granted the altar in the village called Crusciniacus to the monastery of Saint Remigius, for the remedy of my soul, for the glory of God and also out of love for our blessed Father and predecessor Remigius. I clearly recognized that it was fitting to yield to just petitions and that the Lord is honored in the veneration of his holy confessor.

For I did not consider it right to deny the requested gift to the apostle and patron of the Franks, under whose protection we hope always and everywhere to be defended. But so that my action in granting the altar might not be considered rash or unauthorized,[Note: Altars were first granted to monasteries under a vicarial arrangement of persons, as Guido here grants Crusciniacus to the Remigians; later they were given by bishops free from every personal tenure in favor of religious, as is clear from the charter of Elinand, bishop of Laon, in the *Historia Dionysii*, fol. 463. Likewise, concerning the altar of Saint Thomas granted by Archbishop Manasses in 1096: “I assigned the altar of blessed Thomas to Saint Remigius, and, in order that brethren serving God might be gathered there, I granted it to be held without a person.”] with the consent and counsel of Beroldus, bishop of Soissons, and at the urging of our clergy and laymen, I granted the aforesaid altar to Saint Remigius to possess by perpetual right, on the condition that, when one title-holder died, another would be presented by the abbot of the place and the altar returned to him without any payment, and that such succession of title-holders would continue forever.

It is nevertheless required that, in recognition of it, he pay eighteen denarii annually at the synod, as the other altars do, both to me and to my successors.

Wishing the agreement of this grant to remain inviolate, I have taken care to commit it to writing for posterity’s preservation. Indeed, by the authority of God almighty, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and with the merits of the blessed Virgin Mary, Saint Remigius, and all the saints assisting, we excommunicate the violator of the aforesaid agreement, with these witnesses present.

Guido, archbishop.

Albricus, provost.

Constantinus, dean.

Beroldus, bishop.

Guntrannus, chorbishop.

Richardus, Odalricus, and others.

Executed at Reims in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1040, indiction 8, during the twelfth year of the reign of King Henry and the seventh year of the episcopate of Lord Guido. The chancellor Vauterannus wrote and subscribed it.

[Note: The seal displays the archbishop’s half-length image with the inscription: “Seal of Guido, Archbishop of Reims.”]

### III. Agreement of Guido, Archbishop of Reims, with Richard, Abbot of Saint Vannes of Verdun  
*(Year 1040.)*

*[Varin, Archives administratives de la ville de Reims, p. 206, from the chartulary of Saint Vannes of Verdun.]*

I, Guido, by God’s gift archbishop of Reims, wish it to be known to all the faithful of our Church, present and future, that I granted the altar of Wivariis to the monastery of Blessed Peter and Saint Vannes in the suburb of Verdun, with the following matter attached to the grant.

Richard, the abbot, and the brothers of the same monastery complained to me that my predecessor, Lord Ebalus, had unjustly taken the Mouzon mint from the aforesaid monastery, although they lawfully held it by a gift of Emperor Henry, also through the intervention of Count Herimannus, whose benefice it had been. For Ebalus had joined it to the Reims mint.

Although the lord abbot Richard and his brothers had frequently petitioned me concerning this matter, I refused to return the mint they were claiming, lest I seem to diminish the advantage of our own revenue and make the Reims mint less valuable by reducing it. After taking counsel with our faithful clergy and laymen concerning the restoration of the Mouzon mint, and because God is honored through acts of service, I granted the aforesaid altar to the person presented by them, with this provision of the privilege: when the title-holder died, the altar would be returned, for the monks’ use, to another person without any payment, and such succession of title-holders would continue forever.

We have taken care to confirm this decree of our authority by writing it as an official instrument, so that no one might henceforth presume to violate it. If anyone should attempt to do so, let him beware lest he close the gates of heaven to himself by inflicting an injury upon the doorkeeper and taking away his property.

Given in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1040, indiction 8. Executed at Reims during the second year of the reign of King Henry and the seventh year of the episcopate of Lord Guido. Odalricus the chancellor wrote and subscribed it.

### IV. Charter of Guido, Archbishop of Reims, Concerning the Altar of Germereium for the Monastery of Mouzon  
*(Year 1043.)*

*[Mabillon, De re diplomatica II, 603, from the original charter.]*

In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Let it be known to all the faithful, present and future, that I, Guido, archbishop of Reims, with the support of Odo the archdeacon and likewise of the community of canons, and at the request of Lord Abbot Rodulfus and the other brothers, have granted an altar in the village called Germereium to the abbey of Saint Mary of Mouzon, for the remedy of my soul.

The condition is that, when the title-holder of that altar dies, another person presented by the abbot, whomever he may choose, is to be canonically installed without any gift or payment. And so that this may remain firm and stable forever, we strike the violator and breaker of this arrangement with the dart of anathema and bind him with the chain of excommunication.

Sign of Guido, prelate of Reims.

Sign of Odo the archdeacon. Sign of Albricus the provost. Sign of Warinus the archdeacon. Sign of Constantius the dean. Sign of Richardus the cantor. Sign of Richerus the presbyter. Sign of Albertus. Sign of Rotgerus. Sign of Gerardus. Sign of Erlebardus. Sign of Hugo. Sign of Widricus. Sign of Odo. Sign of Sigebertus. Sign of Herimannus. Sign of Leuvinus. Sign of Hugo. Sign of Manasses. Sign of Rodericus. Sign of Rotbertus.

Executed at Reims in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1043, indiction 11, during the seventeenth year of the reign of Henry, king of the Franks, and the eleventh year of the episcopate of Lord Guido, archbishop. Odalricus the chancellor wrote it.

### V. Archbishop Guido of Reims Confirms the Gift of Manasses, His Nephew, to Herimarus, Abbot of Saint Remigius, of Certain Lands Situated on the Border of the Castle of Saint Remigius, by This Charter Subscribed by Noble Neighbors  
*(Year 1053.)*

*[D. Marlot, Metropolis Remensis, II, 110.]*
In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity.

At the boundary of the estate of Saint Remigius there is land adjoining the neighboring lands in the village of Saint Remigius, on the side called Viridate (Vrilly), belonging to a certain viscount of Reims named Manasses Calvus, nephew of Archbishop Wido. Therefore, wishing to build there near the aforementioned village a small residence called Tollensvia—so named because it took away a road that was customarily used, since this land was contiguous with and intermingled among the other lands of Saint Remigius, lest the people cultivating those lands should at some time suffer any trouble from the lord possessing the land mentioned above [Col. 1408D]—the lord Abbot Herimarus asked Manasses Calvus, in the presence of Archbishop Wido, to give it to Saint Remigius for the remedy of his own soul and those of his sons.

He, however, refused to do this unless one hundred solidi were given to him every year during his lifetime and afterward to his heir. Herimarus, having taken counsel with Count Manasses, who was then present, and with the other landholders acting on the instruction of the aforementioned archbishop, refused to agree to give him the stated payment of one hundred solidi except for as long as he lived. Finally, at the urging of everyone present, indeed at the entreaty and command [Col. 1409A] of his uncle, the archbishop named above, he ultimately consented that Manasses should have one hundred solidi as long as he lived, but after his death Saint Remigius should possess both the land and the money by undisputed right.

Accordingly, Archbishop Wido ordered this agreement to be committed to writing in his presence, and, so that it might remain unshaken through the passage of succeeding ages, he confirmed it with the seal of archiepiscopal authority and with the testimony of the clergy and laymen who were present.

The sign of Lord Wido, archbishop.

[Col. 1410A] The sign of Odo, archdeacon.

The sign of Herimarus, abbot, and others.

Among the laymen, the sign of Manasses, count. The sign of Roger, count. The sign of Rainold, count of Soissons. The sign of Wido, knight.

This was enacted at Reims, in the church of Saint Mary, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1053, indiction 6, while Henry, king of the Franks, was reigning in the twenty-fourth year of his reign, and in the twentieth year of Wido’s archiepiscopate. Odalricus, chancellor, wrote this.

[Col. 1409]

## EPITAPH OF GUIDO

(D. Marlot, *Metropolis Remensis*, II, 111.)

O fleeting honor of the world, nobles! Why should you be loved?

While it remains, it torments; and afterward, see what comes to pass.

For twice eleven years, together with two months,

Wido possessed the archbishopric of Reims.

He stands pious and humble at the summit of nobility.

Alas for his wretched lot! His rotting flesh makes him a worm,

But may Jesus cherish his soul through the power of his name,

As he left his earthly prison on the Kalends of September.

## Around the Year of the Lord 1054–1057: Anselm, Monk of Saint Remigius of Reims

[Col. 1409]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE

(*Histoire littéraire de la France*, vol. VII, p. 477.)

[Col. 1409B] Anselm has this in common with several other writers: we know him almost exclusively through the works of his pen. If we are to trust Trithemius (*Chronicon Hirsaugiense*, vol. I, p. 202; *Scriptores*, ch. 333), he was a man versed in every kind of liberal learning, especially in understanding the sacred Scriptures. What is certain is that he was a man of merit and possessed enough talent to write fairly well for his age.

At Saint Remigius of Reims, where he was a monk, he had several fellow brothers who were men of learning and virtue, some of whom were raised to the highest dignities of the cloister (Mabillon, *Annales*, I, p. 63, n. 88). Nevertheless, he was the one whom Herimarus, their abbot, chose in preference to give an account of what had occurred at Saint Remigius during the dedication of the church, [Col. 1410B] performed in 1049 by Pope Leo IX (Mabillon, *Acta*, vol. VIII, p. 713, n. 1).

Since Anselm had witnessed these events and possessed the qualities just mentioned, he was well suited to succeed in this undertaking. He did not, however, carry it out until several years later, and at the earliest in 1056, when Gervais had already become archbishop of Reims after having been bishop of Le Mans—a change that took place the preceding year. Although his work bears simply the title *History of the Dedication of the Church of Saint Remigius of Reims*, Anselm nevertheless incorporated into it, with detail as pleasant as it is instructive, several celebrated events that preceded and followed the ceremony.

One may distinguish five or six parts in the body of his account, almost all of which are announced [Col. 1411A] in the preface addressed to the monks of Saint Remigius. First, the author describes the construction of the new church that was dedicated and makes known the one that had previously existed. He then recounts the journey undertaken by Pope Leo IX from Rome to Reims to perform this dedication, carefully marking everything memorable that occurred along the way. For this reason Sigebert (*Scriptores*, ch. 152) gave Anselm’s entire work the title *The Itinerary of Pope Leo IX from Rome into Gaul*, while Trithemius (*Scriptores*, ch. 333) called it *The History of What This Pope Did in France, in the Holding of Councils and Other Assemblies*. From there Anselm proceeds to describe the dedication and the translation of the body of Saint Remigius, which took place on [Col. 1411B] the second day of October in the already mentioned year 1049. This portion of the history, like the rest, is written with a noble simplicity, an orderliness, and a detail that delight the reader. After this comes the account of the great council held on the two following days, the third and fourth of October. This is the most fully detailed and also the most interesting part of the work. Sigebert and Trithemius had not read it attentively, since, when discussing the events of that assembly, they attribute to the bishop of Freising what the account says happened to Hugh, archbishop of Besançon. Finally, Anselm concludes his work with several miracles that had occurred since the dedication, to which he appended the Pope’s letter to the French, urging them to celebrate [Col. 1411C] the feast of the translation of Saint Remigius on the first of October.

[Col. 1412A] Baronius was the first to print Anselm’s work (Baronius, *Annales*, vol. XI, Appendix, pp. 1055–1070), but without the author’s name and after removing the first part. Dom Marlot subsequently published it in full, except for the preface and a few lines immediately preceding the letter of Pope Leo IX (Marlot, vol. II, pp. 88–104). The continuators of Bollandus also incorporated several passages into their learned observations on the Life of the same pope (Bollandists, 19 April, pp. 642–644). The *General Collection of Councils* likewise contains everything that Baronius had already published from the same work (Collection of Councils, vol. IX, pp. 1028–1045). The best edition is that published by Dom Mabillon from the manuscripts of Saint Remigius of Reims, with [Col. 1412B] historical and critical observations (Mabillon, ibid., pp. 711–727). On the basis of this edition, the celebrated Abbé Fleury made an extensive extract from the work, one of the finest passages in volume XII of his *Ecclesiastical History* (Fleury, *Histoire ecclésiastique*, book LIX, nos. 59–63).

At the beginning of Anselm’s text, in a manuscript of Saint Martin of Tournai (Sanderus, *Bibliotheca Belgica*, manuscript, part I, pp. 126–127), there is the purported letter of the great Saint Benedict to Saint Remigius, bishop of Reims; following it is another letter from the monks of Saint Remigius to those of Monte Cassino, assuring the latter that the preceding letter is genuine and informing them about its transmission from Italy to France. There seems to be [Col. 1412C] no reason to doubt that this second letter too is a work of Anselm.

[Col. 1411C]

# HISTORY OF THE DEDICATION OF THE CHURCH OF SAINT REMIGIUS AT REIMS, BY ANSELM, MONK AND CONTEMPORARY OF THAT PLACE

(Mabillon, *Acta Benedictina*, vol. VIII, p. 711.)

## PRELIMINARY OBSERVATIONS

[Col. 1411D] 1. More than once in these *Acts* we have already spoken of the renowned archmonastery of Saint Remigius at Reims; but no occasion has yet arisen that commended its dignity so greatly as the dedication of its basilica, performed by blessed Leo IX, supreme pontiff. The most holy pope omitted absolutely nothing that could make it renowned, coming into Gaul especially with the intention of openly demonstrating before the whole world the profound religious devotion with which he was bound to blessed Remigius. Accordingly, after announcing a synod to be held in the same basilica, he invited bishops [Col. 1412D] and the leading men of both orders to assemble for this celebration. Although, through the envy of certain ill-disposed persons, the king of the Franks—occupied with suppressing rebels—was not present at the solemnity, such a multitude of every order nevertheless gathered for it that the broadest streets of the city and the spacious basilica could scarcely contain them.

That people came here from almost all the nations of Europe is expressly affirmed, among other authors, by Wibertus the archdeacon, who was the blessed pontiff’s constant companion. For, besides Italians and [Col. 1413A] Germans, who were present in large numbers, he speaks of the other peoples in Book II, chapter 4, of the *Life of Saint Leo*:

> “Pope Leo was invited by Herimarus, abbot of the venerable monastery of the holy pontiff of Reims, to consecrate the church built in his honor. There it is not easy to say how great a multitude came from the ends of the earth—Spaniards, Britons, Franks, and English—to behold his presence. A considerable gathering of pontiffs was also present on that occasion.”

2. Anselm, a monk of that same monastery of Saint Remigius, deliberately described this solemnity. At the command of Abbot Herimarus, he published a separate little work on the subject under the title *The Itinerary of Pope Leo*, in which he sets out individually everything he had seen and heard as a participant. [Col. 1413B] Trithemius mentions this author in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, where he writes that Anselm was extremely well versed in the divine Scriptures and had published other short works besides the *Itinerary*. Concerning the *Itinerary*, he says:

> “He gathered into a single volume the deeds accomplished by Pope Leo IX throughout Gaul in councils and assemblies, to make known with what authority he celebrated a synod at Reims and in other cities, with what diligence and subtlety he examined ecclesiastical cases, with what severity he corrected sinners, and how divine power cooperated with him,” and so forth.

Trithemius borrowed this from Sigebert, who has exactly the same words in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*. Marlotus too mentions Anselm, after the publication of other authors, in volume II of his *History of Reims*, among the illustrious men who flourished at Reims under Archbishop Gervais. Since this little work has already been published almost piecemeal, it seemed appropriate to publish it here in full from the Reims manuscripts, lest the account of a celebration so distinguished—and perhaps the greatest ever held for the dedication of a church—be absent from these *Acts*.

3. Besides Anselm, other writers also celebrated in their works the dedication of the Remigian basilica and the council held there. William of Jumièges, in Book VII of his *History of the Normans*, has an entire chapter, chapter 15, on this subject. There he relates certain matters about Ivo, bishop of Séez, that are not reported in Anselm’s little work [Col. 1413D] and that therefore seemed worth presenting here:

> “At that time Saint Leo, pope, went to Gaul, consecrated the church of Saint Remigius, bishop of Reims, and transferred his body into the newly dedicated church. Then the same pope held a great council at Reims and sharply rebuked negligent bishops or abbots. Among them, as they say, he said to Ivo because of the burning of a church: ‘What have you done, traitor? By what law ought you to be condemned, you who dared to burn your mother?’ The eloquent Ivo openly confessed that he had indeed done wrong, but that he had been compelled to commit this crime under severe pressure, lest worse things be done by criminals against the sons of the Church. He then accepted penance according to the command of the discerning pope and set about restoring the church of Saint Gervais. From there he went to Apulia and [Col. 1414A] then to Constantinople . . . . . Upon returning to Séez, he began to build such a large church,” and so forth.

Ivo had not, however, maliciously set fire to his church, as is clear from chapter 13 of the same book. Rather, when it had been occupied by rioters, the neighboring houses were set on fire; and, as the wind blew, the blaze grew so fierce that the church too was burned together with them.

Orderic Vitalis also mentions this dedication and the council held on that occasion, in Book V of his *Ecclesiastical History*, where he observes that from that time priests gradually abandoned the custom of carrying weapons.

> “Then,” he says, “he held a general council there and, among the other benefits for the Church that he instituted, prohibited priests from carrying weapons and having wives. From then on the deadly custom gradually began to disappear. Priests have indeed gladly ceased carrying weapons, but they still refuse to abstain from mistresses and to adhere to chastity.”

It is surprising that nothing is said about priests living with concubines among the canons of the council reported by Anselm, unless perhaps the canon issued against incestuous unions is understood to concern them. It is nevertheless certain that priests’ marriages were prohibited at that council, as other authors besides Orderic also observed. Alberic, in his *Chronicle*, notes that Pope Leo, on the advice of Saint Hugh, abbot of Cluny, prohibited priests’ marriages at the Council of Reims. Indeed, Raynaldus, abbot of Vézelay, writes in the Life of that same Saint Hugh that blessed Leo “held a synod at Reims to eradicate from Gaul the heresies of the Simoniacs and Nicolaitans.” And in another Life of the same saint, which Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, dedicated to Pontius, abbot of Cluny, it is reported that Leo IX held a general synod at Reims and that, at his command, Hugh delivered there “a holy and grace-filled speech, by which both the Simoniacs were expelled from the improperly obtained dignities and fornicating priests were forbidden access to the Lord’s sanctuary.” Other writers of Hugh’s Life also speak of this speech delivered at the Council of Reims, but nothing of it survives. Moreover, before these authors, Herman the Lame had already noted in his *Chronicle* that “Pope Leo held a great synod at Reims in the autumn with the bishops of Gaul.”

4. A fragment of the book on the foundation of the monastery of Ramsey in England is too important for us to omit. From it we learn that Pope Leo summoned to the Council of Reims not only bishops of Gaul but also those of other nations. It is therefore unsurprising that ancient authors commonly called it a general council. Spelman published this fragment in volume I of his *English Councils*, under the year 1049; it reads as follows:

> “This occurred after the aforementioned Ramsey abbot Alfwin had returned to his homeland, coming back from the great council celebrated at Reims by Pope Leo in the year 1049 of the incarnate Word. King Edward had honorably sent there Duduc, bishop of Wells, and Alfwin himself, abbot of Ramsey, together with Wilfric, abbot of Saint Augustine, to bring back the decrees of Christianity established there by the holy Fathers. Nor must it be passed over in silence that the aforementioned Abbot Alfwin found such favor in the eyes of Lord Pope Leo at the aforesaid Council of Reims that, at his prayers and persistent request, the Ramsey church was endowed with the privilege of the Apostolic See’s generous protection; and by the authority of his letters he fortified its rights and possessions—both those it then held and those it would later acquire lawfully—against the attacks of evildoers.”

From this fragment we learn the name of Duduc, or Duduco, who attended the Council of Reims with two English abbots, sent by [Col. 1415B] King Edward. Duduc is counted as the fourteenth bishop of Wells, a see that he held for more than twenty-seven years. Although Roger of Hoveden, in the first part of his *Annals*, reports that King Edward of the English sent two abbots to the Synod of Reims, he says nothing about a bishop sent with them. He does observe, however, that the prefect of Rome and other leading men of the city accompanied Leo on this journey. These are his words:

> “In that same year”—that is, 1049—“Pope Leo, at the request of Herimarus, abbot of outstanding piety, came to France, having in his retinue the prefect and all the more distinguished men of the city of Rome. He dedicated with the greatest honor the monastery of Saint Remigius, apostle of the Franks, established at Reims. Later, in that same city, he held a great synod of archbishops, bishops, and abbots for six days. At this synod were Aldwin of Ramsey and the abbot of the monastery of Saint Augustine, sent by Edward, king of the English. At this synod, ‘divine religion, which had grown excessively lukewarm, was diligently restored,’ as Odalricus, provost of the church of Reims, who had attended it, testifies in his testament, which we possess from a manuscript codex of the church of Reims.”

5. Finally, other authors too celebrated the dedication of the church of Saint Remigius in various writings; to list them individually would be too laborious. Here, however, we cannot omit that on this occasion the feast of Saint Remigius, already celebrated on the Kalends of October, became more solemn thereafter by order of blessed Leo. In this matter the most holy pontiff restored to its former vigor the ancient devotion of the Frankish Church toward its apostle, which perhaps had been somewhat diminished by the disturbances of war, issuing a bull on the subject that our Anselm inserted at the end of his little work.

But when this ancient veneration for the most holy bishop had again grown lukewarm in many places in Gaul, it was rekindled by a decree of the general assembly of the Gallican clergy. This decree was issued through the efforts of the most pious bishop Félix Vialart, bishop of Châlons and legate of the province of Reims, on 17 March 1657. From it letters were issued in the name of the Gallican clergy to all the bishops, announcing that it had been established that throughout the kingdom of Gaul the feast of blessed Remigius should be celebrated as a solemn feast with double rite. We shall present these letters in full below, together with the privilege of the Remigian altar.

6. Moreover, not only did the feast of blessed Remigius become solemn as a result of Leo’s decree, but also [Col. 1416C] the anniversary feast of the Dedication itself. Besides the Reims martyrologies, other external sources also commemorate it. Ferrarius included it in his *General Catalogue of All the Saints* under the second day of October, as did Andreas Saussayus in his *Gallican Martyrology*, Hugo Menardus in his Benedictine work, Bucelinus in his *Menologium*, and others.

# PROLOGUE ON THE DEDICATION OF THE CHURCH OF BLESSED REMIGIUS OF REIMS

[Col. 1415]

[Col. 1415D] 1. To the beloved brothers in Christ who serve God under the protection of blessed Remigius: the author of the following little work offers the great multitude of boundless sweetness that God has promised to those who fear him.

Since our life on earth is a time of trial, because it is weighed down by the burden of age and decay, we ought to be lifted toward the joy of renewal in the height of charity, which God commended to us through the humility of his only-begotten Son. Therefore, at the command of Lord Abbot Herimarus, I will not allow the account of the dedication of this church of the most holy Father to be obliterated by silence. But since it was accomplished, by God’s favor, by Pope Leo IX of blessed memory, I shall commit it to writing all the more worthily, insofar as my modest intellect permits.

First, therefore, I shall briefly indicate through whose efforts the earlier church was built and for what reason this present church—which now, by God’s favor, survives and has taken [Col. 1416D] its beginnings—arose from the former church, which was already threatening ruin through old age. I shall also add that, because many disturbances were stirred up by the ministers of the devil on the occasion of this dedication, and because many useful outcomes subsequently emerged from the synod held there by that same pope, I shall then append, at the end of this little work, the miracles that I learned by sight or hearing to have been performed after the dedication through the precious patron of the Franks, Remigius.

But you, brothers, whom the fervor of sincere devotion makes dwell together in divine unity in the house . . . . . accept this small service, whatever its measure, with fraternal goodwill. Do not consider in it only the charm of elegant and polished speech. Therefore do not be reluctant to read it sometimes: although you possess many golden and silver vessels in the house of your God, from which you draw the lofty and sweet-flowing cups of the Holy Spirit, nevertheless this water, even though it comes from an earthen vessel, may sometimes refresh you.

# THE ACCOUNT BEGINS

[Col. 1417]

[Col. 1417A] 2. The basilica distinguished by the body of the glorious confessor of Christ, Remigius, which endured down to modern times, was begun through the efforts of former archbishops of Reims and completed by their successor, Hincmarus, of venerable memory. It was dedicated by him in the year 852 of the incarnate Word.

It was not strengthened with sufficiently solid or elaborate construction, since the barbarian peoples who were ravaging this province at that time hindered the aforementioned prelates from carrying out such an undertaking through their frequent incursions. Thus, within 152 years, it had been so worn down by age that, already approaching collapse, it seemed to demand restoration.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1005, in the sixty-second year after the restoration of monastic discipline carried out there by the pseudo-bishop Hugh, Arnulf, archbishop, appointed Airardus abbot of that place after Hincmarus [Note: [Col. 1417D] He was the first regular abbot, elected in 954, since previously the bishops of Reims had been both archbishops and abbots, although this was contrary to the original institution. For Epiphanius is mentioned as abbot of Saint Remigius in the time of Archbishop Aegidius by Saint Gregory of Tours, Book X of the *History of the Franks*, chapter 19.], sixth in succession, a man of exceptional goodness and energetic in the cenobitic order.

When Airardus carefully considered that in his own time several pastors of the Lord’s flock had flourished throughout Gaul who had worked to restore their churches from old age to a better condition, he too resolved to devote himself to renovating the church entrusted to him. Accordingly, after bringing in men reputed to be skilled in architecture, he began to raise the structure of the future temple from squared stones, starting at the foundations. It was much more elaborate than those churches previously mentioned as having been renovated in the kingdom of Gaul, and more ambitious; for that reason it seemed impossible to complete, both to him and to the people of his age.

After administering his pastoral office for nearly twenty-eight years, he died, worn out by old age and without bringing the work he had begun to completion.

3. During his time, divine power displayed itself through many miracles at the tomb of blessed Remigius. I have decided to insert two of them into this account, since I myself witnessed them as a boy. Your affection must grant pardon if, beyond what the prologue promised, I interpose certain matters whose knowledge will nevertheless not be useless.

In the village of Saint Denis the Martyr called Curtis Superior (Consevreux), there was a certain beggar who, by the hidden judgment of God, was afflicted by so grievous a calamity that his feet denied him the support needed for walking, while his heels were bent backward and seemed naturally attached to his buttocks. Therefore, as is customary with other crippled persons, since he was unable to drag himself across the ground on little stools to beg, his brother conveyed him in a certain vehicle through holy places, both to seek the desired alms and to recover his health.

Thus it happened that he was also brought to the basilica of our frequently mentioned protector Remigius. At the hour when the sacred solemnities of Mass were being celebrated, his same brother carried him before the holy altar. When the ministers were already receiving that undefiled feast, a gift of healing flowed from the inexhaustible fountain of mercy.

In an instant his heels began to be torn away from the backsides to which they had been attached. As they returned, by divine command, to their proper position, streams of blood flowed from them as a sign of the miracle. The brothers who were present, observing these mighty works of God, struck the bells and sang devoted praises to the majesty that had worked the miracle.

4. Devotion is added to devotion, and the power of the Almighty declared the merits of his beloved Remigius through a corresponding miracle. After the same poor man had gradually gained strength and was standing on his feet, behold, another cripple arrived, dragging himself with little stools. Having learned of the novelty of the divine work performed upon the disabled man, he entered hurriedly, so that he too might deserve to enjoy the benefit of recovered health.

Nor was the hope of the man who hastened there empty for long. Before he reached the tomb of the saint, the desired healing was present: the tendons beneath his knees, which had long been contracted and stiff, were extended. He who had arrived bent over began, through heavenly grace, to raise himself by the previously unfamiliar use of his feet, and entered before the sacred limbs of the saint, through whose intervention healing had come to him, in order to give thanks.

When the assembly of the brothers saw this, it redoubled its divine praises, and those nearby who heard what had happened flocked joyfully to so delightful a spectacle. They saw there two poor men, shortly before shackled by the misery of human infirmity, though by different afflictions, now set free. Praising God, who is wondrous in his saints, they happily returned to their homes.

One of them, who had been delivered from the greater misfortune, became especially attached through love of his intercessor and remained in the monastery’s service until death. The other, after providing assistance to the bakers for some time, eventually departed.

5. Leaving these matters aside, let us return to the sequence of the account proposed. After Abbot Airardus [Note: [Col. 1418D] According to Marlot, Airardus died in 1031; his successor Theodericus died in 1048 and was succeeded by Herimarus. Their epitaphs may still be seen in the monastery of Saint Remigius; see their publication in Marlot, *Metropolis Remensis*, vol. I, book III, ch. 14.], as has been stated, had been removed by death, Theodericus succeeded him, having been appointed there by Wido, archbishop of Reims. Since he was resolved to arrange many things beneficial to the Church, he decided to place the finishing hand upon the restoration of his church, which his predecessor had begun.

But because the undertaking already begun was far too burdensome and difficult for him to complete, his plan too seemed unlikely to succeed if he attempted to carry it through. Therefore, with the advice of those considered wiser among the people entrusted to him, and of the elders of the province of Reims, he undertook with difficulty to demolish the work already begun. When it had been almost entirely demolished, leaving only certain foundations that the architects judged necessary for future buildings, he began to construct the house of God with a simpler design, but not one that was less fitting, as is easy to see by looking at it.

After this work was successfully begun in the fifth year of his appointment, many Catholic men were inflamed by the fervor of divine religion. They strove, as far as they could, to provide appropriate assistance for the work, both for the remission of their sins and for the repose of their parents, whose bodies had been buried there. Some members of the ecclesiastical household also offered their assistance with ready goodwill, bringing on their carts and oxen loads suitable for so great an undertaking.

Thus, after foundations had been laid wherever there had been none, and columns from the demolished earlier building had been properly arranged, arches carefully rolled over them began to rise, and the structure of the basilica began to grow brighter in the hands of the craftsmen. Then, once the walls of the vestibules had been raised on every side and the upper parts of the inner temple had been lifted higher, the old church dedicated in ancient times by Archbishop Hincmarus, as has been stated, was completely demolished. In the meantime, a humble temporary roof was constructed over the brothers’ choir, where they could devote themselves to divine praises without disturbance from winds and rains.

A crypt was constructed above the tomb of blessed Remigius. Although small and therefore disproportionate to his entire body, it was nevertheless beautifully supported by columns and arches.

The aforementioned abbot, constantly present as an earnest encourager, exerted himself with the greatest determination so that the work might rise to the full perfection of its design during his lifetime. He burned with the greatest desire that, if possible, he might summon the Roman pope to Gaul and have the church consecrated by apostolic blessing. [Col. 1419D]

Although this desire arose from pious devotion, divine providence, postponing its fulfillment, reserved it for his successor. Overtaken by premature death, he ended his final day, leaving the misfortune of the deepest grief to those who loved him, after completing eleven years and eight months in the government of the monastery.

Although he possessed the nobility inherited through his ancestors, he also flourished in extraordinary nobility of character. He humbled himself with exceptional gentleness before those who showed him reverence. He cultivated his subjects, especially lovers of holy religion, with devoted devotion; he was approachable to great and small alike. He was therefore loved by very many nobles of the Franks. As far as he could, he exalted and wished to exalt the honor of the Church entrusted to him.

But since the intervention of death removed the fulfillment of his pious desire, he designated as his successor the provost of that place, named Herimarus, who was still alive [Marlot: “young”]. He believed that the man who had been his assistant and collaborator above all others in carrying out the aforementioned work, and who had supplied the greatest resources from the revenues of the villages entrusted to his administration, would energetically complete what he himself had desired.

6. He was therefore appointed in place of the deceased Father, by the nearly unanimous decision of the brothers and through the ordination of the aforementioned Wido, archbishop of Reims. He did not allow the memorable undertaking of his predecessor to remain interrupted for long. First, he had the right-hand transept of the basilica, already begun to a considerable extent, and the left-hand transept, which had nothing beyond its foundations, built together with spiral stairways by which one could ascend to the upper parts.

The crypt constructed above the tomb of blessed Remigius was too small, as has been related above, and therefore seemed disproportionate to the rest of the work. He had it demolished and replaced with another, more elevated one. He then had timber brought from the forest situated near the monastery of Orbais, and the upper parts of the same church were completed. Thus the entire structure appeared as a most fitting house in all its parts [Note: [Col. 1419D] This church was later enlarged again by Peter, abbot of Celle, commonly called Peter of Celle, who was subsequently appointed successor to John of Salisbury as bishop of Chartres. He testifies that he undertook this work in his letter to the brothers of Monte Dei. Cardinal Lenoncourt also added certain elements, [Col. 1420D] and thus the mass of the church, through various additions, grew into the spacious basilica seen today.].

[Col. 1420C] **7.** Therefore the same abbot Herimarus began, together with certain wise men of the province of Reims, to deliberate with prudent counsel how, by having it consecrated with apostolic blessing, he might satisfy the devout desire of his predecessor. And, so that he might not lack the opportunity to carry out what he wished, the favor of divine providence supplied a suitable occasion. [Note: [Col. 1420D] These matters are reported more fully in the Life of Saint Leo, below under the year 1054.]

For Pope Damasus, who had been bishop in the city of Brixen, in the province of Istria, and had been enthroned in the Apostolic See, had lived there only thirty days. After sending a delegation to the emperor Henry to inform him of his death, the Romans asked that another be appointed by him to the Church, now widowed of its shepherd. Seeking the advice of the bishops and nobles of his empire concerning this matter, he found among the others that Lord Bruno, bishop of Toul, was suitable for undertaking this office, since he appeared distinguished by the maturity of his age, the excellence of his character, and the brilliance of his learning, and was also close to him by blood relationship.
