Accordingly, the insignia of apostolic dignity were assigned to him, and the emperor ordered him to visit the Roman walls in order to receive these according to the ecclesiastical regulations. But because the solemn days of the Nativity of the Lord were approaching, he arranged to celebrate them with the clergy of which he had been shepherd, and, when they had been celebrated, to depart as he had been commanded. [Col. 1421A]

The aforementioned abbot Herimarus had become acquainted with this pontiff in a conference held not long before by the aforesaid emperor and the king of the Franks, for the purpose of confirming peace and friendship. From him he had also received a promise that, during the forthcoming Lenten fast, he would visit the tomb of Saint Remigius without the assistance of a horse, because, when he had once been carrying familiar messages between those same kings and had passed through the neighboring region, he had neglected to visit the holy man’s shrine for the sake of prayer.

The abbot, recalling this carefully in his mind, sent him a letter suggesting that, since he intended to go to Rome for the office of apostolic primate entrusted to him, if at any time he were recalled to neighboring regions for a definite benefit to the Church, he should not render void the promise he had made to the apostle of the Franks. He also sent him as a gift a vessel suitable for drinking, beautifully decorated inside and out with gold, indicating to him his own desire, together with his request, concerning the dedication of the church of that saint.

In reply, the same bishop graciously stated that, even if no other benefit to the Church recalled him, or even if it were solely out of love for Saint Remigius, he would return to Gaul and dedicate his basilica, if divine goodness permitted it. Therefore, after celebrating the two days of the Nativity of the Lord in the see of the city of Toul, on the third day he bade farewell to his clergy and set out on the road leading to Rome.

When he arrived there, he was honorably received with the favor of the whole people, invested with the insignia of apostolic dignity, enthroned on the Feast of the Presentation of the Lord in the chair of Saint Peter, and, in accordance with Roman custom, named Pope Leo. Faithfully administering the duties of his office and diligently arranging whatever seemed advantageous to divine religion, he completed the fasts of Lent and celebrated there the succeeding solemnities of the Lord’s Resurrection. When these had passed, he summoned a synod of the bishops of Italy; there he either corrected whatever perverse practices were sprouting in their dioceses or urged them to correct them.

**8.** After some time had passed, both the promise made to blessed Remigius and his concern for orthodox faith—which had grown so cold in those regions—persuaded him to revisit Gaul. Having obtained permission from the Romans, he traveled through certain cities of Latium and arranged in them many things suitable to ecclesiastical propriety. At length he went to the emperor Henry, who was staying in Saxony.

Meanwhile, the aforementioned abbot, confident from the pope’s own promise that his desire would be fulfilled, went to meet the king of the Franks as he came to Laon on the solemnity of Pentecost. He sought his counsel and favor concerning the consecration of the aforesaid church with apostolic blessing, advising and requesting that he present himself for this undertaking and bring with him the bishops and princes of his kingdom.

The king graciously assented for the present [al., “to the prayers”] and declared that, unless some impediment intervened, he would attend so great a festival. The abbot, rejoicing in this promise, returned. Then, when the pope arrived at Cologne with the emperor on the feast of the Apostles Peter and Paul, the abbot went to meet him. The abbot carefully asked him about the time and order of his coming to the territory of Reims and of the actions to be carried out there.

The pope informed him that he had first decided to come there on the eighth day after the saint’s feast, which is celebrated with the greatest solemnity on the Kalends of October; after dedicating his monastery, he would then celebrate there a synod assembled from the bishops of Gaul. But, having changed this plan, he announced that he would come to the same place on the solemnity of Saint Michael the Archangel and would celebrate the sacred rites of Mass on that same day in the church of the Blessed Mary at Reims. He assigned the feast of the glorious Father Remigius to the elevation of his precious body, the following day to the consecration of the basilica, and then the remaining three days to the celebration of the synod. [Col. 1422B]

After hearing this, the abbot returned to his monastery and sent his letters throughout Francia and the neighboring provinces, inviting the faithful of Holy Church to gather with the greatest readiness to share in so great a joy, both out of love and veneration for their patron and so that they might merit to be strengthened by apostolic blessing.

The pope, meanwhile, departing from Cologne, came to Toul on the Feast of the Exaltation of the Lord’s Cross. From there he ordered letters bearing his authority to be sent to the bishops and abbots of the surrounding regions, commanding them to meet him on the appointed day for the celebration of a synod in the basilica of the aforesaid apostle of the Franks, so that, through the one by whom they had received the first instruction in orthodox faith, they might in his presence obtain the restoration of the divine religion that had grown cold within them. The devout faith of the faithful rejoiced at these commands and diligently prepared itself to fulfill what was proclaimed to it by the decree of apostolic dignity.

**9.** But the venomous serpent, which from the beginning of the world has desired the ruin of the human race, endeavored to oppose an obstacle to this salutary plan through its schemes. To accomplish the purpose of its faithlessness, it stirred up certain powerful laymen who, by engaging in incestuous marriages and entangling themselves in the wicked practices of other crimes, were violators of ecclesiastical propriety. They therefore feared that the hidden places of their offenses would be brought to light.

It also joined to them certain bishops and abbots who had entered the Lord’s sheepfold from elsewhere, not through the door, and who had allowed various things contrary to the decrees of the Catholic Fathers to sprout in their churches. They feared that these things would be exposed and cut away by the examination of the announced synod. For, as it is written, “Everyone who does evil hates the light” (John 3:20), and therefore he applies ever greater concealment and obscurity to his sins.

Thus, instructed by the crafty suggestions of their instigator, men of such perversity told the king of the Franks that the dignity of his kingdom would be destroyed if he permitted the authority of the Roman pontiff to dominate in it, or if, meeting him as he had promised, he offered the support of his presence for convening the council.

They added that none of his predecessors was ever known to have granted that, for a similar reason, a pope should be allowed to enter the cities of France. Moreover, they said, such undertakings required times suited to peace and tranquility, whereas the condition of his kingdom was in considerable disorder: certain powerful men were rejecting the yoke of his rule and alienating various lands and castles from his jurisdiction.

Therefore, they said, it was appropriate to the royal dignity that he should wisely attend to the welfare of the commonwealth [Note: [Col. 1423D] The edition reads, “that he should wisely attend to the welfare of his own commonwealth.”] rather than devote himself to synods; that he should mobilize his princes and the strength of his entire army against the rebels; and that even the bishops and abbots, in whose hands lay the greater part of the kingdom’s resources, ought not to be exempt from this expedition. Before all others, they named the abbot of Saint Remigius, who, as though presuming upon the abundance of his possessions, had, for love of empty glory, summoned the pontiff of the Roman city to dedicate his monastery.

The king, softened by this deceitful persuasion and turned from his honorable purpose toward the byways of seduction, sent word to the pope through the bishop of Senlis that he and his bishops, together with the abbots, were being compelled to suppress the obstinacy of those resisting him, and therefore could not meet him at the appointed time to carry out the council. He should consequently postpone his arrival in France to another time, when, freed from such affairs, the king could receive him with the honor due to him.

The pope replied that he could not render void the promise made to blessed Remigius, but would certainly come to dedicate his basilica; and, if any lovers of divine religion gathered there, he declared that he would hold the synod with them. [Col. 1423C]

When the king had received a report of this message, he nevertheless set out against the rebels, assembling into one body a huge force of his army. Bishops and most of the abbots went there against their will; the perverse rulers of the churches also voluntarily thrust themselves into that undertaking, having contrived this fatal stratagem so that they might escape the examination of their actions by the vicar of the Supreme Shepherd when he came.

The aforementioned abbot of Saint Remigius was brought along with them, exceedingly sorrowful and groaning, as though he would not see the fulfillment of his desire. But the power of divine consolation did not fail his grief. For scarcely had a day and a half of the journey been completed when he was granted permission to return. He immediately went back and sought the Roman pontiff, who was still staying at Toul. Learning that the pope, in accordance with the king’s message, had not altered the plan he had long conceived, he returned joyfully to the monastery and hastened to prepare the things necessary for the assembly of so great a Father and of the sons of Holy Church who were flocking together.

For the appointed time was already near—the limit assigned for completing the arrangement described above. [Col. 1424A]

**10.** Finally, the lord pope, departing from the city of Toul, set out on the road leading to the city of Reims. Having received lodging at suitable places each night, he came on the eve of the feast of Saint Michael to the village of Courmelles [Note: [Col. 1423D] This is the place commonly called Courmeloy.]. The aforementioned abbot met him there and abundantly supplied him and his entire company with everything required for their needs.

On the following day he arrived at Saint Remigius, accompanied by three archbishops—those of Trier, Lyon, and Besançon—and by other distinguished men, among whom were John, bishop of Porto, Peter, a deacon of the Roman Church, and the prefect of the city itself.

At once the entire community of the brothers gathered together, and with them an innumerable [al., “numerous”] crowd of abbots, monks, and clerics who had already streamed in from many regions. From all these a most orderly procession was arranged in the basilica’s atrium. Three bishops—those of Senlis, Angers, and Nevers—preceded the widely ordered ranks, carrying the Gospel book, blessed water, and the fragrance of spices.

Thus arranged, they received the approaching pope. As he entered the church, they sang the responsory *Let the heavens rejoice* with fitting melody. While he prayed before the altar of the Holy Cross, they concluded by singing another responsory, namely *To the Most Holy Trinity*. When he had proceeded as far as the altar of Saint Christopher and had completed his prayer before the tomb of the venerable apostle of the Franks, they again broke into the hymn *Te Deum laudamus* with a harmonious outburst of joyful voices.

After sitting for a short while in the seat suitably prepared for him, he gladdened those standing by with apostolic blessing. Then, as he departed, the same choirs of singers escorted him with divine praises as far as the walls of the city. [Note: [Col. 1423D] At that time the monastery of Saint Remigius lay outside the city walls; for about three hundred years now, after the city’s surrounding boundary was extended, it has been enclosed within them.]

The clergy of Reims, proceeding to meet him with their archbishop and several other bishops, arranged numerous ranks of a splendid procession in the atrium of Saint Dionysius the Martyr. [Note: [Col. 1424D] Frodoardus reports that the burial place of the canons of Reims was there, *History of Reims*, book II, chapter 15, although in the year 1067. Gervasius raised this basilica into an abbey by placing regular canons of Saint Augustine in it; it still survives as such.]. There, with suitable hymns sung for the reception of so great a pontiff, they accompanied him with the greatest rejoicing to the church of Saint Mary.

There, after he had completed his prayer before the altars of the Holy Cross and of the same Mother of God, he sat for a while in the archiepiscopal seat, with the archbishop of Reims sitting at his right and the archbishop of Trier at his left. Then, after the altar ministers had been prepared according to the requirements of their offices, he himself, girded with priestly insignia, proceeded to celebrate the solemn rites of Mass.

When these had been completed and the people present had been strengthened by apostolic blessing, the archbishop of Reims supplying him and his company with the necessary expenses, he received refreshment in the great palace situated beside the church.

**11.** On the following day, fearing that he might be hindered by the crowds of surrounding peoples, he returned to Saint Remigius accompanied by only two chaplains, while the brothers were completing the nocturnal vigils. He had a bath prepared, washed, and was tonsured, since he intended to celebrate on the following day the solemnity of so great a Father and planned to transfer the venerable relic of so precious a gem. He sought to remain in seclusion in a certain house prepared for him next to the church, because he feared to appear in public.

For such a multitude of people, summoned as if from the whole world, was gathering at the saint’s tomb that the spaciousness of the temple could scarcely accommodate those entering. Countless people of both sexes flew there from nearby and distant regions. Harsh Francia poured forth, in honor of its glorious apostle, peasants, townsmen, and citizens; Gaul also sent here thousands of people from almost all its regions.

Among them came noble throngs of bishops, abbots, monks, and clerics. The lowly did not know how to yield to the noble, nor the poor to the rich; instead, all pressed together with one devout intention. They impressed sweet kisses upon the tomb containing the heavenly pearl and each offered, according to his ability, the gifts of his offerings.

Those who were driven back by the force of the tightly packed crowd and could not approach more closely—alas, how they groaned at being deprived of the fulfillment of their desire!—hurled from a distance the gifts they had brought, and with pious devotion covered the saint’s tomb with them as though with stones. [Col. 1425C]

Before the doors of the basilica there is a spacious atrium. Whenever it could no longer contain their density, the multitude of such great gatherings spread out there, drawn by their eagerness to see the vicar of blessed Peter himself. For, after seeking the aid of blessed Remigius, they yearned above all to behold him.

To satisfy the generous desire of those longing to see him, the pope climbed to a more elevated gallery of the house in which he was staying, so that he could look upon those standing below, be seen by them, and be heard while speaking. He gladdened them with apostolic blessing. As some departed and others successively filled the atrium in groups, he gave them salutary words of exhortation three times that day, clearly explaining what they ought to avoid and what they ought to seek for the salvation of their souls.

Finally, he had the sacred mysteries celebrated for him in the same house, because nowhere was there a suitable place for him to enter the church, and the brothers, because of the press of the crowds, could not perform their customary divine office there.

Meanwhile night arrived, yet the multitude of those gathering did not diminish; rather, its abundance grew ever greater. The lord pope feared that those serving God in the sacred vigils might be prevented by the crowd from carrying out the solemnities of divine service, and also that he might be prevented from transferring the precious body of the saint and dedicating the church. He therefore sent his clerics to the abbot of that place and ordered the temple to be completely emptied. After the doors had been carefully locked, all access to it was to be barred.

He also ordered that this be announced to the people in his name: they were to withdraw for a time and allow those serving God to celebrate the solemn watches of that night with fitting devotion, without being disturbed by any rush of the crowd. He promised without fail to satisfy their desires on the following day and to display before their eyes the treasured object they sought. But if they refused to obey his commands, he would depart without accomplishing the undertaking for which he had come.

When this had finally been obtained with the greatest difficulty, a very large crowd nevertheless kept vigil outside with abundant lights, awaiting the fulfillment of the promise. The church was illuminated within by the profusion of candles, shining like the splendor of many stars, while the choirs of those serving God most fittingly passed the hours of that night in spiritual songs.

**12.** When morning came, the holy martyr Cornelius was received by the lord pope within the church. The clerics of Compiègne had brought him there, together with other holy relics, because of the many acts of violence that their church was suffering from certain evildoers.

Then, about the third hour, the same apostolic pontiff, crowned with priestly insignia, proceeded to the tomb of the glorious Father Remigius with thuribles and crosses. Four archbishops accompanied him—those of Reims, Trier, Lyon, and Besançon—together with certain others, as well as the abbot of that place, Lord Hugh, the venerable Father of the monastery of Cluny, and many men of his order.

After the litany had been performed and a considerable fragrant cloud of incense had been kindled over the holy body, he sang the responsory *Let my prayer be directed*. When its verse had been completed, he moved the saint’s bier slightly from its place, so that, once fitted with the prepared instruments, it might be made suitable for carrying, and he sang the antiphon *Remigius, Confessor of the Lord*.

When everything had been suitably arranged as the matter required, he himself, before all others, together with the aforementioned archbishops and abbots, placed his shoulders beneath it and devoutly, weeping, lifted it. He began the responsory *This is he from the heights*. The choirs of singers following his voice burst forth in an exultant dance of jubilation. And, O, how many people’s faces were drenched by the overflow of abundant tears from the joy of their hearts! How many minds were moved to sighs of blessed groaning as they sought the intercession of so great a Father!

The lord pope then entrusted the same precious treasure to the vows of those who thrust themselves forward, and withdrew from the disturbance of the crowds into the oratory of the Holy Trinity. This had been suitably constructed on the southern side within the enclosure of the church through the efforts of a certain monk of that place named Harduin. [Note: [Col. 1425] He flourished under the emperor Louis the Pious. See Frodoardus, *History of Reims*, book II, chapter 19, and Marlot, volume I, *Metropolis of Reims*, book III, chapter 2.] It contained an elegant representation of the Lord’s tomb, modeled on that of Jerusalem, in which our salvation rested.

There, on that same day, he had the archbishop of Trier consecrate the oratory in his presence, with the consent of the aforesaid archbishop of Reims, and with relics of many saints placed there.

Finally, when the monastery doors had been opened, the heavenly gem was exposed to the sight of the people who desired it. Then one could see the common crowd, in excessive exultation, clapping its hands; countless people burst forth in joyful acclamation into divine praises; the powerful and the powerless, the noble and the lowly, each strove with all his strength to draw near and touch joys so greatly desired.

Great was their faith, surely worthy of a great reward; lest it be deprived of so great a benefit, not even the danger of impending death drew it back. Some, driven headlong by the excessive haste of their desire, fell among the tightly packed wedges of people and, unable to rise, died suffocated and trampled.

The reliquary containing the precious body was seized and thrown about rather than carried, as the immense crowd pressing from every side drove it this way and that, like a ship tossed by the violence of sea waves. Now one group, now another, wrested the blessed gift away for itself. To sum up much in a few words, lest the attention of readers fail through lengthy digression, a joyful struggle unfolded along the entire stretch between the city and the saint’s own castle.

The clergy of Reims, together with a multitude of citizens, were striving to carry their apostle to the walls of their own city. They had scarcely torn him away from the force of such a dense crowd when they brought him into the church of the Holy Mother of God. [Note: [Col. 1427D] This is the metropolitan church of the Blessed Mary, which the holy bishop had enriched with many estates.] While alive in the body, he had acquired many benefits for that church through the worthy labors of his earthly life and had added appropriate distinctions of Catholic religion; now, by the presence of his bones, he might grant it the joy and sanctification of even a single night’s stay.

After he had been placed upon the altar of the Holy Cross, the archbishop of Besançon proceeded to the altar of the Blessed Mary and celebrated the solemn rites of Mass with the same clergy on the feast of that glorious Father.

When these rites were completed and the devotion of those who were gathering grew ever denser, the day passed and night followed. Yet the darkness of that night in no way obscured the inner parts of the basilica. Numerous joyous gatherings, bearing in a certain sense their own daylight, made lights glitter everywhere.

The monks kept joyful vigil there around their patron and completed the matutinal office with its twelve lessons and responsories. After them the canons took up the same vigils and solemnly performed them; completing the matins with nine lessons, they prolonged them until daylight.

When morning came, they sang Prime, Terce, and Mass with Sext earlier than at the customary times, and carried the venerable body with divine praises from the church of the Blessed Mother of God. Bearing it joyfully around the city, they made the appropriate stations at the appointed intervals.

When they came to the place where there had once been a gate, called in the ancient language *Patens*, through which the same saint, while still living in the flesh, expelled by his prayers the enemy of the human race, who was raging in that city through visible devastation by fire, they laid down the precious remains there. With worthy devotion and spiritual songs they commemorated that miracle.

As a memorial of this event, a basilica was built there in modern times. A certain servant of God named Constantius elegantly completed it at his own expense, and, while he lived, gathered as many servants of God as he could for its service. He had it consecrated in honor of Saint Mary Magdalene and Saint Remigius. [Note: [Col. 1427D] Concerning this Constantius, a canon, see the *Chronicle of Verdun* by Hugh, abbot of Flavigny, where he is praised at length. At his urging Saint Hugh delivered a speech at the very synod against simoniacs and fornicating priests, as is recorded in the Life of Saint Hugh. Moreover, the church he built is now held by the Knights of Malta. On its principal gate an old inscription from the time of its foundation still survives.] [Col. 1428B]

**13.** While this procession was taking place outside the city walls, the lord pope summoned the bishops into the inner recesses of the monastery that was to be dedicated and assigned each of them a separate altar to consecrate.

He appointed the archbishop of Reims to make a threefold circuit outside, with crosses and relics of the saints, according to ecclesiastical order, and there to complete the rite of consecration. He himself remained inside with those necessary for him and energetically and carefully carried out the sanctification of the divine tabernacle.

When they had reached the place where, according to the decrees of the orthodox Fathers, the relics of the saints and all sacred objects were to be received into the dedicated church, the aforementioned canons, having carried the body of blessed Remigius around the city, the castle, and the neighboring town as described, reached the monastery gates with it.

There such a multitude of thousands had gathered that, because of their density, access to the house prepared for the glorious Father was blocked. The pope himself had ordered those doors not to be opened, lest the rush of those entering with the saint bring danger to him and impede the completion of the dedication that had begun.

Therefore they sought some passage by which he could be brought inside. At length, after he had scarcely been withdrawn from the disturbance of the crowds, he was lowered through a window above the oratory of the Holy Trinity. The apostolic lord received him with the greatest devotion and spiritual songs, but did not at once restore him to his proper place. Instead, he placed him upon the principal altar, which he had consecrated in honor of the Apostles Peter and Paul, the martyrs Clement and Christopher, and blessed Remigius.

He then gave a worthy explanation of the reason for which he had decided to do this: so that, when the synod was celebrated, he might be visibly and conspicuously present before everyone’s eyes. If anyone should presume to assert something erroneous, frivolous, or contrary to ecclesiastical religion, the man of God would display against him, through the presence of his body, the power of that virtue which he had displayed while still living in the world against the Arian heretic.

That heretic had attempted, in an assembly of bishops, to obscure the light of the Catholic faith with the shadow of a murky doctrine. At the saint’s arrival, divine power deprived him of the use of his voice. But shortly afterward, when he humbly acknowledged his guilt, the saint granted him health of soul and body and admitted him among the children of adoption.

The pope’s intention in this discourse, proceeding from heavenly inspiration, was in no way without effect, as this little work will declare in its proper place.

For this reason, then, after the body of blessed Remigius had been placed there, and the entire [al., “numerous”] companies of bishops, abbots, monks, and clerics had been most suitably arranged in choirs, the same pontiff celebrated the solemn rites of Mass for the feast of the dedication.

After the Gospel had been read, he ascended the pulpit and delivered a sermon of exhortation to the people standing around. A great number of them, as has been said, had made their way in through the windows after the monastery doors had been locked.

He preached many useful things to them concerning the sanctification of that church and ordered that the day be celebrated throughout the boundaries of the bishopric of Reims. He condemned under penalty of anathema all who, on the occasion of this solemnity, should inflict any impediment or harm upon those coming annually to that place or returning from it. [Col. 1429C]

He also established that, at the altar which, as stated above, he had consecrated in honor of the Apostles Peter and Paul, the martyrs Clement and Christopher, and the glorious confessor Remigius, the sacred mysteries should not be celebrated indiscriminately by anyone, as had previously been the case. Instead, following the custom of the Roman Church, only seven priests, those regarded as the more distinguished in that congregation, were to be assigned to this office.

The power to celebrate Mass there was granted solely to the archbishop of Reims and the abbot of that monastery, as well as to anyone to whom the abbot granted permission, certainly whenever a reasonable occasion required it. The clergy of Reims were also granted this power twice a year: on the Monday of the Paschal feast and on the vigil of the Lord’s Ascension, when, according to ancient tradition, they hold solemn stations there.

So that these decrees might never be invalidated by the passage of time, he ordered them committed to writing and sealed with the seal of his authority. [Note: [Col. 1429D] The bull is found below. Moreover, the same pontiff granted a similar privilege to the altar of the principal church of Cologne, where those seven priests are called cardinals; this practice is also observed by our Remigians. This arrangement, ordered by the pontiff, is still religiously maintained today in the basilica of Remigius.]

Then he absolved the aforementioned people, who, according to the words of his institution, made a public confession of their sins. After the divine offices had been completed, he sanctified them with apostolic blessing and dismissed them.

He ordered the pontiffs, the heads of the monasteries, and the other ministers of the sacred order who were present there to return to the same place on the following day, so that he might hold with them the synod he had appointed.

# THE FIRST DAY OF THE SYNOD.

14. On the following day, which was the fifth day before the Nones of October, twenty bishops assembled in the aforementioned basilica, together with nearly fifty abbots and many others of the ecclesiastical order. There the old dispute between the clerics of the archbishops of Reims and Trier was immediately renewed. The former argued [Col. 1430B] that the archbishop of Reims was primate in Gaul and that the organization of the synod therefore belonged to him; conversely, the latter endeavored to attribute the same dignity to the archbishop of Trier and to secure for him the first place after the bishop of the Roman Church in the celebration of the council.

[Note: [Col. 1429D] Gerbert calls the church of Reims the head of all the churches of the kingdom. King Charles calls it their mother. Others, in different words, have expressed the prerogatives of the distinguished see of blessed Remigius, apostle and patron of our kings and people. Manasses writes in a letter to Pope Gregory VII that it belongs to the archbishop of Reims to summon all the bishops of Gaul to council; Ivo of Chartres admits that he possesses “the diadem of the kingdom,” and so forth. Hence, according to Saint Bernard, by virtue of the privilege of his see he placed the royal crown upon the king’s head throughout all the churches of Gaul, as was then customary on each feast day. Two crosses always preceded him, according to the ancient Ritual of the church of Reims. Fulco, the successor of Hincmar, writes that the primacy over all Gaul was conferred upon the church of Reims by blessed Peter; others prefer to refer this dignity to Saint Remigius’s apostolic vicariate. Today the bishop of Reims is called the born legate of the Apostolic See and primate of Belgic Gaul, and among the nobles of the kingdom he enjoys the title and prerogatives of the first duke and peer of France.]

But the lord pope, not judging the time opportune for a suitable conclusion to be imposed upon these arguments, and rather fearing that such a controversy might break out into the scandal of contention, ordered the bishops’ seats to be arranged in the form of a circle and his own throne to be placed in their midst. He sanctioned the manner of this arrangement to be carried out at the discretion of the archbishop of Reims. The latter, having summoned the archdeacons and the leading members of his clergy, and acting with their counsel, had the bishops’ seats and the insignia of the apostolic see arranged in the aforementioned circular form.

When these arrangements had been made, the lord pope, crowned with priestly mitres as though for the celebration of Mass, proceeded from the oratory of the Holy Trinity with the cross and the book of the Gospel. Ministers of the sacred order preceded him, and six others walked before him. In front of the holy altar they sang the antiphon *Exaudi nos, Domine* in its entirety. When it had been completed, together with the psalm and the *Gloria*, the archbishop of Trier performed the litany. When this was finished, the deacon admonished the assembly to pour forth prayers to God; then, with the apostolic lord reciting an appropriate prayer, the Gospel was read: “Jesus said to Simon Peter: ‘If your brother sins against you.’”

After this all took their seats [Col. 1430D] in the order arranged by the archbishop of Reims. The lord pope sat in the middle of the choir, as stated, his face turned toward the tomb of blessed Remigius. Before his eyes, on the eastern side, Wido of Reims sat on the right, while Eberhard of Trier sat on the left.

After the archbishop of Reims, the following sat in the order written below: Berold of Soissons, Drogo of Thérouanne, Rollandus [or Frollandus] of Senlis, and Adalbero of Metz. On the southern side sat Aylenard, archbishop of Lyon; Hugh of Langres; Joffrid of Coutances; Ivo of Séez; Herbert of Lisieux; Hugh of Bayeux; Hugh of Avranches; and Theodoric of Verdun. On the northern side sat Hugh, archbishop of Besançon; Hugh of Nevers; Eusebius of Angers; Pudicus of Nantes; the bishop of the English; and John of Porto.

[Note: [Col. 1431D] It is strange that the Sammarthani omitted this Pudicus from their catalogue of the bishops of Nantes, although, apart from our Anselm, others also wrote about him. See what Peter Le Baud reports about him from the *Chronicle of the Church of Nantes* in *History of Brittany*, chapter 22, where he calls him the son of Bishop Gualterius. The same is stated below, no. 16.]

[Note: [Col. 1432D] Namely, Duduco, bishop of Wells, as we noted in the preliminary observations.]

Behind them the abbots likewise sat in a circle, in the following order: the lord Herimarus, abbot of Saint Remigius; the lord Hugh of Cluny; Sigefrid of Gorze; Folco of Corbie; Robert of Prüm; Rainold of Saint-Médard; Girvin of Saint-Riquier; Godfrey of Vézelay; Arnold of Pultares; Rodulf of Mouzon; Oylard of Châlons; Milo of Der; Norgaud of Altvillar; Albert of Saint-Thierry; Stephen of Saint-Urbain; Wlfricus of Saint Augustine of Canterbury; and Alwinus of Saint Benedict in the land of the English.

[Note: [Col. 1432D] Alwinus was abbot of Ramsey in the county of Huntingdon. The church of that monastery, in honor of Blessed Mary, all the holy Virgins, and Saint Benedict, was consecrated by Saint Dunstan, archbishop of Canterbury, and Saint Oswald, archbishop of York, in the year 974.]

Then came the others who, as reported above, were present, nearly fifty in number.

When they had taken their seats, silence was ordered. At the command of the lord pope, Peter, a deacon of the holy Roman Church, rose and, in a concise address, explained [Col. 1431C] the matters that were to be discussed in the same synod. These were the many unlawful practices being carried on in the regions of Gaul contrary to the provisions of the canons: the heresy of simony; ecclesiastical offices and altars held by laymen; the wicked customary payments exacted by them in churchyards; incestuous marriages; those who, abandoning their lawful wives, became entangled in adulterous remarriages; monks and clerics abandoning their holy profession and habit; clerics devoted to worldly military service; robbery and unjust seizures from the poor; the Sodomitic vice; and certain heresies that had begun to arise in those same regions.

After presenting these matters, he admonished all who were present to deliberate with him prudently about what counsel they might offer the lord pope, with suitable assistance, and how these weeds, choking the seed of God’s harvest, might be uprooted. Then, turning his address to the bishops, he warned them under threat of the anathema of apostolic authority that if any of them had reached sacred orders through simony, or had promoted anyone to the same dignity in exchange for payment, he should disclose this by public confession.

Accordingly, the archbishop of Trier first rose at these words and replied that he had neither given nor promised anything in order to obtain the episcopate, nor had he sold sacred orders to anyone. Then the bishops of Lyon and Besançon rose and declared themselves free from such guilt. The aforementioned deacon then turned to the archbishop of Reims and asked what he had to say about those matters from which the others had purified themselves. Rising, he requested a postponement until the following day, saying that he wished to speak privately with the apostolic lord. When this had been granted, all the others rose in order and, following the words of their predecessors, cleared themselves of such suspicion, with only four exceptions: the bishops of Langres, Nevers, Coutances, and Nantes.

Since their case was left for examination that day, the deacon turned his speech to the abbots who were present and admonished them to confess lest they too had entered the Lord’s fold from elsewhere, not through the door. Herimarus, abbot of Saint Remigius, rose first and cleared himself of such guilt with an appropriate response. Then the lord Hugh of Cluny followed and added this account of his purification, saying:

“For obtaining the honor of the abbacy, with God as my witness, I gave or promised nothing—though the flesh desired it, the mind and reason resisted.”

After him, certain others endeavored to excuse themselves suitably … [lacuna] Others, however, made no reply, preferring to conceal their guilt rather than disclose it.

Then the bishop of Langres rose and bitterly accused Pultares, his diocesan abbot, alleging that he lived in the stench of lust and was involved in many scandals. He had also refused to pay each year the customary due owed to blessed Peter and his vicar, the pontiff of the Roman Church, whose abbey it was; and, although excommunicated for this reason, he had presumed to celebrate the sacrament of Mass and, still subject to excommunication, had attended the same synod.

When examined, he was unable to overcome the charges brought against him and was therefore deprived of the dignity of his office.

When these matters had been settled, it was decreed under the anathema of apostolic authority that if any of those seated there asserted that anyone other than the bishop of the Roman see was primate of the universal Church, he should make this known through public satisfaction. When all remained silent in response, the judgments formerly promulgated on this matter by the orthodox Fathers were read, and it was declared that the pontiff of the Roman see alone was primate and apostolic of the universal Church.

After this the lord pope prohibited, under pain of excommunication, anyone from departing without his permission before the third day of the council’s celebration had come to an end. As night was already approaching, he then dismissed the assembly.

## SECOND DAY OF THE SYNOD

[Col. 1433A]

15. On the following day, when the bishops had assembled at the aforementioned basilica with the abbots and clergy, the lord pope withdrew with some of them into the oratory of the Holy Trinity. There the archbishop of Reims had a private conversation with him concerning his confession, and they discussed at length the advancement of ecclesiastical discipline.

The apostolic lord then proceeded from there in the same order as on the previous day. After the antiphon had been sung and the litany performed by the archbishop of Trier, the deacon read the Gospel: “Every good tree.”

When everyone had taken his appointed place, the aforementioned chancellor admonished the archbishop of Reims to give an account of the simony about which he had obtained a postponement the previous day. He also accused him of many crimes which, as he claimed, he had learned through public report.

The archbishop rose and requested that he be granted an opportunity to deliberate. Having obtained this, he summoned the bishops of Besançon, Soissons, Angers, Nevers, Senlis, and Thérouanne and held a confidential consultation with them. On returning, he obtained from the lord pope permission for the bishop of Senlis to plead his case.

The bishop of Senlis rose and replied that the same archbishop was not guilty of the heresy of simony. On hearing this, the apostolic lord ordered the archbishop to prove the truth of the matter by an oath. He also ordered the sentence to be read by which blessed Pope Gregory had decreed that Maximus, bishop of Salona, who had been charged with a similar fault, should clear himself in the same manner.

[Col. 1433C]

The archbishop, however, requested the canonical period of postponement and promised that, when it had expired, he would do what the requirements of his purification demanded. This was granted to him, and it was determined that he should attend the council to be held at Rome in the middle of April.

[Note: [Col. 1433D] Wido retained his see until his death, which occurred in the year 1055. He was buried in the church of Saint Remigius.]

As for the other charges brought against him, since they appeared to lack the accusation of a legitimate accuser, it was decreed that they should remain unexamined for the present.

When this matter had thus been settled, the lord pope complained about the abbey of Der, because it had been removed from the episcopate of Toul. He demonstrated, by having the privileges that he possessed concerning it read aloud, that the abbey belonged to the possession of that church. The archbishop of Reims, however, replied that the abbey belonged rather to his jurisdiction and said that he could establish this by means of more ancient privileges of his church.

Since the documents whose reading could settle the dispute were not then present, the pope ordered them to be sought in the archives of the church of Reims and brought before the assembly on the following day.

Then the clerics of Tours, through the archbishop of Lyon, brought a complaint against the bishop of Dol in Brittany, who had withdrawn himself and seven suffragan bishops from the archbishopric of Tours and had unlawfully claimed for himself the name of archbishop.

[Note: [Col. 1433D] This controversy, which had been disputed for so many centuries, was eventually settled by Pope Innocent III in a celebrated decree, by which the bishops of Dol and the other bishops of Lesser Brittany were placed under the metropolitan of Tours. The acts of this controversy have recently been printed by our Edmund Martene in the new *Collection of Ancient Writers*.]

[Col. 1434A]

He was immediately summoned by apostolic authority to the council which, as stated above, was to be held at Rome in the middle of April, so that the judgment of this case might be considered there.

After this the aforementioned deacon attacked the bishop of Langres, accusing him of having obtained episcopal dignity through simony, of having sold sacred orders, of having committed murders by unlawfully carrying weapons of war, of having violated the rights of another’s marriage, of exercising tyranny over his clerics, and of having been polluted by the Sodomitic crime.

Many informers who were present testified to these charges. Among them, one cleric asserted that, while he himself was still a layman, the bishop had violently taken away his wife and, after committing adultery with her, had made her a nun.

A certain priest also appeared [Col. 1434B], complaining that he had been captured by the same bishop and handed over to the power of his henchmen. They had tortured him with many punishments and, more wickedly still, had pierced his genitals with very sharp nails, extorting from him by such violence ten pounds of denarii.

On hearing this, the bishop requested permission to deliberate. Having obtained it, he summoned the archbishops of Besançon and Lyon, confided to them the secret of his deliberation, and asked them to act as his advocates.

But the bishop of Besançon—who, entangled in so many crimes and seeing the beam in another’s eye more than in his own, had accused his brother, however guilty, at the previous synod and had himself deservedly sought that brother’s condemnation—not only could he not excuse himself from the charges brought against him [Col. 1434C], but, so that he could not say anything in the bishop’s defense, he was divinely deprived of the use of his tongue [or: of the movement of his tongue].

While the bishop of Besançon was pleading the man’s case and putting forward certain unsuitable proposals in an attempt to excuse the criminal, he unexpectedly felt that the assistance of speech had been denied him by divine power.

Beyond doubt, the great father Remigius, who had been displayed before the eyes of the synod for this very reason, as stated above, here too shone forth with the power of that same virtue for the blessed faith, which he had once exercised, while still living as a pilgrim on earth, in frustrating the schemes of that Arian.

At that time he condemned to silence the heretic who was preparing to babble blasphemies against the Catholic faith, so that he would not accomplish what he had attempted but would instead repent and become faithful. Now he deprived a man who, although faithful, would have sinned by defending a criminal, of the use of speech.

Indeed, the incomprehensible power of divine majesty wonderfully manifested itself in both events: there it granted such power to the glorious soul, although it was still enclosed in bodily bonds; here it plainly showed, around his lifeless body, how much glory had already made that soul blessed.

When the aforementioned bishop of Besançon recognized that such a miracle had prevented him from continuing his attempt, he indicated to the bishop of Lyon that he should plead the case of his brother in his place.

The latter rose and stated that the bishop of Langres admitted having sold sacred orders and extorted the aforementioned money from the priest, but denied having subjected him to the tortures he claimed to have suffered. As for the other charges brought against him, he said that the bishop entirely denied them.

When these things had been said, the lord pope, seeing that the matter could not be fully examined that day—for night was already approaching—ordered only that the decree concerning sellers of sacred orders be read. After the judgment had been read, at his command, from the Council of Chalcedon, specifically its second canon, the synod was dissolved, and judgment in this case was postponed until the following day.

## THIRD DAY OF THE SYNOD

[Col. 1435B]

16. When morning came, the bishops again assembled at the same place with the abbots and the other orders of the Church. As the lord pope proceeded toward them, the antiphon *Exaudi nos, Domine* was not sung, as it had been yesterday and the day before, but at his arrival the clergy sang most fittingly the hymn *Veni, creator Spiritus*. When this was completed, together with an antiphon for Saint Remigius, the bishop of Besançon performed the litany, after the apostolic lord had recited the Collect for the Holy Spirit. Then the Gospel was read: “I am the good shepherd.”

When all had taken their customary places, the aforementioned deacon of the Roman Church said that it was appropriate to begin the examination of the case where the previous synod had ended—namely, with the case of the bishop of Langres.

When summoned, the bishop was found to have withdrawn from the synodical examination. He was therefore called a third time by the same deacon, in the name of God and of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and of his vicar who was present.

The bishops of Senlis and Angers were also sent to his lodging to see whether they might find him there and recall him to the council. While they hurried to carry out what had been commanded, the speech of the aforementioned chancellor was addressed to those who had not yet made the required purification from the simony they were accused of.

The bishop of Nevers rose and confessed that a great deal of money had been given by his relatives for his episcopate, although without his knowledge. After obtaining it, he had committed certain acts contrary to ecclesiastical discipline; he therefore said that he feared the vengeance of divine retribution. Accordingly, if it seemed proper to the lord pope and the present assembly, he wished to relinquish the office rather than destroy his soul by retaining it.

When he had said this, he placed his pastoral staff at the feet of the apostolic lord. The latter, moved by the devotion of so great a man and with the approval of the synod, made him prove by oath that the money had been given without his consent. He then restored the pastoral staff and episcopal office to him through another pastoral ministry.

Meanwhile, the privilege of the church of Reims concerning the abbey of Der was brought before the assembly. From its reading it was established that the abbey belonged to the jurisdiction of the archbishop of Reims.

Finally, those who had been sent to recall the bishop of Langres returned and reported that, fearing examination of his crimes, he had sought refuge in flight. Then, at the pope’s command, the judgments promulgated on such a matter by the orthodox Fathers were read, and by the judgment of the entire council he was condemned to the penalty of excommunication.

[Note: [Col. 1435] For his penance and death, see the *Life of Saint Leo*, book II, chapter 4, under the year 1054.]

When the archbishop of Besançon heard this, he rose and disclosed before the same assembly how, on the previous day, while trying to excuse this guilty man, he had been condemned to silence by divine power through the merits of blessed Remigius. He devoutly sought pardon for having concealed the novelty of this miracle so negligently until then.

The lord pope, moved by pious devotion and heartfelt joy, burst into tears and said:

“BLESSED REMIGIUS STILL LIVES.”

Then, at his command, everyone rose and prostrated himself with him before the tomb of the same saint. They sang the antiphon *Sancte Remigi* in its entirety with the greatest devotion.

After this the bishop of Coutances rose and confessed that, without his knowledge, his episcopate had been purchased for him by one of his brothers. When he learned of this, he had wished to flee rather than accept the appointment unlawfully; but his brother had seized him by force and conferred episcopal dignity upon him against his will. Ordered to prove this by oath, and offering no resistance, he was judged not to have incurred the crime of simony.

Finally, the bishop of Nantes approached and confessed that his father had been bishop of his city, that during his father’s lifetime he had received the gift of the episcopate, and that after his father’s death he had been substituted in his place through the payment of money.

Therefore, by judgment of the synod, after his ring and pastoral staff had been removed [Col. 1436C], he was deprived of episcopal office; but, at the intervention of the bishops, he was allowed to retain only the office of priest.

When their cases had been settled in this manner, the lord pope admonished the archbishops who were present that, if they knew any of their suffragans to be guilty of the simoniacal plague, they should not hesitate to make this known before everyone.

When they all denied knowing of any such person, discussion turned to the bishops who, although invited to come to the same synod, had refused to appear and had sent no written explanation for their absence. Accordingly, after the relevant judgments of the Fathers had been read, they were condemned to the penalty of excommunication, together with all those who, fearing the pope’s arrival, had gone on campaign with the king for this reason.

The persons named were the archbishop of Sens and the bishops of Beauvais and Amiens, as well as the abbot of Saint-Médard, because he had departed from the council’s assembly without permission.

The archbishop of Santiago in Galicia was also excommunicated because he unlawfully claimed for himself the dignity of the apostolic name.

After this, at the request of those who were present and loved holy religion, the lord pope renewed by the authority of his command many decrees of the holy Fathers that had already, through negligence, been treated as worthless. He also prohibited under anathema many unlawful practices being carried on in the Gallican Church, so that they should not occur again. These were as follows:

[Col. 1437A]

No one was to be advanced to the governance of a church without the election of the clergy and people.

No one was to buy or sell sacred orders, ecclesiastical offices, or altars; and if any cleric had bought any of these, he was to return it to his bishop with an appropriate satisfaction.

[Note: [Col. 1437D] Some divide this canon into two at the words “And if any cleric …”]

No layman was to hold an ecclesiastical office or altar, nor was any bishop to consent to this.

[Note: [Col. 1437D] The manuscript of Saint Remigius reads *consentirent*. Baronius has: “of the bishops to whom they would consent, or anyone who would consent to them.”]

No one was to presume to exact any customary payment in churchyards except the bishop and his minister.

No one was to exact anything for burial or baptism, for the Eucharist, or for visiting the sick.

No cleric was to carry military weapons or serve in worldly military service.

[Col. 1437B]

No cleric or layman was to practice usury.

No monk or cleric was to apostatize from his rank.

No one was to dare to inflict any violence upon persons of sacred order while they were traveling.

No one was to harass the poor with robberies or seizures.

No one was to enter into an incestuous union.

No one was to abandon his lawful wife and marry another.

Because new heretics had arisen in the regions of Gaul, he excommunicated them, together with those who accepted any gift or service from them or offered them any kind of protection or defense.

[Col. 1437C]

In the same way he condemned sodomites. He also excommunicated Counts Engelrai [Engelrai] and Eustace on account of incest, and Hugh of Braina because he had abandoned his lawful wife and taken another in marriage.

He also forbade Count Baldwin of Flanders to give his daughter in marriage to William the Norman, and forbade William to take her.

He summoned Count Theobald because he had abandoned his wife. He also summoned Godfrey of Anjou to the future synod at Mainz, where he was to be excommunicated unless he released the lord Gervasius, whom he was holding captive. Gervasius was then bishop of the see of Le Mans; later, after being freed from the power of that tyrant, he was appointed by King Henry of the Franks, after the death of Archbishop Wido, to govern the church of Reims.

[Note: [Col. 1438D] He administered the church of Reims with distinction from 1055 to 1067.]

Finally, he excommunicated those against whom the clerics of Compiègne had lodged a complaint, on account of whose injustice they had brought there the body of the holy martyr Cornelius. He also excommunicated those who might cause any hindrance to anyone returning from that synod.

He confirmed the privilege that he had granted to Saint Remigius, having it read aloud there before everyone, and decreed that it should be preserved inviolably for all time, exactly as it was written. Then, after giving his blessing, he dissolved the council.

17. In this manner, therefore, the devoted pontiff of the Roman see celebrated the fourth translation of blessed Father Remigius [Col. 1438A] and, on the sixth day before the Nones of October, happily completed the consecration of the divine house. As has been explained, he also honored it by continuing the celebration of a synod for three days, in the year 1049 of the most blessed Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Accordingly, as he had determined, having by divine providence attained the fulfillment of his desire, on the day after the conclusion of the synod he came into the chapter house [manuscript: *capitolium*] of the brothers and announced to them that he wished to hasten his return. He delighted them with spiritual conversations, devoutly sought and received their fellowship, and, when they humbly requested it, bestowed his own upon them. He absolved those who had prostrated themselves for public confession and, kissing them all in order, sanctified them with the apostolic blessing.

After this he went out, summoned the bishops and abbots and the other members of the ecclesiastical order who had not yet departed, and entered the church with them, where he had the solemn celebration of Mass performed.

When this had been completed, he approached with humble devotion the tomb of the saint which, as stated above, he had placed upon the altar of Saint Christopher after the dedication of the basilica. Having completed his prayer there, he devoutly lifted it from the place on his shoulders and set it down amid divine praises at the station prepared for it.

There, prostrating himself again and again with tears, he eventually set out on his journey. He was accompanied as far as the entrance of the castle by the brothers and an innumerable [Col. 1438C] [or: numerous] gathering of people, with spiritual songs. He took leave of everyone and departed.

On leaving, he carried away, as a recompense for his labor, the fruit of a great reward: namely, in the hidden chamber of his devoted heart, a fire of extraordinary love, by which from that time onward he is known to have burned intensely toward the same glorious Father Remigius. He himself admits this in a letter later addressed to the bishops of France, which we shall place in its proper position below.

From this grace he also obtained the benefit of another grace, when divine power inflicted punishment upon certain people who had attempted to hinder his arrival in Gaul, through the merit of the saint whom he had served.

To pass over the many others who opposed him, Bishop Gibuin of Laon [Col. 1438D] and Hugh of Braina Castle, who stood like standard-bearers among his detractors, both ended their lives by an ignominious death in that same year.

The former, because he had suggested to the king a deadly stratagem in order to avoid the apostolic presence, fled far from his own see when most of his clergy were devoutly seeking that presence. He died alone, by divine judgment, outside the boundaries of his bishopric like a stranger, without being sanctified from his wickedness by the viaticum of the Lord’s Body and without the comfort of a final visitation from his own clergy.

The latter, because he had threatened to cut off the head of Christ’s minister, was mutilated by the cut of an enemy’s sword in the very mouth with which he had uttered his impious words.

18. It is fitting to add to the foregoing, for the memory of posterity, another miracle that divine power worked through the hands of this pontiff, because of the devotion with which he burned toward our Patron.

In the second year after the events related above had been completed, while he was staying in Rome, a certain vessel was broken through an accidental act of negligence by the cupbearer. This was the vessel mentioned at the beginning of this little work as having been given to him by the aforementioned abbot Herimarus.

When he learned this for certain, he took it rather badly. Although he possessed many vessels of greater value, he loved this one above the others because he said it had been sent to him on behalf of Saint Remigius at the beginning of his apostolate. For this reason, he had been accustomed to find it more pleasing than all the others in his service when he drank.

While he was therefore complaining about this loss with a calm expression, as was always his way, in the company of certain spiritual men who were present with him, he ordered that a skilled goldsmith be sought to repair such a fracture. Some of those present, jesting with him, said seriously but cheerfully that this saint, whose devotion had led him to cherish the vessel so greatly, possessed such merit before God that through his intercession he would restore the same vessel to wholeness.

He replied with spiritual joy that he had no distrust in the matter. After praising the saint’s virtues at length, he ordered the broken vessel to be brought to him. When it had been brought, he replaced the fragment that had been torn away, and, as though it were being kept for a goldsmith to repair, ordered it to be put away, carefully impressing upon it, as is said, the sign of the cross.

When it was brought before him the following day, ostensibly to be repaired, it was found whole through divine action, so that no trace of the fracture could be discovered on it.

When the venerable pope saw this, he praised the omnipotence of God and attributed the novelty of the miracle to the merits of blessed Remigius, through whose intervention he had deserved to obtain this result by the efficacy of his faith.

But lest we be accused of lying on account of this account, and lest the memorial of this writing be considered frivolous, we produce three reliable witnesses, through whose testimony [or: judgment] we later came to recognize that it had happened.

They were Hugh, bishop of Nevers; Hugh, a deacon of the church of Reims; and a certain cleric named Benedict, formerly chaplain of Aylenard, archbishop of Lyon.

The first two attended the council held by the same pope at Rome, as was his custom, on the fifteenth day after the Sunday of the Resurrection. From those who had seen it happen, they learned that what we have reported was true. The third was present with his lord and later, when we asked him about it after several [Col. 1440B] years, reported to us what he had learned by seeing it himself.

[Note: [Col. 1439] Add to these Victor III, book III of the *Dialogues*; Bruno of Segni; Wibertus; and others.]

Finally, the venerable man, cultivating the aforementioned apostle of ours with still more fervent love and earnestly desiring to honor him and ennoble his monastery by his authority, sent a letter filled with his praise to the sons of the holy Church established in France. In it he decreed that the feast of that saint, celebrated on the Kalends of October, should be solemnly observed among them.

He also ordered many matters relating to ecclesiastical welfare, which he had treated in the aforementioned synod held in the saint’s basilica, to be arranged among them in the form of chapters and numbered among the orthodox canons.

Since the order of the narrative seems to require it, we have judged it worthy to insert the text of that letter into this work. Its form is as follows.

## Letter of Blessed Pope Leo

[Col. 1440C]

Leo, bishop, etc.

(See in Saint Leo IX, *Patrologia*, volume CXLIII.)

## Privilege of the High Altar of the Church of Saint Remigius of Reims

Leo, bishop, etc.

(See the reference given above.)

[Col. 1439]

## Letter of the Gallican Clergy for the Renewal of the Feast of Saint Remigius
[Col. 1439D] To all the bishops throughout Gaul, the assembly of the Gallican Church sends greetings in the Lord.

Although the festive celebration of Saint Remigius, archbishop of Rheims, has been splendidly established for so many centuries both by the councils of the Gallican Church, by decrees of the supreme pontiffs, and by the capitularies of our kings, nevertheless it has unfortunately happened that what ought rather to have been commended by its antiquity has been obscured—or almost entirely forgotten—because of the cooling devotion of the peoples; or at least the memory of so great an apostle and teacher of the Franks has grown cheap, being celebrated with honors not worthy of him.

For he, as your charity very well knows [Col. 1440D], like a second Sylvester, having subjected our Chlodovech, clothed in mortal purple, to Christ the King, taught him, as a new Constantine, after rejecting his empty gods, to adore what he had burned and to burn what he had adored. Finally, after the peoples had been led to communion with the faith through miracles and teaching together with their prince, and after the stain of the Franks—namely, the leprosy of the old idolatry—had been washed away in the saving bath, he dedicated the first fruits of this Christian kingdom to Christ under its most Christian kings, and gave birth to its firstborn sons and defenders for His Church.

And while Greece rejoiced because it alone possessed a ruler of our law, he showed that the rest of the world was not without its own glory, since a new radiance of new splendor shone forth in a king in the western regions. Certainly, if at any time the ruins in faith of neighboring peoples, set before their eyes, have led them to fall suppliantly before their heavenly patrons, what service of devotion will the piety of the Franks not render to Saint Remigius, their apostle, with united and most earnest prayers, when—alas!—the fire of heretical depravity has spread from the surrounding regions, and, as God avenges sins, religion has been driven away and withdrawn?

Therefore we exhort your charity that, after stirring up the devotion of your subjects, we may labor with one accord to honor Saint Remigius with a more solemn rite on the first day of October [Col. 1442A]; and that, following the example of so great a prelate—who, as Hormisdas testifies, gave evidence of a supreme Pontiff, both doing things worthy of proclamation and not delaying to make them known—we may diligently devote ourselves to this end. Thus, by practicing righteousness, which conquers kingdoms, let us make both ourselves and those who hear us safe.

Paris, 22 May 1657.

Your most devoted servants and fellow brothers, the archbishops, bishops, and ecclesiastical men assembled in the general assemblies of the Gallican clergy.

Claudius, archbishop of Narbonne, president.

By order of the most reverend and most illustrious archbishops, and in the name of the whole ecclesiastical assembly of the clergy of France gathered together:

Henri de Villars, secretary.

Joannes de Montpezat de Carbon, secretary.

# INDEX TO SAINT BRUNO’S COMMENTARY ON THE PSALMS

Beginning of this volume.

(Bibliotheca Patrum XVIII, 68, from the edition of Joannes Cochlaeus.)

## JOANNES COCHLAEUS TO THE READER

[Col. 1441] Although the commentary on the 150 Psalms is in itself brief and concise, pious reader, it has nevertheless seemed useful to add an index for those who are either too occupied to read everything, or who do not have the passages of the Psalter memorized. They may thus have, arranged in alphabetical order, a very brief handbook of notable passages and subjects, as well as of statements, for manifold use and benefit.

If a passage has been read, cited, or brought forward elsewhere, and you wish to learn its genuine exposition and its correct and pious meaning from the sacred doctors rather than rashly conjecture them through confidence in your own ingenuity, consult this index, which will direct you very briefly where you wish to go. If, while praying or singing psalms, you encounter a more obscure passage whose sound meaning you desire quickly to grasp, here you will promptly be shown where to look. If, having been assigned the task of teaching or writing, you wish to expand and enrich the subject you are treating, this storehouse will immediately suggest to you a variety of material; by searching through it, you will understand your subject more clearly and explain its purpose more fully.

If simple people and those not thoroughly practiced in the Scriptures should wish to heed the advice of my simplicity, they will not merely read this index as an index, but will read it through as a little compendium from beginning to end, with the intention of learning from it, in the briefest possible form, how to speak and write piously and appropriately about sacred matters. For here they will find many statements about which previously they may have been uncertain, or may not have known how they ought either to be suitably expressed or soundly understood.

You now have, reader, the reasons for this additional labor of ours, by which we wish to provide for the simpler. Take it in good part, and farewell.
